# Patrologia Latina, volume 154 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 154

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library ... of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III ... SECOND SERIES.**

Volume front matter

Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III: a chronological reprinting of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, very carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the fullest editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following either individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal that nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on each text of each book of Scripture and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others when one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the whole course of the work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Graeco-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 francs; the Graeco-Latin for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, Western as well as Eastern; the latter, however, are furnished in it only in Latin translation.**

# At the Close of the Century

## Hugh, Abbot of Flavigny

[Col. 0009]

# Hugh’s Chronicle

*(Most recently edited by Dom Pertz, in the Historical Monuments of Germany, Writers, vol. VIII, p. 278.)*

## Preface: Hugh’s Age, Homeland, Birth, and Deeds

[Col. 0009A]

The author of the lengthy chronicle, which we are now presenting to our readers because of its remarkable abundance of material relevant to the history of the eleventh century, was Hugh, descended from a family that claimed kinship with the emperors Otto III and Conrad II [Note: [Col. 0009B] He himself states that this was his lineage; but its fabulous character is already shown by the fact that he represents Conrad as assigned to Otto III in the position of a son.], born in 1065 [Note: [Col. 0010B] On folio 137, under the year 1096, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, he writes that he was then living in the thirty-second year of his age. If his birthday fell between the tenth day before the Kalends of December and the Kalends of January, he must have been born in 1064.] at Verdun [Note: [Col. 0010B] He calls it his homeland under the year 1085.] or in the vicinity of that city. He came as a boy into the monastery of Saint Vannes, which at that time flourished in the suburb of Verdun, under Abbot Rudolph, and was instructed in both sacred and secular literature [Note: [Col. 0010B] Besides the Holy Scriptures and the Fathers, he knew the classical authors; he cites Seneca’s *On Benefits*, Gregory’s *Moralia*, Saint Benedict’s Rule, Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore, and Fortunatus.]. Soon afterward he professed obedience to Saint Vannes and to Abbot Rudolph.

The disputes that had arisen at that time between the priesthood and the empire had broken out into open wars and were raging everywhere throughout Germany and Italy. Upper Lorraine was not free from that stain either. Although its bishops—Egilbert, Hermann, Theodoric, and Pibo—remained faithful to the king, Gregory VII employed chiefly the abbots Rudolph of Verdun and Jarenton of Dijon to attack them and draw them over to his side.

Rudolph indeed went to Rome twice and undertook a papal mission. In 1080, carrying letters from Gregory, he established Hermann, bishop of Metz, in fidelity to the Church; and in 1085, returning from Rome once more, he hoped to reconcile Theodoric of Verdun with Gregory. But in the meantime Rome had been occupied by Henry, Gregory had been driven to Salerno, and Theodoric decided to embrace the party of Clement and compelled Rudolph to resign.

Perhaps Jarenton, too, had then returned to Dijon. He was a man most intimate with Gregory, who, at the pope’s command, had summoned Robert Guiscard to Rome with other legates and afterward accompanied Gregory in his flight to Salerno; Gregory then sent him as legate to Coimbra.

After examining the state of affairs, Jarenton advised Rudolph to leave Verdun and, together with his monks, to move first to Flavigny, the estate of Saint Vannes situated in the territory of Toul, and then to Dijon. Among the others, Hugh followed the abbot. In the nineteenth year of his age, he left his known relatives, his homeland [Col. 0010B] and the nest in which he had grown up, with the intention of gladly devoting his body, soul, and entire substance to what he believed to be God’s cause, and of choosing to expend whatever strength his youthful body possessed in God’s service.

Because of this fervor of faith, he was greatly commended to Jarenton. From the beginning he enjoyed Jarenton’s favor and goodwill, and shortly after he, together with the abbot and the other brothers, promised obedience to the monastery of Dijon, he was admitted into the fellowship of their life and counsels. Thus, when Bishop Theodoric died and Abbot Rudolph returned to Verdun in 1092, Hugh decided to remain attached to Jarenton.

Among the principal men of the papal party with whom our Hugh became acquainted, he visited Hugh, abbot of Cluny, as Jarenton’s companion. He pleased Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, so greatly that the archbishop took him into his service and employed him in his affairs. He enjoyed such intimacy with him that the archbishop considered Hugh bound to him by an indissoluble bond.

Stirred by the example of such men and moved by the importance of the affairs in which he had taken part, the young man turned to writing history, with the intention that, if he himself could not hear of brave deeds, he might at least investigate the good actions of brave men and rescue them from oblivion [Note: [Col. 0011D] Under the year 1100.]. He therefore undertook to compose a chronicle that would carry the history from the Nativity of Christ down to his own time.

After gathering a great many sources, he set his hand to the work around the year 1090 [Note: [Col. 0011D] Most of the book had already been written when the author was elected abbot of Flavigny in 1096. Nor were the passages in which he relates his flight and the obedience he rendered to the abbot of Dijon written many years after 1085: folio 97 was written after 1086, folio 129 after 1087, and folio 124 after the year 1090. I therefore believe that he began writing around 1090.].

In the two books that he composed, he carried the history in the first down to the beginning of the eleventh century and in the second down to his own time. In general he followed chronological order; but, as his sources continued to increase here and there after the work had begun, he never ceased revising what he had written with diligent care, adding what had been omitted, placing notes in the margins of the pages, and inserting entire leaves.

He obtained the sources he first used—those of Lorraine and Burgundy—from the resources of the abbeys of Saint Vannes and Dijon. Other materials were added later, such as catalogues [Col. 0011C] of the archbishops of Lyon and the bishops of Clermont. Finally, materials from Flavigny were added in the margins and on inserted pages, evidently after he had assumed the governance of that monastery.

At the beginning of 1095 or 1096, when Jarenton was sent by Pope Urban to Normandy and England to restore the authority of the Church and reconcile King William and Duke Robert, the brothers, Hugh accompanied his abbot. When their mission had achieved nothing and Jarenton and Hugh were returning, they were brought into mortal danger by a violent storm at sea, but eventually reached Bayeux, where Hugh, overcome by a severe illness, barely escaped death a second time.

After he recovered, and after Jarenton had restored concord between Duke Robert and his brother, Hugh accompanied the duke, who intended to go to Jerusalem with the abbot, as far as Pont-de-l’Arche in September 1096 [Col. 0011D] [Col. 0012A]. Returning to Dijon, he agreed—at the urging of Haganon, bishop of Autun, and by the choice of the canons and laymen—to assume the abbacy of Flavigny.

Released only with difficulty by Hugh, the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0011D] The archbishop writes as follows: “whose diligence we trusted, indeed whose tongue was our voice.”], he entered Flavigny on 22 November 1096 and was consecrated on the following day.

During the nearly three years in which he governed the abbey, he devoted himself to its affairs and spent two thousand solidi on the church’s construction. But when Haganon, the diocesan bishop, died in 1098, Hugh found an adversary in his successor, Norgaud.

On 28 March 1099 Abbot Rudolph died. Hugh was present at his death, read the Passion of the Lord, and accompanied the dead man’s funeral to Verdun [Note: [Col. 0011D] Bishop Rudolph was buried on 2 April; Hugh was at Flavigny on 10 April.].

In September of that year Hugh departed from Flavigny, giving way to certain hostile monks [Col. 0012B] and to Norgaud. For some time he worked in vain with Norgaud and with Hugh, the archbishop, to return.

At the beginning of 1100 he again went to England. In August he once more wrote unsuccessfully to his adversaries at Flavigny. Finally, near the end of September, he was restored to the abbey by papal legates at the Council of Valence and returned to Flavigny.

Even then, however, he was unable to win over the offended attitude of the brothers, who suspected that he intended to subject the abbey to Dijon. Thus, in 1101, Norgaud was given the opportunity to install another abbot: Hugh was expelled and appealed to Rome in vain.

These are the last things that Hugh himself wrote about his own life. He therefore seems to have remained at Dijon with Jarenton, whom alone among all his friends he had found constant and faithful [Col. 0012C]. He extended his book intermittently and without following any fixed order, according as his inclination led him, down to the year 1102.

What happened to the author afterward is uncertain. It nevertheless seems clear that he abandoned the ecclesiastical party with which he had stood for so long, left the monastery of Dijon, was excommunicated by the abbot of Dijon, and, when in 1111 Richard, bishop of Verdun and a partisan of Henry V, expelled Paschal’s loyal abbot of Saint Vannes, who had again fled to Jarenton, was installed in that man’s place by the bishop [Note: [Col. 0011D] This account comes from a letter of Laurence, the expelled abbot of Saint Vannes, in which he replies to the writings of his adversaries, perhaps of Hugh himself; see Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. V, p. 685, col. 1. “He [Richard] presumes to take away ... granting or removing at his pleasure the abbeys of the Lord, to whomever he wishes, of whatever sort he wishes, and in whatever manner he wishes. Among these is the man who, rejected from the abbey of Flavigny, fled from the church of Dijon, to which, at the command of his lord Abbot Rudolph, he had made his profession; excommunicated by the abbot of Dijon, he presumed to receive the pastoral staff with which he ought to be scourged eternally. Those who entrusted pastoral care to so infamous a person, and those who allowed it to be entrusted to him, have made themselves partners in his presumption. He himself also composed a book furnished with authorities against those who resist the Roman Church; and we believe that now, in accordance with what the peasants say—that a knife has two edges—he will compile another book,” etc. The book praised by Laurence seems to have been our *Chronicle*.].

This could readily be believed of a man of passionate character who had suffered the greatest injustice, although Hugh’s name is not explicitly given.

If he was indeed the man whom Laurence, abbot of Saint Vannes and Rudolph’s successor, hints at [Col. 0012D], he governed the abbey for only three years, until Laurence [Col. 0013A] was recalled from exile by Richard [Note: [Col. 0013D] Laurence’s continuation of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*.].

Around the year 1140 Laurence of Liège, the continuator of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, reported these events. He states that he wrote his book very reluctantly, compelled by the excessive insistence of the venerable Hugh, monk of Saint Vannes.

There were some who thought that this Hugh was our own Hugh. The fact that the latter would then have been seventy-five years old would not stand in the way; and some support is supplied by the fact that the writer chose to conceal the name of the abbot substituted for Laurence, and that he seems to have known Hugh’s book.

If these things are so, one might suppose that Hugh resigned the abbacy after Abbot Laurence’s return and spent the final years of a life tossed by so many storms peacefully in the nest in which he had grown up as a boy. But these matters are genuinely unknown.

[Col. 0013B]

In the surviving book, we rightly praise above all the remarkable and indefatigable care with which Hugh sought out from every quarter the most extensive sources for his work, as well as his unceasing zeal for adding and correcting.

He had at hand books, documents, and letters drawn from the archives and libraries of Verdun, Dijon, and Lyon, access to which had been provided by the abbots Rudolph and Jarenton and by Hugh, the archbishop. To these were eventually added the materials of Flavigny, namely:

Jerome; Prosper; Hydatius; Victor of Tunnuna; Bede’s *On the Six Ages*; Regino’s *Chronicle*; Aethicus together with the *Itinerary of Antoninus*; Orosius; Victor; Victor of Vita; Jordanes; Nennius; Fortunatus; Gregory of Tours; *Deeds* and catalogues of the Roman pontiffs; Isidore’s *Etymologies*; unpublished Lives of Saints Sanctinus, Mansuetus, Maximinus, and Pulchronius [Col. 0013C]; Sigismund; Chrothildis; Lupus of Troyes; Antidius; Leodegarius; Praejectus; Bonitus; Lambert; Lupus of Sens; Goericus; Balthildis; Agericus, unpublished; Carilefus; Magdalveus, unpublished; the translation of Saint Gorgonius; Fredegar; the *Deeds of the Franks*; Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards* and *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*; the genealogy of the Carolingians; Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*; the *Petavian Annals*; the annals of Einhard, Fulda, Saint Vaast, and Lyon; perhaps also those of Flavigny; Ado’s *Chronicle*; Hincmar’s letter on the *Life of Sanctinus* and the *Life of Remigius*; Bertarius’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun* with its continuations; Flodoard’s *Annals*; Richer; the unpublished *Life of Deodoric of Metz*; the works of Simeon; Rudolph Glaber’s *History* and *Life of William of Dijon*; the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon*; the *Life of Robert*, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu; catalogues of the bishops of Auvergne and the archbishops of Lyon; charters of Saint Vannes, Dijon, and Flavigny [Note: [Col. 0013D] He also mentions the Rouen armarium; folio 89.]; decrees and letters of the Roman pontiffs, bishops, and clerics [Col. 0014A]; many canonical collections; acts of councils; letters of Henry IV, his mother Agnes, Countess Matilda; and various other materials.

He used these sources by excerpting them, copying most of them, or transcribing them in full, and inserting them into his history together with what he himself had seen or had heard from other witnesses of events. But because the text was often carelessly copied [Note: [Col. 0013D] Compare, for example, Nicholas II’s decree on the election of the pope and what I noted there; the Lateran canons of 1078, folios 102 and 103; and the letters, which are very often without dates.], it does not entirely inspire confidence.

In general he followed chronological order, but he often wanders more widely, either drawn away by the abundance of material or indulging his own inclination. Since he inserted many newly discovered items into the older text and very frequently revised the book after long intervals of time, without taking care to rewrite it in full, it was inevitable that he should leave a narrative rich in material but lacking in uniformity and clarity [Col. 0014B]. For example, he reports the death of one and the same man [Note: [Col. 0013D] Abbot Rudolph.] in three places.

Otherwise, he was a learned and diligent man, though not of especially discerning judgment; credulous of marvels and open even to false rumors [Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, he makes Emperor Conrad II the son of Otto III; he assigns the death of William of Utrecht to 1076 instead of 1080; nor does he report the events of 1077–1079 [Col. 0014D] in their proper order. On folio 95 he writes that Alexander III succeeded Pope Alexander II; on the following folio he correctly reports that Gregory VII succeeded Alexander.]. He was also liable to error in arranging events, sometimes talkative and more verbose than was appropriate. He wrote as might be expected of a man angry with the enemies of the Church but candid, and he did not conceal the faults of men on his own side.

Although, in matters preceding his own time, he preserved some information worthy of remembrance by relying on documents now lost, and although in the history of his own time—especially of Lorraine—he reported much that was unknown to others, we do not altogether agree with the first editor of the work, who praised the book as an incomparable treasure of ecclesiastical history, particularly of the eleventh century [Col. 0014C]. We do not hesitate to prefer to Hugh the historians Lambert, Berthold, and Bernold, who belonged to the same age. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that Hugh rendered the study of history an excellent service and that his work should often be consulted with good results.

Our author seems, like other writers from Lorraine, to begin the year from the day of the Incarnation, 25 March, or rather from Easter [Note: [Col. 0014D] He assigns the Roman Council to 1074 on folio 97, although it was held at the end of February 1075. He writes that a comet appeared in 1065, whereas Bernold says that it appeared on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, the author of the Beneventan Annals on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, Adam of Bremen at III, 50, around the days of Easter, and others on the following days of 1066.].

His style is lucid, although his prose sometimes resolves itself into rhythmic clauses [Note: [Col. 0014D] Compare, for example, folios 52 verso, 55, 74, and 96 verso.], as we have already observed in several writers of the eleventh century.

Hugh’s book, difficult to read, may not have been unknown to Laurence of Liège. In general, however, it may be said to have remained hidden until it was printed in 1657 by Philip Labbe in volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*.

The editor used the autograph manuscript of his own college, namely that of the Society of Jesus at Clermont, which was then flourishing in Paris. The text he published was generally reproduced well, but he placed some material in the wrong locations, omitted quite a few passages that were more difficult to read, and cut out other passages that seemed to him useless and commonplace [Col. 0015A], such as the authorities of pontiffs and Fathers in defense of Gregory VII.

Nor can he be absolved from the further fault that, out of deference to the Roman Curia, he altered the text in several places. The text had been concealed beneath two centuries of silence and was then brought to light for the first time. For, as our late Knust once observed, nothing remains hidden forever.

Many writers of ecclesiastical and secular history made use of this first edition. It is worth naming the editors of the *Acts of the Saints*, volume II for June, pages 976 and following; the *Life of Richard, Abbot of Saint Vannes*; Mabillon, *Sixth Century*, part I; the *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, pages 185 and following; the *Life of Frederick, Provost of Arras*; certain passages concerning Simeon the Recluse, page [Col. 0015B] 368; and the explicitly printed *Life of Abbot Richard*, page 557 and following.

Also noteworthy is Bouquet and his continuators, who excerpted our work in volume III, pages 353–365; V, 372–374; VI, 231–232; VII, 246–248; VIII, 286–297; X, 205–210; XI, 142–147; XIII, 617–628; and XIV, 797–804, and attempted to illuminate it here and there with observations.

After we first began considering a new edition of the book, we decided that we ought to investigate its sources. This inquiry was carried out with the greatest possible diligence by our associate, the distinguished scholar Rudolph Koepke, in both the ancient text and the literary materials employed [Note: [Col. 0015D] See the discussion in our *Annals*, vol. IX, p. 240, where many matters are explained more fully and may be omitted here.].

In 1844 I traveled to England, where I had learned that the autograph manuscript, after being sold from the public sale of the manuscripts of the Clermont College, had been transferred to the Meermann Library and, in our own age, to the very extensive treasury of manuscripts belonging to the distinguished Thomas [Col. 0015C] Philipps, baronet of Middle Hill [Note: [Col. 0016D] Sir Thomas Philipps himself copied folios 17–41.].

When I appealed to him, a man distinguished by generosity of spirit, love of letters, and courtesy of manners, he not only permitted me to examine the manuscript but voluntarily invited me to inspect the other treasures of his very rich library that might be useful for the publication of the *Monuments of Germany*.

Once I had been given access to the manuscript and had ascertained that it was genuinely the author’s autograph, I set about correcting Labbe’s text. I left only those passages for which I had not then had sufficient time to make a copy; later I received copies of them from the distinguished scholar. Thus we are now able to present readers with a truly complete text of the book.

The parchment manuscript was written in a small folio format and bears a hand from the end of the eleventh century. It was not written all at one time, but with the pen very frequently laid aside and then taken up again as the material to be written allowed.

After several years had passed, the text was repeatedly revised: in some places it was erased, in others enlarged by sentences and entire pages added and interpolated. The small script up to folio 69, and up to the chronicle’s year 950, is the hand shown on the accompanying page [Col. 0015D]. From folio 69 onward it gradually becomes smaller and smaller. The writing in the margins and in the added pages, as well as in the corrected sentences, is smaller still. From page 123 onward—that is, from the year 1079—the script again diminishes. The passages written at Flavigny from page 138 to the end of the book display an even smaller hand. We have copied a specimen of the final pages.

Everything relating to the history of Flavigny before folio 138 is found either in the margins or on inserted pages.

The parchment consists for the most part of gatherings in the following order: folios 1–6, 7–14, 15–22, 23–33, 34–41, 42–49, 50–63, 64–72, 73–85, 86–92, 93–95, 96–110, 111–119, 120–128, 129–136, [Col. 0016B] 137–142, and 143–148.

The opening gathering is a ternion and quire, folios 1–3. The Flavigny calendar occupies folios 5–6; a table of eras, folios 3–5; excerpts from canons and medical prescriptions, and folios 7, 8, 9, and 9b contain excerpts from canons written on leaves that had first been left blank and were inscribed later.

The *Chronicle* begins on folio 10 and fills the remainder of the book.

The pages interpolated into the *Chronicle* are 9b, 12b, 26, 27, 28, 29, 29b, 30b, 33b, 35b, 57, 58, 58b, 60b, 62b, 81–83, 86b, 93, 94, 95, 100, 101, 103b, and 130b. Perhaps, in addition, some other leaves containing the history of Madalveus were interpolated into the gathering comprising folios 50–63, besides 57, 58, 58b, and 60b.

The leaves that Labbe reports as having been prefixed to the *Chronicle* are missing, for the most part worn away by age. They contained the series of the abbots of Flavigny, which may also be thought to have been written by Hugh, since the same series is inserted in various places in the *Chronicle* [Col. 0016C].

After four intervening pages, Labbe read a necrology. It had not been accurately compiled from earlier documents and now stands at the beginning of the codex. From the handwriting it can be inferred that it is owed to Hugh, and we too shall place it before the *Chronicle*, since it has not yet been printed [Note: [Col. 0016D] Mabillon excerpted a few items from it.], while assigning the series of abbots to the end of the *Chronicle*.

We have not thought it necessary to reproduce again the excerpts from the charters of Flavigny that Labbe transcribed from Sirmond’s papers on pages 269–273.

We have chosen to add only a very small number of notes to so lengthy a work; those owed to our colleague Koepke are distinguished by the letter K.

[Col. 0016D]

It remains for me to mention that, in the necrology, a few items were added by Hugh in a different ink, and that, beneath the catalogue of the archbishops of Lyon, Hugh’s successors down to Humbert were appended. Since Humbert held office from 1147 to 1153, it may be conjectured that Hugh reached that period and spent his old age beyond the age of eighty.

[Col. 0017]

# Necrology

[Col. 0019]

[Col. 0019A] January Kalends. (2) Agrippinus, bishop of Autun. January Nonas 2. Gregory of Langres. January Ides 7. Eugemonius, bishop of Autun. January Ides 5. Paschasia, virgin [and martyr 2.], at Flavigny. Milo, abbot of Der, a monk of Verdun. February Kalends 8. Saint Prejectus, martyr. February Nonas 2. Serotinus, confessor of Flavigny. Translation of Saint Simphorianus. February Ides 4. Rainaldus died, brother of the duke, abbot of Flavigny. February Ides 3. Frederick, a layman, died, my brother. March Kalends 8. Installation of Lord Zachon as abbot. March Kalends 6. Galdricus of Colticum, brother of Lord Hagano, bishop, a convert and monk of Flavigny, [Col. 0019B] died. March Kalends 5. Charles the Great died [Note: [Col. 0019D] February Kalends 5.], who granted to the church of Flavigny, in perpetuity, all the tolls throughout his entire kingdom and everything belonging to the right of the fisc from all the lands of that same church. March Kalends. Gyrardus of Semur died; he gave the cell of Semur to Saint Prejectus. March Ides 7. Wido, abbot of Melun, a monk of Flavigny, died. March Ides 6. King Lothair died (985). April Kalends 16. Aymo, count of Grin. and monk, who gave Saint-Germain of Latifolium. April Kalends 14. Wido of Pothières [Note: [Col. 0019D] Pothières, in the diocese of Langres.], abbot and monk of Flavigny, died. April Kalends 13. Walter, a monk of Flavigny and a convert, died. April Kalends 11. Eupharius, priest of Flavigny. April Kalends 5. Rodulfus, abbot, died. April Ides 4. Evgilis, holy archbishop of Sens, first abbot of Prüm and thereafter of Flavigny, who is renowned for many miracles. [Col. 0020A] June Kalends. Walo, monk and priest of Flavigny, died. June Nones. Reception of the body of Saint Ursinus, martyr, at Flavigny. July Kalends 18. Richard, abbot. July Kalends 14. Robert, king of the Franks, died; he gave the church of Saint John within Autun (1031). July Kalends 12. Louis the Pious, emperor, died; throughout his entire kingdom, in cities, villages, markets, and ports, he granted to the church of Flavigny the toll levied on persons, and gave it to that same church (840). July Kalends 10. King Louis died [Note: [Col. 0020D] June 22; June Kalends 10.], the last of the royal line, brother of Arnulf, bishop of Reims (987). July Kalends 7. Bishop Hagano died, of blessed memory. [Col. 0020B] July Kalends 4. Geylo, bishop of Langres, abbot and monk of Flavigny, died. July Kalends 2. Arveus, bishop of Autun and abbot of Flavigny. July Kalends. Liudo, bishop of Autun, died. July Nones 4. Salocho, bishop of Dol, a monk of Flavigny, died. July Nones 3. Translation of Saint Sanctinus from Meaux to Verdun. Hugo, abbot of Melun, a monk of Flavigny, died. July Nones 2. Gervinus, bishop and abbot of Flavigny, died. July Ides 6. Helmuinus, abbot of Saint Peter’s at Sens, a monk of Flavigny, died. [Col. 0020C] July Ides 3. Henry the Great, emperor, died (1024). August Kalends 17. Hermannus, a canon of Liège, died at Jerusalem. August Kalends 11. Milo, viscount of Tilly, died; he gave the cell of Prisciacum. August Kalends 9. Magoaldus, abbot of Flavigny, died in the eleventh year of Clovis, son of Dagobert. August Kalends 5. Grimoldus, abbot of Verdun, died. [Col. 0020D] September Kalends 10. Ursinus, martyr, at Flavigny, and Flavianus, bishop of Autun. September Kalends 7. Odo I, abbot of Flavigny, died. September Nones 4. Siagrius, bishop of Autun. September Ides 8. Wifardus, abbot of Flavigny, brother-in-law of Emperor Louis, died. [Col. 0021A] September Ides 7. Saint Regina, virgin and martyr, at Flavigny. September Ides 5. Theophilus, martyr, at Flavigny. September Ides 3. Jonas, bishop of Autun, died. September Ides 2. Evantius, bishop of Autun. September Ides. Nectarius, bishop of Autun. October Kalends 10. John, abbot. October Kalends 5. Florentinus, bishop of Autun. October Kalends 4. Lothair, emperor and monk, died (855). October Nones 6. Saint Leodegarius, martyr and bishop of Autun. October Nones 5. Saint Widradus, the first abbot of Flavigny. October Nones 4. Madelveus, bishop of Verdun. [Col. 0021B] October Nones 3. Henry III, emperor, son of Conrad, died (1056). King Louis, son of Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0021D] “King.”], grandson of Charles the Bald, died (882) [Note: [Col. 0021D] He died on August 5.]. October Nones 2. Charles the Bald, emperor, died, and Theobald II, bishop of Langres, monk and prior of Flavigny (877). October Nones. Charles the Simple died (929). October Ides 3. Hugo the Younger, abbot of Melun, a monk of Flavigny, died. November Kalends 17. Gerardus, a layman, died, my brother. November Kalends 16. Dada of Mount Walcherius, my mother [Note: [Col. 0021] “my mother” is written above the line.], died, Crothildis, daughter [Note: [Col. 0021] “C. daughter” added; cf. December Nones 4.]. November Kalends 12. Decia died, sister of Saint Widradus, who founded the monastery of Saint Andochius at Autun; [Col. 0021C] and another sister founded the monastery of Faverniacum. November Kalends 9. King Pippin died, father of Charles the Great (768). November Kalends 5. Gunterus, priest and monk of Flavigny, died. November Kalends 4. Walter, bishop of Autun, died; he restored to the church of Flavigny nineteen altars of churches, together with their furnishings and tithes, and the protections of the villages belonging to the abbot’s treasury. November Kalends 2. Proculus, bishop of Autun. November Kalends. Girardus the Younger, monk and priest [Col. 0021D] of Flavigny, died. [Col. 0022A] November Nones 4. Commemoration of Saint Benignus. November Ides 5. Vito, bishop of Verdun. December Kalends 15. Gregory, bishop of Tours. December Kalends 14. Simplicius, bishop of Autun. December Kalends 11. Eusebius, priest of Autun. # BOOK ONE OF THE CHRONICLE

[Col. 0021]

[Col. 0021D] Folio 10. In the year [Note: [Col. 0021] Written in the margin of the page, marked 9b, are the following words: “In the nineteenth year of Octavian Caesar we find that Lugdunum was founded [Col. 0023] according to Gregory of Tours. Saint Austremonius, first bishop of the Arverni. Urbicus. Legonus. Saint Hildius. Saint Nepotianus. Artomius of Trier. Venerandus. Rusticus. Saint Namatius. Saint Eparchius. Saint Sidonius. Patiens of Lyon. Saint Aprunculus, formerly of Langres, in the time of Chilperic I. Saint Eufrasius, in the time of Clovis I. He died in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate; he lived four years after his death, and Apollinaris [lived] six months. Saint Quintianus, first bishop of Rodez. Saint Gallus, who protected his people by prayer from bubonic plague, paternal uncle of Saint Gregory, bishop of Tours, in the time of Theudebert. Cautinus, in the first year of King Theudewald. Saint Genesius, who founded the monastery of Magnilocus and appointed Evodius abbot. Felix. Garivaldus, [bishop] for twenty days. Saint Prejectus was martyred in the year of the Lord 580, in the tenth year of Chilperic’s reign; he presided for eleven incomplete years. Saint Avitus converted the Jews in the second year of Childebert; he presided for fifteen incomplete years. Saint Bonitus, his father, under King Theoderic. Norbertus, for fifteen years. Proculus.”] from the creation of the world 5198 [Note: [Col. 0021] Or, according to Augustine, 5227.], and from the foundation of the City 752, in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, [Col. 0022D] indiction 4, concurrent 5, epact 11, feria 1, moon 13: Jesus Christ, Son of God, was born at Bethlehem of Judaea, in the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus and the thirty-first year of Herod, king of the Jews, when Carullus and Quintilianus were consuls. [Jerome.] In the year 3 from Christ’s birth, the forty-fifth of Augustus, in the thirty-fourth year of Herod’s reign, when he had learned of Christ’s birth through the signs given by the Magi, he ordered all the infants of Bethlehem to be killed; and in the following year he died miserably, worms swarming throughout his body, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign.

In the fifteenth year from the beginning of the Lord, 5213 from the creation of the world, Augustus, in the seventy-sixth year of his age, died; Tiberius succeeded him and reigned for twenty-two years. [Cf. Jerome.] In his fifteenth year the word of God came to John, son of Zachariah, in the desert; and the Lord Jesus, having completed his thirtieth year of age, was baptized by John in Tiberius’s fifteenth year, under another Herod, king of the Jews, on January Ides 8, which was the seventh feria, indiction 3, moon 15; and in the following year John was beheaded.

Thus, in the year 5232 from the creation of the world, 784 from the foundation of the City, concurrent 7 of the third line, 33 from the beginning of the Lord, Jesus Christ himself, Son of God, came to his Passion for the salvation of the world, in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, on April Kalends 8, Thursday, moon 14, when Gaius Caesar for the fourth time and Junius Saturninus were consuls. In the thirteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, after celebrating the typical Passover with his disciples, he was handed over by his disciple to the Jews during the night. Around morning he was led to Pilate, handed over to the soldiers, beaten with whips, smeared with spittle, and wearing a purple garment and a crown of thorns on his head. He was led away to be crucified on April Kalends 7, moon 15, and on the sixth feria he mounted the cross for the salvation of the world. [Col. 0023C] [Jerome.] An earthquake occurred throughout the whole world, and there was an eclipse of the sun, so that even the stars appeared in the sky, at the sixth hour, in the ninth part of Aries. He rose from the dead on April Kalends 5, moon 17 [Note: [Col. 0023] The remainder is written in the margin of the page.].

Pilate was brought to Rome by Volusianus, together with Saint Veronica, who had been healed by Christ from an issue of blood. Tiberius condemned him so that throughout his entire life he would enjoy neither fire nor water nor food cooked by fire, on account of the death of the Lord Jesus; and he was bound and sent into exile in the city of Amaria in Tuscany. Later recalled by Nero, he was again condemned and died because of the circumcision he had performed upon himself. Veronica, having become wealthy in possessions and riches, [and] the image of the Lord which she herself had painted, and which she herself had accompanied when it was brought to Tiberius, were enclosed in gold. After her death, she rests honorably buried at Rome. Tiberius, meanwhile, in a vision of the image [Col. 0024A] of the Savior, was healed of a fistula [Note: [Col. 0023D] “Perhaps a fistula?”].

In the year 34 from the beginning of the Lord, according to the Latins, who begin the year in January, Paul, as he was going to Damascus, was called from heaven by Christ. But according to the Hebrews, who begin the year in March, in that same year, in the eleventh month of the Lord’s Passion, on February Kalends 8 [Note: [Col. 0023] The second hand adds: “Tiberius was baptized nine months before his death and, healed of a fistula, died.”] [Regino].

In the year 39 from the beginning of the Lord, Gaius reigned for four years, ten months, and eight days. If, therefore, we add to these months the six that remained from the fifty-sixth year of Octavian, there will be sixteen months. Subtracting four from these leaves one complete year, which seems to be inserted at this point.

In the year 44 from the beginning of the Lord, Pilate killed himself.

In the year 45 from the beginning of the Lord, Claudius reigned for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. If we add to these the four months and seven days that remained above, there are eleven months and seven days; adding twenty-eight days gives thirty-seven days, that is, one year and six days, which seems to be added to these periods.

In the year 47 from the beginning of the Lord, James, the brother of John, was beheaded; Peter was sent to prison. Herod was struck by an angel. Paul and Barnabas were set apart by the Spirit for the preaching of the Gospel.

In the year 48 from the beginning of the Lord, Paul and Barnabas went up to Jerusalem, as he himself writes to the Galatians: “After fourteen years,” he says, “I went up to Jerusalem.” Let the number of years therefore be reckoned. We know that Peter held the episcopal see of the city of Rome for twenty-five years. It follows, therefore, that we should believe he came to Rome in the second year of Claudius, which was the fifteenth year from the Lord’s Passion; and in that same year Paul came, fourteen years after the Lord’s Passion. By this calculation we find that Paul came to the faith in that same year of the Lord’s Passion. Fourteen and twenty-five therefore make thirty-nine, which was the year from the Lord’s Passion in which Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom, because in Nero’s second year Paul was sent there in chains, and he contended for the faith for eleven years together with Peter, suffering with him in the twelfth.

(Folio 10 verso.) After God and our Lord Jesus Christ had freed from eternal death, by his own death, the human being whom he had made, and had carried into the heavens the captivity of our flesh, which he had raised from the dead, in that same year Stephen, the protomartyr, was stoned to death for his confession of the truth, in the fifth month, on the third day of the month, which is August Nones 4. The church of the faithful, which was at Jerusalem, was scattered, so that the word of salvation, which had been sent to the Jews and rejected by them, might be received by the nations. As the apostles and their disciples, their followers, therefore departed wherever they could, Peter [Col. 0025A] [Note: [Col. 0025] Cf. *Life of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January II, 918.] went down to Antioch and, over twice seven [Note: [Col. 0025] “Seven”; corrected to “twice seven” by the corrector.] years, founded and governed the church of Antioch, so that Christians were first given that name at Antioch. From there, in the second year of Claudius, when Vinicius and Cornelius Asiaticus and Silvanus were consuls, he came to Rome and, as head of the body of the Church after Christ and through Christ, brought the standard of divine preaching to the Roman citadel (cf. *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*). Having founded the church there, he announced Christ’s Gospel to the Romans; by preaching and confirming his preaching with signs, he held the papacy of that City for twenty-five years. Rome marveled because it had not learned that the unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity ought to be venerated; but at last, through the frequent testimony of miracles, it learned to submit its hearts and necks to the one Trinity.

That same first shepherd and apostle, Peter, had determined to plow with the plowshare of the word the lands of the entire West, to entrust the seeds of teaching to the furrows of minds, so that he might restore to the threshing floor of the Lord who was to come sheaves of grain yielding a hundredfold. Choosing men proved in faith, powerful in work and speech, patient in tribulation, long-suffering in hope, and instructed in all that the Lord Jesus had done, he sent to the city of the Mediomatrici Saint Clement, a patrician of the Roman commonwealth and his own disciple, and Saint Mansuetus, born of the renowned stock of the Scots, eminent in faith and teaching, to the city of the Leuci ( *Life of Mansuetus*). To Reims he also sent Saints Sixtus and Sinicius; to Châlons, Saint Memmius; and to Trier, which is the metropolis and one of the chief cities of Gaul, and to nearby Cologne, he sent Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus. (Folio 11.) Along with these there were many others who, sent by that same prince of the apostles, dispelled the darkness of the West with the shining ray of the true Sun and, endowed with faith and courage, preached the name of Christ, which had not yet shone in those places, to an unbelieving people. At Rome he himself taught the word of God, shaking the wall of unbelief by the force of the Gospel and overthrowing, like a battering ram, the tower of confusion and idolatry by devout confession and belief. He opposed and held himself against the barrier wherever the more violent enemy had taken his stand, whose tyranny he strove, with Christ as his leader, to overthrow.

For the consolation of so great a shepherd and the advancement of preaching, Paul, after many dangers of travel, labor, and hunger, was sent in chains to Rome in the second year of Caesar Nero, in the year 61 from the beginning of the Lord, 28 from the Passion, indiction 4, when Silvanus and Paulinus were consuls—not because Jews and gentiles had desired it, but because Christ had preordained and willed it so that each might be a consolation to the other. Who could resist these sons of thunder? Who could oppose them? It was Simon the Magus who alone seemed to resist the truth. If, after the apostolic triumph and the disgrace of his own downfall and unheard-of arrogance, he had been allowed to recover breath, his own punishment alone would have given him understanding, so that he would not presume to do such things again. But because the magician died condemned in the depths of the pit of the abyss and, as Nero hoped, did not rise again, Nero, seeing himself deprived of the consolation of so faithful a friend, condemned the apostles of God—one to the punishment of the cross, the other to capital sentence—on July Kalends 3, Thursday, moon 23, in the year 72 from the beginning of the Lord, 39 from the Passion, when Vespasian was consul for the seventh time and Titus for the sixth, in the 212th Olympiad.

After Peter, Clement, consecrated by Peter himself, undertook the government of the church (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*). As blessed Clement himself testifies concerning himself in a letter sent to James, the brother of the Lord, saying ( *Interpolated Letter*, in Rufinus, Mansi I, 91): “I appoint this Clement bishop for us; to him alone I hand over the chair of my preaching and teaching. He was my companion in all things from the beginning to the end, and therefore he came to know the whole truth of my [Note: [Col. 0025] “teaching” has dropped out.] doctrine.”

(Folio 11 verso.) Let us examine what should be thought against this, since there are some who attempt to assert that Linus took up the governance of the Roman church after Peter, and that Cletus succeeded Linus. It is said: Pope John, writing to all the bishops throughout Gaul and Germany, states: “Although Peter, prince of the apostles, took Linus and Cletus as assistants, he did not nevertheless entrust to them, by pontifical authority, the rule of binding and loosing, but to his successor Clement, who deserved, after him and with the blessed Peter conferring upon him the apostolic seat and pontifical authority, to hold it. Linus and Cletus administered external matters, while Peter, prince of the apostles, devoted himself to the word and to prayer.” And shortly afterward: “We never read that Linus and Cletus did anything with authoritative power through the pontifical ministry; they did only as much as was commanded them by blessed Peter.”

Linus, therefore, an Italian by nation, of the region of Tuscany, son of Herculanus, ordained by Peter, sat at Rome while Peter was still alive for eleven years, three months, and twelve days. Cletus likewise, a Roman by nation, of the district of the Vicus Patricii, son of Aemilianus, ordained by Peter himself, sat while Peter was still alive for twelve years, one month, and eleven days. Between Cletus and Clement, therefore, twenty days are reckoned (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*).

As has been said, Clement, third after Peter, undertook the priestly office while Peter was still alive. He was Roman by nation, from the district of Caelian Hill, son of Faustus. He sat for eleven years, two months, and two days [Note: [Col. 0025] The *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* give nine years, two months, and ten days.]—until the year 70 from the beginning of the Lord and the eleventh year of Nero’s reign, when Vespasian was consul for the fifth time and Titus for the fourth. From that time until now there has been no one in the entire catalogue of Roman pontiffs who, having exercised the priesthood during his lifetime for twenty-five years, equaled the first pontiff in that number of years. This blessed pontiff, therefore, established in the government of Peter, to whom he had always adhered and whose inseparable companion he had been, after learning of and rejecting the ravings of Simon the Magus, took every possible care to complete what his teacher had begun: namely, to send suitable preachers of the truth to the Western world [Col. 0027A], so that the light of preaching might shine upon the nations (cf. Hincmarus’s letter). (Folio 12.) For this reason he sent Saint Dionysius to the peoples of Gaul. By preaching and giving credibility to his preaching through miracles, Dionysius reached Paris under the Lord’s guidance [Note: [Col. 0027D] The author drew a large part of the narrative from Hincmarus’s letter to Emperor Charles, written in 876 or 877; the letter survives complete in *Acta Sanctorum*, October V, 586. In his letter Hincmarus incorporated a certain *Life of Sanctinus*, which he himself had written as a young man from the little notebooks that Wandelmarus, abbot of Saint Sanctinus, had found in the place entrusted to him, very badly worn and with what was written in them about the life and deeds of blessed Sanctinus almost obliterated. Flodoardus explicitly proves in *History of Reims* III, 18, that Hincmarus truly wrote such a letter to Charles; therefore Calmet should not be followed, *History of Lorraine* I, p. 32, who considers it spurious. K.], and he assigned him many companions: men trained in divine law, noble by birth, eloquent in speech, outstanding in faith, and filled with God’s grace. Among these was Saint Sanctinus (*Life of Sanctinus*), first shepherd of the people of Meaux and Verdun. Born of distinguished nobility, he sought the borders of Gaul with the aforementioned apostle of Gaul, destined to become a shining lamp in the Church, one that would not be hidden under a bushel but would shine for all, set upon a lampstand. For the memory of the fathers handed down that he was one of the seventy-two disciples and that, at the supper, he was appointed to provide water for washing the disciples’ feet and hands and to prepare a towel for the Savior.

When Saint Dionysius therefore came to Paris, he sent his companions through various regions to destroy the devil’s deceits and acquire peoples for the Lord (Hincmarus’s letter). Because Sanctinus excelled in prudence and chastity and was chosen by the most blessed Dionysius, he received the highest priestly office; consecrated as bishop, he was divinely appointed as a light to the peoples of the nations (*Life of Sanctinus*).

The aforementioned Dionysius also gave him, as a consolation in his labor and office, Antoninus, a holy and good man. In him God revealed the great merit of the blessed Sanctinus through a miracle of remarkable and extraordinary action, as will be shown later. And because God had determined to glorify his saint, blessed Dionysius sent him with his aforementioned companion to Chartres to enlighten the people who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, because the sun of justice had not shone upon them, nor had the light of truth dawned for them. When this blessed man arrived there, he grieved that the people were devoted to idolatry. Armed with faith in the Holy Trinity, despising the empty sect of the princes of the earth and their threats, he preached Jesus to the crowds of unbelievers. His preaching was poured forth together with works of power, and, illumined by divine grace, it softened the fierce minds of the pagans with saving teaching. With divine clemency cooperating with him, it came to pass [Col. 0027D] that the people of Chartres recognized the way of the Lord and did not refuse to bear the Lord’s gentle yoke upon the submissive shoulders of their wills. When blessed Dionysius observed this, praised the grace of divine power, and recognized how greatly Sanctinus prevailed in the work of preaching, he appointed him shepherd and teacher of the citizens of Meaux [Col. 0028A]. (Folio 12 verso.) This was not because the people of Meaux already recognized the way of truth—for they were all held fast by the bonds of idolatry—but so that the Lord might deign, through his faithful servant, to open for them the gates of righteousness. Entering through them by believing in his divinity and humanity, they would confess his name, because he is good and because his mercy endures forever.

Blessed Sanctinus, therefore, prepared to endure everything for the Savior’s name, neither fearing the threats nor the blows of the raging pagans. Because his trust was in the Lord, he pressed on with his preaching, watering the minds of his hearers with waters flowing from the belly [Note: [Col. 0027D] Thus in the corrector’s copy; Labbe reads “from the mind.”] of Jesus. Thus, preaching at opportune and inopportune times, he taught them to despise Jupiter, Saturn, Mercury, and Neptune; to reject all the portents of demons, not gods [Col. 0028B]; and to shatter their statues. He demonstrated through the clear evidence of his teaching that no divinity dwelt in them, but only complete falsehood and demonic deception. The nations could offer no reply to these things, since the greatness of the signs bore witness to the novelty of the words, and he who preached new things performed new deeds. Thus it came to pass that they themselves received the word of the Lord, and now venerated and honored as their shepherd and teacher the blessed man whom they had once judged worthy of reproach, mockery, and rejection (*Life of Sanctinus*). They rejoiced to be washed in baptism by his hands and anointed with holy chrism. The Gallic buskin was humbled beneath the feet of the holy man, and the stiff-neckedness of the Gauls, formerly ignorant of divine truth, now humbly hastened to baptism and confession of Christ’s name. The altars of the demons were thrown down; a church was built by the newly adopted people and consecrated by blessed Sanctinus in honor of God.

At that time Domitian held the insignia of the Roman Empire. He was devoted to luxury, tormented by avarice, and cruel in his actions; by excessive cruelty he had stained the imperial majesty. Like an unfed lion thirsting for the blood of the saints, he stirred up the second persecution against Christians after Nero (folio 13), and during the fifteen years in which he unlawfully held the Roman Empire he so crushed the commonwealth that no more cruel man is found in the entire number of Roman emperors. To demonstrate his sacrilegious devotion to the worship of the gods, in the fifth year of his reign he built, without the admixture of wood, a temple which he called the Pantheon. He was so lifted up by pride that he ordered himself to be called god and lord. When he heard (Hincmarus’s letter) of the fame of blessed Dionysius in destroying idols and converting peoples to Christ, he sent lictors into Gaul [Col. 0029A] to find and arrest him and either compel him to sacrifice to idols or kill him after subjecting him to various punishments. When blessed Dionysius learned that they were approaching the borders of Paris, he ordered Sanctinus and Antoninus to be summoned to him (*Life of Sanctinus*). Handing over to them the office of preaching, he admonished them to remain firm in the faith and, hastening to Rome as quickly as possible, to ask the bishop of the apostolic see for fellow workers in the word and teachers, because in the abundant harvest of the Lord’s sowing there were very few laborers to entrust the seed of the word to the furrows of minds. He added that he himself was already hastening to the joys of his Lord and desired that the pious Lord grant him the reward of his labor and burden.

Therefore, when blessed Dionysius had completed his course through the palm of martyrdom [Col. 0029B] in the year 97 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, but 64 from his Passion, at about the ninetieth year of his age, when the sixteenth year of the reign of the emperor Domitian was beginning (Hincmar, Letter), Sanctinus and Antoninus, obeying their master’s commands, were compelled by the thunder of the storm of persecution to withdraw from place to place while preaching. They came into the territory of Belgic Gaul and, with divine grace leading them, wherever they went they proclaimed the mighty deeds of Christ.

Belgic Gaul [Note: [Col. 0029] “Belg” had already been erased in the manuscript.] is a part of Gaul (fol. 12a), so called from the city called Belgis, which is Trier [Note: [Col. 0029D] “which is Trier” is absent in Isidore.] [Cf. Richer I, 1]. Gaul, however, was named from the whiteness of its people: *gala* [Note: [Col. 0029] already erased.] means “milk” [Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV, 4, 25]. For mountains and the severity of the climate exclude the sun’s heat from that region. To the east the ranges of the Alps protect it; to the west the Ocean encloses it [Note: [Col. 0029] “encloses” had already been erased.]; to the south are the precipitous Pyrenees; to the north, the waters of the Rhine and Germany. Its beginning is Belgica, while its end is Aquitania.

It is [Note: [Col. 0029] “It is, however, a region” was erased.] a land of fertile soil and abundant pasture, suitable for the use of living creatures, as those who have described the geography of the earth relate; watered by rivers and springs, it is drenched [Note: [Col. 0029] “perf.” was erased.] by two great rivers, the Rhine and the Rhône. Cisalpine Gaul lies around the Alps [Note: [Col. 0029] *citra*, “on this side,” in Isidore]; Transalpine Gaul lies beyond the Alps toward the north; Rhaetia [Note: [Col. 0029] “Rhaet” was erased.] lies beside the Rhine (ibid. 26). Aquitania was named from the slanting waters of the river Loire, which almost encircles it [Note: [Col. 0029D] What is read here and below about Aquitania is found in the same words in Heriger, *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* 41, MGH SS VII. K.] (ibid. 27).

Nature makes the Gauls fierce by temperament and keener in disposition because of the nature of the climate [Note: [Col. 0029] “and” was erased.]. Aethicus, describing the geography of Gaul, asserts that it has four provinces [Col. 0029D] [AETHICUS]: Belgic Gaul, Lugdunensis Gaul, Narbonensis, and Aquitania. He says that Belgic Gaul has as its boundary to the east the river Rhine and [Note: [Col. 0029] an erased word.] Germany; toward the southeast, the Pennine Alps [Note: [Col. 0029] The author adds an *A* and corrects this to “Appeninas”; i.e., “Pennine.”]; to the south, the province of Narbonensis; to the west, Lugdunensis; toward the northwest, the British Ocean; and to the north, the island of Britain [Col. 0030A] [Note: [Col. 0029] “to the north” was erased.].

Lugdunensis Gaul, extending lengthwise and bending narrowly, half encircles the province of Aquitania. It has [Note: [Col. 0029] “h” was erased.] Belgica to the east; to the south, part of the province of Narbonensis, where Arles is situated, and the Gallic Sea, into which the Rhône flows. The province of Narbonensis [Note: [Col. 0029] “pro” was erased.] has the Cottian Alps to the east; Spain to the west; Aquitania toward the northwest; Lugdunensis to the north; Belgic Gaul to the north [Note: [Col. 0029] “Belgic Gaul” was erased.]; and to the south the Gallic Sea, which lies between Sardinia and the Balearic Islands.

Aquitania has toward the northwest the Ocean called the Aquitanian Gulf; Spain to the west; Lugdunensis to the north and east [Note: [Col. 0029] “Lugdunensis” was erased.]; and toward the southeast and south it borders the province of Narbonensis.

According to Pope Pelagius, a province is properly one that has ten or [Note: [Col. 0029] “or” was erased.] eleven cities [Col. 0030B], one king, an equal number of lesser authorities under him, one metropolitan, and ten or eleven suffragan bishops as judges; all cases of bishops, priests, and cities are referred to their judgment.

After the Vandal destruction, which almost completely ruined the empire of the West and East, Pope Leo distributed the provinces. According to modern authorities, however, the provinces of Gaul are seventeen:

1. The first see of Gaul is Lugdunensis, with its three provinces:  
2. Rotomagensis,  
3. Turonensis, and  
4. Senonensis;  
5. Belgica Prima, which is Trier;  
6. Belgica Secunda, which is Rheims;  
7. Germania Prima, Mainz;  
8. Germania Secunda, Cologne;  
9. Maxima Sequanorum, Besançon;  
10. Alpes Graiae [Note: [Col. 0029] that is, “Graian Alps.”], Darantasia;  
11. Viennensis;  
12. Narbonensis Prima;  
13. Narbonensis Secunda, Aix;  
14. Aquitania Prima, Bourges;  
15. Aquitania Secunda, Bordeaux;  
16. Alpes Maritimae, Embrun;  
17. Novem Populana, Auch (*Provincial Register*).

In the province of Belgica Prima there stood a city on the border of Neustria and Austrasia, called Verdun. The ancients, and also people today, customarily call it the City of Nails. Antiquity itself, which alone preserves knowledge of past events, has indicated to us the etymology of this name—“City of Nails”—namely, that it was so called because it was built with immense care and labor from enormous stones fastened and joined together with iron and lead.

When we searched the Scriptures for a longer time to discover why it was called Verodunum, the only explanation that occurred to us was this: when Julius was conducting a levy of soldiers throughout Gaul, a certain Verolus received the aforementioned city, which had been attacked, into a treaty; from him it took its name, so that it was called Verodunum, as though Verolidunum, just as the Aedui were called Augustodunum from Augustus. Later, when the letter *o* was changed into *e*, it was called Veredunum [Col. 0031A], as Fortunatus attests [Note: [Col. 0031D] Book III, chapter 29.]. Modern authorities, however, derive the name Virdunum from its green meadows, or because it is almost always green, as though “green hill-fort.”

Rejecting all these conjectures, Aethicus in his *Cosmography*, in the *Itinerary of the World*, calls it Virodunum, because it was widely celebrated for the industry of brave men [Note: [Col. 0031] “These” through “celebrated” appears twice.]. The site of the city itself is pleasant by its very position: the river Meuse flows past it, and by its own fertility it is delightful, with the grassy plain of its green meadows (Life of Sanctinus). The people of the city were savage, devoted to the worship of demons, and ignorant of all truth. No herald of truth had come to them, although divine splendor was already shining upon the cities situated around them (fol. 13r).

When blessed Sanctinus therefore reached this city with his companion [Col. 0031B] (cf. Bertar, chapter 2), and saw all its inhabitants devoted to idolatry and without the true God, he prostrated himself on the ground and earnestly prayed to God to show the light of truth to the people sitting in the region of the shadow of death.

O prayer pleasing and beautiful to God! Beautiful, I say, and sweet it became in the sight of the glory of the most high God. Carried aloft on twin wings—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—it sought heaven in free flight and became before the Redeemer like incense of wondrous fragrance. Did it not become a smoke of good odor, when from the hand of the angel holding the censer the smoke of spices ascends, which are the prayers of the saints? And in the Apocalypse the twenty-four elders stand before the throne, holding golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints? But now let us see the fruit of this prayer.

The two men had just risen from prayer when, behold, they saw three doves perched in a single tree, shady with branches and lofty in height, but profaned by the worship of demons, for there the pagan country people offered vows and celebrated sacred rites to Fauns and Satyrs. The doves signified that it was the divine will that the triune and one God should be preached in that very place. Trusting, therefore, in the mercy of God, whose abundant benefits toward his future adopted children they foresaw, they gave thanks with the deepest affection of their hearts and humbly prayed that God might be glorified in his servants.

The place where this prayer had been offered to God [Col. 0031D] was a mountain situated on the northern side of the city. On its summit it has borne ever since a church dedicated by that man of God in the name and through the merits of the apostles Peter and Paul. This consecration took place in the year 98 of the Incarnation of the Word, namely, the thirteenth year of the emperor Domitian, in the consulship of Trajan for the seventh time and Maximus. There he also blessed a courtyard and established it as the cemetery of the church of Verdun. There that lord, together with his successors, the holy bishops, has his place of rest, except for those who glorify churches dedicated to them by their bodily presence, or who built them, or who repaired churches once built and later ruined in their own time. How this happened with his own most sacred body, when he completed the course of his own labor in the city of Meaux, the following account will explain in its proper place.

Blessed Sanctinus, seeing that the people of the city were numerous but blinded by the error of idolatry (fol. 14), and foreseeing in the spirit that a great and evident door had been opened to him in the Lord, resolved to remain for a while in that place with his companion. This was not a transgression of his master’s commands, if he could both win these people and faithfully fulfill the commands of his master.

Placing his hope in the Lord and entrusting himself to him, with a contrite and humbled heart he went forth to the people [Col. 0032B] and proclaimed again the gospel of Jesus Christ. They marveled at the poverty of his clothing, the dignity of his countenance, the eloquence of his speech, and the effectiveness of his miracles; yet they could not endure hearing that they must abandon the worship of demons, shatter the golden, silver, marble, plaster, and wooden images of their gods, and overthrow their altars.

Who could recount how often he was beaten by them, how often insulted, how often thrown half-dead from the city? Only the examiner of hearts knows this—he who, because he witnessed the sufferings and labors, became the merciful rewarder of his soldier and giver of his prizes. Nevertheless, the number of believers increased. From day to day, through the merits of his servants, the church of the faithful multiplied; the error of the pagans was destroyed; holy faith was taught everywhere; the grace of baptism was granted [Col. 0032C]; and the gifts of the Holy Spirit multiplied among the believers.

Blessed was the church, worthy of the governance of so great a shepherd, for it was enlightened by miracles and teachings. He became all things to all people, so that he might win all. Although he was insulted while preaching Christ, he willingly endured the torments, reproaches, and mockery inflicted upon him by evil people, so that he might make children of those whom he suffered as persecutors and return to the Lord the souls whom the devil was trying to take away.

When, by the merciful providence of God, many of those who had once been vessels of wrath destined for destruction became vessels of mercy through the sacrament of baptism, and he saw that the church of the faithful had reached the point where it could now advance by itself, he feared that, if he remained there much longer [Col. 0032D], the mission of obedience entrusted to him might be frustrated. He therefore strengthened the brothers in the Lord, promising more promptly that he would return, bade them farewell, and commended them to the Lord. While they pursued him with tears, he departed for Rome (Letter of Hincmar; fol. 14r).

When they came into Italy, Antoninus was seized by a severe fever. Blessed Sanctinus remained several days in his service, but, with the counsel and consent of blessed Antoninus himself, he resolved to continue the journey he had begun, lest the command of blessed Dionysius be hindered in any way. After leaving the head of the household sufficient provisions and respectable linens, he begged and adjured him by God that, if Antoninus recovered, he should thereafter minister to him abundantly; but if he died, he should bury him with the greatest honor. Thus he made every effort to continue the journey he had begun.

When Sanctinus had already reached the territory of the Romans, Antoninus died. The head of the household, keeping everything entrusted to him for Antoninus’s service, lifted the boards of the stable in which his animals lay, threw Antoninus into a pit where the dung and urine of the animals flowed, and replaced the boards over him.

Blessed Sanctinus learned all this through the Holy Spirit when he had already entered Roman territory. He returned with great haste [Col. 0033B] to the house where he had left Antoninus lying, and arrived weeping and grieving. He asked the head of the household, “Where is Antoninus, my dearest brother?”

The man, with feigned groans and sighs and simulated sorrow, replied, “He is dead. I buried him most honorably, using what you had entrusted to me.”

Sanctinus said to him, “You lie, son of the devil. You threw that holy and righteous man into the dung heap. Now come with me to the stable into which you threw him.”

Struck with fear, the man did not dare resist and came with him to the place where he had thrown Antoninus. When they lifted the boards from there, Sanctinus cried aloud with tears:

“Antoninus, brother, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose name and love the glorious martyr Dionysius suffered, rise, and let us together complete the obedience which that same glorious shepherd and our master jointly commanded us.”

Immediately Antoninus rose, covered with filth. Blessed Sanctinus drew him from the pit of the stable, washed him with the utmost care, and clothed him in clean and respectable garments. Then, offering the sacrifice of praise to the Lord, with complete devotion of mind and compunction of tears, they partook of the Eucharist of the body and blood of Christ. After receiving food, they were strengthened. Then they resumed the journey they had begun and, with the Lord’s help, reached Rome (fol. 15).

By then blessed Clement had been crowned with martyrdom. In the same see, after Anacletus [Note: [Col. 0033D] “after Anacletus” and “from Peter” appear in a twice-erased place.], they found Evaristus, consecrated pontiff fourth after blessed Peter. To him, exactly as blessed Dionysius had commanded, they recounted the course of his deeds and martyrdom [Col. 0033D].

Here I would like to linger for a little while on the subject of prudence, which our fathers, and especially the moral teacher Ambrose, define as consisting in knowledge of the truth and as infusing a desire for fuller knowledge. Prudence is to know God, fear God, and seek God. This is knowledge of the truth. There is also a desire for fuller knowledge, which has three kinds of understanding: if you find some difference in the statements of our predecessors, you should engage in the investigation of truth, so that in these matters you may show reverence for learning and imitation, not the cunning of disputation.

Therefore, as we consider here the disagreement among the written sources [Col. 0034A], let us hold fast to the citadel of this virtue. Let us not rely on our own strength, but, supported by the authorities of sacred Scripture, let us see—under the guidance of Christ God—what truth favors.

We read in the records that, when blessed Sanctinus came to Rome at the command of blessed Dionysius, he found Anacletus, pope of the Roman see, a Greek by nationality from Athens, and reported to him the course of Dionysius’s life and the deeds of his martyrdom. How absurd this is can easily be understood if one examines the succession of the Roman pontiffs and the date of the blessed Dionysius’s martyrdom, reckoning by indictions and years.

According to the historical accounts, blessed Peter presided over the city of Rome for 25 years, 2 months, and 8 days. During that period, as was related above, Linus governed the church under him for 11 years, 3 months, and 12 days. He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. Cletus immediately succeeded him and governed the church under Peter for 12 years, 1 month, and 11 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*).

Thus the pontificate of Peter had already reached 23 years, 4 months, and 23 days. If the 20 days inserted between the death of Cletus and the ordination of Clement are added to these, the total is 43 days, that is, 1 month and 13 days; on the final day of those days Clement was consecrated by Peter.

As for the fact that Clement is said in one place to have governed the church for 11 years, and elsewhere for 9 years, 2 months, and 2 days, there is no doubt that both statements are true. He sat under Peter for 1 year, 8 months, and 25 days; when this number is added to Peter’s 25 years of episcopate, together with the months and days, the full period is accounted for. After Peter’s death, Clement governed for 9 years, 2 months, and 2 days (fol. 15v).

Anacletus held office for 43 years, 10 months, and 7 days. He died on the third day before the Ides of July, and the episcopate remained vacant for 14 days. Evaristus likewise held office for 9 years, 7 months, and 2 days.

Therefore, when Peter died, it was the year 72 from the Lord’s Incarnation. Adding Clement’s 9 years gives 81. Adding Anacletus’s 14 years gives 95; adding Evaristus’s 9 years gives 104.

Now add Peter’s 2 months and 8 days; Clement’s 2 months and 2 days; Anacletus’s 10 months and 7 days; the 14 days between Anacletus and Evaristus during which the episcopate was vacant; and Evaristus’s 7 months and 2 days. These make 19 months and 33 days. One year must also be inserted, and thus the total becomes 105 years, 9 months, and 33 days up to the death of Evaristus, which occurred on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

In the second year of Evaristus, blessed Dionysius suffered martyrdom. In the sixth year after his Passion, blessed Sanctinus came to Rome; that was the year 103 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation. Anacletus had therefore already died, and Evaristus had already succeeded him. How, then, could Sanctinus have found a man who had already died?

It remains, therefore, that faith should be given to the earlier account. Since it rests upon truth, there is no doubt that, when we are taught by the authority of sacred Scripture that this is so, we should hold fast to the truth, strengthened by the virtue of prudence and having obtained the teaching of fuller knowledge—the truth to whose investigation prudence, the first of the principal virtues, itself urged us.

Let us therefore return to what came before. Since we know the year in which, according to the historical accounts, Sanctinus came to Rome, and also which pope he found in the Roman see, let us explain the matter briefly, so that we may speak without offending anyone [Col. 0035A].

While blessed Sanctinus (Life of Sanctinus) was delayed by the demands of travel, by preaching to the new plantation of Verdun, and by the illness of his companion, he found Pope Evaristus already in the ninth [Note: [Col. 0035D] “IX year” appears in a twice-erased place.] year of his pontificate. Evaristus received him with due honor and held him in the place of highest veneration.

Sanctinus explained that the reason for his undertaking such labor was the obedience owed to his master, blessed Dionysius. At the completion of Dionysius’s course, the Gallic church was suffering a great shortage of preachers, and Sanctinus and Antoninus had therefore come so that Evaristus might send some ministers of the word to the church. These were the final commands his master had given him: to make known to the Roman pontiff the circumstances of his master’s completion, and that Evaristus, whose responsibility it was to provide for the churches, might send laborers to cultivate the field of the Lord’s sowing.

When the blessed pontiff rejoiced in the Lord and stretched himself beyond his own capacity in his eagerness to carry out the request, unwilling to suffer any delay in doing what was asked, he nevertheless decided to keep the holy man with him for some time, both for his own consolation and for the refreshment of his labor and journey.

Sanctinus himself remained with him only a few days. Amid the pleasant consolations of mutual conversation, he humbly reported what divine grace had accomplished through them and how the new church of Verdun was bearing fruit. Evaristus therefore gave thanks to God from the depths of his heart and gave Sanctinus three men of proven authority as companions and fellow workers in the word. Although their names are not found in writing, the fact that they were sent is not concealed. We do know, however, that blessed Maurus the priest, who succeeded Sanctinus in the order of the pontificate, was one of their company and number [Col. 0035C].

Meanwhile the church of the faithful at Verdun grew and was strengthened, and with devout and expectant hearts its members awaited their teacher. News of the resurrection of the dead man had already reached them, and this had kindled them more intensely in faith in God and love for their master.

The pious father, remembering that the hearts of his sons—those of Meaux and Verdun—were anxiously awaiting his return, and that almost six years had now passed since the Passion of blessed Dionysius, while the sixth year itself of blessed Evaristus’s pontificate was the eighth [Note: the source’s computation is retained as printed], requested and received a blessing (fol. 16) and resolved to return to Meaux.

Yet he did not wish to pass by without visiting the new adopted sons whom he had regenerated for Christ at Verdun through the water of baptism. He therefore hastened his journey there as quickly as possible, intending to leave there the companions whom he had received from the apostolic see and return to Meaux himself, so that he might govern his own sheep, for whom he had been appointed shepherd and ruler.

When he arrived at Verdun, the brothers received him devoutly. Contrary to the expectations of the citizens, he was chosen as their pastor, and all alike—both the leading men and the common people—asked and obtained that he should preside over them.

The father rejoiced at the hundredfold increase in the number of his children and delighted in the devotion of the citizens. He did not delay in fulfilling what they requested. A church was prepared for the regeneration of the new faithful people, and many were regenerated by the holy bishop’s hands through the saving bath. The temples and shrines of the demons were destroyed, the idols cast down, and, since the first church was insufficient, a new church was built through the remarkable devotion and industry of the citizens. When it had been completed, the necessities for its dedication were prepared, and it was consecrated by the blessed bishop in honor of the Mother of God and the Virgin in the year 104 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, which was the seventh year after the Passion of blessed Dionysius, in the consulship of Gallus and Bradua, in the 220th Olympiad [Col. 0036B]. It was established as the mother church and episcopal see.

When these matters had been completed, Sanctinus admonished the people and carefully instructed them with salutary teachings, strengthening them with blessings. Then he returned to Meaux. There, devoting himself to preaching and holy works (Hincmar, Letter), when he realized that the day of his calling was approaching, he sent letters of exhortation and consolation to the sons of the church of Verdun (Life of Sanctinus). In them he foretold that his calling was near and that they would not see his face again, and he advised and commanded them to choose as his successor the priest Maurus, a man Catholic in faith and most learned.

At first, when they saw the messenger with the letters, they rejoiced and consoled one another in the thought of their father.
