But when mention was made of the shepherd’s departure and their own abandonment, immediately there arose a cry and mourning among them all [Col. 0036C]. There was one voice among the sorrowful. They grieved because they were losing their dearest father and gentlest shepherd. Their sight of mind, worn down and crushed by the force of grief, could scarcely consider that death was for him the road to his homeland, where the end of labors and the reward of eternal prizes awaited him. From there he would be able to help and support them all the more effectively, the closer he would be to God—whom he had served, in whom he had hoped, and whom he had confessed—once he had laid aside the burden of the body.

Faith indeed forbade them to weep, but affection forced groans from them. May he, therefore, now present there, hear us, his most humble servants, praying here; may he govern and protect the church entrusted to him as it is tossed amid the storms of the world, the church which he advanced by his labor to its present state (fol. 16v); and may he offer the prayers and tears of his children before the sight of God the Father of all [Col. 0036D].

It is certainly read in the older accounts of his life [Note: [Col. 0035D] Calmet, *History of Lorraine* I, p. 32, states that in the monastery of Saint-Vanne he read a *Life of Sanctinus*, written after 952, in a twelfth-century manuscript entitled: “Here begins the Life of Saint Sanctinus, first bishop of the city of Cloves. After the glorious triumph of the victory of heaven,” etc. That Hugo had this *Life* before his eyes can scarcely be doubted, as is shown by his own account when compared with the summary of the *Life* given in French by Calmet. Yet everyone can see that not these *Deeds*, but those written by Hincmar, were earlier.], that when he had returned from Meaux, he rebuked a tyrant because he had plundered church property. In a sudden fit of anger, the tyrant took up a sword and sent the blessed man into eternal life.

Even now, as those who saw it and handled his most holy bones have reported, a sword-cut is visible on the head of this most blessed man. The middle part of the head—namely, the front part in which the windows of the eyes are placed—is not joined to the rest of the body, and the rear part appears to have been cut and divided from the front as if by a sword.

How God called his servant to himself is known to him who chose him before the ages. We believe that, although the sword of the persecutor did not take away his soul, he nevertheless did not lose the palm of martyrdom, because the whole course of his life was a continual struggle with the prince of this world.

The Lord took this holy bishop to himself in the city of Meaux, after many dangers of labor and countless exercises of good works, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0037B], while Trajan ruled the earth.

If the diligent reader wishes to learn more fully, let him note that in the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign—the year in which Peter and Paul gloriously died, which was the year 72 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation—Vespasian was sent by Nero to Judaea with an army.

After Nero died in the following year, before Vespasian returned to Rome, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius ruled for one year and six months. Vespasian was therefore proclaimed emperor in Judaea. He also built the Capitol. [Note: [Col. 0037D] “In the consulship of Vespasian for the sixth time and Titus for the fifth, Judaea was destroyed,” in the margin.] In his second year the kingdom of the Jews came to an end, when, from the first building of the Temple under Solomon to its final ruin under Vespasian, 1,202 years are reckoned [REGINO].

Vespasian therefore reigned for 9 years, 11 months, and 22 days. If the 7 months of Nero are added to his 11 months, they make 19; and if his 28 days are added to those 22 days, they make 50 days, that is, 1 year, 7 months, and 20 days. One year is inserted here.

Titus also reigned for 2 years and 2 months. Domitian reigned for 15 years and 5 months. If we add the 7 months of Vespasian to these 5 months, a year is completed, and that year is inserted here.

After Domitian, Nerva reigned for 1 year, 4 months, and 8 days. If, therefore, we add the six months of Otho, Galba, and Vitellius to Titus’s two months and Nerva’s four months, a year is completed, and it is inserted here.

After Nerva, Trajan reigned for 19 years, 6 months, and 15 days. In his second year blessed Sanctinus departed to the Lord: it was the year 105 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, the tenth month and eighteenth day, in the consulship of Africanus and Crispinus, eight years after the Passion of blessed Dionysius, while Pope Evaristus was governing the Roman church in the ninth year of his pontificate.

Nevertheless, the year arising from the calculation of the months must be inserted, so that the number of pontifical years may be preserved exactly; and from the death of blessed Sanctinus until the death of Evaristus, who died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, one full year and seventeen days are to be reckoned [Col. 0037D].

He was buried with fitting honor by the faithful in the church of Saint Peter (fol. 17), which he himself had built from its foundations. This church was enlarged by Saint Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0037] The following is written in the margin: “In the year 167 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Lucius, king of Britain, sent an embassy to Pope Evaristus and received the faith of Christ, together with all the rulers of his people.”], who succeeded him in the episcopate, and was dedicated in honor of that same master of his.

There, for many [Col. 0038A] years, the heavenly treasure lay hidden within the enclosure of the tomb. Finally, when it had been discovered and elevated through divine revelation, amid the great rejoicing of the citizens and the peoples who flocked together, his most sacred body was honorably placed by the bishops upon the altar, in the heavenly mercy-seat, to appease God on behalf of wretched mortals.

There it remained through the succession of many years, carefully guarded and honorably preserved by the watchers, until the time of the emperor Louis, the son of the equally emperor Lothar, while God glorified his saint through innumerable signs and wonders.

After this, because God so willed, it was translated and placed at Verdun in the church of Saint Peter and enclosed in a silver shrine. There, through his merits and prayers, divine blessings continue to abound to this present day [Col. 0038B], by the grace of Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

After him blessed Antoninus governed the church of Meaux for many years. Distinguished by pious works of virtue, he departed to the Lord on the second day before the Kalends of October (Hincmar, Letter), by the grace of Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever. Amen.

After Domitian died, Nerva assumed the empire and reigned for one year and four months. Under him the apostle John was recalled from exile.

Trajan succeeded him. Under Trajan, Zacharias, bishop of the church of Vienne, was crowned with martyrdom. For Crescens was the first and Martin the second of the disciples of the apostles to occupy the see of Vienne.

Trajan reigned for 18 years, 6 months, and 15 days. If we add to these 6 months the 28 days left over above, and the 15 days of Trajan, the total is 43. After Zacharias, Verus flourished as bishop of Vienne. In the third year of his reign, the blessed apostle himself was taken up, in the year 68 after the Passion of the Lord, indiction 14, epact 6. In Trajan’s sixth year blessed Sanctinus departed to the Lord, and the priest Maurus, a man of honorable life and praiseworthy in every respect, took over the governance of the church. [HIER.]

When Trajan began a persecution against Christians, Symeon, bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified; Ignatius was handed over to wild beasts; and Pope Alexander, after governing for 11 years, 7 months, and 2 days, was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan on the fifth day before the Nones of May (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*). He decreed that the water used for sprinkling should be blessed with salt.

After him Xystus held office, a Roman by nationality, son of Pastor, from the district of the Via Lata, for 10 years, 2 months, and 1 day [Col. 0038D] [ADO.]. He decreed that sacred ministries should be touched only by ministers. Justus, bishop of Vienne, flourished [Note: [Col. 0037] “Justus, bishop of Vienne, flourished” appears in the margin.].

In the year 121 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, Hadrian, the son of Trajan’s cousin, reigned [BEDA, HIERON.]. In the ninth year of his reign, when the persecution had been relaxed, he was called “Father of his Country,” and his wife was called Augusta. He reigned for 21 years.

Telesphorus, a Greek by nationality and formerly a hermit, held office for 11 years, 3 months, and 21 days (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*). He endured a distinguished martyrdom on the fifth day before the Nones of January [Note: [Col. 0037] “He endured … January” appears in the margin.]. He decreed that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter (fol. 17v), that Masses should be celebrated on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, and that “Glory to God in the highest” should be sung. He died on the third day before the Ides of January [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the third day before the Ides of January” appears in the margin.].

Yginus succeeded him, a Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher from Athens. He held office for 4 years, 3 months, and 8 days. He organized the clergy and distributed the ecclesiastical ranks. He died on the third day before the Ides of January [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the third day before the Ides of January” appears in the margin.].

In the year 142 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation [BEDA], Antoninus, surnamed Pius, reigned with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for 22 years and 4 months.

Pius, an Italian by nationality, son of Rufinus and brother of Pastor, from the city of Aquileia, held office after Yginus for 19 years, 4 months, and 3 days (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*). He died on the fifth day before the Ides of July [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the fifth day before the Ides of July” appears in the margin.]. At the prompting of an angel, he decreed that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.

There were 29 days between Pius and Anicetus. Anicetus, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, from the village of Emesa [Note: [Col. 0039] “Invisa” is corrected to “Emesa” in the manuscript], held office for 11 years, 4 months, and 3 days [BEDA]. He died on the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the Kalends of May” appears in the margin.]. Under him Polycarp came to Rome and corrected many people who had been corrupted by the heretical stain of Valentinus and Cerdo.

In the year 164 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, Marcus Antoninus Verus reigned with his brother Aurelius Commodus for 29 years and 1 month. Photinus of Lyon and Justus of Vienne were crowned with martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0039] “Photinus … were crowned” appears in the margin.]. Polycarp was crowned with martyrdom under Anicetus, in the consulship of Verus for the fourth time, Quadratus Apronianus, and Paulus (*Deeds of the Pontiffs*).

Many others in Gaul were also killed for Christ. Pope Anicetus decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July” appears in the margin.].

There were 21 days between Anicetus and Soter. Soter, a Campanian by nationality, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, took up the governance of the Roman church in the year 168 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, the ninth year of Marcus Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus. He held office for 9 years, 7 months, and 21 days.

He decreed that no nun should touch the consecrated pallium or place incense in the church. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May” appears in the margin.]. There were 21 days between Soter and Eleutherus.

In the year 177 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, Eleutherus, a Greek by nationality, son of Abundius, from the town of Nicopolis, held office for 15 years, 3 months, and 2 days. He decreed that Christians should reject no food that is rational and human. To him Lucius, king of Britain, sent a letter asking to become a Christian, and obtained his request. Eleutherus died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0039] “He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June” appears in the margin.].

After Commodus died, his brother Antoninus made his son Commodus a partner in the kingdom. Commodus reigned for 15 years after his father’s death. In his time the Marcomannic War was conducted by God’s providence [Note: [Col. 0039] “In whose time” through “aid” is added in the margin.].

For when barbarian peoples rose up against the Romans in innumerable numbers—namely, the Marcomanni, Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Suevi, and almost all Germany—and the Roman army had advanced as far as the territory of the Quadi, it suffered a danger more grievous than that of the enemy because of the scarcity of water. When the soldiers, with great steadfastness of faith, suddenly invoked the name of Christ, such a force of rains burst forth that it restored the Romans most abundantly, while the barbarians, terrified by repeated strokes of lightning, were put to flight. As the Romans pursued them in their retreat, they obtained a bloodless victory through the powerful aid of Christ.

Under this emperor Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, flourished, as did Dionysius of Vienne. After him Helius Pertinax reigned for six months. When he died, Severus reigned, beginning in the year 198 from the Lord’s Incarnation. He reigned for 18 years.

Victor, an African by nationality, son of Felix, held office for 12 years, 2 months, and 10 days (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*). Like Pius, he decreed that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, from the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month through the twenty-first day of that same month. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

In the year 206 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, Zephyrinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Abundius, held office for 18 years, 6 months, and 10 days. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0040B] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 216 [BEDA], Antoninus Caracalla reigned for 7 years. After him Macrinus [reigned] 1 year, and after him the emperor Marcus Aurelius 4 years. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 202, the fourth year of Severus, when an inquiry had been held concerning the observance of Easter, Victor, pope of Rome; Narcissus, [bishop] of Jerusalem; Polycrates, [bishop] of the Ephesians; and Irenaeus, [bishop] of Lyon, published in writing how Easter ought to be observed.

[Note: [Col. 0039] “In the year …” and “to be noted” are added in the margin.]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 210, under Severus, the martyrdom of blessed Irenaeus and his companions took place (fol. 18).

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 224, in the first year of Marcus Aurelius, Callistus, a Roman by nationality, son of Domitius, from the city of Ravenna, held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 10 days (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). He was crowned with martyrdom under Alexander, on the fourteenth day before the Ides of October, in the third year of Alexander. Urban succeeded him, a Campanian by nationality, son of Pontianus. He held office for 7 years, 10 months, and 20 days; he died on the ninth day before the Kalends of June.

[Note: “He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of June” is in the margin.]

Between Urban and Pontianus there were 30 days. Pontianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Calpurnius, held office for 9 years, 5 months, and 2 days. Pontianus, under Maximinus, was beaten with clubs and died on the third day before the Kalends of November.

[Note: “Pontianus … November” is in the margin.]

After Aurelius had died, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 228, Alexander succeeded [him] [BEDA]; he reigned for 13 years. Between Pontianus and Anterus there were 10 days.

In the thirteenth year of Alexander’s reign, from the Incarnation of the Lord 236, in the fifteenth indiction, with an epact of 9 and a concurrent of 6, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Pontianus, Easter was celebrated for the first time in the manner in which it has hitherto been observed by us. For until that time it was observed on the fourteenth day of the moon, according to the custom of the Jews.

[Note: “In the year … of the Jews” is in the margin.]

[Col. 0040D] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 241, Anterus was ordained on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December. He was Greek by nationality, son of Romulus. He held office for 1 month and 17 days; he died on the fourth day before the Nones of January (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs).

[Note: “He died on the fourth day before the Nones of January” is in the margin.]

After Alexander, Maximinus began to reign [BEDA] and launched a persecution against the Christians. Under him Pontianus and Anterus were crowned with martyrdom. Maximinus reigned for 3 years, and after him Gordianus for 6 years. Under Gordianus, Florentius, bishop of Vienne, flourished.

[Note: “Under him … flourished” is in the margin.]

[Col. 0041A] After him Philip [reigned] with his son Philip for 7 years [ADO]. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian, and in his third year the thousandth year of the city of Rome was completed. Therefore, when the city had been crowned and the Roman people were celebrating solemnly and offering sacrifices, the emperor, together with his son and with Pontius, his contemporary—a noble and freeborn man, though secretly a Christian—was proceeding to the temple (The Acts of Pontius?).

But, recalled by blessed Pontius and instructed in the teachings of the Church, he was baptized with his son. Blessed Pontius, because he had taught the Roman emperors to believe in Christ, received the crown of martyrdom. After a long time his body was translated; it now rests honorably and is venerated in the monastery called Tomerias.

[Note: “Philip … approving” is in the margin.]

On the day of Easter, that is, during its vigil, when the emperor Philip wished to partake of the [Col. 0041B] mysteries, Pope Fabianus, who had assumed the pontificate in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 241, did not permit him to do so until he had confessed his sins, stood among the penitents, and by penance expiated the faults that were very widely alleged against him. He willingly accepted what the priest had commanded, demonstrating by his conduct and actions that divine fear and the fullest religious faith were present in him.

His humility attacks the arrogance of our kings all the more sharply because, in so tender a Christianity [text supplied conjecturally], he undertook penance [text supplied conjecturally] more devoutly than [text supplied conjecturally] these men, in a mature Church [text supplied conjecturally] and [text supplied conjecturally] one spread [text supplied conjecturally] throughout the world [text supplied conjecturally], consent even to hear of it.

[Col. 0041C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 257, Decius assumed the empire, which he held for 1 year and 3 months [BEDA; REGINO].

[Note: “To these …” is in the margin.]

To these 3 months of Decius add 3 of Antoninus Pius, 1 of Marcus Antoninus, and 6 of Helius Pertinax; the year stated here results. One month and 28 days of the time mentioned above remain.

After Pope Anterus had been crowned with martyrdom, Fabianus succeeded him. A Roman by nationality, son of Fabius, he held office for 13 years and 11 months (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). Between Anterus and Fabianus there were 13 days. Decius killed many thousands of saints. When Pope Fabianus was crowned with martyrdom under Decius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, the episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 254, at the time when Lupicinus of Vienne flourished, Cornelius succeeded him, a Roman by nationality, son of Romanus [ADO]. He held office for 5 years and 3 days. He was crowned with martyrdom under Decius.

[Note: “He was crowned … under Valerian” is in the margin.]

At the request of Lucina, he raised the bodies of the holy apostles; Paul’s body he placed on the Ostian Way, where he had been beheaded, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of [Col. 0041D] October. Between Cornelius and Lucius there were 35 days.

During his time the heresy of the Novatians arose from a certain Novatus who, from [lacuna] the Church by the ordination of Novatianus, and though God had wished Cornelius to be enthroned, withdrew from the Church and established the heresy bearing his own name. At that time Cyprianus the martyr, primate of Africa, presided at Carthage. He outlived Cornelius until the time of the lord Pope Lucius, and he was crowned [with martyrdom] on the same day on which Cornelius suffered martyrdom in the persecution of Valerian [text supplied conjecturally].

Lucius, a Roman, son of Porphyrius, held office for 3 years, 3 months, and 3 days [Col. 0042A] (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). He decreed that in every place two priests and three deacons should not abandon the bishop. He died on the third day before the Nones of March and was buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [BEDA]. Between Lucius and Stephen there were 25 days.

Gallus reigned with his son Volusianus for 2 years and 4 months. Stephen, a Roman, son of Jobius, held office for 6 years, 6 months, and 2 days. He decreed that priests and Levites should not have sacred vestments for everyday use (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). He was beheaded under Valerian and Gallienus on the fourth day before the Nones of August, and the episcopate remained vacant for 22 days.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 261, Valerian and Gallienus reigned for 15 years [BEDA]. When Valerian had begun a persecution against the Christians, he was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians (fol. 18), and, deprived of his eyes, grew old in wretched slavery [ADO], so that he prepared his [Col. 0042B] back as a mounting-stool for Sapor when the latter mounted his horse. Terrified by this, Gallienus restored peace to the churches [BEDA].

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 276, Claudius reigned for 1 year and 9 months [REGINO].

[Note: “To these … 1 month” is in the margin.]

Add to these 9 months 4 of Volusianus; the year counted here results, and 1 month remains. Aurelianus succeeded him and reigned for 5 years and 5 months. He persecuted the Christians. Under him the martyr Benignus suffered with his companions. After his death Tacitus reigned for 6 months [BEDA; REGINO].

[Note: “To these … 18 days” is in the margin.]

Add these 6 months also to Aurelianus; the year results, and 88 days of Florianus remain. Join to these the 28 days that remained above: they amount to 108 days, or 3 months and 18 days. Add the surplus 2 months: the total is 5 months and 18 days. After him Florianus [reigned] for 88 days [BEDA]. After him Probus reigned for 5 years and 4 months.

[Note: “To these … 3” is in the margin.]

Add to these 6 months of Tacitus and the [Col. 0042C] 5 years stated above [REGINO]; the year results, and 3 months remain.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 264, in the third year of Valerian and Gallienus, at which time Simplides, bishop of Vienne, flourished [ADO], Xystus, a Greek, ordained from having been a philosopher, [was ordained] on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August. He held office for 1 year, 11 months, and 5 days. He suffered under Valerian on the eighth day before the Ides of August (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). Between Xystus and Dionysius there were 5 days.

[Note: [Col. 0041] “Thirty-five” is corrected to “five” in the manuscript.]

Dionysius, formerly a monk, whose lineage I have not been able to discover, held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 4 days. Carus reigned with his sons Carinus and Numerianus for 2 years. Diocletianus succeeded him in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 290 [BEDA]; he reigned for 20 years with Maximianus and Constantius, and after Diocletianus’s death Maximianus reigned with Severus, Galerius, and Maximinus [BEDA].

Pope Dionysius established parishes and dioceses and [Col. 0042D] assigned churches to priests (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs).

Felix, a Roman, son of Constantius, succeeded him and held office for 4 years, 3 months, and 1 day. He died on the third day before the Kalends of June. He decreed that Masses should be celebrated above the memorials of the martyrs.

Eutychianus, a Tuscan, son of Marinus, from the city of Luna, held office for 1 year, 1 month, and 1 day. Under Aurelianus he was crowned with martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of August and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself also buried 342 martyrs with his own hand, and the episcopate remained vacant for 8 days.

[Note: “Under him … 8” is in the margin.]

He decreed that the produce of beans and grapes should be blessed upon the altar.

Gaius the Dalmatian, son of [Col. 0043A] Gaius, of the family of Diocletianus, held office for 11 years, 4 months, and 12 days. He was crowned with martyrdom on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. In his time Saint Sebastian flourished. Between Gaius and Marcellinus there were 11 days.

Marcellinus, a Roman, son of Prejectus [Piectus in manuscript C], held office for 9 years, 4 months, and 17 days. Between Marcellinus and Marcellus there were 25 days.

Marcellus, a Roman, son of Benedictus, from the Via Lata, held office for 6 years, 7 months, and 25 days.

The emperor Diocletianus took Maximianus into partnership in the empire and made Valerius and Constantius Caesars. He ordered that he himself be worshiped as God [HIERON]. Constantius Caesar killed 60,000 Alemanni who had rebelled near Lingones. In the eighteenth year of Diocletianus’s reign a new persecution began, and in the month of March, during the days of Easter, which fell on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, all the churches were overthrown.

In the twentieth—that is, the final—year of his reign, which [Col. 0043B] was the third year of the persecution from the Incarnation of the Lord 310, Diocletianus and Maximianus laid down the purple at Milan. Diocletianus died. Maximianus, fleeing at Massilia, while plotting against his son-in-law, was strangled and died. Constantius Caesar, the grandson through his daughter of the emperor Claudius and the father of Constantine, died in the third year of the persecution, a man of the highest civility and gentleness [BEDA]. Maximianus and Severus were made Caesars (fol. 19).

Maximianus added his sexual outrages to the persecutions of the Christians. Once begun, the persecution raged up to the seventh year of the rule of Constantine; thus, within a single month, 17,000 martyrs are found to have suffered.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 310 (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs), Constantine, son of Constantius and Helena, was made emperor in Britain [Col. 0043C] on the fifth day before the Nones of May. He reigned for 30 years and 10 months. Add to these the 3 months remaining above: the year results, and 1 month remains [REGINO].

Under him Saint Agric[i]us, confessor and bishop of Trier, flourished; his successor was Saint Maximinus (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs).

After Marcellus, in the first year of Constantine, Eusebius, a Greek formerly a physician, held office at Rome for 7 months. Under him the cross of the Lord was discovered. He died on the fifth day before the Nones of October, and the episcopate remained vacant for 7 days [BEDA]. Between Marcellus and Eusebius there were 20 days.

In the fourth year of the persecution, Maxentius, the son of Maximianus Herculius, was proclaimed Augustus at Rome. Constantine fought against him in the sixth year of his own reign; after Maxentius had been killed near Rome, Constantine recovered the city.

Helena, the most Christian mother of Constantine, accompanied her [Col. 0043D] son as he set out for war. She left the city of Trier with a great retinue and came to Besançon. In the little church of Saint Stephen situated on the mountain, shedding continual tears and undertaking prolonged fasts for the safety of her son, she appealed most humbly to the ears [aures*] of the Lord and of blessed Stephen in prayer.

Because that place was very small, she made a vow to repair and enlarge it into a new church; and she did so, sending masons and providing expenses suitable for the construction of the basilica.

Constantine the emperor, having obtained victory [Col. 0044A] through the banner of the holy Cross shown to him from heaven, sent his mother to Jerusalem to seek the Lord’s wood. She found it and had it cut in half, so that she might carry one cross to her son and preserve the other cross at Jerusalem. She acted with wise counsel, so that where the Lord’s limbs had been fitted to it in punishment, there it might, glorified, be venerated by the peoples.

[Col. 0044A] Melchiades the African held office at Rome for 4 years (The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). At that time Paschalius, bishop of Vienne, flourished. He decreed that no one should fast on Sunday or on Friday. He died on the third day before the Ides of December, and the episcopate remained vacant for 17 days.

Anno Domini 315. Sylvester of Rome, son of Rufinus, held the see for 22 years, 10 months, and 11 days. He established that chrism should be prepared, that the baptized should be confirmed, that they should be clothed in dalmatics [Col. 0044B], and that the sacrifice should be wrapped in linen cloth.

In the second year after Constantine, having defeated the tyrant Maxentius, son of Maximian Herculius, and recovered the City, was converted to the faith of Christ in the tenth year of the persecution through the preaching of Pope Sylvester. At Rome, where he was baptized, he built the basilica of blessed John the Baptist, which is called the Constantinian [BEDA].

[Note: [Col. 0043] “This”—“he ordered” in the margin.]

This is the privilege by which Pope Sylvester, through the intervention of the empress Helena, endowed the church through Agricius, patriarch of Trier; Archbishop Volusianus ordered it to be copied out [Note: Cf. *Gesta Treverorum*, chapter 19]:

> “Just as, in your former pagan state, by your own virtue you obtained the distinction, so now at Trier you possess primacy * over the Gauls spiritually and precedence over the Germans. Peter, the head of the Church, marked you out through his staff as one who should possess this rank among the first teachers of the Christian religion—namely, Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus—placing you before all the bishops of these peoples [Col. 0044C] and, in a certain sense, lowering his own dignity in order to make you a participant in it.
>
> “In what manner, then, shall I, Sylvester, his unworthy servant and successor, renew and confirm this through the patriarch Agricius, in honor of the empress Helena, a native of that same metropolis? That blessed woman herself magnificently enriched and specially advanced it through the apostle Matthias, transferred from Judaea, and through the other relics of the Lord.
>
> “Let the newly ordained clergy who rival this privilege be cut off from communion, for they are stained by anathema [Note: EP&Rbar;. Here the note repeats that Archbishop Volusianus ordered it to be copied out.].”

He also built another church for blessed Peter in the temple of Apollo (fol. 19'), and another for blessed Paul, enclosing the bodies of both with bronze, five feet thick [Col. 0044D] (*ibid.*). He also built the basilica in the Sororian palace, which is so called, where he placed a piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross. At the request of his daughter he built the basilica of the holy martyr Agnes, and there a baptistery in which his sister Constantia was baptized together with her daughter Augusta. He also built a basilica for blessed Laurence the martyr on the Tiburtine Way, in the Veran field. Likewise, on the Lavican Way, between the Two Laurels, he built a basilica for the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, and a mausoleum where he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus. He also built a basilica in the city of Ostia, beside the harbor of the city of Rome, for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and Saint John the Baptist [Col. 0045A]. Likewise, another for Saint John the Baptist in the city of Alba. Likewise, another in the city of Naples [BEDA].

The same Constantine, restoring the Bithynian city of Drepanum in honor of the martyr Lucian, who was buried there, named it Helenopolis after his mother [Note: [Col. 0045D] “depravan,” corrected to “Drepanum.”]. He ordered the pagan temples to be closed. Establishing a city bearing his own name in Thrace, he called it Constantinople, and wished it to be the seat of the empire and the capital of the entire East.

He also made a privilege for the holy Roman Church, which he established for blessed Pope Sylvester and all his successors in the pontificate forever, and placed it above the body of blessed Peter the apostle. It will not be burdensome to insert it here [Col. 0045B]. It is as follows (Decretal):

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The emperor Caesar Flavius Constantine, faithful in Christ Jesus to the one and same person of the Trinity, our Lord and God the Savior, merciful, gentle, great, beneficent, Alemannic, Britannic, Hunnic, pious, fortunate, victorious and triumphant, ever august, to the most holy and blessed father Sylvester, bishop and pope of the city of Rome, and to all his successors who shall sit as pontiffs on the see of blessed Peter the apostle until the end of the age; and likewise to all the most reverend and God-loving Catholic bishops subject [Col. 0045C] throughout the whole world to that same holy Roman Church through this our imperial constitution; and also to all their successors appointed for all future times: grace, peace, joy, patience, and mercy from God the almighty Father, and from Jesus Christ his Son, and from the Holy Spirit, be with all of you (fol. 20).

> “Our most gentle serenity has endeavored, by a clear account in the pages of this our imperial constitution, to spread for the knowledge of all peoples throughout the whole world what our equal Savior and Redeemer Jesus Christ, Son of the most high Father, through his holy apostles Peter and Paul, with the intervention of our patron Sylvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope, has deigned wonderfully to accomplish. First, we bring forth, with heartfelt confession for the instruction of all minds, our faith, which we have learned from our aforementioned teacher Sylvester, universal pope and pontiff [Col. 0045D], and then we proclaim the mercy of God poured out upon us.

> “For we wish you to know that, as we signified by our earlier sacred pragmatic order, we have withdrawn from the worship of idols, from mute and handmade images, from diabolical compositions, and from all the pomps of Satan, and have arrived at the complete faith of Christians, which is the true light and everlasting life. We believe, according to what that most life-giving supreme father and teacher Sylvester instructed us, in God the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible [Col. 0046A]; and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, through whom all things were made; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life to every creature.

> “We confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that in the perfect Trinity there may be the fullness of divinity and the unity of power. The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and the three are one. Thus there are three persons but one power. For God has always brought forth from himself the Word, which always existed and was begotten for the ages. And when by the single Word of his wisdom he formed the whole creation, everything was with him as he ordered it by his hidden ministry.

> “Therefore, after perfecting the powers of heaven and all the materials of the earth, by the gracious command of his wisdom he first fashioned man from the clay of the earth in his own image and likeness, and placed him in the paradise of delight [Col. 0046B]. The ancient serpent and ancient enemy, the envious devil, through the bitterest tasting of the forbidden tree, made him an exile from those same joys. After his expulsion, the devil does not cease, in many ways, to extend his poisonous darts, persuading the human race, by drawing it away from the way of truth, to serve the worship of idols—that is, the creature and not the Creator—so that those whom he is able to entangle in his snares may suffer with him the eternal punishment of burning.

> “But our God, having mercy on his work, sent his holy prophets, through whom he announced the light of the life to come, namely, the advent of his Son, our Lord, God, and Savior Jesus Christ. He sent that same only-begotten Son, the Word of wisdom [Col. 0046C]. Descending from heaven for our salvation, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. He did not lose what he had been, but began to be what he had not been: perfect God and man—God, performing miracles; man, enduring human sufferings.

> “As our father Sylvester, supreme pontiff, preaches this, we understand it, so that we do not deny that he was true God and true man. With twelve chosen apostles he shone forth through miracles before them and before an innumerable multitude of the people. We confess that this same Lord Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, suffered, was crucified, rose from the dead on the third day according to the Scriptures, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom shall have no end.

> “This is our orthodox faith, delivered to us by the most blessed Sylvester, supreme pontiff. Therefore we exhort all peoples and the various nations of the world to hold, honor, and preach this faith; to receive the grace of baptism in the name of the holy Trinity; and to adore with devoted heart the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for infinite ages, whom Sylvester, our most blessed father, universal pontiff, preaches.

> “For the Lord our God himself, having had mercy on me, a sinner, sent his holy apostles to visit us and shed upon us the light of his splendor [Col. 0047A]. Rejoice that he has drawn me out of darkness and brought me to the knowledge of his true light and his name.

> “For when, some time ago, the dreadful disease of leprosy had invaded the flesh of my whole body, and the care of many physicians assembled for me had been applied, it did nothing for my healing. Then the priests of the Capitol came, saying that a pool ought to be made for me in the Capitol and filled with the blood of innocent children, and that I could be completely cleansed in its warmth. In accordance with their instructions, when many innocent children had been gathered and the sacrilegious pagan priests wished to slaughter them and fill the pool with their blood, our serenity saw the tears of their mothers. At once I rejected the crime, and, taking pity on them, restored their own children to them. Providing vehicles and granting gifts, we released them all joyfully to their homes [Col. 0047B].

> “After that day had passed, when night had fallen and the time of sleep had come, the holy apostles Peter and Paul appeared, saying to me: ‘Because you have put an end to crimes and rejected the shedding of innocent blood, we have been sent by Christ our Lord to give you counsel for recovering your health. Hear our instructions, therefore, and do whatever we indicate to you. Sylvester, bishop of the city, fleeing your persecutions to Mount Seraptim, is sheltering in caves with his clergy. When you have brought him to you, he himself will show you a pool of salvation. When he has plunged you into it three times, all the disease of leprosy will flee from you. When this has been done, repay this favor to your Savior, so that by your command churches throughout the whole world may be restored [Col. 0047C]. Purify yourself in this matter as well: abandoning every superstition of idols, adore and worship the living and true Lord, who alone is the true God, so that you may attain his will.’

> “When I awoke from sleep, I immediately carried out what I had been instructed by the holy apostles. I summoned that distinguished and magnificent father and enlightener, Sylvester, universal pope, and reported to him in words everything commanded by the holy apostles. I asked him who these gods, Peter and Paul, were (fol. 21).

> “He replied that they were not truly called gods, but the apostles of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Again we began to ask the same most blessed pope whether he possessed painted images of them, so that from the paintings we might recognize that these were the men whom the revelation had shown me. Then that venerable father ordered images of the same apostles to be brought out by his deacon. When I looked at them and saw in those images the faces of those whom I had seen in my sleep, I confessed with a great shout before all my officials that these were the men I had seen in my sleep.

> “Thereupon the most blessed Sylvester, that same father of ours, bishop of the city of Rome, prescribed for us a period of penance within our Lateran palace, in fasting and sackcloth, so that we might obtain from our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, through vigils, fasts, tears, and prayers, the forgiveness of everything we had wickedly done and unjustly ordered. Then, under the laying on of the hands of the clergy, I came to the pontiff himself [Col. 0048A]. There, renouncing Satan’s pomps and works and all handmade idols, I declared that I believed in God the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, of things visible and invisible, and in Jesus Christ, our only Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. I confessed this of my own will before all the people.

> “When the font had been blessed, the water of salvation purified me there by a triple immersion. When I had been placed in the basin of the font, I saw with my own eyes a hand from heaven touching me. Rising cleansed from it, know that I was purified from all the foulness of leprosy (fol. 21').

> “When I had been lifted from the venerable font and clothed in white garments, he applied the sevenfold Spirit of the Holy Spirit in confirmation. With the anointing of holy chrism and the sign of the holy cross he marked my forehead, saying: ‘The Lord marks you with the seal of his faith, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in the confirmation of faith.’ All the clergy replied: ‘Amen.’ The pontiff added: ‘Peace be with you.’

> “Thus, immediately after receiving the mystery of holy baptism and after the healing of my body from the foulness of leprosy, I recognized that there is no other God except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whom the most blessed father Sylvester preaches: Trinity in unity, unity in Trinity. For all the gods of the nations whom I had hitherto worshiped are proved to be demons, works made by human hands.

> “Indeed, that same venerable father explained to us most clearly how great a power the Savior himself bestowed upon his apostle Peter in heaven and on earth. Finding him faithful in his questioning, he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.’

> “This is exceedingly wondrous and glorious: to bind and loose on earth, and for what is bound and loosed to be so in heaven. When I understood these things through the preaching of the most blessed Sylvester, and had been restored to complete bodily health through the benefits of that blessed Peter, we judged it expedient, together with all our officials, the entire senate, and all the people subject to the glory and empire of Rome, that just as the vicar of the Son of God appears to have been appointed on earth, so also the pontiffs who act as substitutes for that prince of the apostles should possess, as granted by us and our empire, a greater power of principate than our earthly imperial clemency appears to have [Col. 0048D].

> “We therefore chose that the prince of the apostles himself, or his vicars, should be firm patrons for us before God. And just as our earthly imperial power honors his most holy Roman Church, we have decreed that the most sacred see of blessed Peter be gloriously exalted above both our empire and our earthly kingdom, granting it power, glory, dignity, strength, and imperial honor.

> “We decree and sanction that it possess primacy both over the four principal sees—Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople [Col. 0049A], and Jerusalem—and also over all the churches of God throughout the entire world. The pontiff who at any time presides over that most holy Roman Church shall be higher and chief among all the priests of the world, and by his judgment whatever things are to be arranged for the worship of God and the stability of the Christian faith shall be ordered (fol. 22).

> “For it is just that the holy law hold the headship of the principate [Col. 0049B] where our Savior, the institutor of the holy laws, commanded the blessed apostle Peter to possess the chair of the apostolate; where, enduring the punishment of the cross, he drank the cup of blessed death and appeared as the imitator of his teacher and Lord. There let the nations bend their necks in confession of Christ’s name, where their teacher Paul, with his neck extended for Christ, was crowned with martyrdom. There let them seek their teacher until the end, where the holy body of the teacher rests; and there let them, prostrate and humbled, serve the office of the heavenly King, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, where they had served the proud earthly king.

> “Meanwhile, we wish all the peoples of every nation and race throughout the whole world to know that within our Lateran palace we have built from the foundations a church for our Savior, the Lord God Jesus Christ. Know also that we ourselves carried twelve baskets of earth from its foundations upon our own shoulders, according to the number of the twelve apostles. We decree that this most holy church be called, honored, venerated, and preached as the head and summit of all churches throughout the whole world, just as we have established by our other imperial decrees [Col. 0049C].

> “We have also built churches for the blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and enriched them with gold and silver. There we deposited their most sacred bodies with great honor, constructing their shrines from electrum, which no force of the elements can overcome. We placed a cross of the purest gold and precious gems over each of their shrines and fastened it with golden nails. For the arrangement of the lights we bestowed estates upon them and enriched them with various possessions.

> “By our imperial command we have granted them sacred property in the eastern and western regions and in the northern and southern quarters—namely, in Judaea, Greece, Asia, Thrace, Africa, Italy, and various islands—on the express condition that everything be administered through the hands of our most blessed father Sylvester, the pontiff, and his successors [Col. 0049D].

> “Let all peoples and nations throughout the whole world rejoice with us. We exhort you all to render with us immense thanks to God and our Savior Jesus Christ, for he is God above in heaven and below on earth. Visiting us through his holy apostles, he commanded us to receive the sacrament of holy baptism and made us worthy of bodily health (fol. 22').

> “For this reason we grant to those holy apostles, my lords, and through them to blessed Sylvester, our father, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the city of Rome, and to all his successors, the pontiffs who shall sit on the see of blessed Peter until the end of the world, and from the present we transfer to them our Lateran palace, which is preferred to and surpasses all palaces throughout the whole world [Col. 0050A].

> “Next, we transfer the diadem, namely the crown of our head, together with the Phrygium, and also the superhumeral, namely the band with which the imperial neck is customarily surrounded; likewise the purple cloak, the scarlet tunic, and all imperial garments; and the entire procession of the imperial eminence, together with the dignity of the imperial presiding horsemen. We also bestow imperial scepters, lances, and standards [blanda], and all the various imperial ornaments, as well as the glory of our power.

> “We decree that the most reverend clerics of various orders serving that same most holy Roman Church shall possess the eminence, distinction, power, and excellence with which our most extensive senate appears to be adorned: that is, that they be made patricians and consuls, and that we proclaim them adorned with the other imperial dignities [Col. 0050B].

> “And just as the imperial army is adorned, so we decree that the clergy of the holy Roman Church be adorned. As the various imperial offices of chamberlains, doorkeepers, and all the guards are decorated, so we wish the holy Roman Church to be honored and to shine forth most fully with pontifical splendor.

> “We decree this also for the clerics of the same holy Roman Church: that their horses be adorned with linen coverings of the brightest whiteness and that they ride in this manner, and that, just as our senate uses footwear with udones—that is, with white linen—they too be distinguished, so that heavenly things [Col. 0050C] may be adorned just as earthly things are.

> “Above all, we grant permission to our most holy father Sylvester, bishop and pope of the city of Rome, and to all the most blessed pontiffs who shall succeed him in perpetuity, for the honor and glory of Christ our Lord, to choose from among our illustrious men anyone whom he wishes, by his own considered judgment, to clerk and number among the religious clergy of the same great Catholic and apostolic Church of God, with no one among them presuming to act arrogantly.

> “We have therefore decreed this also: that our same venerable father Sylvester, supreme pontiff, and all his successors shall use the diadem, namely the crown from our head which we have granted to him, made of the purest gold and precious gems [Col. 0050D], and wear it upon their heads to the praise of God and in honor of blessed Peter (fol. 23).

> “But the blessed pope did not at all permit himself to use that crown of gold above the clerical crown which he wears to the glory of blessed Peter. With our own hands we placed upon his most sacred head the Phrygium, shining with white brilliance and signifying the Lord’s resurrection, establishing that all his successors should use this Phrygium individually in processions in imitation of our empire.

> “Therefore, so that the pontifical summit may not be debased but may rather be adorned with greater dignity and glory than the power of the earthly empire, behold: both our palace, as aforesaid, and the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places, and cities of Italy and of the western regions, we transfer and relinquish to the aforementioned most blessed pontiff, universal pope and our father Sylvester, and to the power and authority of him and his pontifical successors [Col. 0051A].

> “By this imperial judgment, through our divine, sacred, and pragmatic constitution, we decree that these things be administered and that they remain under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church. Therefore we have deemed it fitting that our empire and the power of the kingdom be transferred and moved to the eastern regions, and that in the province of Byzantium, in a suitable place, a city bearing our name be built and our empire established there. For where the principate of the priests and the head of the Christian religion have been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not right that the earthly emperor should possess power there.

> “All these things, then, which we have established and confirmed through this sacred imperial decree and through our other divine decrees, we decree shall remain undefiled and unshaken until the end of the world [Col. 0051B].

> “Therefore, before the living God who commanded us to reign, and before his terrible judgment, through this imperial constitution we adjure all our successors, the emperors, and all the nobles and officials, the most extensive senate, and the entire people throughout the whole world who are now or in future subject to our empire, that none of them in any way be permitted to oppose, break, or in any respect undermine what has been granted by our imperial sanction to the most holy Roman Church and to all its pontiffs.

> “If anyone, however—which we do not believe—should prove to be a violator or despiser of this, let him be bound under eternal condemnations, and let him experience the holy princes of God, the apostles Peter and Paul, as his adversaries both in the present life and in the life to come; and, burned in the lowest hell, let him perish with the devil and all the impious (fol. 23').

> “Strengthening the page of this imperial decree with our own hands, we placed it upon the venerable body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and there promised that we would inviolably preserve everything for that apostle of God. We leave this command to our imperial successors, and, with the assent of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, we hand it over to our most blessed father Sylvester and through him to all his successors, to possess perpetually and happily [Col. 0051D].

> “Amen. May the divinity preserve you for many years, most holy and most blessed fathers.

> “Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of our lord Flavius Augustus for the fourth time and of Gallicanus, most illustrious men.”

Ambrose, in his book *On the Death of Theodosius*, says that although Constantine, when he was approaching the end of his life, had all his sins forgiven through the grace of baptism, nevertheless, because he was the first of the emperors to believe and left to the rulers who followed him an inheritance of faith, he attained a place of great merit [Note: “Ambrosius”—“found it” in the margin.].

[ADO] In the year after the beginning of the Lord’s incarnation 625: the sixth synod [Col. 0052A] at Arles, of 600 fathers, under Marinus, bishop of that city, and Claudius of Vienne [Note: “Anno”—“Viennense” in the margin.].

In the ninth year after Constantine accepted the faith of Christ, the pestilential disease of Arius spread throughout the world, from which the Arian heresy arose [HIERON.]. To destroy its impiety, 318 bishops were assembled at the city of Nicaea by Alexander I, in the 35th year, in the year from the beginning of the Lord 319 [Note: CCCXXIIII corrected to CCCXVIIII]. They met at the command of Pope Sylvester, and the king himself was also present. There they destroyed the machinations of the heretics by the opposition of the *homoousion* [the doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father] (Gesta p. R.).

Pope Sylvester also convened a council in the city of Rome, with the emperor’s approval, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. It consisted of 267 bishops [Note: “Congregavit”—“for 15 days” in the margin]. He again condemned Calixtus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. He established that they should not receive a repentant Arian presbyter unless the bishop of the place designated him; that chrism should be prepared by a bishop; that bishops should confirm the baptized because of the heretics; that, in the event of the danger of death, a presbyter should anoint a baptized child with chrism; and that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric [Col. 0052B].

He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the day before the Kalends of January, truly Catholic and a confessor; and the episcopate was vacant for 13 days [HIERON.]. Constantine died in the sixty-fifth year of his life and the thirtieth year of his empire.

In the year from the beginning of the Lord 341, Constantius, together with his brothers Constantine and Constans, reigned for 23 years, 5 months, and 13 days.

In the year from the beginning of the Lord 338, Mark, a Roman by nationality and son of Priscus, presided over the Roman Church for 2 years, 7 months, and 20 days [Col. 0052C]. He died on the sixth day before the Nones of October; the see was vacant for 21 days (Gesta p. R.).

Julius of Rome succeeded him, son of Rusticus, and held the see for 15 years, 2 months, and 7 days. He died on the second day before the Ides of April; the see was vacant for 26 days.

In the thirteenth year of Constantius [HIERON.], Constans was killed, after which Constantius alone obtained the empire. In the same year Liberius assumed the pontificate of the Roman Church and held the see for 6 years, 3 months, and 4 days (Gesta p. R.).

Thereafter the impiety of Arianism, supported by the power of Constantius, persecuted first Athanasius and then all bishops who did not belong to its party through exiles, imprisonments, and various kinds of affliction [HIERON.]. Athanasius, fleeing throughout the whole world, was received by Maximinus of Trier (Gesta p. R.).

Pope Liberius was first sent into exile by Constantius for confessing the faith. This occurred in the third year, and Felix was appointed in his place with his consent [Col. 0052D]. He was a Catholic man and an opponent of the Arian heresy. He held a council of 48 bishops and deposed the presbyters Ursacius and Valens, who were in communion with Constantius.

Later Valens and Ursacius, with the support of that same emperor Constantius, an Arian, deposed him by holding a council with the heretics. They brought Liberius back from exile to Rome after corrupting him and converting him to their error, in the consulship of Limenius and Catulinus. Persecution then arose against the clergy, so that many were crowned with martyrdom [Note: “et”—“Felix” in the margin.].

Bishop Felix lived on his own estate, where he also rested in peace on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. Thus Liberius, consenting to the Arian emperor Constantius, was not only rebaptized but also gave his assent to him, and afterward presided over his faction for seven years. All the years are happily counted in Liberius’s sequence. After Liberius, the see was vacant for six days.

Felix succeeded him, a Roman by nationality and son of Anastasius. He held the see for 1 year, 3 months, and 2 days. He declared the emperor Constantius a heretic and said that he had been rebaptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia at the estate of Aquilone near Nicomedia. For this charge he was beheaded on the third day before the Ides of November, and the see was vacant for 38 days. He was buried on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December.

Constantius killed Gallus Caesar, his nephew [HIERON.]. Thereafter he made Julian Caesar and sent him into Gaul. Eusebius of Vercelli, Dionysius of Milan, and Lucifer of Cagliari were regarded as distinguished men [PROSPER].

Paulinus of Trier, living in exile in Phrygia, died while Constantius was consul for the ninth time and Julian for the second time. When Lucifer of Cagliari did not relax the rigor of justice toward those who had fallen, he withdrew from communion with his own people [Note: “descivit,” corrected to “deseruit.”] [Note: “Lucifer”—“bishop of Vienne” in the margin.].

Priscillian, bishop of Galicia, founded the heresy bearing his own name in the consulship of Gratian for the sixth time and Theodosius. When Priscillian realized at the synod of Bordeaux that he was to be condemned, he fled to the emperor Maximus. He was handed over to the sword by Evodius, prefect of the praetorium. The bishops Ithacius and Ursacius, Priscillian’s accusers, were deprived of communion because of his death, in the consulship of Arcadius for the second time and Rufinus [ADO]. At that time Nectarius, bishop of Vienne, was flourishing.

[Col. 0053C] [HIERON.] When Hilary of Poitiers had presented a book on his behalf to Constantius at Constantinople, he returned from exile to Gaul, and nearly all the churches of the entire world were polluted under the name of peace through association with the emperor and the Arians.

(fol. 24) In the twentieth year of his reign Constantius entered Rome. In the twenty-second year, a synod was held at Ariminum and afterward at Milan, at which the ancient faith of the 318 bishops was recited. Thereafter the Arian heresy was condemned by the authority of all the bishops. Constantius died in the forty-fifth year of his life [REG.].

After him Julian, the thirty-fifth emperor from Augustus, reigned for 2 years and 8 months. Add to these the six who remained; the total becomes … years … months remain 2, days 28 [Note: “His”—“finivit” in the margin.] [HIERON.].

When Magnentius seized power at Augustodunum [Col. 0053D], Constans was killed not far from Spain, in the fortress of Helena. Because the state was thrown into confusion by this, Vetranio was made emperor at Mursa and Nepotianus at Rome, in the consulship of Sergius and Nigrianus [HIERON.]. The head of Nepotianus was carried on a spear around the city of Pisa; Vetranio was stripped of the imperial insignia at Naissus. Magnentius was defeated at Mursa after the consulship of Sergius and Nigrianus. Magnentius killed himself in a palace at Lyons. His brother Decentius, whom he had made Caesar to defend Gaul, ended his life by hanging at Sens.

This man turned to the worship of idols and persecuted Christians [Col. 0054A]. In his first year, blessed Martin, abandoning military service and baptized by blessed Hilary, became an outstanding soldier of Christ.

Julian’s persecution was mild, more enticing than coercive, and many fell of their own accord. Julian therefore set out against the Persians. After his victory, he was separated from the opposing enemy and died when one of his own men pierced his side with a spear.

On the following day Jovinian became emperor of the Christians. Julian the Apostate had deprived him of military service because he had refused to sacrifice to idols [BEDA]. Jovinian recalled Athanasius. His joyful and honorable beginnings were marred by premature death; he died in the eighth month of his reign.

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 367, Valentinian succeeded Jovinian together with his brother Valens [Col. 0054B]. Valens, rebaptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop of Nicomedia, persecuted Christians; he reigned for eleven years [ADO].

Hilary of Poitiers and Nectarius of Vienne died [Note: “Hylarius”—“day 6” in the margin.] [BEDA]. Gratian, the son of Valentinian, was made emperor at Amiens in the third year of Valentinian and Valens [HIERON.].

Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted Christians and killed many; he drove the rest from their own homes and expelled them into Roman territory.

In the third year of Valentinian and Valens, Damasus, after Felix, assumed the pontificate of the Roman Church. He was the son of Antonius, and this occurred in the year from the beginning of the Lord 379 (Gesta p. R.). Ursinus was ordained together with him. After a council had been held, Damasus was established in the apostolic see, and Ursinus was made bishop of Naples [Col. 0054C].

Damasus held the see for 18 years, 2 months, and 6 days. The deacons Concordius and Addiscus, or Callistus, maliciously accused him of adultery. When he nevertheless cleared himself at a synod of 244 bishops, they were condemned and expelled from the Church, and fell into the noose they had prepared for him.

At his request, Jerome, laboring greatly in the service of God, established that psalms should be sung in the church by day and night. Since they were sung indiscriminately, by the command of Damasus blessed Jerome arranged them so that at the end of the psalm everyone would say, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” He later added, “as it was in the beginning,” and what follows, in order to refute the most wicked growth of the Arian heresy.

In the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Damasus [Note: “Sexto”—“day 31” in the margin.], in the fifth year of Gratian and Valentinian, the second synod of Constantinople was held. Pope Damasus died on the day before the Ides of December, and the see was vacant for 31 days (ibid.).

In the time of the emperor Tiberius, a certain people came forth from the island of Scandinavia and settled along the Rhine (Life of St. Sigismund). In the time of Valentinian, advancing as far as the Rhine, they called the fortified camps that they established there *burgas* [Note: [Col. 0053] *burgus* corrected to *burgas* in c.], and for this reason received the name Burgundians [FREDEGAR]; previously they had not even been named. There they presumed to do nothing except whatever [Col. 0055A] they received as pay from the Germans by purchasing it at a price. After they had remained there for two years, they were invited by envoys of the Romans and Gauls who lived in the province of Lugdunensis, in Cisalpine Gaul, so that they might refuse the public taxes (fol. 24′); they were ordered to settle there with their wives and children (Life of Sigismund). There they remained, having raised over themselves King Gundioch, who was of the lineage of Athanaric, the persecuting king of the Goths (cf. Life of St. Chrothildis).

Valentinian, in the eleventh year of his reign, was overthrown in Britain [Note: [Col. 0055] “overthrown” in the margin], and died by vomiting blood [JEROME]. Valens succeeded him with Gratian and Valentinian, the sons of his brother; he reigned four years [Note: [Col. 0055] “reigned four years” in the margin]. He also issued a law that monks should serve as soldiers; those unwilling to do so he ordered to be killed.

Justina [Note: [Col. 0055] “Justina—Italy” in the margin], the wife of the elder Valentinian, persuaded the boy Valentinian [Col. 0055B] to incline toward the heresy of the Arians, for she herself was also an Arian. Accordingly, by imperial orders, the churches were handed over to the Arians, and in the church of Milan [Note: [Col. 0055] *ecclesiae* corrected in c.] the heretic Auxentius was promoted.

After his late death, when Ambrose had been appointed bishop by divine providence, and when the royal commands were raging against him, a basilica was requested in which the Arians might assemble, but it was not granted. The people of the city watched over Ambrose, lest he be forcibly dragged from the church and bound in exile. He delivered a sermon which he entitled *On the Handing Over of the Basilicas, against Auxentius*. Since we know that it corresponds to our own times, we shall append it to this work [Note: [Col. 0055] Ambrose, Letter 21 to Valentinian; *Sermon against Auxentius* II, 863.].

For blessed Ambrose labored and toiled so greatly in the Church of God [Col. 0055C], while he was beset on every side by the plots of Justina, the Arian queen, and of the king, that through him all Italy was finally brought under the rule of the true faith.

The nation of the Huns, long shut away among inaccessible mountains [OROSIUS], suddenly inflamed by a mad fury, burst upon the Goths and drove them, scattered and thrown into confusion, from their ancient settlements. The Goths, fleeing across the Danube, were received by Valens without laying down their arms [BEDE]. Soon, however, compelled by hunger to rebel through the avarice of the general Maximus, they poured into Thrace; and after defeating the army of Valens, they spread slaughter, fires, and plunder everywhere [JEROME].

The emperor himself, after his men had been slaughtered to the last, fled wounded by an arrow. Since he repeatedly fell from his horse because of extreme pain, he was carried to the hut of a nearby little farmstead [BEDE]. When the barbarians pursued him, they burned the house, and he was deprived of burial, having the same place [Col. 0055D] for his death and his grave, in the year of the Lord 377.

Gratian, however, reigned with his brother Valentinian for six years. Theodosius was chosen by him for the imperial office, and in great and numerous battles he routed those immense Scythian peoples, namely the Alemanni, Huns, and Goths. Since the Arians could not endure his courage and concord, after forty years they abandoned the churches which they had held by force.

[Col. 0056A] [ADO] At that time Nicetas, a most distinguished man, governed the church of Vienne, and Justus the church of Lugdunum. The latter, brought up under Paschasius and made deacon by Bishop Claudius, was transferred to govern the church of Lugdunum. A synod of 150 fathers was assembled in the royal city under Pope Damasus and the emperor Gratian against Macedonius and Eudoxius [IDATIUS]. Several battles were fought between the Romans and the Goths.

[PROSPER] In the third year of Theodosius’ reign, Athanaric, king of the Goths, surrendered himself to Theodosius. Coming to Constantinople, he was honored with great distinction by the emperor, and died on the thirteenth day. Alaric succeeded him, during the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus [IDATIUS]. In the eleventh year of his reign he entered Rome with his son Honorius and corrected the Roman laws by a complete revision [BEDE].

Maximus [Col. 0056B], a vigorous man worthy of the imperial dignity, except that he rose through tyranny against his sworn allegiance [Note: [Col. 0055] *eversisset* in c.], was unwillingly made emperor by the army in Britain in that same year. He crossed into Gaul, and there, having surrounded Gratian Augustus by deceit, killed him at Lugdunum. Hence Jerome says: “The walls of your Lugdunum bear witness to the traces of bloody hands” (Letter 60) [Note: [Col. 0055] *Lugduno* in c.]. He drove his brother Valentinian from Italy and appointed his own son Victor, who was killed by Arbogast in the same year in which Maximus was killed [BEDE; PROSPER].

[Note: [Col. 0055] “He therefore Maximus—lost” in the margin.] Ambrose therefore excluded Maximus from communion, admonishing him to do penance for the blood he had shed—of his lord, and, what was more serious, of an innocent man. But when he, proud in spirit, rejected penance [Col. 0056C], he lost not only future salvation but also that of the present life.

Theodosius fought against him, and after killing him restored Valentinian to the kingdom [OROSIUS], 5,690 years having elapsed from the beginning of the world. The following year Valentinian was killed at Vienne by the crime of Count Arbogast (IDATIUS, Letter 60). Jerome also says concerning him: “The young Valentinian, almost still a boy, after flight, after exiles, after recovering the empire at the cost of much blood, was killed not far from the city conscious of his brother’s death; and his lifeless body was disgraced by hanging” [Note: [Col. 0055] *Frnae* in c.; BEDE].

For eleven years Theodosius ruled the East while Gratian and Valentinian were alive; after their deaths he reigned for six years. The aforementioned admirable doctor Ambrose also prohibited him from entering the church and from communion in the sacraments on account of certain offenses [Note: [Col. 0055] “He himself—killed” in the margin]. The most merciful emperor accepted this so willingly and gratefully that he did not shrink from performing public penance.

After Valentinian, of august memory, was killed in the years of his youth, Eugenius assumed the empire. Because he involved himself in sacrilege concerning the restoration of the altar of Victory, Ambrose rejected his gifts and expelled him and his accomplices from the church [Col. 0057A]; afterward he never saw his face [IDATIUS]. Eugenius was killed with all his followers by Theodosius. Theodosius died at Milan in the seventeenth year of his reign.

In the year of the Lord 397, Pope Siricius, the fortieth after Peter, son of Tyburtius, sat for fifteen years (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). He ordered that penitents not be denied viaticum at the end of life. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, and the episcopate was vacant for twenty days (fol. 25). Ninety days later Anastasius the Roman succeeded him, son of Maximus.

He decreed that whenever the Gospel is recited, priests should not sit but stand bowed. Jerome speaks of him in his letter to Principia as follows [JEROME, Letter 127]: “Not much time passed before the distinguished man Anastasius succeeded to the pontificate, whom Rome was not permitted to possess for long [Col. 0057B], lest the head of the world should be mutilated under such a bishop; rather, for this very reason he was snatched away and transferred, lest he attempt by his prayers to bend a simulated judgment.” He clearly indicates that Anastasius was carried off before the invasion of the City under Alaric [PROSPER].

At that time Arcadius was emperor with his brother Honorius. In the seventh year of Arcadius, the discovery of the proto-martyr Stephen took place on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. In his eleventh year, St. Martin died on the third day before the Ides of November, on the first day of the week, with the moon fifteen days old, in the seventy-first year of his age and the twenty-third of his episcopate (ibid.).

Arcadius reigned thirteen years. Honorius succeeded him with the younger Theodosius. In the latter’s time, in the year of the Lord 433, the sixth year of Pope Celestine, the third synod of Ephesus was held, with 200 fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the royal city [Col. 0057C]. After completing his thirtieth year, he died [IDATIUS], and Theodosius succeeded with Valentinian. Before the fourth consulship of Theodosius, Rome was captured by Alaric [PROSPER].

In the seventh year of Theodosius’ reign, Aetius was named patrician and commander of both armies. He subdued the Burgundians, who were rebelling against the Romans [IDATIUS], killing 20,000 of their army and 7,000 Goths who were aiding them [JORDANES]. The nation of the Vandals came forth from the sheath of its dwelling and invaded Gaul.

After Innocent, Zosimus the Greek, son of Ebrannus, occupied the Roman see for three years, three months, and twenty-six days (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs). He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; the see was vacant for eleven days. After him came Boniface the Roman, son of the presbyter Jocundus, for three years, eight months, and seven days. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; the see was vacant for nine days.

He was ordained amid a dispute with Eulalius, and there was dissension among the clergy. For this reason the emperor Honorius and the empress Placidia, together with their son Valentinian, agreed that Boniface should be bishop of the City, while they sent Eulalius away to Campania. After him, in the year of the Lord 428, came Celestine the Roman, son of Priscus, for eight years, ten months, and seventeen days [IDATIUS]. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of April; the see was vacant for twenty days.

Honorius [Note: [Col. 0057] “Honorius—twenty-two days” in the margin] made the patrician Constantius his partner in the empire at Ravenna. Constantius also took Placidia, his sister, as wife; from her he begot Valentinian. Pope Anastasius died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, and the see was vacant for twenty-one days (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs) [Col. 0058A].

Innocent the Albanian succeeded him, son of Innocent; he sat for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of August; the episcopate was vacant for twenty-two days. By him Palladius, the first bishop, was ordained and sent to the Scots who believed in Christ, in the year of the Lord 431, the eighth year of the reign of the younger Theodosius.

Eudoxia, wife of the emperor Theodosius, traveled to Jerusalem [BEDE] and received from a certain Jew the chain with which the apostle Peter had been bound by Nero in prison; she brought it to Rome with many other relics. Theodosius died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, and Marcian succeeded him in that same year [Note: [Col. 0057] “A.D. 449” in the margin]. Having taken Theodosius’ sister in marriage, Marcian ruled the eastern regions for seven years [IDATIUS].

Valentinian and Placidia remained at Rome and could scarcely prevail to defend and protect their own frontiers from the incursions of barbarian peoples [Col. 0058B]. In the time of Valentinian and his mother Placidia, St. Germanus of Auxerre flourished, in the time of Zosimus and Boniface, of Pope Celestine, of Xystus, of Hilary of Arles, while Eucherius was bishop after Senator governed the church of Lugdunum, and of Hesychius of Vienne, followed by Claudian [PROSPER].

In the consulship of Theodosius for the thirteenth time and Valentinian for the second, Germanus went to Britain. For Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, devastated Sicily and all the lands belonging to the jurisdiction of the empire; nor could Valentinian defend his land from the attacks of the barbarians (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs).

After Celestine, Xystus, a Roman pope, succeeded at Rome, son of Xystus, for eight years and fourteen days. After one year and eight months, a certain Bassus brought a charge against him. When the emperor Valentinian Augustus heard this, he ordered a council to be assembled [Col. 0058C]. At the meeting, Xystus was cleared by fifty-six bishops, while Bassus was condemned by the synod, though with the provision that on the final day viaticum should not be denied him, out of regard for humaneness and mercy [PROSPER].

In the consulship of Aelius [Note: [Col. 0057] “Aelius—might be proved” in the margin] and Valerius, Pope Xystus was ordained with the remarkable peace and consent of the whole world. After his death, the Roman church remained without a pastor for forty days and more, awaiting with remarkable peace and patience the arrival of the deacon Leo, whom Gaul was then detaining while he arranged peace between Aetius and Albinus—as though he had been kept away for this purpose, so that the worthiness of the man elected and the judgment of those electing him might be tested (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs).

But the emperor Valentinian Augustus and his mother, the empress Placidia, moved by rage, condemned Bassus by proscription [Col. 0058D] and handed all his estates and possessions over to the church. By divine providence Bassus died within three months. Pope Xystus, handling and preparing his body with linen cloths and spices, buried it at St. Peter’s in the chamber of his parents (fol. 25′).
