At his supplications, the emperor Valentinian, together with his mother Placidia, offered many ornaments at the confession of blessed Peter and continually advanced and exalted the Roman church.

In the year of the Lord 445, Leo the Tuscan succeeded, son of Quintianus. He sat for twenty-one years, one month, and twenty-eight days. He detected two heresies [Col. 0059A], and for this reason sent word to the faithful emperor Marcian. After conferring with that emperor, bishops were summoned in the second year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord 452. A council was held in the city of Chalcedon. Two hundred and fifty-six priests were assembled, together with others whose written subscription numbered 354; joined together, they made 600 priests, along with the subscription of Pope Leo and of the emperor Marcian. They set forth the Catholic and apostolic faith concerning two natures in Christ, simultaneously God and man.

In that place the most pious emperor, together with his wife Pulcheria, having laid aside the imperial dignity, set forth his faith before the sight of the priests. Explaining it in his own written subscription, they asked the holy council that it be directed to the most blessed Pope Leo. There [Col. 0059B] the heretics Eutyches, Nestorius, and Dioscorus were condemned.

This blessed Leo sent many letters on the faith to Marcian, to the emperor Leo, and to Bishop Flavian; they are preserved in the archives of the Roman church [ADO].

In the time of Marcian and Valentinian, Hesychius, bishop of Vienne, distinguished himself after Mamercus; he instituted the Rogation observances. In Hesychius’ days Severus the presbyter came from India to Vienne. Eucherius of Lugdunum was also held in high esteem.

Therefore, as we are about to say a little about the life and virtues of our blessed father Pulchronius, let us first deal with the matters above, and briefly investigate, for the praise of this priest and for the edification of his hearers, how grave and dangerous his times were. So that the truth of the matter may shine forth more fully, let us relate from the history of the Italians [Col. 0059C], of the Goths and Romans, and also of the Vandals and Sueves, what antiquity records concerning these times, what Jerome records in his letters, and finally what peoples and kingdoms bear witness through their own dangers and the wretchedness of their calamities.

Under the emperor Constantine, who alone possessed the monarchy of the empire and decreed without opposition from any man that the temples of the pagans should be closed, the Church of God, having obtained the liberty for which it had long hoped, began to spread and grow. But while it took excessive delight in its prosperity, it neglected too greatly to root out the luxuriant growth of vices within itself.

For the perfidy of Arius [Note: [Col. 0059] “Arius—to be torn out” in the margin] disturbed the established peace of the Church; and through that very disturbance it so destroyed the grace of Catholic communion that under Constantius [Col. 0059D], the son of Constantine, as it crept everywhere, almost the whole world marveled at itself as Arian.

That plague was followed, as by its mother, by every kind of crime. These infected almost everyone to such a degree that no mortal had ever seen more dangerous times. Yet because God is nowhere absent from the purpose of instruction, and the concern for our correction nowhere departs from him, he provides different remedies for different times and causes, by which the seedbed of wickedness might be altered and expelled (fol. 30).

For the uprooting of this evil from the same mass of iniquity, he prepared a threshing instrument for Arian savagery [Col. 0060A]—namely, emperors and bishops stained with Arian filth—through whom he taught that it was better for his Church to grow and spread under the persecutions of Constantius, Julian, and Valens than to luxuriate in peace.

Therefore, when his children groaned beneath the rod with filial affection and asked for help amid tribulation, he mercifully pitied them and tempered the scourges under the emperor Theodosius. At that time the Arians, unable to endure the virtue of that emperor, abandoned the churches which they had held by force for forty years.

The Christian people, exhilarated by this sign of divine mercy, again began to indulge excessively in a harmful peace. Since, from an abundant and overflowing supply of possessions, they cared too eagerly for their bodies, they were deceived by security. Having shaken the yoke of the fear of the Lord from their necks, they rushed headlong into [Col. 0060B] crimes, pursued every deviation and slippery path, and, despising their ruler, wallowed in the filth of luxury. They did not fear, though swollen with satiety and sluggish with idleness, to be plunged into the foul abyss of the horrible and detestable impurity of Sodom.

God saw and was grieved. Stirred to anger, his wrath blazed like fire, because those who had once been his sons and daughters had provoked him—now they were a house of the provoking and exasperating Samaria.

At that time Innocent governed the Roman church, while throughout the cities of Gaul and Germany bishops fervent in the love of Christ, distinguished in faith, teaching, and miracles, presided over the churches. Nevertheless, there were very few churches over which bishops presided, for many were without pastors (Life of Antidius).

The holy Nicasius governed the metropolitan church of Rheims; [Col. 0060C] the holy Desiderius presided over the city of Langres; and the holy Antidius adorned the see of Chrysopolis with faith, magnanimity, and the practice of good works. There were many others as well, both then and now, shining lamps in the house of the Lord.

Although these men therefore urged the sheep entrusted to them through continual admonitions not to depart from the way of God, the people—who in earlier times, through Arian perfidy, had possessed an immature freedom without a leader, ruler, or governor [Note: [Col. 0059] *moratore* in c.]—although they heard the words of God, were choked by the riches and pleasures of the world like thorns and disdained to produce the fruits of good works.

Therefore the angry Lord handed all Gaul and almost the whole West over to be struck down by the sword of the Vandals, Alans, Sueves, Sarmatians, and Huns [Col. 0060D] [Note: [Col. 0059] much has been erased here].

But [Note: [Col. 0059] “this”—in the margin of fols. 30 and 30′] someone may perhaps ask where these peoples arose or from where they derived their names [ISIDORE, *Etymologies* IX, 2].

The Wandelicus is also a river bursting forth from the remotest borders of Gaul; it is certain that they lived near it and were therefore named from the river Wandalo. The Lanius, however, is a river beyond the Danube, named from the Alans, just as the Lemannus is named from the Alemanni.

The Sueves were named from Mount Suevo, which begins Germany at its eastern boundary; they inhabited its regions. Many have handed down that they consisted of one hundred districts and one hundred peoples. Genoa, moreover, is a part of Germany.

[Col. 0061A] Germany had very many peoples, savage in spirit and always untamed, varied in dress [Note: [Col. 0061] *amicis* in c.], differing in arms, discordant in languages, and uncertain in the origins of their names: the Tolosates, Ansivari, Quadimgi, Marcomanni, Bructeri, Camasi, Blangiani, and Tubantes. Their monstrous barbarity signifies a certain horror even in their names [OROSIUS].

According to the author Orosius, in Germany, where the Sueves live, there are fifty-four peoples. Europe has Alania in the east, whence come the Alans; in the middle, Dacia, whence come the Danes; there also is Gothia, whence come the Goths; then Germany [PAUL THE DEACON].

From this populous Germany, as is found written in the *History of the Italians*, book I, chapter 1, many peoples have often gone forth, because it produces so many populations that it can scarcely feed them. These peoples afflicted the regions of Asia and especially neighboring Europe [Col. 0061B]. The cities destroyed throughout Illyricum and Gaul bear witness to this.

For the Goths, Vandals, Rugians, Heruli, and Turcilingi, as well as other savage nations, came forth from there. In the same way, the nation of the Winili [Note: [Col. 0061] *Winilorum* corrected to *Windorum* in c.], that is, the Lombards, deriving its origin from the Germans, came from the island called Scandinavia.

One may also ask what circumstance caused so many peoples of such great ferocity to unite, when they had often ravaged one another through different massacres. This history is very well known [OROSIUS VII].

Although the elder Theodosius had routed these savage and untamed peoples in great battles, after his death crimes and battles were added to them, and the insolent spirit of their souls … vices. He had entrusted the care of the children—namely Arcadius [Note: [Col. 0061] *Archadius* corrected to *Archadii* in c.] and Honorius [Note: [Col. 0061] supplied conjecturally]—and the administration of the palace to highly experienced men: Rufinus for the Eastern Empire and Stilicho for the Western. But the one sought royal elevation for himself, the other for his own son, and so disturbed the state.

Thus, after the former’s death, the Vandal count, in order to clothe his son Eucherius, who from childhood thirsted for the slaughter of Christians, in the purple, gave over the blood of the entire human race. He summoned and stirred to arms Alaric and the whole Gothic nation, together with the other peoples already mentioned—the Alans, Sueves, and Vandals, intolerable in their forces and strength, and the Burgundians, set in motion by that same upheaval—to terrify the state, hoping that barbarian peoples could be restrained as easily as they could be aroused.

When this was reported to Honorius, he raised an army. Stilicho was killed [Col. 0061D], as was Eucherius, along with a few attendants who had been the authors of such vast schemes. Nevertheless, after the man who had been the first cause of the evils was killed, the seedbed of iniquity blossomed again.

For two years before the invasion of Rome, which was carried out by Alaric, aroused by that same Stilicho, the aforementioned peoples—the Vandals, Alans, Huns, Sueves, Burgundians, and many other nations, as we have said—[fol. 30′] overthrew Gaul; churches and cities were burned, peoples were slaughtered and destroyed to the last, and, because of the sins of the inhabitants, almost the whole West was reduced [Col. 0062A]. As those who wrote about the dangers of those times report, there was no city or fortress in Gaul that escaped their indignation.

Forming themselves into bands, they entered the rivers Po, Rhône, Rhine, Loire, Seine, Garonne, and the others. Attacking the cities situated along their banks by naval and land warfare, they brought everything to ruin with intolerable audacity and cruelty.

Those who advanced along the Rhine destroyed 103 cities situated on the Rhine. From there, proceeding to the cities situated on the rivers that flow down into the Rhine, they overthrew seventy-five of them in the same manner.

Those who came by way of the Rhône crushed Arles, Nîmes, Viviers, Valence, Die, Grenoble, Vienne, Lugdunum, and all the neighboring regions of Italy. Those who came by way of the Po, Loire, Garonne, Seine, and the remaining rivers consumed both the cities and everything situated nearby. Thus, by land and sea, in one assault and at one time, though under many kings and leaders, they threw everything into confusion together [PROSPER].

In the consulship of Arcadius for the sixth time and Probus, the Vandals and Alans crossed the Rhine and entered Gaul on the second day before the Kalends of January, during the consulship of Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius for the second [OROSIUS].

In the year of the Lord 407, while Honorius and the younger Theodosius were emperors, during the consulship of Stilicho and Aurelianus, the fourteenth year of Honorius’ reign and the first of Theodosius’, in the fifth indiction, they rose from the Ocean, where they had wandered as pirates, invaded Gaul, and reached the Pyrenees. Repulsed for a time by the barrier there, they spread through the provinces. Inflamed by the pride of their minds, they believed that no people could resist them, undertook great enterprises, and, under King Croscus, planned to bring all lands under their power (cf. Life of Antidius).

Their most powerful king and leader was Croscus [Note: [Col. 0061] “The king—that they might be punished” in the margin], swollen with pride and cruel in his deeds. Almost the whole West proclaims this: the very ruins of ancient, strongly fortified, and powerful cities do so. The more these cities rejoiced in the advantageous proximity of the neighboring rivers, the more grievous and cruel they found the barbarians in their destruction, so that the prophetic saying already seemed partly fulfilled: “The universe will fight on his behalf against the senseless” (Wisdom 5:21).

For what had once been incentives to luxury became fuel for their ruin, so that in the very things in which they had sinned more gravely, they might be punished more severely.

To increase the savagery of his spirit [Col. 0062D], there was also his impious mother, embittered by the gall of bitterness and the rage of viperous fury [FREDEGAR]. Breathing out dreadful poison and hissing words of impiety, she said to her son:

“If you wish, my son, to magnify yourself, extend your name, and do something new, destroy what others have built. Kill the peoples whom you have overcome. Draw your sword against Christians, so that those who have not seen your face may fear your name.”

Fired by these provocations into excessive fury, the tyrant crossed the Rhine at Mainz and devastated that city together with its people. (Cf. *Deeds of Trier* 35.) From there he attacked the city of Trier [Col. 0063A], thirsting for the destruction of the city and the blood of Christians. (Life of Antidius.)

The people of Trier, however, were saved in the city’s sand quarry, which they had fortified. Thereafter, his innumerable army, surrounding many cities of Austrasia, destroyed the cities and overturned the forts, then encircled Metz in a siege. It repeatedly battered the strength of the walls with a ram. But unless the sins and crimes of the inhabitants of the land had hindered it, the city of the blessed proto-martyr Stephen, made illustrious by his blood and fortified by the intercession of Bishop Auctor, would not have feared ruin.

Since their efforts achieved little during the long siege, they abandoned the city. After they had pitched their camp twelve miles from the city, a wall collapsed by divine providence and opened an entrance for the Vandals. They plundered the city and set it ablaze, except for the oratory of St. Stephen [Col. 0063B]. Then the barbarians departed, taking Bishop Auctor and many captives with them.

Soon, terrified by a divine miracle, they allowed him to depart with all the captives from his city and with immeasurable booty, fearing greatly that heavenly fire would consume them because of the insult done to so great a man. Thus the holy man, desiring to die for his sheep, by his own captivity loosed the bonds of the captives.

Meanwhile their army, joined by the Huns who had descended along the Rhine and the river Meuse, reached Verdun. They surrounded the city with a siege and established a fortified camp on the nearby hill opposite the city, from which they disturbed the townspeople with frequent attacks.

An all-devouring flame consumed all the surrounding villas; ruin crushed every building. No age was spared: old and young, small and great, mothers with their children, masters with their household—all were carried off by the sword.

The barbarians, however, after attempting, considering, and examining the city’s strength for a long time, and observing the courage of the citizens defending themselves and their possessions, lost hope of taking it by their own strength. It was enclosed by an unbreakable wall, constructed from stones joined and bound with lead and iron. Just as they were about to move on to other places, they captured and destroyed the city.

Croscus, sweeping through all the cities of Gaul, destroyed some and burned others. Shaking the supporters of the Christian law with wicked and unheard-of persecutions, he dragged some through various tortures and cut down others with a swift blow of a double-headed axe. There was no limit to madness among the barbarians, no place for mercy; his hand was always unceasingly ready for slaughter.

Jerome, mentioning this time in his letter to Agerochia on monogamy [Note: [Col. 0063] “Jerome—monogamy” in the margin], says:

“I shall pass briefly over the present miseries: the fact that we few remain here to this day is due not to our merit but to the mercy of the Lord. Innumerable and most savage nations have occupied all Gaul. Whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, whatever is enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, the Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Alans, Gepids, Heruli, Saxons, Burgundians, Alemanni, and—O lamentable state!—Pannonian enemies have devastated.

“For indeed Asshur came with them. Mainz, once a noble city, has been captured and overthrown, and many thousands of people have been slaughtered in the church. The Vangiones have been destroyed by a long siege. The powerful city of Rheims, the Ambiani, the Atrebates, and the Morini, the most remote of peoples, have been ravaged. Tournai and Strasbourg have been transferred into Germany; Aquitania, Novempopulana [Note: [Col. 0063] *Novempopulana* corrected to *Novempobulana* in c.], and the provinces of Lugdunensis and Narbonensis have likewise been devastated.

“Apart from a few cities, everything has been laid waste; and even those cities are devastated from outside by the sword and within by fear. I cannot mention Toulouse without tears: the merits of St. Exuperius have preserved it from falling even to this day.

“Even the Spains tremble, already destined to perish, recalling the invasion of the Cimbri and suffering continually in fear what others endured only once.”

*(Life of Antidius.)* Thus, while Croscus was ravaging Lyon Gaul and besieging Arelate, he was captured by the governor Marius, bound in chains, and led back through the cities he had devastated as a reproach. After many tortures, he ended his impious life by a miserable death. After him Fredebald reigned over the Vandals [IDAT.]. Constantius the patrician—whom Honorius had made his colleague in the imperial power at Ravenna and to whom he had given his sister Placidia, by whom he fathered Valentinian—cleverly captured him and sent him to Honorius; Gunderic succeeded him [OROS. VII, 40].

While the Vandals were therefore raging through Gaul, Gratian, a usurper, was created in Britain and killed, and Constantine was chosen from the lowest military ranks, solely because of the hope attached to his name [Col. 0064C], without any merit of virtue. He soon crossed into Gaul and, often deceived by the barbarians through uncertain treaties, wished to send judges into Spain. But when he was repelled by the Pyrenean passes, fortified by the guard of soldiers, he sent there his son Constans, made Caesar from a monk, together with certain barbarians admitted into alliance and enlisted for military service, who were called Honoriaci.

After those who were guarding the Pyrenean Alps with a private garrison had been killed, permission to plunder in the fields of Palestine was granted to these barbarians as though it were a pious reward for victory. Thereafter the responsibility for guarding the aforesaid mountains was entrusted to rustic inhabitants, whose loyalty and usefulness were trusted. But, having become accustomed to plunder and enticed by abundance, so that their crime might remain more unpunished and they might plunder more freely, they betrayed the Pyrenean guard, opened the passes, and introduced the peoples [Col. 0064D] who were wandering through Gaul, letting them into the provinces of Spain [Note: [Col. 0063] *provincias* corrected to *provinciis* in the manuscript.]. They themselves joined them, and after severe devastation of property and people, they settled there once the possessions had been distributed. There Gunderic killed many Christians.

Jerome, writing to Heliodorus about the condition of the times (*Letter* 60), says: “My mind shudders to pursue the ruins of our times. For twenty years and more, Roman blood has been shed daily between Constantinople and the Julian Alps. The Goth, Sarmatian, Quade, Alan, Hun, Vandal, and Marcomannian lay waste to, drag away, and plunder Scythia, Thrace, Macedonia, Thessaly, Dardania, [Col. 0065A] Dacia, Epirus, Dalmatia, and all the Pannonias. Bishops have been captured, priests killed, churches overthrown, and the relics of martyrs dug up” [IDAT.].

When Gunderic therefore plotted against the churches of God, he was struck down by God’s judgment and died in the fourteenth year of his reign. His brother Gaiseric succeeded him. With the Vandals and all their households, he crossed from Spain into Africa by wading through the sea [Note: [Col. 0065] *nadando* corrected to *vadando*.] (*Victor of Vita*), which is said to be twelve thousand paces wide there. It was discovered that eighty thousand Vandals had crossed. Whoever wishes to know how much was then done against the churches of God should read the *Acts of the Vandal Persecution*.

Then that great and ancient city, Carthage, was captured and entered by the Vandals [Col. 0065B] [BEDE]. At that time also the teacher Augustine, while his city was being besieged by the Vandals, took to his bed with fever in the third month of the siege and departed to the Lord in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 430.

When Gaiseric died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign, in the third month, Huneric succeeded him—an even more savage man. After him, seven years and five months later, Gunthamund succeeded. He recalled the Catholics from exile; after him, twelve years later, Thrasamund succeeded.

The beginnings of sorrows therefore date from the time of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger, when Gaul—indeed the whole West—was worn down by so many and such great disturbances because of the insolence of a sinful people. God’s power permitted the savagery of the barbarians to prevail, so that the people who shortly before had gloried in the slaughter of many nations and in the victory by which they had overthrown them might, by one terrible, immense, and [Col. 0065C] horrifying onslaught of barbarians, be trampled down and become the enemy’s prey and mockery.

This devastation lasted for one hundred years, while the Vandals, polluted by Arian depravity, pressed upon the Catholic Church—from the time of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger until the time of the emperor Justin, who succeeded Anastasius; that is, from the time of Gunderic, the Arian king, until the time of their king Chilperic, who was also called Gylimer, in whom their kingdom came to an end.

Nor was Rome free from this and a similar devastation [OROS. VII, 39]. Alaric, king of the Goths and successor of Athanaric, besieged, terrified, and invaded trembling Rome in the 1164th year from the founding of the City and in the year 412 from the Lord’s incarnation. While slaughter was taking place everywhere, all who fled to the thresholds of the apostles were granted mercy. It also happened that the blessed Innocent, bishop of that city, like the righteous Lot taken away from Sodom, was staying at Ravenna and did not see the destruction of the sinful people (*Letter* 127).

Jerome, in his letter to Principia concerning the life of Marcella, after mentioning the heretical madness raging so fiercely against the Catholic Church that it spared neither itself nor any good person, also recalls this invasion later in the letter [Col. 0066A], in these words: “While these things were taking place, a terrifying report was brought from the West: Rome was being besieged, the safety of its citizens was being bought with gold, and those who had been stripped were again surrounded, so that after losing their possessions they might also lose their lives.” And shortly afterward: “The city that captured the whole world is captured—or rather, it perished from hunger before the sword, and scarcely a few were found to be captured. The fury of the starving broke out into unspeakable foods, and they tore one another’s limbs, while a mother did not spare her suckling infant and received back into her womb what she had shortly before brought forth.”

If anyone therefore asks why this just severity of divine punishment was kindled and raged so fiercely against the Christian people, let him acknowledge that God’s judgments are indeed hidden and incomprehensible, but never [Col. 0066B] unjust. Since he leaves these matters hidden from us, let us nevertheless venerate them as just, in accordance with the psalmist: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

After many years had passed, when peace had been restored to the churches of God and the uproar of wars had abated, the few Christians who remained, seeing that divine vengeance had been justly exercised against them and giving thanks for God’s propitiation, submitted themselves with a readier spirit to the fulfillment of God’s commands. Since many churches were vacant—some bishops having been killed by the sword, others having been overtaken by human fate, and no others having been appointed in their place—the few priests who remained gathered together, took counsel concerning great matters, and began to discuss among themselves how they might provide for Catholic peace [Col. 0066C] [OROS.].

At that time, through Constantius the patrician, the Romans and Goths having been joined by treaty, Caesar Constantine was killed at Arelate, and his son, a Caesar formerly a monk, was killed at Vienne. After them Jovinus and Sebastian, invading the state with equal rashness, perished by an equal fate.

Thus at that time the church of Verdun (fol. 31), deprived of a shepherd as one misfortune followed another, lay crushed and oppressed under a long succession of calamities, and, after being without a bishop for a long time, earnestly sought one. And rightly so. For antiquity has recorded that for three hundred and forty years and more [Note: [Col. 0065] The original wording was: “and three years up to this present year of which he speaks.” The words following “years,” up to the erasure, were deleted; the words placed in the text above them were written by the same hand and in the same ink.]—from the death of the blessed Sanctinus up to that time—only three bishops had been in that city: namely, Maurus, Salvinus, and Arator, according to the testimony of the earlier fathers [Col. 0066D] [Note: [Col. 0065] Namely, of Bercarius in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*.].

Whether there had been more bishops there, whose names and deeds oblivion had erased or the scarcity of written records had neglected, or whether the violence of persecution had prevented bishops from being appointed, we do not know, because we have been unable to find this anywhere. The more so since even the younger and modern people of today did not know where the bodies of these three aforementioned saints had been buried [Note: [Col. 0065] *Nomina* corrected to *corpora* in the manuscript.] or by what end they had departed to the Lord—unless divine favor had revealed it to the blessed Ageric, who after a long interval, namely after the succession of five bishops, had himself succeeded them as the sixth, through a most precious revelation at night by the ministry of angels [Col. 0067A].

Those who were present at the translation performed at that time by the blessed Ageric told later generations about the blessed Maurus, and later writers transmitted the account down to our own knowledge: blessed Maurus, afflicted by various kinds of punishment, had borne witness to the truth and fallen in martyrdom for the faith of Christ, just as they themselves had seen in the dead man and, while the holy body was not yet dissolved, had touched his sweet wounds with devout kisses.

But perhaps someone will say: Why, then, did the blessed Ageric and the faithful of that time not institute [Col. 0067B] the celebration of his memory under the name and honor of martyr, since today he is venerated under the name of confessor? Whoever raises this objection should answer it himself: Why did Pope Gregory of Rome, when instituting the memory in the church of his predecessors, the Roman bishops crowned with martyrdom, as it is still sung today, ennoble them by the name of confessors rather than martyrs, although we certainly know that they suffered the most severe torments for Christ and purchased the rewards of life with their blood? [Note: [Col. 0067] *Affectos* corrected to *afflictos* in the manuscript.]

For our part, according to the measure of our small intelligence, we answer: At that time such glory belonged in the Church to any teacher who labored in the word of instruction, watched over those entrusted to him in word and deed, converted erring peoples without the true Lord to the way of truth, and by such services obtained the joys of life, that it was as great as the glory of bowing the head and extending the neck beneath the stroke of an axe or the approaching sword. Anyone from the people whose heart the Lord had prepared by enlightening it could suffice to attain the glory of martyrdom; but among so few Christians very few could be found to whom the priestly office might be entrusted—to plow the hearts of unbelievers with the plowshare of the word, scatter the seeds of divine teachings, and bring forth varied admonitions worthily and prudently according to the quality and capacity [Col. 0067C] [Note: [Col. 0067] “And capacity” is written above the line.] of the hearers.

What of Clement, the third after Peter? Was he not immersed in the depths of the sea and thereby completed his martyrdom? What of Marcellus? Did he not end his life in the house of the matron Lucina, which she had consecrated to God, after being assigned there to guard the animals of the public stable on plank beds? What greater insult to the Christian name could there be than to call or make the supreme priest of God and ruler of the holy Church the guardian of mute animals?

Thus these men—to say nothing meanwhile of many others—reached eternal happiness through the crown of martyrdom; yet when their memory is recalled in the celebration of Mass, the dignity of the priesthood is honored. [Col. 0068A] In saying this, we do not profess that confessors are equal to martyrs, whose steadfastness followed Christ’s footsteps in his Passion. But at the beginning of the newborn Church, when the savagery of the raging adversary made many martyrs of the truth for us, very few teachers and doctors of the churches were found.

Now, because the name of Christianity flourishes in the world, and because, with peace restored to the Church of God, the onslaught of hostile enemies has been crushed, and because the number of priests adhering to the Lord in the purity of an innocent life has increased through the long duration of peace, so that many churches—illumined by the title of many blessed bishops—are scarcely supported by the patronage of a single martyr, it happens that some among the common people almost disdain what they possess and desire what they do not possess. They judge martyrs worthy of every honor, as is right, but venerate and honor the priests of the Lord whom they have as patrons with lesser devotion.

Although the sword of the persecutor did not take away the souls of these priests, they nevertheless did not lose the palm of martyrdom, since by the steadfastness of unconquered faith, hope, and charity they overcame the enticements of the flesh and the devices of the invisible enemy. The people must be taught, not followed. Let martyrs be honored as the noblest warriors in the divine battle and defenders of the Christian name; let confessors also be honored as rulers and teachers of faithful souls; and in each place let the priesthood of those through whom we received the beginning of salvation be honored with special devotion.

But let this suffice concerning these matters. Now let a brief and lucid account, with the help of Christ the Lord who protects and instructs us, set forth what we have found in writings or learned through the truthful report of the faithful concerning the blessed Pulchronius, whom the city of Verdun deserved to have as its ruler at that time [Col. 0068C] [Note: [Col. 0067] In the margin is written: “Turn back four leaves and read.” By these words we are referred to leaves 26, 27, 28, and 29, which were later inserted by Hugh between leaves 25 and 30.].

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0067] The author took what follows from the now-lost *Life of Saint Pulchronius*.], while Honorius and Theodosius the Younger were ruling (fol. 26), the latter made Valentinian, the son of Constantius and Placidia, his colleague in the imperial power [Note: [Col. 0067] *Fecerunt* corrected to *fecit* in the manuscript.], and the blessed Pulchronius was born in the city of Trecassina to Christian parents from the household of the Church.

The beginnings of his birth were marked by divine clemency with heavenly auspices. For, long before his conception, it had been revealed to his parents that they would have such a son as would be a shining lamp of God’s holy Church before the Lord, and that at the proper time he would become the reconciliation of God’s anger and the appeasement of his wrath [Col. 0068D].

His parents were religious and renowned among their people for their grace, full of faith, devoted to almsgiving, attentive to the care of their household, ruling their family piously and justly, walking in God’s commandments and ordinances, hospitable to the poor and strangers, and devoted lovers of the churches. It was therefore rightly granted to them, insofar as human judgment can say, that they should have so great and such a son [Col. 0069A].

The boy was born, initiated into the heavenly sacraments, and in baptism was named Pulchronius or Policronius. O worthy foreshadowing in the name! If you wish to interpret it by resolving it through Greek, it means “city of time” [Note: [Col. 0069] *Interpretatam* corrected to *interpretatum*.]. And what does this name signify except that this holy boy would become in his deeds what was signified by his name?

For if you refer it to the time of his life, when all the wars were destroying everything, he became the city of that time when he was predestined to protect and fortify all who wished to adhere to God. He became the city of that time when he was appointed bishop to gather and preserve the souls of believers.

Let us nevertheless consider the force of this name in a deeper mystery. For when his feet were set on the path to proclaim peace, and while he stood with steadfast foot in the courts of Jerusalem, which is built as a city, he became “the city of the city of eternal time,” because his participation is in that same place where the tribes of the Lord went up to confess the name of the Lord.

Therefore he is also the city of time, and the city of the city of time—not transitory but eternal: the city built not of insensible stones but of living ones. In it the stone rejected by the builders was placed as the cornerstone; it was cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut, and it filled the whole globe of the earth.

Let us therefore contemplate the building of this city of time. And, so that we may be worthy to see it, let us invoke its builder, the Holy Spirit, that he may place the word in our mouth and in our heart, so that our mouth may be in our heart and we may be able to speak what is worthy.

After he had been weaned and the week of babbling infancy had passed, he was handed over to letters and attempted to learn their first rudiments. Once their elements had been committed to memory in a short time, he was already hastening to climb toward higher things.

Given over, therefore, to the leisure of wisdom, he drank in the springs of learning. He was slow in speech, though clear in intellect, since he was not one who possessed great eloquence or even great wisdom [Note: [Col. 0069] *Quam* corrected to *quum* in the manuscript.]. For the breath of eloquence gives little pleasure by pleasing the ear; but as soon as the speaker’s sound ceases, the hearer’s progress also ceases.

Therefore the energetic boy, striving with all his strength toward greater perfection, applied himself to the wisdom that does not fly about in words [Col. 0069D] but consists in virtues. “Good understanding belongs to all who practice it,” not to those who speak of it and preach it.

*(Fol. 26 verso.)* After spending the years of childhood simply at home, in the manner of the patriarch Jacob, when he was already entering the forked path of wavering adolescence, he was placed in a school community. He did not surrender his chastity to the allurements either of age or of his peers, but, as though entrusted to him by the Lord, preserved the seal of purity intact (*Life of Lupus*).

At that time the blessed Lupus was in the same city of Troyes, renowned for the integrity of his morals, distinguished by the gift of holiness, [Col. 0070A] praiseworthy for piety, remarkable for patience, conspicuous for wisdom, overflowing with charity, patient in hope, exemplary in faith, venerable in dignity, upright through zeal for justice toward offenders, near to others through compassion, most patient in adversity, cautious in prosperity—in him every praise may safely be sung.

After living in the world [Note: [Col. 0069] “Hi . . . inscla” in the manuscript; reading uncertain.] for seven years with his wife Piminola, sister of Saint Hilary, archbishop of Arelate, he sought the monastery of Lérins. From there he was taken up into the episcopate, and, having established a monastery for himself in view of the city [Note: [Col. 0069] *Orbis* corrected to *urbis* in the manuscript.], he pursued the same dignity of morals and the same discipline of humility and lowliness, attending there to divine contemplation with those who were with him.

The blessed Pulchronius was entrusted to him by his parents to be educated in the monastery. He began to imitate his teacher and to shape himself, by whatever means he could, according to what he saw him doing [Col. 0070B]. He had cheerfulness in his face, gravity in speech, discernment in obedience, humility in service, diligence in showing respect, modesty in countenance, reverence in his bearing, sweetness in his voice, and constancy in action. He was loved by everyone, praised by all, and honored by everyone. If there were anyone who did not love him, that person would rather condemn himself by failing to love him.

He also made it his concern to fear God, venerate his elders, preserve chastity, not disdain humility, and love modesty and clemency—ornaments of a younger age [Note: [Col. 0069] “He had … up to age” is written in the margin.]. Already then, certainly by the hidden judgment of divine providence, he was being educated so that nothing would be lacking in the apostolic bishop he was soon to become.

For he was one of the clean animals—those that know how to chew the cud and call the word [Col. 0070C] of God back to memory, and that are also fit for divine sacrifices and altars. He circumcised from himself everything that is unfit either for food or for sacrifice, whatever is covered and concealed in a human being by the defect of human nature.

He was preparing himself for the endurance of death, and his earliest age was already meditating on martyrdom. He weakened his tender body with fasts and subdued the fires of the flesh by frequent hunger, knowing that a flame does not require abundant fuel, nor does an unruly beast require more plentiful food to become more unruly, when the body’s own wickedness was enough for it.

He read continually and sang psalms frequently, so that the devil might always find him occupied; for the devil seeks out the idle and flees from the occupied. But if anything through the enemy’s cunning had slipped into the young man, he sought the baptism of tears; there [Col. 0070D], without doubt, he was baptized by fire.

O young man preferable to old men! O disciple whom the priests themselves desired to imitate! The blessed Lupus rejoiced at the progress of his disciple, and his parents also rejoiced at their son’s diligence and purpose: he was perceptive in the Scriptures, reasonable in faith, restraining and directing his course toward the fixed lines of God’s commands, and—what is most difficult at that age—turning neither to the right nor to the left, but walking firmly along the royal road.

*(Life of Lupus, p. 81.)* His fellow disciples under the instruction of the aforementioned father were Severus, later the holy bishop of Trier; Albinus, also of Châlons; the holy Emilianus; and likewise the holy Aventinus, later bishop of Troyes, together with many others. All of them shone through God’s grace with innumerable miracles, so that the merits of the disciples might make clear how great the holiness of their teacher must have been, since he formed such disciples in the way of God [Note: [Col. 0071] *Domini* corrected to *Dei* in the manuscript.] (fol. 27).

A society exceedingly blessed and pleasing to our Lord, in which one could see tranquility of spirit, devotion to gentleness, the grace of moderation, care for decency, and regard for beauty! Among these virtues modesty had truly laid the first foundation in them.

But just as the companionship of equals is sweeter among equals, so the companionship of elders is safer. The young men clung inseparably to the company [Col. 0071B] of the blessed Lupus, who, by a kind of instruction and teaching, colored the morals of the adolescents with his own way of life and dyed them, as it were, with the purple of integrity.

This the great man, full of God, accomplished by the greatest grace, seeing them follow their father’s commands with eager spirits [Note: [Col. 0071] *Alacres illorum animos* corrected to *ut in textu* (“as in the text”).]. Even the rigor of a more demanding purpose did not deter them from what they had begun, since youthful energy always turns toward those studies it considers more worthy of applause.

Among these companions, therefore [Note: [Col. 0071] *Contubernales* corrected to *contribules* in the text above.], the blessed Pulchronius shone with the lamp of his merits. He gleamed with the beauty of decency, taking every care that each person, and especially the best man, should think well of him; therefore he showed every good person the reverence owed to them.

He guarded against the impulses of youthful emotion, observing and examining himself, and restraining and curbing with a certain force of mind the desires that broke forth within him, lest desire either outrun reason or abandon it—lest, by outrunning it, desire disturb and exclude reason, and, by abandoning it, leave it helpless.

Thus, preserving the proper manner of each action, and guarding the order and consistency of his words, the moderation of his deeds, he devoted himself to that decorum which the moral teacher Ambrose attests to be both general and particular in his book *On Duties*, saying:

“Decorum,” he says, “is what stands out; its division is twofold. For there is a kind of decorum, as it were general, which is spread throughout the whole of moral excellence and is viewed, as it were, in the entire body. There is also a particular decorum, which stands out in some part of the body. It is general if someone possesses the whole of moral excellence in every action [Col. 0071D], so that his entire life agrees with itself and does not differ in any matter. It is particular if he has one action [Note: [Col. 0071] *Aliquam virtutem* corrected to *aliquem actum* in the manuscript.] standing out among his virtues [Note: [Col. 0071] *Actibus* corrected to *virtutibus* in the manuscript.].”

The distinguished youth was adorned with these marks of virtue. The splendor of his morals had also advanced him, and divine piety was preparing to exalt him, now dedicated to ecclesiastical service and enlarged by the ministry of the divine order.

When he had traversed the path of adolescence and passed into mature manhood, he began to labor with more fervent service of God, growing stronger day by day and advancing from virtue to virtue. Forgetting what lay behind and reaching forward to what lay ahead [Col. 0072A], he desired to be buried with Christ through the mortification of the flesh, so that through him he might deserve to be raised again to the glory of the Father in the power of the Spirit through the practice of good works.

Thus, living in the flesh, he served not according to the flesh, taking care and observing that, whether by sinning or by being placed under suspicion of sin, he should not become an obstacle or scandal to his brothers (fol. 27 verso). For from the Gospel he had understood how severe a punishment from the Lord is established for one who causes even one of the least to stumble.

That saying of the Lord was fixed in his heart: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Therefore he strove to be humbled on earth, so that he might deserve to be exalted by the Lord in heaven.

Nor could the hidden lamp remain concealed beneath a bushel. Rather, it was placed on a lampstand to dispel the darkness of error and illuminate many [Col. 0072B]. When it pleased him who calls the elect to eternity, justifies those called, and rewards those justified, to exalt his servant who placed his trust in him, he inspired the heart of the blessed Bishop Lupus to promote him to the priestly order as a support in his labor and ministry.

Chosen, therefore, by the common vote and praise of clergy and people, he received the honor of the priesthood and adorned it by his morals. He was powerful in word and doctrine, and used that power, with the apostle, for building up, not for destroying, so that sinners who had been corrected might be built up through repentance—those for whom destruction through guilt already seemed imminent.

He prayed for the sins of the people, and, harming no one, desired to benefit everyone, knowing that it is the duty of a priest or minister to benefit all, if possible, and harm no one [Col. 0072C]. The etymology of his name was already being fulfilled in him, and what had been foretold through the name was already resounding in his actions.

For he was a city of a time that was indeed most grave and dangerous, when almost the entire world was shaken by the roar of battles. He was also a refuge for the poor, a guardian of orphans, a defender of widows and children, a comforter of the oppressed, and a most compassionate receiver and helper of all who fled to him.

O unconquerable city, incomparable protection, invincible defense, dwelling of the divine, propitiatory of the Most High, in which wisdom reigns and justice dictates laws; which fortitude inhabits, prudence governs, and temperance orders; in which the image of God shines and effaces the images of vices [Col. 0072D]! Receive us also, your most humble lovers, and protect us under your defense.

When, therefore, the blessed Pulchronius was being extolled with such great praises for his good works, and his holiness had become evident to all, he was sought for the episcopate of the city of Verdun. As we have said, that city had been so worn down by calamities and burdened with evils that scarcely a few people could be found there who served divine worship.

We have explained the causes of the calamity above. But when he could not be prevailed upon to consent to the wishes of those who sought him, the remaining citizens turned all their hope toward the blessed Lupus, and they repeatedly urged him with tearful complaints to come to the aid of the wretched city, which was almost deserted and already abandoned [Col. 0073A]. The supplication of neighboring priests was added—priests who sighed for and were already rejoicing in the consolation of a future colleague.

Nor could the most holy man resist such devoted petitions from his fellow priests and the people, since he knew the Lord’s command: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10:27), and that a faithful soul is commanded not to seek its own interests but those of Jesus Christ.

*(Fol. 28.)* He therefore yielded and entrusted his devoted disciple to the devoted citizens as their shepherd and bishop. The church of Verdun embraced that day, solemn with the celebration of holy joys, joyful through the cheerfulness of pious hearts, and made glorious by the election and promotion of the blessed man; and to this day it continually experiences the benefits of that day [Col. 0073B].

Heaven rejoices and earth exults, because in this event the entire mystery of divine dispensation converged: those who until then had been vessels of iniquity destined for destruction were converted to repentance through the blessed man and became vessels of righteousness for sanctification.

Consecrated, therefore, as bishop with the wondrous devotion and favor of all, he strove to increase his works of piety, now that he had been advanced by the episcopal fillet. He assumed the name and habit of a priest and strove to be both the priest and the sacrifice of the Most High God.

For he presented himself as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God, offering him a sacrifice of praise and a contrite spirit—the one sacrifice God seeks, with all others rejected and despised. He also strove by the example of his progress to invite and draw others toward virtue, especially through the pattern of humility given to us by God.

By long and continual meditation he had become accustomed always to look upward and to restrain the material substance of the flesh, lifting it by tighter reins. He knew that it is the special duty of a priest to become the mediator of the people before God. For that reason he had refused to preside over those whom he feared he might know to be purer than himself.

At that time the once-fruitful vine, formerly joyful in its branches, had been turned into bitterness; the vine wholly rich in fruit, the diadem of beauty and crown of glory, had become confusion and disgrace, because nearly the whole West was already filthy with Arian dregs, which [Note: [Col. 0073] “Which—had loosened the reins” is written in the margin.], wherever they settled, always left behind foul traces of crime [Col. 0073C].

Although Belgic Gaul had always imitated the faith of Peter and rejected profane novelties of speech and the errors of schisms [Col. 0073D], it had nevertheless then loosened the reins far too much on vices that are nourished by quiet and idleness.

The pious shepherd reproved the erring with a father’s gentleness and mildness, and with the severity and authority of a bishop, knowing that Eli had been condemned for the wickedness of his sons because he had rebuked them with insufficient severity.

With Jeremiah (9:1), he also sought water for his head and a fountain of tears for his eyes, so that he might worthily mourn the wickedness of those who had sinned and had not done penance for their uncleanness and iniquities.

Even amid the remnants of Vandal captivity and destruction, while its memory was still recent [Col. 0074A], the seedbed of Arian iniquity nevertheless remained vigorous. The most blessed man wept over the sins of the people, preached healing, and urged the compunction of repentance, so that those who came to their senses might be converted to the Lord, who is good and whose mercy endures forever.

With the apostle, he taught them to flee fornication, because whoever commits fornication sins against his own body, and because wisdom does not dwell in a body subjected to sins.

Nor could the declaration of so great a preacher be empty and fruitless. On the contrary, the city of Verdun felt, and to this day recognizes, how much had been granted to it in such a bishop: his life was the people’s support, his teaching was medicine for souls, his rebuke was a correction of morals, and his eradication of vices.

[Col. 0074B] (fol. 28'.) Meanwhile, through these pious exercises of divine service, God began to make his servant known to the world by many miracles, so that everyone might recognize that his manner of life was pleasing to the angelic spirits. For he restored sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and hearing to the deaf, and by the power of his word drove away every bodily affliction. (Life of Lupus, p. 70.) Over demons, too, he had received such power from the Lord, and, as is read in the Life of the blessed Lupus, such grace of healing flourished in him that by a mere command he drove demons from possessed bodies; at the first order of his voice all their dark power vanished, and strength returned to every limb. Another writer, recounting the miracles of the aforesaid blessed Lupus and commemorating his disciples, also bears witness to this; he remembers our blessed father as well, in these words: (Life of Lupus, p. 81.) “One of these,” he says, “was Saint Polochronius, bishop of the city of Claves, whose life, full of holiness and distinguished by the gift of virtues, is shown by the performance of miracles, through which he shone forth more than can be believed.” For the wretched, whom a dreadful condition of madness tormented so that they had to be bound with iron chains by men, he obtained from the Lord, through his prayers, release from their madness, so that at his sole command demons also were driven away with their poisonous weapons, and they were freed from the fantasies of ghosts and specters. Nor did he shine only in such matters, but also in various others like them, which the little book written about his life explains more fully to those who wish to know. [Note: [Col. 0073] “These … church” in the margin.] These are the testimonies to the holiness of the blessed man, which the holy Church of God everywhere, both then during his life and now after his death, celebrates, venerates, and proclaims. O man most worthy of every praise, to be revered with every devoted love! O fitting temple of the Holy Spirit, sober through fasts, watchful through vigils, cleansed by prayers, most resplendent in chastity! O fortified city against the ambushes of the devil, sanctuary of God, propitiatory of the heavenly oracle, tower of David built with bulwarks, in which thousands of shields hang, every weapon of the mighty! There are no damp places in it, no shade of reeds beneath which the dragon’s torpid softness may recline. [Col. 0075A] O dwelling of virginity, shrine of piety! Such a minister truly befitted the holy Mother of the Lord; such a bishop worthily adorned her holy church, governed her household, and at the proper time distributed to his fellow servants the measure of the Lord’s grain. We rightly acknowledge him as the apostle of the church of Verdun, yet without diminishing the prerogative of due honor belonging to our first pastor, the blessed Sanctinus. For Saint Sanctinus cultivated the Lord’s field worthily, when it had not yet been marred by the plow of a wicked cultivator or occupied by the prior sowing of evil seed; and by constant passage he made a strange and untrodden road, previously trampled by no footsteps, worn and smooth. But afterward, when that same field had been covered both by the violence of persecution and by the scarcity of cultivators with nettles [Col. 0075B] and brambles, and when the enemy had sown weeds over the seed of faith and truth—that is, evil teaching and perverse doctrines—the labor of the blessed Polochronius was in a certain sense doubled. He first had to thrust out and expel the forms of wickedness previously conceived in people’s hearts, and to pull up and eradicate every harmful thing; then he had to entrust the seed of right faith once more to the furrows of their minds and, as though nothing had been done, renew everything from the beginning. For as many kinds of corruption as there had been, so many kinds of restoration were also required. But knowledge and discipline concerning all these things were handed down by him from the Lord of knowledge himself, by whom he had been chosen, before secular times, for the task of instructing souls. In saying this, we do not diminish the authority of the honor and devotion due to the blessed father Sanctinus; rather, we increase it, since, as an addition to the fullness of his devotion and praise, it was granted him to have such a successor—one who would not depart from the integrity of his faith and would prove no sluggish executor of his teaching and preaching. We embrace him with all the marrow of our bones, as is fitting for a father and dearest lord, through whom we have deserved to obtain this: that such a bishop should be given to us, one who can heal both souls and bodies. For it redounds to his glory that the church of Verdun bears fruit in holy faith. The praise of a teacher is the grace of his church. We also honor blessed Pulchronius not only with words but with the affections of our hearts, because he himself deserved more worthily to be honored by us: he bravely steered the rudder of the ecclesiastical ship, which he had cleansed of the filth of sins, amid worldly dangers, and to this day he has not ceased to steer it through prayers and assistance; nor, with God’s favor, will he cease. But now let us return to the order of the narrative.

The man of God, renowned for such great insignia of virtue, had so won the affection of everyone that he was venerated with extraordinary devotion by kings and princes, as well as by the rich and the ordinary. He was modest in his appearance, movement, gesture, and gait, so that in him one could see the condition of the inner man reflected in his outward bearing. His gait [Col. 0076A] was dignified, his movement pure and simple, his gestures becoming, his appearance chaste and devout, his speech gentle and calm, full of goodwill and grace when he spoke of the teaching of faith, the mastery of life, moral discipline, the confession of sins, the shame of the wicked, the glory of eternal life, and the hope of eternal reward.

How splendidly he adorned the temples of God, since it was always his concern that God’s hall should shine with fitting ornament, we can infer from the cultivation of his mind, where wisdom had established her seat. For he would not have obtained so important a place in the Church if, while he lived, he had not adorned it with appropriate splendor. He took especially devoted care of his children, that they might walk in holiness of heart and righteousness, do penance for their sins and guard themselves against future ones, [Col. 0076B] please God worthily, walk in the paths of innocence, and be lifted by hope toward heavenly things. He loved the clerics as his own members, and devotedly supplied them with the nourishment of life, lest they should fail on the road as they journeyed toward Christ. He was merciful toward all, and toward all extended a brotherly affection; toward his disciples he was like a nurse cherishing her little ones. The lame, the blind, the withered, the epileptic, and all who were held oppressed by various kinds of illness were brought to him from different regions of the world. Just as it is exceedingly difficult to distinguish their forms, so it is also difficult to know their names. An innumerable crowd of them kept watch day and night before the bishop’s house, and the healing hand of God cured them all through his prayers. Some departed healed; others came to be healed. Among those tormented by unclean spirits—many of whom were brought there when reports of his holiness had spread—it was painful to see bloodshot eyes, gnashing teeth, twisted necks, a tongue speaking a foreign language, hands bound in chains (fol. 29), trembling lips, a many-voiced sound, an enemy raging within, and outside a wretched person powerless over himself. Yet this madness withdrew more swiftly than speech at the one command of the man of God, and in that same moment health was bestowed. Everyone called the people blessed who were protected under the rule of so great a bishop, and the populations of neighboring cities preferred to have one of the holy man’s companions—namely, a disciple of the blessed Lupus—given to them as bishop. Since the metropolitan city of Trier had no bishop, it received Saint Severus, a man of outstanding holiness and most renowned in word and teaching, who, together with the blessed Germanus of Auxerre, was sent to recall the island of Britain from the Pelagian heresy a second time by the power of the word, since the blessed Lupus was excused by old age. The city of Châlons, however, chose Saint Albinus, whom it rejoices to possess as its patron to this day.

[Note: [Col. 0075] The following, through the end of folio 29*, Hugo inserted from his own Life.]

While the Gallican Church was flourishing through the preaching and industry of such great men, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 450, the first year of the reign of the emperor Marcian, who had succeeded Theodosius the Younger, the persecution and fury of the Huns grew strong, in the consulship of Valentinian for the seventh time and of Avienus. [Note: [Col. 0075] “Valentiniano … consulibus” in the margin.] [Col. 0077A] According to the authority of the histories, forty-five years are reckoned from the Vandal invasion to that year in which, under the kings Bleda and Attila, the army of the Huns spread through Gaul, as follows. In the fourteenth year of Honorius’s principate the fury of the Vandals boiled over, and afterward Honorius reigned for sixteen years. After him Theodosius the Younger reigned for twenty-seven years, and the emperor Marcian succeeded him; in the first year of Marcian’s reign the Huns occupied Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0077] “This seems to require supplementation.”]

We read in the history of the Goths [JORDAN. 21.] (fol. 29*) that, while the rival city of Rome was being founded by Constantine, forty thousand Goths under the kings Ariaric and Adaric came to that emperor’s aid [Note: [Col. 0077] “provenisse” corrected to “praevenisse” in c.] (ibid., 22). After their departure, when Wisimar, king of the Vandals, was attacked by Geberic, king of the Goths, as the historiographer Dexippus relates—he says that they had scarcely reached our frontier from the Ocean within the space of a year because of the immense extent of the lands—while the Vandals were dwelling in the regions where the Gepids now live, on the bank of the Marisia River they were defeated and overthrown by Geberic. Abandoning that homeland, they sought Pannonia from Constantine; there, having served the emperors according to their decrees for sixty years and more, they were afterward summoned by Stilicho, master of the soldiers and patrician, and occupied Gaul, where they did not establish dwellings fixed by God. After some further intervening material, he adds this as well [Note: [Col. 0077] “subdet,” perhaps “subdit,” in c.]:

(Ibid., 24.) “After no long interval, under King Hermanaric, who had succeeded Geberic, the nation of the Huns, with Balamir ruling over them, blazed up against the Goths—the Ostrogoths, that is, the eastern Goths—with a ferocity more savage than any other.”

(Ibid., 25.) “When the Visigoths saw this, they sent envoys to Valens, the brother of the elder Valentinian, promising that, if he gave them Thrace or Moesia, they would become Christians. Imbued by him with the Arian treachery in which he himself was held, the Visigoths handed on that same treachery, as though because of kinship of origin, to the Ostrogoths and Gepids; and, crossing the Danube, they settled in Dacia, Moesia, and Thrace with permission.”

(Ibid., 26.) “When they wished to hold all the northern regions as far as the Danube, they were attacked in war by that same Valens and became victorious; and when the wounded emperor had taken refuge in a nearby house, they set it on fire and burned him, while Fridigern ruled the Goths after Hermanaric. Athanaric succeeded him, and Alaric succeeded Athanaric.”

(Ibid., 28.) “But when Theodosius came to power together with Gratian, he made peace with them and treated them kindly. Later, however, when his sons dealt with them differently and they invaded Italy, under King Alaric and in the consulship of Stilicho and Arilianus, Gaul was given to them” (ibid., 30), “so that they might defend it against the Vandals. When Stilicho fought them treacherously at Pollentia, the enraged Alaric returned to Rome, invaded and plundered it, and, passing through Campania and Sicily to Africa, died and was buried in the river Barintus.”

(Ibid., 31.) “Athaulf succeeded him and again stripped Rome and Italy of private and public wealth. Taking Placidia, the sister of Honorius, as his wife, and leaving Italy because of their kinship, he went to Gaul, which was being grievously harassed by the Vandals under their leader Cresco, and also by the Alans and Burgundians. For at that time the Vandals, abandoning Pannonia out of fear of the Goths, were pressing upon Gaul and trying to establish fixed settlements there. The enormity of this evil is sufficiently and more than sufficiently clear to all. Nevertheless, fleeing before his face, they shut themselves up in Spain, where they were defeated by the Goths.”

(Ibid., 32.) “When Wallia, the fourth after Alaric, had succeeded him, and the Vandals again harassed Gaul during the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur, he moved an army against them and compelled them to migrate to Africa under their king Gaiseric.”

(Ibid., 34.) “When Wallia died, Theodoric succeeded him in the kingdom of Gaul and Spain. Against him the patrician Aetius, after breaking the peace, moved an army into Gaul with the Huns as allies” [Col. 0078B] (ibid., 35), “whose kings were Bleda and Attila, while Theodosius the Younger was emperor and Theodosius and Felix were consuls. After both sides had given pledges, they withdrew; thereafter Attila, having killed his brother and subjected the entire people of the Huns to himself, began to aspire to rule the whole world.”

From these statements of the historiographer Jordanes [Note: [Col. 0077] “Jordanis” corrected from “Jornandis” in c.] we clearly gather that the empire of the West was first shaken by the inundation of the Vandals and afterward by that of the Huns.

(fol. 29*.) [NENNIUS X, 13.] Adam, the creation of the living God, begot Seth; Seth begot Enos; Enos, Cainan; Cainan begot Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel also begot Jared; Jared, Enoch; Enoch, Methuselah; Methuselah [Col. 0078C] begot Lamech; Lamech begot Noah; Noah begot Japheth, who extended his boundaries in Europe; Shem in Asia; Ham in Africa. Japheth begot Johan; Johan, Lobath; Lobath, Bath; Bath also begot Hisrau; Hisrau, Esraa; Esraa, Ra; Ra begot Abyr; Abyr, Ooth; Ooth, Ethech; Ethech, Aurchact; Aurchact, Ecthactus; Ecthactus also begot Mayr; Mayr, Semion; Semion, Boib; Boib, Thoy; Thoy, Ogomuin; Ogomuin, Fetuyr; Fetuyr, Alanus. [Col. 0078D]

At this point especially, I wish to set out the genealogies of the peoples as they have been read in manuscripts from the beginning of the ninth century; they are as follows:

1. Royal Codex Parisinus no. 609, from the beginning of the ninth century. [Col. 0079A] “Who were those who begot the nations?” Answer: “Three brothers: Ermenus, Ingus, and Etscius. Ermenus begot the Goths, Vandals [the manuscript has V::::ndalos], Gepids, and Saxons. Ingus begot the Burgundians, Thuringians, Lombards, and Bavarians. Scius begot the Romans, Britons, Franks, and Alamanni.”

2. Codex Sangallensis no. 732, quarto, parchment, from the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century, fol. 142. “When Adam was 130 years old, he begot Seth,” and so through six ages up to fol. 154: “and from that point Lord Charles alone took up the kingdom and, with God’s protection, governs it prosperously to the present year, which is the forty-third year of his reign and the tenth of his empire. The total number of years from the beginning of the world to the present year is 4762. HERE BEGINS THE GENEALOGY OF KINGS. THE FIRST KING OF THE ROMANS, ANALEUS: Analeus begot Papulus; Papulus begot Egegius; Egegius begot Egegius; Egegius begot Fadiru, and the Romans lost him. There were three brothers from whom the nations descend: Erminus, Inguo, and their brother Istio. Erminus begot the Goths, Walagoths, Vandals, [Col. 0079B] Gepids, and Saxons. These are five nations. Their brother Inguo begot the Burgundians, Loringians, Lombards, and Bavarians. These are four nations. Their brother Istio begot the Romans, Britons, Franks, and Alamanni. These are four nations.”

3. Royal Codex Parisinus no. 4628 A, from the tenth century, and Ottobonianus 3081, from the fifteenth century. “ALSO CONCERNING THE KINGS OF THE ROMANS. The first king of the Romans was called Allanius. Allanius begot Pabolus; Pabolus, Egetius; Egetius begot Egegius; Egegius begot Siagrius, through whom the Romans lost their kingdom.

“Three men were so called: the first Ermenius, the second Ingo, the third Escio. From them thirteen nations increased. The first, Ermenius, begot the Goths, Walagoths, Vandals, Gepids, and Saxons. Ingo begot the Burgundians, Thuringians, Lombards, and Bavarians. Escio begot the Romans, Britons, Franks, and Alamanni.”

[Col. 0079C] 4. British Museum manuscript among the Harleian manuscripts, no. 3859; Nennius, eleventh century. “The first man who came to Europe from the line of Japheth was Alanus, with his three sons, whose names were Hessitio, Armenon, and Negue. Hissitio had four sons: Francus, Romanus, Britto, and Albanus. Armenon had five sons: Gothus, Valagothus, Gebidus, Burgondus [the manuscript has burgandus; ‘longobardus’ corrected from ‘burgondus’; ‘langobardus,’ likewise below], and Langobardus. Negue had three sons: Wandalus, Saxo, and Boguarus. From Hissitio arose four nations: the Franks, Latins, Albans, and Britons. From Armenon, five: the Goths, Walagoths, Gepids, Burgundians, and Lombards. From Negue, four: the Bavarians, Vandals, Saxons, and Thuringians. These nations were divided throughout all Europe.”

5. From a codex of the monastery of Cava containing Lombard Laws, from the beginning of the eleventh century. “King Mulius had three sons, whose names are these: Armen, Tingus, and Ostius. Each begot four generations. [Col. 0079D] Armen begot the Goths, Vandals, Brigids, and Saxons; Tingus begot the Tuscans and Lombards, Burgundians, and Bavarians; Hostius begot the Romans, Britons, Franks, and Alamanni.”

6. Vatican Codex no. 5001, about the year 1300, fol. 140: “There were three brothers, from whom thirteen nations descend. The first, Ermenius, begot the Butes, Walagoths, Vandals, Gepids, and Saxons; Ingo begot the Burgundians, Thuringians, Lombards, and Bavarians; Escio, the Romans, Britons, Franks, and Alamanni.”

He [Alanus] was the first to come to Europe with his three sons, Ysichion, Armenon, and Neugio. Ysichion begot four sons: Francus, from whom came the Franks; Romanus, from whom Rome came; Alamannus, from whom the Alamanni came; and Brittonus, from whom the Britons came. Armenon begot five sons: Gothus, from whom came the Goths; Walagothus, from whom came the Walagoths; Cibidus, from whom came the Gepids; Burgundus, from whom came the Burgundians; and Langobardus, from whom came the Lombards. Neugio had four sons: Bogarus, from whom came the Bavarians; Wandalus, from whom came the Vandals; Saxo, from whom came the Saxons; and Taringus, from whom came the Thuringians. They were called Alans from their father Alanus. These nations were divided throughout Europe.

[Col. 0079D] (Cf. GREGORY OF TOURS, II, 5.) When the Vandals had withdrawn from Gaul and a report had spread that the Huns wished to burst into Gaul, the inhabitants of the Gallican cities who remained, distrusting their ability to resist those whose barbarity had already terrified them powerfully, sought out strongly fortified places where they believed they could protect themselves against the dreadful assaults of the marauding enemy. Many occupied hills naturally defended, fortifying themselves with towers, engines, and other instruments of war, so that these might be objects of fear to the enemy and sources of strength to their own people. Others made cities that had no natural defenses impregnable with ditches and the solidity of walls, repairing breaches and restoring what had been destroyed. The priests, together with the clerics, took refuge in the aid of prayer and by continual supplications struck at the ears of the Lord and Savior, asking that he might be propitiated toward his people, drunk [Col. 0080B] not with wine or strong drink but with the force of the plague he had brought upon them. For such fear of the invading enemy had seized everyone that everything seemed to threaten death itself. The enemy had thrown everything into confusion, so that nothing seemed better than to flee from the midst and hide. All was blindness; desolation and ruin, calamity and the sword had filled everything. Human weakness might be astonished at how, under so many teachers of the Christian faith—namely, the holy bishops with whom the Gallican Church of that time had zealously fortified itself—it had endured such dangers, trampling, and insults, unless it believed that the judgments of the Lord are incomprehensible; to wish to investigate the great depth of them, as it is, is folly for a human being. Indeed, Scripture shows that whenever the fury of the ancient enemy fell more violently upon the churches of God, the Lord provided them with invincible leaders of spiritual camps, who both resisted the devil’s contrivances powerfully and raised up a horn of salvation for the suffering people of God. This was done by divine dispensation so that the approved might be made manifest and, once unbelief had been wiped away, truth might shine more and more brightly into the light itself.

While all Belgica was therefore wavering at this time, the blessed Pulchronius, foreseeing and knowing in advance that, because of the sins of the people who inhabited it, a very large part of Gaul would be overthrown, offered for the sheep entrusted to him whole burnt offerings rich in marrow, with the fat of lambs and rams, lest they should honor God with their lips while their hearts were far away, and, professing faith in words, deny it by their deeds. [Col. 0080D] He urged them to redeem the flames of their sins by almsgiving and to cleanse by confession and penance the crimes with which almost all Gaul was then still burdened—crimes sprouting from a full belly, security, and idleness—saying [Note: [Col. 0079] Superscript.] that whoever is accused by the testimony of conscience vainly attempts to escape the eyes of God beneath shade and leaves. Miracles were also joined to his preaching, which God deigned to work through his servant, so that those for whom preaching alone was insufficient might be terrified by a miracle—or rather invited to recognize, restrain, and eradicate their wickedness. But what will unpunished wickedness not dare? Nothing could restrain the sinners from the monstrousness of their crimes, until the avenging sword of heavenly wrath came and struck everyone with an irrevocable sentence.

[JORD.] Attila [Note: [Col. 0081] “Attila … historian” was later added by Hugo in the margin; it was not in the Life of Pulchronius.], as we have said, king of the Huns, relying on an army numbering five hundred thousand, son of Munzuccus, a man born into the world for its upheaval, the terror of all lands, terrified everything by a wondrous destiny, with a dreadful reputation spread about him. He was proud in his gait, with lively eyes, so that his arrogance and power were apparent even from the movement [Note: [Col. 0081] “nutu” corrected to “motu” in the manuscript.] of his body. A lover of wars, restrained in the use of his own hand; strong in counsel, approachable by those who begged him, favorable toward those once received into his allegiance, short in stature, broad-chested, with a rather large head, small eyes, a thin nose, and a repulsive complexion, he bore the marks of his origin. Although his nature was such that he always presumed great things, the sword of Mars, which had been found and was always kept among the kings of the Scythians, added confidence to him. Through it he believed that he had been established as ruler of the world and that, as a subtle man, power over wars had been granted him. Before he waged wars, he fought by strategy. Hence he thirsted for dominion over all cities and kingdoms. With him was also Walamer, king of the Ostrogoths, and Ardaric, king of the Gepids, whom Attila loved above the other petty kings because of their shrewdness; the remaining crowd of kings and leaders of different nations served Attila’s nods as attendants. He himself, king of all kings, was concerned for everyone above everyone else, devastating and crushing everything like an inundating whirlwind. Gaul learned this sufficiently through her own misery. For with an unheard-of power before him, he alone held the Scythian and Germanic kingdoms and terrified both empires of the Roman world by capturing cities; and, so that the rest might not be destroyed, he accepted an annual tribute, as the historiographer Jordanes relates.

Thus, when wolves were rushing into the Lord’s sheepfold—that is, when the Huns were raging among the Lord’s people—their innumerable army invaded the cities of First Belgica [Note: [Col. 0081] “Gaul” corrected to “Belgica” in c.], attacking the populations that had escaped the hands of the Vandals and could scarcely yet breathe. They cried out from the depths of their misery: “Hunger presses upon these, iron upon those; death claims some, captivity others.” Wretched, utterly pitiable was the condition: to see populations deprived of every defense, [Col. 0081D] robbed of every consolation, in whose innermost parts the fury of the Vandal persecution was still boiling in fresh memory, now trembling beneath the yoke of the Huns, their faces pale with fasting, dying in the service of cruel masters, and girls, consecrated virgins if any remained, matrons [Note: [Col. 0081] “matr. … bodies” in the margin.] as well, and every free and noble body thrown down for the mockery of a brothel; for them it would have been preferable to be killed by the sword than subjected to such disgraceful slavery. Captured bishops were made a spectacle for beasts; priests were killed; the various offices of clerics were destroyed; churches were overturned; horses were stabled at Christ’s altars. If only we could ascend into the watchtower of the mind and behold the kinds of such great miseries! We would see nations colliding with nations and kingdoms with kingdoms; some tortured, others killed, others overwhelmed by the waves, others dragged into slavery. Everywhere mourning, everywhere groaning, and the image of death in abundance. How many monasteries captured, how many waters of rivers changed by human blood, cities devastated, and herds of captives dragged away! Because of the sins of the people, the barbarians were made strong; through the vices of Christians [Note: [Col. 0081] “his” corrected to “Christians” in c.] the army of the Huns prevailed.
