God was offended, and his fury was kindled [Note: [Col. 0081] “and his fury was kindled” is written over an erasure.]. The heart of the children of men had been blinded, and, except for a few old men, all those born in captivity and under siege did not desire the liberty they did not know [Note: [Col. 0081] After this six or seven words were erased; the fourth was “crowd.”].

Meanwhile the holy bishop saw what he grieved over; the people now recognized what they deserved. There was no counsel, no hope of escape, no refuge except in God’s mercy. He urged his children at least on the day of vengeance to come to their senses, to confess and mourn the crimes they had previously neglected, now that the sword was already threatening their necks, so that they might turn God’s anger—already present, already hanging over them—into gentleness; so that the sword devastating outside and crushing within through fear, when it had reached even to the division of soul and body, might become, for those who endured patiently, a propitiation of the wrath of the Most High; and so that, after they had been reborn in the saving bath, the second death might not possess them, and the enemy exult over the damnation of body and soul. Thus instructing everyone with saving teachings and strengthening them with priestly blessing, he urged all toward the crown of martyrdom, so that, anointed through penance and in a certain sense incorporated into the divine will, they might deserve to become a whole burnt offering for the eternal King, purified in the furnace of tribulation.

[Note: [Col. 0081] “They had fortified … nations” in the margin, in different ink.] They themselves had fortified the suitable places of the city, difficult of access and fit for defense, and every honorable man and man of strength had withdrawn there to frustrate the enemy’s assaults, imitating the valor of the Maccabees. When they were pressed by a similar distress, they regarded their cause as being for the sake of their souls, the sword as defense and protection, zeal as the means of preserving life, and every labor as necessary lest they should, through cowardice, be overthrown as before [Note: [Col. 0081] After this the ink changes.]. Nor was it very difficult for the Huns to extend the madness of their fury and slaughter far and wide. Therefore the people, listening to the voice of the priest who gave saving admonitions, learned that it was good to look from afar toward the nearest good; and the ways of life that they had despised because of innocence they now held through penance [Note: [Col. 0081] “ways” was written over an erasure, “and he despised.”]. They awaited with panting spirit the sword hanging over their necks, and it was most welcome to them to die in this way, while they dreaded the captivity of barbarian domination and plunder, heavier than every sword.

The day of trumpet and [Col. 0083A] blast, of uproar and wailing, had now arrived. The hostile battle line spread out; massacres of Christians took place; rivers of blood flowed, poured out by hostile cruelty, running not with the blood of beasts but of human beings. No one pitied the old men who remained [Note: [Col. 0083] “who remained” was added later; “captives” is read at the side.]; the young were slaughtered without restraint. No modesty, no shame was preserved for mothers and virgins; children and infants were not spared. The sword reached even to the soul. When I bring before my eyes what happened, my voice itself is choked by the bitterness of grief, because amid such devastation of God’s people the mind mourns, the heart is tortured, and the spirit is distressed. Have mercy, Lord, on your people, the portion of your inheritance! Do not abandon your share or give it over to the trampling of the nations.

Only God’s knowledge can count the number of the slain, because, with cities and castles recently destroyed and left exposed by Vandal cruelty, scarcely any place of retreat remained and scarcely any avenue of escape lay open. If some had hidden themselves in secluded forests, their wasting bones grew pale from fasting, especially since even there someone was not lacking who searched out those in hiding, dragged out those he found, and struck down those he had dragged away. Thus the greater part of Gaul became the prey of the enemy, and some cities were reduced almost [Note: [Col. 0083] Superscript.] to the condition of having no inhabitants. Those who escaped drag out—or rather scarcely lead—their lives in hidden mountain places and caves in the rocks. So fiercely did the wrath of the Most High rage in the destruction of the sinful people.

Nevertheless, many priests [Note: [Col. 0083] “Many priests … are” in the margin.], together with the peoples entrusted to them, were delivered by divine protection and human defense from every danger in the fortifications to which they had fled and which they had carefully strengthened [Note: [Col. 0083] “from … peoples,” perhaps, in c.]. At this time the blessed Lupus gave the clearest signs of his holiness; as it is sung in his hymn, while all wars were destroying everything, he fortified Troyes by prayer. In every place devastated by them, whatever wealth was found became booty; the rest was consumed by fire or redeemed by an annual tribute. What [Note: [Col. 0083] “What” with the article in the margin.] they did in each individual city and place is sufficiently and more than sufficiently attested by the affliction of each city and place. Let us briefly see what the end of his boldness was, and then turn the narrative toward recounting the death of the blessed man.

After a great deal of bloodshed, they reached Orléans. At that time the city of Orléans was governed by Saint Anianus, its sixth bishop, who, after Saint Evantius—who had succeeded Definianus in the time of the emperor Constantine and Pope Silvester—had received that city’s episcopal chair [Note: [Col. 0083] “He governed … had received” in the margin.].

[JORD. 37.] When [Note: [Col. 0083] Written over an erasure.] the patrician Aetius, who governed Gaul under the emperor Marcian, learned that Singibanus [Note: [Col. 0083] “Singibanus, king of the Vandals, who was staying there and favored Aetius’s party” is written in another hand in the margin, with “Aetius’s party” superscript.]—the king of the Vandals who was staying there and favored Aetius’s party—wished to hand over the city of Orléans, over which, as stated, the holy bishop Anianus [Note: [Col. 0083] “whom Saint Anianus the bishop governed” is written over an erasure; “as stated” is superscript.] [Col. 0084A] presided, he sent to Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, asking for help against the Huns. If they prevailed over the Huns, he would give the Goths half of Gaul.

[FRED.] Theodoric agreed to this. He also sent other messengers to Attila, king of the Huns, asking for aid against the Goths, who were attempting to invade Gaul. If they prevailed over the Goths, he would give the Huns half of Gaul. When Attila also agreed, the Goths and Huns engaged in a fierce battle on opposite sides for the possession of Gaul.

[JORD. 41.] In that battle two hundred thousand Visigoths were killed, together with their king Theodoric, and one hundred and fifty thousand Huns, apart from ninety thousand Gepids and Franks, who fell by wounds inflicted by one another before the general engagement: the Franks fighting on the Roman side and the Gepids on the side of the Huns [Note: [Col. 0083] “apart from ninety thousand Gepids and Franks, who fell before the encounter” in the margin.].

[FRED.] Thus, through the prayers of the blessed Anianus and the skill of the patrician Aetius, the city of Orléans was freed. The Huns, however, remained with the Ostrogoths in the plain of Mauriac. Thorsimund, who had succeeded his father as king, gathered the whole army of the Visigoths and, desiring to avenge his father, engaged the Huns in battle on the Mauriac plain.

[JORD. 38.] They fought continuously for three days, with Sangibanus always placed in the middle so that he would not turn toward Attila; and an innumerable multitude fell [Note: [Col. 0083] “Sangibanus is always placed in the middle, lest he turn toward Attila” in the margin.]. Aetius, strong in counsel, came by night to Attila and said: “I had hoped that by your valor I could free this region from the assault of the Visigoths; that cannot possibly be done. For tonight Theodoric, the brother of Thorsimund, has arrived with the largest Gothic force, and you will not be able to defeat him in battle—if only you may escape.”

[FRED.] Then Attila gave Aetius ten thousand solidi, so that with his help and skill he might be able to return to Pannonia. That same night Aetius went to Thorsimund and fabricated a similar story about the arrival of a very large force of Huns from Pannonia, adding that Thorsimund ought to beware lest, while he delayed, his brother Theodoric seize his kingdom. In the same way, after receiving ten thousand solidi from him, Aetius promised assistance against the Huns, and thus the Visigoths withdrew secretly. When they had fled, and the Huns likewise withdrew on the other side, Aetius joined the Franks to himself and directed his men behind the Huns. He pursued them as far as Thuringia, and thus, through his valor and ingenuity, Gaul was freed from its enemies.

When this stratagem was reported to Thorsimund and the Goths and they demanded the portion of Gaul that had been promised, Aetius sent them a small golden object weighing five hundred pounds [Note: [Col. 0083] “Five hundred pounds” written above the line], adorned with gems as a means of settlement; it is still preserved in the treasuries of the Goths as an ornament.

[JORD. 40.] [Note: “[Narrat—inglorius]” are written in the margin of the preceding leaf, marked with Θ. That they belong here is shown by the words “Turn the leaf at the sign Θ,” written above the later passage.] The history of the Goths relates that Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, was roused to war against the Pannonian enemies by the younger Valentinian, who ruled in the western regions. Leaving four sons at home, he went into battle with Thrasimund and Theoderic. Aetius, on the other hand, advanced against Attila with such care and prudence that he met the immense host with a force not unequal to it. It was a savage, manifold, monstrous, stubborn war, such as antiquity records none like: the blood overflowed like a stream, flooding its low banks in the manner of a torrent. During this battle Theoderic, riding around and exhorting his men, was thrown from his horse, trampled under the feet of his own men, and died.

After this, the Visigoths, separated from the Alans, would almost have slaughtered Attila himself, had not nightfall ended the battle when Attila enclosed his men within the defenses of the camp. The battle had begun around the ninth hour of the day. Yet he would have been surrounded there had not the archers to whom he had entrusted the defense resisted them in turn.

Thorismund, after attending to the funeral rites and desiring to avenge his father, consulted Aetius about what he should do. Aetius, fearing that, once the Huns had been completely destroyed, the Roman Empire might be crushed by the Visigoths, advised him to return to his ancestral seat and seize the kingship, lest his brothers, having taken possession of their father’s resources, invade the kingdom, and lest he have to fight a more serious war with his own people than with foreigners. Having received this answer, he returned to Gaul.

When Attila learned of his departure, he turned his attention to the oppression of the Romans and besieged the city of Aquileia, the metropolis of Venetia. Thorismund, carried in royal majesty into Tolosa, entered the city through the Catalaunian Fields, where he had also fought.

After capturing Aquileia and cruelly destroying and ravaging it, Attila raged through the remaining cities of Venetia. Milan was overthrown, Ticinum destroyed, the neighboring places struck down, and almost all Italy demolished. As he was about to proceed against Rome, he was dissuaded by the example of King Alaric: Alaric had not long survived after breaking Rome. Pope Leo himself approached Attila, and, appeased by him, Attila withdrew beyond the Danube under a treaty of peace, declaring that he would inflict still worse evils upon Italy unless Honoria, the sister of Valentinian and daughter of Placidia, together with a portion of the royal wealth, were sent to him; Honoria had indeed made this demand. (The same work, 43.)

When he attempted to subdue the Alans living beyond the Loire, he withdrew ingloriously from the Visigoths, against whom he had intended extermination, because the Alans came to their aid. (The same work, 44.)

Thus, after defeating the Huns and arranging peace among his people, Thorismund died, and his brother Theoderic succeeded him. Theoderic, together with the Burgundian kings Gundioc and Chilperic as auxiliaries, struck down and annihilated Rechiarius, the Suevic king who was invading Spain. After Rechiarius was killed, Recismund succeeded him under Gothic rule. (The same work, 47.)

Theoderic also died, and his brother Euric succeeded him. Euric brought Arles and Massilia under his own authority. (The same work, 48.) [Note: “Gothis—est redditus” in the margin.] He lived until the time of Theodemir, king of the Ostrogoths, when the Goths were entirely subject to them and obeyed Attila’s empire.

No Scythian people could otherwise be separated from the empire of the Huns unless Attila’s death, desired by all nations, had come first. His death was so contemptible that his life had been remarkable. After taking a young woman as his wife following innumerable wives, he became excessively relaxed with festivity at the wedding and, weighed down by wine and sleep, lay on his back. Blood that flowed unawares from his nostrils, obstructed in its customary passages, slipped by a fatal route into his throat and killed him as he slept.

An additional marvel is reported by the historian Priscus: while the emperor Marcian of the East was troubled by concern over so savage an enemy, the divinity standing beside him showed him Attila’s broken bow that same night.

When his death became known, a remarkable spectacle was displayed. His corpse was placed in the middle of the fields, within a silken tent. Chosen horsemen from the entire Hunnic nation surrounded the place where he had been laid and celebrated his deeds with a funeral song, holding a great feast and expressing funeral mourning mingled with joy.

They enclosed the corpse in a coffin and reinforced it first with gold, second with silver, and third with common iron: iron because he had subdued nations by force of arms, but gold and silver because he had received the adornment of both realms. Weapons taken from slain enemies were added, together with precious saddlery glittering with varied gems and insignia of different kinds by which some distinction is honored. (Compare the same work, 30.)

To prevent human greed from reaching such great wealth, they slaughtered those assigned to this task with a detestable reward, burying them so that death would be instantaneous both for those who buried and for the one buried.

His burial place was a most enormous river, diverted from its bed and spread into seventy channels. When the full force of the river was flooding there, he was committed to burial; then, after the channels were blocked, the river was returned to its bed.

Thus Gaul was at that time freed from the Huns’ ravaging. The few Christians who remained, seeing that divine vengeance had justly been exercised against them and giving thanks inwardly for God’s propitiation, submitted themselves with a more willing spirit to the fulfillment of God’s commands.

[BEDA.] Aetius, too, the patrician, the great salvation of the western state and the terror of King Attila, was treacherously killed by Valentinian’s own hand. Valentinian was later killed by the deceit of Maximus through two of Aetius’s closest associates, in the thirtieth year of his reign and the fourth year of Marcian.

[FRED.] Maximus, the tyrant who succeeded him, took Valentinian’s widow as his wife. In the fourth month he was killed in a military uprising, and Avitus succeeded him. Avitus was first proclaimed emperor by the Gallic army at Tolosa and afterward at Arles by the Goths. He was deprived of both empire and life in the third year of his reign, and Marcian obtained sole rule.

After Marcian died in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 457, Majorian in Italy and Leo at Constantinople were proclaimed emperors.

[Note: After these three or so words, text has been erased.] In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 435, therefore, before Avitus became emperor, Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, summoned by Valentinian’s widow, entered Rome. Enriched with the Romans’ wealth, he returned to Africa, taking with him Valentinian’s wife, two daughters, and Gaudentius, the son of the patrician Aetius. [ISID.] Gaiseric reigned for 37 years and 3 months; after his death Honoric succeeded him.

[JORD. 50.] [Note: Here begin various additions contained on a small inserted scrap of parchment, very difficult to distinguish, since scarcely any coherence of subject matter offers guidance and the painted signs have sometimes disappeared. I have followed the signs as carefully as I could and indicated them everywhere. Ulrichs.] After Attila’s death, while all his successors desired to rule, they all lost the empire together. Ardaric, the most famous king of the Gepids, was the first to rise against Attila’s sons. A battle was fought in Pannonia, with various peoples whom Attila had ruled—Goths, Gepids, Sueves, Huns, Alans, and Heruls—joining the conflict. Ardaric’s sword killed thirty thousand of them; the rest were put to flight.

[Note: “In—were” on a small slip.] In that battle Elac, Attila’s elder son, was killed. The others were driven toward the shore of the Pontic Sea, where the settlements of the Goths had previously been. The victorious Gepids occupied the borders of Dacia, the Goths the Pannonias, the Huns Illyricum, and the Alans Lower Scythia. Erma, Attila’s younger son, took for himself the farthest settlement of Little Scythia and held it during the reign of Marcian.

The blessed Pulchronius, bishop of the city of Clavero, having completed the course of his life, departed on the second day before the Kalends of May and migrated to the Lord. His body was buried in a church dedicated with honor in the name of Saint Amantius. Many, however, maintain that, out of fear of the enemy, he was buried beside the public road, because he had been carried off amid the very turmoil of the wars so that he would not see the destruction of the city and its people; later, when the wars had abated, a church was built over him by devout men.

After several years had passed, therefore, by divine will his most sacred body was raised and honorably reinterred in the church of Saint Peter, as befitted a saint. Saint Possessor succeeded him; of him we know with certainty that he pleased God and was found righteous. He too died in December, on the first day, and was buried in the church of Saint Peter.

[Note: The words written in the upper margin in the same ink but with faint strokes seem to belong here: “Severus … fuco [uncertain], died in the fourth year.”]

Of the holy memory of these men we find in the writings of the Fathers that their merits were pleasing to God and that they were numbered among the citizens of the saints. (Bercarius, *Gesta*, bishop of Verdun.) The day of the translation of their relics is celebrated annually with solemn remembrance on the fourth day before the Nones of May.

[JORD. 53.] [Note: “Ostrog.—empire” in the margin.] After Valamer, the king of the Ostrogoths was Theodemir; after him his son Theoderic became a very powerful king. At the age of seven he was given to Marcian as a hostage and brought to Constantinople to Leo. At that time the Goths utterly crushed the Huns and destroyed the nation of the Sciri. In that battle Walamir died, while his brother Theodemir ravaged and subjected the Sueves, Sarmatians, Gepids, and Alans. The emperor Leo then returned his son to him. (The same work, 56.)

Theodemir sent his brother Vidimer to Italy, where Vidimer died, leaving an heir who bore his name. After receiving great gifts from the emperor Glycerius, this heir came to Gaul and, joining forces with the Visigoths, defended Gaul under his own authority, since it was being oppressed by neighboring peoples.

Theodemir invaded Pannonia and Thessalonica. After receiving gifts from the patrician Hilary, they obtained places in which to dwell and so remained at peace. Theodemir died, leaving Theoderic as his heir, as has been said, during the reign of Zeno. (The same work, 57.)

Theoderic was invited by Zeno, made consul, and adopted as a son. He was sent to Rome to free it from the tyranny of the king of the Torcilingi and Rugians. In the third year after his entry into Italy he obtained the kingdom and was crowned with the royal diadem. At that time Alaric ruled over the Visigoths, Sigismund in Burgundy—who also had Theoderic’s daughter as his wife—Clovis in France, Ermenfrid in Thuringia, and Thrasamund over the Vandals. (The same work, 58.)

Alaric had a son, Amalaric. While he was ruling in Gaul and Spain, he was killed by the Franks at Barcelona and lost both kingdom and life. Afterward Theudis ruled among the Visigoths and left the kingdom to Agila. Against Agila, Athanagild rose up with Liberius, the Roman patrician.

Among the Ostrogoths in Italy, after Theoderic, Athalaric, his grandson, ruled; Theodahad succeeded him. After Theodahad was deposed, Witigis was made king. With him the kingdom ended and passed to the Roman Empire.

Let us now return to the succession of Roman emperors and pontiffs. Majorian was killed in the fifth year of his reign while preparing to march from Rome against the Vandals, and Anthemius became emperor in the seventh year of the emperor Leo. (The same work, 45.)

[Note: “Anthemius—the year of the Lord 596” on a sewn-on slip.] Anthemius the emperor was killed in an internal war by his son-in-law Ricimer and left the kingdom to Avitus. Avitus voluntarily withdrew, became bishop of Placentia, and left the kingdom to Olybrius. Olybrius too died by the swords of eunuchs. Glycerius was made Caesar at Ravenna; after scarcely one year had passed, he was ordained bishop at the Roman port by Nepos, the son of Marcellinus’s sister. Nepos fled from Orestes, who had made his son Augustulus emperor at Ravenna, and withdrew to Dalmatia. Augustulus succeeded him, but Odoacer, king of the Heruls, deprived him of the imperial dignity and obtained the empire. Thus that imperial eminence, which had begun with Octavian, perished at Rome in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 475, in the 522nd year of the empire, and in the 1214th year from the founding of the city.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 466, Hilary sat at Rome for 6 years, 3 months, and 10 days. Simplicius succeeded him and sat for 15 years, 1 month, and 4 days.

During Simplicius’s episcopate a report came from Greece from Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, declaring that Peter, bishop of Alexandria, had become an Eutychian heretic. Simplicius then condemned Peter of Alexandria because Acacius asserted innumerable crimes against him, while reserving a period for repentance.

Simplicius died and was buried in the church of blessed Peter on the sixth day before the Nones of March. The episcopate remained vacant for six days.

[FREDEG.] After Rome had been captured, the Gothic kingdom was divided in two. Those who remained in Italy surrendered themselves to imperial rule; the rest established the city of Tolosa in Aquitaine as their seat. They chose Adolphus as king, and he also took Placidia as his wife, as has been said.

[ISID.] After Adolphus was killed in the seventh year, Vallia succeeded him; then Theodoric succeeded Vallia, Thorismund succeeded Theodoric, Theoderic succeeded Thorismund, and Euric, his brother, succeeded Theoderic. Euric subjected Spain, Gaul, and all Burgundy to himself and died at Arles in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. Alaric succeeded him, against whom Clovis fought.

[FREDEG.] The Goths who possessed the land of Italy and had surrendered themselves to the rule of the emperor Leo were continually ravaged by Odoacer, king of the Heruls, and by neighboring peoples. Through ambassadors they therefore asked the emperor Leo to appoint Theoderic as their patrician, so that he might resist their adversaries.

Emperor Leo graciously agreed. With the advice of the senate, he sent Theoderic to Rome, where the Romans and Goths gloriously received him with the honor of the patriciate.

Theoderic was of Macedonian descent. The patrician Idacius and his wife Eugenia were childless, but they had in their service two purchased children, Theodorus and Lilia, Macedonians who had been brought from there when they were little children. They joined the two to each other in marriage.

Eugenia ordered the girl to report to her whatever she saw in a dream on the night when they were to be joined. The girl then saw a dream in which a tree sprang from her and was so tall that it pierced the clouds. When she had related this to her husband, he said to her: “When you stand in the presence of your mistress, tell her that you saw this night a horse and a mare of extraordinary beauty, followed by a small horse, all walking in the midst of your masters.”

When Eugenia heard this, she reported it to her husband. Thinking that a child would be born, they immediately ordered both of them to be free and enriched them with many possessions.

Lilia then bore a son named Theoderic. Because he was handsome, prudent, strong, and tall, Idacius and Eugenia adopted him as their son. After their deaths, Theoderic was ordered by the emperor Leo to serve as a soldier. He served for twelve years and fought battles with such strength and skill that he was loved by everyone.

Finally, the palace senators pursued him with such hateful jealousy that they sought a way for him to perish by the emperor’s command. A certain senator, Ptolemy, however, formed a friendship with him and preserved it until the day of his death.

The Romans and Goths therefore received Theoderic, and he fought many battles against Odoacer, who had obtained Rome, and against the Heruls.

[FREDEG.] One day, when battle had been joined, Theoderic entered Ravenna with the Goths in flight. There he found his mother Lilia. She seized him and reproached him, saying that he had nowhere to flee except to enter again the womb from which he had been born. Overwhelmed with shame, he went out again with a few men to meet Odoacer and the Heruls.

Finding them scattered, he defeated them with a few men. He pursued Odoacer, captured him, and killed him together with his wife and children. He destroyed the nation and kingdom of the Heruls.

[ISID.] After the Vandals had crossed over into Africa, the Sueves received Galicia by lot. Their king Erenric reigned for 32 years; after him Rechila reigned for 8 years. Rechila’s son Rechianus succeeded him, became a Catholic, and reigned for 8 years. After he was killed, Maldra, Frumarius, and Reccimund were appointed kings.

Since many Suevic kings remained in the Arian error, Theodemir finally received the kingdom and immediately restored the Sueves to the Catholic faith. Maro succeeded him and reigned for 14 years. Eboric succeeded Maro, but Audeca, having seized power as a tyrant, deprived Eboric of the kingdom and made him a monk.

Leovigild, king of the Goths, fought against Audeca, captured him, tonsured him, and made him a presbyter. Thus the Suevic kingdom was transferred to the Goths; it had lasted for 177 years. The kingdom of the Goths afterward lasted for 380 years.

Reccared succeeded Leovigild, king of Spain, who had succeeded Alaric. Reccared’s brother Hermenegild was crowned with martyrdom by his father. Reccared was secretly baptized and brought all the Goths, assembled at Toledo, back to the Catholic faith in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 596.

[ADO.] [Note: “During—years” in the margin.] During the time of Leo, Hilary of Arles and Claudian of Vienne were renowned. Piaminiola, the sister of Saint Hilary of Arles, was the wife of Saint Lupus of Troyes, whose disciple was Saint Pulchronius of Verdun. They were together for seven years.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] During the reign of King Odoacer, Felix, a Roman by birth and the son of Felix the presbyter, sat at Rome for 8 years, 11 months, and 18 days. He continued until the time of Theoderic.

During his pontificate a report again came from Greece that Peter of Alexandria had been recalled by Acacius of Constantinople. In a council Pope Felix condemned Acacius together with Peter.

Emperor Leo died in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 474, after completing 17 years in the empire. Another Leo succeeded him and died in the same year.

[ISID.] Zeno then became emperor and held the empire for 16 years. During his reign the body of the apostle Barnabas was discovered. From him a report came that Acacius should return as a penitent.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] Pope Felix then sent two bishops, Messenus and Vitalis, so that, if they found Acacius to be Peter’s accomplice, they might condemn him. Corrupted by money, they did not act according to the command of the apostolic see.

At the same time a synod was held. It found that both bishops had been corrupted by money, and they were expelled from communion. Felix was buried in the basilica of blessed Paul, and the episcopate remained vacant for five days.

After him Gelasius, an African by birth and the son of Valerius, sat for 4 years, 8 months, and 9 days. He loved the clergy and the poor and delivered the city from danger and famine. During his time the Manichaeans were discovered in the city, deported into exile, and their books burned.

He restored Messenus to communion after he had made satisfaction, and Messenus, having been cleared, was received again. Gelasius condemned Acacius and Peter forever unless they repented. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December. He composed treatises and hymns.

[BEDA.] After Zeno, Anastasius ruled, beginning in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 490, for 27 years. Because he persecuted Catholics and favored the heresy of Eutyches, he perished by lightning.

[ISID.] [Note: “Thrasamund—son” in the margin.] Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, closed the Catholic churches and sent 220 bishops to Sardinia. He reigned for 27 years and 4 months. Ilderic, the son of Honoric, succeeded him.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] Anastasius, a Roman by birth, sat at Rome for 1 year, 11 months, and 24 days. Many withdrew from communion with him because, without the counsel of the Catholic Church, he had entered into communion with a Thessalonian deacon named Photinus, who was in communion with Acacius.

When Anastasius wished secretly to recall Acacius, who had been condemned by his predecessors, he could not do so, because he died, struck down by divine judgment.

Symmachus, the fifty-third bishop after Peter, succeeded him. A Sardinian by birth and the son of Fortunatus, he sat for 15 years, 7 months, and 27 days. He lived during the time of Anastasius and Theoderic.

He established that on Sundays and the birthdays of the saints the *Gloria in excelsis* should be sung. Among his many works for the churches, he supplied the necessities every year to all the bishops throughout Africa and Sardinia who had been confined in exile.

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 509, Saint Benedict died. He lay at Monte Cassino for 15 years, and afterward his body was transferred to Gaul in the year 660. During the time of Anastasius, Antony was renowned.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] Symmachus and Laurence were ordained with the intention of both being appointed on the same day. Symmachus was confirmed, and, out of consideration for mercy, he ordained Laurence bishop in the city of Nuceria.

After four years, certain members of the clergy and senate, moved by zeal, accused Symmachus, and evils worse than the earlier ones arose. Some senators, acting as though they were giving wiser counsel, sent to King Theoderic asking him to appoint someone who could be ordained pope after both men had been deposed.

Against the sacred canons, Theoderic sent them Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum. Symmachus, however, gathered a universal synod of 125 bishops. First he cleared himself of the charge brought against him; then both he and all the bishops condemned Peter, sent by the king, as an invader of the apostolic see, and likewise condemned Laurence, who appeared to be intruding into the papacy with the support of the seditious.

Strengthened in the Lord, Symmachus remained pope until the day of his death.

Let those who place the favor of an earthly ruler before the will of God listen and understand that the sentence of this condemnation extends and reaches even to them—the sentence which, as we read, was issued by blessed Pope Symmachus and the other 125 bishops against Peter and Laurence.

[Note: “At least—place before” in the margin.] Let those who have invaded the apostolic see and inflicted prejudice upon the Roman Church, who place the favor of an earthly ruler before divine authority, learn from this striking example that they themselves are liable to condemnation. Let them not prefer to walk about with the impious in circles, or to defend the dizziness of their own head, which is plain for all to see, rather than simply confess their error and accept the teaching.

[Note: The following material is in the margin.] Zeno and Anastasius, Eutychianist emperors, are said to have been the first to subject the holy Catholic Church to themselves, confining Catholic bishops in exile and, setting apostolic tradition aside, appointing men agreeable to themselves in their sees.

Before their time, indeed, heretical emperors are said to have harassed Catholic bishops in many ways, but nowhere are they said to have meddled in the election or promotion of any pontiff. Under these same Eutychianist emperors, however, both at Constantinople and in the other cities, an innumerable multitude of the faithful—clergy and people—is said to have been entirely unwilling to receive their false bishops, because it was evident that, without their own election and in contempt of God and for the advancement of their error, the aforesaid rulers had promoted them.

As Anastasius, librarian of the holy Roman Church, relates in the chronicle of Theophanes and George, worshipers of God, which he himself translated from Greek into Latin:

[ANAST.] “In the twentieth year of the reign of Anastasius, after John of Niciu, the heretical bishop of Alexandria, had died, Dioscorus the younger was appointed bishop of Alexandria. When he had received the laying-on of hands, the crowds of country people withdrew, saying: ‘Unless he becomes bishop as the holy canons prescribe, he will not be received.’ For the rulers had enthroned him.

“Dioscorus then came to Saint Mark. When the clergy came, they clothed him again and consecrated him a second time. Thus he came to Saint John and completed the assembly.

“When Theodosius, son of Calliopius the prefect, and Acacius, the commander of the army, were there, the disturbed crowds began to abuse the prefect’s son because he praised the emperor Anastasius. Some of them leapt upon him, drove him from his seat, and killed him.

“Acacius, the commander of the army, killed as many as he was able to capture. When the emperor heard this, he became angry. Dioscorus, however, appeased him. When Dioscorus came to Constantinople to intercede with the emperor on behalf of the Alexandrians, he was publicly attacked with insults by the orthodox. For this reason, although he too had interceded on account of the homicide, he withdrew in haste.”

Behold by what first examples of their rulers these princes seek to promote their own pontiffs in the Church of God.

Following the examples of these heretics, certain Greek emperors, while imposing their own bishops upon the cities of their kingdom, spared the city of Rome this treatment. They decreed that the electoral decree received from the clergy and senate should be sent to them before the future pontiff was consecrated.

Although this is often said to have been sent, nowhere is it said that they changed or rejected the Romans’ election.

Later emperors, however, superior in religion, entirely rejected this practice because it was contrary to the Lord: the Church should not be left without a pontiff while the bearer of the decree went and returned. We can clearly recognize this in the commands of Emperor Constantine to Bishop Benedict, the clergy, and the Roman people.

Therefore, whoever observes that the other Greek emperors did not wish the decree to be sent to them should also observe that they never changed the election; and should further observe … .

[Note: Here certain words cannot be distinguished.]

After Anastasius, Justin the Elder assumed the empire in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 517; he reigned for 9 years.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] [Note: “During—Ysielnus” in the margin.] Hormisdas of Campania sat at Rome beginning in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 511. He sat for 8 years and 14 days; his father was Justus of Frusione. He organized the clergy and instructed the presbyters.

[BEDA.] After him came John of Tuscany, the son of Constantius, who sat for 2 years, 8 months, and 15 days. When he came to Constantinople, at the gate called the Golden Gate, he restored sight before everyone to a blind man who asked him for it.

[Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.] When John had returned and come to Ravenna, Theoderic, moved by jealousy because the Catholic and devout Justin had received him honorably, killed him and his companions through the suffering of imprisonment. In that same year he had killed the patricians Symmachus and Boethius; after this crime, he himself perished by a sudden death on the ninety-ninth day.

[BEDA.] The bishops return from the exile in which they had been held throughout Africa and Sardinia, after 74 years of heretical profanation.

[ADO.] Julian, bishop of the church of Vienne, was renowned.

[ISID.] Childeric, also called Ilderic, the son of Honoric and born from Eudocia, the captive daughter of Valentinian, obtained the kingdom of the Vandals after Thrasamund.

Bound by the oath that, for as long as he held the kingdom, he would not recall the bishops from exile, he recalled the Catholic priests whom Thrasamund had condemned before he received the kingdom. Gilimer, having seized power as a tyrant, deprived him of the kingdom. Gilimer was also called Childeric and obtained the kingdom.

[FREDEG.] Not long afterward Justin began a war against the Persians. When he had crossed Chalcedon, he died of illness, and Justinian was raised to the kingdom.

After Justinian had captured the Persian king, overwhelmed and bound, he honorably ordered him to sit in a chair and asked him for the cities and provinces of the empire. When the king said, “I will not give them,” Justinian answered in rustic speech, “Denras.” For this reason the city founded in that place received the name Denras.

After recovering many provinces and cities, Justinian allowed the Persian king to resume his kingdom and returned to Constantinople in great triumph.

Because he loved Belisarius with a unique affection, he appointed him patrician over those parts of Africa that had not been occupied by the Vandals. The senate, moved by jealousy, suggested to the emperor that Belisarius was plotting his own deposition so that he might himself be raised to the kingdom.

For this reason, bearing jealousy against Belisarius, Justinian ordered him to attack the Vandals, by whom many legions of soldiers had often been slaughtered.

Fearing the Vandals, Belisarius, encouraged by his Christian wife Antonina, vowed a vow to God that he would become a Christian if he could overcome the Vandals.

The Vandals pitched their camp along the seashore. Belisarius, on the other hand, prepared to advance by land, while Antonina prepared to proceed by sea. When the clash was already near, Antonina went out with her men and destroyed all the women and children of the Vandals, allowing none of those creatures to remain alive.

When Childemer heard this, he returned to the camp. Belisarius and Antonina destroyed the battle formation, and, surrounded on land and sea, Childemer and all his men were slaughtered.

Fleeing with only twelve Vandals, Childemer took refuge in a secure fortress. There, hemmed in, he asked Belisarius not to present him bound to the emperor. When Belisarius promised that he would bind him neither with iron, nor wood, nor a strap, nor bronze, Childemer surrendered himself.

Belisarius bound him with a silver chain, killed his companions, and presented Childemer to Justinian. Justinian ordered him to live in his palace, but subjected him to spitting and grievous insults.

Childemer appealed to the emperor, saying: “The inhabitants of your palace oppress me with spitting and insults. If you ordered twelve of them and me alone, with the horse I previously possessed, to come armed before your majesty and fight, you would learn which of us possessed strength and which cowardice.”

When Justinian ordered twelve soldiers to fight him, Childemer attacked them, pretending to flee, and killed them all one by one.

[ISID.] Afterward, by order of the emperor, he was made a eunuch and appointed patrician in the neighboring provinces against the Persians. Thus the kingdom of the Vandals ended in the ninety-seventh year after their entry into Spain, and it had lasted for 113 years.

[FRED.] The senate again made Belisarius hateful to Justinian. For this reason he was removed from the honor of the patriciate. Belisarius again attempted to raise a certain Florian to the empire and depose Justinian.

When Florian sent to Belisarius asking him to help him, Belisarius pretended to honor Florian, surrounded him with his own servants, struck Florian with a sword, and killed all his enemies who were with him. Then, taking the crown from Florian’s head, he placed it on Justinian’s head and restored his kisses to him by the hand.

[FRED.]

A.D. 525. Justinian, the emperor and grandson of Justin the Elder, reigned for 37 years. After Justinian’s death, Justin sought the empire at Constantinople in the year 563; he was an unjust and greedy man.

[ADO.] [Note: “During—flourished” in the margin.] During the time of Justin, Pantagathus was bishop of Vienne for five years; Ysielnus succeeded him. During the reign of the emperor Justinian, Domninus flourished as bishop of Vienne.

[FREDEG.] Theoderic, king of the Goths, whom we mentioned above, had refused during the reign of the emperor Leo to submit to imperial rule. He reigned with great success for thirty years.

All the years during which he ruled in Italy amounted to 32 years. His kingdom extended from the borders of Pannonia to the river Rhône, and from the Tyrrhenian Sea to the Pennine Alps and the river Isère.

In the fourteenth year of his reign he built the basilica of Saint Julian at Brioude, adorned with marvelous columns. He had all the cities he ruled restored and fortified with astonishing workmanship and great skill. He ordered a most splendid palace to be built at Pavia, which is called Ticinum, and also at Ravenna and Verona.

His daughter was the wife of Sigismund, king of the Burgundians. [Note: “After—empire” in the margin.] After him his daughter’s son Athalaric received the kingdom, and after Athalaric came Theodahad.

[JORD.] After Theodahad was deposed, Vitiges was made king. He was defeated and overcome by Justinian through Belisarius, brought to Constantinople, and made a patrician. Thus, after 2,300 years, the kingdom of the Goths passed to the Roman Empire.

Amator [Note: [Col. 0095] Everything that follows up to the end of the catalogue of the bishops of Lyons is on a sewn-in leaf.] the bishop, to Pope Silverius (Mansi IX, 7): [Col. 0095B] “From certain persons, most beloved Father, we have heard that you were unjustly expelled from the See of Saint Peter and condemned to exile. Since we felt this very grievously, we sent you thirty pounds of silver for the support of you and your people.”

Pope Silverius to Bishop Amator: “The entire patrician party was hostile to me because I would not restore Anthemius, formerly patriarch of Constantinople, whom my predecessor Agapitus had deprived of office on account of his merits. Moreover, under pressure from the command, false witnesses came forward, alleging against me crimes in which I had never shared. But while many persisted in that accusation, our patrician Wilisarius became afraid and ordered me to come peacefully to him in the prince’s palace for certain ecclesiastical arrangements. At the first and second curtains he detained all the clergy and people who were coming with me [Col. 0095C] and permitted no one to enter except me alone and our Vigilius. But after I had been detained by force and brought before the aforesaid patrician, they sent me into exile, where I am supported by the bread of affliction and the water of distress.

“For this reason I dismissed two of my attendants, and I do not relinquish my office. Rather, together with the bishops whom I was able to assemble, I anathematized those who had acted so against me, and together with them, by the synodal authority of the apostolic see, I decreed that no one should ever be deceived as I was deceived; and if anyone should thereafter deceive any bishop in this way, let him be anathematized—*anathema maranatha*—in the sight of God and the holy angels.”

Silverius to Vigilius: “Because, against the canonical laws, in the time of Pope Boniface and while he was still alive, you attempted to have his successor designated—unless the justice of the most exalted Senate had opposed you—then, by your pastoral foresight, your already execrable vices ought to have been cut away. But because a small wound in you was neglected, an incurable apostasy grew. Unless it is cut deeper with the sword, it will not be able to feel the medicine of poultices.

“For, conceiving in the audacity of the most wicked spirit the frenzy of ambition, you strive to heap insult upon that apostolic physician to whom the power of binding and loosing souls has been entrusted; you strive once more to introduce a new crime of error; and, after giving money and driving me away—whom, with the Lord’s favor, I have presided over that see for three full [Col. 0096A] periods—you strive in my lifetime to seize it, after the manner of Simon, whose disciple you show yourself to be.

“Therefore, together with those who will be with you, accept the sentence of full condemnation; recognize that your name and the office of your priestly ministry have been taken away, condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the apostolic authority of anathema. For thus the faith of the holy Fathers ought to be preserved in the Catholic Church: whoever assumes through wicked presumption what he did not receive must lose what he possessed.”

(H. Misc.) In the third year of his reign Justinian promulgated that no one except Catholics should serve in the army, granting heretics a period of respite unless they turned themselves toward conversion. Pope Agapitus approached him to make certain requests; but when he perceived that Justinian had become an Eutychian, he rebuked him, and when Justinian threatened him harshly, the pope said: “I desired to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor, but I found a Diocletian.” But when Justinian saw his unwavering and unflattering steadfastness, he returned to the Catholic faith together with many others.

He also publicly deprived Anthemius, the bishop of the royal city and defender of the aforesaid heresy, of communion; and not long afterward he died in that same city. Silverius succeeded him. Belisarius afterward captured Carthage, after the Vandals had held it for ninety-five years, and destroyed the entire Vandal kingdom and stock.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) When Silverius was therefore asked to restore Anthemius, he refused. For this reason he was seized by Belisarius, who was unwilling to do so, at the command of the empress Theodora, and died in exile on the island of Ponza.

## Names of the Bishops of Lyons from the Beginning

[Col. 0096C] Photinus, martyr. Irenaeus, martyr. Zacharias. Helius. Faustinus. Verus. Julius. Ptolemy. Vocius. Maximus. Tretradius. Verissimus; he was present at the Council of Sardica, the fourth. Saint Justus. Saint Alpinus. Martinus. Saint Antiochus. Elpidius. Senator. Saint Eucherius. Salonius. Saint Veranus. Saint Patiens. Saint Lupicinus, at the time of the Vandal persecution. Rusticius. Stephanus. Viventius. Saint Lupus, in the time of Sigismund and Clovis. Lyconcius. Saint Sacerdos, in the time of Childebert. Saint Nicetius, in the time of that same Childebert. Saint Priscus; he was the author of the twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth synods. Saint Aetherius; blessed Pope Gregory wrote to him. Secundinus. Arigius. Tetricus. Gandericus. Viventius. Saint Aonemundus, [Col. 0096D] martyr. Saint Genesius. Saint Lamdebertus; in his time Saint Bonitius died and was buried at Lyons. At the royal palace of Clichy, he consecrated Saint Ansbert of Rouen as bishop. Saint Gudinus. Fulcoaldus [Note: [Col. 0095] “fulc.” deleted.]. This is Fulcoaldus the bishop, who returned the body of Saint Bonitius [Note: [Col. 0095] the word is deleted.] to the people of Auvergne. Madalbertus. Ado. Eldoynus. Leitfradus, in the time of Charlemagne; he restored the church of Lyons after the destruction by the Vandals. Agobardus, distinguished for his learning, in the time of Louis the Pious. [Col. 0097A] Amolo, in whose time—as he himself testifies, together with Egilmarus of Vienne, Bartholomew of Narbonne, Stephen of Belgica, Alteus of Autun, and Odolmannus of Mâcon, in a letter sent to Rodulfus, archbishop of Bourges, and to all the bishops of Aquitaine, Novempopulania, and Narbonensis Prima—the Church of Lyons, having possessed the primacy of the churches in Gaul for nearly three hundred years from the times of the apostles, held the place of the Roman pontiffs by reason of its holiness [Note: [Col. 0097] *optinet* seems to be the reading.]. Remigius, in the time of Charles the Bald. Saint Aurelianus, legate of the Roman See; after him came Agrinius of Langres, who is not included in the number. Aluvala. Bernardus. Austerius. Remigius. Anschericus. Wido. Amblardus. Old Burchard. Young Burchard. Saint Odelricus. [Col. 0097B] Halinardus. Saint Gebuinus. Hugo [Note: [Col. 0097] The following are added by other hands or in other ink: Parvus Josorrandus. Humbaldus, abbot of Vézelay. Rainaldus. Falco. Petrus. Amedeus died on the journey to Jerusalem [*itere* corrected to *itinere*.]. Hunbertus, who is still living; see above, p. 282.].

[FREDEG.] The people of the Lombards, before they were called by this name, came out of Scatanavia, which lies beyond the Danube and the Ocean, and crossed the Danube. When they were questioned by the Huns about what people had dared to violate their borders and were attempting to enter into war with them, they ordered their women to bind the hair of their heads down to their cheeks and chins, so that they might resemble the appearance of men and terrify the enemy by their very multitude, since the women’s hair appeared extremely long, like beards. And they all cried out: “This is the people of the Lombards.” Thus they entered the battle, defeated the Huns, and seized part of Pannonia.

The patrician Narses, being a eunuch, [Col. 0097C] received from Sophia, the wife of the emperor Justin, a woman’s garment made of gold, so that he might spin and deal with wool-work rather than govern the people. Enraged, he replied: “I shall spin a thread which Justin and his wife will not be able to bring to a head.” [PAUL THE DEACON.] He [Note: [Col. 0097] “He … Campania” in the margin.] killed Totila, king of the Goths; but when accused through the Romans’ envy, he withdrew to Naples in Campania.

[FREDEG.] Inviting the Lombards from Pannonia into Italy, he introduced them with their king Alboin, who took Glodesinda, daughter of King Chlothar, [son] of Clovis the Great, as his wife. When she [Note: [Col. 0097] “When she … devastated” in the margin.] died, he took another wife, whose mother he had killed; and by her he himself perished by poison. As has been said, he invaded Italy and besieged and devastated Rome [lacuna].

The Lombards therefore raised over themselves a king named Cleph [Note: [Col. 0097] The letters “e. r. s. s. C. n.” are written above the line.] and, attacking Gaul, killed the patrician Amatus [Col. 0097D] and inflicted many massacres. In his place Mummolus assumed the office of patrician.

[PAUL THE DEACON.] In those days, when Justin had died at Constantinople from the madness that had overtaken him, in the seventeenth year of his reign, Tiberius—who had ruled the kingdom together with Justin’s wife Sophia—seized the empire and held it for six years, ten months, and eight days. He was also exceedingly generous in almsgiving.

Sophia, plotting against Tiberius, wished to raise Justinian, the grandson of Justin, to the throne. [Col. 0098A] When Tiberius perceived this, he stripped her of her treasures, separated the children from her, and ordered her to be confined in custody. Later, after rebuking Justinian, he loved him with great affection.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) After Pope John, whom King Theodoric killed by the affliction of imprisonment, Felix, a Samnite by nationality and son of Castorius, occupied the see for four years, two months, and thirteen days. After him Boniface the Roman, son of Praejectus of the Caelian Hill, occupied it for two years, four months, and six days. John [Note: [Col. 0097] “John … five” in the margin.], also called Martin, succeeded Boniface and held the see for two years, four months, and six days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June; the episcopate was vacant for five days; and Agapitus the Roman succeeded him, son of the presbyter Gordianus, for eleven months and nineteen days.

Between Agapitus and Silverius: twenty-nine days. Silverius of Campania, son of Hormisdas, was bishop of Rome for one year, five months, and eleven days. In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 538, indiction 1, Vigilius the Roman, son of John the consul, occupied the see for eighteen years, six months, and twenty-six days. In the fourteenth year of Pope Vigilius’s episcopate, indiction 14, in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 552 [Note: [Col. 0097] “The year … died” in the margin.], the fifth synod was held at Constantinople.

In the twenty-seventh year of Justinian, grandson of the elder Justin, Vigilius was thrust into exile by Justinian. Recalled while returning to Rome, he died at Syracuse in Sicily from the pain of stones.

Pelagius the Roman, son of John the vicarius, occupied the see for eleven years, ten months, and eighteen days. He was ordained by two bishops and one presbyter. Between Pelagius and John: twenty-six days. John the Roman, son of Anastasius, held the see for twelve years, ten months, and twenty-six days. He restored the cemeteries of the martyrs and established offerings and lights for Sundays. Benedict the Roman, son of Boniface, occupied the see for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days. Between him and Pelagius: five days.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 582, the emperor Maurice succeeded Tiberius and reigned for sixteen years. After Benedict, Pelagius the Roman, son of Unigildus, occupied the see at Rome for ten years, two months, and ten days. During his rule there were rains such that it seemed that the Flood had returned. There was a calamity such as no one remembered ever having existed in the world; during it Pope Pelagius died, and Gregory the Teacher, elected by the clergy and people, assumed the pontificate of the Roman Church, in the tenth year of the emperor Maurice, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 592, indiction 10, epact 21, concurrent 7. A Roman by birth and son of Gordianus, he occupied the see for thirteen years, six months, and ten days.

He arranged that Mass should be sung over the body of blessed Peter the Apostle. In the fourth year of his pontificate, indiction 13, a synod of twenty-four bishops was assembled; in the church of blessed Peter the Apostle he dealt with matters necessary for the Church. By sending Augustine, Mellitus, John, and many other monks to Britain, he converted the English to Christ.

[ADO.] In the time of Leovigild, Renatus, bishop of Vienne, flourished; he died in the same year in which Justin became insane [Note: [Col. 0097] “In the time … died” in the margin.].

[BEDA.] Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Goths, was deprived by his Arian father of the insignia of the kingdom on account of his confession of the Catholic faith and was thrown into prison. On the very night of the Lord’s Resurrection he was struck on the head with an axe and entered the heavenly kingdom as king and martyr. His brother Reccared, king of the Goths, was first baptized secretly; afterward, in the fifth year of Gregory’s pontificate, he ordered all the Goths who were then Arians to assemble at Toledo and to present to him all the books of the Arian sect. He had them burned and ordered all the Goths to be baptized.

[ADO.] Philip also, bishop of Vienne, flourished (fol. 36). He was succeeded by Evantius, a holy man, who, together with Saint Priscus of Lyons, Artemius, Senonicus, Remigius of Bourges, and other holy bishops, as well as Siagrius of Autun, confirmed twenty chapters. [Col. 0099B] He was succeeded by Verus, whose deacon was Saint Desiderius of Autun; Verus was succeeded by Domnolus, energetic in redeeming captives; and Domnolus was succeeded by Aetherius in the time of the emperor Heraclius.

[FREDEG.] In that year, the wife of Arnulf, emperor of the Persians, leaving her husband with four boys and as many girls, came to Constantinople to Saint John the bishop. She said that she was one of the common people and was baptized. The wife of the emperor Maurice received her from the holy font. Since she was repeatedly sought through envoys, who did not know that she was his wife, the empress, seeing that she was extremely beautiful and suspecting that she might be the woman being sought, showed her to the envoys. When they saw and recognized her, they could hear no answer from her unless they were first baptized. [Col. 0099C] They willingly accepted the grace of baptism. She replied to them that she would not return to her husband unless he first received the grace of baptism.

When this was reported to the emperor of the Persians, he sent an embassy to the emperor Maurice, asking that Saint John come to Antioch, from whom he might receive the baptism of salvation. Maurice ordered this to be done with an immense display. There the emperor of the Persians was baptized together with sixty thousand men and was received from the font by Saint Gregory of Antioch. He then asked the emperor Maurice for bishops with a sufficient clergy; Maurice granted this, and thus the whole of Persia believed in Christ the Lord with the greatest speed.

At the same time, in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 598, the seamless tunic of the Lord was found in the city of Zaphat. After a three-day fast, Gregory of Antioch, Thomas of Jerusalem, and John of Constantinople, together with many other bishops, lifted it up with its marble chest. The chest had become so light that it seemed to be made of wood. It was carried on foot with the greatest devotion to Jerusalem and placed in triumph at the place where the Lord’s cross is worshiped.

In the time of the emperor Maurice, while Pope Gregory was administering the pontificate of the Roman Church, the construction of the monastery of Flavigny in the aforesaid fortress was undertaken for Lord Widradus [Col. 0100A] and Magoaldus was ordained abbot, in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 601, indiction 5 (fol. 37). In the first year of King Theodoric, which was from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 606, and in the third year of the emperor Phocas, the same Lord Theodoric confirmed with his seal the testament of Lord Widradus concerning the fortress or monastery of Flavigny, which had been made, and ratified it at Semur, in the second year after the passing of Saint Gregory, that is, in the first year of the papacy of Savinianus, while Secundinus was presiding over the church of Lyons as archbishop.

In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 602 [Note: [Col. 0099] Thus corrected from letters with some erasures.], Phocas, duke and patrician, returning victorious from the Persians, killed the emperor Maurice and assumed the empire. He reigned for eight years [Note: [Col. 0099] Added above the line in somewhat darker ink.]. In that year Aetherius, archbishop of Lyons, died; Secundinus was appointed in his place. [Col. 0100B] In the second year of Phocas, indiction 8, epact 26, concurrent 4, from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 605 [Note: [Col. 0099] These last words were added above the line in darker ink.], blessed Gregory departed to the Lord, while Theodoric and Theodebert, brothers, were reigning in Francia.

After twenty-two days, Savinianus of Tuscany, son of Bonus of the city of Blera, succeeded him in the episcopate of the Roman Church. He occupied the see for one year, five months, and eight days (Gesta pontificum Romanorum). He added lights in the church of blessed Peter. After him Boniface III, the Roman, son of John [Note: [Col. 0099] Some material has been erased here.], occupied the see for eight months and twenty-two days. He asked the emperor to establish that the Roman Church was the head of all the churches, since Constantinople was writing that it was first.

Boniface IV, from the city of Valeria, of the Marsian nation, son of John the physician, occupied the see for six years, eight months, and thirteen days. It is related of him in ecclesiastical history that he obtained from Phocas the gift to the Church [Col. 0100C] of Christ’s temple at Rome, which was called the Pantheon [Note: [Col. 0099] A lacuna of approximately seven words in an erasure.], whose papacy [Note: [Col. 0099] One word appears to have been erased.] … in the year Phocas died.

[FREDEG.] Since Heraclius was patrician of all the provinces of Africa, while Phocas was ruling the empire most wickedly and, in a fit of madness, was throwing treasures into the sea, saying that he was giving gifts to Neptune, the senators, seeing that he wished to destroy the empire through folly, seized Phocas by the hands and feet through Heraclius’s faction, cut off his limbs, tied a stone around his neck, and threw him into the sea. With the consent of the Senate, Heraclius was raised to the kingship in the year 607 [Note: [Col. 0099] The numerals are written above the line.].

[BEDA.] Since many provinces of the empire had been devastated by Persian attacks in the times of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, in Heraclius’s time the Persians, after devastating the city of Chalcedon, also endeavored to destroy Constantinople, the seat of the empire. They invaded many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself, destroying churches and profaning holy things; among their other spoils they also carried away the standard of the holy cross [Note: [Col. 0099] “many … carry away” in the margin.].

[FREDEG.] Heraclius drew up his army against them, and the two commanders of the armies engaged in single combat while everyone on both sides awaited the outcome. Heraclius was victorious, cut off the Persian’s head, and forced the entire Persian army to return to its own settlements. After this, having embarked on ships, he entered Persia; after devastating Persia for approximately three years, he subjected it to his rule and brought back the wood of the Lord’s cross. Later he again defeated the Persians when they rebelled and subjected them to himself.

Although he was extremely handsome in appearance, very strong, an outstanding warrior, and also highly educated in letters, when he saw in the signs of the stars that the empire would be devastated by circumcised peoples, he sent messengers to Dagobert, king of the Franks, asking him to order all the Jews in his kingdom to be baptized. Heraclius himself also decreed that this should be done throughout all the provinces of his empire.

In the fifth year of the reign of Heraclius [Note: [Col. 0101] “The year … the city was” in the margin.], Muhammad was born. When he was still an infant and his father and mother had died, he attached himself to a widow who also nurtured him. When he had grown up, he began to attend the schools and lecture halls of Christians, and he reported at home to the people of his own nation what he had heard there. They marveled at the wisdom that was already in him when they heard from him the things he had heard.

One day, as he was returning from the lecture hall, he met the devil, who had a golden mouth and said that he was the archangel Gabriel, sent by God to him so that he might preach to his people what he had heard and knew. Then Muhammad began to preach that they should abandon idols made by hand and worship the Creator who made all things. When many followed him and regarded him as a prophet, he gathered those who were with him, took up arms, and, as king and prophet, subjected to himself as many as he could. He reigned in Damascus, and the city of Babylon was the capital of his kingdom.

[FREDEG.] The people of the Hagarenes, who are also called Saracens, being circumcised, came out from the side of Mount Caucasus above the Caspian Sea. When they had gathered into an immense multitude, they eventually took up arms and attacked the provinces of the emperor Heraclius to devastate them. Heraclius sent an army against them. But the Saracen soldiers defeated the soldiers and slaughtered them heavily with the sword, so that they killed 150,000 soldiers.

They offered their spoils to Heraclius, but he refused to accept them, wishing to take vengeance on the Saracens. He sent an embassy and ordered the gates that Alexander of Macedon had commanded to be made of bronze and fastened across the Caspian Sea—because of the invasions of savage peoples who lived beyond the heights of the Caucasus—to be opened. From there he sent one hundred thousand warriors, hired with gold, into battle against the Saracens.

When the two armies had pitched their camps not far from one another, intending to fight at dawn, that same night, by God’s power, Heraclius’s army was struck down: fifty thousand of them died in their beds. After this, the soldiers were terrified and returned to their own country. The Saracens, as they had begun, devastated the provinces.

When they had already drawn near to Jerusalem, Heraclius, seeing that he could not resist them, was seized by overwhelming grief and bitterness. Finally, unhappy man, he followed the heresy of the Eutychians and abandoned the worship of Christ. He had as his wife the daughter of his sister; and after the twenty-seventh year of his reign he ended his life cruelly.

Heraclonas [Note: [Col. 0101] “Heraclonas … indiction 7” is written in the margin in two lines.] reigned with his mother Martina for two years. He was succeeded by Constantine, son of Heraclius, for six months, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 634, while Honorius was pope, indiction 7. (Ibid.) Constantine’s son, who was also called Constans, succeeded to the throne while still of tender age and under counsel. In his time the state was excessively devastated by the Saracens.

This devastation lasted for forty-seven years, until the time of the Constantine mentioned above. Then Jerusalem was captured and the other cities were overthrown; Upper and Lower Egypt were invaded; Alexandria was captured and plundered; all Africa was devastated; Asia and Europe were shaken; and all kingdoms bordering the sea were overrun. Only Constantinople, together with the province of Thrace, a few islands, and the Roman province, remained under the rule of the empire.

[Fragment:] “. . rius, an Apollinarist pope, . . us est” [Note: [Col. 0101] Perhaps: “Pope Honorius began the basilica of Saint Apollinaris”?].

In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 651, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, the ordination of Lord Widradus as abbot took place, after Magoaldus the abbot had governed the foundation at Flavigny for forty-eight years [Note: [Col. 0101] These words are written in the margin.].

In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 665, under Pope Vitalianus, Benedict came to Gaul. At Tequemio, Saint Amandus, bishop of Tongeren, died; Saint Remaclus succeeded him in the twenty-second year of the reign of Constantine, and Theodardus succeeded him, while Saint Lambert succeeded Theodardus.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) Twenty-five days after Pope Boniface, Deusdedit the Roman, son of Stephen the subdeacon, succeeded him and occupied the see for three years and twenty-three days. After him, when five months and twenty-six days had elapsed, Boniface V, a Campanian, son of John, occupied the see for five years. He decreed that no one should be dragged from a church.

After thirteen days, Honorius of Campania, son of Petronius the consul, succeeded him and occupied the see for twelve years, eleven months, and eighteen days. On June 14 he rebuked by letter the error that had arisen among the Scots concerning the observance of Easter. John, a Dalmatian by nationality, son of Venantius, succeeded him and occupied the see for one year, eight months, and eighteen days. He sent large sums of money through Istria and Dalmatia for the redemption of captives.

[BEDA.] While he was still only elected, he rebuked the Scots concerning Easter and the Pelagian heresy. Theodore the Greek, son of Theodore, bishop of the city of Jerusalem, succeeded him after five months and thirteen days and occupied the see for six years, five months, and eighteen days.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) He condemned Pyrrhus, bishop of the royal city, who, together with Cyrus of Alexandria and his predecessor Sergius, had revived the heresy of the Acephali [Col. 0102D]. [BEDA.] For he came with a pretended repentance, as later became clear, and offered the same pope a booklet of repentance; but after returning home he went back to his vomit. Therefore, in the presence of the clergy and the Roman people, he was bound by the bond of anathema, as we have said.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) After Theodore, Martinus of Todi in Tuscia occupied the see for six years, five months, and twenty-six days.

[BEDA.] Constantine, deceived by Paul, bishop of the royal city, just as his great-grandfather Heraclius had been deceived by Sergius, composed a book against the Catholic faith. Therefore Pope Martinus, having assembled a synod of 110 bishops at Rome, condemned under anathema the aforesaid heretics Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul.

For this reason the emperor sent the exarch Theodore, who removed Martinus from the church of Constantiniana and brought him to Constantinople. Later he was confined at Cherson, where he ended his life, continuing to shine in that place down to the present through many signs of virtue.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 640, indiction [lacuna], Pope Martinus [lacuna] his papacy [lacuna]. This synod was held in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 650, indiction 8, in the ninth year of the reign of Constantine, who afterward reigned for nineteen years and died in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 669, indiction 12.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) Eugenius the Roman, son of Rufinianus, occupied the see for two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. After one month and twenty-eight days, Vitalianus of Signia in the province of Campania, son of Anastasius, succeeded him and occupied the see for fourteen years and six months.

He preserved the ecclesiastical rule and discipline in every respect, as was customary. Shortly after his ordination, Constantine sent blessed Peter Gospels of gold, ornamented with white gems and of marvelous size. Vitalianus sent many preachers of the divine word to Britain, and they enriched the churches of the English with abundant fruit of the divine word.

The emperor Constantine became tributary to the Saracens and for three years and more paid one thousand gold solidi each day into the Saracen treasuries (ibid.). At last, having recovered his strength, he refused the tribute; after inflicting many extraordinary devastations upon the provinces, he was killed and perished in a bath. He had reigned for twenty-eight years.

Not long afterward Vitalianus sought the heavenly kingdoms. After three months and thirteen days Adeodatus the Roman, formerly a monk, son of Jobianus, succeeded him and occupied the see for four years, two months, and five days. After four months and fifteen days Donus the Roman, son of Mauritius, occupied the see for one year, five months, and ten days. After two months and fifteen days Agatho the Sicilian succeeded him, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 666, indiction 5, and occupied the see for two years, six months, and four days.

[BEDA.] In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 670, indiction 13, epact [lacuna], concurrent [lacuna], Constantine, son of the elder Constantine, began to reign and reigned for seventeen years. At Constantine’s request Pope Agatho sent his legates to the royal city to bring about the union of the holy churches of God. Constantine received them most graciously and ordered them to conduct peaceful discussions concerning the true faith.

When 150 bishops were seated, with George of Constantinople presiding and Macarius of Antioch, a debate took place. George was corrected, and Macarius with his followers was condemned. Such grace accompanied the Catholic legates of peace that John, bishop of Porto, one of them, celebrated a public Mass in the church of Hagia Sophia before the emperor and patriarch on the eighth Sunday after Easter.

This was the sixth universal synod, held at Constantinople and written in Greek, in the time of Pope Agatho, in the third year of his pontificate [Note: [Col. 0103] The material expressed here in spaced-out letters was supplied later by the author above the line; it is not found in Bede.], while the emperor Constantine was carrying out his office and sitting inside his palace, in the fourteenth year of his reign, from the Lord’s Incarnation 668, indiction 11, with the legates of the Apostolic See and 150 bishops likewise seated.

The first synod was held at Nicaea, with 318 Fathers, against Arius, in the time of Pope Sylvester of Rome, Macarius of Jerusalem, and Alexander of Alexandria, under the emperor Constantine.

The second was held at Constantinople, with 150 Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, in the time of Pope Damasus, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Nectarius of Constantinople, under the elder Theodosius and the emperor Gratian.

The third was held at Ephesus, with 200 Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the royal city, who asserted two persons in Christ, under the younger Theodosius and Pope Celestine, in the time of Juvenal of Jerusalem and Cyril of Alexandria.

The fourth was held at Chalcedon, with 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo and the emperor Marcian, in the time of Juvenal of Jerusalem and the bishop of Constantinople, against Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who proclaimed that the Word of God and the flesh have one nature.

The fifth was held at Constantinople against Theodore and all the heretics, in the time of Pope Vigilius, under the emperor Justinian.

This is the sixth, of which we have spoken.

[ADO.] At that time Sindulfus of Vienne flourished. He was succeeded by Hecdicus, a man of great religious devotion, who remained in office until the final period of Justinian and died under him. Cadoldus succeeded him and endured until the time of King Theodoric. Dodolenus succeeded Cadoldus, and Bobolinus succeeded Dodolenus in the time of John, who succeeded Pope Sergius. George, a bishop of great virtue, succeeded Bobolinus [Col. 0104C].

After Agatho, Leo II the Sicilian, son of Paul, assumed the Roman See. One year, six months, and six days intervened between Agatho and his ordination; he occupied the see for seven months and seventeen days. After eleven months and twenty-two days Benedict II, the younger, a Roman by nationality, succeeded him and occupied the see for ten months and twelve days.

(Gesta pontificum Romanorum.) He received the commands of the most merciful emperor Constantine addressed to the Roman clergy and people: whoever was elected to the Roman pontificate was to be consecrated immediately, and the emperor’s further approval and command were no longer to be awaited.

After him, following an interval of two months and fifteen days, John V, a Syrian from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, occupied the see for one year. After two months and eighteen days Chonon, son of [Col. 0104D] Tracesius and raised in Sicily, succeeded him and occupied the see for eleven months.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 688, in the third year of the Roman empire, indiction 1, [lacuna], Sergius assumed the pontificate of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0103] “Incarnation … Sergius” in the margin.].

After him Sergius, a Syrian born in the region of Antioch, son of Tiberius of Palermo in Sicily, occupied the see for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-three days. He established that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung by the clergy and people, and the litanies at the Lord’s *Hypapante*.

By the Lord’s revelation he found in the sacristy of blessed Peter a silver chest, and in it a golden cross ornamented with gems. Beneath four petals a portion of the saving wood was concealed. From that time onward, on the day of its Exaltation, it has been venerated and kissed by all the people in the basilica of the Savior.

[BEDA; CHRONICLE OF SAINT BENIGNUS.] He ordained Saint Willibrord, also called Clement, bishop for the people of the Frisians, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 696. Pippin, mayor of the palace, sent him there with companions after he had conquered Frisia and driven out its duke Radbod.

In the third year of Justinian, Pippin began to reign and retained the office of mayor of the palace for twenty years under Justinian, Leo and Tiberius, then again Justinian, Theodosius, and Leo. He died in the sixth year of Leo’s reign; Charles Martel succeeded him and died in the seventh year of Constantine.

[BEDA.] In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 678, indiction 2, epact none, concurrent 5, Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine, began to reign and reigned for ten years. He ordered Pope Sergius to be seized from the church and transported to Constantinople, because Sergius would neither favor nor subscribe to the emperor’s errant synod, which he had held in the royal city.
