But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions anticipated the king’s orders and expelled his envoys from the city of Rome. Justinian, deprived of his kingdom on account of his faithlessness, withdrew into exile in Pontus. After him Leo ruled for three years. Tiberius fought against him, expelled him from the kingdom, and kept him in custody in that same city during the time in which he himself reigned.

After Sergius, John VI, a Greek by nationality, occupied the Roman Church for three years, two months, and [lacuna] days, after an interval of one month and thirteen days (Gesta pontificum Romanorum). During his time, when Gisulf, duke of the Lombards, was devastating Campania with fire, sword, and captivity, and there was no one to resist him, the pope himself sent priests and clerics to him with many gifts, redeemed all the captives, and made the enemy return home.

[BEDA.] John VII, a Greek by nationality, son of Platon, succeeded him and occupied the see for two years, seven months, and twenty-seven days. Constantine the Syrian, son of John, occupied the see for seven years and fifteen days (Gesta pontificum Romanorum).

[PAUL THE DEACON, VI. 46.] At that time the people of the Saracens crossed over from Africa at a place called Septem, invaded Spain, and, ten years later, entered Aquitaine with their wives and children. When Charles, together with Eudes, prince of Aquitaine, attacked them, 370,000 were killed by the Franks, while only 1,500 of the Franks fell. Eudes likewise attacked them and killed many in the same manner, and the fleeing Saracens, with an immense army, besieged Constantinople for three years.

[BEDA.] Justinian, whom we previously said had been deprived of his kingdom, recovered it with the aid of Terbel, king of the Bulgars, held it for six years, and killed the patricians who had expelled him, as well as Leo, who had usurped his place, and Tiberius, Leo’s successor, who had kept him in custody after expelling him from the kingdom.

He sent the patriarch to Rome with his eyes torn out and gave the bishopric to Cyrus, who had been an abbot in Pontus and had supported him while he was in exile. He ordered Pope Constantine to come to him and received him honorably. On Sunday he ordered the pope to celebrate Mass for him and received communion from his hand; then, prostrated on the ground, he asked him to intercede for his sins and renewed all the privileges of the Church.

When he sent an army into Pontus to arrest Philippicus, whom he had confined there, the army turned around, made Philippicus emperor, and, returning with him to Constantinople, fought against Justinian. After Justinian was defeated and killed, Philippicus assumed the kingdom and held it for one year and six months.

[ADO.] At that time Deodatus, bishop of Vienne, flourished, a man of great frugality. Blidranus succeeded him, and he was succeeded by Coldus, a bishop who also increased the resources of the church of Vienne; for he was related to the kings of the Franks. Bobolinus succeeded him, and Austrobertus, an energetic and noble man, succeeded Bobolinus.

(Gesta p. R.) He sent Pope Constantine a letter containing erroneous doctrine, which the pope rejected by judgment of the Apostolic See. The Roman people decreed that no one should accept the name, documents, or image on a coin of a heretical emperor. Consequently, neither was his likeness brought into a church nor was his name recited during the solemnities of Mass. During his reign Anastasius ruled for three years; he captured Philippicus, deprived him of his eyes, but did not kill him.

[BEDA.] He sent Pope Constantine a letter in which he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy Sixth Synod. After Constantine, Gregory II, a Roman, son of Marcellus, took the see from Peter 92, in the sixteenth year, ninth month, and twelfth day.

(Gesta p. R.) He decreed that a fast should be held on the fifth day of the week during Lent, which had not previously been done, and established the celebrations of Mass.

[BEDA.] At his urging, Liutprand, king of the Lombards, confirmed for a second time the donation of the patrimony of the Alps, which King Hereberecht had made and which Liutprand had reclaimed. At that time Echbert, a holy man of the English people, converted many provinces of the Scottish nation to the canonical observance of Easter by his pious preaching, in the year 717 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Theodosius was therefore chosen emperor in the year 708. He defeated Anastasius in a severe battle at Nicaea and, after receiving his oath that he would become a cleric, had him ordained a priest. He reigned for one year. Since he was Catholic, he restored in the imperial city to its former place the image on which the holy Sixth Synod had been depicted and which Philippicus had cast down. After him Leo ruled in the year 709, for twenty-six years.

[PAUL, DIAC.] [Note: “Here”—“was driven from his see,” in the margin.] He removed and burned the images of the saints and sent word to the Roman pontiff that he should do so if he wished to retain his favor. The pontiff rejected this. Everyone resisted such commands with one accord, and unless the pontiff himself—namely, Gregory IV—had restrained them, they would have set up an emperor over themselves. The pope nevertheless later deposed him. Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, refusing to consent to the emperor’s error, was driven from his see.

The Saracens came to Constantinople with a great army and besieged the city for three years. But when the citizens returned to God with great earnestness, many of the Saracens perished from hunger, cold, and pestilence, and thus, weary of the siege, they abandoned it. From there they attacked the Bulgars; defeated by them, they recovered their ships. But while they were making for the open sea, a storm arose and they were drowned. [Note: “Within Constantinople”—“perished,” in the margin.] Within Constantinople itself, three hundred thousand people perished from pestilence.

When Liutprand heard that the Saracens were defiling those places where the bones of Saint Augustine had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the barbarians, he sent men and, after paying a great price, transferred them to Pavia with due honor.

Gregory III the Syrian, son of John, occupied the see for ten years, eight months, and twenty-five days.

(Gesta p. R.) [Note: “He removed”—735, in the margin.] He removed Rome, Italy, and all the rights both of the commonwealth and of the Church in the western regions from obedience to Leo and to the empire established under him.

(Hist. Misc.) John also—neither pope nor bishop, but a Damascene monk and priest and an excellent teacher—anathematized that same Leo together with the bishops of the East; this is written in Book 23 of the Roman History. Leo died in the year 735 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

[Note: “After”—“Leo succeeded,” in the margin.] After Leo, the impious Constantine assumed the empire in the year 736 from the Incarnation of the Lord. In the year of his reign … [Note: An erasure; at its beginning the letter *p* can be distinguished.] Pope Stephen came to Francia. He ruled for forty-three years. His son Leo succeeded him in the year 770 from the Incarnation of the Lord; he reigned for five years and slightly less than six days. Irene, wife of the elder Constantine, then succeeded him together with her ten-year-old son Constantine, in the year 775, indiction 13. [Note: “d. a.” is written above.] [Note: After this, approximately five words have been erased.] In the year 787 a synod was held at Nicaea, in the first indiction, under Pope Adrian. Constantine was killed through his mother’s faction; she assumed the empire herself in the year 792. Nicephorus succeeded her in the year 795, Michael succeeded Nicephorus in the year 804, and Leo succeeded Michael. (Hist. Misc.)

Pope Gregory died on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the third indiction, on the tenth day; the episcopal see was vacant for eight days. (Gesta p. R.) After him came Zacharias the Greek, in the year 742 from the Incarnation of the Lord, son of Polychronius, for ten years, three months, and fourteen days.

(Ann. Fuld.) Pippin, mayor of the palace in the kingdom of the Franks, sent an embassy to him and asked about the kings of the Franks descended from the ancient stock of the Merovingians. They were indeed called kings, but all the power of the kingdom was held by the mayor of the palace, except that documents and privileges were written in the king’s name. The man who was called king was carried once a year to the Field of Mars in a wagon drawn by oxen, seated in an elevated position, and was shown to the people. Public gifts were solemnly presented to him, while the mayor of the palace stood before him and announced to the people what was to be done during the coming year. The so-called king then returned home, while the mayor of the palace administered all the other affairs of the kingdom.

Pippin therefore asked that it be determined which of them ought justly to be called and to be king: the one who sat safely at home, or the one who bore responsibility for the kingdom and endured all its hardships. Zacharias, by apostolic authority, commanded the Frankish people that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the name. Thus Childeric, the last king of the Merovingian line, was deposed and thrust into a monastery. Pippin, however, was anointed king by Saint Boniface the archbishop in the city of Soissons and elevated to the honor of the kingdom.

[Note: “Pope Zacharias died”—indiction 5, in the margin.] Pope Zacharias died on the Ides of March, in the fifth indiction. (Gesta p. R.)

[Note: “After [he had] died”—“he died,” in the margin.] After the most blessed Pope Zacharias had died in Christ, the Romans elected a certain presbyter named Stephen, and he was consecrated pope. On the third day, however, as he rose from sleep and was arranging his household affairs, he was struck by a sudden illness, lost his speech, and died the following day.

In the year 752 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fifth indiction, with concurrent 1 and epact 6, Stephen the Roman, son of Constantine, occupied the see at Rome for five years and twenty-nine days. (Hist. Misc.) Because of the attacks of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, he came to Pippin in Francia, appointed him defender and prince of the Roman Church, and consecrated him king. (Fol. 39.) From that time Rome was removed from subjection to the empire of the Greeks.

Since, therefore, by God’s gift we have now reached the point at which it seems appropriate to continue with the kings of the Franks, let us briefly clarify, following the statements of the Fathers, what preceded this and at what times kings began to reign in the land of the Franks, who they were, and from where they originated.

Priamus, the first king of the Franks. Frigus. Francio. Turchot. Then they were under dukes until Marcomir the duke, in the time of Theodosius. Marcomir fathered Faramund. Clodio, his son. Merovingius, his son. Childeric, in the time of Maurice. Clovis, the eighth king from the first. (Hist. Franc. epit., c. 2.)

[Note: “Priamus, eighth from the first,” written in the margin in the same ink as the text. The beginnings of the lines—*Pr, Fri, Fr, Tur, Dein, us, duc, Ma, Clo, Me, Chi, Cl*—have been cut away.]

In the year 446 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fourteenth indiction, epact 9, concurrent 1, and the second year of the pontificate of Pope Leo the Great, kings began to reign in the land of the Franks. The first of them, named Clodio, reigned for twenty years. [FREDEG.] Then Childeric, son of Meroveus, drove Aegidius, the Roman duke, from the kingdom and killed him; he seized the kingdom in the year 466 from the Incarnation of the Lord and reigned for twenty-four years. From Basina, queen of the Thuringians, he fathered a son named Clovis, a most warlike and powerful man, at first a pagan and afterward a Christian.

When Childeric died, Clovis succeeded him. [Note: We owe the text of folios 31–40 to the distinguished scholar D. Urlichs, royal professor at Greifswald, who copied them this year in the library at Mediomontana, with the most gracious assistance of D. Thomas Phillipps, Baronet.]

In the fifth year of his reign, Syagrius, son of Aegidius, the Roman duke, had his seat at the city of Soissons, and Clovis attacked him. But when Syagrius saw that his army had been defeated, he hastened swiftly to Toulouse, to Alaric, king of the Goths. [GREG. Tur. II, 27.] When Alaric received the king’s messengers, and, as is the custom of the Goths, trembled at the threat of punishment, he handed the bound Syagrius over to the envoys. Clovis ordered him to be placed under guard and, after obtaining his kingdom, secretly commanded that he be struck down with the sword. [HINCMAR. Vit. Remig.]

At that time blessed Remigius governed the church of Rheims. Through him the Lord restored to reconciliation a people who were already almost in despair, at a time of anger. After vengeance for crimes had been carried out by the Lord through the slaughter of Gaul—first through the cruelty of the Vandals, then of the Huns—the mercies of heaven began to distill, when, to soften the wrath of the Most High, they brought forth Remigius as a bishop for the world.

[FREDEG.] At that time Gundebaud ruled in Burgundy. He was the son of King Gundioc and belonged to the line of Athanarchus the persecutor. Gundioc also had other sons: Godegisel, Chilperic, and Godemar. Gundebaud killed his brother Chilperic with the sword, drowned his wife by fastening a stone around her neck, slaughtered their two sons with the sword, and condemned their two daughters to exile. The elder of them, Sedeleuba, changed her clothing and devoted herself to the Lord; the younger was named Chrotildis.

King Clovis of the Franks sought her, asking that Gundebaud, her uncle, hand her over to him. Since he did not dare refuse, the Franks came and received her from Gundebaud, sending her with many treasures to Clovis. (Fol. 40.) But Gundebaud, recalling the advice of his counselor Aredius and remembering the evil he had done—namely, that he had killed Chrotildis’s father, mother, and brothers—and fearing that, if Chrotildis prevailed, she would avenge the death of her parents, sent an army after her to retain the wagon and treasures. The girl, however, was lifted onto a horse by the Franks and sent to Clovis. Taking her with royal honor, he loved her with consummate affection and married her. (Hist. Franc. epit.)

Clovis already had a son by a concubine, named Theodoric, who reigned after him for twenty-three years. [FREDEG.] He also had three other sons by Chrotildis: Clodomer, Childebert, and Chlothar, who reigned after him. [GREG. Tur.]

After Gundebaud died, his son Sigismund obtained the kingdom of Burgundy. He had as his wife a daughter of Theodoric, king of Italy. [FREDEG.] When she died, he took another wife and, through the stepmother’s plotting, ordered the son of his former wife to be killed. He ordered the boy, made drowsy with wine, to sleep after midday. While he slept, a scarf was placed beneath his neck and tied under his chin, and thus two servants, pulling in opposite directions, strangled him. [GREG. Tur.]

But later, repenting too late, Sigismund threw himself weeping bitterly upon the lifeless body. He returned to Lugdunum after asking forgiveness for many days in the monastery of the Agaunian saints, which he himself had constructed from its foundations with marvelous workmanship, and after establishing a choir of psalm-singers. Divine vengeance immediately followed him. Theodoric, son of Clovis, married his daughter.

[GREG. Tur. II, 30, 31.] Queen Chrotildis was deeply Christian, whereas Clovis followed pagan laws. She repeatedly urged him to abandon empty idols and acknowledge the true God, in whose hand is the heart of kings and the ordering of all powers. He refused to agree until, after undertaking war against the Alamanni, he was compelled by necessity to confess what he had previously denied by choice.

When his army was being slaughtered almost to annihilation, he invoked the name of Jesus, the Son of God whom Chrotildis preached, and obtained victory. When he returned home and reported this to his wife, she secretly summoned blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, and urged him to introduce the word of salvation to the king. Remigius did so. He was a man of outstanding learning and especially well trained in rhetorical studies. With divine grace leading the way, the king believed and was baptized together with his army in the fifteenth year of his reign, during the consulship of Albinus V. C., in the year 502 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

[GREG. Tur. I, 32.] At that time the Burgundians, adhering to the Arian sect, lived around the Arar and the Rhône, which flow beside the city of Lugdunum. Their leaders were the brothers Gundebaud and Godegisel. (II, 34.) Gundebaud killed Godegisel. Although Saint Avitus, archbishop of Vienne, urged him to confess Christ, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit equal to the Father—for he was an Arian—he secretly sought to be anointed. But Avitus urged him not to fear a popular uprising and not to be ashamed to confess in this world the one who reigns forever. Gundebaud, however, confounded by this argument, remained in his madness until the end of his life; Sigismund succeeded him. (Fol. 40′.)

Clovis, then, was a man distinguished in arms and renowned in holy faith. Seeing that the Goths, whose prince and king was Alaric, and whose dominion extended beyond the Loire, were corrupted by the Arian plague and perversity, he wished, with divine assistance, to defeat them and bring their land under his own authority. He therefore directed his army toward Poitiers, where King Alaric was staying. (II, 37.)

Alaric, on the other hand, came out with his men to meet the enemy at the tenth milestone from the city. When they engaged in battle on the plain of Vouillé, Clovis obtained victory over the Arians. [FREDEG.] He killed Alaric together with a great number of Goths and occupied his kingdom from the Tyrrhenian Sea and the River Loire as far as the Pyrenees and the Ocean. Taking Alaric’s treasures from Toulouse, he brought them with him to Paris.

(II, 38.) At about the same time he received from the emperor Anastasius letters patent for the consulship, together with a golden crown and a purple tunic. From that day he was called consul and augustus. [GREG. Tur., II, 40.]

While he was staying in Paris, Clovis considered adding to his dominion the kingdom of his kinsman Sigibert, whose royal seat was the city of Cologne and who had been his faithful ally in the war against Alaric. He acted deceitfully, sending messengers to Theodoric, Sigibert’s son. The son had taken part in the aforementioned war because his father, wounded in the knee while fighting against the Alamanni, was lame. Clovis urged him to kill his father, who was sleeping at midday in his tent, as though he himself were about to possess his father’s kingdom. (II, 40.)

When Theodoric sent messengers to Clovis, pretending to rejoice at his father’s death, and asked him to send trusted men to carry away from his father’s treasures whatever pleased his eyes, Clovis again acted deceitfully. While Theodoric was showing his father’s treasures to the messengers, and while he bent down and put his hand into a small chest to search everything, one of them struck him in the brain with an axe. Thus he received the same treatment he had inflicted upon his father.

When Clovis heard this, he came to the same place and, pretending to be innocent of his kinsmen’s blood, satisfied the people and was established as king. The inhabitants of certain cities, however, bearing this indignantly, tried, if possible, to rebel against him. (Vita Maxim., p. 582.) Among them, the citizens of the town of Verdun are said to have planned defection and armed resistance against him.

[GREG. Tur., II, 41.] After this Clovis captured King Chararic and his son, his relatives, by deceit. He had them bound and tonsured, and ordered the father to be ordained a priest and the son a deacon. But when he learned that they were trying to let their hair grow again, he ordered both of them to be put to death and acquired their kingdom, together with its treasures and people.

(Vita Maxim., p. 582.) When the defection of the people of Verdun was heard, and he judged that such matters should not be postponed, Clovis gathered forces from every direction and came to the same city with a strong military force, intending to avenge the insult. He surrounded its walls with a ring of soldiers, built embankments, leveled obstacles, arranged everything useful for capturing the city, stationed guards at the gates, and with great and sustained effort prevented anyone from safely leaving.

(Fol. 41.) At that time Firminus, bishop of the same city, a man of remarkable holiness, ended his life. Born in the territory of Toul and appointed shepherd of the city of Verdun after Saint Possessor, he had possessed such holiness, had kept such vigilant watch over the flock entrusted to him, had been so compassionate toward his subjects and so terrifying toward the reprobate, that the miracles repeatedly performed at his tomb bear witness to it. It is also found written in the *Gesta* that the people of Verdun rebelled at his instigation.

He died in the month of December, on the second day, in the year which, as far as we can determine, was 504 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Anastasius was reigning in his fourteenth year, in the third year after Clovis’s conversion, during the consulship of Atheus V. C., while blessed Pope Symmachus was presiding over the Roman see. After the siege was lifted, his most sacred body was buried at the right side of the altar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There this delightful treasure lay hidden for many years—from the time of Clovis, that is, until the time of Otto the Great. But let us return to the matter at hand.

(Ib.) The besieged, then, since, as we have said, they were shut in and had lost confidence in their strength, and since, after the bishop’s death, no one seemed likely to be found who could appropriately present the people’s prayers before the prince, who was burning with anger, unanimously agreed to send to the prince the holy man Euspicus, who lived in the same city under the title of presbyter, to present the prayers of the wretched citizens and implore his mercy.

Filled with the Lord and with compassion, Euspicus did not reject the requests of his fellow citizens. Trusting in the one who said to his disciples, “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should say,” he prepared to go to the prince as requested.

When he had humbly prostrated himself before the earthly king, he was respectfully ordered to rise and state the reason for his arrival. He is said to have addressed him as follows:

“Most noble and most pious of all kings, your goodness, by which I entreat you to hear me patiently as I present the prayers of my fellow citizens and implore your mercy, is almost universally celebrated throughout the world. The wickedness of certain men has indeed arisen among us; it has stained the ignorance of many and removed the foolish insolence of the young. We do not deny that we are worthy of your punishment. But for the Lord’s sake I beg that, for the moment, the penalties due for our faults be withheld and mercy be extended to the undeserving.

“Our plea would not be unworthy of your victory, because, since you are victor over men, you will also be a stronger victor over your own passion if you choose to exercise the powers of patience rather than stain your triumph with the blood of your citizens.”

When the king heard these words and perceived their force and the gravity of the man, the vigor of his spirit began to be softened and the bitterness of his gall to be sweetened. God was surely directing this, for before his strength monstrous things yield and hard things crumble.

(Fol. 41′.) Finally, touched by divine direction, the king was so moved that he granted the request and bestowed forgiveness upon the citizens, although they were ungrateful. Thus the saying of the Wise Man concerning him was fulfilled:

“This also,” he says, “I saw under the sun and considered it a great matter: a small city, and few men in it; a great king came against it, besieged it, and built siegeworks around it, and the siege was completed. But a poor wise man was found in it, and by his wisdom he delivered the city.”

Therefore, when the man of God gave the order and held the king’s hand, the barriers of the gates seemed to be drawn back and the gates opened. The clergy also were ordered to come forth to welcome the king with praises and songs worthy of God, through which they might offer the Lord a dance of thanksgiving for their deliverance and show the prince their devoted obedience.

After the king, through the agency of the Lord’s servant, recognized that his anger had cooled and that he had been rescued from a monstrous offense, he gave thanks to God in the church. Having granted the citizens royal pardon, he turned, as was customary, to restoring his body with royal banquets. After indulging in these for two days and seeing that his army had recovered after its labors, he wished to lead it to attend to other similar affairs. He ordered the holy man Euspicus to be brought before him and urged—and in urging him, requested—that he take pastoral charge of the city whose defender he had been and which he had rescued from imminent danger.

But the man of God, mindful of the words, “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before the Lord,” humbly refused the honor offered to him—or rather, the burden of the priesthood. Indeed, foreseeing the brevity of his own life, which was soon to end, he preferred to withdraw so that another might succeed him.

Then the king immediately summoned the multitude of the faithful into one place and ordered them to bring forward their judgment concerning the appointment of a pastor. For he knew that, according to the decree of Pope Leo the Great, no principle permitted those to be counted among the bishops who had not been elected by the clergy, requested by the people, and consecrated by the bishops of the province with the judgment of the metropolitan.

He also knew that, although he presided with secular dignity, he ought nevertheless, as blessed Pope Gelasius writes, devotedly to bow his neck before the leaders of divine affairs, seek from them the means of his salvation, and recognize that in the ordering of religion he ought to submit to them in conferring and arranging the heavenly sacraments, rather than preside over them.

He also wished to obey the decree of the aforesaid Leo the Great, in which he writes to Rusticus, archbishop of Narbonne, among other things:

“When the election of the chief priest is under consideration, let the one whom the unanimous agreement of the clergy and people has requested be placed before all others. Let no one be given to those who are unwilling and do not ask for him, lest a city either reject or hate an unwanted bishop and become less devout because it was not permitted to have the one it wanted.”

Celestine likewise says in his decrees: “Let no bishop be given to those who are unwilling; the desire of the clergy, the people, and the ecclesiastical order must be sought.”

(Fol. 42.) Clovis therefore killed King Ranacharius, whose royal seat was the city of Cambrai, his relative, with his own hand and by deceit, as well as his brother Racharius. [FRED.] He had given the traitors certain ornaments—not gold, but bronze and gilded metal. [GREG. Tur., II, 42.]

After their lord’s death, when the traitors discovered that the gold they had received from the king was not genuine but counterfeit, and told the king this, the king is said to have replied: “He rightly receives such gold who, of his own will, brings his lord to death.”

Their third brother, also a relative of Clovis, was killed at the city of Le Mans on his order. After these men had died, Clovis acquired their entire kingdom and treasures. Having also killed many other kings and close relatives whom he suspected of intending to take the kingdom from him, he extended his own kingdom throughout all Gaul.

He died at the city of Paris in the year 518 from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirtieth year of his reign and at the age of forty-five. He was buried in the basilica of the holy apostles that he had built. At that time Hormisdas was presiding over the Roman Church as pope, and Justin, the successor of Anastasius, was ruling the empire.

(III, 1.) The four sons of Clovis therefore divided his kingdom among themselves in equal portions: Theodoric, Clodomir, Childebert, and Chlothar. [FREDEG.] The seat of Theodoric’s kingdom was the city of Metz, that of Clodomir was Orléans, that of Childebert was Paris, and that of Chlothar was Soissons. [GREG. Tur., III, 1.]

At that time Theodoric already had a son named Theudebert, an elegant and capable man, and a daughter whom Amalaric, king of Spain and son of Alaric, took as his wife. He was killed by the Franks at Barcelona. [FREDEG.] There was always great conflict between Theodoric and Childebert, which afflicted many cities. [GREG. Tur., III, 15.]

Theodoric was an ingenious and crafty man. Later, however, he made a treaty with his brother, and after exchanging oaths that neither would move against the other, they exchanged hostages. But when discord again arose between the kings, the sons of senators who had been given as hostages were assigned to public servitude. For whoever received them for safekeeping made them his slaves. (Vita Carilefi.)

In the time of Chlothar and Childebert, Saint Avitus and Saint Carilephus left the monastery of Menat in Auvergne and sought the monastery of Miciacum, which Saint Maximinus, brother of Saint Vitonus, had founded, and submitted themselves to it.

[FREDEG.] After her husband’s death, Queen Chrotildis urged her sons to avenge the death of their father, mother, and brothers. For this reason they attacked Burgundy and defeated Sigismund, son of Gundebaud, and Godemar in battle. Clodomir captured Sigismund as he fled to the monastery of the Agaunian saints and killed him together with his wife and children. Godemar fled and went into hiding; having recovered his strength, he retained the kingdom of Burgundy.

Avitus, abbot of the monastery of Orléans, foretold to Clodomir that he himself would suffer repeatedly what he had done to Sigismund. When the Franks engaged the Burgundians in battle at Vézeronce, Clodomir was beheaded. He had been deceived by the forces of Theodoric, king of Italy, whose daughter Sigismund had married; after her death, as we stated above, he took another wife. [GREG. Tur., III, 18.]

Since Chrotildis loved Clodomir’s sons with undivided affection, Childebert, driven by envy, incited Chlothar to kill the boys.

(Fol. 42.) [FREDEG.] When they had gathered at Paris as though they were going to elevate the boys to their father’s kingdom, Chlothar deceitfully received them from their mother and killed Theodald and Gunthar. The third, Clodoald, was tonsured as a cleric; miracles take place at his tomb.

[GREG. Tur., III, 13; III, 16; III, 12.] Theodoric, hastening to plunder the territory of Auvergne, ordered Sigivald to move there with his entire household. Sigivald committed many evils and later met an evil end himself. The aforementioned king inflicted such devastation on that region that nothing belonging to either the younger or the older inhabitants was left to them except the land itself, which the barbarians could not carry away with them. He also besieged Autun and completely plundered it.

[Col. 0115A] Thus, when blessed Vitonus had been taken up into the joy of the Lord and, in return for faithfulness in few things and gain, had been set over many and everlasting goods [Note: [Col. 0115D] Surius published a brief Life of Vitonus from a very ancient manuscript of Utrecht in *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. VII, p. 820. [Col. 0116D] Miracles by Rudolf, abbot of Saint-Vitonus, are found in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, sixth century, p. 565.], Desideratus succeeded him in the episcopal care, which required great vigilance and was surrounded by the anguish of anxieties. For Theoderic, being stubborn and ill-disposed, and having afflicted many cities because of the disagreement between himself and his brother, as we have related above, [GREG. Tur., III, 34] Desideratus himself, after many losses, exiles, hardships, and insults had been inflicted upon him, had now, at the Lord’s command, returned to freedom and was exercising the office of bishop at Verdun, as we have said. For in the world he had been of very noble birth, having a wife and a son named Syagrius. (III, 35.) But after he had been accused before the aforesaid king by a certain Syrivald, he had not only been stripped of his possessions but also [Col. 0115B] subjected to punishments. Later, when he had been tonsured and, by the election of clergy and people, had been placed over the church of Verdun, Theoderic, retaining perpetual hostility toward him because he did not consent to his wicked deeds, grievously crushed the city and its inhabitants. Moreover, by divine judgment, a severe famine came upon the city’s feeble people; weakened by it, they were reduced to extreme affliction. (Ib.) And since Theoderic had made him a stranger to his own possessions, and he had nothing of his own with which to comfort his needy and abandoned citizens, he grieved and was saddened. (III, 23, 25.) When Theoderic died in the twenty-third year of his reign, in the year 541 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and his son Theodebert had assumed the kingdom—and, against the will of Childebert and Clothar, had been established and strengthened in the kingdom by his own *leudes*, and afterward had been adopted as a son by Childebert after receiving the greatest gifts—he showed himself great and outstanding in every virtue. For he ruled the kingdom with justice, honored priests, endowed churches, relieved the poor, and bestowed many benefits upon many with pious and most gracious goodwill. He also mercifully remitted the taxes that were paid to the treasury by the churches situated in Auvergne. (III, 26.) He had a wife named Deuteria and a daughter who had already reached maturity. But Deuteria, fearing that, after abandoning her, the king might take her daughter in marriage, placed the girl in a wagon and drove her over the bridge at Verdun with untamed oxen yoked together; she gave up her spirit in the river itself. (III, 34.) Accordingly, when Desideratus saw the goodness and clemency of King Theodebert toward everyone, and the people were already dispersing while the city was being reduced almost to a wilderness, he went to the king and lamented the people’s pitiable misery. By a kindly petition he bent the royal heart, asking him, in compassion for their calamity, to avert it from his treasures, restrain the famine, preserve the perishing people, and, once the danger had been overcome by grace, receive back with the gratitude of God and men what had been lent.

(III, 31.) For he had received fifty thousand gold pieces from Theodahad, king of Italy and successor of Theoderic, together with his uncle Childebert, as compensation [Col. 0116A] for the death of the daughter of Clodoveus’s sister, who had been married to the aforesaid Theoderic and, after his death, had married a slave contrary to her birth (fol. 43). Because her mother, enraged, had attacked her with an army, killed the slave, and brought her daughter back home, the daughter, in anger, placed poison in the cup from which her mother was about to drink—for they had been held in the Arian error—and, as soon as the mother had drunk it, she died. For this reason the Italians, enraged, cast her aside and made the aforesaid Theodahad king. He had her shut in a bathhouse heated to a fierce temperature; she collapsed onto the floor amid the dreadful vapors and died. (III, 32.) For this reason Theodebert also invaded Italy; but because his army was afflicted by various fevers, he left a commander there with part of the army. That commander brought all Italy under his authority, as well as Sicily, and sent him countless treasures. (FREDEG.) Great indeed was the king’s good fortune in all these matters, because he feared the Lord and venerated his priests and churches. (GREG. Tur.) When the bishop of Verdun’s petition had been heard, the king agreed, moved to compassion, and, handing him seven thousand solidi, added the condition that it should be distributed among the needy in such a way that, once the dominion of famine had been overcome by this aid, his own money should be returned to him in full, with thanks.

(III, 34.) The bishop received the money and distributed it among his citizens, and as a result they became merchants and are still renowned today. When, instructed by this relief and having advanced through experience of danger to a better understanding of the finest moderation, they had learned that it was good to look toward the future, they eagerly gathered the money [Col. 0116C] and offered it to the king through the mediation of the bishop, with grateful praises and votive thanksgivings. When the king perceived their relief, he saw the greatness of their joyful devotion; gathering together the royal spirit and the spirit that ruled the money, he granted it to them, both to increase their good name to the highest degree and to preserve a praiseworthy memory for the present and future generations.

(III, 35.) Syagrius, however, the son of Bishop Desideratus, remembering after Theoderic’s death the injuries suffered by his father—injuries inflicted by Theoderic’s instigation and through the accusation of Syriwald—took companions and went to his estate in the territory of Dijon, whose name was Floriacus. At daybreak, when a dense fog prevailed, they entered the house and killed one of his companions, thinking that he was Syriwald. But when they learned [Col. 0116D] that he was not Syriwald, they surrounded the house again, dug through the wall, and killed him. This happened after the death of Bishop Desideratus.

*(Life of Agericus.)* But, to return to the earlier subject and examine more closely God’s abundant mercy toward his own image, divine providence had determined to come to the aid of the church of Verdun from the fountain of mercy and to extend a helping hand to it, endangered by the countless misfortunes of the calamities mentioned above. On the day and at the time he willed, from the highest and most serene counsel of his goodness, he found this new path [Col. 0117A] of salvation: he sent a holy angel from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven to announce to the parents the future birth of a child through the mercy of the One, to indicate the appointed time when it should occur, and to assign the name by which he should be known.

Indeed, because of the excessive love with which he loved his own image in man, he pitied mortal beings suffering under the heavy yoke borne from the first father. In his universal mercy he restored this people, whom sins had especially crushed. First he touched and troubled them and inflicted a bruise with a father’s rod; afterward, looking upon them, he healed them by a wondrous remedy. The messenger of the divine counsel came, delivered the command, proclaimed the decree, and, addressing the parents of the chosen child, raised the horn of salvation for the suffering citizens. “After three years,” he said, “the deferred expectation will be fulfilled; the son himself shall be called Agericus.”

It is an indication of a greater and surpassing privilege before God for God to confer or change a name as a title for anyone. Great, therefore, is the gift; great the graciousness of favor; great the confidence of the promises. What is dictated from the tribunal of the eternal King, with the heavenly messenger proclaiming it, cannot be changed. “He shall be called Agericus,” he said. It is an unusual name, not attached to the pages of Scripture; but the more unknown it is among men, the more worthy it is of divine consideration, and the more acceptable to God, the more beneficial to man. No one can doubt that even now the language of heaven has not forgotten itself, and that heavenly Scripture eternally preserves what heaven has inscribed upon earth. Therefore let earth not reject what heaven approves.

[Col. 0117C] The child was born after three years; the parents’ long expectation was extended into fulfillment; he was delightful in his saffron-colored garments and sweet in his cradle. He passed beyond the seven years of infancy, growing toward the service of speech. He became a boy in bodily growth and a boy in innocence; he adorned his tender nature with a shining disposition. For the angel who had foretold him was always present to guard him. The little boy was given over to the pursuit of wisdom, joined the fellowship of scholars, drank in the springs of knowledge, continually sucked at overflowing breasts, and diligently imitated inward pleasures and better spiritual gifts. For the inner Teacher who had instructed him displayed, as his age advanced, clear signs of his virtues. He had been foreknown before the womb and sanctified in the womb, and he increased holiness and magnificence in the sanctification of God.

He was loved by everyone; by the sublimity of the grace that surpassed all, he overcame everyone’s envy and slander. He advanced in the same city of the people of Verdun until he reached the full maturity of his growth, adding virtue to virtue and bearing in his body the marks of Christ’s Passion. With indescribable joy he ran along the way of God’s commandments. When he was already thirty years old, he was led in the city of Verdun to the church of Saint Peter, had his head tonsured, and was dedicated to Christ. He flourished in the courts of the Lord’s house like a palm tree, and like a cedar in Lebanon he filled the entire house with good fragrances. The beauty of his character advanced him, and he served the bishop in the levitical order. Then, behold, clergy and people, desiring to promote him to the honor of the priesthood, led him to the same church [Col. 0118A] and had him ordained there with joy and praises of thanksgiving. All sang, as if with one voice: “I have exalted one chosen from my people; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Psalm 88:20), because he had been chosen by Christ the Lord to be strengthened with the oil of spiritual grace.

(Fol. 44.) Meanwhile, Desideratus died in name, office, and life, and the vacant see of the church sought a suitable successor. There was no long search for what was at hand, nor was the better decision delayed long in the night of ignorance. All came together as one; all agreed upon one in the election; all demanded that Agericus be ordained and invested with the episcopal insignia. One man attempted to resist the many and labored greatly to excuse himself, but, with God strengthening it, the judgment of clergy and people prevailed. [Col. 0118B] For God was cooperating among the people to repair the protection of the weakened city and to raise the horn of salvation against wickedness.

Three years after completing his tonsure, Agericus was seized by the people of Verdun and led into the church of the great holy Mother of God; there he was consecrated bishop by bishops. He received the pastoral staff for governing the Lord’s sheep and did not show himself a tyrant to the sheep, but truly a shepherd. He did not allow his land to cry out against him while its furrows mourned, but diligently devoted himself to God’s cultivation, so that by his work he might render what he confessed by his name. He kept the faithful advocate, the Lord Jesus Christ, before his eyes and entrusted himself and his people to him through constant prayer.

He offered rich holocausts for the sheep, lest they honor God with their lips while their hearts were far away, provoke him with their hands, and deny by their actions the faith they professed in words. Always watchful, he struck down the lurking lion with prayers, redeemed the flames of temptations with almsgiving, and guarded the treasuries of virtues in the stronghold of humility. He terrified enemies by preaching, brought hidden vices into the light, and shattered the deadly weapons of the enemy with the sharp point of powerful doctrine. Always made stronger than himself through Jesus and the great High Priest, he triumphed on every side.

Indeed, he avoided and greatly feared committing anything for which, accused by the testimony of his conscience, he would be forced to flee beneath the shade and leaves. Always fearful, always solicitous while he devoted due care to the sheep entrusted to him, once the enemy had been overcome he cheerfully subjected himself to the service of justice and freedom from vices.

[Col. 0118D] He often spoke with his herald, the holy angel, both in writing and in words, and sent to the Lord, through the angel’s counsel, the precious deeds of a faithful athlete. He frequently counted the talents entrusted to him, lest, having received more, he should return less in profit and, repenting too late, be delivered, poor and naked, into the bonds of darkness. He also performed signs which, although they may be held in common with the reprobate, he performed with a credible and simple eye and a clear body, compelled by the need of his sheep and of the whole world.

For when the just and holy God was angered against the offending people, and the elements fought on his behalf against the senseless, the clouds withdrew, the air grew hot, the earth dried up, the green of the grasses withered, and the water abandoned the veins of the springs. (Fol. 44'.) Thus, as the elements withdrew, the desolate world grew faint. For wickedness nourished by habit, unless softened by a hard blow, grows hardened against returning to knowledge of itself. Hence it happened that, when the blessing of rains had been withheld for three years, the sky was stretched over them like iron. They endured the first year in expectation, the second in despair, and in the third they collapsed.

When they could find no counsel among themselves, at last the transgressors, returning in a sense to hearts that had forgotten themselves, rushed to the bishop and called upon the shepherd to reconcile the angered God to their sins, remove the punishment, obtain forgiveness, and restore the parched lands to the dying farmers. The saint was moved by the universal necessity and advised that the common danger be removed by common prayer. Accordingly, he proclaimed a three-day fast, ordered litanies to be celebrated throughout God’s churches, and crosses to be carried in remembrance of God’s most merciful [Col. 0119B] mercy, so that Christ, who had suffered for sinners, might be reconciled to them through the intercessions of the saints. He proclaimed and ordered this, and he was the first to do what he had ordered.

They went out indiscriminately barefoot, wrapped themselves in ashes and sackcloth, cried aloud for the mercy of the saints and the propitiation of God, beat their breasts, and shed tears, lest God, executing judgment, should seize the sinners in the works of their hands. On the first day of the litanies, therefore, the shepherd himself walked with his sheep and, in the presence of the crowds, turned his eyes toward heaven. In his heart he moved God, who rested there, to mercy; and suddenly, when the air had been overshadowed by dense clouds, the waters flowed. Thus, as the rains fell throughout those three days, the earth received vigor, the grasses greenness, the springs their flow, the trees life, and the world full [Col. 0119C] abundance.

Nor was it hidden from the people: they saw and marveled at how great a concern the holy shepherd had with God. For while he walked under the open sky and everyone was drenched by the descending waters, God himself made an umbrella for him in the rain. Here and there, wherever he was, the commanded water fell, but it prevented him from being touched by the water—he who does everything whatsoever he wills.

When, according to pastoral custom, he was wearing down the threshold of the principal church of Saint Mary, a certain man named John, loosened in his limbs, dried up in his sinews, dead in strength but with his soul still present, possessing power only through the use of his tongue, implored the bishop with the weak sounds he could produce, saying: “I beseech you, holy man of God, to have mercy on me.” The priest, in a sense bending down and becoming weak with the sick man, replied: “What do you want me to do for you?” The sick man answered: “That you have mercy on me.”

Then the priest, rich in God, brought forth a little from his purse and gave it to the sick man from the abundance of his good heart. For, giving him sustenance for the flesh, he bestowed at the same time strength for the body. The dried-up man received the priest’s gifts together with faith in Christ and, with the same gift, deserved to receive health.

By these and similar signs God glorifying his servant, it began to be evident to all that holy Agericus was Christ’s fosterling. So abundant was the supply of virtues that flowed from him that, if any sick person received a blessing (*eulogia*) from his hand, he immediately recovered health.

(Fol. 45.) When he was treading the threshold of the aforesaid basilica and, as usual, devoting himself to spiritual exercises [Col. 0120A], he displayed the most pious goodness that he carried in his mind through the greatness of a miracle. At the very entrance he encountered a little woman named Theresind, who, guided by a staff, was searching for the way in the blindness of her wandering and following a guide because her eyes had been desolated. Immediately, by the simple remedy of the holy cross, he drove away the darkness of fifteen years and, shining with the light of faith, restored the long-absent light at once. Power radiated through the cross, and it radiated through the bishop. Piety reigned in the bishop; power in the cross. Nor would piety have achieved anything unless it had prevailed through faith in the cross.

For such was the power in the cross that it not only illuminated the woman’s deprived face but also poured unfailing light throughout the whole world. After the Light of the World had hung upon the cross, the regions of the world shone, and night did not follow. The night of the devil lost its kingdom; the day of the cross obtained dominion. Hence the holy bishop prevailed so greatly, because he nourished light in his heart through faith in the cross and through love. He made the sign of the cross over the blind woman’s eyes, because the Holy Spirit was in the finger through the power of the cross.

What more is there to say? The woman rejoices, marvels at the sun, curses the darkness, venerates the physician, and adores God, wondrous in the diversity of his works—she who previously had known only confusion and night. Thus God, through a true Israelite, illuminated this woman and stirred the wondering people to his praise and glory.

At another time, when the lover of mercy and worshiper of piety, the watchful shepherd of the sheep, saw a certain girl named Childuis seized and possessed by an evil spirit, he pitied her misery and, mindful of his office, immediately went up against it. He set himself as a wall against the raging enemy and, showing himself to be one of those dogs of whom it is said, “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies themselves” (Psalm 67:24), extended a healing tongue of aid to the wretched girl and bared against the hostile possessor the teeth of commanding zeal. Barking with the Lord’s voice—which is gentle and patient, does not cry out, and is not heard in the street—he terrified the ever-swollen wickedness and restored to freedom the image of God that had been violently enslaved, not to the Lord.

After he had said, “I command you, unclean spirit, to come out of her [Col. 0120D] and never again enter her,” the spirit, struck by the power of omnipotence, was cast into the foul abyss of its dwelling, as the fiery foam vomited by the girl revealed: the furnace and kiln in which it had secretly possessed and burned the wretched girl. Once she had been calmed and recognized herself, she sat down exhausted. Having lost the armor of the enemy that had grown fat within her, she became gentle and, a wonder to everyone, was now amazed at herself in fear. She began to possess herself, whereas she had been possessed, and, cleansed little by little of the alien spirit, recovered the spirit of her own nature.

The servant of God dismissed her, freed from the service of wickedness, and commanded her to serve the legitimate Lord of all—the one whom the lying servant and murderer from the beginning had stolen away. O most powerful, most victorious, most merciful God, may your powerful, victorious, and merciful servants render to you what they have from you, and may they always possess you and all things.

Thus far we have followed the Lord as though walking upon the earth, describing, as it was granted to us [Note: [Col. 0121D] The Bollandists testify that they had before them two Lives of Agericus: one shorter and more ancient, the other longer. See *Acta Sanctorum*, September, vol. II, p. 222. That Hugh followed the longer one is evident [Col. 0122D] from a certain passage of the shorter Life, which is found at the cited location. That the other Life flowed from this source is proved by Hugh’s narrative. K.], his holy servant exercising works of piety and mercy in mortal bodies. (fol. 45') Now the life-giving Spirit compels us to raise the revolving wheel of Scripture higher and to mark a spiritual miracle with bodily and visible pen.

*(Longer Life of Agericus.)* Blessed Agericus, keeping in his heart and fulfilling by his deeds the apostle’s command, “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things,” happened one night to lie upon his bed, mindful of the Lord. Secretly, with a sweet and gentle delight, he kindled himself with chaste meditations, and, rising above the weight of his own body through the lightness of the spirit, suddenly the lamp burning before him went out. He remained fully awake and sober, hindered neither by sight nor hearing nor by any obstacle of the five bodily senses.

When he was wholly with himself and extended his whole self toward God, and his holy soul, pressed down by the weight of the body, expanded into God through contemplation, as he ascended toward the heights out of desire, the heavenly household descended to him. A multitude of angels entered and traversed the holiness of his dwelling. His bedroom shone with the splendors of holy angels, and as many ministers of glory as there were, so many were the lights of glories. They sang hymns with their fellow citizen and companion, and sounded ineffable harmonies to the glorious God of gods in his saints.

He drew in and tasted a sweetness too great for the vessel of his fragile body; weak flesh could neither comprehend nor contain the overflowing gifts of God. The holy angels praised God’s grace and mercy toward his saints and his regard for his elect. As the heavenly choir displayed so many joys before the bishop, he revealed, for the advancement and strengthening of the whole holy church, his holy predecessors in the episcopate: the bishops Maurus, Salvinus, and Arator—the senate of the saints. Their souls belonged to the heavenly fellowship, while their bodies, entrusted to the earth, lay hidden in obscurity. These gifts, these most precious tokens, the heavenly fellow citizens left in munificence to their host and fellow citizen. They had governed the church of Verdun many years before him, and, united to God, they were also united in the tomb.

After so wondrous a visitation, when the light and the angels had withdrawn to heaven, those who were in the chamber with him were so stunned by the miracle that they were almost deprived of life through divine astonishment. The holy man of God, with the greatest severity, forbade them to make these things known to anyone by telling them, so long as he himself remained in the course of this life.

The bodies of the saints, therefore, more precious than refined gold, were lifted up and honorably and most reverently placed by that man of God in the church consecrated under the name of the holy apostle Peter by blessed Sanctinus, where they had possessed the seat of their repose, on the day before the Nones of September. The day of their translation and revelation was marked in succeeding times by the honor of annual celebration. Their merits are displayed by the frequent miracles occurring at their tombs.

Since he has now taken the better road and has already been led to the homeland of eternal happiness, it would please us to proclaim something, with secure and devoted humility, about so glorious a mercy, to the praise of God and the glory of his faithful servant. Finally, pleasing and clinging to God in the land of the living, he left us an example and offered aid in the land of the dead, so that we might shape our works according to the rule of justice and bring forth words from just deeds.

(Fol. 46.) He prayed without [Col. 0122B] ceasing, fulfilling the Lord’s command: “One ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke 18:1). But how did he pray without growing weary? Because he blessed the Lord with holy prayers and holy works, just as David said of himself: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2). And Tobias said to his son: “Bless God at all times” (Tobit 4:20), and so forth.

For just as by evil works we deny the faith, so conversely by good works we establish it; and he prays well who, by prayer or good work, builds up his neighbor. Since, then, just as those evangelical shepherds watched over their flock, so this man devoted himself through prayers acceptable to God to the guardianship of those entrusted to him, he deserved to be visited by angels and, while still mortal, to enjoy heavenly light.

And just as those shepherds announced glory to God in the highest and peace to people of good will, so these angels glorified God in his holy bishop. Just as those shepherds signified the birth of Christ for the salvation of the world, so these angels showed the bodies of the saints for the salvation of the church. Therefore, by angels, by holy souls, and by us also, insignificant as we are in the body, let glory be sung to the immortal, invisible King of the ages, who is blessed forever. Let what we have said for the glory of God and the admonition of those listening suffice; from here let us return to the matter.

In the year 157 after the passing of Saint Martin, Saint Eufronius, bishop of Autun, [held] the see of Tours . . . while Clothar was reigning, who, after Aribert’s death, brought Sigebert into his see.

[GREG. Tur., IV, 9.] When King Theodebert had therefore departed to the heights, his son Theodebald succeeded him, a very unjust man and of evil disposition, who died in the seventh year of his reign. Clothar received his kingdom. Childebert also died at Paris, and thus Clothar obtained sole rule. *(Carolingian Genealogy.)* This Clothar joined his sister in marriage to Ansbert, who fathered Arnold; Arnold fathered Arnulf, bishop of Metz; Arnulf fathered Anchises, also called Ansegisus; Ansegisus fathered Pippin; Pippin fathered Charles.

[GREG. Tur., IV, 20.] At that time Clothar ordered his son Chramn, who was rebelling against him and plotting revolution, to be burned by fire, after he had first been captured and bound. After this, Clothar hastened to the threshold of Saint Martin on account of his sins. Returning from there, he died at the estate of Compiègne in the year 569 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninety-fifth year of his age and the fifty-first year of his reign. His four sons divided his kingdom among themselves.

*(Life of Praejectus.)* Chilperic obtained his father’s kingdom, with his seat at Soissons; under him [Note: [Col. 0123D] “under him . . . Theoderic succeeded” is added in the margin.] Saint Praejectus, martyr and bishop of the people of Auvergne, suffered and was killed by his own citizens in the year 580 from the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 0123B] and Saint Avitus succeeded him. He presided for not quite fifteen years [Note: [Col. 0124D] He held the office for nearly three times five years. Avitus in the *Life of Saint Bonitus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. I, p. 1071.], and Saint Bonitus succeeded him in the first year of Theoderic. (Life of Bonitus.)

Aribert held the kingdom of Childebert, with his seat at Paris; Guntrannus held the kingdom of Clodomer, with his seat at Orléans; Sigebert held the kingdom of Theoderic, with his seat at Metz.

[FREDEG.] The Huns invaded Gaul. Sigebert defeated and routed them, and afterward made peace with them. Meanwhile Chilperic invaded the city of Reims and other cities belonging to Sigebert’s kingdom, and civil war arose between them. Sigebert attacked Soissons, captured Theodebert, Chilperic’s son, and bound him in exile; he defeated Chilperic and recovered the cities. After a year he returned the son to him and established peace.

Guntrannus, reigning in Burgundy, was a good man devoted to almsgiving. Sigebert, however, seeing that Aribert and Guntrannus were taking low-born wives, married Bruna, also called Brunichildis, the daughter of Athanagild, king of Spain. Through her counsel much evil and bloodshed occurred in Francia. Chilperic also married her sister Gachilissinda, abandoning Fredegund and the other wives whom he had. Later, after breaking the oath he had given to the Goths not to remove her from the kingdom, he had her beaten and so took Fredegund back; she afterward ended her most cruel life by a death she deserved.

[GREG. Tur., V, 29.] This man, worse than Nero and Herod, devastated the churches of God and killed many saints. He imposed extremely severe assessments throughout his entire kingdom [Col. 0123D]. When almost the whole kingdom had paid them, the man who bore them was intercepted and killed by the people of Limoges, and the assessments were burned.

*(Life of Praejectus.)* Hector, the patrician of Marseille, was also killed by him, because Saint Praejectus had previously been unjustly accused before him and, as he had said, had been unable to prove the case for which he had been accused.

[FREDEG.] In the year 566 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Sigebert began to reign and reigned for fourteen years. Guntrannus also subdued the Lombards, who had invaded his kingdom, with such slaughter that only forty men from their entire army returned to Italy.

(Fol. 46'.) After this Chilperic and Sigebert conspired to kill Guntrannus and take his kingdom. But, when their plan was changed by the will of the Lord, Sigebert attacked Chilperic. Chilperic fled to Tournai, while Sigebert came to Paris, where Saint Germanus of Paris urged him to desist from pursuing his brother; but he refused to listen. The bishop said to him: “It is written: ‘He who prepares a pit for his brother falls into it first.’”

Coming to Vitry, Sigebert received all the Neustrian people into submission. There he was treacherously killed by two youths, who were themselves also captured and killed; thus Chilperic recovered the kingdom.

[GREG. Tur., IV, 41.] Sigebert died in the thirteenth year of his reign, at the age of forty, and his son Childebert reigned in his place in the year 582, in the fifteenth indiction.

[FREDEG.] Brunichildis was being held at Paris in custody together with her son Childebert. But the boy was lowered through a window in a sack, and at Metz was raised to his father’s kingdom by the commander Gundebaud.

[GREG. Tur., V, 1, 2.] By Chilperic’s order Brunichildis was condemned to exile at Rouen in the first year of Childebert’s reign. In that year Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, died, and Regnamund succeeded him.

Chilperic therefore sent his son Meroveus with an army to Poitiers. Meroveus abandoned his father’s arrangements, joined himself to the commander Guntrannus Boso, went to Rouen, and married Brunichildis. When Chilperic heard this, he came to Rouen and, after a few days, returned to Soissons with Meroveus. Not long afterward, suspecting him because of his union with Brunichildis, he stripped him of everything and committed him to custody.

(V, 3.) While he was being held in custody, Meroveus was tonsured; his clothing was changed, and he was ordained a priest. He fled and sought refuge in the church of Saint Martin near the city of Tours, where these events took place.

(V, 14.) He remained hidden in that basilica for two months. Afterward he returned to Brunichildis, but was not received by the Austrasians. When he was hiding in the Campania of Reims, he was treacherously captured by the people of Arras. Fearing that he might be handed over to his father, he urged his companion to attack him. When the king arrived after this had been done, Meroveus was found dead.

[Col. 0124D] (V, 31.) In those days, when Justin died in Constantinople in a state of madness, Tiberius became emperor and was generous in almsgiving. (V, 38.) In the fifth year of Childebert, a great persecution of Christians took place in Spain. (V, 35.) A dysenteric illness also seized Gaul; as it grew worse, Chilperic lost three grown sons in a single year. The fourth, who survived, named Clovis, was committed to prison [Col. 0125A] and, through his mother’s intrigue, was killed by his father with a knife. Childebert the king gave his sister in marriage to Herminigildus, son of the king of the Visigoths; at his wife’s urging and through the preaching of Leander, bishop of Seville, he was converted to the faith of Christ. [FREDEG.] After Tiberius, Maurice assumed the empire. From him Childebert received fifty thousand solidi of gold to drive the Lombards from Italy. He therefore entered Italy, and all its inhabitants submitted to his authority; he also established friendship with them and returned from there in glory.

*(Life of Agericus.)* Since he was supposed to hold a hearing and assembly of many people at Verdun, and honored this blessed Agericus, of whom we are speaking, with embraces of affection and veneration, he could not bear to burden him with the necessary provisions. He therefore removed the obligation of service and transferred the hearing [Col. 0125B] to the city of Metz. When, at a later time, he passed through that city, and had been received with kindly sweetness by the holy bishop, while the hospitality of his household was also offered him with every care and attention, the steward in charge of all his affairs approached him amid the very bustle of royal service and said:

“And if, my lord, we abound in other provisions, we cannot provide wine as befits royal majesty, because, apart from one medium-sized vessel, commonly called a *tonna*, we have nothing.”

Then the man of God, distressed in bodily circumstances but enlarged in heart in the Lord, said:

“Do not grow weak through despair, but bring me some of that same liquid. God is able to change the sadness of our poverty into the joy of abundance.”

*(Fol. 47.)* He spoke, and when wine had been brought to him, he took a little. [Col. 0125C] Raising his eyes to heaven, he said:

“Lord, I ask that this wine be increased.”

When, at his command, it had been poured back into the vessel mentioned above, wine began to be served abundantly; it began to flow in abundance. The more the vessel was emptied to satisfy the drinkers, the more it increased, overflowing at the Creator’s command and by his power.

For the Almighty, who had made wine from water at Cana of Galilee, was able also to make wine from wine through the sincere word of the petitioner and his unquestioning faith.

What more need be said? They drank like Gauls, and there was no measure in the distribution. For many days they tried to empty that wine-vessel, and in a sense they seemed to be pouring wine into it while they persisted in drawing it off. The small blessing grew as many drank deeply, and, by God’s command, surpassed the limits of nature. At last, when the service was finished and the wine had not diminished, the king, astonished at the miracle, humbled himself before the bishop and revered God in him. He displayed royal generosity, and he who had drunk the wine of power offered vineyards and estates to the church out of love and devotion for the bishop; by privilege and thereafter by firm authority, the church has possessed them down to the present day.

Indeed, the wine of power, served by the holy prelate from the God of powers to the king and his companions, so gladdened the devout hearts of the people at that time that they built an altar at the place where the abundance had flowed forth through the blessing, so that future generations might know by such a sign the excellence of the merit by which blessed Agericus [Col. 0126A] shone before God in eternal glory.

A certain man also of very high rank, who was destined to be deprived of life by the king because of his crimes, was saved through the prayers of the blessed bishop. Therefore that man gave his own allod to the church of Verdun and confirmed the gift in writing.

*(Fol. 46'.)* Guntramnus [Note: [Col. 0125] “Guntramnus—orphanos” in the margin of fols. 46 and 47.] Boso, the duke, being hated by the queen, began to go about among bishops and nobles and to beg forgiveness. [GREG. Tur., IX, 8.] For when Childebert was still a young man, Boso had assailed the queen with insults and reproaches, and therefore the king ordered him to be pursued. Seeing himself in danger, he went to Verdun, thinking that through the blessed Agericus, who was the king’s father from the baptismal font, he could be saved. The bishop, intending to intercede for him, hastened to the king.

Since the king could not refuse this, he said:

“Let him come, and, after giving sureties in the presence of my uncle, let him undergo judgment.”

He was therefore brought in, stripped of his arms, and thrown prostrate before the king. He was ordered to rise and was entrusted to the holy priest until the presence of Guntramnus. (IX, 9.) After this Childebert hastened, with his mother, sister, and wife, to meet his uncle. When they had come together, Guntramnus Boso was presented without anyone’s defense, for the holy bishop had arranged it thus; the bishop, however, remained behind.

But when Boso was judged guilty on various counts, he fled to the bishop’s residence. When his killers pursued him there, and he would not allow himself to be torn away from the holy man, and when messengers sent by the bishop to the king—abbots and clergy acting as intercessors—were not heard, [Col. 0126C] by Guntramnus’s command fire was set to that house, so that if the bishop refused to come out, he too would be burned with it. *(Fol. 47.)* Hearing this, the clergy broke the door by force and drove the priest out.

But the wretched man, seeing himself pressed by the flames and finally attempting to leave, was seized by his enemies and killed. The priest grieved this greatly.

(IX, 12.) When certain leading men of the kingdom had discussed the deaths of the kings—namely, the uncle and the nephew—and were discovered and killed, one of them, named Bertefredus, fled to the city of Verdun. When his enemies pursued him, they surrounded with an army the church-house in which the bishop was staying and to which Bertefredus too had fled. Climbing onto the roof, they killed him and three boys by striking them with the roof tiles and timbers.

The holy [Col. 0126D] bishop grieved this greatly, because he had been unable to defend him and had also seen the place where he used to pray, and where he had gathered many relics of the saints, polluted with human blood. Childebert sent many gifts to recall him from his grief, but he could not be consoled.

(IX, 23.) He began to fall gravely ill from the sorrow of his long-lasting bitterness, especially because he kept Guntramnus’s sons with him, weeping every day for them, left orphans with him alone.

*(Life of Agericus.)* Once this holy man was passing through the city of Laon, and behold, a certain man met him, bound at the wrists and in fetters. With the torturer preceding him, a dark prison was being opened for him. *(Fol. 47'.)* He went on, but the unhappy man was driven forward more violently, filling the streets with his cries; by wailing and groaning he called upon all whom he encountered to help him.

Such is the repayment of sinners: repentance, always too late, is received amid torment, and the allurements of pleasures are punished by harsh and bitter endings.

When the pitiable man saw the merciful one, he asked, as best he could, for refuge and that he offer him the support of prayer. Mercy heard him, and the bishop, inwardly touched by grief and compassion, approached the torturer with many prayers and humble pleas, asking that he be moved and grant the wretched man the gentleness of pardon.

The torturer refused and rejected him, and in no way consented to hear him. The man’s crimes and misdeeds restrained the judge’s mind, preventing mercy from moving him. The bishop asked a second and a third time, [Col. 0127B] but was rejected. He repeated his prayer three times, yet was not heard.

What could compassion do? Where could it turn? A man could neither compel nor persuade another man, yet compassion continued to increase.

Therefore, turning to the Lord, he lifted his vows to heaven. He hastened to the fountain of mercy, so often experienced, praying that it might come to the aid of the wretched man, and that the invisible and almighty command might release what the proud and insolent judge had despised:

> The Almighty heard, and suddenly loosed the bindings;  
> The fetters fall, and no one is seen to release the chains;  
> No hand, no force—only God’s command.

When the judge, astonished, saw this, overcome by confusion and fear, he fell at the holy man’s feet, bound by the fetter of disobedience. He now asked and implored for himself the pardon that he had refused to grant to his neighbor when the latter begged for it. He forgave the man bound through guilt, while himself, released through pardon, asked only for the grace by which he might be set free.

Thus God worked upon his servant: he freed one by removing guilt and the other by granting pardon.

We have recorded in writing, for the knowledge and salvation of those who come after us, these few miracles of divine power shown to us through the holy man, according to our limited ability. We worship the finger of God, through which Egypt was oppressed, through which the enemy was driven out, through which the measure of faith exists, and through which the distribution of divine gifts is made, as it worked in these events.

We portray the outward matters, because they are visible, as though painting the beautiful and fair face of this our father and shaping it with the colors of lowly words. But if, with sweat and labor, we scarcely reach the door—that is, an understanding of outward things—what shall we do with inward things? How shall we penetrate what is closed and hidden?

Certainly, the servant of God served God most earnestly and attentively in this respect, because he listened with all his inward being to the voice that he heard proclaimed in the Gospel:

“When you pray, enter into your room and, having shut the door, pray to your Father.” (Matthew 6:6.)

What wonder, then, if we cannot recognize his secrets, since we are compelled to keep watch outside the door? Surely he considered it a cause of loss if even a friend came to know his secrets. He had read that King Hezekiah had imprudently offended God in this matter: when the envoys of Babylon came, he was found and reproved for showing them his treasures and storerooms of spices.

He feared and watched anxiously lest, if an enemy lying in ambush should break into his house while the doorkeeper slept carelessly, he himself, overwhelmed by the sleep of death, should perish through negligence. Therefore he guarded his heart with all vigilance, preserving within himself God’s holy temple unharmed and undefiled and cleansing it, and adorning it with the varied flowers of good works.

The people gathered, and the whole city streamed together daily, so that through him, from God’s sanctuary, they might receive oracles of salvation, as the ancient people received them through Moses, and responses concerning life. The priest himself, as high priest, frequently offered sacrifices to God both for himself and for those entrusted to him, and from the chair of the church taught the law of God thoroughly, so that it might be practiced. [Col. 0128B]

Thus, performing a spiritual service in the precious and holy garments of Aaron, he offered himself as a holy sacrifice pleasing to God, as the vicar of the Lord Christ, for the salvation of the people and for the acquisition of eternal praise.

God himself made him such a man and heir of singular glory. Before he was born, God had chosen him; through illustrious ministers of his house he was with him at all times and visited him through frequent encounters.

These bundles of honor, these insignia of the eternal city, this civic crown of the heavenly Jerusalem—how can a son of man, a worm, grasp them? *(Fol. 48.)* If you say that he too is a son of man and a worm, you speak truly; but the miracles especially performed by the Son of God and Man in his friends surpass such things and must not be compared with servile things and Adam’s poverty.

For the moment I shall speak—shall speak of myself—because, pressed down by the little burdens of ancestral corruption, I shall neither attempt to reach the root of his charity fixed in heaven nor claim myself worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. Yet I shall follow his footsteps by proclaiming them, if God should deem it worthy to reveal anything through his enlightened servant.

When, therefore, the man of God was filling his days with the extraordinary virtues mentioned above, and faithfully gathering a good profit for his good Lord from the talents entrusted to him, while diligently performing the duty of hospitality according to the apostle’s command, it happened that a cleric named Fortunatus once came to him. [PAULI Hist. Lang. II, 13; BERT. VI.]

When this same Fortunatus was in Italy, namely in the city of Ravenna, and was suffering greatly from pain in his eyes, he came to a certain monastery within that city’s walls, dedicated to the holy John and Paul. In it an altar of blessed Martin had also been constructed, and nearby there was a window in which a lamp had been placed. He was accompanied by Felix, bishop of the city of Tarvisium, who was likewise suffering from pain in his eyes.

It seemed to Fortunatus that they should anoint their eyes with oil from the lamp burning before the altar, invoking the name of Saint Martin. When he had done this, both immediately received the restoration of their sight through the saint’s merits.
