[Note: [Col. 0127] “etiam alta, construc, uam, n qua, ituta, lice, episcopo, dolorem deleta.” The supplied note preserves damaged or deleted readings; the sense of the affected passage is as translated above.]

Burning with the desire to see the tomb of Saint Martin, Fortunatus came from Italy into Gaul, and his route took him through Verdun. The bishop, whom canonical law commands to receive everyone, welcomed him kindly, served him humanely, and, according to his custom, opened to him the full resources of holiness and compassion.

Fortunatus, thinking of a reward for the service he had received, later returned to Poitiers and lived there. He was ordained priest and afterward bishop of that same city. Since he was learned in the grammatical arts, he composed there a poem in praise of Agericus, skillfully arranged in hexameter and pentameter verses. We have thought it worthwhile to append them here.

Thus the poem is set forth:

> City of Verdun, although enclosed within a narrow sphere,  
> You are made spacious and pleasing by the merits of your bishop.
>
> Greater grace shines forth within a confined circuit—  
> Yours, Agericus—which honor has increased still more.
>
> You have poured out many seeds of great praises,  
> Which by your work you will reap mature in fruitful abundance.
>
> In the present age you distribute sustenance to the needy;  
> From this the coming day will increase your riches a hundredfold.
>
> Shepherd, you unlock the inner chambers of hidden teaching;  
> You feed your flocks not only with food but also with your mouth.
>
> You renew ancient temples and construct new ones more splendidly;  
> The house of the Lord is more splendid when you serve him.
>
> You fill the noble fonts of sacred baptism;  
> So piously filled with the divine fountain, you perform your ministry.
>
> This bright hall shines with sincere and radiant serenity;  
> Even if the sun flees, here a close-pressed daylight remains.
>
> People eagerly hasten from everywhere to the new temples,  
> And you give the peoples more of God in love.
>
> The needy has earned you as his consolation, the naked as his clothing;  
> Alone, you remain drink and food for all.
>
> Happy are you, lover of eternal light through your merits,  
> Preparing now at small cost ages that shall not die.
>
> As Phoebus suspends his lofty course in the ether  
> And scatters everywhere his pure, fiery radiance,
>
> Pouring out his rays, he claims the whole world for himself,  
> Filling mountains and plains, possessing the low and the high.
>
> So, bishop, you shine with the splendor of your soul like the sun;  
> He gleams with his rays, and you yourself with yours.
>
> Sacred Agericus, through whose cultivated speech  
> The fields of the Church delight in their fertility,
>
> Sterile in earthly things, fertile in heavenly matters,  
> Denying all that is perishable, rich as you go toward the heavens.
>
> Pure from allurements, rejecting the world’s wanton delights,  
> You, from whom the bitter love of the flesh has stolen nothing.
>
> Slippery guilt perishes, and death does not rejoice in crime  
> When it sees your members freed from sins.
>
> By dwelling in holy temples you are held so pure  
> That your hearts, father, are holy temples of God.
>
> Christ chooses to be concealed in such a vessel;  
> He himself possesses the house that he purified for himself.
>
> There is no deceit upon your lips, nor savage clouds in your mind;  
> With a sincere mind, daylight blooms in your speech.
>
> You pour back a river of learned speech from its leaping source,  
> And nourish barren minds by watering them with your voice.
>
> You open the lofty mysteries of heaven to the earth;  
> Through you one knows, fears, prays to, and loves the Lord more.
>
> Victorious in divine teaching, eloquent bishop,  
> As a shepherd, by your admonitions you ensure that error does not oppress the sheep.
>
> You refresh with the delights that heaven, field, and water provide,  
> And food satisfies the peoples from one side, faith from the other.
>
> The poor receive help, the sorrowful hope, the naked clothing;  
> You make everything you possess belong to everyone.
>
> May lasting health remain with you here, even though the future lies beyond;  
> And may you long remain a shepherd, offering prayers for your flock.

When, therefore, he had patiently endured for a long time the prolonged sojourn of this life, awaiting death with delight, and had tirelessly carried the burden imposed by the day and its heat in the hope of salvation, and had made the tears of his daily increasing desire into the bread of good and joyful consolation, seeing his enemies—the vices—as the footstool beneath his feet, his soul rejoiced in the Lord, and his spirit exulted in God his Savior.

He bore heavily the bonds of earthly weight, and the more he was deprived of bodily strength, the more greatly he thirsted for the promised freedom, saying with the apostle:

“I desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better.” (Philippians 1:23.)

What, as an old and wearied man, he had held as through a mirror in an enigma, he burned to see face to face. But the good Lord delayed the cutting of the harvest because he knew and arranged the proper ripeness.

He had seen that during that harsh winter the man had swiftly labored with sweat; that he had overcome the winds of temptations, the frosts of tribulations, and the scorching heats of pleasures. As a provident farmer of holy virtues, God delayed cutting down the manifold fruit of the good soil, accumulating its fullness through patience.

The evening of death therefore drew near. Rejoicing and, in a sense, forgetful of what lay behind, he stretched himself toward what lay ahead, asking from the head of the household the denarius of prepared rest, the reward that had been promised and long awaited.

The anchor of hope, firm amid every danger, did not deceive him, and the truth emerged from the shadow of promise into the light. Touched by the combat of nature and knowing that the separation of body and soul was approaching, he trusted in God, who can destroy and save both soul and body. He ordered all the sons of his church to be summoned, especially the better members of the church, and, repeating his customary teachings of salvation and commending himself to them, at last he announced what was to come:

“On the coming Saturday, dearest sons, know that great serenity of heaven will come. For the Lord of the serene Sabbath will give me, his faithful servant, the Sabbath of rest, and, weary from the labor of the six days of this world, he will transport me, free from every labor, into the seventh day without evening.

“Therefore give back to Mother Earth what belongs to her; for God, my life, will receive what he breathed into my face as the breath of life.

“I also beg you, brothers—and now I am concerned for you—that the Lord, who is always and everywhere with you, never depart from your memory.”

He said these and similar things. As though preparing himself for the approaching Easter, he washed away, through sacred and manifold admonition, the filth and contagion of those standing around him and mourning—at one moment restraining them by correction from the things he was leaving behind, at another urging and impelling them toward the things to which he was migrating.

The Saturday he had foretold arrived. And behold, suddenly, in the room where the sick man lay reclining, a multitude was heard; voices were heard that no human tongue could pronounce and no mortal voice could render. Tears ceased; astonishment and ecstasy seized everyone, and all remained silent, held by wonder and fear.

Songs of different kinds, distinguished by the various sexes, were heard, but no one, in dark and fragile bodily form, was able to see who the singers were. Amid this festival, this symphony of joy, amid the rejoicing of the citizens above, the soul of the most holy bishop was taken from its corruptible prison into the hands of the holy angels. Like a snowy dove, it flew forth before all who saw it—those whose eyes God had opened so that they might be deemed worthy to see.

There the happy and blessed soul received eternally and happily from that same Lord the one thing that the Savior teaches in the Gospel to be necessary. [GREG. Tur., IX, 23.]

He died, as we said above, weighed down by the gall of those causes of bitterness, and especially consumed by hunger. His most sacred body was cared for with the pious diligence of his sons and, according to the father’s final instructions, was committed to the earth in the church consecrated in the name of Saint Andrew and blessed Martin. There, through his merits and prayers, divine benefits overflow, and the mercy of God heals everyone.

He rested in the month of December, on the first day, which was a Saturday. He was announced by an angel in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 518; born three years later, in 521; ordained bishop in the thirty-third year of his age, from the Incarnation of the Lord 553, in indiction 3, in the thirteenth year of Theodebert’s reign, two years after the Fifth Council of Constantinople, while Vigilius was acting as pope of the Roman Church and Justinian the Younger, nephew of Justinian the Elder, was emperor in his twenty-eighth year.

He lived in the episcopate for forty-seven years and died at the age of eighty-one, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 602, in indiction 5, which was the thirty-third year of Guntramnus, in the twelfth year of the papacy of the lord Pope Gregory.

(BERT. VII.) A certain abbot named Butiovaldus, seeking the episcopate, obtained nothing because he was proud. The royal authority, with the consent of the citizens, agreed that Caramerus, the referendary, should become a priest. After him there appeared . . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0131D] A place erased and left blank, amounting to one third of a line.] *(Fol. 49'.)* Ermenfridus, of whom we have no other record except that they are found among the bishops in the order of bishops. But for now, let this suffice concerning them.

[Col. 0131D] [GREG. Tur., IV, 46.] Chilperic, worse than Nero and Herod, after the many evils, wars, killings, and new and most burdensome exactions that he carried out throughout his kingdom, was returning from the hunt at the estate of Celles near Paris when night had already begun to darken. As he was being helped down from his horse and held one hand upon a boy’s shoulder, a certain man named Falco, sent by Brunichilde, approached and struck him with a knife beneath the armpit. With a second blow he spilled his life.

[FREDEG.] He devastated many regions, cursed bishops, destroyed many charters of the churches, never loved anyone, and was loved by no one. [GREG. Tur., IV, 46.] When he had breathed out his spirit, he was left alone. Madelulfus, bishop of Senlis, buried him at night. He died in the year 588, in the year . . . of Childebert, son of Sigebert.

[FREDEG.] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 593, while Guntramnus was reigning, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign, the lord King Guntramnus himself built a church in the suburb of Chalon in honor of Saint Marcellus. He enriched it with many possessions and, assembling a synod of forty bishops, decreed that monks should live there after the manner of the monastery of Agaunum.

When he was informed that his brother Chilperic had been killed, he went to Paris, took Chilperic’s son, named Clothar, from the baptismal font, and established him in his father’s kingdoms.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, a son was born to Childebert, named Theodebert, and in the following year Theoderic. Guntramnus adopted Childebert as his son because he had no sons. In that same year the Persian people believed in Christ, and the Persian emperor was baptized by Saint John of Constantinople together with sixty thousand of his people.

In the thirtieth year of his reign, which was the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 598, the seamless tunic of our Lord Jesus Christ was discovered. Gregory of Antioch, Thomas of Jerusalem, John of Constantinople, and many others lifted it from the city of Zafati together with a marble chest, carried it on foot to Jerusalem, and placed it in triumph at the place where the cross is worshiped.

After Guntramnus had held the kingdom of Burgundy for thirty-three years, he died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April and was buried [Col. 0132C] at Chalon. Childebert assumed his kingdom, held it for four years, and died in adolescence, in the seventeenth year of his reign, at the age of twenty-five, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 605.

His sons assumed the kingdom: Theodebert, that of the Austrasians, with his seat at Metz; Theoderic, Guntramnus’s kingdom in Burgundy, with his seat at Orléans. These two kings took up arms against Clothar, son of Chilperic. Clothar was defeated there and made peace under whatever terms he could.

*(Fol. 50.)* In the year . . . of Theoderic, which was the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 602, Phocas, duke and patrician, killed the emperor Maurice and assumed the empire. Sons, Sigebert and Childebert, were born to Theoderic.

Brunichilde and Protadius, mayor of the palace, stirred Theoderic against his brother. For this reason Protadius was killed by Theoderic’s army, and the brothers were reconciled. At the counsel of his grandmother Brunichilde, Theoderic condemned Saint Desiderius, archbishop of Vienne, to exile and, after he had been recalled from exile, had him stoned to death.

He also drove Saint Columban from his kingdom; Clothar, son of Chilperic, received him, for he was a lover of wisdom.

Again, through Brunichilde’s counsel, strife was stirred up between the brothers, and with a gathered army they fought in the plain of Toul. Theoderic, victorious, pursued Theodebert as far as Cologne, where Theodebert, having reassembled his army, renewed the war. So great a slaughter took place there that, because of the multitude of the slain, the corpses of the dead had nowhere to fall. From Tolbiacum to Cologne the defeated army covered the earth.

Theoderic, victorious, pursued his brother and, after Theodebert had been captured through the treachery of his own men, sent him to his grandmother Brunichilde. She had him tonsured as a cleric and shortly afterward killed him.

*(Expanded Life of Goericus.)* During the reign of King Theodebert, the holy Goericus, the last king of Aquitaine, a man powerful in upright conduct, was struck with blindness by the Lord. Through an angelic revelation he came to Metz, which was governed by Saint Arnulfus, his relative. He was given sight by Saint Stephen and constructed the church of Saint Peter. In the time of Dagobert, when Saint Arnulfus withdrew to the wilderness, Goericus was appointed bishop in his place and governed for eighteen years. He died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October and was buried in the monastery of Saint Symphorianus.

*(Life of Lupus of Sens.)* In the time of Theoderic and Brunichilde, Saint Lupus of Sens flourished. He was the nephew of Austerius, bishop of Orléans, and Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre.

[FREDEG.] In the sixteenth year of his reign, which was the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 615, Theoderic, wishing to attack Clothar, died at Metz from a flux of the bowels. Brunichilde installed his son Sigebert in his place. Clothar attempted to recover the boundaries of the kingdom that were owed to his authority. Sigebert met him; Clothar captured and killed him through the treachery of his own men and seized his five brothers together with Brunichilde.

He killed the boys separately and condemned Brunichilde to a miserable death, having her tied to the tails of untamed horses, [Col. 0133C] in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 623. She was also buried at Autun.

Clothar obtained the monarchy of the three kingdoms in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, just as blessed Columban had foretold. In the thirty-eighth year of his reign he made his son Dagobert his associate in the kingdom.

In the forty-second year of his reign, a serious dispute arose between Clothar and his son because Clothar wished to retain for himself everything that belonged to the kingdom of the Austrasians. Therefore twelve judges were chosen from among the Franks, among whom was Saint Arnulfus, bishop of Metz. Through their counsel the father was reconciled with his son.

In the preceding year, when Dagobert was already governing the kingdom of the Austrasians vigorously, a certain man named Haroaldus incurred his displeasure. [Note: [Col. 0133D] Read *Chrodoaldus*. Fred., chapter 52.] The lord Arnulfus and Pippin, mayor of the palace, became intercessors for him, but not long afterward he was killed at Trier.

In the year 630 Clothar died, and Dagobert obtained the monarchy in the fifteenth year of his reign. Bereft of his father, he ordered the Austrasians whom he ruled to advance their army, sending envoys into Burgundy and the other parts of the kingdom so that they might choose him as their king. When he came to Reims, they all surrendered themselves to him.

His brother Aribertus sought to establish that he could assume the kingdom, but his intention achieved little because of his simplicity. After Dagobert had obtained the kingdom, however, he acted with wise counsel and granted his brother Toulouse, Quercy, Agen, Périgueux, and Saintonge, together with the territory extending from these places toward the Pyrenees. Aribertus reigned in Provence and Aquitaine, and after three years he conquered all Gascony and subjected it to himself.

[BERTAR.] In the year of the Lord 582 Saint Germanus of Paris died, and in 630, under Dagobert, Saint Paul of Verdun, his brother, flourished. If, as it is written, this is so, he lived sixty years and more after him. They were born in the territory of Autun, in the village of Lausia; in the farmhouse of their birth neither dog nor bird can seize prey without immediately dying. This has been proved by experience.

That place retains to the present day a little church distinguished by the name and power of Saint Germanus. [Col. 0134B]

[BERTAR.] In Dagobert’s time, after Bishop Ermenfridus, Saint Paul of Verdun was brought from the monastery of Theolegium. He was the brother of Saint Germanus, bishop of the church of Paris, and was consecrated bishop in the church of Verdun; his memory is eternal.

While leading a monastic life, he had been assigned obedience in the brothers’ bakery. Fearing that, when the appointed hour came, the brothers might not have bread, he removed the fire from the oven, entered inside it himself, cleaned the oven in his cowl, and arranged the bread there for baking. He came out unharmed and, at the appointed time, distributed the holy bread to the brothers in the refectory.

When he had been ordained bishop, Grimo, a nephew of King Dagobert, a deacon also called Adelgisus, who had been reverently educated by Saint Paul from childhood, out of love for the bishop gave his property—namely, the monastery of Theolegium—to Saint Mary at Verdun. He confirmed the gift by his own written charter and by the charters of many faithful people, and established with every authority that the church of Verdun should possess that monastery forever.

For the sustenance of the brothers, Grimo assigned the estate of Frasindus as an act of his piety. Saint Paul also purchased the estate of Basonis from his revenues. He drew up the canonical privilege of that church from the older estates and confirmed it under divine attestation by his own authority and that of other bishops.

While holding the episcopate, he performed many miracles. After his death, when he had been placed in the basilica of Saint Saturninus, he granted many benefits of healing to all who asked in faith. He gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and freed the sick from various illnesses.

And what more? He enlarged the church entrusted to him with temporal possessions, adorned it with the flowers of good works, and the almighty Lord causes his soul to rejoice with the saints in eternal glory.

He rested in the month of February, on the ninth day. After him Gisloaldus became bishop, then Gerebertus. [Note: [Col. 0133D] What followed has been erased.]

[FREDEG.] In the sixth year of his reign, Dagobert entered Burgundy, and the bishops and all the nobles of Burgundy were so shaken with fear at his arrival that everyone marveled at him because of the justice he practiced. *(Fol. 51.)*

He came first to Langres, then to Dijon, and, remaining at Latona for many days, administered such justice that no one came before him who returned without receiving justice. From Latona he came to Chalon, then to Autun, from there to Auxerre, then to Sens, and from there to Paris, out of love for the administration of justice. He neither allowed sleep to reach his eyes nor satisfied himself with food.

In the seventh year of his reign, a son was born to him, named Sigebert, whom his brother Aribertus took from the baptismal font. Aribertus himself died the following year. He had a young son, Chilperic, who died not long afterward and is said to have been killed through Dagobert’s intrigue. [Col. 0135B]

In the tenth year of Dagobert’s reign, the Wends were ravaging Thuringia. When they pressed their attack vigorously, Dagobert came to Metz and, on the advice of the bishops and nobles, made his son Sigebert king. He established his seat at Metz and appointed Cunibert, bishop of Cologne, and Ansegisus, the duke—also called Anschisus—to govern the palace.

*(Genealogy of the Carolingians.)* This Ansegisus fathered Pippin, and Pippin fathered Charles. He handed over to his son a sufficient treasure, raised him appropriately to the summit of the kingdom, and confirmed by an edict what he had granted him. They usefully defend the kingdom of the Austrasians and the frontiers of the Frankish kingdom.

In the eleventh year [Note: [Col. 0135] In the margin.] of Clovis, son of Dagobert, Magoaldus, abbot of Flavigny, died, and the lord Widradus was ordained abbot on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. [Col. 0135C] He governed for twelve years.

In the twelfth year of Dagobert’s reign, a son was born to him, named Clovis. After his departure, his father granted him Neustria and Burgundy, while he granted the kingdom of the Austrasians to Sigebert.

In the thirteenth year of his reign Dagobert decisively defeated the Gascons, and in the following year the Bretons and Gascons submitted to him after giving oaths.

He died in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 641, in indiction 14, in the twentieth year of his reign. He was buried in the church of Saint Denis at Paris, which he enriched with such great treasures that anyone who saw them marveled.

His son Clovis succeeded his father in the government. In the second year of his reign, Pope Martin assumed the pontificate of the city of Rome. *(Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.)*
[REGINO.] Clovis, uncovering the body of blessed Dionysius, broke off and stole a bone of the arm with insufficient reverence; immediately, struck with stupor, he fell into madness, and after two years ended his life together with his kingdom. He had three sons, Chlothar, Theuderic, and Childeric, whom he begot by Queen Balthild. Ega, guardian of the palace and tutor of the kingdom, governed the palace and kingdom worthily.

In the third year of Clovis’s reign Ega died, and Erchinoald became mayor of the palace, a patient man, full of every virtue and a lover of peace and justice. Pippin [Col. 0136A] likewise, after the death of his father Anchises, vigorously governed the kingdom of Austrasia together with Bishop Cunibert, as mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Sigebert, and was loved by everyone. He received at the estate of Compiègne the portion of Dagobert’s treasures that belonged to Sigebert, and transported it to Metz.

After this Sigebert died. His son Dagobert took over his kingdom. Since Pippin and Grimoald, Pippin’s son, judged him unfit to administer the kingdom, they had him tonsured as a cleric. (Life of Wilfrid.) Balthild, having sent soldiers, killed Dalfinus, bishop of Lyon, in the year 661; by him Saint Vulfridus, bishop of Eboriacum, was consecrated. He was the first to preach in Frisia, before Saint Willibrord. (Second Life of Balthild.)

Clovis, after completing seventeen years in the administration of the kingdom, [Col. 0136B] died in the first bloom of youth, leaving three sons with Queen Balthild. [Note: [Col. 0135] in the margin.] His archchaplain was Saint Genesius, abbot, who was subsequently appointed archbishop of the church of Lyon. He died before the queen and, at the very moment of her death, appeared to her with great light, together with angels and archangels, and led her to the dwelling of everlasting peace. After him Saint Landebertus, abbot of the church of Fontenelle, presided over the metropolitan church of Lyon. By him Saint Ansbert, bishop of Rouen, was consecrated in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 678, in the fifth indiction, in the ninth year of Theuderic’s reign.

The year of the Lord’s incarnation 682; the second year of Pope Agatho; the thirteenth year of Theuderic, son of Balthild.

(Chronicle of Dijon.) Chlothar, the elder, obtained his father’s kingdom of Neustria and Burgundy, [Col. 0136C] while Childeric received the kingdom of Austrasia and Germany in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 658, in the first indiction. Chlothar reigned for four years and died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 662, in the fifth indiction. (Life of Leodegarius.) After his death a dispute arose among the leading men concerning the kingdom. (Fol. 51′.) Ebroin, mayor of the palace, favored Theuderic; Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, and the others whose judgment was sounder favored Childeric. The better opinion prevailed, and Childeric was established as king of the Franks, because he would govern the kingdom of Austrasia energetically. (Deeds of the Franks.)

One of the writers reports that Theuderic was first raised to the kingdom of the Franks, with Ebroin installed as mayor of the palace, [Col. 0136D] but that, because of their wickedness and cruelty, they were expelled and Childeric was installed in their place. (Life of Leodegarius.) Leodegarius, therefore, under Childeric, administered the affairs of the kingdom well and usefully, so that whenever he found anything contrary to the laws of the ancestors, whose life had been praiseworthy, he corrected it and restored it to its former condition. [Note: [Col. 0135] in the margin.]

Lord Widradus, abbot, died on the fifth day before the Nones of October, and in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 663 Bishop Gayroinus succeeded him. During his time [Note: [Col. 0135] Pippin, mayor of the palace; compare Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova*, I, 269.] Pippin transferred to that church [Col. 0137A] Glennon with its dependencies. He died on the day before the Nones of July during the emperor’s expedition. At the same time Bajo gave Saint Praejectus Pulligny with its church, Magniacum, and Pruiniacum; and his wife gave Puteoli, Opiemariacum, and Cleriacum, in the seventh year of Childeric. [Note: [Col. 0137] On the Sunday before the middle of the month of May; same source.]

In those days the aforementioned Leodegarius governed the church of Autun, Gerebertus the church of Verdun, whom we have already mentioned, and Saint Theodardus the church of Tongeren. (Life of Lambert.) At King Childeric’s court was Saint Lambert, a young man of good character, who, after Saint Theodardus, received the bishopric of Tongeren with the consent of the nobles and leaders.

While Childeric was energetically and prudently ordering the affairs of the kingdom, discord increased among the leading men, at the prompting of the envy of the evil devil, [Col. 0137B] and that celebrated prince was killed in the year 670 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction, after completing twenty-two years in the administration of the kingdom. His brother Theuderic succeeded him. (Life of Leodegarius.)

In those days there was such tribulation in the Church, through Ebroin’s wickedness, that it seemed to surpass in cruelty the times of Nero and Decius. [ADO.] Then Saint Leodegarius was killed, together with his brother Gerinus, by Ebroin himself; Saint Lambert was killed by Count Dodon. Ebroin, raging with cruelty, was killed by Ermenfrid the Frank.

At that time there was a man whom Ebroin himself had deprived of his sight, on an island called Barbara. While he was sitting at night by the bank of the Arar for the sake of prayer, he heard the rush of sailors. When he asked where that vessel was heading, he heard the reply: “It is Ebroin, whom we are carrying to Vulcan’s cauldron; there he will pay the penalty for his deed.”

(Chronicle of Dijon.) By then, as the kings were failing from their former vigor, the administration of the kingdom was carried on by the mayors of the palace. Thus, after Theuderic died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 692, in the fifth indiction, his son Chlothar succeeded him and reigned for one year. Among the dukes and nobles of the kingdom Pippin was preeminent, and the greater part of the kingdom was in his hands. After Chlothar’s death, his successor Childebert reigned for thirteen years. (Deeds of the Franks.)

Berthalamus, bishop, governed the church of Verdun; by his zeal and industry he acquired a great many estates for the church entrusted to him. [BERTAR.] After his death [Col. 0137D] Bishop Abbo succeeded him.

When King Childebert, who was surnamed “the Just,” had been removed from this life in the year 711, his son Dagobert succeeded him while still a child in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 712. He reigned for five years and died in 715. (Deeds of the Franks.) Daniel the cleric, also called Chilperic, succeeded him and reigned for more than five years.

[BERTAR.] In the year 711 from the Lord’s incarnation, Lord Madeleveus was born in the city of Verdun, from a family belonging to the church.

Pippin died in the year 714 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the month of December; his son Grimoald also died, and Charles succeeded in his father’s place. (Chronicle of Dijon.) [Col. 0138A] In those days the Franks laid one another low in mutual slaughter, and drove Theobald, Grimoald’s son, into flight by pursuing him. Rainfred was elected as mayor of the palace; from his hands, through many wars, Charles seized that office, and Rainfred died in the year 731. (Deeds of the Franks.)

In the year 717 Daniel, also called Chilperic, died at the estate of Attigny, was buried at Noyon, and Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, succeeded him. (Chronicle of Dijon.) After Theuderic’s death, Chlothar succeeded in 725; Childebert succeeded Chlothar; and Childeric succeeded Childebert. With him the line of King Clovis came to an end, the line that had ruled until then. (Fol. 52.)

[REGINO.] Charles, rescued by divine mercy from the prison in which he was held, fought against the enemy with a small force two or three times during the twenty-seven years in which he held the chief power under the kings mentioned above, and at first withdrew. At last, at Vinchy, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, he fought against Rainfred, prince of the Franks, in the year 717, the third year of his principate. Having been victorious there, and granting him only one place to inhabit—namely, the city of Angers—he ruled the entire people of the Franks; devastated Saxony and Bavaria; entered Provence as far as Marseille; invaded Gascony; devastated Frisia; and crushed Alemannia. (Chronicle of Dijon.)

He was therefore called *Tudites*, which means “the smith’s hammer,” because just as all iron tools are beaten by a hammer, so he crushed all the kingdoms neighboring him. He also fought the Saracens not far from Narbonne and slaughtered a great number of them. [Col. 0138C] When they invaded Provence again and had captured Arles, Charles, joining forces with Liutprand, king of the Lombards, drove them out of those regions. [PAUL THE DEACON.]

At that time Peter, bishop of Pavia, flourished in life and deeds, adorned with the glory of virginity. He had once been exiled by King Aripert to Spoleto. Charles sent his son Pippin to the aforementioned King Liutprand so that he might cut his hair. When Liutprand cut his hair, he became his godfather; and, having enriched him with many gifts, he sent him back to his father.

While Leo was emperor, in the time of Pope Gregory III, the monastery of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino was restored at the urging of Duke Petronax, almost 110 years having already passed since its destruction. Pope Zacharias also contributed many things to it, among them granting the Rule that Saint Benedict had written with his own hand.

[BERTAR.] At that time Bishop Peppo presided over the church of Verdun. In the rebellion that we said had arisen between Rainfred, prince of the Franks, and Charles *Tudites*, Peppo supported Charles’s side; for that reason, by payment made to Charles and to one of his noble vassals, he obtained the estate of Calmont with all its dependencies. After God had secured the kingdom of the Franks for Charles, he added many other possessions as well, as the record of the charters shows. After Peppo’s death, Volchisus became bishop, and after him Bishop Agroinus, [Col. 0139A] who presided over that church for very few years.

(Chronicle of Dijon.) In the year 741 from the Lord’s incarnation, Charles died, and his sons Carloman and Pippin took over the government of the kingdom. But in the seventh year after his father’s death, in the year 747 from the Lord’s incarnation, Carloman, leaving the care of the kingdom to his brother Pippin, went to Rome and established a monastic dwelling on Mount Serapti. Later, unable to endure the disturbances caused by those who visited him frequently, he moved to Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino. (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.)

At that time Pope Zacharias governed the Roman Church. He had succeeded Gregory III in the year 742 and governed that church for ten years, three months, and fourteen days. [REGINO.] Having received an embassy from Pippin through Burghard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad, Pippin’s chaplain, concerning the unworthiness of the kings descended from the ancient stock of the Merovingians, as we have briefly indicated above, Zacharias instructed the people of the Franks that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the title.

(Annals of Fulda.) Thus Childeric, the last king of that stock, was deposed, thrust into a monastery, and Pippin was elected king and consecrated by Boniface, bishop of Mainz, at Soissons, in an estate, in the year 752. (Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.)

Stephen, who had succeeded Zacharias, also, because of the attacks of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, left Rome on the fourteenth day of October, in the seventh indiction and the second year of his pontificate, in the year 754 from the Lord’s incarnation. He came to Pippin in Francia, appointed him defender and prince of the Roman Church, confirmed him as king by his own anointing, and anointed his two sons, Carloman and Charles. (Annals of Fulda.) From that time Rome was removed from subjection to the Greek Empire.

In the year 755, [Note: [Col. 0139D] in the margin.] after Gayroinus, Manasses was appointed abbot of the church of Flavigny, during the time of Pippin, formerly mayor of the palace and then king of the Franks.

In the year 753 from the incarnation of the Word made human, Lord Maldeveus assumed the bishopric of the church of Verdun. He was born in the same city of Christian and distinguished parents. Immediately reborn from water and the Spirit in the seven stages of baptism, he received the seven gifts of the Paraclete Spirit. Thereafter he received the flesh of the spotless Lamb together with its blood, a candidate adorned with the garment of virginity and the lamp of immortality. [Col. 0139D] (Fol. 52′.)

At that time all Belgica was burning with the daily pressure of wars. [EINH. Life of K.] For the royal dignity, which had taken its beginnings from King Merovech and had continued through King Childeric—who, at the command of Stephen, Roman pontiff, was tonsured and thrust into a monastery—was at that time without any vigor and displayed in itself nothing except the empty name of king. Wealth and abundance of revenues, the administration of the kingdom, and everything that had to be done or arranged either at home or abroad remained in the hands of the prefects of the palace, who were called mayors of the palace.

Through the license of these prefects, insolence of character grew, the cruel power of the lords increased, and envy was not lacking—envy that brought the rights of kingdoms to ruin. One man was puffed up against another; each seized the royal title. As this discord increased, cities were depopulated, churches burned, divine services suppressed, monasteries of men overthrown, those of women violated, and everything laid waste. At that time there was no less lamentation in the churches than in the times of Decius and Diocletian. [BERT. 12.]

In this storm the city of Verdun, after Bishop Agroinus had died, remained vacant for many days, deprived of its shepherd.

In those days, after the noble boy Madelveus had been weaned, he was entrusted to religious men to be instructed in letters. Having quickly committed their elements to memory, he applied himself to understanding the precepts of the grammatical art, through which he might recognize truth and be able to avoid faults. After this he ascended the tribunal of rhetoric. But because a rhetorician is a transmitter of eloquence, while eloquence without wisdom is usually exceedingly harmful and never beneficial, he abandoned the practice of speaking and devoted all his effort to the most upright and honorable studies of reason, referring the study of right reason to divine matters and the study of honorable duty to human affairs.

From this he understood that all things which are dealt with in speech, action, and the whole world are ten in number—those that are called the categories. With an alert mind he distinguished the disguises of arguments and the perplexities of syllogisms, and sharpened the edge of his teachable intellect in them to the utmost. From there he entered the quadrivium, where, with an acute mind, he grasped the cubes of arithmetic, the sounds of music, the modes of geometry, and the rays of astronomy, [Col. 0140C] and attained the perfection of the twofold thesis, that is, of theory and practice.

Thus, after passing his childish years simply at home, like the patriarch Jacob, he advanced and knocked at the doors of adolescence, progressing and pleasing both God and men. Indeed, after the flowers of rhetoric and the serpents of syllogisms, he entered the fields of divine Scripture. There, hearing from the Apostle, “Everyone who lives chastely is a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 6:19), and likewise in the Apocalypse, “Those who have not been defiled with women follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4), he immediately consecrated his earliest age to Christ the Lord. Longing with his whole heart to please and serve him, whose portion and inheritance he is, and reflecting on his ways, he turned his feet toward the testimonies of Jesus, seeking to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

At last, having obtained the honor of the clerical state, he received blessing from the Lord and saving mercy from God. For by daily advancement he went from virtue to virtue. Horrified by the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and following the narrow and constricted way by which one goes to the stars, he pierced his flesh with the fear of God, putting his members to death together with vices and desires; walking by the spirit and not fulfilling the desires of the flesh; devoting himself to works of mercy; afflicting his body with vigils and fasts; persisting in prayer; attending to meditation; restraining his ears from evil speech; turning his eyes away from vanity; striving to be a good odor to God in every place; guarding his mouth from excessive or empty speech; shaking his hands free from every gift; always directing his counsel and work toward God; and seeking in every action not his own glory but God’s.

> As a youth the righteous man lived by these studies,
>
> Answering the sacred orders with fitting conduct.

After this, advancing to greater things, he was elected to and received the honor of the priesthood, and, justified, attained it. Thus, by unanimous agreement and the election of all, he was established as rector and abbot of the church of Saint Vitonus. By the zeal of spiritual exercise and by temporal resources he improved it, and by example and teaching kindled it to love the service of God.

For he was outstanding in humility, abundant in charity, remarkable in prudence, praiseworthy in sobriety, distinguished in justice, and admirable in courage. Although he surpassed everyone in dignity, he was nevertheless subordinate to all in obedience, approved in patience, and made wholeheartedly an example for the flock, so that in him every subordinate might recognize the rule of life he ought to adopt.

This reputation of his spread almost everywhere; this report was continually on everyone’s lips. The piety and goodness of Madelveus illumined the provinces, filled the streets, and knocked at palace doors. With these merits preceding him, he was elected by the votes of all to the episcopate of the city of Verdun. Although, full of fear of God, he rejected it with all his heart and refused it with every effort, the opinion of the many nevertheless prevailed, with the grace of God going before it. By the unanimous agreement of clergy and people, and by the judgment of the bishops, he was deemed worthy and raised to the episcopal chair, [Col. 0141C] confirmed by blessing and consecrated by anointing.

(Deeds of the Bishops of Metz.) At that time Stephen II governed the Roman Church, while Pippin, son of Charles *Tudites*, ruled the Franks. Having been made king from mayor of the palace and prefect of the palace, Pippin sent to Rome Chrodegandus, an outstanding man worthy of every praise, who had been brought up in the palace of the aforementioned Charles and had served as his *referendarius*. Chrodegandus had been chosen by Pippin and all the Franks to summon the aforementioned Pope Stephen to Gaul, as everyone earnestly desired. (Fol. 53′.)

He did so; and Stephen also consecrated him bishop of the church of Metz in the presence of the king and the people, and granted him the pallium together with the title of archbishop. It is also read that this had occasionally been granted to certain bishops of the church of Metz because of the many devastations of the mother church of Trier.

Although Trier had received the primacy at the request of Queen Helena from Pope Sylvester of blessed memory, through the body of the apostle Matthias and through the staff of blessed Peter—and although it had possessed this from ancient times, because before the Lord’s coming the primates of the provinces had been located where the heads of secular law were, to whom those who could not or were not permitted to flee to the emperors’ courts for oppression or injustice used to have recourse—the apostles and blessed Pope Clement, as his blessed successor Pope Anacletus reports, ordered patriarchs or primates to be appointed and established in those same places, holding one form of office although their names were different, in accordance with divine law.

Nevertheless, it was so often worn down, as its sins demanded, that, while it lay vacant, the bishops of Metz exercised metropolitan office and dignity. Godo, a venerable bishop, also presided over the people of Toul. He obtained for his church from the aforementioned King Pippin the city’s immunity and the recovery of charters consumed by fire.

Among these men blessed Madelveus shone with the beauty of virtues and adorned the pontifical dignity with the splendor of good works. Although he received this office at an inexperienced age, he approached it suitably, with the accustomed abundance of his goodness. He devoted himself to preaching, strengthened the people with blessings, and urged them toward better things through sacred exhortations. What he taught in words, he demonstrated by examples.

At that time the city itself had been battered by barbarian attacks and wars, wearied by sieges, and filled with calamities. The temples of God within it had been polluted, the sanctuaries burned, the services violated, and the daily and nightly offices neglected. Some clerics had been driven away, some killed; those who remained were weighed down by great poverty and attended more to their own or earthly affairs than to heavenly ones.

Moved by this, the man of God was bitter in spirit and placed his hope in the Lord, crying to him with a humbled spirit: “All that you have done to us, Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we have sinned against you and have not obeyed your commandments” (Dan. 3:31). Immediately the Lord said to him: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will rescue you, and you shall honor me” (Ps. 49:15). But he replied in humble prayer: “My God, my mercy, you are my refuge [Col. 0142C] from the tribulation that has surrounded me, my joy; rescue me from the distresses and necessities of my children that surround me” (Ps. 31:7).

Without delay consolation came from the mouth of Truth: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). (Fol. 54.) Then he, rejoicing, said: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice” (Ps. 50:10).

He therefore entered the church with swift steps, summoned the clergy and people, and made known the true judgments of God. He urged them to confess their crimes and sins to one another, to produce fruits worthy of repentance, to attend the church, to devote themselves to prayer with tears, to hear the praises of God in silence and reverence, to give alms willingly according to their means, to practice hospitality without murmuring, to restore those at odds to peace before sunset, not to offer a false peace, to fear Gehenna, and to hope for eternal life. He then instituted by ecclesiastical sanction that the clerics should live according to rule, praise God seven times a day, and rise at night to confess to him; and, as far as he could, he arranged their daily sustenance from his own resources.

[EINH. Life of K.] Meanwhile he went to the court and informed Pippin—who, by the authority of Pope Stephen, had been made king from prefect of the palace [Note: [Col. 0141] “from prefect king,” written above the line, or “from prefect,” as the copy has it.]—of the devastation of the city and the calamity of the people whom he had undertaken to govern. He sought and obtained assistance from him through royal generosity [Note: [Col. 0141] “tradition” written above the line, or “generosity,” as the copy has it.] [Col. 0143A].

(BERT.) Through a contribution from the faithful he received certain estates, namely the estate of Wasnau or Warnunci, also Ramisbatium, and many others. He inserted them with his own hand into charters, which the king’s ring authenticated, and which the church of Verdun has not lost from that time onward. (Fol. 57.) Moreover, the king’s munificence did not fail the citizens: he gladdened the clergy, adorned the church, and restored the bishop, who had been rewarded, to the rejoicing people. [Note: [Col. 0143] “thus,” as the copy has it.] [Note: [Col. 0143] Turn three leaves, and seek what is missing here under this sign, as the copy has it.]

(BERT.) There were many things, however, that ought to have kindled him to love, promote, and enlarge that church: namely, the abundant love of Bishop Peppo for his father Charles *Tudites*, his gratuitous loyalty, and, during the time of the rebellion against Rainfred, prince of the Franks and Charles’s rival, their undivided partnership in undertaking labor and danger, on account of which the same Peppo also suffered many adversities.

But something more particular impelled him to the love, restoration, and common protection of all the churches. It seems not irrelevant to insert it in praise of this father of ours in this little work, both to restrain the pride of the kings and princes of the earth and to make clearer what had been the cause of the desolation of the churches of Trier and Verdun.

(Chronicle of Dijon.) Those who have read histories and searched the writings of the ancients know the deeds and battles of this Charles *Tudites*, who was called *Tudites*, “the smith’s hammer,” because just as all iron tools are beaten by a hammer, so he crushed all the kingdoms neighboring him.

For during the twenty-seven years in which he held the chief power under the kings Dagobert the Younger, Chilperic, Theuderic, Chlothar, Childebert, and Childeric [Note: [Col. 0136D] Neither Childebert nor Childeric was king of the Franks during Charles’s time.], after he had seized that office in the kingdom of the Franks from the hands of Rainfred, mayor of the palace, through many wars, he crushed all the kingdoms neighboring him—namely Saxony, Bavaria, Provence as far as Marseille, Gascony, and Frisia, and Alemannia—with such devastation that many churches still lament to this day the desolation inflicted upon them under him, and no passage of time has been able to erase from them the calamity of that tribulation.

(Fol. 57′.) For the entire treasury of the public treasury was squandered with such lavishness, and he gave so much to the soldiers, whom custom established as being called *soldarii* [Note: [Col. 0144D] From Germanic *sold*, pay or stipend.], who flocked to him from every part of the world for the sake of profit, that their troublesome and wicked class began in his time, and the treasure of the kingdom did not suffice for him; nor did the plundering of cities, the many devastations of foreign kingdoms, the stripping of churches and monasteries, or the taxes of the provinces.

When these resources failed, he even dared to seize the lands of churches and hand them over to those fellow soldiers. [Col. 0144A] Finally, he did not hesitate to give the bishoprics themselves to laymen, namely to his supporters and associates. Thus a certain Milo, a cleric in tonsure but a layman in conduct, dress, and behavior, irreligious, held and ravaged the archbishoprics of Trier and Reims for a long time. The bishopric of Vienne also, and many other bishoprics throughout various lands, were possessed by laymen, as the histories relate, and were conferred through lay hands.

If there were any bishops, they either supported him entirely, or ecclesiastical property was plundered, or, when they died, some novice—or someone whom the canonical sanctions do not admit—was substituted in their place. From this plunder, however, the city that supported him or provided him with assistance was somewhat exempt; for whichever city he relied upon, he protected through himself and his own men.

This is why, among the countless churches he had battered, he enriched the church of Verdun with estates during the episcopate of Peppo, because Peppo, as was reported above, supported his side and served him more closely during the time of the dispute. Nevertheless, after Peppo’s death, that church also experienced what the others suffered.

The aforementioned metropolis of Trier was so afflicted by this devastation that, because of its many calamities and humiliation, while it lay vacant the bishops of the city of Metz subsequently exercised the dignity and title of archbishops.

[ADO.] After the province of Lyon and Vienne had likewise been devastated and dispersed, each church remained for several years without bishops. For Wiliarius of Vienne, who had succeeded Austrobertus, seeing the church of Vienne disgracefully humbled because of the disaster of the Saracens threatening the provinces of Septimania, Vienne, and Lyon, while laymen sacrilegiously and barbarously possessed sacred property, abandoned his bishopric and sought the monastery of Agaune. There he led a venerable life, and this occurred in the time of Pope Stephen, who had succeeded Zacharias. After him Bertericus governed the church of Vienne; Paul succeeded him.

After Charles had died and been buried at Paris, and Pippin had obtained the office of mayor of the palace—he being a brother who preferred spiritual things to earthly things—and had subsequently, through his own efforts and with the consent of the Roman pontiff, as has been said, been raised to kingship, the merciful God, wishing to bind him to himself by many benefits and to frighten him by threats, so that he might learn to hope in God rather than presume upon himself, and so that, when prosperity followed, he might remember the Lord his God and not wish to imitate his father, who was known to have thirsted for the ruin of the churches, placed him near the city of Orléans and showed him what was being done with regard to Charles and what reward was being repaid to him for such great labors—not, as we fear, for the refreshment of the dead man, but for the edification of the living.

[Col. 0145A] In that same city there was a bishop named Eucherius [Note: [Col. 0145] Concerning what follows, compare the letter of the bishops to King Louis, year 858, III, 117; Sirmond, *Councils of Gaul*.], praiseworthy for the honesty of his life and admirable for the integrity of his conduct. While he was celebrating the solemn Mass on Easter Day, sitting on the episcopal throne, a thought arose in him concerning how many labors Charles had endured for the protection and enlargement of the kingdom, how many battles he had fought, how, after so many dangers, he had attained peace and ended his life in peace, and how his son had now been granted the honor of the kingdom.

As in silent thought he called the man fortunate because of such prosperous outcomes, sleep briefly played upon him while he was wavering in this thought. He was carried away in an ecstasy of mind and, led by an angel, was brought before the tribunal of the Judge. (Fol. 58.) In that heavenly assembly he heard the sweetness of spiritual melody, and he clung there in astonishment, amazed at the immense greatness of the vision.

There he also wondered whether, among those distinct choirs of blessed spirits, he could see Charles, lord of all Francia and father of the kingdom. The one who presided, answering his silent thoughts, ordered him to be led to the place where Charles was being kept.

He was therefore led into hell. While he marveled at the souls of the wretched, wasted by continuous, indescribable, and infinite torment, filthy, squalid, and stained with the utmost horror; while he feared the kinds of punishment and had almost forgotten Charles amid the terrible sounds of weeping and the gnashing of teeth, he saw Charles placed amid torments, turning as if in the middle of fire: now scorched by fire, now grinding his teeth in icy cold, now rising from the fire only to be tossed about in ice, and now, after being drawn out of the waters, returning to fiery vapors.

What a pitiable spectacle! He who shortly before had ruled Francia, who was called lord of the earth, victor over cities, conqueror of peoples, and subduer of kingdoms, so that he might enlarge his power had troubled the whole world:

> He burns in flames which no stream can hold,
>
> And is gripped by ice which flames cannot dissolve.

As he silently wondered at these things and anxiously turned over in his mind what they might mean, his guide, seeing him hesitate, said: “Behold the subject of your thoughts; behold the one about whom you were anxious in the house of the Lord. See what worldly power is worth; consider what the rule of the world can do, what it foretells, and toward what it tends. Behold Charles, the prince,

> By whom Francia once swelled, to whom she always remained subject,
>
> Who gave new laws, who took away each person’s own,
He is burned by flames; everlasting fire remains for him, because he put the Lord second and did not shrink from the shame of the churches. Announce this to his son, King Pippin, so that he may learn not to be proud or to put his hope in uncertain riches, but in the Lord God, who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna. And if he does not believe you, tell him to go to Paris and open his tomb [Col. 0146A], to look upon his father’s bones; from what he finds there he will put faith in your words.

He had said this, and the priest, returning to himself under the angel’s guidance, was astounded. Praising God and magnifying his incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways, he completed the solemn celebration of the Mass. Afterwards he related to the king and the nobles what he had seen and heard, and how he had been led by his thoughts to see and hear these things. He declared that this vision had been shown to him so that the punishment of his father might begin to benefit the king, and so that he might learn not to blaspheme [Note: [Col. 0145D] *blasphemare* c.], not to desire acts of robbery, and not to place his hope in iniquity; and although riches abounded for him, he should not set his heart upon them, because power belongs to God and mercy to the Lord, so that he may repay each person according to his works.

When Pippin had heard this, he began to become increasingly devoted to God [Col. 0146B], to venerate priests, to honor churches, and to guard himself with all his strength from those things in which he had learned that God had been offended by his father. When he came to Paris, therefore, he ordered his father’s tomb to be opened in the presence of his bishops and nobles; a sulphurous odor mixed with smoke issued from it. (Fol. 58'.) When it had been opened, they saw fire and dark, foul smoke, together with the remains of the consumed body. The tomb too had been blackened by smoke and fire, so that it was plainly understood that the priest’s vision had been true, that the man had been punished with a grievous penalty in the underworld, and that his body had been consumed in the tomb by a sulphurous fire through so extraordinary a miracle.

Great terror arose from this in the king and the people, and great devotion toward Christ and his priests [Col. 0146C] grew in everyone. All were zealous in piously restoring monasteries and churches. Hence it is that in his time so many bishops are found burning with the love of Christ who, having obtained the desired peace and secured the king’s friendship, devoted themselves to restoring churches and worked to nourish and care for souls, because they rejoiced that they had gained some measure of peace and quiet from the great oppression by which the churches had been crushed under the mayors of the palace.

For he loved all the priests of the Lord with the most devoted affection, and submitted himself with the readiest service of humility to those whom he saw to be closer to God through their works of piety. Among them he honored the blessed Madelveus with a devotion all the more devoted, the more clearly he recognized that Madelveus adhered to Christ God with the nobility of a cultivated mind [Col. 0146D]: adorned with good character, a good teacher, pious, reasonable, having children subject to him in all goodness, and prepared to give everyone an account of the hope that is in us.

(Fol. 58b.) Although for this reason he sometimes labored diligently in restoring churches, nevertheless the mass of the evil and the frenzy of greed were so great that the aged corruption of this wickedness endured until the time of Charlemagne, while each person strove to retain even more wickedly whatever he had seized unlawfully and unjustly [Col. 0147A]. Therefore, when the complaints of the churches were brought before the apostolic see and they demanded justice from it, Pope Adrian, meeting Charlemagne before the body of blessed Peter, obtained that everything should be corrected.

Accordingly, he sent a letter to all the archbishops and bishops of Gaul, which we have decided to place here, considering that it contains great authority concerning the churches of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0147D] Mansi, vol. XII, p. 847.]:

“Adrian, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Bertherius, bishop of Vienne, greetings.

“Our beloved and illustrious, religious son, Charles, king and patrician of the Romans, came to Rome and celebrated the Lord’s Passover with us at Saint Peter’s. Among other matters, we admonished him concerning the honor of the metropolitans and concerning the cities that had been handed over to laymen; for episcopal dignity had been trampled underfoot by the Franks for nearly eighty years. When the glorious king had heard this and similar matters, he promised before the body of the blessed apostle Peter that everything would be brought to correction at our request.

“Therefore it pleased us to send to all archbishops and bishops the authority of our letters, so that, just as the individual metropolitan cities were established by ancient privileges, so they might remain, and each metropolis might have its subject cities, which blessed Leo and his other predecessors and successors, after the Council of Chalcedon, assigned to the individual metropolitans. Nor should any metropolis suffer prejudice because we or our predecessor, at the request of devout Frankish dukes, granted the pallium to one of its suffragans.

“Nor should a church suffer any injury to its rank [Col. 0147C] because, through the injustice of whatever prelates and the devastation of barbarians, it lost and forfeited for sixty, seventy, eighty, or even more years its ancient dignity, strengthened by the firmness of the Roman bishops, when it had enjoyed that dignity for almost countless years by the ordering of the Spirit of God.

“Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have restored to each metropolitan his power according to ancient custom. We also asked our glorious and renowned son, King Charles, before the body of blessed Peter, to ensure that all the metropolitans should possess their ancient dignity. For this reason we have sent this letter of our authority to all; we wished you also to have it, so that you might know that the privilege of your church, which it possessed from the time of blessed Pope Leo, has been completely restored.

“Given on the Kalends of January, in the tenth year of the reign of the most pious Augustus Constantine, and in the first year of the patriciate of the most pious king Charles, crowned by God.”

Let what we have said here, as an admonition to those who hear it, concerning the peace of the churches of God restored under Pippin and Charles suffice. We do not think that this addition to the present work, in praise of our father, will weary the faithful; for although the discourse may add nothing to grace, the sequence of truth, expressed with a certain brevity, will nevertheless contribute very greatly to instruction [Note: [Col. 0147] “Return to the later material and repeat what you left out,” c., in the margin.]

(Fol. 54.) Thus the distinguished priest, making the rounds of the episcopal district with pastoral concern, built churches where none had existed, restored those that had fallen into ruin or old age, ordered the divine offices, instructed the congregations in saving doctrine, and confirmed them by episcopal blessing and the anointing of sacred chrism.

He always cherished and advanced the church of Saint Vitonus, in which he had been appointed pastor and rector before receiving the grace of the episcopate, with such great affection that he did not abandon its care even after he had assumed the bishopric. Rather, with every effort and by divine services, he made it illustrious, enlarging it also with estates and ecclesiastical furnishings, out of blessed remembrance of his predecessors who rested there. He did not wish to be separated from them either in body or in spirit, but desired to be buried with them in their place of repose.

He therefore gave to that church, from his own property, the estate of Raherei [Note: [Col. 0147D] Riecourt], with its appurtenances, for the burial of his body, as well as many other possessions, as the record of the charters shows. A certain man named Sartius, too, when approaching death and asking to be buried in the atrium of the aforesaid church, made a will by which he appointed that church heir to his possessions in the district of Verdun, in a place called Ex, beside the river of that name, which flowed there [Note: [Col. 0147D] Apparently Axona]. Thus Saint Vitonus, our father the blessed Madelveus, bishop and abbot, and the guardians of the holy body would be their perpetual heirs.

(Fol. 54'.) Following his example and moved by love for this blessed father, Grimbert, himself also owner of part of that estate and participant in its hereditary right, donated to the basilica of Saint Vitonus everything he possessed in that place: mansions, fields, ploughed lands, meadows, pastures, cleared lands, forests, waters, and the outlets and courses of waters. [Note: [Col. 0148D] *Olca*, German *Esch*: a portion of arable land enclosed by ditches or hedges.]

Afterwards, when a lease in precarium had been made, he received those same possessions from the holy man by beneficiary right, at a specified annual rent of twenty pounds of oil, to be delivered each year on the feast of Saint Vitonus for the lights of his church, in which that precious confessor rests; a definite period was also prescribed during which the saint was to receive them improved. The blessed bishop and abbot confirmed this charter of the precarium by his authority in the third year of the reign of Karlomannus, who was the brother of Charlemagne, on the Kalends of July, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 770, in the eighth indiction.

Aquitaine too received the great works of his holiness. It was often traversed by his footsteps, watered by his tears, strengthened by his teachings, and glorified by his miracles. (BERT.) For he frequently visited the possessions that the church of Verdun had possessed from ancient times in that region, and he carried with him the Lives and miracles of his episcopal predecessors, so that through their merits he might possess those properties more freely, or might be dearer in his lordship to the inhabitants and more humble toward his subjects.

These possessions were as follows: the abbey of Saint Amantius in the city of Rotenia [Note: [Col. 0149D] Rodez], together with its appurtenances; also the royal fisc of Maderniacus, and another called Puliniacus, granted for the use of the servants of Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus through the generosity of that blessed Amantius [Note: [Col. 0149D] In the year 952, Bishop Berengarius of Verdun eventually donated certain possessions of Saint Amantius to the Vitonians by charter, which Hugo himself inserted below in the text.]

(Fol. 54 in the margin.) In the thirteenth year of his ordination, which was the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 765, the bodies of the saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius were brought from the city of Rome by the venerable Grodegandus, archbishop of Metz. They had been granted to him by Stephen’s successor, Pope Paul, in the ninth year of his pontificate; in the following year both men departed from this world, in the fifth indiction. Grodegandus was buried and venerated in the monastery called Gorze, which he himself had built. There the body of Saint Gorgonius was later placed, in the fourth year after Grodegandus’s death, namely in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 768, when the sons of Pippin, Karlomannus and Charles, were already reigning. (Translation concerning Gorgonius? Compare the Annals of Fulda.)

(Fol. 54'.) While he was burning with a manifold desire for virtue, the thought came to him of going as a pilgrim to Jerusalem, to the tomb of the Prince of Life. He therefore hastened to fulfill by voluntary undertaking what he had conceived in his mind through divine inspiration. While everything necessary for the conduct of the journey was being foreseen, the principal church, because of the sins of the people, caught fire and was consumed by a raging blaze [BERT.].

The congregations are thrown into confusion; voices rise to heaven.

[Col. 0149C] One grief fills the city; a common horror grips the citizens.

Then Madelveus’s mind was torn in different directions, his spirit was distressed, and his heart disturbed. At last he came to himself, and remembering that proverb: “He is not great who thinks it a great matter that wood and stones collapse,” he bore the temporal loss patiently and immediately ordered the building to be restored to a better condition. After making an agreement with the craftsmen, appointing guardians, and arranging the necessary expenses, he urged, begged, and commanded them to begin the work promptly, hasten it attentively, and complete it diligently.

When these matters had thus been arranged, a change was made to his plans. (C. 780.) The expenses and vehicles necessary for so great a journey were prepared, and companions burning with the love of Christ were chosen [Col. 0149D]—humble in prosperity and strong in adversity. (790.) The metropolitan’s favor was sought, the consent of the provincial bishops was requested, and it was not refused.

(Fol. 55'.) They grieved at the absence of so great a companion [Note: [Col. 0149D] Thus the codex], but rejoiced in his justice; they prayed that Christ’s presence would accompany him and that the grace of the Holy Spirit would not be lacking. When asked, they requested his blessing; when greeted, they returned the greeting. Finally, on their advice, the church was ordered and the entrusted congregation commended. Thus, having received and given the blessing [Col. 0150A], the new pilgrim departed with joy in his heart.

He is supported by bands united by the love of devotion;

Tears wet their faces, sobs shake their breasts.

The pious man weeps, looking upon the flock that follows him in weeping;

He compelled them to return, but they press upon him more fervently;

They clasp his face, hands, and feet, and he consoles the mourners.

Again and again they cry: “Hail, farewell, and happy journey.”

Only after many prayers had he escaped their hands; then once more he strengthened them with blessings, earnestly warning and beseeching them to attend diligently to divine worship and to seek the salvation of souls with greater devotion. Finally, commending them to the Lord, he proceeded along the public road, relying on God’s help.

After traversing his native Gaul, he was received by Italy beyond the rough and trackless routes of the Alps, which led him to Rome and the thresholds of the apostles [Col. 0150B]. There, seeking the help of prayers at the various cemeteries of the martyrs, he spent the nights in continual vigils and frequently revisited the oratories of blessed Peter.

At that time Adrian, an apostolic man, presided over the Roman church. Madelveus, the most holy pilgrim, was announced to him. He received him kindly, kept him for many days even more kindly, and, when his intention had been tested, dismissed him with the apostolic blessing in the kindest manner.

After passing through the province of Nursia, Campania received the new pilgrim; from there the church of the archangel on Mount Garganus embraced him. Keeping vigil before its doors for several nights, he was strengthened by angelic consolations and gladdened by divine revelations.

Apulia awaited him joyfully, spreading abroad the marks of his holiness. When it saw him, it proclaimed in wonder with the Psalmist [Col. 0150C]: “As we have heard, so we have seen” (Psalm XLVII, 9).

After turning aside through various places, he entered the Pontic shores [Note: [Col. 0150D] That is, maritime shores]. From there turbulent waves threatened, and stormy winds came against him. They received Madelveus, the religious pilgrim-bishop, glorious in innocence. He paid the fare for the ship, entrusting himself to the danger of the sea and nourished by the heavenly sacrifice.

The voyage continued for many days. The priest persisted in preaching and instructed the sailors in saving doctrine. He fasted on successive days and passed the nights in vigils and prayers. But one day, when the sailors were singing their customary *celeuma* and making a noisy din with their nautical chatter, a sudden storm arose. The ship was tossed amid the waves [Col. 0150D] and its timbers were coming apart. With everyone’s spirit thrown into confusion and all hope of safety removed, only the fear of death remained.

(Fol. 55'.) Then the most blessed bishop—no fugitive exposed by a lot like Jonah, but distinguished by holiness, a proven servant of the Lord—at the request of everyone struck heaven with sobs and called upon Christ with groans. Immediately the sky opened to his prayers, and his prayer reached the heights and was heard. Without delay the serenity of the air and the calm of the sea returned, together with joy of spirit [Col. 0151A].

From there they reached the port of Byzantium rejoicing. In those days Constantine ruled the empire of Constantinople with his mother Irene. He was vigorous in military affairs and most devoted in divine worship. When he learned that the just man Madelveus had arrived, he ordered him to be sought out and brought into his presence. After hearing many useful things from him that contributed to his own salvation, he humbly asked him to pray to God’s mercy on his behalf. He offered him precious gifts, but Madelveus rejected them all; the emperor dismissed him with reverence so that he might continue on his desired journey.

Greece received him as a pilgrim and marveled at him as a philosopher among its own people and a divine philosopher beyond them. For he was truly wise, powerful in word and teaching. Honey proceeded from his mouth; the sweetness of honey was on his tongue [Col. 0151B]; honeycomb dripped from his lips, and through the sweetness of his speech he kindled in everyone the fire of love.

Meanwhile he descended to Ephesus to pray at the tomb of John the Theologian. There he poured out streams of many prayers, carrying in his mind the words, “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1), recalling and teaching that “the Word became flesh” (ibid., 14).

From there he reached Joppa, considering, amid the various perils of the journey, the tunics, garments, and alms of Dorcas; and with Peter he marveled at the linen sheet sent down from heaven by its four corners. He was commanded in it to slaughter quadrupeds and reptiles of the earth, signifying the mortification of vices, and to eat, producing fruits worthy of repentance (Acts IX, 39; X, 11).

After this he reached Jerusalem, long desired and now offered to his longing heart. He entered its tabernacles and frequented every holy place [Col. 0151C] in faith and love, worshiping above all the God who is in them. Every day he watered with a shower of tears the tomb of Jesus of Nazareth, who had been crucified, and glorified and worshiped Christ rising from the dead.

Meanwhile the patriarch Eusebius, who at that time governed the holy church of Zion, was informed of Madelveus’s most reverent devotion toward Christ, his daily visits to the holy places, his constant vigils, and the mortification of his own flesh. As soon as he heard this, he could not endure delay in seeking him. When he had found him, he immediately embraced him, marveling at his angelic countenance, modest speech, gentle step, and venerable attire.

Afterwards he brought him into his mother’s house and into his mother’s chamber, and gave him a cup of spiced wine and pomegranate juice (Song of Songs VIII, 2). As he was considering keeping him for all the days of his life, he was warned by a divine revelation not to be so intent upon his own wishes that he begrudged benefits to others, nor to wish to retain as a pilgrim one whom his children longed to have as an evangelical father.

Struck by this thunderbolt, he said to him trembling:

“It was my wish, my brother, that you should never be separated from me. But since we cannot resist God, return, my beloved; go out and follow the tracks of the flocks; feed your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents; catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards. Sit beneath the shade of the one whom you desired, who brought you into the wine cellar, ordered love within you, supporting you with flowers and surrounding you with apples. Let your beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his apples; let his left hand be beneath your head and his right hand embrace you.”

After saying these things [BERT. 12.], he brought forth many precious relics of the saints, together with a crystal chalice carved with wondrous workmanship, and offered them to him, saying:

“Receive, my dear one, this pledge of mutual love. May Christ the Lord, with the intercession of these and the other saints, grant that we may see each other again with joy in the heavenly places.”

At last, kissing each other’s faces, hands, and eyes and praying for good fortune and prosperity, they parted from one another in tears.

Madelveus then visited again and again the Lord’s tomb and the place of his ascension, where his feet had stood, and decided, rejoicing and exulting, to revisit his native land, asking and entreating God to direct his aid toward him [Col. 0152A]. From there, after a long and varied journey, he returned to his native borders.

The happy Gallic land received its foster child; the happy people of Verdun came out to meet their shepherd. “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult”: voices from city and countryside joined in harmony. Tears flowed full of joy; cheeks were wet with gladness; the city was crowned, the streets filled with happiness, and the churches with delight.

The outstanding bishop, supported by God’s help and laden with the relics of the saints, entered the church devoutly and prayed to the Lord, prostrate upon the ground. Rising, he ascended the episcopal throne, greeted clergy and people, gave everyone the kiss of peace, and added the seal of blessing.

Each person returns to his own affairs; the bishop visits the shrines;

He deposits the relics, then returns to his own dwelling.

He inquires into everything: whether there is peace, whether life is healthy;

He immediately hears that all he desired has prospered,

And with his mouth he gives thanks to God, with his heart he offers praise.

On the following day, after inspecting the structure of the new church, praising the craftsmen’s skill, and rewarding the diligence of the guardians, he appointed a suitable time and day for the consecration, venerable to all in their religion. When that day dawned, the bishop, together with the sacred orders, performed everything properly according to ecclesiastical rite, inside and outside, and reverently placed the Jerusalem relics in suitable locations in the principal apse.

(ibid.) Those that had been in the older church he appropriately arranged on the right side of the altar in an underground crypt.
