This most blessed bishop was pure through his devotion to chastity, strong through the discipline of abstinence, filled with the nourishment of doctrine, humble through the endurance of patience [Col. 0152D], upright through the strength of authority, kind through the grace of compassion, and strict through the severity of justice.

(Fol. 56'.) Keeping watch over the flock entrusted to him with pastoral concern, he instructed some by words of heavenly doctrine, strengthened many by examples of religious life, healed very many from every affliction of illness, and even freed certain people from demonic spirits. To everyone he presented himself as a model and mirror of complete holiness.

When the time of his departure drew near, and he had learned by divine revelation that he was to be freed from worldly turmoil, he chose the place of his burial in the church in which he had grown up through daily progress in virtue, in which he had first been appointed pastor and rector, and from which he had also been promoted to the episcopate [Col. 0153A].

Although he labored for the benefit of all the churches, he nevertheless cherished, enlarged, and advanced this one above all sacred places after the first, which is the episcopal see. We know that all his predecessors did the same, since, with very few exceptions, they all have their place of rest there.

This church itself received the privilege from the blessed father who must be named with due honor, Sanctinus, its founder and the first teacher of the Christian religion and name in that city: after the mother church, it was to be the head of all the churches of the diocese of Verdun, from which the mother church itself had received its beginning. Since ancient times—that is, from the very beginnings of the church’s birth—it has also been the cemetery of bishops and of the other faithful Christians [Col. 0153B].

That privilege has remained and continues so unshaken that nearly all the bishops of the same city are recorded as having been fitted there for divine service, tonsured, nurtured, taught, and consecrated, with the sole exception of the actual conferral of episcopal dignity, which plainly belongs to the mother church. More often, those who had served there as abbots were enthroned in the episcopal seat because of their devotion to virtue.

And rightly is that place venerated by all; rightly is it sought; rightly is it loved. The summit of so great a dignity raises it up. For although those who gather there to pray, who serve God there, or who ask to have their bodies buried there under the patronage of the saints may lack goods acquired by merit, they can be satisfied with what will be granted by the holy founder of the place, Sanctinus, and by the saints resting there, though only in proportion to the faith of those who ask [Col. 0153C].

The memorable antiquity of Lord Bertarius bears witness to this affirmation of ours. Recounting the deeds of the holy bishops of Verdun, he also mentions this basilica in these words (BERT. 4):

“The basilica in which the aforesaid bishops rest is built in honor of Saint Peter. It contains the tombs of many bishops and is for this reason greatly to be venerated by the faithful.”

(Fol. 57.) In the penultimate year of his life, the blessed Madelveus acquired for this place, through the gift of Teuthardus [Note: [Col. 0153] *geuehardi* corrected to *teuthardi* c.], certain properties situated in the district of Verdun, in the place called Offelini Curtis, and in the territory of Bettiliniaca, as well as in the territory of Virelinse. Teuthardus possessed them by hereditary right, having received them from his father Guntherus [Col. 0153D], and they consisted of lands, mansions, fields, meadows, pastures, forests, waters, and the courses of waters. He also gave the basilica of Saint Martin constructed in the same village of Bettiliniaca [Note: [Col. 0153D] Bettinville]. All these possessions, just as he had and possessed them, he granted perpetually to Saint Vitonus and to this father of ours, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 775, in the fourteenth indiction, while Charlemagne was reigning in the eighth year of his reign, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, namely on the feast of our holy father Vitonus.

He was loved by all the leading men of the entire kingdom [Col. 0154A], and by the most excellent King Charles himself, since it was fitting that one whom the Lord had suffused with grace should be loved by everyone. He strove to please everyone in every way—not in the manner of those who please human beings, “whose bones God will scatter, so that they may be filled with shame because of his indignation,” but in the manner in which the Apostle pleased everyone in every way, seeking not what was useful to himself but what was useful to many, so that they might be saved.

Therefore, with a good conscience, he could say to his hearers with that same Apostle: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians IV, 16; XI, 1). He wished, of course, to be without offense toward the church of God, teaching that conduct within it should be so regulated that no one might suffer scandal there [Note: [Col. 0153] “Turn back two leaves and look for the following material under this sign,” c.].

(Fol. 58.) But why do we attempt to praise him when we are not sufficient to explain his praise? He himself is his praise, he who is praiseworthy in his saints. Where, then, is our discourse leading us? Why do we delay? Why do we entangle ourselves in recounting his blessed departure from the world? May he himself be favorable toward us, so that we may be able to speak worthily; may the Holy Spirit breathe into our heart through his merits and be poured into our inmost being.

Let us therefore say what he himself, of whom we speak, has granted us, and briefly investigate how he departed from the world to Christ, whom he had devoutly served.

The time of his departure had already arrived, and the blessed man had gone to a certain estate of the episcopal district to consecrate churches. There, struck by the fierce struggle imposed by nature, he began to be worn down by sharp pain.

O blessed, truly fortunate man, who, knowing that the day of his departure was approaching [Col. 0154C], compelled his failing limbs to serve the spirit, considering it the good completion of his virtues if, in so pious and renowned a service of God, he spent what remained of the strength of his weakened body!

He had therefore fulfilled his vows. He consecrated the churches of that village, and that consecration remains effective to this very day. For the authority of the holy man was then, and still is, so great that none of the bishops, however holy or just, dares to repeat or alter that consecration. The dedication then performed remains perpetual among all and will remain so forever.

With the whole city, indeed the whole region, standing by and hanging upon the word of his mouth, he addressed everyone concerning the feast of the church. He announced to them that the Saint of saints had personally come there and forbade them to repeat the consecration [Col. 0154D].

At last he bade everyone farewell and foretold that his departure would soon take place. How great was the lamentation of all at these words! What sighs from the young, what groans from the grieving! Who would not weep when so great a man announced his departure from the world? Who could restrain his tears when everyone was so utterly bereft by the absence of so great a father?

Repeating his customary lessons of salvation and commending himself to them, he blessed everyone, admonished them to remember the Lord God, and, having completed his duty, returned home [Col. 0155A]. As his illness grew worse, he began to be tormented more severely.

Then he was carried back to the church and awaited the hour of his departure with joy, announcing words of life to everyone. The church was full of tears, full of groans, full of mourners and grief. He alone rejoiced; he recognized where he was being called and commended his calling in prayers.

When everyone cried out, “Why are you abandoning us, Father? To whom are you leaving your desolate sheep?” he pitied them all and sympathized with everyone. He taught them all to restrain their tears, saying that he must go more swiftly to his rest [Note: [Col. 0155] “*us eundum*,” or something similar, has been cut away in c.].

Not long afterward the hour came that was desirable to the saint, welcome to the angelic spirits, and mournful to his little children. After his long struggles, Christ invited his servant to his rewards.

In the presence of the sons of his church [Col. 0155B], after sweet instructions for life and the final words of consolation, nourished by the heavenly viaticum, he gave peace to everyone and, in a good confession, surrendered his spirit to God. He was gathered to his fathers, having obtained the better portion, which shall not be taken away from him, because “in peace was his place,” and “his dwelling is in Zion.”

(Fol. 59.) [BERT. 12.] The blessed Madelveus lived from the time of Pippin, who, descended from Ansegisus, begot Charles Tudites, who was the father of Pippin, from whom Charlemagne was born. This just man lived until the time of Charlemagne, leading a sober life in youth, chaste, and completing the course of his present life in a good old age (Life of Charles).

By “old age” we mean the period extending from a man’s fiftieth year to his seventy-seventh, when human strength begins to decline and grow weak from its former condition. For the age that extends from the seventy-seventh year toward life’s setting is called senility and decrepitude; at that point even what remains is marked by weakness and horror [Note: [Col. 0155] The author inserted the following and later deleted it: “Infancy ends at seven years; boyhood at fourteen. The following period, adolescence, consists of two seven-year periods because of understanding and action [c: the two were not yet in the text]. This age extends from the fifteenth year to the twenty-eighth. Youth consists of three seven-year periods because of understanding, action, and bodily strength; it begins with the twenty-ninth year and ends with the forty-ninth. Old age is completed in four seven-year periods, because of the heaviness of mind and body that occurs in those three periods; it begins in the fiftieth year and ends in the seventy-seventh. Old age declining from youth into senility, which is called decrepitude, breathes its last toward the end of life.”]

This distinction is made so that a simple reader, hearing that the blessed man completed the course of his life in a good old age, may not think that he lived to the final stage of old age. For it is clear that each person, when the allotted span of time has been completed and the appointed hour has arrived in the sight of the Lord, finishes his course by dying. It makes no difference whether someone fulfills his appointed course in old age, youth, or infancy: it may still be said of him, “He has completed his course.”

[BERT. 12.] He died while the earth wept and heaven applauded, at a nearby episcopal estate called Novavilla [Col. 0155D], on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the sixty-sixth year of his life, at the very beginning of his whitening old age. He cast off the corruptible garment of flesh and put on the divine robe of immortality.

When this declaration was received, the entire city was thrown into confusion and all the people were afflicted with grief. Without delay, people of every age and both sexes rushed indiscriminately to meet the body, poured out showers of tears, and struck the air with their laments [Col. 0156A].

Nor were heavenly ministers of the funeral rites absent from the funeral of the blessed body. As they surrounded the blessed funeral with their own array, they spread a most sweet fragrance by their presence, so that it was plainly understood by all that the very Author of sweetness had also arrived there. And indeed, the merciful Divinity himself was present, consoling the tears of the mourners and making known what piety, how great a simplicity, and what purity of heart had been found in the deceased.

For immediately after he returned his spirit to heaven, two doves, whiter than snow, descended from the sky before everyone’s eyes and settled upon the cross that stood before the body. They remained there throughout the whole funeral, until he was handed over to burial; then, as everyone watched, they once more sought the hidden places of heaven.

With so great a presence of the heavenly host [Col. 0156B], the body of the father was prepared through the devoted care of his children. Then, with every mark of veneration, it was carried on the shoulders of his sons to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. That church lies on the northern side of the city, where the precious confessor of the Lord, Vitonus, rests with many of his holy episcopal predecessors and successors. There, after the solemn office had been celebrated according to custom, and with the bishops of the neighboring cities attending, the body was committed to the earth with glory.

Happy is the church, worthy of the burial of so great a father! Happy is the place enriched by the gift of so great a treasure! Blessed, I should say, is the people raised up by the governance of so great a shepherd, protected by his blessing, and gladdened by his miracles.

For if the glory of a church is the praise of its teacher, how great were—and indeed how great are—the glories of this church, whose teacher Almighty God approves with so great a praise [Col. 0156C]? Behold, heavenly ministers kept vigil at his funeral, so that it might be recognized on earth how great a glory God had granted him in heaven.

(Fol. 59′.) Truly blessed was the funeral procession, worthy of the visitation of such witnesses! And what else does it mean that doves came from heaven, offered service and consolation at the funeral, and then, while all were watching, sought the secrets of heaven again, except that Christ wished plainly to show the faithful people mourning the death of their father and grieving their own abandonment—under the form of a harmless bird—that the man whose funeral it was had lived in innocence and simplicity; that he had passed his pious, God-fearing, circumspect, watchful life free from the gall of bitterness, eager for the fellowship of the saints, unstained by every blemish of wickedness; and that by pious devotion he had merited the company of the saints in the glory of the heavenly court?

Let still greater miracles be added, and let God be glorified in his saints, who is wondrous in his works. For after the father’s body had been buried, so that it might be shown that he always lives in heaven for the display of his illustrious merits, divine miracles took place at his tomb. And because God’s merciful goodness had washed him from childhood from every defilement of the flesh, and, purifying his mind, had powerfully protected him from demonic delusion, and because he had served God with a pure heart and chaste body, God manifested this more clearly after his death. For just as his mind had remained inviolate from lust, so his flesh remained uncorrupted by decay.

Indeed, although his tomb flourished with the daily wonders of miracles and was frequented by the continual vigils of the people, it was nevertheless situated with less care than the honor of due veneration required. Therefore, at that time the bishop, together with all the clergy and people, judged it worthy to move it to a more fitting place.

At that time Bernard was bishop of the church of Verdun, a Catholic and religious man, highly renowned in the holy faith, while Lothar, son of Louis the Pious, was emperor. His kingdom comprised Italy with the city of Rome and that part of Francia enclosed between the Meuse and the Rhine. When they were striving to carry out what they had resolved to do and to place him in a sarcophagus that had been dug out, a suddenly immeasurable vision was shown to them. For when the covering of the tomb had been removed, they saw the corpse, dead for forty years, as though it were a living man asleep, suffused with the whiteness of lilies and the redness of roses, defiled by no stain or sign of death.

At the sight of this miracle, and overcome by its exceedingly sweet fragrance, they began to weep for joy. Then, lifting the saint’s body with reverence and jubilation, they transferred it to a prepared mausoleum, where from that time divine power has been at work and God’s mercy heals everyone. There every illness is put to sleep, blindness is driven away, crookedness is straightened, weakness is strengthened, and health is restored to all.

Blessed Vitonus now has in heaven as a companion and fellow citizen the man whom he once had on earth as a pupil and devoted successor. He has been joined in glory to the saints whom he devotedly served in this laborious life. Let us too seek him as our patron and protector, and, together with the other saints, as a merciful intercessor with God—the man whom we were privileged to have as teacher and herald of the truth. May he, placed there, hear us here as we pray, guard and protect us, and obtain that those who have him on earth as suppliant worshipers may be his fellow citizens in heaven.

(Fol. 60.) Therefore, if a diligent reader, led by love for this blessed man, earnestly desires to learn at what time he was born and when he was promoted to the episcopate, how many years he lived before becoming bishop and how many as bishop, and when he put off his human life, let him consult the chronicle of his memory; by following the times of the successive kings and Roman pontiffs, he will find what he seeks.

It was related above that before his ordination the people of Verdun had been without a shepherd for many years. For the wicked license of the prefects—who were also called mayors of the palace—did not allow the churches to enjoy their own freedom, even though they had also grievously afflicted the cities themselves, and Verdun above all. Situated on the frontier of Neustria and Austrasia, it lay open on both sides to the incursions and plundering of raiders.

This devastation lasted for many years, from the time, namely, of Theuderic and the ruler Ebroin. Their bestial and inhuman savagery stained the kingdom of the Franks with the blood of nobles and magnates until the second year of King Pippin, in which he was established as king of the Franks by Pope Stephen, just as his predecessor Zacharias had ordained—a year which was A.D. 754 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Then, when the dreadful darkness of the storm had first been dispelled, a new light seemed to arise for the peoples of Gaul, and the peoples who lacked a shepherd eagerly seized their own shepherd, each for itself. In that year this blessed man was enthroned by the authority of Pope Stephen and with the acclamation of Prince Pippin.

Since the chronicle reports what happened from the time of Pippin, born of Ansegisus, who fathered Charles the Hammerer (*Karolum Tuditem*), through the time of Charles, let us reckon from the year A.D. 712, in which this blessed man was born, in the thirteenth indiction. By counting upward from this point, we shall obtain the years during which Pippin survived; also the twenty-seven years during which Charles held the principate after his father; the six years during which his sons Carloman and Pippin jointly ruled after him; the four years during which he alone held the principate before his anointing; and the year itself in which he was raised to kingship. Adding the total, we shall find that he was consecrated in the forty-fifth year of his age, namely in the year in which Pippin was made king by the pope.

Counting again the fifteen years during which Pippin subsequently ruled alone, and the eight years of Charles’s reign—for in the ninth year this blessed man put off his human life, while Charles was besieging Tarvisium, a city of Italy—we shall find that in the fifty-fourth year of his pontificate he exchanged perishable things for heavenly and eternal ones and migrated to the Lord at the nearby episcopal estate called Novavilla, on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the sixty-eighth year of his age, in the fifteenth indiction, with an epact of twenty-eight, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian [Note: [Col. 0157D] Thus in the copy.]—from the Incarnation of the Lord in the year 777, in the time of Constantine and Irene, in the sixth year of their reign, one year before the Seventh Synod.

Thus blessed was the origin of Madelveus, more blessed his course of life, and most blessed his end, through the grace of Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

(Fol. 60′.) (Chron. Div.) In the year A.D. 754, therefore, King Pippin entered Lombardy, and Pope Stephen returned to Rome. In the year A.D. 760 he also went to Wasconia, and in the following year, together with his sons Charles and Carloman, he captured Aquitaine and Bourges. In the year 762 he went again to Aquitaine and conquered the city of Limoges. When he went there for the seventh time by way of Vienne, he gave the bishopric of Vienne to Berteric, one of the household servants of the church.

After this, in the year A.D. 768, he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; and in the same year, on the following day, Charles and Carloman were anointed kings. The Franks divided the kingdom in such a way that Charles received the portion which their father Pippin had held, while Carloman received the portion which their great-grandfather Carloman had possessed.

(Fol. 59′.) In the year A.D. 755, in the eighth indiction, after Bishop Gayroinus, who died on the emperor’s expedition, Lord Manasses was ordained abbot at Flavigny by the gift of Emperor Pippin. He brought into his church the body of the blessed martyr Praejectus, carried from Volvic, on the eighth day before the Ides of November. He also obtained from Emperor Carloman a site at Corbigny, wishing to establish a cell there, but he did not do so. He died in A.D. 787, on the Nones of November, in the thirty-third year of his ordination.

(Fol. 60′.) Adalbert succeeded him. Charles the Great granted to God, to Saint Peter, to Saint Praejectus, and to Abbot Manasses that no person belonging to the church of Flavigny anywhere in his kingdom should pay a toll in cities, markets, villages, estates, bridges, or ports—not the road toll, bargaining toll, dust toll, changing toll, river toll, salutation toll, bidding toll, or crossing toll [Note: [Col. 0159] *riu* deleted; *tra* deleted.]—nor on anything that men customarily carry on their backs. Whatever belonged to the right of the treasury, he remitted to them; and from all the monks’ lands throughout his empire he granted them complete exemption from toll, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0159D] Bouquet V, 732.].

(Chron. Div.) Carloman, therefore, after jointly administering the kingdom for four years, departed in A.D. 771, on the day before the Kalends of December; Charles held the kingdom alone. In the second year of his reign, while his brother was still alive, he completed with such success the Aquitanian war begun by his father but not yet finished that he retained and subjected to himself all Aquitaine and Wasconia.

After Stephen, therefore [Note: [Col. 0159] In the margin: “Stephen V died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction.”], Paul sat in Rome for ten years and one day; he died in the year A.D. 767. After him Stephen sat for three years, ten months, and twenty-eight days.

(Gesta pont. Rom.) Adrian succeeded him. Under Adrian, a synod of 350 fathers was held at Nicaea by the five patriarchs, in the time of Constantine and his mother Irene, in the seventh year of their empire, the tenth year of the reign of Charles the Great, from the Incarnation of the Lord in the year 778. Adrian sat for twenty-four years, three months, and seventeen days. He died in the year A.D. 796, and Leo succeeded him.

(Chron. Div.) After Charles had settled affairs in Aquitaine, and his associate had died, he began, at the request of Adrian, the Roman pontiff, a war against the Lombards. In the year 772 Charles entered Italy and took up the war which had been undertaken by his father at the urging of Pope Stephen. Some of the leading Franks, however, resisted his will so strongly that they openly declared that they would abandon the king and return home.

Nevertheless, the enterprise was begun. Charles compelled Desiderius, king of the Lombards, after a siege lasting only a few days, both to give hostages and to restore what had been seized from the Romans, and to confirm by oath that it would not be reclaimed. Pavia was surrendered in A.D. 774, the seventh year of Charles’s reign.

The end of the war was therefore the subjugation of Italy; Desiderius was assigned to perpetual exile in Francia; his son Adalgisus was driven from Italy; and the property seized by the Lombards was restored to Pope Adrian. Having subjected Lombardy and secured it by oath, Charles appointed his son Pippin over all Italy in that same year, which, as stated, was A.D. 776, and resumed the war against the rebellious Saxons.

(Ann. Petav.) (BERT. c. 14.) In the year A.D. 776, which was the ninth year of Charles’s reign, Bishop Madelveus died while Charles’s army was besieging Stabilinus, the father-in-law of Chrotgaud, in Tarvisium, a city of Italy. Chrotgaud had rebelled against Charles and, because of this, had been killed in the war when Charles entered Italy. In that same city was Peter, an Italian man, by whom the city was surrendered; for this reason he was honored with the bishopric of Verdun.

(Fol. 61.) At that time Fretmodus, a deacon and abbot, presided over the church of Saint Vitonus in the name and office of abbot. After Saint Madelveus, he had undertaken the administration of that place.

In the time of Fretmodus—that is, in the fourteenth year of Charles’s reign, which was A.D. 781 from the Incarnation of the Lord—a certain nobleman named Becco, a canon, gave to the saint and to those serving him, for the sake of his own soul and that of his brother Amlingus, buried in that cemetery, the property which he possessed in the county of Verdun, at a place called Gailanae Curtis on the river Agira: namely, a church in honor of Saint Christopher, together with everything that appeared to belong to that estate, as is contained in the charter.

Later, through the intervention of Bishop Peter [Note: [Col. 0159] Almost the entire word has perished.], Fretmodus made a precarial grant of the estate of Raherei and its dependencies to a certain Abbot Betto, who . . . . Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus, and who also i . . . . . the estate of Garani with its appurtenances; and after his death the saint possessed those improved estates V . . . dinus.

[BERT. 13.] At that time the bishopric of Verdun was vacant for twelve years. But a certain servant of God named Amalbert, made chorepiscopus according to the custom of that age, governed the church; and in an oratory dedicated to all the apostles he led an almost solitary life.

At that time the church itself lost certain possessions which had once been granted to it and which it had held, and this occurred in the time of Charles the Great.

(Ib., 14.) Although the aforementioned Peter, the Italian, had been honored by him with that bishopric for surrendering Tarvisium, traitors are always regarded with suspicion, and therefore he was not admitted to the bishopric during the prescribed period. Nevertheless, so that the king’s word should not be empty and void, after the prescribed interval of years he was permitted to enter the city and take possession of the bishopric in the year A.D. 788 [Note: [Col. 0159] The final stroke has perished.]. He held it for twenty-five years [Ib.] and suffered many adversities.

Indeed, they even accused him of disloyalty to the emperor, and for that reason he did not dare to see the emperor for twelve years. Later, however, having been rightly cleared before the prince by the sons of the church, he approached the emperor’s presence. During his days the church not only did not acquire anything for itself but also lost very much. For it is difficult that things begun with evil beginnings should end well.

The city of Verdun demonstrates this ruin of its own. Fortified by a very solid [Note: [Col. 0161] I have supplied an excised word.] circuit of towers and walls, constructed of stone joined with lead and iron—and from this it acquired its name, being called the City of Nails—it was destroyed by Charles because of the instability and proven disloyalty of this Italian, whom it had been built to protect. Now it displays only the signs of a great . . . [Note: [Col. 0161] Perhaps “fortification”], and scarcely retains any . . . of its ancient strength [Note: [Col. 0161] Perhaps “traces”], teaching everyone by such misfortune of its own that what belongs to God must be sought from God.

The insensitive king also perceived the ruin of so great a calamity, so that no enemy—unless one approached with prior deliberation—would be less destructive here than the Vandal plague had once been. And rightly so: from the earliest beginnings of the faith until that time, the election of the bishop by the clergy and people had always prevailed in the name of God. Although princes are sometimes recorded as having offered favor and consent, they are nowhere reported to have forbidden the election of a bishop who was to be ordained or to have altered an election already made.

He was buried in the church of Saint Mary before the altar of Saint Peter. From the devastation of the city of Verdun by the Vandals until its desolation under Charles, nearly 380 years are reckoned. The chapel at Aachen was built from the squared stones of the ruined city.

[BERT. 15.] After his death, in the year 815, the clergy and people chose for themselves as bishop from the king’s palace Austrannus, its cantor, a vigorous man, through whose diligence the merchants of Bracium were brought under the authority of that church. He survived for five years. He died in the year A.D. 819 and was buried in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter with his predecessors.

(Chron. Div.) The war undertaken by Charles against the Saxons was conducted for thirty-three years, with greater loss to the Saxons than to the Franks. When the Saxons saw that they could not resist, they sought peace, and a multitude of them was baptized.

In the year A.D. 780, therefore, Charles came to Saxony, to a place called Paderborn. There he held a great assembly, and there the Saxons gathered for baptism, on the condition imposed by the king that Franks and Saxons should be one people. In two battles they were so crushed that thereafter they neither challenged the king nor dared to resist him when he came. Many nobles, however, were killed in that war.

In the year 788 he attacked Spain and subjected it to himself, as well as Brittany. For during the forty-seven years in which he reigned, he enlarged the kingdom of the Franks so greatly that, although it had previously been large and strong, he added an equal amount to it.

Above all sacred places he venerated the church of Saint Peter at Rome, to which he also gave much gold and silver. He always labored to ensure that the Roman city should shine with its ancient authority through his efforts. Although he loved it so greatly, he went there only four times during the whole period of his rule. [EINH. Vita K.] When the death of Adrian, the Roman pontiff, was announced to him, he wept as though he had lost his dearest brother.

(Fol. 60*.) Lord Manasses brought the body of the holy martyr Praejectus, carried from Volvic, into the church at Flavigny, which he had founded in honor of Saint Peter and that same martyr. His reception is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of November. He obtained from Carloman [Note: [Col. 0161] This is a charter of King Charles, issued in the eighth year of his reign, without day or place. Plancher, *Histoire de Bourgogne*, vol. I, proofs, p. 5.] permission to build a small monastery at the estate of Corbigny.

(Series abb. Flav.) He died in the thirty-third year of his ordination, on the Nones of November. Adalbert, a venerable man, succeeded him in the twenty-first year of Charles’s reign. He died in the fifth year of his ordination, and Zacho succeeded him; Zacho died in his fourth year. Alcuin then succeeded him and died in his seventh year. Thus, in the thirty-fifth year of Charles’s empire, Lord Apollinaris was appointed abbot by the gift of the emperor.

He also governed the abbeys of Dijon and Réomé, increased their churches’ possessions, and honored them with the relics of the saints. Above all, however, he advanced and enlarged the church of Flavigny. He died on the day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth year of Louis’s empire. He attended the council held at Aachen in the fourth year of that same Louis. Two years later, in the fourteenth year of Louis, Abbot Vigilius succeeded him.

[ADO.] At that time Ursus governed the church of Vienne, and Ado governed that of Lyon. After Ado, his nephew Hilduin held the church of Lyon for a short time, though he was not a bishop; when he withdrew, he became a monk at Lérins. After him Laidradus assumed the church of Lyon, useful to the public order.

Vulferus the Bavarian governed Vienne for eleven years, and Bernard succeeded him. Laidradus, at the beginning of the reign of the emperor Louis, went to the monastery of Soissons, and Agobardus, chorepiscopus of that same church, was substituted in his place, with the consent of the emperor and of the entire synod of the Gallican bishops.

Some who wished to defend this action said that he had been ordained in the see of Lyon by three bishops at the command of Laidradus. Agobardus and Bernard of Vienne were then accused before Louis. Abandoning their churches, they withdrew to Italy to Lothar. But through the intervention of the pious emperors, each recovered his own see.

After a few years Agobardus died at Saintes while on a royal expedition. Bernard also died, and Agilmarus was substituted for him. Amolo likewise assumed the bishopric of Lyon. His authority, and Charles’s affection for him, had great influence with the holy Pope Leo, as Leo himself testifies in a letter sent to him.

[Col. 0163A] (Fol. 61.) (Gesta p. R.; Chron. Div.) After Adrian, Leo succeeded to the Roman pontificate in the year A.D. 796 from the Incarnation of the Lord. He sat in the same see for twenty-two years, five months, and fifteen days.

The Romans seized him during the Greater Litany, inflicted many injuries upon him, tore out his eyes, and cut out his tongue. In the year A.D. 799 they compelled him to appeal to the protection of the king. [ADO.] He was sent into custody, but at night escaped over a wall to the church of Saint Peter. From there the Franks led him to Spoleto, and finally the king received him honorably at Paderborn; he then had him escorted back to Rome with honor.

(Chron. Div.) This was the reason for Charles’s final visit to Rome, to restore the condition of the church. He spent the entire winter there. During that time he assumed the name of emperor and Augustus, in A.D. 799, in the eighth indiction—something he had at first strongly rejected. [ADO.] Then an inquiry was held concerning those who had treated Pope Leo so dishonorably and insulted him by deposing him; the king ordered them, as guilty of treason against majesty, to be punished by death. The pious pontiff intervened on their behalf, and the king pardoned their lives and limbs, although they were sent into exile.

In the year A.D. 803 the emperor sent an embassy to Rome to investigate whether, as was reported, the blood of Christ had been found at Mantua. For this reason Leo came to Francia. The emperor received him at Reims and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with him. When Leo wished to travel through Bavaria, the emperor had him escorted as far as Ravenna, after giving him very great gifts.

[ADO.] In the year A.D. 806 the bodies and bones of Saint Cyprian were brought from Carthage, together with the relics of the Scillitan martyrs, Speratus and his companions, and were placed at Lyon in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

(EINH. Ann.) In the year A.D. 810 Pippin, king of Italy, died. In his kingdom Charles installed his son Bernard, his own grandson, and decreed that he should be called king.

In the year A.D. 813 certain leading Romans conspired to kill Pope Leo. They were arrested and, on his order, put to death. When he had completed the twenty-first year of his pontificate and was gravely ill, the Romans gathered a force, first plundered all the estates that he had recently built in the territories of the individual cities, and then burned them. Bernard, king of Italy, prevented them from carrying out their undertaking, and in that same year Pope Leo died.

(Chron. Div.) At the end of his life, after assembling all the leading men of the Franks, Charles made his son Louis his partner in the kingdom and heir to the imperial name, placing a diadem on his head. [BERT.] At that time Herilandus assumed the bishopric of Verdun, a very simple man and exceedingly weak. After completing seven years as bishop, he died at Aachen. His body was brought back from there and buried beside Austrannus in the basilica of Saint Vitonus.

(Chron. Div.) Charles also died in the year A.D. 815, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-seventh of his reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February. He was buried at the palace of Aachen, in the church which he himself had built.

Louis, surnamed the Pious, succeeded him. For twenty-five years he ruled the empire with great moderation, and by bravely resisting his enemies he powerfully terrified them.

[EINH. Ann.] In the year 816 Pope Leo died. Stephen succeeded him and died the following year; Paschal succeeded him.

In the year 817 Louis held a council concerning abbots and monks. Apollinaris, abbot of Flavigny, attended it, and died in 826.

(Ep. Hincm.) In the eighth year of Lord Louis, A.D. 823 from the Incarnation of the Lord, his son Charles was born in the new palace at Frankfurt. There, on the day before the Ides of June, Drogo, son of Charles the Great, was ordained and was given the bishopric of Metz; the episcopate of Meaux was entrusted to Humbert, the palace precentor.

Humbert found in that church several little books concerning the life of Saint Santinus, but they were badly damaged. In that same year, in the territory of Toul, at the estate of Commarciacus, a girl began to fast on Holy Saturday after receiving Communion. She remained for three years without taking any food or drink, and in A.D. 826 began to eat again.

(Chron. Div.) Louis had three other sons, Lothar, Louis, and Pippin, and by another wife a younger son, whom we have mentioned, Charles.

[EINH. Ann.] In the year 824 Pope Paschal died, and Eugenius succeeded him. After administering the Roman pontificate for three years, he left the see to Valentinus, who died in the same month; Gregory IV succeeded him. (Gesta p. R.) He sat for nineteen years.

(A. Fuld. 833, 834.) During his time, as is read in the *Deeds of the Franks*, Louis went to Alsace. His sons met him there together with the aforementioned Gregory, Roman pontiff. By the judgment of the bishops he laid down his title and lived for some time deprived of his rank and confined, doing penance.

[ADO.] In the year 828, while the whole power of the Franks was enjoying leisure through the efforts of Louis the Pious, certain people who could not endure so great a hope of good [Note: [Col. 0163] I have supplied *bonis*.] sent the emperor’s wife under guard from his side into Aquitaine. The entire people also defected from the king and went over to his sons; he himself was handed over to custody, and his wife likewise was placed under guard.

But by God’s will, after so many [Note: [Col. 0163] *p. t. a.* supplied.] adversities prosperity follows; the people are converted to penance [Note: [Col. 0163] *peniten* supplied.], restore him to his former rank, and exalt him; his sons send messengers to ask pardon and bring back their mother. [REGINO.] The princes ordered Lothar, already emperor, that he should not [Note: [Col. 0163] *ut extra* deleted.] proceed outside Italy unless his father commanded it [Note: [Col. 0163] *procederet* deleted.]. This happened through divine [Note: [Col. 0163] *divina* deleted.] mercy and grace, because the emperor himself [Note: [Col. 0163] supplied.] was subsequently reconciled to penance by the judgment of the bishops. This deposition [Note: [Col. 0163] *dejectio* deleted.] was largely brought about by the many acts of fornication of Judith, his wife.

[BERT.] In the year 839 Lothar, leaving Francia, went to Italy. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, was deposed, and many others were condemned to exile because they had conspired in the emperor’s deposition.

After Bishop Herilandus died, part of the clergy and people of Verdun went to the emperor Louis in the year A.D. 827 and asked that Lord Hildinus of Alemannia be given to them, a good and holy man who built many churches in his bishopric and performed many good works.

(Chron. Div.) Louis, dividing his kingdom among his sons, gave to Lothar, the eldest, the empire and kingdom of Italy, the part of Francia divided by the Meuse and Rhine, and part of Burgundy. To Louis he gave Bavaria, Saxony, and the kingdoms which Charles had conquered. To Pippin he gave Aquitaine, Wasconia, and the land subject to him as far as Spain. Charles, the youngest, called the Bald, received Francia, Burgundy, and Neustria.

(Fol. 62.) His brothers therefore became indignant, because they did not wish him to be their equal, or because the better part of the kingdom had been granted to him. After their father’s death a serious war consequently arose among them, but they were unable to alter their father’s arrangements.

In the end Charles also obtained Aquitaine. For Pippin had died before his father, leaving a son named Pippin. Since he was less capable of governing the kingdom, the leading men transferred their allegiance to Charles, and Charles the Bald reigned for . . .

In the year A.D. 839 the body of Saint Bartholomew was carried to Benevento. Apollinaris, abbot of Flavigny, died on the day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth year of Louis. Two years later Vigilius succeeded him and held office for fourteen years; after him Arewaldus was appointed in the twenty-fifth year of that same Louis.

Louis died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the year A.D. 840 [ADO.], the twenty-fifth year of his empire. His body was carried from Metz by his brother Drogo and placed in the church of Saint Arnulf. Lothar succeeded him in the kingdom.

[REGINO.] In the year A.D. 841 there was at Fontenoy a very serious battle between the brothers, the sons of Louis; Charles and Louis won, but not without great loss among their own men.

(Ann. Lugd.) In the same year Agobardus, bishop of Lyon, died. That memorable work which had stood from the time of the emperor Trajan and was called the Old Forum collapsed at Lyon.

(Chron. Div.) While each man was looking to his own interests and taking care that the other should not be preferred to him, they divided the united kingdom of the Franks by a shameful partition and gave foreign nations an opportunity to rebel. For when the Normans, Danes, and Bretons invaded, massacres of Christians, plundering, devastation, and burnings took place.

For this reason the kings made peace among themselves; and because they could not redeem themselves by arms, they ransomed themselves with money.

(Ann. Prud.) In the same year, which was A.D. 842 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0165D] Correct to DCCCXLI, 841.], the Normans—that is, the northern peoples—devastated Rouen, in the first year of Lothar and Charles.

(Gesta p. R.) In the year 844, after Gregory’s death, Sergius succeeded as pope. After administering the priesthood for three years, he left it to Leo IV; after . . . years Benedict III succeeded him for two years, and then Nicholas I. After completing ten years in the priesthood, Nicholas left the chair to Adrian in the year A.D. 868.

(Chron. Div.) Lothar, the elder, holding the empire, was content with that part of the kingdom which we mentioned above, together with the city of Rome and Italy. The fifteenth indiction was the thirty-third year of Lothar’s rule in Italy and the thirteenth in Francia.

[ADO.] He had a son, Louis, who during his father’s lifetime was crowned at Rome by Pope Sergius and called emperor.

[BERT.] At that time the aforementioned Bishop Hildinus, a man praiseworthy in every respect, governed the church of Verdun. But after the battle fought at Fontenoy, he was greatly hated by the emperor Lothar and died in this city in the year A.D. 851, on the Ides of January, amid great pain and sorrow, after completing twenty-four years as bishop. He was buried in the crypt of Saint Vitonus.

After his death Lord Hatto was ordained in that church. Because of the aforementioned emperor’s hostility, he found the tunic of Saint Mary torn and rent in many places—that is, he found that the possessions of the aforementioned church had been excessively taken away and alienated. To recover these alienated possessions and relieve his people’s affliction, he rose up with all his strength against the enemies of the church, until, through God’s mercy, he restored and renewed everything to its former condition.

[Col. 0166C] Moreover, he obtained from the younger Lothar, king, very many estates and properties, as the evidence of the charters shows. His intention and enormous labor were directed toward exalting the church entrusted to him and enabling it to enjoy peace. This he accomplished during the lifetime of the younger Lothar.

He received a portion of the relics of the holy confessors and bishops Maurus, Salvinus, and Arator. Their bodies had been revealed to Saint Agericus, who had honorably and most reverently arranged them in that same church where they had first been buried, a church consecrated under the name of the holy apostle Peter. But Bishop Hildinus had transferred them to the new church of Saint Medardus. Hatto placed them in the monastery called Theolegium, subject to his church.

He deposited the arm of Saint Maurus beneath the altar in the church which he himself had built in the new castle, now called Hattonchâtel after its founder [Note: [Col. 0165] Hattonchâtel, on the right bank of the Meuse, not far from the town of Saint-Mihiel], for the salvation and protection of posterity.

(Fol. 62′.) When the younger Lothar, son of Lothar, died in the year A.D. 874, in the month of August, Hatto also died on the Kalends of January. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Vitonus, in the crypt beside the body of Bishop Hildinus, after completing twenty-three years as bishop.

[BERT. 18.] He also began the new church of Saint Mary and constructed a large part of it.

At that time Adventius was presiding over the church of Metz, Hatto over that of Verdun, and Remigius over that of Lyon. He sent a letter to Ado, bishop of Vienne and vicar of the Roman Church, and to Pope Nicholas on behalf of the same bishops of Trier and Cologne who had been deposed. [Note: [Col. 0167D] Compare the Annals of Hincmar, the Fulda Annals, and Regino.] The clergy of Cologne likewise sent him a letter, which is included in the catalogue. But although many people labored on the matter in different ways, both from fear of the king and from affection for those men, the pope could in no way be persuaded that they should be restored.

After blessed Nicholas had died and Adrian had succeeded him while Louis was emperor, Adrian sent a letter to the bishops of Gaul instructing them not to ordain any other bishops except those to whom the aforesaid emperor granted a bishopric and ordered to be ordained. The venerable bishops did not consent. Rather, they assembled together and, having drawn up a common letter, informed the pope that they wished faithfully to observe the decrees of the holy fathers and to consecrate bishops according to the provisions of the canons. The text of this letter is found in the catalogue of sacred writings. (Fol. 62b.)

He also wrote another letter to Duke Gerard, Count Rofrid, and all the counts of Gaul, asking them not, out of favor or goodwill toward any man, to permit other men of the ecclesiastical order to consecrate bishops in the bishoprics of all Gaul and Burgundy, except those whom the emperor Louis ordered. The aforesaid venerable bishops of Gaul opposed him with considerable clarity and propriety, examining that letter word by word, [Col. 0167C] and humbly pointing out that its contents were not consonant with the decrees of the holy fathers. At the end of their reply they inserted a letter of Pope Nicholas, his predecessor, which he had sent to a certain bishop of Gaul. Among other matters, it expressed with pious clarity the matter of holy orders in these words:

“But, dearest brother, that sounded ridiculous which you wrote when, commending to us the bearer of your letter, you declared that he was the priest of the illustrious Count Gerard. Yet what your prudence wished to say by writing this, or what you understood by such a statement, I confess that we do not know. Did Count Gerard consecrate him as a priest? Is he of Gerard’s diocese? Where did you read this? Where did you learn it? Unless it is because priests are not ordained, according to the sacred Scriptures, specifically for the church of a city, or for a church’s estate, or for a martyr’s shrine, or for a monastery, but are established in the houses of laymen and associate so closely with secular persons that they are now said to belong neither to God nor to any church, but to that count and that duke; so that what is said through the prophet has been fulfilled: ‘And it shall be: like people, like priest’ (Hosea 4:9).”

“That is perhaps one of these matters. Since we have assembled unanimously in the name of the Lord [Col. 0168A] for this very purpose, it will be appropriate that it be corrected with due propriety and cut off like poisonous hellebore.”

And after a few words they added this:

“What do we think the most blessed Pope Nicholas would have written, and with what grief would he have been moved, if in his own days he had heard that, in letters falsely represented as coming from the Apostolic See, lay counts did not permit bishops to be ordained in the cities except those whom secular power had sent from its own side? What lamentations would he have uttered when he saw the most sacred order treated so unlawfully, and someone daring to rush into such great wickedness as to write from the Apostolic See things so inappropriate and altogether foreign to ecclesiastical practice?”

Such were the bishops in Gaul at that time.

**[REGINO.]** In the year from the beginning of the Lord 855, Lothair divided the empire among his sons: to Louis he gave Italy, and also called him emperor; to Lothair, the kingdom that was named after him; and to Charles, the kingdom of Provence. After arranging the affairs of the kingdom, he became a monk in the monastery called Prüm and ended his life in that same year, three days before the Kalends of October.

In the year 856, indiction 4, Lothair took Teutberga as his wife.

In the year 858 King Charles of Provence died. A dispute then arose over his kingdom between Lothair and his uncle Charles, the son of Louis. Lothair gave Hubert the duchy between the Jura and Mount Jovis because he had Hubert’s sister.

(Fol. 62.) In the year from the beginning of the Lord 860, the Bretons invaded Francia. Charles fought against them, entered Brittany, and fled shamefully defeated.

[Col. 0168C] In the year from the beginning of the Lord 862, the king of the Bretons was struck down by God’s will, and in the following year the Bretons submitted to him.

In the year from the beginning of the Lord 866, Rollo entered Normandy and was later baptized, receiving the name Robert in baptism.

(Fol. 62'.) In the year 868, indiction 1, during the time of King Lothair, a severe famine occurred in the land of the Franks, Gaul, and Burgundy, together with a mortality among human beings and a plague among animals (compare the Annals of Saint Columba). It raged against the people by God’s just judgment with such force that many were compelled to abandon their homeland and migrate to other lands, so that many cities of Francia were scarcely inhabited.

(Fol. 62b.) In the year from the beginning of the Lord 864, the body of Saint Regina, virgin and martyr, was transferred from the city of Alesia to the fortress or monastery of Flavigny. The place was then governed by Aigilo, abbot, later archbishop of Sens, and the city mentioned above belonged to his jurisdiction; Charles the Bald was reigning. This is Aigilo, abbot of Flavigny, who established the cell of Corbigny and placed twelve monks there. [Note: [Col. 0167D] The document of this foundation is itself demonstrated in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, century IV, 2, p. 240. It was written in the year 864, on the day after the burial of the body of Saint Regina the martyr, eleven days before the Kalends of April. In that same place, situated in the county of Avalinse or Nevers, at Ammondas, Abbot Manasses, as the document testifies, wished to build a monastery. An anonymous author described the translation of Regina in Mabillon, *loc. cit.* Isaac, bishop of Langres, granted the same Aigilo several altars in certain churches of the Attorian district on Saturday in October 865, in the twenty-fifth year of King Charles (in October 865, the twenty-sixth regnal year was already running). *Ibid.*, K.]

Two hundred and fifty-eight years had passed since the church of Flavigny had obtained Corbigny. (Fol. 62b.) After Vigilius, in the year 839, indiction 2, Adrevaldus succeeded; Marianus flourished in year 1 of Charles. Vulfaldus died in year 8; Count Warinus [Note: [Col. 0169D] While the illustrious Count Warinus was reigning, Charles the Bald confirmed the immunity of the monastery of Flavigny on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth year of his reign, indiction 12, at Osenivilla. Bouquet VIII, 500. K.], and under him Sarulsus the dean, died in year 10; Gotserus died in year 15; Hugo succeeded. Saint Ezgil, in year 24, indiction 11, transferred the body of Saint Regina in 857. Geylo succeeded him; in the twenty-sixth year, from the beginning of the Lord 866, he was promoted to the bishopric of Langres, and Sigardus succeeded him in 870, the thirtieth year of Charles. Then Wilfrid, nephew of Emperor Louis II, in 880 [Note: [Col. 0169D] It is established that Pope John VIII was staying in Gaul in 878. In letter 97, Mansi XVII, p. 84, he himself writes: “We excommunicate the priest Aduvardus, who ministered to us in the monastery of Flavigny, because his men stole a silver dish of Saint Peter’s—I do not know whether with his consent or not—as punishment for the sacrilege of the theft.” K.], indiction 13, in the second year of the reign of Prince Karloman, obtained permission from Pope John and eighteen bishops to carry out the consecration of the church of Flavigny; in that same year 880, indiction 13, he produced a charter between the abbot, his vassals, and the monks [Note: [Col. 0169D] Hugo seems to have rendered the chronological signs less accurately. There survives a letter of Pope John VIII, dated the fourth day before the Kalends of June, indiction 10, while Lord Charles was emperor in his second year, by which Flavigny is granted perpetually to Adalgar, bishop of Autun, and his successors, and the property of the brothers is confirmed. Mansi. K.].

Adalgar obtained the abbey from Charles the Simple [Note: [Col. 0170D] Rather from Charles the Bald, as the letter shows: a letter of Emperor Charles dated the seventh day before the Kalends of March, indiction 10, in the thirty-seventh year of his reign and the twenty-sixth year of his empire, that is, 877. Bouquet VIII, p. 657. It was confirmed at the synod of Ravenna on the sixth day before the Kalends of December 877. Plancher I, preliminary matter, p. 11. K.]. Because he had seized the church’s property, he was summoned to Rome and died at Tournus in 893 [Note: [Col. 0170D] A certain donation made by Ardrad on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the third year of the reign of Charles the Simple, would prove that Adalgar was still alive in 895; Labbe I, 271. But in the acts of the Synod of Chalon (Mansi XVII, p. 310), it is read that on the Kalends of May, in the year 897, indiction 12, bishops assembled to institute an inquiry into Gisfrid, a monk of Flavigny, who was accused of having removed Adalgar by poison. K.].

There was also Bishop Walo, excommunicated by Pope Silvester for invading that same church, as is found in the letters of Aquinus, bishop elected before Walo. In the year 856 Adalgar became bishop; he presided for thirty-three years. [REGINO.] During this period the empire was divided and broken apart among many rulers: Boso held the kingdom of Provence, Wido the empire, Odo the kingdom of Francia under Charles the Simple, Rudolf the Jura, and the younger Charles the empire. In the first year after the translation of Saint Regina, Salocho, bishop of Dol and a monk of Flavigny, died; his body was found incorrupt after two hundred years.

**(Chron. Div.)** After the younger Lothair, his uncle Charles, surnamed the Bald [Note: [Col. 0170D] Uncle.], obtained the empire and the kingdom of Francia. But Louis, king of Italy and the other brother, desiring to seize the monarchy of the kingdom, again stirred up war against Charles, summoned the Normans and other peoples against him, and Charles defeated them and expelled his brother from his territories.

**(Leg. I, 534.)** In the year 876 Charles held a council at the palace of Pavia, attended by Berhard, bishop of Verdun. Edatius of . . . [Col. 0170A] ricum, Agelmar of Auvergne, and . . . nius of Langres were condemned and deposed. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Bishop Achard, in a document dated the sixth day before the Ides of April, while King Lothair was reigning, in year 12 (867), ordered the altar of Saint Martin in the estate of Chidiviacum to be ceded to Flavigny. Labbe I, 270, K. —But this name, as well as the see of Edatius, remains hidden.] He granted a privilege to the church of Flavigny. Under Pope Nicholas I, an eighth synod was held at Constantinople with five patriarchs and 150 fathers, at the request and in the presence of Basil the Great, emperor.

**(Chron. Div.)** Emperor Charles, surnamed the Bald, died in the year from the beginning of the Lord 877, indiction 11, on the day before the Nones of October. Queen Hermentrude died in the territory of Lyon, and he was buried at Nantoade in the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul. But, following an angelic warning, he was transferred to Paris and buried royally at Saint-Denis. Louis succeeded his father and reigned for four years; Louis, the grandson of Charles, succeeded him and held the royal title for scarcely two years. He so thoroughly subdued the Danes that scarcely anyone remained who could report it.

Pope Adrian was succeeded by John VIII in the year of the Lord 870. John came to Louis in Francia and spoke with him. This Louis died in the second year of his reign, in 882. Charles, who was called the Simple, remained in his cradle, deprived of his father. Therefore, in the year 888, indiction 6, because the Normans were threatening, the Franks chose Odo, son of Robert, count of Anjou, as guardian of the kingdom and of the child, and, although he resisted, made him king under Charles. As long as he lived, he vigorously restrained the enemies; and after Charles had grown up, he patiently restored his kingdoms to him, receiving from him a share of the kingdom.

Remigius, the forty-ninth bishop of Lyon, and Ado of Vienne sent a letter to the aforesaid Pope John concerning simony and because unworthy men were being promoted to the episcopate by lay hands. (Catalogue of pontiffs.) Marinus succeeded this John in the year of Christ 880, and Adrian sat in year 1. [Note: [Col. 0169] One letter is missing.] Stephen succeeded him in 885, indiction 3. Because of the rashness of Frotharius, bishop of Bordeaux, he sent a letter to Aurelian [Note: [Col. 0169] “Relia” supplied.], archbishop of Lyon, instructing him to take one or two bishops from the same province, go to that church, and consecrate its bishop. If they could find no one among the bishops of that province, they were to rely on their own authority and consecrate a bishop themselves. [Col. 0171A] Formosus succeeded Stephen; he was the one who became Silvester II. He restored Augrimus [Note: [Col. 0171] “Augr.” supplied from the list of abbots.] of Langres, who had been substituted in his place after Aurelian of Lyon had died [Note: [Col. 0171] Thus restored from the list; “repaired” seems to be read in the manuscript.]. Formosus entrusted his responsibilities to Barnoinus of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0171] “Ommisit,” deleted.], who was the brother of King Boso.

**(List of the abbots of Flavigny.)** Pope Formosus excommunicated Walo, who was claiming the bishopric of Autun for himself, because the archbishop of Lyon who had been deposed by Pope Stephen but restored by Formosus did not possess his pallium or the dignity restored to him: who, then, could consecrate a bishop? Bishop Teutbold, acting on the pope’s behalf, opposed the consecration. Walo was excommunicated because he had invaded the church of Saint Peter of Flavigny. Duke Richard, Manasses, and Ingelbert were also excommunicated for invading churches, especially those of Autun, until satisfaction should be made. This is found in the letter of Aquinus concerning Walo, the sought and elected bishop of Autun.

And Tedaldus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year from the beginning of the Lord 856, indiction 4. Isaac succeeded him in 880, indiction 13. Geylo succeeded Isaac; he had been promoted from the abbey of Flavigny to the bishopric of Langres in the year from the beginning of the Lord 880, indiction 13 [Note: [Col. 0171] The number has been lost.]. Teutbald succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0171] The beginning “Teut-” is missing.], and Augrimus succeeded Teutbald. Warnerus died in 908.

In the year 879, indiction 12, Boso received the kingdom of Provence at Vienne on the Ides of October, after . . . ; his son Louis succeeded him in 891, still a young man, by the authority of Pope Stephen, under the guardianship of Duke Richard and the queen.

[Col. 0171C] **(Chron. Div.)** In the regions of Bavaria, Saxony, and Italy, Louis, son of the emperor Louis the Pious, and Lothair, son of the emperor Lothair, held power. After their deaths, the sons of that Louis reigned. For the younger King Lothair died without sons.

**[BERT.]** In the time of Louis, in the year from the beginning of the Lord 875, indiction 8, after the death of Lord Hatto, the lord and most holy man Berhard was made bishop of Verdun by the acclamation of clergy and people. His most holy purpose and endeavor was to bring the basilica that had been begun to completion. By God’s mercy he did so. He established there large and honorable bells as well as very fine smaller ones, pontifical vestments, and many ecclesiastical ornaments, and he presented the bier containing the relics of the saints of his church. [Col. 0171D] He compelled his canons to live canonically; he courageously showed the rural priests the way of justice; and he instructed boys in divine and human books, both personally and through others, with the greatest charity. He died in the monastery of Theolegium, where his body was also buried, on the day before the Kalends of January. He had been bishop for ten years.

**(Chron. Div.)** Louis, the just and holy emperor, son of the elder Emperor Lothair and brother of the younger Lothair, died on the fourth day before the Ides of April in the year from the beginning of the Lord 878. His son Karloman succeeded him; his brothers were Louis and Charles. He reigned for five years and died on the Nones of December in the year 884, in which year the Normans invaded Burgundy. [REGINO.] When Charles, surnamed the Bald, heard of his brother’s death, he entered Italy, but, terrified by his nephew Karloman, fled; and in that same year, as we have said, he died.

(Fol. 63.) Karloman died on the Nones of December in the year 884. In the following year Charles became emperor, and when he died after one year, another Charles, the Simple, assumed the empire and reigned for twenty-nine years. Louis, the brother of Karloman, who had been made king of the Saxons, entered Bavaria while that same brother was still alive.

**(Chron. Div.)** In the year from the beginning of the Lord 881, on the Nones of August, Louis, son of King Louis, fought against the pagans and crushed them [Note: [Col. 0171] Thus I supply the text.]; he reigned for three years.

[Col. 0172B] **[REGINO.]** After these two brothers, namely Louis and Karloman, had died within five years, supreme power came to the younger Charles, who was consecrated emperor by Pope John.

**(Chron. Div.)** The year 885, indiction 4, was the fifth year of Emperor Charles in Italy, the fourth in eastern Francia, and the first in Gaul.

**[BERT.]** In the time of King Louis the German, Dado assumed the bishopric of the city of Verdun in the year from the beginning of the Lord 885, under whom Dado acquired very many things. After Dado’s death, Charles, as we have said, acquired the monarchy. Before becoming bishop, Dado had presided over the abbey of Saint Vitonus, and he did not abandon it even after receiving the bishopric. He acquired many possessions for that church, in whose cemetery Bertharius, a canon of the same church, lies buried.

[Col. 0172C] In the year from the beginning of the Word 887, the pagan Normans entered the fortress or monastery of Flavigny and killed eight monks together with their servants [Note: [Col. 0171] “V ::: c.”]; they remained there for fourteen days [Note: [Col. 0171] I supply this; in the manuscript only V seems to be visible.], from the third day before the Ides of January until the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

**[BERT., Preface.]** During the pontificate of Lord Dado, when through his good zeal and illustrious reputation many favorable things had come to the church entrusted to him over thirty-five years, in the thirty-sixth year the principal church was consumed by fire, and most of the books and records of the holy fathers had been destroyed. Therefore Bertharius the priest, so that the sacred memory, venerable zeal, and holy work of the pontiffs of Verdun should not be wholly consigned to oblivion, gathered into a concise account what he had read concerning their holy deeds, pleasing to those present and useful to posterity.

**(Chron. Div.)** Charles, having obtained the empire of Italy and Saxony, after subjecting the Normans who had worn down Paris with a seven-year siege, died in the year from the beginning of the Lord 888, indiction 6, on the day before the Nones of October, in the fourth year of his empire. [REGINO.] After him Arnulf, his nephew, received the kingdom in the year from the beginning of the Lord 888, indiction 6—that is, in the same year—the son of Karloman, son of the just and holy Emperor Louis.

**(Chron. Div.)** The Normans again rose up in the kingdom of the Franks. In the year from the beginning of the Lord 891, indiction 9, they ravaged Gaul, Spain, Italy, Francia, and the whole kingdom of the Christians. The cities of Paris, Beauvais, Chartres, Meaux, and the other cities everywhere were likewise plundered, devastated, and overturned. The bodies of the saints were brought within the walls out of fear of the enemy. The body of Saint Benignus, patron of the church of Dijon, is said to have been brought to Langres. Saint Santinus of Meaux, placed in the principal church, had already been carried to Verdun by the people of Verdun at great cost during the time of the earlier flight [Note: [Col. 0173] “f. ::: c.”], in the year 866.

The Normans ranged throughout Gaul, went to Spain, entered the river Rhône, devastated Italy, and destroyed the whole kingdom of the Christians. Meanwhile the leaders of Francia assembled and held a council concerning important matters. As we have said, they made Odo king under Charles, although he resisted. **(Annals of Saint Vaast.)** Indiction 10 was the first year of the empire of Wido Augustus. He had been made king through Galon, bishop of Langres. When he heard that Odo had been made king, he fought many battles against Berengar, king of Italy; returning victorious, he was created emperor. In that same year, at Toul and around the Alps beyond the Jura, Rudolf was made king in year 92. [Note: [Col. 0173] “At” is deleted.]

**(Chron. Div.)** In the year from the beginning of the Lord 893, indiction 11, while Odo reigned in Francia and Arnulf in Italy and Saxony, Charles, now a young man, reclaimed the scepter of the Franks. The aforementioned Arnulf seized the monarchy of the empire, captured Rome with the consent of Pope Formosus, and was promoted by him to be emperor.

**[REGINO.]** Then for the first time the empire was transferred from the kings of the Franks to foreigners, because the leaders of the kingdom held Charles in contempt on account of the slowness of his mind.

**(Chron. Div.)** Zendebold was made king by Arnulf in the presence of his father, King Odo. Arnulf gave him the kingdom of Lothair; afterward his son was killed, and he himself died in the year 901.

**(Annals of Saint Vaast.)** When Odo died in the twelfth year of his reign, in the year from the beginning of the Lord 899, the waves of Normans and Danes again arose. The Hungarians from the north, and the Saracens bursting forth from the south and from the borders of Spain, clashed in the destruction of Gaul. **(Chron. Div.)** The sword raged everywhere; everything was given over to fire; the holy places were delivered to destruction.

(Fol. 63'.) In that year Burgundy was devastated by the Normans. Duke Richard the Justiciar met them, defeated them in battle, and forced them to turn back. Again, near Chartres, Richard fought the Normans together with Duke Robert, the brother of King Odo, and killed a vast multitude of them. He had three sons: Rudolf, who became king of the Franks; Boso, who received the kingdom of upper Gaul, called Comata—that is, Burgundy; and a third, Hugh Capet, who became duke of lower Burgundy.

**[REGINO.]** In the year from the beginning of the Lord 904, there was a war between Duke Conrad and Adalbert. Conrad fell in it, and in the following year Adalbert was executed by beheading.

**(Catalogue of pontiffs.)** Boniface, Stephen, Theodore, and John IX succeeded Formosus.

In the year 910 the monastery of Cluny was built, and in 918 William, the duke who built it, died.

**(List of the abbots of Flavigny.)** In the year 913 Walo, bishop of Autun, died. He had presided for twenty years under Charles the Simple. Herveus succeeded him.

**[FLOD.]** In the year 919, extraordinary hail fell at Reims, exceeding a hen’s egg in size and measuring half a palm in breadth. In the following year honey was found in the ears of grain, and flowers appeared on trees whose fruits had already ripened.

In the year from the beginning of the Lord 917, Rudolf was made king, and in the twenty-first year of his reign he was killed by the Hungarians, that is, the Saracens, together with Ebbo, duke of the fortress of Dol. Duke Hugh then invaded the kingdom, taking Charles, son of Rudolf, into custody; and he reigned until the year from the beginning of the Lord 981.

In that same year, which was the year from the beginning of the Lord 920, Rollo, leader of the Normans, died, and his son William succeeded him. William was killed by treachery in the year 943, and his son Richard succeeded him.

**(Chron. Div.)** When discord arose between Charles and the leaders of the kingdom, disputes and wars, plundering and fires, and innumerable evils raged everywhere. At last, repenting of what he had done, the king moved the leaders toward reconciliation and established the peace he desired with them.

Richard, therefore, who had acquired his surname from the execution of justice, remained faithful to King Charles throughout his life. After Richard’s death in 922, and after King Odo had also died, on the Kalends of January his brother Robert, hoping and desiring to obtain that part of the kingdom which Odo himself had held, because Charles the Simple—the lord of the entire kingdom—did not return it to him, openly seized power as a tyrant. By cajolery and partly by threats, he extorted from certain bishops a royal crown and the insignia of the royal scepter. But this presumption did not have a happy outcome.

**[REGINO.]** In the year from the beginning of the Lord 900, Emperor Arnulf died, and his son Louis succeeded him. After administering the empire for twelve years, Louis died and left the scepter of the kingdom to Conrad, son of Duke Conrad, in the year from the beginning of the Lord 911. Conrad also reigned for nine years, and Henry I, the great emperor, succeeded him in 920.

**[FLOD.]** In that year there was a dispute between Bishop Hilduin and Abbot Richarius over the bishopric of Tongeren. The king had given that bishopric to Richarius because Hilduin, to whom he had previously given it, had defected from him. But Herimann, archbishop of Cologne, with the clergy choosing and the people supporting him, and also with the support of Giselbert, whom many of the Lotharingians had appointed as their prince after abandoning Charles, ordained Hilduin bishop there. Charles, however, even after the Lotharingians had returned to him together with Duke Giselbert, was supporting Abbot Richarius in that bishopric. Therefore both men went to Rome.

[Col. 0175A] In the year 921 a synod was held at Trosly, presided over by Heriveus, archbishop of Reims, and attended by Charles. From there Charles departed for the kingdom of Lothair. After making an agreement with Henry, the ruler beyond the Rhine, he returned to Laon and later established peace with him.

The Normans accepted the faith of Christ under compulsion from Count Robert. In that same year Richard the Justiciar died.

**[FLOD.]** In the following year the kingdom of Lothair was devastated because of the persecution carried out by Giselbert and Otto, through plundering, sacrilege, and fires, even during Lent. Richarius, who had gone to Rome because of the bishopric of Tongeren, returned after being ordained bishop by Pope John IX; Hilduin had been excommunicated by that same pope. Drogo, bishop of Toul, died; Gauzlin succeeded him and was also ordained on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

(Fol. 64.) In that same year Robert, having been consecrated king, openly seized power as a tyrant, as we have said. Heriveus, archbishop of Reims, died on the third day after Robert’s consecration, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, before completing the twenty-second year of his episcopate. Seulfus, then archdeacon, succeeded him.

Robert sent his son Hugh into the kingdom of Lothair. After receiving hostages from certain Lotharingians, Hugh returned to his father. Charles had besieged the fortress of Château-Thierry belonging to Giselbert; Hugh had been sent to relieve it, and when Charles learned this, he abandoned the siege.

In the year from the beginning of the Lord 922, three suns seemed to appear in the sky at Cambrai, or the sun seemed to have three disks at a distance from one another. Two spikes and two posts were also seen approaching one another until they were covered. An earthquake occurred as well.

**(Catalogue of pontiffs.)** Benedict, Leo, Christopher, Sergius, Anastasius, Lando, and John X succeeded Pope John IX.

**[FLOD.]** In the year from the beginning of the Lord 923, indiction 11, Robert went into the kingdom of Lothair, made an agreement with Henry, and, after gifts had been exchanged on both sides, they departed. There certain Lotharingians also gave hostages to Robert and received a truce.

But Charles, crossing the Meuse with his Lotharingians, who had broken the truce, went beneath the city of Soissons, where he had learned that Robert was staying. On the following day, Sunday, after the sixth hour had passed, when the Franks did not expect a battle and many of them were eating, Charles crossed the Aisne and fell upon Robert. Robert, however, armed the men who were with him and advanced against Charles. When battle had been joined and many had fallen on both sides, Robert himself was pierced by spears and fell.

Those who were with Robert—namely his son Hugh, Count Herbert of Vermandois, and the others—nevertheless gained the victory and put Charles and the Lotharingians to flight. But because their king had died, they stopped pursuing them and held the field. The peasants carried off the spoils.

The Lotharingians, leaving Charles within the kingdom of Francia, returned to their own land. Charles sent many embassies to Count Herbert and Archbishop Seulfus, begging them to return to their own country.

[Col. 0176A] **(Chron. Div.)** When they refused, they sent into Burgundy for Rudolf, son of Richard the Justiciar. He soon came to meet them with a large force of his own men. When Charles fled across the Meuse, Rudolf himself was established as king at the city of Soissons. His brother Boso was made king of upper Gaul, called Comata—that is, upper Burgundy—and Hugh Capet was made duke of lower Burgundy.

The companions of the revolt were not at all frightened by Robert’s death and did not abandon their obstinacy in treachery. Rather, Herbert, by the unspeakable crime of betrayal, captured his lord and king, Charles, king of all Francia, by deceit, ensnared him in chains, and took him to Parrona to shut him away in the dark dwelling of a prison.

Since the kingdom was being governed without a prince and was therefore falling into uncertainty—and especially since the youth of Hugh, son of Robert, who later earned the name “the Great” through his honorable deeds, prevented him from taking up the royal insignia, while Herbert’s conduct stirred everyone’s hatred, particularly those whom compassion for the suffering of the prince moved toward mercy—finally, as we have said, Rudolf was placed in charge of governing Francia, and thus the kingdom of the Franks was transferred to a foreigner.

After obtaining the throne, he was both a severe avenger against evildoers and most skillful in restraining enemies and defending the kingdom. In his days the armies of the Danes and Normans came again and ranged not only through Francia but also throughout Burgundy. Rudolf took up arms against them and so checked their insolent attacks that, even to the present, he has kept Gaul quiet from their incursions.

At that time the body of Saint Benignus the martyr was brought within the walls of the fortress of Dijon and preserved there in the church of Saint Vincent.

**[FLOD.]** While occupied with these matters, Rudolf received envoys from the Lotharingians, who submitted themselves and their possessions to him.
