(Fol. 64'.) When the Lotharingians met him near Mouzon, they were received by Wiger, bishop of Metz, while his wife Emma, daughter of King Robert, was meanwhile consecrated queen by Seulfus. Rudolf returned after receiving hostages from certain Lotharingians.

In that year Dado, bishop of Verdun, died after completing thirty-eight years in the episcopate and earned a worthy burial among the tombs of his predecessors, the bishops, in the church of Saint Vitonus. Rudolf the king granted the bishopric of Verdun to Hugh, who was afterward consecrated at Reims by Archbishop Seulfus.

In the year 924, indiction 12, the Hungarians, led by King Berengar, whom the Lombards had driven back, ravaged Italy. They also burned Pavia, an extremely populous and wealthy city, destroying innumerable riches. Forty-four churches were consumed by fire. The bishop of the city and the bishop of Vercelli, who was with him, were killed by fire and smoke. Of that almost countless multitude, only two hundred are said to have survived; from the remains of the burned city, which they had gathered among the ashes, they gave the Hungarians eight bushels, thereby buying their lives and the walls of the deserted city.

After these things had been completed, they proceeded through precipitous places and reached the ridges of the Alps. Rudolf, king of Cisalpine Gaul, and Hugh, king of Vienne, trapped them amid the narrow Alpine passes. Escaping unexpectedly through remote paths, they attacked Gothia. The aforementioned leaders pursued them and struck down those whom they found.

Meanwhile Berengar was killed by his own men. The Normans made an agreement with the Franks, and the land of Maine and Bayeux was given under the peace treaty. The Hungarians, however, almost all perished from swelling of the head and dysentery.

In the following year Seulfus, archbishop of Reims, died after completing three years and five days in the episcopate. Rollo, prince of the Rouen Normans, broke the peace after ravaging Francia, and the Franks captured the fortress of Eu against him.

All the Lotharingians also entrusted themselves to Henry. He granted the bishopric of Verdun to Bernuin, nephew of Bishop Dado, who, after expelling Hugh, to whom Rudolf had given it, was ordained bishop there in the year 925, indiction 13. From that time Verdun and the other cities defected from the kingdom of the Franks.

Hugh the priest, driven out of Verdun, died in the following year. In that same year, out of fear of the Hungarians, the body of Saint Remigius and the relics of other saints were carried from Reims.

Hugh, son of Berta, was made king of Italy after Rudolf, king of Cisalpine Gaul and invader of the kingdom, was expelled. Four years earlier Rudolf had been chosen by the Italians after they had rejected King Berengar. The year 928, indiction 1, was the first year of that King Hugh.

Hugh the Great, son of King Robert, also took as his wife the daughter of Edward, king of the English, who was the sister of Charles’s wife.

In the year 927, a plague resembling a fever combined with mortality and a cough spread among all the peoples of Germany and Gaul. Widricus, bishop of Metz, was struck by it and died. Count Herbert and Hugh the Great, son of Robert, were summoned across the Rhine to a conference with Henry. After peace had been established, they honored Henry with gifts, and he honored them in return.

There Henry, disregarding the election of the citizens, gave the bishopric of the city of Metz to a certain servant of God, as it was reported, named Benno. Herbert released Charles from custody and led him with him as far as Saint-Quentin. At Metz and throughout Gaul, people were driven to flee from fear of the Hungarians, specifically through Francia and Lotharingia.

[Col. 0177D] (Fol. 65.) In the following year, when Rudolf heard that Charles had been restored, he came from Burgundy into Francia with a hostile force, plundering and burning certain places. Hugh, son of Robert, prepared to meet him. When they came together on the Oise, Hugh stood between King Rudolf and Count Herbert as mediator and intermediary.

Herbert, after giving hostages, came with Charles to the appointed meeting at Reims. From there he sent a letter from Pope John concerning the restoration and honor of Charles, as the pope had ordered him under threat of excommunication.

But when the messenger returned, he announced that Pope John himself had been shut up in prison by Wido, the brother of King Hugh, because of certain disputes that had arisen between them.

**[FLOD.]** After this Herbert commended himself to Rudolf, while Charles was again returned to custody, and Herbert went with Rudolf to meet Hugh, king of Italy.

Bishop Benno of Metz was attacked by an ambush, castrated, and deprived of his eyesight.

King Rudolf, however, sent messengers and made peace with Charles, restoring Attigny to him and honoring him with gifts.

In the year 929, Pope John X died in custody. John XI succeeded him. Charles likewise died at Péronne, having freed his soul, though not his body, from custody. (Chronicle of Dijon.) While he lived, he was called “the Simple” because of his kindness of spirit; now he may rightly be called holy, since, unjustly afflicted by his faithless and perjured subjects with the foulness of prolonged imprisonment, he was transferred to eternal life. He left a son, Louis Overseas, [Col. 0178B] born of Eadgifu, daughter of the king of the English. Fearing to be drawn into the storms of his homeland’s calamities, Louis withdrew among the Anglo-Saxons, on account of his maternal kinship. Counts Herbert and Hugh marched against Boso, King Rudolf’s brother, and for this reason Boso was compelled to swear peace to Henry. Adalbero obtained the bishopric of Metz, while an abbey was granted to Benno as a means of support. The Alpine passes were then blockaded by the Saracens, by whom many wishing to travel to Rome were hindered and forced to turn back. After this, Boso, the king’s brother, abandoned King Henry and returned to Rudolf.

In the year 932, Bernuinus, bishop of Verdun, and Boso, the king’s brother and king of Gaul, which is called Comata, raged among themselves with burnings and plundering, [Col. 0178C] and consequently the city itself suffered greatly.

[FLOD.] In the following year, Vienne was surrendered to King Rudolf, William, prince of the Normans, became his subordinate, and King Hugh of Italy besieged Rome. Fulbert was ordained bishop of Cambrai by Artald, archbishop of Reims.

In the following year, fiery ranks were seen moving across the sky, like a serpent of fire, and certain darts of iron were seen to fly on the morning before sunrise, on the day before the Ides of October. Soon afterward a pestilence followed, afflicting human bodies with various diseases. Struck by this plague, a certain deacon of Verdun named Adelmarus, overcome by illness, died. But before he was placed upon the bier, he returned and rose up so vigorous that he seemed to himself to have suffered no illness. He testified that he had seen various places of punishment and refreshment, and that he himself had been assigned to a place of punishment but, through the prayers of the Mother of God and blessed Martin, had been restored to the present life in order to perform penance. [Col. 0178D] (fol. 65'.)

Moved by this example, certain canons of Saint Mary abandoned the world. Since there was no monastic community in that same city [Note: [Col. 0177] Cf. *Gesta episcoporum Virdunensium*, Continuation C, 2, and John of Gorze, *Life*, chap. 21, 23 ff., *SS*, vol. IV.]—for clerics served in the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus—they went to Toul and, having changed their habit in the monastery of Saint Aper, endeavored to abandon the world and be incorporated into Christ the Lord, like faithful members into their head. This matter caused the bishop great sorrow, as well as the remaining canons and the leading men [Col. 0179A] of the people, because they wished them rather to serve in that same episcopal church than to migrate elsewhere. Nevertheless, through their good and praiseworthy endeavors and examples, the religious observance of the monastic rule and the fervor of the order were restored in that monastery and in certain others throughout the kingdom of Lotharingia.

Meanwhile, when the year had passed, Boso, the king’s brother, made peace with Henry and was received by him. King Rudolf of France and King Rudolf of the Jura likewise entered into friendship with him. Boso died during the expedition to besiege the castle of Saint-Quentin and was buried at Saint-Remigius in Reims.

(Fol. 64.) The Hungarians spread through Burgundy, raging for a short time with plunder, burnings, and slaughter; but when they learned of King Rudolf’s arrival, they crossed over into Italy. (Cf. the *Life of the Abbot* of Flavigny.)

When Bishop Herveus died, Romundus was substituted in his place under King Rudolf. He destroyed the abbey of Coltice [Note: [Col. 0179D] Couches.] and built the castle of Coltica, and likewise constructed Cursum, pierced through with a rock, and gave the possessions of the churches and the castles he had made to his sons and descendants [Note: [Col. 0179D] Walter of Autun records that Bishop Romundus, held down by illness and unable to resist the secular men who were plundering the monastery’s goods, confirmed the goods recovered from Amadeus, abbot of Flavigny, in the fifteenth year of King Robert. Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, century IV, p. 644. K.]. After perpetrating many evils, he died, scourged by Saint Gregory.

(Fol. 65'.) In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 936, King Rudolf died without children, for his son Louis, whom he had by Queen Emma, had died before his father. (Chronicle of Dijon.) [FLOD.] Count Hugh the Great sent overseas to summon to the royal throne Louis, son of Charles. His maternal uncle, King Athelstan, after receiving an oath from the envoys of the Franks, sent him toward France with certain bishops [Col. 0179C] and other faithful men. Hugh went to meet him with the leading men of the Franks. On the sandy shore near Boulogne, they placed themselves under his authority, as had been agreed on both sides. From there Louis was conducted to Laon, enriched with royal blessing, and anointed and crowned by Artald, archbishop of Reims, in the presence of the kingdom’s leading men and more than twenty bishops.

Soon they went into Burgundy and besieged Langres, which Hugh Capet, King Rudolf’s brother, had captured. When its defenders fled, they received the city without a battle. After taking hostages from the bishops and leading men of Burgundy, they returned to Paris. Hugh the Great and Hugh Capet, son of Richard, divided Burgundy between themselves and made peace. (Chronicle of Dijon.) After Hugh Capet, Gislebert obtained the duchy.

When Louis wished to exercise the administration of the kingdom under his own authority, it proved exceedingly burdensome to him, both because of his capture by Theobald, count of Chartres, and, after his recovery of the kingdom, because of the various outcomes of unstable fortune. [FLOD.] In those same days the great emperor Henry died, and a dispute concerning the kingdom arose among his sons. Nevertheless, supreme authority over affairs fell to Otto, the eldest.

Pope John also died, the brother of the patrician Alberic, and Leo V succeeded him. King Hugh of Italy withdrew from Rome after making peace with the patrician Alberic. [Col. 0180A]

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 937, King Louis separated himself from Hugh’s guardianship. In that year a portion of the sky seemed to burn, and from the same quarter there followed an incursion of Hungarians. Villages and fields were laid waste, houses and basilicas were burned, and a multitude of captives was carried away. Nevertheless, when they set fire to certain churches, they could not burn them.

In the church of Saint Basolus, when one of the Hungarians tried to climb upon the altar and had applied his bow to it with his hand, his hand adhered to the stone and could not be torn away at all. Only after the others had cut the stone around the hand itself was the pagan, to everyone’s amazement, compelled to carry away that portion of stone.

A certain priest was captured by them and bound in chains, but was freed by divine revelation. After he had returned to his homeland and house, he reported that a certain monk named Hucbald, of the monastery of Orbais, had been in the same captivity. The pagans repeatedly tried to slaughter him, but could not cut his flesh. They therefore placed him naked in their midst and attacked him with arrows, yet could not even pierce his skin. The arrows rebounded from his body as though repelled by a diamond, and no mark appeared on his skin. They tried with all their strength to strike him with a sword, but nevertheless his flesh remained unharmed.

Radulf, king of cisalpine Gaul in the Jura, died; Conrad succeeded him. Hugh, son of Robert, also took as his wife the sister of Otto, daughter of King Henry. (Chronicle of Dijon.)

In the second year of Louis, [Col. 0180C] son of Charles the Simple, lord Fulcher was ordained abbot of Flavigny; he also governed Dijon for fifteen years. (Life of the Abbot of Flavigny.) In the eighth year of his rule he went to Jerusalem and, returning with precious relics, enriched his church. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of May. Milo Magabrensis succeeded him and obtained a privilege from the pope.

In the year 939, Bernuinus, bishop of Verdun, died. The Lotharingians abandoned their king Otto and prepared to place themselves under Louis, who delayed receiving them because of the friendship that had been agreed between himself and Otto. Again, the leading men of the kingdom—Duke Gislebert and many counts—came to him and placed themselves under his authority. The bishops, however, did not abandon Otto, who was holding their hostages with him. After crossing the Rhine, Otto traversed the kingdom of Lotharingia and devastated certain places with fire and plunder.

When he had returned across the Rhine, Louis attacked the district of Verdun and, after being received by certain bishops and leading men, returned. Duke Gislebert, having crossed the Rhine to plunder, was returning when his adversaries pursued him. He leapt into the Rhine with his horse and was drowned; afterward he could not be found. Louis took as his wife Gislebert’s widow, Otto’s sister. Otto obtained the duchy. Otto then compelled all the Lotharingians to return to him, and in the following year captured Conrad, king of Burgundy, by treachery and made peace with the remaining leading men.

In the year 940, indiction 13, lord Berengarius, born from the lineage of the magnates of Saxony, was enthroned in the pontificate of the city of Verdun.

And, made a companion and equal of apostolic honor,

With the praise of clergy and people,

He led an apostolic life in deeds and in name.

For he was chaste in body, devoted in mind, affable in speech, distinguished in counsel, endowed with prudence, temperate in judgment, firm in inward strength, steadfast in the discipline of justice, constant in long-suffering, strong in patience, gentle in humility, a companion of offenders through compassion, yet raised up against them through zeal for righteousness. [Col. 0181B]

(Fol. 66'.) In his words there appeared an unshaken constancy of mind, and in his actions and conduct the insignia of the virtues shone forth.

He offered to everyone an extremely generous welcome,

No one was excluded; no one suffered rejection.

Loving Christ with all his inmost being and overflowing with the depths of inward charity, he was always concerned for the poor. Since, like Martha, he could not provide Christ with bodily services, he daily refreshed him in the needy. His speech was seasoned with salt; and the briefer and rarer it was, the more precious it was considered for its prudent sweetness.

Among the other members of Christ, he loved lord Fulbert, bishop of Cambrai, with sincere and unanimous affection. With him he always had the constant task of attacking the enemies of truth with all his strength, as anyone can observe in what follows. (Gesta of Verdun 2.)

He lived in the time of Otto, of whom it was said that “Otto began to grow toward the triumph of the Church.” A second Otto succeeded him in the empire, so that the world might flourish.

[FLOD.] In the very year of his ordination, the instigator of wickedness, Hugh the Great, together with certain bishops and leading men of France and Burgundy, besieged the city of Reims. After obtaining it, on the sixth day of the siege he compelled Bishop Artald by oath to renounce the administration and authority of the bishopric, granting him the abbey of Saint Basolus and the monastery of Avenay. Having left at Reims Hugh, son of Heribert, who had long before been elected to the bishopric, he hastened to besiege Laon. [Col. 0181D]

When Louis returned from Burgundy and took Bishop Artald with him, he crossed the Aisne and proceeded toward Laon. Hugh and his men abandoned the siege, went to meet King Otto, and placed themselves under his authority. Otto entrusted the kingdom of Lotharingia to his brother Henry and, with a multitude of various peoples, pursued Louis as he was going into Burgundy. With him he had Conrad, son of Rudolf, king of the Jura, whom he had captured by treachery some time before and was keeping with him. After receiving hostages from certain men, he returned to his own territories.

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 941, the bishops of the diocese of Reims assembled at Soissons in the church of Saints Crispin and Crispinian to deliberate concerning the condition of the church of Reims. The clerics and noble laymen complained that the see had long been vacant of a pastor. They determined that, since Bishop Artald had sworn that he would never concern himself with that bishopric, he ought not to return to its governance, and that Hugh, son of Heribert, who had previously been summoned to that bishopric at the request of the clergy and people, should be ordained bishop.

Thus the bishops went to Reims and consecrated Hugh as bishop. The canons of Montfaucon, as they asserted, weighed down by the oppression of the bishop of Verdun, abandoned their monastery and brought the body of their patron, Saint Baldric, to Reims.

Artald, having lost everything he possessed, gave oaths to Bishop Hugh and to Heribert as they demanded. After the abbeys of Saint Basolus and Avenay, together with the villa of Vindenissa, had been restored to him, he made peace with them and went to Saint Basolus to live.

Not long afterward, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 942, the legate of Pope Stephen, named Damasus, bishop of Rome, who had been ordained for carrying out this legation, brought letters from the apostolic see to the princes of the Franks, ordering them to receive their king Louis. (Fol. 67.) If they neglected this and wished to continue persecuting him as an enemy, he threatened them with the punishment of excommunication.

The legates of the church of Reims, who had likewise been sent to Rome, returned reporting the same thing: the king was to be received by them before Christmas, under threat of anathema. They also brought the pallium for Hugh from the apostolic see. [Col. 0182C]

Louis therefore went to meet King Otto and established friendship with him. Otto also reconciled Hugh the Great with the king.

In this year, lord Odo, the venerable restorer of many monasteries, died at Tours after laboring greatly to establish peace between Hugh, king of Italy, and Alberic, patrician of the Romans. He was buried at Saint Martin, and Heimardus, a venerable man, succeeded him. At that time there was a great famine throughout France and Burgundy.

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 943, William, son of Rollo, was killed, and Richard I succeeded him. Richard obtained Normandy as a gift from King Louis. Hugh the Great fought against the Normans who wished to return to paganism, and in that year Louis granted him the duchy of France.

In the following year Heribert died. His sons were received by Louis through the mediation of Otto, duke of Lotharingia, Adalbero, bishop of Metz, and Duke Hugh. Hugh was received by Louis on the condition that another bishopric would be provided for him and that Reims would be restored to Artald. After this, Otto, duke of Lotharingia, died, and Conrad obtained the duchy.

In the year 946, Pope Marinus died and Agapitus succeeded him. In the preceding year Louis had besieged the city of Reims; after receiving hostages from Hugh as a pledge that an account would be rendered concerning matters about which he was to be questioned, he had withdrawn from the siege.

[FLOD.] From there Louis proceeded to Rouen, where he was captured by his own supporters through treachery and held in custody. Hugh of Italy was also driven from the kingdom by his own men; his son Lothair succeeded him.

Because Hugh the Great was striving to free the king, Louis was released after hostages had been given. Hugh entrusted him to Theobald, count of Chartres, and after a year restored him to the kingdom.

Louis and Otto joined together and surrounded the city of Reims with a siege. On the third day of the siege, Bishop Hugh came out with his men. Robert of Trier and Frederick of Mainz restored Artald to the see, since the authority of the Roman see had so decreed.

In the following year both kings celebrated Easter at Aachen. A synod announced for the middle of November was held at Verdun, presided over by Robert of Trier together with Artald of Reims, Berengarius of Verdun, Odalric of Aachen, Adalbero of Metz, Goslenus of Toul, Hildebaud of Transrhenish territory, and Israel the Breton, in the presence of Bruno, abbot and brother of King Otto, Agenoldus and Odilo, and certain other venerable abbots.

This synod was announced at Verdun for the following reason: so that the aforementioned Berengarius of Verdun might at least attend the assembly of the bishops, since his authority was so great that it seemed improper for the authenticity of his most steadfast nobility not to lend support to the proceedings.

Hugh was summoned to it, and bishops Adalbero and Goslenus were sent to bring him, but he refused to come. The entire synod adjudged the bishopric to Artald of Reims. A further synod was then announced for the Ides of January. On the appointed day it was held in the church of Saint Peter, before the fortress of Mouzon, by lord Robert and the other bishops of the diocese of Trier, together with certain bishops of Reims.

When Hugh came to it, he refused to enter but sent a letter under the name of Pope Agapitus through his cleric, who had brought it from Rome. The letter contained only this: that the bishopric of Reims should be restored to him. (Fol. 67'.)

Since Robert of Trier had received the mandate of the apostolic legation before the kings and the bishops of Gaul and Germany, with Frederick of Mainz presenting it, and had already fulfilled part of the instruction, it was decreed by common decision that what had been regularly begun should be completed canonically.

Accordingly, after chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage, concerning the accused and the accuser, had been read, it was determined according to the meaning of that chapter that, while Artald held the parish, Hugh should abstain from communion and governance [Col. 0183D] until he appeared at the universal synod on the Kalends of August to clear himself. This chapter was written out in a document and sent to him, together with the decision.

On the following day he sent it back and declared that he would in no way obey. Meanwhile, lord Artald sent letters of complaint to the Roman see. Therefore Pope Agapitus sent his vicar, Bishop Marinus, to King Otto in order to convene a general synod. Letters of the pope were also sent individually to certain bishops of Gaul and Germany, ordering them to assemble for the same synod.

The aforesaid synod was therefore assembled in the royal palace at Ingelheim, in the church of Saint Remigius, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the year 948, indiction 6, in the third year of the papacy of lord Agapitus, in the thirteenth year of the reign of King Otto and likewise the thirteenth of Louis. Its purpose was to address the greatest dissensions between King Louis and Prince Hugh, and also between Artald, archbishop of Reims, and Hugh, the bishop unlawfully substituted in his place; these dissensions had disturbed the entire kingdom of the Franks.

Thirty-two bishops of Gaul and Germany assembled at this synod. We judged it worthy to record them below:

Robert of Trier, Artald of Reims, Frederick of Mainz, Wigfrid of Cologne, Adaldoch of Hamburg, Hildebold of Minden, Goslenus of Toul, Adalbero of Metz, Berengarius of Verdun, Fulbert of Cambrai, Rudolf of Laon, Richo of Worms, Reimbold of Speyer, Poppo of Würzburg, Conrad of Constance, Oderic of Augsburg, Tethard of Hildesheim, Bernard of Halberstadt, Dudo of Paderborn, Farabert of Tongeren, Lioptacus of Ribe, Michael of Regensburg, Doddo of Osnabrück, Everis of Minden, Baldric of Utrecht, Herold of Salzburg, Adalbert of Basel, Starchannus of Eichstätt, Horath of Schleswig, Wichard of Basel, and Liefdac of Rips.

(Fol. 68.) After these prelates had taken their seats in the aforementioned church, following the prayers customarily offered at the celebration of a council and the readings from sacred authority, the glorious kings Otto and Louis entered and sat together. After Marinus, the legate of the apostolic see, had delivered his address, King Louis rose from the side and seat of lord King Otto. Publicly before the legate and the other seated bishops, he presented the grievance of his appeal, explaining how he had been summoned from regions across the sea by the envoys of Hugh and the princes of France to receive the kingdom of his paternal inheritance; how, after being consecrated amid the votes and acclamations of all, he had been elevated to the royal throne; and how afterward he had been attacked by the aforementioned Hugh through treachery, captured, and held in custody for an entire year.

If anyone should object that he had suffered all these evils because of his own crime, he declared that he would either clear himself of them according to synodal judgment and the command of King Otto or defend himself by single combat.

After this, Artald of Reims stated the case of the dispute between himself and Hugh, the bishop unlawfully substituted in his place.

Then a certain cleric of Hugh, brought forward into the assembly, produced a letter, asserting that it had been given to him by the vicar himself at Rome. It stated that all the bishops of the diocese of Reims had sent the same letters to Rome in support of Hugh’s restoration.

But Artald of Reims, Fulbert of Cambrai, and Rudolf, who were named in the same letter, immediately refuted this, asserting that they had never before heard or seen it and had given no consent to its delivery.

After the bearer had therefore been publicly confuted, he was deprived of the diaconate in accordance with the judgment of the canons and departed from the synod’s assembly rejected.

The bishopric of Reims was therefore adjudged to Bishop Artald according to the institutions of the canons and the decrees of the holy fathers.

On the second day of the session, at the proposal of Robert of Trier and Berengarius of Verdun, synodal judgment was carried out against Hugh, the invader of the see of Reims. According to the institutions of the holy canons and the decrees of the blessed fathers Sixtus, Alexander, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Symmachus, and the others, they excommunicated him and expelled him from the bosom of Mother Church until he should come to repentance and offer worthy satisfaction.

On the remaining days of the synod, they dealt with incestuous marriages and with churches that were granted—or rather sold—to priests in the regions of Germany, and that were illicitly given to laymen. It was prohibited and decreed that no one should presume to do this at all. Many other matters beneficial to the Church were also discussed.

[Col. 0185B] Meanwhile, at Louis’s request, King Otto sent Duke Conrad with the Lotharingians to his aid. While the army was being assembled, Artald remained with the bishop of Trier, King Louis with the duke, and Rudolf of Laon with Albero of Metz.

The Lotharingian army captured Mouzon and the fortification called Mons Acutus before Laon. Then the Lotharingian bishops came to Laon, summoned Hugh on Marinus’s behalf, and returned to their own territories.

(Fol. 68'.) Prince Hugh attacked the city of Soissons, burned the mother church together with part of the city, burned villages with their inhabitants in the territory of Reims, and committed many evils. For these and many other offenses, and because he had refused to come when summoned to the council, he was excommunicated at Trier by Marinus and the other bishops of France together with Robert of Trier at the following synod. None of the remaining bishops of Lotharingia and Germany was present there.

After completing these matters, Marinus went to Saxony for the consecration of the monastery of Fulda and then returned to Rome.

In the following year, lord Pope Agapitus held a council at Rome, at which he confirmed what had been done at the aforementioned synod.

[FLOD.] After this, Louis and Hugh made peace with one another through the mediation and arbitration of Duke Conrad, Hugh the Black, and Bishops Adalbero and Fulbert.

King Otto also subjugated the Wends and the Hungarians to himself.

A certain Berengarius, prince of Italy, having, as is said, poisoned King Lothair, the son of King Hugh, became king of Italy. King Otto then captured Pavia. When he went into Italy, Berengarius fled at his arrival; the king entered the same city and took as his wife Adelaid, the widow of King Lothair and sister of King Conrad of the Jura.

After the insolence of the wicked had been somewhat quieted, lord Berengarius, made for the sheep entrusted to him an example and mirror of every kind of religion and holiness, strove first to cut away from himself, and then from his subjects, what was harmful and superfluous; to correct what was corrupt; and to seek what was holy, honorable, and useful.

He always preferred what was honorable to what was useful. He thought that one must not turn aside from the truth because of any terror, fear, or flattery. He did not shrink from exile, because he knew that for the wise person the homeland is not the world. He did not fear poverty, because he knew that the wise person lacks nothing and that the whole world is a place of riches for him.

He praised the man who could not be moved by gold, who held wealth in contempt, who, as though from a certain citadel, looked down upon human desires, and with the prophet exclaimed in his praises:

“Who is he,” he said, “and we will praise him? For he has done wonders in his life.” (Ecclesiasticus 31:9.)

He said that the man who despised riches was worthy of admiration, since most people had preferred them to their own salvation.

He avoided greed and devoted every effort to ensuring that he did nothing against justice, but guarded it in all his works. He rebuked offenders and accepted no person’s status in judgment; favor was absent, and he judged cases according to their merits. He considered it a most serious offense to accuse an innocent poor man and excuse a rich man guilty of wrongdoing.

In God’s cause, where he knew that there was danger to communion, he said that even concealing sin was no light matter. He cultivated his reputation with every diligence, so that the mouths of all who wished to speak evil might be stopped.

Everyone regarded him with admiration for his wisdom and love of justice. He possessed the prudence to refute and convict the guilty by the testimony of his words, and also the justice to punish the guilty and rescue the innocent.

His spirit abounded in direct simplicity for every matter. In all his works, honorable conduct conquered utility, not utility honorable conduct. Nothing in him was elicited by artifice; nothing was contrived by deceit that lacked the merit of simplicity.

(Fol. 69.) He observed as naturally as possible the rule of justice implanted in him: not to depart from the truth, to possess his vessel in holiness, and to prefer honor to wealth, honors, and dignities. He allowed nothing simulated or fabricated to exist in himself—something which, though it might flourish at the beginning, would later disperse and wither like a little flower—but only what was true and sincere, founded upon a deep root.

Thus, through the practices of good works, he gave his subjects a model for striving toward the happiness of eternal rest.

In the twelfth year of his episcopate, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 951, indiction … [Note: [Col. 0185D] The number IX is missing in C.], seeing his sons like fertile earth sown with a pure grain of wheat and promising a richer and more abundant harvest, returning many times over what they had received, and grieving that some of them, inflamed by the most fervent desire for a more perfect life and love of a higher calling, were moving into neighboring dioceses [Col. 0186D] to seek elsewhere the monastic order, since it was not found in the city of Verdun itself (Gesta of Verdun 2), he chose, after consulting the clergy and leading men, to gather a community of monks in the aforementioned church dedicated in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, where the precious confessor of the Lord, Vitonus, rests and is venerated together with his predecessors and successors.

He did this so that the monks might serve the divine worship more devotedly and provide a model of humility and patience to all who wished to adhere to Christ. Thus those who had before their eyes a prepared example of religious life would not be compelled to withdraw elsewhere.

By the cooperation of divine grace, and as it searched the inmost recesses of the heart of its priest, it came to pass that the holy desire conceived through long meditation, and strengthened by delay, happily and swiftly attained its fulfillment. As many witnesses as there were to his desire, so many did he find as collaborators and helpers.

Having therefore expelled the clerics, he introduced monks. From his own property and from the goods of the mother church, he arranged for them annual revenues and the necessities of food and clothing, and prepared suitable dwellings for their workshops, hiring master craftsmen and supplying expenses. Thus he might find rest for his soul after labor in the courts of Jerusalem, which is built as a city, and whose fellowship is in unity.

He also appointed Humbert, a religious man from the monastery of Saint Aper, as their abbot, as is found in a charter signed by his own hand. We have judged it worthwhile to append it here. It is as follows:

“Let the diligence of all Catholics, both present and future, know that I, B., bishop of the holy church of Verdun in name, though not by merit, in the twelfth year of my ordination, mindful of the brothers of our church—most of whom frequently followed the Lord’s words saying, ‘Sell what you possess and give alms’ (Luke 12:33), ‘and you will have treasure in heaven, and follow me’ (Luke 18:22)—fleeing earthly things and loving heavenly things, were attempting to leave the place of our congregation, undertake the monastic life, and go to monasteries outside our parish.

“Lest afterward our church suffer loss from its own treasure, with the favor of our most glorious elder, King Otto, and of Conrad, the magnificent duke of the kingdom of Lothair, and with the faithful clerics and laymen of our church assembled by equal vote and common counsel, we decreed, with God’s assent, that a certain monastery should be established within our episcopal jurisdiction. In it, the brothers of our church who were fleeing the active life might in future be able to find the consolation of the contemplative life.

“Then, by common counsel, we summoned lord Humbert, a religious abbot, who had been raised in our church from the earliest beginnings of his childhood, had enjoyed a prebend of our canonry, and had been baptized and enrolled as a parishioner of our bishopric. Later, following the example of the other brothers written below, he undertook the monastic life in hope of eternal reward.

“By the concord of the clergy and people, and of those of our canons who at that time were striving to undertake the monastic life elsewhere, we granted him a certain monastery, established for the building of a community of monks in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. In it rest the bodies of the holy confessors and bishops Vitonus, Pulcronius, Possessor, Firminus, and Madelveus, together with all the possessions belonging to the same abbey.

“Six and a half manses adjoining Scantia belong to that monastery, together with four mills and the ban of that villa, which we have hitherto held and now, for the love of God, have granted entirely to the place; also the jurisdiction over thieves who have fallen under the ban, or over blood that has been shed, and the office of the vice-lord, the court, and the course of the water, and the correction of all measures, except for the allods held by men subject to the general court and the passage of the public road.

“At the court of Ballo, six manses; at Frasnidum, four manses; at Crux, one church; at the court of Casto, one church; at Novavilla, one church with its two chapels, together with one church situated in the villa of Marculfus and belonging to the abbey of the aforementioned Novavilla; in the same court of Marculfus, three manses with woods and meadows; and at Novavilla, four manses with woods and meadows belonging to the same church, one vineyard and one mill situated on the little river Elna.

“At the villa called Parridus, one church with sixteen manses situated between Cosantia and Bunia, together with one mill, woods, and meadows; at the villa of Harbodus in Vapra, one church, two manses, and one quarter-manse; at Liniacum, one quarter of a church, one mansus, three quarters of a mansus, and half a mill with woods and meadows; and in the county of Bar, two manses in the villa called Villare.

“We have also given on behalf of our church, from the abbey of Saint Amantius, ten manses with the dwellings belonging to those manses; at Flavigny, the entire fishery, and another fishery belonging to Tilliacum; the tithe of those rams that are paid to our church from the hundred of Brac; and the tithe of the wine customs of our city.

“We have also given the church situated in the villa of Amonzeia, and the villa of Flavigny with one church, its fishery, mills, woods, meadows, and all the appurtenances belonging to the same villa. (Fol. 70.) Twenty-six manses belong to that villa. And at the villa of Marleia, situated near the city of Metz, one church built in honor of Saint Brictius.

“In like manner, for the preparation of a hospice, we have assigned to the same monastery the church of Saint Peter situated in the suburb of the fortress of Verdun, with five manses, one meadow, and all persons of either sex belonging to the same church; in Piet, one church; in Donnaus, one church; in Morvilla, one; and in Marva, one.

“We have handed over all these things to the place for the salvation of our soul and the absolution of our sins, and by firm authority and legal right we confirm, strengthen, and establish them. We also beseech our successors’ fatherly generosity that, always cherishing a pious disposition toward the aforementioned place, they may allow what we have done for the redemption of souls to remain valid, may not diminish what we have given, and may moreover strive to add from their own possessions, preserving our grants in such a way that they may wish their own decrees also to remain forever.

“But if any bishop or prince, incited by a diabolical spirit, should in any way wish to withdraw or scatter these things, let him first be struck by our anathema and entangled in a hundred curses; let him, made the companion of Dathan and Abiram, incur the anger of almighty God, and, delivered over to eternal fires, suffer inexpiable punishments in hell.

“Therefore, so that this grant of our authority may possess a firmer force, we have decreed that it be strengthened in our presence by the hands of our faithful.”

“Annals. From the Incarnation of the Lord 952, indiction 10, council 4, epact 22, this charter was confirmed, strengthened, and written, [with Pope Adrian presiding over the Roman Church, in the sixth year of his pontificate] [Note: [Col. 0189] inserted in p. R. e. p. A., year 6], while Otto, the august emperor, was reigning: in the first year of his reign in Italy, in France the sixteenth, and in the twelfth year of our episcopate. I, Berengar, unworthy bishop, have subscribed. The signatures are those of Abbot Humbert, Abbot Wodo, Abbot Berard, Provost Bernerius, Provost Alard, and the other clerics and monks devotedly supporting this charter, and of the noble laymen Count Godefrid, Givard, Adelard, and the others.”

In that same year certain men of Verdun were deprived of their offices by Duke Conrad.

**FLOD.** In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 952, King Otto subdued Berengar, king of Italy, and all Italy under himself. In the following year he removed Duke Conrad from the duchy of Lotharingia, besieged Mainz, where Conrad had taken refuge, and captured it; Conrad withdrew to Metz. This discord arose between Otto and his princes because Otto promised the kingdom to his son born of his present wife, although before he went to Italy he had assigned it to his son Liutolf and had made his leading men swear allegiance to him. Liutolf, after committing many crimes on this account, died in the year 957. The king then made peace with Duke Conrad.

[Col. 0189C] (fol. 70′.) In the year 953, Wigfrid, bishop of Cologne, died, and Bruno, King Otto’s brother, succeeded him; Otto entrusted the Lotharingian kingdom to Bruno.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 955 [Note: [Col. 0189] DCCCCLIIII corrected to DCCCCLV], Louis, king of the Franks, died, and Pope Agapitus died, with Octavian succeeding him. There was also a war between Otto and the Hungarians, in which the Hungarians were defeated on the fourth day before the Ides of August of the following year; in that war Duke Conrad died, having by then been reconciled with Otto. (Chronicle of Dijon.) The aforementioned King Louis of the Franks, dying in that same year, left two sons, Lothair and Charles, whom Gerberga, sister of the Emperor Otto, had borne him. Charles, who was called “the Younger,” lived out his old age in obscurity, while Lothair succeeded to the whole inheritance. Lothair betrothed his sister Matilda [Col. 0189D] to Conrad, king of Burgundy, and gave him Lyon as her dowry. It lies on the boundary of the kingdom of Burgundy and at that time belonged by right to the kingdom of the Franks.

From this Matilda was born Rudolf, king of Burgundy, who succeeded his father Conrad in the kingdom of Burgundy. There was also Berta, whom Odo, son of Theobald of Chartres, took as wife [Note: [Col. 0189] thus in the copy]; she bore Odo, who died at Bar. Theobald of Chartres, whose surname was “the Trickster,” and who treacherously killed William of the Normans, fathered this Odo by the sister of Heribert, count of Troyes [Col. 0190A]. This Odo took Berta as wife, and from her was born Odo, who died at Bar. From the same Matilda was born Gisla, whom the Emperor Conrad later took as wife; she bore the third Emperor Henry. King Rudolf, whose wife was Ermengard, being without children, appointed this Henry as heir to the kingdom of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0189D] He appointed Henry II as heir]. Thus the kingdom of Burgundy passed into the dominion of the emperors.

**[FLOD.]** In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 956, Hugh the Great died, and his son Hugh obtained the duchy of France. Robert, bishop of Trier, also died of pestilence, as did Fulbert of Cambrai, and Hairic succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0189] “and F.” inserted]. Otto subsequently defeated the Sarmatians in war.

[Col. 0190B] In the year 961, the boy Otto was raised to be king, and his father Otto, coming to Rome in the following year, was made emperor by Pope Octavian. In that same year Artald, bishop of Reims, died, and a synod was held in the district of Meaux, at Meaux, on the Marnes River. There Wigfred was ordained bishop of Verdun, although Lord Berengar, bishop of Verdun, was still alive and occupying the episcopal see.

They ordained him without the metropolitan’s knowledge because they were hostile to Lord Berengar: he would not attend their councils and disapproved of certain of their actions. Thus, when the administration of the Church of Reims, of which they were suffragans, fell to them, they took the opportunity to ordain him as well, so that they might have him as a companion in their councils [Col. 0190C] and a participant in their enterprise—as though they regarded as nothing the man who presided there, since they saw that he was in no way inclined toward them. [Note: [Col. 0189] “allum” in the copy.]

There too Hugh, the usurper of Reims, was cast out and excommunicated by the Roman synod, while Odelric was enthroned by Wido of Soissons, Rorico of Laon, Gibuin of Châlons, Wigfred of Verdun, and Aistulf of Noyon.

When Pope Octavian was accused of irreligious conduct, he left Rome in 962, and John XII was substituted in his place. But after Emperor Otto returned from Rome, the Romans received Octavian back; he died not long afterward. John, meanwhile, came with the emperor to Pavia. During this time the Romans elected Benedict, who had agreed with John’s election and had always been subject to him [Col. 0190D]. But when Otto returned to Rome, he restored John to his see by synodal judgment. Benedict, however, because he had ascended his father’s bed, was deposed and taken with Otto to Saxony.

Otto issued a privilege for the Church of Saint Vannes concerning all things justly granted or to be granted to it, at the request of Lord Berengar, bishop, and confirmed the church itself, or monastery, to the Church of Verdun. He decreed and promulgated that the sons of the Church of Verdun who wished to renounce the world should receive the monastic habit there and should not depart to external monasteries.

Lord Berengar himself also endeavored to fulfill this arrangement. Rejecting the burden of the prelacy, so that he might still be justified as a just man, he received the monastic habit in that same monastery, serving God in the incorruptibility of a modest and tranquil spirit. Nevertheless, he continued to watch over the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, at the request of the people who did not wish to be subject to another during his lifetime, since they were protected by a vigorous shepherd who, the closer he drew to the Lord, gave increasingly certain signs of his vigor and benevolent purity.

What, then, caused a bishop of such authority and favor to submit himself to the monastic rule—he whose life was a mirror of holiness, a light to souls, an ornament to the devout, and a terror to the reprobate? Since we have reached this point, following the sayings of the fathers, we shall explain it briefly. It was customary for the blessed man to anticipate the nocturnal office with the diligence of vigils and prayers, so that through the daily labor of his vows he might provoke the heavenly Watcher to turn his eyes upon himself and upon the flock entrusted to him through the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled spirit.

(Cf. *Deeds of Verdun*.) As he was preparing for this task one night, and, accompanied by only one companion who served him in the role of lamp-bearer, was entering the principal Church of Saint Mary, (fol. 71.) he proceeded cautiously, believing that there was no one there whom he might strike against, since everything was silent; and even if there were hidden worshipers there, he thought they would withdraw at his arrival. At the very entrance to the choir, [Col. 0191C] however, while he was being less careful, he stumbled against a cleric named Bernerius, provost of that same church. Bernerius happened at that moment to be lying prostrate on the ground, singing the morning course of the Blessed Virgin; as later became clear, he had been wholly lifted by the wings of devotion toward higher things and was extending himself in praises of the Mother of the Lord.

The bishop, not seeing that the man lying on the ground had risen for him, struck him with his foot and ordered him to withdraw—perhaps, I fear, not without some irritation of spirit. The man obeyed the command, withdrew to one side, and continued attending to what he had begun.

After the morning office had been completed, when the bishop had laid his weary limbs upon his bed, the Blessed Mother of God appeared, accompanied on her right and left by the blessed virgins Agnes and Thecla. She appeared in such dress and becoming adornment that everyone could recognize her as the mother and bride of the King of all things, the salvation and sweetness of the faithful.

When she had stood beside his bed, and his mind, astonished and clinging to the novelty of so great a vision, was dumbfounded, that queen of virgins gently asked him why he had struck with his foot his cleric, devoted to her, speaking with her, and wholly absorbed in her, and had forced him to leave the place where he had been standing beside her, thereby obstructing his devotion, with which he had been wholly present to her.

He remained silent, fearing in his trembling conscience to look upon the face of the Mother of Mercy, yet not despairing of her mercy. Then she, the unique refuge of the wretched, the hope and consolation of the humble, said:

“You have indeed served me well, and you have labored well in my church; but now you have erred as a human being. It is better that you now receive the punishment for your error, where every punishment has an end, than in the future, where punishment increases and the human spirit is renewed day by day for punishment. Therefore let the foot with which you sinned suffer punishment, so that all may recognize in you that I love those who love me and do not cease to protect those who make remembrance of me.”

Having said this, she ordered the blessed virgin Thecla to strike with the rod she carried the foot with which he had struck the cleric. It appeared so to the bishop, and he felt himself being struck; for immediately his foot withered, and he limped on it for all the days of his life.

O astonishing mercy of the Mother of the Lord! She praised her bishop, who served her faithfully, because he served her faithfully; yet she did not wish to leave unpunished the sin he had committed against a fellow servant, although that man was inferior to him in priestly rank. By this sign she demonstrated that she is near to those who cry out to her and that, if they are injured, she is prepared to avenge their injuries even upon her household servants.

Thus the bishop limped because the foot that had been moved to injure his neighbor was punished, and his steps were made unsteady. Yet in that very infirmity he learned to make straight steps, where he had endeavored to correct through humility what he had done wrong through arrogance.

For when morning came, and temporal punishment gave credibility to his words, he summoned in the assembly of the church the cleric whom he had injured, acknowledged the guilt of his error, confessed it, and publicly declared what he was suffering and why he was suffering it. Thus each began to profit from the correction of the other, so that what harmed one might benefit both—and, through their example, everyone.

For after only a few days had passed, the bishop went to the monastery and, clothed in the garment of humility, served the poor, himself poor in spirit. He did not, however, abandon care of the bishopric; the love of the clergy and people required him to retain it. Rather, the gains of virtue increased in him to the extent that he adhered to the Lord of virtues with more fervent resolve.

The aforementioned cleric, provost of that city, remained in love of the Blessed Virgin and continually devoted to her service. He persevered in devotion in her church, cherishing the monastery of Saint Peter with great affection because of the dignity of the place, and bestowing countless gifts of gold and silver, vestments, and books. He also gave to that church what he possessed at Exio: vineyards, fields, waters, and watercourses. Therefore, after his death, in recognition of his holiness, he deserved honorable burial in that same church among the tombs of the bishops, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

(Fol. 71′.) Lothair, fifth king of the Franks after Charles the Bald, had a younger brother named Charles and a wife named Emma, daughter of Lothair, king of Italy, and of Adelaid, later empress. By her he had a son, Louis, who, while still a boy, took Blanche as his wife. [RICH. III, 92.] He also had another son, Arnulf, by a certain noble girl. Arnulf was born first and later became archbishop of Reims.

The insolence of his sister-in-law and the poverty of his household resources compelled Charles to leave his ancestral territory and surrender himself to Otto, emperor of the Saxons. After Lothair’s death, his son Louis succeeded him, but died in the first flower of youth. With him the line of kings descended from the family of Charlemagne came to an end, and King Hugh from another family succeeded.

Arnulf, the cleric and brother of Lothair, taking this heavily, as we have said, brought his uncle Charles back into Francia, and captured and retained Laon. Adalbero, bishop of Laon, fleeing from the custody in which he was held, came to Hugh and reconciled Arnulf to him. When the archbishop of Reims died, the king bestowed the archbishopric upon Arnulf in order to reconcile Charles to himself.

While seeking easier means by which to reconcile Charles to the king, Arnulf handed the city over to him. For this reason Hugh publicly denounced him as a perjurer and traitor. Not long afterward, Adalbero of Laon, in whom Arnulf trusted, captured him; both Arnulf and Charles were handed over to Hugh.

Arnulf was told either to confess voluntarily that he was a perjurer or to be deprived of his eyes. He proclaimed himself a perjurer and begged forgiveness. He was then immediately deposed, and his deacon Gerbert was substituted in his place. Gerbert had first been raised in the monastery of Saint Géraud, but was expelled because of the insolence of his conduct. Later expelled from the archbishopric as well, he went to Emperor Otto.

Charles lived out his old age in obscurity, and Arnulf recovered the episcopate. His sister was Matilda, mother of Rudolf, king of Burgundy; her daughter, whom Emperor Conrad, son of Otto III, took as wife, was called Gisla and was the mother of Emperor Henry III. His daughter Berta was also the mother of Odo, who died at Bar [Note: [Col. 0193] Eight lines erased here.]

(Cf. *Life of the Abbot of Flavigny*.) In the year 968, Remigius, bishop of the Eduans, died.

(Fol. 72.) “JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants [Col. 0193C] of God, sends to our brother BERENGAR, bishop of the Church of Verdun, and to all those entrusted to him by God, the reward of eternal recompense.

“It is fitting for apostolic governance, through benevolent charity, to favor those distinguished by pious religion and to grant the minds of petitioners assent with eager devotion. From this, above all, we shall obtain the reward of profit from the Lord, Creator of all things, if venerable holy places, suitably ordered, are brought by our authority to a better condition.

“Therefore, since among the other exercises of holy conduct we have learned that you, dearest brother, have built a certain monastery in your bishopric beside the city of Verdun, in the Church of Saint Peter, for the love of God, in which rest the bodies of holy confessors and of the former bishops of the aforementioned Church of Saint Mary—Wito, Pulchronius, Possessor, and Firminus—and since, with prudent consideration, you have supported it from the goods of your church, so that whenever the sons of your church, moved by divine love and despising earthly things, wished to flee to the perfection of the contemplative life, they might not appear wholly separated from your church, but might find in the monastery, which is a member of that same church, a refuge of consolation under the religious habit and might serve God there in quiet tranquility:

“Let the diligence of all the faithful, present and future, know that we wish the same monastery, built under your administration, together with all its property established for it by royal decrees with your counsel, to remain forever unshaken, namely: Scancia with its appurtenances; the abbey of Saint Amantius and everything belonging to it; Novavilla with its dependent properties; the court of Amantius, with everything pertaining to it; Parridus with its adjacent properties; the village of Harbodus with its appurtenances; the church of the court of Casto with the things belonging to it; the church of Marleius with its adjacent properties; the church of the court of Marculfus with its adjacent properties; the church of the village of Amonzeius with its adjacent properties; together with lands, vineyards, mills, male and female servants; the abbey of Saint Peter and the church of Maroa; at Liniacum, everything belonging to that place; and at Novavilla in the county of Bar, everything belonging to that place.

“All these aforesaid places, with all their appurtenances in general and in particular, and whatever, with God’s help, shall be granted to this monastery in the future by the vow of the faithful, we confirm perpetually through this apostolic privilege, for you and your successors. Moreover, by this privilege of our authority we wish them to be strengthened, so that the same Church of Verdun—which until now was deprived of sons whom it had received from the earliest beginnings of infancy into its own bosom whenever they fled to external monasteries—may henceforth and thereafter rejoice that, in the member subject to it, their holy conduct has been exalted through the counsel of its bishop and the care of the glorious Abbot Humbert.

“But if any person, great or small, of whatever order or power, should attempt with rash boldness to act against this apostolic command of ours, let that person know that he is excommunicated by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, bound by the chain of anathema, and excluded from the kingdom of God, condemned together with all the impious to eternal fire and punishment.

(Fol. 72′.) “But whoever proves himself an observer of this command of ours may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful Lord our God.

“Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the holy apostolic see, in the month of January, in indiction 14. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January by the hand of Marinus, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the tenth year—first month—of the pontificate of Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal Pope XII, with God’s favor, in the most sacred see of the blessed Apostle Peter, indiction 14, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 971.”

The following things were added—or rather, some were restored—to the aforesaid monastery after this privilege had been received: the church of Boccon’s Mountain; the church of Donnatus with its mill; the church of Maurivilla; four manses at Rivaldus; thirty manses at the court of Raherius, the court of Gisleus, and Novavilla, with a church and chapel; vineyards at Arnold’s village, which were given by Duchess Richuara, Adelard, Amalric, Albert, Warner, Gyrulf, and Lambert the canon; one mansus with vineyards at Florinchingas; half a mansus with a vineyard at Saint Julian; three manses at Flabasius; a church at Soliacus; and a church at Buslan’s village.

In the second year after this privilege was issued, which was the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 972, Emperor Otto the Great died in the tenth year of his imperial rule, and Otto the Red succeeded him. Abbot Humbert also died on the second day before the Nones of December, and Adilmar was substituted in his place.

Thus, as we have said, Otto the Second succeeded the first Otto. He was also called “the Red,” concerning whom the proverb was spoken: “Otto the Second succeeded to the empire, so that the age might flourish.”

Lord Berengar lived until the time of Otto III. He died on the second day before the Ides of August and was honorably buried inside the church at the entrance to the cloister, which, it is established, he both sought and ordered to be built. (Cf. *Deeds of Verdun* 2.)

At that time Rudolf, son of Conrad, ruled the kingdom of Burgundy. Rudolf’s sister Gisla was the wife of Emperor Conrad, also called Cono. (Chronicle of Dijon.) Burchard had been promoted to the episcopate in the Church of Lyon. He was the brother of King Rudolf and the son of Conrad by a concubine. By him Bruno was ordained bishop of Langres, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 981, indiction 9. Burchard had obtained the bishopric of Lyon in infancy.

(*Deeds of Verdun.*) In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 983, Otto the Second, called the Red, died at Rome after reigning twelve years. He was brought back by his people and buried at Aachen. Otto III, twelve years old, succeeded him; from his cradle he assumed the scepter of the Romans, under whose rule there was salvation for the world and glory.

At that time Wigfred was bishop of the Church of Verdun. One day he left the city and came to the village of the brothers called Wandersala. There he was captured and released by Count Sigifrid. From the money he received as compensation, he adorned the Church of Saint Mary with so many crowns that if one touched the first by hand, all of them, even the last, would move.

Following the example of his predecessor Lord Berengar, he built a monastery in the suburb of Verdun. After gathering a company of monks, he had the body of Saint Paul, bishop, raised from the place where it lay and placed in a silver coffin. He provided food from the revenues of the bishopric for the brothers who served the Lord in that place.

Among his other good works, he also granted the mansus of Ravandus to Saint Firminus. When Wigfred [Note: [Col. 0195] Seek on another page under this sign as far as: “Heimo succeeded him c.” We have restored the order as indicated.], bishop of Verdun, died on the second day before the Kalends of September and was buried in the monastery he himself had built, Hugh was substituted in his place.

After entering the city, Hugh asked how he was to live. For King Lothair of the Franks, since the commonwealth was under a young Roman prince, besieged Verdun after Bishop Wigfred’s death, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 986, but he did not capture it. Nevertheless, he devastated everything around the city. The men who went out to fight against him were defeated, and many of them were captured [Col. 0196A]. It is said that, to secure their release, Gotbert carried the keys of the city to the king.

For this reason, when Hugh discovered that the resources of the bishopric had been exhausted, he marked down the revenues of the villages and soon departed. After he left, they received, without a royal grant, Adalbero, son of Beatrice, the mother of Duke Theodoric. He remained in the city for a short time, then went to Metz after the death of its bishop, leaving this place.

Adalbero, son of Count Godefrid and grandfather of Duke Godefrid, succeeded him. After taking Boniface’s wife, he later became margrave. In that same year he went to Salerno for the sake of healing; on his return he died in Italy on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, and his body was brought back and buried at Verdun. He lived in the episcopate for three and a half years, and Heimo succeeded him in 988.

[Col. 0196B] **[RODULF GLABER I, 4.]** At the beginning of the reign of Otto III, the pope died. Otto ordered another to be ordained in his place, but John Crescentius, one of the Roman nobles, expelled him and substituted another. Otto returned, however, and, after the deposed pope’s hands and ears had been cut off and his eyes torn out, and after Crescentius had been killed, ordered Gerbert to be ordained pope.

**[RICHER, III, 43.]** Gerbert had been raised in the monastery of Saint Géraud at Aurillac and educated in grammar. The abbot of that place entrusted him to Borellus, duke of Citerior Spain, so that he might be instructed in the arts; Borellus handed him over to a certain Bishop Hatto for instruction, and under him Gerbert devoted himself extensively to mathematics.

When the aforementioned duke later went to Rome with the bishop, Gerbert went with them. He became very well known to the pope, who commended him to King Otto [Col. 0196C], and Gerbert came with Bishop Adalbero of Reims to Reims.

**[ibid.]** At that time Otricus was regarded as eminent among the Saxons. The following year Adalbero of Reims was traveling to Rome with Gerbert. At Pavia he found the emperor with Otricus. The emperor received him magnificently and, taking him by ship down the Po, brought him to Ravenna.

Because in the preceding year Otricus had represented himself as Gerbert’s critic in a certain diagram involving a manifold distribution of different things, the emperor ordered all the learned men of the palace to be gathered inside the palace. The archbishop was also present, along with Abbot Adso of Dervus and a considerable number of scholars. When the disputation had begun and they had already consumed almost the entire day, the emperor’s nod brought it to an end.

There Gerbert was splendidly rewarded by the emperor and returned to Reims with the archbishop [Col. 0196D]. Later, after the bishop Arnulf had been deposed, he used certain stratagems to have himself promoted to the archbishopric of Reims by Hugh, son of Hugh the Great, king of the Franks, who had succeeded Louis from another family.

(Fol. 73.) After some time had passed, however, when he realized that Arnulf was trying to seize the episcopal see from him and bring the people back to himself, he fled by night to Otto. Not long afterward, by means of certain stratagems, he had himself promoted by Otto to the archbishopric of Ravenna. Later he was made pope and called Sylvester. He died in the year 999, and Gregory V succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0197] Not at all; in that year Sylvester II succeeded Gregory V.]

**[RODULF GLABER II, 5.]** In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 988, an image of the Lord on the cross, placed in the monastery of the Apostles at Orléans, wept, while everyone wondered what this sign might portend. In the same city, one night a wolf came and entered the church at the hour of matins. It seized the rope of the bell in its mouth, shook it, and caused it to sound; they could scarcely drive it from the church.

In the following year the entire city, together with its churches, was consumed by fire. But the venerable Bishop Arnulf, having found money in the foundations of the Church of the Holy Cross, restored that church in improved form.

[Col. 0197B] **[ibid. II, 7.]** In the year 991, Saint Odilo entered the religious life at Cluny, and in the fourth year Saint Majolus died. At that time Rome was largely consumed by fire. The Temple of Saint Peter was also set alight, and its beams, covered with iron and bronze plates, were already burning. The entire Roman people ran to the tomb of the Apostle. When human assistance could accomplish nothing, they awaited divine and apostolic aid; and immediately the fire, which was already licking the beams, was extinguished.

At that time also died Odo, count of Tours; Heribert, count of Meaux and Troyes; William, count of Poitiers; Manasses, bishop of Troyes; Gislebert, count of Paris; and Gebuin, count of Châlons.

[Col. 0198A] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 995, Saint Odilo assumed the governance of the Church of Cluny.

**[ibid. II, 1.]** After Lothair and Louis, kings of the Franks, had died, King Hugh was established, as we have said. His brothers were Otto, duke of Burgundy, and Henry. (Chronicle of Dijon.) When Otto died in adolescence without children, Henry succeeded him. Henry’s son was Odo of Beaune, and his stepson was William the stranger, father of Count Rainald.

After Henry, Henry, son of King Robert by Constance, obtained the duchy. After Henry became king, his brother Robert the Elder succeeded him; after Robert, Hugh, duke and later monk, succeeded. Hugh was the son of Henry, who was himself the son of that Robert. After Hugh’s death, his son Robert succeeded him and took Constance as wife, a relative of Hugh, bishop of Auxerre and count of Chalon.

**[GLABER III, 2.]** In the year from the Incarnation 996, Duke Henry died at Poliacum on the Saône, and Richard, duke of the Normans, died.

**[ibid. II, 8.]** In the following year King Robert took with him Richard II, the younger count of the Normans, together with thirty thousand Normans. Because Burgundy had defected from him, he devastated it and finally subdued it.

**[ibid. II, 9.]** At that time a severe famine lasted for five years throughout the Roman world. At that same time the distinguished Father William presided over the Church of Dijon in the office of abbot. Whoever wishes to know his deeds may read them in his life, composed by the monk Rodulf.

**BOOK TWO** [Note: [Col. 0197] The title is absent from the manuscript.]

[Col. 0197]

[Col. 0197C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1002, Otto III, the young emperor, died after completing nineteen years in the kingdom, and Henry succeeded him. In that year, around sunset, a dragon was seen flying through the air; fiery battle lines were seen in the sky; and, at the full moon after the beginning of Lent, the moon was turned to blood from midnight until sunrise. Around midday the sun was divided into two parts.

**[Catalogue of Pontiffs.]** In the following year Pope John XIII died, and Benedict succeeded him.

(Fol. 73′.) In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1010, Heldric, abbot of Flavigny, died on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, and Lord Amadeus succeeded him. (Cf. *Life of the Abbot of Flavigny*.) After resigning the abbacy, Amadeus went to Cluny. Later he acquired the cell of Coltilcus [Note: [Col. 0197D] from Helmuin, bishop of the Eduans, in the thirtieth year of King Robert’s reign, as a charter attests; Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* IV, 652, K.], and recovered those of Semur, Bellevaux, and Corbigny [Col. 0197D] [Note: [Col. 0197D] From the same Helmuin, by a diploma written in the year from the Incarnation 1034, in the fifth year of King Henry; Mabillon, loc. cit., p. 659.].

He captured the fortress of Sarmatia, destroyed Passavant, and obtained the altars of nineteen churches, together with their tithes and customary dues [Note: [Col. 0197D] Two charters of donation to Amadeus are extant: one from King Robert, on the third day before the Kalends of March 1018; Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* IV, 238; the other from Count Rainald, in 1037; Labbe I, 270. K.]

When Abbot Adelmar of the monastery of Saint Vannes died on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, Adelard was substituted in his place. When he too died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, Ermenric succeeded him and enlarged the place as much as he was able. When he too had been taken to the heavenly realm, Rohard succeeded him on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, and Lambert succeeded Rohard.

After Lambert, Lord Fingenius, descended from the people of the Scots, was brought from the monastery of Saint Felix at Metz. Since that place had been somewhat neglected under lay administration, he was ordained abbot there to restore it. Whoever desires to know more fully about his arrival, pilgrimage, and conversion may learn of them in the life of Theodoric, the distinguished bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0198D] The author of the *Life of Richard* praises this Life; see Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, sixth century, 1. See also *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* IV, p. 696. K.]. [Col. 0198D]

When he too had died, and after Adalbero, Heimo had obtained the bishopric of Verdun, Lord Richard undertook the governance of that place. Our humility desires to describe his life, character, deeds, noble lineage, beginning of conversion, devotion to religion, and perseverance in perfection, although our understanding is limited and our speech rustic; for if we are anything, although we are nothing, everything must be attributed after God and his saints to his merits.

Therefore we must invoke the Holy Spirit, distributor of spiritual gifts, so that he may proclaim his blessedness through his own understanding but by our mouth, so that he may be praised in his works and appear wondrous in his saints.

**1.** [Note: [Col. 0199] The chapter numbers are found in the manuscript.] He was born of the noblest stock of the Franks, his father being [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0199] The place is blank], and his mother [lacuna] [Col. 0199B] [Note: [Col. 0199] The place is blank.] [Note: [Col. 0199] His father’s name was Walter, and his mother’s Theodrada, as the author of the *Life of Richard* testifies; see Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, sixth century, 1. K.] From the very beginnings of childhood he was instructed in the liberal arts in the Church of Saint Mary at Reims.

At that time this church flourished with such a glorious ornament of religion and took pride in such an honorable number and fitting dignity of noble and religious persons whom it had itself raised within its walls that it surpassed all the churches of Belgica in religion. It served as a model for all of honorable living and right conduct—in chastity, knowledge, discipline, correction of morals, and the performance of good works.

This is demonstrated by the pious, steadfast, and faithful constancy of Lord Constantius, truly a saint and a canon of that same church, and likewise by the other Constantius, whose praiseworthy generosity toward the poor and dispersal of his entire patrimony deserve imitation and remembrance.

The first of these men is commended by his religious life and works of mercy; the second is so celebrated by the compassion of the poor that they alone were found to praise the merit of so great a man while mourning his death. With grateful diligence they arranged his funeral; at the solemn masses they offered whatever small gifts they could for his repose; and, all gathered together around his body, they mourned their desolation and repeatedly lamented their deprivation of so great a giver of alms.

In marvelous praises they exalted his life; and if anything in him had been corrupted by the weakness of human nature, they covered and concealed it with their tears.

For this reason we have inserted here the constancy of these men as an example for the faithful, so that whoever reads may recognize that so many and such great men in the training-ground of the holy Church of Reims labored neither without teachers nor in such isolation that they escaped the prison of the flesh without leaving behind some witnesses and fellow workers of their way of life, who both imitated their footsteps and embraced the strength of their faith.

## 2.

In this church, then, Richard, a boy of religious character, was entrusted to the study of letters and, for his instruction, quickly passed through each of the subjects that the teachers’ skill had marked out for study. He began already to contemplate higher things and, with the liveliness and penetration of a teachable intellect, attentively to investigate what he had not learned from his teachers, so that everyone might recognize that he would become a man of great renown: such was the keenness of his understanding, capable of grasping hidden and mystical matters, with the grace of God both assisting and preceding him. ([fol. 74.])

Thus he advanced in that same city until he reached the full maturity of his growth. Being keen-minded, he established for himself a rule of life, cutting out in himself the faults that he reproved in others with vigilant care. His religious manner of life and his continual rebuke of evils prove this. His straightforwardness of mind was so abundant that, out of zeal for God and love of righteousness, he was entrusted with the office of precentor and archdeacon, and the administration of the church of Rheims was placed under his direction.

How energetically, prudently, and skillfully he kept watch over this office, we have decided to pass over in silence, lest we perhaps be found excessive in praising him—especially since that very silence is itself his praise. For if we were to stretch our whole substance beyond its limits in praising him, what we could say would still fall short of what ought to be said. The church of Rheims therefore rejoices in his praises, since his devotion itself, by which he labored faithfully in it, is his praise.

He used the authority entrusted to him for building up, not for destroying. He had the freedom, according to his judgment, to refute and convict the guilty by his speech, and to show partiality toward no person in judgment. By these qualities he was so well known to everyone that, even when absent, all feared him out of reverence for him and for his unbending constancy. Old and young alike revered Richard’s impartial and unsparing judgment of character.

He was truly religious, devoting himself to continual prayers. It was also his custom to recite the Psalter each day in sequence. He recited the first fifty psalms standing, with his hands bent toward the ground; the next fifty standing upright; and the next fifty prostrate with his whole body, but suspended and supported on the joints of his feet and hands. He would also say a daily prayer before the cross, all of whose verses began as follows: “I adore you, Christ, ascending the cross, and I bless you.”

One day, after he had recited these prayers with great persistence, he rose from prayer and, looking with tears at the crucified one, heard a voice saying to him: “You blessed me on earth, and I bless you.” Then the one who was in the form of the cross raised his right hand and blessed him. Pierced by the sweetness of this experience, he gave thanks to the supreme priest and began to contemplate perfect things with all the greater intensity, inasmuch as he recognized the sweetness of the merciful God’s graciousness toward him.

We heard this while staying at Rouen from religious men who themselves confessed that they had heard it from Hugh, surnamed the Grammarian, an energetic and religious man, archdeacon of the church of Rouen, who was present at Rheims in the church of Saint Mary when these things occurred.

## 3.
