But as, with each passing day, he was lifted toward higher things on the wings of devotion by the fervor of his religious purpose, and as he admired those who despised the world and denied themselves, venerating God placed in the figure of the cross, he recalled that God invited his followers to himself, saying: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII, 26). He remembered that it was little to serve the Lord if there were no perfection in it unless one also followed him. He chose, therefore, to adhere more firmly to God, because he is good, and blessed are those who hope in him.

He therefore began with a generous hand to distribute among the poor what he had around him. Although from his earliest years works of compassion had shone forth in him, still, the more he despised the misery of the world and its deceptive grace, the more earnestly he devoted himself to works of mercy, so that he might follow Christ naked and, being poor, imitate the poor one who, for our sake, was made a little lower than the angels and wished to be born among the poor and laid in a manger, so that he might become food for pious animals.

When everything had been disposed of, however, and his desires had not been lulled to sleep by delay but rather increased—for they were holy—and when, by a violent effort, he had calmed the flood of thoughts that a faithful soul striving for perfection endures, he reached the harbor of rest and fixed the anchor of hope. Yet, because he had now resolved to depart, he began again to be anxious about where he should go and what place of settlement he should choose, so that, planted there, he might grow green within the pleasantness of his heart.

He wished literally to fulfill what had been said to Abraham, the father of our faith: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Genesis XII, 1; Acts VII, 3). But he considered that it would not be without fruit if, remaining among his own people and becoming for them an example of an honorable life, he offered them an example of following Christ by attaining the religious vocation.

On the other hand, he considered it extremely difficult to undertake a more demanding purpose among acquaintances and relatives. There, the path of danger is sometimes certain, while that of salvation is uncertain: the love of relatives draws back a man already approaching God, and the affection of the flesh obscures the sharpness of the gaze with which he ought to behold God. So too do the many stings of the world, which are not felt as severely by one who avoids and shuns the opportunity to feel them.

Amid these and the many other deliberations of flesh and spirit contending against each other, the help of the Almighty was present. He offered consolation to his servant, laboring in the arena of glorious combat, through one of his faithful men who, beneath the cloak of worldly dignity, concealed a most proven soldier of Christ. ([Col. 0201D])

The man’s name was Frederick; his descent was sufficiently noble and exalted. (Cf. *Deeds of Verdun*, 9.) He flourished in the dignity of a count, and—what is most important—he adorned his comital rank with the character of his mind. His father was Godefrid, a man renowned among the magnates of the kingdom for his probity, favor, wealth, and honors.

He also had other sons: Adalbero, bishop of Verdun, whom we have mentioned; Herimannus, also called Hezelo [Note: [Col. 0201D] The aforementioned Hezelo.], a most noble count; and Godefrid and Gozelo, both dukes. Herimannus, also called Hezelo, married Matilda, by whom he fathered two sons, trees of good hope, Gregory and Godefrid, and a daughter, Odilia, who was abbess of the servants of God in the monastery of Saint Odilia. He also had another son by a concubine, named Godefrid.

Godefrid the duke grew old in wealth and glory without children. Gozelo the duke left as his heir his son Godefrid, who, after taking Boniface’s wife, later became margrave.

Born, then, from this noble stock, Lord Frederick, placed in the heights of honor, kept watch over the limits of his station, lest he put his foot on the precipice [Note: [Col. 0201D] “precipice” (the manuscript has *pcipio*).]. For this reason he attained the good end of his purpose: he did not wander beyond his boundaries.

He was terrible to his enemies, admirable because of his love of justice, generous and lavish in gifts to the poor; merciful in sparing and severe in punishing. Although he frequented the palace, he nevertheless sat with blessed Job on the dung heap (Job II, 8), for if he did anything unlawfully there, he brought it back before the eyes of his mind through repentance.

He sat on the dung heap because, when he saw before him the dung of sins, if any pride had arisen in his heart, he bowed himself down. And the more he considered himself dust and ashes while speaking with God, the higher he ascended toward the honor of divine converse. Hence he was truly humbled, so that he could genuinely rise to the heights of virtue.

For the pious mercy of God acts thus toward his elect: the more they despise themselves beneath themselves, the more sublimely they are lifted toward the love of God; and the more they are restrained by the virtue of true humility from thinking highly of themselves, the more clearly they see the glory of God.

## 4.

As he therefore grew wholly inflamed, through long meditation, with desire for his Creator, and now openly wished to despise the blandishments of the world and adhere to God with undivided purpose, he saw that, as a man established in the world, it was absolutely necessary for him to reveal this desire to some religious person, whose counsel might relieve him and whose prayers might strengthen him.

By divine clemency, it therefore seemed to him that he should seek out a man of outstanding renown for religion—namely Richard, who is the subject of this present account (cf. *Deeds of Verdun*, 8)—and entrust himself to him as to another self, sharing with him the secrets of his heart. He believed Richard to be a counselor who possessed nothing deceitful, nothing pretended, nothing favorable to corrupted peace.

He came, therefore, and as the will of one was disclosed, the desire of both was revealed and strengthened toward completion by their mutual confirmation. It was therefore decreed by common consent, and by a decision reached on both sides, that some poor place should be chosen in which the honor of God and the strictness of the rule might be preserved, where new lovers of Christian poverty could be trained and might finally instruct others in the exercise of spiritual service.

The place chosen was therefore the city of Verdun, and in it the monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Vitonus, confessor of Christ. It had been founded in ancient times, was glorious through the patronage of the saints, and was distinguished by the order of its religious life.

There were good and religious men there, although very few, under the discipline of Abbot Fingenius, a native of the regions of the Scots, who had gathered there for the sake of religion. (Cf. *Deeds of Verdun*, 9.)

When they had decided to go there, they nevertheless came together first to investigate the place, so that, if they were to shut themselves up in that monastery, they might rely less on reputation and attend to what their eyes showed them. ([fol. 75.])

There was another monastery in the same city, built by Bishop Wigfrid, which, because of the suitability of its location, seemed to them a better place for them to enter. The former monastery was less commendable because of the narrowness of the site and the harshness of its position, although the strictness of the order was better preserved there.

Not trusting their own judgment too much, they resolved by common consent to seek the monastery of Cluny. It appeared preeminent in religion and exceedingly rich in wealth. They intended to seek the counsel of Abbot Odilo and to accept his decision; or, if it seemed wiser to the holy man, to remain there under him.

They went, therefore. But the holy man, full of the spirit of prophecy and overflowing with the virtue of charity, gladly received these distinguished men, fervent in the love of Christ, and sent them back to their own place. He urged and commanded them to fulfill their vows to God in the monastery they had first chosen and where they had devoted themselves, especially since the fervor of the order flourished there.

He added that, in the course of time, it could come about through them that the dwellings of God’s servants, now small, would later grow, and that through their industry the very place would become distinguished, although it now seemed narrow and contemptible.

## 5.

It is plainly a pleasure to contemplate the flame of charity in the heart of blessed Odilo. Through blessed Job this is called the manifold law of God (Job XI, 6), because when it has fully seized a person’s mind, it kindles that mind in many ways toward innumerable works.

It was through this charity that the blessed man imagined doing for another what he would expect another to do for himself. Through it also he loved his neighbor as himself, bestowed upon his neighbors the good things he was able to provide, and did not become proud in doing so.

Through this same charity, the holy man enlarged himself in the love of God and neighbor alone and therefore remained ignorant of whatever deviated from righteousness. Through it, loving others as himself, he rejoiced whenever he saw what was right in them, as though it were an increase in his own advancement.

Which of the prelates today would do what this most holy man is known to have done then? Who, if men so distinguished and celebrated everywhere should happen to turn toward him, would advise them to move to other places instead of trying to retain them for himself by favor, influence, prayers, or any other device? Even if he could not retain them, he would nevertheless dismiss them unwillingly and against his will, grieving as though he were losing men whom he had never possessed.

How many prelates in the church of God do we now see who, when they observe another’s advancement and see that it is not their own, grow resentful? We rightly judge blessed Odilo preferable to all of them. To his glory it belongs if, through those whom he assigned to us, the church to which they were assigned flourishes in order and religion. [Note: [Col. 0203D] sic.]

The new recruits of monastic religion therefore returned to Verdun and, falling on their knees, begged admission to the monastery. When the father of the monastery saw them and judged these men of virtue too delicate and little suited to endure insults, trampling, and blows, and when he compared the poverty of the place with their wealth, he granted consent only with difficulty, because he did not know that their minds had been strengthened in divine love. Had he known this, he would not have delayed their entrance for even a moment.

At last he yielded and, granting consent to their request, allowed them to enter, since it was God’s will that what they desired should quickly come to pass. Once joined to the monastery’s congregation, they became for everyone examples of patience and humility, so that all might clearly recognize that the grace of God the Creator had preceded them.

Illuminated by the grace of divine protection, they began to love their heavenly homeland with an ardor considerably greater than that with which they had previously burned in their love of earthly things. For God, whose true inheritance is light and in whom there is no failure of that light, had so illuminated them with his love and so filled them by refreshing them with his vision that their minds, breathed upon by the spirit of a new hope, forgot what they had been in their former way of thinking. Nothing now pleased them except what is eternal, and, despising transient things, they sought only what endures. ([fol. 75’.])

Since, however, the venerable Richard had assumed the monastic habit without the permission and authorization of the archbishop of Rheims, the bishop complained that a canon of his church had departed from it improperly. For this reason he attempted to reclaim him.

When this reached the ears of Abbot Fingenius, he summoned Richard and explained the matter in due order. Then, consoling the father, he sent a letter to the archbishop of Rheims containing the following: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.”

When the archbishop received it and carefully considered the force of the words, he rightly said: “He who has been led by the Spirit of God has departed, and for that reason he is not to be reclaimed by us.”

Thus the accusation of those seeking to reclaim him was refuted; indeed, the devotion of many was further inflamed to imitate him.

At that time Arnulf governed the church. He was the son of King Lothair, who was fifth in descent from Charles the Bald. Arnulf was called “the Traitor” because he returned the city to his uncle Charles, grieving that the kingdom had been given to another lineage and taken away from his own.

## 6.

As time passed, Abbot Fingenius was taken to the heights above on the eighth day before the Ides of October (1004) and was buried in the monastery of Saint Felix. When the election of a successor abbot was being considered in the presence of Bishop Heimo, and, as usually happens in such matters, different people held different opinions and various candidates were being chosen, the lord Richard was suddenly elected at the questioning of the bishop. The unanimous voice of the boys praised him, while the bishop burst into praises of God and said: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise, Lord God” (Psalm VIII, 3).

The bishop’s pronouncement was entirely fitting, for an election made by the mouth of infants and nursing children was praise and glorification of God, who was to be praised and glorified in his faithful servant. (Cf. *Life of Richard*, 6.)

After the election had been confirmed and strengthened in writing, the new Jacob was led away by the bishop in the joy of his heart. After the customary solemn blessing had been given, he was placed over the custody of the Lord’s flock.

The time had now come for the prophecy of the blessed man Odilo to be fulfilled: through Richard and Lord Frederick, the previously very small place would become distinguished, so that blessed Odilo himself might rejoice in their advancement as though it were his own.

Having undertaken the burden of the prelacy, Richard took care to avoid pride and boastfulness. For he knew that he ought to benefit his brothers rather than rule over them. God granted him such great grace that kings and princes, rich and poor alike, loved him with extraordinary affection; for it was fitting that the man whom God had suffused with grace should be loved by everyone.

He was ordained by the hand of Lord Heimo, bishop of Verdun, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1004, when Henry, his kinsman, had already been ruling for the second year after Otto III and was made emperor in the ninth year of his reign.

Lord and Father Richard was compelled to visit the court of this prince on certain business. He took with him the venerable Frederick, who was descended from imperial blood and was very well known to the princes of the kingdom, so that, through Frederick’s favor, he might obtain what he distrusted his own ability to secure—since, when Frederick had been in the world, the entire court had once obeyed him.

When the places had been arranged, and bishops and abbots were seated, with the leading men of the kingdom also standing nearby, the most gentle father was seated far below. His memorable monk, however, as a kinsman of the king and the princes, was expected to take part among the foremost in the palace counsels and to sit in a more distinguished place.

Thinking that it would not benefit him to sit above the father to whom he was subject, Frederick performed an act memorable and worthy of imitation by later generations. Rising from the prince’s side and carrying his own footstool, he approached his abbot. He placed the footstool at the abbot’s feet and sat upon it himself, giving all monks who would come in all succeeding ages an example of true humility and showing that the person who willingly humbles himself for God is truly exalted.

This deed of his was regarded by everyone as a marvel and a cause for praise—not praise of men, but praise for divine service and reverence toward his father. The royal magnificence, embracing the humility of his noble birth and devoutly venerating Christ in his servant, invited Frederick to come nearer. When he refused to be drawn away from his father’s feet, the king, admiring the man’s prudence and intelligence, summoned the abbot to sit beside him and ordered Lord Frederick’s seat to be placed after the abbot’s.

Thus Lord Abbot Richard gained the friendship of the king and the princes. In a short time his wisdom, counsel, cleverness, prudence, and honorable conduct became manifest to all, so that in arranging courtly affairs no one was judged more useful, no one wiser, no one more capable or more acceptable than he. ([fol. 76.])

The prince’s generosity toward him proves this. Out of love for him, the prince loved the monastery at Verdun over which he presided, bestowing upon it great gifts of gold and silver, cloaks, and sacred vestments, and pouring himself so completely into affection for it that anyone who witnessed it would marvel.

## 7.

Having obtained what had caused him to leave, the religious abbot returned to his monastery. He began to desire to become as much closer to God as, through God’s grace, he was more acceptable to the king and princes, bishops, and every kind of powerful person.

He began to devote himself more diligently to divine worship, keeping watch day and night over the Lord’s praises, and training those entrusted to him in religious conduct. Thus the sound of his holiness spread throughout Neustria and Austrasia, France and Burgundy, and his sanctity became manifest to everyone.

There was a great gathering to him from every direction. Some submitted themselves to his instruction, having set aside the blandishments of the deceitful world; others offered him their sons to be educated. His monastery now seemed comparable to the monasteries of Nitria [Note: [Col. 0205D] A district situated above Memphis.] or Egypt because of the multitude of faithful flowing there. They flew from every direction like bees to their hives, carrying minds laden with different kinds of virtue, just as bees carry the undifferentiated qualities of honey and wax on their thighs and feet.

Oh, what great and excellent men shone under his instruction! How precious and devoted to God was the congregation entrusted to him, illuminated by his teachings and thoroughly formed through the practice of a stricter way of life!

The bishops, dukes, and counts of Gaul and Germany prove this. Fervent in the love of Christ, they appointed men from his monastery and discipleship as abbots over the monasteries they possessed, though under his protection and discipline. Or, if they were unable to obtain abbots from there, they selected men from among their own people to make abbots and sent them first to Verdun to be tested, instructed, and trained in good conduct.

Among these men, although we are younger and belong to a later generation, we saw many religious and exceptionally accomplished in every kind of spiritual contemplation, men venerable in angelic face and habit. From the formation of the disciples it was evident how great in religion, gravity, and perfection their master had been, for the excellence of his instruction shone clearly in the conduct of his disciples.

As the number of disciples increased, so did the measure of his honors. (*Life of Richard*, 9.) Richard’s name shone everywhere, his holiness was everywhere proclaimed, and the name of God was glorified through him.

When he saw that the ancient roofing of his church was already nearly ruined [Col. 0206D], he chose, once it had been demolished, to lay broader foundations and to build a new basilica on a better and more noble plan. This was accomplished soon afterward. Lord Frederick built the church’s towers at his own expense, as well as the cellar and the brothers’ refectory. (*Deeds of Verdun*, 9.)

When the dormitory was being rebuilt after its demolition and the necessary building work was being prepared, the old structure had to be cleared before the new one could be built. The men whose work and diligence were required to complete this task were summoned. When some of them, as people commonly do, were ashamed and avoided putting their hands to hauling away the material being cleared, Frederick, a man of humility and grace and truly a monk, came forward as a digger of the earth and carried away what had been excavated, making it into a load. ([Col. 0207A])

Who would now be ashamed to do something similar when he saw that Frederick, the son of a count, the brother of two dukes, and a kinsman of the emperor, had done it without shame?

He performed a similar service in the construction of the towers. When the structure was already rising to a considerable height, and there were very few people to carry the device called an “oiseau” [Note: [Col. 0207D] Still called *oiseau* by the French today.], which was fitted for transporting mortar, those assigned to this task being occupied elsewhere, the man of blessed memory saw one of the nobles standing nearby. He urged him to take up the wooden instrument and carry the mortar on his neck, as was customary.

When the man was ashamed and declared that such an act was unworthy of his birth, the most gentle man first placed his own neck beneath the instrument and fulfilled what he had asked. ([fol. 76’.]) Then he handed the same instrument to the young man and, by his own example, taught him to do what the count’s son had done, and not to be ashamed if anyone reproached him for an act that the count himself had once clearly been the first to perform.

One day this same memorable man was sitting in the brothers’ kitchen and performing some task, washing bowls and cleaning other vessels. Suddenly his brother, Duke Godefrid, arrived at the kitchen door and asked for admission. One of the servants who happened to be there opened it for him. Seeing his brother occupied with the work he had begun, the duke bowed his head and, making a play on the word “count,” said: “It is not fitting for a count to do such things. Names and actions, noble birth and the performance of labor, do not suit one another.”

As the duke was leaving, Frederick followed him out. When he found an opportunity to speak, he said to his brother: “You have spoken excellently, O duke, for the dignity of this office is so great, and the one to whom it is rendered is so great—namely, the blessed apostle Peter and Saint Vitonus the confessor—that it is not fitting for my insignificance to presume to serve them as though on account of the nobility of my birth. Nor is my humility so great that I deserve to be assigned by them to the company of those who are considered worthy of this office.”

Such was the abasement and contempt for himself in the soul of that faithful man that his humility was praised and was a marvel to all who knew the nobility of his birth.

On another occasion, when he was sitting in private and needed to remove his shoes, one of the brothers wished to serve him out of charity. His name was John; I myself saw him as an old man and heard these things from him when I was a boy. John was kneeling down to serve him, but Frederick was astonished and, with a certain religious obstinacy, refused to accept his service. He stopped him, saying:

“What benefit is it to me, brother, to have left behind the honors of the world if I accept from the brothers, when there is no need, the service that I would have had in the world? I came here to serve; how can I accept a service that is unnecessary?”

By saying this, he restrained his brother’s impulse and gave everyone the greatest lesson in patience, humility, and the desire to embrace lowliness.

Let this much be said in passing, to make known to everyone the abasement of his blessed mind. Now let us turn back to the order of the narrative.

[Col. 0208A] **8.** Therefore, once the new church had been built on a larger plan and with more elegant workmanship, it was necessary that the bodies of certain holy bishops should be moved. Then the body of Saint Madelvey was found incorrupt and was decently placed in a marble vessel in the crypt of Saint Mary beneath the altar. At that time also the translation of the two bishops Hildinus and Hatto took place, on the Nones of May, and their relics were placed on the right side of the monastery’s cross—namely, on the right side of the altar of Saint John the Baptist. (*Life of Richard*, 8.)

The body, however, of Lord Berengerius, bishop and monk, was found at the entrance to the cloister, still within the monastery, incorrupt except for the foot that had withered during his lifetime. His chasuble and sandals were removed from his body and placed in the church’s treasury with the relics [Col. 0208B]. His most holy body was moved higher up, toward the choir screen, and honorably provided with a new chasuble and sandals; opposite his tomb was placed the altar of Saint Firminus, which had been discovered by him in his own time.

The body of Lord Dado, bishop, was honorably buried opposite the two bishops mentioned above, on the left side of the monastery’s cross—namely, on the left side of the altar of Saint Martin. The bodies of the remaining bishops are contained beneath the choir, and above them a floor was made of cut and squared stones. Nevertheless, we have heard from many that the bodies of five bishops are contained beneath the pulpit from which the Gospel is read, although we do not know their names. (Folio 77.)

It is sufficiently certain that the pulpit was made of bronze, repeatedly beaten and worked into plates and panels, then gilded, with great precision and elegance. Across twelve panels, images of the twelve prophets and figures of the twelve apostles bearing them aloft were engraved in carved and polished work [Note: [Col. 0208D] multicolored]. These were placed on the western side, namely, at the back of those standing and singing.

On the northern side, however, four representations of the rivers flowing forth from Paradise rise in four sections. Around the circumference, beneath which the reader of the Gospel is shaded as he stands, images can be recognized of Abraham offering his son, Abel with the lamb, Isaac blessing, Jacob supplanting, Tobit burying, and David the strong-handed; they were assembled in similar workmanship. On the front appear the Lord Jesus seated on a throne of majesty, the Virgin Mother, and John the Baptist together with the four Evangelists. [Col. 0208D] To the right and left of the Lord, angels and archangels, with Cherubim and Seraphim, offer service to the Redeemer.

The instrument prepared to receive the text of the Gospel is adorned by John the Evangelist in the likeness of a flying eagle. On the rim and summit of the work, the supreme devotion of Father Richard is recorded in verses arranged in gold hexameters. Truly, the bodies of the saints adorn the mercy-seat, by whose merits the church flourishes.

In the very high and prominent ciborium at the center, Saint Vitonus rests, his forehead crowned with the purest gold and most precious gems, by which the unbounded and incomprehensible majesty of God is enclosed [Col. 0209A]. At his right is a projecting golden image of blessed Peter, and at his left one of the same blessed Vitonus, made in repoussé work. These are surrounded by columns [Note: [Col. 0209] thus in the text] produced from the purest electrum, with silver bases, by casting and relief work.

The ciborium itself is adorned with repoussé insignia of the Lord’s resurrection, appearance, and wondrous ascension. Before it stands a consecrated altar in honor of Saint Vitonus and all confessors. To the left is a consecrated altar in honor of Saint Pulcronius and all martyrs, together with its own ciborium, containing the body of that same blessed Pulcronius and decorated with gold and silver. To the right there is an altar in honor of Saint Possessor and all virgins, with a ciborium, likewise ornamented, in which his body is contained [Col. 0209B].

The greater altar is consecrated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, because of the privilege of this church, which in ancient times was both built and consecrated in honor of that apostle. Before it stands a golden panel, very densely set with purest gold and most precious gems, made with marvelous workmanship and repoussé art. It displays the image of the Lord holding the sign of the cross and walking upon the asp and basilisk, together with images of the apostles Peter and Paul, made in the same workmanship and metal.

At their feet one would see the images of Lord Father Richard and the worthy-to-be-remembered Mathildis, extending suppliant hands and praying—as though asking that this offering of theirs, made from the resources of one and the devotion of the other, might be accepted as pleasing. (Cf. C. of Verdun, 9.)

A portable altar was also made of the purest gold, wonderfully fashioned within in similar workmanship through the zeal and generosity of Lord Count Herimannus. It was joined and fitted together in the form of panels; when it is opened, it becomes an altar, and the panels open out. If one examines them carefully, the object, gloriously decorated with images of Moses and Aaron, presents the figure of the Lord’s cross. It has at its four hinges four representations of the Evangelists—the man, lion, ox, and eagle—made of silver by casting, carrying the aforesaid altar and looking at one another with turned faces.

Upon this altar the arm of Saint Pantaleon is placed, wrapped in a silken cloth and enclosed in wood [Col. 0209D], decorated with silver and gold. The arm was brought, together with the saint’s body, from Nicomedia by Gero, bishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0209D] Gero], after being obtained as a gift from the emperor of Constantinople (folio 77′), when he had been sent as an envoy to that emperor, by order of Otto II, concerning the marriage of the emperor’s daughter to Otto. He went with two bishops, dukes, and counts.

When he had obtained permission to return after accomplishing what he had gone to arrange, and when the emperor had offered many gifts to him and his companions, but they had refused to accept them, the archbishop asked the emperor for the body of Saint Pantaleon [Col. 0210A], obtained it, and brought it back to Cologne.

A certain kinsman of his, the lord of the castle of Commarceium [Note: [Col. 0209D] Commercy], had accompanied him on that expedition. By much entreaty he obtained from him the arm of Saint Pantaleon’s body, which he placed in the church of the aforesaid castle. After several years had passed, the castle was besieged, destroyed, and burned. When the flames were falling upon the roofs of the church and, in victorious globes, licking its interior, the grieving priest, distressed by the burning of the holy relics, informed one of the armed men that he should enter the church and remove the relics from the altar.

He immediately entered, took the relics, and set them aside. While Abbot R. was present there, he sold the arm of the saint to him, in the priest’s presence, for a mark [Col. 0210B] of silver. Abbot R., knowing for certain that it was a relic of the martyr, joyfully brought it to Verdun; encased in silver and gold, it is placed upon the altar on feast days.

He also made many other ornaments: Gospel books furnished with gold and silver; three crosses of the purest gold; two silver fans; one Epistle book furnished with silver; one missal; and one collectary, likewise furnished with silver. (Cf. G. of Verdun, 11.)

Emperor Henry also gave one very large golden chalice with most precious gems and a paten of the same metal; one dish of beryl; and one onyx pyx, in which the Lord’s body was to be kept hanging above the altar. In addition, he gave countless gifts of gold, silver, estates, and sacred vestments, as well as golden, silver, and crystal reliquaries containing the relics of saints; one gold chest marked with the relics of the twelve apostles; and two ivory horns, likewise filled with relics.

The distinguished Father Richard also made two crowns of silver and gold, and a third, a small one, from which the cords of the bells might hang. Countess Adverada likewise gave Saint Peter a green chasuble with gold embroidery, and many people gave many things, which would take too long to enumerate. Thus that place quickly became distinguished. (G. of Verdun, 8, 9.)

Moved by his example, the descendants of Lord Frederick renounced the world, attached themselves to the discipleship of the aforesaid father, and gave their estates and inheritances to the church. Count Godefridus gave Borracum; later, when his son Adalbero, bishop, had been brought back from Italy, and when his parents had ordered that he be buried in the church of Saint Vitonus but he had instead been buried against their wishes in the church of Saint Mary, they gave Forbacum to Saint Vitonus [Note: [Col. 0210D] Forbach] for the repose of his soul.

Herimannus, also called Hezelo, offered his son Gregory to God in childhood and directed all his devotion toward that place. He gave Haslud, with its church, to Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus; one church at Fesseca; twelve manses at Rotgericort; and one church at Ermefredegehen [Col. 0211A]. After his death these properties were exchanged, and Count Baldwin of Flanders gave in return Bonvillare with half a church; Hevenges, likewise with half a church; vineyards at Vitereium with a certain part of the church; and at Harvia, thirty manses with a large household. (G. of Verdun, 9.)

Apart from this exchange, he also transferred Monnau and the church, together with an extensive forest, to the aforesaid church; and Fontagiam, with its household and an excellent vineyard. He also gave, for the soul of his son Godefridus, born of a concubine and buried in the cloister, though not beside the brothers and his father, two churches, one called Ham and the other Gengeavia.

**9.** He also made very precious sacred vestments for the church. After enriching that church above all mortals with his goods and possessions, he finally offered himself to God and became a monk, so that he might reign with Christ forever.

His worthy-to-be-remembered wife, Mathildis, distinguished by good virtues and devoted to works of mercy, died in the cloister of that monastery and now rests there honorably buried. At her head their daughter Odilia, a most holy virgin, has her burial place. (Folio 78.)

A story was told about her, and we heard it from our elders: having left the borders of Bavaria, she came to Verdun on the Wednesday before the holy day of Easter, wishing to celebrate Easter with her father, mother, and brothers. When the man of God Richard saw her, he asked amid gentle words of consolation whether she was suffering from any illness.

When she answered that she was well and felt no burden of sickness, he, filled with the spirit of prophecy and foreseeing that the time of her calling was near, said: “Farewell, daughter, truly a daughter of eternal salvation. For tomorrow at this hour you will be taken up in glory, and you will receive from God everlasting rewards for your good conduct. God has chosen you to be the companion of the holy virgins, because in your heart you have prepared for him a joyful dwelling place of virginity.”

The servant of God was astonished at these words of her pious father. Because she believed that a man of God could not lie, she trusted his words and began to reflect on her end, to examine her transgressions, and to ask him for the support of consolation and prayer. He inclined her holy head upon his breast and, caressing her as though she had already been transformed through the incorruption of body and spirit [Col. 0211D], strengthened her spirit in the Lord, declaring that she would be blessed, since it was certain that she was hastening to the wedding feast of the Lamb.

After this he ordered that she be refreshed, while everyone wondered how he could have predicted that she, healthy and vigorous, would die the next day. On the following day, after he had anointed her with the liquid of holy oil, and while she suffered no heaviness, she took part with him in the washing of the poor’s feet. Seeing the blessed man in the very place where he had washed the poor’s feet, she said: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall await the day of the Lord.” [Col. 0212A]

She then went to the solemn celebration of Mass. After receiving the life-giving mysteries, she was stricken by a slight pain, returned to her cell, and, when the man of God arrived with the brothers, asked that her passing be fortified by their prayers. Thus, reclining in his hands upon ashes and sackcloth, she joyfully breathed out her spirit amid the words of prayer.

When the blessed soul departed, such a fragrance of scent poured forth there [Note: [Col. 0211] thus in the text] that no one could doubt that the author of sweetness had come there. Her body was duly cared for through the pious attentiveness of the religious and was preserved in the church until the third day with pious solicitude and industry. Thus, on Holy Saturday, it was committed to the earth with glory. (Cf. G. of Verdun, 9.)

In this monastery, Lord Count Liethard of Marceium, coming to conversion, bestowed Bailodium [Col. 0212B]. After living for many years in a holy way of life, he eventually died and was buried at Châlons, where obedience had sent him; afterward he was brought back to Verdun and buried in the cloister. (*Life of Richard*, 9.)

Godefridus, duke and brother of Gozelo, was buried there. He gave twenty-nine manses at Beurunes and greatly enlarged the place with his furnishings. Dodo, too, of the Count’s castle, rests there at the entrance to the monastery beside Count Theodoric. There is also Louis, count and monk. (G. of Verdun, 9, 11.)

Count Hildradus, presenting his son Richard to the blessed father to be baptized after he became bishop, gave the court of Baro to Saint Vitonus; after his death he deserved to be buried in the galilee [Note: [Col. 0211D] an area, in our language “gallery”].

It is not easy to relate how many people from various parts of France, Neustria [Col. 0212C], and Austrasia, despising the allurements of worldly vanity, submitted themselves to monastic religion under the discipline and teaching of Father Richard. Kings, bishops, and powerful men had so poured themselves into his love that they venerated him with the deepest affection and called him “father of the fatherland,” because of his fatherly affection toward all, by which he cherished and lifted everyone up.

He was pious in countenance, reverend in his bearing, severe toward the reprobate, gentle toward the well-disposed, honorable in appearance, measured in conduct, always preferring what was honorable to what was useful. No fear and no flattery could turn him from the truth. He was most fervent in observing the rule, most prudent in correcting vices, most illustrious in chastity, and most perfect in the performance of good works [Col. 0212D].

**10. (1020)** Since Baldricus, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0211D] Wolbodo; cf. *Annales Laubienses*, MGH SS IV, 18; *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium*, book 3, chapter 15, MGH SS VII, 470], loved the blessed man uniquely, he entrusted to him the monastery of Lobbes, exceedingly rich in wealth, to govern, so that through his diligence its religious way of life might be reformed, since it appeared to have departed from its former rigor.

Delighted and moved by his admirable example, when he saw his religious conduct in good and holy ways and rejoiced in amazement that the growth of religion and monastic perfection was increasing in that monastery [Col. 0213A], he began to contemplate greater things. He decided that a monastery should be built in the suburb of Liège in honor of the martyr Lawrence. He therefore summoned the same abbot, disclosed his desire to him, urged him to become a collaborator in its fulfillment, and entreated him, adding that his house could greatly advance perfection if, through his zeal and industry, a house of God were built in which the praise and glory of God might be devoutly celebrated day and night.

The man of God consented. Artisans were assembled and the necessary expenses assigned; with Christ the Lord assisting and blessed Lawrence cooperating, the work was energetically completed and dedicated. Brothers who would serve God daily were brought from the monastery of Saint Vitonus. Lord Stephen, who had held the office of cellarer in the aforesaid monastery, was placed over them as provost [Col. 0213B].

Touched by a similar desire for good devotion, Lord Rotgerius, bishop of the city of Châlons, built from the foundations, through the industry and labor of that same Father Richard, a monastery in the suburb of Châlons in honor of Saint Peter. From the aforesaid monastery he brought brothers, together with the necessary books and ornaments, to serve there; during his lifetime he himself personally governed both monasteries. (*Life of Richard*, chapter 12.)

A remarkable event is related about this. When the towers of the church of Saint Lawrence had already been raised high and lifted to their summit, they subsequently appeared to lean, and the church’s collapse through their ruin seemed certain [Note: [Col. 0213] thus in the text]. The man of God arrived and gently consoled the brothers in their distress, which arose from the weariness of having to bring down and rebuild the tower [Col. 0213C].

At night he entered the church and, after spending a long time in prayer, came out when the doors had been opened. Then, having again devoted himself to prayer, he rose, made the sign of the cross, and immediately the towers that had appeared to be leaning, recoiling into themselves with a tremendous crash, settled into place. As is evident to those who saw it, they recoiled into themselves in such a way that it was made clear to everyone that this had been accomplished by angelic service.

The cracking of the structure as it recoiled into itself was so great that the monastery’s brothers, unaware of such a mystery, rose from their beds in the greatest fear, thinking that the part of the church they had feared would fall had collapsed with the towers. The man of God invited them to the customary office of Matins [Col. 0213D] and took part in it with them. When morning came, he showed them the Lord’s benefits with their own eyes and wonderfully stirred them to love the giver of so great a benefit.

The entire city of Liège is witness to this miracle. The fathers who saw it told it to their sons, and the sons to their sons, so that a later generation might know it.

At that time Robert ruled the Franks, and he married Constance. Three times he entrusted the abbey of Saint Peter of Corbie to our blessed father to govern, so that through his instruction and vigor the rule of Father Benedict might be preserved there and the rigor of monastic discipline restored.

Baldwin of Flanders, moreover, entrusted several abbeys to him: the abbey of Saint Peter of Ghent, the abbey of Saint-Amand, the abbey of Saint Bertin, the abbey of Saint Richarius, and the abbey of Saint Josse. He also governed very many other monasteries: Bretigny, Humiliers, Saint-Quentin of Monte, Saint-Wandrille, Saint-Hubert, Saint-Remaclus, Malmedy, Waulsort, Beaulieu, Saint-Urbain, Saint-Vincent of the island of Metz, and many others that do not come to mind. He restored all of them to a better condition and, once they had been improved, appointed abbots from among those whom he had chosen.

He himself governed during his lifetime the monasteries of Beaulieu, Saint Peter of Châlons, and Saint-Urbain [Note: [Col. 0213] partly erased]. At that time the venerable bishop Gerard presided over the churches of Cambrai and Arras.

He assigned to our father, whom he loved uniquely, the church of Saint Vedast, situated in the suburb of Arras, which had been reduced from the greatest wealth to the greatest poverty, in the year 1008 from the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0214B]. In it the man of God did and suffered so much that, if each matter were written down, it would, as I fear, produce weariness in the reader and disgust in the listeners. Yet a few things must be said from among many, and perhaps they will prove more useful.

Let us therefore say what happened that reduced a place of such wealth to poverty. We report this not from what we saw, but from what we heard from our elders.

**11.** One of the servants of Saint Vedast had broken out into such insolence [Note: [Col. 0213] “propterviam” in one copy], and had grown to such arrogance, although he was somewhat necessary to the church, that he built himself a house within the monastery courtyard, of great height and strength, supposedly for the protection of the place [Col. 0214C].

But when he found an opportunity to exercise his insolence, provoked by the excessive idleness of secular life within the monastery, he raised defenses, strengthened weaker points, and began to rebel no longer for the place but against the place and against God. He plundered the church’s goods, gathered male and female servants to himself, brought in a crowd of dogs and a foolish throng of entertainers and buffoons, and did not keep them from entering the cloister (folio 79). Rather, he himself continually sat there surrounded by bands of attendants and profaned the dwelling places of God’s servants through illicit acts.

When the man of God undertook the governance of the monastery and was welcomed by the brothers whose minds were sounder, he could not endure seeing such desolation in the house of God [Col. 0214D]. Instead, he devoted himself entirely to rescuing it.

He nevertheless considered whether he might soften that freedman’s hardness of mind and soothe his insolence with the sweetness of words [Note: [Col. 0213] “dulcenide” in one copy], so that he would cease oppressing and trampling the church, to which by obligation and the law of nature he ought rather to be subject than to preside over it.

But a wicked servant is not broken by words but by blows, as Wisdom says: “For he who is hard of mind will receive wounds” (Proverbs 28:14). Although the words of the wise are like nails driven deep, the fool did not listen to words of prudence, because he did not say what was occupying his heart [Col. 0215A]. For Solomon’s truthful proverb had been fulfilled: “He who pampers a servant will find him rebellious” (Proverbs 29:21).

What could the man of God do? Where could his anxious mind turn? He wrapped himself in sackcloth, sprinkled himself with ashes, and, spending sleepless nights in watchfulness over the flock entrusted to him, prayed more earnestly that God would protect his church from the oppression of the enemy and his members, have mercy on the little ones, and shield them from scandal. He also prayed that God would make him, whom he had set over them, such that toward his subjects he would display both the tenderness of a mother and the discipline of a father, so that there might be in him both a mercy that rightly gives counsel and a discipline that chastens piously.

When an opportune time had come, he assembled the people. After speaking briefly, as the matter and time required, against arrogance, and after delivering some further exhortation concerning the pursuit of the religious vocation, he saw that the people’s minds had turned toward him. He approached the fortress that was troubling him and destroyed it utterly. He then captured the man who, swollen with injustice, was behaving arrogantly, and established him in the alms-house of Saint Vedast, where he would sit and live from the alms. Thus he rescued the place from the harassment of that man and his attendants.

He therefore began to devote himself to religious pursuits with still greater fervor. He brought from Verdun brothers tested in the novitiate of spiritual discipline and entrusted the care of the place to them. Among them was Rothardus of Liège, highly renowned for wisdom and religion. He did this because he knew it was beneficial both for himself, who presided, and for those who were subject to him.

But because his chaste life and holy conduct were distasteful to the inhabitants, and because it seemed harsh to them that, in their old mind, they were being forced to contemplate new things, some of them, emboldened by rebellion, attempted to plot his death [Col. 0215C].

**12.** As the season of Lent approached—for it was the monastery’s rule that during those days each person should mortify himself through stricter abstinence—and as they were compelled to this with more determined care and fervor, the envy concealed in their hearts began to creep upward more deeply and daily to drive their tortured minds toward completing what they had desired.

Why delay over many details? The most sacred day of the Lord’s Supper arrived. Although it was a day of peace and concord, reconciliation and mercy, for these factious men it became a day for carrying out betrayal and wickedness. They had decided that, when that day was over, after the blessed man had completed the saving ministry and relaxed his weary limbs in sleep, they would kill him with swords while everyone slept [Col. 0215D].

O rash presumption! O shameless audacity! What madness, after that victim of the Paschal Lamb had been offered, to condemn anyone to death, however guilty, on that day or night?

That deadly plot of evil did not remain hidden from the blessed man. He heard that he was to be killed by the impious that night, but he was not afraid. The pure fear of the Lord, which endures forever and ever, expelled the fear of death from his mind, because he knew that no power would be granted to anyone over him except insofar as the Lord permitted it.

Entrusting himself entirely to the Lord, he went to bed with his head uncovered, ready, if God willed it, to offer his throat [Col. 0216A]. Then, before Matins, while everyone was resting after their labor, the two men whose deed and intention it was to slaughter their father secretly rose and left the dormitory. Girded with swords, and encouraging one another as they declared their devotion to the crime they were about to commit, they finally agreed that one of them should cautiously circle each bed in the dormitory, lest anyone remain awake whom they feared might detect them.

When this had been done and he had returned to his companion, having seized the opportunity to carry out their wickedness, they approached Father Richard’s bed together and saw the man sleeping with his head uncovered. (Folio 79′.)

When one of them, the bolder in crime, had brandished his armed right hand to strike him, his arm stiffened, and he experienced divine mercy toward himself: the mercy that did not allow the father to be destroyed, since he was destined to send many to the eternal inheritance [Note: [Col. 0215D] L corrects *extera* in c. to *exerta*.] [Col. 0216B]. His right hand remained extended, unable either to strike or to put back the sword.

O marvelous proclamation of God! O wondrous patience! O piety worthy of praise! Our Jesus could have turned those athletes of his away from their sinful intention; he could have punished them with death as soon as they attempted to put their thoughts into action. But he endured the sons of wrath with great patience in order to make them sons of mercy.

Fear, together with fever, seized the wretched man, and he withdrew from the father’s bed, which the grace of the Almighty was protecting. Not long afterward, when the signal had been given, they went to the church. The man whose conscience tormented him attended the nocturnal assembly with the others, although trembling, although ill, although weighed down by the goads of a biting conscience.

When they came to the “darkness” section of the service, while “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy”—was being sung with its verses, the wretched man, pierced in heart, threw himself at his father’s knees and himself cried out to his father: “Lord, have mercy”—that is, asking him to have mercy on him, just as he was praying that God would have mercy on him [Col. 0216C].

The holy man was astonished when he felt the brother fall at his feet, and he had no idea what had happened. Nevertheless, he received him and moved aside with him, completed the prayer, and, after light had been given and the others had returned to their beds, kept some of the brothers with him.

Withdrawing to a suitable place, when the opportunity for speaking had come, he asked the trembling and weeping brother—who had thrown his whole body to the ground and was striking the earth with his head—what was afflicting him. Breaking off his words with a groan, the man said:

“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I did not wish to be called or to be your son; I have become your persecutor.”

Then, drawing a sword from beneath his cowl, he said: “Behold the sword that I extended tonight to strike you, but your Jesus protected you. I wanted to destroy you, but your protector, the Lord, defended you. I drew the sword against you, but he whose power and authority it is restrained the sword. He saved you from death and saved me from the destruction of my soul and from murder.

“Therefore, spare me, because I am ready to turn back, obey your admonitions, and submit to the institutions of the rule. Only forgive me what I have done against you, and pray to God for me” [Col. 0217A].

It was not difficult for the blessed man to forgive those who sinned against him, since he was most patient regarding personal injuries. With his whole body prostrate, he therefore gave thanks to his protector, God. Then he kindly forgave the brother whatever he had done against him, greatly consoling him and insisting that he confess his sins to the Lord.

He said that sin is sometimes both a sin and the punishment of sin, and that all these things could be avoided by one who devoted himself to confession. After speaking briefly, as the time allowed, he dismissed the consoled brother, instructing him to return to him when morning came and to do whatever was commanded him. Thus they parted.

Father Richard went to the oratory and spent what remained of the night in praise of the Creator. When day came, after Prime had been said and the customary office completed [Col. 0217B], as soon as a suitable time was available, the son sought out the father. After making his confession and receiving penance, he left him cheerful and unharmed, saying that it greatly benefited him that the Lord had claimed him for himself on this occasion.

From that time onward this man became Father Richard’s sweetest son and inseparable companion. He shared in his counsels, for he was born of noble parentage and highly educated in letters, and he displayed penance together with modesty.

When they came to the chapter, he performed public penance with his companion, with a contrite and humbled heart. The brothers glorified God, who had turned this sin away from them. They began to hold the holy man in even greater veneration, knowing that he was dear to God, unafraid of death, contemptuous of himself, forgiving of injury, and therefore had God as his defender and protector [Col. 0217C].

If there was now anyone who had at some time been hostile to the man of God, he rose in their midst and confessed whatever it was, fearing greatly lest divine indignation should rage against him also. They all prayed together to be forgiven, because they had not treated him as they ought, as father and lord. Thus there was the downfall of two and the spiritual resurrection of many. (Folio 80.)

The man of God then granted everyone a general pardon, and afterward he was loved by all with such affection that the saying was rightly applied to him: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11).

**13.** Afterward, having organized the church with its personnel and necessary expenses, he returned to Verdun, bringing with him the aforesaid brother, because he understood that he would become a useful vessel in the house of the Lord [Col. 0217D]. Nor was his hope deceived.

For the man became wholly changed. He began to contemplate more perfect things, love honesty, cherish order, put everyone before himself, place himself after everyone, and shape himself in every way toward whatever befits an honorable man. Therefore he was loved by the man of God and was urged by daily admonition to pursue better things.

The man’s name was Leduinus. He is that Leduinus who afterward, by the command and obedience of the aforesaid father, governed the church of Saint Vedast under him for many years.

Yet this seems remarkable in our father: he loved with such affection the man whom he knew had plotted his death. Here one must consider his piety and unconquerable patience, which knew not how to repay those who injured him in kind. His direct simplicity of spirit abounded in him to such a degree that he believed the man whom he had endured as an enemy to be a faithful friend to himself.

O mind truly full of God! Simplicity without pretense! Charity without rivalry! But let these things suffice for the moment; we must hasten to what remains. We cannot describe all the virtues of his spirit. Some matters must be passed over so that we may devote ourselves to the more important.

For now, let us say what we can about his beneficence, since we cannot say everything. He had so bound the hearts of his sons to himself that he was said to be mindful of gratitude and forgetful of injury. He considered the feelings, needs, and circumstances of each person [Col. 0218B], and thus met everyone with a marvelous grace of words and countenance, adding good words to good deeds and commending himself through kindly and humane praise, so that his disposition was valued more highly than whatever it was that had been requested. (Cf. Seneca, *On Benefits* II, 2.)

Just as, for the sick, the timely provision of nourishing food is health, and water given at the proper moment serves as a remedy, so his benefits, although small, because they were at hand and met the recipient’s desire, surpassed in graciousness a costly gift that was slow and long deliberated. They were especially welcome because they were ready, easy, and forthcoming, when the only delay lay in the recipient’s hesitation.

For he knew that the best course was to anticipate each person’s desire and follow close behind it; better still, to forestall it before one was asked [Col. 0218C]. For, as Seneca says in Book II, chapter 1, *On Benefits*, when shame closes a good man’s mouth as he prepares to ask, and blush spreads across his face, whoever removes this torment multiplies the gift. Nothing, indeed, costs more dearly than what is purchased by prayers.

Hence Saint Benedict, speaking of giving necessities, says: “Let the abbot consider the infirmities of those in need, not the ill will of those who envy.” By commanding that infirmities be considered, he teaches that one should anticipate prayers and discern each person’s need, so that the necessity of asking may be removed.

Moreover, this also aided the beneficence of our father: if anyone confessed to him the secrets of his soul or the inner movements of his mind, there was in him such kindness of mind, such sweetness, and such compassion [Col. 0218D], that the one who had come alone to reveal himself believed that the man to whom he was confessing was another self; not without reason, he joined his mind to him as to another self and trusted himself to him.

For he met the other’s desire and conformed himself to him so completely—suffering with the one who suffered and applying a spirit likewise troubled to the one who was distressed—that the visitor marveled to find, as it were, one soul present in two bodies, while he regarded the other as his own self.

This quality is most welcome to ordinary people and most useful to the little ones, who make use of the affection by which they see that those to whom they speak or confess are inclined toward them.

[Col. 0219A] **14.** Now, whenever anyone heard his discourse in the chapter-house [Note: [Col. 0219D] i.e., in the chapter meeting], everyone trembled, everyone was agitated, and everyone applied to himself the sharpest spur of compunction for self-reproach, as though he saw before his eyes the fires of Gehenna prepared and every kind of punishment distributed, until consolation proceeded from the mouth of the speaker, his tongue became sweetness of honey, and a honeycomb dripping from his lips! (Song of Songs IV, 11.) (Fol. 80'.)

For he did not conceal the sins of offenders; rather, whenever the subject was vices, he expressed their filth, uncleanness, and stench so precisely in words that anyone who heard him marveled and, recoiling from such things, utterly detested becoming involved in them. In him there was mercy that gave just counsel and discipline that exercised godly severity. For, as the most gentle teacher Gregory says in the *Moralia*, mercy or discipline is greatly weakened if either is maintained without the other. Affection displayed the father, kindness the mother, reverence born of fear the lord, and discipline the teacher; and all of this proceeded from the fountain of beneficence.

He did not wish his gift to be wasted, since he was always ready to give. Therefore, in conferring a benefit, whether bodily or spiritual, he observed time, place, and persons with common and rational judgment, since certain moments are both pleasing and displeasing. [SENECA, *De beneficiis* II, 1.] A benefit is displeasing when it remains too long in the hands of the giver, when someone parts with it reluctantly, or when he seems to give it as though he were snatching it away from himself. For this reason the blessed man, whenever his sons asked something of him that bodily or spiritual necessity required, did not hesitate, lest he should be close to one who refuses and confer no gratitude [Col. 0219C] (ibid. II, 5), knowing that nothing is so bitter as waiting too long, since some people endure having their hope cut off more calmly than having it dragged out.

What gift, moreover, is as sweet to a human being as to help with counsel, share labors, participate in sorrows, relieve an anxious spirit, rejoice with one who rejoices, and weep with one who weeps? Through these gifts and benefits he had drawn the affection of his sons toward himself, so that they considered his injury their own and believed his joy to be their own. His kindness was so great that, whenever he came and was permitted to remain for some time in any community, when he departed there was no one who did not joyfully boast that he had been helped, relieved, supported, and strengthened.

Now there is no need to praise his generosity, since it is no small part of generosity to consider in every matter how each thing should be said or done. For every kindness that proceeds from generosity hastens, and it is characteristic of one who acts willingly to act quickly. (Ibid. II, 5.) Whoever helps slowly, putting off one day after another, does not act from the heart; thus he loses two very great things, time and the proof of friendly goodwill, because to wish slowly is characteristic of one who does not wish. At times, moreover, a spirit brought to weariness begins to hate a benefit while it waits.

What benefit, however, is greater than to return gratitude to the dead, to provide and care for their repose, from whom you have received alms? This is the highest generosity: to remember those who, while they lived, entrusted themselves to you; by whose living labors and blood you are nourished; who, placing their confidence in you after God, lent their possessions to God through your hands when they generously gave them to you for love of him.

This gratitude was not lacking in our father. Indeed, in all the monasteries that he governed, as soon as he was able he established by perpetual right that, in a calendar, the names of each brother and of the church’s benefactors who had departed from this world should be written on separate pages, and that their anniversaries should be recited each day in the chapter-house. It was to be carefully recorded what each person had contributed to the church, so that, while the brothers recalled their benefits in the present through this most diligent record, their memory might grow warm within them, and they might be remembered with greater gratitude the more acceptably the representation of their benefactions was made.

To make this more acceptable, he delivered a discourse about it before the brothers. He ordered that, after it had been taken down, it should be written at the beginning of the calendar in which these matters were recorded. Anyone who carefully considers it can discern his sweetness and piety, his charity and mercy. Those who are accustomed to observing it know with what affection and zeal he instituted the commemoration of these dead—that is, the office we call the vigil—and the celebration of Masses.

In every respect he was most kind regarding the memory of the dead. For he knew that nothing reaches its fruit unless equal cultivation follows it from beginning to end. Therefore, with pious diligence he carried out his care for those entrusted to him both in life and in death.

What shall we say about his fortitude and temperance, by which his spirit was so governed that they seemed innate in him? Since fortitude without temperance is material for wrongdoing, in him one was so seasoned by the other that it was altogether impossible to see or wish to distinguish one without the other. Justice, moreover, had established a private dwelling for itself in his breast together with prudence; and piety, useful for all things, was not lacking, fortified by the discernment of knowledge.

There is no knowledge if it lacks the usefulness of piety, because whoever neglects to carry out the good things he has recognized binds himself more tightly for judgment. Since the man of God knew this, he had acquired for himself the distinctive qualities of each virtue; armed with them, he overcame the allurements of the deceiving world.

But let us return to the order of the narrative.

[Col. 0220D] **15.** In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1011, the venerable father Richard went to Rome and, having been joined in friendship to Pope Benedict, became most intimate with him. In that same year, when he was already a well-known man in the monastery of Saint Vedast, over which he presided in the office of rector, revelations were made to him in that same monastery. He himself sent their text to all the sons of the Church, and it was also thought proper to record them here.

[Note: [Col. 0219] Fols. 81–83, inserted in the same hand, written in pale ink in minute letter-forms, of which not a few have almost vanished. The individual pages contain between 67 and 75 lines. Thus V. Cl. Ulrichs, to whom we owe the apograph of fols. 81–83.]

(1011, April 17.) «To the orthodox and united elect of the Church of God, members united in the unity of the body under Christ the head, Richard, by the favor of God, although unworthy abbot, sends to those who read this the joys of everlasting salvation.

(Fol. 81.) Taught by evangelical truth and founded in Christ upon the authority of the whole evangelical faith, joined to you, most beloved brothers, by a certain paternal concern, I bring to your charity, as an example, a matter divinely accomplished, which we can infer that divine grace wished to be made manifest to us through a certain brother of ours, who was seized in spirit, as though in an ecstasy of mind, for the space of six hours, for the consolation of your admonition.

Although this matter continually instructs us through hidden and scarcely graspable lessons of the divine Scriptures, in many ways, so that we cannot oppose spiritual things, nevertheless, because we are dulled by constant habit and expose the relaxations of our impatient bodily nature to the enemy of destruction who lies in ambush opposite us, as though through security, we are brought by God’s evident mercy through this vision back to the inward subtlety of our mind and examination, insofar as each of us, with the most subtle eye of mind and discernment, compares and transforms this vision’s meaning into himself for his own benefit through the invincible discernment of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists.

It is also clear to everyone that what is manifested for our salvation through the display of divine mercy is not concealed under the cover of silence without harm. To narrate the works of the Lord is honorable; to suppress them in silence is dangerous.

For what is more salutary and useful than that someone should make a singular gift of divine generosity common by sharing it with others? When this is done, the command of the Savior is fulfilled, in which he says: “What I tell you in the darkness” (Matthew X, 27), and so forth. Considering the force of this command and wishing with all the zeal of our minds to fulfill it, we bring into the open for the benefit of many what we heard in darkness and in the ear—that is, in secret.

Let no one suppose that anything false has been mixed into this account, or believe it in any respect alien to the truth, for, just as we heard and saw, we have touched upon it in a faithful narrative, without the embellishment of falsehood. Now, therefore, let us turn our style to the narration of what happened.

While, with the reverence due to religion, we were completing for ourselves the fifty-day Paschal solemnities in this monastery situated in the city of the people of Arras, honorably dedicated to the most precious confessor of Christ, Vedast, in whose service, by God’s authority, I devote myself to the instruction and discipline of monastic continence, the following vision occurred divinely.

One of our brothers, overtaken by bodily weakness, was confined to a bed of illness. After two days had passed, the moment of the night of the third day itself arrived, when, because of the excessive pain of his anguish, he seemed to be compelled to depart completely from this world. When the brothers appointed to keep watch there saw this, they signaled for me to come quickly. Joined by the service of two brothers, I arrived as soon as possible. Since, after the bed had been laid out, the spirit was struggling with the separation of its departure, I summoned the whole community to be present, applying themselves to psalmody and litanies.

When these had been completed, while we were occupied with the funeral rites, and since it could scarcely be determined by those standing around whether he had completely breathed out his spirit, I began, saying, “Come to his aid, saints of God,” and to cleanse his mouth. Meanwhile, when he had already been disturbed by sudden [Note: [Col. 0221] Was something omitted below? U. Perhaps *motibus* or something of that kind has fallen out.], I brought myself close to the dead man’s body and, applying my hand with the most delicate examination to his mouth, breast, and vital parts, perceived that a spirit was present, like the breath of the thinnest and most delicate air. After the prayer of commendation had been recited, we began to await what would happen.

After an interval of about one hour, his lips began to tremble with a very faint and scarcely perceptible sob and breath. Then his tongue began to emit from its surface an inarticulate sound, as if of someone sighing and grieving, and afterward, as though wishing to form words like the cries of infants, it began to shape a distinct sound. Thus the matter advanced until he formed words intelligible to our hearing.

But please pay attention: he moved only his tongue. In all the other members of his body—by which I mean the head, eyes, and hands, hips and feet—there was no spirit at all, as though a spirit had been present in a piece of wood. The touch of the brothers who were present and numerous bore certain witness to this. Yet the tongue alone formed words that appeared there and were spoken to our hearing. Later, when he returned to himself, he believed that no human being under heaven could know them.

A notary attended him and, impressing the same words in writing, marked them down. Later, when he made use of bodily speech, he testified that he had seen and spoken no other things than those he had seen and spoken in heaven. When you hear him in what follows, reader, do not think that any of these matters can be doubted. Rather, you will marvel more that a wholly dead body could form words by human means; and since the most truthful testimony of both Testaments compels belief, you will not doubt that what he reports was seen by him.

As the soul was leaving the body, three evil spirits, terrifying in their very appearance, stood before it. Attacking it as though with a dreadful assault, they said that they would have it tortured in infernal punishments, bringing forward testimony of its sins: namely, a small knife belonging to one of our brothers, which he had long before lost through forgetfulness and negligence. Although the fault seemed very small, he had neither confessed it earlier nor been absolved by pardon.

Michael, the angel of peace and light, also appeared, a most serene protector against the hostile invasion. When both sides had assembled, in an instant they stood at the gates of hell. There a huge fire, utterly exceeding every measure of size, had been appointed for the torment of souls in those places. It emitted black and exceedingly foul-smelling flames. In it the betrayer of the Lord, Judas, bound tightly with chains on every side, is kept to be tortured with still greater punishments on the day of judgment.

The soul, expecting to be assigned to that place, was gripped by the immense terror of present death and punishment. In a frequent and mournful voice it repeated that God and the holy apostles Peter and Paul, John the Baptist, and the great confessor of Christ Vedast, whom it served, should have mercy on it. But those beings accused it of having delayed a true confession of its earlier sin, testifying against it in order to condemn it.

At last, anticipated by God’s mercy and trusting in the angelic fellowship, it was separated from the unclean spirits. From there they proceeded alone to investigate greater matters. Suddenly, behold, they came to a place of another and distinct kind of torment, where there was a chasm of the lower hell, broad and of immeasurable depth like a well. It displaced flames belching smoke from a furnace, as clouds are heaped together in rain.

The soul was set above this place as though upon a cliff at a precipice [Col. 0223B]. The angel, however, turning his face in another direction, asked it to look inside. Obeying his command out of great fear, it looked in and recognized Albert, prefect of the county of Namur [Note: [Col. 0223D] He died around 1010; cf. *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS VII, p. 439; book VII, XLVIII, p. 440; book XIV, p. 473; book V.], whom many of our people had known, being tortured there.

While it trembled there in great uncertainty about its own destruction, it was lifted up by the angel. After not a very long interval, they came to water that could be gathered from the excessive and foul-smelling frost as being cold. Around it a very large multitude of people sat immersed as though to the depth of half their bodies. Although they had possessed some good, nevertheless, because they had departed from the world impure, they were to be cleansed until the future judgment by the punitive waters of cold and stench, in proportion to their venial sins.

Then they came to another place, which rolled before the eyes, in boiling and bubbling waters, innumerable clamorings of mourners. Their torturers, bearing the likeness of horses, dogs, and almost every kind of creeping creature, rejoiced in their pitiable destruction with shameless gestures of voice and body, because they had been guilty of more serious sins—homicide, fornication, adultery, and sacrilege.

After passing through these places under angelic guidance, they emerged onto a plain of such great extent that it was green with the variety of its most beautiful flowers. Even if the entire globe of the earth, made level, could be gathered within the sight of one person, it could not be compared with this place. One part of it contained places of refreshment, while another was marked by various fires of punishments and flames, so that those oppressed by lighter punishments, as though gold purified by fire, withdrew separately to be refreshed.

In this place of refreshment he recognized Notker, the bishop [Note: [Col. 0223D] He died in 1008]. In the punishments he recognized another bishop, whose name he did not mention. A chain was fastened around his neck and passed down his back, and his torturers were trying to pull out with fiery tongs the tongue with which he ought to have preached to the people [lacuna] a dragon from its mouth, nostrils, and ears deadly flames into the face [lacuna] the priests Eucharius and Rainbold, and also his own little brother named Peter, being burned at his side; and he saw another sister, contracted in every part of her body throughout her life, who had already withdrawn separately and been freed [Note: [Col. 0223] “ex . . csp . . . c.”].

He also saw a layman—the father of a certain brother of ours who was standing there—of whom, because we know his life, we have no doubt, and many others whom memory made known but whom the present circumstances, in many ways, made unknown.

From this point, reader, please attend carefully. As soon as this soul had emerged from the unclean spirits and had been freed from the dangers of the punishments it had seen, and had been sweetly refreshed by the serene guide who accompanied it, familiarity with him increased its desires to investigate and examine still greater matters. It repeatedly extorted from him whatever could be imagined by saying, “O holy lord Michael, kind father, tell me!” You will be able to hear what follows in writing.

Because, with each response of the angel, it anxiously [Note: [Col. 0223] Perhaps *haec*?] troubled him again and again with its questions, crying, “O holy lord Michael, tell me still more!”, we shall take care to write what remains in the form of the soul’s questions and the angel’s replies, with the notary sitting attentively beside him, as we have said above. We have not mixed or altered the Latin, either in wording or expression; everything that they spoke alternately was echoed to us, who were on earth, by the Holy Spirit through the tongue of the dead body. Whenever you find the mark impressed among the letters, transfer to yourself the feeling of the questioning soul, so that you may more easily understand the angelic reply:

**Soul:** O holy Michael, let me go to my brothers, and I will tell them everything.

**Angel:** I will not let you go. Come, follow me. Look.
