**Soul:** O lord, how beautiful are these dwelling places! Tell me who ought to live in them. O what a beautiful dwelling place! O holy Michael, tell me.

**Angel:** Soul, you cannot know. This one is good.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me what this other dwelling place is. Tell me who ought to live here.

**Angel:** Frederick [Note: [Col. 0224D] Provost of Saint Vedast and count of Verdun, about whom Hugh reports more; see above, cols. 201–202].

**Soul:** O lord, there is a small place of refreshment in this dwelling.

**Angel:** It is not yet right.

**Soul:** I see, lord: the dwelling is beautiful, if it had been complete. O lord abbot, the Lord shows many wonders through you. Great Frederick, strong and praiseworthy. O lord, do not permit me to remain here; let me go to my brothers, and I will tell them everything I have seen.

**Angel:** No. It is not in my power, but in the Savior’s.

**Soul:** O lord, how long is the road to where paradise is?

**Angel:** Let us go; follow me.

**Soul:** I follow you. O lord, tell me what this is.

**Angel:** There is one paradise.

**Soul:** O Adam, why did you believe your wife? O Eve, why did you deceive your husband? O wicked serpent Leviathan, why did you lead the woman astray? O holy Peter, holy Paul, holy John, great holy Vedast, have mercy! O pious Mary, holy and glorious Mary, have mercy! O lord, let me go.

**Angel:** Soul, [Col. 0225A] I will not let you go. Sit, sit, sit.

**Soul:** Why do you not let me go?

**Angel:** I will not let you go until we come to the Savior.

**Angel:** Come, let us go.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me what this other dwelling place is.

**Angel:** It is another paradise.

**Soul:** O lord, who is this man?

**Angel:** The two saints, Elijah and Enoch.

**Soul:** O lord, what are they doing here?

**Angel:** They await the judgment of God.

**Soul:** O lord, what will they do then?

**Angel:** They will remain there until Antichrist comes.

**Soul:** When Antichrist comes, O lord, what will they do then?

**Angel:** Then they will rise.

**Soul:** Where will they go?

**Angel:** To the earthly ages.

**Soul:** O lord, who is that Antichrist?

**Angel:** He is the great devil. He himself will say, “I am Christ.” Elijah will say no, and Enoch likewise.

**Soul:** O holy Michael, what will they do then? Tell me.

**Angel:** I tell you: they will be witnesses of the Savior, and they will give his testimony, and their testimony is true.

**Soul:** O all nations, do not believe him; believe me, because the Savior is in heaven. Whoever does not believe this will not have eternal life. O all nations, do not believe this deceiver; he will have no power. O Antichrist, why do you deceive the nations? Your words are not true. O holy Michael, what will they do then?

**Angel:** I tell you: they will prophesy their testimony, because the Savior will come. Whoever believes this will be saved. I tell you: many will believe through Elijah and Enoch.

**Soul:** O holy Michael, what will they do then?

**Angel:** I tell you: they will prophesy everything truly until death.

**Soul:** By what death will they die?

**Angel:** They will be killed for the love of God.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** O soul, stop.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, kind father, tell me.

**Angel:** Then the whole earth will burn.

**Soul:** What shall we do then, lord? Tell me.

**Angel:** Then the Savior will come.

**Soul:** Kind lord, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Then Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John will come. They will say: “Dry bones, arise; hear the word of the Lord.” Then we shall come before the Savior; then there will be a new world and a new earth.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, kind father, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** I tell you.

**Soul:** Tell me, in what form shall we come?

**Angel:** O soul, stop; you have heard enough of the prophets. The whole people will have the form of thirty-year-olds—children, young men, adolescents, and old men alike.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Then you will have new flesh. Then all of us, angels and archangels, will come before the Lord, and then the twelve apostles.

**Soul:** What will they do?

**Angel:** They will sit upon twelve seats and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, kind father, what shall we do then? Tell me.

**Angel:** Every person will have all his works in his hand.

**Soul:** O lord, when will the Savior come?

**Angel:** He has not yet come.

**Soul:** O lord, when he comes, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Then Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, will come and say: “O brothers, let all the nations sit down.” Then the great Jesus, Savior and Redeemer, will come.

**Soul:** O lord, how great an anguish shall we see then? [Col. 0226A] Lord, tell me, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** I tell you: then he will come prepared upon the cross.

**Soul:** O lord, tell me, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** I tell you: then the Savior will say: “O all nations, angels, archangels, apostles, O all nations, see my pains; touch and see. See my Passion, my hands. Just as I was on the cross for your sake, so I am before you. O all nations, I did not give gold and silver for your sake, nor any human being, but my body. O all nations, I loved you; I handed over my body for your sake. See my pains.”

**Soul:** O lord, what will they answer then?

**Angel:** All your works will answer for you.

**Soul:** O lord, what afterward?

**Angel:** Then the apostles will sit at the right hand, and all the angels.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Good.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Soul, why do you not stop?

**Soul:** O kind lord, holy Michael, tell me.

**Angel:** You know the truth; you can know the truth, because Peter was the first to speak.

**Soul:** Lord, what will Saint Peter do?

**Angel:** He will judge first, Paul second, John the Baptist third; then all the apostles; then the holy hermits will judge; then the perfect monks.

**Soul:** O lord, what will they judge then?

**Angel:** The good bishops will then give an account of their entire flock.

**Soul:** O lord, what then?

**Angel:** Then the good priests will come, and they will judge.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Then the good laymen will come, and they will judge all good things. Those who are farmers have labored at many good things, have labored at all good things, and have received all good things.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** Then the women will come.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** I tell you. He who said, “Go, woman; now sin no longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14), will judge them.

**Soul:** O lord, have mercy! What shall we do then?

**Angel:** I tell you. Then the King and Savior will say all good things to those who are at his right hand, and all evil things to those who are at his left. Then he will be a great and mighty king, and the whole people will be humbled. Then the Savior will say: “O all nations, I loved you; I wished you to come from your home, but you did not wish to.”

**Soul:** O lord, what will those who have done good answer then?

**Angel:** I tell you: then the righteous will answer: “Lord, when did we see you? We never saw you; we saw neither you nor your least ones.”

**Angel:** Then the Savior will say: “When you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matthew XXV, 40).

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** The righteous are good—truly good. Then the King will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34). Then great glory will be upon them.

**Soul:** Afterward, lord, what will those on the left do?

**Angel:** O soul, stop.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me.

**Angel:** I tell you: they will go into eternal punishment.

**Soul:** O holy Michael, tell me where they are going. Will there be any remission for them afterward?

**Angel:** O soul, I tell you: God’s indulgence will come to their aid, and God’s angels will make a rapture over them. All the saints will intercede with God for them.

**Soul:** O lord, will they all be freed?

**Angel:** We can come to their aid. It is little.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me, who will make the rapture?

**Angel:** I tell you [lacuna] and the twelve apostles will make the rapture, and all the angels.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, [lacuna]

**Soul:** O lord, those who are not freed—what will they do?

**Angel:** Certainly, evil.

**Soul:** O lord, [lacuna] then what will they do [Note: [Col. 0227] The voice disappeared.]?

**Angel:** O soul, why do you not stop? Do you wish to hear what they will do? God, God will render to them recompense according to their works. After he says to them [Note: [Col. 0227] The voice disappeared.], “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew XXV, 41), “Return your works to your angels, whom you served!” there will no longer be any mercy. There will be a mournful and dark dwelling.

Then the Savior will come.

**Soul:** O lord, what will the Lord God do?

**Angel:** O soul, why do you not stop?

**Soul:** [Note: [Col. 0227] The voice is missing.] O lord, tell me, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** I tell you. Then the Savior will say: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI, 28). “You who followed me will sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX, 28). “Now come to me; I give you eternal joys, in which you will remain.”

**Soul:** O lord, what will those who hear that voice do?

**Angel:** I tell you: they will rejoice without end.

**Soul:** O lord, holy Michael, what shall we do then?

**Angel:** [Col. 0227C] O soul, why do you not stop?

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, tell me still more.

**Angel:** Follow me.

**Soul:** O holy Michael, where should I follow you?

**Angel:** I tell you. I will still show you great good things, a great paradise. Look.

**Soul:** O holy Michael, O lord, how beautiful this dwelling is! What is this, lord?

**Angel:** I will not tell you now; look at another.

**Soul:** I see, lord, that this dwelling is beautiful, because the paradise is beautiful. Tell me, lord, what is this?

**Angel:** This is the refreshment of righteous souls. You cannot see the third one.

**Soul:** O holy lord Michael, have mercy.

**Angel:** I tell you: you will not see the third until the day of the Lord’s judgment comes.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do?

**Angel:** Now we shall go to hell.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do there?

**Angel:** I will show you the punishments.

**Soul:** O lord, do not permit me to enter.

**Angel:** I tell you: there is no human being on earth who ought not to see it. Follow me. Look.

**Soul:** O lord, what are these?

**Angel:** Dwelling places where devils live.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do?

**Angel:** Follow me. Now we shall come to a great and mighty body of water.

**Soul:** O lord, why do you not let me go?

**Angel:** Come, and I will show you. Look.

**Soul:** O lord, what are they doing here?

**Angel:** Here the sick will sit until the day of judgment [Col. 0228A].

**Soul:** O lord, what sort of sick?

**Angel:** Those who do not have sufficient excuse for their sins. They will sit upon this stream.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do?

**Angel:** Come, I will show you. Look.

**Soul:** O lord, what is this?

**Angel:** These are punishments. The impure will sit there, repenting there upon this stream until the day of God’s judgment.

**Soul:** O lord, these punishments are great. What shall we do?

**Angel:** Come, I will show you. Follow me. Look at the great fire.

**Soul:** O lord, who is that?

**Angel:** Look at Judas, who betrayed God.

**Soul:** O Judas, why did you sell the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ? Why did you betray your lord? Why did you do this?

**Angel:** He did many evil things; therefore he will receive all evil things. Do you see these people?

[Col. 0228B]

**Angel:** He was rich; now he is poor.

**Soul:** O lord, what will he do [Note: [Col. 0227] So in the manuscript.]? Will he receive remission for his sin?

**Angel:** Not until the judgment; then all his sins will be forgiven him.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do?

**Angel:** I tell you. Let us leave this danger. Follow me. Now I will show you great wonders that you have not yet seen. Look.

**Soul:** O lord, what is this?

**Angel:** The evil hell. Adulterers, perjurers, false bishops, false priests, and false monks sit there; they will remain there until God’s judgment.

**Soul:** O holy Michael, what shall we do?

**Angel:** Follow me. I will still show you all evils.

**Soul:** O lord, what are they?

**Angel:** I will show you still more. Do you see how many souls there are?

**Soul:** O lord, where did they come from?

**Angel:** This is the whole earth. It is not yet full; they are not yet all here. Do you see that great one who is bound with chains?

**Soul:** Lord, I see him.

**Angel:** He was the great bishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0227D] He seems to indicate Everger].

**Soul:** O lord, who was he?

**Angel:** He was a shepherd—not a shepherd, but a hireling. He was a wolf.

**Soul:** O lord, have mercy! Will he receive pardon?

**Angel:** No. He was a great shepherd, but he did not keep the Lord’s commandments.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do?

**Angel:** Let us go; now I will show you. Follow me. Now sit, soul, sit.

**Soul:** O lord, why do you not let me go?

**Angel:** I will still show you many wonders. Follow me. Look.

**Soul:** O lord, what is this?

**Angel:** These are those who have labored at all good things, and they sit here [Col. 0228D] until the judgment of God.

**Soul:** O lord, why do they not go into the kingdom of God?

**Angel:** Soul, I tell you: no one will enter until the judgment of God.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall we do?

**Angel:** Sit. Do you wish me to tell you more?

**Soul:** I do.

**Angel:** I tell you. There are many people in the world [Note: [Col. 0227] So in the manuscript.] who have not seen what you see.

**Soul:** O lord, what?

**Angel:** I tell you: there are many people who have not seen what you see.

**Soul:** O lord, let me go to my brothers, and I will tell them everything I saw.

**Angel:** Not unless the Lord Savior wills it. I tell you: just as a roaring lion, so the devil is among your brothers. The Lord’s mercy was upon them when, six nights ago, the devil wished to strangle a living boy from among your brothers.

**Soul:** Now I recognize that this is true, because I was present. Lord, has he been freed?

**Angel:** No, because he does not wish to make a true confession. Many say, “We serve the Lord,” but they serve the devil. They reveal all their stains—whatever they do—through a true confession. If they do not, I tell you, you will soon see great danger. Let the great murmurings in that place cease. I tell you: there is an old man who is not acceptable before God.

**Soul:** O lord, who is he?

**Angel:** Be silent, soul; you must not know everything.

**Soul:** O lord, if you let me go to them, I will tell them everything.

**Angel:** You must not know everything; there are many [Col. 0229B] who do not wish to believe you. The Lord is showing you this.

**Soul:** O lord, they loved me so much. O lord, what will my brothers do? There are four of them. O lord, what will the lord abbot [Note: [Col. 0229D] Richard] do?

**Angel:** Everything will be well. He is truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.

**Soul:** O lord, what will lord Frederick do? In God’s name, tell me.

**Angel:** O soul, stop. In God’s name I tell you: he will do all good works, but they are not yet complete.

**Soul:** O lord, tell me something good about the other brothers.

**Angel:** I can tell you something good: true confession will come to their aid.

**Soul:** O lord, what will he do . . . . . .

**Angel:** Why do you not stop? I will not tell you.

**Soul:** O lord, what will my own blood and flesh do? Tell me.

**Angel:** Everything will be well.

**Soul:** Lord, what about those two brothers who fled, Gotmund and Baldwin?

**Angel:** I tell you: dwelling places in hell have been prepared for them.

**Soul:** O lord, tell me.

**Angel:** I tell you: the lord abbot did wrong because he excommunicated them.

**Soul:** Lord, tell me about my brothers.

**Angel:** I tell you: the Lord chose twelve apostles, and one of them was the devil. Among your brothers there are the highest good and the highest evil.

**Soul:** O lord, what shall I do?

**Angel:** I will tell you.

**Soul:** [Uncertain: Why do you release the physician of indulgence], so that I may go to them and tell them everything?

**Angel:** It is not within my authority, but the Lord’s.

**Soul:** O lord, what will my brothers do? I loved them so much.

**Angel:** What can I tell you? They have a shepherd.

**Soul:** O lord, tell me.

**Angel:** [Col. 0229D] I would tell you the truth, but they do not wish to believe you.

**Soul:** O lord, they will believe well.

**Angel:** If one believes, another does not believe. Whoever is from God believes; whoever is not from God does not believe. They all know the punishments, but they do not understand; their heart is closed [Note: [Col. 0229] Here a space of two lines is left blank.].

“**Soul.** Who is the serpent?

**Angel.** They are laymen; but they hear that it is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in a human being.

**Soul.** Who is it that could come to the brothers’ aid?

**Angel.** Listen, soul. Albric is a great serpent; like a roaring lion he goes about seeking someone to devour. [Col. 0230A]

**Soul.** Lord, I did not see him; where is he?

**Angel.** He does everything he thinks of. He says that he is faithful, but he is unfaithful.

**Soul.** O Lord, who is the one from long ago?

**Angel.** I tell you: if he does not amend, I shall soon reveal him before the people by God’s sword, with great power.

**Soul.** Woe to him! O Lord, who is the man? Who are the monks who do not obey the lord abbot?

**Angel.** Do you wish to hear? The lord Robert obeys.

**Soul.** What is he doing now?

**Angel.** I tell you: he is now at the altar [Note: [Col. 0229] *aira* in the codex] before God. Tell me, what are you thinking? Why did you not disclose everything you thought through a true confession?

**Soul.** Lord, I did not think of anything evil.

**Angel.** Reveal your thoughts.

**Soul.** Lord, it is my fault; I thought of enough.

**Angel.** What did you think? [Col. 0230B] Give a true confession.

**Soul.** Lord, it is my fault; I thought of all sorts of evil things.

**Angel.** No—but it would be good if only you were now able to fulfill it.

**Soul.** Lord, I thought that the Lord would visit the place of Saint Bertin.

**Angel.** I tell you, there are many sins there; God’s mercy will visit that place.

**Soul.** Thanks be to God, thanks be to God.

**Angel.** I tell you, there are very many evil spirits in that place. [lacuna] to the Savior.

**Soul.** Where is the Savior? [lacuna]

**Angel.** He will come now. [lacuna] Lord and Savior and Redeemer of the world, come to my aid with mercy.

**Savior.** What are you seeking?

**Soul.** O Lord, mercy and pardon for all my sins. Ask about the master; look. [Col. 0230C]

**Savior.** I tell you: when Saint Bertin came there, there were many devils, yet there have never been so many as there are now.

**Soul.** O Lord, [lacuna] concerning that place and all the brothers who are in it.

**Savior.** I tell you, they are as though destined to follow the world.

**Soul.** O Lord, let me go to them; I shall tell them to leave [Note: [Col. 0229] Thus in the codex; perhaps *relinquant*, “that they should leave”?] the world. Let me go to the bishop; I shall tell him to look after that place. [Note: [Col. 0229] Thus in the codex; or should it read *respiciat*, “that he should look after”?]

**Savior.** Keep this word secret.

**Soul.** Let me go to the lord abbot; I shall tell him alone.

**Savior.** If you tell it to others, you shall die the death. Now go in peace; keep all these secrets.”

“Having thus ended, the soul returned to the body, and in an instant, as we watched, that brother rose up, though he spoke while concealing some of these things. (Fol. 82′.) This occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1011.

“(4 July 1012.) While, in the customary order of religious observance, we were carrying out the purpose of our holy profession in the aforementioned city of Arras, in the monastery of the most precious confessor of Christ, Vedast, in the month called July, on the fourth day—thus in the year following the preceding vision—it happened that one of our brothers, overcome by a grave bodily illness, fell sick for a considerable number of days. As the pain of his illness grew exceedingly severe, he was brought to the very day of his summons, the first day of the August Kalends (1 August), which is devoted to the veneration of the chains of blessed Peter. In the presence of the brothers, he was carried away in a trance of mind and, having wholly departed from the body as though dead, he saw many things while revisiting the regions of hell. In the presence of witnesses, he confirmed these things to us as true, recounting them with his tongue while his spirit alone was absent. Afterwards, when a full period of three hours had passed, he returned to himself and confirmed the things he had seen even more truthfully while conscious, so that this little page, which we wrote down without his knowledge as a witness, would later give an account of them.

“When the soul departed, princes sent from the office of darkness received it. Ready to escort it, they arrived with greater speed than words can tell at the infernal enclosures. They introduced it into a house, intending immediately to exact the punishment it deserved; and, as could be understood more clearly from the excessive density of darkness and foul-smelling smoke, this was an immense city of immeasurable size. Its walls and inner fortification, constructed as though of masonry, appeared on every side within to be painted with letters. From the beginning of the whole world it contained the sins of humanity, except those remitted by sincere confession and repentance; yet it preserved the memory of certain sins of the living that had been trampled down only so that they might be repeated.

“When the devil had brought the soul there, he seized it and began to shake it with a most horrible assault, to shear it, and to strike it with the heaviest blows of rods. Besides this, he threatened to apply the torment of fire and reproached it for its sins, producing certain little sheets and notebooks which it had negligently and without the prior’s permission handled for its own use. He also pointed out that many other things, by his authority, had been retained and inscribed on the aforementioned wall. Yet, throughout his life, that brother had never been able to recall them in confession. As various scourges of torment were inflicted for these things, he confessed only to the guilt of which he was conscious and, in misery, begged divine clemency to come to his aid. For he knew that he deserved this because of the sins demanded by his guilt, and that for this reason he had been deprived of the assistance of the angels and left alone.

“But the devil mocked him still further, saying that by the right of human warfare he ought to become his and serve him, and that he could in no way be freed from the torments inflicted unless he worshiped him, from whom he would never afterward be separated. In reply, that soul, recalling the sacraments of God’s immeasurable mercy, trusted with a certain hope and confidence of belief, spat in his face, and at the same time uttered insults appropriate to one so deserving, answering each of his words with a corresponding word. It said:

“‘You are the spirit of all pride and destruction, you who deceived Eve. You have done many evils, which through you have been inflicted upon the human race. I do not worship you, because you are a thief and a robber. Now you have such power over me, but you would not have it unless it had been given to you from above. God is strong and powerful and of immeasurable mercy, and I worship him who suffered for me. O Lord my God, why have you forsaken me? You formed me and created me. My sins are many; Lord, it is my fault.’

“To this the devil replied: [Col. 0232A] ‘It shall not be so; you did not confess those sins. I am God. For I know everything you have done, and there is no neglect of sin that has occurred among your brothers in which I have not taken part. Worship me; indeed, I have you in my power, and one of your brothers as well. Ha! Did you not see me there a little while ago, where, because you were in my power, you perceived my horrifying presence, and where I had to suffocate your brother by a sudden death so that I might destroy him for myself? You too have done the things you saw inscribed on this wall. But if you wish to be freed from these torments, worship me, whom you recognized as an angel of God.’

“Then that soul, already overcome unto death by the lashes and the fire applied to it, said: ‘O Lord God, mercy! I am burning, Lord; it is my fault. Holy Michael, help me! Why, Lord, have you forsaken me? My sins are many, I know, Lord; the lord abbot knows them. O God, how great are your judgments! O Satan, why do you not let me go? I do not worship you. I too know that you know everything, but the Lord’s power is in heaven and on earth, and let it judge between you and me. But if you are God, where are your angels? Show me your face.’

“‘Pah! You are lying! I saw another angel; you are lying! You are not an angel. I recognize you; you are the devil. I know that you were an angel, but you fell from heaven through your pride. Therefore, if I am in your chains, it is by the Lord’s power and will, not yours. And tell me, who is my brother—the one whom you possess?’

“And because the earthly soul, when released from this dwelling, possesses all knowledge and memory, it remembered—for it had been present—that nine days earlier, after the completion of Matins, that brother had lain down for a short while in bed with the others. Without our knowing from what illness, but with the danger of his death already upon him, he had been sent out of bed by the brothers and had scarcely recovered the breath of life after the space of one hour. Grieving all the more over his sudden death, the soul reproached the enemy’s deadly ambushes, saying:

“‘O Satan, you drag everything to yourself. Why did you deceive him? In this too you are lying, because he will not be your servant. He is very gentle and humble, and greatly obedient and compassionate toward everyone; therefore he will be converted and live. Since God’s mercy has no limit, and he desires not the death but the repentance of the sinner, he will not be yours; he will be converted and live. O brother, beware, beware of his ambushes, lest he deceive you. Savior of the world, help me. Holy Michael, [Col. 0232D] why have you forsaken me? Holy Father, mercy! Lord, I am burning, I am burning. O Satan, why do you punish and punish me all day long?’

“These and many other things of the same kind we disdain to burden readers with, since the wearisome abundance of such material is less suitable for those who grow tired of novelties. While the soul and the devil were engaged in such conversation and an unwearying contention on opposite sides, and while it had been consumed by the lashes and was almost confessing itself defeated and ready to worship him, an angel began to approach from far away for its aid, like the onset of a burning and shining fire. When the soul’s strength was restored through the grace of his most peaceful presence, it pressed its abuse more vigorously, resisting the enemy’s lying presumption and saying:

“‘O Satan, Satan, many evils await you on the day of the Lord, because you are the destruction of the human race and the cause of destruction. Now you shall not hold me; you shall no longer rejoice over me. Now I do not worship you. You lie when you claim to be God; you have no further power over me. O holy Michael, where are you? O Lord, mercy! It is my fault, Lord; I see my evil, because I did not obey your commands. O holy Michael, mercy! I shall amend, Lord, I shall amend. I promise God, and Saint Peter, and Saint Paul, and all the saints, that I shall do everything you ask. Help me, Lord; I am burning!’

“To him the angel said: ‘Be silent; this is God’s will. But follow me.’

“And she said: ‘I follow you, lord, and I am ready to go with you even unto death. But tell me, lord, what will become of that brother of mine about whom the devil told me that he had deceived him? O holy Michael, pardon and mercy, lord, for him! Let me go to my brothers; they will amend. Tell me, lord. Can I speak to him?’

“‘Everything is well.’

“Immediately, when the spirit had returned to the body, he sat up and, calling by name the brother who was present there, said: ‘Take care that the devil does not deceive you, because through him you were nearly [lacuna]’

“While the spirit remained with the angel and the body lay dead as before, he said: ‘O holy Michael, I went to him [lacuna] I saw all the brothers.’

“To him the angel said: ‘Follow me.’

“And she said: ‘I follow you, lord.’

“When these things had been said, [lacuna] of darkness [lacuna] proceeding from there under the angel’s guidance, he was again brought into another house. Because it shone with exceedingly great light and serenity, [lacuna] he was astonished at its beauty and could neither be satisfied with it nor filled to his desire; but, looking about in amazement and trembling, he understood what its purpose was and for what it was possible to possess that place of light.

“For on the surface of its walls he saw written the good works of the whole human race, and also whatever is useful to human needs among all created things: gifts of alms that can be spent on the poor of Christ for the salvation of souls; and, as though expressed in a kind of substantial material, horses and beasts of burden, donkeys and sheep, and various kinds of different animals; gold also, silver, clothing, and very many precious gifts of that sort; lodging for pilgrims, bedding for the poor, and other benefits freely bestowed for Christ’s name; bundles of straw and hay; old companions and green plants of vegetables, suspended above as though by a thread; and also a drink of cold water, concerning which the Lord himself testifies that the faithful do not lose their reward in eternal life.

“Moreover, since it would be lengthy to recount everything, he saw here these and many other gifts of holy alms bestowed upon Christ in his members. Their memory alone is preserved before God in return for eternal life, so that greater confidence might be given to God’s future and present people—namely, that God is forgetful of no benefit, however small, if anyone has offered something in the honor and glory of his praise, with holy charity as the source of every virtue. [Col. 0234A]

“Meanwhile, having seen this miracle worthy of holy remembrance, they withdrew to another place, urged on by the angel’s peaceful admonition. After they had advanced a little farther, the angel said:

“‘See, O soul, the things granted to you by God’s mercy, so that you may see the torments of hell, which, although they are incredible to the human race, nevertheless know that they have been foretold as such through the sacred teachings of the Gospel.’

“And she said: ‘I see, lord, that there are many sins and evils. But let me rest for a little while, because I have suffered much. For the devil scourged me severely.’

“And the angel said: ‘Soul, do you wish to sit? Sit.’

“Terrified by the magnitude—so great and unheard-of—of the torments then present, and by the excessive sufferings and lamentations of that wondrous and innumerable multitude, she was moved by a certain feeling of compassion. Within herself she recalled the day of that judgment and how many punishments the Judge, when he comes, will then heap upon those whom she still saw enduring such torments from almost the beginning of the world. And she cried out:

“‘What will you do, O wretched ones, wretched ones, when the irrecoverable hour and unrepentant day of God’s strict and final judgment comes upon you? That day is the day of wrath, the day of calamity and misery, a great day and exceedingly bitter!’

“Indeed, that place of punishments was so vast in immeasurable extent, and the confusion and unremembered multitude of the grieving peoples were so great, that no kingdom of any empire is or contains such a multitude; nor did he think that even the whole world, with humanity, could be compared with it. There, with many kinds of torments distinguished, the individual ministers standing beside them from the devil’s legion presided over their respective orders in such a way that some people were held in dreadful darkness with its stench; another group was shut up in pitch-black flames; others were tormented by pure fires; and still another group was increased among sinners tortured by cold and frost like that of winter.

“Thus, according to each person’s merits, punishment was prepared for each by its own attendants. Another part of that place threatened souls with useless cooling, as though in certain constructed dwellings. Besides these things there were unending worms, the fires of eternal death, and a great fire nearby, made not from material wood but from the frequent sins of those still living and their daily offenses.

“When he saw this and was not sufficiently confident of his own danger, he heard the angel say: ‘Come and see.’

“And he said: ‘I see, lord, that it is evil; I see everything, and all the evils here. But tell me, lord, what is this, or what does it signify?’

“When the angel had told him that this was being prepared for Count Baldwin of Flanders and was his lot, he suddenly marveled at the man’s imposing appearance, not unequal to royal splendor, and at his power, marked by wealth and human prosperity. If so great a man was to receive such a punishment after passing honors and miserable glory, and the misery of a deadly and deserved death, he cried out in these words:

“‘O lord, does he have evil deeds?’

“And the angel said: ‘Because he did evil, he will receive evil.’

“Again he said: ‘Lord, if you let me go, I shall announce to him that he should be converted and live. Holy Michael, have mercy on him; the Lord does not despise sinners. I know and believe that he himself said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should [m. o.] [Col. 0235A] and live.” Therefore, lord, let me go; I shall come to him and tell him to recognize himself and do penance.’

“To him the angel said: ‘It will do no good, because he does not believe.’

“But he said: ‘Yes, lord; he has much gold and silver, and also many resources on earth. He could easily make amends.’

“And the angel said: ‘I tell you, they are not his but the devil’s. But, soul, follow me; come and see.’

“There was spread out through an immense expanse, with spaces of wondrous size adjoining it, something like a pool of exceedingly cold water. Its waves were freezing, and through rising, foul-smelling frost it seemed to belch deadly vapors up to the heavens. In countless ranks it contained the punishment of this place for the female sex alone—namely, an assembly of prostitutes. Through the incontinence of their own flesh, committing adultery and exceeding the proper measure of human nature, they had not feared, through a merchant’s greed, to corrupt laws and rights. Their breasts, as well as their dreadful front and rear parts, had been taken for devouring by monsters of many kinds and by a very great multitude of serpents dwelling with them.

“When he had surveyed these things, he replied to the angel’s preceding words, saying:

“‘I follow you, lord, and I see that the torments are great. But tell me, what are those groups sitting upon them, and what was their sin?’

“‘These are the prostitutes whom you see. Their breasts are torn by twisting serpents [Note: [Col. 0235] Perhaps *tortiles*, “twisted”?], because they sinned through the flesh and committed great adulteries.’

“But he said: ‘Woe to you, women! Why did you come into this life by being born? Lord, will they sit here until the judgment?’

“The angel said: ‘I tell you: it will be more lenient for them on the day of judgment.’”

“To him he said again: ‘Come, follow me, and pay careful attention to the things that will be shown to you.’

“And he said: ‘Lord, wherever you wish, I follow you.’

“After they had gone forward a little, the angel said: ‘Sit here, because you will still see many other things.’

“Standing there, he saw the father of one of our brothers [Note: [Col. 0235] superscript *c*.], whom the first vision had revealed, still placed in the torment of fire. Concerning him he said to the angel:

“‘I told his friends and announced that he would be punished with the insoluble punishments of hell, but they did not believe my words.’

“There also, in accordance with his sentence, punishments having been added, a person who appeared worthy of whatever rank was being enveloped in torrents of flame. Delivered to certain powers of demons, he was continually compelled to undergo greater punishments. [Col. 0235D]

“When he discussed his case with the angel and investigated more carefully who and how great this person could be, he heard:

“‘The one about whom you ask is the rich Sciherus [Note: [Col. 0235D] Perhaps *Seiherus*; compare *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium* I, ch. 121, *MGH Scriptores* VII, p. 454], avaricious in all the things by which he shone forth, and truly wholly a son of the devil. After these many torments that you see, many others, still more severe, remain in store for him.’

“And he said: ‘Lord, will he receive remission?’

“The angel said: ‘I tell you, no one knows except the Lord God Christ.’

“His young brother also was still being held there, to be purified by the torment of fire. There was likewise such a multitude of people as one would think the whole world could not contain. Mourning the punitive end of all of them, and hoping that they might receive some measure of remission at the Judge’s coming, he said:

“‘Holy Michael, what will sinners do, or when will God’s judgment come?’

“The angel said: ‘Soul, be silent; come, follow me, and see what I shall show you.’

“Leaving behind the stations of hell and the places of punishments, they ascended in the opposite direction and downward, and reached the very summit of a lofty mountain, rising above all peace, light, and rest. There, amid most delightful spaces extending on every side, a dwelling destined to remain in eternal rest was built for each according to his merit.

“When he asked in the gentlest conversation what this was and for whom those dwellings of such magnificence were being built, the angel replied:

“‘Soul, were you not here earlier, and do you not recognize yourself? You have no understanding? These are the dwellings of your brothers, which long ago I named for you according to each one’s merit.’

“And he said: ‘Lord, do we all have dwellings?’

“The angel said: ‘You have them according to your works.’

“And he said: ‘Lord, make known to me still more concerning my brothers.’

“The angel said: ‘I tell you: you wish to know everything, but you cannot. Yet follow me. Come; I shall show you what eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart’ (1 Cor. 2:9).

“Accordingly, after they had crossed somewhat higher spaces, they stood among the summits of such light and radiance. There a dwelling, something like a tiny chamber, solid as though made of the purest gold, shone forth, bathed and encircled by flaming rays. At times it [lacuna] imitated a globe, a mirror of divine power to the world [lacuna].

“When he saw this spectacle of divine transformation [lacuna], he pressed the angel to learn through his answer what it was. The angel said to him:

“‘O soul, what you see is a certain most secret secret of the heavenly mysteries.’

“He broke the seal of God’s words and, approaching more closely, appeared to open a little door in it. With it there issued such a fragrance and the scent of lilies and roses [Note: [Col. 0236D] I.e. *fragrantia*], that it surpassed the most precious kinds and varieties of every spice.

“Burning with the desire for this immeasurable heavenly vision and peace, and longing far more intensely to enjoy the joy of immeasurable and everlasting delight, that soul said:

“‘Holy Lord Michael, how many blessings of every happiness there are here! How wondrous is this sweetness to those who have not experienced it!’

“The angel said: ‘Approach, soul; follow me, come, see, and read.’

“Attending to these things, he said: ‘Lord, I cannot read.’

“Again the angel said: ‘Look, soul, and read.’

“And he said: ‘I cannot, lord, unless you speak.’

“When a somewhat sharper light of the eyes had been brought to bear, because of the excessive brilliance with which the things there shone, he could scarcely read what was inscribed in this manner:

“‘The day of the Lord will come, it will come quickly, like a thief.’ [Col. 0237A]

“And he said: ‘What, lord, what will sinners do then? Or how many years remain before the new world must stand before the Judge who is to come over all things?’

“And the angel said: ‘Soul, read what follows and learn things wondrous to all who behold them.’

“When she saw letters expressing numbers, but was unable to derive a number from them, she nevertheless perceived that only a short time remained until that point and said:

“‘Yes, lord, there are few.’

“And the angel said: ‘There are no more. But today it has been revealed to you how near is the end of this world. Concerning that day, it is not granted to any creature, not even to the angels, to know; it belongs only to God the Father. But, soul, come, follow me.’

“From there they proceeded, and with the angel holding her and leading the way, they came to Saint Peter. The angel handed her over to his authority and withdrew. Saint Peter bound her in chains and, demanding the debt of a certain vow that she had once promised him for the return of her health on the anniversary of that feast but had not fulfilled, fastened her in a place suited to such torments, so that she might be punished.

“Many inhabitants of that place, where this brother had once been a canon, knew the following. Two years earlier, when he was anxious about his health and life and was greatly troubled about how he might leave the world and bind himself to live for God alone, moved by this desire he approached the man of God in that same place. He did not delay in making his vows, asking, with him as counselor, witness, and confidant before God, that he should not wear wool, eat meat, or refrain only partially but wholly abstain from the unlawful desires of the world, and that this should be confirmed by the testimony of blessed Peter. The present day was at hand for the fulfillment of that vow in the memory and veneration of the saint.

“This was indeed done at the time; but afterward, enticed by youth and recalled by its allurements, he wholly repudiated that agreement. Yet divine mercy had not abandoned him. When the feast of blessed Peter returned again, he was weakened by illness in the greatest despair of life. But once more, after making a vow to blessed Peter that he would visit his threshold, he was restored to health. Again he did not fulfill it, having been forestalled by God’s mercy, which led him to the perfection of monastic life. Not forgetful of his conscious guilt in this matter, he raised his voice in tears and, hoping that it might somehow be beneficial to him if he promised amendment, cried out:

“‘O holy Peter, it is my fault before you concerning my sins. I shall amend, lord. Holy Peter, mercy! Lord, I shall amend! I believe no human being concerning my promise and salvation, but the Lord alone. Lord, I shall amend. And, O holy Michael, why have you forsaken me? Good shepherd, holy Peter, I can no longer endure this evil. Holy Peter, I know that my thought was evil; nevertheless, I told and confessed everything to the lord abbot.’

“After he had said this, through the operation of divine power and grace the spirit returned again to the body. As we watched, the face of a living man settled upon him, and immediately he called the brothers whom he saw to be present and said in conversation:

“‘My dearest brothers and lords, have pity on me. Pray for me, because Saint Michael handed me over to blessed Peter, and after leaving me alone he bound me in torments and chains in a place such as you see.’ [Col. 0238A]

“Soon, while the brothers were offering the sacramental rites of the Mass, as the spirit was returning to the body he saw an angel coming from far away to his aid, and he cried out:

“‘O holy Michael, come, lord, come! Be my witness; I want your help with Saint Peter. And why, lord, have you forsaken me?’

“To him the angel said: ‘It was the Lord’s will. Come, let us go to Saint Peter.’

“But when he saw him, he repeated his many prayers, saying:

“‘O holy Peter, mercy! If you let me go, lord, I shall make a firm commitment to you, and I promise you, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, that, doing penance, I shall seek the house where your bodily presence is.’

“The angel said: ‘Will you grant that you will amend? For do you wish to make the promise?’

“And he said: ‘I do, lord, I do.’

“The angel said: ‘And what of what you promised Saint Peter?’

“To him he said: ‘Lord, it was not within my power, but it was the will of the lord abbot. And if I cannot amend, I shall come here again to pay the punishment I owe. And behold, I swear to you by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit that I shall fulfill all these things in this way.’

“When this had been completed, the angel led her out, saying:

“‘Soul, go in peace.’

“Having thus ended, he appeared with the same words; and just as we had written these things while he was unaware, so afterward we confirmed them in writing when he himself reported them. Amen.”

(Fol. 84.) In the same year, that is, from the Lord’s incarnation 1011, and in the seventh year of his rule, while Henry was in the ninth year of his reign, he was raised to the imperial dignity by Pope Benedict. [Rodulfus Glaber, Book III, Prologue.] When the instability of the Lombards had already established a certain Arduin as their king, they finally submitted to him, not without a great slaughter of their own people. Thus Henry came to Pavia and had a palace of marvelous workmanship built for himself by them.

“He also built the city of Bamberg and obtained permission from Pope Benedict for its church to be dedicated; by the pope’s authority he appointed a bishop there. For he was truly Catholic and an outstanding lover of religion. He adhered to the moral counsel of the elders, by whose purity and brilliance Lorraine flourished, Saxony was illuminated, and Swabia and Alemannia were directed. Therefore, under his rule there was salvation for the world and glory.

“Among these men he held in the greatest affection Odilo, the most devout father of the church of Cluny, and William, the vigorous ruler of the church of Dijon, outstanding in religion. Although they were not of his kingdom, they were joined to him in friendship, and through their prayers the affairs of the kingdom were conducted in peace. Nor was Pandulf of Agaunum absent from his intimacy, a man renowned for his life, character, religion, and holiness; the fame of his virtue made him commendable to the king and to the nobles.

“Moreover, of his kingdom, almost as many bishops and leading men of the churches as there were served as incentives to virtue for him, since he was strengthened by them, while they in turn were restrained from illicit things by his authority and urged toward more perfect things.

“Among these he held our father as his dearest, eminent among the foremost, praiseworthy for his compassion, and commendable for his religion. God had endowed him with such grace in every respect that many people, because of his innate kindness and the acceptance of his life and speech, and because of an elegance that was not affected but bestowed by grace, called him by the surname Richard, ‘Grace of God.’ Thus Saint Odilo, because of his inborn compassion, was called ‘the Pious,’ and William, because of the severity of his more fervent purpose, was called ‘Above the Rule.’

“His associate in handling and arranging royal affairs was also the lord Ermenfrid, a canon of the church of Verdun, whose life commends itself sufficiently by the light of his deeds.

“Those were happy times for the church of Verdun, distinguished under Bishop Heimo by such men that, even to the present day, it shines with the brilliance of their deeds—so great indeed that no antiquity can erase it. Under him, Amicus the provost built the church of the Holy Cross; Dudo the provost built the church of Saint Lawrence; and Ermenfrid the prefect built the church of Saint Mary Magdalene, gathering into it a company of canons, for whom he provided sufficient sustenance from royal generosity and the gifts of the nobles.

“And the venerable Richard, having raised from its foundations the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul and of blessed Vitonus the confessor, endowed it afterward with so great a wealth of possessions and religious resources, and endowed the other churches with such brilliance, that he rightly ought to be called the father of the city, the light of his homeland, and the glory of the church. His wonderful life made the lives of many wonderful; his exemplary conduct trained many others to become exemplary through good works.”

16. Nor did Lord Heimo himself leave his mind idle from good works. Rather, he restored and improved the church of Saint John, situated in sight of the city, in which the holy confessors Maurus, Salvinus, and Arator lie at rest; and in it he established a congregation of nuns living according to a rule under the direction of Father Richard. For them, on his advice, he provided a mother, Adelberga, a faithful handmaid of Christ, who was called Ava, whose memory is eternal.

For, like a most prudent bee, imitating her father’s example, she visited the monasteries of God’s servants out of devotion to good zeal and the magnanimity of faith, in order that she might emulate their better spiritual gifts. She went to Cluny, and when the man of God, the blessed Odilo, was informed of her arrival—for piety itself possessed his heart—she was received with great affection. Although it was the custom of the church and held as law that no woman’s foot should tread the monastery cloister, she, because of her religious devotion and because of Father Richard’s undivided fellowship with Saint Odilo, not only entered the cloister but also gained admission to the chapter assembly and was received into procession with the brothers on the Lord’s Day. This remains a memorial in that monastery to the present day.

This was done because of blessed Odilo’s especially ardent affection for his dearest son and most devoted fellow brother, his overflowing love, and the charity flowing from that fountain from which a channel of such perfection has been derived for us—namely, our own father, who was given to us by that same blessed man.

Nor was generosity lacking toward the place over which Lord Heimo presided. Rather, he bestowed upon it the bridge of Masmelli, established a market to be held in the suburb adjoining the same monastery, and had a wall constructed around the monastery at his own expense.

*(Fol. 84'.)* After completing thirty-six years in the episcopate, he died on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1024, and was buried in the church that he himself had built *(Gesta of Verdun)*.

Rambert succeeded him in the episcopate. He honored the aforementioned father with no lesser affection; indeed, he increased, advanced, and elevated with devoted and benevolent affection the devotion begun by his predecessors and transmitted down to himself. Yet it does not seem irrelevant, while we admire his associates and the glory of the kingdom that existed under him, to examine also what the emperor’s end in life was.

*[Rodulfus Glaber III, 1.]* In his time, the king of the Hungarians became a Christian together with his people. He also gave him his sister in marriage to Stephen, who was so named at baptism. Then, the following year, as his illness worsened—for he was without sons—and seeing that many dukes and counts were aspiring to the summit of the kingdom, he chose Conrad, once suspected by him but vigorous, who was called Cono. Thus, with glory, he died as monarch, Caesar Augustus, on the third day before the Ides of July—that is, in the very year in which it was noted above that Bishop Heimo had died.

King Stephen of the Hungarians, when the time of his calling approached, was summoned to the heavenly realm. He is now buried in the church where he rests, and shines forth illustriously through miracles.

Henry reigned twenty-four years and six months. Conrad, described as the son of Otto III [Note: “O. III. f.” was added in the margin.], succeeded him and took as his wife Gisela, sister of Rudolf, king of Burgundy, and daughter of Conrad and Matilda. By her he begot the third Henry, who counted the venerable Richard the abbot among the foremost men of his palace.

*[Ibid. III, 2.]* At that time Odo, son of the treacherous Theobald, and William, stepson of Duke Henry, rebelled against Robert, king of the Franks. Bruno, bishop of Langres, whose sister William had married, and Landric, count of Nevers, favored him. Rainald, the son of the aforementioned William, took as his wife Adelaide, sister of Richard, duke of the Normans.

That William, although an outsider, grew so strong in wealth and military power that no equal to him could be found in the country. Yet Hugh of Auxerre, who was called the abbot-count, strongly resisted him. Robert had married Hugh’s kinswoman Constance.

*[Ibid. IV, 1.]*

17. Thus, after Pope Benedict, in the year 1023, his brother John was ordained from the lay order as a neophyte through the expenditure of money. The archbishop of Constantinople then requested that his church, like the Roman Church, be called universal. He attempted to bend the Romans and those who presided over the papal court with countless gifts, to such an extent that they secretly tried to grant what he requested. Because of this, all Italy was stirred with the greatest violence.

But the bishops and abbots of Gaul tried to oppose the matter: some in person, others by letters sent while visiting the apostolic see. By bringing forward authorities against which it was not permissible to argue, they drove from the Roman Church so great a reproach and disgrace. Nor was the authentic presence of Father Richard lacking among them. Indeed, he strove with all his strength to silence the Constantinopolitan presumption once it had been refuted, showing himself to be a son of the Roman Church even as he safeguarded his mother’s honor.

Among the others, the outstanding abbot William also sent the pope a letter brief in bodily form but immense in substance and rich in language. We do not hesitate to insert it here:

“By the grace of God and through reverence for blessed Peter, I have obtained the most excellent see in the world, Pope John. I, William [Note: “W.” in the margin.], servant of the cross of Christ, wish you the seat of judgment with the apostles and the crown of the kingdom.

“We are instructed by the words of the Teacher of the nations that an elder is not to be rebuked. Yet elsewhere he says: ‘I have become foolish; you compelled me.’ Therefore, in the diligence of filial affection, we urge your common fatherhood to imitate in one respect the Lord and Savior, who sees through the thoughts of human beings: ask someone who is of one mind with you, as he himself asked Peter, ‘What do people say about me?’

“If his answer is given in faith, consider how it sounds. If it is clear, take care that it not become obscure. But if it is obscure, the light of the world must be entreated, so that you may shine in such a way as to provide light to all who are established in the bosom of the Church, enabling them to walk along the way of God’s commandments.

“But there is a report of something that recently occurred among you. Anyone who hears of it and is not scandalized should know that he is far removed from heavenly love. For although the power of the Roman Empire, which once held universal monarchy throughout the world, is now governed by countless scepters in various regions of the earth, the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth rests with the teaching authority of Peter.

“For this reason we have said these things: so that you may recognize that the Greeks have obtained what, as we have heard, they sought from you through nothing other than vainglory. For the rest, we desire that, as befits a universal bishop, you may be vigorous in correction and in the discipline of the holy and apostolic Church, and may live eternally and happily in Christ.”

*(Fol. 85.)* Thus the presumption of the Greeks was refuted. In that same year, which was 1024 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Leduinus—of whom we spoke above—was appointed abbot of Saint Vedast by the command and with the obedience of Father Richard.

In the year 1027, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, died, in the seventh indiction. The many proofs of how greatly he loved this father of ours make it evident.

*(Fol. 84'.)* At that time, the bones of an unknown man were collected by a certain merchant from a most contemptible place, placed in a coffin, and deposited by Marquis Mainfred in the monastery of Saint Mary at Seusia under the name of Justus the martyr *(fol. 85).* Although it was demonstrated to religious people through many sound and proven proofs that this was utterly vain and foolish, the unjust common people, venerating the remains as those of Justus, persisted in their error.

[Note: From this point onward, Hugo indicated in the margin by an added letter that the order had been changed, with this note: “According to the determination and order of the letters, you too must preserve the order of reading and of the chapters.”]

*(Fol. 85'.)*

18. By now the burden of his prelacy seemed heavy to the same Father Richard of God’s Grace; he was eager to advance toward what lay ahead and to cling more freely to divine contemplation, because the world had already withered in his heart. Since it was known that certain people who had gone to Jerusalem had died blessedly in Christ—including a certain man from the territory of Autun who, healthy and vigorous and showing no signs of death, had prayed at the place where the Lord’s feet had last stood and had asked to be received by the Lord in peace, but had soon been struck by a slight illness, carried home, and then, as soon as he had been brought back, had surrendered his spirit to God in the very place where he had prayed—a trustworthy report spread this account.

Richard himself, touched by a similar holy desire of good devotion and longing eagerly to visit the Lord’s tomb, sought permission from the prince, the bishops, the leading men of the kingdom, and the neighboring faithful. Only with difficulty did he obtain it. First he arranged for his sons and undertook to care for them in all respects, so that he might receive the holy obligations of pilgrimage with the goodwill of everyone.

He therefore went to Cluny and, as a memorial that remains in the same monastery to this day, brought with him to Verdun the most pious father, Saint Odilo. He kept him with him for many days, showed him the entire organization of the monastery, the customs and life of its inhabitants, entrusted each matter to his judgment and protection, and corrected and confirmed everything according to his decision.

Saint Odilo rejoiced in the Lord, because through those whom he had made his sons and left in that place he was enjoying the fruits of a good fragrance.

*(Fol. 86.)* When he believed that he had satisfied their wishes, he bade farewell to everyone, commended his son to God, and returned to Cluny. There he displayed to his sons and to the Cluniac brothers his joy at the progress of that church.

People of our own time still report what they heard from their fathers: whenever Odilo returned from these regions, he showed himself so grateful for the good things in which he rejoiced in our father and his sons, and praised them so highly, that anyone who saw him considered it a pleasure.

When the necessary expenses had therefore been prepared, companions for the journey appointed, and the care of his sons entrusted to God, after receiving the blessing of the bishop and neighboring prelates, as well as the requests and consent of the nobles and absolutely everyone, the venerable Father Richard of God’s Grace departed with Madelvaeus, a new pilgrim, in joy of heart.

The entire people accompanied him with tears and cries of grief, sorrowing that they were being deprived of the presence of one whom they regarded as the guardian of their salvation and the protector of their lives. The man of God consoled them kindly and urged them to return, commanding them to love God with all their strength, to honor their neighbor, to love their enemies, to cherish charity, to practice hospitality, to attend to almsgiving, and to pray more earnestly to God for him and for those accompanying him.

Thus, after greeting everyone and being greeted in return by all, he was sent forth with favor along the desired road, while everyone prayed and cried out in a loud voice that God might prosper his journey.

Richard, count of the Normans, provided all the expenses of the journey. He was generous in almsgiving, abundant in charity, and distinguished in honorable conduct. There still survive in the island of Brittany and in Normandy noble and proven men who saw this father of ours, Richard of God’s Grace, and who know with what affection the same count loved him. From them we too heard these things; they also used to report that the two were so closely united in undivided affection that one would have thought that a single soul inhabited two bodies.

19. Having therefore undertaken the desired pilgrimage, the man of God Richard took seven hundred pilgrims with him [Note: *Ademar, History* III, 65; *Life of Richard*, 17.], and provided them sufficiently with food from his own resources.

There were also many others in his company, among them two men from the city of Bayeux, father and son, Hubert and Gauzfred, who attached themselves to his company. Hubert was weighed down by a long illness, so that for an entire year he could neither rise from his bed nor turn onto his other side without the assistance of someone supporting him.

One day, while he was lying in the room, an angel appeared to him in the form of a dove and said: “Go, prepare what is necessary, and proceed to Jerusalem, because the Lord commands it.”

When he replied, “What shall I do? I cannot rise,” the angel repeated: “Prepare what is necessary and go, because the Lord wills it.”

The man obeyed. At daybreak he summoned his brothers and relatives and disclosed the Lord’s will, making clear that he too wished to obey it. They were astonished and, because of the infirmity they saw, tried to oppose his desire. While attempting to turn the man away from his right intention, they declared that what he had been told was impossible.

But when he saw his son Gauzfred standing nearby, he said: “Go, prepare the expenses and whatever is necessary for so great a journey, because I shall go, and you with me, with God’s mercy cooperating.”

The son obeyed and, as quickly as he could, prepared what was necessary for so great a journey. He then informed his father that the departure was ready. Rising with the help of his relatives and neighbors, Hubert crossed the bridge situated before the monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene in the same city of Bayeux, near his house, being supported on either side by four men. As soon as he had been placed on a horse, he was made healthy and whole and committed himself to the journey.

With divine grace accompanying him, he came to Verdun. When he heard and saw that the man of God’s departure was being hastened throughout the city, he waited and joined his company, entrusting himself and his son to Richard’s prayers. The man of God regarded them as especially close companions.

They proceeded through Illyricum and came to the wilderness. When they had almost crossed it, one day they saw from a distance a spring that was exceptionally clear and transparent. Father Richard and his companions went down to take a meal. While the crowds were reclining around the spring, the venerable father sat down at a suitable place for the time and, delighted by the spring’s limpid clarity, instructed a servant whom he had summoned to bring him some water from it.

The servant went, filled a vessel with the spring water, and offered it to the man of God. But when he brought the vessel to Richard’s mouth, the Lord changed the water into wine by a wondrous act of power. Thus the man who had desired water received wine.

Astonished, Richard asked the servant where he had obtained the wine. He emptied the vessel and sent him back for water from the spring.

*(Fol. 86'.)* The servant, amazed, drew water from the spring in the sight of everyone and offered it to the man of God. But once again, by divine favor, the spring water was changed into wine. Recognizing this, the man of God gave thanks to God and drank. He also offered some of the same wine in the same vessel to everyone.

Why say more? They all drank and blessed the Lord of power, who alone works wonders *(Psalm 71:18)*, whose kingdom is eternal *(Daniel 7:27)*, and whose power is eternal and shall not be taken away *(ibid., 14)*.

I say, they all drank from that wine, and the wine was not diminished. When everyone had drunk, that single cup remained abundantly available to all, and afterward it did not fail Father Richard.

The man who saw it bore witness—namely, the aforementioned Humbert and his son Gauzfred. We know that their testimony is true because they themselves drank from it while sitting at that hour near the man of God. Moreover, there were as many witnesses of this miracle as there were companions on the journey, for no one in that company was found to whom the man of God did not offer some of this miraculous wine.

This miracle is still regarded as almost new in the city of Bayeux. The fathers who saw it told it to their sons, and their sons to their sons’ sons, so that another generation might know it.

We also heard it from Gauzfred’s son, named Gozelin, a good and honorable man who is now a monk of the church of Dijon. He had already been born and grown up at that time; he heard the story from his father and grandfather and learned from them the form of prayer that Father Richard taught simpler and uneducated people from the world who sought refuge with him to recite when entering churches. It was as follows:

“Let us adore God, the Holy Trinity. Let us beseech his saints, who are called upon for God’s sake, to entreat God to grant us peace and health; true repentance to sinners; true concord to those in discord; peace to the living; and rest to the dead.”

This form of prayer was handed down to the laypeople in all his monasteries.

20. It was customary for the man of God to rise early, praise God, hasten the journey, and render to the Lord on the road the customary daily service. Thus, when the hour of breaking bread was approaching, wherever he might be, he celebrated the solemnity of Mass; when the mysteries had been completed, he sat down to break bread, lest the brothers be burdened by the labor of the journey and the continuation of the fast *(Life of Simeon, 10)*.

He therefore came to Antioch. When the necessity of the journey compelled him to remain there for several days, the man of God Symeon—who now adorns the church of Trier with his body and his virtues [Note: He died in 1035]—joined himself to him in friendship, and to the brothers who were with him, adopting Richard as his father [Note: These are the final words of Eberwin, abbot of Trier, who accompanied Richard on the journey to Jerusalem and composed the *Life of Simeon*. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, sixth century, vol. 1, p. 376. See above.].

In the action of blessed Symeon, we may observe this: the man of God would not have considered Richard his spiritual guide or entrusted himself to his protection unless divine mercy, which had made Symeon alien from the affairs of the world, had revealed to his heart that Richard was worthy to preside over and benefit those subject to him.

The blessed Symeon had been sent by the brothers of the monastery of Mount Zion to collect the alms owed to that monastery from the land of Richard, count of Normandy. Although he knew, by revelation of the spirit, that he would suffer many adversities, Father Richard, fortified on every side by the eyes of discernment, advised him to persist in what he had begun and fulfill his obedience until the outcome should test the matter.

He therefore sent him away weeping and sorrowful, after they had kissed each other’s feet, hands, and knees on both sides, because the grace of the Holy Spirit was in them. For this is the delight of the saints: to love one another, because God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God *(1 John 4:16)*. “Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor can rivers drown it” *(Song of Songs 8:7)*.

Thus the servant of the Lord, having been tested, took the road and praised Christ as the guide of his journey. He entered the land of the Saracens. When he approached their cities, he preached Jesus Christ to everyone, trusting in the Lord his God, because there was no deceit in his spirit.

When he had reached a city, he sang psalms to his Savior before the city wall and celebrated the solemnity of Mass there, while the pagans hurled stones from above in order to strike his head. He had approached the city so closely that the altar table touched the wall.

Although the men watching and mocking him threw many stones from above, Christ protected him so completely that neither the altar, nor the altar table, nor, finally, whatever is placed upon the altar, nor the man himself, who stood fearlessly beside the altar, was struck by the stones. Often the mound of stones falling from above around the altar became so great that, once Mass had been said, Richard could be extracted only by making a path through them.

None of the monks or clerics accompanying him could stand or dwell beside him. They sang from a distance, as far away as a stone’s throw, and responded to him as he sang; he alone remained intent upon what he had begun until, when the Mass was fully completed, he went out—or rather was pulled out.

*(Fol. 87.)* Once extricated, he pitched his tents before the city and, having procured the necessary expenses, lodged there, never ceasing from praising God, for his praise was always unceasing in his mouth.

The pagans, terrified by the miracle and attracted by the grace of his venerable appearance, came to him. Through an interpreter he gladly announced to them the things concerning Jesus and preached that they should restrain their hands from injuring God’s servants.

In a marvelous way, those whom he had found hostile upon his arrival began in turn to serve him with honor and, when morning came, escort him as he departed. For the Lord glorified his servant through signs and wonders, so that his holiness became known to everyone, and the power of Jesus was preached everywhere through him, because the fame of his holiness was carried everywhere.

21. When he came to Constantinople, we shall pass over how honorably he was received by the emperor and with what worthy gifts and services he was honored, since we are hastening toward other matters.

Sent forth with favor along the desired road, he reached through many dangers the places in Jerusalem that he longed for. Entering the city gate, he sang with his companions in the sweetest melody the responsory for Palm Sunday, “When the Lord entered the holy city,” worshiping Christ crucified, who is God blessed above all forever *(Romans 9:5)*, and reverently embracing with the eyes of faith the place of his tomb.

He therefore visited in faith all the places of the Lord’s birth, passion, and resurrection. While his eyes could never be satisfied with looking upon them, his mind was nourished, for he was filled with joy and ineffable gladness at the sight of those wonders of the Lord—so sweetly seen and long desired, already prepared for by his longing heart.

The patriarch of Jerusalem came to meet him as he approached, for he had heard his fame celebrated by everyone. They greeted one another, exchanged the kiss of peace, and rejoiced in the Lord.

When the patriarch saw in Richard an angelic appearance, modest speech, gentle gait, venerable gray hair, and the bearing of old age, revered by all, he rejoiced in spirit and said: “As we have heard, so have we seen” *(Psalm 47:9)*.

He was then brought into holy Zion and celebrated the solemnity of Mass, with the bishop and clergy standing by. Afterward, revisiting the place of the Lord’s tomb with heartfelt devotion and surveying every holy place with pious dedication, he believed that he had satisfied his desire, yet once again nourished his ardent soul with devout longing.

Never ceasing from celebrating Mass, never ceasing from distributing the word of God, but rather announcing everywhere the things of God, he did not desist—neither through fear of death nor through barbarian violence—from displaying the truth and what was right and forbidding evil.

O what devotion he had toward God! What exultation of a contrite and humbled spirit! What jubilation of heart! He saw himself bodily present where Christ was born, where he suffered, where he was buried, and where his feet last stood when he ascended into heaven.

Wherever he knelt in prayer, the earth was wet with tears; the cry of his heart rose to the Lord; his body was worn down and his spirit lifted up. He spent the nights in vigils and weakened his body through fasting. Never was he without tears, never without prayers. Although he rejoiced entirely in the Lord, he displayed the joy of his mind through the serenity of his face.

On the Lord’s Day commemorating the Lord’s arrival in Jerusalem and his reception by the children with hymns and branches of palms and foliage, he entered the city. Throughout the entire week he remained awake at night in the praises of God. Although the whole church was swarming with pagans girded with swords, he feared nothing and hesitated at nothing; ever watchful in prayers and constant in fasting, he rendered to God the things of God.

The gentiles themselves marveled at the persistence of his devotion and revered his steadfastness.

*(Fol. 86b.)* He spent the most sacred day of the Supper in carrying out the Lord’s commandment and refreshing the poor. He washed the feet of the poor, gave them clothing and everything necessary, and conformed and devoted his entire self to the Lord’s service.

Who could recount how he afflicted and tormented himself on Good Friday, crucifying himself with Christ upon the cross? He was entirely in tears, entirely in compunction of heart, contemplation, and self-denial, especially when he saw Jesus’ tomb before his eyes and found in it material for grief and compassion.

Constant in prayers and keeping vigil throughout the night, he compelled his limbs, wearied by fasting, to serve the spirit. On that day and throughout the following night he did not depart from the place of the tomb. Everyone marveled at his persistence, because while the others departed, he did not.

*(Fol. 87.)* What more need be said? Holy Saturday arrived, when the fire from the Lord was expected. The gentiles, armed and guarding the whole church while the Christians were shut inside and awaited the Lord’s gracious will concerning the reception of the fire, had surrounded the church so that, if the fire did not come, they might all be killed by the sword.

Then, behold, at about the ninth hour, while everyone was praying, fire was kindled by the Lord in a single lamp, without the assistance of any mortal. All the gentiles were seized by astonishment and fear, while the Christians were filled with joy and exultation, so that the whole church resounded competitively with the song: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” *(Psalm 146:5)*.

Immediately the blessed man, clothed in sacred vestments and having begun the Mass, proclaimed the solemn “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) in a loud voice raised on high.

*(Fol. 87'.)* He had already completed the lessons and chants, or whatever constitutes the customary office, up to the lighting of the lamps, while awaiting the new light. Then, intoning “Glory to God in the highest” with tears and rejoicing of heart, he brought joy to the Christians and fear and wonder to the pagans.

They stood all around the altar, growling and gnashing their teeth. Yet such was the man’s reverence and such Christ the Lord’s protection over him that everyone, even those who opposed him, marveled at and revered his holiness and religious devotion and considered him worthy of every honor.

Our father of God’s Grace spent that night without sleep, worshiping the Lord as he rose again and desiring, with Mary Magdalene in the garden of his mind—where the plantations of virtues flourished through him—to see Jesus the gardener, so that he might call him by his own name and learn to recognize him as Teacher and Lord. Thus, made a witness of his true resurrection, he might announce to the brothers in the voice of faith: “The Lord has risen.”

When morning came, after completing the customary chants, he celebrated Mass solemnly around the third hour. After the faithful people had received Communion, he returned home with joy, fulfilled the festivity of the day, and spent the entire day speaking more familiarly with the patriarch in jubilation of heart and a voice of exultation.

He always desired to revisit the Lord’s tomb, recalling and admiring that the napkin from the Lord’s head had not been placed with the linen cloths but had been wrapped separately in one place.

22. After the remaining festal days had been celebrated with joy and spiritual rejoicing, the most gentle man determined to consider his return. He did not return without a gift, for the chest of his heart was filled with good devotion.

What was that gift? During the very week before Easter, the pagans moved about on the more fortified parts of the Temple and threw stones at the people celebrating the sacred rites. By chance, a stone came into the tomb and fell there.
