The man of God took it for himself as a great gift and, throughout all those days on which the passion and resurrection of Jesus are celebrated, dedicated it to the Lord through vigils and prayers while it lay inside the tomb.

When he was about to depart, he lifted it with great devotion, kissed the holy place, and placed the stone among the sacred objects, as though he were carrying the entire place away with him. He bade farewell to the patriarch, wished him prosperity, and resolved to depart.

The patriarch groaned aloud as he bade farewell to his beloved. He brought forth the most precious relics of the wood of the Lord, as well as a very large purse woven with gold and filled with relics of the saints, and offered them to the venerable old man with thanksgiving, saying:

“Receive, beloved of the Lord, a gift of goodwill and devotion, a pledge of mutual love; a gift that is never consumed, that always remains and clings, that lives on with a friend; a gift that awakens fading memory, a joyful gift that comes before the mind and never slips from memory.

“May the Lord grant, through the intercession of these and all the saints, that we may see one another again in heaven, where the end of labors and the reward of eternal prizes are found, where we shall never be separated from one another, rejoicing and tasting how sweet and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” *(Psalm 132:1)*.

They therefore parted from one another in tears, though they would have wished to live together and, if it had been permitted, to die together.

Father Richard of God’s Grace proceeded along the public road, burdened with a noble and sweet-flowing burden, entrusting himself and his companions to the God of all with a humble and contrite heart.

The relics of the saints hung from his neck, so that he might have before his eyes a ready image of holiness and that the memory of those whose delightful burden of relics he carried might never be absent from his heart.

What he suffered on the return journey is known by him who endured it; all these things are judged by the one who promised to be the rewarder of labors.

You would have seen the man, venerable throughout the ages, as he traveled, often turning his neck back toward holy Jerusalem, humbling himself, sighing, groaning, revealing the affection of his heart through his eyes, rejoicing that he had seen the holy place of the tomb and grieving that he would not always see it.

Moved by this affection, he addressed the people, showed them the benefits of Jesus with his eyes, and suddenly caused them all, out of devotion, to groan, bless God, remember divine sweetness, and become wholly inflamed to pursue good works.

The Lord’s Passion did not fall from his memory, for it was almost his entire memory. What, indeed, was the whole course of his life except a desire to suffer for Christ, to die with him and be buried with him, so that through Christ he might be granted to rise again with him in glory? Therefore he suffered so greatly, for he had become an exile for the Lord so that he might suffer.

*(Fol. 88.)* And rightly so. To the wise person, the whole world is exile; to the just man, the whole world is a home [Note: the manuscript reads “gift” (*munus*)]. He was wise, because Wisdom herself dwelt in him; he was a just man, because Wisdom does not know how to dwell in a body subject to sins.

23. At last he returned to his own “wrestlers”—that is, the Saracens—and by the road on which he had come he also made his return. Before the walls of the cities he celebrated the solemnities of Mass, fearing neither the customary showers nor the floods of stones.

It was a wholly marvelous and astonishing power, a great mystery, a spectacle worthy of proclamation. The enemies stood above the head of the man of God and directed stones at him, stones so enormous that, had they struck him, they would have crushed not merely his head but his entire body [Note: The word *prorsus* is written in this form throughout]. He remained fearless because he was protected by the stone cut from the mountain without hands.

The stones were directed elsewhere, for they feared striking the living stone who remained in the stone that was rejected and made the cornerstone. If they struck against him, they would be shattered.

The gentiles were dumbfounded by the miracle, yet they were not frightened by its novelty. Rather, their condition became worse through their wonder, because the very wonder they felt was a renewal of sin.

The monks and clerics stood at a distance, as far away as a stone’s throw, as did the pilgrims. He alone entered the place of propitiation. He had received the shoulder and the right portion set apart in sacrifice, because his work was not only useful but also singular. Among the wicked, he not only did what was right but surpassed his obedient subjects who acted well both in the honor of their order and in the virtue of their conduct.

He had received the breast with the shoulder as food, because he not only thought rightly in his heart but also invited his spectators to higher things through the shoulder of his work.

But why delay over his return? Let us restore the father to his sons, so that they may rejoice together and, for the weariness of the absence that they endured, become one another’s consolation.

Let us not, however, pass over Antioch, made illustrious by the presence of Saint Symeon. There the father found his most loving son; there the son received his dearest father; there companions recognized a companion, brothers a brother, and fellow travelers a fellow traveler.

For, despite the many dangers that stood in his way, Symeon could not complete what he had resolved to do, especially since he knew by divine revelation that he would suffer many adversities on that journey. Delighted, therefore, by each other’s presence, the two chose to return together to Verdun, so that they might spend the time remaining to them together in the practice of spiritual philosophy *(Life of Symeon, 10)*.

When they came to the city of Belgrade [Note: Belgrade], which lies on the border of the Bulgarians and Hungarians, the most wretched ruler of the city prevented Symeon from crossing with them. Thus he was separated from the grieving and sorrowful father and brothers, himself grieving and sorrowful.

Lord Symeon went through many dangers to Rouen in order to fulfill his obedience. Father Richard of God’s Grace, after the long and varied labor of the journey, returned to the regions of Belgic Gaul.

## 24

At once, from afar, he was met by a throng of sons rejoicing and exulting at his long-desired arrival. When the report spread more widely that he was approaching, nobles and commoners, rich, middling, and poor alike, flocked to him; wherever he went, there was no lack of joyful people meeting and hastening toward him. With such a multitude, amid such rejoicing by bishops and palace nobles, as well as by clergy and people, he was escorted over a long interval of time all the way to Verdun. When it was announced there that he was present, they rushed out through all the gates to meet him, and the entire city advanced to greet him. Old men with the young, mothers with infants, even the weakest age hastened to meet so great a man; no one remained at home.

The sacred order dedicated to the Lord—the clergy, monks, and nuns—came out to meet the father with crosses and candles and with the various trappings of ecclesiastical rank, awaiting his arrival and scarcely enduring the delay, because nothing could be hurried enough for their eager hearts. When he arrived, and it was permitted to see him approaching, the people raised an outcry, and tears filled with joy flowed. No one was satisfied to have seen him once unless permitted to see him again and again.

He then descended and, received and escorted amid joyful singing, was brought to the monastery, while all clapped their hands and said: “Blessed is the Lord, who alone works wonders.” The brothers’ devotion made that day solemn and full of rejoicing, for it is a just cause for happiness to see a friend joyful; and if a friend, then what of a father? (fol. 88r)

Good people must act so that their good will does not remain hidden but is disclosed and shines forth. Let words cease: if someone is affected as he ought to be, his conscience will reveal itself in his face. Nothing, however, is sweeter than public friendship, and no punishment is heavier than public hatred. For the person who is marked out by everyone’s eyes—and who thinks himself marked out—has lost the understanding of what is best and sweetest, if he lacks the power of sight or has lost the sense of benefits, his ears being blocked by disease. Yet the multitude of sinners removes shame, and a common reproach ceases to be regarded as disgrace. Conversely, the one loved by everyone enjoys an equal and perpetual pleasure.

The arrival of our father, therefore, was a common benefit, because it was a common joy; for even when he was absent, everyone loved him. He occupied the foremost place in the minds of all and was always present to their memory, never so set aside or cast away as to pass into oblivion. Whatever frequent thought exercises and renews is never withdrawn from memory, which loses nothing except what it has not often looked upon.

Father Richard therefore deposited in the sanctuary the relics from Jerusalem and those gathered from elsewhere, with which he had arrived laden. After the reading had been completed, and after receiving and kissing the brothers, he repaid their benefits, rejoicing with those who rejoiced and giving thanks that, strengthened by their prayers, he had passed safely through the labors of the journey and willingly endured them—a thing which it is most pleasant for anyone to recount once he has escaped danger.

After affection had been satisfied and each side had recounted its good fortune—for another day is reserved for reporting whatever adversities there may be in such matters—they came to refresh the wearied body. This was provided abundantly, yet in a manner sufficient for propriety.

Thereafter the venerable father girded himself to repay their benefits. He made the first installment of his repayment by judging, with an outpouring of affection, that they had come gladly to meet him, and by testifying to this everywhere. He began, as though nothing had yet been done, to add benefits to benefits, to examine the needs of each person, and to relieve them by his assistance, so that all might recognize that a father had come to them and that nothing was lacking from the fullness of their joy.

O man worthy of every proclamation of praise! He even went around the beds of the boys himself, to see whether anything needed to be added, renewed, or improved, so that through this too his paternal spirit might be recognized and due affection might be shown to everyone. He strove to cut away everyone’s vices and correct their conduct, so that he might plant the seedlings of virtues.

## 25

Nor should we remain silent about what happened concerning Stephen, whom we have said was placed over the monastery of Saint Lawrence. Since he had been our common shepherd on the Jerusalem expedition and had stayed away for almost an entire year, and since the report had circulated that he was dead, Duramnus, bishop of Liège, who had succeeded Wolbodus, summoned Stephen to himself and officially urged him to preside in the abbot’s place; by his urging, he requested this of him.

When the man of simple character pleaded the obedience owed to his spiritual father—without whose permission and will no one was permitted to presume to do anything—the bishop replied that, at Richard’s departure, he had learned Richard’s intention: namely, that he had chosen Stephen to preside in his place. Since he had now heard through widespread report that Richard was dead, he had resolved, as was fitting, to fulfill that intention.

Why delay over the details? The man was persuaded, and, being insufficiently cautious, accepted the headship of the place and was consecrated to the office of abbot. Not long afterward the man of God returned and, hearing what had happened, grieved over his brother’s error. When Stephen heard that the father was present, he did not dare to go out to meet him, but decided to forestall his presence by confessing. Taking companions, he came to the feast of Saint Vitonius.

When he arrived, he entered the cloister alone, without his companions, said his prayers, sat in the cloister, and, as though he had never been ordained, renounced the headship. Presented before the father, he gave satisfaction and revealed how he had been induced to consent; nevertheless, he always confessed that he had erred and sinned.

His companions were present, among them an archdeacon sent by the bishop, asking the most merciful father to grant pardon for the error and, for love of him, to allow what had been done to remain approved and established. (Fol. 89)

But the most gentle man, speaking briefly after taking counsel, said: “It is honorable to yield to the request of the lord bishop, and it is good to correct a brother who has sinned publicly by a public satisfaction.”

Having said this, he ordered the brother to sit last among the community of brothers until he could discuss in chapter what the bishop had commanded and determine, by general counsel, what ought to be done. The brother withdrew from the father’s presence and obeyed the command with such strength of patience that anyone who saw him would have marvelled at it.

It was the eve of the feast of Saint Vitonius, to which noble and distinguished men and the common people had hastened from every direction in eager rivalry. In the presence of bishops, abbots, monks, clergy, nobles, and commoners, Stephen sat last of all, with good patience; “his countenance was not changed into different expressions” (1 Samuel 1:18).

For this reason his humility made everyone present unanimous in entreating Father Richard for his restoration. On the following day, after publicly confessing his fault before everyone, he obtained remission of his error and carried away grace. He was promoted from the last place to a higher status and, with the grace of his father, was placed over the guardianship of the Lord’s flock; he was now honored at Masses, as an abbot ought to be. He had not regarded the correction inflicted upon him as an injury.

The archdeacon of Liège, however, because his lord’s will had not been carried out in every respect as he wished, returned to him without Abbot Stephen and became a false witness. He was shown to have reported what had happened not as it had happened, nor with the intention with which it had happened. Unable by any force of mind to restrain or curb the desires that burst forth from his spirit, he took the abbey of Lobbes away from the blessed father because matters had been carried out otherwise than he had commanded, and, against right and justice, installed as abbot whomever he wished.

Lord Stephen, however, after spending several days at Verdun, was improved by the correction. For as long as he lived, he loved the father and the brothers with intimate affection; he taught his sons to serve God in fear, and he was an example of religion and discipline to everyone.

## 26

(Fol. 89r)

Turning back, therefore, to the blessed Symeon, let us briefly explain what he did with Richard, prince of Normandy, as it is contained in the Rouen archive, although his little Life is silent about it.

When he came to Richard with his companions, he was commended to a certain most noble man named Gozelin. Gozelin gladly received them as guests and kindly refreshed them after their labor. The most merciful prince Richard, overflowing with charity and rich in compassion, moved by the servant of God’s labor on so long a journey and sympathizing with the need of the servants of God from Mount Sinai, bestowed upon them very great riches. The venerable Symeon sent these through the brothers who had come with him to the brothers.

He himself, together with the aforesaid Gozelin and with only one servant, named Stephen, an equally holy man, remained for two years. At his urging, that same nobleman built the monastery of the Holy Trinity on a nearby mountain of the city of Rouen.

In that place the most gentle man, Lord Symeon, deposited the relics of Saint Catherine that he carried with him, rejoicing that this had been preordained by divine providence: namely, that the western people would rejoice in so great a source of assistance, since they would often deserve to be relieved by its remedy.

This is Saint Catherine, who was crowned with martyrdom by the emperor Maxentius at Alexandria, carried by angels to Mount Sinai, and placed in a dwelling prepared by angelic hands. The dwelling rises high in the manner of a little tower and, with a ladder placed before it, provides access through only one opening. The oil that flows from her body heals all the sick.

At the foot of the same mountain there is an oratory of the holy virgin herself. A great crowd of monks who sing praises to God day and night offers devoted service to the blessed martyr there. It is their custom to ascend the mountain’s summit on Sunday and, after celebrating Mass there, always to leave two or three brothers behind to keep watch over the sacred body. Other brothers succeed them in turn each week. They receive with the greatest reverence the sacred oil, which never ceases to flow from it, placing a glass vessel beneath it so that it may be reserved for the use of the weak.

Not only Christians but also pagans—marvelous to relate—being anointed with it, carry away for themselves the aid of healing. While the blessed Symeon was performing the duty of his week among them, he was deemed worthy to collect, together with that healing oil, three very small bones that dripped from the sarcophagus.

He carefully collected them and preserved them with the oil in a glass bowl, where they would benefit many. Later, as we have said, he presented them to the aforementioned church of the Holy Trinity at Rouen, more precious than gold and silver.

That glass vessel with the relics is still kept in the same monastery: that is, with three small joints of the limbs. Because of the overflowing of the holy oil, the vessel is emptied each week, and the oil is given to those who ask for it as a relic of the holy body. (Cf. above.)

The blessed Symeon, after remaining for two years with the aforementioned Gozelin, finally decided to visit his dearest father Richard the abbot and his companions. Thus, bidding farewell to everyone, he came to Verdun and remained with the same father for many days. He endured everything, though frequently insulted, like a most gentle lamb, and offered himself to everyone as a mirror of complete holiness.

## 27

(Fol. 85)

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1028, the temple of the Lord’s Sepulchre was utterly destroyed at the command of the prince of Babylon, through the wickedness of the Jews. [Glaber III, 7; IV, 4.]

In the same year a famine followed throughout the entire world, and it began to grow so severe that no one had previously seen anything like it. The elements began to fight among themselves, so that for three years, because of excessive rain, no useful furrows for sowing could be found.

At that time, in many places, the price of a modius was sixty solidi, and elsewhere a sextarius cost fifteen solidi. Human flesh was also devoured by human beings, so that it was brought into the market at Tournus as if it were to be sold. The man who brought it was discovered and burned in the fire. The flesh was buried in the ground, but another person dug it up at night and ate it. When he was discovered, he too was burned.

At that time, near the church of Saint John, in a chestnut grove near the city of Mâcon, a certain man had made himself a hut. One night he had received a wandering stranger as a guest. The stranger discovered him eating such food and, fearing for himself, supposed that flight would be his means of escape. When the matter was disclosed in the city, investigators were sent and found him with forty-eight heads of murdered people, whose flesh he had devoured. When he was discovered, he too was handed over to the fire.

The distress of the famine was so great that in those regions people attempted to dig up a white earth resembling clay, mix it with flour or bran, and eat bread made from it. [Note: Col. 0253D; “cantabrum,” that is, bran.]

It was wretched and lamentable to see faces withering from hunger; some falling to the ground, with no nourishment from food to support them; to see others dying; others dying together while performing the funeral rites for them and collapsing upon their bodies; and many lying unburied because there was no one to bury them.

Another plague followed. Because of the great number of corpses left without burial, wolves, attracted by the dead bodies, began to prey upon human beings. Then the God-fearing made charnel houses, in which a father dragged away his son, a brother his brother, and a mother her son when she saw them failing. Sometimes, when someone despaired of life, he was added to the dead, so that it was considered a most welcome funeral service if anyone still breathing were thrown there by anyone at all.

For this reason, church ornaments were sold to meet the expenses of the needy, and the treasures were distributed. For, as the moral teacher Ambrose says, “the Church possesses gold not to preserve it but to distribute it.” Who, however, would have stored it away at that time, when, if the famine had lasted even five years, there would have been no one to enjoy what had been stored?

Nor could everyone be helped, because the ability to act did not support the will. In this crisis, therefore, the bishops of the Gallic cities took counsel about how so great a mass of evil might be relieved. At last they devised the following measure (1028): since, with food already wholly failing, they could not help everyone, and did not want the earth, deprived of its inhabitants, to be reduced to a wilderness, they would support certain people who were known to be stronger by providing, as far as possible, a daily allotment of whatever food could be found.

This was not so that the assistance they were able to give would be withdrawn from others, but so that those who were sustained might be preserved as cultivators of the land, and so that the bowels of mercy would not be denied to others.

May God grant them to find mercy, since in such great distress they showed mercy to those suffering necessity; and may he pardon those who, although they could have acted, provided for the will of the needy not as they ought and could have done.

Amid these hardships, the venerable Abbot Richard, moved to compunction, gave everything he possessed to the poor. He did not spare the treasures of the church; indeed, he sold the more precious objects among them—ornaments and coverings—to the church of Reims and distributed their price to the poor. He also retained for himself a fixed number of people who were provided with daily food so that they might live.

In addition, he sent letters and messengers, and personally admonished kings and princes, as well as bishops with whom he was connected by friendship, to place in the heavenly palaces, through the hands of the poor, the treasures that moth and rust destroy, and to make the bellies of the needy treasuries of eternity for themselves.

He also received a considerable sum of money from the count of Rodez, granting him as a pledge the abbey of Saint Amantius, which belonged by right to the church of Saint Peter. He distributed the whole amount to the poor.

The count, however, after providing the money, seized the abbey for himself together with its revenues and estates. According to the inhabitants of Rodez, before the money had been recovered from the lands of that same abbey, he was overtaken by death, and thus the abbey was retained by his successors. Nevertheless, the inhabitants do not say that the entire abbey of Saint Amantius—which is very extensive and possesses enormous holdings—belongs to the church of Verdun, but only a certain part, namely the abbey of Saint Marius of Utiabra, as people of the present day still testify.

Nor should the memorable deed of William Supra Regula be passed over in silence. When he had returned from the monastery of Fruttuaria, which belonged by right to the church of Dijon, he was received at Dijon in the chapter house, as was fitting, and inquired how the brothers were faring and whether they lacked necessities.

When he heard that everything was abundant and that no place of need remained that could not be closed by a small barrier, he asked about almsgiving. He learned that, although the customary alms were given, the poor were nevertheless not assisted according to the brothers’ means and possessions.

Inflamed by zeal for the one “who devours the flesh of the saints,” he rebuked their hardness. Then he rose swiftly from his seat with a good deal of indignation and anger. (Fol. 85r) Having begun the antiphon by command, “Where is charity?” he did not proceed further but continually repeated its opening. He came to the storeroom and, seizing whatever implement came to the hands of another Phinehas, broke open the vessels in which grain, barley, and wine were stored, while “Where is charity?” was always in his mouth and heart.

After summoning the poor, he filled their containers, continually uttering from heart and mouth, “Where is charity?” and bearing witness by the performance of the deed. His indignation could scarcely be moderated by assisting him to distribute what had been gathered, while “Where is charity?” was constantly repeated and the brothers themselves were reproached as having grown fat, sleek, and swollen.

[Glaber of Reims, Life of William 29.]

Nor did he stop until all that store had been given to the poor. Then, returning to Italy, he waited two years for his departure from the world. At last he was compelled to return. Passing before Dijon, he went around the places entrusted to him; afterward he went to Fécamp [Note: Col. 0255D: Fécamp], where, as the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1031 and the fourteenth indiction approached, he died on the Kalends of January. At his tomb a ten-year-old boy was healed of a very serious illness.

In this year Chono, also called Conrad, came to Francia.

[Glaber of Reims IV, 5]

In the year 1000 from the Lord’s Passion, but 1033 from the incarnation, peaceful serenity began to show the earth the sweetness of its Creator and to announce an abundance of crops. Councils were then held throughout Aquitaine, the provinces of Arles and Lyon, and all Burgundy, and peace was established.

It was also decreed that abstinence should be kept from wine on Friday and from meat on Saturday, unless serious illness intervened; in that case three poor people were to be fed. In that year there was such an abundance of grain, wine, and other crops as no one could have hoped for in the following five years.

But the human race [Note: Col. 0255D: “styrps,” c.], forgetful of God’s benefits, returned like a dog to its vomit, rebelled, and turned toward wickedness. [Cf. Glaber of Reims, Life of William of Dijon 13.]

At that time the younger Richard [Note: Col. 0260D: cf. Glaber of Reims, Life of William of Dijon 13] ruled the county of Normandy, the son of the first Richard. In the monastery at Fécamp, where his father had established clerics, he expelled the clerics and introduced monks under the rule of Abbot William. For their daily use, in ornaments, estates, lands, and revenues, he bestowed such abundance upon them that he seemed to have satisfied their greed.

He was generous in almsgiving, overflowing in charity, a lover of churches, a restorer of the poor, and an outstanding venerator of the servants of God. In his hand almsgiving remained active until someone was found to whom it was owed.

In his time Normandy flourished with religious men, who flocked to him from every direction like bees to their hives. Among them he honored this blessed man with especially profound reverence, loving him with a particular affection and rejoicing to obey his commands and comply with his counsels.

## 28

(Fol. 89r)

Richard, duke of the Normans, also died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1026. Richard III succeeded him and died in the same year. After him Robert obtained the county of Normandy. He counted this thrice-blessed Richard, about whom we are speaking, among his foremost men, and the affairs of the Norman realm were conducted according to his counsel.

At that time there was a certain Breton named Ermenold, a man of perverse mind and detestable reputation, who had devoted his entire life to the devil, as was later established by thoroughly proven evidence. At every hour and moment he spoke with the devil, and whatever he had to do was arranged through that shadowy conversation.

Nourished by the counsels of iniquity until he reached complete wickedness, and having truly become a member of the one who is the source of malice, discord, and every evil, he accused all the nobles of the entire realm before the aforementioned prince, as though they had been plotting his overthrow and death. He so disturbed the condition of the entire land that it was clearly recognized as the devil’s work, his craft, and his invention.

(Fol. 90) The prince was inflamed against the nobles; divisions arose, quarrels were stirred up, and all Normandy raged in one civil war. As this discord increased, Father Richard was compelled to visit the county. Taking Lord Ermenfridus with him, he came to Rouen. After restoring peace among the princes, he brought the aforementioned Ermenold, who had been convicted and corrected and had become somewhat gentler because all diabolical cunning was rendered futile in the presence of the servants of God, with him to Verdun.

He clothed him in monastic garments and taught the man ensnared in the devil’s traps to reject the things of the demon. But wisdom recoils from dwelling in a body subjected to sins. For a time he pretended to be a philosopher, so that those who did not know him might believe him a theosopher; but wisdom recognizes no friend of a fictitious peace.

Consequently, all his cunning and wickedness were soon discovered, and that savage rage, hostile to peace, could not remain hidden among the saints. The enemy left a place that was not his and returned to his own; he employed the most shameless art, and once again Normandy was corrupted by the perversity of his malignity.

He was driven from his hiding places, where he believed himself stronger and more powerful. The blessed man foretold to him that, through the devil’s cunning, he would be led to death, and the prediction was not frustrated.

After he had defeated several of the nobles of Normandy by inventing accusations of conspiracy and challenging them to single combat—men whom the severity of the prince had deprived of their eyes and lands once they had been convicted—he was himself convicted, overcome, and killed by a certain forester. Thus he brought his life and crimes to an end.

In this deed we may observe the sweetness and compassion of the just man. When he saw a true workshop of the devil, convicted and cast down by the devil, he taught the man to flee to the bosom of mercy. But once he had become incorrigible, so that he might not rage longer in his vices, he announced that he would quickly perish as an example to all the lost, so that his punishment after death might be lighter in proportion as vengeance came more swiftly upon the sinner through death.

## 29

(Fol. 89)

Let us now come to the lamentable battle fought at the castle of Bar in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1037. [Glaber of Reims III, 9.] In it fell Odo, son of Odo, son of Theobald of Chartres, whose surname was Tricator. He had treacherously killed William the Norman, son of Rollo, who had begotten Odo—father of this Odo, as we have said—by the sister of Heribert, count of Troyes.

To make the truth of the matter clearer, let us explain the cause of so great a conflict. Conrad, king of Burgundy, married Matilda, sister of Lothair the younger, king of the Franks. Lothair gave him the city of Lyon, the noblest city of Gaul, as her dowry.

From that Matilda was born King Rudolf, who ruled Burgundy after his father; and Gisla, whom the emperor Conrad married and by whom he fathered the third Henry; and also Bertha, whom Odo of Chartres took as his wife and by whom he fathered this Odo.

King Rudolf, being without children, left the kingdom of Burgundy to the emperor Conrad and gave him the lance of Saint Maurice, which was the emblem of the kingdom of Burgundy.

After Rudolf’s death, when Conrad had gained the kingdom, Odo, because he was Rudolf’s sister’s son, began, having assumed tyrannical power, to aspire to the kingship. Being fierce in spirit and savage in character, he repeatedly invaded the borders of Burgundy, gained possession of cities and castles as far as the Jura and Mount Jovis, and became exceedingly powerful.

He also besieged Vienne, which he received into an alliance on the condition that, at a fixed time, he would be proclaimed and crowned king in that same city.

Within this period he launched an expedition against the kingdom of Lotharingia [ibid.] and captured the castle of Bar. Leaving five hundred soldiers there, he turned to other affairs, for he was troubled by countless concerns.

For Robert’s son Henry, king of the Franks, had been opposed by a revolt, and the emperor Conrad resisted his undertakings; their dispute was a great one. Henry sent Duke Gozelo to attack him.

When Odo learned this, he returned and prepared himself for war against the Lotharingians. Gozelo, duke of all First Raetia, attacked him with a very large army. After they had fought for a long time on both sides, he put Odo’s army to flight, and Odo himself fell there miserably.

The venerable Father Richard and Roger, bishop of Châlons, received his mutilated body from the slaughter and returned it to his wife. He was buried at Tours. Count Manasses also fell in that battle, as did Evervinus and Dido; they were buried at Verdun.

Count Walerannus was gravely wounded in the same battle by Godefrey, son of Duke Gozelo. When he was already failing as he fought, he asked for his life and limbs to be spared, so that he might be permitted to be clothed in monastic garments at Verdun under the rule of Father Richard, as he had vowed to God. He obtained this request.

When the battle was over, he returned with the aforesaid father and became a monk. [Note: Col. 0257D: Life of Richard II.]

(Fol. 90)

We pass over the killing and fishing of nine small children in the fishpond, which was marked out by the Holy Spirit while the man of God was in the hidden and rugged ridges of Mount Romaric, which he had already entered for the love of inner quiet. We do this lest we appear to have wronged the holy community of nuns, especially since their dwelling is nearby and this miracle was celebrated with such great frequency throughout the city of Verdun that anyone who did not see it learned of it through report—although the man of prophetic spirit wanted it entirely concealed because of the reproach it would bring upon the impious.

This was the reason that temporarily brought him down from the solitude of that mountain. Accordingly, after he had given correction appropriate to the time and place, he returned there, so that it might be openly understood that he had relaxed the rigor of his purpose for a time unwillingly and as though compelled.

There was this marvelous thing about the man of God: although absent in body, he knew of the event, including the place and the number of the victims, and that the shipwrecked crowd would be dragged out from the depths of the abyss in three successive stages.

At first he lived in a place five miles distant from Mount Romaric, called . . . . ., content with only one companion. Yet in turn he served as lord with Martin. How severely he afflicted his body, and with what contrition of mind he refreshed his soul, only the Judge of inner things knows. He performed the work of the right hand in such a way that the left did not know it, especially since he daily lamented the prolongation of his dwelling among human beings, wishing to be separated from the company of those who inhabit dark Kedar.

After this he withdrew to a place called Rombêchus. [Note: Col. 0259D: Rumbech, according to the Life of Richard, chapter 14.] There he established a dwelling for himself. Although he wished to remain hidden there for a longer time, he could not. People began to flock to him who had developed a similar ardor for the anachoretic life and wished to give themselves over to his discipleship. For them he established a rule of life according to the custom instituted by the holy Fathers.

When the fifth year of his dedicated penance had been completed, the devotion of his holy desire did not diminish; rather, it increased day by day with greater zeal, because he delighted in that very exercise and was nourished by the delight.

For he had inclined the neck of his spirit toward the testimonies of the Lord: humble in conduct, lofty in achievement, brilliant in progress. Because he embraced true philosophy, he was stirred up, kindled, and burned. “Your word is greatly aflame, O Lord, and your servant loved it” (Psalm 118:140).

The bishop and his brothers, who grieved deeply over his absence, repeatedly summoned him back. They often addressed him with the words: “Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may gaze upon you” (Song of Songs 6:12).

But he denied them his return in words, letters, and even by his actions. [Note: Col. 0259: “denegabatur,” according to c.] I myself saw certain letters sent back and forth and read them when I was a boy. In them, when a word of reply was set against him, he displayed such constancy in his responses that, as we have said, at the end of one letter the brothers’ insistence was restrained:

“If you wish to oppose word with words,” they said, “words for those laboring in words will never fail.”

## 30

(Fol. 90r)

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1035, Robert, count of the Normans, went to Jerusalem, carrying an immense amount of money, which he distributed entirely to the poor; on his return he died at Nicaea. William succeeded him while still a child.

[Glaber of Reims IV, 6]

In that year Pope John died, and Benedict succeeded him, the nephew of Benedict and John. William was driven from Normandy by the treachery of his own people and sought Henry, king of the Franks. Henry engaged them in war with force and arms; after the Normans had been defeated and overthrown, he restored the county to William, having passed judgment against the traitors.

[Note: Henry I reigned from 1031 to 1060.]

(IV, 8) Later William married Matilda, sister of Baldwin of Flanders.

He also honored with such affection this venerable man of whom we are speaking that, in those times, he arranged the administration of the palace according to his counsels. Although he honored him, when summoned with difficulty, with every kind of gracious and devoted attention, he rejoiced to have the church of Rouen, together with the bishop of that see and its clergy, adorned by his teaching, as can still be inferred from the faces of many things and also from the common book, arranged according to the forms and order of his institution and secured by a chain behind the high altar.

[Note: Col. 0259: the greater part of folio 90v and all of folio 91 are blank.]

(Fol. 91r)

Rambert, bishop of Verdun, died while going to Jerusalem at Bellagrada in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1038, in the fourteenth year of his pontificate. Later, in the time of his successor Richard, he was brought back by the clerics Bernerus and Bernardus and buried at Verdun in the monastery. (Gesta of Verdun 10)

In this year Amadeus, abbot of Flavigny, also died, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.

[Note: Col. 0259: added afterward.]

### [ROD. GLAB. IV, 9.]

In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 1039, on the Kalends of July, a Friday, when the moon was 28 days old, an eclipse of the sun occurred. For the sun became sapphire-colored. On that same day, the birthday of the Apostles, certain Romans rose up against Pope Clement and, wishing to kill him, since they were unable to do so, drove him from his see. But Emperor Conrad, coming there, restored him to his own see; and in that same year Conrad died in Saxony, and Henry III succeeded him.

Pope Clement too, formerly bishop of Babenberg, whose name was Suicher, died, as did Robert, king of the Franks. After Rambert’s death, in the first year of his reign, Henry granted the bishopric of Verdun to Richard, the man of God [Col. 0260C]. But that very gentle man refused it, and had his own godson in baptism, Richard, son of Count Hildrad, enthroned instead.

### [GLAB. ROD. V, 3.]

At that time, in the month of November, when the moon was 28 days old, an eclipse of the sun occurred; and a star called Lucifer was seen in the evening moving up and down, as though threatening the inhabitants of the earth.

### (V, 5.)

At that time also a certain boy of twelve years had been installed in the Roman see by simony; the disgracefulness of his conduct and life is horrifying to relate.

### (V, 4.)

There was also, in those days already mentioned, around the thousandth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, a very great dispute after the death of Burchard, archbishop of Lyons. The only noble thing he did was to perish for that very episcopate, which many men were arrogantly seeking.

The first of all was Burchard, nephew of the aforesaid Burchard and bishop of Augsburg. Abandoning his own see, he audaciously seized that of Lyons; after committing many wicked deeds, he was captured by the emperor’s soldiers and condemned to perpetual exile.

After him, Count Gerald, relying solely on presumption, arrogantly installed his little son there; but the boy was put to flight and went into hiding.

### (III, 9.)

At that time Henry, son of King Robert by Constance, governed the kingdom of the Franks. For Hugh, who had been crowned while still ten years old [Col. 0261A], was overtaken by an untimely death. When his mother wished to make Robert III king but was unable to do so, she appointed him duke of Burgundy.

### (V, 2.)

There was also a great dispute between Henry himself and the sons of Odo, who had died at Bar—Theobald and Stephen. The king went so far as to take the lordship of the city of Tours from them and give it to Geoffrey Tuditi, son of Fulk, who besieged it for an entire year. When battle was joined, Stephen was put to flight; Theobald was captured with his men and led out before the city. He surrendered it to Geoffrey and remained in captivity. Seventeen hundred men and more were captured in the battle without bloodshed.

### (V, 4.)

At that time, after the emperor had defeated the Hungarians, who had rebelled against him for the second time, he caused bishops to be assembled from throughout his empire and, acting against simony, began as follows:

### (V, 5.)

“I begin to speak to you in mourning, you who have been appointed in Christ’s place within his Church, which he took as his bride and redeemed with his own blood. For just as, in gratuitous goodness, he deigned to come to us through a virgin in order to redeem us from the bosom of the Father, so he commanded his followers and said, sending them: ‘You received freely; give freely.’

“But you, corrupted by avarice and greed, who ought to confer blessing, are accursed in this transgression, both in giving and in receiving. My father too—for the peril of his soul I greatly fear—practiced that same damnable avarice excessively in his lifetime. Therefore, whoever among you recognizes that he is polluted by this stain must be barred from sacred ministry.

“For because of this offense, famine, mortality, and the sword have come upon the children of men. All ecclesiastical orders, from the supreme pontiff down to the doorkeeper, are oppressed through the reward of your condemnation, and spiritual brigandage is raging against everyone.”

At the emperor’s words the pontiffs were struck with astonishment and begged for an opportunity to perform an act of mercy. But the prince, moved by mercy and urging them to pray for his father’s soul, issued an edict that no ecclesiastical rank or ministry was to be acquired for a price; and if anyone attempted it, he was to be stripped of every honor.

“Just as,” he said, “God freely gave me the crown of the empire, so I freely bestow what belongs to religion. I want you to do likewise.”

Thus the boy who was occupying the Roman Church was expelled from the see at the emperor’s command, and Gregory VI, a Roman by birth, was substituted in his place. By his good reputation, he reformed for the better whatever the former man had defiled.

### (V, 4.)

He then arranged for the holy Odilo to be ordained pontiff of the Church of Lyons, and sent him the pallium and ring. But that religious man, devoted to humility, refused this; nevertheless, he kept the pallium and ring, preserving them for a pontiff who would be worthy. They are still kept at Cluny.

Henry, having recovered the kingdom of Austrasia, grieved when he learned of the dispute. At Besançon, in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 1041, he sent Lord Odelric, archdeacon of Langres, whose election had been confirmed by the clergy and people, to the see of Lyons, splendidly clothed. Peace came to the province and joy to the people.

### (V, 1.)

In that same year the Truce of God was first established and confirmed, and that peace itself was called the Truce of God. It was confirmed not only by human safeguards but also by divine terrors.

When the people of Neustria refused to accept it, the man of God Richard preached and admonished them to receive it, because it was the Lord’s will and because this decree had proceeded from God, not from man. Then, by divine judgment, fire began to rage against them—the fire that tortured them. In that year nearly the whole world suffered scarcity because wine and grain were rare. Immediately afterward there followed a very great mortality among human beings, in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 1042.

Many of those who were tortured by the fire came to the man of God and, through his merits and prayers, were healed by God’s medicinal power [Col. 0262B].

The lord bishop of Autun still survives, advanced in years through the longevity of his life [Note: [Col. 0261D] Hagano died in 1098, June 25; see below.]. He was accustomed to relate that, when this peace had been established through divine revelations by Saint Odilo and the others, had been called the Truce of God, and had been accepted by the Austrasians, and when everyone was united in the desire that it should be observed everywhere, this matter was entrusted by all to the zeal of our father Gratia Dei, so that through his devotion and diligence the same peace might be preserved in Neustria.

They were certain of him because his grace toward everyone, and everyone’s grace toward him, was so great that whatever he taught should be preserved would be preserved by all, and whatever he showed should be avoided would be avoided by everyone.

Therefore the venerable father took pains to ensure that so great a good might be gratefully accepted by all. But the perverse will and untamed mind of certain people rejected it as though it were unheard-of, as though they did not wish to violate their fathers’ institutions or accept new and unfamiliar ones.

Hence divine vengeance followed: fire, raging from the Lord against the rebels and the obstinate, tortured those who were not afraid to resist the man of God and despise his commands.

You could see the monastery of that outstanding father filled with crowds of people burning with the fire. He restored them to their former health by sprinkling them with water blessed with the relics of the saints, washing those relics in wine, and giving the wretched people to drink wine sprinkled with the dust scraped from the stone of the Lord’s tomb. Once peace had been confirmed and sworn, they were healed.

For the countless crowds of sick people who flocked there, a vessel of drink was kept ready, so that, if the sick arrived, the drink of salvation would not be lacking and they would not be disappointed if they came at an unsuitable hour; nor would it then be necessary to return to the washing of the relics, which customarily took place after the completion of Mass.

### [GLAB. ROD. V, 1.]

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1045, Henry took as his wife at Besançon Agnes, daughter of William of Poitiers; twenty-eight bishops were present there. Although he was otherwise a good man and everyone longed for his rule, he nevertheless could not restrain his sexual incontinence [Col. 0263A].

At that time Father Richard did not wish to leave the monastery. He could not be drawn away from it by any circumstances that arose, because he knew and had foretold to his sons that the dissolution of his body was approaching.

In earlier years, when that plague of which we have just spoken devastated the people, and when the population was melting away and the city of Verdun was almost reduced to a wilderness, it was thought advisable that the common danger be removed by common prayer. Under the pressure of the misery created by that necessity, it was decided by common agreement that the help of blessed Vitonus should be sought, for they trusted that through the merits of his life they would undoubtedly obtain relief.

It also seemed to Bishop Richard that the most holy body of that confessor ought to be brought out of its coffin and carried in solemn procession before the sight of everyone, so that the people, supported by his protection and seeing the saint’s shrine, might seek his aid more earnestly, knowing that it would not fail them.

Although our most reverent father opposed this, the bishop arranged that what had been decided should be carried out on the following day. The father resisted and said that the people’s misery would indeed be relieved, but that the bishop would not prosper, since he had dared to disturb the saint’s honored body.

That night the father remained sleepless, devoting himself to prayer with tears before the altar of the saint. On the following day the bishop, all the clergy, and the people came. With great fear and reverence they brought out the relics of the holy pontiff, precious above refined gold [Col. 0263C].

When this had been done, the father approached the bishop and said: “You have fulfilled what you wished, but know that from this point you will not see five years in the world. For me also, who consented, the end of life will come likewise before five years; you will follow me shortly thereafter.”

He had spoken, and the event proved his words. Before four full years had passed, the father’s bodily strength began to fail, and he summoned the brothers and announced that the day of his dissolution was near.

He immediately appointed Abbot Odilard to the Abbey of Saint Peter at Châlons; at Belleville he appointed Father Richard; to the monastery of Saint Hubert, Theodoric; and to Saint Urban, Stephen—men highly approved in every aspect of spiritual contemplation and distinguished in preserving the religious purpose. He himself had governed these abbeys personally.

Thus relieved of all the others, he decided to retain only that one to which he had been appointed pastor and in which he had also determined to be buried.

### (Fol. 92′.)

And now, more assiduous than frequent in carrying out the Lord’s commands, one day he saw one of the monastery’s brothers, named Mysac, burning with such a severe fever that his breath seemed almost to be cut off. He took the man’s hand and ordered him, once healed and restored, to give the signal announcing the hour for the work of God. The man, healed at the sound of his command, obeyed the father’s order and was thus freed from all the discomfort of his illness.

This man, therefore, who abounded in such great virtues, fell ill with fever as the day of his calling approached, and was afflicted by that final illness. When the news spread through the city, the bishop arrived, along with groups of monks, clerics, and nuns [Col. 0264A]. Through this solemn visitation they demonstrated their devotion and loving affection toward the father.

The bishop did not return home; rather, clinging to him in daily vigils, he allowed himself to be separated from him neither by day nor by night. Bishops from neighboring cities, abbots, and all the leading men also arrived to visit him and commend themselves to him. They seemed to believe that at his death the whole earth would be shaken and thrown into confusion.

By day and night, a crowd of his sons and other faithful people kept watch before his house. Some wished to bid farewell to the father hastening toward better things and commend themselves to him; others sought bodily health, hoping at least to deserve the water in which he had washed his hands, so that when they were anointed with it they might be refreshed.

When he sensed that the hour of his calling was approaching, he ordered the sons whom he had acquired for Christ to assemble. After being anointed by the bishop with holy oil, having made his confession and been nourished with the heavenly viaticum, he was placed upon a small bed. He lay in ashes and sackcloth, so that the altar of Saint Nicholas was always visible to him.

Then he addressed the brothers, repeating his customary teachings of salvation. He admonished them to serve God and remain attached to him, and asked them, with the deepest devotion, to remember him. Everyone wept together and repeatedly lamented their bereavement, while he restrained everyone’s tears, consoled their grief, and promised that the protection of Christ the Lord would be present.

After this he ordered the relics given to him by the patriarch of Jerusalem to be brought to him. Having greeted and kissed them with great reverence, he brought out the relics that he was accustomed to wear around his neck and ordered them to be placed reverently before him.

Then, invoking the common protection of the saints, he raised his hand and blessed the brothers and everyone present, and asked that he himself be blessed.

After giving his sons permission to leave, he kept his eyes and hands raised toward heaven and directed his attention to the one toward whom he was hastening. The Passion readings were read before him, as well as readings from the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, and his blessed soul clung to the one to whom he had entrusted himself entirely.

When his body had already begun to die from the lower part upward (1046), he took hold of the relics of the saints and sat up on his bed. Placing them at his feet, he gradually drew them upward as his vital warmth failed, and at last stopped them upon his chest. Having laid the relics there, he set them down.

O admirable devotion of the man! O holiness of his, worthy of proclamation in all things! When he had reclined, he placed his hands upon the relics and remained in that position, with his eyes raised toward God, until he returned his spirit to the Creator.

The bishop was present, as were the religious men whom the love and benefactions of the pious father had bound to him. They fortified his passing with continual prayers and psalmody. They scarcely ever separated from his presence, and then only briefly, lest they be absent when his blessed soul departed from the body.

At daybreak on June 14, which is the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, when the third hour was already approaching, in the presence of his sons, as many as the narrowness of the place could contain, while the others stood and sang in the greater church, that holy soul, released from the bonds of the body [Col. 0265A], reached the eternal reality that is one, indivisible, and triune.

The bishop closed the father’s eyes. The funeral attendants [Note: [Col. 0265D] Those who cared for and anointed the dead.] were the abbots Richard, Odilard, Stephen, and Walerannus. They took charge of the most holy body. As was customary, the bishop clothed it in sacred garments—not those which the father had chosen and ordered, since he had selected the most humble things, but those dictated by fatherly love, the most holy and fitting devotion [Note: [Col. 0265D] *Gesta Virdunensia* 10.].

The relics that he himself had entrusted to his breast were placed upon his breast after he had been clothed in the sacred garments. The most blessed body was then carried on the shoulders of bearers. Because the church had been closed against the force of the oncoming and mourning crowd, it was placed before the altar of Saint Peter. After Mass had been celebrated by the pontiff, the monastery gates were finally opened, and behold, an innumerable crowd of both sexes and every rank rushed in with tears and heart-rending cries.

### (Fol. 93.)

The church was full of tears. Everyone together mourned the death of the pious father, as though they saw the destruction of their homeland approaching. O how great was the grief of all! How great the sorrow of the entire city! How devout was their compassion at his death! How complete their bereavement! That whole day was filled with groaning, wholly given to lamentation.

As evening approached, the brothers carried the most blessed body to the principal Church of Saint Mary. There, throughout that very night, the watchmen honored it with the proper offices of vigils and psalmody.

On the following day, after the canons had solemnly celebrated Mass, the body was carried through the remaining monasteries of the city. After vigils and Masses had been solemnly and dutifully celebrated, it was finally brought back to his own monastery and restored to his grieving sons, who mourned his death.

Then the following day arrived, and behold, around the third hour the entire city assembled to bury him. The bishop celebrated Mass and preached to the people about the mutability of this life, how we had come into this valley of tears, what the end of the good and of the wicked would be, what the father’s life had been, and how precious his death was.

After the office had been completed and the solemn prayers had been said, they went to the place of burial. Although only those serving at the funeral, the bearers, and those performing the offices were permitted to enter, while the rest were held inside the greater church, so great was the multitude of those attending that the need to obtain air compelled them to remove the windows through which light entered the crypt [Col. 0265D].

The multitude of lights surpassed the daylight, and the smoke of incense and aromatic offerings filled the entire church. So great was everyone’s devotion toward the father’s burial!

After the body of the gentlest man had been buried, the tomb was closed and its joints were sealed with solid cement. He rests in the underground crypt before the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint John the Evangelist; above him the greater altar of Saint Peter has been established.

In the same crypt, beneath the aforesaid altar of Saint Mary [Col. 0266A], rests the saint Madelveus, transferred there by our same father and reverently buried.

When the burial office had been completed and the others had departed, the united devotion of the sons turned to arranging the man of God’s resting place. Four marble columns were joined to the tomb’s cement-made cover by means of the same marble. Above them a very large marble slab was attached with the same cement. A wall was then built to some height above the cover and strengthened with a solid bond of bitumen.

A linen cloth was placed upon the slab, which extended upward, and a cloak was added over it, so that all who saw it might clearly understand that he was a man of great merit, whose body was honored in this way on earth.

And rightly so. For what had been his concern on earth except to love God, venerate his saints, and adorn the Church of God with fitting beauty? Nor is it surprising that he is honored so abundantly by his sons, whom he knew how to govern—and to govern according to our discipline, which descends from Christian law and leads to God.

Our father rested in the year from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation 1046, in the forty-second year of his rule, while Henry, son of Conrad, reigned on earth.

Bishop Richard survived him until the month of November and died on November 6, just as he had asked the father when he closed his eyes [Note: [Col. 0265D] *Gesta Virdunensia* 10; *Life of Richard* 20.].

“If,” he said, “father, you are going to God, and if the service by which you served him is pleasing to him, obtain that I may not survive you in this world for one year, since I prefer to die with you rather than live.”

He had spoken and was heard, and was added to his fathers. When his relatives ordered that his body be buried beside the body of the man of God, the canons forcibly prevented this and buried him in the Church of Saint Mary Major.

### (Chron. Div.)

In that same year Lord Halinard was ordained archbishop of the Church of Lyons. In that same year Henry went to Rome, and at a council the usurpers of the Roman Church—John, Benedict, and Sylvester—were deposed. Clement was ordained pope, and from him Henry received the imperial crown. In that same year Clement died, and Damasus succeeded him.

Walerannus also assumed governance of the monastery of Verdun. He was a man of the highest nobility in the world, son of Count Gelduin; he had been wounded in the knee during the battle at the fortress of Bar and walked with a limp.

His brother was Hugh, bishop of Langres, later deposed by Saint Leo IX at the Council of Reims. The bishopric of Verdun was assumed by Theodoric, son of Count Wezelo. In the first year of his episcopal blessing, the Church of Saint Mary was burned by Duke Godfrey and Baldwin, its sacred vessels were carried away, and the city was destroyed on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

### (1047.)

How greatly our father was honored by the grace of God among the people of that age, Theodoric, bishop of Basel, a man of great authority and favor, demonstrated by his own action.

When he had been sent by the emperor to Verdun to escort the new bishop [Note: [Col. 0266D] Namely Theodoric, in the year 1047; cf. Hermann of Reichenau, *Chronicle*.], he was eager to visit the holy man’s tomb. After subjecting himself before the tomb to great contrition in tears and recalling the dead man’s piety, sobriety, and gentleness, he adorned the tomb itself with a most precious saffron-colored cloak. By this action he testified that he did not withhold from the dead the love he had shown him while alive; rather, he considered him worthy of even greater honor, since the Lord was now cherishing him in his own bosom.

By then that place had begun to shine with many miracles. Such an abundance of healing grace was poured out upon those suffering from fever that whoever arrived there afflicted with this illness, after sleeping there for a short while, obtained the aid of health and returned with every fever of illness extinguished.

But why do we delay and fail to relate how he was shown to possess such merit that it was declared even by angelic testimony [Col. 0267B]? For the one who saw the testimony bore witness to it, and because there is no doubt about the man’s life, his testimony is believed on account of his merit.

The father Rodulfus of blessed memory, third successor after him in the governance of the Church and, as we believe, heir to his sanctity, now blessed through a happy departure [Note: [Col. 0267D] He held office for two years while Grimoldus was alive, then from 1078 to 1099.], took charge of governing that place. Hearing from those who reported it many things about him worthy of being related, and seeing everyone’s unanimous devotion toward honoring his memory, he embraced what he saw and heard generally from all.

Within himself, however, he burned with a desire to know whether that man had truly possessed such great holiness as people reported. As though he were seeking this through vigilant and carefully ordered thoughts, he asked what merit he had before God.

He himself also used to pray very frequently at the man’s tomb, because he had experienced the ease with which prayers were answered there, and often spent the night there. Then, one night, after the celebration of the nocturnal office, while he was performing his customary vigils to God in that place, the thought repeatedly troubling and returning to him, sleep briefly played upon him.

Before his bodily senses had fully dissolved into sleep, the eyes of his understanding were opened, and he saw an angel standing beside him and addressing him in a gentle voice:

“Your thoughtful curiosity has detained you for a long time, so that you might know what merit before God belonged to the man at whose tomb you are standing. So that I may not prolong your fatigue, I have been sent to settle this matter for you.

“Two men are resting in this crypt and awaiting the day of the Lord, when they will be rewarded with a double robe: Abbot Richard, and the outstanding confessor of Christ, Madelveus, whose feast you honor at its proper time and on its proper day with devout offices, as is fitting. God has counted him among his saints and assigned him a place among the lot of the righteous. And rightly and worthily he is turned into the memory of men, since he has passed into the joy of the righteous.

“But the man whose tomb I am standing beside is to be venerated by you on earth with equal, not lesser, devotion. God has exalted him in heaven, adorned with an equal lot and no inferior glory.

“Much is the reputation of his holiness on earth, although you do not know even half of it, because the man, enlightened by the grace of God, devoted himself to humility and lowliness. He did not wish to reveal his deeds but rather to conceal them.

“But know that you sent before you a great patron, most dear to God, and that what is said about him is true, although greater things could be said. Let the devotion of his sons toward his memory be pleasing to you, and proclaim publicly today to everyone what I, sent by God, report to you, so that they may rejoice at the happy success of their father, whom they have as an advocate and devoted intercessor in heaven.

“Therefore, now that you have learned these things about the blessed man, do not abandon the path you have begun. Be watchful in mortification of the flesh, humility, lowliness, and chastity. Labor to win souls, so that together with this man and others you may be granted the blessedness of eternal joy.”

### (Fol. 94.)

The man of grace was astonished at the vision and the angel’s address. When he saw the angel praising God for these and the other benefits of the father's compassion bestowed upon human frailty, he prepared himself to do the same. As he slept, he rose up with his whole body, and, awakening, paid with mind and body the thanks that he had tried to offer in spirit.

He did not appear slow to proclaim what he had seen and heard. Rather, he made known to everyone the mighty works of God, since what is pleasing to see or hear is reported even more pleasingly and believed by everyone with the greatest gratitude.

When the brothers heard of the father’s magnificence, attested by the voice of such a messenger, we too rendered praise and thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0268D] Hugh, therefore, was present.]. From that day onward, great care was taken that his memory should be recalled with the devotion most worthy of it.

For these and his other benefits, may the name of the Lord be blessed forever [Note: [Col. 0267D] The author continues after some interval.]. The merit of the blessed man still lives and will live forever [Note: [Col. 0268D] Recognize the verses in what follows.], and as long as the age continues to revolve, his merit will always receive increase.

Normandy bears witness to this; Brittany confesses it; all Gaul applauds, proclaiming the father’s mighty deeds. As greatly as it rejoiced and exulted in his most holy way of life while he was in the world, so greatly it now grieves at his death, deprived of such blessed companionship. His life was a mirror of holiness, a support for penitents, a consolation for the sorrowful, and a defense for the wretched.

The emperor and the nobles mourned his death; kings and pontiffs wept for him. The pipe and organ failed, the lyre and psaltery fell silent, and trumpet and drum sounded hoarsely. The cry of the poor rose to God, as did the desire of the needy who repeatedly lamented their bereavement.

And, even more wondrously, the world mourned the death of one in whom, while he lived, the whole world found rest. Although they understood that there was more reason for rejoicing, if the logic of grief permitted it, the monks nevertheless wept above all, as did virgins and widows, and the ecclesiastical order, supported by his special protection, strengthened by his counsel, and refreshed by his conversation.

O merit of the father, memorable through the ages, venerable to posterity, and worthy of imitation by all! No forgetfulness will ever erase his praises; no passage of time will diminish them; no future age will remove them from our mouths [Col. 0269A]. And even if a tribulation more severe than the present should blaze against us [Note: [Col. 0269] These things were therefore written after the year 1096.], nothing will prevent us from confessing that you, father, are worthy of veneration, proclamation, and every form of praise.

To linger over your praises is to be relieved from tribulation, because your praise is a wondrous grasp of joy and peace, a driving away of grief and anxiety.

Five years ago, when we had not yet tasted how great the labor and weariness are of caring for the affairs of others, the venerable abbot Hugh of the Holy Trinity on Mount Rouen, who still survives, reported the following to our humility.

While he was serving the aforesaid count of Normandy, William, already then king of the English, there was once discussion at court about honorable and memorable men of whom the king had personal knowledge or whose fame he had heard. Among the foremost, this admirable man was recalled with the highest praise: his humility, wisdom, discernment, the devotion to God expressed in his spirit and countenance, his eloquence in speech, the refinement of his conduct, and the reverence of his subjects [Col. 0269B].

The king also wondered that in those modern times no person from so distinguished a place came to him, and that no one, as formerly, sought his royal magnificence—the diligence either of the successors of so great a father or of the monks of that place.

Thus, when the same man from whom we heard these things was once sent to Verdun on a certain embassy, the king and his honorable wife instructed him, among other things, to seek out the famous monastery of Saint Vitonus and lodge there, to greet the father and the brothers of the place devoutly on their behalf, and carefully to observe whether the same cultivation of honor and religion still shone there as once before; who was the father of the monastery; whether a model of ancestral fatherhood and gentleness shone forth in him; whether the ancient dignity of gravity and reverence stood out in the sons; whether temporal resources abounded; and whether the grace of spiritual delights, flowing from the abundance of God’s house, made its inhabitants joyful and satisfied.

He was to inspect everything and examine each detail with lively intelligence, then report back to them.

But what intervening circumstance caused the aforesaid man to lodge elsewhere and to bring the king and queen unexpected reports instead of the excellent things they hoped for is not for us to disclose—especially since, at the time when this occurred, our childhood and the schoolmaster’s rod still forbade us to attend to matters of this kind or similar ones.

Let it suffice to note this one point: when the king heard what he had not expected, and recalled to mind the admirable conduct of that distinguished and memorable man, he mourned his death with many repeated lamentations. Again and again he exalted his merit, repeating his praises with wondrous commendation, and continually rehearsing the lax reciprocal observances of negligent sons, unmerited and ungrateful in return for their father’s diligence.

The entire court echoed this lamentation, so that it might be openly understood by all that, if fame had answered their wishes, the church would have been showered with many gifts and honored by the royal generosity with great affection.

### (Fol. 94′.)

We saw a demon-possessed man brought to the monastery of blessed Vitonus who, within only a few days, carried away the joy of complete health. When, at his first arrival, his relatives wished to lead him into the crypt, bound with straps and tightly fastened with ropes, to the memorial of the saints resting there, they could not do so at all. I believe that the demon feared the presence of those saints, through whose merits that church is illuminated and by whose presence it is adorned [Note: [Col. 0269D] The remainder of the page is blank.].

(Fol. 95.) In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1051, Victor succeeded Leo IX, and died in his fourth year. Stephen then succeeded him—also called Frederick, the brother of Duke Godefrid—and in the first year of his papacy, at Goslar, Emperor Henry died. Stephen attended his funeral, and Henry was buried at Speyer in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1056. Empress Agnes remained with her young son, who also obtained the kingdom under the guardianship of the kingdom’s tutor, Anno, Archbishop of Cologne (1056).

Stephen also died in the year 1058 and was buried near the city of Lucca, where, with God’s cooperation, many miracles occur at his tomb (1059). Nicholas succeeded him. In the second year of his ordination he held a council in the Lateran basilica, in April, in the twelfth indiction; there, with venerable archbishops, bishops, abbots, and venerable priests and deacons seated, he issued the following decision concerning the election of the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0269] Compare Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges, vol. II, B, p. 177, and what I noted there.]:

> “Your Beatitude, beloved brothers and fellow bishops, knows—and the lower members have not been unaware of it either—that, after the death of our predecessor, the lord Stephen, of pious memory, this apostolic see, which by God’s authority I serve, has endured how many adversities and, finally, how many blows and repeated hammerings it has suffered at the hands of the money-changers of the Simoniacal heresy, so that the pillar of the living God already seemed almost to totter, and the net of the supreme Fisherman, as storms swelled, to be sunk into the depths of shipwreck.

> “Therefore, if it pleases your fraternity, with God’s help we must prudently forestall future dangers and provide for the ecclesiastical order, lest—God forbid—evils revived should prevail hereafter. Accordingly, instructed by the authority of our predecessors and of the other holy Fathers, we decree and establish that, when the pontiff of this Roman universal Church dies, first of all the cardinal bishops, acting together with the most careful deliberation, shall immediately associate with themselves the cardinal clerics; then the remaining clergy and the people shall proceed to consent to the new election. Thus, so that the disease of venality may not creep in on any pretext, religious men shall take the lead in advancing the pontiff, while the others shall follow.

> “Certainly, this is judged to be the right and lawful order of election if, after examining the rules and acts of various Fathers, that saying of blessed Leo is also recalled: ‘No principle permits those to be counted among the bishops who have been elected neither by the clergy, sought neither by the people, nor consecrated by the judgment of the metropolitan and the bishops of their province.’

> “Because the apostolic see is preferred to all the churches throughout the world and therefore cannot have a metropolitan over it, the cardinal bishops undoubtedly fulfill the office of a metropolitan; they raise the elected prelate to the summit of the apostolic dignity.

> “Let them choose from the bosom of that same Church, if a suitable man is found; but if no such man is found there, let one be taken from elsewhere, without prejudice to the due honor and reverence owed to our beloved son Henry, who is at present regarded as king and is hoped, by God’s granting, to become emperor—as we have already conceded to him—and to his successors, who may personally obtain this right from this apostolic see.

> “But if the perversity of wicked and unjust men should become so powerful that a pure, sincere, and free election cannot be held in the City, let the cardinal bishops, together with religious clerics and Catholic laymen, even if few in number, possess the authority to elect the prelate of the apostolic see wherever they judge it more suitable.

> “Plainly, after the election has been made, if warlike tumult or any human effort, impelled by malicious purpose, should prevent the elected man from being enthroned in the apostolic see according to custom, nevertheless, as pope, let the elected man possess authority to govern the holy Roman Church and to administer all its possessions. We know that blessed Gregory did this before his own election.

> “But if anyone, against this decree of ours promulgated by synodal judgment, should be elected, or even ordained or enthroned, through sedition, presumption, or any contrivance, let him, by divine authority and that of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, be separated from the thresholds of the holy Church of God by perpetual anathema, together with his authors, agents, and followers, and let him be subjected as an antichrist, an invader, and a destroyer of all Christianity. Let no hearing ever be granted to him concerning this matter; rather, from whatever ecclesiastical rank he previously held, let him be deposed without reconsideration.

> “Whoever adheres to him, shows him any reverence as though he were a pontiff, or presumes to defend him in any way, shall be bound by the same sentence.”

(Fol. 95.) “Whoever proves to be a transgressor of this decree or judgment of ours, and attempts by his presumption to disgrace and disturb the Roman Church contrary to this statute, shall be condemned by perpetual anathema and excommunication and shall be reckoned among the impious when they rise for judgment. Let him feel against himself the anger of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and in this life and the next let him encounter the fury of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whose Church he presumes to disgrace. Let his dwelling become desolate, and [Col. 0272A] let no one inhabit his tents. Let his children become orphans and his wives widows [Note: [Col. 0271D] U. e. u. c.].
