Let him himself be removed, together with his children; let them beg and be driven from their dwellings. Let the usurer search out his substance, and let strangers destroy his labors. Let the world fight against him, let all the elements be hostile to him, and let the merits of all the saints who rest confound him and display open vengeance against him in this life.

> “But let the grace of almighty God protect those who observe this decree of ours, and, by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, release them from every bond.

> “I, Nicholas, bishop of the holy and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed this decree promulgated by us. Boniface of Albano has subscribed. Humbert of the holy Church of Silva Candida has subscribed.”

Peter, bishop of Ostia, subscribed, and seventy-six other bishops, together with priests and deacons, subscribed.

Likewise:

> “Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, and faithful laymen, both great and small, dwelling throughout all Gaul—and also among the Aquitanians and Basques—greeting and apostolic blessing [Note: Compare Mansi, vol. XIX, col. 873].
>
> “Whoever, after the institution of our predecessor Pope Leo, of blessed memory, concerning the chastity of clerics, has publicly taken a concubine, or has not dismissed one already taken, whether priest, deacon, or subdeacon, we command on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul—and we strictly prohibit him—from singing Mass, reading the Gospel or Epistle at Mass, remaining in the presbytery for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid constitution, or receiving any share from the Church, until, God granting it, a judgment concerning such matters proceeds from us.

> “We further command and establish that those of the aforesaid orders who, obeying our predecessor and preserving his institution, shall live according to it, are to eat and sleep together near the churches in which they were ordained, as religious clerics ought to do, and are to hold in common whatever belongs to them from the churches.”

(1060.) Walerannus, abbot of Saint Vitonus, then approached Pope Nicholas and, after lodging a complaint against the Rutenian count concerning the lands of the Church of Verdun situated in the Rutenian county, which he was taking away from Saint Vitonus—namely Maderniacum, Puliniacum, and others—obtained from him a letter sent to the aforesaid count in these words:

> “Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., beloved son, the Rutenian count, greeting and apostolic blessing [Note: Mansi, vol. XIX, col. 874].
>
> “Knowing the purpose of your mind, and that, for the sake of the kingdom of God and his justice, you have wished to renounce the temporal eminence of secular occupations, we confidently declare to you that—as we enjoined upon you when we spoke face to face—you should offer yourself as a defender of the churches of God and of the poor, and, by acquiring justice for them, stand acquitted before God, since you do not bear the sword without cause.
>
> “Because it is our duty to admonish you if we learn that you are neglecting anything that ought not to be neglected, we admonish you, both by prayer and by apostolic command, to restore to the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Verdun, which your venerable kinsman Walerannus governs as abbot, the estates which it is known to possess in your territory. Otherwise, God forbid, by retaining them longer you may incur the excommunication invoked by our predecessors against their usurpers, to the perdition of your soul.
>
> “Nor do we want you to say that they were taken from the servants of God by your parents or by your wife’s parents, since the just Lord repays the iniquity of fathers upon their children, to the third and fourth generation. For, as ancient tradition, conscious of the truth, testifies, Saint Amantius, your special patron, handed them over for the use of the servants of Saint Peter.”

After receiving this letter, Walerannus died of poison while returning, at the monastery of Aremare [Note: Moustier-Ramey, near Troyes], and Grimoldus succeeded him. The chapel was retained by its inhabitants, but later, when demanded, it was returned, though not in its entirety. Since, however, after his death there was no one to carry the letter sent to the Count of Rhetel, the abbey and its lands continued to be retained.

Pope Nicholas also died in that same year, namely 1060 from the Incarnation of the Lord; in the following year Walerannus died and was buried at the same place.

In the year 1061, therefore, Alexander II succeeded Pope Nicholas [Col. 0273C], and died in his second year; Alexander III succeeded him [Note: Alexander sat for twelve years and had Gregory VII as his successor.].

In the year 1065, in the third indiction, a star called a comet appeared. In that same year Edward, king of the English, died (5 January 1066); because he had no sons, he appointed his kinsman William, Count of the Normans, to reign after him. But Harold invaded the kingdom, contrary to the oath he had sworn to William. In that same year, in October, William crossed the sea; battle was joined, and on 14 October Harold fell. On Christmas Day William was raised up and crowned king at London.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1063, a cycle of years came to an end [Note: The word is now erased.] which consists of 532 years; in the following year the same cycle begins. At its end there will be toil and sorrow.

Pope Alexander sent Giraldus, bishop of Ostia, who had succeeded Peter, to Gaul and entrusted his legation to him throughout France and Burgundy. At the pope’s command he held a council at Chalon, presided over by Bishop Roclenus, a man thoroughly learned in letters and most devoted to the reading of the divine books [Note: The Council of Chalon was held on 2 March 1072, as the fragments of its Acts testify; Mansi, vol. XX, p. 47. K.].

[Col. 0274A] (1073.) In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1074 [Note: Or rather 1073.], while Pope Alexander presided over the Roman Church, Giraldus, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Roman see in Gaul, returned to Rome after the council held at Chalon. Staying as a guest at the city of Die, he was speaking with the clerics in the church about the welfare of the Church.

There was in that city a bishop named Lancelinus, reputed to be a Simoniac. When summoned to a hearing, he refused to come, defended himself in the episcopal house by armed force, and attempted to retain the bishopric. The legate therefore discussed with the citizens—namely, the canons and the leading men of the people—what should be done with the bishop. Citing Ambrose, he said that the guilt of a sold ministry was inexpiable; and, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers Leo, Gregory, Nicholas, and the others, that no mercy should be shown to Simoniacs in preserving their dignity. Whoever is ordained through money, he said, is promoted in order to become a heretic; and all who consent to him, all who can correct him but do not, and all who do not oppose them but favor them, share with him in the guilt of the crime he first committed.

While these matters were being discussed among them, and, as we have said, the aforesaid bishop was avoiding a hearing, an eligible bishop was being sought according to the institutions of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers—one who would watch over their salvation and conscientiously supervise the souls entrusted to him. Suddenly they heard that the lord Hugh, chamberlain of Lyon, had arrived there and entered the church in which they were gathered for the sake of prayer. He was girded and prepared to ride, for he was going to Rome to Saint Peter.

Without delay, as the grace of the Holy Spirit enlightened the hearts of his people, there arose a cry and a gathering of the faithful. He was found booted and wearing spurs; he was seized and held. With the greatest favor and goodwill of all, he was led before the vicar of the apostolic see. It was acclaimed that he was worthy and able to preside over and benefit the Church.

He protested and sought to resist the wishes of the people, as though he could not and ought not, while the lawful bridegroom was alive, to corrupt the chastity of the Church by a shameful schism. In this devout contention, it pleased the Divinity to declare to his faithful, by the display of light, the will of his gracious presence.

For although the day was cloudy, light in the form of a sphere shone for several hours in the bosom and upon the face of the church [Col. 0274D]. It so inflamed all who were present and had seen it, inspiring them to praise the favor of divine clemency, that all cried out:

> “Blessed is the Lord God, because he has regarded the humiliation of his Church, to visit and enlighten it with such a pontiff!”

Another marvelous sign of divine mercy also occurred [Note: [Col. 0273] “-tatis” erased.]. When the whole Church applauded his election—with the manuscript also recording erasures of “ejus,” “-n voce,” “ap-,” “praecipue,” “esse,” “papae,” “mirum,” and “inquit” [Note: [Cols. 0273–0275] erased readings.]—with one voice of praise and with rejoicing of heart, and especially rejoiced that it had been helped by such a ruler, the pope’s legate, foreseeing something marvelous in him, said:

> “He has indeed been elected and given by God as pastor to this city, but the Most High has destined greater things for him. He will not long perform the office of pastor for this Church, for he will be given a more excellent gibissarium [Note: That is, a purse, or money-bag.], in order to dispense the gifts of divine grace.” [Note: [Col. 0275] The manuscript records erasures of “-em est,” “-us,” “-navit,” “enim,” “-ficium praestabit,” “-sserio dona-,” “-ur-,” “divinae,” “-a,” and “-ae”.]

[Note: He was promoted to be archbishop of Lyon at the end of 1082 or the beginning of 1083. Compare Scriptores, vol. VI, p. 306.]

Thus the heavenly judgment approved the cries and wishes of all. The elected man, who neither could nor wished to resist, in view of so many preceding signs, the divine will, was compelled by apostolic authority to remain, and the election of the clergy and people was confirmed over him.

(Fol. 96.) When this was heard, the man who had invaded the Church through Simony and was attempting to retain it by arms, grieving at the unanimous agreement of the citizens and fearing that the spirit of the rejoicing people, growing hot in their pious wishes, might swell into a most violent assault, abandoned the episcopal house and withdrew.

He was oppressed by waves of care and by the stings of a biting conscience, from which he could not escape, because he found nowhere to flee; nor did he now, as before, take pleasure in his errors (1073), by which he was punished, though unwillingly and unknowingly. Yet he still exulted in his crime, because, by overshadowing old sins with new ones, he imagined that he could somehow help himself. He thought that a lapse into crime was a mark of virtue.

But let his memory now be silent, because he withdrew, because he fled, because he was not expected to surrender what he had usurped unlawfully. Let us turn instead to the joy of the people and to the rejoicing of the clergy, both great and small.

Our elected man was raised with joy and rejoicing of heart to the pontifical throne; he was acclaimed and confirmed as bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clerics, by the support of the people who were then present, and by the fellowship of priests and good men.

He found the city full of anguish and surrounded by tribulations, greatly in need of vigilance, and the bishop’s property plundered, so that he could not find enough even to live for one day from the revenues of the episcopal household. Those who had preceded him had so completely impoverished everything that, out of all the churches of the entire bishopric, the episcopal house—or mother church—barely possessed one, while almost all the others were held by soldiers and various secular persons.

He did not long endure, in his time, to see such devastation and trampling-down of the Church. Rather, he decreed that no layman should possess a church or receive any share of the revenues of churches. By the cooperation of divine clemency, it came about that everyone gladly accepted and obeyed his command, so that, even before his ordination, the Church entrusted to him had received through him these beginnings of improvement.

In that same year Pope Alexander had died, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, and Gregory VII had been substituted for him by the unanimous election of the clergy and people. Under the aforesaid pontiff Gregory had served in that same Roman Church as archdeacon.

Although the privilege of his ordination and consecration had been entrusted solely to the cardinal bishops of Albano, Ostia, and Porto, Giraldus was absent and was not awaited; instead, a substitute was appointed to act in his place. When Giraldus finally returned, among other matters he informed the pope of the election of the Church of Die and strongly commended the elected man to his fatherly care.

Not long afterward the man who had been commended arrived. Since he possessed only the clerical tonsure—for he detested the ordinations of Simoniacs—he was promoted through the hand of the pope to the rank of priest in December. Some Romans objected, bringing forward the custom of the holy Roman Church that no elected prelate should be ordained by the pope unless he served in that same Church. Nevertheless, the lord pope exercised his authentic authority in this man’s case, for his soul had found favor with him.

In Lent, on Saturday, he was ordained priest, and on the following Sunday he was consecrated bishop at Mass. Thus, after eight days of consecration, richly instructed in divine doctrines and abundantly strengthened by ecclesiastical sanctions, he was dismissed with the blessing he had received to govern the sons for whom he had been ordained pastor and ruler.

Nor should we pass over the matter in which the testimony to his probity and to his foreordained and God-pleasing consecration is especially strengthened. After his election, which took place on 19 October, he came to Rome in December to receive the orders. There he found, awaiting a similar expectation, the lord Anselm, the elected bishop of Lucca, a man worthy of every proclamation of praise, now blessed by a happy death [Note: He died on 18 March 1086.], in whom every praise may safely be sung.

He was joined to him by so great a bond of familiarity and affection, and, although they had separate lodgings, they clung so inseparably to one another in the Lateran palace, that those who knew their unanimity thought it strange to see one without the other. So much so that the prefect of the city, with a kind of foreknowledge of the truth, called one of them “day” and the other “light”—for there is no day without light, and light accompanies day.

The splendor of justice and piety shone in their conduct; their constant friendship, knowing no change, prevailed. They were equal in age, though not unequal in charity, and delighted in their union, because the companionship of equals is sweeter and that of elders safer [Col. 0277A]. They were elders not through length of life but through maturity of character.

Would that the one who remains imitate the grace of virtue and faith of the other, whom God has approved and already taken with him into glory, so that, when the appointed times have passed, those whom divine love here made one may be one in the heavens [Note: Hugh died only in 1106.]

(1074.) While they were in Rome awaiting the day of their consecration, messengers of King Henry came to Rome, asking that the lord pope not consecrate them contrary to the custom of his predecessors, since they had received only the election of their bishoprics, not the gift of investiture through the king.

The pope then summoned the cardinals, explained the king’s embassy, and advised them what should be answered and what ought to be done. When they replied that this was the custom of the Church and was regarded as law, although no authority supported them in the matter, he nevertheless yielded to them in the case of the elected man of Lucca, agreeing to defer his consecration until he had received the investiture of the bishopric as a royal gift [Note: Gregory, by contrast, warned Anselm of Lucca in a letter not to accept investiture from King Henry on 1 September, indiction 12 (1073); Gregory’s Register I, 21. K.].

In the case of the man of Die, however, he refused to yield. During the first week of Lent he ordained him priest on Saturday and consecrated him bishop on Sunday [Note: Gregory wrote to the Count of Die concerning Hugh’s consecration in Register I, 69, on VII Kalends of April, indiction 12—that is, on the very day of his consecration, 16 March 1074; Easter was celebrated on 20 April. K.].

Because he saw that it was contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers for the king’s gift to prevail in the canonical election of a bishop—or rather, for it frequently to alter the election itself or even render it void—he prohibited anyone from presuming to do this in the same year [Note: In the following year, 1075, as Pagi demonstrated under this year. K.] at a Roman synod of fifty bishops, with a multitude of priests and abbots present, according to pontifical decrees and canonical institutions, under threat of anathema. He issued the decree in these words:

> “If anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any lay person, let him in no way be counted among bishops or abbots, nor let any hearing be granted to him as bishop or abbot. Moreover, we prohibit him from the grace of blessed Peter and from entry into the Church until he abandons the place which he obtained under the crime both of ambition and of disobedience, which is the sin of idolatry. We establish the same concerning lower ecclesiastical dignities.
>
> “Likewise: If any emperor, duke, marquis, count, or any secular power or person presumes to give the investiture of a bishopric or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the bond of the same sentence.”

In this he followed the examples of the Fathers, although this damnable custom had already grown strong over many cycles of years and had been converted into common practice.

For it is said that, in the seventh universal synod held under Pope Hadrian by five patriarchs and 350 Fathers, chapter 3:

> “Every election of a bishop, priest, or deacon made by princes shall remain void, according to the rule which says: ‘If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.’”

Likewise, in the eighth universal synod held under Pope Nicholas I by five patriarchs, chapter [illegible]:

> “In harmony with the earlier councils, this holy and universal synod establishes, decrees, and promulgates that the promotions or consecrations of bishops are to take place by the election and decree of bishops. No lay prince or powerful layman is to insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and unsuitable confusion or contention arise from this—especially since it is fitting that no layman possessing power should have authority in such matters, but rather should remain silent and attend to his own affairs until the election of the future pontiff is regularly received from the college of the Church.

> “If, however, a layman is invited by the Church to deliberate and cooperate, let him respectfully obey those who summon him to such a task. But whoever among secular princes or powerful men, or any layman of another dignity, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents.”

Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 6:

> “It is entirely manifest that if anyone is ordained without the will and knowledge of the metropolitan, this holy and great council determines that he ought not to be a bishop.”

Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, chapter [illegible]:

> “If any priest or deacon obtains the Church of God through secular dignity, let him be deposed, and let both he and his ordainer be cut off from communion in every way; let them be under anathema, like Simon Magus under Peter.”

In the election and consecration of the lord bishop of Die, therefore, the work of divinity is clearly shown, because through this occasion the truth of ecclesiastical election, which had been obscured for many previous years, shone forth in the holy Church of God under the papacy of the lord Gregory. Let prudent men therefore determine what right is reserved to emperors, kings, and princes in the election of a pontiff.

(Fol. 97'.) He entrusted his authority to him in Gaul, where the wicked plague of Simony was spreading most extensively; for there were exceedingly few who were not either Simoniacs, or ordained by Simoniacs, or invested by a lay hand [Note: Compare Gregory’s letter, Register I, 69. K.]. He strongly impressed upon him not to abuse the power granted to him, so that he might correct what had been corrupted, strike down what deserved condemnation, teach what was holy and honorable, and cause what ought to be taught to be practiced.

He also wrote to the prelates of the Gallican churches belonging to Saint Peter concerning the annual census owed to blessed Peter, in these words:

> “Gregory [Note: Absent from Gregory’s Register. K.], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all abbots and prelates of both monks and canons established throughout Gaul, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We scarcely believe that your fraternity, beloved brothers, is unaware that, according to the institutions of the earlier Fathers, certain churches of yours ought to pay annual censuses to blessed Peter and to us. But because some of you, partly through negligence and partly through stubborn greed, have so far done this less fully than you ought, we exhort them all to strive to amend their conduct and pay what is due [Note: The words “what is due” are erased.]. We admonish everyone to obey the apostolic command: ‘To whom tribute is due, tribute; to whom tax, tax.’
>
> “For each person should seek not what is his own, but what belongs to another. If the one who does not give his own as he ought is rightly rebuked, what sentence does he deserve who neither fears to seize what belongs to another nor hesitates to retain what is owed? The Lord says: ‘Whatever you wish that others would do for you, do also for them.’ And: ‘What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.’
>
> “Now, because we are sending our beloved son Hugh, bishop of Die, into Gaul to carry out our authority in various matters of ecclesiastical usefulness, and because we ought to trust no one more than a man whom we have found to have faithfully carried out everything entrusted to him by us, we command you to pay to him, for delivery to us, whatever you specifically owe us from your churches, and to make satisfaction for what you have retained.”

In that same year, the lord Jerento had taken the monastic habit at Casa Dei [Note: Saint-Robert-la-Chaise-Dieu, in the diocese of Clermont], on 1 November.

(Fol. 98.) Born in the territory of Vienne, to a father named Arnaldus and a mother named Agnes, he had been raised with diligent care and industry by the lord Hugh, father of the monks of Cluny. He was also instructed in letters by those who appeared to possess the greatest authority at Cluny.

When he came of age, however, he clung to the world and became as though deprived of the grace he had acquired, devoting himself entirely to frivolity and rejecting the rule of the canonical profession, while desiring instead the instruments of military life. He sought to grow in the world, not in God. His spirit, impatient of quiet and energetic in labor, could not be subdued.

In him was fulfilled that most truthful pagan testimony concerning a beardless young man [Note: Horace, Art of Poetry 161 ff.], which it is not our task to recall; whoever knows it may remember it. All who knew him testify this much about him: he was exceedingly light-minded in mind and body, yet agreeable, and so devoted to the world that his conversion already seemed miraculous to everyone.

When he saw that he had satisfied his desire, he began at last to grow weary of what had pleased him. Yet again, at the very beginnings of his conversion, while he desired to reach out toward unfamiliar things, he was beaten back in spirit and returned more readily to his accustomed ways. At last fear of death and Gehenna overcame the man.

He believed himself safe enough from danger under the protection of Christ. He set everything aside, abandoned everything, and went to Casa Dei, where at that time there were no riches and no glory; poverty alone was sufficient for its inhabitants. It was a vast wilderness, for twenty years earlier it had known no human habitation.

Saint Robert was its first inhabitant. He was prepared in mind and body to die to the world and live for Christ, as the little book written about his life more fully explains to those who wish to know [Note: Written by Gerald of Vienne and later polished by Marbod; see Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti, sixth age, vol. II, p. 183.].

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1043 [Note: The manuscript has M . . . c.; I have restored the number from the Chronicle of Maillezais.] he came there. He governed the house for nine years [Note: The manuscript reads “d . . . . c.”; namely, the church and the cell built near it.], and, having become a monk [Note: The word is cut off.], governed as abbot for fifteen years [Note: I supplied the number from the Chronicle of Maillezais.]. He departed to the Lord in 1067, designating his successor, Durannus, by name.

When Jerento came to this place, which the aforesaid Abbot Durannus governed after the death of the aforementioned father, he assumed the disposition and form of a disciple. Soon, however, he was compelled to become a teacher and, by order of the abbot and the entire congregation, undertook the office of prior.

He was saddened because he could not be what he desired to be; and because he was asked to preside over others, he marveled at himself and at what had happened to him. He remained in that office for three years under the abbot’s command, providing as far as he was able and knew for the necessities of Christ’s poor and laboring diligently for the welfare of the Church.

He received advancement through the ecclesiastical orders by the hand of the lord Hugh, bishop of Die, from the first up to the seventh. For Hugh, solicitous for the flock entrusted to him and faithfully maintaining the watchfulness required by his legation, held his first council at Anse and his second at Clermont [Note: It was held on 12 August, as is clear from Hugh of Die’s letter to Ralph, archbishop of Tours; Mansi XX, 483. Letters of Gregory to the bishops of Gaul, which appear below, show that this council was convened in 1076. K.].

At this council, after Stephen of Auvergne, the invader of the see of Le Puy, had been deposed because he had wrongly abandoned his see through ambition, and William, likewise a Simoniac and invader of the see of Auvergne, had also been deposed, the aforesaid Abbot Durannus was consecrated bishop of Auvergne (1077), after he had completed ten years of rule at Casa Dei. Two years later, at the request and by the will of the brothers, he relinquished the care of governance to Siguinus.

The third council was held at Dijon. He persecuted the Simoniacs, against whom he waged continual battle and an unending struggle; insofar as he could, he expelled them from the Church and replaced them with orthodox men.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1075, Grimoldus relinquished the abbacy [Note: Saint Vitonus] on Saint Nicholas’s day. Rodulfus succeeded him; his ordination took place on Saint Urban’s day.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1076, on 22 April, an earthquake occurred, on a Friday, under the fourteenth moon. In that year there was also a severe frost, from 7 December until 15 March.

(Fol. 97′.) He held a fourth council at Augustodunum (1077). For what reasons, however, the council at Edua was celebrated may be learned from the letter of the lord pope, whose text is as follows:

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Hugh, venerable bishop of Die, greeting and apostolic blessing. Gerard, the elected bishop of Cambrai, came to us, etc.”

[Note: In Gregory’s Register IV.22, chronological indications are added: “Given beside the Po, in a place called Ficarolo, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction,” that is, in 1077. See Gregory VII.]

(Fol. 98.) In accordance, therefore, with these apostolic mandates, a synod of venerable Fathers was convened at Edua, under the guardianship and protection of Christ the Lord, with the assent and approval of Hugh the duke, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1076 [Note: On the Ides of September. See the letter of Hugh of Die, Mansi, vol. XX, p. 492], in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory VII. Many distinguished men from France and Burgundy assembled there: bishops and clergy, abbots and very many monks.

The just and steadfast Duke Hugh ruled Burgundy. Rainardus, also called Hugh, governed the church of Langres, a man thoroughly trained in rhetorical studies, renowned for his talent, eloquent in speech, learned, approachable in conversation, and prudent in counsel. That same year Adalbero, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, had died; and, as usually happens in such circumstances, different elections concerning the appointment of an abbot were being advanced among the monks of the place. This monastery, adorned by an ancient lineage of religious observance, had flourished under the rule of Abbot William. But at that time, through the violence of Duke Robert, the negligence of the prelates, and the sloth of the subjects, it seemed somewhat diminished from its former rigor.

(Fol. 98′.) And because what had fallen within could not long stand firm without, there was little religious observance within and a heap of desolation without. Amid such difficulties, anxieties, and tribulations, those whose minds were sounder sought a suitable shepherd. The bishop of Langres and the duke, whose responsibility it was to provide for this, were present at the council; for, as has been stated, many honorable men had gathered there from numerous regions.

Among the others, the prior of Casa Dei was also present, to complain of the injuries inflicted upon his church. The bishop of Langres had known him before his conversion; now, seeing the transformation of his manner in both heart and body, he applauded and rejoiced with him, praising the divine power which had restrained, with the bridle of monastic order and regular gravity, the looseness of character he had possessed in the world. In him God had given an example to all who flee for refuge beneath the shelter of his wings: they should not despair of his mercy, since in this adopted son they recognized such abundant gifts of grace.

When the council had begun, and the Fathers were seated around, many matters advantageous to the holy Church were discussed, and their determination was prolonged into a second, third, and even fourth day. Manasses, the simoniacal usurper of the church of Reims, was accused at that same council by the clergy of Reims. He was suspended from office because, having been summoned to the council to clear himself, he did not come.

When he had prepared many ambushes for the canons of the church of Reims, his accusers, as they were returning from the council, he finally broke into their houses, sold their prebends, and plundered their goods. Later, after receiving a letter from Rome ordering him to come and clear himself at the council with six bishops, he went to Rome.

[Note: From Gregory’s Register V.17 it is clear that, besides Manasses, archbishop of Reims, Hugh of Besançon, Richer of Sens, Godefroy of Chartres, Richard of Bourges, and Rodulfus of Tours were accused.]

On the fifth day, because the see of Lyon was vacant after Humbert the simoniac had been expelled and made a monk in the Jura region, the archdeacon Gebuinus was elected, at the side of the lord bishop of Langres, to be placed over the church of Lyon. He was a man handsome in the integrity of his morals.

[Note: Letter of Hugh of Die, in Mansi XX, p. 488.]

The assent of the entire council acclaimed this decision, and the goodwill of the clergy and laymen of the church of Lyon who were present likewise desired it. He was seized from the altar to which he had fled and was carefully guarded, so that on Sunday he might be blessed according to solemn custom.

The bishop of Langres and the Langres clergy who were present grieved over this, because they seemed to have lost a man indispensable in ecclesiastical and secular affairs, upon whom they greatly relied. But the unanimous judgment of the council prevailed, because this had been determined and was pleasing in the sight of the Lord.

On the sixth day of the session, the bishop of Langres rose from among those seated around him. As a noble man of urbane eloquence, arranging his argument and making his hearers attentive and well disposed toward him, he spoke again of the loss inflicted upon the church entrusted to him. It was as though they had torn out his eye when they took away his archdeacon, in whom lay all his hope, in whom he found refreshment, and in whose love he possessed his consolation.

Thus, in an honorable sequence of words, lamenting the desolation of the mother and not concealing the orphanhood of the daughter, he recalled the ancient nobility of the church of Dijon; the zeal of Abbot William in the rigor of justice, the ardor of discipline, and the strict moderation of the order; and how now, after the abbot’s death, almost everything had been reduced to nothing. There was little religious observance within and heaps of tribulation without, so that the church which once had provided suitable pastors and rulers for many churches could not find one of its own to preside over it.

(Fol. 99.) He declared that he was taking refuge in the counsel of God and of good men, so that he might find some relief from his anxiety—since it was his responsibility to provide and arrange this—in appointing a ruler who would truly be called and truly be a ruler.

When he had finished speaking, and the legate had ordered him, with a promise of counsel and assistance, to say whom among those seated around he wished to place in this office, since no one suitable could be found in that church, he pointed with his hand to the prior of Casa Dei, and at the same time fell forward in his words and bent his knees:

“Give me,” he said, “this fish from the fountain of God.”

To obtain what he requested more easily, he joined Duke Hugh with himself in his prayers, so that through the duke’s goodness he might obtain what he distrusted his own ability to secure. All eyes, therefore, were directed toward the man who was being asked.

But the aforementioned legate of the Roman see knew that the man was sharp of intellect and spirit, and he knew the disorder of the inhabitants of the place and the instability of the land. Though he recognized how useful the man would be, he was reluctant to grant the request, out of consideration for him.

Those who had come from Casa Dei with the prior also tried, by whatever means they could, to oppose the election. But because it was the Lord’s will—he in whose hand are the hearts of kings—that the request should be granted, the authority and acclamation of the council proclaimed it.

While those men were making an uproar and preparing to use whatever force they could, the prior secretly prepared to flee and was already slipping away when he was seized and held. Weeping and deeply grieved, resisting and protesting even against his own supporters, he was brought back into the council and, amid the acclamation of those seated around, was handed over to the bishop of Langres. The bishop was ordered to guard him carefully and to have him led away alone, without the assistance of his companions.

When the presiding bishop admonished him to give thanks to God for what had been granted, to assist the man entrusted to him and worthy of honor, and to treat him honorably in all things, he invoked his predecessors—namely Bishop Bruno and Abbot William, whose praiseworthy fellowship and unanimity of charity were celebrated:

“If I do not assist this man, if I do not love him, if I do not treat him with the charity and gentleness with which Bruno treated William, may I be stripped of my honor.”

The brothers from Dijon had attended the council from its first day. Since they were unable to arrange the affairs of their church by themselves, they had permitted the election to be made by their bishop.

It was Friday when these things occurred. Since, as is customary, the consent of the brothers whom the elected man was to govern was required, the council determined that, if the brothers came on Sunday consenting to the election, the elected man should be blessed; if not, the election should be annulled and he should be allowed to return to his own people.

Accordingly, by rapid messenger the bishop and the duke sent word to Dijon. On the appointed day and at the appointed hour the brothers arrived, confirmed the election in writing, and did not hesitate to submit themselves to his obedience. With joy of heart and mouth they praised the Lord and, magnifying him, exalted his name together in one accord.

[Note: “with c.”]

(Fol. 99′.) On one day, that is, on Sunday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, they were consecrated at Edua amid the greatest rejoicing and celebration of all: the lord Gebuinus as archbishop of Lyon by the legate of the Roman see himself, and the aforementioned elected man as abbot of Dijon by the aforesaid bishop of Langres.

Many matters useful and advantageous to the holy Church of God were then discussed and settled in that council. When it was dissolved, each returned to his own place.

The bishop went to Lyon and installed the archbishop, whom the citizens were awaiting and longing to see glorified in heavenly glory. Amid the joy of the entire city, he placed him on the seat of his predecessors, Irenaeus and Photinus, who had lived in times long past.

Nor was the people’s rejoicing vain: it increased day by day and will have no end, because their kind shepherd, now blessed as a priest in the citadel of heaven, adhered while he lived to him who is the crown of the saints and their rejoicing, who is confined by no place, narrowed by no boundary, and enclosed by no end.

[Note: He died in the year 1082.]

Having received from him the reward of blessed immortality, he protects the citizens and all who flee for refuge to him. Since his dwelling has now been established in peace, and his habitation is in the heavenly Zion, let us pray to him that he may draw us also to himself by his holy prayers—we who do not begrudge his blessed joys—and obtain that our course may be directed and completed in goodness. May he, who was elected together with him in the same place and consecrated on the same day—would that it were with an equally blessed lot!—protect us with unwearied prayers and cause those who love and venerate him to be enrolled with him in heavenly glory.

Stephen, the usurper of the see of Le Puy, had prepared many ambushes for Hugh, the bishop of Die and legate of the Roman see. Finally, while Hugh was going to the council at Clermont, Stephen met him with the canons before the altar of Saint Mary and promised that he would obey his decisions concerning the bishopric if the examination of his case were postponed at the council.

The clergy likewise promised that, if the bishop refused to keep faith with his promises, they would abandon him and obey the Roman see.

After the council at Clermont had ended, Stephen was bound by the agreement he himself had made to resign the bishopric within fifteen days after being admonished by the aforesaid bishop of Die. Before the appointed days had elapsed, however, he had already reached Lyon and returned to Le Puy, taking only a few companions with him.

Because everyone suspected the tyranny of that usurper, the lord Hugh, during the celebration of Mass, after the Gospel had been read, fearlessly addressed the clergy and people. Stephen was absent. Hugh informed them of the agreement made with him and prohibited them by apostolic authority from obeying him in the future. He pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the absent man if he dared thereafter to continue to oppress the church.

The lord pope confirmed this excommunication by writing to the bishops of Gaul as follows:

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Gaul and to all the orders established under them, greeting and apostolic blessing, as is due according to their merits. We wish your charity to know …”

[Note: Given at Bibianello on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction, that is, in 1077. Register IV.19. See Gregory VII. A letter was also given on the same day, IV.18, to the canons of Le Puy.]

Our elected man, therefore, accompanied by the bishop of Langres, came to the place entrusted to him and entered the monastery of Dijon, which he had never seen before, on September 21. Since divine mercy had graciously enriched that place with such a provider and shepherd, from that time onward God’s goodness made itself known through many benefits.

He found the fervor of religious observance, which he had learned had existed among his predecessors, grown lukewarm through both the negligence of the prelates and the sloth of the subjects. The dwellings established for the use of the servants of God had become common to laymen entering and leaving; within there was little religious observance, and without heaps of tribulation.

He found the church in need of annual revenues, burdened by debt, and stripped of its ecclesiastical ornaments. He was consumed by the fires of anxiety and shaken by the waves of thought when he saw that he had undertaken to govern a church of great renown, great antiquity, and ancient dignity, while he found himself lacking every good and deprived within and without of every support by which, strengthened according to the rule, he could serve God with those entrusted to him.

This was his greatest and highest refuge: the words of the Lord, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). He knew that, as zeal for religion grew inwardly, an increase of external resources would also follow.

(Fol. 102.) Since his own people did not assist him equally in pursuing this, he went to Cluny and sought counsel and help from the abbot of Cluny. From that place, through his predecessor William, a man worthy of remembrance, the fountain of religious observance had flowed; from it he had afterward given abundant drink to all the neighboring churches, and also to those abroad and far away.

But he did not find there what he wanted. He sought God with a contrite and humbled heart, and he found him; for the Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and a troubled spirit is a sacrifice most pleasing to him.

This man, whom the bishop of Langres had called, at his election, a fish from the fountain of God, therefore returned to the fountain of God. He brought with him eight fish, gleaming with the virtue of the eight beatitudes. I would rightly call them fish because of the diligent meditation on spirituality to which they devoted themselves, as a fish devotes itself to the water of a river. He sent them into the fountain entrusted to him—a fountain he had resolved to cleanse, made marshy by the itching of vices—giving leaps over the waters with the wings of virtues.

From among them he appointed one prior and assigned the others their individual offices, so that by their example he might teach the rest to trample vices underfoot and desire virtues, and might accustom the unpracticed minds of the inhabitants to the ways of religious men.

But why linger over many details? Through his labor and diligence, with God’s grace leading the way, such great things were accomplished that anyone who had previously seen the place confused by the torpor of negligence, but now observed it flourishing through the happy exercise of virtues, would cry out in the joy of his heart: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11).

Many nobles and people of ordinary rank had already begun, at his admonitions, to abandon their possessions, submit themselves to regular discipline, deny themselves, and serve the one true King, God, under his leadership.

(Fol. 100.) The bishop of Die also celebrated a fifth council (1078) at the city of Poitiers.

[Note: On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, according to the letter of Hugh of Die to the pope, Mansi XX, p. 490. See the canons there, p. 498.]

From the letter he himself sent to the lord pope, we can infer how much God accomplished there and how much the devil attempted against the servants of Christ. Its text is as follows:

“To the lord and, by his merits, blessed Pope Gregory, Hugh, humble priest of Die, greeting in the Lord God.

At the council which, by God’s grace, we celebrated at Poitiers with some measure of fruit, we encountered many dangers on the journey, many adversities in the city itself, both in the council and outside it. For behold, the king of the Franks, hostile to himself because he was hostile to the King of heaven, first sent me a letter in which he confessed before the Lord that he earnestly desired to be called my son, and commended the authority of our legation with every glory and honor.

Then he sent letters to the count and also to the bishops under his jurisdiction, adjuring them with every kind of protestation and making them liable to his majesty and fidelity: the count, if he allowed us anywhere to celebrate gatherings and what might be called councils, as he put it; the bishops, if they attended or supported our decrees, by which we were striving to obscure the splendor of his crown and of the princes of his kingdom.

Taking courage from this adversity of the enemy of truth, they nearly dragged to the left those whom I had regarded as being on the right. I looked about me, and there was no one who recognized me.

For behold, the plague and disgrace of the holy Church, the archbishop of Tours, and with him the bishop of Rennes, perversely proud, occupied almost the entire council. The bishop of Rennes was proved guilty because he had been ordained bishop without first having been ordained a cleric. The cape of the pallium had first been promised and afterward given by the bishop of Angers, while the bishop of Rennes knew nothing of it, but before his ordination confessed another matter: namely, that when he was a knight, he had thrown an enemy knight from his horse, and that this man of Rennes, his companion, had pierced the fallen man with a wound; the man died because of that fall and wound.

We, therefore, yielding to the pleas of many, left him not yet deposed but suspended for the time being, because he was useful to his church, to be presented to your mercy and judged by you.

The bishop of Tours, however, was proved to have bought a deanery before becoming a bishop, although by the custom of his church no one could possess it unless he had already been or was about to become a priest. This bishop of Tours, therefore, who had in no way been canonically elected, could not obtain the king’s grant of the bishopric until his nephew had acquired the aforesaid deanery with money.

He was also accused of simony on another charge, because he had promised a forest to a certain knight if the knight would assist him in obtaining the bishopric. When the knight later brought this charge against him, the bishop of Angers was present and gave clear testimony concerning it before us.

It would take too long, father, to enumerate the disturbances and conflicts which this bishop of Tours inflicted upon us—how many, in what manner, and where: at one time speaking on behalf of the bishop of Rennes, never reasoning but always chattering; at another, shouting on his own behalf, with all the chatter and shameless boldness of his clerics.

For when they had almost bent the archbishop of Lyon to their defense, so that he would pray or speak against us on their behalf, their servants broke down the doors of the church and entered with armed hands and axes. They so violently disrupted the council that they would have put Brother T. to death had not the Lord crowned him with the shield of his goodwill.

Thus, leaving us with only a few companions and in disgrace, the bishop of Tours and his suffragans withdrew in proud tumult, disorderly and uncanonically.

On the following day, when a council had begun in the church of Saint Hilary, without any promise or prior offer of satisfaction for the injury, that dragon rose again like a roaring lion. He could not be heard for long. But drawing the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, we struck down his pride, and after issuing the decree in this matter, we also suspended him from priestly office.

Because he appealed to the apostolic see, where he asserted that he would clear himself of simony, we sent him to the apostolic see and left him to be deposed by your judgment.

The abbot of Bergues in Flanders was proved to be a simoniac and was deposed. The archbishop of Besançon appeared neither at the council of Edua nor at that of Poitiers, nor did he send a canonical excuse.

We have referred to you for judgment the bishop of Beauvais, who was accused of simony and who sold prebends after the decree; likewise the bishop of Noyon on account of his case; and also the usurper of Amiens, together with his ordainers, namely the bishops of Laon, Soissons, and Senlis.

We are also keeping silent about certain evils within our own ranks, because, God helping us, we shall come as soon as possible and tell you more conveniently in your ear the persons by whom they were inflicted.

As you instructed, we heard the case of the count of Anjou from his own mouth and judged it almost reasonable. But, not presuming to absolve him, we entrust the determination of the matter to the prudence of your holiness.

If we have written anything insufficiently to your holiness, your son Teuzo, our most faithful fellow worker in the Lord, will give you a fuller account of what we have decided concerning the bishop of Thérouanne together with the bishop of Poitiers.

Let your holiness therefore take care that it not be reproached against us any longer, so shamefully, that simoniacs or any criminals suspended, deposed, or even condemned by us gladly run to Rome; and that where they ought to experience a greater rigor of justice, they instead carry away what seems like mercy according to their own wishes. Those who previously did not dare to sin even in small matters afterward conduct the most profitable business through tyranny in the churches entrusted to them.

Pray for me, most holy pope, the unworthy servant of your holiness.”

(Fol. 100.) “To Lord Gregory, supreme pontiff, my father and lord, M., by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, the faithful submission of service and obedience and the devotion of prayer.

At your intervention and entreaty, lord, I restored to the lady M., the marchioness, everything that her predecessor had held from me; and I faithfully promise—and have promised—to provide my counsel, assistance, and refuge for defending the same. I am ready to carry out everything she had requested concerning the expulsion of G. and the reception of Count A.

To confirm all these matters, I was present in her city during the holy days of Pentecost with our faithful fellow bishop and your servant T., bishop of Verdun, having left behind, because of the necessity of his situation, all my own necessary affairs during that sacred season.

But I, your faithful servant, ready to obey you in all the rights of the Church, earnestly request and implore your counsel and judgment concerning G., the archbishop of Vienne, who degraded priests in my archbishopric and afterward restored them to rank; pretended to be a Roman legate when he was not; and, after filling his purse—not under the name of truth but in imitation of those who, as the Apostle says, consider religion a means of gain—returned from my diocese to his own.

Therefore, for the honor of God and of the Roman Church, correct this kind of presumption and deception as is proper, lest anyone thereafter presume to do anything similar in another’s jurisdiction.

I also inform you that two of my suffragan bishops, those of Laon and Soissons, consecrated the third, the bishop of Amiens, in my archbishopric, without my knowledge, since I was then in Rome. They acted first against your decree, by which you had determined that no one, at least among the archbishops, should consecrate as bishop a man who had received the gift of a bishopric from a lay person—especially since those very men had been present at the council of Augustodunum, where the lord Hugh, bishop of Die, promulgated and established this ecclesiastical decree of yours before everyone.

This act, therefore, in addition to what we have said, was contrary to authority and the canons. It was also unheard of, astonishing to all who think soundly, and more than can be expressed in words. If it pleases you, let it be declared void.

Indeed, since the consecration of a bishop cannot rightly be completed by any fellow bishops without his metropolitan, as you know, I wish you to know that I have prayed and earnestly entreated you to correct, for the honor of God and of yourself and of us, so rash a confusion of ecclesiastical order with the zeal of justice. Thus each man may know how to remain in his own rank and station and not rashly claim for himself what belongs to another.

I also beseech the goodwill of your honor to preserve for me the dignity which your predecessors preserved for my predecessors, the archbishops, and which they left to posterity in privileges and other documents. May you not allow the privilege which you yourself granted me to be annulled or infringed: namely, that I should answer to you when summoned and when not summoned, and to your Roman legates—not to transalpine men who, joined to the Romans, seek what is their own rather than what is Jesus Christ’s, and under honorable names serve their own greed rather than the Church of God.

Therefore, because of the shameful accusations and summonses of such men, may I, who ought to summon all the bishops of Gaul, be permitted to rely upon you without a summons from legates, until, God willing, I come to you at Easter.

Furthermore, I earnestly wish to beg and forewarn you that, since many things were recently done perversely and disorderly in the regions of my diocese during the absence of me, who had been staying with you, I cannot fail to use our ministry to correct them ecclesiastically. If any accusation concerning this is brought against me, do not quickly believe it or take it amiss against me; instead, reserve it until our presence before you, because I in no way wish to exceed the limits of my authority.

Since those who call themselves your legates are doing this, I have far greater right, through you, to correct matters belonging to our responsibility than anyone has to handle what belongs to another.

Concerning Count Ebal, who attempted to accuse me in your presence and, with deceptive words, commended himself and his fidelity to you, you have ample opportunity to know whose fidelity toward you is the more sincere: mine, who am ready to obey God and you in all things, or his, who both in your presence attacks the church of blessed Peter by himself and in our lands, through Manasses and his followers received into his castle, persecutes blessed Mary.

For Manasses, of whom we have spoken, to whom, at your command, we remitted what he had lost against us if he returned to his mother church, is weighed down by the consciousness of his crime. He neither wishes to return to us nor to be reconciled to the peace of the Church. Rather, together with his followers, he does not cease to tear apart the Church and me by words and curses, since he cannot do so by deeds.

Therefore, leaving Ebal aside—for I believe that you are exercising a just and apostolic sentence against him—I earnestly beseech your holiness concerning Manasses: either order him to return to his own church and cease thereafter to attack it, or direct the force of apostolic discipline against him, his supporters, and his accomplices.

Deign also to write a suitable letter to those who harbor them, so that they may either cease to retain them against the rights of the Church or recognize that they themselves have been punished by the same sentence.

One thing remains for me to tell you: the lord Hugh, bishop of Die, interdicted our bishop Drogo of the see of Thérouanne. He is of such advanced age that, after remaining for a long time in the priestly order before becoming bishop, he has now held the episcopal rank for more than sixty years and approaches his end at nearly every moment.

For this reason we wish to entreat you most earnestly to deign, by your command, to restore him to his ministry, lest—as we greatly fear—he die under this interdict.

Concerning your request that I send you some soldiers to escort the bishop of Paris, I inform you that I intended to send them. But Count Fulco of Arlon, returning from the city of Rome, told me on your behalf that you were willing to excuse me from sending the soldiers, so that I might carry out more vigorously and attentively in our region the affairs of the lady marchioness M.

Because this message came from you, the dispatch of the aforementioned expedition was omitted on our part.

May your holiness prosper, most reverend father.”

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ, Hugh, bishop of Die, and Hugh, abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing. Because, by divine disposition, we preside over the holy Church of God, etc.”

[Note: Register VI.3. Given at Saint-Germain on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the first indiction.]

Response of the same pope to Manasses, archbishop of Reims:

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, M., archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you request from the apostolic see those matters … I ask …”

[Note: The text was therefore not at hand. Given as above. Register VI.2.]

[Col. 0290C] He likewise celebrated a sixth council at Lyon, concerning certain matters whose examination the lord pope had entrusted to him, writing to him in these words.

[Note: It is missing from the Register.]

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Hugh, bishop of Die, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because divine mercy has restored peace to your Church, etc.”

See Gregory VII, letter outside the Register, no. 49.

When this letter had been brought to him and the place of the council had been fixed at Lyon, the archbishop of Reims was also invited, in accordance with the tenor of the letter, to come to that council to clear himself. The lord Hugh was then at Vienne for medical treatment.

The messengers of the aforementioned archbishop came to him, wishing to persuade him by many and great entreaties and gifts. For this purpose they offered him on the spot three hundred ounces of the purest gold, along with precious gifts for his household. They further wished to swear an oath that they would reveal this to no mortal: if he would permit the archbishop to clear himself with six bishops whom the archbishop of Reims himself would choose from among his suffragans, with the inquiry into his infamy set aside.

They added what they could scarcely hope for, but nevertheless wished to leave nothing unattempted: if the archbishop were granted the opportunity to clear himself alone, they would swear to give immeasurable treasures of gold, exceeding even any count, and would also swear not to reveal the matter to anyone.

The manly spirit of that legate rejected all of this. When the archbishop saw that the legate’s disposition toward money was unconquerable, he feared for himself, refused to attend the council, and was therefore deposed by synodal judgment—both because he refused to clear himself and because he evaded the hearings at Edua, Poitiers, and Lyon itself.

[Note: The synod was held between January 3 and April 17, 1080. See Gregory’s letters to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, in Register VII.12 and 20; compare also VIII.17–20.]

He also celebrated a seventh council at Avignon. At it Achardus, the usurper of the see of Arles, was deposed, and Gibilinus was elected archbishop of Arles, Lantelmus likewise archbishop of Embrun, Hugh bishop of Grenoble, and Desiderius bishop of Cavaillon. After the council ended, he took them with him to Rome, where they were consecrated by the pope.

[Note: Most of the page is blank.]

[Col. 0291B] (Fol. 102.) Setting these matters aside for the moment, let us now confidently proclaim the glorious deeds of the blessed father Gregory VII, pontiff of the Roman Church, that great Gregory whose flowers of eloquence, both univocal and equivocal, now spread their fragrance throughout the Church. He has now been placed in safety, has crossed the sea of the shipwrecked world, and has attained the secure harbor of eternal rest.

Let us devoutly recount what assaults of tribulation he endured for the holy Church, and how, while enduring them, he overcame them with marvelous and ineffable steadfastness, so that the Church might be free, chaste, and catholic, with divine mercy accompanying him.

He was born in the city of Rome to parents who were Roman citizens and, what is most important, religious; he was to be enrolled as a citizen of the heavenly court. From early childhood he was devoted to ecclesiastical offices. He cultivated his youth in the company of religious persons, not without definite signs that already marked him out as one who would become illustrious.

He mastered adolescence by adopting a purpose of holiness among those who despise the world, not without great indications of perfection. His youth, likewise dedicated to Christian warfare, strengthened by age as well as by sound doctrine and the firmament of truth, he devoted to the public interests of the holy Church under the distinguished guardians and prelates of the entire Christian name.

(Fol. 102′.) Because of the singular excellence of his outstanding intellect, Pope Nicholas promoted him to the archdeaconate of the mother church. Through his vigorous and praiseworthy administration of this office, he soon became known throughout the world and beloved by religious men.

When Pope Alexander died, he was summoned and elected to the highest summit of Christian government. As God, in exalting his chosen one, stirred the common devotion of his servants to bear the yoke he abhorred—a yoke which he had always avoided by flight of spirit and sometimes by flight of body—the gentle animal submitted his neck to his Lord.

He himself publicly announced the election made concerning him, writing to Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, in these words:

“Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, to D., abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino, greeting in Christ Jesus.

The lord Pope A. has died, etc.”

[Note: Given at Rome on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction. Register I.2. Paul of Bernried, Life of Gregory, 28. See Gregory VII.]

### (1073)

Consecrated, therefore, in justice and holiness, keeping watch in a marvelous manner through constant prayers for himself and for the flock entrusted to him, and compelled by the necessity of pastoral office, he strove with all his strength to correct the distorted hearts of the wicked toward the line of uprightness. Without respect of persons, he made God’s truth known to all, winning the love of all good people through the fervor of his zeal for God and the execution of justice.

But since light has no fellowship with darkness, he incurred the hatred and slander—indeed, the fiercest persecution—of ruined men [Col. 0292B]. Nevertheless, unwavering and immovable, he proceeded boldly along the royal road he had once entered, armed with the weapons of justice on the right and on the left.

First, encouraged by apostolic authority and by the truthful judgments of the holy Fathers, he burned with zeal to eliminate the heresy of simony and to command clerical chastity, as duty toward the office entrusted to him required. Let those who wish to hear listen, so that they may be fortified; and let those who do not wish to hear listen, so that they may be put to shame: let them hear with what a free and Catholic voice this champion of the Church thundered against the mad barking of the impious, their impious schemes, and their criminal audacity.

For when almost everyone sought his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and preferred to adhere to the discipleship of Simon rather than preserve Christ’s poverty [Col. 0292C] in the unity of faith; when the ministers of the divine sanctuary likewise refused to cast off the shameful pollution of lustful contagion, usurped and introduced contrary to right and law; and when the investiture of churches was also unjustly usurped by laymen—(1078, November 19)—he, for the common usefulness and necessity of the Church, convened a synod in the Lateran palace. With archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious clerics and monks who feared God seated around him, he deliberated concerning the matters written above and other benefits of the Church, and promulgated these decretal chapters [Note: [Col. 0292D] Mansi XX, 509, and Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores V, pp. 314–315 (Patrologiae, vol. CXLVIII).]:

> Whoever among the soldiers, etc.

These are the synodal decrees of the most blessed pope, suitable for correcting morals, consonant with the decrees of the holy Fathers, distilled as dew from heaven, to be impressed upon, embraced, and upheld by all the faithful; issued at the command of justice, strengthened by courage, promulgated by prudence, and endowed with the virtue of temperance.

But while the perverse stumble over these standards because of the perversity of their lives, they call them altogether impossible—grave, difficult, and, because they do not wish to be corrected, things from which they shrink in fear of amendment [Col. 0293A]. O foolish mind! O filthy wickedness and most wicked filth! If the morals of ruined men, who refuse correction, go astray in folly, will justice be silenced, piety be trampled underfoot, and the sword of ecclesiastical punishment be prohibited from blood?

Woe to the ruler whom the sentence of this curse shall mark! “Cursed,” it says, “is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10). To withhold the sword from blood is to restrain the word of preaching from killing carnal life.

For this reason, since he wished the holy Church of God to be chaste, free, and Catholic; since he wished to expel from God’s sanctuary the heresy of simony and of neophytes, together with the foul pollution of lustful contagion, the members of the devil began to rise against him [Col. 0293B]. They dared to lay hands upon him even to the shedding of blood, and attempted in many ways to overthrow him, so as to disgrace him either by death or by exile. Thus conflict arose between kingdom and priesthood, and the tribulation of the holy Church of God grew more grievous than usual.

### (Folio 104)

For Heinricus, son of the emperor Heinricus, swollen with arrogant pride against God and against the Roman Church, the mother of all Catholics, because his wicked life was hostile to the decrees of the holy Fathers and canonical institutions, rose up against God and against his Christ. He wickedly became a rebel against ecclesiastical sanctions, inciting the members of the devil against him and arming against him, through threats, flatteries, terrors, and gifts, everyone whom he could, after forming a conspiracy with many bishops from Lotharingia and from beyond the Rhine [Col. 0293C].

[Note: [Col. 0293D] “While [the pope was] still appointed”—“confirming,” from Gregory’s letter to the Germans, preserved in Udalric’s codex 146, in the Saxon Annalist, and in Bernried’s Life, chapter 78. Compare Berthold, year 1075.]

While the same most holy pope was still serving in the diaconate, when an unfavorable and dishonorable reputation about Heinricus was being spread everywhere, he was often admonished by letters and messengers—because of the imperial dignity, respect for his father and mother, and hope for his correction—to remember his illustrious lineage and imperial dignity, and to order his life according to conduct appropriate to imperial power, so that he might show himself a king and emperor in his morals and demonstrate it in his deeds.

But as Heinricus’s age advanced, so too did his wickedness. Once elevated to the pontifical order, the pope, by the authority of the office entrusted to him, urged him each day with much greater concern to improve his life [Col. 0293D]. Day after day, Heinricus promised in words that he would accept the pope’s admonitions, making excuses on the grounds of his fleeting and fragile youth; yet in reality, and through the accumulation of his offenses, he utterly trampled them underfoot, following the evil counsel of those in whose hands the court lay.

From this point he became more inclined to crimes, and, rushing from one precipice to another, he was carried along crooked paths. The most blessed pope therefore decided to summon his intimates to penance—those whose machinations, by introducing simoniacal wolves in place of shepherds into bishoprics and monasteries, had defiled the innocence of the Church with a wicked heresy. He would receive those who came, but separate from communion in the body of Christ [Col. 0294A] and from the fellowship of the faithful those who refused, so that in this way he might separate Heinricus from their seizure of power and their evil counsel. He admonished him to expel those whom he had excommunicated from his household, table, every intimacy, and every form of fellowship.

Meanwhile, as the cause of the Saxons against him grew stronger, and he saw the strength and defenses of the kingdom threatening to fail him, Heinricus sent the pope a letter full of supplication and humility. In it he performed penance for his offenses, promised amendment, and pledged his obedience and faithful assistance against the rebels. He later confirmed this before the pope’s legates, Humbert, bishop of Praeneste, and Girald, bishop of Ostia, swearing it upon their consecrated stoles, which they wore around their necks. The text of the letter is as follows:

### (Folio 103b)

> To the most watchful and most desirable lord Pope Gregory, distinguished from heaven with apostolic dignity, Heinricus, by the grace of God king of the Romans, offers the most faithful expression of due service.
>
> Since kingdom and priesthood, if they are to remain properly administered in Christ, always require one another’s assistance, it is surely necessary, my lord and most loving father, that they should in no way disagree with one another, but rather cling inseparably to one another, joined most closely by the glue of Christ. For thus, and in no other way, the bond of perfect charity and peace, the Christian harmony of unity, and the state of ecclesiastical religion are preserved together.
>
> But we, who by God’s consent now bear the ministry of the kingdom, have not rendered to the priesthood in every respect the justice and honor that were due. Indeed, we have borne not without cause the sword given us by God as the avenger of authority, yet we have not drawn it against the guilty with judicial severity, as was just.
>
> Now, however, touched somewhat by divine mercy and having returned to ourselves, we accuse and confess our former sins to your most indulgent fatherhood, hoping in the Lord from you that, absolved by your apostolic authority, we may deserve to be justified.
>
> Alas, we are criminal and unhappy! Partly through the incitement of flattering youth, partly through the imperious freedom of our power, and partly through the deceptive fraud of those whose excessively misleading counsels we followed, we have sinned against heaven and before you; and now we are no longer worthy to be called your sons.
>
> For we not only invaded ecclesiastical property, but also sold the churches themselves to any unworthy persons, embittered with simoniacal gall and entering not through the door but from elsewhere; nor did we defend them as we ought. But now, since without your authority we cannot correct the churches by ourselves, we earnestly seek your counsel and aid concerning these matters and all our affairs as well. Your command shall be most diligently observed in everything.
>
> At present, especially, we ask that the Church of Milan, which through our fault is in error, be canonically corrected by your apostolic rigor, and that your authoritative judgment then proceed to correct the other churches [Col. 0295A].
>
> We, therefore, by God’s will, shall not fail you in anything, and we humbly ask your fatherhood to be graciously and cheerfully present to us in all things. Before long you shall receive letters from us with our most faithful men, through which, God granting, you shall hear more fully what remains to be said on our part.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Stenzel I, 348, confirms that this letter was written in the middle of the year 1073.]

### (Folio 104)

But after he had engaged in battle and obtained victory [Note: [Col. 0295D] “But”—“could deceive God,” from the letter to the Germans.], he returned to the dog’s vomit, broke his promises, received the excommunicated back into communion and favor, and did not shrink from the Church’s disorder.

The pious pope, however, still believing that Heinricus’s spirit should be tested, sent him admonitory letters, urging him to remember the Lord his God and to remember his promise; not to dishonor the one who honored him, and not to believe that he could deceive God [Col. 0295B]. He added that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Sparing him and preserving toward him the moderation [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-inis* has already fallen away in c.] of apostolic discipline [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-rvans* has already fallen away in c.], he could justly have punished him for this crime alone [Note: [Col. 0295] The word *scelere* has already fallen away in c.] according to the decree [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-retum* has already fallen away in c.] of Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0295D] Mansi VIII, p. 33.], in which, writing [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-ens* has already fallen away in c.] to the emperor Anastasius, chapter . . . , he says:

> Just as no one who has accepted a participant in perversity [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-versitatis* has already fallen away in c.] can fail likewise to be judged perverse [Note: [Col. 0295] The words *non pa-* have already fallen away in c.], so neither can perversity be rejected [Note: [Col. 0295] The beginning *pot-* has already fallen away in c.] when an accomplice, a follower [Note: [Col. 0295] The words *complice sectatore* have already fallen away in c.] of perversity has been admitted.
>
> Certainly, by your laws [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-hus* has already fallen away in c.], persons conscious of crimes [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-cii sus-* has already fallen away in c.] and receivers of robbers are bound by an equal [Note: [Col. 0295] The word *pari* has already fallen away in c.] punishment of judgments [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-ntur* has already fallen away in c.]; nor should he be deemed free from the crime [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-mandus est* has already fallen away in c.] who, although he has not committed it himself, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-en* has already fallen away in c.] has received the friendship [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-em* has already fallen away in c.] and alliance of the perpetrator.

And this was Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0295] The word *papa* has already fallen away in c.].

Moreover, in this father . . . according to what Gregory says in his Decrees [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-tis* has already fallen away in c.], chapter 299, this was worthy of praise [Note: [Col. 0295] The word *erat* has already fallen away in c.]: that he possessed vigilant concern [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *sollicitu-* has already fallen away in c.], not negligent; careful correction [Note: [Col. 0295] The ending *-reptio* has already fallen away in c.], not harsh; yet one was so tempered by the other [Note: [Col. 0295] The words *-c alterum* have already fallen away in c.] that the good had, through love, something they could do [Note: [Col. 0295] The word *boni* has already fallen away in c.; the word *facerent* has already fallen away in c.], and the wicked, through fear, something they could flee [Note: [Col. 0295] The beginning *fu-* has already fallen away in c.].

He also sent special letters, sealed with his bull, to certain bishops of Gaul and Germany [Note: [Col. 0295D] To Manasses of Reims, concerning whom see above; to Isembert of Poitiers, Register I, 73; II, 2, 23; to Roger of Châlons, I, 56; to Dietwin of Liège, II, 61; to Rainer of Orléans, III, 17; V, 9, 20; to Liemar of Bremen, II, 28; to Hermann of Bamberg, I, 84; to Heinricus of Speyer, V, 18. K.], so that their slack hands might be strengthened and their weak knees made firm for raising up the Church from its downfall, eliminating heretical depravity, and restoring the chastity of its ministers [Col. 0296A].

### (Folio 104)

These men, displaying excessive fickleness and taking from the king’s stupidity and from the power of darkness an opportunity to rebel, did not fear to disregard the commands of the apostolic see. They clearly proved themselves not shepherds of sheep but hirelings.

One of them was Otto, bishop of Constance. The authority of the aforementioned Roman pontiff rebuked him for such reckless audacity, sending letters to him and to the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0295D] This refers, unless I am mistaken, to Register I, 60, dated 18 March, indiction 12, and II, 19, to Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, dated 6 December, indiction 13—that is, in 1074. To the same recipient, concerning Hermann, bishop of Bamberg, and Werner of Strasbourg, who favored the king’s party, he wrote letters in Register III, 2 and 4; and to Otto of Constance in Register I, 60, dated 15 March, indiction 13, that is, in 1075. K.].
