When Otto disregarded them, the pope rebuked his obstinate spirit by sending him a second letter, in these words [Note: [Col. 0296D] These letters are lacking from Gregory’s Register; they are preserved in Paul of Bernried’s Life of Gregory, chapters 37–38, and in Udalric’s codex 142–143. K.]:

> “Gregory VII, servant of the servants of God, to Otto, bishop of Constance, greetings and apostolic blessing. It has been reported to us” etc. See the letters of Gregory VII, Patrologia, vol. CXLVIII.

But since Otto had not only dared to command things contrary to the apostolic see, but also wished to resist its commands and refuse obedience, let us hear the letter sent by the pope to the clergy and people of Constance. It clearly states that no loyalty or obligation arising from oaths is owed to anyone who has been disobedient to the apostolic see:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and laity, great and small, residing in the bishopric of Constance, who love the Christian law, greetings and apostolic blessing. We have sent to our brother Otto, your bishop, etc.” See Gregory VII.

### [Col. 0296C]

Likewise, to Robert, count of the Flemings:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., count of the Flemings, greetings and apostolic blessing. On behalf of almighty God and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we ask you, etc.” See the same place.

Likewise, to the laity, for carrying out the statutes stated above:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the dukes Berthald, Rodulf, and Welf, greetings and apostolic blessing [Note: [Col. 0296D] Of Carinthia and Swabia; Welf’s name is absent from Register II, 45, and from Paul of Bernried, chapter 39. Dated at Rome on January 11, indiction 13—that is, 1075. K.]. We know that your prudence,” etc. See Gregory VII.

Likewise, to all clerics and laymen established in the kingdom of the Germans, concerning the same matter [Note: [Col. 0297D] This letter is absent from the Register; it is read in Paul of Bernried, chapter 41.]:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all clerics and laymen established in the kingdom of the Germans, greetings and apostolic blessing. (Folio 106') We have heard that certain bishops,” etc. See Gregory.

Since there are therefore some who say that these commands of the lord pope are unprecedented—namely, that schismatic bishops should be forcibly restrained by secular powers so that they cease from their office, and that their office should not be accepted—let us examine the deeds of the Fathers and see, for the instruction of those who hear, whether anything similar is found in the sequence of the divine Scriptures [Col. 0297B].

Certainly nothing new has occurred here. This is not the first temptation of the devil against the holy Church, nor is this the first medicinal defense against him.

Let us see what Pope Pelagius, a man of great glory in Christ and in the Church, of great authority and grace, says about Paulinus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, ordained by the bishop of Milan contrary to canonical custom. He writes to the patrician John:

> “When rereading the letters of Your Excellency, we were deeply grieved by the injury inflicted upon you through the presumption of wicked men. But because we know that, although your soul was preserved from the contamination of schism through the wickedness and pride of others, we have given thanks to almighty God, who is accustomed to bring good even out of the deeds of wicked men [Col. 0297C].
>
> For we do not believe that it happened without his doing that senseless and most perverse men rushed so far as to prevent you from their pollution, believing their division to be the Catholic Church. Thus, through God’s mercy, even without their knowing it, it happened that, rescued from the fellowship of schismatics, you were preserved in the Catholic Church, which you love.
>
> Although, therefore, your benefit has arisen through their crime, do not permit the presumption of wicked men to grow unchecked. For if what they presumptuously did to your honor is not restrained by punishment, there can no longer be any doubt what they may attempt in lesser matters.
>
> Exercise, therefore, the authority owed in such cases, and let them be restrained by coercion, lest their spirit for committing such things again grow stronger. Indeed, by God’s will they presumed such things against you so that, when you corrected them, you might, with God’s favor, protect others from their crime” [Col. 0297D].

And after some intervening material:

> “Remove such men from that province. Use the opportunity granted you by God to crush the treacherous. This can be done more fully if the authors of the crimes are sent to the most merciful prince—especially the invader of the Church of Aquileia, who, accursed both in schism and by a schismatic, can obtain neither the honor nor the merit of a bishop.”

Pelagius to Valerian:

> “What we asked of you, we now ask again: send Paulinus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, and that bishop of Milan to the most merciful prince under suitable guard [Col. 0298A]. The former cannot in any way be a bishop, since he was made contrary to all canonical custom, and must not be allowed to destroy others as well; the latter, who dared to ordain him contrary to ancient custom, must undergo the punishment prescribed by the canons.”

Likewise, Pelagius to John the defensor:

> “Our brother and fellow bishop Eleutherius complains that his clerics proudly resist him contrary to the canons, and that, although they promised us under a written guarantee deposited in the registry that vigils would be celebrated daily in his church, they contemptuously refuse to fulfill this. Therefore, let your Experience restrain those whom it finds to be obstinate with due rebuke [Col. 0298B], and compel them by every means to keep watch.”

Likewise, Augustine, on John, homily 11:

> “God wishes to stir up the powers against schismatics, against those who destroy the Church, and against those who insult Christ. Let no one be surprised, since God stirs them up so that Hagar may be beaten by Sarah.
>
> Some are surprised when Christian powers are moved against the detestable destroyers of the Church. If they were not moved, how would they render an account to God for their authority? Let your Charity pay attention to what I say, because it concerns the rulers of this age: in their own times they should desire their mother Church, from whom they were born spiritually, to be at peace.”

And shortly afterward:

> “King Nebuchadnezzar decreed, saying: Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be put to death, and his house shall be destroyed. See how a foreign king raged lest the God of Israel be blasphemed—he who was able to rescue three boys from the fire.
>
> Yet they do not wish Christian kings to rage because Christ is insulted—Christ by whom not three boys, but the whole world together with its kings, is rescued from the fires of Gehenna. Who, after this, will blame the secular powers if they restrain schismatics, destroyers of the Church, those who trample upon the divine King, and violators of canonical constitution?” [Col. 0298C]

### (Folio 107)

Heinricus therefore became a despiser of these and of the other holy decrees, failing to restrain the impulse and appetite of his youth and placing excessive trust in the evil counsels of fools. These men, corrupted and made abominable in their iniquities [Col. 0298D], refused to live blamelessly and could not bear to be reproved.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] “He was being sent”—“he compelled him to deny,” from the letter to the Germans.]

Frequent embassies from the lord pope were sent to him, sometimes by letters and sometimes by religious persons and, indeed, by his own faithful men. Through them he was secretly summoned to penance for his crimes—crimes horrible to mention, yet known to many and publicized in many places. For these he deserved not only excommunication, but also to be deprived of every honor of the kingdom without hope of restoration. He was also urged to separate from his association those whom he had excommunicated and whose counsel was driving him headlong into crimes, lest by communicating with those with whom it was forbidden to communicate he pass into their fellowship, whose sacrilegious communion he did not abhor [Col. 0299A].

But he retained the odor with which he had recently been imbued [Cf. Horace, Epistles I, 2, 69].

How much he valued the letters and words sent through the legates is revealed by his deeds [Note: [Col. 0299D] Supply “he valued”], since he could not be recalled from his crimes to amendment. Rather, seized by the madness of a gnawing conscience, he did not desist until he had caused nearly all the bishops of Italy and of the German lands whom he could reach to suffer shipwreck concerning the faith of Christ, compelling them to deny the obedience owed to blessed Peter and to the apostolic see, and the honor granted by the Lord Jesus.

But the just man does not know how to favor the rich, nor does he do anything for the sake of winning approval. Therefore the lord pope powerfully rebuked him who, having strayed from the truth, was behaving arrogantly, knowing that the rule of truth is not to respect the person of the powerful in judgment [Col. 0299B]. Accordingly, because he recognized their crimes, he spoke freely in rebuking them.

Heinricus, however, taking it badly that anyone should reprove or correct him, and seeking occasions to withdraw from his friend—for justice cannot share in iniquity—began to criticize the conduct of that most blessed pope Gregory VII, so that he might turn against Gregory the charges of simony that he feared Gregory would punish in him.

He even dared, surrounded by the officers of a faction, to discuss the expulsion of the Roman pontiff, whom, as Pope Symmachus says, God has reserved without question to his own judgment. The sinner in his pride attempted—shame upon it!—to drive from the judicial seat the one who had been granted power to loosen the bonds of sins and break the fetters of crimes, so that he might put in his place someone like himself, one of his own accomplices [Col. 0299C].

But “there is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30). Human judgments condemn the one whom God approves, and human schemes attack in vain the one whom God protects and approves.

Thus the king—though he should be called not a king but a tyrant—departed from the Roman Church, becoming an unhappy member of him who is king over all the sons of pride.

The prophecy of Jeremiah was truly fulfilled in him, in which Jeremiah, taking upon himself the condition of all human life, complains in lamentation, saying: “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lam. 3:15). For a drunk man does not know what he suffers. Whoever is intoxicated with wormwood both finds what he has consumed bitter and yet does not understand the bitterness with which he is filled [Col. 0299D].

### (Folio 107')

So this man, abandoned to his pleasures and through them delivered over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood: he endures bitter things for love of this world, yet through the blindness of desire and pride, like the insensibility of drunkenness, he does not recognize the bitterness itself.

His counselors became foolish and ignoble, and their slavery of mind drives them from a share in the eternal inheritance. For “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.”

They became ignoble because “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34): always in snares, always in chains, never free from fetters, because always in crimes.

Although they practice the deeds of the wicked, they nevertheless occupy the places of the just [Col. 0300A]. They consider themselves sons of those whose offices they outwardly administer through their desire for honor. Yet they are not sons of those whose places they occupy, but of those whose deeds they perform.

They are therefore foolish because they do not understand true wisdom; they have become ignoble because they are not renewed by any freedom of spirit.

Placed over the faithful, they oppress them rather than govern them, because under the name of shepherds they pursue profits from religion. Under their leadership, God is mocked, faith is made a reproach, truth a crime; and the more just someone is, the more despised he becomes, while the more worthy of praise he is, the more abominable he is considered.

Although they appear to be in the Church, they flee far from it—not in the distance of their steps, but in the quality of their morals.

Who these instigators of evil are, these supporters and accomplices of royal iniquity, these most filthy and reckless corrupters of ecclesiastical chastity, the mother Church has learned sufficiently and more than sufficiently through her own labors, tribulations, torments, and calamities [Col. 0300B].

I mean the bishops—if indeed they should be called bishops—who, unwilling to live blamelessly and refusing to be reproved by their superiors, violate canonical institutions and refuse to be marked by canonical denunciation. They themselves have also prejudiced the universal mother Church and the apostolic see, advancing beyond all doubt even to contempt of the one who speaks to his disciples and, through them, to the rulers of the holy Church, saying: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

They do not remember the decrees of Pope Julius, by which it was established [Col. 0300C] that anything opposed to the authority of the apostolic see should have no force, since that same see, as the voice of truth testifies, first obtained primacy. It would not be called first if it had another above it. It is also the head of all the churches, from which all have taken their origin.

It earned its primacy not through synodal or otherwise contrived institutions, but through the gift of the Lord, who said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

These are the words of Julius concerning the primacy of the apostolic see, to which he said that the final judgments of all bishops and the privileges of convening synods had been reserved.

But the new dogmatists despise apostolic judgments and cast aside the holy Scriptures. They profess what comes from their own hearts and, handed over to the desires of their hearts, receive the reward of their crimes in their own rejection by Christ [Col. 0300D].

At the council held at Worms (1076, January 24), from which all the calamity we suffer arose, they cast off the yoke of discipline [Leg. II, p. 44], although the lord pope had not yet issued any sentence of anathema against them, and they composed a document repudiating holy obedience, renouncing the preeminence of the apostolic see with proud and sudden recklessness.

### (Folio 108)

This first leaven corrupted the entire mass of the Church.

This assembly was held between the Nativity of the Lord and the following Lent, with intervals sufficiently long that whatever was done there could be reported to Rome during the synod.

On the feast of the Nativity of the Apostle Andrew (November 30), before the very feast of the Lord’s Nativity, when Heinricus was at Bamberg, such harmony still prevailed between kingdom and high priesthood that the deposition of the pontiff of that city and the substitution of another would have been regarded as obedience to the lord pope.

Therefore, the man who before the Lord’s Nativity was of such great eminence in the Church that changes of ranks were made at his nod was, only a few days after the Nativity, proscribed without being summoned or heard and, so far as they were concerned, deposed.

From the day on which he had been held in such esteem by everyone, he received no embassy from them until the one arrived in which it was said: “Descend, descend; we forbid you every right of the papacy” [Leg. II, p. 47].

Let heaven hear and be astonished; let earth understand and tremble. Let it be read whether, since the Christian religion began, anyone has presumed such a thing. Let it be stated by what canons, what rules, what reading, or what precedent this was attempted.

It is not read or said to have been heard under heaven that anyone could depose a pope and deprive him of the power granted to him. For the Roman pontiff cannot merely not be deposed; he cannot be judged by anyone at all.

Let the authors, accomplices, and supporters of such great presumption hear what Pope Symmachus thought concerning the privilege of the Roman pontiff. In his decrees, chapter 2, he says:

> “God wished the causes of other men to be settled through men, but he reserved the pontiff of the apostolic see, without question, to his own judgment. He wished the successors of blessed Peter to owe their innocence to heaven alone and to present an inviolate conscience to the scrutiny of the most searching investigation” [Col. 0301C].

Pope Gelasius says:

> “The holy canons have decreed that appeals from the whole Church be brought for examination before this holy see, while the see itself is not to be appealed from by anyone at all. Thus it is to judge the whole Church, but it is not to come under the judgment of anyone; nor have they ever commanded that it be judged by any judgment. They established that its sentence should not be dissolved, and rather commanded that its decrees be followed.”

Writing to the emperor Anastasius, he says in chapter 3:

> “Things established by divine judgment may be attacked by human presumption, but they cannot be conquered. Would that the audacity of those who resist were not as harmful as what was established by the author of sacred religion himself cannot be overthrown by any power.
>
> Let certain men, therefore, cease, I beg you, in your times, under the pretext of the Church’s disturbance, rashly to pursue what is forbidden, lest they in no way attain what they wickedly desire and fail to observe their proper measure before God and men” [Col. 0301D].

Pope Melchiades, in a letter sent to the bishops of Spain, speaks as follows concerning the privilege granted to blessed Peter and his successors in the place of the Lord:

> “The Lord granted this privilege to blessed Peter, his key-bearer, and entrusted it to him alone in his own place. His prerogative is to be inherited and upheld by all his successors for future times, because there was also a certain distinction of power among the apostles.
>
> Although the election of all was equal, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter to take precedence over the others and prudently to arrange the causes and questions that came before him. This was done by God’s ordinance so that later generations would not claim everything for themselves, but would converge upon the one see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and receive there the conclusion of the institutions whose beginning they had received there, lest they ever disagree with their head” [Col. 0302A].

Pope Adrian likewise says in his decrees:

> “The highest prelate shall be judged by no one. For it is written: ‘The disciple is not above his master.’”

### (Folio 108')

Let the inventors and plotters of this new presumption and presumptuous novelty also hear from the words of that same Pope Symmachus what they deserve, so that they may be put to shame and, if only, show reverence in penitence. Chapter 2 states:

> “If any presbyter, deacon, or cleric should attempt, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, to offer a subscription for the Roman pontificate, promise documents or petitions, provide an oath, promise any support, or presume to deliberate and decide the matter in private gatherings, let him be deprived of the dignity of his place and of communion.
>
> Let the same sentence condemn the one who, while the pontiff is alive, is convicted of having sought or attempted the matter in any way, as has been said.”

That apostolic judgments are strengthened by Peter’s equity, Pope Innocent says:

> “Peter’s privilege remains wherever judgment is pronounced according to his equity.”

Gregory likewise says, among other things, in his decree, chapter 10:

> “No one is permitted or able to wish to transgress the commands of the apostolic see, nor the administration of its disposition, which the charity of all ought to follow.
>
> Let anyone who wishes to oppose the apostolic decrees be cast down in sorrow over his ruin and henceforth have no place among priests; let him be expelled from the holy ministry. No one need concern himself with his judgment, since he is already condemned by the holy and apostolic Church and by its authority, and because of his disobedience and presumption there is no doubt that he must be driven out by the greater excommunication.
>
> This is the one to whom the discipline of the holy Church had been entrusted. He ought not only to have obeyed the commands of the ruler of the holy Church, but also to have instructed others not to transgress them. Let him therefore be excluded from divine and pontifical offices, since he refused to obey the apostolic commands.”

### [Col. 0302D]

Pope Sylvester likewise speaks concerning the first see, which is not to be judged, in chapter 6:

> “No one shall judge the first see, which desires justice to be tempered. For it shall be judged by no judge—not by the emperor, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people.”

Pope Boniface, concerning the power of the Roman Church and those who act arrogantly toward it, writes as follows to Eulalius, bishop of Alexandria:

> “From long ago and from the beginning we received such confidence from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that, with the Lord’s help, we have authority to assist the universal Church and to correct and amend by apostolic authority whatever is harmful. For the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be disregarded when he says: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Col. 0303A]. These words are proved by the results of events, since the Catholic religion has always been preserved without blemish in the apostolic see. Desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the constitutions of the Fathers, we anathematize all who, in their arrogance against the holy Roman and apostolic Church, raise their necks, following the apostolic see in all things and proclaiming all its ordinances. And in every respect I hope that I may deserve to be in one communion with you—that communion which the apostolic see proclaims—in which there is the complete and true integrity and perfect solidity of the Christian religion. I promise that all who do not agree with the apostolic see are separated from communion with the Catholic Church, and that their names are not to be recited during the sacred ministries [Col. 0303B]. I condemn both my predecessors and my successors, and all who strive to annul the privileges of the holy Roman and apostolic Church.”

And that no one may appeal from the Roman Church, Gelasius writes to all the bishops, chapter 4 (fol. 109′):

> “The whole Church throughout the world knows that the most holy Roman Church has the right to judge concerning all matters, and that no one is permitted to judge its judgment. For it belongs to that Church to judge concerning every part of the world, while no one is permitted to appeal from it. Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, without any preceding synod, has the power both to absolve those whom an unjust synod had condemned and to condemn those whom it ought to condemn; and this, certainly, because of the primacy which blessed Peter, the apostle of the Lord, both always held and will always hold by the Lord’s word [Col. 0303C].”

Pope Callistus likewise says in his decretals, chapter 1:

> “No act performed without regard for the discernment of justice against the discipline of the Roman Church may be considered valid by any rational judgment.”

Nicholas, presiding over a universal synod, also said concerning contempt for the apostolic see:

> “If anyone despises the doctrines, commands, prohibitions, sanctions, or decrees salutarily promulgated by the prelate of the apostolic see for the Catholic faith, for ecclesiastical discipline, for the correction of the faithful, for the amendment of sinners, or for the prohibition of impending or future evils, let him be anathema. If the one who despises apostolic decrees is anathema, what does he deserve who does not fear to extend an unlawful hand against the majesty of the venerable apostolic name, holy to all [Col. 0303D] [Note: ‘unlawfully’ was deleted.]? And so that at last we may strike with the invincible sword of God [Note: ‘of the sword’—conjectural supplement from an abbreviation], let the assailants of the truth [Note: ‘assailants’ deleted], the defenders of perversity [Note: ‘perversity’ deleted], hear from the words of blessed Peter [Note: ‘Peter’ deleted], the apostle, what they deserve, since they have acted prejudicially against him. ‘If anyone,’ he says, speaking to Clement, ‘grieves this man, he does not receive Christ, who entrusted him with the teaching chair; and just as one who has not received Christ will be judged not to have received the Lord’s brother [Note: ‘brother’—conjectural supplement], so he himself will not be received into the kingdom of heaven [Note: ‘-mquam’ deleted].’”

The same writer [Note: ‘-pra’ deleted], speaking above about bishops, says:

> “Those who harass bishops, or strive to remove or condemn them, appear through the prophet to condemn the Lord himself, and therefore they are condemned until satisfaction is made [Col. 0304A].”

And shortly afterward:

> “Whoever resists these men resists God, and whoever inflicts injury or insult upon them does so against God, by whose legation they are joined.”

Are these things sufficient, or do we still seek further testimonies from the Scriptures to refute the folly of the opposing party [Note: the ending “-ris” was deleted]? Let Jerome also come forward; let him too say what the one who criticizes the judgment of the apostolic see deserves. Let the malicious hear, so that they may be instructed; let the just and well-disposed hear, so that they may be strengthened and confirmed in the Catholic faith. Writing to Damasus, he says among other things:

> “This is the faith, most blessed pope, which we have learned in the Catholic Church and which we have always held. If anything has perhaps been stated in it with insufficient skill or insufficient caution [Col. 0304B], we desire that it be corrected by you, who hold both Peter’s faith and Peter’s see. But if this confession of ours is approved by the judgment of your apostolate, whoever wishes to blame me will prove himself ignorant or malicious, or even, by a non-Catholic designation, a heretic.”

According to these words of the most blessed Jerome, which no believer doubts are founded upon truth, whoever criticizes apostolic judgments is branded with heretical infamy.

Augustine, likewise, when discussing who should and should not be counted among heretics, says among other things:

> “The Apostle says: ‘Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction, knowing that such a person is subverted and sins, being condemned in himself’ (Titus 3:10). But those who defend their own opinion, even though it is false and perverse, without obstinate contentiousness—especially when they have not acquired it through the audacity of their own presumption but have received it from parents who were deceived and had fallen into error—and who seek the truth with cautious diligence, ready to be corrected when they find it, are by no means to be counted among heretics” [Col. 0304C].

These words plainly show that those must undoubtedly be counted among heretics who strive to defend their false and perverse opinion, and the error fixed in their infamous minds and devised through the audacity of presumption, with obstinate contentiousness: rejecting the truth, withdrawing from the embrace of Mother Church, splitting unity, rejecting sound doctrine, rending their mother’s entrails with the thorns of errors, and, by teaching what is foreign to what has been proclaimed to the universal Church, what it holds and teaches, not fearing the apostolic sentence of anathema. Unless they repent, their destruction is certain.

If they say that authority must be obeyed because “there is no authority except from God,” and that “whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance,” let them hear what that same Augustine says in response:

> “‘Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.’ But what if it commands something you ought not to do? In that case, disregard the authority by fearing the authority. Observe the ranks of human dignities themselves [Col. 0305A]. If a governor orders something, must it not be done? Yet if he commands contrary to the proconsul, you do not disregard authority; rather, you choose to serve the greater. The lesser ought not to grow angry because the greater has been preferred. Again, if the proconsul orders one thing and the emperor another, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must serve the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, what do you judge? The greater authority must be obeyed. ‘Forgive me,’ you say: ‘you threaten prison, but he threatens hell.’ From this point you must take up your faith as a shield, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the enemy.”

But perhaps our lords—and would that they were our brothers—had either not read the apostolic decrees and canonical sanctions, or, having read or heard them, had passed them by with deaf ears [Col. 0305B]. Or—and this is more credible—they had both read and heard them and committed them to tenacious memory, but wished to be regarded as faithful assistants and collaborators of their lord, the emperor, to whom they had sworn and to whom they had rendered homage through the laying on of hands and oaths.

Let those who are of this kind consider what Pope Cornelius says concerning the oaths of bishops. Cornelius the bishop to Bishop Rufus:

> “Up to this point we have by no means known that an oath was undertaken in right faith by high priests or by the rest of the faithful [Note: ‘hactenus’ and ‘fidelibus’ deleted], but we have discovered that they swore voluntarily [Note: ‘sed’ (‘but’) deleted]. Therefore we do not know of an oath being offered to bishops [Note: ‘-mentum’ deleted], nor ought it to be made by anyone [Note: ‘a quoqu-’ deleted].”

Pope Pius, speaking about various kinds of oaths [Note: ‘de’ deleted], says [Note: ‘Qui’ deleted]:

> “Whoever swears by the hair of God or by God’s head [Note: the ending ‘-verit’ was deleted], or confesses blasphemy against God in any other manner [Note: ‘confesses against God’ deleted], if he is from the ecclesiastical order [Note: the ending of ‘order’ deleted], let him be deposed; if he is a layman, let him be anathematized. And if anyone swears by created things [Note: ‘swears’ deleted], let him be punished most severely and endure whatever the synod has judged [Note: the ending of ‘endure’ deleted].”

Pope Cornelius also says in the same place:

> “These are the institutions of the holy Fathers [Note: ‘These are, he says’ deleted]. Whoever regards them as worthless or presumes to violate them [Note: the ending of ‘presumes’ deleted] is an enemy of his own soul, because no one does anything against the prophets, no one against the apostle [Note: ‘no one’ deleted], and no one against the Gospel [Note: ‘does anything’ deleted] without danger.”

Therefore let the ministers and stewards of the churches who have passed judgment against the Roman Church hear what Pope Gelasius decrees concerning the privileges of emperors and of all the priests of the holy Church of God:

> “If the emperor is Catholic, let me say this without offending him: he is a son, not a prelate of the Church. He has the privileges of his own power, which he has obtained from God for administering public affairs, and, not ungrateful for God’s benefits, let him usurp nothing against the disposition of the heavenly order. For God wished those matters which are to be arranged for the Church to belong to priests, not to the powers of this world; and, if they are faithful, he wished those powers to be subject to his Church and its priests. Let the emperor not claim another’s right or the ministry assigned to someone else, lest he rashly set himself against the one from whom all things have been established and appear to fight against the benefits of him from whom he has received his own power. The Almighty God wished the clergy and priests of the Christian religion to be ordained, examined, and received—not by public laws or the powers of this world, but by pontiffs and priests—when they return from error. Christian emperors ought to subject their executions of authority to ecclesiastical prelates, not place them above those prelates. These things,” says Gelasius, “he states concerning the privilege of emperors and of all the priests of the holy Church of God.”

We could also draw abundantly from the writings of the orthodox Fathers—Augustine, Jerome, and the very river of Roman eloquence, blessed Ambrose—many examples concerning oaths that are unjust and ought by no means to be observed, against those who say that kings, emperors, and all lords to whom an oath has been sworn must be obeyed, whatever they do and whatever they command. For their error they claim as a defense what is written in Peter’s epistle:

> “Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh” (1 Peter 2:18).

We answer them briefly: we do not deny that a fitting submission is owed to the harsh, but we do not obey harsh masters when they command what is improper [Col. 0306B]. As for what is said, “with all fear,” we understand it as the fear of which it is said concerning its possessor: “Whoever fears God will do good” (Ecclesiasticus 15:1); and: “Blessed is the one who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in [Col. 0306C] his commandments” (Psalm 111:1); and: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 10:10).

Paul likewise says in his Epistle to Titus:

> “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, and to be ready for every good work” (Titus 3:1).

Explaining this passage, blessed Jerome concluded as follows:

> “If what the emperor and governor command is good, obey the will of the one commanding. But if it is evil and savors of opposition to God, answer with the words from the Acts of the Apostles: ‘We must obey God rather than human beings’ (Acts 5:29).”

And, on the Epistle to Titus:

> “Let servants be subject to their masters in all things that are not contrary to God; so that, if a master commands what is not opposed to the holy Scriptures, the servant may submit to the master. But if he commands what is contrary, let the spirit obey rather than the master of the flesh” [Col. 0306D].

Likewise, in the same work, when beautifully commanding servants to obey their masters, he added: “as to Christ,” so that a servant should not listen to his natural master if he wishes to command things contrary to the precepts of the Lord.

Let these few [Col. 0307A] words, then, be said against those who arrogantly and insanely rave against God: they attempted—shame upon them!—to cast down the divinely chosen vicar of the heavenly key-bearer, accepted by all Christendom, distinguished by the holiness of his conduct, and confirmed by the length of his tenure, because they cannot see how to make him conform to their own vices.

Divinity itself destroys their wicked attempts and impious schemes. Like the Egyptian king’s wonder-workers [*significi*, reading uncertain], they strive to obscure by their own deceptions the works performed by God’s power; they transform themselves into angels of light; they display an appearance of piety while denying its power. Corrupted and made abominable in their vanities, “their throat is an open tomb; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Romans 3:13).

“They shall come to nothing like water running away,” because “they have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs” (Isaiah 59:5). It would have been better for them not to receive the counsels of malignant spirits or to hide within the inner chambers of their hearts what they had conceived—things represented by the eggs of asps—than, for the sake of the desires of this world, to carry out temporal deeds of any kind that benefit neither themselves nor others, because they are founded on no stability, as represented by spiders’ webs.

But because they trusted themselves excessively and distrusted the authority of the Scriptures, they did what they ought not to have done, and what the teaching foretold has happened to them. For it follows:

> “Whoever eats of their eggs will die,”

because whoever receives their counsels extinguishes the life of the soul within himself.

> “And what has been laid will break forth into a basilisk [*regulus*],”

because through the counsels of iniquity that have been received and nourished, it grows into the body of Antichrist; through the counsel of their wickedness, hidden in the heart, it is nourished toward complete iniquity. Of such people it is rightly added:

> “They have sucked the head of asps” (Job 20:16),

because they first received the hidden suggestions of unclean spirits through perverse persuasion. But now the tongue of the viper has killed them: captured by the demons’ gentle stealth, they have been slain by the poison of violent temptation.

And why should I say merely that they have been slain? They are already buried; they are already crushed beneath the weight of despair; the faithful are already burdened by the stench of their worst habits and habitual wickedness—for they are four days dead (John 11:39).

Now not only their sisters, relatives, and parents, but also Mother Church, who gave them birth and nourished them with the milk of faith, endures their stench—would that it were not fuel for eternal fire. Yet the right hand of Christ is powerful enough both to raise them up and to restore firm faith in them, for it can raise up children for Abraham from stones [Col. 0307C].

Because Mother Church groans at their condemnation, unable to endure the tortures of her own entrails and the parricidal hands of her former children [Col. 0307D], let us now see what the friend of the Bridegroom did: how he prohibited his children from communion and participation in their society, and finally how, unless they repented, he threatened the guilty with punishment by the sword of anathema.

First, he judged that the malice of their standard-bearer and instigator of evil ought to be struck, and thus that vengeance should be driven into the body of the wicked with the sharpened and unsheathed point of the sword.

Heinricus, then, whose mind had been constricted by the torpor of iniquity, the cause of dissension and the seedbed of malice and wickedness, was excommunicated in the Roman synod by the most blessed pope for his iniquities, together with his accomplices and supporters, and was deposed from the kingdom (February 22), so that affliction alone might give understanding to hearing, and punishment open the eyes that guilt had closed [Col. 0308A].

For impiety does not recognize the evils it has committed until it has begun to be punished for those same evils. All who had sworn allegiance to him, or were about to swear it, were likewise released from the bond of their oath by the permission and authority of apostolic liberty.

Let Agnes, empress and Heinricus’s mother, answer when questioned why and how this was done by the apostolic see. For she writes as follows to Altmann, bishop of Passau:

> “Agnes, by the grace of God whatever she is, sends greetings and most loving affection to Altmann, bishop of Passau. With God’s help, let my safety be known to your fatherhood; yet I am afflicted by the greatest grief because I see the greatest danger threatening the Church, through my son’s excessive credulity toward the words of fools. Since you commanded me to report to you what has now taken place in the Roman synod, I shall report it [Col. 0308B].
>
> “The envoys of my son, the king, came to the synod and said publicly on my son’s behalf to the apostolic lord that he should rise and abandon the apostolic see, which he had acquired not canonically but by robbery. The Romans immediately seized them. Likewise, the archbishop of Mainz and all the bishops of that party sent letters through the same envoys, declaring that henceforth they would show no obedience to the apostolic lord; the bishops of Lombardy decreed the same under oath.
>
> “Therefore the lord pope deprived all who had freely consented of office and communion, while he granted those who had offered their assent under compulsion a delay until the feast of Saint Peter. But he deprived my son the king of his royal dignity and struck him with the sword of anathema, because of these acts, because he communicates with excommunicated persons, and because he refuses to do penance for his crimes; and he released from their oath all who had sworn to him [Col. 0308C]. Farewell.”

(Fol. 111.) Here is a mother’s testimony concerning her son’s presumption, rebellion, and iniquity; her fear concerning the danger threatening the Church; and her refutation and reproach of those whose factious counsels devised and attempted these things. What will the adversaries of the Catholic party say in response to this? What will they answer or bring forward?

Behold, they have accepted as their king the man whom they taught to exalt himself above the heights of the clouds—or rather, whom they taught to rise up against the Lord and Christ—not as a king but as a tyrant of arrogated power.

For, as Isidore says in the book of the *Sentences*, a king is so called from acting rightly. If he rules piously, justly, and mercifully, he is rightly called a king. If he lacks these qualities, he is not a king but a tyrant [Col. 0308D].

And, as the same author writes in the book of the *Etymologies*:

> “In ancient times all kings were called tyrants; but afterward, by ruling piously, justly, and mercifully, they acquired the name of kings. But for those who rule impiously, unjustly, and cruelly, the name applied is not ‘king’ but ‘tyrant.’”

Therefore a man is rightly called a king who knows how to govern both himself and his subjects well and, by governing, to pacify them; who subjects the observance of royal dignity to holy religion; who takes greater delight in serving the Lord in fear than in ruling the people in pride; in whom gentleness moderates anger and kindness adorns power; who [lacuna] holds [them] to be loved rather than feared [lacuna], so that he does not abandon mercy [Col. 0309A]; who remembers above all that he is a son of the holy Catholic Church, so that he makes his rule beneficial to her peace and tranquillity throughout the world.

For how do kings serve the Lord in fear except by prohibiting and punishing with religious severity whatever is contrary to the Lord’s commands? Otherwise, according to Augustine, he serves in one way because he is a human being, and in another because he is a king. Because he is a human being, he serves by living faithfully; because he is a king, he serves by enacting with appropriate vigor laws that command what is just and prohibit what is contrary.

“For no affairs,” says Pope Leo, writing to the empress Pulcheria, chapter 10, “can be secure in any other way unless both royal power and priestly authority defend what pertains to the divine confession.”

If, therefore, the emperor recognizes that he is a sheep of the Lord’s flock; if, among the sacred rites of the altar, he submits himself with reverence to the hands of priests; if the priest preserves the worship of the blessed Trinity through preaching, while the emperor preserves it through his faith; if he boasts not so much that he rules the world as that Christ rules him; if he remembers by whom he was made, to whom he is being invited, how much has been granted to him, and how great a benefaction he owes to God; if he mercifully tempers terror with gentleness and his threats with hope; if he always looks upward; if he obtains mercy from God—then, I say with John Chrysostom, he reigns with Christ; indeed, within Christ’s kingdom he administers human affairs.

It is therefore a royal ministry to govern God’s people and rule them in justice and equity; to be the defender of churches, the guardian of orphans and widows; to free the poor from the powerful and the needy who has no helper [Col. 0309C]; and, with blessed Job, to crush the jaws of the wicked and take away the prey from his teeth; to be a father to the poor, an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame. Whoever does these things will be blessed by the hearing ear, and the widow’s heart will find consolation in him.

This tyrant, then, found the pit of his downfall when he raised himself higher than was fitting to the summit of ostentatious power. For, as the most gentle teacher Gregory says:

> “He becomes like the apostate angel when a human being disdains to be like another human being.”

In saying this we do not attack royal power, which is good in its proper order, but it requires the cautious life of the ruler. It is good if a person knows how to take from it what helps and defeat what tempts him.

Impatience is always a friend to power and even commands power when it is badly subject, because power carries out what impatience itself feels. Would that this power had acted so perversely that it had not passed its poison to others; would that its own death had been enough for it and that, through its poisonous persuasions, it had not also killed the lives of others.

Nevertheless, the lord pope pursued its perversity out of zeal for right striving, not out of the passion of rage. But, in accordance with Jeremiah, “the refiner has refined in vain,” for “the wicked have not been consumed” (Jeremiah 6:29).

For behold, the fire of apostolic excommunication, refining externally, brought the punishment of a harsh burning, and yet it did not burn away the guilt of error [Col. 0309D].

He has been scorched by the fire of anathema and separated from participation in Christian communion; but unless he returns to the unity of Mother Church, from which he had strayed through the error of schism, he can be burned but cannot be cleansed [Col. 0310A]. For there is a place for gold where it is refined; whoever departs from that place, even if he shines, has nevertheless ceased to be gold. Nor does he shine with the splendor of beauty unless, restored and incorporated into the Church, he has first burned in the workshop of charity.

But the Lord did not desire the works of the wicked, and therefore “he brings on night, and they are crushed” (Job 34:25). For the wicked are crushed in the night when they are condemned through the confusion of their preceding sins.

Explaining this, blessed Gregory says:

> “Every sin that is not quickly wiped away by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin. For a sin that repentance does not wash away, by its own weight immediately drags a person to another sin. Thus it comes about that it is not only sin, but both sin and the cause of sin. From that vice the subsequent guilt arises, by which the blind mind is led so that it becomes entangled in something worse. But the sin that arises from sin is no longer merely sin; it is both sin and the punishment of sin, because by a just judgment the Almighty God darkens the heart of the sinner, so that, by the deserving of the preceding sin, he also falls into other sins. This is carried out above according to an ordered disposition, but below in confused iniquity: the preceding guilt becomes the cause of the subsequent one, and again the subsequent guilt becomes the punishment of the preceding one.”

We can observe all of this in this member of the head of all the wicked and in his accomplices. Because, although they knew God, they committed the sin of pride through understanding; they have been blinded so that they do not understand what they are committing. They have been handed over to a depraved mind, so that they think they can tear down the rights of divine authority, destroy the sanctions delivered by the Lord himself, employ presumption unheard of throughout the ages, and profane, overturn, and cast down that divine mystery, whatever it may be [Col. 0310C].

In them, surely, this is taking place: guilt is struck by guilt, so that the very growth of vices becomes the punishment of sinners. Hence the psalmist says concerning the Lord:

> “Dispatches through evil angels; he made a way for the path of his wrath” (Psalm 77:49).

For their hearts, weighed down by their former deserts, were justly permitted to be deceived by subsequent persuasions of malignant spirits; and, as they are deservedly drawn into guilt, their guilt is heaped up in punishment.

(Fol. 112.) Once Heinricus had been separated from communion with the body of the Church and deprived of royal dignity, the principle that the Catholic Church had always held—what had remained stable and unshaken from the beginning of Christianity until these monstrous times, namely, that one must not communicate with the excommunicated—was violated by his supporters and accomplices, men like himself. Thus what is written in the book of Daniel was fulfilled:

> “Iniquity went forth from the elders and judges who appeared to rule the people” (Daniel 13:5).

For these men, who are called heralds of the truth and to whom the words of God have been entrusted for proclaiming to the people, devised an unheard-of destruction of the Church by communicating with a criminal king who had been excommunicated for his crimes, contrary to the decrees of the holy canons and the institutions of the earlier Fathers. By teaching that people should not abstain from him and plunging themselves into the same abyss through such rashness, they failed to understand that those who dissent from the head—that is, from the see of blessed Peter—by adhering to the excommunicated are, according to the sanctions of the orthodox Fathers, bound with them by an equal condemnation.

Thus says the Council of Nicaea:

> “If anyone among the bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any member of the clergy is found to communicate with excommunicated persons, let that person also be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rule of the Church.”

Fabian likewise says in chapter 1:

> “If anyone, knowingly disregarding the rules, speaks with an excommunicated person even in his house, or prays with him, let him be deprived of communion.”

They did not revere Augustine’s statement:

> “Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however laudably he may think he is living, by this one crime alone—that he is separated from the truth of Christ—does not have life in himself; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him.”

This, then, is the deposition of Heinricus, formerly king; this is the excommunication of the tyrant and his supporters. And because, according to the prophetic words, “the rod of God was not for correction over them” (Job 21:9), deceit was directed by their hand, just as Scripture testifies concerning the head of them all:

> “He will act and prosper” (Daniel 8:12).

The more closely they clung to evil, the less they understood the good they were losing. For the light of truth, the more it is neglected where it has been received, the more God permits it neither to be sought nor recovered once lost. And the wicked raise themselves up in empty joy all the more as they grow stronger in worse things, as it is written:

> “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

It belongs to a perverse mind to rejoice in the iniquities over which it ought to weep. A sound mind, by contrast, feels the wound of sin.

Those who rejoice in crimes drag as many as they can toward their own destruction. While remaining beneath sins, or adding sins to sins, they believe they are heaping up an abundance of virtues. Of such people the prophet aptly says that they regard dwelling among thorns as a delight (Job 30:7), because they lift their perverse minds toward joy from the very place where they bear the thorns of sins.

Despising God [Note: “Contempnentes” corrected or noted as “Contepnentes”], they do not at all perceive how great is the evil they are committing. They regard remaining among thorns as a delight because they endure hardships out of love for the present life, and yet, bound by the affection of excessive desire, they consider the labor of that endurance a pleasure.

The tyrant Heinricus’s supporters therefore turned his deposition and excommunication itself into a song, and the lord pope became a proverb among them. When they heard that the king had been excommunicated, they were beside themselves with astonishment; they proclaimed that this was impossible and declared it unheard-of in the world. Let us therefore hear from them that one great secret which either forbids a king to be corrected or refuses to allow a contumacious person to be canonically censured. Why do they shamelessly oppose the pride of kingship to the servants of God? If it lacks justice, that same kingship was certainly called brigandage even by the holy Fathers.

For blessed Augustine says in the fourth book of *The City of God*: “If a good man serves, he is free; if an evil man rules, he is a slave.” And blessed Ambrose says: “Wretched is the slavery of serving sins, and every sin is slavish; innocence is free.” And blessed Augustine, in the same book, shortly afterward says: “When justice is removed, what are kingdoms except great brigandages? For what are brigandages except petty kingdoms?” (Fol. 112'.) The band itself consists of human beings; it is governed by the command of its leader, bound together by an agreement of association, and its plunder is divided according to an agreed law. If this evil grows through the accession of such depraved men to the point that it occupies places, establishes a seat, seizes cities, and subjugates peoples, it more plainly assumes the name of a kingdom. What also contributes to this is not the removal of greed but the addition of impunity.

Who, then, would deny that brigandages must be restrained? If, when justice is removed, kingdoms are nothing other than great brigandages, and the very band of brigands appears to be ruled as though by the command of a prince presiding over crimes, then the prince of brigands must be restrained, and the brigandages themselves must be restrained, so that, with justice added, the laws of kingdoms may be ordered and brigandages cease.

But surely kings were not excepted when the King of kings himself, speaking of ecclesiastical discipline, said to the prince of the apostles: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19), and so forth. Let kings, then, fear being bound on earth by those whose judgment God confirms in heaven. Let them remember that they are not above the Church but within the Church—provided, that is, that they do not, merely because they are called kings, become unrestrained in a whirlpool of vices or in tyranny, but, because they are called Christians, imitate Christ through purity of life and the gentleness of one who rules. For, as blessed Augustine says, the person who is not a Christian according to the true faith and catholic discipline does not follow Christ.

But if the adversaries of the opposing party, mocking us, should ask which bishops have rebuked kings, let them hear what Pope Gelasius says in the letter that he wrote to the bishops of Dardania:

> “The prophet Nathan,” he says, “openly and publicly denounced before King David’s face the error he had committed, did not conceal that he himself had committed it, and subsequently absolved him once he had been corrected through his confession. Ambrose, of blessed memory, priest of the Church of Milan, publicly and openly suspended the emperor Theodosius the Great from communion and brought royal power back to penance. Pope Leo, of blessed memory, freely reproved the emperor Theodosius the Younger when he exceeded the bounds through the brigandage of the Council of Ephesus. Pope Hylarius, of holy memory, publicly and in a loud voice restrained the emperor Anthemius before the blessed apostle Peter, when Philotheus the Macedonian, relying on the emperor’s intimacy, wished to introduce into the city assemblies of various sects, to prevent this from happening—so much so that the emperor promised under oath that these things would not be done. Simplicius, also of holy memory, and after him Pope Felix, of holy memory, are known to have repeatedly rebuked not only the tyrant Basiliscus but also the emperor Zeno for these same offenses. The latter could have been brought to submission had not the instigation of the bishop of Constantinople inflamed him; having become a participant in an alien communion, he necessarily continued to foster the condition into which he had fallen, preferring to resist by the force of his betrayal rather than return, once healed, to what was salutary, as the outcome itself proved. (Fol. 113.) Pope Innocent, also of holy memory, excommunicated the emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom from the Church. (Fol. 112'.) Behold, recently, the great and distinguished priest Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, together with many Catholic priests, steadfastly resisted Honoricus, king of the Vandals, when he was raging, enduring every extreme; even today they do not cease resisting their persecutors. (Fol. 113.) It is also manifest that, when the barbarian heretic Odoacer then held the kingdom of Italy and ordered certain things that ought not to be done, by God’s provision we in no way obeyed him.”

Thus far Gelasius.

It remains for us, too, when examples are sought, to bring forward testimonies suitable to the matter and the period from canonical decrees and authoritative Scriptures, and, if we cannot offer gold, silver, or precious stones in the house of God, at least—since things are going so well for us—to offer goats’ hair. To return, then, somewhat to what was said above: Pope Fabian, of blessed memory, ordered the emperor Philip, the first of all the Christian emperors, to stand among the penitents when he wished to communicate at the Paschal festivals in the life-giving mysteries, until he had washed away through the lamentations of penance the many sins reported against him. That most devout ruler accepted this gladly.

As we have already said elsewhere, his humility attacks the arrogance of our kings all the more sharply because he received ecclesiastical discipline so devoutly when Christianity was so rare and recent, whereas they, in a Christianity already mature and widespread, refuse even to hear it. Blessed Ambrose excluded the great emperor from communion, admonishing him to do penance for the blood he had shed. When the emperor Eugenius involved himself in sacrilege concerning the restoration of the altar of Victory, Ambrose likewise rejected his gifts and expelled him and his associates from the Church.

Pope Gregory III, of holy memory, also removed Rome, Italy, and all rights both of the state and of the Church in the western regions from obedience to the emperor Leo and to the empire established under him. John of Damascus, likewise—not a pope or bishop, but a monk and priest, and an excellent teacher—subjected that same Leo, together with the bishops of the East, to anathema.

Pope Zacharias, of blessed memory, deposed Hilderic, the last king of the Merovingian line, from the kingdom and ordered him to be thrust into a monastery; he decreed that Pippin should be elevated to the honor of kingship. Stephen, the Roman pontiff and his successor, likewise established that same Pippin in the kingdom and absolved all the Franks from their oath of loyalty. (Annals of Fulda, 834.)

The emperor Louis the Pious, having gone to Alsace, encountered there his sons together with Gregory IV, the Roman pontiff. At the judgment of the bishops he laid down his arms and lived for some time in penance, deprived of his position—or, as it is read in the *Deeds of the Franks*, confined. (Ibid., 863 and following.) Let anyone who wishes to know what was done by Pope Nicholas against King Lothar and his accomplices and supporters on behalf of Queen Tietberga, who had been repudiated, and Waldrada, the adulteress who had been introduced in her place, read the same volume.

Germanus, bishop of Paris and of holy memory, also excommunicated King Aribert because, having abandoned his lawful wife, he had joined two women to himself in marriage. Since he was not corrected, he was struck down by God’s judgment and died. Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople and a Catholic man, considering the difficulty of the situation and the intolerable incursions of the barbarians, deposed the emperor Michael because, having engaged the barbarians several times, he had returned without triumph and without glory; together with the empress Procopia and her children, he clothed him in monastic garb.

(Fol. 113'.) To pass over innumerable testimonies, let those who wish to alienate kings from ecclesiastical discipline and thereby from God say whether, throughout the entire sequence of the divine Scriptures—in which the heretics of various sects are read to have been condemned—emperors appear to be excepted. For example, when the Arians are condemned, is the emperor Constantius, or Valens, or any king stained with Arian filth excepted?

But now let the lord pope himself, who cuts rotten and dead members away from the unity of the body, offer and hold out against those who criticize, mock, and hurl curses the shield of defense. Thus, writing to the faithful residing in the kingdom of the Germans who doubted the excommunication of the king, he says:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, dukes, counts, and the other faithful who cherish the Christian faith in the kingdom of the Germans: greeting and apostolic blessing. We have heard that some among you doubt the excommunication that we imposed upon the king,” etc.  
> [Note: This is also found in Udalric’s manuscript 146 and in the Bernried manuscript, chapter 78.]

(See among the letters of Gregory VII, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.)

He also wrote another letter, full of the sweetness of discernment, piety, and mercy, for the reconciliation of certain persons. Thus, if anyone wished to return to God, he would have the remedy of reconciliation prepared before his eyes, lest illness prevent anyone from benefiting because he could not hasten to the apostolic see; and so that there might be no fellowship of communion with the excommunicated:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all brothers in Christ—bishops, abbots, priests, dukes, princes, and soldiers—and to all who truly cherish the Christian faith and the honor of blessed Peter and live in the Roman Empire: greeting and apostolic blessing. We give thanks to almighty God,” etc.  
> [Note: It is found in *Register*, book IV, no. 1.]

Thus, for the reconciliation of the king and of the others alienated from the Church, the devout father gave these instructions to the faithful. Such was the splendor of justice within him that he placed his own safety second, in order to restore the Church, his mother, to her ancient freedom. The dangers to his own safety that he had undertaken, or was about to undertake, for the sake of justice did not move him.

(Fol. 116.) He had so formed his mind that he did not regard riches, pleasures, or honors as the greatest things, nor expend all his effort upon them. Rather, he had set before himself what was becoming and honorable in such a way that, whatever happened to him by which human beings are usually broken, he scarcely felt it, as though he were above it.

According to blessed Ambrose, he was also careful not to do anything rashly or carelessly for which he could not give a credible account. As a good watchman, he kept before his mind that desire should be subjected to reason by the law of nature; it should neither run ahead of reason nor abandon it—lest, by running ahead, it disturb and exclude reason, and by abandoning it, leave it helpless.

But Heinricus’s disturbed mind, driven by an unrestrained desire as though by a wild impulse, did not accept the reins of reason, nor perceive the driver’s guidance; therefore it could not be turned. Nor were there lacking those who reported to him the letters sent by the pope. Yet what he despised doing, he also disdained even to know; nevertheless, from the words of piety he fashioned poisons of iniquity.

[Note: “In” is written above, or “from” another manuscript.]

For it is characteristic of an arrogant man to regard his own evils as good, to perceive good in the goods of others, and to turn the weight of a good action into a stain of crime. While, therefore, he was devising weapons of fury from the condescension and compassion of charity, let us hear how the manly spirit of our father, endowed with the serpent’s cunning and the dove’s simplicity, met his wicked endeavors with prudent forethought, as from the watchtower of the mind. Writing to the same faithful persons as above, he says:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the same persons: greeting and apostolic blessing. After we sent a letter to your fraternity,” etc.  
> (See among the letters of Gregory.)

Do not be surprised that the king is called king although he has been deposed, since even the dead are called by their former designation. Thus Saint Gregory also judged that a bishop irreversibly deposed should be called by the name “bishop,” although he wished to restore nothing of the dignity he had lost.

What the blessed pope also replied to that embassy of the king, who was no longer ruling, on account of which he was likewise deposed in the Roman synod, and how, conceiving the Holy Spirit with his whole mind, he thundered forth, may be set out below (Fol. 116'):

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who desire to be numbered among the sheep of Christ, which he entrusted to blessed Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing. You have heard, my brothers, of a new and unheard-of presumption,” etc.  
> (It is found in *Register*, book III, no. 6.)

(Fol. 116'.) In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1078, indiction 1, in the fifth year of his pontificate, in the month of March, Pope Gregory VII, presiding over a Roman synod of one hundred bishops, said, among other things: “Following the footsteps of the holy Fathers, the ordinations of those who have been ordained by excommunicated persons,” etc.  
(See in Gregory VII, *Acts of the First Roman Synod*.)

(Fol. 116'.) (*Acts of the Council of 1079.*) In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1078, in the month of February, indiction 2, in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII, a council was convened from various parts of the world, with everyone gathered in the Church of the Savior at Rome. A discourse was delivered concerning the body and blood of the Lord.  
[Note: Acts of the council in Mansi XX, 523.]

The greater part of the assembly maintained that the bread and wine are substantially converted, through the words of sacred prayer and the consecration by the priest, with the Holy Spirit working invisibly, into the Lord’s body that hung upon the cross and into the blood that flowed from his side. Some, however, struck by excessive blindness, asserted that there was only a figure.

But when the matter began to be dealt with, before the third day had arrived at the synod, the other party ceased to resist the truth. Finally Berengarius, the teacher of this error, confessed before the council that he had erred after having long taught this impiety, sought pardon, and obtained it through apostolic clemency. He swore as follows:

> “I, Berengarius, believe inwardly and confess outwardly that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are substantially converted, through the mystery of sacred prayer and the words of our Redeemer, into the true, proper, and life-giving flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that after the consecration there is the true body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin, was offered for the salvation of the world, hung upon the cross, and sits at the right hand of the Father; and the true blood of Christ, which was poured from his side—not merely by the sign and power of the sacrament, but in the proper reality of its nature and in the unity of substance—as this brief statement contains, as I have read it and as you understand it, so I believe. Nor will I henceforth teach anything contrary to this faith. So may God help me, and these most holy Gospels.”

Then the lord pope commanded Berengarius, by apostolic authority, never again to presume to dispute or teach with anyone concerning the body and blood of the Lord, except for the purpose of bringing back to the faith those who had departed from it through his teaching.

(Fol. 117.) In this year Grimoldus, abbot of Saint Vito, died while returning from Rome. He was buried at Mantua in the Church of Saint Andrew the Apostle on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, when the lord Abbot Rodulfus had already governed that church for three years, Grimoldus having been excused from the governance of the abbey. For he was of a simple disposition.

In this same year, which was 1078 from the Lord’s incarnation, Siguinus, formerly a canon of Lyon, distinguished by birth and shining with moral integrity, now blessed by a happy departure, received the office of governance at the House of God.

[Note: “He undertook” is to be supplied.]

Under him, Pontius was ordained abbot of the church of Fraxinensis by the lord Pope Gregory.

[Note: “Frainet.”]

After several years, Pontius resigned the abbacy because of the persecution of the aforesaid King Heinricus, having sought and obtained permission from the lord Anselm, bishop of Lucca, in these words:

> “To P., most beloved brother in Christ, from A., the least of all bishops: greeting in Christ. The more your fraternity trusts in our charity, the more diligent and concerned we ought to be for the salvation of your soul, lest—God forbid—our negligence extinguish the holy fervor of your desire, and the almighty Lord demand your blood from my hand at his strict judgment.
>
> “I believed that the obedience owed to the lord abbot and to the holy congregation of the House of God, as well as to our venerable father H., archbishop of Lyon, together with the apostolic blessing of our most blessed father G., was greater than all iniquities and sufficient not only to wipe away every stain of wicked thoughts but also to obtain eternal rest—unless you, by refusing to believe, made yourself unworthy and received God’s grace in vain.
>
> “For whatever is not from faith is sin, so that even in those who seem to deliver their bodies to punishments for God’s sake, death rather than life is at work; through their distrust they in some manner impose upon almighty God a difficulty in accomplishing what he desires, although he wishes all to be saved, as he himself says in the Gospel: ‘You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you.’
>
> “For you, if you obey; for you, if you firmly believe; for you, if you place all your hope in the power of the holy Church, forgiveness has been promised. But if you do something else and pretend something else, no confidence remains for you, even if you hand over your body so that it may burn.
>
> “You know that I have many times received you into my faith, but on this condition: that you should discharge with every care the responsibility of governance entrusted to you, and should not, as you wrongly believed, place the care of your soul before the needs of the flock committed to you; that you should attend not to your own interests but to those of others.
>
> “But, as I see, your mind cannot by any means be recalled from the path of its purpose. Therefore, fearing that even the things that appear good may progress toward something worse, it seemed better to us that the river of your good intention should run its course than that, running against the current, it should be condemned to perpetual dryness.
>
> “For it is more tolerable that you alone should perish than that, together with you, all those entrusted to you should be brought into danger, as has happened until now. Nevertheless, we trust that the Lord will grant you according to your heart, since he did not find you suitable to govern others according to his own heart.
>
> “If another path is more pleasing to you, then with our permission lay down the burden that necessity alone, without charity, imposed upon you, and assist me with your holy prayers as I labor in another ship.
>
> “Through you I greet the lord archbishop of Lyon—provided, however, that reasonable necessity excuses him from the destruction of the whole world. For if, whether through fear, negligence, or love of harmful repose, he delays visiting his mother and freeing her from the hand of death, he will be guilty before the judgment unless he strives to come without delay and assist in everything.”

(Fol. 117'.) The aforesaid pope therefore resolved to descend into the kingdom of the Germans in order to visit and strengthen the defenders of the Christian faith. This had also been requested by those who had sent messengers to me, so that the rule of justice might be made increasingly manifest in his presence. He wrote to all the faithful of blessed Peter in these words:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, margraves, counts, and all who defend and observe the Christian faith, the faith and teaching of blessed Peter, residing throughout the kingdom of the Germans: greeting and, through the blessing of the blessed Peter and Paul, absolution from all sins. I, an unworthy priest of the prince of the apostles,” etc.  
> [Note: It is also read in the Bernried manuscript, chapter 83, and in Udalric’s manuscript 146. (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.)]

(1076.) Many of those whom we have said acted foolishly in the deposition of the Apostolic [man], having recognized the sin of disobedience and moved to penance, returned to God after their error, raising toward God the face of their hearts, from whom they had departed by consenting to iniquity.

Their mouths were filled with reproaches, and as they contemplated the subtle examination of the judging God against themselves, they pursued their sins with laments and reproached themselves in penance for what they had been, pursuing themselves with the bitter accusation of repentance. For it is characteristic of the penitent to mourn his sins when he begins to consider what he has done, and then to consider them more subtly when he begins to mourn them more earnestly.

Having sought and obtained absolution, these men advised the king that, just as they had been absolved, so he too should strive to be absolved from the bonds of anathema. They added that if the year should close before he was absolved, he would be deprived of all their service and would no longer be regarded as king, because they were certain that communion or service with him exposed them to imminent danger of soul.

But he neglected to consider the ugliness of his weakness and instead attended, through the arrogance of pride, to the glory of his power. From the point at which he seemed more glorious to himself, he descended; and from the point at which he judged himself glorious, he fell more disastrously into the depths. For, as that same Heinricus says in the letter addressed to the Romans—although everything in it is full of falsehood and deceit, in this one respect he unwillingly favored the truth—he pretended, under the appearance of divine fear, that he did not consent to their counsels in the truth of Catholic peace.

(Fol. 118.) But we, for whom Christ is faith, Christ is refuge, and Christ is consolation, driving from the memory of all good people his nonsense, vomited from a diabolical mouth, written with the pen of iniquity, and marked with the ink of confusion, let us often hear from the words of our father what he did and how he obtained absolution, so far as concerned the condition of the outward man, since sacred Scripture testifies that those who seek God deceitfully never deserve to find him.

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and the other princes of the kingdom of the Germans who defend the Christian faith: greeting and apostolic blessing. Since, for the love of justice,” etc.  
> See among the letters of Gregory VII, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.

How little the king paid attention to this oath is indicated by the following letter:

[Col. 0319C]

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brothers and sons in Christ, the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and the other princes, together with all the people of the kingdom of the Germans who defend the Christian faith and religion: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “As we informed you in our earlier letters and through the words of our legates,” etc.  
> See the same work, no. 33.

Who these legates of the lord pope were, we learn from the king’s words: namely, the bishops of Padua and Albano.

[Note: They were Bernard, cardinal deacon, and Bernard, abbot of Marseille; see *Register* VI, 23–24.]

[Note: These men were not sent to Heinricus until the year 1079. Berthold’s *Annals*, p. 318.]

A synod was also held by them at Würzburg. Thus, according to what we can gather from the words of the lord pope, the aforesaid King Heinricus was granted only the grace of communion,

[Note: “Only the grace of communion was granted—he could prevail over them” is from the Acts of the Roman Council of 1080. Mansi XX, 534.]

but he was not restored to the kingdom, nor was it ordered that the loyalty of all who had sworn or were about to swear allegiance to him should be preserved for him. (Acts of the council.) This was withheld so that justice or peace might be arranged between him and the transalpine princes who, because of the apostolic command, had resisted him, just as he himself had promised under oath through the two bishops.

(Fol. 119'.) But when the aforesaid bishops and transalpine princes heard that he was not keeping what he had promised, they, as though despairing of him, chose for themselves Duke Rodulfus as king without the counsel of the lord pope.

Rodulfus therefore quickly sent a messenger and declared that he had indeed undertaken the reins of the kingdom under compulsion, but that he was prepared to obey the lord pope in everything. Repeating this same statement continually, he added that he would confirm his promise by oath, giving his son as hostage, together with the son of his faithful duke Bertaldus.

Meanwhile Heinricus also begged the pope to help him against Rodulfus. The lord pope replied that he would gladly do so after hearing the case of both parties, so that he might know to which side justice gave greater support.
