Heinricus, puffed up by empty rumor, disregarded this reply, thinking that he could overcome him by his own strength.

For the more his mind was stirred by the stormy movements of his actions, the more it was separated from the calm and stability of inner wisdom. Since he concealed malice in his heart but displayed flattery with his mouth, since he obscured his thoughts with duplicity, since he judged words of purity to be mere foolishness and turned aside from the straightforward paths of innocence, he could in no way enjoy the tranquility of wisdom.

The lord pope therefore devoted himself entirely to completing what he had begun, seeking a route by which he might cross into the kingdom of the Germans; and the more the condition of the kingdom was disturbed, the more anxious he became. Since he had sent faithful men there as legates who would not be sluggish executors of his wishes, he sent them special letters for this business, writing to them from Italy:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bernard, deacon of the holy Roman Church, and Bernard, abbot of Marseille: greeting and apostolic blessing. We do not doubt that your fraternity knows,” etc.  
> [Note: Given at Carpineto, on the second day before the Kalends of June, indiction 15, *Register* IV, 23. K. (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.)]

And likewise to the other faithful:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and all the faithful of Christ residing in the kingdom of the Germans: greeting and apostolic blessing. We wish it to be known to you, dearest brothers,” etc.  
> [Note: Given as above. *Register* IV, 24.]

Meanwhile Heinricus, because the outcome that followed his desired iniquities favored him, did not cease perpetrating wars, slaughters, and murders through himself and his men. He was intent on the destruction of churches and the disturbance of the Lord’s sheepfold; he drove shepherds from the Church, introducing wolves into the sheepfolds.

He was deceived by his prosperity, because deceit was being directed by his hand. For, having abandoned the way of life and cast himself into the darkness of sins, submerged in the abyss of iniquity and buried beneath the weight of evil habit, he was handed over to a depraved mind, so that he did not know how to weigh the evils he was committing. If only he had followed the paths of life that he had refused to follow through innocence, at least through penance.

(Acts of the council.) Having engaged Rodulfus for the third time, and perceiving that he could not accomplish what he had hoped, he sent two bishops from among his supporters—the bishop of Verdun and the bishop of Osnabrück—to Rome (1078), and through them asked the lord pope in synod to administer justice for him. The messengers of Rodulfus, who were present, approved that this should be done.

(Fol. 121.) It was therefore decreed in that same synod that a conference should be held in the transalpine regions, as anyone can perceive more fully from the words of the lord pope:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, dukes, princes, margraves, and all the greater and lesser persons established in the kingdom of the Germans, except those held under canonical excommunication: greeting and apostolic blessing. We wish it to be known to you, dearest brothers,” etc.  
> [Note: Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of March, indiction 1, *Register* V, 15; Paul of Bernried, 100.]

(Fol. 121'.) For this business he also sent a special letter to the archbishop of Trier, which it will not be burdensome to append here:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udo, bishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing. How great is our concern,” etc.  
> [Note: Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of March, indiction 1. See in Gregory VII.]

Udo, archbishop of Trier, therefore not long afterward rested in a blessed death, and the business of the apostolic legation was interrupted. For this reason the lord pope decided to send other legates to carry out the same business, writing to all the faithful in these words:

[Note: It is also found in the Saxon annalist and in Paul of Bernried, 105. (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLXIII.)]

[Col. 0321C]

(1079, February.)

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops and bishops residing in the kingdom of the Germans, if they are willing to obey: greeting and apostolic blessing. Since from strife and dissension,” etc.

[Note: The Saxon Annals and Paul of Bernried add “and in the Saxon kingdom.”]

[Note: The Saxon Annals and Paul of Bernried have: “and to all princes and all the greater and lesser persons who are not excommunicated.”]

Accordingly, in accordance with the faith of these statements, legates were sent from the side of the apostolic see. When certain unfavorable reports about them were circulated, the lord pope sent them this letter from the city of Rome:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ and fellow bishops, Peter of Albano and Odelricus of Padua: greeting and apostolic blessing. There are many people, although we do not believe them,” etc.  
> [Note: Missing from the *Register*. K. See Gregory’s letters outside the *Register*, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.]

After receiving this letter, they—corrupted by gifts and having deviated from the judgment and purpose of apostolic gravity—did something other than what had been entrusted to them: namely, restoring Heinricus to the kingdom and publicly cutting Rodulfus, as an usurper and invader of the kingdom, off from the Church, although this was wholly opposed to the truth. They also confirmed simoniacal bishops who were openly in communion with Heinricus’s supporters.

When the faithful, having examined the truth of the matter insufficiently, believed and doubted that this had proceeded in such a way from the apostolic see, and when the hesitant speech of those men reached the ears of our father, he sent them a letter in which he both reproved what had been wrongly done, explained that it had been done without his knowledge, and clearly admonished them to persevere in the right faith and unshaken hope. He wrote to them as follows:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Saint Peter residing in the kingdom of the Germans: greeting and apostolic blessing. It has come to our attention that some of you doubt us, as though, in the present necessity, I had resorted to secular fickleness,” etc.  
> [Note: Given at Rome on the Kalends of October, indiction 3, *Register* VII, 3. K.]

How and by which persons that conference was obstructed is made clear in the words of our most excellent father. Heinricus had cast off the yoke of obedience and, by obstructing the conference, had not feared to incur the threatened excommunication. Therefore, for these and countless other evils—murders, perjuries, adulteries, fornications, simony, and the considerable destruction of churches—he was anathematized and condemned in the Roman synod and irreversibly deposed from the kingdom (1080, March 7). We have judged it fitting to append his condemnation here:

(Fol. 123′.) “Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and you, blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, deign, I beg you, to incline your ears toward me and mercifully hear me. Since you are apostles and lovers of truth, help me to speak the truth to you, with every falsehood entirely removed, which you utterly detest; so that my brothers may more readily heed me, and may know and understand that, trusting in you after God and his mother, the ever-Virgin Mary, I resist the wicked and unjust, while I provide assistance to your faithful.

“But you know that I did not willingly enter the sacred order, and that against my will I went beyond the Alps with my lord Pope Gregory; rather, even more unwillingly, I returned with my lord Pope Leo to your special church, in which I served you as best I could. Then, very unwillingly, with great pain, sighing, and lamentation, I was placed—entirely unworthy—in your throne. I say this because it was not I who chose you, but you who chose me, and you placed upon me the exceedingly heavy burden of your Church; and because you ordered me to ascend a lofty mountain, to cry out and announce to the people of God their crimes, and to the sons of the Church their sins, the members of the devil began to rise up against me and even dared to lay hands upon me unto blood.

“The kings of the earth and secular and ecclesiastical princes stood forth; courtiers and commoners also gathered together against the Lord and against you, his anointed ones, saying: ‘Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us.’ And, in order to overwhelm me utterly by death or exile, they attempted to rise against me in many ways. Among them, especially, Heinricus, whom they call king, the son of Emperor Heinricus, raised his heel against your Church, forming a conspiracy with many bishops from beyond the Alps and from Italy, and striving to subjugate it to himself by casting me down.

“Your authority resisted his pride, and your power destroyed him. Confounded and humbled, he came to me in Lombardy and sought absolution from excommunication. When I saw him humbled, and after receiving from him many promises concerning the improvement of his life, I restored to him communion alone; yet I did not restore him to the kingdom, from which I had deposed him in the Roman synod, nor did I command that the fidelity of all who had sworn or were going to swear allegiance to him—whom I had all absolved in that same synod—should be preserved for him.

“And so I detained these matters in order to do justice between him and the princes from beyond the Alps who had resisted him on account of, and at the command of, your Church [Note: [Col. 0323] facere c.], or to establish peace, just as Heinricus himself promised me by oath through two bishops. But when the aforesaid bishops and princes from beyond the Alps heard that he was not keeping what he had promised, they, as though despairing of him, with you as their witnesses, chose Duke Rodulf as their king. King Rodulf then quickly sent a messenger to me and declared that he had been compelled to accept the reins of government, but that he was prepared in every way to obey me. From that time onward he continually sent me the same message, adding that he promised to confirm it by oath, his son having been given as a hostage and with reference to his faithful Duke Bertald [reading uncertain].

“In the meantime Heinricus began to beg me to help him against the aforesaid Rodulf. I replied that I would gladly do so after hearing the case of both parties, so that I might know to which justice was more favorable. But he, thinking that he could defeat him by his own strength, despised my response.

(Fol. 124.) “After he perceived that he could not act as he had hoped, two bishops from among his supporters—namely, Theoderic of Verdun and the bishop of Osnabrück—came to Rome and, in the synod, asked me on Heinricus’s behalf to do him justice; the messengers of Rodulf also approved that this should be done. Finally, with God’s favor, as I believe, I decreed in that same synod that a conference should be held in the regions beyond the Alps, so that there either peace might be established or it might be more clearly determined on whose side justice lay [Note: ‘For I, as you are my witnesses, fathers and lords, have until today resolved to help neither party except the one to whom justice was more favorable’: added in the Acts of the Council, Mansi XX, 535, and in Paul of Bernried, 107; absent from Codex Udalrici 150.]. And because I thought that the more unjust party would not wish a conference to take place where justice would maintain its proper place, I excommunicated and bound with anathema every person—whether king, duke, bishop, or any other man—who by any device should impede the conference from taking place.

“But the aforesaid Heinricus, together with his supporters, not fearing the danger of disobedience, which is the sin of idolatry, incurred excommunication by impeding the conference and bound himself with the chain of anathema. He caused a great multitude of Christians to be handed over to death, caused churches to be destroyed, and gave almost the whole kingdom of the Germans over to desolation.

“Therefore, trusting in the judgment and mercy of God and in that of his most merciful mother, the ever-Virgin Mary, supported by your authority, I subject the often-mentioned Heinricus, whom they call king, and all his supporters to excommunication. Again, on the authority of almighty God and of you, I forbid him the kingdoms of the Germans and of Italy; I take away from him every royal power and dignity; and I forbid any Christian to obey him as king [Note: ‘And I absolve all who have sworn or are swearing allegiance to him concerning the rule of the kingdom from their oath and promise.’ Acts of the Council of 1080, Paul of Bernried, and Codex Udalrici, loc. cit.]. Let Heinricus himself, together with his supporters, obtain no strength in any battle and no victory throughout his life.

“But so that Rodulf may rule and defend the kingdom of the Germans—the man whom the Germans have chosen as their king—I give, bestow, and grant him to your fidelity in your name. To all who faithfully adhere to him, relying on your favor, I grant absolution from all sins and your blessing in this life and in the life to come. For just as Heinricus is rightly cast down from the royal dignity because of his pride, disobedience, and falsehood, so Rodulf [Note: ‘So also’—editorial variant] is granted the power and dignity of the kingdom because of his humility, obedience, and truth.

“Act now, I beg you, most holy fathers and princes, so that the whole world may understand and recognize that, if you can bind and loose in heaven, you can on earth take away and grant kingdoms, empires, principalities, duchies, marches, counties, and the possessions of all men according to their merits. You have often taken patriarchates, archbishoprics, primacies, and bishoprics away from wicked and unworthy men and given them to religious men. For if you judge spiritual matters, what are you able to do concerning secular matters? And if you strike kings who rule over all proud princes, what can you do to their servants?

“Let the kings of the earth and all the princes of this age now learn how great you are and what you can do, and let them fear to disregard the command of your Church. Exercise your judgment upon the aforesaid Heinricus so promptly that all may know that he will fall and be confounded not by chance but by your power—if only unto repentance, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Given at Rome, on the Nones of March.”

[Col. 0325A] (Fol. 124′.) At that time the illustrious lord Herimannus presided over the city of Metz. A son of the Church of Liège, he was, among the foremost defenders of the Catholic faith, a great example of patience, religion, and justice; he had been predestined and granted by God as successor to Adalbero, bishop of Metz, of pious memory.

In the first flower of his youth, during the time of Anno, venerable archbishop of Cologne, guardian and governor of the kingdom, he gained access to the palace and learned nearly everything about that king, so much so that, even before receiving the grace of the episcopate, he often withdrew from the administration of the court because of the king’s insolence. He preferred to be despised for his modest station rather than hope for greater things through association with a faction of corrupt men—especially when he saw the aforesaid Anno, a man of revered memory, mourning and groaning in frequent contrition over the desolate condition of the kingdom under such a prince, the law of imperial rule bent, and the horn of dominion crushed. There was in it only the hope of the overthrow of the Church and the disturbance of Catholic peace: confusion and horror, vanity and destruction, and every proud, slippery, vain, unstable, and impure presumption bringing all things to ruin.

When he obtained the office of bishop, he deeply regretted having received the investiture of the pontificate from that king’s hand. Indeed, he willingly cast off the burden of the prelacy that had been imposed upon him, resigned it of his own will, and made every effort to excuse himself from it, if the authority of the Roman pontiff had permitted. Before that pontiff he did not blush to confess his fault for his transgressions—that is, for having rashly accepted the same investiture, which was contrary to canonical institutions—and thereafter he took great care to avoid communion with the king and his supporters. Because of this he suffered so much that the following saying might seem to have been spoken of him: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:16).

In his first encounter he suffered what belongs to human weakness, so that in the second—an encounter that was continuous and perpetual—he might learn to trust in God rather than in himself. He fell as a man, he stumbled as a man, because he presumed as a man. But the scandal of disgrace was already removed from him, because what had disturbed him was cut away in the goodness of his life; and, as the darkness thinned, the gold shone forth, the finest color gained strength, and the sanctuary-stone in the diadem of the eternal King gleamed.

Thus, at the very beginning of his episcopate, having become an executor of apostolic teaching, he later entered into communion with the wicked king, who had been excommunicated for his crimes. From that communion he had, as was said, suspended himself for some time. He grieved that he had been deceived, and, recovering his strength, sought absolution from the lord pope for his error. The pope also instructed the lord bishop of Die to absolve him, either personally or—if he feared crossing into that place because of the king—through some religious man whose faith and courage he trusted. The bishop, placing this duty upon the abbot of the monastery of Dijon, sent him to Metz; and he was absolved on the very eve of the Nativity of the Lord.

(Fol. 125.) Since he clung with all the marrow of his heart to the apostolic commands, while royal indignation and the deceitful tongues of flatterers directed every adversity against him, they complained that the authority of the holy Roman Church could not depose the king, the son of the emperor, chosen and honored by God; could not separate from the mother Church that holy dignity of royal majesty, honored throughout the ages; and could not deprive him of the power granted to him, since there is no power except from God, and those powers that exist have been ordained by God.

And since he sought from the apostolic see, against the fury of his barking opponents, the remedy of healing, so that he might fortify himself against their attacks with apostolic writings as with a shield of defense, the most gentle teacher sent him this letter from the city (1081) through Rodulf, abbot of the monastery of Verdun. It was so fortified and filled with the authorities of the divine Scriptures and seasoned with the salt of apostolic teaching that this letter alone is sufficient for the faithful to refute the foolish stupidity of their adversaries:

(Fol. 125.) “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, the bishop of Metz [Note: ‘Herimannus’ should be supplied], greetings and apostolic blessing. We do not doubt that the fact that we understand you to be prepared to endure labors and dangers in defense of the truth is a gift of God,” etc. [Note: It survives in the Register, Book VIII, Letter 21, and in Codex Udalrici, no. 156, in Eckhard, *Scriptores* II, 158 ff. We owe this copy to the distinguished scholar Urlichs.].

(Fol. 128.) Receiving this letter, the bishop of Metz was greatly strengthened in the Lord. But let us now, having passed over this matter, return to the order of the history.

When news of the anathemas pronounced by the lord pope reached King Heinricus and his supporters, the tyrant raged. The uproar of the faction thundered forth against the vicar of blessed Peter with shameful and abominable clamor: they called him a magician and impostor, a heretic, murderer, fornicator, and whatever else sound doctrine rejects. They said that the king, the son of the emperor, who did not carry the sword without cause and who ought to be the patrician, guardian, and defender of the Roman commonwealth, ought not to suffer such trampling upon the holy Church of God, so that a man utterly contemptible among all men, one who deservedly ought to be punished for his crimes and rightly expelled from the Church, should attack the supreme majesty of the royal name.

They said that the curse uttered in vain should be turned back upon the one from whom it had proceeded: the man who had prepared a pit of cursing for his lord and king should remain unharmed, while he who was the head and cause of the evil should fall into it first. While the whole court was making this uproar, it was decided by common counsel that the man who had declared the royal majesty, revered throughout the ages, to be an exile from the Church should be separated from the body of the Church; and that the pontiff of the Roman Church, who is above all, should be condemned to excommunication by those who ought to be subject to him.

(Fol. 128′.) O incomparable madness, unspeakable fury, astonishing insanity! Which emperor, I ask, which king has ever dared to rush into such arrogant madness or insane arrogance, as to declare that the vicar of the heavenly key-bearer—whose tongue is the key of heaven—canonically elected, received by all Christendom, living rightly and teaching rightly, should be alienated from the Church?

This assembly was held at Utrecht, where they disputed against God and the Lord. It was a Saturday; and on Saturday evening, as the night giving way to the Lord’s Day was dawning, it was determined and deliberated in the assembly of the wicked that on the following day, during Mass and in the hearing of all, the pope should be excommunicated, because he had dared to excommunicate his king and lord. They held this sentence to be just, so that he might be punished in the matter in which he had sinned.

Theodoric of Verdun and Pibo of Toul, together with many others, were present at that assembly of evil-doers. Although they favored the royal cause, they nevertheless detested this action because it opposed the decrees of the holy fathers and resisted canonical enactments. The king had imposed this duty upon the bishop of Toul because he was timid and highly inconstant in mind, so that he might carry out the matter. But although he feared every detail and did not dare to resist, during the night he entrusted himself, together with the bishop of Verdun and the companions he had taken with him, to the counsel of flight. For this reason the execution of the business was delayed somewhat longer on the following day [Note: The letter of Gregory III, 12, to Udo of Trier, Theodoric of Verdun, and Herimannus of Metz appears to have been written shortly before this. K.].

Only William of Utrecht was found there. While still belching forth the previous day’s drunkenness, he set his mouth against heaven and turned the dart of cursing with his tongue against his lord and master [Note: Lambert relates that this happened at Eastertide in 1076; Stenzel I, 387, noted that Hugh confused the council of Worms with that of Mainz in 1080. K.]. But he did not go unpunished. For when he had performed this deed amid the sacred rites of Mass, and, after committing the crime and being given over to a reprobate mind, was preparing to complete the same rites, so that in this too he might not be separated from Judas the betrayer in fellowship and desert, when he, burdened by an evil conscience, received the Lord’s body against which he had sinned, divine vengeance was revealed.

He was struck by God with an incurable affliction, so that in horror and astonishing bewilderment he cried out: “I am burning! I am burning!” For the body that gives life brought him burning and punishment; it had blazed up within him like fire among thorns, so that the Lord’s vengeance might be made manifest in him. Nor was he given time to repent. As soon as he felt the fire spreading through him, leaning back in his bodily seat, he cried, “Holy Mary!” and ended his miserable life by a miserable death [Note: He died in 1076; compare Berthold, Lambert, Bruno, and Bernold.].

It is certain that these things were seen by us, that this was shown to us so that his punishment might begin to benefit us. Great terror then arose among everyone. Thus the bishop of Verdun, whom we noted had secretly departed, as he approached his city and his clerics came out to meet him with crosses and candles, as is customary, openly forbade the procession. He declared that he had been excommunicated because he had yielded for a time, and then deeply repented that he had shared in the faction’s communion with the lord pope’s excommunication. He openly protested that, unless divine mercy and the prayers of good men had come to his aid, he would have suffered the punishment that William had endured.

For this reason, after sending messengers to the pope—namely, Abbot Rodulf and his companions—and affirming that he was entirely excommunicated because of that communion and had therefore ceased from office, he returned the stole [Note: These letters are lacking from the Register.] and the ring into the pope’s hand by letter.

Although he thus condemned himself, he nevertheless obeyed the king, because it was his hour and the power of darkness. For miracles did not break his long-standing malice, which had become hardened; rather, increases in his vices brought him additions to his torments. Thus what is written was fulfilled in him: “It has been sweated out with great labor, yet its excessive rust has not gone out of it, not even through the fire” (Ezekiel 24:12). The fire of tribulation roared around him in order to purge away the rust of his vices; but he did not lose his rust even through fire, nor was he corrected by scourges, because his malice could not be consumed by the refiner.

(Fol. 129′.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1087, William, king of the English, died.

(1080, October 15.) In the year, therefore, 1079 from the Lord’s incarnation, a battle took place in Saxony, in which King Rodulf fell and Heinricus was defeated in flight. In that same year there were thunder and lightning in January, and the moon appeared black and bloody on the third day before the Kalends of February. In the following year Witbertus invaded the apostolic see, elected as an apostate rather than an apostolic man by the condemned and excommunicated and their kindred.

(*Legg.* II, 51.) This conspiracy was first formed at Brescia, where some bishops of the synagogue of Satan assembled. Given over to a reprobate mind, they cast shameful and abominable things against the faith, which is Peter’s confession, and against his holy see, the Roman Church. To complete their own condemnation, they chose Witbertus, a heresiarch from among their own kind, and by calling him apostolic they made him an apostate, not an apostolic man.

He is therefore worthy of the hatred of all the faithful, because when the princes—namely King Heinricus, who had been deposed, and the other ministers of this perdition—asked who would take up the banner of falsehood against the holy man, Pope Gregory, no one among them was found so bold, presumptuous, desperate, or lost as to choose to undergo the shipwreck of faith, except him alone. We believe that he undertook the business of Antichrist in order to compensate, by accepting the offered danger, for the ruin of the archbishopric of Ravenna, which he had lost by synodal judgment for his crimes while Gregory was presiding.

A great number of condemned men were present in that assembly of the wicked; fellowship in crimes and love of the prince had lured them to persecute the lover of justice. The devil found him alone more ready, and entrusted to him the whole leadership of his malice. Thus he took possession of Satan’s seat and, raised up in the chair of pestilence, sharpened the minds of the ungodly to assault the name of the Lord, becoming for all a pitfall of sin.

But what his advancement or enthronement was, how and how precipitously he ascended to this downfall, by whom he was cursed, what the life and conduct of those men were, and what should be thought about the man ordained and those who ordained him—let Gevehard, bishop of Salzburg, whose life was a mirror of goodness, explain when questioned. For he writes to Herimannus, bishop of Metz, as follows:

“G., bishop of Salzburg, to H., bishop of Metz, greetings. When Witbertus, formerly archbishop of Ravenna, had striven not to observe the obedience he had promised by oath to the apostolic see, but to act with every kind of pride against it, he was irremovably deposed and anathematized in a Roman synod by the apostolic see and by the bishops of the whole Church. Nor did this happen only once, in a single synod, but in every synod that has been held at Rome during the past seven years.

“Thus, having grown old in perjuries and having been irremovably deposed and anathematized for them, he invaded the seat of the Roman pontiff, to whom he had sworn obedience, through the hands of men under anathema, as being his equals, while the lawful shepherd still presided over that see. (1083.) Of those excommunicated men, no one dared to consecrate—or rather, to execrate—him except the former bishops of Modena and Arezzo, both of whom had already been deprived of office and communion for three years because of their crimes.

“But even if they had possessed office and communion, and even if the Roman see had been vacant, they still could not have ordained a pontiff for that see. For the privilege of this ordination was granted by the holy fathers to the cardinal bishops alone: those of Albano, Ostia, and Porto. Therefore, according to the testimony of the most holy Pope Innocent, the bishops of Modena and Arezzo were able to impose upon their Ravennate not a blessing but the condemnation they themselves possessed; and they advanced him not as Roman patriarch but as the most lost of heresiarchs.

“Let every Christian therefore beware of bowing his head to Antichrist, of worshiping the statue that Nebuchadnezzar erected, and thus of binding himself to the pernicious anathema of that heresiarch. For whoever obeys him who said, ‘I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High,’ will most certainly go with him into eternal condemnation. Amen.”

These are the truthful writings about Witbertus by Gevehard of Salzburg, a man certainly most learned and authoritative; no one can rightly prevail against them. Other writings of his, supported by authority and truth, also survive, and the Church of the faithful reverently honors and embraces them because of the man’s merit.

(1084, March 31.) From this Wibertus, whose salt had certainly lost its savor, Heinricus received the imperial crown. He became the unhappy member of him who is king over all the sons of pride, receiving from him a curse instead of a blessing—and quite appropriately. For he was worthy of it, and the matter happened according to his merits: such a king should establish such a pope, and from that pope himself receive a crown of disgrace and a scepter of dishonor.

(Fol. 129′.) At that time, when Gibuinus, archbishop of Lyon, had died [Note: “The deposition of Gebuin, archbishop of Lyon, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May” is recorded in the Necrology of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon. K.], and while various men were being chosen by some, the lord Hugh, bishop of Die, was promoted to be archbishop of Lyon by the election of the clergy and people and by the authority and command of the Roman pontiff, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1082 [Note: In a letter of Gregory to Hugh, Register IX, 18, dated the ninth day before the Kalends of November, Gregory urges him not to hesitate to undertake the government of the Church of Lyon. The letter was written in 1082 if Hugh was consecrated archbishop of Lyon in 1083, and indeed at the beginning of that year, as the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, 109, appear rightly to have inferred from an old charter. K.].

For at that time lord Gregory still presided over the city of Rome, although the conspiracy of the Wibertists had already been formed; their advancement, however, had not yet taken place. But when his advancement was in turn, by its execration, as it were, given official authorization, and it had been decided by the impious and perjured that Rome should be attacked by hostile force, so that the pope—who was protected by the obedience and love of the people with the grace of God—might be driven from his see with insult and disgrace, the king went so far that he marched toward Rome with his pope, supported by an innumerable army. Along the way he compelled as many people as he could to worship the statue and, in it, the image of the beast.

But in a remarkable manner, the more he was carried forward to fulfill the madness of his profane mind, the more heavily he was cast down and dishonored. Once it had been a great thing if someone deserved a royal kiss, and it was considered a favor if someone kissed the pope’s footsteps. Now, with the order of things reversed, whoever was found was detained and not released until he had first kissed the foot of that little pope; only then did he obtain the king’s kiss. Thus the insult was divided equally between the two, though the king’s was much greater, inasmuch as the man at whose feet he bowed was worse.

For what greater madness could there be than for a man highly learned in letters, instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, not ignorant of ecclesiastical law, holding in the Church a position of great dignity and prelacy, to descend into such dullness of mind that he begins to grow proud against God, and, seeking a place of exaltation not in the Church but outside and above the Church, against right and law, strives wholly to imitate the one who said: “I will set my throne in the north; I will sit upon the mount of the testament, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13–14) [Note: At this point it is useful to present a fragment written in a manuscript of the British Museum among the Arundel manuscripts, no. 390, in a hand from the end of the eleventh century, which I transcribed during an English journey in 1844. It appears there on folio 132 and illuminates the pact made between Heinricus IV and the Romans in June 1083:

“Certain men who are called religious and most holy, as they have hitherto been accustomed to do, set themselves against right, tested God, and did what they ought not to have done; because of this they suffered great disgrace. For these are the men who passed judgment on the kingdom and the priesthood. But God, who is most merciful and most compassionate, foresaw what is just.

“For the abbot of Monte Cassino, and the chancellor who is a cardinal of Saint Paul, and the bishop of Porto with his fellow bishops, and Bernard the deacon, and Wimund the monk, who is otherwise called Christian, and Gratian—all these, by the pope’s command, made this law which you are about to hear.

“But first I shall say who blessed the water: a certain man who is exceedingly religious, named Peter the Neapolitan, who is a monk. He, a priest, first observed a three-day fast with the other clergy who were there, and that most holy priest celebrated Mass. When Mass had been completed, he went to the water with the aforementioned men and blessed the water.

“Then, on the king’s behalf, he sent a certain boy into the water, so that God might discern the truth, whether the king himself had justice. As soon as the boy had been sent into the water, he went down to the bottom of the water [Note: ‘downward’—variant]. At this miracle all who were present were amazed, and one of them, named Wimund, who is called Christian, began to say to Gratian: ‘Surely you pressed the boy down so that he would go to the bottom of the water.’ But Gratian himself began to protest and say: ‘I have never done such a thing.’

“Then Wimund went angrily to the pope and said that Gratian had pressed the boy down so that he would go to the bottom of the water. When the pope heard this, he commanded Wimund and said: ‘Go and tell them to send the boy into the water again, so that we may see whether what you say is true.’

“At this command Wimund went and told all who were present, on the pope’s behalf, to send the boy into the water another time. And, at the pope’s command, they sent the boy into the water again, and the little boy went down to the bottom of the water just as before.

“After this, those aforementioned men made the same law on the pope’s behalf and sent the little boy into the water; he began to swim on the surface. They sent him in again, and he likewise floated. Because of this they pushed him beneath the water so that he would go into the depths, but God did not permit it. Indeed, they nearly suffocated him in the water.

“At this miracle they were amazed and did not know what they ought to do. They then took counsel and pledged faith among themselves that, if this matter became known, it should be reported to the king through some person, so that none of them would dare to speak without common counsel and without the pope’s counsel. For he had received an oath from them all that none should dare to speak.

“This happened at Pallaria, in the monastery of Saint Mary, which is the chapel of the abbot of Monte Cassino. This happened to the confusion of those who performed it and for the salvation of your empire, and it took place on the Sunday after the Mass of Advent of the Lord.”]

[Col. 0332A] THE OATH.

“We say to you, King Heinrice [Note: ‘Heinricus’—variant], that within the term which we shall establish with you—fifteen days after you have come to Rome—we shall have Pope Gregory crown you, if he is alive or if he has not perhaps fled from Rome. But if he has died, or if he has fled and does not wish to return, according to our counsel, in order to crown you within the appointed term, we shall elect a pope with your counsel according to the canons, and we shall strive in good faith to have that pope crown you; and we shall strive in good faith to have the Romans swear fidelity to you. We shall observe all these things for you without fraud or evil intent, except insofar as something may be added or diminished by our common counsel and yours.”

.

[Col. 0332A] Meanwhile, returning from the city of Rome, Abbot Rodulf came to Verdun. Bringing from the pope to the bishop of Verdun the grace of communion, he indicated that the bishop should seek absolution from the lord bishop of Metz, to whom the pope’s duties had been entrusted, after first making satisfaction.

But because rumor had already spread that Wibertus had been cursed and that the king was heading for Rome with obstinate intent, the man’s spirit swelled. Disregarding everything he had done and everything he had condemned, he returned to his vomit. He was not ashamed merely to refuse to confess his fault; rather, he did not fear binding himself with heavier chains of sin and obstinacy. For suddenly absolved by himself, he appeared as a pontiff in priestly vestments, celebrated Mass, and did not fear to perform whatever belongs to priestly office, which until then he had avoided. In the new monastery of Saint Mary, which he himself had built with the greatest zeal and care, he brought in relics, blessed and sprinkled water, and fulfilled each of the bishop’s offices.

From this point evils arose in Israel. For in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1084, Heinricus came to Rome, captured the city, overturned its walls, shut Pope Gregory within a tower of the Crescentius family, and established his own pope to sit in the Church of Saint Peter, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be, let the reader understand” (Mark 13:14).

Meanwhile the beast of Verdun, with every semblance of humanity overturned, raged here and there, so that every appearance of religious devotion in him was transformed. The obedience he had previously shown to religious men, who had then flocked to him from Liège and from other regions everywhere and lived under monastic habit in the suburban monasteries, he turned into weapons of fury.

All his speech concerned the empire of Heinricus and the papacy of Clement, so that he publicly ordered the name of that wicked heresiarch to be recited in the canon in the churches. The other bishops of Lotharingia and Lombardy did the same, with very few exceptions who adhered to the teaching of Peter. Although their life was holy, pious, chaste, and Catholic, they were publicly branded with infamy and called insane and heretical. They did not understand Isidore’s saying: “Let him know that he is separated from the communion of the whole world, whoever, on account of any disagreement whatsoever, does not recite the name of the apostolic in the canon.”

Truly admirable is the mercy of almighty God, who, although he sometimes permits his chosen ones to be shaken, does not allow them to be utterly overthrown.

(Fol. 130.) It was not enough for the priests alone to sin; they had all become a snare for the young, so that even without synagogues they caused those who did not share in their works to share in communicating with the excommunicated, in rejecting Gregory, and in asserting Wibertus.

But if anyone was found who communicated with Gregory, he was publicly attacked with insults. He was called a heretic, a destroyer of the kingdom, an advocate of evil, unworthy even of life, and one who incurred the offense of public indignation as a perjurer. By an invented name he was called a Paterine.

Dangerous times had come. The face of the Church was darkened; she did not recognize the sons whom she had brought forth, because she suffered them as enemies, nor did they themselves recognize their mother. Although they afflicted and persecuted her in many strange ways, they did not know how to grieve over her condition.

Blessed are those who, amid this trampling upon the holy Church of God, did not defile their garments; they shall walk in white, because they are worthy.

Nor did the leopard change its spots—namely, Henry did not change his wickedness. Rather, while stationed at Rome, he won over as many people as he could by threats, terrors, blandishments, and promises; making wars, slaughter, and murders through himself and his followers; favoring iniquity with every effort at his command and resisting the truth; and, moreover, sending letters to his supporters in which he falsely fabricated that he had gained possession of Rome, had deposed the pope, and had prevailed over everyone without exception.

But Countess Matilda, [Col. 0333C] daughter of the Roman Church, maintaining the steadfastness of a manly spirit, resisted him all the more forcefully the more she understood his cunning and the pope’s innocence. For she alone at that time was found among women to have disdained the king’s power and to have confronted his craft and might even in armed conflict—so that she deservedly is called a “virago,” since by the strength of her spirit she surpassed even men.

Be present, O Most High God, and do not allow the kingdom of your Church and the strength of ecclesiastical order, which you had established under the direction of your Holy Spirit, to fall from the summit of its glory, nor permit it to be subjected to such great dangers.

This is that woman against whom the crime of incest was brought before the holy pontiff by the detractors of [Col. 0333] the faith and the tramplers upon truth. Even if she lacked the praises of her merits, this one fact alone would make her sufficiently worthy of commendation: that, when she is reproached, when she receives insults, when she hears abuse, she is approved, honored, and praised in connection with such a man. For who contended as she did for the Roman Church? How many and how great things did she endure so that it might enjoy that liberty which was its due?

Several letters of the pope to her are still extant. It will not be burdensome to insert one of them here, so that it may be recognized by what union they were bound to one another; so that every mouth wishing to speak wickedly may be stopped; and so that the well-disposed may be instructed, while the malicious speakers may blush and be confounded:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his beloved daughter in Christ, Matilda. How great is my care, and how great my concern, for you and for your salvation, is understood by him alone who searches the secrets of the heart and knows them far better than I myself. Yet if you do not neglect to weigh the matter, you will perceive, as I think, that I ought to care for you in proportion to the great efforts of charity by which I have detained you, so that you would not abandon them in order to devote yourself solely to the salvation of your soul. For charity, as I have often said and shall say again, following the heavenly trumpet, does not seek what is its own.
>
> “But since, among the other weapons which, with God’s favor, I have given you against the prince of this world, I indicated that the most important was that you should receive the Lord’s body, and since I commanded you to entrust yourself entirely to the sure protection of the Lord’s mother, I have here conveyed to you in writing what blessed Ambrose says concerning the reception of the Lord’s body and blood. For in Book 4 of *On the Sacraments* he says, among other things: ‘If we proclaim the Lord’s death, we proclaim the remission of sins. If, whenever the Lord’s blood is poured out, it is poured out for the remission of sins, I ought always to receive it, so that my sins may always be forgiven. I who always sin ought always to have the medicine.’”  
> [Note: [Col. 0333] Much is missing. The letter was given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction, that is, in 1074; *Registrum* I, 47; Udalric’s Codex 157, K.]
>
> “Likewise, in Book 5 of *On the Sacraments* …”  
> [Note: [Col. 0333] The passage is left blank.]

(Fol. 130′.) Gregory, therefore, shut up within the wall of the Crescentian tower, sent envoys to Robert, duke of Apulia, who at that time happened to be preparing to cross the sea with a fleet equipped, asking him to come and lift the siege. At that time the abbot of Dijon happened to be in Rome, entirely faithful to the lord pope. Because of his innate goodness and the obedience he owed to blessed Peter, the pope embraced him with the deepest affection, so much so that he called him his fellow captive, since the dangers to his life, undertaken for the sake of justice, did not move him to abandon his cause.

He therefore sent him, together with certain cardinals, to summon the duke. The abbot carried out the command without delay, brought the prince, and, after the city had been besieged and an entrance opened, the king was put to flight, the pope was freed, and he was brought back in glory to the Lateran palace.

But because, after capturing Rome and giving it over to plunder, the Normans had perpetrated many evils—violating the daughters of Roman nobles, inflicting equal punishment on the guilty and the innocent alike, and observing no restraint, as is customary with victors, in robbery, cruelty, and pillage—the pope feared that, once the duke had withdrawn, Roman treachery, provoked into renewed fury, might flare up again, and that those whom he had previously regarded as almost faithful friends might prove disloyal. He therefore judged that he must yield to circumstances and withdrew to Salerno.

The king, meanwhile, seeking the protection of flight as the enemy approached, took with him the seal of the lord pope, which he had stolen, and brought along the bishop of Porto, who had once been a familiar of the pope and whom he had won over to himself. Witbertus also fled. Therefore Matilda, fearing that simple people might be deceived by the king’s cunning through the appearance of the seal, forestalled his wickedness by sending a letter to the faithful in these words:

> “Matilda, by the grace of God, whatever I may be, sends greetings to all who dwell in the kingdom of the Germans. We make known to you that Henry, the false king, has secretly stolen the seal of the lord pope Gregory. Therefore, if you hear anything that differs from our message, consider it false, and do not give credence to his lies.
>
> “Moreover, he is taking with him the bishop of Porto, because he was once a familiar of the lord pope. If, therefore, he wishes to undertake anything with you or against you through that man, do not hesitate to regard him as a false witness. Never believe anyone who dares to say anything different from what we say.
>
> “Know that the lord pope has now recovered Sutri and Nepi. Barrabas the robber—that is, Henry’s pope—has also fled. Farewell, and beware of Henry’s ambushes.”

Thus, when the supreme pontiff departed from Rome, the abbot of Dijon did not fail to accompany him. One day, however, when the army had advanced farther than he had expected at the very break of dawn, and he was hastening after it with his companions, he encountered a band of camp-followers who, following the enemy’s rear, were slaughtering with extraordinary swiftness those unsuspecting of trickery and fraud.

Recognizing and guarding against their wickedness, as one experienced in such matters, the abbot warned his companions to hasten their journey. But while they were rapidly moving away, the wicked men slyly shouted from behind them that the road they were following was not the road marked by the footsteps of those who had gone ahead; they claimed to know the correct road and said that they were ready to show it if the others would wait.

Although the abbot contradicted them and exposed their deceit, a brother who was accompanying him, named Walter, stopped and, contrary to everyone’s wishes, sought the road from those men. He was soon killed by them and was about to enter the way of all flesh. This is indeed what happened. For while he was awaiting the one who was hastening after him [Note: [Col. 0335] Thus the codex; Labbe printed *praestolamur*, “we await”], a small spear was cast and directed at him. But while he took too long to protect himself and tried to evade the blow, he received a mortal wound.

As he hastened his step because of the pain of the blow, he followed after the abbot, then fell with his head reclining upon the abbot’s breast as his vital spirit failed, and died in the act of dying. We believe that this harmed him: that he turned away from the pope’s just and holy cause and could not be corrected, although he was often rebuked. May almighty God spare him and grant that the present punishment may bring him both pardon for his sins and an eternal dwelling.

When he had fallen, the wickedness of the evildoers did not cease pursuing the others until the beast carrying the baggage remained behind; then Roman greed found an opportunity to loosen the reins of its innate covetousness, and so their malice was interrupted because of the baggage.

Let us now contemplate the father’s wavering and burning heart over the death of his son, and consider what consolation could have healed his grief. Living among foreign peoples, supported by only two companions and this third one, what do we suppose happened within his heart? What waves of thought, what onslaughts of agitation, what groans of grief, what sighs, what anxiety of mind arose when a companion lost a companion, a father a son, a master a disciple—and when he not only left him without a farewell, but did not even dare to look upon him as he fell, weakened, and died, or perform for him the duties of human compassion?

O you who are fathers, who hold the affection of sons in your hearts, attend and see what the grief of this father must have been. While he thought his son alive and vigorous, he saw him innocently slaughtered before him. In the death of his son, the father suffered.

(Fol. 131.) Whoever has a dearest friend and imagines that he will die knows what this father suffered, although he suffered more than any friend could imagine suffering over a friend. For there is a great difference between what we dream and what we see before our eyes in the present; so too there is an immense difference between what is imagined and what is actually done.

At last, therefore, the abbot came to his companions and, after kissing the pope’s foot, opened his heart’s grief, as his expression revealed his mind. The pope then sent soldiers with weapons to pursue the authors of so great a crime and ordered the body of the lifeless brother to be brought to him. It was found stripped of all clothing and lying in its own blood, and thus a certain cleric from among the companions carried it into the pope’s presence.

Being compassionate, as he was by nature, the pope covered the brother’s body with the cope in which he himself was clothed, gave him absolution, sang Mass for the dead, and thus returned to the earth what belonged to it. He greatly consoled the abbot, so that he might conform his will to that of his God, whose judgments are hidden but never unjust.

His spirit was strengthened in the Lord. Although he had lost everything, he was not provoked to anger, nor did he speak anything foolish against God. The most gentle pope was considering keeping him with him for the rest of his life. But because the abbot had now been anxious for a full year that he had not seen the brothers and sons entrusted to him—although he grieved that he had not dismissed them from him as he ought—when he saw that his mind was set on visiting the brothers, he released him.

He entrusted him with a legation to Coimbra and gave him letters to Sisenand, prince of that province [Note: [Col. 0335D] Neither this letter nor Gregory’s letters that follow are found in the *Register*. K.], so that Sisenand might trust him as another self. He also sent through him, through Peter Igneus [Note: [Col. 0336D] A cardinal.], and through the prince of Salerno, Gisulf by name, whom he was sending to Cluny, a letter to all the faithful. In it he briefly explained both the cause of the calamity of the holy Roman Church and why he had suffered so much and been brought to endure these things, and he urged them to pity him, in these words:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to all the faithful in Christ who truly love the Apostolic See. It has come to us, dearest brothers, etc.”

It is extant among Gregory’s letters, *Patrologia*, volume CXLVIII, column 708.

[Col. 0337A] The abbot of Dijon, therefore, entered the sea at the city of Salerno with Peter Igneus and the prince of Salerno, because they feared to travel by land on account of the attacks of roving enemies. Exhausted by the long voyage, they finally landed at Saint-Gilles [Note: [Col. 0337D] Saint-Gilles in Languedoc.], where his mind began to be troubled by various waves of anxiety: whether he should go straight to Coimbra as the pope had commanded, or visit the sons whom he had not seen for a year already.

Divine compassion therefore provided for him in his indecision, inspiring his heart to visit the brothers and sons after setting aside all doubt. He did so, and did not regret having done it. For if he had not done so, perhaps, on returning from Coimbra, he would scarcely have found anyone left for him to visit.

(1085.) He would also have lost so great a harvest of sonship as he received in that year. Its multiplication was so great that the church of Dijon deservedly ought to count that year with a better stone.

He therefore came to Dijon and found those who had been hostile to him at his departure completely devoted to him. He also found charity divided in some hearts, and healed it as far as he could and as the Lord granted. Not much time had yet passed when he heard of the disagreement between the bishop of Verdun and certain religious men who lived in monasteries outside that city, men who were opposed to Witbertus [Note: [Col. 0337] Thus the codex.] and to those who communicated with the Witbertists [Note: [Col. 0337] Thus the codex.]. He went to Bertiniacum, awaiting and taking precautions in case, with God’s grace, he might be able to capture those brothers and induce them to flee to him, where they could serve God freely in innocence and peace with a modest spirit.

But for now, let this suffice concerning them.

Thus, when the pope came to Salerno, he remained there, serving God devoutly and giving thanks amid the tribulations that had increased upon him. He was strengthened in the Lord and prospered in spirit. For just as the man who displeases himself possesses every adversity, so the man whose simple, pure, and clear conscience does not reproach him lacks nothing good.

He remembered his predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Gregory, Leo, and others, who, the more perfect they had been in the way of God, the more harshly they had been persecuted by the Romans, and therefore had been found worthy. A single eye made the whole body exceedingly bright. He walked securely along the paths of justice, and his conscience bore witness that he was suffering for the defense of truth; therefore he was not troubled.

He saw and carefully reflected within himself that if a pope wishes to be with God, he will become poor and needy; but whoever wishes to be with the world, seeking what is his own rather than what belongs to Jesus, not restraining his hand from simony, favoring iniquity rather than justice, and eagerly gathering money—such a man will become rich in wealth and overflow with abundance.

Therefore he desired all the more the poverty of Christ, who had nowhere to lay his head, which the wicked do not possess in their hearts, because he despised the deceptive and unreal riches of raging and alluring Mammon. He was girded at both shoulders by the covering of the shoulder-piece; against adversity and prosperity he was always protected by the ornament of the virtues. Pressing toward the things that are before him alone, he did not turn aside in any way toward the pleasures below. [Note: [Col. 0337] The rest of the page is blank.]

(Fol. 132′.) Now the time has come for the account of his departure to be related, and for a brief, not wearisome prayer to follow the account of how he migrated to his Lord, for whom he suffered so much.

(1085.) In truth, his end is the praise of the Lord. For if all praise is sung at the end, and since the whole of his completed life is thanksgiving before God, that very completion is an everlasting jubilation in the praises of God.

Knowing, therefore, that the day of his calling was approaching, he summoned long beforehand the cardinal bishops and the other fellow captives and foretold them the day of his death. Then, after completing all the offices of ecclesiastical order, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, under threat of strict judgment and by the command of holy obedience, he bound the aforementioned brothers to speak out without hesitation if they detected anything in him that needed correction.

When they praised both his manner of life and his discipline, his instruction in holy doctrine and formation in morals, and the fervor of his holy zeal according to knowledge, he compelled them, one by one, by apostolic authority to give him their right hands, promising that they would never receive that heretical invader of the holy and apostolic Church unless, perhaps, having canonically repented, he offered the cardinal bishops a sincere confession after being stripped of every dignity of ecclesiastical rank.

He declared and affirmed that all who dared to communicate with Henry the arch-pirate, usurper of the empire, would be condemned together forever, unless, after laying aside the dignity of kingship, he performed fitting penance according to their command and that of the other religious men dwelling in the German kingdom.

Then he confirmed to all his vicars, whom he himself had appointed throughout the world, his office and power of binding and loosing, so that those whom he had bound might be absolved by them after making fitting satisfaction, according to the rule of apostolic faith—not as certain people, deceiving themselves, wandering astray, and drawing others into error, falsely claim, namely, that he had absolved all the excommunicated indiscriminately, as though he could give life to those who do not live.

Next, he divinely understood and foretold that this very delusion would be scattered through many kingdoms. Finally, he absolved all who persevered to the end in this faith that had become known through him from all their sins. Thus, surrendering his spirit to the Creator [Note: [Col. 0337] spm. C. spm. t. c.], he died in the year 1085 from the Lord’s incarnation, a martyr and confessor.

In that same year, wind, hail, lightning, and thunder crushed Gaul on the fourth and third days before the Kalends of July.

(Fol. 130b.) Pope Urban said in one of his letters [Note: [Col. 0339] Compare Udalric’s Codex no. CLXVI, in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, volume V, p. 563, line XLIX and following]:

> “When our lord Pope Gregory, of blessed and worthy memory, was held at Salerno by a serious illness from which he afterward died, the bishops and Roman cardinals who were present there gathered around him, asking and entreating him to show them whom he wished to be substituted as his successor in the pontificate.
>
> “After thinking about it for a little while, he gave them this reply: ‘Whichever of these three you can obtain—the bishop of Lucca, the bishop of Ostia, or the archbishop of Lyon—choose him as pontiff.’
>
> “When he was similarly questioned about the excommunicated, he replied: ‘Except for the aforementioned King Henry and the archbishop of Ravenna, unless perhaps they come to you, as seems appropriate to you, to make worthy and canonical satisfaction—and except for all the principal persons who either by counsel or by aid favor their wickedness and impiety—I absolve and bless everyone who unquestionably believes that I possess this spiritual power in the place of the apostle Saint Peter.’”

(Fol. 132′.) After Gregory, Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, having been raised to the pontificate of the city of Rome, called himself Victor. What his election, elevation, and consecration were like, the lord Hugh of Lyon expressed clearly enough when he wrote to Countess Matilda in these words:

> “Hugh, servant of the holy Church of Lyon, sends to his most beloved sister in Christ, Matilda, the richest grace of divine consolation.
>
> “By how many and how great letters from the holy Roman Church, from the most revered memory of blessed Anselm, and from you—both by embassies and by letters—I was compelled to come to Rome, and how long I remained in the regions of Italy contrary to the purpose of my office, your prudence does not need to be taught.
>
> “You have heard sufficiently about the election of the abbot of Cassino, which took place before I came to Rome. Both I and my other brothers, sons of the holy Roman Church, gave our assent to it according to the weakness of the times, preferring the glory of men to the glory of God.
>
> “After we had remained in Rome for some time, we reached Monte Cassino, where he had already gone ahead. Under his leadership, from our conversations with his intimates—when he did not blush to boastfully recount his most impious acts in the ears of the bishops and cardinals—we necessarily discovered more fully how intolerably we had offended God in his election.
>
> “For who, unless he had heard it from his own mouth, would ever have believed that he had given his faith to the aforementioned King Henry so that he might faithfully help him obtain the crown of the Roman Empire? Or whose accusation against such a man would be accepted, unless he himself, adding it as though to the crowning of his glory, had told us that the aforementioned king had never crossed over into Rome to invade the lands of blessed Peter except at his counsel and persuasion?
>
> “Would not someone seem delirious who chattered that a Roman elect, after receiving absolution from the most blessed Pope Gregory, had been excommunicated—unless that man himself dared not only to proclaim publicly in our common hearing that Cardinal Atto of Milan, elected by the aforementioned pope with that same abbot subscribing, had been publicly excommunicated and had died without penance, but also to pray that he himself might be destined for no other glory than that in which Atto was?
>
> “In all these matters we call as witnesses our most beloved brothers, Cardinals He. and B., whom we believe to be with you. They themselves either heard these things from his mouth or said that they had heard them reported by good men whom they unquestionably trust.
>
> “How often he not only openly disapproved in words of the decrees of his lord Pope Gregory and of the other holy fathers, but afterward destroyed them by manifest actions; in how many places and on what occasions he publicly rejected his own election, declaring that it had been made not according to God but tumultuously, and affirming under a terrible oath that he had never consented to it and never would consent to it; and which persons he said, once the election had been restored to the Church, were suitable to be chosen Roman pontiff—including a certain Hermann of Metz, whom he named to you in writing at the counsel of certain persons—we omit from writing in order, since these matters are largely known to you and their enumeration would exceed the proper form of a letter.
>
> “But now, when at last, after so much labor spent in vain, we seemed to be able to breathe again, and hoped shortly, supported by divine grace and by your counsel and aid, to hold freely an election that had so often been rejected and returned to the Church, a council was convened at Capua under the pretext of electing a Roman pontiff by the one who was apostolic vicar in those regions.
>
> “I, the abbot of Marseille, and the archbishop of Aix, who were staying at Salerno, were invited by the bishop of Ostia, the prince of Salerno, and Cencius the Roman, on behalf of the vicar and the Roman Church, to come and elect a Roman pontiff by common counsel. By coming, we obeyed. The duke also came there, having been youthfully enticed by certain devices of Prince Jordan.
>
> “When we were preparing to discuss the matter at hand, the abbot began, through certain soft and theatrical refusals and gestures, to provoke his supporters—the bishops and the prince—to compel him. Once his trickery had been discovered, and when the aforementioned men were compelling him, as though unwilling, to restore himself, we, the persons named above, held counsel with the bishop of Ostia, the monk Witmund, and certain others concerning how we might oppose his cunning.
>
> “When he was already prepared to resume the insignia of the pontificate and to turn back upon himself the election that had repeatedly been rejected even at that gathering, we, following the counsel of those men and disapproving of such levity and inconstancy of purpose, declared in the hearing of all that we would in no way give our assent unless certain matters that had come to our knowledge about him, damaging his reputation and the dignity of so great an order, were first examined canonically.
>
> “Taking this indignantly, he publicly affirmed that he would neither submit to an examination nor ever accept the election. (1087.) Thus, after he had once again given us permission to elect whomever we wished, and while he was shaking his arms and beginning to withdraw from us, Witmund, on the advice of the bishop of Ostia, publicly cried out that an infamous person ought not to be elected or ordained Roman pontiff, since it was unquestionably established that he had incurred infamy, because he had endured the excommunication of the lord Pope Gregory for a full and uninterrupted year and longer without canonical penance.
>
> “When the gathering had therefore been dissolved, and since night was approaching, we departed, while the duke remained with him, retaining the bishop of Ostia together with the other Roman bishops and cardinals.
>
> “There, when the duke had long persisted in asking the abbot to consecrate a certain Alfanus as bishop of Salerno, but the abbot, because the bishop of Ostia opposed it, did not dare to fulfill the duke’s wish—since Alfanus had been convicted of the most manifest ambition—the duke departed from them in great indignation.
>
> “The abbot, therefore, deprived of favor, and despairing of aspiring to the Roman pontificate without the duke, sent an embassy to the duke deep in the night, while everyone was sleeping. Thus the duke returned to the abbot, and the abbot obtained from the duke the favor by which he might become pope, while the duke obtained from the abbot what he sought: that Alfanus should be consecrated the following day, namely Palm Sunday, with everyone replying that they would do this at the abbot’s command.
>
> “On that same day, after lunch, when the abbot, the duke, and the prince—each of them—had risen from their midday sleep, with the sun declining toward the lower regions but wine prevailing over the upper ones—alas, what grief!—the abbot, as the reward for the most wicked consecration, supported by the duke’s authority, put the cope upon himself, without the knowledge or advice of the bishop of Ostia and of us.
>
> “When these things had taken place, and the bishop of Ostia had in every respect proceeded well with us, he saw that the abbot intended to go to Rome to have himself consecrated through the power of Prince Jordan. Fearing perhaps that he would be deprived of his dignity if another person laid the first hand of consecration upon him, he turned on the day of battle. Forgetful of his purpose and of the promise he had made to us—something shameful to say—he made peace with the abbot and paid him every reverence as pope.
>
> “As for how and in what manner he intends to go to Rome, since the bearers of the present letter and the pilgrims will be able to report to you more fully whatever they saw being prepared for this purpose as they passed through Capua after leaving us, or whatever they learned from the reports of others, we have judged it useless to write about it.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0341] Hugh’s other letter to Matilda concerning the same matter, written after Urban II’s election, was published from the Cluniac cartulary by d’Achery II. K.]

Having therefore been consecrated by the bishop of Ostia, while saying Mass at Saint Peter’s, he was struck down by the judgment of God during the Canon. Although he recognized, belatedly, that he had erred, he deposed himself, summoned the brothers from Monte Cassino who were present with him, ordered that he be carried there, and commanded that he be buried in the chapter house not as pope but as abbot.

(Fol. 133′.) Since these matters have now been arranged, and since we have reached the point at which we must speak of our pilgrimage, let us pray God to pour into our heart knowledge of the word and to bestow the grace of wisdom, so that we may not grow weary while speaking the truth.

The year was 1085 from the Lord’s incarnation, and the furious zeal of Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, in defending and exalting the party of Witbertus of Ravenna, the heretic, was restrained by no moderation of justice from proclaiming that man a holy, just, and Catholic Roman pontiff and from commanding that he be so proclaimed. He even recited solemn prayers for him in the Church, performed ordinations under his authority, and had everything that was owed by right to the holy pope rendered to this man contrary to law and justice.

The simplicity of Abbot Rodulf could not endure this any longer, especially since everyone was raging against him above all others, as though they were grieved that he alone dissented from them—he who ought to have been one of them and among their leaders, but who was now, to their insult, proposing new laws and new institutions against the prince of the kingdom and the priests.

Since concealed hatred was now advancing toward open enmity, he judged that he must yield to circumstances and withdrew to Flavigny. This was a village subject to the jurisdiction of the church of Saint Vito, situated in the territory of Toul. There, somewhat removed from the city, he would wait to see whether an opportunity for remedy might arise, so that, when their anger had somewhat subsided, he might return to the brothers. But the undertaking was fruitless.

He had recently discussed these matters with the abbot of Dijon, and the conclusion of that counsel was that it would be utterly foolish for him to wish to make a pilgrimage with the brothers as he had planned, since the path of danger was open if young and inexperienced brothers, who until then had served God in the monastery under strict custody, were exposed to the world. It would be better for the father, together with his sons, since they could not remain at peace in their own place, to seek some location renowned for religious observance, where they could serve God with grace and tranquility until, once the cloud of that error had passed, they could return to their own place.

The aforementioned abbot added that he was ready to provide them with what they needed—not by giving them what belonged to him, but by gladly assigning to them what was theirs, because the goods of the Church are common to all the sons of the Church. The church of Dijon, endowed with every good, would not fail to provide all religious men with the temporal goods that were in it.

At that time he himself was also nearby, at Bertiniacum, a possession of the church of Dijon situated in the same territory of Toul, ready to make good on his promises. He waited for a long time for Rodulf to come and repeatedly urged him through messengers to do so; and this is what happened.

Seeing that every avenue of return was being closed to him, with evils multiplying on every side, Abbot Rodulf came to him at the aforesaid village of Bertiniacum on the very vigil of the Annunciation of the Lord, and we celebrated that feast there on the same night. On the following day we came to Langres, and on the third day we proceeded to Dijon, where we were honorably and charitably received and joined to the monastery’s community.

It delights us to linger here for a little while in meditation on the memory of the Lord’s wondrous works, which the Lord God has performed with us, he who does great things for his poor, so that our whole substance may confess to him, because he has dealt with us not according to our merits but according to his benefits. It is therefore pleasing to remember the sweetness of his mercy, for he is good, he is sweet; his grace is freely given, his compassion incomparable, his mercy beyond utterance. By it he saves even those who flee from the means by which they ought to be saved, whom your grace, Lord, draws to salvation even against their will.

Yours is the kingdom, Lord; yours the strength and power. To you alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, honor and glory, praise and jubilation, and everlasting thanksgiving are due. You, Lord, made me a participant in this gift of yours. Through your servant, Abbot Rodulfus, you snatched me from the vanity of the world—me who was seeking refuge and foreign things, and who, under the pretext of learning, wished to cling to the world—and appointed me a companion of this pilgrimage. You multiplied your grace in me, so that, though a young man, I did not find it burdensome to leave acquaintances, relatives, my homeland, and the nest in which I had grown up; rather, I rejoiced and gave thanks for whatever your fatherly will desired concerning me, and gladly devoted to you my body, soul, and entire substance, preferring to expend whatever strength there was in my youthful body in your service (fol. 134).

Moreover, though I was lowly and unworthy, you added to me the grace and favor of your servant, the abbot of Dijon. As soon as he saw and recognized me, he took me wholly into himself, with you willing and favoring it, hoping and believing, as I think, that some good would flow from you into us. Would that what he hoped, what he believed, what he sought and seeks from you concerning us, might through your grace come to pass in us, so that he may rejoice in our progress, whom you desired to make him love for love of you. For what was there in us that such a man should love with so great an affection of charity, except your grace, Lord, which he hoped and awaited from you in us?

May the fruitful effect of his devotion, through your grace, come to fruition in us, Lord, so that his sweet soul may rejoice in your kindness, which, by his merits and with your grace cooperating, may deign to strengthen and govern us, so that your mercy may be proclaimed and honored in him and in us. For I do not wish to be ungrateful for your benefits; I do not wish to cast so far away the benefits of this father, which come from you, that they should pass beyond sight. I want frequent reflection to exercise and renew them, so that they may never be removed from memory, which loses nothing except what it has not often regarded. Let them be placed in the foremost part of the mind, so that they may always come before us.

I therefore chose, with more ardent affection and more fervent zeal, to serve you, because I saw your mercy overflowing in me, destroying my iniquity and strengthening my humility. In all things our frail and lowly humility gives you thanks, because you rescued me from the company of the wicked and, in your freely given compassion, delivered me from the tribulations that had increased upon your servants, our brothers, after we had departed from them.

For they were taken captive and, amid reproach and insult, brought before the gaze of that beast of Verdun, to whom the entire senate of the city had gathered. They were questioned as though the matter concerned the faith: which pope they recognized and which king they revered. When they remained silent, the proceedings immediately turned to unheard-of measures. The text of the Gospel was placed in their midst, and judgment was then pronounced that all, from the greatest to the least, should swear that Witbert, surnamed Clement, was a just and catholic pope, and that Henry was an emperor chosen and crowned by God. Whoever would not do this was to be stripped of his clothing and expelled from the city in disgrace and dishonor.

This was done so that those who had been tested might be made manifest. Your mercy knew, Lord God, that servant of yours, Rufus, a pearl of God hidden among stones. Stripped, beaten, and flogged because he refused to swear, he was driven through the middle of the city, yet was not ashamed to bear in his body the disgrace of your cross, Christ.
