Thus naked, wearing only a woolen shirt [Note: [Col. 0343D] A woolen shirt.], he was driven for eight miles. After some servants of God had given him a little clothing, he finally came to Dijon, where he was received with joy and refreshed after his toil.

Meanwhile the number of the brothers who were arriving increased, and, so that harmony and unanimity of peace might be more closely maintained between the two groups, they were admonished to promise stability. This word was exceedingly burdensome to them, because it seemed almost contrary to what was right: they thought that they could neither violate their first faith nor make a second profession while preserving the first they had made. For they feared violating their first vow and first profession, and therefore considered it wrong even to hear talk of making a second, since it seemed wholly intolerable to them to leave, even for an hour, the monastery in which they had vowed stability to God. They would utterly reject such a course if they established a second stability in another church.

Abbot Rodulfus had sought counsel concerning this matter from many people, and Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, gave him the following answer in writing:

“L., archbishop of Canterbury, sends greetings to Abbot Rodulfus. I have been informed that you wish to depart from your monastery and that you are troubled concerning the stability you promised, lest you offend God in the very place from which you ought to please him. Concerning this I offer the following reasoning, and in offering it I give myself as an example. If I, L., had sworn with my own hand that I would not depart from some monastery, but saw that I could not save my soul there, I would leave, and would not incur the crime of perjury. For one who is bound to God for God’s sake is not released from him unless he is released against him. But he is not released from God against God who, for love of him and in order to please him well, migrates from the sons of discord, pride, and distrust—or, to speak more plainly, from the sons of the devil—to the sons of peace, hope, and humility, indeed to the sons of God. For one who passes in this way, does he not flee from the seat of the devil to the seat of God? Who, then, would judge him deserving of condemnation when he flees to God as to a father, as to God and a friend?

“Moreover, one who passes in this way does not pass from one church to another. There are not many churches, but one church spread throughout the whole world; everywhere one God is served, and one king is served as a soldier. Finally, Saint Benedict, who commands that stability be firmly established, orders that a monk coming from one monastery to another be received and, if he is of good life, be urged to establish his stability.”

Strengthened by these and many other plausible arguments and reasons, and obeying the command of their father, some professed stability in the church of Dijon and obedience in the presence of the monastery’s father. Others, however, hesitated and refused to consent to make the profession.

I was one of the hesitant, good Jesus, when your mercy, through your servant our abbot, had already commanded me to attend daily upon your faithful servant, whose soul had taken pleasure in me. Yet I was also afraid of this, because I did not know the man’s modesty, piety, and sweetness. Although I knew his holiness, I revered him. Nevertheless, I kept close to him from a distance and greatly thirsted for his kindness, because I desired to be present with and dwell among good men—and all of this came from you, Lord Jesus.

With exceptional discernment, like a skilled bird-catcher, he hunted my soul, drawing and, as it were, ensnaring my devotion to him—already considerable—with certain gifts and many forms of affection, though none exceeded the bounds of the religious life. Yet again I feared a man whom I did not know, although I had already opened my breast to him and laid bare all the secrets of my soul.

What was in the heart of that faithful servant of yours, Lord Jesus? What was it when he left me so entirely to my own will that he even publicly forbade anyone to criticize whatever I did or said, lest anyone rebuke me, lest anyone even protest in the chapter house? What was it when, as though I were daily prostrate at his feet, and as though I had already been caught, I begged him to rebuke and instruct me, while he seemed to repel me and gave me the option of doing whatever I wished?

And I made my profession, having been led to make it in the following way. By chance I was coming from the cloister while he was sitting in his consistory, and, seeing me, he began to admonish me concerning the profession. When I heard what I did not want to hear, I was ashamed and drew back. But then, as I approached a wooden column, I encountered a serpent coiled in a spiral. Since I did not know what it was and feared nothing of the kind, I extended my foot to discover what it might be; but it stretched out its neck, opened its mouth, and threatened to bite.

When I cried out and stepped backward, at his command the prior came and, crushing the serpent’s head with his foot, threw it down dead, while that blessed man cried out, saying: “Kill it! May the serpent that lies in wait for the salvation of Brother Hugh die in this way!” In my heart I too assented, saying: “So be it. Amen.”

Immediately, good Jesus, when this had been resolved and assented to in my heart, your sweetness mercifully grew strong within me. I felt your love extinguish in me all the serpent’s poisons that were preventing me from fulfilling the obedience of my profession. Why delay? On that same day, when the aforesaid man perceived that our heart had been changed, he approached me alone, as I believe under your inspiration. After he had spoken at length about the simplicity and modesty of our abbot, and had also recalled our irreverence and stubbornness, by which we refused to obey our spiritual father, he brought forward the authority of the Rule, which commands obedience to one’s father even if he should, God forbid, act otherwise, and says that obedience is not to be subjected to examination.

I confess that the authority of the man overcame me, as did the force of his words, supported by reason and authority—and also the fact that, by your grace, I did not wish to resist the truth. In all things I give you thanks, good Jesus, because you protected me, because you sheltered me beneath the shadow of your wings, and because you granted me the grace of your faithful servants.

Thus, under his guidance, I made satisfaction to our abbot for my stubbornness, and on the following day I obeyed their commands. Blessed in every way be the name of your glory, for you dispose all things in tranquility.

I pray, Lord Jesus, that you do not separate me from the number and fellowship of your servants, who abandoned the glory of the world with its pleasures. For I too, when you inspired my heart, willingly set aside and continue to set aside the world and what belongs to it. With blessed Mary as witness and mediator, I devoted and continue to devote my soul and body to you, Lord God, and I prefer to die in your service, because to serve you is to reign (fol. 135).

Mortify in me, Lord, whatever is unfit either for food or for sacrifice, and grant our father, your servant the abbot of Dijon, to see what he desires from us, so that you may be praised in him and in us, you who are powerful, glorious, wondrous, and blessed in your works.

(Year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1088.) When those who remained had been inclined to obey, and all were serving God in peace and moderation, in tranquillity of spirit, suddenly news arrived of the death of Pope Gregory VII [Note: [Col. 0345D]

The following account of the death of Gregory VII is read in a manuscript of the British Museum, among the Cotton manuscripts, Nero C. V., parchment, from the end of the eleventh century, fol. 1:

“‘We wish you to know, you who are concerned with the care of the Church, that the apostolic Hildebrand, now at the point of death, summoned to himself one of the twelve cardinals whom he loved greatly above the others. He confessed to almighty God, Saint Peter, and the whole Church that he had greatly sinned in the pastoral care entrusted to him to govern, having been persuaded by the devil to stir up hatred and anger against the human race. Afterwards, however, he said that he had undertaken the sentence which had been spread throughout the world for the increase of Christianity. Finally, he sent this confessor of his to the emperor and to the whole Church, so that they might seek pardon for him, because he was looking toward the end of his life. He then very quickly put on the angelic garment and released and dissolved for the emperor and for all Christian people, living and dead, clergy and laity, all the bonds of his bans. He ordered his men to leave the house of Theoderic and commanded Henry’s friends to ascend. The archbishop of Mainz bears witness.’

“An account found in the Catalaunian manuscript—not Laon, as it is incorrectly written—may be found above, in volume V of the *Scriptores*, p. 563, lines 42 and following. There, too, at lines 16 and following, are passages expressed incorrectly which we have transcribed here.”]

; the hearts of the brothers were particularly troubled, grieving over the desolation of the holy Church of God, although they knew that they ought to rejoice with him whom the Lord, tested by many tribulations, was now cherishing in his own bosom. Nevertheless, for the absolution and repose of his soul they willingly discharged the customary offering in the offices and celebrations of Masses and in the giving of alms.

For the virtue of charity flourished in our father, the abbot of Dijon, and it was so great that, although that year the violence of the storm had everywhere beaten down and completely ruined the ripe grain in the ears and the grapes on the vines, nothing less was provided in the refectory and in almsgiving. The brothers now almost exceeded a hundred in number, and those who had come from rich and exceedingly fertile land, knowing nothing of suffering want, were supplied with everything in the greatest abundance. Your mercy supplied all things, Lord Jesus.

And rightly so. For to one who has charity, more will be given, and he will abound. What greater charity could there have been than for a man who had been separated from the monastery for an entire year, returning from there to his own place, to find everything confused and utterly ruined, with bread, wine, and provisions all lacking, yet to receive forty brothers with thanksgiving? Though he could in no way provide what was necessary even for his own people, he went away to foreign lands to lead back men whom he did not know, bringing them to their place at his own expense.

These are your marvels, Jesus; these proceed from your fountain. Your servant knew that you would not abandon your own, you who are accustomed to prepare food in the desert and to feed many thousands of people with a few loaves. In your omnipotence you had also foreseen these things for him, supplying him with what was necessary and, moreover, granting him such an increase in the estates and farms of the church in that year and thereafter that the church’s revenue appeared to have been doubled. Furthermore, with you granting it, he will possess the blessing as an inheritance, because he was found faithful in a small matter.

In the following year, during the persecution of the tyrant Henry, Hermann left Metz, and Walo, abbot of Saint-Arnulf, unlawfully usurped his episcopal see. There, by a marvelous judgment of God, when chrism was sought for his execrable consecration and the chrism prepared by Hermann had been brought, the bishop of Verdun rejected and threw away the chrism that was holy. He then brought his own chrism, which he had consecrated contrary to right and law, and used it to complete Walo’s consecration, lest the shameless son should receive his father’s blessing.

Walo, however, because he had mounted his father’s bed, performed public penance. Henry appointed a certain Bruno, a former bishop, in his place; he was later expelled from the city in disgrace and dishonor. Thus, after many dangers of labor and travel, Hermann was recalled by his people from Lombardy, where he had been staying with Matilda. In the fourth year after his departure he was received at Metz with universal affection, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1089. In that same year Odo, bishop of Ostia, was consecrated pope and called Urban (1088, March 12).

As we are now about to speak of the death of Lord Hermann, let us first consider the revelation made concerning the translation of the body of blessed Clement, the first apostle and bishop of the church of Metz, and concerning his death.

Saint Clement appeared to a certain boy named Hugh, of innocent and simple life, and, showing him in the church of Saint Felix the place of his burial, commanded him to go and tell Hermann, bishop of Metz, to raise his bones from there. He also added that Hermann himself would die on the third day after the revelation concerning his body had been made. He further charged the boy to change his way of life and to do nothing childish, but, seeking monastic clothing, to strive to serve God.

When the boy awoke, he summoned his master—for, deprived of both father and mother, he was staying with the man who had his sister—and told him of the vision. He asked to be taken to the bishop. But his master, fearing to do so, took him to the abbot of Saint Felix, to whom the boy reported what he had seen. The abbot disclosed everything in order to the religious persons, and from there they all began to inform the bishop about the translation.

The boy, anxious to fulfill his obedience, wept because he was not being presented to the bishop. But they, indulging in Gallic bombast, attributed the revelation to the abbot of Saint Felix, as though it would thereby have greater authority, keeping silent about the boy. (fol. 135′)

He also requested the monastic habit, as he had been instructed, and, although some judged that he ought to be placed in the monastery of Saint Clement, by his own choice he was taken and received there because he had had two brothers in the monastery of Saint Vitonus, who had already departed from the world. May the Lord grant him a life perfect in all holiness and religious observance, through the merits and intercession of Saint Clement, so that he may see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

(1090.) The venerable Hermann, having been received in his city, began to fall ill during Lent; nevertheless, despite the astonishment of many religious persons at his illness, he did not cease from his episcopal office. For many years previously, certain religious persons had admonished him concerning the translation of blessed Clement, the patrician of the city of Rome, later a disciple and legate of blessed Peter, who had been sent by him and had become the first apostle and bishop of the church of Metz. Some also asserted, on the basis of a sufficiently credible revelation, that God had reserved this for fulfillment in Hermann’s days.

As he was devout, Hermann piously arranged prayers and fasting, postponed the translation until after Easter, and fixed the day. The abbot of Saint Felix partly disclosed and partly concealed the revelation reported to him by the boy. He concealed the fact that the same revelation had fixed the day of Hermann’s death as the third day after the translation of blessed Clement.

Who could adequately recount with what affection he reconciled penitents on the Lord’s Supper, or how devoutly he displayed himself in consecrating the chrism, when, more like an angel than a human being, he shone before the sons of the Church? Although his illness was severe, it could not disturb the dignity of his countenance, the steadiness of his speech, or the firmness of his mind.

When he preached publicly to everyone, he did not remain silent, trusting in the Lord his God, concerning the avoidance of the sacrifices of the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. He explained that, according to blessed Augustine, Nicholas had been judged a heretic by the apostles because, when the apostles reproved him, he refused to give up the use of the wife he had previously had while in the order of the diaconate.

After the divine office had been celebrated at Easter, he fortified himself and the sheep entrusted to him with the sacrament of the body and blood of God. That same evening he began to grow more seriously ill. As the appointed day for transferring the venerable relics approached, however, he regained some strength, with the Lord’s consent. In transferring blessed Clement on the Kalends of May, divine grace fulfilled his desire, with the greatest devotion of clergy and people.

The entire city, indeed the entire region, stood present to hear his preaching, and dew of heavenly sweetness flowed from his mouth. After he had absolved everyone, and everyone had sought absolution from him as though from God himself, he finally expressed his desire in the hearing of all, saying:

“It is enough for me! Would that God would look upon me, bring my labors to an end, and receive my spirit in peace through the intercession of Saint Clement, whose most sacred body, today granted to us from heaven as a magnificent gift, we have been permitted to see, touch, and transfer!”

At these words the people groaned and, grieving with him as he implored the end of his labors, were overcome with compassion.

Two days later, as though foreseeing his approaching departure, he ordered letters to be sent to the faithful of the church, praying and adjuring them by the one who lives forever to conduct the church’s business without deceit and without pretense, in simple and unvarnished truth. He then said his final farewell to everyone, with a marvelous expression in his words and countenance.

On the third day, around the ninth hour, realizing that his departure was near, he ordered the brothers to be summoned. He restrained the sons who stood around him, by voice and gesture, from grieving. When they asked him to whom he was leaving them in their desolation and what he commanded them, he said:

“I commend you to God. Stand firm in the faith and teaching of blessed Peter, as you have both seen and heard from his successors.”

After blessing them all, he armed himself with the sign of the cross. Having invoked the Holy Trinity, commended himself to holy Mary, and implored the common patronage of the saints, he raised his eyes and hands to heaven and, without any sound of voice or movement of body, as though falling asleep, gave up his spirit.

The following night he appeared to one of his beloved companions, whom he had adopted as a son. This man had fallen asleep from grief while the psalms were being sung. Hermann said to him: “Do not be sad; I am safe.” He appeared again to a venerable man and said: “They say that I am dead, but I live.” When these things were reported by abbots and other persons of serious standing, they became known.

The venerable bishop Hermann died on the Nones of May, adorned with the cross, mitre, and pallium, and was buried in the church of Saint Peter with these insignia, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1090.

(1089, May 7.) In the preceding year, Theoderic of Verdun had died on the fourth day before the Nones of May. During his illness, however, he had done penance for his communion with Witbert and for the expulsion of the brothers, and had confessed his guilt. He was absolved by a certain brother named Gerard, formerly a canon and archdeacon of the church of Verdun and then a monk of Saint Vitonus, whom Rodulfus the abbot had piously sent there for this purpose, at the abbot’s command. The abbot had obtained from the Apostolic See the power to absolve those who returned from excommunicated persons. (fol. 136)

From that time Abbot Rodulfus was recalled with the brothers to the monastery entrusted to him. After his departure, rapacious wolves had entered it [Note: [Col. 0349] “rupi.” in witness c], sparing neither place and revering neither God nor man. They so confused and destroyed everything that the memory of that confusion and devastation cannot even today be erased.

In this matter it is delightful to admire the prudence and charity of our father, the abbot of Dijon. When he received such and so many brothers, he rejoiced; when he sent them back to their place, he rejoiced. Indeed, in our times he alone was found who, having retained brothers in a time of necessity, would release them in a time of peace and would not grieve.

The fact that he received them and joined one community to another became a sign against which opposition arose, to such an extent that everyone prayed that these monsters might be turned to good. For Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, disapproved of his action, saying that it would be impossible for three communities to remain in harmony with one another. He therefore gave him the following counsel: if he wished to secure peace for the church entrusted to him, he should retain those who wished permanently to establish stability in the church of Dijon, but should dismiss entirely from himself those who did not wish to do so.

Otherwise the church’s peace could not be secure, since those who had been received or nurtured in the church would disagree with those who had refused to be received, which was contrary to religion. He added that he would do the same if a similar necessity fell upon him.

I heard this from his own mouth when I was with our same father at Cluny. He was already taking me with him so that I might see what surrounded him and devote myself to perfection. When I humbly asked him why he had left me for so long to my own will, he briefly replied:

“I wished to know whether your land would receive the seed of the word, whether, after receiving the seed, it would produce fruit, lest I scatter seed in vain and my labor and expense perish.”

Gathering from his words devotion born of devotion, I gave thanks to you, Christ, and prayed with deep affection that your grace might bear fruit in me, so that he might rejoice in us in you. I remain in that same desire, praying that your favor may be present with us and make us worthy of your mercy, so that, with your mercy working in us, we may be found free from all iniquity, and so that his fatherly affection may rejoice in our sonship.

O God, and O blessed mother of God, receive the cries of his heart on our behalf and gladden his soul concerning us, so that we may be found together in the lot of the glory of the children of God. I do not wish to be ungrateful to a father who gives benefits, nor to give thanks when no witnesses are present. And although benefits bestowed in youth perish because they are never again recalled, I gratefully accept the benefit I have found bestowed. I repay its first installment by judging with gratitude that his affections have flowed toward us, and by bearing witness to this everywhere. If I cannot return the favor, I shall at least never cease to confess everywhere that I cannot return it.

Our father therefore received the brothers with joy and sent them back with joy, because he knew that they were God’s deposit, and therefore willingly obeyed the will of his Lord in keeping and returning them. As blessed Ambrose says in his book *On the Death of His Brother*, it makes no difference whether one rejects a deposit or grieves when it is returned. He therefore did not grieve when it was returned, because he knew the Lord and considered it wrong to oppose his will.

Lord Abbot Rodulfus returned to his monastery with his brothers in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, when Richerus had already been appointed to the church of Verdun and was serving as dean in the church of Saint Stephen of Metz.

After the people of Metz had been deprived of Lord Hermann, they chose a certain cleric from Trier named Poppo, brother of Count Palatine Henry. Without a royal grant, they appointed him to the church by election alone and began to consider his consecration. Since the bishop of Trier was polluted by communion with the Wibertists, they asked that Poppo be consecrated by the archbishop of Lyon, entrusting this task to the vigor of the abbot of Dijon, whose ability they trusted.

Without any hesitation, he led the lord of Lyon, together with two of his suffragans, namely the bishops of Mâcon and Langres, through wars and swords, when everything seemed to threaten death, all the way to Metz. By him Poppo was consecrated with honor in the first week of Lent, and the lord of Lyon then returned home with his companions.

In the following year Richerus [Note: [Col. 0351] Thus in the manuscript.] came to Lyon for his consecration. After purging himself by oath of simony, he was consecrated on Holy Easter Day by the same archbishop, in the presence of the bishops of Mâcon, Chalon, Autun, and Toul, together with the sons of the church of Verdun, and with letters from the lord of Metz concurring in his election.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1094 [Note: [Col. 0351D] Compare Hugh’s letter to Lambert of Arras, Mansi XX, 801. K.], a council of thirty-two bishops was held at Autun under Lord Hugh of Lyon (October 15). Many abbots and religious men also attended.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, on Wednesday, the twenty-fifth day of the moon, the second day before the Nones of April, stars were seen falling from heaven from midnight until dawn. That same night Gerald, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure [Note: [Col. 0351D] La Sauve-Majeure, in the diocese of Bordeaux.], departed to the Lord (fol. 136′).

On that same day the lord archbishop of Lyon also set out for Saint James [Note: [Col. 0352D] Compostela.], accompanied honorably by clergy and laypeople. After staying at Anicium [Note: [Col. 0352D] Le Puy.] for three days, he was drawn away from them only with the greatest difficulty, since many religious people had gathered there to retain him.

He arrived at Saint James on the eve of the holy day of Pentecost, and on the holy day itself publicly celebrated the solemn Mass at the altar of the saint, while a bishop, the clergy, and an immense crowd of people stood by. On the following day, having received permission from the saint, he set out to return home. He arrived at Lyon three days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, where he was received with the favor, praise, and joy of everyone. There he received messengers from Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 0352B]

Concerning the pope’s deeds in Italy, the following account is found in a manuscript of the British Museum, among the Harleian manuscripts, no. 3014, from the twelfth century, on parchment, written by a German or French hand:

“In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the third indiction, a synod was celebrated at Piacenza on the Kalends of March, under the presidency of Lord Pope Urban, with bishops and abbots from both Gaul and Lombardy and Tuscany. A great discussion was held concerning those who had bought churches or prebends, and also concerning those who had been ordained in the Wibertine schism. On the first day, and so forth, until ‘let him himself provide for the offices of the chapels.’ We shall give these matters elsewhere. The account continues:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the third indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, when Lord Pope Urban came to Cremona, King Conrad II went out to meet him and performed the service of the *strator*. Then, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, he gave him security by oath concerning his life, his limbs, his freedom from captivity, the Roman papacy, and the regalia of Saint Peter to be acquired, held, and defended against all men, both within Rome and outside Rome, in good faith, without fraud or evil intent.

“Then the pope received him as a son of the Roman Church and promised publicly that, if the king observed these things as he had promised, he would help him acquire, hold, and defend the kingdom. And when God granted him permission to come to Rome for his coronation, he would give him the imperial crown and help him in his other affairs, for the honor of God, Saint Peter, and the Roman Church—while, of course, preserving the justice of that Church and the apostolic decrees, especially those concerning investitures.”]

who had come from Apulia and was hastening toward Gaul.

(November 18.) He held a council at Clermont, presided over by Bishop Durannus. The devotion of the Cluniacs had been plotting his deposition, but Christ exalted him and manifested in a wondrous way what pleased him.

For when Durannus had accepted the legation of receiving the pope as a guest and supplying what was necessary, and had applied himself to this task with grace, he began to fall seriously ill. Some people maliciously interpreted his illness, although Christ was soon to show his merit to the people.

Certain Cluniac brothers were lying in wait for him because he wished to retain under his authority, subject to the obedience and reverence due to the church of Auvergne, the monastery of Moissiac, which belonged by right to the church of Auvergne and which he had also granted for the restoration of the Cluniac order. For this reason they had accused him before the pope and were attempting to secure his deposition [Note: [Col. 0353D] Concerning another dispute between Durannus and the Cluniacs, there is a letter from Urban to him written in 1094, in Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* V, 314. K.].

When the pope arrived, he visited Durannus and absolved him. As Durannus was already drawing his last breath, he returned his spirit to the Creator on the following night [Note: [Col. 0353D] Baldric of Bourgueil attests this in a double epitaph that he composed: the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. K.], after being washed and cared for with the greatest diligence by his sons—that is, the abbot of Dijon, the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, the bishop of Grenoble, and others.

Before the council began, people from throughout the world hurried to his funeral. He was buried with honor by the pope himself and the bishops of the land, and William of Bafia obtained his see with the approval of clergy and people, by order of that same apostolic lord.

Desiderius, bishop of Cavaillon and abbot of the monastery of Gemmeticum, also died during the same council. In that same year the road of the Christians traveling with arms to Jerusalem was confirmed.

That year also died Rainaldus, archbishop of Reims; Hildebert, archbishop of Bourges; and Landricus, bishop of Mâcon [Note: [Col. 0354D] On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November 1096, Pope Urban issued a bull to Landricus at Cluny. *Gallia Christiana*, Instruments IV, 285. K.].

The extermination of Jews was also carried out that year in many places by men bound for Jerusalem. It may certainly seem strange that this extermination occurred in many places on a single day, through one impulse of fervor, although many condemned the deed and judged it contrary to religion. Yet we know that it could not be prevented from happening, since many priests, after pronouncing a sentence of excommunication, and many princes, by the terror of threats, tried to disrupt it.

### 1096

At that time, in order to establish harmony between the brothers, the sons of King William—namely, William, king of the English, and Robert, count of the Normans—the abbot of Dijon had crossed the sea at the pope’s command. He was to admonish the aforesaid king concerning the many things he was doing unlawfully: the bishoprics and abbeys which he retained for himself without providing them with pastors; the revenues and income of them all, which he appropriated to himself; simony; and the fornication of clerics. He was also to address the fact that the bishop of Albano, whom the pope had first sent to him, had made an agreement with the king that no Roman legate should be sent to England unless the king himself prescribed whom it should be.

Roman authority had become so cheap among the English because of the avarice and greed of the legates that, while the bishop of Albano was present, consenting, and not objecting—in fact, ordering it—the archbishop of Canterbury had sworn fidelity to blessed Peter and the pope, while preserving his fidelity to his own lord, the king. The matter had progressed so far that no one coming on the pope’s behalf was received with the honor due to him; and there was no archbishop, bishop, or abbot in England, much less monk or cleric, who dared receive an apostolic letter, let alone obey it, unless the king ordered it.

When the abbot arrived, he exercised such freedom that the king, having observed his integrity and his unflattering firmness of mind, promised that he would comply with his councils and wishes. All the faithful rejoiced at his arrival, since at his coming the dignity and vigor of the English Church and the freedom of Roman authority seemed to breathe again and rise anew.

### (folio 137)

But what does the insatiable gulf of Roman avarice leave undisturbed? [Note: The manuscript reads “Roman”; Labbe prints “human.”] The king, suspicious of the authority of a man whom he had long heard was coming, had sent ahead a legate of the pope, with ten marks of tested and pure gold in his hand. Trusting in this advance messenger, he delayed answering the aforesaid abbot; meanwhile he retained him with himself through Easter and treated him reverently and honorably.

Then, behold, the legate returned, bringing the king a postponement concerning everything until the Nativity of the Lord. Through a certain little nephew or household servant of the pope, he had obtained this postponement on the assumption that, at the latter’s departure, the payment owed to blessed Peter would mature sooner, as he believed, and that it would be sent to him through the same legate of such great authority, the son of the pope’s sister—or at least part of it, if not the whole.

When he had received this answer, the king became joyful and produced the apostolic postponement granted to him by the aforesaid man. Yet privately and publicly he criticized the pope’s action, because he had treated so dishonorably a man whose fame was celebrated everywhere and who was fortified by the privileges of his authority: he had cancelled his legation through a single layperson, who was equipped neither with apostolic letters nor with the honor of secular learning or rank.

Thus, although the matter remained unresolved, the man departed from him with his reputation, integrity, honor, and wisdom thoroughly commended to everyone. Nevertheless, he remained in Normandy to establish peace and harmony between the brothers. Once peace had been made, and after receiving a pension of ten thousand marks, the count of Normandy entrusted his land to the king of the English to be guarded for three years. He then set out for Jerusalem and was escorted by the same abbot as far as the village called Pontarlier [Note: Pontarlier, at the sources of the Doubs], with Count Stephen of France and Count Robert of Flanders accompanying his retinue.

While we were still in Normandy, the archbishop of Lyon, together with the bishops of Autun and Chalon, had assembled for the funeral rites of the bishop of Mâcon. Berard, the elected archdeacon of Lyon, was consecrated bishop of Mâcon. [Note: On 4 December 1096 he confirmed a certain donation; *Gallia Christiana*, IV, 1067. K.]

There also, Lord Hagano, bishop of Autun, complained greatly about the desolation of the church of Flavigny. Since that church had remained without a pastor for seven years after the death of Lord Raynald, the duke’s brother, he requested me from the archbishop as abbot, since I was, as it were, known to the archbishop; he had very often made this request. [Note: In 1085 King Philip of the Franks, at the request of Hagano, bishop of Autun, and Raynald, abbot of the monastery, had confirmed its possessions. K.] He would scarcely have obtained this, however, had he not enlisted the support of the canons and laymen to request it.

Nevertheless, he succeeded, and the bishop of Chalon was sent to compel the Lord of Dijon, by apostolic authority, to give his consent, and to compel me, in his name, to obey. This was done when we returned.

After the election had been confirmed and the day of consecration fixed, I went to the archbishop and asked what his judgment was concerning the matter. He greatly consoled our anxiety and persuaded us by reason to carry out what had been commanded; he strengthened us by his authority. Thus, after dismissing me, he honored me with a letter, which he sent to the bishop of Autun in these words:

> To our venerable brother in Christ, Hagano [Note: “Ha.” in the manuscript], bishop of Autun, Hugh, servant of the church of Lyon, sends greetings.
>
> Your Reverence remembers well how often you have approached our humility and how often you have asked us to restore the church of Flavigny. With great diligence and insistence you requested from us our dearest brother Hugh, a monk of the church of Dijon, whom we had taken to ourselves and whose diligence we trusted—indeed, whose tongue was our voice. What you requested, you extorted from an unwilling and reluctant man. [Note: *nobis* in place of *a vobis*.]
>
> Therefore, confirming by apostolic authority his election, which was made by you, we impose upon you the obligation of his consecration, being certain that, although we are absent in body, we shall be present in spirit and shall take part, through Christ in the Holy Spirit, in that consecration for the honor of God; and we shall be your faithful fellow-workers.
>
> Now, entrusting to your special protection the aforesaid brother and son of ours, whom we subject to so great a burden, we commit him to your faith. We had always wished to retain him with us, but we have yielded to your insistence. You know with what affection we hold him; for this very reason we entrust him to you. Our counsel and assistance will not be lacking. For his love we are prepared to assist, as duty requires, not only the church of Flavigny but all the churches in your diocese.
>
> Act, then, so that this brother may have reason to give us thanks for the help and consolation bestowed upon him, and so that you may receive grace upon grace.

### 1097

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1097, indiction 5, in the thirty-second year of my age, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December—the feast of Saint Cecilia, 22 November—the seventh day, Saturday, when we entered Flavigny, the consecration was carried out on the following day, and we discussed the advancement of the church. After a few days, we departed from Lord Bishop Hagano, the Lord of Dijon, and the others. [Note: Saint Cecilia’s day fell on a Saturday in 1096 and on a Sunday in 1097; indiction 5 agrees with the year 1097.]

In the same year, on the feast of Saint Peter, in a full court, Aymo returned three solidi in annual rent from the castle called Sacriba and from the lands surrounding the castle belonging by right to the church of Flavigny. He had withheld them for many years, incurred guilt by that withholding, and was absolved. Done on the feast of the Apostles.

A certain Folcuinus, having received fifteen solidi from us, renounced the claim he had against the holding at Galiaco which Waldinus had given. This took place in the presence of the following people: [the text is incomplete]—his kinsman, who received a bridle [Note: so the manuscript reads] worth three solidi for the concession.

For the mares which Wido of Lusignan had seized and carried away, I gave one hundred solidi.

To Odo, viscount of Rubeimont, when he became our man, I gave thirty solidi for certain settlements.

To Girard of Duison I gave eleven solidi for one of our servants from Galiaco; to Artald of Saint-Baudel, twenty solidi.

Hagano of Roca also became our man. In the presence of his uncle Raynald, he abandoned his claim to his fief [Note: The manuscript has *fedi*, that is, *feodi*, “fief”] of Finium, belonging to God, Saint Prejectus, and us, after receiving twenty solidi from us. Done at Flavigny.

### 6 February 1097

Hildegarius of Gurzy also became our man. He increased the alms which his grandfather had given by granting to our church Eremburga, daughter of Hellarda, daughter of William, and all their descendants. He received from us fifty-eight solidi as a charitable gift. Done in February, on Friday the sixth day, the eighth day before the Ides of February.

Aymo Lovel, our liege man [Note: *liius*, that is, *ligius*], granted all his allod to God, Saint Peter, and Saint Prejectus. He renounced the exactions which he made in our estate, after the lawful customs of the estate had been recounted before everyone: two sextarii of oats from the head of the holding and four of wine in protection.

I also made peace with Wolo of Sarmacy. After he became our man, I gave him one hundred solidi, one horse, and one dog.

For the redemption of the church of Fontaines I gave thirty-five solidi. At the saltworks of Salins, I gave forty solidi for a horse.

For the redemption of the land and vineyards which our predecessor, Abbot Raynald, had promised to Walter Frossard, the duke’s man, I gave thirty solidi and retained the land.

To Tebert the provost I gave twenty-five solidi for certain lawsuits, and thirty solidi as a settlement for a stag which his dogs had started and our men had captured and divided against my will. To Bernard of Montbar, at his release, thirty solidi.

For the redemption of a gilded fan and a silver reliquary I gave sixty solidi, and seven for a cope.

A certain knight, Arnulf of Monastery, now a convert, gave our church one holding at Prusiliacum.

Gislebert of Lusignan also gave one holding at Darciacum for his son Pontius, together with all its appurtenances, and three men with their descendants.

Likewise Hugh of Draciacum gave one holding with its appurtenances in the same village for his son. Done at Colchas.

Brutinus, lord of the castle once called Sedunum and now called Blismurus, returned to us the church of that castle with its appurtenances and with everything which it had formerly possessed or then possessed. Because he added certain things from his own property for the sustenance of the brothers, I gave him twenty solidi as a charitable gift.

Aymo, a knight of the same castle and Brutinus’s uncle, coming to conversion during an illness, returned to God, Saint Peter, and Saint Prejectus the lands and men which he had been forcibly taking from us, and renounced his claim.

For the redemption of a cope and a pallium I gave one hundred ten solidi.

### 14 April 1099

The aforesaid Hildegarius of Gurzy, because he had taken Bellus Locus from us and had done us an injustice, was excommunicated by us for a long time. At last he confessed his fault at Coneda and was absolved by us. He acknowledged and renewed his homage, and entirely renounced his claim to that cell. He gave hostages, whose names are these: Hugh, his brother; Raynald of Roca; Deodatus; Girard of Roura and his brother Waldricus; and Gauzfredus of Masiac. To the latter I gave twenty solidi. Done at Coneda on Thursday of Easter week, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Count Pontius of Grimens also, for the homicide he had committed against Pontius, our servant, returned to us a native-born woman (*natalem*) and her niece after receiving one hundred ten solidi, and was absolved on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. Later he seized him and received fifty solidi for his ransom.

### (folio 138)

I made Joffredus of Prumiac, his brother with their wives and sons, the wife of Odo Tuat, the wife of Henry with her children, the wife of John of Polignac with her children, and all their descendants—which are very numerous and excellent—free for Saint Peter, through the mediation of Raynald of Roca and the payment of thirty solidi to Odo, viscount of Rubeimont.

The witnesses to this are as follows: Gislebertus the younger; Teubodus Mant; Raynald of Roca; Gislebertus of Turre; Hagano Roc; Hugh Miscus; Goslenus; Gerard of Duis; Brunardus; Raynald Fla; Raynald.

To William of Turraboit I gave thirty solidi for certain settlements; to Gislebertus, thirty solidi for the ransom of the horse of Grosbof, which he had captured and returned to me.

### 1098

In the same year, 1098 from the Lord’s incarnation, Hagano, bishop of Autun, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of July. [Note: The Necrology of Saint-Bénigne gives the sixth day before the Kalends of July.] The following year, Abbot Rodulf died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

After the venerable Hagano, Norgaudus assumed the governance of the church of Autun; he had served as precentor in that church. [Note: Pope Paschal confirmed Norgaudus’s election in a letter dated the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May 1100, *Mansi* XX, 1017.] He was elected amid opposition.

Nevertheless, since I had often gone to Autun on account of this election—for our voice ought to have been the first in the election—I was eventually invited for the Ascension of the Lord. Since I was in distant parts, I could not attend. I nevertheless sent one of our men to act in my place. Later, when I was free, I alone among the abbots accompanied him to Lyon for his consecration. By doing this I could not calm the anger he had conceived because of my absence, although, on the return journey, I had served him and his entire retinue sufficiently and more than sufficiently for two days at Colchas [Note: Couchy].

When he came to Flavigny, he was honorably received by us. On the same night, the Lord’s Day, after I had served him honorably, his men broke and carried away the benches and market stalls [Note: *banke und scharren*, in German] during the Truce of God. They had been in front of the episcopal house, and the land itself, before there had been a house there, had been assessed to the townsmen for their market. When the men whose property they were demanded them, they were not returned.

While they remained unreturned, one of his men bought an ox for the bishop’s use. When our men, out of reverence for the bishop, wished to slaughter it elsewhere, he forced them to slaughter it in front of the aforesaid house. Our men are prepared to affirm that he promised them defense and protection.

After the ox had been killed, our men, at my command and out of honor for the bishop, dragged it elsewhere. When the men whose land had been assessed saw that I, who ought first to have defended them, was failing them in their custom and usage, they themselves set up their market stalls on their assessed land and replaced the meat.

Because the sticks had been brought and because the men had gathered to defend their customary right, this angered the bishop, and he said that he had been assaulted. Yet they had struck no one, because no one had assaulted them, nor had they assaulted anyone.

When I saw that this displeased the bishop, I myself went to him with certain brothers, nobles, and servants. After taking counsel, I offered him that on the following day I would do as much concerning the matter as was fitting for justice and honor and as much as I could and ought to do. Immediately I went up and summoned the tenants and nobles whom I could, in order to carry out what I had offered.

Meanwhile, he deprived me of Christian communion [Note: that is, he placed me under an interdict], so that those coming from elsewhere for weddings lost the Mass, and a body lost burial. Nevertheless, strengthened by counsel, I wished to fulfill what I had promised. I did not fall short in this, nor did I thereby receive Mass.

He appointed a day for me at Autun, and I accepted it. When he wanted me to bring the men there, I said that I would not do so. I could not, because it was not the church’s custom. I asked for Christian communion, but did not receive it.

Seeing that I would not have it, I offered him a surety of four thousand solidi from the church’s tenants: Walo of Sarmacy, Gislebert of Lusignan, Raynald of Roca, Milo of Frollo, Goslenus of Sinemur, Raynald, and Hugh the provost. The offer was made in the presence of his canons Walter, Stephen, and Duran, and the laymen Aymo and Josbert. Even after doing this, I asked for Mass, but did not receive it.

### 15 July

I went to Autun. At the court, because I had acted in this way, I asked for Mass before anything else, and I did so by judgment of the court. Since I had named and presented lay witnesses from among our men, and since Bernard, our marshal, had named Aymo and Josbert among his laymen, judgment was rendered by both clerics and laymen.

Our men wished to affirm that this surety had truly been offered, so that judgment might even have been rendered by the ordeal of fire or water. The following judgment was made concerning the matter:

> Since the abbot and his men did not name Josbert when the court was summoned, this matter ought to remain in abeyance while the abbot seeks to receive Mass; and therefore he himself ought not to have the matter held in abeyance concerning justice being done to the men.

When I heard this judgment, I was dumbfounded. I sought the counsel of the church which I had previously had, but did not receive it. While I was still remaining in the council concerning the court and the judgment, he broke up the court and went away to lunch. I sent to him and sought a postponement, but did not receive one unless I approved the judgment.

How greatly this court burdened the church may be inferred from the fact that, in the very week in which this occurred, he made me retain one hundred horses at Autun, without their servants, on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Later he wished to bring against us, sworn at Flavigny, the community of the dioceses of Autun and Chalon, but this remained unrealized.

He also wished to place all the cells and properties belonging to us under interdict, but the integrity of the chapter of Autun opposed his wishes. He would have done so had it not opposed him.

At last, after I had come many times to Autun for this cause, presenting justice at times and seeking mercy at others, and after I had received neither justice nor mercy, some of our brothers rose up against me at his counsel and urging, saying that I had been party to the sedition over which these matters had arisen.

For this reason I was summoned to go to Autun. I began the journey surrounded, as I believed, by the counsel of monks, nobles, and servants. Yet I lost them through his influence. Since Bernard of Montfort was his man from the fief of Saint Peter, to whom I had promised thirty solidi, and since he held our property, the bishop forbade him to go with me. When the others saw this, all twenty-five of them withdrew from us.

I presented myself alone, with only one monk and three servants, before the chapter. Behold, around the third hour, certain of our men arrived, with his knowledge, accusing me in the chapter of having been party to the matter and making certain other charges which they could not prove, especially since they were disreputable persons.

One of them, Helinannus, even after abandoning me, sat among the canons, eating, drinking, and riding with him. Although I was prepared to answer and be judged canonically, I canonically requested from the bishop the monk of our house whom he had taken from me, but did not receive him.

Moreover, I saw them accusing me, and I was compelled, lest I appear guilty, to order them myself to speak against me. I saw no abbot there. Nor was the judgment, once begun, carried out, because a certain agreement joined us through the mediation of the bishop of Chalon and the provost Anseric: I was to produce a man who would prove under oath that I had not been party to the sedition, and thus I would recover the bishop’s friendship and return to his favor.

I did so, but received neither his favor nor Mass. Moreover, under threat of anathema, he forbade me to become hostile toward those brothers on account of this matter, and entirely removed them from our jurisdiction, so that I could not even remove them from the obediences over which they presided.

### 6 December

Because of this court I went to Autun seven times, from the feast of the Apostles until the feast of Saint Nicholas. I received neither justice, nor favor, nor Mass, especially since, to satisfy him, I had brought there certain laymen who were being accused, contrary to the custom of the church. I am ashamed to remember how he treated them, especially since there was no occasion for which these things ought to have been done.

### (folio 138)

He also took away our brothers from Dijon, who had been given to me for consolation in my labor and for the preservation of discipline. Using the authority which he could and ought to exercise, he ordered that, unless I returned them to Dijon within three days and recalled those who had been expelled, no divine office was to be celebrated in the church. Thus, early the following morning, he set out for Rome, so that there would be no opportunity for anyone to plead either for receiving Mass or for retaining the brothers.

I, so tightly constrained by this crisis that I was willing to promise still greater things—for I was oppressed by immense weariness, since I was being afflicted by such great tribulations; indeed, from the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul until the very feast day of blessed Nicholas, on which these events occurred, Flavigny had been without divine office and burial, although there was no fault of mine—resolved to submit to him in obedience even in matters contrary and harmful, so that perhaps his obstinacy of mind might thereby be softened and calmed.

While I wished in this way to avoid what seemed a ruin, I fell into the abyss of a monstrous precipice. [Note: The manuscript reads *pcipii* for *praecipitii*.] By this action I recovered neither his friendship, which I had never possessed, nor the affection of our monks. Rather, I offended the unity of our father of Dijon and our brothers, which was precisely what they sought and intended.

And indeed this happened deservedly. For the matter was done according to my merits: I had done evil—it is certain that it was evil for me to send away good men so that a good thing might come, when I had no confidence at all that the good would come, but complete distrust—and, as is now evident, I would have neither the good which I did not believe in nor what I possessed; so that only affliction might give understanding to the hearing.

Later I received absolution from Lyon, though not from him, since it came through the archbishop. Meanwhile, while he was absent, I was at peace, except that I saw everything collapsing for the worse because of the abandonment of discipline, and I could not correct it because I was alone. Then I began to perceive what they had thought, attempted, and contrived, when I could no longer correct it.

Meanwhile I made peace with Raynald of Granciac, who had disturbed all our affairs by frequent incursions and plunderings. Since he had a just claim, I paid him sixty solidi as a settlement.

I also made peace with his brother Wido of Lusignan. For the fief over which he was making a claim, I returned to him two modii and eight sextarii, while he was guardian of the sons of Tebald Rufus. He granted me the fourth part through the approval of his wife and sons, rendered homage, and swore fidelity.

After settling these more serious matters, I gave thirty-five solidi for Walter of Insula, whom Gislebertus Mischius was claiming, and seven solidi for his sister’s son. I made all their descendants free for Saint Peter and Saint Prejectus. Done at Flavigny.

I caused the duke to come to Flavigny concerning the protection payment [Note: *Schutzgeld*] which our men of Galiaco wished to pay him contrary to right and custom. By judgment of our court and his, since he held our fief, he renounced that protection payment. To him I gave a horse worth one hundred solidi as an honorarium.

Arnulf of Grosboes, having received our fellowship and fifteen solidi as a charitable gift, returned to us two families from the fief of Saint Peter at Cleriacum and Agerniacum, and acquired a third for us against Aymo Lovel, our knight. He also returned one holding at Cavanniacum, from the land of Saint Peter belonging to his fief at Flavigny, in the presence of R., the mayor, and Arnulf’s son. Done on Wednesday of the fast in September.

Aymo of Griniac also acknowledged his homage and became our man. Walter of Grinione, for his son who was a monk, gave Saint Prejectus a large piece of land and a demesne meadow of great value beside Corticella. Done on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains.

To Raynerius of Duison I gave thirty solidi for certain settlements by which the land of Empiliacum had been devastated.

Hugh of Asiaco, having received our fellowship and seven solidi as a charitable gift, gave Saint Peter the female dependent of Walo the sacristan, with the approval of his son, and certain other women of his lineage, namely the female dependent of Christianus.

A certain nun of Saint John of Autun, the sister of Aymo Lovel, with that same brother of hers seeing, doing, and approving, placed her inheritance at Agerniacum upon the altar and entrusted it to Saint Peter. It consisted of cultivated and uncultivated lands and male and female dependents. The condition was that, after her death, her niece, the sister of Hugh of Courcelles, should possess it during her lifetime, and after her death the same property should pass into the ownership of the church of Flavigny.

After both women had died, we entered into possession of the inheritance. When the aforesaid Hugh made a claim against it, judgment was given. We produced two legitimate witnesses: the servant of the aforesaid estate who had been given along with it, and the steward of that estate of ours who had been present. They wished to prove that the gift had been made in this manner. It was nevertheless expected that the same judgment would be heard in the higher court. Done at Agerniacum. Thus we obtained the land.

I also redeemed two holdings, one within the court of Laliacum and another outside the court, while Folcuinus was going to Spain, paying twelve denarii each year and two solidi. Done at Flavigny.

I also obtained Adelelmus and his descendants from the same Folcuinus for twelve solidi. Done at Galiaco.

I also redeemed Tapetiolum, called Carlet, for five solidi.

### (folio 139)

I gave the duke a horse worth ten pounds because of the insolence of one of our servants. He approved the gift which any of his knights from his fief might make to the church of Flavigny.

To Walter of Tilly, as assistance for the church of Prisciacum, I gave one horse worth fifty solidi.

To Erleius and Wido, lords of Colchas, I gave forty solidi, and they renounced all bad customs at Colchas.

The following were added to the church treasury:

- One reliquary, given by Walter, a monk of Grin., with a precious and prepared white cloth.
- One curtain, given by Teubodus, together with a cloth.
- Five albs, which Hugh, the monk of Bellus Locus, sent to me when he was dying, together with a silver chalice which is at Bellus Locus.
- Two chalices, one entirely gilded, made by Walo, the monk of Roca, together with one cope of pallium cloth, one chasuble, two stoles, and four albs.
- Two albs made by Girard of Colchas.
- One alb in our chapel, given to me by the wife of Goslenus of Besua.
- An alb given to me by Bovo of Bar, son of Baldric, above Alba, when he became our man.
- One saddlecloth.
- I also redeemed one small pallium for thirty solidi and made from it a border for the pallium in which the body of Saint Prejectus had been wrapped for more than three hundred years.

When the aforesaid Bovo of Bar was at Flavigny asking me for his fief—because he had the daughter of Folcuinus, from the sister of Abbot Odo, who had established that protection arrangement (*casamentum*), that is, the protection of the men of Saint Peter who are in that castle or in the villages around the castle—I did not wish to return it to him in full. I had read a charter which had been made for the men of the castle of Blesum, who belong to Saint Peter, and I feared that these men might be the same or belong to the same group.

Nevertheless, since many witnesses came forward to say that Folcuinus had possessed that same protection, I granted it on the following condition: if I, through our men, after sending a messenger and investigating the matter, or if the men themselves could prove that they had never been under that protection, I would give him nothing, since I loved the church more than him. If the matter proved otherwise, he would have what belonged to his right.

Thus he became our man, but I did not receive an oath, for this reason. Done at Flavigny in the cloister. Witnesses: Gerard the prior, Achadeus, and Helinandus, monks; laymen: Hugh the provost and Raynald; and the servants Raynald, the provost’s son, and Gislerius.

From this protection arrangement I withdrew those men of Arvico from whom I had received rent, namely cheese, and those for whom the charter had been made—all of them, if they could prove it, as I said. He himself also approved this.

Leaving these matters aside for the moment, let us return to the earlier ones. We must not, however, omit the woman whom Deodatus held at Noeirs, who belonged to us, together with half of their father. They had six sons, whom we divided with Hugh, abbot of Saint-Valery: three sons as the mother’s share, and on the father’s side one son and half of another. The mother first sent me the head-tax.

I also received a share in Berenger and his brothers, which Raynald of Colpeium relinquished to us after receiving ten solidi.

When the bishop had returned from Rome, I met him at Sedelocus. I was kindly received, given a kiss, and thanked. On another occasion he summoned me there, and after many injuries I made a settlement concerning everything for ten pounds.

As he was going to the king, he asked me to provide him with a mule. Since I thirsted for his affection, which I knew was difficult to obtain, I offered him an excellent mule. I had bought it directly for one hundred fifty solidi, and I gave it to him.

Thus, when he came to the feast of Saint Nazarius, I served him honorably and returned with his gratitude. For that court and settlement he gave twenty solidi to Stephen, twenty to Hubald, forty to Hugh of Spiriac, forty to Raynald, ten to Teubodus, five to Hugh Misem, and ten to Goslenus.

For the horse of Girard the monk, I gave ten solidi as a settlement to Milo the constable.

I had almost forgotten that a certain Erembert of Massiviac was claiming the village oven, the prebend, and the field of Saint Clement, because his father had given three hundred solidi for them to Abbot Odo, except that he had donated the prebend for his burial.

Since he had burdened me with many lawsuits, and since, because of this burden, he had become the man of the duke and of the provost of Sinemur, he produced certain brothers as witnesses who had seen the matter. When they entirely failed him, we obtained a judgment which brought us peace thereafter.

There, the provost of Sinemur gave one occupied holding at Massiniac, belonging to us, to Saint Peter and Saint Prejectus, out of love for us. It was free from every exaction and owed us all the customary dues. Done at Flavigny.

In total, in the advancement of the church over three years less two months, I gave two thousand solidi, apart from what was expended on bread, wine, and clothing for the brothers; on the provision of hospitality for guests; on oxen, horses, and vineyards; and on all our equipment and expenses.

### 1099

From the Lord’s incarnation in 1099 onward, evils multiplied in our land, but for the moment let this suffice.

In that year, during the first hour of the night, a great light, like a burning fire, was emitted from the north. It lasted almost until dawn and nearly turned night into day.

In that same year, winter raged for eight continuous weeks with greater severity than usual, so that the force of the cold destroyed most beasts, birds, and human beings. [Note: So the manuscript reads; read *extingueret*, “destroyed” or “killed.”]

There were those who said that the light had been given by God for the destruction and overthrow of the Saracens, since he was bringing assistance and granting strength to the men of Jerusalem to strike down and utterly destroy the multitude of the prince of Babylon, who had come to crush those who had captured Jerusalem. Their number was like the sand of the sea. For this reason, they said, the light had been sent by God, so that the Christians who were fighting the battles of the Lord on that day would not also lack light during the night for the crushing of the opposing people.

Whether this was so, or whether that fiery radiance which appeared, and those fiery battle-lines, foretold the shedding of human blood which took place on that day and the next—as we read happened when that grievous war between the sons of Emperor Louis the Pious was imminent—or whether some tribulation was impending over the world, as is said to have happened in the year when King Louis was separated from the guardianship of Hugh the Great, when the same sign appeared and foretold the plague of the Hungarians, which soon became violent—let those whose concern it is investigate and determine. [Note: The manuscript reads *opis*; perhaps *operis*, “work” or “task.”]

The light was seen in the northern part of the sky toward sunset. As the night declined, it seemed to extend eastward when one looked toward it, but it disappeared somewhat before dawn.

In this year Pope Urban died, and Paschal succeeded him. Lord Rodulf, abbot of Verdun, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April (29 July), and Hugh, abbot of Autun, also died. [Note: Turn two leaves and read according to the placement of the letters marked A in the margin.]

(Fol. 141.) Yet when I consider the dispensation of your wondrous and ineffable patience and mercy, whose measure in me is without number, I delight to dwell upon the contemplation of your compassion, although these things, Christ, are beyond me: how, snatched from the breast, you enriched me with the gifts of your superabundant goodness, entrusting me to the companionship of your servants and filling me with the grace of those who love you; how, from my earliest age, when I was already proceeding along crooked and slippery paths and following an age rushing headlong toward destruction, you allowed my troubled heart to breathe again, healing it with the antidote of confession, and recalled me, though fleeing from you, by a certain gentle, unexpected sweetness unknown to me; and how, when by the continual remedy of confession I had been drawn on somewhat and had learned to avoid seductive things, although I was not yet wholly weary of my perversity, so that I understood in mind and deed that “you destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 72:27), you led me—removed and separated from the company of those among whom I had grown up—to foreign lands, unwilling, resisting, and as though unaware; and there, once placed, you enriched me with unexpected and manifold blessing, namely, with the marvelous grace of your servants, who loved in me what I did not know.

Although in these things I understood your gifts, God, even though I was reluctant and had abandoned myself. It pleases me, I say, to recall within myself the sweetness of your mercy, by which you pity all, saving human beings and beasts—that is, saving both those who live rationally and do not forget the dignity in which and for which they were created, and those who live like beasts, becoming “like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding,” restoring through repentance the dignity of their first origin. Among these, you called me also—deformed by the hump of sins and filthy with the horror of vanity and frivolity—to lay aside wickedness, to incline the neck of my heart to the yoke of your service, and to be tamed by your servants; and through the sight of your compassion you made me loathe myself.

O my misery, which did not awaken at so many repeated summonses! Surely my excessive rust had to be smelted away by fire; and therefore, although I tried to rise, I was weighed down by the dross of ingrained pleasure and vicious habit. I had cast my sins behind my back; for my face had been blackened. Yet you, loving your servants, allowed me—not my foulness, but the healing in me that would come from your grace—to proceed and prosper, so that when you recovered these things from one who loved not you but those gifts of yours, given or permitted, in which I prospered, I might be burned by the fire of tribulation, and my wickedness might at least then understand its evils, when it began to be punished for those very evils.

What should I relate about the warnings by which you foretold my amendment, while we were at sea, through the violent wind of our stormy voyage at sea and the tossing of the ship—which was weak in itself and was shaken by the blows of fish—and tried to awaken me, snoring in the sleep of tepidity and negligence? The rudder had broken, the sail was torn by the force of the winds halfway through, the sailors were undone by fear, everything threatened immediate death, and the ship was left to you alone, while it spun in a kind of whirlpool.

O, what sort of person I was then! How credulous, how devoted, how penitent; how diligent, steadfast, and well-disposed in promising correction; how faithful an accuser and judge of my sins; how ready for conversion of conduct and amendment of life! You saw these things, Lord, and delivered me; you heard me and comforted me; and although I was in despair and at the very last extremity, when we had just set out from the harbor, you restored me safely to land, with the ship and all that was in it unharmed. But when I set foot on land, that promise, once so devoted amid the waves of fervor and amendment, grew somewhat cold; yet the fear brought back to my mind did not allow it to grow completely lukewarm, as usually happens.

Immediately another repetition of your compelling summons followed, as soon as I came to Bayeux: namely, an illness by which I was utterly despaired of and, as it were, given up for dead. From this you raised me, holy Jesus, righteous judge of events. What these great deeds of yours accomplished in me, God, or in what way they taught my wretched soul, oppressed by lethargic sleep, to rise and awaken so as to fear you and love you, is attested by our return to our homeland and by my subsequent life—one that could make the pious Lord, once appeased, angry again, but could not suffice to reconcile him when offended.

(Fol. 141'.) And now let whoever wishes read these things of ours, whatever they may be, and mock them as he wishes, provided only that it may please and be permitted me to linger over the memory of your sweetness, you who endure the sinner for the sake of repentance and, by sparing him, invite him to reconcile himself to the patience of the one who endures him.

Immediately thereafter I was advanced to that promotion which is now a horror to me. Whether this happened through your grace, permission, or judgment, I do not know. Once the burden of office had been assumed and had lasted in me for a very short time, its appearance was overlaid and obliterated in so many ways that it became difficult to remember not what I was, but what I had been—either because honors change character, or because this was deserved by the insolence of my conduct, which had not yet been chastised by the rod of satisfaction and healed by the antidote of amendment.

Then came again the warning of illness and the realization of private and public unrest: that collapse—or rather the sudden breaking away—of the dormitory’s upper floor, where planks had failed or been removed. I was so affected that I thought I was about to lose my life. Indeed, blood was drawn from my ears, when your mercy, at the invocation of the name of the martyr Praejectus, and the fulfillment of a good undertaking—in which that very accident found me, for I was making the circuit [Note: [Col. 0365D] Circa, in German, “die runde,” “the round.”] after the morning hours had ended—snatched me from the jaws of death.

At that very time, and in that same month, in our cell at Coltik, two monks likewise fell from the dormitory over a precipice; similarly, in the monastery at Melun, two monks fell. Yet they had not been deprived of confession and communion, though they had not fallen from as great a height as I. Your goodness granted me life; although battered, I was not destroyed in any part of my body, though restored to health only with difficulty, and I still grieve over the fall.

When I recall what thanksgiving I rendered for such great benefits on the day when, lying in bed, I was signed with the sign of your most holy nail and protected by the safeguard of the holy relics, and was given to drink of the life-giving ablution, after a weeklong loss of consciousness, I blush; blushing, I am confounded. What I did not do then I do now, begging that the offering of confession and praise may be acceptable to you, and that amid the scourges of your mercy the very recollection of my error and of your compassion may be acceptable. And because everyone who displeases himself possesses adversity, I desire to please you in this: that, by your gift and your action, I displease myself.

There are still more memorials of your sweetness applied to one who was ungrateful, extending to the circumstances in which my soul is now engaged. Because I did not reverence your face in them, my lyre has justly been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep (Job 30:31). Therefore let the whole substance of our being proclaim to you in a voice of exultation and confession: “All that you have done to us, you have done in true judgment.” Let my entire life proclaim it, I say—sinful before my promotion, rebellious after my promotion: “We have sinned against you and have not obeyed your commandments.” Let it condemn itself entirely by its own judgment, now as though already condemned by human judgment—not in hope of recovering secular status, but from love of provoking against itself the divine punishment justly imposed and destined to be imposed ever more severely; for I am ready for scourging, having sinned through weakness, and therefore seeming deservedly fit for punishment, and my pain is always before me, because I have turned aside from your commandments.

What should I relate as such an evident sign of your compassion—one that scarcely anyone, or almost no one, among the people of Flavigny is unaware of? When I was returning from Semur, surrounded by a company of monks and laymen, amid the crashing and whirlwinds of an overwhelming storm, lightning fell before our eyes. The animal on which I was riding was scorched by the fire itself—its head, breast, and legs—so that for forty days it could scarcely be brought out of the stable; yet your clemency preserved me from injury, although the lightning had fallen only one cubit in front of me.

The next day it was sought and found, and everyone wondered how I had escaped alive or uninjured. Many interpreted it as an evil omen, calling me a sorcerer worthy of death, whom God’s own punishment had shown to deserve chastisement. Perhaps an armed rider was riding before me, close beside me, exposed to the rain with his whole body. He had protected himself with a curved shield held out above him, and, while urging his horse forward with the spurs, he carried a reversed lance at the very moment when the lightning was cast. Its point, while he was terrified and stunned at such a sight, and while his movement was slowed by fear, struck my throat as I was advancing. Unless you, God, had restrained the animal on which I was sitting from its charge, and unless my companions had shouted and forced that man toward the front, it would have deprived me of life.

This twofold rescue of us became a miracle to those who saw and heard it. That attack of ours, related above, had already passed; many other benefits of yours, too numerous to recount, had already taught me, ungrateful though not wholly without gratitude, that you were to be loved and that I must cling to you—if only they had found a teachable, kindly, and humble heart.

What is this, most merciful God? How did the storm of the overwhelming and raging wind of secular life seize me and carry me toward you? I was dragged away and saw it; I was carried off and felt it. I was stolen from myself by myself, and I grieved; before your presence I groaned and thirsted for healing. I desired that you avenge yourself upon me and consume my sins, which I was already punishing in myself by confessing them to you, although not yet to the degree of worthy repentance. For although I grieved that I sinned and was sometimes pierced with remorse, I was not pierced at the end in such a way as to cease sinning—which is the fullness of repentance.

Woe is me! How the mind of those who preside is disturbed by the favor of flatterers! How those who are called blessed are deceived, and the path of their steps is scattered! Indeed, the sinews of Behemoth’s testicles are tangled, his bones are like pipes of bronze, and his cartilage like plates of iron (Job 40:12): for the arguments of the devil are impossible to unravel, his counsels sonorous through sweetness but enervated through pleasure, his vices disguised under the appearance of virtues.

This Leviathan swallows a river and does not marvel, and trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth (ibid., 18); but when his jaw has been pierced by the hook of the Lord’s Passion, he cannot retain what has been chosen, and even if things sometimes flow in of their own accord, he cannot prevent them from flowing out again.

(Fol. 142.) It was a day distinguished by the honor of the Lord’s Resurrection (April 10); the solemn masses were being celebrated, and we were all present. Perhaps an invisible but perceptible pig was allowed to make itself felt as it moved through the choir, and it was perceived by everyone, including me, when I had already indicated the matter to the others in turn by a gesture and immediately sensed it myself and understood what it signified. Then I perceived it again, now being disgusted and truly grieved, and at first indignant with myself on that very account, so that I savagely trampled it as best I could. Driven into flight with a kind of grunt, which could also be heard, it could no longer be perceived.

I groaned in continual sorrow and wept to you alone; my food was tears, my drink sighs. I begged in the silent groaning of my conscience that you might purify me, who had been appointed to purify others, because I saw that the demands of my sins made me as powerless to correct certain serious matters—which I had learned only by hearing—as though they proceeded from the carelessness and sluggish negligence of my own failure. But why do I call them serious, when I could not even correct minor things?
