Thus every virtue, every justice, every severity, and finally whatever it is that befits one who presides had departed from me, as though you were speaking to me through the facts themselves and saying that I must first be healed. For who, or what sort of person, was I then? Surely a man to whom everything was available according to his desire, with every individual thing arranged according to his wish, so that it might plainly be understood that, if I had clung to you and had not loosened the reins of a more relaxed life, with prosperity following on both sides I would have been a king—and truly a king. “For he who rules his spirit is better than he who captures cities.”

But because royal dignity had become worthless to me, and the name that deservedly receives honor had become defiled, my filth made my odor foul, so that the fruits of repentance might give off their own fragrance, while you illumined my darkness and cleansed our conscience. Therefore I did not enjoy the prosperity of my evils for long. For not many days had passed when you visited me with the grace of your compassion, so that I might learn to hope in you, not in the uncertainty of this life. Your omnipotent hand had determined to do this.

The third hour was being celebrated; I myself was present among the choirs of those singing psalms. The thought had crept upon me which, with your permission and gift, belongs to one who displeases himself: that I was a barren tree, occupying the ground uselessly and unwilling to produce the fruit of good works, deserving to be cut down and burned; that those who occupy the places of the saints are not their children, but those who perform their works; and that I ought to be mourned with every fountain of tears, since no one could do greater harm in the Church, because I lived perversely while seeming to possess both the appearance of religion and the position of leadership.

I cried out with no little emotion—inwardly, only with the groaning of my heart and with silent lips—what you were giving and what you had breathed into my heart, even to the flushing of my mouth; and I believe that you heard my voice. For you showed your servant what had to happen soon, speaking with your inward and mystical voice: that my sins were many, and that three choices would be given me for their expiation.

Either a famine would come, so that, as the people scattered and rushed toward death, the whole abbey would be utterly ruined; or the people would suffer the attack of plundering neighbors, and would be so devastated that the mountain itself would be inhabited by scarcely any resident; or I would flee my enemies at an appointed time, they would grow stronger, I would fail completely, and there would be no one at all who recognized me as a friend or did good to me as a friend. Yet in all three forms of this purification my infamy would not remain hidden.

It would be in my power to shorten the time of evil by intensifying the punishment as it poured forth more fiercely, or to prolong it through the delay of some mitigation. I was stunned at the voice that spoke; and when I was pressed for an answer, reflecting that I was the one who had sinned and the one who had acted wickedly, I submitted myself to the justice of God, “for he is good, and his mercy endures forever.”

Fearing that I might fail amid tribulations, I prayed that some friends might be preserved for me, by whose counsels I might be protected. I obtained nothing except the grace of our father, whom I would not even have as mine at the last; and I heard that the duke’s household was especially spreading and magnifying my infamy.

I prayed to be fortified by the virtue of patience, so that I might not succumb, and I was admonished always amid tribulation to give thanks, to praise his true judgments, and to accuse my own evil deeds. This was added: whenever I did so, the weight of evil would be lightened by the approach of consolation. Infamy would cease, grace would return, tribulation would vanish, and consolation would increase. Then I would not forget the Lord, who strikes and heals, casts down and lifts up; whose scourges are acts of compassion, whose blows are acts of reconciliation. I pass over many things that will be fulfilled in their own time.

(Fol. 139'.) It was therefore the third year, and the ninth month of that year since I had come to Flavigny, when domestic malice, repeating its customary attacks, assailed me with accusations, and, God permitting it, disturbed me with greater injuries—the only one it found.

First, after secretly pledging faith to one another, our brothers and sons of this work enlisted as accomplices those who knew of the matter, summoned them as associates, and won supporters to themselves by promises and gifts. Then they themselves came forward as both accusers and witnesses, composing every kind of malicious charge they could devise to tear apart our reputation and discredit our life. They accused me before every sort of person with deadly crimes—things that their own ears would have shuddered to hear.

When I paid little attention to this, believing that they had withdrawn and ceased their attack on us because their efforts had already failed twice, and especially because of their continual service—though it was not sufficiently suitable and was therefore scarcely pleasing, so that I did not even believe those who reported it to me—I finally perceived and experienced a grief that I could scarcely have hoped for.

May God turn this fury away from his Church! May such wickedness end in me; let it be enough that it has come this far. This was the evil that armed the deacon Vigilius for the overthrow of the most blessed Pope Silverius; and when he desired his see, he obtained condemnation by anathema, which he later expiated after being punished by a similar fate.

This plague, to speak only of the particular case—for innumerable examples present themselves—has meanwhile corrupted almost all the monasteries of our time with a general contagion. That fiery serpent of murmuring migrated from the Jewish people into crowds of monks, so that it is now scarcely known by them whether any son at all deserves his father’s blessing. They not only expose the shameful parts of their fathers, not only to brothers but also to mocking outsiders; they even tear apart the very paternal entrails, while ecclesiastical peace is severed by cutting through the bond of charity.

When it became clear that this accusation had arisen from the private counsels of faction-makers who did not regard themselves as sons, it burst from hidden ambushes into open hostility; and what they had spread through associates they proclaimed openly to me without shame [Note: [Col. 0369D] i.e., not being ashamed].

I confess that I blushed. Returning to myself and reflecting that “your judgments, O God, are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7), when I found myself alone among my friends, I rose after rebuking them. Turning over in my mind much of what I had heard but not believed, I understood that a pit had been prepared for me and snares laid. At last I decided to test my fortune, to see whether I could find faith at least among those whom I had placed above the others.

Although I knew their single purpose from many trials, I nevertheless thought that I might bind them to me in this way: by opposing their authority to them and restraining their illicit attempts through the weight of these men. Yet by this effort I accomplished nothing. They gave me words, not counsel, telling me to go to Coltik, where I had not been for a year and more, supposedly to rest there after the work of the harvest and vintage, while they meanwhile labored for our peace and quiet; but in reality they intended to gain through my absence the opportunity and leisure to complete what they had in mind.

I did this—and rather foolishly. After preparing what was necessary and receiving a blessing, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October (September 27) we set out after eating. Some of the brothers and very many of the laymen sat down to table with us; afterward they proceeded with us more carefully than usual and escorted us. The entire populace repeatedly declared what I had not expected: that I was departing and would not return for the present.

I noted each detail. Astonished at the unexpected success of their wishes, and also recognizing within myself many things—almost innumerable things—worthy of scourging and correction, I submitted inwardly to the judgments of divine mercy, recalling the hidden and never unjust judgments of God.

And now, still writing these things, I beseech you, Father of mercies and God of all consolation: give your suppliant sinner a patient spirit, giving thanks in tribulation, acknowledging his errors, and sighing humbly toward you beneath the scourges of your compassion.

From that day I have seen no one from Flavigny, through the manifest and recognized power of God, who orders everything in tranquillity. For all have withdrawn from me; and even when they were with me, they were far from me. If any clung to me in tribulation, when they saw that Flavigny had withdrawn from me, they too departed.

And because, while it was permitted, I abused secular power and honor, your gifts, Christ—for everything came from you—and did not revere you as I ought and could have done, the giver of those gifts: behold, I am alone, and I am not alone, because I do not suffer alone. All fathers suffer with me, all who remember that they possess paternal entrails.

But the one from whom you have turned your face is justly thrown into confusion. With mouth and heart I bless you in all things, my only refuge, who did not abandon me even when I was troubled, but visited my heart in wondrous and various ways, so that I might know that what I suffer comes from you. For although I have sinned, and my sins are many and innumerable, beyond comparison in number and weight with the sand of the sea, they are not, nevertheless, such as those that have been laid upon me.

And behold, I bear the weight of the imposed disgrace [Note: [Col. 0371] a word erased]. The sun grows dark for me in the evening, morning, and midday. Blessed is your dispensation in me.

I therefore came to Dijon, beyond the hope and desire of our brothers and sons. But there too everything was disturbed by the severity of the illness that had seized our father, whom you healed through the prayers of his faithful sons. Nevertheless, that father’s illness was my illness, because I did not speak to him, though I had come to receive his counsel concerning such great tribulation.

I did not judge that the matter should be made known to others, since, as I believed, it was still being conducted secretly. But I went to Coltik, because I thought I could rely sufficiently on the ability of the prior of that place; yet I did not enjoy his good will for long. On the following day I sent him, together with the brother who had come with us, to Flavigny, so that he might restrain the insolence of fools and tame their arrogance.

(Fol. 140.) When they arrived there, they found messengers of the bishop. They entered the village together, but with different intentions. As soon as I had left Flavigny, the sons of the opposing party, not slow to carry out their plan, went to Sedelocus to bring our bishop the first joyful news: that the abbot of Flavigny, an open enemy of the bishop and of the Church, from whom the bishop had suffered so much, had abandoned the church and chosen to take refuge in flight, never to return; that the church was now without a shepherd, the place without a ruler, and the fortress without a guardian.

Let him see to whom it belonged to prevent harm from being done to the mother Church, and prevent the one who had departed from returning, since it was clear that everything would henceforth be endangered by his presence.

The bishop heard this, rejoiced, and publicly announced what he had heard to everyone. Although he ought to have restrained the presumption of the foolish and terrified them by the example of Ham, who, because he exposed his father’s nakedness, inherited a curse, he forgot the faith and peace that had been agreed. He rejoiced at having found what seemed a suitable opportunity to avenge his own injuries, and arranged for our infamy to be publicized to everyone within and outside his court before he had met me by envoys or letters.

Without delay he sent Hubald, one of his own men, accompanied by those brothers who had defamed us, to Flavigny. His envoys and ours, coming from opposite directions, entered the monastery. Our men, assembled as a community, exchanged greetings and spoke briefly, as the time and circumstances required. They reproached the others for being excessively credulous toward young men and offered them, on our behalf, a purgation of the accusations, so that they would not dissent from our subjection and obedience. They were not received.

When those who had been awaited, with the wishes and assent of almost everyone, entered, a thousand insults were hurled against us, reproaches poured out, and taunts multiplied. When I recall them, I shudder; when I shudder, I am stunned, and even daylight itself is hateful to me. Among all those to whom I had done good, not one was found who grieved over our situation or offered even a word on behalf of the father, sinful though he was.

In that assembly the brothers and sons of our holy obedience composed a document of repudiation, offering the bishop, through his envoys, their filial allegiance and promising to preserve the village for him, while renouncing me in every respect.

Your hand, God, had determined that this should happen; and my sins, which had possessed us, Lord, apart from you, had deserved even greater things. Our humility will not be indignant at suffering whatever you have decreed, in view of your mercy.

Then, when our envoys returned to us for the first time without result, I learned that it is better to serve God without Flavigny than to offend God on account of Flavigny. That is what I had done, swollen with the pride of arrogance and softened by crowds of attendants. I did not regard God as I ought, nor keep his fear within my heart.

I confess that I experienced what I could not even believe, much less hope for: I saw myself entirely without friends, although I had always labored, from the time I was able, to gather friends around me. Yet although I had read the blessed Ambrose, that river of Roman eloquence, sounding forth and pouring out the powers of friendship in his books On Duties, I had not yet fully learned what fruit friendship bears. Whoever does not know how to assign an appropriate action to each person is entirely ignorant of this.

Hence it happens that we often wish to gratify the wicked by agreeing with them, and do not fear to plot against an innocent friend—which is outside the proper duty of friendship. When a fool does this, the treaties of peace are violated; and what does not agree in any way with one who behaves thus ought not to be called friendship at all.

Therefore blessed be the name of the Lord, whose judgment gave or permitted these things, and whose mercy took them away.

But who can investigate the ways of a human being? Although mind and reason persuaded me that this was being done by God’s judgment, I nevertheless resolved to go to Lyon—either because, when counsel has been intercepted, no plan remains, or because, when so many adversities succeed one another, it is good to seek counsel, out of charity, from many people, especially the wisest.

I saw that I was being oppressed by my own bishop, and therefore it seemed necessary to have recourse to the metropolitan, according to the decrees of the canons. I was moved also by our ancient intimacy and, as I thought, the indissoluble bond of friendship by which my constant devotion had bound me to his particular service, and by which he had bound me to himself. No one seemed able to sever this bond—not even a hand filled with gifts.

I was moved, too, by the bishop’s obstinate and insolent persistence, by which he had never forgiven any enemy and had spared neither the guilty nor the innocent. The fury of his mind, now inflamed against us, could be healed by no remedy except the censure of a great judgment.

I went, therefore, and would certainly have found what I had hoped for, had not the bishop’s service to our archbishop counted for more than a friendship that was never without a gift. Nevertheless, I was sent back by him to defend and protect our cause before the one whose patronage had snatched me from his protection—namely, the lord of Dijon—so that he himself might confront the bishop, since the bishop had stripped me of the Church’s goods without convening, examining, or hearing me, a course wholly contrary to canonical sanctions.

I therefore came during the very week before the feast of Saint Benignus (November 1), when an enemy’s cry against me was heard throughout the whole land, and I was judged deserving of being driven by my enemies not merely outside the synagogue but outside the common dwelling of all. They too had heard of my misfortune. For what place could there have been to which the good reputation of our house had preceded me, but where the rumor of so great a calamity had not also arrived? Yet the one who had loved more was more deeply distressed, because he had labored more.

Woe is me! What should I relate? See, Lord, for I am troubled; my heart has been wounded by love, because maternal entrails are shaken and torn apart by their children.

(Fol. 140'.) I found everyone’s minds offended, because in the very matter by which I had offended them—namely, in the dismissal of the brothers—I had destroyed myself. Therefore, both through compassion for them and by their deserved judgment, I ought to have been deprived of sympathy.

When I arrived, however, the father received me kindly. I discussed with him the difficulties of both men, and he became a good counselor to me, giving such counsel as befitted him, and giving it better than it would have befitted me to receive it. Since I had told the bishop that I would come to him when I returned from Lyon, and since the bishop—as I had heard and had proved for myself—had stripped me of all my goods, the advice was that I should first go to Flavigny, speak with the brothers, our tenants and servants, and test what feeling they had toward me and what attitude they would adopt. After I had left them, they had said farewell to me and had begged that our return be hastened.

I went, therefore, and, having sent word in advance, I summoned to me at Villiacum the prior whom I had appointed in place of the prior of Coltik, after removing the latter, who had been with me; I also summoned those whom I considered worthy to come with him (October 31).

They came only after considerable delay. Their appearance had changed, and their hearts had withdrawn from me. I was no longer recognized by those to whom I had done every good; I was stunned, because voice and understanding fled from me.

I said that I had come for the festival of the dedication, which was to take place on the following day. They did not receive me, because they had handed the village over to the bishop and had promised not to admit me. I spoke of the infamy imposed upon me, in defense of which I was prepared to go to Autun. When I urged them to go with me, they would not even hear this, claiming, as they said, to fear the bishop.

Seeing that I had been deprived of all the support and assistance of those who had sworn allegiance to me, left alone, and mocked in everything I offered, I resolved to return by myself to our monastery, having tested their fidelity fully and more than fully. The very men who had been with me departed from me the next day, without even waiting for the feast of Saint Benignus.

Blessed be God, who has had mercy on us. He himself will judge my case when he has freed my soul from the sins that have multiplied against us.

I therefore sent the bishop a letter, so that what I could not accomplish in person I might accomplish in writing. Its text is as follows:

“To the most reverend father and lord, N., bishop of Autun, his brother Hugh, servant of the church of Flavigny, greetings.

“Returning from Lyon, I ought to have met you at Autun, as I recently arranged with you there. But because the lord of Lyon, having learned the circumstances of our case, entrusted me to the special protection of our father of Dijon—whose winged protection the bishop had taken me from—so that our entire case might be strengthened and defended by his counsel, I came to Dijon.

“Desiring to go to Flavigny, I had some of the brothers and also some of the nobles and servants come to me at Villiacum, so that they might go with me. They said that they would neither go with me nor receive me within Flavigny, claiming that they were compelled by fear of you. I urged them to travel with me to Autun; they refused.

“Thus deprived and stripped of all support from our people, I withdrew to Dijon. The only thing I could do was send this letter to your fatherhood: a testimony to my dispossession, a plea for restoration, and a presentation of my defense and purgation.

“I therefore ask that you not act toward me otherwise than the holy canons prescribe; for I too am ready to carry out whatever justice dictates in our chapter at Autun. Consider, I beg you, what you owe us, so that you may also cause us to consider what we owe you.

“Farewell.”

I sent this same letter, opened, to the chapter, and from then until now I have remained at Dijon, awaiting your help, Christ—not as abbot, but as though I were one of the brothers, which is safer for me.

The bishop, however, taking counsel from himself, appointed a day for me to appear before him at Autun through a messenger, saying that I had not been stripped of my office and that judgment should be given there as to whether I ought to be reinvested. After taking counsel, I answered in a letter sent in these words:

“To Lord N., bishop of Autun, his brother Hugh, servant of the church of Flavigny, greetings.

“Our humility is astonished that your fatherly discernment has appointed a day for me to travel to Autun, as though to a trial. You also say—and this astonishes us even more—that I have not been stripped of my office.

“No sooner had the report of our infamy reached your ears than, although you ought to have labored to free persons, not to defame them, you sent to Flavigny, ordered the village to be preserved for you, received our brothers and sons into filial allegiance after rejecting our name, and did this without having convened or heard me, while I feared nothing so much as being proscribed.

“Did you not, at Autun, in that honorable council of yours, when I said that I was going to Lyon, make me promise that I would not interfere with the Church’s goods or give anything to anyone—as though this were intended to protect and defend my wickedness? Where are the abbots, the dean, the archdeacon, and the leading men of the clergy, through whom such a person as the abbot of Flavigny ought to have been summoned?

“And behold, I am called to judgment—not for restoration or reinstatement, but to a judgment concerning judgment, as to whether I ought to be invested. Where, I ask, are the apostolic decrees? Where are the canonical enactments, which declare that no one who has been stripped is to be summoned to judgment, since, once naked, there is nothing from which judgment ought to be rendered?

“But alas for wretched me, to whom alone the force and integrity of the canons have perished!

“I cannot therefore attend the appointed day, because I ought not to do so. If a suitable day is assigned, I am ready to appear. Otherwise, I am ready to present myself at the chapter of Lyon.

“If you aim at higher authorities and treat what I have said as nothing, I appeal to the judgment of Rome. Meanwhile, on behalf of God and blessed Peter and his Vicar, and also of the lord of Lyon and our chapter of Autun, I forbid you to take the abbey of Flavigny from me or to introduce anyone into it.”

A copy of these letters was also sent to the chapter; although it had been his will and decision that I should be invested, the bishop refused. Nevertheless, afterward he ordered me to go to Edua on the Monday of the first week of Advent to carry out the investiture, or, on the Wednesday before the Nativity of the Lord, to do justice to him halfway along the road, and he to me. I said that I would go if he sent monks and servants to accompany me, and the matter remained there. (Fol. 141.) Meanwhile, by both public and private satisfaction, I won over the goodwill of the brethren, submitting myself to them in body and will, because I knew that this was expedient for me, since matters went well for me if only I were privately permitted to live among the lowest.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, the archbishops of Lyon, Canterbury, Sens, Tours, and Bourges, and nine bishops—those of Edua, Mâcon, [Col. 0375D] Chalon, Auxerre, Paris, Die, and two others—assembled at Anse. After peace had been established, they spoke about the journey to Jerusalem, separating from communion those who had taken the vow but had not fulfilled it until they should complete their vows. The archbishop of Lyon had sent envoys to Rome, through whom he had shown the pope his wish concerning that journey: he was to go there with the pope’s blessing and absolution. The Roman pontiff assented, advising him to go in person, so that he might entrust to him in Asia the legation which he had administered well in Burgundy; meanwhile, he was to instruct as best he could those legates whom the pope would send from his side to act in his place. For this reason that conference had been arranged with the greatest care, so that, when his envoys returned with letters of absolution, he might also receive provisions for the journey there from his suffragans and his diocese.

In this year Philip, bishop of Châlons, died. That year also there was a great scarcity of grain, and many people were endangered by famine.

(Fol. 142.) Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, on September 30, the legates of the holy Roman Church, John and Benedict, arrived in Gaul. The council, first designated for Edua, was established at the city of Valence on September 30, at which twenty-four archbishops, bishops, and abbots assembled. Envoys of the lord archbishop of Lyon attended, since he himself was ill, although the bishops of his diocese, those of Langres [Col. 0376B] and Chalon—Mâcon, on his return from Rome, had been captured by Wibert and held in custody—were not present, having been forbidden, as was said, by that same archbishop of Lyon. The bishop of Edua, however, was present, because his canons were accusing him of simony and certain other matters; the men of Lyon had assembled there chiefly for his defense.

At the very first entrance to the council I offered a purgation of the charges brought against me. When the accusers fell silent and failed to proceed, by the council’s judgment, at the first word of the abbot of Dijon, I was invested with the abbacy, with the canons of Edua standing by and expressing their approval. I was presented with a cloak and staff, ordered to sit in the circus, and, after the council had been dissolved, was sent back to my own place, fortified with apostolic letters in these words:

“John and Benedict, cardinals and legates of the holy Roman Church, send greetings to the monks, clerics, and laymen belonging to the abbey of Flavigny and obedient to it. We commend to your affection and send back to you our brother Hugh, your abbot, most dear to us, whom the holy synod, by the judgment of the council, has invested with the abbacy. We command you, on behalf of God and blessed Peter, to come to Dijon, receive him as your abbot, and, promising in the hands of our most dear brother, the son of the holy Roman Church, the abbot of Dijon, that you will treat him safely and with paternal care, restore him to the monastery with the honor due to him.

“Those who obey: may you multiply in blessings. Those who disobey: you will hereafter feel the anger of God and will receive from us a fitting sentence for your contumacy. Since it is our duty to guard against and oppose those unwilling or delaying to obey, we place under interdict the divine office for all of you in the village of Flavigny and in every place whatsoever belonging to that abbey, until you obey our commands, which the holy synod has confirmed.”

As that same council was approaching, more than a month beforehand I had sent letters to Flavigny, whose text is as follows:

“Brother Hugh, expelled abbot of Flavigny, to Girard [Note: [Col. 0375] Giru.] the prior and to all who profess themselves sons of the church of Flavigny: monks, clerics, laymen, tenants, servants, nobles and commoners, of whatever age or condition. We have heard, brothers, and we know that a council is to be held by the cardinals of the holy Roman Church on September 30 at the city of Valence, to which archbishops, bishops, and abbots have been summoned.

“We invite you to it on behalf of God and blessed Peter, his vicar, the lord pope Paschal, and the cardinals John and Benedict, who have been sent to carry out the office of that same pope. For our part, with God as protector, we shall present ourselves at the council, if life accompanies us, prepared, with God’s help, to hear, answer, and be judged canonically.

“Let the accusers, informers, and witnesses come—whoever has a case against us; you who consented to our expulsion and dispossession; you who cast us out unheard and uncondemned and, when admonished, scorned to repent. Come: there you will be given an opportunity to make yourselves heard, where, with God’s favor, all matters will be handled justly and canonically.”

After receiving these letters, they sent against me, with their counsel, one of their own conspirators: a man who had killed a boy at school; who, denying Christ, his mother, and baptism, had by his own confession made himself the devil’s servant; and who had been ordained a monk without penance. Later he was handed over to an evil spirit, cured by the prayers of the brethren, and had thereafter made a public confession. Having violated his profession four times, he was finally expelled from the monastery by the people, together with his associates—that is, those six who had conspired against me—for fornication and uncleanness. He had been ordained a priest outside his own church, after, before all these events, he had committed sacrilege in the cell of Coltiac: breaking open a chest, taking money, stealing a dalmatic [Col. 0377C] and adapting it for his own use, and committing certain other acts which it shames me to report.

Nevertheless, in the presence of the bishop and his associates, before anything else I offered a purgation of the charges brought against me before everyone assembled. Since the accusers failed, there was no need to pursue the matter. Thus, in their presence, the abbacy was returned to me by the judgment of the council, and I was restored to my seat. The letters which had been sent were not accepted, although some had read them.

On the feast of the Reception of the Body of Saint Prejectus, celebrated on November 6, two of the Flavigny brethren, sent by the others, came to Dijon. They instructed me to return, saying that the others would obey us. But the counsel of our brethren was that, because of their fear of Sarmatia and Sombornon, whose castle-dwellers were attacking the church of Flavigny, they could not come to us as they ought if those who were present would obey the letters by confessing their fault and promising security and obedience into the hands of the prior—for the lord abbot was absent—who would treat them paternally; and if those at home would likewise promise to do so repeatedly. They proposed that I go to Sarmatia to receive them in accordance with the tenor of the letters.

I went, but none of this was done, although some came to me saying that they would carry it out more honorably in the chapter of Flavigny. I trusted the acclamations of everyone. Yet at our reception I encountered no honor, affection, or reverence; rather, I found disgrace, insult, and every kind of irreverence. Even bread was refused to those who were with me, and a horse to the servant whom alone I had brought with me. No reverence at all was shown me, even by the lowliest. Indeed, those who loved us did not dare, when summoned by me, to come before me, as they themselves protested, because our enemies had forbidden them. Moreover, unless I had left my chamber promptly when warned, intending to go with them to the council, threats, abuse, and the disturbance of the tumultuous crowd would have been directed against me, since I was delayed by the horse of our servant.

(Fol. 143.) On the morning of that same day, in the chapter, I explained to everyone the cardinals’ letters, and, after explaining them, asked whether they would obey. In their words and actions, however, no humility or obedience toward the council’s statutes was found.

Thus, honored in no respect, we hurried toward the council soon to be held at Poitiers. We remained at Coltiac until the fourth day and then took the return road, because they refused to go, since the subject of the investiture was to be discussed, although I had openly professed before them that I had been properly invested, so that I might at least in this way be led by them. They did not even wish to add to our company a single brother who was friendly to us and indispensable to our journey, which was being conducted according to their pleasure, while all of them were enemies.

In truth, they refused to go for this reason: having less confidence in their own party, they feared the justice of the council and the presence of the lord abbot of Dijon and of ourselves. This can be clearly inferred from what followed. After delaying me in this way, they sent one of their own there with letters—and did so without my knowledge. When he arrived, he neither attended the council nor spoke with the cardinals; and, as he had come, so he returned.

This man had been the associate and accomplice of that earlier person whom we have said secretly withdrew from the council at Valence: he had shared in the sacrilege involving the stolen money and dalmatic and in the expulsion for the fornication of nuns, married women, and boys. He was designated abbot, the cause and head of the evil, by men like himself. He had sworn with three others to cause the death of the abbot of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, by whom he had been received after fleeing from the monastery and treated honorably. For that reason he had been expelled to the Cell and abandoned the habit. Later, after his disgraceful expulsion, he was received again by me, but lived dishonorably and utterly depraved, longing for our deposition so that he himself might be substituted in our place.

But what wonder if the desire to rule drives youthful hearts away from what is true and just, when no deeply rooted planting of religious humility or charity restrains them? It even makes minds venerable with the white hair of old age, and minds which from their earliest years have upheld religion, grow accustomed to abandoning that long-standing appearance of monastic gravity and arm themselves against their fathers.

The bishop mentioned above had appointed there as prior an elderly and honored man who had always been with me from the beginning. When he had brought me into Flavigny, he allowed me to be dishonored in his presence by the insults inflicted upon me; and, at the very moment of our entrance, he secretly took away the pastoral staff by force and open robbery. On the following day, after leaving everything in confusion for us, he departed. During the ten days I remained there, I was kept under such strict guard that every access to the public was denied me and everyone was forbidden access to me.

Not only was there no improvement in my investiture; rather, every circumstance concerning me grew worse. In private and in public they went unpunished along crooked and criminal paths and observed none of the statutes of religion. Because of their incorrigible and shameful conduct, and especially because they were disobedient to the apostolic commands, I was compelled to leave until, after the conclusion of the council at Poitiers, where a synodal and canonical decision was expected concerning the case of the usurping bishop of Edua, under whose protection their faction was sheltered, the legates could examine the church’s affairs according to their counsel and judgment.

This was particularly necessary because the leading men in the church of Edua, whose responsibility it was to settle this kind of division among us, had gone to Poitiers to suppress the evil and disastrous rule of that wicked man. Without them, the presumption of the mad could not be restrained.

Miserable and utterly desperate is the presumption of such men, who revere neither God nor human beings, while they scorn the apostolic commands preserved inviolate through the ages and do not fear to usurp the divine office under interdict. There is no doubt that a deserved necessity has driven them to this end: because they despise God and do not consider themselves, they arm themselves against their fathers; and by making their shame public, they violate the rights of paternal piety. Even if, after making them public, they had wished merely to mock what they themselves had done, they would still be hereditary possessors of the curse of Ham.

May it happen to them that their sin—which has not been corrected by a repentant heart—be both sin and the cause of sin; and may that same sin, arising from sin, be no longer merely sin but both sin and the punishment of sin. Let them think that they can abolish the statutes of divine law with impunity while they handle the sacred mysteries of the altar, which are forbidden to them. They do not understand what Saint Leo says in his letter: that if anyone attempts to act contrary to the ordinances of the canons and dares to admit what is forbidden, he should know that he is to be removed from his office, and that he will not share in our communion if he has refused to be a partner in discipline.

How great their blindness and that of those who share their condition is can be understood from this: these very men, expelled from the monastery by lay hands because of their condemned and shameful life, known to everyone, are now, at the dregs of the age, established as its rulers, leaders, and lords. Once publicly disgraced by those who now honor them, publicly despised and rejected, dishonored by beatings and chains in a shameful spectacle, one of them—who, marked by a public confession, ought to have been rejected by the clergy and admitted to communion only at the end of his life—has been promoted as cellarer of the monastery and father of the congregation, so that he may care for everyone. Another, who after denying Christ God and Lord was ordained deacon without penance, has now, after public penance for homicide and denial, been appointed priest and prince [sic].

[Col. 0380A] This, then, was the occasion of the present disagreement: they thought that, because of the permission which the letters required to be given into the hands of the abbot of Dijon, I wished to subject the church of Flavigny to the authority of Dijon. I had neither hoped for nor desired this.

(Fol. 143'.) During the period in which the council of Valence was held, Wibert died, in the twentieth year after he had invaded the apostolic see. He had the bishop of Mâcon and many others of the clerical order in captivity. At his departure he personally absolved them all in exchange for his own absolution, advising the bishop to return to Rome and work before the pope for his release.

When the bishop approached the pope, he found there envoys of the church of Edua complaining about their bishop [Col. 0380B] and reporting the acts of the council and the manner of the accusation:

He had promised Walter the archdeacon, in the presence of Stephen the cantor, in the dormitory at Edua, that, if Walter helped him so that his mother or brother—who possessed great influence—would not harm him in obtaining the bishopric, he would have whatever he wished in the church. Because of this accusation, whose authors were almost all the canons—especially those thirteen leading men of the church who had attended the council as envoys sent by the others, including its two best archdeacons, the provost, the cantor, and others distinguished by nobility, learning, and uprightness—and because I myself had been restored by the council’s judgment, at the complaint of the chapter of Edua, to the seat and position from which I had been removed, controversy arose in the council.

The lord abbot of Cluny raised the matter with particular force through his envoys, and the lord abbot of Dijon in person, because they had experienced all the more harshly the tyranny of the man accused. Those defending the accused replied that the persons were not qualified to accuse, on the ground that sheep have no right to reproach or accuse their shepherd—especially those who had consented to his election and supported his consecration. They had also heard that an anathema had been pronounced against those who knew that his election should be rejected but did not reveal it.

It was also established that the matter had been initiated before his consecration, and that afterward the accuser himself had received from him the office and rank of deacon, while the witness to the accusation had received the office of cantor; and that both had rendered him homage. Therefore, they said, the accusation was insufficient, since one of them was the accuser and the other the witness, and the same person was both witness and accuser.

The legates replied that in a case of simony no person at all, even one of bad reputation or subordinate status, should be excluded from making an accusation, since the lord pope Gregory VII, at the Roman council, had deposed a simoniacal bishop on the accusation of a certain abbot, after first deposing that abbot for the same simony, of which he himself had been a participant and accomplice. They added that one accuser and one witness were sufficient for an accusation.

Those who were bringing the charge also objected, wishing to prove it by oath, that because they were younger and not so well trained in the canons, they had not known that the promised arrangement involved the evil of simony. As soon as they learned this, they had exposed it, thereby deflecting from themselves the dart of excommunication. They further added that his election had been weakened and wholly rejected at the outset by the metropolitan because he had remained excommunicated for a year and a day while holding the office of archdeacon in the church of Langres, and likewise the offices of archdeacon and cantor—although he was not a deacon—in the church of Edua, contrary to the prohibition of that same metropolitan and legate, and while living simoniacally in those positions of authority. After his election had been weakened, they said, he had been ordained deacon at Lyon without the knowledge of the chapter.

The same legates also reported that, once the matter came to judgment, the disagreement had increased. The bishops said that, according to the custom of the Gallican Church—which had, as it were, been confirmed at the council of Clermont in the presence of Pope Urban and likewise at councils held by the lord of Lyon—a purgation ought to be imposed upon the accused, although they were unable to support this with the authority of the canons.

The legates replied in opposition, affirming by canonical argument that it was the accusers’ duty to prove what they had alleged, if they were legitimate accusers; or, in a case of simony, where no legal qualification was required, that the accused had appealed to the Roman see, although they had not assented to his appeal. For while others possessed care in a portion of the responsibility, they possessed it in the fullness of power, since they were the Roman Church and its judges in that Church.

When the bishops delayed giving judgment, the approaching night and the bishops’ expectation dissolved the assembly. The case was postponed and the sentence suspended. On the following day the same matter was debated and contested at greater length but was not concluded. At the request of all the bishops who disagreed about the judgment, a truce was granted until the council at Poitiers, to which both parties were summoned. He was nevertheless suspended from episcopal and priestly office, since on that same night he had sent certain gifts to the bishops in person and through his agents. Some accepted them, while others rejected them. The cardinals were not unaware of this; indeed, in the full assembly they gave thanks to those sitting around them that, although the sacred hunger for gold had tested priestly hearts, it had not entered them.

All this was reported in the hearing of the lord pope while the bishop of Mâcon was present. Letters from the cardinals to the apostolic see concerning the same case were also there, lest the cardinals allow what had been done to the honor of the Roman Church to be overturned.

When the bishop pleaded for his fellow bishop, he was dismissed by the pope with instructions that the cardinals should support justice, and that, before him, a judgment delivered with Peter’s equity would stand confirmed. Thus he returned and attended the council at Poitiers.

This council was assembled in the church of Saint Peter on the day of the octave of Saint Martin—November 18 [Note: [Col. 0381D] Compare the letter of the legates to Lambert of Arras, Mansi XX, 1125. See there also the Acts of the council of 1100, incomplete, K.]—with eighty bishops and abbots present. The bishop of Edua attended with the bishop of Chalon. The bishop of Die was also there; the lord of Lyon had sent him to defend the interests of Augustodunum in his place. Thirty-five canons also arrived to proceed against him.

The charges which had already been brought against him in the earlier council were repeated. The other side resisted them in a remarkable manner, with much supporting material, though not persuasive. The stated controversy remained, and almost the entire council opposed the responses previously given by the cardinals in accordance with the custom of the Gallican Church. They were unwilling either to diminish their authority in any respect or to assent to the appeal.

Nevertheless, he was given an opportunity to purge himself with suitable persons, as the council had desired, and this immediately, without granting the delay of the truce which was requested and without admitting to the purgation the bishop of Chalon, whom he had brought with him, or the bishop of Die, whom the archbishop had sent.

When this had not been done, judgment was rendered, and, although they appealed in vain to the apostolic see, he was asked to return the stole and ring. Meanwhile he withdrew behind the altar with his associates and refused either to obey the judgment or to return to the assembly as he had been ordered.

For this reason he was completely deposed from episcopal and priestly office and, unless he obeyed, was excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church. All who thereafter obeyed or revered him as a bishop, or who helped him persist in his obstinacy, were condemned to eternal malediction.

We must not conceal what intervened here. The archbishop of Tours, the archbishop of Rennes, and many others had initially offered themselves as his defenders and assistants in his purgation, since they belonged to the province of Lyon. In the moment of need, however, they withdrew.

When our canons heard that these men were presenting themselves for a person whose life and character they did not know, they went anxiously to them, privately protesting and publicly warning them not to involve themselves in his communion or in the oath to be spoken—indeed, in perjury—which they would certainly incur through that purgation, if what was being called a purgation was in fact an exaggeration of his crimes. They declared that, unless the others yielded, all the canons would expose their perjury by reasoning and oath and would prove it by the judgment of fire.

This statement prevented them from continuing what they had begun, especially because they saw men of such authority and nobility supporting their case with clear assertion and persuasive evidence.

[Col. 0382D] This, then, is how the matter stands concerning him. Although deposed and separated from the fellowship and communion of the Church, he retained the stole and ring. The clerics, however, administered and disposed of the goods of the bishopric, as they still do, to the great displeasure of the archbishop. He bitterly resented that the bishop whom he himself had consecrated had been accused, judged, and deposed against his will, and that the complaint had been examined outside the province through the hands of the legates rather than being reported to him, who was metropolitan and primate of the province, within the province and according to the canonical ordinances.

Nevertheless, evident necessity grounded in just reason led them to carry out this action and to proceed as they did. For when the cardinals arrived at the very beginning of the scandal, at the urging and entreaties of that same pseudo-bishop, to restore peace to the church—which was being torn apart by a shameful but necessary division—they came to Edua on the feast of Saint Nazarius. After hearing the position of both parties, they pursued and defended his side with such favor, although justice favored the canons’ party, that they brought the great disagreement back toward peaceful unity and joined the parties in such concord that the canons, though reluctantly, assented to it.

When this agreement was finally nullified by his obstinacy, the cardinals, after he had denied justice in the chapter, summoned him to the hearing and judgment of the metropolitan concerning the community’s property, which was the subject of the dispute. He refused. Trusting in the cardinals’ earlier kindness, he invited them to the council designated for Valence, intending to answer and make satisfaction there, and by his invitation compelled them, though they were unwilling, to go.

They rejected his homage, both for the public damage inflicted upon their community and for the private injuries, and they protested that they were openly his enemies, especially because they were being summoned concerning domestic matters to a council outside the province.

Wretched is the misery of a man who has never loved anyone, has been loved by no one, has forgiven no one who sinned against him, has bestowed a blessing on no one after anger, and has placed all his hope solely in the accumulation of money. Let no one believe us if, on this point, the unanimous voice of all does not agree.

It is not ours, even though we have been injured, to repay injury with the curse of retaliation, since we know that we must forgive those who sin against us. Yet neither is it consistent with ecclesiastical truth and piety to fashion falsehoods as truths about those whom he has forgiven when they sinned against him, because true love does not know how to depart from faith in the truth.

May the Lord grant him that, since he sees everything adverse answering his undertakings, he may not add to them by making the end like the beginning. Rather, may he hope in the name of the Lord, not in the uncertainty of riches, and may he rely upon the Lord his God. Amen.

And since we think it most pleasing and useful to all to commend men of virtue to memory, it does not seem inappropriate to us briefly to explain the zeal of these legates against the most shameless adultery of Philip, king of the Franks, corrupted by the sorceries of a second Jezebel and turned away from what is true and just, useful and honorable.

Let no one be indignant with us because it may seem that we are criticizing royal conduct or tearing down the eminent authority of such great majesty or renown. It is neither our will nor our purpose to spend time or exhaust our efforts on these matters. But we do not allow the brave deeds of men—deeds which can scarcely or not at all be remembered without those in comparison with whom they are brave and against whom they contended—to be removed from our labor. If we cannot dare brave deeds, at least let us examine the good works of the brave. (Cf. Leg. I, 196.)

If the little record were silent, all France would cry out, indeed the whole West would thunder with one voice, that the king, having repudiated a lawful marriage; having rejected the wife of royal lineage; having violated the fidelity of the marriage bed; having obscured the splendor of the royal chamber and darkened the brilliance of royal offspring, stole from his count of Anjou his wife—a knight of his own, to whom he had promised faith, and a man related to him by blood.

Thus, on one side they were bound by blood in the third degree of kinship, on the other in the fourth. The bonds of marriage, which the avenging royal sword had until then forbidden to be broken, were dissolved by the king’s shameless and uncontrolled lust; an impudent and irreverent obstinacy, which ought to have been cut off and ended, violated them after so many years.

But what wonder if, in the river of the world, in the torrent of royal pleasure, the ancient Leviathan finds someone whom he may swallow? In the descent of the Jordan he seizes precious and chosen things; among the order of bishops, who ought to preside, he subjects to himself those who ought to preside.

The king, enemy of royal chastity, violent breaker of the royal bed, arrogant trampler of the royal diadem—although he could unjustly cast the queen from her bed and crown—could not establish the adulteress in the royal throne by a blessing unless he found accomplices among the bishops, or, in pitiable desperation, promoted them himself. They would be the executors of his will and the new consecrators of the new queen.

O shamelessness! O miserable scattering of the stones of the sanctuary at the head of the streets! (1092.) If the queen is rejected unjustly, why is the adulteress, joined to a relative while her husband protests and suffers violence, introduced in her place?

(Fol. 144'.) If royal power denies right, overturns what is lawful, and raises up what is unlawful, what, I ask, is it when what is unlawful is blessed; when sacrilege is exalted in the temple, adultery consecrated, and unchastity promoted—and all this through the hands of bishops?

I see nothing more wicked here than what occurred in the time of the blessed Pope Nicholas, when Queen Teutberga was rejected and the adulteress Waldrada introduced by Lothar, son of the emperor Lothar who became a monk. For although there was there a deceitful judgment of the bishops, the expulsion of an innocent queen, the dissolution of a lawful marriage, and the elevation within the royal palace of a concubine who had been made a prostitute [Note: [Col. 0383] “exaltatam” appears to have been written first.], she had not nevertheless been joined to that man by marriage, nor had she been seized from the side of her husband, her kinsman and knight; nor had the bonds of marriage been violated on both sides.

Rather, an insatiable abyss of an old concubinary pleasure, recalled intemperately to memory, loosened the reins of desire without knowing how to draw them back once released. It brought death upon himself, horror upon the kingdom, calamity upon the bishops, and a pitiable death and confusion upon the nobles.

Here everything is confused, everything appalling, everything corrupted by diabolical cunning and malice. This king, I say, found among the bishops men whom he could associate with himself and make ministers of so great a sacrilege: Philip, bishop of Troyes, and Walter, bishop of Meaux. To Walter he gave the bishopric so that he might consent to and serve the consecration for which the bishop of Troyes was to be the agent.

But why should we be angry with bishops to whom apostolic piety grants remission for their error? The lord bishop of Lyon, then legate of the Roman Church, restrained them with much denunciation; and, unless they had guarded themselves, they would have suffered much punishment through his severity. But, as we said above, Roman piety both forgave their errors and overcame their infamy by its remission.

Thus the archbishop was compelled, by letters given to him from Rome, to receive both men into communion and to exchange the kiss with them. Let whoever wishes inquire from what source of piety this flowed, and, if he can, understand it.

He also attempted to separate the king himself, made proud by the prostitution of his concubine, from that condemned union, forbidding him the crown unless he obeyed. (1094.) But impiety does not recognize the evils it has committed until it has begun to be punished for those same sins. (1095.) The matter was discussed for a long time, but he refused to be healed by the apostolic remedy, while truth and judgment hung at the discretion of a woman.

This continued until, after Pope Urban died, Paschal succeeded him and sent these pillars of the Church, of whom we are speaking, to Gaul. That they were rightly called pillars of the Church can be inferred from their very weakness and the unshaken strength of their spirit by anyone who carefully considers their deeds.

After the council of Valence, they themselves summoned the king. When they found in none of his words or actions any correction or penance—like digging around an unfruitful tree and piling up a basket of manure—they could not endure to see such disgrace and trampling in the Catholic Church. At the council of Poitiers they did not fear to cut off the rotten member from the structure of Christ’s body with the sword of anathema.

(1100, October 20.) The count of Poitiers was present, earnestly begging them not to excommunicate his lord. Bishops were also present, making the same request. When they could not obtain what they wanted, the count and his men left the assembly and place of the council, threatening them; some bishops also departed, many clerics, and innumerable laymen.

With the order thus disrupted and peace turned into tumult, those remained who desired to imitate the zeal of Phinehas. Just as he pierced the fornicator of Zamri together with the Midianite woman Cozbi with a sword and appeased the fury of the Lord, so these men, not fearing the roar of the shouting crowd, pierced the adulterous king together with the adulteress with the dagger of excommunication, since they could not correct him, and made him an exile from the life that is in Christ.

This happened when the council was already about to be dissolved. The praise of Christ was already resounding in the mouths of those standing by for the dismissal of the council, as is customary, while the heat of the tumultuous crowd, raging over the excommunication of their lord king, grew hot like the sea.

Then someone from the crowd, standing in the upper part of the church, threw a stone, wishing to strike the cardinals. By its blow a certain cleric who was standing there was felled, his head shattered. The pavements remained bloodstained [Note: [Col. 0385] Thus in the manuscript, in place of *manant* (‘flow’).]. The building was filled with confused shouting, and within and outside the ministers of Satan raged in fury and madness.

The pillars of Christ remained unmoved, awaiting death without fear if the Lord should command it. When the stones flew, they removed their mitres and uncovered their bare heads; they never ceased praising God and preaching the truth, eager, if necessary, to confirm with their blood what they had proclaimed with their voices.

Their devoted steadfastness and most steadfast devotion restrained the fury of the raging people and inclined their hearts toward penance. Thus the counts and all who had previously been raging were humbled before them, after offering satisfaction and professing obedience.

The council also dealt with the unjust expulsion of the abbot of Saint-Remi and the unlawful substitution of Burchard. After the matter had long been examined, his holy manner of life, legitimate entry, promotion, and consecration had been found authentic and canonical—matters also confirmed by letters of the lord pope Urban, to which faith ought rightly to have been given—and since even the opposing party no longer objected to his restoration, it was nevertheless judged necessary to go to the Apostolic See in order to refute certain forged letters, supposedly sent from that See, in which the cardinals recognized neither the Roman style nor Roman parchment, especially since at their conclusion was written “Farewell,” a formula not used by Roman authority. Some of those who had first appealed were distressed that this had not been granted to them; yet they received an answer based on evident reasoning, even if they were not satisfied.

How great a harvest of faith that vigorous defense of the heavenly cause produced may be inferred from this: afterward, when the king had remained for nearly fifteen days in the city of Sens with his queen, all the churches throughout the city having been closed, no Christian worship [Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, Mass.] was celebrated for him. To such an extent did the fury of that Jezebel, employing profane novelty and extending impious hands against God, go so far that she sent officers to break open a church and compelled Mass to be celebrated there for her by people like herself.

O human shamelessness! An unblushing, servile, and unkingly quibble, employing Roman fickleness, now protects its queen; inflamed by disgraceful embraces of error and by the fires of immodesty, it dishonors the dignity of the crown. Although in former times pagan kings both gave laws without the yoke of compulsion in order to entreat God and threatened blasphemers or despisers of God with punishment, this propagator of the Frankish kingdom, this defender of Christian law, acts contrary to the commands of his predecessors and tears down the statutes of holy law and of the Roman pontiffs. Worse still, with those same people supporting him—if one may say what one is ashamed to say—he defends the causes of his own disgrace, puts forward excuses, and, while those who ought to have compelled him to come to his senses should have done so, is instead encouraged by their support to persist in iniquity.

The insatiable abyss of Roman greed does this [Note: [Col. 0385] The word is omitted by Labbe.], which, since it cannot be filled, knows how to protect what ought to be cut away. But enough of this.

*(Folio 145.)* In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s incarnation 1101, John, bishop of Tusculum, was sent by the pope to England on account of the tribute of Saint Peter. This man had been a regular canon of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais; having violated his profession and laid aside his habit, he returned to the world. Unable to endure reproach, he became a monk of Bec. Although Roman by nationality, when Pope Urban came into Gaul he gained his familiarity; he was brought back to Rome, and after the bishop of Labicum had died, although he had already been rewarded with a certain abbey, he was finally promoted from abbot to bishop.

The cardinals had already returned to Rome, openly confirming the sentence of deposition passed against the usurper of the see of Autun and declaring it canonical on the basis of authentic testimony, while the lord of Lyon openly and publicly disapproved their action. As the aforesaid bishop of Tusculum, or Labicum, was traveling to Jerusalem, he encountered him on the road [Note: [Col. 0387] A charter of *Gallia Christiana* IV, 107, shows that Hugh began his journey after the fourth day before the Ides of March in the year 1101. K.], together with the bishop of Chalon and the same usurper of the church of Autun. In the absence of the accusers, Autun’s bishop undertook a purgation outside the province, with the bishop of Lyon prosecuting the matter and confirming it by this oath:

“I believe that this Norigaud, bishop of Autun, has sworn truly, so help me God,”

the bishop of Chalon also agreeing to this and taking the same oath.

I marvel at the gravity of so great a man, everywhere renowned for his innate goodness and honorable reputation, whose unblemished steadfastness the Gallican Church venerates, and that he could have been so deceived by one man that even now he holds, defends, and protects that man’s party, and is almost alone in our world in thinking well and rightly of him, although the generality and universal unanimity of nearly everyone, even of those absent and unknown, oppose his judgment.

This is augmented by another marvel. Before that ill-fated ordination, the lord Hugh of blessed memory, abbot of Saint-Martin of Autun, the provost of that same church of Autun, and the archdeacon Signius had come to him and approved that election, which had been made simoniacally, after deanery, archdeaconry, precentorship, and certain other ecclesiastical offices had been promised and granted, as can now be seen. He said that their words flowed from the source of hatred and compelled the men meanwhile to remain silent about what they had begun, refusing to lend an ear to their statement. Indeed, he even made them make a profession to the man who had been ordained, although they accused him of such manifest ambition. He promised that, if that simony were carried into effect, he would speak otherwise; for one ought not rashly to judge of the hidden matters of another’s heart.

And lest there be anyone who disapproved of the ordination he had carried out, he made all the canons who had assembled promise the same profession that those men had made, and ordered those who had remained at home to do the same. Yet at the beginning he had entirely opposed that election, because it had always been contrary to canonical decrees for him to hold precedence in two churches: namely, two archdeaconries, although he was not a deacon and did not wish to be one, as well as the office of cantor.

After this purgation had been accepted, the aforesaid John brought the bishop of Autun back with him, while the bishop of Lyon proceeded toward Rome. There he also found certain canons of Autun prosecuting their case. For after the cardinals’ departure, the same man had excommunicated them because, after being abandoned by him, they had brought their accusation before the Roman judges; because, in this disagreement, while striving to bring to completion what they had begun, they had somewhat disposed of the church’s property; because, when summoned to judgment on these matters, they had refused to accept a hearing from one whom they knew to be hostile to them; and because they were unwilling to return the episcopal house to him.

When the matter was heard at Rome, they were declared absolved by the pope and were sent back with apostolic letters to the house, while the bishop of Lyon, together with the bishop of Die, proceeded to Jerusalem. Norigaud, however, coming to Autun with John and lodging at Saint-Martin, was not received by the canons. Nevertheless, in that monastery he celebrated Mass, made chrism, and did not fear to attempt priestly ministry, making light of whatever the cardinals had brought against him and trusting in the protection of the archbishop, the apostolic one’s favor, and his own generosity.

But the cardinals, remaining firm in their position, publicly criticized what had been done, declaring that it was not canonical but alien to the equity of Peter. For this reason they withdrew from the pope’s familiarity and counsel, so that John, having left Rome, still remains at Pavia, living regularly with the brothers in the church from which he had been taken to the palace. Benedict, meanwhile, remains in his titular church, withdrawing from the counsel of the curia and disapproving what he had condemned.

Thus, with the church of Autun thrown into turmoil, Norigaud went to Flavigny and appointed Girard, formerly prior of Cluny, abbot there contrary to the prohibition of the chapter of Autun. He thereby received this further reward for his obstinacy: that he saw everything deteriorating during his lifetime. He likewise expelled religious observance from the church of Saint-Martin and introduced secularism, appointing there a man whom the lord archbishop, in name only, forbade. In this way, too, he attained the height of misfortune through the dispersal and destruction of the order, not understanding what is said in chapter 4 of the Council of Sardica:

“When a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who dwell in nearby places, and he has declared that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome, no bishop is to be ordained in his chair after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been settled by the judgment of the Roman bishop.”

Thus Norigaud deposed me, without investigation, hearing, or condemnation, although I had sought a hearing from the chapter of Autun and had appealed to the bishop of Lyon; and when I was not admitted to these proceedings, I also appealed to Rome and opposed that ordination on behalf of God, blessed Peter, and the pope—as far as lay within my power. He himself found what he sought.

Now, therefore, if he acted justly and canonically, let him rejoice in the shepherd whom he appointed and in the flock for which he provided so suitable a shepherd. But if not, let fire go forth from Norigaud and devour him with his own; let fire go forth from Girard and those entrusted to him, and consume Norigaud with his ordinations.

After this, Milo from the monastery of Saint-Albinus [Note: [Col. 0389D] Namely, of Angers.] was sent as legate to France, … bishop. [lacuna: the place of the see is vacant.] He arranged that Norigaud should be received within the city and established a certain reconciliation between him and the canons. He also arranged that he should be received in the chapter of Cluny and acclaimed as bishop, after certain churches had been ceded in that same chapter, in number … [lacuna: the number is missing], without the praise or approval of the canons, or of those who were with Norigaud, or of those who had come against him to prosecute their cases in the presence of the legate [Note: [Col. 0389] The rest of the page is blank.].

*(Folio 145′.)* In the year from the beginning of the Lord’s incarnation 1099, on August 2, Pope Urban died; Paschal succeeded him. William the Younger, king of the English, also died. In that same year, in England, a spring was seen to pour forth real blood, foul and fetid. Almost the entire island ran together to see the spectacle, astonished by the unusual novelty of the event. The aforesaid king came and saw it, but his seeing did him no good.

The common people generally believed that this portent signified the king’s death, and those who reported it told him so as well. But he was a worldly man, one upon whom the fear of God had not fallen, devoted to the pleasures of the flesh and to pride, a despiser and adversary of divine commands. Yet he would have possessed a sufficiently kingly spirit had he not put God second, puffed up by the arrogance of kingship. He did not even think that he would die.

Therefore, although remarkable things occurred in England during his reign, he did not remember the Lord—or even himself—although certain revelations, which nevertheless did him no good, warned him to turn to God. He did not obey them, though terrified by the punishment that divine judgment threatened against him. For what was said was fulfilled in him: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

And because he abandoned God, oppressing the holy Church and establishing it as his servant, he too was abandoned by God. In the forest adjoining the city of Winchester [Note: [Col. 0390D] Winchester.], while he was hunting, he was struck by an arrow shot by someone; he fell and died from the mortal wound, deprived of penance and Communion, and was buried near that city.

During his reign a violent wind rose from the river Thames [Col. 0389D] and destroyed many buildings; no storm of raging winds so great had ever been heard. Striking the monastery of Saint Mary in the city of London, where these events occurred, it tore off the entire roof. It seized nine beams, joined together as they were, carrying them far away through the intervening spaces, nearly fifty paces as far as the marketplace. In that marketplace—something incredible even to relate—it drove them into the ground, with their ends sunk downward, at equal intervals from one another just as they had been joined, so that barely one cubit of their great length appeared above the surface; and this remains so to the present day.

It also caused the squared stones set above the height of the wall, upon which the roof had been supported, to fly as far as seven miles. They can still be seen there. This occurred around the ninth hour of the day.

In that same church a certain sexton was lying in one bed with another man. Between them, while they lay at a distance from one another, one of the beams, driven by the wind through the middle of the bed, entered the ground so that barely its top was visible. It did not injure the men lying there, except that they were almost frightened to death.

In that same spacious and populous city there were many dogs kept to guard the houses. The shorter they were in body, the more fierce and savage they were by nature. As night darkened, they gathered before the house of the great church of Saint Paul, pressing upon passersby if they happened to find anyone alone, helpless, or without a staff, so that no one dared to pass that place without an escort or means of defense—especially since they had already attacked many with their bites. Every night they were carried out for such raids.

Almost no one now traveled by that route, and if anyone happened to have urgent need to go that way, detours were sought. The Londoners, assembled in their court of judgment, made an outcry about this two or three times. An order was given that everyone should shut up and guard his dogs at night; but since even then they could not be called back from their undertaking, a sentence was issued adjudging that all of them should be killed, and a day was appointed for this to be done.

When that day was approaching, however, on the very night preceding it, the entire multitude of those dogs—nearly four thousand—fled and disappeared. It is uncertain whether they threw themselves into the sea, since no one could be found who would say where they had gone or what had become of them. Thus the city was freed.

I am ashamed to relate that unheard-of monster, unprecedented throughout all ages, which occurred at that time on the same island. Yet it must not be concealed, so that whoever hears of it may have his ears ring, be astonished, and blush at becoming entangled in such things—things in which no one has ever been ensnared unless he has been abandoned by God and handed over to a depraved mind. I speak of a male human being impregnated by males, and of that monster, through its shameful formation, developed as far as certain features of a human body.

Worse still, that man was a cleric from the king’s chapel, named Peter. For an entire year and more he was disgraced by this portentous and shameful burden and brought to the point of death. He openly and publicly confessed his sin, which, even if he wished, he could not conceal. He begged that his belly be opened so that the burden of the misshapen prodigy might be removed and extracted, but he did not obtain this. As his madness grew heavier and flared up again, and as he was compelled to endure a woman’s condition while nature resisted, he was brought to the point where he had to die. He thereby gained a shameful death from a shameful life and was buried outside the cemetery, without the Christian rites owed to the dead, although at his own command and request, with the burial of an ass.

When his corpse was opened, it was found to contain precisely what had been reported.

He was the brother of Girard, to whom the aforesaid king later gave the archbishopric of York. His life was sufficiently and more than sufficiently notorious; it was even alleged that he had sacrificed to the devil. There would have been excessive oppression of all his nobles and the friends of demons, and of all their attendants, had not his chamberlain—whom he had ordered to prepare a pig and have it secretly brought to him—wondered what he intended to do and hidden himself in a secluded place. When he had been asked to come out, he nevertheless went to a place from which he could freely see what the other was doing.

There he heard him speaking with a demon, whose voice he heard but whose form he did not see. Later he saw that man carried by the demon through the necessary places, at the demon’s command, and afterward worshiped by him. He also heard certain unspeakable things in that assembly.

Later, when the chamberlain had been summoned and ordered to prepare a banquet, call together as many people as he could for the feast, and prepare for everyone without exception a sort of preliminary tasting from that pig, so that no one would fail to taste it, the chamberlain buried the pig in the ground and tried to fulfill the order with another one. The other man, believing that everything had been done as he had commanded, thought so unless he had been informed by the demon; for the demon disclosed to him everything the chamberlain had done.

When the chamberlain was accused on this account and ordered to be arrested, he—having taken precautions for himself because he feared this—drew his sword and defended himself as he made his way home. Then, mounting the horse he had prepared, he fled to King Henry, William’s successor. He reported everything to him and was ready to prove that what he said was true, if it were judged necessary.

This and certain other monstrous things were reported about him throughout the island in that year, when we were there. A day had also been fixed on which these and other matters were to be debated and judgment given, but we did not await it.

This, however, was known to everyone about him: that he was of bad character and altogether unworthy of the office of bishop, and that his life had been impure from childhood and had never accepted correction.

In that same year the flood of blood was said to have flowed from the aforesaid spring, although we did not see it. In the chapel, however, sodomites are excommunicated on every Sunday and feast day.

*(Folio 146.)* Elsewhere a cow also gave birth to a malformed offspring, two-headed and four-horned. One might marvel at such a novelty in nature, were it not even more marvelous that God patiently endures with such patience the many crimes and sins of human beings, so that scarcely anyone now believes that God either cares for human affairs or exercises vengeance upon evildoers. Thus we see all of us seething in iniquities.
