For what is there now in the world except the emptying out of all justice and the flood of every iniquity and abomination? But for the moment, setting aside these sad matters, let us return to what came a little earlier and relate something that may bring sweetness to the spirit.

We must not pass over the lord Hugh, abbot of Saint-Martin of Autun. He had been brought from the church of Dijon and appointed shepherd there in order to restore that church to its former state of order and religious observance. Although he had suffered many adversities and had no rest by night or day, although he had even seen those whom he had brought with him from Dijon expelled from the monastery for a time, and although afterward, having been struck with an axe, he was almost emptied of his brains, he remained indefatigable. Finally, as is said, he ended his life by poison and obtained the prize of blessed eternity.

At his death, all that religious observance which had begun perished. I refrain from reporting who was appointed as his successor, because this may be reported as an injury to the lord of Lyon and cannot be said without casting blame upon him. For the man whom he had forbidden, in name only, to be enthroned while the abbot was still alive was, as is said, ordained here with his knowledge, acceptance, and consent. But enough of this for now.

In the aforesaid year from the beginning of the Lord’s incarnation 1099, the lord and our father Rodulf, abbot, after many dangers of travel and labors, began to fall ill during Lent, when he was being called to the promised joys of eternal rest.

At that time he was staying at the estate of Flavigny, an honorable and excellent cell of the monastery, either to avoid the troubles of the occupations of those who came upon him or so that he might devote himself more freely to spiritual contemplation and to the welfare of his sons.

Although he was pressed by the most severe anxieties of bodily illness, he nevertheless remained awake through the night in prayers and vigils and attended the divine offices. With religious devotion he had the day or night office celebrated before him, and he always went to Mass in the oratory, supported by the assistance of those who served him.

When, however, the immensity of pain and illness caused him to lie wholly confined to bed, he kept watch entirely upon God with whatever alone remained possible to him: affection, desire, outstretched hands, and his eyes. Firm in mind and faith, he would not allow anything to be diminished from the rigor of his purpose.

The report of his illness had already terrified the faithful who lived nearby and those who were absent, even those who were far away. All hurried together to him—ordinary people, the wealthy, counts, dukes, and even prelates—to be comforted by the conversation and charity of so great a man. They considered it a very great loss if he departed without their having visited him.

He himself urged them to serve one another with such attentiveness, generosity, diligence, and charity that, although almost innumerable people came every day, even those who were received wondered where such abundance, such liberality, and such cheerful, unfailing generosity in every provision could come from.

As is customary with many sick people, he did not refuse the frequent visits of devout people entering and leaving. Rather, with as much affection and courtesy as he could, and with the gesture of his body, he welcomed them, so that there was no one who did not declare that, merely by being allowed to see him, he had been refreshed, consoled, and helped.

He had already sent to Verdun a letter announcing his illness, and the people there had sent throughout the surrounding region to gather the brothers who could come, and to ask those who could not come to seek his recovery from the Lord or to fortify his passing by their prayers [Note: [Col. 0393] Fourteen lines erased.].

When, therefore, people from every direction hastened eagerly to visit him, he exhorted them all, impressing upon everyone the faith which he had held and for which he had been exiled, saying that this was the true faith, the Catholic and apostolic faith, for which no one ought to hesitate to endure adversity, indeed even to undergo death. He asserted that, if they wished and the occasion were suitable, at such a dreadful hour, when the soul hastened to God’s judgment, he was prepared to confirm what he said by an oath, and that for this same faith he would wish to be killed a thousand times, if God commanded it (Mart. 28).

And although he was now wholly laboring toward his dissolution [Col. 0393B], nevertheless all his speech, all his desire, and all his affection were directed toward preserving this faith and guarding it with all his strength and with his whole soul. No one came before him without being exhorted to this end. He said that those whose minds were of themselves driven away from this observance were altogether condemned, if they happened to die without repentance, so that through repentance they might not be restored to the unity of the Church’s body.

After several days had passed, as though foreseeing his imminent departure, he caused the brothers and sons whom he had acquired for Christ to come before him. With marvelous grace in his face and speech, he exhorted them concerning their salvation and admonished them to hope in the Lord. He confessed that he had not governed them well, and had not acted toward them with the paternal affection he ought to have shown, because he was a human being, who never remains in the same condition (fol. 146).

And when he had admonished them sufficiently as a father to remain steadfast in the right faith, just as they had seen him persevere constantly and firmly [Col. 0393C], and had restrained all those standing around from weeping, as far as he could with hand and voice, he said:

“I, who, though unworthy, exercise the place and office of a father, shall first absolve you by the authority of God, of the saints, and of the office entrusted to me; and you shall afterward absolve your dearest father, as most loving and devoted sons. Thus we shall be separated in body, but not in spiritual affection. You will send your father ahead and, with this same affection, escort him to the Lord. I, if God shows mercy to my soul—which I believe and expect—shall be a helper and strengthening support of your faith for all your days, and I shall remember those who remember me through the assistance of God’s grace.”

As he said this, he had a stole brought to him. When they had placed it around his neck, his face, though he was lying down, shone with such grace and beauty, and it suited him so well, that everyone marveled. Even now they affirm that never in his entire life did the arrangement of that garment fit him so gracefully as it did then. In all the days up to that time, scarcely anyone had been found to whom the adornment and placing of sacred vestments suited so well as they suited him—in grace, propriety, stature, and the dignity of his face, speech, and bearing.

When all had prostrated themselves, he absolved them all [Col. 0394A], and was himself absolved by them. Then, after joining everyone in the holy kiss, he saw some nobles standing nearby—religious men who had valued God more highly than the world—and called them to himself and kissed them.

On the other side stood noble women who had turned away from the world: namely, the sister of Richard, bishop of Albano, and another woman of a family of no little distinction. When he had likewise called them to him, and, with the pious affection of a father, declared them to be his daughters and sisters, saying that they too ought to give their father a final farewell, he extended his hand to them to kiss. By this gesture he indicated that their proper union with him should be of this kind, since it is not permitted for women to join priests in a kiss, and especially not religious women with religious men.

When he had also admonished them to attend to what had been said to the others, and to understand that the same words had been addressed to them, and had dismissed them, entrusting them to God’s grace, he received the Lord’s Body. Then, turning wholly toward God, he committed himself and everyone to His mercy. He commanded all that the man whom he named—Lord Godezo, who was assisting him, a man of good reputation and religious conduct—should be chosen as his successor, under obedience, on the very day of his burial, and that they should obey him. If someone else were chosen instead, by disregarding and rejecting him, they were not to obey that person in any way. For he said that he did not wish another to destroy what he himself had built.

When everyone promised that they would comply with this command, he blessed them all with an outstretched hand. With his eyes closed, he prepared himself for the hour of the Lord’s coming, so that he might open to Him, entering with Him and through Him into the wedding feast of the Lamb.

The Lord’s Passion was read before him by someone whom he chose and commanded [Note: [Col. 0393D] The scribe appears to have been the author of these words.]. When the reader recited what they had done to Him and how much they had done, he trembled inwardly [Col. 0394C] so violently that his voice was frequently heard saying: “Why did the enemies of God do this? Did they not recognize God speaking the truth and doing marvelous things? Ah! What punishments they now suffer!”

Then came the hour he had always desired. After remaining silent for a little while, he breathed out his spirit with his eyes closed, as though sleeping.

His body was washed and cared for through the pious diligence of his sons, and, as was customary, clothed in sacred garments. It was carried on the devout shoulders of his sons and laid before the altar of Saint Firmin, where it was honored with the appropriate vigils dictated and made possible by the love of his sons (Mart. 29).

On the following day, after Mass had been celebrated amid the excessive grief and wailing of everyone, they hastened to set out for the monastery where he had ordered himself to be buried, because he had arranged to be buried among his sons in a humble place, just as he had commanded and wished.

They hastened to depart so that, if a duke, count, or any of the other leading men of the region came—men who loved him with extraordinary affection—his body might not be detained by them and its transfer to the monastery forbidden [Col. 0394D]. This would indeed have happened, had those whose concern it was to prevent it not acted in advance, so that when the body was carried out from the village it had already traveled part of the road leading toward its destination.

A crowd of people of different sexes and ages met the honorable funeral procession. Wherever it entered a village, bells were rung; people came together from hamlets and fields and waited for its arrival with crosses, incense burners, and lights.

Even more remarkable was this: when those who were in the fields or among the horse pastures saw the funeral attendants approaching from afar, the peasants left their oxen, the mounted men mounted their horses, and, without being summoned, followed the funeral. So that they would not even appear to burden the bearers with the funeral necessities, they prepared what was needed for themselves and, when it was offered to them, did not accept it.

With such a triumph they came to Toul. The bishop and the abbot of Saint Mansuetus prepared a solemn procession. The whole congregation, clothed in white, raised crosses, banners, and every kind of glorious ornament. The holy body was received, laid before the altar [Col. 0395B], and honored with solemn funeral rites. Thus they spent the night there (Mart. 30).

When daylight came, the devoted love of the brothers prepared itself for Mass. As the faithful hastened to meet them, Mass was celebrated with the greatest devotion, amid the praise of God and the offerings of the faithful.

The canons of the principal church of Saint Stephen expected that the remains of the body would be brought to them, so that they too might honor it with the proper rites and carry it through the monasteries of the city. But those responsible for hastening the journey did not permit this, a decision which the bishop and the canons accepted with considerable displeasure (fol. 147).

That day, with a long procession of those going before and following after, they came to the monastery of Saint Michael, situated on the River Meuse [Note: [Col. 0395D] Saint Michael.], where Lord Odelricus [Note: [Col. 0396D] Odelricus.] then, as now, held the office of abbot [Col. 0395C]. He was a man of good simplicity, a dwelling-place of innocence and religion, taken from that same monastery—where the man of God under discussion had received the monastic habit—and elevated to the governance of souls.

The two men had loved one another with such great affection that one could perceive in them a certain communion of charity and goodwill, and a similar harmony of innocence and religious life. Thus Odelric revered the deceased man with the honor due to a father, while the deceased man embraced Odelric with a tender and irreproachable filial affection, since both were men of good life, good reputation, good conduct, and grace.

When he heard that the little body of his deceased father had arrived, as though he were about to receive the most precious relics of the saints, he arranged a procession with crosses, banners, incense vessels, candlebearers, and every kind of glorious display. Thus, with everything adorned in garments woven with silk and gold, he went forth joyfully to meet the body—except that he did so with tears and groaning. Yet even this is a kind of joy: to celebrate solemnly, with groaning and contrition of heart, the funerals of religious men, especially those who labored in word and deed, whose life is beyond doubt, and in whose esteem our own praise is not endangered.

Some wished to restrain the man’s impulse, but he who knew the innocence of the deceased believed that nothing he did in reverence for him on God’s account could be excessive (Mart. 31).

That night, therefore, he did whatever the fervor of his heart’s affection suggested and enabled. After arranging for a boat and boatmen to carry the funeral by the River Meuse, he himself, present with the brothers [Col. 0396A], guided it toward Verdun until the body, placed aboard the vessel, disappeared from sight. Everyone traveled along the well-worn road and did not abandon the office of psalmody.

They came to a certain populous village called Giniscort, situated above the channel mentioned earlier, three leagues from the city. The men who were carrying the body by the winding and twisting bends of the river were delayed there for a while. Meanwhile, those conducting the funeral had already arrived and were waiting for the rowers. They wished, and urged the clergy of the village—the clergy of its three churches—to go out to meet the body and perform the proper funeral rites, as others had done even without being urged.

But the priests, making malicious and unworthy accusations, could never be compelled to offer the customary prayer of human charity as the procession passed [Col. 0396B]. Instead, they declared him malicious, saying that he had rebelled against bishops and was attempting to drive them from their priesthood and the emperor from his kingdom. They shouted that the hour of his funeral was blessed, since every opportunity for rebellion and dissension had perished.

While they continued to make this noise with rustic babbling, the body passed by, and the crowd following it continued its journey. Divine vengeance immediately pursued the madness of the peasants.

For while they rejoiced that they had done this, and openly and publicly congratulated themselves on having acted rightly, the avenging fire seized the unrepentant men. It is established that, before a month had passed, the entire village was completely consumed by fire. Those will not believe this who do not believe that God repays vengeance upon the enemies of His people and stands ready to avenge the blood of His servants [Col. 0396C].

A messenger announcing the arrival of the funeral had already reached the monastery. The flock of sons, piously devoted to their father, had already hurried out in a long procession to meet the approaching body. After passing through the city, they waited for the arrival of the procession in the church of Saint Victor, in the suburb beyond the walls.

Among that congregation was a brother who might have been of some usefulness, had he known how to restrain the movements of an indignant spirit and break the desires of flattering flesh, so that he might learn to abandon properly what he had often begun improperly. From the beginning, middle, and end of the deceased’s administration, this man had always opposed his arrangements. He was an adversary of nearly all his acts, commands, and constitutions. Yet, because he could not destroy what he was unable to overcome in any other way, he seemed reluctantly to consent.

He also appeared, and claimed, to be somewhat hindered by bodily infirmities. As often happens through indignation and an unhealthy condition, or through the passions of the inner person, the outer person is corrupted and becomes resentful, when no one applies medicine or places a poultice upon the livid wound. This is especially the case with one who delays confessing the soul’s passions to his spiritual father.

While the others were preparing for the journey to meet their father, undertaking the work and preparing what was necessary, this man approached the prior, explained the causes of his infirmity, and asserted that he could not make the journey. He begged to be excused.

The prior, who was not ignorant of his evasions and knew very well on which foot he limped [Col. 0397A], neither granted nor refused his request. Instead, he left everything to him, so that he might decide what to do. He said that the matter stood between God and himself, since God saw the hidden things of the heart; that he should take care lest the impossibility he alleged were false; that God was prepared to avenge every deceit, disobedience, and lie; and that he himself took none of these matters upon himself, but left everything to God and to the man himself (fol. 147′).

They therefore departed, while he remained behind and bore with apparent grief all the preparations made for the deceased.

But the man who delayed going to his father’s funeral was deprived of the service of one who would give him confession, bring him the Eucharistic viaticum, and perform the funeral rites for him when he died. He died a sudden and unexpected death, so that even after a very long interval following his death scarcely anyone arrived to perform the proper rites for his funeral [Col. 0397B]. In this too God avenged the injuries done to His servant.

But, to return to the matter: while the brothers waited in the church of Saint Victor for their father’s body, and the bishop with the clergy and the customary varied display stood on the riverbank, the boatmen arrived with the body. As the entire city hastened to meet it—so that from this rivalry one might understand everyone’s affection for the dead—the funeral was received.

The congregations went before, as is customary at a funeral, while crosses and the rest of the display remained around the body. The procession continued toward the principal church of Saint Mary, with bells ringing throughout the city.

It was possible to see the suburban people, and even the peasants, sharing in the grief of the monks, who mourned their bereavement, and, moved by compassion, breaking into cries with tears, saying: “Good monks, you will never again recover such a devout and beloved father. You grieve rightly; you mourn rightly.”

This was all the more marvelous and honorable to the praise of divinity because the man who had once been called by foolish and less wise people a destroyer of laws and of the homeland on account of the king’s dissension—because he had refused to share with the destroyers of the sacred ordinances of divine law—was now unanimously and without disparagement proclaimed by everyone the father of the city and the region, a man of counsel, a wall and shield of the house of the Lord, who could never again be recovered. The tears and groans accompanying these words seemed to establish their truth.

*(April 1.)*

Thus the body, escorted by his sons and by nearly the entire population of the city [Col. 0397D], was received inside the monastery of Saint Mary by the canons who had come to meet it. After the customary funeral rites had been celebrated, a general Mass with offerings was held.

Then the procession set out for the monastery of Saint Vitus. The brothers of that monastery had gone ahead after the canons received their father’s body. As though they were about to receive a father whom they would possess eternally, they had adorned themselves suitably and taken care that, when the canons departed through the city gate, they should meet them in their own suburb. Receiving the body with the honor due to it, they were to escort it, together with the canons, into the monastery.

After this, the canons departed, and the sons performed the proper rites for the body with even greater devotion. Everything proceeded in such an orderly and well-arranged manner that it was openly evident [Col. 0398A] that, because the man whose funeral this was had lived in an orderly fashion and had conducted himself honorably and orderly, God provided everything appropriate for him in an orderly and well-arranged manner.

When discussion arose concerning the stone with which the tomb was to be closed, and it seemed scarcely possible to find one, craftsmen were sent to the place where one was thought likely to be found. At their first excavation or entry into the earth, they discovered five quarried stones with covers. The one that appeared more worthy, larger, and more suitable was adapted for the reception of the blessed man’s body.

Some said that he should be buried beside Lord Berengarius, the bishop who had founded the monastery, namely before the altar of Saint Firmin, because he had died in the monastery where his precious body rests. But since that place was too far removed from the sight of the congregation, his burial was begun before the altar [Col. 0398B] of Saint Benedict, beside Lord Dado the bishop, where Lord Humbert, the first abbot of that place, was also said to rest.

*(April 2.)*

After this had been carefully expedited, the whole city gathered on the following day to bury him. When Mass had been said and a sermon delivered, he was returned to the earth, to rise again in glory and to dwell with us spiritually forever. He himself had promised this when, as he was about to go to God, he entrusted to God those present who belonged to Him and whom God had committed to his care.

This too may rightly be counted among his merits before God: while he lived, he obtained that he should be buried among the tombs of bishops [25], where, apart from Lord Richard the abbot and the aforementioned Humbert, Ermenric, also an abbot, and Lord Bernerius [Col. 0398C], the provost of the city, to whom that burial place was granted because of his holiness, no one is found to have been buried. The place is otherwise renowned as the burial site of dukes, marquises, counts, and other nobles.

*(April 2.)*

After the burial had been completed, the bishop came into the chapter house with the abbots and the leading clergy to console the brothers. When, after discussion of their father’s death, they were admonished to choose a suitable successor—since delay would diminish their religion and honor, especially because it was established that the deceased had commanded that a successor be chosen for him on the very day of his burial—the bishop left the chapter house, giving the brothers an appropriate opportunity to discuss more freely among themselves the father they should place over them [Col. 0398D].

When everyone had departed and only those to whom the election belonged remained, they prostrated themselves on the ground and sang seven psalms with prayers, beginning: “We are present, Holy Spirit, held back indeed by the enormity of sin, but gathered in your name.” When they rose and sat down, the prior admonished them to choose whomever they judged suitable, declaring that, if he knew the man elected to be suitable, he was prepared to approve the election.

Then the aforementioned brother, a man of good life and reputation both before and after his conversion, rose and delivered faithful prayers on behalf of Lord Abbot Rodulf to the entire assembly (fol. 148).

They marveled and, bending their knees to the ground, gratefully and tearfully received that greeting. He continued: Lord Abbot Rodulf commanded them under obedience [Col. 0399A] to choose as his successor the man whom he himself had named and chosen, and upon whom he had decided that his burden should be imposed.

When they received this command with astonishment, he added that the prior was the man named. In obedience—which had been enjoined upon him just as upon the others—he chose him, lest he be disobedient.

Everyone agreed with him, but the man who had been named did not. “I said,” he declared, “that if a suitable person were chosen, I would consent to the election. But now, since I see that you have chosen a sick and feeble man, whose weakness would provide you with encouragement for idleness, I do not consent. Moreover, your election conflicts with the ordinances of the canons and is invalid for this reason: it is not permitted for a church’s prelate to choose his own successor.”

He said this and many other things, while the brother who had made the announcement repeated only this to everyone: “Lord Abbot Rodulf commands it under obedience.”

Why say more? The election was reported to the laymen, and the command and counsel of the aforementioned father were reported to them, to which the whole congregation agreed. When the laymen accepted the election and everyone acclaimed it with one voice, the bishop was recalled to the chapter house.

When he had sat down with the abbots and the leaders of the clergy, the aforementioned brother rose and repeated to the bishop and the other leading men what he had said to the brothers: namely, that Lord Abbot Rodulf both commanded and requested that the successor he had chosen and named be given to them.

The bishop therefore praised the election as far as he could, and asked whether the convent and the people consented to it [Col. 0399C]. When they acclaimed it together, the elected man attempted to repeat what he had said and similar arguments, and tried to reject the election made in his favor. The brother to whom the command had been given rushed at him, seized him, and, while he was sitting, presented him to the bishop, assisted by the others who had prepared to help him for this very purpose. He was admonished and compelled to receive the pastoral staff; he was not overcome.

When the bishop and those present saw that his spirit was inflexible, the brothers began the antiphon “Confirm this, O God,” and carried him into the church rather than led him. They forced the bells into his hands; he did not ring them. Since resistance was no longer accomplishing anything, he was kissed by the congregation, as was customary, and on the following Sunday he was blessed as abbot [Col. 0399D].

This took place in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, on April 2, a Wednesday, the fifth day after the deposition [Note: [Col. 0399] Namely, the first burial, before the altar of Saint Firmin at Flavigny, on the very day of his death.] of the good-memory father Rodulf.

The tomb of the aforementioned father was carefully closed and coated with bitumen, and a marble tablet was placed upon it. Since it is at the entrance of the choir, before the altar of Saint Benedict, it was decreed that, when the brothers returned from the daily mandate, they should prostrate themselves there and, after completing their prayer, commemorate the father resting in that place [Col. 0400A].

And so that no one might find this burdensome, the memorial that had customarily been said for Lord Abbot Richard after matins—one that had been discontinued, as though because of the brothers’ burden, and whose omission seemed grievous to certain brothers among whom Father Richard’s memory is rightly celebrated—was restored, lest they appear to complain that his memorial had been discontinued and this one begun.

Even to the present day, the good successor of both fathers, passing before the tomb, entrusts again to him the sheep committed to his care. He frequently begs with his mouth, and always with his heart and devotion, that both shepherd and sheep may be ruled and protected by him.

May God grant him faithfully to carry out the care which he undertook unwillingly, so that he may not fear evil report, but hear the Lord’s “Well done,” and deserve to be set over many things.

Whoever wishes to learn what was shown by an angel concerning our father Richard to this father of ours, Rodulf, as it was reported by him to the brothers, should seek it in the life of the aforementioned venerable man Richard, and will find it there.

This same man who was thus appointed was born in the bishopric of Liège, into a family of no little distinction. At the same time as Lord Abbot Rodulf abandoned the world and received the monastic habit, he too received it in the same monastery. When Rodulf was promoted to the abbacy, while this man was prior, he was appointed in his place. Later, when we had moved to Dijon, he was made cloister prior there. Afterward, when the brothers had returned to the monastery, the aforementioned father recalled him and, under and by the authority of that father, appointed him prior of Verdun [Col. 0400C].

Thus, tested in each monastery and office, always rising and making progress, he was chosen to govern souls in the place and according to the wish of the father.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1101, on the feast of Saint Cecilia, a violent wind entered Normandy. It was so violent that it cast down certain buildings and devastated the forests so thoroughly that it uprooted ancient oaks—not merely in certain places, as usually happens, but throughout the entire forest. When one uprooted tree leaned upon another, it broke and threw down the tree upon which it leaned.

This occurred around midnight and lasted almost until midday. In our times no wind of this kind had ever been heard that, wherever it struck, had so completely destroyed everything.

[Col. 0400D] In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1102, Pontius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, was appointed bishop of Anicium, and Aymericus undertook the administration of the abbey of La Chaise-Dieu.

Richard, bishop of Albano, was also sent as legate to Burgundy and France. He had first been dean of the church of Saint Stephen at Metz.

## SERIES OF THE ABBOTS OF FLAVIGNY

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399D] “[lacuna]” [Note: [Col. 0399] We were unable by any means to investigate what precedes this. Labbe.]

Bishop Gayroinus succeeded and died on July 6, 755, indiction 13.

[Col. 0400D] Manasses was appointed abbot by gift of King Pippin. He brought into the church of Flavigny the body of Saint Praejectus, brought back by Volovicus. He died in the year 787 [789], indiction 15 [Col. 0401A], and after him [Note: [Col. 0401] “p [lacuna]” in Labbe] Adalbert was appointed.

He died in the fourth year, and Zacho succeeded him, appointed on the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0401D] On the ninth day before the Kalends of March, according to the Annals of Flavigny]. He died in his fourth year, on the seventh day before the Ides of May (in the year 793).

Alcuin succeeded him (796). In his seventh year he surrendered the see to Apollinaris by gift of the emperor Charles (803). How great and what kind of man he was is set forth in the public records. He died during the time of Emperor Louis, in indiction 4, in 826, and after his death Vigilius succeeded him.

In 839 Adrevaldus succeeded him, and died in the third year. Marianus succeeded in 845, indiction 8, and surrendered the see to Wlfaldus.

After Wlfaldus departed, Count Warinus governed as vice-abbot by gift of the emperor Charles. Under him was Sarulfus the deacon, and after him Gozserus succeeded as abbot.

When Gozserus died, Hugo succeeded in the sixteenth year of Charles, and Saint Eygil succeeded him. He later became archbishop of Sens [Col. 0401B] and transferred the body of Saint Regina.

Sigardus succeeded him. In the fifth year he surrendered the see to Wolfardus, brother-in-law of Emperor Louis II, by the gift of that same emperor.

In the third year of Wolfardus’s appointment, the consecration of the church of Flavigny was performed by Pope John and eighteen bishops, in the year 878, indiction 11. In that same year Emperor Louis died, and Karlomannus succeeded him.

After this, Adalgarius, bishop of Autun, in the first year of Charles the Simple’s reign, sought and obtained the abbey under Odo. Invited to Rome by the pope, he died on the journey at Trenortius in that same year, namely 893. Under him Aquinas was provost.

“[lacuna] with Duke Richard as successor [lacuna], to be ordained” [Col. 0401C]. Argrimus, who had been deposed by Pope John from the bishopric of Langres, consecrated him; but Formosus restored Argrimus in Lyon. Since he did not possess the pallium or the restored dignity by which he could consecrate a bishop, and since Theobald, bishop of Langres, opposed the appointment on the pope’s behalf, Formosus irrecoverably deposed Argrimus and excommunicated Walo and his supporters—namely Richard, Manasses, and the others—for invading the church of Flavigny.

Nevertheless, supported by secular power, Walo obtained the bishopric. Having been made abbot of Flavigny by himself, he retained the casamentum in his own hand and appointed Otbert as provost under him.

Thus the church of Flavigny remained without an abbot for many years. In the same way, while the church’s casamenta passed successively to one another, the bishops of Autun obtained them within their own division.

After Otbert, Girfredus, accused of responsibility for Adalgarius’s death but acquitted by the judgment of the bishops, obtained the prelacy. Raingus, a man of great usefulness and integrity, succeeded him. He died on the Ides of May.

Walo also died in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 913, indiction 15. Herveus succeeded him, retained the abbacy for himself, and appointed Gausarius as prelate under him.

When Herveus nevertheless died, Romundus was appointed in his place. He entrusted the administration of the church of Flavigny to Raino, abbot of Mâcon, in the time of King Rodulf, son of Richard the Justiciar.

When Raino died, Wichardus succeeded him, and Lord Fulcherius succeeded Wichardus in the time of Louis, son of Charles the Simple.

Fulcherius journeyed to Jerusalem in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 944, indiction 2. He brought to his church part of the Lord’s nail, small pieces of His cross, a portion of His belt and burial cloth, and also a piece of the staff. He also governed the church of Dijon.

He brought Saint Paschasia into the church of Flavigny, namely half of her body. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 955, and Milo of Mâcon succeeded him.

When Romundus departed in the year 968, indiction 11, Gerardus succeeded him. Abbot Milo journeyed to Rome and obtained a privilege from Pope Benedict.

Walter succeeded Gerard, bishop of Autun, in the year 978 [Col. 0402B], indiction 6. After Milo’s death, Walter gave the church of Flavigny to Robert, who would have ruined the entire church had precaution not been taken.

Robert was expelled from the abbacy because he was a relative of Landricus, count of Nevers. He was entrusted with the priory of the cell of Corbigny, and Heldricus, a Cluniac monk, was installed as abbot.

Robert, however, came to Corbigny and caused himself to be called its abbot. From that time Corbigny has been called an abbey.

Heldricus died in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1010. Amedeus succeeded him and recovered the cell of Corbigny. He also founded the cells of Coltilly, Semur, and Belloc. He died with great authority and dignity, and Aymo succeeded him.

Accused of simony, Aymo laid down the pastoral staff into the hands of Pope Leo IX. Odo I, a monk of the monastery of Aremar, succeeded him [Col. 0402C], and after two years surrendered the see to Odo II.

Elmuinus, who was administering the see of Autun, also restored Corbigny to our church, since it did not then possess it. When the monks received it with a procession, he unwisely accepted in the procession the pastoral staff which the devilish Robert had possessed. Our brothers vehemently denounced this, and for that reason withdrew from their place in the procession.

For this reason, as the apostolic commands prohibiting any abbot from holding two abbeys grew stronger, he was accused by the same men at the Council of Exoldunum, as though he were governing two churches contrary to the apostolic decrees. He returned the staff, and, when justice was sought concerning his cell—that is, the property of the church of Flavigny [Col. 0402D]—he obtained nothing.

At last, when Bishop Errwinus died and the common election had proceeded in favor of Agano, Abbot Heinricus went to the court of the king of the Franks and disclosed his grievance to the king’s ears. As justice proceeded, the bishop was compelled by oath to promise that, immediately after his consecration, he would restore the rights of the church of Flavigny.

Because the abbot of Flavigny has the first voice in the election of a bishop, which everyone must confirm, the elected bishop came to the chapter of Flavigny and, with a holy kiss, gave the brothers, small and great, a pledge concerning the restoration of the church of Flavigny—that is, the restitution of the cell of Corbigny [Col. 0403A].

But, softened by the attentions of the people of Corbigny, he did not fulfill what he had promised, although he always publicly and privately declared that the right belonged to him.

After Odo’s death, Rainaldus, the duke’s brother and a monk of that same place, was appointed in his place.

He placed the body of Saint Praejectus in a golden casket, fashioned with gems and silver through careful work and labor. For the transfer itself he invited Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny. He also adorned the church entrusted to him with hangings, copes, and various ornaments.

Yet the vigor of his spirit was hindered by illness, so that he could not carry out what he wished. He died in the first flower of youth, before completing seven years in office.

After this the church remained almost seven years without a rector, except that Elmuinus governed it for only two months.

## Around the Beginning of the Century: Blessed Wolphelmus, Abbot of Brunwiller near Cologne

[Col. 0403]

## Life of Blessed Wolphelmus

By Conrad, a monk of the same place and disciple of Blessed Wolphelmus.

*(Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti VI, II, 675.)*

## Preliminary Observations

1. Blessed Wolphelmus, the third abbot of the monastery of Brunwiller, had as the writer of his life one of his own disciples, named Conrad. Conrad faithfully and accurately committed to writing the deeds of his holy master, as he had seen most of them himself and had heard the rest from other trustworthy men.

It is clear that this work was written a few years after the blessed man’s death, both because it is dedicated to Everhard, Wolphelmus’s immediate successor, and from the conclusion of the prologue, where the author speaks as follows:

“If anyone’s faith should waver, as many suitable witnesses remain alive to the present day as there are surviving brothers from that community of that time.”

Trithemius describes Conrad himself in a few words in the Hirsaugiensian Chronicle under the year 1091. Speaking of Wolphelmus, he says:

“Conrad, a monk and his disciple, described his life, full of virtues and signs, in a truthful narrative, for Everard, abbot of Brunwiller, and Hermann, abbot of Saint Pantaleon. Conrad, being not least learned in sacred and secular letters, and having been excellently instructed in every branch of knowledge by a good and highly learned teacher, composed also several other little works by which he transmitted the keenness of his talent to the knowledge of posterity.”

What those works published by Conrad were is unknown to us, except that the same Trithemius, in the Saint Gall edition of the Hirsaugiensian Chronicle and in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men, says that, besides the Life of Blessed Wolphelmus, he published another book on the miracles of the blessed man and several sermons, along with other small works which he admits are unknown to him.

If the book on the miracles praised here by Trithemius was different from the Life presented by the Bollandists, I would readily believe that it has been lost, since it was published neither by Surius nor by the Bollandists, to whom many accounts concerning the saints of Brunwiller were transmitted.

## 2

Moreover, from this Life by Conrad, many authors who followed later composed the eulogy of blessed Wolphelmus. Among the more recent are Yepesius, in volume VI of the *Benedictine Annals*; Bucelinus, in the *Benedictine Menology*; and other historians of our order, including Trithemius himself. In his *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle*, under the year 1091, he writes:

> “In the same year in which Gebhard had been elected abbot—namely, seventy-three days before the death of the holy Father William, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of Christian salvation 1091—the venerable and most holy abbot of the Brunwiller monastery, named Wolphelmus, died. He was a man exceptionally learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, and his most holy way of life benefited many toward salvation. There was a great intimacy between these two most reverend men, William of Hirsau and Wolphelmus of Brunwiller, matched by an equal holiness; it remained inviolate until the death of both of them,” and so forth.

He adorns him with the same praises in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men Who Enlightened Germany by Their Writings*, where he also lists the works published by Wolphelmus:

> “Wolphelmus, abbot . . . , a man learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally well versed in secular letters, devout and most holy in life and conduct, renowned for the performance of many miracles, subtle in intellect and polished in speech, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote several distinguished volumes, but only a few of them have come to my notice. Against Berengarius of Tours, concerning the sacrament of the altar, he published a short but necessary work addressed to Meginhard the abbot, one book. He also wrote many sermons for the brothers and various letters to different people. He composed many elegant poems in different kinds of meter and arranged epigrams on all the volumes in his library. He is also said to have written several other works, which have not at all come to the notice of our reading.”

Conrad included Wolphelmus’s work *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, which Baronius mentions under the year 1059, as chapter 10 of the *Life*. One remarkable point can be observed in it: Berengarius is said to have denied that the Lord Christ entered to the disciples through closed doors—an error that we nowhere find attributed to him by other authors.

## 3

Besides the monasteries of Saint Maximinus at Trier and Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, where blessed Wolphelmus lived a private life, he governed three others, which he distinguished not only by his most holy life but also by pastoral care [Col. 0405] and fatherly solicitude.

The first was Gladbach, in the territory of Jülich; the second was Siegburg, across the Rhine. But when he was burdened beyond measure there with external affairs, he was transferred by Anno, bishop of Cologne, to the monastery of Brunwiller, which lies several leagues from that city. There he persevered until the end of his life.

This monastery owed its origin to Erenfrid, or Ezzo, count palatine, who built it in honor of Saint Nicholas with his wife Matilda, daughter of the emperor Otto II, through the efforts of blessed Poppo, abbot of Stavelot. Poppo installed Ello there as its first abbot, around the year 1024.

The Reverend Father William Wlfrath, prior of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, transmitted to us the Life of Count Ezzo, his wife Matilda, and their children. Since it has already been published by the Bollandists under 21 May, and appears to have been interpolated with certain fables or doubtful matters, it seemed best to omit it.

I wish to note only that six daughters of Ezzo presided over as many monasteries of our order, apart from Richeza, queen of Poland, who was exceedingly generous toward the monastery of Brunwiller. That author lists the monasteries and their names as follows:

> “Adelaide presided in the monastery at Nivelles; Theophanu at Essen; Heilwig at Neuss; Matilda at Dietkirchen and Vilich; Ida in the monastery of Saint Mary at Cologne; and Sophia likewise in the monastery of Saint Mary at Mainz and at Gandersheim. They were placed over the nuns as their rulers.”

## 4

Furthermore, since Wolphelmus has not yet been numbered among the saints by an official decree, and since he is not even publicly honored with an office among our people at Brunwiller—as Henschenius indeed writes—it was sufficient to bestow upon him the title “blessed.”

Nevertheless, in the catalogue of the relics of that monastery, which was sent to us, the head of blessed Wolphelmus is listed among the others. The writer of the catalogue says:

> “Whose remaining bones were scattered and carried here and there through the wars by the violence of soldiers.”

These things certainly indicate that his sacred relics had been raised from the earth and exposed to public veneration. For this reason Gelenius, in book three of *On the Wonders of Cologne Agrippina*, assigns the feast of Saint Wolphelmus, among the special feasts of the monastery of Brunwiller, to 22 April.

On that day his memory is commemorated by the Benedictine Martyrologies of Arnold Wion, Hugh Menard, and Benedict Dorganius; by Molanus in his additions to Usuard; by the German Martyrology; by Philip Ferrarius in the *Catalogue of Saints Who Are Not Found in the Roman Martyrology*; and by various other authors of this kind.

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 0405]

### 1

[Col. 0405A] To the most watchful shepherds and rulers of the Lord’s flock—namely, Everhard, of the Brunwiller monastery, and Hermann, of blessed Pantaleon in Cologne—Conrad, the least of all under the regular discipline, offers the crown laid up by the Lord for those who keep watch.

You, most excellent Fathers, urge us to set forth in writing the life of blessed Wolphelmus the abbot, according to the foreknowledge granted you by God, providing the faithful with no small grace of edification through this work. For you strive that the examples of his virtues, committed to writing and brought to the knowledge of readers, may produce in devout minds principles for living well.

But why, illustrious Fathers, did you choose to impose this task upon us, when neither knowledge is sufficient nor eloquence of speech available? Yet your authority in commanding is so great that, although we fear what you require, we nevertheless consider it wholly wrong to refuse you.

Permit us, by an example drawn from a visible thing, to explain more fully the hesitation by which we have thus far been delayed. You know beyond doubt that the sharpness of the eyes is overcome when struck by the sun’s brilliance; how much more, then, will the spark of our knowledge fail if it presumes to attempt higher things?

Yet, lest by delaying longer we seem to withhold the testimony to his holiness, although we appear to be overwhelmed by the weight of the task, we have nevertheless resolved to obey your wishes as far as our strength permits.

This undertaking is also encouraged and emboldened by the fact that, as we read, each person offered something for the Lord’s tabernacle according to his own capacity: one, gold and silver; another, purple or scarlet cloth; another, red-dyed rams’ skins [Col. 0405C]. We shall have done well if we offer goats’ hair [Col. 0406A].

Since all these things are allegorical, as Catholic teachers explain, distinguishing different kinds of grace by the various gifts, they have wished words of praise to be expressed in certain places by the goats’ hair. Therefore, since by the gift of knowledge or the abundance of merits we cannot attain that perfection signified by gold and silver, purple, scarlet cloth dyed twice, and the other gifts, we wish at least to offer goats’ hair—that is, the calves of our lips—so that we may in some way be found useful in the Lord’s tabernacle and may not appear altogether empty in the sight of the Lord.

Accordingly, when the deeds or triumphs of illustrious men have been entrusted to written memorials, they are found to contain a threefold benefit of usefulness, since by the zeal of imitating their piety very many people are instructed in as many ways by their examples [Col. 0406B].

They are instruments of good works for those who have gone astray, pardon for the penitent, and hope and a crown for those who persevere. Through these three kinds of distinction, the kingdom of heaven truly suffers force (Matthew 11:12), since the one who has gone astray strives to be corrected, the penitent to be justified, and the persevering to be saved.

Divine praises are also raised up when the merits of the saints are recalled to the memory as an example for the faithful. But lest I weary the reader by repeating more, the whole purpose of this discourse is to teach that the merits of the saints continually receive renewed increase through the desires of the faithful, while heavenly grace grants their fruitfulness to minds and supplies the grace of bearing fruit.

Therefore, as we are about to unfold the course of the life of the holy and most blessed abbot Wolphelmus, we intend to pursue absolutely nothing except what we have happened to hear from reliable witnesses [Col. 0406C], or what divine grace has granted us to observe, since for several years they served him or stood beside him [Col. 0407A].

If anyone should hesitate to believe these things, there remain with us as many reliable witnesses as there are brothers from that community who have survived to the present time [Col. 0408A].

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0407]

### 2

[Col. 0407A] Thus the glorious confessor of the Lord, Wolphelmus, born of an illustrious family in the district of the Ripuarians [Note: [Col. 0407D] The Ripuarians were then those who now chiefly inhabit the territories of Cologne and Jülich. Gelenius, in book III of *On the Wonders of Cologne*, traces Wolphelmus’s origin to the counts of Niel.], adorned the line of his noble descent with the title of holiness, through the prevenient grace of God, who freely illumines every just person.

He is rightly recognized as having been called Wolphelm, according to the etymology or the idiom of the language of that region [Note: [Col. 0407D] Henschenius notes that among the people of Cologne *wolf* means “wolf,” while *helm* signifies “helmet” [Col. 0408D].], because, armed with the helmet of salvation, he was destined to engage in battle for the camp of the Lord against the most savage wolf, that is, the devil [Col. 0407B]. How effectively and vigorously he strove to make his deeds correspond to his name, in accordance with circumstance and time, the reader will be able to discover more fully in its proper place.

His father, named Frumold [Note: [Col. 0408D] The same author notes that among the Germans *From* signifies “upright,” while *Olde* refers to “ancient.”], flourished in every kind of action worthy of a good man, as the expression of his name makes clear. He took as his wife a woman named Eveza, fitting him in birth and character. For them, in accordance with the Apostle, the marriage was honorable and the marriage-bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4), since they did not enter into marriage for the satisfaction of lust but for the grace of begetting offspring.

Noble in birth and distinguished among their own people by a certain privilege of innocence, they were most devoted worshipers of the Christian religion, endowed with the wealth of faith, fervent in charity, lovers of piety, and, in the words of the Apostle, doing good to all (Galatians 6:10).

But, to explain the illustrious family and the distinction of her high lineage, Lady Eveza descended from the stock of a very illustrious count named Sicco. He was commended by extensive territories of estates, a numerous household of both sexes, and the boldness of a military spirit.

Because he surpassed others in wealth and nobility, he pursued justice and equity—nothing being more acceptable to God—and exerted all his efforts so that, just as the magnificence of his lineage distinguished his descent, his works of piety might also distinguish him.

From this it is undoubtedly indicated that this just man, a person of such outstanding merit, was born of modest and devout parents, although we read that many just men were born of impious parents, just as roses grow from thorns.

There is no doubt concerning his mother, who, like Rachel, is known to have borne this son in the blessing of Abraham’s seed, in the pain of childbirth and on the right hand, since with Hannah, the mother of Samuel, she merited from God the return of a loan entrusted to her. For she too is found to have offered her son to the Lord with a similar vow.

Concerning her also, we should clearly judge that she pleased the Lord no less in the tabernacle because of the bond of marriage than if she had never been joined to a husband. Indeed, the title of her praise seems rather to be propagated from the fact that she produced the fruit of so fragrant a flower for the establishment of the whole Church than from the fact that she is recognized to have drawn the most illustrious branch of her lineage from the antiquity of her ancestors [Col. 0408A].

In the end, the Almighty approves the mind of each person more than his condition, since slave and free are truly one in the Lord. The only freedom that is pleasing to God, beyond all the glory of the world, is that which no antiquity can remove if we ourselves have done something good or right, or have deserved to have successors devoted to such things [Col. 0408B].

### 3

Blessed Wolphelmus, therefore, ascending the first stage of human growth, passed, with God as his guide, from infancy into the childhood of a good character.

At that age he both undertook the study of the liberal arts and, through the insistence of his family, was associated with the community of the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, at Cologne [Note: [Col. 0408D] This is the metropolitan church of Cologne, over which Saint Heribert presided until the year 1022.].

At that time, after the younger Otto, while Henry II was successfully administering the imperial scepter—a man most powerful in military matters but especially diligent in ecclesiastical disciplines—Saint Heribert, already renowned throughout the world for the fame of his holiness, presided as bishop over the holy Church of Cologne [Col. 0408C].

That most blessed pontiff, already worn out by the old age of his final years, blessed God’s servant Wolphelmus, still small both in body and in wickedness, offered to him according to the custom of the Christian religion, as the Lord had blessed the Gospel child when he was placed in the midst; through the anointing of sacred chrism and the invocation of the Holy Spirit, he transferred him into the company of the children of God.

Moreover, lest the blessing of so great a man be considered empty, vain, or merely accidental, drawn by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, he had already begun to yearn for the contemplative life with the whole desire of his mind. He would have fulfilled his vows if the immaturity of his age had not prevented it. Yet, as his strength increased through natural development, so the desire of his holy fervor grew day by day [Col. 0408D].

### 4

He was chaste in body and sober in mind, possessing such grace in his countenance that his appearance was thought in some way angelic.

In addition to these signs of divine piety, he attained such effectiveness in the study of the Scriptures that whatever he noticed once while reading, he retained forever. This, as we believe, was usually brought about by God’s hidden judgment, lest anything should be lacking in the fullness of knowledge possessed by the most blessed man [Col. 0409A].

Accordingly, apart from the pages of the divine books, whatever the poet sang, the eloquent orator discussed, or the philosopher conceived, he penetrated with a pen of deeper understanding.

Although the young man shone with such great learning, he never fell, exalted by the vice of boastfulness, remembering the Apostle’s words: “Do not be led astray by the empty wisdom of this world” (Ephesians 5:6).

He possessed such gravity and such maturity of character that it was clear to everyone that he was a vessel of election. He would not allow reverence to be shown him on account of his carnal nobility, judging it more useful to display himself as a humble person for the love of Christ than to possess a degenerate spirit.

He also avoided foolish stories and the wantonness of young men, and he abhorred the poisonous tongues of flatterers. He restrained idle talk, frivolity of the eyes, and every movement of the body with the anchor of gravity [Col. 0409B].

The master of the school, observing and weighing his progress in every discipline of virtue, rejoiced that he had devoted himself to teaching one whom he saw to have reached the summit of perfection.

Choosing him, therefore, to be more closely attached to himself and more honorably retained, he took him as a companion and partner in his labor, sharing with him the burden of governing the school’s discipline.

His devotion to the study of Scripture burned magnificently in him through constant exercise. Since the treasure of his knowledge was not hidden away, he became famous everywhere as rumor spread his name. From far away no less than nearby, a crowd of studious clerics sought him out [Col. 0409C], eager by hearing him in person to experience how strongly the wisdom of the true Solomon flourished in him.

Just as no argument could corner him, so no proof of a proposition, however subtle, could be offered that he would not quickly resolve through a fitting historical or allegorical interpretation.

### 5

This man, therefore, bringing forth new and old things from the good treasure of his heart, realizing how impossible it is to serve two masters (Luke 16:13), decided to renounce the world entirely so that he might cling with freer spirit to the one God, for whom to serve is to reign.

Accordingly, in accordance with the Gregorian account (*Dialogues*, book II, chapter 1), drawing back the foot that he had, as it were, placed at the entrance to the world [Col. 0409D], he broke the chains of earthly pleasures. Unable to endure delay, he fled, departed secretly, and sought Saint Maximinus in the city of Trier, where he learned that monastic life was then flourishing under the government of the venerable Father Bernard [Note: [Col. 0409D] Bernard presided over the famous monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier for only two years. He is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Poppo*, whom Bernard had as his predecessor and successor in that same monastery.].

There, having attained the long-desired fulfillment of his vow [Col. 0410A], he professed himself a monk. Clothed with the six wings of the Seraphim, he rejoiced to contemplate with the calm gaze of his mind God supported upon the lofty throne of glory.

Lest this expression seem improperly used, let the reader know that Roman authority decreed [Note: [Col. 0409D] This is the decree of Pope Boniface IV promulgated in the Roman council in the year 610; see Labbe’s volume V of the councils.] that the habit of that order signifies six wings: two by which the height of the whole body is covered; two by which the breadth of the arms is covered; and two upper wings joined to one another as a covering for the head.

Since the holy authority of earlier generations established this, posterity cannot refute it by any argument, especially since the appearance of the same habit seems in every respect to bear the form of the cross.

Blessed Wolphelmus, like another Paul or Anthony, not only assumed this cross outwardly but also bound it indissolubly to the inner man [Col. 0410B]. Freed from the burden of the world, he followed the footsteps of Christ, who draws all things to himself with hands extended upon the wood of his exaltation.

### 6

Meanwhile the people of Cologne, who could not endure lightly being deprived of a man of such holiness, at last heard that he had been sought and was devoting himself at Trier to an angelic way of life. After searching everywhere, they at last learned that he was devoting himself at Trier to an angelic way of life, and conferred among themselves about how they might reclaim him.

They approached Hermann [Note: [Col. 0409D] This was Hermann, son of Ezzo, count palatine and founder of the monastery of Brunwiller, who presided over the Church of Cologne from 1036 to 1055.], who in those days was driving the chariot of God at Cologne. They openly explained their desire to him and, with piously severe indignation, cried out against him: Why did he not reclaim the distinguished man, transferred elsewhere, who belonged to their city?

At that time one could see the leading citizens of the toga-clad city lamenting the departure of their own Gregory [Note: [Col. 0410D] See the *Life of Saint Gregory* by John the Deacon, book I, chapter 6.] [Col. 0410C], because the distress of the Romans at Gregory’s departure was no greater than the trouble agitating the people of Cologne in his absence.

Nor was this unjust. For just as Gregory, making his conduct correspond to his name through good works, watched over his own salvation and that of his neighbors, so Wolphelmus, carrying out works of faith, was worthy of the love and veneration of everyone.

The archbishop, in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man, “He who is feared by many must necessarily fear many,” hastened to yield to the importunities of his subjects. But, suspecting that the people of Trier would be reluctant to return a man of such praiseworthy life, he judged that Wolphelmus should be reclaimed by issuing a summons in the hearing of the whole Church.

### 7

At that time, among the leading figures of the present kingdom of heaven, there stood Henry, abbot of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon [Col. 0410D] [Note: [Col. 0410D] Gelenius says that he was the sixth abbot of that place and records that he departed this life in 1066, on 7 November, although his deposition is noted as occurring on 27 August in the catalogue of the abbots of Gladbach, as Gelenius himself attests. Wolphelmus perhaps became head of the same monastery in the following year.]. He was the uncle of the man mentioned above and often to be mentioned again.

He gladly accepted the recall of his dearest kinsman, but was unable to bear it with equanimity. He sought the bishop’s presence and explained what he thought ought to be done.

The bishop, anxious to avoid appearing to disregard sound counsel, quickly sent to Trier letters sealed with the impression of his seal [Col. 0411A], addressed to Father Bernard, under whose government Wolphelmus was living.

Bernard, reflecting that it made no difference whether he had snatched another’s sheep from the hand of its shepherd or tried to retain it against the shepherd’s will, humbly consented to so important a legation, although he did not surrender so great an ornament of his flock without profound sorrow.

The young man, who ardently desired the monastic life, was thus subjected to the force of the people of Cologne and led into the presence of his bishop. The bishop received him as a son, with the affection due to a father, and, because of the habit of angelic dignity that he had assumed, entrusted him to the care of his uncle Henry.

When Henry saw that Wolphelmus remained devoted to his accustomed solitude and disliked the crowds of those who flocked from everywhere to hear and see him [Col. 0411B], he led him out of the city and placed him over a certain abbey under his jurisdiction, named Gladbach.

No one who believes the accounts of those who came before can doubt how vigorously he devoted the care of his prudence to its interests.

### 8

Meanwhile this same man of God, whose spirit was advancing beyond desire for earthly things and was hastening, swift even without the body, toward the fellowship of the citizens above (Horace, *Epistles* I.12.13), undertook the pilgrimage that he had long contemplated and set out for Rome to fulfill his vows of prayer at the shrine of the apostles.

Although, wherever he was, he had been accustomed to offer the one sacrifice of our salvation each day, he did not wish to abandon this practice even while traveling. The delay of the journey did not seem burdensome, since it was undertaken solely out of love for the heavenly homeland [Col. 0411C].

It happened, however, that some companions on that pilgrimage, sighing in human fashion for the sweet fields of their native soil, left him behind with a few necessary companions, as though by doing so they would have a quicker journey and return.

But they struggled in vain against the Apostle’s judgment, who says that every [progress] belongs not to the one who wills or runs but to God, who has mercy (Romans 9:16). Thus, by God’s hidden will, the holy man’s delay advanced, and their haste was delayed, so that all of them arrived together at the same hour.

For the travelers, who had gained a head start, had not yet entered the threshold of the apostles when the man of God, following behind, pressed upon their footsteps. He showed by deeds rather than words that no human being possesses his path.

Amazed at God’s omnipotence, which they had experienced in this event, they completed their pilgrimage and returned to their own places, from that time intending to hold the man of God in a place worthy of reverence.

### 9

[Col. 0411D] When Hermann, the successor of Pelegrinus, had been removed from life and from the insignia of the pontificate, Anno, archbishop of blessed memory, was substituted in his place with the equal consent of the people of Cologne.

Since Anno, like a great priest in his days, wished to please God and burned with a wondrous love of religion, he devoted no small effort to constructing monasteries, gathering together from every direction those who sought to imitate the law of God for residence in them.

He crowned the other monuments of his pious solicitude with the construction of the monastery of Siegburg [Col. 0412A], and, having learned of the man’s holiness, took care to place the aforementioned man over it.

But when he saw that a man devoted to divine contemplation was entirely inexperienced in the active life, which was absolutely necessary for such beginnings, he led him to a place more suited to his solitude.

Nearby was the abbey of Brunwiller. Since it had been deprived of a pastor, he entrusted its care to the providence of the holy man, who could easily fulfill it without abandoning his purpose.

### 10

In those days France was troubled by Berengarius of Tours, who asserted that the Eucharist we receive at the altar is not truly the body and blood of Christ.

Consequently, many people disputed against him and on his behalf, both orally and in writing. Against him there also survives a letter of this most blessed man [Col. 0412B], addressed to a certain Meginhard, abbot of Gladbach, firmly supported everywhere by an assertion of the truth. Like a son, Meginhard consulted his father in writing concerning the definition of this question.

Although it would be lengthy to append the letter, we have nevertheless considered it appropriate, out of concern for the usefulness of readers, to insert it into the present little work, so that, once transmitted to the knowledge of posterity, the sincerity of his faith may be recognized from it and the faithful may beware of becoming entangled in errors of this kind.

The form or text of the letter is as follows:

## Letter of Saint Wolphelmus on the Sacrament of the Eucharist, Against the Errors of Berengarius

### 11

> “Wolphelmus, abbot by the grace of God, sends greetings to his fellow abbot Meginhard.
>
> Through faith and humility you have more abundantly amassed from heaven the milk of spiritual teaching which you requested from me [Col. 0412C]. Through faith, because you believe that almighty God can work in me what is not in me; through humility, because, though merits and wisdom are lacking, you do not shrink from honoring in me gray hair and the dignity of the order.
>
> How fitting it is that, while what intoxicates is harmful, you should desire as a remedy that which sobers. There is, however, a certain intoxication that is harmful: the heresy of Berengarius. Let us avoid the danger of that intoxication and draw near to breasts better than wine.
>
> And now, with Christ’s help, so that we may be able to destroy the assertion that he seeks to establish—that Christ did not enter to the disciples through closed doors after the resurrection—let the Gospel of John, flowing from the breasts of Mother Church, nourish us [Col. 0412D]:
>
> ‘When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered, Jesus stood in the midst’ (John 20:19).
>
> A little farther on:
>
> ‘After eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them; Jesus came, the doors being closed, and stood in the midst’ (ibid., 26).
>
> Behold: between Berengarius, who says that the Lord did not enter through closed doors [Note: [Col. 0411] Thus Guitmundus, book III; hence correct what we said in the observations, no. 2.], and John, who says that he did enter, there is a dispute. The victor is he to whom, as we know, the whole Church gives its applause when he says that his testimony is true.
>
> For if the Gentiles, when they close their books, applaud those whom they judge worthy of acceptance, [Col. 0413A] much more truly does the Church bear witness to this Gospel (John 21:24) on whose behalf, before it was written, she offered prayers and fasting.
>
> Let Berengarius therefore know that these things are sufficient for him, since, because they come from God, no human being can contradict them.
>
> Henceforth, with the Lord’s help, I shall also come to that concerning which he speaks blasphemy in the sacrament of the Eucharist. But since Scripture teaches that one should answer a fool according to his folly (Proverbs 26:5), let us meanwhile restrain the words of the blasphemy itself and hasten to its source, so that, if the Lord grants us to block it, the corruption of this blasphemy may cease to flow from there to us.
>
> The channel of this spring is that he does not think rightly about the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. While he has bodily eyes with which to look upon the bread and wine in them, he does not apply the eyes of the mind to perceive flesh and blood in those same elements [Col. 0413B].
>
> But, to sharpen our sight and, by sharpening it, to advance until we can behold these things, let us encourage ourselves in this way to preserve the tradition of this truth, once received.
>
> If the one who said, ‘He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created’ (Psalm 32:9), made all things—if, I say, he said of this bread, ‘This is my body’ (Matthew 26:26), and of the wine, ‘This is my blood’ (ibid., 28)—then it must necessarily be so.
>
> For these mysteries alone are not separated from the other things that were made when God spoke or created when he commanded. It is one and the same God who first formed the world and then reforms his image in this sacrament [Col. 0413C].
>
> For if one person made humanity and another redeemed it, the redeemer would claim greater honor for himself. In that case God would redeem only through himself, and humanity could be redeemed only through itself, since whatever God accomplished by assuming something other than a human being would provide no lawful benefit to humanity in its redemption. Thus it is plainly established that the one and same being, God and man, is the redeemer of humanity.
>
> Therefore it must necessarily be so: whatever God says or commands cannot fail to exist.
>
> Behold, we prove this to be true by the authority of the New and Old Testaments. Berengarius adds a third to them, which we reject no less than a third Cato fallen from heaven.
>
> Come, then: after the two Testaments, this third one—and it is a third because it is alienated from them—speaks in the words of its author as follows:
>
> ‘If mice should eat the consecrated body of Christ, Christ will not therefore be in them, nor will they remain in Christ, nor will they have eternal life.’
>
> Oh, if now in the underworld there were sitting the torturer of Horace, mocking this enemy of the Church with these words:
>
> ‘The mountains will labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born!’
>
> We thought that he had been raised up among the mountains and was giving birth to something great, when, behold, we see him summoning mice from their caves to his aid [Col. 0414A].
>
> But now, breaking off this middle section of irony, let us encourage ourselves against Berengarius and on behalf of ourselves, speaking as follows:
>
> If this body of which we are speaking, after being eaten by the apostles and by all the elect—who alone eat it in such a way that Christ remains in them and they in Christ—and not by Judas and all the reprobate, into whom Satan entered after the morsel of bread, producing a very different union between Satan and the reprobate from that which exists between Christ and the elect (for nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham)—if, I say, this body, after being eaten by and joined to the elect, receives itself back to the Father sound and unharmed, living and whole, while they too have been joined to it, then much more is it gathered back into its kingdom without loss or contamination from Judas and all the reprobate, and even from mice and the other filth of the world.
>
> [Col. 0414B] For even this visible sun, created and not omnipotent, draws back to itself, without any pollution, the rays that it has sent into sewers and other filth of the world.
>
> This body, after the communion has been completed in the Catholic manner, receives itself back to the Father sound and unharmed, living and whole.
>
> For the Church of Achaea [Note: [Col. 0413D] In the encyclical letter concerning the martyrdom of Saint Andrew.] also bears witness that blessed Andrew the apostle said:
>
> ‘After all the believing people have eaten the flesh of the Lamb and drunk the blood, the Lamb who was sacrificed remains whole and alive. Although he was truly sacrificed, his flesh was truly eaten by the people, and his blood was truly drunk, nevertheless, as I have said, he remains whole, undefiled, and alive.’
>
> Therefore this body, receiving itself alive, whole, and unharmed from those to whom he is a participant as they are participants in him, gathers itself much more into its kingdom from those [who do not share in his grace] [Col. 0414C].
>
> For the present I think this is sufficient for your charity, while we see whether anything needs to be added to it. Nevertheless, I commend both what I have said and whatever I may say to your prayers and to those of all who think piously of me; for although Jerome’s slanderers are dead, I perceive that the author of this kind of slander is still alive.”

Thus this veteran soldier, armed with the weapons of justice—namely, faith, hope, and charity—standing in the Lord’s battle line, most invincibly defeated Berengarius’s unbelief in its proper place [Col. 0414D].

How great was his devotion in doing this is demonstrated by the prayers and tears he poured forth, so that the deceived might come to their senses, the Catholic faith might remain undefiled, and no corruption might cause it to deviate from the right path.

12. Having given this preliminary account, let the style now turn to describing what labors—or, if it may properly be said, what persecutions—he endured for the good of his church, Cloteno by name. How this property was bestowed upon the church and taken away from it should be briefly explained, since the nature of a matter whose origin is unknown cannot be fully understood.

The lady Richeza [Note: [Col. 0413D] She married Mizecho, king of Poland, and was the mother of Casimir, whom we discussed above. Gelenius wrote an apology for her sanctity against the Polish writers [Col. 0415D]. Her name is also inscribed in various martyrologies; on this matter see the fifth volume of the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, under 21 May.]—whose parents had built the monastery of Brunwiler from its foundations, and who emulated their faith and devotion—made the churches of God heirs to her earthly possessions, so that she might merit becoming both a possessor and heir of the heavenly kingdom. Thus she gave to blessed Peter, at Cologne, Comburg and Salevelt, with all their appurtenances; but to Saint Nicholas, at Brunwiler, the village called Cloteno, with all its revenues.

The present lord bishop Anno confirmed and authorized this donation, made in the presence of many reputable witnesses; and, so that it might remain unshaken throughout the ages, he condemned its violators and robbers to perpetual anathema. When Lady Queen Richeza paid the debt of death, and her body was being carried to be buried in the monastery of Brunwiler, as she herself had arranged while alive—for she had even designated the place of her burial there—the body was forcibly detained by order of the aforesaid archbishop Anno and buried in the church [Note: [Col. 0415D] This church still stands at Cologne. It is called Saint Mary at the Steps and is a collegiate church; concerning it, see Gelenius, Book III of *The Marvels of Cologne*. [Col. 0416D]], which he himself had built from the foundations in honor of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God. After this had been done, he bestowed the aforementioned allod of Cloteno upon that same church, despite the opposition of those to whom, in their zeal for justice, this act of violence seemed grievous to behold. At that time the prudent and most diligent man had been so surrounded by the counsels of evil men that his mind could not suddenly be recalled from what it had begun—especially since, even then, the affairs of the kingdom were arranged at his command.

After these things had been done, when the hour of his death was already approaching, he began to be greatly distressed by the grievous burden of illness.
