Then blessed Wolphelmus visited him, and, introducing a mention of this matter amid words of consolation, admonished him with pious concern to atone for this offense and remove this injustice. He added that, unless he changed what he had done by making restitution, a peril destructive to his soul threatened him.

Since he was a man of open and noble mind, he kindly accepted the admonition, knowing him to be a just and holy man. He humbly commended himself to his prayers, promising that shortly he would either return the same property or restore another in exchange for it. The servant of the Lord, cheered by these promises, returned joyfully to his own place. But, alas, things turned out otherwise than he had promised: overtaken by premature death, he died and left unfinished in the midst of his life what he had promised. Therefore, what we have learned from our predecessors—namely, from the contemporaries or disciples of the most blessed man—we have faithfully arranged in writing. Let us now relate, in the order of his deeds, what was done in our own time and what we ourselves witnessed.

13. After the death of the venerable archbishop Anno, lord Hildolphus obtained the insignia of the episcopate, not without injury to the people of Cologne. The venerable Father repeatedly appealed to him concerning this same matter. Forewarned by the congregation of the aforesaid place, Hildolphus replied that he would in no way take away from the holy Mother of God what a man of such great merit had bestowed upon her out of his devotion.

Then, seeing that he was making no progress with the archbishop, the man of God sought through his envoys to approach the royal majesty and to proclaim the whole sequence of what had been done. King Henry IV, later Augustus of the Romans, who at that time was vigorously governing the monarchy of the kingdom, upon learning of this complaint, promised that he would provide every assistance. He declared that he took the deed gravely amiss and would never, so long as he lived, permit it to stand.

He also perceived that the reputation for goodness of the lord archbishop Anno could be considerably obscured by this transgression of law and justice. Remembering his old friendship with the man—for he had been brought up and nurtured by him—he ordered lord Hildolphus [Col. 0416B], Anno’s successor, to restore Cloteno as quickly as possible to the monastery of Brunwiler. But when Hildolphus gave no definite answer and instead bought time by postponing the matter from day to day, the envoys returned, having not obtained what they desired but rather been disappointed in their hope. Then the man of God, deprived of every human counsel, wavered uncertainly, wondering what he should do and where he should turn; but he sought help and advice from him alone who knows how to assist in dangers and necessities.

14. Then it came into his mind that nothing would be more effective or more prudent than to appeal in this matter to the pontiff of the apostolic see. Made more courageous by this inspiration, he quickly dispatched envoys to the pope, who happened at that time to be staying in the regions bordering the Alps. When they had fully explained before the leading members of the senate and the judges of the Roman Church [Col. 0416C] everything that the archbishop Anno had repeatedly done concerning the aforementioned Cloteno, amazement, together with no small wonder, seized the minds and hearts of all.

Then lord Pope Hildebrand, also called Gregory, by the authority of blessed Peter the Apostle, announced in his letters [Note: [Col. 0416D] These letters are not found among the Gregorian letters preserved in his *Register*.] to lord Hildolphus, Anno’s successor, that he must no longer tolerate Cloteno, which had been violently taken away from the Church of Brunwiler, remaining without restitution. “God,” he said, “does not need anything offered to him from injustice; for, as we read, sacrifices taken by robbery are made to him as though someone were slaughtering a son in his father’s presence” (Ecclus. 34:24).

“We acknowledge our brother Anno, the archbishop, to have been the author of many good works; nevertheless, in this matter he cannot at all be defended as having done no wrong, since what he seized from blessed Nicholas he judged to be a pleasing holocaust to the holy Mother of God. The Lord says through the prophet: ‘For I am the Lord, who love judgment and hate robbery in a burnt offering’ (Isa. 61:8). Nor may the faithful believe that the mother differs from the will of the Son, since it is entirely clear that the same things are proper and common to both: that they will the same things and reject the same things.

“But you, lest by defending injustice you appear to offend God, remove from your midst what Bishop Anno, otherwise a good man, committed here through bad counsel—lest it become both a diminution of his crown and an occasion of guilt for you.”

15. When these paternal admonitions had been received from the authority of the apostolic see, the spirit of the aforesaid pontiff Hildolphus was driven more toward fury than summoned to justice or mercy. At last he summoned the leading men of the Church of Cologne, complaining that he had been defamed and accused before the apostolic pontiff by the man of God.

Then the very gentle man humbly resisted these charges: “Let the evidence of the accusation, my lord, be brought forward, if you please. If I cannot clear myself of what you accuse me of, only then may I rightly be convicted of deserving punishment.”

The bishop, holding the apostolic lord’s letter in his hands, presented it for public reading, thinking that its contents would arm everyone against the servant of God in opposition. When it had been read, many agreed that nothing had been done deserving offense. But a certain Bezelinus, custodian of the house [i.e. the cathedral church] of blessed Peter the Apostle, together with others whose purpose was rather to disturb the matter than to decide it fairly, since they could find nothing else to allege, asserted that the pope ought not to have been approached concerning this affair without their advice.

Although the servant of the Lord could easily have refuted this objection, they insulted and calumniated him out of hatred for the increasingly furious bishop rather than through just judgment. They also assailed him with abuse and reproaches, in a manner unworthy of a man deserving such reverence, and finally threatened, with dreadful oaths, to take away the staff of pastoral care from him.

Then the blessed man, most patient amid insults, strengthened by the virtue of steadfastness and stripped of fear, answered the efforts of his adversaries without trembling—for the mind of the just, which was troubled by no consciousness of guilt, did not know how to be afraid:

“With divine mercy accompanying us, we do not fear incurring prejudice here today, since we bear a pure conscience, entirely innocent of every accusation. This saying appears to be fulfilled where it is written: ‘The just man is confident as a lion’ (Prov. 28:1).”

While the man filled with God spoke these and similar words most powerfully, all his rivals marveled at the grace of his speech and the steadfastness of his mind. As though a kind of night and darkness had been poured into their minds, they wavered uncertainly, wondering what they should do and where they should turn. They grieved that their labor had been expended in vain, finding no way by deed or word to seize him.

16. In the midst of these disturbances and pressures of anguish, two men from among the leading citizens especially favored the blessed man: Bertulfus, a worthy man and provost of the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle, and a certain Wigmannus of Heversbach, a military and noble man, also distinguished for eloquence. These two, standing between him and his adversaries, like the Maccabee once directed from heaven, did not hesitate to oppose injustice in defense of justice; so much so that neither threats nor terrors could shake them, nor any gift induce them to abandon their purpose.

They therefore pressed the matter manfully on the authority of the apostolic mandate, requesting that judgment be rendered for the Church of Brunwiler according to the command and commission of the apostolic pontiff. The bishop, greatly exasperated by their words and insistence, said with heavy indignation: “Take Cloteno for yourselves. It will be my task both to avenge my injury and to recover the more valuable things given in exchange for Cloteno.” Thus the word was snatched from his mouth, and envoys were dispatched with haste to reclaim the same property.

17. After these things had been done, the bishop ordered the man of God to meet him at the castle of Nussium [Note: [Col. 0417] Elsewhere called Novesium, a city under the jurisdiction of the archbishop, commonly called Neuss.], intending by every means that, with no helper or defender standing in his way, he might more easily depose him as he wished. But “there is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30).

As long as this adversity continued, the brothers did not cease to beseech the Lord by the devotional recitation of the seven psalms and the litany, asking that he grant them to find joy from sorrow and gladness from tribulation. The man of God, knowing that secure defense cannot be established through human beings, since the Psalmist says, “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. 117:19), trusting in the Lord’s help, undertook cheerfully and joyfully the journey to which he had been ordered.

When he reached the place, he began to commend himself to God with still greater devotion through works of piety and mercy, after gathering around him a considerable crowd of poor people. While they were seated in the upper room of a certain house, and the man of God was busily moving about, providing what was necessary for his companions, the upper room suddenly collapsed. The entire crowd, together with the man of God, fell into the underground cellar. A substantial part of the house immediately followed and crushed them, but by God’s providence, through the merits of his servant, it injured no one.

The citizens, roused by the crash of so great a noise, quickly rushed from every side and, with great astonishment, drew out alive those whom they had believed already to have perished. One man, who had fallen and been crushed more dangerously than the others, was mourned by everyone as though he were already dead; yet when he was brought out, no part of his body was found to be injured.

The cupbearer of the man of God, named Godecho, was also at that very moment holding two earthen vessels filled with wine in his hands and fell together with the collapsing structure. But, wonderful to say, he suffered no loss—neither of himself, nor of the vessels, nor of the wine. God’s mercy was pleased to display this miraculous event for the reason that it might be revealed to mortals how great the merit of this holy man was in God’s sight.

But the bishop who had compelled him to come was, as is believed, restrained by divine intervention and was then unable to oppose him in any way. Divine providence acted in this wondrous manner toward its servant so that he whom it had determined to magnify by so great a prodigy would not be crushed by the judgment of a mortal man.

From this point the fire of the aforesaid bishop’s fury, far from being extinguished, burned more fiercely. For although he then allowed him to depart, he nevertheless again ordered him to return to Cologne on a fixed day. Meanwhile, while the brothers were concerned for him, as we have mentioned above, in vigils and prayers, the man of God unexpectedly arrived.

What wave of eloquence, what tongue, I ask, could unfold the joy then shared by all? The humility of the flock rightly rejoiced in the presence of its shepherd, whom the Lord had glorified by the testimony of wondrous virtue.

18. At that time a certain Hartmannus [Note: [Col. 0419D] He is said to have been the fifth abbot of this place. Concerning the abbey of Deutz, built near Cologne by blessed Heribert, see Gelenius, *Cologne*, Book III, *Syntagma* 14.] the abbot of Deutz, having given himself over to sleep one night, saw a dream that was certainly a prophecy of future events.

In his vision he saw a man of remarkable appearance and reverend countenance, decently adorned with episcopal vestments, proceeding from the Church of Brunwiler and directing his journey toward Cologne. He saw blessed Wolphelmus the abbot following immediately behind him with a company of brothers, repeatedly chanting the seven psalms with the litanies.

When they reached the doors of the chamber in which the bishop was resting, the locked doors were struck with the staff of the one who went before and opened more quickly than words can tell. Once they had been admitted in this manner, the leader approached the bed of the reclining man and demanded with grave severity why he had rashly presumed to undertake such actions against him.

When he had finished speaking, he struck him heavily on the crown of the head with the staff he carried, in punishment for the injury. The abbot awoke from sleep in terror and made the man of God certain of divine protection and of the consolation of blessed Nicholas.

The dream was not altogether false or meaningless, since what the brothers had been doing in psalms and litanies the Lord had deemed worthy to reveal to him in a vision. The occurrence of the deed also supplied firm confirmation of the vision. For at the very moment when the abbot saw the bishop being struck, the bishop felt himself afflicted by illness.

Thus, in this manner, its hostile intention was divinely repelled and its effort frustrated. As the illness grew stronger, the bishop died a few days later, and Seguinus, a pious man, obtained the episcopal chair. Let it suffice to have recalled these matters; now let the present section turn to describing the subsequent deeds of the man of God.

19. This servant of the Lord, forgetting what lay behind and stretching forward with all his strength toward what lay ahead, following the example of the prophet David, who says, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8), undertook to adorn the house of God with every variety of beauty. Because he conceived this with the most devoted mind, he completed it with wondrous effect.

In brief, to touch upon everything summarily: through his diligence or in his time, the Church of Brunwiler enhanced its condition inside and out by varied ornamental painting and construction, and also by the beauty of mosaic work. Moreover, he expressed the subject of each work in outstanding verses, so that the fullness of its content might be clear to anyone who inquired.

It is also worth mentioning that every year the man of God had the pages of the New and Old Testaments read through in their entirety. Since the four books of the Gospels could not suitably be completed in the same place or order as the others, he decreed that, at the four recurring seasons of the year, each of the four books should be recited by a separate deacon in one of the four wings of the cloister.

The purpose or devotional intention behind this arrangement is clear from the verses he composed below on both Testaments. In them, he attaches a significant reason of usefulness to the completion of both each year. He also touches upon many necessary matters: at one point decently changing the persons in his address, at another proclaiming the salvation of the elect through blows, at another commending the sweet taste of the Scriptures, and finally declaring the healing of the human race through the twofold nature in Christ.

We have given this preliminary account so that, when the reader comes to such passages, he may proceed without hesitation, remembering that he has already learned what follows:

20. Thus widely extended is ecclesiastical custom:

It exercises itself in the two Testaments of the Almighty,

So that it may read both, and complete both every year,

Just as the hymn is brought to an end in the weekly psalter.

But while the appointed order of singing stands on one side,

And that of reading on the other,

Let a preface never be absent that explains the benefit of the reading—

A key by which the threshold is opened to every volume—

So that, once admitted, it may disclose what the abyss cries out to the abyss.

The grace of this practice granted that the clergy be admitted,

Who thereby prepare instruction for the peoples through this ministry.

Yet he does not reveal every inner secret equally to all;

Nevertheless, no one meanwhile refuses the inner things.

Here an angel suspends the sword that strikes.

The blow of the thunderbolt, though it falls more deeply, does not injure;

Neither the rushing fire nor the dreadful face of the demon:

Fierce wrath departs from captive minds.

The vast plague of sickness, which often comes upon the world,

Either does not approach or, if it does, soon departs through prayer.

The Father wills that his chosen sons be prepared

To be touched by blows and afflicted by passing punishments,

By which they are to be frightened away from the harmful covenant of the world.

Yet God does not withdraw the use of these gifts;

Rather, through blows he proves himself to be their Father.

If this lawful rite has been firmly established for them,

So that psalmody and reading are performed as we have said,

Its usefulness is evident outwardly, but a higher usefulness lies hidden within.

The one who has been introduced to this fruit will taste its gifts—

The Lord grants him a mind capable of tasting

The fruit’s greater sweetness than the tongue can reveal.

Nor will there be anyone who can express this taste in writing:

The one who tastes knows better how sweet the grace is,

Which the treasury of the sacred Scriptures preserves

And wishes to diffuse throughout the regions of the world,

So that the human race may be healed by this medicine—

The medicine accomplished by the joining of two natures,

Since from one side God the Father begets, and from the other the unwedded Mother gives birth.

Nothing in heaven is brighter than what comes from there,

Nothing on earth brighter than what comes from here:

In what form is this twofold medicine composed?

Christ, begotten from the Father, is God;

But as man, born from the Virgin.

He is true God with the Father and also with the life-giving Spirit;

May he open to us his merciful heart when our sins have been pardoned,

While he justly examines the ages in judgment. Amen.

21. I thought it useful to insert these verses of the blessed man into this work so that, just as simpler people delight in the nourishment of straightforward prose as it proceeds, so those who are more advanced, investigating spiritual matters with greater discernment, might likewise be refreshed by their spiritual taste and fruit.

Often, when disputing and exhorting the brothers in their assembly concerning the salvation of souls, amid many proposals concerning the virtues, he usually commended the grace of almsgiving and hospitality in this manner:

“It is necessary, as it is written, to have a good testimony from those who are outside (1 Tim. 3:7), and not to neglect hospitality; for we read that some have pleased God by receiving angels as guests. Therefore, brothers, I strongly urge you to devote care to receiving the poor and guests, because whatever is faithfully bestowed upon them is undoubtedly bestowed upon Christ, who wishes to be received in the poor and welcomed in the guest.

“For this reason I have especially presented the grace of hospitality and almsgiving as necessary (Heb. 13:2), because I perceive that neither this place can be extended nor its inhabitants maintained except through almsgiving and constant prayers.

“But, dearest ones, when you see some spark of goodness beginning to glow within you, do not, I beg you, ascribe it to your own merits; for, as it is written: ‘It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy’ (Rom. 9:16). For almighty God anticipates us by inspiring us to will what is good, and follows after us by helping us to accomplish it. Our effort would otherwise be empty unless divine power cooperated with it.

“Thus, when preceding grace and following good will work together, what is the Creator’s gift becomes our merit.”

By frequently irrigating the brothers’ hearts with these and similar exhortations, he urged them to pursue piety. Diligently watching over the winning of souls, he strove to say nothing in words that he did not reinforce by examples, lest the purity of his life wholly contradict his speech.

In this way he avoided the company of hypocrites, who possess the words of holy men but not their life; who beget people through their speech but do not nourish them by their example; and who build them up by their words but destroy them by their conduct and life. The blessed man persuaded not only with his tongue, but also showed through his examples, conduct, and life whatever almighty God had commanded his faithful to observe.

22. He had always been especially concerned for the poor. Accordingly, with prudent provision, he added tithes and vineyards to the hospice, so that the necessities of their food might be supplied without payment.

He was continually at war with vices, because his mind, raised toward the virtues, was not inclined toward vice. He so detested greed and avarice, the root of all evils, that apart from the common and simple fare, he took for himself absolutely nothing that was special or luxurious.

Rather, through an affection for piety, he strove to be loved than feared; hence he unquestionably rejected boastfulness and arrogance. Wishing to disparage no one and hate no one, after extinguishing the torches of anger and envy, he chose to love everyone with brotherly affection.

Always cheerful, always joyful, he displayed in the cheerfulness of his face how sincere and pure his affection was toward God and humanity. Although he was continually suspended in contemplation, he was nevertheless near to each person through compassion; his mind did not turn away from contemplation while piety burned in action.

Thus, in the likeness of the heavenly living creatures, having eyes before and behind, he was bound by the love of both virtues: while he appeared intent upon either one, he nevertheless lacked none of the other’s proper quality.

23. Such was his conduct. Possessing nothing dearer than God, he preferred God above all things, loving him with every affection of heart and mind, and every Christian as himself. He preserved innocence in simplicity, concord in charity, moderation in humility, and discipline in the strictness of correction.

Toward those who acted well, he did not wish to appear as a superior, but as an equal and companion; against the vices of wrongdoers, however, he exercised the privilege of his office.

Who could express in words how carefully he sought to temper all his judgments with discretion, or to moderate them with justice? Whenever correction had to be imposed upon someone for an offense, he first descended into himself, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). He mourned another’s offense as though it were his own guilt.

Thus the mind of his God-devoted heart cultivated itself in every kind of piety, striving to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15)—a truly gentle and just man, who became all things to all people.

For whose sorrow did he not feel sorrow? Who, at the sight of him, did not change grief into joy? Who, inflamed with anger, was not calmed by his speech? Who, troubled by an evil thought, was not healed by him as physician? Who sought consolation and did not find it? Who could express the force of his words or the efficacy of his speech? Who could unfold his piety or narrate his charity?

He had been so deeply rooted and founded in charity that, although he lacked none of the virtues, he was nevertheless its special cultivator.

He also kept firmly in mind that the more numerous his subjects, the greater were the cares with which he was occupied [pluribus. ED.]. He strove in every way to please God through contemplation and to administer the concerns of external affairs solemnly [more probably: diligently] through suitable persons [personas].

Thus, freely devoting himself to the Lord as he desired, he watched over the flock in both respects: within, through his own vigilance; outwardly, through appropriate provision. Since he possessed remarkable gentleness and discretion, knowing that strictness, if it exceeds due measure, gives birth to cruelty, while excessive compassion produces the dissolution of discipline, he exercised such discretion between the two that neither indiscriminate severity became an occasion for his subjects to refuse labor, nor excessive compassion became an immoderate relaxation of discipline.

Following the example of the holy Fathers, he ordered the steps of his actions in such a way that he never allowed his conduct to flow beyond the bounds of justice.

24. For this reason I would rightly call such a man happy and blessed: he firmly maintained the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline, yet never abandoned discretion, the mother of the virtues.

To summarize his conduct and actions: his life was praiseworthy; his speech discerning and useful; his counsel provident; his conduct adorned; his manner of address sweet as honey; he was merciful and kind, ready to forgive and slow to anger.

Through his pious affection he accommodated himself to the needs of all the wretched. In accordance with blessed Job, he was a father to the poor (Job 29:16), a consoler of the sorrowful, and a helper of orphans. He did not despise the needy, nor send the poor away without clothing; he supported some with words of consolation and raised others up through compassionate assistance.

From childhood he learned to fear God; for mercy had grown with him from the womb. His heart’s ark, continually filled with good will, never left his hand empty of a gift. He secured for himself the patronage of the poor before God, making friends for himself from unrighteous wealth, so that they might one day receive him into the eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9).

But lest he appear to love the world more than was right, he used the world only for necessity, not for excessive pleasure. Excluding harmful delights from his mind, he imitated the apostolic teachings: to chastise the body and bring it into servitude (1 Cor. 9), so that, weakened by heavenly disciplines, it might become a vessel fit for sanctification.

For he knew that the mind could not enjoy legitimate rule unless the movements of the flesh had been completely subdued. Finally, in this ritual of sacrifice, he presented himself within the inner sanctuary of his heart as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God (Rom. 12:1), since each day, through the grace of compunction, he slaughtered himself as a holocaust together with the sacred mysteries of Christ’s body and blood.

25. This most blessed man had a full brother named Frumold [Note: [Col. 0423D] Gelenius enumerates Frumold and Oswenna among the other saints in his Cologne calendar, though we do not think that they are entered in the catalogue of saints.], and two sisters who were nuns. One of them, named Oswenda, was a woman of remarkable simplicity and innocence; the other, called Berta, excelled greatly in knowledge of letters.

Berta wrote the life of blessed Adelheid, the first abbess of Vilec, in a very elegant style, and left in that same place abundant fruit of her religious devotion and learning [Note: [Col. 0423D] You will find this Life in Volume I of the present *Age*. [Col. 0424D]].

It is pleasing to relate a miracle performed in our own time concerning her aforementioned sister, Lady Oswenda—a miracle unquestionably worthy of all praise, remembrance, and veneration.

A certain brother from the monastery of Brunwiler, named Udo, was suffering from such a grievous illness that everyone was compelled to despair of his recovery. His entire body swelled miserably, the health of all his limbs was lost, and he appeared more like a trunk than a human body. Moreover, what is usually the clearest sign of death, no remedy applied to him was of any avail. The Lord, as we believe, wished to demonstrate that the more serious the illness, the more powerful the Almighty must be believed to be as physician.

When arrangements were being made only for his funeral, he was seized by a gentle sleep. In a dream he saw Lady Oswenda, already possessing the light of immortality, standing beside him. Moved by compassion, she stroked his entire body with her hand and eased the force of his pain. She then entered the oratory adjoining the sick man’s bed, knelt three times, and prayed. After making the sign of the holy cross over the sick man, she disappeared.

At once divine power followed: after a few days he recovered and regained complete health. Thus, as the vision revealed, there could be no doubt that he had been rescued from the brink of death through the intercession of her merits.

His illness had been so monstrous that from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him. Yet, after the entire skin of his body had been shed—as though he had stripped off the old man—he was clothed with new skin together with restored health.

26. But the aforementioned full brother of blessed Wolphelmus, namely lord Frumoldus, cast off the arms of earthly warfare and refused to become entangled in them any longer, so that he might serve God more freely.

Taking up the discipline of pilgrimage, lest he become an exile from his heavenly homeland, he chose throughout the remainder of his life to exile himself far and wide in order to obtain the patronage of the saints. He was content with only one servant as his companion; yet in return, like another Martin, he often used to minister to that servant himself.

Because he continually practiced this form of divine propitiation with bare feet, we often saw his soles so bruised that he was entirely unable to tolerate footwear.

He also had the solemn custom, whenever he attended the divine office in church, of avoiding every kind of conversation. Instead, whether standing or prostrate on the ground in prayer, he attained such an abundance of tears that he left the pavement wet, as though it had been drenched by rain.

Possessing this grace of compunction through divine mercy, he appointed it guardian of his other virtues; for no sin could ever dominate a man whose mind was assiduously moved to compunction and lamentation.

Who would doubt that he was a most faithful servant of the Lord, when the performance of his commandments provides such evident testimony through his merits? Although he completed his course in the peace of the present life, he nevertheless fulfilled martyrdom, striving to keep the world crucified while he crucified his flesh with its vices and desires. Faithfully following the Lord, he became a pilgrim in the world.

Joined, as we trust, to the assemblies of the just, he lies buried in the church of his own possession. Let these few things that have been brought forward suffice as testimony to the sanctity of the most blessed Fathers Wolphelmus and Frumold, brothers.

27. At that time there was a certain man, noble by birth but nobler in character, named Burchard, of prefectural rank and also exceedingly powerful in arms. He was the brother of the most illustrious man Einehard, [Col. 0425A] bishop of Würzburg. [Note: [Col. 0425D] He is commonly called Ainhard. He succeeded Meginhard in 1088 and administered the see of Würzburg with distinction through the most difficult circumstances until 1104. Bruschio calls him Count of Rotenburg on the Tauber and says that he was the son of Count Richard.]

This man was not a deaf hearer of the Gospel’s words: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21). After abandoning everything he seemed to possess temporally, he had Kanerberch, a fortified castle belonging to him, consecrated to the Lord as a place of prayer. Thus, although he could have been rich in the world, he chose to be poor with Christ. Clad in the garb of a commoner, he visited the places of the saints, diligently seeking the conversation of God’s servants.

In this way he was brought to the attention of God’s servant Wolphelm and was held by him in the highest honor. Just as Jonathan’s soul was once bound to David’s soul, so the love of God joined the two of them. Because of this mutual affection, he was accustomed to visit him frequently [Col. 0425B] and rejoiced to receive from his mouth the sweetest honeycombs of divine speech. He marveled exceedingly at the abundance of divine eloquence granted to him from heaven, so that, just as a stream flows from an overflowing river, divine speech seemed to pour from that honeyed throat.

But what wonder was it that a mind always fixed on heavenly things preferred to discuss divine matters with such subtlety? To continue the account: wishing to reveal to his devout disciple how great a perfection lay hidden in the master, the Lord disclosed to him the following vision during the silence of night.

He saw the One whom Tartarus fears, the abyss worships, the hosts of heaven adore, and whom the ranks of the angels desire to behold. This One, I say, he saw placed in a bath, where He was reverently tended, washed, and wiped by the hands and ministry of the blessed Wolphelm; and there the twelve apostles standing around seemed to assist the one who was ministering. [Col. 0425C]

That most distinguished man, therefore, disclosed the vision shown to him from heaven to God’s man through a monk named Meginhard, a brother who was especially close to him. With a discerning mind, Wolphelm examined the meaning of the dream and began carefully to investigate what the vision seemed to signify. He clearly understood that he was being admonished to preserve vigilantly the course of his good purpose, and to minister to Christ in all His members, according to His own saying: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:45).

The man beloved of God rejoiced that he had pleased the supreme Head of the elect by works of mercy. But wishing to carry out the vision in action, he prepared a bath in the Lord’s place for a needy man, performing in each detail the services required by the order of the vision. When these had been properly completed, the man emerged clean and healthy in his whole body and was completely clothed in new garments.

From that time he merited such grace that he also became worthy to perform miraculous works.

28. At that same time there was a woman in the territory of Brunwiller, named Golda, who lamented that she had fallen into blindness of both eyes. [Col. 0426A] When it pleased the Illuminator of all things to come to her aid through the merits of His servant, she experienced the following vision during the silence of night.

While she seemed to be lightly sleeping, she saw herself assisting God’s man Wolphelm as he celebrated the solemnities of Mass. After the completion of the Mass, she washed her eyes with the water from his handwashing and, after wiping them with the hems of his garments, received the long-desired light.

We conveyed this vision to the servant of God as he was hastening to the divine mysteries, humbly bringing it to his attention and asking him to show compassion toward the poor woman. He did not consent, saying that this was not a merit belonging to him and that dreams, which often deceive, should not lightly be believed. “But,” he said, “if this vision is genuine, may the Lord deign to reveal it a second and a third time.”

Accordingly, while he remained in fasting and prayer with a contrite and humbled heart, [Col. 0426B] the same vision that had first appeared to the woman appeared a second and a third time. What more need be said? At last the Lord’s man was overcome by our persistent requests, and she was admitted secretly, after being ordered to remain outside the little church. For he had not been accustomed easily to admit women into his presence except for a definite reason.

After the solemnities of Mass had been duly completed, he washed and wiped her eyes as the vision had indicated, and she returned home seeing clearly. Then the holy man, unwilling to be lifted up by human praise because of this deed, remembering the Lord’s command by which He ordered the disciples not to disclose the manner of the vision to anyone until the time of the Resurrection had been fulfilled, strictly forbade us, while he remained alive, to reveal or disclose it for any reason or under any necessity.

29. Thus the Lord’s man, increasing from day to day in an abundance of virtues, [Col. 0426C] continually sighed for the joys of heavenly life, which his blessed spirit now rejoices to have obtained in the presence of its Lord. For as long as he lived in the body, he inhabited the world bodily but not mentally, desiring rather to fix his mind where he knew that joy would remain without end.

Therefore he could rightly say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). And also: “We have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14).

Burning with an unceasing and ardent love for the heavenly homeland, he practiced many other virtues; yet his devotion to prayer was so intense that, although he flourished in every virtue, he seemed to possess this one above all. From his constancy in prayer there also grew within him the devotion that, every year during the Lenten fast observed according to the custom of the holy and universal Church, he would visit in prayer not only the places in the surrounding region but also all the holy places throughout Cologne. [Col. 0426D]

30. Since mention of this matter has now arisen, I wish to recount a great danger—or rather, a miracle—that befell us as we were returning to Cologne from Deutz. We had gone to pray at the tomb of the blessed and glorious confessor Heribert. On our return we boarded a vessel; once released from the shore, we sailed with considerable success.

The waves had already carried us far out into the river [Col. 0427A] when suddenly an intolerable storm arose. The Rhine’s calm was shattered from its depths, and waves folding back upon themselves seemed to threaten the heads of those sitting in the vessel like towering rocks. The ship drifted this way and that on the wandering waves; now it hung upon the crest of a swell, now the wave opened up and exposed the earth between the breakers. The sailors, thrown into confusion by fear of death, could scarcely utter a sound.

When we were surrounded by such danger, I approached the man of God, who was sitting at the rear of the vessel, meditating in his customary manner on I know not what secret matter and entirely unaware of what had happened to us. I announced to him that death was threatening us on every side.

He immediately hastened to prayer and most devoutly implored the aid of the saints, adding the supplication of the Litany. [Col. 0427B] Then, frequently making the sign of the holy cross, he began to sing: “Savior of the world, save us.” He continued: “You who redeemed us through the cross and blood, assist us.”

Then, with renewed strength, he urged the men to row steadfastly, not to be shaken by any fear of death, asserting that none of them would perish by God’s providence. Encouraged by this exhortation—and since the matter was one of life for them—they courageously pressed toward the shore and manfully cleaved the waters.

Meanwhile, the pitiable cries of people of both sexes standing along the shore rose to heaven as they watched our danger from afar. What need is there to delay over the details? Caught between the boundaries of death and life, we at last drifted to a place where a multitude of ships occupied a broad inlet of the Rhine. Reaching them and passing from one vessel to another, we all escaped against hope, in accordance with the word of the man of God. [Col. 0427C]

Yet, lest anyone in any way doubt that we had been saved through his merit, the fury of the Rhine immediately made this clear by a divine sign. For as soon as that blessed man set foot outside the vessel, the waves that had shortly before been divinely held back claimed it as their prey. The ship, which previously had been so heavily laden that it could not sink, could not remain afloat once deprived of so great a protector; before our eyes it immediately disappeared beneath the water.

Thus, through the abyss of immense sorrow, the Lord bestowed upon us, through the merits of His servant, the gift of the greatest joy: He both exalted the grace of his virtues and turned away what we feared.

31. At about the same time, one day he entered an oratory in a village of the parish of Brunwiller, called Kyrchedoro, to pray with those who shared his secrets. At that time the place was falsely believed to be an oratory. But when he had prostrated himself on the ground, he learned through a revelation of the Holy Spirit that the place lacked the protection of the saints.

Rising from prayer, he went with the men who were there to the altar. After removing the covering and carefully examining everything, he found absolutely nothing—neither beneath the seal nor in the cracks of the walls—except bats’ nests and spiders’ webs. [Col. 0427D] Greatly—indeed, as was fitting, exceedingly—distressed in mind, he went without delay to the bishop of the Church of Cologne and explained to him in order what had taken place.

[Col. 0428A] The bishop sympathized with his grief and, also providing relics of the saints, sent to him a certain Hezelin, bishop of the see of Scarnensis, [Note: [Col. 0427D] Henschenius thinks that Scardonensis should be restored, since a bishopric of that name exists in Dalmatia, perhaps under whose title that bishop had been appointed—the one whom he calls the chorepiscopus of Cologne. [Col. 0428D]] instructing him, as his representative, to consecrate the aforesaid place to God, since it lay within the diocese of his bishopric, and to dedicate it to His service.

He gladly obeyed the bishop’s command. After gathering a multitude of the faithful, they dedicated the same oratory to divine worship and established two altars there: the upper one in honor of the archangel Michael, and the lower one for the veneration of the blessed confessor Martin.

In this deed, Wolphelm was plainly comparable in the proportion of his virtue to Saint Martin, who, similarly enlightened by divine revelation, freed the people from the deception of diabolical fraud by destroying an altar belonging to a robber, which was being venerated in place of a martyr’s altar. [Col. 0428B]

When these things had been duly celebrated, each returned to his own place, praising God with rejoicing.

32. I think that I should not pass over the miracle that also took place, which we saw with the testimony of all the brothers and which, as rumor has spread, is widely known everywhere.

A certain woman named Adelheidis, afflicted by various illnesses in all her limbs, was brought to the threshold of Saint Nicholas in the monastery of Brunwiller for the sake of recovering her health. She suffered from the loss of the use of all her limbs, from hidden pains in her viscera, and from unbearable tortures, so that she loathed bread of every kind of food to such a degree that she avoided not only tasting it but even touching it. [Col. 0428C]

Through the merits of Saint Nicholas she quickly recovered soundness in her limbs. Nevertheless, by God’s hidden judgment, she continued entirely to abstain from food as before.

After several years had passed, when it pleased divine mercy to release her from this illness, she experienced the following vision during the silence of the dead of night. It seemed to her that the most blessed Wolphelm had blessed a loaf of bread and that, having received it from his venerable hand, she eagerly ate it.

Trusting in the vision and knowing that greater things could be accomplished through him, she begged him in tearful words to bless bread for her. He resisted with all his strength, declaring himself unworthy to perform such a work.

Then one could see the man of God’s spirit become anxiously troubled. He wished to show mercy, but did not wish the act to be performed publicly, lest it bring him boasting and favor. Nevertheless, lest he seem to delay any longer what the divine will had ordained to be fulfilled through him, he blessed the bread that was brought, handed it to the woman, and she ate it in our presence.

Restored completely to health through the merits of the man of God, she devoted herself throughout the rest of her life to serving the needs of that church with all the greater usefulness and devotion, inasmuch as she had deserved to receive the grace of healing more abundantly and distinctly than others.

Although the Lord’s man abounded in such distinguished and exceptional virtues, his spirit never succumbed to pride. He remembered that one should not glory in the power of signs but in fellowship with the company of the elect. [Col. 0429A]

Who could recount individually the kinds of healings bestowed, by divine mercy through him, upon the sick in various places? For very often, when he visited them, health was granted to the ill; yet he absolutely refused to let this be attributed to himself.

Let these examples from the many virtues remembered from him suffice for the faithful. Now let the account turn to describing what his passing from this life was like.

33. After innumerable benefits had been accomplished through him by divine action, the merciful Lord, wishing to console the groans and sighs of His servant, who often said with the Prophet, “When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Psalm 41:3), and, “I shall be satisfied when his glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:15), was pleased to reveal to him the time of his dissolution in the following manner.

One day at midday, as he was sleeping in his customary way—not lying down but sitting—a very handsome young man appeared to him in a vision and admonished him to hasten to follow him as quickly as possible. Accompanying the one who went before him, he was led under angelic guidance to places of great beauty, green with every variety of loveliness, shining with incomparable splendor of light, and fragrant with every kind of sweetness.

There the angel showed him dwellings of various mansions, plainly promised by the Lord to the faithful. At last, the angel of great beauty and stature led him into a certain building and ordered him carefully to contemplate its adornment inside and out. He announced that this dwelling-place had been divinely destined for him.

“According to how diligently and beautifully you adorn it,” he said, “so much more joyfully and happily will you enjoy it when you receive it.” [Col. 0429C]

Thus instructed by the angelic voice concerning the happiness of everlasting glory, he awoke and separately disclosed the vision to certain brothers, adding that he would undoubtedly be dissolved from the body very soon.

They were consequently troubled in spirit in a remarkable manner. Since they had always experienced the benefits of his compassion, they were tortured by an intolerable grief at the prospect of losing him. Wishing to establish the matter with greater certainty, they marked the day, recording it together with the vision. When the cycle of the year had revolved, it happened that on that very day he was released from the prison of the flesh, on which the heavenly vision had been granted to him.

Thus it became clear that the vision had not been a fantastic delusion but a true vision, since it had so clearly indicated both the dissolution of the man of God and his heavenly dwelling.

[Col. 0429D] 34. Throughout the whole intervening year, therefore, he awaited the coming of his Lord—not sleeping negligently, but watchfully devoting himself to good works—and distributed to his fellow servants the talent entrusted to him.

The force of divine love had so pierced his heart that, even if he had wished not to speak about God, he could not remain silent. When he did this with greater urgency and fervor than usual, some began to grow weary and to listen less willingly.

Perceiving this, he did not withdraw from his good purpose. Rather, wishing them to recover their senses, he frequently repeated the Apostle’s words: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). He said this because those whom he had already brought forth by preaching he was again bringing forth with groans by reforming them. He added: “For me, indeed, it is not burdensome, but for you it is necessary” (Philippians 3:1). [Col. 0430A]

When one day he saw that he was making little progress through his paternal admonition, he conceived the Holy Spirit with his whole mind and burst forth in these words of the prophet Amos—or rather, as subsequent events proved, he himself, touched by the spirit of prophecy:

“Days will come,” he said, “says the Lord, and I will send famine upon you—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

Without doubt he knew that just as famine is the withdrawal of bodily nourishment from the flesh, so the silence or loss of divine conversation is famine for the mind.

Therefore, as though narrating future events to them as already past, he declared: “Know that, beyond all doubt, in those things in which I am now burdensome to you or arouse weariness, you will one day desire them greatly, although you will not obtain their fulfillment. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is near” (2 Timothy 4:6). [Col. 0430B]

I have thought these words should not be passed over, lest anyone believe that they were spoken by the man of God in vain, since we do not doubt that every word he uttered was either fulfilled or will certainly be fulfilled in the future.

35. Although he was already approaching the final period of his life, he in no way allowed the rigor of his purpose to weaken by living more indulgently or reducing his labor. He considered the labor of the present time insignificant compared with the recompense of the glory that was to come.

[Col. 0430C] Therefore he did not complain either about the length of time or the difficulty of the labor. Rather, adding labor to labor in every way, he strove to carry out the angelic exhortation.

When his departure was already approaching and he suddenly felt himself deprived of strength and weighed down by illness, he had the most reverend abbot of the monastery of the blessed martyr Pantaleon, a man named Herimannus, distinguished in all uprightness and religion, summoned and had himself anointed with the liquid of consecrated oil.

A few days later, at the first twilight of dawn, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, he died, entering upon the way of all flesh, and happily entered into the joy of his Lord.

[Col. 0430D] He flourished during the reign of the second Emperor Henry, who obtained the monarchy of the kingdom after the death of the third Otto, in the time of the blessed Heribert, archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne. He lived until the thirty-third year of the reign of the fourth Emperor Henry, whose father was the third Henry and whose grandfather was the Emperor Conrad.

He passed away full of days and of the fruits of every good work in the year 1091 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

When his death became known, Herimannus, [Note: [Col. 0429] Herimannus III of this name, who succeeded Sewinus in 1089 and held office until 1099.] then archbishop of Cologne, hastened with the utmost devotion to offer the service of his piety at his funeral and came eagerly to bury him.

Following his example, a crowd of religious men also gathered. Among them were especially prominent and distinguished abbots: namely, Herimannus of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Pantaleon [Col. 0431A] and Reginhardus of Siegburg, of blessed memory. Both had always honored the Lord’s servant with the greatest devotion and zeal.

When the archbishop had completed the solemnities of Mass for his venerable memory, and the sacred little body was to be placed in the tomb, he approached personally and removed the covering by which his sacred face was veiled. And behold, wonderful to relate: although he had already been dead for three days, he appeared not pale as the dead usually are but suffused with a rosy color, full of grace, and sprinkled, as it were, with tiny drops of dew-like sweat. At the sight of this splendid miracle, many wept for joy.

The bishop turned to those standing around and said: “Behold, beloved fathers, how devoted this servant of the Lord must have been, whom such and so great a grace commends through the appearance of his face.”

After the bishop had finished speaking, the body was reverently and fittingly committed to burial beside the altar of the blessed apostle Peter. [Col. 0431B]

There, through the assistance of his merits, the prayers of the faithful are heard and benefits are bestowed upon the sick, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, are honor, power, and glory throughout the endless ages of ages. Amen.

36. Having, as it were, crossed the great sea of the present history, we now breathe again as though we were already seeing the shore, since we perceive that only certain things concerning his miracles remain to be reported.

We must therefore strive to reach the harbor and complete our course. For just as clouds sometimes cover the sun, so sluggish and negligent writers often withhold knowledge of useful matters. [Col. 0431C] Let us therefore begin to recount the miracles that, after his death, were accomplished through him by divine power.

In the territory of Brunwiller, a woman named Wazela had sat down one day to work at weaving when both her hands suddenly began to be tormented by such cruel suffering that she was forced to summon the townspeople with terrible cries.

Because of the enormity of the pain, she was thought to be subject to paralysis. Her hands suddenly became so useless that she could not apply them to any task. As the illness grew increasingly severe, she fell asleep amid the hands of those supporting her, overcome by the excessive torment of pain. Then she sweetly heard the following words in a gentle voice:

“Why are you weighed down by sleep? If you wish to be free of your present suffering, rise quickly and visit the tomb of Lord Wolphelm with an offering of a candle. Through his merits you will obtain the joy of health.”

[Col. 0431D] With lively faith and ready devotion, she hastened to obey the command. She visited the tomb with a burning candle, neither distrusting the merits of the blessed Father nor hesitating to believe the words of the one who had instructed her.

When she had prostrated herself in prayer, she rose shortly afterward healed. Giving thanks to God, she departed safe and joyful.

37. A certain brother from the monastery of Brunwiller, named Heribertus, had been sent after the death of the blessed Wolphelm to the province of Dacia, [Note: [Col. 0431D] Henschenius interprets this as Denmark.] together with several other brothers for the sake of monastic religion.

[Col. 0432A] After he had stayed there for some time and his mind was already urging him to return, he set out on the journey accompanied by honorable and religious men. When they reached the sea, pirates lay in ambush and occupied the inlet of the sea day and night, so that passage was denied them for nearly nine days.

Accordingly, all of them were afflicted together by excessive anguish of heart. From the depths of their being they prayed that the Lord might deign to be present in mercy to those invoking Him. The merciful Lord did not delay the prayers of His faithful but quickly granted assistance.

During the silence of night, the blessed Wolphelm appeared three times in a vision to the aforesaid brother, commanding him to hasten the crossing on the following day. He announced that the sea would be calm and that the attack of the enemy had been restrained.

As a memorial of his deliverance, that worshiper of the Holy Trinity ordered him to pay vows of rejoicing to the Lord with three sets of three psalms. [Col. 0432B]

Thus, when fear of the enemy had been removed, they experienced no small joy because of the divine revelation and gladly entrusted themselves to the sea, since the pirates were entirely unable to harm them.

In this way they were rescued through the merits of the Lord’s servant from the storms of evils that threatened them, and they gave thanks for their divine deliverance. We learned this from the brother himself who experienced it and have related it faithfully.

38. At the same time, a certain lame man named Willemannus, from a village adjoining the place of Brunwiller, called Polheim, recovered the use of his limbs, which had long been denied him, through the intercession of the blessed Wolphelm.

During Lent, he approached the place of the tomb, burning with a desire for health. The groaning of his heart expressed the longing that drew him toward healing, and that groaning revealed the anguish of his heart.

Finally, turning to God with complete devotion, he prayed with tearful sighs that through the merits of His servant he might deserve soundness in his limbs. His hope did not deceive him, for faith provided its encouragement.

[Col. 0432C] The matter quickly made clear what kind of holiness and merit the blessed man possessed. Suddenly the tendons that had long been contracted began to extend, the channels of the veins began to fill with an infusion of life-giving blood, and the limbs that had previously been almost dead were restored to their former strength.

Why delay any longer? Sensing the divine power working within him, the man struggled to rise with a slow effort. Although his step was still unsteady, he stood upright and faithfully explained to those present what had happened around him.

Supported by their hands and led from place to place, he became known to the brothers. God was greatly praised and glorified, He who is “wonderful in his saints” (Psalm 57:36), “glorious” (Daniel 3:52), and “alone does wondrous things” (Psalm 71:18). [Col. 0432D]

As evidence of so great a miracle, his supporting staff remained suspended above the tomb of the most blessed man for a long time.

39. At another time, a similar event occurred, and I wish to relate when and how it happened.

A woman from the village of Geroldeshoven, completely crippled, was brought by her friends to the frequently mentioned place. There she devoted herself assiduously to prayer and visited the threshold of the church with particular attentiveness.

When the most sacred feast of the blessed apostle Peter, chief of the apostles, was being celebrated, [Col. 0433A] she happened to take part in those solemnities with the rest of the people. Weeping profusely and drawing long sighs, she prostrated herself before the tomb of the blessed man and complained bitterly that she was miserable and wretched, that her prayers did not deserve to be admitted and that the afflictions of her body could not be released.

But the One who once wished to delay the prayer of the Canaanite woman also wished to delay this woman’s prayer, so that the persistence of her desire might be a test of her faith. Yet because she did not doubt that she could be saved through the merits of the blessed man, but persevered in asking with faith, she deserved to obtain the result. [Col. 0434A]

Raised upright by divine power, she cried out and broke the silence of everyone with her shouts. When bone joined to bone where the bones had been separated, and the contraction of the tendons became the connection of the joints, it is not surprising that the mind of the weaker female sex was frightened.

Rising from the pavement, restored to strength, she was able to return home safely. Through such effects of miracles this blessed man truly bears witness to the world that he lives with Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0433]

THE LITTLE WORK OF THE BLESSED WOLPHELM ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE ALTAR.

(It appears above, in number 10 of the Life of Blessed Wolphelm.)

[Col. 0433]

VERSES ON THE TWO TESTAMENTS.

(Conrad also inserted these in the Life. Because of the connection by which they adhere to the text, we have likewise chosen not to publish them separately from the little work On the Sacrament of the Altar.)

AT THE END OF THE ELEVENTH CENTURY AND THE BEGINNING OF THE TWELFTH. THE CHRONICLE OF EKKEHARD OF URAUGIA, EDITED BY THE DISTINGUISHED G. WAITZ, PROFESSOR PUBLICUS OF KIEL.

[Col. 0433]

PERTZ’S PREFACE TO VOLUME VIII OF THE MONUMENTA GERMANIAE HISTORICA.

The writers published in the preceding volume, whom we saw to have transmitted universal history in the eleventh century, are now followed by Ekkehardus, Sigebertus, the annalist of Erfurt, and Saxo, who extended the same history as far as the reign of Conrad III.

First and foremost among them, and for the first time rescued from darkness, Ekkehard of Uraugia appears. When, more than twenty years ago, I was seeking a way to publish him, it happened, under a fortunate omen, that I was able to secure for our edition outstanding manuscripts, with whose aid the Annals of Emperors Henry IV and V could be restored to their integrity; also the autograph manuscript necessary for restoring the earlier part of the Chronicle, and another autograph manuscript containing the previously unknown Chronicle of the emperors.

Having thus gathered the richest materials and indicated throughout the sources from which Ekkehard had drawn, I was able to separate the manuscripts into their respective classes and present the plan and method of the new edition in our Annals, volume VII, pages 469–509.

With the way thus opened, I entrusted the completion of the edition to our Waitz, whom, after six years devoted with the greatest benefit to the Monumenta Germaniae, I am pleased to see now honor the office of public professor of history at the University of Kiel. I now present to our readers the edition completed through his tireless labor.

After the work had been printed, when I traveled to Prague in September of the previous year, a quire of an unknown manuscript written in the twelfth century first came into my hands in the Bohemian Museum. In it I was able to read the beginning of Ekkehard’s Chronicle up to approximately the time of Phoroneus. Please therefore add it to the manuscripts catalogued below on pages 14–15. [Col. 0435]

Sigebert of Gembloux, supplied with many but not sufficient resources for a new edition, found our Bethmann as his restorer. When Bethmann encountered at Brussels a manuscript formerly belonging to Gembloux, he recognized it as the autograph of Sigebert himself and of Anselm. He thereby not only laid the foundation of a genuinely new edition but also added supplements, additions, continuations, and the Chronicle of Robert of Monte, copied likewise from the autograph. From these, we trust, scholars of history, both at home and abroad, will derive very great benefit.

I published the Annals of Erfurt, contained in only a few pages, from an autograph manuscript. The Annalist of Saxony, for whom an autograph manuscript—first examined by me in Paris in 1827—provided an equal foundation, will, through Waitz’s work, with the text restored and the historical sources indicated in the margin, be used with greater benefit than has hitherto been possible for investigating the history of the eleventh and twelfth centuries.

Written at Berlin, in the Royal Library, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, 1844.

[Col. 0435]

PREFACE OF THE DISTINGUISHED G. WAITZ.

[Col. 0435A] In our own age we have seen the memory of Ekkehard, the most celebrated historian at the end of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century, almost buried in oblivion. Thus, while Herimannus, Lambertus, Marianus, Bernoldus, and Sigebertus were on everyone’s lips, few mentioned him, and even those few were not sufficiently informed about who he was or what he had written. We trust that, now that his historical works have been published, this will no longer be possible.

For who, at the first sight of this volume, will not recognize its author as a most serious writer, who composed several works in a few years and illuminated with extensive commentaries both ancient history and the history of his own time?

Perhaps the reader will then recall that, in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers, attributed under the name of the anonymous writer of Melk, Ekkehard is praised [Note: [Col. 0435B] Chapter 104.] [Col. 0435B] as “a very learned and religious man, who nevertheless also writes his own chronicle,” and that Helmold refers back to him [Note: [Col. 0435B] Book I, chapter 40, in Leibniz, volume II, page 574.] as an author who narrated the history of Henry IV and Henry V. [Note: [Col. 0435B] From these passages and from Trithemius’s testimony, Bosius (see Struvius, Selected Observations Relating to Universal Literary History, volume I, page 318) and Baluzius (Letter to Schilter, Archiv, volume I, page 344) already possessed knowledge of him.] It is enough to mention that this gave Eccard occasion to attribute that work to Ekkehard, although it was inscribed under the name of the Annalist Saxo. [Col. 0436A]

Martenius had already refuted this and other errors. [Note: [Col. 0435C] For Browerus attributes the catalogue of the bishops of Hildesheim (Life of Godehard, bishop of Hildesheim, Mainz, 1616, quarto, pages 97–101), and Leibniz (Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium, volume I, preface, numbers 46–52) attributes the Chronicle of the Bishops of Hildesheim to Ekkehard. The present writer, however, thinks that Ekkehard was different from the other man whom Helmold praises (same work, volume II, page 514, note; preface, page 52).] [Note: [Col. 0435C] Collectio amplissima, volume IV, pages 2–3. Compare Scheidt, Origines Guelficae, volume III, page 153, note 30.]

After him, Pezius acquired a more accurate knowledge of this author, [Note: [Col. 0435C] Mayer drew from Pezius’s collections what he wrote about Ekkehard and his Chronicle (in Hormayr’s Archiv, 1828, page 806). Almost all more recent scholars appear to have overlooked this.] but nevertheless did not carry out the plan of publishing the Chronicle. Thus only in our own age, after manuscripts from everywhere had been collated, has it become possible to understand the diligence that Ekkehard devoted to composing history and what his books contributed. [Note: [Col. 0435C] See especially what was said in Archiv, volume VII, pages 469–509.]

Yet even in this way we do not have a sufficiently clear understanding of Ekkehard’s life. No one records where or from what parents he was born. Trithemius alone, who mentions him in several places [Note: [Col. 0435C] *Chronicon Hirsaugiense* (of 1559), p. 129; *Annales Hirsaugienses* I, pp. 278, 344, 367, 390; *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, chap. 378.], says that he was a canon of Worms [Note: [Col. 0435C] p. 340: “In the year specified above, Master Eckhard, canon and scholasticus of the church of Worms, moved by the divine Spirit, abandoned the world with its pomp and vanities for the love of Christ and, coming to Hirsau, assumed the habit of holy religious life. He was a man most learned in every branch of knowledge; under his instruction many noble and common men made splendid progress in every kind of learning. Having become a monk, he ordered his life in complete purity, and as his merits increased, after eleven years he was finally appointed the first abbot at Uraugia. …” And p. 367: “In the year likewise specified, Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg, a servant of Christ wholly faithful in all things, among his many works of piety founded anew, at his own expense, a monastery of our order in the diocese of Würzburg, beside the little river Saale, under the patronage of Saint Laurence the Martyr; it is called Uraugia and lies approximately six miles north of Würzburg. Having completed it, he endowed it as best he could for the support of God’s servants, and obtained an abbot with monks from Hirsau. Accordingly, Eckhard, a monk of this Hirsau monastery, was sent as the first abbot to Uraugia by the most reverend Father Bruno, a man most learned in every variety of Scripture. As we stated above under the second year of Bruno’s abbacy, he had first been canon and scholasticus of the church of Worms; afterward he wished to become a monk under Abbot Gebhard, but, being bound by a vow of pilgrimage to the Holy Land, he could not on that occasion fulfill his desire. At length, having returned from overseas regions, he went back to Hirsau and received the monastic habit under the venerable Abbot Bruno. Finally, having become abbot in the aforementioned monastery of Uraugia, he most diligently observed throughout his life the discipline of the rule—which he had learned at Hirsau—in himself as well as in the subjects entrusted to him. For he was firmly rooted in the fear of the Lord and devoted with singular fervor to his commandments, since nothing was ever sweeter to him throughout his life than to devote himself to divine services by night and day alike. Though learned in every variety of Scripture, he never idled in slothful leisure; whenever he could draw breath from temporal cares, he either read something good and holy by which he himself might profit, or wrote something useful that would edify its readers. He endured great want in temporal things, but was rich in humility, patience, and the fullness of the other virtues.”]; but he appears to be mistaken in this.

He goes on to say that Ekkehard had already wished at that time to enter the monastery of Hirsau, but, being bound by a vow to undertake a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, had been unable to do so and had therefore soon set out on his journey. Ekkehard himself relates in his *Chronicle* that this occurred in 1101. He traveled through Bulgaria to Constantinople with a large German army, sailed from there to Joppa, and there barely escaped a great pestilence [Col. 0437A]; afterward he endured the siege of the city and also visited Jerusalem. In 1102, however, he returned by sea to Italy and afterward to Germany.

But he had already been occupied with writing his *Chronicle* in 1099 [Note: [Col. 0437D] See below, no. 27.], and, unless I am greatly mistaken, was living at that time in Bamberg. For the books he used—most of them exceedingly rare—were supplied to him by the Bamberg libraries [Note: [Col. 0437D] See below, cols. 441–444.], and the oldest manuscripts of Ekkehard have been found there [Note: [Col. 0437D] See below, cols. 439, 440, 444–446.]. His account of the foundation of that place and of the events that occurred there is so careful as to indicate an author living in the city itself or in its diocese; finally, the necrology of the monastery of Saint Michael recorded the day of his death.

Ekkehard himself, however, nowhere mentioned Worms; he did not even touch upon Hirsau with a word, although, if we were to believe Trithemius, we should have to suppose that after returning from his journey he lived there for several years [Col. 0437B] and devoted himself to letters, indeed presided over the school. Ekkehard, on the contrary, himself declares that he once lived at Corbie [Note: [Col. 0437D] See the preface to *Erkembert*, col. 449.]; this must have occurred between 1091 and 1107 [Note: [Col. 0437D] For Marquard was abbot during these years; see the *Annals of Saint-Hubert* under the relevant years.].

These circumstances lead me to think that Trithemius—whose reliability everyone agrees is very often unstable—either persuaded himself of these things without reason, or, rather, invented them from his own imagination; perhaps they concern some other monk named Ekkehard of Hirsau, whom he confused with the Bamberg Ekkehard, later abbot of Uraugia. This seems especially likely since he says nothing about the matter in his other books and even appears to agree with us [Note: [Col. 0437D] For in the earlier *Chronicon Hirsaugiense* (Basel, 1559), p. 129, he says: “Eckhart, a venerable monk of the aforesaid monastery of the Mount of Monks, a man …,” where the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount at Bamberg must be understood.], and it is not difficult to understand how he fell into that error [Col. 0438A].

For on this point he returns to the correct path when he says that Ekkehard was afterward ordained abbot of Uraugia. Bishop Otto of Bamberg founded on his estate at Uraugia, situated in the diocese of Würzburg beside the River Saale and now called Aurach, a monastery of Saint Laurence of the Benedictine order. He subjected it to the Hirsau rule and entrusted it to monks taken from Hirsau [Note: [Col. 0437D] This is shown by a letter written by Ekkehard and the other monks of Uraugia to Volmar, abbot of Hirsau, which Trithemius reproduces in the cited work, p. 390:

“To the man of most worthy reverence and most reverend dignity, Lord Volmar, abbot of the Hirsau monks, and to those same foremost members of the supreme Head, Brother Eckhard and the rest of the very small household of Saint Laurence send whatever gifts of the prayers or service of the poor they possess.

“Uraugia, the daughter rightly more despised than the others, gives immense thanks to Hirsau, the spiritual mother of many daughters, though not yet brought to maturity; and she continually entreats even the inward arbiters for rewards for the benefits freely bestowed upon us by your clemency, through which you are accustomed to open your maternal heart both toward us and toward all who suffer need.

“Again and again, prostrate at your feet in mind and spirit, we do not cease to commend our continual petition to the ears of your clemency: do not abandon the young plantation of the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts which you have begun among us, but, returning this act of affection to the Lord Otto the bishop, whose commission we discharge, send us at present some elder whom you know to be such, by whose skill among us what you have graciously planted may be watered.

“We have also sent back the present Brother Conrad, who is weary of our poverty and thirsts with fervent spirit for your spiritual riches, bearing witness for him that, having lived faithfully with us, he has hitherto labored in every way without slackness both for your honor and for our advantage. But now, as he emphatically asserts, fearing the nearness of his death, he desires above all and for the last time to be found in your most holy community.

“May your holiness prosper, flourish, and live forever before Christ; may our humility also now and always find grace in your sight.”

It should be noted that Ekkehard by no means says that he had lived at Hirsau and had been sent from there to Uraugia.];

this appears to have given Trithemius the opportunity to assert that Abbot Ekkehard had also been requested from that monastery. He is mistaken here as well in assigning the foundation to 1118, since documents [Note: [Col. 0438D] In Ussermann, *Episcopatus Wirceb.* *codices probationum*, p. 29. The version is an old German translation of a charter dated 1122.] show that the monastery was begun in 1108 and dedicated five years later, while we see that Ekkehard himself wrote a letter from the monastery of Saint Laurence as early as 1117 [Col. 0438B] [Note: [Col. 0438D] See below, cols. 448–450.].

He was elected by Bishop Otto, whom he praises and honors most highly as though he were his patron [Note: [Col. 0438D] In 1124 and 1125.], and whom he appears to have accompanied earlier on his journeys [Note: [Col. 0438D] See below, cols. 445–447.]. He accepted this office, being at that time, unless I am greatly mistaken, a monk of the monastery of Saint Michael at Bamberg. How many years he lived afterward is not sufficiently certain [Note: [Col. 0438D] In the charter cited as no. 17 he is not himself named, but he appears in another document without a date, in Ludewig, *Scriptores rerum Bambergensium* I, p. 1124.]. He continued the *Chronicle* to 1125; if Trithemius is to be believed, he wrote the letter to Volmar of Hirsau in 1129 [Note: [Col. 0438D] *Annales Hirsaugienses*, cited work, p. 390.]. By then he had devoted himself to letters for thirty years, and therefore appears to have reached approximately old age. He died on 23 January [Note: [Col. 0438D] *Necrologium S. Michaelis Bambergense*, in Schannat, *Vindemiae litterariae* II, p. 29: “The tenth day before the Kalends of February, Eggehardus, abbot of Saint Laurence at Uraugia” (read “Saint Laurence”). Ussermann (*Episcopatus Wirzeburgensis*, p. 418) seems incorrectly to indicate 20 February, that is, the tenth day before the Kalends of March.] [Note: [Col. 0438D] The year is uncertain. In *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, chap. 378, Trithemius’s number 1130 should probably be referred to the preceding rather than the following sentence; compare chapters 377, 381, 383, and so forth. In any case, it is far from the truth. But even if we decided otherwise, we could scarcely rely upon such testimony.].

[Col. 0439A] Let us willingly believe Trithemius that Ekkehard excelled in literary study and devoted his efforts to more than one book. “Eckhard,” he says [Note: [Col. 0439D] *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, cited work.], “the first abbot of the monastery of Saint Laurence, which is called Uraugia, in the diocese of Würzburg, in the Hercynian Forest, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nationality, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters inferior to none among the learned Germans of his time, outstanding in verse and prose. He wrote minor works worthy of being read, in which he displayed the vitality of his intellect. Of these I saw only one distinguished work, composed in a twofold style in imitation of Boethius, highly useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all faithful people who fear God; he entitled it *The Lantern of Monks*, in five books. He composed certain elegant sermons and various letters to different people. He flourished under the emperor Conrad III. In the year of the Lord 1130 he was buried in the middle of the church of the aforesaid monastery.”

Elsewhere he gives a more detailed account of Ekkehard’s written works:

“He wrote minor works of no contemptible authority, by which he made himself useful to those then living and commended himself as memorable to posterity. Among these are said to be the following. He composed a distinguished volume, a *Chronicle* from the creation of the world to the year 1124 inclusive of the Lord’s Incarnation, in which he arranged the deeds of kings and emperors in Germany and abroad in a sufficiently coherent order.
