In imitation also of Martianus Capella and Severinus Boethius, he wrote a work equipped with a twofold style, that is, verse and prose, and entitled it *The Lantern*, or *Mathias*, dividing it into three books [Col. 0439C]. In it Paul, the adopted son in the Lord of a certain sick Mathias, softened the lament of that Mathias with an artfully fashioned consolation.

“He also wrote one letter to the holy abbess Hildegard at Bingen; several letters to Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg; several letters to Volmar, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau; and likewise several letters to various others. He also published sermons for his monks and homilies worthy of attention. The other works he composed have not come to our notice for reading.”

Only one letter survives; no trace remains of the sermons or homilies. Nor has the work seen and more carefully described by Trithemius, entitled *The Lantern*, or *Mathias*, so far become known. Thus it appears that only the historical books have escaped the injuries of time. Besides the *Chronicle* carried down to 1124, Trithemius also reports a brief history [Note: [Col. 0439D] *Chronicon Hirsaugiense* (Basel, 1559), p. 129.] in which Ekkehard described the events occurring in his own time. But by examining all the manuscripts that could be found, it is possible to review each of his works more accurately and determine their dates.

In the final years of the eleventh century, Ekkehard, then a monk at Bamberg, undertook to write a *Chronicle* that would provide, from the creation of the world to his own times, as extensive an account as possible of events, collecting everything he could assemble from historical as well as biblical and theological books and from the writings of other authors [Col. 0440B]. Among the various universal histories of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, I believe I am fully justified in assigning it first place.

He was engaged in this work, as he himself states [Note: [Col. 0439D] Col. 671: “And I brought the times of the Roman pontiffs in sequence from the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 460 up to the year 1099 of that same Incarnation. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1057, Henry began to reign; and when this composition was made, he was reigning in his forty-second year.”], in 1099; yet he should not be thought to have completed it in so short a time. For the text, although printed in this edition in extremely small type, fills for the most part 180 pages; Ekkehard’s autograph manuscript [Note: [Col. 0439D] This has already been demonstrated by Pertz, *Archiv* VII, p. 472.] contained more than two hundred folios.

This manuscript, which I have designated I, is now preserved in the library of the University of Jena, but formerly belonged to “the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount near Bamberg.” We regret that some folios have been cut out; otherwise it presents a genuine text, marred by only a few errors, as Ekkehard wrote it in his own hand, correcting it lightly here and there and enlarging it with several additions. Since we shall publish the complete book below, readers may judge for themselves the arrangement of the material, the method of calculating the years, and the other features by which the author displayed his diligence and skill.

In both the number and the importance of his sources, he surpasses nearly all the writers of his own time, indeed most writers of the Middle Ages, except that exceptionally learned Sigebert. For [Note: [Col. 0439D] The discussions by Gretser (*Opera* XVII, p. 75), Semler (*Versuch*, p. 129), and Schumacher (*Beiträge*, pp. 43–44) concerning the sources of the *Chronicle of Ursberg* belong here; but they confused the matter more than they explained it.], in order to illuminate ancient history, he used, besides the chronicles of Jerome [Note: [Col. 0440D] He copied almost the whole preface from this work.], Prosper [Note: [Col. 0440D] He used both what is called the consular and what is called the imperial *Chronicle*.], Jordanes, Isidore, and Bede, also Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 0440D] Add to this the apocryphal book, the Epistle of Jude the Apostle (col. 502).], Josephus’s *Jewish Antiquities* and *Jewish War*, Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* in the translation and continuation of Rufinus, the works of Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0440D] Below, col. 645.], Jerome [Note: [Col. 0440D] He carefully examined especially the commentary on Daniel (see col. 545 ff.); he also consulted the commentary on Isaiah twice (cols. 509, 541). Later he cites a commentary on Mark, although I have said that Matthew may perhaps be intended there (note 218).], Augustine [Note: [Col. 0440D] Besides *The City of God*, from which he copied especially books 15–18 (col. 505 ff.), he also used the commentary on Genesis (col. 726).] [Col. 0441A], Gregory the Great [Note: [Col. 0441B] He himself cites Gregory’s *Dialogues* (col. 796).], and books of passions [Note: [Col. 0441B] Books of passions (cols. 671, 693, 695) and the *Life of the Fathers* (col. 760) are cited, though I do not know which works are meant; compare col. 668: “so that he may be commemorated not only in martyrologies, but also publicly in the canon of the Masses and in the supplications of the litanies.” The books of the passion of Dionysius the Areopagite and of Pope Alexander are cited at col. 668 (compare col. 679). Ekkehard used the *Life of Saint Basil* at col. 711.] ; he knew the authors of Roman antiquity—Sallust [Note: [Col. 0441B] Cols. 537, 634, 640.], Pliny [Note: [Col. 0441C] Cols. 505, 725. Compare cols. 509–512.], perhaps Livy [Note: [Col. 0441C] Col. 537.] and Virgil [Note: [Col. 0441C] Col. 655. I do not know whether the verse at col. 607 may have been taken from Cicero.]; he borrowed much from Orosius; and in a Bamberg manuscript that still survives [Note: [Col. 0441C]

I shall discuss this more fully in our *Annals* (*Archiv*, vol. IX). It should be noted that Ekkehard copied many of the interpolator’s glosses—for example, at col. 675, the words “which was then a sign of deliverance.” Moreover, take care not to attribute to Ekkehard the errors already committed by that interpolator, for example at col. 721: “he appointed Dagobert to the episcopate” (the Bamberg manuscript has: “Dagoberhtum episcopatu preponit”), and at cols. 709–711 concerning the battle fought between the Saxons and Suevians. I shall give one example of how that manuscript departs from the genuine text:

Paul the Deacon VI, 20:

“Liutbert, whom he had captured, he deprived of life in the bath in the same manner.”

Bamberg manuscript, fol. 183v:

“But Liopert, whom he had seized alive in battle, he sent into the bath and shut the door upon him; and he died from the excessive heat.”

Ekkehard, col. 810:

“He seized Liopert alive in battle … sent him into the bath and shut the door upon him, and thus he died from the excessive heat.”]

he read the history and fabulous letters of Alexander, as well as Aurelius Victor, Jordanes’ *History of the Goths* [Note: [Col. 0441D] Ekkehard’s purer readings can be explained only from this manuscript. To give one example: in place of *familiae balthorum*, the manuscript reads *familia evalthorum*, whence Ekkehard (col. 732) has *familiae Ewaldorum*. Yet he may also have possessed another manuscript from which he corrected certain names. Certainly he did not find Jordanes’ *Chronicle* there in complete form.], the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings*, an abridgment of the *Chronicles*, Paul the Deacon’s book *On the Affairs of the Lombards* [Note: [Col. 0441D] Compare nos. 49, 51.], and other works, as they had been copied and interpolated by some Italian after the language had been changed.

To compose his Frankish history, he also appears to have consulted the second book of Fredegar [Note: [Col. 0441D] Col. 523.], and drew much from the *Lives of Saint Columbanus* [Note: [Col. 0441D] Col. 720.] and Saint Gall [Note: [Col. 0441D] Col. 720.]. In this part of the book he also used the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great* [Col. 0441B] [Note: [Col. 0441D] Cols. 797, 798, 815 ff.], works of Bede [Note: [Col. 0441D] Besides the *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*, he also used the book of which that work forms a part, *On the Reckoning of Time* (col. 555), as well as commentaries on Mark and the Acts of the Apostles (cols. 661, 667), the *Martyrology* (compare no. 53), and the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, which that Bamberg manuscript contains (col. 641; compare cols. 666–667).], Dicuil’s *On the Measurement of the Earth* [Note: [Col. 0442B] What he copied from this work he cites under Bede’s name, although Lappenberg has already noted (*Arch.* VI, p. 890) that it is not found in Bede. I have no doubt that Dicuil’s book was available to Ekkehard, since several manuscripts of it are still found in Germany, for example at Dresden (Ebert, *Geschichte der Dresdner Bibliothek*, p. 283) and Vienna (Endlicher, *Codices philologici Latini*, pp. 231–232). It could easily, like many other works, have been attributed to the famous Bede.], and, above all, the *Roman History* composed by Paul the Deacon [Note: [Col. 0442C] At times he used the text found in that Bamberg manuscript, but for the most part the genuine text, such as we still read in another Bamberg manuscript.], as well as the *Miscellaneous History*, which was compiled a century later from his work and other sources [Note: [Col. 0442C] A complete manuscript of this collection, in twenty-six books, is also preserved at Bamberg (*Arch.* VI, 42). Although I have not yet seen it, I think it was available to Ekkehard. Certainly he possessed a genuine and extensive manuscript from which he copied much that is omitted from the common edition and cited by editors only from either the Hersfeld or the Palatine manuscripts.].

Although he repeatedly drew from these works, especially from Bede’s *Martyrology* [Note: [Col. 0442C] He cites it at col. 669 and often used it from col. 674 onward.], for information about the Roman pontiffs, he nevertheless often departed from these and other authors in determining their succession and dates. He appears to have done this with the aid of a certain catalogue [Note: [Col. 0442C] Compare col. 670. He departs most markedly from the other sources in determining the years.].

When he reached the history of the ninth century, he consulted more authoritative sources: I mean Einhard’s books, both the *Life of Charlemagne* [Note: [Col. 0442C] Compare col. 843.] and the annals. To these he added the *Annals of Lorsch* [Note: [Col. 0442C] Besides Einhard’s *Annals*, he also copied these, as is shown by the years 768 (“the seventh day before the Ides of October”), 773, 783 (“when the vigils of the Ascension were being held”), the beginning of 797, and so forth. Under 823 and 828 he has certain material found only in the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, but he copied it not from those annals, rather from a common source, a fuller manuscript of Einhard.], the *Life of Burchard of Würzburg* [Note: [Col. 0442D] Cols. 837, 839.], the monk of Saint Gall [Note: [Col. 0442D] Cols. 847, 853, 864, 866, 868.], and other works [Note: [Col. 0442D] The passage under 753 concerning Pippin’s coronation was copied not from Regino, whom you see cited in the margin (col. 839), but either from the coronation formula (in Bouquet V) or from some lost source that may also appear to have supplied him with certain material under 799. What is repeated from the *Genealogy of the Frankish Kings* at cols. 871, 876, and 883 should be referred to what is read in the *Chronicle of Würzburg*, col. 493.]; later he also consulted the *Annals of Lobbes* [Note: [Col. 0442D] Col. 871 ff. Note that a manuscript of these annals also exists at Bamberg.].

From Rudolf’s book *On the Translation of Saint Alexander* he illuminated the origins of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0442D] Compare *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, p. 673.], whose historiographer Widukind [Col. 0442B] he afterward had as a most distinguished guide [Note: [Col. 0442D] Compare ibid. III, p. 415.], and he enlarged and corrected Widukind’s account from the histories of Liutprand [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare ibid., p. 272.] and Richer [Note: [Col. 0443B] Compare ibid., p. 566. Everyone knows that the only surviving copy of Richer was found at Bamberg. Nevertheless, I cannot help concluding that Ekkehard had another manuscript of the work at his disposal, not this one. For he often departs from it so far that he should be said to have reproduced the account from memory rather than copied it; this has happened nowhere else. Moreover, he has one passage that everyone will agree bears the stamp of Richer’s style, and he himself attributes it to Richer (col. 900; compare *Jahrbücher*, cited work, p. 198), although it is not found in that Bamberg manuscript. I cannot in any way be persuaded that Ekkehard invented it.], as well as from the *Life of Saint Ulrich* [Note: [Col. 0443C] Col. 897. He possessed the second *Life*, which we owe to Bishop Gebhard; compare *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores IV, p. 389, no. 14. I would not suppose that Ruotger’s *Life of Bruno* was available to him (col. 905).].

From the end of the eleventh century onward, deprived of a more abundant source, he generally repeated what is found in the *Chronicle of Würzburg* that I have mentioned, derived from Hermann of Reichenau. He had already borrowed a great deal from the same work [Note: [Col. 0443C] See col. 443.].

He did indeed copy the accounts of these authors in the manner customary among medieval writers, so faithfully that he sometimes retained their words even when they narrated things they had themselves seen or referred to their own times [Note: [Col. 0443C] For example, col. 680: “Such honor was paid to his memory that down to our own age, in the senate, and so forth,” from the *Miscellaneous History*; col. 731: “I mean ancient Dacia, which the Gepids are now known to possess,” from Jordanes; col. 905: “Bruno, whom we saw exercising the office of supreme pontiff and great commander,” from Widukind. But what must be noted hundreds of times in other authors occurs only three or four times in Ekkehard.]. Nevertheless, he by no means wrote with the carelessness and lack of reflection that we often detect in other works of this period.

On the contrary, although his subject matter was extremely extensive, he never allowed himself to be overwhelmed by it. He arranged each item suitably, carefully collected everything that different authors had written about the same matter [Note: [Col. 0443D] See a particularly clear example on p. 151, where he composed his account most carefully from the *Miscellaneous History* and the *Life of Gregory*. Elsewhere he often took individual words from another source.], corrected one account by means of another [Note: [Col. 0443D] For example, col. 918, where he correctly calls Hugh’s son Lothair (following Liutprand), rather than, with his source Widukind, Louis. Yet Ekkehard himself sometimes committed errors by misunderstanding his books; for example, col. 630: “It is said that from this money he established hospices in which he might receive the poor and pilgrims,” where Josephus is speaking of auxiliary forces, that is, auxiliary soldiers, not pilgrims; col. 673: “He sang the tragedy *Iliad*,” because he read the added words “dressed in tragic costume”; col. 859 under 786, and cols. 881–882, where see the notes.], enlarged it, supplied omissions, and sometimes investigated one matter or another more precisely [Note: [Col. 0443D] He attempted especially to establish the succession of the Jewish kings and the Roman pontiffs, cols. 533, 543 ff., 668.].

I do not claim that he thereby attained the truth, but he certainly did so to the best of his ability, and he candidly acknowledged what he had not sufficiently understood [Note: [Col. 0444B] Col. 535: “Finding these differences in the histories, but not daring, as a man of no authority, to criticize either side, I have recorded the opinion of both, so that I may make the more diligent reader more cautious”; col. 549: “How the agreement of all these matters stands, we leave to more diligent students”; col. 553: “But perhaps we are foolish in proposing these things, while presuming to define nothing rashly; let us yield, as is proper, to the writers of histories, and leave these matters to be investigated by more diligent students”; col. 557: “I have set down these differing opinions of the interpreters so that the wise reader may consider them and see what he should choose”; col. 585: “Let the prudent reader decide which of these things pleases him most”; col. 662: “From these let the prudent reader choose what ought rather to be held”; col. 671: “I do not say all this as though, in my loquacity, I wished to prejudice the opinion of others who surpass me by so much, but as though, driven by a desire to investigate the truth and deserving to be branded with the epithet of foolishness, I were exposing the meaning of my own imprudence. Let every wise person decide according to his capacity what he judges should be held as true, and so forth—I yield most gladly to him who shows himself more desirous of what is certain and true”; col. 693: “How the truth stands concerning these matters rests upon the account of the writers”; col. 890: “It will be for the reader to decide whom he should believe more.”].

He laid at least the first foundations of critical method in that he not only weighed the varying testimonies of writers, but sometimes thought that discrepancies could be attributed to defects in the manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0444C] Col. 535: “Whether this has been corrupted through the fault of scribes who made errors in the variation of the number, or for what reason it has thus varied, we have not yet discovered with certainty; … I do not know whether the *Book of Kings* among us is corrupted or sound …”; cols. 670–671: “It is believed to have arisen through the carelessness and fault of scribes. … Hence it can be sufficiently understood that through the fault of scribes the order was confused because of the similarity of names; … finding many things corrupted through the negligence or incompetence of scribes, because of variations in the numbers represented by letters—for it is easy for the diligent to err in these matters, how much more for those who do not pay attention, when either one letter is put for another or some letter is perhaps omitted”; cols. 693–694: “From this it may be conjectured that the changes in succession were altered through the fault of scribes because of the similarity of names—if, indeed, the book has not been corrupted through the fault of scribes.”].

Besides written sources, he also once or twice appealed to things that were reported in popular songs and sung in verse [Note: [Col. 0444D] Col. 756.]. When he reached periods closer to his own time, he added more material that he may be presumed to have received from contemporaries, especially matters concerning Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0444D] Col. 928 ff.].

He composed the history of the late eleventh century himself, briefly and plainly but with sufficient accuracy, using written materials and other documents [Note: [Col. 0444D] Under 1076 and 1080.]. In this part he displays a mind attached to no faction, a fair and upright judgment, love for his homeland, and the same reverence toward the emperor as toward the supreme pontiff. As I have already said above, he composed the history in 1099 or the following year and ended it with a brief account of the sacred journey undertaken during those years, which he drew from a certain letter of the crusaders [Note: [Col. 0444D] See below, note 278.].

This account, however, is no longer found in the aforesaid manuscript, formerly Bambergensis and now Jenensis, but was afterward altered and continued by the author himself. In another manuscript, also formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Michael at Bamberg and now transferred to the Karlsruhe library [Col. 0445A] [Note: [Col. 0445D] See below, col. 455.], the final part of this *Chronicle*, beginning with the year 1057, is preserved in a form that can readily be understood to be the oldest of all.

For this text, which I have designated A, lacks the alterations and additions that Ekkehard later decided should be made in the autograph manuscript (I) [Note: [Col. 0445D] See the years 1072, 1085, 1096, 1097, 1098, and 1099.]. After 1099, a brief notice for 1100 and 1101 has been added, whether composed by Ekkehard or by the manuscript’s scribe.

In the same volume, before this fragment, another short *Chronicle* is prefixed, neatly written in a different but contemporary hand. It records events from the creation of the world down to 1057, so that this portion of Ekkehard’s book appears in a certain way to follow it. I would certainly think that the two were not joined accidentally [Col. 0445B], although it is clear from the fact that they are not parts of one work that, while the former already recounts the beginnings of Henry IV, the latter begins with the same events, and thus the same thing is read twice in similar words.

I have called that *Chronicle* the *Chronicle of Würzburg*, because I found the succession of the bishops of Würzburg indicated everywhere with accuracy and care. Moreover, almost everything was drawn from well-known sources: Josephus, Orosius, Isidore, Bede, Paul the Deacon’s *Roman History* and *History of the Lombards*, Fredegar, and Einhard’s *Annals*. To these may perhaps be added Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 0445D] Col. 472.] and the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* [Note: [Col. 0445D] Col. 482.]. Above all, however, an epitome such as we know to have been made from the *Chronicle of Hermann of Reichenau* [Note: [Col. 0445D] See *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores V, p. 73.] was copied from beginning to end.

It is evident at a glance that very much from this work passed into Ekkehard’s universal *Chronicle*. Since I saw that the same sources were generally used in both works, that I found almost the same method of arranging the material, and finally that I found both joined in a single volume, I came close to persuading myself that this shorter history too should be attributed to Ekkehard.

What stands in the way, however, is that Ekkehard used neither Fredegar’s continuation nor the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* in preparing his great *Chronicle*; he would scarcely have neglected them if they had been available to him. Further, the order and wording are not always the same. Finally, Ekkehard once appeals to what is read in the *Chronicle of Würzburg* [Col. 0446A] in such a way [Note: [Col. 0445D] Col. 756: “which is recorded in certain chronicles.” What follows is the account given there at cols. 473–475; here, however, it is compared both with popular songs and with Jordanes’ account.] that he seems clearly enough to indicate a work belonging to someone else.

For this reason I think that the *Chronicle of Würzburg*—which I have elsewhere suspected was carried further [Note: [Col. 0445D] See what I said in the preface to the *Saxon Annalist*], and which was read and copied by several medieval writers [Note: [Col. 0445D] By the Saxon annalist and in the annals called Würzburgian (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, p. 239), which you would more correctly call the Mainz annals of Saint Alban. I shall show elsewhere that these were copied in the annals of Hildesheim, Erfurt, and Saint Dysibod.]—should be counted not among Ekkehard’s works but among his principal sources [Note: [Col. 0445D] Hermann of Reichenau’s *Chronicle* can no longer be counted among Ekkehard’s sources (compare *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, p. 238; III, p. 20; V, p. 73). I have already said above, no. 59, that the genealogies of both the Carolingian and Saxon kings and emperors were taken from the *Chronicle of Würzburg*.].

Accordingly, I ask readers to delete his name from pages 17–32 of our edition.

But let us now return to Ekkehard. For he did not remain satisfied with that work for long, but soon undertook to revise and continue it. In 1101 he set out on a journey to the Holy Land; the following year, after returning, he went to Rome, where he heard Paschal proclaiming the ban against Emperor Henry, and from there returned to his homeland. He had then himself seen, or learned from others, many things worthy of being reported; above all, he had gathered much previously unknown to him concerning the first expedition of the Crusaders. This was undoubtedly the reason why, in the autograph manuscript we possess, he erased the History for the years 1098 and 1099 and began a new and more expansive account of the events then taking place [Note: See below, col. 972, and *Archiv* VII, p. 472. He might perhaps have produced a longer History of the Holy War, had he not found in Jerusalem a book on that subject, which he did not wish to copy (col. 972).], which he continued, whether in one uninterrupted act of writing or over the course of time, down to the year 1106. In this part of the book he favors the Church more strongly; he takes the side not of Emperor Henry but of his rebellious sons [Note: Conrad, of whom he had written under the year 1093: “Conrad, the emperor’s son, is accused of having rebelled against his father”; under 1099 he praises him as “a man wholly Catholic and most submissive to the Apostolic See,” and so forth.], and especially extols Henry V, whose first court at Nordhausen in 1105 he attended [Note: See below, col. 991.]. In the same spirit he then also erased or altered certain passages in the first part of the book [Note: See above, no. 83.], and here and there corrected an error [Col. 0446C] [Note: Under 1085; compare 1072.].

Yet the author did not stop there. The old and hated Henry IV had been succeeded by the young Henry V, who, after his father’s death, seemed to be restoring the unity of Church and empire, and was therefore received by all with the greatest applause. This too moved Ekkehard to deny his pen any rest and to devote himself most willingly to describing Henry’s praises. He declares this himself in a preface, which plainly appears to have been written when Henry was not yet emperor, indeed scarcely established as king—that is, in 1106 or 1107 [Note: Below, col. 999. The whole preface demonstrates this. Note especially the words: “You … at last, and scarcely obtained as a head … the Roman world, now awakening from the dust, testifies that the time has come to pity itself,” concerning your character, and so forth. “Blessed will your age be, and it will be brought forth more glorious, if …”]. This is followed by an extensive History of the year 1106 and, unless I am very much mistaken, one written amid the disturbances themselves. For he attacks Henry IV in the bitterest language [Col. 0447A], regards him as a heresiarch, an apostate, and a persecutor of souls, worthy of every insult, and assails his supporters in fiery speech. At that time Ekkehard attached himself to Otto of Bamberg, who had committed himself to the younger king. He seems to have accompanied him when he was sent to Rome in 1106 with the other royal envoys [Note: Below, col. 1001.]; certainly he was present at the council held at Guastalla at the end of that year [Note: Col. 1015.]. At about this time, as we saw above, he was appointed abbot of Aura, and thereafter appears to have been bound by personal familiarity not only to the bishop but also to King Henry V.

Indeed, at the time when the king was about to celebrate his marriage with the daughter of the king of England, he ordered Ekkehard to compose a History—or Chronicle—of the emperors, from the time of Charlemagne down to his own age [Col. 0447B]. Let us hear the author himself on this subject; he prefixed the following preface to the book:

**HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE FOLLOWING CHRONICLE [Note: *Chon. cod.*] WORK.**

Tullius testifies that any commonwealth will be happy if it is either governed by the wise or if those who have governed it happen to devote themselves to wisdom; without wisdom, it is clear that even courage degenerates into nothing more than the name of rashness. We therefore ought to give God greater thanks than other nations, since, after the storms by which we have hitherto been shaken have been calmed, a prince of great wisdom and endowed with great vigor for governing has arisen to rule the Roman Empire. By God’s disposition the whole world, both Roman and Teutonic, rejoices in applauding him with every effort—namely, Henry V, king and fourth emperor, a man composed of manifold [Col. 0447C] virtue, fierce in war, pious and gentle in peace.

Since he shines like a flashing morning star with the splendor of wisdom and breathes the sweetness of every good fragrance, he has deigned to command our smallness to gather for him a chronicle from the times of Charlemagne down to his own, preserving everywhere the truth of history. Although our incompetence refused to undertake this work, his authority and goodwill nevertheless compelled us to bring it to some completion. You therefore have, most serene emperor, through the agency of charity, a chronicle extracted not from our own authority but from that of the ancient chroniclers [Note: *Chon. cod.*]—would that it be not unworthy, I will not say of imperial eyes, but at least of the humblest readers of your court.

Since the entire purpose of this book serves the honor both of the Roman Empire and of the Teutonic kingdom, whose union began with Charles the Frank, we have deemed it necessary to trace more deeply the origin of so noble a people, which proved capable of producing the rulers of Roman power, and thus, by a narrative carried through the generations of the most ancient nobility down to that same Charles, to set out with suitable brevity—excluding the accounts of other chronicles—how he took up a tottering commonwealth, and [Col. 0448A] how thereafter the Roman Empire was governed with the greatest distinction through the succession of kings of this people, down to the present age.

The first book runs from the origin of the Franks through the times of the kingdom of that people. The second book includes, from the empire of Charlemagne, the reigns and deeds and briefly the years of all his successors. The third book begins the deeds and future deeds of this Henry V—which, would that they could not be brought to an end by any limit, or at least that they might end only after many cycles of years, in a good old age well pleasing to God!”

The first book begins, as indicated above, with the chapter “On the Origin of the Franks,” in these words: “The beginnings of the Frankish people emerged from the ancient stock of the Trojans.” [Col. 0448B] For, and so forth [Note: Col. 713.]. Both this passage and what follows generally agree with Ekkehard’s Chronicle so closely that one immediately recognizes the same author, even though, as was his custom, he has concealed his name. Moreover, the unique manuscript also contains a charter relating to the monastery of Aura, and finally the author explicitly refers to the previously written Chronicle [Note: Under 1096, no. ****; under 1101, p. and ****; under 1086, no. *; under 1093, no. *; under 1102, no. *; 220, no. ****.].

The text of this book, which I have designated C., although taken from the earlier Chronicle and pieced together from its individual chapters, nevertheless sometimes departs from it. First, it incorporates a great many passages from the Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux, by which it enlarged its own narrative; then, from the middle of the eleventh century onward, when circumstances had changed, Ekkehard considered that the history too had to be changed. Henry V had appeased his father’s shade and, after the Roman expedition had ended, seemed to himself to have most happily established peace between Church and empire. Therefore Ekkehard now avoided everything that could renew the memory of the ancient discord, and softened what in the first book he had written against the Church, and later, after changing his opinion, had written too harshly against Emperor Henry IV and his adherents [Note: Compare 1072, no. *; 1080, no. *, especially 1105 and 1106. Here and there (col. 953), no. **; 1083, no. *; 1084 and 1085, no. **; he also removed lesser errors (1076, 1089).]. His aim was to present the younger Henry with such an image of past events as would favor no party and offend no one’s mind. This led him to write a new History of the years 1105 and 1106 and to add a continuation composed in the same even and moderate spirit.

There are, moreover, two further recensions of Ekkehard’s Chronicle [Col. 0448D], which agree in many respects with C., although in other respects they depart both from it and from the earlier text. Each presents a preface addressed to the younger Henry and prefixed in 1106; each contains a text written without tables of years but enlarged by many additions taken from Sigebert; and finally each provides a narrative of the years 1070 and following, sometimes altered in the same manner as C. Since this is observed chiefly in passages where harsher words against the Church and the popes have been softened, but not likewise where the author had inveighed against Henry IV, while, on the contrary, the history of 1106 is here retained as having been written in an utterly hostile spirit, one might perhaps consider these recensions older than the history C., indeed already completed in 1106 or 1107 together with that preface and its narrative of the year. I myself would not oppose that view, were it not that Sigebert’s Chronicle was only completed in 1112 and that I find both recensions continued in manuscripts down to 1125. Sigebert is indeed thought to have published a work earlier [Note: Compare what our Bethmann said in his preface to Sigebert. Yet certainly not in 1105: Ekkehard used Sigebert’s Chronicle in 1106 or the following year, which agrees very well with what he noted under no. 47*.]; but the manuscripts also seem to depart in other respects from the original form and to contain the Chronicle as it was later arranged by the author.

These recensions, however, [Col. 0449B] although for the most part agreeing with each other, nevertheless differ in certain respects. The first, which I have called D., takes as its basis the Chronicle begun in 1099 and finished in 1106, but greatly expands it at numerous Sigebertian passages. It omits the History of the Jerusalem War from 1099 onward and relegates it to the end of the volume; from 1106 it proceeds in the manner described above, but continues the narrative down to 1125. The other, called E., likewise follows the traces of the original text and contains almost the same Sigebertian fragments as D.; yet it omits the greater narratives of the History of Alexander [Note: Everything from the words “But since that same Alexander …” (col. 563) to “afterward he reigned for five years” (col. 602) is missing.], of the Franks [Note: 366; cols. 713, 725, 788, 844, 882. The histories of Alexander, the Goths, and the Saxons are also omitted from the principal manuscript of recension D., but were later supplied by the same hand; see below, no. 168.], of the Goths, the Lombards, Charlemagne, and the Saxons [Note: In addition, the passage on the succession of the popes (col. 668).]. It also separates the History of the Crusaders from the Chronicle and reduces it to the form of a separate book, which is entitled *Hierosolymita* (hence designated H.) [Col. 0449C] and dedicated to Abbot Erkembert of Corvey [Note: The Corvey Annals, of doubtful reliability, mention this in Leibnitz II, p. 306.]. To him he also sent the Chronicle, with the following letter prefixed to the book [Note: It was edited from the Paris manuscript (E2) by Martene, *Coll.* V, p. 511; and in *Oesterreichisches Archiv* 1831, *Urkundenblatt* V, p. 17.]:

**HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE.**

To Erkembert, the faithful and prudent steward of Christ’s household, and likewise to that handsome flock, celebrating vigils for Christ’s martyrs Stephen and Vitus under so excellent a shepherd, Brother Ekkehard, together with the other poor men of Saint Lawrence, sends whatever unfeigned charity, pressed beneath such great burdens, is worth sending.

Behold, leaving our own burdens meanwhile in the middle of the road, we have, thanks be to God and praise be to Christ, carried to the goal the great burden imposed upon us by your authority. We ascribe this worthily to charity alone—for since it is God, it can surely do nothing impossible on either side—which, ever extending its hand, enabled us, so small as we are, to accomplish so great a task. [Col. 0450A] For behold, we have supplied, through the service of our style, even for the dregs of our own times, a series of various chroniclers, abridged from the beginning of the world, wishing by this very means to fulfill the desire of your command, though not without danger to our reputation.

Therefore, as a remedy against weariness [Note: The words *reme* and *rimus* were erased in the manuscript.], the work is divided into five little books. The first ends with the foundation of the city of Rome, the second with the birth of Christ, the third with the empire of Charles, the fourth with that of the man who still survives, and the fifth is called “Henry the Emperor.” For it seemed inappropriate that the fifth book should be inscribed with his name, although we have determined that it should end at the discretion of any writer.

At the end we have also added a small book which we call the *Jerusalem Book*, and we have no doubt that it will be a special relief for you, venerable Father, in your pilgrimage, divinely inspired already. There is therefore one thing that we desire with all our wishes, and that we earnestly ask as compensation for our labor: that this volume, the debt of our service, may continually discharge itself in the Corvey monastery, and that it may display in the treasury of Saint Vitus, for the descendants of the poor men of Saint Lawrence, a memorial of the ancient fellowship renewed through it, which we attained under the holy and beloved father Marcward.

Furthermore, burning with an excessive, though not undeserved, affection of charity toward your Reverence [Note: “Our” in the manuscript.], we have sent our like-minded Amel, prior of our congregation, likewise in every respect devoted to you. He will also, Father, as you proceed toward the footsteps of the Savior, bid you an intimate farewell in person on our behalf; as the best-known mediator and suitable witness between the two congregations, he will suffice to confirm face to face our desired brotherhood, and, if anything has been neglected in writing, he will add responses from one side and the other.

We, your unanimous brothers, pray without ceasing that you may always prosper here and live forever.

It is evident that this letter was written during the reign of Henry V, before Erkembert had departed for the Holy Land [Note: Compare *Hierosolymita*, p. 265.], therefore between 1112, when Henry received the imperial crown, and 1117, when Erkembert undertook his journey [Note: *Ann. Hildesh.*, under that year.]. Nevertheless, the manuscripts containing the Chronicle together with this letter and the *Jerusalem Book* present it as extending down to 1125 [Col. 0450D], and do not clearly distinguish the five books indicated in the preface and read by Helmold in his copy [Note: See the passage cited above, II, 40: “Whoever desires to know more fully their deeds—the deeds of Henry the father and the son—and the end of this schism, let him read the fifth book of the master of histories, Eggihard, which, describing it for the younger Henry, he extols with the highest praise of his goodness, while he either entirely suppressed his evil deeds or interpreted them for the better.”] [Col. 0451A] from one another [Note: The fourth book is marked from 801 (col. 865, note 1153), and the fifth from 1105 (col. 999). The others are indicated only by larger initial letters: “Numitor from his grandsons,” etc., col. 537, book 2; “At that time,” etc., col. 657, book 3. It should be noted, however, that the first part has perished from the oldest manuscript of recension E.]. Thus we do not yet possess a genuine copy of the work as it was sent to Erkembert. E., however, seems to come closest to it. Besides the letter, it contains a brief account of the foundation of Corvey [Note: Under 822.], which the other manuscripts, except D., omit, and it presents a text composed from D. [Note: Compare 936, 972, 1024.], but corrected by Ekkehard in his latest revisions [Note: Compare 1110, 1114, 1115, 1119, 1121, and especially 1123, col. 1051.]. Since in some passages of the continuation E. comes closer to C. than to D. [Note: Compare col. 1015, variant reading 2000; col. 1017, variant reading 1989; cols. 1019, 1021.], I consider its earlier part older than C., whether it was composed in 1106 or several years later; but I judge that the Chronicle addressed to Erkembert (E.) was composed around 1117, therefore after C., which we know was completed in 1114, and that first D., and afterward E. as well, were enlarged by a continuation down to 1125 [Col. 0451B].

Moreover, I cannot but attribute to Ekkehard himself the recension in which we possess the Chronicle of 1106, almost unaltered and enlarged only by a few fragments of Sigebert, joined to a continuation down to 1125 (almost the same as D.), which I have called B*, especially since it is established that this too is found in manuscripts of the twelfth century.

These continuations are of the greatest authority and far surpass the rest of the work. For the events which the author himself had seen [Note: See 1099, 1101, 1102, 1105, and 1106. He appears to have attended the royal wedding in 1114.] or had heard from contemporaries [Note: 1099; 1100 (“as we learned from his own [Wigbert’s] mouth”); 1101 (“those who were present commonly testify”); 1106 (“for those who were present report it”); 1118 (“which we confirm by many witnesses”); 1121 (“meanwhile it will be heard, and it is also confirmed by messengers coming from Rome”). Compare 1111 in E.: “as those who were present there at the time affirm to us,” although some of them have a very different opinion about it.], he set out in an accurate and sufficiently full narrative [Col. 0451C]. Nor did he neglect the works of other writers: he used both the lost history of the Roman expedition undertaken by Henry V in 1111 and 1112 by David the Scot [Note: Col. 1019, where I also stated that William of Malmesbury used this book. Trithemius, copying Ekkehard’s words, adds (*Ann. Hirsaug.* I, p. 349): “This David afterward became a monk under Saint Macharius, the first abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Greater in the suburb of the city of Würzburg.”] and Hesso’s book on arranging peace between pope and emperor [Note: 1119, col. 1041.]. He also inserted into his narrative, or briefly reported, letters and other documents of which he had obtained possession [Note: 1106, 1118, 1119, 1122, and 1125.].

It is sufficiently clear that the history of these years was not composed at a single time. We have seen him occupied in composing and altering it in 1106, 1114, and finally around 1117; the remaining parts too, although not year by year, should be thought to have been written over the course of time, and he revised them repeatedly afterward. From all this it is evident that Ekkehard undertook the office of historian in no casual manner; and there is no reason to doubt that everywhere he devoted himself no less to truth. The one accusation that seems justified against him is that he did not judge events and persons with a firm and consistent mind, but allowed himself to be carried away either by partisan zeal or by favor toward a king or pope, so that he later considered that what he had previously written ought to be suppressed and narrated the same matter now one way, now another.

Although I do not entirely deny this, I nevertheless wish readers to remember that affairs at that time were extraordinarily disturbed and changed very frequently, and that between kings and the Roman pontiffs there were, within only a few years, sometimes peace and sometimes the bitterest hostilities. Ekkehard always revered the Church and its head, the Roman pontiff; at the beginning, however, he also considered that the emperor defending the rights of the empire should be excused, perhaps even praised, and he inclined toward the view that is known to have prevailed then among many lovers of their homeland: that obedience was owed both to pope and emperor, although he agreed with neither in everything.

A few years later, after completing his sacred journey and visiting Rome, he went over entirely to the side of the Church [Note: Gretser already perceived this (*Rerum variarum* II, 10; *Op.* XVII, p. 73.)]. He rejoices that the younger Henry, aided by the Church, has been established as king; afterward he bitterly condemns Henry himself when he begins a new schism [Note: 1118.]; then he is filled again with the greatest joy when he sees firm peace established after the storms have been calmed [Note: 1122.]. Yet he grieves that Henry does not fulfill his vows and frustrates the hope formed concerning him; therefore he cannot [Col. 0452C] but judge that the king whom he had greeted in the most joyful words was worthy, at his death, of scarcely moderate praise [Note: 1125.]. Thus he did change his opinion concerning individual persons and events, but he does not seem to me to have fluctuated lightly or to have abandoned fair and just judgment—except in the case of the History of 1106, written amid the storms.

He also published separately the histories of Alexander the Great, the Goths, the Lombards, and the Saxons, which Ekkehard had excluded from the final recension of the Chronicle (E.), and added to them the Life of Queen Matilda, excerpted from that earlier work [Note: *Archiv* VII, p. 486; *Mon. SS.* IV, p. 283.]. Since he had not yet used it in the Chronicle [Col. 0453A], perhaps he only obtained it later. Certainly there is no reason to attribute this collection, found in several manuscripts, to someone else, especially since the words [Note: Leibnitz, *SS.* III, p. 655; *Archiv* VII, pp. 488–489: “When Henry was made king in this manner, how great and what sort of commonwealth he made from one weakened and torn apart, anyone who seeks to know will be able to learn elsewhere—that is, in the succession of kings. Now something must be said, in accordance with the poverty of our little talent, about the life and conduct of his wife, a woman beloved by God. For if we wished to recount all her virtues, the hour would fail us, and even the eloquence of Homer or Maro, if present, would fail.”] with which the Life of Matilda is joined to the history of the Saxons [Note: In two passages a few words from the Life of Matilda also passed into this work (Leibnitz, p. 654: “from his wife called Hadewic,” and “Henry therefore against … concerning which we shall speak more fully shortly”).] seem to breathe the language of Ekkehard.

Although it is now clear that scarcely any medieval writer can be compared with Ekkehard in either the number or the importance of his works, his name nevertheless long remained buried in darkness and consigned to oblivion, since he disclosed it only in the preface to Henry V and in the letter to Erkembert, while adorning his other works with neither a title nor any indication of the author. It is now possible to discover that his narrative was copied by other writers of German history as well. These are the authors whom I have established drew from his books:

The Saxon Annalist (from E. and B*) [Note: Compare Martene, *Coll.* IV, p. 2; Schumacher, *Beiträge*, pp. 57–59; Stenzel, *Fr. K.* II, pp. 110–111; and what I shall say below (preface to the *Annals of Saxony*).];

Otto of Freising (from B.) [Note: He himself appeals to its testimony at VII, 7 and 11. From Otto, Godfrey of Viterbo and Alberic also took these materials (compare Stenzel II, p. 10).];

the monk of Opatowice [Note: Compare Meinert, *Wiener Jahrbücher* XLVIII, p. 36; Palacký, *Würdigung der böhmischen Geschichtschreiber*, p. 65.];

Helmold (from E.) [Note: See above, no. 105; compare Lappenberg, *Archiv* VI, p. 559.];

the Saxon Chronographer (from A. and E.) [Note: Compare Schumacher, p. 65; *Archiv* VII, p. 474.];

Adalbert in the Life of Emperor Henry II [Note: *Mon. SS.* IV, p. 788.];

the short Old Celle Annals (from B*) [Note: In Mencken II, p. 435. The Leipzig autograph manuscript shows that they were written around 1200.];

the author of the Chronicle of Halberstadt (from B*) [Note: It received an addition in the Leipzig manuscript (6), col. 937, no. *2. Compare already Leibnitz II, p. 110, and Schatz in the preface to his edition.];

the monk of Pegau (from B*) [Note: In Hoffmann, *SS. Lus.* I, 1. Its epitome, made in the sixteenth century by a monk of Hamersleben, is the booklet on the foundation of the monastery of Bigau (*ibid.* IV.)];

whoever was the author—whether Godfrey or Otto—of the chronicle of Saint Pantaleon of Cologne (from B.) [Note: Compare Semler, *Versuch*, p. 108; Schumacher, p. 57, 59; Stenzel II, p. 109.];

Burchard of Ursperg [Note: Earlier writers declared Conrad of Lichtenau to be the author of the Ursperg Chronicle (first, Bruschius, *Monast. Germ.*, first century, 1551, fol., p. 168a). It is now established that Burchard, the provost from 1215 onward, wrote all or at least most of it; see Christmann, *Hist. Friderici imp. magni*, Ulm 1790, 4, pp. XII ff., XXXIII, and Braun, *Notitia historico-litteraria de codicibus manuscriptis in bibliotheca monasterii ad S. Udalricum et Afram*, Augsburg 1792, 4, II, p. 92 ff., who used Kuhn’s unpublished dissertation.], who copied almost the entire chronicle (B*) and thereby deprived Ekkehard of the palm for several centuries, so that more recent writers very frequently cite the Ursperg Chronicle [Note: Many nevertheless recognized that an older chronicle had been copied into the Ursperg Chronicle: Bellarmine (*de SS. eccl.*, final edition, Paris 1631, 8, p. 335), Freher, Goldast (see below, no. 154), Gretser (*Rer. var.* II, 10, *Op.* XVII), Vossius (*de H. L.* II, 57), Thomasius (*De plagio litterario*, Leipzig 1673, 4, §§ 585–591), Martene (see above, col. 436), Struvius (*Observationes selectae* I, 20), Schumacher (*Beiträge zur Deutschen Reichsgeschichte*, 1770, 4), Adelung (*Directorium*, p. 79), to omit more recent scholars. I have not seen Moller’s dissertation, Altdorf 1694.], whenever Ekkehard’s book ought to have been cited;

in addition, Albert of Stade (from B.) [Note: Compare Lappenberg, *Archiv* VI, p. 331.];

Hermann of Altaich (from B.) [Note: Compare *Archiv* VII, p. 475. It should rather be called Hermann’s manuscript than Ekkehard’s, since it inserts much into his text concerning the monastery of Altaich—unless I am mistaken, additions made by Hermann when he prefixed this part to his own book—and it should be published together with that work.];

the chronicle extending to 1310 [Note: Unpublished Wolfenbüttel manuscript; compare Ebert, *Archiv* VI, p. 13.];

Henry of Hervord [Note: Compare Bruns, *Beiträge*, p. 15. He seems to have possessed a manuscript similar to E., but enlarged and continued. For Henry cites many passages from Ekkehard that one searches for in vain there, extending even to the time of Frederick II (year 32). Körner drew from Henry; see *Archiv* VI, pp. 763, 592.];

Andrew of Regensburg (from B.) [Note: He found the manuscript in the monastery of Prüfening: *chronicon generale*, in Eckard I, p. 1933; compare p. 2071. He also used this source in the *Bavarian Chronicle* (*SS. Kulpis.*, ed. Schilter, pp. 8, 16, 17.)];

the Bamberg Chronicle “of Henry II and the bishopric of Bamberg founded by him” [Note: See the Hamburg manuscript (*Archiv* VI, p. 242), pp. 156, 157, 185];

Trithemius; and Staindelius.

The monk of Hamersleben reduced Ekkehard’s entire Chronicle (B*) to an epitome [Note: Published by Mader, *Antiquitates Brunsvicenses*, p. 136; Leibnitz I, p. 707. Compare what I shall say about his manuscript in *Archiv* IX.]; excerpts are also found in a certain Hanover manuscript [Note: *Archiv* VIII, p. 641, from a manuscript of Saint Michael’s at Hildesheim.] and elsewhere.

We also see the histories of peoples used in other works, especially the Saxon history: in the booklet “How the Saxons first came to the land of Saxony” [Note: In Ludewig, *Reliquiae manuscriptorum*, VIII, p. 154.]; in the little work “On the Origin of the Suebi” [Note: In Goldast, *SS. rerum Suevicarum*.]; and in the history entitled “Old Celle Annals” [Note: In Mencken II, p. 379: “You will therefore find the deeds of the great and glorious duke Witikind in the histories of Charlemagne and in the chronicle on the origin of the Saxons.” What follows [Col. 0455D] agrees for the most part with Ekkehard.]. Others claimed the History of Alexander for themselves, so that Ekkehard seems to have enjoyed in Germany [Col. 0455A], especially northern Germany, almost the same authority that Hermann had attained in Alemannia, Bavaria, and Austria, and Sigebert in Belgium and Gaul.

Since Ekkehard’s works had become so widely disseminated, it is not surprising that very many manuscripts are still found. I trust that readers will rejoice with me that almost all of them could be used in preparing this edition. They are as follows:

**A.** Codex of the Karlsruhe library, no. 36, parchment, quarto, containing several works written by different hands in the eleventh and twelfth centuries [Note: I shall describe them more precisely in *Archiv*, vol. IX.], now joined in a single volume. At the end, fols. 171–186 contain the Chronicle of Würzburg; fols. 187–197 contain Ekkehard’s Chronicle for 1057–1099 (1101) [Note: See above, col. 445.]. Both were copied most diligently by the highly esteemed Molter; afterward, when the manuscript was kindly sent to us, I collated them myself.

**B.** Of all the manuscripts of this text, the most distinguished is:

**1. Jenen­sis**, parchment, quarto, acquired from the library of Bosius and marked there with number 19. It now contains 199 folios. Concerning Ekkehard’s autograph [Note: It had previously been described by Struvius, *Observationes selectae* I, p. 316, and *Archiv* III, p. 277 ff.] see *Archiv* VII, p. 472 ff., and above, p. 4.

**1b.** I used the name Wolfenbüttel manuscript for the chronicle of Saint Pantaleon of Cologne, described in *Archiv* VII, p. 643 ff. The following should be assigned to the same recension:

**2. Brugensis**, formerly belonging to Blessed Mary of the Dunes, paper, fifteenth century, discovered first by Pertz and examined more carefully by our Bethmann in 1842. From the time of Charlemagne onward it repeats Ekkehard’s Chronicle in the form in which it was completed in 1106, so that the folios missing from manuscript 1 can be supplied from it [Note: At the beginning it provides only an excerpt from Ekkehard and other sources; later it omits at least the histories of the Franks, Goths, and Lombards.].

**3. Vindobonensis**, which ought to be entitled in the name of Hermann of Altaich rather than Ekkehard [Note: See above, no. 136.].

To these may appropriately be added the manuscripts in which a continuation down to 1125 has been appended to this text (B*). All of them mention the monastery of Schwarzach either in several places or in a single passage. If one denies that these notices were added by Ekkehard [Note: I deny it because most of them agree with the Chronicle of Schwarzach, which in turn refers to another, older source (Ludewig, *SS. R. Bamb.* II, pp. 9–12 ff.).], one must conclude that they derive from a copy of that monastery, of the kind we know once existed [Note: In the Paris manuscript containing the compilation of the Saxon Annalist, fol. 219 (under 1116), the following words are written by a fifteenth-century hand: “Likewise, in the chronicles of Eusebius, which are kept in the monastery of Schwarzach, you will find a clearer account of the dispute concerning the bishopric of Würzburg.” Ekkehard’s history is plainly indicated here.], [Col. 0456A] [Note: The common origin of all is also proved by individual readings, for example, col. 639, variant reading 2490; col. 1043, variant reading 1466; and others.].

Besides the manuscript of Freher, later called Heidelbergensis, whose fate is unknown [Note: Freher cites it in the directory prefixed to *SS. R. Germ.*, vol. I, under the name of the Schwarzach Chronicle (compare Goldast, *SS. R. Alam.* I, p. 207; *Apologia pro Henrico IV*, p. 13). Thomasius testifies that it was brought into the Heidelberg library (*De plagio litterario*, § 591). It is now found neither there nor, so far, anywhere in Rome.], the following belong here:

**4. Erlangensis** [Note: Compare Hocker, *Bibliotheca Heilbronnensis*, pp. 86–88; *Archiv* VII, pp. 111, 496, 497.], formerly Heilsbronnensis, parchment, twelfth century, folio. Its distinctive feature is that it does not contain all the shorter additions from Sigebert that were added to this recension, and in other passages as well it comes closer to 1. Otherwise it was written rather carelessly, so that the scribe did not sufficiently restrain himself from changing the wording and arranging it differently. It includes Schwarzach material under 815, 1074, and 1121.

**5. Gothanus** [Note: Compare Jacobs, *Beiträge* II, p. 386; *Archiv* VII, p. 505.], formerly Saint Peter’s at Erfurt, parchment, twelfth century, folio, very well written. Although it contains the complete text of Ekkehard, it can scarcely be counted among his manuscripts, since it has enlarged the work with fragments taken from Lambert and with several other additions; moreover, it has extended the continuation down to 1137, so that the scribe seems rather to have created a new chronicle than to have copied an exemplar of Ekkehard. It places the foundation of the monastery of Schwarzach under 815.

There are several manuscripts that come close to 5 [Note: Compare no. 890, col. 931, no. 238*.], and they agree with one another so closely that there can be no doubt that one was copied from another, or several from a common exemplar [Note: Compare col. 883, no. 231*, and many other passages.]. They not only contain the Schwarzach material under 815, 1074, and 1121, but also mention its abbots under 1095 and 1112. They are:

**6. Lipsiensis**, parchment, twelfth century, folio; see *Archiv* VII, p. 497.

**7. Zizensis**, formerly *Liber sanctae Mariae in Posavia*, parchment, thirteenth century, folio, written fairly carefully, though not by a single hand [Note: It nevertheless omits certain passages under 949, 1033, 1092, and 1115.]. It is distinguished by a continuation which Eccard published under the title *Annals of Posau*. Although this agrees with the Erfurt manuscript (5) down to 1137, Ekkehard’s text departs from it.

**8. Dresdensis** (I 49), paper, fifteenth–sixteenth century, folio [*Archiv* VI, p. 223; VII, p. 499].

9. Three codices, enlarged by a brief continuation extending to 1169 [Note: [Col. 0456D] The numbers 1184 follow. This chronicle was without cause attributed to Guido Calixtus (cf. Archiv. I, p. 111; V, p. 687; VII, p. 499). For in codex 9b, in a sixteenth-century hand, these words are written: “Pope Calixtus II, formerly called Guido, born from the lineage of the counts of Burgundy, composed this history, as you will find in the same history, especially in the Life of Henry IV and V.” But who the author of that history was down to the year 1099 is unknown (Götze, *Merkwürdigkeiten der königl. Bibl. zu Dresden* I, no. 62, p. 483).]: 9a.) Dresden, I, 48, formerly [the book] of St. Mary of Celle, parchment, twelfth century, folio (Archiv. VI, p. 223; VII, p. 498); [Col. 0457A] 9b.) Dresden, F. 60, parchment, fourteenth century, folio (Archiv. VII, p. 499) [Note: [Col. 0457D] Cf. Götze, loc. cit. I; Ebert, Archiv. V, p. 687]; 9c.) Jena II, 65, parchment, fourteenth century, folio (Archiv. VII, p. 498) [Note: [Col. 0457D] Cf. Struve, *Observationes selectae* I, p. 315; Archiv. III, p. 272].

10. Stuttgart, historical manuscript no. 411, folio, formerly Zwiefalten [Note: [Col. 0457D] Concerning it, see Hess, *Monumenta Guelfica*, p. 166; Archiv. I, p. 397; II, p. 310; III, p. 589. The Weingarten codex, about which Dümge thought there was material in the same work, I, p. 43, and (Mone?) 402, did not exist], parchment, twelfth century, defective at the beginning, subsequently corrupted here and there and enlarged by additions, almost all of which were drawn from Bernold [Note: [Col. 0457D] See the years 694, 720, 734, 744, 926, 982, 997, 1045, 1048, 1052, 1055, 1066, 1070, 1074, 1076, 1077, 1087, 1088. Others, at the years 431, 470, and 479, seem to have been taken from Fredegar; a few others from different sources]. Moreover, it contains all the Swarzach material found in the other codices and adds one passage that perhaps concerns the same monastery [Note: [Col. 0457D] Year 1076]. This codex, which I described more accurately in Archiv. VII, pp. 500 ff., had been obtained by

11. Burchard, provost of Ursperg, who, after copying this codex, composed the chronicle extending to 1229, which is in everyone’s hands. I have used the first edition, which the Augsburg printer Johann Miller produced in 1515 from a copy of Conrad Peutinger’s found in the monastery of Ursperg [Col. 0457B] [Note: [Col. 0457D] This is attested by Weissung, canon of Ursperg, in 1524; cf. Christmann, loc. cit., p. XV n. Thus Braun was mistaken (loc. cit., p. 92) when he says that Peutinger used a fifteenth-century Augsburg codex]. [Note: [Col. 0457D] It was later published at Strasbourg in 1537 and 1540; at Basel in 1569; and at Strasbourg in 1609, folio].

This is, so far as I know, the only codex of the chronicle addressed to Henry V in 1114.

C.) Cambridge, Christ’s College no. 373, parchment, twelfth century, Ekkehard’s autograph, carefully written and elegantly ornamented, which Pertz discovered in 1827 and accurately described (Archiv. VII, p. 493). Perhaps it was brought to England by Matilda, the wife of Henry V, and for that reason was never copied in Germany.

D.) The principal codex of this recension is the Royal Parisian no. 4889, parchment, twelfth century, folio. The histories of Alexander, the Goths, and the Saxons had been omitted, [Col. 0457C] but after several leaves were inserted they were later supplied by the same hand; thereafter the quires were numbered in a new order [Note: [Col. 0457D] Fascicles V, XII, XIII, and XX were inserted. In place of XXV, XXVI, and XXVII, the numbers XX, XXI, and XXII were written, which seem to preserve the earlier order]. Although this may seem to indicate the author’s hand, this codex can scarcely be attributed to him, since it was written rather carelessly. At the end, the *History of Jerusalem* is followed by a catalogue of the bishops of Jerusalem. It seems to have been copied from this:

[Col. 0458A] D2.) Paris, Arsenal, no. 6, formerly the book of Green Valley near Brussels [Note: [Col. 0457D] Cf. Sander, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 139, and Hormayr, Archiv. 1828, p. 807], paper, fourteenth century, folio. It begins with the year 576, preceded by the title: “The second part of Eusebius’s chronicle.” At the end it adds a few minor items [Note: [Col. 0458D] Besides brief notices for 1095 and 1100, also these verses:

“Julius . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . burned with triple fivefold light,

When the Franks capture the city by mighty force.

In the thousandth year, and also the hundred and fourth,

The city of Acre is captured by force, which is called Ptolemais.

It is not Accaron, as everyone thinks Acre is;

That is Philistia; this is called Ptolemais.”

Cf. concerning this codex Archiv. VIII, p. 356].

E.) Two codices exhibit the final form of the book:

E1.) Berlin, Lat. no. 295, parchment, twelfth century, small folio, formerly Havelberg [Note: [Col. 0458D] There, on 20 July 1821, it was marked by someone unknown and was rediscovered by the distinguished Riedel (see *Serapeum* I, p. 185)]. On the final page one reads: “This book belongs to St. Mary the Virgin and St. Lawrence the Martyr at Havelberg. The lord Bishop Sichebodo collated it; he held the see from 1206 to 1220.” The codex is lacking seven quires at the beginning (there were formerly twenty-four, now there are seventeen) and two leaves; it is so badly damaged that often individual lines have been erased by decay. Otherwise it is well written, corrected here and there by a contemporary hand, and enlarged in the margin by certain notes concerning the archbishops and abbots of Magdeburg [Col. 0458B] [Note: [Col. 0458D] At the years 937, 968, 981, 1004, 1013, 1023, 1051, 1063, 1076, 1099, 1107, 1113, and 1119]. I incorporated these into the text.

E2.) The Royal Parisian C. no. 4889 A., formerly the book of St. Mary at Rastede [Note: [Col. 0458D] At the beginning and end, a few nearly erased notes about the book’s fate are written: “Brother Conrad, prior of Vechta, redeemed this book at Bremen for five quarter-marks”; and elsewhere: “This book of chronicles [was bought] from Herm . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . of Delmenhorst near . . . . . . . . . . for his son for three and a half solidi”], of the diocese of Bremen, parchment, thirteenth century, folio. It consists of fourteen quires and 111 leaves, the last of which has been cut away. Since it was copied from E1, it supplies the portion lost from that codex and must be cited in its place here and there.

To class D or E belong a codex whose fragment Cramer found and published [Note: [Col. 0458D] *On Some Fragments of Ancient Parchments*, Kiel 1826, quarto, pp. 20 ff.], another that I mentioned above as having been in the monastery of St. Michael at Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0458D] See no. 143], and several others read by medieval writers. I have learned nothing certain about a codex seen by the distinguished Haupt in a Bohemian library; nor do I know to which recension the fragment of the Vienna codex, *Hist. prof.* no. 645, belongs [Note: [Col. 0458D] Cf. Archiv. III, p. 189]. The codices used by the editors of the Ursperg Chronicle also seem to have contained Ekkehard’s Chronicle: the codex of the library of Dalberg, bishop of Worms [Note: [Col. 0458D] It was kept at Ladenburg (see Ullmann, *Memoria I*, Dalberg 1840, quarto, p. 7) and perhaps later came into the Heidelberg collection], and the codex of the library of the Augustinians of Strasbourg, collated by Crato Mylius in 1537 [Col. 0459B], as well as another used in preparing the edition of 1569.

Finally, the codices must be mentioned in which those histories of Alexander, the Goths, the Lombards, and the Saxons, together with the associated *Life of Queen Matilda*, are found: the Vatican–Wolfenbüttel codex, two Munich codices, and the Würzburg codex [Note: [Col. 0459B] Concerning these, cf. Archiv. VII, pp. 486–489]. To these must be added the Royal Parisian no. 6181 (Colbert 3999), paper, fifteenth century, which contains the histories of the Franks, Goths, and Lombards. In other manuscript books only the history of Alexander the Great is found—for example, in the Munich, Hanover, Weimar [Note: [Col. 0459B] Archiv. VII, pp. 490–491], and Jena codices [Note: [Col. 0459B] Ibid. VIII, p. 698].

Using these exceedingly abundant resources, I set out first to publish as faithfully as possible the Chronicle completed in 1106 from the autograph codex, while carefully indicating all the corrections, changes, and additions that Ekkehard is discernibly to have made later. Then I appended the continuations as they appear in codices C, D, E, and B*, retaining the different texts in full wherever I could; the minor differences among them I reported either in the margin or in the notes. Finally, I did not wish to reprint the *History of Jerusalem*, already edited by Martène, since it agrees for the most part word for word with the Chronicle; but I have shared its preface and conclusion with readers and have accurately indicated the form and order of the book [Note: [Col. 0460B] In 1836 I wrote the inaugural dissertation *On the First Part of the Ursperg Chronicle, Its Author, Sources, and Authority among Later Writers*, a specimen of which was printed there. From it I have also transferred some material into this preface].

I cannot help greatly rejoicing that I have now happily completed in my homeland this edition of Ekkehard, to which I first applied myself nine years ago at Copenhagen and afterward at Berlin, and which I continued for several years at Hanover, using the principal codices, some sent there and others copied out during my travels.

[Col. 0460B] Written at Kiel on Easter Day, 1843.

G. WAITZ.

[Col. 0459]

## The Würzburg Chronicle, by Ekkehard, as it seems

[Col. 0459C] God formed the creation of things in six days. First . . . [lacuna]

(H. S.) [Note: [Col. 0459D] I indicate in this way the epitome made from Herimann’s Chronicle, which Sichard published from the St. Gall codex]. In the forty-second year of Octavian Augustus Caesar, and in the twenty-ninth year after Egypt had been reduced to a province and Cleopatra had been defeated together with Antony, but in the 752nd year from the foundation of the City, in the third year of the 190th Olympiad, our Lord Jesus Christ was born at Bethlehem of Judea, after 3,542 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world according to the Hebrew text, and 5,199 according to the Seventy interpreters.

In his forty-third year [Note: [Col. 0459D] In what follows I have omitted the empty years].

In the year 44. Augustus adopted Tiberius and Agrippa as sons. Herod killed the infants.

45. Judas the Galilean urges the Jews to revolt.

[Col. 0459D] 46. The orator Asinius Pollio dies.

47. Herod, king of Judea, dies in great agony; Archelaus reigns in his place for nine years.

48. A great famine occurs at Rome.

50. Tiberius Caesar subdues the Dalmatians and Sarmatians.

53. The gates of Janus, which had already been closed for twelve years by Augustus, are opened.

[Col. 0460C] 55. An eclipse of the sun occurs.

56. Archelaus is banished by Augustus to Vienna, a city of Gaul, and Judea is entrusted to tetrarchs.

(H. R.) [Note: [Col. 0460D] That is, Paul the Deacon’s *Roman History*]. After Octavian returned victorious from the East to Rome, he was then first hailed as Augustus, because he had enlarged the commonwealth, which from that time he alone controlled for forty-four years; previously he had ruled for twelve years with Antony and Lepidus. In his time, on the Lord’s birthday, a fountain of oil flowed from the earth across the Tiber, from a tavern for veterans, throughout the entire day. He was exceedingly merciful toward citizens and faithful to his friends; the foremost among them were Maecenas for his silence, and Agrippa for his modesty and endurance of labor. He also cherished the poets Virgil and Flaccus, devoting himself so intensely to liberal studies that no day passed without his reading, writing, or declaiming. He gloried in the saying: “I found Rome of brick; I leave it of marble.” He was handsome in every part of his body, but his eyes were like the rays of the brightest stars. When a certain soldier turned his eyes away from his face, and was asked why he did so, he replied: “Because I cannot endure the light of your eyes.” He died at the age of seventy-five, in the fifty-sixth year of his reign, at the town of Atella. After his death, the senate judged that he should be honored in many ways, saying: “Would that he had either never been born or never died!”

Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, reigned for twenty-three years.

(H. S.) In the first year of his reign, Herod the tetrarch, son of Herod the Great, held the kingdom of the Jews for twenty-four years.

2. The mathematicians are expelled from the City.

3. The historiographer Livy dies [Note: [Col. 0461] “Luuius” in c.]. The poet Ovid dies in exile.

4. Germanicus, sent by Tiberius, defeats the Germans. Thirteen cities collapse in an earthquake.

5. Germanicus Caesar dies.

6. The poet Fenestella dies.

7. Tiberius summons many kings to him and never sends them back.

[Col. 0461B] 8. Pompey’s theater is burned.

9. Tiberius makes Drusus his partner in the rule; Drusus dies of poison in the same year.

12. Pilate is sent by Tiberius as governor of Judea.

15. Our Lord Jesus Christ is baptized, beginning his thirtieth year according to the flesh.

16. John the Baptist is beheaded by Herod the tetrarch.

18. The Lord suffers and rises again. An eclipse of the sun and an earthquake occur.

19. James, the Lord’s brother, appointed by the apostles bishop of Jerusalem, holds the see for thirty years.

20. Pilate, setting up Caesar’s image in the temple, provokes riots among the Jews.

[Col. 0461C] 21. Sejanus urges Tiberius to destroy the Jews.

22. Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, surnamed Herod, accuses his uncle Herod the tetrarch at Rome and is imprisoned by Tiberius.

23. (H. R.) Tiberius grievously afflicted the Roman people and himself died of poison. Because he was called Claudius Tiberius Nero, he was nicknamed by jesters “Biberius Mero” on account of his drunkenness. Before assuming the empire he was sufficiently prudent in military matters and sufficiently fortunate, possessing literary knowledge and distinguished for great eloquence; but he had a very evil disposition, pretending to want what he did not want. He himself waged no wars; he administered the state with moderation, to such an extent that, when certain provincial governors wished to increase the taxes, he wrote that it was the duty of a good shepherd to shear the sheep, not to flay them. But little by little he changed for the worse, for he killed both his sons and many patricians and consuls. As the arts of war were neglected, Armenia was ravaged by the Parthians, Moesia by the Dacians, Pannonia by the Sarmatians, and Gaul by neighboring peoples. In the twenty-third year of his reign, at the age of seventy-eight, he died in Campania, amid the immense joy of all.

(H. S.—OROS.) Gaius Caligula reigned three years, six months, and eight days. He was a most wicked man [Note: [Col. 0461] “Most heavenly” in c.]. He is said to have exclaimed: “Would that the Roman people had one neck!”

[Col. 0462A] (H. S.) Year 1. Herod Agrippa is appointed king of Judea by Gaius and reigns for seven years.

2. The Jews are defeated at Alexandria; Philo, a most distinguished writer [Note: [Col. 0461] “Most beloved” in c.], appeals on their behalf to Gaius, but accomplishes nothing.

3. Pilate kills himself, overwhelmed by many calamities inflicted by Gaius.

4. Matthew writes the Gospel in Hebrew. Gaius is killed by his guards in the palace at the age of twenty-nine, in the fourth year of his reign. (H. R.—Cf. Josephus, *Jewish War* II.8.) He was the grandson of Drusus and Tiberius, Augustus’s stepsons, and was utterly criminal; he committed sexual offenses with his sisters. Herod the tetrarch, who had been responsible for the death of John the Baptist and had taken part in the Lord’s Passion, also sought Gaius’s friendship and, compelled by Herodias, came to Rome; but after being accused by Herod Agrippa, son of his brother Aristobulus, he lost his tetrarchy and, fleeing to Spain, died of grief.

(H. S.) Claudius: thirteen years, eight months, and eighteen days.

In the first year of his reign:

2. Peter comes to Rome and holds the episcopate there for twenty-five years.

3. Evodius is ordained the first bishop of Antioch. Herod Agrippa is struck by an angel; his son Agrippa reigns in his place for twenty-six years.

4. A great famine occurs. Claudius conquers Britain.

5. A new island, thirty stadia in extent, appears in the sea.

6. The Roman citizens are counted under Claudius and found to number 69,144,000 [Note: [Col. 0461] “LX. VIIII. C. XL thousand IIII” in c.].

7. Thirty thousand Jews are killed during a revolt on the days of unleavened bread.

9. Claudius expels the Jews from the City [Note: [Col. 0461] “Cladius” in c.].

10. A great famine occurs.

11. Claudius appoints Felix procurator of Judea.

12. Simon Magus becomes the author of the heresy of simony.

13. A certain Egyptian pseudoprophet, leading many Jews astray, is suppressed by Felix.

14. Claudius dies at the age of sixty-four, in the fourteenth year of his reign. He was Caligula’s uncle, the son of Drusus, who has a monument near Mainz; Caligula was his nephew. (H. R.—OROS.) In his time the greatest famine seized Rome; the emperor, assailed by insults, was shamefully pelted with fragments of bread by the people in the forum and fled; he died of poison.

(H. S.) Nero: thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. He was the most disgraceful in every respect. He initiated the first persecution of Christians.

1. In the first year of his reign a revolt arose in Caesarea and destroyed many Jews. Festus succeeded Felix.

2. The apostle Paul is sent to Rome by the governor Festus.

3. Up to this point Luke the evangelist brought the book of the Acts of the Apostles, comprising twenty-six years from the Lord’s Passion.

4. The poet Statius is held in high regard.

5. Nero killed his mother Agrippina, his mother’s sister, and his wife Octavia.

6. Nero raged in boundless luxury, debauchery, and sloth.

7. James, the Lord’s brother, is stoned by the Jews. Albinus succeeded Festus; Florus succeeded Albinus.

8. The evangelist Mark suffers at Alexandria.

9. Nero builds the Neronian Baths.

10. Nero sets fire to a large part of Rome so that he might see a likeness of burning Troy.

11. Nero kills Seneca, his teacher.

[Col. 0463B] 12. Vespasian is sent by Nero as commander of the army against the Jews.

13. Peter and Paul are killed by Nero. A pestilence occurs.

14. Nero kills himself. Linus, the first pope after blessed Peter, holds the see for twelve years. Ignatius is ordained the second bishop of Antioch.

(H. R.) Nero disfigured the Roman empire through unprecedented luxury and expenditure, using cold and hot ointments and golden nets for fishing. He also danced and sang on the stage. He dared nothing in war and nearly lost Britain. At last declared a public enemy by the senate, when he was being sought for punishment, he was captured, publicly beaten with rods, and thrown from a rock [Note: [Col. 0463] “Thrown down” in c.]. Fleeing, he killed himself at the fourth milestone from the City, in the suburban estate of his freedman, in the thirty-first year of his life and the fourteenth of his reign. With him the entire family of Augustus was extinguished.

Galba reigned seven months. He was strangled by Otho in the Roman forum and was buried in his own gardens in the seventy-third year of his life, on the Via Aurelia not far from the City.

Otho: three months. When he saw that he was being defeated by Vitellius, he killed himself at Bedriacum in Italy, in the thirty-eighth year of his life, on the ninety-fifth day of his reign. These three seized the empire together after Nero: Galba in Spain, Vitellius in Germany, and Otho at Rome.

(H. S.—H. R.—OROS.) Vitellius: eight months. Vespasian, fighting in Judea, is proclaimed emperor by the army. Vitellius is captured by Vespasian’s commanders.
