He had burned Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, in the Capitol; now he is dragged naked through the City in public, while filth is thrown repeatedly into his mouth, and finally he is strangled and thrown into the Tiber, in the fifty-seventh year of his life, the eighth month and first day of his reign.

(H. R.) Vespasian: nine years, ten months, and twelve days; a man distinguished by military courage, though of obscure birth.

(H. S.) In the first year of this reign, Titus besieges the Jews, tormented by indescribable famine.

2. Jerusalem is destroyed by Titus in the fortieth year from the Lord’s Passion and the 1,089th year from the first foundation of the temple under Solomon.

5. The historiographer Josephus is held in high regard.

[Col. 0464A] 7. A colossal statue is erected, 107 feet high.

9. A pestilence occurs at Rome, and three cities in Cyprus are overthrown by an earthquake.

10. Vespasian dies of a discharge of the bowels at a villa near the Sabines, in the sixty-ninth year of his life, the ninth year of his reign, on the eighth day. (H. R.) Claudius first sent him to Germany, then to Britain; he fought the enemy thirty-two times, added two very powerful peoples, twenty towns, and the Isle of Wight to the Roman empire. He ruled the empire with the greatest moderation, though greedy for money; he unjustly took it from some and gave it especially to the needy [Note: [Col. 0463] “From no one” in c.].

(H. S.) Titus, son of Vespasian: two years and two months; a man admirable for every kind of virtue, so that he was called “the wealth and love of humankind.”

[Col. 0464B] In the first year of his reign, Titus built an amphitheater at Rome; at its dedication he killed 5,000 wild beasts.

2. (H. R.) Pope Cletus, the second, held the see for twelve years. Titus died in the same villa as his father, in the forty-second year of his life, the eighth month and twentieth day of his reign. He was so good that, when one day at dinner he remembered that he had given no one anything that day [Note: [Col. 0463] The text is defective in c.], he said: “Friends, I have lost a day” [Note: [Col. 0463] “illa” corrected to “illo” in c.]. At Jerusalem he fought twelve defenders with twelve arrows.

(H. S.) Domitian, Titus’s brother, reigned fifteen years and five months. Tainted with every crime, he launched the second persecution against Christians.

1. Domitian forbade the creation of eunuchs.

2. Titus is enrolled among the gods by decree of the senate.

[Col. 0464C] 3. Three Vestal virgins are condemned for sexual misconduct.

4. Arianus, the first bishop of Alexandria after the evangelist Mark, dies after twenty-two years. Abilius holds the see in his place for thirteen years.

6. Domitian ordered himself to be called god and lord.

9. The heresy of Menander the magician and many others arises.

10. The Romans suffer many evils from the emperor and from their enemies.

11. Domitian triumphs over the Dacians and Germans.

12. Pope Clement, the third, holds the see for nine years. Cornelia, a Vestal virgin, is buried alive for sexual misconduct.

13. Domitian kills many nobles.

[Col. 0464D] 14. The apostle John, sent into exile by Domitian to the island of Patmos, writes the Apocalypse.

15. Domitian banishes Flavia Domitilla and many others into exile for the faith of Christ.

16. (H. R.) After committing many crimes, Domitian is cruelly killed by his own men in the thirty-fifth year of his life and the fifteenth of his reign. He permitted no statue of himself to be erected in the Capitol except one of gold or silver; he killed his cousins.

(H. S.) Nerva the old: one year, four months, and eight days. By his first edict he recalled all exiles. Saint [Note: [Col. 0463] “Sancte” in 1.] John, returning from exile, wrote the Gospel. [Col. 0465A] Nerva, worn out by illness, dies in the seventy-first year of his life; he reigned one year, four months, and eight days. (H. R.) In private life he had been temperate and energetic, of middling rank; with the help of Petronius, prefect of the praetorian guard, and likewise of Paternius, the slayer of Domitian, he became emperor and showed himself exceptionally just and civil. He adopted Trajan as his successor.

(H. S.) Trajan, a Spaniard by birth: nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days.

1. In the first year of his reign, Cerdo, the third bishop of Alexandria, holds the see for twelve years.

2. The apostle John falls asleep at Ephesus in the sixty-eighth year from the Lord’s Passion.

4. Pope Evaristus, the fourth, holds the see for eight years.

5. Trajan subjects many peoples to the Roman empire.

[Col. 0465B] 6. Simeon, son of Cleopas, bishop of Jerusalem, is crucified at the age of 120. Justus is ordained in his place. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, is delivered to beasts at Rome. Orion is appointed in his place.

8. Earthquakes destroy many cities, and the Golden House perishes in a fire. The Pantheon is also burned by lightning.

9. Pliny Secundus, the distinguished philosopher, softens Trajan’s attitude toward the Christians.

12. Pope Alexander, the fifth, holds the see for ten years.

13. Primus, the fourth bishop of Alexandria, holds the see for twelve years.

14. After Justus, bishop of Jerusalem, Zacchaeus [Col. 0465C] holds the see; after him Tobias; after him Benjamin; then John; after him Matthias; Philip succeeds him.

16. Trajan makes Armenia, Assyria [Note: [Col. 0465] “assyria” in c.], and Mesopotamia provinces.

18. The Jews, stirred up, carry out great massacres; but after being defeated in Alexandria, they are slaughtered everywhere by everyone. An earthquake almost completely destroys Antioch.

19. Trajan dies of a discharge of the bowels in the sixty-fourth year of his life, the ninth month and fourth day, the nineteenth year, sixth month, and fifteenth day of his reign. He alone among all the emperors is buried within the City. (H. R.) His bones, placed in a golden urn, were set beneath the column in the forum he built; the column is 140 feet high. Such honor was paid to his memory that even down to our own age the senators acclaim [Note: [Col. 0465] “acclemetur” in c.] succeeding emperors only with the words: “More fortunate than Augustus, better than Trajan.” At Rome he showed himself equal to everyone, harming no senator, so that throughout his entire reign only one senator was condemned, and that by the senate.

(H. S.) Aelius Hadrian: twenty-one years. Instructed by Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and by Aristides, a wise man, through apologetic books, he became mild toward Christians.

In the first year of his reign, Hadrian restored Alexandria at public expense.

[Col. 0466A] 2. Hadrian again defeats the Jews.

3. Pope Sixtus, the sixth, holds the see for ten years.

4. An earthquake occurs.

5. Hadrian gives a law to the Athenians.

6. Justin holds the episcopate at Alexandria for eleven years.

7. At Jerusalem, Seneca is the tenth bishop; after him Justus, the eleventh; then Levi; after him Ephres; afterward Jesse; after him Judas.

11. Saturninus and two others establish a heresy.

12. Pope Telesphorus holds the see for eleven years.

13. Cornelius is appointed bishop of Antioch.

14. Nicopolis and Caesarea collapse in an earthquake.

15. A temple of Venus is built at Rome.

[Col. 0466B] 17. The Jews ravage Palestine. Eumenes holds the episcopate at Alexandria for thirteen years.

18. The Jews are slain everywhere in great massacres.

19. Jerusalem is restored by Aelius Hadrian and named Aelia after him.

20. Mark is ordained the first bishop of Jerusalem from the Gentiles, after fifteen bishops from the Jewish people had already died.

21. Hadrian dies of dropsy, over sixty years old.

Antonius, surnamed Pius: twenty-two years and three months. He becomes merciful toward Christians.

In the first year of this reign, Pope Hyginus, the seventh, holds the see for four years. Valentinus and Cerdo attack the Church with heresy.

[Col. 0466C] 6. Pope Pius holds the see for fifteen years. Heros is appointed bishop of Antioch.

8. Mark holds the episcopate at Alexandria for ten years.

19. Caeladion holds the episcopate at Alexandria for fourteen years.

21. Pope Anicetus, the tenth, holds the see for eleven years. Cassianus is ordained bishop of Jerusalem, followed by Publius, Maximus, Julianus, Gainus, Symmachus, Gaius, Julianus, and Capito.

23. Antoninus Pius dies at Lorium in the seventy-seventh year of his life.

Marcus Antoninus Verus, together with his brother Lucius Commodus Aurelius: nineteen years and one month. They administered the empire with equal authority.

In the first, second, third, and fourth years of their reign:

[Col. 0466D] Seleucia is captured by the Romans. The Caesars triumph over the Parthians.

6. (H. S.) Many saints are crowned under these emperors. At this time a great plague almost destroyed the Roman army and many other provinces.

7. Pope Soter, the eleventh, holds the see for eight years. The wise man Theophilus is ordained bishop of Antioch.

8. Agrippinus holds the episcopate at Alexandria for eleven years.

14. The emperor Antoninus wages many battles, both personally and through his commanders, against the enemies of the Romans.

16. Pope Eleutherus, the twelfth, holds the see for thirteen years.

[Col. 0467A] 17. Antoninus makes his son Commodus his partner in the rule.

18. Lucius, king of Britain, obtains from Pope Eleutherus that he may become a Christian.

19. Antoninus dies in Pannonia.

Lucius Antoninus Commodus reigns for thirteen years after his father’s death.

In the first year of his reign:

2. Julianus holds the episcopate at Alexandria for ten years.

3. Pantaenus and Clement are held in high regard at Alexandria.

4. Maximus is ordained bishop of Jerusalem. After him come Antonius, Valens, Dulcianus, Narcissus, Dius, Germanio, Gordius, and Narcissus.

5. The Commodian Baths are built at Rome.

[Col. 0467B] 7. Origen is born at Alexandria.

8. Irenaeus of Lyons is held in high regard as a bishop.

9. The Capitol and the library at Rome are burned by lightning.

10. After the head of the Colossus is removed, Commodus puts on it the head of his own image. Pope Victor, the thirteenth, holds the see for thirteen years.

11. Demetrius, the eleventh bishop of Alexandria.

12. Serapion is ordained bishop of Antioch.

13. Commodus, harmful to everyone, is strangled in the house of the Vestal Virgins.

Aelius Pertinax: six months. Julianus kills him and reigns for seven months.

Severus, an African by birth: seventeen years. He defeats Julianus in a civil war and calls himself Pertinax.

[Col. 0467C] 4. In the fourth year of his reign, Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, and many other distinguished bishops are held in high regard.

6. Severus defeats the Parthians and Arabs.

8. The Severan Baths are built at Antioch.

9. Pope Zephyrinus, the fourteenth, holds the see for eighteen years.

10. Severus, the fifth persecutor, crowns very many saints; among them Leonides, the father of Origen, is martyred.

13. Perpetua and Felicity are given to the beasts at Carthage.

15. Severus builds a wall in Britain, 132,000 paces long, from sea to sea.

16. Tertullian the African is held in high regard.

[Col. 0467D] 17. Severus dies in Britain.

Antoninus Caracalla: seven years.

1. Asclepiades is appointed bishop of Antioch.

2. Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, is appointed by Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem.

4. Antoninus Caracalla receives his surname from the type of garment he distributed at Rome.

5. Antoninus builds at Rome baths bearing his name.

6. Antoninus, overcome by lust, marries his stepmother Julia.

7. Antoninus is killed in the forty-second year of his life.

Opilius Macrinus: one year. Macrinus is killed together with his son Diadumenian. [Col. 0468A] Philetus is ordained bishop of Antioch.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus: four years.

1. Pope Callistus, the fifteenth, holds the see for five years.

2. Hippolytus is held in high regard as a bishop.

3. Nicopolis in Palestine, formerly called Emmaus, is founded.

4. Aurelius is killed at Rome in a military revolt.

Aurelius Alexander: thirteen years. Previously he had been uniquely devoted to his mother.

1. Alexander defeats Xerxes, king of the Persians.

3. Pope Urban, the sixteenth, holds the see for eight years. He converts many nobles to the faith.

4. Ulpian, the distinguished jurist, is held in high regard.

5. The Neronian Baths are called Alexandrian.

[Col. 0468B] 6. The presbyter Geminus, Hippolytus, and Herillus are held in high regard.

7. Zebennus, the eleventh bishop of Antioch.

8. Mammaea, Alexander’s mother, had the most celebrated teacher Origen [Note: [Col. 0467D] “celebrat rimum” in c.] summoned to her and arranged to hear him.

10. Pope Pontian, the seventeenth, holds the see for six years.

11. Heraclas, a wise man, holds the episcopate at Alexandria for fourteen years.

13. Alexander is killed in a military revolt.

Maximinus: three years.

1. He launches the sixth persecution after Nero against Christians, especially the leaders of the Church.

2. Pope Pontian and his successor Anterus are crowned with martyrdom after one month in the pontificate.

3. Pope Fabian holds the see for fourteen years. Maximinus is killed at Aquileia.

Gordian: six years.

1. Julius Africanus, the distinguished chronographer, is held in high regard.

2. Origen imbues the brothers Theodore and Athenodorus, later distinguished bishops, with divine philosophy.

6. Gordian, returning victorious from the Parthians, is killed not far from Roman territory.

Philip, with his son Philip: seven years.

1. Philip makes his son Philip his partner in the kingdom.

2. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, is held in high regard; he holds the see for twenty-one years.

4. The thousandth year from the foundation of the City is celebrated as a festival.

[Col. 0468D] 6. During this period Origen the presbyter wrote so much that Jerome says in one passage that he had read 5,000 of his books.

7. (H. S.) Philip the elder is killed at Verona, the younger at Rome.

Decius: one year and three months. He persecutes Christians. Pope Fabian is martyred. Cornelius holds the see in his place for one year. Decius and his son are killed by the Goths in Thrace. Antony the monk is born in Egypt.

Gallus Hostilian, with his son Volusian: two years and four months.

[Col. 0469A] 1. Origen dies at the age of seventy.

2. Gallus and Volusian are killed at Terni.

Valerian, with his son Gallienus: fifteen years. He launches the eighth persecution against Christians.

1. Pope Cornelius is made a martyr. Pope Lucius, the twenty-first, holds the see for three years and is made a martyr. Pope Stephen, the twenty-second, holds the see for one year.

4. Cyprian, the foremost teacher and bishop of Carthage, is martyred. Sixtus holds the see for three years.

7. (OROS.) After initiating a persecution, Valerian is captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and deprived of his eyes. Bending down to the ground, he always lifted up the king, who was about to mount his horse, by offering his back as a step. (H. S.) Thus he grows old in wretched servitude. Terrified, Gallienus restores peace to the worshipers of Christ.

8. The Germans ravage Italy; the Alamanni, Gaul and Italy.

9. (10.) Greece, Macedonia [Note: [Col. 0469] “macediamque” in c.], Pontus, and Asia are ravaged by the Goths, and the incursion shakes many other cities.

12. Maximus holds the episcopate at Alexandria for eighteen years.

13. Hyrmenus is appointed bishop of Jerusalem.

14. Pope Dionysius holds the see for nine years. Gallienus is killed at Milan. Claudius: one year and nine months.

1. (H. R.) He defeats the Goths, who had already been devastating Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years; for this reason the senate decrees for him a golden shield in the senate-house and a golden statue in the Capitol [Col. 0469C].

2. (H. S.) Paul of Samosata [Note: [Col. 0469] “Samosathe” in c.] is convicted of being a heretic as bishop of Antioch. Claudius dies at Firmium. His brother Quintilius succeeds him for seventeen days and is killed.

Aurelian: five years and six months. The 1,027th year from the foundation of the City.

1. He was useful to the state; at first merciful toward Christians, later a persecutor.

2. Timothy is ordained bishop of Antioch. Zenobia, queen of the East, is defeated.

3. When Aurelian celebrates a triumph at Rome, Tetricus and Zenobia precede him as captives.

4. Aurelius builds a temple to the sun and initiates the ninth persecution against Christians.

[Col. 0469D] 5. Terrified by a divine thunderbolt, Aurelius is killed by soldiers between Byzantium and Heraclea.

Tacitus: six months, elsewhere one year (so Isidore). After he is killed in Pontus, Florian reigns for eighty-eight days and is killed at Tarsus. Pope Felix, the twenty-fifth, holds the see for five years.

Probus: six years and four months.

1. Gaul, ravaged by barbarians, is restored by Probus to the Roman empire.

3. The eighteenth bishop of Antioch, Quirillus, is appointed.

5. Pope Eutychian holds the see for ten months. Pope Gaius holds the see for fifteen years.

[Col. 0470A] 6. Theonas holds the episcopate at Alexandria for eighteen years. Probus is killed at Firmium in a military revolt.

Carus, with his sons Carinus and Numerian: two years.

1. Carus, victorious over the Parthians, perished after being struck by lightning beyond the Tigris. Numerian was killed.

2. Carinus was killed by Diocletian at Margum. Up to this point, according to Dionysius, 284 years are reckoned from the Lord’s incarnation.

## Diocletian

Diocletian, in the year 1040 from the founding of the City, reigned 20 years.

1. From this year the Greeks began their paschal cycles. [Note: [Col. 0469] *circulo*, “cycle,” corrected in the copy.]

3. Diocletian took Herculius Maximian into partnership in the rule.

4. Diocletian made Constantius, Constantine’s father, Caesar; he reigned 16 years. [Col. 0470B]

7. Diocletian made Galerius Maximian Caesar.

11. Diocletian ordered that he himself be worshiped as a god.

13. After Pope Gaius was martyred, Marcellinus succeeded him.

15. Constantius killed 60,000 Alamanni.

17. In Alexandria, Peter was bishop for 12 years.

18. Tyrannus was appointed bishop of Antioch.

19. Diocletian in the East and Herculius Maximian in the West overthrew the churches, burned the divine books, and tortured the Christians in the tenth persecution after Nero.

20. Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan voluntarily laid down the purple and the rule because of the decline of old age. After Pope Marcellus was martyred, Eusebius succeeded him for eight months. After he too suffered, Meltiades held the office for four years. Galerius and Constantius were chosen Augusti, and Maximian, persecutor of the Christians, and Severus were chosen Caesars. Constantius Augustus, a gentle man, died in Britain. Constantine, the son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, reigned 30 years and 10 months. He became the first emperor to become a Christian, apart from Philip; from this emperor onward the Christians began.

1. Maxentius, the son of Maximian Herculius, was called Augustus.

2. Maximian Herculius was disgracefully killed at Massilia. After Severus was killed, Lucius was made Caesar.

3. Bishop Quirinus suffered martyrdom. Galerius Maximian, persecutor of the Christians, struck by divine retribution, ordered that the Christians be spared. [Col. 0470D]

4. Caesar Maximinus restored the persecution and himself died. After Pope Meltiades suffered martyrdom, Pope Silvester held office for 21 years.

5. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, was martyred. Achillas succeeded him.

6. Constantine defeated Maxentius in a civil battle at the Mulvian Bridge.

9. A great famine and plague afflicted the persecutors. Diocletian died and was enrolled among the gods. [Col. 0471A]

15. Macarius was appointed bishop of Jerusalem. Alexander was ordained bishop of Alexandria. From him, the presbyter Arius, expelled from the church, drew many into his error and attacked the church with heresy.

17. A council of 318 bishops was convened at Nicaea under Pope Silvester, at which Arius was condemned.

19. The Lord’s Cross was found in Jerusalem by Helena, under Macarius, bishop of that city.

21. Constantine killed his wife Bausia.

22. After Tyrannus, Vitalis was ordained bishop of Antioch. Phylogimius succeeded him, then Paulinus. Eustathius succeeded Paulinus. After Eustathius was sent into exile for the Catholic faith, eleven Arian bishops, one after another, occupied that church. [Col. 0471B]

24. (H. S.) Constantine restored the city of Byzantium, named it Constantinople after himself, and wished it to be the seat of the Roman Empire.

25. Athanasius was ordained bishop of Alexandria.

26. At Rome, Pope Mark held office for eight months. Julius succeeded him for 16 years.

30. Constantia, Constantine’s sister and the wife of Licinius, dying, commended a certain Arian presbyter to her brother. [Note: [Col. 0471] *Lucinii* in the copy.]

31. While Constantine was preparing war against the Persians, he died at Nicomedia in the sixty-sixth year of his life.

## Constantius

Constantius, the son of Constantine, with his brothers Constantine and Constans, reigned 24 years, 5 months, and 13 days.

2. Constantine, making war against his brother, was killed near Aquileia. [Col. 0471C]

3. Earthquakes buried many cities.

5. The Franks were subdued by Constans and received into peace.

7. Maximinus is regarded as a distinguished bishop of Trier. By him Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, who had fled from Constans, was honorably received.

9. Bishop Athanasius returned to Alexandria at the request expressed in Constans’s letter.

10. An eclipse of the sun occurred, together with an earthquake.

11. War was waged against the Persians, with great loss to the Romans.

12. Maximus, bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius, died. After him, Cyril, having expelled Heraclius, and the other Arian bishops occupied that church. [Col. 0471D]

13. Constans was killed not far from Spain, in the thirtieth year of his age.

17. The rhetorician Victorinus and the grammarian Donatus were regarded as distinguished men at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0471] “rhetorician” and “grammarian” abbreviated in the copy.]

18. Julian was made Caesar by Constantine. The monk Antony died at the age of 105. [Note: [Col. 0471] *Julius* in the copy.]

19. Great forces of the Alamanni were destroyed at Argentaria. At Rome Liberius was ordained pope. After he was expelled by the Arians, Felix occupied his place for one year. But Liberius, subscribing to the heresy, returned, and Felix was expelled. Again Liberius and many Catholic bishops were expelled by the Arians. [Col. 0472A]

20. The bones of the apostle Andrew, the evangelist Luke, and Timothy were brought to Constantinople.

21. Paulinus, bishop of Trier, died in exile. Hilary was bishop of Poitiers. Athanasius of Alexandria suffered many evils from the Arians.

23. Constantine took up arms against Julian, abandoned the Parthian war, and died in the forty-sixth year of his life.

## Julian the Apostate

Julian the Apostate reigned one year and eight months. Having been made a pagan from a Christian reader, he persecuted the Christians.

1. After George, the Arian bishop of Alexandria, was burned by the people, Athanasius returned to his see. [Col. 0472B] On the Catholic side, Paulinus was bishop of Antioch. At Sebaste, a city of Palestine, pagans attacked the tomb of John the Baptist, scattered his bones, then gathered them up again, burned them, and scattered them more widely. (Cf. Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* XI, 28.) But some monks from Jerusalem, mingling with those who were gathering the remains, carried what they could to their father Philip. Considering these things of great importance, he sent them to Athanasius of Alexandria through the deacon Julian. Athanasius concealed them behind a hollowed-out wall of the sacristy in the presence of a few witnesses and preserved them, through the prophetic Spirit, for the benefit of a future generation. His prophecy was fulfilled under Theodosius through Theophilus the bishop: after destroying the shrine of Serapis, he consecrated the church of Saint John there. [Col. 0472C] (H. S.) Julian set out for the Parthian war, and, vowing the blood of the Christians to his gods, was killed by God’s judgment in the thirtieth year of his age.

## Jovian

Jovian reigned eight months, elsewhere one year. With his entire army he returned to Christianity. A synod favorable to heresy was held at Antioch. (OROS.) Jovian, reclining in a new chamber, was suffocated by the heat of the coals and the brightness of the walls recently coated with whitewash, and died.

## Valentinian

Valentinian reigned 11 years. Because of his faith in Christ, Julian deprived him of his military tribunate.

1. Valentinian gave his brother Valens the rule of the West.

2. Valens, led astray and baptized by Eudoxius, an Arian bishop, persecuted the orthodox after his brother’s death. An earthquake occurred throughout the whole world. Damasus was ordained pope at Rome. [Col. 0472D]

3. True wool mixed with rain flowed down from the clouds. [Note: [Col. 0471] *Uara* in the copy.]

4. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died.

5. Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted his own people.

7. Valentinian subdued the Saxons in the territory of the Franks by slaughter.

8. Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, died.

9. Peter was ordained bishop of Alexandria after Athanasius.

10. Magnentia, also called Thecla, the most noble woman of the Romans, coming to Jerusalem, became renowned for great virtues and humility. [Col. 0473A]

11. Valentinian died of apoplexy while preparing war against the Sarmatians.

## Valens

After his brother’s death, Valens reigned four years with Gratian and Valentinian.

1. Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a most wise and self-controlled man, but, as they say, proud (cf. Jerome), was regarded as distinguished. (H. S.) Theodosius, the father of the later emperor Theodosius, and many nobles were killed by Valens.

2. Gratian destroyed 30,000 Alamanni. Valens issued a law that monks should serve in the army; when they refused, he ordered them to be killed with clubs.

3. The Goths, expelled by the Huns, spread into Thrace; compelled by famine, the Goths rebelled. [Col. 0473B]

4. Valens, after his army was killed by the Goths, fled and was burned alive in a certain house.

Up to this point Jerome brought the chronicle of Eusebius.

## Gratian

Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, reigned six years after the death of his uncle.

1. At Rome, after Damasus, Ursinus held the papacy for 14 years.

2. From this year Theophilus began the paschal cycles.

3. A synod of 150 bishops was convened at Constantinople against Macedonius under Pope Damasus.

5. Arcadius, the son of Theodosius, was made emperor.

6. Maximus, usurping the kingdom for himself, killed Gratian at Lyons. He drove Valentinian out of Italy. [Col. 0473C]

## Theodosius

Theodosius, who while Gratian was alive had ruled the East for six years, reigned 11 years after his death, at first with Valentinian, whom Theodosius himself, a man full of every virtue, had kindly received after he had been expelled from Italy.

3. Ambrose, bishop of Milan; Martin, bishop of Tours; and Jerome, presbyter of Bethlehem, were regarded as distinguished.

7. Valentinian perished by hanging through the treachery of Arbogast.

10. Jerome brought up to this point the book he wrote on illustrious men of the Church. [Col. 0473D]

11. (H. S.) Theodosius defeated the tyrant Eugenius and himself died peacefully at Milan. Augustine, a most eloquent teacher, was ordained bishop of Hippo Regius in Africa. Up to this point Rufinus brought the ecclesiastical history of Eusebius.

## Arcadius

Arcadius, the son of Theodosius, reigned 13 years with his brother Honorius.

1. John the hermit died.

2. Saint Martin died.

3. Bishop Ambrose departed to the Lord.

4. At Rome Anastasius was ordained pope, the thirty-seventh.

5. The Goths entered Italy under the kings Alaric and Radagaisus. [Col. 0474A]

7. The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed by the Lord.

8. At Rome Innocent held the papacy for 13 years.

13. Arcadius, emperor of the East, died at Constantinople.

## Honorius

Honorius reigned 15 years with Theodosius, his brother’s son.

1. The Vandals occupied the Spains.

3. Attalus was made emperor at Rome, soon deprived of the kingdom, and joined the Goths.

4. Rome was attacked by the Goths under King Alaric in the year 1164 from its foundation; but because he was a Christian king, he used his victory mercifully.

7. The bodies of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Gamaliel, Abibos, and Nicodemus were revealed to the presbyter Lucian. [Col. 0474B]

8. Pope Zosimus held office for three years.

10. An eclipse of the sun occurred. Jerome, presbyter of Bethlehem, died in the ninety-first year of his life.

12. Boniface, the sixtieth pope, was ordained at Rome.

13. At Ravenna, in the tenth year of his reign, Honorius made Constantius his partner in rule. The emperor Constantius died at Ravenna in the third year of his reign. Honorius died; he was the brother of Placidia.

## Theodosius the Younger

Theodosius the Younger, the son of Arcadius, reigned 26 years.

1. Theodosius made Valentinian, the son of Placidia and his cousin, Caesar and sent him with his mother to rule the West.

6. Aetius, after killing many Franks, recovered the part of Gaul that they had possessed.

8. (BEDA.) Augustine, bishop of Hippo and the outstanding teacher of all the churches, departed to the Lord in order not to see the ruin of his city, in the third month of its siege, in the seventy-sixth year of his life and the fortieth of his episcopate. [Col. 0474C]

9. (H. S.) Sixtus was ordained pope at Rome.

11. The third universal synod was convened at Ephesus, consisting of 200 bishops against Nestorius.

13. Aetius defeated Gundicharius, king of the Burgundians; the Huns later killed him.

14. Valentinian took the daughter of Theodosius in marriage.

15. Julian, the Pelagian heretic, was condemned by Pope Sixtus. [Col. 0474D]

16. War was waged against the Goths with the assistance of the Huns.

17. Leo was appointed pope at Rome.

18. Theodosius ineffectively undertook war against the Goths.

20. Briccius, bishop of Tours, died.

21. Eustochius succeeded him.

26. Theodosius, emperor of the East, died.

## Martian

Martian reigned seven years with Valentinian.

1. Aetius, with Roman auxiliaries, defeated Attila.

2. Attila captured Aquileia with great force. [Col. 0475A]

At that time Ermenric ruled over all the Goths, more cunning than all in deceit and more generous than all in gifts. After the death of his only son Frideric, which he himself had caused, he hanged his cousins Embrica and Frithla on the gallows; likewise, at the instigation of his cousin Odoacer, he drove his cousin Theoderic from Verona and forced him to go into exile with Attila.

(H. S.) Attila, king of the Huns, died.

3. The fourth synod, of 630 bishops, was convened at Chalcedon under Pope Leo against Eutyches.

5. Valentinian killed Aetius, a patrician useful to the state, with his own hand. Valentinian was killed in the Field of Mars by Aetius’s friends. In the same year Geiseric stripped Rome of all its wealth. Up to this point Prosper brought his chronicle. [Col. 0475B]

7. Martian, emperor of the East, died.

## Leo

Leo ruled the East for 17 years.

2. Mauronian, emperor of the West, marched into Africa in military array.

11. Anthemius was sent by Leo as emperor of the West.

16. Olybrius, emperor for seven months, died.

17. Leo the Elder died. The Younger succeeded him and reigned for a few months.

## Zeno

Zeno ruled the East for 17 years.

3. Orestes drove out Nepos, the Roman prince, and gave the empire to his son Augustulus. But when he had come to Caesarea for the sake of prayer, he was captured and beaten by the Persians and sent back to their king Chosroes. After being beaten by him a third time, he was finally hung by one hand for three hours and then beheaded, attaining a noble martyrdom with seventy others. [Col. 0478B]

26. (Cf. FREDEGAR, chap. 65.) Heraclius, having become an astrologer, saw that his empire was destined to be devastated by circumcised peoples. He sent to Dagobert, king of the Franks, asked that all the Jews in his kingdom be baptized, and obtained this; he himself also decreed that the same should happen throughout all the provinces of his empire. The Hagarenes, also called Saracens, a circumcised people, devastated Heraclius’s provinces. While Heraclius was fighting them, the Saracens killed 150,000 of his soldiers and sent their spoils back to Heraclius. Unwilling to accept them, and preferring to seek vengeance upon them, he opened the Caspian Gates, which Alexander the Great of Macedon had made over the Caspian Sea and ordered to be guarded because of the incursions of the fiercest peoples. From there he sent 150,000 men armed with gold, together with all the soldiers of all his provinces, to fight against the Saracens. When they were going to fight on the following day, an angel of God struck down 52,000 of Heraclius’s army in the camp that very night. When the survivors were returning and had already approached Jerusalem, Heraclius, seeing that he could in no way resist the violence of his enemies, was overcome by grief and polluted the worship of God with the Eutychian heresy. He had as his wife the daughter of his sister; afflicted by fevers, he ended his life cruelly. [Col. 0478C–D] [Note: [Col. 0477] *heracli*, “of Heraclius,” in the copy.]

1. The younger emperor Charles died. Archbishop Luitpert was succeeded by Sunderolt. On 13 July Arnulf, bishop of Würzburg, was killed in Saxony during the solemn celebration of Mass; he had held office for 36 years, 7 months, and 12 days.

3. King Arnulf completely destroyed the army of the Northmen.

4. Regensburg blazed in a fire.

6. Sunderolf was killed by the Northmen. Hatto succeeded him.

8. Arnulf subjected Italy and Burgundy to his kingdom.

[Col. 0486A] 9. King Arnulf came to Rome and was made emperor.

11. A great famine induced people to eat one another.

12. The emperor Arnulf died. The Pannonian peoples, whom we call Hungarians, ravaged Italy.

Year of the Lord 900. Louis, Arnulf’s son, a very young boy, for 12 years.

1. The Hungarians entered Bavaria, and more than a thousand of them were killed.

2. The Hungarians invaded Carinthia; a battle was fought on Saturday, and they were killed.

6. The Hungarians were killed in even greater numbers. The brothers Berengar, Reginolt, and Gerhard were killed.

7. A battle was fought between Adalbert, their brother, and [Col. 0486B] Conrad, the emperor Louis’s brother; Conrad was killed in it.

8. On 3 August Bishop Rudolf of Würzburg died; he had held office for 17 years, 12 months, and 2 days. Adalbert, deceived through the treachery of Archbishop Hatto and a certain Luitpald, was beheaded at Louis’s command. The Bavarians were killed by the Hungarians.

9. The Hungarians ravaged Saxony and Thuringia. Luitpald was killed.

10. The Hungarians attacked Alamannia.

11. War between the Franks and the Hungarians.

12. King Louis died. Duke Burchard was killed.

Year of the Lord 912. Conrad, son of that Conrad whom Adalbert of Babenberg killed, was raised to the kingdom and ruled for 7 years.

1. The Hungarians were killed by the Alamanni and Bavarians near the River Inn.

2. Comets were seen. King Rudolf died. The Hungarians ravaged Alamannia. Archbishop Hatto died. Heriger succeeded him.

5. Bishop Solomon was captured. The Hungarians ravaged all Alamannia with fire and sword.

6. The brothers Duke Erchanger and Berthold were beheaded on 21 January. Basel was destroyed by the Hungarians.

7. The Hungarians invaded Alamannia, Alsace, and the kingdom of Lothar. Burchard was appointed duke. King Conrad died.

Duke Liudolf of Saxony.

4. King Charles of Gaul came to Francia.

[Col. 0486D] 7. (H. S.) The Blood of the Lord came to the island of Reichenau.

8. The Hungarians devastated all Francia, Gaul, Alsace, and Alamannia with sword and fire. Duke Burchard was killed. Alamannia was entrusted to Hermann. [Col. 0487A]

11. Archbishop Heriger died. Hildebert succeeded him.

12. King Henry attacked Bohemia.

17. [Note: [Col. 0487] “18” erased, c.] King Henry died.

Year of the Lord 937. Otto the Great, son of Henry, for 38 years.

1. The Hungarians, devastating Francia, Alamannia, Gaul as far as the Ocean, and Burgundy, returned through Italy. The monasteries of Saint Gall and Saint Boniface were burned. Arnulf, duke of the Norici, and King Rudolf died.

2. Henry, Otto’s brother, was captured by Eberhard.

3. Giselbert and Adalbert were killed, and the bishops fled.

4. On 25 March Burchard the Younger, bishop of Würzburg, died; he had held office for 9 years, 3 months, and 23 days. There was a severe winter and a pestilence among the animals.

5. Otto attacked Gaul.

6. King Otto and Louis made peace.

8. The Hungarians fought the Bavarians and were defeated. [Note: [Col. 0487] “vicuntur,” c.]

[Col. 0487C] 10. King Otto entered Gaul.

11. Berthold, duke of the Bavarians, died. Henry, Otto’s brother, succeeded him.

13. Hermann, duke of the Alamanni, died. Liudolf, King Otto’s son, succeeded him.

14. King Otto attacked Italy and subjected it to himself; he expelled King Berengar.

15. Berengar came to Otto at Augsburg, to an assembly, to surrender. [Note: [Col. 0487] “deditio,” c.] From there he was led with his wife, Queen Willa, to the castle of Babenberg, where he ended his present life. (H. S.) A fiery stone, like a mass of glowing iron, came flying from the west; and a dragon was seen.

16. King Otto entered Italy together with his son, and a royal wedding was celebrated at Pavia.

[Col. 0487D] 17. Duke Liudolf rebelled against Otto, his father and king. Count Adalbert was killed.

18. The Hungarians attacked Noricum, Francia, and Italy.

19. The Hungarians ravaged all Bavaria; near Augsburg, a city of Alamannia, they were defeated in battle by King Otto and killed in an immense slaughter.

20. Duke Liudolf invaded Italy as an enemy.

21. Liudolf defeated Adalbert in war, and died himself in the same year.

23. Crosses appeared on garments.

24. On 15 February Bishop Poppo of Würzburg died; he had held office for 20 years, 10 months, and 14 days.

[Col. 0488A] 26. King Otto came to Rome and was made emperor. A sign appeared in the sun.

27. Emperor Otto stayed at Pavia for the Nativity of the Lord.

28. Again Otto stayed at Rome for the Nativity of the Lord.

32. And Duke Burchard defeated the rebels in Italy for the emperor. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 21 November.

35. A certain fiery-colored sign appeared in the sky.

8. Emperor Otto, after his army was killed by the Greeks near Calabria, leapt from a ship and escaped. Duke Otto died.

2. King Henry attacked the margrave Henry and others who resisted him with an army.

3. King Henry subdued Italy, Bohemia, and Duke Bolizlaus together with the entire Slavic people.

4. There was a great famine.

6. The bishopric of Babenberg was established by King Henry, and Eberhard was ordained bishop there.

8. Bishop and monk Brun, afflicted by many tortures by the Prussians, and with his hands and feet cut off, was finally beheaded and went to heaven. [Col. 0488D]

17. Bishop Lambert died.

19. Pope Benedict, coming to Babenberg, dedicated the church of Saint Stephen. In the same year Werenher, bishop of Strasbourg, marched with the Alamanni against the Burgun-

[Col. 0489A] 20. (H. S.) A great earthquake occurred on 12 May, a Friday. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, died. Piligrim succeeded him.

21. Emperor Henry took New Troy by surrender, and a great pestilence occurred in the army. [Note: [Col. 0489] “mortalita,” c.]

22. Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, died. Gebehard succeeded him again. [Note: [Col. 0489] “ite,” c.; here “item” may also be read.]

23. Emperor Henry died on 13 July and was buried in the monastery of the apostle Saint Peter, in the bishopric of Babenberg, which he himself had established.

Conrad ruled for approximately 13 years.

1. A great dissension arose in the kingdom against King Conrad.

2. King Conrad made his son Henry king, and, proceeding to Rome, himself was made emperor. [Col. 0489B]

3. Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, and Count Welf carried out raids and burnings against one another.

4. Duke Ernest and Count Welf came to Emperor Conrad to surrender.

5. Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, died. Eberhard succeeded him.

6. Emperor Conrad attacked Stephen, king of Pannonia, with an army. Meanwhile in Alamannia Duke Ernest and Count Werenher, together with many others, were killed on 17 August. [Note: [Col. 0489] “were killed,” c.]

7. King Stephen, sending envoys, made peace with Emperor Conrad.

8. King Rudolf of Burgundy, as he was dying, sent his crown to Emperor Conrad.

[Col. 0489C] 9. On 22 March Bishop Meginhard of Würzburg died; he had held office for 15 years, 2 months, and 21 days. Conrad attacked Burgundy in winter. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 29 June, at the sixth hour.

10. Conrad attacked eastern Francia against Otto. Conrad again ravaged Burgundy. [Note: [Col. 0489] “again,” c.]

11. The pagans called Liuticians seized the castle of Wirbina on the border of Saxony, after killing and capturing many Christians; Conrad attacked them with an army.

12. Italy was suffering from civil discord. Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, died. Gebehard succeeded him again. [Note: [Col. 0489] “again,” c.] The wedding of King Henry. The pagans mentioned above became tributaries of Emperor Conrad. [Note: [Col. 0489] “tributaries,” c.] Piligrim, bishop of Cologne, died. Hermann succeeded him.

13. Emperor Conrad attacked Italy with an army and sent the bishop of Milan into custody; he escaped and rebelled against the emperor. Otto, a prince of the Carolingians, [Note: [Col. 0489] “kalinlorum” corrected to “karlinlorum,” c.] was defeated in battle by Duke Gozzelo and, while fleeing, was killed by a certain soldier.

[Col. 0490A] 14. Queen Cunigund died. Duke Hermann died. Stephen, the Christian king of the Hungarians, died; together with his entire people he was converted to the faith of Christ.

15. Emperor Conrad died on 4 June and was buried at Speyer. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 22 August. Reginbald, bishop of Speyer, died on 13 October.

The pious King Henry, Conrad’s son, began to reign.

2. King Henry attacked Duke Bratislaus of Bohemia in war; but after many nobles and soldiers on both sides had been killed or captured in a forest ambush, he was unable to accomplish anything worthy. King Peter of the Hungarians also sent assistance to that duke against King Henry. [Note: [Col. 0489] “duce,” c.]

3. The Hungarians chose a certain Obo as king for themselves, expelling their own King Peter. As an exile and fugitive, Peter sought and found the favor of King Henry, against whom he had rebelled the preceding year. King Henry entered Bohemia and devastated everything with fire and plunder; he compelled the rebellious duke to give hostages, to come humbly after him to Regensburg to surrender, and to confirm by oath his loyalty and service to him. Obo, king of the Hungarians, because King Henry had received Peter, whom Obo had expelled, ravaged the borders of Bavaria with plunder and fire; but a large part of his army was destroyed by Margrave Adalbero.

4. King Henry entered Pannonia and overthrew two very populous cities, while subjecting several others by surrender. But when the provincials refused to receive King Peter, whom he was bringing with him, he appointed another duke whom they requested; after Henry’s departure, Obo drove this duke back into Bohemia. Empress Gisela, King Henry’s mother, died on 14 February and was buried at Speyer.

5. King Henry invaded Pannonia again and, receiving compensation, hostages, gifts, and confirmation of peace by oath, departed. Returning from there, he attended the synod at Constance, where he remitted all debts owed to him; and after destroying every cause of enmity, by royal authority he confirmed by edict an unprecedented peace both throughout Swabia and in the other provinces of his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0489] “tam” omitted, c.] Then, having Queen Agnes [Note: [Col. 0489] “agnetaen,” c.], daughter of William, prince of Poitou, anointed at Mainz, he joined her to himself in a royal marriage at Ingelheim; from there he allowed an innumerable multitude of actors and entertainers to depart hungry, empty-handed, and grieving. Margrave Luitpald, son of Adalbert, who had wrought the greatest slaughter of the Hungarians, died prematurely. There was a severe pestilence among the livestock. The winter was harsh and snowy. [Col. 0490D]

6. On 27 May Bishop Brun of Würzburg died, in the year of the Lord 1045; he had held office for 11 years, 1 month, and 14 days. (Cf. HERM. for 1044–1045.) King Henry, entering Pannonia angrily for the third time, became victorious through God’s merciful favor and with Blessed Bishop Ulrich commanding. [Note: [Col. 0491] Read “impetrante” (“interceding”).] He drove Obo into exile, together with his wife, sons, and relatives who had a place to escape. He restored Peter to the kingdom and, after subjecting the Hungarian kingdom to himself, returned with the highest honor. Duke Gotefrid of Lorraine, rebelling against King Henry [Note: [Col. 0491] “rege,” c.], was compelled to surrender and confined under guard in the castle of Gibichenstein until he had made suitable satisfaction. [Note: [Col. 0491D] Thus in the Murensian codex of Hermann.]

7. (Cf. HERM. for 1046.) King Henry entered Italy and was received peacefully by the Romans. He deposed synodally three improperly appointed popes and made Suideger, bishop of Babenberg, pope; and on the same day he and his wife, Queen Agnes, were raised to imperial dignity by an imperial blessing. Empress Agnes gave birth to a daughter near Ravenna. The emperor himself, leading his army through Apulia and many provinces in a fortunate victory, returned with great honor. [Col. 0491B]

8. (Cf. HERM. for 1046–1047.) Meanwhile Peter, king of the Hungarians, was captured and blinded by a certain Pannonian tyrant, and the man who had expelled him began to reign. The body of Saint Wido was brought from Italy to Speyer by Emperor Henry in the eighth year of his reign, the first year of his empire, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1047, in the fifteenth indiction. Pope Suideger died in the same year in which he had been appointed. [Note: [Col. 0491] Omitted, c.] Boppo was ordained in his place.

9. (HERM. for 1047–1048.) Otto, duke of Swabia, died. Otto of Schweinfurt arose in his place. Pope Boppo died in the year in which he had been appointed. Bruno, also called Leo, bishop of Toul, was ordained pope. [Col. 0491C]

10. (Cf. ibid. for 1049.) In the third year of his empire Emperor Henry invaded certain parts of Gaul against Gotefrid and Baldwin. After compelling them to surrender and restoring peace to the kingdom in those regions, he returned victorious and with honor. A synod was held at Mainz, attended by Pope Bruno and Emperor Henry.

11. (Ibid. for 1050.) The Hungarians rebelled again. [Note: [Col. 0491] “ite,” c.] Bishop Gebehard of Regensburg, going out to meet them in place of Emperor Henry, put them to flight and afflicted them with no small slaughter; moreover, he had the frontier city of Heimenburg, restored with buildings, fortified with a military garrison. [Note: [Col. 0491] “marchionem,” c.] He himself returned in complete peace. [Note: [Col. 0491] “the margrave,” c.]

[Col. 0491D] 12. (Ibid. for 1051.) Archbishop Bartho died. Luitpold succeeded him. Emperor Henry entered Pannonia again, dividing his multitude of soldiers into two parts and entering from both sides while occupying the region itself, surrounded by forests and especially by accumulations of water. But that people, harsher than the others, acting deceitfully and cowardly together with its king, plundered its own property along with that of others; worn out by hunger, thirst, and many disasters, it escaped by fleeing from our army. [Note: [Col. 0491] “fleeing,” c.] The emperor’s soldiers, after devastating a large part of the province and killing many there besides, returned peacefully, though without success, with the emperor to their own territory. [Col. 0492A]

13. (Ibid. for 1052–1053.) Emperor Henry attacked Pannonia again and returned without success, taking with him in his company Bruno, prelate of the apostolic see. They celebrated the coming Nativity of the Lord together at Worms. In the year 1053 the pope returned to Rome, accompanied by many soldiers from various provinces, sent by imperial command and with the assistance of friends. After Easter he led an army through Apulia against the Northmen—formerly newcomers to that land but then enemies of the Roman Empire. After an innumerable slaughter on both sides, the pope, fleeing with a few men and without victory, returned, leaving there the excellent soldiers of Swabia and Noricum; and he settled in the city of Benevento. [Col. 0492B]

14. (Ibid. for 1054.) Then the devout Pope Bruno, also called Leo, gloriously ended his life in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1054, but in the fifteenth year of Emperor Henry’s reign, and was buried at Rome in the church of Blessed Peter. Conrad, duke of the Norici, rebelled seriously after forming an alliance with the Hungarians. Baldwin and Gotefrid did likewise.

15. Gebehard, also called Victor, succeeded Pope Leo (in the year 1055). Margrave Adalbert died. There was a great famine. Emperor Henry attacked Italy with an army and arranged everything peacefully. On his return he took with him his niece Beatrice, treating her harshly because of a certain arrogance to which she had been accustomed while living after the death of her husband, Duke Boniface. Duke Welf of Carinthia died. Conrad, formerly duke of the Norici, expelled by the emperor, died miserably as an exile in Pannonia. Conrad succeeded Arnulf as bishop of Speyer. [Col. 0492C]

16. Count Hermann of eastern Francia died on 27 January (1056). Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg and uncle of the great Emperor Henry, was discovered to be a very wicked secret enemy; defeated and committed to custody, but treated mercifully, he was sent into exile and restored to his former see. Duke Gotefrid came to surrender. (Cf. BERTH.) A great slaughter was inflicted upon Christians by the barbarians called Liuticians. Some perished by the sword, others while fleeing [Note: [Col. 0491] “figientes,” c.] perished in the water; among them Margrave William was killed. At the same time many princes from various provinces perished. Famine afflicted many provinces. Want and poverty prevailed everywhere. Many evils occurred at that time. Emperor Henry, pierced to the heart by these sufferings, began to fall ill and was brought even to the point of death. Yet, acting with wise counsel, he sought forgiveness from all whom he could, restored to some the estates he had taken, and released all who had committed culpable offenses against him. By the election of the Roman pontiff and the other bishops and princes, he established his son Henry as king. After arranging these and other matters well, as the possibility of life allowed, he ended this present life in God on 5 October. [Col. 0492D–0493A]

Henry, son of Emperor Henry, a very young boy, began to reign in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1057. Agnes, his mother, assumed the duchy of Bavaria. The Roman pontiff Gebehard, also called Victor, after arranging many matters well in Germany and other parts of the Roman kingdom with the advice of bishops and secular princes, returned peacefully to Rome at the beginning of Lent of that year. He too ended his life in the same year. In his place Frideric, also called Stephen, already made a monk, was appointed Roman pontiff by the Romans. The Saxons, having assembled an army, hostilely invaded the fierce people of the Liuticians, [Note: [Col. 0493] so in the codex, c.] afflicted them with various evils, subjected them to Roman rule after receiving hostages and tribute, and returned peacefully to their own territory. At the same time, a certain Frideric and his brothers, exercising tyranny in the regions of Germany against the Roman Empire, were defeated by Empress Agnes and the princes of the kingdom and came to surrender. Frideric, also called Stephen, the Roman pontiff, ended his life. Duke Otto of Swabia died on 28 September. [Note: [Col. 0493] In the codex, the text ends here in nearly the same manner, on an unfinished page. On the following page, the last of the quire, a genealogical stemma is found, which we add.]

[Col. 0497]

EKKEHARD’S UNIVERSAL CHRONICLE. EPITOME [that is, abbreviation] OF EUSEBIUS, FROM THE FOLLOWING WORK.

[PART ONE.]

[Col. 0497A] (HIER.) Learned men have handed down that Moses, leader of the Hebrew people, who first of all the prophets before the coming of the Lord and Savior explained the divine laws in sacred writings, lived in the time of Inachus. Among our own writers are Clement and Africanus, and among the Jews Josephus and Justus, who recount the monuments of ancient history. Moreover, Inachus preceded the Trojan War by five hundred years. Among the pagans, however, that impious man Porphyry, in the fourth book of the work that he composed against us through fruitless labor, asserts that Semiramis lived after Moses; she reigned among the Assyrians for 150 years before Inachus. Thus, according to him, Moses is found to have been almost 850 years older than the Trojan War.

Since these things are so, I have considered it necessary to pursue the truth more carefully, to set the periods of the kingdoms against one another, and to count the years of the individual peoples, so that we may be able to note, in an orderly fashion for the curious, who was contemporary with whom. Nor am I unaware that in Hebrew books differing numbers of years of ages are found, read as more or fewer according as it seemed appropriate to the translators; rather, that reading should be followed which the multitude of copies has drawn into common acceptance. [Col. 0497B]

[Note: [Col. 0497C] The entire preface, with a few changes, has been copied from Eusebius as translated by Jerome.]

But however anyone wishes to calculate it, he will find that in the time of Inachus, whom they say first ruled at Argos, the patriarch of the Hebrews was Israel, from whom the twelve tribes received the name of Israel. It is clear, moreover, that Semiramis and Abraham were contemporaries. For although Moses is younger than those mentioned above, he is nevertheless found to be older than all whom the Greeks consider most ancient—namely Homer, Hesiod, and the Trojan War, and much earlier still than Hercules, Musaeus, Linus, Chiron, Orpheus, Castor and Pollux, Apollo, Asclepius, Liber, Mercury, and the other gods, sacred figures, or prophets of the nations, and even than the deeds of Jupiter himself, whom Greece placed at the summit of divinity.

All these, I say, whom we have enumerated, we prove to have lived even after Cecrops Diphyes [Note: [Col. 0497] In a scraped-away place: “1.”], the first king of Attica. Histories show Cecrops to have been contemporary with Moses and to have preceded the Trojan War by 350 years. So that this may seem doubtful to no one, the following calculation will establish it.

In the forty-second year of Augustus’s reign Christ was born; in the fifteenth year of Tiberius he began to preach. Therefore, if someone counting backward seeks the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, under whom the Temple of Jerusalem, destroyed by the Babylonians, was restored, he will find 540 years from the fifteenth year of Tiberius to Darius. [Note: [Col. 0497C] Ekkehard slightly altered the numbers and the entire computation of years below, though retaining Jerome’s wording.]

For Darius’s second year fell in the first year of the sixty-fifth Olympiad, while Tiberius’s fifteenth year fell in the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad. Thus, between Darius and Tiberius’s fifteenth year there are 136 Olympiads, or 546 years, reckoning four years to an Olympiad.

Then, in Darius’s second year, the seventieth year of the Temple’s desolation was completed. From that point back to the first Olympiad there are 64 Olympiads, or 256 years. The same number is reckoned from the aforementioned year of the Temple’s desolation back to the forty-ninth year of Uzziah, king of the Jews, under whom Isaiah and Hosea lived. Thus the first Olympiad falls within the lifetime of Isaiah and the other prophets who prophesied with him.

Again, if you proceed backward from the first Olympiad to earlier times and as far as the captivity of Troy, you will find 405 years [Note: [Col. 0497] “V,” corrected by the first corrector; Jerome has “VI”], which the exceptionally careful history of the Greeks records.

Likewise, among the Hebrews, from the aforementioned year of Uzziah and the time of the prophet Isaiah to Samson and the third year of the judge Lapdon, you will calculate 405 years [Note: [Col. 0497] “V,” corrected by the first corrector; Jerome has “VI”]. Samson is the man whom later Jewish writers say resembled Hercules in bodily strength. It seems to me that they were not far apart in time, since both lived around the captivity of Troy.

After this, turn back again to earlier times. When the backward calculation has completed 329 years for you, you will find Cecrops Diphyes [Col. 0498C] of the Greeks and Moses of the Hebrews. For from Cecrops’s forty-fifth year to the captivity of Troy, and from Moses’s eightieth year—the year in which he led the Israelite people out of Egypt—to the third year of the judge Lapdon, there are 329 years.

Therefore, without any ambiguity, Moses and Cecrops, who was the first king of the Athenians, lived at the same time. This Cecrops was Diphyes [Note: [Col. 0497] Corrected from “e” by the first corrector], a native, under whom the olive first arose on the citadel, and the city of the Athenians received its name from Minerva. He was the first of all to call upon Jupiter, to establish an altar for him, and to sacrifice an ox. He discovered images of the gods and offered victims, although such things had never before been seen in Greece. The other marvels also celebrated among the Greeks are found to belong to years later than Cecrops.

Let there therefore be this sequence between Cecrops and Moses. After him are described the flood under Deucalion, the conflagration under Phaethon, Erichthonius, son of Vulcan and Earth, and Dardanus, who founded Dardania; the abduction of Libya and of Europa; the rites of Ceres and the shrine of Isis; Triptolemus’s grain at Eleusis; and the reign of Tros,

> Whose gods wished the born Ganymede, carried off to the stars,  
> To pour wine for Jupiter at splendid banquets.

At that time Tantalus and Tityus lived, and Apollo was born. For Latona, Jupiter’s wife, fled through the realms of Tityus; Apollo was the son of Latona and Jupiter.

After them Cadmus came to Thebes,

> Who begot Semele, from whom the fairest offspring,  
> Liber, born of a fitting birth, brought forth the worthy fruit.

Liber and those whom we shall mention immediately afterward lived after Cecrops’s two-hundredth year: namely Linus, Zethus and Amphion, Musaeus, Orpheus, Minos, Perseus, Asclepius, the twins Castor and Pollux, and Hercules, with whom Apollo served Admetus.

After them came the overthrow of Troy, which Homer follows after a long interval. Homer, however, is found to have lived much earlier than Solon, Thales of Miletus, and the others who with them were called the Seven Wise Men. Then Pythagoras appeared, who wished to be called not “wise,” as his predecessors were, but “philosopher”—that is, “lover of wisdom.” He was followed by Socrates, who educated Plato; from Plato philosophy was divided into its famous schools. We shall insert each of these in its proper place according to the order of history. [Col. 0499C]

Moses therefore preceded all those whom we mentioned above, since he has been shown to have lived in the time of Cecrops. From Moses’s eightieth year and the departure of Israel from Egypt, turning back again to earlier times until Abraham’s first year, you will find 505 years [Note: [Col. 0499] “V” corrected from “e” by the first corrector]. Similarly, from Cecrops’s forty-fifth year to Ninus and Semiramis, rulers of the Assyrians, you will calculate 505 years [Note: [Col. 0499] Corrected from “e” by the first corrector].

Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to rule all Asia, except the Indians. Thus it is clear that Abraham was born during the lifetime of Ninus, according to the more abbreviated number which the Hebrew text supplies than the Vulgate edition.

But do not cease your careful investigation. When you have diligently examined divine Scripture, you will find, counting backward, 292 years [Col. 0499D] from Abraham’s birth to the flood of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0499D] Ekkehard altered Jerome’s numbers], and likewise 1,656 years from the Flood to Adam. During those years there is absolutely no Greek or barbarian history—or, to speak generally, no history of any nation—at all.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] Ekkehard added this.] For this reason all writers of history begin their chronological arrangements with Ninus, who, not content with his own kingdom, invaded the territories of others and is therefore said to have been the first to rule.

We, beginning from the very origin of the world’s creation, shall describe the generations of the patriarchs from Adam to Noah, and from Noah after the Flood to Abraham. Then, together with the other writers, we shall pursue the later periods from Abraham and from Ninus down to our own age. At the very beginning of this account, after mentioning Belus, the father of Ninus, and Egialeus, king of the Sicyonians, we shall place Abraham of the Hebrews and Ninus and Semiramis of the Assyrians first, because at that time neither the city of Athens nor the kingdom of the Argives had yet received its name, while only the Sicyonians were flourishing in Greece. Among them, they say, Europes ruled second in the time of Abraham and Ninus. Why we too should think this will be demonstrated below [Note: [Col. 0499] Corrected from “in s.” by the first corrector].

For if you carefully count from Ninus’s forty-third year to the captivity of Troy, you will find 834 years [Col. 0500B] [Note: [Col. 0499] From “a quadr.” to “ad”: corrected by the first corrector; he also altered Jerome’s numbers throughout]. Likewise, in Sicyon, from the twenty-second year of King Europes to the aforementioned period, you will find the same number, 834 years. Among the Hebrews also, from Abraham’s birth to the third year of Lapdon, the Hebrew judge who ruled the people in the time of the Trojans, you will likewise calculate 834 years [Note: [Col. 0499] “t. a. l.” in a scraped-away place: “1.”]. Likewise, among the Egyptians, from the time of Ninus and Semiramis, when the sixteenth dynasty was already ruling the Egyptians, until the twentieth dynasty—that is, the twentieth regime—and Theorus, king of Egypt, whom Homer calls Polypus, under whom Troy was also captured, the aforementioned 834 years are reckoned.

Consequently, in one and the same chronological sequence, we shall place Abraham, Ninus or Semiramis, Europes, and the Thebans of Egypt.

Now we must also take care to divide the years of the Hebrews into four periods: from Abraham to Moses; from Moses to the first building of the Temple; from the building of the Temple to the second building, when it was restored [Note: [Col. 0499] Corrected from “tum est” by the first corrector]; and from its restoration to the coming of Christ the Lord.

From Abraham’s birth to Moses and the exodus of Israel from Egypt, 505 years are reckoned. From there to Solomon and the first building of the Temple, there are 478 years [Note: [Col. 0499] Jerome has “IX”], according to the smaller number contained in the Third Book of Kings; for according to the Book of Judges 600 years are reckoned. From Solomon to the restoration of the Temple, which took place under Darius, king of the Persians, 512 years are gathered [Col. 0500D]. From Darius to the preaching of the Lord Jesus Christ and to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, ruler of the Romans, 547 years are completed [Note: [Col. 0499] Jerome has “VIII”].

Thus, in total, from Abraham to Tiberius’s fifteenth year there are 2,042 years [Note: [Col. 0499] Corrected from “two” by the first corrector; Jerome has “IV”].

Likewise, from Ninus’s forty-third year [Note: [Col. 0499] “Nini” through “DV,” apparently corrected by the first corrector] to Cecrops’s forty-sixth year there are 505 years; from there to the captivity of Troy, 329 years; from the captivity of Troy to the first Olympiad, 405 years [Note: [Col. 0501] Corrected by the first corrector]; from the first Olympiad to Darius’s second year and the restoration of the Temple, 256 years; and from the restoration of the Temple to Tiberius’s fifteenth year and the preaching of Christ, 547 years [Note: [Col. 0501] “VII” corrected to “VIII” by the first corrector].

Therefore, from Ninus and Semiramis [Note: [Col. 0501] “Semirade” in the manuscript] to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar there are 2,042 years [Note: [Col. 0501] “two years” corrected to “IV years” by the first corrector], the same number that we have shown to be reckoned from Abraham to Tiberius.

But lest the long succession of numbers perhaps cause confusion, let us compare the genealogies of the ancient patriarchs from the creation of the first man, Adam, who was formed on the sixth day of the world’s creation, down to Abraham. In this way it will be easy to discover in whose age among Greeks or barbarians the prophets, kings, and priests of the Hebrews lived; likewise, the falsely believed gods of the various nations; which heroes lived; when each city was founded; which philosophers, poets, and rulers were distinguished; which writers produced various works [Note: [Col. 0501] “q. s.” corrected by the first corrector]; and whatever else antiquity considered worthy of remembrance. We shall set all these out in their proper places with the greatest brevity.

(ISID.) [Note: [Col. 0501] Witness 5 adds in red: “Here begins the book called Chronicle or Annals.”] In six days God formed the creation of the world. On the first day he created light; on the second, the firmament; on the third, the appearance of the sea and the earth; on the fourth, the stars; on the fifth, the fish and birds; on the sixth, the beasts and cattle. Finally, in his own likeness he made the first man, Adam. [Note: [Col. 0501] I said that his chronicle was copied word for word in the Würzburg Chronicle. Ekkehard, however, greatly expanded his account here from other sources.]

From Adam’s creation and the creation of the world to the Flood, according to some authorities (JORD. *On the Roman Succession*; BEDA, *On the Six Ages*), 2,242 years are reckoned; according to the Hebrew truth, 1,656. In those years, while human nature was still raw and simple, there were not kings but heads of families, each in his own kind. Their succession was as follows.

(ISID.) In the 130th year of his life Adam begot Seth, who was born in place of Abel. His name is interpreted as “resurrection,” because in him the righteous seed was raised again, namely the stock of the sons of God. Since he was an excellent man, he left behind sons who imitated him and who first discovered the discipline and adornment of heavenly things. When Adam was 930 years old, he died and left the governance of affairs to his son Seth.

(ISID.) In the 105th year of his life Seth begot Enos, while Adam was alive and 235 years old. Enos began—or, as Saint Augustine says according to another translation [Col. 0501D] (*City of God* XV, 18), “hoped”—to invoke the name of the Lord. When Seth had lived 912 years, he died.

(ISID.) In the ninetieth year of his life Enos begot Cainan, whose name is interpreted as “the nature of God,” while Adam was alive and 325 years old. When Enos was 905 years old, he died.

In the seventieth year of his life Cainan begot Malaleel, whose name is interpreted as “planting of God,” while Adam was still alive and 395 years old. After Cainan had lived 910 years, he died.

(ISID.) In the sixty-fifth year of his life Malaleel begot Jared, whose name is interpreted as “descending” or “surpassing,” while Adam was still alive and 460 years old. When Malaleel had lived 895 years, he died.

In the 162nd year of his life Jared begot Enoch, while Adam was still alive and 622 years old. When Jared was 942 years old, he died.

In the sixty-fifth year of his life Enoch begot Methuselah, while Adam was still alive and 687 years old. After Enoch had lived 365 years, he was taken up by God, and therefore no end to his life is found written. It is said that he wrote many things, but antiquity rejected them as writings of suspect credibility [Note: [Col. 0501] “suspectae” corrected to “susceptae” by the first corrector, etc.]. Nevertheless, the apostle Jude gives an example from his words in his epistle.

In this generation the sons of God desired the daughters of men—that is, the sons of Seth desired the daughters of Cain.

In the 187th year of his life Methuselah begot Lamech, while Adam was still alive and 874 years old. In Methuselah’s 243rd year, when his son Lamech was 56 years old, Adam died in the 930th year of his life.

In this generation giants were born. At this time also Jubal, who was of the race of Cain, discovered the art of music; his brother Tubal-cain was the inventor of bronze and iron.

According to the reckoning of the Seventy Interpreters, Methuselah is found to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. For this reason some, holding a false opinion, believe that he remained for a time with his father Enoch, who had been translated, until the Flood passed. It is nevertheless certain, as Saint Augustine says in his book *On the City of God* (XV, 11), that he did not live after the Flood, but died in the very year in which the Flood occurred, at the age of 969.

In the 182nd year of his life Lamech begot Noah. By a divine oracle Noah was commanded to build the ark in the 500th year of his life, when God had decided to destroy human beings because of their wickedness (ISID.; JOSEPH. I, 4).

The people of that time, who through the ingenuity divinely handed down to them had discovered various arts and disciplines over such long spans of life, had been told by Adam, filled with the Spirit of God, that the destruction of all things would come in two forms: one through the power of fire, the other through the force and abundance of water. They therefore made two pillars, one of brick and the other of stone, and wrote upon them the discoveries of their studies, so that what they had wisely found might not be erased from memory. The stone pillar is said to have survived the Flood and to remain to this day in Syria.

(ISID.) When Lamech was 777 years old, he died five years before the Flood. From what has been said above it is plainly evident that the beginning of writing originated with the first man himself, who was still alive when his sons were ardently devoted to the pursuit of wisdom.

When Noah was 500 years old, he begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth [Note: [Col. 0503] Thus in the manuscript], 100 years before the Flood; during those years he also built the ark. In his 600th year the Flood inundated the earth.

Thus, in these ten generations from the beginning of the world to the Flood, 2,262 years are reckoned according to the Seventy Interpreters, but according to the Hebrew truth 1,656, as Saint Augustine attests. Josephus, however (*Antiquities of the Jews* I, 5), gives 2,656. He also says:

> Therefore let no one investigate the limits of the ancients, asking how long each one extended his life with his sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons; let him attend only to their origins and generations.

Nor did these men alone, who are written in this succession, beget children, since it is written of each one that he “begot sons and daughters.” Rather, these alone are selected by Moses, the truthful historian, because Noah derived his origin from them with his sons, and through them the world was to be restored after the destruction of the other human beings in the Flood (cf. AUG. *City of God* XV, 15).

(ISID.) After the Flood had passed, Noah’s ark is reported to have come to rest in the mountains of Armenia called Ararat. Noah had three sons, from whom 72 nations arose: from Japheth 15, from Ham 30, and from Shem 27. Noah lived 350 years after the Flood and died at the age of 950.

(JORD. Cf. BEDA.) From Noah’s rule—or from the Flood itself—to the division of languages, which took place because of the offenses of those building the tower in the plain of Shinar, and to Heber, in whom the Hebrew and ancient language remained because he did not participate in that conspiracy to build, there are, according to the Hebrews, 101 years; according to others, 531.

The latter assign more years to each generation and also place a certain Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah, assigning him 125 years and saying that Arphaxad begot Cainan and Cainan begot Shelah. The evangelist Luke, following the Seventy Interpreters, likewise includes this Cainan in the genealogical succession of the patriarchs in his Gospel [Col. 0503D], saying: “who was of Shelah, who was of Cainan, who was of Arphaxad, who was of Shem.” Saint Augustine (*City of God* XVI, 10) and Jordanes the bishop (MUR. I, p. 222) likewise include him.

Yet in the library of Saint Jerome [Note: [Col. 0503D] That is, the Bible], according to the Hebrew truth, he is not found; rather, Arphaxad is said to have begotten Shelah. This is either because Jerome omitted Cainan for some reason unknown to me, or because of the fault of the scribes, through which the name has remained excessively. The calculation of the years is greatly confused by this matter.

The first age of the world is reckoned from Adam to Noah and the Flood, comprising 1,656 years according to the Hebrews and 2,262 according to the Seventy Interpreters (cf. ABB. *Chronicle*). Then the second age begins (cf. ISID.).

(ISID.) When Shem was 100 years old, he begot Arphaxad two years after the Flood.

In his thirty-fifth year [alternatively 135 [Note: [Col. 0503] So in the margin by the first corrector], Arphaxad begot Shelah, from whom the ancient Samaritans derive their name.

In his thirtieth year Shelah begot Heber, from whom the Hebrews were named.

In his thirty-fourth year [alternatively 134 [Note: [Col. 0503] So in the margin by the first corrector], Heber begot Peleg. In his time the tower was built, with the giant Nimrod, Noah’s grandson—namely, son of Cush, son of Ham, son of Noah—inciting men to outrage and contempt of God.

The height of this tower is said to have extended to a distance of 5,174 paces, narrowing gradually toward the upper levels so that it might more easily bear the weight imposed upon it (cf. Gen. X; ISID.).

History declares that the divisions of languages numbered 72—not because there were only that many people at that time and no more, but because it shows that by then there were that many heads of families descended from Noah’s sons, who founded peoples and nations (cf. BEDA).

From the confusion of languages and the primacy of Heber to the birth of Abraham, who was born in the forty-third year of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, 191 years are reckoned according to the Hebrew truth, but according to others (JORD.) 541.

In the thirtieth year of his life [alternatively 130 [Note: [Col. 0503] So in the margin by the first corrector], Peleg begot Reu. (ISID.) At this time, some say, temples were first built, and certain rulers of the nations began to be worshiped as gods.

In the thirty-second year of his life [alternatively 130 [Note: [Col. 0503] So in the margin by the first corrector], Reu begot Serug. Under him the kingdom of the Scythians arose, where Thanus first ruled.

In the thirtieth year of his life [alternatively 130 [Note: [Col. 0503] So in the margin by the first corrector], Serug begot Nahor.

In the twenty-ninth year of his life—or, as others wish, the seventy-ninth [Note: [Col. 0504D] So consistently in Isidore]—Nahor begot Terah. Under him the kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians arose.

(AUG. ibid. XVI, 1.) In the seventieth year of his life Terah begot Abraham, in the forty-third year of Ninus, king of the Assyrians [Note: [Col. 0503] “who is the 238th year” corrected by the first corrector], approximately the 1,238th year before Rome was founded, as another Babylon in the West.

At the time when Abraham was born, three kingdoms of the nations were prominent: those of the Sicyonians, the Egyptians, and the Assyrians. The Assyrian kingdom was much more powerful and exalted, because that king Ninus, son of Belus, had subjected to this kingdom all the peoples of Asia except India.

Hence he is said to have been the first to rule in the world—not because he was the first king, since his father Belus had ruled for 65 years before him, but because, driven by a desire to rule, he invaded foreign kingdoms.

In Assyria, therefore, the dominion of the impious city had prevailed. Its capital was that Babylon which the giant Nimrod, a contemptor of God, built at the beginning of his reign. The name of this earthly city is entirely appropriate: “confusion.”

In that city the first king was called Belus, the father of Ninus. He ruled among the Assyrians for 75 years, up to the twenty-seventh year of Terah, Abraham’s father (cf. HIER.; OROS. I, 4; AUG. and the same work, chapters 4 and 17).

(HIER.) In the forty-fifth year of Belus, king of the Assyrians, the kingdom of the Sicyonians began. Its first ruler was Egialeus, who reigned for 52 years, up to the forty-ninth year of Terah, Abraham’s father. From his name the land over which he ruled was called Egialia; later it was called the Peloponnese [Note: [Col. 0505] “hactenus G.” in the manuscript].

After Egialeus died, Europes ruled second for 45 years. In his twenty-second year—which was Ninus’s forty-third year and Terah’s seventieth—Abraham was born.

At that time the sixteenth dynasty existed in the kingdom of Egypt, which they call a *dynasty*. From this point the Thebans ruled the Egyptians for 190 years.

In the Assyrian kingdom, when King Belus died in the seventy-fifth year of his reign—which was the twenty-seventh year of Terah, Abraham’s father—his son Ninus succeeded him. Ninus is placed first in the succession of the Assyrian kings because, as has been said, while the other kings were ignorant of deceit and content with the boundaries of their kingdoms (OROS. I, 4), he, from a desire to extend his dominion, carried war abroad. He spent fifty years of his life in bloody warfare, until he subjected all Asia except India to himself.

Finally, after defeating Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians and, as they say, the discoverer of magical art, he killed him in battle. Aristotle writes of him (cf. PLIN. XXX, 1) that the indications in his books show that he composed two million lines (OROS. ibid.). Many centuries later Democritus expanded his art.

Ninus died from the strike of an arrow after conquering the world. After making the Assyrian kingdom more powerful than the others, in the forty-fifth year of his reign he founded the city called Ninus (HIER.), which the Hebrews call Nineveh.
