He reigned for 52 years, ten of them after Abraham was born.

(HIER.) In the forty-third year of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, and the twenty-second year of Europes, the second king of the Sicyonians [Note: [Col. 0505] So in the first corrector; likewise several times], Abraham was born from seventy-year-old Terah. In that same year the Thebans began to rule the Egyptians, and did so for 190 years. From this point all writers of history begin their annals.

[Col. 0506C] Here the reckoning of the second age also ends, comprising 292 years. The two ages together—that is, from Adam to Noah and the Flood, and from the Flood to Abraham—amount to 1,948 years [Note: [Col. 0505] Apparently corrected by the first corrector] according to the Hebrew truth. (Cf. *Abbreviated Chronicle*.) Orosius, however, following the Seventy Interpreters, says that from Adam to Abraham there are 3,184 years, and from Abraham to Christ 2,015 years (I, 1).

[Col. 0505] The third age begins from Abraham to David.

From this point to the departure of Israel from Egypt there are 505 years.

(HIER.) Ninus founded the city of Ninus in the region of the Assyrians, which the Hebrews call Nineveh. The fortieth jubilee begins in Abraham’s third year. One jubilee is fifty years.

Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians and inventor of magical art, became renowned.

(HIER., OROS., HIER., JORD.) Semiramis, the wife of Ninus, ruled the Assyrians for 42 years after him, and innumerable stories are told about her. Not content with the boundaries which she had received from her husband, then the sole warrior, she added Ethiopia to her empire by war and made war upon the Indians—a war into which no one except her and Alexander ever entered.

She restored Babylon with baked-brick walls and built embankments against floods of water. [Note: [Col. 0505] Witness 11 adds [Col. 0506C] (cf. *Gesta Trevir.*): “She expelled her stepson Trebeta from the kingdom. He traveled by sea, the Rhine, and the Moselle, and was the first to build Trier, which the people of Trier say he named after himself. Even up to the present time a small epitaph was found there carved in stone:

> Semiramis of Ninus, made fortunate by so great a husband,  
> Possessed much, but added more to what her predecessors held;  
> Not content with her own possessions, nor with the whole extent of the world,  
> She expelled her stepson Trebeta from his ancestral kingdom.  
> As an exile he founded our distinguished city,  
> Trier, and so forth.”]

Under her, Abraham also grew to manhood in Chaldea; he himself too was a Chaldean by birth.

[Note: [Col. 0507] In what follows I omitted the larger numbers that stand empty.]

(HIER.; AUG. XVIII.) Telchin, the third king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 20 years. Under his rule their times were so peaceful and happy that, when he died, they worshiped him as a god, offering sacrifices and celebrating games which they are said to have instituted for him at that time.

(HIER.) Apis, the fourth king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 25 years. From him that land was called Apia; previously it had been called Egialia, and now it is called the Peloponnese.

2,000 years from the origin.

(HIER.) Zameis, also called Ninias, son of Ninus and Semiramis and the fourth king of the Assyrians, ruled for 38 years.

(JORD.) In his twenty-third year, when Abraham was 75 years old, Abraham left Haran at the Lord’s command and went into the land of Canaan; and God’s promise was made to him.

(HIER.) This was the first year of the promise, from which 430 years are reckoned to Israel’s departure from Egypt. The apostle Paul mentions these years, saying: “Now I say this: the testament…” and so forth.

(HIER.) Cres first ruled the island which was called Crete after him.

Telexion, the fifth king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 52 years.

When Abraham was 75 years old, he received the promise, having been deemed worthy of divine speech. The first year of the promise.

Abraham begot Ishmael by the slave woman Hagar. From him came the race of the Ishmaelites, later called Hagarenes and then Saracens.

Arius, the fifth king of the Assyrians, ruled for 30 years.

When Abraham was 100 years old, he begot Isaac from Sarah, a free woman who was 90 years old, and afterward lived 75 years.

—The word of God first appeared to Abraham, the first of all the prophets, in human form and promised the calling of the nations, which in our time the message of Christ brought to completion through the preaching of the Gospel among all nations.

Aralius, the sixth king of the Assyrians, ruled for 40 years.

Egidrus, the sixth king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 34 years.

[An. 2100.]

Thurimachus, the seventh king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 45 years.

In the sixtieth year of his life Isaac begot twins by Rebecca. The elder was Esau, also called Edom, from whom came the Idumeans; the other was Jacob, who was surnamed Israel, from whom came the Israelites.

[Col. 0507] Xerxes, also called Baleus, the seventh king of the Assyrians, ruled for 30 years.

—From this point the kingdom of the Argives begins. In Argos Inachus first ruled for 50 years. This kingdom lasted 552 years, from Inachus to Eurystheus, the first king of Mycenae. [Note: [Col. 0507] “Quod … DLII” corrected by the first corrector.]

The 100th year of the promise. [Note: [Col. 0507] These years were omitted below.]

Abraham died.

[Col. 0509] Up to this point the Thebans ruled the Egyptians; from then onward the Pharaohs ruled for 103 years. They were also called “shepherds,” because, as we conjecture, Jacob and his sons entered Egypt as shepherds during their time.

Armamitres, the eighth king of the Assyrians, ruled for 38 years.

Leucippus, the eighth king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 53 years.

Shem died 500 years after the Flood. Some believe that he was Melchizedek. The Hebrews relate that from him until the priesthood of Aaron all the firstborn were priests and sacrificed victims to God, and that these were the birthright privileges which Esau sold to his brother Jacob (cf. ISID.; HIER. on Isaiah XLI).

(HIER.—AUG. XVIII, 3; ibid. VIII, 27.) Phoroneus, son of Inachus and Niobe, ruled second at Argos for 60 years. He was the first to write down laws and judgments for the Greeks.

His sister Io became queen of Egypt and was called Isis. Because she had ruled widely and justly, had done many useful things for the Egyptians, and had established writing for them, she deserved divine honors after her death—to such an extent that anyone who said she had been a human being was punished with death.

She was the wife of Osyris, king of Egypt. After sacrificing to the king’s parents, all of whom were said to have been kings, she discovered a crop of barley and showed its ears to her husband the king and to his counselor Mercury. For this reason some wish her to be the same as Ceres.

(HIER.) Io later married Telegonus and begot Epaphus.

Thessalus, son of Graecus, ruled in Thessaly. Greece was called after Graecus, and Thessaly after Thessalus (cf. PLIN. I, 7).

(HIER.) Belochus, king of the Assyrians, ruled for 35 years.

Ogyges founded Eleusis in the province of Attica, which in ancient times was called Acta, and many other cities. In his time a maiden appeared near Lake Tritonis whom the Greeks called Minerva.

[Col. 0509] Jacob took Leah and Rachel in Mesopotamia. Jacob begot Joseph, after ten sons had already been born.

[An. 2200.]

Messapus, the ninth king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 47 years.

A flood occurred in Achaea under Ogyges. There was also a flood in Egypt.

Baleus, the tenth king of the Assyrians, ruled for 52 years.

(HIER.—Gen.) When Joseph was sixteen years old, his brothers sold him into Egypt. He was appointed lord of the land by Pharaoh, and his father, compelled by famine, went down there with his entire household and lived there.

(HIER.) Apis, the third king, ruled at Argos for 35 years. They say that he was Serapis. He appointed his brother Egialeus king of Achaea, while he himself sailed with his people to Egypt.

(AUG. *City of God* XVIII, 5.) When he died there, he became the greatest of all the Egyptian gods, Serapis. When they worshiped him buried in a sarcophagus before a temple was built for him, he was first called Sorapis from what they call a sarcophagus, *soros*, as though *soros Apis* (“Apis’s coffin”); later, with the *o* changed to *e* [Note: [Col. 0509] “e” changed to “o” by the first corrector], he was called Serapis.

It was also decreed concerning him that anyone who said he had been a human being should suffer capital punishment. And since Isis was worshiped in almost all the temples where Serapis was worshiped, there was an image there which, with a finger pressed to its lips, seemed to admonish people to keep silence—obviously so that no one would say that they had been human beings. (Chapter 6.) Apis, therefore, was not an Egyptian but an Argive king, for whom these institutions were established in Egypt.

(HIER.) Apis ruled for 35 years.

The 200th year of the promise.

Memphis in Egypt was founded by Apis.

When Joseph was 30 years old, Pharaoh appointed him ruler of Egypt.

Jacob went down into Egypt with his household.

Isaac died at the age of 180.

After the eighteenth dynasty, Amoses, the first of the Diapolitan kings, ruled for 25 years.

Sparta was founded by Sparto, son of Phoroneus.

Arathus, the tenth king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 46 years.

[Col. 0511] (HIER.) Argus, son of Apis, succeeded his father and ruled for 70 years. From him the people of Argos were thereafter called Argives.

(AUG. ibid., chapter 6.) During his reign Greece began to use grain and to possess cultivated fields, the seeds having been brought from elsewhere. He also deserved divine honors after his death.

When Jacob was 147 years old, he died in Egypt, leaving his son Joseph as ruler of Egypt. Joseph was 57 years old and was in the twenty-seventh year of his administration.

(JORD.) Joseph brought his father’s body back to the land of Canaan with great honor.

(HIER.) Altadas, the eleventh king of the Assyrians, ruled for 32 years.

Chebron, king of the Egyptians, ruled for 13 years.

Prometheus is said to have lived at this time. Poets imagine that human beings were made from clay by him because, being wise, he transformed human savagery and ignorance into humanity and knowledge.

His brother Atlas was a great astrologer. Because he discovered the courses of the stars on Mount Atlas, the occasion gave rise to the fable that he carried the heavens.

(AUG. ibid., chapter 8.) Mercury, too, the grandson of Atlas through his daughter Maia, became famous for his knowledge of many arts, and after his death entered the number of the gods. Many other fictions are also invented in Greece about this period.

(HIER.) Ammenophis [Note: [Col. 0511] “amenosis” corrected to “amenofis” by the first corrector], the third king of the Egyptians, ruled for 21 years.

Plemnaeus, the eleventh king of the Sicyonians, ruled for 48 years.

Maminthus, the twelfth king of the Assyrians, ruled for 30 years.

[An. 2300.]

Meires, the fourth king of the Egyptians, ruled for 12 years.

Joseph died in the 110th year of his life, the eightieth year of his administration. From then onward the harsh servitude of the Hebrews in Egypt lasted 144 years.

The total number of years which the Hebrews spent in Egypt was therefore 215, reckoned from the time when Jacob went down into Egypt with his sons.

[Col. 0511] (HIER.) Mispharmutos, the fifth king of the Egyptians, ruled for 26 years.

Creausus, the fifth king of the Argives, ruled for 54 years.

Machaleus, the thirteenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 30 years. Theomesis, the sixth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 9 years.

Ortopolis, the twelfth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 63 years.

Ammenopes, the seventh king of the Egyptians, reigned for 31 years. At this time Syrus, a native of the region, is thought to have lived; Syria was named after him.

Sperus, the fourteenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 20 years. Moses was born in Egypt.

Mamilus, the fifteenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 30 years. Epidaurus was founded. Phorbas, the sixth king of the Argives, reigned for 35 years. Horus, the eighth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 38 years. Hemon reigned in Thessaly, which was named Hemonia after him. (Cf. PLINY I, 7.)

(HIER.) Hercules is said to have been the first to overcome Antaeus in a wrestling contest. Xanthus, son of Triopas, founded Lesbos.

[Column 0513] (Year 2400.)

The thirtieth year of Moses.

Sparatus, the sixteenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 40 years. Marathius, the thirteenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 30 years.

In the thirty-fifth year of Moses, the kingdom of the Athenians began. Its first king was Cecrops, also called Diphyes, who reigned for 50 years. He was called Diphyes either because of the length of his body or because, although he was Egyptian, he knew both languages, Egyptian and Greek. In Acte, which is now called Attica, he founded Athens, which they also call Diadas; the Euboeans called this city Corcomenon. (AUG. in the same work, 9.) Varro relates the following reason why the city was called Athens—a name certainly derived from Minerva, who is called Athena in Greek.

When an olive tree suddenly appeared there and water burst forth in another place, these prodigies moved the king. He therefore sent to the Delphic Apollo to inquire about the matter. The god replied that the signs referred to Neptune and Minerva, and that it lay within the citizens’ power to decide after which of the two deities the city should rather be named.

After receiving this oracle, Cecrops summoned all the citizens of both sexes for consultation. For at that time it was customary in those places for women also to participate in public deliberations. When the multitude had therefore been consulted, the men voted for Neptune and the women for Minerva. But because one more woman was found [Note: [Column 0513] “fe || || narum” in manuscript 1.], Minerva won.

Then Neptune, angered, ravaged the lands of the Athenians with surging sea waves, since it is not difficult for demons to scatter whatever waters they wish over a wider area. To appease his anger, the Athenians subjected the women to a threefold penalty: they were no longer to cast votes; none of their children was to receive a maternal name; and no one was to call them Athenians.

Thus that city—the mother and nurse of liberal learning and of so many great philosophers, a city than which Greece possessed nothing more illustrious or noble—received the name Athens through demons mocking the quarrel of their gods, the sea and the woman, and the victory of the woman through women, that is, through Minerva. (ISIDORE—HIERONYMUS.)

Accordingly, Cecrops called the Attics Athenians, and the region was named Crecopia [Note: thus manuscript 1; others read “Cecropia.”]. While sacrificing an ox, he was the first to invoke Jupiter and to prescribe that he be worshiped in sacrifice.

From him until the first Olympiad, 17 kings are counted, but 12 rulers whose terms ended only with death. Under them many marvelous things are said to have occurred among the Greeks. For it was then that the Curetes and Corybantes, who founded Cnosus, first devised a measured and harmonious dance in arms. At that time, too, a flood in Thessaly under Deucalion is described. Then also occurred the legendary burning caused by Phaethon; then a temple was built for Apollo at Delphi; and many similar events took place.

From Cecrops [Note: “Cecrope” in manuscript 1; others read “Cecrope”] until the capture of Troy, 329 years are counted.

Cecrops, the first king of the Athenians, reigned for 50 years.

(JORDANES—HIERONYMUS.) The fortieth year of Moses. After killing the Egyptian, he fled into the land of Midian.

Triopas, the seventh king of the Argives, reigned for 46 years.

Acenceres, the ninth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 12 years.

Deucalion began to reign among those who lived around Parnassus.

Achoris, the tenth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 7 years. (HIER.) Marathus, the fourteenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 20 years. Cenchris, the eleventh king of the Egyptians, reigned for 18 years. The flood occurred in Thessaly under Deucalion. Aschatades, the seventeenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 40 years.

(JORDANES—HIERONYMUS.) In the 430th year of the promise, Moses, at God’s command, led the people of Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders, when he was 80 years old; and he expounded the law to them in the wilderness for 40 years.

From this point until Solomon and the construction of the Temple, 478 years are counted; until the capture of Troy, 329 years.

[Column 0513] Acherres, the twelfth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 8 years.

Echireus, the fifteenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 55 years.

Aaron was appointed the first high priest of the Hebrews. Crotopus, the eighth king of the Argives, reigned for 21 years. Gravanus, the second king of the Athenians, reigned for 9 years.

Cherres, the thirteenth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 15 years. Amphictyon, the third king of the Athenians, reigned for 10 years. Armagis, the fourteenth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 5 years. He was also called Danaus. Erycthonius, the fourth king of the Athenians, reigned for 50 years. He first yoked a chariot in Greece. (AUG. in the same work, chapter 2.)

He was found as a child in the temple of Vulcan and Minerva, which the two shared, wrapped around by a serpent; this signified that he would become great. Since his parents were unknown, he was called the son of Vulcan and Minerva on account of their common temple. And because he had been wrapped in a serpent, he is imagined as having been born with serpent-like feet, and for this reason is said to have yoked the chariot.

(HIER.) Stenelus, the ninth king of the Argives, reigned for 11 years.

Remeses, also called Egypt, after whom Egypt—formerly called Acria—received its name, reigned for 68 years. He had a brother, Danaus, who had 50 daughters; Egypt had an equal number of sons. Danaus, by means of his daughters and under the pretense of marriage, killed all of them in a single night except Lynceus, who later reigned at Argos after Danaus and escaped through the compassion of his bride. (OROSIUS I, 11.)

Danaus himself, after driving out his brother, reigned over Egypt; but later, after being driven out in turn, he went to Argos. There Stenelus received him kindly, but Danaus later expelled Stenelus himself and reigned in his place.

(HIER.) Amintes, the eighteenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 45 years.

Danaus, from whom the Danaans also took their name, the tenth king of the Argives, expelled Stenelus and reigned for 50 years. His descendants continued until Eurystheus, son of Stenelus and grandson of Perseus; after him the Pelopids took control, the first of them to reign being Atreus.

At this same time Dardanus founded Dardania, and the temple at Delphi was burned by Phlegeus.

At this time, too, Busiris lived in Egypt, the son of Neptune and Libya, daughter of Epaphus. While exercising tyranny in the regions near the Nile, he killed passing strangers at an altar in a savage crime.

(AUG. in the same work, chapter 12.) During this period—that is, from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt until the death of Joshua—kings established rites for false gods. These rites recalled the memory of the flood that had occurred under Deucalion and of the wretched life of those who moved now to high ground and now to low.

(HIER.) Moses, when he was 120 years old and in the fortieth year of his rule, died. From the creation of the world, his death occurred after 3,730 years according to the Septuagint translation, but according to the Hebrew truth, after 2,493 years [Note: The final figure is corrected in manuscript 1.].

(HIER.) Joshua, also called Jesunave (as Augustine and Jordanes have it), the minister and successor of Moses, brought the people into the Promised Land, divided the land among them, and ruled the people for 27 years.

(Year 2500.) Corax, the sixteenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 30 years.

Joshua died when he was 110 years old. After his death, when the children of Israel had sinned before the Lord, the Lord delivered them into the hands of foreigners for 8 years. Then, when they cried out to the Lord, he gave them the leader Gothoniel, who, as the first judge, ruled for 40 years; those 40 years include the eight years of the Hebrews’ oppression [Note: “Judeorum” is corrected to “Hebreorum” in manuscript 5.]. (Cf. HIER.)

(HIER.) At that time Phinehas assumed the priesthood after Gothoniel. Pandion, the fifth king of the Athenians, reigned for 40 years. His daughters were Progne and Philomela.

Belochus, the nineteenth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 25 years. His daughter Tosa, also called Semiramis, reigned with her father for 8 years.

At this time Jupiter was united with Europa, daughter of Phoenix. The Cretans carried her off in a ship bearing a bull as its emblem. Later Asterius—whom others call Xanthus (AUG. in the same work, chapter 12)—the king of the Cretans, took her as his wife and fathered by her Rhadamanthus, Sarpedon, and Minos. It became more widely reported, however, that they were sons of Jupiter by the same woman.

(HIER.) At that time Cadmus also reigned at Thebes. His daughter Semele gave birth to Dionysus, who was also called Father Liber and Bacchus. Later Cadmus and Phoenix departed from Thebes for Syria and reigned at Tyre and Sidon. Linus, Zethus, and Amphion also became renowned in the art of music at this time. The events related concerning Danae [Note: “Dana” in manuscript 1, for “Danae”]—from whom Perseus was born—also occurred at this time.

Ephyra, now called Corinth, was founded by Sisyphus, and Bithynia by Phoenix. Tarsus and Paphus were also founded.

Epopeus, the seventeenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 35 years. Lynceus, the eleventh king of the Argives, reigned for 41 years.

Menopes, the seventeenth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 40 years.

Bellespares, the twentieth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 30 years (cf. below).

[Column 0517] (AUG. in the same work—OROSIUS, chapter 9.) At this time Dionysus, also called Father Liber, is said to have shown his host the vine in the land of Attica. He also subdued India, drenched it in blood, filled it with slaughter, and polluted it with lust—India, a nation that had never been subject to any human being and had been content with its own native peace.

(HIER.) He had many women in his army, who were called Bacchae; they were strong and noble not so much by valor as by frenzy.

(AUG. in the same work.) At this time Hercules, surnamed Desanaus, was renowned in Phoenicia. But he was not the Hercules whose enormous and innumerable deeds are recounted and whom the Greeks record in their writings as having burned himself alive. As Saint Augustine says, a more hidden history indicates that there were several men called Hercules, Fathers Liber, and Apollos.

(HIER.) At this time Minos also reigned in Crete and Celeus at Eleusis. Arcas, son of Jupiter and Callisto, having received the Pelasgians into submission, named their region Arcadia.

Bellespares, king of the Assyrians, 30 years.

(Cf. HIER.) After the death of Gothoniel, the Hebrews again sinned against the Lord. When he permitted it, the Philistines oppressed them for 18 years, which are nevertheless counted among the years of Ehud.

(BEDA.) Ehud, from the tribe of Ephraim, the second judge of the Hebrews, judged them for 80 years. He used both hands as though they were his right hand.

(HIER.) Erichthaeus, the sixth king of the Athenians, reigned for 30 years. Boreas, son of Astraeus and king of the Thracians, carried off his daughter Orithyia; mythology invents him as having been a wind.

Laomedon, the eighteenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 40 years. Arbas, the twelfth king of the Argives, reigned for 23 years.

(AUG., in the same work, chapter 13.) Lamprides, the twenty-first king of the Assyrians, reigned for 32 years.

(HIER.) At this time the story of Triptolemus, son of Celeus, was invented: that, at Ceres’ command, he was carried on the wings of serpents and brought grain to the needy. In reality, as Philochorus says, he approached various cities in a long ship and distributed grain; the emblem of that ship was a winged serpent.

The story of Proserpina was also invented. Aidoneus, that is, Orcus, king of the Molossians, carried her off. His dog, Cerberus, of marvelous size, devoured Pirithous, who had come with Theseus to abduct Proserpina. Hercules, arriving when Theseus himself was already in danger of death, rescued him as well; for this reason Theseus is said, as it were, to have been snatched from the underworld.

At this time Phrixus is said to have lived, according to the opinion of some. Fleeing with his sister Helle from the plots of his stepmother, he was seen to travel through the air on a ram with a golden fleece. In fact, a ship had been prepared for his flight, and its emblem was a ram. (AUG. in the same work.) Palaephatus [Note: Corrected in manuscript 1; two words were erased, one of them “Philochorus”] asserts that his nurse was called Taurus and that through him Phrixus was rescued.

At this time Latona gave birth to Apollo—not the Apollo whose oracles were customarily consulted at Delphi, but the one who served Admetus together with Hercules. Nevertheless, he was believed to be a god, so that almost everyone supposes that there was only one Apollo.

Lamprides.

(HIER.) Setus, the eighteenth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 55 years; he was the first after the eighteenth dynasty [Note: “VIII” in manuscript 1.].

Proetus, the thirteenth king of the Argives, reigned for 17 years. Sicyon, the nineteenth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 45 years. The Sicyonians were named after him; previously they had been called Aegialeans.

Sosares, the twenty-second king of the Assyrians, reigned for 20 years.

At this time Pelops reigned in Greece, after whom the Peloponnese was named. (OROSIUS I, 12.) He was the son of Pandion, under whom the mysteries of the Greeks began. [Note: “Jerome speaks here of Erechtheus.”]

In Dardania, however, Tros reigned, after whom the Trojans were named. In their time Melampus was recognized as a prophet.

At that time Tantalus ruled the Phrygians, who had previously been called Maeonians. When he had shamefully carried off Ganymede, son of Tros, king of the Dardanians, while hunting, he detained him with the greater disgrace of a violent struggle, as the poet Phanocles confirms; he reports that a great war was stirred up on this account. (HIER. Orosius, in the same work.)

Some say that Tantalus himself, as a companion of the gods, prepared the abducted boy for Jupiter’s lust at an intimate entertainment [the reading *Jenocinio* is uncertain]; he did not hesitate to offer his own son Pelops at Jupiter’s banquets as well. Pelops himself, because he took Hippodamia as his wife, endured great conflicts against the Dardanians and Trojans.

At this same time the adulteries and parricides of Atreus and Thyestes occurred—deeds hated even by heaven. Medea, too, wounded by savage love, carried out the slaughter of her little children; and Eteocles and Polynices perished in mutual attacks.

(HIER.—OROSIUS I, 11—AUG. chapter 13.) Perseus, after killing Acrisius unintentionally, crossed from Greece into Asia. There he subdued barbarian nations in a severe and prolonged war, and finally, as victor, gave his name to the subject land. For from Perseus the Persians were called Persians. Perseus and his wife Andromeda were believed after death to have been carried up into heaven, so that their images were marked among the stars and called by their names.

(AUG. in the same work, chapter 14.) Ino, the wife of Rhadamanthus, and her son Melicertes perished by a voluntary plunge into the sea. Ino was called Leucothea by the Greeks and Mater Matuta by the Latins; Melicertes was called the god Portunus.

(OROSIUS I, 12—AUG. chapter 13.) At that time Oedipus also lived: his father’s murderer, his mother’s husband, his sons’ brother, and his own stepfather. Concerning him mythology relates that he forced a certain four-footed monster with a human face, which they call the Sphinx, to perish by throwing itself down, because he solved the riddle that it was accustomed to propose as though it were insoluble.

Other myths were also invented at this time: concerning the Gorgon, namely, that she had hair of serpents and turned people into stone by the beauty of her appearance; concerning the horse Pegasus, born from her blood; concerning the Hippocentaurs, said to be a mixture of the nature of horses and human beings; and many others.

(HIER.) Ion, a certain exceptionally strong man, called the Athenians Ionians after his own name.

Cecrops, the younger brother of Erichthaeus and the seventh king of the Athenians, reigned for 40 years.

Acrisius, the fourteenth king of the Argives, reigned for 39 years.

Lamperes, the twenty-third king of the Assyrians, reigned for 30 years.

At this time, after the death of Acrisius, the kingdom of the Argives came to an end; it had lasted for 452 years. Thereafter, when power had been transferred to Mycenae, Eurystheus, son of Stenelus, reigned after Acrisius, followed by Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, Aegisthus, Orestes, Tisamenus, Pentilus, and Cometes, up to the descent of the Heraclids into the Peloponnese.

After the death of Ehud, foreigners brought the Hebrews under their control for 20 years; these years are joined to the period of Deborah and Barak.

(BEDA—AUG. chapter 15.) Deborah the prophetess judged the people for 40 years, defeating their enemies through Barak, who was from the tribe of Naphtali. Deborah, however, was from the tribe of Ephraim; her prophecy concerning Christ is less evident and requires a lengthy exposition.

(HIER.) Ramses, the nineteenth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 66 years. Pandion, the eighth king of the Athenians, reigned for 25 years.

Polibus, the twentieth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 40 years. Eurystheus, the first king of Mycenae, reigned for 43 years.

Pannias, the twenty-fourth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 45 years.

At this time Amphion reigned at Thebes. He is said to have moved stones by the sound of his lyre, because his listeners were hard-hearted and, so to speak, actually made of stone.

The events related concerning the Spartoi are also said to have occurred at this time. Palaephatus writes that, since they were from neighboring regions, they stood against Cadmus and, because they had suddenly, as it were, been gathered from the earth and flowed together from every side, were called Spartoi.

Ilion was founded by Ilus.

(AUG. chapter 15.) (H. R.) At this time the Laurentes ruled throughout Italy. Their first king, according to some, was Picus, son of Saturn. Saturn, fleeing his son Jupiter, came from Greece and hid in the city that was called Saturnia after him; its ruins are still visible in the territory of Tuscany, not far from Rome. Because he hid in Italy, the region was called Latium, from his hiding place.

He led the still uncivilized peoples, who hid in the mountains or forests, down to the plains; he taught them to build houses, cultivate the land, plant vineyards, and live according to human customs. Previously they had sustained life like half-wild creatures solely on acorns and had lived either in caves or in huts woven from leaves and branches. Because he taught them to enrich the earth with manure so that it would produce more abundant crops, he was called Stercutius or Sterticen.

(AUG. in the same work—H. R.) He was also the first to establish bronze coins. For these services the ignorant and rustic multitude called him a god.

But according to some, Janus first reigned in Italy, then Saturn, whom Janus himself received as he fled from Greece and, because of his intelligence, admitted into a share of the kingdom [Note: The passage from “whom” to “admitted” was added in manuscript 1; its source is unknown]. Then came Picus, his son. Mythology says that a certain famous sorceress named Circe, because he rejected her love, changed Picus into a bird bearing his own name, since he was an outstanding augur and kept a woodpecker with him in divination. (Cf. AUG. in the same work.)

(H. R.) After him came his son Faunus, who was the father of Latinus. His mother, Carmentis Nicostrata, is believed to have discovered the Latin letters. During their reigns, 150 years are said to have passed.

While Latinus was reigning—he who improved the Latin language and called the Latins by his own name—Troy was captured, when among the Hebrews Lapdon was completing the third year of his rule.

(HIER.) After the death of Deborah, foreigners again brought the Hebrews under their control for 7 years; these years are joined to the years of Gideon according to the traditions of the Jews [Note: “Hebrews” in manuscript 5.]. Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, from the tribe of Manasseh, judged the Hebrew people for 40 years (cf. BEDA).

(HIER.) Aegeus, son of Pandion and the ninth king of the Athenians, reigned for 48 years. (HIER.) Inachus, the twenty-first king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 42 years.

Atreus and Thyestes, brothers, reigned at Mycenae for 65 years.

Menoses, the twentieth king of the Egyptians, reigned for 40 years. Some say that he was Vesoces (OROSIUS). [Note: The words “He is called Vesoces by some” appear to have been added later in manuscript 1.]

(HIER.) Sosarmus, the twenty-fifth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 19 years. At this time some assign the deeds of Father Liber and the events related concerning Lycurgus, Actaeon, and Pentheus.

Abimelech, son of Gideon by a concubine, killed his seventy brothers and judged the Hebrew people for 3 years (cf. HIER.).

Tola, son of Puah, who was Abimelech’s paternal uncle, judged the Hebrews for 22 years (cf. HIER. and BEDA).

(HIER.) Theseus, son of Aegeus and the tenth king of the Athenians, reigned for 30 years.

Mitreus, the twenty-sixth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 27 years.

At this time Orpheus the Thracian was renowned; his disciple was Musaeus, son of Eumolpus.

(AUG. chapter 13.) Linus, the teacher of Hercules, was also famous. Hercules himself performed many contests and killed Antaeus, who is therefore said to have been the son of Earth and, when falling, to have drawn strength from her, because he was highly skilled in the athletic art practiced on the ground.

(HIER.) As for the Hydra that Hercules killed, although others say that it was a marsh overflowing with springs, Plato asserts that it was a woman, an exceedingly clever sophist.

The war between the Lapiths and the Centaurs took place at this time. Palaephatus writes that they were the most distinguished horsemen of the Thessalians and that they were believed and called Centaurs by the Lapiths, (OROSIUS I, 13) because, riding about in battle, they seemed by their speed to form a single body of horses and men.

(HIER.) The events related concerning Daedalus are also said to have occurred at this time. He was thought to have made self-moving statues and to have been the first of all to separate the feet of statues from one another, whereas others made them joined together. It is also related how he fled from Minos by ship with his son Icarus and, because of the extraordinary speed and untraceable course of his flight, was thought to have flown away on wings.

(OROSIUS.) Minos gave laws to the Cretans. His son Androgeus was treacherously killed by the Athenians when he surpassed them in the games. Hence an exceptionally savage conflict arose between the Cretans and the Athenians. After the two peoples had been defeated, the Cretans disastrously pursued a bloodier victory. They cruelly condemned the sons of the Athenian nobles to be devoured by the Minotaur [Note: “Athenians” in manuscript 1.]. Whether this Minotaur was a savage, inhuman, and cruel man or an unnatural monster is uncertain. (Thus Orosius.)

(HIER.) For Philochorus writes in the second book of his *Atthis* that Minos’ teacher was a man named Taurus, inhuman and cruel. Since Minos had established a contest over the death of Androgeus and offered Attic boys as prizes, Taurus, being the strongest, defeated everyone in the contest. But finally he was defeated by Theseus in the athletic arena, and for this reason the Athenian boys were freed from the tribute imposed as punishment.

Theseus gathered the Athenians, who had previously been scattered throughout the region, into a single city. He also carried off Helen, whom her brothers later recovered after capturing Theseus’ mother. Finally, Theseus abandoned Athens as an exile, having been disgracefully expelled.

At this time the Argonauts also lived. With Jason, they traveled to Colchis to seize the Golden Fleece. At that time Laomedon reigned at Troy; after him came his son Priam, under whom Troy was captured (cf. HIER.).

(OROSIUS I, 14.) At the same time Vesoces, king of Egypt, wishing to unite by war or incorporate into his kingdom the southern and northern regions, which were separated almost by the entire extent of heaven and sea, first declared war on the Scythians. He first sent ambassadors to announce to the enemy the terms on which they should submit.

The Scythians replied to the ambassadors that the wealthy king had foolishly undertaken war against the poor, although in a reversal of circumstances he would have more reason to fear them. In war’s uncertain outcomes there were no rewards for him but evident losses; moreover, they did not need to wait for him to come to them, but would go out to meet him of their own accord in pursuit of booty.

There was no delay: words were followed by deeds. First they terrified Vesoces himself and forced him to flee back to his kingdom. Then they attacked his abandoned army and seized all its military equipment. They would have ravaged all Egypt as well, had the marshes of the Nile not stopped them. After immediately returning from there, they subdued all Asia through countless slaughters.

These were the people called Getae or Goths, and in this way and at this time they first came out of Scythia (cf. JORDANES, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*, chapter 6).

Mitreus.

(HIER.) Festus, the twenty-second king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 8 years.

[Column 0523] Jair, from the tribe of Manasseh, judged the people of God for 22 years. He had 30 warrior sons, each a ruler of a city.

Adrastus, the twenty-third king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 4 years. Agamenes, the twenty-first king of the Egyptians, reigned for 26 years.

Phylopides, the twenty-fourth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 31 years.

Thautanes, the twenty-seventh king of the Assyrians, reigned for 32 years.

At this time Minos continued to establish laws and legal institutions. Eventually, when he took up arms against Daedalus in Sicily, he was killed by the daughters of Cocalus.

(HIER.) At that time Hercules also established the Olympic contest. From then until the first Olympiad, 430 years are calculated. Among his great deeds, twelve labors are counted. (Cf. AUG. chapter 12—HIER.)

After he had accomplished many brave deeds, he fell into a fatal illness. To relieve his pain, he cast himself into the flames on Mount Oeta, and thus met his death in the fifty-second year of his life.

During this period Alexander Paris carried off Helen. Because of her, the ten-year Trojan War arose and Troy was captured. He carried her off in the fifteenth year of Thautanes, and Troy was captured in Thautanes’ twenty-fifth year.

Thautanes.

Menestheus, the eleventh king of the Athenians, reigned for 23 years.

After the death of Jair, the Ammonites brought the Hebrews under their control for 19 years; these are counted together with the periods of the later judges according to the tradition of the Jews.

Jephthah judged the Hebrew people for 6 years.

Agamemnon ruled at Mycenae: in his fifteenth year Troy was captured.

Abessan, or Esebon, judged the people of God for 7 years (Judges 12). He had 30 sons and as many daughters; while he was still alive, he gave his daughters to husbands and took wives for his sons.

(HIER.) Theores, the twenty-second king of the Egyptians, reigned for 7 years.

Abdon judged the people of God for 8 years and had 40 sons. In the Book of Judges, however, chapter 12, it is said that after Esbon a judge named Aglaon ruled the people for 10 years; he is not found in the Septuagint translators.

(ISIDORE.) In the third year of Abdon, who was the twenty-fifth year of Thautanes, Troy was captured.

(HIER.) The destruction of Troy; from it until the first Olympiad, 405 years are counted.

The twentieth Egyptian dynasty began immediately after the destruction of Troy and lasted for 177 years. The kings of this period are not recorded among us. The kings of Mycenae, however, are not subsequently written down in order. After Agamemnon, Aegisthus reigned, followed by Orestes, then Tisamenus, Pentilus, and Cometes. Thus, 80 years after the destruction of Troy, the kingdom was transferred to the Lacedaemonians (cf. HIER.).

Demophon, son of Theseus and the twelfth king of the Athenians, reigned for 33 years.

(JORDANES; AUG. chapter 19.) Aeneas, fleeing from Troy, came to Italy with 20 ships, as some say (H. R.; JORDANES), in the third year after the destruction of Troy, although others say that he came in the seventh year (cf. HIER., JORD., H. R., AUG.). He joined himself to Latinus, son of Faunus and king of the Latins, through marriage, taking his daughter Lavinia as his wife. He killed Turnus, son of Daunus, king of the Etruscans, who had been betrothed to her. Thus they called the Phrygians and the Italian peoples together by the name Latins. From that time onward they reigned, although in an extremely poor kingdom and in a narrow region called the Laurentian Plain.

After Latinus died, Aeneas reigned for 3 years and built a fortress, which he called Lavinium after his wife. Because he was an extremely savage and cruel warrior and spared no one, he died, struck by a thunderbolt from God on account of such impiety. [Note: From “Because he was” to “he died,” I do not know from what author these statements were taken. In Uspergensis (11) the following is related of him: “Hence the Roman people trace their origin from Aeneas the exile, whom Virgil himself flatters as a brave man, but whom others represent as a traitor to his country and a necromancer, since he even sacrificed his own wife to his gods.”]

Some say (cf. FREDERIC II, 8.3) that Aeneas and Frigas were two full brothers. Aeneas reigned in Latium and Frigas in Phrygia. From Phrygus there arose a people who, wandering through many regions with their wives and children, chose a king from among themselves named Francio. The Franks are thought to have been named after him because he was exceptionally brave. After he had fought against very many peoples and directed his journey toward Europe, they settled between the Rhine and the Danube.

After Francio died, those whom he left behind fought many battles. Worn down by these struggles, they were reduced to a small number. They then appointed leaders from among themselves, but always refused to bear the yoke of another. From these, those who are still called Franks are thought to have descended.

(H. R.) After Aeneas died, Ascanius, his son, whom Creusa bore to him at Troy and whom he brought with him, assumed the kingdom and reigned for 38 years. Lavinia bore a son after Aeneas’ death and named him Postumus Aeneas. He was also called Silvius, as some say (JORDANES), because Lavinia, fearing Ascanius’ hostility, secretly gave birth to him and raised him in the forest.

(H. R.) Ascanius nevertheless raised him with the greatest devotion. He left Lavinium to his stepmother Lavinia, founded the city of Alba, and reigned there. He fathered a son whom he called Julius, from whom the family of the Julii arose.

When Ascanius had reigned for 38 years and his son was still a child, unfit to govern the citizens, he left his brother Postumus Aeneas Silvius as heir to the kingdom. From him later kings were called Silvii, and from Alba, Albans (cf. JORDANES).

(HIER.) At this time the events related about Ulysses are said to have occurred, including how he fled Scylla in a trireme; she was accustomed to rob travelers. Palaephatus also writes in the first book of his *On Incredible Things* that at that time the Sirens were prostitutes who deceived sailors.

At that time Pyrrhus was also killed in the Delphic temple by Orestes through the treachery of the priest Machareus.

Some say that Homer also lived at that time. Opinions differ concerning his date: some say that he lived 100 years after the destruction of Troy, others 200 years after it, others 180, and others give different figures.

Pelasgus, the twenty-fifth king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 20 years.

After Labdon, foreigners again brought the Hebrews under their control for 40 years; according to the tradition of the Hebrews, these years are counted among the periods of the later judges.

Samson judged the Hebrew people for 20 years. Because he was extraordinarily strong, he was regarded by the nations as Hercules.

Ascanius, the first king of the Albans, reigned for 38 years.

(HIER.) Teuteus, the twenty-eighth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 40 years. In his first year Ascanius founded a city, which he called Alba Longa.

Zeuxippus, the twenty-sixth and last king of the Sicyonians, reigned for 32 years.

Eli was both priest and judge for 40 years. Under him the Ark was captured; when he heard this, he fell from his seat and died.

Onixistes, the thirteenth king of Athens, reigned for 12 years.

Silvius Postumus, son of Aeneas and the second king of the Albans, reigned for 29 years.

Aphidas, the fourteenth king of Athens, reigned for one year.

Thymaetes, the fifteenth king of Athens, reigned for 8 years.

Tineus, the twenty-ninth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 30 years. During his reign, the sons of Hector, after expelling the descendants of Antenor, recovered Ilion, with Helenus providing them assistance.

Melanthus, the sixteenth king of Athens, reigned for 37 years.

The kingdom of the Sicyonians came to an end; it is said to have lasted for 962 years [Note: “1,063” in manuscript 5.].

The prophet Samuel, the judge, and King Saul ruled the Hebrew people for 40 years. From this point kings began to exist among the Hebrew people; Saul was the first (cf. HIER.).

(HIER.) Aeneas Silvius, the third king of the Albans, reigned for 31 years. In another historical account, however, Latinus Silvius is found as the fourth king: he was the son of Silvius and Melampus and the brother of Postumus Silvius. The fifth king—here placed as the fourth—is called Silvius Aeneas, son of Silvius Postumus.

Dercilus, the thirtieth king of the Assyrians, reigned for 40 years. Some say that Homer lived at this time.

At this time the Peloponnesians fought against the Athenians. (AUG. chapter 19.) Codrus, king of the Athenians, voluntarily presented himself to be killed—unknown—to the Peloponnesians, enemies of his city, and thus liberated his homeland.

The Peloponnesians had received an oracle that they would overcome the Athenians only if they killed their king. Codrus therefore put on the appearance of a poor man, approached their camp while gathering firewood, and provoked them with insults until one of them killed him. (AUG. in the same work.) Hence Virgil says: “And the quarrels of Codrus.” The Athenians honored him as a god with sacrifices.

[Column 0525] (HIER.) The kingdoms of the Lacedaemonians and Corinthians arose. The first king of the Lacedaemonians, Eurystheus, reigned for 42 years. The first king of the Corinthians, Alethes, reigned for 35 years.

Codrus, son of Melanthus and the seventeenth king of the Athenians, reigned for 21 years.

Latinus Silvius, the fourth king of the Albans, reigned for 50 years.

Here the third age ends, comprising 940 years; together, the years of the three ages amount to 2,888. The fourth age then begins with David (cf. ISIDORE, *Chronicle of the Abbot*).

(HIER.) David, from the tribe of Judah and king of Israel, reigned for 40 years. During his reign Samuel, Gad, Nathan, and Asaph prophesied in Judea; Abiathar was high priest.

Medon, the eighteenth king of Athens, reigned for 20 years.

Yxyon, the second king of the Corinthians, reigned for 37 years.

Eupales, the thirty-first king of the Assyrians, reigned for 38 years. In his thirtieth year, as some say, Carthage was founded by Carchedon of Tyre, or, as others maintain, by his daughter Dido, 135 years after the destruction of Troy.

Aegis, the second king of Lacedaemon, reigned for one year. After him Echestratus, the third king, reigned for 35 years. Acastus, the nineteenth king of Athens, reigned for 36 years.

Solomon, son of David, the wisest and richest of all the Hebrew kings, took possession of the Israelite kingdom, which his father David had nobly enlarged. At the Lord’s prompting, and with the support of his father’s expenditures, he began to build the Temple in Jerusalem in the fourth year of his reign, and completed the entire work of the Temple in the eleventh year of his reign. He reigned for 40 years. Zadok and Ahijah the Shilonite prophesied.

The first construction of the Temple: from it until its desolation [Note: [Col. 0527] “ad—XX.”: partly corrected and partly added later in 1.], 442 years, 4 months, and 10 days; but until its restoration—that is, until the second year of Darius—512 years, 7 months, and 20 days.

Egelaus, the third king of Corinth, reigned 37 years.

Alba Silvius, the fifth of the Albans, reigned 39 years. Laosthenes, the thirty-second king of the Assyrians, reigned 45 years.

Labotes, the fourth king of the Lacedaemonians, reigned 37 years. Archippus, the twentieth king of Athens, reigned 19 years. The twenty-first dynasty of the Egyptians began, in which Semendes was the first to reign, for 26 years.

Here a disagreement among the histories arises, namely concerning the years of Solomon, who is said in the Book of Kings to have reigned for forty years. Josephus, however, says (III, 11) that he held the kingdom for eighty years and that the whole span of his life was ninety-four years. After Solomon’s death, the kingdom of the Hebrews was divided, and only two tribes remained with Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, who reigned in Jerusalem. These two tribes, because David arose from the tribe of Judah, were called Judah; from this the whole nation of the Jews also received its name. The ten tribes, retaining the ancient name, were called Israel, and chose Jeroboam as their king; he reigned in Samaria (cf. HIER. and AUG. XVII, 21).

(HIER.) Rehoboam, therefore, Solomon’s son, reigned over Judah in Jerusalem for 17 years, although others say 22. In his fifth year, Shishak—so Bede reads—or Susachim [Note: [Col. 0527] “q. s. sive” corrected in 1.], king of Egypt, fighting against Jerusalem, captured it and plundered the Temple. In Judaea, Ahijah, Amos, Joel, and Azariah were prophesying.

Jeroboam, however, reigned over Israel in Samaria for 22 years, and caused Israel to sin with golden calves; this evil prevailed for many years (III Kings XII).

[Col. 0527] (HIER.) Thersippus, the twenty-first king of the Athenians, reigned 41 years.

Primnis, the fourth king of the Corinthians, reigned [Col. 0529] 35 years.

Egyptus Silvius, or Atis, the sixth king of the Albans, reigned 24 years. Doristus, the fifth king of the Lacedaemonians, reigned 29 years.

Pyriciades, the thirty-third king of the Assyrians, reigned 30 years.

At this time Ephesus was founded by Andronicus. Samos also was founded, and Smyrna was enlarged into the form of a city. One of the Sibyls also flourished, since we read of several.

[Col. 0529] Abijah, Rehoboam’s son, reigned over Judah in Jerusalem for three years (cf. HIER. and BEDA).

(HIER.) Pseusennes, the second king of the twenty-first Egyptian dynasty, reigned 41 years.

Asa, Abijah’s son, reigned in Jerusalem over Judah for 41 years. In Judaea, Haggai, Jehu, Amos, Joel, Azariah—also called Abdo [Note: [Col. 0529] “also called Abdo” is in the margin of 1.]—Abdiah, and Micah were prophesying (cf. HIER. and BEDA).

Nadab, Jeroboam’s son, reigned in Samaria for two years. Baasha killed him and reigned in his place (cf. HIER.).

Baasha reigned over Israel in Samaria [Note: [Col. 0529] “Samaria” is written above the line, erased, perhaps by another hand, in 1.] for 24 years.

Three thousand years from the origin of the world.

(HIER. and H. m.) Capys Silvius, who founded Capua, son of the preceding king and the seventh king of the Albans, reigned 28 years.

(HIER.) Agesilaus, the sixth king of the Lacedaemonians, reigned 44 years.—Bacchis, the fifth king of Corinth, reigned 35 years.

Phorbas, the twenty-second king of the Athenians, reigned 31 years. Offractheus, the thirty-fourth king of the Assyrians, reigned 20 years.

Elah, Baasha’s son, reigned for two years over Israel. Zimri killed him and reigned in his place [Note: [Col. 0529] 5 reads “for him” (*pro eo*).]. He reigned for seven days [Note: [Col. 0529] “seven days,” corrected in 1.].

Omri, after killing Zimri [Note: [Col. 0529] “after killing Zimri,” corrected in 1.], reigned over Israel for 12 years. Nefercheres, king of Egypt, reigned four years. Carpentius Silvius, the eighth king of the Albans, reigned 13 years.

Jehoshaphat, Asa’s son, reigned over Judah in Jerusalem for 25 years. During his time Elijah, Elisha, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Micah prophesied.

Ahab, Omri’s son [Note: [Col. 0529] corrected in 1.], reigned over Israel for 22 years.

Ammenophis, king of Egypt, reigned nine years.

Offratanes, the thirty-fifth king of the Assyrians, reigned 50 years.

(HIER.) Osochor, king of Egypt, reigned six years.

Tiberinus Silvius, Carpentius’ son and the ninth king of the Albans, reigned eight years. (H. m.) He fell into the river Albula and drowned; afterward the river was called the Tiber from him.

(HIER.) Megiales, or Migades [Note: [Col. 0529] “or Migades” was added later in 1.], the twenty-third king of the Athenians, reigned 30 years.—Agelas, the sixth king of Corinth, reigned 30 years.

Spinnacheus, king of the Egyptians, reigned nine years.

Agrippa Silvius, Tiberinus’ son and the tenth king of the Albans, reigned 40 years.

At this time, some say, Homer lived. For in the Latin history we find this written word for word (thus Jerome): “Agrippa reigned among the Latins. Homer flourished in Greece,” as the grammarian Apollodorus and the historian Euphorbus testify, 143 years before the founding of the City; and, as Cornelius Nepos says, 138 years before the first Olympiad.

Archelaus, the seventh king of the Lacedaemonians, reigned 60 years.

Ahaziah, Ahab’s son, king of Israel, reigned in Samaria for two years.

Joram, Ahab’s son and Ahaziah’s brother, reigned over Israel for 12 years.—Joram, Jehoshaphat’s son, reigned over Judah in Jerusalem for eight years. At that time Elijah, Elisha, and Micah were prophesying in Judaea. In the seventh year of his reign, Elijah was taken up.

Spusennes, king of the Egyptians, reigned 35 years.

Elijah is taken up.

Ahaziah, or Ochoziah (so Jerome), Joram king of Judah’s son, reigned one year.

Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother, reigned in Jerusalem for seven years. After she had killed all the offspring of her son the king, Jehosheba, Joram’s daughter and Ahaziah’s sister, stole Joash, Ahaziah’s son, and hid him; he later became king (IV Kings XI). (HIER.) This Jehosheba was the wife of the priest Jehoiada, whom the Lord calls Barachiah in the Gospel. He was renowned at that time and is said to have been the only person after Moses to live for 130 years.

Jehu killed Joram, Ahab’s son and king of Israel, in the twelfth year of his reign, and himself reigned over Israel for 28 years.

Joash, Ahaziah’s or Ochoziah’s son, with the support of the priest Jehoiada, reigned over Judah in Jerusalem for 40 years. In the sixth year—or, as some write, in the thirty-sixth year—of his reign (HIER.—cf. II Chronicles XXIV; Josephus IX, 10), he killed Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, forgetting the good things that Jehoiada had done for him.

(HIER.) Elisha dies.

[Col. 0531] Diognitus, the twenty-fourth king of Athens, reigned 28 years.—Eudemus, the seventh king of Corinth, reigned 25 years.

Acrazapes, the thirty-sixth king of the Assyrians, reigned 42 years.

Aremius Silvius, Agrippa’s son and the eleventh king of the Albans, reigned 19 years. He established a fortress of the Albans among the mountains where Rome now is; because of his impiety he was struck by lightning. His son Julius Proculus was the great-grandfather of that Julius Proculus who, migrating to Rome with Romulus, founded the Julian clan.

Sisonchus, king of Egypt, reigned 21 years.

Jehoahaz, Jehu’s son, reigned over Israel for 17 years.

Aristodemus, the eighth king of Corinth, reigned 35 years.

Phe­reclus, the twenty-fifth king of Athens, reigned 19 years.

Aventinus Silvius, Aremius’ son and the twelfth king of the Albans, reigned 36 years. The Aventine Hill was named from him because he was buried there.

Amaziah, Joash’s son, reigned in Jerusalem for 29 years.

[Col. 0533] Joash, Jehoahaz’s son, reigned over Israel for 16 years.—Osorthon, king of Egypt, reigned 15 years. Theleclus [Note: [Col. 0533] “dee”; “Nota” is written in the margin in 5. 9.], the eighth king of the Lacedaemonians, reigned 40 years.

Ariphron, the twenty-sixth king of the Athenians, reigned 20 years.

Tonos Concoloros, whom the Greeks call Sardanapalus, the thirty-seventh king of the Assyrians, reigned 20 years. (OROS. I, 19.) More corrupt than a woman, he moved among crowds of prostitutes in feminine dress, drawing purple thread with a distaff, and was scarcely seen by any of his own people. But his prefect Arbaces, who at that time ruled the Medes, saw him and held him in abhorrence. Soon, having summoned the peoples of the Medes and challenged him to war, Arbaces defeated him. Sardanapalus threw himself into a burning pyre from grief and was consumed. Thus Arbaces seized the kingdom and transferred it to the Medes. The Assyrian kingdom, after 1,219 years from the beginning of the reign of Ninus—or, from the time when his father Belus began to reign, after 1,294 years—came to an end after so long a duration (cf. HIER. and BEDA). Jerome reports, however, that in the meantime, until the reign of Deioces, affairs were conducted without rulers, and that during this interval the Chaldeans in particular prevailed; separate successions of their kings are reported. The other nations likewise used their own kings. This same Sardanapalus founded Tarsus and Anchiale.

At the same time the poet Hesiod flourished, and Pheidon of Argos discovered standards of measures and weights. Lycurgus composed laws for the Lacedaemonians.

Thelegotes, king of Egypt, reigned 13 years. Jeroboam, Joash’s son, reigned over Israel for 41 years.

Agemon, the ninth king of Corinth, reigned 16 years.

Uzziah, also called Azariah, Amaziah’s son, reigned over Judah for 52 years. At this time Hosea, Amos, Jonah, Isaiah, and Micah prophesied.—Ponibastes, king of Egypt, reigned 25 years.—Thespius, the twenty-seventh king of Athens and Ariphron’s son, reigned 27 years.

Thus far the histories report that the Assyrian kingdom lasted from the first year of Ninus for 1,239 years [Note: [Col. 0533] “XXX” corrected in 1; “ten” in 5. 9c.], and that from this point the kingdom of the Medes began (cf. HIER.).

Arbaces the Mede, after killing Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians, transferred their kingdom to the Medes, and himself was the first to reign there, for 28 years.

(HIER.) Procas Silvius, Aventinus’ son and the twelfth [reading: thirteenth, E. P.] king of the Albans, reigned 23 years. Alexander [Note: [Col. 0533] This is absent from 5. 9c.], the tenth king of Corinth, reigned 25 years.

At this time the kingdom of the Macedonians began; its first king was Caranus, who reigned 28 years.—Thalcamenes, the ninth and last king of the Lacedaemonians, reigned 30 years.

Osorthon, king of the Egyptians, whom they themselves called Hercules, reigned nine years.

Agamestor, the twenty-eighth king of Athens, reigned 20 years.

Zechariah, Jeroboam’s son, reigned over Israel for six months. Shallum killed him and reigned in his place for one month; Menahem then killed Shallum and reigned in his place, and thus that year was consumed among different rulers.

Amulius Silvius, Procas’ son and the fourteenth king of the Albans, reigned 43 years. He had a brother, Numitor, whom he deprived of the kingdom. (H. m.) For when Procas, their father, died, he left an inheritance by will to his two sons, Numitor and Amulius, so that one should receive his money and the other the kingdom. Amulius gave his brother Numitor the choice of taking whatever he wished [Note: [Col. 0533] From “Amulius” through “receive” is absent in 5. 9c.]. Numitor took the money, and Amulius obtained the kingdom. When Amulius consulted an oracle, he received the answer that he would be killed by his brother’s offspring; he immediately expelled his brother from the kingdom. Numitor departed and lived on his own estate. He had two children, Sergestus and Rhea, who was also called Ilia. Fearing the oracle, Amulius took Sergestus with him on a hunt and killed him there. He made his sister Rhea a Vestal virgin, so that she could not bear children. (JORD.) When she was discovered to have been violated and pregnant, she tried to excuse her crime by falsely claiming that she had been embraced by Mars. (H. m.) After she had borne twin boys, in the seventh year of her uncle’s reign she was buried alive in the ground according to the law; but the king ordered the infants to be exposed. Faustulus, the royal shepherd of the herd, found them wandering beside the bank of the Tiber and took them to his wife, Acca Larentia. Because of her bodily rapacity and her earnings, and because of her beauty, she was called Lupa by her neighbors. Hence the chambers of prostitutes are still called *lupanaria*. (JORD.) Acca, raising the boys, taught them to associate with the other shepherds. Thus the poets invent the story that they were suckled and raised by a she-wolf in the forest. When the boys, Remus and Romulus, had grown up, they gathered a band of shepherds and robbers, killed Amulius at Alba in revenge for their mother, and installed their grandfather Numitor as king.

There is much disagreement among the histories concerning the arrangement of the kingdoms of Judah and Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0535] “Israel” in 5.; Ekkehard had lingered at greater length here over arranging the times of the kings of the Jews; we did not wish, however, to mark these in another typeface, lest we seem to have devoted too much space to matters foreign to our purpose.], with some saying one thing and others another. Even in the books of the Hebrews whose authority we use—namely, Josephus, the Book of Kings, and the Paralipomena—certain matters are found in this sequence that appear unable to agree with one another: some kings are said to have reigned for so many years, while others are said to have begun reigning before the preceding reigns had yet ended, one earlier than another. Whether this was corrupted through the fault of scribes who erred because of numerical variation, or for what reason the account varies in this way, we have not yet discovered with certainty. This disagreement is found here and in the sequence of the four kings of Israel that follows, down to the destruction of that kingdom, where the Book of Kings and the other Hebrew chroniclers seem to differ greatly.

For, as is recorded in the chronicles with the agreement of many historians (HIER.), Jeroboam, Joash’s son, reigned in Israel from the eighteenth year of Amaziah for 41 years, until the twenty-ninth year of Uzziah, or Azariah, Amaziah’s son. In Uzziah’s thirtieth year, Shallum killed Zechariah, Jeroboam’s son, after he had reigned for six months, and reigned in his place for one month. Menahem then killed Shallum and reigned in his place for ten years, until Uzziah’s fortieth year. From Uzziah’s forty-first year, Pekah, Menahem’s son, reigned for ten years, until the fiftieth year of Uzziah. From Uzziah’s fifty-first year, Pekah, Remaliah’s son, reigned for 20 years, until the second year of Ahaz, king of Judah. From Ahaz’s third year, Hoshea reigned for nine years, until the eleventh year of Ahaz, which was the fifteenth year of Madidus, king of the Medes. In that year, many writers say, the ten tribes of Israel were captured.

Although this is maintained according to the opinion of many and is written in the chronicles in the same way, the Hebrew books—including the Book of Kings, which we possess, though I do not know whether it is corrupted or sound—seem to differ greatly from it. There it is written (II, ch. XIV and following) that the aforementioned Jeroboam, Joash’s son, reigned in Israel from the fifteenth year of Amaziah, king of Judah; and that Zechariah, Jeroboam’s son, began from the thirty-eighth year of Azariah, Amaziah’s son, with nine intervening years omitted. I do not know why this was written in that way.

For since King Azariah of Judah is said to have reigned for 52 years, beginning in the seventeenth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, while Jeroboam is said to have held the kingdom for 41 years, it is clear that Jeroboam’s years ended in Azariah’s twenty-eighth year, since he began to reign in Azariah’s seventeenth year. And since Zechariah, Jeroboam’s son, is said to have reigned for only six months in the thirty-eighth year of King Azariah of Judah, I cannot discover how his succession to his father’s kingdom could have been delayed for so long, with no one ruling in the meantime, so that he took possession of his paternal inheritance only in the tenth year after his father’s death, and was then killed after six months.

For Shallum killed him and, according to this reckoning, reigned for one month in Azariah’s thirty-ninth year. Menahem then killed Shallum, began to reign in that same year, and reigned for ten years, until Azariah’s fiftieth year. His son Pekah reigned for two years in Azariah’s fiftieth and fifty-first years, although according to the earlier calculation he is written in the chronicles as having reigned for ten years. Pekah, Remaliah’s son, killed him and reigned in his place for 20 years, from Azariah’s fifty-second year until the third year of Ahaz, son of Jotham, king of Judah. Ahaz began to reign in Pekah’s eighteenth year and reigned for 16 years.

Hoshea, son of Elah, the last king, reigned in Samaria over Israel for nine years. According to certain chroniclers, he began in the third year of Ahaz, king of Judah, who was the seventh king of the Medes named Madidus, so that the captivity of the ten tribes, which occurred in Hoshea’s ninth year, would fall in the fifteenth year of Madidus. According to the Hebrew books, however, Hoshea began to reign in Israel in Ahaz’s fourteenth year, with ten years somehow omitted between Pekah’s death and his accession, although Hoshea is nevertheless said to have killed Pekah for the sake of the kingdom. Thus, according to this sequence, Hoshea’s ninth year falls in the sixth year of Hezekiah, king of Judah, which was Madidus’ twenty-sixth year; in that year Hoshea himself and all Israel were taken captive. This is according to the Hebrews.

Having found these differences in the histories, but not daring, as a man of no authority, to criticize either side as worthless, I have recorded the opinion of each, in order to make the careful reader more cautious [Note: [Col. 0535] “more studious” in 1.].

I shall now pass through the reigns of the kings as I found them in the chronicles, and, as far as the last of the Israelite kings—that is, Hoshea—I shall follow the authority of the Hebrew books.

(HIER.) Menahem, Gaddi’s son, reigned in Samaria over Israel for ten years.

Sosarmus, the second king of the Medes, reigned 30 years. In his second year Remus and Romulus were born. (JORD.) At that time, after countless—so to speak—kings of Laurentum and Latium, Silvian and Alban kings, who had reigned in Italy for 300 years, though in extreme poverty, Amulius reigned. In the seventh year of Amulius’ reign, these two brothers, who later founded Rome, were born from the daughter of his brother Numitor. (HIER.)—Spamus, king of Egypt, reigned ten years.—Thelestes, the eleventh and last king of Corinth, reigned 12 years.

Pekah, Menahem’s son, reigned in Israel for ten years according to some (HIER.), but according to the Hebrews for two years.—Chinus, the second king of the Macedonians, reigned 12 years.

The end of the Lacedaemonian kingdom.

Bocchoris, king of Egypt, reigned 46 years. He established laws for the Egyptians; under him the lamb also spoke.

Aeschylus, Agamestor’s son and the twenty-ninth king of Athens, reigned 23 years. In his second year, which is reckoned as the 405th after the destruction of Troy, the first Olympiad began. It was first instituted by Iphitus, son of Praxonides, son of Haemon; in it, Chorebus of Elis became victor. Previously, the Eleans held a five-year contest, with four full years intervening, during which they appointed annual officials.

From this time the history of the Greeks is believed to be reliable; before that, they put forward varying accounts according to each person’s judgment.

(OROS. I, 20.) At that time Phalaris of Sicily, having seized a tyranny, was ravaging the people of Agrigentum. Cruel in mind and still more cruel in his inventions, committing every outrage against the innocent, he eventually found someone whom he could justly punish, though he himself was unjust. A certain Perillus, a worker in bronze who sought the tyrant’s friendship, thinking a suitable gift for his cruelty, made a bronze bull and fitted a door into its side, so that when someone was shut inside and roasted over fires placed beneath, the hollow bronze would magnify the sound of his voice crying out in pain, making the bellowing of an animal, rather than the groans of a human being, appear to be heard in the monstrous spectacle. Phalaris embraced the work but cursed its maker, providing both material for his cruelty and an occasion for vengeance. When the opportunity arose, he punished the craftsman himself with his own invention.

(Ibid., ch. 20.) At that time also the greatest war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians was waged with all their strength and spirit. In it, through mutual slaughter, they were driven to the point that, as though defeated, they withdrew from one another and abandoned the war.

At the same time the Lacedaemonians fought against the Messenians for 20 years with unrelenting fury. Although victory often hung in the balance, they finally overcame them. It should be understood that Sparta is the same city as Lacedaemon, and that the Lacedaemonians were therefore called Spartans.

(HIER.) The kingdom of the Lydians begins; their first king, Ardys, reigned 36 years.

The first Olympiad begins.

Pekah, Remaliah’s son, killed Pekah, Menahem’s son and king of Israel, and reigned in his place for 20 years—according to some (HIER.), from the fifty-first year of Azariah, king of Judah; according to the Hebrews, from the following year.

Jotham, Uzziah’s or Azariah’s son, reigned over Judah in Jerusalem for 16 years. In Judaea, Hosea, Isaiah, Micah, Amos, Joel, and Jonah were prophesying.—Tyrimnas, the third king of the Macedonians, reigned 38 years.

Madidus, the third king of the Medes, reigned 40 years. During his time Syracuse and Catina were founded in Sicily. Rome was also founded during his time.

Ahaz, Jotham’s son, reigned over Judah for 16 years. Under him the same prophets as above were active.

Alcmeon, the thirtieth king of the Athenians, reigned two years. After this, the officials who had governed the republic until their deaths ceased to hold office, and the practice of magistracies lasting ten years was instituted; the first was Carobs, Aeschylus’ son.

From this time also, according to some (HIER.), Hoshea began to reign over Israel after killing Pekah; but according to the Hebrew books, this occurred eleven years later, namely from the fourteenth year of Ahaz.

Numitor, restored to the kingdom by his grandsons Remus and Romulus after they had killed his brother Amulius, reigned at Alba for one year. This was the ninth year of Madidus, king of the Medes. In that year the brothers established a small city on the Palatine Hill, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 429 after the destruction of Troy, when 3,211 years had elapsed from the origin of the world.

As they were surrounding it with a wall, Remus criticized the wall, saying that it could not be sufficient protection for the new city, and leapt over its narrow boundary. He was killed by Fabius, Romulus’ commander, with a shepherd’s plough. Some, however, say (cf. LIV. II, 6–7) that the reason for his killing was that, after the city had been founded, the brothers disputed whose name it should bear.

When they had decided to determine this by augury, Romulus, climbing the Palatine Hill, saw seven vultures fly toward him; Remus, on the Aventine, saw twelve. For this reason, it is reported that Remus was killed by Romulus’ soldiers. Romulus then alone obtained the kingdom, named the city Rome after himself, and, having built a temple in it, called it an asylum—that is, a house of refuge—promising immunity to all who fled there (H. m.). For this reason a great multitude flocked to him.

Finally, Latin and Tuscan shepherds, foreign Phrygians who had gathered under Aeneas, Arcadians who had gathered under Evander, and, with them, as Sallust says (Cat. ch. 6), the Aborigines, came together as though into a single body and formed the Roman people. Romulus then chose one hundred of the elders, by whose counsel he would conduct everything; because of their old age he called them senators, and because of the likeness of their care, fathers. He also chose one thousand fighters, whom he called soldiers from their number (JORD.—H. m.).

Since they had no wives, they staged games on horseback and invited the peoples of neighboring cities from the Sabine territory to the spectacle; in the fourth year after the founding of the City, they carried off their maidens. The Sabines, stirred to war because of the wrong done by the abduction of the maidens, surrounded the city (JORD.). Then the Sabines, admitted through gates betrayed by the maiden Tarpeia, began the battle. But some of the abducted women, who had already borne children, came forward with their sons and softened their fathers and kinsmen; thus they made peace between them and their husbands (cf. LIV. I, 13).

(H. m.) Tarpeia, however, was buried beneath shields on the hill that was named Tarpeian after her; the Capitol was later built there. The Romans made a treaty of friendship with the Sabines [Col. 0539], to such an extent that Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, though already old, reigned jointly with Romulus.

(OR.—H. m.) After Titus Tatius died not long afterward—or, as some report, was killed by Romulus himself—the Romans and Sabines became one people. To strengthen this union, the Romans placed Sabine names before their own names, and the Sabines likewise placed Roman names before theirs; from that time the custom endured that no Roman should be without a forename.

Because of this alliance also, since Romulus carried a long spear in the Sabine manner, which in their language was called *cyris*, he was called Quirinus, and from then on the Romans were called Quirites. Thus the Roman Empire, which at its origin was scarcely smaller than any other and which in its growth became greater than any other throughout the world, began from Romulus (AUG. XVIII, 22).

At the time when Rome was founded, the people of Israel had inhabited the Promised Land for 685 years: 27 of these belonged to Joshua, then 308 to the period of the judges, and from the time when kings began to exist there, 350 years had passed. At that time Achaz was king in Judaea.

(AUG. loc. cit., ch. 23.) At this time the Erythraean Sibyl—or, as some wish, the Cumaean Sibyl—is said to have lived; she wrote certain things about Christ plainly.

(HIER.) Numitor therefore reigned over the Albans for one year.—Charobs governed the Athenians for ten years.—Rome began to be built.

Romulus, from whom the Roman Empire began, reigned for 38 years. On the seventh day before the Kalends of August, he was struck by lightning at the Goat’s Marsh and vanished without a trace. At the urging of Julius Proculus, who said that Romulus had appeared to him in a more august form and had ordered himself to be worshiped as a god, he was believed to have passed to the gods and was consecrated as Quirinus (JORD.). Some nevertheless say that, because of his harsh character, he was torn apart by the senate.

Hoshea, Elah’s son, killed Pekah, Remaliah’s son and king of Israel, and himself reigned in Samaria over Israel for nine years. According to the Hebrews, he began in the fourteenth year of Ahaz, king of Judah, eleven years after Pekah’s death; according to others (HIER.), he began in the third year of Ahaz (JOS. XI, 20).

In Hoshea’s ninth year, Shalmaneser, also called Tiglath-pileser, king of the Chaldeans, came up, captured Samaria, took Israel—that is, the ten tribes—captive, and transferred them to the mountain-country of the Medes. The kingdom of Israel in Samaria then ceased, after it had been ruled for 260 years [Note: [Col. 0539] 260 corrected from 261 in 1; 261 in 5. 9c.], 7 months, and 7 days from the time when the remaining tribes separated from the house of David and the tribe of Judah. But from the time when they obtained that province under the leader Joshua, 947 years had passed.

Shalmaneser sent Assyrian settlers to guard the land of the Israelites. They were properly called Cutheans because [Note: [Col. 0539] a word is missing in 1.] they migrated from a certain river called Cutha. Having become imitators of the Jewish law, they were called Samaritans.

Aesimeles governed Athens for ten years. Alyattes, the second king of the Lydians, reigned 14 years.

Hezekiah, Ahaz’s son, reigned in Judaea for 29 years; Isaiah and Hosea were prophesying. In his sixth year, according to the Hebrews, the ten tribes were taken captive, and the kingdom of Israel came to an end.

In Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib, Shalmaneser’s son, came up into Judaea, captured its cities, besieged Lachish, and sent his servants to Jerusalem to blaspheme the name of the Lord. But the angel of the Lord came by night into the king’s camp and struck down 85,000 of his army. The king returned in disgrace to his own land, where he was killed by his own sons (II Kings XVIII, 19). At that time Tobias was in captivity, having been captured by Shalmaneser.

(AUG. loc. cit., chs. 24–25.) At that time Thales of Miletus, one of the seven sages, flourished. The names of the seven who were called sages are these: Thales of Miletus, Pittacus of Mytilene, Solon of Athens, Chilon of Lacedaemon, Periander of Corinth, Cleobulus of Lydia, and Bias of Priene. The tenth Olympiad.

*The kingdom of Israel came to an end, after the ten tribes had been taken captive.* (HIER.) Perdiccas, the fourth king of the Macedonians, reigned 51 years.
