Elidicus governed the Athenians for ten years. Meles, the third king of the Lydians, reigned 12 years.

Sebichus reigned in Egypt for 12 years.—Hippomenes governed the Athenians for ten years.

Cardiaces, the fourth king of the Medes, reigned 13 years.

At that time the Samian Sibyl, also called Herophila, was renowned on Samos.—Nicomedia was founded; it had previously been called Astacus.

Candaules, the fourth king of the Lydians, reigned 17 years.

After Romulus’ death, the senators governed the republic, each for five days, and in this way one year was completed.

Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, reigned 40 years. (H. m.) He waged no war, but benefited the City no less than Romulus. He established laws and customs for the Romans, who, because of their practice of warfare, seemed almost like brigands and half-barbarians. According to some (H. m.), he also divided the year into ten months, whereas previously it had been confused and unregulated. Others say (HIER., Isidore) that under Romulus the year had already had ten months, and that Numa added two, January and February. He built the Capitol from its foundations.

(H. m.) In his time Glaucus first devised the method of joining ironwork.

(H. m.) Leocrates governed Athens for ten years.

Manasseh, Hezekiah’s son, reigned over Judah for 55 years. Among the many evils by which he provoked the Lord, he is said to have ordered the prophet Isaiah to be sawn apart with a wooden saw (cf. HIER., on the end of Isaiah—JORDAN). Therefore, by divine permission, after he had been taken captive by the king of Babylon and bound in iron chains, he is said to have repented; the song of his repentance is also read. Later he was restored to the kingdom, lived well, and left his son Amon as his successor.

(HIER.) Taracus the Ethiopian, king of Egypt, reigned 20 years.

Deioces, the fifth king of the Medes, reigned 54 years. In his time Archilochus, Simonides, and the musician Aristoxenus were renowned.

Absander governed Athens for ten years. Gyges, the fourth king of the Lydians, reigned 36 years. Erixias governed Athens for ten years.

Aethiops, also called Mermes, king of Egypt, reigned 12 years. Argeus, the fifth king of the Macedonians, reigned 38 years. After this, nine men from the noble families of the city [Note: [Col. 0541] “cities” in 1; “city” in 5.] were chosen to govern the Athenian republic annually.

Stephinatis, king of Egypt, reigned seven years.

(ISID.) Tullus Hostilius, the third king of the Romans, reigned 32 years. He was the first of the Romans to use purple and the fasces, and he was the first in the republic to conduct a census. (JORD.—H. m.) He established all military discipline and the practice of war. After training the young men, he waged war against the Albans, who lived twelve miles from Rome, and, after defeating them in the sixth battle, destroyed Alba. He also defeated the Veientes and Fidenates, of whom some lived six miles from the City and others eighteen. By adding the Caelian Hill, he enlarged the City within a circuit of walls. In the thirty-second year of his reign, he and his entire household were consumed by lightning.

(HIER.) Necepses, king of the Egyptians, reigned six years. Necho reigned in Egypt for eight years. From the beginning: 3300.

Ardys, the sixth king of the Lydians, reigned 37 years. Psammetichus, king of Egypt, reigned 44 years.—Pausanias, king of the Spartans, founded Byzantium, later called Constantinople.

Amon, Manasseh’s son, reigned in Jerusalem over Judah for two years according to the Hebrews, but according to the Septuagint for twelve years; the latter figure is also given in the chronicles (cf. HIER.).

Phraortes, the sixth king of the Medes, reigned 24 years (HIER.). During his time Thales of Miletus and the musician Terpander flourished. The hundredth year from the foundation of Rome. Philip, the sixth king of the Macedonians, reigned 38 years.

Josiah, Amon’s son, reigned over Judah for 32 years [Note: [Col. 0541] corrected in 1.]. In his thirteenth year Jeremiah began to prophesy. During his reign Zephaniah and the woman Huldah also prophesied.—(JORD.) He therefore cut down the sacred groves, removed the idols of the nations from his kingdom, and worshiped God with integrity.

(HIER.—Jord.) Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of the Romans and Numa’s grandson through his daughter, reigned 23 years. He enclosed the City with walls and confined the Tiber, which flowed into the City, with a bridge. He established the colony-city of Ostia at the very boundary between sea and river, sixteen miles from Rome, already foreseeing in his mind that the wealth and traffic of the entire world would one day be received there as in a maritime harbor of the City. (H. m.) He crushed the twelve powerful peoples neighboring Tuscia in countless conflicts and enlarged the City by adding the Aventine and Janiculum hills.

Cyaxares, the seventh king of the Medes, reigned 32 years. In his fourth year Epydaunus [Note: [Col. 0541] so in 1.] was founded; it was later called Dyrrachium. During his time Arion of Methymna was also renowned; he is said to have been carried by a dolphin.

Sadyattes, the seventh king of the Lydians, reigned 15 years.

(JORD.) Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of the Romans, reigned for thirty-seven years. Although he was of overseas origin and sought the kingship voluntarily, he received the kingship from the Romans because of his diligence and refinement—indeed, he was descended from Corinth and had blended Greek eloquence with Italian skills (H. m.). He doubled the number of senators, built the Circus at Rome, and established games. He conquered the Sabines and was the first to enter Rome in triumph; he built walls and sewers and began the Capitol. (JORD.) Fasces, the trabea, curule chairs, rings, military decorations (*phalerae*), military cloaks, bordered garments, embroidered togas—in short, all the ornaments and insignia—were first adopted under him from the various peoples he had subdued. (H. m.) In the thirty-seventh year of his rule, therefore, he was killed by the sons of Ancus, whom he had succeeded. (HIER.) In his twelfth year, Pittacus of Mytilene, one of the Seven Sages, competed with Phrinon of Athens in the Olympic contest and defeated him.

[Col. 0543] In these times the poet Stesichorus, Alcaeus, and Sappho—who invented the Sapphic meter—were renowned.

Necho [Note: [Col. 0543] These passages are abrupt in manuscript 1.] the second, also called Necepsus, king of Egypt, reigned for six years.

Jehoiakim, also called Eliakim or Jeconiah, son of Josiah, reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. In the thirty-second year of his reign, his father Josiah engaged Necho, king of Egypt, in battle against Necho’s will and was killed. In his place his son Jehoahaz reigned for three months (2 Kings 23); but Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, came to Jerusalem, removed him from the kingship, and took him with him to Egypt. He appointed his brother Eliakim king in his place and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He is believed to be the one of whom Matthew says (chapter 1): “Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the transmigration of Babylon.” For Josiah fathered three sons—Jehoahaz, Eliakim, and Mattaniah, who was afterward called Zedekiah—just as Eliakim was called Jehoiakim and Jeconiah.

In the third year of Jehoiakim, therefore, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up and captured Judea in the first year of his reign, and Jehoiakim became his tributary for three years (2 Kings 24). (HIER.) Nebuchadnezzar transferred to Babylon part of the vessels of the house of God and many of the Jews, including Ezekiel and Daniel, and also Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, while they were still boys (2 Chronicles 36). Later, when Jehoiakim rebelled, Nebuchadnezzar came against him, captured him, bound him in chains, and led him to Babylon, as is read in the Chronicles (same passage); but according to the Book of Kings (same passage), he is said to have slept with his fathers and to have been killed outside the walls of Jerusalem.

This difference is resolved as follows. He was indeed bound and led out of Jerusalem, but Nebuchadnezzar killed him on the road near Jerusalem. Therefore, because he was killed there, he is said to have slept with his fathers, since he was killed in his homeland; but according to the view of those who saw him being led away from the city, he is said to have been taken to Babylon. It is indeed the custom of the Scriptures sometimes to weave the sequence of a narrative according to popular opinion.

(HIER.) Alyattes [Note: [Col. 0543] These passages are partly abrupt in manuscript 1.], the eighth king of the Lydians, reigned for forty-nine years.

Psammutes, also called Psammetichus, king of Egypt, reigned for twelve years.—Aeropus, the seventh king of the Macedonians, reigned for twenty-six years.

Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim—who was also Eliakim and Jeconiah—reigned in Jerusalem for three months and ten days, just as his uncle Jehoahaz had done (Josephus X, 6). Nebuchadnezzar appointed him in place of his father, whom he had killed, as king of the entire province that he had subjected to himself after defeating Necho, king of Egypt, and taking all Syria from his control.

Afterward Nebuchadnezzar regretted having appointed Jehoiachin in place of his father. For he feared that, remembering the wrong done to him, Jehoiachin might invade his province in revenge for his father’s death. He sent men to besiege him in Jerusalem and came to the city to attack it. Jehoiachin, however, having received an oath that neither he nor the city would suffer any harm, went out to the king with his mother and all his people. The king of Babylon received him in the eighth or ninth year of his reign, but did not keep faith. For he ordered him, his mother, his friends, and all the strong men of Israel to be brought to him in chains. He led them to Babylon and kept them in custody; but he appointed Jehoiachin’s uncle Mattaniah king and imposed on him the name Zedekiah. Thus that year came to an end.

This Jehoiachin did not bear the name Jehoiakim, the final letter of his father’s name having been changed; he had two names. For he was called Jeconiah, just as his father was. And this is the Jeconiah who, after the transmigration, fathered Shealtiel.

After Nebuchadnezzar’s death, as Jeremiah testifies (chapter 52, toward the end), in the thirty-seventh year of the transmigration, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, in that year of his reign, raised up the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah. He brought him out of the prison house, spoke kindly with him, and set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon. He changed his prison garments, and Jehoiachin ate bread before him all the days of his life.

(HIER.) In these times Jeremiah, Baruch, and Zephaniah prophesied.

Zedekiah, also called Mattaniah, son of Josiah and brother of Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim, reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years (2 Kings 25). In the ninth year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar came into Judea, and Jerusalem was besieged until Zedekiah’s eleventh year. When Zedekiah saw that the city was about to be captured, he escaped by flight. The Babylonians pursued and captured him with his wife and sons, and brought him to the king at Riblah—or, as others say, at Arabathah. There, with Zedekiah watching, he ordered his sons and friends to be killed; he had Zedekiah’s eyes gouged out, ordered him to be taken bound to Babylon, and confined him in prison until the end of Nebuchadnezzar’s life (cf. Josephus X, 8).

At this point some think that Jeremiah and Ezekiel contradict one another, because Jeremiah (chapter 38) foretold that Zedekiah would be led to Babylon, whereas Ezekiel (chapter 12) said that he would not see Babylon. Yet the true agreement of both prophecies was fulfilled. He was indeed led bound to Babylon, according to Jeremiah; but because he was led there blind, he did not see it, in accordance with Ezekiel’s prophecy (cf. Josephus, same passage).

(HIER.) Astyages, the eighth king of the Medes, reigned for thirty-eight years.—Solon gave laws to the Athenians.

Apries, king of the Egyptians, reigned for thirty years.

In Zedekiah’s eleventh year Jerusalem was captured by Nebuchadnezzar’s army, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, in the third year after the siege began, but in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, as Jeremiah testifies. He says (chapter 24) that the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, whereas in the Book of Daniel [Col. 0545] (chapter 1) the same king of Babylon is said to have begun to take and plunder Jerusalem in Jehoiakim’s third year.

How these statements agree with one another is a question, unless perhaps each meant the first year in relation to that period—namely, the end of the third and the beginning of the fourth. Nebuchadnezzar sent his military commander Nebuzaradan to Jerusalem. When he came, he plundered the temple and burned it in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah; from the temple’s first construction, 443 years had passed (Josephus X, 8). From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt there had then been 920 years, four months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 0545] These and the numbers that follow are almost all corrected in manuscript 1; Ekk. altered Josephus’s numbers.]; from the Flood, 1,717 years, four months, and ten days; and from Adam’s creation, 3,373 years, four months, and ten days (cf. Josephus).

This people had remained under kings, from Saul and David, for 505 years, four months, and ten days; and under judges for 348 years after the death of Moses and the judge Joshua. These figures are according to the Hebrew truth; Josephus and certain others, however, hold a different view.

King Jehoiakim [Note: [Col. 0545] “Jehoiakim” corrected from “Zedekiah” in manuscript 5.] was blinded and, together with the high priest Josedech and the entire people, was led captive to Babylon. This captivity lasted for seventy years, until the second year of Darius, although Cyrus released many of them.

According to some (HIER.), these years are counted from the third year of Jehoiakim, also called Eliakim, to the twentieth year of Cyrus, king of the Persians. According to others, they run from the thirteenth year of Josiah, Jehoiakim’s father, when Jeremiah began to prophesy, to Cyrus’s first year. According to still others, they run from Zedekiah’s eleventh year to the second year of Darius, the third king of the Persians. The seventy years of the temple’s desolation were completed under Darius.

The prophet Zechariah is a witness to this. In the second year of Darius he says: “Lord Almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, which you have despised? This is the seventieth year.”

Nebuzaradan, the king’s military commander, therefore, after burning the temple and carrying the people away, left certain remnants of the poorer people in Judea to cultivate the land and pay tribute, appointing Gedaliah over them (Josephus X, 9). When Ishmael, from the royal line, killed him, the others, fearing the Babylonians because of his murder, fled to Apries, king of the Egyptians. They dragged the prophet Jeremiah, against his will and despite his objections, along with his disciple Baruch.

In the fifth year of the Hebrew captivity, after Nebuchadnezzar had subjected the Ammonites and Moabites, he proceeded into Egypt and overthrew it. On his return he again led the Jews captive to Babylon, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, leaving no one from them in the province to cultivate it and introducing no other nation, as had been done at Samaria in the captivity of the ten tribes. Therefore all Judea was desolate, and the temple remained desolate for seventy years.

The entire period from the captivity of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes—to the transmigration of the two tribes was 145 years, six months, and ten days.

After the second year of the devastation of Egypt, which was the twenty-seventh year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream about a statue, which Daniel interpreted. Afterward all those events occurred that are read concerning the erection of the statue, the casting of the three youths into the fire, and his second vision, which signified his expulsion from human society for seven years and his restoration again to the kingdom. These events are not distinguished by definite intervals of years in the Book of Daniel. Saint Jerome says in his commentary on Daniel that Nebuchadnezzar reigned for forty-three years in all (cf. Josephus X, 11).

No one should be troubled by our saying that he saw the vision in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, while Daniel says that it was shown to him in the second year of his reign. According to Saint Jerome (on chapter 2), it should be understood from Hebrew tradition that Daniel is not here referring to the second year of the Chaldean and Judean kingdom, which Nebuchadnezzar had held for a long time, but to the kingdom that he afterward acquired after conquering many barbarian nations. This is the second year of his reign in Daniel, the same year that Josephus calls the second year of the devastation of Egypt.

Otherwise, what Daniel says will not stand: that in the third year of Jehoiakim—which they call the first year of Nebuchadnezzar—the same king came into Judea, transferred many people to Babylon, and entrusted Daniel and his companions, still boys, to be nourished and educated, so that after being trained for three years they would stand before him.

Josephus also records (X, 12) that this man’s father was likewise called Nebuchadnezzar and reigned in Babylon for twenty-one years. After his death, this Nebuchadnezzar reigned for forty-three years or more.

He possessed such great strength that Megasthenes, in the fourth book of his *Indica*, attempts to prove that this king surpassed Hercules in strength and the magnitude of his deeds.

After his death, his son Evil-merodach took possession of his kingdom; Josephus calls him Almilmadapachus (same passage), and he raised Jehoiachin from prison. He was succeeded by his brother Belshazzar, according to Orosius [Note: [Col. 0545] Orosius says nothing about these kings.] and certain others. Berossus, however, a gentile writer of history, and Josephus give a different account of his successors, and blessed Jerome (on Daniel, chapter 5) does not disagree with them. He says that Belshazzar was not the son of Nebuchadnezzar.

For Josephus writes as follows (same passage): “After Nebuchadnezzar’s death, Almilmadapachus succeeded to the kingdom. He released King Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, from his bonds. After his death, Egesarius, also called Nergal-sharezer, his son, held the principate. After his death, the rule passed to his son Nabosardachus, whom some call Laborsedech. When he had held it for nine months, after his death it passed to Belshazzar, who was also called Naboar” (Josephus X, 13).

Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Darius, king of the Medes, encamped against this king. While they were besieging him, one night, during a banquet, he saw a hand writing on the wall, as is read in Daniel (chapter 5, toward the end). That very night the city was captured, and Belshazzar himself was killed (Josephus, chapter 14).

Darius, therefore, son of Astyages, whom Daniel (chapter 9) calls the son of Ahasuerus and who was also known by another name among the Greeks, was older than Cyrus—for he was sixty-two years old. Since Cyrus yielded to him by right of kinship, Darius obtained the Chaldean kingdom, and took Daniel with him into Media, treating him with every honor (cf. Jerome on Daniel, chapter 5). For Daniel was one of the three satraps whom Darius had appointed over 360 satraps.

This, then, is what we have learned to have been the end of the Babylonian kingdom as we have described it. But since the kings of Babylon were so powerful and famous, the question arises why they are not included among the number and succession of illustrious kings.

We know that the Assyrian kingdom, founded in Babylonia by Semiramis, the wife of Ninus, remained there for a long period and lasted until Sardanapalus. After he was killed, the Assyrian kingdom was transferred to the Medes by Arbaces, prefect of the Medes. From that time the kings of the Medes are transmitted by historians in order and number, until the kingdom was transferred to the Persians.

Therefore, if the Assyrian kingdom was transferred to the Medes, anyone wishing to know what became of the Babylonian kingdom should recall that Ninus occupied Asia and the whole East as far as India, while his wife additionally subjected the Ethiopians and other nations to the Assyrian kingdom. From this it is clear that when Arbaces defected to the Medes, he seized the greater part and dignity of the kingdom and retained it in Media.

The Chaldeans, however, claimed Babylonia for themselves against the Medes, [Col. 0547] and thus the power of Babylonia was with the Medes, while ownership of the kingdom was with the Chaldeans. But because of the ancient dignity of the royal city, the Chaldeans preferred to call it not by their own dignity but by that of the city. Hence it happened that Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him, down to Darius and Cyrus, who destroyed the Chaldean kingdom and the city of Babylon, although powerful through Chaldean strength, are nevertheless read as famous under the name of Babylonia.

(AUGUSTINE, *The City of God* XVIII, chapter 25.) In these times there were still those Seven whom antiquity celebrated as sages. They expressed certain rather honorable precepts of conduct in brief maxims, but left posterity no writings, so far as literature is concerned, except that Solon gave certain laws to the Athenians, while Thales was a natural philosopher and left books containing his teachings.

(AUGUSTINE VIII, 2.) Pythagoras of Samos, from whom they say the name “philosophy” arose, and who is said to have been the discoverer both of arithmetic and of musical harmonies, is reported to have lived in these same times. For previously those who seemed to excel others were called sages; but when this man was asked what profession he claimed, he replied that he was a philosopher—that is, a student or lover of wisdom—because he considered it extremely arrogant to claim that he himself was wise.

(HIER.) At the same time several others also became famous: Alcman and the poet Stesichorus; Pherecydes, a writer of histories; Xenophanes, a natural philosopher and tragedian; the woman Sappho, famous for many poems; and Anaximander, a natural philosopher whose teacher was Thales of Miletus (cf. Augustine, same passage).

(HIER.) Alcetas, the eighth king of the Macedonians, reigned for twenty-nine years.

The fourth age of the world ends in the captivity of the Hebrews. It contains 486 years, and the four ages together, from the beginning of the world to the captivity, amount to 3,374 years (cf. Isidore). (BEDE.) The fifth age begins with the captivity and continues to Christ.

(H. m.) Servius Tullius, the sixth king of the Romans, reigned for thirty-four years. Although he was born of a noble woman who was nevertheless a captive and therefore a slave, while he was still a boy and was sleeping in the palace of Tarquinius Priscus, Tanaquil, the wife of that king, saw what appeared to be a flame burning on his head. Because of this portent she raised him generously among her own children, and for this reason he attained the kingship.

For after Tarquinius’s death, with the queen’s support, Servius was placed in the king’s position as though temporarily. He administered the kingdom so skillfully, however, that he appeared to have obtained it by right. (HIER. and H. m.) He added three hills to the city—the Quirinal, Viminal, and Esquiline—dug ditches around the wall, and was the first of all to establish a census, which was still unknown throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0547] Thus in manuscript 1.]. When everyone under him at Rome had been registered, the number of Roman citizens, including those who lived in the countryside, was found to be 84,000.

At last he was killed through the crime of his son-in-law Tarquinius Superbus, who was the son of the earlier king whom Servius had succeeded, with the cooperation in his murder of his own daughter, whom Tarquinius had married. While he was still reigning, Belshazzar ruled the Chaldeans; under him Daniel read and interpreted the mystical writing on the wall.

At the same time Claudia, the fifth Vestal Virgin, was accused of sexual misconduct. But she, unwilling to clear herself by ordinary means, went to a ford of the Tiber, boarded a ship, tied the prow with her belt, and said: “If I am a virgin, follow me.” Immediately the ship moved and entered Rome.

(HIER.) Amasis, king of Egypt, reigned for forty-two years.

Croesus, the last king of the Lydians, reigned for twenty-five years.

(JORD.—HIER.) Cyrus the Persian destroyed the empire of the Medes, which had stood for 259 years under eight kings. Transferring it to the Persians, he himself first reigned there for thirty years, from the thirty-first year of the temple’s desolation to its sixtieth year.

There is some disagreement among the histories about how the kingdom of the Medes came to the Persians. Some write as follows (Orosius I, 19). Astyages, the last king of the Medes, being without male offspring, had Cyrus, born among the Persians, as his grandson. But as soon as Cyrus grew up, he gathered a Persian army and challenged his uncle to battle.

Astyages, for his part, had forgotten his crime against Harpalus. Long before, he had killed Harpalus’s only and very young son, served him up for his father to eat, and, so that fortunate ignorance might not deprive the most wretched bereavement of anything, had reproached the father with the infamous meal by displaying the child’s head and hands. Forgetful, I say, of this deed, Astyages entrusted the supreme command of the war to Harpalus. Harpalus immediately handed over the army he had received to Cyrus by treachery.

When Astyages learned of this, he took his forces with him and marched against the Persians, renewing the battle with greater determination. He threatened his men that anyone attempting to withdraw from the battle would be met with the sword.

While the Medes fought fiercely under this compulsion and the Persians gradually gave way, their mothers and wives ran out to meet them, begging them to return to the battle. When they hesitated, the women lifted their garments and exposed the shameful parts of their bodies, asking whether the men wished to flee into the wombs of their mothers or wives.

Ashamed by this, the Persians returned to the battle, and, making an attack, forced those whom they had been fleeing to flee. Astyages was then captured. Cyrus took nothing from him except his kingdom and placed him over the great nation of the Hyrcanians; Astyages himself did not wish to return to the Medes. This was the end of the empire of the Medes.

But the cities that had been tributary to the Medes revolted from Cyrus, and this became for Cyrus the cause and origin of many wars. (HIER. on Daniel, chapter 5.) Pompeius Trogus and certain others testify to this.

Others, however—including blessed Jerome, who appears to agree with them—say that Astyages was Cyrus’s maternal grandfather and that Darius was the son of Astyages and Cyrus’s uncle. Darius destroyed Babylon and the Chaldean kingdom together with Cyrus, and through him they believe that the kingdom of the Medes came to Cyrus as if by hereditary right.

Therefore Bishop Jordanes writes as follows (cited in Muratori I, p. 224): “After Jerusalem had been captured by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, and after the desolation of the temple, the kingdom of the Medes, which had stood for 259 years, was destroyed and transferred to the Persians, because Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Darius, king of the Medes and son of Astyages, were related as nephew and uncle. They attacked Belshazzar, the great-grandson of Nebuchadnezzar and king of Babylonia, and seized his kingdom. After Darius died, Cyrus obtained both his own kingdom—that is, the kingdom of the Persians—and the kingdom of his kinsman Darius, namely, the kingdom of the Medes, together with that third kingdom which they had captured. Afterward he raised up the kingdom and nation of the Persians.” [Col. 0549]

This nation ruled from the aforesaid Cyrus to Darius, son of Arsames, for approximately 230 years, and the kingdom then passed to Alexander. Daniel says that this Darius was the son of Ahasuerus, for some reason unknown to me, unless perhaps Astyages—who is called his father by others—had two names and was also called Ahasuerus.

For Daniel says (chapter 9): “In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, I saw a vision.” And concerning Astyages he says (chapters 13–14): “King Astyages was gathered to his fathers, and Cyrus the Persian received his kingdom, and Daniel was the king’s guest,” and so forth.

Let us leave it to more diligent students to determine how all these matters may be reconciled. We know only this from the histories: Cyrus was the first to reign over the Persians. We find it recorded in the chronicles that he began to reign in the thirty-first year of the temple’s desolation, captured Babylon in the twentieth year of his reign after killing Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, and afterward lived for ten years. He subjected the kingdoms of the Medes and Chaldeans to his own kingdom—that is, to the kingdom of the Persians (cf. Jerome).

In his first year, therefore, the seventieth year of the Jewish captivity coincided, as Josephus reports (XI, 1). But this cannot refer to the captivity in which the temple was burned, since this was its thirty-first year; nor to the captivity in which Jehoiachin, son of Jehoiakim, was taken away, since this was its forty-third year; nor to the captivity under his father Jehoiakim, also called Eliakim, when Daniel and his companions were transferred with the others, since this was its fifty-first year—unless all the years from Josiah’s thirteenth year, when Jeremiah first began to preach about the captivity, are counted as belonging to the captivity.

(JOSEPHUS XI, 1.) When Cyrus was reading the prophecies of Isaiah and found written there that the Lord had said, “I desire Cyrus, whom I have appointed king of many great nations, to send my people back to their own land and rebuild my temple,” he marveled at the name of the Lord, and a certain impulse seized him to fulfill that generous prophecy which Isaiah had foretold 160 years before the temple’s destruction.

(HIER.) He caused nearly 50,000 Jews to return to Judea. After building the altar, they laid the foundations of the temple. When neighboring peoples obstructed the work, it remained unfinished until Darius, son of Hystaspes, with only the altar standing.

Among the Hebrews who had then gone up to Judea from captivity, the high priest Joshua, son of Josedech, and the prince Zerubbabel were prominent. In Cyrus’s fifth year, which was the thirty-fifth year of the temple’s desolation, Haggai and Zechariah prophesied.

The events reported concerning Croesus and his testing of the oracles occurred in these times. In Cyrus’s tenth year Croesus went to war against him. In the twentieth year of his reign Cyrus began the capture of Babylon with his uncle Darius, son of Astyages (cf. Jordanes).

(OROSIUS II, 6; HIER.) At that time Croesus, king of the Lydians and famous for his wealth, came to the aid of the Babylonians. After being defeated, he fled back to his kingdom. Once Babylon had been captured, Cyrus transferred the war to Lydia; he captured Croesus but spared both his life and his property, while destroying the kingdom of the Lydians, which had stood for 230 years (HIER.).

(OROSIUS II, 7.) After Cyrus had subjected very many nations to his rule, he made war upon the Scythians. There he cunningly killed the son of Queen Tomyris, who then ruled that nation, together with a third of his forces. She, in turn, feigning lack of confidence in her despair over the disaster inflicted upon her, gradually withdrew, drawing the arrogant enemy into an ambush.

There, having arranged an ambush among the mountains, she destroyed 200,000 Persians together with the king himself. What was most astonishing was that not even a messenger survived so great a disaster.

The queen cut off Cyrus’s head and ordered it thrown into a leather bag filled with human blood. She reproached him, not like a woman, saying: “Sate yourself with the blood for which you thirsted, you who remained insatiable for fifty years.”

(HIER.) Anaximenes, the natural philosopher, was known in these times; Simonides was renowned; and the poet Stesichorus and Thales of Miletus died.

The Persian kingdom began its origin. Amyntas, the ninth king of the Macedonians, reigned for fifty years. The two-hundredth year from the founding of the city of Rome.

(JORD.) Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, a surname given to him because of his character, was the seventh and last king of the Romans. He preferred to seize the ancestral kingdom, which his father-in-law Servius held, rather than wait for it. Having sent assassins against him, he administered the power acquired by crime no better than he had acquired it.

His wife Tullia was no different in character. In order to greet her husband as king, she drove her chariot over her bloodstained father, making the frightened horses run onward. (H. m.) He was the first to devise fetters, whips, rods, quarries, prisons, shackles, chains, exiles, and mines.

(JORD.) He attacked the senate with slaughter, the plebeians with beatings, and all good men with an arrogance more grievous than cruelty. The Roman people endured the king’s arrogance for so long as it was merely arrogance; but when lust was added, they could not tolerate the insolence of his sons.

(H. m.) For when he was besieging Ardea, situated eighteen miles from Rome, his son Sextus Tarquinius came armed from the camp to Rome by night and raped the most noble Lucretia, daughter of Lucretius Tricipitinus and wife of Tarquinius Collatinus.

She immediately summoned her husband and father, together with other friends, from the camp. Shamefaced and weeping, she complained of the violence she had suffered. When they consoled her and did not regard what she had suffered by force as a crime, she said: “From now on, no unchaste woman shall defend herself by appealing to Lucretia’s example.” Then she suddenly plunged into her entrails the sword that she had concealed beneath her clothing.

Moved by this event, the Roman people, led by Brutus, her father, and by her husband Collatinus, decided that Tarquinius should be deprived of his authority. Soon the army also abandoned Ardea, which it was besieging, together with the king himself, and returned to Rome. When Tarquinius came, the Romans barred the gates and excluded him.

After he had reigned for thirty-five years, he fled with his wife and children. Thus the rule of the kings came to an end.

(JORD.—*Historical Miscellany*.) This was the first age, as it were the infancy, of the Roman people. They spent 243 years under seven kings, while Rome still possessed little more than the area extending at most to the fifteenth mile-marker.

(JORD.—H. m.) After the kings had been expelled, individual senators held the state for one year, each for five days. Thereafter, in place of one king, two consuls were created for one-year terms, for this reason: so that if one wished to be bad, the other, possessing equal power, might restrain him; and so that, knowing they would preside over the people for only a single year, they would not become insolent, but would learn to consult the citizens rather than command them. In this way, during that year they would treat others as they later wished others to treat them.

(HIER.) At first, therefore, there were consuls; then dictators; afterward tribunes of the plebs; and again consuls. This order continued for 408 years, through 916 men, until Julius Caesar, who first seized the monarchy.

(JORD., HIER., H. m.) The first consuls, after Tarquinius had been expelled, were Lucius Junius Brutus, Lucretia’s uncle, who had worked especially hard to drive out Tarquinius, and Tarquinius Collatinus, Lucretia’s husband. Collatinus was immediately deprived of his office, for the Romans decided that no one named Tarquinius should remain in the city. He departed from the city with all his property, and Lucius Valerius Publicola was made consul in his place.

Tarquinius, driven from the kingship, went to Porsenna, king of Etruria, and to the other neighboring peoples, and for three years inflicted many evils upon the Romans.

(H. m.) For, having gathered many nations, he began a war in the same year as his expulsion and fought to be restored to the kingship. In the first battle, the consul Brutus and Arruns, Tarquinius’s son, killed each other, but the Romans nevertheless won.

Valerius Publicola made Lucretius Tricipitinus, Lucretia’s father, his colleague. When Lucretius died not long afterward, he again chose Horatius Pulvillus as his colleague. Thus the first year had five consuls.

In the second year Tarquinius again brought war upon the Romans with the aid of Porsenna, king of the Etruscans. Through continuous attacks he terrified, shut in, and besieged the trembling city. Unless Mucius had driven the enemy away from the city by his steadfast endurance, Tarquinius would either have captured the city or the people would have been subjected to perpetual slavery after restoring the king (cf. Orosius II, 5).

(H. m.) This Mucius had gone down into Porsenna’s camp to kill him. But when he saw one of Porsenna’s subordinate officials distributing pay in purple clothing, he thought that the man was the king and killed him.

(JORD.) When he saw that he had been deceived, he immediately placed his hand in the burning fire on the altar and, intensifying the terror by this ruse, said: “O hand, so that you may know what sort of man has escaped you: three hundred of us have sworn the same oath.” Having done this, he remained unafraid, while the king trembled as though his hand were burning.

One of the maidens, named Cloelia, had been given to the king among the hostages. She escaped from custody, mounted a horse, boldly crossed the Tiber, and returned to Rome.

(H. m.) On another day, when the Etruscans attacked the city across the bridge of the Tiber, a certain Horatius Cocles alone resisted them at the head of the bridge until the citizens destroyed the bridge after it had been dismantled. He then immediately threw himself, armed, into the Tiber and, victorious alike over the enemy and the river, avoided the weapons hurled by the Etruscans.

(JORD.) Terrified by so many and such great displays of courage, the king withdrew and made peace with the Romans.

(H. m.) In the third year, when Tarquinius saw that he could not return to the kingship and that Porsenna would not provide him assistance, he founded the city of Tusculum not far from Rome [Note: [Col. 0551] H. m.: “he withdrew”] and grew old there as a private citizen for fourteen years.

(H. m.) In the fourth year the Sabines brought war against the Romans and were defeated.

(HIER. H. m.) In the fifth year Lucius Valerius, Brutus’s colleague and already consul for the fourth time, died so poor that he was buried at public expense, money having been collected from the citizens.

In the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings, when Tarquinius’s son-in-law had gathered a huge army to avenge the injury done to his father-in-law, a new office was created at Rome called the dictatorship. It was greater than the consulship and resembled the imperial power that the tranquility of the later kingdom possessed, especially since Augustus Octavian and, before him, Julius Caesar also ruled under the title and honor of dictator.

(HIER. H. m.) In the same year a master of the horse was also appointed to obey the dictator. The first dictator was Marcus Valerius, and the first master of the horse was Spurius Cassius.

In the sixteenth year, while the dictator Marcus Valerius was conducting a military levy, the people caused a sedition at Rome, as though they were being oppressed by the senate. They withdrew from the fathers, occupied the Sacred Mount under arms, and created for themselves tribunes of the plebs as their own judges and defenders.

In the seventeenth year the Volscians prepared war against the Romans, but were defeated by Marcus Valerius, and lost Corioli, an excellent city. The same Marcus, expelled from the city in the following year, went angrily to the Volscians. With their aid he made war upon the Romans, often defeated them, and advanced as far as the fifth mile-marker from the city, intending to besiege it. He would have done so had not his mother Veturia and his wife Volumnia come out to him from the city. Overcome by their pleas, he dismissed the army.

He was the second after Tarquinius to become a commander against his own country.

(HIER.) Croesus, king of the Lydians, was captured by Cyrus, and the kingdom of the Lydians, which had stood for 241 years, was destroyed.

Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae killed Cyrus.

Cambyses, son of Cyrus and second king of the Persians, reigned for eight years. He is believed to be called Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes in the Book of Ezra, where it is related that certain people wrote to him to obstruct the rebuilding of Jerusalem and that he consented to their petition (cf. Josephus XI, 2). The same man [Note: [Col. 0551] I do not know the source of these words.], since he hated the Magi, ordered that their ears be cut off. After his death, however, seven Magi secretly killed his son; two Magian brothers among them, because they resembled him closely, reigned, according to some authorities (Jerome), for seven months, but according to Josephus (XI, 3), for one year. Their audacity was quickly detected and suppressed by the sword, because they were found to be Magi with mutilated ears.

Some writers, however, say (Jerome, on Daniel, ch. XI) that the man killed by the Magi was called Smerdis and that he married Pantaptes, the daughter of Cambyses; after he had been killed, Darius took her, together with the kingdom, as his wife and fathered Xerxes by her. Some also say that Cambyses was called a second Nebuchadnezzar (Jerome), under whom the history of Judith both took place and was written, since it is also stated in Roman history (quoted in Muratori, p. 4): “During the time of Tarquinius Superbus, the most chaste Judith killed Holofernes.”

Indeed, Tarquinius was a contemporary of Cambyses, for the first year of Cambyses was his eighteenth. I do not deny that Cambyses may have been called Nebuchadnezzar and that the history of Judith could have been written under him; but how it could have taken place under him, I do not see. For since he is read in the histories to have reigned no more than eight years, and the duration of his reign is likewise recorded in the chronicles, how he could have defeated in the twelfth year of his reign Arphaxad, the exceedingly powerful king of the Medes—who nowhere appears among us in the sequence of kings who ruled the Medes after the kingdom of the Assyrians was transferred to the Medes—or how, in the thirteenth year, he could have sent Holofernes to avenge his wrong, has not yet come within the range of my knowledge. This is especially so since the kingdom of the Medes had recently been transferred from his father Cyrus to the Persians, whether he invaded it after overthrowing Astyages, as some maintain, or, as others say, after the death of Darius, son of that same Astyages—who nevertheless is not placed in the chronicles among the catalogues of kings—and the kingdom came to him by hereditary right, as that of his maternal uncle.

Nor is Eliachim, who in the Book of Judith is read to have been the high priest who exhorted the Jews to trust in the Lord, reported to have lived at this time, unless perhaps he is the same as Joachim. The same book testifies that, after the killing of Holofernes, Joachim came from Jerusalem to Bethulia to see Judith, as the son of Jesus, who is believed to be Joshua. But this Joachim is surnamed Josedech, and his father Jesus also held the dignity of the high priesthood under Darius. Yet perhaps we are foolish to raise these questions while presuming to define nothing rashly; let us therefore yield, as is proper, to the writers of histories and leave these matters for more diligent investigators.

(Hierome—H. m.) In these days Hippicus, a writer of poems, and Xenophanes, a natural philosopher and writer of tragedies, are known. Simonides and Sophocles, Anacreon and Phocylides, lyric poets, are held in renown. Pythagoras too, a natural philosopher and philosopher, was celebrated. He was originally from Samos, lived at Croton, eventually went to Metapontum, and was buried there.

(Jerome.) Darius, son of Hystaspes and third king of the Persians, reigned for thirty-six years, beginning in the sixty-ninth year of the temple’s desolation. He was one of those who restrained by the sword the Magi who wished to rule. While still a private citizen, he prayed to the Lord to receive the kingdom, promising that, if he became king, he would return to Jerusalem all the vessels of God found in Babylon and rebuild the Temple (Orosius II, 8; Josephus XI, 3; cf. 1 Esdras VI; 2 Esdras I).

When he had been made king with everyone’s consent, Nehemiah, one of the Hebrews, found favor before him. When Nehemiah urged him to fulfill the vow he had made to God, in the second year of his reign—which was the seventieth year of the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple—he released the entire captivity, as had been foretold through the prophets (Jerome). Thus permission to rebuild the Temple began under Cyrus, but because of the opposition of enemies it remained unfinished until Darius. In the second year of Darius it was built by Zerubbabel and Jesus, and in the fourth year of the construction—which was the sixth year of Darius—the work was completed; according to Josephus (XI, 6), however, it was completed in the seventh year, which was the ninth year of Darius. The final prophets, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who is called “the Angel” among the Jews, were prophesying at that time.

From the first construction of the Temple under Solomon to its rebuilding under Darius there were, according to some authorities (Jordanes), 512 years; according to Josephus’s account (the same passage), 450.

(Orosius II, 8.) Darius made war against Antyrus, king of the Goths dwelling in Scythia, with seven hundred thousand men, because Antyrus refused him his daughter in marriage; Darius himself lost eighty thousand men. After this he subdued Asia and Macedonia, and fought the Athenians in the plain of Marathon. There, after losing two hundred thousand men from his army, he was defeated and fled back to Persia. As he was preparing to renew the war and take revenge upon the victors, he collapsed amid his preparations.

(Jerome.) In these days the historiographer Hellanicus, the philosopher Democritus, Heraclitus surnamed “the obscure,” Anaxarchus, Diogenes, and Xenophanes, natural philosophers, Aeschylus the tragedian, Hippicus the writer of poems, and Simonides, Anacreon, and Pindar, lyric poets, became famous. Pythagoras died in these days.

In this year [Note: [Col. 0553] This is partly from a correction in manuscript 1.] the Temple began to be rebuilt. From this rebuilding to the forty-second year of Augustus, in which Christ was born, 519 years are reckoned; to the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the preaching of Christ, 547 years.

Among the Romans the royal rule came to an end. From Romulus to Tarquinius Superbus, seven kings had ruled them for 243 years.

Pythagoras died.

A new dignity was created at Rome, namely the dictatorship and the magistracy of the cavalry. Alexander, king of the Macedonians, the tenth, reigned for forty-three years. The plebs seceded from the patricians, and tribunes were then established.

(H. m.) In these times the Fabian family, most glorious in numbers and strength, numbering 306 men, sought a special engagement against the Veientes for a period of ten years, promising that they alone would carry on the entire war. Accordingly, they set out—all nobles, and men who individually ought to have been commanders of great armies—but, having been surrounded by an ambush, they were all slaughtered, except for one survivor who, because he was still a boy, could not be led into battle.

(Jerome.) Xerxes, son of Darius and fourth king of the Persians, reigned for twenty years. Josephus says (XI, 7) that he inherited his father’s goodwill toward the Jews and the Temple of God. Hence Ezra, having obtained his favor, was sent to Jerusalem with many others; Nehemiah too was his cupbearer. Ezra writes that he came down from Babylon by permission of King Artaxerxes, and Nehemiah himself testifies that he was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes.

At that time the high priest was Joachim, surnamed Josedech, son of Jesus. After his death, his son Eliashib succeeded him. Josephus (VIII, 11), however, calls Joachim “Judas.” After Eliashib’s death, Joiada, his son, assumed the priesthood, and his son John succeeded him.

Thus Xerxes is described as having had seven hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand auxiliaries, as well as 1,200 ships equipped with rams and 3,000 cargo ships, when he planned to devastate Greece. It was therefore rightly said that, before that unexpected army and immense fleet, the rivers scarcely sufficed for drinking, the land scarcely for entering, and the seas scarcely for sailing. Hence he is said to have laid a bridge of ships across the sea (cf. Jerome and Orosius II, 9).

(Orosius, same passage.) Against this army, so unbelievable in our own times that its number is now more difficult to establish than it then was to defeat, Leonidas, king of Sparta, opposed himself with four thousand men in the pass of Thermopylae and nearly defeated it. Then Themistocles, commander of the Athenians, overcame his army in a naval battle. Finally, after the war in Greece had gone badly, Xerxes became contemptible to his own people. Returning home, he was surrounded and killed in the palace by his own prefect Artabanus.

(Jerome.) Artabanus reigned in his place for seven months, and afterward Artaxerxes.

(Jordanes.) Artaxerxes, who was called Macrochir, that is, “Long-handed,” reigned among the Persians for forty years, beginning in the fifty-sixth year from the restoration of the Temple. [Col. 0555]

(Jerome.) During his reign Ezra the priest was held in renown among the Hebrews, as the teacher of all in the sacred laws; for he renewed the Law (2 Esdras). Nehemiah completed the walls of the city, while the chief high priest of the Temple was Joiada, son of Eliashib, whom Josephus called Judas.

(Jerome.) Socrates was born. Perdiccas, the eleventh king of the Macedonians, reigned for twenty-eight years.

The three-hundredth year from the foundation of the city of Rome.

In these matters, therefore, historians appear to disagree about the sequence of kings and times. For what is written about Ezra and Nehemiah Josephus (XI, 8) reports as having taken place under King Xerxes, son of Darius—if, that is, the manuscript in which this appears is not corrupt, so that the discrepancy arose more from the negligence of copyists than from the historian’s judgment. For it is written there that Nehemiah was the cupbearer of King Xerxes, that in the twenty-fifth year of that king he came, with his permission, to rebuild Jerusalem, and that in the thirty-eighth year of the same king, in the ninth month, he completed its walls, although neither any other history known to us nor the chronicles record that he reigned for more than twenty-six years.

He also says (same work, ch. 9) that Artaxerxes [Note: [Col. 0555] “Artaxensen” in manuscript 1.]—whom he himself calls Cyrus, under whom the history of Esther took place—was the son of this Xerxes and succeeded him in the kingdom. Yet between them, in the succession of the Persian kings, five rulers are placed: Artabanus, who reigned for seven months after killing that same Xerxes; this Artaxerxes, whom we are now discussing, who was called Macrochir and reigned for forty years; another Xerxes, for two months; Sogdianus, for seven months; and Darius Nothus, for nineteen years. Together these amount to sixty years and four months.

Nehemiah himself, as we read in the Book of Ezra (2 Esdras II), confesses that he was the cupbearer of Artaxerxes and that in the twentieth year of his reign he received permission from him to go down and rebuild Jerusalem; he completed his work over twelve years, that is, in the thirty-second year of the same king (same work, ch. 13; cf. Jerome, on Daniel, ch. IX).

For first, as has often been said, under the rule of Cyrus, Zerubbabel, prince of the Hebrews, Jesus the high priest, and those who wished to go with them came down from Babylon; afterward Ezra and many others came down to construct the Temple and Jerusalem. But when the surrounding nations opposed them, the Temple, after the altar had been built, remained unfinished until the second year of Darius, which was the fortieth year from the first year of Cyrus. With Cyrus’s permission, however, the Temple together with its surrounding wall was completed in his sixth year, while the walls of Jerusalem remained unfinished for sixty-four years after the completion of the Temple. Thus, in the twentieth year of this Artaxerxes, Nehemiah began to build them and completed them in the thirtieth year of the same king.

From that time—that is, from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes—if anyone counts the seventy weeks written of by Daniel, which amount to 490 years, he will find them completed in the reign of Nero. Under Nero, Jerusalem began to be besieged and was captured in the second year of Vespasian. There is much disagreement among teachers concerning the reckoning of these weeks (cf. the same passage).

Some count them from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes to the siege of Jerusalem under Nero, as stated; others from the completion of the Temple under Darius to Hyrcanus, in whom the priesthood came to an end. Their view is as follows:

(Jerome.) Thus the seven and sixty-two weeks, which together make sixty-nine, amount to 483 years. During these years the christs—that is, priests consecrated by anointing—ruled, from the restoration of the Temple under Darius to Hyrcanus, in whom the final chrism and priesthood of the Jews came to an end.

(Jerome, on Daniel, ch. IX.) That the seven and sixty-two weeks, that is, 483 years, may be reckoned from the completion of the Temple—that is, from the sixth year of Darius—to the tenth year of Augustus, we can establish as follows. In the first year of the sixty-sixth Olympiad, that is, in the sixth year of Darius, the construction of the Temple was completed; and in the second year of the 186th Olympiad, that is, in the tenth year of Augustus, Herod assumed the kingdom of the Jews. Between these dates there are 483 years, counting four years for each Olympiad.

Others, reckoning the same weeks from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, wish them to end in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, in which Christ suffered, writing as follows (Bede, On the Reckoning of Time, ch. 7):

“Seventy weeks,” he says, “are shortened concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting justice may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed.” [Note: [Col. 0555] “fiat” in manuscript 1.]

There is no doubt that these words designate the incarnation of Christ, who took away the sins of the world, fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. It is known that seventy weeks, divided into periods of seven years, signify 490 years. But notice that he asserts that these weeks were not simply recorded or counted, but shortened, secretly warning the reader that years shorter than usual are indicated.

“Know,” says the angel, “that from the issuing of the word”—that is, the permission for Jerusalem to be rebuilt—“until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street and the walls shall be rebuilt in the distress of the times.”

From Ezra’s account we learn that Nehemiah, while he was the cupbearer of King Artaxerxes, obtained from him, in the twentieth year of his reign and in the month of Nisan, permission to restore the walls of Jerusalem. The Temple had been constructed long before by permission of Cyrus, and Nehemiah completed this work, as stated, in a time of distress. He was so harassed by the neighboring peoples that, as we are told, each of the builders fought with a sword girded at his side in one hand while rebuilding the wall with the other. [Note: [Col. 0555] “u l.” (uncertain reading).]

From that time, therefore—that is, from the moment when this permission was granted to him by the king—count seventy weeks to Christ the prince, and you will find 490 years of twelve lunar months each, which are 475 solar years. For from the aforesaid twentieth year of Artaxerxes until the death of Darius, the Persians reigned for 116 years; from then until the death of Cleopatra, the Macedonians held power for 300 years; thereafter, until the seventeenth year of Tiberius, the Romans held the monarchy for 59 years. These together, as we have said, amount to 475 solar years, and are contained in twenty-five nineteen-year cycles. For nineteen times twenty-five equals 475.

Since seven intercalary months are added in each cycle, multiply twenty-five by seven, and the result is 175, which are the intercalary months of 475 years. If you wish to know how many lunar years these months can make, divide 175 by twelve. Twelve times fourteen is 168. Thus they make fourteen years, with seven months remaining. Add these fourteen years to the preceding 475, and together they make 489. Add to these the seven surplus months and part of the eighteenth year of Tiberius, in which the Lord suffered, and you will find that, from the predetermined time—that is, from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes—to the Lord’s Passion, the seventy weeks [Note: [Col. 0555] “ebdomades” in manuscript 1.] were shortened: that is, they comprised 490 lunar years but 475 solar years.

At his baptism, however, when the Holy of Holies was anointed, the Holy Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, you will see that not only had the seven weeks and sixty-two weeks been completed, but that part of the seventieth week had already begun.

“And after the sixty-two weeks,” he says, “Christ shall be killed, and his people, who will deny him, shall no longer be his.” [Col. 0557]

Christ was therefore not killed immediately after the sixty-two weeks, but at the end of the seventieth week. For this reason, as far as we can conjecture, he separated that week from the others, because he was going to speak more about it: Christ was crucified in it, and by the faithless people he was denied not only during his Passion but continually from the time when, after being baptized by John, he began to preach.

What follows—“And the people with the coming prince shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed”—does not belong to the seventy weeks. For it had been foretold that the weeks themselves would extend to Christ’s princely rule; but after predicting his coming and Passion, Scripture also showed what would happen afterward to the people who refused to receive him.

By the coming prince it means Titus, who in the fortieth year of the Lord’s Passion so destroyed the city and the sanctuary with the Roman people that not one stone remained upon another. After this anticipation had been introduced, the text immediately returns to explain the outcome of the week it had omitted:

“He will confirm the covenant with many for one week”—that is, the final week itself, during which either John the Baptist or the Lord and the apostles, by preaching, converted many to the faith. “And in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease.” The middle of this week was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when, with Christ’s baptism having begun, the purification of sacrifices gradually began to become of little value to the faithful.

Likewise, what follows—“And in the Temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall continue until the consummation and the end”—refers to subsequent times. The truth of this prophecy is attested by the outcome both of the histories of the ancients and of events in our own times, even today.

I have set out these various opinions of the interpreters concerning the weeks written of in Daniel so that the wise reader may give them attention and see which one to choose.

(Jerome.) Up to this point divine Scripture contains the sequence of times. What was done afterward among the Jews is presented from the books of the Maccabees and from the writings of Josephus and Africanus, who subsequently pursued the whole history down to Roman times.

(Jerome, on Daniel, ch. IX.) Africanus, in the fifth volume of his Chronology, mentions this period as follows: “The work therefore remained unfinished until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes. At that time 113 years of the Persian kingdom had elapsed, while it was the 173rd year of the captivity of Jerusalem. If you wish to count seventy weeks of years from that time, you will be able to reach Christ.”

(Orosius II, 12.) In the 290th year from the foundation of the City, which was the third year of King Artaxerxes, when the war in which the Romans had long been struggling was temporarily suspended, a severe pestilence violently raged throughout the entire city. It killed both consuls, Ebutius and Servilius, along with a great multitude.

In the following year, exiled citizens and fugitive slaves, led by a certain Sabine named Herdonius, invaded and burned the Capitol. When the consul and dictator Valerius bravely resisted them, he was killed.

(H. m.) In the following year the Aequi and Volsci defeated the consul Minucius in battle and surrounded him with sword and famine on Mount Algidus, which lies about twelve miles from the City. The outcome would have been disastrous had not Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus, that outstanding dictator, lifted the siege.

He possessed four iugera of land in the countryside and cultivated it with his own hands. Found plowing at the very moment of his summons, he was called away from the plow and received the bordered toga. Soon, after assuming office and assembling an army, he slaughtered the enemy and returned victorious. He placed the yoke of oxen upon the horses and, holding victory as though it were a plow-handle, was the first to drive the conquered enemies before him.

Nine years later, in the 301st year from the foundation of the City, consular government ceased, and instead of two officials, ten were made the governing authorities. They were called decemvirs from their number, and this measure brought great ruin upon the republic.

(H. R.—H. m.) Since they had governed well in the first year, in the second year one of them, Appius Claudius, after the others yielded to him, continued the authority for himself alone. Immediately afterward a conspiracy of the others followed, so that suddenly they proceeded individually with royal fasces and did everything according to their own pleasure with arrogant display.

Hence the aforementioned Appius violated the daughter of a certain honorable man, Virginius. Because of this, the father, driven by grief for his daughter’s freedom and shame at the dishonor, killed his daughter as she was being dragged off into slavery, in the sight of the people. Moved by the atrocity of this deed and warned of the danger to their freedom, the people occupied the Aventine armed, and did not cease defending their liberty until power had been taken away from the decemvirs and they themselves had been condemned.

After another twenty years—that is, in the thirty-fifth year of Artaxerxes—the Veientes rebelled against the Romans. Furius Camillus was sent against them as dictator and defeated them. When a statue of Juno Moneta was found in the city, he ordered it to be transferred to Rome. One of the soldiers then jokingly asked the image whether it wished to go to Rome, and it immediately replied, “I do.”

Afterward the same Manlius captured the Faliscans as well, a city no less famous. But jealousy was aroused against him, as though he had distributed the spoils improperly, and for that reason he was condemned and expelled from the state.

Then the Gallic Senones, entering Italy under the leadership of Brennus, ravaged everything. When the consul Fabius went out to meet them, he was killed by them. After they had entered Rome, they filled the city with slaughter and fire. Having killed the senators, they shut up the remaining young men—who, it is agreed, then numbered scarcely a thousand—on the heights of the Capitoline hill and surrounded them with a siege.

Recalled by this emergency, Manlius [Note: [Col. 0557] Ekkehard confused Manlius and Furius Camillus with each other and added certain material from the Miscellaneous History.] arrived and, killing many of the enemy, climbed to the Capitol. The Gauls, climbing the Capitol by night, nearly captured it, except that Manlius, awakened by the cry of a goose, resisted them. After besieging them for a long time, however, they received one thousand pounds of gold for their withdrawal and departed.

Manlius pursued them and fought in such a way that he recovered all the gold and brought back all the military standards they had captured. Thus, entering the city in a third triumph, he was called a second Romulus, as though he too had founded the city.

[Col. 0557] (Jerome.) In these times Aristarchus, a writer of tragedies, Cratinus and Plato, writers of comedies, Zeno and Heraclitus, Pherecydes the Younger, a writer of histories, Sophocles and Aristophanes, tragedians, and the famous philosophers Empedocles and Parmenides were known.

Archelaus, the twelfth king of the Macedonians, reigned for twenty-five years.

Xerxes, king of the Persians, reigned for two months. After him Sogdianus reigned for seven months; thus that year came to an end.

Darius, surnamed Nothus, reigned over the Persians for nineteen years, beginning in the ninety-seventh year from the rebuilding of the Temple.

Herodotus, after reading his books before the assembly at Athens, was honored.

Plato was born.

Hippocrates the physician, Socrates the philosopher, and Zeuxis the painter were also held in renown.

The dynasty of the Egyptians arose again. In it the first to rule was Amaritheus the Saite, for six years.

[Col. 0559] The second was Nepherites, king of the Egyptians, who reigned for six years.—Artaxerxes, also surnamed Memnon, son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned over the Persians for forty years, beginning in the 116th year from the restoration of the Temple. [Note: [Col. 0559] Thus in one manuscript: “in the year”—corrected in the first revision.] This is the man whom Josephus’s book (XI, 9) calls the son of Xerxes, with five kings omitted, and this is the one whom the Hebrews call Ahasuerus, under whom the history of Esther took place (Jerome).

(Orosius II, 18.) In these days a civil war among the Persians scarcely ended short of parricide. For after King Darius died, when Artaxerxes and Cyrus, his sons, were contending for the kingdom, the conflict on both sides finally brought great ruin upon provinces and peoples. In the battle, when the two brothers, rushing against each other from opposite directions, exposed themselves to mutual danger, Artaxerxes was first wounded by his brother Cyrus but escaped death through the speed of his horse. Cyrus, however, was soon overwhelmed by the royal cohort and brought the contest to an end.

Thus Artaxerxes, having gained the spoils of his brother’s expedition and possession of the army, secured the power of the kingdom through fratricide. Hence Josephus (same passage) and certain others call him Cyrus.

(Jerome.) Archelaus, the fourteenth king of the Macedonians, reigned for four years.

Amintas, the fifteenth, reigned for one year.

Pausanias, the sixteenth, reigned for one year.—Achoris, the third king of the Egyptians, reigned for twelve years.

Amintas, the seventeenth king of the Macedonians, reigned for six years.

Socrates died after drinking poison.

Argeus, the eighteenth, reigned for two years.

Amintas, the nineteenth, reigned for eighteen years.

Spammutes, the fourth, reigned for one year.

Nectanebis, the fifth king of the Egyptians, reigned for eighteen years.

In these times Demosthenes the orator, Eudoxus the astrologer, and Diogenes the Cynic were known.

Aristotle too, when he was eighteen years old, was a student of Plato, who at that time was renowned together with Xenophon and other Socratics.

Alexander, the twentieth king of the Macedonians, reigned for one year.

Ptolemy, also called Alorites, the twenty-first king of the Macedonians, reigned for four years.

The sixth Egyptian king, Teos, reigned for nineteen years; thus the kingdom came to an end.

Perdiccas, the twenty-second king of the Macedonians, reigned for six years.

(Miscellaneous History, Book II.) In the 365th year from the foundation of the City, which was the eighteenth year of Artaxerxes Memnon, [Note: [Col. 0559] “m. XVIIIus,” corrected in manuscript 1.] the offices of the city were changed. In place of consuls or dictators, military tribunes began to be appointed, and from this point the Roman state began to grow.

For in that year Camillus defeated the Volscian city that had waged war against the Romans for seventy years. He also defeated the city of the Aequi and that of the Sutrini. Titus Quintius Cincinnatus likewise defeated the Praenestines, who had come in war as far as the gates of the City, pursuing them as far as the river Allia; he added to the Romans eight cities that had been subject to them.

The dignity of the military tribunes, however, did not last long. After some time it was decided that none should be appointed, and thus four years passed in the City without any higher magistracies. When consuls were again appointed, Lucius Livius and Quintus Servilius, Camillus died, and an honor second only to that of Romulus was bestowed upon him in the 384th year from the foundation of the City, which was the thirty-seventh year of Artaxerxes.

(H. R.—H. m.) In these times a great pestilence afflicted all Rome continuously for two years. In the following year there occurred a sufficiently grim portent. In the middle of the city forum the earth split open, and when a vast chasm burst open, the underworld yawned forth. Since this remained open for a long time and brought terror upon everyone, the haruspices finally said that it could be closed if a young man who was Rome’s most precious possession were voluntarily sent into it.

Then Marcus Curtius, a Roman knight of distinguished family, took up his arms and, with his horse, leaped into the chasm. Thus it was closed. Afterward, those making sacrifices threw grain into the same place, and soon the earth returned to its natural condition.

Again, a terrifying flood of Gauls advanced near the river Anio [Note: [Col. 0559] “Anionem” in one manuscript?], at the fourth milestone from the City. There Lucius Manlius, a most noble young man from the senatorial class, went out against a Gaul who had challenged him to single combat and killed him. He took the golden torque from the Gaul’s neck and placed it around his own; from that time he and his descendants permanently received the surname Torquatus.

At another time, also in these days, a certain Gaul named Furius [Note: [Col. 0559] Ekkehard took this, with considerable error, from the words of the Miscellaneous History: “under the leadership of Lucius Furius, a certain man from Gaul,” and so forth.] challenged to single combat whichever Roman was the best. Then Marcus Valerius, a military tribune, offered himself. When he advanced armed, a crow settled upon his right arm. Soon, when battle had been joined against the Gaul, the same crow struck the Gaul’s eyes with its wings and claws, so that he could not look straight ahead.

Thus Valerius killed the Gaul and won both the victory and the name Corvinus. Because of this achievement he became consul for twenty-three years. After the Gaul was killed, the remaining Gauls were slaughtered as they fled.

(Orosius III, 7.) At that time night seemed to extend through most of the day, and hail of stone descended from the clouds, beating the earth with real stones. In those same days Alexander the Great was born, truly a devourer of misery and the most savage storm of the entire East.

(Jerome.) In Sicily Dionysius exercised tyranny, and in the nineteenth year he died; his son Dionysius the Younger seized the kingdom.

(Augustine VIII, 3.) Socrates, Plato’s teacher, was then famous at Athens. He is remembered as the first to turn the whole of philosophy toward the correction of morals, whereas before him everyone had devoted himself chiefly to investigating physical, that is, natural, matters. He taught that the good end could be achieved only by living well.

After he had given many examples of the virtues, the envy of uneducated people stirred up the Athenians against him through a defamatory accusation. He drank poison and died, although afterward the entire city publicly mourned him.

(Jerome—Augustine, same work, and VIII, 4, 9, 4.) Since he left behind very many followers of his philosophy, whose zeal was devoted competitively to disputing moral questions—questions concerning the highest good, without which a person cannot become happy—Plato was more eminent than all his disciples in glory and fame. Not without reason, for he had determined that the end of the good was living according to virtue, that this could happen only to one who possessed knowledge of the one God for imitation, and that there was no other cause of blessedness.

Plato was born to an honorable family among his own people, and at Athens surpassed all his fellow students by his remarkable talent. Not content with Socratic instruction, he traveled far and wide, wherever the reputation of acquiring some noble branch of knowledge drew him. Thus in Egypt he learned whatever was regarded and taught there as great; and from there, coming into those parts of Italy where the reputation of Pythagoras was celebrated, he very readily grasped whatever belonged to Italian philosophy.

Because he loved his teacher Socrates with exceptional devotion, he makes him speak in nearly all his dialogues. Since the pursuit of wisdom consists in action and contemplation—hence one part of it is called active and the other contemplative—the active part concerns the conduct of life, that is, the formation of morals, while the contemplative part concerns the observation of the causes of nature and the most unclouded truth, Socrates is said to have excelled in the active part, whereas Pythagoras is said to have devoted himself more intensely to contemplation with all the powers of understanding available to him.

Accordingly, Plato is praised for having perfected philosophy by joining the two. He divided it into three parts: one moral, which is chiefly concerned with action; another natural, which is devoted to contemplation; and a third rational, by which truth is distinguished from falsehood.

Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, reigned among the Persians for twenty-six years, beginning in the 153rd year from the restoration of the Temple.

(Jerome—Jordanes.) He overthrew Sidon, subjected Egypt to his own rule, drove King Nectanebo into Ethiopia, and thereby destroyed the kingdom of the Egyptians; he also devastated the whole of Syria.

(Josephus XI, 14.) The Jewish priest at this time was John, son of Judas, who was also called Joiada. This John had a brother named Jesus, to whom Bagoses, commander of King Artaxerxes, promised the high-priesthood. Confident because of this promise, Jesus quarreled with his brother in the Temple and was killed by him. For this reason the commander entered the Temple, violated it, and inflicted many evils upon the Jews.

(Jerome.) Philip, son of Amintas and father of Alexander the Great, the twenty-third king of the Macedonians, reigned for twenty-six years, during which he constructed a whole heap of bitter deeds and every mass of evil.

(Orosius III, 12, 14, 15.) First, Philip was given as a hostage to the Thebans by his brother Alexander and was educated for three years under Epaminondas, a vigorous teacher and outstanding philosopher. After that Alexander had been killed through the crime of his mother Eurydice, Philip, compelled by the people, assumed responsibility for governing the kingdom on behalf of the young son of his murdered brother.

Soon he made war upon neighboring peoples. After defeating the Athenians and subjecting the Thessalians, he married Olympias, daughter of Auruchas, king of the Molossians, sister of Alexander, king of the Epirotes [Note: [Col. 0561] two folios are missing in the first manuscript.]. By her he fathered Alexander, who was called the Great.

For twenty-six years, throughout all Greece, the conflagrations of cities, the destruction of wars, the subjugation of provinces, the slaughter of human beings, the plundering of wealth, the seizure of livestock, the sale of the dead, and the captivity of the living were driven on by the fraud, ferocity, and domination of one king. In the third year of Arses, son of Ochus, he was treacherously killed by Pausanias, son of Cerastes, who traced his lineage from Orestes. [Note: [Col. 0561] I do not know where Ekkehard found these words.]

The events perpetrated by Philip, preserved in memory, would be sufficient to illustrate the miseries of the world even if Alexander had not succeeded him in the kingdom.

The 400th year from the foundation of the City.

(Jerome—Josephus XI, 14.) Arses [Note: [Col. 0561] “erses,” with the initial letter omitted, in manuscript 4; “arxes” in 9c.], son of Ochus, reigned over the Persians for four years, beginning in the 182nd year from the rebuilding of the Temple.—After John, the Jewish high priest, died, Jaddus, his son, assumed the office. His brother Manasseh built a Temple on Mount Gerizim.

(Jerome.) Plato died in these times. After him Speusippus held the Academy; after Speusippus died, Xenocrates [Note: [Col. 0561] “Zenocrates” in 9c.] succeeded him.—Aristotle was celebrated by everyone’s voice.

Darius, son of Arsames [Note: [Col. 0561] “son of Arsames” in manuscript 4.], the last king of the Persians, reigned for six years, beginning in the 186th year from the restoration of the Temple. [Note: [Col. 0561] The year is missing in 9c.] In his sixth year Alexander, king of the Macedonians, fought against him; after defeating him, he destroyed the Persian kingdom, which had stood for 240 years.

(HIER.)
