Alexander the Great, son of Philip [Note: [Col. 0561] *phylippi* in 4.], as he was thought to be, and son of Olympias, the twenty-fourth king of the Macedonians, reigned twelve years—six while the Persian kingdom still stood, and then another six, which are likewise counted in the chronological sequence. (Cf. JORD.) [Note: [Col. 0561] I do not know where Ekkehard found these words.] He was short in stature, savage by nature, a man of great spirit, impatient of repose, always striving toward higher things, cruel and thirsting for blood. (OROS. III, 18.) Thus he killed many not only of foreigners but also of his own people, among them his cousin Amyntas [Note: *consobri* in 4, 5.], and also Cleitus, advanced in years and closely joined to him in friendship, and Callisthenes [Note: *callastenen* in 4.], a philosopher and his fellow-student under Aristotle, together with very many leading men of the kingdom. (The same, ch. 16.)

After gaining the kingdom, he quickly gave the first demonstration of his courage and valor by suppressing the disturbances of the Greeks, whom the orator Demosthenes had incited to revolt from Macedonian rule. Having subdued the Athenians, destroyed the Thebans, and made the other cities of Greece and Thessaly tributary, and having conquered the Illyrians and Thracians, he set out for the war against Darius, king of the Persians, whom both Greek and Latin histories, as well as those of the barbarians, report to have been the most powerful and richest of men (Cf. HIER., on Dan. ch. IX, and OROS. in the same place).

Alexander had in his army twenty-two thousand infantry, four thousand cavalry, five hundred [Note: *quingentas* in n. 4.] ships; and, with so small a force, whether it is more astonishing that he conquered the whole world or that he dared to attack it is uncertain [Note: *furrat* in 4.]. In his first engagement with Darius, six hundred thousand Persians were drawn up in battle, and they turned their backs, overcome no less by Alexander’s strategy than by the valor of the Macedonians. There was therefore a great slaughter of Persians, whereas from Alexander’s army only one hundred and twenty cavalrymen and nine infantrymen were missing.

Next he besieged and captured Gordium, a city of Phrygia, which is now called Sardis [Note: *sardus* in 4.]. Meanwhile Darius arrived with three hundred thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry. When they joined battle, the fighting was carried on with immense courage on both sides. In the battle both kings were wounded, and the contest remained undecided until Darius fled. At that time, eighty thousand infantry and ten thousand cavalry were killed on the Persian side, and forty thousand were captured; among the Macedonians, one hundred and thirty infantry and one hundred and fifty cavalry fell.

(JOS. XI, 10.) After this Alexander advanced toward Judea and approached Jerusalem. The priest Jaddus came out to meet him wearing a hyacinth-colored and golden robe, with a tiara upon his head and a golden plate; the other priests came forth in linen robes, and the whole multitude in white garments. Alexander alone approached and worshiped the name of God written on the golden plate. First he paid reverence to the high priest, then [Note: *dein* in 4.], ascending to the temple [Note: *in* in 4.], he sacrificed to God according to the priest’s direction, and gave many gifts to the high priest [Note: *sacerdoti* in 4.] and to the other priests.

While all his people were astonished at this, Parmenion, the commander of the army, asked him why he had worshiped the priest of the Jewish nation. “I did not worship him,” he replied, “but God, whose priestly office he exercises. For when I was still in Macedonia and was considering that I could not conquer Asia, I saw him in this very attire, urging me confidently to cross over, and saying that he would lead my army and deliver the power of the Persians into my hands.” [Note: See Julius Zacher, who investigated for a long time and in detail the history of the legends told about Alexander the Great; he observes that this and certain other material can be read in Peter Comestor’s *Historia scholastica*.]

(OROS. in the same place.) Meanwhile Darius, for the third time, having gathered all the forces of the Persians and the assistance of their allies, renewed the war. Alexander, returning from Judea, captured the city of Tyre, invaded Syria and Egypt, and founded Alexandria in Egypt. From there, as he was returning, Darius confronted him at Tarsus with four hundred [Note: “four hundred” in 4.] thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry.

(OROS. III, ch. 17.) There was no delay before the battle: all rushed blindly and furiously upon the weapons; the Macedonians were emboldened by the many victories they had won over their enemies, while the Persians preferred to die rather than fail to conquer. Rarely in any war was so much blood shed. But when Darius saw that his men were being defeated and were ready to die in battle, he was compelled by the urging of his followers [Note: *persuasorum* in 4.] to flee. For twenty-four continuous days Alexander inspected the spoils of the camp. When he heard that Darius was being held by his relatives, bound with golden fetters, he decided to pursue him. But he found him abandoned alone on the road, pierced with many wounds [Note: omitted in 9c.], and dead [Note: omitted in 9c.]; out of empty compassion he had him buried in the tombs of his ancestors.

Thus, when Darius was killed in the sixth year of his reign, and likewise in Alexander’s sixth year, the men of Asia fell [Note: omitted in 4.], and the whole East passed into the power of the Macedonian empire. The kingdom of the Persians was transferred to Alexandria, where rule continued for two hundred and ninety-six years. (Cf. HIER. and OROS. in the same places.) Some call this kingdom the kingdom of the Greeks (JORD.), others the kingdom of the Egyptians (Cf. JOS. XII, 1, and BEDA).

Alexander the Macedonian reigned six years after the death of Darius, in the 186th year from the rebuilding of the temple. For twelve years he held the trembling world beneath him by the sword; but his last six years, during which, after destroying the Persian empire, he held the monarchy of the world, are counted in the chronological sequence, while the preceding seven are reckoned under the Persian kingdom. Having subjected to himself all the kingdoms of the surrounding nations, he advanced into India and subjected it, together with all the kingdoms of the East.

After performing many astonishing deeds and being called lord of diverse nations, in the thirty-second year of his life, near Babylon, while he still thirsted for blood, he drank poison through the treachery of his attendants and died. After his death, the leaders of the Macedonians, having received different provinces, though Alexander himself while still alive had arranged matters, wore one another out in mutual wars. For fourteen years they tore apart the world which Alexander had acquired swiftly and courageously [Note: *ab a.* omitted in 9c.], and, like greedy cubs tearing apart the finest prey brought down by a great lion, they devoured it.

But since Alexander is read to have accomplished many remarkable deeds, which many people take pleasure in knowing, I shall extract something about his life in brief, so that I may in some measure satisfy those who seek such things for their enjoyment (Cf. HIERON., OROS. chs. 19, 20, 23, and JORDAN.).

## EXCERPT FROM THE LIFE OF ALEXANDER THE GREAT [Note: [Col. 0563] omitted in 9c.]

[Col. 0563A] (History of Alexander, Bamb. codex, fol. 193r.) The writings report that the Egyptian people were powerful in mathematical and magical art. Their king Nectanebus, who was a contemporary of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, also called Memnon [Note: *menon* in 4.], was thoroughly skilled in magical art. Thus, when enemies came against him, he did not move soldiers or weapons; instead, entering his palace, he took a bronze bowl and filled it with rainwater. Holding a bronze rod in his hand, he summoned demons by magical arts and investigated the outcome of events.

When he had reigned eighteen years, it was announced to him that many nations had assembled against him [Note: *advenisse* in 9c.]. Dismissing everyone from him, he entered the palace and, as usual, devoted himself to magical consultation. He saw in his bowl that the gods of the Egyptians were steering the ships of the barbarians. He immediately shaved his head and beard to disguise himself, took as much gold as he could [Note: *voluit* in 4.], put on linen garments as though he were an Egyptian prophet and astrologer, and, fleeing from Egypt, came to Macedonia. There, sitting openly, he practiced divination for everyone who came to him. (Fol. 194.)

[Col. 0564A] While he remained there until the time of King Philip, on one occasion, when Philip had gone out to battle, Nectanebus came to the palace. He greeted Queen Olympias, who returned his greeting, and the queen ordered him to sit beside her [Note: *pergit* in 1, fol. 60.], asking whether he truly was an Egyptian. When he said that he was Egyptian, praised the wisdom of the Egyptians at length, and commended himself as highly skilled in divination, he became inflamed with love for her during their conversation and looked at her with desirous intent.

The queen said to him: “O prophet, what have you conceived by looking at me in this way?”

He replied: “I remembered a most beautiful divination that I received from the gods, being close to them. One of the most powerful gods will sleep with you, and you will conceive from him.”

She said: “And who is that god?”

Nectanebus replied: “It is Ammon, who bestows riches on everyone.”

She said: “And what form does he have?”

He replied: “He is neither young nor old, but stands at the midpoint of life; he has gray hair, an adorned beard, and horns on his forehead. Therefore, if it pleases you, prepare yourself for him, because you will see him in a dream, and in that same dream he will sleep with you.”

[Col. 0565A] She said: “If I see this, I shall worship you not as a prophet or diviner but as a god.”

After saying this, Nectanebus immediately went out into the desert. Pulling up herbs and squeezing out their juice, he made a magic charm for Olympias, so that it would seem to her, as truly in a dream, that the god Ammon was sleeping with her. Nectanebus, however, slept with her. When he rose from her, he said to her: “Woman, you have conceived your defender.”

In the morning, when she had risen from her bed, she summoned Nectanebus and recounted to him the dream she had seen. He said: “I know everything. Let us establish some test, because truth is one thing and a dream another. When this god comes to you, he will have the form of a dragon, and afterward a human form resembling mine.”

She said: “You have spoken well, prophet. Take possession of the chamber, and if I see this, I shall regard you as the child’s father.”

When this had happened, as he rose from her, he struck her womb with his hand and said: “May this conception be victorious and in no way be subjected.”

When her womb began to swell, she summoned Nectanebus and said: “Prophet, what will Philip do if he returns?”

He replied: “Do not be afraid; I shall be your aid.”

Thus persuaded, Olympias was seduced by the man as though by a god. Meanwhile Nectanebus [Note: *nectabus* in 1.] performed magical incantations and appeared to Philip as though he saw the god Ammon sleeping with Olympias and saying to her: “Woman, you have conceived in your womb your defender from his father Philip.” He also seemed to see the hidden limbs of the child being sewn together and marked with a golden ring, in which was a stone engraved with a lion’s head, the radiance of the sun, and a sword.

[Col. 0565C] (Fol. 195.) When Philip saw this, he rose and summoned a diviner to interpret the dream. The diviner said to him: “Know for certain, Philip, that Olympias has conceived not from a man but from a god, and the one who will be born will reach as far as the East, fighting and taking cities by the sword.”

After this Philip, having won a victory [Note: omitted in 1.], returned to Macedonia, and Olympias came out to meet him. When he kissed her, he looked at her and said: “To whom have you given yourself, Olympias? You have sinned; against whom? Yet you have not sinned, because you suffered violence from a god. I myself saw all this in a dream; therefore you appear to be free from blame.”

One day, while the king was dining and was very cheerful, Nectanebus transformed himself by magical art into the form of a dragon. He passed through the middle of the dining room and hissed terrifyingly, striking fear into all the guests. Approaching Olympias, he placed his head in her lap. When Philip saw him, he said to everyone: “Truly, I saw this dragon when I was in battle against my enemies.”

After a few days, while Philip was sitting alone, a small bird flew into his lap and laid an egg. When the egg fell from his lap to the ground, it split open, and a very small snake came out. It coiled around the egg and tried to enter it, but before it had inserted its head, it died.

The troubled king summoned the diviner and recounted what had happened to him.

The diviner said: “King Philip, a son will be born to you who is destined to reign and to travel throughout the whole world, subjecting everyone; and before he returns to his own land, he will die.”

The time for Olympias to give birth approached. When her womb began to hurt, she summoned Nectanebus. As he began to calculate, he said: “Raise yourself a little from your seat, Olympias, because at this hour the sun is disturbing all the elements.”

Shortly afterward Olympias gave birth. When the child fell to the ground, lightning, thunder, and an earthquake immediately occurred. When Philip saw this, he said: “Woman, I had decided in my heart that this little child should in no way be reared, because he was not conceived from me. But because I understand that he was conceived by a god, and I see the elements being changed at his birth, let him be raised in memory of me as though he were truly my son, and let him be named Alexander.”

When Philip had said this, they began to raise the boy with every care. His appearance resembled neither his father nor his mother. The hair of his head was like a lion’s mane; his eyes did not resemble one another, but one was black and the other white; his teeth were sharp, and his energy was fierce like that of a lion.

Given over to the study of philosophy, when he sat in school with his fellow students, he often fought with them and defeated them. When he was twelve years old, he was trained with the other soldiers as though for battle. Seeing his speed, the king said to him: “My son, I admire your speed and intelligence, but I am saddened because your appearance does not resemble mine.”

When Olympias saw that he was sad, she summoned Nectanebus and said to him: “Investigate and discover what Philip intends to do with me.”

After calculating, he said: “His intention toward you is pure; the sun is looking upon a certain star that separates its desire.”

Alexander was then there. When he heard this, he said: “Father, do these stars that you calculate appear in the sky?”

Nectanebus [Note: *nectanebus* in 1.] replied: “Yes, my son.”

Alexander said: “And can I see them in the evening?”

Nectanebus replied: “Follow me into the field at night, and I shall show them to you.”

Alexander said: “And do you know your own fate?”

Nectanebus replied: “Yes, certainly.”

Alexander said: “The art is a good one, and I desire to know it. By what death are you destined to die?”

He replied: “I shall die at the hands of my son.”

After saying all this, Alexander followed him at night outside the city.

[Col. 0566D] (Fol. 196.) Nectanebus said to him: “My son, look at the stars and see how sad the star of Hercules is; but the star of Hermes is joyful, and the star of Jupiter is bright.”

While Nectanebus was looking upward in this way, Alexander approached him more closely and, rushing at him, threw him into a pit, saying: “Since you do not know earthly causes, why did you wish to meddle with the heavenly elements?”

Nectanebus replied: “This was known to me, because it had to happen to me in this way; yet I could not escape unless this happened to me.”

Alexander said: “Because I am your son.”

Nectanebus replied: “You are indeed my son.”

When Alexander discovered that he was his father, he hesitated to leave him in the pit, but lifted him onto his shoulders and carried him to the palace.

When his mother saw this, she said: “Son Alexander, what is this?”

He replied: “It is the body of Nectanebus.”

She said: “Nectanebus was your father.”

He replied: “See what your foolishness has done.”

---

[Col. 0567A] (Fol. 195v.) Some men from Cappadocia brought Philip a colt—that is, a large young horse—bound on every side with various restraints, for it ate human beings. The king ordered it to be enclosed behind iron bars, so that rapists, robbers, and other criminals who had been condemned to the wild beasts might be eaten by it.

(Fol. 196.) Alexander, having become bold and courageous, passed one day through the place where that horse was confined. Seeing human hands and feet lying before it, the remains left over from its meals, he was astonished and put his hand through the bars toward it.

The horse immediately stretched out its neck and began to lick his hand. Then, folding its legs beneath itself, it threw itself to the ground, turned its head, and looked at Alexander as though caressing him. Understanding the horse’s intention, Alexander opened the enclosure and began gently to touch its back with his right hand. At once the horse became still tamer, and just as a dog is accustomed to caress its master, so it caressed Alexander.

He mounted it and rode outside, and he called the horse Bucephalus. [Note: Ekkehard took “and he called the horse Bucephalus” from another book.] When Philip saw this, he said: “Son Alexander, now I understand every prophecy concerning you, and I know that you are destined to reign after me.”

[Col. 0567C] Meanwhile, when Alexander was fifteen years old, he said to Philip: “Father, if it can be done, send me out seated in a chariot.”

The king said: “I gladly accept this, my son. I shall give you one hundred horses and forty thousand gold solidi; go with good assistance.”

Accordingly Alexander departed and came into the Peloponnese to fight Nicolaus, king of that province. When Nicolaus saw him, he said: “Tell me, who are you?”

He replied: “I am Alexander, son of Philip.”

Nicolaus said to him: “What do you expect of me?”

Alexander replied: “You are Nicolaus, king of the Arideans; but do not let your heart be lifted up in pride because you possess royal honor. It is often found in human destiny that the greater comes down to smallness and the small rises to greatness.”

Nicolaus said: “You have spoken well. You do not know yourself, whereas my nature is beyond reproach. But tell me the truth: why have you come into these regions?”

Alexander replied: “Withdraw from me, man, because you have nothing against me, nor I against you.”

At this Nicolaus became very angry and said: “See what kind of man I am addressing. By the salvation of my father, if I spit foam into his face, he will die.”

He spat at him and said: “Take this, which you deserve to receive, little whelp, since you are not ashamed.”

But Alexander, restraining himself according to the teaching of philosophy, said: “Nicolaus, by my paternal birth and by my mother’s womb impregnated by God, I shall defeat you by arms and subject your homeland to me.”

[Col. 0568A] Then he withdrew from him.

After a short time the appointed day came, on which the two joined battle. When the trumpets sounded, all Nicolaus’s soldiers advanced together into the fight; Alexander killed them all with his own hand.

Returning in victory, he found that Philip had taken a certain woman named Cleopatra as his companion, having driven out his mother. While Philip was seated at the wedding feast, Alexander entered and said: “Father, receive from me the victorious crown of my first battle. Yet when I celebrate the wedding of my mother, joining her to a husband, you will not be invited to that wedding.”

One of the banqueters, Lysias, said: “Philip, a son resembling you will be born from Cleopatra.”

When Alexander heard this, he struck him with the staff he held in his hand, and Lysias died. Seeing this, Philip became angry, rose, and rushed at him, but fell during the assault.

(Fol. 197.) Alexander said to him: “You who subjected Asia and Europe, why are you not standing on your feet?”

Thus that wedding itself was broken up, and Philip fell ill. After a few days Alexander entered to visit him and said: “Philip, although it is not customary for me to call you by your name, I am not speaking to you as a son but as a friend. Do what is right toward that woman whom you wronged, and do not be troubled because I killed Lysias. I did well; you did wrong in wishing to strike me with a sword.”

Philip wept. When Alexander saw his father weeping, he left him and went to his mother. He said to her: “Mother, do not harbor ill will toward my father. Although your sin is hidden, your reproach will nevertheless remain. It is good that a wife should always be subject to her husband.”

Saying this, he brought her to Philip.

After a few days envoys of King Darius came to Philip, demanding tribute from him. Alexander said to them: “Go and say to Darius: When Philip had no son, a hen laid a golden egg for him; now a son has been born to Philip, and the hen has become barren.”

Saying this, he dismissed them and sent them back empty-handed to King Darius.

After this Armenia rebelled against Philip, and he sent Alexander there with an army to conquer it. In Macedonia there was a certain man named Pausanias, subject to Philip. Desiring Olympias, he plotted against the king, gathered a people around him, and came against Philip with an armed force.

When Philip turned his back on him, Pausanias hurled his spear and struck Philip in the back. Philip did not die immediately but lay half alive in the field. Pausanias, thinking him dead, was elated and entered the palace boldly, where he seized Olympias.

Meanwhile Alexander returned from Armenia and found the greatest disturbance in Macedonia. Olympias came out and began to cry aloud to Alexander, saying: “Where is your victory, Alexander? Where is the destiny that you received from the gods, that you should be victorious and avenge me and your father?”

When Pausanias heard this, he came out to see Alexander. Alexander struck Pausanias with his drawn sword, and he died immediately.

Then a messenger came to Alexander announcing that his father was also dying, and he went to him. When Philip saw him, he said: “Son Alexander, I shall now die happily, because you have taken revenge by killing my enemy.”

Saying this, he died.

Alexander, weeping over his father’s death, went away and buried him. On the following day, seated on his father’s throne, he summoned everyone and said:

“O young men of Macedonia, Thrace, Thessalonica, Lacedaemon, and elsewhere, look and see Alexander, and let the fear of the barbarians be far from you! Let this be my responsibility, for I shall subject them and give them into your service. Whoever among you wishes may take weapons from my palace and prepare himself for battle; whoever does not wish to do so may arm himself with his own weapons.”

The elders said to him: “King Alexander, we have served in the army of your father for many years, and we no longer have the strength to endure hardships. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us be excused from the military service that we have hitherto carried on.” [Note: *habuimus et egimus* in 5.]

Alexander replied: “We prefer to have you in our army rather than young men, because a young man who trusts in his youth brings about his own death, whereas an older man does everything with counsel.”

Saying this, he persuaded them to remain in his army.

(Fol. 198.) After this, having gathered a multitude, he began to march toward Rome, then proceeded into Africa [Note: [Col. 0569D] Ekkehard omitted more material here.], and thus pressed on into Egypt.

When the Egyptians heard of his arrival, they came out to meet him and received him honorably. There he found a royal statue of black marble. When he asked whose it was, he was told that it belonged to King Nectanebus.

He said: “Nectanebus is my father.”

He embraced the statue and kissed it.

From there he proceeded into Syria. The Syrians resisted him bravely, however, and, fighting with him, killed some of his soldiers. Some of them went away to Persia and reported to King Darius Alexander’s presumption.

When Darius asked about Alexander’s stature, they showed him a painted image of Alexander. Darius despised him because of his small appearance and immediately sent him a ball, a curved staff, and a golden cup, together with the following letter:

“King of earthly kings, parent of the sun, which shines together with the gods of Persia, sends greetings to my servant.

“I have heard that you are coming against me through vain glory as a result of your hostility. Therefore I order you to turn your steps back.

[Col. 0569D] “Return, then, to your mother and rest in her lap. I have sent you a ball, a curved staff, and a golden cup, so that you may exercise yourself and think about the reason for play. I know that you are poor and in the greatest need; but quickly recover from the folly and demonic [Note: *daemonii* in 5; *ca.* in 1.] glory in which you are engaged.

“You have gathered some little robbers and wish to fight against the multitude of the Persians. Indeed, consider whether you can count the stars of heaven; and even if you could gather all the people of the entire world, you still could not prevail against the multitude of the Persians, which equals the sand of the sea. There is so much gold in Persia that it surpasses the brilliance of the sun.

“Therefore you ought to repent of what you have done; for if you wish to persist in this folly, I shall send avengers against you to seize you, and I shall order you to be crucified—not as the son of Philip, but as the chief of robbers.”

When Alexander ordered this letter to be read aloud before his soldiers, they were saddened when they heard it. He said to them: “Do not be troubled by the words of this letter. Do you not know that dogs that bark very loudly accomplish nothing? Let us believe, then, that this letter speaks the truth; but we must fight them vigorously and bravely, and not in vain, because their riches compel us to fight.”

When he had said this, he ordered his men to seize the bearers of the letter and crucify them. But they said: “You are doing wrong. What fault do we have?”

He replied: “If I am doing wrong, the words of your elder have compelled me to do it, since he sent you as though to a robber.”

(Fol. 199.) They said: “This is why Darius wrote these things: because he does not know your greatness. But because we have seen an intelligent emperor, if we return, your name will be spread abroad through us.”

Then he ordered them to be released and invited to his banquet. As they sat and feasted with him, they said: “Lord, if it pleases your authority, order one thousand soldiers [Note: *horsemen* in G.] to come with us, and we shall deliver Darius to you.”

He replied: “Let your minds rejoice in what you possess here; but for the betrayal of your own lord, you shall not be given one thousand soldiers [Note: *horsemen* in G.].”

On the following day Alexander sat down and ordered a letter to Darius to be written, containing the following:

“King Alexander, son of Philip and Olympias, to Darius, king of earthly men, nearest to the sun, shining together with the gods of Persia.

“It is a disgrace for so brilliant and magnificent an emperor to send such words to a little man, and to remain every day in fear that you may be harmed by me—though you are the sun’s parent and sit upon a throne as though in the ether, shining together with the gods of Persia. The immortal gods become angry when mortal men attempt to become their companions.

“I am mortal, and so I come to you as one who is going to fight a mortal man. But because, in praising yourself, you said that you possessed immense riches, you sharpened our minds and made us stronger in valor, so that we might acquire your riches.

“If you, who are great, come to fight me and defeat me, you will gain no praise, because you will have defeated a little robber. But if I defeat you, I shall gain great praise, because I shall have defeated a most magnificent emperor.

“Since you sent me a curved staff, a ball, and a golden cup, I understand the curved staff to mean that the most powerful kings bend before me; the round ball to mean that I shall hold the roundness of the entire world; and the golden cup to mean that I am victorious and shall receive tribute from everyone. Thus I, who am small, have received a golden cup from you, who are great.”

After writing this, Alexander summoned the envoys and gave them the golden cup and the letter. When they departed, he prepared himself to set out.

Darius received the letter and, after rereading it, became angry. He wrote the following letter to his satraps:

“Darius, king of the Persians, to his satraps.

“We have heard that Philip’s son, Alexander the Macedonian, has been carried away by folly and has entered the land of Asia, which belongs to me, and plundered it. Therefore I order you to seize him and bring him to me, as befits men so great and strong and as assistants of my empire; I shall flog him like a child and send him dressed in purple to his mother Olympias in Macedonia, because it is not fitting for him to fight, but to remain in his own province and play like a child.”

When the satraps had read the letter, they wrote back to him as follows:

“To King Darius, Primus and Antilochus, satraps, send greetings.

“Let your greatness know that we gathered a multitude and fought with Alexander himself, whom you call a child, and we turned our backs before him, scarcely escaping from his hand. Since you call us assistants of the empire, we must seek your safety; therefore we wish you to know that he will utterly destroy Syria.”

When Darius had read this letter, another messenger arrived announcing that Alexander had encamped beside a river called the Straga.

Again Darius wrote him a letter:

“Darius, king of the Persians, sends this to Alexander.

“Throughout the whole world the name of Darius has been praised; indeed, even the gods praise his name. How have you dared to cross rivers, sea, and mountains and come against me? It would have been a great name for you if, without me, you had retained rule of Macedonia. But you have taken courage, gathered your allies, and gone about fighting and destroying my cities.

“It would be better for you to repent of your evils before you suffer injury from me, and secretly seek refuge with me, who am lord, rather than gather many evils upon yourself. You ought to glory in this: that you have been deemed worthy to receive a letter from me.

“Yet so that you may recognize what my army is like and how great it is, I make it known to you by this poppy seed that I have sent you. (Fol. 200.) If you can count it, then certainly my people can be counted. But if you cannot do this, return to your own land, and do not let such a thing rise again in your heart.”

When the envoys came to Alexander carrying the letter and the poppy seed, he read the letter, stretched out his hand, took some of the poppy seed, and put it into his mouth. Chewing it, he said: “I see that his people are numerous, but they are as soft as this poppy seed.”

Then messengers arrived and informed him that his mother was ill. When he heard this, he wrote to Darius:

“King Alexander to Darius, king of the Persians.

“The many letters that reach me compel me, willingly or unwillingly, to do and say what I am doing and saying. Do not think that I shall withdraw from this place out of fear of your empty glory. Know for certain that I am going to see my mother, who is afflicted with a serious illness; nevertheless, after not much time I shall renew my strength and return.

“In return for the poppy seed that you sent me to represent the immeasurable number of your army, I send you this pepper, so that you may understand that the strength of this very small pepper surpasses the multitude of the poppy seed.”

Alexander gave this letter, together with a little pepper, to the envoys of Darius. When they departed, he himself began to return to his mother.

At that time a certain most powerful man, a commander of King Darius’s army, was stationed with a strong force in Arabia. Moving out from there with his entire army, he took his stand against Alexander and began to fight him fiercely.

The battle began very early and continued until sunset. Neither side proved weak, although many fell on both sides; the fighting continued bravely for three consecutive days.

After this the commander of Darius’s army was defeated and, with those who had survived, fled to Persia so swiftly that he reached Darius before the envoys who had carried Alexander’s letter and the pepper. Darius, holding the letter, questioned the envoys about what Alexander had done with the poppy seed.

They said: “He seized it and bit it, and, despising it, said: ‘They are many, but they are soft.’”

Darius took the pepper and put it into his mouth. Chewing it, he said through his tears: “They are few, but they are harder.”

Seeing this, the commander who had returned from the battle said: “Yes, lord, Alexander has few fighters, but they are strong, and they have killed many of my soldiers.”

Alexander, however, was not elated by his victory; he ordered those of his own men who had fallen to be buried.

After this he arrived in Achaea, where many cities were subjected to him, and he added seventeen thousand men to his army. From there he ascended Mount Taurus and came to the city of Persepolis, in which there are nine Muses. Then he came into Phrygia, to a temple called that of the Sun, in which [Note: *and he sacrificed and made an offering*; the text is defective: *et sacrificavit et o*.] he made an offering.

From there he came to the river Scamander, which is five cubits wide. He said to those who were there: “Blessed are you who possess the praises of the teacher Homer.”

A man named Clytomides stood before him and said: “King Alexander, I can praise your deeds more greatly than Homer could, because you have performed more wondrous feats of valor than those who were at Troy.”

Alexander said: “I would rather be Homer’s student than possess the praise of Achilles.”

After this, returning to Macedonia, he found his mother recovered from her illness, and he rejoiced with her.

After this, leaving Macedonia, he came to a place called Abdira. The inhabitants of that city, however, shut the gates so that he could not enter. Alexander, angered, ordered the city to be burned. When those who were in the city saw the fire, they said: “Alexander, we did not shut the gates in rebellion against you, but through fear of Darius, lest he hear that we had made an agreement with you and destroy us.” (f. 201.) Therefore, when the gates had been opened, he passed through and came to Olynthus; from there he went to Chaldeopolis, and then came to the river called Xenis. A severe famine afflicted them, and the soldiers murmured among themselves, saying: “Our horses have failed.”

Alexander said to them: “My fellow soldiers, even if your horses have failed, have you despaired of your safety? If we live, we shall quickly find horses; but if we die, horses will not be necessary to us. Nevertheless, let us hasten to go to a place where there will be provisions for us and fodder for our horses.” And they began to go to a place called Locrus, where they found abundant provisions and pasture for the animals.

[Col. 0573B] From there they came to a place called Tragachantes, where they found a temple of Apollo. There Alexander wished to obtain an oracle from the virgin priestess Zachora. She said to him: “It is not the hour for divination.” On the second occasion Apollo said: “Heracli.” Alexander said: “O prophet, is my name Heraclius? Then your divination has failed.”

From there he moved his army and, coming to Thebes, said to the Thebans: “Give me four hundred armed men to come to my assistance.” They, however, shut the gates and, armed, went up onto the wall—four thousand of them—and said to him: “Alexander, if you do not withdraw, we shall fight you.”

Alexander smiled and said: “The Thebans are very brave soldiers: they have shut themselves inside the gates, and so claim that they will fight me. Every brave man who wishes to fight goes out into the field; he is not shut inside the city like a maiden.” He ordered his soldiers to attack the city, and after capturing it he burned it. He ordered the wall to be torn down from its foundations and departed.

The Thebans who remained went to Delphi, to Apollo, seeking an oracle as to whether their city ought to be rebuilt. They were told: “The man who will rebuild this city will have three victories, after which he will rebuild it.”

Alexander then set out for Corinth. The Corinthians asked him to compete with them in chariot races, and many people gathered for this spectacle. A tall and renowned Theban followed Alexander; his name was Clytomachus. While they were standing there for the spectacle, Alexander said: “Who will come out to wrestle in this contest?”

Clytomachus said to him: “If it pleases your authority, I shall fight and win.”

Alexander said: “If you defeat three men, you shall be crowned.”

(f. 202.) He therefore fought and defeated two others as well. The herald then said to him: “Tell us your name.”

He replied: “Without a city.”

When Alexander heard this, he said: “O most blessed and most handsome contestant, why are you without a city?”

Clytomachus said: “Great emperor, before you existed I had a city; now, because of you, I have no city.”

Alexander understood this reply and said to the herald: “Proclaim that he is a Theban and that he has the authority to rebuild the city.”

From there Alexander left and came to Athens. He sent the Athenians this message:

“I desire nothing from you except that you serve under my command and regard me as your elder. If you do not wish this, prove yourselves stronger than my men; otherwise, submit yourselves to me, who am stronger than you.”

[Col. 0574A] The Athenians asked Demosthenes the philosopher to give them advice. He nodded, commanded silence with his hand, and said: “My fellow citizens, I shall give you common counsel. If you know yourselves to be such that you can defeat Alexander, fight him; otherwise, let us bend beneath the authority of his hands, because assistance is given to him from heaven.”

After he had made a lengthy speech of this kind, the entire people accepted his advice and decided to send Alexander a victorious crown weighing fifty pounds.

(f. 203.) He said to them: “Because Demosthenes gave you counsel for your salvation and you followed it, from now on take courage and be safe, suffering no opposition from me.”

[Col. 0574B] From there, having taken troops, he proceeded to Lacedaemon. The Lacedaemonians shut the gates, boarded ships, and came out to meet him in a naval battle. Alexander attacked those who were on the walls and wounded them; those who were in the ships he burned by casting fire down upon them. When many had perished, the survivors came to Alexander’s feet and begged for mercy. He immediately granted them their freedom.

Then he entered through Cilicia into the land of the Persians. Darius, therefore, gathered his princes and wise men and held counsel with them about what he ought to do. He said:

“As I see it, this man who advances while fighting in this manner is increasing in strength and victory. I thought he was going about as a brigand, plundering; but he fights like a king and subdues others. The more we wish to exalt ourselves above him, the more his name is exalted. I fear that divine providence is assisting him, wishing to grant him the diadem of the kingdom, so that just as we wished to drive him from Greece, he may drive us from Persia. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us consider our safety and not despise him arrogantly because we hold the Persian kingdom, lest perhaps his smallness increase and our greatness fail.”

When Darius had said this, Ocsiather, the brother of King Darius, said: “You have magnified Alexander by surrendering Greece to him, and by this you have given him confidence to burn more fiercely to enter Persia. Therefore, if it pleases you, do as he does. When he wishes to fight someone, he does not send princes; he goes himself, advances before all the satraps, fights bravely, and wins for himself a name and a victory.”

Another satrap said: “Alexander is exceedingly skilled in everything and commits no fault. In all that he does bravely, he possesses the form and courage of a lion. If it pleases you, send word throughout all your territories and gather the satraps of every nation. We have very many peoples—more than one hundred and fifty—so let us seek aid from the gods.”

While Darius was gathering this multitude and taking counsel, Alexander, delaying in Cilicia, came to a very beautiful pool. He desired to bathe in it, but because of the cold he was seized by a pain in the head and fell gravely ill. When the Macedonians saw this, they became very sorrowful, fearing that Darius would hear of it, attack them, and destroy them.

A certain young man named Philip, whom Alexander loved because he was a physician, promised that he would give him a potion by which he would become well. But a certain military commander who held Armenia hated this physician because the king loved him. He wrote a letter and sent it to Alexander, saying:

“Beware of the physician Philip [Note: [Col. 0575] m. P.: ‘the physician’ in 1], and do not drink his potion, because King Darius has promised to give him his sister in marriage and make him his partner in the kingdom if he kills you.”

When Philip had prepared the potion, he brought it before the king. But before Alexander drank, that letter arrived. He took it and read it before drinking, yet was not disturbed, because he was secure in Philip’s loyalty. Holding the letter in one hand and taking the potion with the other, he looked into Philip’s face.

Philip said to him: “Do not fear the potion, great emperor; drink it.”

He immediately drank it. After drinking, he handed the letter to Philip. Philip read the letter again and said: “I am not guilty, Alexander, as this letter claims.”

When the king had recovered, he summoned Philip, embraced his neck, and said: “Philip, you have learned how much I love you and how much trust I place in you: I drank the potion first and then handed the letter to you.”

Philip said to him: “Have the very man who sent this letter to you brought here, because he himself did not wish me to do such things for your safety.”

He ordered the man to be brought, questioned him, found him guilty, and ordered him to be beheaded.

From there he moved his army and came to Media and Greater Armenia, and subjugated them. Then he traveled for many days and entered a dry, cavernous region in which no water could be found. Passing through a place called Andriacus, he came to the river Euphrates.

He pitched camp, ordered timber to be brought, and prepared a bridge over the river with planks and iron chains. He ordered his soldiers to cross. When they hesitated, he ordered the keepers of the animals to cross with all the equipment and provisions, and afterward ordered the soldiers to cross.

When they still hesitated and feared the river’s powerful current, he himself crossed first, and all the others followed.

(f. 205.) The rivers Tigris and Euphrates flow through the middle of Mesopotamia and Babylonia and enter the Nile. Some say that these rivers are emptied when the Nile floods Egypt, and that when the Nile withdraws, these rivers overflow.

When the entire army had crossed, Alexander turned back and had the bridge cut down. Seeing this, the soldiers began to murmur and say: “If it happens that we flee from the battle, there will be no crossing for us.”

Alexander said to them: “You have encouraged me well when you formed such a thought. For this reason I had this bridge destroyed, so that either you may fight bravely and win, or, if you wish to flee, perish; for victory will not belong to those who flee, but to those who pursue. Therefore, since you will by no means see Macedonia again unless I first defeat all the barbarians, let your minds be strengthened and let the difficulty of battle seem a game to you.”

When they had thus been encouraged, word arrived that a multitude of Darius’s soldiers had assembled on the far side of the Tigris River. Five military commanders were over them. Alexander and his men therefore met Darius’s military commanders in the field, and they fought fiercely.

A certain Persian man of fierce courage put on Macedonian clothing and armor and went to kill Alexander. Mingling with his soldiers behind him, he drew his sword and struck his head so forcefully that he pierced his helmet and wounded his head. Alexander’s soldiers immediately seized him and led him before Alexander.

Alexander said to him: “O brave man, what is this?”

The barbarian replied: “Do not think, my lord, that I am a Macedonian; I am a Persian [Note: [Col. 0576] perhaps ‘of the Persians’; as in the Bamberg manuscript of the History of Alexander, it should be read in manuscript 1]. I promised Darius that I would take your head, and he promised me his daughter in marriage and royal provinces.”

Then Alexander displayed him to all his army and said: “Macedonians, it is fitting for every soldier to possess such courage.” He immediately let the man go, and began to fight bravely. Many of the barbarians fell. When they saw themselves greatly diminished, they fled. Alexander pursued them as far as Bactra and arrived there.

The next day he captured the city. There he found Darius’s mother, his wife and sister, and his two daughters. He established his throne in that city and subjugated all the surrounding cities.

After this, one of Darius’s military commanders dared to come to Alexander and said to him: “My lord Alexander, I am a military commander of Darius, and I served him greatly, yet received nothing worthy from him. If it pleases you, give us ten thousand armed men, and I shall deliver our princes and Darius himself to you.”

Alexander said: “Go and assist your king, because foreigners do not trust a man who wishes to attack his own people.”

Darius’s princes—Fictir, Stapsi, and Nostadi—wrote to Darius about Alexander’s deeds: that he was devastating the land and killing many; that many of Darius’s most powerful men had joined Alexander and received royal provinces and many honors from him; and that Darius should therefore look to himself and to them before Alexander came against him.

Darius, hearing this, wrote to Alexander as follows:

“An account of your arrogance has come into our hands: that you are planning to come near us and speak with us. If this can happen, may all the eastern gods go on dwelling in the West. Let your mind not be lifted up by what you have done. I have prepared myself as though my mother had died and as though I had never possessed a wife. Therefore know that I shall not cease seeking redress for my wrong.

“It has indeed been reported to me that you have shown kindness toward my people. Nevertheless, know this: however much good you may have done them, you will not have me as a friend; and conversely, if you have done them harm, you will no longer have me as an enemy. I have sent you this final declaration.”

Alexander received the letter, read it, and laughed. He sent back a letter of this kind:

“King Alexander to King Darius, greetings. The gods, as I see, hate the arrogance and empty exaltation of your vainglory, because you do not cease blaspheming to the very end.

“What I did for your people, I did not do out of fear of you. Rather, hoping to enter your presence, I showed them my kindness so that you too might receive it with a grateful spirit. But, as I perceive, you are not of a human mind. Let this be my last letter to you. Therefore beware and keep your mind within you.”

When he had sent the letter, he prepared himself and wrote to his satraps who were in Syria, Cappadocia, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Arabia, and the other provinces, ordering each man to prepare one thousand garments and as many animal skins as they could find, and to send them to Antioch. There they were to arrange camels to carry them as far as the Euphrates, so that his soldiers would have garments and footwear.

Darius, meanwhile, wrote to his satraps ordering them to be ready with all their forces to resist the peoples of Macedonia. He also sent to Porus, king of India, asking him to provide assistance. Porus replied that he greatly grieved over Darius’s injury [Note: [Col. 0575] ‘he grieved’ in 1], and that he was indeed ready to come but, being prevented by illness, could not do so; nevertheless, his soldiers would come with the other nations.

When Darius’s mother heard that he was preparing once more to fight Alexander, she sent him this letter:

“His mother sends greetings to King Darius. We have heard that you are gathering other nations and wish to fight Alexander. If you were able to unite the entire world, you would not know what might result from it, because victories have been granted to him. Abandon your lofty pride, and bend down a little; do not presume too much, because you will lose your life.

“As for us, know that we are held in the greatest honor by him. But you bring evil upon us and make us lose the favor we possess. My son, do not prepare anguish for your mother, because I am confident that, if you wish, you may be in good order with Alexander.”

After Darius had read this letter, he was greatly disturbed and wept.

Meanwhile, Alexander moved his army and began to enter Darius’s land. As he approached him, so that the Macedonians could see the highest place of Darius’s city, he ordered his soldiers to uproot grass and branches from trees and tie them to the horses’ feet to raise dust, so that the Persians would see it and be amazed. They were five days’ journey from the city.

When they had come nearer, Alexander said to his wise men: “Let us find a man whom we may send to Darius, so that he may prepare himself and come out to meet us in battle.”

While sleeping there, he saw in a dream the god Hammon in the form of Hermes, wearing a lordly cloak and Macedonian clothing, who said to him: “Son Alexander, whenever assistance is needed, I am ready to announce it to you. See whom you wish to send as a messenger. But I tell you to assume my appearance and go there yourself. It is a dangerous matter for a king to go as a messenger, but because the god is assisting you, you will suffer no hardship.”

When he awoke, he was filled with joy. He recounted the dream to his friends, who advised him to act accordingly. He summoned his most faithful satrap, named Eumilus, and took with him three very swift horses: he himself rode one, that prince rode another, and the third went empty.

The two of them proceeded and came to the river called Stragan. This river freezes at night because of its extreme cold and provides a road throughout the night for those crossing. In the morning, when the sun grows warm, it melts, becomes exceedingly swollen, and swallows those who enter it.

Alexander arrived and found it frozen. Putting on the appearance he had seen in the dream, he left the prince there with two horses, while he crossed with his own. The river was one stadium wide [Note: [Col. 0577] “one stadium,” corrected from another reading in 1].

Alexander went on and, when he reached the gate of Darius’s city, the Persians saw him and marveled at the appearance of his face, thinking that he was a god. When they asked who he was, he replied that he was King Alexander’s messenger. They led him to Darius.

When Darius saw him, he worshiped him as a god, thinking that he was the god Mithras descending from heaven. He asked him: “Who are you?”

He replied: “I am the messenger of King Alexander, sent to announce to you that he is delaying in the field and waiting for you. Therefore, if it pleases you, set a day for battle.”

Darius said to him: “Perhaps you are Alexander, who speaks with such boldness. You do not speak like a messenger but like Alexander himself. Know with certainty, however, that your boldness in no way disturbs me. But dine with me today, since Alexander too sat at dinner with my messengers.”

He extended his hand, took him by the right hand, and led him into his palace. Alexander, however, kept this sign in his heart: that Darius had led him by the right hand, as though he already held his enemy’s palace.

He entered the dining room, where a banquet had been prepared, and sat with the king. Darius’s princes also sat face-to-face with them. The Persians sitting at the banquet looked down upon Alexander’s appearance because he was small, not knowing what strength and courage were contained in such a vessel.

The cupbearers repeatedly carried around cups. During the banquet, when a golden cup had been brought to Alexander and he had drunk from it, he put it into his bosom. He did the same a second and a third time. When the cupbearers saw this, they reported it to Darius.

Darius straightened himself and said: “O most courageous man, what is this that you are doing?”

Alexander replied: “My lord, when he sits at a banquet, gives such vessels to his soldiers in which they drink. If such is not your custom, I shall return everything to you.”

At this all fell silent, thinking that such a custom existed among them [Note: [Col. 0577] another witness lacks “them”; 9c has it].

One of the military commanders, named Anepolis, had once been sent to Philip to demand tribute from him. He now saw Alexander, sitting at the banquet face-to-face with him, and looked closely at his face. He began to think in his heart: “Is this not Alexander?”

Recognizing his voice and his signs, he approached Darius and said: “My lord, this messenger whom you see is Alexander himself.”

Alexander realized that they were speaking about him and recognizing him. He leapt from his seat, took a torch from the hand of a Persian who was holding it, struck him before the king’s table, mounted a horse, and departed.

The Persians pursued him fully armed and with all speed. But he carried the burning torch in his hand and kept to the straight road, while those pursuing him fell into pits, for the night was dark.

Darius, sitting on his throne, saw an ill-omened sign: the house of King Xerxes and his statue had fallen. He grieved.

Alexander came to the river Stragan and crossed it. Immediately the river thawed, and his horse died before it could emerge; the river carried it away. Alexander leapt onto the bank and rejoined the prince whom he had left. He returned to his men, gathered his entire army, went up to a higher place, and encouraged his soldiers, saying:

“Our multitude is not equal to the multitude of the Persians, but let their multitude not disturb us, even if it were increased a hundredfold, because the multitude of flies does not prevail against the smallness of wasps.”

When they heard this, they praised him.

Darius then moved his very large army and crossed the river Stragan to fight Alexander’s army. He had scythed chariots. When both armies had come into the field, Alexander mounted a horse named Bucephalus and stood in the center before all the Persians.

When the Persians saw him, they were afraid to attack him, because some divine power covered him.

(F. 208.) When the two sides had joined battle, they fought fiercely, and many fell, but very many more from Darius’s side. When Darius saw that many of his men had fallen, he took flight. The Persians also fled, but the multitude of scythed chariots killed their own men as they fled, and they lay in the field like a harvest.

Darius came to the river and, finding it still frozen, crossed it. But when the pursuing multitude entered, the ice melted, and very many died. Those who could not enter were killed by the Macedonians pursuing them.

Darius fled and entered his palace. He threw himself face-down upon the ground and, drawing hard sighs from the depths of his chest, said:

“Alas for me! What tribulation has seized Persia, because Darius has been humbled—Darius who subjugated and brought many nations under his power! In the space of one day, in a single moment, it has happened that the humble are exalted above the clouds and the lofty are humbled down to the earth.”

Then he raised himself and came back to his senses, and wrote Alexander a letter of this kind:

“Darius, king, to my lord Alexander, greetings. May your clemency remember that you too are a human being. It is enough for a wise man, when he has obtained victory, that his mind not be lifted up any further.

“Remember, therefore, that the heavenly divinity granted you this victory, and because I flee for refuge to you, show me mercy. You know us, our birth, and our greatness. Grant us my mother, my wife, and my daughters, and I shall give you the treasures I possess in the land of Miniada, at Susa, and at Mactra—treasures which our fathers stored beneath the earth. I shall establish you as lord of the Persians and Medes.

“May you be safe throughout all the days of your life, and may victory be granted to you by Jupiter.”

After Alexander had read the letter, one of the military commanders, Parmenio, said: “Alexander, take all these riches for yourself and return to him those for which he asks.”

Alexander replied: “I wonder whether Darius wishes to receive his mother, wife, and daughters by means of a gift. If Darius has been defeated, let him not promise me a gift; if he wishes to fight again and defeats us, may we be able to save ourselves, let alone retain his mother, wife, and daughters.”

[Col. 0580B] He sent messengers, ordering them to say such things to Darius. He then ordered his soldiers to bury the dead and provide medical care for the wounded. He wintered there for several days, making an offering to his gods. He also ordered his soldiers to burn the beautiful palaces of King Xerxes, but, shortly afterward, repenting, ordered them not to do so.

In those same places were tombs of the dead. When the soldiers dug them up, they found golden and silver vessels. They also found a glass tomb, through which a man’s body and hair could be seen from outside.

They found there as well a tower in which many men had been mutilated, while others were being held in custody. These men cried out to Alexander, begging for mercy and asking him to free them. The place of confinement itself was extremely harsh.

He ordered them to be taken out of that prison. When he saw them, he grieved and wept, and ordered that one thousand drachmas be given to each, restoring their property to them.

Meanwhile, Darius prepared himself once more for battle and wrote a letter to Porus, king of the Indians, as follows:

“Darius, king of kings, to King Porus, greetings. Recently I wrote to you, asking you to provide us aid against those who have attempted to destroy our palace, because this beast that has come against us possesses a savage mind, and his spirit rages like a storm at sea.

“I wished to recover from him my mother, wife, and daughters and offer him gifts, but he refused to agree. Now, although it is against my will, I shall fight him again. Having gathered many nations, I shall contend to the death, because it is better for me to die in war than to see the desolation of my kingdom and people.

“Therefore gather together and prepare yourselves at the Caspian Gates. I shall give payment to all who come with you: to each foot soldier, three solidi per month; to each cavalryman, five. I shall also provide them with food and whatever necessities they require. From the spoils of the captives we shall give you half. The horse Bucephalus and Alexander’s imperial equipment shall also be yours. Wherever you arrive, I shall give you one hundred and eighty young heifers with their ornaments.

“When you have received this letter, hasten to come.”

Darius’s men, fleeing to Alexander, reported all these things to him. When he heard this, he prepared himself and told everyone that he must not be called emperor in any way unless he had obtained Darius’s kingdom.

When Darius heard of Alexander’s arrival, he was greatly afraid. Two Persians, hearing that Alexander was approaching, decided to kill Darius, thinking that they would receive a great reward from Alexander if they killed his enemy.

When they found Darius alone in the palace, they approached him with drawn swords. Darius said to them: “O my dearest men—once servants, now masters—why do you wish to kill me? The Macedonians are more honored than you are. Withdraw from me; my tribulation is enough. Do not inflict this evil upon me.

“If you kill me, and Alexander comes and finds me killed as though by brigands, he will take vengeance upon you. For it is not a joy for an emperor to find another emperor dead through treachery.”

They struck him with their swords, left him half alive, and went away to hide until they heard Alexander’s sentence.

When the Macedonians had crossed the river Stragan, Alexander went and entered Darius’s palace. Finding him lying half alive on the ground, he wept. He removed his imperial cloak, covered him with it, embraced his wounds, wept, and said:

“Rise, my lord Darius, rise. Just as you were once lord of the entire Persian empire, take up your diadem again. I swear to you by the most powerful gods that I truly renounce your empire.”

Then Darius gently extended his hand, embraced him, kissed his hands and breast, and said:

“Son Alexander, do not let your mind be lifted up by the victorious glory you possess. Even if you perform the works of gods and extend your hand to heaven, always remember the final things. Look at me: consider what I was yesterday and what I am today. I was lord of many lands; now I possess no power even over myself, but have been humbled, wretched, down to the dust.

“Let your hands bury me. Let Macedonians and Persians come to my funeral, and from now on let the Persian and Macedonian peoples become one kingdom.

“I commend to you my mother Rodogoni, so that she may be to you as a remembrance of your mother. Let your kindness be shown toward my wife. Take my daughter Roxana in marriage. From good parents, let children be joined as one: you descended from Philip, she from Darius.”

As Darius said this, he gave up his spirit in Alexander’s hands.

Alexander arranged his body in royal fashion. Placing his own neck beneath the bier, he carried it together with the Persians. The Macedonians and Persians, armed, went before it with great ceremony. The Persians wept not so much for Darius’s death as for Alexander’s piety.

(F. 210.) After Darius’s burial, Alexander issued this decree:

“I would indeed rejoice if this people had not failed, but because the god Hammon wished me to become victor over Persia, I ought to give thanks to the gods. I wish there to be princes and governors in each city, as in the time of King Darius, and that they be obeyed. Let all weapons be stored in the royal houses. For I wish this land to be peaceful and full of every good, and from here to Greece let the road be open, so that those who go and return on business suffer no harm.

“Let those who took vengeance upon my enemy Darius come forward, so that I may see them and give them the honor they deserve, because they performed good service for me.”

Then Darius’s killers came before him, expecting a great reward. He ordered them to be beheaded, saying: “Those who kill their own lord—what will they do to a stranger?”

At this there was a great outcry among the Persians, who praised him as though he were a god.

[Note: [Col. 0582B] Add. 5: “Concerning this vengeance, others write as follows: After these matters had been arranged, when Alexander wished to discover who had inflicted death upon Darius, he said: ‘I rejoice that I have subjugated my greatest enemy, Darius, to servitude. Although I myself did not carry this out, I nevertheless have the right to repay with fitting gratitude those who professed their goodwill toward me; and whoever they are, I urge and advise them to reveal themselves. For I swear by the majesty of my father and mother [ [Col. 0581] ‘and of my mother’ in the manuscript] that I shall make them exalted and famous, because they deserve the greatest reward.’

“As soon as Besas and Ariobarzanes heard this, they presented themselves before Alexander, confessed the deed, and asked for the promised reward. He immediately ordered the men to be seized and crucified in the highest place. This was contrary to everyone’s expectation. Nevertheless, he did not regard himself as guilty of perjury, because he had indeed made them exalted and famous before all.”]

There was also Darius’s uncle, named Duriti, whom Alexander appointed, at the request of the entire people, as ruler of Persia.

According to the command of King Darius, he brought Roxana, Darius’s daughter, and took her as his wife. He made her sit with him on the royal throne so that all might worship her as queen.

Then all the Persians raised up their gods and brought them before Alexander, praising and celebrating his name, saying: “Now you have done what pleases the gods.”

Alexander said to them: “I do not wish you to honor me like the gods, because I am corruptible and mortal. Therefore I hesitate to associate myself with them.”

He wrote to his mother, asking her also to celebrate these marriages in Macedonia.

[Col. 0582C] When the days of the wedding celebrations had been completed, he again gathered his soldiers. When he heard that Porus, king of the Indians, had come against him to assist King Darius, he began to go to meet him in India. He traveled through a spacious and deserted land, crossed unfordable rivers, and passed through cavernous hills. He became exhausted together with his soldiers.

They all said: “It is enough for us that we came fighting as far as Persia and subjugated Darius, who formerly exacted tribute from the Macedonians. Why should we wear ourselves out seeking India in places where beasts dwell, forgetting our own land? This Alexander desires to do nothing except go on fighting and subjugating nations to himself. Let us leave him; let him go wherever he wishes.”

When Alexander heard this, he stopped and said to them all: “Separate from one another. Let the Persians be on one side [Note: [Col. 0581] Add. 5: ‘Macedonians and Persians’], and the Macedonians and Greeks on the other.”

Then, looking at the Macedonians and Greeks, he said: “O my fellow soldiers, Macedonians and Greeks, these Persians are opposed to me and to you. But if you too have resolved in your hearts to oppose me, turn back behind me and go to your homeland. Remember, nevertheless, that I alone defeated these men, and wherever I go to fight the barbarians, I shall overcome them.

“You know that when I gave you counsel, your spirits were strengthened. When we came to fight in the field, did I not stand alone before them all and fight alone on behalf of everyone? Did I not go alone for your safety and that of the entire homeland, like a messenger sent to King Darius, and expose myself to many dangers?

“What then? If you wish to go alone to Macedonia, go, because I am not coming with you. You will learn that an army can accomplish nothing without the counsel of its king.”

When he had said this, the soldiers, ashamed, begged forgiveness, saying: “From now on let our lives be placed in your hands. Do whatever you wish.”

They suffered many dangers on that journey and saw many marvelous things, which, as the written accounts say, we shall relate later according to Alexander’s own description.

(Fol. 211.) After some days, in the territory of India, envoys of King Porus met Alexander, bringing him a letter that read as follows:

“Porus, king of the Indians, to the robber Alexander, who seizes cities by robbery.

Although you are a mortal man, what power have you against God? You have afflicted men by persecuting them—men worthy to endure hardship; you fought against weak men who possessed no valor; and because you defeated them, you hope that you are victorious over all men. I too am victorious—not only do men obey me, but also the gods.

Dionysus, the famous one, once came to fight in India, but he turned his back before the Indians and fled, because he could not withstand the valor of the Indians. Therefore, before shame befalls you, I advise and command you to hasten back to your own land.

Before Xerxes existed, the Macedonians paid us tribute; but because we found nothing in that land that pleased the king, as though it were an unproductive land, we disdained it, since everyone desires a broad cause more than a narrow one. Behold, I charge you to return; and where you cannot possess dominion, there you should have no desire.”

When this letter reached Alexander, he read it before everyone and said:

“Fellow soldiers, let the letters of King Porus not disturb your courageous spirit. Remember the words of the letters of King Darius, how arrogantly and with how much boldness he spoke. I tell you the truth: all barbarians share a common mentality and differ little from beasts.”

Having said this, Alexander wrote a letter to King Porus in the following manner:

“King Alexander to King Porus, greetings.

You have sharpened our understanding and furnished us with courage to fight against you. For you said that there is nothing good in Macedonia, whereas India overflows with every sweetness; therefore, with all our strength, we shall fight to acquire it.

And because you said that every man loves a broad cause more than a narrow one, we, who are small, wish to come to the greatness of your majesty. Since your letter said that you are ruler not only of men but also of gods, I am coming to fight as though against a barbarian man who greatly exalts himself, not as though against a god—for the whole world would not be able to withstand the weapons of one god. Indeed, know that your foolish arrogance does not disturb me.”

When this letter had been read, King Porus became angry. He gathered a multitude of his people and many elephants, with which the Indians customarily fight, and went out to meet the Macedonians.

Apart from infantry, whose number could not be counted, his army had 4,800 scythed chariots and 400 elephants carrying towers in which armed men stood ready for battle. When the Macedonians and Persians saw the preparation and multitude of the Indians, they were disturbed and terrified—not so much by the number of men as by that of the wild beasts.

Alexander was carrying with him bronze statues of men. Thinking shrewdly, he put them into a fire so that they would become hot; then, making iron frames to support them, he ordered them to be carried before the army against the elephants. When the elephants saw the statues, they thought that they were men. They stretched out their trunks—that is, their snouts—in accordance with their custom of seizing men, but, being scorched by the statues’ excessive heat, they turned back and died. The others, thrown into confusion, no longer advanced in any way to fight against the men.

When Porus [Note: Col. 0583D, a: Porus 5.] saw what had happened to the beasts, he was greatly troubled. The Persians, however, attacking the Indians with arrows and spears, put them to flight, although a great slaughter of men occurred on both sides.

Alexander, seated on his horse Bucephalus, entered the battle and fought bravely; indeed, the horse himself helped him greatly. They fought against one another for twenty successive days.

When Alexander saw that the people had grown exhausted, he stood alone before the enemy and spoke to King Porus:

“It is not fitting for an emperor to destroy his people uselessly in this manner, but rather to display his own valor by himself. Let your people therefore stand on one side and mine on the other; you and I alone shall fight hand to hand, and whichever of us wins, both peoples shall be counted as his.”

(Fol. 212.) When Porus heard this, he rejoiced, trusting in his height, which was five cubits, whereas Alexander was only three cubits tall. Each army withdrew and stood in its appointed order, and the two men began to fight.

When Porus’s soldiers shouted, he turned his head toward them. Alexander, however, charged at him, leapt upon him with his legs folded beneath him, struck him with his sword, and threw him down to his death.

Then a fierce battle was fought by both armies. Alexander stood and said to the soldiers of Porus:

“Miserable men, why do you fight after the death of your king?”

They replied:

“Because we do not wish to submit our land to you, lest it be laid waste.”

He said:

“Let your fighting cease, and go freely and safely to your homes, because you did not presume to attack us; your king did.”

Having said this, he measured out a camp and ordered Porus to be buried.

Concerning this battle, others think differently, writing as follows (Orosius III.19):

“With Porus, the most powerful king of the Indians, he waged a most bloody war. In it Alexander engaged Porus himself in single combat; after his horse had been killed and thrown down, he escaped the presence of death through the intervention of his guards. Porus, however, pierced by many wounds, was captured; but, in testimony to his valor, Alexander restored his kingdom to him.”

This divergence is also found in the letters said to be Alexander’s own letters to his teacher Aristotle. If they are genuinely his, they express differing views.

In one place it is written (C. B. fol. 215) that, when Alexander came to Queen Candace, Carator, the son of that queen, wished to kill him at the urging of his wife, who was the daughter of Porus, because Alexander himself had killed Porus. Elsewhere, however, the following words are found, presented as his own (Letter to Aristotle, C. B. fol. 231):

“We came,” he says, “to the place where Porus had previously encamped with his army, before we fought with him. He desired to see me and asked some of my soldiers where I was and what I was doing. When they said that they did not know, they came and reported all this to me.

“I removed my royal clothing, put on the garment of one of the soldiers, and went to the fortress, pretending that I wished to purchase meat and wine. When Porus saw me, he called me to him and asked what Alexander was doing and how old he was.

“I said to him: ‘I do not know what he is doing, because I am the herdsman of a certain Macedonian soldier’s animals. As for his age, I know that he is an old man, and perhaps he is now sitting by the fire, as is the custom of old men.’

“Then Porus was filled with joy because he was going to fight an old man, while he himself was young. Elated with pride, he said: ‘Why does he not pay attention to his old age, since he wishes to fight with a young man?’

“Immediately he gave me a letter full of threats, asking and promising a reward that I should give it to Alexander. When I swore to him that the letter would certainly reach Alexander’s hands, I departed. As I read the letter, I laughed greatly at the barbarian’s arrogance and presumption.

“After this I fought with the Indians and defeated them as I wished. I took the kingdoms that Porus had possessed, but afterward I returned them to him. For this reason he became a great friend of the Macedonians and revealed to me his hidden treasures; thus both I and all my companions became rich.

“Afterward he led me to a place where there were golden statues, which Liber Pater and Hercules had set up there; and for a long time he was a companion of our journey.”

I have included this account of the disagreement not only among the historians but also, as they say, in Alexander’s own letters, so that no one may accuse me of falsehood concerning my first description of this battle. For the rest, let the prudent reader choose what he finds most acceptable in these matters.

(Historia Alexandri, Cod. Bamb. fol. 212.) Therefore, after the battle with Porus had been completed, Alexander gathered a great force and departed against the Oxydraces.

The Oxydraces are not proud men, nor do they fight with anyone. They go about naked and are called gymnosophists; they live in huts, possessing neither a city nor other dwellings.

When the king of this people heard of Alexander’s arrival, he sent his nobles to him with the following letter:

“We, the corruptible gymnosophists, write to Alexander the man.

“We have heard that you are coming against us. If you come intending to fight, you will gain nothing, because you will find nothing among us that you can take or carry away; and no one dares to take even what we possess, except insofar as divine providence permits.

“But if you wish to fight, then fight; we shall not abandon our simplicity.”

When Alexander had read this, he sent them word, saying:

“We too shall come to you peacefully.”

Immediately he entered their territory. Seeing that they all went about naked and lived in hidden huts and caves—their sons and wives, however, were separated from them along with the animals—he asked one of them:

“Do you have no tombs?”

The man pointed out his dwelling and said:

“Where I live is sufficient for me.”

When all had been summoned, Alexander said:

“Ask for whatever you wish, and it shall be given to you.”

They replied:

“Give us immortality.”

He said to them:

“Since I myself am mortal, I cannot give you immortality.”

They said:

“And if you are mortal, why do you go running here and there, doing so many such things?”

He replied:

“These matters are governed only by heavenly providence, whose ministers we are, carrying out its command. The sea is not disturbed unless winds enter it. I wish to rest and withdraw from wars, but the lord of my mind does not allow me to do so. If we had all possessed one understanding, the whole world would be like a single field.”

Having said this, he began to depart and became very weary on the journey, because the terrain there was difficult to traverse.

Afterward the Macedonians conquered the Adrestae, Cattheni, and Gangaridae, cutting down their armies. When they reached the Cophides, they fought there against 200,000 horsemen. Though by then they were exhausted by age, troubled in spirit, and weary in strength, they won with difficulty and founded a camp there, more magnificent than usual, in memory of the victory.

(Orosius III.19.) Thereafter Alexander proceeded to the river Agesines, and by way of it was carried into the ocean. There he overwhelmed the Gessones and Sybi, whom Hercules had founded. From there he sailed to the Andri [Note: Col. 0585D: *Andros* as printed, or *Mandros* in witness 1] and Subagri. These peoples met him with 80,000 armed infantry and 60,000 cavalry; after battle had been joined, a long, uncertain, and bloody struggle at last gave the Macedonians a sorrowful and scarcely won victory.
