For when the enemy forces had been routed, Alexander led his army to their city. When he had been the first to climb the wall and thought the city empty, he alone leapt down inside. When hostile enemies surrounded him on every side, it is incredible to relate that neither the multitude of the enemy, nor the great force of their weapons, nor the tremendous shouting of those attacking him terrified him. Alone, he struck down and put to flight thousands.

But when he perceived that he was being overwhelmed by the multitude surrounding him, he protected his rear with the barrier of the wall and more easily held off his opponents until, when the walls had been breached, the entire army entered.

In that battle, after an arrow had pierced him beneath the breast, he continued fighting with one knee fixed until he had killed the man by whom he had been wounded.

Then, having boarded ships and traveled along the shores of the ocean, he came to a certain city ruled by King Ambira. During the assault on the city, however, he lost a large part of his army to arrows smeared with poison. Later, when a herb shown to him in a dream was given as a drink to the wounded and they were thus rescued, he captured the city.

## Concerning the marvelous things that Alexander is said to have seen

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587A] On these journeys, what and how much he endured, and how many marvelous things he saw, he himself, as is reported, wrote to his mother Olympias and to his teacher Aristotle. Of these matters we briefly touch upon some, for the pleasure of learning about marvelous things; for the rest, we leave the truth of the matters themselves to the judgment of the readers.

(Historia Alexandri, C. Bamb. fol. 216.) Thus he writes to his mother that, while he was still in Babylonia, before he departed from that land, there was a certain woman who gave birth to a son. From the navel upward he was like a man, but downward he was like a beast, resembling a dog.

After she had given birth to him, she covered him, brought him to King Alexander, and asked that she be permitted to speak with him privately. When she had been summoned and came, she said:

“Order everyone to leave; I have a secret to reveal to you.”

When everyone had withdrawn, she uncovered the infant and showed him to the king. Seeing him, the king was astonished. He summoned a diviner and asked him what this signified.

The diviner sighed and said:

“O king, your time is approaching, when you will depart from this world. The half of the body that has the appearance of a man is you; the part transformed into a beast consists of the men who will come after you.”

When Alexander heard this, he became sad and said:

“O Jupiter, it would indeed have been fitting for the day of my death to end in peace, so that what I had undertaken might be completed. But since this is pleasing to you, receive me with yourself as an immortal.”

(Fol. 217.) After gathering his people, he departed and came to the Pillars of Hercules, one golden and the other silver, each twelve cubits in length and two cubits in width.

From there they set out and entered a desert. They found cold places so dark that they could scarcely recognize one another.

After traveling for seven days, they came to a hot river. There they saw extremely beautiful Amazon women riding in fearsome garments and holding silver weapons in their hands; bronze and iron are not found there.

When the army joined the river, it could not cross, because its width and depth were exceedingly great, and it was full of reptiles and beasts.

From there they came to the Red Sea and found a very high mountain. When they climbed it, they seemed to themselves to be in heaven.

Alexander considered with his companions how he might construct something by which he could ascend into heaven and test whether this was the heaven that we see. He therefore had a contrived seat made for himself. He captured two griffins, bound them with chains, set poles before them, and placed their food at the tops of the poles.

They began to climb upward, until the whole earth seemed to them to lie beneath them like a threshing floor and the sea to resemble a dragon encircling it.

But divine power overshadowed the griffins and cast them down to earth in a level place ten days’ journey away from the army. Alexander suffered no injury in those enclosures, though he was joined to the soldiers in great distress.

When they saw him, they rejoiced and praised him greatly.

Again it came into his mind to measure the depth of the sea. He summoned astrologers and geometers and ordered them to make a vessel of such a kind that he could descend into the depths of the sea and observe the marvels that were there.

They said:

“Let a glass vessel [literally: ‘an all-glass barrel’] be made and bound with chains, and let the strongest soldiers guide it as it is lowered and brought back up.”

When Alexander heard this, he ordered such a vessel to be made. By this means he investigated the depth of the sea and saw various forms of fish of different colors, and what seemed to be terrestrial animals walking along the floor of the sea, as well as many things that cannot be described.

(Epistle to Aristotle, Cod. Bamb. fol. 228′.) After he had come to Persia and killed King Darius in the month of May, as he himself writes to his teacher Aristotle, he subjected the whole of Darius’s land to himself and placed his nobles over the eastern provinces; and they all became rich.

When the month of July was ending, he came to India Fachiana, where he quickly defeated King Porus and found many riches.

He captured Porus’s city and his magnificent house. In it were 400 golden columns with golden capitals, and the walls of the house were covered with sheets of gold as thick as a man’s finger. There was also a golden vine with crystal grapes, among which fiery and emerald gems had been set.

All the rooms within it were adorned with pearls, unios, and carbuncles. They had doors of white ivory, and coffered ceilings of a wood called ebony, which is black and grows in India and Ethiopia. The chambers were made of cypress wood.

Outside the house stood statues of gold and golden plane trees. Among them were many kinds of birds of various colors, whose claws and beaks were gilded; pearls and unios hung from their ears.

He also found there many vessels of gems, crystal, and gold, but few of silver.

When he had everything under his control, he desired to see the interior of India and to reach the Caspian Gates. As he traveled there with his entire army, they came to a river in the middle of which stood a covered city. Around the city was water extending for about four stadia; the water itself was exceedingly bitter, like hellebore.

(Historia Alexandri, fol. 212′.) When they arrived there at the third hour of the day, thirty-seven of the bolder young men entered the river naked, with their swords drawn. But hippopotami, as the beasts are called, rose from the river and devoured them.

The other soldiers, going around the river on the opposite side, proceeded upstream. They found a sweet-water lake and, settling there, lit fires.

At the third hour of the night, wild beasts suddenly came out of the reeds of the lake and came to drink: lions of extraordinary size, leopards, tigers, and wild boars with teeth one cubit long; there were also elephants and scorpions one cubit in length.

Wild men also came, having six fingers on their hands and feet. They made a great assault upon the soldiers, but the soldiers drove them away with spears and arrows.

They set fire to the reeds in that forest (fol. 213) so that the beasts would flee. And behold, a beast of extraordinary strength came upon them, stronger than an elephant. It attacked them and killed twenty-six of them, but some armed men killed it.

On the following night, foxes and crocodiles came out of the sand and ate the bodies of the dead. Bats as large as pigeons also flew there; their teeth were like those of men, and they bit people, tearing away their noses, ears, and fingers.

Moving on from there, they came to a plain called Actia. A dense forest surrounded it, and there were fruit-bearing trees whose fruits nourished wild men. These men had the form of giants and wore garments of hide. They came out with long spears and killed some of the army.

When Alexander saw this, he ordered his men to shout. When they cried out with loud voices, the wild men became frightened and fled, because human voices were unknown to them.

The soldiers pursued them and killed 634 of them; 127 of the soldiers themselves fell. They remained there for three days, eating the fruit of those trees.

Afterward they came to a certain river in which there was a very wealthy city. As the ninth hour approached, a large, hairy wild man came upon them, covered with hair like a boar.

Alexander therefore ordered his soldiers to seize him. When they attacked him, he neither feared nor fled but stood motionless.

Alexander ordered a girl to be brought and placed naked before him. The wild man attacked, seized her, and stood aside.

When the soldiers rushed forward to take her away, he roared like a beast. With great difficulty they seized him, and Alexander ordered him to be bound and thrown into the fire.

From there they moved on and came to another plain. From the first hour of the day, trees rose from the earth and grew until the sixth hour; from the sixth hour until sunset they descended again into the earth. They bore very fragrant fruits.

Alexander ordered some soldiers to take some of the fruit. But as soon as they approached, demons came out and scourged them. They all also heard a voice, as if from heaven, commanding them not to cut anything from those trees, because whoever did so would die.

There were also very gentle birds, but whenever anyone wished to touch them, fire came forth and burned him.

Moving on from there, they came to the shores of the ocean and heard men speaking the Greek language on a certain island. Some of the soldiers stripped themselves and wished to enter the island, but certain beasts rose from the sea, seized twenty of them, and submerged them in the depths.

From there they came to a certain place where there was a tree bearing neither fruit nor leaves. A bird sat upon it, with shining rays over its head like the sun.

[Col. 0590B] Then they came to a certain mountain, beneath which was a cliff from which a golden chain hung. The mountain itself had 2,500 steps made of sapphire.

Alexander climbed the mountain with some soldiers and found there a palace containing a temple made entirely of gold. In it were drums and cymbals of gold, and a bed with the most precious coverings. Upon it lay a most magnificent and illustrious man, dressed in a white cotton garment adorned with gold and precious stones.

Around him was a golden vine bearing clusters made of precious stones. Alexander worshiped this man and descended.

From that place he continued for fifteen successive days and came to a land called Prasiaca.

When the people of that land learned of his arrival, they brought him gifts: fish skins resembling leopard skins, and eel skins six cubits long.

There was a walled city built without mortar, from stones cut out of the mountain. The chief authority of that kingdom was held by a certain widowed woman named Candace, who had three sons.

Alexander sent her the following letter:

“King Alexander to Queen Candace, greetings.

“I am sending you a temple and a statue of Ammon, so that you may come and that we may go together to the mountains and offer sacrifice to him.”

She replied to him:

“Queen Candace of Meroë to King Alexander, greetings.

“It was revealed to you by your god Ammon that you should go and conquer Egypt, and this was granted to you by the gods themselves. We, however, possess souls that are clear and luminous, more so than those who are with you.

(Fol. 214.) “I am sending your god Ammon a crown of precious stones, namely emeralds and pearls, and ten chains set with precious stones.

“I am also sending you 100 Ethiopian boys, 200 intelligent parrots, 200 sphinxes, 80 rhinoceroses, 3,000 panthers, 400 skins of leopard-lions, thirty golden cups, 1,500 ebony rods, and 450 elephants.

“But you send word back to us whether you have subjected the whole world.”

Among his envoys she also sent a highly skilled painter, who was to examine Alexander’s figure and appearance carefully, paint it, and bring the likeness back to her.

This was done.

One of Queen Candace’s sons, named Candaulis, went with a few horsemen to Alexander’s tent. The guards who were keeping watch over the army seized him and brought him to Ptolemy, who was second to Alexander.

Ptolemy said to him:

“Who are you?”

He replied:

“I am the son of Queen Candace.”

He said:

“Why have you come here?”

He replied:

“I went out with my wife to amuse myself with a few horsemen. The king of the Bebryces, knowing my wife’s beauty, came against me with a strong force and took her from me. When I wished to defend myself, he also killed my soldiers.”

Ptolemy said to him:

“Wait here for the time being.”

He leapt from his tent, went to the king’s tent, awakened Alexander, and told him everything he had heard from the young man.

When Alexander heard this, he rose, took the diadem from his own head, crowned Ptolemy with it, and said:

“Return to your tent, sit upon the royal throne, and say that you are Alexander. Order one of your men to come to you; let him come to me as though he were your man Antigonus, and let him bring me to you as Antigonus. When I come, repeat to me in the young man’s presence everything he told you, and question me in the person of Antigonus, so that I may give you advice concerning this matter.”

And so it was done.

Alexander, speaking in the person of Antigonus, said:

“My lord, if you command it, I shall go against that city by night and set it on fire, and by force I shall have his wife returned to him.”

Candaulis immediately worshiped him and said:

“O most wise Antigonus, it would have been best if you were King Alexander.”

Alexander went out silently during the night and set that city on fire.

When the people of the city awoke, they shouted:

“What is this?”

Alexander said:

“Candaulis is here with a very large army, demanding that his wife be returned to him; otherwise you will all die by fire.”

Those men rushed forward, broke open the gates of the palace, took Candaulis’s wife from there, and returned her to him.

Turning to Alexander, Candaulis said:

“My dearest Antigonus, I beg you, come with me to my mother, so that she may give you a reward worthy of your merits.”

Rejoicing, Alexander said:

“Let us go to Alexander, ask him for me, and I shall come with you.”

He had already informed Ptolemy of this. Candaulis therefore went and asked Ptolemy for him; having received permission, he departed with Alexander.

As they were traveling, Alexander saw high mountains reaching up to the clouds and was astonished. He also saw tall trees bearing enormous fruits and vines with great clusters, so large that one man could not carry one of them. He saw nuts as large as melons, and dragons and many monkeys in the trees.

After a few days, when they had come to the city of Queen Candace, she herself went out to meet them. She was very tall and exceedingly beautiful, wore a golden crown, and welcomed them graciously. She led them into her palace, which was magnificent.

Its roof shone as though it were golden. Its bed coverings were adorned with pure gold; its dining rooms were constructed of onyx stone; the palace columns were of ebony; the tables were ivory; and the bowls and other vessels were made of precious stones.

Beneath the palace ran a river whose water shone as though it were made of gold.

On that day Alexander ate with the queen’s sons. On the following day Candace took him by the hand and led him into a chamber constructed of stones the color of gold. It shone within (fol. 215) as though the sun were shining there.

There was also a triclinium, or dining room, made of *asiptis* wood, which is not consumed by fire. There was also another chamber above enormous pieces of timber with wheels, drawn by twenty elephants.

When Alexander saw these things, he was astonished and said to the queen:

“These things would be worthy of admiration if they were found among the Greeks.”

The queen became angry and said:

“You speak the truth, Alexander.”

When he heard his name, he was greatly frightened.

She said to him:

“Why has your face changed, since I called you Alexander?”

He replied:

“My lady, I am called Antigonus, not Alexander.”

She said:

“I shall show you that you are Alexander.”

She led him into her chamber, showed him his own image, and said:

“Do you recognize this image?”

He began to tremble and grow pale.

She said:

“Why has your color changed, and why are you afraid, destroyer of all Persia and destroyer also of India? You conquered the Indians and the Parthians, yet now, without soldiers and without any battle, you have fallen into the hands of Queen Candace.

“Know therefore, Alexander, that a man’s heart ought never to be lifted up in arrogance, whatever prosperity may follow him, and that he should not think in his heart that he will never find anyone stronger than himself who can overcome him.”

He began to gnash his teeth and turn away.

She said:

“Why are you angry, and why are you troubled? What can your imperial glory do now?”

He replied:

“I am angry because I have no sword.”

She said:

“And if you had one, what would you do?”

He replied:

“Since I have been delivered into your hands by my own will, I would first kill you and afterward myself.”

She said:

“You have spoken as a wise emperor would. Nevertheless, do not grieve, because just as you freed my son’s wife from the hands of her enemies, so I shall free you from the hands of the barbarians. If they learn of your arrival, they will kill you, just as you killed Porus, king of the Indians; for the wife of my younger son is also the daughter of King Porus.”

Having said this, she went out holding Alexander by the hand and said to her sons:

“O my son Candaulis, and you, my daughter Marpissa, let us give some benefit to this man sent by Alexander.”

Her other son Carator replied:

“O mother, it is indeed true that Alexander sent this man, and that he freed my brother’s wife from the hands of her enemies and returned her to him. But my wife compels me to kill this Antigonus in Alexander’s place, because he killed her father, Porus, so that Alexander may suffer grief for him.”

Candace said:

“What reputation shall we gain if we kill this man?”

Candaulis replied:

“This man saved me and returned my wife to me. In good faith I brought him here, and I shall return him safely to his own place.”

Carator said:

“What is this that you are saying? We shall both die here and now.”

Candaulis said:

“I do not wish this; but if you do, I am ready.”

When Candace saw that her sons wished to kill one another, she was distressed. She took Alexander aside and said secretly:

“Alexander, you are not showing any wisdom in this matter, since my sons may be killed because of you.”

Alexander replied:

“Let me go and speak with them.”

When she permitted him, he went to them and said:

“Carator, if you kill me, King Alexander has many soldiers better than I am. But if you want me to deliver your enemy himself to you, give me what I ask: only remain at peace with one another, and I swear to you that I shall bring Alexander here into your palace.”

The brothers believed him, made peace with one another, and promised him many gifts.

Queen Candace then summoned him secretly again and said:

“I would be blessed if I could have you before my eyes every day; through you I would have conquered all my enemies.”

She therefore gave him royal gifts, including a crown of adamant, a breastplate, and a starry cloak.

From there he departed and entered a crypt that Candaulis had shown him, saying that the gods had eaten there.

Before entering, Alexander made an offering and then went inside. He saw a great darkness; amid the darkness he saw a shining star and apparitions of idols. He also saw certain reclining figures whose eyes shone like lamps.

One of them said to him:

“Hail, Alexander.”

He replied:

“Who are you, lord?”

The figure said:

“I am Sesonchosis, who holds the kingdom of the world, subdues the world, and makes everyone subject. Yet I shall not have a name such as the one you will have in the Alexandria that you will build. Enter farther, however, and you will see.”

He saw another darkness and someone seated as though upon a royal throne. He said to him:

“Who are you, lord?”

The figure replied:

“I am the Birth of the Gods. I saw you in the land of Libya, and now you are seen here.”

Alexander said to him:

“Tell me how many years I shall live.”

He replied:

“The matter about which you ask is one that no mortal ought to know. For if a man knew the day of his death, such distress would come upon him as though he had to die every day.

(Fol. 216.) “You will build a city that will stand glorious throughout the whole world. There your tomb will be built, and there your body will rest.”

Having departed from there, he came to his soldiers, moved the army, and advanced against the Amazons [Note: Col. 0593D: witness 5 reads “venit et a.”], sending them the following letter:

**King Alexander to the Amazons, greetings.**

We believe that the battle which we fought with Darius is not unknown to you, nor how we conquered India and the other nations, which were in no way able to resist us. Therefore we write to you to pay us what is owed to us, since we shall not come against you to inflict any harm upon you.

To this they sent the following reply:

**The most powerful Amazons, stronger than all armies, to Alexander, greetings.**

We wrote and informed you, before you come to our borders, so that you may know how you are coming and perhaps avoid suffering disgrace. Know that our dwelling is beyond the river, on a certain island which the river itself surrounds in a circle, having neither beginning nor end; and on one side we have a narrow entrance.

Among us there are 214,000 women untouched by men, for men in no way live among us, but beyond the river, on the other side. Every year we celebrate the festival of Jupiter for thirty days. Thus we cross over to see our men, and they rejoice with us for thirty days. If anyone wishes to remain in happiness with his wife, he keeps her for one year. If the woman, having conceived, gives birth to a male child, the father keeps him with him; if she gives birth to a female child, the father raises her for seven years and afterward returns her to her mother.

When we go to fight against anyone, we number ten times ten thousand horsewomen, while others guard our island. We meet our enemies as far as the mountains themselves, while our men follow behind us; and when we return victorious, our men worship us. If one of us falls, those who survive inherit her property.

Behold, we have informed you of the custom which we observe every year. Consider it, do what is proper, and write your decision to us. If you wish to fight, we shall come out to meet you at the mountains, for we must stand and fight against you. But if you defeat us, you will gain no praise, because you will have defeated women; nor will you find anything to take from us. Therefore beware, emperor, lest some misfortune befall you.

When Alexander read this letter, he laughed and replied as follows:

We have seized three parts of the world and won victory. Therefore, if we do not fight with you when you resist us, it will be shameful for us. Nevertheless, I give you this advice. If you wish to perish and to abandon your land so that it is inhabited no longer, come, as you have said, to meet us at the mountains. But if you do not wish to perish, enter the river, and thus let us speak together. I swear to you by the gods that you will suffer no harm from us.

Send us as many women horse-riders as you wish; we shall give gifts to each of them and, after a time, allow them to return to their own land. Give us whatever tribute you wish to give us. Consider this, therefore, and write to us.

After considering the matter, they sent him ten foals and ten white horses, and he departed from there.

**(Orosius III. 13.)** It is nevertheless read that Halestris, or Minothea, a bold Amazon, came to him with 300 women, moved by a desire to receive offspring from him.

**[Column 0594D] (Letter to Aristotle, Codex Bamb. folio 229.)** When Alexander reached the Caspian Gates and admired that land because it was good, he learned of certain things there which seemed hateful to him. For in those places there were various serpents and beasts, concerning which the inhabitants warned him to be cautious.

He took 150 men experienced in those regions to serve as guides, and proceeded with his entire army in the month of August, under a burning sun and through sandy regions, promising rewards to the guides if they brought him safely through. They reached Bactria, where there are peoples called the Seres. There are trees there whose leaves are like wool, from which the people of that land make clothing for themselves. The guides of the journey also gathered some of it.

One day, while they were traveling, they began to suffer increasingly from thirst. Since Alexander could not endure it, a certain soldier named Zephilus found water in a hollowed-out rock, filled his helmet with it, and brought it to the king, valuing the king’s life more than his own. Alexander then summoned the army and, in the presence of everyone, poured the water onto the ground, lest, when the army saw that he alone had drunk, it should begin to suffer even greater thirst. He praised Zephilus for the kindness he had shown him and gave him excellent gifts.

Thus encouraged, the army began to march. Not far away a river appeared in the desert. On its bank were reeds sixty feet high and as thick as pine trees, from which boards were made for constructing houses. There they set up camp.

When they wished to drink from the same water, it was bitter as gall. The king was therefore more distressed on account of the animals than of the men, because the animals knew less how to moderate their thirst. Some soldiers licked iron, others drank oil, and still others reached such desperate need that they drank their own urine.

Proceeding along the bank of that bitter river, about the eighth hour of the day they came to a fortress situated on an island in the same river, built from the reeds mentioned above. There they saw a few naked men, who hid themselves as soon as they saw the army.

Alexander wished to speak with them so that they might show him water. But when none of them appeared, he ordered a few arrows to be shot, so that they might come out, at least through fear of the arrows. They hid themselves even more.

Then he sent 200 Macedonians in light armor into the river. When they had swum across a quarter of the river, behold, hippopotamuses emerged from the depths, stronger than elephants. While the others watched and mourned, the hippopotamuses devoured the men. Hippopotamuses are half human and half horse. [Note: Col. 0595: witness 1 repeatedly reads *yppotami*; the editor doubts whether *yperpotami* should be read.]

Alexander was angry with those who were leading the army through such places [Note: Col. 0595: witness 1 reads *loco*] and ordered 100 of them to be thrown into the river. The hippopotamuses then began to boil up like ants and devoured them.

Moving on from there, at the eleventh hour of the day they saw men in the river in round little boats made of reeds. They asked them where they might find fresh water. The men indicated to them a lake of fresh water, which they said lay ahead.

They traveled all night, exhausted by thirst, and were in distress because everyone was armed. Lions, bears, and tigers attacked them, and throughout the night they fought with them. On the following day, when they were already weary, at about the eighth hour they reached the lake.

They set up camp there, three miles in length and breadth; the lake itself extended for one mile. They stationed the elephants in the middle of the camp, so that the army could hold its position if anything attacked them during the night. Cutting down the forest around the lake, they made 1,500 fires, and at the eleventh hour they ate their evening meal.

When the moon began to shine, scorpions, serpents, and other wild beasts suddenly came to drink from the lake, and that entire land resounded with the hissing of serpents. The soldiers therefore placed their shields in orderly rows at the front of the camp, held their spears in their hands, and received the serpents that came against them. They killed some of them.

When the serpents withdrew at about the third hour of the night, and they were already hoping to obtain rest, behold, other serpents came down from the mountains, thicker than columns, with their chests raised and their mouths open. Poison flashed from their eyes [Note: Col. 0595: thus Codex Bambergensis, *History of Alexander*; omitted in witness 1 and the remaining witnesses], and their breath was deadly. The soldiers fought them for more than one hour of the night, and thirty servants and twenty soldiers were killed by them.

**[Column 0596B]** After the serpents withdrew, crabs arrived. Their backs were hard like those of crocodiles and could not be pierced when spears were thrown at them. Nevertheless, the soldiers killed many of them in the fire; the rest entered the lake itself.

**(Folio 231.)** The fifth watch of the night had now come, and the army wished to rest. Behold, white lions, larger than bulls, arrived. Shaking their necks and roaring loudly, they charged the soldiers; but the soldiers received them with their hunting spears, and the lions were killed.

After this, pigs of astonishing size arrived, having various colors, and the soldiers fought them in the same way. Meanwhile, one beast appeared resembling a horse, larger than an elephant, armed with three horns. When it saw the camp, before drinking from the lake, it charged the camp. Though the soldiers resisted, it killed twenty-four of them and trampled fifty; nevertheless, they killed it.

Then bats arrived, as it is also written above, resembling doves, but having teeth like human beings. They struck the soldiers in their faces and inflicted wounds upon them. Mice also arrived, resembling foxes; whatever animals they bit died immediately, but human beings did not die from their bites.

As daylight approached, birds resembling vultures arrived, reddish in color, but with black feet and beaks. They filled the entire bank of the lake and, drawing fish from the lake, ate them; they did not harm the human beings.

Alexander, enraged against the guides of the road, had their hands and feet cut off, so that they might be eaten alive by the serpents. He encouraged the soldiers to be brave and not to fail in adversity like women.

**(Folio 232.)** Moving the camp from there, Alexander proceeded as far as the sea, wishing to test whether he could circle the world by way of the ocean. Since the inhabitants of that region said that there were dark and perilous places there, and that Hercules and Liber had not dared to approach those regions, he resolved to circle the left side of India, so that no place would remain unknown to him.

They found a dried-up marsh containing many reeds. When they wished to cross it, a beast emerged from it resembling a hippopotamus. It had a chest like a crocodile and carried what looked like a saw on its back; its teeth were extremely strong. It suddenly killed two soldiers, and spears could not pierce it. They killed it with iron hammers.

Then, arriving at the remotest forests of India, they set up camp six miles in length and two and a half miles in breadth, near a river called the Bucmar. It was the eleventh hour of the day.

When they were already preparing to eat their evening meal, shepherds and wood-gatherers suddenly arrived, announcing that a multitude of elephants were coming out of the forest against them. Alexander ordered the Thessalian cavalry to take pigs with them and ride out to meet the elephants, knowing that elephants feared the grunting of pigs. Thus the elephants were put to flight.

The soldiers pursued them to the sound of trumpets and, hamstringing them, killed 980 of them. They took their teeth and horns and returned to camp. Having spent that night in peace, they began on the following day to travel toward other parts of India.

Finding open plains, they saw there naked men and women whose height was nine feet. They had the custom of living both on land and in rivers. For when some of the army wished to go toward them, they suddenly plunged into the river.

Then they came to a forest full of cynocephali—that is, human beings with dogs’ heads. When these beings wished to strike the soldiers, the soldiers drove them away with arrows.

After this, when those who were with the army from that land said that they would discover nothing new any longer, they began to return to Fasiacen, from which they had come. Alexander ordered the camps to be extended for twelve miles.

When all the tents had already been erected and many fires kindled, so powerful a southeast wind suddenly began to blow that it cast down all the tents. The animals too were greatly tormented, because sparks from the fires struck their backs and harmed them severely.

So they gathered up the tents and found a certain valley, where they set up camp. But heavy snow had fallen, like wool. Alexander, fearing that the snow might grow too deep in the camp, ordered the soldiers to trample it down. Nevertheless, many were overwhelmed by the snow—namely, 500 soldiers, who were also buried there.

**[Column 0597D]** After this they came to a cave where Liber Pater lay. It was said that if anyone entered that cave, he would die of a fever on the third day. They therefore sent in certain condemned men, and found the report to be true.

When they were now taking the road to Fasiacen, two old men met them. Alexander asked them whether they knew of anything new that they could show him. They said that they knew of a marvelous thing, but that the road was long—ten days’ journey—and also narrow, with much water and places full of serpents.

When Alexander gently questioned them about what this great marvel might be, one of them said joyfully:

**[Column 0598A]** “You will see, king, two trees, one of the sun and the other of the moon. The tree of the sun speaks in the Indian language, while the tree of the moon speaks in the Greek tongue. From them you will be able to learn what is destined to happen to you.”

When Alexander heard such an incredible thing, he thought that they were saying it as a joke and had them treated harshly, saying:

“Has my glory spread from west to east so far that these old men dare to make fun of me?”

But they affirmed under oath that they were telling no falsehood and would show that what they said was true. His friends and companions therefore begged him not to neglect seeing such a marvel under any circumstances.

He took 30,000 cavalry with him, sending the rest of the army to Fasiacen with all the wealth he had collected. He himself, with a chosen company of young men, followed those old men through harsh and difficult regions.

When they arrived at the place where the trees were, they saw a broad region full of frankincense and opobalsamum. For there was a forest where these things grew, and the inhabitants of the region lived on them.

Entering the sacred place, they found its priest. He was more than ten feet tall, had a black body and canine teeth, and gems hung from his pierced ears. After Alexander had greeted him, he asked him why he had come.

He replied: “I have come to see the sacred trees of the sun and the moon.”

The barbarian answered: “If you are pure from fornication, you may enter the divine place.”

Three hundred of Alexander’s friends followed the king. The priest ordered them to remove their rings and shoes.

It was the eleventh hour of the day, and the priest waited until the sun set. For he said that the sun usually spoke then and gave an answer. Likewise, concerning the tree of the moon, he said that when the moon rose and shed its light, the tree itself would give an answer.

They therefore began to walk through the forest, which was enclosed by a wall, and saw opobalsamum flowing in great abundance from the trees’ branches. In the middle of the forest were trees resembling cypresses, one hundred feet tall.

Alexander marveled at their height [Note: Col. 0597D: witness 1 reads *altitudinem*] and said that they had grown so large because of the excessive rain. The priest replied that it never rained in that place, nor did any bird, wild beast, or serpent enter those boundaries, because from ancient times the place had been consecrated by the ancestors of the Indians to the sun and the moon.

Alexander wished to sacrifice victims, but the priest forbade him, saying that in that place it was not permitted to kill any animal or to make incense from frankincense. They were only to kiss the trees themselves and ask the sun and moon to give them true answers.

After this they saw the sun’s rays shining above the treetops. The priest said: “Look upward. Whoever wishes to ask about any matter should consider it in his heart and not speak it aloud.”

Then they began to look upward with great care, lest perhaps a magpie or parrot should be among the branches, since such birds commonly imitate the human voice. When they saw no deception, Alexander began to consider in his mind whether he could return in triumph to his homeland, to his dearest mother and sisters.

Suddenly the Indian tree answered:

“As you asked my name, Alexander, you will be lord of the whole world, but you will not return alive to your homeland, because the Fates have determined this concerning you.”

When Alexander asked the Indians whom he had brought with him, they interpreted the speech for him. Then three of his most faithful friends—Perdiccas, Clyton, and Phylotas—began to mourn over this answer.

In the evening the king came to question the tree of the moon. Standing beside the tree, he asked where he was destined to die. When the moon’s radiance touched the tree, it answered and said in the Greek language:

“Your life has already reached its full term, Alexander, but in the coming month of May you will die in Babylon, deceived by one from whom you least expect it.”

Then he began to mourn, as did his friends. When he left the place in sorrow, he refused to eat. His friends begged him not to afflict his body through fasting, and against his will he ate a little. He then lay down in that sacred place, so that he would be ready when the sun first rose.

The following day he rose very early and awakened his friends. The priest, however, lay wrapped in skins, and before him on a table of ebony was placed a large lump of frankincense, which had remained for him from the evening meal.

After the priest had been awakened, Alexander entered for the third time to ask a question, and said:

“Tell me, most sacred tree, whose hands are to kill me, and by what death my mother and sisters are to die.”

The tree said in Greek:

“If I tell you who will kill you, you will kill him, and thus what the Fates have ordained concerning you will be changed. The three sisters—Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos—will be angry with me because I have impeded what they have determined [Note: omitted in witness 1].”

“Therefore, after one year and eight months, you will die in Babylon, not by the sword, as you think, but by poison. Your mother will die a most shameful death and will not be buried; birds and wild beasts will eat her. Your sisters will fare well, while you will be lord of the lands for a short time.

“Now do not question us further. Leave this place and return to Fasiacen.”

The priest also urged him to leave, saying that the mourning and wailing of his friends would cause anger. Alexander therefore returned and told his soldiers to tell no one what they had heard, but to preserve it faithfully.

**[Column 0599D]** Afterward they came to a certain valley in which there were serpents bearing stones on their necks called emeralds. They did not permit anyone to cross that valley. They lived on laser and white pepper, and every year they fought among themselves. When many of them died, the emeralds were released and could be gathered. Alexander’s soldiers therefore took some of them, and they were of considerable size.

From there, amid great dangers, they came to a place where there were beasts with heads like pigs, tails like lions, and two hooves, six feet broad. With these they struck the soldiers violently. Among them were also griffins, which fiercely struck the soldiers’ faces with their beaks; but the soldiers defended themselves with arrows and spears. Nevertheless, 208 soldiers perished in that battle.

From there they came to a river flowing into the ocean, two and a half miles wide. On its bank were reeds so tall and thick that scarcely thirty men could carry one. Making ships from them, they crossed the river and found men clothed in the skins of whales.

These men gave them white and purple sponges and sea-shells holding two or three gallons. They also gave them tunics made from the hides of sea-calves and snails that held a sextarius. They placed before them worms which they had drawn from the river itself, as thick as a man’s thigh; their taste was better than that of any fish. They also gave them red mushrooms and eels weighing 250 pounds, saying that even stronger creatures were found in the ocean.

In that same river there were hairy women. When they saw strangers swimming in the river, they seized them and either drowned them in the river itself or dragged them among the reeds on the banks. Because they were exceedingly beautiful, they made the men lie with them until the men were left without life; or, if the men refused, they killed them in the excess of their anger. Alexander’s soldiers captured two of them. They were white as snow, with long hair spread down their backs.

Departing from there, they came to a place where there were wild beasts whose heads projected serrated bones, sharp like swords. With these they struck the soldiers fiercely and pierced many shields. The soldiers killed as many as 8,450 of them, and thus, with great labor and danger, reached Fasiacen.

There Alexander ordered his soldier Alcon, whom he had placed over Persia, to erect two cast statues of gold in Babylon and Persia, twenty-five feet high, and to write all his deeds upon them. In the farthest part of India, where 100 statues had been placed in honor of Liber and Hercules, Alcon was likewise to erect five golden statues, ten feet high, in Alexander’s honor.

**(Orosius III. 19.)** After Alexander had traversed and subdued India, he came to a rock of extraordinary ruggedness and height, to which many peoples had fled. When he learned that Hercules had been prevented by an earthquake from conquering that same rock, he was moved by rivalry to surpass Hercules’ deeds. With the utmost labor and danger he gained possession of the rock and accepted the submission of all the peoples of that region. He went to the city of Nisa, conquered the Daedalian Mountains and the kingdom of Queen Cleophilis. When she surrendered herself, she purchased the kingdom by intercourse.

**(Orosius III, chapter 20.)** After the whole East had been subdued, Alexander quickly returned to Babylon, where ambassadors from the provinces terrified throughout the entire world were waiting for him: from the Carthaginians and all the cities of Africa, from the Spaniards and Gauls, from Sicily and Sardinia, and also from a very large part of Italy.

For such fear of the commander established in the far East had seized the peoples of the distant West that one might see a foreign embassy coming from the whole world, and scarcely believe that the report had reached so far.

**(History of Alexander.)** Among his princes there was a certain Antipater, who had two sons, Cassander and Yolus. Yolus was the king’s cupbearer. While Alexander was absent, Antipater secretly plotted many things against him; his mother Olympias wrote to him about these matters many times and was deeply distressed.

While Alexander was staying in Babylon, Antipater sent to a certain sorcerer and arranged with him to provide a poisonous potion. The sorcerer made such a potion that no vessel could contain it. Antipater therefore had a small iron cup made and put the potion into it. He gave it to his son Cassander and sent him into Alexander’s service, ordering him to tell his brother Yolus to give the potion to Alexander.

At that time it happened that Alexander struck Yolus on the head, although Yolus was not at fault. The young man, moved by grief, accepted the potion with a willing heart.

When Alexander sat at a banquet with his princes and soldiers, he began to rejoice and be extraordinarily cheerful. In the middle of the banquet, as he became increasingly joyful and spoke at length to his guests, he suddenly asked for a drink. Yolus, the perpetrator of so great an evil, handed him the poison.

When Alexander had drunk it, he suddenly cried out in a loud voice, as though someone had thrust a spear into his liver. Holding himself together for a little while and enduring the pain, he rose from the banquet and asked the princes and soldiers to sit down and continue rejoicing by eating and drinking.

But they were disturbed, rose from the table, and stood outside to see what would happen. Alexander, wishing to vomit, asked for a feather with which he could put it into his throat to induce vomiting. Yolus found a feather, smeared it with poison, and handed it to him. When Alexander put it into his throat, the poison pressed upon him more and more, and he spent the entire night without sleep.

On the following day, realizing that he had been brought into a grave condition, he summoned all his soldiers and urged them to live well and peacefully with one another.

When night came, he ordered everyone to leave the chamber, including his wife Roxana. After they had all gone out, he ordered one of his attendants to open the royal gate **[Note: that is, the door]** which was above the descent of the Euphrates River.

When no one was there, he rose from his bed in the middle of the night, extinguished the lamp, and, since he was unable to walk upright, crawled on his hands and feet across the ground toward the river, intending to drown himself in it.

His wife Roxana, who was awake and saw him making his way toward the river, followed him at the fastest possible pace. When he was already rolling himself near the river, she embraced him, saying:

“Alas, unhappy me! Why are you going, intending to kill yourself?”

He replied:

“I beg you, Roxana, let no one know the manner of my death, since you were not worthy to rejoice with me.”

Although she brought him back unwillingly to his bed, she said:

“If your end has come, first make arrangements concerning us.”

He immediately had a secretary brought in and drew up his will:

“If Roxana, my wife, gives birth to a son by me, let him hold the kingdom, and let the name which pleases the princes be given to him. But if she gives birth to a daughter, let the Macedonians choose for themselves whatever king they wish.

“Ptolemy shall be guardian of my body and governor of Egypt.”

He also arranged the administration of the other provinces and divided them among his young men as he wished while he was still alive. Because I found these divisions written differently, I have omitted them as uncertain.

**(Folio 218´.)** It was announced throughout the entire population that Alexander had died. Immediately all the Macedonians shouted, saying to the chamberlains:

“Know that we shall kill every one of you unless you show us our lord.”

When Alexander heard and understood their disturbance, he ordered them to carry him with the very bed on which he lay and place him in a higher and more spacious location, so that he could be seen by everyone. Sitting on the bed, he struck his breast, weeping bitterly, and cried out in a loud voice:

“Alas, Alexander is dying, and Macedonia will grow weaker! O Macedonians, your name will no longer rule over the barbarians.”

Then all the Macedonians who were present said:

“It would have been better for all of us to die with you, because after your death the kingdom of Macedonia will not endure.”

After this Alexander died. They placed him in his chariot and led him from Babylon to Alexandria. Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, went before his chariot, weeping and saying:

“O strongest Alexander, in your life you did not kill as many as you have in your death.”

The days of his life were thirty-three; the years of his reign were twelve: six before the destruction of the Persian kingdom; in the seventh, after Darius had been killed, he destroyed it; afterward he reigned for five years.

**[Note: Added in witness 5:]** He founded twelve cities, all of which he named Alexandrias after himself:

Alexandria founded under the name of the horse Bucephalus; mountainous Alexandria; Alexandria near Porus; Alexandria in Scythia; Alexandria of Babylon; Alexandria near the Massagetae; Alexandria near Egypt; Alexandria near Origala; Alexandria near the Granicus; Alexandria near Troas; Alexandria near the Tigris River; and Alexandria near the Xanthus.

He therefore marked their walls with the initial five letter-signs, so that the following might be read upon them:

“Alexander the king, of the race of Jupiter, made this,”

using the letters **A, B, Γ, Δ, H**, or alternatively the letters **α, P, C, H, Θ**.

And he whom the whole world could not overcome by iron died, overcome and destroyed by wine and poison. [End of note.]

[Col. 0602D] **(BEDA.)** Therefore, after Alexander’s death, when many were succeeding one another, Ptolemy obtained Egypt; Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, Alexander’s brother, obtained Macedonia [Note: [Col. 0601] “Macedonia”—“of the East” in correction 1]; Seleucus, also called Nicanor, obtained Syria, Babylonia, and the kingdoms of the East; Antigonus, Asia; and all the others received the places assigned to them. [Note: [Col. 0601] Here he continues at 10.]

**(OROS. III. 23.)** But, having drawn different provinces by lot, they exhausted one another in mutual wars, and throughout the entire kingdom of Macedonia—that is, throughout all Asia, the greater part of Europe, and most of Libya—terrible sudden storms of war converged. The cause and origin of the wars was a letter of King Alexander, by which he ordered all exiles to be restored to their fatherland and liberty. But the leading men of the cities of Greece, fearing that the exiles, once their freedom had been restored, would plot revenge, revolted from the kingdom of the Macedonians. The Athenians were the first: having assembled an army of thirty thousand and two hundred ships, they waged war against Antipater, to whom Greece had fallen by lot.

After this, a most serious war arose between Antigonus and Perdiccas. After many provinces and islands had been torn apart because assistance was either refused or provided, it was long debated whether the war should be transferred to Macedonia or waged in Asia. Finally, Perdiccas marched against Egypt with a vast army.

Thus Macedonia, while its commanders moved in two directions, armed itself against its own entrails. Ptolemy, equipped with the forces of Egypt and the troops of Cyrene, prepared to meet Perdiccas in battle. Perdiccas, however, engaged Ptolemy with the utmost ferocity; after losing his forces, he too was killed.

Olympias, Alexander’s mother, was killed by Cassander after the slaughter of very many princes. Hercules, Alexander’s son, who had been placed in custody with his mother Roxana and was already fourteen years old, was killed by the same Cassander. Antigonus, fighting together with his son Demetrius against Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus, who were supported by an alliance with Seleucus, was defeated in battle.

Ptolemy again fought Demetrius in a naval battle, and, after losing almost his entire fleet and army, was defeated and fled to Egypt. Elated by this victory, Antigonus ordered that he himself, together with his son Demetrius, be called king. All the others followed this example and assumed for themselves the name and dignity of kings.

Therefore Ptolemy, Cassander, and the other commanders of the opposing faction, seeing that Antigonus was deceiving them one by one, strengthened one another by letters and agreed upon a time and place for meeting together. They prepared war against Antigonus with their united forces. Since Cassander was entangled in wars with neighboring peoples, he sent Lysimachus, the most distinguished of all the commanders, with a vast force to assist his allies in his place. Seleucus too, departing from Greater Asia, joined them as a new enemy of Antigonus. [Note: [Col. 0603] “as an enemy” in correction 1.]

This Seleucus waged many wars in the East among the allies of the Macedonian kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0603] “Macedonian kingdom,” corrected in witness 1.] At the outset he stormed Babylonia; he subdued the Bactrians, who were rising in new disturbances; then he crossed into India, which after Alexander’s death, as though it had thrown off and shaken the yoke from its neck, had killed his prefects.

After Ptolemy’s forces and those of his allies had been united, battle was joined. The more powerful the array, the more grievous was its destruction. For in that battle almost all the strength of the Macedonian kingdom fell. Antigonus himself was killed in the battle.

But the end of this war was the beginning of another. Since the victors could not agree about the spoils, they were again divided into two factions: Seleucus joined Demetrius, while Ptolemy joined Lysimachus. When Cassander died, his son Philip succeeded him, and thus, as though from the beginning, new Macedonian wars arose.

Demetrius, the son of Antigonus, elated by the enlargement of Greece and of all Macedonia, planned to cross into Asia. Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Lysimachus, having learned in the earlier contest how great the strength of concord was, again made an alliance and, uniting their armies, transferred the war to Europe against Demetrius. King Pyrrhus of Epirus joined them as a companion and ally in the war, hoping that Demetrius could be driven from Macedonia.

[Col. 0604B] Nor was this hope in vain. For after Demetrius’s army had been corrupted and he himself had been put to flight, Pyrrhus seized the kingdom of Macedonia.

Lysimachus, who ruled the Hellespont, after the killing of his son-in-law and the death of his son—stained by repeated acts of kin-murder—was abandoned by his own soldiers. They went over to Seleucus and urged him to wage war against Lysimachus. The spectacle was indeed most disgraceful: two kings, Lysimachus being seventy-four years old and Seleucus seventy-seven, contending to wrest one another’s kingdoms away, standing in battle formation, and taking up arms.

This was the final war of Alexander’s fellow soldiers, preserved as an example of human misery. For, after the deaths of thirty-four of Alexander’s commanders, they alone possessed the whole world, yet, without looking toward the narrow limits of their old age and life, they thought the boundaries of the entire world too narrow for their empire.

**(HIER.)** For Seleucus, after Demetrius had previously been captured in Sicily, destroyed the kingdom of Asia and made one kingdom out of the two. **(OROS. l. l.)** In this war Lysimachus, after fifteen children had previously been lost or killed before this battle, was killed last. Thus Lysimachus was the conclusion of the Macedonian war.

But Seleucus too did not enjoy such a great victory with impunity. He himself did not find the rest of natural death after seventy-seven years; rather, he unhappily ended a life torn from him, as though by a premature death. For, while Ptolemy was pressing him—Ptolemy whose sister Lysimachus had married—he was surrounded by an ambush and killed.

These are the exchanges of kinship and alliance among parents, children, brothers, and companions by which, in fourteen years, they tore apart the world Alexander had acquired swiftly and valiantly, and, like greedy cubs, ripped apart the rich prey struck down by a great lion; provoking one another, they consumed themselves in rivalry over the spoils.

**(H. m.)** In the 422nd year from the founding of the city of Rome, which is the fifth year of Alexander the Great [Note: [Col. 0603] “the fifth year,” in correction 1], Alexander, king of the Epirotes and maternal uncle of this Alexander the Great, crossed into Italy with his forces. As he was preparing to make war on the Romans, he was defeated and killed in Lucania in a great battle by the Samnites, who were supporting the Lucani.

After this the Romans began to grow powerful. They waged war against the Samnites nearly one hundred and eighty miles from the city, under the dictator Papirius. There Fabius Maximus, master of the cavalry, fought most successfully in Papirius’s absence and destroyed twenty thousand Samnites.

Later, after organizing an army with more vigilant care, the Samnites defeated the Romans at the Caudine Forks. The Romans had been enclosed by the narrowness of the terrain and by arms, during the consulship of Titus Veturius and Spurius Postumius, and were defeated with immense disgrace. Their commander Pontius, in the great security of victory, consulted his father Herennius about whether he should kill the enclosed Romans or spare the defeated. He chose to preserve them alive for disgrace.

He ordered the entire Roman army, disgracefully captured and stripped of arms and clothing—only cheaper garments being granted to cover the shame of their bodies—to pass in a long procession beneath the yoke of victory. He accepted six hundred Roman cavalrymen as hostages and sent back the consuls, laden with disgrace, under whatever conditions of peace pleased the Samnites.

But if they had kept faith with the Roman treaty, either they would not exist today, or they would have been subject to the Samnites. For in the following year, at the Senate’s command, the Romans broke faith and forced them into war under the consul Papirius. They did not cease either to yield or to make the Samnites yield until, after the Samnites had been defeated and their commander captured together with seven thousand men, they imposed the yoke upon them.

At that time the censor Appius Claudius brought the Aqua Claudia into the city and paved the Appian Way. Afterward, when the Samnites renewed the war, they defeated Quintus Fabius Maximus, killing three thousand men. Later, when his father Fabius Maximus had been appointed as legate, he both defeated the Samnites and captured many of their towns.

Then Publius Cornelius Rufinus and Marcus Curius Dentatus, both consuls, were sent against the Ramentae [Note: [Col. 0605] Read “Samnites,” from H. m.]. In great battles they destroyed them, demolishing even the ruins of their cities, so that today Samnium must be sought within Samnium itself and is not easily found.

Then the war with the Samnites, which had lasted forty-nine years, was brought to an end. No enemy within Italy had ever wearied Roman valor more.

**(HIER. on Daniel, chapter X.)** After Alexander, Ptolemy, son of Lagus, first ruled in Alexandria for forty years, in the 198th year from the restoration of the Temple. He was an exceedingly prudent man, also extremely rich and powerful, and of such great strength that he restored Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, after he had been driven from his kingdom; acquired Cyprus, Phoenicia, and many cities, islands, and regions; and, after defeating Demetrius, son of Antigonus, restored to Seleucus the portion of his kingdom that had been taken away by Antigonus.

**(HIER.)** After subduing Jerusalem and the Jews by deceit, he transferred many of them again to Egypt, though afterward he treated them kindly. In his time Onias, son of Jaddi, was high priest at Jerusalem. After his death, his son Simeon, surnamed Justus, obtained the high-priesthood. [Note: [Col. 0605] At this point there are already twelve (or thirteen?) quires in witness 1.]

Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, Alexander’s brother, ruled Macedonia for seven years, in the 198th year from the restoration of the Temple.

Here the kingdom of Asia begins; after Alexander, Antigonus first ruled it for eighteen years.

Cassander ruled Macedonia for nineteen years.

The kingdom of Syria begins.

[Col. 0606A] The kingdom of Syria and Babylonia [Note: [Col. 0605] “Babylon,” witness 5] and of the upper regions arose here. After Alexander, Seleucus Nicanor first ruled it for thirty-two years. After capturing Demetrius, son of Antigonus, he destroyed the kingdom of Asia and made one empire out of the two, namely Asia and Syria.

Therefore his son Antiochus, also called Soter, ruled Syria and Asia after him; after him Antiochus, who was called Theos, ruled in turn. Seleucus founded these cities: Antioch, Laodicea, Seleucia, Apamea, Edessa, Beroea, and Pella. He founded Antioch in the twelfth year of his reign and established it as the metropolis of his state.

From this time—that is, from the beginning of Seleucus’s reign—the kingdom of the Greeks is reckoned, according to the Hebrew history of the Maccabees. [Note: [Col. 0605] “was reckoned,” witness 4; *hebraeorum* (“of the Hebrews”), witness 9c.]

Demetrius, son of Antigonus, ruled in Asia for seventeen years.

Antigonus and Alexander, sons of Cassander [Note: [Col. 0605] the final letters are missing in witness 9c], ruled Macedonia for four years.

Demetrius ruled Macedonia for six years. [Note: [Col. 0605] This is absent in witness 9c.]

Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, after corrupting Demetrius’s army and putting him to flight, ruled the Macedonians for seven months. After him Lysimachus ruled for six years. [Note: [Col. 0605] The number is missing in witness 9c.]

**(H. m.)** In the 464th year from the founding of the City, which is the thirty-fifth year of Ptolemy, the Tarentines, who live in the farthest part of Italy, suddenly attacked a Roman fleet passing by, killed all the commanders of the ships, and sold the rest of the men fit for war at a price. Hence a great war arose between them.

**(JORD.)** Tarentum, founded by the Lacedaemonians, was once the head of Calabria, all Apulia, and Lucania. It was remarkable for its wealth, size, walls, harbor, and position itself.

**(H. m.)** The Roman army, therefore, rushing in with the consul Aemilius against the entire territory of the Tarentines, devastated everything with fire and sword, stormed many towns, and cruelly avenged the outrage it had insolently received. [Note: [Col. 0605] “they devastate” corrected to “he devastates,” witness 5; “they storm”—“they avenge,” witness 5.]

The Tarentines, however, were supported by many garrisons of neighboring peoples. King Pyrrhus of the Epirotes, who traced his origin to the race of Achilles, also brought into Italy all the forces of Epirus, Thessaly, and Macedonia, together with elephants—until then unknown to the Romans—in number twenty, as though he were going to avenge a kindred Greek city.

After consulting the oracle of Delphic Apollo, he received this ambiguous response (cf. Cicero, *On Divination* II, 56):

> I say, Aeacid, that you can conquer the Romans.

**(H. m.)** Then for the first time the Romans fought an overseas enemy. The consul Publius Valerius Laevinus was sent against him. After capturing Pyrrhus’s scouts, he ordered them to be led through the camp and shown the entire army, and then released, so that they might report to Pyrrhus what they had seen.

Battle was joined, and the day was consumed in a most grievous struggle, with all on both sides prepared to die and unable to flee. When the Romans saw the elephants brought among the charging ranks—terrible in appearance, oppressive in smell, and terrifying in bulk—they were surrounded and terrified by this unfamiliar mode of fighting. Their horses were especially panic-stricken, and the Romans scattered.

Minutius, however, a centurion of the Fourth Legion, cut off with his sword the extended trunk of one of the beasts. Distraught by the pain of the wound and forced to turn back, the elephants began to throw everything into confusion by their uncontrolled movements.

The battle was ended also by the advantage of night. Laevinus nevertheless fled during the night; his disgraceful flight revealed that the Romans had been defeated. Fourteen thousand eight hundred and eighty infantry are reported to have fallen then, and eight hundred and twenty were captured; among the cavalry, two hundred and forty-six were killed and seven hundred and twelve captured [Note: [Col. 0607] “eight hundred,” witnesses 4, 10, 11], and twenty-two standards were lost.

Pyrrhus treated the Romans whom he captured with the highest honor and buried the dead. [Note: [Col. 0607] This passage is absent in witness 9c; witness 5 reads: “Whom, when he saw them lying even dead, with a wound in front and a fierce expression …”] When he saw them lying there, even after death bearing wounds received in front and fierce expressions, he raised his hands to heaven and said that he could have become master of the whole world if he had been granted such soldiers.

Affixing an inscription commemorating this victory to the temple of Tarentine Jupiter, Pyrrhus wrote:

> These men, who had previously been unconquered, O best father of Olympus,  
> I myself defeated in battle, yet I have been defeated by these same men.

When his own men reproached him for calling himself defeated when he had won, he is said to have replied: “If I win in the same way a second time, I shall return to Epirus without a single soldier.” [Note: [Col. 0607] Absent in witness 9c.]

When envoys were sent to him to ransom the captives, he ordered Lycon and Molossus to go out to meet them. Proceeding himself with his cavalry to the city gate, he received them honorably and released the captives without payment. [Note: [Col. 0607] “without reward,” witness 9c.]

When he saw that one of the envoys, Fabricius, was poor, he promised him a quarter of his kingdom if he would go over to Pyrrhus. [Note: [Col. 0607] “go over himself,” witness 5.] But when Fabricius rejected him, Pyrrhus admired him.

Because of this admiration, Pyrrhus sent to the Romans an envoy of exceptional character named Cineas [Note: [Col. 0607] “foremost,” witness 9c], who was to seek peace on equal terms—namely, that Pyrrhus should retain the part of Italy he had seized by arms. But the peace he offered displeased them. The Senate sent back word that he could not have peace with the Romans unless he withdrew from Italy.

They had ordered that all the captives Pyrrhus had returned should be regarded as disgraced, because they had allowed themselves to be captured while armed. They were not to be restored to their former status until they had brought back to themselves the spoils of enemies they had killed. [Note: [Col. 0607] The remainder of the sentence is absent in witness 9c.]

Thus Pyrrhus’s envoy returned. When Pyrrhus asked him what sort of city he had found Rome to be, Cineas replied that he had seen a city of kings: nearly all the Romans there were such as Pyrrhus alone was thought to be among the Epirotes and the rest of Greece.

A second battle took place between the Romans and Pyrrhus on the borders of Apulia, during the consulship of Publius Sulpicius and Decius. In that battle Pyrrhus, wounded with his arm pierced through, withdrew first from the fighting. Twenty elephants were captured, twenty thousand of the enemy were killed, and five thousand Romans. The legate Fabricius was also wounded.

After a year had passed, the same Fabricius was sent against him. Since their camps were close to one another, Pyrrhus’s physician came to Fabricius by night and promised to poison Pyrrhus if Fabricius would make him some promise. Fabricius sent him back in chains to Pyrrhus and ordered him to be told what he had promised.

The king, admiring Fabricius, is said to have declared: “That is Fabricius, who can be turned from honesty with greater difficulty than the sun from its course.”

The king then departed for Sicily, while Fabricius triumphed after defeating the Lucani and Samnites. Next the consuls Curius Dentatus and Cornelius Lentulus were sent against Pyrrhus. They killed twenty-three thousand of his army and captured three hundred; Pyrrhus himself was driven to Tarentum, and his camp was captured. Curius triumphed during his consulship and was the first to bring four elephants to Rome.

Finally, in the fifth year after he came to Italy, Pyrrhus, defeated, fled. [Note: [Col. 0607] “came fleeing,” witness 9c, repeatedly.] After many wars that he waged in Greece, he was misled by his desire for the Spartan kingdom and died from a blow by a stone at Argos, a city of Achaea.

His right big toe is said—if it is to be believed—to have been a remedy when it was applied to the swollen kidneys of someone suffering from that condition. When Pyrrhus was ordered by the victorious Antigonus to be burned [Note: [Col. 0607] “was,” witness 9c], he burned in such a way that the same toe was found untouched. [Note: [Col. 0607] The clause concerning the swollen kidneys is absent in witness 9c.] It was enclosed in a golden reliquary and placed in the temple of Jupiter. [Note: [Col. 0607] “This finger was enclosed in a golden reliquary and placed in the very ancient temple of Dodonaean Jupiter,” witness 11.]

Ptolemy Philadelphus, son of the preceding Ptolemy, ruled Alexandria for thirty-eight years, in the 238th year from the restoration of the Temple. [Note: [Col. 0608] Cf. Jerome.]

In his time the high priest of the Jews was Eleazar, brother of Simeon surnamed Justus, son of Onias son of Jaddi. He assumed the priesthood for the following reason. **(JOSEPHUS XI, 2.)** When the high priest Onias died, his son Simeon Justus succeeded him. When Simeon died and left behind a young son named Onias, his brother Eleazar assumed the high-priesthood. Ptolemy honored him generously with gifts on this occasion. **(Ibid. XII, 2.)**

Demetrius Phalereus, an orator and philosopher among the Greeks, had been placed in charge of the king’s library, for which the king had great concern. While striving to gather together every volume discovered throughout the world and to acquire anything worthy that he heard of through his own diligence or the king’s will, he was asked how many thousands of books he possessed. He replied, twenty thousand, but that the number could soon reach fifty thousand.

He added that he had been told that the Jews possessed many works worthy of the royal library. At the urging of Aristaeus, a close friend of the king, he persuaded the king to send to Eleazar the high priest at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0609] *Iherosolimam*, witnesses 5 and 9c, regularly; in witness 1 it occurs scarcely once or twice], asking him to send men learned in the Law who could translate it into Greek.

Eleazar selected seventy men, the most learned in the Law of all, and sent them to the king. They were brought to Alexandria, received kindly by the king, and commended to Demetrius.

Demetrius led them into a secluded house suited to this task, situated beside the seashore. There, over seventy-two days, they translated the entire Law with great eloquence, devoting themselves daily to the work until the ninth hour.

When those days had passed, Demetrius gathered all the Jews at the place where the Laws had been translated and read them in the presence of the translators. When the multitude had embraced the Law, and the elders, its interpreters, had praised Demetrius because he had been the discoverer of great things, he asked that it also be given to his officials to read.

The king rejoiced that his desire had been fulfilled. After the Laws had been read again, he was astonished by their meaning and wisdom and said to Demetrius that he marveled that no Greek historiographer or poet had mentioned this Law, since it was so marvelous.

Demetrius replied that no one had dared to touch its composition because it was divine. He added that Theopompus, when he wished to record something about it in his history, had become mentally disturbed for more than thirty days. Finally, suspecting that this madness had come upon him because he had investigated the divine Laws and wished to convey them to impure men, he humbly begged God’s forgiveness in prayer. When he stopped writing, he recovered his senses.

He also related the story of Theodectes, a tragic poet: when he had attempted in a drama to mention something of what is contained in the divine volume, his eyes became clouded. He recognized the cause of his blindness and was freed from the affliction when God granted forgiveness. [Note: [Col. 0609] “Theothectus,” witness 5; “had seemed,” witnesses 9c and 11; “God,” from “a passion,” witness 5.]

Ptolemy sent the same elders back with honor, giving each of them splendid robes, two talents of gold, a cup worth one talent, and the entire couch used at the banquet.

Through them he sent to the high priest Eleazar ten couches with silver feet and suitable furnishings for them, a cup worth thirty talents, ten robes, purple cloth, a splendid crown, one hundred linen garments of fine byssus, as well as gold bowls, a mixing ladle [Note: [Col. 0609] “mixing ladles,” witness 9c], libation vessels, and two gold mixing bowls to be dedicated to God. He also granted freedom to all the Jews whom he found captive in Egypt.

**(HIER.)** After the translators departed, they were also honored by the kings of Asia. **(JOSEPHUS XII, 3.)** For Seleucus Nicanor, in the cities he had built throughout Asia, in Lower Syria, and in Antioch itself, the capital of his state, gave them a status worthy of the state and assigned them equal honor with the Macedonian and Greek inhabitants.

**(H. m.)** In the 470th year from the founding of the City, which is the first year of Philadelphus [Note: [Col. 0609] “the first year; the First Punic War arose. For T. 11.”], the Tarentines, having learned of Pyrrhus’s death, again stirred up fresh arms against the Romans. They requested and received the aid of the Carthaginians through envoys. Battle was joined, and the Romans won. [Note: [Col. 0609] “The Carthaginians were defeated,” witness 11; what follows is taken from the *Historia Miscella*.]

At that time the Carthaginians, although they had not yet been declared enemies, realized that they could nevertheless be defeated by the Romans. This circumstance provided the occasion for wars between the Romans and the Africans. [Note: [Col. 0609] “This circumstance … arose” are Ekkehard’s words.] Both peoples endured these wars, which were prolonged for a long time and excessively savage, although at last the Romans emerged victorious after immense exertion.

Ariminum in Gaul and Beneventum in Samnium were founded by the Romans at this time. In the year specified, prodigies were seen: blood flowed from the earth dug up in many places, and milk descended from heaven like rain.

In the 486th year from the founding of the City, which is the seventeenth year of Philadelphus, the Romans sent the consul Appius Claudius into Sicily when the Mamertines requested aid against Hiero, king of the Syracusans, and against the forces of the Carthaginians, which the king himself had hired.

He defeated them so quickly that the king himself, terrified by the greatness of the kings, declared that he had been defeated before he had even engaged in battle.

Hannibal the Elder, commander of the Carthaginians, had been surrounded by the Romans in a siege at the Sicilian city of Agrigentum and would have been reduced to utter destitution, had not Hanno, the new commander of the Carthaginians, arrived with fifteen hundred cavalry, thirty thousand infantry, and thirty elephants. He thereby delayed the storming of the city for a short time; but it was captured soon afterward, and the Carthaginians were defeated and put to flight. Hannibal escaped with a few men, eleven elephants were captured, and all the people of Agrigentum were sold under the crown.

After this, during the consulship of Gaius Aquilius Florus and Lucius Cornelius Scipio, the Carthaginians appointed Hanno in Hannibal’s place. Hanno, defeated by the consul Scipio, mingled with the densely packed enemy and was killed there.

Hannibal was again placed in command of the fleet. After engaging the Romans unsuccessfully in a naval battle and being defeated, he died when a mutiny broke out among his army and they covered him with stones.

During the consulship of Lucius Manlius Vulso and Marcus Atilius Regulus, the war was transferred to Africa. Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, and another Hanno, commander of the fleet, met them. Battle was joined at sea, and the Phoenicians were put to flight. They lost sixty-four ships. The victorious consuls crossed into Africa and, advancing toward Carthage, ravaged three hundred fortresses or more.

Manlius, departing Africa with his victorious fleet, brought twenty-seven thousand captives to Rome. Regulus remained in Africa and fought against three commanders, including Hasdrubal and Hamilcar, who had been summoned from Sicily.

When he had set up camp not far from the river Bagradas, a serpent of extraordinary size devoured many soldiers who had gone down to the river. Regulus went down with his army to destroy the beast. Since its scales would not receive weapons, he ordered the ballistae used to shatter walls to be brought. Its bones were broken by these, and it was killed. Its hide was brought to Rome and is said to have been stretched over a space of 120 feet.

The Carthaginians, broken by the wars, summoned King Xanthippus of Lacedaemon, among the many men whom they hired for assistance, and placed him in command of the war. When he advanced to battle with the Carthaginian forces organized, thirty thousand Roman soldiers were struck down. The famous commander Regulus was captured with five hundred men and thrown into chains. Finally, in the tenth year of the war against Carthage, he gave the Carthaginians a splendid triumph.

Xanthippus, conscious of so audacious a deed and fearing the changeability of fortune, immediately left Africa for Greece.

After this, exhausted by so many disasters, the Carthaginians decided that peace should be sought from the Romans. For this purpose they thought that Atilius Regulus, formerly the Roman commander whom they had held captive for five years, should be sent above all the other envoys.

When he came to Rome and was led into the Senate, he did nothing as a Roman. He said that from the day on which he had fallen into the power of the Africans, he had ceased to be a Roman. [Note: [Col. 0611] “that he was,” witness 5.]

Thus he kept his wife away from his embrace and urged the Senate not to make peace with the Africans. He succeeded. When they wished to keep him in Rome, he refused, saying that he could not remain in a city where, after having served the Africans, he could not possess the dignity of an honorable citizen.
