He therefore returned to Carthage. After his return, they bound him to a device and forced him always to stand facing the sun. They cut away his eyelids and killed him in sleep. [Note: [Col. 0611] “in a dream,” witnesses 4 and 5.]

Another Atilius Regulus and Manlius Vulso, both twice consuls, later departed for Lilybaeum with a fleet of two hundred ships and four legions. When Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, arrived, they were defeated. After losing most of their army, they themselves barely escaped.

After them, the consul Claudius departed with a fleet of two hundred and twenty ships for the harbor of Drepana against the enemy. There he was soon intercepted by the Carthaginian fleet. Because he fought contrary to the auspices, he was defeated. He himself fled to Lilybaeum with thirty ships; all the others were either captured or sunk. Nine thousand soldiers were killed, and twenty thousand are reported to have been captured.

Meanwhile, the consul Lutatius crossed into Sicily with a fleet of three hundred ships. The Carthaginians met him with four hundred ships and great forces under the command of Hanno. Battle was fought, and the commander Hanno was the first to flee. Seventy-three Punic ships were captured, one hundred and twenty sunk, thirty-two thousand men captured, and fourteen thousand killed.

Afterward they sent envoys first to Lutatius and then to Rome and made peace on these terms: they would withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia and pay the Romans three thousand talents of refined gold for twenty successive years. Thus this Punic War, which had lasted twenty-three years, came to an end.

In these times a silver coin was first struck at Rome.

**(HIER.)** The astrologer Aratus became famous, and the poet Quintus Ennius was born at Tarentum; later he lived at Rome, content with the service of a single female slave.

**(JOSEPHUS XII, 5.)** At this time also, after Eleazar’s death, his uncle Manasses, brother of Jaddi, assumed the high-priesthood. When he died, Onias, son of Simeon Justus, succeeded him—the child whom, as we said above, Simeon had left behind.

[Col. 0612B] **(HIER.)** Ptolemy Philadelphus ruled Alexandria for thirty-eight years.

Demetrius surrendered himself to Seleucus, who, after destroying the kingdom of Asia, made one empire out of the two. [Note: [Col. 0611] “He destroyed the kingdom of Asia and made one empire out of both,” witness 5.]

Ceraunus, also called Ptolemy, ruled Macedonia for nine months; Meleager, for two months; Antipater, for forty-five days.

Sosthenes ruled Macedonia for two years.

Antiochus, also called Soter, son of Seleucus, ruled Syria and Asia for nineteen years.

Antigonus ruled Macedonia for thirty-six years. He obtained Lacedaemon and defeated Pyrrhus.

Aratus is recognized.

A silver coin was first struck at Rome.

After Eleazar, his uncle Manasses assumed the high-priesthood of the Jews.

Years from the beginning: 3700.

[Col. 0612D] **(HIER. on Daniel, chapter XI.)** Antiochus, who was called Theos—that is, God—son of Antiochus Soter, ruled Syria and Asia for fifteen years.

He waged very many wars against Ptolemy Philadelphus and fought with all the forces of Babylonia and the East. Wishing to end the troublesome conflict, Ptolemy, although he himself possessed great forces, gave his daughter Berenice in marriage to Antiochus. Antiochus had two sons by his former wife Laodice: Seleucus, who was surnamed Callinicus, and another Antiochus.

Antiochus said that he wished Berenice to share the kingdom and Laodice to occupy the place of a concubine. But after a long time, overcome by love for Laodice, he brought her and her children back into the kingdom.

Fearing her husband’s uncertain disposition and that he might restore Berenice, Laodice had her husband secretly killed by servants with poison. She handed Berenice, together with the son whom she had borne to Antiochus, over to Icadion and Gennaeus, the king’s leading officials, to be killed. She herself ruled with her elder son Seleucus Callinicus.

**(HIER.)** When the Parthians withdrew from the empire of the Macedonians, Arsaces first ruled them; hence they were also called Arsacids.

The five-hundredth year from the founding of the City.

[Col. 0613B] Ptolemy Euergetes, son of Ptolemy Philadelphus, ruled Alexandria for twenty-six years, in the 276th year from the restoration of the Temple. Under him Jesus son of Sirach composed his book.

**(HIER. on Daniel, chapter XI.)** This Ptolemy [Note: [Col. 0613] Absent in witness 9c], therefore, after the death of his father Philadelphus, in revenge for his father and his murdered sister, entered the province of the king of the north—that is, of Seleucus Callinicus, who ruled Syria with his mother Laodice—with a great army. He captured Syria and Cilicia, the upper regions beyond the Euphrates, and almost all Asia.

When he heard that a rebellion had arisen in Egypt, he plundered Seleucus’s kingdom and carried away forty thousand talents of silver, precious vessels, and two thousand five hundred images of the gods. Among these were also those that Cambyses had carried into Persia after capturing Egypt.

The Egyptian people were greatly devoted to idolatry. Because Ptolemy had brought their gods back after many years, they called him Euergetes, “Benefactor.” He himself retained Syria, but entrusted Cilicia to his friend Antiochus to govern, and the provinces beyond the Euphrates to another commander, Xanthippus.

**(H. m.)** In the 508th year from the founding of the City, which is the first year of Euergetes, a sudden calamity in Rome itself forestalled the Roman triumph.

For during the consulship of Quintus Lutatius Catulus and Aulus Manlius, various disasters of fire and water nearly consumed the city. The Tiber, swollen by unprecedented rains and overflowing beyond all expectation, destroyed all the buildings of Rome situated on level ground.

Different kinds of terrain came together for a single catastrophe: the more severe flood dissolved what it held soaked, while whatever the torrent’s current encountered it knocked down by its force. The gravest disaster of the waters was followed by an even more destructive conflagration. The fire, although it was uncertain where it had arisen, spread through many parts of the city and caused a pitiable slaughter of people and houses.

Then, after devastating everything outside in the surrounding area, it seized the temple of Vesta. Metellus rescued the gods that were about to burn and barely escaped with his arm half burned.

During the consulship of Titus Sempronius Gracchus and Gaius Valerius Falco, the Romans made war on the Faliscans [Note: [Col. 0613] *Falacis*, witnesses 4, 5, and 10; *Aliseis*, witness 9c.], a city that had once been wealthy in Italy. Both consuls completed this war within six days, killing fifteen thousand of the enemy.

In the same year the Cisalpine Gauls also arose as new enemies, and the war against them had varying results. In the first encounter, three thousand Romans fell under the consul Valerius; in the second, fourteen thousand Gauls were killed and two thousand captured. But because of the earlier defeat, the consul was denied a triumph.

In the 517th year from the founding of the City, which is the tenth year of Euergetes, the Phoenician commander Hamilcar was killed by the Spaniards in battle, while he was already secretly preparing another war against the Romans.

(HIER.) Ptolemy Philopator, son of Euergetes, ruled Alexandria for 17 years, beginning in the 302nd year from the restoration of the Temple. [Col. 0614B] (HIER. on Daniel, here and there.) After the flight and death of Seleucus Callinicus, son of Antiochus—whom Euergetes, the father of this Philopator, killed—the two sons of that same Seleucus, namely Seleucus surnamed Ceraunus and Antiochus, who was called the Great, stirred by hope of victory and seeking vengeance for their father, gathered a large army and took up arms against Ptolemy Philopator. When Seleucus, the elder brother, was killed in Phrygia by the treachery of Nicanor in the third year of his reign, the army that was in Syria summoned his brother Antiochus, surnamed the Great, from Babylon to the kingship of Syria, which at that time was held by Ptolemy Philopator. After he had fought against Ptolemy’s commanders—or rather, after he had obtained Syria through the treachery of a certain Theodotus—he grew so bold [Col. 0614C] that he himself initiated war against the Egyptians. Philopator, however, having lost Syria through Theodotus’s treachery, assembled a very large force against Antiochus. When battle was joined near the town of Raphia, which lies on the borders of Egypt, Antiochus lost his entire army and, fleeing through the deserts, was nearly captured. When Syria had been abandoned, the struggle was finally ended by a treaty and an agreement on certain terms.

(JOS. XII, 3.) At this time the Jews were enduring many evils, while their land was subject to various calamities. For when Antiochus had fought against Ptolemy Philopator and his son Epiphanes, the Jews, caught between them, suffered under whichever side was victorious, like ships tossed about and fluctuating amid storms. [Col. 0614D]

[Col. 0614D] (HIER.) Seleucus Callinicus, the elder son of Antiochus, ruled Syria and Asia with his mother Laodice for 20 years.

Demetrius ruled Macedonia for 10 years.

Antigonus ruled Macedonia for 13 years.

The high priest of the Jews was Onias.

[Col. 0615A] Seleucus Ceraunus, son of Seleucus Callinicus, ruled Syria for three years.

Antiochus, who was called the Great, brother of Seleucus Ceraunus, ruled Syria for 36 years.

(H. m. Cf. H. R.) When, therefore, the First Punic War, which had lasted for 23 years, was over, the Romans had already become renowned for the greatest glory, and for a year they rested without military engagements. In that same year the gates of Janus were closed; this had happened only once since the founding of the City, under Numa Pompilius, the successor of Romulus, and afterward did not occur for 450 years. At that time Hiero, the most powerful king of Sicily, came to Rome for the games and gave 200,000 modii of wheat to the people as a gift.

(H. m.) In the 534th year from the founding of the City, which was the first year of Ptolemy Philopator, the Second Punic War was brought upon the Romans by Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians and son of Hamilcar, who had been killed by the Spaniards. This Hannibal, while he was still nine years old, had sworn to his father Hamilcar at the altars that, as soon as he was able, he would fight against the Romans. When he was 20 years old, he began to attack Saguntum, a flourishing city of Spain allied with the Romans. The Romans sent ambassadors to him, asking him to refrain from war, [Col. 0615C] but he contemptuously dismissed them. They sent Fabius to Carthage for the same matter, but when he had received harsh replies there as well [Note: [Col. 0615] “while he was there”: 9c.], he said: “What delay is there? In this fold of my toga I carry peace and war; which do you choose?” When they shouted back, “War!” he said: “Then accept it.” And he shook out the fold of his toga in the middle of the senate-house, as though he were literally carrying war in that fold [Note: [Col. 0615] “carried”: 4, 5.]. Meanwhile the Saguntines were overcome by hunger and, finally captured in the eighth month, were subjected to the ultimate punishments by Hannibal. Then the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio was sent with an army to Spain, and Tiberius Sempronius to Sicily. Hannibal, however, leaving his brother Hasdrubal in Spain, crossed the Pyrenees and opened a road by the sword through the fiercest Gallic peoples. Only on the ninth day did he reach the Alps from the Pyrenees. There, after defeating in battle the mountain Gauls who tried to prevent his ascent, and cutting through impassable cliffs with fire, vinegar, and iron [Note: [Col. 0615] “cut back”: 5.], he delayed for four days and on the fifth, with the greatest effort, reached the level ground. It is reported that he led into Italy 100,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry [Note: [Col. 0615] “120,000”: 4, 5, 10.], and 37 elephants. Meanwhile many Ligurians and Gauls joined Hannibal. Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, learning of Hannibal’s arrival, transported his army from Sicily to Ariminum. Publius Cornelius Scipio first encountered Hannibal at Ticinum. When battle had been joined, his men were routed and almost all defeated; he himself, rescued from death by his son Scipio, still wearing the boy’s toga [Col. 0616A] and barely past childhood, who was later called Africanus, returned wounded to the camp. The same consul then fought at the Trebia [Note: [Col. 0615] “Terebinus”: 9c.] River, and the Romans were defeated again. The consul Sempronius himself also engaged Hannibal and, after losing his army, escaped almost alone. Hannibal, however, was wounded in that battle as well. Later, when he crossed into Etruria in early spring, he was caught by a storm on the summit of the Apennines and remained motionless for two full days, shut in with his army by the snow. There a great number of men, very many pack animals, and almost all the elephants died of the cold. Then, as he came into Tuscany near the River Sarnus, the fog obstructed his view, and he lost a large part of his allies and pack animals. He himself, riding upon the one elephant that alone had survived, scarcely escaped the difficulty of the journey, but lost the eye that had already long been diseased because of the violence of the cold, sleeplessness, and hardship. [Col. 0616B]

In the 540th year from the founding of the City, which was the seventh year of Philopator, the consuls Aemilius Paulus and Terentius Varro [Note: [Col. 0615] “Terentius”: 9c., 10.] were sent against Hannibal. Because of Varro’s impetuosity, despite the opposition of his fellow consul, they lost almost all the strength of Roman hope near the village of Caudinae in Apulia. For nowhere in the Punic War were they more disastrously defeated. The consul Aemilius Paulus perished there. Although wounded, he sat down upon a certain rock, and when Lentulus offered him a horse so that he might escape and survive the disaster, he refused and remained there [Col. 0616C] until he was killed by the enemy. Twenty men of consular or praetorian rank perished there; 30 senators were captured or killed; 300 men of the highest nobility; 40,000 infantry; and 3,550 cavalry. The consul Varro fled to Venusia with 50 horsemen. There is no doubt that that day would have been the last of the Roman state if Hannibal had immediately pressed on to the City after his victory. As a testimony to his victory, Hannibal sent to Carthage three modii of gold rings, which he had stripped from the hands of the Roman cavalrymen and senators who had been killed. Three thousand of his own troops were slain, and many were wounded. Meanwhile Varro returned to Rome, and the Senate thanked him because he had not despaired of the commonwealth. He himself later proved that he had survived not from love of life but from love of the commonwealth. For he let his beard and hair grow, and afterward never again ate while reclining. When honors were also offered him by the people, he refused them, saying that the commonwealth needed more fortunate magistrates. So great, however, was the final despair of the commonwealth among the Romans who remained that they thought a plan should be made to abandon Italy and seek new homes. This would also have been confirmed on the advice of Caecilius Marcellus, had not Cornelius Scipio, then a military tribune and later called Africanus, deterred them with a drawn sword, threatening each man individually and compelling them instead to swear allegiance to his words for the defense of their country. [Col. 0617A]

At this time the Romans were fighting in four places: in Italy against Hannibal; in Spain against his brother Hasdrubal; in Macedonia against Philip; and in Sardinia against the Sardinians and another Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian, whom Titus Manlius, sent to Sardinia, captured alive and brought to Rome. Philip too was defeated in Macedonia by Laevinus. In Spain Hasdrubal and Mago, Hannibal’s third brother, were overcome by the two Scipio brothers. Yet both brothers, the Scipios, were later killed in Spain by Hasdrubal’s brother. Therefore, while everyone hesitated in fear, Scipio—later called Africanus—then 24 years old, volunteered and, having received proconsular authority in Spain, set out chiefly intending to avenge his father and uncle. Crossing the Pyrenees, he captured New Carthage in Spain at the first assault. There were large stores of gold and silver belonging to the Carthaginians and very noble hostages whom they had received from the Spaniards, together with substantial garrisons. There too he captured Mago, Hannibal’s brother, and sent him to Rome with others. Great joy arose at Rome. After Scipio had subdued all Spain from the Pyrenees to the ocean, he was recalled by the Romans and came to Rome in immense glory. Fourteen years after Hannibal had come into Italy—which was the 15th year of Philopator—he was elected consul with Licinius Crassus and sent to Africa. Scipio attacked Africa and by night set fire to the winter quarters of the Carthaginians and the huts of the Numidians, which were not far from Utica. The Carthaginians, alarmed, thinking that the fire had happened by chance, ran unarmed to extinguish it and were easily overwhelmed by the armed troops. In both camps 40,000 men were consumed by fire and sword; 5,000 were captured; and the commanders themselves, horribly burned, barely escaped. Hasdrubal, the commander, fled to Carthage. Soon Syphax and Hasdrubal, having greatly rebuilt their army, engaged Scipio again and were defeated and fled. Laelius and Masinissa captured Syphax as he fled. The rest of the multitude took refuge in Cirta, which Masinissa attacked and received into surrender. He brought Syphax in chains to Scipio, and Scipio handed him over to Laelius to be taken to Rome with immense spoils and very many captives. When Syphax died in custody at Tibur, the Senate ordered that he be honorably buried at public expense. When this became known, almost all Italy abandoned Hannibal. Hannibal himself, ordered by the Carthaginians to return and help his country, which Scipio was laying waste, is said to have left Italy in tears. Thus, in the 17th year, which was the first year of Ptolemy Epiphanes, Italy was freed from Hannibal. The Carthaginian ambassadors were sent to the Senate to seek peace from Scipio, and by Scipio’s decision they received peace. But when Hannibal arrived at Carthage, the peace was disturbed, and the Africans committed many hostile acts. After this Hannibal was defeated by Scipio in frequent battles and himself sought peace and an interview with Scipio. When the two most renowned commanders had gazed at each other for a long time in stunned mutual admiration, they departed without concluding the peace negotiations. Hannibal sent three scouts to Scipio’s camp. After Scipio captured them, he ordered them to be led around the camp and shown the entire army, without asking them anything about the enemy; he also ordered that they be given lunch and, after they had recovered their strength, allowed them to depart. Then battle was joined by both commanders. It was arranged for a long time with great military skill by the leaders and fought with the enormous masses of their forces, a battle such as scarcely any age had seen, since highly experienced men were leading their troops into war. Scipio nevertheless emerged victorious, with Hannibal almost captured. Eighty elephants were captured or killed there. Twenty-five thousand five hundred Carthaginian soldiers were killed. Hannibal, having experienced everything both before and during the battle, escaped amid the confusion first with many cavalrymen, then with 20, and finally scarcely with four; he fled to Hadrumetum and afterward to Carthage. Thirty-six years after he had left there as a little boy with his father, he came before the Carthaginian Senate and persuaded it that there was no hope except in seeking peace [Note: [Col. 0617] “persuaded them to seek peace”: 5.]. When Gaius Cornelius Lentulus and Publius [Note: [Col. 0617] “Publius Aelius Paetus”: 11.] were consuls, peace was granted to the Carthaginians through Scipio, with the consent of the Senate and people. Nevertheless, more than 500 ships were taken out to sea and sunk in sight of the city. Scipio, already surnamed Africanus, entered the City in triumph with every glory. Terentius, [Col. 0618C] who later was a comic poet and was a captive of noble Carthaginian family, followed behind his triumphal chariot wearing the cap of a freedman, which was the sign of the liberty granted to him.

Therefore, in the 552nd year from the founding of the City, which was the second year of Ptolemy Epiphanes, the Second Punic War ended, 19 years after it began. Let Rome boast, if it will, that it defeated Hannibal through victories; nevertheless, a luxurious province overcame him while he lingered amid the pleasures of Campania. While he floated in warm baths, while he gorged himself everywhere on fish and oysters, while he reveled in perfumes, drank, and slept, the relaxation of the baths softened Punic ferocity; and the town of Seplasia in Campania, with its perfumed ointments, weakened and defeated the man whom other hardships had hardened. [Col. 0618D]

(HIER.) Ptolemy Philopator ruled Alexandria for 17 years [Note: [Col. 0617] “17” is absent in 9c.].

Philip ruled Macedonia for 42 years. When he was preparing to rebel, he was first defeated by the consul Laevinus and afterward by Titus Quintius.

Ptolemy Epiphanes, son of Ptolemy Philopator, [Col. 0619A] ruled Alexandria for 24 years [Note: [Col. 0619] “14”: 9c.], beginning in the 319th year from the restoration of the Temple. (HIER. on Daniel, here and there.) After his father Philopator had died, Antiochus the Great broke the treaty and pact he had made with him, gathered an army from the upper regions of Babylonia, and, having made peace with Philip, king of the Macedonians, moved his army against this Epiphanes, who was then four years old [Note: [Col. 0619] “sent”: 9c.]. While Antiochus and the commanders of the boy Ptolemy were fighting one another, Judaea, situated between them and suffering many evils, was divided into opposing factions, just as under Ptolemy Philopator, his father, some favoring Antiochus and others Ptolemy. When Antiochus held Judaea, Scopas, the commander of Ptolemy Epiphanes’s faction, was sent against Antiochus and fought him vigorously; he captured Judaea (JOS. XII, 3). But after a short time Antiochus defeated Scopas, engaging him near the source of the Jordan and striking down many of his army. Later, when Antiochus was capturing Samaria and the cities of Syria that Scopas had held, the Jewish people came to him voluntarily, received his entire army into the city, and offered assistance with willing hearts. Therefore he himself also conferred many benefits upon them, as Josephus describes.

Now Antiochus wished not only to possess Syria, Cilicia, Lycia, and the other provinces that belonged to Ptolemy’s faction, but also to extend his kingdom into Egypt. Having made peace with Ptolemy through Eucles of Rhodes, he betrothed his daughter Cleopatra to him in the seventh year of the young man’s reign and gave her to him in the 13th year, granting her all Coele-Syria and Judaea as her dowry. Yet he was unable to obtain Egypt, because Ptolemy Epiphanes and his commanders, perceiving the deception, acted more cautiously, and Cleopatra supported her husband’s interests more than those of her father. This Antiochus the Great had two sons, brothers of Cleopatra whom he had given to Ptolemy: Seleucus, surnamed Soter, who ruled after him, and Antiochus, who was called [Note: [Col. 0619] “Epiphanes” is absent in 5.] Epiphanes and was given by his father to the Romans as a hostage. After his brother’s death he ruled in his place. He is the Antiochus called illustrious and noble in the Book of the Maccabees (cf. I, 1), who began to reign in the 137th year of the Greek kingdom and inflicted many evils upon the Jews.

[Col. 0619D] (JOS. here and there.) At that time the high priest of the Jews was Onias, son of Simon the Just, brother of Eleazar. This Onias was immature in mind and greedy for money. He did not pay the tax of 20 talents that his fathers had contributed on behalf of the people, and thus provoked King Ptolemy to anger. The king sent an envoy named Athenion to Jerusalem, who accused Onias and threatened that he would measure the land by the acre and send people to inhabit it. When the Jews heard the king’s commands, they were disturbed; but Onias was moved by none of these things because of his greed. When Joseph heard this—Joseph, the young man, the son of Onias’s sister, descended from Tobias [Note: [Col. 0619] “Thobias”: 5.], a very shrewd and noble man among his people—he rebuked his uncle Onias. When Onias paid no attention and refused to go to the king, Joseph voluntarily offered himself as envoy to the king for the people’s welfare, if Onias would permit him. When Onias granted this and the people gave thanks, Joseph received the king’s envoy into his house, treated him magnificently for many days, sent him back to the king honored with gifts, and said that he himself would follow immediately. When Athenion returned to the king and reported everything to him, the king and Queen Cleopatra later received Joseph kindly. He found such favor before the king that he not only freed the people but was also appointed by him commander of Judaea and of lower Syria and the neighboring regions. [Col. 0620B] For 22 years he administered the taxes of Syria, Phoenicia, and Samaria, and brought the Jewish people from poverty and weakness to the most distinguished prosperity. He had seven sons by his wife, and by the daughter of his brother Solinus he had one son named Hyrcanus. When Hyrcanus was 13 years old, he displayed such natural courage and prudence that he aroused even bitter rivalry among his brothers. Joseph, wishing to discover which of his sons was superior in virtue, assigned each of them to the studies of learned teachers, but they returned uneducated through their neglect of learning. After them he sent the boy Hyrcanus to sow a field two days’ journey away in the wilderness. He gave him 300 yoke of oxen but concealed the straps with which they were to be tied. When Hyrcanus arrived at the place and had no straps, the plowmen advised him to send home for some. Unwilling to waste time, he killed the oxen of ten yoke, gave the meat to the workers, cut up the hides, and made them into ties. Having thus sown the land, he returned to his father. Because of this ingenuity of mind, his father received him kindly and loved him excessively, which aroused the envy of his brothers.

After this Joseph was informed that a son had been born to King Ptolemy and that all the provincial rulers were going to Alexandria with the greatest display to celebrate the boy’s birthday. Since old age prevented Joseph from going, he asked his sons which of them wished to go to the king. When the older sons refused and said that Hyrcanus could do it, Joseph consulted Hyrcanus himself. Hyrcanus promised that he would go, provided Joseph sent a letter to Arion, the administrator of the money owed to the king, instructing him to give Hyrcanus the necessary funds. Joseph wrote the letter and sent him away. His brothers, however, wrote to all the king’s friends asking them to kill him. When Hyrcanus arrived in Alexandria, he presented Arion with the letter and, after receiving 1,000 talents from him, secretly approached some merchants. From them he bought 100 boys who knew letters, each for one talent, and 100 girls, each at the same price. He was kindly received by the king and invited to his banquet. Reclining with the leading men of the provinces, he sat last of all, treated by everyone with contempt as a mere boy. When everyone threw the bones of their food onto the table before him, while he remained silent, a certain Tryphon, who was skilled at provoking the laughter of banqueters, stood beside the king’s table at the request of the guests and said to the king: “Do you see, lord, that the bones have been placed before Hyrcanus? From this infer that his father stripped all Syria in the same way as this boy has stripped these bones of their meat.” When the king laughed at Tryphon’s words and asked Hyrcanus why so many bones lay before him, he replied: “Appropriately, lord. Dogs always devour bones together with meat, as these men have done, before whom no bones lie. Human beings, however, eat the meat and throw away the bones, which is what I, like a human being, have now done.” The king, astonished at his answer, so wisely expressed, ordered everyone to applaud and praise his words. The next day Hyrcanus went to each of the king’s friends and to the powerful men of the court and greeted them. When the king’s son’s birthday arrived, the provincial rulers offered gifts to the king—gifts of great value, but none worth more than 20 talents [Note: [Col. 0621] “offered to the king”: 4, 5; “the king’s gifts”: 10, 11.]. Hyrcanus therefore took the boys and girls whom he had bought, gave each man one talent to carry, and presented the boys to the king and the girls to Queen Cleopatra. Everyone admired his generosity. The king honored him liberally, gave him abundant gifts, and sent letters on his behalf to his father, his brothers, and all the magistrates. When his brothers heard that he had earned such rewards from the king and was returning with great honor [Note: [Col. 0621] “returning with honor”: 5.], they pretended to go out to meet him but resolved by every means to kill him. His father knew of this as well and was angry because of the money Hyrcanus had offered the king, but, fearing the king, concealed his anger. When his brothers engaged him in battle, Hyrcanus killed many of their followers together with two of his brothers. The rest fled to their father in Jerusalem. When Joseph came to the city, no one received him, so he departed across the Jordan River and remained there, exacting taxes from the barbarians. At that time Seleucus, who was called Soter, son of Antiochus the Great, was ruling in Asia.

[Col. 0621D] Onias, the high priest, son of Simon the Just, brother of Eleazar and maternal uncle of Joseph, the father of Hyrcanus, died, leaving the high-priesthood to his son Simon. Joseph also died, and after his death the people suffered sedition because of his sons. While the elder sons were waging war against Hyrcanus, the multitude became divided among themselves. Many supported the elder brothers together with the high priest Simon, who was their relative and in-law. Hyrcanus, departing from Jerusalem across the Jordan, built there a very strong tower of white stone. He carved the entire structure down to the ground with various animals and fortified the site with additional buildings. He called it Tyre. He ruled those regions for 12 years, throughout the period when Seleucus, son of Antiochus the Great, ruled Syria. After Seleucus died, his brother Antiochus Epiphanes obtained the kingdom. Fearing that Antiochus would torture him for what he had done against the Arabs, Hyrcanus ended his life by his own hand. Antiochus appropriated his property. Simon the high priest, son of Onias, also died, leaving three sons: Onias, Jesus, and Onias or Ananias. His son Onias succeeded his father in the dignity of the priesthood. This is the man to whom Arius, king of Sparta—that is, of the Lacedaemonians—sent letters, saying that the Jews and Lacedaemonians descended from one lineage of Abraham.

[Col. 0622B] (H. m.) In the 551st year from the founding of the City, which is also counted as the first year of Ptolemy Epiphanes, Titus Quintius Flaminius was sent against Philip, king of Macedonia. After many battles in which he defeated the Macedonians, he granted Philip peace, on the condition that Philip also give his son Demetrius as a hostage. (H. R.) Titus likewise made war upon the Lacedaemonians, defeated their commander Nabis, and received them into allegiance on whatever terms he wished. He celebrated a triumph of immense glory, leading before his chariot the most noble hostages: Demetrius, son of Philip, and Armenes, son of Nabis. After the Macedonian War, the Syrian War followed. (HIER. on Daniel—H. m.) Antiochus the Great, king of Syria, [Col. 0622C] unable to obtain the kingdom of his son-in-law Ptolemy Epiphanes [Note: [Col. 0621] “of his son-in-law”: 4.], turned to Asia. In a naval engagement he captured Rhodes, Samos, and many other islands. Then, preparing war against the Romans, he crossed from Asia into Europe. At that time Hannibal was also ordered by the Senate to be brought to Rome. He secretly departed from Africa so as not to be handed over to the Romans and went to Antiochus, joining himself to him. When he found Antiochus hesitating at Ephesus, he immediately urged him to war. (HIER. here and there—H. m.) But Scipio Nasica met them with his brother Scipio Africanus. Africanus himself held a private conversation with Hannibal, but, since the matter came to nothing, Hannibal withdrew from Antiochus. The following year the same Scipio Africanus defeated and routed Hannibal, who at that time commanded Antiochus’s fleet, in a naval battle. His brother Lucius [Note: [Col. 0621] “Lucilius”: 5, 9c.], consul Cornelius Scipio Nasica, with Eumenes, brother of King Attalus, as an auxiliary, defeated Antiochus in a great battle (cf. HIER.). Antiochus sued for peace and obtained it on the condition that he pay 1,000 talents each year, withdraw from Asia and Europe, remain within Mount Taurus, and surrender Hannibal, the instigator of the war. (H. m.) Hannibal fled to King Prusias of Bithynia. When the Romans demanded him, and he was already about to be handed over, he drank poison. Antiochus, however, voluntarily sent back the son of Africanus, whom he had captured—whether while he was reconnoitering or in battle is uncertain [Note: [Col. 0621] “or in battle”: 9c.]—and also gave his own son Antiochus as a hostage. [Col. 0623A] Returning to Rome, Scipio Nasica celebrated a triumph of immense glory and himself received, in imitation of his brother, the name Asianus because he had conquered Asia. Since Philip, king of the Macedonians, had assisted the Romans against Antiochus, his son Demetrius [Note: [Col. 0623] “of Demetrius”: 5, 9c.] was restored to him. (HIER.) At this time Plautus, from Umbria, of Arpinum, died at Rome. Because of a shortage of grain he had hired himself out to a baker at the hand-mills, where, whenever he was free from work, he used to write and sell plays. Titus Livius was regarded at that time as a famous writer of tragedies. Because of his talent he was given his freedom by Livius Salinator, whose children he was educating.

[Col. 0623B] (HIER.) Ptolemy Epiphanes ruled Alexandria for 24 years.

(H. m.) At this time Scipio Africanus, living for a long time in exile from the ungrateful Roman city, died of illness near the town of Amiternum. He ordered these words to be inscribed on his tomb: “Ungrateful fatherland, you do not even possess my bones.”

Seleucus, also called Soter, son of Antiochus the Great, ruled Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0623] thus in 4, 5, 9c., 10; “Syria”: 11.] for 11 years. At the instigation of a certain Simon, who was superintendent of the Temple at Jerusalem, he sent Heliodorus to take away the money. Heliodorus was struck down by God, as is read in the Book of the Maccabees.

(HIER.) Ptolemy Philometor, the second son of Epiphanes, ruled Alexandria for 35 years, beginning in the 343rd year from the restoration of the Temple. [Col. 0623C]

(JOS. XII, 5 and following.) Perseus, son of Philip, ruled Macedonia for 10 years. Antiochus Epiphanes, that is, “the illustrious,” the brother of Seleucus and son of Antiochus the Great, ruled Syria for 12 years after the death of his brother Seleucus. Ptolemy, who was himself also called Epiphanes, married Antiochus’s sister Cleopatra, by whom he had two sons, whom he left still children when he died. The elder, who ruled in his place, was called Philometor; the other was called Physcon. Antiochus, not content with his own kingdom, resolved to lead an army into Egypt, drawn by his desire for it and despising his sister’s sons as weak and incapable of governing so great an affair. Having arrived at Pelusium with a powerful army and deceitfully surrounding his kinsman Philometor, he seized Egypt. When he had reached the region of Memphis, he captured it. Then he proceeded against Alexandria to besiege Ptolemy, whose uncle he was, but he was driven away by Ptolemy’s commanders not only from Alexandria but from all Egypt (cf. HIER. on Daniel). (JOS. here and there.) Returning from there, he led his army against the city of Jerusalem. When he arrived, he captured it without any battle, because those who knew his intentions opened the gates to him. Entering the city, he killed many who opposed him; but he also killed the very people who had opened the city to him because of the Temple’s riches. After committing all the evils written about in the history of the Maccabees and carrying away many things from the Temple, he returned to Antioch. [Col. 0624A]

(HIER. on Daniel.) Two years later he again gathered an army against Ptolemy and came to Alexandria. When the two brothers, the sons of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, whose uncle Antiochus was, were being besieged in Alexandria, they sent ambassadors to Rome. When the Roman ambassadors arrived in Alexandria, one of whom was Marcus Popillius Laenas, [Col. 0624B] and found Antiochus standing on the shore, they presented him with a decree of the Senate ordering him to withdraw from the friends of the Roman people and to be content with his own authority. When he postponed his response in order to consult his friends, he is said to have drawn a circle in the sand with the staff he held in his hand, encircled the king, and said: “The Senate and people of Rome order you to state at this very spot what course of action you intend to take.” Terrified by these words, Antiochus said: “If this pleases the Senate and people of Rome, I must withdraw.” And he withdrew immediately.

At that time, as Josephus writes (XII.6), Onias, the son of Simon and high priest, died, leaving behind a young son, Onias. Accordingly, Antiochus conferred the high-priesthood upon his brother Jesus, [Col. 0624C] but later, angered against him, took it away and gave it to their younger brother, Onias, or Ananias. For Simon, as we said above, had three sons, to whom the high-priesthood passed in the order mentioned. Jesus, however, called himself Jason, while Onias, or Ananias, was called Menelaus, as Josephus says.

The same Josephus then adds that Jesus—that is, Jason—first stirred up a revolt against Menelaus, and that Menelaus, together with his supporters, abandoned the religion of his fathers, went over to Antiochus, incited him against the Jews, and was later killed by the younger Antiochus at the urging of Lysias. [Note: [Col. 0623] Thus nearly all the manuscripts that I have seen; “to have been killed” with “to have killed” deleted as the alternative wording, 10; “to have been killed,” 11.]

In these words Josephus appears to disagree with the history of the Book of Maccabees, in which it is reported (II Maccabees 3 and following) that Menelaus was the brother of a certain Simon from the tribe of Benjamin, who was superintendent of the Temple. While Seleucus, the brother of Antiochus, was still alive, Simon, out of hatred for the priest Onias, who resisted him lest he contrive some evil in the city, caused Heliodorus to be sent by Seleucus to Jerusalem to remove money from the Temple. When Heliodorus returned in terror, Simon did not cease speaking evil against Onias and incited Apollonius, the governor, against him. Onias, yielding to these attacks, withdrew to the king so that he might live safely under the king’s protection.

[Col. 0625A] After Seleucus’s death, when his brother Antiochus was reigning, what Josephus reports here about Onias and Menelaus is related in this history (chapter 4) about Jason, the brother of Onias. For this Jason, who was also Jesus, gathered impious men, approached Antiochus, expelled his brother Onias by means of money, and received the priesthood. Having obtained permission to build a gymnasium in Jerusalem, he abandoned his religion and adopted the customs of the nations.

After three years Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the aforementioned Simon, carrying to the king the money promised for the priesthood—namely, five hundred and ninety talents. But Menelaus himself, promising the king an additional three hundred pounds, supplanted Jason. Thus Jason, who had expelled his brother Onias, was himself later expelled from his homeland and died in exile, as he deserved.

But when Menelaus did not pay the promised sums, the king took the priesthood away from him and gave it to his own brother Lysimachus. Fearing that Onias might recover the priesthood, Menelaus dealt with Andronicus, a friend of the king whom the king, on departing, had placed in charge of affairs, so that he would kill Onias; and he did so. When Lysimachus too was killed by the Jews on account of his sacrileges, Menelaus recovered the priesthood.

(Josephus XII.14 and following.) After Menelaus was killed by Antiochus Eupator, the son of Antiochus, at the urging of Lysias, a certain impious foreigner, Alcimus, succeeded him in the priesthood. When Alcimus too was struck down by divine judgment, and hereditary successors had failed, Judas Maccabeus assumed the priesthood by the will of everyone.

For Onias, the son of Onias, whom we said above had been left a child when his father died, seeing the evils that were being committed, fled to Ptolemy, king of Egypt. Kindly received by him, he obtained from him the region called Heliopolis. There, with the king’s permission, he built a temple modeled on the Temple of Jerusalem, which remained for many years, until the time of Vespasian. The city itself, which was called Onias, was later destroyed to the ground when the Jews fought against the Romans, [Note: [Col. 0625] “destroyed,” 5.] and no trace of either the city or the temple remains.

Thus, under the pretext of Onias, innumerable multitudes of Jews fled to Egypt. For Onias maintained that the prophecy of Isaiah had been fulfilled in him, when Isaiah wrote: “There shall be an altar of the Lord in Egypt, and a monument of the Lord at its borders”; and that what Ezra [Note: [Col. 0625] “Ezdras,” 5.] had predicted six hundred years earlier had also been fulfilled: that a temple ought to be built for God in Egypt by a Jewish man.

When Antiochus was afflicting the Jews and compelling them, both personally and through his agents, to adopt paganism, Mattathias took up arms against them with his five sons and defended the laws of his fathers courageously. When he died a year later—namely, in the 146th year of the kingdom of the Greeks, which was the thirteenth year of Philometor and the tenth of Antiochus—his son Judas Maccabeus succeeded him. He gathered an army and inflicted vengeance upon the evildoers.

He magnificently restored the Temple destroyed by Antiochus and cleansed it of the filth of the idols by which it had been polluted for three years, in the 152nd year. Hearing also of the Romans’ power, he formed a treaty of friendship and alliance with them. At length, after winning many battles successfully, he fought against Bacchides, the commander of Demetrius, killed many, and was himself killed in the fiftieth year, after ruling the people for [Note: [Col. 0625] “five years”—the words “he ruled” are missing, 4.]

His brother Jonathan succeeded him and ruled the people vigorously for seventeen years. When Jonathan was killed by Tryphon, Simon, their brother, held the leadership for eight years; he assumed it in the seventieth year [Note: [Col. 0625] “the hundredth and seventieth,” 11; and so hereafter he adds one hundred to these numbers.] of the kingdom of the Greeks.

*(H. m. and H. R.)* When Philip, king of the Macedonians, died—he had waged war against the Romans and later brought aid to the Romans against Antiochus—his son Perseus, holding his kingdom, rebelled. His allies were Cotys, king of Thrace, and the king of Illyricum, whose name was Gentium. The Roman allies were Eumenes, king of Asia and brother of Attalus; Ariarathes, king of Cappadocia; Antiochus of Syria; Ptolemy of Egypt; and Masinissa of Numidia. Brusias, king of Bithynia, although he had Perseus’s sister as his wife, maintained an even position toward both sides. [Note: [Col. 0625] “having his sister,” 5.]

The consul Publius Licinius was sent against Perseus and was defeated by him. Nevertheless, the Romans refused to grant peace to the king when he asked for it unless he submitted himself and his people to the Senate. Soon afterward the consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus was sent against him, defeated him, and returned to Rome with great pomp in Perseus’s own ship, which was said to have been of extraordinary size, so that it is reported to have had sixteen banks of oars.

Paulus celebrated his triumph in a golden chariot, with his two sons standing on either side. Two sons of the king were led before his chariot, together with Perseus himself, forty-five years old. Perseus later died in captivity at Alba, while his younger son learned the trade of bronze-working at Rome in order to endure poverty, and died there.

In the six-hundredth year from the founding of the City, which is designated as the twenty-sixth year of Philometor, when an overwhelming fear of the Celtiberians had seized all the Romans and no one among them—neither soldier nor legate—dared go to Spain, Publius Scipio, grandson of Africanus, who was himself later called Africanus, voluntarily offered to serve in Spain, although he had been assigned to Macedonia against Philip.

Having therefore set out for Spain, [Col. 0626D] he inflicted a great slaughter, often performing the duty of a soldier rather than of a commander. Indeed, when a barbarian challenged him to single combat, he engaged him and killed him.

At the same time, the censor Messala ordered the first stone theater to be built in the City. Scipio Nasica opposed its construction with the strongest denunciation, saying that such an invention for nourishing idleness and wantonness would be most hostile to a warlike people. He so moved the Senate that it ordered not only that everything procured for the theater be sold, [Note: [Col. 0625] “procured,” 5, 9c, 10.] but also that benches not be placed at the games, [Note: [Col. 0625] “they prohibited,” 5.] and that neither city-dwellers nor those present from outside within a thousand paces should watch the games while seated, lest their courage grow soft.

At that time, too, Tuccia, a Vestal Virgin, was accused of incest. But she disdained to clear herself by human proofs. She carried a sieve to the Tiber, [Note: [Col. 0627] missing, 9c.] submerged it, [Note: [Col. 0627] “in water” is added in another hand, 10; “into the water,” 11.] and, adding a prayer, said: “O Vesta, if I am pious, if I am a virgin, I shall carry this water from the Tiber to your temple.” And she carried it there.

In the six-hundred-and-second year, the Third Punic War broke out. When the Senate had decided that Carthage must be destroyed, the consuls Lucius Manlius Censorinus and Marcus Manlius set out, and Scipio, then military tribune, established their camp near Utica, on the site of the camp of the elder Africanus.

There, after summoning the Carthaginians and ordering them to surrender their weapons and ships without delay, such a quantity of weapons was suddenly handed over that all Africa could easily have been armed from them. But after they had surrendered their arms and had been ordered to withdraw far from the abandoned city, ten thousand paces from the sea, they turned their grief into desperation, determined either to defend their city or to be buried with it and through it. Soon they appointed two commanders named Hasdrubal, [Note: [Col. 0627] “they appointed commanders for themselves,” 5.] and began making weapons. When bronze and iron ran out, they made them from gold and silver.

The Roman consuls attacked the city. After they had destroyed part of the wall with siege engines, [Note: [Col. 0627] “part of the wall,” 5.] they were defeated and driven back by the Carthaginians. Scipio protected them as they fled, driving the enemy back inside the walls.

He was held in immense fear and reverence by everyone. He was exceptionally ready for battle and extremely prompt in giving counsel, and the Punic commanders avoided nothing more carefully than engaging the Romans on the side where Scipio was fighting.

At the same time, Masinissa, king of the Numidians and a friend of the Roman people for nearly sixty years, died in the ninety-seventh year of his life, having always remained strong in body. He was the man who never covered his head in rain, however heavy, or in cold weather; and he would stand in one place for so long that young men would first yield from weariness before he moved from the spot where he had been standing.

If he stood, he would not move even a limb for the entire day. If he began a journey on horseback, he did not dismount; if on foot, he did not mount. When riding with the army, he was accustomed very often to join day to night, and he entrusted his protection and safety to the fiercest dogs.

After his eighty-sixth year he fathered a son named Methuma, and in his final years he omitted nothing that he had done as a young man. At his death he left forty-four sons, among whom he ordered Scipio to be the divider. After Scipio had divided the kingdom of Numidia among them, he returned to Carthage.

In the six-hundred-and-sixth year from the founding of Rome, which was the thirty-second year of Philometor, when Scipio’s name was illustrious, he was made consul while still a young man. Undertaking, by the final decree of fate, to destroy Carthage, he entered the Cothon.

There, after fighting for six continuous days and nights, the final desperation drove the Carthaginians to surrender. They asked that those whom the disaster of war had left alive might at least be permitted to serve. First a sufficiently pitiable procession of women descended, followed by one more wretched still of men. It is reported that there were twenty-five thousand women and thirty thousand men.

King Hasdrubal surrendered voluntarily and obtained safety only for himself. The deserters were thrown from a precipice by their own choice and consumed by fire. Those Roman deserters whom Scipio was able to seize he crucified; the Latins he struck down with the axe.

When Hasdrubal’s wife saw Carthage burning, she went to meet her husband with her two sons and said to him: “Live, you who can survive Carthage, for you would have pleaded in vain on our behalf.” Then, with her sons willing, in manly grief and feminine fury, she threw herself into the midst of the flames, making the same end in death as the first queen had once made. [Col. 0628B]

The city itself burned continuously for seventeen days and presented its conquerors with a miserable spectacle of the changing condition of human affairs. It was destroyed, every piece of its wall-stone being reduced to dust.

Its situation is said to have been as follows. It was enclosed by a wall twenty-two thousand paces in circumference and was almost entirely surrounded by sea, except for the entrance, which opened for three thousand paces. That place had a wall thirty feet thick, built of squared stone, and forty cubits high. The citadel, called Byrsa, occupied somewhat more than two thousand paces. On one side there was a wall shared by the city and Byrsa, overlooking the sea called the Stagnum Sea.

Thus Carthage was destroyed seven hundred years after it had been founded. The entire multitude of captives, except for a few leading men, was sold. In this way the Third Punic War ended in the fourth year after it had begun. Scipio earned the name that his grandfather had received: on account of his courage, he too was called Africanus the Younger.

In the same year, Corinth, the most celebrated city of Greece, was overthrown by fire by the consul Mummius. Because of the multitude and variety of the statues and images, when the metals of gold, silver, and bronze had flowed together into one mass amid the conflagration of that great city, a new kind of metal was produced. Hence, to this day, whether made from it or in imitation of it, bronze is called Corinthian bronze, and vessels are called Corinthian vessels.

At this time three very celebrated triumphs took place at Rome simultaneously: that of Africanus from Africa, before whose chariot Hasdrubal was led; that of Metellus from Macedonia, before whose chariot Andariscus, also called Pseudo-Philip, king of the Macedonians, preceded; and that of Mummius from Corinth, before whom bronze statues, painted panels, and other ornaments of the famous city were carried.

After Pseudo-Philip, who had usurped Macedonia for himself, was killed, and likewise Pseudo-Perseus, who claimed to be the son of Perseus, the Romans made the Macedonians, who had been masters of nations, tributaries to the Roman rulers, and the kingdom of the Macedonians came to an end. *(Jerome.)*

[Col. 0629A] Statius Caecilius, a distinguished writer of comedies, was held in esteem in these days. By nationality a Gaul—or, as some say, a Milanese—he was first the companion of Ennius and died the year after Ennius’s death. Ennius, however, perished from an arthritic disease in the seventieth year of his life and was buried in the monument of Scipio on the Appian Way, within the first mile from the City. At that time the poet Lucius [Note: [Col. 0629] “Lucilius,” 11.] was also born.

[Col. 0629A] With the kingdom of the Macedonians coming to an end, the kingdom of the Jews began. At that time Judas Maccabeus was the first to hold the leadership, for five years, beginning in the forty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks, which was the fourteenth year of Philometor and the eleventh of Antiochus the Illustrious. *(Cf. Jerome.)*

[Col. 0629B] *(Josephus.)* Antiochus Eupator, the son of Antiochus the Illustrious, reigned in Syria for two years.

Years from the beginning: 3800. Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, the brother of Antiochus the Illustrious, killed Antiochus Eupator, the son of his paternal uncle, [Note: [Col. 0629] missing, 4, 9c; “his paternal uncle,” 4.] and reigned in Syria for eleven years. He had two sons, Demetrius, his namesake, and Antiochus, who was called Sidetes or Soter. [Note: [Col. 0629] The words from “He had two sons” through “Soter” are missing, 10, 11.]

Jonathan, the brother of Judas Maccabeus, assumed the leadership after Judas’s death and ruled the people vigorously for eighteen years. *(Jerome.)* In these times Aristobulus the philosopher wrote commentaries on the books of Moses and presented them to King Ptolemy.

[Col. 0629C] The six-hundredth year from the founding of the City.

Alexander, likewise the son of Antiochus the Illustrious and brother of Eupator, killed Demetrius, the son of his paternal uncle Seleucus, and reigned for four years. He married Cleopatra, the daughter of King Ptolemy, and fathered Antiochus by her.

*(Josephus.)* Demetrius, the son of Demetrius whom Alexander had killed, invaded the kingdom while Alexander was still alive. Ptolemy Philometor joined his daughter Cleopatra, who had been taken away from Alexander, to Alexander. After Alexander was killed, Demetrius reigned for five years, but in the fifth year he was captured by Arsaces, king of the Parthians.

While Demetrius was still reigning, a certain Tryphon, belonging to Alexander’s faction, brought forward Antiochus, the son of that same Alexander, and, although he was still a child, placed the diadem on him so that he might reign. But in the fourth year of his rule Tryphon killed him by treachery and reigned himself.

After Tryphon too was killed in the third year of his reign, Antiochus, the brother of Demetrius, reigned. Cleopatra, the wife of his brother, married him, and by her he had a son named Antiochus, who was called Cyzicenus after the city of Cyzicus, where he was raised. Demetrius too, the brother of Antiochus, had by the same Cleopatra a son of the same name, Antiochus, who was called Gryphus. These two brothers, Antiochus and Antiochus, later contended with one another for the kingdom.

Antiochus, the son of Alexander, after Tryphon had placed the diadem upon him, reigned against Demetrius for four years, but in the fourth year he was treacherously killed by that same Tryphon.

[Col. 0630A] *(Jerome.)* Ptolemy Euergetes II reigned at Alexandria for twenty-nine years, beginning in the year 388 after the restoration of the Temple.

*(H. M.)* In these times, at Rome, a four-footed, four-handed boy was born of a slave woman, with four eyes, an equal number of ears, and a double male nature. In the territory of Bononia, crops grew on trees. [Note: [Col. 0629] “Bononian,” 5.]

[Col. 0630B] *(Josephus.)* Simon, the brother of Judas and Jonathan, ruled the Jewish people for eight years after their deaths.

Tryphon, having killed Antiochus, reigned for three years, but in the third year he too was killed. [Note: [Col. 0629] “he too was killed in the third year,” 5; “in the third year he too was killed,” 9c.]

Antiochus, also called Sidetes, the brother of Demetrius, reigned for fifteen years after his brother had been captured by the king of the Parthians. He freed his brother from captivity, and that brother reigned after him.

*(Josephus XIII.13.)* John, also called Hyrcanus, the son of Simon, held the leadership of the Jewish people for thirty-one years. His father had been killed, together with two sons, at a banquet through the treachery of his son-in-law Ptolemy, who was commander in the region around Jericho. John was called Hyrcanus because he waged war against the Hyrcanians.

*(Jerome—Josephus, Jewish War I.3.)* This man was plainly most blessed. He alone possessed three especially outstanding offices, for he was commander, high priest, and prophet. God spoke with him in such a way that he was completely ignorant of nothing concerning the future. [Note: [Col. 0629] “with God,” 9c.]

*(Jerome.)* He fought many battles, first against Ptolemy, his sister’s husband. Then, after capturing Samaria by siege, he leveled it to the ground; later Herod restored it and called it Sebaste in honor of Augustus.

Antiochus, whom some call Sidetes and others Spondus, the brother of Demetrius, had long been hostile to Simon. In the second year of Hyrcanus, he brought an army and besieged Hyrcanus in Jerusalem. *(Josephus, ibid. I.2.)* But Hyrcanus opened David’s tomb, took more than three thousand talents from it, and, giving three hundred to Antiochus, persuaded him to withdraw from the city.

To lessen resentment over this act, he is said to have established hostels from this money, where he could receive the poor and strangers. After living in great prosperity for thirty-one years and administering affairs very well, he died, leaving five sons.

The eldest of them, Aristobulus, transferred the leadership into a monarchy and was the first among the Jews to place a diadem upon himself, after 398 years and three months had elapsed since the people returned from the Babylonian captivity. His brother Antigonus, second in age, whom he seemed to love, he advanced to equal honor; but he handed the others over in chains to custody. He likewise bound his mother, who had dared to dispute some matter of power, [Note: [Col. 0631] missing, 9c.] and killed her by starvation. Later he also killed his brother Antigonus.

After the murder of his mother and his brother Antigonus, Aristobulus himself was tortured by the most fitting and cruel pain in his entrails and died detestably, having reigned no more than one year. His wife, however, [Note: [Col. 0631] “and at the same age, the others being omitted,” 9c.] released his brothers from their chains and made his brother Alexander king, since he was older in age and seemed to excel in moderation.

[Col. 0631A] Demetrius, the brother of Antiochus, freed from captivity by his brother, reigned for twelve years after his brother’s death.

*(H. m.)* In the six-hundred-and-twentieth year from the founding of the City, which was the eleventh year of Ptolemy Euergetes II, Scipio Africanus the Younger was elected consul for the second time by unanimous consent and was sent with an army to attack Numantia, a city of Spain.

For fourteen years Numantia, with only four thousand of its own men, not only resisted forty thousand Romans but also defeated them and subjected them to disgraceful treaties. When Scipio entered Spain, he did not immediately attack the Numantines as though they were unprepared, for he knew that they were always ready. Instead, for some time he trained his own soldiers, who were corrupt and cowardly because of the guilt of their previous commanders, exercising them rather than punishing them and treating the camp like a school, without harshness.

Then, by a severe order, he commanded that everything kept in the camp for pleasure be removed. In the end, two thousand prostitutes, together with the camp-followers, were expelled from his line of march. Under a strict judge the army made such sudden progress that it would soon level Numantia to the ground, though it had long been most destructive to the Romans.

After spending the whole summer and the entire winter without even attempting battle, however, he made almost no progress through this effort. For when an opportunity to fight arose, the Roman army, overwhelmed by the Numantines’ attack, turned its back as usual. But, provoked by the consul’s rebukes and threats as he confronted them and held them back by force, it finally returned against the enemy and compelled those from whom it had been fleeing to flee.

At that time it was difficult to believe what was being reported: the Numantines had driven away the Romans, and the Romans had seen them fleeing. Therefore, although Scipio was glad because the event had occurred beyond expectation, he nevertheless declared that no further battle ought to be ventured against them.

He therefore enclosed the city with a siege and surrounded it with a ditch ten feet wide and twenty feet deep. Then he fortified the embankment itself, which was faced with stakes, with numerous towers. For this war Micipsa, king of the Numidians, sent Jugurtha to assist Scipio. Jugurtha acted bravely, won glory, and found favor before Scipio.

The Numantines, long shut in and slaughtered by hunger, frequently asked for the opportunity to fight, so that they might be allowed to die like men, but they did not obtain it. Finally, they burst out suddenly through two gates, after first taking a large drink—not of wine, for that region does not produce it, but of a juice made from wheat by a particular process. Because it warms, they call this juice *celia*.

Thus, after their long hunger, they grew warm again through this drink, offered themselves for battle, and suddenly attacked the Romans. The fierce contest lasted long and brought the Romans to the point of danger. The Romans would again have proved, by fleeing, that they were unwilling to fight the Numantines, had they not been fighting under Scipio.

After their bravest men had been killed, the Numantines yielded in battle, but they arranged their ranks and did not return to the city like fugitives. They refused to accept the bodies of the slain when they were offered for burial. In the final hope of desperation, all having resolved upon death, they themselves set fire to the city from within. All alike were consumed by sword, poison, and fire.

The Romans gained nothing at all from these defeated people except their own security. Indeed, after Numantia had been destroyed, they said that they had escaped rather than conquered. Not one Numantine was touched by the victor’s chain, so there was no one to lead in a triumph; and whatever household goods there were, the fire consumed.

Then Scipio asked a certain Celtic leader named Tyresius why Numantia, previously unconquered, had endured, and why it had later been destroyed. Tyresius replied: “Concord brought victory; discord brought destruction.” The Romans accepted this as an example applicable to themselves and spoken about themselves, since news was already being brought to them of the whole City’s dissensions and discord.

For at the very time when these events were taking place at Numantia, the seditions of the Gracchi were being stirred up at Rome. After Carthage and Numantia had been destroyed, a useful debate arose among the Romans concerning provision, but a disgraceful contest concerning ambition.

Gracchus, tribune of the plebs, was angry with the nobility because they marked him among the authors of the Numantine treaty, which had been disgracefully made through the consul Mancinus. He therefore decided that the land that he had previously occupied privately should be divided among the people. When the tribune Octavian opposed him, Gracchus deprived him of his authority and appointed Minucius as his successor. [Note: [Col. 0631] “Gracchus of the Gracchi,” “Gracchus,” in the manuscripts at these places.]

For these reasons anger seized the Senate and arrogance seized the people. Meanwhile, King Attalus of Asia, the brother of Eumenes, died and left the Roman people heirs by a written document. Thus the kingdom of Asia was added to the Roman Empire by testament.

Seeking the people’s favor at a price, Gracchus proposed a law that the money belonging to Attalus should be distributed among the people. When Scipio Nasica opposed him, Pompey too promised that he would prosecute Gracchus as soon as Gracchus left office. Gracchus, however, was striving to remain tribune of the plebs in the following year.

When popular riots broke out on the day of the elections, the nobility, inflamed at the instigation of Nasica, drove the plebs away with fragments of benches. Gracchus fled up the steps above the arch of Calpurnius; when his support was knocked away, he was struck by a piece of a bench and fell. Rising again, he was killed by another blow, a nail being driven into his brain. Two hundred others were also killed in that riot, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. Gracchus’s own corpse likewise decayed unburied.

Two years later, Publius Scipio, who on the previous day had publicly declared in an assembly concerning the danger to his life that he had learned threats were being made against him as he labored for his country by wicked and ungrateful men, was found dead the next morning. This was counted among the greatest disasters of the Romans, [Note: [Col. 0633] “they reckoned,” 9c.] especially since Africanus’s strength and moderation had such influence in that city that it was firmly believed that, while he lived, neither a social nor a civil war could easily arise.

It is said that he was killed by the treachery of his wife Sempronia, who was the sister of the Gracchi, lest, as I believe, a criminal family should be more savage in the destruction of its country amid the impious seditions of men than through the crimes of women as well.

The cause of his death was this. Gaius Carbo, tribune of the plebs, wishing to avenge the killing of Gracchus and stir up the sedition that had quieted down, asked Publius Scipio Africanus, who was returning after the capture of Numantia, what he thought about Gracchus’s death. Africanus replied that he thought Gracchus had been killed justly.

After this, Gaius Gracchus, the brother of that Gracchus who had already been killed in the riot, was made tribune of the plebs amid an upheaval and became a great calamity to the state. For after he had often stirred the Roman people into the bitterest seditions by gifts and excessive promises, he finally withdrew from the tribunate, and Minucius succeeded him.

When Minucius, Gracchus’s successor, overturned his predecessor’s measures and repealed the laws, Gaius Gracchus, accompanied by a huge crowd, ascended the Capitol with Fulvius Flaccus, where an assembly was being held. There, together with Flaccus and his two armed sons, he raised a tremendous disturbance.

On the other side, the former consul Decius Brutus and Lucius Publicius [Note: [Col. 0633] Ekkehardus formed this from the words of H. m.; he altered “from the Publician slope.”] stood against them amid a great struggle. Flaccus fought for a very long time. Gracchus, withdrawing into the temple of Minerva, tried to fall upon his sword, but was restrained by the intervention of Laetorius. [Note: [Col. 0633] “of the lictor,” 11.]

When the battle remained uncertain for a long time, archers sent by Opimius finally scattered the massed crowd. The two Flacci, father and son, having leapt through the temple of Luna into a private house and barred the doors, were pierced and fastened to an [uncertain reading: “aretician grating”] wall. [Note: [Col. 0633] Thus all the manuscripts I have seen—that is, “by an Aretician grating”? In the *Historia Miscella* and in 11 one reads: “They were pierced after the latticework wall had been torn down.”] [Note: [Col. 0633] “to the wall,” 5.]

While his friends fought for him for a long time and perished, Gracchus with difficulty reached the Subsilician Bridge. There, so that he would not be captured alive, he offered his neck to his slave. His severed head was brought to the consul, while his body was carried to the town of Misenum, to Cornelia his mother.

This Cornelia was the daughter of the elder Africanus. After the death of her first son Gracchus, she withdrew to Misenum. Gracchus’s property was confiscated. Flaccus, still a young man, was killed in prison. It is reported that two hundred from Gracchus’s faction were slain on the Aventine Hill.

The consul Opimius, as brave in war as he was cruel in the investigation, had more than three thousand people killed by punishments; among them many innocent people were killed without even having had their case stated. This was the sedition of the Gracchi, and this was its end.

In the six-hundred-and-thirty-seventh year from the founding of the City, which was the twenty-eighth year of Ptolemy Euergetes II, during the consulship of Publius Scipio Nasica and Lucius Calpurnius Bestia, the Senate, with the consent of the Roman people, declared war against Jugurtha, who was invading the kingdom of the Numidians. Sallustius Crispus wrote about this at the greatest length. [Col. 0634B]

In these times the wretched life of Ptolemy Euergetes II produced an even more wretched end to his life. For he first cast off his sister, with whom he had been sexually involved and whom he had then taken in marriage; finally, in an even more shameful act, he rejected the woman whom he had married. He took his stepdaughter—that is, the daughter of his sister and wife—as his own wife. He killed the son whom he had fathered by his sister, as well as the son of his brother. Therefore, detestable on account of such incest and parricides, he was expelled from the kingdom by the Alexandrians in the twenty-ninth year of his reign.

*(Jerome.)* At this time Cicero was born at Arpinum. His mother was named Helvia and belonged to the royal family of the Volscians, while his father was of equestrian rank. The poet Marcus Furius, surnamed Bibaculus, was also born at Cremona.

[Col. 0634C] Ptolemy, also called Physcon or Soter, reigned at Alexandria for seventeen years, beginning in the year 407 after the restoration of the Temple. Later, after being expelled from the kingdom by his mother Cleopatra, he withdrew to Cyprus and returned to the kingdom again after several years.

Antiochus, also called Gryphus, the son of Demetrius, reigned in Syria. But his brother Antiochus Cyzicenus, the son of Antiochus, the brother of Demetrius, by the same woman Cleopatra, expelled his brother and reigned himself. Again, after his brother had driven him out, the former recovered the kingdom. Thus they contended with one another for nineteen years, and as a result that kingdom did not remain independent but passed into Roman control.

[Col. 0634D] Aristobulus, the son of John Hyrcanus, assumed the leadership of the Jews after his father and was the first to place a crown upon himself. He reigned for one year.

*(Josephus, Jewish War I.3.)* Alexander, also called Jannaeus, the brother of Aristobulus, assumed the high-priesthood of the Jews together with the kingdom after his brother’s death and reigned over his fellow citizens with the utmost cruelty for twenty-seven years. [Note: [Col. 0633] “and twenty-eight years,” 9c.]

For in six years of warfare he killed no fewer than fifty thousand of his own people. He also killed one of his own brothers, while he kept the other, stripped of everything, with him in a contemptible life. [Note: [Col. 0635] “one of them,” missing, 5.] When he died in the twenty-seventh year, he left the government of the kingdom to his wife Alexandra, also called Salina, together with her two young sons.

Anyone wishing to know his deeds in greater detail should take care to read the thirteenth book of Josephus’s history of antiquities.

[Col. 0635A] *(Jerome.)* Ptolemy, also called Alexander, after Ptolemy Physcon had been expelled from the kingdom by his mother Cleopatra, reigned at Alexandria for nine years, beginning in the year 424 after the restoration of the Temple.

[Col. 0635B] *(II. m. and H. R.)* In the six-hundred-and-fifty-ninth year, which was the fourth year of Ptolemy Alexander, when almost all foreign wars had ceased—Jugurtha having been defeated in Numidia first by Metellus and then by Marius and Sulla, and the Cimbri and Teutons afterward by Marius and Quintus Catulus—the Picentes, Marsi, and Paeligni stirred up a very serious war in Italy. [Note: [Col. 0635] “of the Picentines,” 5.]

They had already been subject to the Romans for many years. The Romans fought well against them under Gaius Marius, who had already been consul six times, and under Gnaeus Pompey, but especially under Lucius Cornelius Sulla. Among his other distinguished achievements, Sulla routed Cluentius, the enemy commander, with such a large force that he did not lose a single one of his own men. [Note: [Col. 0635] “one man,” 4; “not one,” 11.]

This war, prosecuted amid grave calamity for four years, finally ended in the fifth year through Lucius Cornelius Sulla, then consul, who had previously acted with valor as praetor in the same war.

At that very time dreadful prodigies were seen. At sunrise, a globe of fire flashed from the north with an immense crashing of the sky. At Arretium, during a banquet, blood flowed from loaves as though from wounds in human bodies. For seven continuous days, a storm of stones, mixed also with fragments of pottery, battered the earth over a very wide area. In the regions of Samnium, flame burst from an enormous fissure in the earth and seemed to extend all the way to heaven.

At that time animals of every kind that ordinarily live among human beings also abandoned their stalls and pastures and fled to the forests and mountains with miserable bleating, neighing, and groaning. Dogs, whose nature is such that they cannot exist outside human company, wandered about with tearful howling like wolves.

There was no delay: civil wars followed these grave prodigies.

[Col. 0636A] In the six hundred and sixty-second year from the founding of the City, the Social War was stirred up throughout Italy, with many opposing it, and an internal war was added to it; manifold disasters disturbed the Roman people, although the Romans were already called masters of many nations. The cause of the civil war was provided by Marius, who was consul for the sixth time. For when the consul Sulla was sent to wage war against Mithridates, who had invaded Asia and Achaea, but was still keeping his army for a short while in Campania so that the remnants of the Social War—which, as we said above, had been waged in Italy—might be eliminated, Marius sought to have himself sent against Mithridates when a seventh consulship had been entrusted to him. At this Sulla was angered; he came to the City with his army and, before the City, killed Marius’s lieutenant as though he were the first victim of the civil war. Soon afterward he burst into the City and, fighting against Marius and Sulpicius, killed Sulpicius, put Marius to flight, and, having arranged Gnaeus Octavius and Cornelius Cinna as consuls for the following year, departed for Asia.

But Marius, after unsuccessfully attempting to stir up the nobility, inflame the plebs, and arm the equestrian order against Sulla [Note: [Col. 0635] missing in 9c.], finally withdrew to the Capitol. There, however, he was severely crushed by Sulla’s party; he escaped from them, and, surrounded by the relentless pursuit of his pursuers, hid himself in the marshes of the people of Minturnae. From there, miserably covered with mud and dragged out in disgrace, he was led to Minturnae as a shameful spectacle and thrust into prison. The executioner sent to him was terrified by his mere look. [Note: [Col. 0635] *missus* (“sent”) 5.]

Then, having slipped free of his bonds, [Col. 0636C] he fled to Africa, and, having summoned from Utica his son Marius, who was being held under guard there, he immediately returned to Rome and joined the consul Cinna in a partnership of crimes. Thus, having gathered an army, they entered Rome, killed the most distinguished men of the Senate and men who had held the consulship, and proscribed many others. After Sulla’s own house had been destroyed, they forced his wife and children to flee. The entire remainder of the Senate, fleeing from the City, came to Sulla in Greece and begged him to aid his homeland. He immediately crossed over into Italy.

When Marius had seized a seventh consulship, and Cinna was already consul for the third time, Marius was finally carried off by a lingering death at the beginning of his seventh consulship. Cinna, however, was killed by his own army.

On Sulla’s return, after the consuls at Rome had already been changed, Marius, the son of Marius, and Papirius Carbo had assumed the consulship. Fighting against the younger Marius, Sulla killed 15,000 men and lost 400 of his own. Soon afterward, having entered the City, he killed 3,000 unarmed men despite the pledge he had given. When he was raging with great cruelty against the guilty and the innocent alike, Quintus Catulus said openly to Sulla: “With whom, then, are we ultimately going to live, if in war we kill armed men and in peace unarmed men?”

Thus Sulla pursued Marius, the son of Marius, to Praeneste, besieged him, and drove him to death. After this he celebrated a triumph over Mithridates with immense glory. [Col. 0637A]

(H. m.) Gnaeus Pompey, at the age of twenty-four, triumphed from Africa—a distinction that had been granted to no Roman.

After many crimes, Sulla was made dictator, so that the lust for domination and cruelty might be concealed beneath the reverence attached to an honorable title. At last, however, deprived of power, he died. Thus the two most disastrous wars—the Italian Social War and Sulla’s Civil War—were finally brought to an end.
