Prolonged for ten years, they consumed more than 150,000 Romans.

(HIER.) In these times Terentius Varro, at the age of thirty-five, learned literature with the greatest zeal. Cicero, having defended Roscius against Chrysogonus [Note: [Col. 0637] The manuscripts have *pro Roscio* (“for Roscius”) instead of *Rustico*.], withdrew to Athens; then, after three years, he returned to Rome and, in the twenty-sixth year of his life, also defended Quintius. [Col. 0637B]

At this time Plotius Gallus was the first to teach Latin rhetoric at Rome; Cicero also mentions him. Lucius Pomponius of Bononia, a writer of *catillarum* [“little bowls,” perhaps a corrupt reading; Note: [Col. 0637] the manuscripts have *Atellanarum*], was then prominent. The poet Lucretius was also born. After drinking a love potion, he was driven into madness and wrote several books during intervals of his insanity; Cicero later corrected them. Crispus Sallustius, the historian, was also born. Virgil Maro was born in a village called Andes, not far from Mantua. Portius Cato was recognized as a Stoic philosopher.

At this time Apollodorus of Pergamum, a Greek orator and teacher of Callidius and Augustus, was held in renown. Horace Flaccus was born at Venusia to a freedman father; he later became a satiric and lyric poet. Virgil was educated at Cremona; afterward, having assumed the toga, he crossed over to Milan, and after a short time proceeded to Rome.

(HIER.) Ptolemy Physcon, who had been expelled by his mother, returned from exile and recovered the kingdom, because the citizens expelled Alexander, who had reigned after driving him out, on account of his mother’s murder. He afterward reigned for eight years, beginning in the 433rd year from the restoration of the Temple.

Ptolemy Dionysius, Cleopatra’s brother, reigned at Alexandria for thirty years, beginning in the 441st year from the restoration of the Temple.

When Alexander, the ruler of the Jews, had died, his wife Alexandra, who was also called Salina, [Col. 0637D] held the kingdom of the Jews for nine years. (*Josephus, Jewish War* I.4.) Since she had two sons born to Alexander, she declared Hyrcanus, the elder by age, high priest and appointed him king after her because of his mildness; but she wished the younger, Aristobulus, to live as a private citizen, because he was of a more impetuous character.

While Alexandra was administering the kingdom for nine years, she fell ill. Then her younger son Aristobulus, with his servants—of whom he had many, and all of whom were utterly loyal because of his youthful ardor—seized all the fortresses. Having hired auxiliaries with the money he found there, he declared himself king. Moved by the complaints occasioned by this, Hyrcanus’s mother shut Aristobulus’s wife [Col. 0638A] and children inside a certain fortress; but she died before she could fully avenge Hyrcanus’s wrongs.

[Col. 0638A] Hyrcanus, the son of Alexander Jannaeus and Alexandra Salina, assumed the kingdom of the Jews after his mother’s death, which she had entrusted to him. But his brother Aristobulus, driven by jealousy, attacked and expelled him. This dissension brought about the entry of Roman commanders into Judaea; and, with Pompey’s approval, Hyrcanus recovered the principate. After administering it for thirty-three years, he was captured by the Parthians through the counsel of Antigonus, his brother’s son. Thus the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews came to an end. For Antigonus himself, having received the principate from the Parthians, was killed by the Romans, [Col. 0638B] and the principate was transferred to foreigners. [Note: [Col. 0637] *transiit* (“passed over”) 5.]

Years from the beginning: 3900.

(H. m. and H. R.) In the six hundred and eighty-first year from the founding of the City, which is the ninth year of Ptolemy Dionysius, there were only two serious wars in the Roman empire [Note: [Col. 0637] *in imperio* (“in the empire”) 5.]: the Mithridatic and the Macedonian. The two Luculli were conducting them: Lucius Lucullus the Mithridatic War, and his cousin Marcus Lucullus the Macedonian.

Lucius Lucullus, having crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris, engaged Mithridates and, with a small force of his own men, killed 30,000 of the enemy. Mithridates, accompanied by scarcely 150 men, fled, throwing away his diadem and tiara [Note: [Col. 0637] *cythara* (“lyre”) 9c.] so that he would not be recognized. His camp was plundered, and Lesser Armenia, which he had held, was taken from him. While he was fleeing, he was received by Tigranes, king of Armenia, who at that time ruled with immense glory. Lucullus, pursuing the routed enemy, entered Tigranes’ kingdom as well, and defeated him when he rebelled so completely that he destroyed a large part of Armenia.

The other Lucullus, who governed Macedonia, was the first of the Romans to wage war against the Bessi. After defeating them and many other peoples, he conquered all Macedonia and returned victorious.

At the same time Metellus waged war against the island of Crete for two years and reduced it to the power of the Romans; he exchanged the laws of Minos for Roman laws, and from Crete was therefore also called “Creticus.”

[Col. 0638D] At this time Libya also was being added to the Roman empire by the testament of Appion, who was then its king. In it were the famous cities of Berenice, Ptolemais, and Cyrene.

While these things were taking place, pirates [Note: [Col. 0637] *pyrati* 5.] scattered throughout all the seas not only intercepted the traffic of ships but also devastated islands and provinces. Gnaeus Pompey, to whom the war against them was entrusted, suppressed them within a few months with immense success and remarkable speed.

Afterward, having become Lucullus’s successor, he severely afflicted Mithridates through repeated attacks. At that time Castor, Mithridates’ prefect who was in charge of Phanagoria, killed the king’s friends, seized the citadel, and sent four of Mithridates’ sons to the Roman garrisons. Mithridates, inflamed with anger, erupted into crimes. For, after killing many of his friends, he killed his son Exipodras, although he had already slaughtered another son, Mochares. [Note: [Col. 0639] *suum* (“his”) is missing in 9c.]

Pharnaces, however, his son, terrified by the example of his brothers, won over to himself the army that his father had sent to pursue him, and immediately led it against his father by a just judgment, since he too had contended with his own father over the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0639] *de regno* (“over the kingdom”) is missing in 9c.]. Meanwhile Mithridates, after long and unsuccessfully pleading with his son from the top of a very high wall, when he saw him to be inexorable, is said to have cried out as he was about to die:

“Since Pharnaces commands me to die, I beg you, ancestral gods, that whenever he himself hears this voice from his children, he may suffer the same.”

Then he immediately went down to his wives, concubines, and daughters and gave poison to them all. After he himself had drunk it last of all, he still could not be killed by the poison, because he had often fortified his vital organs against harmful substances with antidotes. As he wandered about in vain, seeking some way by which the infused poison, carried through his veins by the body’s movement, might at last spread, he invited a certain Gallic soldier, who was running about after the wall had been breached, [Note: [Col. 0639] *invasit* (“attacked”) 9c.] and offered him his throat.

Such was the end that Mithridates had: a man, as they say, exceedingly superstitious, who spoke in the languages of twenty-two peoples that he held under his kingdom, so that he never heard embassies through interpreters. He died near the Bosporus, a man of immense judgment and industry. He reigned for forty years and lived for seventy-two, always keeping philosophers and men most skilled in every art with him. He waged war against the Romans for forty years—or, as others say, thirty. [Col. 0639C]

After Pompey received the news of Mithridates’ death, he waged war against Tigranes. But Tigranes surrendered himself to him [Note: [Col. 0639] *se ei* (“himself to him”) 5.] and, having fallen at Pompey’s knees, placed his diadem in Pompey’s hand. [Note: [Col. 0639] *Pompei* (“of Pompey”) 9c.] Pompey returned it to him and treated him honorably, though he took away part of his kingdom and imposed a heavy monetary penalty because he had made war on the Romans without cause. (*Josephus, Jewish War* I.5.)

Meanwhile he sent Scaurus as his lieutenant into Syria and entrusted to him all the affairs to be conducted there. When Scaurus came to Damascus and heard what was being done in Judaea between the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus [Note: [Col. 0639] *agebantur* (“were being conducted”).], he headed there. When envoys of both brothers came to him, he accepted 300 talents from Aristobulus [Col. 0639D] and favored his side, placing justice after money. [Note: [Col. 0639] *postposita* (“placed after”) 5.]

Meanwhile Pompey, after conquering Armenia and all those regions and arranging everything according to his wishes, turned aside into Syria and then came to Damascus. A certain Antipater, an Idumaean by origin, a leading man among his people because of his wealth and abundance of other resources, and long hostile to Aristobulus, urged Hyrcanus to go to Pompey. When Hyrcanus came to him and gave him substantial gifts, he won Pompey over to his side.

(H. m.) As Pompey proceeded toward Jerusalem, resistance from Aristobulus’s party led him to begin a siege. He captured the city only with difficulty in the third month and killed 14,000 Jews. The rest of the multitude submitted. He ordered the city walls to be demolished and leveled to the ground; their circuit is said to have been 4,000 paces. (*Josephus, Jewish War* I.5.)

Pompey entered the Temple with his companions—a deed over which the Jews nevertheless grieved most deeply—and inspected everything inside: the sacred vessels, the candelabra, and the accumulated mass of spices and sacred money, amounting to nearly 2,000 talents. Yet he touched neither these things nor anything else belonging to the sacred treasures. On the following day after the destruction, he ordered the Temple attendants to cleanse the Temple so that it might contain no filth and so that the solemn rites might be celebrated.

He himself struck with the sword those who had been chiefly responsible for the war, but he rewarded with splendid gifts those who had acted bravely with him. He declared Hyrcanus high priest and imposed tribute on the other Jews.

After this, entrusting all affairs from the Euphrates River to the borders of Egypt to Scaurus, Pompey himself hastened to Rome, taking with him Aristobulus as a captive, together with his two daughters and two sons. One of them, Alexander, escaped on the journey; the younger, Antigonus, was brought to Rome with his sisters and father. (*ibid.*, chapter 6.)

Alexander, having gathered a force of about 10,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry, pressed Hyrcanus hard and ravaged Judaea. Meanwhile Gabinius, sent into Syria as Scaurus’s successor, fought against Alexander with a strong force. After losing 6,000 men in the battle, Alexander took refuge in the fortress of Alexandrium. There, surrounded by a siege, he was compelled to ask for pardon and surrender the fortress.

Gabinius, however, destroyed all the fortresses and, on the advice of Alexander’s mother, brought Hyrcanus to Jerusalem. He entrusted the care of the Temple to him and placed the leading men in charge of the other parts of the state. He divided the entire Jewish people into five judicial districts: one at Jerusalem, another at Doris, the third at Amathus, the fourth at Jericho, and the fifth at Sepphoris, a city of Galilee. Freed from the single domination of one man, the Jews willingly allowed themselves to be governed by the leading men.

(H. R.) In the six hundred and eighty-ninth year from the founding of the City, which is the seventeenth year of Ptolemy Dionysius, during the consulship of Marcus Tullius Cicero, the orator, and Gnaeus Antonius, the events that Crispus Sallustius wrote about Catiline and his associates took place.

[Col. 0640D] (H. m.) In the following year, which is the 690th from the founding of the City, during the consulship of Decimus Junius Silanus and Lucius Murena, [Note: [Col. 0639] *decio* 4, 10, 11.] Metellus celebrated a triumph over Crete, and Pompey over the pirate and Mithridatic wars. No triumphal procession had ever been like it. The sons of Mithridates, the son of Tigranes, and Aristobulus from Judaea were led before Pompey’s chariot. An immense quantity of gold and an unlimited amount of silver were carried in procession. At this time there was no serious war.

In the 693rd year from the founding of the City, Gaius Julius Caesar, who afterward ruled, was made consul with Lucius Bibulus. [Col. 0641A] Transalpine Gaul, Cisalpine Gaul, and Illyricum were assigned to him, with ten legions granted for five years; Long-haired Gaul was afterward added by the Senate.

Caesar therefore set out for Gaul and fought many battles with the Gauls and Germans. Though often defeated and more often victorious, he subjected all Gaul, the Suebi—a most savage people, whom many writers report to have had 100 districts—and all Germany to Roman rule. For nine years he subdued almost the whole of Gaul, which lies between the Alps, the Rhône, and the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0641] *renumque* 4, 9c, 10, almost always], and the Ocean, and whose circuit is said to extend for 3,000,000 paces from these boundaries. Then he came to the Marini [Note: [Col. 0641] *morinos* 4; *marinas* 10, 11], from whom the nearest and shortest crossing to Britain is found, and he made war on the Britons [Note: [Col. 0641] thus the manuscripts], to whom even the name of Rome had previously been unknown. [Col. 0641B] There he was first wearied by a bitter battle, but at last defeated them, not without great danger to his men, in the year 50 before the Lord’s incarnation, as Bede writes (that is, A. 1. 2.). Suetonius Tranquillus explained this history most fully.

In the 697th year from the founding of the City, which is the twenty-fifth year of Ptolemy Dionysius, Marcus Licinius Crassus, colleague of Gnaeus Pompey the Great in his second consulship, drew by lot the province against the Parthians. A man of insatiable greed, having heard of the wealth of the Temple of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0641] *templi* (“of the Temple”) is missing in 9c.], which Pompey had left untouched, he turned aside into Palestine, went to Jerusalem, entered the Temple, and plundered its riches.

From there, proceeding through Mesopotamia into Parthia, wherever he traveled he imposed levies of auxiliary troops on allied cities and exacted payments. As soon as he crossed the Euphrates, he encountered Bajasen [reading uncertain], a lieutenant sent to meet him by Orodes, king of the Parthians [Note: [Col. 0641] *Herode* 4, 9c, 10]. Bajasen fiercely rebuked him for crossing the Euphrates, driven by greed and contrary to the treaty of Lucullus and Pompey, and warned that before long he would be loaded with Parthian iron in exchange for Seric (silk-country) gold [Note: [Col. 0641] *syrico* 9c, corrected to *sirico* or *serico* 5.].

When they had come near Carrhae, the Parthians suddenly attacked with Surena and the prefects Salaces, and overwhelmed the Romans with arrows. Many senators fell there, as did several former consuls and former praetors. Crassus’s son also, an exceptionally distinguished young man, was killed in the battle. In addition, four cohorts with the lieutenant Vargunteius were caught in the middle of the plain and killed.

Surena, taking the cavalry, began to pursue Crassus. After surrounding him and killing him when he unsuccessfully sought a conference—although Surena would have preferred to take him alive—he left only a few survivors, who escaped by night and fled to Carrhae. (Cf. Orosius VI.13; cf. Jordanes, *De rebus*.)

For the greed of one man grew into such a crime that twelve Roman legions were either captured, with only a few escaping, or slaughtered together with their commanders. Crassus’s head, together with his right hand, was carried to the king and became an object of mockery to those watching. The king ordered gold to be poured into the open mouth of Crassus’s head, saying: “Let the Parthian gold that burned you while you were alive burn you now.”

Made more arrogant by this success, the Parthians decided to cross into Syria. (*Josephus, Jewish War* I.6.) Cassius bravely received them in ambush and drove them from the borders of the province entrusted to him. Then he invaded Judaea and, after destroying Taricheae, sold 30,000 Jews into slavery.

Antipater, whom I mentioned above as a supporter of Hyrcanus, took as his wife a woman named Cypros, born to the most distinguished rank among the women of Arabia [Note: [Col. 0641] *arabias* 9c.]. By her he had four sons—Phasael, Herod, Joseph, and Pheroras—and a daughter named Salome. Having won the favor of Gabinius through gifts and services, he also gained Cassius’s friendship. For the sake of so many sons, he became a distinguished man, able to win by gifts an alliance with powerful men.

[Col. 0642B] Josephus gives this testimony about him. But Africanus, the leading historian (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* I.4), says:

“They say, those who carefully investigated the matter, that a certain Antipater was the father of Herod the Ascalonite, and that this Antipater himself had been the son of a certain Herod, a sacristan of the Temple of Apollo. This Antipater, captured as a very young boy by Idumaean brigands, remained with the robbers because his father, being unable to support his household, could not ransom his son. But the boy, having been trained in the life and customs of robbers, became a friend of a certain Hyrcanus, the Jewish high priest. From him was born Herod, the one who lived in the time of the Savior.” [Note: [Col. 0641] *is* (“the one”) 9c.]

This is Africanus.

(H. m. and H. R.) In the seven-hundredth year from the founding of the City, which is the twenty-eighth year of Ptolemy Dionysius, a fire of uncertain origin invaded a very large part of the City. They report that the city had never before been seized and devastated by so great a conflagration, for they say that fourteen of its districts were consumed.

After this there followed a civil war, detestable and lamentable, which had already long been prepared by dissensions and schemes. In addition to the disasters that occur in wars, the fortune of the Roman people was also changed. For Caesar, returning victorious from Gaul, demanded that a second consulship be decreed to him in his absence. But the consul Marcellus opposed him, with Pompey and Cato [Note: [Col. 0641] *cattone* 5.] supporting the opposition. Caesar was ordered to come to Rome only after dismissing his armies [Note: [Col. 0641] *non nisi dimissis* (“only after dismissing”) 9c.], and, by the authority of the consul Marcellus, Gnaeus Pompey was sent with military command to the legions that were at Luceria.

[Col. 0642D] Because of this injustice Caesar withdrew to Ravenna. Marcus Antonius and Publius Cassius, tribunes of the plebs, intervened on Caesar’s behalf, but were barred by the consul Lentulus from the senate house and the forum; they therefore went to Caesar, accompanied by Curio and Caelius.

Caesar came against his homeland with the soldiers he had. After crossing the Rubicon River, as soon as he reached Ariminum [Note: [Col. 0641] *arriminum* 5.], with the five cohorts that alone he then possessed—“with which,” as Livy says, “he attacked the whole world”—he explained what needed to be done, lamenting his wrongs and declaring that the cause of the civil war was the restoration of the tribunes to their homeland.

Then, through Antonius, he received from Lucretius the seven cohorts that were stationed at Sulmo [Note: [Col. 0643] *Salmonem* 9c.]. He brought over to his side the three legions that were stationed with Domitius at Cornificium. The consuls, however, together with Gnaeus Pompey, the entire Senate, and all the nobility, fleeing from the City and crossing into Greece, prepared a war against Caesar at Dyrrachium; many kings of the East [Note: [Col. 0643] *reges orientis* (“kings of the East”) 5.] were gathering there with auxiliaries.

Caesar entered the City when it was empty, made himself dictator, and, after breaking open the doors, seized the money from the treasury that had been denied to him. From it he brought out 4,135 pounds of gold and nearly 900,000 pounds of silver.

From there he came to Massilia. Leaving Trebonius with three legions to besiege it, he hastened to Spain, which the Pompeian commanders Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius, and Marcus Varro controlled. After defeating Petreius and Afranius in many battles, he dismissed them under an agreed settlement; in Further Spain he received two legions from Marcus Varro.

Similarly, his commanders expelled Cato from Sicily, Valerius expelled Cotta from Sardinia, and Varro expelled Tubero from Africa.

After settling his affairs, Caesar came to Dyrrachium and unsuccessfully besieged Pompey, since Pompey had access to the sea. Pompey destroyed a certain fortress near the sea where Caesar’s garrisons were stationed and killed the soldiers. Caesar, however, abandoned the siege and turned against Pompey. Torquatus, bursting forth, immediately pursued him as he retreated [Note: [Col. 0643] *aversus* (“turned away”) 5; *adversum* (“opposing”) 9c]. Thus Caesar’s soldiers, terrified by the danger on both sides, fled despite Caesar’s vain efforts to stop them. Caesar nevertheless escaped because night intervened and Pompey was unwilling to continue the pursuit.

Caesar said that Pompey did not know how to win, and that he could have been defeated only on that particular day.

In that battle 4,000 of Caesar’s soldiers were killed, as were twenty-two centurions and several Roman knights. Sceva, Caesar’s bravest soldier, was struck there; his shield is said to have been struck by 120 blows.

From there Caesar marched rapidly through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompey followed with the greatest forces, and battle was joined. It was a sight to behold and lament: the gathered forces of the Romans stood ready on the plains of Pharsalus for mutual slaughter. Had concord governed them, no peoples and no kings would have been able to withstand them [Note: [Col. 0643] thus 9c; *finire* (“bring to an end”) 4, 5, 10, 11].

On Pompey’s side there were eighty-eight cohorts, more than 40,000 infantry, [Note: [Col. 0643] *XL* (“40”) 9c.] 600 cavalry on the left wing and 500 on the right, as well as many kings, senators, and Roman knights. On Caesar’s side there were fewer than 40,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry.

For a long time both sides fought under uncertain fortune. On one side Pompey said, “Spare the citizens,” though he did not do so; on the other, Caesar did what he was pressing others to do, saying, “Soldier, strike the face.” At last Pompey’s entire army fled, and the camp was plundered. [Col. 0644A]

In that battle 15,000 Pompeians and thirty-three centurions were killed.

Pompey, fleeing, found a merchant ship at the mouth of the Peneus River and crossed into Asia. From there, by way of Cyprus, he headed for Alexandria, intending to receive aid from the king of Egypt, whom the Senate had appointed his guardian because of the king’s youth. But the king, following fortune rather than friendship, killed Pompey and sent his head and ring to Caesar.

When Caesar saw them, he is said to have shed tears as he looked upon the head of so great a man, once his son-in-law, and ordered it, after being covered with perfumes, to be burned. Pompey’s wife and sons fled. The rest of the Pompeian fleet was plundered, and everyone aboard it was cruelly slaughtered. Pompey the Bithynian was also killed there; Lentulus, a former consul, was killed at Pelusium.

After settling affairs in Thessaly, Caesar came to Alexandria, where Achillas, the king’s commander [Note: [Col. 0643] *regis* (“of the king”) 5.], having once been stained with Pompey’s blood, was also plotting Caesar’s death. For, when ordered to dismiss the army under his command—nearly 20,000 armed men—he not only refused but also drew up a battle line.

In the battle itself, the royal fleet was ordered to be hauled ashore and burned. When the flames spread to part of the city as well, they consumed 400,000 books stored in nearby buildings—a truly singular monument to the zeal and care of our ancestors, who had collected so many works of so many illustrious intellects.

Afterward Caesar captured the island where the Pharos is located. Achillas came there with the Gabinian soldiers. A great battle was fought, and a large number of Caesar’s soldiers fell there. All the assassins of Pompey were also killed.

Caesar too, pressed by the force of the attacking enemy, boarded a small boat. When it was soon weighed down and sunk by the burden of those following, he reached a ship by swimming for 200 paces, holding one hand above the water because it held his papers.

Soon afterward, attacked in a naval battle, he defeated or captured the royal fleet with great success. When the Alexandrians requested their king, he restored him to them, warning him that he should strive to test Roman friendship rather than arms. [Note: [Col. 0643] *studerent* (“they should strive”) 5.]

As soon as the king was free, however, he made war. He himself was immediately destroyed together with his entire army. For 20,000 men are reported to have been killed in that war, while 12,000, with seventy long ships, surrendered. Five hundred of the victors are said to have fallen.

[Col. 0644D] The young king himself, having boarded a small boat in order to flee, was drowned and killed when many people leaped into it. His body was washed ashore and recognized by means of his golden breastplate. Caesar, having sent it ahead to Alexandria, compelled all the Alexandrians to surrender in despair and gave the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra, Ptolemy’s sister, with whom he maintained an illicit relationship. She later entered the City with royal attendants.

Cleopatra, Ptolemy’s sister, reigned at Alexandria for twenty-two years, as Jordanes the bishop says (*De r. s.*). Tertullian, however, writes (*Against the Jews*, ed. Semler II, p. 296) that she reigned for only twenty years. He says that she reigned jointly with Augustus for thirteen years and that Augustus himself afterward reigned for another forty-three years, making fifty-six years of Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0645] *anni Augusti* (“years of Augustus”) 4, 10, 11; missing in 5.]

Although Cleopatra’s reign is said to have lasted so many years, in the sequence of kings only two are counted, because in her third year Gaius Julius Caesar seized the Roman empire. (Jordanes, cited above.)

This Cleopatra was later taken up by the Roman commander Antonius and joined to his side; he rejected Octavian’s sister and fought against his own fellow citizens. Octavian Augustus defeated him in battle on the Actian shore and compelled both spouses to kill themselves. Thus their kingdom passed into the Roman empire. There, even to the present and until the end of the world, according to the prophecy of Daniel, the succession of the kingdom is destined to remain.

[Col. 0645B] The Roman empire began with Gaius Julius Caesar.

(HIER.) Octavian, [Note: [Col. 0645] “These words are absent in 4 and 11.”] who was afterward called Augustus, the son of Atia, the sister of Julius Caesar, reigned for fifty-six years after Julius. From him Roman emperors were called Augusti.

From this time [Note: [Col. 0645] these words are absent in 4 and 11.], namely from the tenth year of Augustus, the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews, and the Christ—that is, the Anointed One—came to an end and have remained absent to the present time: Hyrcanus, the high priest, having been captured by the Parthians through the counsel of Antigonus, the son of his brother Aristobulus; Antigonus himself having been killed by the Romans; and Herod, a foreigner, having been established as king.

Antonius and Cleopatra killed themselves, and Egypt, reduced to a province, had Cornelius Gallus as its first Roman governor.

The kingdom of Alexandria came to an end. [Note: [Col. 0645] “The end of *Defecit regnum Alexandrinum* (‘the kingdom of Alexandria came to an end’) is absent in 5.]

(HIER.) Gaius Julius Caesar, from whom Roman rulers are called Caesars, was the first among the Romans to seize sole power, and he reigned for five years, from the founding of the City in its 705th year [Note: [Col. 0645] add “in the fifth year.”]. (H. m.) Having returned from Alexandria through Syria, he defeated Pharnaces, the son of Mithridates the Great; returning to Rome, he made himself dictator and consul for the third time together with Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, who had previously been his master of cavalry on account of the dictatorship. Then he set out for Africa, where an immense number of Roman nobles had renewed war against him at Thapsus together with King Juba of Mauretania. The Roman commanders were Publius Cornelius Scipio, of the ancient family of Scipio Africanus and also the father-in-law of Marcus Pompeius; Marcus Petreius Varrus [Note: [Col. 0645] “Varus” in 4.]; Marcus Porcius Cato; and Lucius Cornelius Faustus, son of the dictator Sulla.

When battle was joined against them, Caesar emerged victorious after many people had been slaughtered; their camp was plundered, and sixty elephants were captured. Cato killed himself with poison at Utica; Juba offered his throat to his executioner for a price; Petreius pierced himself with a sword [Note: [Col. 0645] “he pierced himself” in 5.]; and Scipio, in the ship by which he was fleeing toward Spain but which, driven by the wind, had returned to Africa, cut his own throat. Torquatus was also killed on the same ship. Caesar ordered the grandsons of Pompey the Great and his daughter Pompeia [Note: [Col. 0645] “Pompeia, and together with them the grandsons” in 5.] to be killed, along with Faustus, the son of Sulla, and Petreius and Afranius.

After a year he entered Rome with four triumphs, was created dictator and consul for the fourth time, and alone assumed the monarchy of the entire realm. From this arose the continuous succession of Roman emperors. Having thus restored and reorganized the state, he immediately set out for Spain against Gnaeus Pompeius and Sextus Pompeius, the sons of Pompey the Great, and waged many wars with varying success. The final war was fought at the river Munda, where the struggle was so fierce and the slaughter so great that Caesar himself, when even his veterans did not hesitate to give way, wished to kill himself, lest after so much military glory he should fall into the power of young men, being then sixty-six years old.

At last, after his forces had been reorganized, the army of the Pompeians suddenly turned and fled. Titus Labienus and Attius Varus were killed in battle; Gnaeus Pompeius fled with one hundred cavalrymen; and Sextus Pompeius, his brother, having rapidly gathered a considerable band of Lusitanians, engaged Cesonius, was defeated, and was killed while fleeing. This war was fought on the same day on which their father Pompey had earlier fled from the City in order to wage war, and for four years this civil war thundered throughout the world.

Thus, when Caesar had settled the civil wars throughout the world and was returning to Rome, he began to act more arrogantly, contrary to the custom of Roman liberty [Note: [Col. 0645] “to act more arrogantly” in 5.]. Since he bestowed honors according to his own will, although previously they had been conferred by the people, and did not rise for the senate when it came to him, and since he did other royal and almost tyrannical things, a conspiracy was formed against him by more than two hundred and sixty senators and Roman knights. The chief conspirators were the two Brutuses, descendants of that Brutus who had first been consul at Rome and expelled the kings; Gnaeus Cassius; and Servilius Casca.

One day, therefore, when the senate had assembled in the curia and Caesar had arrived, he was stabbed with twenty-three senatorial daggers. The authors of the murder immediately withdrew to the Capitol with drawn daggers. When the people were thrown into confusion, it was long debated whether the Capitol, together with the murderers, ought to be burned. The people seized his body and, driven by grief, burned it in the forum with fragments of platforms and benches.

On the very night preceding his murder, his wife Calpurnia saw in a dream that he lay in her lap, pierced by wounds. She begged him not to go to the senate in the morning, but he, often disregarding the words of omens, scorned the dream; the outcome, however, confirmed its meaning. A few days earlier, an ox had been sacrificed according to custom, but its heart was not found among the entrails. When the haruspex Spurinna declared that this concerned a danger to his life, Caesar, remembering his own steadfastness, said: “Are you surprised that an ox has no heart?” But shortly afterward his life came to an end.

The same Spurinna had told Caesar nearly a few years earlier that he should beware the Ides of March. When that day arrived, Caesar said to Spurinna: “The Ides of March have come.” He replied: “But they have not yet passed.” On that same day Caesar was stabbed—the man who had distinguished himself in war more than anyone ever had. Under his command, 1,192,000 men were killed. He did not wish to record how many he had destroyed in the civil wars. He fought fifty times in pitched battle, surpassing Marcus Marcellus alone, who had fought thirty-nine times [Col. 0647B]. No one wrote more quickly, and no one read more rapidly; he even dictated four letters at once. He was so compassionate that those whom he had subdued by arms he conquered more by clemency [Note: [Col. 0647] “might conquer” or “conquered” in 5.].

At the same time, three suns appeared together at Rome and gradually joined into a single circle. Among the other portents that occurred throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0647] “from that time” in 9c.], an ox spoke while plowing in the suburbs of Rome, saying that it was being driven forward in vain, for soon not grain but human beings would be lacking.

Octavian Caesar, later called Augustus—from whom and thereafter Roman emperors were called Augusti [Note: [Col. 0647] “Roman emperors” in 5.]—reigned for fifty-six years: twelve with Antony and Lepidus, but forty-four alone (Cf. HIER.). (H. m.) He was born to Octavius, a senator, and through his mother’s family received descent from Aeneas through the Julian family. He was the son of Atia, the sister of Julius Caesar, who adopted him as his son because he had no legitimate child of his own, left him his heir by his will, and ordered him to bear his name.

After his uncle Caesar had been killed [Note: [Col. 0647] “Julius Caesar” in 5.], when Octavian first entered the City on his return from Apollonia, at about the third hour, a circle suddenly surrounded the disk of the sun in a clear and cloudless sky, resembling a celestial rainbow. It seemed to show that the one who was to be born in his time would himself be the sole and brightest figure in the world, the one who would both create the sun itself and rule the whole world.

In the year 709 from the founding of the City, after Julius Caesar had been killed, the civil wars broke out again. The senate favored Caesar’s assassins, while Antony, the consul and a partisan of Caesar, tried to crush them through civil war. Thus, when the state had been thrown into confusion, among the many crimes Antony committed he shut Decimus Brutus up under siege at Mutina.

For this reason the senate declared him a public enemy and sent two consuls, Pansa and Hirtius, to defeat him, together with the young Octavian, who was seventeen years old [Note: [Col. 0647] “who was born at the age of seventeen” in 5.]. Pansa, arriving first, was severely wounded by a spear and died after several days. Hirtius, bringing aid to his colleague, destroyed Antony’s large forces in a vast slaughter. Caesar Octavian guarded the camp meanwhile. In a second battle against Antony, great slaughter occurred on both sides; the consul Hirtius was killed, and Caesar gained the victory. The armies of both slain consuls were placed under Caesar Octavian.

Antony, having been routed and having lost his army, fled to Lepidus, who had once been Caesar’s master of cavalry and then possessed large forces of soldiers. Lepidus received him, and through his intervention Caesar restored Antony to favor. As a pledge of this reconciliation, he took Lepidus’s daughter in marriage [Note: [Col. 0647] “in marriage” in 5.]. Then, wishing to avenge Caesar his father, whose heir he had been adopted by testament, he marched toward Rome with an army; together with Antony and Lepidus he held the state by force of arms and proscribed the senate [Note: [Col. 0647] missing in 4 and 9c.].

When rumor of the impending proscription arose in the City, Gaius Toranus [Note: [Col. 0647] “Thorans” in 9c.], a praetorian man who suspected nothing of the kind, was killed in his own house when the soldiers burst in. Many other nobles were also slaughtered [Note: [Col. 0647] “very many” in 5.]. But to prevent uncontrolled slaughter from proceeding even more wildly, the names of 132 senators were posted on a tablet: first at Lepidus’s command and under his name, then under Antony’s, and third under Caesar’s.

There Antony proscribed his enemy Marcus Tullius Cicero, as well as Lucius Caesar, his maternal uncle; and, to increase the crime, he proscribed his widowed mother. Lepidus threw his brother Lucius Paulus into the same group of the proscribed. Thirty Roman knights were later added (Cf. OROS. VI, 18.—H. m.). Many and various disasters continued for a long time; the houses of the proscribed were demolished after everything had been plundered.

Meanwhile Brutus and Cassius, the murderers of Gaius Caesar, stirred up a great war, for there were many armies throughout Macedonia and the East that they had seized. (H. R. and H. m.) Caesar Octavian and Marcus Antony therefore set out against them, while Lepidus remained behind to defend Italy. They fought them at Philippi, a city of Macedonia, and were defeated in the first battle; nevertheless Cassius, the leader of the nobility, perished. In the second battle they defeated and killed Brutus and an immense number of nobles. Thus the state was divided among them: Caesar held Spain, Gaul, and Italy; Antony held Asia, Pontus, and the East.

But Lucius Antony, the consul and brother of the man who had fought with Caesar against Brutus and Cassius, had stirred up civil war in Italy. He was defeated and captured at Perusia, a city of Tuscany, but was not killed. At Rome, however, Fulvia, Antony’s wife and Caesar’s mother-in-law, exercised domination like a woman, behaving arrogantly even toward those through whom she had become arrogant. She attacked Caesar with insults and plots; repelled by him, she withdrew to Antony in Greece. Antony, for his part, married Octavia, Caesar’s sister.

Meanwhile Sextus Pompeius, the son of Gnaeus Pompeius, stirred up a great war in Sicily. Caesar Octavian and Marcus Antony fought against him, but at last peace was arranged between them [Note: [Col. 0649] missing in 5, 9c, and 10.]. When Pompeius later broke it, Agrippa fought him at Caesar’s command and defeated him. He sank or captured 163 of his ships. Pompeius barely escaped with seventeen men.

Lepidus too, swollen with the arrogance of possessing twenty great legions, had plundered Messana after allowing it to his soldiers. When Caesar came to him, Lepidus twice rejected him and ordered that he be attacked with weapons. Caesar avoided them by gathering them up with his left arm and warding them off with his cloak. Soon he returned to his own men on horseback, organized his army, and advanced against Lepidus. He forced most of Lepidus’s legions, with only a few men killed, to pass over to his side. At last Lepidus understood where his vanity was leading. He laid aside his military cloak, put on a dark garment, and became a suppliant before Caesar. He obtained his life and property, though he was permanently corrected by exile. (Cf. OROS. l. l.; H. m.)

At this time Agrippa conducted affairs successfully in Aquitania, and Lucius Ventidius [Note: [Col. 0649] “Vendilius” in 9c.] Bassus defeated the Persians who were invading Syria in three battles. He killed the son of Orodes, king of the Parthians, on the very day on which Orodes had once killed Crassus through his commander Surena. Taurus, Caesar’s prefect, also brought almost the whole of Sicily, after it had been thoroughly ravaged by the sword, into submission. At that time forty-four legions were under Caesar’s sole command [Note: [Col. 0649] missing in 9c; “under his command” in 5.].

Because of this, soldiers made arrogant by their numbers had stirred up disturbances in order to receive land. But Caesar, great in spirit, discharged 20,000 soldiers, restored 30,000 slaves to their masters, and crucified 6,000 whose masters could not be found. [Note: [Col. 0649D] From “even then” through “would be punished” are Ekkehard’s words.] Even then he was foreshadowing that in his own time the one would be born through whom the arrogant would be restrained and all slaves restored to their true master—those, at least, who would recognize their master; those found without a master would be punished by the penalty of death. After this Caesar entered the City in an ovation and, so that he might possess tribunician power permanently, received it by decree of the senate.

In those days, across the Tiber, a spring of oil burst forth from a tavern and flowed in a very broad stream throughout the entire day. This signified that, under the perpetual rule of the one who was to be born, Christ would arise in his time, and that throughout the whole day—that is, at all times—those anointed with the oil of sacred chrism would continually proceed from the hospitable and generous Church of the Roman Empire [Col. 0649D] (Cf. OROS. VI, 20).

(H. m.) Antony, who held Asia and the East, captured Artabanes, king of Armenia, through treachery and deceit. Having bound him with a silver chain, he forced him to disclose the royal treasures. After capturing the city in which the treasures were located, he carried off a great quantity of silver and gold [Note: [Col. 0649] “gold and silver” in 5.]. Elated by his wealth, he declared war on Caesar, announced his repudiation of Octavia, Caesar’s sister, and ordered Cleopatra to meet him from Alexandria; he took her as his wife.

Soon he stirred up a great civil war, compelled by Cleopatra, who in her womanly desire wished also to rule in the City. Caesar therefore set out from Brundisium in Calabria toward Epirus against Antony, who already blockaded the entire coast of Actium with fleets. Caesar’s fleet consisted of 230 beaked ships and thirty triremes without beaks, with eight legions stationed aboard the fleet, apart from five praetorian cohorts. Antony’s fleet consisted of 170 ships; although inferior in number, it surpassed Caesar’s in size, for they rose ten feet above the sea.

This was a famous war. From the fifth hour until the seventh the outcome was uncertain, but for the rest of the day and through the following night it turned toward Caesar’s victory. Queen Cleopatra fled first with sixty swift ships. Antony too, after removing the standard from his praetorian ship, followed [Note: [Col. 0649] missing in 9c.] his fleeing wife. When day was already dawning, Caesar completed the victory.

Antony then pierced himself with a sword and, half alive, was carried to Cleopatra in the royal mausoleum, where she had shut herself away in preparation for death. Cleopatra, adorned with various ornaments, came to Caesar, hoping to entice him by her appearance, as she had done with others, into lust. But he confined himself within chastity, rejected her, and ordered her to be guarded. (JORD. De r. s.) When she understood that she was being reserved for the triumph, she escaped from custody and withdrew into her mausoleum. There, dressed in her richest garments, as was her custom, she placed herself beside Antony on a couch filled with perfumes. Applying serpents to her veins, she was released from life as though from sleep [Col. 0650C], although Caesar vainly sent in snake-charmers, who usually suck the poison of serpents from human wounds.

Thus Caesar Octavian gained possession of Alexandria, the richest of cities, together with the whole of Egypt. He placed Cornelius Gallus over Egypt, of whom Virgil writes. (HIER.—H. R.) Egypt had him as its first Roman governor.

(H. R. and H. m.) In the year 725 from the founding of the City, Caesar returned victorious from the East and entered the City on the eighth day before the Ides of January in a triple triumph. The children of Cleopatra, Sun and Moon, were led before his chariot. Then, for the first time, after all civil wars had been quieted, he closed the gates of Janus.

On that day Caesar was first hailed as Augustus, because he had increased the public realm. From that day the highest authority and power began to be in the hands of one man and remained there; the Greeks call this a monarchy.

In the following year Caesar Augustus, realizing that what had been undertaken in Spain over two hundred years had achieved little if he allowed the Cantabrians and Asturians, the two fiercest peoples of Spain, to live by their own laws, opened the gates of Janus again and himself set out with an army for Spain. There, near Tarraco [Note: [Col. 0649] “Tarragona” in 5.], a city of Hither Spain, envoys of the Indians and Scythians [Note: [Col. 0649] “Scythians” in 5.], having crossed the whole world [Col. 0651A], finally found him and transferred to Caesar the glory of Alexander the Great. For just as an embassy of the Spaniards and Gauls had approached Alexander in the middle of the East, at Babylon, in contemplation of peace, so the suppliant Indian and northern Scythian came to Caesar in Spain, at the westernmost end of the world, and prayed for peace.

After the Cantabrian war had been completed over five years and all Spain had been brought into everlasting peace, Caesar returned to Rome [Note: [Col. 0651] “approached” in 9c.]. He bestowed this honor on the Cantabrian victory: he again shut the gates with their bars. Thus Janus was closed a second time by Caesar, and for the fourth time since the founding of the City.

At no time before him did the Roman state flourish more, for he himself, both personally and through his commanders and envoys, added greatly to it by war. He personally added Egypt, Cantabria, Asturias, Dalmatia, Pannonia, and Aquitania to the Roman Empire. His stepson Drusus, having taken charge of Gaul and Raetia, subdued the greatest and strongest peoples by arms. He conquered the Susipeces, Teucteri, and Chatti [Note: [Col. 0651] “Chatti” in 9c; “Catthi” in 5; “Catti” in 10, 11, and t.] and drove them beyond the river Elbe, which in barbarian territory lies far beyond the Rhine. He nearly destroyed the Marcomanni. Later he defeated in a single war, though a difficult one for his own men, the strongest nations, whose power was given them both by nature and by their accustomed experience of their strength [Note: [Col. 0651] missing from all the manuscripts I have seen.]: the Cherusci, Suebi, and Sicambri.

Their courage and savagery can be judged from this: whenever their women were caught among their wagons during a Roman attack, if their weapons or any other object that their fury could use as a weapon failed them, they threw their little children, dashed against the ground, into the faces of the enemy.

Tiberius, Drusus’s brother, destroyed the Pannonians, who were swelling with a new uprising, in a most bloody slaughter. He immediately also took up war against the Germans and brought back 40,000 captives in victory. This was truly a great and terrifying war, conducted with fifteen legions over three years; as Suetonius testifies, scarcely any greater war had occurred after the Punic War.

At the same time, Quintilius Varus, propraetor with three legions, behaved with astonishing arrogance and greed toward his subjects beyond the Rhine. He was destroyed by the rebelling Germans together with his tribunes and legions. Caesar Augustus bore this disaster of the state so heavily that, disfigured by his clothing, hair, and all the other signs of mourners, and often in the force of his grief striking his head against a wall, he cried out: “Quintilius [Note: [Col. 0651] “Quintilian” in 9c.] Varus, give back the legions!”

In Africa also, Cossus, Caesar’s commander, confined the Musolani and the widely wandering Gaetuli within narrower boundaries and compelled them by fear to remain within the limits imposed by the Roman soldiers [Note: [Col. 0651] the manuscripts read this way; 11 has “to refrain from the boundaries.”]. Piso too was sent against the Vindelici. After subduing them, he came victorious to Caesar at Lugdunum.

Marcus Agrippa conquered the Bosphorans and, restoring in war the Roman standards that they had once taken from Mithridates, compelled the defeated people to surrender [Col. 0652A]. He recovered Armenia from the Parthians. The Parthians, as though they were being marked out in the eyes of everyone because the whole world had either been conquered or pacified and the entire force of the Roman Empire would have to be turned against them alone—for they were tormented by the memory of avenging the earlier killing of Crassus—voluntarily sent back to Caesar the standards they had taken after Crassus was killed. After giving hostages, they earned a firm treaty through faithful supplication [Note: [Col. 0651] “entered into” in 9c.].

Galatia too was made a province under him, although previously it had been a kingdom; Marcus Lollius was the first to administer it as propraetor. Caesar Augustus was held in such affection even among barbarians that kings, as friends of the Romans, founded cities in his honor and called them Caesareas after his name. Many kings also came from their kingdoms to serve him and, wearing Roman dress—that is, the toga—ran beside his carriage or horse.

He himself so detested crowds, wars, and quarrels that, except for just causes, he never declared war against any people. He said that to endanger the safety of citizens through the uncertain outcomes of battles, for the sake of triumphal ambition and a laurel crown—that is, fruitless leaves—was the mark of a boastful and very shallow mind, and that nothing was less fitting for a good commander than recklessness. Whatever was undertaken for the common good was completed sufficiently quickly [Note: [Col. 0651] the manuscripts read this way, instead of “conveniently,” which is found in the Historia miscella]. Arms should never be taken up unless there was hope of greater gain, lest a victory sought through slight profit resemble fishermen using a golden hook: if the hook breaks and is lost, the loss cannot be compensated by any profit from the catch.

Once established in power, he exercised tribunician authority personally. In the end, he was exceedingly merciful toward citizens and exceptionally faithful toward his friends. The chief among them were Maecenas, because of his discretion, and Agrippa, because of his modesty and endurance of labor. He also loved the poets Virgil and Flaccus, and devoted himself so intensely to liberal studies that no day passed, even on campaign, without his reading, writing, or dictating.

He issued some new laws in his own name and others corrected under his name. He enlarged and adorned Rome with many buildings, boasting in the saying: “I found a city of brick; I leave a city of marble.” He was gentle, agreeable, and civil in disposition; beautiful in his whole body, but especially in his eyes, whose gaze flashed like the brightest stars. When a certain soldier turned his eyes away from his face and was asked why he did so, he replied: “Because I cannot bear the lightning of your eyes.”

Yet so great a man was not free from faults. He was somewhat impatient, mildly irascible, secretly envious, openly factional, and extravagantly desirous of ruling; he was also devoted to dice. Though he abstained greatly from food and wine, and to some degree from sleep, he nevertheless indulged his lust to the point of becoming a reproach even in common rumor. For he was accustomed to recline among twelve catamites and an equal number of girls.

After putting away his wife Scribonia, he became possessed by love for another man’s wife and joined himself to Livia, as though her husband had granted her to him. Livia already had two sons, Drusus and Tiberius. Although he was devoted to luxury, he was nevertheless an exceedingly severe avenger of that same vice, like certain people who are harsh in punishing the faults to which they themselves give great indulgence. Thus he condemned the poet Ovid, also called Naso, to irrevocable exile because he had written three books on the art of love. He also took pleasure in every kind of spectacle, especially wild beasts of unfamiliar appearance.

In his time the outstanding wise men at Rome were Virgil, Horace Flaccus, Livy, Sallust, Ovid, Hortensius, Athenodorus of Tarsus, and Sitio of Alexandria.

## The Years of Augustus

1. In the 710th year from the founding of the City, Octavian Caesar began to reign. He reigned with Antony and Lepidus for twelve years and afterward alone for forty-four, making fifty-six in all. In his first year, at the command of the senate, he waged war against Antony and defeated him. (HIER.) In the same year, while many were being killed in vengeance for Caesar, Cicero was killed at his Formian estate by Herennius and Publius, in the sixty-fourth year of his life. In that same year Ovid Naso was born in the Pelignian territory.

2. Curtius Salassus was burned alive on the island of Aratus with four cohorts because he collected the taxes too harshly.

3. With the senate intervening, Octavian returned to friendship with Antony.

4. The poet Cornificius perished after being abandoned by the soldiers whom he often called “helmeted hares” when they fled. His sister was Cornificia, whose distinguished epigrams still survive.

5. The second separation of Caesar and Antony.

6. Cornelius Nepos, a famous historical writer, was held in high regard.

7. Formius was famous together with his son Formius, but the son, who had been a consul, died before his father [Note: [Col. 0653] missing in 9c.].

8. Brutus and Cassius, having assembled large armies, met near Athens and devastated the whole of Greece. Caesar and Antony, reconciled once more, pursued them into Macedonia and drove them to death. For, driven to despair, they inflicted premature death upon themselves before the end of the war. When the executioners had been summoned [Note: [Col. 0653] missing in 9c.], Cassius offered his head and Brutus his side [Note: [Col. 0653] missing in 5.].

9. The poet Varus, whom Virgil mentions in the Bucolics, died in Cappadocia.

10. Herod the foreigner, son of Antipater the Idumaean and Cypros the Arab woman, was made king of the Jews by the Roman senate at Antony’s urging. He reigned for forty-seven years [Note: [Col. 0653] “thirty-seven” in 5; “forty-eight” in 1b.].

To make himself more acceptable to the Jews [Note: [Col. 0653] “to make himself more acceptable to them” in 5.], he put away his wife, who was called Doris and by whom he had a son named Antipater, and joined himself to the royal line by taking Mariamne, daughter of Alexander, son of Aristobulus, the brother of Hyrcanus, the high priest and king. That same Alexander had fathered her by the daughter of Hyrcanus, his paternal uncle (Cf. HIER.—JOS. De b. J. I, 11).

(HIER.) From this year, which was the tenth of Octavian Caesar and the 718th from the founding of the City, but from the beginning of the world the 3,922nd, the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews ceased up to the present time, and the Christ—that is, the Anointed One—whom the Scripture of Daniel signifies, came to an end. (EUS. H. e. I, 5.—HIER. on Dan. ch. IX.)

For until Hyrcanus, son of Alexander Jannaeus, judges, priests, and kings ruled over the Jewish people in succession. But his brother Aristobulus expelled Hyrcanus from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0653] missing in 9c.]. Pompey, the leading Roman, restored him with the support of Antipater, Herod’s father, but took Aristobulus captive to Rome. When Hyrcanus was captured by the Parthians through the counsel of Antigonus, son of his brother Aristobulus, and that same Antigonus [Note: [Col. 0653] “the same” in 9c and 11.] was installed by those same Parthians in place of his uncle, but soon was himself captured and killed by the Romans or by Herod, (HIER.) Herod received the kingdom. From then on, high priests were no longer appointed by succession through the priestly line; instead, men of low birth and different individuals at different times held the office, and some purchased the priesthood for a single year or only a little longer.

Thus Herod summoned a certain Ananelus from Babylon and appointed him high priest. After a short time, however, he gave the office to Aristobulus, his wife Mariamne’s brother and Hyrcanus’s grandson through his daughter. After a year, Aristobulus was drowned in water by Herod’s own scheme, and Herod again restored the priesthood to Ananelus. Thus, through the various successions of outsiders, the priesthood of the Jews ceased to follow the succession of the priestly line.

The angel foretold all these things to Daniel in the following words:

“And you shall know and understand: from the beginning of the word about the restoration and rebuilding of Jerusalem until Christ the Leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two; and after seven weeks and sixty-two the anointing shall perish, and there shall be no judgment, and the people of the coming leader shall corrupt the temple and the sanctuary.” And so forth.

The seven and sixty-two weeks, which together make sixty-nine, amount to 483 years. During these years the christs—that is, priests consecrated through anointing—ruled from the restoration of the temple under Darius until Hyrcanus, in whom the anointing and priesthood of the Jews finally ceased. (HIER. on Dan. ch. IX.)

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Compare the same words above, col. 554.] That the seven and sixty-two weeks, that is, 483 years, are counted from the completion of the temple—this is [Note: [Col. 0653] “this is” missing in 9c.] from the sixth year of Darius—until [Note: [Col. 0653] missing in 5.] the tenth year of Augustus, we can establish as follows. In the first year of the sixty-sixth Olympiad, that is, in the sixth year of Darius, the building of the temple was completed; and in the second year of the 186th Olympiad, that is, in the tenth year of Augustus, Herod received the kingdom of the Jews. Between these dates there are 483 years, counting four years for each Olympiad.

## The Years of King Herod

11. 1. (HIER.) Sallust died four years before the Battle of Actium. The course of the moon was discovered this year according to the Romans.

12. 2. Antony, joined to Cleopatra, gave her Arabia.

13. 3. The beginning of the third disagreement between Octavian and Antony, because Antony, having repudiated Caesar’s sister, had married Cleopatra.

14. 4. Nicetes and Theodorus were regarded as teachers of the art of rhetoric.

15. 5. Antony and Cleopatra killed themselves, and Egypt became a Roman province. Until Cleopatra, those called the Ptolemies ruled it for 273 years [Note: [Col. 0655] “283” in 9c.]; Cleopatra herself ruled for twenty-two years, making 295 years in all.

16. 6. Nicopolis was founded near the promontory of Actium.

17. 7. [Note: [Col. 0655] “6. 4.” and thereafter the years are numbered one lower.] Octavian Caesar entered Rome in a great triumph. Cleopatra’s children, Sun and Moon, were led before his chariot, and on the same day he first received the name Augustus as the name of his triumph. In the same year the philosopher Marcus Terentius Varro died, nearly ninety years old.

18. 8. The poet Cornelius Gallus of Forum Julii, whom Virgil mentions in his final eclogue and who was the first to govern Egypt after it had been made a province, killed himself with his own hand in the forty-fourth year of his life.

19. 9. Augustus made Calabria and Gaul tributary.

20. 10. Marcus Gnatius Plaucius, Cicero’s pupil, was regarded as a distinguished orator. While governing Gallia Comata, he founded Lugdunum.

21. 11. Quintilius of Cremona, a friend of Virgil and Horace [Note: [Col. 0655] “Horace” in the manuscripts.], died.

22. 12. Pylades the Cilician, a pantomime performer, was the first at Rome to have a chorus and flute play before him.

23. 13. Tiberius, sent by Augustus, occupied Armenia.

24. 14. Herod built many large buildings at Jerusalem.

25. 15. Virgil died at Brundisium and was transferred to Naples. His tomb was marked with the following inscription [Note: [Col. 0655] “whose title” in h. and 9c.; a word seems to be missing.] which, they say, he dictated as he was dying:

> Mantua gave me birth; the Calabrians carried me off; now Parthenope holds me.  
> I sang of pastures, the countryside, and commanders.

26. 16. Herod built at Paneas what is called the temple of Pan.

27. 17. Augustus granted freedom to the Samians.

28. 18. Herod raised Samaria, which had long been lying in ashes, from its foundations and, in honor of Augustus, called it Sebaste—that is, Augusta.

29. 19. In Cyprus, parts of many cities collapsed in an earthquake.

30. 20. Varus and Tucca, companions of Virgil and Horace, were regarded as illustrious poets. Augustus later entrusted them with the books of the Aeneid to be corrected, on the condition that they add nothing of their own.

31. 21. Agrippa captured the Bosphorus.

32. 22. Augustus was named chief pontiff by the senate.

33. 23. Herod founded Caesarea in the name of Caesar; it had previously been called the Tower of Strato.

34. 24. Horace died at Rome in the fifty-seventh year of his life.

35. 25. Julius Hyginus, surnamed Polyhistor, was regarded as a distinguished grammarian.

36. 26. Herod killed Hyrcanus, who had once been priest and king of the Jews and had returned from Parthian captivity at Herod’s own request because of their former friendship [Note: [Col. 0655] “while he was reigning” in 9c; corrected to “at his request” in 1b.], fearing that he might recover the kingdom.

37. 27. Herod ordered Aristobulus, his wife Mariamne’s brother, to be strangled (Cf. JOS. XV, 3).

38. 28. (HIER.) Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson but already adopted as his son, triumphed after destroying the Vindelici, Armenians, and Pannonians.

39. 29. Augustus condemned his daughter Julia to exile after discovering her in adultery. Marcus Tullius Tiro, Cicero’s freedman, who was the first to devise shorthand notation, grew old at his estate near Puteoli and died there at nearly one hundred years of age.

40. 30. Porcius Latro, a Latin declaimer, killed himself out of weariness from a double quartan fever.

41. 31. (H. m.) Quirinus was sent to Judaea by decree of the senate and recorded a census of the people and their possessions. Augustus, having counted the inhabitants of the city of Rome by neighborhoods, found 137,000 men.

42. 32. In the forty-second year of his reign, which was the 750th from the founding of the City, Augustus Caesar, after arranging all nations in a single peace from east to west, from north to south, and throughout the entire circuit of the ocean to which Roman power extended, himself closed the gates of Janus for the third time. From then on they remained shut in the most peaceful leisure for nearly twelve years, so continuously that even rust marked them; afterward they were never opened except in Augustus’s extreme old age, when the uprising of the Athenians and the disturbance of the Dacians compelled it.

(H. m.) After the gates of Janus had been closed [Note: [Col. 0655] “already” in 4 and 9c.], Augustus devoted himself to nourishing and enlarging by peace the state that he had won by war. He was the first to establish laws by which the human race might conduct itself with free reverence; but as a man he avoided the title “lord.” For while he was watching the games, when a certain mime declared, “O just and good lord!” and everyone joyfully applauded as though the words had been spoken about Augustus himself, he immediately restrained the indecorous flattery with hand and expression. The next day, by a very severe edict, he rebuked everyone and afterward would not allow himself to be called “lord,” seriously or jokingly, even by his children or grandchildren [Note: [Col. 0657] 5 adds in red: “Here the years of the Lord’s incarnation begin.”].

(Chr. W. [Note: [Col. 0657D] That is, the Würzburg Chronicle edited above.]—H. m.) At that time, therefore—that is, in the forty-second year of Octavian Caesar Augustus, but in the twenty-eighth year from the reduction of Egypt to a province and the defeat of Cleopatra and Antony—when Caesar Augustus, by God’s providential ordering, established the firmest peace, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God [Note: [Col. 0657] “and man” is lacking in 9c.], was born in Bethlehem of Judah. This peace served him. The date was the 3962nd year from the beginning of the creation of the world according to the Hebrew text; according to the Seventy interpreters and their followers, the 5201st; the 2306th from the Flood; the 2014th from Abraham’s birth; the 1509th from Moses and the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt; the 1031st from Solomon and the first construction of the Temple; the 519th from its rebuilding under Darius; the 751st from the foundation of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0657] “of Rome” in 9c.]; and the third year of the 194th Olympiad [Note: [Col. 0657] lacking in 9c.] (cf. Bede).

| 34 | 44 | In the third year of the Lord, Herod kills the infants. |

[Note: [Col. 0657D–0658D] Ekkehard did not find this material thus in Josephus, but seems himself to have compiled it from various places (cf. also above, year 10).]

Herod had many sons by different wives, for he had married several. He had Antipater by Doris [Note: [Col. 0657] “Dosia” in 9c.], whom he had married before he became king; Aristobulus and Alexander, and two daughters, by Mariamne, the granddaughter of Hyrcanus through his daughter, whom he had taken in marriage from royal stock after he himself became king, having cast aside Doris and her son Antipater. Later, after they and others had brought accusations, he killed Mariamne; and he also killed her sons Alexander and Aristobulus, as though they were indignant at their mother’s death (cf. Josephus, *The Jewish War* I, 18).

Alexander had two sons, Tigranes and Alexander, by Glaphyra, daughter of Archelaus, king of Cappadocia. Aristobulus’s sons were Agrippa, who became king under Gaius, and Herod and Aristobulus; his daughter was Herodias, by his cousin Bernice, that is, the daughter of Salome, the sister of Herod, his father.

Herod also had other children: Antipas, Archelaus, and a daughter named Olympias by Martha the Samaritan; Herod by the daughter of Simon the high priest; Herod and Philip by Cleopatra of Jerusalem; and Phasaelus by Pallas.

After he had killed his sons Alexander and Aristobulus, who were of royal descent, he proposed by testament to leave Antipater, who had pleased him by accusing his brothers, as heir to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0657] Here begins the Berlin manuscript (E1.)]. But when Antipater himself was also said to be plotting his father’s death, Herod ordered him, after he had been thrown into prison [Note: [Col. 0657] “prison” is *carcere* in 5, 10, and 11.], to be killed when he was almost at the point of death; and, having changed his will, he named Archelaus as successor to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0657] “successor to the kingdom” is lacking in E1.].

Herod reigned thirty-four years after Antigonus was killed, and thirty-seven years from the time he had received the kingdom from the Romans. Thus, after many crimes, he died an evil death.

## Years of Archelaus

[Note: [Col. 0657] The years of the kings above are lacking in D and E.]

| 1 | 48 |
|---:|---:|
|  | (H. m.) In the seventh year of the Lord, which is Augustus’s forty-eighth, a famine arose at Rome so severe that Augustus ordered all foreigners and the great majority of slaves, except physicians and teachers, to be driven out of the city [Note: [Col. 0657] “ordered” is “might order” in E1.]. |

[Note: [Col. 0657] “A famine arose” is *r. f. est* in E1.]

It is believed that this famine was sent by divine agency because, when Augustus was sending his grandson Gaius to organize the provinces of Egypt and Syria, Gaius, passing from Egypt through the territory of Palestine, refused to worship at Jerusalem in the Temple of God, which was then holy and renowned. When Augustus learned this from him, he used a perverse judgment and praised him for having acted wisely. Thus divine vengeance struck the people together with their sinful ruler, and the nature of the punishment revealed the measure of the offense.

2. 49. (HIER.) In the eighth year of the Lord, Tiberius, having already become Caesar, brought the Dalmatians and Sarmatians back under Roman authority.

3. 50. (H. m.) In the ninth year of the Lord, which is Augustus’s fiftieth and the 758th from the foundation of Rome, fire consumed fourteen districts of the city; it is uncertain where the blaze began.

4. 51. (HIER.) In the tenth year of the Lord, the Athenians plot a revolt against the Romans.

5. 52. In the eleventh year of the Lord, the orator Messala Corvinus, two years before his death, lost his memory and understanding to such an extent that he could scarcely put a few words together.

6. 53. (Chr. W.) In the twelfth year of the Lord, the gates of Janus, which had now been closed for twelve years, were opened by Augustus.

7. 54. (HIER.) In the thirteenth year of the Lord, Satio [Note: [Col. 0657] “sitio” in 9c; “satio” corrected to “sitio” in 4.] the philosopher of Alexandria, Seneca’s teacher, became prominent.

8. 55. In the fourteenth year of the Lord, Augustus, conducting a census at Rome with Tiberius, found 9,370,000 inhabitants.

9. 56. In the fifteenth year of the Lord, which is the fifty-sixth of Augustus’s reign, Archelaus, accused of arrogance, was banished by Augustus to Vienne in the ninth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0659] lacking in 9c.], and Judaea was entrusted to tetrarchs: Herod, Antipas, Lysanias, and Philip.

In the same year Augustus entered Nola, was seized by illness, and died at the town of Atella in Campania in the seventy-fifth year of his age. The Senate decreed that he should be honored in many ways, saying: “Would that he had either never been born or, having been born, had never died” (cf. Bede, Chr. W., HIER., H. m.). 10. 11. add.: He was buried at Rome in the Campus Martius.

[Col. 0659B] In the sixteenth year of the Lord’s incarnation, which is the 766th from the foundation of Rome, Tiberius, son of Livia, stepson of Augustus, then his son-in-law and finally his adopted son, acquired the Roman Empire. He was the second emperor after Augustus and reigned for twenty-three years.

Because he was called Claudius Tiberius Nero, he was wittily nicknamed by the jesters “Caldius Biberius Mero” on account of his drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0659] “Claudius” in 1b and 10; corrected from “e” in 11.]. Before taking the imperial power, he was sufficiently prudent in warfare and sufficiently fortunate under Augustus [Note: [Col. 0659] “so great under” in 1b.] that the administration of the state could reasonably be entrusted to him. He possessed literary knowledge and was highly distinguished for eloquence, but he had a very bad character: savage, greedy, and treacherous. He pretended to want what he did not want and not to want what he did; he acted as though hostile toward those whose interests he wished to promote, while appearing friendly toward those whom he hated; and he was better in spontaneous replies than in prepared ones.

Finally, when the principate was offered to him by the senators—a position he had indeed obtained through cunning—he pretended to refuse it, carefully probing what each man said or thought [Note: [Col. 0659] lacking in E1.]. This destroyed all the better men. For, thinking that he sincerely wished to avoid the burden of imperial power, they expressed their opinions according to what they believed to be his will and consequently fell into the most extreme disasters.

He waged no wars personally, nor did he wage any serious wars even through his generals, except that the disturbances of peoples, once detected in certain places, were quickly suppressed (cf. Orosius VII, 4). He restrained the brigandage of the Gaetulians and cunningly outmaneuvered Maroboduus, king of the Suebi.

For most of his reign he governed the state with great and serious moderation, so much so that when certain governors advised increasing the taxes of the provinces, he wrote to them that it was the duty of a good shepherd “to shear the sheep, not to flay them.” But little by little he changed for the worse.

(H. m.) For he killed by poison his adopted sons Drusus and Germanicus [Note: [Col. 0659] “adopted” singular in 9c.], the sons of his brother Drusus; he killed his prefect Sejanus when Sejanus was plotting a revolution; and of the twenty senators whom he had chosen as his counselors, he scarcely left two alive [Note: [Col. 0659] “fathers” in E1.], killing the rest on various pretexts.

He himself had a son named Drusus. After Drusus died, Tiberius adopted his son Tiberius, surnamed Gemellus, and Gaius, the son of Germanicus, the son of his brother Drusus [Note: [Col. 0659] “the son of his brother” in 5.]. Gaius succeeded him in the kingdom (cf. Josephus XVIII, 13).

In the time of this Tiberius, Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, who was the son of Herod—the Herod who had killed Aristobulus together with his brother Alexander—was living at Rome and became a friend of Drusus, Tiberius’s son. When Drusus died, his father Tiberius, unable to bear his grief, forbade all his son’s friends to come before him, lest seeing them should renew his sorrow [Note: [Col. 0659] “his son’s” in 5.].

Agrippa therefore went down to Judaea and, after some time, returned to Rome. Through the favor of Antonia, the wife of Drusus, Tiberius’s brother, who was very fond of Bernice [Note: [Col. 0659] “Bernicen” in E1 and 11.], Agrippa’s mother, he was received into Tiberius’s friendship. Tiberius ordered him always to remain close to his grandson Tiberius and to cultivate his favor with the utmost effort. But Agrippa loved Gaius, Antonia’s grandson, more, and therefore incurred Tiberius’s displeasure.

For when one day he wished Gaius, after Tiberius’s death [Note: [Col. 0659] lacking in 9c.], to deserve to see him as lord of all, this was reported to Tiberius. He immediately threw Agrippa into chains, where he remained until the time of Gaius.

10. Added in the margin, received by 11: It is said that he strangled a certain Quendambrus [the name is uncertain], who had discovered how to make glass and bend it according to his will, saying to him: “If you live and teach this to others, gold and silver will become worthless.”

## Years of Tiberius

2. (HIER.) In the seventeenth year of the Lord’s incarnation, which is Tiberius’s second, Asinius Gallus, son of Asinius Pollio, was put to death by Tiberius with dreadful punishments.

3. In the eighteenth year of the Lord, the historian Livy died at Padua [Note: [Col. 0659] “Lucius” in E1, which has this material after “Ovidius” and before “died.”]. The poet Ovid also died in exile [Note: [Col. 0659] lacking in 9c.].

4. (H. m.) In the nineteenth year of the Lord, Germanicus, son of Drusus and father of Caligula, celebrated a triumph over the Germans, against whom he had been sent by Augustus when Augustus was already advanced in age.

5. (HIER.) In the twentieth year of the Lord, Germanicus Caesar was killed by poison by his uncle Tiberius.

6. In the twenty-first year of the Lord, the historian and poet Fenestella died in the seventieth year of his life and was buried at Cumae.

7. In the twenty-second year of the Lord, Tiberius summoned many kings to himself by flattering promises and never sent them back, including Archelaus of Cappadocia. He also reduced Archelaus’s kingdom to the form of a province and named its most distinguished city, Mazaca, Caesarea after himself.

8. In the twenty-third year of the Lord, Pompey’s theater was burned. The 200th Olympiad.

9. In the twenty-fourth year of the Lord, Tiberius made Drusus, his brother’s son, a partner in the kingdom, but killed him by poison in the same year.

10. In the twenty-fifth year of the Lord, Servius Plautus, accused of corrupting his son, killed himself in court.

11. In the twenty-sixth year of the Lord, Philip the tetrarch named Paneas, where he had constructed many buildings, Caesarea Philippi.

12. (Chr. W.) In the twenty-seventh year of the Lord, Pilate was sent by Tiberius as governor of Judaea.

13. In the twenty-eighth year of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0661] The intervening empty years were later omitted.].

14. (Josephus, same work, chapter 4.) In the twenty-ninth year of the Lord, Herod the tetrarch, Philip’s brother, attained great favor with Tiberius and built a city, which he named Tiberias after him.

15. (Gospel.) In the thirtieth year of the Lord, John began to baptize the people. Our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized by his baptism in the Jordan and, in the thirtieth year of his age according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0661] “according to the flesh” in 5.], began to perform signs and preach, proving by his works that what he said was true (cf. Chr. W.).

16. In the thirty-first year of the Lord, our Lord Jesus Christ chose disciples and instructed them in the mysteries of the Gospel.

John the Baptist was beheaded by Herod the tetrarch, the son of that Herod under whom the Lord was born. His wife Herodias, whom he had taken from his brother—Mark says Philip—was the instigator. Bede writes (Commentary on Mark, *Works*, ed. 1688, V, p. 123; cf. Chr. W.) that this same Herodias was the daughter of King Aretas, and that Aretas first gave her in marriage to Philip but later took her away and gave her to Herod, his brother, because Herod himself was richer and more powerful.

Josephus, the author of the *Antiquities*, agreeing with neither account, writes in Book XVIII, chapter 9, as follows:

“At this time a great quarrel also arose between Aretas the Petræan and Herod, because of the following circumstance. Herod the tetrarch had married the daughter of Aretas, with whom he had lived for a considerable time. When he was summoned to Rome, he passed through the house of Herod and was received there. This man was also his brother, though they were not born of the same mother; for Herod had been born of the daughter of Simon the high priest.

While he was staying there, he fell in love with Herodias, the wife of the other Herod. She was the daughter of Aristobulus and sister of Agrippa the elder.
