He dared to speak with the woman about entering into marriage. When she accepted, the agreement was confirmed: once he had returned from Rome, she would receive the rights of marriage. It was included in the agreement that he would send away the daughter of King Aretas.

After these agreements had been concluded, Herod traveled to Rome. When he returned, having carried out at Rome the business for which he had been summoned, his wife, who had faithfully learned everything that had been arranged between him and Herodias [Note: [Col. 0661] “and Herodias” is “and with Herodias” in 9c.], before he realized that she knew everything [Note: [Col. 0661] lacking in 9c.], asked her husband to send her to Machaerus, where the boundary between the territory of Aretas and Herod lay. She revealed none of her intention to him [Note: [Col. 0661] lacking in 9c.].

Herod readily granted this request and sent his wife away, believing that she had understood nothing. But she—having long before sent word to her father that everything necessary for the journey should be prepared for her at Machaerus [Note: [Col. 0661] ‘everything’ for ‘all things’ in 5.]—was received by Aretas’s guides and immediately entered Arabia. From those guides she was passed to others and from those again to others, and with the greatest speed she was brought to her father, to whom she disclosed Herod’s entire intention.

He then took this as the beginning of hostilities. The armies of both sides were assembled, and battle was joined in the region of Gamala—not in the presence of the kings themselves [Note: [Col. 0661] ‘by the kings themselves’ in 9c.], but through commanders sent by both sides. After the battle, when Herod’s army had been defeated through the treachery of deserters who had come from the tetrarchy of Philip to Herod as though to offer assistance, Herod wrote these things to Tiberius.

Tiberius, indignant that Aretas had committed such acts [Note: [Col. 0661] ‘Aretas’ in E1.], wrote to Vitellius, then governor of Syria, ordering him to wage war against Aretas without delay and either bring him to him alive in chains or at least cut off his head.

Tiberius therefore charged the governor of Syria to do this. Some of the Jews, however, thought that Herod’s army had perished because divine indignation had justly arisen against him in vengeance for John, who was called the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0661] ‘was called’ in 5.]. For Herod had killed this very good man, who urged the Jews to practice virtue, cultivate justice, preserve piety toward God, and come together through baptism.”

Thus far Josephus’s words. They show that Herodias was neither Aretas’s daughter nor Philip’s wife. For earlier, in Book XVII of the *Antiquities* [Note: [Col. 0661] XVIII in 9c.], chapter 2, Josephus likewise writes that Herod the elder, moved by remorse over the killing of his sons Alexander and Aristobulus, showed clemency toward their children. He married Alexander’s elder son to the daughter of his brother Pheroras; Aristobulus’s son to Antipater’s daughter; Antipater’s son to Aristobulus’s daughter Mariamne; but his other daughter, namely Herodias, to his own son Herod. “This son,” he says, “was born to him by the daughter of the high priest.” Yet he later adds that Herod and Philip were born by Cleopatra of Jerusalem, and that the high priest’s daughter was named Mariamne.

From these facts, let the prudent reader choose what should be held more firmly. It is difficult not to believe the words of the evangelist, while everyone agrees that Josephus was a truthful narrator of the *Antiquities*. Unless, perhaps, it is said that the evangelist changed the names because of the relationship between the persons [Note: [Col. 0661] “changed the names because of their relationship” in 5.], and did not take much care to distinguish among so many sons of Herod, since he is said to have had two sons with the same name [Note: [Col. 0661] lacking in 9c.].

We think Bede should be excused for saying that Herodias was Aretas’s daughter, because, being occupied with writing many things, he perhaps could not retain every detail of the many histories, especially if he had also happened to read that blessed Jerome held the same view in his commentary on Mark [Note: [Col. 0661] That work no longer exists; cf. Commentary on Matthew, *Works*, ed. Vallars, VII, p. 100.].

17. In the thirty-second year of the Lord’s incarnation, Christ’s disciples, instructed in the teachings of the Gospel, preached the word of faith throughout the cities of Judaea, being sent by Christ himself.

18. (Cf. Chr. W.—HIER.) In the thirty-third year of his incarnation, our Lord Jesus Christ suffered in the flesh and rose again. In connection with his passion, many miracles occurred, as writers even among the Gentiles testify.

Josephus also writes, among the other astonishing events that occurred at that time, that the priests of the Temple first heard movements of the place and certain noises, and then a voice burst forth from the inner sanctuary: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

He also writes about Christ himself as follows (XVIII, 6):

“At this time there was Jesus, a wise man—if indeed it is lawful to call him a man; for he was a worker of marvelous deeds and a teacher of people who gladly receive what is true. He won over many Jews and many also of the Gentiles; this man was the Christ.

When Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men of our nation, had condemned him to be led to the cross [Note: [Col. 0663] ‘on the cross’ in 9c.], those who had loved him from the beginning did not abandon him [Note: [Col. 0663] ‘him’ in 9c.]. For he appeared to them alive again on the third day, just as the divinely inspired prophets had foretold these and countless other miracles concerning him. To this day the tribe of Christians, so called after him, has not disappeared, nor has the name.”

19. (Chr. W.) In the thirty-fourth year of the Lord, James, the Lord’s brother, was appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles and held the office for thirty years.

20. In the thirty-fifth year of the Lord, Pilate, wishing to set up an image of Caesar in the Temple, provoked riots among the Jews.

21. (HIER.) In the thirty-sixth year of the Lord, the prefect Sejanus urged Tiberius to destroy the Jews. Persius was born at Volaterrae.

22. (H. m.) In the thirty-seventh year of the Lord, Pilate wrote to Tiberius about the Lord’s passion and resurrection and about his powers, through which, as the faith of many increased, God was believed.

Tiberius, with the support of great popular favor, brought the matter before the Senate so that Christ might be regarded as a god. But the Senate, angered that the proposal had not first been brought before it according to custom, so that it might itself decide beforehand whether worship should be accepted [Note: [Col. 0663] “whether it should first decide” in E1.], refused to consecrate Christ and decreed that Christians should be expelled from the city [Note: [Col. 0663] E1: “that the Christians should be expelled from the city.”], especially since Sejanus, Tiberius’s prefect, most stubbornly opposed the adoption of the religion [Note: [Col. 0663] lacking in E1. In what follows, I shall give only the principal readings of this manuscript and of codex 9c.].

Nevertheless, Tiberius threatened Christ’s accusers with death and proscribed many senators, forcing them to die. (Josephus XVIII, 7.)

When Pilate had completed his tenth year in Judaea, he was accused by the Jews before Vitellius, who then governed Syria. Vitellius ordered him to go to Rome so that he might clear himself of the charges before Caesar [Note: [Col. 0663] lacking in 9c.]. But before Pilate reached Rome, Tiberius departed from human life.—See above.

In the same year Agrippa, son of Aristobulus and surnamed Herod, came to Rome and was treated kindly by Tiberius through the favor of Antonia, the mother of Germanicus and Claudius and the wife of Drusus, Tiberius’s brother. But when Agrippa was accused of wishing Tiberius to die sooner and the kingdom to be given to Gaius, Tiberius threw him into chains, and he was not released while Tiberius lived.

23. (H. m.) In the thirty-eighth year of the Lord, Tiberius, who had severely oppressed the Romans, died by poison through the plot of Caligula, amid immense joy on everyone’s part, in Campania, in the twenty-third year of his reign and the seventy-eighth year of his life.

## Years of Gaius Caligula

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Caligulus” in 5.]

## Years from the beginning of the world: four thousand

1. (H. m.—HIER.) In the thirty-ninth year of the Lord’s incarnation, and the 789th from the foundation of Rome, Gaius Caligula, the third emperor after Augustus, assumed the empire and reigned for three years, ten months, and eight days.

He was the son of Germanicus and grandson of Drusus, who was Augustus’s stepson and Tiberius’s brother. Because Gaius was born in the army, he was nicknamed Caligula after the soldiers’ footwear. He was raised with great affection by his grandmother Antonia and was held in high honor (Josephus XVIII, 13).

Tiberius adopted him as a son together with Tiberius, the son of his own son Drusus [Note: [Col. 0663] lacking in 9c.]. The two were brought up at court and thoroughly educated in the liberal arts. The people loved Gaius because of the virtue of his father Germanicus.

When Tiberius had reached old age, he prayed to the ancestral gods to show him a clear sign of who would succeed him in the empire [Note: [Col. 0663] “would succeed” in 4 and 9c.], since he was eager to leave the principate to his grandson.

He was told that the one who came to him first of all on the following day would reign. Tiberius therefore sent for his grandson’s tutor and ordered him to bring the boy to him early in the morning, thinking to overcome the divine will by some device.

When day broke, he ordered Evodus to summon to him first any of the little children who might be outside. Evodus went out and found Gaius in front of the tent, for Tiberius had not yet arrived, being delayed by eating. Unaware of everything that was happening, Evodus said, “Come, your father is calling you,” and brought Gaius inside.

When Tiberius saw the power of the heavenly majesty, he blamed himself for having asked for that omen. But, unable to resist the divine ordering, he addressed Gaius kindly, entrusted the empire to him, and warned him to be well disposed toward his grandson Tiberius.

Having received the kingdom after Tiberius, Gaius was the most wicked of all his predecessors and wiped away the disgrace of Tiberius. (H. m.) Before his principate he was acceptable to everyone; in the principate he became such a man that it was rightly said that there had never been a harsher master.

To summarize his cruelty briefly, he is said to have exclaimed: “Would that the Roman people had a single neck!” He also often complained about the circumstances of his times, because they were marked by no public calamities. He did many things whose memory I do not know whether it is proper to preserve [Note: [Col. 0665] lacking in 9c.], except perhaps because it is useful for us to know everything about rulers, so that wicked men may at least avoid such actions through fear of their reputation.

(Jordanes, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Romans*.) In the palace he publicly subjected noble matrons to his lust; he committed adultery with his three sisters and even violated the daughter born from one of them. He compelled Memmius Regulus to give him his wife as though she were his daughter, to call himself her father, and, as her father, to draw up the marriage contract. He condemned his sisters, with whom he had committed adultery, to exile on islands.

(HIER.—H. m.) He was the first to put on a diadem, order that he be called “lord,” and command that he be counted among the gods.

As soon as he received the kingdom after Tiberius’s death, he released Agrippa, surnamed Herod, from the chains into which Tiberius had thrown him. He gave him the tetrarchy of his deceased uncle Philip and named him king; later he added to it the tetrarchy of his uncle Herod (cf. Josephus, same work—Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* II, 4).

This is the Herod called Herod in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter XIII. He killed James, imprisoned Peter, and later was struck by an angel and died, swarming with worms. His children were King Agrippa, his namesake, and his sister Bernice.

He reigned for seven years and died in the third year of Claudius (cf. Eusebius II, 10).

His uncle Philip died in the twenty-second year of Tiberius. He had ruled the regions of Trachonitis and Gaulanitis for thirty-two years [Note: [Col. 0665] lacking in 9c.].

2. In the fortieth year of the Lord, which is Gaius’s second, the Jews—who at that time were already being harassed everywhere by disasters deservedly suffered because of Christ’s passion—were defeated and driven from Alexandria after a riot had broken out there.

On their behalf Philo, a man of exceptional learning, came to Rome for a second time and pleaded before Gaius, but accomplished nothing. While remaining there, he is said to have spoken with the apostle Peter and to have enjoyed his friendship (cf. Eusebius II, 5).

3. (Chr. W.) In the forty-first year of the Lord, Pilate, oppressed by many calamities inflicted by Gaius, killed himself.

4. In the forty-second year of the Lord, Matthew wrote the Gospel in Hebrew.

Herod the tetrarch, who had been responsible for the killing of John the Baptist and had taken part in the Lord’s passion, was the son of Herod the Great, under whom Christ was born (see above). He came to Rome at the urging of his wife Herodias, whom he had taken from his brother (Josephus, *The Jewish War* II, 8).

When Herodias saw that her brother Agrippa had been made king by Gaius, she began to reproach Herod for his sluggishness, because, by refusing to sail to Caesar, he was deprived of a higher honor. For, since Gaius had undoubtedly made Agrippa a king from a private citizen, he would certainly have raised Herod from tetrarch to an equal honor.

Moved by this, Herod came to Rome, followed and accused by Agrippa, the son of his brother Aristobulus [Note: [Col. 0665] “but Gaius” after “followed and accused” in E1.]. Gaius harshly rebuked him for greed, took away his tetrarchy, and entrusted it to Agrippa. He himself banished Herod into perpetual exile at Lugdunum.

When Gaius learned that Herodias was Agrippa’s sister, he wished to grant her wealth and everything that belonged to her. But she rejected everything for her husband’s sake, followed him into exile, and there they both perished (cf. *Jewish Antiquities* XVIII, 14).

(H. m.) In the same year, while Gaius was raging against everyone with immense cruelty, he was killed by soldiers in the palace, in the thirty-eighth year of his life and the fourth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0665] “of his age” in 9c.].

After he was killed, two books were found hidden among his papers. On one was marked a dagger as the symbol of its title, and on the other a sword. Both contained the names and identifying notes of the finest men of both orders, namely the senatorial and equestrian orders, who had been designated for death.

A huge chest of various poisons was also found. When these were thrown into the sea at the command of Caesar Claudius, the waters were reportedly polluted, causing a great slaughter of fish, whose bodies were washed by the tides onto the nearby shores.

## Years of Claudius

(H. m.—HIER.) In the forty-third year of the Lord’s incarnation and the 793rd from the foundation of Rome, Claudius, the fourth emperor after Augustus, obtained the empire. He reigned thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-eight days.

(H. m.) He was the uncle of Gaius Caligula and the son of Drusus, Augustus’s stepson, who has a monument near Mainz; Caligula was his nephew.

When the Senate had decreed that the family of the Caesars should be exterminated, Claudius was found hiding in a disgraceful hiding place. Because he was mentally weak, he seemed very mild to the foolish. He was carried off by the soldiers and made emperor, with the support of Agrippa, who had happened at that time to come to Rome and had been summoned by the Senate for consultation. Claudius later made Agrippa’s son king. (H. m.)

Claudius, obedient to his belly, wine, and foul lust, was mentally weak, almost witless, and timid, and he was subject to the commands of his freedmen and his wife (Orosius VII, 6; Bede I, 3). Nevertheless, wishing to show himself a ruler useful to the state, he moved his army against Britain. He crossed to the island, which no one before Julius Caesar and no one after him had dared to approach, and within a few days, without battle or bloodshed, received a very large part of it into submission. He also added the Orkney Islands beyond Britain to the Roman Empire and returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure.

(HIER.) Thus he celebrated a triumph over the Britons and named his son Britannicus.

(H. m.) Claudius’s wife Messalina [Note: [Col. 0665] “Messalia” in 5 and 9c.] first engaged openly in adultery with anyone who wished. As a result, many men abstained through fear, and many were killed. Then, inflamed more fiercely, she selected the noblest married women and virgins as though they were prostitutes and arranged them for herself; their husbands were compelled to be present. If anyone recoiled from such acts, a fabricated charge was brought against him, and violence was inflicted upon him and his entire household [Note: [Col. 0665] “against his entire family” in 9c.].

Thus her freedmen, having acquired supreme power, polluted everything with adultery, exile, murder, and proscription. From their number he appointed Felix prefect over the legions of Judaea; after the British triumph he gave the eunuch Posidonius, counted among the bravest of the military, distinguished arms as though he had shared in the victory; and he allowed Polybius to walk among the consulars as their equal. Narcissus stood above them all.

After this Claudius took as his wife Agrippina, daughter of his brother Germanicus, sister of Caligula, and mother of Nero. Seeking power for her son, she first surrounded her stepson Britannicus in the palace with various plots and then killed her husband himself with poison.

1. Therefore, in the first year of his reign, when Claudius was being established in the kingdom through Agrippa’s counsel [Note: [Col. 0665D] I do not know from what source Ekkehard drew this.], Claudius gave Agrippa, as a reward, everything that Augustus had given Herod [Col. 0667B] [Note: [Col. 0667] “as a reward” added in E1.], and also another kingdom, said to have belonged to Lysanias.

2. In the forty-fourth year of the Lord, the twelve apostles, who until then had preached only in Judaea, were divided throughout the whole world, in accordance with the Lord’s command, as Bede writes, in the twelfth year after the Lord’s passion.

Therefore Peter, having first founded the church at Antioch [Note: [Col. 0667] “the church of Antioch” in 5.], set out for Rome. Some think this happened in this year (Bede, *Martyrology*); according to others (HIER.), it happened in the fourth year of Claudius.

3. (Chr. W.) In the forty-fifth year of the Lord, Evodius was ordained the first bishop of Antioch.

Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, was struck by an angel in the seventh year of his reign, leaving a son named Agrippa and three daughters, Bernice [Note: [Col. 0667] “Bernicen” in E1.], Mariamne, and Drusilla.

Then Claudius, as Josephus testifies (*Jewish Antiquities* XIX, 8; cf. *The Jewish War* II, 10), reduced his kingdom to a province, and Cuspius Fadus was sent to govern it.

4. (HIER.) In the forty-sixth year of the Lord, Claudius celebrated a triumph over the Britons.

In the same year a very severe famine occurred throughout Syria, which the prophet Agabus had also foretold, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter XII, 28). Helena, queen of the Adiabenians, supplied the needs of the Christians at Jerusalem with great generosity, bringing grain from Egypt.

Bede thinks that the following event also took place in this year, namely Claudius’s fourth year [Note: [Col. 0667] lacking in E1]. It is read in the Acts of the Apostles:

“They decided that Paul and Barnabas and certain others from among them should go up to the apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem.”

He believes this ascent to have been the one about which Paul himself writes to the Galatians:

“Then, after fourteen years, I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also.”

After inserting some material about this ascent [Note: [Col. 0667] “with material inserted” in E1.], Bede continues:

“We should therefore believe that blessed Peter came to Rome in the same fourteenth year after the Lord’s passion, in which Paul met him at Jerusalem—that is, in the fourth year of Caesar Claudius. At the same time, unless I am mistaken, we establish by this interpretation that the apostle Paul came to the faith in the same year in which the Lord suffered and rose again.”

Nearly all writers on sacred chronology testify that Peter came to Rome in Claudius’s fourth year. Some think that in this year he assumed the pontificate in the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0667] “pontificate” in 5, 9c, and 10.]. This is inferred as true from the fact that Peter is said to have held the Roman see for twenty-five years (HIER.), and that the final year of Nero, in which Peter is said to have suffered, is counted as the twenty-fifth from Claudius’s fourth year [Note: [Col. 0667] “XXV” is supplied in the margin; the passage beginning “and the final year” is lacking in 9c.].

It therefore appears sufficiently clear that in the same year in which he came to Rome, he also received the pontifical see.

Concerning the succession, order, and dates of the Roman pontiffs, from the beginning onward, different people hold many different opinions. I therefore think it is not irrelevant to set down their views here in summary, so that both the more sluggish and negligent among those like me may be roused to attend to the truth of the matter, and the more prudent may be challenged to investigate it more carefully. [Note: [Col. 0667] The material concerning the order of the pontiffs is lacking in D? E.]

Some write—and ecclesiastical history also appears to agree with them (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 12 and following)—that Linus assumed the governance of the Roman see after the passion of the apostle Peter, who presided over it for twenty-five years; that after twelve years of his own administration, in the second year of Titus, he handed the pontificate over to Anacletus; that Anacletus likewise, after twelve years, handed the see to Clement, which appears to have occurred in the twelfth year of Domitian; and that Clement himself, after nine years of his pontificate, suffered martyrdom under Trajan. Evaristus succeeded him in the fourth year of that same Trajan, and Evaristus was succeeded by Alexander, Alexander by Sixtus, and so on with the others. [Col. 0668B]

Others, however, write that Linus and Cletus served under Peter, and that Peter himself, as soon as he received the pontificate, appointed Linus to act on his behalf in ecclesiastical affairs, so that he might devote himself more freely to preaching. When Linus died after twelve years, Peter substituted Cletus for him; and when Cletus likewise died after twelve years, in the year and at the time when Peter himself suffered martyrdom—that is, in the fourteenth year of Nero—Peter entrusted the see to Clement. Finally, he handed over to Clement and his successors the power of binding and loosing, just as he himself had received it from Christ. After Clement suffered under Domitian, Anacletus succeeded him; Evaristus succeeded Anacletus, Alexander succeeded Evaristus, and so on with the others. [Note: The words following “suffered” are lacking in 9c; they are lacking in 5 after “under Domitian.” Note: “and so on” appears in 9c, 10, and 11.]

Since these accounts prove to differ greatly from one another, we must ask which should be judged more worthy of belief. Let us therefore consider their discrepancies. [Col. 0668D]

If it is accepted that Linus left Anacletus as his successor, and Anacletus left Clement, as the first account testifies, Cletus is entirely excluded from the catalogue of pontiffs. Yet his veneration is so renowned throughout all the churches that he is not only given a place in the martyrologies, but is also publicly recited in the canon of the Mass and in the petitions of the litanies between Linus and Clement.

If, however, Cletus is counted after Linus, then Clement, and after Clement Evaristus and Alexander, there is no place where Anacletus can be admitted. For Bede says in his *Martyrology* (*Works* III, p. 300) that Anacletus occupied the see as the fourth after Peter and suffered under Domitian, so that Linus was first, Cletus second, Clement third, and Anacletus fourth. [Col. 0669A]

But if Anacletus is placed after Clement and is accepted as having suffered under Domitian, according to Bede, it necessarily follows that the claim that his predecessor Clement suffered under Trajan must be rejected. For it is clearly proved that Clement suffered under Domitian if it is not denied that his successor Anacletus was killed by that same emperor.

There is still another argument. If, according to some, Linus and Anacletus, or, according to others, Linus and Cletus, each held the pontificate for twelve years after Peter’s martyrdom—which took place in the fourteenth year of Nero—the twenty-four-year period extends into the twelfth year of Domitian. In that case Clement is in no way shown to have received the see and the authority to bind and loose from the apostle Peter, as some assert. [Col. 0669B]

This too must be added: Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, a disciple of the blessed apostle Paul and bishop of Athens, when he heard—as is related in the book of his passion (*Acta Sanctorum*, October IV, p. 792)—that the blessed apostles Peter and Paul were being held in Rome, appointed a bishop at Athens and hurried to reach Rome as quickly as possible. He earnestly desired, if God so willed, to die together with those holy apostles. But divine providence anticipated his wishes: the holy apostles were crowned with the glory of martyrdom before he reached Rome. When he finally arrived, he found Clement, his fellow disciple, already presiding over the Roman see; Clement sent him as a preacher to Gaul. [Col. 0669C]

What, then, was the urgency of so great a desire if he could be prevented from reaching Rome from Athens for twenty-four years or more by no obstacle at all? It is no counterargument that he is said to have been delayed for some time because, once the door of faith had been opened to him, he was engaged in sowing the word of God. Even if, eager to preach, he had scattered the divine seeds through neighboring parishes, nevertheless, burning with the desire for martyrdom, he could have hastened from Athens to Rome within twenty-four years.

Moreover, since this same Dionysius is described as having suffered in the ninety-sixth year of the Lord’s incarnation, which is the fourteenth year of Domitian, while Clement, who sent him to Gaul, is said—according to the opinion of the preceding account—to have received the see in the twelfth year of that emperor, it may seem astonishing how all these events could have been completed in a year that was not yet finished, or had scarcely ended: namely, that Dionysius should travel from Rome to Gaul, subjugate to the yoke of faith a stiff-necked people who did not yet know him and regarded him as a stranger, build a basilica, and accomplish the many other things read about him; that the report of priests stirred up over these matters should return to Rome; and that, once the persecution had become known, a prefect should be sent from there to Gaul and kill Dionysius with various punishments. [Col. 0669D]

The book of the passion of Pope Alexander also testifies (*Acta Sanctorum*, May I, p. 371) that in the order of the Roman pontiffs Clement is regarded as the first after Peter, that is, the second after him. For it is written there:

“Alexander received the chair of the Roman Church as the fifth from the blessed apostle Peter,” and so forth. [Col. 0670A]

If Linus is called the second after Peter, it is necessary that both Cletus before Clement and Anacletus after him be excluded from the numbering, so that Alexander may be found to be fifth: Peter being first, Linus second, Clement third, Evaristus fourth, and Alexander following in fifth place. Otherwise Alexander is not counted as fifth after Peter. If Linus is second after Peter and Cletus or Anacletus is placed before Clement, Alexander will be sixth; but if Cletus is placed before Clement and Anacletus after Clement, Alexander is counted seventh—unless Clement is numbered second after Peter. [Col. 0670B]

Having brought forward these and similar arguments, I judge for the present that, in view of the agreement of the facts and dates, we should follow those who say that Linus and Cletus served under Peter, and that they administered the office which rural bishops (*chorepiscopi*) hold under a bishop. [Note: 5 reads *corepiscopi*; 10 corrects it to *coepiscopi*, as does 11.] Clement, however, succeeded by legitimate right when Peter himself handed the office over to him. [Note: 5 reads “Peter himself.”] For this reason some call him the first pope, because he is said to have received the pontificate from Peter by a kind of hereditary right, together with the power of binding and loosing. [Note: 9c reads “through” for “for this reason.”] Others, however, call him the third after Peter, because Linus and Cletus preceded him in the priestly office under that apostle. [Note: “were under Peter” appears in 5.]

This is enough concerning them. [Col. 0670C]

In what follows, the same matter produces an accumulation of error concerning the order of succession and the sequence of dates. This is believed to have arisen through the similarity of the names given to the persons, owing to the carelessness and corruption of scribes.

Pope Fabian is said to have suffered under Decius. [Note: 5 reads “is said under Decius.”] After him came Cornelius, and after Cornelius, in the catalogue of pontiffs and also in some chronicles, Lucius, Stephen, Sixtus, and Dionysius are found listed. Since Fabian is said to have suffered under Decius, and Sixtus too—under whom Lawrence held the archdeaconate—is proclaimed throughout all the churches, both in readings and in song, to have suffered under that same emperor; and since Decius is said to have reigned no more than thirty months, that is, two and a half years, or according to some even less—one year and three months—if Lucius and Stephen are placed between Cornelius, Fabian’s successor, and this Sixtus, as some prefer, the sequence of events cannot stand. [Note: The words from “as some” through “the others” are lacking in 10 and 11.] For the one is said to have suffered under Decius, the others under Valerian and Gallienus; and ecclesiastical history says that Cornelius presided over the Roman see for three years, Lucius for eight months, and Stephen for two years. [Note: 5 reads “for two years.” Note: “under Decius” is lacking in 10 and 11.] [Col. 0670D]

It can therefore be understood clearly enough that, through the fault of scribes and because of the similarity of the names, the order was confused: Sixtus succeeded Cornelius and Dionysius succeeded Sixtus; Lucius succeeded Dionysius, Stephen succeeded Lucius, Sixtus in turn succeeded Stephen, then Dionysius again, and so the remaining succession continued in order. [Col. 0671A]

I do not say all this as though, through my own loquacity, I wished to prejudice the judgment of others far more excellent than I. [Note: 9c reads *meae* for *me*; *satis* (“sufficiently”) is lacking in 4, 10, and 11.] Rather, in my desire to seek the truth, I expose the understanding of my imprudence, deserving the label of folly. Let every wise person, according to his capacity, deliberate and judge what should be held as true.

But I, seeing so many and such great variations in historians, and considering them as I pondered and wondered over them according to the weakness of my little intellect, carefully went through, to the best of my ability, the histories, books of passions, and copies of chronicles that I was able to obtain. Finding many things corrupted through the negligence or ignorance of scribes, especially because of the variations in the numbers represented by letters—for diligent people easily make mistakes in these matters, and how much more those who are inattentive, when one letter is substituted for another or some letter is perhaps omitted—I corrected certain things as far as my rusticity and lack of authority permitted. I also connected the dates of the Roman pontiffs as carefully as I could with the dates of the emperors.

Beginning with the forty-sixth year of the Lord’s incarnation, which is the first year of the blessed apostle Peter’s Roman pontificate, although I could not find the years of each individual bishop, I nevertheless set out the order of all of them, as it has been transmitted to us, in sequence down to the one thousand and ninety-ninth year of that same incarnation. [Note: “of the individual pontiffs” appears in 5.] If, by the judgment of the wise, my simple diligence is pleasing and no one begrudges the truth, thanks be to God; but if someone who demonstrates something better should arise, I, as one most desirous of certainty and truth, gladly yield to him. (Cf. Josephus, *Antiquities* XX, 5.)

—Alexander succeeded Fado.

## The Years of Alexander

1. 5. (Jerome.) A.D. 47. Domitius is regarded as a famous orator; later, under Nero, he died at dinner from an excess of food.

2. 6. (Historical miscellany.) A.D. 48. Between Therassia and Thera in the Aegean Sea, a new island emerged, extending over a distance of thirty stades. A certain Cumanus succeeded Tiberius Alexander as procurator of Judaea. (Cf. Josephus, the same work.)

3. 7. (Historical miscellany.) A.D. 49. Under Cumanus, procurator of Judaea, such a great riot arose at Jerusalem during the days of Unleavened Bread through the fault of a single soldier that, when the people were hemmed in at the gates, thirty thousand Jews are said to have been struck down and crushed in the slaughter.

4. 8. (Josephus, the same work.) A.D. 50. Herod, king of Chalcis and brother of Agrippa the Elder, died, leaving three sons: Aristobulus, born of his former wife; and Berenicianus and Hyrcanus, born of Beronice, the daughter of his brother Agrippa. Claudius gave his kingdom to the young Agrippa, Agrippa’s son, because he had already reduced his father’s kingdom to a province, since Agrippa himself was still a child when his father died.

—(Historical miscellany.) In this year there is said to have been such a great famine at Rome that the emperor, seized by the people in the middle of the forum and disgracefully assailed with insults and pieces of bread, scarcely escaped the fury of the mob. At that time Paul found at Athens an altar inscribed “To an unknown god.”

5. 9. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 51. Claudius expelled the Jews from the city of Rome.

6. 10. (Historical miscellany.) A.D. 52. A phoenix was seen in Egypt. It is said to be a bird that flies from Arabia to the place mentioned once every 654 years.

7. 11. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 53. [Note: “LIII” is corrected to “LIIII”; in the margin is supplied: “In the year of the Lord 53, Simon … arose”; 10 and 11 received this material in this form.] Claudius appointed Felix procurator of Judaea.

8. 12. A.D. 54. Simon Magus became the founder of the Simoniac heresy. —(Historical miscellany.) Apollonius, born in Italy, a Pythagorean philosopher, was influential at Rome, so much so that Philostratus and others of keener intellect describe him as having himself been Pythagoras.

9. 13. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 55. A certain Egyptian pseudo-prophet, leading many Jews astray, was crushed by Felix.

10. 14. (Historical miscellany.) A.D. 56. Claudius was killed by poison, as is said, by his wife Agrippina, in the sixty-fourth year of his life. His funeral, like that of Tarquinius Priscus in former times, was concealed for a long time; while guards corrupted by feminine cunning pretended that he was ill, his stepson Nero, Agrippina’s son, assumed the rights of the empire. [Note: 9c adds: “Jerome’s chronicles arrange the years differently down to Constantine the Great and Silvester.”]

## The Years of Domitius Nero

(Historical miscellany—Jerome.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 57, and in the 807th year from the founding of the City, Domitius Nero, son of Domitius Ahenobarbus and Agrippina, the sister of Caligula, fifth after Augustus, assumed the empire and reigned for fourteen incomplete years, namely thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. (Josephus XX, 10.) His mother Agrippina was the daughter of Germanicus, the brother of Claudius; his father Domitius Ahenobarbus came from one of the noblest Roman families. When Domitius died, Claudius loved Agrippina and, because of his love for her, killed his wife Messalina, by whom he had a son, Britannicus, and a daughter, Octavia. He also had a daughter, Antonia, by his first wife, named Paetina.

After marrying Agrippina, Claudius adopted her son Domitius as his own son, called him Nero, and betrothed his daughter Octavia to him. Agrippina, fearing that Britannicus might receive the kingdom from his father, planned Claudius’s death. When Claudius had died, she suddenly sent the military commander Burrus, together with powerful tribunes, and they brought Nero from the camp and hailed him as emperor. Having received the empire in this way, Nero secretly killed Britannicus by poison, and then killed his own mother, thus repaying her in kind.

—(Historical miscellany.) For the first five years he appeared to be a good ruler, to such an extent that some writers said Trajan used to remark that all emperors were far inferior to Nero’s five-year period. (Orosius VII, 7; Aurelius Victor.) During the rest of his life, which extended beyond those five years, he followed the example of his uncle Caligula—or rather surpassed it—so completely that it is shameful to say to what wickedness he attained.

He killed a very large part of the senators, nearly destroyed the equestrian order, and was an enemy to all good people. He was so driven by lust that he is not reported to have abstained even from his mother, sister, or any respect for blood relationship. He took a man as his wife, himself dressed in the appearance of a bride, summoned the senate to deliberate on the matter of the dowry, and, while the wedding ceremonies were being celebrated, was led away almost as a wife by a husband, covered with a skin.

He committed many parricides, killing his mother, brother, sister, wife, and other relatives. He burned the city of Rome for six days and nights, so that he might see what the fire of Troy had been like. Standing on a very high tower, he happily watched the flames and, dressed in theatrical costume, sang the tragedy *The Iliad*.

In military affairs he dared nothing at all and nearly lost Britain. The recklessness of his impiety toward God increased the mass of his crimes. For he was the first to launch a persecution against Christians throughout his entire kingdom and, desiring to eradicate the very name, killed Peter and Paul, the leaders of the apostles. He sent Vespasian with his son Titus to destroy Jerusalem.

Meanwhile Galba, praetor of Spain, and Gaius Julius seized the empire. Nero, detested by everyone, was declared an enemy by the senate. It was decreed that a fork should be inserted into his neck, that he should be led naked through the streets, beaten with rods until death, and thrown from a cliff. When Nero heard this and at the same time learned of Galba’s arrival, he fled from the palace and left the City in the middle of the night.

Phaon, Epaphroditus, Nephitus, and the eunuch Sporus followed him. Nero had once castrated Sporus and tried to transform him into a woman. When Nero had come to the suburban estate of his freedman, located between the Salarian and Nomentan roads at the fourth milestone from the City, he wished to strike himself with a sword, but his trembling hand could not complete the act. Finding no one by whom he could be struck, he cried out: “Can it be that I cannot have either a friend or an enemy?” (Aurelius Victor.)

Seeing this, Sporus assisted his trembling hand, and Nero thus perished in the thirty-first year of his life and the fourteenth of his reign. In him the entire family of Augustus was brought to an end.

—(Historical miscellany.) In Nero’s time Seneca the tragedian and philosopher, Musonius and Plutarch the philosophers, Juvenal and Persius the satirists, and Lucan, the son of Seneca’s brother, together with Statius, were prominent at Rome.

## The Years of Nero

1. 11. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) In Nero’s first year, Festus succeeded Felix as governor.

2. 12. (Jerome.) A.D. 58. The apostle Paul, explaining the principles of his religion before Festus in the presence of King Agrippa, was sent by Festus himself in chains to Rome. There Peter, who arrived, met Paul. (See above.) Since Linus had already died, Peter substituted Cletus in his place; Cletus governed the Church for twelve years, while Peter devoted himself to preaching. [Note: The words “Peter … devoted himself” appear to have been erased in 10; they are lacking in 11.] (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) Thus far Luke the evangelist brought the book of the Acts of the Apostles. [Col. 0674A]

3. 13. (Jerome.) A.D. 59. Probus of Beirut, a most learned grammarian, flourished.

4. 14. A.D. 60. Statius Sursulus, a celebrated poet of Colossae, was prominent.

5. 15. A.D. 61. An earthquake and an eclipse of the sun occurred at Rome.

6. 16. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 62. Albinus succeeded Festus as governor of Judaea.

7. 17. (Jerome.) A.D. 63. James, the brother of the Lord, was stoned by the Jews, and his brother Symeon was appointed in his place. [Note: “Simon” in 4, 9c, 10, and 11.]

8. 18. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 64. Mark the evangelist suffered martyrdom at Alexandria.

9. 19. A.D. 65. (Jerome.) Persius died in the twenty-ninth year of his age. [Note: “of his age” appears in 9c.] A thunderbolt fell before Nero’s table.

10. 20. A.D. 66. The poet Annaeus Lucan of Córdoba, discovered in the Pisonian conspiracy, offered his arm for the cutting of his veins.

11. 21. A.D. 67. Nero burned Rome in imitation of Troy.

12. 22. A.D. 68. Annaeus Seneca of Córdoba, Nero’s tutor and Lucan’s uncle, was ordered by Nero to choose the manner of his death and perished by cutting his veins and drinking poison. His brother Junius Gallio, an outstanding declaimer, killed himself with his own hand. [Note: “killed himself” appears in 5.] Their brother Lucius Annaeus Mela obtained from Nero the property of his son Lucan.

13. 23. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle—cf. Josephus, *The Jewish War* III.) A.D. 69. [Note: A leaf is lacking in E1.] Vespasian, commander of the army against the Jews—who were rebelling because they could not endure the greed of Gessius Florus, Albinus’s successor—was sent by Nero. Among other cities he captured Jotapata, a fortified city, and there seized Josephus, also called Josippus, a Jewish commander who had directed the war there. When Josephus was about to be killed by the Romans, he foretold to Vespasian that Vespasian himself would become emperor, and thus won his life. This is the author of the *Antiquities*.

14. 24. A.D. 70. After completing the period of his preaching, the apostle Peter came to Rome again. [Note: “came to Rome again” appears in 5.] When his disciple Cletus had died, Peter entrusted the Roman chair to Clement, giving him and his successors the power to bind and loose, just as Peter himself had received it from the Lord. In that same year Peter was crucified at Nero’s command, while Paul was beheaded.

Clement occupied the see for nineteen years and five months and suffered martyrdom under Domitian, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, although some contend that he suffered under Trajan (Bede, *Martyrology*, p. 351). According to ecclesiastical history (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 12), Linus, the first after Peter, assumed the Roman Church in this year and governed it for twelve years.

After the killing of the apostles, Nero killed himself in the manner described above, as it is related in Roman history, although some write that he wandered in a forest and was devoured by wolves. (Aurelius Victor.) The Persians loved him so greatly that they sent envoys to Rome, earnestly requesting permission to build him a tomb. All the other provinces, however, and Rome as a whole rejoiced excessively at his death, so much so that everyone, wearing the caps of manumission—which at that time signified liberation—celebrated victory as though they had been freed from an impious master. [Col. 0675A]

—(Jerome.) Ignatius was ordained the second bishop of Antioch, Evodius having preceded him.

## Galba

25. (Historical miscellany.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 71, and in the 821st year from the founding of the City, Galba, a senator of the most ancient nobility and descended from the family of the Sulpicii, while in his seventy-third year, was chosen by the Spaniards and Gauls and soon gladly accepted as emperor by the entire army. As soon as he heard of Nero’s death, he came to Rome. As the sixth after Augustus, he reigned for seven months.

His private life was distinguished by military and civil achievements. He was often consul, often proconsul, and often commander in very serious wars. He treated his soldiers so severely that, when he entered the camp, one man was said to say immediately to another: “Learn to be a soldier: Galba has come, not Getulicus.”

After gaining the empire, however, he offended everyone through greed and sluggishness. He adopted as his son and heir a certain noble young man, Piso; but in the seventh month he himself was beheaded in the middle of the Roman forum through the plotting of a certain Otho, who seized the kingdom after him. (Cf. Orosius VII, 8; Historical miscellany.) [Col. 0675C]

## Otho

Lucius Otho, after killing Galba and Piso, seized the Roman empire. He was born in the town of Ferentinum, nobler on his mother’s side than on his father’s, though neither side was obscure. In private life he was soft and, especially in his youth, disgraceful, and he was a close associate of Nero. In power, however, he was unable to demonstrate what he was made of.

For at the same time that Otho had killed Galba, Vitellius had also been made emperor by the Germanic armies. Otho undertook war against Vitellius and emerged victorious in three minor battles: one near the Alps, another around Placentia, and a third near the place called the Castors. In the fourth battle, when he had been defeated in a minor engagement near Bedriacum in Italy, although he still had enormous forces available for the war, he voluntarily killed himself after completing thirty-eight years of age and on the ninety-fifth day of his reign, that is, in the fourth month.

He was so beloved by his own soldiers that many of them, when they saw his dead body, killed themselves with their own hands.

## Vitellius

Vitellius entered Rome as a victor and obtained the empire by force. He was born of a family more honorable than noble. (Cf. Orosius, the same work.) His father, Lucius Vitellius, was not born with great distinction, yet he held three ordinary consulships.

—(Roman History and Historical miscellany.) Vitellius ruled with great disgrace and was notable for much cruelty and other vices, especially gluttony and voracity. He is said to have dined as often as four or five times a day. [Note: The phrase “four or five” is lacking in 9c.] One particularly famous banquet has been committed to memory: his brother Vitellius gave it for him, and, besides the other expenses, two thousand fish and seven thousand little birds were served. [Note: “birds” appears in 1b and 11.]

Meanwhile, while Vespasian was besieging Jerusalem, he heard of Nero’s death and was proclaimed emperor by the soldiers. When Vitellius heard this, he killed Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, together with many others, after setting fire to the Capitol.

Thereupon Vitellius was defeated in a battle fought beneath the walls of the City by Vespasian’s soldiers. He had shut himself inside a small room near the palace, but he was disgracefully dragged out. With his hands bound behind his back, his head thrown backward and a sword held beneath his chin, he was led through the forum for the crowd to see. As many threw dung and filth into his face, he was mutilated by repeated small blows; then he was dragged away with a hook and thrown into the Tiber. He was in the fifty-seventh year of his life and the eighth month of his reign. [Col. 0676B]

—(Jerome.) These three seized the empire after Nero: Galba in Spain, where he had been sent with an army; Otho at Rome; and Vitellius in Germany. They reigned for one year and six months.

—Ignatius was ordained the second bishop of Antioch.

## The Years of Vespasian

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 72, and in the 822nd year from the founding of the City, Vespasian was sent by Nero into Judaea with an army. When Nero’s death became known, the army made Vespasian emperor. Leaving his son Titus in Judaea to besiege Jerusalem, Vespasian himself traveled through Alexandria to Rome. There, having received the empire, he was the seventh after Augustus and reigned for nine years. [Note: In these numerical entries Ekkehard thereafter follows Jerome, from whom he also noted the years and months of each reign.] He was of obscure birth (Historical miscellany and Roman History), but outstanding in military courage and comparable with the best—for when sent by Claudius first to Germany and then to Britain, he fought the enemy thirty-two times and greatly enlarged the Roman Empire. [Note: “Britain” appears as “Britthania” in 5.]

He conducted himself moderately in power. Among his other good qualities, he possessed this gracious trait: he did not retain enmities in his heart. Thus he gave the daughter of the aforementioned Vitellius, his enemy, richly endowed with wealth, to a most noble husband.

When his friends warned him to beware of Tametius Pomposianus, concerning whom a rumor was spreading that he would become emperor, Vespasian made him consul, joking with this quip: “When he receives the kingdom, he will remember such a kindness.” He often calmed the anger of his friends with such playful remarks.

While repairing Rome, which had been left ruined by fires and old collapses, and adding much to the Roman realm, he celebrated a triumph over the Jews together with his son Titus and remained beloved by everyone. Exhausted by a flux of the bowels, he died at his own villa among the Sabines, in the seventy-ninth year of his life. [Note: “of his life” appears in 9c; “69” in E1.]

26. 1. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle—Historical miscellany.) In his first year, Titus, his son, afflicted the besieged Jews with an indescribable famine, pressing them with various instruments of war.

2. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 73, Jerusalem was captured by Titus, not without much bloodshed among his own men. After overthrowing the city, he killed six hundred thousand Jews, as Cornelius and Suetonius report. [Note: The number is lacking in 9c.] Josephus, also called Josippus, one of the Jews who commanded the war there, writes that eleven hundred thousand perished from famine and the sword, and that one hundred thousand captives were publicly sold.

—(Jerome.) He reports that the reason such a great multitude was found at Jerusalem was the feast of Unleavened Bread, on account of which Jews from every nation had gathered at the Temple and were shut inside the city as though in a prison. It was necessary that they be killed during those same days of Passover on which they had killed the Savior. [Note: “in” is lacking in 5.]

The entire period is reckoned from the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius and from the beginning of the evangelical preaching: forty-two years to the second year of Vespasian and the final destruction of Jerusalem; two hundred years from the captivity that the Jews suffered under Antiochus; 590 years from the second year of Darius, when the Temple was rebuilt; [Note: 5 reads “indeed” for “however.”] and 1,102 years from its first construction under Solomon.

3. A.D. 74. Vespasian began to rebuild the Capitol.

4. A.D. 75. A revolt arose in Alexandria.

5. A.D. 76. The Colossus was erected, having a height of 107 feet.

6. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 77. Josephus the historian became prominent.

7. (Jerome.) A.D. 78. Three cities of Cyprus collapsed in an earthquake.

8. A.D. 79. So great a pestilence occurred at Rome that nearly ten thousand people died within a few days.

9. A.D. 80. Vespasian died from a flux of the bowels.

## The Years of Titus

(Roman History and Historical miscellany.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 81, and in the 831st year from the founding of the City, Titus, son of Vespasian and Domitilla, the eighth after Augustus, assumed the empire and reigned for two years and two months.

He, too, was called Vespasian after his father’s name. He was extremely eloquent in both languages, Greek and Latin; exceptionally warlike; most moderate; and remarkable for every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called “the Love and Delight of the human race.”

He was so generous that he refused nothing to anyone who asked him for something. When his friends reproached him and asked why he acted in this way, he replied that no one ought to leave an emperor saddened.

One day, as he recalled during dinner that he had granted nothing to anyone that day, he said to those sitting with him: “Friends, I have lost a day today.”

He died in the forty-second year of his age, in the same villa where his father had died. Such was the mourning in the city of Rome at his death that it seemed as though they had been left orphans by their father. [Col. 0678A]

1. (Jerome.) In the first year of his reign he built an amphitheater at Rome, at the dedication of which he killed five thousand wild animals. [Note: “five thousand” appears in 5.]

—(Historical miscellany.) A.D. 82. A sudden fire lasted for three days at Rome. [Note: The words from “According to” through “deny this” are lacking in E.] According to ecclesiastical history (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 12, 14), when Linus had died, Anacletus was ordained pope and sat for twelve years; but others deny this. [Note: 9c adds: “Jerome’s chronicles say Cletus, who is also Anacletus.”]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 83, and in the 833rd year from the founding of the City, Domitian, son of Vespasian and Domitilla and younger brother of Titus, the ninth after Augustus, began to reign and reigned for fifteen years and six months.

—(Historical miscellany.) At first he pretended to be merciful and modest; soon, however, becoming more like Tiberius, Caligula, or Nero than like his father or brother, he advanced into every kind of vice. For all his crimes, he was the second persecutor of Christians, the first after Nero.

During this persecution he exiled the apostle and evangelist John to the island of Patmos because of his preaching of the divine word. He also exiled Flavia Domitilla, the daughter of the sister of Flavius Clemens, to the island of Pontia, together with many others, and killed many nobles of Rome.

He ordered himself to be called and written of as “lord and god,” and permitted no statue of himself to be set up in the palace unless it was made of gold or silver. He fell into such mental idleness that, after sending everyone away, he alone in the palace hunted swarms of flies. When someone asked him whether anyone was in the palace, he replied: “Not even a fly.”

Since he was hated by everyone, he was killed in the palace in a conspiracy of his own people. His wife Domitia was brought into the plot because of her love for the actor Paris. He died in the thirty-fifth year of his life. His funeral was carried out by undertakers with great disgrace and he was buried ignominiously. The senate decreed that his name should be erased, so that no one would call him emperor.

He was so skilled in archery that he could shoot an arrow between the fingers of a man standing at a distance.

1. (Jerome.) In his first year he prohibited the making of eunuchs.

2. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 84. By decree of the senate Titus was reckoned among the gods.

3. (Jerome.) A.D. 85. Domitian sent many senators into exile. [Note: “sent” appears in 5.]

4. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 86. Anianus, the first bishop of Alexandria after Mark, died after the twenty-second year of his episcopate. Abilius succeeded him as the second bishop.

5. (Jerome.) A.D. 87. Quintilian of Calagurris in Spain [Note: The manuscripts read “Quintianus” here instead of “Quintilianus.”] was the first at Rome to maintain a public school and receive a salary from the treasury.

6. A.D. 88. Domitian expelled mathematicians and philosophers from the City.

7. A.D. 89. Anacletus, third after Peter, succeeded Clement. He sat for twelve years and ten months and suffered under Trajan, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

8. (Jerome.) A.D. 90. Domitian built a forum and many buildings.

9. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 91. The heresy of Menander and many others arose.

10. A.D. 92. Domitian celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Germans.

11. A.D. 93. Domitian prohibited the planting of vines in cities. [Note: 9c reads “to be done”; 5 has “vines to be planted in cities.”]

12. (Jerome.) A.D. 94. Domitian launched the second persecution against Christians, the first after Nero. [Note: The material from “According to” through “he held” is lacking in E1.] According to ecclesiastical history (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 14, 34), at Rome, after completing twelve years in the episcopate, Anacletus handed the priestly see over to Clement, who held it for nine years.

13. (Jerome.) A.D. 95. Domitian destroyed many noblemen.

14. (*Life of Saint Dionysius.*) A.D. 96. Dionysius the Areopagite, the first bishop of Athens appointed by the apostle Paul and later sent as a preacher to Gaul, was beheaded at Paris together with Rusticus and Eleutherius, under the prefect Sisinnius, in the sixty-fourth year after the Lord’s Passion.

15. (Jerome.) A.D. 97. Flavia Domitilla was exiled to the island of Pontia.

16. (William of Malmesbury’s Chronicle.) A.D. 98. Domitian was killed by his own people.

## Nerva
1. (H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 99, but in the 849th year from the founding of the City [the manuscript E1 omits “of the City”], Nerva Cocceius, born in the town of Narnia, of middling nobility, a very old man, the tenth after Augustus, assumed the imperial power and reigned for one year, four months, and eight days. In private life he was temperate and energetic; in power he showed himself most civil and equitable. (HIER.) By decree of the senate he established that whatever Domitian had ordered should be void, and by his edict he recalled all the exiles. (H. m.) Hence Saint John the Apostle, returning from exile to Ephesus and finding the church disturbed by heresies, wrote the Gospel at the urging of the brethren, thereby confirming the true faith (cf. BEDA, CHR.). Nerva, however, having adopted Trajan as his successor, died, worn out by illness, in the fifth month of the second year of his reign, at the age of 72 (cf. HIER.).

## The Years of Trajan

[The manuscripts omit this heading.]

(H. m.) In the hundredth year of the Lord’s incarnation, but in the 850th year from the founding of the City [the number 850 is absent in manuscript 5], Ulpius Trajanus Crinitus, born in the city of Tuder, Spanish by race, from an old rather than illustrious family, although his father was consul, was made emperor at Agrippina, a noble city of Gaul. He was the eleventh after Augustus and reigned for 19 years, 6 months, and 15 days.

He administered the state in such a way that he deservedly surpassed all emperors. For since two qualities are sought in outstanding rulers—holiness at home and courage in arms, with prudence in both—there was in him such moderation in the greatest matters that he seemed to have blended his virtues by some kind of tempering, except that he was somewhat addicted to food and wine. He was enduring of labor, both a discoverer of justice and human and divine law and a guardian of ancient customs. (AUR. V.) He added much to the Roman Empire and bestowed many benefits throughout the whole world; for he was warlike and devoted to every good pursuit.

(H. m.) When his friends censured him for being too familiar with everyone, he replied: “An emperor ought to be toward his subjects as he himself, when a private citizen, would wish emperors to be toward him.”

Thus Trajan’s rule was believed to have been divinely given as a remedy for the Roman senate, ruined and cast down, because very many remarkable signs had announced it [manuscript 5 reads “pronounced” instead of “foretold”]. Among these, the chief was that a crow, from the summit of the Capitol, cried out in the Attic language: *kalos*—“good” or “beautiful.”

Later, deceived by error, he began the third persecution against the Christians. Pliny the Younger, who, as Tertullian reports, had been appointed one of the judges and persecutors, informed him that these people did nothing deserving death except that they did not sacrifice to the gods, and that before dawn they rose and praised Christ as though he were God, while abstaining from every evil. Trajan wrote back that Christians were in no way to be sought out on account of their faith; thus the persecution was quieted.

Accordingly, after the immense glory he had won in war and at home, Trajan, returning from Persia, died at Seleucia in Isauria from a flux of the bowels, in the 63rd year of his life, in the first month, on the fourth day, in the seventh month of the twentieth year of his reign [in manuscript 9c, the text from “month” through “his” is absent].. The ashes of his cremated body were brought to Rome in a golden urn and buried in Trajan’s Forum beneath his column, whose height is 140 feet. His image was placed beneath it and carried in procession in the manner of a triumph, with the senate and army leading the way. He alone of all men was buried within the City. So great was the honor paid to his memory that, even in our own time, emperors were hailed in the senate only with the words: “More fortunate than Augustus, better than Trajan” (cf. H. R.).

1. (Chr. W.) In his first year, the Apostle and Evangelist John fell asleep at Ephesus, in the 68th year from the Lord’s Passion and the 99th year of his life. (HIER.) At Alexandria, Cerdo was ordained the third bishop; he remained there for 11 years.

2. A.D. 101. Nerva was enrolled among the gods by order of the senate [manuscript 9c. adds: “The Passion narratives agree with Jerome that Clement suffered in the third year of Trajan”].

4. (Chr. W.) A.D. 103. Evaristus was ordained the fourth pope; after sitting for eight years, he suffered under Trajan on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

5. A.D. 104. Trajan subjected many peoples to Roman rule.

7. A.D. 106. Trajan celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Scythians.

8. (HIER.) A.D. 107. Four cities of Asia were destroyed by an earthquake.

10. A.D. 109. Trajan began the fourth persecution [manuscript 9c. reads “third”] against the Christians. In it Symeon, son of Clopas, who held the episcopate in Jerusalem after James, was crucified at the age of 120; in his place Justus was ordained. (Chr. W.) Ignatius also, the second bishop of Antioch, was brought to Rome and handed over to the beasts; in his place Heros was appointed as the third bishop. (HIER.)

11. A.D. 110. Pliny the Younger was held in high esteem and acted on behalf of the Christians.

12. A.D. 111. Alexander was ordained the fifth pope of the Roman Church. After sitting for ten years, he suffered with Eventius and Theodulus on the fifth day before the Nones of May under Hadrian, under the prefect Aurelian (cf. Chr. W.). At Alexandria, Primus was ordained the fourth bishop and remained for 12 years. (HIER.)

14. A.D. 113. Three cities of Galatia collapsed in an earthquake.

15. A.D. 114. In Jerusalem, Zacchaeus was ordained the fourth bishop. After him came Tobias, the fifth; Benjamin, the sixth; John, the seventh; Matthias, the eighth; Philip, the ninth; Seneca, the tenth; Justus, the eleventh [the initials “I. u.” are absent in manuscript 9c.]; Levi, the twelfth; Ephrem, the thirteenth; Joses or Joseph, the fourteenth; and Judas, the fifteenth. These fifteen, from the Apostles until the destruction and restoration of Jerusalem, which occurred under Hadrian, ruled Jerusalem from the circumcision and continued for almost 106 years after the Lord’s Passion.

16. A.D. 115. Trajan made Armenia, Syria, and Mesopotamia provinces.

18. A.D. 117. The Jews destroyed the city of Salamis in Cyprus.

19. A.D. 118. Trajan died of a flux of the bowels. At this time, in Asia, Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostles and bishop of the church of Smyrna, still survived and flourished; likewise Papias was serving as a priest at Hierapolis.

## The Years of Hadrian

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 119, in the 870th year from the founding of the City, Aelius Hadrianus, an Italian by race, the son of Hadrianus, who was Trajan’s cousin, from the city of Adria in the territory of Picenum—from which the Adriatic Sea also takes its name—was made emperor. He was the twelfth after Augustus and reigned for 21 years.

Although he was Trajan’s cousin’s son, he nevertheless did not wish to adopt him [the words are absent in manuscript 9c.]. He became emperor without Trajan’s consent, though Plotina, Trajan’s wife, worked on his behalf. Hence, envying Trajan’s glory, he abandoned the three provinces that Trajan had added: Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia.

He was extremely learned and eloquent in both Greek and Latin. He was exceedingly sharp in questioning and answering, giving ordered answers to ordered questions, jokes to jokes, insults to insults, songs to songs, and pretenses to pretenses, so that one might believe he had prepared himself in advance against everything. In all things he followed every pursuit of the Athenians: in speaking, singing, chanting, learning the art of medicine, music, and geometry. (AUR. V.) He also possessed knowledge of painting and pottery, and learned all these things perfectly, along with many others, so that there was scarcely anything he had not experienced. He retained in his memory more than could be believed [manuscript 4 reads “could retain,” manuscript 5 “can”]: places, things, cases, and soldiers; and he called by their proper names people whom he had never seen. He was a changeable, versatile, and multiform man, a dissembler in good and evil [manuscript E1 reads “in evil”]; and, to make himself appear good, he cleverly concealed the vices he possessed.

(H. m.) Through Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles; Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom; and the legate Serenus Granianus, who instructed him with books composed on the Christian religion, he became more kindly disposed toward Christians. (JORD. DE R. S.—H. m.) He endured many labors by traveling throughout the world and restoring many things. He rebuilt Alexandria and Jerusalem, which had long before been destroyed, and subdued the Jews, who had rebelled again, by a final slaughter. He deprived them of permission to enter Jerusalem, which he himself restored to a better condition at the place where the Lord was crucified outside the gate [manuscript 5 reads “where the cross is”], and called it Aelia after his own name.

(BEDAE CHR.) He died in Campania, at Baiae, from a subcutaneous disease, in the 62nd year of his life and the 21st year of his reign, in the tenth month.

1. (Chr. W.) In his first year he restored Alexandria at public expense [manuscript 9c. reads “publicly”].

2. (HIER.) A.D. 120. The senate enrolled Trajan among the gods.

3. (Chr. W.) A.D. 121. Pope Alexander suffered. Sixtus, the sixth pope, succeeded him; he sat for nine years and suffered under Hadrian on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

4. (HIER.) A.D. 122. Justus was ordained the fifth bishop of Alexandria.

8. A.D. 126. Saturninus and two others founded a heresy.

10. (Chr. W.—HIER.) A.D. 128. Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles, and Aristides of Athens, our philosopher, composed books on the faith.

12. (Chr. W.) A.D. 130. Pope Telesphorus was ordained the seventh pope; after sitting for ten years, he suffered under Hadrian on the Nones of January. (BEDAE MART.) He established that Masses should be celebrated on the night of the holy Lord’s Nativity and that, at the time of the sacrifice, *Gloria in excelsis* should be sung. (HIER.) At Antioch, Cornelius was ordained the fourth bishop.

13. (Chr. W.) A.D. 131. Nicopolis and Caesarea collapsed in an earthquake.

14. (HIER.) A.D. 132. Eumenes was ordained the sixth bishop of Alexandria [the readings are: “the sixth is ordained; he sat”; manuscript 5: “the sixth was ordained and sat for 13 years”; manuscript E1: “was ordained sixth and sat”]. He remained for 13 years.

19. (Chr. W.) A.D. 137. Jerusalem was restored by Aelius Hadrian and called Aelia after his name.

20. (HIER.) A.D. 138. Mark was ordained bishop of Jerusalem, the first from the Gentiles, whereas previously there had been fifteen from the circumcision.

21. (JORD. *De r. s.*) A.D. 139. Hadrian died from a subcutaneous disease. During his reign, Aquila of Pontus translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek.

## The Years of Antoninus

The years from the beginning: 4100.

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 140, in the 891st year from the founding of the City, Antoninus Fulvius Boionius, later surnamed Pius because of his clemency, of noble though not very ancient family, the thirteenth after Augustus, received the imperial power and reigned for 22 years and three months. [The words concerning his family are absent in manuscript E1.]

(AUR. V.—H. m.) He had been adopted by Hadrian as his son and was also his son-in-law. He was an outstanding man, deservedly comparable with Numa Pompilius, just as Trajan is compared with Romulus. He lived in great dignity as a private citizen, and was even greater in power: harsh toward no one, kind to all; in military affairs he moderated his pursuit of glory, preferring to defend the provinces rather than enlarge them, and seeking just men to administer the state [manuscript E1 reads “thus”; the remaining manuscripts omit the phrase].

Although for 22 years he ruled the world by authority alone, without any war, all kings, nations, and peoples feared and loved him so greatly that they regarded him more as a parent or patron than as a lord or emperor. Like a favorable heavenly power, they all wished him well and asked him to judge their disputes. He died in the 77th year of his life.

1. (Chr. W.) In the first year of his reign, Hyginus was ordained the eighth pope. He sat for four years and died on the fourth day before the Ides of January. (BEDAE MART.) He established the clergy and distributed its grades.

2. (Chr. W.) A.D. 141. Valentinus and Cerdo attacked the Church with heresy.

3. (HIER.) A.D. 142. The same heresiarchs came to Rome.

4. (BEDA.) A.D. 143. Justin the philosopher presented Antoninus with a book composed on behalf of the Christian religion and made him favorably disposed toward Christians.

5. (Chr. W.) A.D. 144. Pope Pius, the ninth pope, sat for 15 years; he departed on the fifth day before the Ides of July [manuscript E1 reads “and departed”].

6. (HIER.) A.D. 145. Heros was appointed the fifth bishop of Antioch.

7. A.D. 146. At Alexandria, Mark was ordained the seventh bishop and remained for ten years [manuscript E1 reads “he sat for ten years”].

11. A.D. 150. Apollonius the Stoic of Chalcedon became famous.

14. A.D. 153. A certain Crescens, a Cynic philosopher, began a persecution against Justin, a philosopher of our doctrine, because Justin exposed him as a glutton and a betrayer of philosophy. In this persecution Justin shed his blood gloriously for Christ.

15. A.D. 154. (EUS. H. e. IV, 13.) Antoninus, moved by the heresy of Crescens, wrote a letter on behalf of the Christians to all the peoples of Asia.

16. A.D. 155. (HIER.) At Alexandria, Celadion was ordained the eighth bishop [manuscript 1b reads “Peladion”]; he sat for 14 years.

20. A.D. 159. (Chr. W.—HIER.—BEDAE MART.) Anicetus was ordained the tenth pope and sat for ten years. Under him Polycarp came to Rome and corrected many whom the error of Valentinus and Cerdo had overthrown. This Anicetus established that the clergy should not grow their hair long. He suffered under Marcus and Severus on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

21. A.D. 160. (HIER.) After Mark, Cassianus was ordained the seventeenth bishop of Jerusalem; then Publius, the eighteenth; Maximus, the nineteenth; Julianus, the twentieth [manuscript 5 reads “Julius”; manuscripts 9c. and 10 read “Julius XXI”; manuscript 10 also reads “Symmachus”]; Gaianus, the twenty-first; Symmachus, the twenty-second; Gaius, the twenty-third; Julianus, the twenty-fourth; and Capito, the twenty-fifth.

22. A.D. 161. Antoninus died at his own estate, the villa of Dorius.

## The Years of Antoninus Verus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 162, in the 913th year from the founding of the City, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Verus, the fourteenth after Augustus [the words “after Augustus” are absent in manuscript 9c.], obtained the imperial power and reigned for 19 years.

He was unquestionably of the noblest birth, since his paternal ancestry went back to Numa Pompilius, while his maternal ancestry derived from King Solentius. (AUREL. VICT.) He possessed every virtue and a heavenly intelligence. In public calamities he became a kind of defender; and if he had not existed in those times, Roman glory would undoubtedly have perished.

(H. m.—H. R.) With a new act of benevolence he made his kinsman Lucius Annius Antoninus Severus, who was the son-in-law of Antoninus Pius, his partner in the imperial power. Then, for the first time, the Roman state obeyed two men administering the empire with equal authority, whereas until then it had always had single Augusti. They waged war against the Parthians. Lucius Annius Severus, however, went to that war and accomplished many great deeds personally and through his generals. Returning victorious, he died in Venetia in the eleventh year of the imperial power; thus Marcus Antoninus once again held the empire alone.

1. (HIER. and H. m.) In the first year of his reign, Vologeses, king of the Parthians, rebelling for the first time after Trajan’s victory, ravaged the Roman provinces neighboring his own. Lucius Annius marched against him.

2. (HIER.) A.D. 163. When Lucius Caesar was sacrificing at Athens, a fire in the sky was seen to be carried from west to east.

3. A.D. 164. Fronto, a distinguished orator, was held in high esteem. He instructed Marcus Antoninus in Latin letters.

4. A.D. 165. The city of Seleucia in Assyria was captured by the Romans together with 300,000 people.

6. A.D. 167. When the fourth persecution reckoned from Nero arose, Polycarp, Penius, and many others suffered under these emperors.

8. (Chr. W.) A.D. 169 [the entry is absent in manuscript 9c.]. Soter was ordained the eleventh pope; after sitting for nine years, he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. (HIER.) Agrippinus was ordained the ninth bishop of Alexandria.

9. A.D. 170. The wise man Theophilus was ordained the sixth bishop of Antioch.

10. A.D. 171. (EUS. H. e. IV, 21–22.) Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, was renowned, as were also Pinytus, bishop of Crete; Melito of Sardis; Philip [manuscript 9c. adds “the philosopher”]; Apollinaris; Musanus; Modestus; and especially Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon. Hegesippus also flourished at this time. Coming to Rome under Pope Anicetus, he remained until the time of Pope Eleutherius and left behind many monuments of his learning.

11. A.D. 172. (See above.) Lucius Annius Antoninus Severus died, and Aurelius Marcus Antoninus Verus obtained the empire alone; but he made his son Lucius Commodus his partner in the kingdom. (HIER.) [Manuscript 5 supplies “Antoninus” in the margin; manuscript 9c. omits it; manuscript 4 reads “Antonius.”]

12. A.D. 173. Melito, bishop of Sardis, presented the emperor Antoninus with an apology on behalf of the Christians.

16. A.D. 177. Maximinus was ordained the seventh bishop of Antioch.

17. A.D. 178. Eleutherius was ordained the twelfth pope; after sitting for 13 years, he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. Lucius, king of Britain, sent him a letter asking to be baptized, which he obtained (cf. Chr. W. and BEDA).

19. A.D. 180. (Chr. W.) Antoninus died in Pannonia.

## The Years of Commodus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 181, but in the 932nd year from the founding of the City, Lucius Aurelius Commodus Antoninus, son of Marcus Antoninus Verus, the fifteenth after Augustus, received the imperial power and reigned for 12 years and 8 months. He possessed nothing of his father except that he too fought successfully against the Germans.

He attempted to transfer the month of September to his own name, so that it would be called Commodus. He lived in luxury and every kind of filth. He killed many senators [manuscript 9c. reads “many senators indeed”], especially those whom he saw to excel in nobility and wisdom. Among them he killed Salvius Julianus, the legislator.

His wife was Martia, of freedman origin, distinguished by her beauty and her courtesan’s arts. After she had completely bound his mind to her, when he had left the bath she offered him a cup of poison; then, having sent in a very strong wrestler, she had him strangled in the house of Vestilianus, in the 32nd year of his life. He was so hated by everyone that, even dead, he was judged an enemy of the human race.

1. (HIER.) In the first year of his reign he celebrated a successful triumph over the Germans. Julianus was ordained the tenth bishop of Alexandria and sat for ten years.

3. (Chr. W.) A.D. 183. Pantaenus [manuscript 4 reads “Pantherus,” manuscript 5 “Pantheus”; manuscripts 10 and 11 omit the entire entry] and Clement became famous at Alexandria.

4. (HIER.) A.D. 184. At Jerusalem, Maximus was ordained the twenty-sixth bishop. After him came Antonius, the twenty-seventh; Valens, the twenty-eighth; Dulichianus, the twenty-ninth; Narcissus, the thirtieth; Dius, the thirty-first; Germanio, the thirty-second; Gordius, the thirty-third; and again Narcissus, mentioned above. The years and periods of their episcopates are not known [manuscript 5 adds “note”].

8. (Chr. W.) A.D. 188. Origen was born at Alexandria.
