10. (HIER.) A.D. 190. Serapion was ordained the eighth bishop of Antioch [the words from “Serapion” through “eighth” are absent in manuscripts 10 and 11].

11. (Chr. W.) A.D. 191. Victor was ordained the thirteenth pope; after sitting for ten years, he suffered under Septimius Severus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [manuscript 5 reads “Septimius”]. (HIER.) Demetrius was ordained the eleventh bishop of Alexandria and sat for 43 years [manuscript 9c. reads 42].

12. A.D. 192. Serapion was ordained the eighth bishop of Antioch [this entry is absent in manuscript 1b and manuscripts 4 and 5; cf. the entry for A.D. 190].

13. (Chr. W.) A.D. 193. Aurelius Commodus, troublesome to all, was strangled.

## Helvius Pertinax

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 194, in the 945th year from the founding of the City, Helvius Pertinax, the sixteenth after Augustus, assumed the imperial power and reigned for six months. [Manuscript 5 reads “Helius,” and does so likewise below.]

(H. m.) Born in Liguria of a freedman father, while administering the prefecture of the City and already seventy years old, he was compelled, by decree of the senate, to assume the imperial power, though unwilling and resisting. Hence he was called Pertinax. Through many labors he rose to the highest honors and struggled so fiercely that he was called “the ball of Fortune.”

(JORD. *De r. s.*) When the senate urged him to call his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, he said: “It ought to be enough that I myself have ruled unwillingly, since I did not deserve to do so.”

In the seventh month—or, as others maintain (H. m.), on the eighty-first day—Didius Salvius Julianus killed him in the palace. Julianus was a jurist from Milan, a nobleman, and the grandson of that Salvius Julianus who composed the laws under the deified Hadrian. He was factious, rash, and greedy for the kingdom.

After killing Helvius Pertinax, Julianus himself seized the state, but did not reign for more than seven months [manuscript 9c. reads “not without reason”]. At this time Niger Piscennius at Antioch and Septimius Severus at Savaria in Pannonia were elevated as emperors. Julianus was defeated by Severus in civil war at the Milvian Bridge. He fled to the palace, was captured, and, with his neck stretched out in the manner of condemned men, was beheaded.

## The Years of Severus

(H. m. and H. R.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 195, in the 946th year from the founding of the City, Septimius Severus [manuscripts 4 and 5 read “Septimius”; manuscript E1 corrects “Septimus”; manuscript 1b reads “Septunius”] obtained the imperial power. He was the seventeenth after Augustus and reigned for 17 years and 3 months.

He came from Africa and was the only emperor from Africa in the memory of all. First he was an advocate of the treasury, then a military tribune; thereafter, through many and varied offices, he rose to the administration of the entire state. Because he avenged Helvius Pertinax upon Julianus, he wished to be called Pertinax.

He fought many successful wars, the greatest of which was in Britain. There, in order to keep the recovered provinces secure [manuscript 5 reads “to possess”], he built a very strong wall, reinforced with numerous towers, extending for 132 miles from sea to sea. He died there at Eburacum, in the 65th year of his life and the 18th year of his reign.

He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Geta, however, was declared a public enemy, while he left Bassianus as his successor and wished the name Antoninus to be bestowed upon him.

During his reign the fifth persecution against the Christians took place, and many were crowned for the faith of Christ. Among them was Leonides, the father of Origen, who was martyred.

(Chr. W.—JORD. *De r. s.*) During his reign a certain Samaritan named Symmachus, who had become a proselyte of the Jews, likewise translated the divine Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek and produced his own edition. But, as is read in the *Ecclesiastical History* (VI, 14), he was an Ebionite, that is, a member of the heresy asserting that Christ, born of Joseph and Mary, was a mere man and that the law was to be observed according to Jewish rites. He also composed certain commentaries in which he attempted to confirm the authority of his heresy from the Gospel according to Matthew.

(JORD.) Almost three years after him, Theodotion of Pontus likewise produced his own edition of the same work [manuscript 9c. reads “into an edition”].

1. (HIER.) In the first year of his reign Severus killed Julianus and ordered himself to be called Pertinax.

2. A.D. 196. Clement, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, and Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher, still flourished. They were most eloquent in disputing our doctrine.

3. A.D. 197. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theophilus of Caesarea, as well as Polycarp and Bachilus, bishops of the province of Asia, were held in high esteem.

4. A.D. 198. (BEDA, *Chr.*) A question arose among the bishops of Asia whether, according to the law of Moses, Passover ought to be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month. Pope Victor, issuing widely circulated treatises, decreed that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, as his predecessor Eleutherius had also done, from the fourteenth moon of the first month through the twenty-first. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, together with the other bishops who were present at that council, supported his decrees and wrote a very useful synodical letter against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews [manuscript 9c. reads “against” rather than “to”; the reading “celebrate” was corrected to “celebrated” in manuscript 9c., while manuscripts 10 and 11 retain “celebrate”].

6. (Chr. W.) In the year 200, Severus defeated the Parthians and Arabs.

9. A.D. 203. Zephyrinus was ordained the fourteenth pope; after sitting for 18 years, he departed on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

10. A.D. 204. The fifth persecution against the Christians took place. In it, among many others, Leonides, the father of Origen, suffered for Christ [manuscript E1 supplies: “as was said, having suffered for Christ, while Origen himself…”]. (EUS. H. e. VI, 3.) Origen himself, being eighteen years old and making progress in many disciplines, was also teaching grammar to the Gentiles and converting many to the faith. Among these were Plutarch and his brother Heraclas. Plutarch obtained the palm of martyrdom, while Heraclas was placed in charge of Alexandria after Demetrius.

11. (HIER.) A.D. 205. Alexander was held in high esteem on account of his confession of Christ.

13. (Chr. W.) A.D. 207. Perpetua and Felicitas were assigned to the beasts at Carthage.

15. (HIER.) A.D. 209. Severus transferred the war to the Britons [manuscripts 4 and 5 read “Britons”; manuscript 9c. reads “Britannians”].

16. A.D. 210. Tertullian was celebrated by everyone’s voice.

17. A.D. 211. Origen was studying at Alexandria.

18. A.D. 212. Severus died at Eburacum in Britain [manuscript 5 reads “Septimius Severus”].

## The Years of Antoninus Caracalla

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 213, in the 965th year from the founding of the City, Marcus Antoninus Bassianus Caracalla, son of Severus, the eighteenth after Augustus, succeeded his father in the imperial power and reigned for six years and two months [manuscript E1 reads “two months”].

He was called Bassianus from the name of his maternal grandfather; at his father’s request, the senate called him Antoninus. (AUR. V.) Because he brought many garments from Gaul and made from them long tunics called *caracallae*, and ordered the people, dressed in these garments, to enter and greet him, he was called Caracalla.

(H. m.) His character was somewhat harsher and more threatening than his father’s. He was incapable of restraining his lust, to such an extent that he took his stepmother Julia as his wife. When he saw the body of Alexander the Great, he ordered himself to be called Magnus and Alexander. He had been led to this by the deceitful flatteries of his courtiers, so that, walking with a grim face and his neck turned toward his left shoulder, he imitated the feature they had noticed in Alexander’s face and persuaded himself that his likeness was perfect.

While preparing an expedition against the Parthians, he withdrew at Edessa to attend to his natural functions. There he was killed by a soldier who had followed him as though to guard him, in the 44th year of his life [the age is absent in manuscript E1].

1. (HIER.) In the first year of his reign, Asclepiades was ordained the ninth bishop of Antioch.

2. (EUS. H. e. VI, 7.) A.D. 214. When Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, was traveling toward Jerusalem out of a desire to visit the holy places, Narcissus, the bishop of that city, was still alive. Narcissus was its thirtieth bishop, a man of very advanced age; and Alexander himself was ordained bishop there, the Lord commanding by revelation that this should happen.

This Narcissus was a man of extraordinary holiness. Among his many distinguished virtues, during the Easter vigil, when oil was lacking for the lamps, he ordered water to be poured in; after blessing it, he made it into oil.

Later, after certain men conscious of wrongdoing had feared his judgment, he was defamed by them through a disgraceful accusation. One of them swore that he was telling the truth so that fire would not consume him; another, so that he would not be corrupted by jaundice; and a third, so that he would not lose his eyesight. Although no one who knew his life believed them, even though they swore to it, Narcissus nevertheless, unable to endure the troubles and loving a quiet life, withdrew and hid for years in more secluded places.

The first witness, when a small spark set fire to his house at night, was consumed by the flames with his entire household. The second was corrupted by jaundice from foot to head. The third, seeing the end of the others, finally confessed his guilt and continued in tears until he was deprived of his eyesight [the words in brackets occur only in manuscript E1].

Since Narcissus could not be found, it seemed necessary to the bishops to ordain another in his place, named Dius. After a short time Germanio succeeded him, and Gordius succeeded Germanio.

(EUS. H. e. VI, 8.) Then suddenly Narcissus appeared, as though returned from the dead, and, at the request of the brethren, was restored to his former position. Alexander succeeded Narcissus, now 116 years old and still alive, by divine instruction and governed the Church diligently together with him.

7. (JORD. *De r. s.*) A.D. 219. The edition that we call the fifth was found at Jerusalem.

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 220, in the 971st year from the founding of the City, Opilius Macrinus, who had been prefect of the praetorian guard, the nineteenth after Augustus, was made emperor by the army together with his son Diadumenus. After reigning for one year and two months, he was killed together with his son at Archelaïs by that same army, which was in mutiny. (HIER.) Philetus was ordained the tenth bishop of Antioch.

## The Years of Aurelius

(H. m. and H. R.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 221, in the 972nd year from the founding of the City, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Varus, who was believed to be the son of Antoninus Caracalla, secretly begotten through adultery with his cousin, the twentieth after Augustus, was made emperor and reigned for four years.

(JORD. *De r. s.*—H. m.) His maternal grandfather was Bassianus, a priest of the sun, whom the Phoenicians call Heliogabalus. Hence this man too was called Heliogabalus, himself a priest in the temple of Heliogabalus.

When he came to Rome amid the immense expectation of the soldiers and senate, he polluted himself with every disgrace and, living most shamelessly, omitted no kind of obscenity. Thus, transferring to himself the desire for sexual intercourse which, because of a natural deficiency, he was not yet able to fulfill, he ordered himself to be called by the feminine name Basiana instead of Bassianus [manuscripts 5 and 9c. read “Bassiana”]. He joined a certain Vestal virgin to himself as though in marriage and, after cutting off his genitals, consecrated himself to the Great Mother.

He made his cousin Marcellus Caesar; Marcellus was later called Alexander. After three years and eight months from the beginning of his reign, he was killed at Rome in a military uprising together with his mother, in the sixteenth year of his life. His body was dragged by the soldiers through the streets of the City like a dog’s corpse. With military mockery they called him the puppy of untamed and rabid lust.

(BEDA.) Hippolytus, bishop and author of many short works, brought the chronological canon that he had written down to this point. He also discovered a sixteen-year cycle of Easter, thereby giving Eusebius, who composed a nineteen-year cycle, the occasion for his work.

1. In the first year of Aurelius, Callistus was ordained the fifteenth pope. He sat for five years and suffered under the emperor Alexander on the second day before the Ides of October (cf. Chr. W.).

3. (HIER.) A.D. 223. Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, was founded, with Africanus, the chronicler, undertaking the embassy on its behalf.

4. (Chr. W.) A.D. 224. Aurelius was killed in a military uprising.

## The Years of Alexander

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 225, in the 976th year from the founding of the City (cf. JORD. *De r. s.*), Aurelius Severus Alexander, of humble fortune, the twenty-first after Augustus, was made emperor. He was still a very young man, named Caesar by the army and Augustus by the senate, and reigned for 13 years.

He loved his mother Mammaea piously and uniquely, on account of which he pleased everyone [the phrase is absent in manuscript E1]. She, however, exercised great power over him and compelled him to such an extent that even the very small portions left over from her table, although partly eaten, were reserved for another meal.

(BEDA.) Nevertheless, she later took care to hear the presbyter Origen and, when he was summoned to Antioch, treated him honorably. After hearing him, she became a Christian.

(H. m.) Alexander, having undertaken war against the Persians, defeated their king Xerses with the greatest glory. He maintained military discipline with the utmost severity and was also popular and beloved at Rome.

During his reign Taurinus assumed imperial power in the East, and Julianus Maximus in Gaul. Alexander, stationed at Mainz, when he saw that the soldiers were abandoning him, wished that someone would kill him. When one of them came toward him with a sword, Alexander covered his head and offered his neck; he immediately perished, in the 26th year of his life and the 13th year of his reign.

(JORD. *De r. s.*) During his reign, the edition that we call the sixth was likewise found at Nicopolis Actiaca, that is, in Epirus.

1. (Chr. W.) In the first year of his reign he defeated Xerses, king of the Persians.

2. A.D. 226. Urbanus became the sixteenth pope. After sitting for eight years, he converted many to the faith and exhorted them to martyrdom [manuscript 9c. reads “was constrained”]; he himself suffered under Alexander on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

4. (HIER.) A.D. 228. Ulpianus, a legal expert and Alexander’s assessor, became famous.

7. A.D. 231. Zebennus was appointed the eleventh bishop of Antioch.

10. (Cf. Chr. W.) A.D. 234. Pontianus was ordained the seventeenth pope. He sat for six years and suffered under Maximinus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December. (HIER.) Heraclas was ordained the twelfth bishop of Alexandria.

11. A.D. 235. Origen moved from Alexandria to Caesarea in Palestine.

13. A.D. 237. Alexander was killed at Mainz.

## The Years of Maximinus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 238, in the 989th year from the founding of the City, Julius Maximinus, a Thracian by race and a soldier by rank, the twenty-second after Augustus, was made emperor solely by the will of the soldiers and without the authority of the senate. He reigned for three years.

He carried out the sixth persecution after Nero against the Christians. During his reign the two Gordians, father and son, seized the imperial power, but one died after the other. Maximinus, having undertaken and successfully completed a war against the Germans, was killed at Aquileia by a certain Puppianus together with his still young son [manuscript E1 reads “little son”]. All the soldiers shouted in the camp that, from so vile a stock, not even a puppy should be kept.

## 2. A.D. 239

Maximinus launched the sixth persecution against the Christians. During it, when Pope Pontianus [Col. 0691C] had died, Antheros succeeded him as the eighteenth pope; but after one month and thirteen days he too suffered martyrdom, on 3 January (cf. Chr. W.).

## Years from the beginning: 4200

### 3. A.D. 240

Pope Fabianus, the nineteenth, was ordained [Note: [Col. 0691] “and holding office,” E1.]; he held office for thirteen years and eleven months and suffered martyrdom under Decius, on 20 January. The emperor Maximinus was killed at Aquileia. (HIER.) At Antioch, Babillas was ordained the twelfth bishop.

## The Years of the Gordians

(H. m. and H. R.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 241, and 992 from the founding of the City, Gordianus, the grandson of Gordianus through his daughter, born at Rome of a most illustrious father, the twenty-third from Augustus, was made emperor and reigned for six years. [Col. 0691D] When he had come to Rome, the brothers Puppianus and Balbinus, who had seized the empire after killing Maximinus, were killed in the palace; they were of peasant origin. Gordianus, still very young, married Tranquillina [Note: [Col. 0691] “tranquillam,” E1.] at Rome and set out for the East, making war upon the Parthians. Having conducted it successfully, he afflicted the Persians in great battles; but while returning, he was killed by Philippus, who reigned after him, in the twentieth year of his life [Note: [Col. 0691] “of his age,” 9c.].

### 1. (BEDA.)

In his first year, Julius Africanus, a chronographer distinguished among ecclesiastical writers, was held in esteem [Col. 0692A]. In the chronicles that he wrote, he reports that he hurried to Alexandria, summoned by the renowned reputation of Aradas, whom rumor proclaimed to be most highly trained in divine, human, and philosophical studies, as well as in every branch of Greek learning.

### 2. (EUS. H. e. VI, 22.) A.D. 242

Origen, at Caesarea in Palestine, imbued with divine wisdom Theodorus, surnamed Gregory, and his brother Anthenodorus, later distinguished bishops of Pontus.

### 3. (H. m.) A.D. 243

Porphyrius, a hearer of the Platonist philosopher Plotinus, was held in esteem at Rome.

### 4. (H. m.) A.D. 244

Theopompus of Chaeronea [Note: [Col. 0691] “of Chaeronea,” E1.] and Nicanor the sophist were distinguished at Athens.

### 5. A.D. 245

Gordianus made war upon the Parthians (cf. Chr. W.).

### 6. A.D. 246

Gordianus was killed by Philippus. [Col. 0692B]

## The Years of Philippus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 247, and 998 from the founding of the City, Marcus Julius Philippus, the twenty-fourth from Augustus, seized the empire after killing Gordianus and reigned for seven years together with his son, Gaius Julius Saturninus Philippus. These were the first of all the emperors to become Christians at Rome [Note: [Col. 0691] omitted in E1.]. During the very vigils of Easter, when they wished to join in the sacrifices and receive communion, they were not permitted to do so by Fabianus, the Roman pontiff, unless they first confessed their sins and stood among the penitents. Accepting this most willingly, they demonstrated by their conduct and actions that they possessed fear of God and the fullest faith of Christianity [Note: [Col. 0691] “demonstrated,” E1.].

(HIER.) In the third year of their rule [Note: [Col. 0691] “already,” omitted in 9c.] [Col. 0692C] the thousandth year from the founding of the city of Rome was completed. After it had been solemnly celebrated by everyone, innumerable beasts were killed in the Great Circus, and theatrical games were held in the Campus Martius, while the people kept vigil for three days and nights. (H. m.) Then both of them—the father and the son—were killed by the army: the father at Verona, with the middle of his head cut off above the rows of his teeth, and the son at Rome, when he was twelve years old. He was of such severe character that, from the age of five, no joke of anyone’s could make him laugh; and when his father laughed too boisterously at the Secular Games, he marked his disapproval, although still a child, by turning away his face.

### 1. (Chr. W.)

In the first year of his reign, Philippus made his son Philippus [Note: [Col. 0691] “his son,” 5.] his partner in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0691] “makes him,” 5, 10, 11.].

### 3. (HIER.) A.D. 249

At Alexandria, Dionisius was ordained the thirteenth bishop. (Chr. W.) The thousandth year from the founding of the City was joyfully celebrated at Rome. [Col. 0692D]

### 6. (HIER.) A.D. 252

Philippus built a city bearing his name in Thrace.

### 7. A.D. 253

Philippus the elder was killed at Verona, and the younger at Rome.

## The Years of Decius

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 254, and the thousand and fifth from the founding of the City, Decius, born at Bubalia in Lower Pannonia, the twenty-fifth from Augustus, seized the empire after the two Philippi—that is, the father and the son—were killed through his treachery. He reigned for thirty months [Note: [Col. 0693] omitted in 10 and 11.], that is, two and a half years.

(HIER.) Some, however, write that he reigned for only one year; but this is greatly at variance [Note: [Col. 0693] omitted in E1.] with the martyrdoms of the saints who are said to have suffered under him. (JORD. *De r. s.*) For since Pope Fabianus is read to have received martyrdom in the fourteenth year of his episcopate under him, and Cornelius succeeded him in the see for three years and is likewise said to have suffered under the same emperor, as did Sixtus, Laurentius, Hippolytus, and very many others, it cannot be maintained that he slaughtered so many successive occupants of the Roman see in one year—especially since Cornelius, as ecclesiastical history teaches (EUS. H. e. VII, 3), held the see for three years.

Hence the succession of those pontiffs also raises a question: how, while Decius held the kingdom for either one year or two and a half, did Cornelius hold the Roman episcopate for three years according to ecclesiastical history, followed by Lucius for eight months, Stephanus for two years, then Sixtus for eleven years, and afterward Dionisius for nine years, when throughout the Church Cornelius and Sixtus, whose deacon was Laurentius, are proclaimed to have suffered under Decius, while Lucius and Stephanus are read to have been martyred under Valerianus and Gallienus? From this it may be inferred that, through the fault of scribes and because of the similarity of names, the turns of the successions were altered. It is probable, however, that the authority of the Catholic Church, handed down to us, ought to be followed.

But, to return to what was stated above: (H. m.) Decius made his son Decius Caesar [Col. 0693C] and launched the seventh persecution against the Christians after Nero, taking as his pretext hatred of the Philippi whom he had killed. Many saints suffered in that persecution.

(HIER.—H. m.) In his time, when very many Goths crossed the river Hister and devastated the cities of the Romans, Decius attacked them in battle with his son and killed thirty thousand of them, though he also lost many of his own men. His son too was killed, and he himself was drowned in the whirlpool of a certain marsh amid the confused masses, so that even his corpse could not be found. This occurred in the third year of his reign and the fiftieth year of his life.

In the book of martyrdoms, however, the following is found: after Pope Sixtus and his archdeacon Laurentius and others had been killed, and afterward Hippolytus and his companions, on the twenty-seventh day after the saints’ martyrdom Decius and the prefect Valerianus, sitting in a carriage and still deliberating about the death of the saints, were seized by demons. In Decius’s presence Valerianus expired; Decius, returning to the palace, was tormented for three days and died in the presence of his wife Tryphonia. How the truth of these matters actually stands may be left to the judgment of the writers.

### 1. (Chr. W.)

In the first year of Decius, when the persecution against the Christians had begun, Pope Fabianus, the nineteenth, suffered martyrdom, on 20 January. Cornelius, the twentieth, succeeded him and held office for one year [Note: [Col. 0693] “one year,” 5.], seven months, and several days, although ecclesiastical history (VII, 3; cf. VI, 29) states—provided that the book has not been corrupted through scribal error—that he held the see for three years; this does not appear to accord with the chronology of Decius (cf. HIER.—EUS. H. e. VI, 9).

Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem and successor of Narcissus, completed his good course; Azabbanes succeeded him. The bishop of Antioch, likewise contending with Alexander, died in prison; after him Fabianus, the thirteenth, was appointed.

### 2. A.D. 255

Pope Cornelius, the twentieth, suffered martyrdom on 14 September. Sixtus, the twenty-first pope, succeeded him and held office for ten months. [Col. 0694B]

### 3. A.D. 256

Pope Sixtus suffered martyrdom on 6 August together with others. In this year Polychronius the bishop suffered with many others, as did Abdo [Note: “Abdon,” 9c, 11.], Sennes, Olympiades, and Maximus; Laurentius suffered after Sixtus; Hippolytus with his companions, and very many others, also suffered (cf. *Mart.*).

Dionisius, the twenty-second pope, was ordained after Sixtus and held office for two years and five months [Note: [Col. 0693] “two years,” E1; this form frequently differs from the others.].

## The Years of Gallus and Volusianus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 257, and the thousand and eighth from the founding of the City, Virius Gallus Hostilius, the twenty-sixth from Augustus, was made emperor by the army [Note: [Col. 0693] “was made,” with 5.] and reigned for two years and four months with his son Volusianus.

(BEDA.) Dionisius, bishop of Alexandria, recalled this reign as follows: “Nor could Gallus either see or avoid the evil of Decius; but, stumbling against the same stone of offense, he persecuted holy men.” [Col. 0694C]

(AUR. VICT.) In these times a certain Aemilianus was raised to the imperial office in Moesia. Both men—the father, that is [Note: [Col. 0693] “the father,” 5.] and the son—marched against him and were killed by their own army. The father was forty-seven years old; Aemilianus, a Moor by birth, was killed after four months [Note: [Col. 0693] omitted in E1.].

### 1. (BEDA.)

In the first [Note: [Col. 0693] “but in the first year,” E1.] year of the reign of Gallus and Volusianus, Origen the presbyter died before completing his seventieth year and was buried at Tyre. He was so diligent in writing that Jerome says in one place that he had read five thousand of his books. (HIER.) At Antioch, Demetrianus was appointed the fourteenth bishop.

### 2. A.D. 258

Gallus and Volusianus were killed. Pope Dionisius, the twenty-second, departed [Note: [Col. 0693] “departed to the Lord,” 5.] on 27 December. He assigned churches to presbyters and divided the parishes. (BEDA, *Mart.*) [Col. 0694D]

## The Years of Valerianus and Gallienus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 259, and the thousand and tenth from the founding of the City, Lucinius Valerianus, surnamed Colobius, while serving in Raetia and Noricum, was made emperor by the army and soon was called Augustus, the twenty-seventh from Augustus. At Rome, Gallienus, his son [Note: [Col. 0693] omitted in E1.], was called Caesar by the senate. They reigned together for six years, while Gallienus afterward reigned alone [Note: [Col. 0695] “afterward alone,” 5.] for nine, making fifteen years in all.

Valerianus was indeed noble by birth [Note: [Col. 0695] “was noble,” 5.], but very foolish and [Note: [Col. 0693] omitted in E1.] inactive, and unsuited by judgment or conduct to any use of public office. Gallienus at first reigned successfully, but afterward, living luxuriously [Note: [Col. 0693] omitted in E1.], nearly destroyed the empire. Valerianus therefore made his son Gallienus Augustus, and appointed Cornelius Valerianus, Gallienus’s son, Caesar.

As soon as Licinius Valerianus began to reign, he launched the eighth persecution against the Christians after Nero. Later, while waging war in Mesopotamia, he was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians [Note: [Col. 0695] omitted in 9c.], deprived of his sight, and grew old there in miserable slavery.

(Chr. W.) For as long as he lived, he always lay bent toward the ground and lifted onto his back the king when he was about to mount his horse. (BEDA.) Therefore [Note: [Col. 0695] “therefore, and Gallienus,” 5.] Gallienus, terrified by so clear a judgment of God, granted peace to our people; nevertheless, whether because of his own lust or his father’s warfare against God, he suffered countless losses to the Roman state as the barbarians rose up.

(H. m.) At last he set out against his own general Aureolus, who had attempted to rule at Milan [Note: [Col. 0695] omitted in 9c.]. He captured him at the bridge which, after his name, was called Aureolus, and besieged Milan. But while he was living luxuriously there, he was killed by his own men through the contrivance of that same Aureolus, in the fiftieth year of his life [Note: [Col. 0695] “of his age,” 9c.] (cf. OROS. VII, 22).

In this persecution, which took place under his father, some affirm that Cornelius, Lucius, Stephanus [Note: [Col. 0695] “Lucius and Stephanus, and,” 5.] and Sixtus, the Roman pontiffs, suffered, although Cornelius [Col. 0695C] and Sixtus, as stated above, are read in the books of martyrdoms to have suffered under Decius.

### 1. (Chr. W.)

In the first year of his reign, Licinius Valerianus launched a persecution against the Christians. Lucius, the twenty-third pope, was ordained; he held office for eight months and suffered on 4 March. Stephanus, the twenty-fourth, succeeded him, held office for two years, and suffered on 2 August.

### 4. A.D. 262

Sixtus, the twenty-fifth pope, was ordained, held office for eleven years, and suffered on 6 August [Note: [Col. 0695] “6 August” is absent in E1, as noted in the margin.].

(BEDA.) Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage and a distinguished teacher, whose extremely learned treatises remain, was crowned with martyrdom on 14 September.

### 5. A.D. 263

Theodorus, surnamed Gregory, whom we mentioned above under the year 242, bishop of Neocaesarea [Col. 0695D] in Pontus [Note: [Col. 0695] “of Gneocaesarea,” 5.], was renowned for the great glory of his virtues. By his prayers he dried up a certain lake and moved a mountain so that it would provide sufficient space for a church.

### 6. (HIER.) A.D. 264

At Antioch, Paulus of Samosata was ordained the fifteenth bishop.

### 7. (Chr. W.) A.D. 265

Valerianus was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians.

### 8. A.D. 266

Gallienus, terrified by his father’s fate, granted peace to the Christians.

### 12. (HIER.) A.D. 270

Ysmeneus was ordained bishop of Jerusalem [Col. 0696A]. At Alexandria, Maximus was appointed the fourteenth bishop.

### 13. A.D. 271

At Antioch, Domnus was ordained the sixteenth bishop [Note: [Col. 0695] “bishop XVI Domnus,” 5.].

### 15. (Chr. W.) A.D. 273

Dionisius, the twenty-sixth pope, was ordained and held office for nine years. Gallienus was killed at Milan.

## The Year of Claudius

(H. misc.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 274, and the thousand and twenty-fifth from the founding of the City, Claudius, whom many say was appointed by Gordianus, the twenty-eighth from Augustus, was chosen by the soldiers and called Augustus by the senate. He reigned for one year and nine months. He was frugal and moderate, steadfast in justice, and suitable for governing the state.

He was designated emperor by the decision of the dying Gallienus, to whom the latter sent the imperial garments while he was stationed at Ticinum. After Aureolus had been killed by his own men, Claudius received the legions and defeated in a great battle the Goths, who had already been devastating Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years. Then, fighting against thirty thousand Alemanni not far from Lake Benacus, he routed such a multitude of them that scarcely half remained.

When he died of illness within two years, the senate honored him so greatly that he was called divine; a golden shield was placed for him in the senate-house and a golden statue on the Capitol. His brother Quintilianus, a man of exceptional moderation and civility, and the only one preferable to his brother, was chosen by the soldiers and, with the senate’s agreement, called Augustus [Note: [Col. 0695] “was called,” 9c.]. He was killed at Aquileia on the seventeenth day of his reign. [Col. 0696C]

### 2. (BEDA.) A.D. 275

Paulus of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, was convicted by many bishops of being a heretic, teaching that Christ had merely been a human being of common nature. Against him, Malchion, a most eloquent presbyter of the church of Antioch—since he had taught rhetoric in that same church—argued in the presence of notaries; that dialogue still exists today.

(HIER.) After Paulus had been deposed, Domnus was appointed in his place as the sixteenth bishop of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0695] “of the Antiochene church,” 5.].

## The Years of Aurelianus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 276, and the thousand and twenty-seventh from the founding of the City, Aurelianus, born of a modest father and, as they say, the son of a colonist of the senator Aurelius, the twenty-ninth from Augustus, was chosen emperor. He reigned for five years and six months. He was powerful in war, but of immoderate temperament and inclined toward cruelty, so that he condemned many nobles and even killed his sister’s son.

Nevertheless, he was to a great extent a corrector of military discipline and dissolute morals [Note: [Col. 0695] omitted in E1.]. He vigorously defeated the Goths and was not unlike Alexander the Great or the dictator Caesar. For he recovered the Roman Empire from its invaders in three years, whereas Alexander reached India through great victories over twelve years [Note: [Col. 0695] “over five years,” 9c.], and Gaius Caesar conquered Gaul in ten years and fought against his fellow citizens for four.

He was the first among the Romans to place a diadem on his head and to use garments woven with gold and gems, something previously unknown to the earlier Romans. He also introduced the use of pork as food for the people.

After he had launched the ninth persecution against the Christians after Nero [Note: [Col. 0697] “was launching,” 5.], lightning fell before him, greatly terrifying those standing around; not long afterward he was killed by soldiers between Constantinople and Heraclea.

### 2. (HIER.) A.D. 277

At Antioch, Tymeus was ordained the seventeenth bishop.

### 4. A.D. 279

Eusebius of Laodicea [Note: [Col. 0697] “Laodicene,” 5.] was held in esteem as a distinguished bishop.

### 5. A.D. 280

Aurelianus was killed. [Col. 0697B]

## The Year of Tacitus

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 281, and the thousand and thirty-second from the founding of the City, Tacitus, the thirtieth from Augustus, assumed the empire. He was a man of exceptionally good character [Note: [Col. 0697] “well-mannered,” 1b; “well-mannered or of good character,” E1.] and suitable for governing the state; but he was able to accomplish nothing, because he was killed after six months in Pontus.

Florianus succeeded him, but he too did nothing worthy of remembrance, because he lived in power for only two months and twenty days [Note: [Col. 0697] “only two months,” 5.]. For while a large part of the army was choosing Equitius Probus, an experienced soldier, Florus [Note: [Col. 0697] “Florianus,” 9b.] held the empire as though in play for sixty days [Note: [Col. 0697] “forty,” 4, 5.]. Then he cut open his own veins and died from the loss of blood (cf. H. m., HIER., JORD. *De r. s.*, and H. R.).

## The Years of Probus

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 282, and the thousand and thirty-third from the founding of the City, Probus, the thirty-first from Augustus, obtained the empire and reigned for six years and four months.

(AUR. VICT.) Born to a peasant father, Dalmatius, an exceptionally devoted cultivator of gardens, Probus advanced to public administration through military glory. (H. m.) He restored Gaul, which had been occupied by barbarians, with great success in battle. He was an energetic, vigorous, and just man, waging many wars; he equaled Aurelianus in military glory and surpassed him in civic virtue. He was killed in a military riot at Sirmium.

(HIER.) In these times Anatholius, an Alexandrian by birth and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, trained in the disciplines of the philosophers, was celebrated in many writings. (BEDA) [Col. 0697D] The greatness of his intellect can be recognized most clearly from the book he composed on Easter and from his ten books on the study of arithmetic [Note: [Col. 0697] “and from the ten books,” E1.] [Note: [Col. 0697] “most fully,” 5.].

### 1.

In Probus’s first year [Note: [Col. 0697] omitted in 9e.], Felix, the twenty-seventh pope, was ordained. He held office for five years and died on 30 May. He established the celebration of Masses over the memorials of martyrs (cf. Chr. W.; BEDA, *Mart.*).

### 2. (EUS. H. e. VII, 27.) A.D. 283

A certain Manes arose, a Persian by birth [Note: [Col. 0697] “a Persian,” 5.], barbarous in life and morals, and so keen in intellect that he seemed either to be insane or filled by a demon [Col. 0698A]. From him arose the insane heresy of the Manichaeans.

### 4. (HIER.) A.D. 285

Cyrillus was ordained the eighteenth bishop of Antioch.

### 6. A.D. 287

Pope Euthicianus, the twenty-eighth, was ordained. He held office for ten months and died on 8 December. Gaius, the twenty-ninth, succeeded him, held office for fifteen years, and suffered under Diocletian on 22 April (cf. Chr. W.).

At Alexandria, Theonas was ordained the fifteenth bishop.

(HIER.—BEDA.) Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed in the Syriac language a book containing the disputation he held against Manes, the founder of the heresy; translated by Greeks, it is possessed by many.

## The Years of Carus

### 1. (H. m.) A.D. 288

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 288 [Col. 0698B], and the thousand and thirty-ninth from the founding of the City, Carus, born at Narbo in Gaul, the thirty-second from Augustus [Note: [Col. 0697] add: “made emperor,” 1b; this appears to be missing], soon made his sons Carinus and Numerianus Caesars and reigned for two years with them.

When the disturbance of the Persians was reported to him, he set out for the East. While he was staying near Antioch, his son Numerianus wished to enter a church and investigate the rites of the Christians. When the holy bishop Cyrillus forbade him, saying that one polluted by sacrifices to idols was not permitted to see the divine mysteries, he became angry and killed him.

Carus, while vigorously routing the Persians in battle [Note: [Col. 0697] “while,” 5.] and capturing their most famous cities, set up camp beside the river Tigris and died from a stroke of lightning.

His son Numerianus, while suffering from an eye disease and being carried in a litter, was killed through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper. Since his death was concealed until Aper could seize the kingdom, the stench of his body exposed the crime.

Meanwhile, Carinus, left in Italy, killed Sabinus Julianus, who was invading Italy, in the Veronese fields. He himself, however, polluted himself with crimes, killing many through false accusations and forcibly corrupting noble matrons. Hated by everyone, he was not long afterward slaughtered by the hand of a certain tribune whose wife he is said to have violated.

### 2. A.D. 289

Carus perished by lightning, and his sons were killed (cf. Chr. W.).

## The Years of Diocletian and Maximian

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 290, and the thousand and forty-first from the founding of the City, Diocletian, the thirty-third from Augustus, was made emperor by the army and reigned for twenty years. He was of very obscure origin in Dalmatia.

Some say that he was the son of a certain Dalmatian scribe; others, that he was the freedman of the senator Anulius. (AUR. V.) He was born in the city and to a mother from Dioclea, and therefore, until he assumed the empire, he was called Diocles. (H. m.) Once he assumed the empire, he converted his Greek name into a Latin one, so that from Diocles he would be called Diocletianus.

He was shrewd, perceptive, and possessed a very subtle intelligence. In his time, when certain peasants called Bagaudae were causing an uprising in Gaul and had Amandus and Aemilianus as their leaders, Diocletian made Maximianus [Note: [Col. 0699] “Aurelius Maximianus,” E1.], surnamed Herculius, Caesar and sent him against the rebels; he easily defeated them.

This Maximianus was born in Pannonia, of peasant stock, uncivil in character, savage, cruel, and signifying the harshness of his nature even by the horror of his face. He was luxurious and foolish in counsel. By Eutropia, a Syrian woman, he fathered Maxentius and Fausta, the wife of Constantine. To Constantius, Constantine’s father, he gave his stepdaughter Theodora, by whom Constantius had six children, Constantine’s brothers. Constantine had been born in Gaul to the concubine Helena.

(HIER.—H. m.) Meanwhile, throughout all the Roman frontiers, disorder arose: a certain Carausius, having assumed the purple, occupied Britain; Julianus occupied Italy; Achilleus, Egypt; the Quinquegentiani, Africa; and Narseus, king of the Persians, the East.

For these reasons Diocletian made Maximianus Herculius emperor, while he appointed Constantius and Galerius Maximianus Caesars. Constantius was the grandson of Claudius through his daughter. Galerius, however, was born in Dacia Ripensis to farming parents [Note: [Col. 0699] omitted in 10 and 11.] and had been a herdsman; hence he was called Armentarius. He was nevertheless sufficiently admirable: handsome in body, great, and a strong warrior. He took Valeria, the daughter of Decius, as his wife [Note: [Col. 0699] “took as his wife,” d. f. v.; “a wife,” 5.].

After seven years, Carausius was treacherously killed in Britain by his associate Allectus. Maximianus Herculius defeated the Quinquegentiani in Africa. Constantius experienced both misfortune and good fortune on the same day in Gaul near Lingones. For when he was suddenly forced to shut himself inside the city because barbarians had burst in, scarcely five hours later, when the army arrived, he killed nearly sixty thousand Alemanni [Note: [Col. 0699] “Alamanni,” 5, E1.].

Diocletian, meanwhile, defeated and killed Achilleus, who had been besieged at Alexandria, after approximately eight months. Constantine, the son of Constantius, was with him. Although still a young man, Constantine acted bravely in battles and always showed consideration toward Christians. When Diocletian saw him advancing in intelligence and bodily strength, and realized that he would become the destroyer of his tyranny, he was moved by envy to plan his death by deceit. But God unexpectedly saved him and restored him to his father.

Galerius Maximianus, fighting against Narseus, king of the Persians, was at first defeated and, fleeing, came to Diocletian in Mesopotamia. Diocletian treated him harshly, even making him run for some time before his chariot. After gathering his soldiers again, Galerius returned and won a great victory.

(H. m. and BEDA.) In the nineteenth year of his reign, Diocletian in the East and Maximianus Herculius in the West launched the tenth persecution after Nero against the Christians. It afflicted the Church continuously for ten years and was more severe than the others, although they had always previously persecuted Christians as well.

Then such a cruel, savage, and frequent persecution raged that within one month seventeen thousand martyrs were found to have suffered for Christ [Note: [Col. 0699] “suffered,” 4; “were killed,” 9c.]. Crossing even the boundary of the ocean, it condemned Albinus, Aaron, and Julius, together with many other men and women of Britain, in a glorious death.

The presbyter Pamphilus also suffered, a close associate of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea; Eusebius himself set forth his life in three books (cf. OROS. VIII, 25.—H. R.).

In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian, seeing that because of old age he was less fit to govern the empire, said to Maximianus Herculius that it seemed good to him for them to entrust the administration of public affairs to younger and stronger men and to live quietly themselves in leisure. Although Maximianus did not do this with complete willingness, he nevertheless consented, and on one day they laid down the purple and the power of the kingdom: Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximianus at Milan. Diocletian withdrew to Salona, and Maximianus to Lucania. The persecution nevertheless continued until the seventh year of Constantine, the son of Helena.

### 1.

In Diocletian’s first year, the Bagaudae caused an uprising in Gaul (cf. above).

### 2. (HIER.) A.D. 291

Diocletian made Herculius Maximianus Caesar.

### 3. A.D. 292

Carausius, having assumed the purple, occupied Britain.

### 4. A.D. 293

The Quinquegentiani harassed Africa.

### 5. A.D. 294

Achilleus occupied Egypt. [Col. 0700C]

### 6. A.D. 295

Diocletian made Maximianus Herculius Augustus and his partner in the kingdom; he appointed Constantius, Constantine’s father, and Galerius Maximianus as Caesars.

### 9. A.D. 298

Diocletian was the first to order that he be worshiped as a god [Note: [Col. 0699] “ordered himself to be worshiped as a god,” 5.].

### 12. A.D. 301

Zabda was ordained bishop at Jerusalem.

### 13. A.D. 302

Victurius, master of the soldiers, persecuted the Christians; from that time the persecution against our people gradually increased.

### 14. A.D. 303

Pope Marcellinus, the thirtieth [Note: [Col. 0699] omitted in 9c.], was ordained. He held office for four years and suffered on 26 April.

### 16. A.D. 305

At Jerusalem, Thermon was appointed bishop. At Antioch, Tyrannus was ordained the nineteenth bishop.

### 17. A.D. 306

Petrus was ordained the sixteenth bishop of Alexandria.

### 18. A.D. 307

Pope Marcellus, the thirty-first, was ordained. He held office for one year [Note: [Col. 0699] “one year,” 9c, 11.] and eight months and suffered on 16 January [Note: [Col. 0699] “suffered under Diocletian,” E1.].

### 19. (Chr. W.) A.D. 308

When the persecution had been proclaimed everywhere, Diocletian in the East and Maximianus in the West overthrew the churches, burned the divine books [Col. 0701A], and afflicted the Christians in the tenth persecution after Nero.

### 20. (HIER.) A.D. 309

Diocletian and Maximianus laid down the purple. After Pope Marcellus had been martyred, Pope Eusebius, the thirty-second, succeeded him. After Eusebius suffered eight months later, Melciades, the thirty-third, succeeded him; he held office for four years and died on 10 December (cf. Chr. W.).

## The Year of Constantius and Galerius

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 310, and the thousand and sixty-first from the founding of the City, after Diocletian and Maximianus had withdrawn from the kingdom, Constantius and Galerius were made Augusti for the administration of the state.

The Roman world was divided between them so that Constantius held Italy, Gaul, and Africa, while Galerius held Illyricum, Asia, and the East. But Constantius, content with the dignity of Augustus, refused the administration of Italy and Africa and retained only Gaul. He was an excellent and gentle man of outstanding civility, not merely beloved but also revered by the Gauls, especially because under his rule they escaped the suspicious prudence of Diocletian and the bloodthirsty recklessness of Maximianus.

Galerius, a well-mannered man [Note: [Col. 0701] “well-conducted,” 1b.] and distinguished in military affairs, seeing that Italy too had been added to his administration, with the permission of his colleague Constantius, created two Caesars: Maximinus, whom he placed over the East and who was himself also a persecutor of Christians, and Severus, to whom he gave Italy, while he himself remained in Illyricum.

Constantius made his son Constantine Caesar [Note: [Col. 0701] “Constantius made his son Caesar,” 5.] and entrusted Gaul to him. He himself died at Eburacum in Britain in the third year of the persecution, which was the sixteenth year of his reign.

After his death, Galerius made Licinius Caesar. Licinius was born in Dacia and was known to him from their long-standing association in the war that he had waged against King Narseus (cf. BEDA). (H. m.) He was energetic in labor and well regarded in his duties.

Meanwhile, at Rome, the praetorians raised a riot and proclaimed Maxentius, the son of Herculius Maximianus, Augustus. When his father Maximianus Herculius heard this, he was stirred by the hope of recovering the principate, which he had unwillingly surrendered at Diocletian’s urging. He hurried to Rome from Lucania and also encouraged Diocletian by letter to resume the power he had laid down. Diocletian treated these letters as void and rejected them.

Galerius sent Severus with an army against Maxentius. Severus came to Rome and besieged it; but, abandoned through the treachery of his soldiers, he fled to Ravenna and was killed by Herculius on the way (cf. H. R.).

After this, Herculius Maximianus attempted, in a confrontation between the armies, to strip his son Maxentius of the imperial power. But when the soldiers insulted and abused him, he set out for Gaul, contriving the deception that he had been expelled by his son so that he might join his son-in-law Constantine. He was also plotting to kill Constantine himself, if he could find an opportunity, and seize his kingdom, for Constantine was already ruling in Gaul with immense support from both soldiers and provincials.

(H. m.) When his plots were exposed by his daughter Fausta, who informed her husband of the deception, Maximianus fled from there. But Constantine pursued and captured him at Massilia. With his neck broken by a noose, he paid the penalty for his treachery in the sixtieth year of his life.

## The Years of Constantine [Note: [Col. 0701] This section is absent from the manuscripts.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 311, and the thousand and sixty-second from the founding of the City, Constantine, the son of Constantius by a less respectable marriage—that is, by the concubine Helena—was made emperor in Britain after his father’s death, on 27 July. All who were present supported him, especially Crocus [Note: [Col. 0701] “eroco,” corrected to “eric,” 9c.], king of the Alemanni, who accompanied him in the capacity of an ally. He was the thirty-fourth from Augustus and became the most eagerly desired governor in his father’s place [Col. 0702B]. He reigned for thirty years and ten months [Note: [Col. 0701] “and ten months,” E1.].

He brought his sister Constantia together with Licinius, whom he had summoned to Milan. In those same days he made Caesars his son Crispus, born at the town of Arles to the concubine Minervia, and Licinianus, the son of Licinius, then about twenty months old.

Meanwhile Galerius Maximianus, as he himself aggravated the persecution begun by Diocletian and Maximianus with even more savage edicts, was touched by divine vengeance. His chest rotted inwardly and his vital organs disintegrated. He vomited worms as well as the horror of a condition beyond human suffering; and when the physicians could no longer endure the stench, they were repeatedly killed at his command.

A certain physician, deriving courage from despair, rebuked him, saying that his punishment came from God and that therefore he could not be healed. Soon afterward, having sent edicts throughout the provinces, Galerius recalled the Christians from exile; but, unable to endure his torments, he brought his life to an end.

Meanwhile the Roman state was held by four new emperors: Constantine and Maxentius, sons of the Augusti, and Licinius and Maximinus, men of new standing. Nevertheless, in the fifth year of his reign Constantine made civil war upon Maxentius and routed his forces in many battles; yet, because of the magical arts [Note: [Col. 0701] lacking in 9c.] that Maxentius greatly loved, he feared him. And while he hesitated greatly to engage him and sought help from heaven—although he was still a pagan—he saw during sleep, toward the eastern part of the sky, the sign of the cross shining with fiery brilliance; and, terrified by so great a vision, he saw angels standing beside him and saying: “Constantine, by this you shall conquer.” It is also reported that Christ himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the cross, and commanded him to make one like it. This he did, having it painted upon his standards.

Accordingly, Constantine came to Rome and pitched camp against Maxentius near the Milvian Bridge. And behold, Maxentius burst forth from the gates, with the others following, and ran ahead armed; Constantine, however, ordered the cross that he had fashioned to be carried before him. When the battle was joined, those who were around Maxentius were defeated; Maxentius himself, fleeing a little above the Milvian Bridge, where he had previously constructed what was meant as a trap—a kind of bridge [Col. 0703A] made from boats [Note: [Col. 0703] “rods,” E1.] with planks laid across them—when he tried to enter that same bridge from the side, was submerged in the depths when his horse slipped, and his body was scarcely found. It was then Constantine’s seventh year. Meanwhile the Roman citizens crowned the city and received Constantine, the victor, and the life-giving cross with rejoicing.

—(EUSEBIUS, Ecclesiastical History IX, 10.)—

Meanwhile Maximinus, himself also an exceedingly savage persecutor of the Christians, having undertaken a rebellion in the East against Licinius, was leading an army against him when, suddenly, by divine judgment, he was seized with pains in his internal organs and began to be violently tormented. Then this man, previously always gluttonous and filled with wine, could neither taste food even with his lips nor smell wine. Thus, after his flesh had been consumed by hunger and dryness [Col. 0703B], the unfortunate man achieved only this: that he confessed the justice of God’s vengeance upon him. Finally, after his flesh had first been destroyed by disease [Note: so E1; “eyes” in 1b; lacking in the remaining witnesses.], he met the end of his life.

(H. m.) Valens too, having been proclaimed emperor by the army in the East, was killed by Licinius. A certain Alexander also, having been made emperor at Carthage, was butchered by Constantine’s army. Thus all imperial power came to Constantine and Licinius. Licinius, although at first he showed himself upright and apparently devoted toward the Christians, later, seeing the advancement of the emperor Constantine, was driven by envy and attempted by secret plots, especially through his associates and ministers, to deceive the prince. When this made little progress, he declared open war against him and prepared to persecute the Christians with personal and particular hatred, making this a grievance: that they did not keep watch in prayers for him as they did for Constantine.

Constantine prepared to oppose his crimes; and, after Licinius had been defeated, he alone, together with his sons, obtained sole rule of the empire, in the fourteenth year of his reign.

(H. m.) Thereafter, having himself also, as they say, been changed through arrogance and become more cruel, he first killed his sister’s son, a young man of outstanding character; then he ordered Crispus, his son by Minervina, to be killed, allegedly at the urging of his wife Fausta; next he killed Fausta herself [Note: [Col. 0703] lacking in 9c.] by throwing her into a bath of boiling water, when his mother Helena rebuked him [Note: [Col. 0703] “him,” m. h. n.; “grief,” 5.] in excessive grief for the killing of her grandson; afterward he killed countless friends. And [Note: [Col. 0703D] I do not know who supplied this to Ekkehard.] although he was committing many crimes, he nevertheless possessed many virtues of character. Having been struck by leprosy through divine agency, he was converted to the faith and baptized by Pope Saint Sylvester, together with his mother and many others. Soon he transferred all his zeal to the advancement of the Church, established Christian laws [Note: [Col. 0703] “laws,” 9c.], and built many basilicas.

He also built a city bearing his name, Constantinople, which had previously been called Byzantium; he wished it to be the seat of the Roman Empire and the capital of the entire East. He also built a bridge on the Danube. He made everyone learn the liberal arts, especially literary studies; he himself devoted much effort to reading, writing, and meditation.

(EUSEBIUS, Ecclesiastical History IX, 7.) His religious mother Helena, instructed by divine visions, went to Jerusalem and asked the inhabitants for the place where Christ had been crucified [Note: [Col. 0703] “had suffered and been crucified,” 5.]. This place was difficult to find because ancient persecutors had set up an image of Venus there, so that if anyone wished to worship Christ [Note: [Col. 0703] “if anyone,” 5.], he would appear to be worshiping Venus in that place [Note: [Col. 0703] so E1; “would worship,” 4; “would see,” the remaining witnesses.]. For this reason the place was scarcely visited and had almost fallen into oblivion. But Helena, arriving there, found the place divinely indicated to her; after the rubble had been cleared away to a great depth, she discovered the holy cross under Macarius, bishop of that city.

(OROSIUS VII, 28.) During the reign of this same emperor, Arius, a presbyter of the Church at Alexandria, deviating from the truth of the Catholic faith, established a destructive doctrine for many. But he was soon expelled from the city by Alexander, bishop of that same city. When he also incited the people whom he had led into error to revolt, a gathering of 318 bishops was held at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, under Pope Sylvester; through them the destructive Arian doctrine was openly exposed and condemned.

(EUSEBIUS, Ecclesiastical History IX, 11.) After the emperor’s mother Helena had departed from this light, Constantia, then abandoned by Licinius, enjoyed the consolation of her brother the Augustus. A certain presbyter, secretly favoring the party of Arius, came to her notice. At first he did nothing of this sort with her, but when great familiarity gave him the opportunity, he gradually began to commend Arius to her, until he won Constantia’s mind over to his own. When she was visited by her brother as she lay dying, she asked of him a final favor: that he receive this same presbyter into his confidence and listen to what he suggested to him for his salvation [Note: [Col. 0703] “suggested,” corrected to “might suggest,” E1. But the reading preserved by the other manuscripts appears to be what Ekkehard wrote.]; for she said that she was concerned for his salvation.

Trusting his sister’s words, her brother lent an ear to the presbyter and, at his urging, ordered Arius to be recalled from exile so that he might explain his view concerning the faith. When Arius wrote about the faith, the emperor, astonished, again referred him to the council’s judgment, asking that, if his faith were approved, they should treat him with a merciful judgment—provided, however, that the assent of his bishop Alexander were obtained. When he came to Alexandria, all his undertaking was frustrated.

Meanwhile, while these matters were being conducted at Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0703] “were conducted,” E1.], Constantine, having well ordered the state and having made his three sons—Constantine, Constans, and [Note: [Col. 0703] lacking in E1.] Constantius—and his brother’s son Dalmatius Caesars, was seized by illness. Since his son Constantius, to whom he had assigned the rule of the East [Note: [Col. 0705] “had entrusted,” 5.], was absent [Note: [Col. 0705] so E1; “was present,” 4; “held it,” 10 and 11; lacking in the remaining witnesses.], he made a will for him. Having secretly summoned the presbyter commended to him by his sister, he gave the will to him, ordering that he give it to no one except Constantius (cf. H. m.—EUSEBIUS, in the same place).

When the presbyter carried this out after the emperor’s death, he also obtained great influence with Constantius. Some writers, however, say that the emperor Constantine fell into the Arian heresy and was rebaptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia. Ecclesiastical history does not teach this; rather, it states that he died in great devotion.

(EUSEBIUS, Ecclesiastical History, in the same place.) He died in a suburban villa of Nicomedia, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the sixty-sixth year of his life and the thirty-first of his reign, and was buried at Byzantium in the basilica of the Apostles.

1. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) In his first year Maxentius, son of Herculius, was proclaimed Augustus.

2. A.D. 312. Maximianus was disgracefully killed at Marseilles.

3. A.D. 313. Quirinus Suscianus, bishop, suffered gloriously.

4. A.D. 314. Pope Sylvester, the thirty-fourth, was ordained; after sitting for twenty-two years and ten months, he departed on the second day before the Kalends of January.

5. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 315. Constantine made war upon Maxentius.

6. A.D. 316. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, was martyred.

7. (Jerome.) A.D. 317. Achillas was ordained the seventeenth bishop of Alexandria. Macarius was ordained the thirty-ninth bishop of Jerusalem. Maxentius perished.

9. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) Diocletian died.

10. (Jerome.) A.D. 320. Licinius began a persecution against the Christians.

13. A.D. 323. Licinius was killed. Alexander was ordained the eighteenth bishop of Alexandria.

17. (Cf. Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 327. A council of 300 bishops was convened at Nicaea.

19. A.D. 329. The Lord’s cross was discovered by Helena [Note: [Col. 0705] “discovered at Jerusalem,” 5.].

20. (Jerome.) A.D. 330. Up to this point Eusebius writes the histories; thereafter Jerome.

21. A.D. 331. Vitalis was ordained the twentieth bishop of Antioch [Col. 0705D] [Note: [Col. 0705] lacking in 10 and 11.], after whom came Phylogonus, the twenty-first, then Paulinus, the twenty-second, and after him Eustasius [Note: [Col. 0705] “Eustasius, the twenty-third.” Quo, E1.]. When Eustasius was exiled for the faith, eleven heretical bishops succeeded him.

23. A.D. 333. Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter, composed the Gospels in verse.

24. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 334. Constantine restored the city of Byzantium and called it Constantinople after his own name. Athanasius was ordained the nineteenth bishop of Alexandria.

28. A.D. 338. Pope Mark, the thirty-fifth, sat for eight months and rested on the Nones of October.

29. A.D. 339. Pope Julius, the thirty-sixth, sat for sixteen years and died on the second day before the Ides of April. The years from the beginning: 4300.

30. A.D. 340. Constantia, Constantine’s sister and Licinius’s wife, while dying, commended a certain Arian presbyter to her brother. (Jerome.) While the emperor Constantine was preparing war against the Persians, who were harassing Mesopotamia, he departed from Constantinople and died near Nicomedia.

## The Years of Constantius

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 341, in the 1092nd year from the founding of the City, Constantius, Constantine’s son, the thirty-fifth emperor after Augustus, obtained the empire and reigned for twenty-three years with his brothers Constantine and Constans. Among Constantine’s successors there was also Dalmatius, the son of his brother Dalmatius, whom Constantine himself had adopted into partnership in the kingdom. Constantine himself assigned each of them a separate part to govern: Constantine received everything beyond the Alps; Constans, Italy, Illyricum, and Africa; Constantius, Asia and the East; and Dalmatius, Thrace, Macedonia, and Achaea [Note: [Col. 0705] “a part of the kingdom,” 5.].

Dalmatius, however, a man of very promising character and scarcely unlike his uncle, was killed not long afterward by the soldiers, with his cousin Constantius permitting it rather than ordering it. After this, discord arose between Constantine and Constans over Italy and Africa [Note: [Col. 0705] “arose,” E1.]. Constantine, therefore, while striving to invade his younger brother’s territories, made war against him; but when he rashly entered battle near Aquileia, he was killed by Constans’s soldiers and thrown into the river called the Alsa, not far from Aquileia. Thus the rule of the Roman Empire came to Constans in the western regions, but to Constantius in the eastern.

Constans’s rule was vigorous and just for some time; afterward, when he began to associate with worse friends, he became intolerable to the provincials and displeasing to the soldiers. Therefore, while wandering through the forests and mountain passes near Gaul in pursuit of hunting, he was killed by the soldiers at the instigation of a certain Magnentius, who desired the kingdom, in the thirtieth year of his age [Note: [Col. 0705] “of his age,” 9c.] and the seventeenth of his reign; he had been Caesar for three years. (AURELIUS VICTOR, chapter 42.)

Magnentius seized his kingdom and made his kinsman Decentius Caesar—or, as some wish [H. m.], his brother. Constantius made his cousin Gallus Caesar, gave him his own name, and sent him to Antioch in Syria, so that he might live there and guard those regions. Nevertheless, he later ordered Gallus to be killed.

After this Constantius made war upon Magnentius. When battle was joined, Magnentius alone fled to Lugdunum. There, being hemmed in, he secretly obtained a sword from a part of the wall and, pierced through, died in nearly his fiftieth year and the fourth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0707] “third,” E1.]. When Decentius heard of his death, he ended his life with a noose made from a band. These events took place in the sixth year of Constantius’s reign.

At that time Constantius alone ruled the Roman Empire as prince and Augustus. He was a man of outstanding calm, excessively trusting toward his associates and friends; he was devoted to the love of his wives, but, content with them, did not defile himself with illicit or unjust desire. Of all the wives he had—for he had several—he especially loved Eusebia. At her urging he also made Julian, Gallus’s brother, Caesar and admitted him into partnership in the kingdom.

(Cf. RUFINUS, Ecclesiastical History X, 15.) After this, since the ancient enemy, always envious of the Church’s peace, was at work, Arius and his followers gained a place in Constantius’s confidence, and they drew him into participation in their error.

(BAEDA.) Thus Arian impiety, supported by Constantius’s protection, first persecuted Athanasius and then all the bishops who did not belong to its party, through exiles, prisons, and various forms of affliction.

(H. m.) Meanwhile Constantius, preparing war against the Parthians, heard that Julian was aspiring to the empire. Abandoning the Parthian expedition, he returned and died between Cilicia and Cappadocia from a very severe fever, which indignation intensified, in the forty-fifth year of his age and the twenty-third of his reign.

1. (Jerome.) In the first year of Constantius, James of Nisibis is recognized as bishop; through his prayers the city was often delivered from danger.

3. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 343. Constantine, making war upon his brother, was killed near Aquileia.

5. A.D. 345. Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was held in high regard; Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, a fugitive from Constans, was honorably received by him.

9. A.D. 349. Bishop Athanasius returned to Alexandria in response to a letter from Constans.

13. A.D. 353. Constans was killed not far from Spain, in the thirtieth year of his age.

14. (Jerome.) A.D. 354. Gallus, Constantius’s cousin, was made Caesar.

15. A.D. 355. Liberius, the thirty-seventh pope, was ordained. When the heretics drove him into exile on account of the faith, his deacon Felix was substituted in the priesthood as the thirty-eighth pope. When Felix proved to Constantius that he was a heretic [Note: [Col. 0707D] This is of unknown origin.], he was deposed by him after a year and, as some say (the Martyrology of Bede), beheaded on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. Liberius, overcome by the weariness of exile, subscribed to the heresy and entered Rome as though victorious (cf. Chronicle of Würzburg—Rufinus X, 23).

6. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 356. Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian were considered distinguished at Rome.

17. A.D. 357. Julian was made Caesar by Constantius.

18. (Jerome.) A.D. 358. Eusebius of Vercelli, Dionysius of Milan, and Lucifer of Cagliari were exiled.

19. A.D. 359. Abbot Antony departed in the 105th year of his age.

20. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 360. The bones of the apostle Andrew and of Luke the Evangelist and Timothy were brought to Constantinople.

21. (Jerome.) A.D. 361. Paulinus, bishop of Trier, died in exile. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, exiled by Constantius to Phrygia at the instigation of the Arians, together with Dionysius of Milan and Eusebius of Vercelli, was permitted to return in the fourth year of his exile after he had presented Constantius with a book concerning the faith.

23. A.D. 363. Constantius died in the forty-fifth year of his life.

## The Years of Julian the Apostate

(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 364, in the 1115th year from the founding of the City, Claudius Julianus, already Caesar and the thirty-sixth emperor after Augustus, received the empire and reigned for two years and eight months. Something must be said about his lineage and education, how he became an apostate, and how he came to the throne.

Constantine the Great, who founded Constantinople, had two brothers by the same father but not the same mother, Constantius [Note: [Col. 0707] “Constantius … born,” lacking in E1.] and Dalmatius. The elder Constantius had two sons, Gallus and Julian; Dalmatius had Dalmatius, whom Constantine, as stated above, left as heir to the kingdom together with his sons. When the soldiers killed Dalmatius after Constantine’s death, Gallus and Julian nearly suffered the danger of death along with him, had not illness—which was thought incurable—saved Gallus, and Julian’s infancy saved Julian; for he was eight years old.

When the emperors’ fury toward them had subsided, Gallus was with teachers near Ephesus, where he also possessed estates inherited from his forefathers. Julian, meanwhile, as he grew up in the lecture halls of Constantinople, was trained in the basilica where the teachers were, appearing in private dress. He had a eunuch tutor named Mardonius, a grammarian from Nicomedia in Laconia as his teacher, and he studied rhetoric under the sophist Eubulus, later the teacher of Basil, the bishop.

Julian was a Christian from the beginning. As he advanced in learning and a rumor spread among the people that he might also govern the state, he caused anxiety to the emperor Constantius. For this reason Constantius removed him from the imperial city and sent him to Nicomedia, ordering him not to meet the sophist Libanius the Syrian, supposedly because Libanius was a pagan; nevertheless Julian made use of his books by reading them.

As Julian advanced in rhetoric, the philosopher Maximus came to Nicomedia—not the Byzantine Maximus, the father of Euclid, but the Ephesian Maximus, whom the emperor Valentinian later ordered killed for practicing magical arts. He came to Nicomedia for no other reason than that he had been drawn by Julian’s reputation. When Julian had tasted philosophical discourse in his presence, Maximus also began to implant in his mind a desire for imperial power.

When these things did not escape the emperor’s ears, Julian, caught between hope and fear and wishing to conceal his suspicion, had his hair cut and pretended to live the life of a monk [Note: [Col. 0709] lacking in 9c.]. Secretly he practiced philosophy, but publicly he read the sacred books of the Christians. Finally, he was appointed lector in the church of Nicomedia and read the divine books while the people listened, so that under this guise he might avoid the emperor’s fury, although he by no means abandoned the hope he had conceived in his mind. He used to say [Note: [Col. 0709] E1 reads “dicebat quam” (“he said that”).] to many of his friends that the times would be happy when he himself possessed power [Col. 0709B].

A little later, when Gallus had been killed, Julian suddenly became suspect to the emperor, who even ordered him to be kept under guard. When Julian escaped, he was saved by wandering through various places. At last the emperor’s wife Eusebia found him in hiding and entreated the emperor that he should suffer no harm but rather be sent to Athens to study philosophy [Note: [Col. 0709] lacking in 9c.].

While traveling throughout all of Hellas in his desire for the kingdom, Julian sought seers who would give answers, asking whether he would attain his wish. He found a man who professed that he could tell him what he desired. This man led him to a certain place of idols and, bringing him inside, summoned deceptive demons. When they appeared, Julian, compelled by terror, made the sign of the cross upon his forehead. At its sight the demons suddenly disappeared.

For this reason the magician began to blame Julian. Julian indicated that terror had seized him and said that he had been stunned by the power of the cross, because the demons vanished when they saw it. The magician replied: “Do not suppose, good man, that they were afraid of this; rather, they departed because they abhorred it” [Note: [Col. 0709] “departed,” 5.]. In this way he seized the wretched man and filled Julian with hatred of the Christian sign.

After this Constantius summoned Julian, made him Caesar, gave him Helena, his sister, as wife, and sent him against the barbarians in Gaul. When Julian entered a certain city, a laurel crown of the sort with which cities are customarily decorated, hanging between the columns [Note: [Col. 0709] “colunnans” (“columns”), 5.], fell upon his head after its cord broke and crowned him most appropriately. When they saw this, everyone shouted that it was a sign of imperial power.

Julian acted bravely against the barbarians, captured their noble king Nodomarius, and sent him to Constantius. He also fought against the Alamanni living beside the Rhine River and captured their most powerful king, Badomarius. Decorated with a celebrated victory, and being pleasing to the soldiers because of his moderate way of life and gentleness, he was proclaimed Augustus by them.

Since an imperial crown was lacking, one of the standard-bearers took the torque he had around his neck [Note: [Col. 0709] lacking in E1.] and placed it around Julian’s head. In this way Julian became emperor [Note: [Col. 0709] “became emperor,” 5.].

After this, thinking no more about Constantius, Julian rewarded with honors the judges whom Constantius had appointed and stirred up hatred against Constantius’s name. Thus, having suddenly changed his religion, while his own people still thought him a Christian, he named himself chief priest. He went to the temples of the pagans and sacrificed; he urged his subjects to worship such things; and he endeavored to cleanse Christian baptism through sacrifices, invocations, and the offering of blood.

While Constantius was staying at Antioch because of the Persian war, Julian, hoping that he could retain Illyricum without war, went there, saying that he wished to give satisfaction to Constantius, as though he had not willingly but under compulsion from the soldiers taken up the imperial insignia.

When Constantius heard of his arrival, he abandoned the war and came to Constantinople; but, on the journey itself, he died, as stated above. After his death Julian already held Thrace, and not long afterward, when he came to Constantinople, he was proclaimed Augustus.

He soon began to consider how he might please the people and win their favor, and he accomplished this by the following device. He knew well that Constantius was hated by all the orthodox, since they appeared to have been expelled from the churches and their bishops confiscated and sent into exile. He also knew that the pagans had been saddened by the prohibition of sacrifices and desired the time when their temples would be opened [Note: [Col. 0709] “when their temples would be opened,” 5.].

Thus, commending himself to both groups under an artful disguise, he first disparaged Constantius’s cruelty toward his subjects and, reproving it before all the people, ordered the bishops who had been deported into exile to be recalled and their confiscated possessions restored. He also ordered the temples of the pagans to be opened, as though they were necessary to him. By doing many such things, he reconciled himself to both groups, although he secretly favored the pagans above all.

For a long time he had been striving to spread paganism throughout all his dominion and to exterminate Christianity. First, he ordered the children of the Galileans—for thus he called the worshipers of our Savior—not to study the disciplines of poets, rhetoricians, or philosophers. “According to the proverb,” he said, “we are wounded by our own feathers; for armed with our writings, they wage wars against us.”

The temples, therefore, were open, and the sacrifices of the pagans proceeded throughout the cities according to his will.

Meanwhile the Persians, hearing of Constantius’s death, began to rebel and invaded the Roman frontiers [Note: [Col. 0709] “devastated,” 5.]. Julian set out against them, but was divinely killed in the very course of the war.

Different people have different opinions concerning his death. Some say [Note: [Col. 0709] E1 reads “enim” (“for”).] (H. m.) that he was led for three days through the wilderness by a certain deserter, fell into an ambush, and, surrounded on every side by the Persians, was struck by one of them with a spear; carried back to his tent, he gradually weakened as he lost blood. Others say that a javelin suddenly thrown pierced his arm and ran down into his side; others, that a single Ishmaelite shepherd killed him; others, that soldiers exhausted by hunger and the journey killed him; others, that one of the invisible beings did this.

But whether it was a man or an angel, it is clear that he served divine commands.
