Calistus [Note: [Col. 0711] “callistus,” 5.], who served among his attendants and composed his history in heroic verse [Note: [Col. 0711] “wrote,” 5.], says that he was wounded by a demon. Libanius, the Syrian sophist, however, writes among other things about his life, and at the end of his book says:

> “Julian, fosterling of demons, disciple of demons, and observer of demons.”

But in the book on the life of Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea, we read with certainty (Acts of the Saints, June II, p. 944) that, while Basil and his people were praying and fasting—for Julian had threatened them with evils as he went to war against the Persians—Julian himself was killed at the command of the holy Mother of God Mary, by the martyr Mercury, who was resting in that same city.

It is also reported [Note: [Col. 0711] E1 reads “Ferunt” (“they report”).] that Julian filled his hand with blood, scattered it into the air, and said: “You have conquered, Galilean; you have conquered.”

He perished in the third year of his reign, but in the seventh year after Constantius had made him Caesar, and in the thirty-first year of his life. After his death his magical arts [Note: [Col. 0711] E1 reads “magiae” (“magic”).] were found at Carrhae. For while traveling through that place, he had entered a pagan temple, closed the doors, and performed certain sacrilegious rites. After his death, those who entered the temple found a woman hanging by her hair, with her hands extended; her womb had been opened so that he might inspect the outcome of the war in her liver.

When his death was announced in that city [Note: [Col. 0711] E1 reads “esset” (“was”).], everyone held a public festival, all shouting together: “You greatest of fools, where are your prophecies? God and his Christ have conquered you.”

He was highly educated in the liberal disciplines, possessed immense eloquence and a very tenacious and extensive memory, was physically strong but short, had a long beard, and eyes that wandered and were directed here and there [Note: [Col. 0711] lacking in E1.]. He was bolder than is fitting for an emperor, a superstitious worshiper of idols, and a zealous persecutor of the Christian religion.

Thus, after Julian became emperor, he turned to the worship of idols and first attempted to seduce Christians through a flattering persecution, enticing rather than compelling them to sacrifice; consequently many were deceived (cf. JEROME).

2. (RUFINUS, Ecclesiastical History XI, 28.) A.D. 365. At Sebaste, a city of Palestine, pagans invaded the tomb of Saint John the Baptist, scattered his bones through the fields, and, after collecting them again, burned them and scattered them more widely. But some monks from Jerusalem, mingling with those who were gathering them, brought whatever they could collect to their father Philip. Considering these relics too great for himself, Philip sent them through the deacon Julian to Athanasius at Alexandria. Athanasius, with a few witnesses, enclosed them beneath a hollowed-out wall of the sacristy and, in a prophetic spirit, preserved them for the benefit of a future generation.

His prophecy was fulfilled under Theodosius through Theophilus the bishop, who, after destroying the shrine of Serapis, consecrated a church of Saint John in the same place.

(RUFINUS, Ecclesiastical History X, 34.) Athanasius returned to Alexandria. The impious Julian, having set out for the Persian war, was struck down by divine judgment in the eighth month of the third year of his reign; but on the following day, without any delay, Jovian [Note: [Col. 0711] “Jovinianus,” 1b, 5, 9c.] was crowned by the soldiers [Col. 0712B] (H. m.).

## The Year of Jovian

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 366, in the 1117th year from the founding of the City, Jovian [Note: [Col. 0711] “Jovinianus,” 1b, 9c.] assumed the empire as the forty-first emperor after Augustus [Note: [Col. 0711] “thirty-seventh,” E1.] [Note: [Col. 0711] Ekkehard now takes the numbers of the emperors not from Jerome but from the Miscellaneous History.]. He reigned for eight months. His father was Barronianus, a resident of the province of Pannonia.

Since his father repeatedly lost children, he was told in a dream to call the child who would be born when the birth was imminent “Jovianus” [Note: [Col. 0711] “Jovinianus” throughout, 9c.]. Jovian was distinguished in body, cheerful in disposition, devoted to learning, and strong in his powers. He was a soldier at the time when Julian had proposed a law to the soldiers that they must either sacrifice or leave the army. Jovian chose rather to lose his military belt than to obey the emperor’s commands; but Julian, because of the needs of the war, retained him among the soldiers.

When the soldiers forcibly dragged him to the imperial office, he shouted that he did not wish to rule pagan men, since he himself was a Christian. When everyone’s voice cried out together that they too were Christians, he accepted the empire.

Then, as he hurried to Constantinople, he came to the estate of Dadasta. There, in winter, overcome by illness, he lay in a new room and was suffocated by the heat of the coals and the brightness of the walls recently coated with lime. He died in the eighth month of his reign, in the thirty-third year of his life [Note: [Col. 0711] “of his life,” 9c.], on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September.

(OROSIUS VII, 1.)

## The Years of Valentinian
(H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 367, the 1,118th year from the founding of the City, Valentinian, the 42nd [Note: [Col. 0711] XXXVIII. E1.] after Augustus, was proclaimed emperor. He was an excellent man, most worthy of the imperial dignity, and reigned for 11 years. He was Pannonian by birth, from the city of Cibalae. His father Gratianus, born of humble stock, was called Funarius because one day five soldiers were unable to wrest from him a rope that he was carrying for sale. For this achievement he was enlisted in the army and rose as far as the rank of praetorian prefect. On account of his recommendation, the army offered the imperial power to Valentinian, who was resisting it [Note: [Col. 0713] absent in E1.]. [Col. 0712D] [Col. 0713A]

When Valentinian was tribune of the Scutarii under Julian the Apostate and maintained the true faith, Julian one day entered the temple of Fortune. The temple attendants, standing on either side of the doors, purified those entering by sprinkling water, as they themselves claimed. Then Valentinian, walking before the emperor, saw a drop of the sprinkling on his cloak. Indignant, he struck the temple attendant with his fist, saying that he was being polluted rather than purified. Seeing this, the emperor ordered him to be thrown into custody, saying: “Either let him sacrifice, or let him leave the army.” He immediately withdrew voluntarily.

Soon afterward, Julian was killed and Jovian died, and Valentinian assumed the imperial power in the place of his persecutor. When he reached Constantinople, after thirty days of his reign he associated his brother Valens with himself in the government, granting him the eastern regions while retaining the western for himself. When he had already completed his third year with his brother, he created his son Gratianus—still not fully grown—Augustus at the urging of his mother-in-law and his wife Serena [Note: [Col. 0713] thus the manuscripts].

He also had another young son, Valentinian, by another wife, Justina. He is said to have married her in the following manner while Severa was alive, though not repudiated. Justus, Justina’s father, when he was governor of Picenum in the time of Constantius, saw in a dream that he had brought forth imperial purple from his right thigh. When this vision reached Constantius’ ears, he feared that an emperor would be born from him, and sent men to kill Justus. His daughter Justina, remaining a virgin, eventually came to Severa’s attention. Severa loved her so much that she even bathed with her. Enchanted by her beauty and captivated by affection, she told the emperor that Justina was so beautiful that she deserved to be the emperor’s wife.

Having conceived this plan, Valentinian considered taking Justina as his wife without repudiating Severa. He publicly promulgated a law throughout the cities that anyone who wished might lawfully enter into two marriages with impunity; for, he said, nations were populous because this was customary among them. After issuing this law, he himself married Justina. By her he had Valentinian and three daughters, Justa, Grata, and Galla. Two of them remained virgins, while Theodosius the Elder married Galla; by her, Placidia, his daughter, is known to have been born. (JORD. *De r. s.* II. m.) He had Arcadius and Honorius by Placilla, his earlier wife.

After Auxentius, the Arian bishop of Milan, had died, Ambrose, who was administering the city’s government and had not yet been baptized, was chosen bishop by the common consent of the citizens. By Valentinian’s order he was baptized and ordained bishop as one deemed worthy. [Col. 0714B]

Valentinian fought many battles against various peoples. Among them, the Alans rebelled against the Romans (G. *Franc.* c. 2). Valentinian led a Roman army against them, killing many; the survivors entered the Maeotian marshes. Then Valentinian told his armies that if any of them entered the Maeotian marshes and drove the Alans out, he would allow them to remain free of tribute for ten years.

Some men from Sicambria then entered and fought against the Alans. After winning the battle, they expelled them. Because of this victory Valentinian called them, in the Attic language, *Franks*, that is, fierce, hard, and strong. Since this people has now been mentioned, and its kings are often commemorated in the books of the saints, although I may seem to be making a digression, for the sake of knowledge of the matters I shall, having recalled the origin of this same people, describe the succession of its kings as briefly as I can. [Note: [Col. 0713] The following history of the Franks is absent from E., and is also omitted in 2.]

## On the Origin of the Franks

[Col. 0713]

[Col. 0713C] (G. *Franc.*, Bamberg manuscript.) The beginnings of the Frankish people arose from the ancient stock of the Trojans. For at the time when Aeneas came to Italy after the destruction of Troy, certain of those same Trojans, exiles in a similar manner, reached the region around the Maeotian marshes. Settling there, they extended their boundaries as far as Pannonia. They built the city of Sicambria, and after living there for many years they greatly increased in number; they were first called Sicambri.

Because they expelled the Alans from the Maeotian marsh, as has been said, Valentinian called them Franks, and for this victory they were granted exemption from tribute for ten years. When the ten years had passed, Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0713] *valentinianus*, 5.] sent a certain commander to them to collect the taxes. But since they were fierce, they scorned thereafter to submit to tribute and killed the men sent to them.

At that time they had leaders bearing the insignia of ancient names, Priam and Antenor. When the emperor heard of their action, he became exceedingly angry and ordered the entire Roman army, together with many other foreign peoples [Note: [Col. 0713] *plurimis ceteris*, “very many others,” G. 5.], to fight against them. Battle was joined, and when many fell on both sides, the Franks were finally unable to withstand the multitude and fled. Their king Priam died there.

Leaving Sicambria, they came into the land of Germany, among a people especially hostile to the Romans. They lived for some time in Thuringia with Marcomer, the son of Priam, and Sunno, the son of Antenor. All the peoples living on that side of the Rhine were called Germans because they had large bodies and were always exceedingly strong and untamed.

Meanwhile, after Sunno’s death, the Franks took counsel among themselves to have one king, as the other peoples did. On Marcomer’s advice they made Faramund, his son, king. From that time they began to have laws, which their pagan counselors Wisogast and Salegast composed. From Salegast the Salic Law is also said to have been devised and named. The Franks were pagans.

Finally, when Faramund died, his son Clodius, the Long-Haired, succeeded him; from him the Frankish kings were called Long-Haired. Beyond the Rhine as far as the Loire lived the Romans; beyond the Loire the Goths held power; and the Burgundians lived beside the Rhône, where the city of Leudunum was later built.

The Franks therefore crossed the Rhine from Thuringia and attacked in war the Romans, who at that time ruled Gaul through their magistrates. They drove them as far as the Carbonarian Forest, defeated and killed them, and thus harshly avenged the injury inflicted upon them by the Romans.

Entering the Gallic cities of Tournai and Cambrai, they first violently seized the entire coastlands lying between the rivers Scheldt and Sambre. Advancing and retreating little by little, they brought Rheims, Soissons, Orléans, Cologne, and Trier under their control, and finally subjected to themselves all Gaul and Germany from Aquitaine to Bavaria.

Those who were mixed with the Teutons [Note: [Col. 0715] *theutonicis*, 5; *theotonicis*, 9c, throughout] were called Franks by their proper name; those who were descended through intermarriage from the Gauls were called Frank-born. Clodius [Note: [Col. 0715] absent in 9c.] reigned for twenty years and then died. Meroveus succeeded him, from whom the Frankish kings were called Merovingians [Note: [Col. 0715] “were called,” 5]. When he died, his son Childeric assumed the kingdom.

Because Childeric lived dissolutely and fornicated with the daughters of the people, they did not wish to kill him but expelled him and set a certain Roman, Aegidius, over themselves. After eight years, however, they repented of this action and recalled Childeric. He became, through his power, greater than all the earlier Frankish kings.

In his time the Franks captured the city of Cologne after killing many Romans on the side of Aegidius; they called it Cologne. They also seized Trier, burned it, and devastated the whole region.

After Aegidius died, his son Syagrius succeeded him and sat in the city of Soissons, where the royal seat was. But Childeric arrived with an army and plundered the entire region, adding the cities of Orléans and Angers to his kingdom.

After reigning for twenty-four years, Childeric died, and his son Clovis received the kingdom. He fought Syagrius, who fled to Alaric, king of the Goths. Clovis sent an embassy demanding his surrender [Note: [Col. 0715] *repoposcit*, “demanded again,” 9c.]. When Syagrius was handed over, Clovis killed him and subjected his entire kingdom to himself, destroying the Romans so completely that no trace of them is found today in Gaul.

He took as his wife Gothehild, or Rothild [Note: [Col. 0715] *Rothildam vel Gothehildam*, “Rothild or Gothehild,” 9c.; variant reading absent in 4, 10, 11], the niece of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, had four sons: Gundobad, the father of Sigismund and Godegisel; Hilperic, the father of Gothehild; Godegisel; and Gothemar.

After the elder Gundobad died, the younger Gundobad killed his brother Hilperic and ordered his wife to be drowned, with a stone tied around her neck. He sent the other two brothers into exile. While Gundobad had his niece Gothehild, the daughter of Hilperic [Note: [Col. 0715] *helperici*, 9c., and often], with him, envoys of King Clovis happened to be sent there. Seeing her beauty, they praised her to their lord. Clovis then sent a certain honored servant of his, Aurelian, and took her as his wife. She was a Christian girl.

She often preached Christ to him, but he refused to believe. In the fifteenth year of his reign, he went to war against the Alamanni. When he was nearly defeated, he promised at Aurelian’s urging that he would believe if, with God’s help, he conquered the Alamanni. He immediately defeated them and subjected their entire land to himself [Note: [Col. 0715] absent in 9c.]. Then, instructed by Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, he was baptized with his whole people.

After this he went to the city of Poitiers, where King Alaric lived. Fighting him, he killed him in the twelfth year of that same Alaric. Amalaric, Alaric’s son, fled to Spain and later wisely recovered his father’s kingdom.

Five years after this victory Clovis died peacefully, in the thirtieth year of his reign and the 112th year from the passing of Saint Martin. King Clovis had four sons: Clodomir, Theoderic, Hildebert, and Chlothar. They divided his kingdom equally among themselves and rose to great power.

At that time Theoderic had a son named Theudebert, an energetic and capable man. Amalaric, son of Alaric, king of the Goths, asked for their sister Rothild in marriage. They did not refuse her and gave her to him with great honor [Note: [Col. 0715] absent in 9c.]. But when he later treated her disgracefully as an Arian, she sent a messenger from Spain to her brother Hildebert, who was residing in the Auvergne, and complained to him of her injuries.

Angered by this, Hildebert marched into Spain with a large army. After killing Amalaric, he carried off his sister with great treasures. She was overcome by illness and died on the journey.

In those days Queen Gothehild came to Paris and said to her sons: “My sons, I do not regret having raised you tenderly; only be indignant at my injury and avenge the death of my father and mother.” Immediately moved by anger, they marched with a great army into Burgundy against Sigismund and Gothemar, the sons of Gundobad, who had killed Gothehild’s father and mother.

At that time Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, built the monastery of Saint Maurice and his companions at Agaunum, where they had also suffered martyrdom. The Burgundians gathered an army and went out to meet the sons of Gothehild and Clovis. Battle was joined, and the defeated Burgundians fled.

As Sigismund was fleeing to the saints at Agaunum, Clodomir overtook him. He captured him with his wife and sons, took them to the district of Orléans, and imprisoned them. Later he killed them and threw them into a well at a place called Columnabicus.

Afterward Clodomir again gathered an army and marched into Burgundy against Gothemar. Gothemar resisted but fled. While Clodomir pursued him and rode ahead on a very swift horse, he was struck from the opposite side, fell, and died. When Chlothar heard this, he took Gundeuca, his brother’s wife, in marriage.

King Theoderic reigned for twenty-three years and then died. His son Theudebert succeeded him. After reigning for fourteen years, Theudebert died, and his son Theudebald succeeded him. When Theudebald died seven years later, his uncle Chlothar took his kingdom, together with many treasures.

Queen Gothehild, abundant in almsgiving, lived in great abstinence and sobriety. Full of days, she departed to the Lord at the city of Tours and was buried by her sons Hildebert [Note: [Col. 0717] The manuscripts variously have *hildib.*, *hildeb.*, *sigib.*, and *sigeb.*; I have accepted the former reading from numerous passages.] and Chlothar in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter beside her husband Clovis, where the most blessed Genovefa also rests.

King Chlothar had seven sons by different wives. By Queen Ingund he had Gunthar, Childeric, Sigibert [Note: [Col. 0717] The manuscripts variously have *hildib.*, *hildeb.*, *sigib.*, and *sigeb.*; I have accepted the former reading from numerous passages.], Guntramnus, Heribert, and a daughter, Glodesinda. By Regingunda, Ingund’s sister, he had Hilperic.

Because he loved Ingund, since she was beautiful and attractive, and because he himself was exceedingly lustful, he married her sister Regingunda as well. He also had Gratian by Gusina. Gratian was exceedingly handsome, fierce, and cunning. He rebelled against his father, but after being captured and brought before him [Note: [Col. 0717] *ductus*, “brought,” 5], he was ordered to be burned in a certain hut.

Hildebert, Chlothar’s brother, died after a long illness at Paris, and King Chlothar obtained his kingdom and treasures. In those times the blessed bishop Medard, full of miracles, departed to the Lord. King Chlothar had him buried with great honor in the city of Soissons.

After this King Chlothar was seized by fever and died in the fifty-first year of his reign. His four sons divided his kingdom among themselves: Heribert, Guntramnus, Hilperic, and Sigibert.

Heribert received the kingdom of his uncle Hildebert and established his seat at Paris. Guntramnus received Clodomir’s kingdom and established his seat at Orléans. Hilperic possessed his father Chlothar’s kingdom and set his seat at Soissons. Sigibert received Theoderic’s kingdom, namely Austrasia, and placed the royal seat [Note: [Col. 0717] *s. r.* (*sedem regni*, “royal seat”), 5.] at the city of Metz. (PAUL. DIAC. III, 33.)

Of these, King Guntramnus was peaceful and praiseworthy in every respect for his goodness. He led his life in holy conduct. It is pleasing to insert one of his remarkable deeds into this work.

Once, while he was out hunting, all his companions scattered through the forest, leaving him alone with only one especially faithful attendant beside a stream. When heavy sleep pressed upon him, he laid his head in the lap of his faithful servant and fell asleep.

Suddenly the servant saw what seemed to be a small animal emerge from the king’s mouth, move toward the stream, and try with great effort to cross it. When it found no way across, the man who saw this drew his sword from its sheath, laid it across the stream, and enabled the creature to cross. After crossing the stream, it entered a nearby opening in a mountain. It returned by the same route and, after one hour, entered the king’s mouth again.

The king immediately awoke and related that he had seen a great vision. He said that in a dream he had been traveling toward a great river, which he crossed by an iron bridge. Then, coming beneath a mountain, he saw a great quantity of gold there.

When he told this to his faithful servant, and the servant in turn related everything that had happened, they went to that place. Digging, they found many weights of gold that had been hidden there in ancient times [Note: [Col. 0717] absent in 5]. The king afterward ordered a large ciborium to be made from this gold and decorated with various gems. He wished to send it to Jerusalem, to the Lord’s Sepulchre, but when he could not carry this out, he ordered it to be placed over the body of the blessed martyr Marcellus, buried in the city of Chalon. It is said that no other object like it can be found. [Note: [Col. 0717] Some manuscripts read *ad Iher.*, “to Jerusalem”; others read *illud ad*, “that object to,” 9c.]

[Col. 0718C] (G. Fr.) Hilperic took as his wife Audevora, who bore him three sons, Theudebert, Meroveus, and Clovis.

Heribert married Ingoberga. She had two girls who were exceedingly beautiful and were the daughters of a certain poor man. The king fell passionately in love with them. Because the queen hated them, the angry king repudiated her, took one of the girls in marriage, and afterward joined the other to himself as well.

For this reason Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, excommunicated both of them. Since the king took no account of this and did not dismiss her, she was struck down by divine judgment and died; not long afterward the king himself also died.

King Sigibert, seeing his brother’s wickedness and scorning such marriages, sent an embassy to Spain and asked for and received Brunhild, the king’s daughter, a beautiful and intelligent girl. Since she was subject to the Arian faith, he ordered her to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity. By her he had a son, Hildebert.

At this time Saint Columban came from Ireland to Gaul, and King Sigibert received him kindly. Hilperic, Sigibert’s brother, seeing him elevated by a royal marriage, asked for the hand of Brunhild’s elder sister, named Galswintha, although he already had several wives. Through his envoys he promised that he would dismiss all the others.

After she had been betrothed and brought with many treasures, Fridegund, one of his numerous wives, low-born but beautiful and cunning, strangled her in his bed during the night. Through a most evil plan she also separated Audevora, his earlier wife [Note: [Col. 0719] *andoveram*, 9c.], from him, and herself succeeded to their place as though she were the lawful wife.

At that time the emperor Justinian died at Constantinople, and Justin sought the imperial power.

Afterward Hilperic sent his son Theudebert [Note: [Col. 0719] *Theodericum*, 9c.] across the Loire into the kingdom of his brother Sigibert with an army. He immediately invaded Tours, Poitiers, and the other cities; he burned churches, destroyed monasteries, and killed clergy.

Sigibert moved his army against him and killed him. Hilperic, however, fled with his wife [Note: [Col. 0719] *u. sua*, 9c.] Fridegund to Tournai. Sigibert then took the cities beyond Paris. When the Franks who had formerly been subject to the elder Hildebert [Note: [Col. 0719] *a. qui Franci quondam*, “and the Franks who formerly,” 9c.] wished to make Sigibert their king and abandon Hilperic, he was killed through the plots and counsel of Fridegund, who was exceedingly cunning, in the fourteenth year of his reign and the fortieth year of his age [Note: [Col. 0719] *a. suo*, 9c.].

Brunhild was then residing at Paris with her sons. Cundoald, a duke and mayor of the palace, secretly carried off Sigibert’s young son Hildebert during the night and fled with him. Gathering the peoples over whom his father had ruled, he established the boy as king.

At that time the blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, full of great miracles [Note: [Col. 0719] absent in 9c.], departed to the Lord.

All Hilperic’s sons whom he had by Fridegund also died [Note: [Col. 0719] *s. a.*, “and also,” 5]. Finally, Hilperic fathered Chlothar, who later became a great king; he fathered Dagobert.

Meanwhile great disputes arose between Hilperic and his nephew Hildebert, Sigibert’s son. Fridegund and Brunhild continually provoked them on their respective sides.

At that time the illustrious King Guntramnus, a man of good memory, died. He was Hilperic’s brother and had reigned for thirty-one years. His kingdom, Burgundy, was received by his nephew Hildebert.

After Fridegund committed adultery with a certain Landeric and this became known to King Hilperic, she feared him and took counsel with two young men. When the king returned late from hunting, they killed him as soon as he dismounted, shouting that the ambush had come from Hildebert’s side. Thus she held the kingdom with her young son Chlothar.

Hildebert, Sigibert’s son, reigned for twenty years and then died. He had two sons: the elder, Theudebert, by a concubine, and the younger, Theoderic, by the queen. The elder Theudebert received the kingdom, namely Austrasia; his grandmother Brunhild sent the younger Theoderic to the kingdom of King Guntramnus, namely Burgundy.

At that time Fridegund died. Brunhild supplied her grandson Theoderic with wicked counsel, saying: “Why do you not demand your father’s treasure and kingdom from Theudebert, since he is not your brother but was born from a certain prostitute, your father’s concubine?”

Hearing this, Theoderic, whose character was harsh, sent a very large army against his brother. When they met in battle, Theudebert was defeated and fled to Cologne. Theoderic pursued him, devastating everything. When the people cried out to him to spare his subjects, he said: “If you want me to spare you, bring Theudebert to me alive, or bring me his head.” [Note: [Col. 0719] *auferte*, “take away,” 5.]

They entered the city and urged Theudebert to surrender the treasure so that his brother might withdraw. Believing their words, he entered his treasury. While he was searching for the most precious objects, one of them struck him in the back of the neck with a sword and cut off his head.

Theoderic then seized the city and took many treasures. Returning to the city of Metz, he carried away Theudebert’s exceedingly beautiful daughter with her two young sons. He killed the sons and wished to take the daughter in marriage.

When Brunhild said to him, “You ought not to marry your brother’s daughter,” he became angry and said: “Did you not tell me that he was not my brother? Why have you brought this sin upon me, author of his death?” Drawing his knife, he wished to stab her, but she was rescued by those standing nearby.

Afterward, filled with great hatred, she sent him a poisoned potion through her servants. He drank it and died.

Thus the history of the Franks relates the matter. But in the *Book of the Acts of Saint Columban* (ch. 57 and following) it is written that they fought at Tolbiac, that Theoderic pursued the defeated and fleeing Theudebert, captured him, and brought him to his grandmother Brunhild. She asked that he be made a cleric, but wickedly killed him not many days later.

Theoderic, while staying in the city of Metz, was consumed by divine fire. Let writers decide concerning this controversy.

After Theoderic died, his son Sigibert succeeded to the kingdom. He is the one of whom it is read in the *Book of the Acts of Saint Gall* that he betrothed the daughter of Duke Gunzo, whom the same blessed Gall liberated from a demon. (Vit. Col. l. l.)

Chlothar, son of Hilperic, gathered an army and attempted to recover the territories of the kingdom that were owed to his rule. Sigibert met him with an army. Chlothar captured and killed him, and likewise killed his five brothers, the sons of Theoderic. (G. Fr. l. l.)

After this, the Burgundians and Austrasians made peace with the Franks and raised Chlothar as king in the monarchy of the entire kingdom.

When everyone cried out that Brunhild deserved the most disgraceful death, Chlothar first had her carried around the entire army on a camel; then he ordered her to be tied to the feet of untamed horses. Her tomb was fire.

Chlothar had a son named Dagobert, an able and energetic boy, exceptionally skillful in everything. When he had grown up, the king sent him, together with Duke Pippin, to rule in Austrasia.

Chlothar reigned for forty-four years, died full of days, and his son Dagobert alone obtained the monarchy of the three kingdoms. He was exceedingly strong, the nurturer of the Franks, most severe in ecclesiastical judgments, a distinguished giver of alms, and established peace throughout his kingdom while inspiring fear in the surrounding peoples. Like peaceful Solomon, he ruled his kingdom in tranquility.

At that time, when Gundoald, mayor of the palace, died, Dagobert appointed the illustrious man Erchinoald in his place.

The same king had by Queen Mahthilda [Note: [Col. 0721] *Nacthilda*], of Saxon descent [Note: [Col. 0721] *sagonum*, 5], two sons, Sigibert and Clovis. He sent the elder, Sigibert, to rule in Austrasia under Duke Pippin and Saint Cunibert, bishop of Cologne; he kept the younger, Clovis, with himself.

This Sigibert gave the episcopal see of Utrecht to Saint Romachus [Note: [Col. 0721] The manuscripts have *romocho* in 10, *remaclo* in 9c., and likewise in 5, by a later hand].

Duke Pippin was the father of Saint Gertrude the virgin and of Begga. Begga married Ansegisus, son of Saint Arnulf, a great man beloved by God. For love of God he renounced the world and devoted himself to divine service; later he became bishop of Metz. Then, loving the hermit’s life, he departed to the Lord full of virtues.

This Saint Arnulf’s father was Arnulf, an illustrious man, son of Ansbert and Blithild, the daughter of King Chlothar. (Cf. *Vit. S. Rem.*, *S. Arnolf.*, *S. Gertr.*)

(G. Fr.) King Dagobert reigned for thirty-four years and then died. His son Clovis reigned in his place over the Franks. He took as his wife Mahthild, of Saxon descent [Note: [Col. 0721] *sagonum*, 5], a beautiful and intelligent woman [Note: [Col. 0721] *Balthildem*, “Balthild,” 4, and likewise below]. She bore him three sons, Lothar, Childeric, and Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0721] absent in 9c.].

Sigibert, Clovis’s brother and king of the Austrasians, appointed Grimoald, Pippin’s son, mayor of the palace after Duke Pippin died. Sigibert himself had a young son named Dagobert.

In due course Sigibert died. Grimoald tonsured his son Dagobert, exiled Dido, bishop of the city of Poitiers, to Scotland, and placed Dagobert over the bishopric.

The Franks were indignant at this. They set an ambush for Grimoald, captured him, and brought him before Clovis. Clovis handed him over in chains to prison, where he ended his life as he deserved.

At that time Clovis, instigated by the devil, cut off the arm of the holy martyr Dionysius. From that time the Frankish kingdom collapsed through destructive calamities.

After Clovis died in the fifteenth year of his reign, the Franks established his brother Lothar to reign in his place with their mother Mahthild. Lothar made Saint Leodegar bishop of Autun.

At the same time, after Erchinoald, mayor of the palace, died, Ebroin succeeded him.

Not long afterward Lothar died. Ebroin, mayor of the palace, wished to make his brother Theoderic king. But because Ebroin had already become hateful to the Franks, they rejected his counsel and established his other brother Childeric [Note: [Col. 0721] *fr. e.*, “his other brother,” 5; [Note: [Col. 0721] absent in 9c.], who already ruled the Austrasians, as their king.

When Ebroin saw this, he went to the monastery of Luxeuil with his head tonsured, as though he were to remain a monk permanently. After some time, when Childeric was fickle and acted thoughtlessly in everything, he was killed by certain men together with the pregnant queen [Note: [Col. 0721] absent in 9c.]. Theoderic was again recalled to the kingdom.

Ebroin then burst out of the monastery, reached the king, and recovered his former office. He exercised great tyranny over the Franks, who hated him, and among them he killed Saint Leodegar.

After Theoderic died, his sons Clovis and Hildebert reigned. After them came the younger Dagobert. Hilperic and Reginfrid succeeded him, but were overthrown by Charles, the son of Pippin; Lothar was substituted in their place. After him Hilperic reigned again, and after him Theoderic.

When Theoderic died in the twentieth year of the emperor Leo, and Charles died in the first year of Constantine, Leo’s son, five years passed after Theoderic without a king. Finally, in the sixth year, Pippin and Carloman, the sons of Charles, established Childeric as king. He was the last of the ancient line of kings. (Cf. *gen. Kar.*)

During the time of the earlier kings, after Ebroin’s death, Ansegisus [Note: [Col. 0721] *ansgisus*, corrected to *angisus* in 10 and likewise in 11], the son of Saint Arnulf, became mayor of the palace in the Frankish kingdom. They say that he derived his name [Note: [Col. 0721] [Col. 0722C] from the Trojan Anchises, the father of Aeneas] from that Anchises. [Note: [Col. 0721] *anchiso*, 5.]

After him came Pippin, his son and the son of Begga, the sister of Saint Gertrude. After him came his son Charles, surnamed the Strong, who through many battles seized the chief power from Reginfrid.

Pippin fathered this Charles by Albhaida, the sister of his household officer Dido. He took her in addition to his lawful wife Plectrud, by whom he had Druogo and Grimoald. When Saint Lambert [Note: [Col. 0721] *Lantpertus*, C.] the bishop condemned this action, Dido killed him, with Pippin’s alleged consent [Note: [Col. 0721] This, however, is not found in the *Life of Saint Lambert*, nor could I find it elsewhere; cf. Hirsch’s learned discussion of the matter, *De Vita Sigeberti*, p. 295 and following; cf. SIGEB. *Vit. S. Lamb.*], while Hildebert, son of Theoderic, was reigning.

[Note: [Col. 0723A] C. adds: “Dido himself, shortly afterward afflicted by a most grievous illness, was consumed by worms and, because of the intolerable stench [ [Col. 0723] *foctoris*, C.], was drowned in the river Meuse; and all the accomplices in this flight were divinely punished within a year.” From Sigeb. G. a. 699.]

After Charles died, his sons Pippin and Carloman jointly held the chief power for four years; afterward Pippin held it alone for seven years. At that time kings of the ancient stock still reigned in Francia in name alone and possessed none of the dignity of kingship. Finally, by the authority of Pope Zacharias, Childeric—who then falsely bore the name of king—was tonsured and confined to a monastery, and Pippin was raised from prefect of the palace to the kingship.

Thereafter, through his successor Pope Stephen, Pippin was consecrated with royal anointing together with his wife Bertrada and his sons Charles and Carloman, and was confirmed in the kingdom, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 754. (Cf. EINH. c. 1.)

Having said these things about the Frankish people and kings, whether for the sake of information by repeating what came before or anticipating what follows, and as though by a kind of digression, let us now return to what we began.

## The Years of Valentinian

[Col. 0723B] (Chr. W.) In the first year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s incarnation 367, Valentinian gave his brother Valens the eastern kingdom, while he himself held the western.

A.D. 368. Pope Damasus, the thirty-ninth, was ordained and sat for twenty-six years [Note: [Col. 0723] XVIII. 5. 10. 11], though amid a schism, because Ursinus, a certain deacon of the Roman Church, usurped the priesthood. (BEDAE *Mart.*) Damasus established that psalms should be sung in the church day and night.

(Chr. W.) A.D. 369. Real wool mixed with rain [Note: [Col. 0723] *vero*, “true,” 5, 10; absent in 9, 11] flowed from the clouds.

A.D. 370. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died.

A.D. 371. Athalaric, king of the Goths, persecuted the Christians among his people.

[Col. 0723C] (HIER.) A.D. 372. Eusebius of Vercelli and Lucifer of Cagliari died.

(Chr. W.) A.D. 373. Valentinian subdued the Saxons in Francia by slaughter.

(HIER.) A.D. 374. Didymus of Alexandria composed many works concerning our doctrine.

A.D. 375. Saint Martin was ordained bishop at Tours.

(Chr. W.) A.D. 376. Magnentia, also called Thecla, the most noble of the Romans, came to Jerusalem and became renowned for great miracles and humility.

A.D. 377. Valentinian died when a recently opened vein ruptured [Note: [Col. 0723] 9c. adds: “From this point there is an error in the years up to Charlemagne.”].

(History Miscellany.) Valens [Note: [Col. 0723] At the heading, 5: “Concerning Valens.”], brother of Valentinian, therefore, while by his brother’s concession he ruled with him in the Eastern Empire—that is, at Constantinople—for eleven years, ruled there for four years after his brother’s death, while Gratian and Valentinian, his brother’s sons, held the Western Empire, that is, the Roman imperial power. This Valens, therefore, as soon as his brother had departed from him, was rebaptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, at the urging, as they say, of his wife Dominica; and he would immediately have begun a persecution against the Christians, had he not feared his brother (cf. Orosius VII.32). Remaining at Antioch, however, for a very long time, he gave everyone permission to celebrate his own sacred rites—pagans, Jews, and all heretics alike; he was hostile only to those who preached the apostolic teaching.

After his brother’s death, he fulfilled by his deeds the impiety that he had conceived in his mind. (Jerome—Bede—Jordanes, *On the Roman Successions*—History Miscellany.) For he exiled the Lord’s priests, compelled monks to enter military service, and ordered those unwilling to serve as soldiers to be killed. Meanwhile, wishing, at the devil’s prompting, to discover who would reign after him, he practiced necromancy. But the devil, exploiting his audacity and cruelty, gave him not an explicit but an oblique response, through which he craftily killed many people. For he showed him four letters—θ, ε, ο, δ—saying that the person whose name this formed would receive the highest power of the empire after Valens. Therefore, driven by jealousy, he killed many whom he judged likely to seize the tyranny.

Thus Theodatus, Theodorus, Theodotus, Theodunculus, and everyone who had these letters at the beginning of his name were killed. Because of this fear, very many [Note: [Col. 0723] E1: “many.”] changed their names, denying under oath the names they had previously borne, so that they might escape danger. Among the others, Theodosius too was killed, a brave man descended from Spain, the father of the later emperor Theodosius. This Theodosius, sent to Africa by Valentinian, the brother of Valens, forced a certain Firmus, who was raising himself up to royal power, to his death, and subjected all Africa and Mauritania to the Roman Empire. But when Valens, out of envy, ordered him to be killed, he first asked to be baptized for the remission of his sins, and thus willingly offered his throat to the executioner.

At that time the nation of the Huns, long shut away among inaccessible mountains, suddenly, driven by savage fury, burst forth against the Goths and, throwing them into confusion, expelled them from their ancient settlements. They crossed the Danube and came to Valens; he received them without any treaty and granted them Thrace as a place to inhabit. Then, when the same emperor did not provide them with what was sufficient, they could not endure hunger, seized their weapons, and, marching through Thrace, freely ravaged and burned everything (cf. Jordanes).

When Valens heard this, he departed from Antioch and gathered an army to fight the Goths. (History Miscellany.) First delaying at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0723] Omitted in 5.], he sent Trajan, master of the army, against them; Trajan was defeated and returned in disgrace. When he reproached Valens for his softness, he said:

“I have not been defeated, O emperor, but you have, since, by fighting against God, you are winning His favor for the barbarians. Do you not know whom you expelled from the churches and to whom you handed them over?”

Stirred by tardy repentance, Valens ordered the bishops and the other holy men to be recalled from exile. Meanwhile the barbarians were roaming throughout Thrace [Note: [Col. 0723] 5: “through Trachia.”], and already, with no one preventing them, were burning the suburbs of Constantinople. Therefore, departing from Constantinople, he led his army to the city of Adrianople. When battle was joined with the Goths, at the first attack the Roman cavalry abandoned the exposed infantry, whom the Goths soon surrounded and overwhelmed with clouds of arrows as they fled here and there.

The emperor Valens himself was wounded by an arrow and put to flight. When, because of his excessive pain, he fell from his horse, he was carried into a wretched hut. The Goths then arrived and, not knowing that he was there, set fire to it and burned him alive [Note: [Col. 0725] 9c adds: “himself.”], in the fiftieth year of his life [Note: [Col. 0725] 5 and 9c: “of his life.”] and the fifteenth of his reign—eleven of those years having been spent reigning with his brother, and four after him.

By God’s just judgment he was therefore burned by those whom he himself had inflamed with the fire of treachery. For earlier, when the Goths had asked him to send them preachers and teachers who might instruct them in the Catholic faith, he sent Arian teachers, and thus that entire nation became Arian.

After Valens died, the Goths, now secure, advanced to the city of Constantinople, where Dominica, the wife of Valens, was then residing. She distributed rewards from the public treasury to those who fought bravely and defended the city with masculine courage.

(Jerome.) Around this time Apollinaris of Laodicea, a bishop, composed many writings on our religion; afterward, having deviated from the faith, he established the heresy named after him.

Since the Goths have been mentioned not only in this place but also frequently earlier, and will be mentioned still more often in what follows [Note: [Col. 0725] 5: “will be mentioned here.”], it does not seem superfluous to trace their origin farther back to the beginning and insert here, as briefly and truthfully as possible, something about who they were and from where they came. For the Huns, who are reported to have expelled them from their settlements, are also said to have derived their origin from them; and the Gepids and Amazons are likewise recorded as having sprung from them.

# HISTORY OF THE GOTHS [Note: [Col. 0725] 5: “of the Goths.”]

[Col. 0725]

(Jordanes.) Claudius Ptolemy, outstanding in his description of the world, reports in the second book of his work that in the waters of the northern ocean there is a certain large island called Scanzia, stretched lengthwise like a leaf, with its sides spread wide. Pomponius Mela likewise reports that it lies in the gulf of the Codanian Sea, whose shores the ocean floods.

It lies opposite the mouth of the Vistula River. This river rises in the Sarmatian Mountains and, in sight of Scanzia, pours itself in three branches into the northern ocean, marking the boundary between Germany and Scythia. Many other islands are also said to be situated there; if wolves cross to them over the frozen sea because of the excessive cold, they are said to be deprived of their eyesight. Thus these lands are inhospitable not only to human beings but also cruel to the beasts of the earth.

On the island of Scanzia many different nations dwell. Ptolemy lists seven of them. One of these, called the Adogit, lives in the northern part of the same island and is said to have continuous daylight for forty days and nights in midsummer; likewise, in the middle of winter, for the same number of days and nights, alternating sorrow with joy, it is said not to see clear daylight.

This occurs because during the longer days they see the sun returning toward the east along the edge of the celestial axis, whereas during the shorter days it is not seen among them in the way southerners believe they see it. To us the sun seems to rise from below; to them it seems to circle the edge.

No one should regard this as incredible, since Pliny (II.75), the most learned of secular writers, testifies that the same thing occurs on the island of Thule around the summer and winter solstices, although only for certain days.

The venerable Bede also confirms this, saying [Note: [Col. 0725D] This passage is sought in vain in Bede’s works, but is found in Book VII.2.6 of Dicuil’s *On the Measurement of the World*; Lappenberg had already noted this in *Archiv* VI, p. 890.] that he had been told by certain clerics who had been on that island from the Kalends of February to the Kalends of August that, on the days around the summer solstice, in the evening hour the sun hides itself as it sets, as though behind a small hill, so that during that brief interval there is no darkness at all, but whatever a person wishes to do can be done as though in the presence of the sun. And if they had been on the heights of the mountains of that same land, perhaps the sun would never have been hidden from them [Note: [Col. 0725] 5: “from them.”].

In the middle of that brief interval, however, midnight occurs in the middle of the inhabited world. Blessed Augustine too, in the discussion made in the church concerning the sun, speaks about the sun’s circuit (*On Genesis*, Book I, in the Froben edition of his works, III, p. 506):

“Therefore, when the southern part has the sun, it is day for us; but when, circling around, it reaches the northern part, it is night for us. Yet it is not the case that it is not day in another part where the sun is present—unless perhaps we should incline our minds to poetic fictions and believe that the sun plunges into the sea and, having been washed there, rises in the morning from the other side. Indeed, if that were so, the abyss itself would be illuminated by the sun’s presence, and there would be day there; for it could also illuminate the waters, since they could not extinguish it. But it is monstrous to suppose this.”

(Jordanes.) There is another nation there called the Suehans. The people of this nation use excellent horses, and they are the ones who, through commercial exchange and by way of countless other peoples, transmit to Roman use the skins called *saperinae*, famous for the beauty of their black pelts. Although they live in poverty, they dress most richly.

The Suetidi are also there, known among this nation and taller in body than the others, although the Danes, who sprang from their stock, expelled the Heruli from their own settlements. Among all the nations of Scanzia, the Heruli claim a distinguished reputation because of their extraordinary height [Note: [Col. 0725] 4 and 10: “affectent”; 9c: “afflectent.”].

From this island of Scanzia, which others call Scandinavia [Col. 0727A] (Paul the Deacon I.2; cf. chapter 1), as from a workshop of peoples—or certainly like a sheath of nations—various nations emerged: Danes, Dacians, Heruli, Rugi, Turcilingi, Vandals, the Winih, who are also called Lombards, and those who were afterward called Burgundians, along with many other barbarian nations.

(Jordanes.) From the same island, the Goths—also called Getae—are likewise remembered to have departed long ago with their king, named Berich, in only three ships. Those who were in one ship were somewhat slower, as commonly happens, and, unable to follow the others, came to an island of the Vistula River. There they settled until they could find better dwellings and gave their people a name derived from their slowness (ibid., chapter 17).

For in their language slowness is called *gepanta*, and the people themselves, the name gradually becoming corrupted through this defect of character [Col. 0727B], later received the designation Gepids. I do not believe this is wholly false, for they are slower in understanding and heavier in bodily movement.

(Chapter 4 and following.) The others, who were in the two ships, as soon as they reached the nearer shore of the ocean, gave their name to the place, which is said still to be called Gothiscandza. From there they soon advanced to the settlements of the Ulmerugi, who at that time occupied the shores of the ocean, and pitched their camp against them. After engaging them in battle, they expelled them from their own settlements. Then, subduing their neighbors the Vandals, they added them to their victories.

When the population had greatly increased, and nearly the fifth king after Berich was already reigning, Filimer, son of Gadaric the Great, decided that the army of the Goths should advance from there with their families [Note: [Col. 0727] Omitted in 5.]. While seeking suitable settlements and appropriate places, he reached the lands of Scythia, which in their language were called Oium [Note: [Col. 0727] 5: “oium,” and likewise below.].

Delighted by the great fertility of the regions, he transported his army across a certain river by means of a bridge. After half the army had crossed, the bridge by which they had crossed the river is said to have collapsed irreparably, and no one was thereafter permitted to go or return. For that place, as they say, is enclosed by a surrounding chasm and trembling marshes, which nature has made impassable through this double confusion.

Nevertheless, even today the testimony of travelers, although they hear from far away, is accustomed to report that the sounds of cattle can be heard there and traces of human beings can be detected.

Those who, under Filimer, are said to have been transported into the land of Oium after crossing the river, took possession of the desired soil and immediately came to the people of the Spali. Engaging them in battle, they gained the victory.

From there, like victors, they hastened to the farthest part of Scythia, which is close to the Pontic Sea. This is also celebrated collectively in their ancient songs, almost in the manner of historical narrative, and Ablavius, an outstanding historian of the Gothic people, confirms it as a most truthful account. Some of the ancients agreed with this view and became accustomed to calling them Scythians.

Scythia is contiguous with Germany as far as the place where the Ister River rises [Note: [Col. 0727] 5: “Hister”; 4: “Hyster.”] or where Lake Marsianus spreads out, extending as far as the Danube and Mount Taurus—not the Taurus of Asia, but the one belonging to Scythia—around the whole circumference of the Maeotian marsh. The circuit of that marsh is 1,144 miles [Note: [Col. 0727] 9c: “army.”], and nowhere does it sink to a depth greater than eight cubits.

In this Scythia, the first people from the west are the Gepids, who are surrounded by great and astonishing rivers; inland lies Dacia, fortified in the form of a crown by steep Alps. Then, across immense expanses, the populous nation of the Veneti is settled. Although their names now vary among different families and places, they are principally called Sclaveni.

The first settlement of the Goths on Scythian soil was beside the Maeotian marsh; the second was in Moesia, Thrace, and Dacia; the third was above the Pontic Sea. While they lived in their first settlement beside Maeotis, they had Filimer as king. In the second settlement—that is, on the soil of Moesia, Thrace, and Dacia—they had Zalmoxes, whom they testify to have been a man of extraordinary philosophy and learning.

Most writers of annals, however, report that they first had an instructor named Zeuta, afterward Dicineus, who came to them at the time when Sulla held the Roman principate. After Dicineus they had the wise Comosicus, who, because of his expertise, was regarded among them both as king and as high priest; fourth, they had Zalmoxes.

Nor were there lacking men who instructed them in wisdom. Thus the Goths became wiser than nearly all barbarians and almost equal to the Greeks, as Dio reports. He composed their histories and annals in the Greek style and also says that they first called those who stood out among them for noble birth *Tarabostei*, and afterward *Pilleati* [Note: [Col. 0727] 4: “existebant”; 9c: “existabant.”]. From these they appointed their kings and priests.

The Getae were so highly praised that they claimed that Mars, whom the deceptive art of poets declares to be the god of war, had been born among them. Hence Virgil says:

“And Father Gradivus, who presides over the Getic fields.”

The Goths always appeased Mars with the harshest worship, namely by the death of captives, believing that the commander of wars ought properly to be appeased with human blood [Note: [Col. 0727] 9c: “aptly”; 4 omits it.].

While the Goths—who were also called Scythians—were dwelling in this way, Vesoces, king of Egypt, who reigned at the time when Sosarmus ruled the Assyrians and Inachus the Sicyonians, was the first to bring war against the Goths. Their king at that time was Tanausis, who met Vesoces, defeated him decisively, and drove him in flight all the way to Egypt (Orosius I.14). He attacked the abandoned army and seized all its war equipment [Note: [Col. 0727] 4 and 9c: “he attacked.”]; he would have devastated the whole of Egypt if the marshes of the Nile had not prevented him.

The Goths then returned and made nearly all Asia, subdued through countless massacres, tributary. They remained there for fifteen years without a treaty, until at last they were recalled by the appeals of their wives, who announced that, if they did not return, they would seek offspring from neighboring peoples.

(Jordanes, chapter 7.) During the period in which the men remained in Asia, their women were attacked for plunder by a neighboring people. But, instructed by their husbands, they took up arms and resisted bravely, driving off the attacking enemies with great shame.

Therefore, some people suppose that these women were the ones called Amazons. But this seems inconsistent with the fact that the husbands of these women are recorded as having recalled them after fifteen years, whereas the husbands of the Amazons are said to have been killed partly in war and partly by the Amazons themselves. The origin of the Amazons, however, is said to have been as follows.

# CONCERNING THE AMAZONS

[Col. 0729]

(Orosius I.15.) During the middle period of the Goths’ residence in this settlement, two royal youths, Plinus and Scolopetius, were driven from their homeland among them by a faction of the nobles. They led a great body of young men with them and settled on the coast of Cappadocia Pontica, beside the Thermodon River, bringing the Themiscyrian fields under their control.

While they were ravaging the neighboring regions, nearly all of them, together with their companions [Note: [Col. 0729] Omitted in 9c.], were slaughtered in an ambush through a conspiracy of the neighboring peoples.

Their wives, moved by exile and widowhood, seized weapons. To make all hearts equal through a similar condition, they killed the men who had survived; then, inflamed against the enemy, they exacted vengeance in their own blood by destroying the neighboring peoples who had killed their husbands.

(Jordanes, chapter 8.) Having sought peace through weapons, and fearing that they would become weakened as their offspring diminished, they entered into sexual unions with men of neighboring nations. They arranged such meetings once a year, so that, returning on the same day of the following year, they handed over to the fathers whatever male children they had borne, while they trained whatever was female in the arts of war.

Their maidens did not keep a distaff for any kind of work; instead, they trained themselves in horsemanship, weaponry, and hunting. Some say that when they gave birth to males, they destroyed the unfortunate infants through stepmotherly hatred, and that childbirth was therefore detestable among them, although everywhere else it is recognized as a thing desired. This cruelty greatly increased the terror inspired by them among neighboring peoples through the widespread report of it. For what hope, I ask, would there be for a captive when it was considered impious to spare even a son? (Orosius, same passage.)

They burned the right breast of their girls so that the shooting of arrows or the throwing of javelins would not be hindered. Hence they are also called Amazons, that is, “without a breast.”

(Jordanes, chapter 7.) They had two queens, Lampedo and Marpesia. Choosing them as braver than the others, they submitted themselves to their rule. Dividing their army into two parts, they alternated in taking responsibility for warfare and guarding the home.

While Lampedo defended their own territories at home, Marpesia, taking an army of women, led this new kind of force into Asia. Overcoming various peoples in war and reconciling others by peace, she came to Mount Caucasus. After remaining there for a certain period, she gave the place the name Marpesian Rock.

Hence Virgil says:

“And if the hard Marpesian rock remains.”

From there they departed, crossed the Etalus River, and took possession of Armenia, Syria, Cilicia, Galatia, Pisidia, and many regions of Asia. After ruling there for a long time, they founded Ephesus and other cities and military camps and dedicated them to their own name. At Ephesus they also built a temple of Diana with extraordinary beauty, because of their devotion to archery and hunting, the arts to which they had given themselves.

(Orosius, same passage.) In this way, by such a turn of fortune, the women of the Scythian nation held the kingdom of Asia for one hundred years. Then a large part of the army, burdened with an exceedingly rich spoil, returned to their companions at the Marpesian Rocks. The rest, left behind to defend the empire of Asia, were slaughtered along with Queen Marpesia in an attack by the enemy.

Her daughter Sinope took her place. She increased her exceptional glory in virtue through perpetual virginity. When this reputation had stirred up the nations, such fear and admiration seized them that even Hercules, when ordered by his master to bring him the weapons of the queen of the Amazons, as though he were being sent toward unavoidable danger, gathered a select and noble youth from all Greece and prepared nine long ships. Yet, not even then satisfied with an assessment of his forces, he preferred to attack them unexpectedly and surround them while they were unprepared.

At that time two sisters, Antiope and Orithyia, ruled the kingdom. Hercules arrived and overcame the Amazons, who were unsuspecting, unarmed, and made sluggish by their unconcern for peace. Among the many who were killed and captured, two sisters were held: Melanippe by Hercules and Hippolyte by Theseus.

Theseus took Hippolyte as his wife, while Hercules returned Melanippe to her sister and received the queen’s weapons as the price of her ransom. After Orithyia, Penthesilea gained the kingdom. We have learned of her most famous demonstrations of valor among men during the Trojan War, in which she is said to have been killed by Achilles.

There were seventy thousand Amazons with her, of whom only a few returned. After Penthesilea, Thalestris held the kingdom; she made peace with Alexander the Great. The Amazons are said to have ruled for many years, down to Julius Caesar.

We have inserted this account of the Amazons into this history to show that they too descended from the stock of the Goths. We now return to the history of the Goths itself, which we had begun.

(Jordanes, chapter 9 and following.) Dio the historian, a most diligent investigator of antiquities, who gave his work the title *Getica*, records that after a long interval they had a king named Telephus, son of Hercules [Note: [Col. 0729] 4: “of Belus”; 9c: “of Heracles”; 11: “of Hercules.”]. He was tall in body but even more formidable in strength. Equaling his father’s courage through his own virtues, he resembled Hercules in his knees and in the likeness of his appearance.

His ancestors called his kingdom Moesia. He was joined in marriage to a sister of Priam and waged war against the Danaans. In that battle he killed Thessander, the commander of Greece. When he attacked Ajax in hostility and pursued Ulysses with blows, his horse fell and he himself fell with it. Wounded in the thigh by Achilles’ spear, he could not be healed for a long time. Nevertheless, although wounded, he drove the Greeks from his borders.

After Telephus died, his son Eurypylus succeeded to the kingdom. He was born of the sister of King Priam. When, out of love for Cassandra, he took part in the Trojan War in order to bring aid to his parents and father-in-law, he was soon killed.

After a long interval, Queen Tamyris ruled over the Goths together with her son. She killed Cyrus, king of the Persians, when he brought war against the Scythians.

After this Antinus ruled the Goths. Darius, son of Hydaspes and king of the Persians, sought his daughter in marriage. When he was rejected, he brought war against the Scythians with seven hundred thousand armed men, but, after losing eighty thousand, he fled.

After him Xerxes, his son, believing that he would avenge his father’s injuries, marched against them with seven hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom, three hundred thousand auxiliaries, one thousand warships, and three thousand cargo ships. But, not daring even to test their courage in battle, he returned in shame.

Philip too, the father of Alexander the Great, crossed into Scythia with his son, intending to plunder it. When battle was joined and the Scythians were superior both in number and in valor, they were defeated by the deceit of the exceedingly crafty Philip.

In that battle twenty thousand boys and women of the Scythian nation were captured, and a great quantity of livestock was driven away; no gold or silver was found [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “twenty thousand.”].

Afterward, having concluded a friendship treaty with them, Philip took Medumpa, daughter of Gudila, king of the Goths, as his wife, so that, strengthened by such an alliance, he might secure the Macedonian kingdom [Note: [Col. 0731] 5: “the Macedonian kingdom.”].

Then, while Borbista was reigning among the Goths, Dicineus came to Gothia, at the time when Sulla held the Roman principate. Borhista welcomed Dicineus and gave him royal power. On his advice the Goths ravaged the lands of the Germans [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “of the Romans”], which the Franks now hold.

This was beneficial, advantageous, and desirable for them: whatever Dicineus, their counselor, commanded, they sought in every way to carry out.

(Jordanes, chapter 11 and following.) Seeing that their minds obeyed him in all things and that they possessed a natural intelligence, he instructed them in almost every branch of philosophy. He selected the most noble and prudent men from among them, taught them theology, persuaded them to venerate certain divinities and shrines, and made them priests. He gave them the name *Pilleati*, because, with their heads covered by tiaras—that is, caps—they performed sacrifices. He ordered the rest of the people to be called *Capillati*, “long-haired.”

The Goths accepted this name as a great distinction and still recall it in their songs.

When Dicineus died [Note: [Col. 0731] 4, 5, and 10: “when he declined”], they held Cumosicus in nearly equal veneration; he was not inferior in skill. Because of his expertise, he was both their king and their high priest, and he ruled the people with the highest justice.

When he too departed from human affairs, Zalmoxes, king of the Goths, ascended the throne and ruled his peoples in Dacia for forty years. By Dacia I mean the ancient Dacia now known to be possessed by the Gepids. This country lies opposite Moesia, beyond the Danube, and is encircled by a crown of mountains. It has only two approaches: the first, Dacia; the second, Gothia, now called Gepidia.

(Chapter 5.) The Goths now had their third settlement above the Pontic Sea, more civilized and more prudent. Their peoples were divided among families: the Visigoths, that is, the western Goths, belonged to the family of the Balthi; the Ostrogoths, that is, the eastern Goths, were subject to the illustrious Amali.

Their practice was first among neighboring peoples to bend the bow with sinews, as Lucan testifies when he says:

“Stretch the Armenian bows with Getic sinews.”

They also sang the deeds of their ancient ancestors to the accompaniment of songs and lyres: those of Erpantala [Note: [Col. 0731] 4: “Arpantale”; 5: “Erpantanae”; 10: “Expantanae”; 9c: “Herpantalae.”], Hannala, Fridigern [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “Frigdigerni”], Widigoja, and others whose reputation is great among this people—men whom antiquity, in its wondrous boasting, scarcely declares to have been heroes.

(Chapter 11.) The Goths therefore ruled for a long time—so long, indeed, that Caesar, who first claimed the Roman Empire for himself and had subjected nearly the whole world to his power, repeatedly attempted to subjugate the Goths but could not. Although Gaius Tiberius was already reigning as the third Roman emperor, the Goths nevertheless remained unharmed in their own kingdom.

(Chapter 13 and following.) When Domitian had been reigning for the eleventh year after Augustus, the Goths devastated the bank of the Danube, which had long been occupied by the Romans, after destroying the Roman soldiers and their commanders. Oppius Sabinus was then in charge of that province after Agrippa, while Dorpaneus commanded the Goths.

When battle was joined between them, the Goths defeated the Romans, cut off the head of Oppius Sabinus, and publicly plundered many cities and forts belonging to the emperor.

Driven by this necessity, Domitian hastened with all his forces to Illyricum. He appointed Fuscus commander of the army and ordered him, with the best men, to cross the Danube against Dorpaneus’s army by means of ships joined together like a bridge.

The Goths were not slow to take up arms. In the first engagement they defeated the Romans, and, after killing the commander Fuscus, they plundered the military camp. Having gained a great victory, they began to call their nobles not ordinary men but demigods, *Anses*.

To run briefly through their genealogy: the first of these heroes was Capul, who begot Ulmal. Ulmal begot Anguisath. Anguisath begot the one called Amala, from whom the lineage of the Amali descends. Amala begot Hisarna; Hisarnis begot Ostrogotha; Ostrogotha begot Hunul; Hunul begot Athal; Athal begot Achiulf and Odiulf; Achiulf begot Ansila, Ediulf, Witulf [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “Withulf.”], and Ermenricus; Witulf [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “Withulf.”] begot Walaradans; Walaradans begot Hiarius [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “Hiarrus.”] and Venetharius; Venetharius begot Wandalaricus; Wandalaricus begot Dietmar [Note: [Col. 0731] 4 and 9c: “Dichtmar”], Walamir, and Witimar [Note: [Col. 0731] 9c: “Withmar.”]; Dietmar begot Theodoric; Theodoric begot Amalasuintha; Amalasuintha, by her husband Eutharic [Note: [Col. 0731] “In writing these names I have followed the authority of the manuscripts.”], begot Athalaric and Matasuintha. Eutharic was related to her through this family connection.

The aforementioned Ermenricus [Note: [Col. 0733] 9c: “c.”] son of Achiulf begot Hunimund; Hunimund begot Thurismund; Thurismund begot Herimund; Herimund begot Betericus; Betericus begot Eutharic, who, having been joined to Amalasuintha, begot Athalaric and Matasuintha.

Athalaric died in childhood, and Matasuintha was married to Witigis; she had no son by him. When Witigis departed from human affairs, Germanus the patrician, nephew of the emperor Justin, took her in marriage, made her an ordinary patrician, and begot by her a son named Germanus. After her husband Germanus died, she decided to remain a widow.

The relationship of Ermenricus and Theodoric was as follows: Ermenricus and Witulf were sons of Achiulf.

[Col. 0733B]

Ermenricus | Witulf |

Hunimundus | Walaradans [Note: [Col. 0733] 9c: “Vualaradus.”] |

Thurismundus | Winitharius |

Herimundus [Note: [Col. 0733] 5: “Herismundus.”] | Wandalaricus |

Betericus | Dietmarus |

Eutharicus | Theodericus. |

Eutharic took Theodoric’s daughter Amalasuintha and begot Athalaric and Matasuintha, joining together the stock of the Amali, which had already been almost divided.

Having inserted this material, let us, as we believe appropriate, return to the order of the history.

(C. 14 and following.) After Dorpaneus, king of the Goths, had died, Ostrogotha succeeded him. That part of the Goths which held the eastern region took the name Ostrogoths, either from the king or from the region; the others, who were in the western part, were called Visigoths. Both divisions, however, were subject to King Ostrogotha. And, remarkably, as they prospered, the Vandal lay beneath their right hand, the Marcomannus stood under tribute, and the prince of the Quadi was reduced to servitude.

When Philip was ruling the Romans—he alone, before Constantine, became a Christian together with his son, likewise named Philip—Ostrogotha crossed the Danube with his people and ravaged the Roman provinces. To fight against him, the senator Decius was sent by Philip. When he arrived, he removed from military service the Roman soldiers whom he found and made them live as private citizens, as though the Goths had crossed the Danube through the soldiers’ negligence. Having, as he thought, taken vengeance on his own men, he returned to Philip.

But when the soldiers saw that after all their exertions they had been expelled from the army, they fled to the aid of King Ostrogotha. He received them, and, inflamed by their account, immediately led out three hundred thousand of his own men armed for war. After crossing the Danube, they ravaged Moesia and besieged Marcianopolis, the metropolitan city of that province, which Trajan had once founded and named after his sister Marcia. After a long siege they accepted payment, were enriched, and returned to their own lands. They lived successfully in their homeland for as long as Ostrogotha remained their prince.

After his death, Oniba succeeded him. When he led an army and was ravaging the Roman territories, the emperor Decius, now accompanied by his son, confronted him. Battle was joined, and Decius’s son, himself also called Decius, was killed by an arrow. The father too was slain while attempting to avenge his son [Note: [Col. 0733] *u. f.*, 5].

After Decius, Gallus and Volusianus gained the imperial power and made peace with the Goths. Before long, Gallus and Volusianus having both fallen, Gallienus [Note: [Col. 0733] *galienus*, 9c] seized the principate. When he had been undone by dissipation, the Gothic leaders Respa, Veducus, and Thurbar crossed the Hellespont and plundered many cities of Asia. They burned the celebrated temple of Diana, founded at Ephesus by the Amazons. Returning with much booty, they again destroyed Troy, which had scarcely been rebuilt to any extent after the war of Agamemnon. Thus, after devastating Asia, they came into Thrace; and, taking pleasure in the baths of hot waters near the foot of Mount Haemus, they remained there many days before returning to their own country.

(Jordanes, chs. 20 and following.) After this, when summoned by Herculius Maximianus to assist the Romans against the Parthians, they fought loyally and drove away Narses, king of the Persians and grandson of the great Sapor. Summoned also by the emperor Constantine, they rendered much assistance, and the Goths took part in the construction of the city which he founded in his own name as Rome’s most famous rival. After making a treaty with the emperor, they offered him forty thousand of their men as support against various peoples; their number and military service are still recorded in the state, namely, as the federates. At that time they flourished under the rule of their kings Ariaricus and Arioricus.

After these kings had departed, Geberich succeeded to the kingdom, outstanding in courage and nobility. Born to Hilderic and grandson of Hovida, with Nida as his great-grandfather, he matched the glory of his lineage with his deeds. At the beginning of his reign he immediately declared war on the people of the Vandals, who at that time lived where the Gepids later settled. He defeated their king Wisamar together with a large part of his people, and, having plundered the Vandals, returned victorious.

The very few Vandals who remained, abandoning their unfortunate homeland, sought Pannonia, which the emperor Constantine had granted them [Note: [Col. 0733] omitted in 9c]. Having established their settlements there, they served for sixty years as inhabitants, in accordance with imperial decrees. Then, after a long interval, invited by Stilicho, master of the soldiers, former consul, and patrician, they occupied Gaul. There they plundered the neighboring peoples and did not establish very secure settlements.

When Geberich, king of the Goths, had departed this life, after some time Ermenricus, the noblest of the Amals, succeeded to the kingdom. He subdued many warlike northern peoples and compelled them to obey his laws; for this reason some rightly compared him with Alexander the Great.

[Col. 0735A] He held under his authority the Golthes [Note: [Col. 0735] *golthos*, 4, 9c, 11; *gothos*, 10], the Citathiudos [Note: [Col. 0735] *cithatindos*, 9c], the Inanxos [Note: [Col. 0735] *manxos*, 9c], the Suasi, the Narboncae [Note: [Col. 0735] *narboneas*, 4; *narbunxas*, 9c], the Merentes, the Mordentes, the Ymniscaros [Note: [Col. 0735] *inniscatos*, 4], the Roscathaizantes [Note: [Col. 0735] *roscathazantes*, 9c; *ios. cathaizantes*, 4], the Athaalos, the Mavegones, the Rubegenae, and the Holdae.

And although he was renowned for the service of so many peoples, he did not rest until he had also subjected the people of the Heruli, over whom Alaric ruled. This people lived beside the Maeotian marsh; from the stagnant waters, which the Greeks call *helle*, they were called Heruli, as though “Helluli.” They were a people as proud as they were swift. Indeed, at that time there was no people that did not choose from among them light armament for its battle line [Note: [Col. 0735] *legem*, 5, in place of *levem*]. Yet although their speed often protected them from other peoples with whom they fought, they were subjected to the steadiness and slowness of the Goths. The strength of the latter brought it about that the Heruli served Ermenricus, king of the other Getic peoples, among the remaining nations.

After the slaughter of the Heruli, Ermenricus likewise took up arms against the Venethi. They were powerful in numbers and at first attempted to resist, but numbers avail nothing in war when God permits it and an armed multitude of strong men has arrived. The nation of the Venethi, as we have said above, is populous. Sprung from one stock, they gave themselves three names: Venethi, Antes, and Sclaveni—the last being their principal name. Although later, because of the sins of certain people, they raged everywhere, at that time they all served Ermenricus.

He also subdued the nation of the Hesti, who occupied the longest shore of the Germanic Ocean. He ruled all the peoples of Scythia and Germany as though they were his own household.

After this, the people of the Huns, more savage than every form of ferocity, broke out against the Goths and expelled from their ancient settlements those who had previously been a terror to the other peoples.

We have learned from antiquity that they came into being as follows.

# On the Origin of the Huns

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735B] Filimer, king of the Goths, son of the great Gadaric, who, after their departure from the island of Scandza, held the kingdom of the Getae in the fifth place, and who, as stated above, entered the Scythian lands with his people, found in his army certain magical women whom they call *alirunae* in the Gothic language. Suspecting them, he expelled them from his midst while they were already pregnant, as some say (Jordanes, ch. 24), and forced them to remain far away from the army in the wilderness.

Others, however (the same source?), say that when the wild men whom they call *Faunos ficarios* (“fig-tree fauns”) saw them wandering through the desert, they mingled with them in sexual intercourse and produced this exceedingly savage race. At first it was small, repulsive, and meager, like a human race, among the Maeotian marshes, and it was known by no other voice except that it exhibited the appearance of human speech.

From such a stock, then, the Huns were created and came to the borders of the Goths. Their nation, as has been said, according to the historian Priscus, occupied the farther shore of the Maeotian marsh and devoted itself only to hunting. It experienced no other labor, except that, after it had grown into a people, it disturbed the peace of the neighboring nations by frauds and plundering.

The hunters of this people, as is their custom, were searching for game along the farther shore of the Maeotian marsh when they noticed a hind unexpectedly presenting itself to them. Entering the marsh, now advancing and now stopping, it showed them the route.
