The hunters followed it and crossed on foot the Maeotian marsh, which they had thought impassable; immediately they entered the land of Scythia without knowing where they were.

They had known nothing of another world beyond the Maeotian marsh. Struck with amazement at the land of Scythia, and being ingenious, they returned to their own people, believing that the route previously unknown to every generation had been divinely shown to them. They reported what had happened, praised Scythia, and all together hurried into Scythia by the path the hind had shown. They killed all the Scythians they encountered and subdued the rest after destroying them.

For as soon as they had crossed that enormous marsh, they immediately swept away, like a kind of whirlwind of peoples, the Alpizuros, the Alcizuros, and the Itimaros, and then the Arsos and the Boiscos, who lived along the Scythian bank. They also wore down and subdued the Alans, who were their equals in battle but inferior in civilization and different in appearance, through repeated conflict. For even those whom they perhaps could not overcome in war they drove into flight by instilling extraordinary fear through the terror of their faces. Their appearance was frightening because of the blackness of their complexion; and, if it may be said, they had a kind of shapeless lump instead of a face, with something more like points than eyes; their grim appearance betrays the confidence of their spirits.

They also rage against their sons on the very first day of their birth. As soon as they are born, they cut their cheeks with iron, so that before they receive the nourishment of milk they are forced to endure the wound. Thus they grow old without beards and are unbeautiful youths, because the face furrowed by iron removes the timely grace of hair with its scars. They are indeed small in stature, but agile in their sharp movements and extremely ready for riding, with broad shoulders prepared for bows and arrows [Note: [Col. 0735] *parati*, “prepared,” 9c], firm necks, and always raised in pride [Note: [Col. 0735] *erecti*, “upright,” 9c].

Under the appearance of human beings, they live with bestial cruelty. When the Goths saw this exceptionally mobile race, which had overcome many nations, they were terrified and deliberated with their king about what they should do.

Although Ermenricus, king of the Goths, had been, as we related above, the conqueror of many peoples, he was troubled as he considered the arrival of the Huns. The faithless people of the Rasomoni, who at that time rendered him service among the other nations, deceived him on this occasion.

The king, enraged at her husband's treacherous desertion—a woman from that people named Suanihilda—ordered her to be bound to fiercer horses [Note: [Col. 0735] *ferocioribus*, “fiercer,” 5] and torn apart in various directions by their rushing course [Note: [Col. 0735] *ferocioribus*, “more savage,” 5]. Her brothers Sarus and Ammius, avenging the death of their sister, attacked Ermenricus’s side with a sword. Wounded by this blow, he contracted a sickly life through weakness.

When Valamber, king of the Huns, heard of his grievous condition, he moved his army against the Ostrogothic territory. The Visigoths had already been separated from their alliance with the Ostrogoths by a dispute among themselves.

Meanwhile, Ermenricus, unable to endure either the pain of his wound or the invasion of the Huns, already advanced in age and full of days, died in the 110th year of his life. His death gave the Huns the opportunity to prevail over those Goths whom we have said occupied the eastern region and were called Ostrogoths. Unable to resist the Huns, once the Visigoths had been separated from them by the death of their king Ermenricus, the Ostrogoths returned to their ancient homeland of Scythia, subject to the authority of the Huns.

Nevertheless, Winitharius the Amal, son of Ermenricus's cousin, retained the insignia of leadership.

(Jordanes, ch. 48.) He imitated the courage of his grandfather Witulphus, who was Ermenricus’s brother. Although inferior to Ermenricus in good fortune, he nevertheless bore with difficulty being subject to the power of the Huns. He withdrew from them for a little while and, attempting to display his own courage, marched with an army into the territory of the Antes. Attacking them [Note: [Col. 0737] *pro agg.*, 9c, for *agrediens*], he was defeated in the first engagement; but afterward acting bravely, he nailed their king, named Booz [Note: [Col. 0737] *boz*, 9c], to a cross together with his sons and seven hundred nobles, as an example intended to inspire terror, so that the corpses hanging there might redouble fear among those who had surrendered.

But although he ruled with such freedom for scarcely a year, Valamber, king of the Huns, did not permit it. He led an army against Winitharius. After a long struggle, Winitharius won the first and second battles, and no one can adequately recount the slaughter of the Huns that he inflicted. In the third battle, however, Winitharius was killed. Thus the king of the Huns possessed the entire Gothic people, subdued into peace, though in such a way that the Gothic nation always had its own petty kings, albeit with the counsel of the Huns.

After Winitharius’s death, Hunimundus, son of the once most powerful king Ermenricus, succeeded to the kingdom. When he died, his son Thurismundus reigned after him. Adorned with the vigor of youth, he led an army against the Gepids in the second year of his reign and won a great victory over them; but, it is said, he was killed by an accident.

The Ostrogoths mourned him so deeply that for forty years no one else succeeded him, so that his memory might remain among them for a long time. His son Herimundus, despising the kingdom of the Ostrogoths because of the domination of the Huns, went with his son Betericus to the western peoples. Under Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, of whom we shall speak shortly, he served with great glory while concealing his relationship to his lineage.

After a long interval, therefore, Walamir [Note: [Col. 0737] *walmir*, 5, 9c], son of Wandalaricus, who was the son of Winitharius, received the kingdom together with his brother Dietmarus and also Witimarus. In these three there was a pleasing spectacle:

[Col. 0738A] When the remarkable Dietmarus [Note: [Col. 0737] *f. et w.*, 9c, for *pro fratre Walamiro*] served his brother Walamir in ruling, Walamir in turn commanded for the advancement of the other, while Witimarus supported both and served, as it were, both. They protected one another with such mutual affection that none lacked a kingdom: both held what they possessed in peace. Nevertheless, they served the authority of the king of the Huns, who was now Attila.

(C. 35.) After [Note: [Col. 0737] omitted in 9c] Valamber [Note: [Col. 0737] *valaber*, 5] had died, the king of the Huns was Mauzuchus, Attila’s father. After him came his brothers Hoctar and Roas; after them [Note: [Col. 0737] omitted in 9c], Attila together with his brother Bleda, who ruled over a large part of the Huns. But Attila, after killing his brother Bleda, subjected the entire people to himself. He was a man born into the world to shake nations and terrify all lands, who, by I know not what fate, terrified everyone, as a dreadful reputation about him spread everywhere.

He was proud in his bearing, casting his eyes this way and that, so that the power of his arrogance appeared even in his bodily movement. He was a lover of wars, although he himself refrained from fighting with his own hand; he was extremely strong in counsel, merciful to petitioners, favorable to those whom he had once received into his trust, short in stature, broad-chested, large-headed, with small eyes, a beard sprinkled with sparse gray hairs, and a dark complexion displaying the marks of his origin.

Although his nature was such that he always trusted in great things [Note: [Col. 0737] *m. s.*, 5], the sword of Mars, discovered among the kings of the Scythians and always held by them, nevertheless added to his confidence. The historian Priscus recounts that it was discovered on the following occasion.

A certain shepherd saw one heifer of his herd limping and could find no cause of its pain, except that he saw it had been wounded. Anxiously following the trail of blood, he finally came upon a sword hidden in the grass, which the heedless cow had stepped on while grazing. He dug it out immediately and brought it to Attila.

Attila rejoiced greatly at the gift. In his magnanimity, he considered himself appointed ruler of the whole world, and believed that through the sword of Mars the power of war had been granted to him.

From that time, waging war against many nations, he subjected them to his rule. He also subdued the famous king of the Gepids, Hardericus.

The Ostrogoths, as has been said, had been possessed by the Huns from the beginning (Jordanes, ch. 48). They were not permitted to refuse battle against their kinsmen, the Visigoths, nor could that Scythian nation be separated from the rule of the Huns in any other way than by the death of Attila—an event desired by all nations in common and by the Romans as well. How this came about we shall relate below; for now let us return to the history of the Visigoths.

(C. 25.) [Note: [Col. 0737] rubric added: “On the Visigoths.”] When the Visigoths therefore, after the death of Ermenricus, withdrew from the Ostrogoths and saw that the latter were being oppressed and expelled by the Huns, they were greatly terrified and anxiously deliberated what they should do about themselves because of the Hunnic people [Note: [Col. 0737] *h. g.*, 5]. After long consideration, they finally agreed by common consent to send ambassadors to Valens, the brother of the elder Valentinian, who was then ruling at Constantinople, as has been written above [Note: [Col. 0739] “said,” 9c], asking him to give them a portion of Thrace or Moesia to cultivate. They promised that they would live according to his laws and commands.

To make him more confident in their good faith, they promised to become Christians if he would send them teachers of the faith who knew their language. When Valens learned this, he immediately assented with joy, because they had asked for what he himself had wished to offer [Note: [Col. 0739] omitted in 9c]. He received the Getae in the regions of Moesia and stationed them as a kind of wall of his kingdom against the other peoples.

Because at that time the emperor Valens was afflicted by the Arian error and hated all the priests of our party, he sent preachers who supported his own party. When they arrived, they immediately poured the poison of their error into the uneducated and uninstructed people.

Thus, through the emperor Valens, the Visigoths became Arians rather than Christians. Thereafter, out of affection for their kinsmen, both the Ostrogoths and the Gepids, they preached to them. Through their Arian bishop Ulphilas, who first devised Gothic letters and translated the divine Scriptures into their language (Jordanes, same passage), they invited the entire nation speaking that language everywhere to observe this sect.

They themselves, as has been said, crossed the Danube and settled in Dacia Ripensis, Moesia, and Thrace with the permission of the ruler.

(C. 26.) It happened to them, as commonly happens to a people not yet firmly established in a place, that they were pressed by the scarcity of famine [Note: [Col. 0739] *strigerentur*, 5]. Their leaders, who ruled them in place of kings—Fridigernus, Alatheus, and Saphrach—began to grieve over the army’s need and to request a commercial exchange from Lupicinus [Note: [Col. 0739] *lupicinio*, 4, 5] and Maximus, the Roman commanders.

Compelled by greed, the Romans began to provide them not only with the flesh of sheep and oxen but even with the carcasses of dogs and unclean animals, to such an extent that they would purchase a single slave for one loaf of bread or ten pounds of meat. When the slaves and all their household goods had been exhausted, the greedy merchant demanded their children.

But the parents, concerned for the safety of their pledges, decided that freedom should more easily be sacrificed than life: someone who was to be mercifully fed might be sold and thereby preserved rather than allowed to die. They handed over their children [Note: [Col. 0739] *qui*, 9c, for *quis*].

At that time it happened that Lupicinus, commander of the Romans, invited Fridigernus, the petty king of the Goths, to a banquet and, as the outcome later showed, plotted a deception. Fridigernus, unaware of the trick, came to the banquet with a few companions. While he was dining in the praetorium, he heard the cries of wretched people dying. In another part of the building, the soldiers of the commander Lupicinus, on his orders, were attempting to slaughter his companions, who had been shut inside.

When Fridigernus realized this, he drew his sword and, with great boldness, quickly left the banquet. Having rescued his companions from death, he incited them to kill the Romans. Seizing this welcome opportunity, they chose to die in battle rather than perish from hunger and immediately armed themselves for the death of the commanders Lupicinus and Maximus.

That day deprived the Romans of their security and the Goths of their hunger. The Goths began to command the inhabitants, no longer as foreigners but as citizens and masters, and to hold all the northern regions [Note: [Col. 0739] *septentrionalis*, 5] as far as the Danube under their own authority.

When Valens learned this at Antioch, he made war against them. He himself was wounded in the fighting and fled into a small hut. Since the Goths did not know that the emperor was hiding in so mean a dwelling, they set fire to it, and he was burned. This was plainly the just judgment of God: he was burned by the very people who, seeking the true faith, he had turned toward error, and he had twisted the fire of charity into the fire of Gehenna.

(Jordanes, chs. 27 and following.) After this great triumph, the Visigoths obtained Thrace and Dacia Ripensis and began to inhabit them as their ancestral soil, until Theodosius, son of the Spanish Theodosius, was chosen by the emperor Gratian and appointed to the eastern principate in place of his uncle Valens.

Sharp in intellect and distinguished in courage and counsel, he exercised military discipline and removed the cowardice and sluggishness of the earlier rulers. When the Goth perceived this, he was alarmed; and the Roman soldiers, gaining confidence under a better prince, attempted to attack the Goths and expelled them from the borders of Thrace.

After this, when Theodosius was sick almost to the point of despair, the Goths again grew bold. The army was divided: Fridigernus departed to plunder Thessaly and Achaia, while Alatheus and Saphrach made for Pannonia.

When Gratian heard this—he had then withdrawn from Rome to Gaul [Note: [Col. 0739] “Gaul,” singular, 5]—he immediately gathered an army and went against them. Yet he did not rely on arms; he intended to overcome them by favor and gifts. He made a treaty with them and granted them provisions.

When Theodosius recovered, he learned that the Romans and Goths had made a treaty. He accepted this gladly and himself concluded a treaty with Athalaric, who had succeeded Fridigernus in the kingdom, inviting him to Constantinople.

Athalaric readily agreed in every respect. As he entered the royal city and was received by Theodosius with complete joy and affection, he saw the magnificence of the buildings, the crowds of people adorned as though for a festival, the situation of the city, and the traffic of ships. Then, entering the emperor’s palace and seeing the attendants and various services, he was greatly amazed and said:

“Behold, I see what I often heard but did not believe. Without doubt the emperor is an earthly god; and if anyone raises his hand against him, he himself will be guilty of his own blood.”

Supported by the prince with still greater honor in this state of amazement, he departed this life after a few months. The prince, honoring him out of affection almost more in death than in life, himself preceded his bier at the funeral and committed him to a worthy burial.

When his entire army saw this, it remained in the service of Theodosius because of his great kindness. Submitting itself to Roman rule, it became, as it were, one body with the Roman soldiers. The military force that had formerly been restored under Constantine as the federates was revived, and they themselves were called federates.

From among them the emperor brought more than [number omitted in the printed text] thousand armed men [Note: [Col. 0741] *armatosis*, an uncertain reading, 5] against the usurper Eugenius, who had occupied Gaul after killing Gratian. Recognizing them as loyal and friendly to him, he gained the victory and exacted vengeance.

After Theodosius had departed this life, his sons began to reduce both states to nothing through luxurious living and to withhold the customary gifts from their auxiliaries, the Goths [Note: [Col. 0741] *auxiliariisque*, 5]. The Goths soon grew disgusted with them. Fearing that a long peace might dissolve their strength, they established Alaric as king over themselves.

After the Amals [Note: [Col. 0741] *Hamalos*, 9d], Alaric possessed the second rank of nobility, and his lineage came wonderfully from the Balthi, whose first member had long before received among his people the name Baltha—“the Bold”—from his daring courage.

Alaric therefore immediately deliberated with his people and persuaded them that they should seek a kingdom by their own labor [Note: [Col. 0741] *p. s.*, 5, for *suo potius*] rather than be subjected through hatred to another army. Thus he entered Italy through Pannonia. With no one resisting at all, he arrived at the Candidian Bridge, which was three miles from the royal city of Ravenna. Its former inhabitants, as the elders relate, were called Enethi, that is, “the praiseworthy.”

When the Visigothic army had reached the vicinity, Alaric sent an embassy to Honorius, the son of Theodosius, who was then there, asking him to give them a place [Note: [Col. 0741] omitted, 9c] where they could live with their army. Honorius granted him Gaul and Spain, which Geiseric, king of the Vandals, had by then almost entirely devastated.

As the Goths were making their way there, they remained for some time in a certain place. Then Stilicho, count and patrician and father-in-law of the emperor Honorius, suddenly attacked them on the very sacred day of Easter, when they suspected no harm, and killed many of them.

The Goths were at first thrown into confusion, but soon, recovering their strength, they seized their arms, killed many of Stilicho’s army, and put the rest to flight. Inflamed with great anger, they no longer wished to proceed into Gaul. Abandoning the journey they had begun in a rage, they returned to Liguria, which they had already crossed, and plundered it. They likewise devastated Emilia and Flaminia, then ranged through Tuscany as far as Rome, carrying off as booty whatever lay on either side.

When they came to Rome, they seized it, devastated it, and set it on fire. Alaric nevertheless ordered that anyone who fled to holy places should suffer no harm; and although the city was plundered, no one was to be killed.

Rome was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths, 1,144 years after it had been founded.

The Goths then left the City and proceeded through Campania, Lucania, and Bruttium. When they wished to cross into Sicily, many of them perished at sea.

As Alaric was deliberating what he should do, he died suddenly at Consentia. His people mourned him with extraordinary affection. They diverted the Busento River from its channel, buried their king Alaric in the middle of the river together with many riches, and returned the river to its channel. To prevent anyone from ever learning the place [Note: [Col. 0741] *i. l.*, 5], they killed all the captives who had diverted the river.

They then set up Athaulf [Col. 0742A] as king over themselves, Alaric’s kinsman. Returning to Rome, he scraped away whatever remained, like locusts. With no one resisting, he carried off Placidia, the sister of Honorius and daughter of the emperor Theodosius, and joined her to himself in marriage.

When she softened her husband’s heart with her entreaties so that he might make peace with the Romans, he set out for Gaul. The neighboring peoples were terrified, and the Vandals were driven from there into Spain. In the third year after he had subdued Gaul and Spain, he was killed through the treachery of his own people.

After him, Segeric received the kingdom; but he too was killed by his own men [Note: [Col. 0741] *o est*, 9c] and surrendered his life together with his kingdom.

Then Vallia, the fourth king after Alaric, was established. He was exceedingly prudent. Against him the emperor Honorius sent Constantius, a man distinguished for military skill, promising him that if he brought his sister Placidia back, whether by peace or by any other means, he would give her to him as his wife.

In accordance with this agreement, Constantius proceeded joyfully to Spain with a large force of armed men, and Vallia met him with no smaller an army. But, after envoys had been sent by both sides, they reached an agreement: Vallia would return the emperor’s sister and would not deny his assistance to the Roman state.

In the twelfth year of Vallia’s reign [Note: [Col. 0741] omitted, 5, 9c], when the Huns too had been expelled from Pannonia by the Romans and Goths after fifty years, Vallia saw that the Vandals were behaving recklessly within his borders. He led an army against them and expelled them into Africa. He would have pursued them there as well, had not the accident that had earlier overtaken Alaric when he was heading there recalled him.

After Vallia’s death, Theoderic received the kingdom. To him, as stated above, Herimundus, son of Thurismundus and grandson of Ermenricus, had come after despising the kingdom of the Ostrogoths because of the domination of the Huns.

(H. R. and H. m.) Meanwhile, while Marcian was reigning in the East and Valentinian in the West, Attila, king of all the Huns and sole ruler of nearly all the Scythian peoples, relying on the multitude of the strongest nations whom he had subjected to himself, had devastated Macedonia and Moesia, Achaea and both Dacias, Thrace and almost the whole of Illyricum. He then resolved to come and destroy the Western Empire, that is, the Roman Empire.

Under his authority was the very renowned king of the Gepids, Hardericus [Note: [Col. 0741] “r. g.” 5.], more distinguished than the one whom he served; and the king of the Ostrogoths, Walamir, with his brothers Dietmaro [Col. 0742D] and Witimaro [Note: [Col. 0741] “withmaro” 9c.]; as well as the very powerful peoples—the Marcomanni, Suevi, Quadi, Heruli, Turcilingi, Rugi, and other barbarian nations who dwelt in the northern regions. All these were his auxiliaries, and the number of his army was five hundred thousand.

Proud of his dominion over all these peoples, Attila desired above all to subject to himself the foremost nations of the world, namely the Romans and the Visigoths. Although he hoped that, through the strength of so many nations, he could do whatever he wished, he also sought to conquer by cunning. For he feared that the Goths who lived within Gaul might join the Romans [Col. 0743A] in offering assistance. Since he was exceedingly crafty and subtle, he sent messengers to Valentinian, declaring that he was in no way coming against the Romans as an enemy, nor did he wish in any respect to violate the friendship of the commonwealth, but that he had causes of conflict with Theoderic, king of the Visigoths (cf. JORD.).

Similarly, he sent to Theoderic, saying that he had no quarrel with the Goths but with the Romans, and that he was making every effort to remain at peace with the Goths. He did this deceitfully and through cunning, so that, if he separated the Romans and Goths from one another, he could afterward easily conquer both.

But the patrician Aetius, who was then in command of the army, understanding Attila’s cunning and deceit, sent envoys from the emperor Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0743] “Valentini” 5; corrected to “Valentiniani” 10.] to Theoderic, king of the Goths, who at that time was reigning at Toulouse [Note: [Col. 0743] omitted in 9c.], so that he might establish peace with him. Theoderic agreed to this and made peace with Aetius, promising that he would fight against Attila together with him.

The Burgundians, Franks, Alans, Saxons, Riparioli, Briones, Sarmatians, Armoricians, and Luticians [Note: [Col. 0743] “luciani” 9c.] came to the aid of the patrician Aetius. An innumerable multitude of Visigoths was also brought forth by King Theoderic. Leaving his four sons at home—namely Frideric, Euric [Note: [Col. 0743] “et e.” 9c.], Retemir, and Imneric—he took with him only the two elder ones, Thurismund and Theoderic.

Thus they came together on the Catalaunian Plains, also called the Mauriac Plains, extending for one hundred Gallic leagues [Note: [Col. 0743] “leugas” 4; 9c.], as the Gauls customarily measure them, in length and seventy in breadth. This makes one hundred and fifty miles in length [Col. 0743C] and one hundred and five miles in breadth. For one Gallic league [Note: [Col. 0743] “leuga” 9c.] is measured as one thousand five hundred paces.

(JORD.—H. R.—H. m.) When they had come to the place where they were now supposed to fight, Attila asked his diviners what they foresaw concerning that battle.

(JORD.) These men, as was their custom, sometimes examining the entrails of animals and sometimes certain veins in scraped bones, pronounced an unfavorable outcome for the Huns: namely, that Attila would not have the victory. Yet they foretold this small consolation: that the chief commander on the enemy’s side would fall in the battle.

(H. R.—H. m.) Attila, believing that this referred to the death of Aetius, whose death he thirsted for [Note: [Col. 0743] omitted in 9c.], did not hesitate to engage in battle even at the cost of his own men, provided that he could destroy Aetius, who was resisting his efforts with great strength.

He therefore joined battle around the ninth hour of the day, when the day was already declining toward evening, so that, if he were defeated, he might conceal himself from the enemy in the darkness of the approaching night. Thus the bravest nations gathered on both sides, the battle lines closed, and an exceedingly fierce and stubborn battle began, such as scarcely any history records [Note: [Col. 0743] “in ulla” 9c.]. They did not cease their ardor for fighting until the coming of night deprived them of the opportunity to continue.

In that battle, 170,000 men are said to have been killed [Col. 0744A] [Note: [Col. 0743] omitted in 9c.], and so much blood was shed that a little stream flowing there, suddenly swollen with the blood of the slain, carried away the bodies of the dead.

But Attila’s suspicion regarding the death of Aetius deceived him, for King Theoderic of the Visigoths fell, while Aetius escaped unharmed. Although neither army had yielded in this battle, it is nevertheless agreed that Attila was defeated. (JORD. ch. 40.)

Then the Visigoths [Note: [Col. 0743] “et w” 9c.], separating from the Alans, attacked the host of the Huns and would almost have slaughtered Attila, had he not prudently fled beforehand and immediately shut himself and his men inside the enclosure of the camp, which they had fortified with wagons. Thus, although the fortification was fragile, those for whom shortly before no rampart could withstand them sought there a means of preserving their lives [Note: [Col. 0743] omitted in 9c.].

On the following day, while remaining within the wagon-fortifications, Attila did not dare to come out; yet he did not cease making noise with trumpets and shouting, as though threatening an assault, in order to trouble the victors while he remained shut in. Thurismund, son of King Theoderic, grieving over his father’s death [Note: [Col. 0743] omitted in 9c.], decided to press Attila with a siege and destroy him and his men utterly.

(H. R.—H. m.) Then, despairing of his life, Attila built a great pyre from cavalry saddles, so that, if the Goths should press upon him, he could set fire to it, climb onto it, and burn himself, lest anyone rejoice over his wound or a king of so many nations fall into the power of his enemies.

Aetius, however, fearing that, once Attila had been killed, the Romans might afterward be crushed by the Goths with impunity, and that thereafter, should necessity arise, no assistance might be found against the Goths, persuaded Thurismund—as though taking thought for his interests [Note: [Col. 0743] “consulturus” 5.]—to return home as quickly as possible and take possession of his father’s kingdom. Otherwise, if he were attacked by his brothers, he would be completely dispossessed, and it would afterward be more grievous for him to contend with his own people than to fight with foreigners.

Thurismund gladly accepted this advice, as though it had been offered for his own safety. He returned home and received his father’s kingdom. But Aetius contrived all this in order to remove Attila from the pressure exerted by Thurismund, with the intention stated above—alas, unaware of how great a loss he inflicted upon his country by this precaution, while trying to avert one danger.

For when Attila saw that the enemy had left him and returned to their own lands, his courage revived. He went back to Pannonia, gathering an army much stronger than before [Col. 0744D]. In fury he entered Italy again and first began to attack Aquileia, situated at the very entrance to Italy [Note: [Col. 0743] “a pr.” 9c.].

After besieging it continuously for three years, he made no progress against it, since the citizens were bravely resisting. When he heard the murmuring of his army, which could not endure the scarcity of food and wished to depart, he went around the city one day, seeking to discover from which side he might more easily capture it. Suddenly he saw birds accustomed to build nests on the gables of buildings—these are called storks [Col. 0745A]—flying out of the city in a single movement and carrying their young outside, lifted in their beaks.

Being exceedingly shrewd, he said to his men: “Look! Birds who know the future are abandoning the city that is about to perish and leaving the towers that will fall when danger approaches.”

Immediately he brought up siege engines, encouraged his men, attacked the city fiercely, and captured it without delay. Its wealth was plundered, its citizens were taken captive or slaughtered, and whatever remained after the plundering was consumed by fire.

Afterward that savage enemy burned and destroyed many forts in the same region, killing or capturing their inhabitants. He did the same to Concordia, Altinum, or Patavium, cities neighboring Aquileia. From there the Huns raged through the various cities of Venetia—Verona, Vicentia, Brixia, Bergamum, and the rest. They also plundered Mediolanum [Col. 0745B] and Ticinum in the same manner, yet refrained from fire and the sword. Then, after similarly stripping the cities of Aemilia, they finally pitched their camp at the place where the river Mincius flows into the Po.

There Attila halted and wavered in his mind over whether to go to Rome or desist—not out of concern for the City, against which he was hostile, but because he feared the example of Alaric, who did not long survive the capture of the City. Suddenly the most holy man, Pope Leo, went to him in person. When he had entered the presence of the barbarian king, he obtained everything he desired and carried back safety not only for Rome but for all Italy.

For Attila had been terrified by a divine sign and was unable to say anything to the priest of Christ except what the priest himself desired. It is therefore reported that, after the pontiff’s departure, Attila was asked by his men why he had shown such extraordinary reverence to the Roman pontiff. He replied that he had not revered the person who had come, but had seen standing beside him another man in priestly dress, of more august appearance and more venerable with his white hair, who, with a drawn sword, threatened him with death if he did not fulfill everything the pontiff requested.

Thus Attila, restrained in this way from his savagery, abandoned Italy and returned to Pannonia. Honoria, sister of the prince Valentinian, who was being strictly guarded by her brother for the sake of her chastity, sent her eunuch to him to ask her brother to give her to Attila in marriage.

When he received the message, and had already crossed beyond the borders of Italy and could not immediately turn back with his exhausted army, Attila sent word to the emperor Valentinian that he would soon inflict worse things upon Italy if he did not at once send him his sister together with a portion of the royal wealth.

After returning to his own territories, he took a very beautiful young woman as wife in addition to the many wives he already possessed. Because of this marriage he held lavish banquets. While he was drinking as much wine at once as he had never before drunk [Note: [Col. 0745] “n. a. b.”], he lay sleeping on his back and was suffocated by an excessive flow of blood, which was accustomed to run from his nostrils.

That same night at Constantinople, the emperor Marcian was shown in a dream that Attila’s bow had broken—the weapon, of course, most characteristic of that people. (JORD. ch. 49.)

On the following day, when a large part of the day had passed, the king’s servants broke down the doors amid great shouting. They found Attila dead without any wound, killed by the discharge of blood, and the young woman sitting with downcast face and weeping beneath her veil.

Then, as was customary among that people, they cut off part of their hair and disfigured their faces with wounds, so that this outstanding warrior might be mourned not with women’s lamentations but with a manly procession. His funeral rites were honored by his people with many displays of grief.

In the middle of the fields, after his body had been placed inside a silk tent, chosen horsemen from the whole nation of the Huns rode around it in races and celebrated a funeral song. Then, over his burial mound, they celebrated what they call a *straba*, holding a great feast; joining together opposite things, they expressed funeral mourning mingled with joy. In the secrecy of night they committed the body to the earth.

They enclosed the coffin first with gold, second with silver, and third with the hardness of iron, signifying by this arrangement that everything was appropriate to so powerful a king: iron because he had subdued nations, gold and silver because he had received the ornaments of both commonwealths. They also added weapons acquired by the slaughter of enemies, trappings precious with varied brilliance of gems, and insignia of diverse kinds with which the splendor of the royal court is honored.

And so that human curiosity might be kept away from such great riches, they slaughtered those assigned to this task with a detestable reward.

Afterward a dispute over the kingdom arose among Attila’s successors. Because they desired to rule without judgment, they all lost the empire at once. For his sons, whose unlawful lust had almost made the whole people their offspring, demanded that the nations be divided among them by lot, so that warlike kings might be assigned to the peoples as though to households.

When Hardericus, king of the Gepids, learned this, he was indignant and was the first to rise against Attila’s sons. The fortunate outcome wiped away the shame of servitude that had been imposed upon him, and by his withdrawal he liberated not only his own people but also the other nations that were being oppressed in the same way, because all readily desire what is attempted for the benefit of everyone.

Thus they armed themselves and joined battle in Pannonia beside the river called the Neoda. There a clash occurred among the various peoples whom Attila had held under his authority [Note: [Col. 0745] “illuc” 9c.]. After many conflicts, an unexpected victory favored the Gepids [Note: [Col. 0745] omitted in 9c.]. For Hardericus killed nearly thirty thousand, both Huns and members of other peoples who had brought assistance to the Huns [Col. 0746D], and he killed Attila’s eldest son, named Hella. His father is said to have loved him so greatly that he wished to place him above all his other children in the kingdom.

After Hella was killed, his remaining brothers, together with the Huns, were driven toward the shore of the Pontic Sea, where the Goths are recorded to have dwelt previously. The success of Hardericus brought good fortune to the various nations that had unwillingly served under the rule of the Huns, and it lifted their long-dejected spirits toward the joy of their desired freedom [Col. 0747A].

Many of them therefore came to the emperor Marcian and were received by him with the greatest favor. They were assigned settlements in which to dwell. The Gepids, courageously claiming for themselves the settlements of the Huns, took possession as victors of the whole territory of Dacia, asking nothing else from the Roman Empire but peace.

The Sarmatians and Cemandri, together with certain people from the Hunnic side, settled at the city of Materna in Illyricum. The Scyri and Adagarii [Note: [Col. 0747] “adagatarii” 9c.] received Lesser Scythia and Lower Moesia. The Rugi and several other nations [Note: [Col. 0747] “atque aliae” 5.] took possession of Bizim and Arcadiopolis. Hernach, too, the younger son of Attila, chose for himself and his people a settlement at the extremity of Lesser Scythia. His kinsmen Hemmezur and Bulzindur [Note: [Col. 0747] “birzindur” 9c.] took possession of Hedisco and Halmo in Riparian Dacia. Different peoples sought different places.

The Goths, however, seeing that the Gepids were claiming the Huns’ settlements for themselves and that the people of the Huns were occupying their ancient settlements, preferred to ask the Roman kingdom for land rather than invade another people’s territory at the risk of conflict. They received Pannonia and dwelt there under King Walamir and his brother Dietmar [Note: [Col. 0747] “ediethmaro fratre” m. 9c.], separated in territory but united in counsel.

Walamir lived between Scarniunga [Note: [Col. 0747] “scaniungam” 9c.] and the Black Water; Dietmar lived near the place [Note: [Col. 0747] The manuscripts read this way in place of “lacum,” “lake.”] of Pellois; Witimar remained with both of them.

It happened that Attila’s sons came against the Goths as though against deserters from their rule. Without the knowledge of their other brothers, they attacked Walamir alone. Although he had only a few men, he received them and, after wearing them down for a long time, defeated them so thoroughly that scarcely any part of them remained.

At that time, when he had sent a messenger to his brothers Dietmar and Witimar concerning this achievement, the messenger arrived at Dietmar’s house and found there even greater joy. For on that very day Theoderic, his son, a little boy of good promise though born of a concubine, had been born.

After not much time had passed [Note: [Col. 0747] “longum” 9c.], King Walamir and his brothers Dietmar and Witimar, although they continued to observe the treaties of peace, delayed receiving the customary gifts from the emperor Marcian. Envoys sent by them to the emperor saw Theoderic, son of Triarius, who was indeed of Gothic birth but descended from a different family than the Amals, flourishing altogether with his people and enjoying the friendship of the Romans, while they themselves were completely disregarded.

They reported this at home, and immediately the Goths, stirred by rage, took up arms and devastated almost the whole of Illyricum by plundering. But when the emperor Marcian died and Leo received the kingdom, Leo soon returned to the former friendship with the Goths, granted both the gifts that had been withheld and those currently due, and received Theoderic, the young son of Dietmar, as a hostage.

When Dietmar delayed handing him over, his uncle Walamir made the promise, so that peace might thereafter remain more secure between the Romans and the Goths. Thus Theoderic was taken as a hostage to the city of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0747] “ad u.” omitted in 9c.], and because he was an attractive child, he won the emperor’s favor.

After firm peace had been made between the Romans and Goths, the Goths saw that what they had received from the emperor was not sufficient. At the same time, wishing to display their customary courage, they began to plunder neighboring peoples [Note: [Col. 0747] “depredare” 9c.]. First they took up arms against the Satagi, who possessed inner Pannonia.

When the Hunnic king Dinzich, son of Attila [Note: [Col. 0747] “attalae” 5.], learned of this, he gathered whatever men he still had, although they were few, and began to plunder Pannonia. When the Goths learned of this, they abandoned the expedition that they had undertaken against the Satagi and turned against the Huns. They drove them dishonorably from their territory so completely that from that time onward the Huns who remained feared Gothic arms.

When at last the Hunnic people had been quieted by the Goths, Chunimund, king of the Suevi [Note: [Col. 0747] “suevorum” in 4, 9c, 10, and 11 throughout.], invaded the territory of Dietmar, brother of Walamir, king of the Goths. He plundered it and, carrying off all the herds, returned to his own land.

Dietmar grieved not so much over the loss of the herds as he feared that, if the Suevi gained this advantage with impunity, they would go on to greater license. He therefore kept watch over their crossing so carefully that, in the silence of the dead of night, he attacked them while they were sleeping beside Lake Pellois. An unexpected battle was joined, and he defeated them so completely that he even captured King Chunimund and subjected him, together with his defeated army, to Gothic servitude.

But since he was very merciful, after taking vengeance he granted them pardon. Reconciled with the Suevi, he adopted as his son the man whom he had captured and sent him back with his people to Suavia.

That man, however, forgetful of his father’s kindness [Note: [Col. 0747] “g. i.” 5.], after some time devised a plot and incited the Scyri, who were then settled along the Danube, to gather together and attack the Gothic people.

Then, while the Goths suspected no evil from their neighboring friends, war suddenly arose against them. Forced by this unforeseen necessity, they fled to arms, engaged in battle, and avenged both themselves and the wrong done to them.

In that battle, King Walamir of the Goths was mounting his horse to encourage his men and was riding ahead of the battle line when his frightened horse fell and threw its rider. He was immediately wounded by the spears of the enemy and killed [Col. 0748D].

The Goths, avenging both the death of their king and the wrong done to their people, destroyed them all so thoroughly that scarcely anyone of the Scyri remained except those who bore that name with disgrace.

Again Chunimund, together with the Suevi, relying on the aid of the Sarmatians and the remnants of the Scyri, and having also gathered substantial support from the Gepids and Rugi, brought war against the Goths.

After Walamir’s death, the Goths turned to his brother Dietmar and made him king. (JORD. chs. 54 ff.) Although he had long reigned together with his brother, he now assumed the insignia of greater authority [Note: [Col. 0749] “amplioris” 9c.]. Compelled to take part in the war, he sprang to arms with his brother Witimar. When battle was joined, the Gothic side prevailed, so that the field of the fallen enemy was drenched with blood and appeared like a red sea; weapons and corpses, piled up like hills, filled the field—more than ten thousand of them.

From there Dietmar returned victorious with the Goths to his own settlements. He gratefully received his son Theoderic, whom he had given as a hostage and whom the emperor Leo had sent back with great gifts.

When Theoderic was already eighteen years old, he chose for himself from his father’s retainers and people nearly six thousand men. Without his father’s knowledge, he crossed the Danube, attacked the king of the Sarmatians, killed him, plundered his household and wealth, and returned victorious to his father.

Afterward he attacked the city of Singidunum, which the same Sarmatians possessed, and subjected it not to the Romans but to his own authority.

When the plunder of the neighboring peoples began to fail, food and clothing also began to run short among the Goths. Peace became burdensome to men who had previously lived by war. They all therefore approached Dietmar with a great outcry and begged him to lead the army wherever he wished, because they could no longer remain there any longer [Note: [Col. 0749] “possent” 5.].

He summoned his brother, cast lots, and the lot assigned Italy to Witimar and Illyricum to Dietmar [Col. 0749C]. Thus they abandoned Pannonia: one took Italy and the other Illyricum. But as soon as Witimar entered Italy, he died, leaving the kingdom to his son, who bore the same name as himself.

Licerius, who happened to be emperor at that time, transferred him to Gaul by means of gifts, so that he might reign through the Visigoths, his relatives. After receiving gifts from Licerius, Witimar set out for Gaul, joined himself to his Visigothic relatives, became one body with them, and, holding Gaul and Spain, defended them by his own right so that no one else could prevail against him. (C. 43–47.)

After Theoderic, who fell in the war fought by the Romans and Visigoths against Attila, king of the Huns, his son Thurismund ruled the Visigoths. When he died, his brother Theoderic succeeded to the kingdom. In the thirteenth year of his reign he too died, and their brother Euric then assumed the kingdom. In the nineteenth year he was deprived of both life and kingdom, leaving as successor to the kingdom his son, named Alaric. This Alaric was the ninth king of the Visigoths descended from that great Alaric.

(C. 58.) Dietmar, crossing the river Saus, threatened war against the Sarmatians if anyone opposed him. When they remained quiet and were unable to resist such a great multitude, he crossed into Illyricum. Proceeding successfully everywhere and subjecting many cities to himself, he advanced toward Thessalonica, where Helarianus, a patrician sent by the emperor, was staying with an army.

When Helarianus saw that Thessalonica was being fortified and that he could not resist their efforts, he sent an embassy to King Dietmar with gifts and asked him to turn away from destroying the city. A treaty was then made between the Roman commander and the Goths, and Helarianus voluntarily handed over to them the places they had already inhabited. There the Goths, laying down their arms, remained at peace with their king.

Not long afterward King Dietmar was seized by illness. He summoned the Goths, made his son Theoderic heir to the kingdom, and soon afterward died [Note: [Col. 0749] omitted in 9c.].

(H. R. and H. m.; cf. JORD.) At that time the emperor Zeno held the Eastern Empire. When he heard that Theoderic was king of his people, he received the news with favor [Note: [Col. 0749] “gratulans” 9c.] and ordered him to come to Constantinople. He received him honorably and placed him among the nobles of the palace. After some time, adopting him as his son, he raised him to the consular fasces—the first dignity after the imperial rank—and not only this: he also set up before his palace an equestrian statue of him, in honor of so great a man.

But while Theoderic was enjoying such delights at Constantinople, his people—that is, the Ostrogoths—were suffering severe want. Because the binding force of their treaty prevented them from carrying out their customary plundering, and the stipends offered by the emperor were nevertheless insufficient for them, they were compelled by no small poverty to condemn the treaty they had made and denounce the agreement as useless.

They immediately sent to Theoderic men who would tell him what hardships of want they themselves were enduring while he feasted extravagantly at Greek banquets. They urged him, if he wished to take thought for his people and for himself, to return quickly, so that he might provide for the whole nation before it perished and was forced to seek new lands in which to live.

Not many years earlier, a certain Odoacar [Note: [Col. 0749] “odoaccar” in 4, 5, 9c, and 10 throughout; but 1 later writes “odoacar”], departing from the farthest regions of Pannonia with a very powerful multitude of Heruli, and relying additionally on the aid of the Turcilingi or Scyri, had come to Italy. Since no one resisted him, he occupied all Italy and Rome and ruled there for fourteen years.

When Theoderic learned of the complaints of his people, he approached the emperor Zeno, explained the poverty of his people and complained of their condition, demanded his release, and requested that Italy be given to him. He added that, if he could defeat Odoacar and obtain Italy, this would redound to the glory of the one by whom he had been sent; but if he were defeated in war, the emperor’s gains would nevertheless increase, since he would be rid of the collectors of the daily stipends.

When Zeno heard these things, although he was reluctant to endure Theoderic’s departure, he nevertheless reached a considered decision, looking to the advantage of the commonwealth. He granted Theoderic’s requests, gave Italy to him, entrusted the senate and Roman people to his authority, and allowed him to depart enriched with great gifts.

Theoderic therefore left Constantinople and returned to the Ostrogoths. He immediately urged them to prepare as quickly as possible and to set out as though they were going to take possession of Italy.

When they all joyfully obeyed, he departed with the entire multitude of the Ostrogoths and all their belongings. Before reaching Italy, he defeated in battle and killed Trapestila, king of the Gepids, who was plotting an ambush against him. He also overthrew Busan, king of the Bulgars, together with his forces.

Then he came to Italy and first pitched his camp near the river Sonuum [reading uncertain], which flows not far from Aquileia. While he remained there to restore the strength of the men and animals exhausted by the length of the journey, Odoacar confronted him with a great army and all the forces of Italy.

Theoderic met him eagerly, defeated him in a great battle, and put him to flight. Moving his army from there, he reached Verona. Odoacar again opposed him with no less preparation for war.

Theoderic engaged him not far from Verona and crushed his army with a very great disaster. As Odoacar’s men, seized with fear of flight, threw themselves headlong into the river Adige, many of them became entangled in its swift currents and were drowned.

Theoderic, pursuing the fugitives in the same charge, immediately attacked Verona, while its citizens were panic-stricken [Note: [Col. 0751] “c. p.” 5.]. Odoacar, fleeing with those who had escaped, made for Rome, but when the gates were immediately closed, he was shut out.

Seeing that entrance was being denied him, he consumed by sword and fire everything he could reach, then entered Ravenna and prepared a fortified position there.

Theoderic, departing from Verona, reached Milan. While he remained there, a great multitude of soldiers and many peoples of Italy gathered to him [Col. 0751C]. But after a few days, the army that had surrendered to him again went over to Odoacar’s side, instigated by a certain man named Tustra.

This event so terrified Theoderic that he fortified himself and his army at the city of Ticinum, now called Pavia. Seeing these changes of fortune, Gundebaud, king of the Burgundians, entered Liguria with a huge army. He plundered everything he could find according to the will of the plunderers and led an immeasurable multitude of captives with him to Gaul.

Theoderic therefore kept his army for some time inside the fortifications [Note: [Col. 0751] “tenens” 9c.]. Finally, leaving there his sisters, his mother, and the entire multitude of the common people [Note: [Col. 0751] “ibi. r.” 5.], and placing complete confidence in the faith of Epiphanius, a most holy man and bishop of that city, he set out with lightly equipped bands of armed men to besiege Odoacar at Ravenna.

When he had pitched his camp at a place called Pineta, not far from the city, he besieged Odoacar for almost three continuous years. Odoacar frequently went out of the city at night with his men and harassed Theoderic’s army. Finally, making a nighttime assault on the camp, he struck down Theoderic’s army with great slaughter (H. R.).

But when the Goths resisted bravely, Odoacar was at last defeated and fled back into the city. Not long afterward he sent an embassy, begging pardon, and was received by Theoderic as though under a pledge of good faith [Col. 0752A]. But afterward Theoderic killed him cruelly.

After three years the Goths departed from Ticinum. The Rugi immediately attacked the same city, devastating for two continuous years all the surrounding regions as well as the city itself. At that time the most blessed Epiphanius was still alive, and through his holiness the afflicted citizens were sustained amid such dangers.

Theoderic sent him to Gaul, to Gundebaud, to redeem the captives. In addition to the innumerable multitude for whom he paid a ransom, Epiphanius brought back with him six thousand captives, granted to him solely out of reverence for his sanctity.

Thus Theoderic, after Odoacar had been killed at Ravenna, gained possession of the whole of Italy. Not long afterward he set out for Rome and was received by the Romans with great joy.

To each of them he granted one hundred twenty-six thousand *modii* of wheat as assistance for food [Col. 0752B]. (JORD.) After this, in order to strengthen the power of his kingdom, Theoderic sent an embassy to Clovis, king of the Franks, and requested his daughter Audofleda in marriage. Clovis willingly granted her.

He gave his sister Amalfrida in marriage to Huneric, king of the Vandals and son of Geiseric. He gave the daughter of that same Amalfrida, Amalberga, to Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians. His own daughters, whom he had fathered in Moesia, he joined in marriage to neighboring kings: one, Thiudegotha, to Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, and the other, Ostrogotha, to Alaric, king of the Visigoths. Amalric was born from this Alaric.

While her grandfather Theoderic was raising Amalric, who had been deprived of both parents in childhood, he learned that Eutharic, son of Beteric [Col. 0752C], grandson of Herimund and great-grandson of Thurismund, descended from the stock of the Amals. Eutharic was in Spain, in the vigor of youth, distinguished for prudence, strength, and bodily integrity. Theoderic ordered him to come to him and gave him his daughter Amalsuinda in marriage. She bore Athalaric to him.

There was no neighboring people of Italy that had not been joined to Theoderic either by the affinity of marriage or by the bond of a treaty. After the emperor Zeno died in the seventeenth year of his reign, Anastasius succeeded him in the empire and reigned for twenty-seven years. Theoderic, meanwhile, reigned peacefully in Italy for the same length of time. At Rome he constructed remarkable buildings, and in each of the more celebrated places he built royal residences for himself.

When Anastasius died—he too a heretic—Justinus obtained the empire. Since he was orthodox, and saw that in the eastern regions the Arian heresy still prevailed everywhere, he strove with the zeal of the Catholic faith to destroy the heretics. In the sixth year of his reign he ordered Catholic bishops everywhere to consecrate the churches of the heretics.

When Theoderic heard this—polluted as he was by the Arian taint—he sent Pope John, together with Theodorus and Agapitus, men of consular rank, and another Agapitus, a patrician, to Constantinople to the emperor Justinus. He sent a threatening message, declaring that unless the emperor promptly returned their churches to the heretics and allowed them to live in peace, Theoderic himself would destroy all the people of Italy by the sword.

When they arrived before the emperor and were received by him with the honor that was appropriate, they earnestly and tearfully begged him to listen favorably to the substance of their embassy, although it was unjust, and to take thought for Italy, which was destined to perish.

Moved by their tears, Justinus granted them what they requested and left the Arians under his authority. While these envoys were delayed on their journey, Theoderic, driven on by the madness of his wickedness, slaughtered with the sword the patrician Symmachus and the senator and former consul Boethius.

In those same days, after Alaric, king of the Visigoths, had been killed by the Franks, Theoderic, through his count Hibba, slaughtered more than 30,000 Franks. After Alaric’s death [Note: *generis* (“of the family”) 5.], he appointed Thiodem, Alaric’s arms-bearer, guardian of his grandson Amalric. [Col. 0753B]

Pope John, returning from Constantinople, came with his traveling companions to Theoderic at Ravenna. But Theoderic, through the wickedness of his impiety and cruelty, because they had been honorably received by Justin, the defender of the Catholic faith, handed them over to prison and killed them by the affliction of hunger. Divine retribution soon followed this most savage cruelty: on the ninety-ninth day after this crime, he died a sudden death. As Saint Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*, a solitary man of great virtue near the island of Lipara saw his soul being led, stripped of belt and shoes, between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, and plunged into Vulcan’s cauldron. [Col. 0753C]

**(JORD.)** Before this, while he was still strong but already advanced in age, he summoned the Goths and the nobles of his people, made Athalaric, the son of Amalsuintha, who was scarcely ten years old, king, and urged his people to honor the king, love the senate and Roman people, and always seek to keep the ruler of the East appeased and favorable. **(H. R. and JORD.)**

After Theoderic’s death, the Goths, as he had ordered, placed Athalaric and his mother over the kingdom, observing the command that had been given. Athalaric and his mother reigned for almost eight years. After the emperor Justin had died in the eighth year of his reign, Justinian, his sister’s son, succeeded him in the empire. Athalaric commended both his own youth and his mother’s widowhood to him, but shortly afterward he departed from human affairs.

When the Goths despised the weakness of the female sex, she herself, after deliberation, summoned her cousin Theodahad from Tuscany—where he lived as a private man in his own household—and, on account of their kinship, placed him on the throne. After some time, however, forgetful of their relationship and of the favor she had shown him, he had her dragged from the palace and banished to an island in Lake Bolsena. There, after spending very few days in sorrow, she was strangled in a bath by his attendants. When the emperor heard this, he was inflamed with great anger against Theodahad. **(H. R.)**

Theodahad, perceiving this, sent the blessed Pope Agapitus to Constantinople so that through him he might obtain the emperor’s favor. When the pontiff came to the emperor, he began to converse with him [Note: *c. h.* (“conversation with him”) 5.] [Note: *cis* (“with him”) 9c.] about the faith, and discovered that he held the teaching of Eutyches. When the pontiff rebuked him for his error, the emperor attacked him with threats. But the pope stood immovable in the Catholic faith and said to the emperor:

“I desired to come to the most Christian emperor Justinian, but, as I see, I have found Diocletian.”

When the emperor saw his steadfastness, he yielded, by God’s will, to his admonitions. Not long afterward, however, the same pontiff died there.

Justinian sent the patrician Belisarius, already triumphant over the Vandals in Africa, against Theodahad [Note: *deodatum* (“Theodahad”) 5.], so that he might also free Italy from the service of the Goths. **(JORD.)**

When Belisarius came to Sicily, all the Goths who were there, together with their leader Sinderith, voluntarily surrendered themselves to Belisarius. Theodahad sent his son-in-law Evermund with an army to guard the strait where the exit from Sicily lies. But when Evermund heard what had happened in Sicily, he voluntarily cast himself at the feet of the arriving Belisarius [Note: *venientis* (“of the arriving man”) 9c.], wishing to serve the Roman rulers.

When the Gothic army learned this, it loudly demanded that the suspected Theodahad be driven from the kingdom, and raised Witigis, who had been his arms-bearer, to rebel and assume the kingship. Once raised to the throne, Witigis entered Rome and, after sending trusted men ahead to Ravenna, ordered Theodahad to be killed. A few days later he himself came to Ravenna and forcibly took Mathesuinda, the daughter of Amalsuintha, as his wife.

[Col. 0754C] **(H. R.)** Belisarius, however, turned the military forces he had assembled against Theodahad against Witigis. Departing from Sicily, he came to Rome. The Goths who lived there went out of Rome by night, leaving the gates open, and fled to Ravenna.

When Witigis learned of this, he came to Rome with a large army. But Belisarius, seeing that the time was not suitable for fighting because a great famine had afflicted the world that year, shut himself inside Rome and stationed guards to watch it on every side. The Goths, devastating everything outside, besieged Rome for an entire year; then, struck by fear, they fled to Ravenna.

Again Witigis gathered an army and came to fight Belisarius. When battle was joined, many on Witigis’s side were killed. John, master of the army, pursued Witigis as he fled, captured him alive, and brought him to Rome to Belisarius. Belisarius took him with him to Constantinople. When Justinian saw him, he rejoiced, and not long afterward made him a patrician. Witigis remained there for more than two years and then died.

**(JORD.)** The emperor gave his wife Mathesuinda to his brother, the patrician Germanus. A son named Germanus was born to them, in whom the line of the Anicii and the Amali was joined, and in whom the hope of both families and peoples was placed.

**(H. R.)** After Witigis had been captured, the Goths beyond the Po made Heldebad their king; he was killed that same year. Erarius succeeded him, and before the year was complete he too was slaughtered. Then they placed Baduilla, also called Totila [Note: “missing” 5.], over themselves. Soon, having gathered an army from every direction, they invaded all Italy.

**(H. m.)** From there, as they passed through Campania, Totila came to the monastery of the blessed Father Benedict, who at that time shone with great miracles on Mount Cassino. From him he heard these words:

“You do many evil things; you have done many evil things. Now cease from your wickedness. Indeed, you will cross the sea, enter Rome, reign for nine years, and die in the tenth.”

Departing from there through Lucania, Totila invaded Sicily. Returning from there, he made for Rome and enclosed it in a siege. Since the Romans were suffering from hunger and were no longer able to defend the walls, Totila entered through the Ostian Gate.

Wishing to spare the Romans, he ordered trumpets to sound throughout the entire night, so that they might either protect themselves from the swords of the Goths in the churches or hide themselves by whatever means they could. He lived with the Romans for some time, like a father with his children. But, as may reasonably be inferred, this kindness of spirit was granted to a man previously marked by excessive cruelty through the admonition of the blessed Benedict.

Some senators who had escaped from the city hurried in distress to Constantinople and reported to the emperor the calamities to which Rome had been subjected (cf. P. D. II, 4). He immediately made the eunuch Narses, his chamberlain, exarch of Italy, and sent him to Rome with a strong force so that he might quickly aid afflicted Rome.

When Narses came to Italy, he sent envoys to Alboin, king of the Lombards, who at that time lived in Pannonia and were friendly to the Romans. He instructed Alboin to provide assistance when he fought against the Goths. Alboin then sent a large and select force from among his people. They were transported across the Adriatic Gulf and, joining the Romans, entered into a great struggle with the Goths.

When the Goths had been almost completely destroyed, Narses killed their king Totila, who had already ruled over them for [Note: “missing” 5.] ten years. He sent his bloodstained garments [Note: *cruenta* (“bloody”) 9c.] and crown, adorned with precious stones, to the imperial city; these were cast at the emperor’s feet in the presence of the senate.

Afterward, taking possession of their two fortified cities, Verona and Brixia, he restored all Italy, together with the city of Rome, to the jurisdiction of the republic. He sent the Lombards, honored and laden with great gifts, back to their own country. For the entire period during which they possessed Pannonia, they had been helpers of the Romans against their enemies.

Thus the famous kingdom and the strongest people of the Goths, who had ruled for a long time, were finally conquered after [Note: “missing” 5.] one thousand forty years [Note: “XL years—and earlier he wrote twice” 4.] by the emperor Justinian, victorious over diverse peoples—first through Belisarius and afterward through Narses—and all Italy, freed from their servitude, was restored to its former liberty. [Note: [Col. 0755] In 5, the words from *per Narsetem* (“through Narses”) to *historiae Gothicae finem* (“the end of the Gothic history”) are missing, leaving almost an entire page blank. 6–9 likewise omit nearly the same material, ending with these words: *post per Narsetem vicit* (“afterward he conquered through Narses”) (N.: “he subjected them to his rule,” 6; N.: “the eunuch, his chamberlain, destroyed them,” 7).]

[Col. 0756A] A certain grammarian named Jordanes, descended from the same Gothic stock, wrote about the origin of the Getae and the nobility of the Amali. He did not, as he himself says [Note: *dixit* (“he said”) 4.], include everything that is written and reported about them [Note: *amulorum nobilitatem* (“the nobility of the Amuli”) 4, 10.], but I have inserted this account more briefly into this little work, for the sake of knowledge of the events.

After these matters have been read and carefully examined, let anyone who knows how to distinguish consider how the following claim can be held to be valid—a claim that is used not only in popular storytelling and the singing of songs, but is also recorded in certain chronicles (see Chr. W. above, col. 475): namely, that Ermenric ruled over all the Goths during the reign of the emperor Marcian; and that, at the instigation of Odoacer—also, as they say, his cousin—he drove Theoderic, the son of Dietmar [Note: *diethmari* (“of Dietmar”) 4, frequently.], his own cousin, from Verona and compelled him to live in exile with Attila, king of the Huns.

The historiographer, however, says that Ermenric, king of the Goths, ruling over many kings, reigned during the time of the brothers Valentinian and Valens; that he was wounded by two brothers, Saro and Ammio, whom we conjecture to have been those commonly called Sarelo and Hamidiech [Note: *hamidiech* 4, 10.]; and that, at the beginning of the Huns’ departure through the Maeotian marshes, whose king was Valamber, he died from both the pain of his wound and the incursion of the Huns.

He says that afterward, more than seventy years later, under Marcian and Valentinian, Attila fought with the Romans, the Visigoths, and Aetius, the Roman commander, and departed from kingdom and life under those same emperors.

Thereafter, when Walamir was ruling the Goths, Theoderic, the son of his brother Dietmar, was given to the emperor Leo, already seven years old, as a hostage for the sake of faithfulness. Later, Leo returned him to his father, who was then ruling the Goths. After his father’s death, Theoderic succeeded him in the kingdom. Soon afterward, however, he was summoned to Constantinople by the emperor Zeno and treated as a friend; he received the kingdom of Italy, which Odoacer then possessed, against Zeno’s will, together with the Toringi, Rugians, and other nations. After many battles, Theoderic killed Odoacer, who had surrendered.

From this, the careful examiner of events should consider how Ermenric [Note: *e.* and another *t.* 4.] could have compelled Theoderic, the son of Dietmar, to live in exile with Attila, since, according to this historiographer, he was not his contemporary. Therefore, either this author wrote falsehoods, or popular opinion is mistaken and misleading, or another Ermenric and another Theoderic must be understood as contemporaries of Attila, in whom such an agreement of events could be accepted.

For this Ermenric is read to have died long before Attila, whereas Theoderic is said to have been born after Attila’s death, or at the very time of his death, descended in the fifth generation from Witulph, the brother of Ermenric.

Dietmar, his father, is not recorded to have had any brothers other than Walamir and Witimar. The former, while reigning under Attila, withdrew himself from the dominion of the Huns after Attila’s death; and, dying without sons, left the kingdom to his brother Dietmar. The latter had a son, also named Witimar, who, after his father’s death, abandoned Italy and withdrew into Gaul.

### 1. (Chr. W.) A.D. 378

While Valens was reigning after the death of his brother Valentinian, together with Gratian and Valentinian, the sons of that same brother, Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a most wise and temperate man, flourished; but, as they say, he suffered from the vice of pride. [Note: The words “but … he suffered” are missing in 5, apparently erased.]

### 2. A.D. 379

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria [Note: “missing” 5; *Anastasius* 1b.], departed in the sixty-sixth year of his priesthood and left Peter as his successor (cf. Rufinus).

### 3. (Chr. W.) A.D. 380

The Goths, driven out by the Huns, spread throughout Thrace.

### 4. A.D. 381

The Goths, compelled by hunger, rebelled against Valens. He attacked them in war, but after his army was killed, he fled and was burned alive in a certain hut, in the fifteenth year of his reign. Of his fifteen years of rule, he reigned eleven together with his brother and four after him (cf. H. m.).

## The Years of Gratian

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 382, and the 1,133rd year from the founding of the City, Gratian, the son of Valentinian, the thirty-ninth emperor from Augustus [Note: *XLIIIus* (“forty-third”) 1b.], was chosen to rule after the death of his uncle Valens. He reigned with his brother Valentinian for six years, having previously reigned for four years with his uncle.

At that time the blessed Ambrose at Milan [Note: “flourished” 5.] first composed hymns to be sung in the church [Note: missing 10, 11; “who E.”]. At Tours, the blessed Martin [Col. 0757C] shone with great miracles [Note: *lampabant* (“they shone”) deleted in 10 and thus missing in 11.]. Throughout the whole world, men renowned for doctrine and knowledge shone: Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory Nazianzen, and Jerome at Bethlehem [Note: The words in parentheses appear to have been taken from Sigebert by Ekk. and added afterward. In D? E, the final words “throughout … shone” are omitted.]. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, compiled a paschal cycle covering one hundred years, which he called a *laterculus* [Note: “of Alexandria” E1.]. Throughout the world, men renowned for doctrine and knowledge shone; at Bethlehem, the blessed presbyter Jerome, and at Hippo, a city of Africa, the holy bishop Augustine, shone.

**(H. R. and H. m.)** Gratian, then a very young man, saw an immeasurable multitude of enemies pouring into Roman territory. Trusting in the power of Christ, although greatly inferior in the number of his soldiers, he threw himself against the enemy and killed more than 30,000 Alamanni near Argentaria, a town in Gaul.

Then, hearing that Thrace, Dacia, and Pannonia—their native lands, as it were—were possessed by the Goths and by the Huns and Alans, more savage than every kind of destruction, he came to Pannonia.

At that time Theodosius, the son of Theodosius, was regarded as a man of great renown, both because of the nobility of his parents and because of his own courage. But, worn down by the envy of those unlike him, he was living in Spain, where he had been born and raised.

When the emperor saw that his brother was still a child and hesitated about what to do—since the barbarians, elated by their victories, appeared unconquerable—he summoned Theodosius from Spain and made him master of the army, just as Nerva had once chosen the Spaniard Trajan, through whom the republic was restored. He sent Theodosius against the barbarians with an expedition.

Theodosius went and fought bravely with those great Scythian peoples and triumphed successfully. Then, as an excellent commander, he dispersed his army among the cities and quickly returned to the emperor, himself becoming the messenger of his own triumphs.

When the emperor, overcome with wonder, did not believe this, the envious said that Theodosius had fled and lost the army. But he asked that those who disparaged him be sent to see the multitude of the slain. Moved by these words, the emperor sent men to report to him what had happened.

Meanwhile, the excellent commander saw in a vision that Saint Meletius, bishop of the city of Antioch, clothed him in an imperial cloak and adorned his head with a crown. When he reported this in the morning to one of his friends [Note: *cum retulisset* (“when he had reported it”) E1.], the friend said that the dream was clear and contained nothing enigmatic or doubtful.

A few days later, those who had been sent returned and reported that many thousands of the enemy had been killed. Therefore the emperor Gratian rejoiced and, with everyone’s support, clothed Theodosius, who was in his thirty-third year, in the purple at Sirmium and placed him over the empire of the East and Thrace together [Note: *fecit* (“made”) 9c.].

Theodosius then entered Constantinople in triumph. So that he would not weary the Roman people by fighting continually, he made peace with Athalaric, king of the Visigoths, and kindly received him when he came to Constantinople [Note: “honorably” is missing in 9c.]. He had him buried there with honor after his death and, by this kindness, subjected all the Goths to the Roman Empire [Note: missing in 9c.].

When he came to Thessalonica, he fell ill. Wishing to be baptized, he asked Anatolius, the bishop of that city, what faith he held. Anatolius replied that the Arian plague had not been able to enter Illyricum, but that they preserved inviolate the faith of the Council of Nicaea. The emperor gladly accepted his words, was baptized [Note: “and was” 9c.], and was freed from his illness [Note: missing in 9c.].

Meanwhile, he made his son Arcadius his partner in the empire. In Italy, since Valentinian was still a sufficiently young boy, the former consul and prefect Probus held the administration.

Justina, the mother of Valentinian, was an Arian. While her husband was alive, she could not harm orthodox Christians. But after his death, when her son was still very young, she came to Milan and was hostile to the bishop Ambrose, to the point of ordering him to be sent into exile.

When she ordered him to leave the church, Ambrose said:

“I do not do this willingly, lest I appear to hand the sheepfolds over to wolves or to those who blaspheme God. If you wish, kill me here; in this place I will willingly receive death.”

At that time Maximus was a brave man, worthy of the empire if he had not risen through tyranny against his sworn obligation. Against his will, he was made emperor by the army in Britain, crossed into Gaul, and was welcomed by the legions hostile to Gratian. He terrified Gratian by a sudden attack when Gratian was planning to cross into Italy, deceived him, and killed him at Lyons. He drove Gratian’s brother Valentinian, together with his mother Justina, out of Italy. **(BEDE.)**

Nevertheless, Maximus paid the most just penalty with his mother, who had both polluted him with the Arian heresy and harassed Ambrose, the most eminent teacher of the Catholic faith, through a treacherous siege. **(H. m.)**

Valentinian came to Constantinople and was received by Theodosius with paternal affection and restored to the empire. But certain Eugenius, formerly a grammarian and then a soldier in the palace, and a certain criminal Arbogast corrupted the chamberlains with money. While Valentinian was sleeping, they strangled him, and then suspended him by a noose so that it might be thought that he had inflicted voluntary death upon himself.

### 2. (Chr. W.) A.D. 383

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 383, which was the second year of Gratian, Theophilus began the paschal cycles. [Note: “Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea, died.” D? E. 4–10, from Sigebert.]

### 3. A.D. 384

A synod of 150 bishops was assembled at Constantinople against Macedonius under Pope Damasus [Col. 0759C], who ruled the church for twenty-six years. [Note: *XX tribus* (“twenty-three”) 1b; *XVIII* 5, 10, 11. D? E place this under 386 and continue: “Here it was decreed that the bishop of Constantinople, after the Roman pontiff …” In Gaul, Priscillian, a bishop, formed an error bearing his own name from the doctrine of the Manichaeans and Gnostics. He was heard at councils of bishops, together with his other followers … Ithacius … refusing to share communion with the Ithacians. From Sigebert.]

### 4. A.D. 385

[Note: 4–11 add: “At this time Priam and Antenor ruled the Franks.” From Sigebert.]

### 5. (BEDE.) A.D. 386

Theodosius the father made Arcadius his partner in the kingdom. [Note: D? E place this under 385.]

### 6. (Chr. W.) A.D. 387

Maximus came from Britain into Gaul, usurped the kingdom for himself, and killed Gratian at Lyons; he drove his brother Valentinian out of Italy.

## The Years of Theodosius

### 1. (H. R. and H. m.)

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 388, and the 1,139th year from the founding of the City, Theodosius, born of Theodosius his father and Thermantia his mother [Note: *theremantia* 9c; *terremantia* 1b.], the forty-fifth emperor from Augustus [Note: D? E give “fortieth,” and likewise thereafter], obtained the Roman Empire alone after Gratian had been killed by Maximus. He remained in it for eleven years [Note: *vixitque* (“and lived”) 9c; “forty” 9c.], although he had already ruled for six years in the eastern regions while Gratian was alive.
