Nevertheless, he allowed Valentinian, Gratian’s brother, to reign for as long as he lived.

Theodosius himself undertook war against Maximus, who at that time was stationed at Aquileia [Note: *aquilegiae* 5.]. When Maximus’s own soldiers could no longer withstand the emperor’s force, they captured and handed him over, and Theodosius killed him. He also killed Victor [Note: *victoremque* (“and Victor”) 5.], his son, whom his father, while still a child, had placed over Gaul.

After the victory had been completed, Theodosius came to Rome with Valentinian. Honorius, still a very young boy, was also with them; after the victory his father had summoned him from Constantinople. Theodosius, therefore, while staying at Rome, greatly benefited the City, providing some things and taking away others. After this, he left Valentinian at Rome and himself returned to Constantinople with Honorius.

When Valentinian was crossing into Gaul to organize the affairs of the state, he was suffocated in his sleep by chamberlain eunuchs bribed with money through the treachery of his count Arbogast and the grammarian Eugenius. Then, after Eugenius had been chosen ruler by Arbogast, they gathered a multitude of Franks and Gauls and prepared themselves for battle against Theodosius.

When Theodosius heard this, he assembled a military force and made his son Honorius emperor. He sent his most faithful eunuch Eutropius [Note: *fidissimum* (“most faithful”) E1.] to John, a monk renowned for foreknowledge in the Thebaid. The account of John is found in the *Life of the Fathers*. Eutropius was to bring John if he wished to come, or, if he did not wish to come, ask him about the outcome of the war.

John did not wish to come, but sent him this message: after the tyrant had been killed, Theodosius would gain the victory, but he himself would die in Italy.

Theodosius left both sons in the city of Constantinople and proceeded against Eugenius. Soon afterward an army of more than 20,000 Visigoths met him [Note: missing in E1.]. Eugenius and Arbogast held the Alpine passes, while Theodosius, stationed on the highest Alps, devoted himself to fasting and prayer.

Around cockcrow [Note: *cantum gallorum* (“the crowing of the cocks”) 5.], overcome by sleep, he saw in a dream that he was lying in a field and that two men stood beside him, seated on white horses and clothed in white garments. They ordered him to have confidence and to prepare his soldiers for victory at first light. They said that they had been sent to encourage him. One said that he was John the Evangelist, the other Philip the Apostle. This vision was also revealed to a certain soldier [Note: missing in 9c.].

When the vision became known, Theodosius shed still more abundant tears in prayer. On the following day battle was joined, and a tremendous whirlwind rose from Theodosius’s side against the enemy. It hurled back at the enemy the weapons they themselves had cast, while those thrown from Theodosius’s side were carried through the vast empty space beyond the measure of a human throw and struck the enemy forcefully.

Eugenius fell at the emperor’s feet and begged for mercy, but the soldiers standing around the emperor cut off his head. Arbogast killed himself with his own hand [Note: *se* (“himself”) P. 5.], in the third year of Arcadius’s consulship and the second of Honorius’s.

In praise of Theodosius for his distinguished victory, a certain poet named Claudian—although a pagan—sang these verses, among others, as a testimony to God and man:

> O greatly beloved of God, for whom the heavens wage war,  
> and the conspiring winds come to the trumpet-call.

Theodosius then came to Milan. Exhausted in body after his public labor, he fell ill. Expecting that he would die, he thought instead about the state, considering what usually happens to human beings when an emperor dies.

He therefore quickly summoned his son Honorius from Constantinople and appointed him emperor at Rome. When Honorius came to Milan, his father, having recovered somewhat from his illness, celebrated the victory at the circus. Before lunch he put on a spectacle as if he were well; after lunch, however, he was suddenly overcome and could not attend the spectacle, though he ordered his son to be present at the games. When night came on, he died, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventeenth year of his reign and the fortieth year of his life.

He was a promoter of the republic and an outstanding defender, merciful and compassionate, accessible to all, differing from others only in dress, honorable toward everyone and especially generous toward the good. [Note: “missing” E1.] As great as his gentleness toward human beings was, so great was his humility before the Lord.

This is sufficiently demonstrated in the example of obedience which, it is said, he displayed toward the holy bishop Ambrose, or rather toward God through him. Since the matter is worthy of being reported and remembered, although not in its proper place, I have decided to recall it, both for the benefit of readers and for the reputation of his virtues. [Note: “This is proved in him by the example of obedience, which is widely read, but which we omit here for the sake of brevity: how he submitted to the blessed Ambrose, who forbade him to enter the church because of the unconsidered killing of certain innocent people. The emperor also had another …” D? E.]

Thessalonica is a large and populous city. While Theodosius was there, a riot arose, and certain judges were dragged out and stoned. One of the soldiers, whom he loved, was also killed, as they say (Rufinus XI, 18; H. m.).

For this reason Theodosius became angry. As human passions work, he did not restrain the weakness of his anger, but mingled immense cruelty with righteous fury. He therefore ordered the citizens to be invited to the circus games and suddenly commanded swords to be drawn against all alike, so that the guilty might be killed together with the innocent.

About 7,000 people are said to have been killed there—not after a judicial proceeding, but at the dictation of a furious mind.

When Ambrose heard of this disaster, full of lamentation, and when the emperor came to Milan and wished to enter the church solemnly, Ambrose met him outside at the doors and prevented him from entering the sacred threshold with these words:

“You do not know, emperor, how great is the magnitude of the slaughter you have committed; nor does your mind, after daring such great madness, recognize the weight of so great a presumption. Perhaps the power of the empire prevents you from acknowledging your sin; nevertheless, reason ought to overcome power.

“You must know human nature, its mortality, dissolution, and the dust of your ancestors—from which we were made and to which we shall be reduced—and not, trusting in the purple bloom, remain ignorant of the weakness of the body that it covers.

“You are emperor over your equals and fellow servants; for there is one Lord of all, the king and creator of everything. With what eyes, then, will you look upon the temple of the common Lord? With what feet will you tread his holy pavement? How will you extend hands from which innocent blood still drips? How will you receive the holy body of the Lord with such hands? With what presumption will you receive the cup of precious blood with your mouth, while so much blood has been unjustly poured out by the fury of your words?

“Withdraw, then; withdraw, and do not attempt to increase your former wickedness by a second sin. Accept the bond with which the Lord of all has now bound you; for it is the greatest medicine of healing.”

The emperor obeyed these words. He had been nourished by divine instruction and clearly knew what belonged to priests and what belonged to kings. Groaning and weeping, he returned to the palace.

When eight months had passed continuously, the feast of the Nativity of our Savior drew near. The emperor, sitting in the palace and engaged in constant lamentation, shed unceasing tears.

Then the master of the army Rufinus entered. He possessed exceptional confidence with the emperor and, seeing him prostrate in mourning, approached and asked the reason for his tears. The emperor groaned most bitterly and shed still more tears:

“You, Rufinus,” he said, “are at play and do not feel my misfortune. But I lament and groan over my calamity, because the temples of God are open to slaves and beggars, and they may enter freely to beseech their own Lord; but I have no entrance to him. Indeed, the heavens themselves are closed to me.”

As he said this, each word was broken by sobs.

Rufinus [Note: *Rufinus vero* (“Rufinus, however”) 5.] said: “If you wish, I will run and persuade the bishop by my prayers to release the bond with which he has bound you.”

The emperor replied: “You will not persuade Ambrose. I know that his decree is just, and he will not respect imperial power so as to transgress the divine law.”

When Rufinus used many words and promised that Ambrose could be moved, the emperor ordered him to go quickly. After a short time, the emperor himself followed, relying on Rufinus’s promise.

But as soon as the admirable Ambrose saw Rufinus, he said:

“You have imitated the boldness of dogs, Rufinus [Note: *es* ordered differently in 9c.], being the author of so great a slaughter. You wipe shame from your brow and are neither ashamed nor afraid to bark against the divine image.”

When Rufinus pleaded and said that the emperor was coming, Ambrose, inflamed with heavenly zeal, said:

“I tell you, Rufinus, that I will prevent him from entering the sacred threshold [Note: *prohibeo* (“I prevent”) 5.]. If he changes his imperial authority into tyranny, I will gladly accept death [Note: *suscipiam* (“I will accept”) 5.].”

Rufinus heard these and many other words and reported them to the emperor, advising him not to leave the palace.

But when the emperor learned this while already in the middle of the street, he said:

“I will go and accept just insults in the face.”

When he reached the sacred threshold, he did not presume to enter the holy basilica. Instead, finding the bishop seated in the place of greeting, he begged him to release his bonds.

Ambrose said that his presence was tyrannical, that he was raging against God, and that he was trampling on God’s laws.

The emperor replied:

“I am not rising up against ecclesiastical ordinances, nor am I attempting to enter the sacred threshold unjustly. I ask you to release my bonds, to beseech the mercy of the common Lord on my behalf, and not to close against me the door which our Lord has opened to all who practice repentance.”

Then the bishop said:

“What repentance have you shown after such great wickedness? With what remedies have you healed incurable wounds and injuries?”

The emperor replied:

“It is your task to teach and prepare the medicines; it is mine to receive what is offered.”

Then Saint Ambrose said:

“Because you entrusted your judgment to fury, and because anger rather than reason delivered the sentence, write a law that will annul the decrees of fury. For thirty days let the sentence of death and confiscation remain only in writing and await the judgment of reason. When those days have passed and anger has subsided, let reason, judging the case within itself, determine according to truth what it has understood.

“During those days you will learn whether the sentence you pronounced is just or unjust. If reason proves that what was pronounced is unjust, it will tear it up; if just, it will confirm it. The number of days will be sufficient for examining these matters.”

The emperor accepted this admonition willingly and, confident that it was excellent, immediately ordered the law to be written and confirmed it in his own hand. When this had been done, Ambrose released his bond. This law is observed at Constantinople to the present day. It is as follows:

> “The emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augustuses, to Flavian, prefect of the praetorium of Illyricum [Note: *pretorio* (“of the praetorium”) 9c.].
>
> “If, having regard to the nature of a case, we order that certain persons be punished more severely than is our custom, we do not wish them immediately either to undergo punishment or to receive sentence. Rather, for thirty days their fate and fortune shall remain suspended as to their status.
>
> “Let the accused, indeed, be placed in bonds, and let them be carefully watched under custody and by vigilant guards.”

Thus the most sacred emperor, daring to enter the holy precinct, did not remain standing to beseech the Lord, nor did he bend his knees; rather, lying face down on the pavement, he proclaimed the Davidic words: “My soul clings to the pavement; revive me according to your word.” With his hands he tore out his beard and hair, struck his forehead, and sprinkled the pavement with drops of tears, asking forgiveness. When the time approached at which he was accustomed to offer a gift at the altar, he rose with tears and entered. But when he had made the offering, as was his custom, he stood inside the chancel.

Ambrose, however, again did not consent, but explained the distinction between the places; first, he asked what the emperor was waiting for there. When the emperor said that he was waiting to receive the sacred mysteries, Ambrose sent him this reply through his archdeacon: “O emperor, the innermost places have been assigned only to priests; the others are not permitted either to enter them or to touch them. Go out, therefore, and share this waiting with the others. Purple makes emperors, not priests.” [Col. 0763: “an emperor, not a priest,” 5.]

Then the most faithful emperor, gratefully accepting this rule as well, replied: “I did not remain inside the chancel out of presumption, but I learned that this was the custom in the city of Constantinople. Therefore I give thanks for such a remedy.” Thus both bishop and emperor shone forth in such great virtue. I, for my part, admire the work of each: the confidence of the one, the obedience of the other; the fervor of the one’s zeal, the purity of the other’s faith.

Moreover, the rules of piety that he had received from the great priest he observed, upon returning, even in the city of Constantinople. For when he had proceeded to the church at the time of a feast, he immediately went out after he had offered the gifts at the altar. [Col. 0763: “the altar,” 9c.; “to the altar,” 4.] When Nectarius, then bishop of the church, had sent to ask why he had not wished to remain inside, the emperor sent him this reply: “Only with difficulty could I learn what distinction there is between an emperor and a priest; only with difficulty did I find a teacher of truth. [Col. 0763: m. v., 5.] For I know only Ambrose who deserves to be called a pontiff.”

The emperor also had another opportunity for usefulness, through which he might triumph in good works. For his wife frequently admonished him concerning the divine laws, although she had first thoroughly instructed herself. She was not raised up by the heights of royal power, but rather inflamed by divine love. The greatness of the benefit, indeed, gave her a greater longing for the benefactor. As soon as she came to the purple, she showed the greatest care for the lame and the weak, using neither servants nor other attendants [Col. 0763: “maidservants,” 9c.]; instead, she acted personally, coming to their dwellings and providing each with whatever he needed. She also went through the guest-houses for the sick attached to the churches, ministering to the infirm with her own hands: wiping their pots, tasting their broth, offering spoons, breaking bread, serving food, washing cups, and doing everything else that it is customary for servants and attendants to perform.

To those who tried to dissuade her from such activities she said: “Distributing gold is the work of imperial office; I, however, offer this work in return for the empire itself, to him who has bestowed all good things upon me.” [Col. 0765A.] She often said to her husband: “You ought, my husband, always to consider who you once were and who you are now. If you always consider this, you will not prove ungrateful to your benefactor; rather, you will govern the empire you have received lawfully and appease the author of these things.” By these words she offered her husband a kind of excellent usefulness and an abundance of virtue.

When Theodosius died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, his body was brought to Constantinople on the sixth day before the Ides of November and committed to burial by his son Arcadius. [Col. 0765: “by him,” 9c.] He left the kingdom to his two sons, Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West, but entrusted responsibility for its administration to very powerful men: Rufinus for the eastern court and Stilicho for the western.

A few days later, when Theodosius’s body was transferred—that is, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December—the army that had been with him against Eugenius also returned. While the emperor Arcadius had gone out to meet the army at the gates, the soldiers killed the prefect Rufinus. [Col. 0765: omitted, 9c.] For he was suspected of planning to seize a tyranny and to summon Huns or Goths into [Col. 0765: omitted, 9c.] the Roman provinces against the emperor.

In the time of this same Theodosius, in the province of Palestine, in the fortress of Emmaus, a sound and fully formed child was born, but divided above the navel, so that he had two chests, two heads, and every sense in duplicate. When one ate and drank, the other did not eat; one slept, the other kept watch; sometimes they slept together, played together, wept at one another, and each struck the other. [Col. 0765: “the other,” 5.] They lived for approximately two years: one died, while the other survived for four days.

### 2

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 389, which is the second year of Theodosius after the death of Gratian, the same Theodosius, a man full of virtues, restored Valentinian to the kingdom after Maximus had expelled him from Italy (cf. Bede). (Chronicle W.—Bede.) The relics of the saints Gervasius and Protasius were discovered by Ambrose.

### 4

(Prosper, Imperial Chronicle.) A.D. 391. Augustine, [Col. 0765C: “Augustine, converted from the Manichaean heresy to the catholic faith through Ambrose.” D? E., from Sigebert.] having been converted to the faith, was baptized by Ambrose.

[Col. 0765D.] ### 6

A.D. 393. John the hermit flourished.

### 7

A.D. 394. Pope Siricius, the fortieth, sat for eight years and died on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. [Col. 0765D: D? E. adds: “Paula and Eustochium, [Col. 0765: “Eustochium,” E1.] her daughter, serve Christ at Bethlehem.”]

### 8

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 395. Jerome brought up to this point the book that he wrote concerning illustrious men.

### 9

A.D. 396. [Col. 0765D: D? E. 4–11 adds: “Didymus died at Alexandria. [Col. 0765: omitted, 9c.] The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed. From Sigebert. D? E. continues: ‘Constantinople … destroyed,’ from the same source.”]

[Col. 0766A.] ### 10

A.D. 397. Valentinian was killed through the treachery of Arbogast. [Col. 0765: “Arbogastus,” 9c.; “Arbogast,” 10, 11.] Eugenius seized his place.

### 11

A.D. 398. Theodosius overcame the tyrant Eugenius. Arbogast [Col. 0765: so E1; the other witnesses have “Arbogastes”] killed himself with his own hand. [Col. 0765: omitted, 9c.; “killed himself,” E1.] Theodosius, however, rested in peace at Milan. Augustine, a most eloquent teacher, was ordained bishop of Hippo.

Thus far Rufinus brought the ecclesiastical history of Eusebius. [Col. 0765: “of Eusebius,” 9c.; “Thus far … brought,” omitted in E1.]

## The Years of Arcadius and Honorius

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 309, the 1,150th year from the founding of the City, Arcadius and Honorius, the sons of Theodosius, held the empire jointly, in the forty-sixth position from Augustus, dividing only [Col. 0766B: “however,” 1b.] their residences: Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West. [Col. 0766A: D? E. adds: “The emperors … destroyed. From Sigebert.”] (Jordanes, On the Reign of Successors.)

At that time the patrician Rufinus, plotting against the emperor Arcadius, secretly sent money and invited Alaric, king of the Goths, to ravage Greece. But Rufinus was exposed and, as stated above, was beheaded by the soldiers before the gates of Constantinople. His head, together with his right hand, was carried through the city for mockery. After his wife had been exiled, the eunuch Eutropius acquired all his wealth. [Col. 0765: “and his wife,” E1.; D? E. adds: “At Rome … removed. From Sigebert.”] (Historical Miscellany.)

Gildo, count of Africa, who had earlier been appointed by Theodosius, learned of his death and, judging that there was little hope in children, began to claim Africa for himself. His brother Mascezel, however, being loyal, exposed his brother’s treachery. Gildo killed his brother’s two sons when their father departed. The same Mascezel was sent against him as against an enemy, and when he pressed him very hard, Gildo turned to flight and was strangled a few days later.

(Jordanes.) In the reign of the emperor Honorius, Radagaisus, a most savage Scythian, first poured into the western region with two hundred thousand Goths. He had sworn to drink all the blood of the Roman people. (Historical Miscellany.) Against him the Romans hired two pagan leaders of the Huns, Huldin and Sarus. But since God did not wish the cause of his power to be overcome through human strength, Radagaisus was terrified by divine action. Fleeing to Mount Fesulanus, he was enclosed by immense fear on every side. [Col. 0765: “by fear on every side,” 5.] While suffering from hunger and thirst, and wishing to escape, he was captured alone by the Romans [Col. 0765: “by the Romans,” 5], sent to prison, and died there. So great was the multitude of Goths captured that they were sold like cheap livestock; individual Goths were sold for individual gold pieces. (Jordanes.)

After Radagaisus, Alaric, king of the Goths, entered Italy and, as it is written above in the history of the Goths, inflicted many evils upon the Romans and others; he died at Consentia. [Col. 0765: omitted, 9c.] (Historical Miscellany.) Athaulf, his kinsman, succeeded him, wiped away whatever Alaric had left, and, taking Placidia, the sister of Honorius, married her.

(Historical Miscellany and Jordanes.) The count Stilicho, who was born of the treacherous and deceitful people of the Vandals and was the father-in-law of Honorius—his two daughters, Maria and Hermantia, having been betrothed successively to the emperor Honorius, although both died as virgins—forgot his benefactions and his kinship and coveted his kingdom. He assembled against him the peoples of the Alamanni and Suebi by means of payments, because he planned to make his son Eucherius, who from childhood had always plotted against Christians, Caesar. But Honorius, gathering an army and fighting them, killed both groups. In that same year Arcadius, the eastern emperor, died after reigning thirteen years following his father’s death, in the thirty-first year of his age. He left a son named Theodosius, eight years old, whom he appointed emperor before his death. Succeeding his father, Theodosius reigned for forty-one years: fifteen with his uncle Honorius and thereafter twenty-six, making forty-one years in all. In his time the poets Claudian and Prudentius were renowned (cf. Prosper, Imperial Chronicle).

## The Years of Arcadius

### 1

(Chronicle W.) In the first year of Arcadius and Honorius, which is the year of the Lord’s incarnation 399, John the hermit died.

### 2

A.D. 400. Saint Martin departed to the heavenly realms.

[Col. 0767C.] ### 3

A.D. 401. Saint Ambrose was released from the flesh.

### 4

A.D. 402. Anastasius, the forty-first pope, was ordained. After sitting for three years, he departed on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. [Col. 0767: “died,” E1.]

### 5

A.D. 403. [Col. 0767C: D? E. adds: “In Britain, P. d. e. e. m. n. [abbreviated in the source], teaching, among other things, that a human being can be saved without God’s grace by his own merits (s. g. d. p. s. s. m.) and that a human being is born without original sin (p. o.). From Sigebert.”] The Goths under the kings Radagaisus and Alaric plundered Italy.

### 6

A.D. 404. (Prosper.) A synod was held at Alexandria on account of the teaching of Origen.

### 7

A.D. 405. Innocent, the forty-second pope, was ordained; he sat for fifteen years and died on the fourth day before the Ides of March. [Col. 0767D: D? E. 4–11 adds: “He established that the kiss of peace should be given at Mass. From Sigebert.”]

[Col. 0767D.] ### 9

(Prosper.) A.D. 407. Severus wrote the life of Saint Martin.

### 10

A.D. 408. [Col. 0767D: D? E. adds: “John Chrysostom, compelled by the empress Eudoxia, resigned the episcopate; Arcadius … attempts. From Sigebert. 4–11 adds: ‘John Chrysostom died in exile. The death of the empress Eudoxia followed.’ From Sigebert.”]

[Col. 0768A.] ### 13

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 411. The emperor Arcadius died at Constantinople. [Col. 0768A: D? E. adds: “Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, turned toward the heresy that separates God from man in Christ.”]

## The Years of Honorius

(Historical Miscellany and Jordanes.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 412, the 1,163rd year from the founding of the City, after his brother’s death Honorius continued to reign with Theodosius, his brother’s son, for fifteen years. Seeing the state declining daily, he selected the brave and warlike Count Constantius and sent him to Gaul.

A certain Constantine had occupied Gaul and seized the empire. Two wealthy young men, his enemies, Didymus and Verenianus, took their own servants and household dependents and attempted to defend themselves and their homeland. They captured Constantine’s son Constans and made him a monk. His father made him Caesar after he had become a monk and sent him against them.

But Constantius, sent by Honorius, immediately upon entering Gaul shut Constantine up at Arles and killed him. His son Constans was killed at Vienne by Gerontius, a count of Constantius. Forgetful of their fate, Jovian and Sebastian likewise attempted to seize power in Gaul, but they too were soon killed.

Count Heraclian, also of Africa, came with three thousand armed men and seven hundred ships to plunder Rome. Count Marinus went out against him and so terrified him that Heraclian fled to Carthage with only one ship. He was killed there soon afterward.

In those days, therefore, by order of Honorius and with the assistance of Constantius, firm peace was restored to all the catholic churches throughout Africa, for as long as the illustrious teacher of the Church, Augustine, flourished at Hippo Regius. [Col. 0767: “Hippo,” 5, E1.]

Meanwhile Vallia, king of the Goths, made peace with Honorius [Col. 0767: omitted, 9c.] and returned to him his sister Placidia. Honorius gave her in marriage to the patrician Constantius, who had recovered her.

After Honorius had reigned fifteen years with Theodosius, his brother’s son, and had left the state pacified, he died at Rome.

### 4

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 415. Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome.

### 7

A.D. 418. The bodies of the saints Stephen, Nicodemus, and others were revealed. [Col. 0767: “were revealed,” E1.]

[Col. 0768D.] ### 9

A.D. 420. Zosimus, the forty-third pope, was ordained; he sat for one year and died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. [Col. 0767: “the forty-second,” 5; “the forty-third,” correction of “the forty-second,” 4.] He established that the deacon should cover the left side.

### 10

A.D. 421. Boniface, the forty-fourth pope, sat for three years and eight months.

### 12

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 423. Saint Jerome departed in the ninety-first year of his life.

### 13

A.D. 424. At Ravenna, Honorius made Constantius his associate in the kingdom.

### 14

A.D. 425. Pope Celestine, the forty-third, sat for nearly nine years [Col. 0769: omitted, 1b, 9c.] and died on the eighth day before the Kalends of April (cf. Bede’s Martyrology). He established that the Sanctus—“Holy, Holy, Holy”—should be sung. [Col. 0769: “He established … that the Sanctus should be sung,” 4.] [Col. 0769A: D? E. adds: “He established that the psalms of David … should be sung; cf. Sigebert.” D? E. also: “He established that the psalms … be recited. He also sent … to the Scots … to Christ. From Sigebert.” 5–11 adds: “He also established that the psalms of David [Col. 0769: omitted, 9c.] should be sung; cf. Sigebert.”]

### 15

A.D. 426. Honorius died at Rome in the thirtieth year of his reign [Col. 0769: “twenty-first,” E1, 5, 9c.; “thirty-first,” 4, 10, 11], of which he reigned two years under his father, thirteen with his brother, and fifteen with his brother’s son Theodosius (cf. Historical Miscellany). Faramund, son of Marcomer, reigned in Francia (cf. Prosper, Imperial Chronicle).

The presbyter Paulus Orosius brought his historical book, from the creation of the world, up to this point. [Col. 0769: “This is absent,” E1.]

## The Years of the Younger Theodosius

[Col. 0769B.] (Historical Miscellany.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 427, the 1,178th year from the founding of the City, Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius and grandson of Theodosius the Great, held the empire alone, in the forty-seventh position from Augustus. Previously he had reigned fifteen years with his uncle Honorius; afterward he ruled for twenty-six years, making forty-one years. (Jordanes—Historical Miscellany.)

After Honorius died, a certain John seized the western kingdom and sent an embassy to the emperor Theodosius, begging to be accepted. Theodosius, however, thrust the envoys into prison and sent the praetorian prefect Arduburius against him. John attacked and imprisoned Arduburius at Ravenna.

When Theodosius learned this, he made Valentinian, the son of his aunt Placidia by Constantius, Caesar and sent him with his mother to recover the western kingdom. He sent Aspar, the son of Arduburius, ahead of him against John.

An angel of the Lord, appearing in the guise of a shepherd, led Aspar and those who were with him through the marsh that lay beside Ravenna and had previously been impassable [Col. 0769: “impassable,” E1.]. At that time God made it passable. When they reached Ravenna, they found the gates open; entering, they killed the tyrant John and released Arduburius from his bonds.

Valentinian, therefore, came to Italy and, with the consent of all, was made emperor. For this reason, by decree of Theodosius, he was called Augustus.

At the same time there were Goths and many other great peoples beyond the Danube, inhabiting the northern regions. Of these, the more rational groups were four: the Goths, the Hypogoths, who are also called Visigoths, the Gepids, and the Vandals. They changed only their name and nothing else, and used one language; all, however, held the Arian faith.

Under Arcadius and Honorius these peoples crossed the Danube and were settled in the Roman provinces. The Gepids—among whom the Lombards and Avars were later divided—inhabited the villages around Singidunum and Sirmium. The Visigoths, after laying waste to Rome under Alaric, went into Gaul and took possession of what was there. The Goths, who are also called Ostrogoths, first inhabited Pannonia; then, in the nineteenth year of the reign of the younger Theodosius, they inhabited the villages of Thrace. After dwelling there for fifty-eight years, they also gained the empire of the West.

The Vandals, joining the Alans and the Germans who were then called Franks, crossed the river Ninus under the leadership of Modigisclus and settled in Spain.

At that time there were two praetors, Aetius and Boniface, whom Theodosius sent to Rome at Valentinian’s request. When Boniface received command of Africa and conducted himself there gloriously, Aetius, moved by envy, accused him before Placidia, the mother of Valentinian, of planning rebellion. But he wrote to Boniface: “If you are summoned, do not go; you have been accused, and the emperors are calling you deceitfully.”

Believing him, Boniface delayed going when summoned. Then the emperors accepted Aetius as though he were loyal and sent two commanders, Mavortius and Galbio, against Boniface; Boniface killed them. Sigiswaldus was again sent against him.

Boniface, seeing that he could not retain Africa, crossed over to Spain to the Vandals and Alans. Since Modigisclus had already died, he persuaded his sons Guntharius and Geiseric to come to Africa and possess it. They came and devastated nearly all Africa with sword, fire, and plunder. [Col. 0769: “almost all,” 9c.]

Amid this storm, the most blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, departed to the Lord in the third month of the siege, lest he should see the ruin of his city, having completed seventy-six years of life, forty of which he had spent in the clergy or episcopate.

Meanwhile certain senators, friends of Boniface, informed Placidia of Aetius’s false accusation and showed her the letter that Aetius had written to Boniface. Astonished, she did not harm Aetius, but sent Boniface an encouraging message, together with oaths, telling him to come without fear. When he came, he dispelled the suspicion and was made master of the soldiers; not long afterward, however, he died of illness.

Then the Romans gave the Vandals part of Africa for habitation and made peace with them. When Guntharius died [Col. 0769: omitted, 9c.], Geiseric became emperor of the Alans and Vandals. [Col. 0769: “of the Alans and Vandals,” with the form “dalorum,” as in manuscript 1, fol. 87.] Since he was an Arian, he initiated a persecution against Christians within the boundaries of his settlement in Africa, wishing to overthrow the catholic faith. He persecuted many catholic bishops so severely that he expelled them from their cities, depriving them of the legal possession of their churches. Then, invading Carthage under the pretense of peace, he carried away all the ecclesiastical wealth and ornaments.

The emperor Valentinian Augustus, son of Constantius and Galla, traveled to Constantinople to visit his cousin Theodosius. He married Theodosius’s daughter Eudoxia, whom Eudoxia had borne him, and returned to Rome.

In the thirtieth year of Theodosius’s reign, great earthquakes occurred at Constantinople for four months, so that the frightened inhabitants of Byzantium remained outside the city in a place called the Campus, together with Bishop Proclus, crying out to God in litanies.

One day, while the earth was quaking and the entire people were crying out more intently, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), around the third hour, in the sight of everyone, a certain young man was lifted into the air. He heard a voice telling him to announce to the bishop and the people that they should make litanies and say this: “Holy God, holy mighty one, holy immortal one, have mercy on us,” adding nothing else.

When this was done, the earthquake ceased. The blessed Pulcheria, Theodosius’s sister, greatly marveled at this miracle with her brother and decreed that this hymn should be sung throughout the world in this manner. Around these same days Rome was shaken by such a great earthquake that many buildings collapsed.

[Col. 0771B.] During this period, while Attila, king of the Huns, was ravaging Thrace and Illyricum, Theodosius was compelled to send an embassy to him, pay him six thousand pounds of gold for his withdrawal, and promise an annual tribute of one thousand pounds.

After this Theodosius, consumed by illness, died at Constantinople in the forty-first year of his reign. He was very wise and surpassed everyone in patience and clemency. He was so merciful that whenever someone committed an act deserving death, the person would not reach the city gates on the way to execution before his clemency, following close behind, recalled him.

When one of his associates asked why he subjected none of those who injured him to death, he replied: “Would that it were possible for me even to restore the dead to life.”

Yet this man was not free of faults. He was fickle, surrounded by every wind; consequently, he would sign documents without reading them through.

After his death, before it had yet been publicly announced, the blessed Pulcheria, his sister, summoned Marcianus, an elderly man devoted to religion and chastity and a suitable candidate. [The text repeats: “an elderly man and a suitable man, summoned to her.”] She said to him: “Since the emperor has died, and I have chosen you from the entire senate as one pleasing to me, give me your word that you will preserve my virginity, which I have vowed to God, and I shall proclaim you emperor.”

When he promised this under oath, she summoned the patriarch Anatolius and the entire senate and proclaimed him emperor of the Romans. In his time Saint Servatius flourished.

[Col. 0771D.] ## The Years of Theodosius

### 2

A.D. 428. [Col. 0771: “The numbers of the years are almost all corrected in manuscript 1.”]

### 5

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 431. Aetius, after killing many Franks, recovered the part of Gaul that they had possessed. (Prosper.) Clodius, son of Faramund, reigned in Francia for twenty years.

[Col. 0771D: 10, 11 add: “While this man was sitting with his wife near the sea in the heat of the day, a sea beast, as is said, resembling an equitaurus (equitauro) [Col. 0771: the word in 10 appears to have been deleted, hence ‘and gold’ in 11], attacked his wife as she was going to bathe. Immediately, whether she conceived from the beast or from the man, she bore a son who, from the sea and his spotted face, was called Meroveus—that is, Merefech. From him the kings of the Franks were afterward called Merovingians, that is, Merevingilingi. [Col. 0771: ‘and from him they were,’ 10.] His son Childeric begot Ludovicus, who was also called Clovis. Cf. Fredegar, Epitome of History, chapter 9.”]

A.D. 434. Pope Sixtus, the forty-sixth, sat for eight years and died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

### 10

A.D. 436. Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, flourished.

### 11

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 437. [Col. 0772A: D? E. adds: “Cyril … noted it. From Sigebert.”] The third universal synod of two hundred bishops was convened at Ephesus under Pope Sixtus against Nestorius.

### 12

A.D. 438. [Col. 0772B: D? E. adds: “Eudoxia … on the Kalends of August. From Sigebert.”]

[Col. 0772B.] ### 13

A.D. 439. Aetius defeated Gundicharius, king of the Burgundians, and granted him the pardon he requested; the Huns later killed him (cf. Prosper).

### 14

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 440. Valentinian took the daughter of Theodosius.

(Historical Miscellany.) A.D. 441. Julianus, the Pelagian heretic, was condemned by Pope Sixtus. Great earthquakes occurred at Constantinople.

A.D. 442. Pope Leo, the forty-seventh, was ordained. He sat for sixteen years and departed on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

### 18

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 444. Theodosius unsuccessfully undertook war against the Vandals. [Col. 0771: the folio is missing in manuscript 1.]

### 19

(Prosper, Imperial Chronicle.) A.D. 445. The Alans took possession by force of the territory of further Gaul.

### 20

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 446. Saint Brictius, bishop of the Touronians [Col. 0771: apparently “of the Tunorians,” corrected to “of the Touronians,” 5; “of the Tunorians,” corrected to “of the Touronians,” 10], departed.

### 21

A.D. 447. [Col. 0772C: D? E. adds: “The seven sleepers at Ephesus, after 192 years of sleep, rose from sleep and, having affirmed the faith in the resurrection, again slept in Christ. Cf. Sigebert.”] Eustochius succeeded Brictius.

### 23

(Prosper, Imperial Chronicle.) A.D. 449. Bleda, king of the Huns, was struck down through the treachery of his brother Attila.

### 25

A.D. 451. Meroveus, son of Clodius [Col. 0771: “Merovecus,” corrected to “Meroveus,” 5; “Meroveus,” 4], reigned in Francia for ten years.

### 26

(Historical Miscellany.) A.D. 452. The younger Theodosius, emperor of the East, died in the forty-first year of his reign, of which he reigned fifteen years with his uncle Honorius and twenty-six with his cousin Valentinian.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 453, the 1,204th year from the founding of the City, Marcianus, the forty-eighth from Augustus, was placed in command of the eastern court as emperor and reigned seven years with Valentinian. The times of Valentinian, however, whether of this emperor or of the preceding one, will be assigned in their proper sequence.

Valentinian, therefore, ruler of the western empire, established peace with Geiseric, Africa being divided between them. [Col. 0771: “ruler of the empire,” 5.] But while Geiseric was growing proud even among his own people because of the success of his affairs, a powerful conspiracy of his own people was formed against him. When it was discovered, he killed many of them by various punishments.

(Jordanes, On the Reigns of Successors.) Marcianus, a deeply religious man who bestowed many benefits upon the needy, restored by divine providence the kingdom that his pleasure-loving predecessors and ancestors, ruling it in turn for nearly sixty years, had diminished, so that immense rejoicing increased among all. For he established peace with the Parthians and Vandals, who were greatly troubling the kingdom; he checked Attila’s threats; and through Florus, administrator of the city of Alexandria, he expelled from the Roman borders the Novades [Col. 0773: “nomads,” 9c.] and the Blemmyes, who had poured out of Ethiopia.

(Historical Miscellany.) Meanwhile the blessed Pulcheria fell asleep in Christ. [Col. 0773: omitted, 4, 5.] She had done many good works and left all her possessions to the poor; the emperor Marcianus, although they were considerable, distributed them eagerly.

During this period Attila, king of the Huns, ravaging Gaul and planning to invade Italy, was defeated by Aetius and Theodoric, king of the Goths, as is written in the history of the Goths.

But since virtue always produces envy, the emperor Valentinian, fearing Aetius’s prosperous successes, killed him, together with the most noble senator Boethius. With them, the empire of the West and the safety of the state collapsed [Col. 0773: “the safety of the state,” 9c, 10, 11] and could not afterward be restored.

The death of Aetius, however, did not go unpunished for Valentinian. For in the following year he too was stabbed to death by Transtila [Col. 0773: “Strantila,” 10, corrected in 11], a soldier of Aetius, through the counsels of the patrician Maximus. This occurred in the thirtieth year of his reign, of which he had reigned twenty-five years with his father-in-law Theodosius and five with Marcianus.

After his death, Maximus seized the empire and forcibly joined himself to Eudoxia, the wife of Valentinian. Believing that no help would come from Constantinople, since her father Theodosius and her aunt Pulcheria were dead, she sent an embassy and invited Geiseric from Africa. He suddenly entered Italy by sea with a great multitude, while the blessed Leo still governed the Roman pontificate.

The Romans were terrified at Geiseric’s arrival, and many fled from the City. Among them was Maximus, who, while fleeing, was torn apart limb by limb by the Romans. [Col. 0773: “among them also Maximus,” 10, 11.] This occurred in the third month of his tyranny.

Geiseric, finding the City empty, invaded it. The blessed Pope Leo met him outside the gate and, by divine prompting, so softened him through his prayers that, although everything had been handed over to his power, Geiseric abstained from burning, killing, and punishments.

For fourteen days they emptied Rome of all its wealth. [Col. 0773: omitted, 5.] They carried away many captives from there, including Eudoxia, who had invited Geiseric to this evil, together with her two daughters. [Col. 0773: “sons,” 5.] They deported them to Africa. [Col. 0773: “they deported them,” 5.]

In this way Rome was captured for the second time after Alaric invaded it, forty-three years having elapsed since that time, and 1,207 years since its foundation. [Col. 0773: omitted in E1, 5.]

After leaving the City, the Vandals spread through Campania and consumed everything with sword and fire. They destroyed the most renowned city of Capua; they also overturned the very wealthy city of Nola and many others. They were unable to capture Naples because it was extremely well fortified, but they nevertheless ravaged everything outside it.

Amid these hardships, the most holy Paulinus, bishop of Nola, having spent everything he possessed on the redemption of captives, surrendered himself in order to ransom a widow’s son, as the blessed Gregory writes more fully in Book III, chapter 1, of the Dialogues. [Col. 0773: “continues,” manuscript 1.]

After Geiseric had returned to Africa enriched by the wealth of Italy, he gave the daughter of the emperor Valentinian, Eudoxia, whom he had taken from the City as a captive, in marriage to his son Trasamundus. [Col. 0773: “Eudoxia, daughter of Valentinian, whom he had taken from the City by the lot of captivity,” 1b.] Hilderic was born from this marriage; he was the fourth to reign over the Vandals after Geiseric.

Geiseric had three sons, and before his death he arranged the kingdom for them in such a way that one would reign after another according to age. After him, therefore, Huneric reigned first, Gunthemandus second, and Trasamundus third. After Trasamundus, his son Hilderic reigned fourth; following his mother’s instructions, he was catholic (cf. Jordanes, On the Reign of the Goths, chapter 33).

(Historical Miscellany.) The emperor Marcianus, after reigning seven years at Constantinople, was killed through a conspiracy of his own people.

(Historical Miscellany—Bede.) In his time John the Baptist revealed his head, which had been buried near the former dwelling of King Herod, to two eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. It was afterward carried to Edessa, a city of Phoenicia, and honored with fitting reverence.

[Col. 0774C.] ## The Years of Marcianus

### 1

(Chronicle W.) In the first year of Marcianus, which is the year 452 from the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0773: “451,” 9c; “452,” corrected to “453,” 5; “453,” 1b], Aetius defeated Attila. [Col. 0774C: D? E. adds: “Earthquakes … the consequences. From Sigebert.”]

### 3

A.D. 453. The fourth synod, of 630 bishops [Col. 0773: “530,” 5, 9c, 10, 11], was convened at Chalcedon [Col. 0773: “convened,” apparently read as “congregato” in 1 and likewise in 5 after correction; “was convened,” 1b; “is convened,” E1, 10, 11, and Chronicle W.] under Pope Leo against Eutyches. [Col. 0774C: D? E. adds: “Here it was decreed … to have begotten. From Sigebert.”]

### 4

A.D. 456. Valentinian killed the patrician Aetius.

### 5

A.D. 457. Valentinian was killed by Aetius’s friends.

[Col. 0774D.] ### 6

(Bede.) A.D. 458. Hilary, the forty-eighth pope, was ordained. He sat for seven years and died on the fourth day before the Ides of September. During his pontificate Victurius composed a paschal cycle of 532 years.

### 7

(Chronicle W.) A.D. 459. Marcianus, emperor of the East, was killed.

(Jordanes.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 460, the 1,211th year from the founding of the City. (Historical Miscellany.) Leo, born of Bessian stock, was chosen emperor from the rank of military tribune and crowned by the patriarch Anatolius. He was the forty-ninth from Augustus, received the eastern kingdom, and held it for sixteen years. Later, in the following period, he made his son Leo his associate in the kingdom.

As for the Western empire, a certain Mauronianus—or Majorianus [Col. 0775: “M. v.” in 1 and E1, written above the same word by the same hand; “M. v.” absent in 4, 5, 9c, 10, 11]—received it at Ravenna. But in the fourth year he was killed not far from the city of Dertona. Immediately afterward Severus became emperor at Ravenna without Leo’s authorization and was called Augustus; he too died at Rome after four years.

(Jordanes.) After his death, by the consent of the entire army, the emperor Leo made Anthemius, son-in-law of the deified Marcianus, Caesar from the rank of patrician and sent him to Rome to rule.

(Historical Miscellany.) In the following year Servandus, who was prefect in Gaul, wishing to seize the empire, was sent into exile by Anthemius. [Col. 0775: “by Anthemius,” with correction in 1.] Again, a year later, the patrician Romanus attempted by deceit to take the empire and was killed on the order of Anthemius. [Col. 0775: with correction in 1.]

In these times the emperor Leo made Zeno, his son-in-law, master of the whole East, and appointed Basiliscus, the brother of his wife Verena, master of Africa. Thus Emperor Leo made peace with the Ostrogoths, who were then ruled by Walamir, and took as a hostage Theoderic, son of Walamir’s brother Dietmar, already in his eighth year; nevertheless, he later returned him to his father with honor (cf. JORD. *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*, ch. 53).

(H. m.) During this period a great source of discord arose between the emperor Anthemius [Col. 0775C] and his son-in-law, the patrician Ricimer, who was then stationed at Milan and governed Liguria. Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, a man distinguished for his holiness, intervened between them and recalled them to concord. But because Ricimer belonged to the treacherous race of the Goths, he broke the peace. Marching toward Rome with a strong force, he killed Anthemius, who was then in the fourth year of his reign; but he did not long rejoice in his treachery, for after three months he died in agony from illness.

Meanwhile Olybrius, sent by the emperor Leo, came to Rome and, while Anthemius was still alive, attained the imperial dignity. He married Placidia, daughter of the emperor Valentinian. After holding the empire for seven months, he died a natural death at Rome. After [Col. 0775D] his death, Licerius was made emperor at Ravenna; but in the following year the patrician Nepos, son of Nepotianus, came with an army, expelled Licerius, and, taking the empire himself, appointed him bishop in the Dalmatian city of Salona (cf. JORD.).

(H. m.) At that time Euric reigned at Toulouse over the Visigoths. He was the son of Theoderic, who had fallen while fighting Attila together with Aetius.

[Col. 0776A] Therefore Emperor Leo, after ruling the Eastern Empire for sixteen years, appointed as emperor Leo, his grandson through his daughter Ariagne and the son of Zeno, and brought his life to an end. (JORD.) When the younger Leo had ruled the empire for a few months, he crowned his father Zeno with his own hand and appointed him emperor, then departed this life.

(H. m.) Soon Basiliscus, master of Africa, was acclaimed emperor; he made his son Marcus Caesar and crowned his wife Zenobia as empress. Meanwhile Zeno, master of the whole East, arrived at the imperial city with his wife Ariagne and was received by the people and the senate. Basiliscus, however, fled to a church; having placed the imperial dignity—that is, the crown—upon the divine table, he himself and his wife Zenobia fled to the baptistery. Zeno immediately obtained the imperial dignity and took possession of the empire.

## The Years of Leo

1. In the first year of Leo, which is the year 459 from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0775] 460 in manuscripts 1b, 5, E1.], the body of Saint Anastasia was brought from Sirmium and placed in her church in the porticoes of Domninus.

2. A.D. 461. Childeric [Note: [Col. 0775D] In recording the names of the Frankish kings, Ekk., who added this material in a second revision, does not everywhere agree with the *Deeds of the Franks*, but seems to have possessed another catalogue of kings.], son of Merovech, reigned in Francia for twenty-four years (cf. *Deeds of the Franks*).

[Note: [Col. 0776B] D? E. add: Symeon, standing on a pillar, is renowned at Antioch. From Sigebert, under the year 458.]

3. A.D. 462. [Note: [Col. 0776B] D? E., 4–11, add: The Franks drive Childeric from the kingdom because he conducted himself arrogantly and luxuriously. From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0776C] 6. A.D. 465. Pope Simplicius, the forty-ninth, occupied the see for twelve years and died on the sixth day before the Ides of March. [Note: [Col. 0776C] D? E. add: He condemned Peter, bishop of Alexandria, convicted of the Eutychian heresy. From Sigebert.]

8. (H. m.) A.D. 467. A certain painter, having presumed to paint the Savior in the likeness of Jupiter, had his hand wither; when he confessed his sin, Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, healed him.

9. A.D. 468. The prophet Elisha was transferred to Alexandria and placed in the monastery of Paul the Leper, who healed a leper, made a leper, and was transferred to the place where the lepers were.

10. A.D. 469. [Note: [Col. 0776D] D? E. add: Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, instituted the litanies before the Ascension of the Lord because of an impending calamity. From Sigebert. 4–11 add: Mamertus of Vienne, bishop, became renowned; he instituted the litanies before the Ascension of the Lord. Manuscripts 10 and 11. From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0776D] 11. A.D. 470. [Note: [Col. 0776D] Manuscripts 10 and 11 add: Queen Basina, having rejected the king of the Thuringians, joined herself in marriage to Childeric because he was more powerful and wealthier. But on the first night she said to him: “My lord, do not sleep with me until you see something in a dream that will benefit you.” He consented and saw in a dream a lion walking about in the palace. She interpreted this to mean that she would bear a powerful son. And so it happened, for she bore Clovis, a very powerful man. Cf. Fredegar, *Epitome of History*, ch. 12.]

[Col. 0777A] 16. (Chr. W.) A.D. 475. The elder Leo died [Note: [Col. 0777] “Leo … reigned” occurs in an erased place. Manuscript 1.]; in his place the younger Leo reigned for a few months.

## The Years of Zeno

1. In the year 476 from the Lord’s incarnation, and in the 227th year from the founding of the City, Zeno, of Isaurian origin and son-in-law of the emperor Leo, obtained the Eastern Empire, fiftieth in succession after Augustus, and reigned for sixteen years. In the West, Nepos held the empire at Rome.

(H. m.) The patrician Orestes drove him from the throne and made his own son Augustulus emperor. In the following year he concluded a treaty with Geiseric, king of the Vandals.

While these events were taking place at Rome, Odoacer, of Rugian origin, relying on the hordes of the Thuringians, Scyrians, and Heruli, set out for Italy from the farthest borders of Pannonia. While he was still leading his army through the countryside of Noricum, he learned of the fame of Severinus, the servant of God, who was then living in those regions, and approached him to seek his blessing. Having received the blessing, he was leaving the cell; and as he bowed his head so as not to strike it—for he was tall in stature—he heard from the man of God, who knew the future:

“Go now to Italy, Odoacer; go, for the present clothed in the cheapest skins of animals, soon to distribute much more abundantly to many.”

The outcome proved these words true, for afterward he reigned throughout all [Col. 0777C] Italy. When Odoacer entered Italy, the patrician Orestes immediately met him at the borders of Liguria. But when he saw that he could not withstand so great a multitude, he shut himself up in fear within Ticinum, which is now called Pavia. Odoacer came, entered the city after conquering it, ravaged everything with plunder, and slaughtered Orestes, whom he had captured, with the sword. From there the barbarians, dispersing, rapidly subjected all Italy to their authority.

Seeing his successes increase, Odoacer immediately seized the royal dignity. Augustulus, however, seeing all Italy subjected to Odoacer’s power and terrified by unprecedented fear, voluntarily and miserably cast off the purple and laid down the imperial majesty after barely eleven months in possession of the state.

Thus the Roman Empire, revered throughout the whole world, and that august eminence which had begun under Augustus Octavian in the 709th year from the founding of the City, perished in this Augustulus in the 227th year from the founding of the City, in the 524th year from Caesar, who first seized sole rule in it, and in the year 477 from the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0778A] D? E. add: The heresy of the Acephali arose; they opposed the three chapters of the Council of Chalcedon without naming an author. For this reason they were called Acephali, that is, “headless.”]

After Augustulus had been deposed, Odoacer entered Rome and obtained the kingdom of all Italy. He held it for fourteen years without disturbance, until Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, entered Italy with the permission of the emperor Zeno, intending to possess it. How this occurred may be read above in the history of the Goths.

Thus the emperor Zeno, after presiding over the Eastern kingdom for seventeen years, reached the end of his life. His brother Longinus attempted to seize the empire but was repulsed by Ariagne. Anastasius, the palace officer, was then chosen by the entire senate and people at her urging; clothed in purple, he took Ariagne as his wife.

2. In the year 477 from the Lord’s incarnation, Pope Felix, the fiftieth, occupied the see for eight years. [Note: [Col. 0778B] D? E. add: He condemned Acacius … condemned. From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0778B] 3. (Chr. W.) A.D. 478. Odoacer entered Italy.

4. A.D. 479. The body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of the apostle Matthew, written in his own hand, were discovered. [Note: [Col. 0778B] Manuscripts 10 and 11 add: Clovis, in love with Rothild, daughter of the king of the Allobroges, who are now called Burgundians, was unable to approach her openly because of the plots of his enemies. Secretly, through his faithful man Aurelianus, sending her a ring while disguised as a pilgrim, he betrothed her. But when he was approaching the borders of Burgundy, he persuaded those who were escorting her to burn and plunder twelve miles on both sides, so that she might at least witness one act of vengeance against those who had killed her father, drowned her mother with a stone tied around her neck, driven her brothers into exile, and thrown her cousin King Sigismund, together with his wife and sons, into a well. And this was done. Saint Remigius baptized him, and he reigned for thirty years. Cf. Fredegar, *Epitome of History*.]

8. A.D. 484. Clovis [Note: [Col. 0777] “Clovis … Remigius” ends in manuscripts 10 and 11.], son of Childeric, reigned in Francia for thirty years. Saint Remigius baptized him [Note: [Col. 0777] “Him … Remigius” ends in manuscript 4.].

9. A.D. 485. Pope Gelasius, the fifty-first, occupied the see for four years and eight months and died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December. [Note: [Col. 0778C] D? E. add: He acted against the Manichaeans … accomplished. From Sigebert.]

10. (BEDA.) A.D. 486. Huneric, king of the Vandals and son of Geiseric, exiled more than 334 Catholic bishops and cut out the tongues of some of them; nevertheless, they spoke, as blessed Gregory mentions in the third book of the *Dialogues* (III.32).

14. A.D. 489. [Note: [Col. 0778D] Manuscripts 4–11 add: Avitus, bishop of Vienne, converted the Gauls. From Sigebert.]

15. A.D. 490. [Note: [Col. 0778D] D? add: Avitus, bishop of Vienne, converted the Gauls from the worship of idols and composed books on Catholic faith in verse. From Sigebert.] Pope Anastasius, the fifty-second, occupied the see for one year and ten months.

17. [A.D. 492. [Note: [Col. 0777] In codex 1 Ekk., as almost always, corrected the numbers. In the form we have printed, he first wrote the year 492 (and so did manuscripts 5 and 9c.), then changed the following year, 493, to 492, and therefore erased this line, writing the words “Symmachus … XIV” somewhat lower in the margin. Manuscript 491; manuscript 4. These words are absent from E.] ] Pope Symmachus, the fifty-third, occupied the see for fourteen years.

## The Years of Anastasius

1. (H. R.) In the year 492 from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscripts 493, 5, 9c, and 11; 492 corrected to 493 in manuscript 10.], and in the 243rd year from the founding of the City, Anastasius obtained the empire and reigned for twenty-seven years, fifty-first in succession after Augustus.

(H. m.) Theoderic, however, presided over the Roman Empire with the Goths: the former was an Arian, the latter an Eutychian heretic. At this time great discord arose at Rome on account of Symmachus and Laurentius. Some, contrary to Roman custom, chose Laurentius; others, of sounder judgment, chose the deacon Symmachus. Because of this, many Roman citizens, clerics, and priests were killed at Rome for approximately three years, until Theoderic the ruler came to Rome. Although he was an Arian, he held a synod and confirmed Symmachus as bishop of Rome, while ordering that Laurentius be installed as bishop in the city of Nuceria. Laurentius, however, did not in any way remain quiet, but stirred up seditions; he was deposed by Symmachus and sent into exile in Dalmatia. [Note: [Col. 0779B] D? E. add: On account of whom … to be sung in exalted places. From Sigebert.]

At the same time Trasamund, son of Geiseric, who was already reigning over the Vandals, followed the impiety of his father and brother, closed the churches of God, and exiled 220 bishops to Sardinia. Blessed Pope Symmachus supplied them with daily assistance.

Amid these storms blessed Fulgentius, the bishop, became renowned for his confession of the faith and his learning.

In these same days, while a certain Arian named Olympius was bathing in Africa and speaking disgraceful and blasphemous words about the faith of the Holy Trinity, a fiery sword suddenly came from heaven and struck him.

The Arian bishop Deuterius was baptizing a man named Barbas of Byzantium. While asserting, contrary to the rule of faith, that the Son and the Holy Spirit were lesser than the Father, he said, “I baptize you, Barbas, in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.” Suddenly the water in which he was supposed to baptize disappeared completely. When the man who was to be baptized saw this, he immediately hurried to the Catholic church and received baptism according to the custom of the true faith.

At this same time, after Alamundar, prince of the Saracens, had been baptized, two Arian bishops came to him, urging him to agree with their sect. Having been baptized and instructed by orthodox Christians, he memorably rebuked them with the following story. He said:

“Today I received a letter saying that the archangel Michael had died.”

When they replied that this was impossible, the prince said: “And how, according to your belief, was Christ crucified while alive, unless he had two natures, since not even an angel has died?”

Thus the bishops departed in confusion.

During the reign of this Anastasius, Clovis reigned in Francia. He killed Alaric, king of the Goths, and received from Anastasius letters conferring the dignity of the consulship (cf. *Deeds of the Franks*).

(H. m.) Since Anastasius persisted in the heresy into which he had fallen, Pope Hormisdas, the successor of Symmachus, sent to him Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, with other Catholics, to restore him to the rule of the Catholic faith. But he not only rejected their salutary admonitions; he also expelled them from his presence with insult and ordered that they be placed on an old and fragile ship and forbidden to enter any city throughout Greece. Divine vengeance soon followed his impious arrogance. For when he was completing the twenty-seventh year of his reign, he died. Some say that he was struck by lightning.

4. (Chr. W.) A.D. 495. Theoderic killed Odoacer and himself held the Western kingdom for thirty-one years.

[Col. 0780B] 7. A.D. 498. Trasamund, king of the Vandals and son of Geiseric, closed the Catholic churches and sent 220 bishops into exile.

12. A.D. 503. The consul Boethius left at Rome, through his writings, many monuments of his intellect.

14. A.D. 505. Theoderic came to Rome and built many remarkable structures there.

15. A.D. 506. Pope Hormisdas, the fifty-fourth, occupied the see for nine years and died on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

20. A.D. 511. [Note: [Col. 0780B] Manuscripts 5–11 add: The virgin Genovefa of Paris, eighty years old, departed to God [“the Lord” in manuscript 9c]. From Sigebert.]

21. A.D. 512. [Note: [Col. 0780B] D? E. add: Genovefa, virgin of Paris, an octogenarian, departed to the Lord. From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0780C] 22. A.D. 513. King Clovis died, leaving four sons as heirs of the kingdom (cf. *Deeds of the Franks*).

23. A.D. 514. Lothar, son of Clovis, reigned for fifty-one years.

24. A.D. 515. Pope John, the thirty-fifth, occupied the see for two years and nine months. [Note: [Col. 0780C] D? E. add: King Sigismund … for the sake of healing. From Sigebert.]

25. (Chr. W.) A.D. 516. Theoderic gave his daughter Amalasuntha to Eutharic.

27. A.D. 518. Pope Felix, the fifty-sixth, occupied the see for four years and died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

(H. m. and JORD.) In the year 519 from the Lord’s incarnation, and in the 270th year from the founding of the City, Justin, an Illyrian by birth, a Catholic and very old and experienced man, commander of the guards, advanced from the soldiers to the senate. He obtained the empire by the senate’s election, fifty-second in succession after Augustus, and reigned for eight years.

A man of outstanding holiness, Germanus, bishop of the city of Capua, was sent to him by the Roman pontiff for the restoration of the faith. He was worthily received by Justin and strengthened the wavering hearts of many in the faith.

At that time, after Trasamund, king of the Vandals, had died in Africa, Hilderic, his son by Eudoxia, the captive daughter of Valentinian, assumed the kingdom. Following not his Arian father and grandfather but his Catholic mother, he became a worshiper of the true faith. He caused all the bishops who were in exile to return and ordered them to restore the churches that had been destroyed during the seventy years from Geiseric to Hilderic.

In the sixth year of his reign, Emperor Justin, zealously contending for the Catholic faith, ordered the heretics to be dispersed and directed that Catholic bishops consecrate their churches everywhere. When Theoderic, himself an Arian, heard this, he sent Pope John to Justin, ordering that he either return their churches to the heretics [Note: [Col. 0781] A leaf has been cut out of codex 1.] or he himself would put the entire population of Italy to the sword.

After John had departed, Theoderic meanwhile killed the patrician Symmachus and the senator Boethius with the sword, and when the pope returned, he killed him by starvation. Therefore, by divine judgment, he died a sudden death on the ninety-ninth day thereafter. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript 9c reads “by divine vengeance.”]

When Emperor Justin had already held the imperial dignity for eight years, he began to fall ill in April, in the fourth indiction. While he was still alive, he advanced Justinian, his sister’s son, to the empire; Justinian ruled jointly with him for four months. In August Justin himself departed this life at Constantinople.

## The Years of Justin

1. (JORD.) In the first year of his reign he killed Amantius, the chief officer of the palace, and others who were aspiring to his kingdom.

4. A.D. 522. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscripts 523 and 4; the manuscript that numbers from the year 520 through 527 gives the higher number.] Pope Boniface, the fifty-seventh, occupied the see for two years.

6. A.D. 524. John, also called Mercury, pope [Note: [Col. 0781] “Pope John, also called Mercury” in manuscript 5.], the fifty-eighth, occupied the see for two years and died on the fifth day before the Kalends of June. When he was sent by Theoderic to Justin at Constantinople, he restored sight to a blind man upon reaching the Golden Gate (cf. BEDA).

7. A.D. 525. King Theoderic [Note: Absent from E1.] slaughtered Boethius and Symmachus with the sword, killed Pope John by starvation in prison, and himself died ninety-nine days later.

8. (Chr. W.) A.D. 526. Justin, appointing Justinian as his partner and successor in the kingdom, died. Pope Agapitus, the fifty-ninth, occupied the see for ten years and died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

(H. m.) In the year 527 from the Lord’s incarnation and the 278th year from the founding of the City, Justinian, the son of the emperor Justin’s sister, obtained the empire alone, fifty-third in succession after Augustus, and reigned for twenty-eight years.

As soon as he assumed the imperial authority, he devoted himself to restoring the condition of the state. First he sent the patrician Belisarius, a great man, against the Persians, who had invaded the Roman borders; Belisarius defeated them courageously.

Meanwhile Gretes, king of the Heruli, came to Constantinople with his people, asking to be baptized. The emperor received him from the font after he had been baptized on the Epiphany, and Gretes promised to assist him in everything.

In the same year a certain woman from the Huns, a widow, joined the Romans, bringing with her one hundred thousand Huns. At that time also Gorda, king of the Huns who live near the Bosporus, approached the emperor, became a Christian, and was received by him. After giving him many gifts, the emperor sent him back to his own region to guard Roman interests and the city of Bosporus, which was called Bosporus after him because he supplied the Romans with oxen each year in exchange for money.

The emperor renewed the laws, making a separate code and calling it the *Novella Constitutions*. In the same year Antioch suffered great earthquakes and storms. Everyone performed litanies barefoot, crying, “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.” It appeared in a vision to a certain worshiper of God that he should tell everyone to write on their lintels: “Christ is with us; stand firm.” When this was done, the anger of God ceased.

Meanwhile Athalaric, Theoderic’s grandson and king of the Goths, was overtaken by premature death after reigning for a few years. His mother Amalasuntha took her cousin Theodahad as her partner in the kingdom. But after a few days he, forgetful of the favor bestowed on him, ordered her to be strangled in a bath. Since she had commended herself and her son to the ruler while she was alive, the emperor, hearing of her death, burned with great anger against Theodahad.

Sensing this, Theodahad sent Pope Agapitus to Constantinople as an intermediary. When Agapitus arrived and began to confer with the emperor, he discovered that the emperor had fallen into the doctrine of the Eutychians. After restoring him to the rule of the faith, Pope Agapitus publicly convicted Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, who defended the same heresy; he deprived him of communion and persuaded the emperor to send him into exile. After this, not long afterward, the same pontiff Agapitus died there. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript 5 reads “there in that place.”]

Meanwhile, since the Vandals had held Africa for many years, the emperor sent the patrician Belisarius against them with an army. Belisarius arrived and attacked them for three months, from the Kalends of September to the Kalends of December. After killing many, he finally defeated them, entered Carthage, captured Gelismer, king of the Vandals, alive, and subjected all Africa to the Roman Empire, freeing it from Vandal rule after ninety-six years.

Then, sent against Theodahad, he came to Sicily. After Theodahad was killed, Witigis seized his kingdom, but Belisarius captured him and brought him to Constantinople.

(P. D. I.25.) The same Belisarius also fought many other battles and defeated many peoples in war. On account of his many victories he earned various surnames, so that he was called Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, and Africanus. [Col. 0783A] He also attained great glory and honor with the emperor and all the leading men.

(H. m.) While he was staying at Rome, the empress Theodora ordered him to drive Pope Silverius, convicted on the accusation of false witnesses, into exile, because Silverius had refused to absolve Anthimus, the heretical bishop of Constantinople whom Pope Agapitus had excommunicated. Although unwilling, Belisarius carried this out and exiled him to the island of Pontiana, where he also died.

Similarly Pope Vigilius, his successor, was taken to Constantinople by the scribe Anthimus because of the same resentment and was sent into exile from there (P. D. ibid.). Under Pope Vigilius, Arator, a Roman subdeacon, flourished and wrote the *Acts of the Apostles* in verse.

In these times Cassiodorus also became renowned at Rome for both secular and divine learning. Among the other good works he wrote, he interpreted the hidden meanings of the Psalms with great excellence. He had formerly been consul, then senator, and finally a monk.

At this same time Dionysius the abbot, residing in the city of Rome, wisely composed the paschal cycles. Priscian of Caesarea also investigated the depths of grammar.

(IB. II.9.) Felix, bishop of the church of Tarvisium, and his fellow student Fortunatus also lived at this time. Fortunatus came from a place called Duplabilis, not far from Tarvisium, and learned grammar and rhetoric at Ravenna.

When he suffered from toothache, and his companion Felix likewise, they both went to the church of Saints John and Paul in the same city of Ravenna, where there is also an altar of Saint Martin. Beside it was a window where a lamp used to be placed. They put some of its oil over their eyes and recovered their health.

For this reason Fortunatus loved blessed Martin so greatly that, leaving his homeland, he came to his tomb at Tours before the Lombards entered Italy. From there he proceeded to Poitiers and remained there, composing many accounts of the sufferings of the saints, some in verse and others in prose. There he first became a priest and later a bishop.

(IB. I.26.) In these same times the holy father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0783] “Our father” in manuscript 1b.] [Col. 0783D] after the eremitical life that he led in the place called Subiaco, became renowned on Mount Cassino for his teaching and miracles.

When he first set out for that place, having left his former dwelling at divine command, three ravens that he fed every day followed him constantly in flight, as is written in the history of the Lombards. When he came to a certain fork in the road, two angels appeared to him in the form of two young men and showed him which road he ought to take.

In that very place a certain servant of God was living, and a voice from heaven said to him: “Spare these places; another friend is present.” This is expressed more clearly as: “Friend, leave this place, because another friend ought to live here.”

When blessed Benedict came to the summit of the mountain, he imposed on himself a severe abstinence. After building a monastery, he lived there, as is read in the *Dialogue* (II.1).

(H. m.) At this same time the people of the Lombards, then friends of the Roman people, lived in Pannonia. Audoin governed them at that time. Throughout the entire period during which the Lombards lived in Pannonia, they assisted the Roman state against its enemies.

Therefore Alboin, son of Audoin, at the request of Narses—whom Justinian had made exarch of Italy and sent to defend the Romans against Totila, king of the Goths—sent him a strong force as auxiliaries. Relying on this force, Narses defeated Totila and thereafter freed all Italy from Gothic power.

The patrician Belisarius was accused before the emperor of having conspired against him. After all his possessions had been taken away, he was sent into custody; but after a short time he was released and recovered everything.

After reigning for thirty-eight years [Note: [Col. 0783] Absent from manuscript 1.], Emperor Justinian departed this life.

## The Years of Justinian

(H. m.) In the first year of his reign, the patrician Belisarius, sent against the Persians, routed them in great battles and entered Constantinople in triumph by the ruler’s command.

2. A.D. 528. A great earthquake occurred at Antioch.

[Col. 0784C] 3. A.D. 529. Justinian promulgated a decree that pagans and heretics should not serve in the army, granting them three months as a period for conversion.

6. (Chr. W.) A.D. 532. Dionysius, the Roman abbot, began the paschal cycles from this year.

8. (H. m.) A.D. 534. At Pompeiopolis, a city of Mysia, the earth was split by an earthquake. The middle of the city, together with its inhabitants, was buried, and their voices were heard from beneath the earth crying out for help. The emperor gave much money to bring them out and generously freed those who were still alive.

In the same year Justinian handed over to the church for chanting the hymn that is sung: “The Only-Begotten Son and Word of God.”

10. A.D. 536. Pope Silverius, the sixtieth, occupied the see for two years and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July.

[Col. 0784D] 11. A.D. 537. Theoderic, son of Clovis and brother of Lothar, died in the twenty-third year of his reign, leaving his son Theudebert (cf. *Deeds of the Franks*).

12. A.D. 538. Pope Vigilius, the sixty-first, occupied the see for fourteen years.

13. (H. m.) A.D. 539. A certain Mundus, of Gepid origin, joined the Romans.

The years from the beginning of the world: 4500.

15. A.D. 541. The celebration of the Lord’s Presentation began to be observed at Byzantium, since there was a great mortality there that year.

17. A.D. 543. A great earthquake occurred throughout the whole world. In the same year a certain man named Andreas appeared from the region of the Italians, running through the villages. He had a red and blind dog, which performed marvelous things at his command.

When he stood in the marketplace and a crowd gathered around him, the gold, silver, and iron rings of those standing nearby were secretly carried off by the same dog and placed on the ground, which the dog covered. At his command the dog then took them up and gave each person his own.

Similarly, he held out mixed coins of various emperors, identifying them by name. With the crowd standing around, he was asked about people and pointed out those who were pregnant, fornicators and adulterers, the greedy and the high-minded; and whatever anyone asked about each person, he revealed truthfully. Therefore some said that he possessed the spirit of the Python.

18. (BEDA.) A.D. 544. The sea spread across Thrace for four miles. (Chr. W.) The body of Saint Antony was discovered and placed in Alexandria.

20. (H. m.) A.D. 546. The empress Theodora died. Arator the subdeacon publicly read his book before Pope Vigilius.

(Chr. W.) In these times Cassiodorus flourished at Rome, and at Constantinople Priscian of Caesarea presented his book on the art of grammar to the consul Julian.

21. (Chr. W.) A.D. 547. The Fifth Ecumenical Synod was convened at Constantinople under Pope Vigilius against Theodore and all heretics.
