23. (H. m.) A.D. 549. The dedication of the church of the holy apostles took place at Constantinople in June. The relics of the apostles Andrew, Luke, and Timothy were deposited there. Bishop Menas proceeded with the holy relics, seated in the emperor’s golden, jewel-studded chariot, holding three reliquaries of the holy apostles on his knees, and thus celebrated the dedication.

25. (Chr. W.) A.D. 551. Victor, bishop of Capua, wrote a book on Easter and refuted the errors of Victorius. Theudebert, son of Theoderic, son of Clovis, died in the fourteenth year of his reign. His son was Theudebald (cf. *Deeds of the Franks*).

26. A.D. 552. Pope Pelagius, the sixty-second, occupied the see for twelve years.

27. (H. m.) A.D. 553. A terrible earthquake occurred at Constantinople and in the surrounding cities for forty days.

29. A.D. 555. A fire appeared in the sky in the form of a lance.

[Col. 0785D] 30. A.D. 556. [Note: [Col. 0785D] D? E., 5–11, add: Saint Medard died. From Sigebert.]

31. A.D. 557. [Note: [Col. 0785D] D? E. add: Queen Radegund, formerly the wife of King Lothar, having changed her clothing, became renowned for the nobility of her holiness. Manuscripts 4–11 add: Radegund, queen, formerly wife of King Lothar, became renowned for her holiness [manuscript 5: “for the glory of holiness”]. From Sigebert.]

32. A.D. 558. [Note: [Col. 0785D] D? E., 4–11, add: Gregory, formerly urban prefect and then a monk, flourished at Rome. From Sigebert.]

33. (Cf. *Deeds of the Franks*.) A.D. 559. Theudebald, son of Theoderic, died in the eighth year of his reign.

[Col. 0786A] 37. A.D. 563. Hilperic, son of Lothar, began to reign.

38. (Chr. W.) A.D. 564. Pope John, the sixty-third, occupied the see for thirteen years. [Note: [Col. 0785] Manuscript 5: “thirteen years.”] Emperor Justinian died. Lothar, son of Clovis and king of the Franks, died in the fifty-first year of his reign, leaving four sons (cf. *Deeds of the Franks*).

Up to this point Bishop Jordanes brought his chronicle from Adam [Note: [Col. 0785] “John … thirteen” and “Up to this point … Adam” are absent from E1.] (cf. Chr. W.).

(H. m.) In the year 565 from the Lord’s incarnation and the 316th year from the founding of the City, Justin the Younger, Justinian’s nephew, of Thracian origin, obtained sole rule, fifty-fourth in succession after Augustus, and reigned for eleven years. His wife was named Sophia, whom he crowned empress; he himself was crowned by Eutychius, the patriarch.

Since he was pious and orthodox, he adorned the churches that Justinian had built, giving them treasures and all their revenues. He sent the monk Photinus, the stepson of the patrician Belisarius, granting him authority over every person and every matter, so that he might bring all the churches of Egypt and Alexandria to peace.

As has been said, he was good at the beginning; afterward, however, he fell into every form of greed. He became an exactor from the poor and a despoiler of senators, making iron chests in which he stored whatever talents of gold he plundered.

In the eighth year of his reign peace was broken between the Romans and the Persians because the Homerites had sent an embassy to the Romans and the emperor had sent Julian, the master, with a letter to Arethas, king of the Indians.

Arethas received him with great joy, evidently desiring the friendship of the Roman emperor. When Julian returned, he related that when King Arethas received him, the king was naked, wearing a girdle around his loins and linen garments woven with gold. Around his belly he wore torn clothing sewn with precious pearls. On his arms he had five rings, and on his hands golden bracelets. On his head he wore a jeweled cloth, with four plaited cords hanging from either fastening, and around his neck a golden torque.

He stood upon four elephants, which stood bearing a yoke and four wheels; above them was a tall chariot covered with golden petals. He himself stood above it, carrying a very small gilded shield and two golden spears. His entire senate was armed and sang musical melodies.

[Col. 0786D] When the Roman envoy had been brought in and had bowed down, Arethas ordered him to rise and be brought to him. When he had received the emperor’s sacred letter, he kissed the seal that bore the emperor’s bust. After receiving the gifts, he rejoiced greatly.

When he had read the letter, he found that he was being asked to arm himself against the king of the Persians and lay waste to his kingdom. He did this immediately. Taking Julian by the head, he gave him the kiss of peace and dismissed him with great goodwill and many gifts.

(P. D. II, 1 ff.) In these times Narses, formerly the emperor Justinian’s *cartularius* but made patrician because of his good service, killed Totila, king of the Goths, with the Lombards assisting—at that time friends of the Romans, though still settled in Pannonia—and exterminated the Gothic people from Italy. The same Narses also killed Buccellinus, a Frankish commander sent by King Theuderic to devastate Italy; he captured Sindoald, king of the Brendri, who remained from the race of the Heruli whom Odoacer had led into Italy, and hanged him from a high beam. Thus he made all Italy free from its enemies.

For he was a most wise man, Catholic in the faith of Christ, generous toward the poor, a restorer of churches, and constant in vigils and prayers, so much so that he gained victory more by prayer than by arms. In his time a great mortality occurred in Italy, beginning in Liguria, so that that land was almost deprived of its inhabitants. Meanwhile Justinian died, and Justin succeeded him.

But when Narses the patrician, having overcome the Gothic people, already held Italy securely, the Romans, out of envy, directed an accusation against him to the emperor Justin and his wife Sophia, saying: “It would be better for us to serve the Goths than the Greeks, where the castrated Narses rules and oppresses us with servitude, while our most holy prince does not know this. Either free us from his hand, or else we shall surrender the city of Rome and ourselves to foreign peoples.”

When Narses heard this, he wrote to the emperor, saying: “If I have done evil to the Romans, may I meet with evil.” But the emperor, angered against Narses, immediately sent Longinus to Italy as prefect, to take Narses’ place. The empress Sophia also wrote to the Romans concerning him, among other things: “I shall put that eunuch in the women’s quarters [Note: [Col. 0787] *de genetio* in 1b], so that he may spin combed wool with the girls.”

To this Narses replied: “I shall weave for her such a web that, as long as Sophia herself lives, she will be unable to lay it aside.” Since he feared returning to Constantinople, he withdrew to Naples and sent his envoys directly to the Lombards, bringing them into Italy. In order that we may describe more clearly the arrival of this people in Italy and its settlement there down to the present, let us insert here, in abbreviated form, some account of its origin and of the succession of its kings.

# HISTORY OF THE LOMBARDS

[Col. 0787]

(P. D. I, 1 ff.) The northern region, the farther it lies from the sun’s heat and the colder it is because of continual snows, always has healthier people and is consequently more suited to multiplying peoples. Hence it happens that such a multitude of peoples is born in that region that they cannot remain there to live: some are sold for a price into the southern region, while others depart of their own accord.

For this reason, as was said in the history of the Goths, many peoples departed from those same regions: the Goths, Gepids, Rugians, Vandals, Heruli, Turcilingi, Huns—who are also called Avars—and likewise the Winili, who are the Lombards.

There is therefore a certain island in the regions of the northern ocean called Scandinavia or Scanzia. Some say that it is not situated in the ocean, but that, because of its flatness, the surging waves of the sea surround it. When a great population had grown there, so that it could not remain living in the island, the whole multitude, after taking counsel [Note: [Col. 0787] a word erased before *c* in 1], was divided into three parts. By casting lots they sought to determine which part should leave its homeland and seek new settlements.

Accordingly, the part whom the lot ordered to depart appointed two brothers as its leaders, Ibor and Aio: young in age, but greater and stronger in body than the others. Their mother, Gambara, was exceedingly wise and an excellent counselor, and everyone had great confidence in her prudence.

After kissing their parents and friends, they began their journey. They came to the region of Scoringa and remained there for several years. At that time Ambri and Assi, leaders of the Vandals, were harshly oppressing the neighboring regions. Since they were already boasting of many victories, they sent word to the Winili [Note: *ita* in 1], who are the Lombards, ordering them either to pay tribute or to prepare for battle.

Then Ibor and Aio, following the counsel of their mother Gambara, decided that it was better for them either to die fighting or to defend themselves by arms than to submit shamefully to tribute. They sent envoys to the Vandals, declaring that they were more ready to fight than to serve.

When battle was joined, the Winili [Note: *ili* corrected from *e* in 1], fighting bravely for the glory of liberty, won the victory. But afterward they suffered a great famine in that same province of Scoringa and were greatly humbled. Departing from there, they came to Mauringa, and from there in turn to the province of Godoland, where they remained for some time.

Meanwhile their leaders Ibor and Aio died. The Lombards, now unwilling to have leaders over them, established Agelmund as their first king, after the manner of other peoples. He ruled over them for thirty-three years. Agelmund was the son of Aio, of the race of the Thuringians, a people said among them to be the best and strongest.

In those days a certain prostitute gave birth to seven sons in a single delivery and, more cruel than a wild beast, threw them into a pond. When the aforementioned Agelmund happened to pass by the pond and saw the infants, he felt pity. He thrust in his spear and rolled them about in the water. When one of them grasped the king’s spear, the king, moved by compassion, lifted him from the water, saying: “This boy will become great.” With every care he gave him to be reared.

Because he had lifted him from the pond, and because in their language water is called *lama*, he gave him the name Lamissio. When he grew up, he became a most powerful warrior and a very wise man, and after Agelmund he himself reigned.

After King Lamissio died, Lethus reigned as the third king. Having ruled for forty years, he left his son Childeoc as the fourth king. When Childeoc died, Godeoc reigned. After his death, his son Calpho reigned as the sixth king. When Calpho died, Tado reigned as the seventh.

After this the Lombards left Rugiland, which in Latin speech is called the homeland of the Rugians, and lived in open fields, which in the barbarian language are called *felt*. After they had lived in that place for three years, a conflict arose between Tado and Ruodolf, king of the Heruli, who had previously been friends. This was the evil from which discord entered between them.

The brother of King Ruodolf had come to Tado for the sake of peace. When he wished to return to his homeland, he passed before the house of Rumetruda, the king’s daughter. When she saw many noble men traveling with him, she asked who he was, and she was told that he was the brother of King Ruodolf.

Then she sent a girl to invite him to drink with her, if he would deign to do so. When he heard this, he came with a simple heart. But because he was of small stature, the proud and boastful girl despised and mocked him. Unable to endure such shame, he insulted her still further.

Burning with feminine anger, she carried out the evil she had conceived in her mind. She pretended, patiently, to be pleased and, inviting him to sit, made him sit in a place where there was a window behind his back. So that he could have no suspicion of danger, she ordered a most precious cloth to be stretched before the window. She told her servants that, as soon as she said, “Mix,” they should pierce him from behind with spears.

And so it was done. When this was reported to King Ruodolf, he was exceedingly angry at the wicked death of his brother. He broke the peace that he had maintained with King Tado and declared war against him.

When both sides had come onto the open field, Ruodolf ordered his men into battle. He himself sat in his tent playing at a board game, confident of his victory. The Heruli were highly trained in warfare, and, so that they might be light for battle, they fought naked, covering only the private parts of their bodies.

The king, relying without doubt on their valor, sat safely playing at the board, as we have said. Nevertheless, he ordered one of his men to climb a tree and report the victory of his people to him, promising to cut off his head if he reported that his Heruli were fleeing.

But when the man saw them fleeing and the Lombards pressing them hard, the king asked him what the Heruli were doing. He replied: “They are fighting very well.” He did not dare to report the evil that he saw until all the Heruli had turned their backs.

Then, although late, he raised his voice and said: “Woe to you, wretched Herulia, struck by the wrath of the heavenly God!”

When Ruodolf heard this, he was alarmed and said: “Perhaps my Heruli are fleeing.”

The man replied: “It is not I who have said this, but you, king.”

Then, as usually happens in such circumstances, the king himself and all who were with him were thrown into confusion and did not know what to do. The advancing Lombards killed the king and all who were with him.

As the Herulian army fled here and there, such wrath came upon them from heaven that, when they saw green bushes in the field, they thought they were water; and when they stretched out their arms as though to swim, they were cruelly cut down by the enemy.

The Lombards therefore became victorious and divided a great booty among themselves. Tado received King Ruodolf’s standard and helmet, which he afterward always carried in battle.

From that time the valor of the Heruli was so humbled that they no longer had a king over them. The Lombards, however, having become wealthy through this victory, began of their own accord to seek battles and to spread their glory and valor everywhere.

After this Tado did not rejoice greatly in his victory, for Wacho, the son of his brother Zuchilo, fell upon him and killed him. Then Hildegis, the son of Tado, fought against Wacho, but Wacho defeated him. Hildegis fled to the Gepids and died there. For this reason the Lombards were enemies of the Gepids from that time onward.

Wacho had three wives. The first was Ranigunda, daughter of the king of the Thuringians. Then he took Austrigosa, daughter of the king of the Gepids, by whom he had two daughters. One was named Wiselgarda, whom King Theudebert of the Franks took as his wife. The other was called Walterada, whom Chusabald, king of the Franks, also took as his wife; but because he hated her, he gave her in marriage to one of his men named Garibald.

Wacho’s third wife was Salinga, daughter of the king of the Heruli. By her Walthari was born, and after his father’s death he ruled the Lombards as their eighth king.

All these belonged to the Lething family, a stock regarded among them as most noble. Walthari reigned for seven years and died. After him Andoin reigned as the ninth king. Not long afterward he led the Lombards into Pannonia.

He had a wife named Rodelinda, who bore him a son, Alboin, who was strong and clever in every respect.

When the Gepids quarreled with the Lombards, both sides prepared for battle. When the battle was joined and both sides fought bravely without either turning its back, it happened that Alboin, son of Audoin, and Thurismodus, son of Thurisind, king of the Gepids, encountered one another in the battle. Alboin struck Thurismodus with his sword and threw him from his horse, and thus Thurismodus died.

When the Gepids saw the king’s son dead—the man in whom they had placed great confidence—they immediately fled. The Lombards pursued them vigorously, struck down many of them, and turned to seize the spoils.

When the victory was complete and the Lombards were returning to their own places, they asked King Audoin to allow his son Alboin to sit and dine with him at table, since they had won the victory through him, so that just as he had shared his father’s danger, he might also share his banquet.

But his father Audoin answered them: “I cannot do this, for I would break the established law of our people. You know that we have such a custom among us: the king’s son may not dine with his father until he has received arms from a foreign king.”

When Alboin heard this from his father, he took forty young men with him and went to King Thurisind, against whom he had previously fought. He explained to him why he had come.

The king received him graciously and invited him to dinner. He made him sit at his right hand, where his son Thurismodus, whom Alboin had killed, customarily sat.

When they had become cheerful, King Thurisind saw his son’s killer sitting in his son’s place. He drew a deep sigh and revealed the grief in his heart, saying: “This place is dear to me, but the person who sits there is very painful for me to see.”

Then another son of the king, hearing his father’s words, was inflamed with anger and began to insult the Lombards greatly. Because they wore white bands around their legs, he mocked them, saying: “You have white shins down to your feet, and you are like various-colored beasts that produce offspring.”

Then one of the Lombards answered him: “Go to the field called Asfelt, and there without doubt you will learn what sort of men these are whom you have said resemble beasts, and how they can kick. For there you will find the bones of your brother scattered in the midst of the meadows, as though they belonged to some worthless beast.”

When the Gepids heard this and could not endure such disgrace, they became exceedingly angry and wished to avenge so manifest an insult. The Lombards, for their part, preparing for battle, all seized their swords.

But the king rose from the table, placed himself between them, and restrained his own men from anger, swearing that he would kill the first man who dared to begin the fight. For he said: “That victory is not pleasing to God in which someone kills an enemy who has been received peacefully in his own house.”

Thus peace was made between them, and they again began a joyful banquet. When the meal was finished, King Thurisind took the arms of his son Thurismodus and handed them to Alboin, then dismissed him safely and peacefully.

Alboin returned to his father and became his table companion. As he sat at table with his father, he told him everything that had happened to him. Everyone present marveled and praised Alboin for his courage and Thurisind for such great fidelity.

In these times the emperor Justinian ruled the Roman Empire. Through the patrician Belisarius he achieved many victories, renewed the laws, repaired the churches, and also built the basilica called *Ad Agyam Sophyam*, that is, “Holy Wisdom.” Its workmanship is considered so much more excellent than all other buildings that no equal to it is found across such vast expanses of the earth.

At that time Cassiodorus, Dionysius, and Arator were distinguished at Rome; Priscian flourished at Constantinople; and Saint Benedict also shone forth through his miracles.

Audoin then died, and his son Alboin received the kingdom. Since he was very famous and exceptionally brave, King Clothar of the Franks gave him his daughter, named Glotsuinda, in marriage. By her he had only one daughter, named Albsuinda.

Meanwhile Thurisind, king of the Gepids, died, and Chunimund received the kingdom. Wishing to avenge the wrongs done to the Gepids, he broke the peace with the Lombards and loved battle more than peace.

Alboin, however, made a firm peace with the Avars, who were first called Huns but afterward were called Avars from the name of their king. Then he went to war against the Gepids.

When the Gepids advanced against Alboin, the Avars immediately entered their land, as they had agreed with Alboin. For this reason, when sad news came to Chunimund, he was deeply distressed and began urging his men first to fight the Lombards and afterward to return to drive out the Avars.

When battle was joined, Alboin killed Chunimund. From his head he afterward made a drinking vessel, which among them is called a *scala* and among the Latins a *patera*. He also led away his daughter Rosemund, together with a great multitude of men and women, as a captive.

The Gepids were so completely destroyed that from that time onward they no longer had a king of their own. When Queen Glothsuinda, the daughter of Clothar, died, Alboin, as will be related below, took Rosemund, the daughter of Chunimund, as his wife—to his own destruction.

Meanwhile Emperor Justinian died, and Justin the Younger succeeded him in governing Constantinople. As was written above, the patrician Narses had been accused before him. Emperor Justinian had sent Narses, in place of Belisarius, to defend Italy. To avenge the injury done to him, Narses sent envoys to his friends the Lombards, saying: “Leave the poverty of Pannonia and come to fertile Italy, full of every kind of wealth.”

To stir them further to come, he sent them every variety of fruit and everything delightful that he could imagine among the riches of the land. When the Lombards heard this, they received it gladly and made preparations for their journey.

Immediately signs appeared in the sky over Italy, namely fiery armies, signifying the human blood that would afterward be shed.

Alboin therefore sought the aid of the ancient Saxons, his friends, so that he might enter spacious Italy with a large force. More than twenty thousand Saxons joined him, and according to his wishes they entered Italy with him, together with their wives and children.

At that time Alboin left Pannonia to his friends the Huns, on the condition that, if it should ever become necessary for the Lombards to return, each person would return to his own place.

The Lombards lived in Pannonia for forty-two years. They departed from Pannonia with their women, children, and all their possessions in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 568, in the first indiction, on the second day after Easter; that holy Easter was celebrated on the Kalends of April.

In those days, when the Lombards invaded Italy, Clothar, king of the Franks, died, leaving four sons: Heribert, Guntrammus, Helperic, and Sigibert.

At this time a holy man, Pope John, governed the Roman Church; after him came Benedict. Blessed Paul, the patriarch, governed the city of Aquileia and its people. Fearing the cruelty of the Lombards, he withdrew from Aquileia to the island of Grado and carried away with him all the treasure of his church.

Narses, having returned from Campania to Rome, died not long afterward. They placed his body in a leaden chest together with all his wealth and sent it to Constantinople.

Alboin entered Liguria in the third indiction, on the third day before the Nones of September, and in the time of Honoratus, archbishop of Milan, he entered Milan. He then seized the remaining cities of Liguria.

He besieged the city of Ticinum, now called Pavia, for three years. When those years had passed, the city was surrendered into his hands several months later.

When he entered through the gate called Saint John’s, on the eastern side, the horse on which he was sitting stopped in the middle of the gate. Although he struck it with his spurs and all those standing around beat it, the horse could not be moved at all.

Then one of the Lombards said to the king: “Remember, my lord king, what you vowed; break this harsh vow, and you will enter the city. For truly the people in this city are Christian.”

Alboin had previously vowed that he would kill with the sword the entire population that refused to surrender to him. When he broke this vow, the horse immediately moved, and thus he entered the city.

When peace had been granted, all the people at last ran to him at the palace that King Theuderic had once built.

After Alboin had ruled in Italy for three years and six months, he was killed through the plot of his wife, for the following reason.

When Alboin was dining at Ravenna and had drunk more than was proper, he ordered wine to be brought to Queen Rosemund in the vessel he had made from the skull of her father, King Chunimund. He told her to drink happily with her father.

Because of this she conceived the greatest grief in her heart and considered how she might kill her husband and avenge her father. She discussed the matter with Helmichis, the king’s arms-bearer, who was of the same age as the queen.

Helmichis advised her to enlist Peredeus, a certain strong man who was accustomed to sleep with the queen’s wardrobe attendant. When she disclosed her intention to him and he refused to consent to the murder of his king, the queen, during the night, placed herself in the bed of her wardrobe attendant, whom Peredeus loved.

When Peredeus came, the queen committed adultery with him. After this was done, she began to say to Peredeus: “Who do you think I am?”

When he named his beloved, she replied: “It is not as you think; I am Rosemund. Certainly you have now done something such that, unless you kill Alboin, he himself will kill you.”

When he understood the evil he had done, he consented, although unwillingly, to the king’s death.

Then Rosemund, more savage than any beast, when Alboin had surrendered to sleep at midday, ordered profound silence throughout the palace and had all the weapons removed. She firmly tied his sword to the head of the bed, so that it could neither be drawn nor taken up, and thus admitted his killers.

Alboin, awakened from sleep and understanding the danger that threatened him, quickly reached for the sword that had been tied down. Unable to draw it, he seized a footstool and defended himself for some time. But his attackers overcame him and killed him.

Helmichis took Rosemund as his wife and struggled to seize Alboin’s kingdom, but he could not do so, because the Lombards, deeply grieving over Alboin’s death, sought to kill Helmichis.

Meanwhile Rosemund sent word to Longinus, the prefect of Ravenna, asking him to send a ship quickly to carry them away. When he had sent one, Helmichis and Rosemund entered the ship in the silence of night, taking with them Albsuinda, the daughter of King Alboin, and the entire treasure.

The prefect Longinus persuaded Rosemund to kill Helmichis and take him as her husband. When she agreed, one day, as Helmichis was going to the bath, she went with him to attend him, carrying poison with which to kill him.

When he came out of the bath, she handed him the poison in a cup, saying: “If you drink this, you will gain great health from it.”

When he drank and realized that it was poison, he seized his sword, grabbed Rosemund by the hair, and forced her to drink the poison that remained. Thus, by God’s judgment, both of them perished by poison.

The prefect Longinus sent Albsuinda with the entire treasure to Constantinople, to the emperor Justin.

The Lombards, after taking counsel among themselves, made Cleph, a most noble man of the Lombard people, king in the city of Ticinum. He killed some powerful Romans and drove others from Italy. For at that time the Romans did not possess enough strength to resist the Lombards, since both the mortality that had occurred under Narses and the famine that came afterward had devastated all Italy.

After Cleph had reigned for one year and six months, he was killed with a sword by a certain boy, one of his household, using a weapon that had been kept at the table for his service.

After his death the Lombards had no king for ten years, but had dukes, each city having its own duke. Some of these dukes entered Gaul with many warriors and plundered it. Against them the patrician Amatus, who belonged to the party of King Guntrammus, advanced with an army, but was killed by them; they themselves returned with much booty.

After they had departed, the king summoned Eunium, also called Nummulus, to himself and made him patrician. Again the Lombards entered Gaul. Nummulus, joining himself to the Burgundians, went against them and, surrounding them with an ambush, killed many of them and forced the rest to return empty-handed.

After this the Saxons who had entered Italy with the Lombards, seeing that the Lombards ruled and unwilling themselves to live under them, returned through Gaul with all their possessions. With the assistance of King Sigibert, they made their way back to their homeland.

When they arrived there, they found the Suebi and other peoples occupying it. They therefore rose against them and fought to drive them out. But those peoples gave them a third of the region, saying: “We can live together in common.”

When the Saxons refused to agree, the others again gave them another third, so that they themselves might retain one third. But when the Saxons in no way consented, they joined battle. In it, twenty thousand Saxons were killed, while of the others four hundred thousand and eighty died. Thus the Saxons gained possession of their land.

[Col. 0795A] At this time Sigibert, king of the Franks, was killed through the treachery of his brother Helperic, and his son Hildibert received the kingdom together with his mother Brunihilde.

Justin the Younger also died after reigning for eleven years, at about the same time, leaving Tiberius Constantine as his successor. When Tiberius died seven years later, Maurice succeeded him in the empire.

After the Lombards had been under dukes for ten years, they later agreed together to appoint Authari as their king, the son of the aforementioned Calpho, the prince who had reigned before Tado. As a great honor they called him Flavius, and afterward the Lombard kings commonly used this praenomen.

The dukes who were then in office, for the restoration of the kingdom, gave half of all their possessions for the expenses of the commonwealth, so that there would be enough for the king himself to live on, for those who served him, and for those who came to him.

This was remarkable in the kingdom of the Lombards: no one used violence against another; there was no deceit; no one unjustly compelled anyone to forced service; there were no robbers; each person traveled safely wherever he wished.

At this time the emperor Maurice sent fifty thousand solidi to Hildibert, king of the Franks, so that he might drive the Lombards from Italy. When Hildibert arrived with a large army, the Lombards entered their cities, sent gifts to King Hildibert, and made peace with him. He returned to Gaul.

When Maurice heard this, he began demanding back the solidi he had given Hildibert for the destruction of the Lombards. But Hildibert, trusting in his own strength, gave him no answer.

Meanwhile Hildibert fought against the Spaniards and defeated them. This was the cause from which they began to fight one another: King Hildibert had given his sister, named Ingund, in marriage to Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Spaniards.

Hermenegild, through the preaching of Bishop Leander and the exhortations of his wife, had been converted from the Arian heresy, which his father practiced, to the Catholic faith. For this reason his wicked father ordered him struck with an axe on the very feast of Easter.

His wife, fleeing from Spain, wished to return to her homeland. But Roman soldiers who were stationed in those regions seized her with her little son and brought her to Sicily, where she died. They sent her son to Constantinople, to the emperor Maurice.

Again Emperor Maurice sent to Hildibert, asking him to direct an army into Italy against the Lombards. Hildibert, hoping that his sister was still alive and in Constantinople and wishing to recover her, fulfilled the emperor’s wish and sent a Frankish army into Italy. But the Lombards fought against them repeatedly.

After this the Franks and the Alamanni quarreled with one another. They left Italy and returned to their own lands.

At this time a flood of waters occurred in Italy, about which blessed Gregory writes in the *Dialogue* (cf. III, 19), as well as the pestilence for which, while he was already archdeacon, he established the sevenfold litany and reluctantly accepted the Roman pontificate.

After this King Authari sent his envoys to Garibald, king of the Bavarians, asking for his daughter in marriage. Garibald received the envoys kindly and promised them his daughter, named Theodelinda.

When the envoys reported this to Authari, he desired to see his betrothed. He chose a few exceptionally brave young men, together with one very faithful man to act as though he were the lord, and hastened with them to Bavaria.

When they stood in the presence of King Garibald, and the man who appeared to be the senior had completed his speech, Authari said to the king: “My lord Authari sent me especially for this purpose, so that I might see your daughter, our lady, and be able truthfully to report to my lord what her appearance is like.”

The king immediately had her brought in. When Authari was pleased with her, he said to the king: “If it pleases your authority, let her give us a drink from her own hand, as she will also have to do afterward.”

When the king ordered this to be done, she lifted a cup full of unmixed wine. She gave it first to the man who appeared to be the senior, and then extended it to Authari, not knowing who he was.

After he had drunk and returned the cup, he secretly touched her with his finger and drew his hand across her face, with no one seeing. Blushing, she reported this to her nurse. The nurse replied: “If he were not your king and betrothed, he would never have dared to touch you. But let us be silent, and let your father not hear of this. A man who has such a bearing is worthy both to possess an empire and to take you as his wife.”

For Authari was a very handsome young man and well proportioned.

Afterward they asked the king for permission to depart and returned to their homeland. When Authari had reached the borders of Italy, accompanied by some Bavarians, he approached a tree standing beside the road. He raised himself on his horse as high as he could, struck the tree with the axe he carried in his hand, and left the axe embedded there, saying: “This is how Authari usually strikes.”

When he had said this, the Bavarians understood that he himself was Authari.

Some time later King Garibald was disturbed by the arrival of the Franks. His daughter Theodelinda, together with her brother named Gundoald [Note: [Col. 0795] in a place erased in 1], fled to Italy and sent word to her betrothed Authari to come meet them.

He was delighted. Making great preparations, he went to the field called Sardis, above Verona, and welcomed her joyfully.

Among the other Lombards there was at that time Agilolf, duke of the city of Turin. Suddenly the atmosphere became disturbed, and it began to thunder and flash violently. At once lightning struck a tree that had been placed within the king’s enclosure.

Agilolf had a certain boy who, I do not know by what art, understood what this signified. He secretly said to Agilolf: “This woman whom the king has just taken as his wife will soon be your wife.”

Angrily he replied: “If you say this another time, I shall cut off your head.”

The boy answered him: “It is true that you can cut off my head; but it is also true that this woman has come to this homeland so that she may be your wife.”

And so it happened afterward.

Meanwhile King Authari sent peaceful words to Guntrammus, king of the Franks and uncle of King Hildibert, asking him to make peace with him. Guntrammus received Authari’s envoys gladly and sent them to his nephew Hildibert, so that, according to his wishes and counsel, he might make peace with the Lombards.

King Guntrammus was peaceful and endowed with every virtue.

While the envoys were delayed in Francia, Authari died at Ticinum, reportedly by poison, after reigning for six years. Immediately the Lombards sent to King Hildibert to announce Authari’s death and ask him for peace. He received them kindly and granted the peace they requested.

Because Queen Theodelinda was pleasing to the Lombards, they allowed her to continue reigning, telling her to take as her husband whichever man she loved, provided that he was worthy to rule the kingdom.

After consulting wise men, she chose as her husband the duke Agilolf, a wise man, a warrior, and in every respect suited to rule. She immediately sent word for him to come to her, and she herself went to meet him at the fortress called Laumellum.

When they were conversing with one another, the queen ordered wine to be brought. She drank first and gave the cup to Agilolf. When he received it, he honorably kissed her hand.

Smiling, she said: “You should not kiss my hand, because you will be my king and husband.”

She then embraced him and disclosed everything that had been arranged, according to the counsel of the wise men, concerning the government of the kingdom and their marriage.

Meanwhile the wedding was celebrated with great joy. Agilolf, who was a kinsman of King Authari, began to reign at the beginning of November. Later, when the Lombards had assembled together at Milan in the month of May, he was confirmed in the kingdom.

Agilolf, also called Agio, having his royal dignity confirmed, sent Bishop Agnellus of Trent to Francia to recover those people who had been taken captive by the Franks from the castles of Trent. When Agnellus arrived, Queen Brunihilde ransomed many of them at her own expense and gave them to him to bring back.

[Col. 0797D] In these days blessed Gregory, pope of Rome, wrote the *Dialogue* and sent it as a gift to Queen Theodelinda, because he knew that she was most Christian and God-fearing. Through her, indeed, many good things were accomplished in the Church of God.

For while the Lombards were still held in the error of paganism, they had carried off almost all the possessions of the churches. But she, through her prayers, brought the king himself also to the Catholic faith, bestowed many possessions on the churches, and restored to their proper dignity the bishops, who previously had no honor.

At this time Tassilo was appointed king in Bavaria by Hildibert, king of the Franks, and immediately marched with an army into the territory of the Slavs. Having won a victory, he returned to his own land with great booty. [Col. 0798A]

Thus, while the Lombards ruled throughout all Italy, when Agilolf came into the Roman territories, blessed Gregory was so terrified by his arrival that, as he himself testifies, he ceased writing his exposition of Ezekiel. He began frequently to admonish Queen Theodelinda through his letters, urging her to persuade her husband Agilolf to maintain peace with the Romans. This was indeed done. Therefore that venerable priest, giving thanks, sent letters to the same queen and to King Agilolf; these are found written in the book of his Life.

At this time King Hildibert was killed by poison, as they say, together with his wife. King Guntrammus also died. [Col. 0798B]

Around this time the Lombards destroyed the monastery of Saint Benedict at the fortress of Cassino. For they entered it by night and carried everything away, but, in accordance with the prophecy of the man of God, they could seize none of the monks. The monks fled and came to Rome, carrying with them the book of the holy Rule, which the same blessed father had composed, as well as other writings, and also a weight of bread and a measure of wine, together with whatever else they had been able to carry away from there. After blessed Benedict, Constantine governed that monastery; after him, Simplicius; after him, Vitalis; after him, Bonitus, under whom this destruction took place. [Col. 0798C]

In these days Queen Theodelinda built the church of blessed John the Baptist at Modicia, which is twelve miles from Milan. She adorned that church with many ornaments of gold and silver and granted it many estates. In the same place King Theodoric of the Goths had once built a palace, because the place is temperate and agreeable in summer; indeed, it lies near the Alps.

At that time a son was born to Agilolf and Queen Theodelinda in the palace at Modicia. He was baptized there and was named Adolandus; Secundus, a servant of God from Tridentum, received him from the sacred font.

Until this time the city of Padua had been rebellious against the Lombards, because the soldiers stationed there resisted with the utmost force. But afterward they cast fire there and set the city ablaze; by order of King Agilolf it was overturned to the ground. The soldiers who were in it, however, were permitted to return to Ravenna. [Col. 0798D]

During the reign of this Agilolf, blessed Columban came to Italy and founded the monastery called Bobium in the Cottian Alps.

Thus Agilolf, also called Agio, after reigning for twenty years, died, leaving his son Adolandus, still a child, in the kingship with his mother Theodelinda. After he had reigned for ten years, he lost his reason, and they expelled him from the kingdom. In his place they appointed a certain Arioald, whose ancestry is not recorded. [Col. 0799A] After he had held the kingdom for twelve years, he died, and the kingdom was taken over by Ruotheri, a strong and vigorous man, but stained by the Arian perfidy. In his time there were, in nearly all the cities of his kingdom, two bishops: one Catholic and the other Arian.

This King Ruotheri of the Lombards composed laws and called the book itself an edict. It was already the seventy-seventh year since the Lombards had come to Italy. After reigning for sixteen years and four months, he died and left the kingdom to his son Radoald. He himself was buried beside the church of blessed John the Baptist.

After some time a certain man, driven by wicked greed, opened his tomb by night and took all the ornaments from his body. Blessed John then appeared to him in a vision and said: “Why did you dare to touch the body of this man? Although he did not believe correctly, he nevertheless commended himself to me. Since, therefore, you presumed to do this, you shall never again enter that church.” And so it happened. For whenever he tried to enter that church, he suddenly fell backward, as though someone intended to strike him in the throat with a great knife.

Accordingly, after his father’s death, Radoald took possession of the kingdom and married Guntbirga, the daughter of Agilolf and Theodelinda. This Guntbirga built the church of Saint John the Baptist in the city of Ticinum, just as her mother had done at Modicia; she adorned it with ornaments and enriched it with possessions, and was herself buried there.

When she was accused before her husband that Carellus, her servant, had committed adultery, Carellus asked the king to permit him to fight in single combat against the man who had defamed his mistress. Fighting him before the whole people, he threw him down; thus the queen recovered her former honor. [Note: A folio is missing in MS 1.] [Col. 0799C]

King Radoald [Note: “Rodoaldus” in witness 9c], however, as they say, committed adultery with the wife of a certain Lombard and was killed by that man, after he had reigned for five years and seven days. Aripert succeeded him, the son of Gundoald, who had been Queen Theodelinda’s brother. He built a church in honor of the Lord and Savior at Ticinum, adorned it with various ornaments, and enriched it with possessions.

Thus the emperor Maurice, after reigning for twenty-one years with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine, was killed by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus; Phocas himself then reigned. After he had ruled for eight years, Heraclius, who governed Africa, rebelled against him, came with an army, killed him, and assumed the empire.

After Heraclius had died twenty-seven years later [Note: “after five years” in the manuscript], his son Constantine assumed the empire. But when Constantine had been killed by poison after four months, his brother Heracleonas and their mother Martina seized the kingdom. After they were soon deposed, Constans, the son of Constantine, reigned for twenty-eight years. [Col. 0799D]

King Aripert, after ruling the Lombards at Ticinum for nine years, died and left the kingdom to his two sons, Perhtari [Note: “Perthari” in witnesses 4, 5, 9c, 10, 11, and so thereafter] and Gotepertus [Note: “Gotebertus” in witnesses 9c and 10; “Godebertus” in witness 4 and thereafter]. Gotepertus sat at Ticinum, and Perhtari at Milan.

Finally, through the agency of wicked men, hatred and discord arose between the two brothers, to such an extent that each strove to take the kingdom from the other. For this reason Gotepertus sent Garibald, duke of Turin, to Grimoald, duke of Benevento, asking him to come and assist him against his brother and promising to give him his sister in marriage if he helped him.

But Garibald betrayed his lord and gave Grimoald [Note: “Grimaldus” in witness 4; “Grimoldus” in witness 9c, consistently] the advice that he should come and seize the kingdom of the Lombards, which the two brothers, being young men, were squandering. Grimoald was already of mature age and was good in counsel and strong in valor. Hearing this, Grimoald immediately turned his mind toward taking the Lombard kingdom. He appointed his son Romoald duke in Benevento, then himself set out toward Ticinum with a chosen multitude of men. He sent messages through all the cities and made friends for himself, so that he might obtain the kingdom.

He sent Trasemund, count of Capua, through Polentia and Tuscany to invite all the Lombards in those regions to come to his assistance [Note: “a. ejus” in witness 5]. Trasemund did so, and met him near Emilia with substantial support. [Col. 0800B]

When Grimoald reached Placentia, he sent Garibald ahead to inform Gotepertus [Note: “Gotebertus,” now also in witness 5] of his arrival. Hearing this, Gotepertus asked Garibald [Note: “Geribaldus” in witness 9c] for advice about where he should prepare lodging for Grimoald. Garibald replied that it was fitting for Grimoald, who had come on his account and was to receive his sister, to have lodging inside the palace.

This was done. Then the aforementioned Garibald, the sower of malice, said to Gotepertus: “When you come to confer with Grimoald, wear a coat of mail beneath your clothing, because he is seeking to kill you.” He then said the same words to Grimoald.

When they came together on the following day to confer, Grimoald saw that Gotepertus was wearing a coat of mail. He drew his sword, killed him, and seized his kingdom. Gotepertus had a little son named Reginpert, whom his loyal followers took away and secretly raised. Grimoald did not bother to pursue him, because he was still a child. [Col. 0800D]

When Perhtari, who was ruling at Milan, heard that his brother had died, he fled as quickly as he could and went to Cacan, king of the Avars. Grimoald sent his wife, named Rodelinda, and his little son, named Chunibertus [Note: “Cunibertus” in witness 5], into Benevento.

After this, the wicked man Garibald, through whose counsel all these events had occurred, did not long rejoice in them. There was in the city of Turin a certain little man, a very small fellow, born of Gotepertus’s own people. Knowing that Garibald would come on the most holy day of Easter to pray in the church of blessed John the Baptist, he went and climbed onto the sacred font of the baptistery. With his left hand he held onto a small column beside which Garibald would have to pass, while with his right he concealed a drawn sword beneath his clothing.

When Garibald came near him, the little man [Note: “pergit” in MS 1] drew his sword and struck him in the neck with all the force he could muster, cutting off his head. Garibald’s men inflicted many wounds on the attacker and ultimately killed him. Although he died after being punished in this way, he had nevertheless avenged the injury and death of his lord. [Col. 0801B]

Grimoald, having been confirmed in the kingdom at Ticinum, killed Chunibertus, the son of Gotepertus [Note: “Godepertus,” corrected to “Gotepertus” in witness 1], and married Gotepertus’s sister [Note: so in witness 1], the daughter of Aripert. He sent the Beneventan army with which he had seized the kingdom back to its own territory, enriched with great gifts, although he retained some of them and granted them very generous estates.

When he heard that Perhtari had fled to Scythia and was staying with Cacan, king of the Huns, he sent word to Cacan that if Perhtari remained in his kingdom, he could no longer maintain peace with the Lombards as he had until then. When Cacan heard this, he said to Perhtari: “Go wherever you wish, because you cannot remain in my kingdom, lest on your account I incur the hostility of the Lombards.”

When Perhtari heard this, he chose to return to Grimoald, because he had heard that Grimoald was most merciful. When he reached the city of Lodi, he sent Unulf, a man most faithful to him, to Grimoald to announce his arrival. When Grimoald heard this, he rejoiced greatly and sent him word, promising that he would suffer no harm if he came to him.

Accordingly, when Perhtari entered Grimoald’s presence, he wished to throw himself at his feet. But Grimoald did not allow him to do so; he held him back and kissed him. Then Perhtari said to Grimoald: “I am your servant. I could indeed have lived among the pagans, but when I heard that you were most Christian and most merciful, I came to you for the sake of your good name.”

Then the king promised him under oath before everyone, saying: “By him who caused me to be born, since you have come under my protection, no harm shall come to you.” He gave him an excellent house and ordered his servants to ensure that he had, from the public treasury, an abundant supply of everything he needed.

Then all the people of Ticinum began to flock to him and greet him as though he were an acquaintance. Immediately, malicious speakers approached Grimoald and said to him: “Unless you kill Perhtari quickly, you will not possess the kingdom. Everyone is flocking to him, and because of him they may perhaps kill you.” [Col. 0802A]

Trusting these words, Grimoald forgot the oath he had sworn to him and discussed with his men how he might kill him. Finally, on the advice of his counselors, he sent him various foods, excellent wine, and various drinks for dinner, so that when Perhtari lay as if dead through the night, he could be killed more easily.

When he sat down to dinner, however, one of his former servants came to him, bringing the food which the king had sent. After placing it on the table, he pretended to greet Perhtari and, putting his head beneath the table, secretly informed him of Grimoald’s plan.

Perhtari immediately called his cupbearer and ordered him to mix his drink in a golden cup, but always to put only water into it. Then the king’s messengers, acting on his orders, urged him to drink cheerfully and empty the entire cup in honor of Grimoald. He said that he was drinking the whole cup gladly and emptying it in Grimoald’s honor, but he drank nothing except water.

The king’s servants continued to go and report to him that Perhtari was drinking a great deal of wine and was already drunk. Grimoald said cheerfully: “Let that drunkard drink today; tomorrow he will vomit out those same wines together with his blood.”

Meanwhile Perhtari called Unulf, his most faithful servant, and disclosed to him the king’s intention and plan. When Unulf heard this, he summoned his own servant and ordered him to prepare a bed beside Perhtari’s bed.

After dinner, when the king had sent men to guard Perhtari so that he could not escape, Perhtari entered the bedchamber where he was to sleep with Unulf and his most faithful chamberlain. He informed the chamberlain that the king was plotting his death and said: “If I am able to escape, pretend, by speaking to the king’s men, that I am sleeping in this room; perhaps, by escaping from their hands, I shall free myself.”

When the chamberlain gladly promised to do this, Unulf took a mattress and a bearskin, placed them on Perhtari’s back, and began to beat him as though he were a peasant servant, striking him with a bar and driving him with his fist at the neck out through the palace [Note: i.e. “door,” as is frequently found in the Bamberg manuscript of Paul, which Ekk. used].

When the king’s soldiers asked what this meant, Unulf said: “This peasant servant made my bed beside Perhtari’s bed. Perhtari is so drunk that he is sleeping as though he were dead.” When they heard and believed this to be true, they were pleased and allowed Perhtari to leave as though he were a peasant servant.

The most faithful chamberlain remained in the room, closed it, and firmly secured it. When the king’s servants saw this, they returned to their lord.

Unulf lowered several men by a rope to Perhtari, his lord, so that they could go with him. They began fleeing together, and when they found horses in a meadow, they seized them, mounted them, and reached the city of Asti that same night. There Perhtari had very loyal friends [Note: “amie” in MS 1], because the city had not yet submitted to Grimoald.

From there Perhtari fled to the city of Turin and reached Francia. Thus almighty God saved the innocent Perhtari from death and prevented Grimoald from committing murder.

On the following day Grimoald, expecting Perhtari to be sleeping in his lodging, sent men to bring him. From that place to the palace he stationed men on both sides, so that Perhtari could not escape by any stratagem.

When the king’s messengers arrived, they began shouting at the palace door where the chamberlain was staying, in order to awaken Perhtari. The chamberlain said: “Have mercy on him and let him sleep, because he is tired from the journey and is still sleeping deeply.”

When they reported this to the king, he said: “He was so drunk last night that he still cannot wake up.” He sent again, ordering that Perhtari be brought more quickly.

They came to the door where they expected him to be sleeping and shouted loudly to awaken him. The chamberlain again begged them to let him sleep a little longer. Angry, they said: “That drunkard has slept long enough.” They kicked in the palace doors, entered the room, searched the bed, and, not finding him, asked the chamberlain what had become of him.

The chamberlain replied that he had fled. They seized him by the hair, beat him with clubs, tied his hands behind his back, and led him to the king, saying: “This man knows how Perhtari escaped, and therefore deserves death.” [Col. 0803C]

The king ordered them to untie him and commanded him to explain in detail how Perhtari had escaped. He recounted everything as it had happened.

Then the king asked those standing around him: “What does this man deserve, who has done such a wicked thing?” They all replied that he ought to die a cruel death.

But the king said: “By him who caused me to be born, this man ought to be treated well, for he was willing to give himself over to death for his lord.” He then ordered that the man become one of his chamberlains, promising him many rewards if he kept such faith with him as he had kept with Perhtari.

Then the king asked what had happened to Unulf. The answer was: “He fled to the church of Saint Michael the Archangel.” The king immediately sent for him, promising that he would suffer no harm if only he came to him quickly.

When Unulf heard this, he hastened to the palace and immediately threw himself at the king’s feet. When the king asked him how Perhtari had escaped, he told him the whole truth of the matter.

Then, praising his prudence and loyalty before everyone, the king placed all his wealth at his disposal, so that he might be the most honored man in the palace.

After several days the king asked him whether he would rather remain with him or with Perhtari. Unulf began to swear that he would prefer to die with Perhtari rather than live anywhere in the greatest luxury.

Then the king summoned that chamberlain and ordered him to say whether he thought it better to remain in the palace or to go into exile with Perhtari. The chamberlain gave the same answer that Unulf had given earlier.

When the king heard this, he rejoiced greatly and praised their loyalty. He said to Unulf: “Take whatever you wish from my household—men, horses, or anything else—and go to your lord without suffering any injury.” He said the same to the chamberlain.

They took everything they needed and, with the permission of King Grimoald, went to their most beloved lord Perhtari in the territory of the Franks. [Col. 0804A]

At this time Dagobert held the kingdom of the Franks, with whom Grimoald maintained firm peace. The Roman Empire was taken over by Constantine, the son of Constans, and he held it for seventeen years [Note: “XVII” corrected to “XVII” in witness 1].

After this Grimoald underwent bloodletting in the palace. When, nine days later, he wished to shoot at a dove, a vein in his arm burst and he died. In the edict that King Ruotheri had composed, he added several chapters. He was very large in body and extremely bold, bald-headed, with a long beard, and foremost in counsel and valor. He was buried in the church of Saint Ambrose, which he himself had built.

He left his son Garibald, whom he had had by the daughter of King Aripert, as heir to the kingdom, though still a child; his son Romoald, however, he had already appointed duke in Benevento. [Col. 0804B]

When Perhtari was in Francia, fearing Grimoald because Grimoald was allied with the Frankish king, he wished to flee to Britain. As he sailed across the open sea, he suddenly heard someone from the shore saying: “If Perhtari is in this ship, tell him to return to his own country, because it is already three days since King Grimoald died.”

When Perhtari heard this, he sailed close to the shore to see who was speaking. But when he found no one, he realized that an angel had spoken these words. He immediately turned back, came to Ticinum, and found there a multitude of Lombards, who received him joyfully.

He expelled the child Garibald, Grimoald’s son, from the kingdom, and in the third month thereafter the Lombards appointed him king over themselves. He was a just man, upright in the faith of Christ, and a nourisher of the poor. [Col. 0804D]

He sent to Benevento and brought from there his wife Rodelinda and his son Cunibert, whom Grimoald had sent there into exile.

After this Perhtari built a monastery at the very place from which he had previously fled. He had it dedicated in honor of God and the holy virgin Agatha, gathered many virgins there, and gave it many ornaments and possessions.

His wife Rodelinda also built a church in honor of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary outside the walls of Ticinum, at a place called Ad Perticas, adorning it with marvelous ornaments. [Col. 0805A]

Thus Perhtari, after reigning alone for seven years, in the eighth year appointed his son Cunibert to share the kingdom with him. They ruled together for ten years.

While they were reigning in complete tranquility, the son of the devil, named Alachis [Note: “Alahis” corrected to “Alachis” in witness 1], from Tridentum, rose up against them. But Cunibert, the king’s son, who was fond of Alachis [Note: “Alahis” in witness 1], restored him to his father’s favor.

The king often wished to kill Alachis [Note: “Alahin” corrected to “Alachin” in witness 1, and likewise thereafter], but Cunibert always pleaded for him, hoping that at some time he would become loyal to him. Moreover, he did not cease asking his father to give Alachis the dukedom of Brescia.

Perhtari said: “You are asking for your own destruction, by giving Alachis such power that he may be able to reign. The city of Brescia has always possessed a multitude of noble Lombards.” For this reason Perhtari feared that Alachis would rule there.

After Perhtari had reigned for eighteen years, he died and was buried beside the church that his father Aripert had built.

After his death, his son Cunibert married a woman named Ermelinda, of the race of the Anglo-Saxons.

But Alachis forgot all the benefits that Cunibert had done for him. He joined himself with Aldo and Grauso of Brescia and with many Lombards. When Cunibert was not in Pavia, Alachis entered his palace and rebelled against him.

When Cunibert heard this, he fled into Lake Larius near Como. Great distress then arose among all who loved him, especially the clerics and priests, whom Alachis hated. [Col. 0805C]

At that time there was in the church of Ticinum a bishop named Damianus, a most holy and most wise man. Seeing that Alachis possessed the palace, and fearing that either his church or he himself might suffer harm, he sent to him, with the blessing of his church, his deacon named Thomas, a wise and religious man.

When Alachis was informed that Deacon Thomas was coming to him with the blessing of his bishop, he—because he hated all clerics—sent him this message: “If he has clean femoralia, that is, clean breeches, let him enter to me; otherwise let him remain outside.”

Thomas replied: “Tell him that I have clean femoralia, for today I put on freshly washed clothing.”

Alachis sent back to him: “I am not speaking about his femoralia, but about what he has inside his femoralia.”

To this Deacon Thomas replied: “God alone can find fault with me in these matters; he cannot.”

When Alachis had him brought in, he spoke to him with great anger. When all the clerics heard this, they were exceedingly afraid, expecting that, because of his cruelty, they would be unable to live in that city. They began to desire and love their King Cunibert as greatly as they heard Alachis described as cruel and proud.

Therefore his cruelty and pride did not last long. One day, when he was counting solidi on his table, a tremissis fell. The young son of Aldo picked it up from the ground and returned it to him.

Alachis, supposing that the child still understood nothing, said: “Your father has many of these; if God wills, he will soon be giving them to me.”

When the little boy returned home in the evening, his father asked whether the king had said anything to him. After the boy reported everything that had been done and said, Aldo became extremely afraid. He went to his brother Grauso and reported the king’s words to him. At once they both began to consult with their friends about the king’s destruction. [Col. 0806A]

In the morning they went to the palace and spoke to Alachis as follows: “Why do you consent to remain in the city forever? Look: the entire city and all the people are loyal to you, while that drunken Cunibert has been so thoroughly humbled that he can no longer possess any power against you. So leave the city and go hunting with your young men. We, together with your other loyal followers, will defend this city for you. We also promise you that soon we shall bring you the head of your enemy Cunibert.”

Persuaded by their words, Alachis left the city and went into the forest to hunt with his men.

Aldo and Grauso, however, went to Lake Como, boarded a ship, and proceeded to King Cunibert. Throwing themselves at his feet, they asked forgiveness for what they had done against him, and told him what harm Alachis had intended to do to them and what advice they had given him.

When King Cunibert heard this, he rejoiced greatly. They exchanged an oath with one another and set a day on which Cunibert would come to Ticinum and they would admit him into the city.

When the appointed day came, Cunibert arrived, and they received him gladly, as they had promised. Then everyone—the bishop, priests, and clerics, young and old—ran to him joyfully, giving thanks to God for his return. Some embraced his knees and others his feet; he in turn kissed as friends as many as he could.

Suddenly a messenger came from there to Alachis and told him that Aldo and Grauso had brought not merely Cunibert’s head, as they had promised, but his whole body, and had placed it in the palace.

When Alachis heard this, he was greatly distressed. He departed in furious anger, went through Placentia and many cities, seizing some by persuasion and others by force, and gathered everyone he could in order to fight Cunibert. [Col. 0806D]

When Cunibert, for his part, gathered his own men, the two forces met in a field called Coronatus, where they took their positions.

Cunibert sent a message to Alachis: “Why should such a multitude of men perish? Let you and I fight, and let the victor possess the kingdom.”

Alachis refused.

One of his people, a Tuscan by birth, said to him: “Why do you not fight him? You are the strongest and boldest of men. Why do you not go forth courageously and fight him?”

Alachis replied: “Although Cunibert is a drunkard, he is nevertheless very strong. In the time of his father, when we were boys, there were larger rams in the palace. Cunibert would seize any one of them by the wool on its back and carry it with one hand, which I could not do.”

When that Tuscan heard this, he said: “If you cannot fight him, you shall no longer have me as an ally.” Immediately he left Alachis, went to Cunibert, and told him all these things. [Col. 0807A]

When the time had nearly come for the two sides to join battle, a certain deacon named Seno, who loved Cunibert greatly and feared that he would die in the battle, said to him:

“My lord king, all our hope rests in you. If you die in battle, that most cruel Alachis will kill us all by various tortures. Therefore accept my advice: give me all your armor, and I shall go and fight this adversary. If I die, you will recover your cause; if I win, you will have the greater glory, because through your servant you will gain the victory.”

When Cunibert absolutely refused this, his most faithful followers who were present asked him to consent. Then he agreed, clothed the deacon in all his armor, and sent him into battle in his place.

When the two sides were fighting, Alachis kept watching for the place where Deacon Seno stood. Thinking that he was Cunibert, he attacked and killed him. Then, rejoicing, he ordered his head to be cut off. Raising it on a spear, he gave thanks to God that he had killed Cunibert.

But when they removed the helmet from the man’s head, it became evident that he was a cleric. Then Alachis cried out in great anger: “Alas for me! We have accomplished nothing by engaging in this battle, in which we have killed a cleric.” He immediately made this vow: if he gained victory over Cunibert, he would fill a well with the testicles of clerics.

Cunibert, seeing that his men were giving way because they thought he was dead, showed himself to them, encouraging them and saying: “Do not be afraid; now we must conquer our enemies.”

Again both sides prepared for battle. When they were already close to joining combat [Note: the passage is absent in witness 1; “conjungeret” in witness 1], Cunibert once more sent a message to Alachis, saying: “Why should the people perish? Let the two of us fight, and let the victor rule over all this people.”

When Alachis’s men asked him why he would not fight him, he replied: “I cannot do this, because I see the image of Saint Michael the Archangel among his spears, where I swore an oath to him.” [Col. 0807D]

One of them said to him: “Through fear you see something that is not there, and it is already too late for you to say this.”

When the two sides engaged, many fell on both sides. Alachis also fell, and Cunibert, with the Lord’s assistance, gained the victory. Alachis’s head and legs were cut off, and only his mutilated trunk remained. The king returned to Ticinum with joy and victory.

While these things were happening among the Lombards beyond the Po, Romoald, the son of Grimoald and duke of the Beneventans, gathered an army and began to attack Tarentum and Brundisium; he brought the whole region under his control. His wife Diederada built a monastery in honor of the apostle Saint Peter outside the walls of the city of Benevento, where she established a community of maidens dedicated to Christ.

After Romoald had reigned for sixteen years, he died. His son Grimoald governed Benevento for three years and married Wigilinda, the daughter of King Perhtari and sister of Cunibert. After Grimoald’s death, his brother Gisolf became duke and held the dukedom for seventeen years. He had a wife named Winibirga, the daughter of Duke Radoald. [Col. 0808A]

Around this time, after the monastery of Saint Benedict on Mount Cassino had lain abandoned for many years, Franks from Celmania and Aurelia came to the same place. Pretending that they were lying in the very place where the bodies of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica lay, they took their bones and carried them to their own country. There two monasteries were built: one in honor of Saint Benedict and the other in honor of Saint Scholastica.

But we firmly believe that the venerable mouth which was always meditating on divine words, and the eyes which were always seeing heavenly things, together with his other members, although dissolved, remained in the same place. For only the Lord’s body did not see corruption; the bodies of the other saints, although they are to be restored in eternal glory, were nevertheless dissolved in this world. [Col. 0808B]

While these events were taking place in Italy, a heresy arose at Constantinople. It was stirred up by George, patriarch of Constantinople, and by Macarius, Pyrrhus, Peter, and Paul, who separated divinity and humanity in Christ.

For this reason the emperor Constantine had one hundred and fifty bishops assembled. Among them were two legates of the holy Roman Church, sent by Pope Agatho: John the deacon and John, bishop of Porto. After the council had been held, they condemned the aforementioned heresy.

At that very hour such a great mass of spiders’ webs fell in the midst of the people that everyone marveled at it. This was seen to signify that the heresy would be emptied out. The aforementioned patriarch George was admonished and corrected by the bishops; the others, however, who remained in their perfidy, were anathematized by all the bishops. This is the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, that is, the synod which the whole world accepts. [Col. 0808D]

In these same times, during the eighth indiction, an eclipse of the moon appeared. On the second day of the beginning of May, an eclipse of the sun occurred at the tenth hour of the day; afterward, in July, August, and September, there was a great mortality.

At that time two angels, one good and the other evil, visibly appeared to many people walking through the City by night. The evil angel held a spear in his hand, and, at the command of the good angel, struck the door of whatever house he approached; on the following day all the people in that house died. [Col. 0809A]

After this, a good man was told in a vision that the mortality would not cease unless an altar were dedicated in the church of Saint Peter called “Ad Vincula,” in honor of the martyr Saint Sebastian. When this was done, the mortality ceased.

Meanwhile King Chunibert consulted with one of his most trusted men about how he might kill Aldo and Grauso. While they were speaking to each other about this matter, standing near a certain window, a fly suddenly settled on that window. When Chunibert wished to kill it, he cut off only one of its feet with the knife he was holding. As Aldo and Grauso were making their way to the king’s palace and had already drawn near, [Col. 0809B] a man with a mutilated foot met them and told them that King Chunibert wanted to kill them. When they heard this, they fled into the church of Saint Romanus the martyr and hid behind the altar of that church. When this was reported to the king, he immediately summoned his trusted servant, the only man to whom he had confided the matter, and said to him: “Why did you disclose my plan to someone?” Trembling, the man replied: “My lord king, you know that after you spoke to me I never went out of your sight; how, then, could I have told this to anyone?”

Then the king sent word to Aldo and Grauso, asking why they had fled into the church. They replied: “Because we heard that the king wanted to kill us.” Again the king sent to them and asked who had reported this to them, saying that they would not have his favor unless they revealed it to him. Then they disclosed everything that had happened, saying: “A man met us whose foot had been cut off up to the knee, and he himself told us this.” Then King Chunibert understood that the fly had been the devil and that he himself had reported this to them. He immediately summoned them, restored his favor to them, and honored them until their death.

Meanwhile the Emperor Constantine died, and his younger son Justinian held the kingdom for ten years. Against him came a certain Leo, seized him, mutilated his nose, expelled him from the kingdom, and himself reigned for three years, exiling Justinian to a certain island. Again Tiberius expelled this Leo from the kingdom, held the kingdom himself, and placed Leo in custody. After this Justinian recovered his kingdom with the assistance of Terebellus, king of the Bulgars, and had Leo and Tiberius beheaded publicly in the middle of the circus.

In those days Cedoaldus, king of the Anglo-Saxons, who had fought many battles in his homeland, was converted to Christ. Journeying toward Rome, he came to King Chunibert, who received him with great honor. He then went to Rome and was baptized by the blessed Pope Sergius, receiving the name Peter. While he was still in his baptismal robes, he died and was buried in the church of Saint Peter.

At this time there was in the kingdom of the Franks a man named Arnulfus, beloved of God, who later abandoned the world and became a bishop.

Cunibert, after reigning alone for twelve years following his father’s death, died and left the kingdom to his son Liopert, who was still a small child. He appointed the wise man Asprandus as his guardian. After eight months Reginpert, duke of the people of Turin, came with an army against Asprandus and Ruotharius, dukes of Pergamum. Fighting them, he defeated them and seized the kingdom; but he died that same year. His son Aripert then fought against King Liopert at Ticinum and captured Liopert alive in battle, while his guardian Asprandus fled to the island of Comacina.

When Duke Ruotharius had returned to Pergamum, Aripert besieged and stormed the city with [Col. 0810B] a large army. After capturing Ruotharius, he had his head and beard shaved and exiled him; Ruotharius died after some time. As for the boy Liopert, Aripert sent him to the bathhouse and shut the door upon him, so that he died from the excessive heat.

When Aripert was now reigning securely, he seized Sigibrandus, the son of Asprandus, blinded him, and afflicted all his relatives with various tortures. He kept Liutprandus, Asprandus’s younger son, in prison; but because he was still a very young child, he thought little of him and did not wish to harm him. Instead, he allowed him to go to his father.

Liutprandus therefore went to his father in Bavaria, where Asprandus had long before fled from that same Aripert, to Duke Theodebert. Asprandus remained with him for nine years. When Liutprandus arrived, he was received with great joy.

At this time in Gaul, in the kingdom of the Franks, Ansgis, the son of the aforementioned Arnulfus, held power under the title of mayor of the palace. He seems to derive his name from Anchises the Trojan.

After Asprandus had remained in Bavaria for nine years, he stirred up Theodepert, duke of the Bavarians, who came into Italy with an army. He fought Aripert, and many men from both sides died. Although night brought the battle to an end, it is nevertheless certain that the Bavarians fled and that Aripert returned victorious to the camp. Since he did not wish to remain in the camp but [Col. 0810D] went to Ticinum, he caused his own people to despair and gave courage to his adversaries.

After he had entered the city and realized that the people were angry with him because of this act, he resolved to flee to Francia. He took as much gold as he wished from the palace and departed. When he attempted to swim across the river Ticinum, weighed down with gold, he was suffocated by the water and died. The next day his body was found and buried in the church of the Lord Savior.

After his death Asprandus held the kingdom of the Lombards and reigned for only three months. He was altogether a good man, and few people could equal his wisdom. When the Lombards saw that Asprandus was dying, they made his son Liutprandus king while his father was still alive.

[Col. 0811A] Philippicus killed the Emperor Justinian and held his kingdom for one year and six months. Anastasius, also called Artemius, rose up against him, expelled him from the kingdom, and caused his eyes to be torn out.

When Anastasius sent ships to Alexandria against the Saracens, the soldiers who had turned aside to Constantinople sought out Theodosius, an orthodox man, and compelled him by force to assume the kingdom. The same Theodosius left Constantinople for Nicaea, fought against Anastasius, and defeated him. He extracted an oath from him, ordered him to become a cleric, and afterward had him ordained a presbyter. After Theodosius died one year later, Leo became emperor.

[Col. 0811B] At that time Pippin reigned in the kingdom of the Franks. He was exceedingly bold and always gained victory over his enemies. He had sons, among whom Charles proved to be the best; he succeeded his father in the kingdom.

About this time, moved by divine love, Petronax of Brescia came to Rome. At the urging [Note: [Col. 0811] “and p. e.” [uncertain abbreviation], in an erased place in manuscript 1.] of the blessed Gregory, who was then pope, he went to the fortress of Cassino and began living there with the simple men who at that time resided there. They subsequently made this venerable man Petronax their abbot. Many noblemen immediately began to flock to him. With the assistance of divine grace and through the merits of the blessed father Benedict, he restored the former dwellings [Col. 0811C] and, living with everyone under the yoke of the holy Rule according to the order of the blessed Benedict, brought that holy monastery into a good condition.

The pope Zacharias, beloved of God, gave this venerable man much assistance, providing him with books of Holy Scripture and other things useful to the monastery, as well as the Rule that the blessed father Benedict had written with his own hands. From the time that that place was destroyed until the aforesaid abbot Petronax, one hundred and ten years had elapsed.

In Francia, after Pippin’s death, his son Charles, through many battles, took the principate from the power of Reginfrid. Meanwhile King Liutprandus, hearing that the Saracens were plundering Sardinia, paid a large price and sent men to Sardinia.
