He had the bones of Saint Augustine the bishop brought from there and placed them honorably in Ticinum.

After this Charles, king of the Franks, sent his son Pippin to King Liutprandus, so that Liutprandus might cut his hair and thereby become his godfather. Liutprandus did so and sent the boy back to his father with many gifts.

King Liutprandus then built many churches in various places. He built outside the walls of the city of Ticinum a monastery of the blessed apostle Peter called the Golden Heaven. High in the Alps, in his own estate, he built a monastery called [Col. 0812A] Barcetum; likewise, in his own estate of Alonna, he built a monastery in honor of Saint Anastasius the martyr. He also built a church of the Lord Savior in his palace and appointed priests and clerics there to celebrate the divine offices daily—something no other king before him had done.

After reigning for thirty-one years and seven months, he died and was buried in the church of Saint Adrian the martyr, where his father was also buried. He was wise and strong, a lover of peace, merciful toward those at fault, chaste, devoted to prayers and vigils, and generous in almsgiving. He did not know letters, yet he was so wise that he might be compared with philosophers.

Up to this point, it is sufficient to have given a brief account of the origin of the Lombard people, their entry into Italy, and the succession of their kings, while also briefly touching upon the names and times of the Roman emperors who reigned in the meantime. Now let the narrative return to the arrangement of the sequence begun earlier, from which we digressed for a little while.

(H. m.) The Emperor Justinus made Tiberius, commander of the imperial guards, his son, called him caesar, and appointed him his associate. The emperor suffered from an ailment of the feet and therefore spent much of his time lying in bed. Afterward, when he fell ill but shortly thereafter recovered from his sickness, he summoned both Euticius the pontiff and the senate, as well as all the priests and citizens. Having brought in the caesar Tiberius, he publicly called him emperor before everyone, using these words:

“Behold, God has done you a favor; God has given you this position, not I. Honor him, so that you too may be honored by him. Honor your mother, who was once your mistress; you know that at first you were her servant, but now you are her son. Do not rejoice in bloodshed, and do not share in murder. Do not repay evil with evil, lest you become like me in the evil of enmity. Do not let this position raise you up as it raised me. Regard everyone as you regard yourself. Know what you have been, so that you may not become proud, and you will not sin. All these are your sons and servants; when you look upon them, you see all who belong to the commonwealth.”

When he had said this, and after the patriarch had offered a prayer and everyone had said “Amen,” the caesar fell at the emperor’s feet and said to him: “If you wish, I am; if you wish, I am not.” The emperor replied: “May God, who made heaven and earth, place in your heart all that I have forgotten to say.”

While the emperor was speaking these words, the entire assembly was filled with tears. After this Justinus died in the eleventh year of his reign, leaving Tiberius as his successor.

The Years of Justinus.

[Note: [Col. 0811] Absent in manuscripts 1 and 4.]

1. (Chr. W.) In the first year of Justinus, which is the year 565 of the Lord’s incarnation, the Armenians received the faith.

3. (H. m.) A.D. 567. The Augusta Sophia summoned the notaries and ordered the debt acknowledgments and registers to be brought to her, and forgave them all their debts. [Note: [Col. 0811] “after” is supplied in one manuscript.] (Chr. W.) In the same year Narses the patrician killed King Totila and scattered the Goths.

[Col. 0813A] 4. A.D. 568. The Lombards, making for Italy, departed from Pannonia (cf. P. D.).

6. A.D. 570. [Note: [Col. 0813A] D? E., and at the end of year 5, add: “Saint Vedastus died.” However, 9c. is missing in [Col. 0813]. Cf. Sigeb.] The Lombards entered Milan.

7. A.D. 571. [Note: [Col. 0813A] D? E. 4–11 add: “Gregory of Tours, bishop, shines in Gaul.” [In [Col. 0813], 4–11 are missing at “in Gaul.” Cf. Sigeb.]]

11. (Chr. W.) A.D. 575. The Emperor Justinus died. Some writers state (P. D. III, 11) that he fell into the Pelagian heresy and therefore, by God’s just judgment, lost his reason and ended his life in madness.

The Years of Tiberius.

(H. m.) In the year 576 of the Lord’s incarnation, and in the 1,327th year from the founding of the City, Tiberius Constantine, a Thracian by origin, receiving the empire as the fifty-fifth ruler after Augustus, was crowned by Euticius the patriarch and reigned for seven years.

He sent for his wife Anastasia and brought her to him, and crowned her. When she was being crowned, the factions shouted: “Anastasia, may you conquer! Save, O Lord, those whom you have commanded to rule.”

When Sophia, the wife of Justinus, heard this, she was deeply shaken, for she did not know that Tiberius had a wife. She herself wished to marry Tiberius and remain Augusta. Some said, however, that while Justinus was alive she had become intimate with Tiberius and had persuaded Justinus to make him caesar (cf. P. D. III, 2).

While Tiberius still presided over the palace during Justinus’s lifetime, and, as a true Christian, distributed to the poor the great treasure that Justinus had amassed wrongly and stored even more wrongly in iron chests, the Augusta Sophia frequently rebuked him, saying: “What I accumulated over many years, you are spending in a short time.” He replied: “I trust in the Lord, because money will not be lacking in the royal treasury, provided only that the poor receive alms and captives are redeemed.”

When he was about to receive the imperial crown and the people were awaiting him in the circus, according to custom, where kings used to be crowned, certain adversaries laid an ambush for him and wished to elevate Justinian, Justinus’s nephew, to the empire. Tiberius first visited the holy places. Then, summoning to himself Euticius, the city’s pontiff, together with the consuls, prefects, and the other dignitaries, he entered the palace [Col. 0813D]. He clothed himself in purple, placed the crown upon his head, sat upon the imperial throne, and was confirmed in the glory of the kingdom with great acclamations.

(H. m.) When his adversaries saw this, they were covered with great confusion. After a few days Justinian came, threw himself at Tiberius’s feet, and gave him fifteen hundredweight of gold in order to secure his favor. Tiberius, who was always patient, received him kindly and ordered him to remain perpetually in the palace.

Sophia, too, forgetful of the promise she had once made to Tiberius, attempted to plot against him. When he went out to his estate, in order to enjoy the grape harvest with his people for thirty days according to imperial custom, Sophia secretly summoned Justinian and sought to elevate him to the kingdom. When Tiberius heard this, he hastened back to Constantinople. He seized Sophia, stripped her of all her possessions, and left her only enough to live on. He took all her servants and replaced them with men from his own household to serve her, ordering that none of those who had previously served her should approach her.

As for Justinian, Tiberius reproved him only with words, but afterward loved him so much that he promised his daughter to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son. For some reason, however, this did not come to pass. (P. D. l. l.) Since Tiberius therefore gave many alms every day, God showed him much gold.

(H. m.) One day, as he was walking through the palace, he saw on the pavement a stone on which the sign of the holy cross had been carved. He said: “We ought to sign our foreheads and breasts with the Lord’s cross, and behold, we are treading it under our feet.” He ordered it to be removed. When it was lifted, they found another marked in the same way. When he ordered this one also to be lifted, a third appeared. When they had lifted that one as well, they found more than a thousand hundredweight of gold. After it had been removed, he distributed a great deal of it to the poor.

The patrician Narses also had a large house. In it he built a cistern and concealed a great quantity of gold and silver there, killing everyone who knew of the matter except one old man. From him he exacted an oath and entrusted everything to him. After Narses died, the aforementioned old man came to Tiberius and told him about the money. Tiberius rejoiced and sent his servants with him. When they opened the cistern, they found so much money that they could scarcely carry it away over many days. In his customary manner, he distributed almost all of it to the poor.

When Rome was suffering from famine during the pontificate of Pope Benedict, while the Lombards were devastating everything, Tiberius sent many thousands of measures of grain by ship from Egypt and relieved the city out of his zeal for mercy.

In the third year of Tiberius, the king of the Persians gathered a large army against him. Tiberius sent an army under the command of Maurice, who defeated the Persians. When Maurice returned victorious, Tiberius received him with honor, gave him his daughter Constantina, and made him his son-in-law. Likewise, he joined his daughter Charito in marriage to Germanus the praetor, making both men caesars.

(P. D. III, 13.) To this Tiberius King Helpericus of the Franks sent his envoys and received many gifts, as well as gold coins, one of which weighed a pound. On one side they bore the emperor’s likeness and the inscription around it: “Of Tiberius Constantine, the perpetual Augustus.” On the other side there was a chariot and a man driving it, with the inscription around it: “The Glory of the Romans.”

[Col. 0815A] In these times the blessed Gregory, then archdeacon, had been sent to Constantinople by Pope Pelagius. At the request of the brothers living with him, especially Leander, bishop of Hispania, who had also been sent there at that time, he wrote the *Moralia on Job*. In the presence of Tiberius Augustus, he convicted Euthicius, the bishop of that city, of having erred concerning the faith in the resurrection (cf. *Life of Gregory* and Bede).

(P. D. III, 15.) After Tiberius had reigned for seven years and, having fallen ill, perceived that death was near, with the counsel of the Augusta Sophia he chose his son-in-law Maurice, a Cappadocian by birth, for the empire and granted him the principate, saying: “Keep in mind that you must always love uprightness and justice.” After saying this, he departed from this life. All the peoples [Col. 0815B] mourned him greatly because of his goodness. He was of the highest goodness, ready to give alms, just in judgments, extremely prudent in discernment. He despised no one but received everyone with goodwill; and because he had loved everyone, he was loved by everyone.

The Years of Tiberius.

[Note: [Col. 0815] One year is missing.]

In his first year a great treasure was found beneath the pavement of the palace and in the house of the patrician Narses, as stated above.

2. A.D. 577. Pope Benedict, the sixty-fourth, occupied the see for four years. [Note: [Col. 0815B] D? E. add: “From this Gregory … was ordained.” Manuscripts 4–11 add: “From this Gregory was sent to preach to the English,” from Sigeb. [Col. 0815C] A.D. 575.]

[Col. 0815C] 3. (cf. G. Fr.) A.D. 578. Sigibertus, son of Lotharius, was killed in the fourteenth year of his reign.

6. A.D. 581. Pope Pelagius, the sixty-fifth, occupied the see for ten years and two months.

7. (Chr. W.) A.D. 582. Tiberius Constantine died.

(H. m.) In the year 583 of the Lord’s incarnation, and in the 1,334th year from the founding of the City, Maurice, a Cappadocian by birth, the fifty-sixth ruler after Augustus and the first of Greek descent, obtained the empire and reigned for twenty-one years.

In the second year of his reign he was called consul and gave many treasures to the City. He promoted a certain Philippicus to be praetor of the East and gave him his daughter Gordia in marriage. Nevertheless, afterward he regarded him with suspicion as a possible usurper of the kingdom.

(*Life of Gregory.*) During Maurice’s reign, and through his support, the blessed Gregory was advanced to the rank of Roman pontiff. Gregory himself had previously received Maurice’s son from the baptismal font. Later, however, Maurice became extremely hostile to Pope Gregory. He was devoted to great avarice and rapacity, for which Gregory rebuked him as much as he could. Because he did not fear the emperor, Maurice strove to proceed in exercising tyranny against Gregory.

(H. m.) In that same year, which was the nineteenth of Maurice’s reign, a certain man dressed in monastic garb and holding a sword in his right hand ran from the marketplace to the bronze statue of the gladiator [Col. 0816A] and announced to everyone that the emperor would die by the sword.

(JOHN, *Life of Gregory* IV, 3, and H. m.) When Maurice heard this, he restrained himself from inflicting tyranny upon Gregory. Coming to his senses, he reflected that nothing is hidden from God and that he repays everyone according to his works. He also recognized the excess he had committed in imprisoning many people—for he had waged many wars in various parts of the world through his different commanders—and judged that it would be better for him to receive the punishment for his sin in this life rather than in the next.

He therefore composed written prayers and sent them to Gregory, to all the patriarchal sees, and to all the cities and monasteries, whether in cities or in the wilderness, together with candles, incense, and money. He begged them to intercede for his sins, asking above all that he receive here, and not in the future, what he deserved.

When he himself had also sought this earnestly for a long time with tears, one night, while sleeping, he saw in a vision that he was standing before a large crowd at the bronze gate of the palace, before an image of the Lord Savior. He heard a terrible voice coming from that image, saying: “Hand over Maurice.” The ministers of judgment seized him and placed him beside the purple omphalos that stood there. The same voice, in the form of an inscription, said to him: “Where do you wish me to repay you for the evils you have done—in this world or in the future age?”

He replied: “Lover of mankind, Lord and righteous judge, repay me here rather than in the future.” Then the divine voice ordered that Maurice, his wife Constantina, his children, and all his kin be handed over to the soldier Phocas.

Maurice awoke, summoned the man who was sleeping before him [Note: [Col. 0815] “after” is added in manuscript 1.], and sent [Note: [Col. 0815] *misitque* corrected to *misit* in manuscript 1.] for his son-in-law Philippicus, whom he had long suspected of wanting to steal the kingdom from him. Philippicus, supposing that he was being summoned to his destruction because of the aforementioned suspicion, called his wife Gordia to him, bade her farewell as though he would never see her again, received the sacrament of communion, and went to the palace. Entering the emperor’s chamber, he fell at his feet.

The emperor rose to meet him but likewise fell at his feet, saying: “Forgive me, I beg you, for God’s sake, because I have sinned against you. Now I know with absolute certainty that you have not sinned against me. But if you know of anyone in our ranks who is called Phocas, tell me.”

Philippicus reflected for a long time and said: “I know one man of that name. Recently appointed commander by the army, he opposed your authority.” When the emperor asked about his character, Philippicus replied: “He is indeed young and rash, yet timid.”

Then Maurice said: “If he is timid, he is certainly also a murderer,” and he recounted to Philippicus the dream he had seen.

That same night a star called a comet appeared. The following day Magistrianus came, having been sent to the hermits, and brought back this response from them: “God, having accepted your repentance, will save your soul and place you with your entire household among the number of the saints. But you will depart from the empire with disgrace and danger.”

[Note: [Col. 0818D] This note appears at the foot of column 818, but its callout number (*) is not printed in the text. D? E. add: “The books of Gregory … testimony,” from Sigeb.]

When Maurice heard this, he glorified God magnificently and indeed maintained his repentance; but he did not abandon the evil of avarice. He ordered the army to winter in dangerous places and to seek provisions from outsiders at risk to themselves, so that he would not have to provide them with public supplies.

When the army heard this, it rebelled. They raised the centurion Phocas upon a shield and acclaimed him as exarch. When a great tumult arose in Constantinople, Maurice changed his clothing and boarded a dromon at night with his wife and children. Fleeing, he came to Saint Anthemius.

Phocas arrived with the army on the seventh day and became emperor. He sent Maurice, together with his wife and children, to Chalcedon, where they were beheaded.

Maurice endured his misfortune patiently, invoking God in everything and frequently saying: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.” Some say that after he was killed, milk flowed together with his blood, so that everyone who saw it wept bitterly. Thus the emperor, raised even above the laws of nature, exchanged this life for another. From that time onward, various great calamities were never absent from the Roman Empire.

4. (Chr. W.) A.D. 586. Leovigild, the Arian king of the Visigoths, had his son Hermenegild killed with an axe on the holy Lord’s Day of Easter, on account of the Catholic faith that he had received from Leander the bishop. (BEDE.) Hilperic, one of the four sons of Lotharius, died in the twenty-fourth year of his reign (cf. G. Fr.).

6. A.D. 588. Lotharius, son of Hilperic, began to reign.

[Col. 0817C] 9. A.D. 591. Gregory I, the sixty-sixth pope, was ordained. He occupied the see for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, and departed this life on the fourth day before the Ides of March in the second year of the Emperor Phocas.

13. (Chr. W.—BEDE.) A.D. 595. [Note: [Col. 0817C] D? E. add: “In Italy … Pelagius. For this reason Gregory the deacon instituted a sevenfold litany, and shortly afterward became pope. He, among … recited.” From Sigeb., A.D. 591–592. They continue: “He also held a synod,” etc.] Gregory the pontiff gathered twenty-four bishops in synod at Saint Peter’s and issued decrees concerning the needs of the Church.

14. A.D. 596. Gregory sent Augustine to preach to the English. [Note: [Col. 0817] E. reads “to preach.”]

15. A.D. 597. King Guntrammus, son of Lotharius, died in the thirty-third year of his reign, leaving two sons, Theodebertus [Col. 0817D] and Theodericus (cf. G. Fr.). [Note: [Col. 0817] The words “leaving two sons, Theodebertus and Theodericus” are absent from E.]

17. A.D. 599. Hildibertus, son of Sigibertus, died after reigning for twenty years.

18. A.D. 600. [Note: [Col. 0817D] D? E. 5–11 add: “Saint Goar, coming from Aquitania, flourishes in Gaul.” From Sigeb.]

19. A.D. 601. [Note: [Col. 0817D] D? E. add: “The dispute … died.” From Sigeb.]

21. (Chr. W.) A.D. 603. Gregory, having sent the teachers Augustine, Mellitus, John, and several others, converted the English to Christ.

The Lord’s tunic, over which the soldiers cast lots, was found at Zaphath, far from Jerusalem, in a marble chest. Gregory, bishop of Antioch, Thomas of Jerusalem, and John of Constantinople, together with many other bishops, after undertaking a three-day fast, carried it on foot in that same chest to Jerusalem and placed it in the church where the Lord’s cross is worshiped.

Maurice, paying in this life the penalty for his crimes, as he himself had prayed, was disgracefully beheaded by Phocas.

The Years of Phocas.

1. In the year 604 of the Lord’s incarnation, and in the 1,355th year from the founding of the City, a certain Phocas, formerly, as they say, groom of the patrician Priscus, later promoted to military service, then appointed commander by the people, and finally, while the Emperor Maurice was still alive, elected emperor by the army, seized the empire as the fifty-seventh ruler after Augustus and reigned for eight years. [Note: [Col. 0817] “in a place erased” in one manuscript.] He had a wife named Leontia.

(BEDE.) In the second year of his reign the blessed Pope Gregory departed to the Lord, and Sabinianus was chosen to the pontificate in his place. After him came Boniface, at whose request Phocas established the Roman and apostolic Church as the head of all the churches; previously, the Church of Constantinople had styled itself first among all.

After him came another Boniface, the fourth after the blessed Gregory. At his request the same Phocas ordered [Note: [Col. 0817] *ut* added and then deleted in manuscript 1.] that the old temple called the Pantheon, after its idolatrous defilements had been removed, should be made a church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and all the martyrs. Thus, where once the worship of all—not gods but demons—had taken place, the memory of all the saints might thereafter be honored.

During his reign Cosdroe, king of the Persians, waged extremely severe wars against the Roman state, seized many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself, destroyed churches, and profaned holy things. Among the ornaments of the places, whether holy or secular, that he carried away, he also took away the standard of the Lord’s cross. [Note: [Col. 0817] The words “and seized … carried away” are absent from manuscripts 10 and 11.]

(H. m.) After Phocas had committed many murders and other evils among the people, Priscus the patrician, his son-in-law, grieving over these deeds, wrote to Heraclius the patrician and governor of Africa, asking him to send his son Heraclius to come against the tyrant Phocas. Heraclius came with an army, fought him, and defeated him. The populace seized Phocas, killed him, and burned him in the fire at the Taurus.

2. (Chr. W.) A.D. 605. Saint Gregory the pope departed to the Lord.

3. A.D. 606. Pope Sabinianus, the sixty-seventh, occupied the see for one year and five months.

[Col. 0819A] 4. A.D. 607. Pope Boniface, the sixty-eighth, occupied the see for one year and eight months. (Chr. W.) At his request Phocas made Rome the mother of the churches.

6. A.D. 609. Pope Boniface, the sixty-ninth, occupied the see for six years and eight months. At his request Phocas gave the Pantheon to the Church.

7. A.D. 610. [Note: [Col. 0819A] D? E. add: “At Alexandria … obtained the name *eleymon*, that is, almsgiver.” From Sigeb.]

8. A.D. 611. Phocas was killed.

The Years of Heraclius.

1. (H. m.) In the year 612 of the Lord’s incarnation, and in the 1,363rd year from the founding of the City, Heraclius, the fifty-eighth ruler after Augustus, received the empire after Phocas had been killed and reigned for twenty-seven years.

He was crowned by the patriarch Sergius in the oratory of Saint Stephen, which is in the palace, together with Eudoxia, who had been betrothed to him. They received the marriage crowns at the same time, and on one and the same day Heraclius was presented both as emperor and as bridegroom.

In the following year a son was born to the emperor by Eudoxia, the younger Heraclius, also called the new Constantine, and the Augusta died that same year. Then, in the next year, Heraclius illicitly married his niece Martina, the daughter of his sister. She was crowned Augusta by the heretical patriarch Sergius. By her he fathered a son, Heraclonas.

In the eighth year of his reign Heraclius sent envoys to Cosdroes in Persia, seeking peace. Cosdroes rejected them, saying: “I will not spare you until you deny the crucified one whom you confess to be God and worship the sun.” In the following year Chaianus, king of the Avars, directed his forces against Thrace; but after Heraclius sent envoys, he made peace with him.

In the twelfth year of his reign, having assembled all his forces, Heraclius moved his army into Persia. Engaging in many battles with various commanders, he devastated and conquered Persia for six years. After Chosdroe had been killed, he returned to Constantinople in the seventh year, bringing from Persia the life-giving wood of the cross. Soon afterward, in the following spring, he set out for Jerusalem, bringing the precious wood back there in order to give thanks to God.

[Note: [Col. 0819C] D? E. add: “Desiderius … is martyred,” from Sigeb., A.D. 612.]

[Col. 0819D] (BEDE.) During Heraclius’s reign the Persian monk Anastasius suffered a noble martyrdom for Christ. Born in Persia, he learned magical arts from his father as a boy. But when he learned the name of Christ from Christian captives, he soon turned to him with his whole heart. He left Persia, sought Christ at Chalcedon and Hierapolis, and then went to Jerusalem.

After receiving the grace of baptism there, he entered the monastery of the abbot Anastasius, four miles from that city. Living there according to the Rule for seven years, he came to Caesarea of Palestine for the sake of prayer. He was captured by the Persians, suffered many beatings for a long time amid imprisonment and chains under the judge Marzobanas, and at last was sent to King Chosdroe.

The king had him beaten three times at intervals. Finally he was suspended by one hand for three hours and then beheaded, completing a noble martyrdom with seventy others. Soon afterward, a demoniac wearing his tunic was cured.

Meanwhile Prince Heraclius arrived with an army, defeated the Persians, and brought back the Christians who had been taken captive, rejoicing. The relics of the blessed martyr Anastasius were first brought to his monastery and afterward conveyed to Rome. They are venerated in the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul, called *Ad Aquas Salvias*.

(H. m.) In the fifteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, Muhammad, the leader of the Arabs—who are also called Saracens—was held in high regard. He was a false prophet, but among them he was considered great, to such an extent that at the beginning of his appearance they even thought that he was the one whom they were awaiting, [Col. 0820B] namely, the Christ. He was descended from the line of Ishmael, the son of Abraham.

Since this Muhammad was poor and orphaned, it seemed good to him to enter the service of a certain wealthy woman, his relative, named Cadiga, as a hired man, in order to conduct trade with her camels in Egypt and Palestine, as was customary in those regions. Gradually, however, he gained the confidence of the woman, who was a widow, married her, and acquired her camels and all her property.

When he came into Palestine, he associated with Jews and Christians and obtained certain writings from them. Moreover, he suffered from epilepsy, that is, the falling sickness [Note: [Col. 0819] “cadicum” or “cadiuum,” 1?; “cadiuum,” E 1.]. When this became known, his wife was deeply distressed, being a noblewoman, [Col. 0820C] that she had joined herself to such a man—namely, a poor and epileptic one.

But he sought to calm her by saying: “I behold a vision of the angel Gabriel, and, unable to bear the sight of him, I lose consciousness and fall.” She, however, had another such associate of hers, who was living in exile there because of his unbelief. She told him all her husband’s words and the name of the angel. Wishing to reassure her, he said: “He has spoken the truth; for this angel is sent to all prophets.”

Thus she was the first to believe him after receiving his words, and she proclaimed to the other women of her kin that he was a prophet. In this way the report passed from the women to the men, first to Hebuber, whom he also left as his successor; and Hebuber retained a part of his heresy and his inheritance.

He taught his hearers [Col. 0820D] that whoever kills an enemy, or is killed by an enemy, enters paradise. He declared that paradise was filled with bodily food, drink, and intercourse with women, and that there were rivers of wine, honey, and milk there, together with abundant pleasure and many other things full of luxury and folly, which seemed delightful to fools and therefore credible.

—(Chr. W.) Heraclius, having been deceived by the patriarch Sergius, by a certain Anastasius, and by other heretics, fell into the Eutychian heresy. Having become a mathematician and astrologer, he saw that his empire was destined to be devastated by circumcised peoples. He sent to Dagobert, king of the Franks, asking and obtaining that all the Jews in his kingdom be baptized; and he himself decreed that the same should be done throughout all the borders and provinces of his empire.

After this, the Hagarenes, who are also called Saracens, a circumcised people, devastated Heraclius’s provinces. While Heraclius was fighting against them, the Saracens killed 150,000 of his soldiers and sent their spoils back to Heraclius. He refused to accept them, however, and sought vengeance against them. He opened the Caspian Gates, which Alexander the Great of Macedon had constructed beside the Caspian Sea and ordered to be closed because of the multitude of the fiercest peoples; from there he sent 150,000 men armed with gold, together with the soldiers of all the provinces, into battle against the Saracens.

When they were to fight on the following day, on that very night the angel of God struck down 52,000 from Heraclius’s army in the camp. When the survivors, returning, had drawn near Jerusalem, Heraclius, seeing that he was in no way able to resist, was overcome with grief, became dropsical, and died (H. m.).

2. [Note: [Col. 0821] thus, 1.] A.D. 613.

2. [Note: [Col. 0821] thus, 1.] A.D. 614. [Note: [Col. 0821B] 5–11 add: “Saint Columbanus is driven out by King Theoderic at the instigation of his grandmother Brunhild.” From Sigeb.]

3. (Chr. W.) A.D. 615. Anastasius the Persian became a monk.

4. A.D. 616. Pope Deusdedit, the seventieth, held office for seven years. [Note: [Col. 0821B] D? E. add: “Lupus … descended.” From Sigeb.]

6. A.D. 618. Edwin became king of the English.

11. A.D. 622. Anastasius suffered martyrdom.

12. A.D. 623. Pope Boniface, the seventy-first, held office for five years.

[Col. 0821C] 16. A.D. 627. [Note: [Col. 0821C] 4–11 add: “Isidore of Seville, the teacher, [ [Col. 0821] “teacher of Spain,” 4.] shines forth. D? E. add under A.D. 628: “I. H. shines forth in learning.” From Sigeb.]

17. (BEDA.) A.D. 628. Pope Honorius, the seventy-second, held office for ten years, eleven months, and seventeen days. Edwin, king of the English, was baptized by Bishop Paulinus in the eleventh year of his reign; the arrival of the English in Britain was 180 [years earlier].

18. (Chr. W.) A.D. 629. After killing Chosroes, king of the Persians, Heraclius brought the Lord’s cross, which Chosroes had taken away, to Constantinople, and in the following year restored it to Jerusalem with due veneration. [Note: [Col. 0821C] D? E. add: “The celebration … of the cross …” From Sigeb., under A.D. 631.]

[Col. 0821D] 19. A.D. 630. [Note: [Col. 0821D] 1, 10 (in another ink), and 11 add: “Saint Gall built his cell.”] 1.

20. A.D. 631. Lothair, son of Chilperic, died in the forty-fourth year of his reign, leaving his son Dagobert as his successor (cf. G. Fr.).

27. (H. m.) A.D. 638. Heraclius died after becoming dropsical. Pope Severinus, the seventy-third, held office for one year and two months.

## The Years of Constantine

1. In the six hundred and thirty-ninth year of the Lord’s incarnation, and the one thousand three hundred and ninetieth year from the founding of the City, Constantine, son of Heraclius and Eudoxia, the fifty-ninth from Augustus, assumed the empire. After reigning for four months, he was poisoned by his stepmother Martina and by Pyrrhus the patriarch. When he had been killed, she ruled with her son Heraclonas.

Therefore the entire senate of Constantinople, together with all the people, was aroused by just indignation and expelled Heraclonas. After Martina’s tongue and Heraclonas’s nose had been cut off, and after they had been sent into exile, they elevated Constans, son of Constantine and grandson of Heraclius.

(BEDA.) Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, and Pyrrhus of Constantinople, together with many others, revived the heresy.

(H. m.) But the senate and the whole city expelled Pyrrhus as an impious man, together with Heraclonas and his mother; and while Constans was reigning, Paul was consecrated bishop, and he too was a heretic. John, however, the Roman prelate, having gathered a council of bishops, anathematized all the supporters of this heresy.

When John died, Theodore was consecrated pope in his place. Pyrrhus, traveling toward Africa, was brought before the presence of Maximus, at that time a most religious abbot, and of the holy bishops residing there. They rebuked and persuaded him and sent him to Pope Theodore at Rome. But after he had presented the pope with a written statement of orthodoxy, he was received by him—though, as later became clear, his repentance was feigned. [Note: [Col. 0821] What follows [lacuna] to A.D. 642 was written in 1 after other material had been erased.]

As soon as he departed from Rome and reached Ravenna, however, he returned like a dog to his vomit. When the pope learned this, he summoned all the priests [Col. 0822C] and clergy into the church of the prince of the apostles and condemned him under the bond of anathema.

Pope John, the seventy-fourth, held office for two years, nine months, and eighteen days.

## The Years of Heraclonas

1. A.D. 640. [Note: [Col. 0821] XL, with DC omitted, 1.] [Note: [Col. 0822C] D? E. add: “Saint Arnulf … is enslaved.” From Sigeb.] Heraclonas [Note: [Col. 0821] “Heraclonas” corrected to “Heracleonas,” 1.], son of Heraclius, after killing his brother Constantine by poison, seized the kingdom and reigned with his mother Martina for two years.

From the beginning of the year 4600.

2. A.D. 641 [Note: [Col. 0821] XLI, 1.]. Heraclonas was disgracefully deposed together with his mother.

## The Years of Constans

[Col. 0822D] 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 642, and the one thousand three hundred and ninety-third year from the founding of the City, Constans, son of Constantine and grandson of Heraclius, the sixtieth from Augustus, was chosen to the kingdom. Heraclonas [Note: [Col. 0821] “Heracliona,” apparently corrected to “Heraclona,” 1.] was deposed together with his mother, and Constans reigned for twenty-eight years.

(BEDA.) During his reign, as stated above, Paul, a heretic, was consecrated bishop in place of the heretic Pyrrhus. He too was a heretic and afflicted the Catholics not only with the mad doctrine of his predecessors but also with open persecution, including the representatives of the holy Roman Church who had been sent to correct him—some with imprisonment, some with exile, and some with [Note: [Col. 0823D] [ [Col. 0823] This note appears at the foot of column 823, but the callout number (*) has not been printed in the text.] D? E. add: “Oswald, king, son of King Æthelfrith, killed by P. r., departs to the Lord as king and martyr.” 4–11 add: “King Oswald is killed.” From Siceb.] [Col. 0823A] beatings.

He also destroyed their altar, consecrated in the venerable shrine in Placidia’s house, forbidding them to celebrate Mass there. [Note: [Col. 0823D] D? E. add: “Constans the emperor, deceived by Paul … that Christ may be …” From Sigeb., under A.D. 652.]

(H. m.) Therefore Pope Martin, who succeeded Theodore, having been inflamed by the aforementioned Abbot Maximus, who came from Africa to Rome, gathered a synod of 110 bishops and anathematized Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Cyrus.

(BEDA.) When Constans learned of this—he had been deceived by Paul, just as his grandfather Heraclius had been deceived by Sergius, the bishop of the same royal city—he sent Theodore the exarch and had Pope Martin and Maximus brought to Constantinople. After subjecting them to insults, he had them exiled to Cherson. There the blessed Pope Martin died, shining forth with many signs of virtue.

Constans, however, moved by zeal for God, himself summoned a holy synod under Pope Vitalian, who had recently been ordained, and renounced the heresy. He sent to the blessed apostle Peter golden Gospels, ornamented around the edges with extraordinarily large white gems. Several years later he came to Rome and offered upon the altar of Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold, while his entire army entered the church with candles.

(H. m.) He also wished to transfer the kingdom to Rome, because he had become hateful to the Byzantines: he had treated Pope Martin disgracefully and exiled him; he had cut out the tongue and severed the hand of Maximus, a most learned man; he had handed two of Maximus’s disciples, both named Anastasius, over to torture and exile; and he had condemned many of the orthodox [Note: [Col. 0823] “orthodorum,” 1.] to beatings, confiscation of property, and exile. Because of such actions, he became hateful to everyone and spent six years in Sicily.

There, one day, when he had entered a bath, a certain Andrew entered with him to attend him. When the emperor had begun to be rubbed with French soap, Andrew took a bucket, struck him on the head with it, and immediately fled. While the emperor remained delayed in the bath, those who were outside rushed in and found him dead.

After he had been buried, they made a certain Armenian named Miziz emperor, compelling him by force. He was very handsome and attractive. When his son Constantine heard of his father’s death, he entered Sicily with a large fleet, attacked Miziz, killed him and his father’s assassins, put the West in order, returned to Constantinople, and ruled over the Romans with his brothers Tiberius and Heraclius.

During the reign of this emperor, holy Gertrude, daughter of the prince Pippin, died. [Note: [Col. 0823] “Hujus … principis” was written in the margin by the same hand; 9c lacks it; 10 and 11 lack it; D, E.]

[Col. 0823D] Pope Theodore, the seventy-fourth, held office for seven years. [Note: [Col. 0823D] D? E. add: “Dagobert … grants.” From Sigeb.]

2. A.D. 643.

[Col. 0824A] 4. A.D. 645. King Dagobert sent his son Sigibert, destined to reign in Austrasia, to Pippin and Saint Cunibert (cf. G. Fr.).

6. A.D. 647. [Note: [Col. 0824A] D, E, 5–11 add: “Pippin dies. His son Grimoald becomes mayor of the palace in his place.” From Sigeb.]

7. A.D. 648. [Note: [Col. 0824A] D? E. add: “Saint Furseus … attacked, after several years found rest in Gaul. 5–11 add: ‘Saint Furseus shone forth in Ireland.’” From Sigeb.]

8. (Chr. W.) A.D. 649. Pope Martin, the seventy-fifth, held office for ten years. Having gathered 110 bishops, he condemned Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul. (H. m.) For this reason he was exiled by the emperor Constans, who had been deceived by them, to Cherson.

9. A.D. 650. [Note: [Col. 0824B] D? E. add: “Hitta … appointed him prefect. 5–11 add: ‘Hitta, Pippin’s widow, at the instigation of Saint Amandus founded the monastery of Nivelles.’” From Sigeb.]

11. A.D. 652. Ash descended from heaven, and great fear arose among the people. [Note: [Col. 0824B] D? E. add: “Pestilence … they were dying.” From Sigeb., under A.D. 654.]

13. A.D. 654. [Note: [Col. 0824B] D? E. add: “The Saracens … were burdened.” From Sigeb.]

17. A.D. 658. Pope Martin departed at Cherson on the fourth day before the Ides of November.

18. A.D. 659. Pope Eugenius, the seventy-sixth, held office for two years and [Col. 0824C] nine months.

21. A.D. 662. Pope Vitalian, the seventy-seventh, held office for nine years and six months.

24. A.D. 665. Dagobert, son of Lothair, after reigning for thirty-four years [Note: [Col. 0823] “34: Clovis succeeded him … Austrasia,” 9c.], died (cf. G. Fr.). [Note: [Col. 0824C] D? E. 4–11 [ [Col. 0823] 9c is nevertheless lacking.] add: “Saint Gertrude died.”]

25. A.D. 666. Clovis, his son, succeeded him. His brother Sigibert reigned in Austrasia. [Note: [Col. 0823] The reference “Cui … frater” for Dagobert is read in 4 from A.D. 665; 11 lacks it.]

28. (Chr. W.) A.D. 669. Constans was killed in the bath. [Note: [Col. 0824C] D? E. add: “Theodore the abbot, sent by Pope Vitalian to Alexandria, convened a synod … useful things. He also wrote … faults.” From Sigeb., under A.D. 668 and 674.]

## The Years of Constantine

[Col. 0824D] (H. m.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 670, and the one thousand four hundred and twenty-first year from the founding of the City, Constantine, son of Constans, the sixty-first from Augustus, reigned with his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius.

When certain men from the eastern regions came and said, “If we believe in the Trinity, let us also crown three men,” Constantine, who alone had been crowned, was disturbed. Through the patrician Theodore he summoned the leading men among them, as though to a conference and council in order that their will might be fulfilled, and hanged them on a gallows. When the others saw this, they fled. He himself reigned with his son Tiberius for seventeen years.

(BEDA.) During his time Agatho, pontiff of the Roman Church, sent his legates to the royal city to admonish the holy churches of God. Among them was John, then archdeacon of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0825] “archidianus,” 1.], but not long afterward its bishop.

They were received most graciously by Constantine, the most reverent defender of the Catholic faith. They were instructed, setting aside philosophical disputes, to investigate the true faith through peaceful discussion, and were given from the Constantinopolitan library all the books of the ancient fathers that they requested.

A universal synod of 150 bishops was assembled—or, as some books have it (H. m.), 289—under the presidency of George, patriarch of Constantinople, and Macarius of Antioch. These men were reviving the heresy of those who asserted one will and one operation in Christ. They were convicted of having falsified the sayings of the holy fathers in many places.

(BEDA.) When the dispute had ended, the patriarch George was corrected. Macarius, however, together with his followers and his predecessors Sergius, Cyrus, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, was anathematized. The abbot Theophanius of Sicily was made bishop of Antioch in his place.

Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, who was one of them, publicly celebrated Mass in Latin in the church of Saint Sophia before the prince and the patriarch on the Sunday of Easter week.

This is the sixth universal synod, celebrated at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, during the pontificate of Pope Agatho, with the most devout prince Constantine conducting and presiding over it within his own palace, while the legates of the apostolic see and 150—or 289—bishops were seated together.

The first universal synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, with 318 fathers, under the emperor Constantine and during the pontificate of Pope Sylvester.

The second was held at Constantinople with 150 fathers against Macedonius and Eudoxius, during the pontificate of Pope Damasus and the reign of the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city.

The third was held at Ephesus with 200 fathers against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the emperor Theodosius the Great and Pope Sixtus [Note: [Col. 0825] “and S. p.” in an erasure, 1.].

The fourth was held at Chalcedon with 630 fathers under Pope Leo, during the reign of the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, the most impious Manichaean [Col. 0825D] prelate [Note: [Col. 0825] “and S. p.” in an erasure, 1.].

The fifth likewise took place at Constantinople, during the pontificate of Pope Vigilius and under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics.

The sixth is this one about which we have just spoken. [Note: [Col. 0825D] D? E. add: “Among the Saracens … fifty noble horses.” From Sigeb., under A.D. 679.]

At this time Chunibert held the kingdom of the Lombards, and Clovis that of the Franks (cf. P. D. VI, 16 and 23). [Note: [Col. 0825] In an erasure, 1.]

At this time [Note: [Col. 0826A] In place of this, D? E. have: “At this time in Gaul, in Francia, Ansgisus, son of Saint Arnulf, governed under the name of mayor of the palace. He was called … Him Gundwin later killed, whom … had promoted. His widow Begga, daughter namely of Pippin, formerly prince of the Austrasians, sister of Grimoald and Saint Gertrude, founded herself and her possessions …” From Sigeb., under A.D. 685–686.] there was also in Gaul a powerful man beloved by God named Arnulf. After renouncing the world, he later became bishop of Metz. His son Ansgisus, who is believed to have been named after Anchises the Trojan, later held the chief authority in the kingdom of the Franks under the title of mayor of the palace.

At this time Saint Lambert succeeded Saint Theodard in the episcopate of Maastricht, under Childeric, king of Austrasia. [Note: [Col. 0825] “e” corrected, 1.]

—(BEDA.) At the same time the holy and perpetual virgin of Christ, Æthelthryth, daughter of Anna, king of the English, was first given in marriage to another very distinguished man and afterward to King Ecgfrith. After preserving her marital bed undefiled for twelve years, she assumed the sacred veil and, from being a queen, became a nun. Before long she also became a mother and nurse to pious virgins. Her merits, still living, are also attested by her dead flesh, which, sixteen years after burial, was found incorrupt together with the garment in which she had been wrapped.

## The Years of Constantine

3. A.D. 672. Pope Adeodatus, the seventy-eighth, held office for four years.

7. A.D. 676. Pope Domnus, the seventy-ninth, held office for one year and five months.

9. A.D. 678. Pope Agatho, the eightieth, held office for five years and [Col. 0826C] six months.

12. (Chr. W.—cf. P. D. VI, 4, and G. Fr.) A.D. 681. The sixth universal synod was assembled at Constantinople under Pope Agatho, who succeeded Donus. When the heretics had been condemned, such a web of spiders fell in the midst of the people that everyone understood and marveled that the filth of the heresies had been expelled.

Clovis, son of Dagobert, died. His son Lothair succeeded him.

14. A.D. 683. Pope Leo, the eighty-first, held office for one year and ten months.

16. A.D. 685. Pope Benedict, the eighty-second, held office for ten months and died on the Nones of May. [Note: [Col. 0826C] D? E. add: “The Ravennate … to be ordained.” From Sigeb.]

[Col. 0826D] 17. (Chr. W.) A.D. 686. The emperor Constantine died. Pope John, the eighty-second, held office for one year. Pope Conon, the eighty-third, succeeded him and held office for two years and eleven months; from him Saint Kilian received pontifical authority. Sergius succeeded Conon.

—Among the Gauls, in Francia, Ansgisus held the chief authority under the title of mayor of the palace. [Note: [Col. 0826D] In place of this, D? E. have: “Saint Leodegarius, bishop, was … by E. t.; at last … the cutting off.” From Sigeb.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 687, and the one thousand four hundred and thirty-eighth year from the founding of the City, Justinian, son of Constantine, the sixty-second from Augustus, assumed the kingdom and reigned for ten years.

(BEDA.) He made a firm peace with the Saracens for ten years, on land and sea. The province of Africa was also brought under Roman rule, although it had been held by the Saracens.

Because the blessed Sergius, pontiff of the Roman Church, refused to support and subscribe to the erroneous synod that Justinian had held at Constantinople, Justinian sent his protospatharius Zacharias and ordered Sergius to be transported to Constantinople. But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions forestalled the emperor’s wicked command and drove the same Zacharias from the city of Rome with insults and injuries. [Note: [Col. 0827] “Zachariam,” thus in 1; “Zachariam,” E 1; etc.]

(H. m.) The same Justinian demanded from the patriarch Callinicus that he offer a prayer for the destruction of the church of the holy Mother of God situated beside the palace, which was called the Metropolis, [Col. 0827B] because he wished to construct buildings there where he might be received by the people.

The patriarch said: “We have a prayer for establishing a church, but we have not received a prayer for destroying a church.” When the emperor compelled him and demanded it in every way, the patriarch said this prayer: “Glory to God, who continually endures and suffers, now and forever and unto all ages of ages.”

When they heard this, they destroyed the church. Since he also did many other reckless things, he aroused the hatred of the people against himself.

Therefore the patrician Leontius, whom Justinian had once made praetor and commander of the eastern armies but whom he had now kept in custody for three years, was brought out and sent into exile. Leontius turned against him and, joining many others to himself, seized Justinian. After cutting off his nose, he exiled him to a certain island and himself reigned.

## The Years of Pippin. The Years of Justinian

2. (Chr. W.) A.D. 688. Saint Kilian suffered martyrdom with his companions.

1. 3. A.D. 689. Pippin, son of Ansgisus, became mayor of the palace in Gaul and administered the kingdom of the Franks for twenty-seven years. His years and those of his successors thereafter are recorded in the catalogue of kings.

2. 4. A.D. 690. Pope Sergius, the eighty-fourth, held office for sixteen years and eight months and died on the fifth day before the Ides of September. He established that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung during the sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 0827C] 10 and 11 add: “He found a large portion of the holy cross [Col. 0827D] in a reliquary [ [Col. 0827] “in ipsa” corrected to “in capsa,” 10; 11 lacks it.].]

[Col. 0827D] 4. 6. A.D. 692. Clovis, son of Theoderic, brother of Dagobert, began to reign with his brother Hildibert (cf. G. Fr.).

6. 8. A.D. 694. Saint Remaclus, bishop of Maastricht, departed this life. [Note: [Col. 0827D] 10 and 11 add: “The two English priests Ewald, Black and White, suffered martyrdom and were buried at Cologne by Pippin.” From Bernold.]

7. 9. (Chr. W.) A.D. 695. Willibrord, also called Clement, was ordained bishop by Pope Sergius [Note: [Col. 0827] “to preach to the nations” is lacking in 4.] for the preaching of the nations.

[Col. 0828A] 8. 10. A.D. 696. Justinian was deprived of the kingdom and exiled because of his treachery.

## The Years of Leo

9. 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 697, and the one thousand four hundred and forty-eighth year from the founding of the City, Leo, also called Leontius, the sixty-third from Augustus, seized the kingdom after Justinian had been deposed and reigned for three years.

(BEDA.) In the first year of his reign, Pope Sergius found, by divine revelation, in the sacristy of the blessed apostle Peter, a silver reliquary that had lain for a very long time in a dark corner. In it he found a cross adorned with various precious stones. After removing four panels in which gems had been set, he saw within them a portion of the Lord’s cross of extraordinary size. Every year, on the day of its Exaltation, all the people venerate it in the basilica of the Savior, which is called [Col. 0828B] Constantinian.

11. 3. A.D. 699. Saint Cuthbert, bishop, died after having been a hermit. His body was found intact eleven years after his burial. [Note: [Col. 0827] “His body … was found” is lacking in 4.]

(H. m.) While Leontius was established at Constantinople, Tiberius, also called Apsimarus, came with many men to the opposite side of the city. After the city had been betrayed to him, he seized Leontius, cut off his nose, placed him under guard in the monastery of Dalmatia, and himself reigned.

## Tyb.

12. 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 700, and the one thousand four hundred and fifty-first year from the founding of the City, Tiberius, also called Apsimarus, the sixty-fourth from Augustus, seized the empire after Leo had been deposed and reigned for seven years.

(BEDA.) During his reign the synod held at Aquileia hesitated to accept the fifth universal council because of ignorance of the faith, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to this together with the other churches of Christ.

During his time Saint Lambert, the bishop, was killed under King Hildebert (cf. H. Fr. above). [Note: [Col. 0827] “During his time … under the king” in the margin, 1.]

15. 4. (Chr. W.) A.D. 703. A synod was assembled at Aquileia under Pope Sergius.

18. 7. A.D. 706. Pope John, the eighty-fifth, held office for three years.

The venerable Bede [Note: [Col. 0827] “Bede … brought it up to this point” is lacking in D, E, 9c.] the English priest brought the chronicle of his shorter book up to this point.

## The Years of Justinian

[Col. 0828D] 19. 1. (BEDA.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 707, and the one thousand four hundred and fifty-eighth year from the founding of the City, Justinian, son of Constantine, whom we said above had been expelled from the kingdom by Leo, recovered the kingdom with the help of Terbelis, king of the Bulgars, after Constantinople had been conquered, and afterward reigned for six years.

(H. m.) After recovering the kingdom, he gave Terbelis many gifts and royal vessels and dismissed him in peace. Apsimarus, also called Tiberius, fled from the city, but was captured during the pursuit and brought to Justinian.

When Leontius, who had deposed him, was also brought in, Justinian had both of them bound in chains and, while the horse-games were being held, dragged through the streets. After they had been dragged publicly before his feet while he sat on his throne, he threw himself upon their necks and trod them down forcefully, while the entire populace shouted: “You have walked upon the asp and the basilisk, and you have trampled underfoot the lion and the dragon!” Thus he ordered them to be beheaded. He also had an innumerable multitude of those who had sided against him killed by various deaths.

(P. D. VI, 32.) Because they had cut off his nose, whenever he wiped away with his hand a drop of rheum that was running from it, he ordered one of them or another to be slaughtered. (H. m.—cf. BEDA.)

He exiled the patriarch Callinicus to Rome after gouging out his eyes, and promoted Cyrus to the episcopate in his place. Cyrus had been an abbot in Pontus and had supported Justinian in exile and foretold that he would be restored to the empire.

A son was born to Justinian in the same year in which he recovered the empire, by Theodora, daughter of Chaianus, whom he had married while he was in exile. He named the son Tiberius, crowned him together with his mother, and they reigned with him.

(BEDA and P. D. VI, 31.) Justinian summoned Pope Constantine, received him honorably, prostrated himself on the ground, and asked him to intercede for his sins. Renewing all the privileges of the Church, he sent him back with honor.

When Justinian sent an army into Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, Pope Constantine strongly opposed him, but could not change his mind. The army he had sent, however, went over to Philippicus, made him emperor there, and returned with him to Constantinople. Philippicus fought against Justinian twelve miles from the city, defeated and killed him, and received the kingdom.

(H. m.) Justinian’s son, who was still a boy, was also killed by those whom Philippicus had sent ahead.

21. 3. A.D. 709. Pope John, the eighty-sixth, held office for two years and seven months.

22. 4. A.D. 710. Dagobert the Younger began to reign (cf. H. Fr.).

23. 5. A.D. 711. Pope Sisinnius, the eighty-seventh, held office for twenty days. Pope Constantine, the eighty-eighth, succeeded him and held office for six years.

24. 6. A.D. 712. Justinian was killed by Philippicus (cf. H. m.).

## The Years of Philippicus

[Col. 0829D] 25. (H. m.) 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 713, and the one thousand four hundred and sixty-fourth year from the founding of the City, Philippicus, the sixty-sixth [Note: [Col. 0829] D, E have LX, so that from this point onward they depart from the text as printed by six years.] from Augustus, seized the empire after Justinian had been killed and reigned for one year and six months.

Before he became emperor [Note: [Col. 0829] 5 has “before he was made emperor.”], he had a certain monk as a friend, an enclosed monk who was a heretic but also a seer. This monk said to him: “The empire is yours.” Philippicus was troubled. The enclosed monk said to him: “If God commands it, why do you resist?”

“I tell you this,” he continued, “because the sixth synod was wrongly conducted. Therefore, if you reign, reject it, and your empire will become strong and long-lasting.”

Philippicus swore that he would do this. When he became emperor, he held a synod of pseudo-bishops in accordance with the words of that false, enclosed monk, and rejected the holy and universal sixth synod. In that same year the vain enclosed monk was struck blind.

Philippicus then found a certain John who agreed with him and made him prelate of Constantinople. He deposed Cyrus and ordered him to return to his monastery.

(P. D. VI, 34, and H. m.) In his disputations Philippicus appeared reasonable and prudent, but in his actions he proved everywhere to be blameworthy, ending his life dishonorably and unworthily. For he was a heretic and an adulterer.

(BEDA.) He sent Pope Constantine a letter containing false doctrine, which Constantine rejected with the counsel of the apostolic see. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0829] “For this reason” is in an erasure, 1.] Constantine made paintings in the portico of Saint Peter depicting the acts of the six holy synods. Similar paintings were also kept at Constantinople, and Philippicus ordered them removed.

The Roman people decreed that they would accept neither the name nor the documents nor the coin-image of the heretical emperor. Therefore his image was not brought into the church, nor was his name pronounced during the solemn Masses.

(H. m.) On the Saturday of Pentecost, while Philippicus was bathing in a public bath, Rufinus, chief of the *stratores*, entered with cavalry and musical instruments. After Philippicus had dined with citizens of ancient lineage and was resting at midday, Rufinus suddenly entered through the Golden Gate with the patrician Theodore. Hurrying to the palace and finding Philippicus resting, he seized him and tore out his eyes.

On the following day, that is, Pentecost, after the people had assembled in the great church, Artemisius was crowned and changed his name to Anastasius.

## The Years of Anastasius

26. 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 714, and the one thousand four hundred and sixty-fifth year from the founding of the City, Anastasius, the sixty-seventh from Augustus, obtained the empire and reigned for three years.

Some books, however, have it [*] that Philippicus reigned for two years and nine months, while Anastasius reigned for one year and three months.

(H. m.—P. D. l. l.) After Anastasius received the kingdom, he sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome by the patrician Scholasticus, in which he declared and demonstrated himself to be a supporter and defender of the Catholic faith and a preacher of the holy sixth council.

While he was reigning, certain men conspired against him and marched with an army against the royal city.

(H. m.) When they had reached Adramyttium [Note: [Col. 0829] “had ascended Ramium,” 1b.] and were without a leader, they found there a native named Theodosius, an inactive and ignorant man who collected public taxes. They urged him to become emperor.

He fled and hid in the mountains. When they found him, they extolled him with praises as emperor and compelled him by force.

When Anastasius learned this, he went to Nicaea and fortified himself there.

(P. D. VI, 36.) Theodosius followed him and defeated him in a great battle. After receiving an oath from him, he made Anastasius a cleric and afterward had him ordained priest.

27. 2. (Chr. W.) A.D. 715. [Note: [Col. 0831A] D, E add: “Saint Giles … shines forth in Gaul.” From Sigeb. 5. (6–9? [ [Col. 0831] not legible in 9c.]–10, 11 below after “succeeded his father”) add: “Saint Giles shone forth.”] Pippin the Elder, mayor of the palace, died; his son Charles succeeded him. King Dagobert of the Franks died.

## The Years of Charles the Elder

1. 3. A.D. 716. Charles, son of Pippin the Elder, succeeded his father in the administration of the kingdom, while kings still remained in Francia but reigned with little authority (cf. Hanc. Frist. above, col. 000).

[Col. 0831B] In the Roman Empire too there were still emperors at Constantinople, but they had been almost completely weakened by internal and external wars alike and possessed little power.

Charles administered the kingdom of the Franks for twenty-seven years. When a certain Ragamfred opposed him and tried to hold the kingdom, Charles, after many battles and struggles, took the leadership from his hands.

(P. D. VI, 42.) For while Charles was being held in custody, he escaped from there under the protection of divine mercy. First he fought against the same Ragamfred three times; afterward, after a great struggle, he defeated him. He nevertheless allowed him the city of Angers as a place to live, while he himself held authority over the entire Frankish people and fought many battles against the Saracens in Wasconia, Saxony, and [Col. 0831C] Frisia.

—Ekbert, a holy man of the English people, taught the Scots to celebrate Easter lawfully.

—(Chr. W.) Pope Gregory, the eighty-ninth, held office for ten years and departed on the Ides of February. He ordained Saint Boniface bishop. [Note: [Col. 0831C] D, E add: “He established … previously. Petronax also, a citizen … had been.” From Sigeb., under A.D. 714.]

## 2. 1.

In the year 717 of the Lord’s incarnation, but 1,468 from the founding of the City, Theodosius, elected by the soldiers, received the Roman Empire, sixty-eighth in succession from Augustus, and reigned for one year. (H. m.) Leo, who was commander of the eastern forces, since he was supporting Anastasius, did not submit to Theodosius. Therefore, coming to Nicomedia, he seized Theodosius’s son, together with all the royal equipment and the chief men of the palace, and came to Chrysopolis. When Theodosius heard this, after receiving counsel from Germanus the patriarch and the senate, through that same patriarch he obtained from Leo a promise of security and of preserving the churches without disturbance; and so they entrusted the empire to him. Theodosius himself, however, together with his son, became a cleric and spent the remainder of his life peacefully.

—(Chr. W.) In this year the Tiber left its bed and overturned many buildings in Rome, rising in the Via Lata to a height of one and a half fathoms. (BEDA.) It remained so for seven days, until, after the citizens had held frequent litanies, it finally returned to its channel on the eighth day.

## 3. 1.

In the year 718 of the Lord’s incarnation, but 1,469 from the founding of the City, Leo, commander of the eastern forces, a Syrian by origin, sixty-ninth in succession from Augustus, was elevated to the Roman Empire and reigned for twenty-four years. (H. m.) Earlier, when Justinian was reigning, he had been exiled by him to Mesembria in the region of Thrace. Later, when Justinian was reigning for the second time, Leo came to meet him together with the Bulgarians and offered him gifts, namely five hundred sheep. Justinian was appeased, made him a *spatharius*, and treated him as a close friend. Consequently, certain men, driven by envy, slandered him as though he were aspiring to the empire; but when an inquiry was held, they were found to be lying. Later, however, Justinian grew suspicious of him, though unwilling to injure him openly, and sent him with money to Alania to stir up the Alans against Abasgia. When many things prospered for him there, and after Justinian had been killed and Philippicus blinded, Anastasius became emperor and promoted Leo to commander of the eastern forces. After Anastasius was driven out by Theodosius, while Theodosius was reigning, Leo also expelled him and himself became emperor. But he was impious toward Christians, the churches of God, and holy religion. (P. D. VI, 49.)

Indeed, he first ordered—[Note: He gave this order, deceived by a certain Beser, an apostate from the faith; D. E.; cf. Sigebert, year 725.]—in Constantinople that whoever possessed images of the Lord and Savior, or of his holy mother, or of other saints, should bring them to him; and he had them burned in the middle of the city. Because many of the people did not consent to this impiety, they were beheaded. The patriarch Germanus was also removed from his see, and the presbyter Anastasius was appointed in his place. He also sent to Pope Gregory, ordering him to do likewise; but Gregory refused and prohibited the payment of all the taxes of the city of Rome and of Italy to him.

(H. m.) In the third year of his reign, a son was born to him by his wife Maria. He named him Constantine; this son proved more impious than his father and became a precursor of Antichrist. Later Leo joined him in marriage to the daughter of Chaianus, king of the Scythians, and, making her a Christian, gave her the name Irene. After she had learned the sacred writings, she devoted herself to piety and often reproved these men for their impiety.

[Col. 0832D] **5. 3. A.D. 720.** [Note: D. E. add: “Constantine … scandal,” from Sigebert, year 720.] [Note: **10. 11.** add: “Saint Otmar became abbot,” from Bernold.]

## 6. 4.

(P. D. VI, 47.) **A.D. 721.** The Saracens besieged Constantinople. After remaining there for three years and devastating many provinces, they were finally driven away by famine and plague, when the people cried out to God; many also perished from cold, the sword, and shipwreck.

[Col. 0833A] Theoderic reigned in Francia for sixteen years (cf. G. Fr.).

## 8. 6.

(P. D. VI, 48.) (S. BEDA.) **A.D. 723.** Luitprand [Note: Thus in witness 1, and not “Liutprand.”], king of the Lombards, hearing that the Saracens, after laying waste Sardinia, had also desecrated the places where, at some earlier time because of the devastation of the barbarians, the bones of Saint Augustine had been transferred, sent men and brought them back for a price to Ticinum, where he reburied them honorably, as was fitting.

—(H. m.) The emperor Leo compelled the Jews and the Montanists to be baptized. The Jews, however, washed off the chrismal anointing, partook of the sacraments after eating, and contaminated the faith. The Montanists, after appointing a day for themselves, entered houses assigned to their error and burned themselves alive.

## 9. 7.

**A.D. 724.** [Note: D. E. add: “A certain Jew … died shortly afterward,” from Sigebert.]

[Col. 0833B] ## 10. 8.

(Chr. W.) **A.D. 725.** Saint Pirmin entered Augia and cleansed it of snakes.

## 11. 9.

**A.D. 726.** Up to this point Bede carried his chronicle forward in his larger work. [Note: “Up to this point … carried forward” is absent from D. E.]

## 12. 10.

**A.D. 727.** Pope Gregory, the ninetieth, occupied the see for eight years and died on the fourth day before the Kalends of December. He added to the canon: “And also all those saints whose solemnity [today is] in the sight of your majesty …” [Note: D.: “whose solemnity is today in the sight of your majesty …”; E.: “whose solemnity is today in the sight of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.”]

## 15. 13.

(Chr. W.) **A.D. 730.** Pirmin came from Augia into Alsace.

## 16. 14.

(H. m.) **A.D. 731.** The most holy patriarch Germanus, seeing Leo’s impiety, renounced the highest priesthood, handed over the pallium, and devoted himself to quiet in his own house. He had exercised the priesthood for fourteen years and five months. In his place Leo appointed Anastasius, formerly his disciple but now consenting to impiety. Saint Gregory, bishop of Rome, anathematized him; and, rebuking Leo by letters as one acting impiously, he caused Rome and all Italy to withdraw from Leo’s rule. Bede, the venerable presbyter of the English, died.

## 17. 15.

(Chr. W.—P. D. VI, 53.) **A.D. 732.** Charles sent his son Pippin to Luitprand, king of the Lombards, to have his hair cut. Luitprand did this and sent him back to his father with many gifts. [Note: D. E.: “presents.”]

[Col. 0833D] ## 18. 16.

(Chr. W.) **A.D. 733.** Charles, mayor of the palace, devastated Frisia.

## 19. 17.

**A.D. 734.** Charles invaded Vasconia.

[Note: **10. 11.** add: “Eto, abbot of Augia, having been made bishop of Strasbourg, built the monastery of his own name, Ettenheim,” from Bernold.]

## 20. 18.

(Chr. W.) **A.D. 735.** Pope Zacharias, the ninety-first, occupied the see for eighteen years. He translated the four books of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory into Greek.

## 22. 20.

**A.D. 737.** Theoderic, king of the Franks, died (cf. G. Fr.).

[Col. 0834A] ## 24. 22.

(P. D. VI, 54.) **A.D. 739.** When the Saracens again invaded Gaul, they captured the city of Arles. Then Charles sent to Luitprand, who came to him with the entire Lombard army. When the Saracens heard this, they fled from that land.

**Years from the beginning: 4,700.**

## 25. 23.

(Chr. W.) **A.D. 740.** Charles entered Saxony.

## 26. 24.

(H. m.) **A.D. 741.** The impious emperor Leo died.

### The Years of Constantine

## 27.

(H. m.) **1.** In the year 742 of the Lord’s incarnation, but 1,493 from the founding of the City, Constantine, Leo’s son, seventieth in succession from Augustus, assumed the Roman Empire and reigned for thirty-four years, two months, and twenty-six days.

[Col. 0834B] He was most destructive, savage, and uncivilized, a persecutor of the laws handed down by the Fathers. He exercised his imperial power tyrannically, not lawfully. At first he turned away from God, from his undefiled mother, and from all the saints; he delighted in magic, sorceries, debauchery, bloody sacrifices, and invocations of demons. From early youth he also lived amid effeminacies and all things that corrupt souls. He increased in persecutions of the holy churches, executions of monks, violations of monasteries, and various evils—no less than Diocletian and the other ancient tyrants.

(EINH. Ann.) In the first year of his reign, which was the year 742 of the Lord’s incarnation, Charles, son of Pippin and mayor of the palace in the kingdom of the Franks, died, leaving three sons: Pippin, Carloman, and Grifo. Grifo, the youngest of them, had as his mother Suanahild, niece of Odilo, duke of the Bavarians. By an evil plan she incited him to hope for the entire kingdom, to such an extent that he immediately seized the city of Laon and declared war on his brothers. They quickly gathered an army, besieged Laon, and accepted their brother’s submission. From there they turned their attention to organizing the kingdom and recovering the provinces that had defected from the Frankish alliance after their father’s death. Since they were setting out abroad and wished to leave everything at home secure, Carloman had Grifo confined in a new fortress [Note: “in no fortress,” 1b.] situated near Auvergne. He is said to have remained in this custody until the time when Carloman departed for Rome.

### Pippin and Carloman

## 1. 2.

**A.D. 743.** Pippin and Carloman, having obtained the principate, first wishing to recover Aquitaine, entered that province with an army against Hunold, its duke. After capturing a certain fortress called Lucas, and before withdrawing from the province, they divided between themselves the kingdom they jointly held, at a place called Old Poitiers. Carloman received Austrasia, Alamannia, and Thuringia; Pippin received Burgundy, Neustria, and Provence. Thus Carloman ruled until the sixth year, and Pippin until the eleventh (Chr. W.).

Neustria is a part of Celtic Gaul [Note: “cellicae” in witnesses 1, 5, and 9c; D.: “celticae”; 10: “cellicae”; E. corrects “cellicae” to “celticae.”], namely that which lies between the Seine and the Loire.

(RICHERUS I, 2.) For all Gaul is divided into three parts: Belgica, Celtica, and Aquitania. Belgica extends from the Rhine—which separates Germany from the ocean and, because it produces many peoples, received its name from “germinating”—as far as the river Marne. On both sides it is bounded, on one by the Apennine Alps and on the other by the sea; through the surrounding waters the island of Britain is formed. Celtica stretches lengthwise from the Marne to the Garonne; its sides are bounded by the British Ocean and the island of Britain. Whatever extends from the Garonne to the Pyrenees is called Aquitania, bounded on one side by the Rhône and the Saône and on the other by the Mediterranean Sea. Thus the whole extent of Gaul is enclosed in the east by the Rhine, in the west by the Pyrenees, in the north by the British Sea, and in the south by the Mediterranean Sea.

All the peoples of Gaul are therefore greatly carried away by their innate boldness and are extremely intolerant of insults. (Ibid., c. 3.) When provoked, they rejoice in slaughter and, becoming fiercer, attack with excessive violence. Once they have accepted something as persuasive and established by argument, they scarcely know how to refute it. The Belgians are especially distinguished in arranging affairs; they are not inferior in strength and courage. They seek the greatest things more by intelligence than by force; but if they fail in what they seek by intelligence, they use force boldly. They are also exceedingly moderate in food and drink.

The Celts and Aquitanians, however, are very strong both in counsel and in courage and are suited to seditious undertakings. The Celts are more cautious, while the Aquitanians act rashly and are carried away especially by desire for food, so innate is this in them that they desire nothing contrary to nature. Hence Sulpicius Severus: “Gluttony,” he says, “is appetite among the Greeks, but nature among the Gauls.”

Histories report that all these peoples of Gaul conducted themselves with almost complete success even in paganism. Later, after being baptized by Saint Remigius, they are said always to have emerged with splendid and illustrious victory against every assault of foreign nations. Their first Christian king is said to have been Clovis, a bold and vigorous man, than whom no one after him ever shone more brightly in piety and in wars.

(G. Fr.) Once, when he had come to Tours to wage war against Alaric, king of the Goths, he offered many gifts to the church of Saint Martin, including his swiftest horse, which he loved dearly. After seeking the aid of that same saint against the unbelieving nation, he promised still greater gifts if he should return victorious through the saint’s intercession. When he returned in victory after Alaric had been killed, he came to the same church and offered many gifts to fulfill his vow. For the horse, however, which he had left there, he gave the church’s keepers one hundred solidi so that they would return it to him. When the money had been paid, the horse would not move at all. He then said: “Let another hundred be given.” When these too had been paid, the horse immediately broke free and departed. Then the king said joyfully: “Truly Saint Martin is good in help and dear in business.”

(RICHER.) From this Clovis onward, through successive periods, the commonwealth of the Franks is recognized to have been governed by outstanding emperors, down to the recent times of the Pippins and Charleses. In those times it had declined somewhat through the frivolity of the kings, but through these excellent men, of whom we are now speaking, it was restored more magnificently to its former dignity.

(EINH. Ann.) Finally, when we began to write about the brothers Pippin and Carloman, as soon as they had returned home from Aquitaine, Carloman entered Alamannia—which had likewise defected from the Frankish alliance—with an army and devastated it with sword and fire.

Hilderic, king of the Franks, began to reign (cf. H. Fr.).

## 2. 3.

(EINH. Ann.) **A.D. 744.** Carloman and Pippin set out with their combined forces against Odilo, duke of the Bavarians. After battle was joined, they routed his army. But after returning from the slaughter, Carloman set out with his men for Saxony in the same year, captured the fortress called Hochseoburg [Note: “Hochscoburg,” 1b.], and received Theoderic the Saxon, the leading man of that place, into submission.

[Note: **10. 11.** add: “Saint Boniface established two bishoprics from his own diocese of Mainz, Würzburg and Eichstätt,” from Bernold.]

## 3. 4.

**A.D. 745.** Carloman and Pippin again entered Saxony with a joined force [Note: So in witness 1. In the Annals of Einhard and D. E. it reads “with joined hand.” Other witnesses read “with a force joined together.” This could easily have been misread in witness 1.], and captured the aforementioned Theoderic the Saxon.

(Chr. W.) The foundation of the monastery of Fulda.

## 4. 5.

(EINH. Ann.) **A.D. 746.** Carloman disclosed to his brother what he had long been considering: namely, that he wished to abandon the world [Note: “to leave it,” witness 5.] and serve God in the monastic habit. For this reason they undertook no expedition that year. Instead, both prepared themselves: Carloman to fulfill his journey and vow, and Pippin to send him away honorably.

## 5. 6.

(Chr. W.—EINH. *Life of Charles*, c. 2.) **A.D. 747.** [Note: D. E. add: “Rachis … his brother was appointed in his place,” from Sigebert, year 749.]

Carloman, inflamed by divine love and heading for Rome, presented himself to Pope Zacharias. The pope made him a cleric; after changing his clothing, he took the monastic habit. In a monastery built on Mount Soracte, or Syraptis [Note: “on Mount Serapte,” 1b; “on Mount Syrapti,” 4], near the church of Saint Silvester, he enjoyed the desired quiet for several years with the brothers who had come there with him for this purpose.

But when many nobles from Francia traveled to Rome to fulfill their vows and would not pass him by as though he had once been their lord, interrupting the leisure he valued above all by their frequent greetings, they compelled him to change his residence. When he saw that such crowds were hindering his purpose, he left the mountain and withdrew to the province of Samnium, to the monastery of Saint Benedict situated in the fortress of Cassino. There he completed the remainder of his life.

## 6. 7.

(EINH. Ann.) **A.D. 748.** Grifo, unwilling to remain subject to his brother Pippin, although he was living honorably under him, fled to Saxony. After gathering a Saxon army, he settled above the river Oker at a place called Orheim. Pippin, however, went with a Frankish army into Thuringia, entered Saxony against his brother’s schemes, and settled above the river Missaha at a place called Scahaningi. No battle was fought between them; instead, they withdrew by agreement.

## 7. 8.
