**A.D. 749.** Distrusting the loyalty of the Saxons, Grifo went to Bavaria with the forces that had flocked to him from Francia and brought the duchy under his own control. He received Tassilo and Hiltrude into submission and welcomed Suigger, who had come to his aid. When Pippin heard this, he came to Bavaria with a very large army and captured his brother Grifo together with all his men. He restored Tassilo to the duchy and, returning home, granted Grifo, in the manner of dukes, twelve counties. But Grifo was not satisfied with such a benefit and, in the same year, fled to Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine.

## 9. 10.

(Chr. W.) **A.D. 751.** [Note: D. E. add: “In Mesopotamia the earth split open, and from it rose a mule-like animal … the Arabs,” from Sigebert, year 753.]

Saint Burchard received the bishopric of Würzburg, in which he occupied the see for forty years.

(EINH. A.) This Saint Burchard and Folrad the chief chaplain—whom some call an abbot (*Life of Burchard*), while others call a presbyter (EINH. A.)—were sent to Pope Zacharias of Rome to consult him about the kings who at that time existed in Francia, possessing only the name of king and no royal power.

[Note: E. adds: “This is Folrad, who is said to have transferred the body of Saint Vitus the martyr from Rome to Gaul”; and continues: “S. Fr.”]

[Col. 0837D] (Life of Burchard.) The Franks had traditionally had kings from the ancient line of kings. They were called Merovingians from Meroveus, son of Clodius, their second king. Their genealogy continued down to Hilderic, then king, and ended with him. Although it might appear to have ended in that man, it had long since possessed no strength and displayed nothing distinguished in itself except the empty title of king.

For both the wealth and power of the kingdom were held by the prefects of the palace, who were called mayors of the palace and to whom supreme authority belonged. Nothing else was permitted to the king except, content with the royal name alone, to sit on his throne with his hair flowing and his beard hanging down, to create the appearance of a ruler, to hear ambassadors arriving from every direction, and, when they departed, to give them from his supposed authority the replies he had learned or been ordered to give. Apart from the useless name of king and the precarious allowance for his living, which the prefect of the palace supplied him according to his discretion, he possessed nothing else—except one small estate, and that a very small one, in which he had a house and from which he had a few servants to provide what he needed and render him service.

Wherever he had to go, he traveled in a cart drawn by yoked oxen, with a rustic ox-driver acting as driver. Thus he used to go to the palace and to the public assembly, which was held annually on the Kalends of May for the benefit of the kingdom [Note: Supplied in the margin by the same hand, witness 1]. There, presiding before the whole people, greeting everyone and being greeted by them, and honored with the proper services, he would return home. He would remain at home with his retinue until the following May.

The prefect of the palace, however, managed the administration of the kingdom and everything that had to be done or arranged either at home or abroad. At that time, when the aforementioned envoys were sent to Rome, Pippin—son of Charles and father of Charles the Great—was already exercising this office as though by hereditary right.

Pope Zacharias, consulted about this matter, sent back the reply that it was better for the man in whom supreme power resided to be called king. By his authority he ordered that Pippin be made king.

[Col. 0838C] ## 10. 11.

**A.D. 752.** Pippin, elected to the kingship according to Frankish custom by the authority of Pope Zacharias, was raised to the royal throne through the hands of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, in the city of Soissons.

—(Chr. W.) The translation of Saint Kilian took place.

—Blessed Pope Zacharias found the head of Saint George the martyr stored in a chest in the venerable patriarchal residence and transferred it to the city of Rome.

## 11. 12.

**A.D. 753.** Pope Stephen, the ninety-second, was ordained and occupied the see for five years and twenty-eight days.

### The Years of Pippin’s Reign

## 1. 13.

(EINH. A.) In the year 754 of the Lord’s incarnation, King Pippin entered Saxony with a large army. Although the Saxons resisted him with the greatest determination, they were nevertheless driven back and withdrew, while he advanced as far as the place called Rimie beside the river Weser. During this expedition Bishop Hiltigarius was killed on the mountain called Viburg [Note: “Wiburg,” 1b.]. As the king was returning from Saxony, a messenger brought news of the death of his brother Grifo, and of by whom and in what manner he had been killed.

In the same year Pope Stephen, after suffering much harm at the hands of Haistulf, king of the Lombards, came to King Pippin at the estate called Carisius [Note: “Carisius,” later corrected to “Parisius,” 1b.]. He urged him to defend himself and the Roman Church against the Lombards’ attacks.

Carloman also came, the king’s brother, now a monk, at the command of his abbot, so that he might oppose, before his brother, the entreaties of the Roman pontiff. He is thought to have done this unwillingly, because neither could he disregard his abbot’s commands, nor did that abbot dare resist the orders of the king of the Lombards, who had commanded him to do this.

(REGINO.) Pope Stephen, after being ill for some time near Paris and recovering again through Saint Denis, received from King Pippin a firm pledge of protection for the holy Roman Church. He then confirmed Pippin, by sacred anointing, in the dignity of kingship, and consecrated with him his two sons, Charles and Carloman, together with their mother Bertrada.

After sanctifying the Frankish nobles and the people together with an apostolic blessing, he bound them by the authority of blessed Peter the Apostle and declared that neither they nor anyone born from their descendants in the course of successive generations should ever set over themselves a king from another stock, but only from the lineage of those whom divine providence had then deigned to raise up for the defense of the Church.

(EINH. *Life of Charles*—*Life of Burchard*—Chr. W.) Thus Pippin, elevated and anointed from the office of prefect of the palace to the royal seat by apostolic authority, reigned afterward for fifteen years. The same Pope Stephen released him from the oath that he had sworn to King Hilderic together with the other leading men of the kingdom.

Hilderic, who had falsely borne the name of king, was tonsured and sent to a monastery. [Note: In witness 1, one and a half lines have been erased.]

## 2. 14.

(EINH. A.) **A.D. 755.** [Note: D. E. add: “Constantine … acts as a tyrant,” from Sigebert.]

At the invitation and request of the aforementioned Pope Stephen, King Pippin entered Italy with a strong force to exact from Haistulf, king of the Lombards, the justice due to the blessed Apostle Peter. The Lombards resisted and defended the mountain passes of Italy, and fierce fighting took place at the very passes. When the Lombards gave way, all the Frankish forces entered.

King Haistulf shut himself up in the city of Pavia. King Pippin besieged him until he received forty hostages as security for the fulfillment of justice to the holy Roman Church.

After these hostages had been given and the promises confirmed by oath, Pippin returned home, while he sent Pope Stephen back to Rome with the chaplain Folrad and a considerable Frankish force.

Carloman, the king’s brother, who had remained with Queen Bertrada in the city of Vienne, was seized by a fever and died before he could return. By the king’s order his body was taken to the monastery of Saint Benedict, where he had been a monk.

Saint Boniface suffered martyrdom. (Chr. W.) [Note: “Saint … suffered martyrdom” was added later in witness 1.]

## 3. 15.

(EINH. A.) **A.D. 756.** Since Haistulf, king of the Lombards, had fulfilled none of the things he had promised after giving hostages and swearing an oath, King Pippin again came into Italy with an army, besieged him in Pavia, and compelled him by the siege to fulfill his promises. After Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and the whole exarchate belonging to Ravenna had been restored to him, Pippin gave all these to Saint Peter. After completing these matters, he returned to Gaul.

After his departure, Haistulf began again to consider changing what he had promised. He fell from his horse while hunting and, becoming ill as a result, died within a few days. Desiderius succeeded him.

## 4. 16.

**A.D. 757.** The emperor Constantine sent gifts to King Pippin, among them an organ. They reached him at the estate of Compendium, where he was then holding the general assembly of his people.

There Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, also came with the leading men of his nation. He promised loyalty by oath both to King Pippin himself and to his sons Charles and Carloman over the body of Saint Denis. Not only there, but also over the bodies of Saint Martin and Saint Germanus, he confirmed the same oath with all his leading men.

## 5. 17.

**A.D. 758.** King Pippin attacked Saxony with an army. Although the Saxons resisted with great strength and defended themselves with fortifications, he defeated the defenders in battle and entered the rampart they had constructed to defend their homeland. After battle was joined everywhere, he killed a very large number of them and compelled them to promise that they would do everything he ordered and would give three hundred horses every year as a mark of honor.

When these arrangements had been made and confirmed according to Saxon custom so that they would be binding, he returned to Gaul.

—Pope Paul, the ninety-third, occupied the see for ten years.

## 6. 18.

**A.D. 759.** [Note: D. E. add: “Saint Gingulf was killed in Burgundy by a certain cleric because that cleric had committed adultery with Gingulf’s wife, whom he loved.”]

A son was born to King Pippin, whom he wished to be called Pippin after himself. But the child was overtaken by premature death and died in the third year after his birth.

## 7. 19.

**A.D. 760.** Since Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, refused to return the property of the churches that was in his power and belonged to churches established under the authority of King Pippin, and since he scorned to heed the king, who admonished him about these matters through his envoys, his defiance stirred that same king to undertake war against him.

The king therefore gathered forces from everywhere, entered Aquitaine, and declared that he would exact the property and rights of the churches. When he had pitched camp and settled at a place called Tedoad, Waifarius, not daring to engage in battle, sent an embassy to the king and promised to do what was ordered and to restore the rights of the churches. He also gave two hostages from the leading men of his people, Adalgarius and Itherius.

(Chr. W.) After accepting them, the king refrained from war and returned home.

—Saint Otmar, having been exiled to the island called Stein, departed to God. [Note: He died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifth month.]

## 8. 20.

(EINH. A.) **A.D. 761.** Although Waifarius had given hostages and sworn oaths, he nevertheless judged it preferable to exact vengeance for the war brought against him in the previous year. He therefore caused an army that devastated Frankish possessions to advance as far as the city of Chalon.

When this was reported to King Pippin, who was holding a general assembly at the estate of Düren, he gathered counsel from every side, entered Aquitaine with a great preparation for war, and laid everything waste with sword and fire. He captured some towns and fortresses by force, while others voluntarily surrendered to the victor.

When he had reached Limoges while devastating everything, he returned and, after spending the winter again at Carisius, celebrated Christmas and Easter there. On this expedition his first-born son Charles was with him; after his father’s death, supreme authority over the entire empire came to him.

## 9. 21.

**A.D. 762.** King Pippin, wishing to bring to an end the war he had undertaken, entered Aquitaine for the third time. After capturing the city of Bourges and the fortress of Thouars, he returned and spent the winter at the estate of Gentilly.

## 10. 22.

**A.D. 763.** After holding an assembly at Nevers, Pippin entered Aquitaine for the fourth time. Having laid waste everything outside the fortifications as far as the town of Cahors [Note: “Carducia,” witness 16], he turned back through the Limousin with his entire army in order to return to Francia.

(Ann. Laur.—EINH. A.) Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, setting aside the oaths he had sworn and forgetting all the benefits his uncle King Pippin had bestowed upon him, deceitfully withdrew from this expedition by pretending to be ill and returned to Bavaria. Having resolved to defect, he renounced coming any further into the king’s presence. The king, however, dismissed the army and spent the winter at the estate of Longlier.

## 11. 23.

**A.D. 764.** King Pippin, torn in different directions by two wars—namely, the Aquitanian war already undertaken and the Bavarian war to be undertaken because of the defection of Duke Tassilo—held an assembly of his people at Worms. Since the expedition was postponed to the future, he remained at home that year.

[Col. 0841D] ## 12. 24.

**A.D. 765.** Pippin held a general assembly at the estate of Attigny. But, undertaking no expedition anywhere that year either, he spent the winter at Aachen.

—The bodies of the saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius were transferred from Rome to Francia. [Note: “The bodies … to Francia” was added later in witness 1.]

## 13. 25.

**A.D. 766.** The Turks, having come out through the Caspian Gates, went to war with the Avars, and many from both sides perished.

Pippin, intent on completing the Aquitanian war, held an assembly at Orléans and set out for Aquitaine for the fifth time. He rebuilt the fortress of Argentomagus, which Waifarius had destroyed, stationed a garrison there and in the city of Bourges, and returned.

## 14. 26.

**A.D. 767.** [Note: D. E. add: “Constantine … and H., king of the Saracens, equal … the deep,” from Sigebert, year 766.]

A dispute arose between the Eastern and Western Church—that is, between the Greeks and the Romans—concerning the Holy Trinity and the images of the saints. King Pippin held a synod at the estate of Gentilly [alternative: Salency [Note: So in the margin of witness 1, apparently by the same hand; “Sal.” is written above “Gent.” E1: “salmonciaco vel gentiliaco”; D.: “salmonciaco or gentiliaco”; 1b omits this and reads “another synod”; 4: “Salmontiaco”; 5, 9c, 10, 11: “Salmontiaco.”].

After the dispute had been debated, he set out for Aquitaine after Christmas, for the seventh time, to complete the aforementioned war. After capturing many fortresses and villages, he returned to Vienne, celebrated Easter there, and refreshed the army. In August he set out to continue the war. Coming to Bourges, he held an assembly in the open country. From there he advanced to the river Garonne and captured many fortresses, rocky strongholds, and caves in which a very large number of the enemy were defending themselves. Returning to Bourges, he dismissed the army into winter quarters.

15. 27. A.D. 768. Pippin celebrated Christmas at Bourges, and as soon as he saw that the time was suitable for waging war, he summoned an army from every quarter and hastened toward the city of Saintes. After capturing Rimistein on the way, when he had reached the aforesaid city, Waifarius’s mother, sister, and nieces were brought to him. He received them kindly and ordered that they be kept in custody, then set out for the Garonne River. There Heriwigus [Note: [Col. 0841] *herwicus* in 1b.] met him together with another sister of the aforesaid duke, and surrendered himself and her to the king. After several matters had been successfully accomplished, the king returned and celebrated Easter in the castle called Sels. Taking his wife and household with him, he came again to the city of Saintes. Leaving his wife and household there, he resolved with all his forces to pursue Waifarius, and did not intend to desist before either capturing him alive or killing him in his rebellion.

After Waifarius had been killed in the territory of Périgueux and the Aquitanian war had been brought to an end, Pippin returned to Saintes. Remaining there for some time, he fell ill; nevertheless, he was carried to Tours, where he prayed at the shrine of Saint Martin. From there he came to Paris and died on 8 Kalends of October [24 September]. His body was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis.

His sons Charles and Carloman were then both made kings by the agreement of all the Franks (EINH. ch. 3), with this condition stipulated beforehand: that they should divide the entire kingdom equally. Charles received the part that their father Pippin had held, while Carloman received the part possessed by their uncle Carloman; and Charles received the insignia of kingship on 7 Ides of October [9 October] in the city of Noyon, while Carloman received them at Soissons. (EINH. Ann. and Laur.)

Charles, who was the elder by birth, went to Aachen and celebrated Christmas there, and Easter in the city of Rouen. (EINH. [Col. 0843A] same passage.) Thus the conditions were accepted on both sides, and each received the portion of the divided kingdom according to the arrangement proposed to him. This harmony remained, though with great difficulty, since many on Carloman’s side wished to break up their partnership, to such an extent that some even planned to bring them into armed conflict. But the outcome of events itself proved that there had been more suspicion than danger: after Carloman’s death, his wife and sons, together with some of his leading men, fled to Italy and, disregarding her husband’s brother without any valid reason, placed herself and her children under the protection of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. (EINH. ch. 4.)

Carloman, after jointly administering the kingdom for two years, died of illness. Charles, however, after his brother’s death, was made king with the consent of all the Franks. Concerning his birth and infancy or boyhood, Einhard, the writer of his deeds, who had been brought up by that same prince, says that nothing had ever been set down in writing about these matters, nor had anyone been found in his time who claimed to possess knowledge of them. But concerning his deeds, character, and the other parts of his life [Note: [Col. 0844A] He set out very clearly many remarkable and highly memorable deeds, surpassing those of almost all emperors. E; all the following material through “he dared to enter” (col. 853) is absent.] he explained matters as follows.

DESCRIPTION OF THE DEEDS OF CHARLES THE GREAT.

[Col. 0843]

[Col. 0843B] (EINH. Life of Charles.) Of all the wars which he waged, he first undertook the Aquitanian war, begun by his father but not yet finished, because it seemed capable of being completed quickly. While his brother was still alive, he undertook it, having even requested his assistance; and although his brother, through the machinations of certain evil men, disappointed him of the promised aid, he carried out the expedition he had undertaken most vigorously and did not desist until he accomplished what he had set out to achieve. For he compelled a certain Hunold, who after Waifarius’s death had seized Aquitaine and attempted to renew the war, now almost concluded, to leave Aquitaine and flee into Gascony. Not allowing him to remain there either, Charles crossed the Garonne and ordered Lupus, duke of the Gascons, to surrender the fugitive, declaring that, unless he did so promptly, he would demand him by war. [Col. 0843C] But Lupus, adopting the sounder counsel, not only surrendered Hunold but also submitted himself, together with the province over which he ruled, to Charles’s authority.

(EINH. Ann. for 773.—Life. Ann.) When this war had ended, at the request and entreaties of Hadrian, pontiff of Rome, who could not endure the insolence of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, he undertook war against the Lombards. Dividing the forces which he had brought, he ordered one part, with his uncle Bernard, to proceed by way of Mount Jupiter; he himself led the other by way of Mont Cenis and entered Italy. (Life.) He did not desist until he had received King Desiderius, exhausted by a long siege at Pavia, into surrender and sent him into perpetual exile; compelled his son Adalgisus, in whom all hope seemed to rest, to depart not only from the kingdom but also from Italy; restored all that had been taken from the Romans; crushed Routhgisus, prefect of the duchy of Friuli, while he was plotting innovations; subjected all Italy to his rule; and set his son Pippin as king over the land he had subdued.

After the end of this war, the Saxon war, which had seemed as though interrupted, was renewed. No war was undertaken that was either more prolonged, more savage, or more burdensome to the Frankish people, because the Saxons, like nearly all the peoples of Germany, were fierce by nature and devoted to the worship of idols; nor did they consider it dishonourable to violate or transgress either divine or [Col. 0844B] human laws. [Note: [Col. 0843] After “idols,” 1 supplies.] War was therefore undertaken against them and was waged for a continuous thirty years with great spirit on both sides, though with greater loss to the Saxons. It could indeed have been ended sooner, had Saxon perfidy permitted it. It is difficult to say how often, when defeated and suppliant, they surrendered themselves to the king, promised to do what was commanded, gave without delay the hostages demanded, and received the envoys sent to them. At times they were so tamed and softened that they even promised to abandon the worship of demons and submit themselves to the Christian religion; but, as they were at times ready to do these things, so they were always hasty to overthrow them again. The king’s magnanimity, either in person or through his counts, sent an army and always avenged their perfidy, until, after all who were accustomed to resist had been crushed, he removed ten thousand persons from among those who inhabited both banks of the River Elbe, together with their wives and little children, and distributed them in many divisions throughout Gaul and Germany. It is established that the war, prolonged for so many years, was ended on this condition: that, abandoning the worship of demons, they should receive the sacraments of the Christian religion.

Although this war was drawn out for so long, Charles himself engaged the enemy in battle no more than twice: once near the mountain called Osneggi, at the place named Theotmelli, and again near the River Hase, both within one month, with only a few days intervening. Yet in these two battles they were so thoroughly defeated [Col. 0844D] that thereafter they did not dare either to provoke the king or to resist him when he came, unless defended by some natural fortification. Nevertheless, in that war many men of the highest rank among both the Franks and the Saxons, and men who had held the highest offices, perished. At length it was ended in the thirty-third year. Meanwhile he also subdued Spain; for he first subjected Aquitaine and Gascony. He likewise subdued the Bretons and, dispatching an expedition, compelled them to do what was commanded.

—He afterwards entered Italy with an army and, passing by way of Rome, came to Capua, a city of Campania. Having pitched camp there, he threatened the Beneventans with war unless they surrendered. This was forestalled by Aragisus, duke of that people [Note: [Col. 0845] *arasgilfus* in 1b.], who, sending his sons Rumold and Grimold to meet the king with a great sum of money, begged him to accept his sons as hostages and promised that he and his people would do what was commanded, with this sole exception: that he himself should not be compelled to appear before him. The king, considering the advantage of the people more than the duke’s obstinacy, accepted the hostages offered to him and, as a great favour, granted that he should not be compelled to appear before him. Retaining the younger son as hostage, he restored the elder to his father; and, having sent envoys with Aragisus to exact oaths of fidelity from the Beneventans, he returned to Rome. After spending several days there in the veneration of the saints, he returned to Gaul.

—Then the Bavarian war arose suddenly [Col. 0845B] and was brought to a swift conclusion. It had been stirred up by the pride and indolence alike of Duke Tassilo, who, at his wife’s urging—she was the daughter of King Desiderius and thought that she could avenge her father’s exile through her husband—had made an alliance with the Huns, who border Bavaria on the east, and was attempting not only to refuse what was commanded but to provoke the king to war. Since the duke’s obstinacy seemed excessive, the king’s spirit could not endure it; accordingly, having gathered forces from every quarter, he came to the River Lech, which divides the Bavarians from the Alemanni, intending to invade Bavaria. Having stationed his camp on its bank, he decided, before entering the province, to test the duke’s disposition through envoys. But Tassilo, judging it neither useful for himself nor for his people to act obstinately, submitted himself as a suppliant [Col. 0845C] to the king, gave the hostages required, including his son Theodo, and moreover gave his pledged word under oath that he would not consent to revolt from Charles’s authority at anyone’s persuasion. Thus the war, which had seemed likely to be very great, was brought to a most speedy end.

Tassilo, however, was afterwards summoned to the king and was neither permitted to return nor was the province he had held thereafter entrusted to a duke; rather, it was committed to counts. (Life, Ann. for 788.) For when Duke Tassilo had been judged guilty of treason and condemned to death, the king’s clemency granted him his life; his dress was changed and he was sent to a monastery. His son Theodo too was tonsured and assigned to the monastic life.

—(Life.) When these disturbances had been thus settled, war was brought against the Slavs, who in our usage are called Wilci but in their own language Weletabi. [Col. 0845D] In this war the Saxons served, as auxiliaries among the other nations, though with feigned and less than devoted obedience; and in this single expedition these same Slavs were so subdued that thereafter they did not resist commands.

The greatest of all the wars undertaken by Charles, apart from the Saxon war, followed this war: namely, that waged against the Avars or Huns. He conducted it more vigorously than the others and with a far greater preparation. Yet he himself made only one expedition into Pannonia—for that people inhabited that province—and entrusted the completion of the rest to his son Pippin, to the prefects of the provinces, [Col. 0846A] and also to counts and envoys. When these had carried them out most vigorously, the war was at last concluded in the eighth year. How many battles were fought in it and how much blood was shed, Pannonia, left almost empty of every inhabitant, bears witness, as does the place where the Cagan’s royal seat stood, so deserted that not even a trace of human habitation appears there. In this war all the nobility of the Huns perished, all their glory fell, and all their money and treasures amassed over a long time were plundered. Human memory can recall no war raised against the Franks by which they were enriched and increased in wealth more greatly, for until that time they had seemed almost poor. So much gold and silver was found in the royal residence, and so much precious spoil was taken in battle, that it may deservedly be believed that the Franks justly took from the Huns what the Huns had formerly unjustly torn from other peoples.

—Description [Note: [Col. 0845] These words are written in red in the margin. 1.] of the land of the Huns: For the land of the Huns, as narrators of ancient times attest (Mon. Sang. II, 1), was enclosed by nine rings, which the Germans call *haga*. Each of these was so constructed of oak, beech, or fir posts that it extended twenty feet in width from edge to edge and rose the same number of feet in height; its entire hollow was filled either with the hardest stones or with most tenacious clay [Note: [Col. 0845] “city” 4; “ci city” 9c.], while the surface of these same ramparts was covered with the most perfect turf. Within their boundaries small trees were planted which, as we are accustomed to see, when cut down and cast aside put forth the foliage of branches and leaves. From the first ring to the second there extended twenty German miles, and similarly thence to the third, and so on to the ninth, although the rings themselves were each much narrower than the preceding. Between these embankments villages and country houses were so placed that a human voice could be heard from one to another. Opposite these buildings, however, gates of no great width had been constructed amid impregnable walls, through which not only those outside but also those within customarily went out for the purpose of plundering. From ring to ring, moreover, possessions [Note: [Col. 0845] *possiones* 1.] and dwellings were arranged in every direction so that the sound of trumpets could be distinctly [Note: [Col. 0845] “more distinctly” 4, 5, 9c, 10, 11.] perceived between each separate place.

To these fortifications, for two hundred years and more, they brought together whatever wealth existed in all the West; and, while both the Goths and the Vandals disturbed the peace of mankind, they left the western world almost empty. Then the most unconquered Charles so completely subdued them in eight years that he permitted not even the slightest remnants of them to remain. But he withdrew his hand from the Bulgars because, the Huns having been destroyed, they seemed likely to do no harm to the Frankish kingdom. Moreover, he distributed the booty found in Pannonia with the greatest liberality among bishoprics and monasteries.

(EINH. Life of Charles.) Only two of the leading Franks perished in that war. Eric, [Col. 0847A] duke of Friuli, was caught in an ambush laid by the townspeople in Liburnia near the maritime city of Tarsatica; and Gerold, prefect of Bavaria, was killed in Pannonia, by an unknown assailant, together with only the two men who accompanied him as he rode about encouraging each man, while he was drawing up the battle line to fight the Huns. Otherwise this war was almost bloodless for the Franks and had a most successful outcome, although it was drawn out by its magnitude for a rather long time. After it, the Saxon war too received an end commensurate with its length.

—The Bohemian and Linonian wars, which arose later, likewise could not endure; both were completed in a short time under the leadership of Charles the Younger.

—Finally, war was undertaken against the Northmen, who are called Danes. At first they practised piracy; then, with a larger fleet, they devastated the coasts [Col. 0847B] of Gaul and Germany. Their king Godfrey was so inflated with vain hope that he promised himself dominion over all Germany; he regarded Frisia and Saxony no differently from his own provinces. He had already reduced his neighbouring Abodrites to his dominion and made them tributary to himself. He even boasted that he would shortly come to Aachen, where the king’s court was, with very great forces. Nor was all credit denied to his words, vain though they were; indeed, it was thought that he would have begun something of this sort had he not been forestalled by a swift death. For, killed by his own retainer—or, as some more truly judge (Mon. Sang. II, 13), by his own son, whose mother he had repudiated and another woman married—he put an end both to his own life and to the war he had begun. [Col. 0847C]

(EINH. Life of Charlemagne) These are the wars which the most powerful king conducted with the greatest prudence and success over forty-six years—for he reigned that many years—in various parts of the world. Through them he so nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks, which he had received from his father Pippin already great and strong, that he made it almost twice as large.

For whereas previously the power of the Frankish kingdom extended over no more than that part of Gaul which lies between the Rhine, the Loire, the Ocean, and the Balearic Sea; that part of Germany which lies between Saxony, the Danube, and the River Saale, which divides the Thuringians from the Sorbs and was later inhabited by the Franks called Eastern Franks; and, besides these, the Alemanni and Bavarians, he himself, through the wars mentioned above, first conquered Aquitaine and Wasconia, together with the entire range of the Pyrenees, as far as the River Ebro—which rises among the Navarri [Note: [Col. 0847] so in the manuscripts], cuts through the most fertile fields of Spain, and joins the Balearic Sea beneath the walls of the city of Tortosa. Next he conquered all Italy, from Augusta Praetoria to lower Calabria, where the territories of the Greeks and Beneventans meet. Then he conquered Saxony, which is indeed a large part of Germany and is thought to be twice as broad as the part inhabited by the Franks, though it may be comparable to it in length. Next he conquered both Pannonias, and Dacia, lying on the opposite bank of the Danube; also Histria, Liburnia, and Dalmatia, except for the coastal cities, which he allowed the emperor of Constantinople to retain because of their friendship and the treaty concluded with him. Finally, he completely subdued all the barbarous and wild peoples who inhabit Germany between the Rhine and Vistula, the Ocean and the Danube—peoples almost similar in language but very different in customs and appearance—and made them tributary.

He also increased the glory of his kingdom by joining certain kings and peoples to himself through friendship. He bound Alfonso, king of Galicia and Asturias [Note: [Col. 0847] “Alfonso and Asturias,” 1b], so closely to himself by an alliance that whenever Alfonso sent him letters or envoys, he ordered that he be called before him no otherwise than “his own man.” [Col. 0848B] He also inclined the kings of the Scots so favorably toward his will through his generosity that they never declared him to be anything but their lord, and themselves his subjects and servants. With Aaron, king of the Persians, who, except for India, held almost the entire East, he maintained such harmonious friendship that Aaron preferred his favor to the friendship of all the kings and princes in the whole world, and judged that he alone deserved to be honored with respect and generosity.

The emperors of Constantinople also—Nicephorus, Michael, and Leo—voluntarily sought his friendship and alliance and sent many envoys to him. With them, however, because he had assumed the title of emperor and was therefore viewed with great suspicion, as though he wished to seize their empire, he established the firmest possible treaty, so that no occasion for any discord might remain [Col. 0848C] between the parties. For the power of the Franks had always been suspect to the Romans and Greeks. Hence there remains that Greek proverb: “If you have a Frank as a friend, you have no neighbor” (τον φρανκον φυλον κεχις, γυτονα ου κεχις).

Although he was so great in enlarging his kingdom and subduing foreign nations, and was constantly occupied with such enterprises, he nevertheless began many works in various places that contributed to the dignity and usefulness of the kingdom, and completed some of them. Among these, the most notable may rightly be considered the basilica of the holy Mother of God at Aachen, constructed with marvelous workmanship, and the bridge over the Rhine at Mainz, five hundred paces long—for the river is that wide there. Yet the bridge was consumed by fire one year before his death and could not be rebuilt because of his sudden death, although he had been considering replacing the wooden bridge with one of stone.

He also began palaces of outstanding workmanship: one not far from the city of Mainz, beside a villa called Ingelheim, and another at Nijmegen above the River Waal. Above all, wherever throughout his kingdom he found sacred buildings collapsed through age, he ordered the bishops and abbots responsible for them to restore them, taking care through envoys that they fulfilled his commands. Such, it is clear, was his conduct in enlarging, defending, and ordering the kingdom. Let us now speak of what he was like in domestic matters.

After his father’s death, when he divided the kingdom with his brother, he endured his brother’s hostility and envy with such patience that everyone found it astonishing that he could not be provoked by him even to anger. Later, at his mother’s urging, he married the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards; after a year he repudiated her and married Hildigard, a woman of the Suebi and of the highest nobility. By her he fathered three sons—Charles, Pippin, and Louis—and an equal number of daughters—Ruothrud, Bertha, and Gisla. He also had three other daughters: Theodrada and Hiltrud, two by his wife Fastrada, who was of the race of the Eastern Franks, that is, the Germans, and the third, Ruotheide, by a concubine. After Fastrada’s death he married Luitgard, an Alemannian, by whom he had no children. After her death he had three concubines: Gersuinda, of Saxon descent, by whom he had a daughter named Adaltrud; Regina, who bore him Drogo and Hugh; and Adelinda, who bore Theodoric.

His mother Bertrada also grew old in great honor with him. He revered her greatly, and no disagreement ever arose between them except over the divorce of Desiderius’s daughter, whom he had married at his mother’s urging. She eventually died after Hildigard’s death, when she had already seen three grandsons and three granddaughters in her son’s household. He had her buried with great honor in the same basilica at Saint-Denis in which his father was buried [Col. 0849C] [Note: [Col. 0849] *humare* (“to bury”) corrected to *humari* (“to be buried”), 1].

He had one sister, named Gisla, who from girlhood had devoted herself to a religious life. He honored her with the same affection as his mother. She too died a few years before his death in the monastery where she had lived.

He decreed that his children should be educated in such a way that both sons and daughters would first be instructed in the liberal studies to which he himself also devoted attention. Then, as soon as their age permitted, he had his sons taught to ride in the Frankish manner and trained in arms and hunting; he ordered his daughters to become accustomed to wool-working and to devote themselves to the distaff and spindle, so that they would not grow slack through idleness, and to be instructed in every honorable pursuit.

Of all these children, he lost only two sons and one daughter before his death: Charles, who was the elder; Pippin, whom he had placed over the kingdom of Italy; [Col. 0849D] and Ruothrud, the firstborn of his daughters, who had been betrothed to Constantine, the Greek emperor, son of Leo and Irene. Pippin left one son, Bernard, and five surviving daughters. In these he displayed a notable example of his affection, arranging that his grandson should succeed his father and that his granddaughters should be raised among his own daughters.

He took such great care in raising his sons and daughters [Note: [Col. 0849] MS 1 reads *tantum* (“such,” neuter), perhaps corrected to *tantam* (“such,” feminine); 9c, 10, and El. read *tantum*.] that, whenever he was at home, he never dined without them and never traveled without them. His sons rode beside him, while his daughters followed behind; a troop of guards specially assigned for this purpose protected the rear of their procession. Although they were exceedingly beautiful and he loved them very much, it is astonishing that he did not wish to give any of them in marriage to anyone, whether one of his own people or a foreigner. Instead, he kept them all with him in his household until his death, saying that he could not do without their companionship. For this reason, although otherwise fortunate, he experienced the indignity of adverse fortune; yet he concealed it so completely that one might think no suspicion or rumor of any disgrace concerning them had ever arisen.

He had a son named Pippin, born of a concubine, whose mention among the others I postponed. He was handsome in face but disfigured by a hump. While his father was wintering in Bavaria during the war he had undertaken against the Huns, Pippin conspired against him with certain leading Franks who had enticed him with a vain promise of the kingdom. After the plot had been discovered and the conspirators condemned, his hair was cut off, and he was allowed to devote himself to a religious life in the monastery of Prüm.

Another powerful conspiracy had previously been formed against him in Germany. Its leaders were partly blinded, while the others remained unharmed but were all carried into exile; none of them was killed except three, who, when they defended themselves with drawn swords so as not to be captured and had even killed some people, were slain because they could not otherwise be restrained. The cruelty of Queen Fastrada is said to have been the cause and origin of these conspiracies. In both cases, therefore, the king was plotted against because, by consenting to his wife’s cruelty, he seemed to have departed from the kindness and gentleness of his own nature.

For the rest, throughout his entire life he conducted himself at home and abroad with such great love and favor from everyone that no one ever brought against him even the slightest charge of unjust credulity. He loved foreigners and took great care in receiving them, so much so that their multitude seemed, not without reason, burdensome not only to the palace but also to the kingdom. Yet, because of his greatness of spirit, he was not at all weighed down by such a burden; indeed, he balanced even immense inconveniences with the praise of generosity and the reward of a good reputation [Note: [Col. 0849] *onere* (“burden”), 5].

He had a large and sturdy body, and a tall stature, though not excessive—for it is established that he measured seven of his own feet in height. His head was round at the crown, his eyes very large and lively, his nose slightly longer than ordinary, his hair attractively gray, and his face cheerful and bright, giving his appearance authority and dignity whether he stood or sat. Although his neck seemed thick and short and his belly somewhat protruding, the proportion of his other limbs concealed these features. His gait was firm, and his whole bodily bearing manly. His voice was clear, though it suited the form of his body less well. His health was good, except that for four years before his death he was frequently seized by fevers; at the end he also became lame in one foot.

He was rich and fluent in speech and could express whatever he wished with complete clarity. Nor was he content with his native language: he applied himself to learning foreign languages as well. He learned Latin so thoroughly that he was accustomed to pray in it as in his native tongue; Greek, however, he could understand better than he could speak. He cultivated the liberal arts with the greatest zeal, revered their teachers greatly, and raised them to positions of high honor. In grammar he studied under Peter of Pisa, an elderly deacon. In the other disciplines he had as his teacher Albinus, surnamed Alcuin, likewise a deacon from Britain, a man learned in every field. With him he devoted much time and effort to learning rhetoric and dialectic, and especially astronomy.

He also studied the art of calculation and, with keen attention, examined the courses of the stars with the greatest curiosity. He attempted to write as well: he used to carry writing tablets and notebooks around with him in bed beneath his pillow, so that whenever he had free time he could train his hand in forming letters. But the effort had little success, since it was begun too late and in the wrong order.

He constantly practiced riding and hunting, which were traditional to his people, since scarcely any nation on earth can be found that equals the Franks in this art. He also delighted in naturally hot waters, exercising his body through frequent swimming. He was so skilled at it that no one could rightly be placed before him. For this reason he built a royal residence at Aachen and spent the final years of his life there continuously, until his death.

In food and drink he was temperate, but more temperate in drink, so that at dinner he rarely drank more than three times. He could not abstain from food to the same extent, and he often complained that fasting was harmful to his body. He very rarely gave banquets, and then only on the greatest festivals, though on those occasions with a large number of people. His daily dinner consisted of only four courses, besides the roast meat that the huntsmen used to bring in on spits; he preferred this to every other kind of food. During dinner he listened either to some entertainment or to a reader. Histories and the deeds of ancient men were read to him; he also delighted in the books of Saint Augustine, especially those entitled *The City of God*.

With regard to supporting the poor and the free generosity that the Greeks call almsgiving, he was exceedingly devoted. He took care to practice it not only in his homeland and his own kingdom but also overseas—in Syria, Egypt, and Africa, at Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage—wherever he found Christians living in poverty. Taking pity on their want, he used to send them money. For this reason above all he sought the friendship of overseas kings, so that some relief and support might come to Christians living under their rule.

Among sacred places he especially honored the church of the blessed Apostle Peter at Rome, in whose treasury he amassed a great quantity of money. Throughout his entire reign he considered nothing more important than restoring the city of Rome, through his own work and exertion, to its ancient authority, and ensuring that the church of Saint Peter, through him, would not only be safe and defended but also, through his works, more richly adorned and endowed than all other churches.

Although he valued it so highly, during the forty-six years of his reign he went there only four times, for the fulfillment of vows and for prayer. On his final visit, these were not the only reasons: the Romans had compelled Pope Leo, who had suffered many injuries—his eyes having reportedly been torn out and his tongue cut off—to appeal to the king for protection. Therefore, when he came to Rome to restore the condition of the church, which had been greatly disturbed, he spent the whole winter there.

At that time he received the title of emperor and Augustus. At first he disliked it so much that he declared that, had he been able to foresee the pope’s intention, he would not have entered the church on that day, even though it was the greatest festival. Nevertheless, he endured with great patience the resentment caused by the title he had assumed, while the Roman emperors were indignant about it. He overcame their arrogance through the greatness of spirit in which he was undoubtedly far superior to them, sending them frequent embassies and calling them “brothers” in his letters.

After assuming the imperial title, he noticed that much was lacking from the laws of his people—for the Franks have two laws, very different in many places. He considered adding what was missing, uniting what was inconsistent, and correcting what was wrong or improperly expressed. But he did nothing further in this matter except add a few chapters, and those incomplete, to the laws.

Nevertheless, he had the laws of all the nations under his rule that had not been written down committed to writing and recorded. He also had the barbarous and very ancient songs written down and preserved in memory—songs that celebrated the deeds and wars of ancient kings. He began a grammar of the native language as well. He also assigned names according to their own language to the months, which until then had been called among the Franks partly by Latin and partly by barbarian names. He called January *wintermanoth*, February *hornung*, March *lencinmanoth*, April *ostermanoth*, May *vunnemanoth*, June *brahmanoth*, July *howimanoth*, August *arnmanoth*, September *witemanoth*, October *windemanoth*, November *herbistmanoth*, and December [Col. 0852D] *heilicmanoth*.

He likewise marked the twelve winds with their own names, whereas previously scarcely more than four names for winds could be found: the southeast wind he called *osterwint*; the east-southeast, *ostsundroni*; the southeast-south, *sundostroni*; the south wind, *sundroni*; the south-southwest, *sundwestroni*; the southwest, *westsundroni*; the west wind, *westroni*; the west-northwest, *westnordroni*; the northwest, *nordwestroni*; the north wind, *nordroni*; the northeast, *nordostroni*; and the east-northeast, *ostnordroni*.

He cultivated the Christian religion, with which he had been imbued from childhood, most devoutly and with the deepest piety. For this reason he built at Aachen a basilica of extraordinary beauty and adorned it with gold, silver, lamps, and grilles and doors of solid bronze. Since he could not obtain columns and marble for its construction elsewhere, he arranged for them to be transported from Rome [Col. 0853A] and Ravenna.

He diligently attended the church morning and evening, during the night hours, and at the time of the sacrifice, as long as his health permitted. He took great care that everything done there should be carried out with the utmost propriety, repeatedly warning the doorkeepers not to allow anything indecent or filthy either to be brought in or to remain there. He provided such an abundance of sacred vessels of gold and silver and priestly vestments that, when the sacrifices were celebrated, not even the doorkeepers—the lowest-ranking officials—needed to serve in their ordinary clothing.

He diligently corrected the discipline of reading and singing. He was highly skilled in both, although he himself neither read publicly nor sang except softly and in unison. (Monk of Saint Gall I.5, 7.) It was customary in his basilica for the choirmaster to assign each person on the preceding day which responsory he was to sing during the night office. But no one assigned the readings to anyone else, nor did anyone mark the end with wax or impress even the slightest sign with his fingernail. Rather, everyone took care to make all the readings so familiar to himself that, whenever he was unexpectedly ordered to read, he would be found faultless in the king’s presence.

By extending a finger or staff, or by sending someone from his side to those sitting at a distance, he indicated whom he wished to read. He signaled the end of a reading with a sound from his throat. Everyone was so attentively dependent upon this signal that, whether he indicated the end of a sentence, the middle of a distinction, or a subdivision, no one dared begin either above or below, however inappropriate the ending or beginning might seem. In this way it came about that, even if they did not understand what they were reading, all the readers in his palace were excellent. No outsider, and no newcomer either, unless able to read and sing, dared enter his choir.

At the end of his life [Note: [Col. 0854B] E continues: “The same emperor, when he was now already afflicted by illness, etc.”], when he was already weighed down by illness and old age, he summoned to himself his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, the only surviving son of Queen Hildigard. Having solemnly assembled the leading men from the entire Frankish kingdom [EINH. Life of Charlemagne], he appointed Louis, with the consent of all, his associate in the whole kingdom and heir to the imperial title. Placing a diadem on his head, he ordered him to be called emperor and Augustus. All who were present received this decision with great approval, for it seemed to them divinely inspired for the welfare of the kingdom. The act increased his majesty and struck no small terror into foreign nations. [Col. 0853D]

He then sent his son back to Aquitaine. He himself, according to his usual custom, although exhausted by old age, went hunting not far from the royal residence at Aachen. After spending the remainder of the autumn in this activity, he returned to Aachen around the Kalends of November. While wintering there, he was seized by a severe fever in January and took to bed. Immediately, as he was accustomed to do during fevers, he imposed abstinence from food upon himself, believing that by this restraint the illness could be driven away or at least eased.

But when pain in his side was added to the fever—a condition the Greeks call *pleuritis*—and he continued to fast, sustaining his body only with very infrequent drink, he died on the seventh day after taking to bed, after receiving holy communion, in the seventy-second year of his age and in the forty-sixth year from the beginning of his reign [lacuna], in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0853] “Indiction 7,” written above in the same hand, 1], on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, at the third hour of the day.

His body was washed and prepared according to customary ceremony, carried into the church amid the greatest mourning of the entire people, and buried. At first there was uncertainty about where it should be laid, because he himself had given no command about this while alive. At last everyone agreed that he could nowhere be buried more honorably than in the basilica which he himself had built in that same place at his own expense, out of love for God and our Lord Jesus Christ and for love of his holy and eternal Virgin Mother. He was buried there on the very day of his death, and a gilded arch was erected above the tomb, with an image and inscription. The inscription was composed as follows:

“Under this tomb lies the body of Charles, the great and orthodox emperor, who nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks and ruled it prosperously for forty-six years.”

[Note: [Col. 0854B] D and E add: “Rome—Paul—scandal”; “This [Col. 0854C] through zeal—private”; and, after 28, “This man, so—chrism,” and *Venerationem s. i. c. e. p. a.* [a title abbreviated in the source], from Sigibert, years 767 and 768.]

Pope Stephen, the ninety-fourth, held the see for three years, five months, and twenty-eight days. [Note: [Col. 0853] “Stephen—28” added afterward by 1.]

[Col. 0854C] [Years of Constantine.] 28. [Year of Charles.] 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 769, Charles the Great, son of Pippin, began to reign with his brother Carloman after the kingdom had been divided following their father’s death; he reigned for forty-six years—three with his brother and afterward forty-three alone (EINH. Annals). In his first year, a certain Hunald invaded Aquitaine, which had fallen to Charles’s share, and, stirring up the inhabitants to new rebellion, renewed the war which his father Pippin had seemed to bring to an end by killing Waifar. Charles marched against him and requested his brother’s assistance, but was unable to obtain it because evil men prevented it. Nevertheless, after meeting with him, Charles set out to pursue Hunald and, by sending an embassy to Lupus, duke of Wasconia, received the fugitive together with his wife. Lupus himself and all Wasconia having submitted to him, Charles returned.

29. 2. A.D. 770. King Charles held a general assembly in the city of Worms. Bertrada, mother of the kings, stationed with her younger son Carloman [Note: [Col. 0853] *Kalrlomanno*, 1] at Salussa, set out for Italy for the sake of peace. After completing the business for which she had gone, and after also venerating the thresholds of the holy Apostles at Rome, she returned to her sons. (Chronicle of W.) The body of Saint Othmar was found incorrupt for ten years on the island where he had died, and after being removed was buried in the basilica of Saint Gall.

30. 3. (EINH. Ann.) A.D. 771. Carloman died at a villa called Samoussy on the second day before the Nones of December. King Charles, intent on taking possession of the entire kingdom, came to the villa of Corbeny. There Bishop Williharius of Sion, the priest Fulrad, and many other priests, as well as counts and leading men of his brother, came to him. Carloman’s wife, however, set out for Italy with her sons and part of the nobility.

31. 4. A.D. 772. King Charles, having assembled a general gathering at Worms, decided to attack Saxony by war. Entering it without delay and laying waste everything with sword and fire, he captured the fortress of Eresburg and overthrew the idol called by the Saxons Irminsul. While he remained in the same place for three days during its destruction, it happened that, because of the continual clearness of the sky, all the streams and springs of that place dried up, and water could not be found for drinking. But suddenly, as is believed, by divine intervention, while everyone was resting at midday, such a quantity of water burst forth from the hollow of a certain torrent that it was sufficient for the whole army. Then, after destroying the idol, the king came to the River Weser; there he received twelve hostages from the Saxons and withdrew.

Pope Adrian, the ninety-fifth, was ordained and held the see for twenty-four years. [Note: [Col. 0855] MS 1 gives “Adrian—24” in the margin; D and E place it here; 5 places it at the end of the year 771; 4 and 9 omit it.]

32. 5. A.D. 773. [Note: [Col. 0856A] 1 and 11 add: “In that year the most devout Irene, together with Constantine, received the empire gloriously and by divine will. In the first year of this empire, when Constantine was ten years old, a certain man digging in the Long Walls of Thrace found a stone chest. After cleaning and opening it, he found a man lying in it and letters skillfully joined together, containing the following: ‘Christ will be born of the Virgin Mary, and I believe in him. Under the emperors Constantine and Irene, O sun, you will see me again.’ See also A.D. 782, no. 1.”]

Pope Adrian, unable to endure the arrogance of King Desiderius and the oppression of the Lombards, sent an embassy to Charles and implored his aid. Charles came with an army, besieged Desiderius inside Pavia, and spent the whole winter in that siege, undertaking many operations.

While these events were taking place in Italy, the Saxons, taking advantage of the king’s absence, ravaged the neighboring territory of the Hessi. They came to a place called Fritzlar and attempted to burn the church dedicated by Saint Boniface, which the holy martyr himself had foretold through the spirit of prophecy would never be violated by fire (Annals of Lorsch). As they tried with great force to burn it, two young men in white appeared to some Christians and pagans, and they protected the church from the fire. By divine command, terror was sent among the attackers, and they all fled, although no one pursued them from outside.

Later, one of those same Saxons was found dead beside the church, kneeling forward, holding wood and fire in his hands, and seeming to blow with his mouth in order to burn the basilica. (EINH. Annals.) The king, however, leaving an army behind to besiege and conquer Pavia, went to Rome to pray. After fulfilling his vows, he returned to the army and compelled the city, exhausted by the long siege, to surrender. The other cities followed its example and submitted themselves to the king’s power.

After subduing Italy and arranging its affairs for the time being, the king returned to Francia, leading King Desiderius captive. His son Adalgis, distrustful of the fortunes of his homeland, withdrew to Greece to Emperor Constantine, where he ended his life in the rank of patrician.

[Note: [Col. 0856A] D. E. add: “Pope Adrian [here D.]—consolidated,” from Sigibert, year 772, and continue: “The same pope,” etc.] 1

[Col. 0856B] 33. 6. A.D. 774. After returning home, Charles sent a threefold army into the regions of the Saxons before they learned that he had arrived. The army devastated everything with plunder and fires, killed many who attempted to resist, and returned with immense booty.

54. 7. A.D. 775. After taking counsel, King Charles resolved to enter Saxony and remain there until the Saxons either submitted to the Christian religion or were utterly destroyed. He therefore marched into Saxony with all the forces of the kingdom. On his first advance he captured the fortress of Sigiburg, where a Saxon garrison was stationed; he fortified the fortress of Eresburg, which the Saxons had destroyed, and placed a Frankish garrison in it. After inflicting a great slaughter and receiving hostages from them and from the Westphalians, he returned.

The bodies of Saints Gordian and Epimachus were transferred from Rome to Alemannia. (Chronicle of W.; H. m.) The emperor Constantine, son of Leo, persecutor of Christians and destroyer of churches and of the law [Note: [Col. 0856C] “destroyer … plague of the worst … dies miserably,” D. E., from Sigibert, year 776], died.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 776, and in the 527th year from the founding of the City, Leo, son of Constantine the persecutor, assumed the Roman empire as the seventy-first emperor after Augustus and reigned for five years. For a short time he appeared to be devout and a friend of the holy Mother of God and of the monks; therefore he placed metropolitans drawn from the monks in the principal sees and greatly enlarged many religious orders in the city.

For this reason all the leading men, entering with a great multitude of people, asked for his son Constantine to be made emperor. When Leo said that Constantine was his only child and still a little boy, and that he feared that, if something human should happen to him, they might kill Constantine and promote another, they all swore that they would admit no other emperors except Leo and Constantine and their descendants, and they confirmed this in writing. Thus Constantine was crowned emperor on the holy day of Easter.

Leo, however, after reigning for five years, died, and his son Constantine reigned in his place with his mother Irene.

[Col. 0857A] [Years of Leo.] 1. [Years of Charles.] 8. (EINH. Ann.) In the first year of Leo, which was Charles’s eighth, Charles was informed that the Lombard Ruotgaud [Note: [Col. 0857] “Ruotgaud,” corrected to “Ruovtgaud,” 1], whom he had appointed duke of Friuli, was planning a rebellion in Italy and that several cities had defected to him. Marching there immediately, Charles killed Ruotgaud, recovered the cities that had defected from him, placed Frankish garrisons in them, and returned. As soon as he heard that the Saxons had rebelled, he marched there; but finding them once again submissive, he granted them pardon. He baptized those who wished it, received hostages, and returned again to Francia.

2. 9. A.D. 777. King Charles, having held an assembly at a place called Paderborn, entered Saxony again [Col. 0857B] and found them all deceitfully devoted. For everyone came to him except Witikind, one of the leading Westphalians, who, conscious of many crimes, feared the king and fled with a few companions to Sigefrid, king of the Danes. The others who had come placed themselves so completely under the king’s power that they deserved pardon on the condition that, if they violated his decrees thereafter, they would be deprived of their homeland and liberty. A large multitude was also baptized—people who, although falsely, had promised that they would be Christians.

3. 10. A.D. 778. King Charles, making for the regions of Spain, subdued certain cities and received hostages from the Saracens. But on his return, through the treachery of the Wascones, many members of his household were killed in an ambush.

Meanwhile, when the Saxons learned that he had withdrawn so far, they took up arms and advanced as far as the Rhine. Unable to cross the river, they laid waste with sword and fire everything consisting of villages and estates from the city of Zülpich to the River Moselle. The enemy’s anger had spared no distinction of sex or age, so that it was plainly evident that they had entered Frankish territory not to plunder but to take revenge.

When the king, stationed at Auxerre, heard this, he immediately sent Eastern Franks and Alemanni to repel them. Hearing of their arrival, the Saxons withdrew. The others followed them closely and found them in the region of the Hessi beside the River Eder. Attacking them at once at the river ford itself, they struck them down in so great a slaughter that scarcely a few returned from the immense multitude.

[Col. 0857D] 4. 11. A.D. 779. Duke Hiltibrand of Spoleto came to Charles at the villa of Verzenay with great gifts. Charles received him kindly and, after presenting him with gifts, sent him back to his duchy. Charles himself, intent on marching into Saxony, crossed the Rhine with his army at the place called Lippe. When the Saxons attempted to resist him at a place called Bocholt, they were defeated and put to flight. The king entered the region of the Westphalians and accepted them all into submission. From there he came to the Weser and pitched camp. There the Angrarii and Ostphalians gave hostages and swore oaths. After this was completed, the king withdrew to Worms for the winter.

[Col. 0858A] 5. 12. A.D. 780. When Charles came to Saxony, all the Saxons of the eastern regions came to meet him, and many of the people were baptized. When he came to the place where the Rivers Havel and Elbe meet, he organized the affairs of both the Saxons and the Slavs. Returning to Francia, he held a council, then went to Rome with his wife Hildigard and his children for the sake of prayer, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Pavia.

Emperor Leo died.

(H. m., compiled with EINH. Life, ch. 19.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 781, and the 532nd year from the founding of the City, Constantine, son of Leo, the seventy-second emperor after Augustus, assumed the kingdom with his mother Irene and reigned for seventeen years. He had been betrothed to Ruothrud, daughter of Charles and Queen Hildigard, but his mother was joining him to another woman against his will.

[Col. 0858B] [Years of Constantine.] 1. [Years of Charles.] 13. (EINH. Ann.) In his first year Charles came to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Adrian. While he was celebrating holy Easter there, the same pontiff baptized his son Pippin, received him from the sacred font, anointed him king of Italy, and placed a crown upon him. He anointed Charles’s other son Louis king of Aquitaine and placed a crown upon him.

After departing from Rome, the king came to Milan. There his daughter Gisla was baptized by Archbishop Thomas, who also lifted her from the sacred font. Pope Adrian sent Bishops Formosus and Damasus, together with the king’s envoys Richolf, a deacon, and Eberhard, master of the cupbearers, to Duke Tassilo, to remind him of the oath that he had once sworn to Pippin and his sons. When they arrived, they softened his heart so that he came with them to Worms to the king. There he gave twelve hostages [Note: [Col. 0857] *obsidionibus* (“sieges”) in place of *obsides* (“hostages”), 1] and swore loyalty to the king. But when he returned home, he did not remain faithful for long.

2. 14. A.D. 782. Charles decided to go into Saxony and to hold there, as in Francia, a general assembly every year. After crossing the Rhine at Cologne, he came to the source of the Lippe and, having set up camp there, among his other business heard and dismissed the envoys of Sigifrid, king of the Danes, and those whom the princes of the Huns, Caganus and Jugurrus, had sent to him ostensibly for the sake of peace. When the assembly had been concluded and he had returned to Francia, Witikind returned to his homeland and persuaded the Saxons to rebel.

It was reported to the king that the Sorabian Slavs, who inhabit the lands lying between the Elbe and the Saale, had entered the neighboring territories of the Thuringians and Saxons for the purpose of plundering [Note: [Col. 0857] 1 reads *causi*.]. When he had sent three of his officers against them with the eastern Franks, those men, hearing of the Saxon uprising, turned aside toward the Saxons. But acting incautiously, they were surrounded by the Saxons and almost all were killed [Note: [Col. 0857] *interfecti*, “killed,” in D and E, instead of *occisi*, “slain.”]. When the king came to investigate this matter, everyone proclaimed Witikind the author of the crime. But since they were unable to hand over Witikind, who had fled, they surrendered as many as 4,500 of the others who had consented to him, and all were beheaded on one day by order of the king.

[Col. 0859A] [A note appears here whose callout number (*) was not printed in the text: D and E add, “In Constantinople someone found a stone coffin, and in it a man lying with this inscription: ‘Christ will be born of the virgin Mary, and I believe in him; under the emperors Constantine and Hyrene, O sun, you will see me again.’ From Sigeb.” The note appears in column 839.]

3. 15. A.D. 783. When the king had prepared himself for the Saxon expedition, before he moved the army, Queen Hiltigardis, his wife, died on 30 April, when the vigil of the Ascension was being observed. After he had paid the customary solemn rites at her funeral, he headed for Saxony and, fighting them at a place called Theotmelli, defeated them. From there, coming to Paderbrunnen, he heard that they were again prepared for battle in the territory of the Westphalians. Marching against them, he fought with them with the same success as before.

Returning from there to Francia, he married Fastrada, the daughter of Ratolf, count of eastern Francia, by whom he had two daughters.

In the same year Berhtrada, queen and mother of the king, of good memory, died on 12 July.

4. 16. A.D. 784. Charles crossed the Rhine at a place called Lippeheim and ravaged the districts of the Westphalians. Coming to the Weser, and finding that a flood of waters prevented the crossing, he left his son Charles in the territory of the Westphalians, while he himself turned aside through Thuringia and devastated the regions around the Elbe; then he returned to Francia.

The Saxons, however, assembled and fought with his son Charles. But after inflicting great slaughter, he returned victorious to his father at Worms.

[Note: [Col. 0859] In 1, *in* is superscribed.]

5. 17. A.D. 785. Witikind and Abbio came from the region beyond the Elbe to King Charles at Attigny, brought by Amalwin, one of the palace officials [Note: [Col. 0859] 1b reads *amalwico*]. There they were received into favor and baptized. The obstinacy of Saxon treachery ceased for several years.

6. 18. A.D. 786. When the king heard that the Angles and Saxons had invaded Britain [Note: [Col. 0859] “Ekkehard has greatly confused Einhard’s account at this point”], he sent there with an army Audolf, provost of the royal table. Coming there, he quickly suppressed the defiance of the treacherous people and brought hostages, together with many of the leading men of the population, to Worms before the king.

When peace had been established everywhere, the king decided to go to Rome and bring under his authority that part of Italy which lies around Benevento, most of which he had already subjected to himself after capturing Desiderius. Accordingly, coming into Italy, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Florence, a city of Tuscany.

7. 19. A.D. 787. King Charles came to Rome and was honorably received by the apostolic lord Hadrian. After remaining there several days, he proceeded with the same pontiff to Benevento.

When Aragisus, duke of Benevento, heard this, he sent his son Rumold to the king with great gifts, asking him not to enter that land. The king refused this request, however, and kept Rumold with him. He came to Capua and, intending to wage war, set up camp there.

Aragisus, meanwhile, abandoned Benevento, which is the capital of that land, and withdrew to Salerno as to a more strongly fortified place. He sent an embassy and offered both his sons to the king, promising to obey him in everything, provided only that he not be compelled to appear in the king’s presence.

(EINH. *Life of Charles*—*Annals.*) The king granted his request, kept the younger son, named Grimold, with him, and sent the elder back to his father. He also received eleven hostages from the people and sent envoys who were to bind both the duke himself and the whole Beneventan people by oath.

After this, he spoke with the envoys of Hyrene and her son Constantine, who had been sent to request his daughter. After dismissing them, he returned to Rome and celebrated holy Easter there with great rejoicing.

Then envoys of Duke Tassilo came to the pope—Arn, bishop, and Hunricus, abbot—asking him to deign to become a mediator of peace between them and the king. When the pope earnestly attempted this and the king said that he desired it, the envoys were asked in what manner they wished to establish peace. They replied that they had received no instruction from their lord concerning this matter.

The pope, therefore, angered, decreed that they should be struck with anathema as deceitful and fraudulent men if they abandoned the loyalty once promised to the king. He sent this message to the duke and dismissed them without peace having been made.

The apostolic lord and the king then took leave of each other and departed. After receiving the pope’s blessing, the king returned to Francia, where at Worms he found his sons and daughters with his wife Fastrada.

There, after holding a general assembly, he narrated before his nobles everything that had happened during his journey. On their advice he sent envoys to Tassilo (A. Laur.) to discover whether he intended to obey the apostolic lord’s commands and preserve faith with the king.

(EINH. *Annals.*) When Tassilo despised the commands, the king decided to proceed against Bavaria with a three-part army. He ordered his son Pippin, with the Italian forces, to assemble in the valley of Trent; the army of the Saxons and eastern Franks to assemble above the Danube at a place called Pheringa; and he himself, with the army he had brought, took up position above the river Lech in the suburb of the city of Augsburg.

Seeing that he was surrounded on every side, Tassilo came humbly to the king and asked to be forgiven for his former deeds. The king, who was always mild, spared the suppliant; after receiving his son Theodo and twelve other hostages from him, he returned to Francia.

8. 20. (A. Laur. and EINH.) A.D. 788. While Charles was celebrating Easter and holding a general council at Ingelheim, Duke Tassilo arrived, as did the other leading men of the kingdom. But he was accused by the Bavarians of having failed to keep faith after recently giving hostages, and of having, at the urging of his wife Liutburga, daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, called in the Avars to destroy the kingdom. He was also accused of many other hostile words and deeds. Since he could not deny these charges, he was judged guilty of treason.

While everyone was condemning him with one voice to capital punishment, the king, wishing to free him out of love for God and because he was his kinsman, asked what he now wished to do. Tassilo asked that permission be given him to repent of his sins. He was tonsured and sent to a monastery. His son Theodo was treated likewise. The other accomplices in his treachery were condemned to various exiles.

[Note: [Col. 0861A] D and E add: “At the insistence of Tharasius … he is deposed.” From Sigeb.]

9. 21. A.D. 789. Leading an army against the people of the Slavs called the Wilzi, Charles joined the banks of the Elbe by means of two bridges. He fortified one of them at both ends with a rampart, upon which he placed a tower of wood and earth. Entering the land of the Wilzi, he laid waste everything with sword and fire until he subjugated them.

(H. m.) In this year the empress Hyrene, having broken the peace of the marriage alliance with the Franks, sent for and brought a girl named Maria from Armenia and joined her to her son, the emperor Constantine. Constantine was greatly saddened because of the affection with which he burned for Charles’s daughter, to whom he had previously been betrothed.

10. 22. (EINH. *Annals.*) A.D. 790. Charles undertook no expedition. Residing at Worms, he received the envoys of the Huns and sent his own men to their princes. They were negotiating concerning the boundaries of their kingdoms; this matter became the seed of a future war.

[Col. 0861C] 11. 23. (Chr. W.; cf. H. m.) A.D. 791. Saint Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, died on 2 February.

In the same year disagreement arose between Constantine and his mother Hyrene, through the instigation of evil men, to such an extent that she wished to deprive him of the kingdom.

(EINH. *Annals.*) Charles, setting out from Worms, headed for Bavaria with the intention of making war on the Huns. Dividing his army, he ordered Count Theoderic and his chamberlain Meginfrid to proceed with one part along the northern bank of the Danube, while he himself descended with the other along the southern bank. Coming to the river Enns, which is the boundary between Pannonia and Bavaria, they set up camp and performed litanies there for three days.

(A. Laur.) When the Huns saw the army [Note: [Col. 0861] 1b reads *exercitus*, “army,” instead of *exercitum*, “the army”], holding both banks, they were struck with divinely sent terror. Abandoning their fortifications, they fled, and each army entered freely and devastated a large part of Pannonia as far as the river called the Rába.

(EINH. *Annals.*) The king then decided to return by way of Savaria; the other part of the army returned by the route along which it had come.

12. 24. A.D. 792. While Charles was staying at Regensburg from the Nativity of the Lord through the summer [Note: [Col. 0861] the reading is in an erased place in 1], certain Franks conspired against him, as did his son Pippin, born of a concubine, and others, because of Queen Fastrada, whose cruelty the Franks said they could not endure.

When this conspiracy had been exposed by Fardulf the Lombard, he was rewarded for preserving his loyalty by being given the monastery of Saint Denis. The authors of the conspiracy were partly cut down by the sword and partly hanged on the gallows.

While the king was at Regensburg because of the war undertaken against the Huns [Note: [Col. 0861] 1, 4, 5, 9c, and 10 have *sedente*, “while he was sitting”; D and E read *sedens*, “sitting.”], some people persuaded him that it would be entirely practicable to sail from the Danube to the Rhine if a ditch were dug between the rivers Radantia and Altmühl, since one of these rivers flowed into the Danube and the other into the Rhine.
