The king immediately came with his entire retinue to a place suitable for this work. After a great multitude of men had been assembled, he spent the whole autumn on it. A ditch was therefore dug between the aforesaid rivers, two thousand paces in length and three hundred feet wide. But the effort was useless, for, because of the continual rains and the soil, which is naturally marshy, the work could not hold. As much earth as the diggers removed by day sank back again at night as the soil collapsed.

While he was occupied with this work, news arrived of the complete revolt of the Saxons and the slaughter of many Franks by the Saracens. Moved by these events, he returned to Francia and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Saint Kilian’s—that is, Würzburg—beside the river Main. He celebrated Easter on the same river at the village of Frankfurt, where he had also wintered.

13. 25. A.D. 793. While Charles was celebrating Easter at Frankfurt, a great synod of bishops was assembled from all the provinces of the kingdom. Envoys of Pope Hadrian were also present in his place.

At this synod the heresy of a certain bishop named Felix was condemned. He said that Christ, insofar as he is man, was the adoptive son of God. A book was composed against this teaching by the common authority of the bishops, and all subscribed to it.

The synod which, a few years earlier, had been assembled at Constantinople under Hyrene and her son Constantine, and which they themselves had called the seventh and universal synod, was also rejected by everyone as superfluous, so that it was to be called neither the seventh synod nor anything else.

Queen Fastrada also died there and was buried at Mainz, at Saint Alban’s.

14. 26. A.D. 794. The king, dividing the army between himself and his son Charles, entered Saxony with a great force. The Saxons, however, revering his presence as usual, gave hostages and swore that they would obey him in everything.

15. 27. A.D. 795. Not forgetful of the Saxons’ treachery, the king held a general assembly at a village called Cuffesstein [Note: [Col. 0861] 1b reads *cusfestun*], across the Rhine opposite Mainz, beside the river Main. From there he entered Saxony with an army and traversed almost the whole country, devastating it. After again receiving hostages, he returned to Gaul.

16. 28. A.D. 796. Pope Leo, the ninety-sixth, was ordained and held office for twenty years; others say twenty-five (EINH. *Annals.*). He made Charles emperor [Note: [Col. 0863] “Leo … made emperor” is in an erased place in 1].

As soon as he had been ordained, he sent King Charles the keys of the confession of Saint Peter and the banner of the Roman city, together with other gifts. He asked Charles to send one of his nobles to bind the Roman people to him by oath.

Angilbert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius, was sent for this purpose. Through him Leo also sent a large part of the treasure which Duke Hericus [Note: [Col. 0863] 1b, 4, 9c, and 11 read *Heinricus*] of Friuli had brought to the king from Pannonia in that same year after plundering the royal palace of the Huns, which was called the *ringus*. The king distributed the remainder generously among the nobles, palace officials, and those serving the palace.

After this the king set out for Saxony and sent his son Pippin, king of Italy, into Pannonia. He himself, after devastating Saxony, returned to Aachen. Pippin, having driven the Huns beyond the river Tisza, returned to his father with the remainder of the Hun treasure (cf. A. Laur.).

17. 29. (EINH. *Annals.*) A.D. 797. An expedition was made into Saxony. The army crossed as far as the ocean, beyond all the marshes and impassable places. Returning from Hadoloha—for that is the name of the place where the ocean washes Saxony—the king received the entire Saxon people into submission by means of hostages.

Returning to the palace at Aachen, he received Abdella the Saracen, son of King Ibimauga, who had been driven out by his brother and had commended himself to Charles. The envoy of Nicetas, who at that time ruled Sicily, also came there, bearing a letter from the emperor Constantine. The king received him magnificently and dismissed him after a few days.

In the middle of November he entered Saxony with the army to winter there. Having set up camp beside the Weser, he ordered the camp to be called Heristal. Envoys of the Huns came there with great gifts.

From there he sent Abdella the Saracen with his son Louis back to Spain, sent Pippin to Italy, and devoted the entire winter to organizing Saxony. He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there and Easter of the following year there as well.

30. (A. EINH. and Laur.) A.D. 798. The Saxons beyond the Elbe, having raised a revolt, seized the king’s envoys who had then been sent to administer justice. They killed some and held others for ransom.

Therefore the king, having assembled an army [Note: [Col. 0863] apparently *exercitum*, “army,” rather than *exercitu*, “with an army”], proceeded to a place called Minida. After holding a council, he traversed all Saxony between the Elbe and the Weser, devastating it.

The Transalbian Saxons, elated by pride, took up arms against the Abodrites, who had always remained faithful to the king. But their duke Thrasico engaged them in battle, killed four thousand of them [Note: [Col. 0863] *occisit*, with the letter *s* erased in 1], and forced the rest, disgracefully put to flight, to surrender to the king.

The king, returning to Francia, heard at Aachen the envoys of the empress Hyrene, who were negotiating peace. Her son Constantine had been captured by his own people because of his insolent behavior and blinded; or, as some more truthfully admit (H. m.), this had been done on the advice of his own mother, who was striving to hold the kingdom alone.

(A. EINH. and Laur.) After the king dismissed these envoys, envoys came from Spain from Hadefonsus, king of Galicia and Asturias: Basyliscus and Froia. They brought gifts which Hadefonsus had arranged to send to the king from the spoils he had taken as victor at Lisbon, the last city of Spain, which he himself had conquered—namely, seven Moors, with an equal number of mules and coats of mail. The king received them kindly and, after honoring them with suitable gifts, dismissed them.

(H. m.) The emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0863] “C.” and the rest of the phrase are in an erased place in 1], son of Leo and Hyrene, died a short time after he had been blinded on his mother’s advice. Thus his mother ruled thereafter for five years.

At that time the sun was darkened for seventeen days, so that ships wandered at sea, and everyone said that the sun had been darkened because the emperor had been blinded.

31. (EINH. A.) A.D. 799. Pope Leo was blinded by the Romans. For while the Romans gloried in their security, their hearts were lifted up according to their usual custom, and they wished to claim for themselves what belonged to imperial authority.

(H. m.) When Pope Leo resisted, certain relatives of Pope Hadrian of blessed memory stirred up a sedition among the people and incited them against the pope.

(A. Laur. and EINH.) It therefore happened that during the greater litany, when he was proceeding from the Lateran to the church of Saint Lawrence called the Craticula, riding on horseback, he encountered the ambush which the Romans had arranged near that church. They threw him from his horse, tore out his eyes, as it appeared to him, and cut out his tongue. Naked and half alive, he was left in the middle of the street.

(Mon. Sang. I, 26.) Some say that they tore out only one of his eyes; others that they tore out neither, but cut through the middle of his eyes with razors without, however, taking away his sight.

(EINH. A.) Then, by order of those who had planned this crime, he was sent to the monastery of Saint Erasmus the Martyr. At night, through the care of a certain chamberlain of his named Albinus [Note: [Col. 0863] D and E omit “Albinus … was lowered”], he was lowered over the wall. Winigis, duke of Spoleto, who had hastened to Rome upon hearing of this crime, received him and led him to Spoleto.

When the king received news of this, he ordered that Leo himself, as the vicar of Saint Peter, be brought to him with the highest honor. Nevertheless, he did not interrupt his journey, which he had planned into Saxony.

After holding an assembly on the Rhine at a place called Lippeheim, he crossed the river and, coming to Paderbrunnen [Note: [Col. 0863] in an erased place in 1], awaited the pontiff’s arrival there. In the meantime he sent his son Charles with an army to the Elbe to arrange certain matters with the Wilzi and Abodrites.

When he had awaited Charles’s return, the pontiff came. The king received him honorably, and Leo stayed with him for several days. After making known to the king all the reasons for which he had come, he was escorted back with honor by the king’s envoys and restored to his position.

(A. Laur.) In the same year the Avars, who are also called Huns, defected from the loyalty they had promised. Gerold, prefect of Bavaria, fought against them and was killed in battle.

[Note: [Col. 0865A] D and E add: “Concerning him, through envy … let it be.” From Sigeb., under the year 800.]

32. (EINH. A.) A.D. 800. King Charles went to Tours for the sake of prayer and remained there several days because of the illness of his wife, Lady Luitgardis, who died and was buried there on 4 June.

At the beginning of August, coming to Mainz, he announced his journey into Italy.

(A. Laur.) As he was heading toward Rome, Pope Leo met him the day before he entered the city at Nomentum, twelve miles from Rome. The pope dined with him and left him there for the night, while he went ahead to the city.

(A. EINH. and Laur.) On the following day, having arranged crowds at suitable places, Leo himself stood on the steps with the bishops and clergy and received Charles honorably. While everyone sang psalms, he led him into the basilica of Saint Peter. This took place on 24 November.

Seven days later the king summoned an assembly and disclosed to everyone the reasons for his coming. Chief among them was the examination of the crimes charged against the pontiff. To make themselves appear more completely justified, his accusers had brought a capital charge against him.

When the king investigated this matter and no one could prove the crime, the pontiff, taking up the text of the Gospel, mounted the pulpit before the king and all the people. With the accusers standing by, he invoked the name of the Holy Trinity and cleared himself of the charges brought against him.

Up to this point the Roman Empire, from the time of Constantine the Great, son of Helena, had remained at Constantinople under the Greek emperors. From this point it passed through Charles to the kings—or rather emperors—of the Franks.

[Note: [Col. 0865] E1 adds in red: “Here begins the fourth book.”]

[The Years of Charles’s Empire.] 1. [The Years of His Reign.] 33. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 801, and in the 1,552nd year from the founding of Rome, Charles the Great, king of the Franks, son of King Pippin, was consecrated Roman emperor, in the thirty-third year of his reign, being the seventy-third ruler after Augustus [Note: [Col. 0865] D and E give LXVII, “sixty-seven”]. Thus he ruled as emperor for fourteen years.

[Col. 0865D] (EINH. A.—A. Laur.) When he came to Rome because of the accusations brought against Pope Leo and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there, on that most sacred day he went to the solemn mass. As he rose from prayer before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, Pope Leo, when Charles least expected it, placed a crown upon him, proclaimed him Roman emperor, and the entire Roman people acclaimed him:

“Life and victory to Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor of the Romans!”

(EINH. A.) After these praises the apostolic lord anointed him and, according to the custom of the ancient princes, adored him. The title of patrician was removed, and he was called emperor and Augustus.

A few days later, after the case of the pope’s adversaries had been heard, they were condemned under Roman law as guilty of treason and sentenced to beheading. The pope, however, intervened for them with pious compassion; their lives and bodily integrity were spared, but because of the magnitude of their crime they were carried into exile.

Some say (Mon. Sang. I, 26) that three hundred of their leading men were beheaded in a single day in the Lateran field [Note: [Col. 0865] *lateransi*, “Lateran,” in 1].

The Lord so demonstrated the innocence of blessed Pope Leo that afterward he granted him clearer eyes. Yet, as a sign of his ordeal, a most beautiful scar, shaped like the finest thread, adorned his dove-colored eyes with snowy brightness.

(EINH. A.) After arranging not only the public affairs of the city of Rome, the apostolic lord, and all Italy, but also ecclesiastical and private matters, the emperor left Rome on 24 April. This was the thirty-third year of his reign and the first of his empire.

2. 34. (A. EINH. and Laur.) A.D. 802. The empress Hyrene sent her envoy, named Leo, from Constantinople to Emperor Charles to establish peace between the Franks and the Greeks. The emperor in turn sent Jesse, bishop of Amiens, and Count Helmgaud to Constantinople for the same purpose, and also to ask the empress Hyrene (H. m.) to marry him.

She would have agreed to this if Aecius the patrician had not prevented it, since he was powerful and was striving to transfer the empire to her brother Nicephorus. For while Charles’s envoys were still in the city, Nicephorus seized the empire and banished Hyrene to a monastery which she herself had built on a certain island.

3. 35. (EINH. A.) A.D. 803. The envoys of Emperor Charles returned from Constantinople. With them came the representatives of Nicephorus, who at that time governed the state among the Greeks: Michael, bishop; Peter, abbot; and Callistus, a candidate. They found the emperor in Germany on the river Saale, at a place called Salz, and received in writing the agreement for establishing peace. From there, returning to Rome with the emperor’s letter, they went back home.

4. 36. A.D. 804. [Note: [Col. 0867A] C adds: “Charles administers justice throughout the whole empire and establishes twenty-nine chapters of laws.” From Sigeb., under the year 802.]

The emperor wintered at Aachen. In summer, leading an army into Saxony, he transferred all the Saxons who lived beyond the Elbe, with their women and children, into Francia, and gave their territories beyond the Elbe to the Abodrites.

At the same time Gotefrid, king of the Danes, came with his fleet and all his cavalry to a place called Scliesdorph [Note: [Col. 0865] “or Slieswich” in the margin of E1; “Selieswich” in the text of E2], on the boundary of his kingdom and Saxony. He had promised to come to a conference with the emperor, but, frightened by the advice of his people, he did not approach more closely. Instead, he sent through envoys whatever message he wished. The emperor was sitting above the river Elbe at a place called Holdunsteti (cf. A. Laur. and EINH. A.).

That same summer it was reported to the emperor that the blood of the Lord had been found in the city of Mantua. He sent to the pope so that he might investigate the truth of this report.

The pope, finding an opportunity to leave, first set out for Lombardy, supposedly to investigate the matter. From there he suddenly took the road to the emperor and sent him word in mid-November that he wished to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord with him.

The emperor immediately sent his son Charles to Saint Maurice and ordered him to receive the pope honorably. He himself went to meet him at Reims and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the estate of Quierzy. From there he led him to Aachen and, after presenting him with great gifts, had him escorted as he wished to travel through Bavaria, as far as Ravenna.

[Col. 0867B] 5. 37. (EINH. A.—cf. A. Laur.) A.D. 805. The emperor sent his son Charles with an army into Bohemia. After devastating everything, Charles killed the duke of that land, named Lecho. Returning from there to his father, he found him occupied with hunting in the Vosges forest.

6. 38. (EINH. A.) A.D. 806. After holding an assembly, the emperor took counsel with the leading Franks concerning the establishment and preservation of peace and the division of the kingdom among his sons into three parts, so that each of them would know which part he ought to defend and govern if he outlived his father.

A testament concerning this division was drawn up and confirmed by oath by the nobles.

[Col. 0867C] 7. 39. A.D. 807. Envoys of the king of Persia came to the emperor, bringing him gifts: a pavilion and three tents, made in varied colors, of astonishing size and beauty, all of fine linen, both the tents and their ropes.

They also brought many costly silk garments, perfumes and balsam, and a clock of brass, wonderfully constructed by mechanical art. In it, the course of twelve hours turned by means of a water clock, with twelve bronze balls which fell when the hours were completed and, by their falling, caused a cymbal placed beneath them to ring. In the same clock were also added twelve horsemen who emerged through twelve windows when the hours were completed. As they came out, they caused an equal number of windows, which had previously been open, to close.

There were also many other things in the clock which would take too long to enumerate.

8. 40. A.D. 808. When the emperor heard that Gotefrid, king of the Danes, had crossed into the territory of the Abodrites with an army, he sent his son Charles against him with a strong force of Franks and Saxons, in case Gotefrid should attempt to attack the borders of Saxony.

Gotefrid captured several Slavic strongholds but returned with great loss to his forces. He had lost the bravest of his men, among them his brother’s son Reginold.

9. 41. A.D. 809. King Ludowicus, the emperor’s son, entered Spain with an army and besieged the city of Tortosa. Unable to capture it, he abandoned the siege and withdrew into Aquitaine.

10. 42. A.D. 810. King Pippin of Italy, the emperor’s son, urged on by the treachery of the Venetian dukes, ordered an attack on Venetia by land and sea. After subjugating Venetia, he received its dukes into submission.

The emperor, who was still at Aachen and planning an expedition against King Gotefrid, received news that a fleet of two hundred ships from Normandy had landed in Frisia and ravaged all the islands adjoining the Frisian coast. The army was already on the mainland.

He gathered forces as rapidly as he could and hastened straight toward them. Having set up camp near the Weser, he awaited the outcome of Gotefrid’s threats. The proud king, inflated by the utterly vain hope of victory, had boasted that he wished to engage the emperor.

While the emperor was holding his stationary camp, messengers came to him bearing various reports: the aforesaid fleet had returned; King Gotefrid had been killed by one of his own retainers—or, as some say (Mon. Sang. II, 13), by his own son, whose mother Gotefrid had abandoned after recently taking another wife; the stronghold of Hohcburi, situated beside the Elbe, in which Outo, the emperor’s envoy, and the eastern Saxons were stationed, had been captured by the Wilzi (EINH. A.); and his son Pippin, king of Italy, had died on 8 July.

When he heard these things, he arranged the affairs of Saxony as circumstances required and returned home.

In that year the sun and moon were eclipsed twice: the sun on 7 June and 30 November, and the moon on 21 June and 15 December.

Ruothdruth, the emperor’s eldest daughter, died on 8 July.

After Gotefrid, king of the Danes, died, Hemming, his brother’s son, succeeded to the kingdom and made peace with the emperor.

11. 43. A.D. 811. The emperor [Note: [Col. 0867] E2 lacks the history of this year], after making peace with Hemming and holding a general assembly at Aachen, sent three armies into three parts of his kingdom.

He sent one beyond the Elbe against the Linones; it ravaged them and restored the stronghold of Hohcburi, which the Wilzi had destroyed in the preceding year. He sent another into Pannonia to settle the disputes between the Huns and the Slavs, and a third against the Britons to punish their treachery. All accomplished their tasks successfully.

Charles, the emperor’s eldest son, died on 4 December.

[Col. 0868D] 12. 44. A.D. 812. The emperor Nicephorus of Constantinople was killed while fighting against the Bulgarians, and Michael, his son-in-law, obtained the empire.

Michael received and dismissed the envoys of Emperor Charles who had been sent to Nicephorus. With them he sent his own envoys, through whom he confirmed the peace begun by Nicephorus.

13. 45. A.D. 813. After holding a general assembly at Aachen, the emperor summoned his son Ludewicus, king of Aquitaine, to him. Placing a crown upon him, he made him his associate in the imperial title.

He appointed his grandson Bernhard, son of his son Pippin, over Italy and ordered him to be called king.

Councils were also held throughout Gaul by order of the emperor, with the bishops assembled to correct the condition of the churches. One was held at Mainz, another at Reims, a third at Reims [Note: [Col. 0869] so in 1, 1b, 5, 9c, and 10; T and R omit it; D and E have “at Tours,” as does Einhard], a fourth at Chalon, and a fifth at Arles.

The emperor Michael attacked the Bulgarians but met with no favorable success. Therefore, returning home, he laid aside the diadem and became a monk. Leo, son of the patrician Bardas, was appointed in his place.

(EINH. *Life of Charles*, ch. 32.) The bridge over the Rhine at Mainz, which the emperor had constructed of wood over ten years with immense labor and astonishing workmanship, so that it seemed capable of lasting forever, burned down accidentally in May within three hours. Apart from the part covered by water, not even a single splinter remained.

14. 46. (EINH. A.; cf. *Life*, ch. 31.) A.D. 814. While Emperor Charles was wintering at Aachen, he was struck by fever and pleurisy—that is, pain in the side—and departed this life on 28 January, at about seventy-one years of age, in the forty-sixth year of his reign, the forty-third year after the subjugation of Italy, and the fourteenth year since he had been called emperor and Augustus.

(EINH. A.) When his son Ludewicus, who was in Aquitaine, received news of this, he came to Aachen on the thirtieth day after it had occurred. With the unanimous consent and favor of all the Franks, he succeeded his father. Turning his attention to the administration of the kingdom, he first received and dismissed the embassies that had come to his father, among which the most important was that of Leo, the emperor who had succeeded Michael.

After holding a general assembly at Aachen, he sent envoys into every part of the kingdom to administer justice. Of his sons, he appointed Lothar over Bavaria and Pippin over Aquitaine.

The Years of Ludewicus’s Reign.

1. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 815, and in the 566th year from the founding of the City, Ludewicus, son of Charlemagne, reigned as the 74th [Note: [Col. 0869] LXVIII. D. E.] ruler after Augustus, and held the kingdom for 26 years. In the first year of his reign it was reported to him that certain leading Romans had conspired to kill Pope Leo and that, when this information had been conveyed to the pontiff, all the leaders of that faction had been slaughtered at his command. [Col. 0869D] Since Ludewicus was distressed by this, he summoned his nephew Bernhard, king of Italy, to him and sent him to investigate what had been reported. When Bernhard reached Rome, he fell ill. Concerning the matters on account of which he had come, he sent word to King Ludewicus through Count Herold, who had been assigned to him as legate, reporting everything he had discovered. The pontiff’s legates followed him and fully satisfied King Ludewicus regarding the accusations brought against their lord.

[Note: [Col. 0870A] Lines 4–10 add: In that same year the monastery of Swarzach was built by Count Megingaud [ [Col. 0869] *meginguado*, lines 10–11] and his wife Ymma, in honor of our Lord and Savior, the holy Mother of God, Saint Sebastian, and Saint Felicitas the martyr, under the first abbot of that monastery, named Benedict, with the condition that it be free from every form of servitude and exaction. Later, after the first monastery had collapsed, it was restored in honor of the holy Mother of God, Saint Felicitas, and her seven sons. Compare the Swarzach Chronicle in Ludewig, *SS. Bamb.* II, p. 3.]

[Col. 0870A] 2. A.D. 816. The Lord Pope Leo departed this life in the twenty-first year of his pontificate, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June; and the deacon Stephanus was ordained pope in his place, the 97th, and sat for seven months. Thus, not yet two months after his consecration, he hastened to come to the emperor by whatever routes he could travel most rapidly, while in the meantime sending two legates to inform the emperor, as it were, on behalf of his consecration. When the emperor heard this, he met him at Reims and sent men to escort him there; he received him honorably. The pontiff immediately explained to him the reason for his arrival. Then, after celebrating the solemn Masses according to custom, he crowned him by placing the diadem upon him and proclaimed him emperor of the Romans, in the second year of his reign, according to others in the seventh.

Years of his imperial rule

3. 2. [Note: [Col. 0869] The first year of the empire is entered in the margin as A.D. 816.] (EINH. *Ann.*) A.D. 817. Pope Stephanus died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, before three months had yet elapsed since he had come to Rome. Paschalis was elected as his successor; after his ordination had been solemnly completed, he sent the emperor gifts and a letter of apology, asserting that the honor of the pontificate had been imposed upon him even though he not only did not want it but deeply regretted it. Pope Paschalis, the 98th, sat for seven years, according to others nine. [Note: [Col. 0869] *Paschalis*—later added as *VIIII*.]

The emperor, holding a general assembly at Aachen, made his firstborn son Lotharius his associate in name and imperial rule, while he designated the other two as kings, appointing one to Aquitaine and the other to Bavaria. After this he was informed that his nephew Bernhard, king of Italy, had planned tyranny on the advice of certain wicked men and had already secured all the entrances into Italy, which are called *clusae*, by placing garrisons there, and that all the cities of Italy had sworn allegiance to him. This was partly true and partly false. When the emperor came swiftly with a large army to suppress these disturbances, Bernhard, despairing of his position, laid down his arms and surrendered himself to the emperor at Chalon-sur-Saône.

4. 3. A.D. 818. When the conspiracy had been exposed and all the rebels reduced to his power, the emperor returned to Aachen. After the Lenten fast had ended, a few days after Holy Easter, he ordered the leaders of the conspiracy and the king himself, who had been condemned to death by the judgment of the Franks, merely to be deprived of their sight. [Note: (Geneal. *SS.* II, p. 314.)] Queen Irmingard died on the fifth day before the Nones of October. She had borne the emperor Lotharius, Pippinus, and Ludewicus. [Note: [Col. 0871] *quae*—“who”—followed by *Ludewicum* is added in the margin; absent in manuscript 1b.]

5. 4. A.D. 819. An assembly was held at Aachen after the Nativity of the Lord. Much was discussed there concerning the condition of the churches, and certain highly necessary chapters that had been lacking were also added to the laws. (Geneal. II, 314.) When this had been completed, the emperor, having inspected many of the daughters of noblemen, took as his wife the daughter of Count Welf, named Judith. She bore him Charles the Bald. [Note: [Col. 0871] *quae*—“who”—followed by *Calvum* is added in the margin.]

6. 5. A.D. 820. Because of continuous rains and air dissolved by excessive moisture, great misfortunes occurred. For pestilence afflicted both human beings and cattle, and the grain and legumes were also spoiled.

7. 6. A.D. 821. The emperor Ludewicus was informed of the death of Leo, emperor of Constantinople: in the previous year he had been killed in the basilica of the holy Mother of God within the palace, through a conspiracy of certain of his nobles and especially of Michael, count of the household troops. Michael, with the support of the praetorian soldiers, assumed the imperial insignia and reigned for nine years. [Note: [Col. 0871] *secundum*—“according to”—followed by *successit* is added in the margin; four words are absent.]

According to some, Pope Leo died and Stephanus succeeded him.

8. 7. A.D. 822. In the land of the Thuringians, in a certain place beside a river, a sod of earth fifty feet long, fourteen feet wide, and one and a half feet high was found cut and lifted from the ground without human hands, lying twenty-five feet away from the place where it had been taken up. Likewise, in eastern Saxony, near the borders of the Sorbs, in a deserted place beside a lake called Arnse, the earth swelled up like an embankment and, within the space of a single night, raised itself in the form of a rampart without human labor, extending for the length of one league. [Col. 0871C]

Pope Stephanus died; Paschalis succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0871] *Stephanus*—followed by *successit*—is added in the margin; four words are absent. Above, after *inventus est*, manuscripts 5, 9c, 10, and 11 read this passage.]

The Lord emperor sent his son Lotharius to Italy to administer the affairs of the kingdom. In the preceding year he had joined him in marriage to Irmingard, daughter of Count Hugo. [Note: [Col. 0871] *cui*—“to whom”—followed by *junxit* is in a damaged place.] [Note: [Col. 0871] The phrase meaning “he joined [her] to him,” or another similar expression, is absent.] From her he had Lotharius, later excommunicated, Ludewicus, who reigned after him, and Charles. (EINH. *Ann.*)

The emperor sent his son Pippinus to Aquitaine and joined him in marriage to the daughter of Count Theodoric of Matriacum. [Note: [Col. 0871D] D. E. add: The beginning of the new monastery of Corbie in Saxony by Saint Adelhard, abbot of old Corbie in France.]

9. 8. A.D. 823. In May, when an assembly had been held at Frankfurt, among the other embassies of barbarians there came to the emperor two brothers from the kingdom of the Wilzi, Milegast and Celeadrogo, sons of Liubit, king of the Wilzi. [Note: [Col. 0871] *liuthit* in manuscript 1b.] When their father had died fighting against the eastern Abodrites, the people of the Wilzi made his elder son Milegast king. But when he did not administer the kingdom suitably according to the custom of the nation, they rejected him and conferred the royal honor upon his younger brother. For this reason both came into the emperor’s presence. When he saw that the will of the nation inclined more toward the younger brother, he decided that the latter should hold the kingdom. Nevertheless, he sent both of them back to their homeland, enriched with gifts and confirmed by oath.

[Note: [Col. 0872D] D. E. add: Paschalis—“transferred”; from Sigebert, A.D. 821.]

When Lotharius had arranged the affairs of Italy and was now preparing to return, he came to Rome at the request of Pope Paschalis. Received honorably by him, on the holy day of Easter at Saint Peter’s he received both the crown of the kingdom and the name of emperor and Augustus. Thus, in June, he came to his father.

The emperor appointed his brother Drugon, who was living under canonical discipline at the church of Metz, as its head, with the clergy of that city consenting and electing him; he judged that Drugon should be advanced to the rank of bishop.

Ceadrogo, prince of the Abodrites, came to the emperor with certain leading men of his people and gave a not implausible account of the reason for his delayed arrival, for which he had been accused. Although he was blameworthy in certain matters, nevertheless, because of the merits of his parents, he was not only left unpunished but also enriched with gifts and permitted to return to his kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0871] Thus in all the manuscripts I have seen: *celeadrogo* in manuscript 11.]

It is reported that certain portents occurred in this year. The most notable were earthquakes in the palace at Aachen and, in the territory of Toul near the village of Commerciacum, a girl of about twelve years who, after receiving Holy Communion at Easter from the hand of a priest, completed a full two years and half of the third without any desire for food, taking no nourishment whatsoever into her body. She began to fast at Easter in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 823, and in 825, around the beginning of November, after the fast had ended, she began to take food and live by eating in the manner of other human beings. [Col. 0872C]

In Saxony, in the district of Firihsaze, twenty-three villages were burned by heavenly fire, and lightning was seen in clear weather and fell from the sky during the day.

In the territory of the Italian city of Como, in the village of Gravedona, in the church of Saint John the Baptist, an image of Saint Mary holding the child Jesus in her lap had been painted in the apse of the same church. Because of extreme age it had become dark and almost entirely faded, but it shone with such brightness for two days that it seemed wholly to surpass, by the beauty of its radiance, all the splendor of a newly made painting. Images of the Magi offering gifts had also been painted beside it, but that brightness illuminated them not at all, apart from the gifts they were offering.

[Col. 0873A] 10. 9. (EINH. *Ann.*) A.D. 824. Pope Paschalis died. Since two men had been elected to his place amid a popular dispute, Eugenius, a priest of the titular church of Saint Sabina, nevertheless prevailed because the nobles’ party won, and was ordained the 99th pope. He sat for three years.

Legates of Michael, emperor of Constantinople, came to the emperor Ludewicus with gifts and letters to confirm the peace, and, after receiving a fitting reply, were dismissed. [Note: [Col. 0873A] D. E. add: “Among the other gifts … healed there,” from Sigebert.]

In this year, a few days after the summer solstice, it is said that in the territory of Autun, when the air suddenly changed into stormy weather, an enormous fragment of ice fell together with hail. It is said to have been fifteen feet long, seven feet wide, and two feet thick.

[Col. 0873B] 11. 10. A.D. 825. When an assembly had been held at Aachen, envoys of the Bulgars came to the emperor to establish the boundaries between the Franks and the Bulgars. After receiving a reply, they returned.

12. 11. A.D. 826. Hilduvinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis near Paris and archchaplain of the sacred palace, sent to Rome and, with Eugenius’s consent—for Eugenius was then bishop of the apostolic see—received the body of Christ’s most blessed martyr Sebastian. He placed it in the basilica of Saint Medard at the city of Soissons. While it still lay unburied in the casket in which it had been brought, beside the tomb of Saint Medard, such a multitude of miracles appeared that no mortal could either comprehend them in number or relate them in words. Some are said to have been so astonishing that they would exceed human credulity, unless it were certain that the Lord, for whom Sebastian himself suffered, can do all things.

13. 12. A.D. 827. Pope Eugenius died in August. In his place Valentinus, a deacon, was ordained by the Romans as the hundredth pope, but he scarcely completed one month in the pontificate. [Note: [Col. 0873] “He was also called Leo IV,” written above the line in manuscript E 1; *recepit* in E 2.] After his death, Gregorius, priest of the titular church of Saint Mark, was elected the 101st pope, but he was not ordained until an imperial legate had come to Rome and examined the character of the people’s election. After Gregorius’s death, Sergius succeeded as the 102nd pope; after him came Leo, the 103rd. [Note: [Col. 0873D] D. E. add: “He decreed that the octave … was celebrated. He also decreed that, while … no one except the ministers of the altar should presume to do so,” from Sigebert, A.D. 847; and: “Rabanus, second to none in knowledge of letters … sent him,” from the same, A.D. 824; and: “He also composed treatises …,” from A.D. 827.]

The bodies of Saints Marcellinus and Peter were transferred from Rome to Germany in November and glorified by miracles. [Note: [Col. 0873] *corpora*—“bodies”—followed by *sunt*, and several earlier words of this year, are in a damaged place.]

14. 13. A.D. 828. In the region of Gascony beyond the Garonne, in the district of Agen, they say that grain descended from heaven like rain. It had grains resembling wheat but somewhat shorter and rounder. Concerning it, a report was brought to the lord emperor at the palace of Aachen. [Col. 0874A]

(Chronicle of W.) Wettinus, a monk of Reichenau, was carried away in spirit and saw a marvelous vision.

15. 14. (EINH. *Ann.*) A.D. 829. During Lent itself, a few days before Holy Easter, an earthquake occurred at night at Aachen, and a wind arose with such violence that it stripped not only the lower houses but also a considerable part of the very basilica of the holy Mother of God, called the chapel and roofed with leaden tiles.

16. 15. A.D. 830. The emperor Michael died.

17. 16. A.D. 831. According to some (Chronicle of W.), Pope Paschalis died and Eugenius succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0874B] D. at the beginning of the year and E. at the end add: “Amularius … published concerning kings,” from Sigebert, A.D. 827.] The bodies of Saints Valens, Senesius, and Theopontius were brought to the island of Reichenau. Theophilus, son of Michael, reigned for twelve years.

19. 18. (A. Lob.) A.D. 833. The emperor gave Alamannia, Rhaetia, and part of Burgundy to his son Charles, born of Judith, to the indignation of his other sons.

24. 23. A.D. 838. Pippinus, the emperor’s son, died.

25. 24. A.D. 839.

26. 25. A.D. 840. The emperor Ludewicus died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July and was buried in the church at Metz. [Note: [Col. 0873] “The church of Saint Arnulf at Metz,” manuscript 1b.]

1. (Chronicle of W.—A. Lob.—Compare Chronicle of W.) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 841, and in the 592nd year from the founding of the City, Ludewicus, son of the earlier Ludewicus, began to reign as the 75th [Note: [Col. 0873] LXIX. D. E.] ruler after Augustus, and reigned for 36 years.

(A. Lob.) After the death of his father, the emperor Ludewicus, his brother Lotharius, returning from Italy, and Pippinus, son of his paternal uncle Pippinus, wished to deprive Charles, Judith’s son, surnamed the Bald, of the portion that his father had granted him, and to divide the kingdoms among themselves into three parts according to the testament that their grandfather Charlemagne had established. For this reason a serious battle was fought between them in the district of Auxerre, at a place called Fontenay, and the fighting was conducted with great slaughter; neither side achieved victory.

(Chronicle of W.) At last they were reconciled and divided the kingdoms into four tetrarchies. In the division of the kingdoms, Lotharius, with the imperial title, possessed Italy; Ludewicus, Germany; Pippinus, Aquitaine; and Charles, Gaul. [Note: [Col. 0873] *in*—“in”—followed by *Galliam*—“Gaul”—is added in the margin.]

Theophylus, emperor of Constantinople, died; his son Michael reigned for 26 years. [Note: [Col. 0874D] D. E. add: “The king of the Bulgars … persisted in Christianity,” from Sigebert, A.D. 865.]

4. A.D. 844. There was war between Pippinus, son of Pippinus, and Charles.

7. A.D. 847. The empress Judith, wife of Ludewicus the Earlier, died. [Note: [Col. 0873] This is absent in manuscript 5.] [Note: [Col. 0875A] The note appears in column 0875, but the callout number has not been printed in the text.] D. E. add: “A certain Gottschalk, when Rabanus had already been ordained archbishop of Mainz, … but under error,” from Sigebert, A.D. 849. [Note: [Col. 0875] *Gothescalcus* in D 1.]

10. A.D. 850.

15. A.D. 855. [Note: [Col. 0875A] D. E. add: “By earthquakes, unusual agitation of the air, whirlwinds, and many calamities, people are shaken. A certain man also … remaining,” from Sigebert; and they continue: “The church also …”]

The church of Saint Kilian at Würzburg was burned by lightning. Lotharius the emperor, having received the tonsure and monastic habit, died at Prüm (from A. Lob.); his son Lotharius succeeded him together with his brother Ludewicus. [Note: [Col. 0875] “When Lotharius of Prüm had died, Lotharius his son …,” manuscript 5.] The body of Saint Martin was raised from its tomb.

[Col. 0875B] 17. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 857. Pope Leo died; Pope Benedict, the 104th, succeeded him and died in the same year. Queen Hiltigart died.

18. A.D. 858. Pope Nicholas, the 105th, was ordained and sat for nine years.

22. A.D. 862. [Note: [Col. 0875B] D. at the beginning and E. at the end of the year add: “Archbishop Rabanus died.”] Saint Meginrad the hermit was killed.

25. A.D. 865. The Huns attacked the name of Christianity.

27. A.D. 867. Basil, after killing his lord Michael, reigned for twenty years.

28. A.D. 868. Pope Hadrian, the 106th, sat for five years.

30. (A. Lob.) A.D. 870. Lotharius, son of the emperor Lotharius, having taken another woman in addition to his lawful wife, was summoned to Rome. When he refused to obey the pope, he was excommunicated, and thus, while returning, died at Piacenza. [Note: [Col. 0875C] D. E. add: “Earlier, Guntharius, archbishop of Cologne, and Dietgaudus, archbishop of Trier, because they had consented to him in the adultery committed, were examined and convicted at Rome by Pope Nicholas; the episcopate … was granted,” from Sigebert, A.D. 863.]

32. A.D. 872. John, the 107th pope, was ordained. [Note: [Col. 0875C] D. in the margin and E. add: “To him John … with booklets,” from Sigebert.] [Note: [Col. 0875C] Manuscripts 10 and 11 add: “He was poisoned by one man and struck with a hammer by another; he died, and immediately his attacker died, untouched by anyone.” [Col. 0875D] The words *statimque*—“and immediately”—through *moritur*—“dies”—are absent in manuscript 11.] After him came Marinus, the 108th; Hadrian, the 109th; Agapitus, the 110th; Basil, the 111th; and Stephanus, the 112th.

[Col. 0875D] 35. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 875. Ludewicus, son of the emperor Lotharius and brother of Lotharius, died, and King Charles, heading toward Rome, was made emperor by Pope John. [Note: [Col. 0875D] D. E. add: “King Ludewicus … did not strive. In Italy … it is reported. A very great army of locusts, possessing six wings, six feet, and two teeth harder than stone, devastated Gaul, and a famine followed so severe that it almost consumed a third of the human race,” from Sigebert.]

[Col. 0876A] 36. A.D. 876. [Note: [Col. 0876A] D. E. add: “A comet … its trace,” from Sigebert.] The emperor Ludewicus died. [Note: [Col. 0876A] D. E. add: “in Italy.”]

Years of Charles the Younger

1. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, and in the 628th year from the founding of the City, Charles, younger son of Ludewicus, who was Charlemagne’s grandson, began to reign as the 76th [Note: [Col. 0875] LXX. D. E.] ruler after Augustus, and reigned with his brothers Karlomannus and Ludewicus for eleven years (Geneal. *SS.* II, 314). Ludewicus, they say, held East Francia, Charles Alamannia, and Karlomannus Bavaria; the latter’s son Arnolfus later obtained the monarchy.

2. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 878. King Charles of Gaul, surnamed the Bald, brother of Ludewicus the Second, died.

3. A.D. 879. Ludewicus the Stammerer, son of Charles, died.

4. A.D. 880. [Note: [Col. 0876B] D. E. add: “The sun … appeared,” from Sigebert.] Ludewicus, Charles’s brother, entered Bavaria while his brother Karlomannus was still alive. Karlomannus died.

5. A.D. 881. Charles the Younger was elevated with imperial blessing together with his wife Rihegarda.

6. A.D. 882. King Ludewicus of the Franks, brother of the emperor Charles, died.

10. (RICHER I, 5.) A.D. 886. Outo, a military and energetic man, was created king by the princes of Gaul in the palace of Compiègne. His father was Ruotpert, from the equestrian order, and his paternal grandfather was Witichinus, a refugee from Germany. They advanced him to the kingdom for this reason: Charles, son of Charles, grandson of Charles the Bald, king of Gaul, to whom the kingdom belonged (I, 4), was scarcely three years old. His father had died when he was two, while his mother survived him by scarcely four years.

11. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 887. The emperor Charles relinquished the kingdom while still alive. Basil, the emperor, died.

Years of Arnolfus

1. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 888, and in the 639th year from the founding of the City, Arnolfus, son of Karlomannus, brother of Charles the Younger, assumed the kingdom as the 77th [Note: [Col. 0875] LXXI. D. E.] ruler after Augustus and reigned for twelve years, but was emperor for five. In his first year, the younger emperor Charles, having first relinquished the empire, died.

Leo and Alexander, the sons of Basil, held the Constantinopolitan kingdom for 22 years; afterward Alexander for one year; then Constantine Porphyrogenitus, son of Leo, for six years with his mother Zoe; afterward Romanus the Armenian with the same Constantine for 26 years; after this the same Constantine with his son Romanus, still a child, for fifteen years.

(LIUDPR. I, 5, 13.) Thus King Arnolfus ruled powerfully over the Bavarians, the Swabians, the Eastern Franks, and, after the death of Charles the Bald, the Lotharingians and the bold Saxons. Zuentebald, duke of the Moravians, resisted him bravely.

Until this time the people of the Hungarians, whose ferocity almost every nation has experienced, had been separated from us by certain extremely difficult barriers, which the common people call *clusurae*, so that they had no opportunity of going out either toward the south or toward the west. Since King Arnolfus could not overcome the aforementioned Zuentebald, he had those fortifications, alas, removed and called the Hungarian people, eager for crimes, to his aid—if it can be called aid, since shortly afterward, when he died, it brought grave danger, indeed destruction, both upon his own people and upon the other peoples living in the south and west.

After Zuentebald had been defeated, Arnolfus securely possessed the kingdom. Meanwhile the Hungarians, observing the exit and examining the region, were devising in their hearts the evil that later appeared openly. [Note: [Col. 0877] *servato* corrected to *observato* in manuscript 1.]

2. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 889. Sunderold succeeded Archbishop Liutpert. Arn, bishop of Würzburg, was killed in Saxony during the celebration of Mass. He had sat for 36 years and seven months.

3. A.D. 890. King Arnolfus destroyed an army of Northmen.

[Col. 0877C] 4. A.D. 891. Regensburg burned in a fire.

6. (WIDUK. I, 22.) A.D. 893. Archbishop Sunderold was killed by the Northmen. In his place Hatto was ordained, obscure indeed by birth but sharp in intellect, and one about whom it would be difficult to determine whether he was better or worse in counsel.

7. A.D. 894. [Note: [Col. 0877C] D. E. add: “Arnolfus … of the Lotharingians,” from Sigebert, A.D. 896.]

8. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 895. Arnolfus subjected Italy and Burgundy to himself.

Years of Arnolfus’s imperial rule

9. 1. A.D. 896. King Arnolfus came to Rome and was made emperor.

In his time Formosus was the 113th pope.

[Col. 0877D] 10. 2. (RICHER I, 12 ff.) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 897, Charles, now fifteen years old, was made king of Gaul while Outo was still alive and concealing the injury done to him; nevertheless, Outo died in that same year. His brother Ruotpert, whom Charles appointed duke of Celtic Gaul, later sought the kingdom and was killed by Charles’s soldiers. His son Hugo, always hostile to the king because of his father’s death, acted through everyone he could influence so that Ruodolfus, son of Richard of Burgundy, might be made king, despite Ruodolfus’s strong opposition, and so that King Charles might be captured by ambush by Heripert, a kinsman of that same Hugo, and committed to prison. There he died after five years, in the 36th year of his reign and the 54th of his life. [Note: [Col. 0877] “The 53rd,” manuscript 1b.]

That same Charles fathered by the sister of Adelstan, king of the English, a son named Ludewicus. During the disturbances of his father’s reign, while still an infant, he was brought across the sea to his maternal uncle Adelstan. After the death of his father and of Ruodolfus, he ruled his paternal and ancestral kingdom.

He also took as wife Gerbirga, daughter of Heinricus, duke and later king of the Saxons, and sister of Otto the Great, after her husband Gisilbertus had died. [Note: [Col. 0877] *quam*—“whom”—followed by *persuasit* is in a damaged place.] By her he had a son, Lotharius, who succeeded his father in the same kingdom.

11. 3. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 899. A great famine compelled people to eat one another.

[Col. 0878B] 12. 4. (LIUDPR. II, 1, 2.) A.D. 900. The emperor Arnolfus died. [Note: [Col. 0878B] D. E. add, from Sigebert, A.D. 902: “The emperor Arnolfus, after a long …, died.”] As soon as the Hungarians heard of his death, they gathered a very large army and invaded and seized the people of the Moravians, whom the emperor Arnolfus had subjected to himself with their help. They also occupied the borders of Bavaria, demolished fortresses, consumed churches with fire, slaughtered the peoples, and, to make themselves more and more feared, drank the blood of those they had killed.

(LIUDPR. I, 28, 29, 30, 36, 30, 31.) In the time of this Arnolfus, Pope Formosus was severely harassed by the Romans, at whose urging King Arnolfus had also come to Rome. When he entered the city, he ordered many Roman nobles who were hastening to meet him to be beheaded, taking vengeance for the injury done to the pope.

The cause of the quarrel between the Romans and Pope Formosus was this. After Formosus’s predecessor had died, one faction of the Romans elected as pope a certain Sergius, a deacon of the Roman church, while another faction, not inferior in birth, eagerly desired to make Formosus, bishop of the city of Porto, pope because of his true religion and his knowledge of divine Scripture and doctrine.

When Sergius was about to be ordained, the faction favoring Formosus, amid considerable disturbance and violence, drove Sergius from the altar and established Formosus as pope. Sergius therefore withdrew into Tuscany, intending to obtain the powerful assistance of the margrave Adelbertus. This was accomplished. For after Formosus had died, and after Arnolfus had perished in his homeland by a miserable death—namely, from worms called lice, which poured forth in such abundance that no medical treatment could diminish them—the man who had been appointed after Formosus’s death was expelled, and Sergius was made pope through Adelbertus.

Once established, Sergius, being impious and ignorant of sacred doctrine, ordered Formosus to be dragged from his tomb, dressed in priestly vestments, placed upon the seat of the Roman pontificate, and then beheaded. He also said to him: “Since you were bishop of Porto, why, driven by a spirit of ambition, did you usurp the universal Roman see?” Then he ordered him stripped of his sacred vestments, three fingers cut off, and his body thrown into the Tiber. He also deposed all those whom Formosus had ordained from their proper rank and ordained them again.

How badly and unjustly he acted in this can be understood from the fact that even those who had received salvation or apostolic blessing from Judas the traitor before his betrayal were not deprived of it after his betrayal and the hanging of his own body, except those whom perhaps shameful crimes had defiled. For the blessing bestowed upon Christ’s ministers is poured out not by the priest who is seen but by the one who is unseen. Neither is the one who waters anything, nor the one who plants, but God who gives the growth.

From this we can gather how great Formosus was in authority and religion: when he was later found by fishermen and carried to the church of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, certain images of the saints inclined themselves and reverently greeted him as he lay in the casket. The most religious men of the city of Rome testified to this.

After Formosus, John became the 114th pope; Stephanus succeeded him as the 115th.

1. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 901, and in the 652nd year from the founding of the City, Ludewicus, son of the emperor Arnolfus, still a very young boy, assumed the empire as the 78th [Note: [Col. 0879] LXXII. D. E.] ruler after Augustus and reigned for twelve years (compare Chronicle of W.).

(LIUDPR. II, 2–5.) In his first year the Hungarians ravaged Bavaria. But Ludewicus, unable to endure the devastation of his people, gathered a great army and fought them beside the river Lech, killing more than a thousand of them.

When the battle had already continued until the seventh hour and the king’s victory was thought assured, the cunning Hungarians, having set an ambush opposite, pretended to flee. As the king’s soldiers, ignorant of the trick, pursued them with great force, the ambushes emerged from every side and, though apparently defeated, killed the victors themselves. The king was astonished to find himself, from a victor, defeated, and an unexpected and more grievous disaster befell him. The Hungarians, to satisfy the rage of their treachery, traversed the kingdoms of the Bavarians, Swabians, and Franks, devastating and burning everything.

In this period Adelbertus, no ordinary man but a great hero among the leading men, son of the sister of Heinricus, duke and later king, and grandson of Otto, duke of Saxony, was waging considerable hostility against the public authority in the castle of Babenberg.

(WID. I, 22.) For since there was enmity between Chuonradus, father of Chuonradus who later became king, and Adelbertus, Adelbertus’s brother was first killed by Chuonradus; in revenge for him, Chuonradus was later killed by Adelbertus. None of the kings could calm the immense war that had arisen between such eminent men.

(LIUDPR. book I.) Since Adelbertus was also in rebellion against King Ludewicus, the king often gathered everyone and attacked his castle. But the aforementioned hero prepared for battle not near the castle, as most men do, but at a distance from the fortification.

Before the king’s soldiers had tested his valor in action, they went ahead of the king and planned, as a prelude to the battle, to draw him out of the fortress and kill him. But he, not only fully aware of such a preliminary maneuver but even intoxicated by it, had advanced to meet them so far from the castle that the soldiers did not recognize him as an enemy until his sword, impatient of slaughter, raged through their necks. [Note: [Col. 0879] *virtutem*—“valor”—is written above the line in manuscript 1.]

Thus, when the hero Adelbertus had carried on this rebellion for nearly seven years, Ludewicus, knowing that he could overcome his courage and audacity only by some stratagem, consulted Hatto, archbishop of the see of Mainz, about what ought to be done. Since Hatto was full of cunning, he said: “Stop worrying; I shall make you safe through my efforts. I shall arrange for him to come to you; you must ensure that he does not return.”

Thus Hatto, encouraged by the confidence of spirit with which he had turned certain misfortunes to advantage, went to Babenberg, ostensibly to advise Adelbertus concerning his affairs. After much conversation, he deceitfully persuaded him to come to the king, promising him on oath either that he would make peace for him with the king or that he would restore him unharmed to his own place.

(WID. I, 22.) Having agreed to these terms, Adelbertus asked the bishop to honor him by dining with him, for the sake of faith and friendship. (LIUDPR. and WID.) Hatto refused under this pretext of cunning, and they immediately left the city, the bishop holding Adelbertus’s right hand.

When they had passed through the town with their entire retinue, the bishop is said to have exclaimed: “Alas! How often he begs who rejects what is offered! I am weary of the longer road and the later hour, for we cannot walk all day fasting.” [Note: [Col. 0879] *jam*—“now”—in manuscript 1b.]

Hearing this, and suspecting no evil, Adelbertus happily bent his knee before the pontiff and begged him to return into the city so that he might eat something. The pontiff returned into the city with Adelbertus, considering himself released from the bond of his oath because he had restored him unharmed to his own place.

Afterward, when he went out with the pontiff, Adelbertus was presented by him to King Ludewicus. A judgment was immediately held, and by the decree of the princes who were present he suffered the death sentence. He received burial in his own castle of Tharissa.

[Col. 0880D] 2. (Chronicle of W.) A.D. 902. The Hungarians invaded Carinthia and, after a battle fought on Holy Saturday, were killed. [Note: [Col. 0880D] D. E. add: “The Saracens … defeated them,” from Sigebert, A.D. 910.]

3. A.D. 903. [Note: [Col. 0880D] D. E. add: “Ludewicus … should come,” from Sigebert, A.D. 911; “Zuendebaldus … arranged,” from Sigebert, A.D. 903.]

6. A.D. 906. The Hungarians were killed more bitterly. Berenger, Reginolt, and Gerhart, brothers by birth, were killed. [Note: [Col. 0879] “Berengir, Reinold, and Gerhard, twin brothers,” manuscript 1b.]

[Col. 0881A] 7. A.D. 907. A battle was fought between Adelbertus, their brother, and Chuonradus, brother of the emperor Ludewicus. [Note: [Col. 0881] *i. erat*—“it was”—in manuscript 4; *committitur*—“is fought”—in manuscripts 9c, 10, and 11.] Chuonradus was killed in it.

8. A.D. 908. Ruodolfus, bishop of Würzburg, died. Adelbertus, deceived by the treachery of Archbishop Hatto and a certain Luitpaldus, was beheaded at the command of King Ludewicus. The Bavarians were killed by the Hungarians.

9. A.D. 909. The Hungarians ravaged Saxony and Thuringia.

10. A.D. 910. The Hungarians attacked Alamannia. Leo, emperor of Constantinople, died.

11. A.D. 911. The Franks fought with the Hungarians.

12. A.D. 912. King Ludewicus dies. According to some, he is called the last of the Carolingians who ruled among the eastern [Col. 0881B] Franks; according to others, Chuonradus, who ruled after him, is counted the last. His father, Chuonradus, who was killed by Adelbertus, is thought to have been the brother of this Ludewicus. But let the error of this divergence be attributed to the writers of the kingdoms. (WID. I, 16.) Ludewicus, then, having taken as his wife a woman named Mahthilda, the sister of Bruno and of the great duke Otto, did not live many years thereafter. Their father was Luitolfus, who went to Rome and brought back from there the relics of Pope Innocent. Bruno, after administering the duchy of all Saxony, led an army against the Danes and, surrounded by a sudden flood and having no place in which to fight, perished with the entire army, leaving the duchy to his brother, younger indeed by birth but much greater in every virtue. Since King Ludewicus had no son, after his death the entire people of the Franks and Saxons sought to place the royal diadem upon Otto, but he, as though already burdened by age, refused the burden of rule. Nevertheless, at his counsel, Chuonradus, formerly duke of the Franks, son (from Chr. W.) of that Chuonradus whom Adelbertus killed, was anointed king; yet supreme authority was always and everywhere exercised by Otto. (WID. I, 17.) A son was born to that same Otto, Heinricus, an excellent man, necessary to the world, who was the first to rule Saxony with unrestricted authority. When his father died, he left him the duchy of all Saxony, while Chuonradus had already been elevated to the kingship.

[Col. 0881D] (Chr. W.) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 913, but in the 1664th year from the founding of the City, Chuonradus, son of Chuonradus whom Adelbertus killed, descended from the Frankish people, an energetic man and trained by experience in war, received the kingdom by the election of all, in the 79th [Note: [Col. 0881] D. E. have LXXIII.] place from Augustus, and reigned for seven years. (LIUDPR. II, 17, 18, 19.) Under him the most powerful princes were Arnoldus in Bavaria, Burchardus in [Col. 0882A] Swabia [Note: [Col. 0881] Thus, in letters running beyond the line, by a later hand in 1 and the other copies.], Eberhardus [Note: [Col. 0881] “Evrardus” in 1b.] the most powerful count in Francia, and Gisilbertus duke in Lotharingia. Among them Heinricus, the exceedingly powerful duke of the Saxons and Thuringians, shone brightly. In the second year of his reign the princes mentioned above rebelled especially against him; he overcame them both by the force of wisdom and by the strength of courage, and brought them over to his loyalty. Arnolfus, however, compelled by excessive fear, fled with his wife and sons to the Hungarians, and remained there until Chuonradus’s death.

## The Years of Chuonradus

1. (Chr. W.) In the first year of King Chuonradus, Hungarians are killed by the Alemanni [Note: [Col. 0881] “alamannis” corrected to “alemannis” in 1.] and Bavarians beside the river Enus [Note: [Col. 0881] “enim” corrected to “eni” in 1b.], which is commonly called the Ine.

2. (LIUDPR.---Chr. W.---RICHER II, 1 ff.). A.D. [Col. 0882B] 914. The princes mentioned above rebel against the king. King Ruodolfus dies. After him Ludewicus, son of Karolus, is brought back from overseas to Gaul and raised to his father’s kingdom on the advice of Duke Hugo, son of Ruotpertus; the same Hugo, however, later opposes him. At this time Marinus was the 116th pope. [Note: [Col. 0881D] Ekkehardus here regards King Rudolfus as the first king of Burgundy of this name and also as king of Gaul.]

3. (Chr. W.) A.D. 915. The Hungarians devastate Alemannia. Archbishop Hatto [Note: [Col. 0881] “a. Mogontinus” in 5.] died; Heriger succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0881] “the tenth archbishop” in 5.].

5. A.D. 917. Bishop Salomon was captured. The Hungarians devastate all Alemannia [Note: [Col. 0882B] “While devastating all the land, they reach Fulda.” D. E., from Sigeb., a. 917.] with fire and sword.

6. A.D. 918. Duke Erkengerus and Berhtolfus, brothers by birth, are beheaded. Basel is destroyed by the Hungarians.

[Col. 0882C] 7. A.D. 919. The Hungarians, passing through Alemannia and Alsace, invade Lotharingia. Duke Burchardus [Note: [Col. 0882C] “B. duke”; “duke” is absent in E., where the following is read: “King Cuonradus, dying before the princes of the kingdom, designates as king Heinricus, son of Otto, duke of the Saxons, by Luitgard, daughter of Emperor Arnulfus. The entire history of the Saxons is absent.”] is appointed. King Chuonradus dies, and by his counsel and command Heinricus, duke of Saxony, son of Duke Otto, is advanced to the kingdom (cf. WID.). But since, with the Carolingian line failing in the kingdom of the Franks, the kingdom is now transferred to the Saxons through Heinricus, let us briefly set out the genealogy of the Carolingians for the sake of remembrance; then let us describe something about the origin of the Saxon people, whose account is disputed, and so proceed to the beginning of the reign. [Note: [Col. 0882D] 5 adds these verses:

**Kings from the stock of Karolus**

The stock of great Karolus, venerable to the whole world,  
Was formerly illustrious, but at last began to grow rare.

**Of the stock of the Saxons**

Then the Saxon kings began to give laws;  
Heinricus was king, first among them in name.  
That stock reigned until it drew near its end.

If his lineage does not decline, his race still endures.]
