# ON THE ORIGIN OF THE SAXONS

[Col. 0885]

[Col. 0885A] (WIDUK. I, 2.) There is a disputed opinion concerning the origin of the Saxon people. Some think that they derived their origin from the Danes and Northmen; others, among whom the Greeks are also said to agree, think that they were remnants of the Macedonian army, which, following Alexander the Great, was scattered throughout the whole world after his premature death. We find, however, in the writings of a certain author (Transl. S. Alex.) that, according to a tradition handed down from ancient times, they departed from the Angles, the inhabitants of Britain, and, sailing across the Ocean, landed on the shores of Germany because of their desire and necessity to seek settlements, at a place called Hathuloga. This occurred at the time when King Theodericus of the Franks, fighting against Irminfridus, duke of the Thuringians, devastated their land cruelly with sword and fire.

(WID. I, 3 ff.) When they had first come ashore, the inhabitants of that land, who are said to have been Thuringians, deeply resenting their arrival, took up arms against them. The Saxons, however, resisting fiercely, secured the harbor. After they had fought among themselves for a long time, with many falling on both sides, at last both parties agreed to negotiate peace. A treaty was made on these terms: the Saxons would have the opportunity to buy and sell, but otherwise they would abstain from the fields, from killing people, and from plunder. That treaty stood inviolate for many days.

When the Saxons’ money had already run out, and they had nothing with which to buy or sell, they judged the peace useless to them. At that time, then, it happened that a certain young man came out of the ships, loaded with much gold, a golden necklace, and golden bracelets as well. A certain Thuringian met him and said: “What is the meaning of such an enormous quantity of gold around your hungry neck?” “I am looking for a buyer,” he replied. “I carry this gold for no other purpose. If I am dying of hunger, what pleasure does gold give me?”

When the other asked about the quality and quantity of the price, the Saxon said: “I have no fixed price; whatever you give, I shall regard as acceptable.” The other, smiling, said: “What if I fill your bosom with that dust?” There was, in fact, a great deal of earth dug up at that spot. Without hesitation, the Saxon opened his bosom and accepted the earth, immediately handing the gold over to the Thuringian. Both returned happily to their own people.

The Thuringians extolled their Thuringian to the heavens with praises because he had deceived the Saxon by a noble fraud. They called him fortunate beyond all mortals, since for a paltry price he had acquired such an enormous amount of gold. For the rest, confident of victory, they were already celebrating a kind of triumph over the Saxons.

Meanwhile the Saxon, stripped of his gold but loaded with much earth, approached the ships. When his companions came to meet him and wondered what he was doing, some of his friends began to mock him, others to reproach him, and all alike considered him mad. But he asked for silence and said: “Follow me, best of Saxons, and you will prove my madness useful to you.”

Though doubtful, they nevertheless followed. Taking the earth, he scattered it as finely as he could over the neighboring fields and occupied the sites of the camps. When the Thuringians saw the Saxon camps, the situation seemed intolerable to them. They sent envoys and complained that the treaty had been broken and the agreement violated by the Saxons.

The Saxons replied that they had kept the treaty inviolate up to that point, but that they wished to retain in peace the land purchased with their own gold, or else defend it by arms. When they heard this, the inhabitants began to curse Saxon gold, and they acknowledged that the man whom they had shortly before proclaimed fortunate was the author of their own destruction and that of their country.

Then, inflamed by anger, they rushed upon the camp in blind combat, without order and without counsel. The Saxons, however, being prepared, received the enemy, struck them down, and, after their affairs had prospered, acquired by right of war the neighboring lands all around.

After they had fought one another for a long time, and the Thuringians saw that the Saxons would prove superior to them, they sought through intermediaries to make peace with them and granted them possession of the land they had taken.

(G. Franc. c. 19.---WID. I, 9 ff.) At that time, after Clodoveus, king of the Franks, had died, his four sons divided his kingdom equally among themselves. When Theodericus had received Austrasia, whose royal seat was at the city of Metz, he arranged to send an embassy to Irminfridus, king of the Thuringians, for the sake of peace and concord. He instructed him that he did not wish to be his lord but his friend, not his emperor but his kinsman, and that he wished to preserve inviolate the rights of kinship—for Irminfridus had married Theodericus’s sister—asking only that he not depart from the concord of the Frankish people, who had made him king.

When Irminfridus answered kindly that the Franks’ arrangements pleased him and that he greatly desired peace, but that concerning the matter of the kingdom he wished to defer his answer until the presence of his friends, the queen heard that her brother’s envoy had arrived and had spoken with the king about the kingdom. She therefore dealt with Iring, one of the king’s warriors, a bold man, strong of hand, keen in intelligence, sharp in counsel, persistent in carrying out undertakings, and ready to persuade others to whatever he wished. He had thereby attached the king’s mind to himself. She urged Iring and the king together to persuade Irminfridus that the kingdom had come to him by hereditary right, since she was the daughter of a king and queen; that Theodericus was his servant, as though born of a concubine; and that it would therefore be disgraceful ever to extend a hand to one’s own servant.

The princes and necessary friends were then summoned, and Irminfridus repeated the envoy’s words in their presence. They unanimously advised him to favor what belonged to peace and concord, since he could not withstand the Franks’ assault, especially because he was also being pressed from another side by fiercer enemies.

But Iring, gratifying the wishes of the wanton woman, advised Irminfridus [Col. 0887A] that he ought not to yield to the Franks, that he had the stronger claim in the matter of the kingdom, and that, with his broad empire, the hands and weapons of his soldiers, and his other resources of war, he and Theodericus were by no means evenly matched.

Persuaded by these words, Irminfridus answered the envoy that he did not deny the friendship and kinship of Theodericus, but that he could not sufficiently wonder how Theodericus wished to usurp rule before liberty—being born a servant, and yet seeking dominion over his own people. He could not extend his hand to his own servant.

The envoy, greatly angered by this, said: “I would rather hand this head of mine over to you than hear such words from you, knowing that they must be washed away in much Frankish and Thuringian blood.” Saying this, he returned to Theodericus and concealed nothing of what he had heard.

Theodericus, hiding excessive anger beneath a calm expression, said: “We must hasten to serve Irminfridus, so that, deprived as we are of liberty, we may at least enjoy an empty life.”

As he approached the borders of the Thuringians with a large army, he found Irminfridus also waiting for him with a strong force at a place called Runiberg. When battle was joined, the fighting continued with uncertain outcome for two days. On the third day, Irminfridus was defeated, yielded to Theodericus, and, fleeing, finally withdrew into a city called Schidinga, situated on the river Onestrod [Note: [Col. 0887] “Unstrut” in 3.].

Theodericus then gathered the leaders of his army and asked their opinion: did they think Irminfridus should be pursued, or should they return home? Theodericus had a sufficiently clever servant whose counsel he had often tested as sound and to whom, for that reason, he was bound by a certain intimacy.

When some advised that the dead should be buried, the wounded cared for, and that they should return home to gather a larger army, the servant, asked for his opinion, said:

“In honorable undertakings I have always thought perseverance most beautiful. Our ancestors valued it so highly that they rarely or never abandoned enterprises once begun. Yet I would not consider our labors equal to theirs, for they overcame enormous forces of peoples with small forces.

“Now the land is in our power. By our departure, shall we provide the defeated with an opportunity to conquer? I too would embrace returning home and attending to our familiar needs, if I knew that our enemy would be idle during that interval. Perhaps our wounded need such a thing; but I think the labor of the camp, for energetic spirits, is the greatest pleasure.

“Our army has been severely weakened by the slaughter of the multitude. Have all the enemies escaped? Certainly, very few. The duke himself, like some little animal protected by its hiding place, is surrounded by the enclosure of the city and does not dare even to look safely upon the gathering, compelled by fear of us.

“But he is not without money with which barbarian nations may be hired; nor is he without a body of soldiers, although tired. Yet all these things are restored by our absence. It is disgraceful for victors to give the defeated an opportunity to conquer.

“Are we strong enough to supply garrisons for each city? We shall lose them all while going and returning.”

As he continued in this vein, Theodericus and all who thirsted for victory decided to remain in the camp and send to the Saxons, ancient enemies of the Thuringians, asking them for aid on the condition that, if they defeated Irminfridus and captured the city, he would grant them the land as a perpetual inheritance.

The Saxons did not hesitate, but sent nine dukes, each with a thousand soldiers. The nine dukes entered the camp, each with a hundred soldiers, leaving the rest of the multitude outside the camp. They greeted Theodericus with peaceful words. Received cheerfully by him, they gave and received right hands, declaring that they had been sent by the Saxon people as his devoted men, ready for everything, and that they wished either to conquer or not to live.

As they spoke these words, the Franks admired the men, excellent in body and spirit; they also admired their unfamiliar dress, their weapons, and their long hair flowing over their shoulders, and above all their immense steadfastness of spirit. They were dressed in cloaks and armed with long spears. They stood leaning upon small shields and had large knives at their waists.

Some of the Franks, however, said that the Franks had no need of such great and remarkable friends, that this was an untamed people, and that, if they inhabited the present land, they would undoubtedly be the ones who would someday destroy the Franks altogether [Note: [Col. 0887] “Entirely” in 5.].

Theodericus, looking to his own interests, received the men into his confidence and instructed them to prepare to attack the city. Returning from the king, they pitched their camp on the southern side of the city, in meadows adjoining the river. The next day, rising at first light, they took up their weapons, attacked and set fire to the town, and immediately drew up their battle line opposite the eastern gate.

Those inside, shut in by the walls, saw the lines drawn up and realized that they were reduced to the last extremity. They boldly burst through the gates and rushed upon their opponents in blind combat. After missiles had been thrown, the conflict was carried on with swords.

As a severe battle arose, many fell on both sides: the defenders fought for their country, their wives and children, and finally for their lives, while the Saxons fought for glory and to acquire the land. When slaughter and wailing were occurring everywhere, and neither army gave ground, the late hour brought the battle to an end.

That day many Thuringians were killed and many wounded; among the Saxons, six thousand dead were counted.

Iring was therefore sent by Irminfridus with a suppliant embassy and all his treasures to Theodericus, seeking peace and voluntary surrender. When Iring approached, he said:

“Your former kinsman, now your servant, has sent these things to you, asking that, if you do not pity him, you at least pity your wretched sister and your nephews, who are placed in the greatest danger.”

When he had said this with tears, the intervention of the leaders, corrupted by gold, added that royal clemency required Theodericus not to reject such an embassy or forget their common nature. It was better to receive into his allegiance one whom he had already defeated and crushed so completely that he could never rise against him again than to preserve that untamed and indefatigable race, from which the Frankish empire could expect nothing but danger. It was therefore better, once the Thuringians had been received, to drive the Saxons from their borders together with them.

Although unwilling, Theodericus was bent by these words and promised that on the following day he would receive Irminfridus and expel the Saxons.

When Iring heard this, he threw himself at the king’s feet. Praising the king’s decision, he remained in the camp that night, and, having sent an eagerly desired message to his lord, filled him and the city with the joy of security.

Meanwhile, as the city had been made more secure by the promised peace, a certain man went out with a hawk, seeking food along the bank of the river mentioned above. One of the Saxons on the farther bank caught the bird after it had been released.

When the owner asked that it be returned, the Saxon refused. The other said: “Return it, and I will reveal to you a secret useful to you and your companions.”

The Saxon replied: “Tell me, so that you may receive what you seek.”

“Because the kings have made peace between themselves,” the other said, “they have decided that if you are found in the camp tomorrow, you will either be captured or certainly killed.”

The Saxon answered: “Are you speaking seriously, or in jest?”

“The second hour of the coming day will prove,” he replied, “that you should not treat this as a joke. Therefore look to your own interests and seek safety in flight.”

The Saxon immediately released the bird and reported to his companions what he had heard. They were greatly disturbed and could not at once decide what they ought to do about it.

There was then in the camp a certain veteran soldier, already advanced in age but still vigorous with a healthy old age. Because of his good qualities he was rightly called the father of fathers. His name was Hatugato.

Seizing the banner that was held sacred among them, marked with the figure of a lion, a dragon, and above them a flying eagle—so that it might display the effectiveness of courage and wisdom, while his bodily movement declared steadfastness of spirit—he said:

“Until now I have lived among the best of the Saxons, and age has brought me nearly to this final old age. I have never seen my Saxons flee; how, then, am I now compelled to do what I have never learned? I have learned to fight; I neither know how to flee nor am able to do so.

“If fate does not permit me to live longer, at least let me die with my friends in the way that is sweetest to me. The virtues of my fathers are my example, as are the bodies of our friends lying around us—men who preferred to die rather than be defeated, and to surrender their energetic spirits rather than yield their ground before the enemy.

“But why must I prolong an exhortation concerning contempt for death? Behold, we shall go against men who are secure, for slaughter only, not for battle. Secure because of the promised peace and our grievous wound, they suspect nothing adverse. Fatigued also by today’s battle, they remain without fear and therefore without watchfulness or their customary guard.

“Let us therefore rush upon the unsuspecting, buried in sleep. The labor is small. Follow me as your leader, and I give you this gray head of mine, if what I say does not come to pass.”

Encouraged by his excellent words, they spent the rest of the day restoring their bodies. Then, at the first watch of the night, when deeper sleep is accustomed to seize mortals, they gave the signal, took up their weapons, and, with their leader at their head, rushed upon the walls. Finding the defenders without guards or sentries, they entered the city with a great shout.

Roused by this, some of the adversaries sought safety in flight; others wandered like drunk men through the streets and along the walls of the city; others fell upon the Saxons, thinking them fellow citizens. The Saxons handed over to death all those of full age, but preserved the underage as booty.

When a search was made for Irminfridus, it was discovered that he had escaped with his wife, his sons, and a small retinue.

When Theodericus heard this, he arranged for him to be recalled by deceit and for Iring to kill him, so that Theodericus might stand as though innocent of his death. Iring accepted this unwillingly, but, overcome by deceptive promises—as though he were to be given great gifts and raised to great power in the kingdom—he finally consented and promised to obey his will.

Irminfridus was therefore recalled and prostrated himself at Theodericus’s feet. Iring, standing beside him like the king’s armor-bearer, drew his sword and slaughtered the prostrate lord.

Immediately the king said to him: “Because you have killed your lord, and are deservedly hateful to all mortals for such a crime, you have an open road to depart from us. We do not wish to share in any portion or part of your wickedness.”

Iring replied: “I deservedly appear hateful to everyone, since I obeyed your deceit. Before I depart, however, I shall cleanse myself of this crime by avenging my lord.”

As he stood there with his sword drawn, he struck down Theodericus as well. Taking the body of his lord, he placed it upon Theodericus’s corpse, so that the man who had been defeated while alive might at least conquer in death. Then, making his way with his sword, he departed.

Whether any credence should be given to these words is for the reader to decide. Yet we cannot sufficiently marvel that the story’s fame should have prevailed so far that the Milky Way in the sky is still marked by Iring’s name, “Iringesstraza.”

In the deeds of the Franks it is read (c. 22) that Theodericus, having given his word to Irminfridus, caused him to come to him at the city of Tolbiac; while they were conversing above the city walls, Irminfridus was compelled to fall from the wall to the ground [Col. 0890D] and thus died, and Theodericus ordered his sons to be killed.

(WID. l. l.) After the war had ended, the Saxons returned to Theodericus in the camp. They were well received and sufficiently praised by him, and were given the present land as an everlasting possession. They were also called allies and friends of the Franks. They soon first inhabited the city, which they had spared from fire as though it were protected by their own walls.

(Transl. S. AI.) Dividing the land they had received by lot, they could not occupy all of it, since many of them had fallen in the war and their numbers were too few. They therefore assigned part of it—especially the part facing east—to settlers to cultivate under tribute, while they themselves possessed the remaining places.

To the south they had the Franks and that part of the Thuringians which the preceding hostile storm had not touched; these were separated from them by the bed of the river [Col. 0891A] Unstroda. To the north they had the Northmen, exceedingly fierce peoples; to the east, the Obodrites; and to the west, the Frisians. From these they necessarily defended the extent of their boundaries without interruption, whether by treaty or by conflict.

They were indeed exceedingly restless and hostile to the settlements of their neighbors, but at home they were peaceful and, with tranquil kindness, concerned themselves with the interests of their fellow citizens. They also took the most careful concern for their lineage and nobility, and were not easily tainted by marriages with any other peoples, or with peoples inferior to themselves. They strove to make their own people pure, unmixed, and resembling themselves alone. Hence their clothing, the size of their bodies, and the color of their hair were almost the same in nearly all of them, despite their great number.

That people therefore had four distinctions within its order: nobles and free persons, freedmen, and slaves. It was confirmed by laws that no class should cross the boundaries of its own rank in joining marriages, but that a nobleman should marry a noblewoman, a free man a free woman, a freedman a freedwoman, and a slave a female slave.

If any one of them took as wife a woman unsuited to him and superior in birth, he was to make satisfaction at the cost of his life.

They also made excellent use of laws for avenging wrongdoers, and strove to possess many useful and honorable practices, in accordance with the law of nature, in the integrity of their customs. These might have helped them to attain true blessedness, if they had possessed knowledge of their Creator.

For they worshiped those who were not gods by nature, especially Mercury, to whom on appointed days they also made offerings with human victims. They did not consider it permissible, on account of the greatness and dignity of divinity, either to confine their gods in temples or to make them resemble any human form. They consecrated groves and woods, calling them by the names of the gods, and contemplated that secret place with reverence alone.

They observed omens and lots with the greatest care. Their practice of casting lots was simple. They cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree into small twigs and, marking them with certain signs, scattered them randomly and by chance upon a white cloth.

Then, if the consultation was public, the people’s priest; if private, the head of the household himself, after praying to the gods and looking up toward heaven, took up three twigs at a time and interpreted them according to the sign impressed upon them beforehand. If the signs forbade it, no further consultation about that matter took place on that day; if they permitted it, confidence in the outcome was still required.

It was characteristic of that people to question the voices and flights of birds. They also tested the omens and movements of horses, observing their neighing and snorting, and no omen was trusted more than these—not only by the common people but also by the nobles.

There was another practice of observing omens by which they used to investigate the outcome of serious wars. They would take a captive, intercepted by whatever means, from the people with whom they were to fight, and set him against a chosen man from their own people, each armed with the weapons of his homeland. They regarded the victory of one or the other as a forecast of the future.

How they also believed that it was most auspicious to begin undertakings on certain days, when the moon was beginning or becoming full, and how they observed countless other kinds of vain superstitions by which they were entangled, I pass over. I have recalled these matters, however, so that the prudent reader may recognize from how many shadows of error they were freed by the grace of God.

They were, like all the peoples inhabiting Germany, naturally fierce, devoted to the worship of demons, and opposed to the true religion. They did not think it unlawful or dishonorable to transgress either divine or human laws.

Thus it happened that they had disputes and conflicts with their neighbors, especially with the Franks, because there were causes that could disturb the peace every day. The boundaries of both peoples touched one another almost everywhere across open country, except in a few places where great forests or mountain ridges intervened and separated the lands of both by a fixed limit. In these regions killings, plundering, and burnings did not cease to occur alternately.

The Franks were so provoked by this that they no longer intended merely to return each injury in kind, but deliberated on undertaking open war against them.

War was therefore undertaken against them. It was waged for thirty continuous years, with great hostility on both sides but with greater loss to the Saxons. It could have ended sooner, if the Saxons’ treachery had permitted this.

For it is difficult to say how often, after being defeated, they surrendered themselves as suppliants to the king, promising to do what was commanded; how often they gave without delay the hostages demanded; how they received the envoys who were sent; and how, at times, they were so subdued and softened that they even promised that they wished to abandon the worship of demons and submit themselves to the Christian religion.

But just as they were sometimes inclined to undertake these things, so they were always precipitous in turning away from them. Nor is it easy to judge toward which of these two courses they could more truly be called the more ready.

They showed reverence to leafy trees and springs. They also worshiped a large tree trunk raised upright in the open air, calling it in their native language Irminsul, which in Latin means “universal column,” as though it supported everything.

(EINH. *Vita Kar.* c. 1.) Therefore, when Pippin died—after King Childeric had been deposed and sent to a monastery, he being the last of the Merovingians whose rule had ended, and after Pippin, formerly master of the palace, had alone obtained the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom through the authority of Zachary, Roman pontiff—his son Charles succeeded him. Charles renewed the war against the Saxons, which had seemed almost interrupted by his father’s death (cf. above, under the year 758). [Col. 0892D]

(EX EINH. *Ann.* et *Transl. S. Al.) For his father had previously imposed upon them, after their defeat, an annual tribute of three hundred horses. After Charles renewed the war against them, scarcely a year passed in which they did not alter their treaty; but the king’s magnanimity and his constant firmness of mind, alike in adversity and prosperity, could neither be overcome by any of their changes nor wearied by the measures he had begun. For he never allowed them to perpetrate anything of this kind with impunity, but either led an army himself or sent one through his counts, avenged their treachery, and exacted an appropriate penalty from them. This continued until, after all who were accustomed to resist had been defeated and reduced under his power, he transferred ten thousand men from those who inhabited both banks of the River Elbe, together with their wives and little children, and distributed them here and there throughout Gaul and Germany in many separate settlements. The war, which had lasted so many years, is said to have ended on the condition that they abandon the worship of demons and accept the sacraments of the Christian religion. And this was done.

Witikind also, who stood out among them both for the distinction of his lineage and for the extent of his wealth, and who had been their tireless author and instigator of treachery, came of his own accord to Charles’s faith. He was baptized at Tiniacum and received by the king from the baptismal font; and thus all Saxony was conquered and subjected. Witikind’s son Wigbert, a devoted practitioner of the Christian religion, fathered a son whom he named Waltbert. He too was religious from childhood; and when he had become a man, he journeyed to Rome for the sake of prayer and the acquisition of relics. [Note: [Col. 0893] “Rum tetendit” in an erased space.] Receiving from Pope Leo, then reigning, the intact body of Saint Alexander, son of Saint Felicity, he brought it to Saxony and placed it in the place called Wigaltingohuson. [Col. 0893A–B]

From the stock of this same Saxon people there arose a noble and very illustrious man named Luitelfus, who likewise went to Rome for the sake of religion and brought back from there the relics of blessed Pope Innocent.

(WID. I, 16 ff.) He had two sons, Brun and Otto. The elder, Brun, after administering the duchy of all Saxony, led an army against the Danes; he was killed there and left the duchy to his brother Otto. They had a sister named Luitgart, whom King Ludewicus, son of the Emperor Arnolfus, took as his wife; but she did not live long thereafter. When he died without sons, the entire Frankish and Saxon people wished to place the royal diadem upon Duke Otto. When Otto, as though already weighed down by old age, refused it, Conrad, duke of the Franks, was made king at his advice; nevertheless, supreme authority always and everywhere remained with Otto. [Col. 0893C]

Otto had a son named Heinricus, who was the first to rule in Saxony with unrestricted power. Since he adorned his life with every kind of virtue from his earliest youth, his father, observing the young man’s prudence, left him the army against Dalmatia, against which he himself had long waged war. But the Dalmatians, unable to withstand his attack, brought the Avars against him—whom we now call Hungarians. Some think that they are remnants of the Huns, who, as is read in the history of the Goths, came forth from among the Goths and inflicted much harm upon neighboring peoples. Later, while inhabiting Pannonia, they were defeated by Charles the Great, who, as is said, confined them within a huge rampart and prevented them from their customary devastation of nations. The Emperor Arnolfus destroyed this work and led them out as auxiliaries against Zuentebold, king of the Moravians. How great a slaughter and how much injury they later inflicted upon the Frankish kingdom is still attested by the cities and regions lying desolate. These same men, summoned by the Dalmatians, also inflicted great disaster upon Saxony and carried away much booty. [Col. 0893D–0894A]

Therefore, when Otto, the great father of his country and duke, died, he left the duchy of all Saxony to his illustrious and magnificent son Heinricus. [Note: In 1, the reading “the father … and the great duke Otto having died, his illustrious and magnificent son Heinricus … the duchy (received?)” is corrected to the text printed.] King Conrad, however, having often tested the new duke’s courage, feared to entrust him with all his father’s authority. As a result, he incurred the hostility of the entire Saxon army. When the king saw that their expression toward him had become harsher, and judged that he could not crush their duke in open war because of the army’s enormous numbers, he arranged that the duke should be killed by treachery in some manner or other. For this purpose, as is reported, he had an especially suitable agent in the bishop of the Mainz see, named Hatto, by whose counsel Adelbert of Babenberg had also been deceived. [Col. 0894A–B]

This man, approaching the aforesaid duke by treachery, had a golden torque made for him and invited him to a banquet, where he intended to honor him with magnificent gifts. Meanwhile, the bishop entered the goldsmith’s workshop to inspect the work. When he saw the torque, he is said to have groaned. When the goldsmith asked the reason for his groan, he replied that the torque ought to be dipped in the blood of an excellent and very dear man—namely, Duke Heinricus. Having heard this, the goldsmith concealed the matter in silence. When the work was finished and delivered, he asked for and received permission to depart; meeting the duke as he was going about his business, he told him what he had heard.

The duke, however, becoming extremely angry, summoned the bishop’s envoy, who had already arrived to invite him, and said: “Go and tell Hatto that Heinricus does not have a harder neck than Adelbert, and that we have judged it better to remain at home and discuss his service than to burden him with the multitude of our retinue.” [Col. 0894C]

He immediately returned and seized throughout Saxony and Thuringia everything that belonged to himself by right. He also so afflicted Burchard and Bardo—one of whom was the king’s son-in-law—that they abandoned the land, and he divided all their possessions among his own soldiers. Bishop Hatto, seeing that his stratagems had been brought to an end, was overcome after not many days by excessive grief and illness together and died. There were also those who said that he had been struck by lightning and, shattered by its blow, had perished on the third day.

The king sent his brother Eberhard with an army to ravage Saxony. When he approached the city called Heresburg, he spoke arrogantly, as they report, saying that he had no greater concern than the fact that the Saxons did not dare to show themselves before the walls, so that he could fight them. The words were still in his mouth when, behold, the Saxons met him one mile from the city. Battle was joined, and the Franks suffered such slaughter that people mocked the matter with a declamation asking where that great hell could be which could contain so large a multitude of the slain. The king’s brother was freed from his fear of the Saxons’ absence, for he saw them present and departed, shamefully routed by them. [Col. 0894D–0895A]

When the king heard that his brother had fought badly, he assembled all the strength of the Franks and set out to seek Heinricus. Learning that Heinricus was in the stronghold of the city called Gruona, he attempted to besiege it. First sending an embassy to propose voluntary surrender, he promised that, if Heinricus surrendered, he would thereby become his friend rather than find him an enemy.

Dietmarus intervened in this embassy on behalf of the eastern Saxons. He was a man highly skilled in military discipline, versatile and great in counsel, and by his native cunning surpassed many mortals. When he arrived and found the king’s envoys present, he asked the duke where he wished the army to encamp. Heinricus, already persuaded to yield to the Franks, took confidence from hearing about the army, believing the statement to be true; but Dietmarus was speaking deceitfully, for he had come with only five men. When the duke asked about the number of legions, Dietmarus replied that he could field nearly thirty legions. Thus deceived, the envoys returned to the king. Dietmarus defeated by his cunning those whom Duke Heinricus could not defeat by the sword. For before dawn, the Franks abandoned their camp, and each man returned to his own place. [Col. 0895A–B]

(LIUDPR. II, 20.) In the seventh year of his reign King Conrad began to fall ill. Recognizing that the time of his calling had arrived, he summoned the princes of the kingdom, except Heinricus, and addressed them as follows:

“I recognize that the time of my calling has come, and, as you see, it is at hand. Therefore I beg you again and again to pursue peace and concord. When I, a mortal man, depart, let no ambition to rule inflame you. Choose Heinricus, the most prudent duke of the Saxons and Thuringians, and establish him as king and lord; for he is powerful in wisdom and abounds in the judgment of just severity.” [Col. 0895B–C]

(WID. I, 25.) When they agreed to these words, he summoned his brother Eberhard and addressed him as follows:

“I perceive, brother, that I can no longer continue to hold this life. Therefore consider your own position, and, in what chiefly concerns you, provide for the entire Frankish kingdom, attending to the counsel of me, your brother. We have the resources to assemble and lead armies; we have cities and weapons, together with the royal insignia, and everything that royal dignity requires, except fortune and character. Fortune, brother, yields to Heinricus, together with the noblest character; supreme authority over public affairs is now with the Saxons.

“Therefore take these insignia—the lance, the golden bracelets, the cloak, the ancient sword of the kings, and the diadem—and go to Heinricus. Make peace with him, so that you may have him as an ally forever. For what need is there that the Frankish people should fall with you before him? He will truly be king and emperor of many peoples.”

After these words, his brother replied through tears that he consented. Thereafter the king died, a brave and powerful man, excellent at home and in war, gracious in generosity, and distinguished by every mark of virtue. He was buried in his own city, Wilinaburg, amid the mourning and tears of all the Franks. [Col. 0895C–0896A]

(WIDUK. I, cc. 25–26.) As soon as the king had died, Eberhard approached Heinricus, surrendered himself to him together with all the treasures, made peace with him, and earned his friendship, which he maintained faithfully and familiarly to the end. Then, after assembling the princes and the elder men, he designated Heinricus king of the Frankish army at the place called Friteslare, before the entire Frankish and Saxon people.

## The Years of Heinricus

### 1.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 920, in the 671st year from the founding of the City, Heinricus, a Saxon by birth and son of Duke Otto, was elected king in the eightieth place after Augustus [Note: The same is found in D; LXXII in E; LXXV in A and S.], and he reigned for seventeen years. [Note: E continues.]

Although he had not enjoyed the favor of his predecessor, King Conrad, that same king, because of Heinricus’s upright character and strength of spirit, chose him at the point of death, as stated above, passing over his own brother, and advised that all the princes should carry out this decision. [Col. 0896A–B]

(WID. I, 26–27.) When anointing and the diadem were offered to him by the supreme pontiff, who at that time was Herigerus, he neither rejected nor accepted them, saying: “It is enough for me to be called and designated king before my elders, with God’s approval and through your kindness; let the anointing and diadem remain with those better than we are. We judge ourselves unworthy of so great an honor.”

This speech pleased the entire multitude. Raising their right hands toward heaven, they repeatedly saluted the new king’s name with a loud shout. (LIUDPR. II, 50; RICHER. I, 47.) [Col. 0896B]

Having become king in this manner, Heinricus proceeded with his entire retinue to fight against Burchard, duke of Alamannia. Burchard’s daughter had been married to Ruodolfus of Burgundy, who, after King Ruotpert of Gaul—the father of Duke Hugo and brother of King Otto—had been killed, was elevated by the enemies of King Charles as king, just as his predecessor Ruotpert had been. [Note: With an exceptional error, Ekkehard confuses the contemporary kings Ruodolfus of Burgundy and Gaul with one another.] [Note: “Ruotperti” appears as “ruperti” in 1b.] [Note: “Outonis” appears as “ottonis” in 1b.]

(WID. l. l.) Duke Burchard, although he was an invincible warrior, nevertheless, being very prudent, realized that he could not withstand an encounter with the king. He therefore surrendered himself to him together with all his cities and people. [Col. 0896C]

(LIUPR. II, 21.) At the same time [Ann. of the Lord 921, E.], Duke Arnolfus returned from Hungary with his wife and sons and was honorably received by the Bavarians. He was not merely received but was also earnestly entreated by them to become king. [Col. 0896C–D]

When King Heinricus saw that, among all the princes of the kingdom who obeyed him, Arnolfus alone was resisting, he assembled a very powerful army and proceeded to Bavaria. According to some accounts (WID. l. l.), he besieged Arnolfus in the stronghold of the city of Regensburg. Seeing this, and judging that he was not strong enough to resist the king, Arnolfus went out through the open gates to meet the king, surrendered himself together with his entire kingdom, and, honorably received by him, was called the king’s friend.

Others, however, write (LIUDPR. l. l.) that Arnolfus did not allow the king to await his arrival in Bavaria [Note: What follows is absent from E.], but, assembling whatever forces he could, advanced to meet him in battle. When they were on the point of beginning the war, King Heinricus, as a wise and God-fearing man, reflected that irreparable harm might occur on both sides. He therefore sent word to Arnolfus that he wished to speak with him alone. Arnolfus, thinking that he was being summoned to single combat, arrived alone at the appointed place. Heinricus, prudent in mind and powerful in speech, addressed him in wise words, rebuking him for resisting God’s ordinance when he knew that Heinricus had been chosen by the entire people [Note: written above the line in 1.]—for nothing could happen except by God’s arrangement. He declared that, if the people should likewise choose Arnolfus unanimously, he himself would be the first to acclaim his election. In this way, soothing Arnolfus’s spirit with an abundance of eloquence, he returned to his own men. [Col. 0896D–0897B]

Arnolfus likewise returned to his men and reported Heinricus’s words. They replied that it was true that they had heard Solomon say that kings reign through wisdom and that the wise discern justice. Indeed, the spirit of the entire people could not become one in Heinricus’s election unless it were clear that God had chosen him. They therefore thought it fair and good that Arnolfus should not dissent from the others but choose Heinricus as king—on the condition, however, that Heinricus grant him what his predecessors had not possessed: namely, that all the bishops of Bavaria should be subject to his authority [Note: “Bojoariae,” thus in 1.], and that, when one died, he should be permitted to appoint another.

Arnolfus therefore agreed with this counsel of his men, became Heinricus’s vassal, and was honored by him, as stated, with the bishops of all Bavaria granted to him. [Col. 0897B–C]

This is that Arnolfus concerning whose designation a sword without a hilt was shown to Saint Oudalricus, bishop, as is read in the book of his deeds. Arnolfus, desiring in vain to become king, became an invader of the kingdom; and for this ambition, after destroying churches, he granted their revenues to his soldiers as benefices.

(WID. I, 27–29.) King Heinricus, advancing and growing from day to day, was regarded as ever stronger and more distinguished. When he gathered, pacified, and united the kingdom, which had been disordered on every side by civil and foreign wars under his predecessors, he moved his standards against Gaul and the kingdom of Lotharius.

Lotharius was the eldest son of the Emperor Ludewicus, who had been born to the great Charles. His brothers were Pippinus [Note: Ekkehard has added the words at greater length to Widukind’s account; cf. above.], Charles, and Ludewicus. Under these brothers a famous war was fought at Fontenay before the division of the kingdom took place. After the division, Spain fell to Pippinus; the kingdom of Aquitaine and Wasconia fell to Charles, bounded on the west by Barcelona, a city of Spain; on the north by the British Sea; on the south by the Alpine mountains; and on the east by the River Meuse. [Col. 0897C–D]

Between the River Meuse and the Rhine, Lotharius received a kingdom together with Italy, which he had received to govern while his father was alive. From the Rhine to the borders of Illyricum and Pannonia, as well as to the River Oder and the boundaries of the Danes, all Germany was the kingdom of Ludewicus. This division among them remained inviolate until, by hereditary right, all these kingdoms passed to Charles, son of Ludewicus, who was the son of Charles called the Bald [Note: written above the line in 1.]. [Col. 0897D–0898A]

To this Charles, to whom we have said that the kingdoms passed by inheritance, there came a man named Outo from the eastern Franks. Received by him, and being a brave and prudent man, Outo used his counsel to bring about a war against the Danes, who had already been troubling Lotharius’s kingdom for many years. When battle was fought against them, it is reported that one hundred thousand of them were killed in a single day (WID. l. l.).

From this event Outo was regarded as distinguished and eminent, and as second to the king, although when he came to him he was content with only one servant as his companion. When Charles was dying, he asked Outo to remember his benefaction and not to deny his son, if one should be born, the mercy that Charles had shown him. For Charles did not yet have a son; according to some (WID. l. l.), the queen was still pregnant, while others (RICHER. I, 4) say that the son was already nearly two years old. [Col. 0898A–B]

When Charles died, Outo proclaimed his son both in the kingdom and in his father’s name. But the Emperor Arnolfus, who expelled the elder Charles from Germany, claimed the whole of his kingdom for himself after Charles’s death. Outo offered him the diadem, scepter, and the other royal ornaments, and obtained the kingdom for his lord through the favor of the Emperor Arnolfus. This is according to the account of some (WID. l. l.).

Others (RICHER. I, 4), however, say that, because of the boy’s infancy, the princes, driven by excessive greed for power, strove to surpass one another, each enlarging his own possessions as much as he could, while no one sought the advancement of the king or the protection of the kingdom. When they saw this, enemies attacked the kingdom from every side. At last the princes regretted what they had done and assembled together; since the boy was still scarcely three years old, they appointed Outo to defend the kingdom because of his wisdom and courage—not as deserters, but as men angered by the enemy incursions.

But since Outo is said to have obtained the kingdom itself from the Emperor Arnolfus, from that time down to the present (WID. l. l.) there has been a dispute concerning the kingdom between the line of Charles and Outo’s descendants, and likewise a contest between the Carolingian and eastern Frankish kings over the kingdom of Lotharius. [Col. 0898B–C]

For this reason King Heinricus also moved his camp against Charles when Charles, already fifteen years old, was elevated to the kingdom, and he repeatedly defeated his army; fortune aided the brave man.

When Outo died in the tenth year of his reign, the princes of Gaul were bound to Charles by loyalty and oath. Ruotpertus also, brother of the deceased King Outo, a capable man, submitted himself to Charles, who appointed him duke of Celtic Gaul. When Charles had already gathered almost the whole kingdom, he began to elevate a certain Haganon from among the middle ranks and to love him above all the princes, so much so that, while all the nobles stood at a distance, Haganon alone clung to the king’s side and diverted much royal property to his own possession. [Col. 0898C–D]

The leading men, therefore, indignant and unable by any means to turn Charles away from his affection for Haganon, sought to expel Charles from the kingdom. After plotting much against him, they finally assembled and made Ruotpertus, brother of Outo, king.

When Charles prepared war against him and they met in battle, Ruotpertus was killed. On his side 11,349 men fell, and on Charles’s side 7,118. (RICH. II, 1–2.) [Col. 0899A]

Hugo, son of Ruotpertus, still a young man, persuaded as many as he could, especially his kinsman Heribertus, one of the nobles, that another king should be created in his father’s place to depose Charles. He himself did not wish to be advanced, since his father’s killing argued against it. The princes were therefore summoned and made Ruodolfus, son of Richard of Burgundy, king, although Ruodolfus strongly protested. He was a vigorous man, educated in the liberal arts, who, as stated above [Note: Ekkehard again, through a great error, attributes the deeds of the kings of Burgundy and Gaul to one man.], married Bertha, daughter of Burchard, duke of Alamannia [Note: “superscript” in 1.]. [Col. 0899B]

Later he was summoned by the Italians against Berengarius the Elder. After Berengarius was killed, Ruodolfus held the kingdom of Italy for some time, until, when his father-in-law was summoned to aid him against those same rebels who again resisted him and was killed there by them, Ruodolfus abandoned Italy and returned to Burgundy. [Note: “Aliquandiu” in 1.]

Hugo, count of the people of Arles, was summoned by the Italians and received the kingdom. By his wife, named Alda and descended from the line of the eastern Franks [Note: “superscript” in 1.], he fathered a son whom he named Lotharius and made king when he had grown up. But after both of them were expelled, Berengarius ruled; he was later carried to Babenberg and died there (cf. LIUDPR. II, 60 ff.; III, 13 ff., 16, 20; IV, 2; V, 27 ff.). (RICH. I, 47, 65.) [Col. 0899B–C]

After Ruodolfus had been elevated to the kingdom of Charles, as stated, the aforesaid Heribertus, on the advice of his kinsman Hugo, son of Ruotpertus, captured Charles by treachery and placed him in custody, where he also ended his life (cf. WID. I, 30). Charles had a son named Ludewicus by the sister of King Adelstan of the Britons. In the storm of his troubles he sent the boy to that same maternal uncle. Thus, after King Ruodolfus’s death, Ludewicus was brought back at the advice of the aforesaid Hugo and received his father’s kingdom; but that same Duke Hugo later rebelled against him. [Col. 0899C]

[Col. 0899D] (WID. I, 30.) At that time King Heinricus, hearing of Charles’s downfall, grieved and marveled at the common fortune of human mutability. He judged that he should indeed refrain from arms, but thought that the Lotharingians should instead be overcome by strategy, since they were a changeable people, accustomed to stratagems, ready for war, and quick to embrace novelties.

At that time there was a certain Lotharingian named Cristianus. Seeing that everything was prospering for King Heinricus, he sought a way to be honored by the king with greater favor. Pretending to be ill, he summoned Gisilbertus, to whom the principality of the region had passed by paternal succession. When Gisilbertus came, Cristianus captured him by a stratagem and sent him under guard to King Heinricus. [Col. 0899D–0900A]

Gisilbertus was born of noble lineage and an ancient family. The king received him with great pleasure, thinking that through him alone he would possess the whole kingdom of Lotharius. Then, observing that the young man was extremely capable and distinguished by birth, power, and wealth, he began to treat him generously. Finally, after betrothing to him his daughter Gerbirga, he joined Gisilbertus to himself alike by kinship and friendship, entrusting to him the whole kingdom of Lotharius.

This is according to the account of a certain monk of Corvey [Note: D1 identifies him as Witikind of Corvey], who wrote about the origin of the Saxons and the deeds of these kings. But there is another historian (RICHER.) who arranges the times of this Charles—whose memory we now have before us—and of his successors. He writes that Gisilbertus married Heinricus’s daughter before Heinricus became king, while Heinricus was still administering the duchy; that Heinricus himself had received the Saxon duchy from Charles; and that Heinricus and Ruotpertus, who later became king, were among the first of the princes who defected from the king on account of Haganon, as stated above.

For he says as follows (I, 14):

> “After Celtic Gaul had been granted to Ruotpertus, Charles withdrew into Saxony. Traversing its cities and royal residences, he obtained them without resistance; there too he granted to Heinricus, a duke distinguished by royal lineage and descended from that stock, everything.”

And shortly afterward [Note: The following passages are absent from Richer’s text; cf. the preface.]:

> “Meanwhile, after the cities and towns of Gaul had been firmly secured, as the solemnity of Easter approached, the king withdrew to the palace at Aachen (cf. ib. I, 16). From all Gaul the princes flocked here; here too the men of lesser rank assembled with great enthusiasm. The dukes were also present: from Saxony, Heinricus; from Gaul, Ruotpertus. Every day they remained beside the doors of the royal bedchamber; every day they awaited the king’s departure from the inner chambers of the palace. But when the king gave them no answer for four days, Heinricus, bearing this very grievously, is said to have remarked either that Haganon would one day reign together with Charles, or that Charles would fall with Haganon to a condition of mediocrity. Indignant, he departed without consulting the king. The king, taking this badly, wished to recall him and sent Heriveus, metropolitan of Reims, for this purpose.” [Col. 0900B–D]

(RICHER. I, 22–24.) Persuaded by Heriveus’s eloquent and friendly speech, Duke Heinricus returned to the king. He was admitted before him with great honor and received with the utmost familiarity in the foremost place of favor. (I, 34.)

At this time Ragenerus, a noble man and the most faithful guardian of Charles’s party, reached the end of his life. Charles attended his funeral, and after it was completed, he most generously conferred his father’s honor upon Giselbertus, Ragenerus’s adult son, before the assembled princes. [Col. 0900D–0901A]

(I, 35 ff.) Since Giselbertus was distinguished by wealth and lineage, and was quite fortunate in his marriage to Gerberga, daughter of Heinricus beyond the Rhine, he was being driven by excessive arrogance into reckless audacity and was plotting many things for the king’s overthrow.

When Charles learned of this, he returned from Celtic Gaul with an army and prepared to make war upon the Belgians, whose duke was Giselbertus. The Belgians soon did not attempt to resist Giselbertus in open battle, but quickly shut themselves up in their towns and fortresses. The king sent envoys to them and promised that he would grant them everything they had previously held from Giselbertus as benefices, if they came over to him.

Captured by this promise, they soon returned to the king by oath and rose together against Giselbertus. He, however, was shut up with a few men in the town of Harburg, which was bounded on one side by the River Meuse and on the other by the River Geul; on its remaining sides it seemed exceedingly secure because of its immense ravine and the dense, terrifying thickets. [Col. 0901A–B]

The king hurried there with his forces and established a siege, by water on one side and the other and elsewhere by cavalry. When he pressed the siege more violently, Giselbertus secretly slipped over the wall, crossed the river by swimming, and, traveling with two retainers across the Rhine in exile, spent several years in exile with his father-in-law Heinricus, deprived of his patrimony.

The townsmen, left without their duke, surrendered to the king. After some time had passed, Heinricus persuaded the king to receive Giselbertus back into favor, but on this condition: Giselbertus would lack those benefices which he had insolently distributed and which the king had afterward granted to his supporters for as long as their holders lived; those whose holders had died during the years of his exile, however, he would recover through the king’s mercy. [Col. 0901B–C]

Thus he recovered Traiectum, Juppila, Harstalium, Marsna, Littam, and Capremont, which, having been abandoned by their deceased holders, lay vacant. But he harassed the others who still held their possessions with great slaughter until he recovered everything that had been his.

Afterward, plotting many things against the king, he went to his father-in-law and strongly urged him to cease supporting the king. He asserted that Celtic Gaul alone could suffice for the king, whereas Belgium and Germany greatly needed another king. By a variety of arguments he therefore tried to persuade Duke Heinricus not to refuse to be made king himself.

But when Heinricus perceived that Giselbertus was urging an unlawful course, he strongly resisted the adviser’s words and repeatedly warned him to desist from his wicked designs. When Giselbertus could make no progress with his father-in-law and could not secure the kingdom for himself, he withdrew to Celtic Gaul and crossed into Neustria. There he conferred with Ruotpertus, brother of King Outo and duke of Celtic Gaul, about the same matter, suggesting to him that he accept the kingdom and depose Charles [Note: A quire is missing in 1.]. [Col. 0901C–D]

The tyrant rejoiced and immediately supported the adviser. They therefore deliberated and bound themselves to one another by oath. In due course, after assembling the princes, Ruotpertus was made king in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 922.

These are the words of that Gallic historian. If they differ in any respect from the preceding statements of the Saxon writer, let the careful reader weigh the matter. The year in which Ruotpertus [Note: D1 consistently reads “Rutpertus.”] is said to have been elevated to the kingdom is the year entered in our records as the third year of Heinricus’s reign. Ruotpertus was afterward killed by Charles’s soldiers, but Ruodolfus [Note: D1 frequently has “rudolfus”] was substituted in his place. Charles was then captured and committed to custody.

(WID. I, 33.) This was the time when, as written above, Heinricus was advancing to enlarge his empire over the Lotharingians [Note: 9c. reads “Lotharingos”]. For during that expedition, when he had crossed the Rhine, an envoy of Charles met him and, after greeting him in the most humble words [Note: 5 reads “ei,” “to him.”], said:

> “My lord Charles, once endowed with royal power but now deprived of it, has sent me to you, asking that, since he is surrounded by enemies [Note: 2 reads “friends” (amicis)], nothing could be more pleasing or sweeter to him now [Note: 10 and 11 omit “now”] than to hear something of the glory of your magnificent advancement and to be consoled by the report of your virtues. He has sent you this token of faith and truth.”

He then drew from his breast [Note: “drew out” (protulit) is the reading of D1] the hand of the precious martyr Dionysius, enclosed in gold and gems, and said:

> “Have this as a pledge of perpetual alliance and vicarious love. This portion of the one consolation of the Franks who inhabit Gaul—after Saint Vitus [Note: 2, 10, and 11 omit “Saint martyr Vitus”] deserted us to our destruction and visited Saxony for your perpetual peace [Note: 10 and 11 read “our” rather than “your”]—has chosen to share itself with you [Note: D1 omits “to share with you”]. For ever since his body was translated, neither civil nor foreign wars have ceased among us. In that very year the Danes and Northmen invaded our region.”

The king received the divine gift with every expression of gratitude, prostrated himself before the holy relics [Note: 2 reads sancti, “holy,” in the singular], and, kissing them, venerated them with the highest reverence. [Col. 0901D–0902C]

As for Saint Vitus, about whom Charles’s envoy spoke, a certain man named Foliadus brought him from Rome and placed him in the region of Paris. During the reign of the Emperor Ludewicus, his relics were transferred from there to Saxony. As that envoy confessed, from this time the fortunes of the Franks began to diminish and those of the Saxons to expand.

(LIUDPR. IV, 24.) Ruodolfus, king of the Burgundians, who ruled the Italians for several years, had received from a certain count named Samson as a gift a lance which they said had belonged to Constantine the Great, son of Saint Helena [Note: 9c omits “to have belonged.”]. Unlike the appearance of other lances, it had been fashioned in an unusual manner, with novel workmanship and design. Along the middle of its spine, on both sides, it had something like a window; and in the middle of the spine were crosses made from the nails with which the hands and feet of our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, had been fastened. [Note: 9c. reads “crucis,” “of the cross.”] [Col. 0902C–D]

When King Heinricus heard this [Note: D1 reads haec, “this”]—that Ruodolfus possessed so heavenly a gift—he, being a man who feared God and loved all religion, sent envoys to try whether he could acquire it through some rewards [Note: 4 and D1 omit “it” (illud)]. When King Ruodolfus declared in every possible way that he would never do so [Note: “Quod cum rex” (“when King …”) is read by 2 and D1 and omitted by the remaining witnesses], King Heinricus, since he could not soften him with gifts [Note: 9c omits “him” (hunc)], took great care to frighten him with threats. For he threatened that he would lay waste to his entire kingdom with slaughter and fires. [Col. 0902D–0903A]

But because the gift being requested was one that had joined earthly things to heavenly ones, God softened King Ruodolfus’s heart [Note: D1 reads “Deus cor,” “God [his] heart”] and immediately caused him to hand it over to the just king [Note: 2 omits “just king”], who was justly and rightly making the request. For where peace is present, there is no room for hostility.

How greatly King Heinricus loved the aforesaid heavenly gift became clear in many matters, but especially in this: he honored the giver not only with gifts of gold and silver [Note: 2 reads “of silver and gold”] but also with a very substantial portion of the province of the Suebi [Note: 5 adds “and bestowed it upon him”].

On this occasion—or rather, by God’s will—King Heinricus obtained the holy lance. Through it he often triumphed over his enemies, and when he died he left it, together with the kingdom, to his son Otto the Great. We believe that it is the lance which from that time down to the present is customarily kept under the protection of the emperors. [Col. 0903A–B]

(LIUDPR. II, 24. WID. I, 32.) When the Hungarians heard of Emperor Conrad’s death and Henry’s succession to the kingdom, wishing to test whether the new king would pay the customary tribute, they ranged throughout Saxony, set cities and fortified places on fire, and everywhere inflicted such slaughter that they threatened utter devastation. The king, however, was stationed in the fortress called Werlahon and did not trust the still inexperienced soldiers, unaccustomed to public warfare, against so savage a people.

[Note: [Col. 0903] *cuonradi* is read in D1.]

It happened that one of the Hungarian princes was captured, defeated, and brought to the king. The Hungarians had loved him so greatly [Note: [Col. 0903] *deest* (“is absent”) in 9c.] that they offered countless weights of gold and silver for him. [Note: [Col. 0903] 9c reads *innumerabilia* (“countless”); manuscripts 2 and 4 read: “many weights of gold and silver were offered for him.”] The king, however, despising gold, demanded peace and finally obtained a firm peace settlement for nine years. [Note: [Col. 0903] *tandem* (“finally”) is read by manuscripts 10 and 11; *tandemque* is the principal reading.]

(WID. I, 35.) During this truce he first selected every ninth man from among the agricultural soldiers and made him live in the cities, so that he might build dwellings for his other eight companions, receive a third part of all the crops, and store it. The other eight were to sow and reap, gather the crops for the ninth man, and put them in their proper places. [Note: [Col. 0903] Manuscripts 2 (uncertain), 10, and 11 read *cum familiaribus* (“with household members”) for *confamiliaribus* (“fellow members of the household”).] He ordered councils, all assemblies, and banquets to be held in the cities, so that in peacetime they might learn what they ought to do when enemies arrived. Outside the cities there were either paltry fortifications or none at all. [Note: [Col. 0903] Manuscript 2 reads *aut ulla* (“or any”).] [Note: [Col. 0903] *moenia* (“walls”); another hand corrected it to *menia*; manuscripts 10 and 11 read *munia*.]

As he accustomed his citizens to such a law and discipline, he suddenly attacked the Slavs called the Hevelli. Wearied by many battles, he finally captured, in a most severe winter, with his camp placed upon the ice, the city called Brennaburg by famine, the sword, and the cold. Having gained possession of that city and the entire surrounding region, he turned his standards against Dalmatia, against which his father had long ago left him the military command. [Note: [Col. 0903] The words after *contra* are absent in manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 0903] *dalmatiam* is read in manuscripts 2 and 9c.] Besieging the city called Grana, he captured it at last on the twentieth day. The city’s booty was handed over to the soldiers; all adult males were killed, while the boys and girls were preserved for captivity.

After this he went to Prague, the city of the Bohemians, and received its king into submission. [Note: [Col. 0903] *plagam* is read in D1 for *Pragam*.] [Note: [Col. 0903] 9c reads *boemorum* (“of the Bohemians”) for *Boemiorum*.] He was the father of Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 0903] Manuscript 2 reads *bolizlai*.] and remained faithful and useful to the king for as long as he lived. Bohemia having thus become tributary, the king returned to Saxony.

(WID. I, 38.) When the period of the truce had passed, ambassadors of the Hungarians approached the king for the customary payments, but he rejected them, and they returned empty-handed to their own land. Since he now had cavalry tested in battle, he dared to enter combat against his ancient enemies.

When the Avars heard this, they delayed no longer but hastened to invade Saxony with a hostile and formidable force. Passing through Dalmatia, they sought assistance, as though from their ancient friends. But those people, knowing that the Avars were hastening toward Saxony and that the Saxons were prepared to fight them, threw them a very fat dog as a gift. Since there was no opportunity to avenge the insult while they were hastening toward another battle, they followed their friends farther with sufficiently ridiculous shouting. Thus, with as sudden an assault as they could make, they entered the territory of the Thuringians and ravaged the whole land in a hostile manner. [Note: [Col. 0903] 9c reads *autem* (“however”).]

(LIUDPR. II, 25.) King Henry was being held by a very serious illness, and he was informed that the Hungarians’ arrival was near. He immediately sent messengers through Saxony and gathered a very strong army within four days. [Note: [Col. 0903] 9c reads *colligit* (“he gathers”) for *collegit* (“he gathered”).] Although weak in body, he mounted his horse, strengthened by courage of spirit, and went to meet the enemy.

A swift messenger came running and reported that the Hungarians were at Merseburg, a fortress on the frontier of the Saxons, Thuringians, and Slavs, [Note: [Col. 0903] One witness reads “which is a fortress”; D1 reads “which is a fortress.”] and that they already possessed considerable booty of boys and women, while they had inflicted an immense slaughter of men. [Note: [Col. 0903] Some witnesses omit *esse* (“to be”); others omit *jam* (“already”) and related words. Manuscript 5 reads *stragem* (“slaughter”) in the relevant phrase.]

The king, steadfast in spirit, was not frightened by such reports but urged his men more and more to fight for their fatherland. Without delay the battle began. From the Christian side “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) was sung; from the other side an ugly and diabolical cry, “Hui, hui, hui,” was heard. [Note: [Col. 0903] D1 reads *kyriel.* for “Kyrie eleison.”] [Note: [Col. 0903] The cry “hui, hui, hui” is absent in D1.]

When the battle had begun, by God’s command the Hungarians were cut down and put to flight; the king and his men were adorned with victory; an immense crowd of captives was released; and the voice of lamentation was changed into a song of joy.

The king ordered this triumph, worthy of both praise and remembrance, to be depicted by a painter in the upper dining room of the royal palace at Merseburg, so vividly that you would judge the representation to be a true event rather than merely a plausible one. [Note: [Col. 0903] Manuscript 5 reads *merseburg*.]

(WID. I, 39.) The victorious king returned and in every way rendered thanksgiving to divine honor, as was fitting. He dedicated to divine worship the tribute that he had been accustomed to give to the enemy and determined that it should serve the needs of the poor. [Note: [Col. 0905] Manuscript 2 reads *dari* (“to be given”) for *dare* (“to give”). Manuscript 2 and D1 thus read: “the tribute which he had been accustomed to give”; manuscripts 4–11 read *consuevit* (“he had been accustomed”).]

After this the army called him father of his country, lord of affairs, and emperor, and he spread the fame of his power and virtue far and wide among all kings and peoples. [Note: [Col. 0905] D1 reads *dominus rerum* (“lord of affairs”).] [Note: [Col. 0905] 9c reads “kings and peoples”; manuscript 4 omits “and peoples.”]

For this reason nobles from other kingdoms also approached him, seeking to find favor in his sight; they valued the loyalty of so great and distinguished a man. Among them was Heribert, son-in-law of Duke Hugh. When King Rudolf opposed him, Heribert begged Henry to serve as his protection before Rudolf. Henry was indeed such a man that he refused nothing to his friends.

He therefore went to Gaul, and one king addressed another. When the business had been completed, he returned to Saxony.

King Hugh of Italy also sent ambassadors to him and sought his friendship with the greatest eagerness (cf. LIUDPR. III, 21; IV, 14).

King Henry had a wife and partner in the kingdom, distinguished and most noble, named Matilda, daughter of Theoderic and of the same Saxon people. Her brothers were Witikind, Immod, and Reginbern.

Reginbern was the man who fought against the Danes, who had long ravaged Saxony. [Note: [Col. 0905] D1 reads *vastantes* (“ravaging”).] He defeated them and freed his fatherland from their incursions up to the present day.

These men were descended from the line of the great Duke Witikind, who waged a powerful war against Charlemagne for nearly thirty years (WID. and LIUDPR., passim).

Before he assumed the kingdom, Matilda bore Henry a daughter, Gerberga, whom he gave in marriage to Giselbert, Duke of Belgium, and also a son, Otto, “the love of the world.” After he had attained royal dignity, she bore a second son, whom he named Henry after his father: a brave and energetic man, sufficiently adorned with wit, prudent in counsel, and gracious in the beauty of his face. She also bore a third son named Bruno, whom we saw exercising the office of supreme pontiff and great duke (RUOTGER, *Vita Brunonis*, chapters 5 and following, 11, 18, 20).

His brother Otto, while ruling the empire after their father’s death, made Bruno, who was imbued with every branch of learning, bishop of Cologne. Afterwards, when great disorder arose in the kingdom, so that even the king’s son Liudolf joined the opposition against his father at the urging of wicked men, King Otto withdrew to the eastern regions to organize the kingdom and entrusted the western regions to Bishop Bruno for administration.

Thus Bruno exercised the priestly office with great religious devotion and, when necessity required it, fulfilled by the king’s command the task of a great-hearted duke. [Note: [Col. 0905] Manuscript 5 reads *itaque* (“therefore”).] [Note: [Col. 0905] The statement that he exercised the priestly office is absent in D1.] [Note: [Col. 0905] The statement that he fulfilled the ducal task is absent in 9c.]

(WID. I, 31.) Let no one declare him blameworthy for this, since we read that the holy Samuel and many other priests were likewise judges.

(LIUDPR. IV, 16.) Otto, the king’s son, while his father was still alive, took a wife from the most noble race of the English, the daughter of King Athelstan’s brother. Some call her Otgit, others Edith. [Note: [Col. 0905] The name is absent in manuscript 2.] She bore him a son whom he named Liudolf, whom he loved greatly. But later Liudolf rebelled against him.

(WID. I, 39.) While King Henry was advancing his people, there was scarcely any notable man, or none at all, throughout Saxony whom he did not promote either with a splendid gift or with some office. He possessed immense prudence, and the beauty of his body also added dignity to his royal rank. In the exercises of sport he surpassed everyone by such excellence that he inspired terror in the others. In hunting he was so vigorous that on one occasion he captured forty beasts or more. Although he was quite cheerful at banquets, he diminished nothing of royal discipline. He inspired so much favor and fear at once that even while he was playing, people did not believe that they could abandon themselves to any frivolity.

Having subdued the surrounding peoples, he finally decided to set out for Rome; but, seized by illness, he interrupted his journey.

(LIUDPR. IV, 14.) He fell ill in the fortress called Hiemelewa, which lies between the frontiers of the Saxons and Thuringians, and there he also died.

(WID. I, 41.) When he realized that his illness was growing heavier, he summoned the whole people and designated his son Otto as king. He distributed estates and treasures among his other sons, but placed Otto himself—who was the eldest and best—over his brothers and over the entire Frankish empire. [Note: [Col. 0905] The words “over his brothers” are missing because a folio has fallen out in manuscript 6.]

(LIUDPR. IV, 15.) His wisdom and religious devotion can be demonstrated by the fact that he appointed as king the man whom he knew to be the most capable and most religious, although he had not been born into the empire.

(WID., passim.) After making his testament lawfully and arranging all his affairs properly, he died in the seventeenth year of his reign and about the sixtieth year of his life. [Note: [Col. 0905] Manuscript 2 reads *legitimo* (“lawful”) for *legitime* (“lawfully”).] His sons transferred his body [Note: [Col. 0905] “His sons” is absent in D1.] to the city called Quedlinburg and buried it in the basilica of Saint Peter before the altar, amid the mourning and tears of many.

The blood of the Lord came to the island of Reichenau. [Note: [Col. 0907A] Manuscripts 10 and 11 add “from a certain matron,” from Bernold.] [Note: [Col. 0907A] These words are absent in D and E, where one reads: “King Henry, after defeating the Slavs and Danes and reducing them to tribute, makes his name famous. Berengar … they set on fire,” from Sigebert under the year 925.]

### A.D. 930

Heriger, archbishop of Mainz, died; Hiltibert was appointed in his place. [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscript 5 adds “of Mainz.”] [Note: [Col. 0907] The name appears as *hiltipertus* in manuscript 4, *hildibertus* in manuscripts 5 and 9c, and *hildibertus* in manuscripts 10 and 11; likewise below.]

King Henry marched against Bohemia. [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscripts 5 and 10 read *poemiam*.]

### A.D. 933

[Note: [Col. 0907C] D and E add: “Arnold … useful things,” from Sigebert under the year 932.]
