Henry killed the Hungarians. [Note: [Col. 0907C] D and E read: “The Hungarians are killed or captured by the army of King Henry,” from Sigebert.]

### A.D. 935

Noting, bishop of Constance, died; Conrad succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0907C] D and E add: “In Genoa … emptied,” from Sigebert.] [Note: [Col. 0907C] Manuscripts 10 and 11 add “most distinguished by birth.”]

### A.D. 936

King Henry died. [Note: [Col. 0907D] D reads: “He died, although he had received …,” from Sigebert under the year 937. E reads: “King Henry fell ill in the fortress … amid the tears of many,” as above.]

After Pope Martin, Agapetus presided over the Roman see as its 117th pontiff; then Octavianus, the 118th; Leo, the 119th; Benedict, the 120th; and John, the 121st. [Note: [Col. 0907D] The words “Leo … 121st” are absent in D1.] [Note: [Col. 0907D] E1 adds in another hand in the margin: “In this year King Otto made a royal abbey at Magdeburg” (absent in E2).]

[Col. 0907D]

### A.D. 937

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 937, and from the founding of the City 1688. [Note: [Col. 0907] The words concerning the City are absent in manuscript 2 and perhaps in manuscripts 10 and 11.]

Otto the Great, son of Henry, eighty-first in succession from Augustus, was elected king by the entire people of the Saxons and Franks, and reigned for thirty-eight years. [Note: [Col. 0907] D and E read seventy-fifth; D1 reads thirty-six.]

(WID. II, 1.) He was elected at Aachen, where he was immediately anointed king by the supreme pontiff of the Mainz see, named Hiltibert, a Frank by birth and a monk by profession. Raised in the monastery of Fulda, he was deservedly advanced first to become abbot of that place and then to the summit of the supreme pontificate of the Mainz see.

He was a man of remarkable holiness and, in addition to natural wisdom of spirit, quite distinguished in literary learning. He is also said to have received, among his other gifts of grace, the spirit of prophecy. [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscript 2 reads *prophecisse* (“to have prophesied”).]

After receiving the anointing of blessing, the king showed himself so wise in administering the kingdom, so brave in fighting his opponents, and so energetic in religion that it cannot easily be described.

(WID. II, 3.) First, when the barbarians were raging in their efforts to bring about a revolution, Boleslaus struck down his brother, a Christian man, faithful to the kingdom and, as they say, a devout worshiper of God. [Note: [Col. 0907] D1 reads *bolizaus* for *Bolizlaus*.] [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscript 5 reads “his brother Wenceslaus” for “his brother.”]

When the king sent an army against Boleslaus to avenge this, our forces at first proved victorious. [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscript 2 reads *dum* (“when”) for *cum* (“when”).] Then, acting too confidently because of their recent victory, they were all killed in a sudden attack by him. [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscripts 2, D, and E read *bolizlauum*; the other manuscripts read *bolizlaum*.] This war continued until the fifteenth year of the king’s reign; from that time Boleslaus remained a faithful and useful servant to the king.

After this the ancient enemies, the Hungarians, came to test the new king’s courage. Entering Francia, they decided, if possible, to enter Saxony from the western side. When the king heard this, he delayed no longer but met them with a strong army and drove them from his borders. When external wars ceased, civil wars began to arise.

(WID. II, chapters 8, 9, 1, 11, 10, 11, 12.) Duke Arnulf of Bavaria died, and his sons, lifted up by pride, refused by the king’s command to go to the county court. [Note: [Col. 0907] 9c reads *comitatu* (“county court”); the other cited reading is also *comitatu*.] The king gave his duchy to his brother Berthold. [Note: [Col. 0907] The name appears as *Berhtoldo*, *Berhctoldo*, *Bertholdo*, *Bertholfo*, and *Berchtolfo* in the cited witnesses.]

Count Sigefrid, the best of the Saxons, also died. He had administered Saxony second only to the king. Because of kinship, Dankmar, the king’s brother on his father’s side but not his mother’s, claimed Sigefrid’s office for himself, but the king’s royal gift transferred it to Count Gero. Dankmar was therefore afflicted with great sadness.

He was quick-handed, keen in intellect, skilled in warfare. His mother was the daughter of Count Sigefrid’s maternal aunt; from her King Henry had begotten him, and he enriched him with many estates apart from those that had belonged to his mother. [Note: [Col. 0907] 9c reads *mater sua* (“his own mother”).]

Count Eberhard, angry with a certain Bruning, one of the leading men, gathered a force and burned his city, called Elmeri, killing all the inhabitants of that city. [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscript 2 reads *bruniggum*.] [Note: [Col. 0907] Manuscript 2 reads *elmari*.]

For this presumption the king condemned him to pay one hundred talents. All the nobles who had helped him in this were condemned to the humiliation of carrying dogs as far as the royal city called Magdeburg. [Note: [Col. 0909] Manuscript 5 reads *adjuvabant* (“were helping”).] [Note: [Col. 0909] D1 reads *magedeburc*.]

Angered by this, Eberhard joined Dankmar. Gathering a powerful force, they attacked the stronghold called Badiliki, in which Henry, the king’s brother, was still a young man. [Note: [Col. 0909] The words “still a young man” are absent in manuscript 2.] After giving the booty of the city to his soldiers, Eberhard took Henry with him as though he were a worthless slave.

Then Dankmar began to occupy the city called Hereburg. He remained there and carried out many acts of brigandage. Although unwilling, the king went there with a large retinue to repress his insolence.

The citizens of the city opened its gates and admitted the king’s army. Dankmar, fleeing into the church of the blessed apostle Peter and standing beside the altar, laid down his weapons upon it and was pierced from behind through a window by someone.

Eberhard, however, kept Henry with him. When he heard of Dankmar’s death, he was broken in spirit, fell at the feet of his captive, and begged forgiveness. He wickedly obtained it on the condition that Henry join him in a conspiracy against his lord and brother and, if possible, place the crown upon his own head. At that time Henry was still much too young and was burning with desire to reign.

(LIUDPR. IV, 20, 22.) Eberhard had indeed separated Giselbert, duke of the Lotharingians, from his loyalty to the king, and with Giselbert’s help he resisted the king considerably. [Note: [Col. 0909] The words “from the king’s loyalty” are absent in manuscripts 10 and 11.]

Although Giselbert had the king’s sister as his wife, he too preferred to resist the king in hope of obtaining the kingdom rather than to assist him as he ought.

The king had several large and very strong forces, namely Herman, duke of the Suevians, his brother Otto, and Conrad, surnamed the Wise. Although they were related to Eberhard by kinship, they preferred, if necessity arose, to fall justly with the just king rather than triumph unjustly with their kinsman.

Eberhard therefore did not cease to separate Giselbert from the king’s allegiance until Giselbert promised that he would make him king. Giselbert, however, wished to deceive Henry by this scheme: after defeating the king with Giselbert’s assistance, he himself would obtain the throne. [Note: [Col. 0909] 9c arranges the words differently, with “he wished by this scheme to deceive Henry.”]

But Eberhard had planned something quite different. If he could defeat the king, he intended to deprive both Giselbert and Henry of the kingdom and usurp it for himself, as we may infer from the words he spoke to his wife shortly before he was killed. While he held her in his lap, he said: “Rejoice in the embrace of the count; before long you will rejoice in the embraces of the king.” [Note: [Col. 0909] Manuscript 2 reads *sinu* (“lap”) for *gremio* (“embrace” or “lap”).]

[Col. 0910A]

(WID. II, 15.) Henry, burning with desire to reign, held a celebrated banquet at the place called Saalfeld. Since he was great and powerful, possessing royal majesty and authority, he gave many gifts to many people and thereby won many accomplices to his faction. [Note: [Col. 0909] D1 reads *crebre* (“frequently”) for *celebre* (“celebrated”).]

(LIUDPR. IV, 23; WID. passim; LIUDPR. passim.) Then he went into Lotharingia to Giselbert, duke of Belgium, and with Giselbert and Eberhard together began to prepare war against his brother.

When this was reported to the king, he did not initially believe it. But as soon as he was informed with certainty, he hastened in the opposite direction joyfully, not frightened by their numbers but trusting in God’s mercy.

When he reached the Rhine with his men and his troops had already begun to cross the river, Henry and his followers were unexpectedly so close that they could already be seen by them. [Note: [Col. 0909] D1 reads *preparat* (“he prepares”) for *properat* (“he hastens”).] [Note: [Col. 0909] D1 reads *tamque* for *jamque*.] [Note: [Col. 0909] D1 omits *jam* (“already”); another witness reads *jam non* (“no longer”).]

At last, only a very few had disembarked from the boats and could scarcely mount their horses and clothe themselves in armor, when the opposing troops were not announced as approaching but were seen before their eyes, already present.

(WID. II, 17.) The king, still remaining with a multitude on the farther side of the river and observing this, did not conceal his grief of spirit in the movement of his body, because there were no boats by which he could cross the Rhine. The suddenness of the battle allowed those stationed on the farther bank to consider nothing else except either that they must fall before the enemy or certainly defend their lives with their weapons.

(LIUDPR. passim.) Remembering the people of the Lord, who had defeated the Amalekites opposing them through the prayers of Moses, God’s servant, he immediately dismounted from his horse. Weeping, he prostrated himself with all the people before the lance in which the victorious nails that had been driven through the hands and feet of our Redeemer were enclosed. [Note: [Col. 0909] 9c reads “had fastened”; manuscript 5 reads “were fastened.”]

How much the prayer of a just man avails, as James says, was proved by the event itself.

(WID. passim; LIUDPR. passim.) The men who were on the farther bank were transferring their baggage and every kind of impediment to the place called Xanten. Encouraging one another, they attacked the enemy at a headlong pace. [Note: [Col. 0909] 9c reads *exhortati* (“having exhorted”) for *cohortati* (“having encouraged”).]

(WID. passim.) Since there was a marsh between them and the enemy, separating the Saxons from the enemy, one group rushed against the enemy from the front, while another followed from behind. Pressing upon the enemy in the middle, a few men fiercely harried the many. [Note: [Col. 0909] Manuscript 2 reads *hostes* (“the enemy”) for *hos* (“these”).] [Note: [Col. 0909] D1 reads *saxoni* (“the Saxons”).] [Note: [Col. 0909] 9c reads *divisa* (“divided”).] [Note: [Col. 0909] Manuscript 5 arranges the words as “one part rushed against the enemy from the front.”]

It is said that there were not more than one hundred armed men on our side, whereas the enemy army was quite large. But since they were pressed from both front and rear, they had no opportunity to guard against the place where they ought most to have been on their watch. [Note: [Col. 0909] Some witnesses omit the phrase “from the front.”]

(LIUDPR. passim.) While the king was praying, none of his men fell, and all the enemy were put to flight. Some of them did not know why they were fleeing, because, owing to the small number of their pursuers, they could not see the enemies who were chasing them. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 5 has a different reading for the phrase concerning the small number of pursuers.]

(WID. passim.) Among our men there were also some who knew how to speak the Gallic language. Raising a loud cry in French, they urged the adversaries to flee. The enemy supposed that these men were shouting to their comrades and, as soon as the cry was raised, began their flight.

(LIUDPR. passim.) After many had been killed, Henry was struck severely in the arm. Although the strength of a triple coat of mail prevented the sword’s edge from reaching the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 5 reads “the iron” or “the sword” instead of “the sword’s edge.”] the force of the harsh blow nevertheless turned his arm so livid that no medical treatment could heal it completely, and he felt great pain throughout the whole of that year.

(WID. II, 18 and following.) A certain Thuringian named Teti sent word to the commanders of the cities that were in Henry’s eastern territory about the king’s victory and the fact that Henry himself had fallen in battle. He acted cleverly so that they all surrendered to royal authority.

Only two cities of all the rest remained to them: Merseburg and Schidungen. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 5 reads *merseburg*.] [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 2 reads *scidingon*.]

When Henry heard of the defection of his cities and, broken in spirit, learned of the king’s recent victory, he set out with only nine armed men. [Note: [Col. 0911] D1 reads *noie*.] Approaching Saxony more slowly, he entered the city of Merseburg. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscripts 5 and 4 read *mersburg* and *mesburg*.]

When the king learned this, he too returned and besieged the city in which his brother was. Since Henry could not resist a stronger force, after about two months he surrendered the city and came out to the king.

A truce of thirty days was granted to him, so that he could withdraw from Saxony with the soldiers attached to him. If any of them wished to approach the king, they would have the opportunity to receive pardon.

Henry therefore departed from Saxony, went again to the Lotharians, and remained for some time with Duke Giselbert. [Note: [Col. 0911] 9c reads *lotharingos* (“Lotharians”) for *Lotharios*.]

(WID. II, 22.) An army was again led against Giselbert, and the entire region subject to his authority was given over to fire. Besieged in the fortress of Kievermont, which means “Goat Mountain,” he escaped from there by flight. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 2 reads *presidio* (“stronghold”) for *obsidio* (“siege”).]

Since the siege made little progress because of the difficulty of the terrain, the region having been devastated on every side, the king returned to Saxony.

(LIUDPR. IV, 26.) On the frontier of Alsace there is a fortress called Brisach, from which the whole neighboring district is called Breisgau. It is said once to have belonged to those who were called the Harelungi. At that time it was under Eberhard’s authority.

There he stationed a multitude of his soldiers. Through their terror he not only claimed for himself a large part of the aforementioned province but also cruelly slaughtered the king’s faithful followers all around.

(WID. II, 24; LIUDPR. passim.) The king set out to besiege it and established his camp. Then, allegedly on the advice of Frederick, archbishop of the Mainz see, many bishops set up their tents around the camp but abandoned them during the night and deserted the king’s cause, secretly returning home. Frederick, it is said, remained there deceitfully. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 2 reads *ferunt* (“they say”); D1 reads *fert* (“he says”).]

That same Frederick was the successor of the aforementioned holy man Hiltibert. As far as human judgment could determine, he was devoted to good works, except that he favored the side of his lord the king’s adversaries. Many people reported this, but Frederick himself denied it with every effort.

(LIUDPR. passim.) The king’s soldiers, observing the bishops’ departure, advised him to return to Saxony and abandon that region himself. Undaunted, he answered them, as Judas Maccabeus once said to his men: [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 5 reads: “Judas, who once said such things to his men.”]

“Do not speak such things. If our time has come, let us all die courageously and not bring disgrace upon our glory. It is better to undergo death for true justice than to live dishonorably by fleeing.”

With these and similar words he not only turned them away from their intention to flee but also strongly encouraged them to fight.

(LIUDPR. IV, 27.) A certain count was then with him, and the multitude of his soldiers adorned the king’s battle line. Seeing that many were defecting from the king, the count reflected that, because of the present necessity, the king would refuse him nothing. He therefore asked that the abbey of Lorsch be granted for the use of himself and his men.

But the king understood what that request signified and said to him before everyone:

“One must obey God rather than human beings. What sane person does not understand that you have said this not with the humility of a petitioner but with the authority of a threat? It is written: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs.’ Although this is proclaimed to be understood spiritually, I nevertheless judge that I would be giving what is holy to dogs if I took away the estates of monasteries, which religious men have offered to God, from those who serve God and handed them over to those who serve the world.

“But to you, who so brazenly demand what is unjust, I declare before the testimony of the entire people that you will never receive from me either this or anything else. If it is in your heart to fly away with the other faithless men, the sooner you do so, the better.”

[Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 5 reads *me sanctum* (“what is holy from me”).]

When he heard this, the count, flushed with shame, fell at the king’s feet and publicly repented that he had sinned.

(LIUDPR. IV, 28, 29.) Eberhard and Giselbert, hearing that the king was in the regions of Alsace, gathered a very large army, crossed the bed of the Rhine at Andernach, and proceeded to destroy the king’s faithful followers everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 5 reads *in partibus esse* (“to be in the regions”).]

Otto, the brother of Herman, duke of the Suevians, and Conrad, surnamed the Wise, were themselves in those regions. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 2 omits *etiam* (“also”).] But because their forces were inferior to the forces of Eberhard and Giselbert, they were afraid to meet them. Nevertheless, they followed them from behind as they returned with much booty. [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscript 2 reads *Odo*; 9c reads *Udo*.] [Note: [Col. 0911] Manuscripts 4 and 5 read *Herimanni* (“of Herman”).]

After they had advanced a little, a certain priest met them weeping and lamenting. They asked him where he had come from and why he was weeping. He replied:

“One possession that was the sole comfort of my poverty—a beast of burden—has been taken from me by these robbers.”

They asked him whether he had seen Giselbert and Eberhard or where they were. He answered:

“After all the booty had been conveyed across the Rhine, they alone, with their chosen men, are taking food—may it not turn out well for them.”

When they heard this, they rushed upon them with the greatest speed. Eberhard was immediately killed. Giselbert leaped from his horse into the current and was submerged in the waters. Since he could not swallow them, he died as his soul departed. [Note: [Col. 0913] Manuscript 5 reads *poterat* (“he could”) for *potuit* (“he could”).]

Of the others, not one escaped: each was either captured alive or beheaded with the sword.

When the messenger of this event met the king as he was accustomed to go in the morning to the church, which lay far from the camp, the king immediately dismounted from his horse and, giving thanks to God with tears, devoted himself to prayer. When the prayer was completed, he began his journey and proceeded to the church.

(RICHER, II, 17, 18, 19. [Note: Compare the readings added from Ekkehard in the notes to Richer’s edition.]) Nevertheless, that Gallic writer whom I mentioned above [Note: “we mentioned,” 9c.] relates the outcome of this affair differently, saying as follows [Note: Omitted in 10 and 11.]:

“Ludewicus [Note: *Luodewicus*, 5.], son of Charles, who, recalled from overseas and then reigning in Gaul, was, together with Prince Hugo of Cisalpine Gaul, annexing in the Alsatian district the Outer Belgians, who had not yet come over to his side, and compelling those who favored Otto’s party to flee beyond the Rhine. For he had learned beforehand [Note: *enim*, 5; *praesens enim erat*, 4.] that Otto wished to transfer Belgica into his own jurisdiction. Therefore, acting with still greater ferocity against him, he expelled from Belgica all whom he saw to be Otto’s supporters; those who agreed with himself, however, he bound to him by oath on the advice of Giselbert, duke of Belgica, and Count Theoderic.

“Now when Otto discovered that the Belgians had defected from him and flocked to Ludewicus [Note: *Luodewigum*, 5, and so frequently thereafter.], he crossed the Rhine and entered Belgica with an army, devastating many of its places with fire and immense plunder. For he was striving to become prince of Belgica, as though by hereditary right [Note: Omitted in D 1.]. But this was denounced as contrary to law, since his father had been appointed duke only of Saxony, which is part of Germany, because Charles, the father of Ludewicus, to whom supreme authority was due, was at that time still a child in his cradle.

“Thus Otto, carrying off much plunder, crossed the Rhine. Duke Giselbert, hastening to avenge the insult of this disgrace, gathered an army and pursued the enemy. Crossing the Rhine, he devastated that land to the ground with enormous fires; his army also gathered and carried off an excessive amount of plunder in cattle and livestock.

“They were now preparing to enter the river, and behold, Otto brought against them troops gathered from all Saxony [Note: *ex t. S. Otto*, D 1.]. The Belgians, therefore, resisting without hesitation together with their duke, entered the battle with hostile standards against the Germans beside the river, and many fell on both sides. On that day, although the Germans’ victory was hard won, it nevertheless shone forth [Col. 0913A]. For when two-thirds of their forces lay defeated, and Giselbert thought that his own men had failed while the enemy remained unharmed [Note: Omitted in 2.], he tried, amid such confusion, to escape the danger by flight and leapt into the current on his horse. But when the horse could not swim across the deep river, overcome by the force of the waters [Note: *in unda*, 2.], it perished and submerged its rider.

“Meanwhile the Belgians, unaware of their duke’s death, fought with all their strength and continued to exert themselves with such force that, after a dreadful and immeasurable slaughter, some of those who remained were captured and others drowned in the river.

“But King Ludewicus, learning that Giselbert had perished, felt deep compassion at his death. He set out for Belgica and took his wife Gerbirga, Otto’s sister, in marriage.

“Thus, although the circumstances differed, both writers—the Gallic and the Saxon—testify to the duke’s death, which had one and the same end [Note: *exitu*, 2, 9c, 10, D 1.]; but it will be for the reader to decide whom he should believe more.”

(LIUDPRAND, IV, 30, 31, 32, 33.) At this time [Note: Omitted in 2.] Bertholdus [Note: *Bertholdus*, D 1, 10, 11; *Berchtoldus*, 5; *Bertoldus*, 4, 9c.], duke of the Bavarians and brother of Duke Arnolf, a vigorous man, supported the king’s party with all his strength. Therefore, since the king wished him to share in present joy just as he had shared in past tribulation, immediately on the following day, as soon as he heard of the death of his adversaries, he informed him through messengers of what the Lord had done for him. Since he was not at all bound by marriage, the king, to increase his joy, required him under oath that, if he could obtain his sister—that is, Giselbert’s widow—he should marry her; but if this could not be arranged, he should marry Giselbert’s daughter, born of that same sister of his and then in the king’s keeping, already nearly of marriageable age [Note: *illi*, 5, 9c, 10, 11; *ei*, corrected from *illi*, 4; *conjungeret*, 5.]. On hearing this, Bertholdus was filled with immense joy and chose rather to await the daughter, who was not yet marriageable, than to take the mother, who had already married.

Archbishop Fridericus, therefore, in order that the treachery he secretly harbored might become evident to all, left the king ten days before the death of the men mentioned above and hastened to Mainz [Note: Omitted in 2.]. After lingering there for no time, he went to the city of Metz. For Heinricus, the king’s brother, had arranged that, when Eberhardus and Giselbertus returned, he should gather an army there with the same Fridericus and thus prepare a great war against the king, who was staying in Alsace.

As the same archbishop was traveling there, messengers unexpectedly met him and announced the death of those men so often mentioned. On hearing this, he was thrown into confusion and did not know what to do. Meanwhile the king, abandoning Alsace, occupied Francia. Terrified by fear of him, the citizens of Mainz did not receive the returning archbishop within the city walls. As a result, not long afterward he was captured by one of the king’s loyal men, brought into the king’s presence, and handed over to custody in Saxony. After remaining there for a short time, he was restored, through the king’s compassion—for he was exceedingly merciful—to his former dignity.

Heinricus, compelled by fear of his brother, wished to enter the castle of Kievermont, fortified not only by human ingenuity but also by nature itself [Note: *sed*, 4, D 1.]. But his sister, Giselbert’s widow, forbade him, saying to him:

“Are you not ashamed of my sufferings, which I endure because my husband has been killed? Do you even wish, by enclosing yourself in my fortifications, to pour the king’s anger over this region like water [Note: *infundas*, 2.]? I will not allow it. Nor will I be so foolish as to seek your advantage from my own misfortunes.”

On hearing this, Henricus abandoned Lotharingia and withdrew into the kingdom of Ludewicus.

(WIDUKIND, II, 26.) The king appointed Otto, son of Richwinus, over the region of Lotharingia, so that he might govern the kingdom and raise his nephew, Giselbert’s son, a promising young boy named Heinricus.

(LIUDPRAND, IV, 34.) Heinricus, the king’s brother, not knowing what else to do, took with him certain bishops whose assistance he might have and, one day, came barefoot to the king’s feet without the king’s knowledge. As a suppliant, he begged for mercy. The king said to him:

“Your unworthy deed does not deserve forgiveness; yet because I see you humbled before me, I will not bring evil upon you” [Note: *te video*, D 1.].

The king therefore ordered him to go to the palace at Ingelheim and to be kept there under diligent guard until, when the distress of his mind had somewhat subsided [Note: *paulum*, 9c.], he could determine, with the counsel of wise men, what should be done with him.

(WIDUKIND, II, 29, 36, 37 and following; 35, 33.) After this, his ever-present clemency granted him several neighboring cities for his use and allowed him to live in the region of Lotharingia. Later, after Berhtoldus, duke of the Bavarians, had died [Note: “Berthold,” D 1.], at the urging and intercession of his holy mother he appointed Heinricus to that same kingdom, making peace and an agreement with him, in which Heinricus also remained faithful to the end.

Heinricus himself was married to the daughter of Duke Arnolf, a woman of remarkable beauty and extraordinary prudence.

Thus, when both internal and external wars had ceased and divine and human laws prevailed with authoritative force, a severe persecution arose against the monks in those days. Certain bishops maintained that it seemed better for a few men illustrious in their way of life to exist in monasteries than for many negligent men, and therefore that their manner of life ought to be examined throughout the monasteries and those who did not live well expelled. They had forgotten, I think [Note: Omitted in 9c.], the judgment of the householder, who forbade his servants to uproot the weeds from the wheat, but ordered both to be left to grow until the harvest, lest, when one was rashly uprooted, harm should be done to the other.

That is precisely what happened in this matter. For many who were conscious of their own weakness avoided the grave burden imposed by the priests by laying aside their habit and abandoning the monasteries [Note: *relictis monasteriis*, D 1.]. There were many who thought that the supreme pontiff Fridericus had brought this about not sincerely but deceitfully [Note: *non pure*, D and E.], in order, if he could somehow do so, to dishonor the venerable and king-loyal abbot Hademarus of Fulda [Note: *regique fidelem*, omitted in 2.].

For that abbot was a man of great prudence and ability. During his time the famous church of Fulda was consumed by fire, but he restored it in an improved form. He held this same pontiff, who was guilty of a second conspiracy, under guard—at first honorably, but, after he had criticized letters written by the pontiff, quite strictly. The pontiff, once released, sought revenge but could not prevail against so great a man. He therefore decided to test the humblest monasteries, to see whether he might perhaps proceed equally against the most distinguished [Note: Omitted in 9c.].

But such schemes were poured out in vain [Note: *incasse*, D 1; *incassum* corrected above *incasse*, E 1.]. For the abbot remained in the king’s favor and friendship [Note: D 1 and E 1 add *et abbas*; here the text continues in 1.], and, amid the intervening disputes, the pontiff did not accomplish what he wished.

The king, however, advancing from day to day and not content with his paternal kingdom, went into Burgundy and brought its king and kingdom under his authority. After Otto, governor of Lotharingia and the king’s nephew Heinricus, son of Giselbertus, had died [Note: Everything up to the years of Otto is lacking in E.], The king granted the duchy of that region to Chuonradus and also betrothed to him his only daughter, Luitgarda. He was a vigorous and brave young man, excellent at home and in war, and dear to his fellow soldiers. Luitolfus, the king’s son, became closely attached to him through an excessive intimacy of affection.

(RICHER, II, 29.) After this, King Otto was reconciled with King Ludewicus through the intervention of ambassadors, a reconciliation which is shown to have benefited Ludewicus greatly afterward.

(WIDUKIND, II, 39.) The king’s sister Gerberga bore Ludewicus two sons, Karolus and Lotharius, who later succeeded their father.

(RICHER, II, 47, 48; WIDUKIND, II, 39, 41; III, 1 and following.) Ludewicus, therefore, surrounded by his dukes, was first captured by the men of Rouen, among whom Hairoldus, son of Thurmodus, prince of the men of Bayeux, had entered alone as a fugitive. He was handed over to Haioroldus but released after giving his younger son as a hostage. Immediately afterward he was captured by Duke Hugo and sent under public guard to Lyon.

When the king heard this, he grieved deeply over the misfortune of his friend and ordered an expedition into Gaul against Hugo for the following year. That year was made notable by the death of Queen Edith, who died on the seventh day before the Kalends of February. Born of the English people, she shone no less through holy religion than through royal power. She shared the kingdom for ten years and died in the eleventh; she lived in Saxony for nineteen years. She left a son named Luitolfus, who at that age was second to none in every virtue of mind and body, and also a daughter named Luitgarda [Col. 0917A], who had married Duke Chuonradus. She was buried in the city of Magdeburg.

After her death the king transferred all his attention to his son and, having made a will, created him king after himself. He was then still a young man, sixteen years of age.

As the king set out on an expedition into Gaul, he hastened to enter the kingdom of Karolus, in order to avenge the injury done to his friend Ludewicus. When Hugo heard this, he sent an embassy and swore by the soul of his father that he possessed such a quantity of arms as the king had never seen. He also expressed contempt in vain and boastful speech for the Saxons, because they were unwarlike and because he could easily swallow seven Saxon weapons in a single drink.

To this the king gave a sufficiently famous reply: there would be such a multitude of felt (*feninus*) caps to be presented to him as neither he nor his father had ever seen; and in truth, although the army was very large—“thirty, indeed, of two legions,” as the text reads [uncertain]—not one person was found who did not wear a felt (*feninus*) cap, except the abbot of Corvey with three of his followers.

Ludewicus, therefore, released, met the king and joined his army with his own men.

(RICHER, II, 54.) King Chuonradus of the Genauni also met them with a large expedition; Ludewicus had summoned him as an ally. They therefore went together to Lyon, but, unable to capture it because of the roughness of the terrain, they proceeded to the city of Reims, where Hugo, nephew of Duke Hugo, had been unlawfully and improperly installed as bishop while the legitimate bishop was still alive.

(WIDUKIND, III, 3.) They captured the city by force of arms, expelled the unlawful priest, and restored the legitimate bishop to his own see.

After three months, therefore, the king returned to Saxony with his army intact [Note: A superscript correction in 1.] and left with King Ludewicus everything that had been won by arms. Hugo, having experienced the power of the king and the valor of the Saxons, did not allow them thereafter to enter his territories in a hostile manner. The following year, when the king was going on the same expedition, Hugo met him near the river called the Kar and, by the king’s command, made an agreement with his lord Ludewicus, surrendered himself, and afterward remained useful.

(LIUDPRAND, V, 1.) As nobles from every direction were gathering to the king, there also came the very wealthy duke of the Suebi, Herimannus. After courteously exchanging congratulations, he addressed the king in these words:

“It is not unknown to my lord that, although I am very rich in the extent of my estates and the immensity of my wealth, I am without children; and, when I die, no one except my only little daughter will be heir to my property. Therefore, may it please you, my lord king, to adopt your son Luitolfus as my son, so that, joined in marriage to my only daughter, he may become magnificently endowed with the inheritance of my possessions.”

The king approved the duke’s proposal and fulfilled what he requested without delay.

(WIDUKIND, III, 6, 7.) Shortly afterward the father-in-law died, leaving the entire duchy and all his property to his son-in-law. Having received this power, Luitolfus discarded the tranquil disposition he had possessed as a boy and, leading an armed force into Italy, captured several cities there and placed them under guard; then he returned to Francia.

At that time a savage and greedy man, who sold every act of justice for money, Berengarius, ruled in Lombardy after usurping the authority. He had once come to King Otto, fleeing King Hugo of Italy, and had been treated kindly by him; although Hugo wished to pay a large sum of money for him, Otto did not surrender him.

(Compare LIUDPRAND, V, 12, 13; WIDUKIND, III, 7.) Later, when Berengarius reigned after Hugo had been driven out, he feared the singular prudence of Queen Adelheidis, left by Lotharius, the son of Hugo, and afflicted her in many ways, in order either to extinguish or at least obscure the glory of so great a splendor.

She was the daughter of King Ruodolfus of the Burgundians, who had also reigned in Italy, and of Queen Berhta, daughter of Burchardus, duke of the Alamanni. After Ruodolfus’s death, King Hugo married Berhta and joined her daughter in marriage to his son Lotharius.

(Compare LIUDPRAND, IV, 12; WIDUKIND, III, 8 and following.) At that time the king set out on campaign against Bolizlavus, king of the Bohemians. When the city called Nova was about to be captured, in which Bolizlavus’s son was shut up under siege, the prudent king brought the battle to an end, lest any soldier should incur danger while taking the enemy’s spoils.

When Bolizlaus had considered the king’s valor and the army’s innumerable multitude, he left the city and preferred to submit to such majesty rather than suffer utter destruction. Standing beneath the standards, listening to the king and giving his answers, he finally obtained pardon. The king, therefore, gloriously victorious, returned to Saxony.

Since the king was aware of the virtue of the queen mentioned above, he pretended that he was going to Rome. When he entered Lombardy, he tried to test the queen’s love for him by gifts. Having tested it faithfully, he took her as his wife and, together with her, obtained the city of Pavia, which is the seat of the kingdom.

When his son Liutolfus saw this [Note: Thus in this passage in H and L.], he departed from him in sadness. He went to Saxony and stayed for some time at Salaveldon, a place ominous for deliberations. The king, however, after celebrating the wedding in Italy with royal magnificence, set out from there in the splendor of his new marriage, intending to celebrate the coming Easter in Saxony.

King Berengarius, persuaded by Duke Chuonradus, to whom Pavia had been left to guard with a military garrison, followed the king into Germany, intending to make peace with him and obey his commands in everything. When he came to the royal city, he was ordered to remain in the lodging prepared for him; for he did not obtain the privilege of seeing the king’s face for three days.

Chuonradus, who had brought him, took this badly, as did Luitolfus, the king’s son, who shared his view. After this the king spoke with Berengarius, who was received into the favor of the king and queen. He gave a pledge of surrender and designated a day and Augsburg as the place for a voluntary treaty.

When the assembly took place there, Berengarius clasped the hands of his son Adelbertus in his own and, before the entire army, submitted himself and his son to the king’s service. He was then dismissed and returned to Italy with favor and peace. There, a stone of extraordinary size, hurled from heaven by thunder and storm, provided a great marvel to many who saw it.

(WIDUKIND, III, 12, 18 and following.) The king’s sons were born of the most serene queen: the firstborn, Heinricus; the second, Brun; the third, Otto, designated by the majesty of his paternal name, whom the whole world already hoped would be lord and father after his father; and a daughter, marked with the name of his holy mother.

Luitolfus, the king’s son, and Chuonradus, his son-in-law [Note: *Chuorandus*, 1.], began to devise new schemes against the king. When this did not escape his notice, he moved his army against them around the Kalends of July. He captured the cities of the opposing side that lay in his path either by force of arms or by surrender, until he reached Mainz, which his son had already entered with an army and where, pitiable to relate, he awaited his father in arms.

There a war began more bitter than any civil war and every other calamity. Many siege engines were brought against the walls, but the townsmen destroyed or burned them; there were frequent battles before the gates, while the besiegers’ positions were rarely routed. They delayed because they feared the ruler of the kingdom outside and his successor within.

When the siege had lasted nearly sixty days, discussion of peace began. Accordingly, the king’s cousin Ekbertus was given as a hostage to the city, so that access to the camp might be open to them. The son and son-in-law entered the camp and prostrated themselves at the king’s feet, promising that they would endure everything for their crime, provided that their allied friends suffered no harm.

The king, however, unable to determine how to inflict the deserved punishments upon his son, demanded that the supporters of the conspiracy be produced. They, bound by reciprocal oaths and somehow constrained by the craft of the ancient enemy, denied everything absolutely, and so, having accomplished nothing, returned to the city.

Ekbertus, who had been given as a hostage to the city, turned against the king with persuasive words, since he had already been angry with him because of his rebukes.

On the following night the Bavarian counts of Heinricus, the king’s brother, abandoned him and joined Luitolfus. With them Luitolfus proceeded and captured the royal city of Regensburg, together with the other strongly fortified places in that region. He divided all Duke Heinricus’s wealth among his soldiers and compelled Heinricus’s wife, children, and friends to leave not only the city but also the region.

All this was done on the advice of Arnolfus the younger and his brothers, because Heinricus himself possessed the hereditary duchy.

The king, following his son, surrounded Regensburg with a siege. But since the multitude did not allow siege engines to be brought up to the city, the two sides sometimes fought fiercely enough before the walls. The townsmen, worn down by repeated battles, also began to be endangered by hunger.

Therefore Luitolfus left the city with the leading men and asked for peace, but did not obtain it because he refused obedience to his father. Returning to the city, he attacked with weapons Gero, who was besieging the eastern gate, a man famous for as many victories as battles.

From the third hour until the ninth, while fierce fighting was taking place before the city gate, Arnolfus’s horse fell. Its rider, disarmed and immediately pierced by weapons, died. Two days later, a woman fleeing the city because of hunger reported his death, which had previously been unknown.

The townsmen were greatly dismayed by his death and began to negotiate peace. Accordingly, through the intervention of the nobles, Luitolfus again left the city and, after it had been besieged for a full month and a half, obtained peace until the appointed day on which these matters would be judged. The place of the council was designated as Fritzlar.

The king returned from there to his homeland, while Heinricus obtained Nova Civitas. On the following night Regensburg was almost entirely burned.

After this, while the king was hunting for exercise at a place called Sweldon, his son fell prostrate at his father’s feet with bare soles. Deeply touched by repentance, he moved first his father’s tears and then those of all who were present. Received into favor through paternal love, he promised that he would obey his father’s every will.

Meanwhile it was announced that the supreme pontiff Fridericus had fallen ill, and therefore the king’s decision was postponed for a short time. After the pontiff’s death, a general assembly of the people was held. After a year and a half, Mainz, together with all Francia, was handed over to the king. The son and son-in-law were received into favor, which they faithfully enjoyed to the end.

As the king entered Saxony around the Kalends of July, he encountered ambassadors of the Hungarians, apparently visiting him on account of ancient loyalty and favor, but, as some thought, actually observing the outcome of the civil war. After he had kept them with him for several days and dismissed them in peace with a few gifts, he heard from messengers of his brother, the duke of the Bavarians:

“Behold, the Hungarians are spreading out and invading your territories; they intend to engage you in battle.”

When the king heard this, as though he had endured no labor the previous year, he began to march against the enemy, taking with him only a very few Saxons because the Sclavonic war was already pressing upon him.

After the camp had been established near the boundaries of the city of Augsburg, the Frankish and Bavarian armies met him. Duke Chuonradus also came to the camp with a strong cavalry force. At his arrival the soldiers were heartened and now wished the battle not to be delayed.

For that duke was naturally bold in spirit and—what is rare among the bold—good in counsel. Whether he went against the enemy on foot or on horseback, he was an unconquerable warrior and, at home and in war, dear to his comrades.

Thus, from the raiding bands of both armies, it was reported that the two armies were not far from one another. A fast was therefore proclaimed in the camp, and orders were given that everyone should be ready for battle on the following day.

At first light they rose. After peace had been given and received, each first promised his service to the duke and then, under oath, to the others. With the standards raised, approximately eight legions proceeded from the camp.

The army was led through rough and difficult places so that the enemy would not have the opportunity to harass the columns with arrows, which they used with great skill, while thickets protected the army.

The Bavarians led the first, second, and third legions, commanded by the prefects of Duke Heinricus; he himself was absent from the battle because he had been suffering from bodily illness, of which he also died. The Franks arranged the fourth legion, whose leader and commander was Duke Chuonradus.

(WIDUKIND, III, 44 and following.) In the fifth legion, which was the largest and was called the royal legion, the king himself was present. He was surrounded by picked men from all the thousands of soldiers and by vigorous young men; before him stood the banner called the Angel, and he was enclosed by a dense mass of troops.

The Suebi formed the sixth and seventh legions, commanded by Burchardus, whose wife was the daughter of the king’s brother. In the eighth were one thousand chosen Bohemian soldiers, equipped more with weapons than with good fortune. All the baggage and equipment were placed in this legion, as though it were the safest because it was the last.

But events turned out otherwise. For the Hungarians, without delay [Note: *junctantes*, 1.], crossed the river Licus, called the Lech, and, surrounding the army [Note: *circuentesque*, 1.], began to harass the rearmost legion with arrows. Then, making a charge with tremendous shouting, they killed some, captured others, seized all the baggage, and compelled the armed men of that legion to flee.

In the same way they attacked the seventh and sixth legions and, after routing many of them, put them to flight. But when the king perceived that battle was being offered from the front while the rearmost columns were in danger behind, he sent Duke Chuonradus there with the fourth legion. When he arrived, he rescued the captives, recovered the booty, and threw the enemy’s raiding bands into confusion.

After the enemy raiders had been routed everywhere, the duke returned to the king with victorious standards. In a remarkable turn of events, while the veteran soldiers, accustomed to the glory of victory, were astonished, he achieved triumph with the new soldiers, who were almost inexperienced in warfare.

When the king saw that the whole weight of the battle was now in front, he addressed his men to encourage them, reminding them of their ancient victories and of their repeated success in noble deeds. He urged them not to yield now in their own homeland, since they had so often been victorious in foreign lands. After saying many such things, he concluded:

“I would say more, my soldiers, if I knew that words could increase the courage or boldness in your hearts. Now let us begin to act better with swords than with tongues.”

With these words, taking up his shield and sacred lance, he himself was the first to turn his horse against the enemy, performing the duty of a most courageous soldier and excellent commander.

The bolder of the enemy first resisted; then, when they saw their comrades turn their backs, they were stupefied, became mingled with our men, and were killed. Of the rest, some entered the nearest villages on exhausted horses and, surrounded by armed men, were burned together with the buildings; others, swimming across the adjacent river, were overwhelmed and perished when the farther bank did not support them as they climbed it.

Duke Chuonradus, fighting bravely, was overcome by the fervor of his spirit and by the heat of the sun, which was excessive that day. He loosened the fastenings of his coat of mail, and, while seeking a breath of air, fell from a wound caused by an arrow fixed in the front of his throat.

By the king’s command his body was honorably gathered and carried to Worms, where it was buried amid the weeping and lamentation of all the Franks.

On that same day the camp was attacked and all the captives rescued. On the second and third days, the remaining multitude from the neighboring cities was so thoroughly destroyed that scarcely anyone escaped.

Three dukes of the Hungarian people were captured and presented to Duke Heinricus; they were punished with the evil death they deserved, for they burst apart on the gallows.

The king, made glorious by a celebrated triumph, was called by the army “father of his country” and “emperor.” After honors and worthy praises had been decreed to the supreme divinity in every church, and after he had likewise entrusted this duty by messengers to his holy mother, he returned to Saxony amid rejoicing and the greatest joy and was received most willingly by his people. No king before him had rejoiced in so great a victory within two hundred years.

When affairs had thus been properly settled throughout all Francia, Saxony, and the neighboring peoples around them, he resolved to go to Rome and proceeded into Lombardy. How he besieged Berengarius, king of the Lombards, who was inflicting many evils upon the churches of God together with his son Adelbertus, for two years; how he captured him and sent him into exile with his wife and sons; how he defeated the Romans in two battles; subjected the dukes of Beneventum; overcame the Greeks in Calabria and Apulia; opened veins of silver in Saxon territory; and magnificently extended the empire together with his son, who bore the same name, is too great a task and therefore cannot be written by us.

(LIUDPRAND, History of Otto.) This alone must be briefly noted: when Pope Johannes had earnestly entreated him by letter to free, for the love of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, the holy Roman Church from the jaws of Berengarius and his followers, and when he had been moved by the complaints of many other bishops, of another order, and of laymen, he made his son Otto king, contrary to the custom of his predecessors, while still in childhood, and left him in Saxony. He himself, having gathered his forces, came swiftly to Italy. He sent Berengarius, together with his wife Willa and his son Adelbertus, as captives into exile at Babenberg, where that same Berengarius later died and was buried.

He himself, coming to Rome, was received with magnificent ceremony and raised by the apostolic Johannes through imperial anointing and blessing; he was called emperor and augustus. After remaining for some time in those regions, he summoned his son Otto to him. Otto received the crown of the kingdom from the apostolic on the day of the Nativity of the Lord.

He also sent an embassy to Constantinople and brought from there the emperor’s daughter, named Theophanu, whom, after celebrating the wedding in Italy, he joined in marriage to his son.

(Compare the Chronicle of Würzburg; LIUDPRAND, the works cited; WIDUKIND, III, 70–73.)

(WIDUKIND, III, 75, 76.) After this, Emperor Otto returned from Italy with his son the king [Note: “Co-emperor,” E; “co-emperor,” A, 972.] and entered Gaul, intending to cross from there into Germany and celebrate the coming Easter at Quedlinburg. After remaining there for seventeen days, he descended from there to celebrate the Ascension of the Lord at Merseburg.

On the Tuesday before Pentecost he came to a place called Memleben. After the following night had passed, at the appointed hour he sat down cheerfully at table. When the time for evening praises arrived, he attended them; but when the singing of the Gospel had ended, he began to grow feverish and weary. When the nobles standing around him perceived this, they placed him on a seat.

As he inclined his head, as though he had already collapsed, they revived him. After he had requested and received the Lord’s sacrament, he gave up his spirit to the Lord without a groan and in great tranquility, on the Nones of May, the Wednesday before Pentecost.

He was then carried into a chamber, and when it was already evening, his death was announced to the people. His body was carried by his son, who had now become king [Note: “His son, his namesake,” etc., E; “his own son, his namesake,” etc., in the other witnesses.], amid the great funeral rites of the mourners, to the city he himself had built and named Magdeburg; there it was honorably buried.

## The Years of Otto the Great

1. (Chronicle of Würzburg.) In his first year, which is the year 937 from the Lord’s incarnation, the Hungarians, devastating Francia, Alamannia, and Gaul as far as the ocean, as well as Burgundy, returned through Italy [Note: The words “The Hungarians … returned” are lacking in D and E; there one reads “The monasteries … are burned” after “Rudolfus … died”; at the end they add “Inger … ordered it.” From Sigebert, year 936.]. The monasteries of Saint Gall and Saint Boniface were burned. King Ruodolfus of Burgundy and Duke Arnolfus of the Noricans died.

2. A.D. 938. Heinricus [Note: D and E have: “Against Otto … they return,” from Sigebert.], the brother of King Otto, was captured by Count Eberhardus.

3. A.D. 939. King Otto, while his soldiers were fighting against his brother Heinricus, Gisilbertus, and Eberhardus, won the victory [Note: D and E have: “Eberhardus and … the son of Arnolfus,” from Sigebert.].

From the beginning of the year 4900.

4. A.D. 940. While the king was besieging the castle of Brisach in the region of Alsace, certain bishops withdrew at night, abandoning their tents. Count Eberhardus [Note: “Duke Giselbertus” erased before “Eberhardus,” 1.] was killed by Uto [Note: *Otto*, D 1.] and Chuonradus beside the Rhine; Duke Giselbertus was drowned in the water [Note: D and E have: “King Otto … fled to the king,” from Sigebert.]. Bishop Burghardus of Würzburg died.

5. A.D. 941. King Otto set out for Gaul [Note: D and E: “King Ludewicus [*Luodewicus*, E 1, frequently] … put them to flight,” from Sigebert.].

6. A.D. 942. Kings Otto and Ludewicus were reconciled [Note: D and E: “Giselbertus and … wounded,” from Sigebert.].

7. A.D. 943. [Note: D and E place here the events listed above under 940: “The king … was drowned.”]

8. A.D. 944. The Hungarians fought the Bavarians and were defeated [Note: D and E: “Stephanus … followed,” from Sigebert.].

9. A.D. 945. [Note: D and E add: “Otto subdued …,” as others place it under 946, “while [someone] resisted … for sixteen years.” From Sigebert. D and E also add: “In Italy a comet of extraordinary size appeared, foretelling the famine that followed.” From Sigebert.]

10. A.D. 946. [Note: D and E add: “Heinricus, the king’s brother, having been cast out … was excluded,” from Sigebert. D and E also add: “King Otto subjected all Lotharingia to himself,” from Sigebert.]

11. A.D. 947. Bertholfus [Note: “E. R. O. B. … is entrusted.” D and E, which add: “Berengarius … returns,” from Sigebert.] duke of the Bavarians, brother of Duke Arnolfus, died, and the duchy was entrusted to Heinricus, the king’s brother. Queen Edith died [Note: “E. R. C.” is lacking in 4.].

12. A.D. 948. [Note: D and E add: “The king … tyrannizes,” from Sigebert.]

13. **A.D. 949.** Herimannus [Note: [Col. 0923] These words are lacking in 7.] duke of the Alamanni died; in his place Luitolfus, son of King Otto, was appointed duke. [Note: [Col. 0924B] D. E. add: Taxis … receives. From Sigebert.]

14. **A.D. 950.** King Otto [Note: [Col. 0924B] D. E. read: Through the regions … they were made. From Sigebert.] went to Italy and subjected it to himself; and on his return he entrusted Pavia to Chuonradus [Note: [Col. 0923] *chuorado* in 1.], duke of the Lotharingians, to defend.

15. **A.D. 951.** Berenger, king of the Lombards, at the urging of Chuonradus, came with his son Adelbert at Augsburg to surrender; having been made the king’s man, he was sent back into his kingdom in peace. [Note: [Col. 0924C] D. E. add: From Mainz … he was released. From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0924C] 16. **A.D. 952.** King Otto entered Italy on account of Queen Adelheida; and, having taken her as his wife, celebrated the wedding at Pavia.

17. **A.D. 953.** Duke Luitolfus [Note: [Col. 0924C] “At the instigation of Duke Chuonradus … War took place … he described it in detail.” D. E. from Sigebert.] rebelled against his father, and Duke Chuonradus with him.

18. **A.D. 954.** The Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0924C] D. E. read: Ratherius … Farabertus. “They return with Liutolfus.” “To Ludewicus … 32 years.” From Sigebert, years 954–955.] invaded Italy, Noricum, and Francia.

19. **A.D. 955.** The Hungarians, ravaging all Bavaria, were defeated in battle by King Otto near Augsburg, a city of Alamannia [Col. 0924D], and were slaughtered in an immense massacre. [Note: [Col. 0924D] D. E. read: Fridericus … a bishop is substituted. From Sigebert, year 956.]

20. **A.D. 956.** Duke Luitolfus [Note: [Col. 0924D] D. E.: “Luitolfus, son of the king, enters … and defeats Adelbertus, but dies that same year. The Hungarians again … perished. Archbishop Brun built a monastery …” From Sigebert, year 957.] entered Italy in a hostile manner.

21. **A.D. 957.** Luitolfus [Note: [Col. 0924D] D. E., who place these events under 956, have for this year: “Brun … did.” From Sigebert, year 958.] defeated Adelbertus, and died himself that same year.

[Col. 0925A] 22. **A.D. 958.** Crosses appeared on men’s garments. [Note: [Col. 0925A] D. E. add: “Brun … fled for refuge to the king.” From Sigebert, year 959.]

24. **A.D. 960.** Poppo, bishop of Würzburg, died. [Note: [Col. 0925A] D. E. add: “At Constantinople … ten years. Gaul and … he directed himself.” From Sigebert, year 961.]

26. **A.D. 962.** At the request of Pope John and because of the complaints of many who were proclaiming accusations against Berenger and his son, Otto [Note: [Col. 0925] This was written under 961 and later assigned to 962.] proceeded to Rome [Note: [Col. 0925A] “King Otto, having traversed Italy, reached Rome”; [Col. 0925B] “and there …” D. E.; cf. Sigebert, year 963]. There he was made emperor by that same pope [Note: [Col. 0925B] “by Pope John,” D. E.], captured Berenger, and sent him with his wife, named Willa, to the castle of Babenberg, where he also ended his present life.

[Col. 0925B] 27. **A.D. 963.** The Emperor Otto celebrated Christmas at Pavia. [Note: [Col. 0925B] D. E. add: “After this he left Italy. Adelberone … is substituted.” From Sigebert, year 964.]

28. **A.D. 964.** The Emperor Otto stayed in Rome for Christmas; there his son Otto was also crowned. [Note: [Col. 0925B] D. E.: “The emperor celebrated Pentecost … to be equaled. Otto returned to Italy. Brun … is brought back.” From Sigebert, year 965.]

31. **A.D. 967.** [Note: [Col. 0925B] D. E.: “The younger Otto … is blessed as emperor by the pope on Christmas Day. Willihelmus … died,” from Sigebert, years 968 and 966. “Likewise Queen Mathildis, mother of that emperor, full of good works [Col. 0925C] and almsgiving, died.”] The Emperor Otto returned from Italy.

[Col. 0925C] 32. **A.D. 968.** [Note: [Col. 0925C] D. E. add: “A certain … intimate associate … deserved.” From Sigebert, year 969.] [Note: [Col. 0925C] E1. (in another hand) and 2, in the margin, read: “In this year the royal abbey at Magdeburg was changed into an archbishopric.”]

33. **A.D. 969.** Mathildis [Note: [Col. 0925C] D. E., who place these events under 967, have for this year: “Theodericus … gathered, and he placed this with part … granted in Gaul …” From Sigebert.] mother of the emperor, died.

34. **A.D. 970.** [Note: [Col. 0925C] D. E. add: “At … Nicephorus ruled.” From Sigebert.]

35. **A.D. 971.** A certain sign of fiery color appeared in the sky. [Note: [Col. 0925D] D. E. add: “Otto … joined to himself.” From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0925D] 36. **A.D. 972.** [Note: [Col. 0925D] D. adds: “The elder Otto … wrote.” From Sigebert. “After John … the 123rd,” as below under 974. E. adds: “The emperor, having returned from Italy … was buried,” as above. “Whose life …” as in D.]

37. **A.D. 973.** [Note: [Col. 0925D] D. E. have the material found in the other manuscripts under A.D. 975.]

38. **A.D. 974.** [Note: [Col. 0926A] D. E. only: “Saint O. … 50.” They add: “Raginerus, younger son of Raginerus … returned, and with Count Warnerus, who had received his father’s county from the emperor, fought at Perrona; after Warnerus was killed with many others, Raginerus recovered his paternal inheritance. Ratherius died at Lobbes [ [Col. 0925] lacking in D1.], whose own monostich is: ‘Ratherius the bishop, but thrice Ratherius the exile’; he caused this epitaph to be inscribed on his tomb: ‘Trample underfoot, O men, the salt that has lost its savor.’ Frost … winter …” From Sigebert, years 974, 973, and 975.] The Emperor Otto died on the Nones of May. In the same year Saint Oudalricus departed this life, in the year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0925] “After … the 123rd” is lacking in 4.] After Pope John, Benedict was ordained the 122nd pope [Col. 0926A], and after him likewise Benedict, the 123rd.

## The years of Otto II

1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 975, but from the founding of the City 1726, Otto II, son of the Great Otto [Note: [Col. 0925] “of Otto the Great,” 5; D. E.], began to reign, eighty-second in succession from Augustus, and reigned for nine years. [Col. 0926B] (WID. III, 76.) Having been elected to the kingdom while his father was still alive and adorned at Rome by the apostolic crown of the kingdom, as soon as his father died he was again elected by all who were present and placed upon the royal throne. [Note: [Col. 0926B] Since these words stand under A.D. 973 (1724), this year is vacant in D. E.; “the seventy-sixth … ten years” is read.]

“In the nineteenth year of his reign, the Emperor Otto—whom the wife of Crescens had enticed into love for her with the hope of reigning—while, against his will, he was drawn away from Italy by an unwilling woman at the urging of his army, died, consumed by poison sent to him by her, while returning through Italy, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February … first, as above. In the eighteenth year of his reign, the Emperor Otto III died on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, namely in the year which is designated as 1001 from the Lord’s incarnation. His intestines were buried at Augsburg, and the rest of his body at Aachen.

[Col. 0928C] ## The years of Heinricus II

1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1001, but from the founding of the City 1752, Heinricus II, at first duke of Bavaria and afterward, when Otto III had died without sons, raised to the summit of the kingdom, eighty-fourth [Note: [Col. 0927] Seventy-eighth, D. E.] in succession from Augustus [Col. 0928D], received the kingdom and reigned for twenty-three years and five months: twelve years under the title of king, and eleven with the dignity and title of emperor.

Having been elevated to the royal throne, after he had overcome the Margrave Heinricus and others who resisted him at the beginning of his reign, subjected Italy and Bohemia, and Bolizlaus with the whole race of the Slavs, and after the Lord had granted him rest, he considered that he would have no children; for, as many testify, he never knew his consort Cunigundis but loved her as a sister. He therefore chose the Lord, giver of all good things, as his heir. [Col. 0929A] In the sixth year of his reign, with wise counsel [Note: [Col. 0929] “Using wisdom,” E.] he established the bishopric of Babenberg in honor of Saint Peter and Saint George, and most abundantly endowed the place itself with the wealth of estates and every adornment, as it is seen at the present day. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Cf. the Life of Heinricus, published in Volume IV, whose author copied this material but illustrated it with charters and other documents.]

In the southern part of the city he also built a monastery under canonical rule in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr; on the other side, that is, toward the north, he established another monastery under the monastic rule in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel and Saint Benedict the abbot. Thus, for himself and his city—founded upon the rock of apostolic firmness and fortified and adorned with a wall and the strongholds of the merits of Saint George and the other saints—he prepared a tower of strength in Stephen against the assaults of vices [Col. 0929B], and against the cooling blasts of him who in the north, whence all evil is spread, resolved to establish his seat, a secure refuge in angelic protection [Note: [Col. 0930D] That is, of Saint Michael.], so that, enclosed on the right and on the left by the weapons of righteousness, the ambusher might in no way prevail.

To other holy places also throughout the breadth of the kingdom he imparted the generosity of his munificence no less, as necessity required: restoring some things that had already fallen into ruin for the better, and adding to others what they lacked.

The king’s brother was Brun, bishop of the see of Augsburg. Envious of his brother’s fortunate deeds, he inflicted upon him, as far as he could, many injuries of adversity; and where he could not do so himself, he joined himself to those inflicting them, or, by encouraging others to inflict them, drove them on with goads of provocation. [Note: [Col. 0930A] “And … subdued him” is lacking in E.]

His brother, however, not only did not repay him in kind, but, instructed by brotherly [Col. 0929C] love, strove to overcome him by good, concealing everything and enduring it patiently. [Note: [Col. 0930A] D. E.: “He strove to overcome him by the goodness of brotherly love and patience.”]

Their sister, a woman of blessed memory named Gisela [Note: [Col. 0929] In the margin of 1.], was sought in marriage by the king of the Hungarians, who was called Stephanus [Note: [Col. 0930A] D. E.: “Who was afterward called Stephanus at baptism.”]; but he did not obtain her as his wife until he promised that he would receive the rudiments of the Christian religion and the sacrament of holy baptism with his entire people. When he fulfilled this promise in deed, he afterward remained religious and devoted to God in the performance of good works. Divine mercy demonstrated this after his death by evident signs, through miracles of signs performed at his burial.

[Note: [Col. 0930A] “King … monastery” is lacking here in E. (see below, A.D. 1024).]

King Heinricus, after he had caused the fragrance of a good reputation to spread far and wide, and after he had brought to perfection the place he loved by enriching, adorning, and cultivating it together with the other monasteries, entered, by divine calling, upon the way of all flesh and happily, as we believe, gave his soul back to God on the third day before the Ides of July, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, the eleventh of his empire, and the fifty-second of his life. He was buried at Babenberg [Col. 0930A] in the episcopal church built by him, in the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle.

[Col. 0933A] ## The years of Chuonradus II

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1025, but from the founding of the City 1776, Chuonradus, one of the leading men of the kingdom but previously opposed to the kingdom through rebellion, while the princes disagreed over his election, but Archbishop Aribo of Mainz and Eberhardus, bishop of Babenberg, supporting him, eighty-fifth [Note: [Col. 0933] Seventy-eighth, D. E.] in succession from Augustus, received the kingdom and reigned for fifteen years.

Having been elevated to the royal throne, he began, on the advice of Brun, bishop of Augsburg and brother of the Emperor Heinricus—who, as stated above, was always envious of his fortunate deeds—to plot the destruction of the bishopric of Babenberg, because that same Bishop Brun had promised Queen Gisela that he would hand over to her son Heinricus all the estates belonging to her by hereditary right.

[Col. 0933B] A place and time were therefore appointed for an assembly at which this matter was to be brought to a definite conclusion. On the night preceding the day on which these matters were to be debated, Bishop Eberhardus secretly approached the tent of the aforementioned Brunus. Sitting beside his bed, he earnestly addressed him at length with admonitions and entreaties, impressing upon his mind the memory of his brother, and anxiously pleaded with him.

When he had departed after a considerable part of the night had passed, and sleep had overcome the bishop, who had been troubled by what he had heard, his brother, the Emperor Heinricus, seemed to stand beside his bed and present to him his face, disfigured by having the beard shaved off on one side.

When he was astonished and amazed at this and asked who had dared such an outrage against him, the emperor said: “You have done this, since you intended to despoil me and the saints of God, whom I endowed with the possessions granted to me by God. Beware hereafter of such presumption, lest you pay for what you have begun with great misfortune.”

At this, awakened and greatly terrified by the vision, he was also severely seized by horror and trembling of his limbs. When morning came, and he did not come to the assembly of the nobles, though he had long been expected, the queen, anxious for her son, sent messengers and earnestly begged him to come and fulfill his promise.

He, however, declared that he was weighed down by such serious illness that he could neither rise from his bed nor move his foot anywhere. When he was asked to allow himself to be carried in his bed to the assembly, so that even in this way the promise might be fulfilled, he utterly refused, and finally proclaimed in a clear voice that he had sinned against God, his saints, and his brother.

Thus divine mercy, through the merits of its servant, lest the hope he had placed in it should be disappointed, suppressed all the devices of that wicked conspiracy, and, by confirming what had been well begun by him, thereafter continually advanced it toward better things. [Note: [Col. 0934B] E. continues: “Therefore, in the first year of his reign, King Chuonradus completed, in his own castle called Lintburg … A great dissension at that time against Chuonradus in the kingdom …”]

In the second year of his reign, King Chuonradus made his son Heinricus king; then, proceeding to Rome, he received the imperial blessing. After this he joined to his son the daughter of Knuth, king of the Danes, named Cunigundis, and devoted himself more earnestly to doing good.

For in his own castle, called Lintburg, formerly pleasing to him for other purposes, he built a monastery; enriching it with an abundance of estates, he introduced there a community of monks under the care of an abbot. [Note: [Col. 0933] Cf. the charter in *Acta palatina*, VI, p. 274.] He also resolved to advance the bishopric of Speyer, but, not reaching the end of his life, entrusted the fulfillment of his will to his son Heinricus. He himself began the work magnificently, but his son, likewise Heinricus, completed it still more magnificently.

1. **(Chronicle of Würzburg.)** Therefore, in the first year of King Chuonradus, a great dissension arose against him in the kingdom, but it was quickly calmed by divine intervention.

2. **A.D. 1026.** Heinricus, son of King Chuonradus, was made king; but Chuonradus, proceeding to Rome, was raised by the imperial [Col. 0934C] blessing.

3. **A.D. 1027.** Brun, bishop of Augsburg, and Count Welefo carried out plundering and burnings against one another.

4. **A.D. 1028.** Duke Ernest of the Alamanni and Count Welefo came to surrender to the Emperor Chuonradus.

5. **A.D. 1029.** Brun, bishop of Augsburg, died; Eberhardus succeeded him.

6. **A.D. 1030.** The Emperor Chuonradus marched with an army against Stephanus, king of Pannonia. Meanwhile in Alamannia [Col. 0935A] Duke Ernest and Count Werinherus, together with many others, were killed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

7. **A.D. 1031.** King Stephanus was reconciled with the emperor through envoys.

8. **A.D. 1032.** [Note: [Col. 0935A] D. E. add: “Rutpertus [ [Col. 0935] ‘Rodbertus’ in E.] and Richardus, departing from Normandy, went to Apulia and vigorously fought the natives.” From Sigebert.] King Ruodolfus of Burgundy, dying, sent his crown to the Emperor Chuonradus.

9. **A.D. 1033.** Meginhardus, bishop of Würzburg, died. In winter the Emperor Chuonradus marched against Burgundy. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the third day before the Kalends of July, at the sixth hour. [Note: [Col. 0935] The words “at the sixth hour” are lacking in 7.]

10. **A.D. 1034.** The emperor marched against Outo into Francia. He also devastated Burgundy. [Note: [Col. 0935] “He also … devastated” is lacking in 4–11.]

11. **A.D. 1035.** The pagans called Liutici seized the castle of Wirbinam, situated on the borders of Saxony, after killing and capturing many Christians. The emperor marched against them.

12. **A.D. 1036.** Gebehardus II, bishop of Regensburg, died; Gebehardus III succeeded him.---Heinricus, son of the emperor, was joined in marriage to the daughter of Knuth, king of the Danes.---The Liutici became tributaries of the emperor.---Piligrinus, archbishop of Cologne, died; Herimannus was ordained in his place.

13. **A.D. 1037.** The Emperor Chuonradus marched into Italy with an army and sent the bishop of Milan into custody; the latter escaped and rebelled against the emperor.---Outo [Col. 0935C], a prince of the Carolingians, was defeated in battle by Gozelo, duke of Lotharingia, and, fleeing, was killed by a certain soldier.

14. **A.D. 1038.** Stephanus, the devout king of the Hungarians, died.

15. **A.D. 1039.** The Empress Chunigundis, mother of the poor, herself rich, passed to Christ the Rich One on the fifth day before the Nones of March.---Herimannus, duke of the Alamanni and son of the Empress Gisila, died. The Emperor Chuonradus died on the second day before the Nones of June and was buried at Speyer. Reginboldus, bishop of Speyer, died on the third day before the Ides of October.---An eclipse of the sun occurred on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September.

## Years from the beginning: 5000

## The years of Heinricus III

[Col. 0935D] 1. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1040, but from the founding of the City 1791, Heinricus III, son of the Emperor Chuonradus, who had already long before been made king while his father was alive, eighty-sixth [Note: [Col. 0935] Eightieth, D. E.] in succession from Augustus, succeeded his father and reigned for seventeen years. Eberhardus [Note: [Col. 0935] “Eberhardus … died” is lacking in 4 in the margin.] the first bishop of Babenberg died.

2. **(Chronicle of Würzburg.) A.D. 1041.** King Heinricus marched against the duke of Bohemia, Fratizlaus, in battle; but, after many nobles and soldiers had been killed or captured in the forest ambush on both sides, he could accomplish nothing worthy of remembrance.---Peter [Col. 0936A] also, king of the Hungarians, sent auxiliaries to that duke against the king.

3. **A.D. 1042.** The Hungarians made a certain Ovonus their king and expelled their king Peter. As a fugitive and exile, Peter sought and found the favor of King Heinricus, against whom he had rebelled the previous year.---King Heinricus entered Bohemia, devastated everything with fire and plunder, and compelled the rebellious duke to give hostages, to come after him to Regensburg for the most humble surrender, and to confirm his loyalty and service to him by oath.---Ovo, king of the Hungarians, because King Heinricus had received Peter, whom he had expelled, devastated the borders of Bavaria with plunder; but a large part of his army was destroyed by Margrave Adelberone.

4. **A.D. 1043.** King Heinricus entered Pannonia [Col. 0936B], overthrew two very populous cities, and subjected many others to himself by surrender.---The Empress Gisela died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March and was buried at Speyer.

5. A.D. 1044. King Henry, invading Pannonia once again, accepted satisfaction, hostages, gifts, and confirmation of peace by oath, and withdrew. Returning from there, he attended the synod at Constance, where he remitted the penalties owed by all who had offended against him; and, after abolishing every enmity, he confirmed by royal edict a peace previously unheard of throughout all Swabia and in the other provinces of his kingdom. Then, having Agnes, daughter of William, prince of Poitiers, anointed queen at Mainz, he joined her to himself in a royal marriage at Ingelheim [Col. 0936C]. From there he allowed an innumerable multitude of actors and jesters to depart empty-handed and grieving, not only without gifts but also without food and drink. —Margrave Liutpold, son of Adelbert, the greatest disaster of the Hungarians, died prematurely. —There was a very great pestilence among the cattle; the winter was harsh and snowy.

6. A.D. 1045. Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. Adelbero was appointed in his place. —King Henry entered Pannonia for the third time and, by God’s gracious favor, emerged victorious. He drove out Ovo with his wife, sons, and relatives who had a place to flee; restored Peter to the kingdom; and, after subjecting the Hungarian kingdom to himself, returned with the highest honor. —Gotefrid, duke of the Lotharingians, rebelling against King Henry, was forced to surrender and was confined in the castle of Gibichenstein [Col. 0936D] until he had rendered an appropriate satisfaction. [Note: [Col. 0936D] Numbers 10 and 11 add: Otto became duke of Swabia. From Bernold.]

7. A.D. 1046. King Henry entered Italy and was received peacefully by the Romans. He canonically deposed three popes who had been improperly appointed and made Suidger, the second bishop of the church of Babenberg, pope. By him Henry himself and his wife Agnes were elevated by the imperial blessing on the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 0937A]. The empress Agnes, returning from there, gave birth to a daughter near Ravenna. The emperor, however, leading his army successfully through Apulia and many provinces, returned with great honor. Pope Suidger died on the seventh day before the Ides of October; in his place Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, was appointed.

[Note: [Col. 0937] “Suidger … is appointed” is absent in four witnesses.]

8. A.D. 1047. Peter, king of the Hungarians, was captured and blinded by a certain Pannonian tyrant; the man who had expelled him then began to reign.
