9. A.D. 1048. Pope Poppo [Note: [Col. 0937B] P., who is also Damasus, in D and E.] died before completing the year from the time he had been appointed. In his place Bruno, bishop of Toul, who was later called Leo, was appointed pope. [Note: [Col. 0937B] C, D, and E add: “This man, cousin of the emperor Conrad, when … affliction, you will call upon me and I will hear you, and I will bring back your captivity from all places. ‘Among other things, this is read concerning him: when he … a poor man … he was astonished. This man, learned in every field, composed chants for certain saints with sweet and regular melody, namely for Pope Gregory, Cyriacus the martyr, Gorgonius the martyr, and others; he also made and wrote many other things useful to the Church. He also, in Gaul … improved …’ From Sigebert, for the years 1048–1049.”]

[Note: [Col. 0937B] In the margin, witness 6 has: “This Bruno was educated in the liberal disciplines under Saint Albewin, master of the schools at Hersfeld and afterward abbot of Nienburg in Saxony.”]

Duke Otto of Swabia died; in his place [Note: [Col. 0937] “In his place” is absent in witnesses 1 and 5.] Otto, count of Schweinfurt, arose. [Note: [Col. 0937B] Numbers 10 and 11 add: “The blood of the Lord is revealed at Mantua through a blind man.” From Bernold.]

[Col. 0937C] 10. A.D. 1049. In the fourth year of his imperial reign, Emperor Henry invaded certain parts of Gaul against the dukes Gotefrid and Baldwin. After forcing them to surrender and pacifying the kingdom in those regions, he returned victorious and with honor. A synod was held at Mainz, attended by Bruno the apostolic bishop and Emperor Henry.

11. A.D. 1050. The Hungarians rebelled again. Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg and the emperor’s uncle, came against them in the emperor’s place; after putting them to flight, he inflicted a considerable slaughter upon them. He also restored the buildings of the city of Heimenburg, situated in the march, and had it fortified with a military garrison. He himself returned in the greatest peace [Col. 0937D].

12. A.D. 1051. Barto, archbishop of Mainz, died peacefully; Luitpold, provost of Babenberg, succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0938A] D and E add: “Nourished in monastic profession at the monastery of Fulda, he was promoted from there, on account of the merit of his life, to the pontifical dignity and rested in Christ, renowned for his virtues.”] [Note: [Col. 0938A] D and E add: “The things received by the Greeks … were received among the Greeks.” From Sigebert, for the years 1053 and 1054.]

Emperor Henry again went to Pannonia. Dividing his army into two parts, he entered while occupying the region on both sides, which was enclosed by forests and especially by accumulations of water. But that people, harsher than the others, acted treacherously with their king and, plundering their own possessions along with those of others, escaped while fleeing from the emperor’s army, which had been weakened by hunger, thirst, and many hardships. The emperor’s soldiers, after devastating a large part of the province and killing many there, returned peacefully, though without accomplishing their purpose, to their own country with the emperor. [Note: [Col. 0938A] E1, in another hand, and 2 add: “Hunfrid, sixth archbishop of Magdeburg, died.”]

13. A.D. 1052. The emperor again attacked Pannonia and returned without accomplishing his purpose, accompanied by Bruno, prelate of the apostolic see. When this pope came to Regensburg, he examined the relics of Saint Dionysius the martyr, whose presence there had long been doubted, in the presence of envoys from Paris, and established that they were indeed kept there. He also raised Saint Wolfgang, bishop of that city, from his tomb. Passing from there through Babenberg with the emperor, he ordered the privileges of that place to be examined and proclaimed before the emperor and the people by his chancellor Frederick, who later succeeded him; and by his own authority he confirmed them. [Note: [Col. 0937] See Leo’s charter issued on this matter in Ussermann’s proofs concerning the bishop of Bamberg, p. 36, and *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, IV, p. 802.]

From there, traveling together toward the regions bordering the Rhine, they celebrated the approaching Nativity of the Lord at Worms.

[Note: [Col. 0938B] The following is absent in witnesses 10 and 11, which add: “The relics of Saint Zeno were brought to Ulm by Walter, bishop of Verona.” From Bernold.]

14. A.D. 1053. While the pope and the emperor were celebrating the Lord’s Nativity at Worms with divine and royal ceremony, and after the apostolic bishop had properly completed the celebration of the Mass on the holy day, on the following day he assigned this office to Luitpold, archbishop of the see of Mainz, since he was the principal prelate in his own diocese. After the procession had been completed and the prayer for that occasion had been said, Luitpold took his seat. One of his deacons, named Humbert, then chanted the lesson, as many customarily do out of reverence for that feast.

Certain Romans attending the pope criticized this and complained to the pope that it was not being done according to Roman custom. They persuaded him to send word to the same deacon and forbid him to continue the chant. When the young man disregarded this, the pope sent word again and forbade it. The deacon immediately continued, with the same tone of voice as before, reading the lesson decorously to the end [Col. 0938D]. When it had ended, the pope summoned him and, as though for the insolence of disobedience, degraded him.

The archbishop sent to him, asking that he return his minister. When the pope refused, the bishop, being a man of ancient discipline, endured it for the time being in silence, although with difficulty and patience. After the Gospel had been read and the offertory chanted, when the time of the holy sacrifice arrived, the bishop sat in his own seat and solemnly declared that neither he nor anyone else would complete the service unless he received back the minister of his procession. When the apostolic bishop understood this, he yielded to the bishop and immediately sent back the minister after restoring him to his office. Once he had received him, the prelate undertook the duty proper to him.

In this matter both the authority of the bishop and the humility of the apostolic bishop are worthy of consideration: the one strove to defend the dignity of his office, while the other, although of greater dignity, recognized that he nevertheless had to yield to the metropolitan in the latter’s own diocese.

After this the apostolic bishop returned to Rome, accompanied by many soldiers from various provinces, sent by imperial command and supported by his friends. After Easter, leading an army through Apulia, he fought against the Normans, formerly newcomers to that land but at that time invaders of apostolic possessions and enemies of the Roman Empire. After an immeasurable slaughter on both sides, the pope fled with a few men and returned without victory, leaving behind the best soldiers of the Swabians and Noricans [Note: [Col. 0939] “German soldiers there” in manuscript 1b.], and settled in the city of Benevento, where at that time Oudalric, a Norican by birth, held the bishopric.

15. A.D. 1054. The religious pope Bruno, also called Leo, ended his life gloriously on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May. He was magnificently buried at Rome in the church of Saint Peter and became renowned for miracles. —Cuono, duke of the Noricans, rebelled gravely after allying the Hungarians to himself. Likewise Baldwin and Gotefrid. [Note: [Col. 0939] “Cuono … rebels” is absent in four witnesses.] [Note: [Col. 0939B] Numbers 10 and 11 add: “Hermann Contractus died.”]

16. A.D. 1055. Gebehard, also called Victor, bishop of Eichstätt, succeeded Pope Leo. [Note: [Col. 0939C] D and E add: “He was ordained bishop at Cologne.” From Sigebert; the remainder is absent in A.] [Note: [Col. 0939C–D] Numbers 10 and 11 add: “When his deacon had put poison into the chalice, he was unable to lift the chalice from the altar. While the people prayed for this, the deacon was tormented by a demon; after confessing his crime, he was freed, and the chalice, together with the sacraments, was enclosed in a certain altar as relics.” From Bernold.]

Margrave Adelbert died. There was a great famine. —Emperor Henry went to Italy with an army and arranged everything peacefully. On his return he brought with him his niece Beatrice, mother of Matilda, treating her harshly because of certain insolences to which she had become accustomed after the death of her husband, Duke Boniface. —Welefo, duke of Carinthia, died. —Cuono, formerly duke of the Noricans, was expelled by the emperor for the crime of his treachery and died miserably in exile in Pannonia. —Conrad succeeded Arnolf, bishop of Speyer.

[Col. 0939D] 17. A.D. 1056. Hermann, count of eastern Francia, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of February. —Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg and Emperor Henry’s uncle, was discovered and convicted as a secretly most dangerous enemy. He was committed to custody but treated mercifully, sent into exile [Col. 0940A], and restored to his former see. —Gotefrid surrendered. —A great slaughter of Christians was carried out by the Liutizi; some perished by the sword, others while fleeing into the water. Among them Margrave William was killed.

At the same time many princes of various provinces perished. Famine afflicted many regions; want and scarcity prevailed everywhere, and many evils occurred in those days. —Emperor Henry, pierced to the heart with grief over these events, began to fall ill. As death approached, he acted with wise counsel: he sought pardon from everyone from whom he could; restored to some the estates he had taken from them; and released all who had committed punishable offenses against him and his kingdom. He also established his son Henry as king through the election of the Roman pontiff and all the bishops and princes of the kingdom.

Having arranged these and other matters as far as the possibility of life allowed, he ended this present life in God on the third day before the Nones of October. [Note: [Col. 0940C–D] C adds: “Both the apostolic bishop and all the leading men of the kingdom buried his body at Speyer with immense honor beside his father. He was in every respect most worthy of so great a dignity: handsome in body, tall in stature, exceptionally vigorous in arms and spirit according to the times, yet sufficiently tempered by patience and humility, abundantly instructed in letters, and always showing the greatest reverence to Christ’s priests—indeed, to every clerical rank—while bestowing on all persons the beneficence appropriate to each.”]

After his death, because his son Henry was still a very young boy, the lady Empress Agnes, the boy’s mother, held the kingdom under her care for some time and governed it wisely and energetically. Then certain princes, driven by envy, took the boy away from his mother and removed her from the government of the kingdom. Among them was Lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne, who placed the boy on a ship at the place called Werida [Note: [Col. 0939D] Kaiserswerth] and took him away from his mother (in the year 1062).

We cannot discern with what intention he did this or how it pleased the divine judgment. We are certain, however, that many disadvantages arose from that time onward and continued to increase. For dissensions in the kingdom, disturbance of the Church, destruction of monasteries, contempt for the clergy, and the trampling underfoot of all justice and religion both began and continue.

The empress herself, considering the changes in her circumstances, went to Italy (in the year 1069), and for some time led a religious life at the monastery called Fruttuaria. Later she died at Rome and was honorably buried in the church of Saint Petronilla.

[Col. 0940D] The Years of Henry IV

1. In the year 1057 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0939] LVIII corrected to LVII in A.], but 1808 from the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 0939] The “e” is corrected in witness 1], Henry IV, son of Emperor Henry, succeeded his father while still very young and began to reign [Note: [Col. 0942C–D] C, D, and E add: “Pope Stephen died; Gerard, also called Nicholas, succeeded him. Henry, king of France, died, and his son Philip reigned in his place. From Sigebert.”] [Col. 0941A]. At the time this account was written he had reigned for forty-two years [Note: [Col. 0941] Forty-two is written as fifty-two in witness 4.] [Note: [Col. 0942B] Fifty in D.], being eighty-seventh in succession from Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0942A–B] C has: “Henry IV, son of Emperor Henry, still a very young boy, succeeded his father and began to reign, eighty-seventh in succession from Augustus, and reigned for fifty years. Empress Agnes, his mother, assumed the duchy of Bavaria. Through the mediation of Pope Victor, Baldwin and Gotefrid were restored to the king’s favor, and all the disturbances of war were quieted. A certain Frederick and his brothers … came, as above. In Frisia … they are restrained. From Sigebert. In the same year the aforementioned apostolic bishop returned to Rome and ended his present life. Duke Otto of Swabia died, and Rudolf, who was later made king, received the duchy.”]

(Chronicle of Würzburg.) Empress Agnes, his mother, assumed the duchy of Bavaria.

Gebehard, also called Victor, Roman pontiff, having arranged many matters in Germany and in other parts of the Roman kingdom with the counsel of bishops and secular princes, returned peacefully to Rome at the beginning of Lent in that year. He too ended his life in the same year. In his place Frederick, brother of Duke Gotefrid, who had already become a monk, was ordained pontiff by the Romans and called Stephen.

The Saxons, having gathered an army, hostilely invaded the savage people of the Liutizi [Note: [Col. 0941] “Leutici” in A.], afflicted them with various evils, subjected them to Roman rule, and, after receiving hostages and tribute, returned home.

At the same time a certain Frederick and his brothers, exercising tyranny in the regions of Germany against the Roman Empire, were defeated by Empress Agnes and the princes of the kingdom and came to surrender.

Otto of Schweinfurt, duke of Swabia, died on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and Rudolf of Rheinfelden, who later sought to become king [Note: [Col. 0942B] “Was made king” in D and E], received the duchy. This became a great seedbed of the disturbances by which the kingdom was troubled.

While Duke Otto was still alive, Emperor Henry had promised that same duchy to Count Berhtold [Note: [Col. 0941D] “Of Zähringen”], who later received the duchy of Carinthia, and had given him his ring as a reminder of this arrangement. Berhtold carefully preserved it and, after the death of both the emperor and the duke, presented it to the empress Agnes, who was then governing the empire, reminding her of the duchy promised to him when she recognized the ring.

But since the aforementioned Rudolf, shortly after the emperor’s death, married the emperor’s daughter, who had been entrusted to Rumold, bishop of Constance—whether she was abducted by design or by trickery is unknown—the empress, having now received Rudolf back into favor, gave him the duchy on account of her daughter [Note: [Col. 0941] “On account of the daughter” is absent in A]. This greatly disturbed Berhtold.

To alleviate this agitation, the duchy of Carinthia was entrusted to him (in the year 1061). Later, at his request, King Henry entrusted it to his son, who had the same name as Berhtold. Subsequently, however, at the instigation of certain people, he gave the same duchy to his kinsman Liutolf [Note: [Col. 0941] “Liutold” in A], thereby treating father and son with contempt and offending them.

Thus, as though an earlier injury had been renewed, when Duke Berhtold was stirred to action he turned all the devices of his counsels, in which he was very powerful, toward taking revenge on both Rudolf and the king: on the former because he had supplanted him in the duchy promised to him, and on the latter because he had deprived him of what he had received [Note: [Col. 0941] “Because he had deprived him” is absent].

Meanwhile many causes, then handled imprudently, converged with him and provided opportunities for this plot. Duke Otto of Bavaria was deposed; Conrad, a Swabian by birth, was killed by the king’s soldiers (in the year 1070), and the crime was charged against the king as though it had been ordered by him.

Otto therefore conspired in Saxony and Berhtold in Swabia. Disturbances and assemblies took place in both regions, in which hatred and envy against the king were stirred up. Many other things were also happening meanwhile in the kingdom, and these turned both peoples away from adhering to the king for reasons that seemed just and necessary. Matters were brought to such a point that Rudolf invaded the kingdom to his own condemnation and sought to depose or kill his lord, the king (in the year 1076). But even peasants are not unaware of what outcome this affair would have.

[Col. 0942B] 2. A.D. 1058. Frederick, also called Stephen, Roman pontiff, ended his life. [Note: [Col. 0942C] C has: “Frederick, son of Duke Gothelon, a cleric of Saint Lambert of Liège, whom Pope Leo, because he was hated by Emperor Henry and exiled out of hatred for his brother Gotefrid, had taken to himself as seventh levite and chancellor of the Roman Church; after the embassy to Constantinople he became a monk among the Cassinese and was promoted to abbot of Monte Cassino. He was elected pope by the Romans, and, changing his name, presided over the Church as Stephen. From Sigebert.” The year is omitted in E.]

Alexander, bishop of Lucca, succeeded him. During his time Hildebrand, later pontiff, held the office of archdeacon at Rome.

3. A.D. 1059.

[Col. 0942D] 4. A.D. 1060. Luitpold, archbishop of Mainz, died [Note: [Col. 0942D] M has “bishop.” C, D, and E have: “He died; Sigifrid F. was appointed in his place”; the remainder is absent there.]; Sigifrid, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him; he later joined with others against his lord, the king.

6. A.D. 1062. [Note: [Col. 0942D–0943A] C adds: “Anno, archbishop of Cologne, with the counsel of the leading men of the kingdom—who, as though they were unwilling to endure that public affairs should be governed by a woman, the empress, in an unmanly fashion—violently and cunningly seized the boy king and placed him under his own guardianship, removing the government of the empire from his mother. After giving an account of this matter before everyone, he regained the favor of his lord the king, and through the son himself returned to the favor of his mother.

“Empress Agnes, turning necessity into willingness, so that she might close the mouth of those speaking wickedly, not long afterward rejected not only the honor of the kingdom but also the burden of worldly affairs. She went to Rome, to the threshold of the apostle Peter, and there, until the end of her life, became an example and a marvel to all through every kind of virtue. From Sigebert.”]

[Col. 0943A] D. 1063. [Note: [Col. 0943A–B] C, D, and E add: “Pope Nicholas died; Alexander, bishop of Lucca, succeeded him. A certain bishop of Parma, however, shamefully sought the papacy and scandalized Christ’s Church even to the shedding of blood. But much later, through Anno, bishop of Cologne, who was then serving as legate in the transalpine regions, and all the bishops of Italy, this controversy was resolved: the bishop of Parma was deposed, and Alexander, as justice required, was confirmed. Compare Sigebert.” [Note: [Col. 0943B] E1, in another hand, and 2 add: “Eggilhard, seventh archbishop of Magdeburg, died.”]]

[Col. 0943B] 8. A.D. 1064. Sigifrid, bishop of Mainz; Gunther, bishop of Babenberg; William, bishop of Utrecht; and many other prelates and nobles, traveling toward Jerusalem with a large retinue, suffered many attacks from barbarians. At last, having achieved the desired arrival, they returned greatly reduced in number and possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0943C] “And William of Utrecht” is absent in C.]

9. A.D. 1065. Gunther, bishop of Babenberg, died in Pannonia while returning from Jerusalem. His body was carried to Babenberg and buried there; after him Hermann was appointed. —Count Gozwin, exercising tyranny in the bishopric of Würzburg, was killed by the retainers of Bishop Adelbero.

10. A.D. 1066. A comet appeared for a long time throughout the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0943D] C adds: “Harwich … twenty-one years.” From Sigebert; the remainder of this year is absent.]

In the same year England was miserably afflicted and finally subdued by William the Norman, who himself became its king. He soon condemned nearly all the bishops of that kingdom to exile and the nobles to death; he reduced the common people to servitude under his soldiers; and he subjected the wives of all the natives to marriage with newcomers. [Note: [Col. 0943D] Numbers 10 and 11 add: “Conrad, born at Pfullingen near Trier, was elected; after suffering at the hands of Count Dietrich, he was buried at Dole.” From Bernold.]

11. A.D. 1067. [Note: [Col. 0944A] C, D, and E add: “Conrad, principal cantor of the church of Cologne, designated bishop of Trier by King Henry, was captured by Theoderic, count of that city. His retainers led him into a forest, threw him three times from the top of a mountain, and, when he was still unharmed, pierced him through with a sword. From Sigebert.”]

King Henry took Bertha, daughter of a certain Italian Otto and Adelheid, as his wife, celebrating the wedding at Tribur.

12. A.D. 1068. King Henry, enjoying the freedom of youth, began to inhabit Saxony alone among all the territories of the Roman Empire; to despise the princes; to oppress the nobles; to support the lower orders; and, as he was accused, to devote himself more to hunting, games, and other exercises of this kind than to the administration of justice. He married the daughters of distinguished men to persons of obscure birth and established private garrisons, evidently because he did not sufficiently trust the powerful men of the kingdom.

From these seeds of discord it happened that very many plotters against both the king’s life and his kingdom grew up against him. Yet, since he had not fully reached the years of maturity, there were those who judged that not so much he himself as Adelbert, archbishop of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0943] “Adelbero” in A], should be blamed, because he did all these things on the archbishop’s advice.

13. A.D. 1062 [Note: [Col. 0943] The history for the year 1069 is read in witness 4 after the year 1070.] Empress Agnes, mother of King Henry, afflicted with weariness, or rather pierced by divine prompting, laid down the duchy of Bavaria. Repenting and despising the government of the kingdom for Christ’s sake, she went to Rome. There, serving with marvelous humility the worthy fruits of repentance [Col. 0944C], she ended this present life in the Lord after several years. [Note: [Col. 0944C] C adds: “The Hungarians … are restrained.” From Sigebert.]

14. A.D. 1070. [Note: [Col. 0943] In the margin of witness 5, in another hand: “Note: from this point the modern chronicle begins.”]

Margrave Teti began a tyranny in the royal territories, not without the counsel of the princes of Saxony. It was soon restrained by both heavenly and earthly majesty: the king destroyed his castles at Bichlingen and Schidingen [Note: [Col. 0943D] Compare Lambert above, under the year 1069]; his son, likewise a warrior, was killed by his own servant; and Teti himself soon died an ordinary death. [Note: [Col. 0944C] Numbers 10 and 11 add: “Rudolf, bishop of Constance, died.” From Bernold.]

15. A.D. 1071. Otto lost the duchy of Bavaria. This man was a Saxon by birth, of the highest nobility, and scarcely comparable to anyone in prudence and military matters. He was held in such high esteem among all the leading men that the king—already wholly mistrusted and hated by the Saxons—feared that, if affairs went otherwise, Otto might be elevated against him to the summit of the kingdom [Col. 0944D]. [Note: [Col. 0943] “By the Saxons” is absent in A.]

Taking advantage of this opportunity for perversity, a certain Egino, born in a middling station and very poor in possessions but sufficiently notorious for audacity and wickedness, entered the court with the support of certain royal loyalists. He invented the claim that the great hero, whom he had never known, had discussed the king’s murder with him. As is customary, Egino also offered himself as a pledge to the royal power until he could prove the truth of his report by fighting the duke in a champion’s duel.

What more is needed? At royal hearings or conferences, one appointed at Mainz and the other at Goslar, Otto scorned to fight with Egino, as a duke with a robber and a leading man with a person of low birth. Yet either his innocence or Egino’s wickedness was by no means concealed. Thus Otto lost the duchy of Bavaria as one accused of treason against the majesty of the ruler [Note: [Col. 0945] “Otto” is absent in A]. A certain distinguished, vigorous, and warlike Swabian by birth, Welefo, received it.

This became the seed of such a great discord between the ruling powers that, alas, it sprouted and grew into the lamentable fruits of perpetual wars and rebellions, plunder and fires, even schisms and heresies, and deaths.

[Note: [Col. 0945B] The continuation beginning “If affairs …” is absent in C, D, and E; C continues: “A certain Egino …”]

16. A.D. 1072. The king pursued Otto everywhere [Note: [Col. 0945D] This belongs to the year 1071], destroyed very many of his fortifications, devastated his estates, and planned to eliminate him entirely as a true enemy of the state. Otto, on the other hand, equipped with picked soldiers, himself also very strong-handed and excessively fierce in spirit, because he could not engage the royal forces directly, strove to avenge his injuries wherever chance offered, now by plunder, now by fire, now even by the sword [Note: [Col. 0945] “Wherever …” is absent in A; witness 1 has “as chance offered”].

Finally, through his agency, the Saxon people, fierce in spirit as they are, did not cease to confirm by unanimous conspiracy a plot against the king, to bring blasphemous and unheard-of accusations against him to the apostolic see, and to enlist allies for themselves from throughout the Teutonic kingdom by letters and messages.

First they made Sigifrid, metropolitan of the see of Mainz; Adelbert of Worms; Adelbero of Würzburg; Gebehard of Salzburg; and many other prelates [Note: [Col. 0945C] C has “prelates or princes who supported them”] their supporters, and then, through these men, even Pope Alexander [Note: [Col. 0945C] A adds “as they say”; Ekkehard himself deleted it in witness 1] was made their supporter. Some also assert that Anno, archbishop of Cologne, a man of the highest sanctity, was involved in the same conspiracy.

Terrified by their plots, the king withdrew from Saxony and devoted himself to conducting affairs in other parts of the kingdom.

[Col. 0945D] 17. A.D. 1073. Anno, bishop of Cologne, and Hermann of Babenberg were sent to Rome to gather the money owed to the king. After completing their embassy and returning, they brought letters from Alexander the apostolic bishop [Note: [Col. 0945D] Compare Bonizo, in Oefelius II, p. 810, concerning the synod held by Alexander at Rome that year], summoning the king to give satisfaction for the simoniacal heresy and for several other matters deserving correction that had been heard about him at Rome [Col. 0946A].

After this the Saxons also began to construct many fortifications—for Saxony as yet did not possess more [Note: [Col. 0946A] This note appears in column 946, but its callout sign (**) was not printed in the text: “is absent in C.”] fortifications [Note: [Col. 0945] “Saxony” is absent in A.] [Note: [Col. 0945D] “The same thing as Liudprand attests in Book II, chapter 24, of the fifth century.”]. Moreover, they utterly destroyed the castles that the king had formerly built. Among them they demolished the prominent castle called Harzburg [Note: [Col. 0945] “Harzesburg” in A] and, acting with great audacity, razed to the ground the monastery and the canons’ cloister that stood there. What is unspeakable, they threw from the tomb the bones of an innocent son of the king who had been buried there, in insult to his father. [Note: [Col. 0946A] C adds: “Two brothers … to acquire.” From Sigebert.]

[Col. 0946B] 18. A.D. 1074. After Pope Alexander of blessed memory had died [Note: [Col. 0946D] More correctly, Ekkehard, revising his work in a second edition, placed this under the year 1073], Hildebrand, later called Gregory [Note: [Col. 0946B] “Gregory VII” in D and E], a monk by profession and an archdeacon, succeeded to the Roman see. Under him the Roman state and the whole Church began to be endangered by new and unheard-of errors of schism.

Because he had ascended this height without the king’s consent and solely with the support of the Romans, there are those who maintain that he was not canonically appointed but had tyrannically usurped the papacy for himself. For this reason he was also deposed by certain bishops [Note: [Col. 0945] “By some bishops” is written in a space erased in witness 1].

He summoned King Henry once again to synodal judgment by repeated messages and letters. [Note: [Col. 0946C] C adds: “For the simoniacal heresy and several other matters deserving correction that had been heard about him at Rome.” C, D, and E add: “In 1074 Pope Gregory held a synod and anathematized the simoniacs—that is, sellers and buyers of the gift of the Holy Spirit. He decreed that the Nicolaitans, namely married priests, were to be removed from the ministry of the altar, and forbade laypeople to hear their Masses. C continues: ‘By a just judgment, certainly, but by a new precedent and, as many thought, an ill-considered prejudice.’ From Sigebert.”]

[Note: [Col. 0946C] Numbers 4 and 6–11 add: “In this same year the monastery of Schwarzach was dedicated by Adelbero, bishop of Würzburg, in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Felicitas the martyr, under Ekkebert, the venerable abbot of that monastery.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Witness 4 has “Erkebert”; it is corrected to “Ekebert” in 7 and to “Eckebert” in 9c.] Numbers 10 and 11 preface this with: “Margrave Hermann, son of Duke Berhtold, died a monk at Cluny.” From Bernold.]

[Col. 0946D] 19. A.D. 1075. King Henry, having gathered a strong force from Alemannia, Bavaria, Germany, and Bohemia, attacked the Saxons and engaged them near the river Unstrut. After a considerable slaughter on both sides, he finally obtained victory and returned.

There Rudolf, duke of Alemannia and Burgundy, who later invaded the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0947A] “Held” in D and E], was observed to have fought bravely with his men on behalf of the king.

Hermann of Babenberg was deposed from the episcopate by the authority of Pope Hildebrand on account of the simoniacal heresy, and Ruotpert was appointed in his place by the king.

Anno, archbishop of Cologne, full of the merits of holiness [Note: [Col. 0947] “Of works and merits” in witness 5], died and was laid to rest in the monastery of Siegburg, which he himself had built. Hildolf succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0947A] The continuation is absent in C: “After this crushing defeat all the princes, bishops, dukes, counts, and other powerful men of the Saxons were handed over by surrender to royal authority and were compelled to make peace. The Hungarians, etc. From Sigebert. Anno, etc.”] [Note: [Col. 0947A–B] Numbers 10 and 11 add: “Lord Ekkebert, abbot of this community, departed to the Lord on the seventh day before the Kalends of December.”]

[Col. 0947B] **20. A.D. 1076.** [Note: [Col. 0948C] E. 1. Another hand adds in the margin: “Bernhard the Elder, eighth abbot of St John the Baptist, died.”] A council was held at Worms, where, in the presence of King Heinricus, nearly all the German bishops except the Saxons renounced Pope Hiltibrandus [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “king”], sending him a letter which, after many accusations brought against him, concluded as follows [Note: [Col. 0947D] This letter was published in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges* II, p. 44]:

> Since, therefore, both your entrance into office was initiated by such perjuries, and the Church of God is endangered by so grievous a storm through the abuse of your innovations, and you have dishonored your life and conduct [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “and conduct”] with such [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “has”] manifold infamy, we announce that we neither promised you obedience nor intend henceforth to observe any; and since none of us, as you publicly proclaimed, has hitherto been your bishop, you likewise shall henceforth be apostolic for none of us.

[Note: [Col. 0948C] C continues: “On the contrary, Pope Hiltibrandus inveighs at length against the king and his supporters—and tries to turn them away,” from Sigebert. “Therefore, when he had been summoned by the Apostolic See under threat of excommunication to come and make satisfaction, he disdainfully refused,” with the rest omitted.]

In that same year, around the 18th [Note: [Col. 0947D] Lambert and Bernold have “17 Kalends of October.”] day before the Kalends of October, a great assembly was held at Oppenheim. There nearly all the princes of the kingdom, but especially those of Saxony and Alemannia, renounced subjection to the king, alleging as their reason that, although summoned by two apostolic authorities to make satisfaction, he had not come, and that for this contempt he had received a sentence of excommunication from the pope at a Roman synod, even though he himself had been unheard and absent.

Compelled by this upheaval, the king set out for Rome humbly, intending to seek pardon from the apostolic authority, contrary to the expectations of his enemies. Finding the pope at the town of Canossa, he remained there for three days before the castle gate, having laid aside all royal attire, barefoot and clothed in wool. Nor did he cease imploring, with much weeping, the aid and consolation [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “consolations”] of apostolic mercy until, through the prayers and tears of all who were present, the bond of anathema was finally loosened and he was received into the grace of communion and the bosom of Mother Church, after receiving from him many assurances concerning the correction of his life in the future. [Note: [Col. 0947D] This is copied word for word from a letter of Gregory VII, *Registrum* IV, 12.]

The whole world already bears witness to the upheaval caused by these events. But since some say that Ruodolfus was elevated to the kingship by the pope’s authority and counsel, while others deny that King Heinricus was excommunicated by him, it seems appropriate to record certain statements of that same pope, especially on these matters. For in a letter sent to all the princes of the German kingdom he says [Note: [Col. 0948D] See this letter in Bruno, chapter 72, and elsewhere, though not in the *Register*]:

> We have heard that some among you doubt concerning the excommunication which we pronounced against the king [Note: [Col. 0947] A has a corrupt reading here: “dubita … feci”], and ask whether he was excommunicated justly or unjustly. We admonished him to do penance for his deeds. But he, taking it badly that anyone should rebuke him [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “that he should be … by anyone”], could not be recalled from his offenses to amendment; rather, seized by greater fury, he did not desist until he had caused nearly all the bishops of Italy, and as many as he could in the German lands, to suffer shipwreck concerning the faith of Christ, by making them deny the obedience and honor owed to blessed Peter and to the Apostolic See, which had been granted by our Lord Jesus Christ. For these reasons—first, because he refused to abstain from the communion of those who had been excommunicated for sacrilege and the crime of simoniacal heresy; and then because, for his criminal acts, he was unwilling not merely to undertake penance but even to promise it—we excommunicated him [Note: [Col. 0947] A omits “him”] by synodal judgment.

Likewise, in another letter, after the reconciliation had been granted [Note: [Col. 0948D] See the excommunication of the king pronounced at the Roman council of 1080 in Mansi XX, p. 534], he says:

> I restored communion to him alone,

[Col. 0948C] but did not restore him to the kingdom, from which I had deposed him at the Roman synod.

And after inserting certain material he says:

> The bishops and princes from beyond the Alps, hearing that he did not keep what he had promised me, and as though they had despaired of him, elected Ruodolfus as king for themselves without my counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0948C] Numbers 10–11 add: “A certain Roman citizen named Centius, one of Heinricus’s supporters, seized Pope Gregory while he was celebrating Mass [Note: [Col. 0947] Number 10 reads “Mass” in the nominative] at cockcrow on the Nativity of the Lord, dragged him grievously wounded from the altar, and imprisoned him in his tower. The people, angered by this, destroyed Centius’s tower that same day, and, with difficulty sparing his life, restored the pope to his place. Beforehand, however, the Mass had been completed at the altar, with the pope supported, although he had begun it earlier and had not yet finished it. Cf. Bernoldus.”]

[Col. 0949A] **21. A.D. 1077.** [Note: [Col. 0949] “Year” and “native” are in an erased place.] Ruodolfus, a native of Swabia, a land entirely foreign to royal descent [Note: [Col. 0949] Number 4 omits “a land entirely foreign to royal descent”], was elevated as king at Forchheim through the agency of Sigefridus, metropolitan bishop, and Adelbero, bishop of Würzburg, together with Berhtolfus, duke of Carinthia, the aforementioned Otto, and several other princes, in the presence of certain legates of the Roman See who gave their assent unwillingly.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] C has this for the year: “A frost lasted until the spring equinox,” from Sigebert, under the year 1076. “King Heinricus crossed the mountains and, with the pope stationed in the castle of Canossa, made satisfaction with the utmost humility; after receiving absolution and communion, he made peace. But how soon that peace between the kingdom and the priesthood was broken, the whole world, greatly stirred by it, now knows.” Meanwhile, while these things were occurring, the Saxons and Alemanni, with their bishops and princes, through the mediation of Sigefridus of Mainz, Adelbero of Würzburg, and Welefo, duke of Bavaria, elevated Ruodolfus, duke of Swabia and Burgundy, as king over themselves. Certain legates of the Apostolic See gave unwilling assent, and later, as he himself habitually did, excused the Apostolicus for this consent. “He was then led to Mainz, but, terrified by Heinricus’s arrival, withdrew,” as above, somewhat more briefly. “He himself crossed the Alps,” etc., from Sigebert. “Heinricus fought,” as above. “Heinricus displayed courage,” from Sigebert under 1078. “Berhtolfus, formerly duke of Carinthia, now an old man and regarded as the wisest man in the kingdom, by whose counsel a king was set over the king, at one of his towns, Lintperg,” etc.]

He was led from there to Mainz and was anointed king by Bishop Sigefridus in the middle of Lent, on the 12th [Note: [Col. 0949D] Read with Bruno: “7 Kalends of April, Laetare Sunday.”] day before the Kalends of April. There, on that same day, under a most evil omen, a revolt broke out, and a great crowd of common people was killed by his soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0950A] M. adds: “But he himself, leaving Mainz with the metropolitan bishop Sigefridus, went into Saxony, where, having gathered a large army, he …” The Würzburg material and the remainder are omitted.]

The populace consequently became inflamed against them, struck down many with heavy blows, drove the rest into the palace courtyard, and tried to set fire to the royal buildings, except that Bishop Sigefridus offered himself as a hostage to secure Ruodolfus’s swift departure. Thus Ruodolfus and all who had come with him were expelled; Bishop Sigefridus himself was also driven out amid great blasphemies and never again entered Mainz.

Afterward, having gathered a large army from Saxony (August), Ruodolfus besieged the people of Würzburg, who remained faithful to King Heinricus and despised both their bishop Adelbero and themselves. But once various engines had been prepared for the assault on the city, he withdrew without accomplishing anything, terrified by King Heinricus, who had returned from Italy around the [Note: [Col. 0949] “Around … Italy” is in an erased place.] Kalends of July.

King Heinricus, however, marched into Alemannia with an army [Col. 0949C] (in 1078). There he defeated, not without great devastation of that province, a certain native named Hugo [Note: [Col. 0949D] Of Tübingen; see Stalin, *History of Württemberg* I, p. 561. These events and those that follow belong to 1078.] and others who had rebelled against him there.

Berhctoldus [Note: [Col. 0949] A has “Berhtolfus”] of Zähringen, formerly duke of Carinthia, had taken refuge in one of his naturally fortified towns, Lintperg [Note: [Col. 0950D] Near Kirchheim in Württemberg], and, seeing everything laid waste with impunity at the king’s command, is said, from grief of mind, to have been seized by the illness which physicians call frenzy. He survived for seven days afterward, uttered many senseless words as though delirious, and so ended his life. [Note: [Col. 0950B] C, D, and E have: “Overcome by grief of mind and bodily illness, he ended his present life.”]

During that expedition Uto, archbishop of Trier, died. [Note: [Col. 0950B] Numbers 10–11 add: “Agnes, mother of King Heinricus, died at Rome after twenty-nine years of widowhood and was buried in the church of Saint Petronilla,” from Bernoldus.]

[Col. 0950B] **22. A.D. 1078.** King Heinricus met Ruodolfus, who was advancing against him with a large army, near the Strow. After battle had been joined (August 7), not a few on both sides were struck down, and victory remained uncertain, with both sides fleeing in haste to their own territories.

There, Wecil, archbishop of Magdeburg, was killed in flight by common men—or, as some say, was hanged. Duke Magnus was stripped of his possessions; Herimannus, Magnus’s uncle, and Adelbertus, bishop of Worms, were captured; and many of the Saxon soldiers were disgracefully killed. On King Heinricus’s side [Note: [Col. 0949] A reads “On King Heinricus’s side”], Poppo [Note: [Col. 0950D] Of Henneberg], a remarkably brave man, fell. [Note: [Col. 0950C] Number 5 adds: “Hildolfus, archbishop of Cologne, died; Sigewinus succeeded him.”]

**23. A.D. 1079.** War again broke out between Heinricus and Ruodolfus at a place called Fladehcheim [Note: [Col. 0950D] Flarcheim, near Mühlhausen], during an exceptionally harsh winter (1080, January 27). At the first encounter the Saxons turned their backs. [Note: [Col. 0949] E2 has: “The emperor turned his back,” written by another hand in an erased place.]

There Duke Fratizlaus of Bohemia acquired Ruodolfus’s royal lance. Thereafter, by permission of King Heinricus, it always preceded anyone of that people who bore the insignia of the dukedom in every festive procession.

King Heinricus, however, returned to his own camp and found scarcely any of the armed men he had left there. One of the Saxon legions, abandoning the battle at the first encounter because the air was dark, secretly invaded the king’s camp, captured many boys, strangled them, and, carrying off much plunder, fled. The king, having dismissed his army, turned aside into eastern Francia with a few men.

[Note: [Col. 0951A] Number 5 adds: “In this same year the city of Erfurt was burned by the army of King Heinricus. As the multitude, as is customary, fled for refuge into the churches, the churches of the saints were burned. Among them was the monastery of Saint Severus, called the Upper Monastery, which was burned with a multitude of people and afterward destroyed; another, smaller monastery was later rebuilt on the same site. On the mountain at the same place, the monastery of Saint Peter, which King Tagobertus of the Franks had built long ago [Note: [Col. 0951D] Compare the passage edited in the same manuscript, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* III, p. 33, line XLVIII], was also burned. Thereafter, weakened by age and fire alike, it collapsed and was destroyed, and another of larger construction was built.”]

[Col. 0951A] **24. A.D. 1030.** When an assembly of thirty bishops, together with an army of nobles—not only from Italy but also from Germany—was being gathered at Brixina in Noricum by order of King Heinricus (June 25), all agreed against Pope Hiltibrandus, called Gregory VII. Declaring him a pseudo-monk, the destructive leader of every madness, and especially an invader of the Holy Roman See, they judged that he should be expelled from the Apostolic See, although absent, and elected Wigpertus, archbishop of Ravenna, to be substituted for him.

The conclusion of this decree [Note: [Col. 0952C] C omits “The conclusion of this decree … famous for miracles.”] [Note: [Col. 0951D] The complete text is in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges* II, p. 51] is as follows:

> Since, they say, it is clear that he was not chosen by God but, through fraud and money, was most imprudently thrust forward by himself; since he subverts ecclesiastical order, disturbs the kingdom of the Christian empire, threatens bodily and spiritual death to the Catholic and peaceful king, defends a perjured king, sows discord among those who are united, quarrels among the peaceful, scandals among brothers, divorces among spouses, and has shaken whatever appeared to stand securely among the pious and peaceable: we, gathered together by God’s authority, relying on the legates and letters of the nineteen bishops assembled at Mainz on the holy day of the previous Pentecost, judge that the same most insolent Hiltibrandus—who preaches sacrileges and conflagrations, defends perjuries and murders, calls the Catholic and apostolic faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord into question [Note: [Col. 0951] A omits “concerning the body and blood of the Lord”], is the ancient disciple of the heretic Berengarius, a worshiper of divinations and dreams, a manifest necromancer, afflicted by a pythonic spirit, and therefore deviating from the true faith—must canonically be deposed and expelled, and, unless he withdraws from that See after hearing these charges, condemned forever.

These things were done on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, Thursday, in the third indiction.

After this Anshelmus, bishop of Lucca, wrote a letter to the same Wigpertus [Note: [Col. 0952C] “The aforesaid,” D and E], in which he calls him a transgressor and proud, adding among other things:

> To speak, then, of blessed Gregory, our father, what blessed Cyprian wrote concerning Cornelius: he became bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clergy—or, more truly, of all of them—by the support of the people who were then present, and by the company of the ancient priests and good men, when no one had been made bishop before him, when the place of Alexander—that is, the place of Peter and the rank of the priestly chair—was vacant. Once it had been occupied and he had been ordained by God’s will and by the consent of all of us, whoever thereafter wishes to become bishop must be outside; nor does he possess ecclesiastical ordination who does not preserve the Church’s unity. Whoever he may be, even if he boasts greatly of himself and claims much for himself, he is profane, alien, outside. Since after the first there cannot be a second, whoever has been made after the one who alone ought to exist is no longer a second but nothing.

Anshelmus, a bishop highly learned in letters, exceptionally acute in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and—greater than all these qualities—renowned for fear of God and holy conduct, wrote this in strong opposition to his earlier judgment. He was so celebrated that he is reported to have been famous for miracles both during his life and after his death.

After these events, war again took place between King Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0951] A omits “King Heinricus”] and Ruodolfus near the river Elster (October 15). Ruodolfus fell there, but his men carried him alive to Merseburg; he died shortly afterward and was honorably buried there. [Note: [Col. 0951D] On his tomb, which still stands there, see Dethier in Forstemann, *Mittheilungen* I.2, pp. 22 ff. It bears this inscription:]

> Here lies King Ruodolfus, slain for the law of his fathers,  
> Deservedly mourned, buried in this tomb.  
> If a king like him should rule in a time of peace,  
> In counsel and in sword, he would not have been inferior to Charles.  
> In the battle in which his followers were victorious, he fell here, a sacred victim of war;  
> His death was life for him, but for the Church he fell.

It is nevertheless reported [Note: [Col. 0952C] C, D, and E omit “It is reported … you might have led”] that, when he was near death and looking at his severed right hand, he said with a deep sigh to the bishops who happened to be present:

> Behold this hand, with which I confirmed my loyalty by oath to my lord Heinricus. Behold, I am now abandoning his kingdom and this present life. See to it—you who made me mount his throne—that you might have led me along the right path as I followed your counsels.

In this battle also, on King Heinricus’s side, Count Ratpoto [Note: [Col. 0952D] Compare Moritz, *Neue historische Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie* V, p. 548], a man very loyal to the king, died.

**25. A.D. 1081.** [Note: [Col. 0953A] D and E add: “Magnus … foretelling, as some thought, the approaching … grieved and still grieves,” from Sigebert.] King Heinricus marched into Italy with an army and, reaching Rome on the vigil of Pentecost (May 22), set up camp before the castle of Saint Peter, while Pope Hiltibrandus and the Romans resisted him. There, although the townspeople harassed him with frequent attacks for two years, he accomplished many brave deeds with a small force.

[Note: [Col. 0953A] C, D, and E add: “Mainz was largely consumed by fire, with the principal church and three monasteries burned. Compare Sigebert and p. 205, note [1].” Numbers 1b and 5 add: “The monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz, with three adjoining monasteries, was burned, and nearly the whole city was destroyed. Heinricus the fifth of this name, who deprived his father of the kingdom, was born. Compare the Würzburg Annals.”]

The monastery of Babenberg was burned on the Easter vigil (April 3). The Saxons and Alemanni, having come to an assembly in eastern Francia, returned only after suffering great losses in that province.

A battle was fought in eastern Bavaria between Chuonradus, the brother of the duke of Bohemia, and Luitpoldus [Note: [Col. 0953] “Luitboldus” corrected to “Luitpoldus” in 1; A has “Liutpoldus”], the margrave, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

Another battle was fought between the Alemanni and Bavarians on the third day before the Ides of August near the Danube at Hochstein [Note: [Col. 0953D] Hochstedt; compare the *Annals of Augsburg* and Bernoldus under this year], where Chuono, the son of Count Palatine Chuono, was killed.

[Note: [Col. 0953A] Numbers 1b and 5 repeat: “The monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz, with three adjoining monasteries, was burned, and nearly the whole city was destroyed. Heinricus the fifth of this name, who deprived his father of the kingdom, was born. Compare the Würzburg Annals.”]

[Col. 0953B] **26. A.D. 1082.** A certain Herimannus, a powerful and noble man from Germany, was made king by the Saxons and Alemanni [Note: [Col. 0953D] Already in 1081, August 9.]. With his supporters in those regions—that is, in Lorraine or Germany [Note: [Col. 0953B] C omits “that is, in Lorraine or Germany”]—no one could equal him in military matters or wealth. Yet, once he had assumed the royal title, he soon began to be despised by both his own people and outsiders.

**27. A.D. 1083.** Herimannus invaded eastern Francia with a few men in a hostile manner. An army of horsemen also seemed to be racing throughout that region, though their tracks could in no way be identified.

King Heinricus celebrated Easter at Santa Rufina. Soon afterward, advancing toward Rome, he established his camp where he had done so previously, on the western side of the castle of Saint Peter. The city was captured on the fourth day before the Nones of June, the Friday before the octave of Pentecost.

At that time Pope Hiltibrandus, confined in the castle of Crescentius, commonly called the House of Theoderic, awaited the outcome. The king, meanwhile, constructed a fortification on the Palatine Hill and lost not a few of the men he had stationed there, as an unusually intense summer heat grew oppressive. Many others in the army were also carried off by the same mortality.

At the same time envoys of the Greeks arrived, bringing many large gifts of gold and silver, vessels, and silks.

The Romans, giving the king twenty hostages [Note: [Col. 0953] At this point one leaf is missing in 1], chosen from among the nobles, asked that a day be appointed on which the pope and all the senators would come into his presence [Note: [Col. 0953] “Would assemble,” 2]. He appointed the Kalends of November and himself climbed into the mountains at the beginning of July. Remaining there until the appointed time [Note: [Col. 0953] A omits this], he returned to Rome in November; but the pope did not come into his presence. [Note: [Col. 0954A] C, D, and E add: “He came, but secretly,” with the remainder omitted.]

The Romans, therefore, becoming agitated, surrendered to the king, while they unanimously deposed Pope Hiltibrandus [Note: [Col. 0953] “By unanimous consent,” 4]. He fled secretly, withdrew to Salerno, and remained there until the day of his death. [Note: [Col. 0953] 1 has “there until”; 4 has “there”; 10–11 have “remained there.”]

In the same year Welefo, formerly duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0954A] C omits “formerly”], entered the city of Augsburg very early in the morning [Note: [Col. 0953] “The city,” 4]. Bishop Sigifridus barely escaped [Note: [Col. 0953] “Sigefridus,” 5, 10, 11], and Welefo enthroned a certain Wigoldus, a canon of that place.

**28. A.D. 1084.** Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0953] E has “King Heinricus”] celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome in Saint Peter’s. Around the Kalends of February he crossed into Campania and captured it [Note: [Col. 0953] “And it,” 4] and a large part of Apulia.

Afterward, when the Romans asked through envoys that he return peacefully, he returned to Rome and set up camp at the Lateran Gate. He received all who surrendered [Note: [Col. 0953] “All the surrendering people,” D1; “those who surrendered,” 4; “accepted them into surrender,” 11; A and S], and, at their request, because Hiltibrandus, having been deposed by them, had fled [Note: [Col. 0953] Number 2 omits from “that” through “had fled”; number 4 omits from “because” through “bishop”], he appointed Wigpertus [Note: [Col. 0953] “Wehebertus,” 2], bishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0953] “Ravennate,” 9], as their pope [Note: [Col. 0954C] C, D, and E omit from “at their request” through “as their pope,” continuing “and on the eleventh day before the Kalends”]; he entered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0954D] The following day seems more correct; compare Stenzel II, p. 283], the Friday before Palm Sunday, accompanied by many and with great glory, bringing with him the aforesaid bishop. [Note: [Col. 0954C] C, D, and E have “the aforesaid Bishop Wigpertus.”]

On the following Sunday (March 24), he was reverently enthroned by many bishops, dedicated to the apostolic name and taking the name Clement [Note: [Col. 0953] “Bishops,” 4; C, D, and E add “at the chair of Peter.”]. From him the king, together with Queen Berhta [Note: [Col. 0953] 4 omits “with Queen”; E1 has “Bertha”], was elevated by imperial blessing on holy Easter Sunday [Note: [Col. 0953] “On Easter Day,” 4]. [Note: [Col. 0954C] C, D, and E read: “was elevated to the imperial title.”]

After this Emperor Heinricus departed from Italy, besieged and captured the city of Augsburg, which had been invaded by the Alemanni [Note: [Col. 0953] “The city,” 4; “received,” 10–11]. After Archbishop Sigifridus of Mainz died, Wecil succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0953] D1 has “Wezil”; 10–11 have “Wicil”; 2 has “Wicil.”]

[**The first year of Emperor Heinricus IV**]

**29. 2. A.D. 1085.** A synod was held at Mainz (May), attended by the emperor. In the presence of envoys of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0956B] C, D, and E have “the Wigpertine envoys”], all the bishops who were hostile to the emperor were judged worthy of deposition [Note: [Col. 0953] “Restoration,” 4]; the others were condemned by anathema, as it seemed [Note: [Col. 0953] Number 4 reads “the others, as it appeared, were condemned to anathema”; A omits “as it seemed”]. There, by common consent and counsel, the Peace of God was also established. [Note: [Col. 0954D] Published in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges* II, p. 55.]

Not long afterward, after the emperor had appointed bishops throughout the dioceses in place of those who had been deposed, Meginhardus, commendable in conduct and scarcely inferior to anyone in learning, intellect, and eloquence [Note: [Col. 0955] 4 omits “in learning”], was ordained bishop of the Church of Würzburg in place of Adelbero. [Note: [Col. 0956B] D, E, and 5–11 add: “worthy to have been bishop in another age.”]

After Emperor Heinricus had been peacefully received by the Saxons, a certain margrave, Eggibertus [Note: [Col. 0955] “Ekkibertus,” 5; “Egelbertus,” 2], also the emperor’s kinsman [Note: [Col. 0955] 4 omits this], vigorous in arms, spirited, and exceedingly rich, again stirred up tyranny against the emperor in Saxony. When the emperor learned of this, he quickly returned to Francia.

In the same year, a conference agreed upon by both the emperor’s enemies and his friends [Note: [Col. 0955] “By his enemies and friends,” 6], was held in Thuringia (January 20), at a place called Berchach [Note: [Col. 0955] “Bergbach,” A; “Berchac,” 4; “Bercha,” 9c] [Note: [Col. 0955D] Berkach on the Werra]. From both sides came all who were considered the wisest among the nobles, intending to prove by the authority of the canons which side justice favored. The emperor, however, was absent, for he had consented to this arrangement.

After suitably learned and eloquent men had been chosen—on one side Wecil [Note: [Col. 0955] “Wecelone,” A, and below], archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0955] Number 5 reads “Maguntino” (of Mainz), and likewise below; A has “Moguntino” (of Mainz)], and on the other Gebehardus [Note: [Col. 0955] 2 has “Everhardus of Salzburg”], archbishop of Salzburg—the debate began.

Gebehardus affirmed, after Wecil had first proposed the matter, that the emperor had been deprived both of the kingdom and of communion by a just judgment of the Apostolicus. Wecil, on the contrary, contended that his lord had suffered prejudice no less from the pope than from the princes, since, while he was at Canossa making satisfaction—or rather, after he had already been received into communion by the pope—they had elevated another king over him.

The man of Mainz also added that the emperor, long since driven from Saxony and deprived of the opportunity to rule even by that dissension which is recorded as having taken place before Ruodolfus, ought not canonically to have been summoned, judged, or condemned.

Gebehardus, attempting to disprove this, asserted that no one was thereby absolved from the divine laws if he happened to have been stripped of some part of his property; still less was this true of a king, since Saxony was not merely his own possession but the Lord’s kingdom, and, as Daniel—or King Nebuchadnezzar himself—testifies (Daniel IV, 14), God gives it to whomever he wishes. Moreover, before losing Saxony, the king had first been summoned by Alexander and afterward by Hiltibrandus, yet had refused to make satisfaction.

Thus each side favored and applauded its own position, and they departed. [Note: [Col. 0956B] C omits from “It is nevertheless known” through “the laws.”]

It is nevertheless known that the emperor’s opponents pursued this same opinion with such zeal that, at a council later held at Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 0955] “Quedlinburg,” corrected from “Quitilingoburg” in A; E1 has “Quitilingeburg”; other copies have various forms] (April), at which Otto, bishop of Ostia, was present as legate of Pope Hiltibrandus, they discussed Wecilo’s view at length and called him a heresiarch [Note: [Col. 0956B] A adds “which is dreadful to say,” later erased], accusing him of having taught doctrine contrary to the faith: namely, that so long as someone had been stripped of his possessions, he was not subject to the divine laws.

Pope Hiltibrandus, also called Gregory VII, died at Salerno (May 25) and was buried there in the church.

With the consent of the Normans, of Mathildis, that most powerful woman throughout Italy, and of all who espoused such a sect [Note: [Col. 0956B] C adds “and of the Romans,”], Desiderius, a Roman cardinal and abbot of Monte Cassino, a true servant of Christ, was substituted for him, although he resisted greatly in both heart and body (1086). [Note: [Col. 0956B] C adds: “and he was called Victor.”] But since he was suffering from a severe illness and was advanced to this highest dignity against his will—or rather as a captive—he obtained through prayers that within not many days he should be taken from this life (1087). [Note: [Col. 0955D] Elected May 24, 1086; died September 16, 1087.]

After this, through the same electors and ordainers, the aforesaid Otto, bishop of Ostia, was appointed to the same office (1088). Changing his name according to Roman custom, he was called Urban. [Note: [Col. 0956B] A has instead: “After this man had died, a certain Urbanus was appointed to the same See by them.”]

[Col. 0956C] **30. 3. A.D. 1086.** [Note: [Col. 0955] Number 1 omits “of the Lord.”] Emperor Heinricus devastated Saxony. Würzburg was besieged by the Saxons and Alemanni (July). To free it, the emperor gathered a large army of infantry and cavalry. After a battle near Bleihefeld (August 11), he withdrew without victory. Soon the city was captured by the enemy, Bishop Adelbero was brought in, and, after a military garrison had been left with him, each side returned to its own territory. A short time later the same city was recovered by the emperor; Adelbero and his men were expelled, and Meginhardus was restored.

**31. 4. A.D. 1087.** Herimannus [Note: [Col. 0956D] These events should be assigned to 1088], having laid aside the false title of king [Note: [Col. 0956D] C has “the vain title”; D and E omit this], returned to his own lands with the emperor’s permission and died a few days later during the siege of a certain town. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Numbers 10–11 add: “He was buried at Metz,” from Bernoldus under 1088.]

[Col. 0957A] **32. 5. A.D. 1088.** Empress Berhta died and was buried at Speyer.

Buggo, bishop of Halberstadt, was killed at Goslar. [Note: [Col. 0957D] Compare Stenzel II, p. 290.]

The city of Augsburg was captured through a plot by the Swabians on Maundy Thursday [Note: [Col. 0957D] The *Annals of Augsburg* under this year indicate the preceding day, the second day before the Ides of April (April 12)] and destroyed on the second day of Easter (April 13–17). [Note: [Col. 0957] A has “on the first day of Easter.”] Sigifridus, bishop of that city, was committed to custody. Wigoldus, the invader of the same church, died within a few days.

Meginhardus, bishop of Würzburg, died; Emehardus succeeded him, while Adelbero was still alive. [Note: [Col. 0957] A has “Adalbero.”]

Wecil, archbishop of Mainz, died; Ruothardus succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0957A] C, D, and E add: “Gebehardus, archbishop of Salzburg, died”; D and E add: “the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July” (E: “the seventh”).]

[Note: [Col. 0957A] Number 5 adds: “There was a great earthquake on the fifth day before the Ides of May.” Numbers 10–11 add: “Peter, bishop of Albano, died. Passing unharmed through an enormous pyre by the judgment of fire, with even his garments flying through the flames yet in no way damaged, he declared Peter, bishop of Florence, to be a simoniac; hence he himself was afterward called ‘the fiery one,’” from Bernoldus under 1090.]

[Col. 0957B] **33. 6. A.D. 1089.** Otto, bishop of Regensburg, died; in his place the young Gebehardus was appointed.

The emperor celebrated his wedding at Cologne, taking as his wife a certain widow of Uto [Note: [Col. 0957C] C, D, and E have “of Heinricus,”] the margrave, the daughter of the king of the Russians.

Afterward, having gathered an army, he besieged a certain very strongly fortified town belonging to Margrave Eggibertus in Thuringia, called Gliche [Note: [Col. 0957] A omits this] [Note: [Col. 0957D] Gleichen; these events took place toward the end of 1089].

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, which fell on a Sunday, when a large part of the leading men had already departed because of the feast, Eggibertus, taking thought for his own men, boldly attacked the emperor. Although the emperor resisted vigorously at first, Eggibertus finally compelled him to yield. There Burchardus, bishop of Lausanne, who was carrying the emperor’s sacred lance that day, was killed. [Note: [Col. 0957] A has “was killed”; elsewhere it has been corrected to “is killed” or “was killed.”]

**34. 7. A.D. 1090.** Emperor Heinricus again entered Italy and remained there for nearly seven years.

The aforementioned Eggibertus was found by certain loyal men of the emperor in a mill where he had stopped to rest and was disgracefully killed.

Adelbero of Würzburg, long since driven from his See, died in Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0957] A omits this] and was buried there in his monastery at Lambach. [Note: [Col. 0958D] Compare the *Life of Adalbero* by a monk of Lambach in Pez, *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum* II.]

**35. 8. A.D. 1091.** In many regions there appeared exceedingly strange little worms flying not far above the ground—that is, so near that they could be touched by hand or rod. They were about the size of flies in thickness, but considerably longer. Their swarm was so immense that they seemed to occupy nearly one mile in width and two or three in length; by their density they even concealed the sunlight from the earth.

Some interpreted this portentous apparition as a figure of the expedition to Jerusalem that took place four years later.

### 36. 9. A.D. 1092

A great pestilence occurred among human beings and livestock. [Note: Six words are missing in the source.]

### 37. 10. A.D. 1093

Fratislaus [Note: *Fratizlaus* in A.] duke of Bohemia suddenly fell from his horse while hunting and died an abrupt death. [Note: On 15 January.]—Chuonradus, son of the emperor and of the empress Berhta, was accused of having rebelled against his father. [Note: “It is reported” in C, D, and E.]—A certain radiance, like a flying torch, was seen passing through the air from east to west.—An eclipse of the sun occurred on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, at the third hour, and a great mortality followed.

### 38. 11. A.D. 1094

The Church was incredibly devastated by an immense mortality; moreover, it was grievously afflicted by pestilence, whirlwinds, inundations of rain, and various disasters.

### 39. 12. A.D. 1095

Ladizlaus, king of Pannonia, full of works of mercy, ended his life in the Lord.—Luitpold, likewise margrave, and Heinrich, count palatine, also died. [Note: C omits this.] [Note: B adds: “Burchard, abbot, also passed to the Lord on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.”]

### 40. 13. In the Year of the Lord 1096

Welefo, formerly duke of Noricum, who had long before renounced allegiance to the emperor and had therefore lost the duchy, returned to his favor and recovered the duchy.

A sign appeared in the sun on the fifth day before the Nones of March, the Monday beginning Lent. It was also reported everywhere that the world had brought forth various portents. [Note: “An eclipse …” through “14” appears here below in C, D, and E.] Soon from almost every part of the earth, but especially from the regions of the western kingdoms, innumerable bands of kings and nobles, as well as common people of both sexes, began to proceed under arms toward Jerusalem. [Note: “They seized” instead of “they began” in E. Concerning this expedition, some specialized works already exist. E omits the remainder of this year.] They had been stirred up, evidently, by frequent reports concerning the oppression of the Lord’s sepulchre and the desolation of all the churches of the East, which the extremely savage people of the Turks, having subjected them to their rule for several years, had now almost entirely destroyed amid unheard-of calamities. [Note: 5 omits this passage; 9c reads “of the regions”; in 11 “of the East” is written above the line; A omits it.] [Note: The words from “For these …” to “return to their homeland” are absent here in D.] Since they had resolved to assist them, as has been said, they hastened in separate groups and, for the most part, under different and uncertain leaders. [Note: P adds: “We refrain from recounting more about this expedition, because, as so great a matter requires, we have elsewhere sufficient elegant accounts of it.” C omits the rest.]

The first, following a certain monk named Peter, whom many later said had been a hypocrite, were estimated at fifteen thousand. They passed peacefully through Germany and thence through Bavaria and Pannonia. Very many others traveled by ship along the Danube or overland through Alamannia; others, numbering about twelve thousand, were led through Saxony and Bohemia by a certain priest named Folcmar [Note: *Folemaro* in A.], while some were led by the priest Gotescalc through eastern Francia.

These people also treated the most abominable remnants of the Jews as the true internal enemies of the Church: in the cities through which they passed they either utterly destroyed them or compelled them to seek refuge in baptism. Yet very many of them later returned, like dogs to their vomit. [Note: “It must be left to them to determine by what judgment of God this was done,” A adds. Another copy adds: “It must be left to them to determine by what judgment of God, or in whatever manner it may have pleased Him”; this was later erased.]

When those travelers reached Hungary, laden with many spoils, they became, as it seemed, objects of hatred to the inhabitants on account of certain disturbances; but in reality, by their abundance of possessions, they inflamed those half-barbarous people to greed. By order of their king Colomannus [Note: *Cholomannus* in A.], they were captured by deceit rather than by arms. Many were punished with death; a few, stripped of their arms and possessions, gained flight as their greatest profit.

Nevertheless, a very large multitude of both groups was led astray by a certain military man named Emicho—or rather, like the Israelite army of old, deceived by the spirit of fornication. Finding only a few men barring their entrance into Pannonia at the fortress of Miesenburg [Note: Wieselburg.], they returned to their homeland in flight, with no one pursuing them. [Note: Ekkehard later discovered that this account, written in 1099, was otherwise; see what he added for 1099 after his return. For this reason he omitted this passage from the *Jerusalem Book*.]

An eclipse of the moon occurred on the sixth day before the Ides of August, when the moon was fourteen days old.

### 41. 14. In the Year of the Lord 1097

The emperor Heinrich, returning from Italy, came to the Bavarian city of Regensburg. After staying there for some time, he granted the Jews who had been compelled to receive baptism permission to observe the Jewish rite. [Note: The first hand reads “to use their own laws, as is reported,” in A and 1; after “as is reported” was later erased, the expression “the rite of practicing Judaism” was substituted for “to use their own laws.”] (May–June.)

[Note: From “Meanwhile” through “he settled under siege” is absent in C, D, and E.] Meanwhile Gotefrid, duke of Lotharingia, a man highly distinguished by birth, arms, and intelligence, had set out the previous year through eastern Francia after converting all his possessions into money and equipping himself with numerous soldiers and no small degree of faith. He was not terrified even by the flight of those people from Hungary; with permission both of the emperor Heinrich and of King Colomannus [Note: *Cholomannus* in A.], he had crossed Pannonia and Bulgaria [Note: *Bulgariamque* was corrected to *Bulgariasque* in 1]. He entered into alliance with the emperor of Constantinople and, supported by his garrisons, reached Romania. There, joining to himself the armies of Sicily and Greece, of the Danes, the Northmen, and other overseas peoples—or rather, the assistance of all nations worshiping Christ—he began, through frequent engagements, to wear down the barbarians. At last, after Romania had been occupied, he settled under siege at Antioch. [Note: R reads: “Having subdued Romania, he settled at Antioch”; A corrects the text to the reading printed here.]

The emperor Heinrich held a conference concerning peace with the princes at Mainz around the Kalends of December, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Strasbourg. [Note: The words from “and” through “celebrated” are absent in C, D, and E.]

A comet appeared.—That year the summer was exceedingly fertile, but the winter was mild and pestilential; the inundations of rains and rivers increased greatly.

### 42. 15. In the Year of the Lord 1118

[Note: C, D, and E read: “While the emperor was inquiring at Mainz into the property of the Jews who had been killed, and both the bishop and his relatives were accused concerning this money, the angered bishop withdrew with his followers to Thuringia. Heinrich, however, appropriated all the revenues of the bishopric to his own use and ordered the possessions of the fugitives to be confiscated and the walls demolished. Welefo, etc.”]

When the emperor had conducted an inquiry at Mainz concerning the property of the Jews who had been killed, certain relatives of the archbishop were accused among those who had seized it. When the emperor sought them and they did not appear before him, the bishop, wishing but unable to defend their case, departed from the city in indignation and withdrew with them to Thuringia, as though he would thereby better protect his own interests and, from his proximity to the emperor, bring some terror upon the emperor through the rebels and so exact vengeance for his anger. There were, however, people who said that the bishop himself had received a large share of the confiscated money and had therefore devoted himself so zealously to defending the others. [Note: A adds: “But when the emperor saw the bishop abandoning his seat so foolishly, he appropriated to his own use all the revenues of the bishopric and its various administrative functions, and ordered the possessions of the fugitives to be confiscated and the walls to be demolished. Thus the bishop, while arrogantly and imprudently contemplating how to protect others, was himself, like his predecessor, deprived of many advantages by wandering about. These words also appear in 1, but were later erased by the author.”]

Welefo, again duke of the Bavarians, reconciled his sons—who themselves had attempted to rebel—to the emperor’s favor and obtained permission for the duchy to be entrusted after him to one of them. [Note: Migne printed an asterisk instead of three asterisks.]

[Note: This brief account of the holy war is taken from the letter of the princes to Paschal II, which appears under the year 1100 in the *Annals of St. Disibod* (commonly attributed to Dodechin).]

A adds the following:

Gotefrid, duke, and the others associated with him in the journey and undertaking described above, when they departed after the capture of Nicaea, had more than three hundred thousand armed men. Although this immense multitude could have occupied all Romania, drunk up its rivers, and grazed down all its crops in a single day, God nevertheless provided such an abundance of life’s necessities that a ram could be bought for one coin and an ox for scarcely twelve. Moreover, although the Saracen princes and kings rose up against them, by God’s will they were easily defeated and trampled underfoot.

Because certain men grew arrogant over these successful events, God opposed Antioch to them, a city impregnable by human strength. There, after keeping them under siege for nine months, He humbled them so greatly that all their pride was crushed. Once they had thus been humbled, so that scarcely a hundred good horses could be found in the entire army, God opened the abundance of His blessing and mercy, led them into the city, and handed over the Turks and all their possessions to their power. When they obtained these things as though they had acquired them by their own strength, and did not adequately magnify God, who had bestowed them upon them, they were besieged by such a multitude of Saracens that no one from so great a host dared leave the city. Moreover, famine had become so severe within the city that some scarcely abstained from eating human flesh. It would take too long to recount the miseries that occurred there.

But the Lord, looking upon the people whom He had scourged for so long, mercifully comforted them. First, as though in satisfaction for their tribulation, He offered them His lance, with which He had been wounded on the cross—a gift unseen since the time of the Apostles—as a pledge of victory. Then He so strengthened human hearts that He infused the power to take up arms and fight manfully against the enemy into those whom sickness or hunger had deprived of the strength to walk.

Afterward, when the army, having defeated its enemies, was weakened at Antioch by hunger and weariness, especially because of dissensions among the princes, they set out for Syria and conquered the Saracen cities of Barram and Marram, taking possession of the region’s fortresses. When they decided to remain there, such hunger prevailed in the army that the Christian people ate the already-fetid bodies of Saracens.

Then, as they advanced by divine direction into the interior of Spain, they had with them the most generous, merciful, and victorious hand of the omnipotent Father. For the citizens and castle-dwellers of the region through which they passed sent envoys ahead to them with many gifts, prepared to serve them and surrender their towns. But because the army was not large and they were hastening unanimously toward Jerusalem, they took hostages and made those people tributary—especially since one of the coastal cities had more inhabitants than there were men in the Christian army.
