When it was heard at Antioch, Laodicea, and Edessa that the hand of the Lord was with those who had departed, many from the army that had remained there followed them as far as Tyre. Thus, with God as their companion and fellow-worker, they reached Jerusalem.

When the army suffered greatly during the siege of that city, especially because of the lack of water, a council was held. The bishops and princes proclaimed that the city should be circumambulated barefoot, so that He who had entered it in humility for the sake of humankind might, through their humility on His behalf, open it to them for judgment upon its enemies.

The Lord, pleased by this humiliation, handed the city over to them on the eighth day after their humiliation, precisely on the day when the primitive Church had been expelled from it, when many faithful celebrate the feast of the Dispersion of the Apostles.

If anyone wishes to know what was done with the enemies found there, let him know that in the portico called Solomon’s, and in his Temple, the victors rode through the blood of the Saracens up to the horses’ knees.

After it had been decided who should retain the city, and others wished to return out of love for their homeland and affection for their families, it was announced to them that the king of Babylon had come to Ascalon with an innumerable multitude of pagans, intending to lead the Franks who were in Jerusalem into captivity and to attack Antioch, as he himself had said. But the Lord had determined otherwise.

Accordingly, when those who were in Jerusalem had truly learned that the Babylonian army was at Ascalon, they went out to meet it, leaving their baggage and their sick at Jerusalem with a garrison. When their army and that of the enemy came into view of one another, the Christians knelt and called upon God, asking that He who had confirmed the law of the Christians in their other necessities might, in the present battle, shatter the strength of the pagans and the devil and extend the kingdom of Christ and His Church everywhere, from sea to sea.

Without delay, God was present when they cried to Him and supplied such strength for their courage that anyone who saw them rushing upon the enemy would have judged them a sluggish deer thirsting for a spring of living water. This was marvelous indeed, since the Christian army had no more than five thousand cavalry and fifteen thousand infantry, whereas the enemy army might have contained one hundred thousand cavalry and four hundred thousand infantry.

Then God appeared wondrous in His servants. Before they even engaged, He put that multitude to flight by the mere force of their attack and seized all their arms, so that if they afterward wished to resist these men, they had no weapons in which to place their hope.

As for the spoils, there is no need to ask how much was captured, since the treasures of the king of Babylon were seized. More than one hundred thousand Moors [Note: Or “armed men,” as C adds.] fell there by the sword. Such fear seized the others that about two thousand were suffocated at the city gate. There is no number for those who perished in the sea; the thickets also captured many of them. Certainly the whole world fought on behalf of the Christians. Had the spoils of the camps not detained many of them, few of so great a multitude of enemies would have been able to report the outcome of the battle.

On the day before the battle, the army captured many thousands of camels, oxen, and sheep. When, at the order of the princes, the people released these animals as they advanced to battle, marvelous to relate, the camels formed many and various companies, and so likewise did the oxen and sheep. These animals accompanied the army in such a way that they stood when it stood, advanced when it advanced, and ran when it ran. Clouds also protected the Christians from the sun’s heat and cooled them.

After the victory had been celebrated, the army returned to Jerusalem. Leaving Gotefrid there as leader, Reginmund, count of Saint-Gilles, Ruotpert, count of Normandy, and Ruotpert, count of Flanders, returned to Laodicea. There they found the Pisan fleet and Boemundus.

When the Pisan archbishop had reconciled Boemundus and the others who were in disagreement with him, Reginmund decided to return for God and for the brethren. A great multitude, as has been said above, attempted to return to its homeland; the others who remained retained the land in peace to this day, by God’s disposition.

[Note: This had also previously been written in 1, and there it still survives through the words “nor did they adequately magnify God,” which are underlined. The remainder, on folio 184 and following, was either written, erased, or wholly lost when the folio was cut out.]

### A.D. 1119

[Note: Copies 4, 5, and 10 add the numbers “43. 16,” which 1 omits.] [Note: What follows was added by Ekkehard after his return from the Jerusalem expedition, after he had erased what he had previously written for 1098. He retained only a few passages from the earlier version.] [Note: E and 1 add in another hand in the margin: “Hillibold, the tenth abbot of St. John the Baptist, was appointed; he established the Hirsau order.”]

Heinrich the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne; but at Epiphany, at Aachen, he made his younger son Heinrich V king, rejecting his elder son Chuonrad, whom he had previously crowned. [Note: C omits this.] [Note: C omits everything that follows here.]

[Note: A continues as follows: “After this, proceeding toward Bavaria, he commended that same son whom he had made king to those who had previously not been present, so that they might recognize him as king.—Meanwhile the count palatine Ratpoto and his cousin Oudalric, whom they called very wealthy, died.—The emperor, celebrating the feast of the Apostles at Bamberg, earnestly admonished the princes of those regions to preserve peace faithfully and bound them under oath to pursue and punish without hesitation those who practiced robbery and theft. He also utterly forbade the advocates to appoint subordinate advocates under themselves for the plundering of the people and churches. But, alas, this command had little force, because the princes, unwilling to lack bands of soldiers whom they had chiefly won over to themselves through such benefices, immediately after the emperor’s departure resumed their customary and ancient practice.—Jerusalem was captured by the Christians on the Ides of July, a Friday.—Chuonrad, bishop of Utrecht, was killed by his own people during these days.—Heremann, archbishop of Cologne, died.—Pope Urban died; Paschal succeeded him, while Pope Wigbert, also called Clement, was still living.”]

Chuonrad, revealing the cause of his rebellion to only a few of his most intimate associates in the kingdom, took with him a certain man from his father’s ministerial order, also named Chuonrad, a very strong and prudent man. Through certain regions of Italy he maintained the name and dignity of king for nearly nine years, spreading meanwhile such a fragrance of his character throughout the Roman world that no religious or wise person doubted that the welfare of the commonwealth ought to be entrusted to him. [Note: 1 and D1 read *salutem rei publicae* (“the welfare of the commonwealth”); 5 reads *salutem rem publicam*; 6, 9c, 10, and 11 read *saltem rem publicam* (“at least the commonwealth”).] For he was in every respect catholic and most subject to the Apostolic See; he was devoted more to religion than to insignia or arms. Nevertheless, he was sufficiently and more than sufficiently equipped with courage and boldness. He preferred to devote himself to reading rather than to games. He drew near to the wretched of every kind, but especially to soldiers oppressed by poverty, through compassion and the fruit of mercy. Inflicting contempt, violence, or injury upon no one, he was gracious to every person and every condition; and therefore, not undeservedly, he was always beloved by God and by human beings.

Although he had resolved to preserve the modesty of celibacy perpetually, he was nevertheless compelled by his people to marry the daughter of Ruotker, duke of Sicily, a man almost the most famous of our age. He used her companionship with such chastity that it could scarcely be believed that he had ever known her. [Note: Nevertheless, this woman, endowed with faith like a turtledove [Note: *Turturnina* in 1b.], detested a second embrace so greatly that after only her head had been taken from her body, she devoted the rest of her life to labor as the fruit of the sixtyfold. This passage, written in 1, was erased by Ekkehard when the widow later married King Baldwin of Jerusalem; see below in the *Jerusalem Book*. In 1 it can now be read only with the aid of chemical reagent; in 1b it remains.]

[Note: C, under the year 1101, supplies: “In accordance with that legal precept.”] He observed that legal precept, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” (Leviticus 18:7), and likewise, “Honor your father” (Matthew 19:19): he never allowed to reach his own ears the murmuring that throughout the Roman Empire tore apart his father’s character and had become for him the cause of his father’s offense and of his own separation from him. He always called him his lord and Caesar or emperor. He treated all who came from his father’s court, even the lowliest, with social kindness, addressing them as fellow servants.

In addition to the virtues of his mind and the composure of his conduct, he was exceptionally handsome in body and tall in stature.

In that same year Gotefrid the duke, Reginmund count of Saint-Gilles, Ruopert count of Normandy, and Ruopert count of Flanders reached Jerusalem with the troops under their command, after very great difficulty, now in the fourth year since they had voluntarily crucified themselves in this army for Christ, who had been crucified for them. The rest of the multitude, except those who had remained with Boemundus at Antioch or had gone with Baldwin to Edessa, had stayed at Laodicea and Tyre or had scattered through the various surrounding regions.

[Note: The following account of the Jerusalem war is absent here from D and E, which add a separate narrative and, at this point, together with C, give only this: “In that same year our Lord Jesus Christ opened Jerusalem, the city of His rest, to His faithful, and, by the greatness of His power, expelled the impurities of the pagans and mercifully restored there the free practice of Christian devotion.”]

Here my impassioned spirit is moved to add something to what has been written above concerning the cause of this military expedition—not so much humanly as divinely ordained—especially in response to the rebuke of certain imprudent, indeed shameless, people. Content with their ancient error, they dare with reckless speech to criticize this new development, already necessary for a world growing old and nearly perishing. In the Epicurean manner, they embrace the broad rather than the narrow path of divine service [Note: 5 wrongly supplies *tam latam* (“so broad”); the author appears to have intended *potius latam* (“rather broad”).], regarding the desire for the world as prudence, contempt for it as folly, the prison as a homeland, darkness as light, evil as good, and death as life—shamefully considering all these things with utterly blind hearts. [Note: H reads “wrongly discerning” instead of “considering with utterly blind hearts.”]

The corruption of affairs, now disordered everywhere but especially in these regions, encourages them and supplies them with such audacity. Here wisdom is hated above all, every virtue is detested, religion is despised, humility is trampled, cunning wins primacy, vice gains love, cruelty breeds fear, and pride commands honor. [Note: H adds “extorts.”]

But trusting in the Lord alone, longing not for present things but for those to come, and although sluggish spectators, nevertheless benevolent supporters, let us praise those glorious men of our time [Note: H reads “let us praise certain other men.”] who conquered the kingdoms of the world; who, leaving wives and children, kingdoms and riches for the sake of the pious seeker of the hundredth sheep, placed their souls in their hands; who, zealously zealous for the Lord God of hosts, properly armed with both kinds of courage, entered the service of their heavenly king. [Note: Copy 5 adds in red: “Concerning the Jerusalem expedition.”]

During the time of Heinrich IV, Roman emperor, and Alexius, prince of Constantinople, in accordance with the Gospel prophecy, “nation rose against nation and kingdom against kingdom,” and there were great earthquakes in various places, pestilences and famines, terrors from heaven, and great signs. Since the evangelical trumpet of the just Judge was already proclaiming His coming to all nations, behold, the universal Church also observes the entire surrounding world displaying the foretold signs.

Jerusalem, now possessed by Saracen inhabitants, was subject to Babylon [Note: That is, Cairo.], which is now the seat of the Egyptian kingdom. The small remnant of Christian worship there bought its daily freedom through tribute. Bethlehem, the house of the angels’ bread, had become a stable for cattle, and all the churches throughout the surrounding regions had for many years been subjected in every way to the mockery of the pagans.

Meanwhile, when a disastrous war arose among the Eastern Christians—that is, the Greeks and Armenians—the Armenians, being inferior in kingdoms and numbers, enlisted as allies warriors of renowned reputation from Persia, the Turks. With their assistance, having quelled the revolt according to their own wishes, they dismissed them to their homes, though the Turks had been strongly attracted by the abundance and fertility of those lands.

After several years, a plan was therefore formed, and many forces of the aforementioned pagans emerged from the northern region, from the land of Gorrizene, which is said to be more fertile in human beings than in provisions. Divided among four sultans—for that is what they customarily call their satraps—they were subject to one Persian emperor almost as though to a god. They spread through Armenia, then Cappadocia, all Romania, and Syria.

First they conquered Nicaea, once the strongest tower of the catholic faith. After slaughtering the Christians whom they had captured there, they installed one of their own, a tyrant named Solomanus, with garrisons. They utterly devastated all the surrounding regions as far as the marsh or inlet of the sea called the Arm of Saint George, sparing no Christian soul, no church or monastery, and not even the images of the saints.

For we have seen—and it remains a pitiable spectacle to see—in the half-ruined oratories of those regions the paintings of our Savior, of His most glorious mother, and of whichever of the elect were depicted there, their noses or ears, hands or feet cut off. They visibly display, as it were, the mourning of the desolated churches and exhibit the vigilant rod of divine judgment over them, with wounds seemingly always fresh.

These swords, O most noble Constantinople, were not warded off from you by the thousandfold cunning of your king, nor by the countless multitude of your citizens. The crowds at your markets and your endless heaps of gold did not redeem you. Neither the multitude of your Varangians, nor of your Turks, nor of your Pincernas, nor your fleets defended you. Only the intervening waters of the aforementioned strait afforded you protection; indeed, only the Creator’s work fortified you.

Powerful Antioch of old was subjected to these attacks, and, not to delay with many details, all Syria and Palestine together surrendered their right hands.

Thus, once the Promised Land had been subdued, Jerusalem, the mother of our redemption and faith, was weighed down by the double yoke of captivity. The consolation, however, was exceedingly small: the Saracens who oppressed it were themselves punished by an equal fate by the Turks, a much more disgraceful people.

After a sultan and numerous soldiers had been stationed there, the monasteries outside the city were destroyed in order to restore the outer wall [Note: *Mural* was corrected to *antemural* in 1.] that is still visible, along with whatever other buildings there were. The Lord’s sepulchre alone was left intact, solely for the sake of revenue. The Temple of the Lord, most famous and, as I believe, comparable to no human structure, was reserved for the sacrilegious worship of the pagans. They always held it in such great reverence that they never entered it except with bare and washed feet; yet they permitted none of the Christians—whom they judged especially unclean—to enter even its court throughout all those many years, whether under Saracen or Turkish rule.

While these conquerors now labored at arms, as circumstances required, and now indulged themselves in games and pleasures, as people transplanted from barren gravel into especially fertile soil, it is scarcely credible to anyone inexperienced what torments, what crosses, and what miseries the surviving worshipers of Christ endured in their service. Yet this can easily be understood from the very frequent embassies and letters, some of which we ourselves saw, in which they mournfully called upon the universal Church for aid to the Church of Jerusalem. [Note: Copy 5 reads: “through continual embassies and very frequent letters.”]

The aforementioned emperor Alexius of Constantinople also sent no small number of letters to Pope Urban concerning these same barbarous plunderers, who had already spread through most of his kingdom. In them he lamented that he was unable to defend the Eastern churches and implored that the entire West, which was now wholly reckoned as Christian, if possible be summoned to his aid. He promised that he himself would supply by land and sea everything necessary for those who would fight.

Moved by this, the Apostolic See and the entire Roman Church [Note: H reads: “the Church in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096.”] caused a general council to be assembled on the border of Spain [Note: At Clermont.] or, as some say, at Paris. [Note: The words “or, as some say, at Paris” are written in the margin of 1 and superscribed in D; they are absent from 1b and H.] He himself, arriving there after a very arduous journey, proclaimed with the most eloquent speech all that has been set out above and much more besides to the countless peoples who had gathered there and to the envoys of various kingdoms.

Soon, when so many thousands were dissolved in tears and the lamentations of various languages had risen high, this eminent teacher promised them remission of all sins if, renouncing everything they possessed and unanimously bearing the cross after Christ, they would bring aid to their fellow Christians in danger.

When all their spirits had been stirred by this promise, about one hundred thousand men were designated for the Lord’s army at that time: from Aquitaine, Normandy, England, Scotland and Ireland, Britain, Galicia [Note: *Galacia* in 1b.], Gascony, France, Flanders, Lotharingia, and the other Christian peoples whose names do not now come to mind.

This truly crusading army wore the sign of the cross on its garments as a reminder of mortification, believing that by this sign, in accordance with the vision once revealed to the great Constantine [Note: See above.], it would triumph over the enemies of Christ’s cross.

By the marvelous and incomprehensible dispensation of God, so many members of Christ, differing in languages, tribes, and nations, were suddenly joined and grew together into one body through the love of Christ. They all had one king, Christ, while individual peoples were placed under individual leaders: Gotefrid of Lotharingia and his brothers Baldwin and Eustace; Ruopert of Flanders; likewise Ruopert of Normandy; Regimund, count of Saint-Gilles; Hugh, brother of King Philip of France; and the other warriors of equal energy, nobility, and courage.

The Apostolic See appointed over all of them a man of venerable holiness and wisdom, Bishop Hademar [Note: Of Puy.]. It also granted him, to exercise in its place, the power of binding and loosing inherited by the Roman See from blessed Peter. After marking the army with the sign of the heavenly army and sealing it with the Apostolic blessing, and after the time of departure had been fixed by all, he himself returned to Italy with a considerable band from the same expedition.

Finally, when each envoy had returned to his own country, this report spread throughout the whole world on both sides of the sea and immediately stirred it. Moreover—and it is marvelous to relate—flying with customary speed even beyond the limits of the ocean, it caused the seas themselves to overflow with the fleets of the islanders for the service of the heavenly King.

For, as we have learned with complete certainty, the ocean poured forth peoples so unknown that no inhabitant of this shore could recognize, from them or even from their sailors, I will not say their customs and appearance, but not even their language. It brought forth others whose only customary food was bread and water, and still others who used silver in place of iron for all their implements.

Thus from every direction the number of those marked with the cross increased daily all around, and, as we have already said, the entire world burned with zeal for such an expedition, was wholly shaken, or rather seemed to be transformed.

The western Franks could easily be persuaded to leave their own lands, for Gaul had for several years been grievously afflicted now by civil unrest, now by famine, now by pestilence; finally, that plague which arose around the church of Saint Gertrude at Nivelles [Note: Nivelle] had terrified them almost to despair of life. It was of the following kind. Anyone touched by an invisible fire, on whatever part of the body, burned for so long in a perceptible—or rather incomparable—and even incurable torment, until either he lost his life amid torture or lost the tortured limb together with the torment. To this day some testify to it, having had their hands or feet amputated by this punishment.

The common people and other individuals of the remaining nations, apart from the apostolic decree, declared that some had recently been called to the land of promise by certain prophets who had arisen among them, or by heavenly signs and revelations [Note: superscript 1], while others confessed that various hardships had compelled them to make such vows; for a considerable part of them set out burdened with their wives, children, and all their possessions.

But this trumpet-call sounded not at all among the eastern Franks, Saxons and Thuringians, Bavarians and Alamanni, chiefly because of that schism which, from the time of Pope Alexander until today, has so confirmed both us and the Romans as hateful and hostile to one another—alas! Hence, at the beginning of this expedition, almost the entire German people, ignorant of its purpose, mocked the many legions of cavalry, the many companies of infantry, and the many bands of peasants, women, and little children passing through their land, as though they were raving in unheard-of folly: people who, grasping at uncertainties in place of certainties, were foolishly abandoning the land of their birth, seeking the uncertain land of promise at certain peril, renouncing their own possessions and coveting those of others.

Yet although our people is much more insolent than the others, the German fury was finally inclined, through divine mercy, to accept the word of this renunciation [Note: *ad* corrected to *e*], once the matter had been fully explained by the crowds of travelers.

Moreover, the sign in the sun mentioned above [Note: Above, under the year 1096], which was seen in the year 1096, and many portents that appeared both in the air and on the earth, roused not a few who had previously been sluggish to such undertakings. We have thought it most useful to insert some of these here, although to relate them all would take too long.

At that time, around the Nones of October, we ourselves saw a comet standing in the southern region and extending its brilliance obliquely like a sword. Three years afterward, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, we saw another star in the east repeatedly changing its position by long intervals and leaps (perhaps in the year 1098) [Note: “VI Kal. Mar.” written above the line]. We also saw blood-red clouds rising both in the west and in the east and meeting one another in the middle of the sky; again, almost in the middle of the night, fiery gleams rising from the north; and frequently, as we establish by the testimony of many people, torches flying through the air.

Not many years earlier, a venerable priest named Suiggerus, a man of holy life, saw at about the ninth hour of a certain day two horsemen meeting in the air and contending for a long time. One of them, who also carried a considerable cross with which he seemed to strike, appeared victorious over the other.

At the same time, the priest G., who now under monastic profession pays Christ, in place of his firstborn, the sheep that is due for a donkey [Exodus 13:13], was walking in a forest at midday with two companions. He saw a sword of extraordinary length carried aloft by a whirlwind, though it was unknown from where it had been lifted; and until its height disappeared from sight, he distinguished both a crash with his ears and metal with his eyes.

Some who were keeping watch over the horses’ pastures reported that they had seen the appearance of a city in the air, and had also observed various crowds hastening toward it from different directions, traveling both on horseback and on foot. Some people even displayed the mark of a cross divinely impressed upon their foreheads, ropes, or any other part of their bodies, and believed that by this very stigma they had been appointed to the Lord’s same military service.

Likewise, when others had been suddenly pricked in mind or instructed by a nocturnal vision, they decided to sell their estates and possessions and sew the sign of mortification onto their garments. And while crowds of people were running in groups to the churches in all these matters beyond anything that could be believed, priestly blessing distributed swords together with staves and little bags in a new ritual.

What shall I say of the events of those times? A certain woman, pregnant for two full years, finally, when her womb burst open, gave birth to a speaking son. There was also a little child entirely double-bodied, another with two heads, and some lambs born with two heads. Mares even produced, at the very moment of giving birth, larger teeth—the teeth commonly called equine teeth—which nature grants only to three-year-old horses.

While the whole creation was urging itself into the Creator’s service by signs of this and similar kinds, that enemy did not delay—the enemy who, though the others were sleeping, was always fully awake to sow his own weeds over the good seed, to raise up false prophets, and to mingle false brothers and dishonorable women among the Lord’s armies under the guise of religion. Thus, through the hypocrisy and lies of some, and through the wicked impurities of others, Christ’s flocks were so disgraced that, according to the good Shepherd’s prophecy, even the elect would be led astray [Matthew 24:24].

From this arose that fabricated story about Charlemagne, supposedly raised again for this very purpose from the dead, together with some other person who had likewise returned to life; and that frivolous tale about a goose leading its mistress, along with many stories of the same kind.

Yet the same seducers, just as each has been recognized by his own fruits and as wolves have been marked beneath sheep’s clothing, must be identified—especially those of them who still survive, if they can be found [Note: superscript 1]. That is, they must be asked at which harbor, in accordance with their promise, they crossed the sea without a ship; in what battles or places they struck down many pagans with a small force; which of their fortifications they immediately captured; and on what part of Jerusalem’s walls they finally pitched their camps, and so forth. Since they have nothing to answer, both for the offerings they hypocritically received from the faithful and for the crowds they killed in order to plunder what they had deceived, and especially for their own apostasy [Note: “maxima” corrected to “maxime”], they must necessarily be compelled to do penance.

For, as was stated above [Note: Above, under the year 1096], when the people of Folcmar, following through Bohemia, had reached Nitra, a city of Pannonia, and had been destroyed there partly by captivity and partly by the sword after a revolt had broken out, the very few who survived still commonly testify that the sign of the cross appeared above them from heaven and delivered them from the impending slaughter.

But Gotescalcus, not a true servant of God but a false one, after entering Hungary with his followers, not without damage to eastern Noricum, established a fortification in a certain castle under the admirable appearance of false religion and, after placing garrisons there, began to ravage the Pannonian lands on every side through the remaining populace. When the natives promptly captured that stronghold, slaughtering and taking captive a great number of people and scattering the rest of the band, he himself—the mercenary, not the shepherd—was shamefully driven into flight.

At that same time there also arose a certain military man, Count Emicho, from those regions around the Rhine. He had long been extremely notorious for his tyrannical conduct, but now, like another Saul, was summoned, as he claimed, by divine revelations to this kind of religious undertaking. Usurping command over nearly twelve thousand marked men, he led them through the cities of the Rhine, the Main, and the Danube. Wherever he found the detestable Jewish population, he strove—serving Christian zeal even in this matter—either to destroy them utterly or to force them into the bosom of the Church.

When they had multiplied and reached the borders of Pannonia with innumerable forces of both sexes, they were forbidden to enter that kingdom, which is enclosed partly by marshes and partly by forests, because its fortified defenses had been firmly secured. For the report of King Coloman had already struck their ears [Note: “praemonuerat” in H; “perculerat” in the margin; variants include “vel praemonuerat,” “vel premoverat,” and “vel permonuerat”]. They knew that, in the minds of the Germans, there was no difference between the slaughter of pagans and that of Hungarians.

Therefore, while they labored for six weeks to storm the fortress of Misenburg, they suffered many hardships there. Among other things, they were shaken by a most foolish civil discord over which of them, in the name of the king of Pannonia, should possess the lands.

Thus, while they were exerting themselves in the final assault—when the walls had already been breached, the townsmen were already fleeing, and the army of the natives was already ravaging its own property with fire—the army of the pilgrims nevertheless, by the wonderful will of almighty God, turned its back in victory. After abandoning their baggage, no one carried away any gain except his wretched life [Note: “subpellectilibus” corrected to “suppellectilibus”].

So, indeed, so were our people, who possessed zeal for God but not according to knowledge [Romans 10:2], restrained by divine mercy through the blood of their brothers. For in the military service which Christ had provided for the liberation of Christians, they had begun to persecute other Christians. The Hungarians too were delivered. This is why certain simpler brothers, ignorant of the matter and consequently scandalized, judged the entire effort of this expedition to be vain and frivolous, acting as excessively hasty judges.

Yet when such straw had been winnowed from the Lord’s threshing floor, we saw grains of wheat enduring by the weight of their natural solidity: namely, Gotefridus and the other leaders of the Lord’s true army mentioned above. Each of them, with his followers, obtained peace and favor from all the rulers of the peoples through whose lands they passed, beneath camps beautiful beyond the entire arrangement of the stars, by the example of humility and charity, as true disciples of Christ, until, after Bulgaria had been crossed amid various difficulties of the routes [Note: corrected in one witness], they reached the fortresses of Constantinople.

We read a little book from Jerusalem that pursues the whole sequence of this history with great care from the present point and brings the many labors of God’s people over three years to their most joyful conclusion in the victory of captured Jerusalem. Therefore, from this point we shall provide only a few items out of many.

Alexius the emperor made such heroes his friends by entirely fictitious favors, but afterward bound them by extracted oaths lest they use force against his kingdom (1096–1097). Yet it is clear that, while they delayed there, having each of the first companies wait for the others who were arriving, he would have killed them by treachery had the prudence of Duke Gotefridus not watched more carefully over the Lord’s flock. The revolt itself, which he then destroyed in the suburbs, and the bridge which he stormed bear witness to this.

Why say more? For nearly two months the army received new recruits from Byzantium every day. Of these, when the multitude of common people, children, and women had been excluded, 300,000 fighting men were finally counted. The companies that had followed Peter, however, having been transported earlier at Alexius’s command, had already become a laughingstock to the pagans.

Having therefore moved their camp, they came to Nicaea in May, stormed it in June after driving out the aforementioned prince Soliman, and handed the captured city over to the emperor’s garrisons. For they had confirmed their oaths in such a way that, if they conquered any cities taken from his empire, they would restore them to their former authority; and in turn they did not doubt that, within the same boundary, they would be supported by both royal arms and subsidies.

From there, advancing through the kingdom of Constantine—a most prosperous land—they reached the sea of Russia. Thus, as the letter brought by Count Ruopert reports [Note: See the note already given above, no. 278, cited in the Annals of Saint Disibod under the year 1100; Ekkehardus retained everything through column 974, celebrating it among the faithful and retaining it from this source], Christ led his army with such abundance of provisions that a ram was sold for a coin and an ox for a shekel.

“Moreover,” he says, “whenever the kings or princes of the Saracens rose up against us, with God willing they were easily defeated and trampled down.”

Because some had grown swollen with pride over these successes, God set Antioch before them in October—a city impregnable by human strength. There he detained them for nine months in its siege and humbled them so greatly that all the swelling of their pride melted away.

After they had been humbled in this way, so that scarcely a hundred good horses could be found in the entire army, God opened to them an abundance of his blessing and mercy, brought them into the city, and delivered the Turks and everything belonging to them into their power (1098, June).

When they possessed these things as though they had acquired them by their own strength, and did not duly glorify God, who had bestowed them, they were besieged by such a multitude of Saracens that no one from so great a crowd dared leave the city. Moreover, famine had grown so severe in the city that some could scarcely refrain from inhuman fare [Note: “ut vix ab inhumanis dapibus se aliqui continerent”; a variant reads “humanis” (“human fare”)].

It would take too long to recount the sufferings that occurred in the city. But the Lord looked upon the people whom he had scourged for so long, and kindly consoled them. First, as though in satisfaction for their tribulation, he offered them his lance, with which he had been wounded on the cross, as an unseen gift since the time of the apostles and as a pledge of victory. Then he so strengthened their hearts that even those whom illness or famine had deprived of the strength to walk were infused with the power to take up arms and fight courageously against the enemy.

After the enemy had been defeated on June 28, the army, weakened at Antioch by hunger and weariness, especially because of disagreements among the leaders, set out for Syria. They stormed Baraa and Marrā, cities of the Saracens, and captured the region’s fortresses in November. When they decided to remain there, such famine afflicted the army that the Christian people ate the bodies of Saracens who had already begun to stink.

From there, advancing by divine will into the interior of Syria [Note: A region of Syria] in the year 1099, they had with them the most generous, merciful, and victorious hand of the omnipotent Father.

For the citizens and castle-dwellers of the region through which they advanced sent envoys to them with many gifts, ready to serve them and surrender their towns. But because the army was not large and they were hastening unanimously toward Jerusalem, the pilgrims accepted pledges of security and made those people tributaries, especially since one of the many cities along that coast contained more inhabitants than there were men in the Christian army.

When it was heard at Antioch, Laodicea, and Edessa that the Lord’s hand was with them, many from the army who had remained there followed them and caught up with them at Tyre. Thus, with God traveling and working alongside them, they reached Jerusalem.

When they were struggling with its siege, chiefly because of the scarcity of water, a council was held. The bishops and princes proclaimed that the city should be encircled barefoot, so that he who had entered it for our sake in humility might, through their humility on his behalf, open it to them for judgment upon its enemies.

The Lord was appeased by this humility [Note: one witness reads “satisfaction”], and on the eighth day after their humiliation he handed the city over to them (1099, July 15), on the very day when the primitive Church had been cast out from there and when many of the faithful celebrate the feast of the Apostles’ Dispersion.

Meanwhile, it seems that the following must not be passed over: while the army was staying at the siege of Antioch, all the nations throughout the East were struck with fear. Messengers and scouts ran from every part of the world, some arranging peace and others plotting war. Even envoys of the king of Babylon presented themselves at the assembly of the princes, promising among other things that, if the pilgrims defeated the people of Antioch and also drove the Turks from Jerusalem, they would have their lord as brother and friend together with all the Saracens. For, as stated above, the Turks had long before taken Judea, Jerusalem, and all Palestine away from the Saracens.

For this reason, after receiving assurances of security, not a few of the finest soldiers were sent toward Babylon. The barbarians were astonished by their courage, stature, appearance, bearing, and every aspect of their elegance. They acknowledged that the Franks—as they customarily call all the western peoples—were more than human, that is, gods, and declared that it was not at all surprising that such warriors sought to subject the whole world to themselves.

Finally, after taking counsel, the king of Babylon besieged Jerusalem. He displayed his envoys and declared that he was allied with the Franks, threatening that, if the inhabitants did not surrender the city to him, they themselves would be handed over to the Frankish swords.

By these deceptions, the barbarian king recovered the city—not through fear of himself but through fear of the Franks—and, dismissing the Turks with all their belongings, fortified it with every effort, engines, and soldiers against the arrival of the Christians. Thus it came about that Jerusalem was captured twice in one year: first by the Saracens, then by the Franks.

As for what was done with the enemies found there, let anyone who wishes to know understand this: in the portico called Solomon’s, and in his temple, the victorious riders rode in the blood of the Saracens up to their horses’ knees.

Afterward, when it had been arranged who should retain the city, and some wished to return out of love for their homeland and devotion to their parents, word was brought to them that the king of the Babylonians had come to Ascalon with an innumerable multitude of pagans. He intended, as he himself had said, to lead the Franks who were in Jerusalem into captivity and to storm Antioch. But the Lord had ordained otherwise.

When those who were in Jerusalem learned for certain that the Babylonian army was at Ascalon, they hastened to meet it, leaving their baggage and their sick in Jerusalem with a garrison. When they saw the enemy’s innumerable army on August 14, they fell to their knees and called upon God, asking that he who had always been present to help them in their other necessities might, in the present battle, shatter the strength of the pagans and the devil and extend Christ’s kingdom and Church everywhere from sea to sea.

There was no delay. When they cried out to him, God came to their aid and supplied such strength of courage that anyone who saw them run against the enemy would have judged them a sluggish deer thirsting for a spring of living water. This was astonishing, since there were no more than five thousand cavalry and fifteen thousand infantry in the Christian army, while the enemy army may have contained one hundred thousand cavalry and four hundred thousand infantry.

Then God appeared wondrous in his servants. Before they engaged in battle, by their mere advance he put that multitude to flight and seized all their weapons, so that if they afterward wished to resist these men, they would have no arms in which to place their hope.

As for the spoils, it is unnecessary to ask how much was captured, since the treasures of the king of Babylon were seized. More than one hundred thousand Moors fell there by the sword. Their fear was so great that about two thousand were suffocated at the city gate. There is no count of those who perished at sea; even the thorn bushes captured many of them.

Certainly, the whole world fought on behalf of the Christians. And if the spoils of the camp had not detained many of them, only a few of so great a multitude of enemies would have been able to report back from the battle.

On the day before the battle, the army captured many thousands of camels, oxen, and sheep. When the people, at the command of the princes, had released them and advanced to battle, the camels, astonishing to say, formed many and various companies [Note: “multas” and “et” are absent in H]. Oxen and sheep did likewise. These animals accompanied the army in such a way that they stood when it stood, advanced when it advanced, and ran when it ran [Note: another reading says that the same animals accompanied the army in this manner].

Clouds also protected the Christians from the heat of the sun and cooled them [Note: one version has “protected” singular and “cooled”].

After celebrating the victory, the army returned to Jerusalem. Gotefridus was left there as duke, while Count Reginmunt of Saint-Gilles, Count Ruotpert of Normandy, and Count Ruotpert of Flanders returned to Laodicea. There they found the Pisan fleet and Boimundus [Note: “Boimundus with his men”; the witnesses add: “For a considerable multitude, apart from those who had remained with Boimundus at Antioch, gone with Baldwin to Edessa, remained at Tyre, or had been scattered through the surrounding regions, had assembled there”].

When the Pisan archbishop had reconciled Boimundus and the others who were at odds with him [Note: one version continues: “When he had done this, a very large multitude hastened to return to their homeland. As has been said, Gotefridus governed the people who remained in Jerusalem. Thus that great-hearted duke…”], Reginmunt decided to return for God and for his brothers. A great multitude, as stated above, hastened to return to its homeland; the others who remained, through God’s providence, retained the land in peace to this day.

The great-hearted duke, scarcely matched by anyone in religious devotion, supported by a small force yet attempting great things in the Lord, pursued the remnants of the pagans wherever they remained; established garrisons in suitable places; restored Joppa, which had long been destroyed, together with its long-deserted harbor; repaired churches and clergy as far as he could [Note: a later hand wrote “destroyed” in place of this word]; gathered monks elsewhere; and most devotedly bestowed many gifts both upon monasteries and upon the hospital in Jerusalem, which had never failed.

He maintained the firmest peace with the people of Ascalon and Damascus for the sake of commerce. He honored the soldiers of our people above all other warriors [Note: that is, of the German people; a folio is missing at this point in one witness], and, commending their ferocity to the French knights through the gentlest courtesy, he softened the envy that naturally exists in some way between the two groups through his innate mastery of both languages.

In this year Chuonradus, bishop of Utrecht, was killed by his own people. Herimannus, bishop of Cologne, died, and Fridericus succeeded him.

Rapoto, count palatine, and Oudalricus, his cousin, whom they called very wealthy, died. While the emperor was holding a conference with the princes at Regensburg in April, a pestilence suddenly arose and carried off the two aforementioned magnates, along with many more of the lower orders. It also caused considerable slaughter among the common people throughout the cities and regions. An unexpected famine likewise grew severe in many places.

Pope Urbanus died on July 29. While the upheaval among the churches lamentably continued [Note: the words “hactenus… manente” are absent in H], he had convened many councils and promulgated many decrees [Note: one witness has “indeed”]. Among these, after nearly two hundred bishops had been summoned to the city of Piacenza [Note: in 1095; compare Bernoldus under this year and Mansi XX, pp. 801 ff.], he declared the emperor Heinricus deprived of communion both by himself and by his predecessors.

This was done especially at the testimony of Queen Adelheit, the emperor’s wife, who was present and testified many disgraceful things against him before the ears of the entire synod [Note: the witnesses vary between “Adelheit,” “Agnès,” and related forms].

But before he departed this life, instructed by the divine Spirit, he designated Rainerus, cardinal of Saint Clement, a Roman nobleman, abbot of holy conduct and good reputation, to be elected to the apostolic government [Note: one witness reads “kingdom”]. He had also been marked out by other revelations [Note: some witnesses read “others”]. The whole Roman Church consecrated him as its pastor, although unwilling, calling him Paschal [Note: one witness has “they called him”].

## A.D. 1100

Under Duke Gotefridus, who was defending the Church of Jerusalem, a great assembly was held in Jerusalem by all the Christians living in the East, especially by the pilgrims who had settled either at Antioch or in Syria, Edessa, or Palestine. It was so great that, during the very feast of the Lord’s Nativity, many bishops were consecrated in the neighboring regions [Note: one witness reads “in many neighboring regions”; another has “were consecrated” rather than “would be consecrated”]. The mystical prophecies had by then been turned into visible histories:

“Arise, shine, Jerusalem” [Isaiah 60:1];

and:

“Rejoice, Jerusalem, and celebrate the feast, all you who love her” [Isaiah 66:10], and so forth.

After this, as summer grew hot, the air throughout Palestine was corrupted by the stench of corpses. Some also say that springs had been infected by the barbarians with poison, or cisterns with the gore of the slain. From this a pestilence arose and killed many of our people, who were serving as soldiers under a foreign sky. Among them, it took from God’s people Gotefridus himself, whom the whole Catholic Church must mourn with tears: he had cared for the people entrusted to him with a father’s solicitude and cherished them with a mother’s tenderness.

He governed God’s people for only one year. Overcome by a prolonged illness, he ended his present life in Christ, full of faith and good works, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Apart from, or leaving unmentioned, all the virtues in which he excelled [Note: the remainder of this passage is absent in C], he had joined himself with such gentleness to both natives and fellow-pilgrims [Note: another reading: “with pilgrims”] that it was scarcely noticeable whether he was mourned more by the Franks [Note: one witness has “by the Franks”] than by the Syrians or Greeks. His mausoleum stands before Mount Calvary, in the vestibule of the church of Golgotha, constructed of Parian marble.

At this time Count Balduvinus had settled in Edessa [Note: D and H add: “which is thought to be the city of Rages of the Medes”], an illustrious city—or rather a kingdom—and part of Armenia [Note: variants read “royal” rather than “a region”]. He had already obtained the principate of that people, since the great old Christian ruler who had attached himself to Balduvinus from Antioch as his defender, and who had fought many battles bravely, adopting him as his son and heir, had meanwhile died.

Although that broad city had always been attacked from ancient days, it had never surrendered to the pagans, because it was fortified by walls stronger than human workmanship could normally produce, by a river boiling within them, and by every natural feature, as well as by the fertility of its people and provisions.

It is not the place or time to commit to writing how often that aforementioned man, with a small force, struck down a great multitude of barbarians there, and sometimes even, though defeated, conquered [Note: the phrase is absent in one witness]; how, after losing his army, he brought another from the siege of Antioch; and finally how, by the tricks of a certain supposedly allied Turk named Balduc, he freed himself and captured and killed Balduc himself. Anyone wishing to write all this down would be abandoned by time before being abandoned by subject matter.

Nevertheless, when he heard of the death of his brother Gotefridus, he entrusted the city and its people to the younger Balduvinus, his kinsman. He himself set out for Jerusalem with nearly three hundred men, eluded the thousands of pagans lying in ambush for him, engaged them, defeated them, and entered Jerusalem in triumph, laden with spoils, in November.

When all asked and praised him to be their prince, he consented [Note: one witness reads “he consented to their petition”]. Not long afterward, bowing his head over the tomb of the Lord’s sepulchre, he subjected himself perpetually to the Lord’s service.

After this, so that greater fear of the Christians might be instilled in the pagans [Note: the words are absent in one witness], he was crowned on Pentecost, May 21, 1101, having received the royal blessing through a legate of the Apostolic See [Note: some witnesses omit “having received”]. Then he subdued the coastal cities of Arsuf and Caesarea, killed the Saracens who were there, and enlarged his kingdom at the expense of the king of Babylon.

Wigbertus, archbishop of Ravenna, who had been placed over Hildebrand, Gregory [Note: the phrase is absent in some witnesses] and was called Pope Clement, died. He was a man distinguished by considerable intelligence, eloquence, nobility, and personal dignity. At that time he was well received neither in Rome nor in Ravenna. Although, as they say, he had been compelled to rise above one living pope, he himself outlived three successors who followed one another in turn [Note: one version reads “three who succeeded one another”]. Exiled from both sees, Rome and Ravenna, he preferred—as we learned from his own mouth—that he had never accepted the name “apostolic” [Note: some witnesses omit “name”; in one witness a description of the city of Jerusalem is inserted].

## A.D. 1101

Chuonradus, the youthful king, in the ninth year after he had left his father’s court, was related by blood and household association to Mahthildis, that great and most noble woman whom some also call religious. In arranging affairs throughout Italy, he always made use of the counsel both of that woman, of the lord pope, and of other God-fearing persons [Note: one witness continues the preceding phrase differently].

Struck down by an untimely death, he is believed to have passed from the transitory kingdom to the eternal kingdom with complete faith and a good confession. Some also say that he died by poison.

Those who were present commonly testify that they saw the sign of the cross suddenly appear on the arm of his lifeless body, and that his funeral rites were honored by certain miracles [Note: C adds: “And not undeservedly. For so great was the promise of his character that he was lovable. In accordance with that legal command, ‘Honor your father,’ the murmuring with which many tore apart their father’s conduct—and which is thought to have been the cause—reached the ears of the princes, as above under the year 1099.”]

[Col. 0979B] A fire, resembling a city of no small size, was seen by one of our household flying from west to east. [Note: The remainder of this year is missing here in D.] An incredible army of little worms, called “butterflies” because of their resemblance to tents, flew for three continuous days, as though from the borders of Saxony toward Bavaria. [Note: The remainder of this year is missing in E.]

Soon a populous expedition followed, almost equal in number to the preceding one. After the unexpectedly favorable reports of what had been accomplished at Jerusalem had been heard, it was being prepared anew by the peoples remaining throughout the whole West, especially by those whose earlier vows had been hindered by fear or distrust, poverty or weakness. [Note: We have written elsewhere more fully concerning the outcome of this matter. C. omits the rest.] First, 50,000 Lombards took the cross under the bishops of Milan and Pavia and the other Lombard peoples; then came Germans from various provinces; finally Aquitanians, under William of Poitiers, numbering about 30,000 armored men besides the common people.

With Duke Henry’s permission [Note: H. 1 and the others], the Lombard common people crossed through Carinthia. While they wintered in the cities of Bulgaria [Note: i.e. Bulgaria], leaving the Hungarians behind them, they began to diminish in number. At length, when they reached Constantinople, they were transported to the opposite bank—Alexius, that accursed man, customarily hastens this service for pilgrims [Note: A. 1, more than once]—or rather, they were exposed to the arrows of the pagans.

For the Turks, having discovered the Lombards’ sluggishness, wore them down as one wears down straw, so that the German army, which followed the same route and reached that metropolis around the Kalends of June, could in no way discover what had happened to those who had gone before, since no survivor returning from Romania remained. From the entrance, or the first city, of Bulgaria all the way to Alexius’ seat, messengers of his “peace” continually met us; yet sometimes, going ahead of us or accompanying us, they vanished like fading sparks.

The army of his soldiers, whom they call Pechenegs, now inflicted damage upon us from behind, now attacked us from the flank, now joined battle with us in a direct line from the front, and now attempted to break into the camp at night. Thus they were always close to us and hostile for twenty days, until, enjoying the station mentioned above, we were gathered to the number of 100,000 over fifteen days, together with Duke Welf’s troop and William’s army, as well as forces flowing in daily from different places. [Col. 0980A]

Alexius received the leaders of all these separate troops, according to his custom, under the title of “sons.” After receiving their homage and securing their oaths, he distributed gifts among them, as he had done to the earlier armies. To the poor outside the city he ordered alms to be given and a market to be prepared. Because of his suspicion, however, entry into any city, fortress, or stronghold throughout his empire was permitted to only a very few persons—and even to them only for a price and secretly.

For this same reason, when William was prevented from passing with his army through the middle of Adrianople, along which the imperial road runs, the Aquitanians, soon swelling with their native pride, raised a tumultuous cry, set fire to the suburbs, and invaded the city. While they were pressing the assault fiercely, they encountered from behind the army of the Pechenegs, which, as stated above, was always watching that very road at the emperor’s command. Engaging them, they struck down many and lost many; finally they proceeded along the road they had previously despised.

Thus that entire and enormous people planned to direct its march through Romania. Each person bought what was necessary for himself in the wilderness. We were transported across that arm of the sea called Saint George’s, both those compelled to go and those who went willingly; but we awaited with great anxiety what outcome the daily meetings of the leaders and their daily conversations with the emperor would have. [Col. 0980C]

But suddenly an unwelcome rumor arose: the emperor favored the party of the Turks rather than that of the Christians, and, after investigating what was happening around us, he was encouraging them against us with frequent messages.

“This,” they said, “is that treacherous Alexius who, after expelling his lord Michael with the aid of certain hired Germans, usurped his empire [Note: “kingdom,” 5], and had the very men who had shared in his crime killed after condemning them to exile. Now he says that he values Franks fighting with Turks as highly as dogs biting one another.”

When anyone attempted to hire ships, he heard that the emperor had also laid ambushes for pilgrims at sea and had previously sunk many ships by the same crime. Therefore everyone cursed and anathematized him; everyone called him with his tongue not emperor but traitor.

It is incredible to relate, and terrible for those who experienced it to remember, how great was the wavering in our company—that is, the German company, which was the smaller of the groups—when one saw father separated from son, brother from brother, companion from friend, by a separation far more bitter than that by which death separates life: one entrusting himself to the land, another to the sea.

Again, some, after paying the fare and spending one or two nights on a ship, gathered up their belongings and leapt ashore at great loss. They bought back, at a higher price, the horses they had recently sold and hastened toward death in fleeing from death. [Note: “in fleeing,” superscript in 1.]

We too, troubled for a long time and greatly by the same wavering of spirit, finally, among those who had dared to entrust themselves to the open sea, reached the port of Joppa after six weeks, divine mercy governing our sufferings. (August.) Blessed in all things be Jesus Christ!

The united army, having received from the emperor 300 Turcopoles to lead the troops by a suitable route, turned toward Nicomedia. From there, turning aside into Romania, it proceeded toward the northern region, against the land of Chorizana, which is the homeland of the Turks.

For the places in Romania situated around the public road had been devastated by the perjured Alexius, since he had not dared to bring aid, as he had sworn, to our people long besieged in Antioch; for this reason he was already suspect both to the Franks and to the Turks. Moreover, he had proposed that this army should make a name for itself among the nations, as the earlier army had done. But, as the outcome of events proved, this did not please divine predestination.

For only a few days earlier those same pagans had hardened their swords, previously blunted by the scarcely cooled blood of the Lombards, as has been stated; emboldened by this, they dared to resist so innumerable a multitude of warriors.

There were scarcely more than four thousand Turks. Yet these were picked men, mounted on very swift horses and exceedingly well equipped with arms, weapons, and skill in archery. They came to test their fortune or valor against the unknown army, preferring to investigate by reconnaissance rather than to engage openly.

First, like plunderers, they seized the rear of the common people; then they captured or retreated; next, running ahead through the crossroads, they devastated the fodder by fire or by whatever means they could. Sometimes, even while the army was moving through reed beds or marshes, they harassed it throughout the whole day with flames or smoke. At other times they blocked springs [Note: “springs … to harass” is absent in D. H.] or cisterns, attacked from safer positions with missiles, and at night broke into one or another part of the camp, causing disturbance everywhere.

Yet amid all this they never engaged in a direct battle or met us openly in the manner of fighting men. They yielded when resisted, fled when pursued, and followed again when the pursuers turned back.

If we attempt to recount fully those miseries, more pitiable than all miseries, we exceed both our ability and the limits of the account, when we report that so many nobles shamefully fell, so many rich men through want, and so many strong men without weapons; that the servant present could not help his master, nor the man adequately supplied with money the wealthy man, nor was the strong man permitted to fight.

For those places were narrow, impassable, and uninhabitable; they were known to the enemy and unknown to our people. Through them the devices of the traitor Alexius imprisoned the people of God. [Col. 0982A]

Why delay? For nearly twenty days they were exposed like a target to arrows; every day they were regarded as sheep for slaughter. At last, already reduced to the extremity of their fortune, they entrusted themselves by night to the forested ravines, striving to hasten for themselves a lingering but certain death. Escape brought advantage to very few, except that it brought to completion the final destinies of all, though they had been delayed.

For out of that innumerable people of God—alas, alas!—we do not believe that a thousand men survived. We later saw them scarcely clinging to their bones at Rhodes, Paphos, and the other ports, and only a few even at Joppa. Among them Count Bernard and Count Henry of Regensburg died at Jerusalem; Duke Welf, dying on the return journey, was buried at Paphos.

Amid the very long history of their sufferings, which even the character of this concise work does not permit us to set out here, they reported that among our countrymen Archbishop Thiemo of Salzburg [Note: T. 1.] had been captured, the margravine N. had been slaughtered, and two noble men, canons named Bruno, had perished from hunger and thirst. Of the Latin princes, they said that William, Raymond, Stephen, and some of the others had survived.

While these things were taking place, the Christians who were in Judea were not spared either. Daily raids were carried out by the men of Ascalon and Damascus, while wars were prepared by the Babylonians.

After the Kalends of May, the Babylonian army pitched camp not far from Ramla. King Baldwin drew up his line against it [Note: D. H. read, “Baldwin drew up the battle line”] and urged his men not to yield to the multitude of the enemy, just as, a few days earlier, by God’s grace, they had carried away much booty from Arabia with a small force.

“Let us live at their expense,” he said, “or die at their peril! Behold the war, good soldiers, which we once desired [Note: “once” is a correction in 1], for which we despised homeland, parents, and peace [Note: D. H. read “peace”]. To fight for Christ’s inheritance against invaders and foreign plunderers is honorable; to conquer such men is by no means uncertain; to die is glorious.

“Their homeland provides them with flight; our exile provides us with victory. Let us now prove what they themselves reproach us for: that the Franks do not fear death, indeed, that Christ’s pilgrims wish either to conquer in Christ [Note: D. H. read “in Christ”] or to die for Christ!”

After he had delivered many such words and had raised the spirits of his men, by the wonderful will of almighty God the immense Saracen host yielded to a force of only one legion, or slightly more, so completely that they did not even dare to engage. After spending several days in the same station, they returned shamefully and without accomplishing anything.

Again, around the Kalends of September, when the report of the approaching Christians whom we mentioned had terrified the kingdoms of Babylonia, the enemy took counsel and planned to bring about the annihilation of our people—that is, of all who were then found in Judea or throughout those regions. They sent letters to Damascus, Tripoli, Gibelet, and the other barbarian cities, mutually encouraging one another by whatever agreement they could reach against the Christian name.

An army of 40,000 therefore went out from Babylon, first making for Joppa to seize it. Not far from Ascalon, after taking allies from there, it settled in camp.

Baldwin, however, who was not ignorant of the plan, summoned his men from every direction: from Jerusalem, Neapolis [Note: “Nicomedia,” D. H.], Mount Tabor, Hebron, Caesarea, and Arsuf, to Joppa, where at that time a considerable crowd of pilgrims was staying.

In those days we saw—and barely escaped—the great mortality spreading among the people. As many as 300 corpses were carried out of Jerusalem each day, while at Joppa a vast field was covered with graves within a few days.

Finally, on the third hour of a certain day (September 7), the whole people assembled outside the city of Joppa, with the wood of the Lord’s cross preceding the king. In the preceding year certain Syrians had shown this cross, long hidden in the earth, to Duke Godfrey. [Note: G. 1.]

At the king’s command, Arnold, a certain honorable [Note: “venerable,” H.] and well-educated cleric, began thus in the midst of the assembly:

“Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen” (Psalm 32:12). [Note: D. H. add “for an inheritance for himself.”]

“You, dearest brothers, are that blessed nation; that holy nation. You are that people belonging to Christ as an inheritance, that people acquired by him, who, having abandoned everything—homeland, parents, and possessions—have carried your daily cross after Christ. You have given your bodies [Note: D. H. omit “your bodies”] over to suffering for Christ. You appear to have fought, but Christ, through the blood which you willingly sacrificed to him and through the precious death of your brothers and fellow soldiers, has deigned to cleanse the place of his sanctification. He wished, through your devoted service, to free Jerusalem, the city of his rest, after so many years of bondage to the most filthy people.

“‘This is my rest for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it’” (Psalm 131:14).

“Against the hope given to us by divine promise, behold, by God’s will the letters of the pagans have been seized from messengers captured the day before. They report prophecies uttered by demons: that we are to be destroyed by their attacks this year; that Jerusalem is to be utterly destroyed; and—something even more horrifying to say than all their other abominations—that the stone of the Lord’s glorious tomb itself is to be broken layer by layer, carried by camels to the sea, and sunk in the most distant waters, where Christians will never be able to recover it. [Col. 0983D] [Note: This is absent in D. H.]

“Therefore, people devoted to Christ, consider what must be done; weigh what end this great presumption will finally have!”

He wished to discuss further matters, but an interrupting uproar immediately silenced him. As though from one mouth, the unanimous voice of all resounded:

“Events stand at a critical point. Our counsel is brief and, in a manner, concise: for Christ, Christ’s laws, and our holy things, we must either fight bravely or die shamefully. Either we must die gloriously and live eternally, or we must yield most shamefully and purchase perpetual death by a brief and shameful life.

“Nor may anyone live either temporally or eternally who is unwilling to fight against so profane and blasphemous an audacity of pagans!”

Immediately, before the cross of our redemption, they made a unanimous act of humility by confessing their sins. After receiving the indulgence pronounced by the apostolic legate, who happened to be present at that time, and receiving his blessing, they called upon the Lord for help and were restored to the fortress with cheerful spirits.

At dawn they were counted: 7,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry. With great joy they were presented for the immense danger.

When they saw the barbarians’ position, wonderful to relate, their faith began to burn so strongly that each man did not doubt that he alone could strike down so many legions. Consequently, when they rushed upon the enemy in disorder and with insufficient caution for nearly a mile, the first cohort was attacked from the flank and immediately fell as a whole.

Baldwin, enraged by this, charged them with such a force of cavalry that, although they resisted more fiercely than ever before, assured by the responses of their idols that they would be victorious, they melted before him like wax before the face of fire.

The venerable Abbot Gerard, who at that time always carried the Lord’s cross close beside the king, told me that he had never seen such a dense multitude of snow or rain as the multitude of missiles flying against the king at that time. But after the precious wood had been shown, none of the enemy entrusted himself to missiles or weapons; all committed themselves to flight for protection.

Thus, after the victory had been granted them by God—“for it is no harder for him to save by many than by few” (1 Maccabees 3:18)—while they were plundering the enemy’s camp and booty, a messenger arrived from the people of Joppa, reporting that the city was besieged by land and sea.

Immediately, weighed down with spoils and committing the remainder to the flames, they hastened as quickly as possible to our aid. We had already blocked the gates from within and were surrounded on land by many horsemen and at sea by forty-two ships with rams.

After so many attacks by the enemy and such sufferings of poverty and pestilence [Note: Witnesses 1, 4, 5, and 10 read “such great”; 9c reads “such great … misery”], they caused us to complete with the greatest rejoicing the feast of the Nativity of the Mother of God (September 8), which we had begun that very day in sorrow.

On the following day (September 9), thirty ships brought us an abundant supply of grain and all kinds of provisions, together with the pilgrim brothers, estimated at 12,000. When the enemy fleet attempted to attack them, the marvelous power of God, through the virtue of the holy cross—which, since no bodily assistance could be brought from the city, was raised high in the air at the king’s command—so restrained them that both pagans and Christians marveled greatly that neither force nor skill in rowing could move even one of all those ships from its position.

Nor should we pass over in silence what we learned had happened there in the same year, as the venerable priest Herimann, who was then living on the Mount of Olives, reported in these words:

“On the day of the most sacred Sabbath, when, after the baptism had already been consecrated, we were devoutly awaiting the heavenly light to be bestowed upon us according to the Lord's ancient consolation, we continued until evening in our customary prayers. Then, because of our sins, we were altogether deprived of the desired heavenly gift, which Christians before us had always been accustomed to receive publicly before the eyes of the nations. We passed that night of the Lord’s resurrection mourning and grieving, without any service of festive assembly.

“At dawn, barefoot and with litanies, we proceeded from the Lord’s tomb. We entered the temple of the Lord, at the place—that is, Mount Moriah [Note: H. reads “on Mount Moriah”], at the threshing floor of Araunah (2 Samuel 24:23)—where we read that David was heard in his greatest tribulation and that all who pray there with devoted hearts were promised to be heard by Solomon.

“Immediately after prayers and tears had been poured out, lest Christ, by abandoning us, prepare blasphemy against his name among the nations, we had not yet left that famous court when suddenly we heard the sound of bells and high praises echoing toward us from those who had remained behind. Entering the aforesaid church, we saw, filled with immense joy, two lamps kindled from heaven.

“What more need be said? Beginning with the baptismal service, from which we had abstained the previous day, we paid to the Lord, with the most joyful devotion, the whole obligation of our service that had long been withheld, until the completion of Mass. After we too had gone out, other lamps were divinely kindled during the Mass of the Syrians, who always sing in the same choir after our departure. Before Vespers and during the Vespers praises themselves, the number of such visible lights increased to sixteen.

“Thus it happened that scarcely any Christians or pagans remaining within Jerusalem could be found who did not testify that they had seen so evident a manifestation of Christ’s power.”

**A.D. 1102** [Note: Witness 3 prefixes the marginal numbers 46 and 19.]

Emperor Henry [Note: H. 1 repeatedly], after conferring with the princes, announced that he would go to Rome and summon a general council there around the Kalends of February, so that, after both his own case and that of the apostolic lord had been canonically examined, the Catholic unity between kingdom and priesthood—which had remained divided for so many years—might be restored. [Note: C. continues: “He began to consider whether it might be possible for him to set out for Rome around the Kalends of February, so that unity might be confirmed. But since he was prevented by other affairs, after half the—,” etc.]

It is nevertheless clear that he did not come according to the agreement, nor did he send messengers professing submission to the apostolic dignity. Nor is it hidden that he attempted, if possible, to set up another pope over Lord Paschal, but did not succeed.

After half of Lent had passed, when all the bishops of Apulia, Campania [Note: Omitted in D1], Sicily, Tuscany [Note: C reads “Tuscia”], and Italy as a whole had assembled, together with the legates of very many fathers from beyond the Alps, a great synod was held at Rome (March). In addition to the ancient regulations of the Fathers, reverently confirmed according to custom, the oft-mentioned schism of our time was also counted among the principal heresies and condemned forever, together with its authors and followers, by the following signed profession:

“I anathematize every heresy, and especially that which disturbs the condition of the present Church, which teaches and asserts that anathema is to be despised and the bonds of the Church rejected.

“I promise obedience to the pontiff of the apostolic see, Lord Paschal, and to his successors, under the testimony of Christ and the Church, affirming what the holy and universal Church affirms, and condemning what it condemns.” [Note: The remainder of “I promise … they contain iniquity” is absent in C.]

There too we learned from the mouth of the same apostolic lord Paschal [Note: P. 1 repeatedly], at the Last Supper of the Lord (April 3), in the Lateran church, what sentence he had promulgated against the emperor, or Roman patrician, Henry [Note: The reading was corrected in witness 1]. This was after we had entrusted ourselves at Joppa to the waves of the sea on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and, through Christ’s grace, had been brought to Rome during the aforesaid Holy Week, amid countless throngs of peoples from different nations.

“Because,” he said, “he did not cease to tear Christ’s tunic—that is, to devastate the Church with plunder and fires and to defile it with lusts, perjuries, and murders—he was first excommunicated and condemned by Pope Gregory of blessed memory, and then, because of his disobedience, by the most holy man Urban, my predecessor. We too, in our recent synod, by the judgment of the whole Church, have consigned him forever to anathema. We wish this to be known to all, and especially to those from beyond the Alps, so that they may keep themselves from his iniquity.” [Col. 0986B] [Note: The profession from “I promise” through “keep themselves from his iniquity” is absent in C.]

Hartwig, archbishop of Magdeburg, died, a man praiseworthy in many respects, but especially popular, and laboring greatly to expand the interests of the Church over which he presided. In the oft-mentioned schism he was also an indefatigable mediator, striving to restore peace between the two sides. [Note: D. and E. arrange the remainder of this year as follows: “Erbo … lord. Ruotpertus … religious. Hartwig … indefatigable.” C. has only this: “Ruotpert, bishop, is appointed in his place, a man wholly religious and, above all, more faithful to the emperor than anyone else, even unto death and not without great dangers. Hartwig, bishop of Magdeburg, died.”]

Bishop Ruotpert of Bamberg died. In his place Emperor Henry appointed Otto, his chancellor, a man believed to be religious.

Aerbo, now advanced in age, a noble prince of Carinthia and formerly count palatine in Bavaria, departed in the Lord.

A battle was also fought (July) by Baldwin and the Jerusalemites who were with him against an innumerable multitude of Saracens. Since the affair was conducted rashly, our men, already greatly reduced in number and surrounded by the multitude of archers, were compelled to withdraw within the walls of the nearby city of Ramla; the king, they say, escaped with three horsemen.

When the barbarians appeared to have more men than the fortress had stones [Note: “to be enclosed,” added by 11, who did not understand the passage], they soon demolished the entire wall. After capturing and killing all whom they found, they sent the captives, together with messengers announcing their victory, on to Babylon. They then safely pitched their own camp in the open country, as though they intended to possess that land, acquired by their swords, while awaiting the return of their king’s messengers.
