But that victory did not go unpunished for them. It had been won not by their own strength but by divine disposition among those whom God wished to inhabit paradise rather than any longer dwell upon earth. On the third day Baldwin arrived with a large army, which he ought to have awaited earlier, and destroyed them with such slaughter that their victory neither pleased nor benefited them.

That new army was led both by Raymond of Tripoli, whom Baldwin had recently defeated, and by Tancred, who was bringing forces from Antioch. For his uncle Bohemond, captured by the Turks through treachery two years earlier, had left him the principality of Antioch. [Note: This entire battle notice is missing at this point in D. and E., and is not found in C.]

**A.D. 1103** [Note: C reads: “While Emperor Henry was celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz and discussing with the princes all necessary matters concerning the state of the realm, a rumor suddenly spread that he would entrust the supreme power to his son King Henry and visit the Lord’s tomb, thereby making satisfaction to Christ for his sins. Accordingly, some prepared themselves, with the greatest favor, to join his company. Cuono, etc.”]

Cuono, son of Otto, duke of Northeim and Bavaria [Note: Otto is identified as duke of Northeim and Bavaria], one of the great princes, and second to none in all human distinction—pre-eminent in birth, knowledge of letters, courage, and wealth, and beloved and approachable by all good men for his elegance and eloquence—was attacked and killed at night, while traveling, by a conspiracy of certain murderous men. He left the nobles of the realm in immense grief and suspicion, since such great crimes are attempted by the lowest against the highest.

Three years earlier, Henry the Fat, Cuono’s own brother and elder [Note: C. 1 and E1 read “Chunradi”; D. reads “Cuonradi”], while traveling to conduct affairs in the Frisian march over which he presided, was surrounded by an ambush laid by the common Frisians, to whom the yoke of his rule was burdensome. While demanding their obedience, he was surrounded by their ambush. When the matter became known, he fled toward the sea, but was wounded by sailors and at the same time suffocated. The death of this great man, who held the principality of all Saxony second only to the king, was deeply mourned throughout the entire Teutonic realm; and now, as we have said, that grief was doubled by the killing of his brother Cuono.

Henry, margrave of Ilburg [Note: C., D., and E. identify him as “of Ilburg”], the most powerful man of his time in Saxony, died.

**A.D. 1104**

Henry the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Regensburg. While he remained there for some time, a rumor first arose among the Bavarian princes because Saxons and Franks were treated there by the emperor with greater familiarity and honor than the natives.

Count Sigihard, who was especially marked out by this suspicion, gradually began to become disliked by the emperor. This was especially because, alone among all the princes then present, he had brought a larger number of soldiers and appeared to have fortified himself in order to resist, should anything go wrong at court.

Several days later, when the same count had become more secure and had allowed his troops to disperse, a furious uprising was stirred against him. The conspirators included both the townsmen of Regensburg and men of the ministerial class from various regions. [Note: Compare Stenzel I, p. 582, on this passage, and the constitution concerning the law of advocates, Mon. Legg. II, p. 62.] The revolt could not be calmed, even when the emperor’s own son intervened.

At length, after being besieged in his lodging from the third hour of the day until the ninth, the doors were broken down. He first made confession, received the viaticum of the Lord’s sacrament, and then was beheaded and died. [Note: The remainder of “Concerning this crime … the city itself” is absent in C.]

We refrain from reporting more about this crime, especially since the punishments and other evils that followed are still before our eyes, and we cannot know what end they will have.

Apart from these events, however, the land enjoyed considerable peace everywhere, together with fertility, pleasant weather, and bodily health. [Note: “Sanitata” was corrected to “sanitate” in witness 1.] Some palmers returning from Jerusalem also announced that Acre, which is also called Accaron, had been conquered by our people. They reported many other favorable events concerning the condition of the Church of Jerusalem, which would bring us great joy.

Count Boto, surnamed the Strong, brother of that Aerbo whom we mentioned above [Note: A.D. 1102, col. 986], died full of days not far from Regensburg. He was conveyed to the monastery of Theres [Note: Theres near the Main], which he had richly endowed from his own resources and estates, and was buried there.

These two brothers, Aerbo and Boto, drew the most ancient nobility of the Noric people from their paternal bloodline, namely from the famous Aerbo whom, pierced by a bison while hunting, the songs of the common people still celebrate. He was the son of Count Hartwig the Palatine, who was the brother of that Frederick [Note: “Frederick.” Since Ekkehard wrote this name when revising the book, it should be preferred. The genealogy is of this sort: D. E.] who had fathered Sigihard, the man killed at Regensburg.

On their mother’s side, their lineage came from Saxony, from the distinguished tribe of the Immedingians, which is also said to have been related to the illustrious line of the Ottos. For the Saxon history mentions that same Immid in these words: [Note: Widukind I, 3.]

“There was,” it says, “a famous and most noble queen of singular prudence, namely Mahthildis, mother of the great Otto, daughter of Theodoric, whose brothers were Witukind, Immid, and Reginbern. Reginbern himself was the one who fought against the Danes, who for a long time devastated Saxony, and defeated them, freeing his homeland from their incursions to this very day. These men belonged to the lineage of the great Duke Witukind, who waged a mighty war against the great Charles for nearly thirty years.”

As we have said, from the seed of these most illustrious princes, the noble Friderun, mother of Aerbo and Boto, was born from Reting, son of Boto, son of Reting, born from the second Boto. After Hartwig’s death she immediately consecrated herself under the veil of widowhood, while Aerbo was still a small child and she was pregnant with the posthumous Boto.

We know that both men made considerable progress in letters, arms, and worldly affairs. Yet the people of almost the whole of Germany and Italy testify that Boto, just as he was taller and more handsome in body, was also more outstanding and renowned in military matters. Pannonia admits that it once experienced him as such a great man that he is truly believed among them to have been one of the ancient giants.

There would be ample opportunity to report more about him, if the purpose of this concise work did not forbid it.

John, bishop of Speyer, afflicted with some ulcer around the genitals, about which certain notable reports were also being spread, weakened by a long illness, was buried in the city itself. [Note: The bishop died and was buried in his monastery at Sunnisheim [Sinzheim in the grand duchy of Baden], which he himself had built. E. reads: “in the monastery of Sunnisheim,” which he himself had built; witnesses 4–11.]

Cuonrad, a young man and son of Margravine Beatrix, after abandoning the study of letters, in which he had been especially well instructed [Note: “educated,” C.], devoted himself to arms. In accordance with Christ’s prophecy—“he who takes the sword will perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52)—he perished by the sword.

Not long afterward Beatrix herself also died and was buried beside her father, Duke Otto, in the fortress of Schweinfurt. [Note: C. omits the passage from “And beside her father” through “might be seen.”]

Around the summer solstice, when the air changed into stormy weather, ice is said to have fallen among the hailstones in the district of Würzburg, of such size that, after being divided into four pieces, each piece seemed too heavy for four men to carry.

In the bishopric of Speyer, blood appeared to flow from loaves of bread; it was also found prodigiously in a dish of lentils. This was interpreted as a portent of civil, indeed intestine, war, by analogy with an ancient story of Roman history. [Note: Compare above, col. 635.]

**A.D. 1105** [Note: Witness 5 adds in red: “The years of Henry V,” with the marginal numbers 49, 22, 1.]

While [Note: [Col. 0992A] C reads as follows: “King Henry, touched by the innate greatness of spirit of his youth, began, amid the many hardships—despite the good foresight of his father, and also because of his frequent bodily ailments—to perceive the instability of fortune and the variability of affairs. Taking precautions lest perhaps the unexpected death of his father should find him not yet fully provided with friends or soldiers, or even specially distinguished in military matters, and thus bring upon him some difficulty in ruling, he was not content with his father’s palace, nor with the common household, although it was in every respect most august, but withdrew to Bavaria. There he allied himself with the princes of that region, some of whom had been drawn by kinship on his mother’s side, and insisted on managing the affairs of the state himself, as king and son of a king. First, therefore, through Gebhard, bishop of Constance, at that time the representative of Pope Paschal, he was united to the Roman See by a profession of due obedience; then, taking with him certain Noricans, as well as some nobles from Alemannia and eastern Francia, he turned to the Saxons. Received honorably by them, and celebrating Easter at Quedlinburg, he soon gained possession of all the cities of Saxony and was sufficiently honored with royal dignity by the leading men. There are those who say that this division had been arranged through the enterprise of the emperor himself, whose prudence scarcely anyone could equal, so that by means of a pretended discord he might cleverly draw into his son’s fellowship that part of the kingdom which was defecting from the father—namely, lest there be any place or opportunity for his adversaries truly to make another head for themselves. We, however, believe that the whole matter was undoubtedly accomplished through divine dispensation, and, with God’s assent, we shall confirm the matter itself by its good result. For, instructed by letters from Pope Paschal and by the counsel and service of Ruothard, etc.”] Emperor Henry celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz; Henry, his son, called King Henry V after that name, was plotting rebellion against his father in Bavaria, with the margrave Diotpald, Count Bernger, and a certain nobleman Otto, related to him on his mother’s side. With their counsel and assistance he had departed from his father’s side a few days earlier. First, indeed, he anathematized the heresy mentioned above and professed the obedience owed to the pontiff of the apostolic See; then, allied with the Norican princes and with certain nobles from Alemannia and eastern Francia, he turned to the Saxons. Received honorably by them, and celebrating Easter at Quedlinburg (April 9), he soon gained possession of all the cities of Saxony and was sufficiently honored with royal dignity by the leading men.

Nevertheless, by the counsel and service of Ruothard of Mainz and Gebhard, bishop of Constance—namely, representatives of the lord Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0992C] “representatives of the lord Pope Paschal” is absent in C, D, and E.]—he reconciled all Saxony to communion with the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0992C] absent in D and E]. He also summoned the bishops and clergy to a general assembly in the royal estate called Northusun, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, where the already corrupted discipline of ecclesiastical institution was to be discussed.

In that council, after the decrees of the Fathers concerning the matters at issue had first been reread, those things which could laudably be corrected at that time were corrected, while certain matters which seemed more serious were deferred to the apostolic hearing. The heresy of simony, condemned by the custom of the Fathers, was rejected; likewise, the fornicating intercourse of the Nicolaitans was there renounced by all. The fast of the month of March was ordered by the aforesaid bishops, on apostolic authority, to be observed according to Roman custom in the first week of Lent [Note: [Col. 0991] “first” is read thus in E; “in the same week” in 1a; C and D have “of Lent”; a word has been erased here in 1; “first” is absent from 4 and the remaining witnesses.], while the fast of the month of June was to be observed in the very week of Pentecost. The Peace of God was confirmed. To those who had been consecrated by pseudo-bishops, reconciliation through the imposition of the Catholic hand was promised for the next fast [Note: [Col. 0992C] The words “but to these … is promised” are absent in C; [Col. 0991] written above the line in manuscript 1.].

Meanwhile we saw something which we cannot pass over in silence: King Henry publicly displayed considerable hope of good character, together with great humility and authority. For, although he wished to attend the assembly of the servants of God only when summoned—for a great crowd had gathered there with the bishops and clergy, including abbots and monks, all thirsting for ecclesiastical unity—he was at last brought forward in humble attire and stood in a more elevated place. There, in accordance with the decrees of the princes, he reasonably renewed all their laws and rights. If anything unreasonable was requested, he refuted it with an extraordinary prudence beyond his years and with ancestral greatness of spirit. In all this he wonderfully preserved the modesty proper to youth while also displaying reverence worthy of Christ’s priests.

Amid these events, with tears arising, he called upon the King of Heaven himself and the whole heavenly host as witnesses that he was not usurping his father’s rule out of any desire to reign, nor wishing his lord and father to be deposed from the Roman empire [Col. 0991D]; rather, he continually showed due compassion for his obstinacy and disobedience. If his father wished to subject himself to Saint Peter and his successors according to Christian law, he promised either to yield the kingdom or to submit to him in servile obedience.

When the whole multitude heard this, they praised it together and began to pour forth tears and prayers both for the father’s conversion and for the son’s prosperity, proclaiming aloud, “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.” At that same hour, the bishops Uto of Hildesheim, Henry of Paderborn, and Frederick of Halberstadt, prostrating themselves at the feet of the metropolitan, surrendered themselves to apostolic obedience, with the testimony of the metropolitan, of the king who was standing there, and of the whole church present. The matters entrusted to them were nevertheless reserved for apostolic judgment, with only the suspension of their office imposed upon them.

[Col. 0992C] When these matters had been properly arranged [Note: [Col. 0991] “these matters were thus properly arranged” in D1. There appears to be an error here: the council is said to have been held on 29 May, whereas Pentecost begins on the 28th.], the same king, celebrating Pentecost at Merseburg (May 28), had Henry, long designated archbishop of the church of Magdeburg but rejected by the emperor’s followers, consecrated [Note: [Col. 0991] “Magdeburg” corrected from “Megdeburg” in 1]. Not long afterward he moved an expedition against Mainz, intending to restore the bishop expelled there. His father was awaiting the outcome inside the walls with a considerable troop of soldiers and with several princes who were not, however, entirely trustworthy to him.

Just as the intervening Rhine and the removal of the ships denied these men access to the city, so consideration of the oaths made both by son and father forbade them a parricidal war. Nevertheless, many messengers traveled back and forth; the leading men of the kingdom weighed many plans among themselves [Col. 0993A]. The father promised a division of the kingdom and confirmation of hereditary succession, while the son demanded nothing except the achievement of submission to the apostolic authority and ecclesiastical unity.

Thus departing at night [Note: [Col. 0993] “at night” corrected from “at once” in C], he reached Würzburg (July) [Note: [Col. 0994C] C reads: “He reached Würzburg, and there pitched camp outside the city. In that same year, after the death of Bishop Emehard, Erlung, a canon of the church of Bamberg, a man of singular integrity and exceptional prudence, succeeded him. He had been most carefully educated and thoroughly trained in the liberal disciplines by his maternal uncle, Meginhard, a highly learned man who had formerly been bishop of the same see. Because of the good fragrance of his reputation, he had been summoned from the Bamberg cloister to the palace and had competently discharged the office of chancellor for several years; then, by the consent of both clergy and people, he obtained the bishopric of Würzburg. Considering perseverance to be the virtue of a good work, and since he had not yet been consecrated, he preferred to yield his place rather than be marked by even the slightest disloyalty toward the emperor, whom he had served until then with unfailing sincerity. When he withdrew, the king appointed Ruotpert, etc.”]. Expelling a certain Erlung [Note: [Col. 0994D] D and E read “Erlung,” whom the emperor had designated bishop after the death of Emehard], whom the emperor had formerly designated as bishop, he enthroned Ruotpert, provost of that church, who had previously and now alike been elected by clergy and people, through the archbishop Ruothard [Note: [Col. 0995A] “and, both previously and then, elected” is absent in C, D, and E]. Thus, after that church had been reconciled to apostolic communion and he had received security from the townspeople, he dismissed the Saxons and turned with the Bavarians toward the siege of the castle of Nuremberg. After taking it successfully two or more months later (August–September), he disbanded the army and withdrew to Regensburg.

His father followed immediately, restored Erlung to the people of Würzburg after driving out Ruotpert, and, laying waste to everything belonging to his son’s supporters, finally, with the treacherous assistance of the people of Regensburg, drove his son from the city. Remaining there, he appointed to that see a certain youth named Oudelric [Note: [Col. 0993] “Oudelric” in 1; C, D, and E read: “he appointed a certain youth, whose name was Oudelric,” with variants in the manuscripts]. For Gebhard, who had occupied the place of shepherd there miserably for sixteen years, had died that same year, slaughtered by one of his own soldiers whom he had treated with excessive cruelty; and thus he was doubly worthy of lamentation.

Having gathered an army from every direction, the emperor advanced and devastated the march of Diotpald, chiefly through the cruelty of the Bohemian people [Note: [Col. 0995A] C, D, and E add: “The emperor, having gathered an army from every direction, advanced and devastated the march, etc.”]. Nor did the king’s soldiers remain any longer with their lord without making an expedition everywhere, repaying the imperial fires and plunder from behind, and finally seeking an engagement with ten thousand chosen young men divided into five legions.

[Col. 0993C] With the camps now set against one another, in a spectacle of extreme horror, for three continuous days the standards of the emperor flew on one bank of the Regen River and those of the king on the other. Frequent skirmishes already raged in the riverbed itself; during one of them Count Hartwic fell on the emperor’s side [Note: [Col. 0995A] The words “and … fell” are absent in C, which continues, “not a few”; D and E add: “Count Sigihard is captured.”]. Nor did the uncertain lot of Mars carry off only a few from either side. Yet on the day preceding the one on which a general engagement was most certainly expected, the princes who seemed to be the heads and strength of both armies, after mutually granting peaceful conferences and laboriously debating among themselves the cause of the present war, at last, as is believed, taught by the divine Spirit, considered unanimously that such a harsh and dangerous undertaking contained little justice and little advantage [Col. 0993D]. Accordingly, they judged with one accord that the brothers—namely, the Christian people on both sides—ought to be spared, or rather that the parricidal battle ought to cease.

The young king, too, when bloody Mars had already begun, as we have said, to roar amid battle lines ordered on every side, is said to have cried out mournfully, his heart stirred by grief for his father:

“Thanks, good fellow soldiers,” he said, “I offer you the greatest thanks for your affection toward me. If circumstances require it, I do not refuse to repay each of you in equal measure. Yet let no one wish or believe that I am allied with him for this purpose: that he may boast of having killed, or ever consider killing, my lord and father [Col. 0994A].

“I wish, if it pleases the ruler of all things, to hold the kingdom entrusted to me under Christian laws as heir and successor of the emperors. But I do not wish to be called or to be a parricide. If my father submits himself to the yoke of apostolic obedience, I shall immediately be content with those things which his clemency alone grants me. Meanwhile, you should know that I am not the assailant of my father but the defender of my father’s kingdom.”

[Note: [Col. 0995A] C reads: “I desire to hold the inheritance of my fathers and of the holy emperors, if the ruler of all things grants it, and to possess it by the law of nations; but I do not wish to be called or to be a parricide. But if my father subjects himself to apostolic obedience—which is indeed the point at issue—you are to know that I am rather the defender of my father’s kingdom.” Several words in this reading are printed only as initials. It continues: “Meanwhile, as evening was already falling, the royal companies returned to camp. But while the emperor, as though certain of a battle on the morrow, was instructing his men, he heard from the princes that neither battle nor the wish to fight was permissible there. Informed that a conspiracy had been made against him by his own men, he secretly withdrew from the camp with a few men. As the dark night allowed, each hastened back to his own place. But the king, granting mercy to his disordered enemies, won the city of Würzburg to his side …”]

As the day was now growing late, the royal phalanxes withdrew from the field, loudly declaring that they wished to show reverence to the imperial majesty. But while the emperor was arranging his forces in the camp for the next day’s expected battle, he heard from the princes—through the duke of Bohemia and Margrave Liupald, contrary to expectation—that there was neither a battle nor any desire for battle on their part.

Immediately dismayed in spirit, he humbly sought their assistance but did not obtain it. He was also informed by the secret messages of his son that his own men had conspired against him. He therefore slipped away secretly from the camp with only a very few men. Thus, by divine providence, while one man was saved, the blood of many—which was believed would have to be shed—was spared. For as soon as the emperor’s absence became known throughout the entire camp in every direction, each man hastened to return to his own place, especially since the darkness of night offered a safe means of turning aside into hiding.

But the king, while he could have used his disordered enemies at will, decided to spare rather than pursue them. Because of the city’s earlier breach of the treaty, he secured it for himself under a stricter agreement. He deposed Oudelric [Note: [Col. 0993] “Hartwic … enthrones” appears in the margin of 1] and enthroned Hartwic, a proven Catholic and noble man [Note: [Col. 0994C] C, D, and E read “a certain youth named Oudelric,” with manuscript variants]. He also won over certain bishops and princes of his father’s army whom he found inside the walls. Then, returning to Francia, he made the treacherous Würzburgers drink from the same cup.

Among these events was the following: the aforementioned Erlung [Note: [Col. 0995B] C reads: “Here the bishop Erlung, who had received the episcopate there from the emperor, considering with indignation, as a prudent and discerning man, the wheel of fortune, surrendered himself to the king as he restored Ruotpert; thereafter, since he had long been especially well known, he was treated among the king’s chaplains with great and particular honor. After this, arriving at Speyer, the king appointed Gebehard, abbot of Hirsau, bishop there; he also restored Ruothard, who had been driven from his see for eight years, to noble Mainz, and thus reconciled both its people and clergy to apostolic communion. Then, turning toward Burgundy, he was recalled by messages from his faithful men; and, forestalling certain deceitful schemes of Count Sigefrid, by which, with the emperor, he was said to be trying to hinder the princely assembly appointed by all the princes of the kingdom concerning the present matter, he found his father at Bingen around the Ides of December. Face to face, the son admonished his father concerning those things which seemed worthy of correction—though the order was reversed, it was necessarily changed—and promised to render the obedience due, provided that the latter did not refuse God.”], who had usurped the name of bishop there, frustrated in the hope he had conceived, yielded his see to Ruotpert and surrendered himself to the king. Thereafter he was considered equally faithful among the king’s chaplains.

[Col. 0995C] Meanwhile, hearing that his father had been found with Wigpert, a most illustrious and prudent man [Col. 0995D], who ruled over the regions inhabited by the Sorbs, the king allowed him to govern that man’s duchy as far as the Rhine—for this was what his father himself requested through ambassadors. Nevertheless, lest he be harassed there by any plot of his father’s, he promptly departed from Würzburg and crossed the aforesaid river, not without danger, near Speyer. Soon, having gained possession of the city itself and of the treasures of his father stored there (October 31), he appointed as bishop of Speyer Gebhard, abbot of Hirsau, a wise and noble man, distinguished by the reputation of his holy way of life and by the excellence of his character, and beloved by all sound-minded men.

In those days the venerable Archbishop Ruothard, escorted from Thuringia—where for eight years he had avoided the tyrant’s madness—by the protection of Catholic princes, was restored to his see at Mainz amid the greatest rejoicing of the nobles. Reconciling both the people and the clergy to the apostolic Church, he was honored by everyone not only as an aged father but also as one risen again from the dead.

When affairs around the Rhine had been settled, King Henry turned toward Burgundy (December). But, recalled by messengers from his faithful supporters, he forestalled with remarkable speed the plots which his father was contriving with the assistance of Count Sigefrid. For, as his father was making for Mainz and attempting to impede the princely assembly, agreed upon by all the king’s princes concerning the present matter and expected at the Nativity of the Lord, the son found him at Bingen around the Ides of December [Col. 0996B]. Face to face, the son admonished his father concerning the bond of anathema and the other offenses he had arrogantly committed against the state. The order of the matter was reversed, but necessarily so; he promised him the obedience due, provided only that he should deign to repent.

The elder deferred these and many similar pronouncements to the hearing of the leading men and the decision of the senate in the approaching assembly. Thus, each company, peaceful toward the other, turned together against the oft-mentioned metropolis.

Meanwhile, while the king’s faithful supporters reported through secret messengers that the father was attempting certain actions incompatible with this agreement and peace, it seemed best to them that the father should separately await the assembly of the princes with his own men in some exceedingly secure castle [Col. 0996C], especially since the bishops of Mainz and Speyer, together with the others who were present, publicly protested that they could not grant him communion within their churches, which had only recently been reconciled.

These arrangements having been made, and guards having also been assigned to prevent anything new from proceeding from him or reaching him [Note: [Col. 0995] Ekkhard omits a word, perhaps “take precautions”], the king went to Mainz for the public assembly of the princes. But popular folly spread the report everywhere that the father had been captured by his son through deceit and handed over to custody [Note: [Col. 0996C] C and E add: “On the day before … was on his side,” in the passage below].

In this year King Baldwin, surrounding Ascalon from the sea with a very large multitude of ships and from the land with a considerable army, compelled it through a long siege to become tributary to him. After several months, the divine power struck down before him the strength of fifty thousand Saracens who had unexpectedly invaded him, with one commander—who appeared to be second to the king of Babylon—captured, and another killed amid the rest of the multitude.

As the mercy of Christ prospered his pilgrims at Antioch, in Syria, throughout Palestine, and throughout all Asia, and as their service drove barbarous filth from every side, Alexius, hitherto an envious and hidden persecutor of the Church, unsheathed the long-concealed, poison-tainted madness of his treachery. He most securely allied himself with the Turks, for whom scarcely any hope of ruling remained in the East, and—O most shameful deed!—returned to the sons of the tyrant Soloman Nicaea, which we previously described as a tower of our faith, long ago acquired at the cost of much Christian blood [Note: [Col. 0997] D and H read “redeemed”]. He established guards on land and sea to prevent the pilgrims’ passage [Note: [Col. 0997] D and H read: “he stirred up the Babylonian king against our people and established guards”], and by frequent messages encouraged the king of Babylon against us.

His fleets, sent against the people of Antioch, were captured by the Antiochene forces in battle. They cut off the noses and thumbs of all Alexius’s men, loaded one of their boats with this kind of fare, and sent it to that king, a murderer of many thousands [Note: [Col. 0997] D and H read: “His numerous fleets of beaked ships against the Antiochenes …”].

Bohemond, too, released by divine providence after three years of captivity, came by ship to Italy [Col. 0997B]. There, arranging for fleets to be built, he himself traveled as far as the kingdoms of Spain and began gathering, by whatever means he could, all the military force he was able to assemble against the aforesaid tyrant.

Duke Frederick died, a man sufficiently renowned for prudence, character, and nobility, but adorned by his marriage to Adelheid [Note: [Col. 0997] C corrects this to “Agnes”], a woman of the most distinguished and singularly illustrious reputation, namely the emperor’s daughter, and by offspring of remarkable character born from that union [Note: [Col. 0997B] C, D, and E read: “Duke Frederick, a man … adorned, died.” C adds: “His duchy was assumed by Frederick, his eldest son, while still a boy, and he was always treated with great and fitting honor and affection by his maternal uncle, the king. END OF BOOK TWO.”].

On the day before the vigil of the Nativity of Christ, a fire appeared to flame among the stars in the west with such magnitude that it would have been thought to be the sun’s radiance had it been in the eastern part.

A. [Note: [Col. 0997] Added: “50. 23. 2.”]  
D. 1106.

During the reign of the younger Henry [Note: [Col. 0997] “The remainder from 1. Likewise, in 4–11 they are extant. What C, D, and E have follows below], such a great assembly of the entire Teutonic kingdom was held at Mainz on the Nativity of the Lord as had nowhere been seen for many years. Those who were present report that fifty-two leading men, or even more, were then there, so that only Magnus, duke of Saxony, was noted as absent, since his already advanced age prevented him from attending.

There the legates of the apostolic See arrived—namely, Bishop Albanus together with the bishop of Constance—and, testifying in writing and speech to the sentence of anathema against the elder Henry, called emperor, repeatedly proclaimed by so many successive apostolic authorities, they confirmed that the entire multitude, indeed the whole Church spread throughout the world, had for many years been separated from his communion by the authority of Christ and blessed Peter [Col. 0998A] [Note: [Col. 0997] “separated” is read thus in 1].

For this reason, when he attempted to present himself at Mainz from the castle where he was staying, the princes, in order to prevent an uprising of the common people—who were accustomed to favor his side rather than his son’s—went to meet him at Ingelheim (December 31, 1105). At last, surrounding him by a general agreement, they brought him to a confession of guilt and a declaration of satisfaction.

Since the legates could not at that time restore to him communion or establish a form of penance without the judgment of a general synod and apostolic examination, he, yielding to the counsels of both parties, handed over to his son’s authority the royal or imperial insignia—namely, the cross and lance, the scepter, the orb, and the crown—wishing him prosperity, commending him to the leading men amid abundant tears, and promising that from then on, in accordance with the decrees of the supreme priest and the whole Church, he would attend to the welfare of his soul.

In this manner Henry V, first elected king by his father and then by all the princes of Germany, now for the second time, and also confirmed as a Catholic by the imposition of hands of the apostolic legates, began to reign after receiving the oaths both of bishops and laymen according to the custom of the country: in the 88th year after Augustus, in the 50th year of his father’s reign, in the 1857th year from the founding of the City, in the 5058th year from the origin of the world, and, as has been said, in the 1106th year of the incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0997] Read “1857”]. [Note: [Col. 0997] The reading is thus in witnesses 5 and 10; in 4 the numeral is “LVIII”; in 1 part of the numbers has been cut away, though “VIII” seems legible; V, CCC, V in 1b, 6, 9c, and 11. According to Ekkhard’s computation (see the year 1039), the year should be written as 5067.]

When the embassies of the Roman See had been reported before the king, all the leading men and bishops of Germany, and the entire clergy together with the people, concerning the various and long-standing defilements of the churches of this kingdom, and when, on the other hand, universal correction had been unanimously promised, both the king and the leading men decided to send from these regions to the holy mother, the Roman Church, such and so important legates as would be capable of properly answering the charges, carefully investigating uncertainties, and wisely providing in every respect for ecclesiastical interests.

For this task men full of the spirit of wisdom were selected, distinguished in rank, birth, elegance, and wealth, and not unworthy of veneration before either God or the world: from Lotharingia, Bruno of Trier; from Saxony, Henry of Magdeburg; from Francia, Otto of Bamberg; from Bavaria, Eberhard of Eichstätt; from Alemannia, Gebhard of Constance; from Burgundy, the bishop of Chur; and also certain nobles from the king’s entourage belonging to the lay profession. Among other instructions, they received this principal mandate: if it could be accomplished, they were to obtain the presence of the lord apostolic in the lands beyond the Alps [Note: [Col. 0997] A fifteenth-century hand at the end of manuscript 1 adds: “In the year of the Lord 1457, Ladislaus, king of Bohemia, died.”].

PART TWO. THE YEARS 1106–1125.

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 0999A] In your golden times, O king destined to live forever, I, Ekkihard, such a tiny little man, restored after long sufferings, and after the works of various chroniclers had been stripped bare, now, by watching the vessel bearing the course of time from the very beginning of the ages, finally brought into the harbor of your glorious empire through the manifold threats of Charybdis and Scylla, rejoice beyond all measure of human estimation. I therefore, I think not inappropriately, refuse the reward of freedom to my pen, though now utterly weary it earnestly desires it; rather, for as long as these limbs are governed by life, I most devotedly subject it to serving your praises with all my strength and beyond my strength.

Why should I not? You, lord of the nations, the head whom those long seated in sorrow have at last, and only with difficulty, obtained from the Father of spirits through many tears, are therefore deservedly supported with every favor within its power by every Catholic and orthodox member of that same Church [Col. 0999B]; and the Roman world, now awakening from the dust, from sea to sea—indeed the whole world from the rising of the sun to its setting—congratulates you with indescribable rejoicing.

In you all hearts sound in wisdom behold the righteous branch of David raised up. Above all, the people serving God, emerging everywhere from their hiding places, testify that the time has now come for God to show mercy, calling you a light risen for them in darkness and drawing from you certain divine prophecies. Every holy soul confidently judges that whatever is just or holy which it hears concerning your character is the fruit of its service toward Christ the King.

Your age will be blessed and will be produced more glorious than even the magnificence of your ancestral and maternal lines, if the Spirit makes his dwelling in your most august heart—the Spirit whom all the prayers pleasing to God both desire and implore for you day and night [Col. 1000B].

[Col. 0999] THE PROLOGUE ENDS [Note: [Col. 0999] “the prologue” is absent in D1].

[THE TEXT BEGINS.]

Manuscripts D, E, 4–11. [THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS]. [Note: [Col. 0999B] The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0999B]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1106.

[Year 1105, December 25.] During the reign of the younger Henry, such a great assembly of the entire Teutonic kingdom was held at Mainz on the Nativity of the Lord as had nowhere been seen for many years [Note: [Col. 0999] Manuscripts 4–11, from “until the presence was obtained,” agree with the text printed above in 1]. Those who were present report that fifty-two leading men, or even more, were then there [Note: [Col. 0999] D1 reads “were there”], so that only Magnus, duke of Saxony, was noted as absent, since his already advanced age prevented him from attending.

There the legates of the apostolic See arrived—namely, Bishop Albanus together with the bishop of Constance—and, testifying in writing and speech to the sentence of anathema against the elder Henry, called emperor, repeatedly proclaimed by so many successive apostolic authorities, they confirmed that the entire multitude, indeed the whole Church spread throughout the world, had for many years been separated from his communion by the authority of Christ and blessed Peter [Col. 0998A].

For this reason, when he attempted to present himself at Mainz from the castle where he was staying, the princes, in order to prevent an uprising of the common people, who were accustomed to favor his side rather than his son’s, went to meet him at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0999] E2 reads “Ingelheim”]. At last, surrounding him by a general agreement, they brought him to a confession of guilt and a declaration of satisfaction.

Since the legates could not at that time restore to him communion or establish a form of penance without the judgment of a general synod and apostolic examination, he, yielding to the counsels of both parties, handed over to his son’s authority the royal or imperial insignia—namely, the cross and lance, the scepter, the orb, and the crown—wishing him prosperity, commending him to the leading men amid abundant tears, and promising that from then on, in accordance with the decrees of the supreme priest and the whole Church, he would attend to the welfare of his soul.

In this manner Henry V, first elected king by his father and then by all the princes of Germany [Note: [Col. 1001] “by all the princes of Germany” is absent in E2; in E1 more than half a line has been erased, and it could easily have been overlooked], now for the second time (January), and also confirmed as a Catholic by the imposition of hands of the apostolic legates, began to reign after receiving the oaths both of bishops and laymen according to the custom of the country: in the 82nd year after Augustus, in the 50th year of his father’s reign, in the 1858th year from the founding of the City, in the 5058th year from the origin of the world, and, as has been said, in the 1106th year of the incarnation of the Lord.

[Col. 1001B] When the embassies of the Roman See had been reported before the king, all the leading men and bishops of Germany, and the entire clergy together with the people, concerning the various and long-standing defilements of the churches of this kingdom, and when, on the other hand, universal correction had been unanimously promised, both the king and the leading men decided to send from these regions to the holy mother, the Roman Church, such and so important legates as would be capable of properly answering the charges, carefully investigating uncertainties, and wisely providing in every respect for ecclesiastical interests.

For this task men full of the spirit of wisdom were selected, distinguished in rank, birth, elegance, or wealth, and not unworthy of veneration before either God or the world: from Lotharingia, Bruno of Trier [Note: [Col. 1001] “Lotharingia” is spelled “Lutharingia” in E2; “Trevirensis” is corrected to “Treverensis” in E2]; from Saxony, Henry of Magdeburg, archbishops [Note: [Col. 1001C] The syntax is difficult; the plural may reflect the transmitted text]; from eastern Francia, Otto of Bamberg; from Bavaria, Eberhard of Eichstätt, both designated bishops; from Alemannia, Gebhard of Constance; and several other bishops, as well as a number of nobles from the king’s entourage belonging to the lay profession. Among other instructions, they received this principal mandate: if it could be accomplished, they were to obtain through them the presence of the lord apostolic in the lands beyond the Alps.

Thus, indeed thus, the orthodox light, obscured for so many years, began to rise in our regions [Note: [Col. 1001] “in our regions” is read thus in 7 and 9c]. The Wigbertine or Heinrician heresy [Note: [Col. 1001] “Heinrician” is written “Neinrician” in 4] was exposed and brought into the open, judged [Note: [Col. 1001] “dejudged” in 10 and 11] and convicted, declared foul and rejected, condemned and anathematized. The heretics were renounced or driven away [Note: [Col. 1001] “heresy” in 5, 6, and 10; “heresies” in 11; corrected from another reading in 7], while Catholics were appointed to episcopal sees, and some of them were even consecrated during the very festivals.

Finally, zeal for the divine law suddenly grew so fervent that even the corpses of the pseudo-bishops were expelled from the churches. All those whom they had ordained were suspended from their offices until the general hearing.

For the Roman Church, now divinely exalted with horns [Col. 1001D], had determined to cast out, in order to strike fear into all the members of schisms everywhere, even the bones of the head itself—namely, of the so-called Pope Wigbert—from his tomb, which he had occupied for six years in the church of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1001] “six” is absent in V, 10, and 11]. It had decreed that all his institutions be annulled, as those not of a truly apostolic priest but of an apostate usurper [Note: [Col. 1003] “his institutions” is read “and his institutions” in 7; “already not” in 5; “but of” is absent in 10 and 11].

Meanwhile Werinherus (variants: *Werenherus* 6, 9c; *Wernherus* 4, 5, 7, 10, 11), a certain man from the king’s ministerial order who was in charge of the march in the regions of Aquina [the manuscript has *marchie* 9c; *est* is present in E but absent from the other witnesses], as though about to revive that same heresy, gathered forces from everywhere throughout Italy and also corrupted several Romans with a great deal of money (n. r. E.). While the apostolic lord was staying in the territory of Benevento, he set a certain pseudo-abbot from Farfa—shameful to relate!—upon the *kathedra* of Saint Peter, and wanted him to be called pope under Caesar’s designation, Silvester. Nevertheless, shortly afterward he was disgracefully expelled by the Catholics, as he deserved (*elimanatus* 10.), and he received the reward of his madness: the loss of the badly acquired and even worse scattered money (*aeris*; variant *eritis* 4.). Apart from the loss to the faith, the wretched man did not grieve this with his blind heart.

[Col. 1003A] Moreover, while the aforementioned nobles were gathering from their respective regions in the valley of Trent and spending the night at the city of the same name—that is, Trent (February)—a certain young Adelbertus, prominent among those factions by a certain comital retinue, fell upon them early in the morning, since they were unarmed and strangers, together with armed citizens; he stripped them, captured them, and handed them over to custody (the variant is *tradidit*, “handed over,” 7.). He proved that this had been entrusted to him through embassies from his lord, Heinricus, namely the former emperor (the reading *Heinrici* is frequent; *N.* occurs sometimes in 6; *scilicet* is supplied by E; *imperatoris* is found in 4, while E² has deleted *ex* from *eximperatoris*).

For that same Heinricus, employing his customary devices, had secretly filled whatever cities and provinces of the kingdom he could with plaintive letters and messengers—[the witnesses variously read *clam*, “secretly”; *nam*, “for”; or *clanculis iam et querelosis...*, “already with secret and plaintive...”], lamenting that he had suffered violence from the princes, indeed that he had been driven from the empire by his only son; and he warned all fathers everywhere that the kingdom, confused amid his own miseries [variants: *et fusum*, “and poured out,” 6; *effusum*, “cast forth,” 7c.], ought to fear an example of the same fate [*patribus*, “fathers,” in the text; *partibus*, “parties,” 6; the phrase “of that same fate” is absent in 4].

For this reason the same legates could no longer find any free passage through Italy [*liber transitus* is absent in 7]. Only Gebehardus, bishop of Constance, entering by more hidden paths through the Alps, reached the apostolic presence under the protection of the countess Mahthildis—the other Deborah, of course (the name appears as *Mathildis*, *Mathilde*, *Machthildis*, *Mehtildis*, *Mechtildis*, and *Methildis* in the witnesses). Compare the *Life of Saint Hugh of Grenoble*, *Acta Sanctorum*, April I, p. 39: “Countess Mathildis too, outwardly possessing a woman’s appearance but inwardly possessing a man’s courage, knew how, like the prophetess Deborah, wisely to calm the tumult and dangers of human affairs and bravely to endure them.”

The other magnates, as we have said, were treated disgracefully, as though captured by a most foolish captor, except for Otto, bishop of Babenberg, whom the same Adelbertus was obliged to spare because he was his vassal-knight (the variant *videbatur*, “he seemed,” occurs in 7). Through him, Bruno, bishop of Trier, and Count Wigbertus (variants: *Wibertus* D¹; *Wicpertus* 4, 7; *Wigpertus* 9c.) were also released, on the condition that they should meet the former emperor in order to make peace with him and return to report what he himself ordered concerning the others.

But Jesus, who is always near to those who call upon him, and near to those who are troubled in heart [the witnesses variously add or omit *se omnibus*, “to all”; “with all” is also attested], suddenly brought against these same rebels Duke Welefo of Noricum, as though a sword drawn from its sheath (the name appears as *Welfo* in witnesses 4–11). Arriving on the third day, he broke through the barred and blocked barriers with a strong force (*de* is absent in 9c.; *clusas*, “barriers,” is read as *clausas*, “closed [things],” in 10, 11).

He compelled the citizens to receive Gebehardus, a proven man appointed by the Catholic king as the new bishop of the church of Trent, although the citizens themselves had conspired never to accept him. He also terrified Adelbertus and his accomplices in crime so thoroughly that they brought out the princes whom they had imprisoned and surrendered the fortress itself to the new bishop; moreover, they went barefoot and asked pardon from those whom they had afflicted.

Then also, from the first week of Lent—the week during which we too suffered these events—we observed a comet of immense brilliance until the Passion of the Lord (February; March). On our return, both poor and rich, each at no small personal loss, learned from sinister rumor that our king Heinricus had suffered some misfortune at the hands of certain rebels and seditionists against him in Alsace (the witnesses read *seditionis*, “of sedition,” in 4, 5, 7, 10, 11; *famam sinistram*, “sinister report,” in 7). We also learned that the king’s father had drawn considerable assistance to himself against his son: namely, the bishop of Liège, Heinricus duke of the Lotharingians (variant: “Lotharingian,” 7; “Lotharian,” 9c.), Cologne, Jülich, Bonn—which is also Verona—and the other towns of that faction. These events threatened no small degree of instability to the Catholic faith.

[Col. 1005A] In addition, King Heinricus, strengthened by confidence in God and no less encouraged by his inborn magnanimity, turned toward Liège, intending to hold the Easter court there, as though he were about to humble the hostile faction. After Palm Sunday had been celebrated quite joyfully at Cologne, when the enemies withdrew (March 18; the witnesses variously read “celebrated,” “about to celebrate,” or “he celebrates”), he set his army in motion. Once again he felt Fortune turning her wheel against him, since matters were being conducted with insufficient deliberation [the text has *res* according to E and C.; *inconsultus*, “undiscerning,” occurs in 6 and 9c.].

For when he learned of his father’s stratagem—that his father, as a warrior from his youth [this phrase is absent in 6, 7, 9c., 10, 11], was preparing, with considerable forethought, to resist him by means of troops hired for the city where, as we stated above, the court had been announced—he nevertheless, inflamed by youthful boldness, pressed on in the direction in which he had begun to go, although his father was surrounded by only a small force.

Accordingly, after sending ahead three hundred men to guard the bridge built over the river Meuse at a place called Wegesaz (variants: *Uuegezaz* 6, 7, 9c.; *Wegesaza* 4; a note identifies it as Visé or Weset)—for the enemy had already blocked all the crossings of that river—, while the king was celebrating the Lord’s Supper at the palace of Aachen (March 22), Duke Heinricus attacked the royal soldiers at the bridge with the imperial army. They resisted bravely, but by a particular cavalry tactic, which that people uses more than any other [the variant is *caeteris*, “than the others,” 4], he drove them into more open ground [some witnesses read “higher ground,” 10, 11], surrounded them with the multitude of his legions, overwhelmed, struck down, and captured them (some witnesses read “struck down and overwhelmed,” 6, 7, 9c.). The river also swallowed several who were fleeing.

You might have seen the bravest Maccabees in the battle for Catholic peace, after inflicting a great slaughter upon the apostate people, commending their souls in great faith and joy to Christ, who had suffered for them, and consoling one another that on that same day of indulgence they had obtained forgiveness for their earlier transgressions.

Through these deceptions of Fortune—or rather, by the disposition of the supreme Judge—the minds of the heretics began to swell, but the hope of the orthodox did not diminish. For during the very Easter festivities (March 25), which he was then celebrating at Bonn on account of the outcome of the affair [one witness reads “for the king,” 4, 10], King Heinricus deprived Duke Heinricus of his duchy, judging him guilty of treason and an enemy of the commonwealth, and, having received an oath from the princes, proclaimed and prepared a general expedition against Lotharingia throughout the whole kingdom.

When he thereafter proceeded into the upper regions, his father surrendered himself to the people of Cologne; after expelling the bishop, he very magnificently fortified the city itself with ditches, ramparts, and every means of resistance. He himself withdrew with his most faithful followers to Liège [the phrase appears in E as “he withdrew to Liège”; the manuscript notation indicates March].

[Col. 1007A] Thus, in the month of June, when it was already nearly halfway through [the Annals of Hildesheim say: “after the feast of Peter and Paul,” June 29], King Heinricus besieged Cologne Agrippina with a large army, namely twenty thousand men [some witnesses read “with his own army,” 4, 10, 11]. But since, as has been said, it was strongly fortified in every respect [this is absent from 4, 5, 6, 10, 11], he spent three or four weeks there in almost fruitless labor, except that, as commonly happens, the young men, impatient of delay, sometimes rushing out before the walls, drove one another away in cruel sport or struck one another down [the witnesses read either *alterum*, “one another,” or *alterutrum*, “each other”].

There too Count Dietericus, most faithful to the king, oppressed by illness, departed in the common destiny of death. He was a man born of the noblest Saxon stock, devoted to every kind of religion and to the defense of the Catholic faith in no ordinary degree, and also somewhat educated in letters.

Meanwhile, envoys of King Heinricus’s father arrived from Liège before King Heinricus, bearing letters both for him and for the princes of the kingdom. We thought it not inappropriate to insert a copy of them here (the variant is *inferri*, “to be brought in,” 4), in order to demonstrate that man’s many-sided evasion—by which, throughout his entire life, he had made himself superior to all who resisted him by means of feigned submission:

> Heinricus, by the grace of God august Roman emperor, sends grace and affection to the bishops, dukes, margraves, counts, and all the other princes of the kingdom who deign to receive it.
>
> We complain to almighty God, to the holy Lady Mary, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and our patron, and to all of you princes, that we have been treated unjustly, inhumanely, and cruelly, relying as we did upon that fidelity about which we ought not to have doubted. We have been stripped, contrary to divine and human law, both of the honor of the kingdom and of our possessions and everything we had, to the disgrace and reproach of the kingdom, so that absolutely nothing has been left to us except life alone (the witnesses often read *nil* for *nichil*).
>
> When nearly all of you were present, a large part of you seemed to grieve and mourn; but, alas, your sorrow did nothing for us, except that the hateful will of our enemies might satisfy itself against us. And because, with the counsel and at the request of our son, after first receiving from him a pledge of our life and honor [this phrase is absent in 10, 11], we were confidently and eagerly proceeding to Mainz into the presence of the Roman legate and the princes, so that by their decision we might deal both with the condition of the Church and the honor of the kingdom, as well as with the salvation of our soul, he did not hesitate, in this intention and obedience, to seize us contrary to his pledged faith and nearly lead us to the point of death (E² reads *deducere*, “to lead down”; the text has *ducere*).
>
> We did not dare trust him so far that he might treat us, as before, with injuries and insults according to his will. Therefore we earnestly ask and urgently entreat you, for fear of God, for the honor of the kingdom, and for your own dignity, to deign to strive to determine how, through you, we may recover justice for the wrong inflicted upon us while we were in your hands. For our part, in accordance with your counsel and that of the other religious men who do not hate us, we are prepared willingly to make amends both to our son, if we have offended him in any respect, and to anyone else in the kingdom.
>
> Furthermore, just as we were prepared to obey the lord pope in the presence of his legate and of you, so now too we are prepared, with sincere heart and devotion, to show him in person every due reverence and obedience, and, according to your counsel and that of our spiritual father, Hugh, abbot of Cluny [variant: “our religious father,” D¹], and of other religious men [*aliorumque*, “and of others,” in 10; *aliorum*, “of others,” in 10], to arrange, as far as lies within us, the condition of the Church and the honor of the kingdom.
>
> Since, therefore, we are prepared for all these things, we ask and urgently entreat you, for God’s sake and for the honor of the kingdom and your own honor, earnestly to admonish our son that, since according to the aforesaid judgment no occasion hostile to us remains for him [the witnesses vary the word order], he should henceforth cease to persecute us and our faithful, and should permit us to live quietly and peacefully, so that the matters mentioned above may be completed in their entirety and with tranquility.
>
> But if he refuses, we appeal to you by the authority of the Roman Church, to which we entrust ourselves, and by the honor of the kingdom, not to come against us and our faithful; for it is manifest that he began this not out of zeal for divine law or love of the Roman Church, but out of desire for the kingdom, having unjustly deprived his father of it. If, with him, neither your intervention nor any other intervention can presently avail, we appeal to the Roman pontiff and to the holy universal Roman See and Church.

After these letters and others had been read before the multitude—letters differing little in wording and not at all in meaning or intention from the earlier ones, though addressed especially to the person of the son (see the version from the Udalric codex, no. 214, in Eccard II, p. 220, and in Urstisius I, p. 398, where the earlier letter is also read)—King Heinricus, on the advice of the nobles, sent a counter-embassy to his father. Before doing so, however, he had it publicly proclaimed by the archbishop of Magdeburg, Heinricus [the witnesses read *Magadeb.* in E²; *episcopum* rather than *archiepiscopum* in 4? and 7]. By this action he greatly strengthened the courage of his supporters. The embassy was as follows:

> After the Roman Empire had been divided for a long time—approximately forty years—in a division that has nearly abolished both divine and human laws [one witness reads *obolevit*, “has weakened,” 10], and that, apart from every kind of death, sacrilege, perjury, plunder, and arson, has reduced our kingdom not only to desolation but almost to apostasy from the Catholic faith, or even to paganism itself, divine mercy has at last looked upon its Church. We, the children of that same bride of Christ, have through the Holy Spirit returned with steadfast hearts to the unity of the faith [the witnesses variously read *resipuimus*, “we have come to our senses,” or *respuimus*, “we have rejected,” 4, 5, 7, 9c., 10], and, out of zeal for God and obedience to the apostolic faith, have deposed from office that incorrigible head of those schisms, namely our emperor Heinricus. Although he was born of his stock, we have elected as our king one who is Catholic [the witnesses read *eligimus*, “we elect,” 7, 9].
>
> Seeing that the beginning of this king’s reign was his own end, he himself also praised it as though voluntarily—but, as his letters now confess, much against his will—returned the royal insignia, and, weeping, entrusted the care of his son together with the kingdom to our faith [the phrase “of his son” is absent in 6, 7, 9c.]. For the future he promised that he would seek no pomp of the kingdom but rather the healing of his soul [one witness reads “the healing of his soul,” 4].
>
> But now, behold, returning to his former evasions, he complains throughout the world that he has suffered wrong. He plans to drive swords belonging to the Gauls, English, Danes, and other neighboring peoples into our hearts [one witness reads “of the Danes and others,” 4], and he asks that justice be recovered for the injuries inflicted upon him. He also promises that henceforth he will obey our counsels more readily [this is absent in 10, 11; the witnesses read *promptius*, “more readily,” or *promptum*, “ready”]. In reality, however, by his customary devices he strives to scatter this camp of the Lord, to disarm Christ’s army [the words “he has begun to disarm” are absent by themselves in 4], and—as is plain—to ravage anew the Lord’s vineyard, which has only lately begun to blossom [this phrase is absent in 6, 7, 9c.], both personally, as a singularly savage beast, and through foxes, namely the pestilential men who adhere to him [this whole phrase is absent in 6, 7, 9c.]. He seeks to destroy it through the sacrileges of the priests of Belial and to return it to a renewed anathema—or rather, what is shameful to say, he intends once again to crucify in the hearts of all Christ, who has now risen again in his own Church [one witness reads “Christ risen again”].
>
> Therefore it is pleasing to the king and to all the princes of the kingdom, indeed to the entire orthodox army, that the same elder, so that no just complaint may be open to him against us, should bring his case before the present assembly and people, in whatever security he chooses and at whatever place he prefers; that he should receive justice and render justice. Thus, after all the causes of the seditions from the origin of the schism have been examined on every side—as though nothing had yet been settled concerning them—his justice may answer to both son and father, while the condition of the Church and kingdom may cease to waver, not, as he himself proposes, after long delays, but immediately, once these controversies have been resolved [the witnesses read *regni*, “of the kingdom,” rather than *regnique*; *in provintiarum* occurs in 10; *direptis*, “plundered,” in E²].

When Albuinus and Riwin, priests of proven and exceptional prudence (variants: *Albuwinus* in A. Saxo; *Albuinus* D, 5, 6, 9c.; *abb.* in 7?; *Albero* 4; *Richwin* and related forms in the witnesses; *presbiteri* is also written *prespiteri* in D¹ and E¹), together with certain religious men in lay dress, had been entrusted with this embassy by the king, all the princes, and indeed the entire army, they delivered it to the oft-mentioned former emperor. They had scarcely obtained access to his presence and permission to speak when they were treated—horrible, or, as E reads, incredible, to relate—with what immense danger to their lives for six days [the witnesses read *sex*; the phrase is unclear] because they had refused in any way to join that assembly of evildoers. At last, when the crowd broke into the custody in which they were staying, they were released by popular action and returned without any protection from the duchy to the camp situated around Cologne.

They brought back, however, this principal point among the elder’s replies (see the letter in Urstisius I, p. 399): that for the present there should be a withdrawal from arms, and that in the future a courtly conference should be summoned concerning such disputes [the word *universaliter*, “universally,” is supplied by E].

[Col. 1011A] It is also reported that the former emperor Heinricus and the former duke Heinricus are gathering an army from every quarter and are preparing by every means to try their fortune once more (the variant is *fortunae*, “of Fortune,” 10). Therefore the entire king’s army, indeed Christ’s army, resolving at least to bring matters to an end by the sword—for it was absolutely certain that the townsmen would assist the imperial party against them—lifted the siege. Moving against Lotharingia, they meanwhile plundered the fortifications and other possessions of the rebels (the witnesses read *munitionem*, singular, in 6, 7, 9c.). They sent ahead a second embassy to the elder Heinricus, to present him with the following choice: either to come shortly to Aachen to meet his son and settle the matter according to the previously stated agreement for making peace, or not to doubt that war was threatening him.

When these envoys too were handed over to custody, he secretly prepared by every means to resist. But after several days, when the same envoys had been released, an unexpected report followed them—no news could have been more welcome to that camp—that the emperor Heinricus himself had died [the witnesses read *d. a.*, “after several days,” in E¹ and E²].

It is nevertheless pitiable to relate that a man of such a name, such dignity [E reads “nobility”], and such spirit, who had gained the world for so long under the profession of Christianity, did not deserve from any person among so many Christians even the pious or compassionate mourning ordinarily given to a poor man at his death. Rather, the report of his death filled the hearts and mouths of all true Christians, both there and everywhere else, with an exceedingly boundless rejoicing.

Israel did not sing more loudly to the Lord when Pharaoh was drowned, nor did Rome ever applaud a triumph more grandly for Augustus himself or for any of the emperors. For the bridle that was in the jaws of the peoples (Isaiah 30:29) was turned for them into a song, like the voice of a holy solemnity [one witness reads *nox*, “night,” instead of *vox*, “voice,” as Isaiah has it; another reads *sollemniter*, “solemnly”].

Therefore, since at last the exactor ceased and the tribute was quieted [variants: *quievit*, “was quieted,” 5, 11; *acquievit*, “came to rest,” 10], all those who, solely for the sake of profit, had hitherto placed their souls up for sale by adhering to that prince of darkness [*tenebrarum*, “of darkness,” is supplied by E], promptly submitted both to the king’s authority and to Catholic communion.

Otbertus of Liège and his fellow bishops were received into communion on this and other conditions of penance: they were to exhume the body of the excommunicate, which they themselves had buried the previous day in a monastery, and lay it down in an unconsecrated place without any share in burial or funeral rites (the witnesses variously read *ulla*, “any,” rather than *ullo*, “any,” and *in loco*, “in a place,” in 6). The archbishops and bishops who were present approved this, because those to whom the Church does not communicate while they are alive cannot be admitted to communion by her even when dead (the witnesses read *posset*, “could,” in 6, 7, 9c.).

After this had been done, the body itself was later carried, with the king’s consent, to the city of Speyer in a stone sarcophagus (one witness reads “to the city,” 4), and there it remained unburied outside the Church for five years [E adds: “unburied there for several years outside the Church”].

Here was the end, here the destruction, and here the final fate of Heinricus, whom his own people called the fourth Roman emperor [the manuscript column changes at this point]. But by the Catholics—that is, by all who preserve their faith and obedience by Christian law toward blessed Peter and his successors—he was rightly called both arch-pirate and heresiarch, as well as apostate and persecutor, of souls more than of bodies. For, not content with natural and customary crimes, he was infamous for having devised and practiced new crimes, unheard of for centuries, and therefore in some respects incredible.

If anyone should wish to write these things, at the discretion of those who judge the deeds of emperors—whether very wicked or virtuous—worthy of being committed to writing, we yield the place to him, especially since we do not doubt that some of these matters are more worthy of oblivion than of memory (E¹ and E² read *memoriae*, “of memory”).

We shall nevertheless be able to prove through many witnesses that in our times no one seemed more suited than this man to the imperial insignia by birth, intellect, strength, boldness, stature, and the whole elegance of his body [the final phrase is absent or otherwise represented in witnesses 4–11], if only, in the struggle against vice, the inner man had not degenerated or succumbed.

Moreover, since not a few men still survive—and indeed occupy high positions—whose cooperation in that man’s deeds rebukes them, we offer one suggestion, though with excessive timidity: let them turn the example of his condemnation into a remedy for themselves. Let them attend not to the flower of the honor they wrongly obtained, but to the seed, and let them judge it better to toil at uprooting evil plantings than later to pluck from them the fruit of everlasting death.

Otherwise it is utter folly to believe that a wound filled with iron can be healed, or to wish to serve both God and Mammon. It is like a monster to usurp the dignity of apostolic humility from the height of Pharisaical pride—having climbed, as they say, by the reward of sacrileges—and to hope for the fruit of a hierarchy from the seed of apostasy (variants: *hierarchiae* D¹, E¹, E²; *ierarchiae* 10; *tetrarchiae* 6, 7, 9c.).

Thus far. But thanks be to God, who, though late, nevertheless granted his Church victory on a magnificent scale. To that Church, the same Galilean who once conquered Julian turned the fiftieth year of that Nebuchadnezzar’s exaction into a jubilee.

If anyone is so zealous that he does not wish the day of Heinricus’s death—like the day of Haman’s destruction—to be unknown throughout the posterity of the Church [the witnesses read *Aman* in 6, 7, 9c.; the text after *per* is uncertain in 4–11], let him know that it was the seventh day before the Ides of August, on which day, attacking his mother Church at Unstruot, he sent countless souls to hell (a note observes that this battle occurred on June 9, 1075, whereas another battle at the river Strow occurred on August 7, 1078). It was the same Tuesday on which he was accustomed to undertake all his battles, plainly under a pagan auspice [one witness reads *Martius*, “of Mars,” 6, 9c.; another reads “all his own battles,” 5].

[Col. 1013A] After this, in the fourth week of October [variants: *ebdomade quarte*, “of the fourth week,” 6c.; *menses octo*, “eight months,” 6, 9c.; E⁴ corrects the reading to “the month of October,” and *quarta* is explained as “the fourth,” namely of the month], a general council was held in the province of Lombardy (October), on the bank of the river Po, at a place called Warstallis. There, with the truly apostolic man Paschal II presiding in every respect, and before a very great multitude of clerics and laymen who had gathered from the churches of various kingdoms [the witnesses variously omit or retain *et* and read *convenerat*, singular, in E¹ and E²], and with envoys of the lord King Heinricus also present, many things were uprooted according to canonical equity, as weeds of the enemy; many structures founded upon sand were destroyed; still more nurseries of the faithful seed were planted more deeply and watered; and several strong defenses of the safest fortification were built throughout the churches.

For when, on that same Sunday, which was the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, he had consecrated Chuonradus for the people of Salzburg and Gebehardus for those of Trent as bishops [see the acts from the codex of Cencius and others in Mansi XX, p. 1209; also compare the *Translation of Saint Modoaldus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 67, to be inserted in another volume of this collection], it would take long to recount how indefatigably that prudent and faithful steward of the supreme householder refreshed his fellow servants every day with the wheat of God’s word in abundance, deposed pseudo-bishops [this is absent in 6, 7, 9c.], established Catholics, granted pallia to archbishops and privileges to monasteries, instructed the present shepherds of Christ’s sheep with honey-sweet addresses and the absent with letters of fatherly admonition [variants: *commonitorum*, “of admonition,” 5, 6, 9c.; E² corrects this to *commonitoriis*, “letters of admonition”; E² also reads *commonitoniorum*], reincorporated into the Church certain members that had once been cut off, and, by excision through anathema, cut away others that had seemed incurable.

Concerning ordinations made during the times of the schism, about which very great controversies were being debated, he promulgated a decree skillfully medicated with the discretion of maternal compassion, in these words:

> For many years now the extent of the Teutonic kingdom has been divided from unity with the apostolic See. In this schism such danger has arisen that—as we say with grief—scarcely a few Catholic priests or clerics are found throughout so vast an expanse of land.
>
> Since so many sons are therefore lying in this slaughter, the necessity of Christian peace demands that the maternal bosom of the Church be opened over them. Instructed, then, by the examples and writings of our fathers [this phrase is absent in 6, 7, 9c.; D¹ reads “the examples and writings of the holy fathers”; Cencius has *scripturis*, “Scriptures”], who at various times received Novatians, Donatists, and other heretics into their orders, we receive the bishops of the aforesaid kingdom who were ordained in the schism into the episcopal office, unless they are proved to be invaders, Simoniacs, or criminals [Cencius reads “unless they are proved criminals”]. We establish the same concerning clerics of whatever order whom life and knowledge commend.

[Col. 1015B] Rejoicing in the splendors of these and similar things, like the dawn of divine light rising over the Church—for surely the time of having mercy upon her had at last come—and strengthened by apostolic blessings, each of us returned to his own place. We, however, that is, those who had crossed the Alps [this is absent in 7, 9c.], were lifted above all others by a particular joy, because we were certain that the apostolic lord’s departure had been arranged in such a way that, following our journey very soon, he would celebrate Christmas at Mainz in the presence of our new king together with all the princes of the kingdom.

This year Duke Magnus of Saxony died, and Lotharius arose in his place. Likewise Uto, margrave of Saxony, died (August 23) [the name appears as *Uoto* in 4; *Uto de S. m.* in 7]. Ruotpertus, bishop of Würzburg (variants: *Ruotbertus* E²; *Ruopertus* 4, 7, 10; *Rupertus* 11), died on the journey while traveling to the council. After his death [E² initially read *descendente*, “descending,” then corrected to *decedente*, “after his death”], Lord Erlungus—who had earlier been unjustly removed but had now, by God’s just judgment, been restored—was urgently demanded by both the clergy and the people of Würzburg as their true shepherd [E gives: “Erlungus, formerly expelled, was urgently demanded by both the clergy and the people of Würzburg”]. Granted by both king and pope, he was received through envoys of the Roman See with great expectation and the incredible rejoicing of the whole city and many peoples, and was enthroned with the highest honors.

**Codex C: HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK.**

[Col. 1000B]

Through the younger Heinricus, so great an assembly of the whole Teutonic kingdom was held at Mainz on the Nativity of the Lord as had nowhere been seen throughout the course of many years. For those who were present report that 52 [Col. 1000C] nobles, or even more, were then there, so that only Magnus, duke of Saxony by name, was noted as absent, since advancing age now hindered him. There the legates of the Apostolic See arrived—namely, the bishop of Albano together with the bishop of Constance—and brought forward, both in writing and orally, the judgment of the apostolic shepherd, which accused the lord emperor of many transgressions. For this reason, when he himself attempted to present himself at Mainz from the castle where he was staying, the princes, to avoid an uprising of the populace—which was accustomed to favor their side rather than that of the son—met him at Ingelheim. At last, surrounding him by common counsel, they brought him to a profession of satisfaction. When the legates declared that they could not grant him absolution [Col. 1000D] or prescribe the form of his penance without the examination of a general synod and the judgment of the Apostolic See, he, agreeing to the counsels of both parties, handed over to his son the royal or imperial insignia—namely, the cross and lance, the scepter, the orb, and the crown—praying prosperity for him, commending him to the nobles amid much weeping, and thereafter promising, in accordance with the decrees of the supreme priest and the whole Church, to take thought for his own soul.

In this manner Heinricus the Fifth of that name, first elected by his father and then for the second time by all the princes of Germany as king (January), also canonically confirmed by the apostolic legates through the laying on of hands, and having received the customary oaths from both bishops and laymen according to the custom of the fatherland, began to reign: in the 88th place from Augustus, in the 50th year of his father’s reign, in the 1857th year from the founding of the City, in the 5053rd year from the beginning of the world, and, as has been said, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Col. 1002B]
