Accordingly, when the legations of the Roman See concerning the kingdom’s churches—variously and long corrupted—and the correction thereof unanimously promised by all had been reported before the king, all the nobles and prelates of Germany, and the whole clergy and people, it pleased both the king and the leading men to send from these regions such and so many legates to the holy mother Church of Rome as would be capable both of properly answering the charges brought against them, intelligently investigating matters of uncertainty, and wisely taking counsel in every respect for ecclesiastical interests. Men full of the spirit of wisdom were chosen for this task, distinguished in rank, birth, refinement, and wealth, and unworthy of veneration neither before God nor before the world: Bruno of Lorraine, archbishop of Trier; from Saxony [Col. 1002C], Heinricus, archbishop of Magdeburg; from eastern Francia, Otto of Bamberg; from Bavaria, Eberhard of Eichstätt, both of the latter designated bishops; from Alemannia, Gebehard of Constance; and several other prelates, together with many nobles of the king’s household belonging to the lay order. Among their other instructions they received this especially important one: that, if it could be achieved, through their efforts the presence of the apostolic lord might be obtained for the Cisalpine regions.

Thus, indeed thus, through the entrails of the mercy of our God, as so great a morning star arose for us, the ecclesiastical light, clouded for so many years, began to shine forth. To conclude briefly what is very extensive: while Heinricus took up the governance of the state and defended the Roman See, the special flower of the whole world [Col. 1002D], the scandals of schisms were everywhere removed completely; the rent tunic of Christ was repaired, and, once the good had been chosen for the vessels of the Church, the evil fish were cast out of Peter’s net.

[Col. 1004A]

Meanwhile, when the aforementioned nobles, each arriving from his own region, assembled in the valley of Trent and spent the night near the city of the same name, namely Trent (February), a certain young Adelbertus—though he was distinguished by a considerable comital position in those regions—early in the morning fell upon them, unarmed and foreign as they were, with armed citizens; he robbed them, captured them, and handed them over to custody, proving that this had been commanded to him through legates of his lord the emperor. But Jesus, who is always near those who invoke him and close to those who are troubled in heart, suddenly drew forth against those most foolish captors of so many great magnates Welf, duke of Noricum, like a sharpened sword from its sheath. Arriving on the third day with a strong force, he broke open the blocked gates, compelled the citizens to receive Gebehardus—an entirely [Col. 1004B] praiseworthy man appointed by our king Heinricus as bishop of the Church of Trent, whom those citizens had sworn never to accept—and so terrified Adelbertus himself and his accomplices in crime that they released the princes whom they had imprisoned and surrendered the castle itself to the new bishop. Moreover, they themselves, barefoot, sought pardon from those whom they had afflicted.

At that time also, beginning with the first week of Lent, during which we suffered these events, we observed for two weeks a comet of immense brilliance. As we returned, both poor and rich, each not without personal loss, we heard through an evil report that our king Heinricus had suffered some misfortune at the hands of certain rebels who had revolted against him in Alsace. In Lotharingia [Col. 1004C], too, Duke Heinricus and Otbertus, bishop of Liège [Note: The codex reads “O.”], were arming themselves against the king, while Cologne, Jülich, and Bonn—which is also called Verona—and the other towns on this and that side of the Rhine were preparing to resist.

[Col. 1006A]

But King Heinricus, strengthened by confidence in God, turned toward Liège, intending to humble the hostile parties there and to hold his Easter court in that place. After Palm Sunday had been celebrated quite joyfully at Cologne, when the enemies withdrew (March 18), he set his army in motion and again felt Fortune’s wheel turning against him. For matters were being handled too rashly: he himself, inflamed by youthful ardor, attempted, even with a small force, to approach the court he had announced despite the opposition of his enemies.

He therefore sent ahead three hundred men to guard the bridge constructed over the River Meuse at a place called Wegesaz—for the enemy had interrupted all the crossings of that river. While the king celebrated the Lord’s Supper at Aachen (March 22), Duke Heinricus attacked the royal [Col. 1006B] troops at the bridge with an army. When they resisted vigorously, he drew them out into the open by a certain equestrian tactic in which that people excels above others, surrounded them with a larger force, overwhelmed, struck down, and captured them. The river also swallowed some who fell.

You would have seen the bravest Maccabees in the war of Catholic peace, after a great slaughter had been inflicted upon the apostate people, commending their souls in great faith and joy to Christ, who had suffered for them, and consoling one another that on that same day of indulgence they had obtained such forgiveness for the remission of their former offenses. Through these deceptions of Fortune—or rather by the disposition of the supreme Judge—the minds of the schismatics began to swell, yet the hope of the orthodox did not diminish. For while the king was celebrating the Easter festivities at Bonn because of the outcome of the affair (March 25), he deprived Duke Heinricus—declared by the judgment of the nobles guilty of treason and an enemy of the state—of his duchy, and, having received an oath from the princes, announced and prepared throughout the whole kingdom a general expedition against Lotharingia [Col. 1006C].

[Col. 1008A]

Thereafter, around the middle of June, he besieged Cologne Agrippina with nearly twenty thousand fighting men. But since the city had already been most magnificently fortified with a moat, defenses, abundant soldiers, and every means of resistance, he spent three or four weeks there in almost fruitless labor, except that, as commonly happens, the young men, impatient of delay, sometimes rushing out before the walls, drove one another away or struck one another down in cruel play. There also Count Dietericus, most faithful to the king, oppressed by illness, departed this life, a man born of the noblest Saxon stock and devoted in no small degree both to every kind of religion and to the defense of the Catholic faith; he was also by no means uneducated in letters.

[Col. 1012A]

At that time, while the king’s father was staying at Liège—for the people of Liège remained faithfully attached to him with their ancient affection—frequent messages and letters were passing back and forth. In the midst of these events, when nothing less was expected, word spread that the emperor was ill and, after a brief sickness, had died in the camp. Those who were present report that he ended his life after a good confession and not without great confidence. Having arranged all his affairs in every respect, and sent messages both to the apostolic pontiff and to his son the king, he received the viaticum and expired as though falling asleep.

For fifty years he held the reins of the Roman Empire. At times he piously cared for the Romans, when they were willing; at other times he necessarily resisted the ungrateful, who sought to humble both him and the Teutonic kingdom. He was a vigorous and warlike man, accustomed to bestow upon every person, every age, and every matter whatever was fitting for each, and scarcely willing to permit himself to be ignorant of anything. Following the custom of his father, he wished clerics, and especially learned men, to remain close to him. Treating them honorably, he occupied himself more familiarly with them, sometimes with psalms, sometimes with reading or discussion, and sometimes with the investigation of Scripture and the liberal arts.

We shall also be able to demonstrate through many witnesses that in our times no one seemed more suited to the imperial insignia in birth, intellect, strength, courage, stature, and the whole elegance of his body. Above all the churches of his kingdom he cherished Speyer, and enlarged it with royal and magnificent building and honor. There, now in the presence of his son and all the princes of the kingdom, honorably buried beside his ancestors, he rests.

[Col. 1014A]

After these events, in the fourth week of October, a general council was held (October) in the province of Lombardy on the bank of the River Po, at a place called Warstallis. There, with the truly apostolic man Paschal II presiding, before a very great multitude of both laymen and clerics who were serving as legates of various kingdoms or churches, and with the legates of the lord king also present, many things were uprooted, as canonical equity demanded, from the tares of the enemy, and many more plantings of genuine seed were set more deeply. Structures founded upon sand were destroyed; the defenses of the safest fortification were built throughout the churches.

For since on that Sunday—which was the twelfth day before the Kalends of November—he had personally consecrated certain prelates, it would be lengthy to recount how tirelessly that prudent and faithful steward of the supreme head of the household daily nourished his fellow servants most generously with the wheat of God’s word; how he deposed pseudo-bishops, appointed Catholics, granted pallia to archbishops and privileges to monasteries, instructed the shepherds of Christ’s sheep who were present with honey-sweet addresses and those absent with paternal [Col. 1016A] letters of admonition; how he restored to the Church certain limbs formerly cut off, and amputated others, which seemed incurable, by the excision of anathema. Concerning ordinations made during the time of schism, about which very great disputes were being raised, he promulgated a decree artfully medicated with the discretion of a mother’s compassion:

[Col. 1016B]

Rejoicing in the glad splendors of these and similar things, as though in the dawn of divine light rising over the Church—for at last the time of having mercy upon it had come—and strengthened together by apostolic blessings, each returned to his own place. We, however—that is, those who had crossed the Alps—were carried away by a particular joy beyond all others, because we were certain that the apostolic lord’s journey had been arranged in such a way that, following our own journey as soon as possible, he would celebrate the birthday of the Lord at Mainz, with our new king Heinricus present together with all the princes of the kingdom.

In this year Magnus, duke of Saxony, died; in his place Lotharius arose. Likewise Outo, margrave of Saxony, died (August 23). Ruotpertus, bishop of Würzburg, died on the way while traveling to the council. After his death, Lord Erlungus was earnestly requested by both the clergy and the people of Würzburg as their true shepherd—formerly unjustly taken away from him, but restored again by God’s just judgment—and, granted by both the king and the pope, was received through the legates of the Roman See with great expectation and the unbelievable rejoicing of the whole city and many peoples, and was enthroned with the highest honor.

*(In the years that follow—1111. Codex C agrees with the remaining codices.)*

A. [Note: Witness 5 adds “years of reign III”; witness 10, “II indeed”; and so thereafter.] D. 1107.

[Col. 1015]

King Heinricus celebrated the Nativity [Note: Witnesses 7 and 9c read *natale*, “the Nativity,” in the neuter.] of the Lord at Regensburg, in the presence of the legates of the apostolic lord Paschal, whose arrival he had for some time been awaiting at Augsburg, the metropolis of Alemannia [Note: Witnesses 4 and 7 read *alamannie*], and in the other upper regions. But the apostolic lord, avoiding, as it were, the arrogance of the Teutons at the advice of his own men, especially because of a certain seditious disturbance [Note: Witness E2 reads *seditionum*, “of disturbances”] that had previously confronted him while he was lodging at Verona [Note: Witness 5 reads *veroni*. [Col. 1015C] “At Bonn?” See above.] [Note: Witness D1 reads *hospitandi*, “of lodging,” rather than *hospitanti*, “while lodging”], and because certain men further suggested to him that our people would not easily accept that decree [Note: Witness 4 reads “that our people would not easily accept”] which forbids laymen to receive any ecclesiastical investiture from the hands [Note: “*accipi*” is so read in Codex C] of laymen, and also because of the spirited heart of the young king, which was not yet in every respect amenable to the yoke of the Lord—this man of God, I say, perceiving and considering these and many things of that kind, and declaring with a groan that the door had not yet been opened to him in the German regions [Note: Witness 10 omits “and”; witness E2 supplies it after the indicated omission], turned his journey with the legates of Spain through Burgundy toward Gaul, and greatly increased the joy of the Nativity of the Lord among the people of Cluny [Note: Witness 4 reads *cloniacensibus*] by his presence. From there [Note: Codex E1 adds here in the margin: “Heinricus, tenth archbishop of Magdeburg, died.”], withdrawing, he was received by all the churches of those regions as a true disciple of Christ and vicar of the apostles with immense honor [Note: Witness 4 reads *s. h.*, “such honor”], treated with worthy reverence, and heard as though he had been sent from heaven as a lawgiver. Thus, for several months, as a faithful and prudent steward, caring daily for all the churches, he finally held a considerable council at Troyes around the Ascension of the Lord [Note: The Ascension fell on June 2. The council, however, was held on May 23.]. There, among many matters which he corrected according to the time and necessity, he promulgated, in accordance with the decrees of his predecessors, a judgment concerning the free election of shepherds and the restraint of laymen’s presumption in ecclesiastical dignities [Note: See Mansi XX, p. 1223. The text, corrected from the codices, will be published in its proper place with Bennone.].

But King Heinricus, after traversing the regions of Saxony, following the celebration of Easter at Mainz (April 14) [Note: Witnesses C and E read *postquam*, “after”;], presented himself near that council, though not in attendance, together with certain bishops and nobles [Note: Codices 6, 7, and 9c omit the words; in one hand, “*vicinum*” is added after the neighboring word.]. After taking counsel with them, he sent honorable legates to the apostolic lord, through whom they were to inform both him and the whole synod of the authority to appoint bishops granted by apostolic privileges to Emperor Charles [Note: On this matter, see what S. Hirsch discusses in *De Vita et scriptis Sigiberti*, pp. 42–48.]. Since Heinricus, as he was beginning to possess the Roman scepter, did not allow anything to be decided concerning this question in another kingdom [Note: Witness 6 reads *in alieno*, “in an alien realm”], a truce was granted to him for the whole interval of the following year, so that he might come to Rome and debate the same matter in a general council. At that time the lord pope also punished certain bishops from our regions with suspension from office because they had not attended that council [Note: Witness 9c omits “not”]; nevertheless, not long afterward, when they had given satisfaction, he mercifully absolved them.

Again, having complained sufficiently that he still could not find in German hearts the humility he sought, he arranged not to visit us at all, as he had intended, but to return with his retinue to the Italian regions [Note: Witnesses 10 and 11 read *disposuit*, “he arranged.”]. Although he reached them slowly [Note: That is, “having delayed,” “late”], he was received with such rejoicing by both the Roman clergy and people [Note: Witnesses 10 and 11 read *t. suis*, “with such rejoicing of his own”] that they seemed to believe he had returned alive from the dead.

But the king, having returned to the eastern regions, held a conference with the Bavarians at Regensburg [Note: Witness 4 reads “having held a conference with the Bavarians”; witness 10 omits “held”; witness 7 adds it afterward], at which he organized an expedition against Ruotpertus in Flanders (October) [Note: Witness E2 reads *ruotbertum*; witnesses 4, 5, and 10 read *ruopertum*; witness 7 reads *ropertum*; and so repeatedly]. When it was undertaken around October, he entered the land of the rebels and devastated it for more than a month, not without serious loss to his army [Note: Witness 4 reads “his people”], until, through intermediaries, the matter was deferred to the next court and the dispute was brought to an end [Note: Witness 9c reads *rebellum*; witness E2 reads *vestat*, apparently for *vastat*, “devastates.”].

A. D. 1108.

King Heinricus, celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz [Note: Witness 4 omits “King Heinricus.” [Col. 1018] The note states that he celebrated it at Aachen; see Stenzel II, p. 312. The diploma was dated there on December 28.], received the aforementioned Ruotpertus back into favor [Note: Witness E1 reads “Rodbertus” here.].

At that time a quarrel arose between Colomannus, king of Pannonia, and his kinsman Almūs, because each contended that the royal dignity properly belonged to himself according to the law of that people [Note: Witness 5 reads “each of the two”]; Almūs, stripped both of his possessions and of the duchy in which he had been distinguished among the Hungarians [Note: Witness D1 reads “Hungarians”], and in which, as was fitting for the king’s brother, he had been honored as second to the king, approached King Heinricus. In the hearing of the entire senate [Note: Witness 4 omits this], he lamented his miseries no differently from how Atherbal, formerly the brother of Hiempsal [Note: So in Codex C], once did [Note: Witness 10 reads “Atherbar.” [Col. 1018] See Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chapter 14], and sought to bend the magnificence of the Roman Empire toward compassion and his defense.

Moved by these complaints, and moreover because the same Colomannus had invaded the borders of our kingdom, namely in the coastal regions [Note: Compare Thomas of Split, *Historia Salonitana*, chapters 17 and 51.], King Heinricus attacked Hungary with an army (September) [Note: Witness 4 reads “with an army.”]. But since the adversaries had prepared themselves in many ways, especially by blocking the river fords everywhere, after a prolonged and fruitless siege of the fortress of Bratislava (November) [Note: Witnesses 4 and 7 read “Bresburg”; witness 7 also reads “Bresburch”], he returned with the undertaking almost unfinished [B. “He returned with the business unfinished.” Codex C].

A. D. 1109.

King Heinricus celebrates the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz, and shortly afterward, after a meeting of the nobles had been held at Frankfurt [Note: Witnesses 5, 6, 7, 9c, 10, and 11 read “Frankfurt”; witness 4 reads “Frankenvurt.”], he committed Count Sigifridus, the palatine, to custody with the bishop of Würzburg [Note: Witnesses 4, 5, 10, and 11 read “Sigefridus”], because—through the betrayal of Heinricus, formerly duke [Note: Witness 5 reads “formerly duke”] of Lotharingia, now restored to the king’s favor—he had plotted to rise up against the king’s life [Note: Witnesses 6 and 9c read “in place of”] and kingdom. There also, after Gotefridus [Note: Witness D1 reads “Gothefridus”; witnesses 5 and 10 “Godefridus”; witness 7 “Godefridus”] had been deposed as abbot of Fulda, he appointed Wolfhelmus [Note: Witness 5 reads “Wolfelmus”] over them from the same congregation [Note: Witnesses 4–11 read “appointed” rather than “appoints.”].

After this he moved his army against Poland [Note: Witness 7 reads “Pollonia”], a distant people, and, laboring there with much and prolonged exertion [Note: Witness 4 omits “and”], exacted the tribute owed by that land, which had long been denied [Note: [Col. 1019A] On this expedition see what Martinus Gallus, book III, chapters 2–15, relates in the edition of Bandtke.].

Ruothardus, archbishop of Mainz, died.

A. D. 1110.

Codices D, 4–11.

King Heinricus, celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Bamberg, is unexpectedly stirred by adverse reports: [lacuna] [Note: Witness 7 adds in the margin: “the son of Bozwi, son of Vratizlaus.”] that Prague, the metropolis of Bohemia [Note: Witness 6 reads *bargam*; witnesses 7, 9c, E1, and E2 read *pragam*.], had been occupied with an army and that the duchy of that people had been usurped against the king’s will. [Codices C and E: “While King Heinricus was celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Bamberg, he is unexpectedly stirred by adverse reports: Werinherus [Note: So in Codex C; the note [Col. 1019A] states that the matter ought to concern Boriwoi; see Cosmas of Prague, *Historia Boemorum*.] had occupied Prague, the metropolis of Bohemia, with an army.”] Immediately inflamed in spirit, he sent against him his most faithful princes with a strong force (January) [Note: Witness 7 reads “most faithful”; “he sent them there with a strong force.”]. Their enterprise prospered wonderfully and swiftly: they captured the city together with the enemies found inside it and met the king, who followed step by step, in triumph.

At the Epiphany of the Lord, Heinricus, holding a conference with the princes at Regensburg [Note: Codex C omits “Heinricus”; witness 9c has “Heinricus at Regensburg.”], disclosed to them the purpose of his mind: namely, that he wished to present himself in the regions beyond the Alps, so that he might receive the imperial blessing from the supreme pontiff in Rome, which is the head of the world, and bring the broad provinces of Italy into the fellowship of the German kingdom in brotherly peace, justice, and accordance with the ancient laws. Moreover, he wished to show himself ready, at the command of the apostolic father, for everything that ecclesiastical defense might require.

When the spirits of all were aroused in approval of the pious foresight of the prudent consul and already unquestioned lover of his fatherland, no man would have been thought a man if he attempted to withdraw from participation in so manly an enterprise [Note: The words “so manly an enterprise” are absent in witness 4]. Accordingly, after those present had confirmed the matter with a very willing oath [Note: Witnesses 4–11 omit this phrase], the eager king did not cease to discuss such an expedition persistently throughout the individual provinces of Germany. Although the appearance of an unlucky comet terrified the minds of some for nearly six months, he, generous in royal munificence, distributed everywhere stipends of immeasurable sums of money and ordered an army to move from all sides around August. Some crossed the Alps with him by Mount Jovis, others through the valley of Trent [Note: Witness 5 reads “Tridentina.”].

Now the king, second to no king of the world in all foresight, had provided for this. He knew that the Roman state had once been accustomed to be governed not so much by arms as by wisdom [Note: Witness 6 omits this; witness 7 adds it in the margin], and that he needed to fortify himself not only with armed men but also with learned men [Note: The form *literati* occurs here and often in Codices C, E1, E2, and 10; it is known from the autograph that Ekkehard sometimes wrote it], prepared to give an account to anyone who demanded one.

Codices D, 4–11. [Note: The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1019A]

Among these there was a certain notable Scot-born man named David [Note: Witness 6 omits “certain.” Witnesses D1 and 10 read *Scothigena*]. While he was directing the schools at Würzburg [Note: Codex C reads “Wirciburg”], the king, on account of his good character, took him as his chaplain. At the king’s command, this man arranged the entire sequence of this expedition and of the events that occurred in it in three books, in a style so easy that it differs almost nothing from ordinary speech [Note: Compare William of Malmesbury, book V, §420, Hardy’s edition, London 1840, II, p. 646, who himself used this book of David], thereby also accommodating lay readers and others of lesser learning who might be able to grasp the meaning of these things [Note: Witness 4 reads “also in this.”].

Accordingly, according to the testimony of the aforementioned historian—

Codex C.

[Col. 1020A]

Among these there was a certain notable Scot-born man named David, whom the king, while he had long been directing the schools at Würzburg, took as his chaplain on account of his good character and complete mastery of the liberal arts. At the king’s command, he arranged the entire sequence of this expedition and of the events that occurred in it in three books, in a style so easy that it scarcely differs from ordinary speech, thereby also accommodating lay readers and others of lesser learning whose understanding might grasp these things.

Accordingly, according to the account of the aforementioned historian—

[The words *inter quos* (“among these”) and *hystoriographi* (“historian”) are absent in Codex E.]

After overcoming the harshness of the mountains with great difficulty (August–September), the king arrived with his men, joyful and unharmed, at Ivrea. The other army, having previously captured certain castles, received him joyfully at Viruncalia [Note: These are otherwise called the Roncaglia fields. I do not know whether they have already been mentioned. I would either attribute the constitution edited in *Monumenta Germaniae*, Laws II, p. 38**, to a later period or regard it as interpolated; compare nevertheless the Annals of St. Nicholas for the year 1136, which call Runcania the ancient resting-place of the emperors.] after he himself had conquered Novara, as had been agreed (September).

After remaining there for a few days, he crossed the Po successfully [Note: Witness 4 reads “crossed” in the perfect tense], pitched camp at Piacenza, received abundant gifts and great loyalty from the citizens, remained in those regions for three weeks [Note: Witness 4 reads “weeks,” and likewise below], and, arriving at Parma (October–November), granted the countess Matilda [Note: Witness D1 and 10 read “Mahtildem”; E1 and E2 “Maththildem”; witness 4 “Mathildam”; witness 7 “Machtildem”; witness 9c “Mechtildem.”]—who had submitted to him through intermediaries [Note: Witness 6 reads “submitted,” feminine singular]—his favor and her own rights [Note: Witnesses 4–11 read “her own.”].

After this, severely afflicted by an exceedingly harsh winter (December), he crossed Mount Bardone [Note: “Monte Pardonis”; the note identifies it as Monte Bardone] with the greatest loss to the army and a pitiful shortage of supplies and horses. Immense rains fell incessantly upon them, as was appropriate to the character of that climate. After suffering these conditions for seven weeks [Note: Witness 4 omits “these”], they finally reached Florence, greatly afflicted, as the feast of the Lord’s Nativity approached.

A. [Note: Witness 7 adds “the first year of Emperor Heinricus V”; witness 5 adds the same, and so thereafter.] D. 1111.

After King Heinricus had arranged matters successfully throughout Lombardy and Tuscany [Codices C and E omit “successfully”], he celebrated the joys of the Lord’s Nativity at Florence with immense rejoicing among his men and with a splendor and honor wondrous and never before seen by the citizens of that region [Note: Witnesses 9c and 10 read “wondrous”; witness 4 “celebrated.”]. From there he set his army in motion toward Aricia. When he reached it, he was received kindly by the clerics but deceitfully by the citizens [Note: Witness 4 reads “by the civil authorities”; witness 7 “by the laymen.”] (December 27, in the year 1110 [Note: The printed figures are corrupt: “27 34”]). He thoroughly and abundantly subdued their insolence: their city [Note: That is, their castle or fortress] was utterly demolished, together with the towers they had prepared for resisting the king [Note: Witness 4 omits “for resisting the king”; witnesses 5 omit the entire phrase from “utterly” through “had taken away”], while all the Church’s rights, which those same citizens had violently taken away, were restored at the petition of the clerics [Note: Witnesses 5 and 9c read “at the clerics’ petition.”].

From there he advanced to Aquapendente [Note: See Stenzel II, p. 316], where he found his legates, previously sent from Aricia, bearing good news from the apostolic lord. He sent back other messengers with the Romans who had met him there as suppliants, and proceeded gradually to Sutri. There the apostolic legates [Note: Witness 4 reads “the legates of the lord”] arrived together with the king’s envoys (February 9) [Note: Witness E2 has the singular “arriving”; E1 corrects it to the plural]. They announced that the pope was ready for the consecration and for every honor and wish of the king, provided that the king himself would grant liberty to the churches, forbidding lay investiture, while nevertheless receiving from the churches the duchies, marches, counties, advocacies, mints, tolls, and the totality of the other royal rights that they possessed [Note: Witnesses 5–10 read “of the remaining” or “of the other royal rights”; witness 7 reads “the sum of the rights which they possess.”].

The king gave his assent, but on condition that this alteration be established by firm and authentic reasoning, with the counsel and agreement of the whole Church and the consent of the princes of the kingdom; and it was believed that this could scarcely or in no way be done. When this agreement had been made, the legates and hostages on both sides were dismissed [Note: “*missis*” is so read in Codices C and E], and the king hastened joyfully toward the City. The apostolic lord, meanwhile, together with all the clergy, indeed all Rome, prepared to meet him (February 11–12) [Note: Codices C and E supply “the apostolic lord.”].

It would be very lengthy to recount what happened afterward: with what immense honor he was received and led through the Silver Gate as far as the central wheel, according to the ancient custom of the Romans [Note: Witness 4 reads “the ancient Romans”]; how the privileges were publicly read there; how the princes, in tumult, complained without end about the despoiling of the churches and thereby the removal of their benefices [Note: Witness 9c reads “the offering of their benefices”]; with what great danger and varied debate that entire day was consumed; and finally how the apostolic father was guarded by bishops and other faithful men of the king [Note: Witness 7 omits “was”], until the peaceful and ecclesiastical consecration of the emperor, in imitation of the patriarch Jacob, who said to the angel: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26) [Note: William of Malmesbury, book V, cites the same passage from David].

When these matters had been completed during the Sunday of Lent [Note: Witness 4 reads “the Sunday of the fiftieth day”; the note states that “of the fiftieth day” should be written], the Romans, having gathered throughout the night, attacked the king’s army from every side early in the morning [Note: Witnesses D1, 7, and 9c read “from every side”]. After a battle had been joined for some time (February 13) [Note: Witness 6 reads “when battle had been joined”], it became necessary for the king himself to come to the army’s aid. He did so energetically and, acting as a very brave soldier and excellent commander until the day was already declining, by God’s grace brought victory to his men and flight upon the enemy after a great slaughter [Note: Witness 5 reads “after much slaughter.”].

Three days later he withdrew from Rome (February 16) [Note: Witness 4 reads “he withdrew from Rome”], taking the apostolic lord with him and keeping him with whatever honor he could, until, after arranging the affairs which circumstances required throughout the regions and pacifying all his adversaries [Note: Witness E2 reads “paying” rather than “pacifying”], he celebrated the approaching Easter not far from the City in his camp (April 2). There, after the long-standing dissensions between himself and the apostolic lord, between the kingdom and the priesthood, had been calmed, following the Easter octave, amid the immense rejoicing of the Roman people—indeed of the whole Church—and of the immeasurable army, before the confession of Saint Peter, he received from Christ the august name and imperial authority. He himself, properly anointed and consecrated with chrism and crowned amid the most august pomp, received them (April 13) [Note: “As those who were present there at the time affirm to us; although some people far away report the matter quite differently.” Codex E. [Note: In the margin of E1, in another but equally contemporary hand: “Note the fictional defense of the dictator.”]].

In the presence of the assembled Church, he was also granted by the hand of the apostolic lord, under its testimony, a privilege concerning ecclesiastical investiture [Note: See it in *Monumenta Germaniae*, Laws II, p. 72; from David, through William of Malmesbury, p. 659], in accordance with what had pleased and remained customary for the predecessors of both parties. The lord pope immediately confirmed its unshakable stability under anathema. Thus, on that day, the glory “to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will,” so to speak, was recovered, when the scandals of schisms, so long established and until then incorrigible, were removed from the kingdom of Christ.

Not long afterward Heinricus, with imperial generosity, distributed so many and such great gifts to his spiritual father, Pope Paschal, and to each of his cardinal bishops and to the greater and lesser clerics, that to those absent it is altogether unbelievable to recount [Note: Witness 5 reads “he gave”; Codex D1 “such and so great”; witnesses 4–11 read “memorable” or “to be remembered.”]. Thus, with both the apostolic lord and all the others wishing prosperity for him, and escorting him for some time with an immense bond of love [Note: Witness E2 reads “posterity” rather than “prosperity”; witness 10 adds in the margin “the first year of the reign of Heinricus V”], he returned safely through Lombardy to the Alps and from there to the German lands.

After his return (July), certain matters, both by the emperor himself and by the bishops who accompanied him, which seemed to require correction, were smoothed out according to what the supreme pontiff had granted [Note: Witness 6 reads “had agreed to”] or imposed upon each person, and what was corrupted was refined to purity. Thus, with Christ looking favorably upon the earth from his holy heaven, just as Christian devotion and religion began everywhere to increase, so also prosperity, abundance of crops, and new rejoicing began to grow all around.

Therefore, in the month of August, Emperor Henry summoned to Speyer very many bishops and abbots, and also some princes [Note: [Col. 1023] 4 reads “some abbots”; 4–11 read “summons” (*vocat*).] With their agreement and cooperation, he celebrated the anniversary of his father with extraordinary magnificence. For the communion connected with burial and prayers, which for a full five years had been suspended by apostolic authority, was then granted (August 7) by those same priests who had also given testimony at Rome before the pope concerning his penance [Note: [Col. 1023] 6 and 9c read “exhortations” (*ortationum*); the fuller text has “the communion of burial and prayers suspended by apostolic authority,” while 4 onward read “and prayers.”]. And with funeral expenditures more splendid than those of any emperor, he was buried beside his ancestors in the church [The entire passage from “Therefore” through “he was buried” is absent from C.].

After this, at a court held at Mainz (August 15) [Note: [Col. 1023] Absent in C.], he invested his chancellor Adalbert—who had long before been elected to that same see [Note: [Col. 1023] 5 reads *ad eandem kathedram*, “to that same see.”]—with staff and ring [Note: [Col. 1023] 4–11 read “clothed.”].

A.D. 1112.

Codices D, E, 4–11.

[Note: [Col. 1023A] The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

He dismissed Count Siegfried, who had been afflicted by a sufficiently long imprisonment, reconciled to him in accordance with the counsel and petition of the princes, and began to treat him kindly, to such an extent that he received his son from the baptismal font and promised that he would forget the injuries of the past [Note: [Col. 1023] 4–11 omit “from”; 9c reads “into oblivion”; 4 omits “that he would do so.”].

At that time the lord apostolic suffered many injuries from the Roman Church, since people reproached him for having, contrary to the institutions of the whole ecclesiastical discipline, raised King Henry—who was a tyrannical devastator of the state [Note: [Col. 1023] E2 reads “the tyrant and devastator of the Roman state.”] and destroyer of churches—to imperial dignity by his blessing, and, moreover, for having granted him that sacrilegious privilege. Therefore, compelled [to act], at the council held at the Lateran on March 18 in the church of Constantiniana [Note: [Col. 1023] “Constantiana” 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1023A] Compare the Life of Paschal in Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum* III.1, p. 363, and William of Malmesbury V, §426 ff., p. 661 ff.; it is easy to understand that the latter also drew these passages from the same source as Ekkehard. It is clear that both had at hand the acts, whether from David or elsewhere. For such acts, see the copies made from the Codex of Saint Justina at Padua in Mansi XXI, p. 67.], on the last day of the council, after making a profession of the Catholic faith before everyone, so that no one might doubt his faith, he said:

“I embrace all the divine Scripture of the Old and New Testament, the Law written by Moses and [the writings of] the holy prophets; I embrace the four Gospels, the seven canonical epistles [Note: [Col. 1023] “the canonical epistles” 9c.; E1 corrected “epistles,” and E2 has the same.] of the glorious doctor, blessed [Note: [Col. 1023] Absent in 4.] Paul the apostle [Note: [Col. 1023] 4 adds: “again, the epistles”], the holy canons of the apostles, the four universal councils [Note: [Col. 1023] D1 reads “all the councils”] just as [I embrace] the four Gospels [Note: [Col. 1023] E2 reads “evangelical”]: the Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 1023] E2 reads “Nicetum”], Ephesus, Constantinople, Chalcedon, and Antioch; and the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs, and especially the decrees of my lord Pope Gregory VII and of Pope Urban, of blessed memory.

“Whatever they praised, I praise; whatever they held, I hold; whatever they confirmed, I confirm; whatever they condemned, I condemn; whatever they rejected, I reject; whatever they interdicted, I interdict; whatever they prohibited, I prohibit—in all things and through all things. And in these things I shall always persevere.”

When this had been completed, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 1025] D1 reads “Gebehardus”; 7 reads “Gerardus”; D1 and 4–11 have “Engelismensis.”], legate in Aquitaine, rose and, with the common agreement [Note: [Col. 1025] E and William of Malmesbury read “agreement”; the others, “consent.”] of Lord Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 1025] P and D1 read “of Pope Paschal.”] and of the entire council, read the following document aloud before everyone:

“That privilege—which is not a privilege but truly ought to be called a *pravilege* [Note: [Col. 1025] 4, 6, and 9c read “privilege.”]—extorted by the violence of King Henry from Lord Pope Paschal for the liberation of the Church’s captives: we all who are assembled in this holy council [Note: [Col. 1025] Omitted in 7.] condemn it by canonical censure and ecclesiastical authority [Note: [Col. 1025] 4–11 read “the authority of the Church.”], and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit declare it invalid; and, so that it may have absolutely no authority or effectiveness, we entirely excommunicate it. It has been condemned for this reason: that the privilege contains the provision that no one canonically elected may be consecrated by anyone unless he has first been invested by the king. This is contrary to the Holy Spirit and to canonical institution.”

After the document had been read, everyone acclaimed: “Amen, amen!” The archbishops John, patriarch of Venice, and Sennes of Capua, together with nearly one hundred other bishops, signed.

On this occasion the archbishop of Vienne, with his accomplices, attempted to sow a new schism among our people and to extend the sword of anathema against the emperor [Note: [Col. 1025] 4 reads “against the emperor.”]; but because his undertaking seemed to lack both apostolic and therefore all ecclesiastical authority [Note: [Col. 1025] 4 reads “his undertaking is.”], [Note: [Col. 1025] See the synod which he held at Vienne in Mansi XXI, pp. 73–77], it was scarcely able to gain strength for the time being. Nevertheless, from the seedbed of that same dissension, the evil of envy began to creep everywhere [Note: [Col. 1025] 7, 9c, and 11 read *seminate* (“seed”); 5 and 10 read *seminare* (“to sow”); 4 reads *seminarium* (“seedbed”); 5 omits *invidiae* (“of envy”), while 4 reads *et inv.*], so that some people, plotting something against the state, were considering seizing the material of this affair as a shield for their own agitation. Among them was the aforementioned Adalbert, designated bishop of Mainz, who had always been second only to the king in every respect and without whose counsel he usually did nothing. He was accused—something scarcely anyone would have believed—of conspiring against the emperor with certain princes. When the matter became known, the emperor handed him over to imprisonment [Note: [Col. 1025] “by him” is absent from 4–11.].

At this time one of the princes of Saxony, named Odalricus [Note: [Col. 1025] 5 reads “Uodalricus.”] [Note: [Col. 1025] From Weimar; see the Saxon Annals. Compare Stenzel I, p. 654.], died. He had formerly been the son-in-law of Count Louis [Note: [Col. 1025] “of Louis” 5 ff.], but had by then become hated because of his repudiation of the count’s daughter [Note: [Col. 1025] “of his daughter” 4–11.]. The aforementioned Siegfried claimed his possessions for himself by hereditary succession, but the lord emperor was attempting to draw them into the jurisdiction of the kingdom. This affair began to provide fuel for renewed discord. For the same count, magnifying his former sufferings by those that followed, filled almost all Saxony [Note: [Col. 1025] 9c omits “almost”]—his own homeland—with such great complaints that he drew both Duke Lothar and Margrave Rudolf, Count Palatine Frederick, Wigbert [Note: [Col. 1025] 4 reads “Wicpertus.”], and [Note: [Col. 1025] 9c and 4 omit “and”] Louis [Note: [Col. 1025] 5 reads “Lodewicus”; E1, E2, and 10 read “Luodewicus.”] and several others away from allegiance to the emperor [Note: [Col. 1025] Absent in 10.]. The bishop of Halberstadt also, as well as Gertrude [Note: [Col. 1025] E1 and E2 read “Gerthrudis”; 9c reads “Gertrudis.”], that exceedingly powerful widow throughout Saxony [Note: [Col. 1025] E2 has the accusative *viduam*; E1 corrects it to *vidua*.] [Note: [Col. 1025A] Widow of Henry the Margrave.], complained that she too was suffering violence from the emperor’s wrongs through the seizure of her estates [Note: [Col. 1025] E reads “she was likewise suffering.”]. These and similar weeds of scandal aroused endless murmuring in the kingdom, which had recently been pacified. [Note: [Col. 1025] 6–11 add: “Abbot Altmann died.”]

Codex C.

[Col. 1024A]

He dismissed Count Siegfried, who had been afflicted by a sufficiently long imprisonment, reconciled to him in accordance with the counsel and petition of the princes, and began to treat him kindly, to such an extent that he received his son from the baptismal font and promised that he would forget the injuries of the past. At that time the aforementioned Adalbert, designated bishop of Mainz, who had always been second only to the king in every respect and without whose counsel he usually did nothing, was accused—something scarcely anyone would have believed—of conspiring against the emperor with certain princes. When the matter became known, he was handed over by him to imprisonment.

A.D. 1113.

[Col. 1025]

Codex C.

[Note: [Col. 1025A] The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Emperor Henry celebrated Christmas at Erfurt. Duke Lothar, the aforementioned Siegfried, Margrave Rudolf, the elder Wigbert, Count Palatine Frederick, and Count Louis prepared a rebellion against the emperor. He himself, pursuing them without delay with an army, did not cease to harass them by burnings and the destruction of fortifications, until fortune—or rather the grace of Christ—brought the affair to an end: Siegfried was killed by the emperor’s followers, Lothar and Rudolf were reconciled, and Frederick and the elder Wigbert were justly captured and committed to imprisonment.

[Col. 1027A] In the same year [Note: [Col. 1027] The following words are written in somewhat darker ink.] the emperor, unwilling that any discord should arise in his kingdom, invaded with an army a certain Reginold of Munzun [Note: [Col. 1027C] Mousson. Compare Stenzel I, p. 657.], who was resisting him and devastating the property of his bishoprics. He besieged him at Bar, his castle; and while Reginold was defending himself and the castle valiantly, the emperor pressed him still more vigorously with many leading men of that region, and burned the castle itself with fire.

Codices D, E, 4–11.

[Col. 1026A]

Emperor Henry celebrated Christmas at Erfurt [Note: [Col. 1025] 6, 7, and 9c read “Erpherfurt”; 4 reads “Erphuurt”; 10 and 11 read “Erphesfurt.”]. When the aforementioned princes of Saxony had not attended the court there, the emperor, greatly angered, ordered their property to be plundered and their possessions devastated by fire, even during the festival itself [Note: [Col. 1025] 6 reads “carried out.”]. Not long afterward he destroyed, after a long siege, the exceedingly well-fortified castle of Hornburg [Note: [Col. 1025] 4 and 7 read “Hornburc”; 9c reads “Honburg.”] [Note: [Col. 1025A] On the River Ilse.]. Then, leaving his loyal men in garrisons, he afflicted his opponents by ambushes and encounters. Among these, the oft-mentioned Count Palatine Siegfried, a most noble man and in his time second to no one in every virtue [Note: [Col. 1025] “in his time” is absent in 10 and 11.], fell; Wigbert [Note: [Col. 1025] 4, 5, and 9c read “Wicpertus.”] was captured; Louis [Note: [Col. 1025] 5 reads “Loudewicus”; 7 “Lothewicus”; 10 “Luodewicus.”] was compelled to surrender. Thus, for the time being, a measure of peace—although a small one—was granted. [Note: [Col. 1025] E1 adds in the margin: “Abbot Hildebold died.”]

[Col. 1028A] After this, a certain Reginold [Note: [Col. 1027] “Reinoldus” in E1, corrected in E2, and in 7.]—count of the province of Burgundy and, as they say, a kinsman of the emperor—began, driven by youthful insolence, to exercise tyranny against the state. When Henry Augustus came upon him with a strong force [Note: [Col. 1027] 7 reads “uálica.”], Reginold was captured and lost the stronghold in which he placed his greatest confidence, Mousson [Note: [Col. 1027] 9c reads “Munzun.”] [the name is absent in E]; and thus, the dispute being quickly settled [Note: [Col. 1027] E2 reads “seized” instead of “settled.”], he was handed over to imprisonment.

A.D. 1114.

[Note: [Col. 1027A] At this point there is a table depicting the emperor’s wedding.]

[Note: [Col. 1027A] The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

The emperor Henry celebrated Christmas at Bamberg, having arranged his wedding at Mainz for the coming Epiphany. For three years earlier he had become betrothed to Matilda, daughter of Henry, king of the English: a virgin in character, noble, beautiful, and graceful [Col. 1027B] in appearance, who was regarded as the glory and ornament of both the Roman Empire and the English kingdom. She was descended on both sides from a long line of magnificent nobility and royal lineage. In her speech and conduct, an abundant pattern of future goodness shone forth, so that everyone wished her to become the mother of the heir of the Roman Empire.

For the wedding itself such a multitude of archbishops, bishops, dukes and counts, abbots and provosts, and highly learned clerics assembled that no old man of that age could remember or in any way testify that he had seen—or even heard of—so great a multitude of such dignitaries gathered in one assembly. At the wedding itself there were five archbishops, thirty bishops, and five dukes; among them, the duke of Bohemia served as chief cupbearer. The number of counts, abbots, and provosts could not be reckoned by any person present, however astute. The gifts that various kings and innumerable leading men sent to the lord emperor at the wedding, and those that the emperor himself distributed among an innumerable multitude of jesters, performers, and people of various kinds and nations, could no more be counted by any chamberlain who received or distributed them than they could be recorded in writing by any chronicler of that same emperor.

[Col. 1027C] In that same year, at the same wedding, the princes swore that they would undertake an expedition against the Frisians in the second week after Pentecost. For they had refused to render the lord emperor the submission that was owed and to pay the tribute that they were legally bound to pay each year. Inflated by insolence and relying on the fortifications of their region, they disdained to submit to any lord or to carry out the command of anyone, however powerful.

When the army began to move against them, the archbishop of Cologne, together with certain other princes, obstructed its advance and began fiercely to resist his lord the emperor with his own citizens, a large body of soldiers, and the support of various counts, harassing his men day and night. Therefore, on the advice and with the agreement of the princes, the emperor returned to Mainz, his undertaking unfinished and his labor and that of his followers frustrated. Those who had contrived this rebellion against the emperor had no other grounds on which they could accuse him except that they claimed that one of his ministeriales was exercising lordship too ferociously in his own territories [Note: [Col. 1029] Thus ends this work.].

[Col. 1028A] The lord emperor celebrated Christmas at Bamberg with the greatest magnificence and an abundant multitude of princes; and he did not do so without reason, because he regarded the man of God Otto, bishop there, with some suspicion, since Otto was unwilling to attend the court on account of certain scandals already arising in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1027] “Certain scandals already arising” is absent in 4; “the scandals already arising” in 7 and 9c.]. Otto himself, sparing no transient possessions for the sake of ecclesiastical concord, gloriously overcame the king’s hostility by his tireless benefactions. Accordingly, having summoned an assembly at Mainz [Note: [Col. 1027] “At Mainz” 4.] (January 7), the emperor arranged the wedding with the greatest solemnity after the Epiphany of the Lord. There he also wished scarcely any, or certainly none, of the magnates to be absent. With their counsel or consent [Note: [Col. 1027] E1 and E2 read “agreement.”], he lawfully took to himself the daughter of the king of England, named Matilda [Note: [Col. 1027] D1, 4, and 10 read “Mahthilda”; 5 “Machthilda”; E1 and E2 “Mathilda,” and likewise below.], who had long before been betrothed to him [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in 7.], and made her partner of the kingdom.

[Col. 1028C] Then the emperor undertook, with much effort, a naval expedition against certain people inhabiting marshy regions beyond the Frisian islands [Note: [Col. 1027] E2 reads “the Frisian.”] [Note: [Col. 1027] “A naval expedition” is absent in 6 and 7; 7 corrects in the margin to “a naval battle.”]. As he was proceeding against them, he found Cologne, the city of Agrippina, in rebellion against him, with very many Transrhenians and Westphalians agreeing with it. The most renowned among them were Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Duke Godfrey [Note: [Col. 1027] D1 reads “Gothefridus”; 7 and 10 “Godefridus.”]; Henry [Note: [Col. 1027C] Of Limburg.], formerly a duke; and Frederick of Arnsburg [Note: [Col. 1027] 4 reads “Arnsburc”; 7 “Arnesburch.”].

He therefore abandoned the expedition. Desiring to turn his force against the enemies present, he settled in the region of Cologne; but, unable to overcome the remarkably fortified city [Note: [Col. 1027] 9c reads “fortified.”], he devastated the surrounding countryside and, finally, after disbanding the assembly [Col. 1030A] [E reads “army”], declared a renewed expedition against the same rebels [Note: [Col. 1029] D1 omits “against the same”; E2 omits “rebels.”]. When it had been assembled around the Kalends of October, he attacked Frederick’s possessions [Note: [Col. 1029] E1 and E2 read “possession.”]. After the entire region had been devastated and a strong castle had been built in its midst, furnished with soldiers, arms, and provisions, winter came on and he withdrew from military operations.

A.D. 1115.

[Col. 1029]

The emperor, observing that Saxony was now openly defecting from him [Note: [Col. 1029] 5 reads “now”; the repeated “now” varies among the witnesses.], came against it both enraged and armed. From those whom he had brought with him and those whom he found there willing to support him, he established considerable camps. The Saxons, seeing that their dangers were being brought upon them [Note: [Col. 1029] 4–11 omit *de* (“by/from”); 4 reads *Saxones vero periculis se angi*, “the Saxons, however, were distressed by dangers.”], stationed their forces at different places [Note: [Col. 1029] 5–11 read *ex diverso* (“in different places”).]. They were compelled not by the audacity to fight against their lord, but by the necessity of defending themselves, as they themselves affirmed to the emperor through messengers [Note: [Col. 1029] Absent in 4, 7?, 10, and 11.].

[Note: [Col. 1029] In the margin of E1, in another hand: “Here he gives a crafty and fraudulent account of King Henry.”]

While for several days each side threatened the other and refrained from battle [Note: [Col. 1029] 9c spells *Cumque* as *Comque*; 5, 6, 9c, and 10 read *haberi*; 4 omits it; 7 adds *abheri certamen* (“a contest”).], a brave man named Hoger [Note: [Col. 1029] 4, 5, 6, and 9c read “Hoiger”; 10 and 11 “Hogiar.”], who had previously made himself most famous at the king’s court, among many warlike deeds, by the killing of Count Palatine Siegfried [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 omits “by the killing of Count Palatine Siegfried”; 4 reads “had made himself”], having taken with him all the selected young men [Note: [Col. 1029] 6, 7, and 9c omit “all”; 7 omits “selected”], who, like himself, could not bear delay, boldly attacked the Saxons, his fellow countrymen (February 11). Fighting with leonine ferocity [Note: [Col. 1029] 7 reads “ferocity.”], he proved by his own death, while many fell with him, the desire for glory with which he burned [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 and 5 read “which.”].

Bishop Reinhard of Halberstadt took part in this conflict—indeed, as they say, in some sense presided over it [Note: [Col. 1029] 7 reads “in this conflict.”]—although he had previously been wronged not a little by the emperor. He proclaimed to his own men great consolation through justice and even forbade communion at burial for those who had been killed on the emperor’s side.

Thus the lord emperor, greatly angered, turned toward the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1029] 6, 7, and 9c read “he turned.”]; while the agreement of the Saxons to resist him grew stronger and stronger [Note: [Col. 1029] “To him” is absent in 6, 7, and 9c; 6?, 7, and 9c read “their agreement grew stronger.”]. In addition, they summoned through messengers a Roman cardinal named Dieteric [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads “Dietricus”; 7 “Tiedericus.”], who had served as legate in Pannonia [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads “Pannonia.”]. When he proclaimed both the proceedings of the aforementioned council and the emperor’s excommunication [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads “proclaiming.”], the archbishop of Magdeburg and the bishops of the other churches [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads “of the remaining churches.”] received reconciliation. Thus, with the kingdom again torn apart [Note: [Col. 1029] 7 reads “torn.”], new developments arose everywhere; each side plotted every kind of opposing action against the other.

Meanwhile, messengers sent from Italy announced the death of the illustrious Matilda [Note: [Col. 1029D] She had died on June 24.] and invited the emperor to take possession by hereditary right of her very extensive lands and estates. Just as no one in our time was richer or more famous than this woman [Note: [Col. 1029] E2 reads “more beautiful.”], so no one under a lay profession was found more distinguished in virtues and religious devotion.

After this, compelled by the counsel of his friends—or rather by the complaints of the entire kingdom [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads *nimiis*, “excessive”]—the emperor arranged for a general court to be held at Mainz on the Kalends of November. There he promised everyone a free hearing, satisfaction concerning the charges brought against him [Note: [Col. 1029] 4, 5, 9c, 10, and 11 read “concerning the matters submitted.”], and, by decree of the senate, correction concerning his extraordinary or youthful conduct [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads “extraordinarily.”].

When the appointed time arrived, while he himself was present at Mainz and vainly awaited the announced assembly—for no prince except a few bishops was arriving—the people of Mainz, perceiving that a favorable opportunity had presented itself, suddenly surrounded the palace, armored and armed. Others rushed furiously into the courtyard and gathered themselves into bands and wedges; filling everything with tumult and all things with shouting, they presented the courtiers with a terrifying spectacle.

Why say more? There is no doubt that, unless the emperor, after giving hostages for the present, had immediately affirmed that he would do what was being imposed upon him, the palace itself, together with all who were in it, might have collapsed at once in a most savage slaughter [Note: [Col. 1029] E2 reads “confirmed” instead of “affirmed.”]. Thus, when the exceedingly fierce fury of the soldiers and populace had scarcely been calmed, the emperor withdrew from the city. A few days later he sent Adalbert—whom he had already held under the strictest imprisonment for three years, scarcely clinging to his bones [Note: [Col. 1029] Absent in 4.]—back to his see, as he had been compelled to promise [Note: [Col. 1029] Absent in 4.] [The E version reads: “The emperor withdrew, and, in accordance with the agreement, on the third day he sent Adalbert, whom he had already held under the strictest imprisonment for three years, scarcely clinging to his bones, back to his see.”].

Not long afterward Adalbert submitted himself by messengers and letters to Dieteric, legate of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 reads “of the apostolic see, Dieteric.”], and asked him and several other bishops to meet him at Cologne [Col. 1031], where they could jointly receive the pope’s instructions that Dieteric had brought and where Adalbert could obtain his own consecration—long prevented—with such authority. This assembly was held as the feast of Christmas approached, not without the emperor’s indignation [E reads “the king’s”], since he was not yet fully willing to consent to that ordination [Note: [Col. 1031] 7 omits the passage from “This assembly” through “ordination.”]. [Note: [Col. 1031] 7 corrects “his instructions” to “the instructions of the pope”; 4 reads “which he had brought.”].

A.D. 1116.

[Col. 1031]

The emperor celebrated Christmas at Speyer with a few bishops and princes and took harshly the things meanwhile being done at Cologne. For he heard that very many people had assembled there—not only metropolitans but also other bishops and the leading men of the kingdom—with the principal purpose of publicly proclaiming the sentence of excommunication against him. Yet the cardinal himself [Note: [Col. 1031] Dieteric.], on whose authority these proceedings had been initiated [Note: [Col. 1031] 7 and 9c read “initiated.”], had already died on the journey and had been brought there for burial rather than for taking part in the council’s proceedings [Note: [Col. 1031] The remainder of this sentence is absent in 4–11.].

Nevertheless, the bishop of Würzburg, who had been sent there by him, was granted neither a hearing nor communion except after reconciliation. After returning from the legation he refused again to communicate with the man who had sent him; but, compelled by danger to his life, he celebrated Mass in the presence of the king. Thereafter, grieving until his death, he secretly departed. Thus, reconciled once more to his former communion with many tears [Note: [Col. 1031] 4 reads “to the former communion.”], he was deprived both of the emperor’s presence and of his favor.

Inflamed also by this agitation, the emperor entrusted the duchy of eastern Francia—which by the ancient succession of kings belonged to the bishopric of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1031] Absent in 6, 7, and 9c.] by hereditary succession [Note: [Col. 1031] All manuscripts read this; the Saxon Annals read “by concession.”]—to Conrad [Note: [Col. 1031] D1, E2, and 10 read “Chuonrad”; 4 “Cunrad”; 7 “Conrad.”], the son of his sister [Note: [Col. 1031] On this famous passage, compare Montag, *Geschichte der staatsbürgerlichen Freiheit* II, pp. 141–186.]. Avoiding the scandals of the princes, he himself went to Italy with the queen and his entire household (March) [Note: [Col. 1031] Absent in 4.]. Occupying himself with the affairs of the kingdom around the Po, he humbly sent envoys to the apostolic lord to settle the disputes that had again begun to disturb the kingdom and the priesthood. The abbot of Cluny [Note: [Col. 1031] 4 reads “Cloniacensis.”], said to be a kinsman [Note: [Col. 1031] 5 reads “kinsman.”] of the lord pope [Note: [Col. 1031] Pontius. Compare *Gallia Christiana* IV, p. 1134, and the passage there cited from Book XII of Orderic Vitalis.], held first place in this embassy. As a faithful and diligent *apocrisiarius*, he labored with many arguments to promote the peaceful settlement of matters between the two sides [Note: [Col. 1031] Absent in 7, 10, and 11; E1 adds it above the line.] [Note: [Col. 1031] Absent in 6 and 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1031] D1 reads “and” instead of “faithful and.”]

In that same year, which was the eighteenth of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II, on 6 March, at Rome in the Lateran basilica, in the church of Saint Saviour called the Constantinian Church, a universal synod of the council was celebrated, with bishops from various kingdoms and provinces assembled there, together with abbots, Catholic dukes and counts, and very many legates of all the provinces. [Note: [Col. 1031] “and abbots” in 4; “by all Catholics” in 6, 7, 9c.]

Accordingly, on the first day, which was Tuesday of the third week of Lent (6 March), a controversy was aired between the Milanese bishops Grosulanus and Jordan: one was accused of invasion, the other of having deserted his church. [Note: [Col. 1031] “Grosulanus” in 4–11.] [Note: [Col. 1031] “had existed” in 9c.] The lord apostolic postponed the hearing of this case, to be handled with the advice of the cardinal bishops.

On the following day (7 March), much was discussed concerning the same case, but the matter was not concluded. [Note: [Col. 1031] “the matter was discussed first” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1031] “not at all” in E1, 2.] [Note: [Col. 1031] “not unfinished” in 9c.]

On Wednesday (8 March), however, the bishop of Lucca brought a charge against the Pisans concerning land belonging to his church. While the Pisan defended his people, a lengthy dispute was conducted between the two sides, with the support of both peoples. [Note: [Col. 1031] “against either side,” “with the support of both peoples” in 6, 7, 9c; “with the force of both peoples” in s. 4; “between both sides” in 5, 10; “against the law of one side” in 11.]

Then one of the bishops rose from the middle of the council and began as follows:

“It is fitting that the lord pope should remember why the holy multitude of this present and general council has been summoned and has gathered by sea and land through every kind of danger: namely, to discuss there not spiritual or ecclesiastical matters, but secular matters in an inverted order. What they have chiefly gathered to accomplish must first be settled, so that it may become clearer what the lord apostolic thinks and what they should return to preach in their churches.”

Then the apostolic explained the purpose of the council and the intention of his heart in these words:

“After the Lord had done with his servant what he willed and had delivered me and the Roman people into the hands of the king, I saw daily, everywhere, robberies and fires, killings and adulteries being committed. I wished to avert these and similar evils from the Church and the people of God; and what I did, I did for the liberation of the people of God. Yet I did it as a human being, because I am dust and ashes. I confess that I acted wrongly, but I ask all of you to pray to God for me, so that he may forgive me.

“But that evil document which was made in the tents, which because of its wickedness is called a ‘wicked privilege,’ I condemn under perpetual anathema, so that it may never be held in anyone’s good memory; and I ask all of you to do the same.””

Then all cried out: “Let it be! Let it be!” [Note: [Col. 1033] “They shouted” in 4.]

Bruno, bishop of Segni, then began in a louder voice:

“We give thanks to almighty God that we have heard with our own ears the lord Pope Paschal, who presides over this council, condemning that wicked privilege, which contained wickedness and heresy.” [Note: [Col. 1033] “Pope Paschal” in 4–11.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “who presides over this council” in 4.]

To this someone added mockingly:

“If that privilege contained heresy, the man who made it was a heretic.”

John Gaetanus, moved by this, replied to Segni: [Note: [Col. 1033] “Gaetanus” in 4, 5, 6?, 7, 9c, 10.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “to this” in 10; “moved, he said to Segni” in 4.]

“Are you, here and in the council, in our hearing, calling the Roman pontiff a heretic? The document which the lord pope made was indeed evil, but it was not heresy.”

Another then added:

“Indeed, it ought not even to be called evil, because if it is good to liberate the people of God, what the lord pope did was good. To liberate the people of God is good by the authority of the Gospel (John 10), by which we are commanded to lay down even our lives for our brothers.” [Note: [Col. 1033] The words “which is good even to the end” are found in 6 and supplied in the margin.]

At this, the patience of the lord pope, provoked by the dreadful name of heresy, was roused. Signalling for silence with his hand, he quieted the cries and murmurs of the dissenters in these words: [Note: [Col. 1033] The words are absent from E1, 2, A, S.] [Note: [Col. 1033] Compare the passage quoted from Gerhoh of Reichersberg’s *Book on the Building of God* by Mansi XXI, p. 151.]

“My brothers and lords, listen to me! This Church has never had heresy; rather, all heresies have been shattered here. Here the Arian heresy, which flourished for nearly three hundred years, was annulled. From this see the Eutychian and Sabellian heresies were crushed, and Photinus and the other heretics were destroyed. For this Church the Son of God prayed in his Passion when he said: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail’ (Luke 22:32).”

On Thursday (9 March), the pope did not sit in the council, being occupied with many matters, especially those of the king, by the lord of Cluny, John Gaetanus, Peter Leonis, the prefect of the City, and the other supporters of that party. [Note: [Col. 1033] “of Cluny” in 4, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “Gaetanus” in 4; “Cajectanus” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “Leon” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “and” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “the others” in 4.]

On Friday (10 March), the apostolic turned his attention to the general cause of all the churches. When John Gaetanus, Peter Leonis, and the other royal loyalists openly resisted the aforesaid Cuono of Praeneste, who repeatedly wished to set forth the word “excommunication,” he restrained the murmuring with these words and with a gesture: [Note: [Col. 1033] “Friday” in E2; “from Friday” in E1.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “the pope” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “Gaetanus” in 4; “Cajactanus” in 4, “Cajectanus” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “Cuono” in E2; “Chuono” in 4; “Chuno” in 7, 9c.]

“The primitive Church flourished before God, not before human beings, in the time of the martyrs. Then kings, Roman emperors, and princes were converted to the faith; like good sons, they honoured their mother Church by granting the Church of God estates and landed properties, secular honours and dignities, and also royal rights and insignia, as Constantine and the other faithful did. Thus the Church began to flourish both before human beings and before God.

“Therefore let our mother and mistress, the Church, have what has been granted to her by kings or princes; let her administer and distribute it to her sons as she knows and wills.

“Wishing to erase the privilege of investiture which he seemed to have granted in the tents, he repeated the sentence of Pope Gregory VII and again excommunicated the investiture of ecclesiastical things by a lay hand, under anathema both of the giver and of the receiver.” [Note: [Col. 1033] “privilege” in 4, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “to have granted” in 7, 9c.]

The cardinal, the lord Cuono of Praeneste, then made the pope the following appeal concerning his own legation and one appropriate to those disturbing the present matter: [Note: [Col. 1033] “made an appeal to the pope” in 5.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “indictment” in 6, 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1033] “to the legation” in D1.]

“Lord father, if it pleases your majesty, and if I was truly your legate and you wish what I did to be considered valid, declare it with your own mouth in the hearing of this holy council, and strengthen my legation by your authority, so that all may know that you sent me.”

The apostolic replied:

“You were truly sent as a legate from our side; and whatever you and the rest of our brothers, the cardinal bishops, legates of God and of the apostles Peter and Paul, have done, approved, and confirmed by the authority of this see and by ours, I also approve and confirm. Whatever, however, they condemned, I condemn.” [Note: [Col. 1033] “approved and confirmed” in 4–11.] [Note: [Col. 1033] The words “whatever, however, they condemned” are absent in 4–11.] [Note: [Col. 1033] The words “legates of God” are absent from E1, 2, A, S.]

Thereupon the lord of Praeneste added how, while carrying out the legation of that see in Jerusalem, he had heard that King Henry, after oaths, hostages, and kisses in the very church of blessed Peter, had held the lord pope captive and treated him disgracefully; that the more important members of the Church, namely the cardinals, had been stripped, dragged about, and badly treated; that noble Romans had been killed and taken captive; and that slaughter had been inflicted on the people. Hearing this, he had groaned; and for such crimes, moved by zeal for God and on the advice of the Church of Jerusalem, he had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the king. He had renewed and confirmed the same sentence in Greece, Hungary, Saxony, Lorraine, and France, in five councils, with the counsel of the aforesaid churches. [Note: [Col. 1033] Compare what G. Cossart published from the manuscript of Mont-Dieu concerning the council of 1114: “In the year of the Lord 1114, on 6 December, Cuono, bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Apostolic See, anathematized King Henry at Beauvais in his council. And in the following Lent, on Laetare Jerusalem, 28 March, he condemned the same Henry at the council celebrated at Reims. Likewise Cuono condemned King Henry at Cologne in the church of Saint Gereon on the Monday of the following Easter. At Châlons, after holding a fourth council, Cuono condemned the aforesaid king on 12 July.” For these councils see Mansi XXI, pp. 121, 129, 135 ff.]

He had confirmed that sentence anew, with the counsel of the aforesaid churches, in five councils: in Greece, Hungary, Saxony, Lorraine, and France. Finally, he asked that, just as the lord pope had confirmed his legation, so the fathers and bishops of the present council should unanimously approve it.

The legates and letters of the lord of Vienne made the same request.

While the assent of so varied and discordant a multitude was being sought in this manner and order, no one from the sounder side contradicted truth or open reason; a few muttered beneath their breath, but none of the bishops or abbots raised an objection. [Note: [Col. 1035] “It was so” in E.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “and abbots” in E.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “objected” is corrected from “redeemed”; 6 has “redonated.”]

Finally, on Saturday (11 March), the controversy between the Milanese bishops was settled by the following dispensation. Pope Paschal explained that the translation of bishops occurs in two ways: through necessity or through usefulness. But in the case of this translation of Grosulanus, the usefulness appeared to have been turned into harm for souls and bodies. He therefore restored Grosulanus to the place from which he had been transferred, but granted Jordan to the Milanese. [Note: [Col. 1035] “translations of bishops occur in two ways” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “or” is replaced by “and” in 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “Grosulanus” in 4–11 and consistently thereafter.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “which therefore” in 6, 9c; “which he saw” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “from which he had been transferred” in 7; “from which he was transferred” in the other reading.]

To those who had visited the threshold of the apostles because of the council and for the salvation of their souls, and who were performing penance for capital offenses, he granted forty days of penance and with the apostolic blessing laudably concluded the council’s six-day session. [Note: [Col. 1035] “who had performed penance” in D1, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “he enclosed” in 9c.]

Meanwhile the Teutonic kingdom was being torn apart, although it had rested in concord for nearly ten years or a little more. Since the king was absent, each person did not do what was right but what seemed pleasing to himself. [Note: [Col. 1035] “had gone away” in 10, 11.]

At first, therefore, each side began, through continual assemblies, to ravage the other’s fields and strip the peasants; and this plague grew especially in the bishopric of Würzburg through Cuonrad, the brother of Duke Frederick. Afterward, once the opportunity had arisen, bandits sprang up everywhere. Showing no distinction between times or persons, as the saying goes, they strove to rob and plunder, attack and kill, and leave the defeated nothing at all.

It would be a long task to set down in writing the machinations of the bishop of Mainz against the king’s loyalists; their treacherous raids against him; the seditions of certain townsmen; the cities deprived of their bishops by these disasters; fortifications constructed in unusual places; the many castles destroyed one against another; regions devastated by plunder and fire; mutual battles and killings carried out by the horsemen of both sides; and the oppression and captivity of the poor and of travellers, inflicted in barbarian fashion by Christians upon Christians. [Note: [Col. 1035] “in places” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “destroyed” in 4–10; “constructed” in 11.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “and the poor” and “and travellers” are absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “inflicted” in 4, 7.]

For neither the Peace of God nor the other agreements confirmed by oaths are being observed. Rather, except for the men of ecclesiastical profession—who now have scarcely anything left but their wretched souls—all the rest, I say, of every condition and age, are raging with bestial fury at this time. [Note: [Col. 1035] “confirmed by the sacraments” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “others” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “are raging” is written “are raging” with an erroneous initial letter in 4.]

Thus, with fields ravaged everywhere, villages depopulated, and some towns and regions reduced almost to wilderness, and with the clergy’s daily provision failing throughout the churches, certain churches ceased their clerical offices. And—O cup of God’s wrath poured out!—that exceedingly wealthy and most famous principal monastery of Fulda throughout Germany was reduced to the extreme poverty of even necessary food.

A.D. 1117.

[Col. 1035]

While all the surrounding kingdoms of the nations, content with their own boundaries and possessions, were at last returning their swords, long wet with blood, and their other instruments of death, to the sheath of concord; and while the universal mother Church, after the numerous wars of persecutions, heresies, and schisms, was already placing her limbs, exceedingly weary beneath the true vine Jesus, in the service of the divine commandments through abundant acts of thanksgiving—alas! only the Teutonic fury, unable to lay aside its stiff-neckedness and unwilling to learn how great peace is for those who love God’s law, indeed how through the tranquillity of present prosperity one may reach the vision of eternal peace—only, I say, the people of our nation, while it remained incorrigibly obstinate in its ingrained perversity above all the peoples of the earth, caused perjury and falsehood and the other things lamented by the prophetic voice (Hosea 4:2) to overflow, so that blood touched blood. No less than once the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah, cries of this kind entered the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

Therefore, amid the very feasts of the Lord’s Nativity, on 3 January in the evening, the earth was shaken and trembled, stirred by such contempt for divine judgment—obviously by the anger of the Lord’s wrath—that no one was found on earth who did not confess that he had never felt so great an earthquake. Many buildings were overturned by it, and they say that certain cities in Italy were even thrown down. [Note: [Col. 1035] “from the anger” is absent in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “that no one was found” in E1.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “who had ever felt” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “cities” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “certain cities were thrown down” in 4.]
