Moreover, on 30 January, extremely terrifying thunder was heard with a great whirlwind, and flashes of lightning were frequently seen at the same time. [Note: [Col. 1035] “thunder” and “terrifying” are transposed in 4.]

Liège is a city of Lorraine, especially renowned under the patronage of the blessed martyr Lambert, once its bishop, and especially famous above other places for its devotion to learning. [Note: [Col. 1035] “Saint” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1035] “Lambert” in 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “handsome,” corrected to “famous,” in 7.]

There, while on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension (2 May) the entire clergy—namely, the members of ten communities—had assembled according to custom inside the mother church, and were singing the evening office, and had already completed the first psalm, suddenly the clearest air turned stormy and discharged such terrible thunder and lightning, with sulfurous fires, that no one present doubted that the final hour of the Last Judgment was already at hand. Two clerics and one noble soldier were consumed by the storm inside the sacred building. [Note: [Col. 1037] “the tenth” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “and” in 4–11.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “and had already” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “into a whirlwind” in 4, 6, 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “fires” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1037] The words “already” are absent in E1, 2, A, S, 6, 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “the final” in 4.]

Fifteen days later, from a nearby mountain of the same bishopric, where no water had ever been seen except rain, a great river burst forth. It flooded no small part of the city and, to the greatest detriment of the people of Liège, poured into the territory of Utrecht. [Note: [Col. 1037] “of the same bishopric” is abbreviated in E1, 2.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “from which” in 4, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “which” is absent in 10, 11.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “of the people of Liège” in E1; “of the people of Liège” in E2.]

On 17 February in the evening, we saw fiery or blood-red clouds rise from the north and, extending themselves across the middle of the firmament, strike the world with no small terror. For, as we learned afterward, the same glow seemed so near to every city that it was thought to be threatening the end of all things there. [Note: [Col. 1037] E1, 2 read “fiery clouds”; the words are absent in 4, 6, 7, 9c; 5 has “as though”; 10, 11 have “as if.”] [Note: [Col. 1037] “to threaten” is written “to imitate” in E2.]

Wounded to the heart by these and similar disasters, King Henry did not cease sending conciliatory embassies to the Apostolic See, although he himself was laboring intensely amid Italian troubles; nevertheless, it is clear that they achieved nothing. For the lord apostolic denies that, on account of the security he had granted the king, though under compulsion, he had bound him with the bond of anathema. Yet he denies that he can dissolve the excommunication attached to the Church’s more important members except on their advice, while the right of synodal hearing had been granted to both sides. [Note: [Col. 1037] “though unwilling” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “he denies” appears as “he disputes” in E2.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “he had bound himself” in 5.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “granted” in E1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9c, 10.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “hearing” in 6.]

He asserts that he is driven to this daily by letters from across the Alps, especially by the metropolitan of Mainz. For this reason the seditions begun on both sides do not cease raging everywhere, particularly in the lands beyond the Rhine; indeed, many are falling in the city of Mainz itself, and the noblest regions are being ravaged on every side. [Note: [Col. 1037] “for this reason the seditions on both sides do not cease” in 4.]

Count Emicho is killed by the soldiers of Duke Frederick. [Colomannus, king of the Pannonians, died. E.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “Is this the same man who, in 1099, gathered crusaders around Ravenna?”]

A.D. 1118.

[Col. 1037]

The lord apostolic Paschal II, purified by a long illness, ended his present life in the Lord (21 January). [Note: [Col. 1037] “divine” in 7, 9c; E1, 2 read “purified by a long illness.”] [Note: [Col. 1037] The words “his present life in the Lord” are absent in E1, 2.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “he ended his life” in 5.]

In his place John Gaetanus, a prudent and venerable man who had always collaborated irreproachably with that apostolic in the Roman Church, was elected and duly consecrated by the unanimous agreement of all Catholics. [Note: [Col. 1037] “Gaetanus” in 4, 5, 10; “Cajetanus” in 4; “Cartanus” in 6, 7, 9c.]

Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, while engaged in an expedition against the Arabs, perceived that the illness which had afflicted him for a long time, though mildly, had reached his vital organs. He designated another Baldwin of Rhaïs as king in his place, and surrendered his soul, full of faith and with a good confession, to the Lord Christ, for whom he had already fought many battles. [Note: [Col. 1037] “Baldwin” in 5, 10, 11; “Baldwin” in E2.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “of Rhaïs” in 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “in his place” in E1, 2.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “had come” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “Baldwin” in E1, 2; “Baldwin” in 7; “Baldiwin” in 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1037] The words “for whom he had already fought many battles” are absent in 4.]

On Palm Sunday (7 April), near his brother Godfrey, he was received into a mausoleum at the place of Calvary, very similar to his brother’s tomb, amid the greatest lamentation of various peoples. [Note: [Col. 1037] “near his brother” is absent in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “Godfrey” in E1, 2, 7.]

Very early on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection (14 April), the sky opened on the southern side and poured out such an abundance of light that it outshone, with an incomparable brilliance, the light of the moon, which was then extraordinarily bright, and remained brighter than all the light of the sun for one hour or more—as we confirm through many witnesses. [Note: [Col. 1037] “so much” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “which was then very bright” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1037] “we prove” in 4.]

During that same interval, a sizeable cross appeared hanging through the same opening; the variety of its gold and gems could be clearly distinguished.

Emperor Henry, while staying in the region of Padua, heard of the apostolic’s death and hurried to Rome. At first he gave his assent to the election of the lord John, also called Gelasius II; afterward, when Gelasius withdrew from his communion, Henry, not without the support of certain Romans, imposed another man, Burdinus, who had arrived from Spain, upon the Apostolic See. Thus the schism, which had already been expected to have died out, cruelly revived. [Note: [Col. 1037] “he withdrew himself from his communion” in 5.]

For when Gelasius had freely taken possession of the Roman chair, he, together with the cardinals who had gone away with him and the other Catholics whom he could gather, condemned the emperor at Capua, together with his idol, as letters sent by him in every direction attest. From there he travelled through Campania with his followers to Burgundy and arranged for a synod to be convened at Vienne. [Note: [Col. 1037] “to be convened” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1039] The alternative text reads: “Not without the support of certain Romans he imposed another man, Maurice, who had arrived from Spain, upon the Apostolic See; thus the schism, which had already been expected to have died out, cruelly revived. For when Gelasius had freely taken possession of the Roman chair, he, together with the cardinals who had gone away with him and the other Catholics whom he could gather, condemned the emperor at Capua, together with his pope, as letters sent by him in every direction attest.” [Note: [Col. 1039] In A.S. “idol” is nevertheless read.]

A.D. 1119.

[Col. 1039]

The lord apostolic Gelasius II convened a synod at Vienne. After it had been completed, he ended his present life in the Lord a few days later at the monastery of Cluny. Having been honourably buried there, as was fitting, he later described in a letter to Archbishop Adelbert of Mainz how the lord Milo, archbishop of Vienne, had succeeded him: [Note: [Col. 1039] “after it had been completed” in E1, 2.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “of Cluny” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1039] The alternative wording reads: “how Archbishop Milo had succeeded him, he later made known to the bishop of Mainz in these words.”]

“Our lord Gelasius, of blessed memory, departing from Vienne, instructed me to hasten to his presence once he himself had reached Cluny. While I was striving to fulfil this after several days, I was informed on the road of his death. In order to offer consolation, as reason demanded, to the brothers who had come with that lord, I proceeded to Cluny in profound sorrow. [Note: [Col. 1039] “to offer” in D1, 6, 7.]

“While I was thinking carefully about their consolation, they imposed upon me a very heavy burden, one entirely beyond my strength. For, on the day after my arrival, the cardinal bishops and one hundred Roman clerics and laymen gathered together and, although I was unwilling and wholly resisting, unanimously chose me as pontiff of the Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 1039] “and” is absent in 10, 11.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “as pontiff of the Roman Church” is absent in 4.]

“At that time Cuono of Praeneste, still serving as Gelasius’s legate, held a synod at Cologne with the Teutons, where he publicly proclaimed the emperor’s excommunication in every respect. [Note: [Col. 1039] This passage concerns events belonging to 1118, as Stenzel observed, II, pp. 329–330. Ekkehard reports it only in this year in order to show the reasons that moved the emperor to return. Compare the letters of Adelbert of Mainz concerning these councils in Udalricus, no. 289–291.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “Cuono” in D1, 9c; “Chono” in 7; “Covno” in E1.] [Note: [Col. 1039] In the margin of 10 and in 11: “Norbert, later founder of the Premonstratensian order, attended this council. At that time he was newly converted and wore a pilgrim’s habit; there he was accused by everyone of many things, to which he prudently offered his defence. Hence it is also written of him: ‘The hand of all these is against him, and he himself is against all these.’”]

“He also summoned another synod at Fritzlar for the same reason. Once it had been held, he confirmed the same excommunication as before. [Note: [Col. 1039] “another” in 4; abbreviated in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “Fritzlar” in D1, 6, 7.]

“When the emperor heard this—and also that the princes had proposed shortly afterward to establish a general or royal assembly at Würzburg, where he was to appear in person for a hearing or, if absent, be deposed from the kingdom—he was inflamed in spirit. Leaving Italy with his forces and the queen, he appeared unexpectedly in the German regions. [Note: [Col. 1039] “obedience” in 7.]

“Since the excess of his anger in no way allowed him to restrain his hand from the injuries inflicted by his rivals, the fury of invasions, plundering, and fires, which had already been expected to be capable of being put to rest, was reawakened by this example—namely, by the universal ruler. [Note: [Col. 1039] “persuasions” in 6; “persuasions” corrected to “persecutions” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “is reawakened” in E1, 2, A, S.]

“In that storm all the provinces were so disturbed by the relentless burden of continual devastation that even the oaths professed for the observance of the divine peace were not kept. [Note: [Col. 1039] “all” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “by the continual burden of devastation” is absent in D1.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “are disturbed” in D1; “are unsettled” in 6, 9c, corrected to “are disturbed” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “so that not even in the very [place]” in E2.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “divine” in E2.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “are observed” in 10.]

“Therefore Henry, compelled by messengers from all the priests and nobles of the kingdom, agreed that a general assembly should be held at Tribur. There he promised, in accordance with the decree of the senate, to make satisfaction for everything imposed upon him. [Note: [Col. 1039] “satisfy” in E1, 2, A, S.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “which they might impose upon him” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “to carry out satisfaction” in 6, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “he promised to make satisfaction” in 4.]

“At this assembly, held in the Rhenish regions, around November, the emperor, taking the counsel of both his enemies and his friends, ordered that everyone throughout the kingdom who had been stripped of his possessions should be restored to his own property. [Note: [Col. 1039] “around November” is so given in E.] [Note: [Col. 1040] That this date is false is clear, since Ekkehard himself says that at this assembly the council appointed for 18 October was commended; compare Stenzel II, p. 332.]

“He temporarily took into his own control all the fiscal possessions of the ancient kings. Peace throughout all the provinces was proclaimed and praised by everyone, but in reality it proved to have achieved little.

“There were also envoys sent by both the Romans and the people of Vienne, indeed by various churches, confirming the election of the lord Calixtus. [Note: [Col. 1039] “Calixtus” in 7.]

“When all our bishops had professed obedience to him and had approved the holding of the synod which was being announced for them around the feast of Saint Luke (18 October), the king himself promised that he would appear there for the reconciliation of the universal Church. The bishop of Châlons and the abbot of Cluny, meeting him at Strasbourg, obtained this from him through many strenuous arguments. [Note: [Col. 1039] “near” in E.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “and” in 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “of Cluny” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “arguments” in 7.]

“Anyone who wishes to know the proceedings of this council in full will be able to find them elegantly explained in the writings of a certain scholar named Hesso. [Note: [Col. 1041] Hesso’s book, edited by Tengnagel, is well known. Compare the acts of the council in Mansi XXI, p. 235.] [Note: [Col. 1041] “was able to find” in 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1041] Codex E gives: “For those who wish to know how the Council of Reims was conducted, it is not difficult to find the writings of a certain scholar named Hesso, who testifies that he was present and describes everything in detail.” E1 adds in another hand: “Adelgotus, archbishop of Magdeburg, died in the eleventh year, and in the same year Hugh the abbot also died,” which E2 incorporated.]

“There one will find how the king agreed that concord should be established between the kingdom and the priesthood; and how, at the same council, on 20 October, the aforesaid Pope Calixtus II presided, surrounded by 426 fathers, before an innumerable multitude of clergy and people. He did not present himself as entirely present, but nevertheless showed himself to be nearby. [Note: [Col. 1041] The words “the king” are absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1041] The words “at which, namely, on 20 October, the aforesaid Pope Calixtus II” are absent in 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1041] “not himself present but nearby” in 4.]

“There, after granting an interview to the lord pope’s legates, he finally sought another postponement so that he might hold a general conference with the princes concerning ecclesiastical investitures, which he was being compelled to relinquish with such insistence. At last the same apostolic, after an agreement had been concluded between himself and the king, confirmed the synodal decrees of his predecessors (30 October) and added several other things which circumstances required. [Note: [Col. 1041] “to the legates” is absent.]

“Thus, after the council had been duly concluded in the power of the Holy Spirit after nearly twelve days, he permitted all who had been strengthened by the apostolic blessing to return joyfully to their own places. He himself also soon afterward turned toward Italy. It is incredible to relate with what rejoicing and with how immense a display—not only by the whole of Rome but also by all the provinces through which he passed—he was received as Christ’s representative. [Note: [Col. 1041] “to say” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1041] “but” in 4.]

“From that time the truly apostolic man himself, and the whole flock of Christ that followed him, began to advance from day to day, until the entire party of Burdinus, whom some customarily call ‘the Idol,’ weakened day by day and ceased attempting to act against the Church. Yet the disturbance that had begun in the kingdom—alas, what a crime!—did not cease at all. [Note: [Col. 1041] “Burdinus” in 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1041] “strengthened in an attempt” in D1.] [Note: [Col. 1041] “alas!” is explained as “ah, crime!” in 4–11.]

“In this year Adelgotus, archbishop of Magdeburg, a young man acceptable both to God and to all good people, was overtaken by an untimely death and ended his present life in the Lord. Canon Ruggerus succeeded him by canonical election. [Note: [Col. 1041] “to all human beings” in 6, 7, 9c.] [Note: [Col. 1041] “Ruggerus” in 4, 6, 7, 9c, 10.]

A.D. 1120.

[Col. 1041]
### Canonical apparatus register

The following entries preserve the supplied manuscript readings wherever the normal English rendering would hide a spelling, inflectional, word-order, or omission distinction. Each entry is keyed to the translated lemma and gives the English sense of the source form.

- **Col. 1031, “was celebrated”:** manuscript 4 has *c. habetur*, “the council is held.” With “abbots,” 4 reads *et abb.* (“and abbots”), while 6, 7, and 9c add *ab omnibus catholicis* (“by all the Catholics”); 4 also adds *et leg.* (“and legates”).
- **Col. 1031, first day / Grosulanus:** *secunda* means “second [weekday]”; f. 4 explicitly reads *est secunda*, “is the second.” The name is *Grosulanum* in the text but *grosolanum* in 4–11; this is an orthographic form of Grosulanus, not a different person. 9c has *existeret* (“might have been”) for *extiterit* (“has proved to be”).
- **Col. 1031, “many matters were discussed”:** 4 abbreviates *tractata sunt plurima*; E1 and 2 read *minime*, “not at all,” for *non*. In the dispute between the parties, 6, 7, and 9c read *utramque*, “each/both,” 4 has *utramque partem vis populi utriusque*, “each party, by the force of each people,” 5 and 10 have *utramque vis*, and 11 *utranque jus*.
- **Col. 1031, “to be discussed”:** E1, 2, A, S, and 10 have *tractari* (“to be discussed”); 4 has *tractatura* (“about to discuss”); 5 has *tractaturis*, corrected to *tractaturi* (“about to discuss”); and 6, 7, 9c, and 11 have *tractatur* (“is discussed”). 9c has *convenerunt*, “assembled,” for *convenerint*, “have assembled.”
- **Col. 1031, “I am dust and ashes”:** D1 has *qui*, “who,” and 4 expands *quia cinis sum et p[ulvis]*, “because I am ashes and dust.” 4–11 read the imperative *orate*, “pray,” rather than infinitive *orare*, “to pray.” 6 and 9c have *per pravitatem*, “through perversity,” for *pro pravitate*, “because of perversity”; *privilegium* is the corrected spelling of *pravilegium*.
- **Col. 1033, Paschal and Cajetanus:** 4–11 read *papam Paschalem*, “Pope Paschal,” and 4 has *p[apa] praesidet c[oncilio]*, “the pope presides over the council.” The personal name is *Cajetanus*; 4, 5, 6?, 7, 9c, and 10 read *Cajectanus*, and 4 later *Cajactanus*. These are spelling variants of the same name. 10–11 read *hec*, “these things,” for *ad hoc*, “at this.”
- **Col. 1033, debate on heresy:** 6? has *Tunc*, “then,” and 7 and 9c *Tu*, “you,” for *Tune*, “do you then?” Manuscript 10 omits *dici*, “to be called”; 6 reads *quod usque bonum est*, “which indeed is good”; 4 omits the clause “is good,” and 7 has *fuit*, “was.” 6 and 9c have *quia*, “because,” corrected to *qua*, “by which,” in E1.
- **Col. 1033, Roman Church passage:** 4 adds *a me*, “listen to me”; 5 has *omnes hic*, “all here”; 4 omits “for almost 300 years,” reads *alii*, “other,” for *ceteri*, “the rest,” and has *Cloniacensem* for *Cluniacensem* (Cluny). 4 and 7 have *Cajactanus* and *Caject[anus]* for *Cajetanus*; 4 has *Leonem* for *Leonis*.
- **Col. 1033, conversion of rulers:** the source is *Dein ad fidem conversi sunt reges* (“then kings were converted to the faith”). 9c has *Deinde*, “then/afterwards”; 6 and 9c have *reversi*, “returned,” for *conversi*, “converted”; and 10–11 omit the *et*, “and,” after “Roman emperors.” 4 has *sive*, “or,” for *sibi*, “for itself,” and expands *sive a principibus*, “or by princes.”
- **Col. 1033, investiture and Cuono:** 4 and 9c spell *privilegium* for *pravilegium*; 7 and 9c have *cessisse*, “to have yielded,” for *concessisse*, “to have granted.” The name is *Cuono*; E2 has *Cunoni*, 4 *Chuononi*, and 7 and 9c *Chunoni*: all preserve the same person’s name in different spellings. 6, 7, and 9c have *indictionem*, “proclamation/announcement,” for *inductionem*, “introduction.”
- **Col. 1033, legation and arrest:** D1 has *legationi*, “to the legation,” for *legationis*, “of the legation”; 4–11 compress *confirmaverunt* to *c[onfirmaverunt] p[robaverunt]*, “approved and confirmed.” Manuscript E supplies the bracketed *et*, “and,” after *captum*, “taken captive.” The long historical note on the five councils is translated in the prose as the councils at Beauvais, Reims, Cologne, and Châlons and its Mansi reference.
- **Col. 1035, Milan settlement:** 9c has *et*, “and,” for *vel*, “or”; 4–11 consistently spell the name *Grosolanus*. 7 has *fuit*, “was,” for *fuerat*, “had been”; D1 and 9c have *egerant*, “had done penance,” for *agerent*, “were doing penance”; 9c has *inclusit*, “enclosed,” for *indulsit*, “remitted.” *Exameron* means the six-day period, hence “six-day session,” not “eighth day.”
- **Col. 1035, German disorders and 1117:** 10–11 have *abierat*, “had gone away,” for *aberat*, “was absent”; E2 spells *colones*, “settlers,” for *colonos*, “settlers” (a case-form distinction). 4–10 have *destructas*, “destroyed,” and 11 *constructas*, “built,” for *instructas*, “fortified.” 4 has *prestat*, “is of use,” for *restat*, “remains,” and *alii*, “others,” for *ceteri*, “the rest.”
- **Col. 1035, peace and earthquake:** E and Peutinger’s conjecture retain *locaret*, “might place/settle”; 5–11 read *caret*, “lacks,” and 4 *cadet*, “will fall.” E1–2 have *prosperitatem tranquillitatis*, “prosperity of tranquillity,” and 7 *visionis pacem*, “peace of vision.” E2’s *numquam* means “never,” against *unquam*, “ever”; 4’s *fat[etur] s[ensisse]* means “confesses that he felt.”
- **Col. 1035–1037, Liège phenomena:** 4 reads *urbes*, “cities,” for *civitates*, and *sancti*, “saint,” for *beati*, “blessed.” 9c spells Lambert *Lantberti*. 7 first wrote *formosa*, “beautiful,” then corrected it to *famosa*, “famous.” 4–11 use *quo*, “in which,” for *qua*, “in which [city],” and 4 has *ad*, “to,” for *et*, “and.”
- **Col. 1037, flood and embassy:** E1 abbreviates *mont[e] eiusdem episcopii*, “mountain of the same bishopric”; 4 and 9c read *quo*, “from which,” and 10–11 omit *qui*, “which.” 7 has *invito*, “unwilling,” for *coactus*, “compelled”; E2 has *dissitetur*, a spelling/error for *diffitetur*, “denies.” 6 reads *audiente*, “hearing,” for *audientiae*, “of hearing.”
- **Col. 1037, Paschal, John, and Baldwin:** 7 and 9c read *divina*, “divine,” for *diutina*, “long”; 4, 5, and 10 have *Caitanus*, while 6, 7, and 9c have *Cartanus*, for *Cajetanus*. Baldwin’s successor is *Balduvinum de Rohas*; 7 and 9c spell the place *Rhoas*. E1–2 have *Baldevinum*, 7 *Balduuuinum*, and 9c *Baldiuuinum*: spelling forms of Baldwin.
- **Col. 1039, election of Calixtus:** the source explicitly reads *in Romanae ecclesiae pontificem Calistum unanimiter assumpserunt*, “they unanimously chose Calixtus as pontiff of the Roman Church.” 10–11 omit *ac*, “and,” before “wholly resisting”; 4 omits the office phrase. E2 adds *autem*, “however,” before “at that time.”
- **Col. 1039, Cuono and Fritzlar:** D1 and 9c have *Cuono*, 7 *Chono*, and E1 *co[v]no*; these are source spellings of Cuono. 4 omits “there,” and 4 reads *Alterum*, “another [neuter],” while 7 abbreviates it, for *Alteram* (“another [feminine] synod”). The place is *Friteslar* in the source, “Fritzlar”; D1, 6, and 7 use *Fritzlar*.
- **Col. 1039, Henry’s return and violence:** D1, 9c, and 10 spell Würzburg *Wirziburg*, 7 *Wirciburc*, and 5 *Wirzeburg*. The phrase is *ab emulorum suorum injuriis manum abstinere*, “to hold his hand back from his rivals’ injuries”; the marginal variant *abstrahere* means “to draw back.” E1, 2, A, and S have present *excitatur*, “is stirred up,” for imperfect *excitabatur*, “was stirred up.”
- **Col. 1039, peace, Tribur, and Reims:** 4 has *omnes*, “all,” for *universae*, “all/universal”; D1 omits “by the continual burden of devastation”; 6 and 9c have *inequitantur*, corrected in 7 to *inquietantur*, “are troubled.” E2’s *ut me in ipsa* is a corrupt reading for “so that not even in the very [place].” E1, 2, A, and S have *consensit*, “agreed,” for *assensit*, “assented.”
- **Col. 1039–1041, closing variants:** 4 has *res*, “the thing itself,” for *re ipsa*, “in fact”; 9c writes *ac*, “and,” for *et*; 4 spells Cluny *Cloniacensis*. 7 uses *Kalixtus* for *Calistus*. 9c has *Burgundini*, “of Burgundus,” for *Burdini*, “of Burdinus.” The successor is *Ruggerus*; 4, 6, 7, 9c, and 10 have *Ruoggerus*, a spelling variant, not a different canonical successor.

The emperor celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Worms in a manner unbecoming an emperor. Afterwards, entering Saxony under the leadership [Note: *dictu* (“in speech”) in witness 7, rather than *ductu* (“under the leadership”)] of Frederick of Arnsberg [Note: *Arnesburg* in E2; *Arnsburg* in witness 4; *Arnesberc* in witness 7], and with the bishops of that region abstaining from communion with him [Note: omitted in witnesses 6, 7, and 9c], he turned toward Francia. There he was regarded as acceptable by some and detested by many others. Nor meanwhile did the Lord himself abhor any less the schism in his seamless tunic. Among the many scourges with which the whole world fought on his behalf, in the bishopric of Trier, in the month of June, he stirred up a storm [Note: *tempestas* (“storm”) in E1; *tempestas in glaciem* (“the storm into ice”) in witness 7] and poured down ice of extraordinary size. It overturned buildings and caused other dangers [Note: omitted in witness 4]. He also scourged Saxony, and especially the bishopric of Halberstadt [Note: *Halberstadensi* in D1 and E1; *Halberstatensi* in witness 2], with dreadful hail, to such an extent that within the boundaries of nine villages it consumed not only the crops but also the beasts of the field together with countless birds.

Stimulated by this chastisement [Note: *correctione* (“correction”) in D1], the Saxons began to hold frequent assemblies for the sake of concord, to reconcile those divided among themselves, to give one another their right hands, to expel robbers, and—suppressing the emperor’s person—to arm themselves unanimously against anyone attempting to invade their territories. In the midst of this, they surrounded in the castle of Wassenburg [Note: *Wassenburg* in witnesses 4, 5, 6, 10, and 11; *Wasseburc* in witness 7; *Wassenbur* in 9c] certain imperial soldiers who were ravaging Thuringia [Note: *Turingiam* in witness 4], enclosing them on every side with separate defensive positions. At last, after they had been weakened by want, they drove them out. Thus, within a short time, they established a most welcome peace in their own districts, although the customary war was raging elsewhere [Note: *in w.* (“in war”) in 9c].

Strengthened also by letters and embassies from the pope [Note: one witness reads “by the pope’s letters and by royal embassies”], they canonically elected pastors to vacant sees [Note: *kathedrae* (“seats”) in witness 10]. Through the assistance of the archbishop of Mainz [Note: omitted in witnesses 10 and 11], who at that time had withdrawn from the king’s anger, they had them consecrated in a commendable manner and in accordance with ecclesiastical liberty.

At this time Count Frederick the Palatine, who had recently separated himself from the others and bound himself to the king’s loyalty [Note: *devixerat* in E2; another reading has “had detached himself from loyalty”], died, already advanced in age. They say that, as was clearly revealed to a certain servant of God, he descended to places of punishment [Note: one witness adds “he descended to the places of punishment”].

Dieggerus [Note: *Dietgerus* in witness 7] of blessed memory, first abbot of the monastery of Saint George and afterwards ordained to the church of Metz through an apostolic legate [Note: *apostolici* in 9c], found rest in the Lord after many injuries inflicted upon him by the king’s supporters. He was buried in the same church [Note: one witness reads “he was buried in the church of the Cluniacs, where a man of outstanding merit presided”; other witnesses abbreviate this differently]. He was exceptionally learned and remained steadfast in holy conduct until the end of his life.

There are in Saxony two fortifications situated not far apart [Note: *longe* (“far”) in D and witnesses 4–11], whose names now do not come to memory. At about midnight, the guards of both castles saw—not in imagination but in truth [Note: omitted in witness 4]—the figure of a man proceeding from the wall of one of the castles and advancing across the entire breadth of the intervening field toward the other. His whole body blazed like a torch or a glowing mass [Note: one witness reads *cadentis*, “falling,” rather than *candentis*, “glowing”], and he disappeared near the opposite castle. This vision appeared in the same way not once but twice or three times [Note: omitted in witness 4].

## A.D. 1121

[Col. 1043]

Lord Thideric [Note: witnesses 4–11 read *Heinricus* (“Henry”); Ekkehardus seems to have corrected this error only in his final revision], who had succeeded Burkhard the Red [Note: *Burchardus* in D and witnesses 4–11] in the episcopal see of Münster through an ecclesiastical election after Burkhard had died long before while serving as Emperor Henry’s legate at Constantinople, was treated shamefully by his own people. He brought a complaint about his injuries before the Saxon princes. Since he was a distinguished man by birth and renowned for his virtues, he gathered an army through Duke Lothar and reclaimed his see, even against the king’s will.

It happened, however, by a hidden judgment of God, that while the citizens were terrified at the sight of the opposing armies and each person was trying to secure his own possessions because of the impending danger, several huts were carelessly set on fire. As the flames gradually gained power, they completely consumed the great basilica, which was the seat of that church [Note: one witness reads *obrui*, “to be overwhelmed,” rather than *comburi*, “to be burned”]. Thus, having gained a pitiable victory, they restored the expelled bishop and contributed a large sum of money for the church’s restoration [Note: omitted in witness 7]. Some interpreted the cause of so great a disaster as nothing other than the revelation that God had not been pleased with the offering of the deceased bishop Burkhard [Note: spelling *Burchardi* in witnesses 4–11], who had amassed many things there through iniquity.

Meanwhile it was heard, and confirmed by messengers arriving from Rome, that the pseudopope Burdinus had been captured after the castle of Sutri [Note: “in the castle” in witnesses 10 and 11], where he was residing [Note: *sidebat* in E2], serving his wretched office, had been destroyed through the zeal of the Roman army (April). After the common people had inflicted many insults and mockeries upon him, the lord apostolic barely rescued him from their hands and relegated him into exile to perform penance [Note: *religatum*, “bound,” in E1 and E2]. There are also those who assert that he was discovered involved in such crimes that we considered it unworthy to commit them to our writings.

Accordingly, after taking counsel with his faithful supporters (June), Emperor Henry planned to afflict the rebels of Mainz [Note: *curavit*, “he took care,” in E1 and E2]. First, he completely cut off the transport of provisions by ship. Then, after fortifications had been established all around, he prevented fairs and markets of this kind from being held and prevented any food supplies from being brought into the city. Finally, he ordered a public expedition to be proclaimed from every side for the siege of that same city.

When Archbishop Adalbert heard this, he stirred up all Saxony, where he was then staying. Since he had previously received an apostolic legation from the pope himself, he frequently summoned the bishops and princes of that province by virtue of this authority for the interests of Mother Church [Note: omitted in witness 4]. There, as an eloquent man who held primacy in many ways in the Cis-Alpine regions [Note: one witness reads *eis alpinis*], he at last aroused the courage of all who professed Catholic obedience for the defense of the metropolis of all Germany [Note: variants include “he aroused,” “he incited,” “he raised up,” and “he inflamed”; some witnesses omit the phrase].

Moreover, the bishops of Speyer and Worms, and any others who, although unable to resist [Note: one witness reads “unable not to resist”], nevertheless professed apostolic obedience [Note: omitted in witness 4], wandered in exile after being expelled from their sees [Note: one reading has “driven out”]. Those same princes, burning with zeal for the Lord God of hosts [Note: omitted in witness 4], intended to restore each of them to his own place.

Finally, around the summer solstice, with grain already expensive everywhere [Note: some witnesses read “with the regions everywhere devastated, grain was scarce”], two armies were assembled for you, noble Mainz, through the ravaged regions: one in Alsace and the other in Saxony. They sought the proud walls of your age-old dignity: one aiming at your destruction, the other at your defense. As though you were saying in lamentation, “The sons of my mother have fought against me!” (Song of Songs 1:5), Christ answered the situation: “Behold, these too have gathered and come to you!” (Isaiah 49:18).

Meanwhile, fasts, supplications, and litanies [Note: *letatue* in E2] were held throughout all the churches. There was no daughter of Zion who made herself free from sharing in so great a danger to her mother. Therefore the Lord looked upon the prayer of the humble and did not despise their petition [Note: *preces*, “prayers,” in witness 7]. Instead, having sent his principal spirit [Note: witnesses 4–11 read simply “his spirit”], the spirit of counsel and the spirit of peace, among the princes of both peoples [Note: one witness reads “the princes and people”], when the two armies had already taken up positions not far from one another and were preparing to direct their lines against each other, he caused the wisest and most religious nobles from both sides to be sent. They began honorably to negotiate their brotherly concord [Col. 1045].

What more is there to say? The spirit of Jesus, fighting for the price of his blood and for the children of his bride [Note: E1 and E2 read “for the blood of the Son”], prevailed so greatly over the spirit of pride and wickedness that, once the minds of all had been joined in a single assent to the divine will [Note: one witness reads “in the assent of the divine will”], the king’s anger was so softened by their counsel, persuasion, and entreaty that he himself decided that the present matter should be settled not by his own judgment but by the authority of the leading men of both parties [Note: *decrevit*, “he decreed,” in witness 4].

Then, while everyone gave thanks to the governor of all things, twelve leading men were appointed from both sides. Possessing hearts occupied by the fear of God, they were able, with no one resisting, to calm the longstanding discord between the kingdom and the priesthood.

For settling these matters, an assembly of the princes of the whole kingdom was approved, at the court of Würzburg [Note: variants include *Wirziburg*, *Wirciburc*, and *Wirciburg*], at the feast of Saint Michael [Note: *Michahelis*; one witness reads *Machaelis*]. Each man confirmed the agreement by placing his own hand in the hand of the other, as though under oath, and they departed in peace and joy.

After almost three months had passed, Emperor Henry came with a great retinue to the city of Würzburg, according to the agreement (September) [Note: variants include *Wirziburg*, *Wirciburc*, and *Wirciburch*]. The princes of Saxony, however, together with the archbishop of Mainz and the other leaders, encamped beside a stream called the Werna [Note: variants include *Werra*; an interlinear note identifies it as the Wernitz], one day’s journey away from the king [Note: one witness reads “at a distance of one day from the king”].

There, security having been arranged on both sides through intermediaries, after three days they met the king at the place already named. Because of the excessive crowd from both parties, they were received peacefully outside the walls [Note: one witness reads *recepto*, “having received”]. From then on, throughout an entire week [Note: one witness reads *ebdomadam*], they gathered each day in the same court, and there they never ceased to deliberate carefully about the present schism [Note: omitted in witness 4], namely, between the kingdom and the priesthood [Note: “the kingdom” is abbreviated in one witness].

Although some who hated peace attempted to sow new scandals over the old ones [Note: one witness reads “attempted”], nevertheless no one was able to resist the purpose of the divine arrangement, by which so many heads of the state had assembled [Note: one witness reads “by which the state had assembled”]. At last Emperor Henry, mindful of his pledge, conceded in every respect that all the questions under discussion should be concluded not by his own judgment or by the contention of any of his men, but according to the decision of the senate.

Since it would be exceedingly long to recount all that was then arranged there with great courage [Note: compare the conditions agreed upon, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges* II, p. 74], it is enough here to record only those matters that were also the principal cause of that assembly [Note: one witness reads “nevertheless” rather than “only”]. Thus, a most firm peace, legally established by all and universally, even at the risk of life [Note: *instituta*, “established,” in witnesses 6, 7, and 9c], was decreed: royal or fiscal properties were assigned to the kingdom, ecclesiastical properties to the churches, estates to those who had been plundered, inheritances to the heirs, and to every person and condition the justice properly belonging to them.

It was also confirmed by unanimous oath that robbers and thieves should be pursued by imperial edicts or restrained by the laws established in ancient times. Whatever scandal and whatever disturbance had everywhere grown throughout the kingdoms of Germany from the enemy’s sowing [Note: one witness reads *vel*, “or,” rather than the second *quicquid*], it was decreed should be eradicated by every means.

Concerning the word “excommunication,” from which almost all the scandals had sprung, nothing was defined [Note: one witness reads “nothing at all was defined”]. Nevertheless, the matter was unanimously deferred in the fear of God to the hearing of the apostolic government [Note: one witness reads *delatum*, “brought,” rather than *dilatum*, “deferred”]. Legates were appointed on the spot to carry all these matters to Rome, so that, when a general council had been summoned by apostolic authority, whatever could not be settled by human means might be determined by the judgment of the Holy Spirit.

After these matters had been arranged reverently, both for the honor and for the advantage of the kingdom, the following were sent at once: Lord Otto, bishop of Bamberg; Duke Henry; and Count Berengar [Note: variants include *Berengerus*, *Bereng*, *Bering*, *Beringer*, and *Beringe*]. They were to announce all these things to the Noric princes, who happened at that time to be absent from the aforesaid assembly because they were occupied with other affairs of state, having been summoned to Regensburg on the Kalends of November. They found them willing in all these matters and confirmed them [Note: E1 and E2 read “they confirmed them”].

[The remainder of this year is absent from witnesses 4–11. In their place, witnesses 4 and 6–11 read the following:]

In the same year, at the monastery of Schwarzach, something memorable occurred in honor and reverence of Mary, his most holy mother and perpetual virgin, and of Saint Felicity, the renowned martyr, and her seven sons. The monastery had been built and dedicated in their honor. Just as the Lord once brought salvation to a man blind from birth, so in these times he performed a similar deed in a young man mute from birth.

We briefly disclose and make known how this happened [Note: one witness reads “how this came to pass”; the final phrase is absent in witness 4]. A poor boy from another province had come there. The brothers’ steward mercifully received him out of compassion, and he served there for many days, being assigned the care of gathering and preserving apples for the brothers [Note: variants include “preserving” and “gathering and preserving”; another correction reads “of gathering and preserving”].

While he remained hidden and served in this duty for a long time [Note: one witness has an extensive marginal addition concerning his service], it happened that the great feast of All Saints drew near. On its vigil, the servant passed the day fasting until evening [Note: *jejunium*, “the fast,” and *jejuniis*, “fasts,” also occur; the phrase means “having spent the day fasting”]. When he had already sat down to eat, suddenly, by God’s will, an overwhelming terror seized him [Note: one witness reads “a new terror”]. He was wholly thrown into an ecstasy and rushed impetuously into the monastery, where the hymn “All the Orders of Heaven” was already being sung with great devotion by everyone at vespers.

Having knelt once and twice in prayer [Note: one witness reads “having bent his knees to God”], he commended himself most attentively to God and his saints [Note: omitted in witnesses 10 and 11]. Then, suddenly, through the regard of almighty God [Note: omitted in witness 4], the bond of his tongue, which until then had been closed, was loosened. He spat from his mouth what seemed like a piece of raw flesh mixed with blood, and he spoke in a clear voice to those standing around him [Note: one witness reads *exsecrans*, “cursing,” rather than *excreans*, “spitting out”].

All the people staying in the church marvelled greatly at the sudden transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High God [Note: variants include “at the great wonder given by the sudden transformation”]. They urged the man who had been healed to ascend into the choir, to stretch himself out in the form of a cross before the principal altar, and to give immense thanks to God himself for his indescribable mercy.

When this had been done, and the service of vespers had also been completed, the brothers and the people alike, with contrition of heart and spirit, raised their voices to the stars and proclaimed Christ’s mighty works with hymns and praises [Note: one witness reads *ymnis*, “with hymns,” without the conjunction]. Nearly all the inhabitants of the province are witnesses to this event, and so too is the entire household that continually renders its due service to that place.

At the monastery of Fulda, the southern tower collapsed and crushed the eastern sanctuary, the crypt beneath it, and the seven altars surrounding it.

## A.D. 1122

[Col. 1047]

Bishop Erlungus of Würzburg [Note: *Erlongus*; variants include *Wirciburgensis*, *Wirziburgensis*, and *Wirceb.*] had been afflicted for four years by elephantiasis. He died on the feast of the Holy Innocents [Note: witnesses 4–11 add “he died on the third day before the Kalends of January”]. Because of the schism, he did not obtain burial in the city but in the monastery of Schwarzach [Note: variants include *Suarza* and *Swarzaha*].

The lord emperor came there to attend to the vacant see. Following the advice of his supporters, he raised to episcopal investiture a certain young man named Gebhard, indeed well-born [Note: one witness reads “a certain well-born man”], but still, because of his scholarly studies, not attached to any ecclesiastical advancement. He did this despite the firm and considerable opposition, as they say, of the sounder part of the clergy and people [Note: omitted in witness 7].

The other party, however, canonically elected another man named Ruggerus [Note: variants include *Ruoggerus* and *Ruggerum], a deacon of that church [Note: omitted in witness 4], who had been brought up there and was a canon. From this arose no small dissension. So great was it that those supporting Ruggerus, abandoning what they possessed in the city, were compelled to avoid the emperor’s anger. Duke Frederick and his brother Conrad [Note: variants include *Chuonradum*, *Cuonradum*, *Cuondradum*, and *Cunradum*], although they vainly consented to the same election [Note: omitted in witness 4], departed in anger from their uncle and lord [Note: one witness reads “departed” rather than “to depart”].

Not long afterwards, however, Frederick and Conrad held a conference with the archbishop of Mainz and several princes of Saxony beside the river Wirraha [Note: variants include *Wira* and *Werra*]. There, against the king’s will, they confirmed the aforesaid Ruggerus as bishop by election and investiture through the authority of Archbishop Adalbert and the other legates of the pope, who had recently returned from Rome [Note: one witness reads “who had recently come from Rome”].

At that very time the bishop of Speyer and the abbot of Fulda had returned after carrying out a legation on behalf of the whole kingdom before the apostolic see. They brought with them the bishop of Ostia, who exercised the authority of the lord apostolic in every respect [Note: one witness reads “the pope’s authority”], together with two cardinals who had likewise been sent by the see of Saint Peter for the reconciliation of the kingdom and the priesthood.

For this reason another courtly assembly was proclaimed throughout the provinces. Its place was Würzburg, and its appointed time was the feast of Saint Peter (June 29?) [Note: the date is omitted in witness 7]. As it approached, the princes and troops of various provinces began to draw near to the appointed city, not without harm to the whole of eastern Francia [Note: the wording concerning the princes and troops is defective in several witnesses].

But when they learned from trustworthy messengers that the lord emperor would certainly not come there, since he was entangled in other affairs around the Rhine, each man planned to return to his own place [Note: one witness has the singular “each man planned”].

Meanwhile Gebhard, having already firmly allied the townspeople to himself [Note: *jam sibi*, “already to himself,” in witness 4], remained within the walls with a large crowd. One afternoon he took a strong force from among those with him and attempted to attack certain men who had already pitched camp scarcely a mile from the city, suspecting no evil. He intended, regarding them as enemies of the kingdom [Note: E1 and E2 read “arguing” rather than “regarding”], either shamefully to drive them away or to strike down the unsuspecting [Note: E2 reads “the unguarded”].

But, roused by the shouting of those approaching, they swiftly drew up two lines against him and, resisting vigorously, defended themselves and their camp [Note: one witness reads the singular *aciem*, “line of battle”]. After a number had been killed, wounded, and captured on both sides [Note: variants include “captured men” and “after many had been killed, wounded, and captured”], as evening came these returned to the city and those to their tents.

Thereupon the princes, inflamed with anger, turned unanimously toward the city, striving to enthrone Ruggerus. But when they realized that this could not be done without bloodshed, they withdrew to the monastery called Schwarzach [Note: variants include *Swarzaha* and *Suarza*]. There, in the presence of the entire council, both the metropolitan and the other Roman legates consecrated him bishop of the church of Würzburg [Note: the wording is elliptical: “consecrating him bishop”]. Then each returned to his own place [Col. 1049; one witness has the singular “he returned”].

From then on, Ruggerus held for his own use that part of the bishopric which lies around the river Neckar [Note: variants include *Necaro*, *Necaro fluvio*, and *Neccaro*]. Gebhard, meanwhile, securely possessed the city and the lands adjoining it.

Meanwhile the archbishop of Mainz, looking everywhere for protection from the emperor’s anger, began with astonishing effort to fortify an ancient castle, almost completely ruined for many generations. It was called Aschaffenburg, either from the stream flowing past it, the Aschaf, or, as some maintain, from its founder Ascanius [Note: variants include *Askenburc*, *Ascenburg*, *Aschenburg*, *Ascenburc*, *Ascafenburg*, *Asafinburc*, and *Asasinburch*; the editorial identification is Aschaffenburg].

The king, judging that this was being done both as an injury to himself and against the public interest, decided in turn to organize a siege. But the benevolent and human-loving Jesus, through the diligence of his servants—the legates of the apostolic see who were then staying at Mainz [Note: E2 reads *ligatorum*, “of the bound,” rather than *legatorum*]—or rather through his Spirit dwelling in them [Note: omitted in witness 7], began to remove from the hearts of the princes the spirit opposed to peace and to pour charity into them as well. For, as is truly believed, after so many rifts in Christ’s tunic and so many civil wars among Christians, the time for having mercy on Zion, which is the Church [Note: the phrase is omitted in witnesses 10 and 11, which read “the Church”], had at last arrived, though late.

Accordingly, a universal assembly was held at the city of the Wangiones (September), which is now called Worms [Note: variant *Warmatia*]. It is as difficult to believe as it is long to recount how wisely, urgently, and in every respect with what anxious care all the leading men struggled for peace and concord for one week or more, until he in whose hand is the heart of the king bent all the emperor’s hostility under obedience to apostolic reverence for the sake of Mother Church, even beyond the hope of most people.

Soon afterwards, both the emperor himself and the entire army subject to him were received into communion by the envoys of the apostolic see. Indeed, through an apostolic act of general absolution granted to all polluted by this schism, the emperor, humbled for Christ before a very great multitude, renounced the ecclesiastical investitures and other spiritual affairs that the Teutonic kings had administered for so long. He had resolved never to relinquish them while he lived, lest the honor of the kingdom be diminished [Note: one marginal note reads “which they had administered for so long, so that the kingdom might not be diminished”; the wording is uncertain in one witness]. He relinquished them into the hands of the lord bishop of Ostia and, through him, into the perpetual right of our Lord Jesus Christ and his Church [Note: *jus* (“right”) is omitted in witness 4]. The following writings will better instruct both parties as to what the apostolic authority in turn granted him for preserving the honor of the kingdom [Note: compare the edition based on the best sources, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges* II, p. 75]:

> I, Henry, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans, august [Note: one witness adds “and ever august”], for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and of Lord Pope Calixtus, and for the salvation of my soul, surrender to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul and to the holy Catholic Church every investiture by ring and staff, and I grant that elections and free consecration be held in all churches.
>
> The possessions and regalia of blessed Peter [Note: witnesses 4 and 9c read “Saint Peter”] that have been taken away from the beginning of this discord until the present day, whether in the time of my father or in my own, and that I possess, I restore to that same holy Roman Church. As for those that I do not possess, I will faithfully assist in restoring them.
>
> The possessions also of all other churches, princes, and other persons, both clerical and lay, which I possess, I will return according to the counsel of the princes and justice [Note: the phrase “which I possess … which I do not possess” is absent in witnesses 10 and 11]; as for those I do not possess, I will faithfully assist in having them returned.
>
> I also grant true peace to Calixtus, to the holy Roman Church [Note: witnesses 10 and 11 repeat *sanctae*], and to all who are or have been on his side [Note: D, E1, E2, 5, and 10 read “and to all who are in his party”]. And in whatever matters the holy Roman Church seeks my assistance, I will faithfully help.

> I, Calixtus [Note: E1 and E2 read *Calixtus*], servant of the servants of God, grant to my beloved son Henry, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans, august:
>
> I grant that the elections of bishops and abbots of the Teutonic kingdom who belong to the kingdom be held in your presence, without simony and without any violence [Note: one witness reads “without all violence.”] If discord should arise between the parties, you shall provide assent and assistance to the sounder party according to the counsel or judgment of the metropolitan and the comprovincial bishops [Note: variants read “provincial bishops”].
>
> The person elected shall receive the regalia from you by the scepter, except for everything known to belong to the Roman Church; and he shall do what he owes you by right from these possessions.
>
> In the other parts of the empire, a person who has been consecrated shall receive the regalia from you by the scepter within six months [Note: one witness spells *sceptrum* as *ceptrum*].
>
> In matters about which you make complaint to me [Note: omitted in witness 4], I shall provide my assistance according to the duty of my office.
>
> I grant true peace to you and to all who are or have been on your side during this discord.

Given in the year 1122, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October.

These documents and counter-documents were read, given, and received before the gathering of the countless multitude in an open place beside the Rhine. Afterwards, after many praises had been offered to the governor of all things [Note: witness 4 adds “of all things”], and after the divine sacraments had been celebrated by the lord of Ostia [Note: *Ostiensis* corrected to *Ostiense* in one witness], during which he fully reconciled the lord emperor through the kiss of peace and holy communion, everyone departed in immeasurable joy.

[Col. 1051]

Not long afterwards, namely on the feast of Saint Martin, the emperor held another conference at Bamberg [Note: variants include *Babenberc*] with the princes who had not been present at the earlier one. When all had agreed to his wishes, and many matters suitable to the honor both of the kingdom and of the priesthood had been settled according to ancestral custom, he sent his own legates together with the Roman legates to the lord apostolic Calixtus, who was now united to him as a most intimate kinsman. He dispatched both groups bearing honorable messages and gifts [Note: one witness reads *utros*, “both,” rather than *utrosque*].

[Moreover, after Lord Erlolf, who presided over the men of Fulda even against their will, had died a few days earlier, Lord Oudalricus, a brother of that community, succeeded him in its governance. A regular election having first been held with the consent of the princes present, he received from the emperor the royal or fiscal properties belonging to the same monastery according to the privilege written above. — E.]

## A.D. 1123

Emperor Henry celebrated Christmas at Utrecht. During the feast itself a certain quarrel arose, namely between the members of the court and the bishop’s ministerials. It progressed to such a point that the entire court and city were thrown into turmoil [Note: the phrase “so that” is omitted in witness 7 and supplied above the line in E1], and armed companies of both sides came together.

A confused uproar arose, as though the people of Utrecht had conspired against the emperor [Note: conjecturally, “as though a conspiracy had been made against the emperor by the people of Utrecht”]. Thus, when some attacked and others resisted, a fierce battle began. Many fell, and more of the townspeople were captured; the rest fled for refuge to a very strong tower that stood there [Note: the relative clause is omitted in witness 4].

The bishop himself, regarded as a participant in the evil counsel and therefore held guilty of treason, was handed over to custody. Afterwards, after being fined a large sum of money, he was scarcely ransomed through the intervention of many leading men of that region [Note: one witness reads “former leaders”], especially Frederick, archbishop of Cologne [Note: one witness reads “bishop of Cologne”].

At that time the seed of the discord also began to sprout which, in the following summer, was to be brought to an end only slowly and with difficulty, and at last only when the emperor himself led a large army there. It caused the greatest harm to that region, commonly called Holland [Note: *Holland* in D1]. There a certain noblewoman, whose name has slipped from memory [Note: the inserted version identifies her as Gertrude], namely the sister of Duke Lothar, relying on whose protection she had rebelled against the emperor [Note: one version reads: “where a certain noblewoman named Gertrude, namely the sister of Duke Lothar, on whose protection she relied, dared to rebel against the emperor.”]

At that time, therefore, first throughout Saxony and then throughout almost all Germany, while external wars were at rest [Col. 1051: the preceding words *totam pene* (“almost all”) are absent in witness 4; witness E reads *ita* (“thus”) for *bellis* (“wars”)], the storm of civil uprisings increased everywhere; and, as the prophet says, “falsehood and perjury have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hosea 4:2; [Col. 1051: a lacuna of six letters occurs in the witnesses]). For brigands, who everywhere abounded under the name of knights, invaded the estates and fields of the churches, robbed the peasants at home and abroad—*colonos* (“peasants”; witness E2 reads *colones*)—and, oh, the crime!, forced those who were accustomed to live on bread and water alone [*et aqua* (“and water”) is absent in witness 4] to provide them with delicacies by means of torture. Thus, as each person avenged his wrongs by plunder and arson, scarcity—indeed, an extreme scarcity—of grain began to grow everywhere.

In the Worms district [*Wormaciensi*; witness 4 reads *warmaciensi*], for several days an armed multitude of horsemen seemed to be going and returning, forming companies now here, now there, as though for appointed conferences, but around the ninth hour returning to a certain mountain from which they also seemed to have emerged. At last one of the inhabitants of that region, fortified with the sign of the cross, approached this strangely prodigious assembly with great fear [*prodigiosae* (“prodigious”); witness E2 reads *prodigione*, “prodigy”]. He adjured one of the figures who came toward him to reveal, in the name of our almighty Lord Jesus Christ [this phrase is manifest in witness 4], the cause of the people who appeared in this way [witness 7 reads *que* for *qui*]. Among other things the figure replied to him:

“We are not phantoms, as you think, nor a crowd of soldiers, as we appear to you, but the souls of soldiers who were killed not long ago. Our weapons and clothing and horses, because they had previously been instruments of sinning for us [*fuerant* (“had been”); witness 9c reads *fuerunt*, “were”], are now the material of our torment; and truly everything that you see in us is aflame, although you cannot discern this with your bodily eyes.”

It is also said that Count Emicho, who had been killed a few years earlier [see the year 1117], appeared in such a company and declared that he could be redeemed from this punishment by prayers and almsgiving [the phrase “from this punishment” is absent in witness 7; “that he could be redeemed” is absent in witnesses 6, 7, and 9c].

Some report that on the night preceding the day of the Lord’s Supper, while they were hastening to the vigils according to ecclesiastical custom, they saw what seemed to be countless stars falling from heaven, so many that in both number and descent they appeared to imitate drops of rain.

At this time Dietericus, bishop of Chur [witness E2 reads *thiedericus*, witness 7 *theodericus*, witness 4 *dietricus*, and witness 9c *dietricus*], distinguished himself: he was highly learned in letters, always a Catholic champion against the schisms that occasionally sprouted in his day, and laboring with every pastoral concern for the welfare of the church entrusted to him [witness 9c reads *pastoralis*, “pastoral,” for *pastorali*].

Accordingly, not far from the suburb or territory of his city [witness 9c reads *sive*, “or,” for *suae*], with the utmost zeal and at great expense for several years, he founded a monastery or abbey on a hill which antiquity had once called Bosowa [the word “once” is absent in witnesses 10 and 11]. When the place had already been brought almost to completion [*ad unguem*, literally “to the fingernail”; witnesses 10 and 11 read *ad ungen*], with a substantial basilica consecrated and a community of monks established there [“also” is absent in witness 4], a certain perverse man was found among those whom we call *conversi* (“converted brothers”; witnesses 10 and 11 read *conversus*, “converted”). He was born of the same people, the Sorabi [the words “of the same people” are absent in witness 9c; witness 7 adds *Sor.*, “Sorabi,” after *progenitus*], and was in every respect subject not to the holy rule but to his own desires.

The abbot frequently rebuked him for his excesses [witness 4 reads *sepe*, “often,” for *frequenter*]; but, since he did not improve, he was brought before the bishop for correction. The bishop himself often rebuked him more severely, as he deserved. The man, however, broke out into such insolence that he stabbed the bishop with a knife while he was standing in prayer before the altar. Consequently, after three days the venerable priest [absent in witnesses 10 and 11] departed to Christ.

## A.D. 1124

[Col. 1053]

Emperor Henry celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen. A lunar eclipse appeared at the Purification of Saint Mary [this occurred on February 1]. As a result, Conrad, the emperor’s cousin, greatly frightened, professed that he would reform his conduct [witness E2 reads *professis*, “having professed”] and vowed that he would go to Jerusalem [witness D1 reads *iher.*, witness E2 *iher.*, witness E1 and witness 7 *ieros.*] and serve Christ there [“there” is absent in witness 7]; hence he gained considerable favor from all who heard this. Some also, previously devoted to wicked pursuits, declared that they would join the same company.

Not long afterward Emperor Henry launched an expedition against those who opposed him in the region of Holland [the witnesses variously read *Hollant*, *Holland*, and *holland*]; after subduing them, though only with difficulty, he proceeded to the upper regions, leaving the queen near the borders of Lorraine [the witnesses preserve different abbreviations for “the queen was left”]. Around the middle of Lent (March), he held a conference at Worms with certain nobles. To the others who were not present—that is, the Saxons, Bavarians [witness E1 reads *bajoriis*, “Bavarians”], and Bohemians—he announced that they were to come to the court at Babenberg [witness 4 reads *babenberch*, witness 7 *babenberc*] on the Nones of May [May 7; witnesses E1, E2, and 4 read *Maii*, “of May”], chiefly because of the insolence of Duke Lothair, who was suspected of plotting something new against the commonwealth on account of the injury inflicted by the emperor upon his aforementioned sister [the phrase “inflicted by the emperor” is absent in witness D1; witness 10 reads *quae* for *qui*].

A considerable assembly was therefore held there (May). The dukes of the individual provinces were present, except for the aforementioned Lothair and a few Saxon princes who agreed with him [“a few” is absent in witness 4]. The venerable Bishop Otto [witness B and witness D1 preserve the initial “B.”] supplied each of them with the expenses they required, either wholly or in part, in addition to the public and anciently established service owed to the imperial majesty, which the courtiers also demanded with excessive insistence [the phrase “from the courtiers” is absent in witnesses 10 and 11, as is the phrase “and the public service” in witnesses A and S].

The same father was reproached by them for visiting the palace less frequently than the other prelates [the witnesses preserve variants meaning “it was noted that he visited the palace less frequently”]. He himself, however, preferred to occupy himself with building and restoring monasteries, distributing alms, keeping vigil in prayer, and laboring at the other studies both practical and theoretical [the witnesses variously read *insudandis* (“to be labored at”) and *insinuandis* (“to be introduced”)].

There were also people who, murmuring that this was motivated by envy, judged that his efforts ought rather to be devoted to public duties [witnesses E1 and E2 add *etiam*, “also,” and “public functions”] and thus tried to stir up the emperor’s anger against the man of God [witness 4 reads *movere*, “to move,” for *commovere*]. But because “the Lord guards all who love him, and destroys the ways of sinners” [witness 4 reads *viam*, “the way,” for *vias*], this man [witnesses E1 and E2 read *ille*, “that man”], not sparing his temporal resources for the time being [witness E2 reads *transitorii*, “transient”], supplied sufficient support to everyone in a marvelous manner, although scarcity was pressing upon every region. He overcame malice by goodness and, through the services of genuine charity, earned the benevolent affection of the whole kingdom.

When the matters of that assembly had been settled, he informed both the emperor and all the leading men that he had been summoned by letters and many messengers from Boleslaus [*Polizlaus*], duke of Poland, and had also been sent with the permission and blessing of Pope Calixtus, specifically to the people of Pomerania, whom that duke had recently subdued as his neighbors [the phrase “as his neighbors” is absent in witness 4] and compelled to seek the refuge of Christianity.

The whole church that had assembled approved [“the church” is absent in witness 4], and the court approved as well, praying for success in his pious endeavors. Only the sons of the church of Babenberg unwillingly left their most beloved father, accompanying him as though escorting a funeral with many tears [witness D1 adds *cum*, “with,” after *lacrimis*].

After sufficient discussion had taken place concerning the confirmation of peace, various legal matters, and affairs of the kingdom, the emperor, indignant at those who had scorned to attend the present court [witness D1 first reads *curam*, “care,” then corrects it to *curiam*, “court”], arranged that a general expedition should be undertaken the following August [the words “one leaf is missing here in manuscript 4”]. In appearance it was directed against Saxony, but in reality against Gaul, into the kingdom of King Louis [the witnesses preserve forms including *Luodewici* and *Luod.*], namely to assist his father-in-law, Henry, king of England, who was contending with that same king of Gaul, Louis, for possession of the province of Normandy [the witnesses preserve *Normanniae*, *Nortmanniae*, *Norimannie*, and *Normantine*].

After the boundaries of that kingdom had been reached [the words *cujus fines*—“whose boundaries”—are marked in the margin of witness 6], once the appointed time had arrived and the German army had begun to approach (August), scouts reported daily that the French, having already assembled a very large army at home, were awaiting—or rather rashly seeking—a battle. The emperor at that time was leading only a small force there [the phrase “he was leading only a small force there” is variously abbreviated in witness 7], because Germans do not readily attack foreign peoples.

Meanwhile, word was brought from behind that the people of Worms, with the assistance of Duke Frederick and against the emperor’s will [witnesses 5 and 9c read *voluntates*, “wills,” in the plural], had restored their bishop Buggo [witnesses E1 and E2 read *contra Buggonem*, “against Buggo”] to his see and had fortified themselves in every way within the city walls for rebellion.

On hearing this, they turned back and attacked the city with the greatest ferocity [witnesses E1 and E2 read *magna*, “great,” for *maxima*]. They did not lift the siege until, after many efforts had been expended on both sides [the phrase *expensis—deficientibus*, “after the efforts had been expended—when they were failing,” is added in the margin of witness 6], many had been captured or killed before the walls, and provisions had finally run out, the townspeople were fined five thousand talents. Leaving the bishop in place, they made an agreement according to the emperor’s wishes.

Pope Calixtus II [the name is absent in witnesses 7, 10, and 11], a man outstanding in birth, character, wisdom, and every arrangement of divine and human affairs [witness 10 reads *divinarumque*, “and divine,” for *divinarum*], ended his life in the Lord.

After his death, one faction of the Romans tried to place the archbishop of Ravenna [Walter], a man sufficiently commended by every testimony of religious conduct, upon the apostolic see; others proposed Lambert of Ostia [witness E2 reads *Lambertum Ostiensem*]. Lambert, when the universal election subsequently concurred [witnesses E1 and E2 read *concordantes*, “concurring”], attained the object of their wish. For this man, long tested in the Roman church and well known on both sides in the legation during which he had previously labored energetically in the German regions for the reconciliation of kingdom and priesthood, was canonically consecrated by the unanimous favor of the priests both near and far [witnesses 10 and 11 read *consecratus*, “having been consecrated”]. In accordance with the custom of that see, and as truly worthy of so great an honor [the words “truly worthy” are absent in witnesses 6, 7, and 9c], he was called Honorius II [witnesses E1 and E2 read “he was called”; witnesses 6–11 add: “Abbot Poppo died”].

## A.D. 1125

[Col. 1055]

Emperor Henry celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the city of Strasbourg, also called Argentoratum [witness E1 reads *Strazburc*, witnesses E1, E2, and 5–9 read related forms], with the princes of Alsace, Lorraine, and the other leading men of the regions beyond the Rhine attending his court [“attending” is absent in witnesses 7 and 9c; the wording is otherwise preserved in witness D1 and witness E1].

At that time there followed a very harsh winter, a stormy spring, an extremely severe famine, and a most cruel mortality. They caused such slaughter throughout all the provinces, especially among the common people, that almost a third of the population is recorded to have perished [“almost” is absent in witnesses 6, 7, and 9c; “a third part” is absent in witness 9c].

At this time, on the very holy Saturday of Easter (March 28), our most longed-for and divinely provided provider, our bishop Otto, returned to visit the flock entrusted to him after enduring many tribulations for Christ. He was received no otherwise than Christ himself, the Anointed of the Lord, and, by rejoicing with his disciples, doubled the joy of the Lord’s resurrection [witness 6 corrects *gavisis* to *gavisus*, “rejoicing”].

That same faithful and prudent steward of Christ ordered the profit gained from the talent entrusted to him to be recorded in writing as a testimony to his faith and devotion. We too have not hesitated to append it here for the instruction of readers [manuscript E omits this entire sentence].

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1124 [witness D1 reads “of the Lord”], in the second indiction, while Calixtus II [witness 7 reads *uo*, apparently *vero*, “indeed”] was presiding over the Roman see, Otto, by the grace of God bishop of the church of Babenberg, admonished by divine inspiration and strengthened by the authority and approval of the aforementioned apostolic lord, undertook the regions of the pagan Pomeranians together with certain cities of the land of Louticia, in order to recall them from their error and lead them to the way of truth and to the knowledge of the Son of God.

“After baptizing and converting them, he built and consecrated churches, and taught them to observe the following according to the institutions of the holy fathers:

“On Friday they were to abstain from meat and milk, according to the custom of the other Christians [witness 7 reads *sexta feria*, “on Friday,” in a different order]. On Sunday they were to refrain from every evil work, come to church to hear the divine office [witness D1 reads *vacant*, “let them be free,” and witnesses 5 and 10 preserve the same reading; witness 6 corrects a duplicated form], and devote themselves earnestly to prayers there.

“They were to observe the solemnities of the saints with vigils [this phrase is absent in witnesses 6, 7, 9c, and 11], or according to whatever might be prescribed to them, with every diligence [witness 5 reads *cum omni*, “with all,” witness 10 *omnia*, “all”]. They were to strive to observe the holy Forty Days with the utmost care through fasts, vigils, almsgiving, and prayers.

“They were to bring their infants for baptism on Holy Saturday of Easter and at Pentecost [witness 5 reads *pentecostes*, “of Pentecost,” and witness 7 preserves a related form], with candles and the garment called the white robe, accompanied by godparents; and, once clothed in the garment of innocence, they were to bring them to church each day until the eighth day of that Saturday [the witnesses variously abbreviate ‘until the eighth day’; witnesses 5–11 preserve the sense], taking care to attend the celebration of the divine office.

“He also enjoined that they should not kill their children, a crime that was especially prevalent among them. Nor were they to hold their sons and daughters at baptism themselves, but were to seek godparents for them; and they were to maintain faith and friendship with the godparents as with blood relatives.

“He also prohibited anyone from taking his godmother as wife, or his own female relative, up to the sixth and seventh generation [witness 10 reads *indixit*, “he prescribed,” for *interdixit*, “he prohibited”]. Each man was to be content with one wife. They were not to bury Christian dead among pagans, in forests or fields, but in cemeteries, as is the custom of all Christians; nor were they to place sticks at their graves.

“They were to reject every pagan rite and depravity; they were not to build houses for idols, consult prophetesses, or practice divination. They were not to eat anything unclean: carrion, anything strangled, anything sacrificed to idols, or the blood of animals. They were not to associate with pagans, nor take food or drink with them or in their vessels. In all these matters they were not to return to pagan custom.

“He also enjoined that, while they were healthy, they should come to the priests of the church to confess their sins. In illness they were to call the priests to them, confess their sins, and receive the body of the Lord.

“He also enjoined that they should do penance for perjury [witness 7 reads “let them do penance for perjury and for…”], adultery, homicide [witness 4 reads *et*, “and,” in place of the expected construction], and other capital crimes according to the institutions of the canons [witness 7 reads “let them do penance”], and that in every Christian religion and observance they should be obedient.

“After childbirth, women were to come to church and receive a blessing from the priest, as is customary.

“Names of the cities: Piriz [witness 6 corrects *Poriz* to *Piriz*; witness 8 reads *Pirif*], Stetin [witness 4 reads *Stein*, witness D1 *Stetun*], Vulin [witness 4 reads *Wilîn*, witness 6 *Ulin*], Gamen [witness D1 reads *Camen*; witness 7 corrects *Gamen* to *Camin*], Colbrech [witness 4 reads *Colberch*], Belgrado, Lubin [witness 4 reads *Zubin* or *Lubin*], Gresch.”

[In the lower margin of witness D1 appear the words “Names of Gresch.” The editor identifies the places as Old Piritz, Stettin, Wollin, Kamin, Colberg, Belgard, Lubzin—apparently—and Garz.]

During these times, throughout the breadth of the Roman Empire [witness 7 reads “of the Roman Empire”], various prodigies and disasters occurred so frequently that neither their number nor their nature can be gathered by any mortal’s knowledge. Nevertheless, I have wished to commit to writing the few things that flying rumor brought to our ears, lest we seem to conceal from the coming generation examples of the divine blows that we endure under manifold scourges [witness 10 reads “divine”; witness 11 “the divine word”].

On the Wednesday of Pentecost week, the cold of a most dreadful frost inflicted great damage both on the new crops everywhere and on the vineyards, which, already swelling with abundant promise of their fruits, were offering the greatest hope. Not long afterward, namely on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [June 16], a storm of such immense force that it seemed to threaten a flood [witness 9c reads “in the sea”; witness 5 preserves a related variant] cruelly devastated certain places [witness D1, witnesses 4, 5, 6, 9c, 10, and 11 read *alicui*, “some place”; witness 7 corrects this to *alicubi*, “in certain places”].

Likewise, certain mists [“mists” is added in witness 7], bursting forth from marshy places, damaged the neighboring crops, especially the wheat, with rust or blight [witness 7 corrects *depravavit*, “it damaged,” to *depravaverunt*, “they damaged”]. The offspring of the bees [witness E1 reads *apum*, “of bees”; witness E2 corrects its form] also almost entirely perished, through some misfortune whose source I do not know. Moreover, several people testified that they had seen various signs in the sun, moon, or stars, each in a different manner [witness 4 and witness 7 read *et*, “and,” in place of *vel*, “or”], so that to some they seemed even to exceed belief.

A boy born in the district of Tullifelt [a district of eastern France; witness 5 preserves an abbreviated form] had his right leg swollen by a lasting livid discoloration.
