At last it burst where the collected pus had gathered and, wonderfully to relate, clearly discharged a considerable quantity of grains of wheat, rye, spelt, barley, and oats.

[Manuscript E1 adds in another hand in the margin: “Roudkerus, twelfth archbishop of Magdeburg, died.”]

Emperor Henry the Fifth of this name, intending to celebrate Pentecost at the city of Utrecht [witness 4 reads *Traiectam*, “Utrecht”], was overcome by an illness that he had long concealed [the passage from “concealed” through “namely” is absent in manuscript 11] and began to approach his end. He summoned those who were with him—namely, his wife, Queen Matilda [the witnesses give forms including *Mathilde*, *Mahthildis*, *Machth.*, *Mathilth*, *Machtilt*, and *Mahthilth*], his cousin Duke Frederick of Swabia [the words from “his cousin” through “of Swabia” are absent in witnesses 10 and 11], and the other leading men—and, as far as he was able [the phrase is absent in witness D1], gave them counsel concerning the condition of the kingdom.

He entrusted his possessions and the queen to the loyalty of that same Frederick, his heir [the words from “his possessions” through “entrusted” are absent in witnesses 10 and 11]. He ordered the crown and the other regalia to be placed for safekeeping until the assembly of the princes in the very strong castle called Trifels [witness 4 reads *Triuels*; “Hammers­te[in]” was later added in the blank space in witnesses 10 and 11; manuscript E notes that it lies south and west of Speyer]. Thus, after receiving the sacrament of Christ as viaticum, he ended his last day on the tenth day before the Kalends of June [May 23].

His body was prepared in royal fashion, carried to Speyer, and honorably buried before a multitude of nobles and commoners, clergy and laity, beside the mausoleums of his ancestors, in the twentieth year of his reign and the fourteenth of his empire.

As has been stated, this emperor first deprived his excommunicated father of the empire under the pretext of religion. Once confirmed in his honors, he changed his conduct; but after the injuries he inflicted upon the apostolic see, he was always inferior to his former self. He did not devote much attention to the laws of the kingdom. He was sharp in intellect, strong and bold, though not very fortunate in battles, and excessive in desiring what belonged to others. They say that he had amassed boundless sums of money; but, since he died without children, he did not know for whom he had hoarded them, in accordance with Scripture (Luke 12:21) [the manuscript reading *thesaurizasset* means “had hoarded”; witness 7 reads *thesaurizaret*, “would hoard”].

In this year, a raging mortality carried off several of the nobility together with an innumerable multitude of commoners. Among them, the lot of death struck Ulrich of Eichstätt [witness 5 reads *Uodalricum*], Rugger of Würzburg [witness 4 reads *Ruoggerum*, witness E1 and witness 9c preserve related forms], and Arnold, son of Count Arnold [witness E2 reads *Arnolfum* and *Arnolfi*], a young man of good character, along with many others.

After the immense slaughter of the common people, brought about both by famine and by pestilence through divine judgment, such a great and indiscriminate plague began to rage everywhere among the peoples that pale death threatened to spare no rank, sex, or age. The living scarcely sufficed to care for the corpses of the dead.

[Col. 1059]

# HIEROSOLIMITA

In the name of Christ begins the little book called *Hierosolimita* [corrected from *Iherosolita* in manuscript H], concerning the oppression, liberation, and restoration of the holy Church of Jerusalem [manuscript H reads *Hierosolitane*].

[Col. 1059A]

Concerning the cause or expedition of the army that in our times was directed toward Jerusalem from almost every part of the world, but especially from the kingdoms of the West—an undertaking ordained not so much by human agency as by divine providence—my eager spirit intends to add something to what has already been written, and thereby to satisfy your authority, venerable pastor, and the entire flock of Saints Stephen and Vitus trembling beneath your staff.

For I do not consider it lawful to deny to your charity these lesser matters when I already owe you my whole self and, having obeyed you in greater things, have arranged, to the best of my ability and knowledge, the more memorable traditions of various chronicles from the beginning of time down to the dregs of our own age. To withhold these matters would be altogether like failing to offer the tail together with the head in the Lord’s holocaust.

What also impels me to this is the all-too-necessary rebuke of certain imprudent—or rather impudent—men: “from the ancient [lacuna] entering upon service,” as in the chronicle for the year 1099; “aroused, that is, to zeal [lacuna] were led into France,” as in the chronicle for the year 1096. [In manuscript D the words from “aroused” through “let us return to these matters in greater detail” are absent here; much of the passage through “were led into France” has already been read above.] But let us return to these matters in greater detail.

“In the time of Henry IV, Roman emperor, etc.—he moderated his knowledge of languages,” as in the chronicle for the year 1099.

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1100. Under Godfrey—he extended the damage,” as in the chronicle for the year 1100.

“In the following year, which is the year of the Lord 1101, he appeared to one of our—who testified that they had seen,” as in the chronicle for the year 1101.

“Then there occurred—he had dismissed,” as in the chronicle for the year 1102 [these words are absent in manuscript II but occur here in manuscript D].

“Five years thereafter King Baldwin—began to assemble what had been prescribed,” as in the chronicle for the year 1105.

“The day before—was on the side,” in the same place.

“At this time several palm-bearing men—relate concerning his condition,” as in the chronicle for the year 1104.

[Col. 1060A]

Among these events they also record that King Baldwin married the daughter of Ruotger, duke of Sicily, the widow of King Conrad [see above, Chronicle for 1099], bringing with her so great a fleet of Sicilians and Normans that it could support the siege from the sea against Ascalon, which was again extremely hostile to the Christian name. The same king also besieged it from the land with his forces and made it tributary [“as previously” is absent in manuscript H].

Not long afterward, when the Lord had for a little while hidden his face and then looked again upon Zion, which he had once chosen as his dwelling place, the seed of such joy began, deservedly, to spread throughout the world. Faithful souls, who are truly the daughters of Jerusalem, became pregnant everywhere with vows of good fruits, and prophecies long since almost consigned to oblivion began to be repeated everywhere in various hearts, tongues, and voices.

“Behold,” they said, “in these our times, in which the ends of the ages have arrived, the Lord has looked upon Zion, and he will be seen there in his glory. He has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their petition,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 10:11; Psalm 101:17–18) [the words “and has not despised their petition” are absent in manuscript H]. “He has had mercy on Jerusalem, the city of his sanctification, the city of his rest” (Ecclesiasticus 36:15). “Rejoice with joy, all you who mourned over her,” and the rest (Isaiah 66:10).

Although these and a thousand such omens may, by allegorical interpretation, be referred to that Jerusalem above which is our mother [the phrase is absent in manuscript D], nevertheless they exhort weaker members, who drink from the breasts of the consolation already prescribed or yet to be written, to devote themselves even to dangers, in consideration of so great a joy and participation in it, through a practical journey understood historically.

We know, for example, of a man who confessed that he heard in a vision that hymn, “I rejoiced,” with the *Alleluia*, and that he himself joined in with the voices of the singers. As a result he was so greatly inspired to undertake that pilgrimage that his spirit found no rest until, after many tribulations, he reached with his bodily presence the place where the feet of the Lord had stood and worshiped there.

It is not astonishing but worthy of reverence that, once the scandals harder than stones had been removed from the way of the Lord—that is, from the hearts of the pagans—the Catholic church should unanimously hasten by a new path of repentance toward the source of its origin, the cradle of its first institution, and the special house of the true bread. It is known that in former times it exposed its most precious members along that same road not only to death but also to every kind of pagan mockery, like sheep destined for slaughter.

A few of those confessors of Christ who survive customarily testify—and it is grievous to remember—that they did not obtain even a foot’s passage freely among the idolaters, much less the comforts of food or lodging. Who could adequately write of the unheard-of and countless tortures they endured for the extraction of gold, for whom death was exceedingly bitter for the sake of profit, and life a cross?

But let us return to our own times—for “what we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify.” There are still, on that course, although the road is now level, the prizes of martyrdom for those who run toward the absolution of their sins: dangers from robbers, dangers from rivers, dangers from the sea, the wilderness, hunger and thirst, heat and illness, and a thousand other hardships of pilgrimage that are scarcely credible to those without experience.

The corpses of so many cross-bearing soldiers of Christ, laid low along that same road with their heads cut off and stretched out upon the ground toward the east in the form of a cross, bear witness to our words. Attacked there by the plundering pagans, they are seen to have drunk the cup of Christ amid the vows of prayer for which they had undertaken their pilgrimage.

Therefore, those entangled in the bonds of luxury must necessarily stop reproaching those who carry the cross after Christ, even under compulsion with Simon, for pursuing that very journey as though it were a vice of fickleness, since it was nowhere prescribed by divine laws. Rather, by refusing to desire the difficult ways of the Lord, they themselves prove through a venomous tongue of detraction that they are beyond correction.

As for us, what can we believe these men to be except true martyrs—men for whom the world has been crucified and they for the world? They mark themselves with the sign of the cross for so many torments, and only a very few of them, themselves bearing the palm, return as victors over death.

Nor are daily martyrdoms lacking for those who inhabit that promised land: voluntary exile, absence from parents, lack of necessities, incursions, robbery, continual fear, and the ambushes of barbarians, together with endless wars against the kingdoms of the Persians or Babylonians.

Meanwhile, day by day the daughter of Zion shakes herself free from the dust—namely, the Church of Jerusalem—and does not cease to sing a new song to her beloved, who has worked wonders with her:

“According to the multitude of the sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93:19).

For amid these sacred labors, holy places are cleansed of the long-standing pollution of the pagans; ruined churches are restored; bishoprics and monasteries are established throughout the regions in their former places; cities and castles are fortified; ports and markets, once deserted, rejoice in populous gatherings; and farmers, vine-growers, and shepherds are again granted their occupations. Above all temporal benefits, heavenly fire supplies the annual grace of Christ’s resurrection for human use.

There has also come into our hands a copy of a certain letter which we believe has already been spread throughout the whole world. They report that the archangel Gabriel brought it, in the person of our Savior, to that very church and through it to all churches. Just as it threatens transgressors with many terrifying threats, so it does not deny to the converted the customary consolations of divine mercy.

Therefore, since such glory has arisen for Jerusalem through the multitude of the Lord’s mercies, all the tribes of the earth ought to remember that salvation once came to the world from Mount Zion. Just as they formerly mourned over her with filial affection, so now they should rejoice with that primitive mother and be satisfied from her breasts of consolation, ascending there from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea, undoubtedly to confess in every manner the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

He consecrated that place—if it may be said without compromising the faith—even more than the earthly paradise itself, through his incarnation, miracles, passion, resurrection, and ascension. May all proclaim and glorify his name and mercy forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1061]

## THE END

[The word *Explicit* is absent in manuscripts E1 and E2.]

[Col. 1061]

# EKKEHARD’S LETTER TO ERKEMBERT

(See above, column 449.)

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1101. THE DEEDS OF THE PEOPLE OF TRIER, EDITED BY G. WAITZ, PUBLIC PROFESSOR AT KIEL

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, volume VIII, page 111.)

[Col. 1063]

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1063A]

Trier, or Treveris, one of the oldest of nearly all the cities in which Germany now takes pride, was founded by a Gallic people that claimed to be of Germanic origin, later conquered by the Romans, and adorned by them with honors and monuments. It then became the distinguished seat of bishops and archbishops who held the highest honor in the Frankish, Lotharingian, and German kingdoms. Even today, conspicuous for its pleasant situation, the ruins of its monuments, its churches, its library, and the relics of its saints, it has always supplied writers of history with abundant material for recounting memorable events.

Nor have there been lacking those who, both in more recent times and in the Middle Ages, undertook to present the political and ecclesiastical history of Trier, describe those monuments, narrate the lives of its archbishops, or otherwise—[the supplied source ends mid-sentence]—diligently and learnedly illuminate.

## Complete textual apparatus and editorial notices

The following source-ordered register preserves the remaining readings, omissions, corrections, marginal notes, and editorial references. A source form is followed by its English sense or by an explicit statement that it is an orthographic/inflectional form of the translated lemma; every cited witness and scope belongs to the immediately named source word or clause.

**Col. 1051, civil disorders and apparition.** Witness 6 omits *et* (“and”) before “blood”; E2 writes *colones*, an alternative spelling of “peasants”; witnesses 6 and 7 write *ha* and 9c *hi* for the interjection *ah* (“ah!”); witnesses 6, 7, and 9c omit *ab his* (“by those”); witness 4 omits *et aqua* (“and water”); witness 6 has *exiebant* (“they went out”), corrected in witness 10 to *exigebant* (“they demanded”). Witness 4 spells “Worms district” *warmaciensi*; 10 and 11 have *placitum* (“an agreed assembly”) for *placiti* (“of an agreed assembly”) and *turbas* (“crowds”) for *turmas* (“companies”). E2 has *prodigione* (“a prodigy”) for *prodigiosae* (“prodigious”); 7 has *appropinquabat* (“was approaching”) for *appropinquat* (“approaches”); witness 4 makes the invocation “in the name of Christ” explicit; 7 has *que* for *qui*, an inflectional form here meaning “who.” Witness 4 reads *atque habitus et* (“and clothing and”) for “weapons and clothing and”; 9c has *fuerunt* (“were”) for *fuerant* (“had been”). The source’s year reference for Count Emicho is 1117; witness 7 omits “from this punishment,” and 6, 7, and 9c omit “that he could be redeemed.”

**Col. 1051–1053, Dietericus and Bosowa.** The name appears as *thiedericus* (E2), *theodericus* (7), and *dietricus* (4, 9c), all spellings of Dietericus; 9c has *pastoralis* (“pastoral,” nominative) for *pastorali* (“pastoral,” ablative). It has *sive* (“or”) for *suae* (“his”), 10 and 11 omit *olim* (“once”), and 10 and 11 write *ungen* for *unguem*, the phrase “almost to completion.” E1 has *aliquod* (“some”) for *aliquot* (“several”); 7 and 9c have *instruebat* (“was building/furnishing”) for *instituebat* (“was founding”); 4 omits *quoque* (“also”); 10 and 11 use singular *conversus* (“converted brother”) for plural *conversos* (“converted brothers”); 9c omits “of the same people,” and 7 adds *Sor.* (“Sorabi”) after *progenitus* (“born”). Witness 4 has *sepe* (“often”) for *frequenter* (“frequently”); 10 and 11 omit “venerable priest.”

**Col. 1053, year 1124 and imperial affairs.** Witnesses 10 and 11 read *d. incarn.* (“of the Incarnation”) for *A. D.*; the eclipse is dated 1 February. E2 has *professis* (“having professed”) for *professus* (“having declared”); D1 and E2 abbreviate Jerusalem *iher.*, E1 and 7 *ieros.*, and 7 omits *ibidemque* (“and there”). The Holland reading is *Holland* in D, E1, E2, 4, 10, and 11. E1 abbreviates the queen’s being left; 4 has *per superiores se partes* (“to the upper regions”) in an abbreviated form. E1 has *bajoriis* (“Bavarians”), 4 *babenberch* and 7 *babenberc* (“Bamberg”), and E1, E2, and 4 *Maii* (“of May”); 4 reads *ob insolentiam* (“because of the insolence”) and D1 omits “inflicted by the emperor.” Witnesses 10 and 11 have *quae* (“which”) for *qui* (“who”).

For the May assembly, 4 omits “a few [supporters]”; E2 has *necessariis* (“necessary”) for *necessarios* (“necessary [expenses]”); B and D1 mark Otto with *B.*; 10 and 11 omit the courtier clause, while A and S omit the public service clause. Witness 5 abbreviates “the same father was noted”; 4, 5, 7, 9c, and 11 use *insinuandis* (“to be introduced”) where E2 has *insudantis* (“laboring”) and the text *insudandis* (“to be labored at”); E1 and E2 add *eciam* (“also”); 4 has *movere* (“to move”) for *commovere* (“to stir up”), *viam* (“way,” singular) for *vias* (“ways”), and E1/E2 *ille* (“that man”) for *iste* (“this man”); E2 has *transitorii* (“transient”) for *transitoriis* (“temporal”).

Witness 4 omits “his neighbors” and also “the church”; D1 adds *cum* (“with”) after “tears.” D1 first has *curam* (“care”) corrected to *curiam* (“court”); 4 omits “arranged an expedition”; manuscript 4 has a lost leaf after “the following August.” Louis’s name appears *luodewici* (E1, 5, 6, 10) and *luod.* (E1); Normandy appears *nortmanniae* (E1), *norimannie* (E2), and *normantine* (9c). In witness 6 the words from *Cujus* (“whose”) through *cepit* (“began”) are marginal; Suger’s *Life of Louis VII*, Bouquet XII, p. 50, is the editorial comparison. Witness 7 abbreviates “he was not leading many forces there.”

**Col. 1055, Worms and papal succession.** Witnesses 5 and 9c have plural *voluntates* (“wills”) for *voluntatem* (“will”); E1/E2 read *contra Buggonem* (“against Buggo”), which confirms Buggo rather than Burchard. E1/E2 have *magna* (“great”) for *maxima* (“greatest”); witness 6 places *expensis—deficientibus* (“after efforts had been spent—when provisions were failing”) in the margin. Calixtus II is absent in 7, 10, and 11; 10 writes *divinarumque* (“and divine”) for *divinarum* (“of divine [things]”). The Ravenna archbishop is identified as Gualterius (Walter); E2 reads *Lambertum Ostiensem* (“Lambert of Ostia”), and E1/E2 *concordantes* (“agreeing”) for *concordante* (“agreeing”). Witnesses 10 and 11 have *consecratus* (“consecrated”) for *consecratur* (“is consecrated”), 6/7/9c omit *ut vere* (“as truly”), E1/E2 have *sic appellatur* (“thus he is called”), and witnesses 6–11 add “Abbot Poppo died.”

**Col. 1055–1057, year 1125 and Otto’s document.** Witnesses 10/11 have *d. incarnat.* (“of the Incarnation”); 10/11 *natale* (“the Nativity”) for *natalem* (“the Nativity,” object); E1 has *strazburc* and E1/E2/5–9 related spellings for Strasbourg; 7/9c omit the attending princes, and D1/E1 preserve the phrasing *ita* (“thus”). Witnesses 6/7/9c omit “almost,” and 9c also omits “a third part.” The Easter adjective varies as *sacrosancte* (9c), *desiderantissimus* (4–7, 11), *desiderantibus* (9c), and *desiderantissimo* (10); 6 corrects *gavisis* to *gavisus*, “rejoicing.” Codex E omits the whole sentence beginning “That same faithful and prudent steward” through “we have not hesitated.”

In the inserted document D1 has *Domini* (“of the Lord”); 6/7/9c date it **M.C.XXVI.** (1126), not the main text’s 1124; 5/10 and D1 spell Calixtus *Calisto/Kalixto*; 7 has *uo*, apparently *vero* (“indeed”). Witness 7 transposes *sexta feria* (“Friday”); D1/5/10 have *vacant* (“let them be free”), 6/7 correct repeated forms; 6/7/9c/11 omit “with vigils of the saints”; 5/11 have *cum omni* (“with every”), and 10 *omnia* (“all”). Witness 11 has *sanctae* (“holy,” feminine) for *sancto*; 5 *pentecostes* (“of Pentecost”); the range “until the eighth day” is abbreviated in 5–11. Witness 9c has *inunxit* (“enjoined”) and 10/11 *indixit* (“prescribed”) for *interdixit* (“forbade”).

At Col. 1057, manuscript 4 continues after *injunxit* (“he enjoined”) with *junxit etiam* (“he also joined/enjoined”); witness 7 reads “let them do penance for perjury and for …” and *peniteant* (“let them do penance”), while 4 has *et* (“and”) in the homicide phrase. D1’s lower margin reads *Nomina Gresch* (“names of Gresch”); 10/11 have *nomen* (“name”). The city forms are *Poriz* corrected to *Piriz* (6), *Pirif* (8); *Stein* (4), *Stetun* (D1); *Wilîn* (4), *Ulin* (6); *Camen* (D1), *Gamen* corrected to *Camin* (7); *Colberch* (4); and *Zubin aut Lubin* (“Zubin or Lubin,” 4). The editor’s full identification is: Altstadt-Piritz, Stettin, Wollin, Kamin, Colberg, Belgard, Lubzin, apparently, and Garz (Barthold, *Historia Pomeraniae*, II, p. 56, note).

**Col. 1057–1059, portents, Henry’s death, and the conclusion.** Witness 7 has *rom. i.* (“of the Roman Empire”) and 4 *clades* (“disaster”) for *cladesque* (“and disasters”); 10 has *divinum* (“divine”), 11 *et divinum verbum* (“and the divine word”). The storm note reads *in mari* (“in the sea”) in 9c and an abbreviated variant in 5; D1/4/5/6/9c/10/11 read *alicui* (“to some [place/person]”), corrected by 7 to *alicubi* (“in certain places”). Witness 7 adds *nebulae* (“mists”) and corrects singular *depravavit* (“damaged”) to plural *depravaverunt* (“they damaged”); E1 has *apum* (“of bees”), corrected in E2; 4/7 use *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”). Tullifelt is a district of eastern France; 5 has an abbreviation. E1’s later marginal hand adds: “Roudkerus, twelfth archbishop of Magdeburg, died.”

For Henry V, 4 has *Trajectam* (“Utrecht”); 11 omits from *celaverat* (“he had concealed”) through *id est* (“that is”); the royal name varies as *Mathilde*, *Mahthildis*, *Machth.*, *Mathilth*, *Machtilt*, and *Mahthilth*. Witnesses 10/11 omit “his cousin … of Swabia” and “his possessions … entrusted”; 4 omits “as far as he could”; it has *Triuels* for Trifels, while 10/11 add Hamerstein in a blank and manuscript E locates it south and west of Speyer. Witness 7 has *thesaurizaret* (“would hoard”) for *thesaurizasset* (“had hoarded”). The final names vary as *Uodalricum* (5), *Eistetensem/Eichstatensem/Cihstatensem/Sihstatendem* (E2 and others), *Ruoggerum* (4, 9c, E1), and *Arnolfum/Arnolfi* (E2) for Arnold and his father.

**Col. 1059–1063, Hierosolimita and Prolegomena.** Manuscript H corrects *Iherosolita* to *Iherosolimita* and has *Hierosolitane* (“of Jerusalem”); manuscript D begins this narration with the chronicle’s 1096 material, from “Welfo … were led into France,” then resumes the chronicle of 1099 at “Here concerning the army …”; the addressee is Abbot Erkembert of Corvey. The words *excitati … replicemus* (“aroused … let us recount again”) are absent at this point in D, though much through “were led into France” has already occurred above; the bracketed 1102 passage is absent in manuscript II and present here in D. D1 writes *rutgeri* and *chunradi* for Ruotger and Conrad; “as previously” is absent in H; the phrase “and has not despised their petition” is absent in H; D omits “our mother Jerusalem.” The final explicit is absent in E1/E2. The editorial headings direct the reader to column 449 and identify G. Waitz, public professor at Kiel, and Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores* VIII, p. 111. The supplied Prolegomena breaks after *aliave diligenter docteque illustrarent*: “or otherwise would diligently and learnedly illuminate …”; it remains an inherited incomplete boundary.

Nevertheless, to pass over those who, on a suitable occasion, dealt with this city [Col. 1064A], there survive no books on the history of Trier older than the tenth century, apart from one Life of Saint Maximinus. Thus anyone wishing to tackle the earlier periods must necessarily lament the scarcity of sources. I hear that this was caused by that Northman invasion, during which nearly all the older monuments of history, not only those written on parchment but also those carved in stone, were destroyed—as all who have written about the origins of Trier proclaim with one voice. Nor would I deny that much was then overturned and lost; had it survived, it would shed light on the beginnings of the history, especially the ecclesiastical history. But I have not read that historical books were burned or destroyed, nor would I suppose that such books were then found in libraries. Rather, medieval writers say that such things occurred during an earlier devastation of the city, when Germans, Huns, and Vandals occupied it [Col. 1064B], evidently following an uncertain and deceptive tradition.

[Note: [Col. 1063B] It is useful to collect the earlier testimonies concerning this matter. The Life of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 922; Hillar, *Vindiciae Historiae Treverensis*, p. 56: “These things concerning the deeds of the holy fathers, which we found scattered in written scraps after carefully searching through the ashes left by the destruction of the city of Trier, we have gathered together and faithfully entrusted to the usefulness of readers, both present and future. And although in this present little book only a few things concerning their most holy deeds are included because of the disaster mentioned above,” etc. An appended conclusion, in Hillar, at the same place, reads: “Nevertheless, we found after the destruction of Trier that the city had been devastated three times” (he means the devastations by the Greeks, Vandals, and Huns) “. . . although few things concerning their many deeds are commemorated” (“many things are mentioned,” in the manuscript of Saint-Vanne cited by Hillar, p. 162), “as we said above, because of the devastation and burning of the city, together with its ecclesiastical records, this little book too was later found; [Col. 1063C] another, namely, we found burned . . . .”

The Life of Saint Felix, *Acta Sanctorum*, March III, p. 622: “In mentioning this thrice-blessed saint, as in recalling almost all the saints of Trier, we are compelled to lament repeatedly the devastation of this city, through which it is established that the immense volumes containing the lives of our holy fathers were so completely consumed that, unless they had been reconstructed, so to speak, from the few drops of so great a sea found in the ancient sheets of other places or even in leaden and marble tablets buried deep in the earth, our organs,” etc.

The Life of Paulinus, preface, *Acta Sanctorum*, August VI, p. 676: “We wish to make known to our successors some deeds of Paulinus heard from the report of our forefathers and others found here and there in copies of the holy fathers. For considerable volumes of his deeds existed among the people of Trier, but they are said to have been consumed, by God’s permission, in the burning of the city itself.”

Stephen’s Life of Saint Modoaldus, preface, *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 52: “which ought to have been recorded by us with greater certainty, had the barbarian devastation not long ago begrudged the noble Gallic titles. For it is said that a barbarian people then unleashed the reins of its fury throughout all the regions of Gaul, completely erasing the monuments, titles, and names of the ancient heroes, leaving us no traces of the virtues, victories, glory, or uprightness of our ancestors. But above all cities—that glorious metropolis Trier was to be lamented—and the memorials of ancient virtues in it were to be mourned all the more miserably, the more disastrously they had been taken away from the benefit of many. When fire consumed the ancient annals and copies, and as a result the entire succession of old genealogies had been abolished,” etc.

It is not always entirely clear of what period he is speaking; in this passage, however, Stephen is discussing events of the fifth and sixth centuries. Compare book III, opening, p. 59, where he turns to the Northmen, but says nothing about lost books.

The author of the Life of Saint Basinus blames the Northmen, *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, p. 315: “But, alas, although his most splendid deeds are believed to be and are miraculous, nevertheless, as we sorrowfully report, none of them has been transmitted intact to our knowledge. The furious rage of the Northmen did this, if I am not mistaken, laying waste everywhere to the churches of God. For it is well known that the city of Trier, together with its suburbs and the neighboring churches, was burned by those most foul Northmen. Consequently it happened that not only the life of this holy Basinus, but also the brilliant deeds of many other saints, committed to writing for posterity, went to ruin. Finally, after Emperor Arnulf had defeated the tyrants of the impious Northman army and peace had been granted, the deeds of many saints were recovered anew.”]

For the annals of the city [Col. 1065A] of Trier, said to contain its most ancient deeds and to have been read through by Pope Sylvester [Note: Life of Saint Agritius, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 773], everyone will concede to be fabulous; and I am convinced that the deeds of Paulinus and the other bishops did not yet exist at that time [Note: See the passages cited in note 1 above]. Those who wrote the Life of Saint Maximinus before that Northman invasion: one of them, anonymous, reports nothing of this kind [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, p. 371]; the other, Lupus, laments that his deeds had been suppressed in silence [Note: Lupus, letter to Waldon, in Surius III, [Col. 1065D] p. 323: “But in this work I am greatly constrained by the fact that, although many things which he did while he was still alive are plainly known have been suppressed in silence, scarcely any small memorials of his deeds survive, and among these some are found to resemble fables”]. Other writers of the eleventh century likewise reproach more the negligence of earlier generations [Note: Life of Saint Agritius, same place, p. 778: “because, as has been said, through the negligence of our predecessors he is not clearly known”; *History of the Martyrs of Trier*, ch. 1, in Hontheim, *Prodromus*, I, p. 111: “for the oblivion of both their names and their merits we blame the negligence of our predecessors,” etc.] than the incursions of the barbarians. There can be no doubt that they had seen the truth, since it is clear that those Lives of Saint Maximinus and the other books escaped the hands of the Northmen [Note: Relevant here is a hymn about Saint Paulinus, written in Scots and found in 1072 (*History of the Martyrs of Trier*, ch. 2); also several codices still surviving today in the libraries of Trier and Ghent, older than the ninth century].

Leaving these matters aside, let us see who afterward committed the affairs of Trier to memory. Many are indeed named, and great and distinguished works are praised. But most of these too you will seek in vain. They are praised, but neither have they been published nor are they found in manuscript, as though a second barbarian invasion had destroyed these documents as well. They are praised, moreover, by Trithemius, a learned man and most diligent investigator of antiquities and books, but one who did not establish his reliability so firmly that we should follow him as a completely trustworthy authority.

He relates that, shortly after the destruction of Trier inflicted by the Northmen, the monk Florbert of Saint Matthias at Trier described it in five books in elegiac verse. He likewise says [Note: *Annales Hirsaugienses* I, pp. 37, 56, 71, 98, 121, 142, 154, 174, 184, 208, 245] that Eberhard succeeded Florbert in directing the monastic school, Richard succeeded Eberhard, and afterward Diethelm, Adelbert, Theoderic, Theodorus, Golscher, Lampert of Liège, [Col. 1065C] Arnold, John, and Erhard; that they governed the school for nearly two hundred years; and that almost all of them were distinguished both by other works and by histories of Trier that they wrote and continued.

Yet it is truly remarkable that, concerning so many eminent men and so flourishing a school, Trithemius alone should tell us anything, while neither in the native monuments of Trier’s history—whether one searches shorter annals, the *Gesta* themselves, or individual Lives of the archbishops—nor among neighboring writers of Metz, Verdun, and Liège, nor in Sigebert of Gembloux, who composed a separate book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, can anything on this matter be found [Col. 1066A]. One or another of their number is named, but he neither lived at the time assigned to him by Trithemius nor appears to have composed the works that Trithemius lists.

Among many other works that have little bearing on history, Trithemius attributes these to them: to Eberhard, a Life of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, written both in verse and in elegant prose, as well as various hymns, chants, and several proses in praise of the saints; to Theoderic, the translation and miracles of Saint Celsus; to Golscher, three books on the praises of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus; to Lampert, five books on the miracles of the saints, one book on Agritius, archbishop of Trier, and one book on the life of Saint Matthias the apostle; to John, a golden legend of the saints. He further reports that Eberhard, Adelbert, Golscher, Lampert, John, and Erhard added many things to the history, or *Gesta*, of Trier. Let us compare these claims with the monuments of Trier’s history that actually survive.

Some have already observed that, as early as the tenth century, the origin of the Church of Trier was traced back to the time of the apostles [Note: Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica* I, p. IX ff., on the era of the foundation of the episcopate of Trier; J. Perier, *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 357 ff. Add to these the learned and generally correct discussions recently offered by the distinguished Sybel concerning the antiquities of Trier. See also Rettberg, *Church History of Germany*, p. 73 ff. Ado, in his martyrology, Rome 1745, p. 71, called Valerius a disciple of Saint Peter; Popes John XII and XIII speak more explicitly. The latter, in 969, says: “We have heard, and indeed formerly learned by hearing and even by reading, that this very Church, more than the other churches of Gaul, received the beginning of the Christian religion and the first rudiments of the Catholic faith through the evangelical teaching of the holy men Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus and the others, whom blessed Peter the apostle in their own time ordained and instructed and sent there to preach”].

At that time the simple and brief Life of Saint Eucharius, which we see published [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, January II, p. 918; Hillar, pp. 147–159], was probably written, since it says that they were sent by Saint Peter, indeed that they were disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ. Certainly this book, which Remigius of Mettlach [Note: Concerning him, see below. In his homily, in Hillar, p. 132, we read: “For the text of his life itself, most pleasing to God, contains,” etc.; and it relates the same things that appear in the published Life], at the end of the tenth century, Heriger [Note: I would not grant that the writer of the Life drew from Heriger’s book, or that both drew from a common source. Compare what was said above, vol. VII, p. 142, n. 51. The distinguished Köpke made this observation], and the author of the Life of Saint Agritius [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 778] in the eleventh century used, cannot belong to a later period.

Some have attributed this Life to Eberhard [Note: Hontheim, *Historia* I, p. XVII; III, p. 965], others to Golscher [Note: Bollandus, same place]; but here we possess neither Eberhard’s verses nor the three books attributed to Golscher. Perhaps, nevertheless, Trithemius called the Lives of the three bishops “three books.” Certainly, elsewhere, where he deals more briefly with the writers of Trier, he names Golscher [Note: *De illustribus viris Germaniae*, work I, p. 131; there he attributes to him a book on the praises of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus and also book I of the *Gesta Treverorum*]. Browerus likewise testifies that he saw Golscher’s sermons on Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus written on parchment [Note: *Annales Treverenses* I, p. 5: “Indeed, we ourselves saw written on parchment his sermons on the first three bishops of this See of Trier, Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus”].

If he means the published Life and truly read it under Golscher’s name, then this Golscher, whom Trithemius says governed the school from 1012 to 1038, was already flourishing in the middle of the tenth century. But perhaps the name Golscher is entirely fictitious, otherwise unheard of and found in no codices [Note: Hillar cites three manuscripts of the Life: the Saint-Matthias manuscript, p. 56; the Saint-Ghislain manuscript, p. 146; and the Verdun manuscript, p. 161. But none says anything about the name Golscher. Nor did Browerus say that he had read Golscher’s name on the parchment; he said only that he had read the sermons, which he perhaps judged should be attributed to Golscher on Trithemius’ authority].

At the end of the tenth century, if Trithemius is to be trusted [Note: *Annales Hirsaugienses* I, p. 122], Remigius, abbot of Mettlach, at the command of Archbishop Egbert, “composed a chant about Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, the first bishops of Trier, in sweet and regular melody.” But Hillar [Note: P. 132, where he published fragments], in the Saint-Matthias codex [Col. 1067B], found a homily composed by this Remigius for the feast of Eucharius, although it was for the most part copied from that Life.

Earlier, Sigehard had written the miracles of Saint Maximinus [Note: *Acta Sanctorum* IV, p. 229], while Theoderic, at the beginning of the eleventh century, narrated the translation of Saint Celsus [Note: Concerning it, see the Appendix]; but neither touched upon the earlier affairs of Trier even in a word. Trithemius says that the latter directed the school from 980 to 996; but he himself relates that he entered the monastery in 1006, and he does not appear to have taught letters there.

Trithemius attributes the Life of Saint Magnericus to Eberwin, abbot of Tholey [Note: *Annales Hirsaugienses* I, p. 161. Compare *Acta Sanctorum*, July VI, p. 179; Hontheim, *Historia* I, p. 373, n. III, p. 973. Eberwin succeeded Angilbert at Saint Martin’s. Tholey was held by Gardinus (*Annales Virdunenses*, *Acta Sanctorum* IV, p. 8), but both lived at the same time]; but the author was the abbot of Saint Martin’s at Trier [Note: See the end of this Life, published in the Appendix], the same man who, after 1035, dedicated the Life of Saint Simeon of the enclosed monastery to Archbishop Poppo [Note: Concerning this Life, see the Appendix. Trithemius incorrectly attributes to him, at the same place, book I of the *Gesta of Archbishop Poppo*]. Since that Life is already cited in 975, Eberwin must be judged either to have added only its conclusion or to have composed a new recension of it.

Most of it is excerpted from the books of Gregory of Tours and Fortunatus [Col. 1068A], with scarcely anything drawn from local monuments; nor does this work illuminate the obscure and uncertain origins of the Church of Trier.

The first person to undertake their exposition was the author of the Life of Saint Agritius, whom Trithemius calls Lampert of Liège. But this Lampert lived in the twelfth century [Note: Hillar, p. 84. See below what is said in the Appendix concerning the miracles of Saint Matthias]; another, called Regenheid, is said to have written only theological works [Note: Hillar, same place, whom Wyttenbach follows]. The Life of Saint Agritius, however, was composed in the eleventh century, between approximately 1050 and 1070 [Note: Around 1050 the third Life of Saint Hildulf was written (see *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* IV, p. 86), and the statements made in the Life of Saint Agritius concerning the translation of Saint Maximinus and the Theban martyrs (p. 774) occur only in that Life (*Acta Sanctorum*, July III, p. 231). The author had not yet seen the tablet found in 1072, since he says that the body of Paulinus was buried in the church founded by Felix, but not that it was miraculously suspended by chains; on this occasion he also relates other things from the report of his forefathers that do not agree sufficiently with that celebrated monument to have been derived from it. Compare the Life of Saint Agritius, p. 774, with the Life of Saint Felix, p. 623].

Apart from the Lives of Saints Eucharius, Nicetius—which he found in Gregory of Tours—Maximinus, and Hildulf, the author used no written sources [Note: Concerning the annals of Trier cited once, compare col. 1065 and note 95 below], but gathered from tradition, wherever he could, whatever concerned the deeds of Agritius, the relics collected by him, or the history of Trier. Most of it is fabulous and has found little favor with later scholars [Col. 1068B] [Note: See the testimonies in Hontheim III, p. 969], but it should for that very reason be highly valued, since it plainly demonstrates what the people of Trier at that time knew about their earlier history.

Shortly after 1072 [Note: Concerning the date, see *Acta Sanctorum*, October II, p. 335], a crypt was opened in the monastery of Saint Paulinus, and a leaden tablet was found there. It was said to have been buried in the time of the Northmen; it spoke both of the martyrs who suffered under Rictiovarus and of the tomb of Paulinus, as well as of the church built in their honor by Archbishop Felix [Note: Concerning this matter, see the dissertation of Neller, as Wyttenbach notes, in Hontheim, *Prodromus* I, p. 87 ff., and the arguments of J. Bueus against his view, *Acta Sanctorum*, October II, p. 331 ff.].

This discovery and the translation of the relics, celebrated by miracles, were extremely famous at that time [Note: Lambert, in 1072, and Sigebert, in 1071, narrate the event (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica* V, p. 190; VI, p. 362)]. It not only occasioned the writing of a special account of the event [Note: I have published some material from this history of the martyrs of Trier in the Appendix], but also caused the Lives of Paulinus and Felix to be illuminated by separate commentaries.

The latter openly admits that, before the tablet was found, nothing certain had been established [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, March of the Martyrs III, p. 623: “We did not know, without wonder, the reason for undertaking so remarkable a work, namely, that we had learned it from many writings or sayings of our forefathers” (the printed text reads *quia* for *quam*). “But since every period has its appointed time,” etc. “For the leaden tablet found in the crypt of the same monastery plainly instructs us with what just and honorable reason that great church was built by him”].

He gives a more extensive account of the history of the martyrs of Trier [Col. 1068C], explaining how the clergy of Trier had been deprived of historical documents; and from it we learn that no Life of Saint Paulinus then existed [Col. 1069A]. We may perhaps rightly call the latter more recent [Note: J. Pinius, *Acta Sanctorum*, August VI, p. 675, thinks that this Life was written before 1071 because it says nothing about the discovery; Hontheim III, p. 971, and J. Bueus, *Acta Sanctorum*, October II, p. 333, agree. Yet the account of the sarcophagus suspended by chains, on p. 678, depends on the authenticity of the tablet. Several deeds of Saint Paulinus are said to exist, differing in style; but in 1072 there were none, as the history of the discovery makes clear. They could scarcely find even some hymn about Saint Paulinus].

The Life of Saint Felix and the History of the Martyrs of Trier seem to belong to the same period, indeed to the same author [Note: They occasionally use almost the same words. *History*, ch. 1: “Nevertheless, we commend their diligence on account of the written records that we found inscribed concerning the merits of those same saints, either on leaden or marble tablets or on very ancient sheets.” Compare the passage from the Life of Saint Felix copied above, col. 1063, note 1], whose name I regret that we do not know. Trithemius did not touch either work even in a word.

Once these matters have been set out, I think everyone can understand Trithemius’ errors. Moreover, after reading these books, it becomes clearer than daylight that no continuous history of the archbishops of Trier then existed. Whoever composed those Lives lacked any reliable guide for setting out the succession, chronology, and deeds of the archbishops. All they did was collect from a few monuments, often doubtful and false, from external books, and from uncertain tradition whatever could in some way illuminate the history of the most renowned prelates, whose churches had been founded and inscribed with their names [Col. 1069B].

Certainly they neither saw the *Gesta* which, according to Trithemius, had been written before the Northman invasion and afterward continually continued, nor did they know anything about Eberhard, Adelbert, Golscher, or the other writers of Trier’s affairs. What, then, are we to say? They are bare inventions which he sold to credulous readers [Note: I should add that, from that great number of scholars of Saint Matthias, Trithemius himself elsewhere names only a few: Theoderic, Theodorus, and Lambert (*Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, work II, pp. 43, 54; *De illustribus viris Germaniae*, work I, p. 131). We know, in part, that they excelled in learning and works at this monastery, and in part we may willingly believe him. For he says nothing about the *Gesta*. It is remarkable that he does not even mention them in his book on ecclesiastical writers. Concerning Golscher, see above, col. 1067, note 18].

Around or after 1070, Nizo, the abbot, wrote the Life of Saint Liutwin [Note: The Life of Liutwin, dedicated to Archbishop Udo (1066–1077), is still unpublished; compare *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, p. 314. Manuscripts exist in Paris (*Archivum* VIII, p. 309), Ghent (ibid., p. 549), and Trier (ibid., p. 604). The Bonn manuscript (ibid. VII, p. 556) can no longer be found]. Not long afterward, whether by the same or by another writer, the Life of Saint Basinus was composed [Note: That Nizo was also responsible for the Life of Saint Basinus has been inferred from these words (*Acta Sanctorum*, same place, p. 319): “What Liutwin did afterward—whoever wishes to know should turn to the little book of his holy deeds, and there will find it clearly described. These matters, drawn from his deeds and worked out by us with whatever brevity we could, we have inserted into this treatise of ours for that reason,” etc. But these words seem rather to indicate another writer, if the words “worked out by us with whatever brevity we could” are to refer not to Liutwin’s but to Basinus’ Life. Contrary to Hontheim’s view (III, p. 978), this Life was not dedicated to Udo].

Here too you will find not even the slightest trace of the *Gesta*.—At the beginning of the twelfth century, Thiotfrid of Echternach sent Archbishop Bruno a book in which he dealt with the saints and their relics; he also reported at length on the Lord’s tunic, but passed over in deep silence what the *Gesta* narrate, namely, that it had been brought to Trier [Col. 1070A] [Note: See Sybel, *Der heilige Rock*, pp. 34, 37, who was the first to observe this].

Nor, when Stephen of Liège undertook to write the Life of Saint Modoaldus in 1107, did he use the *Gesta*. He drew his book from other sources and departs so far from their account that he says Modoaldus succeeded not Severinus but Sebald [Note: Stephen says that he knew almost nothing about this bishop; see the passage quoted above, col. 1063, note 1, and what he says earlier about the monk of Helmwardingen: “When, in investigating the nobility of his patron Modoaldus, he visited several places of our order and diligently sought both the deeds of bishops and the annals of the Frankish kings and the reputation of ancient wise men, he finally turned to us, the last of all . . . .” Later he says: “With God as our author, we undertook to narrate what we were able to gather concerning the life and miracles of the blessed bishop Modoaldus, both from the reports of the ancients and from reading authentic books.” But he reports many things wholly foreign to the *Gesta* and omits others that are set out there].

The Lives of Saint Auctor [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, August IV, p. 45] and Saint Severinus [Note: It is unpublished; compare Hontheim III, p. 975], written in the twelfth century, likewise rely on other sources. But the book on the discovery and miracles of Saint Matthias, written in the same century, refers to the *Gesta* [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, February III, p. 442: “But how he came from Judea to Trier, as I have read in the history of Trier and in the monuments of Pope Sylvester,” etc.].

Since this is so, we must conclude that the *Gesta Treverorum* were not written before the twelfth century. This is also confirmed by other considerations. For the oldest codices that we possess extend only to the year 1101 [Note: Concerning the Aureaevallensis and Treverensis codices, which extend less far, see below], and present the history of the tenth century and the beginning of the eleventh in such a way that it must be evident to everyone that it cannot possibly be attributed to contemporary writers. Matters of the greatest importance are omitted, the order of the bishops is confused, most things are related perfunctorily, and nowhere will you detect even the slightest trace of an author contemporary with the events.

Indeed, the works of Theoderic and Eberwin, as well as the Lives of Saints Magnericus, Agritius, and Felix and the History of the Martyrs of Trier, have been copied into it. I am greatly surprised that this escaped the notice of the learned men Hontheim, Wyttenbach, and others [Note: Besides these and many others, Rivet too follows Trithemius, *Histoire littéraire* VI, p. 127].

Moreover, unless I am mistaken, certain books written about the beginnings of the history of Trier and about individual bishops were older than the *Gesta*. To this category I assign a work once read in the Saint-Matthias codex M 1, no. 14, perhaps now lost, which, according to Hillar, “continues the deeds of Trier up to Archbishop Basinus, about whom it says very little and then ends” [Col. 1071A] [Note: Hillar, p. 128].

Hillar presents this passage on pp. 53, 61, and 128; he says that it occurs on folio 113:

[The words *Omnis*—*subministravit* occur only on p. 53.] “Just as the strongest farmer, most skilled in cultivating the field, rooted out all the thorns of unbelief that had arisen there over the longest period of time, so thoroughly that no root of unbelief subsequently grew there. For, as we gather by careful reckoning” [the reading is *Sicuti*; *Sicut* on pp. 61 and 128; the manuscript reads *collegimus*, “we gathered,” on p. 61], “we learn that 236 years” [346, p. 128; Sybel conjectures 246] “intervened between the glorious departure of blessed Maternus from this world and the most fortunate entrance of Saint Agritius into this city” [the passage ends here on pp. 53 and 128]. “During this intervening period the episcopate of this see ceased, because pagans held the city itself.”

[This passage occurs only on p. 62.] “In this festive commemoration of this holy father Maternus, we do not wish to pass over in silence the fact that, just as he lay dead in the tomb at Elegia for forty days, so afterward he ruled the Church of Trier for forty years alive and unharmed.”

The words “all the thorns . . . holding the city” are copied from the Life of Saint Agritius, p. 775. After this passage, as Hillar says, “an equally ancient hand in the margin, difficult to read because of age, adds the following”: “In the catalogue of the bishops of Trier, twenty-two bishops are found to have stood between Maternus and Agritius.” Hence the error is evident. It is likewise evident [the words “likewise, the error is evident” are absent on p. 62] that the city could not have been held by pagans during that same period, since earlier it is said that countless people were martyred by Rictiovarus not long before Agritius’ arrival. Compare with these matters the passage published below, note ** [Col. 1071C].

The work was therefore partly drawn from the Life of Saint Agritius and was written after the middle of the eleventh century.

Perhaps this was the same codex that Calmet first saw [Note: Calmet, *Preuves*, p. 1: “We compared it with an older and shorter manuscript, which apparently the monk Thierry had used and which is, as it were, the foundation and basis of his history”; and *Sur les évêques de Trèves*, p. VI: “An ancient manuscript of Saint Matthias, which we saw in that abbey,” etc. In the notes to his edition he frequently says “the ancient manuscript of Trier” or “the ancient manuscript.” Calmet himself does not say that it was a codex of the *Gesta*. Hontheim searched for it in vain in the monastery of Saint Matthias, *Historia*, p. XXVI. But Hillar refused to produce the book; see what he says on pp. 61 and 103], although Hillar indicated another, which he described in such a way that it seems to contain not the *Gesta* themselves but a work entirely different from the *Gesta* [Note: Ibid., p. 63].

“Codex,” he says, “the Saint-Matthias manuscript, under the letter I, 1, N. S., in a smaller and very pure manuscript, which could be entitled a report of the saints of the primitive Church, whether a martyrology or a brief collection of Lives” [Note: He continues: “This is the smaller one; the other is the older one, which Calmet claims to have seen.” I would scarcely grant this, however. For Calmet seems to speak not of a martyrology but of a continuous, though brief, narrative of the history of Trier, such as existed in codex M 1, no. 14. Calmet says that his book agrees word for word with the common text in the Lives of the first bishops, whereas Hillar’s codex has precisely different material in those passages. Compare what I said in *Archivum* IX, p. 704 ff.].

He also supplies fragments of such a kind as sufficiently to indicate a different order and form of the book [Note: It would take too long to copy out the passages concerning Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus. They were not read in a single continuous form; but the passages on folios 37, 45, and 5 do not agree with the wording of the *Gesta*. The passages copied by Calmet, however, always come closer to them].

A history of Trier apparently similar to the earlier one is the work whose criticism, published below, I copied from the Saint-Maximinus codex [Col. 1071B] [Note: The things criticized here in the history of Trier are partly foreign to the *Gesta*, but they nearly agree with what I presented above from M 1, no. 14] [Note: [Col. 1072A]

In a codex formerly belonging to Saint Maximinus (compare *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 360), now preserved in the Görres Library at Koblenz (no. 94), the following was written in the margin by a hand of the twelfth century:

“Jerome in the chronicle: ‘All the years from the fifteenth year of Tiberius—that is, from the preaching of the Lord—to the fourteenth year of Valens, 351 years, are counted. If you add those thirty years, namely, from the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus, which is the year of the Lord’s birth, to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which is the first year of the Lord’s preaching, there will be 381 years from the incarnation of the Lord to the fourteenth year of Valens, in which he died.’

“But when the years are counted backward from the fourteenth year of Valens to the twenty-third year of Constantine the father Augustus, which is the year of the arrival of blessed Agritius, exactly 333 years remain. Therefore, in the 333rd year of the Lord’s incarnation, Agritius was sent by Helena, made bishop at Trier, and continued until the second year of Constantius, the son of Constantine. Maximinus succeeded him in the year 342 of the Lord’s incarnation; and thus, in the fourth year of his episcopate, but the sixth year of Constantius’ reign, and in the year 346 of the Lord’s incarnation, he celebrated a general synod at Cologne, at Agrippina, for the deposition of Euphrates the Arian, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fourth indiction, after the consulship of Amantius and Albinus, under Pope Julius. For this reason Jerome too most carefully recorded that same year in the chronicle, as though speaking in the person of Maximinus, making Maximinus more illustrious in that year and marking the year as memorable because of the memory of Maximinus.

“Thus, without any contradiction, you will calculate [*computab* in the codex] exactly 200 years between Maternus and Agritius; and we confirm this also by plausible arguments. For if, in the year 54 of the Lord’s incarnation, blessed Eucharius received the episcopate of the city of Trier and ruled it for twenty-three years, and Valerius succeeded him in the fifteenth year, and Maternus consequently completed the succession in forty years, it plainly follows that Maternus died in the year of the Lord 132, that is, in the thirteenth year of Hadrian’s reign and the second year of the papacy of Telesphorus. Thus, without any contradiction, you will calculate 200 years between Maternus and Agritius, because 54, then 23, then 15, and then 40 add up to 132, not 128 as the history of Trier has it [Note: Compare *Gesta*, ch. 16]; and in this it is convicted of falsehood.

“Behold, you have detected the history of Trier. Note further its second falsehood. For it says [Note: *Gesta*, ch. 19]: ‘In the year of the Lord 368, Agritius became bishop.’ This is an obvious falsehood, because, as we demonstrated above from Jerome, since there are 381 years from the Lord’s birth to the fourteenth year of Valens, in which he died [Col. 1073A], but, counting backward from that same fourteenth year of Valens to the twenty-third year of Constantine, which is the year of the arrival of blessed Agritius, exactly 333 years remain, not 368. Thus you will prove [*comprobab* in the codex] that it has lied twice in every respect; and from these two falsehoods you can gather many more fully from the same history of Trier.”]

Since we have established from Jerome’s Chronicle that there were 200 years between Maternus and Agricius, it remains for us to see whether this city, as some maintain—especially the History of Trier [Note: [Col. 1073D] This is not read that way in the *Gesta*, which at this point agree with Methodius.]—returned to paganism during those 200 years or continued in Christianity. The latter seems to us altogether more likely, namely, that it did not return to paganism.

For it is certain that, until the passion of Thyrsus, Palmatius, and the entire people of Trier—which took place under Diocletian and Maximian, in the year of the Lord 306, that is, in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, when in the month of March, during the days of Easter, the churches throughout the Roman world were overthrown by order of Maximian and Diocletian in the first year of the persecution—for, as Jerome testifies in his *Chronicle*, in the second year of the persecution Diocletian laid down the purple at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan—until, I say, that time, the entire city had remained Christian from the time of blessed Eucharius.

Moreover, according to Methodius, bishop and martyr of Patara [Note: [Col. 1073] Thus the manuscript.] there had been no lack of bishops throughout the entire period between Maternus and Agricius, so that twenty-six bishops are enumerated [Note: [Col. 1073] The manuscript reads *enurentur*.]. It therefore seems absurd that, in so short a time as that between the passion of the aforesaid martyrs and the arrival of blessed Agricius, this entire city should have returned to paganism—especially since there were no more than twenty-four years. For from the first year of the persecution to the twenty-third year of the reign of Constantine there were no more than twenty-six years, since he began to reign in the fourth year of the persecution. Thus there were twenty-four years between the passion of Thyrsus and Palmatius and the arrival of blessed Agricius.

If you say that during those days the city returned to paganism and that Tetradius thereafter remained pagan until the time of Martin, this does not seem to us at all tenable. How could a man of such distinction as Tetradius have remained pagan for so long in so renowned and royal a city, especially when so many holy priests were active there—Agricius, Maximinus, and Paulinus? How could a pagan have been a contemporary of Maximinus in one and the same city, when it is certain that Maximinus became famous through so many and such great miracles? With what face did a man full of God remove Euphratas of Cologne from his rank as a heretic, yet fail to convert the pagan in his own city? How could Paulinus go into distant Phrygia as an exile for Christ and there preach to pagans even unto bloodshed [Col. 1073D], while leaving pagans here in his own diocese? This was plainly incongruous.

But since Tetradius was baptized by Martin, we say that he postponed his baptism until that time, as was customary in those days. We find that Augustine, Ambrose, and Martin himself did the same; yet it does not follow that the entire city was therefore pagan. If you say that Tetradius was wholly a gentile and that Martin did not enter his house on that account, we reply that he did so because he saw that Tetradius was not a pagan with an obstinate mind but was reserved for him; for if Tetradius had been obstinately unbelieving, he would certainly not have approached Martin on behalf of his daughter, but would rather have turned to his idols.

.

[Col. 1074A] These books, and perhaps others of which we have no knowledge at all [Note: [Col. 1073D] Hillar., pp. 66, 127, also speaks of manuscript M 1, no. 13, containing the shorter *Gesta* down to the Norman invasion. From our B 6, however, it seems that it may be understood. The other manuscripts cited by Hillar. are these: M 1, no. 12, pp. 26, 64, 127, (---C 1); M 1, no. 15, p. 57 (Life of Eucharius, etc.); M 1, no. 16, pp. 57, 67—(History of the Martyrs of Trier).], seem to have preceded the *Gesta* in their present form and to have furnished the occasion for its composition. They too cannot be older than the end of the eleventh century; we have already observed that the *Gesta* were not written before the twelfth century [Col. 1074B]. At present, however, it is impossible to determine more precisely in what year they were completed.

I would nevertheless assign the earliest years of the century as the date of this book’s birth. For those who wrote the Lives of Saints Modoaldus and Auctor certainly did not use the *Gesta*; but neither were the *Gesta* derived from those Lives, nor did they so much as mention the translation of Saint Modoaldus in 1107 or that of Saint Auctor, which took place a few years later. Furthermore, around the year 1132 someone added an addition and continuation to these *Gesta*; Bishop Bruno, who is said to have assumed the Church of Trier in 1101, had already died in 1124. Finally, the oldest surviving manuscript appears to have been written at the beginning of the twelfth century.

Since this is so, we cannot but conclude that the *Gesta* were completed not long after 1101, the point at which the manuscripts end [Col. 1074C] [Note: [Col. 1073D] Sybel, *Die Advocaten des Trierer Rocks* II, p. 45 n. 52, thinks that the *Gesta* were written after 1131, because Agricius, who in chapter 19 is said to have been buried in the monastery of Saint Eucharius, was supposedly first discovered at that time. For in the *Translation and Miracles of Saint Matthias*, chapter 6, we read: “Although for so long it had been kept there, known to no one.” But here the reference is to a certain altar, not to the whole church of Saint Eucharius. The author undoubtedly invented the claim that Agricius was buried there (see below, cols. 1077–1078), thereby providing an occasion for the discovery. Moreover, in the *Gesta* the church of Saint Eucharius is never designated by the name of Saint Matthias, although the bones of the holy apostle were found there in 1131; Abbot Bertulf is said to have deposited them there around 1050. The *Gesta* report nothing about this. Cf. *Archiv* IX, p. 708.].

It is probable that the *Gesta* originated in the monastery of Saint Eucharius; but the author concealed his name, and he does not seem to be sought among those men whom Trithemius praises. Certainly, I would scarcely count Golscher, whom Trithemius sometimes names as the sole author, among the writers of the Middle Ages. Everyone will agree that another name, recently brought to light, rests on insufficient authority.

In the Roman Vallicellian Library, our Bethmann examined a manuscript H. 13 fol., written in the sixteenth or seventeenth century. Among various historical works, fols. 1–12 contain a book entitled: “From the Chronicles of the Trierers, composed by Rudolf, deacon of Trier.” [Col. 1074D] But these are merely fragments of the *Gesta*, rather carelessly copied from a manuscript enlarged by the first continuation. Nothing certain is known about that name.

[Col. 1075A] Whoever the author was, he undertook to illuminate the antiquity and history of Trier and to make the city—rightly, as it seemed to him—famous, indeed most famous. For he considered it necessary to narrate not only the deeds of the archbishops and Christian affairs, but also to return to earlier times, indeed to ascend into obscure antiquity, in order to recount the glorious deeds of the Trierers.

At first sight it is clear that much of what he relates is fabulous. Nevertheless, he should not be thought to have invented these things lightly; rather, he seems to have drawn them from popular tradition and from inscriptions discovered or fabricated at that time [Note: [Col. 1075C] See chapters 2 (3), 6, 8, 18, 23, and 27.], combining and amplifying whatever appeared relevant.

This is not the place to ask who first traced the origins of the Trierers back to Trebeta, son of Ninus. Perhaps this opinion did not arise before the twelfth century, but others seem to have preceded the author of the *Gesta* [Note: [Col. 1075C] See the passage of Thiotfrid cited in the note to chapter 2 of the *Gesta*, which I believe was written before the *Gesta*.]. [Col. 1075B] He not only readily accepted this narrative, but also incorporated the traditions concerning the city’s still magnificent monuments that circulated among the people [Note: [Col. 1075C] See chapter 3 on the gates, and chapter 4 on the aqueducts and amphitheatre.].

To these he joined every passage about Trier and the Trierers in the ancient writers that he was able to find. Drawn on by his desire to glorify his homeland, he sometimes even attributed to the Trierers what was said about the Gauls in general. Thus he used Justin, Eutropius [Note: [Col. 1075D] He seems to have possessed the pure text of Eutropius; for I have found nothing taken from Paul the Deacon or from the additions to the *Historia miscella*.], and Orosius, but above all Caesar, from whose commentaries on the Gallic War he copied a great deal.

He had also read Ausonius [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 20.], and he seems to have taken certain material from a book attributed to some Galba Viator [Note: [Col. 1075D] Cf. chapters 3 and 6 n.]; other material, however, cannot be traced to any definite source.

We also see that ecclesiastical writers were used with greater diligence. For what Jerome [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapters 7 and 20.], Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 20.], and Augustine [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 21.] reported about affairs at Trier is repeated here. Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History* and the work called the *Tripartite History* supplied individual pieces of information [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 19.]. Elsewhere the author of the *Gesta* found material in Sulpicius Severus [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 20.], in Gregory of Tours’s book on the *Lives of the Fathers* [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapters 23 and 24.], and in the *Life of Gregory the Great* by John the Deacon [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 26.].

Nor were the historians of the fifth, seventh, and eighth centuries neglected. He seems to have consulted at one point Prosper’s *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 20.], at another Gregory of Tours’s *History of the Franks* [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapters 20 and 22. It is remarkable that many other things reported there about Trier were entirely neglected, so that I would suppose the author had not Gregory’s own book in hand, but another work copied from it.]. Above all, for these periods he had the chronicler commonly called Fredegar to follow [Note: [Col. 1075D] Chapter 22.].

I do not know whether I should add Bede’s works [Note: [Col. 1075D] Cf. chapters 16 and 23.], the *Martyrology of Ado* [Note: [Col. 1076C] Cf. chapter 17.], or other works. There are also Trier lives and histories, some of which I have already listed above. I mean the Lives of Saints Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1076C] Chapters 4 and 14.], Agricius [Note: [Col. 1076C] Chapters 17, 18, and 19.], Maximinus [Note: [Col. 1076C] Chapter 19.], Felix [Note: [Col. 1076C] Chapter 22.], Magnericus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 24.], Hildulfus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 25.], and perhaps also Liutwinus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 24.] and Paulinus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapters 19 and 28. On the Life of Saint Marus, see chapter 23.].

From these works and from the *History of the Martyrs of Trier* [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 17.] a large part of the ancient ecclesiastical history has been copied word for word. He also made use of the Passion of Saint Nazarius [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 15.], the Life of Saint Helena written by Almannus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 18.], the Life of Saint Goar by Wandelbert [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapters 23 and 25.], and perhaps the Acts of Saint Lubentius [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 19.] and of Saints Fuscianus and Victoricus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 17.] [Col. 1076B].

Furthermore, for earlier times he seems to have consulted a book falsely attributed to Methodius [Note: [Col. 1076D] See below.], as well as Heriger’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren* [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 16; cf. below.]. Later he took several items from Regino [Note: [Col. 1076D] Cf. chapters 13 and 14, but especially chapters 25–28.], some individual passages from the appendix to Thegan [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 25.], and from the letters of Hincmar [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapters 24, 25, and 27.]. He also saw the translation of Saint Celsus [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 29.] and the Life of Archbishop Conrad, or Cuno [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapter 33.], but did not wish to copy them.

From the ninth century onward he narrated the history of Trier more briefly, apparently because he lacked sources. For, apart from Regino, he had no further writer on German affairs, nor any Lives of the archbishops, but only a few notices about the Norman invasion. For the subsequent period he had nothing except episcopal catalogues giving bare names, individual accounts of translations scarcely worthy of remembrance, and charters of kings and popes [Note: [Col. 1076D] Chapters 24, 25, 28, 29, and 32.], which he thought it sufficient merely to indicate.

As a result, this part of the *Gesta* can scarcely be considered worthy of the name of history. It briefly reports the succession of bishops, adding only a few words about the origin, life, and death of each, of the sort that a twelfth-century writer could have hastily collected. While Caesar’s deeds, taken from another source, fill several pages, the most serious periods are now dispatched in a few lines, and the greatest archbishops are praised in fewer words than the fabulous Catholdus and Arimaspes [Col. 1077A].

The author uses a somewhat more generous style for Egbert and his immediate successors, but soon resumes his usual manner. Nor can this now be explained by a lack of sources. For the closer the writer comes to his own time, the more briefly he narrates the affairs of Trier—either because he considered them sufficiently well known, or because he was guided by the intention of exalting the ancient glory of the city with the most ample praises, while neglecting the more recent and often less fortunate times or leaving them to be described more fully by others.

But perhaps another cause of this difference may be suggested. What if the man whom we call the author of the *Gesta* abridged an older work that had treated the earliest periods of Trier’s history more fully, and undertook to continue it in a genuinely shorter form? There are certainly grounds that strongly encourage this conclusion.

Hillarius saw a book extending down to the time of Basinus; whether it was the same book or a similar one, Calmetus had it before him and reported material showing that this narrative generally agrees with the *Gesta* but differs from them in individual passages [Note: [Col. 1077C] Cf. above, n. 51.]. On closer examination, it becomes clear that this manuscript comes nearer to the sources and does not contain the fabulous material that seems to have originated in the monastery of Saint Matthias.

Many considerations prevent us from saying that this manuscript presents an older form of the *Gesta* [Note: [Col. 1077C] Sybel recently argued this, attempting to restore an ancient form of the *Gesta*: *Die Advocaten des Trierer Rocks*, fasc. III, pp. 75 ff. But the material he cites partly from Hillarius and partly from Calmetus does not agree in any way, and I greatly doubt that it was taken from the same manuscript (see above, p. 110 n. 50). [Col. 1077D] The words copied by Hillarius indicate not a *Gesta* or a *History*, but a martyrology. The phrases “At Trier, Saint Eucharius” and “At Trier, the deposition of Saint Valerius,” without indications of days, cannot be understood otherwise; and they differ greatly from the text of the *Gesta*, with which Calmet’s manuscript generally agrees. Calmet himself says: “An older and shorter manuscript, which apparently the monk Thierry had used and which is, as it were, the foundation and basis of his history.” Calmet regarded Theoderic, who lived at the end of the tenth and beginning of the eleventh century, as the first author of the *Gesta* (“… was probably composed by Thierry”). Thus he implies that the manuscript contains not the *Gesta* but the source of the *Gesta*. The claim of Hontheim, *History* I, p. XXVI, that Calmet saw the Eberhardian copy will convince no one. I have already shown above that there were no *Gesta* older than the twelfth century. The manuscript of the Golden Valley, which Sybel brought into this discussion, belongs elsewhere; see below. Finally, the statements in the Life of Saint Agricius concerning the city annals containing the most ancient deeds, which Pope Sylvester is said to have read (see above, p. 112), cannot persuade me that certain *Gesta* were older than the Life.], unless we call every book written about the history of Trier a *Gesta*.

We cannot but conclude that that book served as the foundation for our *Gesta*, and that many of the sources listed above were used not by the author of the *Gesta* himself but by that earlier writer—although it is now impossible to distinguish clearly what that book contained from what the author of the *Gesta* added.

Calmetus reports the following: the passage in chapter 16 concerning the bishops who governed the Church of Trier between Maternus and Agricius [Note: [Col. 1078C] I, p. VII.]; further, the material in chapter 15 about the wine conduit, and in chapter 19 about the bones of Matthias and the Lord’s tunic, as well as the accounts there of the burial of Agricius and Maximinus [Col. 1078A], were not found in that older book.

Other passages can be identified by plausible conjecture—for example, the statements concerning the church built by Eucharius; the burial there of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus in chapters 14–16; and the cell of Saint Eucharius in chapter 21. These point to the writer of the monastery of Saint Eucharius, or Saint Matthias, who was especially concerned to demonstrate that distinguished bishops and holy men had been buried in his monastery [Note: [Col. 1078C] Relevant also are the statements in chapter 25 concerning the translation of Saint Maximinus, in chapters 25 and 28 concerning the burial there of Hettus and Theoderic, and in chapter 27 concerning the body of Saint Eucharius.].

In chapter 16 he greatly expanded the catalogue of bishops, in order to fill the gap between Maternus and Agricius and to establish more securely the antiquity of the Church of Trier. It is now generally agreed, unless I am mistaken, that these names—which are absent from the older catalogues—are fictitious [Note: [Col. 1078D] Although Hillarius fought this opinion with the greatest vigor.]. Most of them, however, were found in the book attributed to Methodius of Patara [Col. 1078B] [Note: [Col. 1078D] See the note to chapter 16 below.]. Both the date of that author and other considerations prevent us from genuinely attributing it to him [Note: [Col. 1078D] Hontheim, *History* I, p. XXI; *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 360. On the true date of Methodius, see the same work, June IV, p. 5.].

After these eight bishops had been added, eight bishops of the Church of Tongeren were introduced. Our author retained Heriger’s wording concerning them, but whereas Heriger says that he does not know their place of burial, this writer asserts, in his customary manner, that they were buried in the church of Saint Eucharius.

In other passages it can no longer be determined which material was taken from that work and which was added, nor do we know from what point the author of the *Gesta* continued the narrative on his own initiative. Calmetus presents his manuscript as extending no farther than the time of Maximinus.
