Hillarius says that one manuscript ended with Basinus, while another—the one he identifies with Calmet’s—contained a concise account of the lives of the saints of the primitive Church.

I would suppose that from approximately chapter 23 onward the author was without this guide [Col. 1078C]. Yet I would also attribute to that monk of Saint Matthias the material taken earlier from Gregory and Fredegar, and even the material concerning the ancient city of Trier, compiled partly from books and partly from popular tradition. In the twelfth century he composed these *Gesta* from a shorter history of the archbishops, with the intention of celebrating as fully as possible the glory of his homeland and his Church [Note: [Col. 1078D] Often he adapted the testimony of his sources for his own purposes by adding or changing only a few words. In chapter 22 he changed Roman commanders into princes of the Trierers. He endowed the church of Saint Eucharius with both marvelous antiquity and other precious objects. He boldly made bishops of Tongeren into bishops of Trier. Sybel has also shown that the false diploma of Sylvester was enlarged by him with new additions in order to demonstrate that the Lord’s tunic had been brought to Trier.].

[Col. 1079A] Yet this book did not satisfy everyone’s wishes. For shortly afterward a certain Trierer undertook to continue and enlarge it. At first he added individual notices, sometimes shorter and sometimes longer; occasionally he altered what had been written or omitted it entirely. Later he began a new, fuller, and more accurate history of the archbishops, continued down to the time of Adalbero in 1132.

A different spirit is recognizable at first sight in this writer. With a less tranquil mind and a more abundant style, he follows the affairs of Trier, sometimes using new sources and sometimes following tradition and the reports of his elders. He illustrates the Roman period from Suetonius and Ausonius [Note: [Col. 1079D] On chapter 13.], once also appealing to Gallic history [Note: [Col. 1079D] On chapter 14.], perhaps meaning Caesar’s commentaries [Col. 1079B] [Note: [Col. 1079D] He used these in other passages as well, altering the wording of the old *Gesta*; see the notes to chapters 9, 10, etc.]. He also expressly praises Galba Viator as an author.

When the beginnings of the Christian religion among the Trierers are discussed [Note: [Col. 1079D] Chapter 14.], we see inserted not only a longer history of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, but also a repetition of those fabulous origins of the city, in almost the same manner but in different words from the opening chapters of the *Gesta*. When these passages are compared, it is clear that they were taken not from the *Gesta* but from their sources; yet it may be questioned whether they were composed by that continuator or copied from elsewhere.

Although in this section I seem to detect almost the same style and expressions that occur in the continuation itself, I nevertheless find the following opinion very attractive: first, because I do not see why he would have narrated the same matters twice in one book; and second, because I think this section is closely connected with the preceding history of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, which seems to have been transferred here from some ecclesiastical book, as both the overall tenor of the narrative and individual words appear to indicate [Note: [Col. 1079D] I mean the words: “the following reading demonstrates it.”].

Unless, perhaps, one says that this is the beginning of another history of Trier, later joined to the *Gesta*—a possibility somewhat confirmed by the heading prefixed at this point in certain manuscripts: “Here begins the history of the Trierers.” I would not oppose this opinion; indeed, I was once almost convinced that there had been two books of Trier’s history, later fused into one [Note: [Col. 1079D] Perhaps the same writer who continued the *Gesta* composed such a little book on the origins of the Trierer state and Church, which he later decided to insert into the *Gesta*. Someone might say that these are genuine fragments of the older book from which I said above that the *Gesta* were partly copied; I can scarcely agree.].

I have set this opinion aside, lest I be accused of indulging too much in conjecture and of making these matters more obscure rather than explaining them.

Afterward, that second writer added little to the ancient text and did not enlarge it enough for it to be called a new work. He merely appended a few items drawn from the Lives of Saints Martin [Note: [Col. 1080D] On chapter 20.], Severinus [Note: [Col. 1080D] On chapter 24.], Gertrude, and perhaps Basinus, as well as from charters and other records.

When the history of the tenth century had to be expounded, he too was plainly without sources. We see that he used no book apart from the account of the saints brought from Metz by Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1080D] On chapter 29.]. Rather, from popular rumor he took the generally false traditions about Rotger, Egbert, and other bishops; or they concern churches built or endowed by them; or they are minor matters of scarcely any importance. The stories about Poppo too are full of fables: some were taken from a certain ecclesiastical tradition, others from the Life of Saint Symeon [Note: [Col. 1080D] Addition, chapters 3 and 4.] Subsequently, some material was copied from the Passion of Saint Cuno [Note: [Col. 1080D] Addition, chapter 9.].

From this point onward, however, the author entirely rejected the ancient text of the *Gesta* as too brief. He aimed to narrate more fully and at greater length whatever he could gather both from the reports of his elders [Note: [Col. 1080D] Addition, chapter 1: “as far as the report of the elders came to my knowledge”; chapter 16: “came to our knowledge through the report of the elders”; chapter 25: “as we have learned from the report of our fathers.”] and from charters [Note: [Col. 1080D] Chapters 1, 7, 8, and 17.] and letters [Note: [Col. 1080D] Chapters 5, 12, 13, and 19. He also appeals to Hincmar’s letter in chapter 23.].

Accordingly, he follows the periods of Poppo and Engelbert in a full narrative. With an open mind, but excessively hostile toward the emperor Henry IV, he presents the most serious affairs; and when he reaches times closer to his own, he relates what he himself saw or learned from those who were present [Note: [Col. 1080D] Chapter 24: “which I myself saw and learned from the reliable report of others”; chapter 19: “a memorable event in which it happened that I took part.”].

Everyone will agree that this part of the book possesses great authority. They will judge its style sufficiently cultivated, although excessively adorned with passages from Sacred Scripture and the Fathers [Col. 1080C] [Note: [Col. 1080D] He cites Augustine in chapters 17, 20, and 22; Gregory the Great in chapters 18 and 22; Gelasius’s letter in chapter 14; and canons there and in chapter 20, but generally in passages where he is reporting the words of others.].

Who the author was is unknown; but he must be thought to have lived not long after 1132, when he broke off the thread of his narrative. I would call him a Trier canon, certainly not a monk of Saint Matthias, since he carefully describes Saint Peter’s church rebuilt by Poppo, but says nothing about the restoration of that monastery and nothing about the discovery of Saint Matthias.

There were also men who judged that this form of the *Gesta* should be altered and enlarged. Leaving aside the manuscripts in which we see this continuation added to the first part of the ancient recension, one writer altered individual passages [Note: [Col. 1080D] Chapters 14 and 15.], considering the author’s words at times unjust and excessively harsh. Another undertook to give a fuller account of the period of Archbishop Godefrid from genuine records [Note: [Col. 1081D] See the edition below.]. Finally, another enlarged the text with new additions, fully transcribing charters and diplomas that had been briefly indicated in the ancient *Gesta*, together with many others. The mass of this material sometimes seems to bury the genuine text completely and to present a cartulary rather than a chronicle of Trier.

Some maintain that this was done by Lambert of Liège, a monk of Saint Matthias [Note: [Col. 1081D] Wyttenbach, p. XX, n. 68; on p. 172 he attributes those alterations in chapters 14 and 15 to the same man. On Lambert, see the *Miracles of Saint Matthias* in the Appendix.]. I would not venture either to confirm or deny this. Certainly, the manuscript—unless I am very much mistaken—must be placed in the middle of the twelfth century and seems to have been written by the author himself. It was formerly in the library of Saint Matthias.

Moreover, the note concerning the rebuilding of the church of Saint Eucharius and the discovery of Saint Matthias [Note: [Col. 1081D] Chapter 25.] also shows that it was written in that monastery. The same writer should probably be regarded as having added the continuation from 1132 to 1152, drawn for the most part from the Life of Saint Adalbero. In that manuscript we see it written by the same hand, although not continuously.

The writer did not proceed beyond that year; later, others added further continuations, which we shall discuss more fully elsewhere.

Here we present the oldest *Gesta of the Trierers* down to 1101; the enlarged and continued *Gesta* down to 1132; and, finally, the additions made in the twelfth century. Guided throughout by the authority of manuscripts and more recent writers, we call all of these the *Gesta of the Trierers*. To distinguish the individual works, however, we designate the first by *a*, the second by *b*, and the third by *c* [Col. 1081C].

We shall publish in another volume of this collection the brief continuation down to 1152, together with what was later written at different times about the bishops of Trier.

We shall now briefly describe all the manuscripts that have come to our attention, hoping that in this way we shall not only prepare the path for our edition, but also further confirm and illuminate what we have already set forth. By following the manuscripts, we have been able to detect Trithemius’s errors and to distinguish not only the three forms of the *Gesta* but also their more minor alterations.

(A) 1. A manuscript [Note: [Col. 1081D] Cf. what I have already said about this and other manuscripts in *Archiv* VII, pp. 511 ff.] formerly belonging to “the monastery of Saint Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, of the Order of Saint Benedict,” [Col. 1081D] is in our time preserved in the library of the learned Fichard of Frankfurt.

The book consists of seventy-five leaves in a small format, sixty-nine of which are filled by the *Gesta*. They were written at the beginning of the twelfth century by more than one hand, partly on what are called palimpsest parchments, carelessly and so inaccurately that the scribe seems not to have understood the text sufficiently, but to have made as faithful a copy as possible of another manuscript.

In the individual words he often departs from ordinary usage, displaying such peculiarities as *c* for *t*, *cc* for *ct*, *cum* for *com*, and others. I believe that both these features and the more serious errors should be attributed to the scribe; but I would assign not a few errors to the author of the *Gesta* himself.

A brief notice of the archbishops Adalbero, Godefrid, and Meginher was added in another hand, apparently written during the period of those men. He copied this notice faithfully together with the text of the *Gesta*.

(A) 1b. A manuscript of the British Museum, Harley no. 3773, from the twelfth century, which Pertz had already used several years ago for this new edition of the *Gesta*, has now been copied again with the greatest accuracy by the distinguished Oehler, since the Trier sheets have been lost [Col. 1082B].

It has thereby been established that this book is a copy of manuscript 1. It seems to have been produced in such a way that the scribe took down with his pen the words dictated by a teacher. On this occasion the latter tried to repair the corrupt text of manuscript 1 by conjecture, while the former introduced new errors more serious than the old ones. For the words and sentences have already become so corrupt that even traces of the true reading have often disappeared.

A later hand corrected many passages, sometimes apparently with the help of another manuscript, but more often indulging in mere conjecture.

In the final four leaves of the book, a work of different subject [Note: [Col. 1081D] “The first dedication established by King Solomon”; “On the repentance and liberation of Solomon”; “The disagreement between Ambrose and Jerome.”] has been written.

(A) 2. A manuscript of the British Museum, Arundel no. 270, apparently written in the thirteenth century in quarto format, in which the ancient *Gesta of the Trierers* are found on fols. 1–23 [Col. 1082C].

This book, formerly perhaps kept at Mainz or in the Mainz diocese [Note: [Col. 1082D] For I noted already in *Archiv* VII, p. 512, that a catalogue of the archbishops of Mainz down to the year 1230 is read on the final leaf.], was first examined by the distinguished Lappenberg and more recently copied for our purposes by the distinguished Thorpe.

This copy of the *Gesta*, taken not from manuscript 1 but from another manuscript of this recension, is written accurately, but is by no means free of errors. At times it omits words; at times it adds others or distorts the ancient style through corrections [Note: [Col. 1082D] For example, in chapter 9, “neither … they wanted”; in chapter 10, “with these … they had arrived,” and “who … were setting out” are missing; in chapter 23, *penuria* is written for *penus*, thereby distorting the sense of the passage.]. A very brief continuation, written by the same hand, was added at the end.

Several manuscripts agree with this one so closely that they must have been derived from the same source. Among them two manuscript fragments must be mentioned first, although it can no longer be determined whether they belong to this class:

[Col. 1082D] 3a) A Wolfenbüttel manuscript of the twelfth century, now consisting of only one gathering, in which the beginning of the *Gesta* is written down accurately and neatly as far as the words of chapter 9, “held in the council” [*in concilio habuit cir*].

3b) A manuscript belonging to the distinguished Leopold van Alstein of Ghent, formerly Lammens [Note: [Col. 1083D] Cf. *Archiv* VII, p. 522; VIII, p. 555. Our Bethmann incorrectly says that this fragment forms part of the Leiden manuscript (p. 555, 97).], from the twelfth century, elegantly written on parchment. Only eight leaves of this too survive, extending as far as the words of chapter 12, “the magistrates, which …”

To these may be added the manuscripts which, as I have already said, joined the continuation down to 1132 to the ancient *Gesta* (A), copied as far as the death of Eberhard (+ 1066), and thereby in a certain sense produced a new work. I do not know whether manuscripts 3a and 3b belong here; the others do not extend beyond the thirteenth century and are recommended neither by their age nor by the accuracy of their readings, although they generally agree with manuscript 2.

4) A manuscript of the distinguished Sir Thomas Phillipps, preserved in his exceedingly rich library at Middlehill. It contains the *Gesta* in forty parchment leaves, written in a thirteenth-century hand [Col. 1083B], with reasonable care. The principal readings were noted by the distinguished Lappenberg.

5a) A Hamburg manuscript, *Hist. eccl.*, quarto, no. XXXI [Note: [Col. 1083D] On this, cf. *Archiv* VI, p. 230.], formerly belonging to Uffenbach and later to Wolf, written on paper in the fifteenth century in quarto format. Its 223 leaves contain various historical works: John of Stavelot’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, the *Gesta of the Trierers*, and the chronicles of Eusebius and Prosper, preceded by Sigebert.

The *Gesta of the Trierers* occupy seventy leaves, formerly numbered separately and now designated pages 159–278. From p. 253 (fol. 48), however, a continuation is read, carried down to Archbishop Wernher (1388).

5b) A Hamburg manuscript, *Hist. Germ.*, folio, no. 31b, written in quarto majus by several hands from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century [Col. 1083C], contains an extensive collection of historical books [Note: [Col. 1083D] See *Archiv* VI, p. 240, and what I shall say in volume X.]. Among them are both John of Stavelot’s work and the *Gesta of the Trierers*, the latter written on fols. 175–190 by a fifteenth-century hand, apparently.

Its readings generally agree with those of 5a; the continuation on fols. 186–190 is the same.

5c) The Hamburg Codex, *Hist. Germ. sing. region.*, folio, no. 70 [Note: [Col. 1084D] See *Archiv.* VI, p. 244.], of a later period, which presents in 88 folios the same historical monuments of Trier, and adds to them the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Cologne* (as does 5b). This book is written in a reasonably elegant hand, but is riddled with the foulest errors, which reveal a scribe ignorant of the old script. It agrees very closely with 5a and 5b, yet was not copied from either of them; rather, all three must be traced back to an older exemplar.—Of the same kind.

[Col. 1083D] 5d) The codex of the British Museum, Cotton Titus D. XXV, appears to be one which contains the *Deeds of Trier* down to 1387, as well as the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Cologne and Utrecht* and other material [Note: [Col. 1084D] *Archiv.* VII, p. 75.].

6a) Codex no. 5873 of the Royal Library of Paris, formerly belonging to I. A. de Thou, and earlier “from the books of Jo. Leferon of Charleville.” Three codices of different periods are contained in one volume. The third, begun in the thirteenth century and written in two columns, formerly belonged to another volume, as the quire numbers XXXI–XXXIV show; this is also confirmed by the following note in a more recent hand: “In the old codex there preceded the *Deeds of the Franks* and the *Miscellaneous Histories* of Paul the Deacon, in twenty-four books.” Now nothing but the *Deeds of Trier* is read here, and these are defective because two leaves have already been omitted. But our Bethmann recently found these leaves in Rome, in Vatican Codex Christ. no. 1283, where they occur on fols. 70 and 71.

6b) The Paris Codex of Saint-Germain, no. 77, large folio, thirteenth century, written in two columns, contains the material now missing from 6a, part of the Frankish history written by Hugh of Fleury, the *Miscellaneous History*, and certain fragments concerning Frankish history; to these it adds the *Deeds of Trier*, copied word for word from 6a, as I soon understood from an exact collation of the codices [Col. 1084B].

6b*) The Paris Codex of Saint-Germain, no. 1079, from the sixteenth century, copied from the book of Joan. le Feron of Charleville, that is, from 6a.

6b**) The Paris Codex Baluze Armoire II, p. 5, no. 2, contains a seventeenth-century copy of codex 6a.

6c) The Brussels Codex no. 9178–9187, thirteenth century, folio, contains the same works that were formerly read in 6a and that partly still exist in 6b. The readings of this codex, carefully recorded everywhere by the distinguished Oehler, agree with those of the other codices.

6d) The Lyon Codex no. 127, begun in the thirteenth century, quarto, defective at beginning and end, begins the *Deeds* with the words “which is called the granary” [Col. 1084C]. The opening words of the *Miscellaneous History* follow; the remainder of this book has been torn away. This book too, when compared by Bethmann with the printed editions, comes very close to the other codices of this class. Nor can there be any doubt that all of them flowed from a single source, which had already supplied them with a considerably altered text. For although much is shared with 4 and 5, many peculiar passages are nevertheless read here, showing that the scribe freely and boldly corrected the wording in order to make the sentence easier and more elegant.

I have recorded almost the entire variety of these codices, especially that in which all the codices, or those of individual classes, agreed. I have indicated this by the letters 3, 5, and 6.

The manuscripts that follow present the text of the *Deeds*, enlarged by many additions and continued down to 1132. These too must be divided into two classes: one that preserves the genuine form of this work, and another that has been augmented here and there by new interpolations. Otherwise they agree very closely with one another; and although they sometimes also approach codices 5 and 6, for the most part they preserve the genuine reading of codex 1 [Note: [Col. 1084D] See examples in chapters 9, 10, and many other places.].

The following belong to the first class:

[Col. 1085A] B 1) The Vienna Codex, *Hist. prof.*, no. 1069, twelfth century, octavo, whose readings from the time of Archbishop Poppo onward were transcribed for our use by the distinguished Chmel. At the end are found the metrical *Deeds of Archbishop Albero* and verses on Roman greed. A copy of this book, made for Lambecius, is preserved in the Vienna Library, S. II, 361.

B 2) The Wolfenbüttel Codex [Note: [Col. 1085C] See *Archiv.* VII, p. 515.], formerly “the book of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul at Ilsenburg,” twelfth century, quarto, written in an elegant hand, remarkable for its very good text and for the distinctive history of Archbishop Godefrid.

B 3) The Schlettstadt Codex, formerly belonging to the monastery of Marbach near Colmar, late twelfth century, folio, discovered by Pertz in 1841 and read through by our Bethmann this year, who judged it the best of this recension. Nevertheless, since I had readings recorded only at individual places, I could not assign it first place. Six leaves are missing; others contain Justin.

Three other codices offer a narrative altered or interpolated here and there. Among them are:

B 4) The Stuttgart Codex, of the twelfth century, is the chief: it is older than the others, carefully written, neither abridged at the scribe’s discretion nor deprived of its ending by the ravages of time.

B 5) The Vienna Codex, *Hist. prof.*, no. 686, omits a large part of the *Deeds* (the Addition, chapters 10–14, the beginning of 16, 17, the end of 18, and chapters 19 onward).

B 6) The Trier Codex no. 30, formerly belonging to St. Matthias at Trier, is defective at the end (it ends at chapter 30), and is written so erroneously and carelessly [Note: [Col. 1085C] See *Archiv.* VII, p. 518. It appears to be the same book that Hillarius says, on p. 127—cf. p. 66—is entered under M 1 no. 13 and extends down to the invasion of the Northmen.] that it can be mentioned only last. The material added by the B codices in chapter 14 is absent; all the remaining additions and interpolations, however, are read here, and there can be no doubt about the late date and low reliability of the codex. In the same volume is read a history of the martyrs of Trier. I regret that I did not transcribe it, either when the distinguished Wyttenbach sent this codex to Hanover or while I was staying at Trier [Col. 1086A] to make use of the books of its extremely rich library. Although this work appears to be of a later period, I nevertheless thought that individual passages might shed light on the *Deeds*.

The following must be assigned to this family of codices:

B 7) The Scriverian Codex, edited by Leibniz and, according to his own testimony, bearing at the end the following inscription: “The deeds of the people of Trier end happily, written with the greatest care by the hand of Peter of Wesel, whose soul, after death, may rest in peace with Christ. Amen.” Elsewhere Leibniz [Note: [Col. 1085C] *Accessiones historicae* I, preface.] praises three codices, besides the Wolfenbüttel manuscript mentioned above: one received from Migius, professor at Marburg, and another which he himself possessed. Which of them was the Scriverian Codex is unknown.

Goldast too possessed a similar codex [Note: [Col. 1085D] *Apologia*, pp. 41, 43.], and there may have been others [Col. 1086B] that now remain hidden. Certainly the thirteenth-century Codex of the Golden Valley, seen by Martene and sought by me in vain in the Luxembourg Library, appears to have been destroyed by fire. Although it agrees with Everhard the bishop as far as the ending, including the addition to chapter 8, I am moved to assign it here because Martene says that it agrees with the Leibnizian text [Note: [Col. 1085D] Martene, *Collectio* IV, p. 141: “It is altogether similar to this [the *History of Trier* edited by Leibniz], which we found in a manuscript of the Golden Valley, written five hundred years ago … Or if any difference occurs between the two, it is very slight and lies in this: the Codex of the Golden Valley, ending in its first hand at the year 1047, adds a few remarks about the succeeding archbishops, down to Hillinus, in a more recent but nevertheless old hand.” Martene printed this on p. 171 n.]. A continuation, added in another brief hand and carried down to 1258, was partly drawn from the chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 1085D] Hirsch, *De Vita Sigeberti*, p. 415.—Since the place for the year 1049 has been omitted, it is useful to transcribe the remainder here: “After him Engelbert became archbishop. When he died, Bruno was ordained archbishop. In the year of the Lord 1124, Godefrid was archbishop of Trier for seven years. In A.D. 1131, Albero of Metz became archbishop for approximately twenty years. Here it should be said that Frederick, count of Toul, the brother of Bishop Henry of Liège, who was buried at Huy, had two sons, Count Reynard and Count Peter. This Peter had two daughters. From one was born this Archbishop Albero, and from the other Bishop Peter of Toul. Albero is also mentioned in the *Life of Saint Florbert*. In A.D. 1152 Hillinus became archbishop; he was born in the diocese of Liège, at Fallemannia near Dinant. Concerning this Hillinus it is stated in the *Life of Saint Bernard* that he brought him to the reconciliation of the people of Metz, having sought pardon in the chapter of Clairvaux. Archbishop Arnold follows; then Folmar. Against him, during the schism, the emperor appointed the provost Rudolph; Folmar fled to France and died there near Tours. After him John became archbishop in A.D. 1188 and held office for twenty-three years. He was buried in the abbey of the Cloister. After him Theoderic of Wecla (Weda?) held office for nearly thirty years. He was buried in the church of Saint Peter at Trier. Then his nephew Arnold, in 1242. Radulf, meanwhile, became grand provost. In the year of the Lord 1258, after the feast of All Saints, Arnold, Archbishop of Trier, died intestate in his castle; he was brought back to Trier and buried in the church of Saint Peter.”].

Finally, the codices containing the third form of the *Deeds* must be reviewed. The most distinguished of all is:

C 1) The Trier Codex no. 1341 (XXXI), parchment, large quarto, marked with this inscription: “The codex of Saint Eucharius the bishop and Saint Matthias the apostle. Whoever removes it, may he become forever a participant in the chalice of Judas the betrayer. Amen. Amen. So be it” [Note: [Col. 1086D] Formerly designated M. I, no. 12; see Hillarius, pp. 26, 64, 127.]. This volume consists of two parts, one written in the twelfth (or thirteenth?) century, the other in the fourteenth. The first contains on fol. 197 the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*; on fol. 98, some brief notices [Note: [Col. 1086D] “It should be noted: the bravest of the Gauls are the Belgae,” etc. (see the note below on chapter 16), and: “Let us consider what the authority and use of the pallium may be; what is the pallium,” etc.]; and on fol. 99 and following (fol. 182) [Col. 1087A] the *Deeds of Trier*. These are written in a large and very clear script, ornamented with red initials and headings, and for the most part composed carefully and diligently. We see, however, that the narrative has been enlarged by documents and charters inserted into it, as I said above; individual words have also been added and altered. This was generally done by the hand of a corrector, who reviewed the written book, adding some things, transposing others, and emending still others. Since we see these features passed into every codex of this class, without a single exception, we cannot avoid concluding that the remaining codices flowed from this one as their source; this is plainly confirmed by a more careful comparison of the books with one another. It is therefore probable that this book—the oldest of all, distinguished by many corrections in a contemporary hand, and preserved in the monastery where the author of this recension lived—is the author’s autograph. Other considerations also support this judgment. For in this codex too the history originally extended only to the year 1132; afterward, when certain leaves had been inserted, the same hand, but with different ink, continued the *Deeds* to 1152. That is, the scribe made an epitome from Balderic’s *Life of Albero* and added to it a brief account of the new dedication of the monastery of Saint Eucharius by Pope Eugenius. The person who committed these matters to writing did not copy them from elsewhere but composed them first in this form. He also wrote out the earlier part of the *Deeds* in the form in which it is now read not only in this codex but in very many others. Accordingly, whether one attributes the addition of the documents to him or says that someone else followed him in this part of the book, here certainly lies the origin and source of the form of the *Deeds* that the other C codices present.

The other part of the volume, written in the fourteenth century in two columns, fols. 83–144, contains a continuation of the *Deeds* to 1259, as well as the *Deeds of Henry, Archbishop of Trier*, and of Theoderic, abbot of Saint Matthias; we shall discuss these elsewhere. For now it is enough to have noted that this part is of a later period and was copied from elsewhere.

Of the remaining codices, the following should be briefly mentioned:

C2) The Venetian Codex of the Library of Saint Mark, no. 403, parchment, thirteenth–fourteenth century, formerly the Codex of Saint Martin at Trier, examined by our Kopko. The book was written in one hand down to 1152 and was undoubtedly copied from C 1; afterward it contains continuations by several hands—to 1190 and to 1259.

[Col. 1087D] C3) The Frankfurt Codex, parchment, thirteenth century, folio, written by different hands—to 1190, 1259, and 1286. The first part—to 1152—was copied from C1; but it omits many documents, including some that were already read in the B codices. The history of Henry from 1259 to 1286 is the same as that read in C1, but C3 is older at this point [Col. 1088A].

C4) The Trier Codex no. 1343 (XXXIII), parchment, fourteenth century, folio, formerly the book of the collegiate church of Saint Paulinus, later owned by Hontheim and bequeathed to the public library. The text down to 1152 was copied from C3 (or C2?); from 1152 to 1159 it agrees more closely with the second part of C1. Thereafter a brief *Deeds of Archbishop Henry* is added, extending to 1286 and entirely different from the history mentioned above.

C5) The Trier Codex no. 1344 (LI), parchment, fourteenth century, quarto, formerly the book of the monastery of Saint Agnes at Trier, copied down to 1259 from the first and second parts of C1. Thereafter, on fols. 79–83, it contains a brief *Deeds of Henry*; on fols. 83–101, the *Deeds of Archbishop Boemund* (to 1300). On fols. 77 and 78, which had been left blank, another hand inserted certain material concerning the foundations of Archbishop John [Col. 1088B] (edited by Wyttenbach, chapter 102).

C6) The Paris Codex no. 6036, paper, fourteenth century, fols. 1–244, contains the *Deeds* continued to 1259, the *Deeds of Henry*, chapters concerning Archbishop John, the *Deeds of Boemund*, and the *Deeds of Baldwin* (to 1354). To these have been added certain documents and, from fol. 267 onward, in another hand, that other history of Henry.

Several more codices flowed from these, while the codices of Saint Maximin, seen by Hontheim and Martene and now hidden from view, carried the text further. We shall speak of all these more fully elsewhere. Finally, let us mention two books that present the life of Poppo copied from this edition of the *Deeds* [Note: [Col. 1087D] On this *Life*, see *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, pp. 88, 93 n.; Hontheim III, p. 982.]:

[Col. 1088C] The Trier Codex no. 1151 (963), thirteenth century, folio, where, among other Lives of saints, on fol. 140 verso and following, is read the *Life of Poppo, Archbishop of Trier*, with his miracles.

The Trier Codex no. 1383 (1200), paper, recently written, in fourteen leaves contains the same *Life*, as well as the “Instrument drawn up concerning the opening of the tomb of that same lord Poppo, archbishop of Trier” (1516).

By collating these codices with one another, it has been possible both to perceive the origins, alterations, and continuations of the *Deeds* with the greatest possible accuracy and to publish all their forms from the best and genuine sources.

Until now we see that both medieval writers and more recent authors have used sometimes one, sometimes another, copy of the *Deeds*. The former had these copies in hand more rarely than might be expected given the great number of manuscript books; apart from the author of the *Life of Saint Meinwerc* [Note: [Col. 1087D] Chapter 41. The passage was added later in the autograph codex; it was taken from the B text.], Alberic [Note: [Col. 1087D] A. 52, 71, 91, 128, 143, 157, 174, 319, 345, 357, 368, 385, 397, 446, 450, 511, 546, 577, 592, 617, 647, 681, 723, (765), 784, 796, 810, 837, 851, 864, 884, 905, (921?), 923, 960, 966, 970, 993, 1003, (1007), 1015, (1016?), 1029, (1071?). From B.], Albert of Stade [Note: [Col. 1088D] Edited by Kulpis, pp. 128, 138, 139, 156 (from year 47 onward), 161 (year 314), 165 (year 410).] and the Belgian chronicler [Note: [Col. 1088D] The *Magnum chronicon Belgicum* in the edition of Struve, published by Pistorius, pp. 1, 2, 4 and following, on almost every page. From a codex of the kind represented by 4, 5, and 6.] among foreign writers, no one, so far as I know, used them. For what is read concerning Trier in Sigebert [Note: [Col. 1088D] A. 413, on the founding of the city; 1071, on the discovery of the tablet. See Hirsch, *De Sigeberto*, p. 232 n.], Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 1088D] I, 8, on the founding of the city; III, 15, on Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus; III, 45, on Helena, born at Trier; IV, 8, on Maximinus and Paulinus.], the Zwiefalten Codex of Ekkehard [Col. 1089A] [Note: [Col. 1089D] *MGH SS* V, p. 36, on the founding of the city, apparently from Otto of Freising.] and the annals compiled in the monastery of Saint Disibod from Marianus and other sources [Note: [Col. 1089D] These are attributed to Methodius; concerning him, see above, col. 1078.] appears to have come from elsewhere.

The local writers, however, are all later than the *Deeds* and rely upon their authority: they repeat the narratives and often retain the very words. To these belong the authors of the unpublished *Passion of the Martyrs of Trier* [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Archiv.* VII, p. 517.], the *Life of Saint Matthias* [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Acta Sanctorum*, February III, pp. 442, 445.] and the Trier chronicle—to 1353 [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Archiv.* VII, p. 693. Several codices exist at Trier.], as well as Aegidius, monk of the Golden Valley [Note: [Col. 1089D] In the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, in Chapeaville I, pp. 19, 21, 23.] and John of Stavelot [Note: [Col. 1089D] See his book in the Hamburg codices indicated above under 5a and 5b.], writers on the history of Liège. In addition, there are those who, at the beginning of the sixteenth century, composed new *Deeds* or histories of Trier: the Eberhardo-Clausen monk [Note: [Col. 1089D] Preserved in the Trier Library, no. 1350 (CXVIII).], another anonymous author [Note: [Col. 1090D] Trier Codex no. 1346 (XXIX)—1522. Other Trier histories are preserved there under nos. 1391 (1347)—1537 and 1392 (1346)—1569.], John Enen [Note: [Col. 1090D] Concerning his book, translated into Latin by Scheckmann and published at Metz under the title *Epitome*, otherwise *Medulla Gestorum Trevirensium*, see Hontheim III, p. 989.]. To these may be added Kyriander [Note: [Col. 1089D] Hontheim, same work, p. 990.] and John Linden [Note: [Col. 1089D] Hontheim, same work, p. 991; Wyttenbach I, prologue, p. XL.], who continued the narrative of the *Deeds* down to 1629 [Col. 1089B].

In the sixteenth century Trithemius obtained a copy of the *Deeds* and transferred a very large amount of material from it into his historical works, spreading the book’s fame throughout Germany, so that several soon began to consider publishing the *Deeds*: C. Bruschius, Freherus, and Lambecius [Note: [Col. 1090D] See Leibniz, *Accessiones* I, preface.]. Since no one nevertheless carried out this plan, and Browerus did not share with readers the book that he had used in so many places, Dacherius was the first to publish the *Deeds*, in the form in which he found them in codex 6b (1675, *Spicilegium* XII, p. 196; new edition II, p. 208). Unaware of this, Leibniz soon afterward inserted in the first volume of his *Historical Additions* the B text drawn from three codices (Leipzig, 1698). Then, at nearly the same time, Eccard made public the continuation from 1132 to 1259 (*Corpus historicum* II, pp. 2197–2258, Leipzig, 1723); Calmet, following the Leibnizian edition, arranged for most of the book to be reproduced and noted several readings of the codices (*Histoire de Lorraine* I, *Preuves*, pp. 1–50, Nancy, 1728; second edition, ibid., 1745, pp. I–LXI); finally, Martene and Durand presented recension C, with the earlier chapters abridged but with continuations to 1455 added (*Veterum Scriptorum et monumentorum amplissima collectio* IV, pp. 145–452, Paris, 1729). From this edition some fragments passed into the collection of the writers of Gallic history (Bouquet, continuation XI, p. 194; XVIII, p. 670). After them Hontheim [Col. 1090A] published both recension C, lacking its beginning, from codex C1, and various continuations from the Trier codices (*Prodromus historiae Trevirensis* II, pp. 746–948, Augsburg, 1757). In our own times the distinguished Wyttenbach and Muller, intending to prepare a new edition, used many codices and compiled a rich collection of material concerning Trier from both older and more recent books (3 vols., quarto, Trier, 1836 and following); but, generally following codex C1, they made no effort to distinguish the various forms of the *Deeds*. They nevertheless deserve praise because, from the codices of the extremely rich Trier Library, collected and preserved by Wyttenbach with great diligence, they brought together many noteworthy materials for illuminating passages of the *Deeds*.

[Col. 1090B] In preparing this new edition I have partly used what the very learned men already named above, with their deserved praise, transcribed from the codices; but partly I myself examined the most important codices and handled them with all the diligence I could: the Frankfurt and Wolfenbüttel codices at Hanover, the Paris codices at Paris, the Trier codices in the library of this city, and finally the Hamburg codices at Kiel. I published the most ancient *Deeds* first, generally following codex 1, which alone preserved the true reading in many places [Note: [Col. 1090D] This is clear from several passages in chapters 9 and 10, compared with Caesar; for example, “and having exhorted,” “far from,” “from the Senones and Carnutes,” “to whom … were held,” etc. Codices 2–6 always depart from Caesar; the B and C codices, however, sometimes agree with him because the first scribe of the B codex used Caesar’s book.]. I appended what the B and C codices added, almost everywhere following the readings of codices B2 and C1. What was added in B from the time of Poppo I have called the Addition and the Continuation, and I have published it as the second part of the *Deeds* [Col. 1090C], indicating below the small additions or alterations of codices B4–6 and C. I recorded a sufficiently extensive range of variant readings, nor did I wish to be sparing in elucidating the narrative itself, especially for those periods whose sources can be identified or conjectured. Finally, I appended an Appendix of Trier monuments, in which I collected those materials that appeared useful either for explaining the *Deeds* themselves or for acquiring fuller knowledge of the earlier history of Trier.

G. WAITZ.

[Col. 1091]

# DEEDS OF TRIER

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK ON THE ORIGIN OF THE GAULS OF TRIER

[Col. 1091A] 1. A thousand three hundred years before the founding of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 1091B] The passage from “In the year” to “he perished by the stroke” has been copied, with a few words changed, from Orosius I, 4.], Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians, as historians maintain, driven by a desire to extend his rule, carried arms abroad and lived a bloody life through wars for fifty years [Note: [Col. 1091] Fifty-two.], waging war throughout all Asia. Rising from the south and the Red Sea, he subdued the lands beneath the farthest north by ravaging the Euxine Sea; and he taught Scythia, still barbarous, unwarlike, innocent, and sunk in torpor, to rouse its savagery [Note: [Col. 1091] “To be conquered”; the reading in 2.] and recognize its strength, to live not on the milk of cattle but on human blood, and finally to conquer while he conquered [Note: [Col. 1091] “Until he is conquered” should have been written from Orosius.]. At last he overcame and killed Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians [Note: [Col. 1091] “Of the Bractrians,” 5b.], whom they also say to have been the inventor of the magical art [Note: [Col. 1091] “The art,” 3b.; “magic,” B2.]. Then, while attacking a city that was withdrawing from him [Note: [Col. 1091] “From Asia,” corrected; 6b.], he himself perished by the stroke of an arrow, leaving his wife Semiramis with two sons, Trebeta and Nina [Note: [Col. 1091] Ninus (Nyno), 3b, 4, 5, 6, C3, C4, C5; Ninus is written above the line, or “Ninia,” in C1 and 6.].

[Col. 1091B] Their first son, namely Trebetas [Note: [Col. 1091] Trebeta, 2, 3a, 4, 5, 6.], had been born from a certain queen of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 1091] “Of the Chaldeans,” 5.], whom Ninus had married before Semiramis; Ninas, however, had been born from Semiramis [Note: [Col. 1091] Ninus (Nynus), 3b, 4, 5, 6, C3, C4, C5; Ninus is written above the line, or “Ninias,” in C1 and 6.]. After Ninus had been killed, Semiramis wished to take her stepson Trebeta as her husband. When he resisted and abhorred the proposal [Note: [Col. 1091] “Refused,” 4.], she, driven by jealousy and lust, persecuted him until she expelled him from his homeland [Note: [Col. 1091] “Expelled him from his homeland,” 4.] and kingdom. Thus driven out [Note: [Col. 1091] “Therefore,” 3a, 4?, 5, 6; “and while he was seeking a dwelling for a long time,” B6.], as he wandered for a long time seeking a place to settle and did not find one, he began to grow weary from the fatigue of his prolonged journey and to inquire, by the casting of lots [Note: [Col. 1091] “By order,” 5a. Errors of this kind from this codex will not be noted afterward.], where fate might direct him to rest. The lot offered Europe, which is the third part of the world, although some define it as the second [Col. 1092A] [Note: [Col. 1091] “Some define it as such,” C6.], while others maintain that Africa is not a part in itself but belongs to Europe. After crossing the Mediterranean Sea, which divides Europe from Asia [Note: [Col. 1091] Absent in 3a; absent in B and 2.], he came through vast wildernesses and trackless mountain passes [Note: [Col. 1091] “Trackless places,” 2.] to the Moselle. On its bank he found a lovely valley [Note: [Col. 1091] “Spacious,” C3, C4.], watered by streams, thick with wooded forests, and surrounded on every side by mountains. Captivated by the beauty of the place [Note: [Col. 1091] “Captivated, therefore,” C.], he chose to settle there and founded a city [Note: [Col. 1091] “Built,” 1.], which he called Trier (*Treberis*) after his own name [Note: [Col. 1091] “Called,” 1; frequently so hereafter.].

[Col. 1091] 2. A thousand two hundred and fifty years before the founding of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 1091] Absent in 3a, 4?, 5, 6.], the city of Trier was founded in Europe by the exile Trebeta [Note: [Col. 1091] “Tebeta,” corrected to Trebeta, 1; “Trebeta,” 6b.], son of Ninus, son of Belus [Note: [Col. 1091] “Beli,” C (perhaps “Belis,” corrected to “Beli” in C1).], in the seventh year of the life of the patriarch Abraham [Note: [Col. 1091] Thus 1.].

[Col. 1092B] The people who inhabited it derived their origin from Gomer, son of Japheth [Note: [Col. 1091] “Japhet,” 1b, 3, 5, 6, and likewise below; “Japhet,” B2, but “Japhet” below; “Jafet,” 2 and below.], son of Noah; and from the whiteness of the bodies of the Gauls [Note: [Col. 1091] “Of the Gauls,” B2; absent in B1?, 3, 4, 6, C.] the people and city took their name. They were most ancient, existing before there were peoples or cities in Europe [Note: [Col. 1091] “Nor were there peoples,” 2, 3, 4?, 5, 6.], whereas all those that exist either arose from them or began after them. Noah indeed had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. From Shem were born the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Greeks; from Ham, the Africans and Gaetulians [Note: [Col. 1091] “Getidians,” B2.]; from Japheth [Note: [Col. 1091] “From Japheth, indeed,” C.] the Italians, Gauls, and Spaniards [Note: [Col. 1091] Thus 1, 3a; “Hispani” or “Hyspani” in the others, here and below.]. Shem possessed India, Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine, Armenia, and the remaining provinces of Asia. Ham held Ethiopia [Note: [Col. 1091] Thus 1; “Ethiopia” in the others.], Numidia, and all Africa. Japheth received Spain, Baetica [Note: [Col. 1091] “Betigam”; “Baeticam,” 4; “Betigam,” corrected to “Baeticam,” 5a.], Lusitania, Aquitania, Britain [Note: [Col. 1091] “Britain,” 3, 5, 6, B2.], [Col. 1093A] Germany, Belgica, Gallia Togata [Note: [Col. 1091] “Thogata,” B2; “G. br. t. c.,” 5b.], Gallia Bracata, Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul, Pannonia, Italy, Ruria [Note: [Col. 1093C] Perhaps Etruria?], Liguria, Dalmatia, the region of Illyricum [Note: [Col. 1093C] “Illyricum” should have been written.], Bizemilia [Note: [Col. 1093] “Bihemilia,” 1b; “Bize. milia,” 2; “Biremilia,” 5a; “Biremiliam,” 5b; “Byzemiliam,” B2; “Bizemiliam,” C4, 6.] and all Europe.

[Col. 1093] [Note: [Col. 1093] Chapter III begins, C. Leibniz.] When Trebeta died [Note: [Col. 1093] “Trebete,” corrected to “Trebeta,” 1b; “Trebetae,” 3a, B6, B2; “Trebeta,” 3b, 5, 6, C; “Trebata,” 6c.], his son Hero [Note: [Col. 1093] “His son,” 5, 6a-b, B4.] succeeded him in the rule. Following the ancestral custom of the gentiles, he buried his father, who had been burned by fire, on the summit of Mount Juranus [Note: [Col. 1093] “Uranus,” B2; “Jurani,” corrected to “Urani,” C1, and likewise C3, C4, C5; “Turani,” 6a, apparently corrected.]. He also established altars for him and ordered his subjects to worship him as a god [Note: [Col. 1093] Absent in 5b.]: a great error, invented by Ninus, Hero’s grandfather, who first cast an image of his father Belus [Note: [Col. 1093] “Beli,” 3a, C (perhaps “Belis,” corrected to “Beli” in 1?).] and ordered a human being to be revered as a god [Note: [Col. 1093] “Cast the image,” 5c begins; “cast,” absent in 5b.]. Hero inscribed his father’s merits on a marble tablet [Note: [Col. 1093] “Merit,” 1.] and buried it with him, both in his memory and for the knowledge of future generations, in the form of the following inscription [Note: [Col. 1093] Added in red in B2: “Hero’s epitaph.”]:

[Col. 1093C] This inscription perhaps furnished the occasion for the preceding narrative. A passage cited by Wyttenbach from the *Life of Saint Willibrord* by the author Theotfrid refers to these verses: “The city of Trier, as epigrams discovered in a tomb in our own time declare, was founded and called Trier by Trebeta, the stepson of Semiramis, the wife of Ninus”; cf. Otto of Freising I, 8: “There still remain there monuments of ancient nobility, as they themselves say; among them we have placed below an epitaph that was found in our own time and carved on stone.”

[Col. 1093B]

Semiramis of Ninus, who, happy with so great a husband,

Possessed many things, but added more to what her predecessors had [Note: [Col. 1093] Absent in 5b.];

Not content with her own possessions or with all the boundaries of the world,

She expelled her stepson Trebeta from his ancestral kingdom [Note: [Col. 1093] “From his homeland,” corrected to “from his ancestral kingdom” in 1; “from his homeland,” 5b.],

The exile who founded our distinguished city,

Giving it the name of Trier out of love for its founder;

It is recognized as the head of Europe in antiquity.

His son Hero places these verses about his father [Note: [Col. 1093] Thus 1, 5a, B, 3, C1, C3; “epigrams” in the others.],

For whom here, in funeral rites, Mars with Jupiter holds the altars

Under a harmonious star; peace belongs to him who does not separate.

### Manuscript apparatus for the opening chapters

The following register preserves the printed forms (including spelling and inflectional variants), with an English gloss and the witnesses. It belongs to the immediately preceding lemma in each entry.

- **Title, Col. 1091:** *Inc.* is absent in 1b; 2 has *I. liber de or. Tr.* (“Book I on the origin of Trier”); 3/6 have *I. historia Treberorum* (3b spells *hyst.* and *Treuer.*); 5a has *De origine urbis Treverice et de gestis pontificum ejusdem civitatis* (“On the origin of Trier and the deeds of its bishops”); B1 *Inc. libellus de constructione Treberis*; B2 *Incipiunt gesta Treberorum*; B3 *Inc. historia Trevirorum*; B6 *Inc. de or. Trev.*; C1, C3?, C4 *In nomine domini nostri Jhesu Christi incipiunt gesta Trevirorum*; C6 *Inc. liber primus de gestis Trebirorum*.
- **“A thousand three hundred”:** *CCo* (“two hundred”) in 3b, 4?, 5, 6, B3. **“desire to extend his rule”:** omitted in 2 (which has *dom. suae*, “his rule”); 3a has *p. causa* (“for the sake of”); 3b/4/5 *p. causa*; 6 *p. fame causa* (“for the sake of fame”). **“fifty”:** *LII* (“fifty-two”) in 5; **“years”:** *q. a.* (“which years”) omitted in 3a.
- **“Scythia”:** *scytiamque* in 2, C1, C3; *scitiamque* in 3 and B2; *scithiamque* in 6; *scichiamque* in 5a; *sichiamque* in 5b; *sciticamque* in 4—each a spelling/form of “and Scythia.” **“and”:** *atque* in B6. **“to rouse savagery”:** *sevictam* in 2, a corrupt form. **“finally”:** *extremum* in 5. **“while”:** 2 has *d. v. vincere* (“while conquering”). **“conquered”:** *vincitur* (“is conquered”) is what should have been written from Orosius.
- **“Bactrians”:** *bractianorum* in 5b. **“magical”:** *maice* in B2. **“as they say”:** *fertur* (“it is said”) in 2?. **“art”:** *artem* in 3b. **“withdrawing from him”:** 6b corrects to *Asiae* (“of Asia”).
- **“Nina”:** 3b, 4, 5, 6, C3–C5 read *Nino* (3b *Nyno*); C1 and 6 have *Nino* written above the line or *Ninia*. **“Trebetas”:** *Trebeta* in 2, 3a, 4, 5, 6. **“Chaldeans”:** *Caldeorum* in 5. **“Ninas”:** 3b, 4, 5, 6, C3–C5 have *Ninus* (3b *Nynus*); C1 and 6 have *Ninus* above the line or *Ninias*.
- **“After Ninus had been killed”:** *autem* (“however”) in 5a and B6. **“resisted”:** *renuentem* (“refusing”) in 4. **“expelled”:** 4 has *e. pelleret p.* (“expelled him from his homeland”). **“thus driven out”:** *ergo* (“therefore”) in 3a, 4?, 5, 6; B6 has *i. diuque sedes* (“and, for a long time, a dwelling”). **“as”:** *cum* (“when/as”) in C3–C4. **“far and wide”:** *longe lateque* in 6. **“prolonged”:** *diurni* (“daily”) in 5.
- **“casting”:** 5a reads *jussione* (“by command”); the editor says such errors of this codex are not later recorded. **“offered”:** *obtinuit* (“obtained”) in 6a–b. **“the second”:** C6 has *s. eam* (“it [as] such”). **“define”:** 2 and 6 have *ita* (“thus”); 1 has *affiniant* corrected to *affirmant* (“affirm”); 1b/3a *affiniant*; 3b *affiniant* above the line or *di(ffiniant)*; C1 *afiniant*; C5 *afirmant* corrected; C3–C4 *definiant*; 5 and B *affirmant*. **“which divides Europe from Asia”:** omitted in 3a and in B/2. **“trackless mountain-passes”:** 2 has *sal[t]u loca* (“trackless places”). **“lovely”:** *spaciosam* (“spacious”) in C3–C4. **“captivated”:** C has *captus itaque* (“therefore captivated”). **“founded”:** *construxit* (“built”) in 1. **“called”:** *apell.* in 1, frequently so thereafter.
- **Chapter 2:** the opening date is absent in 3a, 4?, 5, 6; 6a has numeral *MoCoLo* (“1,250”). *Treveris* replaces *Treberis* in C1; *ab auctore* (“by the founder”) replaces *auctore* in 4?, 5, 6, B, C; 1 corrects *tebeta* to *trebeta*, and 6b has *trebeta*. *filio* is omitted in 1, added by another hand in 1b, and *f. N.* (“son of Ninus”) is absent in B and C. C has *Beli*, perhaps *Belis* corrected to *Beli* in C1. 1 and 1b add *aetatis suae* (“of his own age”); *Habrahae* is the form in 1.
- **“The people who inhabited it”:** 1/1b have *incolunt* (“inhabit”); 3b corrects *incoluit*; B2 *incolit Galliam* (“inhabits Gaul”); 5, 6, B3, C *incoluit eam* (“inhabited it”); 6a–b *gens que incoluit eam originem de* (“the people which inhabited it [derived] its origin from”). **“Japheth”:** *Japhet* in 1b, 3, 5, 6 and below; B2 likewise here but later *Japhet*; 2 and below *Jafet*. **“of the Gauls”:** B2 *Galli* (“Gauls”); absent in B1?, 3, 4, 6, C. The derivation is from Isidore, *Origines* IX.2; compare Jerome’s prologue to book II of his commentary on Galatians.
- **“nor peoples”:** 2, 3, 4?, 5, 6 read *neque gentes* (“nor peoples”). **“were”:** C1 apparently corrects to *fuerint* (“have been”), as do C3? and C4; C5 has *fierent* (“came into being”). **“Gaetulians”:** B2 *Getidi* (“Getidians”). **“from Japheth”:** C *inde vero* (“indeed from there”). **“Spaniards”:** 1/3a have *Ispani*; the others *Hispani* or *Hyspani*, here and below. **“Ethiopia”:** 1 has *Ethyopiam*; the others *Ethiopiam*. **“Baetica”:** 4 *Beticam*; 5a *Betigam* corrected to *Beticam*. **“Britain”:** *Britanniam* in 3, 5, 6, B2.
- **Places, Col. 1093:** B2 *thogatam* for *togatam*; 5b abbreviates *G. br. t. c.* The printed *Ruriam* is perhaps *Etruriam*; *Muricum* should read *Illyricum*. For *Bizemilia*: 1b *bihemilia*, 2 *bize. milia*, 5a *biremilia*, 5b *biremiliam*, B2 *byzemiliam*, C4/6 *bizemiliam*. 5b has *totamque* (“and all”) for *cunctamque*. C/Leibniz marks the beginning of chapter III.
- **“When Trebeta died”:** 1b corrects *trebete* to *trebeta*; 3a/B6/B2 *trebetae*; 3b, 5, 6, C *trebeta*; 6c *trebata*. **“his son”:** *filius eius* in 5, 6a–b, B4. **“in the rule”:** *principatum* (“the rule,” accusative) in 3b, 5, 6. **“succeeded”:** *succedit* (“succeeds”) in B2. **“Juranus”:** B2 *Uranus*; C1 corrects *Jurani* to *Urani*, followed by C3–C5; 6a *Turani*, apparently corrected. **“also”:** *et* in 5. **“his subjects”:** 5a omits *et sibi subjectis*; 5b has *subditis* (“subjects”). **“to worship”:** omitted in 5b.
- **“Belus”:** 3a and C have *Beli* (perhaps *Belis* corrected to *Beli* in 1?). **“image”:** 5c begins *mulachrum fudit* (“cast [the] image”); 5b omits *fudit* (“cast”). **“merits”:** *merito* (“merit”) in 1. **“for”:** *ob* (“on account of”) in 5b. B2 adds in red *Epytaphium Heronis* (“Hero’s epitaph”). The Col. 1093C note explains that the inscription may have prompted the narrative and quotes Theotfrid’s *Life of Willibrord* and Otto of Freising I.8; both quotations have been translated above.
- **Poem:** 5b omits *set plura prioribus addit* (“but adds more to what predecessors had”); B and C have *nec* (“nor”) for *non*; 5b *civibus* (“citizens”), an error, for *finibus* (“bounds”); 1 has the corrected reading *a patrio*, “from the paternal,” referring to the father’s kingdom (*regno*). B2 corrects *patria* to *patrio*, while 5b has *patria*: these are different inflections of “paternal,” with *patrio* agreeing with *regno*, “kingdom.” B6 has *Treveris* for *Treberis* (both names for Trier), and often thereafter; 6b *eius Ero* (“his Hero”); 1, 5a, B, 3, C1, C3 have *epigramata*, the others *epigrammata* (“epigrams”).

### 3 [Note: Col. 1093: Chapter IV, Leibniz]

After Heron, rulers and leaders arose from the very stock of the Treberi [Note: Col. 1093: *treberorum* is read in 1, 1b, B5, and C1; the others have *trevirorum*, and so almost everywhere thereafter.]. And now the Treberenses, increased both in number and in wealth, resolved to fortify and adorn their city in every way.

First, therefore, on the northern side of the city [Col. 1094A], they built a gate of squared stones with great towers, remarkable for its own size and threatening height [Note: Col. 1093: *quadris*, “squared,” is corrected from *quadis* in manuscript 1. The verb *construxerunt*, “built,” occurs in C.]. They called this gate the Black Gate and the Gate of Mars [Note: Col. 1093: *appellaverunt*, “they called,” occurs in 5c and 6; manuscript 2 adds “of Mars, who was believed to be the god of war.”] [Note: Col. 1093C: A remarkable monument of antiquity still exists today; in the Middle Ages it was the church of St. Simeon, restored to its original form in 1817. In Poppo’s charter (in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 379), it is already called the gate remembered among the pagans as consecrated to Mars.]. Its stones were joined not with cement but with iron and lead. Mars was believed to be the god of war [Note: Col. 1093: the words from “Mars” through “was believed” are absent in 2, B, and C; C1 adds *a Marte*, “from Mars,” and C2 and the following witnesses do likewise.], and through this gate those who were going to wage war set out. It was called Black because, fleeing from battle, they returned sadly through the same gate [Note: Col. 1093: B and 6 have “through the gate.”].

The field before the gate, spacious in length and breadth, was called the Field of Mars [Note: Col. 1093: this sentence is absent in B, 2, 3, and C1; 1, B4, 6, and C2 read “the field, however.”], where recruits were trained in arms.

Next, a second gate was built toward the rising sun, with handsome towers. Victors returning from war were received there amid the gathering of the whole city and with rejoicing [Col. 1094B]; for this reason it was called the White Gate [Note: Col. 1093: “is called” occurs in 1 and 1b; “called” in 3b; “has been named” in 5 and 6; C3 has “is named.”] [Note: Col. 1094C: It was called *Altthor* in the German language down to our own time. In antiquity it was not a Roman gate, but in the course of time it was built from the ruins of the Roman baths. Wytt. Compare his *New Investigations into the Roman Architectural Antiquities in the Moselle Valley at Trier*, 1835, p. 48. See also Schmidt, *Architectural Monuments of the Roman Period and the Middle Ages in Trier and Its Environs*, especially V.2, 1845.].

A third gate was built in the middle of the city on the southern side, with strong and lofty towers [Note: Col. 1093: this phrase is absent in 2, 3, 4?, 5, and 6.]. For this reason it was called the Middle Gate [Note: Col. 1093: 6 has “is named”; 5c, “is called”; 5b, “is called the gate”; B and 6, “is named.”] [Note: Col. 1094C: For its location, see Wyttenbach, *New Contributions to Epigraphy*, p. 13.]. A very large market for goods for sale was considered to have been established before this gate [Note: Col. 1093: B and C read *forum vero*, “a very large market indeed,” rather than *forum rerum*, “a market of goods.”], as well as the place from which the dead were carried out for burial.

A fourth gate was built toward the west, beside the bank of the Moselle. By its remarkable workmanship and the incomparable beauty of its towers it surpassed the other gates [Note: Col. 1093: *excellabat*, “surpassed,” occurs in 3, 5, and 6; B2 has *excellunt*, “they surpass.”], and for this reason it took the name of the Illustrious Gate [Note: Col. 1093: C has “the name of the Illustrious Gate.”]. They painted this gate wondrously with stars made of gold, which provided the nearest harbor of ships with illumination by night and day [Note: Col. 1093: witnesses 3, 5b, C, and 6c read *die et nocte* (“by day and night”); 5a, 6a, and 6b have *die ac nocte* (“by day and night”).].

There they also built a very large capitolium and a temple of idols [Note: Col. 1093: this phrase is absent in B6], in which no fewer than one hundred idols set up [Col. 1095A] were worshiped generally by the entire population; through them the wretched people were deceived by the responses of demons and by various magic tricks [Note: Col. 1095: *prestigiis*, “deceptions” or “magical illusions,” is a variant spelling in manuscript 1.] [Note: Col. 1095D: This passage is taken from the *Life of St. Eucharius*, *Acts of the Saints*, January I, p. 919: “They came to Trier, where there was such great error of paganism that, apart from the household gods of individuals, in one place in the city one hundred idols were set up, worshiped generally by the people, and through them the wretched were deceived by the responses of demons and magical illusions.”].

They also built, in honor of Mercury—whom they supposed to be the supreme god and, among gods and human beings, as it were a mediator who flew [Note: Col. 1095: B omits “the supreme god”; B and C add “and judge” after “mediator.”]—an arch of immeasurable height [Note: Col. 1095: B and C have “great height.”]. In it they caused an iron image of that same Mercury, of extraordinary size, to hang in the air as though flying [Note: Col. 1095: B and C read “as though flying”], with the following inscription:

> The iron bearer of the caduceus hangs in the empty air.

There was one lodestone joined at the top and another at the floor of the arch. Its natural force drew the iron toward itself from opposite directions, and thus the enormous iron object hung in the air as though hesitating [Note: Col. 1095: one witness has “drew the iron toward itself”; B2 has “drew the iron to itself.”].

Not far from there, over the Moselle, they built a bridge from great stones joined with iron and lead; no age could weaken it and no waters could break it apart [Col. 1095B] [Note: Col. 1095D: Traces of this bridge still survive; see Wyttenbach, *Historical-Antiquarian Investigation into the Age of the Moselle Bridge at Trier*, 1826.].

They also built throughout different parts of the city strong and lofty towers, capitolia, palaces, temples, statues [Note: Col. 1095: C1 has *tuias* written above the line, perhaps an alternative to *statuas*, “statues”; C3 and C6 likewise record *tuias*.], hot baths [Note: Col. 1095: manuscript 5 has “baths, hot baths.”], washhouses, and theaters [Note: Col. 1095: manuscript 5b has a variant spelling.]. Underground, within and outside the city and throughout all their territory, they performed many incredible marvels for those who did not know the truth.

Desiring also to have an abundant water supply, they brought in the stream that modern people call the Olevia [Note: Col. 1095: C reads *Olivia*.] [Note: Col. 1095D: A village now called Olewig bears this name.], beneath Mount Juranus [Note: Col. 1095: manuscript 1b has *Uranus*, with the letter *i* erased.] [Note: Col. 1096D: The mountain opposite the city to the east is meant. Wytt. It was later called Mount St. Martin; see the note to chapter 24.]. Divided into channels, it could scarcely supply half the city for its needs [Note: Col. 1095: the witnesses read “half the city,” “half of the city’s use,” or simply “for use.”] [Note: Col. 1096D: Several remains of this Roman aqueduct, which seems to have been directed to the baths, have been discovered in our own time. Wytt. Compare his *New Investigations*, p. 95.].

Then they brought in another stream, named the Ruoverias [Note: Col. 1095: variants include *Roverias*, *Ruuerias*, and *Rowerias*], two miles from the city, flowing into the other stream, called the Ruovora [Note: Col. 1095: the witnesses preserve numerous spellings, including *Ruoura*, *Riuora*, *Rowora*, *Ruovera*, and *Rovera*], rich in marble [Note: Col. 1096D: “Erubris, famous for marble,” in Ausonius, *Mosella* 359. It is now called the Ruwer; compare Böcking on the Moselle, p. 89.] [Note: Col. 1095: C6 has “flowing” rather than “flowing into.”]. First they led it over the same Ruovora [Note: Col. 1095: the witnesses preserve numerous variant spellings of the name] through stone arches [Col. 1096A] [Note: Col. 1095: 2 and C have *lapideis*, “of stone”; 1b corrects *lapides* to *lapideis*, while all the other manuscripts examined read *lapides*.], then along the sloping sides of mountains and through the depths of valleys [Note: Col. 1095: variants include “different,” “sloping,” and “steep”; 6 omits “sides.”]. They filled the streets of the entire city with living waters [Note: Col. 1096D: This passage concerns another Roman aqueduct, directed toward the amphitheater, whose traces have recently become clearly visible in several places. Wytt.]. Sometimes, swollen by rainwater, these carried all the filth of the streets into the Moselle.

### 4 [Note: Col. 1095: “Then,” in 5a and C.]

Catholdus, a prince, had received by lot the task of bringing in this stream, later called the Ruovora [Note: Col. 1095: one manuscript specifies “the stream named Ruovora,”], and of building the amphitheater at the same time. While he hesitated over how he could lead it such a long distance around so many mountains and valleys, a household servant, taking courage, firmly promised that, if expenses were provided, he would bring it into the city on whatever day his master was to complete the amphitheater.

The master strongly objected and declared that the servant would in no way accomplish this [Note: Col. 1095: one witness has the perfect tense, “he declared”; another has “would complete.”]. At last they ended their dispute on these terms: if, on the appointed day, the servant had failed to fulfill what he had promised, he would be put to death by his master; but if he demonstrated that he had succeeded, the master would likewise be punished by the servant.

The master’s wife had encouraged the servant in this undertaking. She, having repeatedly violated marital fidelity, was committing adultery with him. What more need be said? The work begun was progressing energetically on both sides [Note: Col. 1095: variants include “on both sides,” “of both,” and “both together.”]. Meanwhile the servant was assisted by the opposing interests and expenditures of the married couple: the husband was awaiting the servant’s death as his own life, while the woman was awaiting her husband’s death as the life of her rival [Note: Col. 1095: the final word is absent in 6; the phrase is supplemented in 3b.].

On the appointed day the amphitheater and the aqueduct were finished. But because, through the craftsman’s ignorance, the aqueduct was blocked everywhere [Note: Col. 1095: 1 has *ductus*, “the duct”; 1b has *obstructus*, “blocked”; the reading is materially uncertain], and because it admitted no openings for air [Col. 1096C] [Note: Col. 1095: “in itself” is absent in 3a, 5, and 6], the obstructed waters did not reach their intended destinations [Note: Col. 1095: 1b adds “places.”].

The incestuous woman, seeing that the servant was anxious about this matter [Note: Col. 1095: 1b reads “seeing him anxious,”], hid him beneath the bed on the preceding night [Col. 1097A] [Note: Col. 1095: 1b has “the preceding day,”], where she and her husband discussed the same matter [Note: Col. 1097: some witnesses omit “matter.”].

“Come now,” said the husband, “our servant, who boasted so arrogantly—how cast down and humiliated he is! Yet I know by what means he could quickly help himself.”

The woman then approached her husband, asked him to disclose the method, promised to keep silent, enticed and persuaded him. At last she received this answer from him:

“If,” he said, “in certain places separated from one another by the length of a stone’s throw [Note: Col. 1097: this phrase is absent in 1, 2, 3, 4?, 5, and 6], a small hole were to break into the aqueduct, the water would immediately resume its course.”

Having eagerly taken in this information, shortly afterward, when her husband had fallen asleep [Note: Col. 1097: variants read “after secretly putting her husband to sleep,” “after he had fallen asleep,” or “after her master had been secretly lulled to sleep”], the servant secretly went out. He summoned workmen and very quickly completed what he had been taught; at the same time he brought the water into the city [Note: Col. 1097: this phrase is absent in 5c.].

When Catholdus learned of this in the morning [Col. 1097B] [Note: Col. 1097: “in the morning” is absent in 2, 3, 4?, 5, and 6; B and C preserve it], while the servant shouted, “Master, here is the water!”, he wished to forestall the disgrace of a servile sword at his throat [Note: Col. 1097: 1b reads “the disgrace of the sword”; the wording is otherwise variant]. He pronounced a deadly curse upon his criminal wife, seized her, and hurled her from the amphitheater. He gave the place the everlasting name of Catholdus’s Solarium [Note: Col. 1097: C3 has “for all eternity.”] [Note: Col. 1097C: The Roman amphitheater, and especially its underground passage leading to the arena or enclosure, is called by the local population today *Cas-Keller* (*Caiicella*). Wyttenbach cites Wilthemi, who derives this name from the French word *kaio* or *caio*, “I enclose” or “restrain,” because wild animals were confined there in their enclosures.].

### 5 [Note: Col. 1097: Chapter VI, Leibniz]

Thus the city was not only strongly fortified by human labor, but also naturally difficult and narrow of access, with rivers, forests, and steep mountains opening only a difficult passage [Note: Col. 1097: “difficult” is absent in C3], and it was exceedingly well fortified by the mountains Jure [Note: Col. 1097: the witnesses variously read *Jure*, *Jurano*, and *Jure et Jurano*] and Cebenna. One of these contained a castle built above it for the city’s protection [Note: Col. 1097: some witnesses read “placed beneath.”].

As time passed, and as their wars prospered, they defeated and subjected the neighboring peoples and cities on every side. Among these they subjugated five highly distinguished cities situated on the bank of the Rhine [Col. 1097C] [Note: Col. 1097: B6 omits “on the Rhine”], namely Basel, Strasbourg, Wangia [Note: Col. 1097C: *Wangiones*, that is, Worms.], Mainz [Note: Col. 1097: some manuscripts have *Moguntia*, “Mainz”], and Cologne, together with their peoples [Note: Col. 1097: omitted in B2]. From them they began annually to receive a very large tribute [Col. 1098A] and, through it, to rule far and wide [Note: Col. 1098C: In manuscript 6d the following verses occur at the end:

> Trier, adorned with countless triumphs of war,  
> Had subjected five strong cities and their peoples;  
> From them it was accustomed to extract an immense tribute,  
> By which it began to grow exceedingly wealthy and to rule.]

### 6 [Note: Col. 1097: Chapter VII, Leibniz]

After many years, these five cities, wishing to claim their own liberty, rebelled and refused to pay the tribute owed for thirty continuous years. But hail coming from heaven devastated them, causing the greatest loss to their fields and vineyards [Note: Col. 1097: some manuscripts have the masculine *eos*, “them,” rather than the feminine *eas*; another has “laid waste.”].

From this there arose great rumor and fear among those citizens, who supposed that this storm of hail had been inflicted upon them by the gods of the Treberi [Note: Col. 1097: the witnesses vary between *Treberorum* and *Trevirorum*] because they had withheld the tribute [Note: Col. 1097: absent in 3, 5, and 6]. Therefore, after taking counsel, they brought to Trier the tribute collected for thirty years [Note: Col. 1097: absent in 2] and promised faithfully that thereafter they would pay it every year [Note: Col. 1097: variants include “each year,” “every year,” and “in all years.”].

Then the Treberenses erected a statue of precious marble [Note: Col. 1097: 6 specifies “of precious marble”], and upon it they placed Jupiter, holding in his hand a golden dish two feet wide, inscribed with these words [Note: Col. 1097: *caraxatam* means “marked,” “engraved,” or “inscribed”; variants read “holding a golden dish”]:

> To Jupiter the Avenger: because the tribute of the five cities of the Rhine was withheld for three decades, but was extorted by heavenly fire and terror, an appeasing holocaust.

Likewise:

> The disk, unmixed with fire, burns incense.

This had been made by mechanical art so that, when incense or any other fragrant substance was placed in the dish, it would immediately emit a burning, fragrant smoke without fire [Note: Col. 1097: one manuscript has “without delay”], while the substance itself was not diminished in any way [Note: Col. 1097: one witness omits “in any way”; another reads “equipped” rather than “diminished.”].

In the city of Lingones, to which they had extended their power [Note: Col. 1097: one manuscript reads “had erected”], they also had the following words written on a stone above the gate [Note: Col. 1097: B and C say that the inscription was still legible]:

> Thus far extend the laws of the Treberi.

They entered into a treaty and friendship with the Remenses [Note: Col. 1097: C adds “also”]. For this reason the Remenses built a gate and called it the Treberic Gate [Note: Col. 1097: variants read “Treviran”; B6 has “they built it and called it.”].

### 7 [Note: Col. 1097: Chapter VIII, Leibniz]

The Treberi and the Remenses are the principal peoples in Gaul [Note: Col. 1097: B and C add “Belgic”; B2 has a form corresponding to “warlike.”]. Gaul is divided into three parts [Note: Col. 1097: variants read “in threefold fashion” or “into three parts”: Gaul of the long-haired people, Gaul of the breeches, and Gaul of the toga]—Gaul of the long-haired people, Gaul of the breeches, and Gaul of the toga [Col. 1099A] [Note: Col. 1099C: Compare Orosius VI.7.].

Gaul of the long-haired people was later called Belgic Gaul [Note: Col. 1099: “was later called” is supplied by 6; one manuscript omits “Gaul”], after Belgio, the leader of the Treberi [Note: Col. 1099: C has “after the leader of the Treberi.”] [Note: Col. 1099C: The author devised this from the name Belgion, which he had read in Justin.]. From his name the river Belgis [Note: Col. 1099: B says “a certain river which …”; B and C omit the words from “which” through “Olevia”] is called the Olevia by another name [Note: Col. 1099C: The river is called Belgis below in the text; today it is the Kyll. Compare the passage edited below in the note to chapter 16.].

Together with Belgio, a very large part of the Gauls crossed into Greece in the following manner [Note: Col. 1099C: What follows is taken from Justin XXIV.4 and following, and XX.5, etc.] (Justin XXIV.4; XX.5; XXIV.4–5; XXV.2).

Since the Gauls had such an abundance of people that the lands which had produced them could not contain them [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript has “the land that had produced them could not contain them”], they sent out three hundred thousand men to seek new settlements. Some of these settled in Italy [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript has the accusative *Italiam*, “Italy”], expelled the Etruscans from their own territories [Note: Col. 1099: omitted in 5b], and founded these cities: Milan, Rimini [Note: Col. 1100C: Justin omits Rimini], Como [Note: Col. 1099: C has a variant form], Brescia [Note: Col. 1099: the witnesses preserve variant forms of the name], Verona, Bergamo, Trent, and Vicenza.

Another group, with birds as guides—for the Gauls excelled other peoples in the practice of augury [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript has the spelling *augurandi*, “of augury,” rather than *auguriandi*]—penetrated the Illyrian gulfs through the slaughter of barbarians and settled in Pannonia. This was a harsh, bold, and warlike people [Note: Col. 1099: 6 omits “and warlike”]. It was the first, after Hercules—to whom that achievement gave admiration for his courage and confidence in his immortality—to cross the unconquered ridges of the Alps and places made impassable by the cold [Note: Col. 1099: variants read “impassable places” or *descendit*, “descended,” rather than “crossed.”]. There, after subduing the Pannonians, they waged various wars with neighboring peoples for many years [Note: Col. 1099: some manuscripts have “for many days.”].

Then, encouraged by success, they divided their forces. Some sought Greece, others Macedonia, laying everything low with the sword. So great was the terror of the Gallic name that even kings, when not attacked, voluntarily purchased peace at a great price [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript reads “at a price” rather than “at great expense.”].

Only Ptolemy, king of Macedonia [Note: Col. 1099: the witnesses preserve several variant spellings of Ptolemy’s name], heard of the Gauls’ arrival without fear. Driven by the furies of parricide [Note: Col. 1099: the witnesses preserve the spelling *parricidorum* as well as *parricidiorum*], he went to meet them with a few disorderly troops [Note: Col. 1099: the conjunction “and” is absent in some manuscripts].

Therefore the Gauls, under their leader Belgio, sent ambassadors to Ptolemy to test the spirit of the Macedonians [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript reads “to test the Macedonians”], offering peace if they wished to buy it. But Ptolemy boasted among his men, despite their fear of war, that the Gauls were seeking peace, and he boasted no less arrogantly to the ambassadors than he did among his enemies [Note: Col. 1099: “friends” is written above “enemies” in one manuscript]. He declared that he would give peace only if they gave their leaders as hostages [Col. 1100A] and surrendered their weapons; for he said that he would trust them only when they were unarmed [Note: Col. 1099: C has “he declares that he will trust them only when disarmed.”].

When the embassy had reported this, the Gauls laughed and shouted on every side that he would soon learn whether they had offered peace in their own interest or in his [Note: Col. 1099: variants read “whether they had offered peace for themselves or for him.”].

After several days, battle was joined. The Macedonians were defeated and slaughtered. Ptolemy, wounded by many blows [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript has *sauciatus*, “wounded,” rather than *saucius*], was captured; his head was cut off, fixed upon a spear [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript specifies “fixed upon the spear”], and carried throughout the entire battle line [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript reads “throughout the day”] to terrify the enemy. Flight saved a few of the Macedonians; the rest were either captured or killed [Note: Col. 1099: B2 adds “were killed.”].

At that time the youth of the Gauls was so extraordinarily numerous that they filled all Asia as though it were some kind of swarm [Note: Col. 1099: B6 omits “as though some swarm”; other witnesses vary in the comparison].
