Finally, neither did the kings of the East wage any war without a Gallic mercenary army, nor did those driven from their kingdoms flee for refuge anywhere but to the Gauls [Note: Col. 1099: B4 adds “then.”].

So great was the terror of the Gallic name and the invincible success of their arms [Col. 1100B] [Note: Col. 1099: the witnesses vary in the order of these words] that they thought neither their majesty could be kept secure nor, once lost, recovered without Gallic valor [Note: Col. 1099: variants use “majesty” rather than “sovereignty” and “they supposed” rather than “they thought.”].

Accordingly, summoned to the aid of the king of Bithynia, they shared the kingdom with him after winning the victory, and they called that region Gallo-Greece, a name compounded from Gauls and Greeks.

There, part of the army of the Treberi was sent back to its homeland, while the part that remained fathered a Gallic people [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript reads “the part which had remained”] and thereafter used two languages, namely Gallic and Greek [Note: Col. 1099: B6 omits “that is.”].

Finally, the Galatians, who originated from the Gallo-Greeks [Note: Col. 1099: one manuscript has “from Gauls and Greeks”], except for the Greek language, which all the East speaks [Note: Col. 1100C: This passage, from “Except for” through “time,” is taken from Jerome’s preface to Book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, in Martianay’s edition of the works, IV, p. 255], possess almost the same particularity of speech as the Treberi [Note: Col. 1099: this phrase is absent in 2, 3a, 5, and 6]. It does not matter if some features have subsequently decayed, since the Africans too have altered the Phoenician language in some respects [Note: Col. 1099: 6 adds “in some part”], and Latin itself changes daily according to regions and time.

### 8 [Note: Col. 1099: Chapter X, Leibniz]

Thus the dominion of the Treberi remained secure and unviolated far and wide until the time of the Romans. Then, even after the Romans had subdued the whole world by arms and prudence [Note: Col. 1099: 6 has “power” rather than “prudence”], they entered into friendship and a very firm treaty with the Treberi [Note: Col. 1099: B and C have the singular “friendship”; B has “with the Treverenses”] and called this city, because of its ancient nobility and the dignity of its citizens, which was in a certain sense equal to their own [Col. 1101A] [Note: Col. 1101: the witnesses vary between “dignity” and “nobility or dignity,”], the Second Rome [Note: Col. 1101C: I do not know where this name is first found, but it is useful to cite some passages older than the *Deeds*. *Life of St. Deicolus* (*Acts of the Saints*, January I, p. 201): “Since great Trier, as the Second Rome, necessarily had great teachers.” *Life of St. Conrad of Trier*, chapter 2, below. *Life of St. Agritius* (*Acts of the Saints*, January I, p. 773): “For when the holy bishop Silvester had reviewed the annals of that city, containing its most ancient deeds, he carefully investigated the excellence of its nobility and its ancient dignity, and learned that, both because of the very firm preeminence of its buildings and because of the nobility of its citizens, it so surpassed all the cities of Gaul and Germany that, rightly, in the judgment of the Romans themselves, it received the name of the Second Rome.” Compare our preface, p. 112; likewise p. 778: “Therefore, just as Trier is called the Second Rome because it once rivaled Rome in the marvelous workmanship of its material structure.” *History of the Martyrs of Trier*, in Hontheim, *Prodr.* I, p. 114: “For this city was called the Second Rome not only because of the equality of its buildings, but also because of the rivalry of its dignities.” Add Berengosus, *On the Discovery of the Holy Cross* III.1 (*Bibliotheca maxima Patrum* XII, p. 306): “The most famous city of Trier … which at that time was richer in wealth and possessions in proportion as it appeared more powerful in arms and soldiers. For although it was strong because of the provinces and cities surrounding it on every side, through the grace of God it was stronger among believers, especially since, through blessed Eucharius and his companions, idolatry was rendered barren and faith fruitful, so that it was not undeservedly called the Second Rome.” The diploma of Frederick I cited by Wyttenbach is, however, spurious. (?)].

At that time the Treberi also began to have Roman rights and laws, which they are known to have preserved down to the present day [Note: Col. 1101: 5b omits “down to the present day”; B has “to have” rather than “to preserve.”] [Note: Col. 1102C: Observe that this passage was written at the beginning of the twelfth century.].

At those same times [Note: Col. 1101: “At that time” is absent in 6] Arimaspes, a senator and governor of the city of Rome, came to Trier, wishing to test personally, by his own judgment, the excellence of the Treberi’s virtue, of which he had often heard.

The Treberi entrusted to him the same office of governor that he had administered in the city of Rome, and they treated the excellent man with such generosity and friendship that he no longer wished to return to his homeland [Note: Col. 1101: one manuscript omits “any longer”; others omit “to return to his homeland.”].

While he was still administering Roman law there, it happened that a certain man named Epten, a defendant, was condemned to death by Arimaspes [Col. 1101B] [Note: Col. 1101: variants include “a defendant named Epten was condemned by him.”]. Fleeing the judgment, he wandered uncertainly and in exile here and there [Note: Col. 1101: one manuscript has “here and there and as an exile”; another omits the conjunction].

When, therefore, through spreading report he learned with what honors Arimaspes flourished among the Treberi [Note: Col. 1101: *armaspes* in 1b and 5 is a spelling of Arimaspes; 5 has *volitante qual.* (“as report flew, with what [honors]”)], he became envious. Desiring to avenge the death that Arimaspes had once decreed for him [Note: Col. 1101: one manuscript reads “which he had decreed for him”], he came to Trier. There, since no one recognized him and therefore no one suspected anything sinister in him [Note: Col. 1101: one manuscript reads “suspecting nothing sinister in him”], after laying many ambushes [Note: Col. 1101: the phrase is absent in 1, 1b, and B; one manuscript has “many” rather than “many ambushes”], he found and killed Arimaspes.

Realizing that he could not escape death from this wound [Note: Col. 1101: some manuscripts omit this clause], Arimaspes asked to be buried at the Gate of Mars and had the following epitaph inscribed above his tomb [Col. 1102A] in honor of the Treberi [Note: Col. 1101: 6 has “in honor of the Treberi”; some witnesses omit “above his tomb.” C1 and C3 add the rubric “Epitaph of Arimaspes”]:

> An exile, Arimaspes, I rest in this citadel of Mars.  
>   
> Belgium was worthy of me; Rome was not.  
>   
> For its good law, nobility of merits, and triumphs,  
> May the gods protect it: nothing is its equal except Rome.  
>   
> I, consul and foremost of the senate, am wounded by Epten, a condemned man [Note: Col. 1101: manuscripts 2, 3, and B2 have “senator” rather than “first senator.”].  
>   
> Rejoice here, you who are mine: thus I deserved to die [Note: Col. 1101: 5 has *gaudere* (“to rejoice”) for *gaudete* (“rejoice”).].

## Complete textual apparatus and editorial notices

This source-ordered register supplies the readings, omissions, corrections, marginal additions, and bibliography not fully verbalized in the running translation. Each retained source form is glossed at its exact lemma, and sigla apply only to the immediately described word, phrase, or margin.

**Chapters III–IV, gates, monuments, and waterworks (Cols. 1093–1096).** The chapter heading is “chapter IV” in Leibniz. *Treberorum* is the reading of 1, 1b, B5, and C1; 2 and almost all later witnesses have *trevirorum*, both meaning “of the Treberi.” 6a/b omit “born from the same people”; 1 writes *printipes* for *principes* (“rulers”); 1b has *trehirenses* and corrects *mucro* to *numero* (“number”). B6 has *quidem* (“indeed”); the northern phrase varies as *ad aquilonarem* (“toward the northern”), *aquilonem* (“the north”), *ad quilonem*, and *aquilonalem*; 1 corrects *quadis* to *quadris* (“squared”), C has *construxerunt* (“built”), and 3a has *sibi* (“for itself”). Witness 6 omits from “remarkable for its own size” through “remarkable”; 3b/5 have *mirabilis* (“remarkable”).

The Porta Nigra itself is absent in 5a; 5c abbreviates “Black Gate and Gate of Mars.” 5c/6 use *appellaverunt* (“they called”); 2 explains Mars as the god of war. Witness 6 inserts at “iron and lead”: “remarkable for its own size and threatening height”; 2 omits the Mars clause here, B5 calls Mars *deus belli* (“god of war”), 6 *deus est belli*, and C1 adds *a Marte* (“from Mars”) in the margin, followed by C2 onward. Witness 2 has *Ii* (“they”) and 5 omits “and”; B6 reads *per eandem portam* (“through that gate”). The field sentence is absent in B, 2, 3, C1; 1/B4/6/C2 have “the field, however”; C omits “and” before breadth. C constructs the eastern gate; 5/6 have *revertebantur* (“were returning”), nearly all witnesses but 6 add *totiusque* (“and of the whole”), 6 has *ex* (“from”) and B4 *ab* (“by”) for *ob* (“because of”).

For the Middle Gate, 2,3,4?,5,6 omit “in the middle of the city”; B6 uses *constituta* (“established”), and the title varies as *nominata est*, *vocata est*, and *nuncupatur*, all “was/is called.” B/C write *forum vero* (“market indeed”) for *forum rerum* (“market of goods”). The western gate’s verb is *excellebat* (“surpassed,” 3/5/6) or *excellunt* (“they surpass,” B2); C abbreviates “the Illustrious Gate.” B6 omits the idol temple; 2 has *ydola statuta* (“set-up idols”); 1 spells *prestigyis* (“magical illusions”). The long note at 1095D is from the *Life of St. Eucharius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 919, and quotes the hundred city idols and demonic deceptions in full.

The Mercury account is editorially identified as a relation of an otherwise unknown Galba Viator and as an alternate recension printed below. 6b has *autem* (“however”); B omits “supreme god”; B/C add *et arbitrum* (“and judge”) after “mediator”; B/C have *magnae* (“great”) for “infinite”; B/C write *quasi volantis* (“as though flying”), and 1 *aerae* for *aere* (“in air”). 5b omits “there was,” 1/1b spell *asscivit*, and B2 has *sibi a ferrum* (“drew the iron to itself”). The verse means: “The iron bearer of the caduceus hangs in the empty air.” Chapter V begins at the Moselle bridge in Leibniz; 3/5a/5b have passive *labefactari* (“be weakened”), and the surviving bridge remains are referred to Wyttenbach, *Historisch-antiquarische Forschung über das Alter der Moselbrücke zu Trier* (1826).

For the city works, C’s forms *tuias* are an uncertain superscript alternative to *statuas* (“statues”); 5 has *thermas, balnea calida* (“baths, hot baths”), 5b *ett.* for *theatra* (“theaters”). C spells Olevia *Olivia*; 2 omits “is called”; the modern place is Olewig. 1b has *urano*, with erased *i*, for Juranus; the editor identifies the eastern mountain, later St Martin’s. 5/6 write *dimidie* (“half”) and B2 *usus* (“use”). The first aqueduct’s remains are cited to Wyttenbach, *Neue Forschungen*, p. 95.

Ruoverias is *roverias* (4/5c), *ruuerias* (5a/b/6), or *rowerias* (B2); Ruovora is *ruoura*, *riuora*, *rowora*, *ruovera*, or *rovera*, all river-name spellings. C6 has *fluentem* (“flowing”) for *influentem* (“flowing into”); the modern Ruwer and Ausonius, *Mosella* 359, are cited. The bridge form varies *ruonoram/rouoram/reuoram/ruueriam/rouuram/rouuoram/ruoveram*; 1b corrects *lapides* (“stones”) to *lapideis* (“of stone”), while most manuscripts retain *lapides*. The route is *diversa* (“different”), *deuera*, or *deuexa* (“sloping”); 6 omits “sides.” The note identifies this as another Roman aqueduct, toward the amphitheater, with recently detected traces.

**Chapters IV–VI, Catholdus and the five cities (Cols. 1095–1098).** Chapter IV’s number is *Tunc* (“then”) in 5a/C; the Ruovora name is explicit in 5. Catholdus is *chatholdus* (3b); *dum* becomes *cum* (“when”) in B2/C1/C3 and is absent in B6; 5b omits “master.” B2/C1/C3 have *dubitari graviter* (“to hesitate seriously”), 5/6 *asseveravit* (“declared”), 5b *perfecturum* (“would complete”). The contest’s forms are *certaminis/certamine*; 2 adds “the servant to this”; the wife’s adultery phrase has *utriusque*, *utrumque*, and corrected *utrimque* (“on both sides”). The spouse forms *conjugis/conjugi/conjugium* retain the relation “of/to the spouse(s)”; C3 omits “her husband’s death as the life of the rival,” 6 omits *conrivalis* (“rival”), restored in 3b’s blank.

At the completion, 1 has *inscia* (“ignorance”) and *ductus* (“duct”), 1b *inscientia/obstructus* (“ignorance/blocked”); 3a/5/6 omit *in se* (“in itself”), and 1b adds *loca* (“places”). 1b supplies “seeing him anxious” and “the preceding day”; B/C omit *ejusdem rei* (“of the same matter”). The husband’s variants are *autem inquit/nunc inquit* (“but/now he said”); 5b omits “quickly,” while 2/6/B2 abbreviate “could help himself.” *Tum/Tunc* mean “then”; *illicit/allicit* mean “entices”; 6 adds “in”; 1/1b transpose “is the throw of a stone”; the entire distance phrase is absent in 1–6. The sleep note distinguishes “after secretly putting him to sleep,” “after he slept,” and “after her master had secretly slept.” 5c omits “to the city”; morning is omitted in 2–6 but B/C retain it; 6 omits “Master”; 1b has *servilis mucronis* (“of a servant’s blade”); C3 *in aeternum* (“for eternity”). The amphitheater note gives the current name *Cas-Keller/Caiicella* and Wyttenbach’s derivation from French *kaio/caio*, “I confine/restrain,” because beasts were confined there.

Chapter VI is Leibniz’s heading. 5a omits *valde* (“strongly”), 5b has *valde murata* (“very walled”), C3 omits *arduum* (“steep/difficult”), 5 *tunc* (“then”), and the path forms are *prebentibus/petentibus/pendentibus*. Jure appears *jurano* (2–6) and corrected *jure/jurano* in C1/C3; B3 has “most fortified by Mount Jure and Jurano and Cebenna.” The castle is *suppositum* (“placed beneath”) in 3b/5a/b. “As time passed” is omitted in 1/1b and 5c (the latter through “on every side”), while 6 has *denique* (“finally”). Five cities is absent B3; “on the Rhine” B6; 1/1b have *positas* (“placed”); Wangia is Wangiones/Worms; Mainz is *Moguntia*; B2 omits “with their peoples.” Manuscript 6d appends the four verses on Trier’s five conquered cities and immense tribute, translated in the running text’s quotation.

**Chapters VII–X, Gallic history and Arimaspes (Cols. 1097–1102).** The five cities’ own freedom is *propriam* in 6a/b; 3b/5/6 read *eos* (“them,” masculine) for cities; 1/5a have *depopulabatur* (“was ravaging”), *Treberorum/Trevirorum* are consistent name spellings, 3/5/6 omit *retentum* (“withheld”), 2 omits “collected,” 3a *quodannis* (“each year”), 5 *quotquot annis* (“every year”), 2 “all years,” and 5a/c/B/C omit *fideliter* (“faithfully”). The Galba Viator dependence is repeated here. The statue is “of precious marble” in 6; 3b/5/6 add *et scutulam* (“and a small dish”), and *scittulam/scutellam* are “small dish.” *Caraxatam/exaratam* means “inscribed,” with 5a/5b/6’s explicit gloss “written/marked with characters.” 1b corrects *vincendi* (“of conquering”) to *vindici* (“avenging”); 5b calls the sacrifice *hoc holocaustum* (“this offering”).

The poem’s *haut* (“not”) through *discus* (“dish”) is another hand in a scraped space in 1; its sense is “A dish not mixed with fires burns incense.” Spelling variants *timiamata/thimiamata/thinniamata/thymiamata* all mean “incense”; B/C add *autem* (“however”), 1/1b say the mechanism was made “by art,” 1 *ture* (“incense”), 6a/b “any fragrant substance,” B2 *sine* (“without”), 5b *mora* (“delay”) for *igne* (“fire”), 1/1b omit “in any respect,” and 5b/6 *munita* (“fortified”) for *minuta* (“diminished”). At Langres the inscription reads “Thus far the rights of the Treberi”; B/C reverse “to which extent,” 5 *erexerant* (“had raised”), and the inscription is still readable in B/C. C adds *etiam* (“also”) with Reims; 6 *fecerunt* (“made”) and the Treberic gate name has the Treveric spelling in 1/1b.

Chapter VIII is Leibniz’s heading; B/C add Belgic Gaul, B2 has *bellica* (“warlike”). The divisions are *trifariam/trifarie* (“threefold”), and B/C explicitly “Gaul is divided threefold”; forms include *bracatam/brachatam* (“trousered”) and B2’s added *togata* (“toga-clad”). Belgic is *bellica* in B2, Belgio *belgeo* in 5a; the editor says this derivation from Belgio is the author’s invention. Belgis is the stream now Kyll; B’s stream words are absent in B/C. The Justin citations are XXIV.4; XX.5; XXIV.4–5; XXV.2, and the later material is taken from Justin. The numbers and places vary: *CCCtorum* (“three hundred”) in 2; Italy’s case form, Como *comium*, Brescia *brycxiam/brixium*, and one lost leaf in 6a after Trident. The Pannonian route has *augurandi* (“divining”), 6 omits “and warlike,” *intractabili* (“impassable,” singular), C3 *descendit* (“descended”), and *ubi/ibi* (“where/there”); 3/5/6 have “days” for years. Ptolemy’s forms (*pholomeus/ptholomeus*), *isque* (“and he”), *parricidorum* (“of parricides”), and the reporting/peace variants are spelling or inflectional forms with the same English senses; 1b has *sauciatus* (“having been wounded”), 2 “fixed on the spear,” and 6b “throughout the day.”

Chapter IX begins at “such was the abundance”; B6 omits the swarm comparison, 3b/5/6 have *velut aquilo* (“like a north wind”), and B4 adds *tum* (“then”). The author resumes after the Gallo-Greek notice; *patria* (3a), *remanserat* (1/1b), and *quod* (2) are forms for homeland/remained/that; B6 omits “that is,” and *Gallis et Grecis* means “Gauls and Greeks.” Jerome’s *Commentary on Galatians*, book II preface, Martianay IV p.255, supplies the language comparison; 2/3a/5/6 omit “particularity of speech,” 3b/5/6 omit “and,” and the African/Phoenician spellings retain their English senses.

Chapter X begins in Leibniz. 6b has *potentia* (“power”) for *prudentia* (“prudence”); B/C singular “friendship” and B *Treverenses*; 3b/5/6 omit “of citizens,” while readings use *dignitate* (“dignity”) or “nobility or dignity.” The extensive editorial note documents the title “Second Rome” from the *Lives* of Deicolus, Conrad, and Agritius, Hontheim’s *History of the Trier Martyrs*, Berengosus III.1, and says Wyttenbach’s purported Frederick I diploma is spurious. 5b omits “to the present day,” B *habere* (“to have”), and the note dates the author to the early twelfth century.

### 9. [Chapter XI, Leibniz]

In the fiftieth year before the Lord’s incarnation, when Julius Caesar had been sent from Rome to Gaul (Caesar II.24; II.16; II.24; V.2–3)—what follows is for the most part copied word for word from Julius Caesar’s *Commentaries*—the Treveri, whose reputation among the Gauls is that of exceptional courage, sent Caesar a contingent of cavalry. But when a battle had to be fought against the Atrebates and the Viromandui, and they saw the Roman camp filled by the multitude of the enemy, the legions hard-pressed and almost surrounded, and the camp-followers, cavalry, Numidian slingers, and others scattered and fleeing in every direction, they despaired of the Romans and wished to hurry home. They reported to their state that the Romans had been driven back and defeated, and that the enemy had seized their camp and baggage.

Then, after taking counsel, they neither came to Caesar’s councils nor wished to obey Roman authority, and they began to incite the Germans across the Rhine against the Romans. For this reason Caesar set out against the territory of the Treveri with four legions and eight hundred cavalry. This state was by far the strongest in all Gaul in cavalry and possessed great forces of infantry; as we have explained above, it touched the Rhine. In it two men were competing for supremacy, Indutiomarus and Cingetorix.

As soon as one of them learned of Caesar’s arrival and that of the legions, he came to him and assured him that he and all his people would remain loyal and would not defect from friendship with the commonwealth; he also showed him what was being done among the Treveri. But Indutiomarus began to assemble cavalry and infantry. Those who because of their age could not bear arms he concealed in the Ardennes Forest, which extends through the middle of the Treveran territory from the Rhine to the beginning of the Remi territory and is of immense size [the forest is the largest in all Gaul]. There he began to prepare for war.

Afterward, when certain leading men of that state, persuaded by Cingetorix’s authority and terrified by the arrival of the Roman army, came to Caesar and began to make requests of him concerning their private affairs, since they could not look after the interests of their state, Indutiomarus, fearing that he would be abandoned by everyone, sent envoys to Caesar. He said that he had therefore been unwilling to leave his people and come to Caesar, so that he might more easily keep the state loyal and prevent the common people, through lack of judgment, from going astray when all the nobility departed. Thus, he said, the state was in his power, and, if Caesar permitted it, he would come to him in the camp and entrust the fortunes of the state to Caesar’s protection.

Although Caesar understood the reason for these statements and what circumstance was deterring Indutiomarus from his planned course, nevertheless, so that he would not be compelled to spend the summer among the Treveri, having made all preparations for the British war, he ordered Indutiomarus to come to him with two hundred hostages. When these had been brought, together with all his sons and relatives whom Caesar had expressly summoned, Caesar consoled and encouraged Indutiomarus to remain loyal.

He achieved nothing, however. After summoning the leading men of the Treveri to him, he reconciled them individually with Cingetorix. Although he understood that this had rightly been done by him, he nevertheless considered it of great importance that Cingetorix’s authority should carry as much weight as possible among his own people, since Caesar had perceived his outstanding goodwill toward himself. Indutiomarus took this very badly. His influence among his own people had been diminished; and, since he had already been hostile toward the Romans, he burned with much greater anger because of this affront.

*(Caesar V.24.)*

When the British war had been completed, and grain had become scarcer for Gaul because of the droughts, Caesar was compelled to quarter the army otherwise than in previous years and to distribute the legions among several states. Of these, he ordered one, under Titus Labienus, to winter on the frontier between the Treveri and the Remi; another, under Titurius Sabinus and Cotta, he sent to winter among the Eburones, most of whose territory lies between the Rhine and the Meuse under the authority of Ambiorix.

Indutiomarus, by sending messengers, persuaded Ambiorix to kill the legions that were wintering with their commanders in his territory (cf. Caesar V.26). When Ambiorix had surrounded and utterly destroyed them by an ambush, Indutiomarus, possessing large forces of armed men and having also been informed of the agreement of all Gaul, decided to destroy Labienus and the legion under his command, which he thought would be easy to do, and then, joining the Eburones and Nervii, to proceed to crush Caesar (cf. Caesar V.37–39; Orosius VI.10).

*(Caesar V.47–49, 51–53, 55–58.)*

When Labienus learned of Sabinus’ death and the slaughter of the cohorts, and all the Treveran forces had assembled against him, he feared that, if he made a departure from winter quarters resembling a flight, he would be unable to withstand the enemy’s attack, especially since he knew that they were elated by their recent victory. He sent Caesar a letter explaining the danger involved in leading the legion out of winter quarters. He fully described what had happened among the Eburones and informed him that all the Treveran cavalry and infantry had encamped three thousand paces from his own camp.

Caesar came with astonishing speed to the Nervii, where the forces of Ambiorix were planning to destroy Cicero, the commander, together with the Second Legion. After putting Ambiorix to flight, Caesar quickly defeated them and sent Labienus the swiftest possible messenger announcing the victory.

When this news reached the Treveri, Indutiomarus, who had decided to attack Labienus’ camp on the following day, fled by night and led all his forces back into Treveran territory. Then, throughout the remainder of the winter, they allowed no opportunity to pass without sending envoys across the Rhine, soliciting the states, promising money, and saying that a large part of the Roman army had been killed and that only a smaller portion remained.

Nevertheless, no German state could be persuaded to cross the Rhine. They said that they had learned by experience in Ariovistus’ war, whether just or unjust, that fortune should no longer be tested.

Disappointed in this hope, Indutiomarus nevertheless began to gather and train forces, obtain horses from neighboring peoples, and attract exiles and condemned men to himself from all Gaul with great rewards. By these means he had already acquired such authority in Gaul that envoys flocked to him from every direction and sought his favor and friendship, both publicly and privately.

When he realized that people were coming to him voluntarily, and when on one side the Senones and Carnutes were urging him on to awareness of the crime, while on the other the Nervii and Atuatuci were preparing war against the Romans, and that he would not lack volunteers if he began to advance from his own territory, he summoned an armed assembly.

This is the Gallic custom at the beginning of war: by common law all adult males are compelled to assemble under arms; whoever among them arrives last is tortured in the sight of the multitude and killed after being subjected to every form of torment.

At this assembly he arranged for Cingetorix, the leader of the opposing faction and his own son-in-law—who, as we showed above, had taken refuge under Caesar’s protection and had not abandoned him—to be judged an enemy, and he confiscated his property.

When these matters had been completed, he declared at the assembly that he had been summoned by the Senones, Carnutes, and several other states of Gaul; that he would make this march through the territory of the Remi and lay waste to their land; and that, before doing so, he would attack Labienus’ camp. He issued orders for what he wished to be done.

Labienus, since he was holding himself in a camp strongly fortified both by the nature of the location and by human construction, feared nothing for himself or the legion; he was thinking only that he should not let any opportunity for successful action pass. Thus, having learned from Cingetorix and his relatives the speech that Indutiomarus had delivered at the assembly, he sent cavalry around to the neighboring states and summoned horsemen from every direction, appointing a fixed day for their assembly.

Meanwhile, almost every day Indutiomarus roamed beneath his camp with all his cavalry, sometimes to reconnoiter the position of the camp, sometimes to converse or to intimidate. The horsemen generally hurled their weapons inside the rampart. Labienus kept his men inside the fortifications and increased the impression that he was afraid by every means available to him.

When Indutiomarus approached each day with increasing contempt, Labienus, having brought into the camp one night the cavalry of all the neighboring states whom he had arranged to summon, kept all his men inside the camp under guard with such care that the matter could in no way be revealed or reported to the Treveri.

Meanwhile, following his daily custom, Indutiomarus approached the camp and spent a large part of the day there. The horsemen hurled weapons and, with great abuse, summoned the Romans to battle. Since the Romans gave no response, when it seemed appropriate, toward evening they departed scattered and dispersed.

Suddenly Labienus sent out all his cavalry through two gates. He gave orders and forbade them—since he saw that the enemy would be terrified and thrown into confusion, as indeed happened—that all should attack one man and that no one should wound another before seeing that man killed. He did not want him to escape by gaining time through the delay caused by the others. He offered great rewards to those who killed him and sent cohorts to support the cavalry.

Fortune approved the man’s plan. When everyone was attacking one man, Indutiomarus was caught in the ford of the river and killed; his head was carried back into the camp. The returning horsemen pursued and killed as many as they could. When this became known, all the assembled forces of the Eburones and Nervii withdrew, and, shortly after this event, Caesar found Gaul more peaceful.

### 10. [Chapter XIV, Leibniz]

*(Caesar VI.2.)*

After Indutiomarus had been killed, power among the Treveri passed to his relatives. They did not cease soliciting the neighboring Germans and promising them money. When they could obtain nothing from the nearest peoples, they tried those farther away. After finding several states willing to join them, they bound one another by oath, exchanged hostages, made guarantees concerning the money, and joined Ambiorix to themselves by alliance and treaty.

*(Caesar VI.3, 5–8, 11.)*

When Caesar learned this, he held a council. All the other states except the Senones and Carnutes came; Caesar, wholly inflamed in mind and spirit for war against the Treveri and Ambiorix, made terms with the Senones and Carnutes after receiving their hostages.

The Menapii bordered the Eburones. Protected by continuous marshes and woods, they alone in Gaul had sent no envoys to Caesar concerning peace. Ambiorix had guest-friendship with them, and through the Treveri he had also entered into friendship with the Germans. Caesar thought these sources of aid must first be taken from Ambiorix and the Treveri before he challenged them directly in war.

Having adopted this plan, he sent the baggage of the whole army to Labienus among the Treveri and ordered two legions to proceed to him; he himself marched against the Menapii with five unencumbered legions. The Menapii assembled no force. Trusting in the protection of the terrain, they fled into the woods and marshes and carried their possessions there too.

Caesar divided his forces with Fabius and Marcus Crassus the quaestor. Bridges were quickly built; the three divisions entered the country, burned buildings and villages, and seized a great number of cattle and people. Compelled by this, the Menapii sent envoys to seek peace. Caesar accepted hostages and declared that he would count them as enemies if they received Ambiorix, the Treveri, or their envoys within their territory. After settling these matters, he left Connius the Atrebatian there with cavalry to keep watch among the Menapii.

Meanwhile, the Treveri, having assembled large forces of infantry and cavalry, were preparing to attack Labienus with the one legion that was wintering in their territory. They were already no more than a two-day journey away from him when they learned that two legions had arrived at Caesar’s command. After pitching their camp fifteen thousand paces away, they decided to await the German auxiliaries.

Labienus, having learned of the enemy’s plan and hoping that their rashness would provide some opportunity for battle, left five cohorts to guard the baggage and set out against the Treveri with twenty-five cohorts and a large body of cavalry. After leaving a distance of one thousand paces, he fortified his camp.

Between them and Labienus there was a river difficult to cross, with steep banks. He himself had no intention of crossing it, nor did he think that the Treveri would cross. The Treveri’s hope of receiving reinforcements increased daily.

Labienus openly declared in council that, since the Germans were said to be approaching, he would not place himself or the fortunes of his army in jeopardy, and that at first light on the following day he would move the camp.

This was quickly reported to the Treveri. Moreover, the character of some men among their numerous cavalry naturally inclined them to favor the Gallic cause. During the night Labienus summoned the military tribunes and the senior officers and explained his plan. To make it easier for the enemy to suspect that he was afraid, he ordered the camp to be moved with greater noise and commotion than the custom of a public military undertaking allowed.

By these measures he made the departure resemble a flight. This too was reported to the Treveri by scouts before dawn. Scarcely had the rear of the column moved beyond the fortifications when the Gauls encouraged one another not to let their expected booty slip from their hands. They said it was pointless to await the Germans when the Romans were terrified, and that it was unworthy of them not to attack with such large forces so small a band, especially one that was fleeing and encumbered.

They did not hesitate to cross the river and engage in battle on unfavorable ground. Labienus suspected that this would happen. To draw them all across the river, he used the same pretence of marching and proceeded calmly.

Then, after sending the baggage a short distance ahead and placing it on a certain hill, he encouraged the soldiers and ordered the standards to be turned toward the Gauls and the battle line to be formed. He sent a few squadrons to guard the baggage and stationed the remaining cavalry on the flanks.

The Romans quickly raised a battle cry and hurled their javelins at the Treveri. When the Treveri saw, contrary to expectation, that those whom they had believed to be fleeing were advancing against them with hostile standards, they could not withstand the attack. At the first encounter they were put to flight and sought the nearest woods.

Labienus pursued them with cavalry, killed a great number, captured many, and a few days later recovered the state. For the Germans who had come as auxiliaries, once they learned of the Treveran flight, returned home. The relatives of Indutiomarus who had been responsible for the revolt accompanied them and withdrew from the state. The supremacy and authority were handed over to Cingetorix, whom we showed had remained loyal from the beginning.

After Caesar came from the Menapii to the Treveri, he wished to cross the Rhine for two reasons. One was that they had sent auxiliaries against him; the other was to prevent Ambiorix from having a refuge among them. Leaving a strong garrison at the bridge, so that no sudden uprising might arise among them, he crossed the Rhine with the remaining forces against the Suebi, who had sent auxiliaries to the Treveri.

## Canonical textual apparatus

The following 337 entries follow the supplied source exactly. Each entry identifies the attached source scope, preserves the printed form and witness sigla, and gives its English force. Spelling-only and inflection-only differences are identified as such rather than turned into invented differences of meaning.

### Column 1101

1. **Scope:** `9`  
   **Printed reading and witnesses:** `c. XI. Leibn.`  
   **English meaning:** Leibniz labels this as Chapter XI.

### Column 1102C

2. **Scope:** `. Anno`  
   **Printed reading and witnesses:** `Quae sequuntur ad verbum plerumque ex Julii Caesaris Commentariis descripta sunt.`  
   **English meaning:** The following text is copied mostly word for word from Julius Caesar's Commentaries.

### Column 1101

   **Printed reading and witnesses:** `deest 1.`  
   **English meaning:** The printed scope is omitted in the witnesses stated in the note (is omitted in 1.).

   **Printed reading and witnesses:** `m. f. 6.`  
   **English meaning:** At 'had been sent,' the apparatus gives MS 6’s word order as *missus fuisset*, ‘had been sent.’

### 11. (CAES. VI, 11.)

It does not seem out of place to set forth something about the customs of the Treveri—or of the Gauls—by which customs, evidently, the treaty they had made with the Romans was in part violated. Among the Treveri there were factions not only in every district and territory, but almost even in individual households, and the leaders of these factions possessed, by their judgment, the highest authority. To their decision and judgment the supreme control of all matters and deliberations reverted, and this institution had been established from ancient times for the following reason: so that no one from the common people would lack assistance against a more powerful person. For no one tolerates his own people being oppressed or ensnared. Otherwise, if they acted differently, they had no authority at all among their own people.

The same arrangement existed throughout all Gaul (cf. V, 3). For this state suffered loss for the reason that Indutiomarus belonged to one faction and Cingetorix to the other. Meanwhile, both in it and throughout Gaul, there were two classes of those men who were counted as possessing some standing and honor. The common people were regarded almost as slaves; they dared nothing on their own and were admitted to no council. Most of them, when they were oppressed by debt, the magnitude of their taxes, or the injustice of the powerful, surrendered themselves into slavery to the nobles. Against these all the rights that masters possess over slaves were exercised.

Of these two classes, one was that of the *druids*, the other that of the knights. The former attended to divine matters, administered public and private sacrifices, and interpreted religious matters. A large number of young men flocked to them for the sake of instruction, and they were held in great honor among them. For they used to decide almost all public and private disputes; if a crime had been committed, if a murder had taken place, or if there was a dispute concerning an inheritance or boundaries, they rendered the decision, and fixed rewards and penalties. If any private person or community did not obey their decree, they excluded them from participation. This penalty was regarded by them as most severe. Those against whom the ban had been pronounced were counted among the impious and criminals. Everyone withdrew from them, avoided their approach and conversation, lest they suffer some disadvantage from association with them. Nor was justice administered to them when they sought it, nor was any honor shared with them.

One man presided over all these druids, possessing the highest authority among them. When he died, whoever among the others excelled in rank succeeded him; or, if several were equal, he was chosen by the vote of the druids. Sometimes they also contended for the chief position by arms.

At a fixed time each year they sat within the territory of the Carnutes, a region regarded as the center of all Gaul, in a consecrated place. From every direction all who had disputes assembled there and obeyed their decrees and judgments. Their discipline was thought to have been discovered in Britain and transferred from there to Gaul. Those who wished to learn the matter more carefully generally went there for the sake of study.

### (CAES. VI, 14–15.)

The druids customarily stayed away from war, and they never paid tribute with the others; they enjoyed exemption from military service and immunity from every obligation. Attracted by such great rewards, many came to the discipline of their own accord, and others were sent by their parents and relatives. Thus some remained in training for twenty years. They did not consider it lawful to commit their teaching to writing, although in almost all other public and private matters they used Greek letters.

They seem to have established this practice for two important reasons: because they did not wish the discipline to be spread among the common people, nor did they want those who were learning to rely on writing and thereby devote less attention to memory—for this happens to most people, so that, relying on the aid of writing, they lose their diligence in learning thoroughly and their memory.

Above all, they wished to persuade people that souls do not perish, but pass from one person to another after death; and they thought that this belief encouraged courage, with the fear of death disregarded. They also discussed and taught the young much concerning the stars and their movements, the size of the universe and the earth, the nature of things, and the power and authority of the gods.

The other class was that of the knights. Whenever there was need, and whenever some war arose, which before Caesar’s arrival usually occurred almost every year, whether they themselves inflicted injuries or repelled injuries inflicted upon them, they were all engaged in war. And in proportion as each was distinguished by birth and wealth, so he had around him the greatest number of *ambacti* and clients. They recognized no other influence or power.

### 12. (CAES. VI, 16–17–20.)

The entire nation of the Gauls was so devoted to religious observances that, for this reason, whenever they were afflicted by more serious illnesses, or were engaged in danger and battles, they either sacrificed human beings as victims or vowed that they would sacrifice themselves. They employed druids as ministers for these sacrifices, because they thought that the power of the immortal gods could not otherwise be appeased unless one human life were repaid for another. They also maintained publicly established sacrifices of this kind.

Some possessed images of enormous size, whose limbs, woven from wickerwork, they filled with living human beings. When these images had been set alight, the people enclosed within them were killed by the flames.

They believed that the punishments of those who had been caught in theft, robbery, or any other offense were more pleasing to the immortal gods. But when a supply of such persons failed, they also resorted to the punishment of the innocent. They especially worshiped the god Mercury. They had very many images of him. They said that he was the inventor of all arts, the guide of roads and journeys, and they believed that he possessed the greatest power for acquiring money and conducting commerce.

After him they worshiped Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva. Concerning these they held the same opinion as the other nations: Apollo drove away diseases; Minerva taught the beginnings of crafts and sacrifices; Jupiter held the heavenly command; and Mars ruled wars.

When they were about to fight a battle, they generally vowed to this god the things they had taken in war, and they sacrificed the captured animals that had survived. They brought all the remaining goods together in one place. In many communities it was formerly possible to see heaps of these objects, constructed in consecrated places, and still possible today. Nor did it often happen that, with religion disregarded, anyone dared either to conceal what had been captured or to remove what had been deposited. The most severe punishment, accompanied by torture, had been established there for such offenses.

The Treveri, like all the Gauls, declared that they were descended from Father Dis and said that this had been handed down by the druids. For this reason they measured every period of time not by the number of days but by nights; and they observed birthdays and the beginnings of months and years in such a way that the day followed the night.

In the other arrangements of life they differed from the other nations chiefly in this: they did not allow their children to come openly before them until they had grown up sufficiently to be able to undertake military service. They considered it disgraceful for a son of childish age to stand in public in his father’s sight.

The husbands shared with their wives, on the basis of an assessed valuation, as much property from their own possessions as they had received from their wives in the name of a dowry. An account was kept jointly of all this money, and the profits were preserved, so that whichever partner survived the other would receive the share of both together with the profits of the preceding period.

The husbands possessed power of life and death over their wives just as over their children. When the head of a household born into a more distinguished position died, his relatives assembled; and, if there was suspicion concerning the death, they conducted an inquiry into the wives in the manner of slaves. If the matter was established, they killed them after torturing them with fire and every kind of torment.

The funerals of the Gauls, in proportion to their culture, were magnificent and costly. They placed in the grave everything they thought had been dear to the deceased while alive, including animals. Until shortly before our own memory, slaves and clients whom it was clear the deceased had loved were also burned with him after the proper rites had been completed.

They also had this established as sacred by their laws: if they learned anything from neighboring peoples by rumor concerning public affairs, they were to report it to the magistrate and not communicate it to anyone else. For it was often discovered that rash and ignorant people were terrified by false rumors, driven to crime, and led to take counsel concerning matters of the highest importance.

The magistrates concealed what seemed appropriate to conceal, but disclosed to the multitude what they had judged useful. It was not permitted to speak about public affairs except in a council.

### 13.

Therefore Caesar, as we said above, granted Cingetorix the chief authority among the Treveri, and granted the community its former liberty.

He himself reduced all Gaul—which is enclosed by the Pyrenean range, the Alps, and Mount Gebenna, which lies to the west of the city of the Treveri, and by the rivers Rhine and Rhône—into the form of a province and imposed upon it the name of tribute; it extends around a circuit of 3,200,000 paces. Having thus pacified all Gaul, excepting, as stated, the community of the Treveri because of its very ancient authority and Cingetorix’s outstanding loyalty, he decided to return to Rome.

But when he realized that Pompey and the Senate were denying him a triumph out of envy, he returned to Gaul, enrolled the Germans and Gauls in his alliance, and received large auxiliary forces; the Treveri likewise provided him with support.

The Gauls welcomed this conduct of the war, evidently rejoicing that the war had been brought to Rome, from which it had earlier been inflicted upon them by Caesar. Relying on this multitude, Caesar expelled Pompey and the Senate from Rome, later forced Pompey to his death, and alone gained possession of the Roman kingdom. After several years he died, killed by the senators.

Octavianus succeeded him, his sister’s grandson. He sent his stepchildren Claudius Tiberius Nero and Drusus to Gaul to pacify the rebellious Gauls. This is Tiberius, who ruled after Augustus.

Accordingly, he fought against the Gauls with Drusus at the Rhine, in a place called Bingis. In this engagement Drusus was killed. After the great slaughter of Drusus’s army, Tiberius finally won a most bloody victory. All the forces of the Treveri fell in that battle; the Gauls were destroyed to extinction.

Drusus was carried back to Mogontiacum and was buried there.

In the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus Octavianus, in which that same Caesar had established the firmest and truest peace by God’s ordering, Christ was born. This peace served his coming, and at his birth the rejoicing angels sang in the hearing of the people:

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.

When Caesar died, Tiberius succeeded him. In the fifteenth year of his reign, Christ, already thirty years old, was baptized by John.

Then he chose twelve apostles, and afterward appointed seventy-two disciples for their assistance. After our Lord had suffered, died, and been buried, had risen from the dead, and had ascended into heaven, the most blessed apostle Peter founded at Antioch the first church in the confession of the Christian name, upon the most solid rock. He also enlightened Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and Bithynia with the word of preaching.

### 14. Anno

#### THE HISTORY OF THE TREVERI BEGINS

Accordingly, when the most blessed Peter, appointed by the Lord as prince of the apostles and universal shepherd of the Church, had first founded at Antioch the catholic Church through the faith that is in God, and had governed it for approximately seven continuous years, he resolved to bring the standard of that same faith, through pastoral prudence, to the city which, just as in paganism, so also in Christianity, had obtained the primacy of the whole world through the merits, evidently, of blessed Peter.

For this purpose, in the fourth year of the reign of the emperor Claudius, as we have learned from historians, he went there. With the Lord granting signs and miracles, and with no small harvest of peoples acquired through the word of sacred preaching, he repeatedly lamented that cities and nations everywhere were devoted to the worship of demons—not, one might say, gods. Therefore, as can be believed without any ambiguity, he repeatedly appealed to the Lord in prayer that he would provide heavenly growth for his new plantation, namely, that he would send workers into his harvest.

At last, after reaching a salutary decision, he sent the blessed Eucharius, his fellow disciple, who had followed Peter in holiness from Jerusalem all the way to Rome and who, as his name indicates, was a Greek, raised to the dignity of the episcopate, for this work. He joined to him as fellow-workers in the word men of proven holiness from among his disciples, whom he had begotten as sons of God through his Gospel, so that they might rescue the people from the service of the devil and persuade them to turn to their Creator through sacred instruction: namely, the blessed Valerius and Maternus, Synicius, Mansuetus, Clement, Felix, Memmius, and many others.

He promoted Eucharius, Clement, Mansuetus, Synicius, and Memmius to the dignity of the episcopate in several cities of Gaul, to preach the word of God. He appointed some of the others to the office of deacon or subdeacon.

Nevertheless, over all these men he placed the blessed Eucharius—something which, as we know, was not said without the muttering of envy—in a ministry more extensive and in a privilege of dignity greater than theirs. For, as we have received by tradition from our elders, Eucharius had received from the Lord himself, while he was dwelling in the flesh, the first elements of the sacred faith together with Peter, since he was with him at that most sacred supper at which the Lord entrusted his disciples with the celebration of the precious mysteries of his body and blood. He also deserved, together with the apostles, to see with blessed vision the Lord rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, and received the Holy Spirit and the tongues of all nations in the appearance of fire.

All these holy fathers went to the peoples of Gaul to win them for God through the word of salvation, proceeding along the right way and preaching the teaching to everyone. Then Clement went with Felix to the Mediomatrici, Mansuetus to Toul, Synicius to Reims, Memmius to Châlons, and the others to the places preordained for them by God. The word of God prospered in their hands.

The blessed Eucharius, however, stopped with his deacon, namely Valerius, at Elegia, a large village in the province of Gaul, overwhelmed by the very grave illness of his fellow soldier Maternus. As this illness grew more severe, Maternus gave up his spirit; and the following account shows that this happened for the salvation of many.

After they had committed him to the earth, the holy men, piously mourning his burial, hurried back to Rome and reported to their aforesaid master, the blessed Peter, what had happened on the journey. They added that they had come among a stiff-necked people, and that they would accomplish little in converting it unless the power of our Lord Jesus Christ were manifested through the resurrection of Maternus.

The blessed Peter consoled them and said:

> Do not mourn, my dearest sons, because our Lord God has provided the death of your brother for the life of many. Trust in the Lord and do not despair; for divine mercy will be present to console you in your sorrow.

And he gave Eucharius the staff with which he supported his aged limbs, saying:

> Retrace without hesitation the road by which you came, and carry this staff of mine with you. When you approach the place of the tomb, place the staff upon the excavated body and say: “Maternus, arise in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

After receiving their master’s blessing, they hurried back to Elegia with confidence.

When they arrived there and approached the tomb, a great crowd also came together with them by God’s will, wishing to see what would happen. Eucharius, presuming nothing upon himself but rather commending the authority of his master, first offered a prayer and then said:

> Brother Maternus, my master, the apostle Peter, has commanded you to rise from death in the name of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and to bear witness with us to your Creator before this people gathered around you.

And he, as though awakening from a sweet sleep, rose alive and sound in mind at the name of Christ. He had already lain in the tomb for forty days.

When they saw this miracle, not only all who were present, but also many who lived far away and to whom the report had been carried, renounced their idols at that very hour. They began to flock to the saints of God and to ask them to give them knowledge of the faith of Christ and baptism. In a clear voice they confessed that this was the true and awe-inspiring God to be worshiped by every nation, the God whose servants could perform such miracles when his name was invoked.

After receiving the first elements of the faith and the regeneration of baptism, they immediately built in that very place a basilica in honor and memory of the power of our Lord Jesus Christ. They gave it its name from the resurrection that had been celebrated there, recalling both the spiritual resurrection of their souls and the bodily resurrection of Maternus.

When everyone throughout the surrounding region had been strengthened in the confession of the faith, the holy men prepared to carry the word of salvation also to the peoples of other regions. Having commended everyone to the one to whom they had submitted themselves through faith, they departed, sowing the seeds of life along the way. At last, guided by God, they reached Treveris, which had once been a great city, the metropolis of Belgic Gaul.

At this point, with the reader’s indulgence, I would like to pause for a while to recall something about the antiquity and situation of that city, since the sequence of events that took place there, which we are attempting to relate, will show to some extent that this is not irrelevant.

## Source-ordered textual apparatus and editorial notices

The entries below follow the supplied text and retain the printed column anchors. Latin forms are quoted where spelling, inflection, or word order is the substance of the reading; each is accompanied by its English force.

The source’s anchors occur in this order: [Col. 1109], [Col. 1110C], [Col. 1111A], [Col. 1111B], [Col. 1111C], [Col. 1112A], [Col. 1112B], [Col. 1112C], [Col. 1113A], [Col. 1113B], [Col. 1113C], [Col. 1114A], [Col. 1114B], [Col. 1114C], [Col. 1115A], [Col. 1115B], [Col. 1115C], [Col. 1116A], [Col. 1116B], [Col. 1116C], [Col. 1117], [Col. 1118A], [Col. 1118B], [Col. 1118C], [Col. 1119A], [Col. 1119B], [Col. 1119C], [Col. 1119D], [Col. 1120A], [Col. 1120B], and [Col. 1120C]. Repeated anchors within individual notes refer to the same printed columns.

### Section 11 — columns 1109–1112

- At the opening in column 1109, the editor observes that the Treveri are named here by the Treveran writer, not by Caesar; the same notice is printed again after *In Treberis*. For *habuerant* (“they had made [the treaty]”), 3b and 5 read singular *habuerat* (“it/he had made”). For *Treberis* (“among the Treveri”), 1, 1b, and 3b read *treberi*, an inflectional/spelling variant of “Treveri.”
- In “not only in all districts and parts, but almost even in individual houses,” 3b, 5, B, and C omit *sed* (“but”); 6 omits *pene etiam* (“almost even”), while 3b and 5 omit *et* (“even/also”); 2 omits *in singulis domibus* (“in individual houses”). For *eorumque factionum* (“and of their factions”), nearly all manuscripts seen by the editor support the printed form, while 3b, 5, and 6 read feminine *earumque* (“and of those [factions]”).
- For *summam auctoritatem* (“the highest authority”), 5a reads *summa auctoritate* (“with the highest authority”). At “to whose decision and judgment,” 5 has *judicium summaque* (“judgment and the highest …”), a changed construction. For *consiliorumque* (“and deliberations”), 6 reads *judiciorumque* (“and judgments”). At *rediebat* (“reverted/returned”), 1 corrects *rediebat* to *redibat*; 5a corrects plural *rediebant* (“they reverted”) to singular *redibat*; 5c, 6, and C3 read *redibat*; C1 is also cited with the correction.
- The words *idque ejus rei* (“and this, for that reason”) are absent from 2, 3b, 5, 6, B, and C. After *causa antiquitus institutum* (“established from ancient times for this reason”), B and C add *est* (“was”). For *ne quis* (“lest anyone”), 1 and 1b read *quid* (“anything”). In *auxilii egeret* (“should lack assistance”), 2 reads *auxilio* (“with/by assistance”); 1b reads *egerat* (“had lacked”); 2 also has *suo* (“his own”). For passive *circumveniri* (“to be ensnared”), B2 reads active *circumvenire* (“to ensnare”).
- *Neque enim aliter* (“for otherwise”) is absent from 2, 3b, 5, and 6. For *ullam* (“any [authority]”), 5b reads *et illam* (“and that [authority]”). For *habent* (“they have”), 5a, 5b, and 6 read *haberent* (“they would have”), and 5c reads infinitive *habere* (“to have”). At *Haec eadem ratio* (“this same arrangement”), 1b has *ratione in*, giving the sense “in this same arrangement.”
- For *Cingetorix*, 3b, 5, and 6 have the shortened form *cingetor*, as elsewhere. Leibniz begins chapter XVII at *In*. Witness 6 reads *Interea* (“meanwhile”) for *In ea* (“in it”). For *in aliquo numero* (“of some standing”), 2 reads *in aliquo munere* (“in some office”). Witnesses 1 and 1b omit *et honore* (“and honor”). The editor identifies *plebes* (“the common people”) as the reading of 1, 1b, 2, 3b, 5a, and 5b. Witness 5 omits the whole clause from *quae* through *consilio*: “who dared nothing on their own and were admitted to no council”; 6 reads *audiebat* (“heard”) for *audebat* (“dared”).
- At “all the rights that masters [possess] over slaves,” 5b supplies *in* (“over/against”). The manuscripts spell the genitive “of the druids” as follows: *druudum* in 1b; *drudum* consistently in 6 and here also in 3b; 5a corrects *drudum* to *druidum*; 5b has *drudum*; 5c has *drundum* and continues so later; B2 has *driuitum*. B and C add *id est philosophorum* (“that is, of the philosophers”). After “the other [class],” 6 adds *erat* (“was”).
- At “they attended to divine matters,” C1 corrects *rebus de rebus* to *de rebus* (“to matters concerning divine things”); 6 and C3 likewise read *de rebus*. For *ac* (“and”) between public and private sacrifices, 5a and 5c read *et* (“and”). Witness 1 has ablative *religione* (“in/with religion”) for accusative *religionem* (“religion”). At “they were held in great honor among them,” 2 and 6 put *apud eos* (“among them”) before *erant honore* (“were in honor”); C6 reads *Namque* (“for indeed”) for *Nam* (“for”).
- In the list “if a crime … if a killing … if a dispute about inheritance or boundaries,” 6 repeats *si de* (“if concerning”) before the boundary dispute. For *decernebant* (“they decided”), 6a has the misspelling *decernabant*, and 5b reads *determinabant* (“they determined”). For *si qui* (“if anyone”), 2 reads *si quid* (“if anything”). For *privati* (“private persons”), B2 and C read adverbial *privatim* (“privately”). At “did not obey their decree,” 3b, 5, and 6 have plural *obediebant* (“they did not obey”) and continue *iis aditum interdicebant* (“they denied them access”), making explicit the object of the following ban.
- For “this penalty was most severe,” 5c reads *erat gravissima* (“was the most severe”). The whole sentence from *Quibus* through *habebantur*—“those under the ban were counted among the impious and criminals”—is absent from 2, 3b, possibly 4, 5, 6, B, and C. After *ab his omnes* (“everyone from them”), 6b adds *autem* (“however”). For *decedebant* (“withdrew”), 2, 3b, 5, 6, B, and C read *discedebant* (“departed”); C1 corrects *descedebant* to *discedebant*. In 1b the same hand rewrites *aditum* (“approach/access”) without changing its reading. Witness 2 reads *quid excommunicationi* (“some [harm] from excommunication”) for *quid ex communione* (“some [harm] from association”). For *incommodi* (“disadvantage”), 5b has *comodi*, 5c and 6 *commodi* (“advantage”), and 5a corrects to *incommodi*. For passive *communicabatur* (“was shared”), 2 reads active *communicabat* (“shared”).
- At “over all these druids,” 3b reads *drundibus* (“druids”), here and below. In the succession sentence, 1 reads *haut* (“not”) at *aut* (“or”); B2 reads *si autem erant plures pares* (“but if several were equal”). For singular *allegebatur* (“he was chosen”), 1 and 1b have *allegabatur* with the same meaning; 2, 3b, 5a, and 6 read plural *allegebantur* (“they were chosen”); 5b, 5c, B, and C have plural *allegabantur*.
- Witness 5b omits *certo tempore anni* (“at a fixed time of year”). For feminine *media* (“central”), 1b reads neuter *medio* (“in the middle”). For present *habetur* (“is regarded”), 6b reads past *habebatur* (“was regarded”). For *considebant* (“they sat”), 2 and B2 read *consedebant* (“they sat down”). C3 reads *Hucusque* (“thus far”) for *Huc* (“here”). At “they obeyed their decrees,” 2 reads *eorum* (“their”) without *-que*, while 6 adds *et eorum* (“and their”).
- In “the discipline was discovered in Britain,” 6 reads *Disciplina haec* (“this discipline”), and 1 has the spelling *brittannia*; 5b adds *est*, “was discovered”; B and C read present *existimatur* (“is thought”), agreeing with Caesar, for past *existimabatur* (“was thought”). The whole sentence “Those wishing to learn it more carefully generally went there for study” is absent from 2, 3b, possibly 4, 5, and 6.
- At the column 1112 citation of Caesar VI.14–15, 6b reads *Druides bello adesse* (“the druids were present at war”) for *Druides a bello esse [liberi] consuerunt* (“the druids customarily were free from war”); 5a adds *liberi* (“free”) after the phrase, and C1 adds it, followed by C3 and subsequent C witnesses. Witness 5b omits *-que* (“and”) in “and immunity from every obligation.” For *habebant immunitatem* (“they had immunity”), 1b reads *habebantur immunes* (“they were considered exempt”). At “of their own accord,” 2 reads *sponte sua* (“by their own will/person”). Witness 2 omits *esse* (“to be”) in “they did not think it lawful.” At *in reliquis rebus* (“in other matters”), 6 records the abbreviated variant *f. r.*; the source does not expand it, so its English force cannot be recovered more precisely without conjecture.
- The clause “They seem to us to have established this for two important reasons” is absent from 1 and 1b. For *instituisse* (“to have established”), 1 reads *instituere* (“to establish”) and 1b *instruere* (“to instruct/arrange”). For *in vulgum* (“among the common people”), 5, 6, B2, 4, and C use nominative/accusative *vulgus*, an inflectional change. At *disciplinam efferri* (“the discipline to be spread”), 5, 6, B, and C transpose the words; B6 and C6 read *offerri* (“to be offered”) for *efferri* (“to be spread”). Witnesses 5 and 6 omit the words governing the learners in the next clause. For *perdiscendo* (“learning thoroughly”), 1 and 1b read *discendo* (“learning”), and 5 and 6 *perdocendo* (“teaching thoroughly”).
- At “they wished above all to persuade,” 2, 5a–b, 6, B2, B6, and C read passive *persuaderi* (“that people be persuaded”). Witness 5b adds *et* after *sed*, “but also [pass].” In the phrase rendered “this encouraged courage,” 1 reads corrupt *exeputari* and 1b *exceptari* in place of *exercitari* (“to be exercised/encouraged”). Witness 1b has adjectival *sideriis* (“stellar matters”) for *sideribus* (“stars”). Witness 6 reads *de natura rerum* (“concerning the nature of things”) with reversed word order; 5a reads *atque* (“and also”) for *ac* (“and”).
- At the beginning of the knights passage, 5a reads *ad* (“to”) for *atque* (“and”). For *accidit* (“arose”), 6b reads imperfect *accidebat* (“was arising”). Witness 6 omits *fere* (“almost”). For *quotannis* (“every year”), B2 and C3 read *quod annis* (“which in years”), while 2 reads *omnibus annis* (“in all years”). B6 omits *aut ipsi injurias inferrent aut* (“whether they themselves inflicted injuries or”). For *quisque* (“each”), 5a reads *quisquis* (“whoever”). For singular *amplissimus* (“most distinguished”), 2, 5, and 6 read plural *amplissimis*. For the Gallic retainers *ambactos*, 1b reads *abjectos* (“rejected”), and 2, 3b, 5a–b, 6, B, and C read *abactos* (“driven away”). For singular *habebat* (“he had”), 2, 5, and 6 read plural *habebant* (“they had”).

### Section 12 — columns 1111–1114

- For *adeo dedita religionibus* (“so devoted to religious observances”), 1b reads *debita* (“bound/owed”), and 5b omits *adeo* (“so”). At *quo erant affecti* (“when/by which they were afflicted”), 5a reads *quod? q* (“because/which?”), 3b, 5b–c, and 6 read feminine *qua* (“by which”), and C6 reads *quae* (“which”). For plural *in periculis* (“in dangers”), 1b reads singular *in periculo* (“in danger”). Witness 5 reads *atque* (“and”) for *aut* (“or”). C1 adds and then deletes *a* after *vovebant* (“they vowed”).
- The name “druids” in the sacrificial-ministers clause appears as *driodibus* in 5a–b and 6; 3b corrects *driotibus* to *driodibus*. At *nisi* (“unless”), 5a wrote *ne* (“lest”) and later deleted it; 5b has *ubi* (“where”). For *hominis vita* (“a human life”), 5, B, and C reverse the words as *vita hominis*, with the same meaning. In “the divine power of the immortal gods could not otherwise be appeased,” 2, 3b, 5, and 6 reorder the clause while retaining singular *numen* (“divine power”); B and C have plural *numina* (“divine powers”), except B2’s *nomina* (“names”). At “they had publicly established sacrifices,” 5 and 6 transpose *instituta habebant*, “they had [them] established.”
- For *immani* (“enormous”), C3 and 4 have corrupt *inmanu*. Witness 2 omits *simulacra* (“images”); 5 and 6 read *simulacra habebant* (“they possessed images”), while C1 adds *statuebant* (“they set [them] up”), followed by C3. For *contexta* (“woven”), 3b, 5a, and 6 read *contecta* (“covered”); 5b and 5c read *contenta* (“contained”); 1b reads *fluminibus* (“rivers”) for *viminibus* (“wickerwork”). Witness 2 omits *viminibus membra* (“limbs [made] of wickerwork”). For *vivis hominibus* (“with living human beings”), 1 and 1b read *unius hominis* (“of one human being”), while 5b rearranges the phrase to *membra vivis hominibus* (“limbs [filled] with living human beings”).
- Witness 5b omits *quibus* (“when/with these”). For *succensis* (“having been set alight”), 1b reads *succensi* (“having been kindled”), a masculine nominative plural instead of the ablative plural, 5b and 6 corrupt *successis*, and 5a corrects *succenssis* to the printed form. In “the people enclosed by flame were killed,” 1 and 1b read *homines examinabant* (“the people were examined”), 3b, 5, and 6 *exurebantur* (“were burned”), and 1b also has the reordered *homines examinabant*.
- For *forent comprehensi* (“had been caught”), 1 and 1b read infinitive *comprehendi* (“to be caught”). B2 omits “they thought [such punishments] more pleasing to the immortal gods.” For *innocentium* (“of the innocent”), B2 has the nonstandard spelling *innocentum*. In the Mercury sentence, 6c reads *Deinde* (“then”) for *Deum* (“the god”), and 1b omits the text from *Deum* through *maxime* (“the god … especially”). Witness 2 reads *sacrificia* (“sacrifices”) for *simulacra* (“images”), and *verum* (“true”) before “inventor.” Witness 1b has singular *questum* (“profit”) for plural *quaestus* (“profits/acquisition”).
- Witness 1b reads *Nervam* (“Nerva”) for *Minervam* (“Minerva”), here and below. Witness 2 omits *habebant* (“they held”) in “they held the same opinion.” At “Minerva taught *operam* and the beginnings of sacrifices,” nearly all manuscripts seen by the editor read singular *operam* (“work, skill”); B6 has *ad operam* (“toward work”), and C1 corrects to plural/ablative *opera* (“by works” or “works”), followed by C3. Witness 6 reads *imperium celeste* (“heavenly command”) with reversed word order. For *bella regere* (“to rule wars”), 1b reads *bella gerere* (“to wage wars”).
- For *cepissent* (“they had taken”) in the war-vow sentence, 3b, 5b–c, and 6 read *concepissent* (“they had conceived”); 5a corrects to *cepissent*. C1 supplies *capta* (“captured”) before *animalia* (“animals”) and afterward; C3, perhaps 4, has the reversed *capta animalia* (“captured animals”). Witness 2 omits *reliquas res* (“the remaining things”). Witness 5 reads *congregabant* (“assembled”) for *conferebant* (“brought together”).
- In “heaps of these things erected in consecrated places,” witness 2 omits the phrase identified in the apparatus; 3b, 4, 5, and 6 read *cruciatus … consecratis*, producing “tortures/punishments … in consecrated [places].” The words *olim et adhuc* (“formerly and still”) are an addition by the Treveran writer. B and C read present *licet* (“it is possible”), agreeing with Caesar, for *licebat* (“it was possible”). For *Neque* (“nor”), 3b, 5a–b, and 6 read *Namque* (“for indeed”), and 5c *Nam* (“for”). B2 reads *ut sepe* (“as often” or “so that often”) at *saepe* (“often”). Witness 6 reads *gratissimum* (“most welcome/pleasing”) for *gravissimum* (“most severe”) punishment.
- Witness 5 omits *Treberi se* (“the Treveri [said] themselves”). For *sicut omnes Galli* (“like all the Gauls”), 2, 5a, 5c, 6, B2, 4, and C read *et omnes Galli* (“and all the Gauls”). At *ab Dite patre* (“from Father Dis”), 1 and 1b read *patre abdite* (“from the hidden father”), 2 *abdite patre* (“from the hidden father”), 3b, 5, and 6 *abdito patre* (“from a hidden father”); C1 corrects abbreviated *ab. d.* to *a d.*, restoring “from Dis.” Witness 2 has shortened *prognatos* (“born/descended”) for *progeneratos* (“begotten/descended”). “Druids” is *driodibus* in 3b and 5 and *driopibus* (“Dryopes”) in 6. Witness 3b reads *perditum* (“destroyed/lost”) for *proditum* (“handed down”). For plural *dicebant* (“they said”), 1 and 1b read singular passive *dicebatur* (“it was said”). For *eam* (“that [cause]”), 6 reads *hanc* (“this”).
- For *initia* (“beginnings”) of months and years, 6 reads *curricula* (“courses/cycles”); a second hand in 6c writes *curricula* above the line or alternatively restores *initia*. B2 reads passive *observabantur* (“were observed”) for active *observabant* (“they observed”). For *fere* (“chiefly/approximately”), 1b reads *vere* (“truly”). Witness 2 reverses *suos liberos* to *liberos suos* (“their children”).
- For *venire* (“to come”) openly before their fathers, 3b, 5, 6, B2, and C read *ire* (“to go”; 6 is repeated in the printed witness list). For *puerili aetate* (“of childish age”), 2, 3b, 5a, 5c, and 6 read *puerulum* (“a little boy”); 5b has *parvulum aetate* (“a small child in age”) or *puerulum*; B and C read *in puerili [aetate]* (“in childhood”). For active *turpe ducebant* (“they considered it disgraceful”), 1 and 1b read passive *turpe ducebatur* (“it was considered disgraceful”). B and C, with Caesar, read *viri* (“the husbands/men”) for connective *virique* (“and the husbands”).
- C3 omits *quantas pecunias* (“as much money as”). For *ab uxoribus* (“from their wives”), 5 reads singular *uxore* (“from a wife”), while B and C omit the words. For *tanta* (“that much”), 3b, 5, and 6 read feminine plural *tantas*, an agreement change. Witness 2 reverses *suis bonis* to *bonis suis* (“their own goods”). For *conjunctim* (“jointly”), 5a and 5b read *conjunctum* (“joined/as a single whole”), 5c *convictum* (“living together/as a partnership”), and 6 reverses the surrounding words.
- For singular *superavisset* (“whichever life had survived”), 1b reads plural *superavissent* (“they had survived”). Witness 5 reads *utraque* (“both”) for *pars utriusque* (“the share of each/both”). Witnesses 1 and 1b omit *cum fructu* (“with the profit”). For *sicut in liberos* (“just as over their children”), 2 reads *et in liberos* (“and over their children”). Witnesses 1 and 1b read plural *potestates* (“powers”) for singular *potestatem* (“power”).
- For *decessit* (“died”), 5b reads *discessit* (“departed”), and 6 has pluperfect *decessisset* (“had died”) with reordered neighboring words. At “if it was established,” 2, B, and C read *et compertum igne* (“and established by fire”); in C1 a later hand corrects *compertum* to *coopertum* (“covered”); 3b, 5, and 6 read *et comperta igne* (“and discovered by fire,” with feminine agreement). For *igne atque omnibus tormentis* (“with fire and every torment”), 5a and 6 read *igne et* (“with fire and”). Witness 6a–b has masculine/dative *excruciatis* in place of feminine accusative *excruciatas* (“the wives having been tortured”).
- Witnesses 1 and 1b omit *pro cultu* (“in proportion to their culture”) from the funeral sentence. B2 adds *et* before *omnia* (“and everything”). For *fuisse* (“had been [dear]”), 1 and 1b read *esse* (“to be [dear]”). Witness 1b reads *ad* (“to”) for connective *ac* (“and”). Witnesses 2 and 6 omit *paulo* (“a little/shortly”) from “until shortly before our memory.” For *justis* (“the proper rites”), 5 and 6 read *ustis* (“burnings”), while C1 corrects *hustis* to *justis*. For *confectis* (“completed”), 3b and 6 read *consectis* (“cut up”), 5a–b *confectisque* (“and completed”), and 5c *consectisque* (“and cut up”). Witness 5 reads *habebantque* (“and they had”) for *habebant et* (“they also had”).
- The word *sanctum* (“sacred/established”) is *sancctum* in 2, *sanccitum* (“enacted”) in 5a and 6, *sanxitum* in 5c, *xancsitum* in 5b, corrected from a corrupt form to *sanctum* in C1, and *sanctorum* (“of holy persons”) in C3 and 4. For *de re publica* (“concerning public affairs”), 5a and 6 read *de publico* (“concerning the public matter”), and 5b–c *de publica*, an incomplete/inflectional form. Witness 5a reads *ne* (“not/lest”) for *neve* (“and not”). Witness 1b omits *cum alio* (“with another”), while 5b reads *cum aliquo alio* (“with anyone else”). Witness 5 omits *homines* (“people”). Witness 5b reads *aut* (“or”) for *et* (“and”) before “driven to crime.”
- Codex 3b ends at the word *Magistratus* (“the magistrates”). Witness 6c omits the second *quae*, hence “what they judged useful.” For *nisi* (“except”), 6 reads *non nisi* (“only/except”). Witnesses 1, 1b, and 6 omit *loqui* (“to speak”). C1 supplies *non* (“not”) after the line; 1b reads plural *concedebantur* (“were permitted”) for singular *concedebatur* (“it was permitted”).

### Section 13 — columns 1113–1116

- Leibniz begins chapter XVIII at section 13. For *igitur* (“therefore”), 1b reads *vero* (“however”) and 2, 5a–b, and 6 *ergo* (“therefore”). For *sicut supra diximus* (“as we said above”), 2, 5, 6, B, and C read *sicut praediximus* (“as we stated earlier”); the marginal cross-reference is chapter 9. For *Cingetorigi* (“to Cingetorix”), 2 has *cingetori*, a shortened spelling; 1 spells *Trebirorum* (“of the Treveri”) as *trevirorum*. B and C add after the grant of authority: *ob egregiam in se et bene meritam Cingetorigis fidem et societatem*, “on account of Cingetorix’s outstanding loyalty toward him and his well-deserved fidelity and alliance.” Witness 2 has corrupt *perpr.* for *pristinam* (“former”).
- The editor states in column 1115C that the author added the grant of former liberty himself; it is futile to ask from what source he drew the following material, except that he seems to have had Orosius before him. At *omni Gallia* (“all Gaul”), C1 corrects *gallia* to genitive *galliae*, followed by C3.
- B and C add the entire description and provincial settlement: Gaul, bounded by the Pyrenees, Alps, Mount Gebenna, and the Rhine and Rhône, extends 3,200,000 paces in circuit; Caesar reduced it to provincial form and imposed tribute, excepting the Treveri because of their ancient authority and Cingetorix’s loyalty. The editor says the portion through *imposuit* (“imposed”) comes from Suetonius, *Life of Caesar* 25. The Treveran author added “which is west of the city of the Treveri,” in considerable error, placing this famous Gallic mountain in Treveran territory, although chapter 5 attests another mountain of nearly the same name there. Within the addition, C spells *Gebenna* as *cebenna*; B2, 3, C1, and C3 spell *Reno* (“Rhine”) as *rheno*; C1 twice supplies in the margin the abbreviated sequence *c. p. in c. ad* beside *continetur* (“is bounded”), but the source does not expand it and its exact English force is uncertain; C spells *Treberorum* as *trebirorum*. The addition ends with the unexplained abbreviation *et sic R. r. d.* (“and thus R. r. d.”), whose expansion likewise is not supplied.
- For *Romam redire* (“to return to Rome”), B and C read *Romam ire* (“to go to Rome”). For *Pompeio* (“Pompey”), 1b reads *Pontio* (“Pontius”) and 5b the spelling *Pompeo*. For *et senatu* (“and the Senate”), 5a reads *senatuque* (“and the Senate”). Witnesses 1 and 1b omit *sibi* (“to him”) in “a triumph to him”; 6 abbreviates/reorders the phrase *ob invidiam sibi denegari* (“to be denied him out of envy”).
- B2 omits *sibi* (“to himself”) from “enrolled in alliance with himself”; 2, 5, and 6 place it after *in amicitiam* (“in alliance”). B6 omits the span *magna … solacia*: “large auxiliary forces … support.” For *solacia* (“support”), B2, 4, and C read *auxilia* (“auxiliary forces”). For *Grata* (“welcome”), B and C read *gratis* (“freely/gratefully”). Witness 2 omits *bellum* (“the war”) in “the war was brought to Rome.” For *fuit … illatum* (“had been inflicted”), B and C read *fuerat per Caesarem* (“had been [inflicted] by Caesar”) with changed word order.
- The name *Pompeium* (“Pompey”) is *ponpeium* in 1b and *ponpeum* in 5b. For *Romanum regnum* (“the Roman kingdom”), 5a and 6 read *Romanum imperium* (“the Roman empire”). For *aliquot annos* (“several years”), 1b reads *aliquos* (“some”), while 2, 5, 6, B, and C read *aliquantos* (“a considerable number of”). Leibniz begins chapter XIX at *Huic* (“him”). Witness 5 omits *ejus* (“his”) from “his sister’s grandson”; 1 and 1b reverse *ejus ex sorore* to *ex sorore ejus* (“from his sister”). Witness 2 omits *Claudium Tiberium* from the name Claudius Tiberius Nero.
