Witnesses 5, B, and C omit “rebellious … to pacify,” leaving “sent [them] to the Gauls”; 6 reads *ob rebellantes pacandos*, “to pacify them because they were rebelling.”
- For *Bingis*, 5 and 6 read *Binga*, both forms naming the place. Witness 5b reads *cum Gallis* (“with the Gauls”) for *contra Gallos* (“against the Gauls”). Witness 2 adds *et* before *Tiberius* (“and Tiberius”). The people-name *Trebirorum* is *trevirorum* in 1 and *treberorum* in 5, as elsewhere. Witness 6c omits *usque* (“all the way”) from *usque ad internitionem* (“to extinction”).
- B and C add after the destruction: “There, as Ausonius says”—*Mosella* 3–4—“Unhappy Gaul equalled the Latin Cannae, and helpless bands lie unmourned upon the fields.” C1 supplies *infelix* (“unhappy”) after the line, followed by C3 and later witnesses; 6 reads corrupt *inflecteque* for *infletaeque* (“and unmourned”), reorders the words before *jacent* (“lie”), and reads *arvas* for *arva* (“fields”).
- The place-name *Mogonciam* (“Mogontiacum/Mainz”) is *moguntiam* in 2, *mogunciam* in 5a and B6, *magontiam* in 4 and 6, and *magunciam* in 5b. At *relatus est, ibique sepultus* (“was carried back and buried there”), 5b reads *est delatus et ibi est sepultus* (“was carried there and was buried there”). B and C add *est* and the editorial notice: Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius* 7, says Drusus was carried to Rome and Tiberius followed his funeral on foot.
- Leibniz begins chapter XX with *Anno circiter* (“about the year”) at the printed *Igitur* (“therefore”). Witness 5 omits *Augusti* (“of Augustus”); 6, B, and C read *Octaviani* (“of Octavianus”) immediately after “year of the reign.” The printed forty-second year is XLIII (“forty-third”) in 1 and XL (“fortieth”) in 1b. The clause from *quo* through *voluntatis* is from Orosius VI.22. Witness 1 spells *firmissimam* (“firmest”) as *firmissam*. Witnesses 2, 5, 6, B, and C reverse *ordinatione Dei* to *Dei ordinatione* (“by God’s ordering”). B2 reads *adventu* (“at/by the coming”) for dative *adventui* (“served the coming”); 6a corrects to *adventui*. Witness 2 omits *hominibus* (“people”) from “in the hearing of people.”
- In “when Caesar died,” 5b reads *Caesare Augusto* (“when Caesar Augustus [died]”) and 6 *Augusto* (“when Augustus [died]”). The spelling *Tyberius* occurs here in 1 and repeatedly in 1b and 2. The notice “Thus Regino” supports the fifteenth year of Tiberius. Witness 5 reads *annorum triginta* (“thirty years of age”) for *triginta annorum*; 1 and 1b reverse “was baptized by John” to “by John was baptized.”
- Witness C omits everything from *Deinde* (“then”) through *illustravit* (“he enlightened”), the remainder of section 13. For *apostolos* (“apostles”), B2, 3, and 4 read *discipulos* (“disciples”); B6 reads *discipulos in eorum [solacium] elegit*, “he chose disciples for their assistance.” Witness 6 reads LXII (“sixty-two”) for LXXII (“seventy-two”). Compare Orosius at the place already cited. For *Dominus noster* (“our Lord”), 5 and 6 read *Dominus noster Jesus Christus* (“our Lord Jesus Christ”). Witness 1b reads *surrexit* (“rose”) for *resurrexit* (“rose again/from the dead”). For *beatissimus* (“most blessed”), 1 and 1b read *beatus* (“blessed”). The passage from “the most blessed [Peter]” through “enlightened” is copied from the *Life of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 918.
- For *ecclesiam primam* (“the first church”), 5 and 6 read feminine nominative *prima*, an agreement change. Witnesses 1 and 1b reverse *confessione christiani nominis* to *christiani nominis confessione* (“in the confession of the Christian name”). For *super* (“upon”), 6 reads *supra* (“above/upon”). Witness 1b omits *et* (“and”) before Pontus; 5 and 6 read *ac* (“and”). Witnesses 5 and B omit the second *et* before Galatia. In 6a, *asidiam* (“Assyria,” corrupt) is corrected to *asiam* (“Asia”); 6b–c read *asiam*, and B reads *atque* (“and”) in that position. Witness 2 spells *Bithiniam* as *bytiniam*. Witness 5b adds “Explicit”; after one and a half blank pages it continues, “Chronicle of the Archbishops of Trier. In the year of the Lord ….” Witness 6c adds, “Here begins Book II.”

### Section 14 — columns 1116–1120

- The supplied boundary preserves the isolated word “Anno” (“In the year”). The column 1118A note says that B—except manuscript 5, in which both narratives are absent—and C omit chapter 14 and instead read the following fuller history. B2 titles it *Incipit hystoria Treverorum* (“The History of the Treveri begins”). C1 reads, “The first book concerning the deeds of the Treveri is complete, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The second book concerning the deeds of the Treveri begins,” and the later witnesses are generally similar.
- The editor says the writer again appears to follow a more recent and highly fabulous *Life of Saint Eucharius*; compare the editor’s preface, p. 121. C reverses *apostolorum princeps* to *princeps apostolorum* (“prince of the apostles”). C omits *fide, quae in Deum est* (“through the faith which is in God”). B2 omits *est* (“was/has”) from the clause saying Rome obtained universal primacy. For Peter’s arrival in the fourth year of Claudius, compare Regino under that year.
- B2 spells *Synicium* as *sinnicium*. For Memmius compare also the *Life of Saint Memmius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, August II, p. 13; another Life written by Almannus remains unpublished. Leibniz begins chapter XXI at *Verum*. For the story full of fables concerning Eucharius’s instruction by Christ, compare *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 380. At “who also was present,” C1 corrects *qui et* to *quique* (“and who”), followed by C3. C1 supplies after the line the words governing “at that most sacred supper.”
- At Elegia, C6 reads feminine *quae* (“which”) for masculine *qui*. C reads *invalitudine* (“illness”) for *valitudine* in the phrase “overwhelmed by very great illness.” In the return-to-Rome passage, C6 reads *Animos* (“their spirits/minds”) for *Quos* (“whom”); C reads present participle *consolans* (“consoling”) for perfect *consolatus* (“having consoled”). In “his aged limbs,” C reads *sui* for *sua*, an inflectional disagreement. B2 reads *corpore* (“body,” ablative) for *corpori* (“upon the body,” dative) in the command to place the staff on Maternus’s exhumed body.
- In Eucharius’s command at the tomb, C omits *domini nostri* (“our Lord”) from “the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.” In “all these who were present,” C1 supplies *hii* (“these”) above the line; C3 reads *hii omnes* (“all these”), reversing the words. C1 adds *cognitionem fidei Christi* (“knowledge of the faith of Christ”) in the margin. B2 consistently spells *baptisma* (“baptism”) as *babtisma*. C reads *in honore et memoria* (“in honor and memory”) where the printed text has *in honorem et memoriam*, the same phrase with different case. C reads *civitas est* (“is a city”) for *civitas quondam fuit* (“was once a city”). Finally, C omits the whole sentence from *Hoc in loco* through *esse ab re*: the narrator’s statement that he will pause to discuss the city’s antiquity and location because the ensuing events will show that the digression is relevant.

As Gallic history relates [Note: [Col. 1119] Chapter XXII in Leibniz, II, 2. C.]—what history this may be, no one can say unless one understands by it the *Deeds of the Treverans* themselves or their source [Col. 1120D]. For it generally agrees with what precedes in their text, which was mostly written by another Treveran author. Caesar’s commentaries, which I cited above on p. 121, cannot be intended here.]—in the days of Abraham [Note: [Col. 1119] “Abraham,” C.], the patriarch, the most powerful King Ninus, who built the city of Nineveh, concerning whom the prophet Jonah testifies that it was “a great city, a three days’ journey” (Jonah 3:3), fathered by a certain queen of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 1119] “Chaldeans,” C.] a son named Trebeta. To this queen, I say—whether she was still alive I do not know—he took another woman, named Semiramis, as wife. After Ninus’s death, she wished to marry the same Trebeta. When the young man refused to consent to so wicked a deed, she, being of fierce character, attacked him with many stratagems and poisons; finally, after he had been wearied by countless military persecutions, she drove him from the borders of the entire kingdom. He wandered through many parts of the world and, finding no place in which he wished to remain, at last, guided by lot, chose Belgic Gaul.

After exploring it, he came to the place where Treberis [Note: [Col. 1119] “Treveris,” B2.] now stands [Note: [Col. 1121] “Afterward supplied,” C1.], which [Note: [Col. 1121] “Which also,” C.] greatly pleased him as a place for settlement. And rightly so. For it was, as it is now, delightful to behold, with no harmful climatic inconvenience troubling its inhabitants, sufficiently broad in plain, and—as we may put it briefly [Note: [Col. 1121] “In words” added, C.]—filled with every beautiful delight. It was extremely well defended, being surrounded on every side by high mountains like walls and, above them, by wooded country. Beside it, toward the west, at the foot of the mountain, flowed a river called the Moselle, sweet to the taste and healthful for bathing, rich in fish and navigable by large ships. On its western bank a certain little river, as if looking toward the city, flows into it; it is called Belgis [Note: [Col. 1121D] “Kyll.”], from which the whole province received its name.

When that noble young man had settled in this valley and it pleased him to live there, he relied not only on the aid of his own people who had come with him, but also on others who flocked there from different regions—partly because they had heard of the noble birth and mighty deeds of the newcomers, whose accomplishments fame had spread [Note: [Col. 1121] “Of him,” C3.], and partly because of the strength of the place. He began to build a city which, in the course of time, surpassed many cities in honor and dignity [Note: [Col. 1121] “Excelled,” C.], so that it was called the head of all the regions situated in Europe, the third part of the world. In memory of himself, because he had first begun to inhabit it and, when he died, left it to be governed by his son, named Hero, he called it Treberim [Note: [Col. 1121] “Treberim,” B2.], after the name of Trebeta.

That this same city surpassed many cities of all Gaul in strength and subdued their peoples by arms is testified to this day [Note: [Col. 1121] This is absent from C1 and C3.] by the strong fortifications once constructed by the victors in many places belonging to those conquered cities [Note: [Col. 1121] “Triumphant conquerors,” B4? C.], now ancient ruins, which bear on their surfaces this inscription or one similar to it:

> “Thus far extend the rights of the Treverans” [Note: [Col. 1121] “Treberans,” B2.].

For, as they say, it was the custom of conquerors that, if they captured a people or region by arms, they immediately built fortified towns within its boundaries for the protection of their rule and compelled the people to serve under their laws [Note: [Col. 1121] “Their laws,” B2.], together with their traditional obligations.

Thus [Note: [Col. 1121] Chapter XXIII, Leibniz.] that royal city grew, exalted in every excellence, as has been said, surrounded by walls and a ditch, and defended by high, strong towers. It had four public gates, facing the four regions of the world. The first, facing north, was constructed from square stones joined with marvelous skill—not by mortar, but by iron—and was called the Black Gate, or the Gate of Mars. It was called the Gate of Mars because the men of the city went out through it when they were setting forth for war; Black, either because, when the outcome of war had not favored them, they returned sadly through it, or because the dead of the city were carried out through it for burial.

The second, toward the east, was called the White Gate, because when the citizens returned victorious from war, they were solemnly received there by their fellow citizens with praises and triumphs, riding in on white oxen [Note: [Col. 1121] “Oxen,” B2.].

The third, facing south, was called the Middle Gate, because through it a road opened for those entering through the middle of the city [Note: [Col. 1121] “For this reason,” C.].

The fourth, situated toward the setting of the sun, was made of square stones in a splendid work. At its exits was a station or harbor for ships coming from either direction along the channel of the aforesaid river. To illuminate these ships at night, the gate itself was adorned, as though with the sun, moon, and stars, with gold and precious stones skillfully fashioned. Hence, I say, because of the splendor of its workmanship, it was called the Illustrious Gate [Note: [Col. 1121] The words “by name” are lacking after an apparent correction from *ex* to *est* in C1; the text from this point to here is lacking in C6.].

I would like to continue mentioning further details concerning either the beauty or the strength of this same city, if you, reader, do not mind listening. This city was much older in foundation than Rome. When, as has been said, it had been fortified on every side with walls, gates, and towers, all its inhabitants—people and princes alike—turned their minds to its adornment.

They built a temple in the western part, most carefully decorated inside and outside with gold, dedicating it to the divine powers of many idols. Anyone who still examines their images carefully will find them inscribed there or fixed to the wall [Note: [Col. 1121] “Would find,” B2.]. Because it had been consecrated to countless demons, the common people say that it was called the Hundred-Shrine (*centifanum*).

In its vestibule, a notable arch of squared stone rose. It had an iron image of Mercury hanging in the air—marvelous to relate—while separately there stood a marble Jupiter holding a golden dish in his hands. Incense placed in it gave off a fragrance to the nostrils of those standing nearby as though it had been thrown onto a fire, yet it was not burned.

So that no one may refuse to believe this when it is reported in our words, as though we had invented it, let him hear instead Galba Viator bearing witness to this very thing in these words to Eucinius the sophist, among the other astonishing things he had seen and heard. For he says:

> “Hear also something at which you may marvel. Treberis is a noble city of Gaul, where a certain Senetio, whose hospitality I enjoyed for twelve days, showed me in the suburb of the city an iron image of flying Mercury, of great weight, hanging in the air [Note: [Col. 1121] “Image,” C.]. The same host showed me that there was a magnet above it in the vault and another in the pavement. Their natural force, directly opposite one another, drew the iron toward them, and thus the huge iron object remained suspended in the air, as though hesitating [Note: [Col. 1121] The words “drew the iron toward them, and thus” are absent from B2 and B4, as I believe, and also from other manuscripts of this recension; C1 corrected the text to the form printed here, which C3 and the remaining manuscripts followed.]. I also saw in the same city a Jupiter made of enormous and precious marble, holding a golden dish two feet wide. On it was inscribed:
>
> > “To Jupiter the Avenger of the Treverans [Note: [Col. 1121] “Treberans,” B2.], from the tribute of five cities of the Rhine, withheld for three decades but extorted by lightning and heavenly terror.”
>
> “It had been made by mechanical art. If incense is placed in it as though on burning coals, it gives off a fragrance, yet does not diminish. I proved that this was so.”

When [Note: [Col. 1121] Chapter III, C; Chapter XXIV, Leibniz.] the fame of this most celebrated city had been widely spread everywhere in its own age [Col. 1123A], because it was said to be unconquerable through the courage of its inhabitants and unequaled in lawful right, nobility of achievements, and triumphs—long after Rome had been founded—and while powerful men ruled there, one of their nobles, named Arimaspes, the first consul and head of the senate, went there to see whether what fame had spread about it was true.

When he saw it, he did not return to Rome. Instead, after he had been granted a place there in the council of the great men, he established a council according to Roman customs, with Roman dress, offices, and various names of dignities. That this does not differ from the truth is sufficiently demonstrated by the images and inscriptions found throughout almost the entire city, carved in stone to preserve the memory of consuls, senators, patricians, and other dignitaries and of their names and deeds, buried beneath hills, pyramids, or heaps of stones [Col. 1123B]. The ruins of the theater that still survive also support this claim; as we have said, it was built according to Roman practice for the performance of circus games and athletic exercises.

Thus [Note: [Col. 1123] Chapter IV, C; Chapter XXV, Leibniz.] that Treveran city [Note: [Col. 1123] “Treveran,” C., and below] had risen in the manner we have described. Later, when the Romans resolved to subject the whole earth to their empire and had conquered all the regions situated nearby and far away, this city alone, relying too greatly on its own strength, dared to resist with its dependencies—namely all Gaul, France, and Germany [Note: [Col. 1123] Apparently corrected from *praesumpsit* (“dared”) to *praesumpserit* (“has dared”) in C1, and so in C3.]—at the time when Julius, called Caesar among the Romans, was administering the office of consul [Note: [Col. 1123] “Consulate,” B2.] and had simultaneously received from the senate the order to lead an army against the Gauls and compel them to obey the Romans.

He therefore came and besieged Treberim, the capital of the province of Gaul, whose exceptional reputation for strength, as we have already stated, had spread throughout the whole world. There he labored in vain at warfare for almost ten years. For as long as the inhabitants preserved unanimity and harmony among themselves, they could not be defeated by their enemies; but as soon as they abandoned these, they did not endure.

At that time, through a great misfortune, two nobles who ruled the city, Induciomarus and Cingetorix—one possessing the dignity of a patrician, the other that of consul—contended with each other over primacy, each asking which of them seemed the greater. While such dissension was taking place between them, Cingetorix secretly went outside and approached Julius’s camp. He promised that he would surrender the city if the principate were granted to him. When this had been confirmed at his request, he arranged for the enemy to gain entrance. Thus the pride of that royal city became to a great extent crushed [Note: [Col. 1123] “Became,” C.].

But what benefit is there in recalling the secular glory and royal nobility of that city? It is more useful, and brings more spiritual joy, if we undertake to describe the condition into which it was advanced by the grace of God to a better life [Note: [Col. 1123] Absent in B2.].

But [Note: [Col. 1115] Absent from 2, 4, 5, and 6; “forty-sixth,” 1 and 1b.] in the forty-seventh year of the Lord’s incarnation and the fourth year of the reign of Claudius Caesar [Note: [Col. 1116C] Compare Regino for this year.], by the ordering of divine providence [Note: [Col. 1116C] “Divine providence … ruled,” from the *Life of Eucharius*, same place.], he entered Rome and preached the faith that brings salvation to all believers with the utmost firmness [Note: [Col. 1115] “Blessed Peter” added by 5c.], confirming it with exceedingly powerful signs [Col. 1116C] [Note: [Col. 1115] “Powerful signs,” 5 and 6.] and virtues [Note: [Col. 1115] “And,” 1 and 1b.]. He governed the pontificate of that city with the greatest diligence for twenty-five years.

When the Church of the Roman city had thus been founded and built upon the firmest rock, which is Christ, by the faithful man named Peter [Note: [Col. 1117] “Upon,” 5 and 6a–b; “who,” 6.], and when the shoots of life were already budding throughout all Italy [Note: [Col. 1117] *Pullurarent* is corrected to *pulularent*, “were budding,” in 1, g, v, p, 2, 5, and 6.], he was finally instructed by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1117C] “Finally … ordained,” from the *Life*, same place.] to undertake to bring the word of salvation to Germany and Gaul [Note: [Col. 1117] “Gaul and Germany,” 6.].

For this work there were chosen from among his disciples men of great virtues: Eucharius, who was third in the order of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1117] “Sixty-two,” 6. “Of the Lord” is absent from 5b and from 2; the final words are absent.], Valerius, and Maternus. He immediately ordained Eucharius bishop, Valerius deacon, and Maternus subdeacon. He then sent them to the work of preaching, together with other suitable men: Clement, Mansuetus, Memmius [Note: [Col. 1117] “Caelestem,” 1b; “Mennium,” 2 and 5a; “Innocentium,” 5c.] and many others [Note: [Col. 1117] “And” is absent from 5b.].

After receiving their teacher’s blessing [Note: [Col. 1117] “From the master,” 5.], they hurried to Gaul [Col. 1117B] [Note: [Col. 1117] “They hastened,” 2, 5, and 6.] and brought many people to the steadfastness of the sacred faith through the power of signs.

When they had reached Elegia in Alsace [Note: [Col. 1117] “Ingelheim,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 1117C] The *Life* also names this place. Browerus, *Annales Treverorum*, p. 143: “A very ancient … village of the Triboci is still shown here on the bank of the river Elli or Illa, noteworthy both for Roman antiquity and for Christian religion.” Perhaps Illkirch? Compare *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 382.], and were preaching the word of truth there to the people [Note: [Col. 1117] “To the people,” 5 and 6.], one of them, named Maternus, began to fall seriously ill. As the distress of the illness increased [Note: [Col. 1117] “As the distress of the illness,” 2; “with the illness” in 5.], he died after not many days [Note: [Col. 1117] “Not afterward,” 6.].

Saint Eucharius buried his body in the earth with sighing and mourning. Taking Valerius with him, he quickly returned to Rome [Note: [Col. 1117] “Valerius” is absent in 1? “Quickly” is absent from 2, 5, 6, and B.] and tearfully recounted to his teacher, in order, everything that had happened to him on the journey [Note: [Col. 1117] “On the journey,” 5 and 6; “in order,” 2, 5, and 6.].

He consoled him kindly and handed him his staff [Note: [Col. 1117] Absent from 5b.], commanding that the staff be placed upon the body of the deceased and that, by his command, Maternus be raised in the name of Jesus Christ.

Eucharius, traveling swiftly, reached Elegia on the fortieth day after Maternus’s death [Note: [Col. 1118C] “On the fortieth day” is not found here in the *Life*.]. He dug up the body of his brother and placed the staff upon it. When he had fulfilled the apostle’s words [Note: [Col. 1117] “When he had fulfilled the word,” 5b.], Maternus immediately rose alive and unharmed from the tomb before the assembled crowd [Note: [Col. 1117] “The whole,” 1b; “before the people,” 5 and 6.].

In that place the Christian people built a church and, because of what had happened there [Note: [Col. 1117] Absent from 2, 5, and 6.], gave it the name “Resurrection” [Note: [Col. 1117] “To it,” 6.].

After Saint Eucharius had instructed many people at Elegia in the faith of Christ [Note: [Col. 1117] “To the faith” supplied in 1.], he now prepared to move on to other places. He bade farewell to the brothers at Elegia and departed with Valerius and Maternus. At last, after completing the journey, he reached Treberis [Note: [Col. 1117] “They reached,” 5b.].

### 5 [Note: [Col. 1123] Chapter XXVI in Leibniz, II, chapter 5. C.]

In the fifty-fourth year of the Lord’s incarnation and the nineteenth year of the reign of Claudius Caesar [Note: [Col. 1123] “Reign,” 6; “Claudius Caesar” is absent from C, erased in C1; “nineteenth” corrected from XV to XVIIII in 2; IX in 5b; XI in B2; 6 and C. These numbers do not agree with those read in chapter 14.], and in the eighth year of the episcopate of the blessed apostle Peter in Rome [Note: [Col. 1123] “Of the blessed Peter the apostle” is absent from 1 and 1b; “in the city,” 6; “year” is absent from 6.], Saint Eucharius, third in the order of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1123] Absent from 2; in 5a, “Eucharius, third in the order of the seventy-two disciples,” together with 5b, 5c, and 6.], finally reached Treberim with his companions Valerius and Maternus to preach to the Gallic peoples [Note: [Col. 1123] “Came,” 1b; “Sent to the Gallic peoples,” B and C; “Treveris,” C, frequently; “Treberis,” 5a.].

[Note: [Col. 1123] The passage beginning *Cujus* (“whose”) and ending *Maternus* is absent from manuscripts 1 and 1b, with half a page left blank. In 1b the words from *pontificalem* (“episcopal”) through *multiplicavit* (“he increased”) were also erased in red. A thirteenth-century hand then wrote in the margin: “When he had led a very great people to faith in Christ, had the affairs of the Church well secured and founded, and had himself become old, in the twenty-third year of his pontificate he left the sorrowful world and passed to the joys above. After whose [death Valerius] governed most excellently by preaching. When he died, blessed Maternus, bishop and holy apostle, just as he had lain forty days in the tomb, so presided over the episcopal chair for forty years and increased the talent of the holy Catholic faith.”]

Defeating the ranks of unbelief [Note: [Col. 1123] “Unhappiness,” 5 and 6.] and gaining the stronghold of true religion, he held the pontificate of that city for twenty-three years [Note: [Col. 1123] “Forty,” 5b; “thirteen,” 6a–b.] [Note: [Col. 1123] B2 adds in the margin: “Eucharius died on the sixth day before the Ides of December”; B6 adds: “He died on the sixth day before the Ides of December.”] [Note: [Col. 1125A] C adds: “And, happy, he departed to the Lord on the sixth day before the Ides of December”; above, variant reading 1054.].

He was buried in the church of Saint John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1123] Absent from 2; “of the holy one,” 5 and 6; “the Baptist,” 5.], which he had built before the Middle Gate [Note: [Col. 1123] “Which he had built before the Middle Gate,” 6a–b.], and he had blessed a cemetery around it [Note: [Col. 1123] Absent from B and 6. 5b adds in the text: “Concerning this Saint Eucharius, see more at the beginning of the chronicle of the bishops of Tongeren.”] [Note: [Col. 1123D] I. Pierius also observed that this smells of a fable, *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 380.].

After his death [Note: [Col. 1124D] “After his death … in religion,” from the *Life* cited above, p. 291.] blessed Valerius succeeded him in the priestly ministry [Note: [Col. 1123] “Death” superscribed with the year 76 in C6.], and governed it for fifteen years, living holily and preaching the word of life with the greatest distinction [Note: [Col. 1123] “Most blessedly,” 2, 5a–b, and 6; “most usefully,” 5c.].

His preaching was so persistent that already at that time Christians in Gaul and Germany surpassed the pagans both in number and in religion [Note: [Col. 1123] B2 adds in the margin: “Valerius died … on the first day before the Kalends of February”; 5b adds in the text: “Concerning him, see also earlier in the chronicle of Tongeren.”].

He too was buried in the same church beside the body of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1123] B6 adds: “He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.”] [Note: [Col. 1125B] C adds: “On the fourth day before the Kalends of February.” Compare the variant above, p. 1066.].

After his death [Note: [Col. 1124C] “After his death … the summit, and for forty years,” from the *Life*, same place.] blessed Maternus assumed the pontifical office and faithfully multiplied for forty years the talent entrusted to him [Col. 1125A] [Note: [Col. 1125] “The entrusted talent,” 6.].

He converted the people of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 1125] “Tongrenses,” 5a and C; “Tongerenses,” 5b.] and Cologne [Note: [Col. 1125] “Colienses,” 1b; “Agrippinenses,” B and C; absent from 2.], and presided by pontifical right over these three cities. In each of them, it is said, he celebrated the divine office on the same day of Easter [Note: [Col. 1125] “On one and the same day of Easter,” B and C; “on the day of Pentecost,” 5a; “on the day of Pentecost,” 5b, 5c, 6, and others.].

At this time the Treverans constructed an underground wine-conduit [Note: [Col. 1125] “Wine aqueduct,” B4.] from Treberis to Cologne through the village of Bedonis [Note: [Col. 1125] “Pedonis,” 5a and 6.] [Note: [Col. 1125C] Traces of the aqueduct still remain. Compare Hontheim, *Historia*, I, p. 61.], through which they sent a great quantity of wine to the people of Cologne as a token of friendship [Note: [Col. 1125] “A great quantity of wine,” 2, 5, and 6; the passage from “a great quantity” through chapter 18 is absent from 6a because of a defective folio; these words are from Maxentius.].

In those same days Saint Nazarius came to Treberis preaching Christ [Note: [Col. 1125] Absent from 1b.], but he was denounced to the emperor by the city’s most unfortunate ruler, Cornelius Domitianus [Note: [Col. 1125] Absent from 5b.] [Note: [Col. 1125C] Compare the Passion of Saint Nazarius, *Acta Sanctorum*, July VI, p. 583.].

### 16 [Note: [Col. 1125] II, chapter VI. C.]

Therefore Saint Maternus died an old man at Cologne [Note: [Col. 1125C] C adds: “On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.” Compare the variant below, p. 1090.] in the year 128 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1125] “124,” 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1125] B6 adds: “On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October”; B2 in the margin: “Maternus died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.”].

When his death became known at Treberis, they immediately set out for Cologne, seeking to recover their shepherd [Note: [Col. 1125] Absent from 5b.]. The people of Tongeren were also present, and together with the people of Cologne they strove to retain him for themselves [Note: [Col. 1125] “They wished,” 1b.].

For a long time both sides contended [Note: [Col. 1125] “The contest lasted so long,” 2, 5, and 6; “a contest lasting so long,” corrected in B2; “the contest continued for so long,” B4? and 6; “the contest then continued,” C.] [Note: [Col. 1125] “Between both parties,” corrected by another hand to “both sides” in 1; “a contest was held between both sides,” B2; “the contest was waged,” C.].

Meanwhile a venerable old man appeared in the city [Note: [Col. 1125] “Appeared,” 1.], warning the citizens to desist from the quarrel and obey his counsel [Note: [Col. 1125] “That they should obey,” 2, 5, and 6; “obey,” corrected to “may obey” in C1 and so in C3.]. He instructed them to place the bishop’s body in a ship, push it from the shore into the waves, and allow it to go wherever God wished [Note: [Col. 1125] Absent from B6.].

A marvelous thing! As soon as what the angel had advised was done [Note: [Col. 1125] “Had advised,” 2; “had counseled,” the usual form.], the ship, laden with the sacred body [Note: [Col. 1125] “Laden with the sacred body,” 2; “with the body laden,” B and C.], was guided against the waves by angelic rowing, with no helmsman directing it. After covering a mile in a short space of time, it came ashore at a place which, because of the sorrow of the people of Cologne, was then called Roze [Note: [Col. 1125] “Roze,” corrected from “roce” in 1; “rohe,” 1b; “rouueza,” 5a–b and 6b; corrected “rouuesa” to “rouueza,” 6c; “ronnesa,” 5c; “Rotkiriche,” C1 and C3; “royitkiriche,” C6. In 1b a later hand adds: “Rucukirge.”] [Note: [Col. 1125C] *Roz* means “weeping” in the Germanic language. Later writers identify it with Rodenkirchen; see *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 393.].

Then the Treverans received the body of their bishop, which God had assigned to them, with due thanksgiving, carried it back to Treberis, and honorably committed it to burial in the church [Note: [Col. 1125] “In the aforesaid church,” 5b.], not far from the bodies of Saints Eucharius and Valerius [Note: [Col. 1125] Absent from 6c.] [Note: [Col. 1125] 5b adds: “Concerning this saint, see also much else at the beginning of the chronicle of Tongeren.”].

## Source-ordered English apparatus and editorial notes

**Trebeta and early Treveris (Cols. 1119–1122).** C1 corrects *a* to *ac* at the expulsion clause: the added *ac* means “and.” C has *abrahae* for *Habrahae* (“Abraham”) and *chaldeorum* for *Caldeorum* (“of the Chaldeans”); B2 has *treveris* for *Treberis* (“Trier”). C1 supplies *post* (“afterward”), C has *qui etiam* (“which also”) and adds *verbis* (“in words”), and it calls the river *Kyll* rather than *Belgis*. At the settlement B2’s *herilis* means “lordly,” C3’s *ejus* “of him” rather than *eis*, “of them,” and B2’s *patracione* is the spelling of *patrationem*, “achievement.” C has *praeminentem* (“surpassing”) for *prominentem* (“standing out”); C1/C3 omit the whole sentence beginning “That this city surpassed”; B4? and C read *triumpatoribus* (“triumphant conquerors”); B2 has *treberorum* (“of the Treverans”) and *suis legibus* (“their own laws”).

**The gates and pagan temple (Col. 1121).** C6 has *eis* for *illis* (“them”); C has *idcirco quia* (“for that reason because”), *revertebantur* (“were returning”), and *ideo quod* (“for that reason that”); B2 has *bubus* for *bobus*, both “oxen.” At the Illustrious Gate C1 apparently corrects *ex* (“from”) to *est* (“is”), and C6 lacks the text from after *add* (“adorned”) through *nomine* (“by name”). B2 omits *omnes* (“all”) and reads *reperiret* (“would find”) for *reperiet* (“will find”); C reads *habet* (“has”) for *habuit* (“had”).

**Mercury and Jupiter (Col. 1121).** C reads *effigiem* (“likeness/image”) for *imaginem* (“image”). The exact words *sibi ferrum ascivit, sicque*, “drew the iron to themselves, and thus,” are absent in B2 and B4 and, as the editor believes, other manuscripts of that recension. C1 corrects its wording to the printed form; C3 and the remaining manuscripts follow that correction. B2 has *treberorum* for *Trebirorum*, both “of the Treverans.”

**Arimaspes and Caesar (Col. 1123).** Another hand adds *ucusque vel ususque* (“continually/up to that point”) in C1’s margin; C3 has *ucusque*. C has *treverica* (“Treveran”) for *Treberica*; C1 corrects *praesumpsit* (“dared”) to *praesumpserit* (“has dared”), followed by C3. C omits *quo* (“when”), B2 has *consolatus* (“the consulship”) for *consulatus*, B2 reads *civitatem se* for *se civitatem*, and C has *factus* (“made,” a past participle that yields an incongruous reading here) for *fastus* (“pride/arrogance”); B2 omits *utilius est* (“it is more useful”).

**Peter’s mission and the first journey (Cols. 1115–1118).** 2, 4, 5, and 6 omit *vero* (“but”); 1 and 1b read XLVI (“forty-sixth”) for 47; 5c adds *beatus Petrus* (“blessed Peter”); 5 and 6 have *signis potentissimis* (“most powerful signs”); 1 and 1b have *et* for *atque* (“and”); 5’s *strennue* is the spelling of *strenue*, “vigorously”; and 2, 5, and 6 read *fundata atque edificata* (“founded and built”). 5 and 6a–b have *super* for *supra* (“upon”), 6 *qui* for *quae* (“who” for “which”), and 1, g, v, p, 2, 5, and 6 correct *pullurarent* to *pulularent* (“were budding”). 6 reverses “Gaul and Germany” and has *dirigitur* (“is sent”) for *eligitur* (“is chosen”). The editor attributes “divine providence … ruled,” “finally … ordained,” and the ordination sentence to the *Life of Eucharius*.

**Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus (Col. 1117).** 2 omits *in*; 5 and 6 have *ordinatione* (“ordination/rank”) for *ordine* (“order”); 6 reads LXII (“sixty-two”) for 72; 5b omits *Domini* (“of the Lord”), and 2 lacks the final words. 2 inserts *et Valerius*, “and Valerius,” while 6 has *Valerius quoque*, “Valerius also.” Manuscript 1 corrects *subdiacum* to *subdiaconum*: both identify Maternus as “subdeacon,” the latter being the regular spelling. 5b omits *que* (“and”); 1b has *Caelestem*, 2 and 5a *Mennium*, and 5c *Innocentium* for *Memmium*—alternative proper names, not different offices. 1 has corrupt *magnt* for *magistri* (“of the teacher”), 5 *a magistro* (“from the teacher”), and 2, 5, 6 *properaverunt* (“they hastened”). 2 calls Elegia *Ingelheim*; 6c has *assatie* for Alsace; 5 and 6 have singular *populo*; 5a reads *verbum praedicationis veritatis* and 2/5b *praedicationis verbum veritatis*, both “word of the preaching of truth.” The editor says the remainder is abbreviated from the *Life* and discusses Elegia/Illkirch with Browerus, *Annales Treverorum*, p. 143, and *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 382.

For the illness and return, 2 has *infirmitate molestia* (“with the distress of illness”), 5’s *infirmate non* is a corrupt phrase, literally “illness not,” for “the distress of that illness”; and 6 reverses *non post* (“not after”); 1 perhaps omits Valerius, while 2, 5, 6, and B omit *celeriter* (“quickly”). C has *cuncta*, “all things,” for *cuncta quae*, “all the things which”; 2 has *cunctaque que*, “and all the things which”; and 5–6 *et cuncta*, “and all things.” 5–6 add *acciderant* (“had happened”) to “on the journey,” and 2, 5, 6 omit *per ordinem* (“in order”). At the staff, 5a has *clemens* for *clementer* (“kind/kindly”), 5b omits the staff, 5–6 *eidem* for *ei*, and 6 has *eundem suum … baculum*, “that same staff of his,” rather than simply “that same staff.” The *Life* lacks “on the fortieth day” here. 1b omits *ejus* (“his”) from “his death,” while 5a has *sue* (“his own”); 1b has *cumque* (“and when”) for *dumque* (“while”); 5b *verbi implevisset* (“had fulfilled the word”); 5a *mortuus* (“the dead man”) for the name Maternus; 1b *omni* (“the whole”) before “crowd”; and 5–6 *populo* (“the people”) for *populi multitudine* (“a multitude of people”). At Resurrection, 2, 5, 6 omit *ibi* (“there”), 6 has *ei imposuerunt* (“gave it [the name]”), 1 supplies *ad fidem*, 2 has *tandem*, and 5b plural *pervenerunt* (“they arrived”).

**Chapter 5 and Eucharius’s succession (Col. 1123).** 6 has *imperii* (“empire”) for *regni* (“reign”); C omits “Claudius Caesar,” erased in C1; the date is XV corrected to XVIIII in 2, IX in 5b, XI in B2, 6, and C, which the editor says conflicts with chapter 14. 1b has *epactis II*, “epacts II,” a chronological calculation; 1/1b omit Peter’s title, 6 has *urbe Roma* and omits *anno*, 2 omits *sanctus*, B6 omits “with companions,” and B/C read *gentibus directus* (“sent to the peoples”). 5/6 have *infelicitatis* (“unhappiness”) for *infidelitatis* (“unbelief”); 5b omits *et … tenuit*, 5/6 omit *ejusdem urbis*, 5b reads XL and 6a–b XIII for 23. B2’s margin and B6 say Eucharius died on the sixth day before the Ides of December; C adds that he happily departed to the Lord on that date, referring to variant 1054.

At the burial B6 omits *sepultus est*; 2 omits *beati*, 5–6 have *sancti*, and 5 *Baptistae* for *Evangelistae*. 6a–b has “which he himself had built before the Middle Gate”; B/6 omit *et*; 5b adds the Tongeren-chronicle reference; I. Pierius, *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 380, says the account smells of a fable. The *Life* supplies “After his death … religion.” C6 writes year 76 above “death”; 5b omits *-que*; 2 *perbeatissime*, “most blessedly”; 5a–b/6 *beatissime*, “blessedly”; and 5c *utilissime*, “most usefully.” B2’s margin gives Valerius’s death on the first day before the Kalends of February; B6 and C give the fourth day before those Kalends, C referring to variant 1066.

**Maternus, Bedonis, and Nazarius (Cols. 1124–1125).** The *Life* supplies “After his death … the pontifical summit, and for forty years.” C6’s margin gives year 89; 5b omits *beatus*; 6b has *Martinus*, the alternative name “Martin”; and 6 reads *creditum sanctum talentum*, “the entrusted holy talent,” where the printed text has *talentum sibi creditum*, “the talent entrusted to him.” Forms are *tongrenses* (5a/C), *tongerenses* (5b), *Colienses* (1b), and *Agrippinenses* (B/C): alternative names for the Tongeren or Cologne people; 2 omits Cologne. 6 omits *his* (“these”); 5 reverses *pontificali iure*, “by pontifical right”; 5 has *ferunt*, “they report,” B/C “on one and the same Easter day,” while 5a, 5b, 5c, 6 and others substitute Pentecost.

Calmet says the wine-conduit narrative was added in a later hand in the old St Matthias manuscript. B4 reads *vini conductum* (“wine conduit”); 6 has *usque ad Coloniam*, “all the way to Cologne,” for *usque Coloniam*, “as far as Cologne”; 5a/6 *Pedonis*, an alternative spelling of the village name Bedonis. Traces remain; the separate Bedonis reference is Hontheim, *Historia*, I, p. 61. 5 omits *magnam*; 2, 5, 6 read *vini copiam*, “an abundance/quantity of wine,” so that the phrase is “they sent the people of Cologne an abundance of wine”; 6a lacks from *copiam* through chapter 18 because of a defective folio, and the editor calls those words Maxentius’s. 1 marks the initial *e* as corrected; 1, 1b, 5b read *his*, “these,” for *hisdem*, “these same [days]”; 1b omits Nazarius’s arrival and 5b his denunciation; see the Passion of St Nazarius, *Acta Sanctorum*, July VI, p. 583.

**Maternus’s death and boat (Cols. 1125–1126).** The editor says this account occurs in some *Life* manuscripts but may be copied from the *Deeds*, citing *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 392. 1 corrects *Martinus* to *Maternus*; 6 has *apud urbem Coloniam*; C and B6 give the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, B2 the eighth; 1b reads 124 for 128. 5b omits the Treverans’ departure; 1b omits the Tongeren people and has *cupiebant* (“wished”); 6 says “with the Cologne people,” 5/C “with the people of Cologne.”

2, 5, 6 read *certamen est diu* (“the contest lasted long”); B2 corrects *certamen tam diu*, “a contest so long,” to *certamen tum diu*, “then a long contest”; B4?/6 have *certamen diu*, “a long contest,” and C *certamen tum*, “then a contest.” 1 corrects *utriusque* to *utrisque* (“both sides”); B2 has *utrisque habebatur*, “a contest was being held by both sides,” and C *utrisque geritur*, “the contest is waged by both sides.” 1 corrects accusative *venerandum*, “venerable,” to nominative *venerandus*, “a venerable [man]”; its *aparuit* is a spelling of *apparuit*, “appeared.” 2, 5, 6 have *parerent*, “that they should obey,” where the text has *parent*, “they obey”; C1 corrects that indicative to *pareant*, “may/should obey,” followed by C3. B6 omits “where God wills”; 1b’s *sinitant* is a faulty spelling of *sinant*, “let them allow”; 2 has *consulerat*, “had given counsel,” for *consuluerat*, “had advised”; 5 omits *factum est*; 2 has *onusta sacro corpore*, “laden with the sacred body,” while B/C have *corpore onusta*, “laden with the body”; 1b omits *et*.

For Roze, 1 corrects *roce* to *roze*, 1b has *rohe*, 5a/5b/6b *rouueza*, 6c corrects *rouuesa* to *rouueza*, 5c *ronnesa*, C1/C3 *rotkiriche*, C6 *royitkiriche*, and a later hand in 1b adds *Rucukirge*: all are place-name spellings. The editor explains German *Roz* as “weeping” and identifies the later place-name as Rodenkirchen, *Acta Sanctorum*, September IV, p. 393. 5 has abbreviated *t. r.* at the words “then called Roze” (the source supplies no expansion beyond those initials), and B4?/6 omit *tunc*, “then”; 5b/6/B6 have dative *littori*, “to the shore,” for *litore*, “at the shore,” and C1 corrects to *littori*, followed by C3. Finally, 6b adds *sibi*, “for themselves,” in *debita sibi gratiarum actione*, “with the due thanksgiving for themselves”; 5b has *ecclesia praedicta*, “the aforesaid church”; 6c omits *Eucharii et* (“of Eucharius and”); and 5b repeats the Tongeren-chronicle reference.]

[Column 1126B] Then—[Note: [Column 1125] Chapter XXVII begins in Leibniz.]—[Note: [Column 1125C] Calmet notes that what follows is absent from the ancient manuscript of Saint Matthias at Trier, the source of the *Deeds*; concerning another manuscript, Hontheim makes the same observation, *History* I, p. XXVII. In the same work, pp. XXIII ff., ch. I, Perier has sufficiently demonstrated that these names were copied from the catalogues of other churches or collected from monuments of doubtful reliability. See also Rettberg, *Church History of Germany* I, pp. 180 ff.—In the Life of Saint Agritius it is written (*Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 175): “For, as we have gathered by careful reckoning, we know that 201 years elapsed between the glorious departure from this world of Saint Maternus and the blessed arrival of Agritius in this city; during this intervening period the episcopate of this see ceased, since pagans held the city itself.” See the passage printed above from the manuscript of Saint Maximinus, col. 1073. Nor does the continuation of the *Deeds* know these bishops, but calls Agritius the fourth (ch. 18).—Yet nearly the same words as are read here are presented under the name of Methodius in the Frankfurt manuscript of Marianus (in Pistorius, ed. Struve I, p. 563); there are also found there the words which I have printed below from C, while other passages copied from Herigerus are absent. Finally, in the passage printed above, on the testimony of Methodius, twenty-six bishops are said to have sat between Maternus and Agritius; I think an error lies in that number. From this, however, it is clear that a twelfth-century book was attributed to Methodius, who first indicated these names of the bishops of Trier; the author seems to have followed him and added other material from Herigerus.] A certain Auspicius held the administration [Note: [Column 1125] Absent in 5.] [Note: [Column 1125] “Kingdom” in 5a; “administration of the church of Trier” in 5b; “administration of the church” in B (B6: “administration of the church”). C.] [Note: [Column 1125] C6: “in the year 129.”] Then [Note: [Column 1125] “De insignes,” corrected by another hand to “dein insignes” in 1; “deinde” in 1b, 2, 5, 6c, and B6.—5b has a completely different text: “And Avitus presided over the church of Cologne, and Navitus over that of Tongeren. These three men were disciples of Saint Maternus. In the church of Trier, thirteen bishops were crowned with martyrdom within twenty-one years, because after the death of Saint Maternus a very great multitude fell back into idolatry; but they were removed so quickly that no certainty concerning their times has been handed down” (or, according to the reading *celsitudo*, “no distinction”). “After Auspicius came Celsus; then Felix,” etc.] there arose distinguished men, powerful in holiness and grace, through legitimate succession [Note: [Column 1125] “Celsus” added in 5.] [Note: [Column 1128A] C1 adds in the margin: “The most holy Celsus—Celsus, that is, distinguished by name or merits, lofty in spirit and illustrious by birth, no sluggard in service to his native land, ever flourishing everywhere, pious in affection, serene in dignity and deed; Felix.” This wording was adopted by C3 and the remaining witnesses. In C3’s margin is written: “In these times it happened that nine kings sat in Trier. And it is said that this was performed by mimes before King Tacian in the period between Maternus and Agritius.”—[Column 1128C] These words are also found in Pseudo-Methodius, but seem to have been taken from an epitaph of Celsus discovered in the tenth century. See the *Acts of the Saints*, February III, p. 398. See also Hontheim, *History* I, p. XXI.]—Felix, Mansuetus, Clemens, Moses, Martinus, Anastasius, Andreas [Note: [Column 1125] Corrected from another hand.], Rusticus, Auctor [Note: [Column 1125] “Victor” in 5b.], Fauricius [Note: [Column 1125] “Mauricius” in 1b, 5, and 6.], Fortunatus [Note: [Column 1125] Absent in 2.] [Note: [Column 1128B] C adds: “who died on the fourth day before the Ides of June”], Cassianus, Marcus, Navitus, Marcellus, Metropolus, Severinus, Florentius, Martinus, Maximinus, Valentinus [Note: [Column 1126C] Pseudo-Methodius, in the same passage, omits these eight names and continues: “Marcus and very many others, who in their various times not only in their own province…” The passage is taken from Herigerus’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, ch. 15.] [Column 1127A] The last eight of these are also known to have presided over the church of Tongeren. All of them, at different times, were industrious and illustrious not only in their own province but also in the farthest and most remote regions [Note: [Column 1127] “Distinguished” in 1b; “foreign” in 5b; “extreme” in 6c.] [Note: [Column 1127] “Industrious” corrected from *indrustes* in 1; “diligent” in 6.] They were renowned not only for confession but also for martyrdom [Note: [Column 1127] “Who” corrected to “but” in 1; “but” in 6.] [Note: [Column 1127] “Also” in 2 and 6.] and conquered even the kingdoms of tyrants. These bishops [Note: [Column 1127C] The remainder is absent from Pseudo-Methodius.] are all believed to have been buried in the church of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Column 1127] “All the bishops” in 2; “the bishops, for the most part,” in 5b.]. But under which emperors or consuls each flourished [Note: [Column 1127] “And” in 1b; “or” in 5b.] [Note: [Column 1127] “Consuls” corrected from *cunsulum* in 1.] what end their individual lives had, how many years each administered the office of bishop [Note: [Column 1127] “They had” in 5; “they might have” in B2.] [Note: [Column 1127] *quotque* is written *qotque* in 1, *quotquot* in 5b, *quique singulis* in B2, and *quodque singulis* in B6; C1 corrects *quodque*, apparently, to *quotque*. *amministraverint* is *ammistraverint* in 1.] [Note: [Column 1127C] Herigerus has here: “or where the burial-place of each of them is”; our author could not adopt this because all were believed to have been buried in the church of Saint Eucharius.] or how much each enlarged the revenues of his church [Note: [Column 1127] “Extended” in B6; “how much each expanded the revenues of his church” in 5.]—because the upheaval wrought throughout Gaul by the Huns and Northmen [Note: [Column 1127] “Northmen” in 5; “Normans” in 6b; “Northmen” in B2; “Norwegians” in B6.] has obliterated everything [Note: [Column 1128C] The sentence from “Because” through “inquiry” is taken from Herigerus, with the name of the Northmen added. Note also the passage copied from codex C1, fol. 1, where nearly the same words may be read, though not copied from this text: “It should be noted. The Belgians are the bravest of the Gauls; moreover, among all the Belgians the Treveri have a singular reputation for courage. In the fiftieth year before the incarnation of the Lord, Labienus, Caesar’s legate, routed the forces of the Treveri, having lured them into battle by stratagem, before they could join the approaching Germans; he then took the city itself called Belgae (see ch. 10, §7). In the fifty-fourth year from the Lord’s incarnation, Eucharius received the bishopric of Trier, then Valerius, and afterwards Maternus. As for the bishops between Maternus and Agritius—under which emperors or consuls they flourished, what ends their individual lives had, how many years each administered the episcopal office, where the tomb of each may be, or how much each enlarged the standing of his church—the devastation of all Gaul wrought by the Huns and Northmen has obliterated these things; nor should any reader demand an exact account from us, since even in the dreadful times of the ten persecutions under which they lived, the fame spread by writers’ efforts was scarcely able to perpetuate their memory.”]—nor should any reader demand an exact account from us [Column 1127B] [Note: [Column 1127] “Of any reader” in 5; “of any reader” in C1 and 5b.] when, even during the ten dreadful persecutions [Note: [Column 1127] “Ten” absent in 5a.] under which they lived, the fame of written accounts was scarcely able, through the efforts of writers, to preserve and disseminate their memory [Note: [Column 1127] “The memory of the writers’ fame” in 5a.].

[Note: [Column 1128C] These details were found in Bede or in other chronicles.] For the first persecution of the Christians was carried out by Nero [Note: [Column 1127] “The first was Nero” in 2, 5, and 6.], the second by Domitian, the third by Trajan, the fourth by Marcus Antoninus [Note: [Column 1127] “Antoninus” corrected from “Antunnus” in 1 and likewise in 1b; “Anthonius” in 5a–b; “Antonius” in 5c and B2; “Antoninus,” apparently corrected, in C1 and likewise in C3 and the remaining witnesses.], the fifth by Severus Pertinax, the sixth by Maximinus, the seventh by Decius [Note: [Column 1127] Absent in B6; corrected from another reading in C1.], the eighth by Valerian, the ninth by Aurelian, and the tenth by Diocletian [Note: [Column 1127] “Dioclesian” in 6b; “Declesian” in 5b.] together with Maximian. During the times of these persecutions, therefore, the men mentioned above are shown to have carried out the episcopate of Trier not openly, but, as the Apostle says [Note: [Column 1127] Absent in 1b.], in deserts and mountains [Column 1128A] [Note: [Column 1127] “And in mountains” in 2, 5a, c, and 6; “and in caves” in 2 and 5; “in caves” in 6.] and caves and caverns of the earth [Note: [Column 1127] “And in caves” in 2, 5, and 6.], so that it is rightly believed that their lives, amid the persecution then raging everywhere [Note: [Column 1127] Absent in 5b.] and after the city of Trier had so often been devastated, were handed over to oblivion [Note: [Column 1127] “May believe” in 1b; “may be believed” in 5b.]. The adversary of the human race increased this misfortune. Finally, after the inseparable [Note: [Column 1127] “Inseparable” plural in 1b and 5c; “unconquerable” in 6b; “unconquerable?” in 6c.] [Trinity [Note: [Column 1127] Absent in 1, 2, 5, and 6b; “three” absent in 5b.]] had called to the heavens its three workers of the Gospel, destined for perpetual reward—namely Eucharius, Valerius [Note: [Column 1127] “And Valerius” in 5b.] and Maternus—Trier lost the faithfulness of right belief and, for the most part, returned to its former vomit of paganism [Note: [Column 1127] “Paganism” in 1b; “paganism” corrected from another reading in 5 and 6.].

[Column 1128B] 17. [Note: [Column 1127] Chapter XXVIII. Leibniz II, ch. VII. C adds “concerning the Theban martyrs.”] Therefore, in the year 291 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Column 1127] “Two hundred twelve” in 6c.] the emperor Maximian [Note: [Column 1128C] This narrative is taken from the *History of the Martyrs of Trier* (Hontheim, *Prodr.* I, pp. 111 ff.).], surnamed Herculius, summoned soldiers from the East to his aid because of the frequent revolts of the Gauls. These Thebans had been baptized by the bishop of Jerusalem and had then been instructed by the blessed Pope Marcellinus of Rome [Note: [Column 1129] “By Pope” in 6, B, and C.] how, under the arms of Roman liberty [Note: [Column 1129] “Under the arms of Roman authority,” corrected from another reading in 1; “Roman liberty” in 5.], they ought to preserve Christian innocence.

Two commanders were placed over this legion: one was called Tyrsus [Note: [Column 1129] “Thyrsus” in B2.], the other Secundus [Note: [Column 1129] Absent in 5c; “and the following are absent in 1b.”], and Mauritius, the first centurion of the same legion [Note: [Column 1129] “First standard-bearer” in 1b.—“First-centurion” in 5 and 6, which add this gloss: “It is said that Augustus established the ball on the standard because of the nations subject to him throughout the whole world, so that the staff might display the figure of the world; hence he is called *primipilarius*, as though ‘the first to carry the ball.’”] [Note: [Column 1129D] The *History of the Martyrs* says in book I: “The name of the first centurion of that same legion, as we received it from our predecessors, was Mauritius. Indeed, there were also other army commanders and leaders in that legion; because the names and merits of these men have been forgotten, we blame the negligence of our predecessors, though we commend their diligence for the little written documents concerning the merits of these same saints which we have found inscribed on leaden or marble tablets or on very ancient scraps.”].

Of these, Secundus ended his life by martyrdom at Victimilium, a fortress of Italy [Note: [Column 1129] “Victimi” in 1b; “Victimili” (or “Ructimili”) in 5b; “an Italian fortress” in 5.], while Mauritius, with his companions [Note: [Column 1129] B2 reads “with his very many companions and soldiers,” with the remainder omitted.], was slain for Christ at the town of Agaunum [Note: [Column 1129] “Agauium” in 1; “Agannium” in 2; “Aganium” in 5a; “Agitinum” in 5b; “Auganum” in 6b; “Augaunum” in B2.] [Note: [Column 1129D] See Ado, *Martyrology*, Rome, 1745, pp. 427, 487.]. But Tyrsus [Note: [Column 1132A] B4, 6, and C add “and Bonifacius.”], with his many companions and soldiers, came to Trier [Note: [Column 1129] “Came to Trier” in B6; “came down” in C1; “they resolved” in C3 and C4.], and there pitched camp in the Field of Mars [Note: [Column 1129] “In the Field of Mars” in 1; “in the Field of Mars” in 2.]. [Note: [Column 1129D] Thereafter he copied that history of the martyrs word for word.] There they were received by the most Christian leaders of the city [Column 1129B] [Note: [Column 1129] “By the Christian leaders,” with the rest absent in B2.], who recognized in them signs of Christianity and peace [Note: [Column 1129] “Signs” in 1b; “signs of Christian peace” in 5a–b; “signs of Christianity and peace” in 5c.], in a Christian and friendly manner [Note: [Column 1129] “Christianly” in 6.] and hospitably and honorably, with the supreme love that is in God arranging this reception [Note: [Column 1129] Absent in B2; “the supreme love arranging this” in 5.].

When these men had tearfully recounted to those leaders the reason for their departure from the East and their arrival at this place [Note: [Column 1129] Absent in 2 and 5b.], and had humbly requested both their counsel and their assistance [Note: [Column 1129] Absent in 2.], the hearts of all, citizens and guests alike, were so inflamed with the burning ardor of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Column 1129] “With burning” in 5 and 6; “burned” in B2.] and kindled with the love of God [Note: [Column 1129] “All hearts” in 5b and B2.] that they exhorted one another to offer their lives rather for receiving death out of love for Christ than for worshiping idols or attacking Christians [Column 1129C] [Note: [Column 1129] “Rather than for the worship of idols” in 6c.].

[Column 1130A] Scarcely, therefore, had they armed one another with the weapons of holy exhortation when, behold, Rictiovarus [Note: [Column 1129] “Rictiovarius” in 1 and 5b, frequently thereafter; “Ricciovarus” in 1b.] entered the same city, having been appointed prefect of Trier by the emperor Maximian [Note: [Column 1129] “Maxinian” in 1.] [Note: [Column 1130D] “Prefect of Trier” seems to have been taken from the *Passion of Fuscianus and Victoricus* (Hontheim, *Prodr.* I, p. 95).], accompanied by a very large military force. He first summoned before him the Christians of the Theban legion [Note: [Column 1129] “Legions” in 1b.]—the reason for his coming chiefly being them [Note: [Column 1129] “They had come” in 1b; absent in 6.]—and asked whether they too wished to worship the gods of the Romans and to subjugate their opponents by arms [Note: [Column 1129] The manuscripts vary extensively here: some omit “and”; others read “whether they themselves wished to worship the gods of the Romans”; “their detractors” or “opponents” appears with variant readings; “arms” is absent in 1b.].

When the commander of the legion, Tyrsus, replied that he and all his men, companions, and soldiers preferred to die for the love of Christ rather than be polluted by such sacrilege [Note: [Column 1129] “All his men” in 5a; “such a kind” in 6b; absent in B2.], Rictiovarus, having spread his soldiers throughout the whole field, ordered them all to be killed [Note: [Column 1130D] Compare the *Passion of Fuscianus and Victoricus*, cited above.] and their bodies to be left to be devoured by wild beasts and birds [Note: [Column 1129] “And by birds” in 6b; “their bodies to birds to be devoured” in 5a–b.].

[Column 1130B] Of these countless victims, such a multitude was martyred on the bank of the Moselle beside the Capitol that streams of blood flowing down [Note: [Column 1130D] From the *History*, ch. 2, p. 116.] and mingling with the waters of the Moselle changed it to their own color [Note: [Column 1129] “Changed it” in 5; “changed it” corrected to “changed them” in C1.] [Note: [Column 1132A] B and C add: “as far as the fortress called Niumaga” [Numaga in C]—[Column 1131D] Neumagen. See Hontheim, *Prodr.* I, p. 95.] so that, its natural brightness removed, it appeared red with a foreign rather than its own color [Note: [Column 1129] “The natural clarity of the water” in 5b; “rather” in 5b.]. Even then, while the bodies of the saints remained unburied, the water provided them with a tomb [Note: [Column 1129] “A tumult” in 6c.], which, when the harmonious union of their limbs returned, would present them at the future judgment [Note: [Column 1129] “Would represent it” in 5.].

Later this same Capitol was dedicated in honor of God’s mother and ever-virgin Mary [Note: [Column 1129] “Of the mother of God” in 1b; the genitive is absent in B6.] [Note: [Column 1129] “Ever-virgin Mary” in B and C.], and the place itself, in memory of the martyrs, received the name “Bank of the Martyrs” [Note: [Column 1129] “To the bank” in 1; “the bank of the martyrs” in 1b; see below, ch. 23.] [Column 1130C] [Note: [Column 1130D] Commonly called Mergen; see Hontheim, *Prodr.* I, p. 89. Wyttenbach notes: “We should certainly attribute the origin of the foundations of this monastery to the ancient memory of the Romans. In our own time, splendid remains of Roman workmanship have been discovered in the ruins of our church.”].

Rictiovarus carried out this slaughter [Note: [Column 1129] “Exercised” spelled *excercuit* in 1.], namely that of Tyrsus [Column 1131A] [Note: [Column 1131] “Tyasi” in 1 and 1b.] and his companions [Note: [Column 1131] “And” in 6.], on the fourth day before the Nones of October. On the following day [Note: [Column 1131] “On the next day” in 1; the words “following day” were erased in 1b.] he killed Palmacius [Note: [Column 1131] “Palmarius” in 5a–b; “Palmarem” in 5c.], the consul and patrician of the city, together with eleven of its leaders [Note: [Column 1131] Absent in B and C.]. Their names are these: Maxentius [Note: [Column 1131] “Maxentus” in 1.], Constantius [Note: [Column 1131] “Constantinus” in 6c; 6a continues with the preceding word.], Crescentius, Justinus [Note: [Column 1131] “Melinus” in 1; absent in 1b.], Leander, Alexander [Note: [Column 1131] Absent in 2 and 5, where it appears below after Jovianus; “Ilexander” in 5b; in 5c it occurs here after Crescentius.], Sother, Hormisda [Note: [Column 1131] “Ormisda”; “Papirus” in 1b.], Papirius, Constans, and Jovianus [Note: [Column 1131] “Jovinianus” in 1b and C.].

On the third day Rictiovarus nevertheless carried out another slaughter among the common people of both sexes [Note: [Column 1131] “Of both sexes” in B and C.] and every age, filling the entire city with innumerable Christians whom he had killed [Note: [Column 1131] “Filled” in 2.]. A few Christians [Note: [Column 1131] “A few Christians, therefore,” in B and C.] [Note: [Column 1131D] “A few…withdrew” and “filled a certain…” are taken from the Life of Saint Agritius (*Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 775), where the following precedes them: “as the report of all our ancestors has handed down to our knowledge.”] who escaped the storms of this persecution by flight [Note: [Column 1131] Absent in 6a–b.] after the persecution had abated somewhat [Note: [Column 1131] “After the persecution” is absent in 6; other readings occur in 5.] buried some of the bodies of these martyrs and filled with the bones of the saints a very large well, long neglected through age and drained of its water [Column 1131B] [Note: [Column 1131D] “Now covered by a pavement in the church of Saint Mary at the Martyrs,” adds Eberhardus (sixteenth century), according to Wyttenbach.].

Someone may ask how Rictiovarus killed so great a multitude of citizens and foreigners [Note: [Column 1131] Absent in B6; “citizens and” absent in 5 and 6.] or why the Thebans or the people of Trier were unable to resist him [Note: [Column 1131] “The Thebans or, as they are called, the people of Trier” in 6. “Were able” in 5 and 6.]. But it must be noted [Note: [Column 1131] “It must be noted” in B6.] that this Theban legion [Note: [Column 1131] “Of the Thebans” in 2.] first swore an oath to divine obligations [Note: [Column 1131] “First it swore to divine things”; “to a divine oath and then to the royal oath” in 1b.] and afterward to royal obligations. That it observed both oaths is demonstrated by this: first, it scorned to sacrifice to idols; second, although it was able to defend its innocence with arms, it refused to do so [Note: [Column 1131] “First…second” in 5 and 6; “who” in 1.]. Otherwise, if the Thebans, joined with the people of Trier, had wished to defend themselves [Note: [Column 1131] Various arrangements of “the Thebans joined with the people of Trier” occur in 5 and 6.], they could have resisted not only Rictiovarus but also the power of Maximian [Note: [Column 1131] “They would have remained powerful” in 1b.] [Note: [Column 1131D] See the *History*, p. 113: “They could easily have resisted and even prevailed, especially since we read in Roman and Gallic histories that the Roman emperor Caesar himself, with all the troops he could muster, was wearied for a long time and greatly by the citizens of Trier alone.”]. But he preserved his oath by dying patiently [Column 1131C] [Note: [Column 1131] B2: “He preserved his oath by patiently dying.”], and faithfully invited the citizens of the most powerful city, together with him, to despise death.

[Column 1132A] 18. [Note: [Column 1131] Chapter XXIX. Leibniz II, ch. VIII. C.] After the bloodiest rule of Rictiovarus [Note: [Column 1131] “Empire” or “dominion” (5: “dominion”); alternatively, “at last, civil war,” in 2, 5, and 6.], the civil rule of Constantius [Note: [Column 1131] “Constanti” in 5a; “Constantine” in 5b–c.], first Caesar and thereafter Augustus, was at last restored to us [Note: [Column 1131] “Was found again” in 1b; “was restored” in 5b.]. He showed great clemency toward human beings and the greatest religious devotion toward God [Note: [Column 1131] “Toward God, true religion” absent in 2; “true” in 5a–b.], and he neither stained his kingdom with the blood of the devout [Note: [Column 1131] “Of his predecessors” in 5a.] nor destroyed houses of prayer [Note: [Column 1131] “Prayer” in 2, 5, and 6.], but held the worshipers of God in veneration and honor [Note: [Column 1131] “Of God” in B and C.].

He was not only beloved but also revered by the people of Trier [Note: [Column 1132D] This account is taken from Eutropius X, 1, or from Paul the Deacon; but our author substitutes “the people of Trier” for “the Gauls” and adds the name of Rictiovarus.], especially because they had escaped the suspicious prudence of Diocletian [Column 1132B] and the bloody recklessness of Maximian and Rictiovarus through his rule [Note: [Column 1131] “Of that same man” in 6; “through his rule” in 2.]. He attacked the Alamanni, who had been ravaging the borders of Trier since the time of the emperor Valerian, at the very boundaries of Trier and destroyed them in a great slaughter.

Near Lingones [Note: [Column 1131] “Linganos” in 6c.] he experienced adverse and favorable fortune on the same day [Note: [Column 1132D] From Eutropius IX, 23.]. For when the barbarians suddenly attacked and he was forced inside the city in such desperate haste that, with the gates closed, he had to be lifted onto the wall by ropes, scarcely five hours later, when the army was arriving at midday, he killed nearly 60,000 Alamanni [Note: [Column 1131] “Fourteen” in 5 and 6; “men” in 1b; “of the day” in 5a–c and 6; “at the approach of day” in 5b.], after capturing their kings [Note: [Column 1132D] The account of the capture and exhibition of the kings is taken from Eutropius X, 3, which speaks of Constantine.], whom he also exposed to wild beasts after preparing a magnificent spectacle for the public [Note: [Column 1131] “You might marvel, having prepared…” in 1b; “had prepared” in 6.].

In the sixteenth year [Note: [Column 1132D] From Eutropius X, 1. “Thirteenth” in 1b, following Eutropius; “seventh” in 5a; “sixth” in 5b–c and 6.] of his reign he died in Britain at Eboracum, and from there was brought back to Trier [Column 1132C] and honorably buried in the Field of Mars [Column 1133A] with an epitaph of this kind:

“Elius Constantius [Note: [Column 1133] “Constantinus” in 2 and 5.], a man of consular rank, count and master of both military forces, and patrician, and twice ordinary consul [Note: [Column 1133] “Appointed consul” in 1b.]. Here he left Constantine, his son born to him by Helena, the most noble woman of Trier, as emperor of the Gauls [Note: [Column 1133C] It is now universally recognized that this and what follows are fabulous. Almannus was perhaps the first to call Helena a woman of Trier; at the end of the ninth century he wrote her Life (*Acta Sanctorum*, August III, p. 583). See also the discussion there, p. 549, by Pinius. Our author follows Almannus. I give the beginning of the Life, where it speaks of the city of Trier: “Blessed Helena, therefore, a native of Trier, was of such nobility according to the honor and dignity of the present life that almost the whole city of immense size was reckoned among the fields of her estate. Her house, now still shown, became the greater part of a church dedicated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as the episcopal seat of the metropolis; so that it is called and is the first see of Belgic Gaul, and also became the dwelling of royal ambition in that same city, constructed with wonderful workmanship. For its pavement was laid with Parian stone of various marbles, like the palace of Xerxes, surnamed Ahasuerus; its walls were made translucent with gleaming gold, like glass, as Solomon’s hall had been constructed of the timbers of Tyre; its ceilings, shaped like a crypt, were carved with precious marbles and relief work; and its bedroom was furnished and adorned with golden decorations.” See also Berengosus, *On the Discovery of the Holy Cross* III, ch. 2 (*Bibliotheca maxima Patrum* XII, p. 360), who had this passage before his eyes.], who alone also obtained by great wars the monarchy of the entire Roman empire [Note: [Column 1133] “And emperor” in 5 and 6; the phrases “by great wars” and “alone” are absent in 5 and 6.].

But his most blessed mother Helena went to Jerusalem with a great army [Note: [Column 1133] “With an army” in 5.] and there, with God’s help [Note: [Column 1133] “And of blessed God” in 2.], found the wood of the holy cross [Note: [Column 1134C] See Almannus, cited above, p. 588; Berengosus II, ch. 5 ff.]. After celebrating this discovery [Note: [Column 1134C] What follows is taken from the Life of Saint Agritius (*Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 773).], she approached Pope Sylvester and earnestly begged him to take pity on the city of Trier, related to her by blood [Note: [Column 1133] “Related” in 1 and 1b.], and to deign to illumine the darkness of its unbelief through some suitable preacher [Note: [Column 1133] “Might deign” in 1b.].

[Column 1133B] After a great search had therefore been made for a teacher [Note: [Column 1133] “After a great inquiry” in 2, 5, and 6.], by the counsel of all the faithful Saint Agritius, bishop of the city of Antioch [Note: [Column 1133] “Bishop of Antioch” in 1b.], was summoned and sent by the pope and the queen to Trier with the most precious relics, which we shall name below [Note: [Column 1133] “Which we have named below” in 1b; “which we shall note” in 2, 5, and 6.], together with a privilege which Pope Sylvester himself is known to have written in this manner in honor of the church of Trier [Note: [Column 1134C] This privilege certainly seems to have provided the occasion for this narrative. The author of the Life of Saint Agritius found it there but expanded it in a few words. See Hontheim, *History* I, p. 17, and Sybel, *The Holy Robe*, pp. 25, 37, and *The Advocates of the Holy Robe*, fascicle 2.].

[Column 1134A] “Just as in your own pagan nation you obtain primacy by your own virtue, so now, Trier, you possess first place and precedence over the Gauls and Germans, which Peter, head of the Church, marked out for you to have above all the bishops of these peoples among the first teachers of the Christian religion—namely Eucharius, [Note: [Column 1133] “Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus” in 1; “Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus” in B4?; “Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus” in B6.] Valerius, and Maternus—diminishing his own dignity in some way so as to make you a participant. I, Sylvester, his servant and unworthy successor, renew and confirm this through Agritius, patriarch of Antioch, in honor of the homeland of the empress Helena, a native of this metropolis [Note: [Column 1133] “Metropulis” in 1.], which that blessed woman enriched and specially advanced by transferring from Judea [Note: [Column 1133] “From Judea” in 6; corrected from “Judea” to “from Judea” in C3 and likewise in C4 and C6.] [Note: [Column 1134C] “Together with the nail and the other relics of the Lord, she magnificently endowed [it],” *Life of Saint Agritius*, p. 774. In B5, where this charter, containing chapter 18, is inserted, the text reads: “Having transferred [him], together with the other relics, namely the tunic and nail of the Lord, the head of Pope Cornelius, the tooth of Saint Peter, the sandals of the apostle Andrew, and many other gifts, she magnificently endowed [it].”] the apostle Matthias, together with the tunic and nail of the Lord, the tooth of Saint Peter, and the sandals of the apostle Saint Andrew, and the head of Pope Cornelius [Column 1134B] [Note: [Column 1133] “Of Saint Cornelius” in 2, 5, and 6.] and the other relics, magnificently endowed [Note: [Column 1133] Absent in 1b.] and specially advanced [Note: [Column 1133] “Magnified” in 2, 5, and 6.]. Those harmful rivals who knowingly oppose this privilege [Note: [Column 1133] “Knowingly harmful” corrected from another reading in 1; “harmful” in 5a–b and 6; absent in 5c.] shall be separated from communion [Note: [Column 1133] “Communion” in 1.] because they are stained with anathema [Note: [Column 1133] Corrected from another reading in 1.].”

Source preparation: Exact local canonical restoration; no foreign-text recoveries in this chunk.

## 19

[Note: [Col. 1133] Chapter XXXI. Leibniz II, chapter IX. C. — “Of Saint Agritius” is added in C3. — 6c reads: “End of Book II. Beginning of Book III.”]

In the year [Note: [Col. 1133] “Thus, of the Lord’s incarnation” in 1b.] of the Lord’s incarnation 368 [Note: [Col. 1134D] On this passage, compare the note printed above, p. 117. The year is evidently false. Agritius subscribed the Council of Arles in 314; see Rettberg, *Church History of Germany* I, p. 180.], Saint Agritius became bishop of the Treveri [Note: [Col. 1133] Absent in 1b. “Twenty-sixth in the order of bishops” is added in 5c.]. He rescued the people from their ancient error of idolatry [Note: [Col. 1133] “From the ancient error” in 2, 5, 6.] like another Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1133] “Idolatry” in 5, 6, and others. “Rescued”: *aripuit*, corrected to *eripuit*, in 1.], and [Note: [Col. 1134D] “And … established” is taken from the *Life of Saint Agritius*, p. 779, where it reads: “This is still shown today, since the house of the blessed empress Helena, which at the request of that most holy woman had been dedicated by the blessed patriarch Agritius as an episcopal see of the metropolis in honor of the prince of the apostles, Peter, and which has been nobly enriched and especially honored with a treasure of incomparable worth, namely the nail and the other relics of the Lord, is truly the first see of Gaul and Germany and is so called.”] dedicated the house of the most blessed Helena [Note: [Col. 1135] Absent in 2. “Holy” in 5, 6.]—after removing from it all the impurities of paganism [Note: [Col. 1135] “Of the most pagan [things]” in 1 and B6; corrected in 6b to “of paganism”; “of the pagans” in 1b.]—in honor of Saint Peter, and established it as the head of the church of Treveris [Note: [Col. 1135] “Of the church of Treveris” in 6 and B2.] [Note: [Col. 1135] “Established” is replaced by “constituted” in 5b and B6.].

At that time, at Helena’s command, a church of magnificent ornamentation and construction was built at Treveris in honor of the holy cross [Note: [Col. 1135] “Dedicated” in B6.] and even in the form of a cross [Note: [Col. 1135] “And also in the form of a cross” in 6; “in the form of the holy cross” in 5b.]. At the same time, a monastery in honor of Saint Florinus the Confessor was built at Confluentia [Note: [Col. 1135] “In the fortress” is added in 5, 6; 5 and 6 instead read “a monastery built in honour of the holy Virgin Mary”; 5b omits “built” and continues “and by”.] by a niece of the blessed Helena named Mathilda [Note: [Col. 1135] “Niece” in 1 and 1b.]. The bones of the apostle Matthias were placed beside the bodies of the holy Eucharius and his companions [Note: [Col. 1135] “Eucharius” in 1b. “And his companions” is added after “companions” in 1; “and of his companions” in 5, B, C.], while the Lord’s tunic, together with the nail and the other relics, was deposited in the house of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1135] “The tunic … were deposited” is absent from 5, 6.].

Saint Agritius, having completed the duties of his pontificate [Note: [Col. 1135B]], departed to the Lord and was buried [Note: [Col. 1135] The *-que* is absent in 5.] beside the body of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1135C] “He was buried in the church built in honor of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist; in that church also lies buried the body of Maximinus, bishop of Treveris, resting beside the body of that glorious pontiff. Blessed Agritius was succeeded, therefore, etc.” From the manuscript of Saint Matthias cited by Calmet; the author of the *Deeds* altered Calmet’s account. The *Life of Agritius*, p. 780, does not say where the bishop was buried.]. [Note: [Col. 1135C] Compare Brower, p. 225, and the preface, p. 120.]

Blessed Maximinus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1135] “Succeeded” is written *successet* in 1.], his disciple [Note: [Col. 1135C] This seems to have been taken from the *Life of Maximinus* by Lupus, chapter 5.], who deposed Eufratas of Cologne, a heretic [Note: [Col. 1135] *Eufraten* in 1b; *Eufratem* in 5; *Effratham* in 6. “Of Cologne” in 1b. “Nor should he be called a bishop,” in B and C. 5b adds after “heretic”: “together with many other bishops of Gaul in the time of Saint Servatius, who pronounced his first sentence against Eufratas.”], and substituted Severinus in his place [Note: [Col. 1135] B and C add: “by election of the church.”]. He honorably received Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fleeing the persecution of the emperor Constantius (336–338) [Note: [Col. 1135] 5b adds: “the persecution of the heretic.”], and did so fearlessly [Note: [Col. 1135] Absent in C.].
