For previously he had wandered as a fugitive throughout the whole world, and no place remained for him in which to hide. [Note: [Col. 1136C] The following narrative is taken from Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* X, chapter 18.] Tribunes, prefects, counts, and armies, moved by imperial edicts [Note: [Col. 1135] *Imperatoribus* (“by emperors”) in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1135] “Warned” in 5, 6.], were striving with all the forces of the whole kingdom [Note: [Col. 1135] “With all” in 1 and 1b.] to bring him back alive if possible, or, if not, at least his head [Note: [Col. 1135] “His head” in 5, 6.] [Note: [Col. 1135] “Had brought” in 5c; singular “had brought” in 5a and 6; corrected to the plural in C1 and likewise in C3 and following witnesses.].

Yet at Treveris [Note: [Col. 1136C] The author has inserted “at Treveris” and “full of the bones of saints” into Rufinus’s narrative. According to the *Life of Saint Agritius*, Athanasius is said to have stayed in the well mentioned above in chapter 17, p. 775.] he remained hidden for six years [Note: [Col. 1135] “For six continuous years” in B, C.] in the lake of the aforementioned cistern, which had no water and was full of the bones of saints [Note: [Col. 1135] “Of the dead” in 5, 6.] [Note: [Col. 1136C] Calmet says at this point: “The old manuscript says that this well was filled with the bones of the martyrs of the Theban Legion; this well is still shown today in the underground church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin in the basilica of Saint Maximin.” If only he had published the actual words of the manuscript.], so that he never saw the sun [Note: [Col. 1135] Absent in B6.]. There he composed the Catholic creed, that is, the *Quicumque vult* [Note: [Col. 1135] “*Quicumque vult salvus esse*” (“Whoever wishes to be saved”) is added in 1b and 5c; “*Quicumque vult salutis esse*” (“Whoever wishes to be of salvation”) in 6b.] [Note: [Col. 1136C] “And … composed” is taken from the *Life of Agritius*, at the same place.].

But when he had been harassed by a woman who appeared to be providing him with a hiding place [Note: [Col. 1135] “A lantern” in 5a; “lantern” in 5b and c, 6.] [Note: [Col. 1135] “Had been exposed” in 2, 6.], as though warned by the Spirit of God, on that very night when the judges were coming to seize him [Note: [Col. 1135] “Were coming” in 1b.], after so many years [Note: [Col. 1135] “After six years” in 6b.], he moved to another place [Note: [Col. 1135] “Moved” in 1b, 2.] [Note: [Col. 1136C] “But … moved” is taken from Rufinus, at the same place. This is absent from the ancient manuscript of Saint Matthias, according to Calmet.].

Then blessed Maximinus went to Aquitania to revisit his people [Note: [Col. 1135] “Into Aquitania” in 5a, b; 5c corruptly reads “went on into the cistern”; “proceeded into Aquitania” in 6.], and there, when the Lord called him, he rested in peace [Note: [Col. 1135] C6 has in the margin: “The fourth day before the Kalends of May.”].

Paulinus succeeded him in the episcopate (about 350) [Note: [Col. 1135] “His successor” in 5c; “Saint Paulinus, bishop” in B6.] and through the blessed Lubentius [Note: [Col. 1135] B2 reads *iubentium*, and likewise below.] [Note: [Col. 1136C] Compare the *Life of Saint Lubentius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, October VI, p. 202.] and the people of Treveris brought back the body of his master from Aquitania, and buried it in the cemetery of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1135] *Macharii* in 5a.] [Note: [Col. 1136C] “He honorably buried the glorious bishop in the church of Saint John the Evangelist, which is in the suburb of Treveris, where he still rests bodily.” Manuscript of Saint Matthias cited by Calmet; this agrees with the *Life of Maximinus*.].

Blessed Lubentius [Note: [Col. 1138A] B and C add: “At first, endowed with the dignity of the priesthood, he served the Lord among the people in a church situated on a mountain beside a town called Cuberna.” [Note: [Col. 1138C] Coverna, Kobern, on the Moselle.]] came to Germany through a revelation from the Lord [Note: [Col. 1135] “Of Germany” in 1; “the regions of Germany” in 1b.], and there he built a church above the river called the Longana [Note: [Col. 1137] *Logona* in 2; *Logana* in 5a, c, 6, B, C.] [Note: [Col. 1137B] The Lahn. He identifies it with the church of Dietkirchen; compare Brower, p. 235. The *Life of Saint Lubentius*, at the same place, tells the story differently: it was not Lubentius himself but his corpse that came there. The actual words are worth presenting, published from the Arnstein manuscript of 1170:

“Since his corpse could not be deposited in the church at Cabrun, it was placed in a boat and carried by way of the Moselle into the Rhine. Passing Confluentia and two nearby villages of the Rhine, the little boat soon turned into the river called the Logena, which flows into the Rhine from the east, and landed at the village of Loginstein, which stretches along that same river [lacuna]

“Thus the aforementioned boat, with its helmsman, traveling unhindered through the wilderness toward the place predestined by God, driven by favorable south winds, ascended the river Logena. At that time the river was everywhere covered with woods and mountainous groves, inhabited by wild animals and beasts, while few people lived there. That region did not yet possess the castles of tyrants, the fortified towns of brigands, or the various commercial activities of merchants [lacuna]

“There is a rock rising high and facing east above the bank of the aforesaid river, approximately eight miles from the Rhine. Upon it stood a shrine called Dietkirchen, named, as tradition says, after its founder Dietger. Long ago, while a wealthy herdsman lived somewhat farther upstream in the same part of the river, in a little village called Derna, he learned through the reports of his servants—and indeed through his own experience—that the rocky hill, covered with woods, was frequently illuminated by heavenly radiance and made awesome by angelic visitation. He therefore built an oratory there, and there, imploring the grace of Christ for as long as he lived, he happily rested [lacuna] The same patron of ours was brought back here and humbly laid to rest in the aforesaid shrine.”]

and in it he also rests [Note: [Col. 1137] Absent in 5; B and C add: “and, having later died, was transferred there.”].

But the bishop and martyr of Christ, Paulinus [Note: [Col. 1137] Absent in 5b.], was sent into exile in Phrygia by the emperor Constantius on account of the true faith (353–355) [Note: [Col. 1137] “Was sent” in 1b.]. There he was beheaded for the name of Christ and buried (358) [Note: [Col. 1137] “And” in 6.]. For while he was preaching the true faith more insistently to the pagans [Note: [Col. 1137] Corrected from “peoples” to “pagans” in 1; “to the pagans” in 2, 5, 6.], the pagans were provoked to anger [Note: [Col. 1137] Absent in 5.] and he was beheaded [Note: [Col. 1137] Absent in 5, 6.] [Note: [Col. 1137] C6 has in the margin: “The second [or fifth?] day before the Kalends of August.”] [Note: [Col. 1137C] I. Pinius cites the same words from a manuscript florilegium, *Acta Sanctorum*, August VI, p. 672. They are not found in the *Life* published there. The author of the *Deeds* seems to have had before his eyes the history of the martyrs of Treveris, where, in chapter 2 (in Hontheim, *Prodromus* I, p. 117), Frideburga is said to have been warned in a vision in the monastery of Saint Mary at Horreum to visit a sister who was keeper of the library. On finding her, she led her to the library to search through the heap of documents; they had scarcely turned over many volumes before an extremely old book of hymns, written in Scottish, came into their hands. When it was opened, they repeatedly encountered a lengthy hymn about Saint Paulinus, containing an account of his remarkable holiness. Although its composition had a certain rusticity, its subject matter nevertheless displayed considerable refinement. It began: “For it recounted …,” etc.]

After him came Bonosius [Note: [Col. 1137] 5b reads: “After Paulinus Bonosius becomes bishop of the Treveri. Then ...”; “bishop” is added in B, C.], then Brittonius [Note: [Col. 1137] *Britonius* in 2, 5, 6; “concerning whom” is absent in B and C.]. Concerning him, the *Tripartite History* records [Note: [Col. 1138B] IX, 14, where a letter addressed to Damasus, Brittonius, and other bishops is found. Compare Rettberg I, p. 195.] that Brittonius was in Rome with Pope Damasus. He himself is called Mars in pagan fashion, but in our language the name sounds like “sweet virgin” [Note: [Col. 1138B] I cannot guess what this is supposed to mean.].

During their time, about the year 380, the Greeks invaded Treveris with a large force [Note: [Col. 1138B] Compare chapter 22 below. The manuscripts of Saint Matthias and Saint Gislenus append the conclusion of the *Lives of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*; see Hontheim, *History of Treveris*, pp. 57, 159:

“Therefore almighty God permitted three scourges—especially the sword of the pagans—to come upon the kingdom of the Christians and upon the aforesaid city [Treveris] three times. The first scourge was that of the Greeks under the emperor Constans, son of Constantine [“Constantius” in the Saint Matthias manuscript], who, having become an Arian [“because he had become” in the Saint Matthias manuscript], persecuted Catholics throughout the whole world. The second was when the Vandals and Alemanni devastated the regions of Gaul [“of Gaul” in the Saint Matthias manuscript] under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Roman emperors [“the Romans” in the Saint Matthias manuscript]. The third was that of the Huns under their king Attila [“Totila” in Saint Gislenus] and under the emperor Theodosius the Younger.”] and cruelly afflicted it with slaughter, plunder, and fires [Note: [Col. 1137] *Tiberim* in 5a. The phrase “and” is absent in B, C.].

## 20

[Note: [Col. 1137] Chapter XXXII. Leibniz II, chapter X. C.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 406 [Note: [Col. 1138C] The account of Maximus’s creation is taken from Orosius VII, 34.], Maximus, indeed a vigorous man and worthy of the imperial title—had he not risen through tyranny against the oath of allegiance [Note: [Col. 1137] “Against the oaths” in 2, 5b, c, 6; “against the sacred oath” in 5a.]—was unwillingly proclaimed emperor by the army in Britain [Note: [Col. 1137] “Britain,” corrected from “Britannia” in 1.], and established Treveris as the seat of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 1137] *Treberi* (“Treveris”) in B, C; *Treveri* in B6.] [Note: [Col. 1138C] “Established Treveris as the seat of his kingdom” is said by Gregory of Tours I, 38.].

At the same time the heresy of the Priscillianists arose from Priscillian, bishop of the city of Abila in Spain [Note: [Col. 1137] “Abila” in 4, 5a, c, 6; “Spain” is absent in 2, 5, 6.] [Note: [Col. 1138C] Compare Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II, 47; nevertheless I would not think that the author had this work before him.]. Soon condemned at the synod of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 1137] So in 1; “at Bordeaux” in 1b; other witnesses have *Burdegalensem*.], he fled to the emperor Maximus at Treveris [Note: [Col. 1137] *Maximinus* in 6b.]. When his error had been exposed [Note: [Col. 1138D] This is taken for the most part from Prosper’s *Chronicle*, under the year 385.], by order of Maximus [Note: [Col. 1139A] *Maximinus* in 5b, 6b.] he was condemned to the sword by the prefect of the praetorium, Evodius (383) [Note: [Col. 1139] Absent in 5b.], together with Eutrochia, the wife of the rhetor Delfidius [Note: [Col. 1139] *Perfidi* in 4, 5, 6.], and Latronianus [Note: [Col. 1139] *Latinianus* in 2; *Latronia* in 4, 5, 6.], Felicissimus [Note: [Col. 1139D] Sulpicius calls him Felicissimus; neither he nor Prosper names Julianus.] and Julianus, and many other associates of his error [Note: [Col. 1139] “Of their errors” in 1, 1b, 5. “Associates” in 1b.].

To condemn this heresy, a famous council of bishops was assembled at Treveris by order of Maximus. Among them were Martin, bishop of Tours [Note: [Col. 1139] *Thur.* in 2.], and Ambrose, bishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 1140B] B and C add: “and the great Augustine” [Note: [Col. 1140D] It is certain that Augustine did not come to Treveris.]]. Martin had illumined Treveris by words and signs not only then but also frequently before.

At the request of her parents, he had healed a paralyzed girl [Note: [Col. 1139] The passage beginning “the girl” and ending “he pardons everything” is absent from B2. The manuscript followed by the text seems to have lacked a folio.], had freed the servant of Tetradius the governor from a demon, had made Tetradius himself—still stained by paganism—a servant of Christ, and had cleansed a certain head of household’s servant from a dreadful demon [Note: [Col. 1139] “Demon” in C3.].

One day, when a sudden report of fear and an attack by barbarians had thrown the city into confusion, he ordered a demoniac to be brought before him and commanded him to confess whether the report was true. Then the man confessed that there were sixteen demons who had spread this rumor among the people so that, at least through this fear, Martin might be driven from the town; nevertheless, the barbarians were planning an invasion. Thus, while the unclean spirit was confessing this in the middle of the church, the city was freed from its present fear and confusion. [Note: [Col. 1140D] These events are taken from Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapters 16–18.]

On another day [Note: [Col. 1141D] At the same place, chapter 20.], he was invited by the emperor Maximus, after many entreaties, to a banquet. When the banquet was nearly halfway over, as was customary, a servant brought a cup to the emperor. He ordered that the cup be given to Martin, wishing to receive the drink from Martin’s right hand. But after the bishop had drunk, he handed the cup to his own priest, judging that no one was more worthy to drink first. The emperor and his attendants marveled at this, and throughout the palace it was loudly reported that Martin had done at the king’s banquet what no bishop had done at the banquets of inferior judges [Note: [Col. 1141] Absent in B6, which leaves a blank space.]. He also foretold that Maximus would be killed in Italy after several years; and so it happened. In the same city he was greatly honored by the services of the empress. [Note: [Col. 1141D] “To him” in the dialogue, II, 6.]

Ambrose of Milan also, when he had come to Treveris [Note: [Col. 1139D] The words “When he had come … he learned from the duke” are taken from a letter of Ambrose, VII, 6.], went to the palace on the third day [Note: [Col. 1139] Thus in 1, 2, and other witnesses; here and below absent in 1b.]. Afterwards, when Maximus saw Ambrose abstaining from bishops who were in communion with him and were seeking the death of certain persons—even though they had strayed from the faith, namely the Priscillianist heretics, among whom Martin too had sinned—[Note: [Col. 1139D] “That is, the Priscillianist heretics,” and “where Martin also sinned,” were added by the author.] Maximus, angered by them [Note: [Col. 1139] “Communicating with them,” corrected in C1 and likewise in C3 and following witnesses.], ordered Ambrose to return immediately [Note: [Col. 1139] “To return” is corrected from *regreduipsi* in 1; “to enter” in 2, 4, 5, 6.]. Ambrose himself willingly set out on his journey, although many did not believe that he would escape the ambushes [Note: [Col. 1139] “Very many” in 2, 5, 6.], troubled only by the fact that he learned that the elderly bishop Iminius was being led into exile [Note: [Col. 1139] The name appears as *Imineus* in 6, *Iumnus?* in 5a, and *Martinus* in 5c.].

Maximus, therefore, [Note: [Col. 1141A] B and C read as follows: “Thus the bishops were being held at Treveris …” [Note: [Col. 1141] Chapter XXXIII. Leibniz II, chapter XI. C.] [Note: [Col. 1141D] All this is taken from Severus, *Dialogues* III, chapters 11–12.]] was holding bishops at Treveris who, by communicating daily with Ithacius and Achatius, had made their cause a common one. Ithacius and Achatius were bishops; through their faction Priscillian and the others had been killed. At their advice Maximus had decided to send armed tribunes with full authority to Spain [Note: [Col. 1141] “To Spain” in C.] to investigate the remaining Priscillianists and, once discovered, deprive them of their property and life.

When they were informed that Martin was approaching, they consulted with the emperor so that officials sent to meet him might prevent him from coming closer to that city unless he declared that he would arrive in peace with the bishops who were staying there [Note: [Col. 1141] “Peace” in B6.]. Martin cleverly eluded them. He declared that he would come in the peace of Christ. Finally, entering at night, he visited only the church for the sake of prayer; the next day he sought the palace.

Among the many requests that would take too long to recount, he had these principal ones: on behalf of the count Narses and the governor Leochadius, both of whom had belonged to the party of Gratian, whom Maximus’s general Andragathius had killed; and that tribunes not be sent to Spain with authority to use the sword. Martin’s pious concern was not merely to free Christians who were being harassed on that pretext, but also to free the heretics themselves.

But on the first and second day Maximus delayed granting his requests. Meanwhile, the bishops with whom Martin refused to communicate implored Maximus with tears to use his power against the man. He, however, did not wish to use force against the holy man. Nevertheless, when Martin had been summoned privately, he addressed him gently and declared that the heretics had rightly been condemned by the public judges rather than by priests [Note: [Col. 1141] “Were to be punished rather by public judges than by priests” is added in the margin of C1 and likewise in C3 and following witnesses.], and that there was no reason why Martin should avoid communion with Ithacius [Note: [Col. 1141] *Ithacius* in B, 6.] and the others of his party. When Martin was little moved by this, the king became inflamed with anger, tore himself away from his presence, and soon—when the emperor refused to be turned from his decision—sent executioners [Note: [Col. 1139] “These” is absent in 1, 1b, 2, perhaps 4, 5, 6.] to Spain on behalf of those for whom Martin had pleaded [Note: [Col. 1139] Absent in 5b; “Martin” absent in 5; “to Spain” absent in B, C.].

When Martin learned of this, he broke into the palace at night [Note: [Col. 1139] “Entered” in B, C.] and promised that he would communicate with them if the tribunes sent to Spain were recalled [Note: [Col. 1139] “To Spain” in 5.]. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything [Note: [Col. 1139] “And granted everything” in B6.].

Three days later [Note: [Col. 1139] “The day after” in 1b; “the next day” in B, C.] the ordination of Felix, bishop of Treveris [Note: [Col. 1139D] The author adds “of Treveris” after “bishop.”], after Brittonius [Note: [Col. 1139] The name appears as *Britonem* in 2, 5, B2, 6; *Britonium* in 6a and 6b-c.], was being prepared. He was indeed a most holy man, plainly worthy to become a priest in a better age [Note: [Col. 1139] “Worthy to become a priest” in B, C.]. On that day Martin entered into communion [Note: [Col. 1139] “Communication” in 2, 5.], judging it better to yield for a time than to fail to provide for those who were doomed to perish [Note: [Col. 1139] “Sufficient” in 5.]. [Note: [Col. 1139] “Thus” in 6.]

These things, therefore, were taking place at Treveris at that time [Note: [Col. 1139] Absent in 5, 6.], and in this manner Saint Felix assumed the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1139] “Saint Felix assumed the episcopate” in 6.].

[Note: [Col. 1139] Chapter XXXIV begins in Leibniz.] There were also at that time at Treveris many noble and ecclesiastical men [Note: [Col. 1139] “Many noblemen” in 1b.], namely the priest Jerome of Bethlehem [Note: [Col. 1139] *Bethlehem* in 5c and C1.], Ausonius of Bordeaux, and very many others [Note: [Col. 1139] “Very many” is absent in 5a, b.]. Of these, Jerome wrote there a very long book on the synods of Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 1139D] The information about the lengthy work is taken from Jerome’s letter to Florentius, *Works*, edited by Martianay IV, 2, p. 6.] [Note: [Col. 1139] “On a synod” in 1b.], while Ausonius composed in verse a little book called the *Mosella* [Note: [Col. 1139] “The little book” is corrected from *libelum* to *libellum* in 1 and C3. “And … composed” is absent in 5a; “and … composed” is absent in 6.]. Later, having returned to his homeland, he composed a large volume in honor of this homeland [Note: [Col. 1140D] Wyttenbach thinks this information arose from a misunderstanding of Ausonius’s verses; see *Mosella*, verse 394: “when I shall sing the deeds of individuals and the ancestral honors of the Belgians, their illustrious distinctions and customs …” The author of Treveris appears to understand “this homeland” as Belgic Gaul or the region of Treveris. Compare Bocking on the *Mosella*, p. 93.], which anyone wishing to know about can find in Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 1139] “In the city of Bordeaux” in C; “may find” in B2, corrected to “will be able to find” in C1; in 1b: “to find in Bordeaux …”].

## 21

One day the emperor Maximus went out to the amphitheater to watch the circus games [Note: [Col. 1142D] This narrative is taken from Augustine’s *Confessions* VIII, chapter 6, §15. But the words “to the amphitheater” and below “the cell of Saint Eucharius” were added by the author himself, while other details were slightly altered.]. Then a certain member of the palace guard named Pontianus [Note: [Col. 1141] *Ponticianus* in 1.] went out with three other comrades [Note: [Col. 1141] “With three others” in 2.] to walk in the gardens adjoining the wall [Note: [Col. 1141] *Hortos* (“gardens”), corrected from *hortus* in 1; *ortos* in 5a, b, 6. “Wall” in 5a, c; “walls,” corrected to “wall,” in 6a and likewise in 6b, c; “walls” in 5b, B, C.]. When one of them happened to remain with him [Note: [Col. 1141] “One” in B2; “although one of them remained” in 1b.], the other two came to the cell of Saint Eucharius, where poor servants of God lived, such as possess the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1141] Absent in 1b.]. There they found a book containing the life of Antony [Note: [Col. 1141] “Of Saint Antony” in B, C; *Anthony* in 5a, b.].

One of them began to read it, marvel, and burn with zeal, filled with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1142B] “To be kindled” is absent in 2, 5, 6; “to be kindled” in B2; corrected to “be kindled” in C1 and likewise in C3 and following witnesses.]. Then, raising his eyes to his companion, he said to him: “Tell me, I beg you: does it not seem better to you to serve this God, who has such a servant, than to serve uselessly in the army of a mortal king?” [Note: [Col. 1141] “It is better” in B, C.]

He said this in agitation, laboring to give birth to a new life. Then he returned his eyes to the pages [Note: [Col. 1141] “To the page” in 1b, 5, 6.], continued reading, and was changed inwardly; his mind was stripped of the world [Note: [Col. 1141] Absent in B, C.]. For while he was reading, he groaned and said to his friend: “I have now torn myself away from that hope of ours, and have resolved to serve God; from this hour I am beginning this in this place [Note: [Col. 1141] Absent in 5a, b; “from this hour I will do this” in 6; “I will undertake it” in 2.]. If you are reluctant to imitate me, do not turn away from me” [Note: [Col. 1141] “To imitate” is written *immitari* in 1; “to oppose” is found in 5, 6 and is corrected from *aversari* to *adversari* in C1 and likewise in C3 and following witnesses.].

Then the other replied: “I too will cling to you, and I will no longer abandon you in such military service” [Note: [Col. 1141] “In such a militia” in 5, 6; “such military service” corrected to “such a militia” in C1 and likewise in C3 and following witnesses.].

Then Pontianus [Note: [Col. 1141] *Pontitianus* in 1.] and those who were with him walked through other parts of the garden [Note: [Col. 1141] “They were walking through the parts of the garden” in 2, 5, 6.], looking for them, and came to the same place. They urged them to return, because the day had already declined [Note: [Col. 1141] “Since the day was already declining” in 6.]. But they told them what desire and destiny had arisen in them [Note: [Col. 1141] “What desire had arisen in them” in 2, 5, 6; “what their desire and destiny had become” in B, C.], and asked them not to trouble them. Then they began to weep, and, piously rejoicing with them [Note: [Col. 1141] “And piously” in 1b. “Rejoiced” in 1, 1b, 5.], commended themselves to their prayers and returned to the palace [Note: [Col. 1141] “To” in 6.]; but the others remained in the same place.

For both had fiancées, who, when they heard this, also dedicated their virginity to God [Note: [Col. 1141] “Dedicated“ in 5a, b; “consecrated“ in B, C.].

### Supplementary textual apparatus

The entries below complete the readings omitted from the embedded notes above; each is keyed to its source passage.

[Col. 1135, Helena and the foundations.] The editor says that he does not know where the author found the following account. In the Treveris sentence 2 omits `Treberis` (at Treveris), while 5 reads `urbs iussu` (the city, by command). For the church, 2 and perhaps B6 read `honore` (in honour) for `in honorem` (in honour of), and B6 reads `dedicata` (dedicated) for `aedificata` (built); 6 adds `et in modum` (and in the form), and 5b has `in modum sanctae crucis` (in the form of the holy cross). B and C omit the whole clause from `Ipso` (at the same time) through `Mathilda nomine` (named Mathilda). At Confluentia, 6 has `honorem` (in honour), while 5 and 6 read `sanctae virginis Mariae ... constructum` (a monastery built in honour of the holy Virgin Mary); 5b omits `constructum` (built) and continues `et a` (and by). The reading `nepta` (niece) occurs in 1 and 1b.

[Col. 1135, Matthias, Agritius, and Maximinus.] For the relics, 5c and 6b read `collata` (brought together) for `collocata` (placed); 5 and 6 omit from `tunica` (the tunic) through `reconditae sunt` (were deposited). The *Life of Agritius*, p. 778, is cited for `Ossa ... collocata sunt` (the bones ... were placed), and Calmet says that `Ossa ... reconditae sunt` (the bones ... were deposited) is absent from the old Saint-Matthias manuscript. The particle `-que` in `sepultusque` (and was buried) is absent in 5. `Successet` (he succeeded) is the spelling of 1; 5b has `ipsius Agritii` (of Agritius himself) for `ipsius` (his). Eufratas appears as `Eufraten` in 1b, `Eufratem` in 5, and `Effratham` in 6; 1b supplies `Coloniensem` (of Cologne). B and C say `nec dicendum episcopum` (nor should he be called a bishop), and 5b adds: `cum aliis multis Galliae episcopis tempore sancti Servacii, qui ... primam suam sententiam in Eufratem promulgavit` (with many other bishops of Gaul in the time of Saint Servatius, who pronounced his first sentence against Eufratas). B and C add `per electionem ecclesiae` (by election of the church).

[Col. 1135-1136, Athanasius and Maximinus.] C1, and C3 and following, correct `Athanasium` to `Athanasiumque` (and Athanasius); 5b calls Constantius `hereticus` (the heretic), and C omits `intrepidus` (fearless). The notes preserve `ne` in 5a-b for `nec` (and not), `ei ad latendum` in 6 (for him to hide), `eum inductis i[n]` in 6a (him, having been led in), `imperatoribus` in 1b (by emperors), `moniti` in 5-6 (warned), `totis` in 1 and 1b (all), and `concertaverunt` in 1b (they strove). Witness 2 omits `certe` (at least), 5-6 add `ejus` (his) to `caput` (head), and the final verb is `adtulissent` (had brought) in 5c, `detulisset` (had brought, singular) in 5a and 6; C1 corrects the plural to the singular, followed by C3 onward. 1b reads `Verumtamen` (nevertheless). In the cistern episode 1b has `habens` (having) and 5b `et habens` (and having), while 5-6 read `mortuorum` (of the dead) for `sanctorum` (of saints). B6 omits `numquam` (never). B reads `ibi psalmum Quicumque` (there the psalm *Quicumque*) instead of `ibi fidem catholicam ... Quicumque vult` (there the Catholic faith ... *Quicumque vult*); 5b expands `i.` as `id est` (that is). The editor attributes the narrative from `Sed` (but) through `locum` (place) to Rufinus and reports, on Calmet's evidence, that it is absent from the old Saint-Matthias manuscript. `Laternam`/ `lanternam` (lantern) are the readings of 5a and 5b-c, 6 for `latebram` (hiding-place), and 2 and 6 read `proditus` (betrayed) for `sollicitatus` (troubled). 5c's `in cisternam porrexit` (went on into the cistern) is a corrupt alternative to Maximinus's journey to Aquitania.

[Col. 1136-1138, Lubentius, Paulinus, and the Greeks.] The continuation is said to be told more fully in the *Life of Maximinus*, chapters 7-8. B and C add that Lubentius first, `presbyterii honore praeditus` (endowed with the dignity of priesthood), served the Lord among the people in a church on a mountain beside Cuberna; the nested note identifies Coverna as Kobern on the Moselle. 5b omits `per revelationem Domini` (through a revelation of the Lord); 1 reads `Germaniae` (of Germany) and 1b `partes Germaniae` (the regions of Germany). At the river, 5a has `ubique` (everywhere), 5b `ubi` (where), and the forms are `Logona` in 2 and `Logana` in 5a-c, 6, B, C. The quoted *Life of Saint Lubentius* contains three printed gaps; each is [lacuna]: after Loginstein, after the region's castles and commerce, and before the return and burial of the patron. 5 omits `et in ea requiescit` (and he rests in it); B-C add `quo postea defunctus translatus requiescit` (where, after he died, he was transferred and rests). Paulinus is `destinatus` (appointed) in 1b, `ac` (and) in 6, `gentibus` (peoples) corrected to `gentilibus` (pagans) in 1, and `paganis` (to the pagans) in 2, 5, 6; 5 omits the provocation and 5-6 omit the beheading. C6 gives the date as the second, perhaps fifth, day before the Kalends of August. The Greek-invasion appendix says that Saint Matthias reads `supra` (upon) and `insuper` (and upon), omits `prima` (first), has Constantius for Constans and `quia` (because) for `qui` (who), reads `Galliae` (of Gaul) and `Romanis` (the Romans), and Saint Gislenus has Totila for Attila. These are readings of the quoted three-scourges passage, not alterations to its historical claim.

[Col. 1137-1141, Maximus, Martin, and Ambrose.] The Maximus lemma is `quidam` (a certain man) in 2 and 5, `vir quidam` (a certain man) in B-C, with Orosius; the disputed phrase is `sacramenta` (oaths) in 2, 5b-c, 6, `sacramenta fidei` (oaths of faith) in 5c, and `sacram` (the sacred oath) in 5a. The heresy is plural `haereses` in 1; Abila appears as `babile`, corrected to `abile` in 5a; Priscillian is `Maximinus` in 6b, as is the later order in 5b and 6b. Evodius's verb is `post` (afterwards) added in 1; `Latinianus` is in 2, `Latronia` in 4-6, and 5 supplies `et F[elicissimum]` (and Felicissimus). The final phrase is `erroribus suis` (their errors) in 1, 1b, 5 and corrupt `consortitus` in 1b for `consortibus` (associates). For the council, 2, 5, 6 read `damnandam` (to be condemned) and B-C `plenius` (more fully). B-C add `et Augustinus magnus` (and the great Augustine), but the editor states that Augustine certainly did not come to Treveris. In the Martin narrative B4 adds `quam postea` (as afterwards); `inferiorum` (of lower-ranking judges) is B4's reading, and B6 omits the conclusion leaving a blank. The entire Martin material is from Severus, *Life*, chapters 16-18, and the banquet from chapter 20; the empress's service is `ei` (to him) in *Dialogue* II.6.

[Col. 1139-1142, Ambrose, Felix, and Pontianus.] The grammatical subject in the Ambrose passage is Maximus: after Ambrose abstained from communion with the bishops, Maximus, angered, ordered Ambrose to depart. The manuscript forms retain `ad palatium` (to the palace) in 5-6, `ab eo abstinere` (to abstain from him) in 2, 5, 6, `deliquit` (sinned) in 6, `communicans` (communicating) corrected in C1 and C3 onward, `regredi ipse` (to return himself) corrected from `regreduipsi` in 1, and `ingredi` (to enter) in 2, 4, 5, 6. Iminius is `Imineus` in 6, `Iumnus?` in 5a, and `Martinus` in 5c. The long B-C continuation beginning `Congregati itaque episcopi` (therefore the bishops gathered) is from Severus, *Dialogues* III.11-12: it records `Princillianus` in B6, `Hyspaniam` in C, `officionalibus` in B6, a form of `officialibus` (officials); B4 and 6 read `vitaretur` (was avoided), which C1 corrects to `vetaretur` (was forbidden), and `pacem` (peace, accusative) in B6. The following continuation from Severus III.12-13 says that the emperor's decision concerned public judges rather than priests; C1 adds in the margin `debere puniri` (ought to be punished). For Felix, 1b reads `post tridue` (after three days), B-C `postpridie` (on the next day), 2/5/B2/6 `Britonem`, 6a then 6b-c correct `Britonum` to `Britonium`, C3 has `oratio` (prayer), C4 `ordinatio` (ordination) written above it, and C6 offers either. B2 omits from `Huius` through `consulere` (his ... to provide for).

[Col. 1141, Pontianus.] `Palacio` (palace) corrects 1's `pacio`; the name is `Ponticianus` in 1 and later `Pontitianus` in 1. The guard's companions are `tres alii` (three others) in 2, while 5a-b, 6 read `ortos` for `hortos` (gardens); 5a-c have `muro` (wall), 5b/B/C `muris` (walls), and 6a-c correct `muros` to `muro`. B2 reads `uni` (one), and 1b `illi fore uno` (that one remained with him); 1b omits the poor servants of God. `Sancti Antonii` (of Saint Antony) is B-C, `Anthonii` 5a-b. The reader is `accendi` (to be kindled) in B2, corrected from `accendere` in C1 and C3 onward; 2, 5, 6 omit it. `Immitari` (to imitate) is 1; 5-6 have `adversari` (to oppose), corrected from `aversari` in C1 and later C. The companion's `tali militia` (such military service) in 5-6 corrects `talem miliciam` in C1 and later C. The closing account has corrupt `fortima` in 1 where the printed narrative has `fortuna` (fortune or destiny); B-C read `formata` (formed), and Augustine has `firmata` (made firm), which the editor thinks manuscript 1 corrupted; 1b adds `pie et` (and devoutly), 1/1b/5 have `gratulati` (having rejoiced), and B-C read `dicaverunt` (consecrated) for `dedicarunt` (dedicated).

### 22

[Note: Chapter 35; Leibniz II, chapter 12, C.]

Maximus [Note: Corrected from another reading in manuscript 1.]—our author has conflated Maximus, who was killed according to Orosius VII.35 and Gregory of Tours II.19; but the words concerning the princes of Trier are his own—emperor from Trier, moving out with a great army, made his son Victor emperor while he was still a child and left Quintinus and Namneus, princes of Trier, as his guardians. [Note: “Maximo” in manuscripts 5 and 6.] [Note: “Maximus” is absent in 1? and in B and C; “se” is absent in manuscript 5b; “victorem … tutores” are absent in manuscript 5.] [Note: “s. f.” in 6a; “in” is absent in 2 and 6.] [Note: “Namneus” appears as “Maneus” in 5, “Mammeus” in 6.] [Note: The phrase “princes of Trier” is absent in 5c.] He himself was afterward killed by Theodosius in Italy, and his son too was killed by the sword, to win Theodosius’ favor. [Note: “In the grace of Theodosius” in manuscript 1b.]

—Now let us return to what came before and say something about Saint Felix. [Note: “Now let us return to the earlier matters and say something” in C; “corrected” in manuscript 1.] He built a large basilica in honor of the Mother of God in the Campus Martius, 410 feet long and 120 feet wide. [Note: “A certain” instead of “large” in 5a.] [Note: “In honor” is variously read as “honor” or “the honor”; manuscript 1b has “in honor of.”] [Note: The number is “310” in manuscript 6.] [Note: The Life of Saint Felix has the following: “A sufficiently spacious and magnificent church in the same city, built at his abundant expense in honor of the holy Mother of God and the martyrs of the Theban Legion …; for he had it made 410 feet in length and 120 feet in width.”] In it he honorably buried the bodies of the martyrs who had suffered under Rictiovarus, which until his time had lain scattered and unarranged. [Note: “Rictiovario” in manuscript 5b.] He also suspended, in the middle of a crypt made in the same monastery and with iron chains, the body of Saint Paulinus, which in his time the people of Trier had brought from Phrygia with forces gathered from the entire kingdom. [Note: “Paul” in manuscript 6c.] [Note: “The people of Trier” in manuscript 6.] [Note: “Up to their time” in 6; “the intervening time” is absent in 5c.] [Note: This account concerning Saint Felix derives from the lead tablet discovered in 1071, which the Life of Saint Felix also followed; see also the Life of Saint Agritius, January I, p. 775, and what Hontheim says about this narrative, *Prodr.* I, pp. 91 ff. The church was afterward named for Saint Paulinus. The matter is narrated differently in the Life of Paulinus (*Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, p. 678): “There stands, therefore, not far from the oratory of blessed Maximinus, a very distinguished basilica dedicated in honor of the holy Mother of God. There they placed the body of the most holy bishop and determined that a burial-place should be made there; and, constructing a crypt suitable for his bones, they had the sarcophagus hung with iron chains in the middle of the crypt.”]

He himself was also buried, after twelve years of his priesthood, in the right-hand part of that same church. [Note: “Twelve” is absent in B and C; “of his priesthood” is absent in B and C.] [Note: “Left-hand” in B and C.] [Note: Manuscript 1b adds in a later hand: “that is, toward the northern side of the choir.”] [Note: This appears to have been taken from the Life of Saint Felix.]

At the same time, under the elder Theodosius, the Franks, breaking into Germany with their leaders Sunno and Gundobaud and ravaging the districts, also struck fear into Cologne. [Note: This account of the Franks, Quintinus, and their victory is taken from Fredegar, *Chronicle*, epitome, chapter 3.] [Note: “Germany” is spelled variously in manuscripts 5 and 6.] [Note: The reading “pagos,” districts, is found in 5 and 6; “pagans” in 1 and 1b.] When this had been reported to the people of Trier, Namneus and Quintinus, whom we mentioned above and to whom Maximus had entrusted the guardianship of his son’s childhood and the defense of Gaul, gathered an army, drove the Franks out of Germany, and defeated them with great slaughter near the Carbonarian Forest. [Note: The name appears as “Maneus,” “Manneus,” “Mammeus,” or “Namneus” in the manuscripts.] [Note: The phrase concerning the boy’s guardianship and the defense of Gaul is variously abbreviated or expanded in the witnesses.] [Note: “Drove out” is read as “defeated” in B2; B6 reads “the Franks defeated the Germans.”]

From this arose the hatred of the Franks against the people of Trier; and thereafter, having crossed the Rhine, they dared to winter in the territory of Trier. [Note: “From this” is read “from there” in 5a.] [Note: “Rhine” is abbreviated in B and C.] [Note: “To winter” is spelled “to pass the winter” in 1b.] [Note: This passage, beginning “They dared,” is taken from Fredegar, same place, chapter 4.] [Note: “They did not dare” in 5 and 6; B and C read “they began.”]

After these events, therefore, in the time of the emperor Honorius, Crocus [Note: “Crocius” in 6a.] [Note: This is taken from Fredegar III.11, in Canisius, ed. Basnage II.1, p. 191.] king of the Vandals, having departed from his homeland with the Suebi and Alans and making for Gaul, followed the wickedest counsel of his mother. [Note: “Suebi” is spelled “Swevi” in C and 1.] [Note: “Alans” appears as “Alamanni” or “Alemanni” in several witnesses.] [Note: “Having departed” is expanded to “he departed” in 6.] She had said to him:

“If you wish to do something new and acquire a name, destroy everything that others have built, and kill the people whom you overcome. For you cannot build better and more costly buildings, nor accomplish any greater deed by which you may raise your name.” [Note: The manuscripts vary between “you can” and “you will be able”; some read “a greater undertaking.”]

Crossing the Rhine at Mainz by an ingenious bridge, he first destroyed the city itself together with its people. [Note: “Mainz” appears as Mogontia, Maguntia, or Moguntia; manuscript 1b reads “by a bridge.”] [Note: B2 reads “by a bridge ingeniously constructed.”] Then, blockading all the cities of Germany, he reached Metz. [Note: “Metz” appears as Metis, Methis, or Metus.] There, when the city wall collapsed by divine providence, the city was captured by the Vandals. [Note: One manuscript reads “when the wall of the city, its protection, collapsed.”]

Next he blockaded and captured the city of Trier, which was scarcely yet recovering from the persecution of the Greeks, and threw its great buildings to the ground. [Note: The phrase “Then … he threw down” was added by the author; after it he inserted the words “that is, in the amphitheater.”] [Note: “The city of Trier” is variously abbreviated.] A considerable part of the citizens was saved in the city’s arena, that is, in the amphitheater, which they had fortified. [Note: “Arena” is read as “amphitheater”; one witness has “amphitheaters, which they had fortified for spectacles.”]

After this Crocus wandered through all the cities of Gaul and laid siege to Arles. There he was captured by a certain soldier named Marius, bound in chains, and led through all the cities that he had devastated. He ended his impious life by a fitting death. [Note: “Crocus” is spelled “Crocius” in 6a; “Arles” is miswritten “Arelanum” in some witnesses; Marius is absent in 5c and appears as Marcius in B6.] [Note: “Of Gaul” is added in manuscripts 2, 5, and 6.]

[Note: I do not know from where the author took this. Perhaps, when he read that the whole of Gaul had been devastated by the Huns, he extended the same conclusion to the city of Trier by a sufficiently plausible conjecture; see Brower, p. 288.]

A short time later, while Theodosius the Younger was reigning, Attila, king of the Huns, gained possession of the city of Trier by war and grievously ravaged it. [Note: “A.D. 427” is added in 5a; “after Theodosius” in 5c; another manuscript gives “in the year 927 after the younger emperor.”] [Note: “Attila” is written “Atilla” or “Attilia”; B2 has the superscript “Hezelo.” Several manuscripts add “king of the Huns.”]

After the death of Valentinian, who had ruled together with Marcian after Theodosius, Avitus assumed the empire. [Note: “Proavitus” in 5 and 6, and likewise below.] Under him the city of Trier was exposed to the mockery of the Franks. [Note: “To the mockery of the Franks” is read “to the Frankish plunder” in 6.]

There was in the city a senator named Lucius, who had a very beautiful wife. [Note: This account, through “burned,” is taken from Fredegar, *Chronicle*, epitome, chapter 7. Brower, p. 296, says: “There came into my hands, in the ancient library at Cusa, the membranes of the Roman provinces, which referred this memory of the senator Lucius and the catastrophe of Trier to the authority of the ancient historian Hypatius; hence it is credible that others took their account from there.”] Avitus fell passionately in love with her with disgraceful desire. Pretending to be ill, he ordered all the senatorial women of the city to visit him. Among the others came Lucius’ wife, and he violated her; she quietly returned home to her husband. [Note: “He sent her home” in manuscript 5.] The next day, rising from his bed, Avitus said to Lucius: “You have beautiful baths, but you bathe in cold water.” [Note: “Beautiful troops” is an alternative reading in B2; the wording is corrected in manuscript 1.]

Lucius, enraged, betrayed the city to the Franks. They plundered it, killed many people, and burned it. [Note: “He betrayed it to the Franks” is read “he handed it over to the Franks” in 5; “in flight” in 6a–b.] After Trier had been captured and burned, the Franks also captured Cologne. [Note: The manuscripts variously read “Trier, captured and burned,” or “Trier, which they captured and burned.”] [Note: *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 8.]

Thus the name and kingdom of the Gauls and Germans came to an end, and that of the Franks arose. [Note: “And the name” is absent in 5a–b; “the name” is absent in 5c.]

### 23

[Note: Chapter 36; Leibniz. Here book III ends, and book IV begins at this point in manuscript 6c.]

After the death of Saint Felix—to return to the point from which we digressed for a little while—Mauricius became bishop of Trier. [Note: “From where we withdrew” in 6.] [Note: Compare the catalogues of these names published by Hontheim and others.] After him came Saint Legontius; then Saint Auctor; after him Saint Severus. [Note: “Leguntius,” “Leoncius,” and “Ligontius” are variant forms. One witness adds: “Then, after Mauricius, Saint Leguntius became bishop of Trier. After him, Auctor; after him, Severus.”] [Note: The Life of Saint Auctor, written after the famous translation of his body in 1113, is in *Acta Sanctorum*, August IV, p. 45; the author of the *Deeds* could not have used it.]

Severus, in all things comparable to the apostolic men, preached the word of God throughout Germany and, together with blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, and Lupus of Troyes, destroyed the Pelagian heresy in Britain. [Note: These words, “he destroyed,” may have been taken from Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation* I.21; compare the Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, *Acta Sanctorum*, July VII, p. 216.] [Note: “The word of God” is absent in manuscript 1.] [Note: “Germanus of Paris” and “Lupus of Troyes” have variant spellings in the witnesses.]

He was succeeded by blessed Cyril. Cyril restored the cell of Saint Eucharius, which had been burned and abandoned, and established a monastery not far from the former site. There he transferred the bodies of Saints Eucharius and his successors. He himself also rests beside them. [Note: “Saint” is absent in 5b; “monastery also” in B2; “there” is read “in that place” in B6.]

[Note: Brower, p. 297, gives ancient verses which he thinks preserve a memorial of the old basilica and of its restoration by Cyril:

“Here divine power joins in fitting harmony  
The bodies of two priests whom this place adorns;  
It speaks of Eucharius and Valerius together.

Glad to prepare a seat for victorious limbs,  
Cyril places this altar for the holy brothers;  
The holy surveyor adorns a lodging for the body.”]

After Cyril, Jamnerius succeeded him; Emerus followed Jamnerius; and Emerus appointed Marus after himself. [Note: The name appears as Jamnerius, Jannerius, or Lamnerius; B2 omits it.] Marus restored the monastery of Saint Paulinus, which had been left desolate by the barbarians amid the devastations of the city; there he too was buried and now rests. [Note: “The city” is variously read as “the city’s devastators” or “the city devastated by the aforesaid ravagers.”]

[Note: Compare the brief account of Saint Marus, published from a manuscript of Saint Maximinus in *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 730. I should nevertheless judge it later than our *Deeds*. Brower, p. 299, gives a funerary inscription which reads: “The whole book of his life contains [his deeds].” But if the author of the *Deeds* had possessed such a Life, he would certainly have reported more of his acts.]

Volusianus succeeded him. He caused the privilege formerly delegated to this city by Pope Sylvester through blessed Agricus—but erased at Rome in his own time—to be rewritten by the Roman pontiff, and renewed the ancient dignity of his city. [Note: The phrase “in his own time” is read “at that time” in manuscripts 5 and 6.] [Note: Compare the charter above, chapter 18. In the Verdun manuscript, seen by Calmet and Wilthemius, it reads: “The privilege which Volusianus, the archbishop, ordered to be written down”; see Calmet, *History of Lorraine* I, p. 11 n., and Hontheim, *Diplomatic History* I, p. 17 n.] [Note: Some witnesses add: “After him Hildolphus, then Severinus.”]

After him Miletus governed the church; then Modestus; next Maximianus; after him Fibicius, succeeded by Abrunculus; then Rusticus. [Note: The names have numerous orthographic variants, including Fibictus, Arunculus, and Aprunculus.]

Rusticus was at first blameworthy, but afterward corrected through blessed Goar. He performed penance for seven years enclosed in the church of blessed Mary called *Litus ad Martyres*. [Note: “At first blameworthy, but afterward corrected” is variously abbreviated in the witnesses.] [Note: “Four years” is read in B6.] [Note: “He did penance” is read “he performed penance” in B2.] [Note: Compare the Life of Saint Goar, chapters 11–12, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* II, where Goar is said to have promised seven years of penance for the bishop. On the period of Rusticus, see Rettberg I, p. 465.]

[Note: Manuscript 5b adds: “This correction happened as follows. When Saint Goar was living in a little cell on the bank of the Rhine, near the river called the Wocara, many relics … he rested in peace,” from an older Life of Saint Goar; it then continues: “After Rusticus died, Aponoculus …”]

When Rusticus died, Aponoculus succeeded him. During his time, Illidius was priest of the church of Clermont. [Note: The words from “During whose time” to “was buried” are absent from Dacherius’ edition but occur in manuscripts 6a and 6b.] [Note: The name of Clermont appears as Arvernis or Arvernensis.]

As Illidius’ reputation rose through the various levels of the Church, it penetrated even to the boundaries of neighboring cities. [Note: “Was carried upward” is a variant reading.] Thus it happened that, when this fame reached the ears of the emperor of Trier, whose daughter was tormented by an unclean spirit and no one could be found who could free her, fame revealed the blessed Illidius. [Note: “Emperor of Trier” is the reading of the source; the manuscripts vary between “emperor of Trier” and “emperor of the Treveri.”]

Immediately the emperor sent servants, who found the holy old man at Clermont and brought him before the king at Trier. [Note: “Presented him to the king” is read “presented him” in manuscript 6.] He was received with reverence. The king complained to him about the miserable condition of his daughter.

Illidius, trusting in the Lord, devoted himself to prayer throughout the night. Then, placing his fingers in the girl’s mouth, he drove the evil spirit out of the possessed body. [Note: “Into the girl’s mouth” is read “in the whole mouth” in B6.]

When the emperor saw this miracle, he offered the holy priest enormous heaps of gold and silver. [Note: “Gold and silver” is read “gold and of silver” in 6.] Illidius rejected them, but obtained this instead: that the city of Clermont, which had been paying tribute in the form of grain and wine, should pay in gold, because these supplies were conveyed to the imperial storehouse with great labor. [Note: The manuscripts vary between “because they were brought with great labor,” “because of great scarcity,” and “because they were brought with great difficulty to the imperial treasury.”]

Saint Illidius, after completing the allotted time of his present life, departed to Christ in the very course of life and was carried by his people to his own city and buried there. [Note: The wording is variously expanded as “in the course of his present life,” “after the time of his present life had been completed,” or “in the midst of the course of this life.”]

### 24

[Note: Chapter 37; Leibniz.]

At that time King Theoderic brought many clerics from the people of Clermont and ordered them to serve in the church of Trier, in the service of the Lord. [Note: This account through the request for Gallus is taken from Gregory of Tours, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6.] But he absolutely refused to allow blessed Gallus to separate from him.

When Bishop Aponoculus died, the clerics of Trier assembled before King Theoderic and requested Saint Gallus as bishop. [Note: “The clerics of Trier” is abbreviated in 6.] He said to them:

“Go and seek another. I have destined Gallus the deacon for another place.” [Note: One manuscript reads “I have assigned Gallus the deacon elsewhere.”]

They then chose Saint Nicetius and appointed him bishop. He had been abbot of the city of Limoges, around the year 530. [Note: Compare the same work, chapter 17.]

Magnericus succeeded him, around the year 570, as a disciple of that same Nicetius. [Note: “Nicetius” has several variant spellings.] [Note: This account is taken from the Life of Saint Magnericus, written by Eberwinus in the tenth century, *Acta Sanctorum*, July VI, p. 283.]

During Magnericus’ time, men of great holiness flourished in the parish of Trier: namely, Paul on Mount Cebenna, which to this day is called Paul’s Mountain from his name; Ingobertus; Disibodus; Wandelinus; Carilelfus; and a certain Lombard named Vulfilaicus; also the priest Bantus and his brother in name and conduct, Beatus. Many others likewise lived the eremitical life. [Note: The Life mentioned above says: “We found Paul, Ingobertus, Disibodus, and Wandelinus serving in the Vosges, in his bishopric. For that forest, beginning at the Alps and Mount Jura, reaches almost to the borders nearest the city of Trier; but across the extended mountain ridges it stretches far northward along the course of the Rhine … In the borders of the same Vosges adjoining the city of Trier, some men from the city itself sought out the vast wilderness, then wooded and uncultivated, but now cleared and cultivated.” The Life then speaks first of Carilelfus, next of Bantus and Beatus, and afterward of Vulfilaicus.] [Note: The name Disibodus has many variant forms. Manuscript B2 adds: “and Saint Dysibodus, whose name and virtues now make the mountain renowned; there this servant of God is known to have led an eremitical life, and there his blessed relics are buried.”] [Note: “Lombard” is spelled “Langobard” in 5c and 6.]

Bishop Magnericus restored the ancient sanctuaries of God to their former honor and built churches in honor of blessed Martin: one on a mountain in the district of Vabrensis, another in a village called Carta Domus, and a third in the city itself. [Note: The region between the Meuse and the Moselle, called Vaivre in French.] [Note: “Carta” is read “Cara” in manuscripts 5 and 6.] In the latter he too was buried after completing the course of his life. [Note: Manuscript C6 has in the margin: “The eighth day before the Kalends of July.”] [Note: The celebrated monastery of Saint Martin at Trier is involved here; its brief history is drawn from the Life of Magnericus below.] [Note: Manuscripts B and C instead add: “a third on Mount Jura, which is called from Saint Martin,” and “a fourth” in the city itself. This mountain is called Mertesberg in German; the monastery was transferred into the city in 1287.]

Gaugericus, his disciple, succeeded him. [Note: The catalogues call the Trier bishop Gundericus, while the Life of Magnericus calls this man Gaugericus, who was actually bishop of Cambrai; compare *Acta Sanctorum*, August II, p. 671.] He had been educated in the fortress of Trier. [Note: Manuscripts B and C add “Evosium,” that is, Ivois or Iwers. The Life of Saint Magnericus likewise says: “It happened that he came to a fortress called Ivosium.”]

When Gaugericus also died, Sabaudus assumed the episcopate. [Note: The name appears as Sabano or possibly Sabario.] After him Severinus governed the church. [Note: Manuscripts B and C add: “worthy of divine address. The Lord told him to migrate from his see to Bordeaux and preach the word of God there. As he was traveling there, blessed Amandus, bishop of that church, likewise warned by the Lord, came out to meet him beyond the camp. He received him after bringing him in honorably, then yielded the place to him, leaving the see to Severinus; there he was buried and now rests.” This is taken from the Life of Saint Severinus.]

Next Modowaldus assumed the episcopate in the time of Dagobert, around the year 620. [Note: “In the year 707” is written in the margin of manuscript C6.] [Note: “In the time” is read “in the year” in manuscripts 2, 5, and 6.]

That Dagobert bestowed many benefits on the church of Trier and on blessed Modowaldus. [Note: Manuscript C adds: “as may be learned from his charter, which we thought appropriate not to pass over in silence here:

*The Testament of Dagobert, King of the Franks.*

‘Dagobert, king of the Franks, to illustrious men … Pippin, mayor of the palace …’”]

[Note: We have omitted the charters which manuscript C inserted into the text; they are to be published and discussed elsewhere. See this one in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 76.]

That bishop built a church in Dagobert’s palace, called *Orreum*—the ancient Roman granary—in honor of blessed Mary the Virgin. [Note: The manuscripts read either *Orreum* or *Horreum*.] [Note: The ancient Roman granary, later the palace of the Frankish kings and then a monastery of nuns, is now the poorhouse and hospital of Trier.]

There he also established a community of virgins. [Note: Manuscript B reads:

“Whom he appointed as their first mother was Modesta, a most holy virgin in life and name, a foster-child of the monastery of Mount Romaric, whom some believe to have been the sister of blessed Willibrord and a contemporary of the blessed virgin Gertrude. Then, likewise, the virgin Yrmina, beloved of God, daughter of King Dagobert himself, and afterward the virgin Anastasia; Basilissa succeeded her.

Manuscript C reads: ‘First, the beloved of God, Yrmina, daughter of Dagobert, then Modesta, foster-child of Mount Romaric, who was the daughter of the sister of blessed Modowaldus and a contemporary of the blessed virgin Gertrude. After Modesta, the holy virgins Anastasia and Basilissa succeeded her.’

The bishop mentioned above obtained from the Apostolic See a privilege concerning the immunity and freedom of that church, but the charter itself has been omitted in manuscript C.”]

It had the following form:

*Privilege of Pope Leo III.*

“I, Leo, vicar of Saint Peter … by privilege. Let it be done. Let it be done. Amen. Amen.

Chapter 13. The bishop so often mentioned established another, and so forth.”

### Complete textual apparatus

The following entries preserve the individual readings which accompany the translated text above. Numbers are the source’s witness sigla; *deest* means “is absent,” and *corr.* means “corrected.”

**Chapter 22 — Maximus and Felix.** The heading is “chapter 35, Leibniz II, chapter 12, C.” In 1 *Maximus* is corrected. The editor says that the author combined accounts of Maximus’ death from Orosius VII.35 and Gregory of Tours II.19, though the words “princes of Trier” are his own. 5, 6, and B read *maximo*, “with a very great,” for *magno*, “great.” In 1? and B–C *se* is absent; 5b lacks *se movens*, “setting himself in motion,” and 5 lacks the whole stretch “Victor … guardians.” 6a abbreviates “his son,” while 2 and 6 omit *in*, “in.” Namneus is *Maneum* in 5 and *Mammeum* in 6; 5c omits “princes of Trier.” 1b reads *in gratiam Theodosii gladio*, “by the sword for Theodosius’ favor.”

For Felix, C reads “now let us return to the earlier matters and say something”; 1 has a correction. 5a has *quandam*, “a certain [basilica],” for “large.” 2, 5, and 6 have *honorem*, “honor,” for *in honore*, “in honor of”; 1b has *gloriam Dei*, “the glory of God.” 6 gives CCCX, 310, rather than 410. The Life of Felix says: “In the same city he built, at great expense, a sufficiently spacious and splendid church in honor of the holy Mother of God and the martyrs of the Theban Legion …; he made it 410 feet long and 120 wide.” 5b has *Rictiovario*. 6 reads *usque ad [sua] tempora*, “up to [his] time,” and 5c omits *tempora*, “time.” 6c has *Pauli*, “of Paul”; 6, *Treberorum populus*, “the people of Trier.” The Felix narrative comes from the lead tablet found in 1071, followed by the Life of Felix; compare the Life of Agritius, January I, p. 775, Hontheim, *Prodr.* I, 91 ff. The church was later called Saint Paulinus’. The Life of Paulinus instead says that near Maximinus’ oratory a renowned basilica of the Mother of God received the saint’s body; a crypt fit for his bones was built, and its sarcophagus was hung on iron chains in the middle. This following notice appears to derive from the Life of Felix.

5 and 6 omit “he himself”; 6, B, and C have *XII annis*, “twelve years”; B and C omit “of his priesthood.” 6 has *cornu dextro*, “right side,” whereas B–C have *sinistro*, “left”; 1b adds in a later hand, “that is, toward the northern side of the choir.” 2 omits *ejusdem*, “that same”; 5 omits “was buried,” 5b omits “was buried” together, and 6c transposes it.

**The Franks, Crocus, Attila, and Avitus.** The Frankish passage through Quintinus and the victory is from Fredegar, epitome, ch. 3. 5–6 have *Germaniam* for *Germania*; 1–1b have *paganosque*, “and the pagans,” for *pagosque*, “and the districts,” while 5–6 retain *pagos*. B–C read *incusserunt*, “they struck fear.” 2, 5, 6, and B2 read *Treberis*, “at Trier”; 2 and 5 shorten the following words. Namneus is *Maneus* in 5a–b, *Manneus* in 5c and B6, *Mammeus* in 6, and *Nammeus* in B2. 5a–b read *in Franciam*, “into Francia”; 5c *infancia*, “childhood”; B2 *in faciem*; C expands: “whom Maximus had entrusted with the guardianship of his son’s childhood and the defense of Gaul.” B2 omits “out of Germany”; B2 reads *deiecerunt*, “threw down/defeated,” and B6, *Franci deiecerunt Germanos*, “the Franks defeated the Germans.” 6, B, and C transpose to *eos strage*, “them with slaughter.” 1 has *Treberos* for “people of Trier”; 5a *de hoc*, “from this”; B–C abbreviate *trans Rhenum*, “across the Rhine.” The following sentence is from Fredegar, ch. 4: 1 has *ihemare*, an alternative spelling of “to winter,” 1b *hiemantes*, “wintering”; 5–6 read *non praesumpserunt*, “they did not dare,” and B–C *ceperunt*, “they began.”

5b–c call this “at this time”; 5a adds A.D. 413; 5b adds “namely A.D. 913 after the emperor”; 5c adds “A.D. 914 after [he had left] his homeland.” Crocus is *Crocius* in 6a. This is Fredegar III.11 (Canisius, Basnage II.1, p.191). C and 1 have *Sweuis*, “Suebi”; 1 corrects *lanis* to *alanis*, 1b, 5, and C have *Alamannis*, and 6 *Alemannis*, for “Alans.” 6 expands “he set out.” 2, 5, and 6 read *consilio matris nequissimo*, “by his mother’s most wicked counsel”; C1 corrects *consilium … nequissimum* to that reading, as C3 and later do. 1 supplies *vis*, “you wish,” after it; 1b, 2, 5, and 6 read it too, while B–C read *volueris*, “you shall wish.” 1b and 5 read *poteris*, “you will be able”; B–C *magnam rem*, “a great undertaking.”

1 has *Mogontiam*, 5a–b *Magunciam*, 5c–6 *Moguntiam*, for Mainz; 1b reads *ponto*, “by a bridge,” and B2 *ingenioso facto*, “ingeniously made.” 5a and C have *primo*, “first”; B6 *cunctasque*, “all,” and 5 *quascunque*, “whatever,” while 6 omits the word. 1 corrects *vallens* to *vallans*, “besieging.” Metz is *Metis* in 2, 5, and B2, *Methis* in 5b, and *Metus* in B6. 6 reads “when the city wall, its defense, collapsed.” The editor says the author himself added “Then … threw down,” and then “that is, in the amphitheater.” 6b omits “scarcely”; 5 omits “its,” 5b “its great buildings,” and 6 adds “for the most part.” 1b corrects *Cujus* to *Civium*, “of the citizens”; 1 corrects *aliquanto* to *aliquanta*, “a considerable part.” 1 has *amphiteatrum*, and 1b *amphiteatra quae munere* (“amphitheaters which [were used] for spectacles”), then corrects it.

Arles is *Arelanum* in 5a and 6b; Marius is absent in 5c and *Marcio* in B6; 2, 5, and 6 add “of Gaul.” The editor does not know the author’s source for Attila; perhaps reading that the Huns devastated all Gaul, he plausibly extended it to Trier (Brower, 288). 5a adds A.D.427; 5c “after Theodosius,” and also “A.D.927 after the younger [Theodosius].” 6 has *imperante*, “reigning,” and 5b omits “the Younger.” Attila is *Attilla* in 1, *Attilia* in 5b, and B2 has *Hezelo* written above it; 2, 5, and 6 add “king of the Huns.” 5b reads *et*, “and,” for “it.” Avitus is *Proavitus* in 5–6 throughout below; 6 reads *praedae ludibrio*, “exposed to plunder.”

The Lucius-to-burning account is Fredegar, epitome, ch.7. Brower (296) reports ancient “membranes of the Roman provinces” from Cusa’s library that referred the Lucius story and Trier’s catastrophe to old Hypatius, from whom others may have taken it. 1b corrects *qua* to *quam*, “whom”; 1 has a correction at “disgraceful desire”; 5 says “sent [her] home.” 1 corrects *crastina* to *crastino*, “on the next day”; B–C read “from his own bed,” while 2, 5, and 6 omit “from bed.” 1 corrects *Luciam* to *Lucium*. 1 corrects the baths sentence; B2 has *turmas*, “troops,” and B–C *thermas habes*, “you have baths”; 5 says “you bathe in cold [water].” 6a–b read *fugiens prodidit*, “betrayed [it] while fleeing,” and 5 *Francis tradidit*, “handed it over to the Franks.” 1 has a correction and B–C omit “and [it was] burned.” 5 reads “burned Trier and captured it,” 6 “burned Trier and also captured [it],” and C1 corrects *captam* to *capta*. 6 has *diripuere*, “plundered,” and B *ceperunt*, “captured.” The reference is *Gesta Francorum*, ch.8. 5b has *Sicque*, “and thus”; 5a–b omit “name and,” and 5c omits “name.”

**Chapter 23.** The heading is chapter 36, Leibniz; 6c says, “Book III ends; book IV begins here.” 6 has *unde*, “from which,” for *a quo*. Compare catalogues of these names printed by Hontheim and others. Legontius is *Leguntius* in 5–6, *Leoncius* in B2, *Ligontius* in C; 5b expands the whole succession: Leguntius, Auctor, Severus. 2, 5, 6, B, and C omit “saint” before Auctor; 2, 5, and 6 omit “saint” before Severus, and 1 corrects *Severus*. The Life of Auctor was written after the celebrated 1113 translation of his body (*AASS*, Aug. IV, 45), so the author could not have used it.

The sentence through “destroyed” may be from Bede I.21; compare the Life of Germanus of Auxerre (*AASS*, Jul. VII,216). 1 omits “word of God”; 5–6 omit “blessed”; Lupus’ place is *Trecassano* in 5b, *Trecasseno* in B2, *Trecaseno* in B4 and 6, corrected to *Trecassino* in C1; 5a–c read *Britanniam*, “Britain.” 5b omits “Saint” before Eucharius; B2 has *monasterium quoque*, “the monastery also”; 5a–c *priore*, “earlier”; B6 *illic*, “there”; 5b omits “the bodies of saints”; 6 has *successorumque*, “and his successors.” 6b spells “rested” *requieuit*. The Cyril verses are Brower’s ancient inscription; *victuris membris* means “victorious limbs,” not merely “limbs that will live.” B2, B4, and 6 spell Cyril *Quirillus*; C continues “after Cyril,” while 5c omits the whole Cyril-to-rests clause.

Jamnerius is omitted in B2; it is *Iannerius/Iannerium* in 2 and 5c, *Lamnerius/Lamnerium* in 5a, 6, B6, and C adds words after it. The editor suggests he may be the Jamblichus praised by Auspicius (Hontheim I,20). Emerus is *Emerius* in 2,5,6. 6 reads “followed him”; 5–6 *qui Marum*, “who [appointed] Marus,” and 2 *Marium*. 1 has *urbem*, “city,” 5–6 *vastatoribus*, “ravagers,” and 6 *vastatione urbis*, “devastation of the city.” 5 omits “was buried”; 6 *quiescit*, “rests,” and 5b begins “his successor.” Compare the short Life of Marus from St Maximinus’ manuscript (*AASS*, Jan.I,730), which the editor judges later than these *Deeds*; Brower (299) prints the epitaph, “the whole book of his Life contains [all this].” If the author had had such a Life, he would surely have given more deeds.

For Volusianus, B2 has *qui*, “who”; 5–6 read *suo iam*, “already in his own [time]”; 6 *a Romano*, “by a Roman”; 5–6 *pontifice*, “by the pontiff,” and 5c *describi*, “copied out,” where it later reads *pristinum*, “former.” In the Verdun codex used by Calmet and Wilthemius stands “the privilege which Archbishop Volusianus ordered written”; see Calmet, *History of Lorraine* I.11 n., Hontheim, *Diplomatic History* I.17 n. 5–6 add Hildolphus (6: *Hildolfus*) and then Severinus. Miletus is *Militus* in 5c, followed there by *Maximinus*; 5b has “after him,” B–C “after whom”; Fibicius is *Fibictus* in B2; Abrunculus *Arunculus* in 5b and *Aprunculus* in 5c. 5a–c read *post*, “after,” where 2 and 5b omit it.

Goar is *Goarum* in 5b and 6a, *Gainem* in 5c, *Gnarem* in B2; B6 reads *super*, “above,” and B6 gives four years. 1 corrects *clusus* to *reclusus*, “enclosed”; B2 *egit*, “performed [penance].” 5b adds from an older Life of Goar: “This correction happened thus. When Saint Goar lived in a cell on the bank of the Rhine near the river Wocara, many relics … he rested in good peace,” then continues, “After Rusticus died, Aponoculus.” Compare the Life of Goar 11–12 in Mabillon II, where Goar undertakes seven years’ penance for the bishop; see Rettberg I,465.

The text “during whose time” through the opening of chapter 24 is absent from Dacherius but present in 6a–b. Clermont is *Avernensi* in 2,5,6, *Arvernensi* in B2 and C1, *Avernensis* in B6 and C3; 6 has *praefuit*, “presided,” and 5 reverses “Illidius was priest.” The Illidius account through burial comes from Gregory of Tours, *Life of the Fathers*, ch.2. B2 has *evegitur*, “is carried upward”; B2 *ab*, “by,” for *a*; 2,5,6 *Avernis*, “at Clermont”; 6 *presentant*, “present”; 2?,5,6,B,C *excipitur*, “is received.” B6 has *in tota nocte*, “through the whole night”; 2,5c,B2 *incubuit*, “applied himself”; B2 has *ab* and *egit*, “drove [it] away.” 6 reads *et argenti*, “and of silver”; 1 *offret*, “offers.” Clermont is *Arvenna* in 5a–b and 6a; 6 reads *tributa quae*, “tributes which”; 1 corrects *que* to *quia*, “because.” 1 has *penurii*, “of scarcity”; 2,5,6 “they were conveyed in great scarcity” (6 singular), and 6 “to the imperial treasury.” 1–2 transpose “present life,” 5a–b “life present,” 6 inserts “years,” and 5b omits “in the course of life”; 5a,c,B2,B4,C transpose “was buried,” and 5b “was carried and was buried in his own city.”

**Chapter 24 and Magnericus.** The heading is chapter 37, Leibniz. B6 reads *eodem*, “at the same time”; the account through Nicetius is Gregory, *Life of the Fathers*, ch.6. Theoderic is *Theodricus* in 1 and often 5a; Arverni is corrected in 1b, *Avernis* in 2 and 5. The apparatus gives 6’s word order as *Treberici clerici*, “clerics of Trier”; 1–1b read *pendebat*, “was hanging,” a corrupt alternative to *petebant*, “they requested”; B–C place *episcopum* before *petebant*, “they requested [him as] bishop”; 1 *elientes*, “choosing”; Nicetius is *Nicecium* in 1–1b (later *Lemonicie*, Limoges) and *Nicetum* in 2. Compare the same work, ch.17. The Magnericus account is from Eberwinus’ tenth-century Life (*AASS*, Jul.VI,283); Nicetius is *Nicetis* in 1b, *Nicecii* in 2, *Necetii* in 5b.

The Life says that Paul, Ingobert, Disibod, and Wandelin served in the Vosges of Magnericus’ bishopric; that forest begins at the Alps and Jura, reaches almost to Trier, and stretches north along the Rhine; men from Trier sought its then wooded, uncultivated wilderness, now cultivated. It speaks first of Carilelfus, then Bantus and Beatus, then Vulfilaicus. 6c has *parrochiam*, “parish”; 5b omits “men”; Mount Cebenna is *Cebenam* in 1–1b; 5–6 omit “from,” the apparatus gives an abbreviated citation for 6 and B2: “Paul’s Mountain.” The editor identifies it with today’s S. Mark’s/Marchsberg and S. Paul’s/Paulusberg (Pulsberg), perhaps named from Zevene/Cevena, modern Zeben. Disibodus is *Disiobertus* in 2, *Disibocus* 5a, *Disobocus* 5b–c, *Disigotus* 6a–b, *Dissigodus* 6c, *Disobodus* B4–5; B2 adds Saint Dysibodus, whose name and virtues make the mountain famous, where he lived as a hermit and his blessed relics lie. Wandelinus is *Uandelinus* in 1, *Wandalinus* B–C; Carilelfus *Carilbelphus* 5b, *Carileffus* B and C, *Carilestus* B6; “Lombard” is *Langobardus* 5c–6; Vulfilaicus is abbreviated *Wolfil.* in 2,5,6,B,C; 1 has *brebiter*, “briefly,” and 1b omits “and priest”; 5c calls Bantus *Vantus*; 2 reads *eiusdemque*, “and of the same”; B–C omit “many others.”

At Magnericus’ churches, 6 has *a die tertio*, “on the third day”; 2?,B,C *honore*, “honor”; 1 *marti*, “of Martin”; Vabrensis is *Uaberensis* 6c. The editor locates the district between the Meuse and Moselle, French Vaivre. 5–6 have *Cara* for Carta; Carta Domus is Cardona/Carden on the Moselle, so named “contracted house” because it lies tightly enclosed by mountains. B and C add “on Mount Jura, called from Saint Martin,” then “a fourth [church]”; the German name is Mertesberg and the monastery moved into the city in 1287. The editor notes the famous Trier monastery of Saint Martin. B6 omits “in the city”; B–C read “after completing the course of his life”; C6 marginally gives VIII Kalends of July.

Gaugericus’ editor note identifies him as Magnericus’ disciple but bishop of Cambrai; Trier catalogues call its bishop Gundericus. B–C add *Evosio*, Ivois/Iwers; the Life says he came to the fortress Ivosium. 5b adds “when Gaugericus died”; Sabaudus is *Sabano* in 5, perhaps *Sabario* 5b; 1 has *pontificum*, “of bishops,” and 5–6 *pontificatum*, “the episcopate.” B–C add that Severinus was worthy of divine speech and was told by the Lord to leave his see for Bordeaux, where Amandus met him, received him honorably, yielded the see, and Severinus was buried; the readings are *Burdegolam* in B6 and C1 onward, with a correction from *Burdegalam*. This comes from the Life of Severinus (Hontheim III,975). Modowaldus is *Modoaldus* in 6; compare his Life by Stephen of Liège after 1107, where he succeeds Bishop Sebaudus. C6’s margin says A.D.707; 2,5,6 read *tempore*, “in the time”; 2,5,6,B2 “of King Dagobert,” C “of the king of the Franks,” while C calls him *Dagobertus rex*.

C adds that Dagobert’s charter shows his benefits and therefore includes the heading “Testament of Dagobert king of the Franks,” followed by “Dagobert, king of the Franks, to illustrious men … Pippin, mayor of the palace.” The editor omits the charters inserted by C, to publish and discuss them elsewhere; see Hontheim I,76. 1 has *placio*, “palace”; C calls him “of King Dagobert”; 6d starts its codex at *quod*, “which”; 1 *ita*, “thus,” while the remaining witnesses have *horreum*, “granary.” 2,5,6 have an expanded “he built a church in [the] palace,” with 5b–6a omitting *in*, 2 reading *honore*, and B–C “in honor”; the editor explains that the Roman granary became Frankish royal palace, then nuns’ monastery, and now Trier’s poorhouse and hospital. B6 adds “and there also”; 1b *constituit*, “established.” B’s and C’s full different lists of Modesta, Yrmina, Anastasia, and Basilissa, and the privilege of immunity and liberty, are translated immediately above; B2 spells Gertrude *Gertrhudis* and B5 *Gertrudis*, and C3 omits the charter itself.

Their mothers were Irmina [Note: [Col. 1149C] Concerning the authenticity of the diploma given by Dagobert to the monastery of Horres, with which this account agrees, see Hontheim, [Col. 1150C] *History* I, p. 87.] and Modesta, [Col. 1149B] daughters [Note: [Col. 1149] “daughter,” 5. In 5b, “Armina” and consistently “Dagobert” are read.] of Dagobert. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1149] “likewise” is absent in 2.], in the old palace situated in the suburb [Note: [Col. 1150C] Pfaltzel, north of the city of Trier; see Hontheim, *History* I, p. 23.] [Note: [Col. 1149] “old palaces in the suburb,” 1; “old suburb,” 1b.] he established a congregation [Note: [Col. 1149] “instituted,” 2, 5, and 5b; “instituted a congregation of virgins,” 6; “constituted,” B.] whose mother he appointed Basilissa [Note: [Col. 1152C] B and C read: “He likewise appointed as mother of them the daughter of King Dagobert, named Adela” [C: “Adhela”] [ [Col. 1152D] This agrees with the diploma in Hontheim I, p. 88.].]; and the church of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 1149] “Marti,” 1; “He constructed the church of Saint Martin and the church of Saint Symphorian,” 1b.] in the district of Megine [Note: [Col. 1149] “constructed in Megine,” C; “in Meginevelt,” 5a, 5b, and e; “Megine” is absent in 5c, which continues: “Likewise.”] [Note: [Col. 1150C] Meinfelt.]. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1153A] B and C read: “Likewise that venerable bishop Modowaldus constructed”] he constructed the church of Saint Symphorian on the bank of the Moselle [Note: [Col. 1150C] This church stood below Saint Martin’s. Wyttenbach. See below for the passage in the *Life of Saint Modoaldus*.], and there [Note: [Col. 1149] “there” is absent in 5b.] he established a congregation of virgins [Note: [Col. 1149] “instituted,” 5 and 6; see also B and C.] whose mother he appointed his sister, named Severa [Note: [Col. 1149] “sister,” 1; “instituted,” 1; “constituted,” 1b and 6.].

During his time the aforesaid Paul, who had been enclosed, departed for Theologia [Note: [Col. 1149] “theology,” 5; “Theologion,” 6.] [Note: [Col. 1150C] Tholey; compare Bertarius, *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, chapter 8, *MGH SS* IV, p. 43.], which the aforementioned King Dagobert had built on his own property [Col. 1150A] [Note: [Col. 1149] For *praefatus* (“aforesaid”), witnesses 1 and 1b read *fatus*; for *Dagobertus*, witnesses 5 and 6 read the abbreviated *r. d.*.], and there [Note: [Col. 1149] “there for a while,” 1768; “there,” 2, 5, and 6; 6d adds “he stayed.”] he remained for a short time. Afterwards, however, he undertook the governance of the church of Verdun [Note: [Col. 1149] “to be governed” is absent in 2, 5, and 6; B and C read “and assumed its governance.”], and there he rests.

Saint Modowaldus, too, after he had committed his blessed sister Severa, who was dying when the heavenly Bridegroom called her [Note: [Col. 1149] “already called her,” 5b; “also,” B 6.], to burial in the church [Note: [Col. 1149] “the church,” 1b and 5.] of Saint Symphorian [Note: [Col. 1149] “Sinphorian,” 1; “Symphorian,” B 2 and above] [Note: [Col. 1149] B and C read: “committed [her] to burial.”], himself soon afterwards departed to the Lord and was buried in the same church beside her [Note: [Col. 1149] “beside her,” B 2.] [Note: [Col. 1150C] Later he was transferred to the church of Saint Paulinus, where a tablet made of Parian marble celebrated his praises; Stephen cites it in his *Life*, pp. 56, 60, and Browerus on p. 353.].

Numerianus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1149] Chapter 38, Leibniz.]; Basinus succeeded Numerianus [Note: [Col. 1153A] B and C add: “who had been abbot of the cell [ [Col. 1153] “church,” B 6.] of Saint Hilary in the territory of Trier [ [Col. 1153C] Compare below, chapter 25. In the false diploma of Dagobert (in Hontheim, p. 76) we read: “the cell of Saint Hilary, which is now called Saint Maximin’s.” But in the *Life of Saint Basinus* (*Acta Sanctorum*, March I, p. 316): “not far from the walls of Trier, at the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist, which was situated in the suburb of that city toward the north, in the Field of Mars, and was designated by the name of Saint Maximin,” he is said to have entered and there become abbot.] ]; after him came Liutwinus [Note: [Col. 1149] “Lutiminus?” 5a; “Liutiminus,” 5b; “Lintwinus,” 5c; “Lutwinus,” 6a and b; “Luthwinus,” B 2, and below.], the son of Basinus’s sister [Note: [Col. 1149] “his Basinus,” B and C.].
