He was first duke of Belgic Gaul [Note: [Col. 1150C] These details were doubtless drawn from the unpublished *Life of Saint Liutwinus*, written in the eleventh century by Nithardus, or Nizo, abbot of Mediolacum; see *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, pp. 314 and 319. For the *Life of Saint Basinus*, see the preface, p. 115.] [Note: [Col. 1149] “Belgic,” 1.] and honored all the monasteries of this city with very generous gifts [Note: [Col. 1149] “with the richest gifts,” 5a; “with gifts,” 5a; “with gifts in possessions,” 5b.] and increased their estates [Note: [Col. 1149] “possessions,” 1b.]. Afterwards, on the river Saar [Note: [Col. 1149] “Sora,” 1; “Sora,” B 2; corrected to “Saroa,” 2; “Saroan,” 6a.] [Note: [Col. 1150C] Saar. The monastery is now called Mettlach.] he established a congregation of monks on his own property [Note: [Col. 1149] “on his own,” 6.]; there he himself also took up the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 1149] “monachic,” B and C.].

When his maternal uncle, Bishop Basinus [Note: [Col. 1149] “in the year,” 1; “Basinus,” 5b; “Saint Basinus himself,” e; “himself succeeded,” 1b.], died, he succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1149] “Basinus” added in 6b.]. He was also elected [Note: [Col. 1149] “from this point also elected,” 5b and c; “elected; he also,” 6.] and presided over Reims and Laon [Note: [Col. 1149] The source has *a Remensibus et Laudunensibus*, “by the people of Reims and Laon”; *a* is absent in witnesses 2, 5, and 6.]. In both cities, on the same day, with God’s assistance [Note: [Col. 1149] “by divine predestination,” 1b.], he celebrated the consecration of the sacred orders [Note: [Col. 1149] “of the sacred [feminine] order,” B 2; “of the orders,” 5.].

He died at Reims, and, being brought back by Milo his son [Note: [Col. 1149] “his own son,” 1b; “and by,” 5b.] and by the people of Trier, was buried at Mediolacum [Note: [Col. 1149] C 6 has in the margin: “the third day before the Kalends of September”] by a divine sign [Note: [Col. 1149] “given,” 5a and c.]. Afterwards, when the see of Metz had become vacant [Note: [Col. 1153A] The words “Afterwards ... became” are absent in B and C, which read: “When he had died, Clodulfus” [B 6: “Elodofus”].], the governance of the church of Trier was entrusted to Clodulfus, bishop of Metz and son of Saint Arnolfus. While he governed it, Milo, son of the aforementioned Bishop Liutwinus, occupied it—not, as some say, by ecclesiastical election, but by tyrannical seizure—in which nothing of cl[—the supplied source breaks off here].

Milo, his son, exercised the priestly office at Trier and Reims: at first indeed an imitator of his father, but later he became a tyrant, and in him nothing shone forth of clerical honor or life except the tonsure [Note: [Col. 1153A] B and C continue: “The reason for his seizure was as follows. At that time serious wars arose in this province between Charles and Raginfred, who were contending for supremacy. In order that Charles might obtain it by war, he bestowed bishoprics upon laymen ...”]. At that time [Note: [Col. 1151] “At that time,” 1.]—around the year 720 and thereafter—serious and internal, murderous wars [Note: [Col. 1151] Witness 6 reads *graviora*, “more serious,” for *gravia*; 5b reads *parricidialia*, 6 *parricidia*, and 5c *parricolia* for *parricidalia*, “murderous/civil-war-like.”] [Note: [Col. 1151D] The passage beginning “Wars ... bestowed” is taken from a letter of Hincmar, 6 (edited by Busaeus), p. 112, with a few words added here and there. The author of the *Life of Saint Rigobert* (*Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 177) and Flodoardus (*History of Reims* II.12) likewise followed Hincmar. I read a longer history of this period in Trier manuscript no. XXX; I mentioned it in *Archiv* VII, p. 517.] arose in this province, when the tyrant Charles gave bishoprics to laymen [Note: [Col. 1151] “gave,” 5 and 6.] and allowed the bishops to possess no authority [Note: [Col. 1151] “and” is absent in 1 and 1b.].

Milo, the aforementioned man, went to war with this Charles, being already a cleric only in tonsure, but in habit and conduct an irreligious layman [Note: [Col. 1151] This is absent in 5 and 6.]; after the victory, Charles bestowed upon him the bishoprics of Trier and Reims. During his disastrous time, much was taken from these churches [Note: [Col. 1151] “much was taken away,” B.], the possessions of the bishoprics were divided, the houses of religious persons were destroyed, and ecclesiastical discipline was scattered [Note: [Col. 1151] “lost,” 6; “destroyed,” 6a, c, and d; “dispersed,” B and C.], so completely that clerics, priests, monks, and nuns [Note: [Col. 1151] “and nuns” is absent in 6.] lived without ecclesiastical law [Col. 1151B] and possessed unauthorized refuges.

The evidence of this calamity is apparent in many churches of the parish of Trier [Note: [Col. 1151] “in more churches,” 5 and 6; “in the churches and parishes,” 5.], in each of which there had formerly been a separate congregation [Note: [Col. 1151] “there had been,” 5c and 6; “formerly each had,” 6.]. These congregations, stripped of their possessions by the aforementioned Milo and by other tyrants—not to call them bishops—can scarcely support a single priest [Note: [Col. 1151] “are scarcely able to support one priest,” 2, 5, and 6.]. Such are the church of Saint Medard, situated near the cell of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1151D] Near Saint Maternus, whose basilica was built close to the north of the basilica of Saint Eucharius the Confessor; see the charter of Archbishop Egbert in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 320.]; the church on the Saar called Tavena [Note: [Col. 1151] “of Tavena,” 5c; “Trauena,” 5b, 6a, b, and d; “Rauenna,” 5a and c.] [Note: [Col. 1151D] Taven, a place four thousand paces from Sarrebourg, as Browerus says on p. 565, who notes that this monastery was rebuilt in the eleventh century. The necrology of Saint Maximin says: “On the eighth day before the Ides of May: Wickerus, priest and abbot of our congregation, who built a monastery at Tavana and assigned estates to that place [Col. 1152D] and established twenty prebendaries there.”]; the church of Saint Symphorian, constructed by Saint Modowaldus [Note: [Col. 1152D] See above in this chapter]; the church founded by order of Blessed Helena in honor of the Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 1151] “founded,” 1, B 2, 5, and 6.] [Note: [Col. 1152D] See chapter 19]; the church of Saint Remigius on the bank of the Moselle; [the church [Note: [Col. 1151] These words are absent in 1 and 1b.] by the palace; the church [Col. 1151C] on Mount Saint Beatus [Note: [Col. 1151] “of Saint Beatus the Confessor at Confluentes,” 5 and 6; “Benedictus,” B 4 and 5.]; the church] of Saint Stephen outside the fortress [Note: [Col. 1151] “cloister,” 1 and 1b.] of Andernach [Note: [Col. 1151] “of Andernach,” 5 and 6.].

The market, too, which had been established before the Middle Gate [Note: [Col. 1151] This is absent in 2.] and was quite celebrated and famous because of the large attendance of the inhabitants of the surrounding region [Note: [Col. 1151] “provincials,” 1b and 5c; “and provincials,” B 4 and 6; corrected from “provincials” to “inhabitants of the surrounding region” in C 1.], was transferred from that place to Wagasatia [Note: [Col. 1151] “Vagasacia,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 1152D] Perhaps the estate called Wadegozzinga in charters, not far from the Saar, at the place where the monastery of Wadgassen—Wadegotia—later stood. Wyttenbach.], after a serious quarrel had arisen between the citizens and the merchants [Note: [Col. 1151] “negotiators,” 1; “quarrel,” 1.]. And enough about these matters.

[Col. 1153B] ## 25 [Note: [Col. 1153] Chapter 39, Leibniz.]

Zacharias the pope appointed blessed Boniface, illustrious in teaching and works, as visitor and administrator of spiritual affairs for the churches of Trier and Reims [Note: [Col. 1153] “of the church,” 5; “the churches” is absent in 2.] [Note: [Col. 1153] “visitor,” 1; the words “and administrator of spiritual affairs” are absent in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1153] “appointed administrator,” 5.] while the tyrant Milo held the possessions of both [Note: [Col. 1153C] Compare the letter of Hincmar, cited above.].

Meanwhile Charles, the destroyer of churches, died in the year 741. Concerning him [Note: [Col. 1153C] See the letter of the Council of Quierzy in Baluzius, *Capitularies*, Chiniac edition II, p. 108, from which most historians derived this account. Compare *Acta Sanctorum*, February III, pp. 211 ff., where G. Henschenius discusses the matter more fully.] it was revealed one night to Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans [Note: [Col. 1153] “Eucharius,” 5a and c.], that he was in the lower hell [Note: [Col. 1153] “that he was in hell,” 5a and c; “that he was,” C.]. He summoned Lord Boniface, vicar of the Roman see [Note: [Col. 1153] “legate or vicar,” B 2.], and other men of good reputation [Note: [Col. 1153] “of good testimony,” 1.], and opened Charles’s tomb [Note: [Col. 1153] “his tomb,” 6.]. When the stone had been removed, a serpent of extraordinary size came out of the sarcophagus [Note: [Col. 1153] “sacrophagus,” 1; “sarcophagus,” 6; “sarchophagus,” B 4, 5, 6, and C.], but Charles’s body was not found there [Note: [Col. 1153] B and C: “was not found there.”].

In those days Pope Zacharias, hearing of the faith and teaching of Lord Boniface, appointed him archbishop of the church of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1153C] Compare Hincmar’s letter, cited above. The author’s addition concerning the primacy of the bishops of Worms may have been borrowed from another source.]. Formerly, the bishops of Mainz and Cologne [Note: [Col. 1153] “and Cologne” is absent in B and C.] had been suffragans [Note: [Col. 1153] “suffragans,” 5a and 6a, b, and d.] of the bishops of Worms [Note: [Col. 1153] “of Worms,” 5 and 6 and C.].

After these events, the tyrant Milo, while engaged in hunting, was struck by a boar and died in a village called Arno [Note: [Col. 1153] “Arno,” 1 and 1b; “Iranc,” 2, 6, B 4, 5, and 6; “Irane,” 5; “Yranch,” B 2; “Yranc,” B 3; “Ieranc,” C.] [Note: [Col. 1153D] I have retained this reading, although the people of Trier prefer “Iranc” or “Yranc.” Concerning the place, Wyttenbach remarks: “Today Ehrang, a village below Trier on the royal road leading to Wittlich.”] at the first milestone from Trier [Note: [Col. 1153] “miliary,” B 2; “from Trier” is absent in 1b.], where he was also buried [Note: [Col. 1153] “buried,” 5; “he is buried there,” 5b; “was buried,” 6.] [Note: [Col. 1153D] Wyttenbach cites the following from a dissertation by Neller, printed at Trier in 1779, p. 46: “There still stands on the road by which one ascends from the iron foundry called Quinta, beside a forest situated on the right, a memorial column, whose rough stone and workmanship indicate its antiquity; the forest is still called the Meilenwald—the Forest of Milo. It is said that Milo was hunting there and was struck by the tusk of a boar.”] (in the year 753?) after forty years of his tyrannical usurpation [Note: [Col. 1153] C 3, corrected by a later hand, and C 6 in the margin: “In the year 748.”].

King Pippin [Note: [Col. 1153] “Pippinus,” 1b, 6, and B 6.] then, at the urging of the clergy and people of Trier [Col. 1154B], appointed Hildulfus bishop of the metropolitan church of Trier. Hildulfus was born of the illustrious race of the Nervii [Note: [Col. 1153] “Nerini,” 5b and c; a later hand in C 1 superscribes: “that is, dukes of Carinthia.”] and had been brought up at Regensburg [Note: [Col. 1153] “Regensburg,” 2; “Ratisbon,” 5b.]. He constructed a church [Note: [Col. 1153] “a monastery,” B and C; “church” is absent in 6.] in honor of Saint John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1153] “John,” 1.], beside the cell of Saint Hilary in the Field of Mars. Into it he transferred the body of Saint Maximin from the cell of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1154C] This does not agree with other historical monuments of Trier. The earlier *Life of Saint Maximin* (*Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, p. 373) and the other life by Lupus (in Surius III), chapter 10, state that Maximin had already been buried by Paulinus in the church of Saint John. They add that later Hildulfus and others transferred him from the crypt to the place “where he is now worshiped,” “where he is now situated”; nor does the *Life of Hildulfus* seem to relate the matter differently.], together with the bodies of 300 other martyrs who had suffered under Rictiovarus [Note: [Col. 1153] “Rictionarius,” 5a and b; “Rictouarus,” 5c.] [Note: [Col. 1154C] The third *Life of Saint Hildulfus* (*Acta Sanctorum*, July III, p. 231) relates similarly: “In it were likewise placed the bodies of three hundred martyrs of the Theban Legion; he so distinguished that place with furnishings and estates, and filled it with cenobites, that henceforth it seemed in no way inferior to the bishopric of the city itself.”].

He endowed that place with his own furnishings and estates and filled it with monks [Note: [Col. 1153] “with monasteries,” 1b, 2, and 6c.] numbering one hundred [Col. 1155A] [Note: [Col. 1154D] The passage from “He endowed” through “appointed” is taken from the *Life of Saint Agritius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 775; it too reports the translation of the three hundred martyrs’ bodies.] [Note: [Col. 1155] “filled,” 1, 1b, 2, B 5; “filled,” corrected to “filled [them]” in B 4.]. This cell [Note: [Col. 1155] “church,” 5; absent in C 3.], constructed on the estate of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1155] Absent in B 2 and 6.], remained subject for a long time to the jurisdiction of the bishops of Trier [Note: [Col. 1155C] Compare the *Deeds of Bishop Adalbero*, to be published below.], until one of them, through damnable flattery, gave the same cell as a wedding gift to a certain queen, together with the castle called Sericum [Note: [Col. 1155C] Sirck.] [Note: [Col. 1155] “gave as a gift,” 2, 5, and 6.] [Note: [Col. 1155C] Compare the diploma of Otto I, dated 962, in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 292, and Zyllesius’s book, *The Defense of Saint Maximin*.]. Thus thereafter it was held by kings [Note: [Col. 1155] “by the kingdom,” 1.].

This man, therefore, after some years had relinquished his bishopric, built for himself a cell in the forest of the Vosges [Note: [Col. 1156B] B and C: “He constructed three cells in the Vosges of the parish of Toul; in the middle one he became a monk and served God under the authority of an abbot, and there he rests. Yet while he lived, no one succeeded him in the bishopric. After Hildulfus died [C: “after Hildulfus,”] Weomadus succeeded him [C 3: “Wiomadus”], and he was abbot of the cell [B 6: “church”] of Saint Maximin. He constructed the cell of Saint ...”] [Note: [Col. 1155] “Vosagi,” 5a, b, and 6a, b, d; “Vasagi,” 5c; “Wosagi,” B 2.] and there rested [Note: [Col. 1155] “rests,” 2, 5, and 6a and b.].

Wiomadus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1155] “Wiemadus,” 5 and 6.]. He attempted to transfer the cell of Saint Goar to the jurisdiction of Saint Peter (around the years 760–791), but the violence of King Pippin prevented his attempt [Note: [Col. 1155] “Pippin,” 5b, 6, B 2 and 6, and below; “the king” is absent in 6, as are “his attempt was prevented” in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1155C] Compare Wandelbertus, *Miracles of Saint Goar*, chapter 35.]. Nevertheless, he obtained from that same Pippin a royal decree concerning the cell of Saint Maximin and other possessions of the church of Trier [Col. 1155B], and also from Charlemagne, the son of Pippin [Note: [Col. 1155] “of Pippinus,” 1.]. Whoever wishes to know it will be able to find it [Note: [Col. 1157A] C 1: “Whoever wishes to know it will be able to find it here at present”; after words deleted in C 1, this is absent in C 3 and following. C 1, 5, and 6 add diplomas, which are not found in C 3 and 4:

“In the name of the Lord God ... Pippin ... at Thionville, in the name of God, successfully” [ [Col. 1157D] The diploma is published in Hontheim I, p. 120.].

“In the name of the Lord God ... Charles ... at the palace of Herstal, in the name of God. Amen” [ [Col. 1157D] In Hontheim I, p. 132.].].

After his death Richbodus was ordained bishop [Note: [Col. 1155] “Richboldus,” C 3 and 4.]; then Wazzo [Note: [Col. 1155] “Wazo,” 1b and 2; “Wiso,” 5a and c; “Wizo,” 6; “Watto,” B 2.] [Note: [Col. 1157A] B and C add: “Both of them, succeeding one another, had been abbots of the monastery of Mediolacum” [B 6: “Mediolanum”] [ [Col. 1157D] That Richbodus had been abbot of Lorsch is shown by the *Lorsch Chronicle* (edited by Lemay I, p. 26), where he is said to have presided over the church for ten years and eight months.].]. After him came Hamularius Fortunatus, a Roman cardinal (804–809) [Note: [Col. 1155] Witnesses 5a, 5c, and 6 read *Amularius*; 5b reads *Amualarius*. The edition marks the remaining readings only as *alii* (“others”), without assigning further sigla. “Fortunatus cardinal” is absent in 5c.], who composed a book of offices [Note: [Col. 1155] “compiled,” 6.] [Note: [Col. 1155C] In the ninth-century Trier manuscript of Amularius, Wyttenbach reports the following inscription: “Hamelarius Fortunatus, Roman cardinal, metropolitan of Trier, archbishop by the grace of God of the diocese of Tongeren, composed this venerable work, useful for ecclesiastical orders, so that by this order the Lord may be praised as long as this mortal race endures.” But other scholars seem more correctly to attribute this work to Amalarius of Metz; see Rivet, *Literary History* IV, p. 537.].

He was sent by Charlemagne to Constantinople to establish peace with the emperor Michael [Note: [Col. 1155] “Michael,” 1 and others; “Michahel,” 6.]. That same Charles transported a great quantity of marble and a very large amount of mosaic [Note: [Col. 1155] “marble,” 2; “mosaic” is absent in 4, with space left blank.] from Trier [Note: [Col. 1155] “from Trier,” 2, 5a, b, and 6; “from Treveris,” 5c.] to the palace at Aachen [Note: [Col. 1155] “to the palace,” B 4 and 5; absent in 6.], and in return gave gifts to blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 1155] “numbers,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1155] C 6 has in the margin: “He died on the fourth day before the Ides of June and was buried at Saint Paulinus behind the high altar.”] [Note: [Col. 1155C] See the diploma in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 153.].

After Fortunatus, Hetti presided over the church of Trier (around the year 814), abbot of Mediolacum [Note: [Col. 1155] “Mediolanum,” 1 and 5; “abbot of Mediol ... ensis,” 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1155] “After Fortunatus ... Mediolacensis” is absent in B 2.]. Having been warned in a vision by Saint Maternus [Note: [Col. 1155C] The material beginning “Having been warned ... presented” seems to have been taken from the appendix to Theganus; see *MGH SS* II, p. 603.], in the twenty-third year of Emperor Louis, he transferred the body of Saint Castor from a place called Cardena [Note: [Col. 1155] “called,” 2, 5, and 6; “Caderna,” 6c.] to Confluentes, to the monastery that he himself had built. On the fifth day before the Ides of December he consecrated it in honor of Saint Castor [Note: [Col. 1155] “and of all confessors” is absent in B and C; in C 4 space was left blank; C 6 has it in the margin.] and all confessors, and after the consecration placed the holy body in the church [Note: [Col. 1156C] On this matter see also the *Life of Saint Castor*, *Acta Sanctorum*, February II, p. 666: “After a long time, when it pleased God to grant his confessor Castor still greater glory of honor on earth ... he inspired the archbishop of that time and the other rulers of the lands to divide the relics of Saint Castor and place one portion at Karadonum in the aforementioned church, formerly called the house of Saint Paulinus, and transfer the other to Confluentes, where the river Moselle flows into the Rhine, from which the place also receives its appropriate name. There the site was broader, resources more abundant, and popular access more frequent. In that place a basilica of wondrous beauty was built at royal expense and dedicated to Almighty God in honor of Saint Castor the Confessor.”].

There also Emperor Louis presented many gifts [Note: [Col. 1155] “Louis,” B 2; “Loduwicus,” 5b.]. Some say that he had handed over the possessions of the churches of Saint Eucharius and Saint Liutwinus [Note: [Col. 1155] “Liutunius,” 5a and b; “Lintunius,” 5c; “Lutwinus,” 6a; “Liuttiunius,” 6c; “Luthwinus,” B 2.] [Note: [Col. 1156C] That is, of the monastery of Mediolacum.] as benefices to his princes [Col. 1156B].

After thirty years of his priesthood [Note: [Col. 1155] B and C read: “thirty-seven.”] he died and was buried [Note: [Col. 1155] Absent in 5b.] in the monastery of Saint Eucharius, before the altar of Saint John the Baptist, in the northern apse [Note: [Col. 1155] “apse,” 2 and 5; “abscide,” 5b; “absidia,” C.] [Note: [Col. 1155] “northern,” 1b, 2, 5, and 6.]. On his right [Note: [Col. 1155] “right-hand side,” 1, here.], in the other apse, rests a man illustrious in the nobility of his lineage [Note: [Col. 1155] “a man of great dignity, a noble and distinguished man,” 2; “a man illustrious in noble descent,” 5 and 6; “a very magnificent man,” B and C.] named Ruotgaudus [Note: [Col. 1155] “Rotgardus,” 5a; “Rotgadus,” 5b and c and 6; “Ruothgaudus,” B 2 and C.] [Note: [Col. 1157A] B and C add: “Hetti’s brother.”] [Note: [Col. 1156C] Compare Browerus, *Annals* I, p. 413.].

[Col. 1157A] ## 26 [Note: [Col. 1157] Chapter 41, Leibniz; II, chapter 14, C. C 3 adds: “Concerning Thietgaudus.”]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 851 [847] [Note: [Col. 1157] “951,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1157D] This is taken from certain manuscripts of Regino; see *MGH SS* I, p. 568, note o.] Tietgaudus [Note: [Col. 1157] “Tietgaudus,” 2; “Thietgaudus,” 5c and B 2; “Ruotgaudus,” B 6; “Thiethgaudus,” C.] obtained Hetti’s episcopal seat [Note: [Col. 1157] “Hetti,” 2; “Heti,” B 4; “Hethi,” B 6.].

He was a simple man, led astray by the emperor and adulterer Lothair [Note: [Col. 1157] “Lothair, king and emperor, the adulterer,” 5b; these words are absent in another reading.] and by Gunther, archbishop of Cologne [Col. 1157B] [Note: [Col. 1157] “bishop,” 5, B 2, 4, 5, and C.], and consented to the deposition of Tietberga, the wife of that same Lothair, falsely accused [Note: [Col. 1157] “accused,” 1; “she testified at Metz,” 1b; “defined,” 5a; “defined,” 6; “was first defined,” 5c.]. Indeed, at a synod he declared that she had confessed that she herself had been polluted by incestuous intercourse with her full brother [Note: [Col. 1157] “with her brother,” 6.].

Lothair had fabricated this false disgrace with these bishops, wishing in this way to cast out the queen and bring into the kingdom Waldrada [Note: [Col. 1158B] B and C add: “the sister of that same Gunther, archbishop of Cologne” [B 6: “bishop”].] [Note: [Col. 1157] “Waldrada, whom he had taken as his concubine when he was a young man, ... into the kingdom,” 5 and 6.] whom he himself, as a young man, had kept as a concubine. When he had obtained this through the judgment of the bishops, Tietgaudus and Gunther were summoned to Rome by Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1157] “Nicholas,” 2 and others.] for these reasons, and there they were deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity and deposed [Note: [Col. 1157] Absent in 1b and d; “and deposed,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 1158B] B and C add here: “In the sixth year of this Bishop Tietgaudus, a dog was seen at Trier upon his episcopal chair.” The chapter ends there.].

When they had gone again, and a third time, to the apostolic see in order to obtain restoration [Note: [Col. 1157D] Up to this point, from Regino.], but had accomplished nothing [Note: [Col. 1157] “and had made no progress” is absent in 1 and 1b.], finally, after Pope Nicholas had died [Note: [Col. 1157] Absent in 2, 5, and 6; “Nicholas,” 1b and 6.], Adrian succeeded him. Through Adrian’s liberality [Note: [Col. 1157] “liberality,” 1; “freedom,” 1b.], Tietgaudus obtained lodging in the monastery of Saint Gregory [Note: [Col. 1157] “Saint George,” 1b.].

Saint Gregory appeared to him in dreams once and again and warned him to leave and not disturb his dwelling, because Gregory had determined that this was unlawful [Note: [Col. 1157] “so that he would not disturb it; when he explained that this was unlawful,” 5 and 6.]. Tietgaudus neglected to do this. Then, for a third time, he was rebuked for disobedience and for wearying the apostolic see—[Note: [Col. 1157] The phrase is *de fatigatione apostolica*, “for wearying the apostolic see”; *de* is absent in B 6.]; for the blessed Apostle Andrew had appeared to him, led by a right hand [Note: [Col. 1158C] B and C instead read *ducens dextera manu Andream apostolum*, “leading the Apostle Andrew by the right hand”; B 2 has simply *apostolum Andream*. The source names no person as the leader in this variant.], with the Levite Peter preceding him with a light [Note: [Col. 1157] Witness 2 reads *ita* (“thus”); 1 reads *leuitio* for *levitico* (“Levitical”). Witnesses 5 and 6 preserve the altered sequence *manus Petrus p. c. l. beato Andrea apostolo et responsum* (with the printed abbreviations), literally “hand; Peter going before with a light; to the blessed Apostle Andrew; and an answer.” Here *p. c. l.* abbreviates *praeeunte cum lumine*, “going before with a light”; the altered sequence is grammatically disrupted. Witness 1b reads *pretereunte* (“passing by”) for *praeeunte* (“going before”).], and received the answer that he would indeed be delivered from immediate death, but would be deprived of his homeland together with all that was his [Note: [Col. 1157] “all his possessions,” 5b; absent in B and C.].

When he revealed this to everyone he could, and could not obtain another lodging from the bishop [Note: [Col. 1157] Witness 1 has *aliud ospitium*, “another lodging”; *a pontifice*, “from the bishop/pontiff,” is absent in 2.], he withdrew among the Sabines [Col. 1158B] [Note: [Col. 1157] “departing,” 2 and 5.] and, in that same year, died together with Gunther [Note: [Col. 1158D] “With Gunther,” from Regino, year 865. What follows is from the same source, year 869.] and all his people [Note: [Col. 1157] “with all his people” is absent in C.] [Note: [Col. 1158D] Ancient parchment records of the church of Cardena explicitly testified that he died in the year of the Lord 870. Browerus, p. 423.].

The emperor Lothair, struck by divine judgment, died at Piacenza [Note: [Col. 1157] “at,” B and 5; “Piacenza or Bliesenz,” B 2.] (in the year 869). With him the whole kingdom that from his name is called Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1157] “Lotharingian,” 5a, 6, B 2, 4, 5, and C; “Lothringia,” 5b; “Lotharingia,” 5c; “Lotaringum,” B 6.] also collapsed. The castle of Lothair, not far from Trier on the Saar [Note: [Col. 1158D] Perhaps Heribodesheim, or Herbizheim, which is named in the division of Lothair’s kingdom (*Leges* I, p. 517).], was from that time abandoned [Note: [Col. 1157] “it remained abandoned,” 1.].

In the sixth year of Tietgaudus, a dog was seen at Trier sitting upon his episcopal chair [Note: [Col. 1157] “a dog sitting upon his chair,” 2 and 5; “a dog on the episcopal chair,” 6.] [Note: [Col. 1158D] See the *Annals of Corvey*, year 857, and compare the *Annals of Saint Bertin*, which report a similar portent in the same year.].

[Col. 1159A] **27** [Note: [Col. 1159] Chapter XLII. Leibniz II, chapter XV. C adds: “Concerning Bertolfus, archbishop.”]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1159] 5b reads “in the year of the Lord”] 868 [Note: [Col. 1159] 1b reads 866; 5 reads 873; B and C read 864.], Bertolfus [Note: [Col. 1159] 6 and B2, almost throughout, read *Bertholfus*], abbot of Mediolacum [Note: [Col. 1159] 5b–c read *Mediolanensis*; B2, *Medolacensis*], became bishop [Note: [Col. 1159] Omitted in 6c.] of Treberis [Note: [Col. 1159] 1 reads *Tberis*; 1b reads *consors eius*, “his associate.”], and was a kinsman of Adventius [Note: [Col. 1159] 2 reads *Adventicii*, “of Adventicius,” and below *Adventicius*], who at that time was bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 1159] 1 and 2 read *Metensis*; the other witnesses read *Mettensis* here.] [Note: [Col. 1159D] He follows Regino, who relates these events under 869, yet does not name Hincmar, by whom Charles was crowned, as is sufficiently established from other books and from the acts published in *Monumenta Legum* I, p. 512.].

When Adventius learned that King Lothar had died at Piacenza [Note: [Col. 1159] *Placia* in 1 and 1b; “the king of Piacenza” in 6.], he summoned his brother Charles, who was reigning in Provence, to Metz [Note: [Col. 1159] *Methtis* in B2; *Metis* (*Methis* in 5b); “summoned” in 5 and 6.]. Together with other bishops and Hincmar, archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 1159] Omitted in 5; *Hincmaro* in 5a–b.], he consecrated him king of Lotharingia and Provence in 869 [Note: [Col. 1159] “Consecrated” in 1b.]. He also secured for his kinsman Bertolfus [Note: [Col. 1159] *Bertulfus* in 1; *Bertholphus* here in 5a and 5c; *Barcolphus* in 5b.] the archbishopric of Treberis [Note: [Col. 1159] Added in B and C; *Treberense* in B2.]

He purchased from the royal hand a village called Martia [Note: [Col. 1159] *Marino* in 1; *Maritio* in 1b; “called Marcia (Martia)” in B and C.] [Note: [Col. 1159D] Marcetum beside the Saar, today Merzig. The charter appears to have been lost.].

In Bertolfus’s fifth year [Note: [Col. 1159] “After Bertolfus had died” in 1b; “of Bishop Bartolfus” in 5b.], Adventius, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 1159] “Of Reims” in B6.], died. Walo [Note: [Col. 1159] C adds “and Walo.”] was appointed in his place [Note: [Col. 1159] “Was sustained” in 1.]. In the second year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1159] Omitted in C.], the pallium was sent to him by Pope John [Note: [Col. 1159] “Sent” in 1.], together with a letter explaining on which feasts he was to use it [Note: [Col. 1159D] See it in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 217.].

When Bertolfus, the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 1159] *Metopolitanus* in 1.], heard that Walo was proceeding with the pallium on the holy day of Easter [Note: [Col. 1159] “On the second day” in 5 and 6.], he sent a letter summoning him to Treberis [Note: [Col. 1159] “And to Treberis” in 6.] and asking when, how, or by whom permission had been granted him [Note: [Col. 1159] Omitted in 2, 5, and 6.] to proceed with the pallium.

After Walo had read aloud in the hearing of all who were present [Note: [Col. 1159] “In the ears of all” in 5.] the privilege concerning the use of the pallium that had been sent to him by the pope [Note: [Col. 1159] “Sent” in 1.], he asserted [Note: [Col. 1160D] Hirsch has already noted similar material in Sigebert’s *Life of Theoderic of Metz*, *On the Life of Sigebert*, p. 230. The *Deeds of Sigebert* are later than this work but follow another author.] that he was not the first but the fifth whom the Apostolic See had deemed worthy to elevate with this honor, while preserving in all things subjection to the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 1159] *Metropolitanus* in 1 and 1b; “of the metropolitan” in 5 and 6, corrected in C1; “metropolitan” in 2 and B2.]. The first was Urbitium [Note: [Col. 1159] *Xriαu?* in 1; omitted in 1b.], the second Crodegangus [Note: [Col. 1159] *Crodegandus* in B5 and 6; *Trodegangus* in 2; *Chrodegangus* in C.], nephew through his sister of King Pippin; the third Angelramnus; the fourth Druogo [Note: [Col. 1159] *Drugonem* in 1b, 2, 5, 6, and C.]; and the fifth the son of Emperor Charles the Great [Note: [Col. 1159] “Charles” in 1; omitted in 6.].

Bertolfus, not satisfied by these assertions [Note: [Col. 1159] “Not moved” in 6; “satisfying” in B2.], read a chapter of the canons in which it is asserted [Note: [Col. 1159] “They assert” in 1b.] that no suffragan should presume to introduce anything new that had not been possessed by all his predecessors in his church [Note: [Col. 1159] *Praedecessoo+ribus* is misspelled in 1.] without the counsel and permission of his metropolitan [Note: [Col. 1159] “Of the metropolitan” in 1, 1b, and 2; “the metropolitan’s” in 5a–b.]. He therefore forbade him, by the holy obedience [Note: [Col. 1159] B2 adds “obedience”; the word is omitted below.] which he owed him in all ecclesiastical matters [Note: [Col. 1159] Omitted in B6.], to use the pallium thereafter unless permission had first been requested from him and granted.

When Walo invoked apostolic authority, while the archbishop defended the privileges [Note: [Col. 1159] “Rights” in 6.] of metropolitans, a great enmity arose on both sides [Note: [Col. 1159] 6 reads: “Great enmities arose between them”; 5b: “A great enmity of both parties was formed.”].

Thus the most reverend Hincmarus, archbishop of Reims, distinguished also for his eloquence [Note: [Col. 1159] “Most distinguished” in B and C.], hearing of this disagreement [Note: [Col. 1159] Omitted in 2, 5, and 6; B and C read “hearing of this disagreement.”], sent Walo a letter [Note: [Col. 1160D] Flodoard also mentions this letter, *History of Reims* III.23; I suppose that the author of the *Deeds* had it in his hands.] seasoned with the salt of wisdom and sound counsel [Note: [Col. 1159] *Salus* corrected to *sani* in 1; *sole* in B2.]. Through it he instructed him in obedience to his metropolitan and thus restored concord.

This Bertolfus was exceedingly harsh and impatient with such presumptions by his suffragans, and he would not permit the privilege of his church to be violated in any respect [Note: [Col. 1159] “To be moderated” in 1b.]. He refused to receive letters from the Roman pontiff sent to him on account of Walo’s presumption and also concerning the ordination, against his will, of the bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 1159] *Wirdunensis* in B2.] [Note: [Col. 1159] “Ordinations” in B2; “ordination” in B6.].

In the twelfth year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 1159] Fourteenth in 1 and 1b.], heavenly vengeance came upon Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1159] *Lotharingam* in 1 and 1b; *Lothringiam* in 5b, frequently.], the kingdom of the aforementioned King Lothar, the adulterer and excommunicate.

At last the Northmen [Note: [Col. 1159] 5 and 6 read *Normanni*; B2 and C, *Northmanni*], who had gone forth several years earlier and burned the city of Nantes [Note: [Col. 1161] 1 first wrote *Mettis* (“Metz”), corrected to *Namnettis* (“Nantes”); 1b *Mettensis*; 5a and B5 *Na metis*; 5c *Mammetis*; 5b *Namethis*; B6 *Nammetis*; C1, corrected, and C3 *Na mettis*; C4 *Nammetis*], and had slain its bishop with all his clergy [Note: [Col. 1161] 5 and 6 read “having set [the city] on fire, [they slew] the bishop”] on Holy Saturday while he was blessing the fonts [Note: [Col. 1161] Omitted in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1161C] This is taken from Regino under the year 853.], devastated Angers, Tours, Poitiers, Liège [Note: [Col. 1161C] The account continues from Regino under the years 881 and 882.], Utrecht [Note: [Col. 1161] 1 reads *Tracirectum*], Tongeren [Note: [Col. 1161] 1b *Tungrensem*; 5b *Tungerim*; C *Tungrum*], Cologne, Bonn [Note: [Col. 1161] Omitted in B6.], Zülpich [Note: [Col. 1161] 5a *Tulpaicam*; 5c *Tuspaicum*; 6 *Tulpaicum*; omitted in 2 and 5b], Jülich [Note: [Col. 1161] B2 *Uibacum*], Neuss [Note: [Col. 1161] 2 *Hiusa*; 6 *Nussam*], Aachen, Hinde [Note: [Col. 1161] 5 and 6 *Indam*], Malmedy [Note: [Col. 1161] 1 *Malmumdarium*; 6 “St. M.”; 5a omits “Stavelot, Prüm, Nijmegen”], Stavelot, Prüm, and Nijmegen [Note: [Col. 1161] 1 *Prum ina[a]umago*; 1b *Prumnuam*; 5b–c *Niumago*; 6 *Neomagum regum*; C *Numagen*], a royal fortress, with fire and sword.

The people of Treberis therefore [Note: [Col. 1161] B6 reads “truly”], after taking counsel with the wiser men, concealed in underground caves [Note: [Col. 1161] 1b has the misspelling *subternenis* and *occult*; 5a *occultant*, 5b *ocultant*, 5c *occultare*] whatever ecclesiastical property or ornaments there were in the city, and they thrust even the sarcophagi [Note: [Col. 1161] 1 *scarcophaga*] of the saints deep into the earth [Note: [Col. 1161] 1 reads *itere mergunt*; 1b “they buried [them] more deeply”], lest the relics of the saints [Note: [Col. 1161] 5 and 6 read “that the relics of the saints”; 6 “of the barbarian”] become a mockery of the barbarians’ madness.

There was therefore in the monastery of Saint Paulinus a crypt in which, around the sarcophagus of that saint, suspended by iron chains [Note: [Col. 1161] “Suspended” in 1b; 2 and 5 add “and in which”; 6 reads “in which twelve bodies lay.”], thirteen bodies of martyrs lay. Their names had been inscribed in golden letters on the walls of the same crypt.

The religious Christians who were there at that time, fearing that, as has been said, through the evidence of this inscription the sarcophagi or the very bones of the martyrs might become a mockery to the enemies, adopted a salutary plan: namely, that the names of those martyrs should be removed from the walls and that, in addition, who they had been, whence they had come, when, how, and by whom they had been killed [Note: [Col. 1161] “When and how” in 5 and 6; “when” is omitted in 5b.] should be written together on a lead tablet, where they could at some time be found [Note: [Col. 1161] “Find” in 1 and 1b.], together with the reason for transferring these names [Note: [Col. 1161] “The names or translations” in 1b.] and the names and merits of the martyrs.

They wrote on the lead tablet as follows [Note: [Col. 1161] “On a lead tablet” in 5 and 6; [Col. 1162C] This narrative rests upon the lead tablet which the author himself adduces. It is printed in the *History of the Martyrs of Treberis*, chapter 2, p. 119; in the *Life of Saint Felix*, *Acta Sanctorum*, March III, p. 623; and also in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 221. See also his *Preliminary History of Trier* I, p. 92.]:

[Note: [Col. 1161C] B2, B4, and B5 read: “In this crypt lie,” and the remainder. B3, however, and C give the complete tablet:]

> In this crypt lie the bodies of saints, most noble according to worldly rank, but precious martyrs according to the will of God. For Rictiovarus, prefect of the emperor Maximian, pursuing the Theban legion everywhere at his command, entered this city also because of them. After he had killed innumerable members of it here, he also killed these leading men of this city, confessors of the Christian faith, together with them; their bodies are laid here round about. In their midst the body of Saint Paulinus, most distinguished bishop of the Treveri, is suspended by iron chains; Saint Felix, bishop of this see, honourably suspended it there on 3 May, after it had been brought from Phrygia by the resources of the entire kingdom. He also built this monastery in honour of the holy Mother of God and of those same martyrs. Besides the bodies of these leaders, innumerable bodies of the same multitude are contained in this monastery; their names could not be discovered, just as those of an innumerable and foreign people could not be, except for the name of one leader, who was called Thyrsus. Therefore the names of this man and of those martyrs whose sarcophagi can be seen here had been written in gold letters on the wall of this crypt. The devout Christians then living transferred them here when they foresaw that the Northmen would devastate this city, as they would cities everywhere else. He, therefore, who is laid on the right side of Saint Paulinus was called Palmatius; as consul and patrician he governed this entire city. On his left lies the man called Thyrsus, whose name alone, out of so great a multitude, was recorded because he commanded that same legion. At the head of Saint Paulinus lie seven most noble senators of this city, crowned with martyrdom together with the Thebans: their physician was called Maxentius; next to him on the right lies one named Constantius, after whom is Crescentius, and then Justinus. On the left side of Maxentius lie three full brothers: the eldest, nearest to Maxentius, Leander; next to him Alexander; then Sother. At the feet of Saint Paulinus, placed on either side, are four men most distinguished in birth and virtue. Although in time of peace they worshipped Christ secretly, in time of persecution they defended the Christians’ faith openly and so steadfastly, and opposed Rictiovarus to his face so resolutely, that, after he had grievously afflicted them with diverse kinds of tortures as an example to others, he finally had them beheaded in his presence. Of the two placed toward the south, the inner one is called Hormisda and the outer Papirius. Of those whose sides face north, the inner one is likewise called Constans and the outer Jovianus. Rictiovarus entered Treberis on 4 October, and on that day killed Thyrsus with his companions; on the following day Palmatius with the other leaders of the city; on the third day he carried out slaughter among the populace of both sexes.

> B3 and Leibniz add: When earth from the crypt in which these bodies of saints lie was being removed [the printed reading *potaretur* is uncertain; Leibniz reads *portarentur*, “was being carried away”], a certain bone, carelessly thrown out, shed no small amount of blood. Immediately, in the presence of abbots, clerics, and laymen, it was carried into a little vessel; as often as it was poured out, so often was it filled again with a great flood of gore. This flow continued from the ninth hour of Saturday until the first hour of the second feria [Monday]. It still remains blood-stained.

> In this crypt lie the bodies of the saints whose names are these: Palmacius, Maxentius, Constantius [Note: [Col. 1161] *Constantinus* in 5 and 6.], Crescentius, Justinus, Leander, Alexander, Sother, Hormisda [Note: [Col. 1161] “Hormista Papirus” in 1b.], Papirius, Constans, and Jovianus.

> The body also of Saint Eucharius and of the others buried there [Note: [Col. 1161] “The remaining ones who were buried there” in 1b; “of the rest” in 2.] they buried deeper in the earth. They did the same with the others buried around the city [Note: [Col. 1161] 6c adds: “End of Book IV.”].

[Col. 1163B] **28** [Note: [Col. 1163] Chapter XLIII. Leibniz II, chapter XVI. C.]. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 880 [882] [Note: [Col. 1163] 882, corrected in C1 and likewise below.] [Note: [Col. 1163D] A. 882, Regino. According to Wyttenbach, the same date is written in the margin of the ninth-century Treveran manuscript of Hamelarius: “In the year 882, indiction 15, the people of the Northmen burned Treberis with fire.”], after the emperor Ludowicus had died [Note: [Col. 1163D] “The Northmen … occupied it” is taken from Regino under the year 882.], the Northmen [Note: [Col. 1163] *Nomanni* in 1 and 5a–b; other witnesses have *Northmanni*.], having heard of his death and coming forth with all their forces [Note: [Col. 1163] Omitted in 5b.], occupied the city of Treberis on the Nones of April [Note: [Col. 1163] “Treveris, on the seventh day before the Nones” in 5b.], on the most sacred day of the Lord’s Supper [Note: [Col. 1163] “Most sacred” in 2; feminine “most sacred” in 5 and 6.], while Bishop Bertolfus escaped by flight together with certain citizens [Note: [Col. 1163] “Having escaped” in 2.].

While they rested there until Holy Easter Day, refreshing their bodies wearied by the journey, they demolished the entire territory around the city down to the ground [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Until Easter … they demolished” is taken from Regino.], and killed with the sword everyone whom they found inside or outside the city [Note: [Col. 1163] “Or” in B6; “found” in 1, 1b, and 2; other witnesses have “found again.”]. They also set fire to the city itself and all the monasteries [Note: [Col. 1163] B and C read “they burned them with fire.”].

Although they repeatedly set fire to the monastery of Saint Paulinus [Note: [Col. 1163D] Compare the *Life of Saint Paulinus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, August VI, p. 678, where these events are related differently. Perhaps the author of the *Deeds* used another *Life*, concerning which see the same work, p. 675.], and the fire was extinguished by divine power, they broke the iron chains from which his sarcophagus hung [Note: [Col. 1163] *Sarcophagus* in 2, 5, and 6c–d; *sarcofagus* in 6a and likewise below.]. Nevertheless, when the chains had been broken, the sarcophagus did not sink deeper into the earth at all [Note: [Col. 1163] “The sarcophagus, falling, did not …” in 2.], but remained suspended in the air until, many years later, certain unbelievers forced it down and it sank, not without vengeance being inflicted upon them. For all who served this sacrilege with their hands [Note: [Col. 1163] Omitted in 5; 5b adds “and each.”] received individual afflictions as blows.

Thus, after the Northmen had burned and laid waste the entire city, they prepared to hasten to Metz [Note: [Col. 1164D] “To Metz … fled” is taken from Regino; but the words concerning Remich are added by the *Deeds*. On this matter see *Miracles of Saint Glodesind*, chapter 29, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* IV, p. 237.].

When Walo, bishop of that same city, learned this, he went voluntarily to meet them in battle at Remich [Note: [Col. 1164D] Remich on the Moselle.] together with Bertolfus, bishop of Treberis [Note: [Col. 1163] “Of Treberis” in 5a–b and 6; “archbishop of Treberis” in C.], and Count Adalard [Note: [Col. 1163] *Adelhardus* in 1b and C; *Adalhardus* in 2, B4, and 5; *Adolardus* in 5b; *Adelradus* in B2.].

When battle had been joined, the Northmen won. Bishop Walo fell there, while Bertolfus fled with the others. In that same year, 883, Archbishop Bertolfus [Note: [Col. 1163] “Bishop” in 5b and B2; omitted in C6.] departed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1163] “Died” in 5a and 5c.].

Radbodus [Note: [Col. 1163] *Rabodus* in 1 and 1b; *Raphodus* in 2; *Rathbodus* in 5a and C; *Rathbodo* in 5b–c; *Ratbodo* in 6; *Katbodus* in B5.] succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1163] “Succeeds” in 6.], an abbot of Mediolacum [Note: [Col. 1163] *Medio-lacum* in 2, 5, and 6.], a venerable bishop [Note: [Col. 1163] “Abbot” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 1164D] This is taken from Regino under the year 883.]. In the same year he consecrated Robert [Note: [Col. 1163] *Rubertus* in 2, 5a, and 6c–d; *Ruotpertus* in B2; *Ruotbertus* in B4 and C; *Ruthbertus* in C6.] bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 1163] Omitted in 6.]. (Years 889 and 917.)

He acquired from Emperor Arnulf the abbey of Saint Servatius, called Mastreth [Note: [Col. 1163] *Masetricht* in 2; *Masetreh* in 4 and 6; *Maserch* in 5a–b; *Maserth* in 5c; *Mastreiz* in B2; *Mastretz* in B6; *Mastreit* in B4, 5, and C.] [Note: [Col. 1164B]

> C1 adds: “And he obtained from the same emperor a charter concerning that abbey, in the following form:
>
> **Charter of King Arnulf concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius, confessor of Christ** [Note: [Col. 1164D] The charter was published in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 229.].
>
> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Arnulfus … in the name of God, amen.
>
> **Charter of King Zwentibold concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius** [Note: [Col. 1165D] The following two charters are omitted in C3 and C4.], in Hontheim, p. 237.
>
> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Zwentiboldus … at that very Utrecht.
>
> **Another charter of King Zwentibold concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius** [Note: [Col. 1165D] Not found in Hontheim.].
>
> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Zwentiboldus … in the name of God, amen.
>
> “The aforementioned bishop also obtained these things from Ludowicus …” [Note: [Col. 1165] The continuation is interrupted in the source.]]

Then he also obtained from Emperor Ludowicus [Note: [Col. 1163] “From another Ludowicus” in 1b; “from Lothar” in B2.] these castles, Sericum and Orkesvels [Note: [Col. 1163] Other manuscript readings include *Orkegiels?*, *Horceshinvelt*, *Orceshinvelt*, *Orcesbinvel*, *Orkesveld*, and *Orxvels*.] [Note: [Col. 1164D] Sike and Orsvels between the Meuse and the Moselle. This charter appears to have been lost.], together with the villages dependent upon them [Note: [Col. 1163] “Adjacent to them” in 6 and C.].

[Col. 1165A] [Note: [Col. 1165D] Concerning this collection, see Wasserschleben in Richter, *Critical Yearbooks* (1838), p. 485, and *Contributions*, p. 30. Albericus under the year 905 adds: “to Dado, bishop of Verdun.”]

> B and C add: “After …” [Note: [Col. 1165B]
>
> C has the following: “When Radbodus had resigned, Ruthkerus succeeded him as bishop. He obtained a charter of royal authority concerning the same abbey; it does not seem inappropriate to insert a copy of it here:
>
> **Charter of King Charles of the Franks concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius** [Note: [Col. 1165D] Not found in Hontheim.].
>
> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles … the villa of Theodonis.
>
> **Charter of King Charles of the Franks concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius** [Note: [Col. 1165D] In Hontheim, p. 281.].
>
> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles … at the palace of Eristail.
>
> “This aforementioned bishop, a man of good …” [Note: [Col. 1165] The continuation is interrupted in the source.]]

[Col. 1165A] Bishop Ruotgerus obtained a charter of royal authority concerning the same abbey [Note: [Col. 1165] *Rogerus* in B2; *Rubertus* in B6.]. Being a man of good conduct, he held a general council at Treberis with the suffragan bishops and the rest of the clergy, brought forward a book of canonical decrees composed through his own labor, and confirmed it [Note: [Col. 1165B] C reads: “He confirmed it, and not long afterward departed to the happier life.”].

[Col. 1165B] **29** [Note: [Col. 1165] Chapter XLIV. Leibniz has *Rupertus* in 2, *Ruothpertus* in 4, *Rubertus* in 5a, 6c–d, B3, and 6, *Robertus* in 5b–c, *Ruobertus* in 6a, *Rothbertus* in B2, and *Rutpertus* in B4 and B5. C adds after this: “After him, Rupertus.” “Bishop” is added in 4, B, and C; “and afterward he existed” in 5b; “existed” is omitted in 2.]

Then Rutpertus [Note: [Col. 1165] *Rupertus* in 1b.] held office (in 931) [Note: [Col. 1165D] He succeeded Rotgerus in 931; see the *Annals of Saint Maximin*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* III, p. 6.] [Note: [Col. 1167B] C adds: “He obtained from Otto I a privilege concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius, in the following form:

> **Charter of King Otto of the Franks concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius** [Note: [Col. 1168D] In Hontheim, p. 264.].
>
> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Otto … at Thalahem.”]

[Note: [Col. 1167B] B and C omit the words from “who transferred” through “was buried,” and substitute the following: “This [C: Archbishop Rubertus] was the first, as they report [B2: ‘it is reported’], to attach the church of Treberis to the kingdom called Lotharingia, because his sister had been joined in marriage to the emperor. Until his time it had belonged to the kingdom of the Franks, named after Charles. He took certain goods from Saint Martin, illustrious through many honours” [Note: [Col. 1168D] On this see what I said in *Yearbooks* I.1, p. 60. The Ballerini brothers seek to show from a passage of Ratherius that Rotbert was a kinsman of the Saxon kings; Ratherius appears to say that on the day of his own consecration he ordained Rotbert’s nephew Bruno archbishop; see *Opera Ratherii*, p. 208, note 22.] [Note: [Col. 1167] B6 omits “after Charles”; B2 reads *materno* (‘maternal’) for *Martino* (‘Martin’)].]

He transferred from Italy the body of Saint Severus, of whom it is read in the book of the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 1165] “In the first book” in 1, 4, and 5; “in the book” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 1165D] Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* I.12.]. With a divinely serving helmsman, it was carried along the channel of the Moselle [Note: [Col. 1165] “He carried it across” in 1b.] and arrived at the place called the harbor of Hatton [Note: [Col. 1165] *Hartonis* in 5; “it arrived” in 5b.] [Note: [Col. 1165D] Hatzeport; compare Brower, p. 459, who also gives the *Translation of Saint Severus*.]. There it was received by the brothers of the monastery [Note: [Col. 1165] “Of the monastery” in 1; “brothers of the monastery” in 1b.] of Saint Martin in a district called Megine [Note: [Col. 1166D] Meinfelt.] and honorably buried in that same monastery [Note: [Col. 1165] Omitted in 5.].

After Rutpertus [Note: [Col. 1165] The witnesses give *Rutbertus*, *Rubertus*, *Robertus*, *Ruothpertus*, *Rothbertus*, *Ruopertus*, and *Ruobertus*.], Heinricus presided over the church (in 956) [Note: [Col. 1165] *Henricus* in 2, 5, and 6, consistently.]. He built the regular workshops and cloister around the greater church [Note: [Col. 1165] Omitted in 1b.], and resolved to exercise there the vigor of regular observance [Note: [Col. 1165] “Rigor” in 4, 5, and 6; “to be exercised” in 6a–b and d, B, and C.]. He established a market in the place where it now seems to exist [Note: [Col. 1165] “Where it now does not” in 1b; “where it appears to be” in 2 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 1166D] In the margin of C3, in another hand, is added: “In it he caused a cross to be erected, at whose summit there is now found engraved: ‘In memory of the signs of the cross which had appeared from heaven over human beings in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 968, and in the second year of our episcopate, I, Archbishop Henricus, erected me.’”].

He was present at Rome with Otto [Note: [Col. 1165] “Otto I” in B and C; *Ottho* in 6a and frequently.] in 963 when the magician, not Pope John [Note: [Col. 1165] John XII in 5a and 5c; John XIII in 5b.], was condemned.

Otto also removed the aforementioned abbey from this church by his authority [Note: [Col. 1165] “By royal authority” in B and C.] and assigned to this church another one called Horrea [Note: [Col. 1165] “Which was called” in B4, 5, and C; “which was superscripted or ‘as if’” in C1 and likewise in C3.], as though it were his own [Note: [Col. 1165] “His own” is omitted here.], in exchange for Mastreth [Note: [Col. 1165] The witnesses give *Masetricht*, *Masetrech*, *Masetreh*, *Masetreht*, *Masethre*, *Mastreht*, *Mastreith*, *Mastreit*, *Mastret*, and *Maestrich*.] [Note: [Col. 1166D] See the charter in Gunther, *Rhenish-Moselle Diplomatic Codex* I, p. 74.], although nothing belonging to it pertained to him [Note: [Col. 1165] This clause is omitted in 5a.].

Bishop Heinricus died in Italy (in 964, July 2) [Note: [Col. 1165] “Died” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1167C] B and C continue: “He himself took eighty hides from Saint Martin, and afterward died in Italy.”].

Theodericus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1165] *Theodricus* in 5a; “his successor” in B2.] [Note: [Col. 1167C] B and C continue: “A noble man of great authority, provost of the greater church of Mainz, who …”]. He buried the body of his predecessor, brought back to Treberis [Col. 1166B], in the cemetery of the greater church. He renewed and enlarged the privileges of his church [Note: [Col. 1165] “Privilege” in 5 and 6; “increased the privilege” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 1168A]

> C adds: “Copies of them we have taken care to set down here:
>
> **17. The privilege of Pope Benedict, which he gave to Theodericus, bishop of Treberis** [Note: [Col. 1168D] Not found in Hontheim.].
>
> Benedictus, bishop … in the aforementioned first indiction.
>
> **18. Another privilege of Pope Benedict, which he gave to Theodericus, bishop of Treberis** [Note: [Col. 1168D] The following two charters are omitted in C3 and C4; not found in Hontheim.].
>
> Benedictus, bishop … in the aforementioned third indiction.
>
> **19. Concerning the same: Pope John XIII** [Note: [Col. 1167] “Concerning the same John” in W; omitted in C1 and C6.] [Note: [Col. 1168D] In Hontheim, p. 305.].
>
> John, bishop … in the twelfth indiction. Farewell.
>
> The aforementioned bishop Theodericus gave to the churches, and so forth, as in manuscript B.”

[Col. 1168B] B and C add: “He gave many gifts to the churches of Saint Martin, where Saint Magnericus rests, and of blessed Paulinus, and restored those that had collapsed through age” [Note: [Col. 1167] “Gift” in B5; “collapsed” in B5.] [Note: [Col. 1168D] Compare Theodericus’s charter in *History and Commentaries of the Palatine Academy* III, p. 40, and Pope Benedict’s in Hontheim, p. 316, as well as what we have published below concerning this monastery.].

At Rome he acquired for himself and his successors in perpetuity the cell of the Four Crowned Saints with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1165] C adds “also the cell”; 1 and 5b spell *acquisivit* (“he acquired”) as *acquesivit*; 6 places *acquisivit* before *in perpetuum*, “he acquired in perpetuity.”] [Note: [Col. 1168B]

> C continues: “And he obtained from Pope Benedict a privilege concerning it, in the following form:
>
> **20. The privilege of Pope Benedict, which he gave to Bishop Theodericus of Treberis** [Note: [Col. 1167] The rubric is omitted in C1, where only “six popes” is read.] [Note: [Col. 1168D] In Hontheim, p. 314.].
>
> Benedictus, bishop … in the aforementioned third indiction.
>
> Under this pontiff the regular canons, and so forth.”]

Under him the regular canons ceased to be in the church of Saint Peter. He was buried [Note: [Col. 1168B] B and C continue: “He died at Mainz and was buried in the basilica of Saint Gangulf, martyr” [Note: [Col. 1167] *Gyngulf* in B2.], which he himself built from his own resources and where he established twelve brothers to serve God, supplying them with the necessities of life [Note: [Col. 1167] “The necessities” in B5.].] in the cemetery of Saint Eucharius [Note: [Col. 1165] Omitted in 5b.] (in 977, June 5).

Eckebertus, of eternal memory, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1165] At the name Eckebertus, 1 has *ecb eckebertus*; 5 reads *eketherus*; 6 has *eketbertus eterne memorie*, “Eketbertus of eternal memory,” reversing the order; B5 reads *ekeberdus*, and C *ekebertus*. These are forms of the bishop’s name.] [Note: [Col. 1168B] B and C continue: “Bishop Ekebertus” [Note: [Col. 1167] “Archbishop” in C.] [Note: [Col. 1169A]

> C adds: “Here he obtained from the emperor Otto II a charter concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius, as follows” [Note: [Col. 1169] C3 and C4 omit the introductory notice beginning “Here” and the charter itself.]:
>
> **Charter of King Otto concerning the abbey of Saint Servatius** [Note: [Col. 1169D] In Hontheim, p. 331.].
>
> [Col. 1169B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Otto … Successfully enacted at Ingelheim. Amen.
>
> “Thus [C3 begins chapter 19 here] the aforementioned bishop from Brittannia, and so forth.”]

[The supplied source ends with the editor’s abbreviated continuation, “and so forth.”]

He was born in Britain, the son of Theoderic, Count of Holland [Col. 1168D; cf. the *Life of Adalbert the Deacon*, written at Egbert’s command, *Acta Sanctorum*, June V, p. 102; see also Hontheim, *Prodromus*, I, p. 84, and Kluit, *Historia critica Hollandiae*], and of a woman named Hildegard, foremost among the English in wealth and nobility; and, as we believe, by divine providence he was predestined for this see. For as soon as, with Christ caring for the people of Trier, he ascended this see, he so perpetually relieved its manifold poverty through the charity and mercy that abounded in him that, for as long as this world revolves, his memory must rightly be judged worthy of celebration [Col. 1169; *celebranda* corrected to *celebrando* in B2; B3 reads *celebrando*, while C1’s correction restores *celebranda*].

Immediately, therefore, he sent word to all his kinsmen according to the flesh and the spirit in Britain that they should prepare themselves to visit him and to display the proof of their nobility, and that at the next Nativity of the Lord they should hasten to Trier with every display of pomp and ambition [Col. 1169; B5 reads *preparent*, “prepare”]. When they had diligently and energetically fulfilled this, he, through charity, stripped them of all the goods and money that they had brought [B4 and B5 read “all whom”; B3 and C omit “for them”], and, after they had returned to their homeland [B5 and B6 read *patria*, “homeland”], sent back much more and added more valuable things, “his church …” [the supplied text breaks off here]; “distinguished in nobility and virtue” [a surviving fragment; Col. 1165: *insignitus*, “distinguished,” in witness 2].

He found his church emptied by the plunder of pagans and Christians [Col. 1165; *et Christianorum* is absent in 5a; *rapinis*, “plunderings,” in 6c], and enriched it with the most lavish generosity [*leberalitate*, “liberality,” in witness 1], increasing it with gold and silver crosses, liturgical books [one manuscript reads *planetis*, “chasubles”], chasubles, dalmatics [*dalmaciis* in witness 2], tunics, pallia, capes, veils, curtains [*cortinis*, “curtains,” in witnesses 4, 5, and 6], and possessions [Col. 1166C]. He repaired the monasteries of the city, which had been exhausted of their estates by the plunder of the neighboring inhabitants [*provincialium*, “provincial inhabitants,” in 5c and B and C; the manuscripts generally read *exaustas*, while C has *exhaustas* and 2 and 5–6 *exhausta*], recovering everywhere, by force of authority, the possessions that had been taken away [Col. 1166D; see his charters in Hontheim, pp. 320–321, and the translation of Saint Celsus published below]. He received as a gift the abbey of Saint Servatius from the second Otto [Col. 1165; witness 5c omits “as a gift”; Col. 1166D: “the Third”; see the charter below, col. 1167, note *1*, from C; another manuscript reads “Otto the Second”].

He ordered a fast on account of the drought threatening the land, as well as processions bearing crosses and holy relics around the circuit of the Trier valley [Col. 1169; B and C continue: “A fast [C adds ‘also’] on account of the drought threatening the land, and processions of crosses and holy relics around the circuit of the Trier valley”], to be held by everyone in his parish [*porrochia*, “parish,” in witness 1] in the third week after Easter [Col. 1167A; Col. 1167D: Brower, p. 486, remarks that the fast was afterward called a proclaimed or mandated fast. Compare the *History of the Martyrs of Trier*, chap. 4 (Hontheim, *Prodromus*, I, p. 124), where it reads: “Afterward, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, on which day, according to the institution of Archbishop Egbert, great crowds from the surrounding villages customarily come to Trier with crosses and go around all the monasteries of that city.”]. Moreover, he discovered the body of Saint Celsus the Confessor in the cemetery of Saint Eucharius [Col. 1167; one manuscript reads “in the cemetery of Saint Eucharius”; Col. 1167D: I have published below certain passages from the history of its translation, written by Theoderic].

[Col. 1169B; B and C add:] For this Egbert and Theoderic, bishop of Metz, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 970, while they were staying in Italy for nearly three years with Otto the Great and Most Glorious Emperor Augustus, whose wife is more correctly called Adelheid [Theophanu in the text], gathered many bodies of saints and sent them to their respective sees. Egbert acquired, with the assistance of the king mentioned above [B2: “previously mentioned”], Saint Severus the priest, buried in the valley of Terento, of whom Saint Gregory makes mention in the *Dialogues* [B2: “in the Dialogue”; C1 adds “makes mention,” and the later copies follow it]. He was transported along the bed of the Moselle River [C omits this]. He acquired at the city of Spoleto the bones of Gregory the martyr and of Pontianus the martyr [Col. 1169D: Theoderic is credited with this account], and at the fortress of Turegum the relics of Felix and Regula [Col. 1169D: these are not mentioned in the account from which the following material is taken].

The bishop of Corfinium gave the body of Saint Lucy the virgin to Bishop Theoderic of Metz, testifying, with his hand placed upon the Gospel, that this was indeed the Syracusan Lucy, for whom responsories and antiphons are sung everywhere with the Mass, and that she had been transferred to that place by a certain Foroard, duke of Spoleto [*poletinum* in B6]. The same Theoderic, at the most devout request of Bishop Egbert [C: “archbishop”], gave him half of it [Col. 1169D: this is added by the Trier author].

Through Egbert’s industry the church of Trier also recovered the staff of Saint Peter, which had long been lost. How it had been lost we shall briefly explain [Col. 1169D; Leibniz, chap. XLV. In the *Deeds of the Bishops of Toul* it is related that Saint Peter’s staff reached Toul from Metz in the tenth century. On the staff preserved at Metz, see Brower, I, p. 483. Compare, however, the *Life of Saint Agritius*, p. 778: “It is known that blessed Eucharius brought to this place the staff of the chief of the apostles, Peter, which he had received from his own hand as a consolation in a brother’s death and as an honor of apostolic dignity. Therefore, as the privilege deposited in the Roman archives testifies, no successor of that chief of the apostles in the Roman see uses the support of the staff.”].

In the time of Saint Maximinus, when the Huns were planning to cross the Rhine and invade Gaul, Saint Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, foresaw in spirit the slaughter and fires and the future destruction of all Gaul. He went to Rome for the sake of prayer, so that through the support of apostolic patronage he might mitigate the Lord’s anger. While he persisted there for three days in prayers and tears, he learned by an apostolic response that the Lord’s vengeance would in no way be averted, and that no city or church in Gaul would be left unburned except only the monastery of Saint Stephen at Metz [Col. 1170B; up to this point he appears to follow Heriger, chaps. 22–23, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, VII, p. 173. He now adds a very fabulous narrative copied from an unknown book].

Returning from there to Trier, he reported what he had heard to Saint Maximinus, and not long afterward died at Tongeren. It was therefore decided, on the advice of wise men [C: “of the wise”], that whatever movable relics [B6: “noble relics”] there were in the city of Trier should be taken to Metz for fear of the aforesaid hostility [B2: *mehtthi*; B4: *mett.*]. But before the incursion of the Huns, the people of Trier had endured an invasion by the Greeks [Col. 1170D; see above, chaps. 19 and 22].

Not long afterward that Attila, celebrated in everyone’s report—the king of the Huns, a whirlpool of misery and evil—captured, burned, and devastated all Gaul from the Rhine to Orléans. Then, when peace had been restored and the cities and villages began again to be inhabited as before, the people of Trier sought to recover their possessions from the people of Metz, but labored in vain. It was therefore decided that an annual tribute should be paid from the city of Trier to Saint Stephen, patron of the people of Metz [Col. 1170C], so that, through this act of veneration, they might deserve some restoration of their property.

When the people of Metz returned certain things to them, except for the staff [B2 omits “other”], and it became a source of shame to the people of Trier [C1 corrects the reading to “the people of Trier,” followed by C3 and later copies] that they, once conquerors of nations, should be tributaries of the people of Metz, they broke the agreement and erected an altar in honor of Saint Stephen upon four columns in the Trier court [B6 omits “in honor”], and paid the aforesaid census there every year.

Afterward, when a complaint arose among the people of Metz in the king’s court, and they said that the annual tribute owed to them by the people of Trier had for several years been withheld, while the latter denied that they had ever been tributaries to anyone, the people of Metz requested that the altar set upon the columns in the court should be sent for and inspected as evidence of their good faith and their complaint. When it had been agreed by the judgment of both sides that this should be done, the people of Trier secretly sent a very swift messenger and moved the altar from the columns and placed it in the monastery of Saint Peter.

Thus, when the matter raised by the complaints could not be proved by testimony, the people of Trier gained this victory, but remained deprived of the staff’s presence. This continued until, after the aforesaid invasions and three further very grave invasions by the Vandals, Franks, and Northmen, during the reign of Otto, his brother [Col. 1171B; B4 has “Bruno” in the margin], the most powerful bishop of Cologne, who had also been granted this city, was asked by the people of Trier to compel the people of Metz to return the staff to this church. He extorted it from them, but, wishing to steal it away with the same treachery by which they had stolen the Lord’s nail [Col. 1171C; on this matter see the *Life of Saint Agritius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 777; I have decided to reproduce its passage below], gave it as a gift to the church of Cologne [B2: “with him”].

A few years later, at the insistence of Bishop Egbert [C: “Archbishop”], Bishop Warinus of Cologne cut off the upper part of the staff, keeping the portion with the tip for himself, and sent the remainder here [B2: “to this church”; B5: “this”].

It is said that swallows were cursed by this man, namely Bishop Egbert, so that they would not fly into the church of Saint Peter, or, if they did fly in, would perish, because one day, while he was celebrating the sacred rites at the altar, the head of one of them had touched and defiled him [B6: “on a certain day” and “a certain one”].”

When the feast of Saint Eucharius once arrived [the manuscripts also read “on a certain feast,” “on the feast,” and “on a certain day”], he went to that saint’s monastery to celebrate the divine office there. After the solemnities of the Mass had been completed [6c omits “after”], the brothers earnestly asked him to accept their charity in food and drink [B and C: “food and drink”]. But, lest it perhaps be burdensome to them if he, accompanied by so great a retinue and display, should dine there [the manuscripts otherwise read *reficeretur*; some have *reficeret*], he began entirely to refuse the hospitality offered by the brothers [several manuscripts omit “offered” and “entirely”] and to hasten his return to the city [one manuscript omits “return”].

When he had come to the river Olevia [manuscript forms include *Olevia*, *Oliviam*, *Olivam*, and *Obliviam*], he began to fail from a severe illness. Without delay, he came to his see [B and C: “arriving at his see”] and closed his final day [C6 adds in the margin: “the fifth day before the Ides of December”] (993, December 9).

He was buried there in a small church [Col. 1167B; witness 2 omits “in”] that he himself had built [B and C: “which he himself had built”] in honor of Saint Andrew [one manuscript adds “the Apostle”]. [B and C add: “on the right side of the church. On the left lies the aforementioned Heinrich, his third predecessor, whom he buried there after he had died in Italy and had been brought here.”]

The church stood toward the east of the metropolitan church. The Paris manuscript (C6) added his epitaph, which, as Brower notes (p. 493), had already disappeared in his time, only traces of the tomb being visible. It was as follows.

**Epitaph of Erbertus** [the manuscript reads “Erbertus”]:

> The glory of pontiffs, the church’s most brilliant lamp,  
> The peace and love of the people, the favor of all the clergy,  
> Here lies Egbertus, found in the region of light,  
> The Trier prelate, and founder of this court.  
> He ruled the church for six tens of years  
> [lacuna] nine [surviving term: *novenis*] and days.  
> Commend your beloved patron to God by your prayers.

### 30.

[Leibniz, chap. XLVI.]

Liudolf succeeded him [manuscript forms include *Luoitoldus* and *Hildolfus*]. [B and C add:] By birth a Saxon. He surrounded the church of Saint Peter and the dwellings of the brothers with walls [C6 reads “tabernacles”], and established that the things within them should serve the canons, except those belonging to the bishop [B2 reads “episcopal residence”], so that, just as they were separated from the common people in religion, so also they might be separated in their dwelling. Wyttenbach notes that the ruins of these walls still survived at the end of the eighteenth century and could even then be seen behind the two places popularly called *auf dem Graben*.

During his episcopate, a provost named Adelbero presided over the monastery of Saint Paulinus. He was from Lucelenburg [the manuscripts give *Lutzelenburc*, *Luzeleborch*, *Luzelenburch*, *Luzelenbruch*, and other forms], a powerful and wealthy man, possessing these castles: Sarburg [also *Sareburc*, *Sareburch*, *Saremburch*, and *Sarenbruch*], Bernkastel [also *Herencastel*, *Berencastell*, and *Beronoasdel*], and Rutiche [also *Rutehe*, *Ruteche*, *Ruthiche*, *Ruthice*, *Rustiche*, *Rudiche*, and *Ruothiche*]. [Col. 1171C: Sarburg, Bernkastel, and Roussy.]

After entering into an evil agreement with Archbishop Liudolf [one manuscript reads “with the archpriest”; B2 “with the bishop”; several omit “bishop”], he claimed for himself, partly by force and partly by deceit [some manuscripts read “by gift”], the church of Saint Symphorian, which had been subject to the abbots of Saint Martin, with the bishop—alas!—consenting to him [B5 omits “to him”], and afterward retained it for Saint Paulinus [some manuscripts read “he obtained it for Saint Paulinus”].

When Liudolf died (1008, April 7) [one manuscript reads “when Adelbero died”], Adelbero, relying on the confidence inspired by the fact that his sister had been married to Emperor Henry the Lame [several manuscripts omit this phrase], invaded the bishopric. He compelled the soldiers to swear allegiance to him, occupied the palace situated in the same city, and also fortified the bridge over the Moselle with towers.

But Emperor Henry gave the bishopric to Meingard [manuscript forms include *Megingaudus*, *Meingado*, *Meningaudus*, and *Mangaudus*], provost of the church of Mainz [several manuscripts omit this phrase]. When he prepared to resist Adelbero’s power, he granted Ravenger of Malberg [Col. 1172C: “Malberg”; the manuscripts give *Madelberch*, *Madelburc*, *Maldeberch*, *Madelberg*, *Madelberc*, and *Mailberch*] and Udelbert of Stalle [forms include *Oldeberto*, *Adelberto*, *Adalberto*, and *Uodelberto*; *Stalle* also has variant forms] eighty hides [B and C read sixty] from the possessions of Saint Martin as a benefice, but nevertheless he did not prevail.

Then Emperor Henry came to Trier with an army and besieged the palace from the Sunday after the White Days until the Kalends of September (1008, April 4–September 1) [Col. 1172C; compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg* for this year and Thietmar VI, 25]. During that siege not only was the countryside around the city devastated everywhere [B and C omit this], but the city itself [6 reads “the city itself also,” and some manuscripts omit “already”], which after the Northmen’s devastation had already been adorned with buildings and had to some extent been inhabited again, was reduced to its former desolation [B and C: “was almost reduced”].

Finally, not only did the besiegers, but the besieged men of the palace themselves, by frequent sorties, ravage the besiegers and the areas adjoining the palace [one manuscript reads “the palaces were ravaged”]. One day, a multitude of oxen and sheep [one manuscript reads “oxen, birds, and sheep”], brought down from the summit of Mount Juran [also *Urani*], descended with a military escort [one manuscript reads “with a large escort”] for the emperor’s service. Seeing this from the fortress, the men of the palace suddenly made a sortie, routed the escort, and drove the oxen and sheep before them into the palace. The imperial soldiers pursued them, and, when the gates had been opened, burst into the palace together with them [6: “with the animals themselves”]. Without delay, the men of the palace closed the gates from within, and, hurling stones from the fortress, killed some of all who had entered, severely wounded others, and captured the rest [B6 ends here].

Then the emperor ordered siege engines to be erected from the timber of the city houses around the palace and as far as the fortresses, so that from the same height as the palace he might more easily hem in the men of the palace [one manuscript omits “so that he might”; another reads “so that he might more easily hem in the palace men”]. But while the men of the palace fought back bravely [manuscript forms include “strongly” and “they fought at the doors”], these engines were either set on fire by the introduction of fire or destroyed [variants include “burned,” “overcome,” and “demolished”].

Therefore, since the emperor made no progress in capturing it, he departed on the Kalends of September [one manuscript omits the phrase beginning “since he made no progress”] and ordered the bridge, whose custody Adelbero’s men had held [variants: “the custody of which Adelbero had held”], to be thrown down. He confirmed Meingard in the bishopric. Meingard administered the bishopric from the castle of Confluentia until the end of his life, while the aforesaid usurper Adelbero retained most of the episcopal household.

At last, toward the end of Meingard’s life [several manuscripts omit “of Meingard” or “of his life”], when he was weighed down by a serious illness, he restored everything to Meingard [C reads “returned it”], but retained the palace for himself [B and C omit “for himself”].

When Meingard died (1015, December 23), Emperor Henry appointed Poppo [manuscript forms include *Boppo* and *Poponem*], who had been educated at Bamberg [the manuscripts variously read *Babenberg*, *Babenberch*, *Regensburg*, and related forms], as bishop in opposition to Adelbero, saying: “I must send such a man as will be capable of resisting your madness.”

At last Adelbero, touched by delayed repentance [C reads “late”], and unable to withstand Poppo’s strength, became his suppliant and surrendered to him the palace, his castles, and all his property. [Col. 1173D; Hontheim I, pp. 368 and 371, preserves two charters, from 1036 and 1037, in which he gives various possessions to the monastery of Saint Matthias. The Trier library possesses another charter from 1037, not yet printed, in which this Albero made donations of his villages to various other churches as well—Saint Martin, Prüm, Saint Mary at the Martyrs, and others. Wyttenbach.] He afterward remained in the monastery of Saint Paulinus until the end of his life [some manuscripts omit “of his life”].

But Emperor Henry, to make satisfaction to Saint Peter for the harm he had inflicted upon the city, sent a panel of gold and silver, adorned with precious stones [manuscript variants include “metals” and omit the phrase], equal in size to the altar [some manuscripts read “of the altar”] of Saint Peter [the manuscripts variously read “equal to,” “of the size of,” and “of the magnitude of”].

### 31.

[Leibniz, chap. XLVII; II, chap. XXI, C1. C3 adds the red heading: “Concerning Archbishop Poppo”; thereafter the chapters are not numbered.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1015 [manuscript variants include 1016, 1020, and 1015], Poppo was ordained archbishop of Trier [6 reads “the Trier archbishop”]. Often occupied in military expeditions and campaigns, he took certain things from Saint Paulinus [B1 reads “brought back”; witnesses 5 and later omit the phrase]. From the palace he also distributed sixty prebends for nuns among soldiers as benefices [several manuscripts omit this; one reads “gave”].
