He destroyed Bernkastel [B2 reads *Berencastel*], formerly defended by Adelbero’s brigands, and also cast down to the ground another castle belonging to a certain tyrant named Adelbert, called Sckiva [the name appears as *scriua* or *servia*, *siura*, *suira*, *suura*, *skiva*, and *sisiva*; C6 omits it]. Wyttenbach cites from a later Trier manuscript the words: “Sckiva, which was called Munclerum.” Today it is Monclair.

This Adelbert possessed a castle once built near Trier in honor of the Holy Cross [some manuscripts read “in honor”; others omit “holy”]. No ruins of this castle, formerly situated near Trier, survive today [Wyttenbach].

From there he frequently made sorties with a multitude of soldiers against the bishop’s court, violently carrying away and taking with him whatever was being prepared there for the bishop’s service [one manuscript reads “whatever belonged to his service”]. Ashamed of this disgrace—namely, that he could not defeat an enemy so close to him because of the castle’s fortification—the bishop, after voicing many complaints to his friends [one manuscript reads “to many of his friends”], began to seek counsel and assistance to drive away such infamy [one manuscript reads “to defeat such an enemy”].

There was in his army a man powerful in wealth and strong in bodily strength [6 reads “strong in wealth and strength”], named Sicko [variant spellings include *Sikko*, *Siko*, and *Sicho*], who promised that he would try to discover some means of remedying this evil, if he could somehow do so [the manuscripts variously read “if he could find some way” and “if he could discover a remedy for this evil”].

The bishop rejoiced greatly at this [B2 reads “rejoicing with him”]. Sicko went out, wishing to attempt what he had promised [C reads “to fulfill what he had promised”]. One day he went to the gate of the castle and knocked at the doors [manuscript forms include *fores*, *foras*, and *foris*]. He asked that Adelbert send him a drinking vessel to refresh himself [Col. 1175C: that is, wine casks, in German *Ohm*]. When it had quickly been brought and he had drunk it [6c reads “had obeyed”], he addressed the servant [B and C read “the cupbearer”]:

“Give your master my great thanks, and also take care to tell him these words: while I remain alive, I shall strive to repay this cup to him very soon with grateful goodwill.”

After saying this, he departed.

Then, having chosen a suitable time [the manuscripts read “at a suitable time” or “after suitable planning”], he prepared thirty large vessels [some manuscripts read “casks”], placing in each one an armed soldier chosen from among the best, clad in a coat of mail [one reads “a leather cuirass”], helmeted, and girded with swords. He covered them above with linen cloths [variants include “cloths” and “open cloths”] and arranged ropes on them into which poles could be inserted for carrying them [manuscripts vary between “poles” and “crossbars”].

He also appointed sixty men, likewise chosen and dressed in common clothing [one manuscript omits this], with their swords hidden in the vessels [variants include “in the vessels” and “in the large vessels”], to be their bearers. Without making any person aware of this deception except the men mentioned above [one manuscript reads “except the aforesaid men”], Sicko himself, surrounded by these and a few other soldiers, proceeded to the castle [one manuscript reads “to the palace”] and knocked at the doors.

When the servant asked who he was and what he wanted, he replied: “Tell your master that I am bringing him the wine that I formerly promised him as a token of great affection, since he was not reluctant to send me a cup when I was thirsty.”

When the servant had reported this [variants include “announced” and “proclaimed”], Adelbert ordered the men to be admitted. When they had entered and placed the vessels simultaneously on the ground before Adelbert [one manuscript reads “with two lines”; another has *potentibus*], Sicko entered behind them and ordered the coverings of the vessels to be removed [variants include “the linen coverings” and “the linen cloth.”]. He asked Adelbert to accept the gifts of affection.

The bearers, just as they had been instructed, threw down all the coverings of the vessels at the same moment [one manuscript reads “they put down the burdens”], seized their swords [some manuscripts omit “their swords”], and sprang out of the vessels [one reads “leapt forth”]. They drew their swords and struck fiercely on every side; they cut down Adelbert himself, cruelly slaughtered the other household attendants, and reduced the castle to desolation [one manuscript reads “the castle was directed”].

For this victory Sicko was honored by Poppo with benefices [some manuscripts omit “for the victory”; others read “was enriched”].

[B and C continue:] In the same way, through other leaders, he captured many castles, partly by force and partly by deceit, and to a very great extent restrained the madness of the tyrants, who had long raged with impunity. He mercifully assisted the monasteries, which had been nearly emptied by their violence, as far as he could: to some he gave what they had not possessed, to others he restored what had been taken away. The only exceptions, as we said above, were the two communities of Saint Paulinus and Saint Mary of the Palace. From the former he did not refrain from taking certain things because of Adelbero’s insolence; from the latter, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, about whom we shall speak later [see the Addendum below], he took away everything they had possessed and expelled them from that place.

**Editorial correction (Cols. 1176C–1177C):** This is a very serious error. The Trier author here identifies the archbishop Poppo with the Poppo who preached to the Danes in the tenth century; he has turned King Otto into a Danish count and, to compound the errors, has brought Ansgar into the story.

At the request of a certain Danish count named Otto, he came to Denmark [B1 reads *Dana*, “Denmark”; B2 and B3 correct *Daxia* to *Dacia*, “Denmark”; C1 and 6 have *Dacia* by correction; C3 has *Datia*] and converted the Danish people, who at that time still served idols, to Christ. When unbelievers resisted, he ordered an iron gauntlet to be made and heated in the fire. After covering his hand with it [Col. 1176C], and putting on a linen cloth soaked in wax next to his flesh, he entered a glowing furnace [B2 has *candaentem*, “glowing”; another manuscript reads “burning furnace”]. He emerged from it unharmed, although the cloth had been burned, and by this sign declared that Christ, the Son of God, is the true God [B2 writes the Christogram *xpictum*, “Christ”].

This is still widely proclaimed among the Danes, by whom he is also called Ansgarius [*Ansgerius* in B1]. By this name his memory is celebrated among them on the fifth day before the Ides of September. His tomb at Trier is frequented by the Danes.

But since we have mentioned him in passing, it is agreeable to recall briefly, from the beginning, certain events of his deeds [Leibniz begins chap. XLVIII here; the manuscripts vary between “to narrate” and “to commemorate by narration”].”

Poppo repaired the church of Saint Peter, which had already collapsed, and, after transferring some of the relics of Saint Martin into it [one manuscript reads “into that church”], dedicated it in honor of Saint Martin [one manuscript reads “maternal”]. He also built a tower there [see the Addendum below, chap. 8]. He assigned certain goods to Saint Eucharius and restored certain things that had been taken away [one manuscript omits the phrase beginning “to Saint Eucharius”].

The hermit Saint Symeon [one manuscript reads “Simon”] flourished above the Black Gate at Trier. There he also found rest [the manuscripts read “rests” or “rested”]. Archbishop Poppo established a community there [“of clerics” is absent from manuscripts 2, 4, 5, and 6]. From the ruins of the gate a church of Saint Simeon was built, which stood until our own times. There afterward he himself also found rest at the feet of Saint Symeon [several manuscripts omit “at the feet of Saint Symeon”] (1047).

[Col. 1177A] I have published below a continuation of this text under the title of the Addendum.

### Apparatus retained from the supplied edition

This register gives the edition’s readings in source order. Latin forms are retained only where English cannot show a spelling, case, or inflectional difference; each is paired with an English gloss or explanation. Abbreviated apparatus entries that describe word order are expanded as word-order statements rather than treated as manuscript abbreviations.

**Opening through Celsus.** Col. 1168D identifies Theoderic as Count of Holland and compares the *Life of Adalbert the Deacon*, written at Egbert’s command (*Acta Sanctorum*, June V, p. 102), Hontheim, *Prodromus* I, p. 84, and Kluit, *Historia communis Hollandiae*. Col. 1168C supplies the statement that Hildegard ranked among the foremost English in wealth and nobility. At Col. 1169A the source spells “abounded” *habundavit*. At Col. 1169, B2 corrects *celebranda*, “to be celebrated,” to *celebrando*, “by celebrating”; B3 and 6 read *celebrando*, while C1 restores *celebranda* by correction. B5 has *preparent*, “let them prepare.” B2 omits “when” from “when they had fulfilled this.” B4–5 read “all persons whom” (*omnes … quos*) where the text has “all the things which,” and B3/C omit “for them.” B2, 6, and C6 spell “and to the same persons” *isdemque*; C1 corrects *isdem* to *hisdemque*, followed by C3 and later witnesses. B5–6 use the ablative *patria*, “from the homeland,” where the text has *in patriam*, “to the homeland.” The text itself breaks after *ecclesiam suam p.* (“his church …”); no continuation is supplied. Witness 2 reads *insignitus*, “distinguished,” for *insignis*, “distinguished.”

At Col. 1165, 5a omits “and Christians”; 6c has plural *rapinis*, “plunderings,” for singular *rapina*, “plunder”; 1 writes *leberalitate* for *liberalitate*, “generosity”; 6 reads *planetis*, “chasubles,” for *plenariis*, “liturgical books”; 2 writes *dalmaciis* for *dalmaticis*, “dalmatics”; and 4–6 write *cortinis* for *cortinisque*, “and curtains.” B5 has singular *monasterio*, “monastery,” for plural *monasteria*, “monasteries”; 1b reads *monasteria urbis*, “the monasteries of the city.” For “neighboring inhabitants,” 5c reads *provincialium*, “provincial inhabitants,” and B/C read *et provincialium*, “and provincial inhabitants.” Nearly all manuscripts seen by the editor read *exaustas*, “exhausted”; C has *exhaustas*, while 2, 5, and 6 have singular *exhausta*. Col. 1166C marks the statement that he increased the church’s possessions. Col. 1166D refers to Egbert’s charters in Hontheim, pp. 320–21, and to the translation of Saint Celsus printed below. Witness 5 places “he repaired” after “abbey”; C omits the span from “abbey” through “received.” Witness 5c omits “as a gift.” Col. 1166D reads Otto “the Third,” referring to the charter from C printed below at col. 1167 n. 1; B reverses the base order “second Otto” to “Otto the Second.”

At Col. 1169B, B/C continue the sentence as follows: “He ordered a fast [C adds ‘also’] because drought threatened the land, together with rogations and processions of crosses and holy relics around the circuit of the Trier valley, to be observed by everyone in his parish.” B2 has *sanctorum*, “of saints,” for *sanctarum*, “holy,” and C1 corrects the adjective *Treberici* to *Treberice*, followed by C3 and later witnesses. Witness 1 spells “parish” *porrochia*. Col. 1167D says Brower, p. 486, notes that the fast was later called *bannitum*, “proclaimed” or “mandated,” and compares *History of the Martyrs of Trier* 4 (Hontheim, *Prodromus* I, p. 124): “Afterward, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, on which day, by the institution of Archbishop Ekbert, great crowds from the surrounding villages customarily come to Trier with crosses and go around every monastery of that city.” C reads “the body moreover”; 6c moves “found” before “Eucharius” (*repperit Eucharii*) rather than leaving the verb after the cemetery phrase. Col. 1167D says the editor printed below passages from the history of Celsus’s translation written by Theoderic.

**Relics, Servatius, and the staff.** The relic narrative is added by B/C. Col. 1169D says it was drawn from the narrative about saints brought back by Theoderic (*Acta Sanctorum* IV, p. 473), although that narrative makes no mention of Egbert. B2 spells Egbert *Eckebertus*; C calls him “Archbishop Ekbert”; B4 spells “of Metz” *Methensis*; B5/C omit “in Italy.” Col. 1169D says Otto’s wife is more correctly named Adelheid than Theophanu. The sentence from Saint Severus through his transport is absent from B6. A further Col. 1169D note compares the old text printed above and suggests that the writer may have seen the history of the translation. B2 reads “previously named” for “named above”; B2 has singular “in the Dialogue,” while C1 adds “makes mention,” followed by C3 and later witnesses. C omits the span from “who” through “was transported,” and B4–5 omit “was transported.” C reads “He also obtained”; B6 writes *Poleto* for Spoleto. Col. 1169D says the account attributes the Gregory and Pontianus episode to Theoderic, and that Felix and Regula do not occur in the narrative from which the following material was taken. B5 has singular “responsory”; B6 writes *poletinum* for “of Spoleto.” Col. 1169D says the Trier writer added the gift of half of Lucy’s body; C calls Egbert archbishop. At the opening of the staff episode, Leibniz begins chapter XLV and C adds “also.” B2 has plural “they lost” for singular “he lost.” Col. 1169D says the *Deeds of the Bishops of Toul* relates that Saint Peter’s staff reached Toul from Metz in the tenth century, cites Brower I, p. 483 for the staff kept at Metz, and compares the *Life of Saint Agritius*, p. 778: blessed Eucharius brought there the staff of Peter, prince of the apostles, received from Peter’s own hand as consolation for a brother’s death and as an honor of apostolic dignity; therefore, as the privilege deposited in the Roman archives testifies, every successor of Peter in the Roman see does not use the support of a staff.

C1 and all later witnesses spell the Rhine *Rhenum*; B2 and 6 spell “of all” *tocius*. The Metz monastery is *Methi* in B2, *Metti* in B3/C, and *Meto* in B4–5. Col. 1170B says the narrative so far appears to follow Heriger 22–23, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* VII, p. 173; Col. 1170D says the author now adds a very fabulous story copied from some unknown book. B2 spells Trier *Treberi*; B6 reads “noble relics” for “movable relics”; Metz is *mehtthi* in B2 and *mett.* in B4; C has “of the wise” for “of wise men.” B4 reads “however” for “before” the Hunnic invasion. Col. 1170D refers to chapters 19 and 22 above for the Greek invasion. C3 corrects *exin*, “thereupon,” to *exinde*, “thereafter,” followed by C4 and 6. B5 inserts “already” before “from the people of Metz”; B2 reads “therefore” for “accordingly”; C1 spells the Trier people *Treveri*. B2 omits “other things.” C1 corrects genitive *Trebirorum*, “of the people of Trier,” to accusative *Trebiros*, “the people of Trier,” making them the subject of “were tributaries”; C3 and later witnesses follow the correction. B6 omits “in honor”; B2 has *Treberici*, “of Trier,” for *Treberica*, “Trier,” modifying the court. C1 and later witnesses read “several years” for “some year”; B2 reads “by themselves” for “to anyone.” Col. 1171B records “Bruno” in B4’s margin as Otto’s brother. B2 has *cum*, “with,” for the pronoun *eum*, “it.” Col. 1171C refers to the *Life of Saint Agritius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 777, for the Lord’s nail and says the editor decided to reproduce the passage below. C calls Egbert archbishop; C3–4 omit “for himself”; B2 reads “to this church” for “here,” and B5 reads *hunc*, “this [staff or portion],” for “here.” C reads “or” for “and if”; B2 expands “because” to “for the reason that”; B6/C use feminine *quadam* rather than masculine *quodam* in “on a certain day.”

**Egbert’s death and burial.** For “when … once arrived,” witness 4 has feminine *quadam*, 5c and 6c masculine *quodam*, and B2 “on a certain day”; for “feast,” 5a, 5c, and 6 read *festo*, while 5b reads *festum*. Witness 6c omits “after”; 1 spells “Masses” *misarum*. B/C place “earnestly” after “asked,” and read “food and drink” with an explicit “and.” Witnesses 2, 4, 5, and 6 have passive *reficeretur*, “he should be refreshed/dine,” while 1 and B/C have active *reficeret*, “he should refresh himself/dine.” Witnesses 2, 4, 5, and 6 omit “offered”; 5b omits “entirely,” while 6 places “entirely” before “hospitality”; 1 omits “into” before “the city.” B/C read “river” as *flumen* rather than *fluvium*. The river is *Olevia* in 4–5, *Oliviam* in B2, 6, and C, *Olivam* in B5, and *Obliviam* in C6. Witness 5 places the possessive after “see” (“his see”); B/C read “having arrived” (*perveniens*) for “coming” (*veniens*). C6’s margin dates the death to the fifth day before the Ides of December. Witness 2 omits “in” before “a small church.” Col. 1167D locates that church east of the metropolitan church and says the Paris manuscript C6 added the epitaph, which had already disappeared in Brower’s time (p. 493), when only traces of the tomb were visible. Its manuscript title is *Epitavium Erberti*, “Epitaph of Erbertus”; the supplied row of dots in the sixth verse is a lacuna. B/C order the clause as “which he himself had built in honor of Saint Andrew”; the apparatus adds “the Apostle” after Andrew without assigning a witness. B/C add that the burial lay on the church’s right side (B6 omits this location); on the left lay the aforementioned Heinrich, Egbert’s third predecessor, whom Egbert buried there after Heinrich died in Italy and was brought back. B2 has singular *antecessori* instead of nominative “predecessor.”

**Liudolf and Adelbero.** Leibniz labels the section chapter XLVI. B4–5 call Liudolf *Luoitoldus* and B6 *Hildolfus*. B/C add: “a Saxon by birth.” C6 reads *tabernacula*, “quarters” or “lodgings,” for “dwellings.” B4–6 omit “the things which”; C1 later supplies “the things which,” followed by its successors. B2 reads *episcopium*, “episcopal residence,” for “bishop,” and omits “also.” Cols. 1173D–1174D record Wyttenbach’s note that ruins of the walls survived at the end of the eighteenth century and could still be seen behind the two places popularly called *auf dem Graben*. B/C read “while he was bishop” with *Quo* rather than *Eo*. Witnesses 5–6 read “church” for “monastery” of Saint Paulinus. Lucelenburg is *Lenburch* in 1b, *Lutzelenburc* in 2, *Luzeleborch* in 5b, *Luzelembruch* in 6c, *Luozelenburc* in B4–5, *Luzelenburch* in C1, and corrected to *Lutzlenburg* in C3 and likewise C6. Witnesses 5–6 read “fortresses” (*castra*) for “castles” (*castella*). Sarburg is *Sareburc* in 2, *Sareburch* in 4–5, *Saremburch* in 6a, and *Sarenbruch* (with a doubtful *m*) in 6c–d. Bernkastel is *Herencastel* in 5a–b, *Herencastell* in 5c, *Berencastell* in 6, and *Beronoasdel* in B2. Witness 5b omits “and.” Rutiche is *Rutehe* in 1, *Ruteche* in 1b, *Ruthiche* in 5a/C6, *Ruthice* in 5c, *Rustiche* in 6c, *Rudiche* in B2, and *Ruothiche* in C1. Col. 1171C identifies the places as Sarburg, Bernkastel, and Roussy.

B4–5 move “plan” beside “having entered,” yielding “having entered into a plan with Archbishop Liudolf.” Witness 2 calls Liudolf archpriest; B2 calls him bishop; 5c and 6a omit the office, while 6c reads “with Bishop Liudolf.” Witness 6 adds “and” before “the church.” Witnesses 5–6 read “by gift” for “by deceit.” Witness 5b omits “to him”; 1 misspells “afterward” *deindeps*. Witnesses 2, 5c, and 6 read “he obtained it for Saint Paulinus,” while 5a–b omit “for Saint Paulinus.” Witness 2 spells Liudolf *Luodolfus*; 5b omits “however.” Witness 5 makes Adelbero, rather than Liudolf, the man who died. In the motive clause, 5c has “because” and 2?/6 “because of the fact that” for “with the confidence by which”; B2 omits “his,” while 2, 5, and 6 repeat “his sister.” Witnesses 2, 4, 5, and 6 omit the marriage to Emperor Henry the Lame; 1b has genitive *Heinrici*, “of Henry.” B6 reads “had invaded” for “invaded”; 1 adds “and” to “soldiers.” B/C omit “situated in the same city.” Witness 1 misspells Henry *Neinricus*; 5c omits “however.” Meingard is *Megingaudus* in B/C, *Meingado* in 5b, *Meningaudus* in 5c, and *Mangaudus* in 6a. In 5a, 5c, and 6 the word order is “gave the bishopric to Meingard, provost of the church of Mainz”; 5b places “bishopric” immediately before “gave”; witness 2 omits “gave.” Witnesses 1, 1b, and 2 omit “provost,” and 2 spells Mainz *Mogontiae*. B/C move “resist Adelbero’s power” before “prepared.” B/C read sixty rather than eighty hides. Ravenger is *Ravengo* in 5–6, *Reuengoro* in B2, and *Ravangero* in C3. Malberg is *Madelburc* in 2, *Maldeberch* in 4, *Madelberg* in 5a/5c/6, *Madelberc* in B4–5, and *Mailberch* in B6; Col. 1172C identifies it as Malberg. Witnesses 5–6 omit “and.” Udelbert is *Oldebertus* in 4, *Adelbertus* in 1b/5c, *Adalbertus* in B2, and *Uodelbertus* in B4–5, 6, and C1; 5–6 spell Stalle *Stale*.

**The siege and Meingard’s settlement.** Col. 1172C compares the *Annals of Quedlinburg* for 1008 and Thietmar VI.25. Henry is *Hinricus* in 1 and *Henricus* in 2, 5, and B6; witness 6 regularly uses *Henricus*. B/C omit the devastation of the countryside. Witnesses 1, 1b, 2, and 5 omit “but”; 6 reads “and the city itself”; 2, 4, 5, and 6 omit “already”; C3–4 put *exornatam*, “adorned,” in a different case; 5a omits “and”; B/C read “was almost reduced.” Witness 1 supplements the text from “but” through “the besiegers” after the omission, while 5 reads “but the palace men themselves.” Witnesses 5 and B2 read “incursions” for “sorties”; 1b omits “and”; 2 reads “they ravaged the palaces” instead of “they ravaged the areas adjoining the palace.” Mount Juran is *Urani* in B2/C6. Witness 1b adds birds to the oxen; 4 reads “led down” for “brought”; B5 has singular/ablative *adducto*, so that “with … brought” modifies the escort rather than the multitude. Witness 1 spells “oxen” *bovum*. For the guard, 1 reads *multum*, “much,” for *militum*, “of soldiers,” while 1b reads *multo*, “large,” yielding “with a large guard.” Witness 2 omits “from the fortress.” Witness 6 places “a sortie having suddenly been made” in that order; 1b omits “and” between oxen and sheep; 6 places “the escort having been routed” before “their”; and 6 reads “with the animals themselves” for “with them.” B6 ends after the closing of the gates. Witnesses 2, 4, 5, and 6 read “from the fortress” with *ab* rather than *ex*.

Witness 5c omits “so that he might”; 2 reads “so that he might more easily hem in the palace men,” omitting the intervening explanation about the engines’ height. B2 spells “these” *hec*. Witnesses 1 and 5a–b read *fortibus*, “brave men,” for adverbial *fortiter*, “bravely”; 1b reads “while they fought at the doors.” Witness 6 orders the forms *igne succensae, immisso vel dirutae*: “set alight by fire, or destroyed after it was introduced.” The destructive readings are *diruptae*, “shattered,” in 1b; *domitae*, “overcome,” in 2, 4, 5a, 5c, and 6; and misspelled *deruite*, “demolished,” in 5b; the apparatus notes an omission at the point where “are” would stand. Witness 1b reads “but” for “therefore” and omits “to” before the Kalends; B2 writes *semtb* for September; 5 omits the span from “he made no progress” through “departed.” Witness 5b omits the span from “custody” through “had held.” C1 corrects *custodiae* to singular *custodia* and plural *optinuerant* to singular *obtinuerat*, followed by C3 and later witnesses. Meingard is *Megingaudus* in 1, *Meingaudus* in 1b/5a/5c/6, and *Meingado* in 5b, consistently in those witnesses. Witness 1 has feminine *supradicta* for “aforesaid.” At the end of Meingard’s life, 2 writes *Magengaudi*; 5–6 omit Meingard’s name; 4 reads *vitae*, “of life,” for Meingard’s name, yielding “near the end of life.” Witness 5a writes *Meingado* and 5c *Menigando* for Meingard here and below; C reads “restored” for “gave back”; 5–6 omit “for himself.” At Meingard’s death, 5b writes *Minegando*.

Poppo is *Boppo* in 2 and B4–5 and *Poponem* in 5 and B2. Bamberg is *Babenburc* in 2, *Haberich* in 5b, *Babenberg* in 6, and *Babenbercth* in 4; B2 omits the place and the accompanying alternative-manuscript supplement, while B4–5 have *Regenesburc* and C *Regenesburch*, “Regensburg.” Witness 6 reads “appointed” for “constituted”; B2 puts “prelate” before “constituted.” Witness 1b spells Adelbero *Albero*. C reads “late” as the adverb *sero* rather than adjective *sera*. Witness 6 reads “in” for “until”; 4–6 add “his” to “end of life.” Col. 1173D cites two charters preserved by Hontheim I, pp. 368 and 371 (1036 and 1037) by which Adelbero made various gifts to Saint Matthias, and an unpublished 1037 charter in the Trier library recording gifts of his villages to Saint Martin, Prüm, Saint Mary at the Martyrs, and various other churches; the note is signed WYTT., Wyttenbach. Witness 2 perhaps reads *Hic*, “Here” or “This man,” for “Henry.” B/C omit the entire imperial restitution. Witness 6 orders the phrase “those injuries which he inflicted on the city.” Witness 2 reads *metalli*, “of metal,” for “plated,” while 4–6 omit “and precious stones.” For the panel’s relation to the altar, the base text has *tabulam … equalis*, “a panel … of equal [size],” while 4–6 have accusative *equalem*, “a panel … equal”; the base has *secundum altare*, “corresponding to the altar,” while 6 has genitive *altaris*, “of the altar”; and the base has *magnitudinis*, “of [equal] size,” while 4–5 have ablative *magnitudine*, “in size,” and 6 accusative *magnitudinem*, “size.” Witness 1b omits “sent it to make satisfaction to Saint Peter.”

**Poppo, Adelbert, and Sicko.** Leibniz labels the section chapter XLVII and II.21; C1 has the latter numbering. C3 adds the red heading “Concerning Archbishop Poppo,” after which the chapters are no longer numbered. Witnesses 2, B1, and C date Poppo’s ordination 1016; witness 5 dates it 1020; B2, B4, and B5 omit the year. Witness 2 calls him *Boppo*; 6 orders the title as “the Trier archbishop.” B1 reads “brought back” for “took”; 5 omits the Saint Paulinus clause. Witnesses 2, 5, and 6 omit the nuns’ prebends; 2 reads “handed over” for “distributed.” B2 repeats the spelling *Berencastel*. B/C order the phrase as “a certain tyrant Adelbert.” Witnesses 5–6 read “who” for “which” before Sckiva. Sckiva is *Scriua* or *Servia* in 2, *Siura* in 5a?/6, *Suira* in 4c, *Suura* in 5b, *Skiva* in B1, perhaps B4–5, and C, and *Sisiva* in B2; C6 omits the name. Col. 1174D quotes from a later Trier manuscript, “Skiva, which was called Munclerum,” identifies it with modern Monclair, and says no ruins of the castle once situated near Trier remained in Wyttenbach’s day. Witness 6 and B2/B4?/B5?/C put “honor” in the accusative; 1 omits “holy”; 2 omits “built.” Witnesses 6c–d/B1 read “whence” for “thence.” Witness 1 writes “care” for “court,” and 1b omits “there”; 1b reads “pertained to his service” for “was prepared for his service.” Witnesses 4–6 read “who” for “namely because”; 1b has accusative “many complaints”; 5/B1/C3 spell “of this kind” *hujusmodi*; 2 reads “to conquer this disgrace” for “to dispel this disgrace.” Witness 5e reads “For there was,” while B1/C read “There was, however.” Witness 6 adds “his” to “army” and reads *fortis viribus*, “strong in strength,” after “powerful in wealth.” Sicko is *Sikko* in B1, *Siko* consistently in 6/C, and *Sicho* consistently in 5. Witness 4 reads “if he found some way” for “if somehow he could”; 6 places “could” after “find some remedy for this evil.” Witness 5 omits “the bishop”; B2 has “congratulating him” rather than “rejoicing for himself”; 5b omits “he”; C reads “fulfill” for “attempt.” Witness 1b reads “went” for “goes”; 6/B2 add “and” to “knocking”; doors are *foras* in 1, 1b, and C3 and *foris* in C4. Witness 5 reads “asking” for “he asks”; 1/1b omit “from”; 1b has accusative “Adelbert,” and B1 calls him Albert. Witness 1b places “to be sent” before “cup” (*mitti poculum*). Col. 1175C explains *hamae* here as wine casks, German *Ohm*. B1 reads “while” for “when”; 6c reads “had obeyed” for “had drunk”; B/C identify the messenger as the cupbearer (B5 spells it *pincernum*); 6c has plural “they address”; 6a reads “he said” for “he says”; witnesses 2, 4, 5a, 5c, and 6 read “thanks” as *grates*; 5a/5c read *scilicet*, “namely,” for *sibi*, “to him”; and 2, 4, 5, and 6 omit “very soon.”

Witness 1b omits “having chosen.” Witness 1 has feminine *oportuna* for “suitable”; 4–6 order the phrase “then, after suitable planning [4: at a suitable time], thirty ….” Witness 5 consistently spells the large vessels *amas* for *hamas*. Witness 1 writes *laricatos* for *loricatos*, “clad in mail.” Witness 6 omits “and” before “helmeted.” Witness 1 also has *praecinctos*, “girded” (an orthographic reading in the apparatus); 5b has *precinctis*, “with [them] girded”; and 1/1b replace finite “he places” with plural participle *collocati*, “placed.” Witness 6 omits the span from the second “and” through “he arranged.” B2 has masculine *opertos*, “covered,” for feminine *opertas* agreeing with the vessels; 5c reads *apertas*, “open,” and then singular *funus* for “ropes.” Witness 1 writes *fines*, “ends/boundaries,” for *funes*, “ropes.” Witness 5a omits “poles”; 5c writes *confectes* for *vectes*, “poles.” Witnesses 4, 5a, and 5c have *portandas*, “for them to be carried,” for *ad portandum eas*, “for carrying them”; 2 has present *inserantur*, “may be inserted,” for imperfect subjunctive *insererentur*, “could be inserted.” Witness 1b gives seventy rather than sixty bearers. Witness 1 omits “in common clothing”; 1b misspells “common” *plebeta*. Witnesses 5b, 6, B2, B4, and B5 omit “and” before “their swords.” The swords are hidden *in hamis*, “in the vessels,” in 2, 6, and B2, and *in amis* in 5. Witnesses 1/1b put “hidden” in the feminine accusative *reconditas*, agreeing with an implied object rather than the swords. Witnesses 4–6 read “he made no persons aware …” (5 restores singular “no person”), while B1 has only singular “no”; witness 2 reads “except the aforesaid men” for “except those named above”; B/C omit “the aforesaid men.” Witness 5 reads “that Sicho,” and 6 reads “went” for “proceeds”; 5b reads “proceeds to the palace.” Witnesses 4–6 add “and” to “knocked at the doors.” Witness 2 omits “great”; for the thirsty recipient, 2 misspells *sitienti* as *sic(i)enti*, while 4 reads *sciscienti*, “inquiring.” Witness 2 reads “announced” and 4 “proclaimed” for “reported.” Witness 1 breaks “Adelbert” as *ad delberto* across two lines. Witness 1 reads “being able” for “placing.” Witness 2 reads “entered” for “enters,” and B2 adds “together” before “enters.” For the vessel coverings, 2 writes *lintearum*, 4/6/B1 use neuter *linteorum*, and 5c reads *linteum velamen*, “linen covering.” Witness 1 misspells “asks” *rega*; 1b orders the words “asks Adelbert.” Witness B1, corrected in C3 and followed by C4, reads *portatores*, “bearers,” for *portitores*, “carriers.” B1 orders the passage *onera hamarum deponunt, velamina dejiciunt*: “they put down the vessels’ burdens and cast off the coverings.” Witnesses 5–6 omit “their swords.” Witness 5a reads “snatch away,” 6 reads “seize” (6a corrects this to “receive”), for “snatch up.” Witness 6 reads “spring forth” for “leap out”; B1 adds “their” to “swords”; B/C omit “himself” before Adelbert. Witness 1b reads “the castle is directed” for “they reduce the castle.” Witness 1b omits “for the victory”; 1 misspells “honored” *ilustratus*, 1b uses present “is honored,” and 5–6 omit “was.”

B/C continue: in the same way Poppo captured many castles through other leaders, partly by force and partly by deceit, and for the most part restrained the madness of tyrants that had long raged with impunity; C3 reads “very many” for “many.” He mercifully aided as far as he could the monasteries almost exhausted by their violence, giving to some what they had not possessed and restoring to others what had been taken. The exceptions were the two communities of Saint Paulinus and Saint Mary of the Palace: he did not refrain from taking certain things from the former because of Adelbero’s insolence; from the latter, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, about whom the text says it will speak later, he took everything and expelled the inhabitants. Col. 1176C directs the reader to the Addendum below.

**The Danish error and closing notices.** Cols. 1176C–1177C says the Trier author makes the very serious error of identifying Archbishop Poppo of Trier with the Poppo who preached to the Danes in the tenth century, turns King Otto into a Danish count named Otto, and, to compound the errors, draws Ansgar into the story. Denmark is *Dana* in B1; B2–3 correct *Daxia* to *Dacia*; C1 and 6 have corrected *Dacia*; C3 has *Datia*. B2 misspells “glowing” *candaentem* and writes the Christogram *xpictum*, “Christ.” B1 spells Ansgar *Ansgerius* and omits “his” before “memory”; B2, B3, and C omit “his” before “tomb.” Leibniz begins chapter XLVIII at the tomb sentence. C1 has *narrandum cummemore*, corrected as in the edition to *narrando commemorare*, “to commemorate by narrating.”

Witness 4 reads “maternal” for “Martin”; 4–6 read *ea* for *in eam*, dropping the preposition and changing the case of “it”; 5 reads “a little” for “in part.” Witness 1 perhaps reads “tower” in a different case (*turremque* for *turrimque*). Col. 1175C refers to Addendum 8. Witness 1 omits “to Saint” at the start of the Eucharius clause, then supplies the span from “who/which [goods]” through “restored” later. Witness 1 calls Symeon “Simon”; 5–6 read “above” for “upon” the Black Gate; 4, 5c, and 6 use present “rests” for past “rested.” “Of clerics” is absent from 2, 4, 5, and 6. Cols. 1175C–1176C says Saint Simeon’s church was built from the ruins of the gate and stood until the editor’s time. Witnesses 5–6 omit “at the feet of Saint Symeon”; 5b moves “he himself” later, before “at the feet.” Col. 1177A says the continuation of this text is printed below under the title “Addendum.”

32. Eberhard succeeded him. [Note: *heberhardus* in 4; *heberardus* in 5b.c.; *heberadus* in 5a; *eberardus* in 6; consistently.] He renewed the privileges of his church before the pope. [Note: *privilegio* in 1; *privilegio* in 4 and 6.] He received the pope himself at Trier with honor (1049), [Note: “the pope” is absent from 4, 5, and 6;] acquired many estates, and took more than a thousand talents from the treasury to redeem them. [Note: Compare *l. l.* c. 9, and what Codex C added there.]

Once, while he was touring the dioceses, [Note: *dioceseos* in 1 and 1b; *dioceseo* in 2?] he was captured by Count Conrad of Luxembourg. [Note: *conrado* in 4, 5, and 6; consistently.] His priestly vestments were torn away by the soldiers, [Note: “his vestments” in 4; “the sacred vestments were torn” in 5b;] his pallium was ripped apart, the Lord’s Body was violated and thrown upon the ground, [Note: *terra*, “earth,” in 2, 4, and 5;] the chrism of anointing was poured out, and the bishop was taken to Luxembourg [Note: “to Luxembourg” in 6; the place-name appears as *lucenleburch* in 1, *luscelenburch* in 1b, *luzelenburc* in 2, *luscelemburch* in 4, *luzelenburch* in 5a.c. and 6a, *luzelenborch* in 5b, and *luzelenbruch* in 6c] into custody. [Col. 1177B] [Note: “into custody” is absent from 2, 4, and 6.]

The people of Trier refused to celebrate any of the rites belonging to the divine office [Note: singular “belongs” in 1] until they had appealed to the Roman pontiff through envoys. [Note: *internoncios*, “messengers,” in 1.] Meanwhile, Count Conrad, compelled by many people, released the bishop. [Note: *comes*, “count,” is abbreviated as *c.* in 6; the reading in 1 is defective: *di . . istiti*.] The Roman pontiff excommunicated Conrad and entrusted him to Eberhard to be absolved. [Note: *heberado* in 5b; *heberardo* in 5a.c.; “Eberhard” here.] [Note: *ad solvendum*, “to be absolved,” in 5 and 6; *dimisit*, “released,” in 5.] At last Conrad, repentant, came to Trier, humbly sought and obtained absolution from the supreme pontiff, and, as satisfaction, handed over certain goods to Saint Peter. [Note: *contradido* in 1c, “gave”; *dono* in 1b, “as a gift”; *tradidit* in 5a.c., “delivered.”]

At that time (1053), Emperor Henry transferred the body of Saint Valerius from Trier to Goslar, [Note: *tanrsstulit* in 1, an obvious corruption of “transferred”;] and in exchange gave the estate called Vilmar [Note: “the court called Vilmar” in 1b;] to Saint Eucharius. [Note: *contradidit* in 5b, “gave back.”] [Col. 1178C] Vilmar was beside the River Lahn; see Henry’s charter in Hontheim I, p. 394.

Bishop Eberhard [Note: *Eberardus* in 5a.c.;] completed the tower begun by Poppo. [Note: “completed” was written by another hand in 1; *perficit*, “completes,” in 2.] On Holy Saturday of Easter (15 April 1066), after completing the divine office in the treasury, [Note: another hand in 1 adds *sollemne*, “solemn”; 1b reads: “he had been anointed with oil and, having died, was buried”; the phrase is absent from 2;] he died as he was prepared. [Note: “when he had completed everything” in 6.] [Col. 1178A] He was buried in the monastery of Saint Paulinus. [Note: *sepultusque in*, “and was buried in,” in 4; *est* is absent from 5b.]

33. After his death, Anno, bishop of Cologne, whom the emperor Henry mentioned above had appointed guardian of the kingdom and of his son Henry, [Note: the words “and of his son Henry” are absent from 2;] ordained one of his own clerics, named Cuon, [Note: *cunonem* in 1b and 2;] as bishop and sent him to Trier. When Theoderic, the ruler of Trier, [Note: *comes*, “count,” in 1b;] learned of this, he gathered an armed force, seized him at the fortress called Bideburch, [Note: *biedenburc* in 2;] kept him bound, and not long afterward killed him by a shameful death (1066). Whoever wishes to know about his martyrdom can readily find it. [Col. 1178C] [Note: See it edited below.] When these things had been accomplished, [Note: *Is*, “he,” in 1 and 1b; *pactis*, “agreements,” in 1;] the noble Swabian Udo [Note: *suevs* in 1;] took up the bishopric. [Col. 1178C] [Note: See the Addition below.] When he died, Eilbert, [Note: *egilbertus* in 2;] a bishop worthy of every good remembrance, [Note: “all” is absent from 2;] was appointed in his place (1077). He rebuilt, as far as he was able, the churches throughout his bishopric that had fallen into ruin. [Col. 1178B] [Note: *dirotas*, “destroyed,” corrected to *dirutas*, “ruined,” in 1.] Not long afterward he too was removed from this life, and Bruno succeeded him as bishop (1101). [Note: *Hac*, “this,” in 1 and 2, instead of *ac*, “and.”]

Codex 1 adds in another hand. [Note: 1b continues in the same hand.]

During his days many disasters and dissensions occurred throughout the kingdom, and he himself was not free from involvement in them either by counsel or by action. When he died (1124), Godefrid, dean of the greater church, was appointed bishop; but afterward, accused by his own people of simony, he was expelled, and the bishopric passed to Meginero (1127).

Codex 2 adds:

After him came Godefrid, who was convicted of simony and deposed. Meginher succeeded him; having gone to Rome, he was captured by a certain tyrant named Conrad and killed in captivity by various tortures (1129). After him Adelbero of Metz succeeded to the bishopric (1130).

# FIRST ADDITION AND FIRST CONTINUATION

[Col. 1177]

## 1. [Note: II, chapter XXII, in C1 and 6.]

In the reign of the most serene Henry—Henry the Second as king, but the First as emperor—in the fourteenth year of his reign, after Megingaut, archbishop of the city of Trier, had been removed from this life, Lord Poppo took up the episcopal chair amid the joy [Col. 1178D] and gladness [Col. 1179A] of the entire city (1015). [Note: *meingaudo* in B2. *Ci* appears for *ti* in B2; I have generally retained it.] Truly, I say, amid joy, because, to use the words of a certain schoolmaster concerning him:

“He brought with him the kindly guardian Symeon.”

I shall therefore treat more fully of this in what follows, God willing. First, however, I shall report, insofar as it has come to my knowledge through the accounts of the elders, from which parents and from what region he originated.

His father was named Luopald, [Note: *liuopaldi* in B2 and C1, 3, and 4;] who held the margraviate of the region of Austria. His mother, Richeza, was the daughter of a certain duke of Germany and France. [Col. 1179D] [Note: Whose daughter she was is not yet known; compare Moritz, *History of the Counts of Sulzbach* I, p. 11.] His father’s brother, who bore the same name as his father, [Col. 1179D] [Note: Poppo’s brothers were the margraves Henry and Albert; Luitpold II was Albert’s son and Poppo’s nephew;] after their father’s death, energetically governed the same margraviate.

They therefore entrusted their son—Poppo, I mean, [Note: *bopponem* in B4 and 5, *poponem* in C;]—to the more learned men of the city of Regensburg [Col. 1179B] [Note: *regenesburch* in B2; *genesburch*, later corrected to *regenesburch*, in C1 and 3;] to be educated in literary discipline as he grew older. After a period of time, when he had been sufficiently imbued with literary knowledge and had already grown to manly strength, they presented him to the aforementioned king. He soon became so dear to the king and seemed so suitable that, as I have said, after Megingaut, bishop of the metropolitan church of Trier, had been removed from this life, the king himself hurried to Trier—he had been stationed at Confluence—and, having obtained the consent of both clergy and people, raised Poppo to the pontifical chair.

Accordingly, he was consecrated there by the bishops who had come on the king’s business, on the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1016. One of his consecrators was Theodorus, [Note: *Theodericus*. See Thietmar VII.19 concerning this matter.] the second bishop of Metz.

Then, after not many days had passed, he set out for Rome for the sake of prayer and asked that what the holy Roman mother church owed to her daughter, namely the church of Trier, by the institution of the holy apostles, in honor and grace, might be granted to him. [Note: *postulasset*, “had asked,” in B1.]

Lord Benedict VIII, presiding over the most sacred apostolic see, received him with great honor and showed him every reverence and affection while he remained there, so that he celebrated Masses for him and often ate with him. When Poppo wished to depart, Benedict earnestly admonished him concerning the preservation of his faith, which is directed toward God, the instruction of his subjects, the correction of sinners—not in fury but as a father—and the careful purity of soul and body. [Note: From “and that these…” through the whole of Benedict’s constitution, the text is absent from C3 and 4.]

So that these commands might not fall from his memory, he gave him a written document in the following form:

“Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most blessed brother and bishop Poppo, venerable archbishop of the holy see of Trier, eternal salvation in the Lord and apostolic blessing.

“It is fitting for apostolic concern always to offer benevolent affection toward the brethren and to grant assent to their requests whenever they appear well-founded and reasonable. [Note: The passage is absent from B1; in that manuscript *videntur*, “appear,” was written twice, with one occurrence erased.] Therefore, dearest brother, because you asked me to grant you the use of the pallium according to the custom of your predecessors, we willingly agree to your desire, earnestly admonishing your fraternity to adorn the appearance of the outward garment with the integrity of your conduct, and to show yourself in all things such that you always strive to administer the office entrusted to you with pastoral care.

“For then you will appear conspicuous to all, like a lamp shining in the house of the Lord, if you are adorned inwardly as well as outwardly. You wear the cross of Christ upon your body in the form of the pallium; resolve to carry it within, in your mind, crying out with the Apostle: ‘The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Gal. 6:14), and eagerly adding the words of the prophet: ‘Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear’ (Ps. 118:20).” [Note: In B5, *claves*, “keys,” appears instead of *clavis*, “nails”; the words *clavi a timore* are absent from B1.]

“Therefore, admonishing you with the charity that is your due, we send you the pallium from the apostolic see. By the authority of this privilege of ours we decree that, when celebrating Mass, you may wear it only on these solemnities: the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter and Pentecost, [Note: *in* appears in B, 4, and 5; “Easter” is absent from B4 and 5;] the Ascension of the Lord, the feasts of the holy Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the solemnities of all the apostles, the solemnity of All Saints, [Note: *solemnitatibus*, “solemnities,” in C6;] the feasts of those saints whose bodies and relics are kept in your bishopric, the dedication of your church, the annual day of your ordination, and whenever you decide to confer holy orders in a fitting manner.

“We also grant you, dearest son, permission to have the cross carried before you. [Note: *gestandi* has *vel gestari*, “or to be carried,” written above it in C1.]

“May the Almighty Lord preserve your fraternity, dearest brother, here and in the future, and strengthen our minds in his service, so that for the well-administered office of pastoral care he may reward our labor with eternal blessedness.

“Farewell.” [Note: C has *vale*, “fare well.”]

“Given on the sixth day before the Ides of April, through the hands of Benedict, bishop and legate of the apostolic see, in the fourteenth year of the most unconquered king of the Romans, Henry, and in the third year of his empire, in the fourteenth indiction (1016).” [Note: *imperio*, “imperial rule,” in B2, 4, and 5; *vero*, “indeed,” is absent from B1.]

## 2. [Note: Chapter L in Leibniz.]

After several years had passed, while he was striving to offer his soul immaculate to God according to God’s will and the admonition written above by the Roman pontiff (Lev. 3:1), behold, the devil—who, as Sacred Scripture says, deceives the whole world (Rev. 12:9)—just as by his most wicked art he stripped Adam, the first-formed man, and through him all of us of the garment of immortality by means of a woman, so also attempted by his deceit to overthrow this man’s mind from his purpose of chastity through hidden coverings, [Note: absent from B1,] so that he could not say with the Apostle: “Our glory is this: the testimony of a good conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12), and so forth.

For example: in the suburb of Trier there is a certain town called Aula Palacii, [Note: Palatiolum or Pfalzel; see above, chapter 24,] where, by the foundation of one of King Dagobert’s daughters, the precious virgin Athala, [Note: *athele* in B2, 5, and C,] who rests there, there was a community of girls professing the canonical life. [Note: *congregationis*, “of the community,” in B2, 4, and 5, apparently corrected to *congregatio*, “community,” in C1 and likewise in C3 and following.]

It happened that the bishop sent one of them a piece of the pallium, so that she might make from it stockings for him to wear when he proceeded to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. [Note: *exinde* appears in C3.] She received them and, desiring to make them participants in her own impurity, infected them by some sort of magical poison of her devising and sent them back after sewing them.

As soon as the bishop put them on—strange to say—it seemed to him that he could not continue living in good health unless he immediately had intercourse with a woman. Astonished at such a sudden change of mind and such an unexpected tickling of the flesh—especially since he had resolved not to consent to carnal desires—he quickly took them off and gave them, as I may put it, to one of the chief priests who happened to be present. As soon as that man put them on, he too quickly removed them, wondering at what had happened but saying nothing.

Then the others who were standing nearby, astonished at this miracle, took the same stockings one after another in secret and put them on, and suffered similar effects. Yet none dared, out of shame, to admit what he was experiencing. [Note: *pro* was corrected to *pre* in C1, “before” rather than “out of.”]

At last they came to the prefect of the city. When he put them on at the bishop’s command, he roared with incredible fury and proclaimed that he had been bewitched. [Note: C has *p. esse*, “that he was bewitched.”] When asked who had been the author of this iniquity, the bishop revealed it.

Then all of them, speaking their judgments together, said that this was a very great disgrace to the church: that one who was reckoned as belonging to a canonical, or even ecclesiastical, profession should be marked by such wickedness. [Note: All B manuscripts read *polleret*, “should be powerful” or “should prevail”; C1 corrects this to plural *pollerent*, “should prevail,” and C3, followed by C4, to *pollueretur*, “should be defiled.”] It was proper that the woman who had done this be expelled from the order of religious women; but the others who remained there, lest something so infamous should in some way proceed from them, [Note: *infamie*, “of infamy,” in B1;] ought to change their clothing, wear black instead of white, and devote themselves to a stricter life. If they were unwilling to endure this, it would be better for that place to be without inhabitants than for such persons to live there, carrying out this kind of wickedness under the appearance of religion.

And so it was done. She was expelled. The others, unwilling to change either their habit or their way of life, [Note: *conversionem*, “conversion,” in B1,] were likewise expelled. Some went to the monastery of girls called Horreum, while others moved to other places suitable for their order, and the place remained for some time without the divine praises. [Note: B1 reads “that place.”]

Because of this affair, the bishop afterward, overcome by the deepest repentance and fearing that he might be condemned by the vengeance of the final judgment of God because of this injury, [Note: absent from B1,] with the consent of Lord John, then Roman pontiff, entrusted the church of Trier, under his own testimony, to the bishops of his province—namely, his suffragans—and resolved to go to Jerusalem. Returning from there, he installed religious clerics in the place mentioned above to celebrate the praises of God.

Anyone prudent can clearly perceive how effective and pleasing to God his repentance was when he learns that divine mercy joined the holy and blessed man Symeon to him and brought him back with him. Since mention of him has arisen, although a fuller account of him is given elsewhere, [Note: From this Life by Eberwinus I have presented certain fragments below in the Appendix,] I too wish, however briefly, with God’s help, to touch upon his holiness, so that the memory of the man who brought him here may remain in blessing. [Note: *cum*, “with him,” in B2 and 5.]

## 3. [Note: Chapter LI in Leibniz; II, chapter XXIIII in C1 and 6.]

Meanwhile, Lord Poppo, of whom we are speaking, the energetic administrator of this metropolitan church of Trier, was traveling toward Jerusalem (1028). He arrived at the place where Symeon was staying and begged him to come with him. Symeon consented. When they had reached Antioch together, [Note: *anthiochiam* in C1,] Symeon remained there because of the leading men, among whom he had earlier made himself known, until Poppo, returning from Jerusalem, turned his journey aside near that city. [Note: The words “near that city” are absent from C.]

Then, warned in a dream, Symeon entrusted himself to the aforesaid bishop and came with him to Trier. [Col. 1182D] [Note: Eberwinus tells the story differently; see below.] There Poppo shut him up, at his own request, in a certain deserted tower. Just as once on the summit of Mount Sinai, so now here too he endured grave attacks from evil spirits, but with the Lord’s help he overcame them. [Note: *perpetiit*, “he suffered,” was corrected in C1 to *perpessus est*, “he endured,” and so in C3 and following.]

Finally, after spending seven years confined there, on the Kalends of June in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1035, [Note: *XXXV*, “35,” corrected to *XXXVI*, “36,” in C3,] he returned his soul to the one who had given it.

God glorified him with many signs of virtue, so that, raising our hands upward to God and our hearts likewise, [Note: *a*, “and,” in B5,] we may joyfully sing that evangelical saying: “God has visited his people” (Luke 1:68). Thus, because of the frequent manifestation of miracles, the people of the entire province often begged the aforementioned Bishop Poppo to consult the Roman pontiff, either personally or by letter, concerning the honor of God and of that holy man, and to report the outcome. They asked that, by a decree of authority, the faithful people might also venerate him—whom God commended by evident miracles—with the worthy devotion due to saints, and solemnly celebrate each year the day of his deposition. [Note: “the day of his deposition” is absent from B1.]

After taking counsel with the bishops of his province concerning this matter, the archbishop decided to fulfill what the people subject to him had piously requested. [Note: See the letter in chapter 4.]

## 4. [Note: Chapter LII in Leibniz; II, chapter XXV in C1 and 6.]

But, to return to the order of the narrative, I wish to look back briefly at what came before. While Poppo was occupied with the business of the journey just mentioned and had not yet returned, a certain Count Giselbert of the castle called Luxembourg, together with his son Conrad, acted no differently from a wolf raging among sheep whenever it happens that the shepherd is absent: one claimed this, another that; one seized whomever he could, the other plundered; and so they did not cease committing indescribable evils. [Note: *sicut*, “just as,” in B2; it was deleted in C1 and is absent from C3 and following; *ipse*, “he himself,” in B1.]

When the bishop returned and learned of this—indeed, even while he was present they could not restrain themselves from their wickedness—he was unable in any way to resist them. The most powerful men of the entire province, who ought to have avenged this injury against them, [Note: absent from B1,] were bound to them by a conspiracy of homage. [Note: *homini*, “to a man,” in B2 and 3; *homines*, “men,” in B4 and 5; *hominii*, apparently corrected in C1, and likewise thereafter.]

He repeatedly lodged complaints about their tyranny before Emperor Conrad, [Note: *cunradum* throughout in C,] but could accomplish nothing, as his letter reproduced below records. Therefore he sent many letters both to the king and to the pope. Since it would have been tedious, because of their number, to set down each one, [Note: From *verum* through “below, chapter 8,” the text is absent from B3 because three leaves have been cut out,] and since not all of them came to my knowledge, it will suffice to place this one in place of all the others.

# LETTER OF BISHOP POPPO

[Note: The rubric is absent from B2, 4, 5, and C3. C1 and 6 read “Poppo’s letter to the pope,” where the chapter numbering begins with XXVI.]

“To the most reverend father of fathers, Benedict, venerable in grace and name, Poppo, although unworthy, yet by the divine gift of mercy minister of the holy church of Trier, offers, with every affection of love, the obedience that is due.

“Last year, with the consent of the venerable Lord John, your predecessor in this holy apostolic see, I had gone abroad to Jerusalem out of love for seeing the sepulchre of the God-man Jesus Christ. In our region, however, the wickedness of evil men grew so greatly that even now they cannot withdraw their hands from the wickedness they began; [Note: *nequucia*, a spelling variant of *nequitia*, in B2;] they plunder and devastate everything all around them.

“Regarding this, I very often begged my lord the king to extend to me the hand of his punishment, [Note: absent from B1,] but I accomplished nothing. I also repeatedly petitioned your predecessor, named above, concerning the same matter, nor have I obtained any consolation up to the present.

“Therefore I desire that now at least your fatherhood, beloved of God, bring me consolation, and send me one of your more honored and prudent men, who may support me in my necessities with counsel and assistance—assistance, I mean, against my adversities, and counsel concerning matters that I do not believe can remain hidden from the ears of your holiness. But if these things have until now been hidden from you, I now beg you to give a kindly hearing to my letters.

“A certain man, praised for the holiness of his life, has recently departed from this light among us. If we ought to believe the signs and virtues that the Lord works through him, we have no doubt that he shares eternal blessedness with the saints. Yet it is not so much the signs, which are common to the faithful and the unfaithful, as the power of faith—by which the faithful are separated from the unfaithful—which was especially strong in him while he still remained in the body, that makes us certain of his holiness. [Note: *reddidit*, “made us certain,” in B4 and B5.]

“Therefore both the clergy and the people of our church have summoned us, begging that, by letters sent from us to this apostolic see over which you preside by God’s authority, together with the life and miracles of that holy man, we should ask what we believe worthy of petition: namely, that, if it seems prudent to you, once your apostolic decree has been given to us, we may enroll his name among the names of the saints and render to him the other honors due to the saints.

“Therefore, without a lengthy delay, deign to make known to me what your wisdom decides should be undertaken for my consolation and counsel regarding the relief of our anxieties, arising from this side and that. May your honor and merit before God and human beings always increase.”

But what the pope replied to this, and how kindly he received his letter, does not require my preface. Let us hear what he himself says.

# LETTER OF THE LORD POPE

[Note: The rubric is absent from B2, 4, 5, and C3. C1 and 6 read “Pope Benedict to Poppo.” In the margin of C3 another hand has written: “Canonization of Saint Symeon.” This is chapter LIII in Leibniz and chapter XXVII in C1 and 6.] [Note: Edited from a codex of the church of Saint Simeon; *Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 96, published it, and I have incorporated its readings here and there.]

“Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends to Poppo, [Col. 1185A] [Note: *poponi* in 2; *patri*, “father,” in the *Acta*;] archbishop of Trier, [Note: “bishop” in B2,] equally distinguished by his own merits and by divine grace, his most affectionate greetings with apostolic blessing. [Note: C adds “and apostolic blessing.”]

“Having received your letters of reverence and read them and read them again, [Note: “and read them” is absent from B1,] we placed their force in the depths of our heart, so that we might grant what you requested. For we ought, as far as we are able, to imitate the rule of the Master, who was not obstinate toward those who asked rightly, was not slow toward those who sought him in truth, and did not delay opening to those who perseveringly knocked at his doors.

“Although we have replied later than we wished, [Note: *concupivimus*, “we desired,” in B2,] nevertheless, at the sound of your written page, we respond as we ought, out of affection. For we do not act when we wish to act, [Note: this clause is absent from the *Acta*,] but when we receive from God the power to act, and when heavenly providence has arranged all things in their proper times.

“As you recalled, the apostolic see over which we preside by divine favor is the refuge of all pastoral care in the church. Therefore, since you fled to it with your requests, we have embraced these very words with fitting affection, for it is the origin and foundation of the churches, the Lord thus confirming Peter’s confession: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church’ (Matt. 16:18). It plainly seems right that every Christian fidelity should hasten to it and that it should extend the hand of consolation to all. [Note: B1 reads: “that it should extend to all the hand of the consolation of the pontiff.”]

“Since you are engaged in conflict, fighting against the wickedness of evil men and punishing it with the spiritual sword, and since you have asked us for a fellow bishop as an assistant in the matters divinely entrusted to you, behold, we send you one. [Note: This is absent from the *Acta*; perhaps an initial was written in place of his name.]

“His character is adorned both by moral integrity, as his name indicates, and by the discerning beauty of his mind. We have judged him most suitable for this business because we have recognized him as a faithful and prudent servant of God. He possesses both the cunning of the serpent and the simplicity of the dove. From his lips, as it were, honey flows, filled with the ambrosia of heaven according to the capacity of his hearers. We have separated him from our body like a right arm, invoking health and joy upon him.

“We therefore send him to console you in your necessities, both in the work of consecration and in the anointing of confirmation, and, with God’s favor, in whatever other necessities he may be able to assist according to the will of your holy fraternity. I do not think you need any admonition not to neglect or disregard treating him as is fitting, [Note: *tractetis*, “that you treat him,” in B2; *tractaretis*, “that you would treat him,” in B4 and 5; *detrectetis*, “neglect,” in B1 and the *Acta*,] since your kindness is more abundant precisely where it is holier.

“As for the man Symeon, whom you show as shining with numerous miracles and radiant with divine virtues: it is clear from this that he carried within his fragile body a treasure of spiritual grace, so that he provided not only for his own salvation but also for the manifold healing of others.

“Since he is believed to have reached that eternal blessedness, that perpetual state of supreme happiness, and that heavenly fellowship—as is more frequently revealed through the working of signs—our apostolic authority, following the judgment of divine discernment and supported by the consent of many of our brethren, [Note: I restore *consensu*, “consent,” from the *Acta*. After *nostrorum*, “of our brethren,” another hand added *assensu*, “assent,” in C1; C3 and following adopted it, while the B manuscripts omit the word;] decrees that the same man of God, Symeon, must henceforth always and everywhere be called a saint, and that his natale, like that of the other saints, must be celebrated each year with the greatest reverence.

“For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends (2 Cor. 10:18). Let him therefore [Note: *ergo*, “therefore,” in the *Acta*] be glorified, praised, flourish, please, be celebrated, loved, and honored, and let his name be inserted into the martyrology.

“May he intercede before the most merciful majesty of the divine power for our sins and negligences and for those of the persons entrusted to us, so that the wonders he visibly displays in the bodies of the sick he may graciously display in our souls by a hidden power.”

[Note: C reads: “Farewell, Benedict IX, pope.” “Benedict VIII, pope” was added afterward in another hand in C1.]

Benedict IX, pope (perhaps 1042?). [Col. 1185C] [Note: Papebroch, *Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 97, notes: “In our original manuscript a seal is represented as attached. On one face, otherwise blank, the name + BENEDICTI was written around it; on the other was impressed the head of Saint Peter, over which there was always a +, and beneath it, arranged in a circle, three letters, P P E, meaning PAPAE. Hence it is evident that these words were taken by the author of the *Gesta* from the same source. In the same place the bull of canonization of this pope is published.”]

## Corrections to the preceding translation

Read “with the worthy service due to saints” for “with the worthy devotion due to saints”; the source is *digno sanctis obsequio*, “with worthy service owed to saints.” Read “the hand of consolation” in B1’s variant, without the added words “of the pontiff.”

In the pope’s letter, read: “We believe that you need no admonition not to neglect or disregard treating him as is fitting”; and read “his feast-day (*natalis*)” for the untranslated *natale*. These are direct translations of *nulla credimus admonitione indigetis* and *ejusque natalem*.

## Supplementary apparatus and corrections

These entries preserve the remaining printed readings and editorial notices in the supplied text. Each belongs to the immediately preceding corresponding word or clause.

### Sections 32–33

- At “renewed,” compare the same subject, chapter 9, and what Codex C added there. At “at that time,” 5c reads *Eodem* (“at the same time”); Henry is *heinericus* in 2; and *tanrsstulit* in 1 is a corruption of “transferred.”
- At “and in exchange,” 4 reads *qui* (“who”) and 6c omits the connective; 2 has *contra* (“in return”) for *econtra*. At “estate,” 1b reads *curiam quae dicitur* (“the court which is called”); *Vilmar* is *wilmar* in another hand in 1 and *uillimar* in 1b. The note identifies Vilmar by the Lahn and refers to Henry’s charter in Hontheim I, p. 394.
- The title *episcopus* (“bishop”) after Eberhard is absent in 2, 4, 5, and 6. At Holy Saturday, 1 has *sancte*; at “divine office,” another hand in 1 adds *sollempne* (“solemn”), 1b has *et ita* (“and thus”), and its longer reading says that he had been anointed with oil and, having died, was buried; 2 omits the phrase. At “as he was prepared,” 6 has *e. p.*
- The notice after “after his death” says that what follows from codices 1, 1b, 2–4, 5, and 6 now agrees with B and C; their text is printed below. Theoderic’s name is *n. th.* in 2; “whose martyrdom” is *Quius* in 1. The source says “see it printed below,” not merely that it can be found.
- At Udo, *Suevus* is *suevs* in 1; the editorial note is “see the Addition below.” At “Bruno succeeded,” 1 and 2 read *Hac* (“this”) for *ac* (“and”).

### Addition 1 and Benedict VIII’s privilege

- The chapter heading is II, chapter XXII, in C1 and 6. *Megingaut* is *meingaudo* in B2. The editor notes that B2 repeatedly writes *ci* for *ti* and that he has generally retained it.
- At “consecrators,” C3 and C4 omit the word. The note identifies Theodorus as *Theodericus* and refers to Thietmar VII.19. At “asked,” B1 has *postulasset* (“had asked”). Benedict is *b. papa* (“Pope B.”) in B1; at “every reverence,” C3 and C4 read *omnemque* (“and every”). The clause “so that” is absent from B1.
- At “preservation,” B2 reads *conversacione* (“conduct/way of life”) for *conservacione* (“preservation”). C3 and C4 omit from “and that these” through the end of Benedict’s constitution; B1 omits “these” at “these commands.” The heading of the privilege is chapter XLIX in Leibniz and chapter XXIII in C1 and 6.
- B1 omits the opening sentence of the privilege; there *videntur* (“appear”) was written twice and one instance erased. B1 also omits “yourself” at “show yourself”; C6 reads *in o. te*. At “eagerly adding,” B2, 3?, and 4? read *addens et* (“adding also”).
- In the feast list, B, 4, 5, and C1 read *in* before Pentecost; B4 and B5 omit “Easter,” and B4–B5 omit the following *et* (“and”). At Saint John, B2 has *natifitate* and C1 *natale*; C6 has plural *solemnitatibus* at All Saints. At “to you,” B2 reads *t. e.*; “permission” is absent in B2, 4, 5, and C1. C1 writes above *gestandi* (“of carrying”) *vel gestari* (“or to be carried”).

### Sections 2–4

- At “Scripture,” C (with *sacra* corrected in C1) reads *Scriptura sacra*, “Sacred Scripture.” At “testimony,” C6 omits *testimonium*. Athala is *athele* in B2, 5, and C; *congregationis* (“of the community”) stands in B2, 4, and 5 and appears corrected to *congregatio* in C1 and thereafter.
- At “stockings,” C3 adds *exinde* (“from it”). “Bishop” is abbreviated *epo* in B2, 4, and 5, corrected to *eps* in C1 and followed thereafter; B1 omits *id* (“this/that”) at “continue living.” At the chief priests the source says *indutum dedit*: he gave the stockings on, or to be put on, to one of them.
- The difficult line uses singular *polleret* in all B manuscripts; C1 corrects it to plural *pollerent*, and C3/C4 to *pollueretur* (“should be defiled”). C3 omits “ecclesiastical”; B1 has *infamie* (“of infamy”), *conversionem* (“conversion”) for “way of life,” and *locus iste* (“that place”).
- At the Jerusalem sentence, C repeatedly spells it *Iherusalem*. C3 omits “blessed” before Symeon. The editor says that he has printed fragments below in the Appendix from Eberwinus’s Life. The ambiguous final sentence is retained as an incomplete construction: “Since mention of him has arisen, although a fuller account is available, I too wish briefly, with the Lord’s help, to touch upon his holiness, so that the memory of the man who brought him may be in blessing”; B2 and B5 read *cum* (“with [him]”).
- In section 3 the heading is chapter LI in Leibniz and II, chapter XXIIII in C1 and 6. *Symeon* is *simeon* in B1; C omits “near that city,” B1 omits “city.” At “as he himself requested,” B2 often writes *peciit* for *petiit*, and similarly uses *frequencius*, *sentencia*, and comparable spellings, though not at every occurrence. At “returned his soul,” the source reads “gave [it] back to him who gave [it]”; C3 corrects 1035 to 1036. B2 has *cum* and C omits *eum* at “God glorified him.”
- In section 4 B4–B5 omit *ad* at “to the order”; Giselbert is *gisilbertus* in B4–B5, Luxembourg is *lucelenburch* in B2, *luzelenburc* in B4–B5, and *luzelenburch* in C. B2 has *sicut* (“just as”), deleted in C1 and absent thereafter; B1 has *ipse* (“he himself”).
- At the conspiracy, B2–B3 read *homini* (“to a man”), B4–B5 *homines* (“men”), while C1 corrects to *hominii* (“of homage”). C consistently has *cunradum*; B2 and C6 read *mittebant* (“were sending”), corrected to singular *mittebat* in C1. B3 lacks from *verum* through “below, chapter 8” because three leaves were cut out.

### The correspondence and canonization decree

- At Poppo’s letter B2 has *nequucia* for *nequitia*; B1 omits “his” at “his punishment” and “the life” before “and miracles.” C1 corrects *nichilque* to *nichil* and C3 onward follow it. At “what your wisdom decides,” B2, B5, and C6 have *in eundem*.
- The papal heading is absent in B2, 4, 5, and C3; C1 and C6 title it “Pope Benedict to Poppo,” and C3’s margin reads “Canonization of Saint Symeon.” It is chapter LIII in Leibniz and XXVII in C1/C6. The text was edited from a manuscript of Saint Simeon’s church; *Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 96, supplies readings used here and there.
- At the unnamed envoy, the *Acta* omits “behold, we send”; the editor says an initial may have stood for his name. Papebroch identifies him as Gratian. *Quidem* (“indeed”) remains attached to that man; the *Acta* reads *ut cui* (“to whom”) for *cui*, and *quare et eum* (“therefore also him”) for *quem*.
- C spells “spiritual” *spiritali*; B1 omits *sanctae* (“holy”) before “your fraternity”; the *Acta* has *ut autem* (“but that”) at the next transition. At “treat,” B2 has *tractetis*, B4–B5 *tractaretis*, and B1 and the *Acta* *detrectetis* (“neglect”); *fit* (“is”) occurs in B2, B4, B5, and the *Acta*. B1 reads *innumerosis* (“innumerable”) for *numerosis* (“numerous”).
- C3 omits *et* before the bracketed *consensu* (“consent”). The editor restores *consensu* from the *Acta*; another hand added *assensu* (“assent”) after *nostrorum* in C1, adopted by C3 and later C, while B omits the word. The *Acta* has *ergo* (“therefore”). C ends “Farewell, Benedict IX, pope”; “Benedict VIII, pope” was added later in C1.

5. [Note: [Col. 1185] Chapter LIV in Leibniz; Book II, chapter XXVIII in C1 and C6. In C3 the rubric reads: “Concerning the Lord’s nail.”] I judged it fitting not to pass over in silence a matter very worthy of remembrance, which I discovered had occurred around that time [Note: [Col. 1185] Absent in B2, B4, and B5; *ejus* (“of it”) was added after it in C1, and so appears in C3 and following manuscripts.]. As I have indicated above, when Poppo himself had gone to Jerusalem and remained there for nearly three years—for he had gone as far as Babylon in order to see that most celebrated city, where he also [Note: [Col. 1185] Absent in C.] suffered for some time in captivity—if I remember correctly, a certain bishop of Metz came once to Trier during the fast of June to perform the ordinations in his place. Before leaving the province, he had asked that whichever of his fellow provincial bishops, that is, his suffragans, had been assigned this duty should come to Trier and fulfill his office in his stead. Since this bishop was nearer to Trier than the others, he was consequently more frequently present there for this work [Note: [Col. 1185] *videndi* (“of seeing”), corrected to *vidende* in C1, and so in C3 and following manuscripts.].

[Col. 1187A] But [Note: [Col. 1187D] The *Life of Saint Agritius* tells the same story about Archbishop Bruno. It is useful to reproduce its passage here:

“One thing, however, which that same nail of the Lord gave as a mark of its preciousness, we do not wish to pass over in silence. For when Bruno, called the brother of the emperor Otto—there were three of them—held in his power the better bishoprics of Lotharingia, namely Trier and Cologne, as well as the greater part of this kingdom, he wished, as is evident, moved by no good spirit, secretly, not to say furtively, to carry away this very nail of the Lord of which we speak, the object of festive remembrance and our salvation. Having corrupted the guardian of this divine treasure, he had another made so similar to it that, when both were examined, the true one could scarcely, or not at all, be distinguished from the false by any diligence. Thus, when the guardian, won over by money, had received it from the hand of the aforementioned bishop [Col. 1188D], and thought that he had found a suitable opportunity for the wicked theft, he finally attempted in vain to complete the fraud he had long contrived [lacuna]

The very day on which these divine acts of God’s mercies toward us had been celebrated was immediately recorded in the martyrologies, namely, the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June]. But if anyone should, God forbid, hesitate to lend the ear of belief to this unheard-of miracle of the Lord, he can still see, if permission is granted, both the same cloth bearing marks of blood and the same counterfeit nail in the house of Saint Peter.”]

as I said, intending to perform the ordinations, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July [17 June], he asked that the Lord’s nail, which was kept there through the gift of the empress Helena, be placed before him on the altar, as he regularly did; and, if the testimony of a demon ought to be believed [Note: [Col. 1187] *debat* in B4 and B5; *debe(b)at* corrected to *debeat* in C1, and likewise in C3 and following manuscripts. C1 subsequently adds in the margin, whence C3 and following manuscripts received: “it is proved to be the true nail of the Lord.”], when a certain person was tormented by a demon and this nail had been brought there with other relics of the saints to drive it out [Note: [Col. 1187] *illo* (“there”) is absent in B2; *fuisse* (“to have been brought”) in B1.], that evil spirit declared it to be the very nail [Note: [Col. 1187] *ipse esse* (“it itself to be”) is absent in B5.] which had been driven into the right foot of the Lord hanging upon the cross for the salvation of the human race [Note: [Col. 1187] *fuisset* (“had been”) is absent in B1.], and said that it was compelled to depart by its extraordinary power. Before this, there had been no certainty, but only an opinion, regarding the power possessed by the nail.

After it had been placed on the altar, the aforementioned bishop stood nearby, secretly looking around and searching for a place where, if the opportunity should arise, he could seize it and put it into his bosom. He had ordered another to be made for this purpose and had hidden it beneath his armpit; once the true one had been taken away, he intended to thrust the substitute into its place [Note: [Col. 1187] *et alium* (“and another”) is *et alium* in C6; the words from *alium* through *quem* are absent in B1. *Erepto* (“after this had been seized”) is *erepta* (“after she had been seized”) in B5.]. What more need be said? He hid the one he had coveted in his bosom, as he had desired, and joyfully completed the service he had undertaken.

Thereafter, when he was being led out after the sacred rites had been completed, as the Lord willed, that nail poured forth blood in greater abundance, and it began to seep drop by drop from his bosom onto the ground. His attendants, who surrounded him and were urging him to move more quickly and hurry to undress, saw this and pressed him, supposing that some evil had befallen him. Finally, when he began to remove his priestly garments and saw that his entire white garment was filled with blood, he first stood rigid with terror. Astonished beyond belief at what was happening to him, he eventually came to himself, confessed the crime he had committed, and obtained pardon. After removing his garments, he rolled them all together and advised that they be preserved with the greatest reverence; and this was done.

6. [Note: [Col. 1187] Chapter LV in Leibniz; Book II, chapter XXIX in C1. C1 adds the rubric: “Concerning Poppo’s compassion toward the poor.”] At that time, while the aforementioned servant of God Symeon still breathed the breath of life [Note: [Col. 1187] *auras* (“air, breezes”) is *aures* (“ears”) in B1; cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.388.], that holy man often persuaded the frequently mentioned Archbishop Poppo, his leader [Note: [Col. 1187] Absent in B1.] and host [Note: [Col. 1187] *dei* (“of God”) in B4? and B5?], in private conversation to perform deeds worthy of the future life, so that, while placed in this light, he might strive with God’s help to labor in such a way that after death he might enter into the fellowship of the blessed, whose office he now seemed to exercise [Note: [Col. 1187] *videtur* (“seems”) in B2, B5, and C6; corrected to *videretur* (“might seem”) in C1.].

There was a severe famine throughout this entire region, so that many were dying of hunger.
