The abundance of the winter rains, together with the immeasurable overflow in spring of the river flowing beside the city, had, through its prolonged standing and excessive mud, swallowed almost all the crops [Note: [Col. 1187] *inaestimabili* (“immeasurable”) in B1, B2, B4, and B5.]. The foolish populace blamed Symeon for this calamity, as is read in his *Life* [Note: [Col. 1187] *sua* (“his”) in B1? [Col. 1188D] See the passage below.].

At that time the bishop showed great kindness to the needy, frequently keeping before the eyes of his mind what the divine word says: “Whoever sees his brother suffering want and closes his heart against him, the love of God does not remain in him” (1 John 3:17). One day, during the Easter season in white garments, as he was riding a noble horse toward one of the churches standing in the city to celebrate the divine office [Note: [Col. 1187] “to celebrate” is supplied later in C1.], he encountered in the open country a large crowd of poor people. They begged him, in his customary compassion [Note: [Col. 1187] *solita* (“customary”) in B5 is *solito* (“customarily”).], to give them something as support for life [Note: [Col. 1187] *aliquid* (“something”), corrected to *aliquod* (“some thing”) in C1 and so in C3 and following manuscripts.].

He immediately summoned his chamberlain and ordered that a considerable amount from the treasury be quickly brought to him for distribution among them [Note: [Col. 1187] *exhibere* (“to produce”) in B2.]. All those who were with him, however, pressed him and said that he should first fulfill the purpose for which he had come; then, returning, he could more conveniently show the poor as much mercy as he wished. He replied:

“Do not persuade me of this, dearest ones, because this too is service to God, just as that is. Indeed, our prayer will be more acceptable before the majesty of God if this charity precedes us before we come to him. I firmly believe and am confident that our sacrifice will be presented before the divine presence without ambiguity if it is commended by the poured-out prayer of so great a multitude.”

Meanwhile the chamberlain brought the requested money. As the bishop began to spend it among the poor [Note: [Col. 1189] Absent in C6.], they all began to cry out with one voice that they had no need of coins. For with a coin, each could buy either nothing or very little of any value to himself, since, as the bishop knew, one bushel of grain cost twenty-five solidi.

He replied that he had nothing else at hand with which he could share in their needs [Note: [Col. 1189] *illo* (“with that”) in C3 and C4.]. They answered:

“If you have nothing else to give us at present [Note: [Col. 1189] *non habes* (“you do not have”) is absent in B2; *potes* (“you can”) in B4? and B5.], at least give us some of your well-fed horses, so that our hunger may be appeased, even briefly, by eating their meat.”

Although unwilling, he remembered the saying that has been turned into a common proverb:

“Everyone gives what is dear, who seeks to receive what is dear” [Note: [Col. 1189] *velit* (“who wishes”) in B1.].

He first gave his own horse, then those of the others—not indeed all of them, but only those whom he was able to encourage by his exhortation to this act of piety. They were butchered and devoured immediately before his eyes [Note: [Col. 1189] The words *in eo momento* (“at that moment”) are absent in B4, B5, and C.]. After this, he proceeded to the place appointed.

7. [Note: [Col. 1189] Chapter LVI in Leibniz; Book II, chapter XXX in C1. C1 adds the rubric: “Concerning Bishop Poppo.”] Finally, he was deeply concerned either with building churches or with repairing the ruins of those destroyed by age [Note: [Col. 1189] *de* (“about”) is absent in B2, B4, and B5 and was added later in C1. *Raparandis* is an error corrected to *reparandis* (“being repaired”) in C1.]. A clear testimony to the former is provided by the church of the blessed apostle Peter, which is called both a house and an episcopal see. As they say [Note: [Col. 1189] *fertur* (“it is said”) in B5. [Col. 1189C] See above, chapter 19.], this had formerly been the house of the lady Helena, at whose request it was first dedicated by the blessed Agritius in honor of the chief of the apostles. It was supported by four marble columns of great height, upon which the entire structure rested, consisting of nine arches, distorted this way and that.

But in earlier years one of those columns, worn down by its own length and weighed down by the great mass of its burden, had fallen headlong. As a result, no one dared celebrate the divine office there for fear of collapse. Nor did anyone dare climb up to repair the roof. Through prolonged neglect it had reached such a state that it was no longer called a house of prayer; rather, shepherds were driving their flocks there to pasture [Note: [Col. 1189] *neglecto* (“with neglect”) in B5.].

Poppo restored it through great labor and expense. He fitted bases around the same columns—bases which ordinary speech now calls *pilares* [“pillars”] [Note: [Col. 1189C] German *Pfeiler* (“pillars”).]—and, by a praiseworthy technique, placed new arches beneath the earlier ones [Note: [Col. 1189] *vocat* (“calls”) in B1.]. Thus, not inappropriately, the following words from the Book of Wisdom should resound in his praise: “Behold the great priest, who in his lifetime supported the house and in his days strengthened the temple” (Ecclesiasticus 50:1) [Note: [Col. 1189] *libris* (“books”) in B5; *etc.* is absent in C6.].

After it had been restored and reformed to its former condition [Note: [Col. 1189] “and” is supplied in the margin of C1.], he adorned and dedicated it on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], after the precious relics of the blessed Maternus had been transferred from the place of his burial. The transfer was carried out in the presence of the neighboring bishops assembled there and of the clergy and people of his entire diocese, as though for a synod—one celebrated, so to speak, the day before yesterday, yesterday, and today [Note: [Col. 1189C] Concerning a synod celebrated by Poppo in June 1036, see Hontheim, *Prodromus*, I, p. 318; cf. Brower, I, p. 518.]—there, that is, at Trier [Note: [Col. 1189] *truere* in B2, corrected to *treueri* in C1.]. He magnificently enriched the church, which had been honored by many gifts from the emperors—namely Henry II and Conrad II, and likewise from King Henry III, who was Emperor Henry II—as is contained in their charters concerning Trier [Note: [Col. 1189] *treueri* in B1? and B4?; corrected to *treuerim* in C1 and so in C3 and following manuscripts.].

Afterward it pleased him to enlarge the same church, and he made its circuit one-third larger than it had previously been. As I heard, he ordered the foundation of this structure to be made as deep as the earth now rises above it [Note: [Col. 1189] *facere* (“to make”) in B1?]. While he was applying himself especially diligently to this work, and the construction had already been raised above the ground to the length of a spear, one day, as he was sitting where the work was being done, the sun—being hotter than usual—shone back upon his head, for he was bald, and inflamed his brain. He began to suffer severely from the illness, which grew worse from day to day, as happens with one seized by a fever. Not long afterward, brought to his end, he gave up his spirit on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1067 [Note: [Col. 1189] *MVII* was later corrected to *MXLVII* in B1; *LXVII* was corrected to *XLVII* in C1, C3, and C4. [Col. 1190C] I think the author wrote this for 1047.].

The people of Trier duly arranged his funeral and buried him at the city gate called the Black Gate. There he himself had committed the blessed Symeon, mentioned above, to the earth [Note: [Col. 1189] *mentio facta* (“mention made”) in B1? and B3?; *commendavit* (“had committed”) in C.]. There, religious clerics whom he himself had assigned to that place for the honor of God and of that holy man [Note: [Col. 1190C] On this matter, see a charter of Poppo dated 1042 in Hontheim, *Historia*, I, p. 379: “At the gate which is remembered as having been consecrated by the pagans to Mars, we built a church in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of his glorious and perpetual virgin mother Mary, and of the blessed Simeon, who, resting there, performs innumerable powers and miracles in our midst, and we consecrated it in honor of all the saints.”], pour forth prayers to God day and night for his repose. To him be honor and glory forever and ever [Note: [Col. 1189] “Amen” follows in B2.]. He had sat in the episcopate for thirty years, five months, and ten days.

8. [Note: [Col. 1189] Chapter LVII in Leibniz. In C3 the rubric reads: “Concerning Archbishop Everhard”; C1 has no distinction.] After his death, Bishop Everhard succeeded him in the priestly ministry [Col. 1191A] with the consent of the clergy and people [Note: [Col. 1191] Absent in B1.]. [Note: [Col. 1191] Here the manuscript of the Abbey of Aulne ends.] He was born to Hizelin, count of Alamannia [Note: [Col. 1191] *alamanniae* (“of Alamannia”), with a later hand superscribed in C1: “that is, of Swabia”; and likewise in C6. [Col. 1191C] Brower, p. 524, cites the following from the Trier necrology: “On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April] died Henry, father of Everhard, archbishop of Trier.” The lineage of the counts still seems unknown.]. When he had grown into manhood, his nobility of birth was adorned by great uprightness of character, judgment, and prudence. He became provost of the principal church of Worms [Note: [Col. 1191] “was” is supplied later in C1 and so in C3 and following manuscripts.] under Bishop N. [Note: [Col. 1192C] Arnold.], who governed his subjects with considerable competence.

God granted him favor in the eyes of the aforementioned Emperor Henry and his princes, so that in royal affairs and every other important matter he was regarded as neither the least nor an authority to be despised [Note: [Col. 1191] *que negotiis magnisque* (“and important affairs”) in B1.]. Thus, when Trier had been deprived of its bishop, and those to whom the election belonged yielded to the king’s request [Note: [Col. 1191] *conuentibus* (“having assembled”) in B2; corrected to *coniuentibus* (“consenting”) in C1.], he was appointed bishop of the aforesaid metropolitan church.

This distinguished man was a most prudent ruler of the church of Trier [Col. 1191B]. He increased its possessions and renewed its privileges [Note: [Col. 1192A] C adds: “Anyone who wishes to know these things can find them in the present work.”]. He was also so diligent a guardian of it that he recovered, through the gift of Emperor Henry, the abbeys of Saint Servatius and Saint Maximin, which had been taken away from his predecessors [Note: [Col. 1191] *praedecessoribus* (“predecessors”) in C6; *recepit* (“he recovered”) in B1. [Col. 1192C] I searched in vain for documents issued concerning this matter, and Brower did not see them either; see *Annales*, p. 539.].

He frequently went to Rome to visit the thresholds of the apostles. On one such occasion he returned with great honor and received Pope Leo, who was also called Bruno [Note: [Col. 1191] *vocabatur* (“was called”) in B1.], into the see [Note: [Col. 1192C] This passage and what follows are taken from the older text of the *Gesta*, chapter 32, described above in column 1177.].

Once, while he was traveling through the dioceses, he was captured by Count Conrad of Luxembourg [Note: [Col. 1191] *lucelenburc* in B1 and C; *luzelenburc* in B4 and B5.]. His priestly garments were torn away, his pallium was ripped apart, and the chrism of anointing was poured out. A great sacrilege was committed by wicked men.

When news of this reached Trier, the celebration of all the rights of the divine mystery was suspended until the Roman pope could be consulted about what decision he would make concerning the matter [Note: [Col. 1191] *fieret* (“might be done”) in B1; *definiret* (“might decide”) in B4, B5, and C.]. The pope excommunicated the same Conrad and all his accomplices in a general council, but entrusted the penitent bishop with Conrad’s absolution [Note: [Col. 1191] *et poenitentiam* (“and penance”) in B1.]. He also sent the bishop a pallium to replace the one that his enemies had cut up.

Meanwhile the bishop returned from captivity after hostages had been given. Not long afterward he received the count, who had become penitent, and imposed upon him a pilgrimage to Jerusalem as penance; he died during it.

Next, the bishop declared persecution against the Jews and decreed that they were to be expelled from the city unless they became Christians by the following Saturday of Easter [Note: [Col. 1191] *pasce* in C1.]. Therefore, certain members of that wicked people made a wax image resembling the bishop, with a wick placed inside it [Note: [Col. 1191] *lichnis* (“with a wick”) is corrected from *lignis* (“with wood”) in B4; *licinis* in B5.], and bribed with money a certain cleric from the monastery of Saint Paulinus—Christian in name but not in deed—to baptize it. On that very Saturday, when the bishop was already prepared to celebrate the baptismal solemnities, they set it alight.

When it had already been half consumed [Note: [Col. 1191] *medio* (“half”) in B5; *media jam* (“already half”) in C.], the bishop, while engaged in the sacred rites over the font [Note: [Col. 1191] *altare* (“altar”) in B2.], began to fall seriously ill. He withdrew into the sacristy [Note: [Col. 1191] *sacrario* (“sacristy”) in C.] with the assistance of his ministers and, kneeling in prayer in his sacred vestments [Note: [Col. 1191] “with knees bent” is added here in C. [Col. 1192B] B4, B5, and C add: “before the cross painted there.”], died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May [15 April] (in the year 1006). He was buried in the basilica of Saint Paulinus [Note: [Col. 1191] “of Paulinus” is added from the canon in C6.].

[Col. 1192B] 31. Pope Leo’s privilege for Everhard, archbishop of Trier [the rubric is absent in C3 and following manuscripts] [Note: [Col. 1192C] In Hontheim, I, p. 386.]

Leo, bishop and servant—issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [17 April]—

Leo, bishop and servant—issued on the Ides of April [13 April]—in the second indiction.

32. Concerning L.

In the second indiction.

33. Concerning Pope Victor [Note: [Col. 1192C] In Gunther, I, p. 134.]

Victor, bishop and servant—on the twenty-fifth day.

[C1 adds to the rubric: “Another account belongs at this place.” C3: “Concerning the tearing of the pallium.”] The aforementioned pontiff was also very diligent, and so forth.

9. [Note: [Col. 1191] Chapter LVIII in Leibniz. From this point onward manuscripts 4, 5, and 6 also agree with B and C.] After his death [Note: [Col. 1191] *defuncto* (“having died”) in B4, B5a, and C6.], Archbishop Anno of Cologne—whom the dying Emperor Henry had left as regent of the kingdom and guardian of his son Henry [Note: [Col. 1191] Absent in B5 and B6]—disregarded the counsel and election of the people of Trier. Having obtained the investiture and confirmation of the still-underage king, he sent his nephew Cuono [Note: [Col. 1191] *Cononem* in B5 and B6 throughout.] toward Trier with great ambition and with a military force, if that should prove necessary, in order to enthrone him [Note: [Col. 1191] *intronizandum* (“to be enthroned”) in B4, B5, and C; *misit* (“sent”) in C6.].

As this rash advancement became for that blessed man an occasion of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 1191] *beatae* (“blessed woman”) in B4 and C6; *et martyrii* (“and of martyrdom”) in B4, B5, and C.], so it gave the people of Trier the boldness and opportunity to exercise cruelty [Note: [Col. 1191] *dedit* (“gave”) in B4, B5, and B6. [Col. 1192C] Compare the *Life of Conrad* below in the Appendix.].

Without delay, they incited their ruler Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1191] *Theodricum* in B5a and throughout.] and the other princes [Note: [Col. 1191] “his princes” in B4, B5, and B6.]—summoned to avenge the injury of so great a contempt—with loud voices, saying that if the people of Cologne should prevail in this undertaking [Note: [Col. 1191] *violacione* (“violation”) in B5.], it would bring disgrace and infamy upon all their successors [Note: [Col. 1193] Absent in B5b; *et* (“and”) is added before *infamiam* in B4, B5, and B6.].

What more need be said? An army was assembled. Carrying tree branches so that their weapons would not be revealed [Note: [Col. 1193] *viderentur* (“might be seen”) in B6c and B6d; *ferentes* (“carrying”) in B4; *prae se ferentes* (“carrying before them”) in B2, B4, B5, and C.], they proceeded to meet them on a clear night [Note: [Col. 1193C] “In the month of May” is added in B4, B5, and C.]. They suddenly surrounded them while they were resting in the village of Bedon, suspecting nothing of the sort [Note: [Col. 1193] Absent in B5b.].

Confused by the sound of the approaching multitude, once they realized that the enemy was present [Note: [Col. 1193] The words “that the enemy was present” are absent in B5a.], each chose flight for himself as best he could, by the speed of his feet and the density of the woodland thickets. As they scattered, the enemy attacked them. They captured many, wounded several, and seized all their possessions together with enormous booty [Note: [Col. 1193] *-que* (“and”) is absent in B5 and B6c.].

Lord Cuono himself fell into the hands of impious men [Note: [Col. 1193] The words from *qui* through *commiserunt* (“who entrusted him”) are absent in B1.]. They entrusted him to be guarded by even more wicked men until they could see how matters would turn out [Col. 1193B]. A little later, lest the rash will of the still-young king should prevail [Note: [Col. 1193] Absent in B4, B5, and B6.], they threw him from a cliff and killed him by a miserable death on the Kalends of June [1 June] [Note: [Col. 1193] “Of July” in B5a.].

Because of this, the king was deeply angered and threatened to lay waste to the city of Trier [Note: [Col. 1193] *-que* (“and”) is absent in B5b.]. At last, by God’s gift, his rage was calmed by his wise counselors [Note: [Col. 1193] Absent in B1 and B3.], and through the election of the clergy and people Udo [Note: [Col. 1193] *Udo* in B5 and B6; perhaps B1? and B5.] was enthroned as bishop.

He was descended from the lineage of the Alamanni [Note: [Col. 1193] A later hand in C1 has written above it: “that is, of the Swabians.”], his father being Count Everhard [Note: [Col. 1193C] Of Nellenburg; compare Stalin, *History of Württemberg*, I, p. 553; the charter cited there, p. 554 n. 11; and the *Schaffhausen Annals*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores V, p. 388.], and his mother Ita [Note: [Col. 1193] *Ida* in B4, B6, and B1; *Yda* in B5a and B5b; *Vda* in B5c.]. His parents were the founders of the monastery called Schaffhausen [Note: [Col. 1193] *monasterii* (“monastery”) in B5 and B6; *fundatoribus* (“founders”) in B4, B5, and B6. The place-name appears as *Scafuse* in the main text, with numerous manuscript variants.]. He was a most venerable man, handsome in face, eloquent in speech, and tall in stature; by his merit, the burden of so great a government could be supported upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 1193] *humeris* (“shoulders”) is absent in B5b; *tanti* (“so great”) is absent in B6.].

He completed the works begun by his predecessors, namely the enlargement of the monastery of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1193] “by his predecessors” in B5b.], and restrained the boldness and tyranny of the soldiers of his province [Note: [Col. 1193] “and tyranny” is absent in B4, B5, and B6.].

He died during the king’s expedition, at the siege of the Alamannic fortress called Tuingia [Note: [Col. 1193] *Turingia* in B4; *Tuvigia*, corrected to *Tuuingia*, in B5a; *Mingia* in B5c; *Tumgia* in B6c; *Tuingia* in B4 and B5; *Twingia* in C. [Col. 1194C] Tübingen; compare Bruno, *On the Saxon War*, chapters 61 and 103; Ekkehard, year 1077; and Stenzel, I, p. 437 n.], in the year 1078, on November 13. The people of Trier brought him back and buried him in the monastery of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1193] *monasterium* (“the monastery”) in B5a and B5c; absent in B5b.]. Egilbert succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1193] *Engilbertus* in B5; *Engelbertus* in B1 and thereafter; *Egelbertus* in B2, B3, E, S, B5, and B6.]. It is worth recounting somewhat more fully the circumstances of his election.

10. [Note: [Col. 1193] Chapter LIX in Leibniz. In C1 and C6 the rubric reads: “Another notable account”; in C3: “Concerning Egilbert’s election.” Chapters 10–14 are absent in B5.] At that time, when Gregory, also called Hildebrand [Note: [Col. 1193] *Hildebranth* in B4.], was administering the rights of the Roman pontificate, an ancient decree was promulgated anew: namely, that all those constituted in sacred orders—priests and deacons [Note: [Col. 1193] Absent in B1.]—should, as was proper, abstain from cohabitation with women [Note: [Col. 1193] *distribuerent* (“should distribute”) corrected to *abstinerent* (“should abstain”) in B6a and so in B6b and B6c; *astinerent* in B6b.], or cease from their office [Note: [Col. 1193] Absent in B4, B5, and B6; *vacarent* (“should be free from it”) in B6.].

At the same time, no one of any order—layman or cleric—was to presume to buy or sell, either personally or through an intermediary [Note: [Col. 1193] *vel* (“or”) in B4, B5, and B6; absent in B6c.], a bishopric, abbey, or any other dignity of spiritual gifts. Whoever violated this rule was to lose whatever honor he possessed [Note: [Col. 1193] *quod* (“which”) in B5 and B6.].

When this decree became publicly known, it aroused great envy in the hearts of those who did not walk according to God. Therefore factions arose between the kingdom and the priesthood, and immense hostilities grew on both sides [Note: [Col. 1193] *invidiae* (“envies”) in B5 and B6; *succreverint* (“grew”) in B6c; *succurrerunt* (“came to the aid”) in B1.]. The tinder of this dissension and mutual hatred gained such strength that, if any Caesarian encountered an ecclesiastic—perhaps one who had abandoned the world for love of his heavenly homeland, mortified his flesh, and been weakened by some bodily affliction, or one who, as was then customary, had grown a beard as a sign of religious devotion—they treated them as betrayers of royal honor with insults, mockingly calling them “churchmen” [Note: [Col. 1193] *h. r.* (“royal honor”) in C3.].

At that time no order of canonical sanction was observed in appointing bishops or other ecclesiastical dignitaries. Whoever merely filled the hand of the king [Note: [Col. 1193] The words from *regis* through *sibi* (“for himself”) are absent in B2.] or prince, or rendered some other service pleasing to him, was appointed by royal violence wherever he wished.

But when the king and the princes who agreed with him persisted nonetheless and increasingly practiced the forbidden sale [Note: [Col. 1193] *ac* (“and”) in B6.], the aforementioned pope, unafraid, bound them all with a sentence of anathema [Note: [Col. 1193] *concludit* (“he binds”) in B5 and B6.]. Whoever wished to be counted among the fellowship of Catholics had the following words written for himself:

“I anathematize every heresy of the king called Henry and of all his accomplices [Note: [Col. 1193] *complicum* (“accomplices”) in B5.] and every person who venerates him by reason of his royal name or honor [Note: [Col. 1193] *et* (“and”) in B6; the words “or honor” are absent in B1.], namely Henry, the fourth king of this name [Note: [Col. 1193] The words “the fourth king” are absent in B6.].”

When news of this excommunication reached the emperor’s ears [Note: [Col. 1195] Absent in B4 and B5; “of the emperor” in B5 and B6.], he bore it with the greatest displeasure and added sin to sin. He summoned a council of the bishops, abbots, and men of other orders belonging to his party, and decreed that Gregory should no longer be apostolic for any of them, nor should anyone accept his decrees [Note: [Col. 1195] “Nor should Gregory be apostolic for any of them” in B6.].

Having done this, he went to Italy with all speed and made a certain Wicbert, bishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1195] *Wichbertus* in B5; *W.* in B1.], pope in one of the cities of Italy [Note: [Col. 1195] Brescia.], in place of Pope Gregory, in the year 1080. He named him Clement.

Whenever Gregory went out from Rome to conduct some business [Note: [Col. 1195] *Roma* in B5c; in B6a, *Romam ingressus* (“having entered Rome”) is corrected to *Roma egressus* (“having departed from Rome”); *ingressus* in B6c.], Clement entered in his place; when Gregory returned, Clement fled. The greater part of the ecclesiastical party supported Gregory, while the Caesarian party supported Clement [Note: [Col. 1195] “But the Caesarian party” in B6; absent in B6 and B1.]

But what does this have to do with us? Let these matters return to their proper places [Note: [Col. 1195] The words from *potius* through *prosequamur* (“rather, let us continue”) are absent in C6; *habeant* (“let them have”) in B2 and B3.]. Let us continue the sequence of our subject.

### Supplementary apparatus and corrections

The following notes restore source apparatus that belongs to the preceding passages; each is keyed to its local lemma.

**5. Poppo, the nail.** The chapter heading is chapter LIV in Leibniz and Book II, chapter XXVIII in C1 and C6; C3’s rubric is “Concerning the Lord’s nail.” At “around that time,” B2, B4, and B5 omit the words; C1 adds *ejus* (“of it”) after them, followed by C3 and later manuscripts. *Videndi* (“of seeing”) is corrected to *vidende* in C1 and then C3 and later manuscripts; C omits *et* (“also”). At “fellow provincial bishops,” B1 reads *provincialium* (“provincial bishops”). C1, followed by C3 and later witnesses, adds *erat* (“was”) after “for this work.”

The quotation from the *Life of Saint Agritius* says that Archbishop Bruno secretly wished to transfer, or rather steal, the Lord’s nail; after arranging a close counterfeit, the bribed guardian received it from the bishop, attempted the long-plotted theft, and the text breaks off at a lacuna. It dates the miracle to 20 June and says that the blood-marked cloth and counterfeit nail could still be seen at Saint Peter’s, if permission was granted. The same *Life* (Acta Sanctorum, January I, p. 777) tells the exorcism differently: Winiberga, from the city commonly called Regensburg, experienced it.

At “if the demon’s testimony ought to be believed,” B4 and B5 have *debat*; C1 corrects *debebat* to *debeat*, followed by C3 and later witnesses, and C1 later adds in the margin, “it is proved to be the true nail of the Lord,” whence C3 and later witnesses take it. B2 omits *illo* (“there”), B1 has *fuisse* (“to have been brought”), B5 omits *ipse esse* (“it itself to be”), and B1 omits *fuisset* (“had been”). At “the bishop stood nearby,” B1 omits *astitit ille*. C6 reads *et alium* (“and another”); B1 omits the words from *alium* (“another”) through *quem* (“which”); B5 has feminine *erepta* (“after she had been seized”) for *erepto* (“after it had been seized”).

**6. Famine and Poppo’s charity.** The heading is chapter LV in Leibniz and Book II, chapter XXIX in C1 and C6; C1 adds the rubric “Concerning Poppo’s compassion toward the poor.” B1 transposes *illo itaque* to *itaque illo*; it reads *aures* (“ears”) for *auras* (“air, breezes”; compare Virgil, *Aeneid* I.388), omits *ducem suum* (“his leader”), and may read *dei* (“of God”) for the following word. B2, B5, and C6 read indicative *videtur* (“seems”), corrected in C1 to subjunctive *videretur* (“might seem”). B1, B2, B4, and B5 have *inaestimabili* for *inaestimabilis* (“immeasurable”); B4 has *obsorbuerat* for *absorbuerat* (“had swallowed”); B1 perhaps has *sua* (“his”) in “his Life.” The editorial note directs the reader to the cited passage below.

At “the eyes of his mind,” B2 prints the abbreviation *o. s. m.*, expanded here as *oculos suae mentis*. B5 reads *civitatem* for *civitate* (“in the city”), and C1 corrects *in c. e.*; C1 subsequently supplies *celebraturus* (“about to celebrate”). B5 has *solito* (“customarily”) for *solita* (“customary”); C1, followed by C3 and later witnesses, corrects *aliquid* (“something”) to *aliquod* (“some thing”). B4 and B5 omit *ad se* (“to himself”); B2 has infinitive *exhibere* (“to bring forth”) for *exhiberi* (“to be brought forth”); B1?, B4?, and B5? have *igitur* (“therefore”). C6 omits the words “as he began to spend it among the poor.” C1 subsequently supplies *prae* in *prae manibus* (“at hand”); C3 and C4 read *illo* (“with that”) for *illorum* (“their”). B2 omits *non habes* (“you do not have”), while B4? and B5? have *potes* (“you can”). B1 has *velit* (“wishes”) for *quaerit* (“seeks”); B4, B5, and C omit *in eo* (“at that moment”).

**7. Saint Peter’s church and Poppo’s death.** The heading is chapter LVI in Leibniz and Book II, chapter XXX in C1 and C6; C1 adds “Concerning Bishop Poppo.” B2, B4, and B5 omit *de* (“about”), later supplied in C1; C1 corrects erroneous *raparandis* to *reparandis* (“repairing”). B5 has singular *fertur* (“it is said”); the editorial cross-reference is to chapter 19 above. For the collapsed column and its rebuilding, compare Steininger, *Bemerkungen zur Geschichte des Domes zu Trier* (1839), quarto, p. 1. B5 has *neglecto* for *neglectu* (“through neglect”); B1 reads *circumactis* (“turned around”) for *circumamictis* (“wrapped around”), and *vocat* (“calls”) for *nuncupat* (“names”). The German *Pfeiler* glosses *pilares* (“pillars”). B5 reads *libris* (“books”) for *libri* (“Book”) and B1 *suffulcivit* (“supported”) for *suffulsit*; C6 omits *etc.*

At the dedication, C1 supplies *et* (“and”) in the margin; it corrects *e* to *beati* in “the blessed Maternus’s relics.” C1 corrects *synodus* to *synodi*, followed by C3 and later manuscripts; B1 omits *jam* (“now”); B4, B5, and C read *ibidem Treveri* (“there at Trier”); B2 has *truere*, corrected in C1 to *treueri*; B2, B4, and B5 have singular *translato* (“after the transfer”) for *translatis* (“after the relics had been transferred”). The contextual reference is Hontheim, *Prodromus* I, p. 318, and Brower I, p. 518, on Poppo’s synod of June 1036. C1 later adds *secundo* after Conrad; B1? and B4? have *treueri*, while C1 corrects *treuerim* to *treueri*, followed by C3 and later manuscripts. B1? has *facere* (“to make”). B1 omits *sub die* (“on the day”); B1 first wrote *MVII*, later corrected it to *MXLVII*, and C1, C3, and C4 correct *LXVII* to *XLVII*: the editor judges 1047, not 1067, to be what the author wrote. B1? and B3? read *mentio facta* (“mention made”); C has *commendavit* (“he commended”) for *commendaverat* (“he had commended”). The relevant charter of Poppo, dated 1042 in Hontheim, *Historia* I, p. 379, describes the church built at the gate consecrated to Mars by pagans, in honour of Christ, Mary, Symeon, and all saints. B2 appends *Amen* after “for ever and ever.”

**8. Everhard.** The heading is chapter LVII in Leibniz; C3’s rubric is “Concerning Archbishop Everhard,” while C1 has no division. B1 omits *cum* (“with”) in “with the consent”; the Aura Vallis manuscript ends here. C1’s later hand glosses *Alamanniae* (“of Alamannia”) as *id est Swevie* (“that is, Swabia”), as does C6. Brower, p. 524, quotes the Trier necrology: Henry, father of Archbishop Everhard, died on 14 April; the family of the counts still seems unknown. C6 supplies *et* (“and”); C1, then C3 and later witnesses, subsequently adds *fuit* (“was”), while B4 reads *ecclesiae Wormaciensis* (“of the church of Worms”). The unnamed bishop is Arnold. B1 has *que negotiis magnisque* (“and affairs and great [affairs]”); C1 corrects *non sp.* to *nec spernendus* (“nor to be despised”). C3 reads *treverici*, B1/B2/B4/(B5?) have *orbate*, corrected in C1 to feminine *orbata*, and B2 has *conuentibus* (“having assembled”), corrected to *coniuentibus* (“consenting”). C adds: “Anyone wishing to know these things can find them in the present work.” B1 adds *et*; C6 has *praedecessoribus* (“predecessors”) and B1 *recepit* (“recovered”). The editor found no diplomas on the matter, nor did Brower; see his *Annales*, p. 539.

At Leo’s name B1 has *vocabatur* (“was called”); the passage derives from the older text of the *Gesta*, chapter 32, described above at column 1177. The Luxembourg place-name is *lucelenburc* in B1 and C, *luzelenburc* in B4 and B5; B4 and B5 spell *krisma* for *crisma*. C6 omits *omnia* (“all”) and changes *misterii* (“mystery”) to *ministerii* (“ministry”); B3 continues *pergit*; B1 has *fieret* (“might be done”), B4, B5, and C *definiret* (“might decide”), and B1 adds *et penitentiam* (“and penance”). C1/C6 have *deinde i.* and C3 *deindeis* for *dein*; C4 reads *de judeis* (“concerning Jews”). B5 reads *pasce*; B4 corrects *lignis* (“with wood”) to *licnis* (“with wicks”), while B5 has *licinis*. B5 has masculine *medio*, C *media jam* (“already half”), B2 *altare* (“altar”), C *sacrario* (“in the sacristy”); C adds *genibus flexis* (“with knees bent”), while B4, B5, and C add “before the cross painted there,” and B3 omits *in oratione* (“in prayer”). B5 reads *VII* for *XVII*; C6 adds “of Paulinus” from the canon.

For the intervening entries, C3 and C4 lack the two Leo diplomas. The rubric for Leo’s privilege is absent from C3 and later manuscripts; Hontheim I, p. 386 is the reference. Victor’s item is in Gunther I, p. 134. C1 adds to the rubric “Another account belongs here,” and C3 reads “Concerning the tearing of the pallium.”

**9. Cuono and Udo.** The heading is chapter LVIII in Leibniz; from this point manuscripts 4, 5, and 6 agree with B and C. B4, B5a, and C6 read *defuncto* (“having died”). At Anno, 5c and C read *Suno*; 5b has *archiepiscopus* (“archbishop”). B5 and B6 omit “regent of the kingdom and guardian of his son Henry.” The text reads *Treberorum*; B and C have *treberi*, which the editor says may perhaps be adopted. B5 and B6 consistently have *Cononem*; B4, B5, and C use *intronizandum* (“to be enthroned”), and C6 *misit* (“sent”). B4/C6 have *beatae* (“of the blessed woman”); B4, B5, and C add *et martyrii* (“and of martyrdom”). C has *trebirensibus*, B4 *exerendae*, and B4/B5/B6 *dedit* (“gave”); compare the *Life of Conrad* below in the Appendix.

Manuscript 6 reads *Nam sine mora* (“for without delay”); B5a consistently has *Theodricum*, and B4/B5/B6 *principes suis* (“his princes”); B5/B6 omit *injuriae vocibus* (“with cries [about] the injury”). B5 has *violacione* (“violation”); B5b omits *omnium successorum* (“of all successors”) and the following *esse* (“to be”), while B4/B5/B6 add *et ad infamiam* (“and to infamy”). B5b/B6 omit *coacto* (“having assembled”); 6 omits enclitic *-que* in *frondesque* (“and branches”), 6c/6d have *viderentur* (“might be seen”), B4 *ferentes* (“carrying”), and B2/B4/B5/C *prae se ferentes* (“carrying before themselves”). B4/B5/C add “in the month of May”; B5b omits *subito* (“suddenly”). B5a omits the words from *adesse* through *hostes* (“that the enemies were present”); B5/B6c omit *-que* (“and”) in “enormous booty.” B4/B5/C add *vero* after *ipse* (“Cuono himself”); B1 omits the relative clause “who entrusted him.” B4/B5/B6 omit *videlicet* (“namely”); B5a has *Julii* (“of July”) for *Junii* (“of June”); B5b omits the enclitic in *civitatemque*; B1/B3 omit “by his wise counsellors,” and 5 reads *furore eius* (“his rage”) for *ejus furore* (“by his rage”).

For Udo, C1’s later hand glosses “that is, of the Swabians”; B5 has *ortus* (“born”) for *oriundus* (“sprung from”). The forms for Everhard are *hebrardo* (B5a), *heberhardo* (B5c), *heberhardo* (B5b), and *eberhardo* (B6). The family is of Nellenburg; compare Stalin, *History of Württemberg* I, p. 553, the charter at p. 554 n. 11, and the *Schaffhausen Annals*, *MGH Scriptores* V, p. 388. C1 supplies *matre* (“by [his] mother”); Ita appears as *Ida* (B4, B6, B1, B2), *Yda* (B5a, B5b), and *Vda* (B5c). B6/B1/B3 read *ejusdem*, B5/B2 *ejusdemque*, B5/B6 *monasterii* (“monastery”), and B1/B4/B5/C/C6 give the forms *Scaphuse*, *Scafhusen*, *Scafhuse*, and *Schafhuse* for Schaffhausen; B4/B5/B6 have *fundatoribus* (“founders”). B5b omits *humeris* (“shoulders”), B6 *tanti* (“so great”); B5b has *a suis predecessoribus*, B4/B5/B6 *fecit* (“made”), and omit *et tirannidem* (“and tyranny”). B5/B6 omit *Hic* (“he”); B5a’s other hand corrects the ethnonym to “Swabians,” as does C1’s later hand. Tuingia’s forms are *Turingia* (B4), *Tuvigia*, corrected to *Tuuingia* (B5a), *Mingia* (B5c), *Tumgia* (B6c), *Tuingia* (B4/B5), and *Twingia* (C); the editor identifies it as Tübingen and cites Bruno, *On the Saxon War*, chapters 61 and 103, Ekkehard under 1077, and Stenzel I, p. 437 n. B5/B6 read *dicitur* (“is called”), B5b omits *quod* (“which”), B5a/B5c have *monasterium*, B5b omits the final phrase, and the succession name forms are *Engilbertus* (B5), *Engelbertus* (B1 and thereafter), and *Egelbertus* (B2, B3, and subsequently B5 and B6).

**10. Gregory and Clement.** The heading is chapter LIX in Leibniz; C1/C6 have “Another notable account,” C3 “Concerning Egilbert’s election,” and B5 lacks chapters 10–14. B5 reads *quo* (“when”) for *cum*; B4 has *Hildebranth*. B1 omits “priests”; B6a corrects *distribuerent* (“should distribute”) to *abstinerent* (“should abstain”), followed by B6b/B6c, while B6b has *astinerent*; B4/B5/B6 omit *ab* (“from”), and B6 has *vacarent* (“should be free [of office]”). B5a reads *Similiter ne* (“likewise, that no one”); B5c omits *sive* (“or”), B5a *vel* (“or”), and B6c *per* (“through”); B4/B5/B6 use *vel* for *sive*; B5/B6 have *quod* for *quodque*. B5/B6 have *invidiae* (“envies”), B6c *succreverint* (“have grown”), and B1 *succurrerunt* (“came to the aid”); C reads *alia* (“another”) for *aliqua* (“some”). C3 abbreviates *honoris regii* as *h. r.* (“royal honour”). B2 omits from *regis* (“of the king”) through *sibi* (“to himself”).

B4 omits *ubi* (“when”); B6 has *ac* (“and”) for *et*; B5/B6 have present *concludit* (“binds”) for perfect *conclusit* (“bound”). Witness 6 omits *omnium* (“all”); B5 has *complicum* (“of accomplices”); B6 *et* for *vel* (“or”), B1 omits *vel honore* (“or by honour”), B5/B4 abbreviate *Heinricum nominis* (“Henry, of the name”), and B6 omits *regem quartum* (“the fourth king”). B4/B5 omit *fama* (“report”), B5/B6 omit *ad aures imperatoris* (“to the emperor’s ears”), and B6 omits “nor should Gregory be apostolic for any of them.” B4? omits *ipse* (“he himself”); B5 has *Wichbertum*, B1 *et W.*; B5c omits *quendam* (“a certain”), B4/C3 have singular *civitate*, and the editor identifies the city as Brescia. B5c has *Roma*; B6a corrects *Romam ... ingressus* (“having entered Rome”) to *Roma ... egressus* (“having departed Rome”), while B6c retains *ingressus*; B4 reads *ille* (“that man”). B1 omits *ecclesiastica*, C omits *major*, B6 adds *vero* after *isti*, and B6/B1 omit *caesariana pars* (“the Caesarian party”). Finally, C6 omits from *potius* (“rather”) through *prosequamur* (“let us continue”), and B2/B3 read *habeant* (“let them have”) for *abeant* (“let them go away”).

### 11

[Note: Column 1195: chapter 60 in Leibniz.]

At that time there was in the city of Batavia [Note: Column 1195: *barama* 5b; after correction, *battavia* 5a; *baramia* 5c; *batana* B1; *bathanya* B2; *batava*, corrected to *batavia*, C1. Column 1196C: Passau.] a certain provost of the principal church and schoolmaster, named Egilbertus [Note: Column 1195: B1 consistently reads *Engelbertus*], one of the nobles of Bavaria [Note: Column 1195: *bajoriae* 4, 5, B3; *bawoariae* B2]. On one occasion, when the bishop of that place, like the bishops of the other cities, was proclaiming in his church, by order of the Roman pontiff, the decree mentioned above, Egilbertus rashly resisted him to his face, openly making it understood by everyone that he too was bound by the bond of anathema together with the adherents of Henry [Note: Column 1195: *recitaret* (“should recite”) 6; *intelligere* C1; *quam* B1].

For it is established, with the Apostle bearing witness, concerning evildoers [Note: Column 1195: *fautoribus* (“supporters”), *factoribus* (“wrongdoers”) 4, 5], that those who do the deed and those who consent are to be punished by the same sentence (Romans 1:32) [Note: Column 1195: *testimonio* (“by the testimony”) 5a; *deest* (“is absent”) C6]. Now a person consents who, even if he cannot refuse, nevertheless, by showing favor, shares, so far as lies within him, in the works of the wrongdoer.

He said that the emperor was permitted to bestow freely or for a price upon whomever he wished not spiritual possessions but his royal rights, and that he would not thereby lose communion with the Church [Note: Column 1195: *c. e.* (“and would not lose communion”) 6; *c. non amittere* (“and would not lose”) B1]. Yet these were not properly his own; according to Roman custom they could more rightly be called the royal rights of blessed Peter or of the Church.

But would that those who desire to reach the summit of ecclesiastical dignity did not thrust themselves forward ambitiously, as is utterly unfitting, nor devise for themselves the contrivances of the Simoniacal heresy under the specious guise of an artful invention [Note: Column 1195: *configant* (“fasten together”) B2], asserting that they acquire not spiritual but earthly things through earthly means—although, just as in time, so also in their minds, the animal comes first and the spiritual afterward, and they seek not [so much] pastoral care as temporal honor! [Note: Column 1195: *tam* (“so much”) is absent from almost all manuscripts; it is uncertain whether it appears in 4 and B4.]

After many discussions had therefore taken place between them concerning this matter, when the bishop saw that Egilbertus was incorrigibly attached to the Simoniacal party and in no way assented to the ecclesiastical position, he ordered that he should remain excluded from communion with the Church until, when presented to the universal pope, he might through him be deemed worthy to be reunited to the unity of the Church.

Accordingly, after he had hesitated within himself for a long time, the desire to go to Rome finally occurred to him. Nevertheless, he did not wish to go there without consulting the king. From that king, then, having received a message for the man whom we have called the pope’s superior [Note: Column 1195: *superpositum* 4; *superpositi* 4; *suppositum* 6a; *subpositum* B2], he conveyed it to him and withdrew entirely from the universal pope [Note: Column 1195: *ei voluntas* (“the desire came to him”) 6].

And it happened that, while he was returning after completing the business for which he had been sent by the king, he heard on his way back that Uodo, the archbishop of Trier, a man worthy of faithful remembrance [Note: Column 1195: *treberensium* (“of the Treverans”) 6], had departed this life [Note: Column 1195: one manuscript reads *episcopum* (“bishop”) B2]. For that reason the king had gone to Trier [Note: Column 1195: *treberim advenisse* (“had arrived at Trier”) 5, 6], in order that he might appoint another in his place [Note: Column 1195: *loco* (“in the place”) 5].

When he learned this news, he hastened his journey as much as possible [Note: Column 1195: *tunc* (“then”) 5], thinking within himself that, if he could perhaps arrive there sooner [Note: Column 1195: *posset* (“could”) 5], the honor might succeed to him in return for the service he had so often rendered the king [Note: Column 1195: *subsistere* (“remain”) 6]. And so it happened [Note: Column 1195: omitted in 5]. But how this came about we shall explain to those who do not know [Note: Column 1195: *est* (“was”) 5].

When the emperor had ordered that they should elect as bishop the man whom they recognized as pleasing to him, and the clergy, one after another from their own fellowship [Note: Column 1195: *consortio* (“association”) 4, 5, 6], presented men who were in every respect worthy of this honor, the king nevertheless said that none of those whom they had named pleased him [Note: Column 1196C: “none of them” is omitted in 5; *dixit* (“he said”) 5]. For none of them had anticipated his goodwill with an adequate assessment of their worth.

Three days had already passed in the election [Note: Column 1195: *exactis* (“having elapsed”) 6], and on the fourth day everyone had assembled again for the same purpose [Note: Column 1195: “again” is omitted in 6 and B1]. Then, as though sent by God—if it can be said that the way of a man who by his own fault deserved to be suspended from the communion of the Church was directed by God—Egilbertus came. After saying his prayer [Note: Column 1195: omitted in 6], he spoke to the king about the matters entrusted to him.

When he had finished, the king said: “Since we have now for a long time been unable to agree in choosing a bishop [Note: Column 1195: *quoniam* (“since”) 6; *quamdiu* (“how long”) 5b, 5c, B2, 3, 4, C; *possismus* (“we might be able”) 6c], let us at least agree upon this man.”

Of the bishops who had come for the election [Note: Column 1195: “for devotion” in 5 and 6], only Theodericus, bishop of Verdun [Note: Column 1195: *theodricus* 5a, 5b; *wirdunensis* B2], who was called Magnus by surname, consented to him, together with a certain part of the people of Trier [Note: Column 1197: omitted in C].

The king therefore delayed no longer but invested him, giving him the ring and staff, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1078 [Note: Column 1197: the year is omitted in B2. The editor states that 1079 seems intended, since the twenty-two years, eight months, and three days attributed to Egilbertus’s administration in chapter 17 run from 8 January 1079 to 5 September. The ancient custom of Trier began the year on 25 March. See the dissertation printed at Trier in 1815, entitled *Chronologisch-diplomatische Bemerkungen über die Zeitrechnung der Trierer im Mittelalter* (“Chronological-Diplomatic Observations concerning the Reckoning of Time among the Trierers in the Middle Ages”). See also Wyttenbach; Stenzel I, p. 437 n.; Stalin, *History of Württemberg* I, p. 510.]

The bishops Herimannus of Metz [Note: Column 1197: *Hermannus* 5, B1, C6; *Heremannus* B2] and Bibo of Toul [Note: Column 1197: *Bybo* B2], together with the remaining clergy and people, did not consent, so far as lay within them, because they themselves had presented equally suitable persons [Note: Column 1197: the masculine *idoneos* is corrected to feminine *idoneas* in C1; *exhibuerant* (“had presented”) 5]. Nevertheless, they could not resist the king’s will.

The clergy and people, however, being greatly distressed that violence was being inflicted upon them [Note: Column 1197: “that so much violence was being inflicted upon them” in 6], entreated the bishops who were present and, under threat of apostolic authority, forbade them to consecrate him as bishop [Note: Column 1197: *episcopum* (“bishop”) in B4?], reminding them of the canon of that decree which prescribes that no one is to be consecrated bishop unless canonically elected.

For this reason, when the bishops returned to their own sees, Egilbertus remained without having received the blessing. He desired to be consecrated, but for many days he could not obtain this from any ecclesiastical bishop who had heard of his entrance into office [Note: Column 1197: *catholicorum* (“Catholic”) 5, 6; *audissent* (“had heard”) 4, 5, 6. Column 1198: compare the letter of Theodericus, bishop of Verdun, written to Egilbertus from the Udalrician codex, in Hontheim I, p. 426.]

After nearly three years had therefore passed [Note: Column 1198: the editor says that six years should have been stated], when the matter had become known to the king—who at that time, returning from Rome after much slaughter had been committed there and Pope Gregory had been driven out, was lingering on the far side of the Alps, while this event certainly filled everyone’s mouth with the most famous report of those days (around 1084) [Note: Column 1197: a substantial passage, extending to “if this is indeed so” below chapter 17, is absent from B3 and other witnesses because three leaves have been lost]—he sent letters to the aforesaid bishop of Verdun, who was closely attached to him, and asked him to make every effort to consecrate the metropolitan of Trier as quickly as possible [Note: Column 1197: “bishop of Trier” in B1]. It does not seem out of place to insert here a copy of those letters, which ran as follows [Note: Column 1197: the phrase is omitted in C6; *ab re* (“out of place”) is read *videri ab re* in 6].

### 12

[Note: Column 1197: chapter 60 in Leibniz. In C1 and C6 the rubric reads: “Here begin the letters which the emperor Henry sent to Theodericus.”]

King Henry, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans and august [Note: Column 1197: “ever august” in B1], sends to Bishop Theodericus an affection greater than to anyone.

First, we wish you to know that we trust no one more than you, and that we have sent you the bishop of Utrecht not as an adviser in loyalty, but as a collaborator to manage the honor of the kingdom [Note: Column 1197: *ad hoc honorem* (“for this honor”) 5b].

Next, to each of the matters you entrusted to us we give a separate answer, but a very brief one, since we reserve countless matters to be told you face to face. Concerning what you wrote to us in the margin of your letter about the Roman affair, we say this first of all [Note: Column 1197: *tibi* (“to you”) is abbreviated as *t. d.* in B1].

We entered Rome on the feast of Saint Benedict. How we were received by the Romans, how we stood with the Romans, and how we departed from the Romans, we believe you have heard from many others; we have also indicated it to you in our letters [Note: Column 1197: *indicamus* (“we indicate”) B1, B2, 4, C], which we think you have not yet seen [Note: Column 1197: *credimus* (“we believe”) 5, 6]. Indeed, we would prefer that you learn from someone other than our own mouth what the Lord has done for us [Note: Column 1197: this sentence is omitted in C6].

For it seems incredible, though it has been proved most true, what happened in Rome [Note: Column 1197: “what happened in the city of Rome” in B4?]. To put it so, the Lord accomplished through ten men among us what would have been a miracle to everyone if our predecessors had accomplished it with ten thousand [Note: Column 1197: the words “which was accomplished” are omitted in 5b].

For when, having already despaired of acquiring Rome, we wished to return to the German regions, behold, the Romans sent envoys asking us to enter Rome and promising that they would obey us in everything [Note: Column 1197: *se quoque* (“they too”) 6]. And so they did.

They received us as we entered with the greatest joy [Note: Column 1197: *susceperunt* (“received”) 6a]; they helped us, while we remained among them, with the greatest zeal; and when we departed from them, they escorted us with the greatest triumph and loyalty [Note: Column 1197: the final phrase is omitted in 6 and B1]. Thus we can confidently say in the Lord that all Rome is in our hand [Note: Column 1197: *in manu nostra* (“in our hand”) C3], except for that castle [Note: Column 1197: omitted in 5] in which Hildebrand is shut up [Note: Column 1197: 6 reads *reclusus habitat* (“lives shut up there”); C reads *conclusus* (“confined”)], namely, in the house of Crescentius.

You should know that Hildebrand was rejected by the legal judgment of all the cardinals and the entire Roman people [Note: Column 1197: omitted in B1], and that our pope Clement was elected and raised to the apostolic see by the acclamation of all the Romans [Note: Column 1197: “our pope was elected” in 6]. You should also know that we were ordained by Pope Clement and, with the consent of all the Romans, consecrated emperor on the holy day of Easter, amid the rejoicing of the entire Roman people [Note: Column 1197: *sanctae* (“holy”) 5a, C; the phrase “as emperor” is omitted in 5a, B1, B2; “with the rejoicing of the people” in C].

After these things had been done, we departed from Rome with the blessing of God and Saint Peter and with everyone rejoicing [Note: Column 1197: *itaque* (“therefore”) 5a, 5b, B1]. We are hastening toward these regions as quickly as we can [Note: Column 1197: *quantocius* (“as quickly as possible”) 5c, B1, B2, C; “toward these regions” is omitted in 5a, 5b], and on the road your messenger found us returning.

Let those rejoice who wish; let those grieve who wish. By God’s favor we are here [Note: Column 1197: *gaude autem* (“but rejoice”) C6]. We do not care to know what that lord is doing, but, as you warned us, we shall gladly take precautions so that he may not cause us harm [Note: Column 1197: *innotuisti* (“you made known”) C6].

Concerning the Saxons, the archbishop of Salzburg [Note: Column 1197: *Salebergensi* 5a; *Saleburgensi* 5b; *Saleburgense* 5c], Count Adalbert, and the others who wish to return to us, we answer you this: we gladly accept your counsel, provided only that true peace may be made in our time [Note: Column 1199: “in our regions” in C6], namely, that they be faithful when they have returned to us.

But if you are not troubled to do what we desire, we ask you to come to us at Augsburg after the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul [Note: Column 1199: “we ask you to come” in 6], because, with God’s favor, we shall be at Regensburg on their feast [Note: Column 1199: *Ratisponae villa* (“at Regensburg village”) 5]. Make every effort, therefore, to come to us, so that you may gladden us by your arrival.

Furthermore, Pope Clement and the emperor Henry command you that, just as you love us, so you should hasten to consecrate the archbishop of Trier [Note: Column 1199: *festines* (“make haste”) 5, 6; *diligis* (“you love”) 6a, 6b].

Farewell [Note: Column 1199: *valete* (“farewell,” plural) 5].

### 13

[Note: Column 1199: chapter 62 in Leibniz.]

When the aforesaid Theodericus had read these letters, he did not willingly wish to fulfill what was being requested. Astonished at the magnitude of the events, he did not bring himself to believe that everything was as the letter stated [Note: Column 1199: *non potuit ... ponere in corde suo* (“he could not set it in his heart”) 5c, 6, B3; *non credere* (“not to believe”) B1].

He also remembered that the clergy of Trier had forbidden him, by apostolic authority, to do this, lest suitable accusations should at some time arise against him on that account. He therefore thought it appropriate to send a letter about the matter to the Roman pontiff. In it he also recalled the deposition from the episcopate of the aforementioned Herimannus, bishop of Metz [Note: Column 1199: *Heremannus* B2 and thereafter; *Hermannus* 5, C], and the reconciliation imposed upon him, so that, through the pope’s intervention, Herimannus might be restored to his place. Although he had worked very hard for this, he was unable to obtain it at that time; he obtained it only later [Note: Column 1199: *obtinuit* (“he obtained it”) 6].

The letter which he sent ran as follows [Note: Column 1199: omitted in 5b, 5c]. [Note: Column 1199: C1 and C6 add the rubric: “The letter of Theodericus, bishop of Verdun, which he sent to Pope Gregory.” This letter was written several years before Henry’s letter, as is clear from its statement that the Church of Trier had been widowed for nearly two years.]

[Column 1199: (Around 1080?)]

To Gregory, supreme pontiff, most beloved and most reverend lord, Theodericus, bishop of Verdun, however unworthy, yet his own, sends the affection which a son owes his father, the submission which a subject owes his prelate, and the service which a servant owes his lord.

To be able to obey you is my greatest joy; to be able to serve you is no small gladness. In that in which I honor you, I honor blessed Peter; in that in which, by obeying and serving, I win your favor [Note: Column 1199: one manuscript reads “I reconcile you to myself”], I win the favor of the blessed Apostle [Note: Column 1199: “blessed Peter the Apostle” in 5b and C6].

Admonished by you, I received my confrere, the bishop of Metz, as I would receive you yourself, mindful of that saying of the Lord: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40). I made his cause my cause and regarded his business as my own; the same adversity was ours, and the same prosperity was ours [Note: Column 1199: one manuscript reverses the order: “the same prosperity ... the same adversity”].

Mutual brotherhood, owed charity, and above all your command, your goodwill, and the confidence you have placed in me invited me to this.

Moreover, the Church of Trier, with deep sorrow, throws herself at your fatherly feet [Note: Column 1199: “your feet” in 4, 5, 6], and the daughter knocks upon her lord’s door. Through me she laments that her loss in these times is beyond consolation [Note: Column 1199: “her loss in consolation” in 4, 5, 6]. Widowed for nearly two years [Note: Column 1199: omitted in 5; “for nearly two years” in 6], how much has she suffered and continues to suffer! How afflicted has she been and continues to be afflicted! Outside, battles; within, fears.

She chose from the people a man worthy to be a priest, a suitable father, by common assent—my conscience bearing witness before God and before you—that nothing Simoniacal had occurred in connection with his ecclesiastical office [the precise object of *ecclesiasticum* is uncertain], and that nothing Simoniacal had intervened even when the petition was set aside.

We are astonished that his consecration is delayed [Note: Column 1199: the words “we are astonished that his consecration is delayed” are omitted in 5c]; we are astonished that so grave a delay could have been impressed upon you [Note: Column 1199: *intorculari* (“thrust upon you”) in C], and especially that you allow this desolation to weigh so heavily upon us.

It is a very heavy burden for me to be alone in the midst of a wicked and perverse nation; alone, with that father and brother expelled, and no other consecrated in his place [Note: Column 1199: a later manuscript adds a correcting letter after *patre*].

If you care for the Church and for the condition of Christianity, look upon our situation. If the life of the father, examined in every respect, deserves ordination, then, when you have heard the bishop of Metz and me, let no one’s detraction delay the matter any longer [Note: Column 1199: *Mettense* (“of Metz”) in 5 and B1; *Metensem* corrected to *Metense* in C1 and thereafter; this phrase is omitted in C6].

He will repay you what a son owes his father and what a subject owes his prelate.

After inserting certain further matters, he concludes at the end as follows: “How the king stands with you, and you with the king, only write back to me as your own [servant]” [Note: Column 1199: 6c reads *tui* (“of you”) for “and you”; 5 and 6 omit *modo* (“only”).]

### 14

[Note: Column 1199: chapter 63 in Leibniz.]

Finally, after the matters just recounted had been sent to Rome, as the time approached when the king had instructed Theodericus by the letter quoted above that he would come, Theodericus, as he had been ordered [Note: Column 1199: “as he had been instructed by him” in 5b], prepared to go to meet him.

As he was coming to Mainz [Note: Column 1199: “in Mainz” in B2], he happened to find there several bishops who were going to meet the king [Note: Column 1199: omitted in B4?]. After offering his prayer, he asked them—for they were his confreres, namely, the suffragan bishops of the Church of Trier [Note: Column 1199: omitted in C; “of the Church of Trier” in 5]—the aforementioned Herimannus of Metz and Bibo of Toul [Note: Column 1199: *Bybo* B2; “and Bibo” omitted in 5b]—to cooperate with him out of charity. They had been unwilling, through fear of the king, to take part in the consecration of their metropolitan. He obtained his request.

Taking with him those who seemed more favorably disposed toward him than the others [Note: Column 1201: “who seemed to be more benevolent toward him” in 6], and with the archpriest of that see conniving [Note: Column 1201: variants include “with the archpriest consenting,” “with the archpriest agreeing,” and “with the archbishop having been summoned”], he consecrated Egilbertus as bishop [Note: Column 1201: *consecravit eum* (“consecrated him”) 4].

After he had been ordained, a few days later he came to Trier and began to act tyrannically toward those who, so to speak, had not wanted him to reign over them [Note: Column 1201: “those who did not want him” in 4 and 6], so that thereafter they would desist from opposing him. Against the more powerful, whom he could not harm any further, he instilled fear of the king; but the property of the helpless common people, who could not defend themselves against him [Note: Column 1201: *eum* (“him”) B, 4, C], he plundered on every possible pretext.

Then those who had dared to resist him more than the others [Note: Column 1201: *ausi sunt ei resistere* (“had dared to resist him”) 6] said:

“Since you have come to this honor of the episcopate, both then and now, against our will [Note: Column 1201: *ingratus* (“ungrateful”) B2, 4, C], and since you received episcopal insignia—namely, the ring and staff—from an excommunicated layman, and especially since the canons decree that laymen, however religious, have been granted no power to dispose of anything concerning ecclesiastical affairs [Note: Column 1201: portions of this clause are omitted in 5c and 6], for that reason you cannot exercise the episcopate [Note: Column 1201: *episcopare* (“to exercise the episcopate”) B1, B2, C], nor can we communicate with you.

“But if, in addition, you are to remain in the rank of the honor you have received [Note: Column 1201: *gradum* (“rank”) 5a, 5b], you must submit and obey Gregory, the supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church [Note: Column 1201: “of the apostolic Church” in C3, C4], and renounce entirely that heretic who has been set over you. We call him heretical in accordance with what blessed Pope and martyr Gelasius wrote in a certain letter addressed to all the eastern bishops, concerning such men set over others:

“‘What, then, shall we do about so many cities from which Catholic bishops have been rejected? If Catholics have been substituted, why have Catholics been rejected? [Note: Column 1201: portions of the sentence are omitted in 6a; other witnesses read “if Catholic bishops have been substituted” and omit portions of the question.] But it is plainly evident that, when Catholics were rejected, those who were substituted were not Catholics. It remains, therefore, that whoever succeeded them are not Catholics but heretics.’ [Note: Column 1201: this passage is absent at this point in 6, which adds it elsewhere.]

“Again:

“‘Who does not see that those are Catholics and wholly free from every heretical plague who have been driven from their own cities and reduced to exile, and that those who have dared to become successors while Catholics still survived are not Catholics at all?’ [Note: Column 1201: 6 adds here: “It remains, therefore, that those who succeeded them are not Catholics.”]

“To these add also those who previously joined themselves to the communion of such men [Note: Column 1201: *eos* (“those”) in 4].”

In reply, Egilbertus said that he preferred to give his life rather than be unfaithful to the man who had elevated him to this honor [Note: Column 1201: *provexit* (“elevated”) B2]. He said that he would never obey Gregory so long as Gregory himself refused to enter into friendship with the king [Note: Column 1201: *praeire* (“go forward toward”) 5, 6].

Meanwhile, while they were discussing these and similar matters among themselves, the fast of the Four Ember Days was approaching. At that time it is customary in the Church to promote those who are to be promoted to the clerical order [Note: Column 1201: *movendi* (“to be moved forward”) B1, B2]. Egilbertus was striving with all his might to do this [Note: Column 1201: *visu* (“sight”) 6b, 6c], not out of love of justice, but so that he might bind some one of the greater men to himself [Note: Column 1201: *advincere* (“bind”) 6c; the reading is defective in 5b]. Thus, once consecrated by him, they would afterward be subject to him and would fear their own suspension from clerical rank just as they feared his deposition from the episcopate.

When they learned of his intention, they said:

“Because you have not yet obtained the pallium which is owed by the Roman Church to our metropolitan see [Note: Column 1201: the relative clause is omitted in B2], we do not wish to receive the laying on of hands from you [Note: Column 1201: *recipere* (“receive”) 5; *suscipere* (“accept”) 6], especially since it is decreed in the canons: ‘If any metropolitan bishop presumes to consecrate without the pallium, both the consecrator and the consecrated shall be subject to grave danger to their order’ [Note: Column 1201: the opening words are omitted in 5 and 6c; *est* (“is”) 5].

“If, as you ought, you are to acquire it, you must humble yourself before the pope whom you despise so greatly—Gregory—so that you may deserve to receive it [Note: Column 1201: *Gregorio* is omitted in B2].”

Why say more? After suitable reasons had been set before him explaining why he ought not to perform the ordinations [Note: Column 1201: *ministrare* (“minister the orders”) 5b], he abstained.

A few days later he sent a certain associate of his, named Theodericus, a good man, a schoolmaster, and a monk [Note: Column 1203: B4 and C read: “one of his subjects, named Theodericus, a good man, a schoolmaster, a monk.”], skilled in the black arts—namely, necromancy [Note: Column 1201: *nichromaticus* 6b, 6c; *nichromanticus* 6a, 6d, B2]—but by profession a monk and highly learned in letters, to seek out his pope Clement [Note: Column 1201: “his own pope” in B1] and ask him, once he had found him, to send him the pallium [Note: Column 1201: *ut* (“so that”) 4, C?; variants read “to send it to him” and “that it be sent”].

Clement, for his part, rejoiced that someone was looking to him to receive a blessing [Note: Column 1201: “that someone was looking to him” is *aliquis ipsum*; 6b reads *aliquid* (“something”)], and sent what was requested, together with letters explaining during what periods he was to use it [Note: Column 1201: “saying during what times this was to be” in C]. Since the author does not support these letters but rather weakens them—for no faithful person accepts the decrees of heretics and excommunicated men—we have not thought it necessary to preserve them in our record [Note: Column 1201: the letters are found nowhere else].

### 64

[Note: Column 1201: chapter 64 begins in Leibniz.]

This Theodericus, whom we have already named [Note: Column 1201: the opening is corrected in C1], published two books concerning the frequently mentioned Pope Gregory [Note: Column 1202: Hontheim and Wyttenbach think that this may be the book which Sigebert attributes to Henry, *On the Holy Church*, chapter 160. Henry, he says, while still a schoolmaster at Trier and later bishop of Vercelli, wrote a book under the name of Theodericus, bishop of Verdun, addressed to Hildebrand or Pope Gregory, concerning the discord between kingdom and priesthood. He adds: “Not rebuking him, but entreating him as an elder and father, and, in a friendly introduction, presenting to him, as though with the feeling of one who grieves, everything which rumor, with its loquacity, reported that he had done and said against the law and against religious propriety.” Nor does the book edited by Martène agree with these statements. Compare Stenzel I, p. 510 n.].

In them he compiled many lies [Note: Column 1201: one manuscript transposes the words as “many lies”], which no one knew better than he how to compose [Note: Column 1201: one manuscript reads “continue”]. He made Gregory infamous, while commending the innocence and holiness of the king and of his own pope.

For publishing these works, Egilbertus—the man of whom we are speaking [Note: Column 1203: *Engilbertus* in B4]—gave him the abbey of Saint Martin [Note: Column 1203: omitted in 5a and 5b; “Saint Mary” in 4 and 5c] on the bank of the Moselle, on the very day that Sigibertus, of blessed memory, died [Note: Column 1203: *Sigebertus* 6; *Sigibernus* B2, C; *Sigebernus* B4]. He gave him this reward [Note: Column 1203: variants read “to be governed” or “to be ruled.” B4 and C continue: “which he, as a fortunate abbot, governed as far as he could and restored that church itself. For it itself … was sufficient; but, as sins demanded, in his times it was so stripped that the monks who served God there, unless etc.”].

If he had done no greater evil than this, it would have been enough for his perpetual condemnation. For that abbey had previously been abundantly supplied with possessions [Note: Column 1203: omitted in 5b], but now it has been so utterly reduced to nothing [Note: Column 1203: “it has been so greatly stripped of this” in a note to 5] that even the monks who were devoted to divine service there [Note: Column 1203: “who were there” is omitted in 6], unless they obtained supplies from elsewhere, would not have the necessities of life.

### Complete source apparatus

The following passage-keyed register supplies the remaining printed apparatus. *Deest* means “is absent”; “corrected” records an explicit correction in the witness; all sigla are retained as printed.

**11 (Columns 1195–1198).** Leibniz labels this chapter 60. At *Batavia*: 5b has *barama*, 5a *battavia* after correction, 5c *baramia*, B1 and 3 *batana*, B2 *bathanya*, and C1 *batava* corrected to *batavia*; column 1196C identifies the place as Passau. At “nobles of Bavaria,” 4, 5, B3, and 4 have *bajoriae*, B2 *bawoariae*. B1 consistently calls Egilbertus *Engelbertus*. At the decree, 6 has *recitaret* (“should recite”); C1 has *intelligere* (“to understand”); B1 has *quam* (“that”). At “it is established,” C6 omits *enim* (“for”); 5a has *testimonio* (“by testimony”); at “evildoers,” 4 has *fautoribus* (“supporters”) and 5 *factoribus* (“wrongdoers”); C6 omits *ille vero* (“but that man”).

At “communion with the Church,” 6 abbreviates *consortium ecclesiae* as *c. e.*; B1 has *c. non amittere* (“and not to lose [communion]”). At “summit,” 6 omits *culmen* (“summit”), while 6a writes *honorem* (“honor”) above the line. B2 has *configant* (“fasten/contrive”) for *confingant*, and omits *quod* (“which/that”) before “spiritual.” *Tam* (“so much”) is absent from nearly every manuscript; the editor does not know whether 4 and B4 contain it. At “discussions,” 5a omits *pro* (“about”); 6c has *videret* (“might see”) for *vidisset* (“had seen”). At the resolve to travel, 6 has *ei voluntas* (“the wish came to him”), and omits *inquam* (“I mean”).

At “the pope’s superior,” 4 has *superpositi*, 6a *suppositum*, B2 *subpositum*; the printed text has *superpositum*: these are forms of “one placed over.” At Uodo, 6 has *treberensium* (“of the Trierers”), B2 *episcopum* (“bishop”), and 6 omits *ob hoc* (“for this reason”); 5 and 6 have *Treverim advenisse* (“had arrived at Trier”), and 5 *loco* (“in the place”). At the report, 5b has *Hec fama* (“this report”); 5 *tunc* (“then”); 5 *posset* (“could”); 6 *subsistere* (“remain/succeed”); 5 omits *et* (“and”); and 5 has *est* (“is”) for *fuerit* (“will have been”).

At the election, 4–6 have *consortio* (“association/fellowship”); 5 and C6 omit *nullum eorum* (“none of them”); 5 has *dixit* (“said”), 6 omits *nullus enim eorum* (“for none of them”), and 6 *jam* (“already”). At “three days elapsed,” 6 has *exactis* (“having elapsed”); 6 and B1 omit *iterum* (“again”). B1 has *viam* (“way,” accusative); 5 and 6 *sua* (“his own”); B1, B2, and 4 *meruerit* (“may have deserved”); 5a reads *ab ecclesia et ecclesie communione* (“from the Church and from the Church’s communion”); 6 omits the prayer. At the king’s *Quia* (“since”), 5a has *O*, 5b and 5c *quamdiu* (“how long”), B2, 3, 4, and C *c.* (abbreviated), and 6 *quoniam* (“since”); 6c has *possimus* (“we may be able”). At the bishops’ purpose, 5 and 6 abbreviate *causa electionis*, while C reads *devotionis causa* (“for devotion”). 5a and 5b spell *Theodricus*; B2 *Wirdunensis* (“of Verdun”). C omits “a part of the people of Trier.”

At investment, B2 has *igitur* (“therefore”), 5 and 6 *vero* (“but”); C omits *sub die octavo Idus Januarii* (“on the eighth day before the Ides of January”), and B2 omits the year. The dating note says that 1079 seems intended: the twenty-two years, eight months, and three days assigned in chapter 17 run from 8 January 1079 to the Nones of September; Trier’s old year began on 25 March. It refers to the 1815 Trier dissertation *Chronologisch-diplomatische Bemerkungen über die Zeitrechnung der Trierer im Mittelalter* (“Chronological-Diplomatic Observations on the Trierers’ Reckoning of Time in the Middle Ages”), Wyttenbach, Stenzel I p. 437 note, and Stalin, *History of Württemberg* I p. 510. At the bishops, 5, B1, C6 have *Hermannus*, B2 *Heremannus*; B2 has *Bybo*; C1 corrects masculine *idoneos* (“suitable [men]”) to feminine *idoneas* (“suitable [persons]”); 5 has *exhibuerant* (“had presented”). B1 and B2 omit *clerus et populus* (“clergy and people”); 6 has *tantum sibi irrogari violentiam* (“that so much violence was inflicted on them”); B4 perhaps has *episcopum* (“bishop”).

At Egilbertus’s waiting, 5b omits *cupiens* (“desiring”); 5 and 6 have *catholicorum* (“Catholic [bishops]”); 4–6 have plural *audissent* (“had heard”); compare Theodericus of Verdun’s letter to Egilbertus from the Udalrician codex in Hontheim I p. 426. The editor says that “six,” rather than “three,” years ought to have been stated; C6 omits *fere* (“nearly”); 5, B2, C have *Romam* (“to Rome”) for *Roma* (“from Rome”). B3 lacks the passage from *multa* (“many”) through “if this is indeed so” in chapter 17 because three leaves are lost. 5 and 6 omit *certe* (“certainly”); 6 has *certe ... omnium ora* (“certainly ... everyone’s mouths”); C6 omits *diebus illis* (“in those days”); B2 *moras* (“delays”); 6 *epis* (an abbreviation of *epistolis*, “letters”); 6 *petiit quo* (“asked that”); B1 *episcopum metropolitanum* (“metropolitan bishop”); C6 omits *exemplar* (“copy”); 6 has *videri ab re* (“to seem out of place”).

**12 (Columns 1197–1199).** Leibniz again calls this chapter 60; C1 and C6 add the red rubric: “Here begin the letters which Emperor Henry sent to Theodericus.” 6 omits *et* (“and”) before *augustus*; B1 reads *semper augustus* (“ever august”). 5b has *ad hoc honorem* (“for this honor”). B1 abbreviates *tibi dicimus* (“we say to you”) as *t. d.*. C6 omits from *qualiter* (“how”) through *simus* (“we have been”); 6a has *sumus* (“we are”); B1, B2, 4, C have *indicamus* (“we indicate”), 5 and 6 *credimus* (“we believe”), C6 omits *te* (“you”), and 5b omits *factum* (“done”). At Rome, 6 has *est Romae* (“was at Rome”), B4 perhaps *urbe Roma* (“in the city of Rome”); C6 omits *in nobis* (“among us”); C6 *quae* (“which [things]”); 6 omits *jam* (“already”); 6 has *se quoque* (“they also”); 6a *susceperunt* (“received”); 6 and B1 omit the final escort phrase; C6 omits *in tantum ut* (“so much that”); C3 has *nostra manu* (“our hand”); 5 omits the castle.

At Hildebrand, 5 omits *est* (“is”); 6 reads *reclusus habitat* (“lives shut up there”), C *conclusus* (“confined”); 4 spells *Hildebranth*. B1 omits “of all the cardinals and of the whole Roman people”; 6 has *nostrum papam* (“our pope”); B2 adds *et*; 5a and C *sanctae* (“holy”); 5a, B1, B2 omit *in imperatorem* (“as emperor”); C has *in exultatione* (“in the rejoicing”). At departure, 5a, 5b, B1 have *itaque* (“therefore”); 5c, B1, B2, C *quantocius* (“as quickly as possible”); B2 *possimus* (“we may be able”); 5a and 5b omit *ad has partes* (“toward these regions”), while 5c *prope partes* (“near the regions”); B2 *properantes* (“hastening”). C6 reads *gaude autem* (“but rejoice”); C6 *innotuisti* (“you made known”); 6 has *damnum ne faciat* (“lest he do harm”).

At Salzburg, 5a has *Salebergensi*, 5b *Saleburgensi*, 5c *Saleburgense*; 6a omits *vera* (“true”); C6 has *in nostris partibus* (“in our regions”); 6 has *te rogamus* (“we ask you”); 5 has *quia erimus, Deo favente, in festivitate eorum Ratisponae* (“for, God favoring, we shall be at Regensburg on their feast”); 5 and 6 *festo* (“feast”); B2 *Ratisponae*, 5 *Ratisponae villa* (“at the town of Regensburg”); 5 and C *tuo adventu possis nos* (“by your arrival you may gladden us”); 6a *tibi mandat* (“commands you”); 6 *Heinricus imperator*; 6a and 6b correct *dilĭgas* (“may you love”) to *diligis* (“you love”); 5 and 6 *festines* (“make haste”); 5 *valete* (“farewell,” plural).

**13 (Columns 1199–1200).** Leibniz marks chapter 62. 6 has *litteras* (“letters”); 5 and C *voluit* (“wished”); 5c, 6, B3 *non potuit* (“was not able”); B1 gives *non posuit in corde suo, non credere* (“he did not put it in his heart not to believe”). 5 has *referente scriptura* (“the writing reporting”); 5a and 5b *adversum* (“against”); 5 *ydonee* (“suitable”). B2 has *Heremanni* and thereafter; 5 and C *Hermanni*; 4 *Mettensis episcopi* (“bishop of Metz”), C repeatedly *Metensis*; 6 *obtinuit* (“obtained”). 5b and 5c omit “of the letters”; C1 and C6 add the rubric “The letter of Theodericus, bishop of Verdun, which he sent to Pope Gregory.” The editorial note dates this letter several years before Henry’s because it says Trier had been widowed for almost two years.

In the letter, C has *ac reverentissimo* (“and most reverend”); 6 *mihi est* (“is to me”); C6 *Petrum apostolum* (“Peter the Apostle”); C6 *reconciliabo* (“I shall reconcile”); 5b and C *beatum Petrum apostolum* (“blessed Peter the Apostle”). At the Metz bishop, 6d has *negotium eius* (“his business”); C1 adds *eius* in the margin and C3 onward retain it. 6 reverses the pair as *prosperitas ... adversitas* (“prosperity ... adversity”). 6c reads *Propterea* (“therefore”); 4–6 *vestris* (“your,” plural) for “fatherly”; 6 *provolvitur* (“casts itself down”); 4–6 *in consolatione* (“in consolation”) and 5b *in hiis* (“in these [times]”). 5 omits “for nearly two years,” while 6 has *fere biennio* (“for almost two years”); 5b omits “outside, battles.”

5c omits “we are astonished that his consecration is delayed”; 5a and 5b have *desolationem* (“desolation”) for *dilationem* (“delay”); C *intorculari* (“to be pressed/thrust upon”). 5c omits *solum* (“alone”); 6 *atque* (“and”); 6a adds a correction after *patre* (“father”), retained in 6b, while 6c writes *patre ex...* (defective). 5 *cures* (“you care for”); 4–6 *et cura patris* (“and the father’s care”).
