B1 omits *sit* (“stands”); 6c has *tui* (“of you”); 5 and 6 omit *modo* (“only”).

**14 and 64 (Columns 1199–1203).** Leibniz marks chapter 63. 5 and 6 *termino* (“the appointed time”); 5b *iussu eius facto* (“having acted at his command”); B2 *in Mogontia* (“in Mainz”); B4 perhaps omits *forte* (“by chance”); C omits “suffragans,” while 5 has *Treverensis ecclesiae* (“of the Church of Trier”); B2 *Bybo*, 5b omits “and Bibo”; 5 and 6 *ab* (“from”) for *ex* (“out of”); 6 *sibi eos* (“them for himself”); 5a *Ita* (“thus”); 6 *secum his* (“with these [men]”). 6 has *benigni esse* (“to be favorable”). At the archpriest, B1 and 4 have *connivente archipresulem* (a defective form, “with the archpriest conniving”); C *annuente ... archipresule* (“with the archpriest consenting”); 4–6 *convenit eis archipraesulem* (“the archpriest agreed with them”). 5a, 5b, 6d add *et* before Egilbertus; 4 *consecravit eum* (“consecrated him”). 4 has *his ... qui eum* (“those ... who [did not want] him”), 6 *regnare noluerunt* (“did not wish to reign”), and B, 4, C *eum* (“him”).

At the objectors, 6 has *ausi sunt ei resistere* (“dared to resist him”); 6 *adhuc* (“hitherto”); 5 and 6c *ordinem* (“rank/order”); B2, 4, C *ingratus* (“ungrateful”); 5c omits *cum* (“since”); 6 *et decretis* (“and decreed”); 5 adds *et*, 6 omits the clause, and 5–6 give *de ecclesiasticis rebus aliquid disponendi nulla* (“no power to dispose of anything concerning church affairs”); B2 *aliqua* (“some things”); B1, B2, C *episcopare* (“to exercise the episcopate”). 5a and 5b *gradum* (“rank”); 6 *persistere* (“to remain”); C3 and C4 *apostolicae ecclesiae* (“apostolic Church”); 5a and 6 omit from *heretico illi* (“that heretic”) through *abrenunciare* (“renounce”); 5 omits *beatus* (“blessed”).

B4 perhaps omits *sunt*; 5a and 5b transpose *sunt subrogati* (“have been substituted”), 5a omits from *cur* (“why”) through *qui subrogati* (“those substituted”), 5c omits *subrogati*, and 6 *sunt subrogati*. B2 *rejecti sunt* (“have been rejected”); 5b and 5c omit *quia* (“because”); 5b transposes *sunt subrogati*; 6 lacks *Restat* through *successerunt* at this location; C6 reads *cum* (“since”). In the second quotation 4–6 have *extrusi* (“driven out”); 6 adds “It remains therefore that whoever succeeded are not Catholics” here. B1 omits *his* (“to these”); C3 and C4 *has* (“these”); 4 *eos* (“those”). B2 has *provexit* (“raised up”); 5c omits *ipse* (“he himself”); 5 and 6 *praeire* (“go before/advance toward”).

At Ember ordinations B1 and B2 have *movendi* (“those to be moved forward”); 5b omits *hoc* (“this”); 6b and 6c *visu* (“by sight”); 6c *advincere* (“bind to oneself”), while 5b breaks off *advi....*; 6c *paululum* (“a little”) for *pallium*; B2 omits *quod* (“which”); 5 *recipere* (“receive”), 6 *suscipere* (“accept”); 5 *est* (“is”); 5 and 6c omit the opening of the canonical quotation. 6 omits *necessarium habes* (“you have it necessary”); B2 omits from *papae* (“pope”) through *Gregorio* (“Gregory”); 6 *te convenit* (“it is fitting for you”); 4–6 omit *Quid multa?* (“Why say more?”); 5b omits *ei* (“to him”); 4 *deberet* (“ought”); 5b *ministrare* (“to administer [orders]”).

At Theodericus, B4 and C read *quendam subditorum suorum nomine Theodericum, virum probum, scholasticum, monachum* (“one of his subjects, named Theodericus, a good man, schoolmaster, monk”); 6b and 6c *nichromaticum*, 6a, 6d, B2 *nichromanticum* (“necromantic”); 4 *sui Clementem* (“his Clement”); B1 *papam suum* (“his pope”); 4 and C *ut* (“so that”). 6 *sibi transmittere* (“send to him”); 6b *transmitteret ei* (“should send to him”); 5b *transmitti* (“to be sent”); 5a and 6c *peteret* (“should request”). 5 and 6 omit *inquam* (“I mean”); 6b has *aliquid* (“something”), while 5b omits *ipsum* (“him”); C *dicentibus* (“saying”); 4 *foret hoc* (“this would be”); 6b *auctoritas* (“authority”) for *auctor* (“author”); 5 has *vero* (“indeed”), 5b omits it; 6 *memoriae commendare* (“commit to memory”). The editor says the letters exist nowhere else.

Leibniz begins chapter 64 here. C1 corrects the opening *Hic*; B2 omits *de* (“concerning”). The long editorial note says Hontheim and Wyttenbach think this may be the book Sigebert assigns to Henry in *On Holy Church*, chapter 160: Henry, once Trier’s schoolmaster and later bishop of Vercelli, wrote under the person of Theodericus of Verdun to Hildebrand/Gregory on the conflict of kingdom and priesthood; Sigebert describes it as entreating him as an elder and father, while reporting what talkative rumor said he had done and said against law and religious right. Martène’s edited book does not agree; compare Stenzel I p. 510 note. 5 and 6 read *multis mendaciis* (“with many lies”); 5 *continuare* (“to continue”) for *concinnare* (“to compose”). B4 spells *Engilbertus*. 5a and 5b omit Saint Martin; 4 and 5c read Saint Mary. 6 has *Sigeberto*, B2 and C *Sigiberno*, B4 *Sigeberno*; 6b *eodem* (“on the same [day]”); B4 and C *regendam* (“to be governed”). B4 and C continue: “which he, as a fortunate abbot, governed as far as he could and restored that church itself. For it itself [lacuna] was sufficient; but, as sins demanded, in his times it was so stripped that the monks serving God there, unless etc.” 6b has *sibi* (“for himself”); 5b omits *quidem* (“indeed”); 5 adds *adeo est ab hoc* (“it has been so stripped of this”); 6 has *mancipati erant* (“were devoted/bound”) for the final clause.

[Col. 1203B] **15.** There is also another matter among the deeds of this same Egilbert which, because of the similarity of the deed, I am pleased to insert here [Note: [Col. 1203] *pergit* (“continues”) in B5; *quoddam* (“a certain one”) in 5 and 6; *eg. e.* (“of the same Egilbert”) in 5; *inferre* (“to introduce”) in 5b, B1, and B2; B4, B5, and C read *quod successoribus nostris volumus narrare* (“which we wish to relate to our successors”).]. In the monastery of the virgins at Horrea, although all who served God there resisted, after Imiza [Note: [Col. 1203] *uniza* in 4; *imaza* in B2.], a servant of God of the highest vigor, the mother of the community, had died, he placed in charge a certain niece of his, the daughter of his brother, named Liucarda [Note: [Col. 1203] *liutgardem* in 4; *lugardam* in B1; *liuchardam* in B2; *liugardam* in B4.]. [Note: [Col. 1203] The words “although all who served God there resisted” through “the daughter of his brother” are absent in C. C6 omits “a certain niece of his”; 6 reads “he placed in charge the daughter of his brother.” [Col. 1204B] B3, B4, and C continue: “Liucarda was indeed very young in body and handsome, educated in letters according to her age, and honorable in conduct. Concerning her, etc.”]—which I say with due regard for the peace and dignity of her religious profession; God knows that I am not lying—she was a practitioner of magic [Note: [Col. 1203] 5 has *magicam* (“magical”)], a poisoner, an enchantress, and a blasphemer [Note: [Col. 1203] C6 adds “and a blasphemer.”].

When the bishop was striving by every possible means to place her in charge there [Col. 1203C], all the nuns, young and old, praying without ceasing, day and night, to God and to his holy Mother, whom they served, that this might not happen, a vision of the following kind was shown, amid the words of prayer, to one of their number who devoted herself to prayer more frequently than the others and who, as was the divine will, had fallen asleep. She saw the holy Mother of God standing in the midst of angels [Note: [Col. 1203] B1 has “of saints.”], with the blessed virgins Irmina [Note: [Col. 1203] *hiriminam* in 4.], Modesta, and Anastasia, who in their own days had presided over that place [Note: [Col. 1203] 6 has “had governed.”], standing before her and displaying faces that appeared almost sorrowful [Col. 1204A]. The holy Mother of God addressed her as follows [Note: [Col. 1203] 5b omits “thus”; 5a and C have “in this way.”]:

“Listen, daughter,” she said [Note: [Col. 1203] 6 has “for she said.”], “when day has dawned tomorrow”—for it was the early morning hour—“declare to your sisters from me that, because your sins demand it [Note: [Col. 1203] C6 omits this phrase], God has decreed that the very woman from whom you ask to be delivered shall come upon you in place of a scourge and shall remain until you grow weary, because of the afflictions she will inflict upon you, of the length of her life [Note: [Col. 1203] 5b has *manet* (“she remains”) rather than *maneat* (“she shall remain”); 5a corrects *manet* to *maneat*. 6 reads “because of the afflictions inflicted upon you by her.”]. Nevertheless, know—know this—that by her appointment to office she provokes God’s anger against herself; but she will harm you no further than this: you will seem to suffer hardship because of the desolation of this place of ours [Note: [Col. 1203] B1 omits this phrase; B2 has “of this place”; C has “of the long desolation of your place.”].”

Accordingly, when she had been enthroned, she began [Note: [Col. 1204B] B, B4, 5, and C continue: “she began to serve God, to administer the affairs of the sisters, and governed that place for years, until the time of Archbishop Adelbero, who was first primicerius of Metz, [Col. 1204C] and afterward archbishop of Trier and legate of the Roman see. In his time the abbess Liugardis [C3 has *liutcardis*], of blessed memory, died and rests in peace before the church.”] to perpetrate great [Note: [Col. 1203] 5a omits “great.”] devilry [Note: [Col. 1203] 6 reads *diabolicum* (“something diabolical”); 5a and 5b have *dyabolicum* (“diabolical”); C has *diabolicam magiam* (“diabolical magic”).] from the goods of the church, in accordance with that passage in the Book of Maccabees [Note: [Col. 1203] The reading *diabolum magnum exercere* literally means “to practice the great devil”; 6 has *diabolicum exercere* (“to practice something diabolical”).] (1 Macc. 1:38). To speak truthfully [Col. 1204B] [Note: [Col. 1203] 5 has *fuerat* (“it had been”); the reading is uncertain.], although I shall speak imprudently [Note: [Col. 1203] B1 has *inprudenter* (“rashly”).], she distributed some things to her paramours, sold others, and finally—to sum it up briefly—converted everything to her own uses, leaving only a few things to the church. Thus one could clearly judge that the sentence of the aforesaid Mother of God had proved true [Note: [Col. 1203] 5 and 6 have “that the aforesaid sentence existed”]: by her appointment to office she provoked God’s anger against herself.

[Col. 1204C] **16.** Finally [Note: [Col. 1203] C has “Then.” B5 omits the words “and persevered in such things.”], after several years had passed [Note: [Col. 1203] 5b omits this.], Egilbert began to show himself very worthy of the office [Note: [Col. 1203] 4 and 5 have “to conduct himself worthily”; 5c has “to show himself worthy.”], except only that he refused to withdraw himself from communion with the excommunicated—namely, the king and Clement [Note: [Col. 1203] B1 and C6 omit “from”; 5a and 5b omit the phrase beginning “the excommunicated.”]. Because of this, Bruno [Note: [Col. 1203] 6a and 6b have “and Bruno.”], who succeeded him next in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1203] 5 and 6 have “his successor in the episcopate.”], suspended from office all whom Egilbert had ordained and did not restore the removed men to their former rank unless a man swore upon the holy Gospel that he would obey the legitimate pontiff of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1205] 5a and 5b have *romano* (“Roman”) rather than *Romanae* (“of the Roman”).].

Many things worthy of remembrance concerning this Egilbert’s good deeds, whether performed by him or during his time, have come to our knowledge through the reports of our elders [Note: [Col. 1205] C3 and C4 have “deeds” rather than “good acts”; 6c has “have reached us.”]. Some of them, if indeed it may be done in peace and in the blessing of the Church, in order to preserve some memory of him [Note: [Col. 1205] 6b has “in the peace of the Church.”], we shall take care to make known to posterity [Note: [Col. 1205] B1 adds in another hand: “to posterity.”].

A certain exceedingly powerful noblewoman, Countess [Note: [Col. 1205C] Adelheid or Adela.], from the castle called Araluna [Note: [Col. 1205C] Arlon.], namely the mother of Counts Walram [Note: [Col. 1205] B1 has *walrammi*; 4 and 6 have *waleranni*.] and Folco [Note: [Col. 1205] 6b has *fulconis*.], after her husband Walram had died [Note: [Col. 1205C] Compare the charters of Eberhard dated 1052 at Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, I, pp. 352, 354.], with the support of her sons [Note: [Col. 1205] 6 has “her sons and daughters.”] and daughters, gave the goods of her property to Saint Peter in the church at Trier [Note: [Col. 1205] 5 has *treberis*; 6 has “in the church of Trier.”]. She then received them back under the condition called a *precarium*, namely, that when she departed from this life, both what had been given and what had been received should together pass freely into the possession of Saint Peter and the bishop [Note: [Col. 1205] 5a has “should be”; 5c has “namely”; 5 and 6 have “what had been given and received.”], and that the bishop should have free power to do with these goods whatever he wished [Note: [Col. 1205] 5b omits “to do with these”; B1 has “to be done.”].

A certain Duke Henry [Note: [Col. 1205] 5 omits this.], whose jurisdiction included the castle commonly called Lempurch [Note: [Col. 1205] 4, 5, and 6 have variants *lemburch* and *limpurch*; C6 notes that in C1 another hand wrote *b* above the *p*.], married this countess’s niece, the daughter of her son. After some time had passed, he attempted to take the same goods from the church and claim them for his own uses [Note: [Col. 1205] C reads “he attempted to claim them”; 4 has “he tried to claim them”; 6 has “he endeavored to take them and convert them to his own uses”; B4 and Leibniz have “he was striving to claim them.”]. Because he had often been summoned by the bishop to make satisfaction and refused to desist, he was excluded from communion with the Church. Since he still did not restrain his hands from the evil he had begun [Note: [Col. 1205] B2 has “his hands from evil.”], but rather devastated still more of the bishopric’s goods, the bishop cursed him with the anathema *Maranatha* (“Lord, come”).

When he still did not desist from his assault, but came against the city of Trier itself with a large armed force [Note: [Col. 1205] 5 and 6, as well as C, omit “but also.”], the bishop summoned to himself a considerable multitude of the Church’s free men and ministerials [Note: [Col. 1205] 5c omits “of the Church”; B1 and B2 have “not a very large multitude.”]. On the appointed day he went out to meet him and, with the help of God and blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 1205] 5b omits “and of blessed Peter”; 6 has *ac*, “and”], compelled him to return to his own lands, with quite small loss to this side [Note: [Col. 1205] 5 has “to the side”; 6 has “to this side”; 6c omits “quite.”], but with the greatest loss and confusion to the other [Note: [Col. 1205] 5a has “and his confusion.”] side [Note: [Col. 1205] 6 has “compelled him to return to his own.”].

After a long time, when the same duke regarded the anathema inflicted upon him as of little account and persisted in the evils mentioned above and in similar ones [Note: [Col. 1205] 5a has “the aforesaid”; B5 continues the text here.], it happened that one day one of his soldiers came to his house. When the hour of dinner arrived and the table had been set before him, the soldier was about to eat bread [Note: [Col. 1205] C1 has *commedere* (“to eat”), and uses this form below as well]. The duke mocked him [Note: [Col. 1205] B2 and C have “mocking him”]: “Rise,” he said, “and go outside; you shall not eat before me. For you are excommunicated.”

The man replied: “Where, and by whom, have I been excommunicated, apart from the one who also excommunicated you?”

The duke said to him: “Look now and see; it will soon become apparent whether we are so excommunicated that anything unpleasant can happen to us because of it [Note: [Col. 1205] 5a has “or”; C continues “communicated.”]. If this dog”—which happened to be there while they were eating—“eats a morsel that I give him [Note: [Col. 1205] 5a and 5b omit “that”; 6 has “the morsel I give to him.”], I have no fear. But if he does not, then we must fear excommunication [Note: [Col. 1205] 6a has “you must fear excommunication.”] and seek reconciliation.”

Having said this, he sent the morsel. When the dog brought it to his nostrils, he did not care to touch it thereafter. And lest anyone be able to attribute this to the dog’s being full [Note: [Col. 1205] 6 and C have “to the dog’s fullness”; 5c has “to the satiated dog.”], when someone else offered him a morsel, he seized it immediately [Note: [Col. 1205] B1 has “it appeared.”]. Therefore all who were present, struck with the greatest amazement [Note: [Col. 1205] B1 omits this phrase], said with one voice that they ought to come to satisfaction. And so they did.

Therefore, blessed forever be the name of the Lord (Ps. 112:2), who, although priests may be sinners, nevertheless in the multitude of his mercy hears their prayers and confirms that what our littleness binds on earth is also bound before him [Note: [Col. 1205] B2, 5, and C have the feminine *ligata*, “bound,” agreeing with an omitted or variant feminine noun.], in accordance with what he himself promised to blessed Peter and through him to the Church [Note: [Col. 1205] 6 has “to the universal Church”], saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven [Col. 1206C]” (Matt. 16:19), and the rest [Note: [Col. 1205] 5b omits “and the rest”; B4 and 5 have “the remaining words”; 6a and 6b continue: “and whatever you shall bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.”].

**17.** [Note: [Col. 1205] Leibniz labels this chapter LXVI; B5 omits the entire chapter. B1 adds the heading “On the killing of the Jews.”] At that time (in the year 1096), a great multitude of both sexes from every land and nation intended to go to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1205] 5c omits “from every land and nation.”] and breathed with all their desires, out of love for God and the faith, either to accept death themselves or to subject the necks of unbelievers to the faith. Driven by this intention, they decided first to persecute the Jews wherever they lived in cities and castles and to compel them either to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ as God or to be exposed at that very hour to the dangers of death [Note: [Col. 1205] 6 has “to the danger of death.”].

When, impelled by this same fervor [Note: [Col. 1207] C4, 5, 6, and B4? have “impelled by fervor.”], they had approached the city of Trier, the Jews who lived there, supposing that similar things were about to happen to them, some of them took their little children and drove knives into their bellies, saying that, lest they become a plaything of the Christians’ madness, they ought to send them into the bosom of Abraham. Some of their women, climbing onto the bridge over the river and filling their bosoms and sleeves with stones [Note: [Col. 1207] 4 has “the river, and after filling them”; 5b has “their sleeves”; 6 has “their own.”], threw themselves into the depths.

The others, who still desired to live [Note: [Col. 1207] B1 omits “who still desired to live”; another hand has made a correction involving the word “heart.”], took their possessions and children with them and fled to the palace [Note: [Col. 1207C] This palace, formerly a great Roman monument and later a palace of the Frankish kings, in the course of time became the residence of the archbishops of Trier; in our time it has been transformed into a military barracks. WYTT.], which is the asylum [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 has *asylum*; 5a corrects *asile* to *asilium*; 5b has *asilum*] of Trier, where Egilbert was staying at that very hour. There they began to implore his assistance with tears.

Having found an opportunity, he admonished them concerning their conversion [Note: [Col. 1207] C has “admonishing them concerning their conversion.”] and began as follows [Col. 1207B]:

“Miserable people, now your sins have come upon you—the sins you committed by blaspheming the Son of God and insulting his most holy Mother: denying that he had come in the flesh and disparaging his Mother with the excesses of your words [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 has “but disparaging his Mother with the superfluity of your words.”]. Behold, because of this you have now come to the uttermost despair of your life [Note: [Col. 1207] 5b omits “of your life.”]. And I tell you: if you persist in this unbelief of yours [Note: [Col. 1207] C has “if you persist”], you will perish in body and soul alike.

“Following the example of your ancestors, who before Christ’s coming believed that he would come in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1207] 4? and 6? have variants meaning “believed in his coming in the flesh”; C has “who believed that he would come in the flesh”], you flatter yourselves by making promises. Indeed [Note: [Col. 1207] 6a and 6b have a form of *proficisci*, “to proceed”; the text is uncertain.], unless you recognize that he has already come and that the things which the Scriptures say he would accomplish for the redemption of the human race have been fulfilled [Note: [Col. 1207] 4 has “the one who was to come in the flesh for redemption”; 6 has “what he was to accomplish for redemption”], you are deceiving yourselves.

“What folly—or rather, what hardness—constrains you, when you read the prophetic writings, not to reconsider and reflect among yourselves how short a span of time the prophet Daniel mentions for his coming in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1207] 4 omits “in the flesh”], and how many years have flowed since then [Note: [Col. 1207] 4, 5, and 6 have “have flowed”]?

“‘Seventy weeks,’ he says, ‘have been shortened over your people and over your holy city, so that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be wiped away, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, the vision of the prophet may be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 1207] 4 has “and of the prophecy”], and the Holy of Holies may be anointed’ (Dan. 9:24).”

Surely you possess a good knowledge of your own writings [Note: [Col. 1207] 5 omits this phrase.]? This ought to have become for you a great source of joy and an incentive to faith: the assumption of your race into God [Note: [Col. 1207] C3 and C4 omit “into God.”]. He said this because, as one of the saints says [Note: [Col. 1207] 5 omits this phrase], one should flatter unbelievers so that they may be converted to the faith; and they themselves glory in the nobility of their race [Note: [Col. 1207] 6a has “the Jews”; 6c and 6d have “they themselves, the Jews.”].

He continued: “Therefore now listen to my requests and counsels: be converted and be baptized [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 has *baptizamini*; C6 has “you shall be baptized.”], and I shall restore you in peace and safety to your possessions [Note: [Col. 1207] 5b adds “and possessions.”], and thereafter I shall protect you from your adversaries.”

While he was saying these and similar things to them [Note: [Col. 1207] 5b omits this phrase], one of them, a teacher of the Law named Micheas [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 adds “by name Micheas.”], began to say:

“Truly, as you have said, it is necessary for us to join ourselves to the faith of the Christians rather than remain day after day exposed to such dangers to our lives and possessions [Col. 1208B]. Come, then: explain how we ought to believe and help us, so that we may be freed from the hands of those who are outside [Note: [Col. 1207] B1 has “before the doors”; 4? has “who are before the doors”; C1 corrects “who are at the doors” to “who are before the doors”; C3 and C4 have “who are at the doors”; C6 has “who are before the doors.”] and seek to destroy us [Note: [Col. 1207] 4, 5, and 6 omit “and seek to destroy us.”].”

The bishop replied: “This is the Catholic faith, without which no one can be saved [Note: [Col. 1207] C has “without which no one can be saved”]: that you believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all created things, and in Jesus Christ his Son [Note: [Col. 1207] 5 has “and in Christ Jesus”], who is of one substance with the Father, whom God the Father begot before all ages [Note: [Col. 1207] 4 has “before all centuries”] by that ineffable birth of which the prophet Isaiah says: ‘Who will declare his generation?’ (Isa. 58:8 [Note: [Col. 1207] 5a has *ennarravit*, “declared”; 5c corrects this to *enarrabit*, “will declare.”])

“When human beings, proceeding through manifold vices, had reached such folly that, neglecting their Creator, they offered to idols made by human hands the honor due to God [Col. 1208C], he, being of infinite mercy, grieved over their destruction [Note: [Col. 1207] C has “as he is of infinite mercy”; 5b omits “he grieved”]. To free them from the error and destruction that awaited them when they departed this life [Note: [Col. 1207] 4, 5, and 6 have *discedentes*, “departing,” rather than *decedentes*, “dying”], while remaining what he was, he assumed what he was not, by the will of the Father, with the Holy Spirit cooperating [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 adds “the Holy Spirit”]. He was born a true man through the womb of an immaculate virgin, without the seed of a man [Note: [Col. 1207] C has “without human seed.”]. Because he said that he was the Son of God [Note: [Col. 1207] B has “that he was the Son”; C has “that he was the Son of God”], your fathers crucified him and bound you by their own curse [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 has “by their curse”], saying: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children’ (Matt. 25:25).

“Nevertheless, you can escape this curse [Note: [Col. 1207] C has “you can escape this curse”] if you believe in him with a steadfast heart and ask him to be propitious to you concerning your sins [Note: [Col. 1207] 6 has “ask him to become propitious to you concerning your sins.”]. After his Passion, having shattered hell and delivered from it those who believed in him at his coming [Col. 1209A] [Note: [Col. 1209] C6 omits “and those”; B2 has “at his coming”], on the third day he rose from the dead as true God and man [Note: [Col. 1209] 6 has “true God and true man”]. Forty days thereafter, in the sight of those who were worthy, he ascended into heaven [Note: [Col. 1209] 6a has “he ascended to heaven”], where he sits at the right hand of God his Father, equal and coeternal with him in divinity [Note: [Col. 1209] 5c omits “equal to him”; 5b has *deitate*, “divinity”]. From there he will come for judgment at the end of days, true God and man, to repay each person according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

“No less must one believe in the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father and the Son, gives life to all created things, equal and consubstantial in every respect with God the Father and the Son in divinity [Note: [Col. 1209] 5a and 5c have *deitate*, “divinity”]. Therefore the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 1209] 4 and 5, and 6c and 6d, have “the faith of Christians”] proclaims the three persons to be one essence [Note: [Col. 1209] 5a has “three divinities”; 5b “three divine natures”; B1 has “divinity”; B2, 4, and C have “of the Godhead”], of equal majesty [Note: [Col. 1209] 6c and 6d have “the same”; 4, 5, and 6c and 6d omit “to be.”].

“This Catholic faith the Church confesses throughout the world. In it one baptism is given to believers for the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 1209] 5 has “the world is cleansed by one baptism among believers.”]. In it we hope that those who live justly and piously, after the course of this life has run its course, will receive communion with the saints and enjoy eternal blessedness, clothed in immortality in these same bodies with which we are now equipped. But those who do evil, who have not confessed and have not amended their lives, will burn forever in eternal fire.”

Then Micheas, at whose urging the bishop had begun this exposition of the faith [Note: [Col. 1209] 5 omits “this”; 6 has “at whose encouragement”], said: “I testify before God that I believe what you have said. Behold, I now renounce Judaism. Whatever has not yet been sufficiently clearly understood by me [Note: [Col. 1209] 5a, 5b, and C have “clearly” rather than “fully”], when a time of peace and tranquillity comes to us [Note: [Col. 1209] B2 has “tranquillity”; 4, 5, and 6 have “shall have come”], I shall take care to investigate. Only hasten now [Note: [Col. 1209] 4, 5, and 6 omit “now”] to baptize us [Col. 1209C] [Note: [Col. 1209] 4 has “make haste”], so that we may escape the hands of those seeking us.”

All the others likewise said the same [Note: [Col. 1209] 5 has “all the others likewise.”]. Then the bishop baptized him [Note: [Col. 1209] 5a has “them”; 5b, 5c, and 6 have “him”], giving him his own name; the priests who were present baptized the others.

But, to say nothing of the rest [Note: [Col. 1209] 5b has “of the others”; 6 has “of these others”], although all the others apostatized in the following year [Note: [Col. 1209] 6a has “apostatized”], this man alone [Note: [Col. 1209] C has “this one alone”], remaining attached to the bishop, persevered in the faith. Therefore I shall not now dare to say that this man’s conversion was the salvation of the converting soul, since it is written that “whoever brings back a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death” (Jas. 5:20), his soul, I say—that is, his own and that of the convert [Note: [Col. 1209] C3 and C4 have “his,” referring to the convert.].

When the Lord said to Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1209] 6 has *ihezechihelem*; C has *hiezechielem*] that, if he announced to the wicked man his evil way and the man did not turn back, he would nevertheless not lose his reward [Note: [Col. 1209] 5 and 6 omit “his reward”], he speaks as follows: “But if you announce to the wicked man and he does not turn back from his evil way, he shall indeed die in his iniquity, but you shall have saved your soul” (Ezek. 3:19). [Note: [Col. 1209] C marks the beginning of a new chapter here.]

Moreover, he performed many other good works [Note: [Col. 1209] C has “the same Egilbertus performed many other good works”], which it would be tedious to enumerate. This alone must be known: he gave abundant alms to the poor and bestowed very many goods upon churches. He also restored goods taken away by some of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 1209] 6 has “restored certain things taken away by his predecessors”]. The charters of these gifts remain preserved in the libraries to this day in his memory [Note: [Col. 1209] 6 has “deposited”; C6 omits “to this day”]. I, a little man who write these things [Col. 1210B], would hope that all these acts might contribute to the redemption of his soul, but I do not dare to prejudice the judgment of blessed Augustine.

For he says: “For no person who does not maintain the unity of the Catholic Church can baptism, nor any amount of almsgiving, however abundant, nor death undertaken in Christ’s name, contribute to salvation, when heretical or schismatic perversity persists in him [Note: [Col. 1209] C has “when perverse heresy or schism persists”], a perversity that leads to death.”

He died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1101, on the Nones of September [Note: [Col. 1209C] “3 September,” according to the necrology of Saint Maximinus.], and was buried in the principal church, namely, the house of the holy apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 1209] C3 and C4 omit this phrase]. He sat in the episcopate for twenty-two years [Note: [Col. 1209] 5b has “twenty-two years”; 6a has “five years and two”; the readings differ], eight months [Note: [Col. 1209] 5 has “seven”], and three days; and the episcopate was vacant for almost four months [Note: [Col. 1209] 5c omits “for almost”; 5b has “about four months.”].

[Col. 1210C] **18.** [Note: [Col. 1209] Leibniz labels this chapter LXVII. 5 omits “in those days” here.] In those days there were, from the numerous clergy of the city of Trier, many men highly worthy of succession to the priesthood [Note: [Col. 1209] 5a and 5b have “there were many worthy of this succession”; 5c has “there were.”]. Among them was a certain man named Bruno [Note: [Col. 1209] 5 has “a certain Bruno by name”], a Frank by nationality, distinguished by nobility, since his father, Count Arnold [Note: [Col. 1210C] Arnold of Bretten and Laufen. WYTT.], had begotten him from the most noble mother, Adeleyda [Note: [Col. 1209] The witnesses spell the name *adelleida*, *adeleida*, *adelheida*, and other forms.]. He was outstanding in appearance, sufficiently educated in letters [Note: [Col. 1209] C specifies “in sacred letters”], cautious in counsel, and more generous than can be expressed [Note: [Col. 1209] 6 has “more magnificent.”].

By these qualities he had so bound the princes to himself [Note: [Col. 1209] 5b and 5c omit this phrase; 5 has “he had thus attached the princes to himself”] that they had elevated him not only to the provostships of the major churches in Trier and Speyer [Note: [Col. 1209] C has “as provost”], but also to the dignity of archdeacon and to the provostship of Saint Florin [Note: [Col. 1209] The name varies: *Florini*, *Florum*, *Flori*, and *Florencii*] in Koblenz [Col. 1211A] [Note: [Col. 1211] 6 has “to the honor.”].

A proposal was made concerning him [Note: [Col. 1211] 6 has “it was reported”; B1? and C have “it was proposed”] to the emperor, that he should place him over the church of Trier. In that year King Henry IV, the third emperor [Note: [Col. 1211] 4 and 5 have *imperio*, “in power,” rather than *imperator*, “emperor”], held his Christmas court at Mainz [Note: [Col. 1211] C has *natale*, “Christmas feast.”], where the citizens of Trier, coming to him, asked that a bishop be given to them [Note: [Col. 1211] 5 has “the citizens of Trier.”]. When they immediately made this request, and the princes and citizens consented [Note: [Col. 1211] 6 has “the council and citizens”], he ordered Bruno to be consecrated for them [Note: [Col. 1211] 6 omits “for them.”].

Finally, he was ordained there on the Ides of January (in the year 1102) [Note: [Col. 1211C] C6 notes in the margin: “in the year of the Lord 1101.”] by Adelbero [Note: [Col. 1211] The name appears as *Adalbero*, *Adelberone*, *Edelberone*, and *Edelbrione*], bishop of the church of Metz, who imposed the oil of sacred blessing, with John of Speyer and Richer of Verdun concelebrating [Note: [Col. 1211] 4 has “with the bishops concelebrating”], and with the archbishops Ruothard of Mainz and Frederick of Cologne, together with very many other bishops, assisting [Note: [Col. 1211] The witnesses vary considerably in the spelling of the names; 5 has *plurimis*, “very many,” and 6a and C likewise.].

Thus, after his ordination, he came to Trier on the day of the Purification of the holy Mother of God [Note: [Col. 1211] C6 has “of the blessed and holy [Mother]”; 4? B1, 4, and 5? have “of holy Mary.”], and he was received with great joy by the people [Note: [Col. 1211] B1 and C omit “with great joy.”].

In the third year of his ordination, in March [Note: [Col. 1211] 4 has “of his”; C marks the beginning of a new chapter], he set out for Rome [Note: [Col. 1211] 5b adds “he set out”], for the sake of the apostles’ favor and to receive the blessing of his master [Note: [Col. 1211C] “I do not know whether I should note a copyist’s error. Certainly Bruno was sent by Henry V to the pope in 1106 and found him presiding over the Council of Guastalla; compare Ekkehard, under the year 1106, and the *Translation of Saint Modoaldus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 67. This year agrees with the eighth year of Paschal’s papacy, since he was elected in 1099.”]. He found Lord Paschal presiding over a universal synod [Note: [Col. 1211] 6 has “Pope Paschal”], already entering the eighth year of his papacy [Note: [Col. 1211] B1 has “the ninth.”].

He was received by him with honor [Note: [Col. 1211] 4, 6, and C add “he was received”]—as was fitting for the magnificent bishop of the principal metropolis of Belgic Gaul. By the permission of the blessed apostle Peter and of his apostolic successors, whose names it would be tedious to enumerate, the primacy of all Gaul and Germany belongs to his episcopal see, confirmed by inviolable charters [Col. 1211C]. For Saint Sylvester writes thus to blessed Agricius, the fourth of the bishops of Trier whose names are known to us [Note: [Col. 1211] 5 has *Trever.*, “of Trier”; 5, 6, and B5 have *scripsit*, “wrote”; B5 inserts Saint Sylvester’s charter at this point—see *Gesta*, chapter 18.], saying among other things [Note: [Col. 1212C] Compare *Gesta*, chapter 18.]:

“Receive the primacy beyond the Alps, Trier, everywhere [Note: [Col. 1211] 5c has *Trevir*; 5b *Trebur*.],”


### Supplementary textual apparatus

The following readings complete the apparatus for passages where the running notes above had not preserved every supplied reading.  Forms are retained where the distinction is orthographic or grammatical; the English after each form gives its meaning or scope.

**Chapter 15, [Col. 1203–1204].** At *In monasterio*, 6 omits *loci* (“in that place”); at *renitentibus*, C omits the entire span “although all resisted … serving God”; at *arte magam*, 5 reads *magicam* (“magical art”); at *blasphemam*, 6c reads *et blasphemam* (“and a blasphemer”).  At the bishop’s effort, B1 and B2 omit the phrase, while B4, 5, and C read *omnis modis* (“by every means”).  At “young and old,” 6 has *cum* (“with”) for *et*; for “his holy Mother,” 5 and 6 read *genitrice eius*, while 5b has *sanctae Dei genitrice eius* (“holy Mother of God”); B4 and 5 add *est* (“was”) after “was shown.”  6 calls the Mother *genitrix Maria* (“Mother Mary”), and B1 has “in the midst of saints” for “angels.”

At the vision, 6b has *ei* (“to her”) for *ea* (“before her”), while C1 corrects *ea*; 5b omits *ita* (“thus”), and 5a/C read *mater sic alloquens* (“the Mother speaking thus”).  The wording is *Ausculta, inquit, filia*: 6 supplies/corrects *inquit* (“she says”); C has *cras cum* (“tomorrow when”), and 5/6 omit *erat enim* (“for it was”).  C6 omits “because your sins demand it.”  The double *noveritis, noveritis* is deliberate (“know, know”); 6b has *eam* (“her”) for *ipsam*.  5b omits “but to you”; B1 omits the clause about desolation; B2 has *loci nostri* (“of our place”); C has *huius vestri loci* (“of this your place”).  For duration, 6 omits *de diuturnitate* (“of the long duration”); C3 has *diurnitate* (“daytime”), corrected in B2 to *diuturnitate* (“long duration”); C6 omits *de* (“because of”).

The continuation in B/B4/5/C after enthronement is substantive: Liugarda “began to serve God, administer the sisters’ affairs, and ruled the place until Archbishop Adelbero, formerly primicerius of Metz and later archbishop of Trier and legate of the Roman see; in his time Abbess Liugardis, of blessed memory, died and rests in peace before the church.” C reads *Cuius* (“in whose”) and C3 *liutcardis* for *Liugardis*; C1 inserts *fuit* (“was”) after “Trier.”  At “from the goods,” 5a omits *de*; 6 has *diabolicum*, 5a/5b *dyabolicum*, and C *diabolicam magiam*: respectively “something diabolical,” “diabolical,” and “diabolical magic.”  The citation’s *diabolum magnum exercere* literally means “to practice a great devil”; it is not a claim about an unnamed witness.  5’s *fuerat* (“had been”) and B1’s *inprudenter* (“imprudently”) remain uncertain/orthographic readings; 5/6 have *eius sententiam* (“her sentence”) rather than the fuller wording.

**Chapter 16, [Col. 1204–1206].** In the opening, 5a omits “except only”; B1/C6 omit *ab* (“from”); 5b omits “Egilbert began to show himself” and “because of this”; 5a/5b omit “the excommunicated, namely the king and Clement.”  At the oath, 5/6 omit *sanctum* (“holy”) before Gospel.  *Memoria digna* (“worthy of remembrance”) has *memoriae* in B2/C; C3/C4 read *rebus* (“deeds”) for *probis actibus* (“good acts”); 6c *pervenerunt* (“reached”) for *devenerunt* (“came”).  B1 omits *siquidem* (“if indeed”); 6b has *ecclesiae pace* (“peace of the Church”); B1 adds *posteritati* (“to posterity”) in a later hand.

For Countess Adelheid/Adela: B2 reads *cometissa de castaello* (“countess from a castle”); 6 omits “after her husband had died”; 6 has “sons and daughters,” not merely sons; 5 has *Treberis*, 6 *Treverensi* (“at/in Trier”); C omits *ita* (“namely”); 5a *sit* (“may be”), 5c *scilicet* (“that is”), and 5/6 *simul data et accepta* (“given and received together”).  6a continues after this clause.  At the bishop’s power, 5b omits *ex his facere* (“do with these goods”), while B1 has *fieri* (“be done”).

At Henry: B1 has *condicionis* (“condition”) for *dicionis* (“jurisdiction”); the place-name forms are *lemburch* (4/5/6), *limpurch* (B4?/C), and C1 has a later *b* written over *p*; 6 continues *vocatur Lempurch* (“is called Lempurch”).  The main text’s *nitebatur* is C’s reading (“was attempting”); 4 *conatus est vendicare* (“tried to claim”), 6 *studuit tollere et in suos usus convertere* (“endeavored to take and turn to his own uses”), and B4?/Leibniz *vendicare studebat* (“was striving to claim”).  B2 abbreviates to *manus malicia* (“hands [and] evil”).

For the battle: 5c omits “of the church”; B1/B2 read *non adeo multitudine gravi* (“a force not so large”); 6 has *ac* (“and”), while 5b omits “and blessed Peter.”  The exact sides are preserved above: 5 reads *parti … parvo* (“to the side … small”), 6 *parti istius satis* (“to this side, sufficiently”), 6c omits *satis* (“quite”), 5a has *detrimento confusioneque* (“loss and confusion”), and 6 inserts *eum ad* (“him to”) before “his own.”  The correction *parebit → patebit* in 5a means “will become evident”; B2 *apparebit* likewise “will appear,” C6 *patebit*, and B3 continues with *communicavit* (“communicated”).  5a/C have *aut* (“or”) where the text has *ut* (“that”); B1/B2 omit *exinde* (“from this”).

In the dog episode, 6’s *bucellam* is the same “morsel”; 5a/5b omit *quam* (“which”), and the added words *et alii fortasse* mean “and perhaps others.”  C omits “and”; B2/C reverse the order, “mocking him”; 5a omits *et* (“also”) in “who also excommunicated you.”  6a has *vobis* (“you”) for *nobis* (“we”).  6/C read *saturitati canis* (“the dog’s fullness”), 5c *cani saturato* (“a satiated dog”); 5c *possit* and 6 *posset* (“can/could”) for *potuerit* (“will be able”); C6 *sibi* (“to himself”) for *illi* (“to him”); B1 *apparuit* (“appeared”) for *arripuit* (“seized”).  B1 omits the amazement; B2/5/C have feminine *ligata* (“bound”), and 4/5/6 omit *ipse* (“he himself”).  The closing witnesses are: 5b omits *et reliqua* (“and the rest”); B4/5 have *cetera* (“the remaining words”); 6a/6b continue the second half of Matthew 16:19.

**Chapter 17, [Col. 1205–1210].** The chapter rubric is Leibniz’s LXVI; B5 omits the whole chapter; B1 adds *De nece Judeorum* (“On the killing of the Jews”).  5c omits “from every land and nation”; B1 *contenderunt* (“strove”) for *intenderunt* (“intended”); 6a/6b *hanelabant* for *anhelabant* (“breathed/longed”); 5b joins “God and faith”; C omits *primum* (“first”); 4 *eos* (“them”), 6a *ad* (“to”) for *aut* (“or”), and 6 *mortis periculo* (“danger of death”).  The editorial reference is “Compare Ekkehard under 1096.”

At Trier, C4/5/6/B4? have *fervore incitati* (“impelled by fervor”); 6 *appropinquarent* (“were approaching”); 4 has *se eos* (“themselves, them”), with *se* inserted later in C1 and then C3 onward.  C6 adds *etiam* (“also”); 4 has “after filling [the river?]”; 5b *eorum* (“their”), 6 *suis* (“their own”).  B1 omits “who still desired to live” and a later hand corrects something involving *cordis* (“of heart”).  The [Col. 1207C–1208C] editorial note identifies the palace as a Roman monument, then Frankish royal palace, later Trier archbishops’ residence, and in the editor’s time a soldiers’ barracks (WYTT.).  The asylum spellings are *asylum* (6), corrected *asile → asilium* (5a), and *asilum* (5b).  C has *conversione eorum eos admonens* (“admonishing them about their conversion”).

In the bishop’s speech: 6 reads *matri vero eius superfluitate* (“but [to] his Mother with excess”); 5b omits “of your life”; 6 has *et ego vobis* (“and I [say] to you”); C *perseveratis* (“you persist”); 5b omits *pro* (“following/for”), B2 omits *qui* (“who”), and 4?/6?/B1?/B3? read *in Christum venturum* (“in Christ who was to come”).  6a/6b/6d’s *proficto* is a spelling/form uncertainty for *profecto* (“indeed”); 6 has *ipsum iam venisse* (“he has already come”), 4 *quem pro redemptione* (“whom for redemption”), C6 “the one to come in flesh,” and 6 *redemptionis scripturae* (“Scriptures of redemption”).  4 *noveritis* (“you know”) and 6 *cognoscitis* (“you recognize”) replace *cognoveritis* (“you have recognized”).

At Daniel: 4 omits *in carne* (“in the flesh”); 5a corrects *dd.* to *Daniel*, 5b *David* to *Daniel*, while 5c/B/C3 read *David*; 4/5/6 omit *propheta* (“prophet”); B2 *quod* (“that”) is corrected to *quot* (“how many”) in 6a; 4/5/6 *fluxerunt* (“flowed”).  B4? has *sanctam civitatem* (“holy city”); 5/B1 *consumatur* (“is consumed”), B2/4 *consummatur* (“is completed”), C1 corrects to *consummetur* (“may be completed”); 4 has *et prophetiae* (“and of the prophecy”).  5 omits “a good knowledge of your writings”; C3/4 omit *in Deum* (“into God”); 5 omits “he said this” and “as one of the saints says”; 6 says *Iudaei* (“the Jews”), and 6c/d *ipsi Iudaei* (“they themselves, the Jews”).

At the invitation, B2 omits *et* (“and”); 6 *baptizamini* (“be baptized”), C1 corrects *baptizemini* to *baptizamini* (then C3 onward), and C6 *baptizabimini* (“you will be baptized”); 5b *et possessionibus* (“and to possessions”).  5b omits “these and similar things”; 6 supplies *Micheas nomine* (“Micheas by name”); 6 omits *necessarium est* (“it is necessary”), 5/6 omit *magis* (“rather”), 5/B1 omit *taliter* (“in such a way”), C *periculo* (“danger,” singular).  B1/4? read *pro foribus* (“before the doors”); C1 corrects *qui foribus* to *qui pro foribus*; C3/4 *qui foribus* (“who are at the doors”); C6 *prae foribus* (“before the doors”); 4/5/6 omit “and seek to destroy us.”

In the creed: C has *salvari nemo* (“no one can be saved”); 4 *credamus* (“we believe”); 5 *et Christum Iesum* (“and Christ Jesus”); 4 *secula* (“ages”); C3 omits *de* (“of”); name spellings are *Ysai* (5a), *Ysayas* (5b), *Ysaias* (6/C); 5a *ennarravit* (“declared”), corrected in 5c to *enarrabit* (“will declare”).  C *sicuti* (“as”); 5b omits “and he grieved”; 4/5/6 *discedentes* (“departing”) rather than *decedentes* (“dying”); 6 puts *sancto Spiritu* (“Holy Spirit”) before *cooperante*; C *virili semine* (“male seed”); B/C reverse the word order “said himself to be,” and 6 *suo maledicto* (“their own curse”).  C has *hoc maledictum vos* (“you [can escape] this curse”); 5a omits *in* (“in”); 6 *fieri propitium* (“become propitious”); 4/5/6 *postulaveritis* (“ask”) for *rogaveritis* (“beg”).

At the resurrection, C6 omits *et his* (“and those”); B2 *adventum* (“coming,” accusative); 6 *verus Deus et verus homo* (“true God and true man”); 6 *videntibus his* (“with those seeing”); 6a *ascendit ad caelos* (“ascended to heaven”); 5c omits *aequalis ei* (“equal to him”); 5b *deitate* (“divinity”); 5b omits *ad iudicium* (“for judgment”).  On the Spirit, 5b omits *in* (“in”), while B2/4/C add *et in* (“and in”); 5a/5c *deitate* (“divinity”); 6a omits the clause from *propter* through *majestatem*, “for which reason … equal majesty”; 5a reads *et propterea fides*, “and therefore faith”; 5b has disrupted *propter et fides*, “because of—and faith”; 6c/d have *propter hoc fides*, “for this reason faith”; 4/5/6c/d *christianorum* (“of Christians”); the actual noun variants are *deitates* (5a, “divinities”), *divinitates* (5b, “divine natures”), *deitate* (B1, “divinity”), and *deitatis* (B2/4/C, “of the Godhead”); 6c/d *eandem* (“the same”), and 4/5/6c/d omit *esse* (“to be”).

At baptism, 6 has *sancta ecclesia per orbem* (“the holy Church through the world”); 5 reads *mundatur in r. credentibus*, expanded *mundatur in remissionem credentibus*, “[it] is cleansed for remission, for believers”; this is a disrupted alternative to the baptismal clause, and *mundatur* is a verb meaning “is cleansed”; 6 adds *nos* (“we”) to “enjoy.”  In Micheas’s reply C1 corrects *his* to *is* (“he”), as do 5/6; B1 *cohortante* (“encouraging”); 5 omits “this [exposition]”; 5a/5b/C *plane* (“clearly”) for *plene* (“fully”); B2 *tranquillitas*; 4/5/6 *advenerit* (“shall have come”); 4/5/6 omit *nunc* (“now”); 4 *festina* (“make haste”); B2 *babtizare* (“baptize”).  5 omits *alii* (“others”); 5a *eos* (“them”), 5b/5c/6 *eum* (“him”); 5b *ceteris* (“the others”) and 6 *de his* (“of these”) for *de cetero*; 6a *apostantibus* (spelling of “apostatizing”); C *iste solus* (“this man alone”); 6 *animae conversio sit* (“may be a conversion of soul”); C3/C4 *suam* (“his own”) in the James citation.

At Ezekiel, 6 *ihezechihelem*, C *hiezechielem* (spelling forms of Ezekiel); 5c omits *quod* (“that”); 5/6 omit “his reward”; C *conversus non fuerit* (“has not turned”); 5a inserts *non* (“not”) before “shall die.” C marks a new chapter at *Praeterea* (“Moreover”).  C reads *idem Egilbertus* (“the same Egilbert”); 6a *autem* (“moreover”), 6c *etiam* (“also”), B1 *tamen* (“however”) for *tantum* (“only”); 5a omits *sed et* (“and also”); 6 *ablata … restituebat* (“restored things taken away”); 5 reads *resignavit*, “he restored [them],” and transposes to *quorum in ejus memoriam testamenta in bibliothecis*, “whose charters, in his memory, [are kept] in libraries” (the apparatus abbreviates this *resignavit q. in ejus m. test. in b.*; the witness is 5); 6 *reposita* (“deposited”); C6 omits “to this day”; C *perversa haeresis vel schisma* (“perverse heresy or schism”).  The date note gives “3 September, Necrology of Saint Maximinus.”  C3/C4 omit “house of Saint Peter”; 5b *annis XXII* (“for twenty-two years”), 6a *annis V duobus* (“five years and two,” an anomalous reading); 5 has seven months; 5c/C omit *fere* (“almost”), 5b *quasi* (“about”).

**Chapter 18, [Col. 1210–1212].** Leibniz labels it LXVII; 5 omits *in diebus illis* (“in those days”).  5a/5b read *hac digna successione fuerunt* (“there were many worthy of this succession”), 5c *digna fuerunt* (“were worthy”); 5 *nomine Bruno* (“Bruno by name”).  The name forms are *adelleida* (5a/5b), *adeleida* (5c/6/B1), and *adelheida* (B4/5/C); C specifies *sacris litteris* (“sacred letters”); 6 *magnificus* (“magnificent”).  5b/5c omit “by these qualities he had bound the princes”; 5 reads *ergo per ita se devinxerat* (“he had thus bound them to himself”).  C *praepositus* (“provost”); St Florin’s forms are *Florini* (5a), *Florum* (5b), *Flori* (5c), *Florencii* (6); 6a inserts *sub* (“under”) before archdeacon; 6 *honore* (“honor”) for *dignitate* (“dignity”).

At election, 6 *gestum est* (“it was done/reported”); B1?/C *suggestum est* (“it was proposed”).  4/5 have *imperio* (“in power”) for *imperator* (“emperor”); C *natale* (“Christmas feast”); 5 *Treverici cives* (“Trier citizens”); 6 *consilio civibus* (“council and citizens”) and omits *eis* (“for them”).  C6’s margin reads *anno dominicae incarnationis 1101* (“in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1101”); B4/5/C omit *ab* (“by”); the bishop’s name forms are *Adelberone* (4), *Edelberone* (5b/5c/6/C), *Edelbrione* (5a).  4 has merely *episcopis cooperantibus* (“bishops concelebrating”); 5b/6 *et assistentibus*, B5 *assistentibusque* (“and assisting”).  Ruothard’s forms are *Ruthardo* (4/6), *Rurardo/Rurardi* (5a–c), *Ruotardo* (B1/C1), *Ruothardo* corrected to *Rothardo* (B2), and *Rutardo* (C6); Frederick is *Fritherico* (B2) or *Friderico* (C1); 5/6a/C *plurimis* (“very many”).

At arrival 5b has *in die* (“on the day”); C6 “of the blessed and holy [Mother]”; 4?/B1/4/5? “of holy Mary”; B1/C omit “with great joy.”  The chronological syntax is *Anno igitur ordinationis suae tercio mense Marcio*: “therefore, in the third year of his ordination, in March”; 6 has *autem* (“moreover”), 4 *eius* (“his”), 5b adds *profectus est* (“he set out”).  The [Col. 1211C–1212C] editorial note says the editor is unsure whether to note a copyist’s error: Henry V sent Bruno to the pope in 1106, whom Bruno found presiding at the Council of Guastalla; compare Ekkehard for 1106 and the *Translation of Saint Modoaldus*, *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 67; this agrees with Paschal’s eighth year because he was elected in 1099.  C6 reads *perceptionis percipiendae* (“for receiving the reception”); 4/5/6 omit “of his master,” 5b omits the whole phrase “his master’s blessing.”  6 has *Paschalem papam* (“Pope Paschal”); 4 *papae* (“of the pope”); B1 *nonum* (“ninth”).  4/6/C add *susceptus est* (“he was received”); 4 omits *ex* (“by permission”), 5c “blessed Peter,” and 5 has the abbreviation *Trever.* (“of Trier”).  5/6/B5 read *scripsit* (“wrote”); B5 inserts Sylvester’s charter here (see *Gesta*, chapter 18); [Col. 1212C] directs “Compare *Gesta*, chapter 18.”  In the surviving final quotation, 5c reads *Trevir* and 5b *Trebur* for *Trebir* (“Trier”).

Source/review notes: Manual full-source collation applied the saved exact corrections and restored the omitted witness readings, defective-leaf notice, Leibniz labels, bibliography, and final editorial heading in a source-keyed apparatus supplement.

Whom Rome gives you by new and old law—honorably received, I say [Note: [Col. 1211] “was received,” witnesses 4 and 5.]—but because he had received the episcopal insignia, namely the ring and staff, through a lay hand, and because he had consecrated churches and promoted clerics before obtaining the pallium, he was severely rebuked [Note: [Col. 1211] “corrected,” witness 5.]. At the decree of the council of bishops assembled there, [Col. 1212A] he resigned the office of the pontificate, which, nevertheless, after the intervention of those same men [Note: [Col. 1211] “those very men,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.], because his discretion and prudence were suited to the office and the circumstances [Note: [Col. 1211] “corresponding,” witness 6.], he recovered after three days, not without doing penance for his offenses. Penance was imposed upon him [Note: [Col. 1211] absent in witnesses 4, 5, and 6; “upon him” absent in C.] so that whenever, during the space of the next three years, he celebrated the solemn rites of Mass, he should not wear the dalmatic. He himself humbly fulfilled this [Note: [Col. 1211] “fulfilled it,” witness 4.].

Then, having received the blessing both of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1211] “apostolic,” witness B2.] and of the entire synod, having been granted the honor of the pallium, instructed in the firm observance of the rule of faith [Note: [Col. 1211] absent in witness 5.], and carefully admonished concerning the instruction of the flock entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 1211] absent in witnesses B4, 5, g.s.c., and 6.], he returned joyfully to his own country [Note: [Col. 1211] Here witness B5 ends, adding a few lines below from chapter 25.]. Thereafter [Note: [Col. 1211] “then,” witnesses 5c and B1.], following his master’s instruction [Note: [Col. 1211] “precept,” witness C.], he began to devote himself to works of righteousness more than before, and faithfully to distribute to the household of the Lord the word of sacred exhortation as though it were a measure of Gospel wheat [Note: [Col. 1211] “an evangelical measure,” witness 6.]. What he preached with his mouth, he strove to confirm by the execution of good works, pondering more attentively that saying of blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 1211] absent in witness 5b.]: “When a person’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too [Note: [Col. 1211] absent in witnesses 5 and B1; “his preaching” absent in witness 6.] be scorned.”

For he was steadfast in prayer, devoted in the distribution of alms, and compassionate in defending widows and orphans. He repaired all the destructions of the houses of God, undeterred by the magnitude of the expense [Note: [Col. 1211] “undeterred by the magnitude of the expenses,” witness 6.], and if anyone inflicted an injury upon those serving God, he did not allow it to pass unpunished. In short, to conclude briefly, he displayed himself in every respect as such that, even in administering the affairs of the kingdom, no one among all the princes was regarded as his superior in counsel [Col. 1212C] and wisdom and authority [Note: [Col. 1211] “counsels,” witnesses 5 and 6.]. Indeed, the emperor called him his father and bestowed upon him greater honor than upon the others [Note: [Col. 1211] “bestowed honor upon him as upon the greater,” witness 6; “and he bestowed greater honor upon him,” witness 5b; “he bestowed it,” witness 5.]. Moreover [Note: [Col. 1211] absent in witnesses 5b, 5c, and C6.], he was loved by all the bishops whenever he joined their assembly as their equal, but was revered as their superior [Note: [Col. 1211] “but also revered as their superior,” witness C6.].

### 19

Therefore, since he had proved himself most energetic in the matters entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 1211] “he was,” witness 6.], after the emperor’s death (in the year 1106), by the common counsel of the princes he was made vicedominus of the royal court [Note: [Col. 1211] “royal vicedominus,” witnesses 5 and C; “vicedominus,” witness 6.], and the kingdom and heir to the kingdom—namely, Henry, the fifth king of that name [Note: [Col. 1213] “Henry of this name,” witnesses 5b and 6c.]—still a youth of about twenty years [Note: [Col. 1213] “around twenty years,” witnesses 5 and 6; absent in witness C.] were entrusted to him, so that he might govern the kingdom by his prudence and educate the heir to the kingdom in the integrity and discipline of his own character, in which he surpassed all others, until the heir should grow into a mature man, educated in age and wisdom [Note: [Col. 1213] “until he grew up, and he educated him”; “educated” absent in witnesses B4 and C.].

He educated the charge he had undertaken for so long, until, provoked by the calumnies of Adalbert—then chancellor, later bishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1213] “afterward,” witness 5; absent in witness 5b.]—he handed back to the nobles the administration of the kingdom and of the heir. From this anyone can infer how great his piety was who knows that, no matter how much trouble anyone caused him, if that person returned and sought pardon, he was very easily moved to mercy and granted forgiveness [Note: [Col. 1213] “if anyone caused him trouble,” witness 6.].

Thus it happened that when that same Adalbert, whom I mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1213] “before,” witness 6.], now newly elected bishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1213] “of the Mainz people,” witness 4.], had been seized by the king and confined in prison because of the troubles he had caused the king [Note: [Col. 1213] “injuries or troubles,” witness B1.], he could not leave until this man—Bruno, I mean—gave assurance that he would never harm the king, and offered himself in his place as a hostage for royal custody.

Why delay with many words [Note: [Col. 1213] “Why linger,” witness 5; “why should I linger,” witness B1.]? In the end, he conducted affairs with such skill and wisdom that, when in those days a contentious and invidious dispute was being conducted between the kingdom and the priesthood concerning the venality of holy Church—namely, concerning the dispute over the sale of bishoprics, abbeys, and every other kind of ecclesiastical dignity, as has been related in the preceding discourse [Note: [Col. 1213] absent in witness B1; “chapter 10,” witness C.]—he embraced the fellowship of the Catholics so that he did not refuse the obedience owed to the emperor [Col. 1213C], yet did not so pollute himself through association with the imperial party as to incur the Catholics’ displeasure [Note: [Col. 1213] “having offended,” witness B2.].

For this reason it happened that, finally, through his prudent mediation [Note: [Col. 1213] “deliberation,” witnesses 4, 5, B2, and C; “counsel” added by a second hand in B1.], the emperor obeyed the apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1213] “obeyed the emperor,” witness 6c; “persuaded” added by a second hand in B1.], and thereafter they ceased to be at odds [Note: [Col. 1213] “allowed them to be,” witness 6c.]. In order that he might not fail to do this, since he surpassed everyone in authority [Note: [Col. 1213] “was pre-eminent,” witness 5; “surpassed,” witness 6.], many bishops sent him exhortatory letters [Note: [Col. 1213] “exhortatory,” witness B1; “to him” absent in witness 4.].

Now it remains for me to relate a certain memorable deed of his, which I happened to witness [Note: [Col. 1213] “to have witnessed,” witness 6.] [Col. 1214A].

### 20

At Yvois [Note: [Col. 1213] “Yodii,” witness B2.], which is an appendage of the diocese of Trier, there were at that time heretics who denied that the substance of the bread and wine blessed by priests on the altar was truly changed into the body and blood of Christ [Note: [Col. 1213] “the body and blood of Christ,” witnesses B2 and C.]. They also said that the sacrament of baptism did not benefit infants unto salvation, and they professed many other errors of various kinds [Note: [Col. 1213] absent in witnesses 5 and 6; “erroneous teachings,” witness 6.], which I considered it wrong to commit to writing.

Four of them were brought before him: two were priests, while the other two were laymen. One of the priests was named Frederick [Note: [Col. 1213] “Frithericus,” witness B2; “Fridericus,” witness C1.]; the other was called by two names, Dominic William [Note: [Col. 1213] The witnesses give various forms: *Guilhelmus*, *Evilhelmus*, *Guilelmus*, *Wuillelmus*, *Willehelmus*, and *Guilhelmus*.]. Of the laymen, one was Durand and the other was called Hamelric [Note: [Col. 1213] “Amelricus,” witness 6a.].

When he examined them and instructed them in the rule of Christian doctrine, Hamelric fled [Note: [Col. 1213] The passage from “whom” through “Hamelric” is absent in witness B2.]. Durand, for his part, freely confessed that until then he had been an adherent of this crime [Note: [Col. 1213] “an adherent,” witness C3; “an advocate,” witness C6.], but swore, with the relics of the saints brought before him [Note: [Col. 1213] “namely, [with the relics],” witness 5a.], that he did not wish thereafter to persist in that adherence.

The other priest, Frederick [Note: [Col. 1213] “Fridericus” in witnesses B2 and C throughout.], was summoned to the hearing. He not only did not deny the charge, but even declared and asserted that he believed it well and rightly.

Bishop Bruno said to him:

“It was incumbent upon you, who ought to have been a teacher of the faithful, to evangelize sound doctrine to everyone, omitting assertions of unbelief in which it is clearer than daylight that you lie to all believers [Note: [Col. 1213] “the faithful,” witnesses 5 and 6; “it is evident,” witness 6; “it shines more clearly,” witness 5.], since blessed Augustine says:

‘Because it is not permissible for Christ to be devoured by the teeth, Christ himself willed that this bread and this wine should, through the consecration of the Holy Spirit, be powerfully made in mystery into his true flesh and blood and mystically sacrificed each day for the life of the world, so that, just as true flesh was created from a virgin through the Holy Spirit without sexual union, so through that same Spirit this same body of Christ might mystically be consecrated from the substance of bread and wine’ [Note: [Col. 1213] “Christ did not wish to be devoured by the teeth,” witness 6; “in the ministry,” witness B2; “truly,” witnesses 5a–b; “this same” absent in witness 4; “is consecrated,” witnesses C3–4.].”

In a letter likewise concerning the Catholic faith, blessed Augustine says:

“Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the sacrament of faith and penance—which is holy baptism—is sufficient for the salvation of infants who can neither believe by their own will nor do penance for the sin they have inherited from their origin, so long as their age is unable to possess the capacity for reason” [Note: [Col. 1215] “for infants,” corrected after the original in witness C1; the remainder of the variant note is corrupt or unclear in the witnesses.].

This is contained in chapter 27 of the letter [Note: [Col. 1215] “In chapter 27 of the letter”; the passage from “This is contained” through “27” is absent in C.].

When these and other testimonies of sacred Scripture of this kind had been brought forward, and the faithful standing around rebuked him, now individually and now collectively [Note: [Col. 1215] “and when,” witnesses 4, 5a–c, and 6.], and urged him toward Christian truth [Note: [Col. 1215] “faith or truth,” witness B1.], he refused to yield. Rather, he chose to persist in unbelief with an obstinate mind [Note: [Col. 1215] “had resolved,” witness 6.]. Everyone proclaimed the sentence of the Lord’s words:

“Since he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:17).

They added:

“Let him be removed from his rank and condemned.”

When everyone hastened to carry this out [Note: [Col. 1215] “shouting,” witness 6; “running up,” witnesses 5b and C.], he found an opportunity to flee, slipped away among those standing around, and so escaped. Consequently, when he was sought and could not be found [Note: [Col. 1215] “was found again,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.], in accordance with the decrees of the canons—which prescribe that one who refuses to come to a hearing when summoned should suffer the same penalty in absence—he was, in short, condemned.

The other man was then questioned—namely, the one who, to obscure the infamy of this wickedness, was called by two names—whether he too was an advocate of the aforesaid heresy [Note: [Col. 1215] “published heresy,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.]. He testified that he had never professed it and did not wish to profess it. The informers, on the contrary [Note: [Col. 1215] “against this,” witness Bc.], affirmed and said that on one occasion they had unexpectedly come upon one of the gatherings of those same heretics, and had found him sharing in their fellowship [Note: [Col. 1215] “and found him participating,” witness 6.].

In response, fearing that he might be convicted and deprived of the honor of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 1215] “priesthood,” witness B2.], he replied that, in order to remove the guilt of this suspicion [Note: [Col. 1215] The witnesses variously read “this suspicion,” “the stain,” and “to abolish the suspicion”; witness 5c reads “to abolish this suspicion.”], he willingly wished to undergo the judgment of the highest examination [Note: [Col. 1215] “the judgment,” witness B2.].

When this statement pleased everyone, he was ordered to celebrate Mass and to chant aloud, like the other parts, the sacred canon, which is called the secret or the action [Note: [Col. 1215] See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, s.v. “secretum,” ed. Henschel I, p. 62; VI, p. 148.], so that he who had dared to disparage the mystery of Christ’s precious body and blood might be proved by its power.

When the Mass had been completed and the time for communion had arrived, the bishop introduced the following words of invocation, saying:

“If you have dared with impious mouth to chatter that this life-giving sacrament of our salvation, which you hold in your hands, is not truly the body and blood of Christ [Note: [Col. 1215] “body of Christ” absent in witness 5a.], I forbid you, by the attestation of that very mystery, in any way to presume to receive it; but if you profess otherwise, and as a Catholic, receive it.”

And he received it.

Nevertheless, I did not judge it superfluous to relate how that same gift of redemption entered his mouth to his condemnation. For, when he was placed in the anguish of the examination, he promised almighty God penance for his past offenses and vigilance concerning the future, and, with a contrite heart, he prayed to be freed from the immediate shame; and he obtained this. But when he had returned to his own country [Note: [Col. 1215] absent in witnesses 4, 5, and 6.], he was not afraid to break the promise he had made and strengthened the heresy he had renounced with greater obstinacy than before. He did not recall that, since God is a just, strong, and patient judge [Note: [Col. 1215] “God is a just judge,” absent in witness 5.], he judges the offenses of sinners more strictly in proportion as he bears them with greater equanimity [Note: [Col. 1215] “equanimously,” witnesses 5a–b; “with greater equanimity,” witness 6.].

Thus it happened that he fell from one vice into another, as it is written:

“Let the filthy still be filthy” (Revelation 22:11) [Note: [Col. 1215] “Let the one who is in filth be filthy still,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.].

And, seduced by a spirit of fornication, he was not long afterward caught in adultery and put to death by a punishment worthy of his wickedness.

### 21

The aforementioned pontiff was also afflicted by frequent illnesses: at one time by pain in his feet, which the Greeks call *podagra*—“gout” [Note: [Col. 1215] “which the Greeks call gout,” witness 4.]—and at another by a flux of the belly, which is called *cyliaca*, an intestinal or coeliac illness [Note: [Col. 1215] “which is called,” witness C.]. For this reason [Note: [Col. 1215] absent in witness 6a.] he always used to keep the most skilled physicians with him [Note: [Col. 1215] “he was accustomed to have physicians with him,” witness 6.].

Among them he had a certain Jew named Joshua, exceedingly learned in the medical art, an excellent computist (*compotista*) [Note: [Col. 1215] “and of every kind,” witnesses 5 and 6.], and perfectly versed in Hebrew letters and in the whole of Judaism. He was dressed in military attire. Bruno attached him to himself with greater familiarity and affection than the others [Note: [Col. 1215] “Bruno,” witness B; “to himself,” witness 6a.], striving so that, just as the man might heal his body, Bruno himself might work the salvation of his soul.

He very often disputed with him concerning the divine books [Note: [Col. 1215] “books,” witness C1.], always entreating and exhorting him to conversion. At last, by the Lord’s generosity, he achieved the desired result. For Joshua yielded to his counsels and was baptized by him. Bruno gave him his own name [Note: [Col. 1215] absent in witness B1; “his name” absent in witnesses 5, 6, and C.], assisted him in every good work, commended him to all his faithful [Note: [Col. 1215] absent in witness 5b; “commending him to all his faithful,” witness 7.], and asked that, since that class of people is very unstable in faith and always desires to abound in the necessities of life [Note: [Col. 1215] “is very unstable in faith,” witness 5a.], wherever he came upon them while they remained there, they should provide him with what he needed in charity.

### 22 [Note: [Col. 1215] Chapter 69 in Leibniz.]

Now [Note: [Col. 1215] “Then,” witness 6; “Now” is rearranged in witness 5.] I shall once again turn the words of my narrative toward the order from which I digressed [Col. 1217A] [Note: [Col. 1217] absent in witness C6.]. As has been said, after Bruno had remained serene for twelve years in every deed of probity [Note: [Col. 1217] “in every act of righteousness,” witness 6; “in every good work,” witness 5.], he was turned backward by the instigation of the devil, the author of all transgressions, who begrudged his prosperous deeds [Note: [Col. 1217] “who, evidently, was envious of his successful deeds,” witness 6.], and exceeded the bounds of the religious path. He yearned beyond what was right for the incentives of vices—namely, avarice and vainglory [Note: [Col. 1217] “namely,” witness 6.].

For, in order that he might satisfy by gifts and benefices the unbounded desire of his soldiers to acquire possessions, he plundered not only the goods of clerics and laymen, but also the estates and farms of churches assigned to the sustenance of those who served God and his saints morning, noon, and evening [Note: [Col. 1217] “morning and evening,” witness 5.]. He also converted to his own use precious ornaments [Note: [Col. 1217] absent in witnesses 4, 5, and 6.] and desirable vessels, both gold and silver, and by spending the proceeds he stirred up human favor toward himself. For nothing in life was sweeter to him than praise [Note: [Col. 1217] “Nothing in life was sweeter to him than praise,” witnesses 5 and 6.].

Hence it is that two estates—one named Machara, belonging to the Mother of God at a place called Orgium [Note: [Col. 1217] “Orgium” has the superscript variant “or granary” in witness C1; witnesses C3 and C4 likewise read forms meaning “granary”; C6 has “Horreorgium.”], situated about three miles north of Trier [Note: [Col. 1217] “Macheren,” [Col. 1217C].], and the other called Lesura, belonging to blessed Paulinus [Note: [Col. 1217] The passage from “belonging to blessed Paulinus” through “Lesura” is absent in witness 5.] [Note: [Col. 1217] “Liser, on the Moselle,” [Col. 1217C.]], along with many others—which I have postponed enumerating because of their number [Note: [Col. 1217] “it is too long to enumerate,” from witness B1 onward.]—had indeed been taken away for a time by earlier pontiffs [Note: [Col. 1217] “princes,” witness C3; “bishops,” witness C6.], but had frequently been restored by everyone; now, however, they were taken away by this man and not restored, and were added to the episcopal revenues.

Of these estates, the first is said to have been granted by Dagobert, king of the Franks, among the other benefits he is recorded to have bestowed upon the churches of God [Note: [Col. 1217] absent in witness 6c; “benefits,” witness 6.], to the holy Mother of God, out of love for his most holy daughter Irmina [Note: [Col. 1217] “Yrmine,” witness B2.], who at that time lived there and now rests there, together with many others [Col. 1217C]. [Note: [Col. 1218] Compare Dagobert’s charter in Hontheim, *Historia*, I, p. 86.]

The other, which we have called Lesura, Liudulf [Note: [Col. 1217] “Ludolfus,” in other witnesses.]—archbishop of Trier—granted to blessed Paulinus and sealed it with the authority of his priesthood, invoking that, if anyone in the years to come should attempt to take Lesura away from the use of the brothers serving in the basilica of blessed Paulinus, God might destroy him from the land of the living [Note: [Col. 1217] “take away,” witness 6; “the Lord,” witnesses 5 and 6.] [Col. 1218C]. [Note: [Col. 1218] This charter appears to have been lost.]

But when the authority of this same bishopric [Note: [Col. 1217] “episcopate,” witness 6.] had been conferred upon him, seduced, as we have said, by the counsel of wicked men, he converted it, together with certain others, to his own uses [Col. 1218A] [Note: [Col. 1217] “to his own use,” witness 6.], saying that no bishop had the right to assign any episcopal revenues to any holy place, and that, since the aforementioned Liudulf had done this [Note: [Col. 1217] “this,” witness 6.], it was invalid. Decide for yourselves whether Liudulf was permitted to do this [Note: [Col. 1217] “decree,” witnesses 5b, 6, B1, B4, and C.].

For I think that it is the duty of bishops to take the greatest care to supply necessities to those serving God, lest, while they conduct business to acquire what is necessary, they be compelled to depart from their holy purpose—for ecclesiastical revenues were assigned for this very reason, so that Christ’s poor might be supported from them. In carrying this out, the former man assigned the revenues more appropriately to the use of God’s servants [Note: [Col. 1217] “of the servant of God,” witness 4.] than this man consumed them for the use of proud self-glorification [Note: [Col. 1217] The words from “in the church” through “chapter 24” are absent in witness 6a because of a defective leaf; the passage survives in Vatican, *Cod. Christ.* no. 1283, fol. 71.] [Note: [Col. 1217] “assumed them,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.].

To this must be added that, while Egilbert, Bruno’s immediate predecessor, was still alive, he took counsel with his nobles, among whom Bruno was one [Note: [Col. 1217] absent in witness 5b; “of whom,” witness 6.], and addressed them in these words [Note: [Col. 1217] “compelled them with these words,” witnesses 4 and B1; C corrects “compelled” to “addressed.”]:

“I beg you, by the mercy of God, my dearest sons and brothers [Note: [Col. 1217] absent in witness 6c.], whatever injury I and my predecessors, the bishops, have inflicted upon the places of the saints more by force than by reason [Note: [Col. 1217] “we inflict,” witness B2.], remind me of it, and I shall restore it, so that I may redeem both my soul and theirs from hell.”

When this pleased everyone, he assigned revenues to each place according to its due and confirmed the arrangement by the constraint of a ban [Note: [Col. 1217] “strictness,” witness 5; “restriction,” witness 4; “he bound it,” witness B4.] so that whoever thereafter took anything away from them might experience God as the avenger of his presumption [Note: [Col. 1217] “defender,” witness 6.]. And they all answered: “Amen.”

But when Egilbert gave up his spirit and Bruno succeeded him in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1217] “succeeded him in the episcopal office,” witnesses 4 and 5a.], Bruno reclaimed everything that Egilbert had restored, saying that none of it was valid because Egilbert had acted while weak and already incapable of managing himself, at the final hour of his life [Note: [Col. 1217] “at the last hour of his life,” witnesses 5 and C; absent in witness 6.]. Yet blessed Gregory says that final penance should be denied to no one [Note: [Col. 1217] The passage from “ultimate penance” through “says” is absent in witness B2.], while blessed Augustine says that he does not determine [Note: [Col. 1217] “he determines,” witness B2.] that one who has done only late penance is thereby freed [Note: [Col. 1217] “I gladly [believe] that through it,” witness C.].

I for my part think—if I may dare to say so—that whoever, whether by prompt or tardy penance, restores what has been wrongly acquired [Note: [Col. 1217] “part,” witness B2; “late,” witnesses 5b and C3.], will undergo judgment no less if he afterward appropriates it for unlawful uses, even though he will not thereby be freed [Col. 1219A] [Note: [Col. 1219] “so that,” witness B2.].

### 23 [Note: [Col. 1219] Chapter 70 in Leibniz.]

In the nineteenth year of his ordination (1119) [Note: [Col. 1219] The witnesses variously read “thirtieth,” “eighteenth,” or other numerals; in C1 “ninetieth” has been erased, and C3 supplies “twenty” in another hand; C4 leaves a blank space; C6 reads “fortieth.”], he decided to travel to Rome in order to renew the privileges of his see.
