He was indignant at the arrogance of the aforementioned Adalbert, bishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1219] “bishop” absent in witness 5b.], who was proudly exalting himself on account of the legation of the Roman see granted to him [Note: [Col. 1219] “and proudly,” witness 5c.], especially since, by the grant of earlier apostolic authorities, the bishop of Trier ought to obey no one except the apostolic authority alone or someone sent for the occasion from his side [Note: [Col. 1219] “sent at his side for the present,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.], as Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, recalls in his letter addressed to Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1219] “pope” corrected from “papa” in witness 5a; “pope,” witness B4.] [Col. 1219C; Note: The reference is to the letter mentioned above, praised in *Gesta*, chapter 24.], saying:

“The church of Reims never had a primate, except the Roman pontiff [Col. 1219B] [Note: [Col. 1219] “primacy,” witnesses B2 and C6.], except for the time when, after its bishop had been expelled by the violence of the tyrant Milo in the time of Prince Charles, though without any fault of his own [Note: [Col. 1219] “after he had been cast out,” witnesses 5 and 6; “from him,” witness 6.], and the church was left without a shepherd, it was entrusted for a time to Boniface, legate of the apostolic see, just as the church of Trier was.”

Moreover, at that time a certain Stephen presided over the church of Metz, the nephew through his sister of Pope Calixtus [Note: [Col. 1219] The witnesses variously spell the name *Calixtus*, *Kalistus*, *Calistus*, and *Kalistus* throughout.]. His aforementioned uncle had granted him the right to appear wearing the pallium at the celebration of Masses [Note: [Col. 1219] “to walk,” witness 6b.], while the full authority of the metropolitan church of Trier remained intact [Note: [Col. 1219] “with the authority remaining in the metropolitan,” witness 5c.].

Delighted by the honor of the pallium and, as though confident in the favor of the relationship mentioned above, he exalted himself beyond what was proper. He strove by every means, if somehow he could, to oppress the church of Trier and place his own before it [Note: [Col. 1219] Witness 4 reads the forms “to oppress … to put before … to make.”], and to make his own church a metropolitan see [Col. 1219C], hoping that Calixtus would approve whatever he began [Note: [Col. 1219] “Pope Calixtus,” witness 4.].

We infer this from the fact that whenever he had been summoned by the metropolitan, so that, as is customary for suffragan bishops, he might subscribe to obedience and subjection to the metropolitan church, he scorned to come, saying that his predecessors too had at some time been archbishops [Note: [Col. 1219] “saying that,” witness C; “whenever,” witness C.]. No authority of any writing confirms or declares this [Note: [Col. 1219] absent in witness B2; “a firm proof,” witness B1.]. Only five bishops of Metz are reported to have used the pallium [Col. 1219C] [Note: [Col. 1219] Compare *Gesta*, chapter 27.], and this man is counted as the sixth, while subjection to the metropolitan was nevertheless preserved in every respect.

But not all who use the pallium are archbishops—only those whose metropolitan see presides over other cities and bishops subject to it.

When, therefore, for the reasons mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1219] “for the reasons mentioned,” witness 6.], the aforementioned Bruno was traveling toward Rome and had proceeded as far as Autun [Note: [Col. 1219] The witnesses spell the name variously; [Col. 1220C] identifies the place as Autun.], Pope Calixtus met him there, received him as a friend [Note: [Col. 1219] “and received him as a friend,” witness 6.], and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with him in the same place (in the year 1119).

When the festive days had passed, they proceeded together to Cluny. There Bruno disclosed the reasons for his journey; after producing the privileges of his see before the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1219] The words “and of his church” are absent in witness 5c.], he requested that these be confirmed for him and his church by the security of an apostolic subscription. This he also obtained. For, after granting him indulgence for his sins [Col. 1220B], Calixtus sent him back to his own country, giving him a written charter containing the following:

“Calixtus, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bruno, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 1219] “of the church of Trier,” possibly witness B4.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the custom of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1219] “of the apostolic see,” witness 5.] and the order of reason itself require that we honor and love more greatly wise and religious persons who are devoted to the unity and obedience of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1219] “and devotion,” absent in witness 6; “obediences,” witness 6b; “devoted,” witness C.]. Therefore, dearest brother, we graciously assent to your petition, and, embracing your person in the arms of affection [Note: [Col. 1219] “we embrace you and it,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6.], we absolve you from the authority of any legate, unless he should be sent from our side. For we trust in the Lord that from your wisdom and religious devotion great honor and benefit will accrue both to God and to the Church [Col. 1220C]. Given at Cluny, on the third day before the Nones of January (in the year 1120)” [Note: [Col. 1219] “Ides,” witness 5b.].

### 24

Finally, not long afterward, when his bodily strength was declining toward its end through old age and illness alike, wicked men began to rise up throughout almost the entire surrounding region [Note: [Col. 1219] “and in the surrounding region,” witness C6.]. They ravaged in barbarian fashion the property of the Church that had been entrusted to their protection and, so to speak, their advocacy [Note: [Col. 1219] “advocacy,” witness 6b.]. A certain Count William [Note: [Col. 1219] The name appears as *Vilhelmus*, *Wilhelmus*, *Wilelmus*, and *Gillehelmus* in the witnesses.], son of the aforementioned Count Conrad [Note: [Col. 1219] “the aforementioned count,” witness 6.] [Note: [Col. 1220] Chapter 8.], furnished them with leadership.

Although he frequently invited them to correction, without success [Col. 1221A], at last, since he had no one who could suppress their madness by armed force—for they ought to have resisted these men if barbarians attacked this province—he used against them the vengeance of anathema on a certain Sunday, the eighth day before the Ides of December (6 December), in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1122, the twenty-first year of his pontificate [Note: [Col. 1221] “the twenty-first year of his pontificate” absent in witness 5b.].

The series of the words of this anathema [Note: [Col. 1221] absent in witness 6.] is as follows [Col. 1221C; Note: Edited from the Epternacensis manuscript by Martène and Durand, *Collectio*, I, p. 677, where it is entitled: “This decree was enacted by Bruno, archbishop, in the twenty-first year of his archbishopric.”]

### Complete apparatus supplement

The following source readings supply the forms and omissions that qualify the translated text above.  In this register *absent* means that the stated witness omits the associated source words; quoted Latin is retained only where its spelling or inflection is the point, and each is glossed.

**Opening passage (Col. 1211–1212).** Witnesses 4 and 5 read *susceptus est* (“was received”) for *honorifice … susceptus* (“honorably received”); 4 reads *ita* (“thus”) for *atque quia* (“and because”); 5 reads *correctus* (“corrected”) for *correptus* (“rebuked”). Witnesses 5a–b add *et quod* (“and which”) and 5c *et quia* (“and because”) before the clause about recovering the office; 4, 5, and 6 read *ipsis* (“the very men”) for *eisdem* (“the same men”), 5 has *et* (“and”) for *quia* (“because”), and 6 *congruens* (“corresponding/suited”) for *conveniens* (“fitting”). Witnesses 4–6 omit *ei* (“upon him”), while C omits the same object; 4 reads *illud* (“it”) for *hoc* (“this”). B2 has *apostolica* (“apostolic”) for *apostolicae sedis* (“of the apostolic see”); 5 omits “in the firm observance of the rule of faith”; B4, 5, g.s.c., and 6 omit the admonition about instructing the entrusted flock. B5 ends here and appends several lines from chapter 25 below. 5c and B1 read *tunc* (“then”) for *deinde* (“thereafter”); C *praeceptum* (“precept”) for “instruction”; 6 *evangelicam mensuram* (“an evangelical measure”) for “a measure of Gospel wheat.” 5b omits “pondering more attentively”; 5 and B1 omit *et praedicatio ejus* (“and his preaching”), while 6 omits *ejus praedicatio* (“his preaching”). 6 reads *sumptuum* (“expenses”) for *sumptus* (“expense”); 5 and 6 *consiliis* (“counsels”) for *consilio* (“counsel”); 6 *eum honoravit quasi majorem* (“honored him as the greater”), 5b *et majorem honorem ei impendit* (“and bestowed greater honor on him”), and 5 *impensum est* (“it was bestowed”). 5b, 5c, and C6 omit *porro* (“moreover”); C6 adds *etiam* (“also”) before “revered.”

**Chapter 19 (Col. 1211–1214).** 6 has *erat* (“was”) for the wording that he had proved himself energetic; 5 and C *regalis vicedominus* (“royal steward”), 6 *vicedominus* (“steward”). 5b and 6c call Henry *Henricus hujus nominis* (“Henry of this name”); 5 and 6 *circiter viginti* (“about twenty”), C omits the age. B4 and C omit *et educaret* (“and educate”); 5 reads *postquam crevit et educavit eum* (“after he grew up, and he educated him”). 5 has *postea* (“afterward”) for “later,” and 5b omits the clause identifying Adalbert as chancellor and later bishop. 6 supplies *si quis ei molestiam intulisset* (“if anyone had caused him trouble”). 6 has *prius* (“before”) for “above”; 4 *Moguntini populi* (“of the people of Mainz”); B1 *injurias vel molestias* (“injuries or troubles”). 5 *quid moror* (“why do I delay?”), B1 *quid morer* (“why should I delay?”); B1 omits the preceding-discourse clause, C calls it chapter 10. B2 reads *offensos* (“having offended”) for the Catholics’ displeasure. 4, 5, B2, and C have *deliberatione* (“deliberation”) for mediation, and B1 adds *consilio* (“by counsel”); 6c has *imperatori obedivit* (“obeyed the emperor”) and *eos esse permisit* (“allowed them to be [at odds]”), while B1 adds *persuasit* (“persuaded”). 5 *praeeminuit* (“was pre-eminent”), 6 *excessit* (“surpassed”); B1 *exhortatorias* (“exhortatory”), and 4 omits “to him.” 6 reads *me vidisse* (“me to have witnessed”).

**Chapter 20 (Col. 1213–1216).** B2 reads *Yodii* for Yvois; B2 and C omit “the body and blood of Christ”; 5 and 6 omit the clause about other errors, while 6 calls them *errores* (“erroneous teachings”). B2 has *Frithericus*, C1 *Fridericus*; the William readings are *guilhelmus* (5b), *evilhelmus* (6a), *guilelmus* (6c), *wuillelmus* (4), *willehelmus* (B1), *guillehelmus* (B4), and *guuilhelmus* (C1/3); 6a *Amelricus* for Hamelric. B2 omits the whole span from “whom” (the four accused) through Hamelric. C3 has *sectator* (“adherent”) and C6 *assertor* (“advocate”); 5a adds *videlicet* (“namely”) to the relics. B2 and C consistently write *Fridericus*. 5 and 6 read *fideles* (“the faithful”), 6 *patet* (“is evident”), 5 *lucet clarius* (“shines more clearly”). In the first Augustine citation 6 has the order *Christum non est fas vorari dentibus, voluit*, “it is not lawful for Christ to be devoured by teeth; [he] willed …” (apparatus *c. n. e. f. v. d. voluit*); B2 *in ministerio* (“in the ministry”); 5a–b *vero* (“indeed/however”) for *vere* (“truly”); 4 omits *idem* (“same”); C3–4 *consecratur* (“is consecrated”). C1 corrects accusative *parvulos*, “infants,” to dative *parvulis*, “for infants.” The same printed note gives 5 as *c. v. n. e. f. d. oluit*, an apparently displaced and damaged abbreviation of the earlier Christ-and-teeth clause: tentatively “Christ … to be devoured … is not lawful … by teeth … [he] willed”; the supplied *oluit* is defective. The phrase “This is contained in chapter 27 of the letter” is absent in C, while other witnesses have *In capitulo XXVII epistolae* (“In chapter 27 of the letter”). 4, 5a–c, and 6 read *et cum* (“and when”); B1 *fidem vel veritatem* (“faith or truth”); 6 *destinasset* (“had resolved”). C has *acclamatur* (“is proclaimed”); 6 *acclamantibus* (“while shouting”), 5b and C *accurentibus* (“while running up”); 4, 5, and 6 *reinventus* (“found again”); B2 *pacietur* (“will suffer”). 4 and 5b omit *et* (“and”), C6 omits “and the other”; 4–6 *publicatae* (“published”) for “aforesaid”; 4 *exstiterit* (“had been”), B2 omits the claim of advocacy. Bc reads *contra* (“against”); 5a–b *conventiculo* (“gathering”), 5c *quaestiunculis* (“little questions/disputes”); 6 adds *communicantem invenisse* (“to have found [him] participating”). 5 and 6 omit *ne forte* (“lest perhaps”); B2 abbreviates *presbiterii* (“of the priesthood”); 6 omits *se* (“himself”). The nested note is: B1 reads *culpam* (“guilt”), 6 *notam* (“stain”), B2 omits it; 4, 5a–b, B4, and C1 read *suspicionem abolendae* (“of suspicion to be removed”), after *gratiam* C3 and following add the text received by them, and 5c reads *ob hanc suspicionem abolendam* (“to remove this suspicion”). B2 has *sententia* (“judgment”) and C6 *ut cum* (“when/as”). The editorial note directs the reader to Du Cange, *Glossarium*, s.v. *secretum* (“the secret [of the Mass]”), Henschel I, 62 and VI, 148. 5 and 6 have *hujuscemodi* (“of this kind”); 5a adds *etiam* (“also”) and C6 omits “and blood.” B1 omits *non supervacuum* (“not superfluous”). 4–6 omit *inde vero* (“but thereafter”); 5b omits *cum* (“since”); 5 omits “God is a just judge”; 5a–b *equanimis* (“even-tempered”), 6 *equanimius* (“more equably”); 4–6 read *qui in sordibus est* (“he who is in filth”).

**Chapters 21–22 (Col. 1215–1219).** 4 omits *semper* (“always”); 6 *habere solitus erat* (“was accustomed to have”) for *solebat habere* (“used to keep”); C has *vocant* (“they call”) for *nuncupant* (“is called”). C reads *exquisitos* (“excellent”) for *exquisitissimos* (“most excellent”); 5 and 6 add *et totius* (“and of all”) after computist; 5b omits *prae ceteris* (“before the others”); 6a has *Bruno idem* (“the same Bruno”); 5a–b spell *adnectabat* (“attached”), B1 *annectabat* (“attached”); 5b omits “striving,” C instead has *ubi qua* (“where/by which”). C1 spells *volumininibus* (“books”); B1 omits Bruno’s name, 5, 6, and C omit “his name”; 5b omits “to all his faithful,” 7 *suis eum* (“him to his own [faithful]”); 5a reads *est multum instabile in fide* (“is very unstable in faith”), C omits *in* (“in”), and 6 *in quocumque* (“wherever”).

For chapter 22: 6 reads *tunc* (“then”), 5 rearranges *nunc* (“now”); 6 *cum igitur* (“when therefore”); 5a–c *omnis* (“every [masc.]”), 5b, B2, 4 *omnia* (“all [neut.]”), 6 *actu* (“act”), 5 *auctor* (“author”) for *actione* (“deed”); 6 inserts *videlicet*, “namely,” yielding *qui videlicet felicibus actibus ejus invidebat*, “who, namely, envied his successful deeds”, 5b omits *retro conversus* (“turned back”). 6 has *scilicet* (“namely”); 5 and 6c *multum* (“much”), an anomalous reading for *militum* (“of soldiers”), 4 omits “of acquiring,” 5b omits “and benefices,” 6a omits “evening,” 5 has “morning and evening,” and 4–6 omit precious ornaments. C1 gives the superscript *vel horreum* (“or granary”) for Orgium, C3 the same, C4 *horreorgium*, C6 *quae horreum* (“which [is] a granary”); B2 *nunccupata* (“named”), 6c *machra*, C3–4 *lisura*, C3 calls earlier pontiffs *principes* (“princes”), C6 *episcopos* (“bishops”), 5 *quoque* (“also”), B1 *restituta vel reconsignata* (“restored or reassigned”). 6c omits the Dagobert-benefits phrase and 6 *beneficia* (“benefits”); B2 *Yrmine*; 6 *vero* (“indeed”), 5 omits “blessed Paulinus … Lesura,” B2 preserves *Liudulfus*, others *Ludolfus*, 6a *donavit* (“gave”), 6 *tollere* (“take away”), C *disperdet* (“will destroy”), 5–6 *Dominus* (“the Lord”). The charter is explicitly marked as apparently lost. 6 has *episcopatus* (“episcopate”), *in usus suos* (“to his own uses”), *reddituum* (“revenues”), and *id* (“that”); B4 *Liutoldus*, C *Liudolfus*, others *Ludolfus*; 4 *utrum* (“whether”), C omits “you,” 5b–c, 6, B1, B4, C *decernite* (“decide/decree”), B4 *discere* (“learn”), C *recedere* (“withdraw”), 4 omits “for this purpose,” and 4 *Deo* (“to God”). Witness 6a omits the actual surviving words *in ecclesia ad (infra c. 24.)* (“in the church, to [below, ch. 24]”) because its leaf is defective; the source locates them in Vatican manuscript *Christ. N. 1283*, fol. 71. 4–6 *assumpserit* (“has taken up”) for *absumpserit* (“has consumed”). The printed *temporanea sive scrotina penitentia* means “with timely or [late] penance”; *scrotina* is apparently corrupted *serotina*, “late,” as the preceding reference to late penance suggests; 5b *vel* (“or”), C3 *et* (“and”), B2 *parte* (“part”), B2 *ut* (“so that”).

**Chapters 23–24 (Col. 1219–1221).** The heading is chapter 70 in Leibniz. B1 reads *ergo* (“therefore”), 5b omits “of his ordination,” and the nineteenth year has these exact alternatives: B1 *XXX* (“thirtieth”), B2 *VIIIIno* (literally nine with an ordinal ending, “ninth,” anomalous against the printed nineteenth year), C1 erased *nonagesimo* (“ninetieth”), C3 omits it but another hand supplies *XX* (“twenty”), C4 leaves a blank, C6 *XL* (“fortieth”). C spells Mainz *Mogociensis*; 5b omits “bishop”; 5c *superbeque* (“and proudly”); 4–6 *misso ad praesens* (“sent for the present”); 5a–b *Hicmarus*; 5a has *papa* corrected to *papae*, B4 *papa*, C1 corrects to *papae*. The editorial cross-reference is “in the letter above cited, *Gesta* ch. 24.” B2 and C6 *primatum* (“primacy”), 5–6 *abjecto* (“cast out”), 6 *eo* (“him”) and B6 *violentiam* (“violence”); 6 omits “the church,” and adds *nomine* (“by name”) before Stephen. For printed *Calixti* (“of Calixtus”), 5b/6 read *kalixti*, B2 *calisti*, and B4 *kalisti*, also subsequently; 5 adds *cum jam* (“when already”), 6b *incedere* (“to walk”), 5c *potestate remanente* (“with authority remaining”), 5 *Trever.*, 6 *ut Trevericam* (“as Trier’s”), 4 reads the three infinitives *deprimere—anteferre—facere* (“oppress—prefer—make”), 5b adds *et in metropolim* (“and into a metropolitan”), 5/B2/C6 *quodcumque* (“whatever”), 4 *Calixtus papa* (“Pope Calixtus”). 6 has *ut quotienscumque* (“that whenever”), C omits “saying” and has *quandocumque* (“whenever”); B2 omits the written-authority clause, B1 *firma probat* (“firmly proves”); 5b omits “only,” 5a “five,” 5–6 singular *pallio* (“with the pallium”). For printed *Augustidunum* (“Autun”), 5b reads *augustudinum* and 5c/B1/2/4 *augustudunum*; the editor identifies the place as Autun; B2 has *Kalistus*, 6 adds “and received him as a friend,” B2 *prolatis* (“having produced”), 5c omits “of his see and church,” 6 omits “and obtained it,” 5c *est ei* (“was to him”), C1 corrects *ei*; 6 *remisit eum* (“sent him back”). The privilege begins, in Leibniz, chapter 71. It addresses *Brunoni Treberensi archiepiscopo* (“Bruno, archbishop of Trier”); 5 abbreviates *Trever.*, B4 “of the church of Trier”; 4–6 omit “and,” 5 *apostolicae sedis* (“of the apostolic see”), C omits “and” and 5b *-que*, 6 omits “unity and,” 6b *obedientias* (“obediences”), C *devotos* (“devoted [masc.]”), 5b omits “your person” and “from any legate,” 4–6 *amplectimur et eam* (“we embrace [you] and it”), and 5b *ydus* (“Ides”).

In chapter 24 C6 adds *et in* (“and in”); 6b spells advocacy *advocassie*; For printed *Willehelmo* (“William”), 5/C read *vilhelmo*, 6c *wilelmo*, and B1 *gillehelmo*; 6 supplies *comitis supra memorati* (“the aforesaid count”), 5–6 omit *vulgo* (“commonly”), 4–5 *dicitur* (“is called”), 6 *vocatur Luzel.* (“is called Luzel…”). C1 has a superscript correction on “not”; 6 *resistere debuerunt* (“ought to have resisted”), 6 *eos* (“them”), and 5b omits the twenty-first regnal/pontifical-year clause. Leibniz begins chapter 72 here. The final editorial note is a distinct quotation: “Martène and Durand edited [this] from the Epternacensis codex, *Collectio* I, p. 677, where it is headed: *Hoc decretum sanxit Bruno archiepiscopus, XXI archiepiscopatus sui anno*—‘Bruno the archbishop enacted this decree in the twenty-first year of his archiepiscopate.’”

Because of the continuous oppressions suffered by our church, we decree and confirm, by the judgment and authority of the Holy Spirit granted to us [Note: [Col. 1221] “of the Holy Spirit”: 6, B; “and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit”: omitted in B1.] [Note: [Col. 1221] omitted in C6.], that whoever has hitherto troubled us [Note: [Col. 1221] “has troubled”: C.]—whether by plundering ecclesiastical property, burning any church, seizing any cleric, imposing any unjust exaction, or violating the general or particular peace [Col. 1221B] [Note: [Col. 1221] “or”: 5a; “in a particular peace”: B1.]—shall be canonically summoned to make satisfaction and shall suffer judgment according to his deserts: the obedient shall receive judgment with mercy, the rebellious [Note: [Col. 1221] “the rebellious shall receive judgment without mercy”: omitted in C6.] judgment without mercy.

Moreover, whoever hereafter is found to be a violator of any of the foregoing [Note: [Col. 1221] “of the foregoing violations”: 6.] we condemn in advance by today’s excommunication [Note: [Col. 1221] “that is, on 4 December”: added by Mart.], and we order that he be avoided by everyone as a sacrilegious person, his name being displayed in the church as a sign of the excommunication already pronounced against him and to be repeated every Sunday [Note: [Col. 1221] “on Sundays”: 5b, 6.], so that whoever communicates with him, if a layman, shall be struck by the same anathema, and, if a cleric, shall be deposed from his order. Whoever buys or accepts as a gift property taken as spoil [Note: [Col. 1221] “as a gift”: omitted in B4?; “in a gift”: 5b, where immediately follows “according to the rite.”] shall be subjected to the same condemnation as the one who carried off the spoil.

We also grant congregations permission to pursue with daily excommunication anyone who injures them in the goods allotted for their support [Col. 1221C]. Furthermore [Note: [Col. 1221] The remainder is lacking in Mart.], I grant the archdeacons permission, whenever I am unable to be present because I am occupied with other affairs, to reconcile penitents to the church, provided that the prescribed order is observed in settlements and in the other ecclesiastical customs [Note: [Col. 1221C] Compare the letter written on this occasion by Count William, in Hontheim, *History*, I, p. 507.].

He also performed many other distinguished deeds of virtue [Note: [Col. 1221] Chapter LXXIII begins here in Leibniz.] which I myself saw and learned through the reliable report of others [Col. 1222A]; but, to avoid prolixity, I have omitted listing them individually. This alone should suffice to know: as the end of his life approached [Note: [Col. 1221] “of his life”: B1.], he preceded it with exceedingly praiseworthy works [Note: [Col. 1221] “anticipated”: corrected to “preceded”: 6a; “anticipated”: 6c, d.]. For during the night he was accustomed to go silently around the memorials of the saints, remaining there for a long time in prayer [Note: [Col. 1221] “to persist”: B1.] and earnestly imploring God’s favor, with their intercession [Note: [Col. 1221] omitted in 4, 5, 6.], in abundant tears. He also visited the places where the servants and handmaids of God lived in enclosure, taking only one companion with him; he supplied whatever necessities they had, both food and clothing [Note: [Col. 1221] omitted in 4? B1? 4?], and commended himself to their prayers with the greatest devotion [Note: [Col. 1221] “devoted”: 5, 6.].

### 25.

Nor must it be passed over that, in the diocese of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1221] “of Mainz”: B2; “of Speyer”: 4, 5, 6, B4, C; this appears to be a corrector’s reading.], on his estate called Odenheim [Col. 1222B], he built a monastery [Note: [Col. 1221] “constructed”: B4, C.], where he gathered together monks living under the monastic profession in the service of God, and assigned to them so much of the resources of his estates [Note: [Col. 1221] “of their estates” is absent in B1; added in the margin of C1 and accordingly in C3; “of the estates” is absent in 5.] as could suffice for the daily sustenance of those dwelling there [Note: [Col. 1223B] C adds: “At the same time he restored the monastery of Saint Eucharius, already almost collapsed in discipline and possessions, through Abbot Eberhard of Kamberg, a man of vigorous religious observance. This man, beginning to build a new monastery, demolished the old one; and in the time of the aforesaid Eberhard, Saint Matthias the apostle of the Lord was discovered. See below the account of this matter. How greatly God advanced that place through signs of many miracles is attested by the entire city of Trier, which also displays many indications of its improvement through the merits of blessed Matthias.”] [Note: [Col. 1221C] See the charter of Henry V in Hontheim I, p. 483 n.].

Nor should this be left unmentioned: at Koblenz, too [Note: [Col. 1221] omitted in B4?], he built the basilica of Saint Florinus, consumed by age, in a finer design and on a more spacious plan, from blocks of tufa stone cut and polished [Note: [Col. 1221] “tufa”: 5, 6c, B1.] [Note: [Col. 1221C] German: *Tufsteine*], as it can still be seen to this day [Note: [Col. 1221] omitted in C.] [Note: [Col. 1221C] Compare Bruno’s charter concerning the hospital founded there, Günther I, p. 166.].

He also rebuilt at Trier [Note: [Col. 1222C] In an ancient ritual book once belonging to the metropolitan church one reads: “In the year of the Lord 1121, indiction 15, on 23 October, the new part of this house, which is on the west, with the altar of Saint Nicholas the confessor situated in it, was dedicated by Lord Bruno, venerable archbishop of Trier, in the twentieth year of his pontificate, in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity and of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor, whose relics are contained in it.”] the church in which lie buried blessed Paulinus and the other confessor-bishops of Trier [Note: [Col. 1221] “of the Treveran church”: C1.], as well as many bodies of Theban martyrs who suffered under Rictiovarus [Note: [Col. 1221] “Rictiovarius”: 4; the remainder of the phrase is omitted in 5c.]. As we have learned from the report of our fathers [Col. 1222C] [Note: [Col. 1222C] *Deeds*, chapters 20 and 23.], Saint Felix, bishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 1221] “Treveran”: B2; “of Trier”: C1.], who rests in that very church, first founded it on a large and spacious site [Note: [Col. 1221] “with a large space”: C3.]. Later, when it had been consumed by age, blessed Marus [Note: [Col. 1221] “Maurus”: 6c.], himself bishop of the same city and also resting there [Note: [Col. 1221] “who rests there”: C3, 4.], restored it to its original condition [Note: [Col. 1221] omitted in C3.]. In our own time, moreover, he rebuilt it after it had been destroyed by fire [Col. 1223A] [Note: [Col. 1223C] A.D. 1092, 1 August, *Annals of Saint Eucharius*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, V, p. 10. Compare the passage on this matter from the *Miracles of Saint Modoaldus*, edited below.], through the diligence of Adalbert and Rudolf [Note: [Col. 1223] “Rodolph”: 5a; “Rudolf”: 4, 6, B1? C; “Rudolph”: 5b.], provosts of that church, providing them with the necessary funds [Note: [Col. 1223] “to him”: 5a, c.], not according to the size of its original dimensions but according to the modest limits of their means [Note: [Col. 1223] “measure”: 5, 6, B4, C.].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1124, which was the twenty-third year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in C3, 4; “twenty-ninth”: B4?; the words from “which” to “twenty-third” are omitted in 5b.], on 25 April, a Friday [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 6; omitted in 5.], at the first hour, he gave up his soul. The bishops of the Trier diocese who attended his funeral were Henry of Verdun and Conrad of Toul; they buried him with great honor and amid the mourning of all the clergy and people, not far from the tomb of his predecessor Egilbert. He had occupied the episcopate for twenty-three years [Note: [Col. 1223] “twenty years”: 6c; “three months” added in 6a, b, d.], twenty-four days [Note: [Col. 1223] “twenty-four days”: 6, B1, 3, 4, C; “twenty-three”: 6a; “eighteen”: 5b, c; “twenty-four … two days”: omitted in 5a.], and the episcopate remained vacant for two months and eight days [Note: [Col. 1223] “and days”: C6; C6 adds: “and so forth.”].

### 26.

[Note: [Col. 1223] Chapter LXXIV in Leibniz. In place of this chapter, manuscript B2 contains a fuller narrative, which we publish below.]

After the death of Bishop Bruno [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 6, C6.], Godefrid [Note: [Col. 1223] “Godefridus”: B1.], dean of the major church, succeeded to the episcopate. He was descended from the diocese of Liège [Note: [Col. 1223] “of Liège”: 4, 6a.]. His kinsman Arnulf [Note: [Col. 1223] “Arnold”: 5, 6, B4, C.], provost of the major church—that is, the church of blessed Peter—was a religious man distinguished for the uprightness of his conduct [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 6; “namely”: 5, C.]. He founded the church situated beside the White Gate in honor of the Holy Cross and, having followed him to Trier [Note: [Col. 1223] “Trier”: 5, 6.], was appointed a cleric by Eberhard, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 1223] “Eberard”: 6.].

This Godefrid, like his predecessor—the aforementioned provost—distinguished for the dignity of his conduct and the generosity of his spirit, was first loved by the people of Trier, clergy and laity alike, and enriched by Egilbert and Bruno, bishops of that city, with many ecclesiastical honors [Col. 1224A] [Note: [Col. 1223] “was enriched”: 5b.]. Finally, when Lord Bruno died, as we have said, he was raised to the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1223] “to the episcopal office”: B1; “was elevated”: 4.].

After he had completed one year of his episcopate, certain of his clerics rose against him and challenged his entry into office [Note: [Col. 1223] A.D. 1125–1126]—whether their challenge was just or unjust, God knows; I do not [Note: [Col. 1223] “I do not know; God knows”: C.]—and at length the matter was brought to this point: recognizing that his weakness was insufficient for such a burden [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 5, 6]—for he had already reached extreme old age—and also seeing that fraternal charity was being torn apart in the church on his account, with some adhering to him and others resisting him [Note: [Col. 1223] “resisting him”: 6.], he did not wish to be the cause of this schism and was released from the episcopate near the end of his third year. He held the see for two years, ten months, and eleven days [Col. 1224B]. He then survived for one year, five months, and sixteen days [Note: [Col. 1223] “one year”: 6; “six”: 4, 5, 6.], and died on 14 November, a Thursday [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 5b; “Thursday”: B1.] [Note: [Col. 1224C] 14 November 1128 was a Wednesday.], at the third hour of the night. His successor buried him in the basilica of Saint Peter of the major church, beneath the arch on the southern side [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 4.].

### 27.

[Note: [Col. 1223] Chapter LXXV in Leibniz. C1 adds the rubric: “Concerning Meginher.”]

His successor, named Meginher [Note: [Col. 1223] “Meyner”: 4; “Megenheres”: B1, throughout.], was himself born of noble parents from the same diocese as his predecessor [Note: [Col. 1223] omitted in 5a; “petitioners”: 6c.] and had been educated from childhood in the church of Trier. He would certainly have risen worthily to the honor of the episcopate on account of the uprightness of his conduct and the maturity of his character, had he either attacked the aforesaid Godefrid [Note: [Col. 1223] “Gotefrid”: B4.] less harshly or imposed some limit upon his own severity and indiscretion.

Elected in June (1127), he gathered the Trier militia in the following autumn and, at the first assault, captured the new castle called Bumaggen [Note: [Col. 1223] “Bumage”: 5, 5a, c, 6; “Bunniage”: B4; “Bunnage”: C; “Humage”: 5b; “Huniage”: C6; B2 adds: “the new one, of which mention has already been made, previously.”] [Note: [Col. 1224C] The location of this place is unknown; one should not think of Numagen.]. He compelled Count William to agree to terms of peace and soon restored peace to the homeland [Note: [Col. 1223] “the peace”: omitted in 5b.].

When Lent came (1128), he set out for Rome, where Pope Honorius ordained him [Note: [Col. 1223] “ordained him and …”: 6.] and adorned him with the dignity of the pallium [Note: [Col. 1223] “with the dignity of the pallium”: 4, 5, 6.] [Note: [Col. 1224C] Compare the charter of Honorius, Günther I, p. 200.]. On his return, he was honorably received by the clergy and people of Trier [Note: [Col. 1223] “Treveran”: C.].

Afterward, while in his excessive zeal for righteousness he harshly issued many measures concerning the incontinence of clerics, without the seasoning of discretion [Col. 1225A], he acquired great hatred for himself and incurred an infamy that cannot rightly be spoken of.

### 28.

[Note: [Col. 1225] Chapter LXXVI begins here in Leibniz.]

Perhaps at the same time the political order of the Franks was being greatly disturbed [Note: [Col. 1225] “almost”: 5.]. For a few years earlier, after Emperor Henry, the fifth king of that name, had died without offspring (1125), the nobles of the Franks had raised Lothair [Note: [Col. 1225] “Lotharius”: 4, 5, 6, B4, C.] duke of Saxony to the kingship at Mainz [Note: [Col. 1225] “raised”: B2.], and the Romans had approved their decision. But then Frederick [Note: [Col. 1225] “Frithericus”: B2; “Frid.”: C.], duke of Alamannia and the sister’s son of the same Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in 5c, B1, C.], having formed a conspiracy with certain enemies of justice [Note: [Col. 1225] C1, corrected by a second hand, reads: “the sister’s son, having entered into a plan with certain men favoring him, [set up] his brother”; C5, 6 have the same.], set up his brother Conrad [Note: [Col. 1225] “Conrad”: 5; “Cunrad”: 6, throughout.] as king and thereby aroused a great cause of war and fuel for conflict (1127–1128) [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted, with “the cause” added afterward, in C1; likewise in C3 and following manuscripts.].

When Pope Honorius learned of this, he bound Conrad and all who supported him with the bond of excommunication. He commanded the archbishop Meginher [Note: [Col. 1225] “Meginher”: 5a, b, and so below; “ordained archbishop of Trier”: 5b.]—who had already been ordained and was returning—to excommunicate Conrad in his own see [Note: [Col. 1225] “in his see”: 5.]. Meginher carried this out without delay [Note: [Col. 1225] The words from “This” through “carried out” are omitted in 6a.].

### 29.

[Note: [Col. 1225] Chapter LXXVII in Leibniz.]

After him, the people of Trier elected Bruno, a canon of the church of Trier [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in 5; “of the Treveran church”: 6, B1; “of the church of Trier”: C.], nephew of Bruno, once archbishop, on 7 December. He resisted this with every effort, chiefly because of the poverty of this church [Note: [Col. 1225] The word was erased in C1.]; but the truth, as later became clear, was that he aspired to the greater glory of another episcopate. He did this with the approval of Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 1225] “with the favor of Pope Innocent”: 6; omitted in B1.], who at that time was residing in Gaul and holding councils in various places [Note: [Col. 1225] “holds”: C3.].

For when Bishop Meginher, traveling to Rome, had been captured and handed over to custody [Note: [Col. 1225] “Bishop”: omitted in 5, 6; “Rome”: C.], war also broke out among the Romans over the position of Innocent and Anacletus, after Pope Honorius had died [Note: [Col. 1225] “war was also kindled”: 6.]. The former had succeeded him after being enthroned and consecrated by an authentic election of the clergy and people [Note: [Col. 1225] “authentic”: 5a, 6.]; the latter, through the faction of the Roman nobles, with whom he was influential by kinship, had assumed the dignity of the papacy for himself [Note: [Col. 1225] “for himself”: 6.].

When the greatest tumult had been stirred up on their account [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in B1.], Pope Innocent fled into the church of Saint Peter. Anacletus besieged him there and, employing engines and siege-machines [Note: [Col. 1225] “and engines”: 6; “also with engines”: B2.], drove him from the church and the city. Expelled from Rome, Innocent sought Gaul [Note: [Col. 1225] “to Gaul”: 5, 6.], where the envoys of the people of Trier approached him and asked that he not delay confirming and completing their election [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in 4, 5, 6; “that he confirm and complete it”: 6.]. He replied that they should choose someone else whom they considered suitable for this office [Note: [Col. 1225] “whomever they wished”: 5; “whomever they knew to be suitable”: 6.], for neither they nor the sons of another church could have Bruno as bishop [Note: [Col. 1225] “could have had”: 5, B4, C; “could not have had him”: 4.].

They received this response at Liège during Lent (March 1131) [Note: [Col. 1225] “received”: 5.]. At the following Easter (19 April), when King Lothair [Note: [Col. 1225] “Lotharius”: B2.] and all the princes of Trier [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in 5b, B2; variants include “of Trier” and “of the Treverans.”] had assembled at Trier [Note: [Col. 1225] “at Trier”: 6; “at Treveri”: 5b, B1, B2; other variants.], one faction of the clergy was electing Adalbero, the primicerius of Metz [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in B2; “Alberon”: 4, 5, 6.], but the princes and people fiercely opposed them. When this disagreement had been prolonged for an entire year [Note: [Col. 1225] omitted in C.] [Note: [Col. 1225] “protracted”: 5.], it was finally settled by order of the pope and royal command. At the second Easter, Adalbero was enthroned, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1132 (10 April) [Note: [Col. 1225] “one thousand”: C; “the twenty-second”: 6c, B2; “the thirty-third”: B3. B2 adds: “The book on the history of Trier ends here”; 6d: “The history of Trier ends here”; B2: “The deeds of Trier end here.” Manuscript 5 and the others add a later continuation.].

# DEEDS OF ARCHBISHOP GODEFRID

[Note: [Col. 1227] These are found in manuscript B2, folio 43r.]

[Col. 1227]

### 1.

Thus, after the death of Bishop Bruno, Godefrid [Note: [Col. 1227] “Guothfridus,” with the letter *u* erased in the manuscript.] succeeded to the episcopate. He was born in the diocese of Liège to very noble parents—his father was named Rutfrid and his mother Fridesinda—and came from a village called Falmanies [Note: [Col. 1227] “oriudus,” with the letter *u* erased in the manuscript.]. Following his maternal uncle Arnulf to Trier, Arnulf being provost of the major church—that is, the church of blessed Peter the apostle—he was appointed a cleric by Eberhard, bishop of Trier.

But when he had obtained premature freedom, he immediately learned, under the influence of his peers whose hearts were set on luxury and idleness, to love vices; he was taught to walk along the path of corruption and, like an unbridled horse, despising its driver, to abandon the line of the right road [Note: [Col. 1227] “of the journey,” corrected to “of the road.”].

For this reason he was assigned by the aforementioned Arnulf to the service of King Henry IV [Col. 1227B]: since Arnulf had no regular hope that the irreligiousness of his conduct would permit him to attain any ecclesiastical honor, he intended that, if an opportunity arose—namely, if some ecclesiastical dignitary died—then, if Godefrid could not obtain office canonically, he might at least be intruded into it by royal power.

As time passed, then, the dean of the Trier church died, and not long afterward the office of archdeacon also became vacant when another man died there. When the king learned of this, he immediately sent letters to Bishop Egilbert, commanding him to raise the aforementioned Godefrid to those honors; if he failed to do so, he would offend the king.

Once he had obtained office, whenever he ought to invest someone with a canonry or an altar by gift, he did not do so without receiving a payment. In the diabolical manner, he was unwilling to perish alone; rather, he strove to drag others down with him, especially since, according to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, both those who sell and those who buy ecclesiastical honors have been condemned by anathema.

Since even then he did not seem able to sell canonries freely enough—for the provost, who ranks before the dean, ought to carry out the investiture—he himself also sought to acquire any provostships he might be able to obtain [Note: [Col. 1227] “afterward” supplied by the corrector.].

A certain man named Uodelric, born in the territory of Aquileia, presided over the congregation of Saint Simeon above the city gate. Through a certain Martin, his chaplain, Godefrid so ensnared him that, if Uodelric wished to return to Aquileia, he would appoint him heir to his provostship. Yet ecclesiastical dignities are not to be conferred by hereditary right, but upon those proved by the holiness of their lives, whose conduct should be a model of life for their subjects [Col. 1227D].

### 2.

After scraping together a great heap of treasure from here and there, when Bruno died (1124), Godefrid began to pant with all his desires for the possibility of rising into Bruno’s place [Col. 1228A]. Through his secretaries he sent King Henry 1,100 and, as is said, more than that number of silver marks. In this way he won the king over to himself, so that, when the people of Trier came and requested that a bishop be given to them, and some of them pointed out Godefrid’s incompetence, the king nevertheless did not refrain from appointing him bishop.

For Godefrid was full of senile foolishness and the fury of anger, with very little discretion; he did not even know how to govern his own household [Note: [Col. 1227] “house”: corrected to “household.”]. They feared to choose him bishop for such reasons. Nevertheless, whether they wished it or not [Note: [Col. 1227] “afterward” supplied by the corrector.], he was enthroned on 2 July.

He immediately sent a delegation and instructed the bishops of the churches subject to the metropolitan church of Trier to assemble at Trier and consecrate him as bishop. Although he himself wished this consecration to be expedited, he was hindered by various intervening obstacles [Col. 1228B] [Note: [Col. 1227] “intervening”: the manuscript reading, which I have followed almost literally; I have nevertheless written *ae* rather than *o* at the end of the word.].

For when Stephen, bishop of Metz, heard that Godefrid had entered by the aforesaid procedure, he pretended not to come. He would have come, however, if he had been permitted to wear at the metropolitan’s consecration the pallium with which his uncle, Pope Calixtus, had honored him. He refused to attend the consecration unless he was wearing the pallium.

The reason he was not permitted to wear it was this: he boasted that he wore it as though in insult to the metropolitan church, and he did not wish to show the metropolitan any deference in its use [Note: [Col. 1227] The manuscript reads “to show no regard to him in its use.”].

There is also another reason why he did not wish to attend the aforementioned consecration. A dispute arose between Stephen and Henry, bishop of Verdun, as to which of them would consecrate the metropolitan as bishop. Stephen claimed the primacy of his see, while Henry claimed priority by virtue of his ordination [Col. 1228C]. Let the one who proposed the more just claim explain it—especially since Stephen wished to be the consecrator out of a certain haughty pride, whereas Henry wished to be one by reason of law—unless perhaps the church of Metz possesses a privilege providing that its bishop is to consecrate the metropolitan.

Meanwhile, while these matters were being dealt with, a certain cardinal named William, bishop of Praeneste, happened to arrive. He said that he had been sent by apostolic authority to complete whatever he found unfinished, whether unconsecrated bishops or any other matter of this kind.

When Stephen of Metz learned that William had come to Trier [Col. 1228D], he sent him a letter, first asking him out of charity, and afterward forbidding him by apostolic authority to presume to do anything belonging to Stephen’s office [Note: [Col. 1227] The wording is uncertain: “anything that should be read,” or a word must be supplied after “anything.” P.].

In response, William produced letters of apostolic authority given to him for this work [Note: [Col. 1229] “displayed”: manuscript reading.], containing the following:

> Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved brothers in Christ, the archbishops and the other ecclesiastical orders established throughout Gaul, Germany, and France: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> We are sending to you our brother William, bishop of Praeneste, granting him, with your goodwill, permission that, if there are among you any bishops who have not been consecrated, he may consecrate them; and if there are any other matters of this kind in ecclesiastical affairs that remain incomplete [Note: [Col. 1229] “incomplete matters”: C.], he may complete them all without offending fraternity.
>
> Peace be with you.

After he had recited these letters in the hearing of everyone present [Col. 1229B], he added:

> “If our brother of Metz wishes to attend the metropolitan consecration, I shall be his helper as long as I live; but if he does not hasten to come, then, as the Lord permits, I shall fulfill his role.”

Finally, since Stephen refused to come to Trier for the reasons mentioned above, the aforesaid cardinal, with the cooperation of the bishops Henry of Verdun and Conrad of Toul, consecrated the aforementioned Godefrid as bishop on Sunday, 7 September.

### 3.

Thus, having at last obtained possession of his office, on one occasion, when he ought—as is customary—to announce words of salvation to the faithful from the pulpit and to explain how one ought to understand the Holy Trinity, he discoursed so irrationally and disorderly that those whom he ought to have taught could have judged him a heretic rather than a Catholic [Col. 1229C], had they not attributed it more to his ignorance of eloquence, as was in fact the case, than to heretical perversity.

It is true, as blessed Jerome says: “Fools are those who, although they do not know how to speak, cannot keep silent.”

To explain one of the many errors in his speech: when, as we have said, he had taken his place in the pulpit and wished to expound the words of faith, he said: “Believe that three lords are one lord,” interpreting the persons as lords, although orthodox Christians are forbidden to speak of three Gods or three lords, as blessed Athanasius of Alexandria set forth in his formulation of the Catholic faith:

> Just as Christian truth compels us to confess each person individually as God and Lord, so Catholic religion forbids us to say three Gods or three Lords.

Therefore, lest they be corrupted—for, as the apostle testifies, “bad company corrupts good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33)—one man after another argued among themselves that this speaker was uttering words of a new faith, unheard-of yet heretical, and that none of their teachers had ever said anything of the kind.

Some of the simpler people would indeed have been scandalized and led astray by this, had they not been restored to the right path by the diligent preaching of the clergy and instructed according to the profession of Christian truth: that one and the same God is undivided and uncut, threefold in the distinction of persons, one in the substance of the Godhead [Col. 1230A].

### 4.

Moreover, it was not yet known to many that he had purchased the episcopate for money when suddenly wicked men from the knightly order rose against him, demanding that the benefits he had promised them be given to them—the reward, namely, for their favor, since they had established him more through their own favor than by ecclesiastical election.

Although he granted them many of the episcopal revenues, he did not distribute enough to satisfy them. They therefore left after bringing accusations against him [Note: [Col. 1229] “departed”: C.], and some of them established castles to his injury, while others engaged in plundering and others in burnings, so that even in our own time we lament devastations of this city of Trier such as we read were carried out in antiquity.

Finally, if any members of the clergy—or even of the rest of the population—left the city on their own business and had to turn aside here or there, they were captured, subjected to accusations, and stripped of everything they possessed [Col. 1230B] [Note: [Col. 1229] “from”: omitted in C.].

The author and leader of all this destruction was Count William, mentioned in the preceding discourse [Note: [Col. 1229D] The *Deeds* add: chapter 24], and his son Conrad. Just as he was heir to the patrimony, so too he was heir to and imitator of every form of wickedness. If in any way he was not altogether equal to his father in evil, he surpassed him in the enormity of his crimes rather than falling short in any respect.

Their collaborators were both their servants and their free men—if one may call free a person who is a slave of iniquity and is proved to be so [Note: [Col. 1229] “whoever is called free”: C.]—tearing down churches and, when other materials were not available, building their castles with stones taken from them [Col. 1230C], something so wicked even to say.

One of them, Brunicho, built a tower on the summit of a certain mountain, about two miles from the city. It burned twice when fire came from heaven, yet he did not turn away from injustice.

What I am about to relate is extraordinary and perhaps scarcely credible to the ears of the few. Nevertheless, let them know that, although I myself was astonished by it and reluctant to believe it because of its novelty, the man who reported the matters I am about to relate, calling God to witness that they were true and that he had both seen and heard what he was saying, declared that the aforementioned Brunicho had entrusted this same castle of his—which was indeed a plague and destruction to the surrounding region, so to speak—to the faith and guardianship of Satan.

Satan, with marvelous and unbelievable familiarity, used to run about the castle [Col. 1230D]. And so that this same Satan might not stray far from the castle, Brunicho ordered that provisions sufficient for three men be carried daily at mealtime for Satan’s use and placed in a secret part of the house. As soon as it had been set down, it was consumed in an instant before the man who had carried it there. Yet he did not see the devourer; he heard only a sound like the voices of dogs fighting.

### Complete supplementary textual apparatus

This register supplies source readings not already carried in the running notes. Sigla are retained; forms are glossed, and editorial abbreviations are expanded in context.

**Decree and opening narrative (Col. 1221–1222).** At “by the judgment and authority,” 6 and B read *Spiritus sancti* (“of the Holy Spirit”), while B1 omits *et Spiritus sancti iudicio* (“and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit”); C6 omits *nobis* (“to us”); 6 has *commissa* (“entrusted”) for *concessa* (“granted”), and Mart. has *firmamus* (“we make firm”) for *confirmamus* (“we confirm”). 5 omits the first *sive* (“whether”); 5a has *sive* where the text has *vel* (“or”); B1 has *in speciali* (“in a particular [peace]”); C has future *conturbaverit* (“shall have disturbed”) for *conturbavit* (“has disturbed”); C6 omits “the rebellious shall [receive] judgment without mercy.” Mart. adds “that is, 4 December,” and later “that is, 1122, on a Sunday.” 6 has *violatorum* (“of the violations”); 6a continues after *ad indicium*, while 5a and 6c read *iudicium* (“judgment”) for *indicium* (“sign”); 5b/6 have *diebus dominicis* (“on Sundays”). At “as a gift,” B4? omits *dono* and 5b reads *in dono* (“in a gift”), immediately followed there by *ad ritum* (“according to the rite”). Mart. adds *etiam* (“also”); C has *cottidie* (“daily”) for *cottidiana* (“daily [excommunication]”); Mart. lacks the remainder. In the archdeacons’ permission 5a–b read *nisi* (“unless”) and 5c *si* (“if”) for *ubi* (“when”). The citation directs: “Compare Count William’s letter written on this occasion, in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 507.”

At the virtuous deeds, Leibniz begins chapter LXXIII at *Multa* (“many”); 5b omits *fuit insignia* (“distinguished deeds”); 6 has *ipse ego* (“I myself”); B1 has *suae* (“his”) for “of his life”; 6a corrects *antecedit* to *antecessit* (“preceded”), whereas 6c–d retain *antecedit* (“goes before”); B1/B2/C have *illisque* (“and there”) for *illicque* (“there”), B1 *insistere* (“to persist”) for *persistere*, and 4/5/6 omit *cum* (“with”) before “their intercession.” The printed uncertain witness list “4? B1? 4?” omits *in* (“in”) before clothing; 5/6 have *devotus* (“devoted”) for *devotius* (“more devoutly”).

**Chapter 25 (Col. 1221–1224).** 5a omits *quod* (“that”); B2 reads *Mogontiacensi* (“of Mainz”), while 4/5/6/B4/C read *Spirensi* (“of Speyer”), which the editor calls apparently a corrector’s reading. B4/C have *construxit* (“built”) for *exstruxit*. B1/B2 omit *de* (“from”), C1 adds it in the margin and C3 follows; 5 omits *de rebus* (“from the goods”); 5a omits the subsequent *de* and has *possit illis* (“may suffice for them”). C’s long addition says that Bruno restored Saint Eucharius’ monastery, nearly ruined in religious discipline and property, through Abbot Eberhard of Kamberg, a man of strenuous observance; rebuilding it, he demolished the old monastery; in Eberhard’s time Saint Matthias the apostle was found; see the account below; Trier itself testifies to the site’s many miracles and improvement through Saint Matthias’ merits. C1 reads *strennuae*; the internal editorial reference is “See the account of this matter below.” The other citation is Henry V’s charter in Hontheim I, p. 483 n.

At Koblenz 6a has *neque* (“nor”) for *nec* (“and not”); B4? omits “also”; 5/6c/B1 have *tophis* for *thophis*, both “tufa stones”; the German is *Tufsteine* (“tufa stones”); C omits “to this day.” Compare Bruno’s charter on the hospital founded there, Günther I, p. 166. At Trier, 5 omits *et* (“and”). The ritual-book note reads: “In the year of the Lord 1121, indiction 15, on 23 October, the new western part of this building, with the altar of Saint Nicholas the confessor in it, was dedicated by Lord Bruno, venerable archbishop of Trier, in the twentieth year of his pontificate, in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity and of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor, whose relics are contained in it.” B1 omits *in qua* (“in which”); C1 has *Trevirensium* for *Treverensium* (“of Trier”); 4 has *Rictiouario* and 5c omits “who suffered under Rictiovarus.” 6 reads *sicut relatu seniorum nostrorum* (“as by our elders’ report”); compare *Gesta*, chapters 20 and 23. B2 has *Treverensis*, C1 *Trevirorum*; C3 reads *spatio* (“space”) for *spacioso* (“spacious”); C3 omits *vero* (“however”); 6c has *Maurus* for *Marus*; 5/6 abbreviate “bishop of that same city”; C3/4 have *requiescit* (“rests”) for *quiescit*; B1 reads *reparavit nostris quoque* (“also restored in our times”). The fire note gives 1 August 1092, *Annals of Saint Eucharius*, MGH V, p. 10, and refers to the *Miracles of Saint Modoaldus* printed below. The forms are *Rodolphi* (5a), *Rudolfi* (4/6/B1?/C), *Rudolphi* (5b); 5a/c have *ei* (“to him”) for *eis* (“to them”); 5/6/B4/C have *modum* (“measure”) for *modicitatem* (“modesty”).

C begins a new chapter at *Anno*; 5b omits *autem* (“however”); C3/4 omit “which was the twenty-third year,” B4? reads twenty-nine, and 5b omits the span from “which” through twenty-third. 6 omits “on the seventh day before the Kalends of May”; 5 omits “on the sixth weekday.” The bishops’ name is *Conradus* in 5 and others. C continues *sedit autem* (“he sat/held office”), while 6/B1/C have accusative *annos* (“years”) and 6c reads twenty; 6a/b/d add “three months.” 6/B1/3/4/C have *dies* (“days”); 6a reads twenty-three, 5b/c eighteen, and 5a omits “twenty-four … two days.” C6 omits “the see was vacant,” supplies *et dies* (“and days”), and adds *et cetera* (“and so forth”).

**Chapters 26–29 (Col. 1223–1226).** Leibniz numbers chapter 26 LXXIV; B2 contains a fuller narrative in its place, printed below. 6/C6 omit “after the death”; B1 spells *Godefridus*; 4/6a have *Leodicensi* (“of Liège”); 5/6/B4/C have *Arnoldum*; 6 has *sancti Petri* (“Saint Peter’s”); 6 omits *videlicet* (“namely”), while 5/C have *scilicet* (“that is”); B4 has *honorem* (“honor”) for *honore*; 5/6 have *Treberim*; 6 *Eberardo*; 5b omits *vero*, 6 omits *et*, and 5 reads *primo* (“first”). 5b has *est ditatus* (“was enriched”); B1 has *in episcopatu* (“in the episcopate/in office”) for *in episcopatum* (“to the episcopate”); 4 *sublevatus* (“raised”). B4? has *in* before “against”; C says “God knows; I do not know”; 5b omits “the matter was brought to this point”; 5/6 omit *ad hoc*; C omits *etiam*; 6 has *quod in ecclesia fraterna pro eo [scindebatur caritas]*, moving “because of him” after “in the Church”: “that fraternal charity in the Church was being torn apart because of him”; 6 reads *sibi resistentibus* (“resisting him”). B2 continues from *Obtinuit autem* with its own fuller text; C reads *sedem episcopatus* (“the seat of the bishopric”) for *sedem* (“the see”). 6 has *vero annum* (“but one year”); 4/5/6 read six months, and 5b begins “and he died”; C has VIII for XVIII before the Kalends; 6 omits “day … third”; 5b omits Thursday and B1 gives *feria V*; the editor notes that 14 November 1128 was Wednesday; 4 omits “his successor.”

Leibniz calls chapter 27 LXXV; C1 adds the rubric “On Meginher.” The name forms are *Meynerus* (4) and *Megenheres* (B1 throughout); 4/B4 read *diocesi eius* (“from his diocese”) for *eadem qua decessor parrochia* (“the same diocese as his predecessor”); 5a omits “from noble parents,” and 6c has *petentibus* (“petitioners/people asking”) for *parentibus* (“parents”); B4 spells *Gotefridum*. The fortress forms are *Bumage* (5/5a/c/6), *Bunniage* (B4), *Bunnage* (C), *Humage* (5b), *Huniage* (C6); B2 adds “the new [castle], already mentioned above.” The editor says its location is unknown and it should not be identified with Numagen. 5/C and others have *Wilhelmum*, 6a *Wilelmum*; 5b omits *-que* (“and”) in “and restored peace”; 6 has “he was ordained and adorned by the pope”; 4/5/6 read *pallii dignitate* (“with the dignity of the pallium”); compare Honorius’ charter, Günther I, p. 200. 5 reads *inde* (“thence”), C *Treverico*; 5/6 omit “harshly.”

Leibniz begins chapter LXXVI at *Et forte*; 5 has *fere* (“almost”). The printed *Leodegarium* is opposed by *Lotharium* in 4/5/6/B4/C; B2 has *elevaverunt* (“raised”). Frederick is *Frithericus* in B2 and abbreviated *Frid.* in C; 5c/B1/C omit “the emperor’s”; C1, corrected by a second hand and followed by C5/6, reads “the nephew, having entered into a plan with certain men favoring him, [set up] his brother.” Conrad is *Conradum* (5) and *Cunradum* (6 throughout); C1 and C3 onward omit the clause about war, adding *causa* (“cause”) afterward. 5a/b abbreviate Meginher’s name; 5b says “the bishop of Trier, ordained”; 5 has *sua sede* (“his see”); 6a omits the span “This … carried out,” and 4/5b omit *ille quoque* (“he also”).

At chapter 28 the editor says that Wyttenbach inserted much from Lind. and the Eberhardus Clus. manuscript, but omitted it because it was written in the fifteenth/sixteenth century and judged worthless. 5b omits *iam* (“already”); 6a has *annos* (“years”) for *animos* (“minds”), B1/C6 *que* for *qua*; C has *minor* (“lesser”); the German forms are *Theuthonico* (5a/c), *Teutonico* (C), and *Teuthonico regno* (6); 5b calls Meginher archbishop; 5a/b have *pdictum*, corrected in 5c to *praedictum* (“aforementioned”); 5a has *eundemque* (“and that same [man]”); 5b omits *iam*; B1 has *episcopus vero* (“but the bishop”), omits *ipsi* (“for himself”), and reads *corpus eius* (“his body”).

Leibniz calls chapter 29 LXXVII. The people are *Treverici* (4), *Treverenses* (B1), *Treviri* (C1); 5 omits *ecclesiae Treverensis* (“of the Trier church”), 6/B1 read *Treverensis ecclesiae* (“of the Trier church”), and C *Trevericae ecclesiae* (“of the Trier church”). 6 reads *maximo nisu causa* (“with the greatest effort, because”); C1 has a word erased; 5a omits *autem* and 5 has *postea* (“afterward”); 6 has *gratia Innocentii papae* (“with the favor of Pope Innocent”) for *gratia apostolici Innocentii* (“with the favor of the apostolic [pope] Innocent”); B1 omits the phrase; C3 has present *celebrat* (“holds”). Meginher’s spellings are *Megiherus* (5a), *Meginerus* (6c), *Migeherns* (5b), *Meinherus* (B2); 5/6 omit *episcopus* (“bishop”); C has *Roma pergens* (“setting out from Rome”) for *Romam pergens* (“setting out for Rome”); 6 reads *bellum quoque conflatum est inter Romanos de* (“war also broke out among the Romans over”), preserving the same clause with *quoque* (“also”) moved before the verb. 5a/6 spell *autentica* (“authentic”), an orthographic form of *auctentica*; 6 has *vero* (“but”), *sibi* (“for himself”), and B1 omits “on their account”; 6 omits “Pope Innocent”; 6 reads *et tormentis* (“and with siege-engines”) and B2 *quoque tormentis* (“also with siege-engines”), where the source text has *tormentis quoque* (“with siege-engines also”); 5/6 have *in Gallias* (“into Gaul”), 4/6 *adiit*, 5 *adivit* (“went to”).

The envoys’ forms are *trorum* (5a), *treverorum* (4/5c/6), *trevirorum* (B4/C), *treverenses* (B2), and *canonicorum* (5b); 4/5/6 omit “their election”; 6 continues “that he should confirm (6c: *confirmaret*) and complete it”; 5 abbreviates “choose whom they wished,” while 6 reads “choose the one whom they knew suitable”; 5/B4/C have *potuissent* (“could have”), 4 “could not have had him.” 5 *receperunt* (“received”). B2 spells Lothair *Lotarius*. 5b/B2/3 omit “all the princes,” and the remaining forms are *Rorum* (5a), *treberorum* (5c), *tr.* (6a), *treberenses* (B1), *trevirorum* (B4/C); the place forms are *Treverim* (6), *Treberi* (5b/B1/B2 and others). B2 omits “primicerius of Metz”; 4/5/6 have *Alberonem* (“Albero”) for *Adalberonem* (“Adalbero”), and plural *eligebant* (“were electing”) for singular *eligebat* (“was electing”); C omits “for an entire year,” and 5 has *protractata* (“drawn out/prolonged”) for *protracta* (“having been prolonged”); Adalbero is *Albero* (4/5/6), *Adelbero* (B1/C1). C reads only “one thousand,” 6c/B2 “twenty-second,” B3 “thirty-third”; 6c adds “The book on the history of Trier ends,” 6d “The history of Trier ends,” B2 “The deeds of Trier end,” and manuscripts 5 add a later continuation.

**Gesta of Archbishop Godefrid (Col. 1227–1230).** The heading note states: “These are found in manuscript B2, folio 43r.” *Guothfridus* is written with erased *u* in the manuscript; *oriudus* likewise has an erased *u*; *iteneris* is corrected to *itineris* (“journey/road”); the corrector C supplies *post* (“afterward”); C has *Guthfridus*. In chapter 2 C corrects *domue* to *domui* (“household”) and supplies *post*; its *intercidencium* is followed almost literally, but the editor writes *ae* rather than *o* at the end of the word. C omits *in* (“in”) before “insult,” has *eis* (“them”) for *eius* (“his/its”), and the editorial P. note says that either *quod* should be read or something supplied after *quid*. C has *pretulit* (“presented”) for *protulit* (“brought forth”) and *perfecta quam* (“more complete than”) for *minus perfecta* (“less complete”). In chapter 4 C has *abcedebant* (“departed”) for *abscedebant*, omits *de* (“from”), gives the citation “Gesta, addition, chapter 24,” reads *quis libet* (“anyone whatsoever”) for *quis liber* (“any free man”), and has *cottidie* (“daily”).

5. Thus the Treverans, afflicted by many such tribulations and evils, gathered around the man on whose account all these things were inflicted upon them—namely, the aforesaid bishop Guotfrid—and addressed him as follows:

“How long are we to endure these things?”

He replied: “You know the faithlessness and wickedness of that entire most evil family, which originated from the castle called Lucelenburch [Note: The manuscript reads *dicta*; corrected to *dicto*.], and you know with how many adversities they afflicted my predecessors—men who, in comparison with me, were truly apostolic. To use the prophet’s words: ‘For I am no better than my fathers’ (1 Kings 19:4). Indeed, those who attack us were themselves supposed to be our protectors.”

But they answered: “If you cannot defend us with the material sword, why do you at least not defend us with the spiritual one?”

He said: “Have you not heard how they make light of episcopal authority, saying that I cannot bind or loose anyone by a spiritual bond because I do not possess the honor of the pallium of my predecessors, the archbishops of this see? You see that, in order to obtain it, I cannot approach the lord pope because I am hindered by bodily illness. But, as often before, so now again I beg you: choose from among yourselves prudent men of both orders who may be considered worthy of such an embassy, and I will provide them with the means for their journey.”

They answered him: “What you say is true in part; but those who persecute us suggest something else to us, threatening that we shall not have peace until you pay the gifts that you promised them for your election. Nevertheless, so that it may be clear to everyone that no obstacle lies with us, we shall approach the lord pope in your name and set forth the tribulation of our place. We shall say that, if it seems appropriate to you, since our metropolis does not possess the pallium, this is the reason why you cannot suppress the attackers of this church of ours. We shall add that, for God’s sake, he should remember our tribulation by granting our church its due honor.”

Accordingly, the more distinguished men of both orders of the place [Note: The manuscript reads *honoratioribus viris*; corrected to *honoraciores viri*.] prepared themselves for the journey with these words.

6. When they had reached Rome, the report of the whole affair had already spread there. After they had explained the reason for their arrival to the lord Honorius, then Roman pontiff, he recounted what he had heard concerning that man’s “entry”—for that was how he described it, I mean Guothfrid—and asked whether they were willing to prove by oath that he was innocent of these matters. When they refused, he said:

“That man has stained the holy Church of God, which has neither spot nor wrinkle, with the disgraceful mark of simoniacal depravity [Note: The manuscript reads *infimia*; corrected to *infamia*.]. Therefore, unless he has been cleared, he will not be able to exercise the episcopate in peace with the Church. Behold, I am about to send beyond the Alps our brother Peter, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata, a wise and discerning man, to arrange ecclesiastical affairs in those regions. When he comes to you, obey him as you would me. Let a day and place be established wherever it seems suitable in your province; there, with him seated in the place of judge and with the bishops of the surrounding province and whatever other religious persons may be summoned, let that man be brought to trial. If he is found innocent, let him be released; otherwise, let him be removed.

“As for your church, that ancient and noble Treveran metropolis, by God’s favor we do not deny it its due honor—provided, however, that the same church has been restored to its former dignity.”

After receiving this answer, those who had been sent were dismissed and returned to their own land.

7. Finally, when the matter had nearly come to everyone’s attention throughout the region and all were condemning his installation, he repeatedly reproached those whom I mentioned above as having been sent to Rome on his behalf, saying that it was their fault that such an infamous report had spread about him.

But through the aforesaid presbyter Martin and a certain Bolso—whom he had elevated to the office of archdeacon because, together with the aforementioned Martin, he had gone to purchase the episcopate for him without the others’ knowledge—he corrupted, by money given and promised, a certain Theoderic, deacon of his household, a man sharp-witted and exceedingly ambitious, so that he might become his defender against the others. For Theoderic was more eloquent and influential than the others, but he was also double-minded: he had secured himself on both sides, on the one hand to conduct the church’s case, and on the other to remain his faithful helper.

In the end, after he had repeatedly frustrated the efforts made against Guothfrid and had often encouraged him, Theoderic was, by the just judgment of God, struck by the kind of disease that the Greeks call *lienteria* [Note: *liemeriam*?—that is, Greek λειεντερία, “lientery” or chronic diarrhea]. Unexpectedly, when he had risen to empty his bowels, he died at the same moment as the evacuation.

8. Accordingly, as the appointed time for the council that was to be held concerning this matter approached, a council was announced for Toul on 13 March, during Lent (the year 1127, 13 March). There, with the aforementioned Peter the cardinal presiding, together with Bishops Stephen of Metz, Henry of Toul, and Gerard of Troyes, and with many abbots and the leading men of the region present, Peter first produced and read aloud the letter of the lord pope, which reported to the apostolic see the infamous circumstances of this installation.

Then, after the members of the council had taken their seats in order, he admonished them concerning obedience to the Roman Church—which it is sacrilegious to violate—and ordered them not to omit stating whatever they knew about the matter.

I cannot adequately explain all that he heard at that time, especially since many loudly declared that they had seen these things, while others said that they had heard them. They declared that they were so certain of this that, if anyone doubted it, they were willing to establish its truth by oath.

But when he saw that the situation was almost hopeless and had nothing else with which to evade the matter, he said that, since none of his fellow bishops was present there to accuse him of this deed, it seemed just to him that he should be permitted to clear himself by his own hand alone of the infamy directed against him [Note: *post* supplied by the manuscript correction].

When they denied this and said that he had nevertheless been accused by Catholic and truthful persons—and indeed that, since any person, even a prostitute, as they say, may accuse simony alone, when known to be true, out of zeal for God, he ought to clear himself by the testimony of religious brethren—they read aloud many decrees of the saints concerning this matter.

While these were being read, a certain bearer arrived with a letter subscribed by the bishop of Mainz, in which he called himself a legate of the apostolic see. Those who were present know how indignantly everyone received this. After the letter had been read aloud before them all, Peter addressed Guothfrid as follows:

“Earlier, brother, you complained that violence was being done to you because there was no fellow bishop to accuse you. Now you hear what this man testifies against you.”

9. Since he had no suitable answer to offer, another council was announced at Worms, and he was ordered to appear there and clear himself together with six bishops, himself being the seventh.

But, at the request of everyone who pleaded God’s mercy and the clemency of the lord Honorius, supreme pontiff, they made a more lenient decree: he was to clear himself before three bishops, two abbots, and likewise two priests of good reputation, on the sixty-fourth day from that time, namely, 15 May, the Sunday before Pentecost.

When this period of delay had elapsed and they had arrived at Worms, he had none of the persons appointed to assist him. Two of the bishops mentioned above were present, those of Verdun and Toul, as well as three others: Bucko of that city, Siegfried of Speyer, and Ulrich of Constance, a man of very great religious devotion.

When they had taken their seats, Henry of Verdun, who had also been present at Toul, was asked for his judgment. He declared that, since Guothfrid had not produced the persons named for his purification [Note: The manuscript reads *personis*; corrected to *personas*.], it was just that he should cease from office after being deprived of his episcopal dignity.

At this, Guothfrid became angry and, filled with a spirit of wrath, began urging those who were with him to go outside, seize weapons, return inside, and slaughter the party that had opposed him [Note: The manuscript reads *f. e.*; corrected to *foras egressi*].

It is not irrelevant to report how, by the intervention of God’s grace, they refrained from doing this. For Guothfrid, adding sin to sin, took up the sacred Gospel and swore upon it that he was innocent of the crime charged against him.

After he had done this, his followers came running with great haste, dragged him by the hands, and led him out of the council. As though he had achieved his will and retained his honor, they proceeded along the road singing. Thus that assembly escaped the hands of the wicked.

Then the cardinal, having consulted the bishops and the entire clergy concerning the matter, decreed that on the following day he should excommunicate Guothfrid together with all who had carried him away.

When they heard this, everyone withdrew from his companionship. Thus, although the previous day he had left the council accompanied by a great crowd, when he came after being summoned on the following day, he scarcely had one man to follow him.

Terrified by this, he prostrated himself face down and placed himself at everyone’s mercy. He obtained only that the necessities of life be granted him; and, delaying no longer, though unwillingly because he could not prevail, he laid aside his pontifical insignia on 17 May [16 Kalends of June] 1127.

# APPENDIX OF TREVErAN DOCUMENTS

[Col. 1233]

## FROM THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT CELSUS, BY THE AUTHOR THEODERICUS

### [NOTE]

Theodericus, who entered the monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier in 1006, wrote, at the request of Abbot Richard, a little book on the translation and miracles of Saint Celsus. His style is indeed inflated, but he transmitted to memory much information about Egbert’s affairs and other matters worthy of notice, after prefacing the work with a dedication to Abbot Richard. These materials are repeated from the *Acta Sanctorum*, February, vol. III, p. 396, where they were published from the Budecensian and Treveran manuscripts.

[Col. 1233C] To the most excellent laborer of Christ and most magnificent father Richard, his own last among his own, Theodericus—among monks there is none held more worthless, though he has not forgotten his monastic purpose—offers, with every convoluted apology set aside, the service of true obedience. [Col. 1234C]

For your fatherly piety asks—or rather, enjoins by an unavoidable command—that my littleness should not delay in committing to writing and memory, for the benefit of posterity, the discovery of the most sacred relic of the blessed confessor of Christ, Celsus, whose outstanding merits are proclaimed by the etymology of his name; likewise, the occasion on which, though known to the Divinity before time began, in our foul days the blessed relics of Celsus were solemnly found by Egbert, of pious memory, hierarch of the city of Trier, and finally revealed to mortals for some extraordinary benefit to the Church; and the distinguished evidence of his merits, recognized as having been accomplished more clearly than daylight for the welcome manifestation of so great a treasure, hidden until then.

For you do not think it right that such a radiance of miracles belonging to so great a man, poured forth from heaven for the increase of the salvation of many, should remain buried in the sluggish silence of inactivity and vanish like smoke into the air.

To this I replied: “I am greatly astonished, I confess, and struck by intense amazement that such a prudent man should be minded to do this, and that, setting aside and almost despising so many native servants who act irreproachably at home and in public service, whom you nourish with sacred teaching in the spiritual school of blessed Eucharius, you should prefer to load the inexperienced and weak shoulders of a newcomer with so great a burden.

“For I call upon the all-knowing God as witness—not because I am of such a mind as to wish, which would be wrong, to resist your command even by murmuring—I have found among your labors several brothers of more advanced ability who, if this same burden were imposed upon them under the guidance of obedience, could, to speak truthfully, carry it on unwearied shoulders and fully satisfy your wishes in every respect.

“But what need is there to say more? Monks are specifically destined above others to show no delay in fulfilling the commands of their superiors; and although impossible tasks may be imposed upon them, they should always trust in the Lord’s mercy and know that everything will be possible for them to accomplish.

“Therefore I shall attempt what you command, firmly convinced that blessed Celsus can obtain for me by his prayers that I may deserve to swim across this gray-blue sea with my cargo safely preserved and reach the desired harbor unharmed.”

1. Since it is plainly evident to all who pursue divine and human philosophy that the Treveran metropolis has rightly and deservedly been called the chief church [*archisterium*] of all Gaul, both because of the antiquity of its worldly dignity and because of the cardinal majesty of the Catholic faith, and since by a certain special distinction of apostolic authority it has been exalted more splendidly than all the churches around it, it is surely because of this joyful circumstance: the personal Trinity and essential Unity, God, creator of the universe, deigned to visit and illuminate it with the primordial splendor of the holy Gospel through the perpetually reward-worthy labor of three of his workers.

It would indeed be most inconsistent if the things that he decided to reveal with such merciful regard at the end of time before the court of that same city should evaporate into the air like smoke through the torpor of silence [Note: *jam* supplied by the edition.].

[Col. 1236A] 2. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 978, when Otto II of blessed memory, kinsman of the great Augustus Otto, was vigorously governing the summit of the Roman monarchy as prince upon the throne, the blessed Egbert, an archimandrite of shining virtues and illustrious reputation, presided over the holy Treveran Church, which God was to preserve.
