He was distinguished by the nobility of his family [Note: On this, compare above, *Gesta*, chapter 29.], but even more distinguished by the inestimable gift of complete integrity. Indeed, because he flourished splendidly in this twofold distinction, he surpassed all the bishops and leading men of the kingdom by the very force of his reverence, as due honor demanded.

Finally, he was tall in stature, while his face shone with a radiant beauty more attractively than all the leading men of that time. He was the foremost protector and nourisher of monks and a special lover of regular discipline. For beneath the habit of a bishop he concealed the humble heart of a most devoted monk, and thus, like Martha, he poured himself outward into the frequent service of the Lord, while, like Mary, he devoted himself entirely to the study of the divine word, making himself a pleasing sacrifice to the Divinity: in practical matters a dove, but in rhetoric a turtledove.

What worthy account can I give of his generosity, by which he was uniquely enriched? In him one might see a new John whom they call *Eleemon*, for the wealth that God had bestowed upon him so abundantly he transmitted, as I may say, with a full horn, through the hands of the needy into heaven.

3. The monasteries subject to the Treveran see were, before his time, poor beyond the ordinary condition of those serving God and exhausted by the harshest shortage of provisions and equipment. Consequently, monastic religion suffered no small decline.

As the purifier of perfected morals grew rarer, that fire of divine love which Truth sent into the world and wished to burn intensely, while iniquity was increasing everywhere, began not merely to grow cold but, more dangerously, to be extinguished by every means.

For his predecessor, Theodericus of venerable memory, was indeed a most eloquent teacher and an industrious steward of the household of the Lord. But because the straitness of the times repeatedly constrained him through the many exactions of the state, he was less able to provide for the needs of the monasteries—for he had no resources available to him.

But Egbert, worthy of being named with the highest reverence, walked the royal road neither to the right nor to the left. He did not fear to restrain the ambition of soldiers; as an impartial judge, he suppressed by his authority the tyranny of his fellow provincials; and whatever had been taken from the monasteries by hostile invasion, he gathered back from every quarter by the force of his authority and, with great vigilance, restored it to the monasteries. Like a pious head of a household, he took the greatest care to repair what had been neglected and worn out with age.

4. When he turned his fatherly eyes toward the enclosure of blessed Eucharius and felt deep compassion for the extreme poverty of its monks, he wisely chose first a steward worthy of the monastery, namely an abbot named Gotherus, who had been exceptionally well disciplined at the monastery of Ghent.

He bestowed upon him so much additional income from fields and vineyards, apart from many other gifts useful for adorning the monastery, that, as long as the sphere of the heavens revolves, his perpetual merit might accordingly continue to increase.

How much he granted with a generous hand to the other monasteries equally subject to his pastoral care and nearly collapsing under the pressure of poverty, and how he came to the aid of monastic religion—which at that time seemed everywhere to be ruined—as a chief physician favorable to languishing souls, exceeds all measure and calculation; therefore speech fails when attempting to narrate it.

Finally, charity, the guide of virtues, held the scepter in his heart with such vigorous authority that he could rightly say with blessed Job: “From my mother’s womb charity came forth with me” (Job 31:18).

5. He often grieved and repeatedly drew deep sighs with tearful eyes because the chapel in which the precious chief bishop of the Lord, Eucharius, rests in peace together with his most blessed companions and awaits the Redeemer’s coming had, after so many passing years, continued in an exceedingly humble and poor structure.

Anxiously turning the matter over in the archive of his mind, he considered how, as long as life and health permitted, he might polish the church of the Lord down to its very nails with an adornment worthy, in human estimation, of such patrons, after laying a new foundation and equipping it with every kind of ornament [Note: Budé reads *decreverit*, “he had decided.”].

He regarded our old building as worthless and, obliquely speaking, called it a storehouse of revenues.

6. While he was occupied with this spiritual desire through frequent reflection, it happened on one occasion that he was in the company of the aforementioned prince, who had honored him with the prerogative of apostolic dignity, along with other ecclesiastical leaders in a moral conversation. Among other counsels for the benefit of the Church, he opened to him the doors of this intention.

The emperor, as the most Catholic ruler of the worldly court, rejoicing together with the bishop in so great a desire, burst forth in the excessive joy of his heart with these words:

“Blessed be God upon the throne of his eternal majesty, who has deigned to inspire us with a will so pleasing to him! And blessed be the unanimous company of the monks of blessed Eucharius, through whose necessary prayers the destinies of our entire empire are ruled by the Lord.

“And if divine providence brings this undertaking to fulfillment in our days, I shall now gladly enter upon the way of all flesh, provided that before Jesus Christ, the just judge, I may deserve to find blessed Eucharius, the first pious teacher of the city of Trier, as a patron for my transgressions.

“And now,” he said, “go as quickly as possible and apply yourselves with every effort of the spirit to so pious a labor. For God, who has granted you the will, is able also to supply the power.

“But I do not want you to be unaware of this: if you strive with fervent determination to lay the foundation, then, once I have learned that it has risen to such a height that it displays one cubit above the ground, I shall provide you with such assistance from our treasury that, after a short interval of a few years, its progress will increase through joyful labor until it reaches its summit, beyond all ordinary expectation.”

7. Encouraged by this glorious imperial promise, the blessed bishop, accompanied by divine assistance and eager to fulfill in action what he had conceived in his mind, summoned and assembled a great number of masons and diggers and hastened to the site.

After work had gone on for several days in digging, the excavators suddenly, through unexpected blows, struck—three or four times, as it pleased the Divinity—the tomb of blessed Celsus. [Lacuna.]

The sarcophagus itself, in which the naked grain of resurrection had lain hidden for so many years in preparation for ripening, was made of a stone of marvelous whiteness, which the common people call chalk. Above it was a marble slab on which an inscription, a sign of his sanctity, had been carved. It contained these words:

> Anxious, whoever you are, and desiring to know the tomb,  
> Here lies Celsus, illustrious in name and in merits,  
> Whom the Lord marked with true honor,  
> Ever vigorous everywhere, not sluggish toward his homeland;  
>   
> He drew his lineage and origin from a noble stock,  
> And with pious devotion is buried in this tomb.

8. The workman who first of all came upon the tomb was a peasant, almost incapable of every kind of understanding, as people of that class are known to be. He did not know that blessed Job had said: “I diligently investigated a cause that I did not know” (Job 5:6). Instead, heedlessly giving his hand to rashness, he struck at the slab with a double-headed axe, so that the inscription could scarcely have been read accurately even by learned men. [Lacuna.]

9. When such joyful news had swiftly reached the knowledge of the pious bishop, he blessed God, the giver of all gifts, with abundant praise and thanksgiving. Then, eager and knowing no delay, he rushed to behold the divine spectacle, surrounded by the clergy.

Although he was exceedingly eager for the work he had begun, he nevertheless endured this interruption with the greatest joy, assured by true faith, on the testimony of the inscription, that in his days the regard of the Divinity had graciously descended upon the city of Trier.

After carefully examining everything that had happened with the scalpel of prudence, he did not dare move the tomb of the blessed relic from the place of its deposition. He merely arranged for it to be marked with the seal of his authority under the watch of guards. In the meantime he stationed monks there to sing psalms, so that, on account of the merits of so great a just man, they might offer unceasing praises to the Divinity until he could learn more fully, with the advice of his fellow bishops, what ought to be done about so great a matter.

He then had a copy made of the inscription and entrusted it to the key-bearer of the episcopal household.

10. According to the inviolate statute of so great a shepherd, the brothers continually performed the divine office day and night in the resting place of the just, now under the open sky, now beneath a roof. With urgent prayers they importuned the highest Sun, who undoubtedly fulfills the will of those who fear him and is accustomed to hear their supplication.

Not long afterward, by imperial decree, a solemn synod of very many bishops and abbots was summoned at the royal palace called, in the barbarian language, Engilenheim [Note: Nothing else is known about it. But after 977, when Egbert became archbishop, Otto II did not come to Ingilenheim until 980.]. The fathers of Belgica and Germany were present, and necessary measures for the benefit of the Church were there promulgated sweetly, with the authority of the sacred canons preceding them, and ordered to be observed inviolably by posterity.

The metropolitan of the Treveran Church, the well-deserving Egbert, necessarily attended. His memory, as long as the present age is spoken of, must always be held in blessing, because it is attributed to his pious efforts that the clergy of his church were ennobled by learning and religion.

After many matters demanded by the synodal rubric had been discussed there, when that great archbishop—who held primacy among them all—saw that he had an opportunity to speak, he took up a small tablet on which the inscription of blessed Celsus had been written. In the eloquence of Cicero he set forth before them, in due order, what the divine favor had revealed at his city. He then read the inscription aloud.

When the emperor heard this, he was filled with immense joy and addressed the sacred and God-speaking assembly in these words:

“Rejoice, brothers and fathers, in the Lord, and praise our Lord God from the depths of your hearts, who, through the marvelous grace of his eternal goodness, has deigned to look upon our times by giving his Church at the Treveran metropolis a new patron, blessed Celsus. He was exceedingly full of virtues and full of days, and from the time of his departure from Egypt until now he has dwelt in the heavenly realms among the companies of angels [Note: *Emplumé*, “feathered,” or “winged.”].

“Again I ask you, rejoice, because, to speak truthfully, from that moment not only has our salvation been increased, but also the integrity of the pious shepherd of that city, whom you now see before you, has been clearly revealed.”

When the priests of both orders of the Lord who had attended that sacred synod heard this, they raised their hands toward heaven and poured forth pious tears of joy. They gave immense thanks to the Creator, who had not allowed so glorious a relic to remain buried any longer, but had judged that its merit before him should be made manifest through shining miracles.

For it was not right that the one to whom the Lord had already awarded the crown of righteousness in heaven should lack the service of the ecclesiastical army on earth.

After this, the holy council decided that, with a narrow edict preceding the action [Note: Greek πρόσταγμα, that is, “edict”] and with the indivisible agreement of the bishops accompanying it, the Treveran bishop should promptly revisit his see, raise the body of blessed Celsus from its own tomb together with the subordinate clergy, and place it in an exalted position within a small chest, as though in a treasury of divine riches. Then, with every mark of holiness, he was to place it upon the sacred altar like a member—no ordinary member—of the supreme King.

11. Having received such a mandate and counsel, the blessed archbishop Egbert, like a prudent creature, fortified himself with the blessings and prayers of so many fathers. He also bound himself more firmly to imperial favor, and thus hastened his journey with a prosperous outcome, protected by divine guardianship and accompanied by a crowd of companions.

When he had returned to his own see, after a few days had passed, he summoned to himself all the abbots and monks endowed with wisdom, as well as the priests and clerics belonging to his diocese, and publicly related the event to them.

When he found them all in agreement with the synodal decree, he immediately arranged a solemn procession with crosses, candles, censers, jeweled Gospel books, and every kind of ecclesiastical equipment. The brothers joined together in singing the Lord’s hymn sweetly, and, full of tears of joy, he proceeded slowly to the sanctuary of blessed Eucharius. [Lacuna.]

## MIRACLES

[Col. 1239]

[Col. 1239D] Having at last completed, though in an unpolished discourse and with a rustic pen, what the sequence of the narrative required concerning the discovery of the precious body of Saint Celsus, confessor of Christ, we must now turn our style toward explaining his celebrated miracles. [Lacuna.]

After the sacred relics of blessed Celsus had been kept upon the altar of Saint Eucharius for an entire month after their discovery, it pleased Gunderadus, the father of that monastery, and all the brothers that the chest of Saint Celsus should be carried into the nave of the church and placed upon the altar of the Holy Cross, which is at the entrance of the sanctuary. [Lacuna.] For in the same monastery of Saint Eucharius there was a certain poor man named Richolfus. [Lacuna.]

When the celebration of the Mass had been completed and everything had been duly finished, the bishop gave gifts to blessed Celsus and clothed the man who had been healed—and who had become a wonder to everyone—in the monastic habit. He belonged to the household of the bishop. The bishop imposed upon him the command that, as long as he lived, he should never presume to withdraw his foot from the service of the Church.

This same poor man, renewed in health, served in the monastery for many years as he had been ordered. After his cure, he flourished with such bodily strength and abounded in such vigor that he could find no equal among all the monastery’s servants. It therefore happened that, with the agreement of the brothers, he was assigned to a more important service—namely, the office of fuller—which he diligently performed for many years without reproach and remained beloved by all.

Nor must I conceal in silence what happened in our own presence a few years ago. In the same monastery of Saint Eucharius there grew up a small boy of monastic character named Martin, who had been offered to blessed Eucharius from his mother’s womb. [Lacuna.] When a tutor of boys named Dominicus, a young man of good promise, [Lacuna.]

In the suburb of the same monastery, nearly five years ago, there was a certain young man named Thiezo, who is still alive. Struck by the disease that physicians call elephantiasis, he came close to death. [Lacuna.] Although that plague was raging severely in the same year and had caused no small slaughter among the Christian people, [Lacuna.]

Nor do I judge that the following should be placed in the last position: what Christ, the pious and merciful Redeemer of the world, deigned to accomplish in the days of Liutolf, archbishop of this city of Trier. A certain ministerial of the same monastery had a swineherd named Peter. [Lacuna.]

About four years ago, a seven-year-old boy named Azelinus grew up in the same monastery. He still breathes in good health, and nearly all our brothers know him. [Lacuna.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1007, in the fifth indiction, a certain possessed woman from a neighboring village of the monastery [Lacuna.] was brought there. When the annual feast of Saint Valerius, confessor of Christ, arrived and the people of Trier hurried eagerly to so great a patron, [Lacuna.]

Since we have already committed to writing, as truthfully as we could, some of the miracles of the blessed man that we learned from truthful narrators, we judge it wholly improper that the things which, in our own age, the Divinity chose to perform through that same father should be silenced in sluggish quiet.

In the aforementioned monastery of blessed Eucharius there lived a young man of exceptional character named Burchardus. From almost the time of his cradle, his parents had entrusted him there to be nourished by Almighty God. He is still alive and serves in the office of deacon; moreover, because of his extraordinary usefulness, he is an honor to the monastery above many others. [Lacuna.] The abbot of the monastery was Gunderadus, of blessed memory. [Lacuna.]

Thus far we have dealt with what we learned concerning the powers of the holy man through domestic and familiar report—that is, only those events said to have occurred at suitable times either within the enclosure of blessed Eucharius or in the dependencies of that same monastery.

Now the proper order of the narrative demands that we discuss some events from nearer and farther places that have been brought to our knowledge. [Lacuna.]

There is in the same city of Trier a certain monastery, which in ancient times received the name of Horrei and was consecrated to the Queen of Heaven. From the time of the orthodox King Dagobert, holy women had always been accustomed to serve God there with particular devotion.

There, finally, a certain nun of noble descent named Henza proved to be of no small usefulness, as they say. [Lacuna.]

At another time, in that same monastery of the ever-virgin Mary, there was a certain nun named Geila, born of noble blood and held there in no low position. [Lacuna.]

Nor do we think it permissible to pass over in silence what, within recent memory, the benevolent favor of the Divinity determined to reveal in the same monastery through the celebrated merits of blessed Celsus.

A certain nun of distinguished lineage, who from infancy had lived there, was named Glismoda. [Lacuna.]

Up to this point, on account of the smallness of the spark divinely bestowed upon me, I have merely recorded what I heard, in whatever sort of composition I could manage. Now, at the conclusion of this little work, I would like to bring forth something that divine power has deigned to display in me through blessed Celsus; but, as I think, this is more appropriately recounted if it is assigned to a separate chapter of its own. For just as inserting the benefits bestowed on others into truthful accounts for the increase of divine praise is recognized as bringing great reward, so concealing one’s own benefits is believed to incur no small condemnation.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1006, which is the last year of the twenty-fifth nineteen-year cycle in the second series of the great year called the paschal year, [Col. 1242C] with Christ guiding me I escaped naked from the surging sea of this world and fled, for the sake of hospitality, to the safest harbor of blessed Eucharius. When I had been received with sufficient familial affection by the father of that monastery, a man of the highest veneration named Richard, and treated with every monastic devotion, he ordered me, though unworthy, to be joined to the assembly of the brothers; and he addressed me not as a guest but as a most intimate friend, with gracious speech.

After he had perceived that my small ability possessed no little knowledge of the monastic order—both from his own dove-like simplicity and because, on account of my advanced age, he supposed me to be learned, although I had not been fully instructed even in the first letters, so to speak—he persuaded me with paternal authority not to delay writing something in praise of the Redeemer and concerning the renowned virtues and newly manifested miracles of Saint Celsus, even if with a rustic pen. Thinking that I certainly ought not to resist this persuasion, partly compelled by the command of so great a father and partly by the common entreaty of the brothers, I recently undertook, during the days of Lent, to fashion this little work.

And, to tell the truth, although for three successive years I had been so entangled in gout, through swelling and ulceration of the legs, that I could scarcely support myself with a staff, praise be to God! after I had completed what I had learned about Saint Celsus, through the intercession of so great a patron I was restored so completely that you might think me Asahel rather than a limping monk.

[Col. 1243]

## ON THE ABBEY OF SAINT MARTIN, FROM THE LIFE OF SAINT MAGNERICUS, BY THE AUTHOR EBERWIN

### [Note]

At the beginning of the eleventh century, Eberwin, abbot of Saint Martin at Trier, either first wrote or prepared a new edition of the Life of Saint Magnericus, archbishop, who had founded the monastery over which Eberwin himself presided. The work was published from a manuscript of Saint Martin in *Acta Sanctorum*, July VI, p. 183. At the end he added the following concerning Magnericus’s tomb and the fortunes of the monastery:

[Col. 1243A] His body was buried in the church we have mentioned, that of Saint Martin at Trier, where it is now venerated with fitting honor. Since it had been buried some feet away from the altar, in our time the holy priest appeared in a vision to an honorable man named Berengarius, a monk of that same church, and ordered him to adapt an altar to the tomb. He, treating the matter as the ravings of a dream, paid no attention; but he was warned a second time, and on the third occasion was rebuked by the priest. He reported what he had seen to the most reverend lord Robert, bishop. Then the bishop came to the church and, seeing how matters stood, ordered that, according to the holy priest’s command, a holy altar be fitted to the tomb and that a canopy be constructed over it, as is customary.

[Col. 1243B] That church, having long before collapsed through age and having been burned, together with the city itself, in the Norman devastation, was entrusted by Rabbodo, bishop of Trier, to a certain religious and ecclesiastical man, Abbot Regino [Col. 1243C] [Note: Along with Browerus, *Annales Treverenses*, book I, p. 440, and Bosch, *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, p. 175, I have thought that Regino of Prüm is intended—the man who, expelled from Prüm, lived at Trier and there, at Rabbodo’s command, wrote his books *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*.], in the years 883–917, and by him was restored to its former condition. And, as we find in the most ancient privileges of a certain church, that place had always been under abbots, because there—as in the other principal churches of the city—there was a station, seat, and residence of the bishop; and by tradition from blessed Magnericus the abbots of that place wore the episcopal insignia and performed the bishop’s functions in divine service only when he was absent.

[Col. 1243C] After Abbot Regino’s death, however, it was granted to laymen as a benefice, and that little abbey was divided first among Bertoald, brother of Bishop Rotger, and then among various others. Thus, later, in the time of Duke Albert [Col. 1243C] [Note: Perhaps the same man whom Sigebert names in *Miracles of Saint Maximinus*, chapter 16, *Acta Sanctorum* IV, 233; yet he was not a duke here. Conrad, son-in-law of Otto I, seems to be intended. For there can scarcely be discussion here of the battles between Conrad and Adalbert at the beginning of the eleventh century.], when there was frequent and extreme disturbance and sedition among the kingdoms, the entire episcopal property was so plundered by invaders of the holy Church that nothing within or outside the city remained which the malicious invaders did not claim for themselves or carry away [Col. 1243] [Note: *deriperent* in the edition]. There was then no regard for God’s priest, no reverence for the Church; everywhere there was plunder, everywhere fires. The walls were destroyed and the churches violated. Then that place too, attacked by the enemies of God like rabid dogs and wolves, was so demolished that, apart from the walls of the church, there remained—not merely no buildings—but not even traces of the foundations. The same church, uncovered and deserted, was at times accessible to wild beasts.

Therefore, moved at last by the greatest compassion, the venerable Bishop Theoderic [Col. 1244C] [Note: A.D. 964–975], after he had recovered the place in his own time by royal authority [Col. 1244C] [Note: Compare Otto II’s charter in Hontheim, *History*, I, 310], entrusted its governance to a certain religious abbot, Angilbert, a servant of God, granting him some possessions belonging to the place—namely, so that by establishing a regular life there, a community of monks might thereafter dwell there, and so that it would no longer be granted as a benefice, lest the place be endangered on that pretext, but, serving God and his saints, might be subject to the bishop’s authority rather than that of tyrants.

This abbot, establishing a monastic residence there, gathered a small but honorable community of monks serving God. The bishop, rejoicing in his industry and good works, brought back from Rome an apostolic document [Col. 1244C] [Note: Benedict VII’s. It was published in *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, p. 176, and in Hontheim, *History*, I, p. 316; there the Life of Magnericus is cited, as it appears in his own Life. Certainly a different work must be understood from this one, which Eberwin wrote after the time of Theoderic and Pope Benedict, unless one wishes to say that these passages concerning the monastery of Saint Martin were later added by Eberwin to an older Life. Compare above.], by which that recently restored place, strengthened by the privilege of the aforesaid grant, might thereafter remain secure by its own stability, and, having been granted to the monks, might obey the authority of the bishop and no other; and so that the monks, living according to the rule, might also have the right of election according to the constitution [Col. 1244C] of Saint Benedict.

After the aforementioned man had governed the place for some time, fortified by apostolic decree, he happily departed this life.

After him, with the bishop’s consent and the election of the brothers, we who are writing this, though unworthy, undertook the governance of the same cell, and to this day, as best we can, we labor in the Lord’s vineyard, though useless servants. . . .

[Col. 1245]

## FROM THE MIRACLES OF SAINT SYMEON, BY THE AUTHOR EBERWIN

### [Note]

Eberwin was the abbot who, together with Richard, abbot of Verdun, had accompanied the monk Symeon on his return from the Holy Land, later received him into his own monastery, and remained closely attached to him in friendship until his death. Archbishop Poppo commissioned him to write the Life of the holy man, as it seemed to be. Eberwin undertook this task modestly and carried it out by briefly and simply recounting what he had heard from Symeon or had himself witnessed. He added some miracles performed after the saint’s death and dedicated the entire work to Poppo, prefacing it with this letter:

[Col. 1245A] To the lord and venerable Poppo, archbishop, Brother Eberwin, unworthy to bear the name of abbot, devoted servant of both men.

You urge—or rather command—me, most holy father, though deficient in talent and foolish in expression, to explain something about the life, conduct, and death of the man of God Symeon, and about the miracles that the Lord worked through him, and to make it known to the many who desire to learn these things for the praise and glory of the Lord. I confess that you place a great burden upon me, weak as I am, especially since, being infirm in my whole body, I fear the dreadful judgment of God if I should invent anything false.

Trusting, therefore, in God’s help, I obey your commands, trembling though I am, describing in plain, brief, and simple speech what I myself heard from his mouth or learned from faithful men—whether they had heard it from him or had witnessed the miracles. It is therefore for your judgment to decide whether you wish this little work to be made public, or to entrust it to your learned men for correction, embellishment, and expansion. Whatever is found blameworthy in me must necessarily be attributed rather to you, who commanded, than to me, who obeyed.

### [Note]

[Col. 1245]

This Life, which survives in many manuscripts—several of which I myself saw, though I did not copy them—was published in *Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 89, and in Mabillon, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict* VI, p. 372. Hontheim, *Prodromus* I, p. 665, gives some excerpts.

Eberwin found Symeon at Antioch, sent westward from the monastery of Mount Sinai to collect the money promised by Richard, duke of the Normans. He tells the story as follows:

[Col. 1245B] At that time it happened that Abbot Richard, a man worthy of imitation by the perfect, wished, out of pious devotion, to visit the holy places of Jerusalem. While we were traveling through Antioch and were compelled by the necessities of the journey to remain there for some time, the servant of God Symeon formed a friendship with us, adopting the aforementioned Abbot Richard as his father. After he had explained to him in order what had been entrusted to him and what had happened, he added that no dangers or hardships could restrain him from fulfilling his abbot’s commands to the best of his ability.

So we set out and returned, and found him ready to come with us. Although he was frequently insulted and beaten in our company, he endured it patiently, like the gentlest sheep. When we reached the city of Belgrade, situated on the frontier of the Bulgarians and Hungarians, the city’s most unfortunate ruler forbade him to cross with us. Therefore, weeping and giving thanks to God, he left us sorrowful and in tears.

After [Col. 1245] [Note: *Per* in the edition] many hardships and ambushes by robbers, he eventually returned as far as the sea; having crossed it and continued on a prosperous journey, he reached France by way of Rome. A certain Count William, known to him, received him kindly, and he remained with him for some time. . . . He came to Rouen, the most illustrious city of the Normans, greatly distinguished by the body and merits of Saint Audoenus the confessor. There he found Count Richard already dead, and, since no one gave him an answer concerning the money and tribute owed from Richard’s territory as alms to his monastery, he became somewhat distressed. . . . He asked advice about what he should do.

It then occurred to him that he should visit his dearest father, namely Abbot Richard, and us, his companions; and this he did. He remained with us for a long time, and, to conclude briefly [Col. 1245] [Note: *lightly* in the edition], as long as he stayed with us, he lived irreproachably.

Meanwhile, the lord Poppo, archbishop and energetic guardian of the holy Church of Trier, hearing the prophet devoutly say concerning Christ, “And his tomb shall be glorious” (Isaiah II, 10), went to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. He had this servant of God as his companion and fellow traveler both on the outward and return journeys; and after his return he offered him, and most willingly granted him, the freedom to remain wherever he wished within his diocese.

Symeon, the servant of Christ, therefore, discerning through a revelation from God a place where he could devote himself to prayer in solitude, asked for a small hut in the tower formerly called the Black Gate. There Lord Bishop Poppo enclosed him there in the presence of the clergy and people on the feast of Saint Andrew. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

At that time, because our sins deserved it, an excessive inundation of waters arose. Symeon was blamed by everyone as the cause of this danger: they said that he was a sorcerer and that this evil threatened the world on account of his crimes. Every day the people cried out that he should be removed by the bishop.

At last a mob was assembled from the city, and they hurried to the holy man’s cell. They threw stones upward and blocked the windows of the hut, attempting to stone Symeon. I confess that we saw the broken window; but Symeon, Christ’s athlete, founded upon the firm rock, remained unmoved, and, giving thanks to God, prayed joyfully for his persecutors. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

As the years passed, Symeon, the man of God, foresaw the dissolution of his body (A.D. 1035). At last he asked the lord bishop to send him expenses and workmen to construct a bed for him; he himself prepared a burial place in one part of his dwelling: “This is my resting place forever and ever. Here I shall await the day of the Lord; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it.”

A few days later, I, a humble man, was summoned to him. Although unworthy to kiss his feet, I was admitted by him into the cell. After prayer, embraces, kisses, and tears, we sat down. . . . . . . [Col. 1247B] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

After 105 days had passed, he fell ill on the octave of Pentecost [Col. 1247D] [Note: That is, May 25] and ordered Stephen, who served him, to give him rest for several days, so that he might devote himself more than usual to contemplation. Stephen waited one day. On Tuesday evening Symeon gave a sign and suspended a basket with bread from the window. When morning came, Stephen found it untouched, just as he had left it, and, deeply anxious, went up to him. When questioned, Symeon answered only: “What do you want? Go in peace.”

Fearing, Stephen reported the matter in order to Gozelo, a cleric who was very close to the man of God, saying that Lord Symeon was extremely ill and was not speaking to him as he usually did. The cleric visited him on Thursday. The servant of God gave no answer [Col. 1247C], but nevertheless accepted a drink from his hand and drew himself back onto his bed.

On the eighth day, when the cleric visited him very early, he found him at the point of death and informed me. I ran there quickly. Though infirm throughout his body and especially weak in his legs, I climbed up as if healthy and without pain. I found him still alive and already drawing his final breath. With only two brothers, namely Anselm and Robert, who had come with me, we performed as best we could the funeral rites owed for the absolution of his soul.

Thus, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1035, on Sunday at the third hour, on the Kalends of June, he returned his holy soul to the most merciful Creator whom he had always served.

Immediately everyone gathered. Monks, clerics, virgins consecrated to God, common people of both sexes, and everyone who could hear about it hurried to the funeral of so great a man. Therefore, just as he himself had arranged—or rather foretold—we prepared his little body according to the custom of his homeland and placed it in the tomb with psalms and praises of God.

[Col. 1248A] Leaving the tomb open, we appointed people to serve in the vigils and offices. On the following day the entire city gathered as though it were one man; the inner house was decorated with ecclesiastical ornaments. While the funeral rites were being celebrated by all in common. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . it seemed to everyone that the body of so great a man should not be neglected, but should be guarded in turn by clerics appointed for the following thirty days.

Accordingly, after the ninth hour, the tomb was carefully closed. While the clerics, during their appointed watches, were singing psalms in the cell where the body of the man of God had been buried, one . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

On the thirtieth day after the death of the man of God Symeon, a great crowd began to gather at the tomb with candles and other gifts. A certain old woman. . . . . . . . [Col. 1248B] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

From that time onward the tomb of the man of God was frequented and venerated by the people. When a convenient ascent was being prepared in the tower building, a piece of timber was being dragged by many people; and when it had already been raised to a considerable height, the rope broke and it began to threaten death to the crowd that had gathered and stood below. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Here, too [Col. 1247] [Note: *Quo* in the edition], I would like to insert the miracles which those same people who were healed testify occurred during his life. For a certain woman named Cecilia, after suffering for a long time. . . . . . . It was related by a certain cleric, Gozelo. . . . . . . A certain little boy named Bezelinus. . . . . . . A certain woman born in the district of Metz. . . . . . . . . . . Another. . . a little boy of a certain priest Adelard. . . . . . . . .

On another Sunday, a certain woman from the estate of the brothers called Mandiricium [Col. 1248C] [Note: Perhaps Manderen, four leagues from the city toward the southeast. Henschenius]. . . . . . Suddenly the woman’s parents and the estate’s officials arrived. . . . . . A certain Adalmannus, a priest and citizen of Trier, while traveling. . . . . . A certain woman from the district of Trier. . . . . . A certain servant of the count palatine had a maidservant. . . . . . A certain knight named Bertramnus had a maidservant in his service. . . . . .

On the Kalends of November, when the lord bishop had decided to consecrate an altar in honor of all the saints in the tower building where the body of the man of God had been buried, a great crowd began to gather from every direction. While preparations were being made and the lord bishop was awaited. . . . . .

A certain peasant named Godefridus. . . . . .

[Col. 1248D] At that time, when the city of Trier was renowned for such great miracles. . . . . . There happened to be among us a monk from Alemannia, not moderately trained in the liberal arts. . . . . .

[Col. 1247]

## FROM THE LIFE OF SAINT AGRITIUS

### [Note]

I explained above that this Life of Saint Agritius, which must be counted among the precious historical monuments of Trier, was composed in the middle of the eleventh century. Most of what is narrated here belongs to earlier times; of those matters I have presented below in the notes whatever seemed useful for illuminating the narrative of the *Gesta*. Now I shall add one passage recounting events that took place in the tenth century or at the beginning of the eleventh, following the edition prepared by Bollandus from a manuscript of Saint Maximinus (*Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 773).

[Col. 1249A] Moreover, that he carried other relics of the Lord, no less worthy of veneration than the nail itself, is attested both by the aforementioned privilege [Col. 1249D] [Note: He is speaking of a charter said to have been issued by Pope Sylvester; see above], and by the church in the city of Trier, dedicated by him in honor of the prince of the apostles, which glories in the Lord because these relics are preserved for it in the treasury of its treasure-house.

How astonishing a magnitude of reverence is owed to them, I think, is clearly demonstrated if one sign of their sanctity, which they once gave, is recalled to memory. For we have learned through the most truthful account of our ancestors that, when a certain very religious bishop of that metropolis heard various opinions among people concerning these relics of the Lord—some saying that they were the Lord’s seamless tunic, others that they were the purple garment in which he had been clothed at the time of his Passion, and still others thinking that the pledge of love was the sandals of the Savior of the world—he greatly desired to resolve these opinions by seeking the truth.

After taking counsel with the people, the clergy, and the monastic order, he proclaimed a three-day fast throughout the entire city, humbly asking everyone to pray unanimously that God, in his peace and permission, would grant one of them the privilege of looking upon so great a sacrament.

When the fast had been completed, clergy and people were summoned to the church of Saint Peter, guardian of this treasure. There a monk of outstanding religion and devotion was chosen from the entire multitude to see the Lord’s hidden object and reveal it to the bishop. He opened the chest in which blessed Agritius had placed this treasure.

But as soon as he lifted the covering in order to look inside, the hidden judgment of God, against which there is no counsel, closed his eyes so that he could not see. Consequently, all who among them were of wiser judgment and keener intellect judged, from the blindness inflicted upon so great a man, that this was God’s will: no sinner would ever be admitted to behold it, since its sight would not even be granted to a righteous man.

After that hour had passed, no one attempted to open this chest. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Yet we do not wish to pass over in silence one sign of the preciousness that the same nail of the Lord displayed. When Bruno, called the brother of the emperor Otto I—for there were three of them—held in his power the better bishoprics of Lotharingia, namely Trier and Cologne, as well as the greater part of this kingdom [Col. 1249D] [Note: It is sufficiently established that Bruno did not hold the bishopric of Trier, but possessed supreme authority throughout the whole kingdom of Lotharingia [Col. 1250D]. Others relate a similar story about Theoderic of Metz; see above, *Gesta*, supplement, chapter 5], he was evidently moved by an evil spirit and secretly, not to say furtively, wished to transfer—whither is unknown—this very nail, the nail of our festal memorial and salvation, of which we are speaking.

After corrupting the guardian of this lordly treasure, he had another nail prepared so similar to this one that it could scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be distinguished from the true one by the careful examination of anyone looking at both. When the guardian, induced by payment, had received this counterfeit from the hand of the aforementioned bishop, and thought that he had found a suitable opportunity for the wicked theft, he finally tried in vain to carry out the deception he had long contrived.

Having transferred this adulterous nail into the shrine of the most venerable nail of the Lord, he carefully wrapped the precious testament of our redemption in a clean linen cloth. Placing it in the bosom of his shirt, he prepared to approach his master by a swift route.

But so that it might be plainly understood with what special privilege of love the Lord embraced the Church of Trier, betrothed to Christ through blessed Agritius, the Lord displayed in the very nail of our redemption a miracle rightly to be counted among the Lord’s foremost miracles and to astonish the whole world.

For while that most faithless guardian, like the vilest renegade, corrupted by the price of iniquity, had turned his back on faith and was preparing to carry away its precious pledge from the bosom of the bride, the Church of Trier, an amazing thing occurred: a considerable quantity of blood poured from the nail itself onto the linen cloth, and from there flowed into the bosom of his shirt in such abundance that all the inward parts of that most wretched bearer grew cold with terror.

Confounded by this, he was compelled to confess publicly both his own guilt and that of the bishop. An assembly of everyone was immediately convened, summoned by the prolonged sound of the bells and by the unusual report of so great a miracle—a report unheard since the beginning of the age. With the detestable thief placed in the midst, the bloodstained cloth stretched out before all, and the most sacred nail from which the blood had flowed displayed, one voice of praise was raised by everyone.

After this voice had been repeated again and again for a long time, a suitable sentence of penance for so great a sacrilege was pronounced against the wretched man—though I hesitate to call him a guardian—by the common counsel of the wiser among all those present.

The day on which these acts of God’s mercies toward us had been divinely celebrated was immediately entered in the martyrologies, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [June 20]. If anyone, which God forbid, doubts that this unheard-of miracle of the Lord deserves the ear of belief, he can still see, if permission is granted, both the same bloodmarked cloth and the same counterfeit nail in the church of Saint Peter.

[Col. 1250D] Nor do we think that we ought to remain silent about that proclamation of supreme festivity concerning this most genuine remedy for our infirmity, although we received it from a most wicked witness, the enemy of our salvation, through the mouth of a woman possessed by him. For a certain woman named Winiberga, born in a city commonly called Regensburg. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

[Col. 1251]

## LIFE AND PASSION OF CONRAD, ARCHBISHOP, BY THE AUTHOR THEODERICUS

### [Note]

The Life of Conrad—who in A.D. 1066 was promoted by King Henry IV to be archbishop of Trier but was killed by the people of Trier before he entered the city—was written by a monk of Tholey named Theoderic. Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, arranged for the body of this man, soon numbered among the martyrs of the Church, to be transferred to the monastery of Tholey, where miracles were later said to have occurred at his tomb.

The abbot and brothers of the monastery wished to prevent both these events and the sequence of his Passion from passing out of human memory. At their command [Col. 1251D] [Note: “Compelled by the command of the abbot and brothers,” preface], Theoderic wrote the account, and he also judged it his duty to set forth briefly the Life of Conrad. But he had learned nothing certain about it and therefore committed only a few, and those relatively minor, matters to writing.

He himself appears to have entered the monastery of Tholey only after A.D. 1066, as a foreigner [Col. 1251D] [Note: In the preface he twice calls himself a newcomer], and to have undertaken this work there after A.D. 1073 [Col. 1251D] [Note: Chapters 4 and 8. Before A.D. 1090, when Bishop Theoderic died. Compare chapter 8, where the knight Folcardus is said to be alive], assisted by the reports of the brothers [Col. 1251D] [Note: Chapters 1 and 7], but lacking more accurate knowledge of events and, indeed, knowledge of the German language [Col. 1252D] [Note: Preface, line 1].

At the beginning especially, he uses a more inflated style, excessively embellished with passages from Holy Scripture; but he sets out the miracles he himself witnessed more simply. He praises Bishop Theoderic, to whom he dedicated the book, in exalted terms, but he is strongly hostile toward Pope Gregory VII, whom Theoderic had regarded as an enemy [Col. 1252D] [Note: Compare the supplement to the *Gesta Treverensia*, chapters 11 and following, and Laurence of Liège, *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*]. [Col. 1252D] [Note: Chapter 4]. Nevertheless, several medieval historians followed this author, not only Sigebert of Gembloux [Col. 1252D] [Note: Compare Hirsch, *On Sigebert*, p. 113, who doubted this, and Bethmann, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* VI, p. 361, note 36], who was himself hostile to Gregory, but also the other author of the *Gesta Treverensia* [Col. 1252D] [Note: Chapter 9], who was attached to the ecclesiastical party.

The following materials were used for the edition of the Life:

1. Trier manuscript no. 1384 (CXVI), parchment, quarto, formerly belonging to Saint Martin. It consists of several parts, and in the third position this complete and carefully written Life appears, copied in the thirteenth century [Col. 1252D] [Note: At the beginning of the volume there are images of Conrad and Symeon, the former marked with this inscription:

“Thrice he stood sound, thrust down from the mountain’s summit;

Received and joined to the saints, he was slain by the sword.”]

1a. Vienna manuscript no. 541 (*Ecclesiastical History* III), twelfth–thirteenth century, quarto. It contains the same Life on folios 1–4, together with the miracles on folios 5 and following. This is all that the distinguished scholar Chmel recorded.

1b. The manuscript of Saint Maximinus at Trier, cited by Henschenius, was similar, but lacked the prologue.

2. Paris manuscript, *Supplementum Latinum* no. 870, small folio, folios 78 verso–81. It contains this Life, without the prologue, written in a thirteenth-century hand (see *Archivum* VIII, p. 311).

3. Henschenius was the first to publish Theoderic’s work (*Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 127), from a very ancient manuscript, as he says, given to him (3a). That manuscript, however, omitted the prologue, altered the genuine text in more than one place, and especially enlarged the final part with many interpolations.

The editor also saw the manuscript of Saint Maximinus and another described by Wilthemius, now preserved in Brussels (*Archivum* VIII, p. 503), as well as an abridgment supplied by the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Cologne. Hontheim took the material that he included in his collection of Trier writers from this edition (*Prodromus* I, p. 670).

[Col. 1251A] To Deoderic, the angel of the Lord of hosts, to be revered with the highest veneration [Col. 1251] [Note: *angelorum*, “of the angels,” manuscript 3], from a newcomer of the same name, the least of the hooded company: the immeasurable riches of the surpassing glory of God.

Blessed be the name of the Most High Lord, by whose unrepenting oath you, O glory of bishops, have been eternally adorned with the beauty of an eternal priesthood; certainly not unequal to Melchizedek, assimilated to the Son of God, indeed like and equal to him according to the order of pontifical office.

Because you have always loved the beauty of the Lord’s house, you have deserved, not without reason, to become a sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. His anointing teaches you concerning all things, and teaches how your sublimity knows both to make itself equal to the exalted and to condescend to the lowly [Col. 1251] [Note: *prae*, “before,” manuscript 3].

For this reason, most holy father, I, the reproach of men [Col. 1251B] and the outcast of the common people, have dared to make myself known to your loftiness [Col. 1251] [Note: *ignotesci*, “to remain unknown,” manuscript 1], and to offer this tasteless and rustic dish, seasoned with the salt of your learning, incomparable among those of our own time, [Col. 1252A] so that you may strengthen it by your authority, if you approve, or cancel it if you disapprove.

Insofar as you are one with God, you have been made by him wisdom and justice for us: wisdom, so that you may correct folly; justice, so that you may weigh just and unjust in an equal balance [Col. 1251] [Note: *equilance*, “with an equal balance,” manuscript 1].

As the philosopher Plato says, states would be blessed if either lovers of wisdom governed them or their rulers happened to devote themselves to wisdom. You are one of such men—not because of flattery, to which we do not know how to devote ourselves, but because the truth itself teaches us to confess it, and it is fitting for our order to proclaim this in heart and mouth.

Among those who, according to their ability, offer various kinds of gifts in God’s tabernacle, I have tried not to appear empty-handed [Col. 1251] [Note: *aparere*, “to appear,” manuscript 1]. I have also thought that I would do you a service if I did not allow your martyr, worthy of the style of that Mantuan comic poet [Col. 1251] [Note: *concini*, “of the fellow-comic poet,” manuscript 3], to remain forgotten any longer [Col. 1252B].

Yours, I say, yours, because you, as God’s fellow worker, are responsible for all the glory that he possesses on earth, and to your charity is attributed the fact that he at least has a tomb in the bishopric [Col. 1253A] once entrusted to him [Col. 1253] [Note: *epischopatu*, “bishopric,” manuscript 1].

I have done this not with any arrogance, but compelled by the command of the abbot [Col. 1253] [Note: *abbatis et* are absent in manuscript 3] and the brothers, to whom I am also obliged beyond my strength to obey in all things, since, newly desolate and abandoned for Christ’s name and out of respect for the rule, they deigned to admit me into their fellowship.

Therefore, O both our protection and our sweet honor—“our sweet glory” (*Horace, Odes* I.1.2)—you who, in the catalogue of the bishops of the holy Church of Verdun, through observance of the Decalogue and an angelic life on earth, may receive the denarius of divine reward in the jubilee of eternal rest and of the freedom of the children of God, and on the last day the prize of the eight longed-for beatitudes: graciously receive this spiritual little gift from your fellow-named newcomer.

And because doctrine and truth shine wonderfully in the mystical breastplate of your heart, examine spiritual matters by comparing spiritual things with spiritual, according to the wisdom given you by God. When you have weighed how many vigils and how much sweat this has cost us, if it is not to be obliterated, cut away what is superfluous, fill what gapes, clarify what shines too little, adorn what is unadorned [Col. 1253B]. But if you judge this work more fit to feed moths than minds, deign to forge another work worthy of the merits of so holy a man [Col. 1253] [Note: In manuscript 3 this is badly corrupt: “carefully following these things, according to your…”].

For we do not greatly grieve over the empty labor expended if, before so just and incorruptible a judge, we lose our case—if we receive precious things in exchange for worthless ones, or if, in exchange for a gift of baked brick, we receive pure gold.

By the judgment of all, that man is rightly deemed blameworthy whose inactivity lacks something which, if possessed, would have benefited the honor and advantage of many. Hence that wicked servant too was deprived by divine judgment of the Lord’s grace [Note: [Col. 1253] *divine* corrected to *divino* in 1; *privatus* in 1], because he preferred to hide the talent entrusted to him in the earth rather than, by putting it out at interest, both benefit his fellow servants and serve his master’s purposes. But since we have at hand the means by which, through similar sluggishness, we might incur anger, and by which, through working again, we may deserve grace—if he deigns to be present, without whom we can do nothing, from whom comes all wisdom and every perfect gift, who made the tongues of infants eloquent and, when he wished, made a brute animal articulate—if, I say, he deigns to fill our open mouth and to breathe his Spirit into our heart, who breathes where and when he wills, we desire not to imitate the lazy servant by idling wickedly, but rather, by exercising ourselves a little, to imitate the man who returned to his master the talent doubled through business, gained a good standing, and earned the right to attain greater things [Note: [Col. 1253] *with* in 1].

For this purpose also the most wise Ecclesiastes, consulting the salvation of all, as though speaking to one person, exhorts everyone in one person, saying: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because there is neither work nor reason nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). So that we may never happen to hasten there, may we be aided by the intercession of blessed Cuonrad, our patron. In his praise and honor we labor to send to posterity an account of how the Lord crowned him with glory and honor through the suffering of martyrdom. Here the reader eager for novelty should not seek verbal finery, since we have deliberately striven to render what we write clear and intelligible in ordinary, straightforward language. At times also—and we are not ashamed to admit this—because of intervening incompetence, unpolished and inelegant Latin has accommodated itself to people as unlearned as ourselves. But concerning the variety of his name, it seems appropriate first to satisfy the many who disagree, if we ourselves were not held by the same scruple of uncertainty [Note: [Col. 1253D] These words plainly show that the author was an outsider]. Some call him Cuonrandus; others, especially his countrymen and relatives, call him Cuono; others maintain that he was virtually two-named, bearing both names. We, however, yielding to the opinions of different people and leaving the matter to God’s knowledge—for whatever his name may have been, we do not doubt that he is written in heaven—let us at last, in the name of the Lord, begin the text of the narrative.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE AND PASSION

[Col. 1253]

[Col. 1253D] 1. Blessed martyr Cuonrad [Note: [Col. 1253] *Conrad* in 2 and 3; 3 adds “who is also called Cuno”] was born of noble lineage, from the Swabian town of Pulinga [Note: [Col. 1253] *opido* in 1] [Col. 1254D] [Pfullingen; compare Stalin, *History of Württemberg*, I, p. 566], to his father Eilolf [Note: [Col. 1253] *Eibolf* in 2; *Eylolf* in 3] and his mother Hazzecha [Note: [Col. 1253] *Exizecha* in 2; *Azecha* in 3]. Although, according to the rank of the world, they were by no means insignificant, but wealthy and abundantly supplied with possessions and extended over very extensive estates, this made it understood that their son would become a vessel of love [Note: [Col. 1253] *of election* in 2], because by divine predestination he was assigned not to those worldly things—which, although only temporarily, he could nevertheless have used freely as the heir of such great patrimonies—but to ecclesiastical things; as though the Lord were saying to his parents: “I am his portion of inheritance” (Psalm 15:5).

Accordingly, that first age was given to the holy instruction of letters [Note: [Col. 1253] *given* in 1; 3 adds “by his parents”]. The more he wept beneath the resounding rods, the more he advanced day by day from virtue to virtue [Note: [Col. 1253] 3 adds “with the progress of age toward an increase in moral excellence”], destined one day to see the God of gods in Zion [Note: [Col. 1253] *when* in 2; absent in 3]. His mother too sometimes restrained herself with the moderation of philosophy, and eagerly desired to nourish him with milk and food, as he moved about her household [Note: [Col. 1253] *observantem* in 2], until he attained the strength of a manly spirit.

God’s grace made him so wise that he was not at all among those of whom it is said: “Where is the scribe, where is the wise man, where is the investigator of this world? Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” (1 Corinthians 1:20); rather, he belonged to those whom the Apostle teaches, saying: “I want you to be wise in what is good, but simple in what is evil” (Romans 16:19) [Note: [Col. 1255] 2 has *to be*].

From there he entered Pythagoras’ forked road, avoiding the left-hand branch and proceeding along the right. When, having reached mature age, he became his own master, we have judged it preferable to report different accounts of why he left his native land and how he sought the metropolis of Germany, Cologne Agrippina, since we have learned different things from different people.

Some say that, out of a desire for greater study—as that younger age commonly does—he wished to live abroad in that same city. Others say that he came there out of love for blessed Anno, bishop of that see, who was thought to be closely related to him by kinship and family connection [Note: [Col. 1255] *or* in 2]. Others say that the same bishop brought him with him when he assumed his office, for he too was a Swabian by nation.

Which of these accounts is truer, however, he himself knows better who foreknew him and predestined him to be conformed to the passion of his Son; and whom he predestined, he called; and whom he called, he justified; and [Note: [Col. 1255] absent in 2], as is clear to everyone today, he glorified. Therefore there is no doubt in our hearts that, whatever the cause of his departure from his homeland may have been, it foreshadowed the omen of his blessed passion. And who would doubt that the following words were spoken by the Lord to him, if not openly, at least sent into his heart: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you, and blessing I will bless you” (Genesis 12:2)?

Almighty God showed him that very land, and in it granted him no small measure of grace, as the praise that is now sung at the end attests. For the aforementioned most holy bishop Anno—although the tongue of certain envious people may have kept silent about his praiseworthy works, many buildings of stone will nevertheless cry out [Note: [Col. 1255] “buildings which he built” in one witness], buildings by which he constructed monasteries of his bishopric [Note: [Col. 1255] *for his episcopate* in 2] and enlarged those already built—himself an immigrant, but exalted by God’s right hand, kindly welcomed this blessed newcomer, treated him humanely, and, when he wished and judged him worthy, raised him up and promoted him to a higher rank. Ordering him to stand nearby in the next rank, and elevating him to the dignity of the priesthood, he appointed him second after himself as chief provost of the chief household of his see, that is, of Saint Peter.

This was the first responsibility entrusted to him. He administered it vigorously and capably in the sight of God and human beings, as there still exist as many witnesses as were able to know him.

### 2. [Note: [Col. 1255] I myself established this division into chapters.]

At about the same time, Henry IV [Note: [Col. 1255] *Henry* in 2 and 3], bearing the same name as his father, was still in tender years. His august father had recently been removed from the world, yet he was governing vigorously with the scepter. The aforementioned holy bishop Anno, a man of complete prudence and courtly education, had accepted him for upbringing at the request of his widowed imperial mother [Note: [Col. 1255D] “These things differ greatly from the truth; there is no need for me to point this out”]. He entrusted him to liberal literary studies, instructed him in divine and human matters, and brought him up becomingly, as suited a royal child [Note: [Col. 1255] *that* corrected to *and that* in 1].

On account of this tutorship he sometimes also managed affairs of the kingdom, and, whenever circumstances required, extended the hand of counsel to his pupil. The more he feared the saying, “Whatever a pupil does wrong is attributed to the teacher,” the more carefully he guarded against anything adverse happening to the commonwealth that could be imputed to him. Recalling that saying of Solomon—“Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1:1) [Note: [Col. 1255] *Solomonic* in 1]—he helped to guide the reins of the noble cities with the straight moderation of the laws, to restore civil right to the good, to terrify the guilty, and to distribute each person’s due rightly.

Therefore he advised that all upright and wise men be advanced to govern churches, because he knew it was written: “The multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wisdom 6:16) [Note: [Col. 1255] *for himself, as it seemed to him* in 2]. Hence, when, as it seemed to him, the welfare of the realm required it and the city of Trier had been deprived of its shepherd [Note: [Col. 1256D] Archbishop Eberhard died on April 15, 1066], he judged that the aforementioned Cuonrad, whom he knew to be suitable and capable for this purpose, should be appointed in his place.

Although, by the inscrutable mystery of the Godhead, the promotion of such a man of God became the occasion of his martyrdom, no one can doubt that, if, as is said, he desired this bishopric, he desired a good work; for he sought to be in character what his very name indicates he ought to be [Note: [Col. 1255] *the name itself* in 1, 2, and 3]. Thus, at the prompting and counsel of his aforementioned bishop, the martyr of Christ—destined to be a martyr before he was a bishop—was brought forward and acclaimed as worthy. He received from the royal hand the insignia of the pontificate, namely the pastoral staff [Note: [Col. 1255] 3 adds “the rod indicating governance”] and the church’s nuptial ring, pending his ordination as the Church’s bridegroom through anointing with sacred chrism.

Without delay he was sent, as the agent of that king, to the see entrusted to him—that is, to the city of Trier—with the venerable bishop Eilard of the city of Speyer [Note: [Col. 1255] *Einhard* in 3]. Although Trier had long been distinguished by God with very holy bishops, surpassed by none anywhere on earth, so that it was not undeservedly called a second Rome, nevertheless, because its sins demanded it, we believe that in these latter times it was unworthy of such a bishop; and the outcome of events proves this.

For when his arrival was heard of [Note: [Col. 1255] *when they heard* in 2], the city, which ought through him to have progressed from misfortune toward improvement, instead, through evil counsel, rushed from bad to worse. At once the devil, a murderer from the beginning—through whose envy death entered the world, and whom those who belong to his party imitate—knowing them to be of his faction, inflamed them with the fury of his madness and incited them to imitate him, that is, to murder.

And where in the whole world is there a city, after Rome, in which the devil himself, his worshipers, and the agents of his wickedness once had more followers than there? Although she who had been a teacher of error is now a disciple of truth, nevertheless, alas, he still found some of his members there, whom he stirred up to persecute and kill the members of Christ.

We see similar events to those of the Lord’s passion occurring also in the passion of this holy man. For just as the priests and pontiffs of the Jews, instructed in the Law and the Prophets, incited the unlearned people to kill the Savior, so also—and it is shameful to say it—certain members of the clergy strove all the more to provoke the lay people, whom they ought to have restrained, to such a crime.

They approached Theoderic, the prefect of the city [Note: [Col. 1257] Concerning him, see Hontheim, *History*, I, p. 341. He is called “our count and procurator” in a charter of Archbishop Eberhard from 1065; see the same work, p. 407], and, partly with many persuasive words and partly with various plausible arguments [Note: [Col. 1257] *when* in 2], encouraged him to destroy the blessed man.

Then, raising a tumult and shouting in the popular manner, they swore that the bishop—neither elected nor properly appointed—would never enter their city and would never rule his own; sometimes invoking oaths, sometimes protests, and sometimes curses [Note: [Col. 1257] *curses* written *malectis* in 2]. They flatteringly proclaimed that the same prefect was the city’s defender and patron and ought not to suffer such things.

They said that this man had to be killed; that this was a matter of their honor; that it would please the saints of the place; that this was not a crime but zeal for justice and proper defense. Moreover, they said [Note: [Col. 1257] singular *says* in 2; absent in 3 after “whereby we shall sin in this”]: “We will bear this sin; let it cling to us, let it be charged to us.” This seems almost openly to echo the words: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

The man, supported by worldly glory and enticed by these and similar evil exhortations and foolish promises, sought soldiers and seized weapons. When the herald shouted, “Whoever is not present will offend the governor,” the entire city assembled [Note: [Col. 1257] *assembled* in 2; *came to meet him* in 3]. Even the great signal that had been sounded for the completion of the divine office became a signal for inciting every kind of evil [Note: [Col. 1257] *imitation* in 1 and 2].

It was already a late hour, when the servants of God ought, according to canonical regulations, to have completed their daytime offices [Note: [Col. 1257] *fulfilled* in 2; *celebrated* in 3]. Then these men, whose hearts held the night and darkness of sin, assembled at that very hour with their weapons. Mounting their horses, they went out to meet the coming shepherd—not as sheep, but as ravenous wolves, to devour him.

He had taken lodging four miles from the city in a village called Bithyburg [Note: [Col. 1257] *Bithburg* in 2; *Bideburg* in 3] [Note: [Col. 1257D] Bittburg], and, suspecting nothing of the sort, was spending the night with the venerable bishop to whom we have said he had been entrusted [Note: [Col. 1257D] “A municipality situated on the Moselle” in 3]. The next morning, as was supposed, he was to be presented to the city by that lord in the king’s place and, as customary, solemnly received by clergy and people.

But in vain did the piety of almighty God provide a pious ruler for the widowed and abandoned city; in vain did it say to her in a father’s voice: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, meek” (John 12:15). She preferred to be stained with his blood rather than be ruled by him even for an hour.

When morning came, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June—that is, May 18—once the sun had risen, the crowd of attendants hurried to rise, summoned one another to go out, carefully adorned themselves, as that noble company was accustomed to do, saddled the horses, and decently prepared everything of this kind. Suddenly, unexpectedly and without warning, they found themselves not merely surrounded but besieged by the enemy.

What were they to do? They had committed nothing worthy of death against these men; why, then, were they to die at their hands? At last they too rushed to arms [Note: [Col. 1257] *ran* in 2] and resolved to fight for their lives, if that could be done. But how could one pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight? (Deuteronomy 32:30.)

The many prevailed where the few stood in opposition. After breaking down the doors, they entered the courtyard of the house—not without bloodshed on both sides—and burst into the room where the two elders were resting. Already awakened by the noise, they were awaiting, after the judgment they saw approaching, the mercy of God. God had permitted what he did not wish to happen, but only for the condemnation of these men; and, as we believe, he delayed his mercy because he was reserving greater glory for his servant Cuonrad.

They plundered everything that came to hand—their horses, vessels, clothing, and remaining furniture [Note: [Col. 1257] *household furnishings* in 2]. They allowed the aforementioned bishop of Speyer to depart, though not without injury, since he had been stripped of his belongings.

But they seized and bound blessed Cuonrad and, without mercy or humanity, dragging him with laughter [Note: [Col. 1257] *with mocking laughter* in 1] and insults to a fortress called Urcich [Note: [Col. 1257] *Urtich* in 1b; *Urzich* in 2 and 3] [Note: [Col. 1258D] This fortress, they say, was fortified in the thirteenth century by Wirico of Dune and destroyed by Archbishop Arnold; see the continuation of the *Deeds of Trier*, Hontheim], handed him over to custody—perhaps while they deliberated among themselves what death would destroy him by.

### 3. [Note: [Col. 1257] This chapter is absent in 3a.]

But meanwhile, I think we should pause, so that, together with those who chatter with a dog’s tooth, we may debate the claim that he was not canonically elected [Note: [Col. 1257] *elected and* is absent in 2], and that, because he was not elected, he was therefore not canonically promoted.

We assert not only that a man must be elected both by human beings and by God, but also oppose a defensive front to those who contradict this, insisting that he must not be elected by God alone or by human beings alone [Note: [Col. 1257] “not by God” so in 1 and 2, but it seems more correct to omit it in 3]. In the Song of Love, the bride says of Christ the bridegroom—that is, the Church says of the bishop, the vicar of Christ her bridegroom: “My beloved is chosen from thousands” (Song of Songs 5:10). She plainly indicates that just anyone is not to be readily accepted, but that a man of good reputation is to be chosen from the multitude and by the multitude.

At the beginning of the nascent Church, Matthias was chosen for the apostolate by divine lot; Stephen also was chosen for the diaconate by the election of the apostles, indeed of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1259] *the holy* in 2]. And what purpose would it serve to fill our page with a thousand testimonies?

Those, therefore, who do not believe that this man, promoted by the holy man Anno under divine inspiration [Note: [Col. 1259] *by a holy man* in 2], was elected by God, should, with the same madness of mind, not believe that those whom we have said were appointed by divinely inspired holy apostles were elected by God [Note: [Col. 1259] *elected by God* in 2 and 3].

The holy Fathers also, authors of the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 1259] *of the saints* in 2 and 3], seeing that, as iniquity increased and charity grew cold, men of this kind were entering the holy Church through the heresy of simony—of one such blessed Augustine cries out: “O bishop, if you had not given a hundred solidi [Note: [Col. 1259] 3 adds “solidi,” that is, coins], you would not be bishop today”—decreed in the very sentences of the canons, to use their words: “Wherever a worthy man can be found, let him be appointed wherever there is need.”

We establish this from the canons themselves, from the decrees of the pontiffs [Note: [Col. 1259] *pontiffs* in 1], and from the register of blessed Pope Gregory, with many readings confirming it. We shall also show in the chronicles many such men appointed by royal authority whose appointment was shown afterward, through their deeds, to have pleased God.

Such was the man from whom, as we have said above, our father Cuonrad was promoted: the sound of whose holiness has already gone out, heard throughout the whole earth. Although Agrippina did not know how to choose him, since he had previously been unknown to her [Note: [Col. 1259] *unfamiliar* in 1, corrected], nevertheless she now glories in having been worthy of so great a bishop.

Perhaps those who favor the other side object that they chose from among their own the man whom they judged worthy. But they must beware lest the prophetic saying confront them: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20) [Note: [Col. 1259] *lest* in 2].

For if both those who elected and the man whom they elected had been from God, with God, and in God, they would never, inflamed by envy and desire, have condemned innocent blood. Therefore, whoever, instructed in the conduct of wisdom, is found wholly unlike the pursuits of wicked men [Note: [Col. 1259] *unlike* in 2], should not be surprised if, on this sea of life, the holy are tossed by storms sweeping around them. For the chief aim of such storms is to displease the worst people [Note: [Col. 1259] *to despise* in 1].

Although their army is numerous, it must nevertheless be scorned, because it is ruled by no leader, as we shall say in its proper place concerning the persecutors of this holy man [Note: [Col. 1259] *although* in 1]. Now let us return to our subject and entrust the noble triumph of the martyr to the knowledge of the faithful.

### 4.

For fourteen days the athlete of Christ was held in custody at the aforementioned fortress—not because those men delayed the day of his death out of mercy, since there was no limit to their cruelty, but because the hour had not yet come when he was to be summoned by the one who had formed him even in the womb.

On the fifteenth day, when the sacrilegious prefect Theoderic, utterly unworthy of the Christian name, had been stirred by a frenzy of profane cruelty and desired to be glutted with the blood of an innocent man, he brought Cuonrad out of custody and handed him over to four wicked sons, so that they might mock him. He threatened them under command, declaring that if they took his life by a light punishment, they should know that they would be deprived of his favor [Note: [Col. 1259] *having threatened them* in 2 and 3].

They rejoiced that the opportunity they desired had fallen to them for raging against him and that they could please their master in so slight a service [Note: [Col. 1259] *in every such service* in 1]. Driven by a demonic spirit [Note: [Col. 1259] *demonic* in 2], they led him to the brow of a nearby mountain, which was so dense [Note: [Col. 1259] 3 adds “and high”] that, had he been thrown from it, he would have been torn limb from limb before he could be thought dead.

They set him at the summit, stripped of his clothing, covered only by an undertunic, with his face covered and his hands tied behind his back [Note: [Col. 1259] *behind his back* in 1]. “Look,” they said, “we have to find out whether God chose you for the episcopate. That will become clear when he makes you remain unharmed after this fall” [Note: [Col. 1259] *makes you unharmed from this fall* in 1 and 2; *makes you unharmed in this fall* in 3].

When they did not fear to hurl the reverend man down amid such mockery, divine mercy chose to reveal that he had indeed been chosen by God, but that they were unworthy of him. For, falling from the height downward, he stood not only alive but also unharmed in his entire body. Anyone who wishes to consider the matter will not fail to marvel that his limbs had been battered—unless it is truly established that the Lord had placed his hand beneath him [Note: [Col. 1259] *had placed it beneath him* in 2].

When the wicked saw this miracle, their stony breasts were not moved to pity. Instead, they took him up again: “We shall try this same thing again,” they said. Having tried it a second time, they dared to attempt it even a third. Already tested three times, glorified three times by God, and three times preserved unharmed by him, the blinded mind of the faithless took no account of it, storing up wrath for itself on the day of the Lord’s anger in its unrepentant heart.
