If you seek signs and miracles by which you may rightly acknowledge that this man was holy, consider whether it was not a work of divine power for the mass of a heavy body, so to speak, to fly three times, or to fall from a height to the ground, or at least to turn aside down the steep slopes of a rugged mountain [Note: [Col. 1259] *rough* in 1] amid rocks everywhere, while preserving its integrity—and all this when he had no garment with which he could protect himself even from the spikes of the thorns.

If you have an eye that is not envious but faithful, you will appropriately acknowledge that this Davidic verse should be sung in his praise: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone” (Psalm 90:12) [Note: [Col. 1259] *and in my hands they will lift* in 2].

We likewise read that James, the Lord’s brother, was treated as a plaything by a similar fall; but what that man underwent once, this man underwent three times, because perhaps, being still of lesser merit, he had to have his punishment increased. Yet both were happier in proportion as they were mindful of that saying of the Lord: “A servant is not greater than his master” (John 13:16).

The devil, taking the Lord while he was still young and, through the weakness of the flesh he had assumed, lifting him higher, urged him toward the precipice; afterward the members of that same devil led him to the brow of the mountain to hurl him down.

The executioners of the cruel tyrant were not yet satisfied with punishment. “Because you did not remain standing properly after your leap,” they said [Note: [Col. 1261] *you did not stand* in 2], “our sword shall rule over your flesh.” Then, to complete the measure of their condemnation [Note: [Col. 1261] *to the tomb* in 2 and 3], they attacked him with their swords and, having beheaded him, joined the martyr to the company of martyrs.

Thus that thrice-blessed man, having experienced mockery and blows, and in addition bonds and prisons, died by the killing of the sword. His spirit was taken up by angels [Note: [Col. 1261] 1 reads *by angels*], and he was presented before the face of the Almighty with manifold triumphs. The heavenly court was renewed by the fragrance of his sweetness: on one side, lilies gleamed white from the priestly robe; on the other, blooming roses exuded fragrance from the blood of his passion [Note: [Col. 1261] *would have exuded fragrance* in 2].

They covered the lifeless body with thorns and bushes and went away to announce such joyful news to their master. When he asked them where the bishop was, they said: “We have placed a pontifical mitre on him [Note: [Col. 1261] *a pontifical mitre* in 1], but he will never come to Trier again, nor will he govern a pontifical chair” [Note: [Col. 1261] *pontifical* in 1].

Insulting the holy man with such abuse, they perhaps did not know that a day would come when, groaning from anguish of spirit, they would say among themselves in repentance: “This is the man whom we once held in derision and made an object of reproach; fools that we were, we considered his life madness and his end dishonorable. How, then, has he been counted among the sons of God, and how is his lot among the saints?”

Because, through fear of that same tyrant, no one dared commit the limbs of Christ’s victim to the earth [Note: [Col. 1261] absent in 1], they lay unburied for nearly forty days, exposed, like blessed Stephen the protomartyr, to the birds of heaven and the beasts of the field. But by God’s providence they were touched by none of them.

At last, moved by piety, the inhabitants of the neighboring village, namely Loncscet [Note: [Col. 1261] *Loncsceit* in 1; *Lonseti* in 3; forms as printed in 1b and 2] [Note: [Col. 1261D] Lonset, on the opposite side of the Moselle; Hontheim], secretly lifted them and buried them at that same village, before the church doors, on the eighth day before the Ides of July, with whatever honor they were able to provide.

He suffered, therefore, in the year 1066 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the fourth indiction, on the first day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 1261] *III N II* in 2]. Shortly before his passion, a comet was seen to have appeared in the western region for many nights [Note: [Col. 1261] *comet* in 1; *to have appeared* in 1], plainly an omen of divine vengeance [Note: [Col. 1261D] Compare Lambert and Bernold for this year].

For the voice of his innocent blood, calling upon God for vengeance, raised such a cry to heaven that it still seems to demand vengeance from the hand of the whole world, through the anger of the heavenly Judge. Indeed, no answer was given to it by delay: “Wait a little while.” Rather, immediately, in that same year and at the same time, the holy Church [Note: [Col. 1261] 3 adds “and especially the metropolitan church of Trier”] began to be tossed by so great a storm of dissensions and disturbances [Note: [Col. 1261] *so great* in 1] that, amid the prolonged turbulence of wars and civil war, she seems not to know what peace is.

At once, in accordance with the prophetic judgment—“Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:6)—the venerable pontiff of the Apostolic See, Alexander, departed this life [Note: [Col. 1261] The words from “At once” through “prophetic” are absent in 3]. Hildebrand succeeded him, a destructive man who, during the days of his office, offered the cup of God’s wrath to the whole world. Unless he grants time for mercy, the teeth of his children must still, and in the future, be made numb by its most bitter taste [Note: [Col. 1261] *must be* in 2].

For we are the people and sheep of his pasture (Psalm 99:3) [Note: [Col. 1261] 2 reads: “Of whom we are the people and sheep of the pasture, whom we confess as God and Lord, whom we praise forever and ever”]. We confess him as God and Lord, and praise him forever and ever. Amen.

### 5.

As it is written: “The just man, by whatever death he is overtaken, will be in repose, because God’s grace and mercy are upon his holy one [Note: [Col. 1261] *upon the holy ones?* in 1; 3] and he has regard for his chosen one” (Wisdom 4:7) [Note: [Col. 1261] *his chosen ones* in 3], it pleased God to honor the memory of his martyr and priest with a more worthy tomb and to enrich the monastery of Theologia with such a patron—one who would stand on one side of Mauritius and extend his hand on the other to the poor congregation.

And because “whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matthew 10:41), the venerable bishop Deoderic [Note: [Col. 1261] *Theoderic, venerable bishop* in 2] will not be deprived of this eternal reward, since through his pious and favorable zeal both acts of service toward the martyr came about: his elevation from a lowly place and his translation to a more fitting one.

Wonderful, therefore, is God in his saints: he granted that his faithful Cuonrad [Note: [Col. 1261] *Cunrad* here in 1] receive from two men of the same name but of different rank different gifts of honor—from Deoderic the cruel tyrant [Note: [Col. 1261] *from the cleric Deoderic* in 2] the crown of martyrdom, and from his namesake, the most worthy bishop, the honorable repose of a tomb.

But because he himself, the rewarder of good deeds and avenger of evil, will assign to each of them different recompense according to their merits, after the account of the martyr’s passion let us now write of his arrival among us.

The most honorable Bishop Deoderic of the holy Church of Verdun, while that same year he was attending to affairs at Novallis, a fortress under his jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 1261] “Novrillis” in witness 1; “Novellis” in witnesses 3 and 3a; “s. d.” is absent in witness 1], was celebrating the solemn Mass on a certain day [Note: [Col. 1261] Witness 3 reads: “on the feast of Saint Apollinaris”]. At the time of the sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1261] Witness 3 adds here: “Suddenly he was disturbed by a vision of the spirit of the blessed man of whom we spoke, flying about the circuit of the altar like a bird. During the Canon for the Dead, he was brought to mind—the man whose killing he had heard of.”], remembering the martyr, he was so drenched in a shower of tears that no one present could doubt that he had suddenly been carried away into contemplation. When the same solemn rites had ended, the undergarment [Note: [Col. 1262D] He seems to mean the chasuble, in a rather inappropriate expression. — Henschen] of the stricken priest was wet with many large drops that had fallen upon the breast, and everyone was astonished, yet none dared inquire into the truth of what had happened. The lord himself [Note: [Col. 1261] “Donnus” in witness 1; “dompnus” in witness 2], whose face was still tearful, began to proclaim—not so much with the foolishness of the tongue as by his action [Note: [Col. 1263] Witness 3 adds: “the vision of the aforesaid spirit”]—what had been divinely brought back before the eyes of his mind:

“Because the just man perishes, and no one takes it to heart; for the memory of him is in peace” (Isaiah 57:1).

He immediately summoned a multitude of his household and dependants. Some he bound by oaths, others by words of entreaty, promising that whoever would show him the recently slain man and point out the place where his corpse had been thrown would not lack his favor and subsequent benefaction. Do you suppose that the man who was able in this matter to fulfill the wishes of his superior was happy, when it was clearer than daylight to everyone that, while he was offering the sacrifice, he had received that command from God, who had accepted it, and that from God’s presence the gracious flood of tears had flowed?

Without delay, those who knew the matter approached him more closely, and the faithful strove all the harder to appear to have anticipated the bishop in reporting the truth. “Lord,” they said, “he suffered such and such things and is buried in such and such a village.” [Note: [Col. 1263] “We know the village and the road by which it is reached, but we are completely ignorant of the place of burial. Yet the one who, through the admonition of his spirit, in the form of a bird—as you say—made this known to you will doubtless also reveal the remains of his body by whatever indication.”]

Once he had been informed of these things, the devout man considered how he might bring the hidden treasure into his church, where a place of prayer for the martyr might one day be opened. But because the remoteness of the region prevented his wishes from being carried out, he again turned over in his mind the possibility of transferring the body somewhere—at least somewhere under his jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 1263] “Devotion” in witness 1b]—where it might rest in an honor suitable to him. At last, having found a salutary plan, he decided to bring it to the monastery of Theologia, since there was no nearer place belonging to him; there the memory of noble martyrs was honored, namely of Mauritius and his companions.

He sent an embassy to Abbo, father of that monastery [Note: [Col. 1263] “Lagatione Abdoni” in witness 1], and endeavored to inform him of the whole matter. He ordered him to meet him promptly in the village of Loncscet, where he had heard that the saint was buried, with whatever was appropriate for the funeral rites [Note: [Col. 1263] “Obviari” in witnesses 2 and 3]. Abbo, ready to obey and rejoicing to receive the heavenly gift, took with him several of the brothers and the necessary equipment and hastened on the appointed day to the appointed place.

The venerable bishop, however, uncertain what outcome the discovery would have, had arrived with an armed force. Yet he could not easily obtain what he sought from the inhabitants, because, fearing the aforementioned tyrant, they did not dare admit either that they knew anything about the matter or that the man had been buried among them [Note: [Col. 1263] Witness 3 adds: “But those among them who had sounder judgment, having learned of the martyr’s holiness—which they had experienced through many signs and wonders during the twelve days he was held among them, though they had been as ungrateful as they were untrained in praising God—because they would not consent to his being carried away, drove off that rustic crowd by force of arms.”]. Wherever he went, no one pointed anything out [Note: [Col. 1263] Witness 3 adds: “No one indicated where it was.”]. Nevertheless, with God’s will and through someone who revealed it [Note: [Col. 1263] Witness 3: “through one who had suffered violence”], he obtained what he desired. He raised the lamp from concealment and brought it onto the lampstand of this church, where now, for those entering the house of the Lord, it shines with a clear light.

### 6

With the weakness of our understanding impeding us [Note: [Col. 1263] “Tenuite” in witnesses 1 and 2], we are less able to express how the noble pontiff once again celebrated the funeral rites of the noble man with a fitting and solemn Mass. Yet here one may see whether anything is lacking because of the fault of our language. [Note: [Col. 1263] Witness 3 continues: “Then the sacred body was clothed in priestly vestments—for they asserted that he had exercised the office of a presbyter, as we reported earlier—and, after the limbs had been arranged in order and the solemnities of the Mass completed, they carried that holy funeral in a musical procession to the place of burial and laid it in the sarcophagus with fitting rites. But how the lord bishop adorned it with a cover of metal fashioned by elaborate workmanship, and with a stone engraved with the precious epitaph he himself had composed, no power of our pen is sufficient to recount. Certainly, if anything is missing because of our unskilled language, it may be seen there. This memorial…”]

That same pontiff made this memorial of his name in his own days, and it remains forever before God in remembrance [Note: [Col. 1263] “Memoriam” in witness 1].

### 7

On the eighth day before the Kalends of August, this dwelling was augmented by such a heavenly inhabitant; and what his merit is in heaven, his dead flesh bears witness to on earth. For when the sick come to his tomb, they return restored to health and in possession of what they had prayed for. Therefore, from the hymn-singing choirs of angels, glory, praise, and honor be given to the name of the Omnipotent, who makes this blessed man shine with continual virtues [Note: [Col. 1263] “Coruschare” in witness 2; “v.” and “et” are absent in witnesses 2 and 3] and miracles. Of these we shall relate a few for the benefit of the faithful [Note: [Col. 1263] “Referimus” in witness 2], but we omit very many, which, passed over in silence through the negligence of our predecessors, remain unknown to us, though they are known to God. These, then, are the things that we have seen [Note: [Col. 1263] Witness 3: “which the Lord worked through him, some of them seen by us and others learned from the report of our elders”] or have been able to investigate more carefully.

The fingers of two women, bent downward, were straightened at the invocation of his name. Finally, two lame men were raised upright at his tomb on the anniversary of his burial.

One day the material of his tomb was completely disturbed, and at that same hour a candle appeared, kindled from heaven. [Note: [Col. 1263C] These events are related at greater length in manuscript 3 at the place cited above; but the following words show that the account there belongs to another and more recent writer: “This one thing we received through the faithful report of the brothers of that monastery, and it is proclaimed by those townspeople: at twilight they were found lying flat on the ground. Since no one dared touch them for any ordinary purpose, by common agreement they were hung before the church doors as testimony to so great a miracle. There they hung until, piece by piece, they were carried away by sick people whom the fame of this miracle had summoned, used as a remedy for healing, and consumed for various purposes—thus serving the honor and glory of God more usefully than if they had been burned up by flames.”]

A woman who was blind and paralyzed was restored to health. A certain boy, too, was freed from the affliction of stones.

Here we must speak of the piety he showed when he returned good for evil to a certain soldier, Folcard, who had been one of his enemies. Since Folcard had long been afflicted by divine vengeance, he eventually came to himself and, crying out that he had sinned against God’s saint and confessing his guilt, obtained forgiveness in accordance with the true repentance of his heart. When he recovered, he was not ungrateful for the benefit he had received: he came to fulfill his vows and give thanks, and to this day he does not cease each year to pay the rent owed for his deliverance. Yet a sign of incurable illness appears in him, so that, for as long as he lives, he may pay the penalty for the sin committed against the servant of God. Finally, it is established that, after being captured by his enemies and bound in fetters, he was freed through the invocation of the saint’s name.

A contracted woman was restored to health at his tomb on the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul. I think that, as a kind of recompense, she honored their birthday with the adornment of such a miracle, since he himself had once been their son at Agrippina and was destined to become their vicar in the city of Trier.

The daughter of a certain well-known Reginfrid, deprived of the sight of both eyes; a maidservant of a likewise well-known soldier, afflicted by illness; and another woman whose jaw had been displaced from its proper place—all alike obtained at his tomb the desired joys of healing: the first, the light of her eyes; the others, the soundness of their limbs.

He displayed three benefits in one man. This man had been possessed by a demon and had lost the functions of speech and hearing; at the saint’s tomb he obtained both of these and was freed from the malignant enemy.

Six peasants, whose feet had likewise been fastened in the stocks by an exactor because of their insolence, deserved to be released at the invocation of the saint’s name, although no one laid a hand upon them.

Then a lunatic boy and another boy, a household servant of the soldier Wigeric, whose stomach had already rejected bread for a year, came with the same prayer; both alike experienced the saint’s power through the recovery of their health.

A blind man who came from the household of the blessed Willebrord also experienced a similar miracle through the restoration of his sight. Although that same blessed confessor could easily have granted him this favor, he nevertheless did not begrudge the martyr his glory.

No one should expect to hear from me all the many things that divine grace wished to reveal as evidence of his sanctity. For, as I remember saying above, many things have been obliterated through the negligence of our predecessors, and we deliberately omit still more, partly out of consideration for the envy of many and partly out of compassion for the misery of unbelievers, who give assent neither to writings nor to words unless they see the matter with their own eyes. Let them at least believe one of their own: Count Folcard, in whose presence another blind man recovered the sight he had lost.

### 8

Let whoever wishes strike his forehead against the wall, for we shall not keep silent about what is known throughout the whole world concerning his persecutor, Theoderic. When this man finally heard the praises of so many miracles [Note: [Col. 1265] “Hoc” in witness 2], he in no way gave credence to the words of those who asserted them. With an unbelieving heart, he rashly decided to test for himself whether these things were true.

As he approached the doors of the basilica, not without arrogant pride, where the sacred relics of the man he had martyred were flourishing, he became aware, not without shame [Note: [Col. 1265] “Verecundia” in witness 2], of how great was the divine power present within. For suddenly an invisible barrier prevented the undeserving man from entering the sacred building. He was allowed neither to see the martyr’s tomb nor to touch the threshold of his own oratory.

When he repeatedly tried to enter, and the same power repeatedly opposed him, he finally departed in great confusion, having experienced what he had come to test. The faithful and his relatives urged him, for the sake of his salvation, to make satisfaction to the saint and to give some landed property as alms to his poor church. But the vain man, whose reckoning with heavenly wrath was impending, treated their words with a deaf ear and considered them worthless.

Not long afterward [Note: [Col. 1265D] In 1073; see Bernold of Constance, under this year. Sigebert seems to indicate, less correctly, the year 1068], while traveling toward Jerusalem—by what spirit I do not know—he suffered shipwreck, encountered the storms of the sea, and, descending to the depths below, paid, by an irrevocable fate [Note: [Col. 1265] “Satis” in witness 2], under God’s judgment, the penalty for his crime.

Of the four men who, at his command, killed him, we have preferred to remain silent rather than speak. Let it suffice to say this: they were removed from this light by diverse punishments and manifest evils [Note: [Col. 1266D] Compare Bernold, under the year 1066].

### 9

The blessed father Conrad sometimes corrected those who served him belatedly through reprimands accompanied by signs. Once, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, when a candle placed before him was not burning because of the negligence of the custodians, it was suddenly kindled by divine power. Likewise, as we said above, when on another occasion a lamp was lacking there through the same fault, the entire structure of the tomb was suddenly shaken, and, by that same power, a candle that happened to be present shone with a bright light.

Something similar happened when a candle that had not been fixed securely before him fell upon the sarcophagus covered with a cloth. It lay there burning for a long time, and, burning as it lay, preserved the cloth itself unburned.

Let the pen now set a limit to these matters for eager listeners, because, as blessed Gregory says, signs are to be shown to unbelievers, not to believers; for believers, even fewer words would suffice for salvation. If the faith of those who ask is not lacking, his assistance is never lacking. For what he did not wish to do for himself while still surrounded by the weakness of the flesh, he certainly does not refuse to do for others.

May his continual intercession commend us to the almighty God of gods, to whom be praise forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1265] In manuscripts 1, 1a—written by another hand—and 1b, the following additions appear: “On the Kalends of June, the passion of Saint Cuno, bishop and martyr. On the eighth day before the Ides of July, the discovery of the body of Saint Cuno, bishop and martyr, at the rock where he was beheaded. On the eighth day before the Kalends of August, the translation of the body of Saint Cuno, bishop and martyr, into the basilica of blessed Mauritius and his [s.].”]

[Col. 1267]

## EPITAPH

[Note: [Col. 1267D] Found in Vienna manuscript no. 791 (Lunaelac manuscript no. 8), twelfth century, folio 115.]

[Col. 1267A]

Leader of the flock, harbor, and flower happily sprung forth,

After bearing fruit, he enters this monument;

The flower mentioned above, transplanted into this cloister.

By birth he was from Trier, by monastic profession from Sigeberg [Note: [Col. 1268D] Another hand writes in the margin: “Sigenbergensis,” situated three miles from Nerdelingen.]

He brought here with him a horse venerable to the brothers,

Teaching, character, and every hue of virtue.

Because the conspiracy of wicked servants struck him down,

Though innocent, the sword joined him to Christ:

Therefore, what you had hoped for, martyr, now, though once an abbot,

You were a witness, Chounrade, in the monastery of Christ.

[Col. 1267]

## FROM THE HISTORY OF THE TREVIRAN MARTYRS

### Note

In the year 1072, a Treviran cleric narrated the discovery of a tablet concerning the martyrs killed by Rictiovarus and buried at Trier. He recounted both the passion of those saints, the order of their discovery, and certain miracles performed there, prefacing the work with a prologue that conveyed nothing about himself or about the plan of the work. Yet it is abundantly clear from the whole narrative that he witnessed much of it himself, and he should not be thought to have written long afterward, since his account of the miracles does not extend beyond the year 1072.

I have already noted above that the Life of Felix should also be attributed to him; but here too the author’s name is omitted. The History of the Martyrs was published by Hontheim, *Prodromus*, volume I, page 109, from a Trier manuscript, and was later collated with the manuscript of Saint Maximin and published in *Acta Sanctorum*, October, volume II, page 373. Hillarius saw the Sanmathian manuscript (pages 27 and 67); the Trier library undoubtedly contains others. I reproduce these fragments from Hontheim’s edition.

### 1

[lacuna] We must nevertheless necessarily transmit to posterity, in whatever manner we may write, the way in which, by the ordering of divine predestination, we were gladdened by this manifestation of the saints.

### 2

There were, then, in that congregation of canons of Saint Paulinus certain brothers fervently kindled with zeal for holy religion. While, among their other works of piety, they devoted no little effort to reading the page of Sacred Scripture, they frequently used the eyes of body and mind to represent those things that seemed to concern the honor of the Church of Trier, their mother—perhaps, indeed truly, mindful of the commandment that says, “Honor your father and your mother” (Deuteronomy 5:16), and of other injunctions of this kind that urge a righteous way of life.

Among the many praises of this place, the passion of the holy martyrs Gentianus and Victoricus occurred to them most frequently. Whenever the account of the countless slaughter of Christians perpetrated by Rictiovarus in the city of Trier resounded in their bodily ears, their hearts trembled at once with grief and joy: with grief because the treasure of the saints’ bodies, so great and precious, was unknown; with joy because they had learned the truth of these events through the great authority of Sacred Scripture.

For the passion of these saints reported that, when Rictiovarus entered Trier, such an outpouring of the blood of the saints took place there that streams of gore, mingling with the water beside which they had been killed and flowing into the Moselle, changed it to their own color. Its natural clarity removed, the river became red with a color more foreign than its own. The account continues:

“Although the bodies of the saints were then unburied, the current of water provided a tomb for them, so that, when the structure of their limbs had been restored, it might present them at the judgment to come.”

Placed, therefore, in this distress of mind, they sometimes imposed upon themselves two-day and sometimes three-day fasts, and asked the divine mercy to deign to show them some indication of so holy a deposit, by which his blessed name might be blessed and praised from age to age.

Thus the promise of God might remain unmoved, which says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20)—and there were three brothers devoted to this purpose—they soon perceived that God’s help was being granted to their undertaking.

Before they had completed the three-day fast for the third time, God sent them as an aid a layman of holy conduct named Folbert, blind in both eyes. One of the three brothers mentioned above, Cuono, the custodian of the monastery of Saint Paulinus, received him into his home out of a desire for holy hospitality and supported him with adequate and pleasing attentiveness.

His evening meal consisted of a very small piece of bread, no wider than half a palm, made of two parts flour and one part ash, together with some kind of herbs, either raw or insufficiently cooked and unsalted, and a very small measure of water—certainly not exceeding a small cup.

Greatly gladdened by this consolation of divine assistance and clearly encouraged to hope for greater gifts from God, they disclosed to the brother the plan they had conceived concerning this matter and asked him to supply them with the more fervent assistance of his devotion.

He, being ready to offer everyone all the support within his strength, after the example of the teacher of the nations, who said that he had become all things to all people, intensified his customary fasting for this purpose to such a degree that for three full days he accepted no bodily nourishment at all. During the day he went barefoot, as was his custom, through all the monasteries of this city; at night he spent those same days awake in prayer at the monastery of the aforementioned father Paulinus.

It happened, therefore, that on the third night after the first cockcrow, as he himself later reported to us, while his face was abundantly wet with tears and he was earnestly addressing the Lord with what he called a kind of importunate prayer, he was suddenly seized in an ecstasy of mind and thought that he was standing in a certain underground monastery, very spacious and beautiful.

There, as he saw with the eyes of his mind a multitude that he could not count, walking about and displaying various mutilations of their limbs, he gathered for a while the powers of his mind that he had lost. When some of them, as though solely for the purpose of being questioned by him, presented themselves, he said to them:

“Who are you, lords, and by whom were you slaughtered?”

One who appeared to be the eldest among them answered him:

“We fled here from the persecutions of the pagans, and, when they sought us out for punishment, we suffered the torments that you see.”

Having heard no more words from him, he returned to his former state of sober consciousness. Then, girding himself with all the powers of his mind for giving thanks to God, he earnestly asked God that, if the vision had come from him, he might deign to show it to him a third time.

He obtained this as well. For, falling asleep in prayer twice before daybreak, he was gladdened by the same vision.

When morning came, he summoned the three brothers and related his vision to them in order. With great exhortation he strove to persuade them not to abandon their devoted practice of prayer before they knew that the comfort of divine mercy was present with them. On behalf of him who loves those who persevere in hope, he promised them that within the space of one year divine consolation would come to them in this search.

After giving this exhortation, and thanking God for the welcome of brotherly hospitality that he had found among them, he humbly begged them not to contrive opportunities for him to remain longer in that place, since he wished gladly to complete the journey to Saint James that he had long intended. And so he departed from them.

They, however, burned with an ever-greater desire for the pursuit of this holy investigation. Accordingly, after seeking assistance from monks, canons, and religious women [Note: [Col. 1269] The edition reads “holy nuns”], they devoted themselves to fasts, prayers, and generous almsgiving even more than at the beginning.

It happened that, at midday, a clear voice came to a religious sister of this community named Frideburga, who was resting on her bench in the monastery of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1269D] “At Horrea”], and said:

“Go and search among the most ancient documents, in golden letters, as testimony for them.”

Awakened by the loud sound of this resounding voice, she raised her head from the bench and looked around, but saw no one. She had scarcely lowered her head again into the same resting position when the same voice sounded in her ears a second time, more distinctly than before.

She rose again and fortified herself with the sign of the holy cross. Since she could see no author of the voice, she reclined her head once more—not to sleep, but to await the voice’s coming for a third time.

Then, as she herself reported to us, the same voice came to her with a certain stern imperiousness and greatly frightened her, now awake rather than sleeping.

She rose, therefore, filled more with terror than with distress, and with great haste sought and found the sister who was custodian of the library. After indicating her anxiety, she led her to the storeroom that contained a heap of documents. They had scarcely turned over many volumes of books when an extremely old book of hymns, written in the Scottish script [Note: [Col. 1270D] That is, in Scottish lettering], came into their hands.

When it was finally opened, they repeatedly came upon a fairly extensive hymn concerning Saint Paulinus. Although its composition possessed a certain rusticity, the hymn nevertheless flourished with no little elegance in its subject matter. It related what kind of battle that saint had endured for the Catholic faith against the Arians; how he had been sent into exile by those enemies of the Catholic faith; and how he had converted the Phrygians [Note: [Col. 1269] The edition reads “Frigies”] among whom he was exiled to the faith of Christ by performing signs and miracles before the kings of that land.

The same hymn also contained this: after he had bravely completed the course of this life and received from the Lord there the prize of eternal reward, the precious treasure of his body had been received by the people of Trier by divine command and with the aid of miracles. This, too, was woven into the hymn.

Concerning the revered location of his burial, which took place during his glorious reception, these words were written there:

“They laid him beside the most illustrious and renowned offspring of Trier,

where many bodies of foreigners sleep,

rising again to rewards on the world’s final day,

to meet the Lord in heaven with joy.”

They read and reread these previously unheard testimonies of Sacred Scripture with thanksgiving to God and holy exultation of mind. Yet they did not yet understand whether the warnings of the vision echoed in them, or whether these words indicated that something should be sought on their own.

Therefore they summoned one of the three brothers mentioned above. They told him both of the admonition of the voice—undoubtedly angelic—that the sister mentioned earlier had received, and showed him the book of hymns that, at the prompting of that same voice, they had found among the most ancient volumes of the elders, so to speak.

As soon as he recalled in his mind their common purpose in prayer and the consolation of the divine vision that had been heard and seen, he judged that God’s merciful will lay in this: that he should pray [“he asked,” absent from the edition] that this little book, which made mention of foreigners, might be granted to them, so that it might inspire in us still more strongly the desire to seek them. And this was done.

For as soon as this book of hymns had been brought into the assembly of the brothers and that hymn had been recited there, the hearts of all the brothers present were inflamed to seek further information to such an extent that the single opinion of all the wiser men among them was that the crypt of Saint Paulinus should be broken open for the sake of this investigation.

After consulting with the leaders of the city, they asked the lord archbishop Udo for permission to undertake this, and obtained it only with great difficulty. For the crypt had been deliberately fortified in such a way that, unless the principal altar of the monastery were moved, no place was left through which it could be broken open. Thus the lord archbishop, with good reason and in accordance with his dignity, was not quick to grant permission to break open so great a sanctuary.

When the crypt had therefore been broken open, six sarcophagi were found around the sarcophagus of Saint Paulinus. Two of them had been placed along its sides, while four adhered to its feet in such a way that two stood on each side. In addition, at the head of that same holy father of ours, seven sarcophagi of holy martyrs, fragrant with an equal number of bodies, were placed.

Those who had arranged them had joined everything together in such a way that, after constructing a vault over each pair of sarcophagi, no space was left for moving them unless the monastery’s principal altar was first moved.

Moreover, not the diligent builder of this crypt, but some devoted person concerned with the place and with the holy bodies located there, had constructed a certain small altar at the feet of our holy father, joined to his sarcophagus.

The removal of this altar, followed by some excavation of the earth beneath it, brought full consolation to our expectation. For a marble tablet was found there. When it was lifted, a lead tablet of the same dimensions appeared.

This, too, was raised and, after being cleansed with much water and vigorous rubbing with a pig’s bristle, its engraved inscription reported to us the names of these martyrs and the times of the martyrs, the names of their persecutors, and many other great praises of festal splendor. The engraving on this lead sang all these things to us.

We therefore wished to insert the full text of the engraving here.

In this crypt [Note: [Col. 1271D] See the tablet above, column 1161, note *, edited from the manuscripts of the *Gesta*. Hontheim [Neller?], in the work cited, page 100, sought to prove that it was fabricated after the time of the Northmen; J. Bueus, however, argued for the contrary position in *Acta Sanctorum*, October, volume II, pages 336 and following.] [lacuna]

### 3

This letter was therefore read and soon transcribed onto many sheets, amid the great rejoicing of all the faithful of God who heard it. Yet even within that gathering of God’s faithful there was the dissent of the malignant Church, which did not receive these benefits of divine mercy with the reverence they deserved.

Stirred up by an evil spirit, it dared to tear them apart with livid teeth. But the Lord took care to crush their teeth, since, in the sight of those people, he multiplied through the merits of the precious martyrs—whose discovery they did not celebrate—the signs that, in Paul’s words, are given not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Corinthians 14:22).

Of these signs, therefore, so that we may agree here with the apostolic words, we briefly record some—not so much to instruct Christ’s faithful as to admonish those same ministers of unbelief to embrace the true faith and the reverence owed to God’s saints.

The first of these was so remarkable, so memorable, and indeed so wondrous that not only would whatever minds of unbelievers there were have surely melted away at it, but even the hearts of Christ’s faithful would have trembled greatly. For when, as we have said above, this revelation of the saints had been brought about through God’s mercy and had pleased our lord Archbishop Udo and his leaders, so that the crypt might be suitably enlarged for the placement of the saints’ bodies, it became necessary for a very large amount of earth to be removed from that place. Before this, however, there was on the western side of the aforesaid father Paulinus’s monastery a certain marsh, so harmful to travelers that scarcely the narrowest of paths had been left for those seeking the monastery or wishing to return from it by that route. Therefore it pleased many of the brothers of that place that the same earth, which was being removed from the monastery because of the aforementioned need to prepare the crypt, should be deposited there to dry out the marsh.

When this was being done, and earth had already been deposited there for six days, it happened that, on the seventh day, one of the canons of that place—before whose door the same marsh caused a great inundation—went out from his house in order to level the earth that had been laid there. As he was turning over the soil, he saw some fragments of bones lying there. Taking one of them, he carried it in his hand into his house [Col. 1272C]. He also carefully washed it with water and, after cleansing it, entrusted it to a certain woman for safekeeping until he could find an opportunity to return it to the monastery. She received it contemptuously and, wondering why she should judge it worthy of reverence, nevertheless placed it in her chest among other rags and various items of women’s household use. Some kinds of spices were also stored in the same chest.

When that brother wished to take his evening meal with his companions in the same house, as the observance of the Lenten season required, the young woman to whom the bone had been entrusted began to be tormented by intense pain of the heart. She began humbly and devoutly to beg, through whatever signs of speech she could make—for she was unable to speak in words—for the communion of the body and blood of the Lord, as preparation for her approaching end [Note: [Col. 1271] Or *ut*, as in the edition.]. The brother said to her: “Have your chest brought to you, and if there is there some kind of spice that might help your heart’s pain, look for it.” He said this, and did not delay making the chest available to her so that it might be opened for this purpose.

As soon as it had been opened and its lid slightly raised—wondrous to relate!—so great a quantity of blood poured forth from that very small bone [Col. 1273A] that the woman’s entire face and the right sleeve of her sheepskin garment were astonishingly drenched by it. At that very hour she too was freed from the pain in her heart. Thereupon, struck with overwhelming terror, they immediately implored divine mercy with tearful prayers, asking that, in consequence of so immense a proclamation of his divinity, he not condemn them by any judgment of body or soul.

After this, the same brother ran at full speed to a certain brother whom he knew from experience to be more trustworthy, and brought him to witness the matter. When the latter came and lifted the lid of the chest to inspect it, he said that no one who did not see it could have believed how the blood was still bubbling forth from the same bone, splashing over the entire lid of the chest and everything that was in the chest [Col. 1273B], the instruments of women’s domestic use. Therefore he too, filled with no small amazement, carried the bone hastily to the monastery, together with everything that was in the chest—not henceforth women’s equipment, but rather objects made into sacraments by the sprinkling of such precious blood—and immediately displayed it to all the priors of that place, whom he summoned.

They at once sent messengers throughout all the monasteries of the entire city to announce the event, and at that very hour caused all the abbots and provosts, chorepiscopi and deans, and many other brothers of good reputation to come to them. The lord archbishop was not then in that city. All the other priors of the place, however, quickly gathered in the cloister of Saint [Col. 1273C] Paulinus and rejoiced greatly at the magnificent sign of this miracle.

When the chest was brought into their presence, with the bone pouring out blood without ceasing, one of the brothers took the bloody bone in his hands. Whenever he emptied it repeatedly of the blood that had flowed into the chest, it was filled again, always more quickly than one could say, by a greater flood of blood. The wiser men among those who had gathered then held an inquiry: by what circumstance, they asked, had so great a miracle occurred, and by what divine counsel had those present been struck by the dart of this miracle? From this inquiry one conclusion arose among them all: that, because of this sign, greater reverence should be shown both to the bones of the companions themselves and to their ashes.

They said that an increase of this reverence required that the earth which had been placed around their sarcophagi and, as has been said, had previously been thrown into a muddy place should henceforth be reverently deposited in some clean location. Since its heap would rightly be called Galaath—that is, “heap of testimony”—the miracle performed in the bone that had been placed beneath this earth would speak to all posterity.

When this counsel had been given and approved, the same community of brothers also decided that, after the chest had been carried back into the monastery and placed upon the altar, they should praise the divine wisdom with a common harmony of heart, voice, and bells—a wisdom that does nothing except in great wisdom, as is fitting. Thus men and women of every rank and age from the whole city—young men and maidens, old men with the younger—came joyfully together for this praise of God. When the praise had ended, they returned to their homes, blessing the Lord in amazement at so unheard-of a miracle.

This miracle occurred on the fifth day before the Nones of March, and it was a Saturday [Note: [Col. 1273D] This occurred in the year 1072.]. At the ninth hour that blood began to flow from the bone, and it was not seen to cease until the third hour of the following Monday. The fame of this miracle, flying far and wide, became an occasion of salvation for many, as innumerable people oppressed by various afflictions of illness, aroused from every direction by news of the miracle, came humbly and devoutly to this place. When they had lamented before this sacrament on account of the sins for which they had in some measure been punished, and had tasted, to some extent, the water given to them after it had been consecrated by the dipping of this bone [Col. 1274B], it is credible only to Christ’s faithful how swiftly they were freed from whatever disease afflicted them. But if anyone should curiously ask us for the number and order of these people, let him believe that he is answered by these words of Porphyry: “They are numbered, but not in a finite number.”

### 4.

Moreover, not a few miracles occurred in that crypt where the bodies of the holy martyrs have been laid to rest. Some of these, now coming to our memory, must be briefly indicated. The first of them was this. Although it happens in the memories of very many saints, we nevertheless do not wish to deny a place in these miracles to the one whom the ordering of divine mercy deemed worthy to assign this place.

When the lord archbishop, having heard the report of the miracle of the bone, first came to the monastery of Saint Paulinus for the sake of prayer, there came with him a penitent from the region of Aquitaine whose right arm had been bound with iron. He entered with the lord bishop that excavation—or rather, let me not call it a crypt, since one did not yet exist there. . . . [lacuna]

After this, on the Palm Sunday that was then approaching, a certain woman . . . . [lacuna] It is the custom of the communities of that place that every year, on Palm Sunday, everyone should gather in that same monastery of Saint Paulinus, with a great multitude of people, for the praise of God. When, therefore, on that day, in accordance with this custom, a great number of clergy and people had gathered there and had sung the customary praises to the Lord . . . . [lacuna]

Afterward, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, when, in accordance with the practice introduced by Archbishop Ekbert, large crowds from the surrounding villages customarily come to Trier with crosses and go around all the monasteries of that city, a certain small boy was carried by his parents to the monastery of the often-mentioned father Paulinus, which from that time onward may rightly also be called the monastery of the holy martyrs . . . At that hour the lord archbishop was engaged in prayer in the same monastery with all the communities of the canons of that place . . . [lacuna]

[Col. 1275A] Then, after not much time had passed, a certain girl was brought there . . . [lacuna]

The next miracle in order [Note: [Col. 1275] The edition reads *proximo*.] followed this one. A certain peasant, originally from a village called Saint Aldegundis, whose eyesight had completely failed, was brought there with his priest and a considerable number of his fellow citizens. The priest, taking with him two brothers from that place, led the blind man to the site consecrated to the bodies of the saints. There he had him pledge one denarius as an annual payment to those saints over one of the sarcophagi. After one denarius had been deposited there for the time being . . . [lacuna]

Then another villager from a village commonly called Inda . . . [lacuna]

[Col. 1275]

## FROM THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MODOALDUS, BY STEPHEN.

### [Note.]

When the body of Saint Modoaldus was transferred in 1106 from Trier to the monastery of Helmwardeshusen, a monk of that monastery, who had long sought the saint’s life in vain, approached Stephen, abbot of Saint James at Liège, a man distinguished in learning and works [Note: [Col. 1275C] Compare *Literary History* IX, pp. 522 ff.], with petitions that he complete this gap. In the preface addressed to Abbot Thietmar he writes: “He who, although bodily absent from you for a time, is always present in spirit, while visiting many places of our order in search of the distinction of its patron, and, like a resourceful bee carrying the sweetness of flowers into the liquid of honey, carefully investigating both the deeds of bishops, the annals of the Frankish kings, and the reputation of the sages of old, finally turned to us, the last of all. He begged—not casually but tirelessly and most insistently—that we might deem him worthy to receive from us, for him to carry home, some small gift of our ingenuity concerning the life and miracles of blessed Modoaldus, in readings and responsories.”

“On the one hand, the humility of our profession persuaded us to oppose his suitably importunate petitions, in order to avoid the charge of presumption; on the other hand, the charity within us accused us of hardness toward our neighbor. Considering, without fear, the breadth of the higher way, since we owe wholly to God and to our neighbor what we are, what we live, and what we know, we at last consented to satisfy our friend’s pious desire.”

The author laments that he lacks sources [Note: [Col. 1275C] Compare the passages cited above, p. 112, note 1, and p. 115, note [Col. 1276C] 42.], but nevertheless sets out Modoaldus’s lineage and deeds in a very extensive discourse. Omitting these, we have presented a few of the miracles, following the edition which Henschenius prepared after Surius with the aid of the Corsendoncan manuscript (*Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 51).—The same Stephen received from Thietmar, abbot of Helmwardeshusen, the history of the translation for correction. It belongs in another volume of our collection and will also provide an opportunity to treat Stephen’s writings more accurately.

## BOOK III OF THE LIFE

[Col. 1275B] Since, with God’s favor, we clarified in the first book of this work the noble lineage of blessed Modoaldus, extended through the highest line of royal blood; since in the second we placed before all royal nobility his praiseworthy life, imitable by few, through which he became dear to God and venerable to men; and since we concluded that his glorious passing brought joy to the angelic choirs, we have now judged it not inappropriate, in this third book, to explain very briefly the signs of his holiness—namely, what beginnings of miracles almighty God, in his grace, wished to display after the peaceful dormition of his servant through his relics in the city of Trier . . . [lacuna]

### 1.

It is pleasing briefly to touch upon the extent of the barbarian cruelty and the desolation of the aforesaid city from which that occasion arose through which the merits of the man of God first became known to the faithful. What we discussed in the preface to this little work concerning a similar calamity brought about at another time [Note: [Col. 1276C] See the passage partly transcribed above, p. 112, note 1.] can serve as an argument for understanding what we are about to say here [Col. 1276B].

There we recalled that barbarian nations in general had unleashed the reins of their fury throughout all the regions of Gaul; here, however, we introduce the untamed people of the Northmen, drawn from the sheath of their cruelty, occupying certain parts of Gaul and Germany. Raging through the enormity of their crime, savage against the necks of the faithful like a she-bear whose cubs have been seized, they spared neither sex nor age: they killed venerable old men; they stabbed young men and adolescents defending themselves according to their strength or the time available; they dashed out the brains of little children torn from their mothers’ breasts; they dishonored chaste matrons and modest virgins; they burned the noblest cities with devouring flames; they either overthrew or profaned the sanctuaries of God; and with equal contempt they ruined divine and human things . . . [lacuna]

[Col. 1276C] When the storm of this horrible tempest invaded the city of Trier—in the year 882—all trembled and were terrified. They had no hope either of flight, for which they had not prepared, or of any defense. The image of death hovered before everyone’s eyes; the city’s joyous entertainments passed into lamentation, the choirs of those singing psalms into mourning, and the dances of the girls into wailing. One might have seen the appearance of the entire city transformed, with scarcely any thin remnants of divine religion remaining.

Moreover, the virgins consecrated to God, whom we previously described as serving God in a monastic way of life in the oratory of blessed Symphorianus the martyr [Note: [Col. 1277D] Book II: “Meanwhile . . . he built an oratory on the bank of the Moselle in honor of blessed Symphorianus the martyr, small in workmanship and less ambitious in the elegance of its artful design . . . There he established a community of holy virgins . . . . . . . He also placed his sister, named Severa, over them to maintain the rigor of regular discipline” [Col. 1278D]. Compare the *Deeds*, ch. 24.], fled amid all these forms of death to their accustomed weapons of prayer. They invoked heavenly aid with the most ardent contrition of spirit—not to preserve the present life, which they had despised, but to preserve the chastity they had vowed. All prostrated themselves at the tomb of blessed Modoaldus, asking to be rescued through his protection from the impending danger, and are said to have pierced heaven with prayers such as these or similar ones: “Lord Jesus Christ . . . . . . . .” [lacuna]

[Col. 1277B] When such prayers had been poured forth with great contrition of spirit and a great flood of tears, the action of heavenly hearing was not lacking, nor was the manifestation of miracles by the blessed confessor. Therefore, lest the virgins consecrated to God see the evils they feared on account of the weakness of their sex, or lose the good things they had earned through the observance of chastity—wondrous to hear, even more wondrous to see!—as they lay peacefully in their beds, they all departed from this present life within thirty days. And they did so as happily as they were destined to live eternally: with their lamps adorned, they went out to meet their heavenly bridegroom and entered with him the bridal chamber of everlasting joy.

Their bodies were buried in the same oratory in which the relics of blessed Modoaldus lay, so that, since their souls possessed heaven with their patron through his protecting merits, their bodies might, by the demand of his relics, be buried in the same place. There their prayers flourish, and the benefits of God abound for the memory of the virgins, from that time and now and forever.

### 2.

Since traces of that same tempest still remained and prolonged desolation restrained many of the holy places, it naturally happened that that corner of the saint’s household obtained little reverence in proportion to its dignity, and, abandoned by the negligence of the citizens, lay exposed to injury. But this carelessness of mortals became for our bishop the material of greater glory.

Certain men of Frankish origin, not undistinguished among their people, exceptionally strong in mind and body, had come to the city of Trier out of holy devotion. They had discovered that it was made illustrious throughout all Gaul by the number of its saints and celebrated by the dignity of its antiquity. For some time they attended its homes, delighted by its religious observances, and wore down its sacred thresholds; from being almost unknown, they became very well known. Meanwhile, these naturally shrewd men were seized by the impulse to perform a most splendid crime: by whatever means, through prayers or payment, they might share in the great benefit of Trier through so many relics of the saints . . . [lacuna]

Accordingly, entering the church of Saint Symphorianus under a pretense of devotion and investigating everything that might soon be useful to them, they saw a house neglected and exposed to injury, disregarded by ministers and citizens—indeed, nobler in its merits than the riches of Croesus, but far more obscure than the others because of its poverty of resources . . . . . . when the people began to assemble according to custom for morning prayer . . . [Note: [Col. 1278D] They were discovered while removing part of the body, after blood had been shed. *History* I, p. 76.]

Nevertheless, in order to punish this crime and ensure that pernicious license should not thereafter produce anything similar, they jointly resolved to transfer the saint’s body, which had been left exposed, from the church, and to entrust the heavenly treasure to stronger repositories and a safer treasury. Accordingly, they hastened to prepare a wooden chest, constructed of the strongest boards and reinforced on every side with iron fastenings. They placed the confessor’s relics in it and carried them with the greatest reverence to the oratory of Saint Paulinus, above the altar of the Holy Cross—deliberately, so that like might be joined to like, priest to priest, and that those who came there might be comforted by a double protection.

A slab of Parian marble was added, brought to the highest finish of beauty by the remarkable skill of a sculptor. Found beside his tomb, it bore the name and merit of the buried man, engraved in these words:

“This is the sanctuary of Modoaldus, beloved of God, archbishop of Trier, whose holiness King Dagobert, as is recorded in his charter concerning Trier, magnificently exalted and extended between the Loire and the Rhine” [Note: [Col. 1278D] The date at which this was done is not known.].

This too was mentioned above.

[Col. 1278C] Thus the church of Saint Paulinus, made illustrious by its new guest, soon attained renown; and it is incredible to recount with what devotion the faithful corrected their former neglect, while the poor, together with the rich, hastened to lament their needs before him. But after prolonged repose had produced leisure, and leisure’s security had produced corrupt morals, while contempt for divine things had spread and altered the entire appearance of the city, the judgment of heavenly correction necessarily had to be endured, so that polluted license might be restrained under the bridle of discipline.

Accordingly, in keeping with the prophet’s sentence, “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezek. 9:6), the same oratory was suddenly consumed by fire in the silence of the dead of night [Note: [Col. 1278D] See this false charter in Hontheim.]. Divine judgment brought this about so that, if it had been kindled during the day, the efforts of those running together might not easily extinguish it [Col. 1278D]. Fireballs were carried everywhere, driven by the winds, and the force of the flames ruled with full rein.

Meanwhile, the awakened custodians saw that their affairs were in the greatest danger and that their resources were inadequate to provide help anywhere. Therefore, in the straitened circumstances permitted by so great a crisis, they hurried, ran together, trembled in immense fear, unable either to resist or to remain still, and finally, uncertain whether they should stay or flee [Col. 1279A], testified by their shouting to the unforeseen disaster and uncertain danger.

Their cries roused those who had gathered beneath the dark night, though they were very few. These people nevertheless strove with all their might to protect the gold and silver—which mortals regard as the first of things—and the various equipment of sacred ministry. But they forgot to rescue the saints’ relics and devoted the least attention to those objects.

Thus it happened that the devouring fire, sparing no part of the place, not only completely consumed the dry wooden material but also damaged on every side the marble slabs, wondrous in the dignity of their workmanship. Amid such a desperate situation, who would not have thought that your relics, holy one, would be lost? The mass of the buildings collapsed everywhere; the solidity of the marble burst apart under the force of the heat; and the entire appearance of the sacred buildings [Col. 1279B] was one heap of ashes. Who among all could have believed that the wooden reliquary, most vulnerable to the force of fire, which stood high in the middle of the church’s vault and received the full impact of the collapsing structure, had escaped danger? But the outcome proved that what seemed exceedingly difficult in action to suffering mortals was exceedingly easy for the supreme Administrator of events . . . [lacuna]

### 4.

But since, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we have shown how the blessed confessor was always present for the defense of his relics, it is pleasing to touch upon the rest briefly and to conclude in a few words how he never thereafter failed the salvation of his suppliants. That stone mausoleum, which, as became clear from what was said above, had been broken open and secretly stripped by certain reckless men, was attested by the memory of the elders. After it had been emptied of its precious treasure for the sake of greater security, it was nevertheless arranged in the same church with no less reverence than before and was carefully preserved.

A skilled artisan’s hand had encircled its surface on every side with marble slabs at the front. Firmly joined to one another, these had added usefulness to beauty and beauty to the work. Through their proximity to the saint’s body, so much power and so much saving grace had been divinely added to them that it can scarcely be believed how many human afflictions were relieved through the saint’s benefit.

For anyone consumed to the bone by prolonged fevers, anyone wasted by a lingering disease, who brought here with complete faith the complaint of his sufferings [Col. 1280A], obtained, by mixing scrapings from that marble with water and drinking it, the swiftest remedy for his illness through a most certain cure.

Although even today we see innumerable people hastening from different parts of the world to obtain this aid, and no one seeking the intercession of the pious advocate in vain, it is nevertheless not fitting to pass over in silence one man outstanding in faith and religion.

Mainz, the most celebrated city of all Germany, lies upon the banks of the Rhine. Open to commerce, unfamiliar with poverty, fertile in fields and vineyards, lacking nothing necessary, and sufficiently adorned with men and buildings, it was more blessed still in being distinguished by the venerable order of monks, the most precious kind of religious excellence.

In one of their monasteries, called Saint Alban’s and far nobler than the others [Col. 1280B], there lived in our time a certain provost named Severendus, occupied in heavenly philosophy. He was a man imbued from childhood with the finest disciplines and dear and acceptable to God and men because of his many intellectual gifts.

But a continual illness impeded these happy successes, and the achievement of this eminent man was oppressed by the slow vapors of fevers. His strength exhausted by this most severe disease over a period of three years, he finally believed that nothing could be more healthful than, once the useless efforts of physicians had ceased, to seek the aid of a heavenly hand.

Having learned of the renown of the church of Trier, he traveled there and directed his steps thither. Joining the suppliant people, a humble petitioner but a most renowned obtain­er of benefits, he approached the saint’s tomb and sincerely partook of a drink made from scraped marble. His faithful desire was not frustrated: before long, he was completely restored from sickness and exchanged pallor for renewed color.

Not forgetful of the benefit, he served all the saints with purity but clung more familiarly to his own healer. He had advanced so far in devotion toward him that he sought our place [Note: [Col. 1279C] This can scarcely refer to the monastery of Saint James. Did the monk of Helmwardeshusen add this?], where he had learned that the saint’s relics had recently been transferred, with special affection, visiting it repeatedly and frequently. Previously welcome to our brotherhood, he then became most welcome through the constancy of his residence.

We have rightly judged that the power which he had experienced and which, by his account, had become known to the brothers devoted to him should be inserted into our narrative, fearing not at all that it might be assailed by the weak slander of falsehood, since the patronage of so truthful a man will easily render such slander powerless . . . [lacuna]

[Col. 1279]

## FROM THE INVENTION AND MIRACLES OF SAINT MATTHIAS.

### [Note.]

Trithemius already reported that Lambert of Liège had written books on the life and miracles of Saint Matthias the apostle [Note: [Col. 1279C] Take care not to suppose that he is the same man who wrote the *Life of Saint Heribert* in the eleventh century; see *Literary History* VIII, p. 6; *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, IV, p. 739; *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège* in Martène IV, p. 1067.]. Browerus [Note: [Col. 1280C] II, p. 22.], Hillarius [Note: [Col. 1280C] P. 85.] and others likewise attest this. Therefore, when Henschenius published two accounts of Saint Matthias, buried and discovered at Trier (*Acta Sanctorum*, February III, pp. 441 and 448), he did not doubt that one of them should be attributed to Lambert [Note: [Col. 1281A] *Literary History* XII, pp. 531 ff., agrees with Henschenius.]. He assigned that title to the account which he took from the Saint Matthias manuscript and which is plainly shown at first sight to have been composed shortly after the saint’s discovery.

Hillarius, however, demonstrated that the other account was Lambert’s by pointing out that the preface placed before it in the Trier manuscript contains Lambert’s name. I would not think him mistaken in this matter [Note: [Col. 1281A] This is what Sybel argues, *Die Advokaten* II, p. 43, n.], nor do I see what should prevent us from accepting this opinion.

In indicating Lambert’s date, Trithemius errs in his customary manner [Note: [Col. 1281A] In one place he says that Lambert lived from 1038 to 1047 (*Annals of Hirsau*, as cited); elsewhere he says: “He flourished under Henry IV in the year of Our Lord 1080.”]. Nor do we have any certain knowledge from another source concerning the period in which he lived [Note: [Col. 1281A] One fact is that Browerus, in the passage cited, says that Lambert wrote that he had been freed from fevers in his own time through the aid of Saint Matthias; see note 67. But even this does not conflict with our opinion.], except for that preface, which was sent to Abbot L.—that is, Ludowicus—who governed the monastery of Saint Matthias after the middle of the twelfth century [Note: [Col. 1281A] From approximately 1169 to 1182 he appears in charters preserved by Hontheim.].

The preface, as Henschenius copied it from Lazius’s edition, lacks the names which Hillarius supplied from the Trier manuscript:

“To his most reverend lord, the most worthy abbot L. of the church of Saint Eucharius at Trier, Lambert, a humble Levite, the least of all the brothers entrusted to him, offers the devoted obedience of due submission.

Since you excel, most blessed father, in word and deed, and have drawn many back from secular frivolity to the cloister of contemplation [or society?], among whom you have devoted particular attention to my formation, your daily persistence, admonition, and correction bear witness to this. Although, because of youthful frivolity, I do not receive it readily enough, I do not fail to recognize the piety from which it proceeds when I recall my mind from vanity.

Nor must I pass over the fact that you continually command and encourage me to persevere in reading: lest the enemy find me idle; lest, by murmuring, he occupy my mind; lest detraction serve upon my tongue; and lest my hand persist in work that contributes nothing to the matter at hand.

Therefore your blessedness commands me to expound at greater length the life of blessed Matthias the apostle, over whose bones you preside worthily, translated from a Hebrew volume called the *Book of the Condemned*, because it contains the judgments of those who act against the law, having investigated with eager—or rather extorted—effort the entire truth of the matter.

Although I am marked, as I deserve, for audacity, I nevertheless did this as best I could. Therefore another may be permitted to explain it at greater length and with greater eloquence, and to polish this rustic style more suitably with urban refinement.

May the Lord preserve you unharmed for us, dearest father. Amen.”] [Col. 1281B]

Lambert received his surname from the fact that he was born at Liège, or Legia [Note: [Col. 1281C] The following verses appear in Hillarius, in the passage cited, and in Wyttenbach, vol. I, preface, p. XX, from the manuscript now in the Trier public library, no. 80:

“Liège gave me birth; another Trier cherishes me, in which,  
As a little one, I played little tunes and store up little things.”].

He lived in the monastery of Saint Matthias, where he celebrated the saint’s praises both in verse and in prose. I have not seen the former, which remains unpublished, nor did I read it in the Trier manuscript. This book first presents the life of Saint Matthias, said to have been translated from a Hebrew manuscript [Note: [Col. 1281C] See the letter reported in note 62 and the prologue prefixed to this book:

“When I was burning with great zeal and concern to discover the deeds of blessed Matthias the apostle, which are found in none of the ecclesiastical interpreters, a certain priest named Theoderic saw me wavering and sad, asked the causes of my sadness, and learned them. Filled with great joy because he had discovered this zeal in me, he said that, if I wished to be an interpreter of those same deeds, he would arrange with a certain Jewish acquaintance of his to present me with a book which the Jew himself called the *Book of the Condemned*, because it contained the condemnation of those who act against the law—namely, of Matthias, both Jameses, and Stephen.

At that time I had learned the Hebrew letters from one of the Jews. The man came, bringing the little book. When I read its title, I found written *Sir Hasirim*, that is, ‘Song of Songs.’ I was so enraged that I could scarcely keep my hands off him. For he was trying to deceive me out of the innate hatred he bore Christians.

‘And do you,’ I said, ‘most filthy procurer, attempt to deceive a cleric who has acquired a full knowledge of Hebrew, Greek, and Latin histories? There is certainly nothing in your library, whether Greek or Latin, that I do not know.’

Overcome by fear, especially lest I should harm him with the ruler in whose favor I then stood, he promised under oath that he would satisfy me—and he did so. For when I read the title of the book which he afterward brought, I discovered that it was written *Ay Mathay*, that is, ‘Life of Matthias.’ Finally, believing that I understood everything written below, he nevertheless, though unwilling, disclosed the whole truth to me in order, after receiving from us a payment of twenty-three solidi.

The following year my lord the archbishop discovered that another Jew, who was in danger of losing his property, possessed the matter in precisely this way, except that he said a verse of a psalm alluded to his own name. Later the same thing was revealed to a certain anchoress who had undertaken a three-day fast for this very purpose.

Let it therefore be read without any hesitation of doubt, since it has been found true by such certain proofs, because the Holy Spirit has removed every ambiguity. How it came from Judea to Trier, as I read in the history of Trier and in the records of Pope Sylvester, I shall also explain, together with his subsequent miracles.”]

Afterward it narrates the discovery and miracles that occurred in the twelfth century, but it is for the most part copied from that earlier account and here and there enlarged by a few details, themselves fabulous [Note: [Col. 1282C] I have reported a few of them in the notes.].

I omitted all these matters as being of no value, but preferred to follow that earlier author who carefully set forth what he had received from his forebears or had himself witnessed.

[Note: [Col. 1282C] Chapter 6. The *Gesta* follows the first chapter.]

The miracles said to have been added at the end are now missing; nor did I have at hand the books on the miracles of Saint Matthias written metrically by Lambert, which still seem to exist in the Trier library.

[Note: [Col. 1282C] Concerning these, see Trithemius, cited above. The following also seem to belong here, as Brower, cited above, observed: “Lambert himself, a coenobite not without learning, who also pursued in a written book the works divinely performed there, writes that through the aid of the holy Matthias he was delivered from troublesome and acute fevers in this present age.”]

[Note: [Col. 1282C] See Wyttenbach, cited above.]

Others have been published together with Lambert’s life.

[Note: [Col. 1282C] I do not know whether the brief account of the church of Saint Matthias, dedicated by Pope Eugenius in the year 1140, should also be attributed to the same author (*Acta Sanctorum*, cited above, p. 453); see Hontheim, *History*, I, p. 552, note h.]

Others I transcribed from an Erlangen manuscript of the twelfth century, which also contains the Life of Saint Otto of Bamberg and other works,

[Note: [Col. 1282C] I shall discuss this more accurately elsewhere.]

and from a Trier manuscript of the thirteenth century (no. 547). Although some of these accounts belong to a later period, I judged that they should be inserted into this collection of Trier monuments.

## FROM THE HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERY

[Col. 1283]

[Col. 1283A] We believe it worthy and right, and indeed fitting, that the city of Trier, which contains the blessed bones of Matthias the apostle, should solemnize another day in the glory and honor of the blessed apostle Matthias, in addition to that reverence which Christ’s faithful throughout the whole world offer him on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

[Note: [Col. 1283D] On the Kalends of September. “This day,” says Brower, “the later coenobites observe as a holiday in the divine offices in honor of the discovery of the holy apostle.” Henschen.]

For it is truly pious and appropriate that those to whom the grace of our Lord God has been granted—more familiarly than to other peoples—to enjoy, as it were, his converse and to be daily warmed by his blessing, should honor him with a more devoted reverence than those to whom this grace has not been granted. We judged this especially appropriate on the day of his life-giving revelation. We shall therefore relate in due order, with the Lord’s help and as far as we are able, how greatly we have rejoiced at the joyful translation, discovery, and revelation of his relics, and at the glorification produced by miracles of such and such magnitude.

[Col. 1283B] But at the very beginning we must beseech the blessed Matthias himself, through the Lord Jesus, that by his intercession, guided by our foolishness, we may bring forth nothing other than what is worthy of him and pleasing to God.

### 1

[Note: [Col. 1283D] This chapter is taken from *The Deeds*, chapters 19 and 18.]

In the year 368 of the incarnation of the Word of God, while Constantine the Great, father of emperors and a most Christian ruler, was happily governing the scepters of the Roman name; while blessed Helena, his mother, the august empress, likewise steadfast in her Christian profession, had discovered the Lord’s cross; she, mindful of pious duty toward this, her native country—for she was a native of the city of Trier—sent the blessed apostle Matthias here from Judaea, together with other magnificent relics of which there is no need to speak now, through Agric[i]us, patriarch of Antioch, with the blessing of the blessed Sylvester, then Roman pontiff.

We learned this by reading the examples of the blessed Sylvester himself given to Agric[i]us. Not long afterward, the faithful people then living at Trier reverently placed this blessed Matthias, deeply buried in the earth beside the bodies of the saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, with prudent foresight because of the persecutions of the churches which the Arians and pagans were stirring up. They did this for the sake of the joy and gladness of the sons who would come later. By God’s grace we now enjoy participation in the joy of his revelation.

### 2

[Col. 1283D] A great deal of time had passed—almost six hundred years (1047–1066)—and Eberhard, an industrious man, was governing the church of Trier.

[Note: [Col. 1283D] These matters are related less correctly in the other account, that of Lambert: “In the year 1127 from the incarnation of the Lord, while Henry, the second Roman emperor of that name, was reigning, Archbishop Eberhard governed the Trier see. To him Emperor Henry and the whole church of Trier directed their sacred embassy,” and so forth.]

At that time he was urgently petitioned by the king who then reigned, namely Henry, son of Emperor Conrad II, to give him some relics of the holy apostle Matthias, as well as the bodies of other saints, in order to adorn the church he was building at Goslar; for his church at Trier was reputed to abound in them more than all the churches this side of the Alps.

The bishop refused the petitioner the relics, because he doubted that they were there; indeed, even if they were there, he did not know where they were. Meanwhile, on one occasion, when he had gone to Rome, either for the sake of prayer or because some other reason required it, he happened by chance upon a book containing information about the places where each of the apostles had preached, where and how they had suffered, and where they had come to rest.
