By reading it he learned that Saint Matthias had preached and come to rest in Judaea, that afterward he had been transferred from Judaea by Helena, the mother of Constantine, and sent to Trier through Agric[i]us, patriarch of Antioch, and that there he had been deposited beside the bodies of the disciples of Christ, the Son of God, on the left-hand side, between north and south.

When he saw this, he rejoiced greatly and, showing it to certain men accompanying him who were not entirely faithful to this church of Trier, offered it as a cause for congratulations. These men then reported to the king what they had learned by reading, flattering him in the hope of winning his favor. For the king, as we have already mentioned, did not cease pressing the matter; rather, day by day he insisted more and more that his desire should be fulfilled.

Thus they became informers concerning the magnificent, precious, and most sacred treasures of that church. When the king heard that the bones of Matthias had formerly been deposited beside the bodies of the disciples of Christ—as we have said, there can be no doubt that these were the blessed Eucharius and his companions—he demanded, under threat of withdrawing his favor and affection, that the body of Saint Valerius the bishop be given to him together with however small a portion of Matthias’s relics.

He promised—and did so—to bestow magnificent benefits from his revenues, for the honor of God and, as it were, to placate the father of the household of that monastery, the blessed Eucharius named above, so that he would permit his brother and fellow soldier to be separated from him.

[Note: [Col. 1284D] By a charter issued in 1153, in Hontheim I, p. 395; see *The Deeds*, chapter 32. But in 1151 Henry was at Trier.]

Accordingly, persuaded by the suffragan bishops Adalbero, called “the Saint,” of Metz, and Theoderic, surnamed “the Great,” of Verdun, together with others who happened to be at Trier at that time, the archbishop, although unwilling, permitted the relics to be dug out from the profoundest depth of the earth.

Finally, when the aforesaid bishops and other members of the clergy had opened the tomb, such sweetness of fragrance suddenly issued from it that all were struck with wonder and fear and, as we believe, divinely inspired. They resolved not to deprive this region of so great a treasure, but to close the tomb-cover as quickly as possible.

[Col. 1284D] The bishop Theoderic of Verdun lost the edge of the cope in which he had been solemnly vested that day. For while he was scrutinizing the holy relics too eagerly, in the hope that he might steal something from them, the tomb was quickly closed, and part of the cope happened to be shut inside it. Since he resisted and objected, it immediately had to be cut away with a blade.

A venerable priest who had deserved to handle the bones of the apostle became famous throughout the rest of his life by this testimony: whenever he mentioned any of those relics with someone, the fingers of his right hand, sanctified by touching the holy bones, immediately began, in a wonderful manner, to drip as though soaked in oil.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] Lambert adds: “A certain religious old man told me with tears that he had often seen this happen to his fellow priest, to the astonishment of many.”]

Thereafter, at the petition and on the advice of the people concerned with the bodies mentioned above and with the whole church, the most sacred bones of the blessed apostle Matthias were no longer buried beneath the earth. Instead, they were placed above ground, although they were hidden in walls or altars, lest they perhaps be stolen, or beneath the enclosures of the same basilica, where the faithful could offer the duties of pious devotion and yet no person could easily carry them off by force. Thus the city, fortified by this patron, would not forever be deprived of his benefit.

But where those sacred pledges had then been deposited became unknown when the older generations had passed away and their sons succeeded them.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] The other account says differently: “Here the priest divided the apostle Matthias into three portions and carefully and secretly placed him in three altars, with only a very few of the faithful knowing, lest afterward the city of Trier should be deprived of its own patron by anyone’s violence.”]

### 3

But after almost eighty years had passed, it pleased Lord Eberhard, father of that same monastery of the holy confessors Eucharius and his companions, to destroy the old walls of the monastery and build new ones.

[Col. 1285C]

[Note: [Col. 1285D] On this matter compare what is read in the continuation of the other version of *The Deeds*, to be published later.]

Whatever the occasion on which this work was begun, it was not undertaken without divine dispensation, especially since no pressing ruin of the old buildings had brought about a work so costly and requiring such immeasurable expenditure.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] He relates how the body of Saint Matthias was revealed to several people in dreams. Lambert’s account has other details, including the following: “After this, in the bishopric of Tongeren, now the bishopric of Liège, there is a certain place called Susteren, because nuns live there, whom the common people call sisters. In that place there was a mother of the monastery devoted to religion who, as is customary, decided by lot to choose one of the apostles as her patron. She therefore wrote the names of the twelve apostles on twelve candles and, placing them upon the altar,” and so forth.]

[lacuna] beside the altar which stood apart there, opposite the feet of the confessors, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, [lacuna].

Meanwhile the new structure of the building was rising and being carried forward with very great haste, while the earlier sanctuary still remained standing. When summer had ended and autumn was beginning, as they were setting up the machinery for the altar of the great arches that stand before the sanctuary, they judged it appropriate that the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God, which we mentioned above, should be removed.

[lacuna]

There they found a leaden reliquary, shaped like a small chest, containing the larger bones of the body of the apostle Matthias, as well as a broad marble slab about a palm in width, on which this was engraved: “Saint Matthias the apostle,” together with the relics placed within.

[Note: [Col. 1286D] Lambert explains this occurrence fabulously.]

What more need be said? That building resounded with the unanimous joy of all and with voices praising the Lord. The chest containing the sacred relics was carried into the middle; a wooden case, hastily prepared for the occasion and most securely fastened with iron, together with other safeguards of the kind briefly mentioned above, was locked away with the greatest care.

[Note: [Col. 1285] The passage seems to be corrupt.]

It remained so until, when the new work then in hand had been completed, a common decision could be reached about where it should be placed in a suitable location.

A few days later many sick people began to assemble, and the Lord’s grace followed the apostle’s prayers. For the Lord blessed his land and turned away Jacob’s captivity; after long years of barrenness, deprivation, and famine, the land yielded its fruit, and the Lord prepared a table for his people. The violence of tyrants and robbers was driven away, and pleasant times of peace and rest followed, so that in our rejoicing we may truly say: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke 1:68).

This discovery occurred in the year 1127 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifth indiction, while the most serene worshiper of God, Lothair the Saxon, was reigning, under the pontificate of Meginher, bishop and martyr of Christ, on the Kalends of September, at the first hour of the day, to the praise and glory of Christ.

### 4

But just as, without any preceding merits of good works, and rather through God’s free mercy, we had been magnificently gladdened, advanced, and consoled by the unexpected discovery of this most holy apostle, so afterward, because our sins deserved it and because of the causes mentioned above,

[Note: [Col. 1285] The edited text reads *supermemoravimus*, “we mentioned above.”]

we were grievously saddened and endangered.

Five years after that event—that is, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s incarnation—while the structure of the old monastery of Saint Eucharius was being diligently restored to a new condition, and while the part near the sanctuary had been completed and securely covered with beams and tiles, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June,

[Note: [Col. 1285] There may be an error in the number or the month, since the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June would be the same as the Ides of May.]

when the brothers, after the midday hour had passed, had begun the ninth hour as usual, a tremendous fire suddenly and unexpectedly broke out in the building of the sacristy adjoining the monastery on the north. It sent threatening flames high into the air, and, quickly seizing the roof of the sanctuary, threatened everyone with deadly destruction.

Immediately, sooner than words can say, the entire city was stirred and gathered together as one. They rushed to put out the fire. Having climbed onto the building itself and opposing it from every side, they tried in vain to extinguish the conflagration, which, as the outcome afterward showed, was raging by divine will.

When the fire fell upon their heads—for they could not climb onto the burning roofs—and the entrance through which they had entered was already nearly blocked, so that no exit for escape was open and they were hemmed in on every side by the impending danger, they were forced, against their will, to yield to the raging flames. Some fell through the windows onto the nearby lower roofs; others, lowering themselves by ropes, barely escaped unharmed.

Again rushing together in competition, they quickly destroyed the roofs of the dormitory and cloister, lest the fire, spreading from the monastery, render the place wholly uninhabitable. This would certainly have happened had the merciful compassion of God not been present. For although a house at the very edge of the village, far from the monastery, was set alight by the fire, how much more would the roofs nearest the building have been almost entirely consumed if God’s protection had not intervened?

Therefore we may rightly cry out: “Unless the Lord had helped us, perhaps the fire that arose would have swallowed us alive.”

Who could adequately recount how many tears were shed there, how much weeping and how many sighs, when they thought that the place most beloved throughout the whole kingdom, made famous by God’s grace through the discovery and miracles of the blessed Matthias, was to be destroyed by deadly flames?

But what the Lord deigned to show of mercy and consolation must, with complete justice, be made known.

### 5

First of all, our concern was for the relics of the saints, and especially for the pledges of the holy apostle Matthias, by which the Lord had deigned to glorify this place. We feared that men of malicious intent might devise some scheme through which the place would thereafter be made a laughingstock and an object of contempt.

This would indeed have happened in every respect, had not, as I said shortly before, the mercy of God been present.

For when the fire, as we have said, was consuming everything around it by licking it with its flames, and the little building containing the great altar and the sarcophagus of the saint was already threatened by the fire, certain men of malicious intent gathered together and discussed in common how they might extract the sarcophagus by whatever means they could, remove it from the fire, and carry it into the city.

They said that clear signs had shown that it was no longer the saint’s will to remain there, since the monks had in every way proved themselves unworthy of his protection.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] Lambert says that the monks were unworthy of Matthias because they were black both in clothing and in morals.]

They therefore fastened a very long rope around the sarcophagus and extended it as far as the outer gate, trying with all their strength to rescue it from the fire. But the outcome plainly revealed the intention with which they acted. For although more than a hundred men struck it now with their arms, now with clubs, they could scarcely move it from its place.

At last men of sounder judgment and greater authority arrived. They nullified the others’ plan and, with immense labor, finally dragged it outside and placed it before the doors of the shrine. When, after the fire had ended, they carried it back to its former place, however, it was found to be extremely light: what a hundred men had shortly before been unable to move was now carried back with ease by twelve.

### 6

To those who wish to know from what cause this arose, or why God permitted this fire to prevail, we shall explain the matter as far as we can. It must not be suppressed in silence, because the cause of the fire was greater than the fire itself.

There was a certain monk who had come from elsewhere and had long since been received there.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] Lambert calls him a certain hypocritical Swabian in his account.]

He did not live there according to the rule of the obedience he had promised, but without subjection, and he displayed such a completely false fidelity everywhere that not only were the smallest tasks entrusted to him, but even the obedience of cellarer was unworthily imposed upon him.

Eventually he lost that office, although unwillingly, because he had led a most disorderly life. Then, with the devil surely prompting him, he again seized upon the office of assistant to the keeper, without being ordered to do so, so that by the voluntary assistance he offered he might also be judged suitable for this obedience.

What more need be said? Since it accorded with his own will, he was appointed assistant to the keeper and immediately, against the will of the brothers and despite their frequent objections, set up a bed for himself in the monastery, where he could more conveniently find a place to carry out his madness.

He had a desire to depart, and for this reason he strove by every means, though secretly, to acquire the relics of the saints, hoping that he would be received more honorably if he came with them to another place.

A very large tower remained from the structure of the old monastery. It opened an entrance to those entering the church and had once been built with the greatest care by the venerable abbot Bertulf. On its ascent he had established an altar. Although that altar had been neglected because it had recently been violated by those mentioned above and emptied of its relics at the summit,

[Note: [Col. 1288D] This is not found in the printed editions, but the reference seems to be to the same matter in chapter 3.]

it later became clear that it had been richly marked by the bones and ashes of Saint Agric[i]us, patriarch of Antioch and archbishop of Trier.

Although he had been preserved there for so long without anyone knowing it, we nevertheless heard from the elders that the aforesaid venerable abbot would sometimes secretly climb that tower and devote the entire day there to prayer; very often, too, he would spend the night lying prostrate before the aforementioned altar in vigil.

Perhaps, then, the plan of the work required that this tower be destroyed so that space might be made for the new construction. When its buildings and ceilings had almost all been removed, the aforesaid monk, prompted—I do not know by what spirit—after the hour of supper had passed, seized a tool as the laborers were leaving their work for home and began to break apart the aforementioned altar.

After he had labored for some time at breaking it, he found a small chest carefully stored away with a seal placed upon it. Since he did not know letters, he could not determine whose seal it was. He told us, however, that he recognized only the first letter, which was at the beginning of the name of the aforesaid abbot Bertulf. It was therefore judged to have belonged to Bertulf, who had built the tower and established the altar at the same time.

He brought the chest outside and, after removing the seal, did not hesitate to open it with his rash hand. Taking away a brief inscription written on marble and placed upon the bones, he was able to recognize, by reading as best he could, what was plainly written: “Saint Agric[i]us the archbishop.”

[Col. 1289B]

[Note: [Col. 1289D] Wishing to explain this, Lambert says: “Since he did not fully understand the writing, he began to search whether he could find anything similar anywhere. He did so. For when he found something similar written in a book of his Life, through repeated inquiry he came to know this name.”]

He was delighted, descended with the chest, and carried it away with him. Since he had no secure place in which to keep it, he hid it in a crypt in the cemetery among the bones of the dead, until he could provide himself with a suitable place where he could keep it without fear and without anyone knowing.

It lay hidden there for three days, until, since he was an assistant to the keeper, he carefully prepared a suitable place in the sacristy for preserving relics. The lower part of the sacristy building is vaulted in stone, while the upper part is covered with wood; one ascends to it from below by a spiral staircase.

In this upper section he prepared a place between the beams and the roof, and there he placed the sacred bones after bringing them back from the crypt. He piled a great heap of wood from the old building around them and, going there often and sometimes even sleeping there, did not cease frequenting the place.

Meanwhile he prepared his journey after obtaining permission and sent a message to one of his trustworthy friends, earnestly asking him to come to him. He added that he wanted no one else at all to be present at the matter he wished to discuss with him.

Having placed part of the relics from the chest in cloths he had prepared, he diligently took care that nothing should obstruct his departure, so that, when everything had been properly arranged, he could leave freely on whatever day he wished.

The wretch had devised these things without considering divine retribution. But almighty God, who did not wish Agric[i]us to be separated from his most holy apostle, whose bearer he had once been across so many expanses of land, revealed and nullified his impious plan.

For when, as we have said, he had for some time frequently visited that place with constant care, he descended from it on the day before the event, as was his custom, and prepared to go elsewhere—I do not know where. Suddenly the building itself, consumed by a fire whose origin was unknown, burned down together with the relics and the monastery.

Some people, however, affirm that he had a lamp there in honor of the relics, a claim he entirely denied. Others again say that it happened because of the fire with which candles were prepared there; but this seems unbelievable, since three days earlier the fire there had completely gone out. In truth, the matter had been decreed by divine will.

As the fire shot its flames high into the air, that most wretched man, anxious about the relics, hurried up into the building. He seized the cloth containing the relics, which was already near the fire, and, wishing to drag it away with him, was completely unable to do so. It yielded no further to his wicked hands, but remained there to be consumed.

After he had labored in vain for a long time to pull it away, he opened the chest in despair, so that he might at least take one part from it and preserve it unburned according to his own wishes. But when he looked inside, suddenly fire, as though discharged like a flash of lightning from the sacred bones, set his face aflame, and he fell backward, almost lifeless.

Even then he did not open his mouth to disclose the matter to any of those who came running with weapons and water. Had he done so, the relics could have been rescued from the fire unharmed.

Thus, by God’s arrangement, the bones and dust of Agric[i]us remained in the place from which they had been wickedly removed in order to be stolen. Later, after being diligently sought piece by piece among the coals, they were found for the most part, so that we do not doubt that we possess the greater part of his body.

The dust, carefully purified with a sieve together with the ashes, was placed there to be preserved in one location. Some advised that an altar should be established there in honor of the same Saint Agric[i]us and that a church should be dedicated.

Blessed in every way is God, who, although we are unworthy, did not wish to deprive us of such a patron, whose help we rejoice to enjoy everywhere!

After these things had taken place, the author of this crime, seeing that what God had wished to reveal could not be concealed, brought forward everything he had done or planned. He also showed the place where he had placed the relics.

The brothers carefully searched it and, as we have already said, gathered together as many of the half-burned bones as they could and preserved them honorably for the future.

The wretch then departed with permission, in accordance with everyone’s judgment, since it seemed to us that it was no longer fitting for him to live in this place.

[lacuna]

### 7

[lacuna] I find this sufficiently remarkable: amid so great a danger from fire and conflagration, amid so great a gathering and multitude of people of both sexes, no one at all suffered any injury to life or health, and none of us lost any part of his possessions.

Let these matters, however imperfectly related, suffice. Now let us speak of some miracles of the blessed Matthias which, according to the testimony of many religious men still living, occurred before his discovery; from them we happened to hear these accounts.

[lacuna]

These miracles are absent from the edition.

## FROM THE MIRACLES

[Col. 1291]

### 1. From the Erlangen manuscript

[Note: [Col. 1291D] Some things agree with what is read in Lambert, *Acta Sanctorum*, cited above. But Lambert seems to have used this source.]

[Col. 1291A] Meanwhile, as the renown of the blessed Matthias grew through many signs, very many people, summoned from different parts of the world by the fame of his powers,

[Note: [Col. 1291] *exciti* corrected from *excitati*.]

came and were cured of their illnesses.

One day, as religious men carrying votive offerings were hurrying toward that place, another group came out from there and met them. As they began, as is customary, to inquire more closely whether the apostle’s miracles were truly as they had heard, a certain man of malicious intent—later it became clear that the devil had instigated him—said:

“What? Do you believe in old women’s tales? Do you not know that clerics and monks are exceedingly skilled at fabricating such things, for the sake of profit, and that by their tricks they set traps for our purses and storehouses? So that they may feast, we must fast; so that they may abound, we shall be in want.

“The reason they repeatedly set idols before us—now Martin, now Nicholas, now the others—is not concern for our salvation but greed for our property. As though this were not enough, they now make a new little god of Matthias, so that they may drain the ancestral estate completely.

“Return, then, to your senses and see that these are the ravings of old women rather than true miracles.”

While he was saying this and much else that I have omitted for the sake of brevity, his wife, his sons, and other men of sounder judgment begged him not to disparage the holy apostle, saying that these were divine works, not human fabrications.

But when the unhappy man refused not only to keep silent but also uttered much worse things, he was suddenly handed over to the ancient enemy, at whose prompting he spoke. He tore his cloak and tunic down to his feet, mounted his horse, and sped away with a loud cry through the mountains, valleys, and every trackless place.

He was sought for two days but was not found. On the third day his horse appeared in a certain marsh, but he himself could nowhere be found. By his example many were corrected and became more devout.

At the same time, a certain paralytic from the Ardennes forest, which is the largest forest in all Gaul, [lacuna].

It is the established solemn custom of the Gauls on the fourth day before the Kalends of July for the people of each diocese to gather together and proceed with relics and litanies to the city of Trier, so that they may celebrate with common joy the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.

Since the discovery of Saint Matthias, however, this custom has particularly flourished here; hence it is also often repeated in popular song. While some people were singing in this manner praises of Saint Matthias, which in the vernacular they call *leysos*, one of them,

[Note: [Col. 1291] *usus* corrected.]

moved by youthful frivolity, began to jest rashly and, in place of a song closely resembling the praise, began to sing something similar in order to provoke laughter among those like himself.

[lacuna]

The following year, a certain peasant entered a small boat with his wife and son on the eve of Saint John the Baptist and decided to travel by the Moselle to the threshold of the blessed apostle. On the journey he was captured by a certain tyrant and thrown in chains into prison, while the others escaped by flight.

[lacuna]

In the city of Strasbourg in the province of Alsace, a certain cleric [lacuna].

Another man, while he was a shepherd of sheep, vowed a sheep from his poor fold to blessed Simeon, who rests at Trier by the Porta Marcia, which is also called the Black Gate.

[lacuna]

[Col. 1292B] Two men from a village called Logostein,

[Note: [Col. 1292D] Lahnstein.]

intending to cross the Rhine, entered a fisherman’s boat.

[lacuna]

[lacuna] He also sought the aid of Jews and the charms of old women.

[lacuna]

Likewise, a little boy following his mother, who was walking ahead, fell from the Attila bridge into the waters below.

[lacuna]

Near the triumphal arch of Attila,

[Note: [Col. 1292D] The reference seems to be to the monument still standing in the village of Igel.]

which lies two miles south of the city of Trier, a young man, wishing to wade across the Moselle in midsummer, [lacuna].

A certain soldier born in the territory of Trier was not of the lowest rank, but he was poor in property. Therefore, moved by shame, he left his native land and traveled wherever opportunity presented itself.

He came to Cologne Agrippina, where, because he was pleased with both the constitution and the laws of the city, he chose to settle. He therefore adopted the most powerful men as his lords, so that, after rendering them loyalty and service, he might live more securely through their aid and counsel.

After he had prospered for a long time and no trouble had arisen, an occasion presented itself on which one of his lords, concealing his hatred, summoned him to his house, seized him, and threw him into chains. For nine days, finally, he lay in a certain fortress.

[lacuna]

A certain man of Purgensis, of the same city, [lacuna].

A certain boy, the son of a widow, was struck by illness and brought to the point of death. After he had been sick for fifteen days, he died. He was placed in a coffin and set in the middle of the house, where, according to the custom of the Gauls, people solemnly gathered for vigils and games.

Some played, but the mother wept most bitterly.

[lacuna]

[Col. 1293A] A man of about fifty, a resident of Pulcrum-Mons,

[Note: [Col. 1293D] Beaumont.]

which is in the Ardennes forest, [lacuna] a certain free man, a citizen of the same castle, [lacuna].

In the suburban countryside adjoining Trier toward the north, near the Porta Marcia, [lacuna].

At Fulda, which is in Germanic France, a certain woman was about to cross a bridge over the river.

[lacuna]

There was a certain man who, just as he was rich in possessions, was also rich in vices and of malicious intent. He attacked his neighbors with murders and robberies and violently plundered everything.

One of those whom he had unjustly oppressed set fire to his house and fled. But the tyrant, being as perverse in mind as ever, laid the crime upon a poor man and brought him before the court.

When the poor man, through his advocate, denied having done it, the case eventually came to be decided by a duel.

The tyrant, being exceedingly thirsty for blood, received this with eager spirit. The poor man, however, wanted to submit himself and his possessions to the tyrant’s authority in order to obtain peace. But the tyrant refused.

On the appointed day they both came, entered the place of combat, and engaged one another, their strength unequal though the contest was evenly matched. For the tyrant wore down the poor man almost to surrender, until the poor man, compelled by his own companions, invoked the name of Saint Matthias. Then he struck down and killed the rich man with a single blow.

Thus innocent blood was saved through the merits of the blessed Matthias.

[lacuna]

Near the bridge of the Moselle, a little boy fell from a boat and was submerged. Seeing this, a young man threw off his clothes and leapt into the water. Wishing to find and pull him out, he lost him once and then a second time, as the evil spirit—whom they call Neptune—dragged him back.

[lacuna]

### 2. From the Trier manuscript

[Col. 1293]

[Col. 1293B] **1.** In the year of the incarnation of the Word 1226, in the first year of Pope Gregory IX, while the glorious Emperor Frederick was reigning—God favoring him, who does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses, who brings forth clouds from the ends of the earth (Psalm 134:7)—the preachers, namely, of the Holy Cross, traveling throughout the world and proclaiming the glory of the Cross, marked the servants of God and soldiers of Christ upon their foreheads, from every nation, people, tribe, and language. For the sense and thought of the human heart, which is inclined toward evil at all times, were made, from its youth onward, most ready for the glory of Christ and reverence for the Holy Cross, while multitudes of people were marked for the remission of all their sins and good soldiers were enrolled in the army of heaven.

Therefore the glorious Emperor Frederick, receiving the sign of salvation, wished to glory in nothing but the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ; and all the crusaders rejoiced with exceedingly great joy on account of their faith in and devotion to it. The wicked and inscrutable human heart uttered its voice from the abyss, and the height of earthly dignity lifted its hands to heaven.

One of these preachers, a preacher named Conrad, a native of Hall, [Note: Hall is the emperor’s city in Swabia.] came to the abbot of the Cistercian Order at Walrebach [Note: [Col. 1293D] Walderbach.], an abbey situated in the diocese of Regensburg on the border of the kingdom of Bohemia. The abbot entrusted to the said Master Conrad his authority and the authentic mandate of the lord pope for preaching the Cross, and confirmed this by his letters and seal.

When the aforesaid Conrad came to the city called Cubitus [Note: [Col. 1294D] Elbogen.], belonging to the Prague bishopric and to the royal chamber of the king of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 1293] *boecie* C.], and preached the Cross, so many thousands of knights and multitudes of people received the sign of the Cross that, when the king of Bohemia was proposing to go to war against the duke of Austria and could not resist him—because a large part of his knights had been marked by the aforesaid Conrad and he did not wish to expend his strength in the king’s futile wars—the king, driven by immense fury and agitated by an evil spirit, wished to pour out all his anger upon Conrad. He regarded Conrad as the cause of so great a withdrawal of his army and as having diminished the king’s honor by reducing the number of his soldiers.

Thus, with their passions inflamed, the king summoned his notary, promised him great rewards, and armed him for Conrad’s death. Since all things obey money and gifts even blind the eyes of the wise (Deuteronomy 16:19), the notary, blinded by promises, offered himself for the beheading of an innocent man.

With a multitude standing around like a crown, the king’s notary stood there with drawn sword, while the preacher of the Cross, on account of the word of the Cross, lay stretched out upon the ground in the form of a cross. O unspeakable spectacle! O iniquity proceeding from the face of the earth! A spring muddied by the foot; the just man falling before the face of the sinner. The wicked man stands, the just man lies; and the savage swordsman is present to cut off the just man’s head.

Thus prostrate and near death, Conrad prayed and begged that a little time be granted him in which he might make confession and receive the Lord’s body. While he was pouring forth his prayers, and no one dared to help him through fear of the king—for the king’s command pressed upon them—behold, the king’s daughter, breaking through the surrounding crowd on every side, came with uncovered head, grieving and weeping over her father’s wickedness.

She lifted up the prostrate man, brought him with her into a chapel that was nearby, and piously provided confessors for him. When Conrad had recovered somewhat, before confession he asked the priests to write down the names of the twelve apostles and to place one name upon each candle, so that, whichever name he might draw by God’s will, he might have that apostle as his patron and advocate, favorable to him in so dreadful a danger of death and at the future judgment.

When the confession had been made, he rose, approached, took up, and read the slips, and found written the name of the glorious apostle Matthias. Standing astonished and holding with both hands the little slip on which the holy name of the apostle was written [Note: [Col. 1295] *quo* C.?], he devoted himself wholly, with all his heart and spirit, to the apostle, and begged and entreated him to assist him and become his swift helper in so great a tribulation.

At once the goodness of the most merciful apostle was present, and suddenly there was a change in the right hand of the Most High. For the king’s anger, which had been the messenger of death, was changed, through the intervention and protection of the holy apostle, into clemency; fury into mercy; a great storm into the greatest calm.

Immediately, therefore, the king’s heart was changed, and he repented of his crime. He hurried up amid the great tumult of the soldiers surrounding him, so that Conrad, terrified by the uproar of the surging crowd, feared that he was once again being dragged to death.

When the king arrived, he fell at Master Conrad’s feet and, prostrate upon the ground with his whole body in the form of a cross, most humbly and devoutly begged that pardon be granted him. Conrad, marveling at God’s grace and the celebrated help of blessed Matthias the apostle, was almost in an ecstasy at what had happened to him. He raised the prostrate king from the ground and, granting him his life, joyfully released him from the guilt of his crime.

The swordsman also came, namely the king’s notary, pale and trembling, repentant of his deed; he begged forgiveness and received it. Conrad was immediately taken up by the king and, in the presence of the king and the entire multitude, was set upon a high place; the king ordered him to preach the word of God.

[Col. 1295C] That day there was a market and a forum for goods for sale, where swarms of people ordinarily gathered from various places for the sake of trading. On that very day, with God’s favor and the king’s rejoicing, a great multitude of princes and soldiers, and of men and women of various ages and conditions, was marked with the Cross, and there was great joy among the people [lacuna].

This same Conrad the preacher came to Trier, was in the church of Saint Eucharius, and preached in the cemetery of that church before the tomb of the blessed apostle. He rendered immense thanks to God and to the blessed apostle, his deliverer, and, recounting all these things that had happened to him, asked that they be committed to writing for the glory of God and of the blessed apostle. These events took place in the city called Cubitus, situated in the Prague bishopric, to the honor of the glorious apostle and the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

**2.** In the diocese of Speyer there is a certain city belonging to the lord king, called Gruoninge [Note: Grüningen.], subject to the empire. The inhabitants of this city [Note: The codex reads *habitores*.] had long ago been enrolled and associated as brothers in the brotherhood of the blessed apostle Matthias [lacuna].

**3.** Count Palatine Henry, surrounded by two of his clerks filled with an evil spirit, was induced to attempt to draw into his own legal ownership a certain village called Vilmar, situated upon the river Lahn, which the Emperor Henry of blessed memory had solemnly given, with all its appurtenances, to the blessed apostle Matthias and Saint Eucharius for the remedy of his soul [Note: See above, *Gesta*, chapter 32].

Those same two clerks, in order to win the count’s favor more and more for themselves, promised to make privileges and seals by such an art that the eyes of those who looked upon them would be deceived and that documents made many years earlier would appear ancient and extremely old.

The count’s mind was drawn away and enticed by these clerks’ tricks and deceits. Since he was a noble and powerful man, and the church could not resist him, he said that the aforesaid village was his own. This report reached the ears of the church and struck all the brothers of that church with excessive terror, like the sound of great thunder.

The abbot entered the assembly and, seeing them all greatly dismayed in spirit, consoled them in the Lord, saying: “The Lord of rulers is powerful enough both to touch the count and to restore to you what is yours. God is faithful,” he said, “and will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure.”

Having said this, he went to the count. It happened that he found him seated upon a horse and traveling with a large retinue. The abbot approached the count, explained the church’s case and need, and offered prayers and supplications on behalf of the church. He begged and entreated him, for the sake of God and of the blessed apostle Matthias and Saint Eucharius—whose church was renowned for their relics and miracles [Note: [Col. 1295] *eadem* is written twice in C.]—not to presume to seize the church’s property [Note: [Col. 1295] *res ecclesiae* is written twice in C.], since he could in no way escape the anger of God and of his saints, who were the lords and most faithful protectors of that place.

The count, therefore, lifted up by the pride of temporal glory, rejected and refused the abbot’s prayers, in accordance with the saying: “The simplicity of the just man, like a lamp despised before the face of the sinner, is prepared for an appointed time” (Job 12:4).

The abbot was acting as an envoy on behalf of the church and was being despised; but prayer was being made for him without ceasing by the church to God [Note: [Col. 1295] C reads *au* followed by illegible characters.]. God, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, looked down from his holy height upon the prayer of the humble and did not despise their prayers [Note: The codex has *deest*—“missing”—where *spete* appears in an erasure.].

When the count despised the abbot at his first prayers, the count felt God’s hand somewhat heavily laid upon him. For his horse trembled all over [Note: [Col. 1295] *equs* C.] and, threatening to fall, caused the count a little fear; but none of those present could perceive that this gentle chastisement was being inflicted by God.

As the count proceeded, the abbot again joined him. Adding prayers to prayers, he was again despised. The count’s horse [Note: [Col. 1295] *equs* C.], shaken by even greater terror the second time, collapsed upon its knees and terrified its rider with grave fear.

Then the count’s friends [lacuna; Note: [Col. 1297] C reads “[illegible]gntes.”] and, fearing that this might be the visitation of God and the indignation of his saints, began unanimously to entreat the count to deign to desist from his injustice, since he could not resist the wrath of God and his saints.

But the count, hardened in heart, rejected everyone’s prayers and counsels, and therefore deserved to be chastised more severely. He received correction for his madness, since vexation alone is accustomed to give understanding to the hearing.

The third time, when the same abbot—whom greater concern goaded and urged on—addressed the count, and, having endured much rejection [Note: [Col. 1297] C: *multa p. repusam*], accomplished nothing, behold, suddenly, in the sight of everyone, the count openly experienced the anger of God and his saints, worthy of his deserts. Like a locust, he was violently thrown from his horse, and he fell with it. His body was crushed by a severe impact; almost dead and deprived of consciousness, he lay stretched out upon the ground as though senseless.

At length he was lifted from the ground and carried elsewhere. When he had returned to himself and understood the blows that God and his saints had already inflicted upon him for the third time, fearing that he might suffer worse than before, and admonished also by the gentle counsel of his friends and nobles, he publicly declared before the abbot and many others [Note: The codex reads *pluris*; the remainder is illegible.] that he had wished unjustly to seize the church’s property, confessed that he had no right whatsoever in the church’s possessions, and admitted that he had been dangerously induced to pursue iniquity.

This was the change in the right hand of the Most High, who rules the power of the sea and, according to his will and the character of men, either calms or aggravates the movement of its waves (Psalm 88:10) [Note: The codex reads *potestatis*—“of power.”].

Thus chastised and humbled, the count in turn sought out the abbot and begged him mercifully to pardon his error; that the church might freely and absolutely possess, with all its appurtenances [Note: The codex reads *appenciis*.], the liberty of the village which he had unjustly attempted to seize; and he humbly entreated the brothers of the church to pray for him.

He also offered many thanks and expressions of gratitude to God and his saints, because he had deserved to be chastised in this merciful way and because the saints’ compassion had not handed him over to present death.

Moreover, those two clerks, who ought not to be named, fabricators of falsehood, who had persisted in such wicked deceit against the innocent church and had led the count into this iniquity [Note: The codex reads *aduxerant*.], experienced horribly, as those storing up wrath for the day of wrath, the anger of God and of his saints. Both of them died together by a sudden death [lacuna].

**4.** The lord of the castle of Merenberch, named Hardradus, was at a certain time attacked by his enemies. His adversaries, running about everywhere, devastated by plunder and fire whatever belonged to him, as far as they could.

They therefore came to a certain village called Duorlar, situated not far from the aforesaid castle and belonging to Hardradus, the lord of the castle, intending to do there what they were doing in other places.

In that village there was a certain estate and a granary full of grain, gathered and stored from a certain arable field. The elder Hardradus, namely the grandfather of this younger Hardradus, had bequeathed that field to the blessed apostle Matthias as alms for the remedy of his soul. A certain tenant named Louis diligently cultivated it in the same village and paid the church of Saint Matthias an annual rent from that alms.

When the enemies and adversaries entered the village, they began to carry off plunder, set fires, and burn the village [lacuna].

[Col. 1297]

# THE DEEDS OF ALBERO, ARCHBISHOP.

## Preface

After the history of the archbishops of Trier had been written, through a continuation of the *Deeds*, down to the death of Meginher, the period of Albero followed—a distinguished, strong, and ingenious man whose times raised the church, oppressed by poverty, to a new glory and granted the people of Trier a major role in conducting the public affairs of the German Empire.

It is therefore unsurprising that several men devoted themselves to singing and writing his praises: one, unless I am mistaken, while the bishop was still alive; another under Hillin, Albero’s successor [Note: See Balderic, chapter 11].

The first described the archbishop’s life in hexameter verse down to A.D. 1145, speaking now more briefly, now more fully, about public and ecclesiastical affairs, but everywhere thoroughly acquainted with what he decided to narrate, since he appears to have lived in the city of Trier and to have perceived most things with his own eyes or ears. He also used certain documents [Note: See verses 126, 136, and 158.] and added the whole narrative as a brief supplement to the ancient *Deeds* [Note: What he says above had already been mentioned in verses 19 and 82; these passages are found in the continued *Deeds*, not in the poem itself.].

Balderic undertook the matter more extensively when, several years after Albero’s death, he began to narrate his life. At that time he was master of the schools, having been called to this office by Albero himself in 1147. Born in the diocese of Liège, in the village of Florennes, he had attached himself to the court of Pope Eugene. When Albero had heard him, while the pope was away in Gaul, “arguing cases and often pleading appropriately,” as Balderic himself relates, he brought him with him to Trier and placed him in charge of the school of the church of Saint Peter [Note: Chapter 22].

From that time onward he was familiar with the archbishop and sometimes accompanied him on his journeys [Note: Chapter 26], so that he had a good understanding of the deeds later performed by Albero and could be moved, both by his devotion to truth and by his love for Albero, to entrust them to the memory of posterity.

He lived for several years afterward under Archbishop Hillin and is mentioned in documents, either his own or those of others, in the years 1152, 1154, 1156, and 1157. In 1156 he was provost of the church of Saint Simeon [Note: Hontheim, *History*, I, p. 568: “master of the school”; Gunther, *Rheno-Mosellan Diplomatic Code*, I, p. 348: “master of the schools”; p. 353: “schoolmaster”; Hontheim I, p. 577: “schoolmaster of the main house and provost of Saint Simeon”; p. 588: “master of the schools.”]. Afterward, however, no one mentioned him [Note: Already in a charter of Hillin from 1158, Hontheim I, p. 586, Balderic’s name is absent. Walter, dean of Saint Simeon, is read there; there is no provost, nor is he mentioned in a charter given to the church of Saint Simeon in 1162.].

Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, gave Balderic a notable testimony to his learning and talent when Balderic began to direct the school at Trier [Note: Martène, *Collection*, II, p. 247, and from there Hontheim I, p. 557:

“Brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend Balderic, master: blessing and life forever.

“Now at last, having been freed from those very great occupations which, as you yourself know, long kept us entangled here and there, we have begun to be able at last to greet our friends and, having driven away the anguish of our spirit, to show something of our more tender affection.

“Therefore, greeting your diligence with paternal and intimate affection, we beg and exhort you in the Lord not to allow that noble and most acute intellect of yours, which by God’s favor has been implanted in you by nature and splendidly cultivated in your youth through the best arts, to grow dull through idleness, lest the honor bestowed upon you, as a certain fruit of your labor, on account of the brilliance of your learning, should be able to bring a kind of obscurity upon your excellent disciplines.

“Indeed, you will adorn both the acuteness of your intellect, the glory of your eloquence, and the dignities you have attained with humility, as though with the radiance of gems; and remember that honors must be preserved by the same arts through which you attained them. For, to speak in worldly terms, it may have been fortunate that you ascended, but to govern yourself on high is certainly a mark of diligence.

“Let your presence be a discipline to your hearers; for you will rarely need to chastise if you are constantly present. Your position involves more than the duty of teaching; you must also display the severity of a censor, since you should know that you have been appointed over the correction of morals, a discipline and exercise subtler than all others and more fruitful for everyone.

“For one who knows, little is sufficient—not that we should teach a teacher, but lest we neglect our duty.”]

Nor should Balderic be judged to have disappointed the good opinion of him when he undertook and completed his work. You may judge his style more florid than dry, embellished here and there with passages from the poets Horace and Ovid [Note: Chapters 3 and 12.]; and the author himself openly says that he strives to emulate the praises of ancient writers [Note: Chapter 16].

Nevertheless, he does not appear to have exceeded the limits prescribed for a writer of history, but for the most part narrated what happened appropriately and simply. In a brief but well-composed preface he demonstrated to his readers his love of truth. Although he wished not to remain silent about the archbishop’s praises, but to celebrate the remarkable deeds of an outstanding man, he nevertheless did not allow himself to be carried away by partisan zeal.

In the peaceful and tranquil early years of the Emperor Frederick, unless I am mistaken, he gave an impartial judgment of the dispute between the kingdom and the church in which Albero had been deeply involved, and he inserted into his narrative the letter of the king hostile to Albero [Note: Chapter 3]. Later, he openly acknowledged what he knew less certainly [Note: Chapter 4]; wherever he was able to receive trustworthy documents [Note: Chapter 10: the letter of the Trier clergy concerning Albero’s election, written to Pope Innocent.], he followed them.

In several places Balderic’s narrative agrees so closely with the metrical *Deeds* that one author appears to have used the other [Note: Compare chapter 4 with verses 26 and following; chapter 15 with verses 61 and following; chapter 17 with verses 140 and following.]. Yet each always has material of his own. Since that poet had already completed his book before Balderic’s arrival, whereas Balderic is much fuller and more extensive [Note: The poet also narrated certain matters more fully and accurately: verse 86 concerning the anointing of King Conrad; verse 110 concerning the abbey of Saint Maximin; verses 211 and following concerning the capture of the castle of Rudolfsberg.], I should think that Balderic had indeed seen the poet’s work but used it only in a few places.

After 1145 he had no written sources, and in this principal part of his book he must be highly valued for the abundance and reliability of its material.

The Trier writer who, in the codex of Saint Matthias at Trier, no. 1341, mentioned above as C1, added a brief continuation of the *Deeds* down to the year 1152, possessed both the poet’s book and Balderic’s, but followed Balderic especially closely.

The poet afterward remained hidden for a long time, whereas Balderic was read by Browerus and others, and was edited by Hontheim [Note: Compare the excerpts in the *Collection of the Historians of Gaul*, vol. XIV, pp. 349–360.] (*Prodr.*, II, p. 767) and by Wyttenbach [Note: But here, in his customary manner, he mixed into the text not only what had been added in the continuation but also additions from a later age.] (vol. I, p. 217 and following).

The metrical *Deeds* in the Vienna codex, Hist. prof. N. 1069, mentioned above as B1, were first discovered by Pertz, and at his insistence were copied by the distinguished scholar Chmel; his copy formed the basis for preparing this edition.

The Trier codex no. 1387 (IV), formerly perhaps belonging to Saint Mary *ad Martyres* [Note: Hontheim prepared his edition from such a manuscript. There is now no trace in the codex of this provenance.], a parchment manuscript from the end of the twelfth century, consisting of eight gatherings and three leaves, written more elegantly than carefully, contains Balderic’s *Deeds of Albero*.

In 1840 I accurately compared it in the Trier library with the printed editions, and I have now taken care to reproduce it as faithfully as possible after correcting its errors [Note: In spelling I departed from the codex only in writing *ae* for *e* everywhere at the end of words. The codex is not consistent with itself.].

On a special leaf at the beginning of the volume there is an image of the archbishop, with this inscription added: “Lord Albero, archbishop of the people of Trier.” Another paper manuscript was copied from this codex in the sixteenth century; it is now designated N. 1388 (1281), and I judged that it should be entirely excluded from the edition of the book.

Kiel, the day before the Kalends of May, 1847.

**G. WAITZ**

# THE METRICAL DEEDS BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

I cannot set forth in a tongue worthy of the deeds

Of this bishop; but, asked by my friends,

I arrange a few things in speech as justly as I scarcely can.

Favor me, Muse; beware of error, as you turn over many things.

Shepherd, come forth; say, “Hail, bishop,” as you resolve a few things.

[Col. 1301A] A man had arisen from the famous region of Metz;

Later, as a boy, he was nurtured in that church,

And in his youth he became renowned widely

Throughout the regions of the kingdom. And already then at Rome,

A great error was spreading everywhere, because the emperor held the pope,

Captured by fraud and deceit, and compelled him by oaths

Never to excommunicate himself—having given wicked commands.

But when the pact was broken, and the leaders of the churches compelled it,

A great fire of war had been kindled.

Peace was denied to all good ecclesiastics,

Who were called “the children of the Church”;

While the Heinricians were intent upon slaughter and plunder,

So called after the name of King Henry.

We have already touched briefly upon these matters elsewhere [Note: See the supplementary *Deeds*, chapters 10 and 19];

Therefore it is not necessary, as is clear, to repeat them.

[Col. 1301B] Then Albero, of whom we speak, had grown

Like an unconquerable strength, and began to become known to the clergy.

First he became known to the imperial party, then to the magnates themselves,

By repeatedly undertaking many opposing actions.

He also caused Adelbero, bishop of Metz,

Who was not well disposed toward him, to be deprived both of his office

And of his tomb.

He first secured the holy Theoger as his successor,

Then Stephen, despite the imperial right.

For this reason, while the king raged,

Many received the order that his death was to be arranged.

This pleased many, and they lay in wait for him sufficiently

As he traveled toward Rome or passed through the kingdom.

Yet he often escaped the nearness of death.

[Col. 1301C] Often, as though paralyzed, through hostile enemies,

Placed upon a cart and dragged by a harnessed donkey,

He passed unharmed, with any poor man serving as his guide.

For a face thickly covered with deliberately applied pigment

Concealed him; he also accepted the hospitality

Of those who were planning to slaughter him.

Thus he went to Rome, and thus he went wherever he wished.

The people of Metz, despising the pope’s decrees,

He harassed in such a way that no one buried their dead,

Until that mad people learned that it must never resist

The Roman See.

When he therefore obtained the episcopal see

Of Trier [Note: In the year 1132.], he compelled the aforesaid Stephen,

Formerly bishop of Metz, who until then had been opposed

To these three metropolitans of ours—

Bruno, Godefrid, and Meginher—

And perhaps resisted and refused to obey him,

At last to obey as he wished.

From then on he began to advise concerning his own property,

Restraining his countrymen from plundering by means of the ban.

As he directed the forces of his eyes throughout the bishopric,

He gathered from every side whatever his mind judged useful.

Verse 55.

[Col. 1302A] Nor did he spare his own monasteries in this matter;

And he treated the one named for Eucharius, in the name of Christ,

With excessive severity, oppressing it far too heavily.

Then, directing his mind to recovering the monastery of Maximin,

He undertook the burden of great affairs, and accompanied

The journey of King Lothair, who was hastening to Italy,

Serving him throughout the entire year without ever tiring [Note: In the years 1136–1137.].

There he became dear to the honor both of pope and king,

And was made legate of the churches of Cisalpine Italy.

Upon his return he transferred the body of Meginher,

Formerly bishop and his predecessor, from there,

And buried it in the church of Saint Peter.

Soon the dangers of very difficult cares arose.

[Col. 1302B] For his own castle, called Ararum [Note: Arraz, according to Balderic, chapter 15.],

Had been seized by the treachery of robbers while he was abroad;

And the death of King Lothair [Note: In the year 1137.] had been reported throughout the cities.

Struck by these events, he acted silently for a little while;

But, encouraged, he drew strength and courage from within,

And gathered his soldiery and the citizens of Trier into the castle.

He surrounded it with a siege and captured it after a few days,

Though not without bloodshed;

And he also captured nearby Nanterus [Note: Nantersburch, according to Balderic, in the same passage.], famous by name.

Moreover, having sent servants all around,

He gathered bishops and leading men together [Note: In the year 1138.]

Where the Moselle, the glory of rivers, flows into the Rhine.

There he appointed as king the Conrad I mentioned earlier [Note: The author does not name him at all; in the continuation of the *Deeds*, chapters 27–28, he is called Conrad.],

And honored him with his possessions and expenditure.

Then, when Conrad was hastening to the castle of Aachen,

He followed him so that, according to the custom of the ancestors,

He might bless him. But he could not proceed any farther

In accomplishing his desire, because the bishop of Cologne

Interrupted it, saying that it belonged to his own jurisdiction

To anoint the king.

If anyone wishes to consider the reason for this,

He will quickly recognize that what lacks reason

Can never stand.

For it is clear to everyone that the metropolitan of Trier

Presides by right over all the churches of Gaul and Germany,

So that he may arrange all the highest affairs.

As we read, when Lothair died—

Formerly a false king, but truly a usurper—

And there was no bishop at Trier, since Thietgaud,

The bishop, had died abroad,

Adventius, who was then bishop of Metz,

Set up Charles as king in place of the metropolitan

And consecrated him—he was the third to bear that name [Note: See Regino, under the year 869.].

But perhaps they will say that their bishop had died

At that time as well; and we do not reject this as untrue.

Verse 103.

[Col. 1303A] Nevertheless, he could have more quickly exercised his rights

Over the subordinate districts, if the ancient law had favored him—

The law which modern men trample underfoot through wealth and pride—

So that, because this see of Trier is poorer,

It should therefore be inferior to those richer sees.

Let this suffice for now. Yet Albero strove

To be more ready than all others to serve the king.

The king, too, always honored him above the rest,

Often making fortunate use of his counsels,

Especially when the Saxons, taking up arms,

Prepared to attack him with immense forces.

Albero came against them at great expense and with many soldiers,

And won the palm of praise for his integrity.

Nevertheless, through this mediation, the war was abandoned

By terms of peace, and the people returned home.

For these and other deeds so well performed by him,

And because what had been unjustly taken from the church of Trier—

From whose property and foundation it is truly read to have been built—

As the testaments report under the names of the kings

Dagobert, Pippin, and Charles [Note: See the kings’ charters in Hontheim, *History* I, pp. 76, 120, and 132, all of doubtful authenticity.],

The king restored to him the abbey called by the name of Maximin,

To blessed Peter through him [Note: See the king’s diploma there, p. 541.].

But the monks, having expelled their abbot Gerhard

A few days earlier, immediately substituted another for him,

A man wholly unknown in person and religion.

Having sold the church’s metal, vestments, and sacred objects,

They purchased Roman support with them,

And secured by payments from the apostolic see

That he should be made abbot in the customary manner

And consecrated for themselves.

They urgently demanded that he be confirmed

By the metropolitan’s ban, exempted from jurisdiction,

And that his liberty be protected [Note: See Innocent’s charter there, p. 543.];

And, rejoicing, they brought him back

And secretly installed him in his own see.

A full year passed in these struggles.

From this great event there grew a great concern

For the metropolitan, because such force had been brought against him

And such grave contempt had been shown him by those Romans

Whom he had always loved and by whose strength

He had believed himself able to overcome all who wished to harm him.

But what could he do about it? The mandates

Which they had brought from the pope forbade him to break open the castle,

And entrance was unjustly denied to him and his men.

Nevertheless, he repeatedly recalled the citizens,

Who were inflamed for such wars, from them by threats and prayers.

Moreover, moved because his embassy had been rejected

By certain churches and bishops, he hurried to Rome

At great expense, explained the causes of his journey,

And, with the pope’s favor, obtained what he then wished

And returned victorious.

Verse 153.

[Col. 1304A] Having attained the fulfillment of his wish, namely that the monastery

Should always be subject to him and his successors,

He brought back, as a gift, a charter confirmed in this matter

By the apostolic seal [Note: See another bull of Innocent in Hontheim I, p. 547.].

But afterward matters more serious than the earlier evils arose.

This had been done in the presence of the monks.

The apostolic authority also ordered them to obey

The metropolitan’s commands, while at the same time entrusting to them

The church’s gift—the abbacy—to be received

At the direction of the pontiff and by the hand of the see of Trier.

But when they had rejected the Roman decree and the bishop,

They conspired again against him and denied him entrance.

For this offense they were anathematized.

But the abbot sought pardon and was released from the ban.

The monks, however, created a great tumult over this,

And induced the count of Luxembourg, mentioned earlier,

Who had assumed the name of their defender

And sworn faith and assistance to the pontiff,

To make war, having almost corrupted him with seven hundred talents.

By fraud and deceit, breaking his first faith and treaty,

They made him ready to take up war and arms.

As you know, he was like a most savage enemy:

After many killings, plunderings, and captures,

He profaned sacred things and burned villages and churches.

Alas, it is shameful that armed forces and a proud enemy

Should have carried hostile standards to the gate of Mars

And the doors of Saint Simeon, contrary to the Key-Bearer of heaven!

This place was not defended by a wall, but by a wretched rampart,

And a very few men endured the hostile hand.

Yet the enemy did not escape the disaster unharmed;

He departed having suffered a greater loss among his own.

We saw at the bridge the mad bishop’s army,

Raging with fire, rushing upon houses, and profaning shrines.

The hall of the Mother of God, which King Dagobert had once built,

Was broken into and burned by devouring flames.

The greedy soldier, with drawn sword, slaughtered

The shrines of the saints which he found upon the altars [Note: [Col. 1303] *supra* C.?];

He held the Creator and the relics alike.

We saw fulfilled what Ezekiel reports:

That a messenger would be sent to violate

The secret place of the Lord (Ezekiel 7:22).

But this crime was not committed with impunity.

After the enemy had burned several villages and churches

And ordered many more to be burned,

The bishop followed him with his army from behind,

Overtook him, captured many from his host,

Killed more, disabled some,

And, through the Lord’s mercy, forced him to hasten his flight [Note: Compare Balderic, chapter 20.].

The fifth year of this struggle had now arrived,

And those great men were justly expelled from the place;

Religious monks were appointed in their stead.

Verse 203.

[Col. 1305A] The bishop appointed Sigerus as abbot [Note: In the year 1142.],

Who had first been elected and consecrated by the apostolic authority,

Then anathematized and reconciled.

These battles were fought in the autumn of a two-year period;

They were followed by winters of strong winds and rains,

With great loss and lamentation for the people.

Peace and future quiet were already thought to have been secured.

But the matter turned out otherwise, because the strong castle

Of the aforesaid count remained,

Which lies three miles from us, [lacuna]

By the name of Butolicum [Note: [Col. 1305] Thus the manuscript; perhaps Rutolicum should be read.] [Note: [Col. 1305D] This must be the same place which Balderic, ch. 20, calls Mount Rodolfus, elsewhere known as Roulmont; he briefly relates that it was besieged twice by the bishop and finally captured.] which had previously been besieged by the bishop’s army,

But had been released from the siege,

When the bishop pressed upon the fleeing count’s rear [Note: [Col. 1306D] See Balderic, Book I.].

But the castellan and his men had surrendered themselves or their possessions for peace;

[Col. 1305B] And in the flight the count was compelled to praise this peace.

But when shortly afterward it became clear that he had broken it by fraud and deceit, and that his men had violated it by slaughter and fire,

Thus the wretched populace, driven from its ancestral territory,

Exiled and wandering, perished, scattered in various directions;

Those who remained applied themselves to no work;

Their only concern was to hide from the enemy.

Now the cattle had been driven away and the surrounding region devastated,

The farmers mourned the year’s loss of their stolen young cattle;

Cultivation withdrew from the land throughout the Belgian countryside.

While the enemy wrought evil, God accomplished less;

For the cattle whom fear and dread of the enemy had driven away,

The savage, ravaging wolf seized at night and tore to pieces.

The river near us, called by the name of Kylia [Note: [Col. 1306D] Kyll.],

[Col. 1305C] And which seeks you, Moselle, grew suddenly,

When the rains poured forth and roofs and houses collapsed,

Carrying into the river every kind of cattle and bird found within,

And men together with boys, women, and girls,

Swallowed up in the river of greater renown.

Meanwhile the people of Trier, weighed down by anxieties,

Unaccustomed to such wars, set their efforts to the task,

And undertook the work without a wall. For the city lay open,

Except on the southern side, which the former care of Bishop Bruno

Had enclosed with a long fortification.

They surrounded the walls with a rampart, or strengthened them with masonry,

Placed guards and sentries, or repaired what had fallen;

They prepared weapons, summoned allies, and harassed the enemy.

The latter, excessively elated by plunder and success,

[Col. 1305D] Had already hoped that the whole population would submit to him.

But the appearance of affairs changed and brought them reversals;

When the people of Trier repeatedly made sorties,

Capturing some of these nobles and killing others by the sword,

They balanced the defeats they had suffered with these defeats inflicted in return.

Soon, when grass and herbs emerged in the mild weather,

The bishop, having scraped together whatever gold there was in the churches,

Verse 251.

[Col. 1306A] And, besides, whatever he then found in the great cross

Which the once-fortunate Ekebert had formerly bestowed there [Note: [Col. 1306D] See Gesta, ch. 29],

Again attacked the fortress of Butolicum with all his strength;

But, though he captured it only with difficulty,

it was because he discovered that the hearts of his companions were not loyal to him:

They secretly supplied bread to the castellans, whom hunger was already forcing to surrender,

And the man entrusted with operating the siege engine commonly called a *manga* abandoned his skill at throwing,

Because he had been led astray by the wages he was to receive.

At last, with the utmost care and anxiety,

After many men had died and much blood had been shed,

Surrounded on every side and prevented from receiving provisions,

Already despairing, they began to contemplate surrender,

And sought permission to leave with their possessions and their lives preserved.

[Col. 1306B] The bishop agreed to this and granted them safe conduct.

Then certain of the leading men of Trier,

Who had previously hindered the bishop greatly through their limited loyalty,

But secretly assisted the castellans,

Begged that this fortress might be granted to them unharmed.

When this became known among the people of Trier through these reports,

They grew exceedingly angry, and a great outcry

And widespread tumult arose throughout the camp;

They seized their weapons. “If this fortress,” they said,

“is now to remain unharmed, why did we besiege it?

Why, leaving our homes and children so often,

Did we travel the roads night and day amid dangers?

Why did we endure hunger, thirst, rain and the heat of the sun,

Wounds, bruises, a thousand dangers, deaths,

[Col. 1306C] Expense, exertion, anxieties, and the burdens of toil

For nothing, if we gain nothing from this undertaking?

Here is an escape available to every member of the band of robbers.

Here the marauder who ravages the people is protected in safety.

This man was hostile to our city, hostile to our fathers,

And he barred this road to us as well as to travelers.

Here our blood was shed, and here our relatives

And our companions alike fell in death.

But come, men, break your bonds now;

While there is opportunity, throw off the harsh yoke from your necks!

How heavily it weighs is unknown, because it has become customary;

But once laid aside, it will grant great relief.

Do not look to what each count says, or to what any commander wishes;

Look instead to the face of your own multitude.

There are far more who will follow us and our standards,

[Col. 1306D] Or who will bravely drive back our adversaries with the sword.

The bishop is lord of events; he will aid our wishes

By his nod, if our tongues should perhaps fall silent.”

Thus encouraged, they climbed the heights of the mountain

In a dense column, making way for those whom they had defeated,

And occupied all the entrances to the gates and the walls.

Without delay, secretly applying a broad fire beneath the walls,

Verse 302.

[Col. 1307A] The bishop rejoices, the enemy groans, the whole

Mountain smokes, and this struggle reaches its end in a single day.

When approximately half of the month of October had passed [Note: [Col. 1307B] The year 1144?],

The citizens having been dispersed outside because of the autumn season,

These castellans, driven out by such a fortification,

Together with their prelate commander, again spread fires,

Nor were they reluctant to rush with hostile standards toward the bridge.

At once the city’s youth, prepared for battle,

But without the prudent counsel of wise advice,

Went out barefoot and unprotected against the armored tyrants.

The force of the mad commander, advancing in a headlong charge,

Was driven into thin ranks, and struck them down and routed them.

There had been a few horsemen, and they were routed first;

The wretched foot soldiers suffered deaths and wounds,

While the survivors fled through the closed gates to safety.

[Col. 1307B] The following morning was wholly and exceedingly foggy;

No guard was present at the bridge, and the gates stood open.

Verse 319.

[Col. 1308A] Then the enemy, rejoicing in his earlier success,

Rushed forward and would have captured the city through the open gates,

Had not one of the canons come out to meet him;

By his shout, after gathering a few companions,

He drove him back by a swift advance, closing the gates.

But scattering fires, he destroyed all the houses there;

Then, pursuing the citizens whom we mentioned earlier,

He confiscated their property and burned the village to the ground.

For the bishop brought the king into this region [Note: [Col. 1308B] See the Continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux, under the year 1145, MGH SS VI, p. 389.],

And attacked towers and castles, and pressed the count hard,

And deprived him of the county entrusted to him;

This he assigned to one of the princes and faithful men of the kingdom,

Not because [Note: [Col. 1307] “Not because”—I do not know what he means.] he died not long afterward,

And the welcome benefices returned again to their former holder.

[Col. 1308B] Nevertheless the bishop granted these things with a generous heart,

Rejoicing that he had now brought the bloody war to an end.

Verse 385.

[Col. 1307] HERE ENDS [Note: [Col. 1307] Written twice.].

## Deeds of Archbishop Albero, by the author Balderic

[Col. 1307C] I am about to recount the memorable deeds and sayings of Albero, archbishop of Trier, undertaking a matter which posterity will find less credible than miraculous. In this undertaking, reader, know that I am striving neither for praise nor for blame, but for truth.

### 1

We admire some men for having accomplished great things, but with the favor, assistance, and cooperation of many—such as the rulers of nations who, being heirs and successors of their ancestral kingdoms, enlarged their empire by the arms of subject peoples: Alexander, Julius, Augustus, Charlemagne, and many others, who supplied abundant material for the ancient writers of history.

But this man is especially worthy of admiration in this respect: although he was a solitary and private individual, indeed still poor, he accomplished the greatest things. While still in the first years of his youth, when no ecclesiastical or secular dignity yet shone upon him, he alone among all the people of Metz opposed the summit of imperial majesty for the liberty of the Church.

At the time when kingdom and priesthood were divided by the gravest schism—which began in the days of Pope Gregory VII, formerly called Hildebrand, and of the emperor Henry III, and continued through the times of the apostolic lords Urban and Paschal until the time of Pope Calixtus—this new man, a newly enlisted soldier, began to be a defender of the holy Church through the arms of his remarkable intelligence [Col. 1308C] and counsel.

But so that you may understand more fully and clearly what this man accomplished, of what kind it was, how he accomplished it, and for what purpose, in defending the Church against the emperor’s injury, I must first explain what and of what kind was the cause of this schism.

From the time of the emperor Charlemagne until the time of the emperor Henry III, kings, because of their merits—since by their benefactions they enlarged and defended the churches—gave investitures of bishoprics by concession of the Roman pontiffs and by confirmation of their privileges, and administered the affairs of the churches. But Henry III, whose sins, as we hope, have been covered over because of his many very great good works, was excessively defamed for the sale of bishoprics.

Therefore the aforesaid Pope Gregory VII attempted to take away from that king the investitures of bishoprics [Col. 1308D] [Note: [Col. 1307] The writer’s errors will easily be apparent to anyone. Certainly he did not sufficiently distinguish Henry III from Henry IV.].

When he could not accomplish this, he nevertheless compelled him firmly to promise that he would expel from their sees all those bishops whom he knew had entered them by payment, and that thereafter he would give no one a bishopric for money.

When the aforesaid emperor undertook this matter, he incurred such hatred from almost all the bishops that they adhered to Pope Gregory against the king and, together with the lord pope, excommunicated him. Many of the cardinals, however, joined the king, as did members of the Roman clergy and people. Against Pope Hildebrand there survive many sharply hostile writings from these men [Col. 1309A] [Note: [Col. 1309D] He seems to have in mind especially the book of Benno.].

This Henry was the son of the emperor Conrad. His son Henry, who was called the elder, inherited his father’s conflict with the Roman pontiffs. By imitating his father, he oppressed certain bishops to such an extent that, through their plotting and the authority of the Roman pontiff, he was driven from the kingdom by his son Henry in the fifty-fourth year of his reign, and shortly afterward died at Liège.

When his son, the younger Henry, succeeded him in the kingdom, Pope Paschal—who, after Gregory and after the death of Pope Urban, was seated in the apostolic see—wished to complete what the lord Gregory VII had begun, inflamed by zeal for God.

When the younger Henry came to Rome for his imperial consecration, the pope refused him the anointing unless he renounced the right which he appeared to possess over the investitures of bishoprics. The outcome of this affair may be judged from the letter which King Henry sent throughout the kingdom after returning from Rome (in the year 1111).

### 2

[Note: [Col. 1309D] This encyclical letter has already been published from Udalric of Babenberg and the Annals of Saint Disibod, in *Leges*, vol. II, p. 70. In every individual phrase the present text differs from the published one.]

**Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, to all the faithful of Christ and of the Church.**
