We wish it to be known to your love and discernment how the matters that existed between us and that lord Paschal were begun, discussed, and concluded—namely, the agreement between him and me, and the betrayal of the Romans against me and my men—so that what you hear you may understand, what you understand you may examine, and what you examine you may judge.

Accordingly, when I was wholly prepared to bring myself into conformity with the benefit of the Church and with his wish, if it were just [Note: [Col. 1309] *coponerem*, manuscript reading for *componerem*.], he began assiduously to promise the expansion and exaltation of the kingdom above all my predecessors [Col. 1309C], while deceitfully considering how he might separate kingdom and Church from their proper condition.

This is how he undertook the matter. He wished to take away without a hearing from our kingdom—which for more than three hundred years from Charlemagne, and under sixty-three apostolic pontiffs, had held the investitures of bishoprics and abbeys by their authority and the confirmation of their privileges—the possessions in question. When our envoys asked what would become of us once all these things had been taken away, and on what our kingdom would rest, since almost everything our predecessors had granted and handed over to the churches, he replied:

“Let the brothers of the Church be content with their tithes and offerings; but let the king receive and retain for himself and his successors all the estates and royal rights which Charlemagne, Louis, Otto, and Henry granted to the churches.”

When our men replied that we did not wish to inflict violence upon the churches, lest by taking these things away I incur so many sacrileges [Note: [Col. 1309] Something is missing here; the letter confidently promised something.], his men swore on his behalf, on the Sunday *Esto mihi*, before God, that they would confirm and strengthen all these things with justice and authority, under anathema [Col. 1310A]. Our men likewise swore that, if he fulfilled what had been proposed—and yet they knew that it could in no way be done—I too would renounce the investitures of the churches, as he demanded, as you will be able to see more fully in the charter of agreement.

Concerning the betrayal against us and our men, the matter stands thus. We had scarcely entered the gates of the city when, while our men were moving about safely within the walls, some were wounded, others killed, and all were either robbed or captured.

Yet I, as though unmoved by a trivial matter, proceeded with a good and tranquil mind in procession as far as the doors of blessed Peter. There, to show that no disturbance of God’s churches [Note: [Col. 1309] The letter reads “of God’s churches.”] proceeded from our intention, I proclaimed this decree before the eyes and ears of all who were present:

“I, Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans [Col. 1310B], confirm to God and Saint Peter, to all bishops, abbots, and all churches, everything which my predecessors, kings and emperors, granted or handed over to them; and what they offered to God in hope of eternal reward, I, a sinner, refuse in every way to take away through fear of the terrible judgment.”

After this decree had been read and subscribed [Note: [Col. 1309] “Read by me”; manuscript reading.], I asked him to fulfill for me what was written in his charter of agreement. This is his charter of agreement addressed to me [Note: [Col. 1309] The published edition reads: “If the king fulfills for the lord pope, as is written in the other charter of agreement, the lord pope shall…”; *Leges* II, p. 67.]:

“The lord pope shall command the bishops present on the day of the king’s coronation to leave to the king and the kingdom the royal rights that belonged to the kingdom in the time of Charlemagne, Louis, Otto, Henry, and his other predecessors. He shall confirm in writing, under anathema, that none of them, present or absent, nor their successors, shall interfere with or invade those same royal rights: namely, cities, duchies, marches, counties, coinage, tolls, markets [Note: [Col. 1309] The edition reads *mercatum*.], advocacies, all the rights of the centurions—that is, of the stewards [Note: [Col. 1310D] The Trier scribe appears to have added this explanation.]—estates and villages that belonged to the kingdom, with all their appurtenances, military forces, and castles.

“Nor shall he thereafter trouble the king or the kingdom concerning these matters, and by a privilege under anathema he shall confirm that his successors shall not presume to trouble the king any further. He shall receive the king kindly and honorably, and, following the custom of his catholic predecessors, shall crown him without withholding anything knowingly; and he shall help him to hold the kingdom, with all these things, by the assistance of his office.

“If the lord pope does not fulfill these things for the king, I, Peter Leonis, swear that with all my power I shall hold fast to the lord king. As for the hostages, unless they have escaped, we shall return them on the day after the king’s coronation. If it is because of the pope that he is not crowned, we shall likewise return them. On Sunday, when the king comes to the procession, I shall give as hostages Gratianus, my son, and the son of Wizo, my son, or the son of my sister, if I can obtain him.”

These are the oaths:

“I, Peter Leonis, swear to you that on the coming Sunday the lord pope will fulfill for the king what is written in the charter of agreement.”

These are the oaths sworn on our side:

“I, Count Hermann. I, Count Godfrey. I, Count Frederick. I, Folmar. I, Adalbert the chancellor, swear to you that on the coming Wednesday or Thursday the lord king will cause the princes to swear and will give hostages, as is written in the charter of agreement.”

When, therefore, I persisted in the aforesaid demand—that he confirm to me with justice and authority the agreement he had promised—while all present resisted him to his face and denounced his decree as manifest heresy, namely, the bishops and abbots, both his and ours, and all the sons of the Church, he wished to produce this privilege, if it may be said without offense to the Church:

“Paschal, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son King Henry and his successors.

“It has been established by the institution of divine law and forbidden by the sacred canons that priests should be occupied with secular cares, or that they should go to a court except to rescue the condemned or to assist others who suffer injury. Hence the apostle Paul says: ‘If you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church.’

“But in the regions of your kingdom bishops and abbots are so occupied with secular cares that they are compelled constantly to attend the royal court and to exercise military service—duties which scarcely, or not at all, can be performed without robberies, sacrileges, burnings, or murders. For ministers of the altar have been made ministers of the court, because they have received from kings cities, duchies, marches, coinage, tolls, estates, and other things belonging to the service of the kingdom.

“Thus an intolerable custom has also arisen in the Church: elected bishops could in no way receive consecration unless they had first been invested by the royal hand. For this reason the depravity of simoniacal heresy and ambition has sometimes prevailed so greatly that episcopal sees were invaded without any prior election; at times men were invested while the bishops were still alive.

“Moved by these and many other evils which commonly occurred through investiture, our predecessors, the pontiffs Gregory VII and Urban II of blessed memory, frequently convening councils of bishops, condemned those investitures by the lay hand. If any clerics had obtained churches through them, they decreed that the clerics should be deposed and that those who gave the churches should be deprived of communion, in accordance with that chapter of the apostolic canons which reads:

“‘If any bishop, using the powers of the world, obtains a church through them [Note: [Col. 1311] *illos* is written above the line, or *ipsos* in the manuscript.], let him be deposed and separated, and let all who communicate with him be separated.’

“Following in their footsteps, we too have confirmed their sentence in an episcopal council.

“Therefore, dearest son, King Henry—and now, by the grace of God, emperor of the Romans through our office—we command you and the kingdom to leave the royal rights that manifestly belonged to the kingdom in the time of Charlemagne, Louis, and your other predecessors [Col. 1312A]. We also forbid and prohibit under the strictness of anathema [Note: [Col. 1311] The manuscript reads ‘under anathema.’] that any bishop or abbot, present or future, invade those same royal rights [Note: [Col. 1311] Repeated in the manuscript]: namely, cities, duchies, marches, counties, coinage, tolls, markets, advocacies, the rights of the centurions, and the estates that belonged to the kingdom, with their appurtenances, military forces, and castles; nor shall anyone thereafter interfere with the king’s royal rights except by the king’s favor.

“Nor shall our successors, who will occupy the apostolic see after us, be permitted to trouble you or the kingdom concerning this matter. We decree, however, that the churches, together with God’s offerings and hereditary possessions which manifestly did not belong to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1311] The published edition of *Leges* II, p. 69 omits *non*.], shall remain free [Col. 1312B], just as you promised the almighty Lord on the day of your coronation in the presence of the whole Church.

“It is fitting that bishops, freed from secular cares, should attend to the care of their peoples and should not be absent from their churches for long. For, according to the apostle Paul, they keep watch continually as those who will have to render an account for their souls.”

### 3

As you can judge from the substance of the letter, reader, this matter was not brought to an end. Those who were with the king caused such great discord over it that the king’s army and the Romans fought fiercely at the steps of Saint Peter, and the king brought the pope captive as far as Viterbo, together with certain cardinals.

There, when the king was looking at paintings in a church, he saw Jacob wrestling with the angel. He pointed out the same painting to the lord pope and said, after the example of Jacob: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26) [Note: [Col. 1311D] See Ekkehard, under the year 1111.].

At last, from the compelled lord pope, he extorted not only the imperial anointing (April 13), but also oaths that he would never pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him. Although the lord pope himself, as a man who feared God, firmly observed this, the prelates of the churches, grieving for the suffering of their pious father, abstained from communion with the emperor.

From this point, the emperor was against the churches, and the churches against the emperor.

But perhaps, reader, you will mock me with the words of Horace, saying:

> The amphora began to be formed;  
> why, as the wheel turns, does a pitcher emerge?  
> [Col. 1312D] (*Art of Poetry* 21.)

By this you would mean that, although I promised to recount Albero’s deeds, I have transferred myself to the deeds of Roman pontiffs and kings. But I can easily answer you in Horace’s own words:

> Neither does the beginning disagree with the middle,  
> nor the middle with the end.  
> (*Ibid.*, 152.)

For at that time the lord Albero, a cleric of Metz, stood alone among all the people of Metz—indeed, against all the people of Metz—with the lord pope. By his lively skill and counsel he fearlessly accomplished many things for the honor and benefit of the lord pope and for the liberty of the universal Church. Thus he stirred up against himself the most severe movements of royal indignation, which he very often escaped by marvelous arts [Note: [Col. 1313D] See the *Life of Theoger of Metz*, to be published in another volume.].

### 4

Since the king allowed no liberty to the churches in electing pontiffs, he also expelled the venerable Bishop Poppo from his see in the city of Metz and, by his own will, installed a certain nobleman named Albero as bishop.

The aforesaid lord Albero, by repeatedly going to Rome, finally caused him to be deposed and excommunicated, and, when he died under excommunication, to be buried outside the church [Note: [Col. 1313D] See the *Metrical Deeds*, verse 27]. He also caused the city to be placed under an interdict from divine services by apostolic letters, so that burial was even denied to the dead [Note: [Col. 1314D] See also the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, to be published below.].

When no one dared to bring the lord pope’s letters containing the sentence of interdict to Metz, for fear of the cruelest death, he put on a linen clerical tunic, wrapped his head and face in a woman’s veil, and covered himself with a cloak of gray cloth. In the guise of a foreign woman, as though carrying incense to the altar, he placed the lord pope’s letters on the altar.

Then, returning from there, he summoned to him the canons whom he saw in that very church of Saint Stephen, and ordered them to receive the lord pope’s letters from the altar and read them reverently.

But when they began to recognize him, they hurried to rage and shout, and to stir up the city’s people against him by the ringing of the bell. Before they could seize him, however, he quickly mounted a very swift horse which he had prepared before the doors of the church and fled at the fastest pace.

When the people of that city, horsemen and foot soldiers alike, pursued him as far as the village called Arkenzei, he crossed the Moselle River swimming on the strong horse he was riding and reached his lord at the fortress of Rozeium, which lay in the patrimony of Bishop Poppo himself [Col. 1313C].

By a similar art he escaped the king’s ambushes many times.

### 5

For the king had blocked all the roads for him when he was going to Rome and had ordered all his faithful men to kill him. He had publicly declared him an adversary and enemy of the kingdom.

Albero, however, transformed himself into various forms and passed unknown through the midst of his enemies [Note: [Col. 1314D] See the *Metrical Deeds*, verse 34 and following.]. Sometimes he dressed his servants in his own clothing, while he himself served them in servile dress, cared for the horses, prepared dinner, removed their shoes, and ate the servants’ leftovers. Sometimes he went among beggars as a beggar; sometimes with merchants, as though carrying merchandise. In countless other ways he changed his appearance, not merely by changing his clothes, but also by disguising his face, hair, and beard with pigments.

It is also said—but I do not know whether it is true—that once, pretending to be crippled and sitting on a donkey, he encountered the king and his army and received five solidi in alms from the queen.

It is further added—but I do not know whether it is true—that, on the same journey, after accompanying the king’s progress for a longer distance, he was placed as a beggar under the king’s table. There he heard the king, the queen, and the king’s other faithful men speaking at leisure about the schemes he had devised against the pope, including the ambushes arranged against the lord Albero and how many roads, and which ones, had been closed to him as he traveled to Rome [Note: [Col. 1313] The manuscript corrects *quod* to *quot*.].

Having thus been forewarned, he escaped all the king’s ambushes. When he reached Rome, he sent word back to the queen, offering many and great thanks for the benefit he had received from her; he told her that he was the very man to whom she had given five solidi while he sat on the donkey.

When the king learned that he had reached Rome, he prepared ambushes for him not only by land but also by sea, so that he might not escape on his return. This did not escape the notice of the lord Albero. Thus, when returning from Rome he reached Pisa, and knowing that the king had also sent orders to the Pisans concerning his death, he did not dare approach the harbor of the ships himself, lest he be awaited there by the ambushers who had been prepared.

Instead, his servant hired a ship for himself and his companion as though they were still to arrive. On the day when the hired ship was to leave the shore, his servant boarded it with his belongings. Albero himself did not dare enter the ship, because a great crowd was standing in the harbor to watch, and he feared that his ambushers might be among them.

Therefore he boarded the sea elsewhere in a fisherman’s boat that had been prepared for him, and only with difficulty caught up with the ship ahead of him that same day. When he wished to board it, he fell into the sea. After swimming for some time in the open water, he was finally, and only barely, hauled into the ship by a rope lowered from the stern [Note: [Col. 1313] The manuscript reads *pape*.].

When, in the evening, after his clothes had dried, he ate with the sailors, they began to examine his beautiful hands and infer from them that he was not a common man.

The sailors, moreover, had been compelled by the Pisans to swear that they would not take anyone carrying letters from the apostolic lord into their ship. Therefore they told Albero that they wished to inspect his little chests, lest he be carrying letters against the lord emperor; they also told him how they had received an order from the Pisans concerning this matter and had given their oath.

But the lord Albero had hidden the letters in a locked ivory box, which he had decently wrapped in Tyrian cloth, as though it were a sacred object. He said that it contained relics of the saints, which he was bringing from overseas; he added that, through their intercession, he had been delivered from danger when he had been tossed about at sea.

Terrified by this, and showing reverence toward the sacred object, they did not dare open it [Col. 1315A]. Thus he escaped these and many other dangers.

### 6

On one occasion in the bishopric of Strasbourg, knowing that royal ambushers had been prepared for him on the road he was about to take, and unable now to turn aside elsewhere, he armed himself with shield, lance, and military clothing. Seated firmly on a strong horse, he hurried through their midst, suddenly asking them whether they had seen Albero of Metz, the devil, passing that way.

For the king had suddenly sent him to capture Albero, and he cursed him, saying: “May God give him as evil an hour as I have had all night while pursuing him.”

In this way he was accustomed to elude the king’s ambushes by a thousand devices.

### 7

During this conflict the people of Metz had twice destroyed his house, which he owned in their city, after selling off his possessions. But he in turn twice compelled them to rebuild it and restore what they had taken [Col. 1315B].

### 8

At last, after the aforesaid Bishop Poppo died (in the year 1120), Albero also caused the people of Metz to have another bishop without the king’s consent [Note: [Col. 1315D] Namely Theoger, abbot of Saint George in the Black Forest], a man of wondrous holiness.

When he had been consecrated bishop, he was not received in the city but, within a few days, was transferred to the dwelling of the eternal city.

After him, Albero caused them to have as bishop a man named Stephen, brother of Count Rainald of Monzon. It was thought that he had done this out of love for Count Rainald, for the two men appeared to be a pair united in friendship.

Thus, during the aforesaid conflict, Rainald had also lent him his castle of Monzon, so that Albero might wage war against the people of Metz from there.

At one time Albero secretly entered the city from that castle and withdrew to the house of a certain widow. When morning came, he suddenly mounted a horse and displayed himself in the streets.

When this became known, an outcry arose throughout the entire city, and all who had horses pursued him far beyond the city. Count Rainald, however, kept soldiers in ambush, as he and the lord Albero had agreed; attacking the people of Metz, he captured many of them.

Afterward it happened that Count Rainald allied himself with the people of Metz, having received gifts which blind even the hearts of the wise, and abandoned his friendship with the lord Albero.

The lord Albero bore this indignantly. He hurled severe threats against him to his face, openly predicting that great disgrace would come upon him from this affair. He immediately ordered horses to be saddled in the count’s presence and, hastening to King Henry—into whose favor he had recently and fully returned—by saying many things he brought it about [Col. 1316A] that the king himself went to Monzon.

When the king had besieged it, the count fled by night and escaped to Bari. The king, leaving Monzon, surrounded Bari with a large army and, after forcing the count to surrender, brought him away as a captive [Note: [Col. 1315D] See Ekkehard, under the relevant year.].

But at last the lord Albero was moved by many prayers and brought him back free and released. Thereafter their friendship, which had been dissolved for a time, was strengthened with such steadfast firmness that neither any circumstance nor even death could dissolve it.

### 9

By this time the lord Albero had greatly increased in dignities and revenues. He had already become primicerius of the Church of Metz, archdeacon, and provost of Saint Arnual.

He had also obtained an archdeaconry in the Church of Verdun [Col. 1316B], and in the Church of Toul, from which he originated, he was archdeacon and provost of Saint Gangulf.

I say that he came from the bishopric of Toul, from noble parents [Note: [Col. 1315D] Concerning them, see the passage above, col. 1085, no. 142, edited from the Codex of Aulne.].

In that bishopric, before he was elected by the people of Trier, he had built an abbey on his own patrimony, called Monasteriolum [Note: [Col. 1315D] Montreuil or Monterol. Concerning it Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, II (1746 edition), p. 52, says: “The castle called Monsterol was near the place where the abbey of Belchamp now stands . . . This castle is now entirely ruined; only a few traces remain, but its name still survives in a hill a quarter of a league from the abbey.”].

In it he gathered regular canons, men of great religious devotion and holiness. The cloister is called Bellus Campus [Note: [Col. 1316D] Bel-Champ.].

In our own times no one has shown greater eagerness to draw religious and learned men around him, to love them, and to honor them generously with his benefactions. He was also extraordinarily hospitable, beyond his means, and always accustomed to treat strangers with gentleness and humanity.

[Col. 1316C] **10.** Matters standing thus, it happened that he was elected to the archbishopric of Partonopolis [Note: [Col. 1316D] Magdeburg.] in the time of King and Emperor Lothair II (in the year 1126). Rejecting this office in every way, he brought it about by his own ingenuity that Lord Norbert, a man of renowned religious life, undertook the governance of that church [Note: [Col. 1316D] Compare the *Annals of Saxony* under the year 1126, and the *Life of St. Norbert*.].

In the time of that same emperor, when he had come to the church of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 1315] The manuscript reads *abberstadensem*.], the clergy of that city had already assembled to elect him as bishop to the vacant see [Note: [Col. 1316D] This must have happened in the year 1129, when Bishop Otto had been deposed.]. Since, however, owing to differing factions, they could agree on no individual, and since they heard that so distinguished and eminent a man had arrived, they all unanimously agreed upon him. When he learned of this, he abandoned the meal that had already been prepared for him in the house of a certain venerable man, Conrad the chamberlain, whom King Henry had caused to be blinded at the time of the aforesaid schism. Just as his men had begun to wash their hands and were about to go to dinner, [Col. 1317A] he unexpectedly mounted a horse and ordered his men to follow him immediately; and so he fled.

At last, while Pope Innocent was seated on the apostolic throne and Lothair was reigning, the clergy of Trier, against the will of all the laymen, elected him archbishop (in the year 1131). How the election was conducted you will be able to judge from the contents of the following letter, which the clergy sent to Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript repeatedly has “I.”]. The letter is as follows:

> To the most blessed pontiff of the Catholic Church, the clergy of the Church of Trier offer their devoted service of obedience and ministry.
>
> Reverend Father, it is not hidden from you how the Church of Trier has now been deprived of its own shepherd for two years. You also know that we were unable to have Lord Bruno, whom we had unanimously elected. But now, setting aside the labors and evils that we have endured in the meantime, we announce to you new hardships and dangers, and we desire, through the assistance of your fatherly concern, to obtain their end as soon as possible.
>
> Certainly, when the king was in our city (April), together with the Lord of Albano, the bishops of Metz and Toul, and the barons of our province, a meeting was held to elect a shepherd. We named five men, so that, by agreement, one of them might more easily be elected by everyone. After these men had been named, the barons and all the laymen withdrew from us to one side to take counsel; then, returning to us shortly afterward, they requested—not any one of the five previously named by us, but Gebehard of Würzburg, all with one voice [Note: [Col. 1317D] Gebehard had been expelled from the see of Würzburg.].
>
> Although we pointed out to them a legitimate reason for rejecting him [Note: [Col. 1317] A word appears to be missing, or else a word such as “to provide” is required.], nevertheless they persisted in that demand, shouting and making tumult, to such an extent that many of our brothers began to agree with them. Thus, with the business unfinished, the assembly was dismissed that day.
>
> Later, however, we few, not sufficiently confident in our own strength against so great a multitude, sought counsel from the bishops, namely those of Albano and Metz. At last we placed ourselves and our cause so entirely in their hands and under their counsel that, whatever person they advised us to choose—provided that person was acceptable to you, Father, and that the lord king was willing to invest him—we would elect.
>
> What more is there to say? They spoke with the king. Then, returning to us, they advised us to elect Lord Albero, primicerius of the Church of Metz [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript reads “of the church of Metz.”], and said that he pleased the lord king and that his favor would be with us in this matter.
>
> Encouraged, therefore, by this confidence, when we assembled to carry out the election, the count palatine, who is the advocate of our church, together with the other nobles and the people, as soon as they perceived our intention, utterly disrupted us with uproar and tumult. Then they all demanded that Lord Godefrid, [Col. 1318A] the provost of our church, who was the first named among the five, be given to them [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript has “G.”] [Note: [Col. 1317D] Hontheim incorrectly calls him Gebehard; compare chapter 11. Godefrid, provost of the greater church, is named in several charters; see Günther, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus* I, p. 208 (year 1129), 215, 223; Hontheim, *History* I, pp. 520, 526, 531, 533, etc.].
>
> But because, as has been said above, we were bound by our commitment, and refused to comply with their demand, we postponed the election until the king and the barons had departed. For we did not dare elect the primicerius in their presence. Then, as the king was leaving, he appointed a day for us at Mainz, affirming that he wished to deal with our affair there by the judgment of the bishops.
>
> Meanwhile, we few—namely, the provost of the greater house, the dean, two archdeacons, the provost of St. Paulinus, the master of the schools, the custos, and four other canons of the greater house—assembled in our choir. We elected Lord Albero under the following condition [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript lacks “under the condition.”]: namely, if it pleased you, Lord Father, and if the lord king wished to invest him, as the bishops of Albano and Metz had promised us, by the gift of his authority [Note: [Col. 1318B] The manuscript has “the king” written above the line.].
>
> For we knew, and still know truly, that the anger and fury of the laymen could in no way and by no ingenuity be calmed except by royal power and favor. The reason why we did not summon more of our brothers to the election was the fear with which we feared our fellow citizens: if they had learned of it, they would have fallen upon our throats. We had less hope of the assent of certain of our brothers, since we had seen that previously they had been terrified, as we believe, by fear of death and had favored the laymen. Nevertheless, even then most of them received the election brought to them by us with kindly minds and words [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript has this phrase written above the line.].
>
> Later, when on the appointed day we came to Mainz [Note: [Col. 1318D] On the date of this assembly, see Jaffé, *History of Lothair*, p. 103.], and presented the completed election to the lord king, he, changed by the favor of the laymen, heard us with unexpected kindness [Col. 1318C] and did not support our cause. Finally, when reminded by the Lord of Albano of the promise mentioned above, he testified before all the bishops and princes who were present that he had never promised the Lord of Albano or the Lord of Metz that he would have any favorable disposition toward the election of that person unless it could be carried out with the assent and agreement of all, both laymen and clergy [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript reads “to the Lord of Albano,” rather than “by the Lord of Albano.”].
>
> Thus, ashamed and frustrated, we departed from him. When we reached home, we found almost all the clergy opposed to us, except those of us who had conducted the election. Whenever we addressed them and tried to encourage them, they threatened us with the destruction of the cloisters, the seizure of their prebends, and danger to life itself, and they loudly declared that they could find no remedy for any of these evils.
>
> Therefore, falling at the feet of your Majesty, we beseech you through the charity of Jesus Christ to obtain quickly the favor of the king, which the Lords of Albano and Metz promised us. Otherwise, it remains either that you restore to us our first elect, namely Lord Bruno [Note: [Col. 1318D] Concerning him, see below in this chapter.] [Col. 1319A] or—without prejudice to your fatherly favor—we must necessarily elect another person in whom the votes of clergy and people may agree.
>
> Indeed, we are not so much moved by the evils that we ourselves endure or expect to endure as by the repeated wailing and complaint of our brothers, clerics, monks, nuns, orphans, and widows, who miserably lament that through our fault they have been exposed to every danger.

**11.** As you can judge from the contents of this letter, the laymen, both free men and ministerials [Note: [Col. 1319] The manuscript reads “misterials.”], opposed the election of this person. Among them, a certain Lodoycus, burgrave—that is, prefect of the city—a man belonging to the household of the church, broke into the houses of all the clerics who did not wish to oppose this election [Col. 1319B] and seized all their goods. What is more cruel, he and his men ambushed the most distinguished clerics of the entire church, men adorned with the highest dignities, as they were hastening to Metz to seek the elected candidate, at the bridge of Konz [Note: [Col. 1319D] Near Konz on the River Saar. WYTTENB.]. They stripped them of their horses and clothing and—horrible to relate!—disturbed noble persons with savage blows and beatings.

Nor should it be considered tedious to commit to memory the names of those who tried to defend the liberty of the church [Note: [Col. 1319] The manuscript reads: “who, having tried …”; the printed edition has: “who tried …”]. These were brave men, tested in tribulation and steadfast in faith: Godefrid, provost of the greater house; Folmar, the dean [Note: [Col. 1319D] The same man is mentioned in Hontheim I, pp. 520, 526, 530, [Col. 1320D] 531, 533, etc. He is named in Günther I, p. 223.]; Arnulf, the archdeacon [Note: [Col. 1320D] Compare Günther I, p. 225; Hontheim, cited above.]; Theoderic and Bolso, archdeacons [Note: [Col. 1319] The manuscript reads “archdicons.”]; and Lord Hillinus, at that time still a subdeacon [Note: [Col. 1319] The manuscript first has “subdiconus,” corrected to “subdiaconus.”], who shortly afterward succeeded the aforesaid Lord Albero in the archiepiscopal see [Col. 1319C]. Also among them was Lord Bruno, then provost of Koblenz and later archbishop of Cologne, brother of Count Adolf of Berg. Before the Treverans had named Lord Albero, they had all unanimously elected Bruno archbishop during their tribulation. But he obtained absolution from Pope Innocent only after much effort, putting forward certain hidden reasons. It was said, however, that he had refused the honor offered to him because he desired a richer, although less dignified, bishopric. What happened afterward also made this sufficiently plausible. For shortly afterward, while he was in France pursuing his studies, when the people of Cologne had elected a certain Godefrid, provost of Xanten, by the common consent of clergy and people, Bruno learned of this report, immediately returned, had the election annulled, and accepted that bishopric (December 25, 1131) [Note: [Col. 1319D] The manuscript has “G.”].

**12.** While matters thus stood, a council happened to be assembled at the city of Reims, presided over by Lord Innocent II, pope (October 1131) [Col. 1320A]. To this council the aforesaid Lord Albero and the clerics of Trier came with differing aims. The latter strove to obtain their chosen candidate, despite his resistance, through the coercion of the lord pope; the former labored to be released from this burden and to recover the dignities and ecclesiastical benefices that he had lost because of his disobedience.

For the aforesaid Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 1319] The manuscript repeatedly has “I.”], because Albero avoided this burden after the pope had repeatedly ordered him to accept it, suspended him from every ecclesiastical office and benefice. At this council, therefore, the lord pope ordered that he be raised up, clothed in a cope, and placed among the archbishops; and, taking him to Vienne, he consecrated him archbishop, although Albero was still laboring to obtain release from the office.

When news of this reached Trier, [Col. 1320B] the aforesaid burgrave Lodoycus formed a conspiracy: if Lord Albero ever entered the city of Trier, they would hand him over to death. Lodoycus himself added this oath to the conspiracy, that he would be the first to attack him.

The reason why the aforesaid Lodoycus opposed Lord Albero so violently was this: he had so subjected Lord Godefrid the archbishop by his machinations that he claimed to hold the palace as a benefice, together with all the episcopal revenues that were to be brought into it; he also claimed that he ought to support the bishop and his chaplains, and that everything else belonging to the bishopric was his benefice. He said that the bishop’s responsibility was to celebrate Masses, ordinations of clerics, and consecrations of churches; his own right, however, was to govern the land, arrange everything in the bishopric, and maintain the military force.

Thus, every day he supplied the bishop’s dinner with one sextarius of wine and two sextarii of beer. He himself, with a multitude of men at his table, feasted splendidly every day like a great prince; everywhere he went he was surrounded by a crowd of soldiers, and in every way he lorded it over the entire land. Consequently, the aforesaid bishop incurred the hatred of all the clergy, because, scorning the counsel and companionship of the entire clergy, he had given himself wholly to one layman. They therefore began to work for his deposition [Col. 1320C] [Note: [Col. 1320D] See the *Deeds* published above, col. 1227.].

Overwhelmed by poverty, he succumbed before his adversaries. For the aforesaid Lodoycus had drained away not only his money but also all his wisdom and judgment; in both respects he was deficient, as commonly happens whenever someone who ought to watch over public interests, wishing like a sluggard to languish in sluggish idleness, casts all his care and concern upon another and wishes to be responsible neither for himself nor for anyone else.

For there is a proverb: “Entrust your purse to your client, but keep the prudence of your counsel with yourself.” For a similar reason King Childeric of the Franks was deposed from the kingdom, and the kingdom was given to the man to whom he had entrusted its government—namely, Pepin, the mayor of the palace—with the approval of Pope Adrian.

And because Lodoycus knew Albero to be a man of sharp intelligence, prudent in everything, and not destined to become subject to him, and because he had learned not to bear a lord but to lord it himself, he therefore opposed him. But do you wish to hear the outcome of this affair? Listen:

> “Nor does the bull love the yoke; yet what he hates, he bears.”  
> *(Ovid, Amores III.11.36.)*

When this conspiracy became known, Lord Albero the archbishop—who had previously withdrawn from the city entrusted to him, as though evading the burden of episcopal office—now, like a river which, when blocked by a barrier, had previously flowed on in a quiet and silent course but, as though indignant at the barrier’s obstruction, exhausts the banks with tumultuous roar and foaming waves and bursts through its restraints, came to Trier as an unconquerable and undaunted man, having gathered a large military force.

The clerics came out to meet him at the White Gate [Note: [Col. 1321D] Concerning this, see the *Deeds*, chapter 3.] in solemn procession and received him honorably, with hymns and praises and great eagerness. Lodoycus and his fellow conspirators likewise went out to meet him. When they saw him surrounded by so large a force of soldiers, they were astonished and confused in mind, immediately pretended peace, and Lodoycus, first among them all, hastened to greet his lord with flattering and humble speech and approached to kiss him.

[Col. 1321C] **13.** It should not be passed over in silence that when Lord Albero the archbishop came to Aachen to the emperor’s court (April 1132), King Lothair refused to invest him with the regalia, because Albero had already received episcopal consecration before requesting his investiture. The king would have opposed him altogether, as was generally believed, except that he knew Albero to be such a man that he could easily stir the entire world of his empire against him. Therefore he accepted from Albero a light satisfaction.

For when, following the common counsel of the princes, Albero offered the king an oath that this had not been done to diminish his honor, but that he had approached consecration because he had been compelled by the lord pope, the lord king released him from the oath [Note: [Col. 1321] The manuscript reads “he released the oath to him.”] and granted him the regalia with the royal scepter.

At the same court he also pronounced Simon, duke of Lorraine, the king’s brother [Note: [Col. 1321D] Born to Duke Theoderic and Hadwide, widow of Gebhard of Supplinburg.], excommunicated, and on Holy Easter Day, while the Gospel was being read, compelled him to leave the church [Note: [Col. 1321D] On his reconciliation in 1132, see the charters of Simon and Albero in Hontheim, *History* I, pp. 519–520.] (April 10, 1132).

**14.** Nor should this be omitted: when, after receiving the regalia, he was about to enter Trier, not enough could be found among all the episcopal revenues to prepare a service for him on the first day [Col. 1322A]. Everything belonging to the bishopric was either pledged or was claimed by the aforesaid Lodoycus and his fellow conspirators as a benefice held by them.

Accordingly, Lord Archbishop Albero, making provision against his poverty, had obtained from Lord Pope Innocent permission to retain for three years the ecclesiastical revenues that he had possessed before becoming bishop. When his wine, grain, and other provisions necessary for his sustenance were brought into the palace according to ancient custom, the aforesaid Lodoycus locked everything away and distributed to Albero each day only as much as he pleased, as he had been accustomed to do with Albero’s predecessors. He himself and his companions consumed the rest [Col. 1322B].

After the archbishop had tolerated this for some time, Lodoycus abused his patience to such an extent that one afternoon, when certain outsiders had come to the archbishop’s court and Albero had ordered drink to be served, as was customary, his servants came to the palace for wine. Lodoycus’s steward replied that he would give them nothing unless Lord Lodoycus ordered it.

After he had often endured this and similar treatment, Albero finally judged the situation intolerable. Accordingly, he rebuilt at great expense Palaciolum, the fortress of Julius Caesar situated beside the city, which at that time was ruined and uninhabitable from age and neglect, and ordered his provisions to be brought there. Then he uttered this sarcasm: “Now let Lodoycus have his palace.”

Afterward, while residing there for three years, he devoted all his attention to freeing the episcopal revenues. He redeemed the court of Humahc [Note: [Col. 1321D] Perhaps Hunbach, in a charter of Poppo, in [Col. 1322D] Günther I, p. 124; Hontheim incorrectly reads Limbach.] for 300 marks, which his predecessor Lord Meinerus had pledged. Lord Albero redeemed nearly everything else belonging to the bishopric that had been pledged or granted as a benefice by Archbishop Godefrid.

At last, while Lodoycus kept the palace empty at his own expense, he was reduced to such humility that, barefoot and wearing woolen garments, he prostrated himself at the archbishop’s feet in Palaciolum, asking for mercy and surrendering the palace.

**15.** In those days the lord archbishop, by accumulating many things, became very rich in possessions, and, increasing daily [Col. 1322D], was making preparations for certain great undertakings that he had in mind.

Understanding from ancient privileges [Note: [Col. 1322D] In a forged diploma of King Dagobert, Hontheim, *History* I, p. 76, it is called a church “built on the estate of St. Peter.” It is well known that the archbishops and abbots disputed this matter for a long time.] that the abbey of St. Maximin, situated on the estate of blessed Peter and by ancient right belonging to the disposition of his church, he devoted himself entirely to devising how he might wrest it from the power of the king and restore it to his own church.

For this reason he set out with King Lothair on the Italian expedition (in the year 1136) with one hundred soldiers, according to an estimate [Note: [Col. 1323D] In Conrad III’s diploma concerning this matter, published in Hontheim, *History* I, p. 542, it reads: “when Archbishop Albero had faithfully served that emperor (Lothair) in the expedition to Apulia, at great danger and expense, chiefly to obtain this benefice,” etc.], but in truth with sixty-seven. After King Roger of Sicily had been driven from the parts of Apulia that he had occupied, those lands given to Duke Rainald, and the regalia of blessed Peter recovered, the emperor, as he was returning, fell by the common lot of mortals into death.

Lord Archbishop Albero, however, having been honored by Pope Innocent with the office of legate [Note: [Col. 1323D] See Innocent’s bull in Günther, *Codex diplomaticus* I, p. 226. Compare Hontheim, *History* I, p. 536.], when he was returning (in the year 1137), reached Mount Romaricum [Note: [Col. 1323D] Remiremont.] and heard from a report that Count Otto of Rheineck, from the king’s army in Italy, had sent word to two brothers, Warner and John of Nantersburg [Note: [Col. 1323D] Near Lutzerath, as Hontheim notes.], that they should seize his castle of Arraz by treachery, and that this would be carried into effect.

When he had hoped for rest after many labors and now saw so many great cares again threatening him, he bravely steeled his mind against adversity and swore by his crown that he would never shave his beard unless he had first recovered his castle of Arraz and destroyed the castle of those brothers, namely Warner and John of Nantersburg.

Gathering all the princes of the lands of Toul and Metz, he reached Trier with a large military force. He simultaneously besieged both castles, Arraz and Nantersburg. After destroying Nantersburg and recovering Arraz, he returned to Trier in great triumph.

Nor does it seem proper to deny silence concerning the fact that the aforesaid Lord Albero, returning from the same expedition, forcibly carried away from Parma the relics of his predecessor, Archbishop Meinerus, and brought them with him to Trier [Col. 1323C].

For the aforesaid Lord Meinerus, as a magnanimous man, excommunicated Conrad, later king, when Conrad had been set over Lothair. Therefore, when that same Conrad, later king, was hastening to Rome on the business of his church, he captured him and placed him at Parma as a pledge for a large sum of money. There he also died in prison [Note: [Col. 1323D] See above, continuation of the *Deeds*, chapter 28.].

That same Conrad [Note: [Col. 1323] The manuscript reads “C.”], then king who had been set over Lothair, was reconciled to King Lothair in the aforesaid expedition. Since he saw that the strength and authority of the kingdom rested with Archbishop Albero, he attached himself to him through close friendship and service. At that time they became so closely joined [Col. 1323D] that, after the death of Emperor Lothair, Lord Albero worked with every effort, despite the opposition of nearly all the princes of the kingdom, to have Conrad raised to the kingship [Note: [Col. 1323] The manuscript lacks the word supplied by the edition: “procured.”].

For by his great industry he brought it about that Duke Frederick, the brother of King Conrad, and Burchard, bishop of Worms, came with Conrad to a conference at Koblenz (in the year 1138). Archbishop Arnulf of Cologne also came to that conference. Finally, after much deliberation, Lord Archbishop Albero raised Conrad to the kingship (March 7) and, leading him to Aachen with a great multitude, confirmed him in the kingdom by royal anointing (March 13) [Note: [Col. 1323D] Jaffé, *History of Conrad III*, p. 5.].

Afterward, when the Saxons, together with Duke Henry, the son-in-law of King Lothair, had appointed a day and place at Hersfeld for King Conrad, so that by the hazard of battle they might determine whether or not he had begun to reign rightly, and when the lord archbishop had promised that he would come with twenty soldiers, he brought five hundred soldiers and also brought thirty wagonloads of wine and an immense supply of provisions, carried in almost countless wagons [Col. 1324B].

There Albert the Younger, then bishop of Mainz, worked by every means to make this evil grow into a greater discord. Lord Albero, however, with God’s help, worked so that they separated from one another in peace, although many thousands had assembled in great hatred to fight.

Once everything had been settled peacefully, Archbishop Albero sent each of the princes a wagonload of wine, especially to the Saxons. Here one should note the subtlety of Lord Albero’s intelligence. He perceived that an abundance of wine and other provisions contributed more to victory and to inflaming the courage of men than many thousands of hungry soldiers [Col. 1324C].

**16.** After these events, he received the abbey of St. Maximin from King Conrad for this and other services [Note: [Col. 1323D] The diploma is published in Hontheim I, p. [Col. 1324D] 541.]. For the king restored to him the patronage of the aforesaid church, which he had held for a long time.

When the monks learned of this through the swift rumor of fame, they—who at that time had been living in a highly disorderly manner in the aforesaid church—gathered all the silver and gold that in those days abounded greatly in that monastery, in woven panels, images, and various ornaments, as well as precious stones and gems [Note: [Col. 1324D] In truth, to protect the new prelate, Abbot Sigerus, and his church, they carried away the church’s more precious furnishings; they also broke certain utensils so that they could be transported more easily. The monks dispersed in various directions with the monastery’s older privileges, a considerable portion of which perished in that tumult. From the prologue of the manuscript *Golden Book* of St. Maximin. WYTT.].

Before the archbishop’s return, they gave these things to the Count of Namur, who at that time held the land of Luxembourg [Note: [Col. 1324D] Henry, surnamed the Blind, count of Namur, who had married the daughter of Conrad of Luxembourg and acquired the county of Luxembourg in the year 1136. ID.], so that he might bring them armed assistance and, since he was the church’s advocate [Note: [Col. 1325D] On this, compare Zyllesius, *Defense of the Imperial Abbey of St. Maximin*, chapter 3.], remove the archbishop’s lordship and power from them by force of arms.

Now courage is needed [Note: [Col. 1325D] Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.261.]; now an inexhaustible subject presents itself to us, one that requires not my feeble pen but some great poet. For who could make words equal to the brave deeds of this man Albero and his followers against the aforesaid tyrant, as they fought for seven years with stratagem, sword, fire, famine, and the inexplicable hazards of Mars?

This would be a subject sufficient for Homer’s powers, if Homer himself were sufficient for the subject. If I wished poetically to imitate the celebrated deeds of individual men here and there, the various outcomes of their battles, and the diverse fortunes of those who now yielded and now drove back their opponents; or if, following the skill of historians, I wished to renew each event through artful narration and represent it to you, O reader, as though you saw it happening before your eyes, then either I would succumb to the burden—which is true [Note: [Col. 1325] The manuscript reads “to succumb”—]—or I would be found no inferior to Virgil or Statius, Livy [Note: [Col. 1325] The manuscript reads “Ivvo,” corrected.] or Josephus.

Even if I were equal to the task, it would not be worthwhile for you [Note: [Col. 1325] Some words appear to be missing.]. For the work would be less than the purpose for which it is undertaken. Nor do I think that the one who accomplished this task well would deserve less praise than all those whose deeds he had properly expressed.

But now expect nothing else from me except that I touch briefly upon each matter in summary, lest they be entirely erased by eternal oblivion.

**17.** At that time, therefore, when the church of St. Maximin was vacant of a shepherd, the monks elected as abbot a certain monk from the Church of Liège [Col. 1325C], the brother of certain men who were counselors of the Count of Namur, so that through their counsel the count might be inflamed more fiercely each day in his fury.

They brought him to Rome at great expense and, against the will of the archbishop, had him blessed as abbot by Lord Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 1325D] Sigerus; Pope Innocent confirmed his privileges and immunity in the year 1140; Hontheim, *History* I, p. 543.]. The crowds marveled at so sudden a change of affairs: namely, that the Roman Church had so severely harassed such a great and eminent man, who had endured so many labors and dangers for it and who so recently had stood in such great favor with the Apostolic See. He had even opposed King Lothair so strongly on behalf of Pope Innocent during the expedition mentioned above that the archbishop and the king had departed from one another without friendly feelings [Col. 1325D] [Note: [Col. 1326D] Compare *Metrical Deeds*, lines 140 ff.].

**18.** Moreover, during this war between the archbishop and the count, the brothers of the Church of Koblenz also began to harass him. Against his will they elected as provost a nobleman, Lord Lodoycus of Isenburg [Col. 1326A]. They traveled to Rome with him at great expense and brought back apostolic letters contrary to the archbishop’s wishes.

When they presented these letters to the archbishop as he was seated in synod, he, in a fit of anger, threw them onto the ground. Consequently, after being accused before Pope Innocent, he was summoned by him to the appointed day. Since he did not appear on that day, he was suspended from episcopal office.

All these evils came upon him together, and the Lord freed him from them all. For when he came to Rome, he brought it about that the abbot of St. Maximin promised him obedience and swore fidelity to him, and that the election of the people of Koblenz was annulled (in the year 1140).

These matters settled, let us return to the count.

**19.** At the beginning of this discord, before he had renounced his fidelity to his lord, the count unexpectedly approached the city of Trier with fifteen hundred soldiers. The people of Trier were not fortified, enclosed neither by a ditch nor by a wall; having enjoyed a long peace, they were unaccustomed to war. The archbishop himself was absent, residing at the king’s court.

The count could then have greatly afflicted the city if God had not turned aside this evil. But Count Frederick of Vianden [Note: [Col. 1326D] Vianden.] happened to be in the city at that time. Meeting the Count of Namur, he persuaded him by many arguments to return, showing him that it would be a great and perpetual disgrace if he committed such an act against his lord before renouncing his lordship—especially since it would be an offense against royal majesty if he inflicted any harm upon the archbishop, who was residing at the court by the king’s command [Col. 1326C].

When the archbishop returned from court, he began by every means to work for peace and to recall the count from the fury he had begun. But the count carried out arson, plunder, and killings throughout the bishopric. At last the archbishop began to defend himself.

And since I am now hastening toward the end, passing over many matters, I gather the substance of the events as follows.

### 20

He twice surrounded Rodolf’s Mount [Note: Rudolfsberg was a fortress of Luxembourg, not far from Trier, on the bank of the Saar. WYTT calls it Roulmont; Hontheim I, p. 554; Rodulfisberg, Gunther I, p. 336.] and destroyed it during the second siege—namely, the castle that had seemed impregnable in every respect. He built a new castle called Mercury’s Mount [Note: Montmédy.], fearing that the Namur count might seize that mountain, since it lay almost at the heart of his territory. He captured Manderscheid Castle [Note: Manderscheid.]—a place strongly fortified by nature—and retained it until his death. He captured Gerlanda [Note: No one identifies its location.] and Zolvera [Note: Commonly called Zolver, in the territory of the duchy of Luxembourg, four and a half leagues from Luxembourg. On the hill now called der Zollwerknopf there once stood the castle of this family; today not even the slightest ruins remain. WYTT.], and either captured or destroyed thirty fortifications belonging to the count of Namur. He also captured Echternach, where the count had been accustomed to maintain a garrison.

But between the first and second sieges of Rodolf’s Mount, the archbishop and the count engaged in battle in the open field. It happened as follows. When the archbishop had first laid siege to Rodolf’s Mount, the count invaded Palatiolum and, setting fire to the church of Saint Mary, hoped also to burn the archbishop’s fortification. When this report reached the archbishop, he raised the siege and hastened throughout the night with his army, so that, coming upon the enemy unexpectedly and striking him with unforeseen terror, he might display his strength.

But the count, learning through scouts that the archbishop was approaching, turned to flight and that night withdrew into the bishop’s village of Wittlich. Wishing to refresh his horses and men, and finding nothing there, he burned the entire village. Passing on from there, he wished to rest beside the abbey called “the Cloister” [Note: Namely, Himmerod; cf. Albero’s charter of 1138, in Honth. Hist. I, p. 539: “and we caused that place to be called the Cloister.”] and break bread—for he was hungry—when he was informed that the archbishop’s army was already pressing upon him. He and his men immediately took flight; and, summoning one of the brothers to him, he adjured and charged him to report these words to the pursuing archbishop:

“May God grant him—that is, the archbishop—no better day or night than the two days and two nights I have continually endured. Although I had fasted for two days, when on the third day I wished to refresh myself with a little bread, I was not permitted to do so.”

The archbishop therefore overtook the count and engaged him in fierce battle. The count turned his back and escaped only with difficulty, thanks to a swift horse; many of his men were captured and many others killed. The archbishop then returned to Rodolf’s Mount and, as has been said above, destroyed it (1144?).

At last, exhausted in every respect, the count sought the favor of the lord archbishop through King Conrad, who was then about to depart on the Jerusalem expedition. At Speyer he requested it with great effort and many attempts, and obtained it only with great difficulty. He confirmed it by the solemnity of an oath: that thereafter he would in no way take up arms against the church of Trier on this account; that he would neither rebuild Rodolf’s Mount nor permit it to be rebuilt; and that he would never reclaim Manderscheid by force or any kind of extortion [Note: See the diploma of King Conrad issued concerning this matter, Hontheim, Hist. I, p. 554.] (1146, December; 1147, January).

The lord archbishop, however, returned Echternach and his other castles and fortifications to the count. Of the benefices that the count had held in the territory from the church of Trier, the archbishop restored those which, during the time of this conflict, he had not given to his own supporters. Thus he recovered the abbey and won a glorious victory over the count. After this he accomplished many other things as well.

### 21

For Count Frederick of Vianden had usurped the whole of his own castle of Arraz, although the archbishop had appointed a guardian over one tower [Note: See the noteworthy diploma issued concerning this matter in Hontheim, Hist. I, p. 557.], and had carried out many acts of robbery on the Moselle River. Recovering the castle again, the archbishop expelled Count Frederick from it.

After all these events, being greatly exhausted [Note: “Exhausted”; the manuscript has *exhautus*.] because of the great and varied expenses he had incurred in the war, he thereafter enjoyed peace, since no one attempted to provoke him to war. Gathering together again a great deal of property, he filled his palace and all his castles with abundant wine and every kind of food, so that, if anyone should again provoke him by some injury, he would not be found unprepared.

### 22

In those days (1147) it happened that Pope Eugenius came to France. When the archbishop met him at Provins [Note: Provins.], he celebrated Easter with him at Paris (April 20), and there renewed and confirmed the privileges of his church, concerning the primacy of his church and the restoration of the abbey of Saint Maximin [Note: See the bull of Eugenius in Hontheim, Hist. I, p. 556.]. There he was also honored by the lord pope, by Louis, king of France, and by Count Theobald [Note: Count of Blois, Chartres, and Troyes.] with highly appropriate gifts.

As he was about to depart, he invited the lord pope to his own house. When he heard a certain cleric named Baldricus [Note: The author of this book.], young in age and originating from the bishopric of Liège, from the castle of Florennes [Note: Florennes.], arguing cases at the lord pope’s court and often pleading them aptly, he brought him with him from Paris to Trier and appointed him master of the schools in the house of Saint Peter. As long as he lived, he held him very dear and familiar.

Not long afterward, the aforesaid king of France and Henry, son of Count Theobald, passed through the village of Saint Arnual [Note: In Lorraine.]. The lord archbishop, learning of this, sent each of them separately such great and magnificent service that, when it was offered unexpectedly and without their prior knowledge, they were both greatly astonished.

### 23

In the same year, on the Sunday on which *To you I have lifted up* is sung, Pope Eugenius came to Trier, as he had been invited by the lord archbishop. On the Saturday (November 29) before that Sunday he was honorably lodged in the church of Saint Eucharius.

On that Sunday itself (November 30), with the greatest reverence, he was led into the church by clergy and people, amid an extraordinary processional display and a solemnity worthy of remembrance. Lord Albero led him on the right, and on the left stood Arnold, archbishop of Cologne. Many bishops preceded them—of Germany, Belgium, France, England, Burgundy, Lombardy, Tuscany, and every nation beneath heaven.

Nor does it weary me to enumerate the cardinals who came to Trier with Pope Eugenius [Note: The manuscript has “E. c.”]. They were men honorable in appearance, dress, bearing, learning, and morals, and worthy, because of their great integrity, of everlasting remembrance. These are their names—may they be written more securely in the book of life [Note: Compare the subscriptions in Eugenius’s charters, in Günther I, p. 311, etc.]:

Among the cardinal bishops: Alberic of Ostia and Himerus of Tusculum.

Among the priests: Guido Summanus; Heribert of Saint Anastasia; Master Guidodens, a very learned man and skilled in laws and jurisprudence; Julius of Saint Marcellus; Hugh of Novara; Master Hubaldus; Gilbert of Saint Mark; and John Papiro.

Among the deacons: Octavianus, noble by birth and nobler still in character, distinguished for integrity and generosity, and a special friend of the Germans; Guido of Cremona, a man of high birth, highly courtly and honorable, with sweet eloquence; Odo of Boncase, a most gentle man, descended from noble Romans, affable and compassionate toward all; John of Santa Maria Nova, a man of the sweetest affability, adorned with holiness and refinement of character; and Gregory of Sant’Angelo, a man of lively intelligence, ready and capable in everything conducive to honor and the usefulness of the church of God.

What shall I say of Jacinctus, who surpassed every hyacinth in the splendor of his virtue, who drew everyone to love him by the sweetness of his eloquence, and whose hearing and seeing were lessons in integrity? Nor shall I be silent about Guido of Pisa, a most prudent man and remarkable for his concise speech.

For twelve continuous weeks the archbishop supplied all these men with necessities in such abundance that they themselves admitted that plenty had come to them with a full horn.

What shall I say of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, archdeacons, provosts, dukes, and counts who came to Trier to visit the lord pope, not one of whom he left without a share of his generosity? Who could explain in words the solemn celebration of the Nativity of the Lord held at Trier [Note: The manuscript has *quat*.], so that you who were not present could understand or imagine it?

What pomp do you suppose there was in the procession on the holy day, when the lord pope, riding on a mule, proceeded to the church of Saint Paulinus, with the cardinals preceding him and a multitude of bishops on horses covered in white? Returning from there, he celebrated the solemn Mass amid such a vast crowd of people that throughout the entire church of Saint Peter one could not find even the space of a foot left empty.

What if I were to describe how, on the holy day, after the solemn service had been completed, the lord pope with his cardinals sat at tables on one side, while the lord archbishop with the bishops who had gathered there sat opposite them, wearing their mitres? By what calculation could anyone reckon such numerous and enormous expenses?

I would certainly say that, before the lord pope’s arrival [Note: The manuscript has *adventu*.], within six weeks he built the house called the Pope’s House, which had three stories according to its height, and repaired the house called Jerusalem, which had been almost completely destroyed. But even if I remain silent, the facts themselves will speak and recall it to memory.

### 24

I now turn to the fact that, leaving Trier, Pope Eugenius reached Reims to celebrate a council in the middle of Lent (March 17, 1148). The lord archbishop Albero arrived at that council in such magnificent fashion that he drew everyone’s eyes and opened everyone’s mouth in astonishment.

He was carried between two horses in a little chamber made of leather and neatly lined inside with linen cloth, a sight that seemed marvelous to everyone. He was already burdened by old age and, broken by long labors, was failing.

At this council, therefore, sitting first in rank among all the bishops, he had many privileges concerning the primacy of his see read aloud over all Belgium, Gaul, and Germany. When these had been heard, the archbishop of Reims was greatly disturbed. Consequently, his men, becoming embroiled in a disturbance with Albero’s men, wounded some of them.

The lord archbishop Albero took this very badly and threatened to sit down before Ivois [Note: Ivois.] and devastate the bishopric of Reims. At last the matter was brought to this conclusion: the archbishop of Reims came with the bishop of Soissons to the lodging and handed over to Albero’s authority the men who had committed this offense.

### 25

In the same year, in September, when Count Palatine Hermann had occupied the castle of Treis [Note: Treis.] and strengthened it with buildings, Count Otto of Rheineck gave the aforesaid castle, together with the land belonging to it, to this archbishop and his church, so that he might recover it. Therefore he laid siege to the castle.

The count palatine, gathering all his forces to liberate the castle, came and pitched his camp at the entrance of the forest adjoining it [Note: The manuscript has *costro*]. The archbishop, however, drew up a battle line of horsemen and foot soldiers on the opposite side and awaited his arrival for three days.

There you would have seen shining helmets, coats of mail surpassing daylight in their brightness, and shields surrounding the mountains with reflected sunlight. Oh, what fearless faces of men you would have observed! How impatiently they endured the delay of the hesitating enemy! What preliminary maneuvers of soldiers pretending to fight you would have seen in their armor! How quickly you would have watched a spirited horse being wheeled about! What encounters of soldiers on horseback, and with what clatter you would have seen their lances splintered! What cries you would have heard from those pursuing and those turning their backs!

With what skill you would have observed a feigned flight, how suddenly those who seemed to be fleeing turned back, and how fortune was reversed when those who had been pursuing were driven headlong from behind! There you would have noticed the soldiers at one moment massed together, at another suddenly opening their ranks and, as though yielding, cleverly receiving the attacking enemy into their midst, then closing around him by bending back their wings. A thousand arts and a thousand methods of deception could be learned there.

Meanwhile the archbishop’s scout arrived after examining the palatine’s forces and announced that he was already approaching and prepared for battle. Then you would have seen that old man, already weakened in his entire body, arrange the infantry lines and deploy the cavalry with military skill. He called those he knew individually by name and asked about the unknown men—who they were—in such a way that, from the very question, they seemed to have acquired not merely the notice but even the familiarity of so great a prince.

Then, holding the archiepiscopal cross in his hands, he began to address the armed lines with an exhortation:

“O friends of blessed Peter! O defenders of the holy church! You who today have offered your mortal bodies to the enemy sword for God and for justice, let blessed Peter come to your minds, whose soldiers you are today. Believe that he is protecting you today with invisible shields, together with a great company of saints. Be certain of victory.

“Look upon this sign of the cross—this, I say, terrible sign to the adversaries of Jesus Christ. This is the cross upon which Count Hermann, the count palatine, swore fidelity to me on the day when I appointed him advocate of our church, on the day when I conferred upon him those forces and that power with which he now harasses me.

“Then I told him that in this cross there was a piece of the Lord’s wood, on which he whose most holy image shines here triumphed over the enemy of the human race. I also indicated that this cross contained the venerable relics of many saints.

“The count palatine himself, placing his hand upon this holy image, swore to me in these words:

“‘I give you, lord archbishop, this Lord, this one crucified for us, as guarantor, and I swear to you by his power that I will never do anything against you, and that in all your necessities I will faithfully support you with all my strength and all my power.’

“Know, therefore, all of you, that I shall carry this guarantor—namely, Christ the Lord—in his sacred image before him; I shall place him before his eyes and show him this witness to his oath.

“But now, O faithful ones of Jesus Christ, who are offering your life and blood for the defense of his church, prepare your hearts for the Lord and cleanse your consciences. Since there is no time for you to make your confessions individually, make a general confession of your sins to me, your shepherd. And I, by the authority entrusted to us by God, shall through our office grant you indulgence and remission of all your sins, so that, if anyone is called away today from this temporal and uncertain life, he may pass into the better life, namely, eternal life.”

When he had received the common confession of all, granted indulgence and absolution, and bestowed a blessing upon them, he so inspired everyone that not the slightest sign of fear appeared in any one of them.

The archbishop entrusted the banner to the count of Namur, while he himself carried the cross in his own hands. When matters stood thus, and the count palatine learned through scouts that he was not strong enough to engage such an inspired army in battle, he sent envoys to the archbishop and conveyed words of supplication. To come quickly to the end, he obtained this: that his men who were in the castle might depart unharmed, and that the archbishop might carry out his will concerning the castle.

### 26

Now I wish to say a little about his character and habits, for in all his activities he had unusual and highly exceptional ways. He was slow in body, in action, and in speech. He prolonged everything for an extremely long time. He never, or only very rarely, did anything in haste; rather, he attached such delay to everything that he seemed exceedingly burdensome and slow to everyone, and caused weariness both to his own people and to outsiders. Yet, when any matter he was about to begin had become hopeless because of his excessive slowness, it nevertheless ended in the desired result.

In walking, riding, sleeping, and waking, he did not follow the customary habits of other men. When walking, he had to be led by the hands, for he suffered from sciatica. Because of the same infirmity, when he rode he had stirrups hanging from the saddle-bow, and he kept his left leg over the horse’s neck. Although he did this because of the compulsion of his illness, others thought he did it merely because of its strangeness.

At night he was accustomed to remain in councils or conferences until the curfew or cockcrow, and often until dawn. He very frequently slept until the second hour of the day. He came late to table, after the customary hour, and remained there for a very long time, discussing and conversing with his clerics with great cheerfulness about the sacred Scriptures and the opinions of the holy fathers. He was accustomed to keep a great number of religious and learned men with him.

In the sacred mysteries of the altar he seemed more than human. He never approached them without tears and the greatest contrition. Dressed in pontifical vestments, he seemed an angel of the Lord; his face shone with an angelic appearance, and he handled those heavenly sacraments with such devotion that, when he lingered in secret prayer, he seemed through contemplation and prayer to penetrate the heavens.

When he addressed the people, he could scarcely explain what he had begun: partly because he was slow in speech, partly because, having been born a speaker of French, he was not fluent in German, and partly because he dealt with matters of excessive depth. He said almost everything in proverbs and comparisons, of which he possessed a greater store than any men who have come to our knowledge.

He gave alms most generously and every day. He had considerable knowledge of physiognomy, so much so that from the appearance of different faces he could discern the secrets of minds and character.

When he came to royal courts, he was a spectacle to everyone. He alone seemed worthy of admiration; the magnificence of his retinue and expenditures outshone all other princes. By his pleasant speech and the cheerful insertion of his proverbs, he used to make both the king and the princes happy.

He was the last to come, and the one long awaited, to court or to any conference, and he was the last to depart. At individual assemblies he never disclosed his own counsel until he had heard the others.

I, Baldricus, who composed this little work, attended one court which he approached at Frankfurt under King Conrad [Note: Either in March 1147 or in August 1149; see Jaffé, cited above, pp. 118, 171.] with forty decked ships, besides the light vessels, cargo ships, and cooking boats. At that court he had with him eight counts, Duke Matthew of Lorraine, and Duke Henry of Limburg, as well as such a multitude of clerics and soldiers that he astonished everyone who saw them.

He also took with him in his decked fleet Master Jarland of Besançon [Note: See *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, p. 275.] and Master Theodoric of Chartres [Note: John of Salisbury, *Metalogicon*, book I, chapter 5, remarks that this Theodoric was a most diligent investigator of the liberal arts. WYTT.], two of the most outstanding teachers of our time in fame and glory. He took great delight in their disputations and discussions, and when he returned home from the court, he sent them back to their own places, joyful and richly honored with suitable gifts.

I do not know whether this deserves to be remembered: when he was returning from the aforesaid court, because he hated the people of Mainz and perhaps suspected them, as he approached their city he ordered the banners to be raised on each ship and the soldiers to display themselves in shields shining with gold, coats of mail surpassing silver in brilliance, and helmets. As he approached with the sound of trumpets, horns, and weapons, and with the terrible clamoring of the men, he stirred the entire city.

There you would have seen people rushing together from the whole city and women crying out; and, as though the city were already about to be captured, you would have seen tumult and panic everywhere [Note: The manuscript has *ubrs*].

### 27

At last, as I am about to bring the narrative to an end, I shall say a little about his death, his passing, and his testament.

At the Epiphany of the Lord he had held a great court at Koblenz and had obtained a truce between Count Albert of Molbach [Note: Count Albert of Molbach is named in charters from 1158–1175, in Gunther, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, vol. I.] and Count of Sayn [Note: Sayn.] (January 6, 1152). These men had long been at war with one another over the county of Bonn; nearly all the nobles of the lower region supported one side or the other, and they were about to devastate the entire land if he had not intervened by his counsel.

For he had this as a custom: frequently to assemble his suffragan bishops, princes, and nobles from his province, to provide them generously with stipends, and to deliberate with them concerning the condition of the church and the peace of the fatherland.

To return to what I had begun to say: immediately after the Epiphany, he was inflamed by the dreadful heat of an acute fever and constricted by an attack of pleurisy [Note: So the manuscript.]. Beginning to doubt his life, he summoned religious men—the abbot Richard of Saint Mary of Sprinkenbach [Note: A monastery founded in 1107; see Hontheim I, p. 483.], the abbot Bertolf of Saint Eucharius, and many others.

After confessing all his sins, he was anointed with oil according to the instruction of blessed James. As he was about to receive the most holy body of Christ, he uttered words signifying great fidelity and true catholic faith.

Thus the magnanimous hero, the catholic shepherd, began in a memorable voice:

“Hear me, my dearest brothers. I have summoned you abbots and religious men so that, in the presence of this church and in the universal church that will be gathered at the end of the world from holy angels and human beings, you may stand as witnesses to my true faith and, by your prayer, help this faith to save me.

“I believe that what I now see under the appearance of bread is the true body of Christ, the Son of God, which in the virginal womb of Mary, the undefiled Virgin, with the Holy Spirit overshadowing her, was united—as it remains now—to the Word of God, the true Son of the Most High Father. For us it was abandoned by its soul in temporal death on the cross; but, when its soul descended to hell, it was not deprived of the fellowship of divinity in the tomb, just as the soul was not abandoned in hell, according to what David testifies about him, saying:

“‘For you will not abandon my soul to hell, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption’ (Psalm 15:10).
