“This, I say, is that body of Christ which, on the third day, when its soul returned to it, broke the gates of hell by the divine power it possessed, rescued the faithful of the former age from the devil’s power, and rose from the tomb—thereafter immortal and incapable of suffering. Before his passion, while at supper, holding himself in his sacred hands in this form of bread, he distributed himself to his disciples to eat, giving them one incapable of suffering, though he himself was still destined to suffer, and teaching them to celebrate the mysteries of this sacrament.

“This, I say, is the body of Christ which appeared to the disciples visibly and tangibly for forty days after the resurrection, yet remained incorruptible, according to the power of his will, by which he does everything whatsoever he wills.

“This is the truly glorified and ineffably glorious body which, while the apostles watched, was marvelously taken up in glory. The Lord sits with the Lord, the Son with the Father, at his right hand [Note: The manuscript has *addextris*.], the same Son in the bosom of the Father—that is, in unity of essence.

“Of this sacred and venerable body I can truly say with the centurion: ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’ (Matthew 8:8; Luke 7:6). Yet I ask you, O good Jesus, who deigned to enter the house of Zacchaeus, that you may also deign to enter the inner chamber and secret dwelling of my soul, and heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.

“You who have now come to me through this faith, visit me through the grace that dwells within me. In this faith I receive life in place of life, just as you said: ‘The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world’ (John 6:52), so that it may be my provision for eternal life. Amen.”

When he had received the Lord’s body, he took the chalice and said:

“O most merciful and serene Father, I, a sinner, beseech your most kindly majesty today that, through this true sacrifice of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, through this immeasurable mystery of the redemption of human beings and eternal salvation—which your holy church offers to you in true faith, in loving propitiation, and in the blood of your Son—you may be appeased and favorable toward me.

“And just as I truly believe that this is the true body of your Son, according to the sacred gift of his teaching, so truly today may you pardon me and remove my iniquity. Do not [enter into judgment with me] [Note: The manuscript lacks this phrase.], but, in the truth of this faith, lead me along the straight path into eternal life. Amen.”

### 28

Know, reader, that although I may not have reported the very same words, I have nevertheless reported the meaning and intention of his words.

Now I shall explain as briefly as I can how he arranged his testament. He gave the court at Thure, which he had purchased with his own money from Count William of Glisberg [Note: The manuscript has “W.”], to the brothers of the church of Saint Peter at Trier, so that they might obtain their refectory from its revenues on the anniversary of his death.

He also gave his patrimony at Sule and the court at Bredal to the aforesaid church, with this arrangement: the gilded cross which he had stripped during the aforementioned war was to be repaired from its revenues, certain ornaments which he had pawned were to be restored, and thereafter the property was to pass perpetually by right to the use of the brothers.

He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: Himmerod. His heart and entrails were transferred to this monastery, buried there, and covered with marble bearing this epitaph: “Here are buried the heart and entrails of the venerable Albero, archbishop of Trier, the first founder of our monastery, who died in the year of grace 1152, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.” See Heesius, *Manipulus rerum memorabilium claustri Hemmerodensis*, Cologne, 1641. WYTT.].

Although he fell to his fate according to the common lot of mortals, he was not buried according to the ordinary fortune of men. For when he died at Koblenz, his entrails were buried in the Cloister [Note: He meant to say January 18; see chapter 30.] beside the wall facing north and covered with a marble stone. His body, embalmed with myrrh, aloe, and spices by his highly skilled physician Philip the Lombard—who had also predicted his death three days beforehand by examining his urine—was dressed in pontifical garments and brought to Trier with a great retinue.

Count Palatine Hermann [Note: The manuscript has “Her.”] and many barons of the lower region followed his funeral with a great company. When it reached Trier, the clergy and people went out to meet it at the bridge. It was then carried through the individual monasteries, one each day, in a solemn procession, until the number of days equaled the number of monasteries. Each day the number of nobles gathering from the whole province for his funeral increased.

When they learned of his death, his suffragan bishops came: Stephen of Metz, Henry of Toul, Albero of Verdun, and the cardinal priest Jordan of the Roman church. Jordan had at that time assembled at Metz a gathering of all the abbots of Upper Lorraine, and he came with them to Albero’s funeral.

On the eleventh day after his death he was buried with such honor and amid such common mourning throughout the entire province that everyone present confessed that they had never seen such an honorable funeral.

He lies buried in the church of Saint Peter [Note: The manuscript lacks these words.], on the southern side, beside the altar of Saint Stephen. It is worth noting that, whenever he entered the aforesaid church while alive, he used to pray in the very place where his tomb now stands.

### 29

Lord Jesus Christ, splendor of the Father, wisdom and power, who by your ineffable condescension shone forth in human form so that you might free us, miserable sinners, from the devil’s power through the fellowship of your companionable life among us, may the light of your glory shine today upon Albero, priest of the true sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek.

He frequently offered your venerable and most holy body to your Father in holy faith—the body which you gave to your church, as a pledge of your love, when she sought it from the Father.

For when your Father said to the synagogue, “Shall I drink the blood of goats or calves?” (Psalm 49:13), and David heard this and, as a devout servant, alluding to your Father, answered by speaking of your Father’s good pleasure: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering” (Psalm 39:7; Hebrews 10:5); and when your Father seemed to consent, David, perceiving his will and yours, said in your person—or rather, you said in his person: “Behold, I come” (Hebrews 10:7).

And when your church saw that the rite of the ancient sacrifice was rejected, and saw that you did not delight in the flesh of goats or calves which the synagogue offered to you, she anxiously asked what she could offer you in praise and acknowledgment for all your benefits, and daily said: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115:12).

Then, in wondrous compassion, you fashioned a body for yourself and gave it to your bride, your beloved, your dove—that is, to your church—so that she might sacrifice it to your Father. Therefore she herself rejoicing says: “I shall receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:13).

Therefore, by the power of this sacrifice, deign to grant the radiance of your countenance and eternal rest to him, Lord, who live and reign as God throughout all ages. Amen.

> Albero, greatest of men, Rome weeps, Trier weeps everywhere,  
> > At the death of such a great and wondrous man.  
>   
> Trier weeps for its shepherd, Rome weeps that rigor has fallen,  
> > And that the doctrine of justice, the light of the church, has fallen.  
>   
> You were great among the great, equal to the small, a limit to tyrants,  
> > Glory to the rich, a portion to the poor.  
>   
> Overthrowing the camps of tyrants, you founded  
> > Very many camps of the good; generous, you were a host.  
>   
> Generous and humane. January had completed in due order  
> > Eighteen days. May death be rest for you!

These ten verses are contained in the epitaph of Albero, lord archbishop of Trier; they are written in letters of gold on sheets of copper [Note: These words are written in red ink.].

#### Beneath the arch

> Belgian Rome, your perpetual adornment and glory  
> > Lies here: he who lives as your eternal honor.  
>   
> Albero, light of the world, glory of the city, glory of the clergy,  
> > Ornament of the fatherland, splendor of the church,  
>   
> Here lies the lesser part of him; the greater survives above:  
> > For his mind survives, and his fame will be everlasting.  
>   
> Oh, how great a man is enclosed in so small a cave!  
> > He was not lesser than the world in praises and merits.  
>   
> It was peculiar to this man not to be conquered, to conquer,  
> > To spare the conquered, and to have no equal in generosity. [Note: Perhaps “a generous hand”?]  
>   
> This is the man to whom Germans and Belgians did not think it too much  
> > To submit their necks to his primacy.  
>   
> Through him, kindly Trier became greater; Rome  
> > Sent you Quirites and made them your citizens.  
>   
> Coming here, the head of the world does not deny that here is the heart of the world,  
> > Nor that you are a second Rome.  
>   
> Twice nine times had Janus brought forth the sun for the world  
> > When he took away so great a light from the church.  
>   
> What alone remains, say, reader, with suppliant mind:  
> > “Albero, may God be your light; may God be your life”—  
>   
> He who, as though from a watchtower, visible throughout the whole world,  
> > Raised your name, Trier, to the stars,  
>   
> Confounding the mighty, and an iron rod to the proud,  
> > Skilled at breaking them like a potter’s vessel [Note: The text is uncertain; the edition reads *eras*.],  
>   
> Whom no storm of fortune could make lesser,  
> > For when he was pressed down, he was greater.  
>   
> He, the house of the Lord, a mountain higher than the mountains,  
> > Leaping over the hills, with valleys in his shadow,  
>   
> When Janus had twice nine times brought the sun back to its rising,  
> > Lying like a serene star in the west,  
>   
> Albero said: “Death is nothing to me, for the flesh destined to be glorified  
> > Will rise again, rejoicing with the soul.” [Note: The manuscript has *naque*.]

And this is the epitaph over his remains at Koblenz:

> The venerable bishop Albero, worthy in both offices,  
> > Committed, alas, his heart and entrails to this soil.  
>   
> Ask God, reader, that there—where true peace is yours—  
> > He may be found as a man for you to follow in your allotted lot.

**In the year of the Lord 825–1106. Chronicle of Saint Hubert of Andage, edited by L. C. Bethmann and W. Wattenbach, Doctors of Philosophy.**

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. VIII, p. 565.)*
[Col. 1337]

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1337C] When that immense struggle between kingship and priesthood arose, scattering the seeds of discord throughout each and every episcopal diocese, the same disaster that overtook the other monasteries of the Diocese of Liège also dragged down the distinguished monastery of Saint Hubert in the Ardennes. It had been raised to the summit of prosperity under Theoderic I, but Theoderic II’s dispute with Bishop Otbert completely cast it down from its position. Yet amid the very calamities by which it was shaken, it yielded the fruit of its ancient discipline: a Hubertine monk, brought up under Theoderic I and moderately well instructed in literary studies, undertook to write the history of the monastery and brought what he had begun to completion with such a fortunate result that you will scarcely find a more illuminating author concerning the condition of those times.

He wished to keep his name hidden, but both his intimate knowledge of events and what he tells us in chapter 58, concerning something that happened in the monastery before our own eyes, show him to have been a monk of Saint Hubert. His whole manner of writing reveals that he devoted himself to letters, although at times he departs from the rules of grammar; but [Col. 1339A] I believe that more often the copyist was at fault. He imitated Sallust in his writing, and also borrows his words in chapters 54 and 76. He likewise displays knowledge of other writers—Cicero and Macrobius—in chapters 60 and following, where he reports Lambert’s narratives, but so consistently preserves the authors’ wording that he seems to have read them himself, unless he used some derivative source. In addition, in chapter 1 he inserted a passage from the *Miscellaneous History*; in chapter 78, a letter of Peter Damian.

For writing the early history of his own monastery, although he touched upon it only briefly, he also used local authors: the *Life of Saint Beregisus* [Note: [Col. 1339D] *Acta Sanctorum*, October I, 524.], the *Life of Saint Hubert* [Note: [Col. 1339D] In Surius VI, 45.], the *Translation* [Note: [Col. 1339D] Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* IV, 1, 295.], and the *Miracles* [Note: [Col. 1339D] Ibid., p. 297. Some additions were made at the end; they already exist in Brussels manuscript 14650, of the eleventh century. Our author mentions them in chapter 22.], the *Life of Lambert* by Sigebert [Note: [Col. 1339D] In Chapeaville I, 411, where it is wrongly attributed to Renerus.], and also Fredegar and Anselm’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* [Note: [Col. 1339D] Chapter 2. But this is not certain, for very little could have been drawn from that source.]. He always had the monastery’s privileges at hand, sometimes inserting them whole into his narrative and sometimes only in excerpts.

After setting out the monastery’s beginnings, he left untouched the intervening period between Altuenus and Adelard—825–1034—about which he had learned nothing certain; he says, “let us go through again the events that we have heard and seen in our own times.” These words should not be interpreted literally, for in 1034 he may scarcely yet have been born, and he reports little about Adelard; but he knew Theoderic I well, who governed the abbey in 1055–1087, and added much to what he received from the life of Theoderic written by another contemporary monk [Note: [Col. 1339D] After Mabillon, *Acta* VI, 2, 557, it was more accurately edited from the Alnensis manuscript in *Acta Sanctorum*, August IV, 848.]; elsewhere he gives a somewhat different account.

For while that other writer is wholly occupied with praising the abbot’s piety and adduces miracles, touching on the remaining matters briefly as though they were foreign to his subject, our author is less concerned with miracles—borrowing a concise account of them from the author of the *Life*—but treats the entire condition of the monastery, its external affairs, and its relations with the powerful men of those regions in detail. He gathered these matters both from the monastery’s privileges and from what he himself saw; for in chapter 58 he reports that Duke Frederick (+ 1065) carried a boar into the church, “before our eyes.” Moreover, he also seems to have used Rupert’s *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence* [Col. 1339C], chapters 28–30.

He then advances to the history of the deeds performed under Theoderic II, which occupies more than half the work. It is written so accurately and supported by so many documentary letters that we readily recognize him as a close friend of Theoderic, apparently his companion in exile, although he sometimes criticizes him freely. Heribrand, abbot of Saint Lawrence of Liège [Note: [Col. 1339D] Reinerus, *On Famous Writers of Monasteries*, in Pez, *Thesaurus* IV, 3, pp. 20 ff., chapter 7.], wrote a *Life of “Theoderic the Younger, Abbot of Saint Hubert”* (1115–1130), but no trace of it remains. In chapter 70 our author mentions Heribrand, a monk of Saint Lawrence, who, in my opinion, is the same man who wrote the *Life*, though perhaps he wrote it after our author. For our author’s work ends in A.D. 1106, but its ending was lost through the injury of time.

Chapter 96 [Col. 1340A] says that Manasses later became archbishop of Reims, and that Rodulf became provost after Manasses. Since, after Manasses died in 1106, Rodulf was elected archbishop, the first editors concluded from this that the work had been written earlier [Note: [Col. 1339D] They say, before 1108, but Rodulf had already been elected in 1106.]. I concede that this has the appearance of truth; but if he had already begun writing at that time, he added what follows only later. For he speaks so freely of Abbot Theoderic (+ 1109) that I can scarcely believe the work was published while Theoderic was alive; and in chapter 88, speaking of Bishop Otbert, he says, “as long as he survived thereafter,” words that certainly seem to have been written after Otbert’s death (+ 1118).

Nevertheless, I recognize no conclusive argument either here or there, and I acknowledge that these matters must remain uncertain. Let it be enough for us to know that the author of the work was a man involved in public affairs, keen in judgment, and devoted to truth. His entire manner of expression, and his plain and sincere narration of events, suggest this.

Toward the end of the century Gislebertus borrowed from our author in chapter 24 [Col. 1340B]. Later Aegidius seems to have known him (see chapters 24, 28–30), but since he intended to report only laudable things about the bishops of Liège, he adopted very little from him; he consulted him only later, when, deprived of Anselm, he was looking around for other authors.

The autograph manuscript of the work was lost at an early date. For it is clear from the fact that, in 1550, it was no longer in the monastery that, when a lawsuit arose between Charles V and the Bishop of Liège concerning jurisdiction over Andage, and the monastery’s history had to be produced in court [Note: [Col. 1339D] Thus Robaulx, from the manuscript *Foundation of the Monastery of Andage*, written around the end of the seventeenth century and preserved in the church of Saint Hubert.], Remaclus, then abbot, finding nothing in the domestic archives, appealed by letter to Orval. From there the manuscript of Aurea Vallis was sent on condition of its return [Note: [Col. 1339D] A copy of this condition is found at the end of manuscript 1*, written as follows:

“We, Brother Dominique [Col. 1340D] Robin, by the permission of God humble Abbot of the Church and Monastery of Notre-Dame d’Orval, of the Cistercian Order, Diocese of Trier and County of Chiny, and we, the entire convent of that same place, hereby make known to all whom it may concern that around the year 1550 our predecessors, the late Abbot and Convent of Orval, lent to the late Lord Dom Remacle, in his time Abbot of Saint Hubert, a very ancient handwritten book entitled *Cantatorium*. This book was found in our archives; it is very old, complete, and authentic, fit to be trusted in court and outside it. The said late Lord Abbot of Saint Hubert had promised to return and restore the book in the same condition and manner in which he had received it from our said late predecessors. In witness whereof we, the aforesaid Abbot and Convent, have caused our abbatial and conventual seals to be affixed to these presents on 8 March 1569, Trier style.”

Below this was written:

“Collated with the original and found to agree, on parchment, with two seals in green wax, this second day of March 1570, Trier style, by me.”

Below this was signed:

“N. Brutkens.”]

Nevertheless, neither the abbot nor his successors fulfilled that condition. Rather, the manuscript remained at Saint Hubert until the monastery was suppressed in 1796 and its library dispersed. After various vicissitudes it finally came into the possession of the distinguished Theodorus Geoffroy, then a cavalry lieutenant in the Belgian army, a friend of the Muses amid the arms. In 1841 our Bethmann met him at Bruges for this very purpose, and he graciously made both the manuscript and his home available for our use, with a courtesy for which we can never praise him sufficiently. We hope that these lines may remain a monument both of our grateful spirit and of his own enduring kindness toward us.

The manuscript is on parchment, of small format, written by several hands in the thirteenth century. After the *Lives of Saints Judocus, Basil, Leodegarius, Eupraxia, Radegund, Balthildis,* Gillebertus’ letter to Anselm, Gillebertus’ disputation with a Jew, and the *Lives of Anastasia, Theoderic the Martyr, Gengulf,* and *Corbinian,* it contains this history [Col. 1341A], written continuously by a thirteenth-century hand and bearing the title:

“Here begins the book called the *Cantatorium*.”

Two leaves, 52 and 53, in the middle, have fallen out; Romualdus Hancar was still able to read them two hundred years ago. One or more leaves at the end, which were already missing at that time, have also disappeared. The copyist did not always avoid errors. When he saw that material supplied from the autograph manuscript on slips apparently sewn into it had been inserted into the manuscript, he sometimes placed it in the wrong position [Note: [Col. 1341D] Chapters 1, 8, and 62.]; he omitted other material [Note: [Col. 1341D] Chapters 76 and 78.]. I also believe that most of the years’ numbers displayed in the text of our manuscript had been written in the margin of the original.

1*) Around 1630 Romualdus Hancar, a monk of Saint Hubert, transcribed the Aurea Vallis manuscript quite carefully onto paper. This copy, enriched by his own marginal notes, later entered the registry archive of Saint Hubert. In 1834 it was transferred to Brussels, to the Burgundian Library, no. 14,600, and, while we were preparing this new edition, was most courteously sent to us so that from it we might more accurately supply the two omitted leaves [Col. 1341B].

1**) Linotte de Poupehan, magistrate of Bouillon, possessed another copy made in 1737 from 1*, according to Ozeray, *History of the Duchy of Bouillon*, p. 310.

1***) Robaulx, p. 4, mentions two other copies made in 1563 from the original 1 and given to the procurator of Luxembourg and the legate of the Bishop of Liège. One of them may perhaps be the same copy that Dewez says he saw in Mirwart Castle, *History of Liège* I, 54.

The first edition was prepared by Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio* IV, 914, from the manuscript itself, 1; but it was excessively disfigured by errors, and they imposed their own division into chapters. Dom Bouquet XI, 149, 635; XIII, [Col. 1342A] 564, gave excerpts only. A second edition was produced by P. de Robaulx de Soumoy, *Chronicle of the Abbey of Saint-Hubert*, Brussels, 1847, octavo, from Brussels manuscript 1*, with a French translation. He appended to it a history of the monastery from the end of the *Cantatorium* down to his own time, together with notes that are genuinely useful and rich in good material, from which we learned much.

The editor used Romualdus Hancar’s manuscript history of the monastery, which Hancar himself had governed as prior and had composed from our *Cantatorium* and other local sources; the *Foundation of the Monastery of Andage*; the *Andaginian Antiquities*; the *Titles of the Possessions of Saint Hubert*; and several other manuscripts from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Thus he provided his book with great usefulness. Thirdly, L. B. De Reiffenberg, director of the Burgundian Library, *Monuments to Serve the History of Namur, Hainaut, and Luxembourg*, Brussels, 1847, quarto, did possess manuscript 1, but rarely used it. He was content to publish a new edition from its copy, 1*, which he adorned with a reproduction [Col. 1342B] of manuscript 1.

Finally, we present the *Cantatorium* from the manuscript itself, 1, supplying its lacunae from 1* and leaving its spelling intact, except that we have changed the simple *e* to *ae*, a spelling that only began to be used everywhere in the thirteenth century. We have retained the division into chapters instituted by the copyist himself, not by numbers but by initial capital letters in red, while adding Martène’s numbers in brackets for the convenience of readers. In the notes we have excerpted as briefly as possible whatever useful material Romualdus Hancar, Martène, and De Robaulx had already supplied, religiously adding their sigla H., M., and R. everywhere as a mark of gratitude; the rest is ours.

[Col. 1341]

## CHRONICLE OF SAINT HUBERT OF ANDAGE

### HERE BEGINS THE BOOK CALLED THE *CANTATORIUM*: HOW THE ABBEY OF SAINT HUBERT WAS FOUNDED

[Col. 1341C] **1.** In the Ardennes district there was said to be a certain fortress called Ambra, because it was the head of the Amberlacum fisc [Note: [Col. 1341] Thus corrected by a recent hand in place of *ablacensis*.] [Note: [Col. 1341D] I have found no other mention of the fortress of Ambra, but the trace of the name remains in the village of Amberloux, near Saint Hubert.]. It had been utterly destroyed when the Huns ravaged Gaul and, left deserted for nearly three hundred and thirty-seven years [Note: [Col. 1342D] It should be corrected to 237. Hancar.], had come to nothing. (*Miscellaneous History.*)

This people, long secluded among inaccessible mountains, invaded the lands of the Goths in a sudden frenzy during the time of the emperor Valens. Their king Filimer had earlier entered the lands of the Getae and Scythians with the Goths and found there certain women skilled in magic, whom they call *alirumnas*. Suspecting them, he drove them out and expelled them into the wilderness. There they joined with wild men whom they call *fauns of the fig trees* and produced, among the Maeotian marshes, a most savage race. It was foul and emaciated, scarcely resembling a human figure, and inflicted excessive terror on those who saw it by the horror of its face, since it was deformed and of accursed blackness.

The cheeks of the males were dried out [Note: [Col. 1341] “Cut off,” according to the *Miscellaneous History*.] before they were suckled, so that even then they were forced to endure hardship. They were small in stature [Col. 1342C], but quick and nimble in their movements and extremely ready for riding; broad-shouldered, skilled in bending bows and shooting arrows; strong-necked and always holding their heads erect in pride; possessing the fiercest spirits and living like beasts.

While these men, with their king Athala, were serving the necessities [Note: [Col. 1341] Perhaps “commands”? The reading is uncertain: *nibus* in 1; *jussibus* in 1*. corrected.] of divine vengeance, as they devastated the cities, fortresses, and churches of Gaul alike, they also destroyed this fortress as they passed through. (*Life of Beregisus.*)

In the time of Pippin, who was mayor of the palace under King Theoderic, his wife Plectrudis was preparing to visit Amberlacum, a fisc belonging to her jurisdiction. Passing through the aforesaid place, exhausted both by the weariness of the vast solitude and by the heat of summer, she decided to rest there for a while in the green meadows. After she had refreshed herself, her companions were weighed down by a longer sleep. Being more watchful about the grazing horses, lest they wander through the woods, she rose alone without waking anyone.

When she had gathered the horses together and was already more tired, she sat upon a heap of stones that happened to have been piled there and was astonished to see a small document fall before her, as though it had glided down from heaven. Although frightened, she seized it; but, not daring to entrust the secret to any of her companions, she resolved to return to her husband as quickly as possible. When she had related the miraculous event to him in order, he summoned the venerable man Beregisus, who at that time served them in their daily affairs, and handed him the document to interpret.

The priest of God, consulted, replied that the place where the document had fallen had been chosen by God, since the souls of many were destined to pass from there to the kingdoms of heaven. When Pippin then asked what he thought ought to be done, Beregisus seized the opportunity. He had long been deliberating within himself how, after abandoning the world, he might devote himself more freely to God. He therefore suggested to the prince that he should not, so far as lay in his power, fail the divine plan, and that he was ready to cultivate that wilderness if Pippin would grant it to him.

Pippin approved Beregisus’ proposal [Note: [Col. 1343D] The author of the *Life* relates what follows more briefly; the man who forged Pippin’s privilege adds more, in a manuscript formerly of Saint Hubert, now Namur, no. 5, fol. 89, published in Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* II, 1125.], although he was greatly distressed to send away someone so dear to him. Nevertheless, when Beregisus repeatedly urged him to hasten the matter, Pippin came with his court officials to the place where the heavenly document had been found. There, after making a legal donation and confirming it in the presence of his nobles, he donated the place itself to Beregisus to possess forever. He surveyed the boundaries of the donation and marked out definite limits by the following borderlands:

To the south, between the Divisiones [Note: [Col. 1343] *diusiones* in 1.] [Note: [Col. 1343D] “Stone markers formed the boundary between the lordship of Neufchâteau and several villages of the provostship of Bastogne.” Robaulx, from the *Andaginian Antiquities* written in the mid-seventeenth century. The same author explains the following names: Mochamp—Champlon—Halleux—a line of iron-ore heaps between Champlon and Halleux—Nassogne—Awenne—the Masblette, a stream crossing the valley of Font-à-Bulat—the Sulmont rock—the Lomme.], to the east, Mollem campellum; to the north, between Campilon and Halet, Ferreummons, between Nasania and Awana [Note: [Col. 1343] *Awanna* in the privilege.], the Fountain of the Table; and to the west, the Sulmonian rock and the River Lomme.

But Beregisus, persisting in unremitting labors and aided also by the assistance of certain faithful people, cleared the wooded wilderness and made it habitable. He did not stop until he had rebuilt from the foundations the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, which had formerly been utterly destroyed in the aforesaid fortress. Having gathered religious clerics around him, who served God there under the name and office of abbot, he presided over them. (*Translation of Saint Hubert.*)

After he departed to the Lord at the end of the labors of this pilgrimage [Note: [Col. 1344D] Still in the fifth year of Theoderic, that is, 724 or 725, he received a donation from Count Grimbert, according to the author of the *Life* in its prologue.], his successors continued there for a long time in the clerical order, until, while Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, was emperor, divine providence enlarged that place in the following manner.

**2. (4.)** In his time a bishop of venerable memory, Gualcaudus, presided over the Church of Liège. He was exceedingly devoted to restoring [Note: [Col. 1343] “Administering” is superscribed in the same hand; or “restoring,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1343] “Energetic” is superscribed; or “devoted,” 1.] ecclesiastical affairs. And, in order to say what must necessarily be said by way of digression concerning the See of Liège itself: Blessed Bishop Hubert had formerly transferred that episcopal see from the city of Tongeren, which had been moved to Traiectum, from that same village to the Legia. Since in his own time he flourished with great industry and power, he raised a modest little village into a most noble city and episcopal see, and there established the laws of the public courts and the judicial measures that still survive.

When, through divine revelation, he had also brought back the bones of his predecessor, blessed Lambert the martyr, and, burying him at the place of his martyrdom, had built a fitting church over him, he likewise constructed a temple at the foot of Publicimons in honor of blessed Peter the apostle, where he ordained that his own body should be buried when he departed to the Lord. Since frequent miracles declared his holiness, in the sixteenth year after his departure [Note: [Col. 1344D] The third year of Carloman; the seventy-five years that he took from the history of the translation end with the establishment of the monks, not with the second translation.] he was transferred from the aforesaid church of Saint Peter to the church of Saint Lambert (A.D. 743), where he was venerated for seventy-five years.

**3. (5.)** (*Translation of Saint Hubert.*) In the year 825 of the Incarnation of the Word, while Louis the Pious was reigning as stated, that same prince, being devoted to ecclesiastical affairs in his kingdom, either founded communities of saints or enlarged those founded earlier. By his example he instructed the bishops of cities and the rulers of provinces to do the same.

Meanwhile the clerics of the aforesaid cell of Saint Beregisus, since they were already almost failing, being situated in so vast and barren a wilderness, took the opportunity to look after themselves. They went to Gualcaudus, Bishop of Liège, and reported to him how divine providence had chosen the aforesaid place for them and what necessities they suffered there.

He rejoiced that he had found an opportunity to provide for his own salvation by cooperating with the divine will in that place. He took upon himself the care of carrying this out with complete determination and, with God’s help, raised the place to its present condition. For, changing the clerical order, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 817, on the fourth day before the Ides of August [Col. 1345A], the feast of Saint Lawrence the martyr, he established there a religious community of monks. He assigned them possessions, legally confirmed for the future, sufficient for the needs of those serving God there.

It was also established by common decree that, from the revenues of the donations made to Saint Beregisus, the administrators should bring an offering annually to that place on the same day, so that by this the ecclesiastical possession of the earlier acquisition and the later assistance might thereafter be distinguished.

As more people gathered there, wishing to devote themselves to God in that remote wilderness with greater freedom and secrecy, some of the more distinguished clerics from the church of Saint Lambert also came there. Changing their habit, they bravely girded themselves for contempt of the world.

After deliberating among themselves [Col. 1345B] how they might raise the same place to still greater honor—and especially since they hoped that the bishop’s favor would support them in this—they asked him to transfer the body of Saint Hubert there, asserting that the city had sufficient protection in Saint Lambert.

Although this undertaking seemed far too difficult for the bishop because of its magnitude, divine grace, for which nothing is impossible, hastened to grant effect to their just petitions. For a provincial synod of bishops was assembled at the church of Saint Mary in the palace at Aachen, and Louis, the pious and religious emperor, wished to be present at the ecclesiastical arrangements that were to be made there.

When Gualcaudus there reported the proposal to transfer the body of Saint Hubert to the place of Andage, he obtained, by divine disposition, the voluntary consent of the aforesaid prince and of the entire synod. A condition was imposed upon him: he was to enlarge the honor appropriate to so great a bishop and, after gathering the brothers there, both those present and those to come or follow, ensure that every necessity was excluded.

When the appointed day for carrying out the matter had arrived, the prince himself came to Liège. Accompanied both by a throng of courtiers and by the common people, he most devoutly followed the holy body, which was being transferred with its stone coffin, and carried it across the Meuse amid divine hymns and praises (A.D. 825, September 30). He also bestowed many gifts upon it with royal generosity. Although they have perished either through the antiquity of time or through the dispersal caused by ravagers, some of them nevertheless survive in the church even in our own day.

There remains an excellent text of the holy Gospels, adorned with gold and jewels. There remains a psalter written in gold, divided into groups of ten psalms by capital letters [Note: [Col. 1345D] A most precious psalter, elegantly written in gold, is preserved to this day in the monastery of Andage—not by Louis the Pious, as the author believes, but given by his son Lothair, as the verses found at the beginning of the manuscript prove. Martène. “It is believed that this psalter still exists today in the village of Boevange, canton of Mersch, Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, in the possession of Mr. Neuman, heir of the prior of Saint Hubert.” R.]; there remains, in one very large volume, Augustine’s exposition of the entire Psalter; and there remains his book entitled *On the Trinity*.

There had also remained two volumes of homilies for the whole year. After they were renewed, the winter volume was given as alms to the church of Giviniacum [Note: [Col. 1346D] Juvigny, a monastery of virgins in the Wabrian district, near Martisville.], while the summer volume was sent to the cell of Pirum [Note: [Col. 1346D] Pries, across the Meuse near Mézières.].

As for the translation of Saint Hubert, we have decided to say nothing further, since the proper account of that translation recounts these matters more clearly and at greater length. Yet since this too was certainly accomplished by the arrangement of divine grace, it may reasonably be believed that the same blessed bishop also wished gratefully to rest in the place where the venerable Beregisus lay.

Indeed, they were diligent fellow-workers at the same place and contemporaries. It was therefore fitting that, just as familiarity between them had flourished while they remained in the body, so the fellowship of their blessed bodies should also be venerated by the devotion of the faithful in one and the same place.

That they were contemporaries, if anyone wishes to know more certainly, can be proved from the deeds of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1346D] That is, from Fredegar, from whom what follows was drawn, together with the *Life of Lambert* by Sigebert. The name of Idda was added because she is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Gertrude*.], through the times of their kings and princes.

Pippin, the first of that name, was duke and mayor of the palace under King Lothair, who was the son of Chilperic by Fredegund. He administered the affairs of the kingdom together with Cunibert, Archbishop of Cologne. He continued to conduct himself nobly and wisely under Kings Dagobert and Sigibert. By his noble and religious wife Idda he fathered Grimoald and Begga, as well as blessed Gertrude.

Begga, married to Duke Ansegisus, gave birth to this Pippin, the second of that name, in the time of Kings Childeric and Theoderic. Under Childeric, blessed Lambert flourished at Traiectum [Note: [Col. 1345] Thus in 1; “in the episcopate of Traiectum” in 1*.]. King Theoderic, however, being of rather dull intelligence, was greatly despised among the Franks through the abuse of the wicked Ebroin, who was his mayor of the palace.

Not long afterward Childeric, who was more powerful, perished while hunting, intercepted by a certain nobleman named Bodilo, whom he had unlawfully ordered to be beaten while tied to a stake. After Theoderic had received the whole kingdom in his place, in the third year [Note: [Col. 1346D] I do not know where he obtained “in the third year.”] the aforesaid Pippin, son of Ansegisus and Begga, became duke of the Austrasians and grew in power.

Through Ebroin’s prompting and the faction of the Bishop of Cologne, blessed Lambert had been expelled from the episcopate. Pippin drove out Faramund and restored Lambert to his see after seven years of that unjust expulsion. The holy bishop himself soon afterward, as is read in his deeds, was crowned with martyrdom and died in defense of truth and chastity. Blessed Hubert succeeded him in the episcopate.

At that same time Beregisus undertook to cultivate the place of Andage, divinely designated, through a gift from the aforesaid Pippin and his wife Plectrudis. And since blessed Hubert, out of care for the souls entrusted to him, strove throughout the whole Ardennes—as is read in his life [Col. 1347A] [Note: [Col. 1347D] In Surius VI, p. 47.]—to abolish the idolatry that still remained there, it is clear that, because of their frequent journeys and contacts, the two men were very well known to each other and shared love and devotion toward God, as well as cooperation in this place chosen by God.

Through the zeal of both men’s preaching, unbelief faltering in that territory, the Christian religion gained increase. Therefore, by the Lord’s gift, it was granted that those whom the province itself had deserved to have as teachers while they remained in the flesh should, now reigning with Christ, be its special patrons and defenders.

**4. (8.)** If anyone wishes to know with what and how great ingenuity that same Bishop Gualcaudus strove to enlarge the place, from what revenues of possessions, whether from his own patrimony and that of his brother Erohengoldus [Note: [Col. 1347] Perhaps Erchenboldus? P.], or from estates [Note: [Col. 1347D] That is, fiefs.] taken away from certain laymen, he secured a permanent means of support for those living there in the future as well as in the present, he can learn it fully by rereading his privileges.

Although he seemed to have drawn up these privileges from the impulse of great devotion, he did so only after prolonged deliberation and the repeatedly discussed consent of the clergy, senate, and all the nobles and wise men of the Church of Liège, as well as after consulting his metropolitan, Hildebold, Bishop of Cologne, and with the authority of Pope Leo of Rome and the attestation of Louis [Note: [Col. 1347D] Thus between A.D. 814 and May 816, when Leo died.], the most pious emperor and son of the great emperor Charlemagne. He established them and strengthened them by canonical confirmation.

To insert something from those same privileges, he says:

“We assign with the firmest legal right the properties and possessions that have hitherto been assigned to that same place: namely, Aprovilla [Note: [Col. 1347D] Arville—Louville, Naomé, Palizeul, Gemelle, Telin, Lesterny, Revogne, Frandeux, Givet, Anseremme, Romedenne, Maissin, Martelanges, Boulaide. R.], Lotvilla, Nelina, Palatiolum, Gamedella, Telins [Note: [Col. 1347] Thus below, chapter 32, and in the privilege of Innocent II, in Miraeus IV, 170. The manuscript reads *Teluis*.], Lesternivis [Note: [Col. 1347] Or *Lestermius*; below, *Lesterneias*.], Ruvonia, Frandilionis, Gabelium, Anseromia, Rumendinis, and the churches of Melsun, Martilinges, and Builaidas, with all their appurtenances.

“Likewise, with the consent of our brothers, we have granted and wish to remain with the same cell other properties from the possessions of our church, which were not held directly by the lord but had been granted as benefices: namely, Tervonia, Teuledum [Note: [Col. 1347D] Terwagne, Tilleur, Marloie, Aye, Avent, Nettine, Florzée, Wanlin, Ardenne, Braz, Vesqueville, Lizere, Evernicourt, Soulpy, Noyers. R.], Marlida, Aldamum, Alventium, Nentina, Florias, Wowonium, Arduanium, [Col. 1348A] Bractis, otherwise called the bishop’s estate, Lisura, Evernicorten, Sulpiacum, Nogarias, Buthesaim; three vineyards in the fortress of Huy; one house at Liège, built by us; and also one vineyard with the mansus belonging to it in Liège territory, called Vingitis, with all its appurtenances.

“Likewise, in the same privilege, a little later:

“‘By divine counsel, as we believe, and with the consent of our faithful, we give to the aforesaid monks every year twenty pounds of silver, and a tenth of the cheese from all our estates held directly by the lord, and a tenth of the wine from three estates, namely Goganheim, Berthahem, and Cuneron.

“‘After this we add two estates to them, namely Tavernas [Note: [Col. 1347D] Taviers, Ernau. R.] and Ernau, so that, living there according to the rule, they may have sufficient and abundant food and clothing.’

“We cede all these things in their privilege before our clergy and laymen and wish them to remain both in our time and in that of our successors.”

After these arrangements, rationally ordered in every respect by the grace of God, had reached the imperial ears, the emperor rejoiced with great joy. He transferred, with the firmest legal right, the monastery called Suguilis [Note: [Col. 1347D] Suguile. H.], in which women dedicated to God were living, to the jurisdiction of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert with all its appurtenances, so that the See of Tongeren should not appear diminished in any respect because of the properties we had granted to the servants of God in the aforesaid monastery.

Moreover, he transferred to the aforesaid cell a certain forest called Wangisisusmons [Note: [Col. 1347D] Wagimont. H.], and confirmed and sealed the same legal donation by an imperial privilege.

Most of these possessions have long since been lost to this church, not only through the violence of laymen but also through that of the Bishops of Liège. Bishop Gualcaudus appointed Altuenus as abbot to preside over the place and confirmed forever, by a legal privilege made for the church, the possessions and revenues by which the brothers were to subsist, believing that whatever was done there to the end of the world would bring special benefit to himself.

But who succeeded the aforesaid abbot, how long they presided, or how the place itself either prospered or declined under each of them, we have neither read nor learned from anyone’s more reliable account [Note: [Col. 1347D] Romualdus Hancar compiled their catalogue from catalogues of the abbots of Prüm, from the Martyrology, and from other local sources in a handwritten *History of the Monastery of Saint Hubert*, which was possessed by P. de Robaulx. We present here an excerpt of this catalogue from his very useful book:

Alveus died 16 November 828.

Tancradus, Abbot of Prüm, died 11 February 829.

Marcuardus, Abbot of Prüm, resigned in 836.

Sevoldus died 13 January 855.

Saint Egilo, Abbot of Prüm, resigned in 860.

Saint Ansbaldus, Abbot of Prüm, resigned in 860.

Saint Ansbaldus, Abbot of Prüm, died 10 March 887.

Farabertus, Abbot of Prüm, died on 1 May, in an unknown year.

Regino, Abbot of Prüm, was deposed in 894.

Richarius resigned in 920.

Hildrardus.

Fridericus died in 942.

Albertus died in 966.

Heribertus died 20 May 990.

Vulbertus died 14 July 1004.

Vulbertus died in 1006.

Witericus died in 1027.

Albertus died in 1033.

Reinwardus died in 1034.]

Therefore, passing over these matters, let us return to the events that we have heard and seen in our own times.

5. (9.) In the year of the Incarnation of the Word [1034] [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 1349] The number is missing in one manuscript.]—when Abbot Renuard died, Lord Adelard succeeded him, appointed abbot by Bishop Raginard of the church of Saint Hubert. He had been scholasticus and treasurer of the monastery of Saint Trond. Being an energetic and prudent man, although he was burdened by a long and severe famine, by the prolonged and inexorable revolt between Emperor Henry and Duke Godefrid, and by the most grievous siege, decreed by the emperor and conducted by nearly all the princes dwelling on this side of the Rhine, of the castle of Mirvold [Note: [Col. 1349D] Mirwart on the river Lomme.], which pressed hard upon the church (1045), he nevertheless held firmly the place entrusted to him—which, given the dangers of the time, was most difficult [Col. 1349B]—so that it might not be utterly destroyed. Indeed, he enlarged it in possessions, adorned it with vestments and ornaments, and dignified it with buildings. He built the brothers’ refectory with a dormitory, and the abbot’s chamber with a palace.

He retained by vigorous defense the church of Alventia [Note: [Col. 1349D] Avent.], which Bishop Gualcaudus had once bestowed upon the place from his patrimony and which certain invaders had attacked. He purchased from a certain nobleman named Robert a fourth part of Calviciacum [Note: [Col. 1349D] Chauvency-Saint-Hubert, near Montmédy. R.] belonging to the fisc; half of it, in every respect, had belonged to the church from ancient times [Note: [Col. 1349D] Concerning this matter, the following is related in the *Miracles of Saint Hubert*, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, ch. 20: “In the year 955, the twentieth year of the reign of Otto I, Count Stephen gave to the church of Andage, as a lawful gift, whatever right he possessed at Calventiacum, in the presence of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, and Balderic, bishop of Liège. Since he was bound to blessed Hubert by great affection, he obtained from Abbot Albert and the brothers that his body be carried to the aforesaid fisc, and there publicly confirmed the investiture of that allod before Counts Raginard and Gislebert and many princes of the realm.”]. Count Stephen had given it to the church in satisfaction, because he had violently and unjustly fortified the castle of Mirvot upon ecclesiastical property.

He also secured for the church, at the conference held at Evodius [Note: [Col. 1350D] Ivois; compare Hermann of Reichenau, year 1048.] [1048] [Col. 1349C] between Emperor Henry and Henry, king of the Franks, a market confirmed by the emperor’s ban and authority. Throughout his lifetime he obtained by customary and prescriptive right all its jurisdictions, tolls, ban, county court, jurisdiction over thieves [Note: [Col. 1350D] That is, jurisdiction in cases of theft.], market dues [Note: [Col. 1350D] A tax paid in the marketplace.], and the profit or claims arising from any litigation; and he left the entire abbey intact to his successors, to be held without any challenge.

While the justice of public law still prevailed in his time, no advocate of the whole abbey attended any lawsuit except at the three general sessions held each year [Note: [Col. 1350D] “The place before the abbey of Saint-Hubert, where the pleas were held, is still called *Place-plaids*.” R.]. If, in these proceedings, any pledge or fine arose by judgment of the lay assessors, its payment was likewise determined at their discretion—not according to the will of the lords, but according to the means of the persons concerned. [Col. 1350A] From this common revenue the advocate received the food allowance due to him; if the proceeds were insufficient, the church made up the difference. Moreover, if the advocate compelled a rebel to submit to justice, he received his *decaterva* [Note: [Col. 1349] Thus in one manuscript; another has *decaterna*; compare Du Cange.].

6. (10.) In the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1055, in the twenty-second year of his appointment, when he had died, Lord Theoderic, a monk of the monastery of Lobbes, succeeded him by God’s providence (*Life of Theoderic*, ch. 2). He had been trained by Abbot Richard [Note: [Col. 1350D] Richard, abbot of Saint-Vanne at Verdun, an incomparable man and reformer of many distinguished monasteries; his Acts may be found in Mabillon’s *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century VI. He held the abbacy of Lobbes from 1020 to 1027.], and was subsequently ordained priest by Gerard, the venerable bishop of Cambrai. He was highly learned in letters, which he also adorned with honorable conduct, so that by the liveliness of his intellect and his moral integrity he was regarded as admirable and inimitable by both young and old. Most remarkably, he attained glory without provoking envy, and was equally dear to everyone.

Thus famous in philosophy and summoned by the abbots of neighboring communities, through pious rivalry, to direct their schools, he taught many both liberal studies and upright conduct: at Stavelot under Abbot Poppo; then at Verdun under Abbot Gualerannus, successor to Lord Richard [Note: [Col. 1349] One manuscript reads *successori*, “to the successor.”]; and finally at Mouzon under Abbot Rodulfus. We later saw many of his pupils become imitators and defenders of that same master, men of the highest probity.

Later, with permission from his abbot, Hugh of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 1350D] He died in 1053. The Annals of Lobbes state: “In the same year Deoduinus was at Rome”; see *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, VII, 150.], he attempted to go to Jerusalem [1053], but was prevented from crossing Pannonia. He turned aside to Rome, as though he were to sail across the Adriatic Sea, and there, contrary to expectation [Note: [Col. 1349] Martène supplied the word *spem*, “expectation”; it is absent in one manuscript. Another manuscript places *ibidemque* after *Deoduinus*.], found Bishop Deodignus of Liège in the church of Saint Peter, together with certain men known familiarly to him. At their urging—or rather, pressed by the bishop’s friendly prohibition against proceeding farther—he returned with them toward his homeland. On the journey back, the bishop perceived what knowledge, seriousness, and perfection he possessed [Note: [Col. 1349] One manuscript reads *perspectus*, “seen through” or “perceived.”] and honorably restored him to his monastery.

7. (11.) [See *Theoderic*, ch. 3.] Not long afterward, Emperor Henry ordered Bishop Deoduinus to procure for him a monk trained by Abbot Richard, whom he could appoint scholasticus at the monastery of Fulda. The bishop summoned Theoderic from the monastery of Lobbes [1055], having found him suitable for this purpose during the journey from Rome to Liège, and kept him with him as though he were about to be presented to the emperor.

Meanwhile, in accordance with the bishop’s order, the abbots and archdeacons were summoned to appoint a father for the church of Saint Hubert, which had been left without one. Theoderic himself came with the others, unaware of the appointment that was to be made for him [Note: [Col. 1351D] That is, suspecting nothing.]. When the bishop consulted them about who should be placed over the deserted church, a certain Godiscalcus, a man of honorable dignity, and Anselm, dean of Saint Lambert’s—whose authority in arranging such matters was especially strong—replied, after first conferring with the council, that such a provision would be entirely fitting for Brother Theoderic.

When the others applauded them for having judged rightly [Note: [Col. 1351] One manuscript reads *id*, “this.”], the bishop himself willingly agreed. Lord Theoderic was summoned, and the bishop began insistently urging him to become abbot. Theoderic, on the contrary, resisted with all the strength he could, pleading his inability and insufficiency, protesting that he was unequal to so great a burden, and even bearing witness with tears that his heart did not differ from his lips.

The bishop, however, pressed him to yield; the entire assembly urged him on, lest he appear to resist the divine call and will. At last, overcome by the authority of so many and forcibly brought forward by Gonzo, abbot of Florennes, and Stephen of Saint Lawrence, he accepted the charge entrusted to him. He was consecrated abbot on the Feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, ever-virgin, and then proceeded to the church entrusted to him accompanied by the aforementioned Stephen, abbot of Saint Lawrence.

When he saw its height from a distance, since the winter was then exceedingly harsh, he fell to the ground amid the snow and called upon God with a groan to be his helper. With his head covered and his feet bare, he continued on to the monastery.

8. (12.) Received by everyone with due favor, he strove rather to benefit the brothers than to preside over them, and to labor for the winning of souls more by example than by teaching. The brothers whom he found there were: Robert the elder; Ermenfridus, dean; Evrardus, precentor; Guillelmus, provost; Alfridus, treasurer; Lietbrandus, chamberlain; Lambertus, organist [Note: [Col. 1351D] This passage deserves particular attention, since organs were then extremely rare in monasteries. On this matter, see what we said in the commentary on chapter 19 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. M.]; Gualerannus, cellarer; Robertus, armarius; Stepelinus, external scholasticus [Note: [Col. 1351D] The external scholasticus was the person who directed the schools outside the monastery, or who instructed secular boys in the disciplines; the internal scholasticus instructed the monks. M.]; and the internal scholasticus, Balduinus, together with Lambertus, Guerizo, Engenulfus, Renuardus, Otto, and Gualterus.

Often opposed by those who, compelled to form new thoughts in an old mindset, nevertheless bore such adversity patiently and silently, he worked skillfully and steadfastly to nourish, educate, and even convert as many as he could. Among the many whom the same abbot taught from childhood to fear God, he nurtured Gislebertus, later dean of that church, diligent in writing and renewing books; Afridus, cellarer and custodian, later prior of the cell of Mirwart; Liebertus, the first prior of the cell of Bouillon, later provost of the greater church; and Arnulfus, chaplain. (*Life of Theoderic*, ch. 3.)

A certain Lambertus was excessively proud of his nobility. Although the abbot endured him as a particularly hostile man, he did not cease exhorting him to come to his senses [Note: [Col. 1351] One manuscript reads *resipiscente*, “when he came to his senses.”] and praying to God to give him a spirit of contrition. On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, when Lambertus was to read at the nocturnal vigils, he intended to pass before the abbot without bowing reverently. Suddenly he was terrified to see, between the abbot’s arms, a child of glorious appearance, rejoicing cheerfully with the abbot but angrily threatening Lambertus.

While Lambertus trembled and could scarcely remain at his reading, he returned and made the most humble bow to the abbot. To everyone’s amazement, he was so dissolved in tears that he could not cease sobbing and sighing. After the vigils he fell at the abbot’s feet, confessed his sins completely, and asked him to impose exile upon him as penance, to be endured by voluntary begging.

The abbot urged him to remain with him and promised to work with him in his penance. Lambertus replied that it did not seem useful for him, after regretting having lived with them, to wish henceforward to live with them [Note: [Col. 1351] One manuscript reads *nolle*, “not to wish.”], and that nothing more remained for him in that place, as though it were conscious of his error. Thus punishing himself with a salutary obstinacy, he bound himself with iron around his belly, arms, and legs [Note: [Col. 1351D] This was formerly the penance imposed upon those who had attacked close relatives with a sword: the penitent’s body was enclosed in a circle made from the same iron, and he was ordered to make pilgrimage to holy places until the iron circle broke of its own accord. Lambertus undertook this penance upon himself as a spiritual parricide. Martène. In the *Life of Theoderic* the story is not told in precisely the same way. Nevertheless, the whole passage seems to have been taken from it, and perhaps was inserted here incorrectly by the scribe, for immediately afterward the sentence that had previously been interrupted is continued.], and, with the abbot following him in tears, left the monastery.

At last, in great exhaustion, he reached Mouzon on foot. Since strict observance of the Rule flourished there at that time under Abbot Rodulfus, he was retained by him and stayed there. After persevering for almost two years in mourning and penance, he died.

By his example, certain of those who had remained at the place were moved to compunction, became more concerned for their salvation, and grew more submissive in obedience to the abbot.

Lambertus, whom divine grace raised from extreme poverty to great glory, was for a time precentor and scholasticus of that church; afterward, at the request of Raginoldus, bishop of Reims, and Abbot Henry, he became scholasticus of the church of Saint Remigius, as well as a cardinal [Note: [Col. 1352D] At the church of Saint Remigius, “cardinals” were the seven monks designated by the abbot who alone possessed the right and power to celebrate the principal Mass, by a privilege of Pope Leo IX, who dedicated the church. Martène. See below, ch. 46.], and dean.

He also nurtured Fulco, who became precentor after Lambertus, skilled in illuminating initials and carving wood and stone; Gozelinus, quick in literary knowledge and counsel but desirous of no earthly administration; Guiredus, provost of the cell of Ebernach, later appointed abbot of the church after Theoderic II; Stephanus, Remigius, and Rodulfus, outstanding in the study of writing; Gerardus, later provost of Ebernach after Guiredus; Quintinus and Heribrandus, exceedingly learned but exposed by Theoderic II to external duties too prematurely; Herbertus, a painter, overtaken by an untimely death, a matter greatly to be mourned; Guido, scholasticus and precentor, distinguished in knowledge and conduct; Fulcuinus and both Bernards, capable in ecclesiastical functions; Hugh of Macerias [Note: [Col. 1353D] Mezières, on the Meuse.], praiseworthy for nobility and simplicity; Helbertus of Liège, triumphant in arithmetic and music; Raginerus of Huy; Alsemannus; Gualterus; Godefridus; and Brother Benedictus, brother of Abbot Berengerus.

9. (13.) Under him the following men, who professed the monastic life, were converted: Albertus the priest, later provost of Ardennes [Note: [Col. 1353] One manuscript, corrected, reads *Arduennensis*, “of Ardennes.”]; Theodericus, likewise a very energetic man, provost of Condroz [Note: [Col. 1353D] Le Condroz.], and afterward abbot, appointed by Bishop Henry; and Lambertus, called “the Elder,” educated from childhood in that same church.

When he was already a young man, the marchioness Beatrice took him to Lombardy, where he studied philosophy for some time under Drogo of Parma. After the death of Marquis Boniface [1052], when he was returning to his homeland, the friendship of the same abbot drew him in, and he became a monk under him. How greatly his counsel and assistance benefited the church will scarcely seem credible to posterity in later times.

Under him Berengerus and Adalbero were converted; not long afterward each of them held the office of abbot [Note: [Col. 1353D] At Saint Lawrence in Liège and Saint Vincent in Laon.]. Then came Robertus, a canon of the church of Verdun, afterward provost of the cell of Chauvency [Note: [Col. 1353D] Compare R.]; Raginerus of Macerias, later provost of the cell of Pierrepont; Obertus the German, who administered Lesura for the church as long as he lived [Note: [Col. 1354D] Liser. R.], well born in that region; Everardus of Dion; Stephanus of Namur; Emmo; Alardus; Ebremundus; Guarnerus; and Dominicus of Huy; Fulcaudus of Mons, surnamed John the Apostle because of his good conduct; Fulcherus; Richerus and Gonterus, both of Portus [Note: [Col. 1354D] From the castle or district of Porcianum, Saint-Nicolas-à-Port in Lorraine. R.]; Arnulfus of Valenciennes; Almannus; Godefridus; and Adelo of Wavre [Note: [Col. 1354D] The land of Voivre, one of the four divisions of Luxembourg. R.].

10. (14.) Over all these men, serving God under the discipline of the Rule [Col. 1354A], the abbot presided like a commander skilled in military leadership [Note: [Col. 1354D] Similar matters are related in the *Life of Theoderic*, though the accounts do not entirely agree.]. He became all things to all of them [Note: [Col. 1353] That is, *is*, “he.”], adapting himself to each until Christ might be formed in them. He judged no one by fortune or social condition, but by conduct and religion.

Having been religiously trained from early youth and having lived modestly and chastely, he established for himself this continued manner of life: he would always eat only once a day, and then so sparingly that he remained continually hungry. He did this without eggs or cheese and without any seasoning of fat. During the appointed observances of Advent and Lent, he secretly afflicted himself with fasts of two or three days.

Besides the monastery’s common almsgiving, he fed twelve poor persons every day. After washing their feet and hands and providing them with a sufficient meal, he prostrated himself before them on the ground with great humility, as before Christ. He rested briefly upon a very cheap bed covered with a hair shirt; then he rose secretly and always anticipated the common vigils. Thus, with genuflections and tears, he sacrificed himself to God in prayer. (*Life of Theoderic*, ch. 3.)

One night, while anticipating the vigils according to his custom and devoting himself to prayer, the devil appeared to him in the likeness of a doe and began to disturb the focus of his prayer by stamping its feet. Believing that it truly was a doe, he rose indignantly to see whether the door of the cloister had carelessly been left open late, through which the doe, driven by its nocturnal wandering from the neighboring forest, might have entered.

The doe attacked him fiercely, at one moment going before him and at another following him, until both reached the cloister door [Col. 1354C], which was carefully barred. At last the abbot, stunned by the horror of the devil’s pursuit, raised his eyes to God and opposed to it the sign of the holy cross, saying: “Behold the cross of the Lord; flee, hostile forces.” The devil vanished with such a great din that the entire dormitory of the brothers, beneath which the aforesaid door stood, seemed to be torn from its foundations. (Chapter 4.)

Not long afterward, while he was weary from frequent genuflections and was praying prostrate before the high altar around midnight, suddenly an immense light shone from heaven throughout the entire church. With that light a dove of wondrous beauty appeared and began flying around, surveying every corner of the basilica. After it had cheerfully greeted each of the saints’ altars with joyful clapping of its wings and a certain sweetness of voice [Col. 1354D], it finally glided gently to the place where the venerable man lay and remained there until, when the vigils were sounded, it disappeared together with the withdrawn light.

The brothers who were keeping watch over the monastery saw this and, on the following day, reported it to the abbot as though he knew nothing, with amazement and joy. He rebuked them indignantly and ordered them not to tell anyone of it as long as he lived.

Besides the canonical hours, which he carefully rendered to God as his due, he sang vigils and all the hours of the day individually in honor of the blessed Trinity, the glorious ever-virgin Mary, the apostle Peter, and all the saints. He also recited the entire Psalter between night and day, either singing it himself or arranging for someone to sing it on his behalf.

It belongs to Him alone who weighs the hearts of all human beings to judge with what groans and what contrition of heart he stood at the daily solemn celebrations of Mass, about to offer sacrifice to the Lord. Every ecclesiastical dignity admired the humility of his clothing, the gravity of his walk, the evenness of his expression, and the propriety of his conduct; even the proud secular power, irreverent toward others, admired them. It magnificently praised his absence and humbly honored his presence.

11. (17.) Often summoned by the religious Anno, bishop of Cologne, he was received with affectionate reverence. Compelled to remain for some time in the closest familiarity with so great a man, he delighted in the mutual exchange of divine Scriptures, as though reclining upon Solomon’s golden couch spread in the midst of charity.

Once, in the course of their conversation, the abbot put it to the bishop in a friendly and cheerful spirit why he did not use his episcopal authority to restrain certain barbarians of his parish who lived beyond the Rhine from eating eggs, milk, and cheese during Lent. The bishop replied that he entirely approved, attested, and praised ecclesiastical abstinence and religion. But, he said, differences in food did not greatly harm those who were firm in the faith, since the Lord had fed Elijah in the desert through a raven—not with fish, but with meat. He had often prohibited this practice, but without success. He rejoiced greatly that they were willing to be called Christians, rather than driving those same barbarians away from the Christian faith by any form of force.

And because the abbot was dearer to the bishop in proportion as the latter recognized in him a greater capacity for honoring virtue, he never returned from him without gifts, which were entirely appropriate both to the giver and to the recipient. (*Life of Theoderic*, ch. 4.)

On one occasion the same abbot, drawn both by the grace of prayer and by affection for the bishop, was traveling to Cologne. He wished to lodge at the castle of Jülich, named after its founder Julius, and there, in the morning, proceeded to the church to celebrate Mass.

A certain woman was ill in that place. Entirely deprived of food, drink, and sleep, she was weary even of her relatives because she was still alive. During the night, while she was awake, a venerable person stood beside her and instructed her to be carried to the church in the morning, ask for blessed bread from the hand of the abbot who would celebrate Mass there, and trust that she would be healed through his prayers.

Her parents carried the sick woman to the church and petitioned the abbot on her behalf. The abbot, who was not accustomed to speak until he had completed the Psalter, resisted as far as he could by turning away and indicating through signs and gestures that this was not his concern. At last, overcome by the tears and prayers of those assembled, he blessed five hosts and placed them in the woman’s mouth. Immediately she recovered the ability to eat and was restored to health. The abbot, avoiding human praise, quickly fled and did not wish to pass through the same place again except secretly.

12. (19.) Whenever he appeared before Lord Adalbero, bishop of Metz, on matters concerning the church, the bishop afterward marveled, when recalling it, at the humility with which a man of such nobility and power bowed before him, and at the kindness with which he compelled him to sit and dine with him.

Once, during the meal, the first pears of the season were brought to the bishop. He began handling them, smelling them repeatedly, and putting them back on the table. As though under the pretext of some pleasure, he tortured himself by touching them without tasting them.

The abbot entirely abstained from them and divided them among the others. He carefully observed what the bishop had done and, when they were sitting alone together, humbly asked the reason for it. The bishop sighed deeply and groaned. Since he remembered that in his youth he had taken excessive pleasure in these things and had sinned, he replied that he had resolved to punish himself by abstaining from those very things through which he had sinned.

Edified by this example of abstinence, the abbot often rejoiced among his familiar companions that it had later benefited him greatly; and, so that he would not exceed the bounds through unlawful things, he steadfastly restrained himself even from lawful ones.

13. (20.) In the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1071 [Note: [Col. 1355] The words “in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1071” are written after *episcopus* in one manuscript. They seem to have entered the text from the margin.], Lord Helinandus, bishop of Laon, who delighted in the abbot’s friendship, advised and assisted him in building a cell in his bishopric, namely before Neufchâteau on the Aisne [Note: [Col. 1355D] Neufchâteau on the Aisne. The matter is mentioned more briefly in the *Life of Theoderic*, ch. 3, §37. Later, on October 15, 1082, Helinandus gave six of those altars to Saint Hubert; see the privilege in Martène and Durand, *Collectio Amplissima*, I, 501.].

It was at Eberneicourt, where the church of Saint Hubert had long possessed fifteen manses besides the demesne land. With the consent of his archdeacons Fulcardus and Ebalus and of the entire chapter of the church of Laon [Col. 1356D], the bishop granted for the use of the aforesaid cell the altar of the mother church of that village, substituting nine other altars for it: one at Brienne, one at Pugneicourt, one at Midiville, two between Provasy and Provasily, one at Guignicourt, two at Juvignicourt, and one at Ranlicourt.

He confirmed all these gifts in perpetuity to the church of Saint Hubert situated in the Ardennes, by duly ratified and binding privileges, excluding also the persons who held those altars [Note: [Col. 1357D] Brienne, Pugnicourt, Midiville, Provasy, Provasily, Guignicourt, Juvignicourt, Ranlicourt. The donation is reported by Bertholet, *History of Luxembourg*, III, 36. R.].

Not long afterward, the church of Laon was given a return for this donation by the church of Saint Hubert: namely, one volume containing the whole of the Old and New Testaments. Bishop Helinandus saw this library, newly written by Lord Gislebertus, when he was returning from Cologne with Josfridus, bishop of Paris, and turned aside to visit us. His clerics praised it, and he desired it; he obtained it as a gift for himself, as a token of special and perpetual friendship between the church of Laon and ours.

He had a kind of amusing [Note: [Col. 1357] One manuscript has *jocundi* superscribed, or *jocosi*, “amusing.”] event involving a miracle as the reason for turning aside to us. Abbot Theoderic had heard that both bishops were passing through Huy on their way to Cologne. He sent them a letter asking them to return by the church of Saint Hubert.

The letters were lost at the place called Mala Leuga, between Huy and Liège. When the bishops returned along the same road nearly twelve days later, a traveler presented them with the very letters, which he had just found there. Considering the event a miracle of the divine will, they did not dare in any way to disregard the abbot’s command.

When they arrived, the abbot welcomed them with a most ceremonious procession, detained them for two days, and abundantly refreshed them. During the meal, to the astonishment of those who saw it, he presented them with carp [Note: [Col. 1357] One manuscript reads *capris*, “goats”; the reading is *carpis*, “carp.”] and live fish.

Afterward, when they departed, he ordered them to be escorted at the church’s expense all the way to Mouzon. They gave thanks to God for the charity they had experienced and for the noble and venerable religious observance they had witnessed in that place—something they declared they would never have believed from those who told it, had they not tested it with their own eyes.

14. (22.) In the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1074, King Philip of the Franks, at the request of the same abbot, acknowledged and restored to its mother church, Saint Mary’s at Eberneicourt, all the chapels of Neufchâteau, which he then held. By a privilege of his authority, he confirmed those chapels, together with the aforesaid cell, for perpetual possession by the church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert.

15. (23.) In the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1068, the cell of Pierrepont came from the patrimony of Count Arnulf of Chiny [Note: [Col. 1357D] Chiny. The author of the *Life* calls him “the count of Warcq,” 3, 37, where he briefly touches upon these matters.].

Although he was young, he was nevertheless moved by the highest reputation and love of Abbot Theoderic, and also drawn by the fragrance of its excellent religious life to establish his burial there. He lawfully gave the aforesaid cell in perpetuity to the church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert, adding whatever right he possessed between Marbais and Fainon [Note: [Col. 1357D] Marbais and Fainon. The donation charter, undated, was published in *Collectio Amplissima*, I, 472, and in Miraeus, *Opera Diplomatica*, IV, 504.], as is more fully contained in the privilege drawn up for that donation.

The abbot, having granted an exchange of prebends to the clerics who had previously served there, substituted his own monks in the same place with the consent of Lord Manasses, bishop of Reims, on the eighth day before the Ides of that year [Note: [Col. 1357] The name of the month is missing.]. (*Life of Theoderic*, ch. 4.)

When the same abbot entered the church of Saint Hilary at cockcrow for the sake of prayer, it happened that a candle was kindled there by divine power, so that it might make clear that the Son of Light had arrived, before whose arrival heavenly light had shone there. [Note: [Col. 1357D] In the village of Pierrepont.]

16. (24.) The aforementioned Bishop Manasses, moved by his regard for the religious abbot and with the consent of the clerics of the church of Reims, gave to the church of Saint Hubert the altar of Saint Hilary at Guisliac, together with the chapel at Warcq, and also the altar of Saint Mary at Nouvion on the Meuse [Note: [Col. 1358D] Guillais, Warcq near Mézières, and Nouvion-sur-Meuse. The privilege was published by Martène and Durand, *Collectio Amplissima*, I, 499, dated 1079. But an earlier document must have existed, since the conclusion of the chapter shows that these events occurred before the time of Henry, bishop of Liège, who held the see from 1075 to 1091.].

Excluding forever the persons who held those altars, he confirmed his gift to the church of Saint Hubert by lawful privileges publicly drawn up and recognized in his councils.

Not long afterward it happened that Adeladis, the wife of Arnulf [Note: [Col. 1358D] Count of Chiny.], but the sister of Ebalus of Roussy [Note: [Col. 1358D] Roussy on the Aisne.], died and was buried at the entrance of the church toward the cloister. Manasses, the brother of that same Arnulf, was also compelled by a divine scourge to become a monk and died there less than a month later, where he was laid.

There were also four brothers—Hugh and Louis, Roderic and Riquinus—the sons of Richezo and Lieggarde, the paternal aunt of Count Arnulf. One of them, Riquinus, was killed by Heribrandus of Bouillon and buried at the head of the aforementioned Adeladis.

As a result, Arnulf and his nephews became more devoted to the place. The nephews, on behalf of their brother, gave the church whatever they possessed at Ligny and Carnière, as well as their fourth part of the bridge at Givet [Note: [Col. 1358D] Ligny, Carnière, and Givet. R.].
