Arnulf, besides the cell of Pierrepont, which, as stated, he had given to Saint Hubert, permanently remitted to the church certain exactions that the unjust officials of his predecessors had fraudulently and wrongfully imposed upon our property at Givet: namely, forty *modii* of oats according to our measure; one cartload of hay and another of straw, which were exacted to feed the count’s horse; fourteen sheaves from the demesne cultivation, seven of spelt and seven of oats, which were given to the lay assessors; and one *modius* of grain assigned to the steward.

When the bridge-men injured the church’s officials while transporting the tithe, violently taking the better sheaves for themselves, Count Arnulf, at the urging of Provost Theoderic, ordered them to come before the court of Saint Hubert. He had with him, from among his nobles, Riquinus and Algoldus, Theoderic and Albertus. After summoning the entire jurisdiction of Givet by a bannal summons, he adjured the oldest and best men, under oath to the fidelity they owed him, to tell him the truth about this custom.

After conferring together, they replied to the count through Provost Roderic and Steward Gobertus, exactly as they had been adjured: these exactions had been invented by the unjust officials of the lords and imposed upon the church unjustly and fraudulently. Therefore, in their judgment, if justice were observed, they ought by every means to be annulled [Note: [Col. 1359] One manuscript reads *omnino*, “entirely.”].

When the count heard this, he made Vido, chief of the lay assessors, carry on his own neck the sheaves taken from the demesne cultivation, in the sight of everyone, and return them to the granary of Saint Hubert.

There is a certain fishing weir, called a *radius*, in the Huia [Note: [Col. 1359D] The Houille, a tributary of the Meuse that rises above Gedinne. R.]. Whatever catch of fish was taken there from the ninth hour of Sunday night until the following day’s vespers is the church’s own property by ancient custom [Note: [Col. 1359D] That is, “property,” a manner of speaking frequently found in this work; see ch. 19 at the end and ch. 27 at the beginning.]. Whenever our steward secured the weir [Note: [Col. 1359D] “Closed” or “fastened.”], the count’s steward demanded his food allowance.

The count forbade, by bannal authority, that any of these injustices should ever again be exacted. He ordered the bridge-men to take one sheaf from each cartload of tithe that they transported; if anything less than a full cartload was involved, they were to receive half a sheaf [Note: [Col. 1359] One manuscript reads *illis*, “to them.”], according to the church official’s decision, and without any dispute.

Then, for these and other injustices [Note: [Col. 1359] One manuscript reads *justitiis*, “justices.”] which he acknowledged had been committed against the church either by himself or by his people, the count publicly confessed his guilt. Taking his son Otto with him, he came to the monastery and lawfully gave Flohimont [Note: [Col. 1359D] Flohimont. H.] to Saint Hubert, together with its household and mill, to be held permanently.

He placed his son’s right hand upon the high altar of Saint Peter and dictated to him an oath, which he himself swore aloud in the presence of certain of his nobles, confirming that everything he had donated to that church, as well as the unjust exactions and customs he had annulled, had been given and abolished by right.

Since we have once entered Givet in our account, it seems useful to inform posterity—although this interrupts the order of the narrative—what happened there in the time of Lord Henry, bishop.

Every tithe, wherever it might lie within the bannal boundaries of the whole of Givet, is known to have belonged from ancient times to the church of Saint Hubert. At the village of Feschaux [Note: [Col. 1360D] Feschaux. R.], however, after clearings had been cut in the forest, a fertile crop had grown there. Raguenus, the priest of that village, had secretly entered this crop, attempting to take the tithe of the clearings for himself. After carrying away twenty sheaves, Provost Theoderic arrived and, with the greatest indignation, firmly brought what remained of the tithe into the church’s granary. He ordered Raguenus to accompany him to the bishop’s court.

The older neighbors were summoned, and both men appeared before the bishop, who was staying at Saint Hubert. There, in his presence, the truth was established by the oath of truthful witnesses. By the judgment of Boso, the archdeacon, the priest Raguenus rendered public satisfaction to Abbot Theoderic; and, at the bishop’s command, he transported the tithe he had taken back in his own vehicle and replaced it with his own hands in the church’s granary.

17. (24.) The hundred-court jurisdiction of Anseromia was subject, though unjustly, to the county of Namur, and the church’s household was grievously oppressed by the violence of the viscounts. [Col. 1360B] William of Vierve, together with Herman and his brother Rudolph of Hontheye, came there on the appointed day to conduct the case concerning this exaction. [Note: Up to the words “remit it to the church,” these matters are also found among the *Miracles of Saint Hubert*, ch. 28; there I think they were added from our text.] Finding a pig in the manorial court, they ordered it killed and prepared for their supper. A very large fire was heaped beneath the boiling meat, but it could not be cooked in any way; and when the servants, as usual, tried it, the meat inflicted upon them its rawness and bloody horror. The lords, who were to dine, grew weary of waiting and ordered the meat, whatever its condition, to be served to them. But that supper was their last: William was seized by a demon and, carried back to Vierve in a litter, miserably expired; Herman and Rudolph, however, survived for some time in great pain before wasting away without repentance or recognition of God.

When these events had been proved, Count Albert of Namur, while staying in the Ardennes forest for the sake of hunting, turned aside with his wife Ida, formerly the wife of Duke Frederick [Note: Of Lorraine, who died in 1065.], out of reverence for the place, to the church of Saint Hubert. Abbot Theoderic obtained from them that they should permanently remit the county of Anseromia to the church (around 1066). [Col. 1360D] The remission was made, however, on this condition [Note: *conditio* in witness 1.]: that every year the provost of Anseromia should pay twenty *modii* of oats according to our measure to the county, while the steward of the village should collect from every household within that jurisdiction one *modius* of oats, to replace the aforesaid twenty *modii* in the manorial court. This condition was confirmed especially at the insistence of the villagers, who were being excessively burdened by the county’s exactions from outsiders.

At this same time [Note: This passage is absent in witnesses 1 and 1*.] William, count of the Normans, after conquering the English, became their king. So that he might not prove ungrateful for the honor bestowed upon him by God, he summoned religious teachers from all the monasteries throughout England and either established or reformed the order of perfect religion; and through public laws governing external administration [Note: *amministrationes* in witness 1.] he cultivated the dignity of civil life.

The same king, generous in gifts, once saw a certain knight fail to make an offering with the others during the solemnity of Easter. He summoned him and asked why he did not offer. When the man replied that he lacked anything he could offer, the king ordered one hundred pounds in coin to be brought to him. The knight received them in his cloak and, without holding anything back, offered all of them to God upon the altar. The king, amazed, together with the others standing by, at the faith of the offerer, returned to the knight whatever Easter gift had been brought to him there.

[Col. 1361A] When a certain Breton cleric, Marbod, was reclining at King William’s dinner, a silver vessel in the shape of a ship was brought for drinking [Note: *aurea*—“golden”—is written above *argentea*, “silver,” in witness 1. The words from *Britannico* through *psallere digne* are placed in witness 1 with their letter-signs transposed.]. While holding it in his hand, he pronounced this verse about it:

> This silver ship needs neither pitch nor nails.

When Bishop Hugh of Langres [Note: Also called Rainardus, 1065–1085.] was about to go to Jerusalem, he approached the same king to request assistance for the journey, and presented him with the following greeting, as a fitting compliment:

> If anyone looks ahead and surveys you, from you  
> He infers: formerly a count, now a king, he will be emperor.

This praise, expressed and commended with the approval of many, pleased the king; it would take too long to recount with how many and how great gifts he honored the bishop.

The same Hugh, having ordained a certain boy as an exorcist, was judged by Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Roman Church, to have acted too indiscreetly; the archbishop declared the ordination invalid and repeated the orders the boy had once received, conferring them anew by his own ordination. The bishop removed this insult through a biting jest and flung these witticisms in the archbishop’s face:

> If you know how to renew ancient orders like poems,  
> So that every hostile person prejudges me as guilty,  
> I now see that you can alter whatever I do;  
> But I grieve that I cannot even know what you are.  
>
> If love of ancient piety had held you back,  
> And you had not abandoned the servant who was yours,  
> You would not have had to act on behalf of an excellent boy,  
> Nor so deprive a bishop without judgment.  
> What was hidden? What was the reason? The order was useful:  
> Through me it was a fourth; through you it became a tenth on the ten-stringed instrument.  
>
> What is now a tenth will be able to tithe, and, most generously,  
> It will be able to confer three orders and chant worthily.

18. (26.) Count Gozilo of Bohania [Note: Béhogne, a dependency of the town of Rochefort, which was the chief place of the deanery of Bohania; Marloye. R.] violently broke into the manorial house at Marloye. Having abused whatever he found there for his own purposes, he allowed his retainers to plunder even the property belonging to the church’s household. While he prolonged the night after dinner with jokes and conversation, he was suddenly struck by divine vengeance and ended his life at twilight (1064).

His wife Ermentrude sent word through her nobles to Saint Hubert and the abbot that she humbly sought satisfaction for her husband’s offense, and requested that his body be buried there. On the advice of the brothers, the abbot consented both to the satisfaction and to the request. After Gozilo had been buried, he acquired by lawful donation for the church the allod of Summeium, together with its mother church and household, from his wife Ermentrude and from his sons Cono, Rudolph, Wido, and Henry [Note: The charter was published by Bertholet, *III, Preuves*, p. 29.].

At the same time the crown of eight towers was begun, as were the church in the meadow in honor of Saint Giles, the wall around the monastery—which had almost entirely collapsed through excessive age—the cloister, and the crypt.

19. (27.) Countess Adeladis of Arlon was the most noble daughter of Duke Theoderic and sister of Sigifrid [Note: Rather, of Frederick; she was the widow of Waleran, count of Arlon or Araeleon.], the father of Margravine Beatrice. One of her chamberlains was bitten and infected by a rabid dog. As his only remaining remedy for salvation, he fled to the protection of Saint Hubert. For, through the merits of the saint before God, that place possesses the singular privilege of proven efficacy that anyone infected by the bite of a rabid dog, wolf, or any mad animal, if he flees there and is cut according to its rite of incision and observes that rite [Note: This rite of incision still continues at Saint Hubert—*la taille*. Those bitten by a rabid animal, after confessing their sins to a priest and being refreshed by holy communion, receive a small incision made with an instrument in the forehead; a piece of Saint Hubert’s stole is inserted into the wound. The bitten person wears it for nine days, tied to the forehead with a linen cloth, while observing a prescribed way of life, and returns undoubtedly cured. The author of the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Hubert* also mentions this rite, chapter 14, in John Roberti. M.], undoubtedly escapes the danger of certain death.

To prove by an extraordinary example that what we say is true, we ourselves have seen in our own time two young men from the Hasbanian district who had been infected by a certain rabid dog. They were misled by a certain priest so that they would not flee to the merit of Saint Hubert. He promised them certainty of recovery through certain incantations and medicines; after receiving payment for this, he made them remain at home, while others who had been infected by the same dog fled to the church of Saint Hubert. When those others returned healthy, the aforesaid young men, tormented by madness and pain, began to rave—to howl like wolves and bark like dogs. They were scarcely brought to the monastery, and there they died, striking fear of the greatest horror into those who saw and heard them. But that is an extraordinary example.

Adeladis’s aforesaid chamberlain, having been cut according to the custom and having paid the head-payment [Note: The payment required from every person who underwent *la taille* and thereby obtained the title of pilgrim of Saint Hubert.], became a servant of the saint and was led to the morning Mass to receive communion. He observed the brothers standing in orderly and reverent fashion, their heads bowed and their eyes never lowered elsewhere; he admired their orderly devotion in making the offering and their composed dignity in going and returning. As a secular man, he saw in them something like an image of mortification. On returning to his lady, he reported to her what he had seen.

She immediately sent a message to the abbot and, with great entreaty, obtained that he come to her. When he came, he sent ahead a messenger to announce his arrival to the countess. On seeing the messenger, the woman, who possessed a manly spirit and, conscious of her own nobility, cared nothing for the rank or person of anyone of that time, rose quickly to meet the abbot. Her sons Fulco and Waleran were astonished at the reverence she showed toward this novelty. Supported by their arms, she went out to meet the abbot; and when he had come near enough for her to be heard, she honored him with a most humble greeting, bowing her head. After the prayer, when she could speak with him more freely, she said:

“I give thanks to you, venerable father, for I have heard so much of the religion of your sons and of the remarkably rare fragrance of the holy reputation of our time.”

As she recounted what her chamberlain had reported, and they took delight in the Lord for some time through mutual conversations of edification, she offered the abbot the church of the estate of Anslaro [Note: Anlier. R.] to be held perpetually for the use of the brothers. Her aforesaid sons praised and confirmed this gift.

The abbot, seeing a supply of large stones in the foundations of what had once been an old city, now reduced to the walls of a castle, requested—at the suggestion of Lambert the mayor—that she donate from those stones as much as would suffice for building the crypt or cloister. She willingly granted what was requested; moreover, she promised lodging and food for the church’s workmen for as long as they remained there.

The abbot gave thanks to almighty God, respectfully took leave of Adeladis and her sons, and returned to the monastery. Soon, having hired stonecutters from Liège, he brought the crypt and cloister to their present state. Columns from Arlon were transported there with their capitals and bases, as well as altar tables. He also enlarged the chapels on the right and left sides of the church. On the right he transferred the memorial of blessed Mary to the central altar of the new crypt and substituted there an altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. On the left he left the memorial of Saint Martin as it had been and built outside it a new chapel called “Holy Jerusalem,” because it contains an exact likeness of the Lord’s burial and resurrection.

He also illuminated the chapels he had built with splendid windows, employing a certain Roger from the city of Rheims, a very capable man who was highly skilled and exceptionally proficient in this art. He built an altar in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity at the feet of Saint Hubert, where he also deposited very great relics of the saints.

Not long afterward Bishop Henry, taking with him Bishop Franco of Belgrade [Note: I have found nowhere who this was. Bishops of Alba Maritima—Old Zara in Dalmatia—and of Alba Julia—Karlsburg in Transylvania—used that name; I do not know whether it was also used for Alba Regia, Stuhlweissenburg. Could this be Belgrade? See above, column 1245.], who at that time was staying with him at Liège, dedicated all these works with great glory and joy.

The aforesaid abbot also completed the golden panel before the high altar, which is in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. Abbot Albert had begun it earlier, intending to use a twenty-pound golden chalice that had remained there until then and had once been donated to Saint Hubert by Louis the Pious, son of the emperor Charlemagne.

Many more gifts—not only in silver and gold, but also ornaments woven with gold and books—had been bestowed upon that place by the aforesaid prince and by Bishop Gualcaud. The simplicity of those who lived there, or the recklessness of foreign abbots [Note: The abbots of Prüm are said at some times to have governed Andage.] or provosts, dissipated them, or an unrestrained license, shameless through abuse and greed, carried them away.

In our own time we ourselves saw certain men, whom we judged should not be named, burn many of those same gold-woven ornaments, ostensibly on the pretext that they were old and no longer worth preserving, but in reality because they sought to seize the gold from them.

What need is there to speak of the dispersal or sale of the books, when even the psalter written in gold, which had belonged to the emperor Louis himself and was marked at the beginning with his image, was sold at the city of Toul, as though it could be hidden there more securely in a foreign province?

Yet divine providence restored it to its own church in this way. The mother of Pope Leo IX [Note: Wibert calls her Heilewide; she is said to have been countess of Dasburg.] found it for sale and bought it. She gave it to her son, then called Bruno, so that he might learn the psalms from it. But although he read correctly and easily returned what he was learning in any other psalter, in that one he constantly made such mistakes that, overcome by excessive weariness, he seemed unable to continue reading.

For the Holy Spirit did not wish that boy—who was destined to become a chosen vessel—to be contaminated, even unknowingly, by contact with some sacrilege. When his mother wondered that her son was so opposed to the psalter, she heard through common report that it had belonged to the church of Saint Hubert and that its public recovery was being proclaimed under many anathemas throughout various regions. She did not delay long before hastening to the place, taking the boy with her. Humbly requesting absolution for her ignorance, she returned the psalter to the church.

As satisfaction, she also offered one book of sacraments, which was later given to the church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, which is Saint Hubert’s own church at Gabelium [Note: That is, its own church.].

20. (28.) The advocate, Thiebold, wanted to oppress the church’s household with certain new injustices. Because he could not overcome this resistance while the abbot opposed him manfully, he sought opportunities to avenge himself on the abbot. Accordingly, he approached the elder Duke Godfrey and insistently urged him to impose an unjust forced labor upon the men of Saint Hubert, requiring them to strengthen the rampart of his castle of Bouillon [Note: Thus in witness 1, but thereafter consistently *Buloniensis*.].

The duke, meanwhile, did not wish to disturb the abbot, whom he truly revered with humility, and so remained silent for the time being, until he came to the monastery and asked to be received there. He was honorably received and remained in the place for two days with the abbot. During their conversation, he reported Thiebold’s suggestion to the abbot, with Thiebold himself also present.

The abbot summoned Heribrand the elder, castellan, and Engo, Walter, Roderic, and Hugh. With Lambert the mayor explaining the ancient customs of the province, he carefully investigated the truth of the matter. With the testimony of the aforesaid nobles, he firmly established before the duke that the entire household of the church—scarcely sufficient to restore and maintain the services and fortifications of the monastery—was free from this exaction.

When Thiebold tried to resist the abbot, the duke understood his malice and, being a man of vehement temper, became gravely angry with him:

“This is your loyalty toward me, that you satisfy your wickedness and greed through my sin, while by your lie you provoke me to sin against God and against his household.”

Then, sitting as he customarily did in the hearing for administering public justice, he established this sentence by the counsel and testimony of his nobles and by lawful judgment. To ensure that it would never be removed by anyone, he confirmed that the entire household of the church should henceforth and forever be free from this exaction, whether it was owed or not owed.

21. (29.) In the year 1074, at about the same time, a dispute arose between the abbot and the advocates concerning the county of the abbey. In the presence of the same duke [Note: But he died on 21 December 1069. Therefore the year assigned here is incorrect.] and his son Godfrey, it was adjudicated wholly to the abbey and confirmed to it, to the church, and to its ministers, for them to use as they wished.

22. (30.) Three times each year, around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, the church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert is solemnly honored by offerings commonly called the Falmenian [Note: Famène, Palizeul, in the Ardennes. R.], Palatine, and Ardennian crosses.

Anyone who wishes to learn more fully by what necessities the people of the region were compelled to vow these customs to God and Saint Hubert, and by what proven consolations they established them lawfully for themselves as an enduring obligation, should reread the text of the miracles of the aforesaid patron [Note: Chapter 6, where they are said to have been instituted in 837.]. We know that these offerings were imposed there by an edict of Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, and by the synodal ban of Gualcaud, bishop of Liège; and that they were defined by fixed boundaries and confirmed by a lawful privilege.

In the year 1075, in our own time, Godiscalc, abbot of Hastière [Note: The monastery of Hastière on the Meuse, in the diocese of Liège and under Walcourt, to which it was subject; see Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, I, 343.], had deceitfully attempted to diminish the Palatium crosses. By bribing the village priests and seducing them, he had drawn to his own church, away from ours, Harnie, Gabelium, Wilerceias, both Bursivas, both Letires, Nevies, Gedina, and Granthes [Note: Hancar renders these names Harnie, Wileursie—whence another hand wrote Willerey—old and new Borsine, Loitte, Naomé, Gedine, and Grandhez. He adds: “Note. These villages are bound to pay annually cheeses and the obol commonly called *Priquette*. In addition to these villages, the following places in the same deanery of Gradensis are likewise bound: Palizeux, Villance, Maissey, Vencymont, Jehonville, Ochamps, Offaigne, Sansareux, with their dependencies; Bouillon, Noirfontaine, Crufoz, Briahan, Vcymont [sic], Bothasart, Belnaux with its dependencies, Fays-les-Veneurs, Assenoy, Graide, Rienne, Hoffays, Oisy, Gembre, Bièvre.”].

When Abbot Theoderic learned of this presumption, he took it very seriously and summoned him through Freduard, dean, to answer for it before the council of priests called at Graide [Note: Now Graide, west of Saint Hubert; it gave its name to the deanery of Gradensis, in which were the villages of Villance, Palizeul, and others.]. There, in the presence of Boso the archdeacon and Ernetbold, advocate of the altar, Godiscalc was convicted by judgment and amid the outcry of the entire council. He publicly acknowledged that what belonged to the church of Saint Hubert had belonged to it from ancient times. Rising before Abbot Theoderic, he handed him the pledge of justice through the sleeve of his tunic; as security for it, he was required to deposit ten pounds in pledges. From then on he ceased his presumption.

23. (32.) (A.D. 1069; cf. the *Annals of Berthold*.) Duke Godfrey fell ill in Italy and, having been brought back thence to Bouillon, when he had already despaired of his life, sent envoys to Abbot Theoderic and very humbly requested him to visit him. For the abbot did not readily leave the monastery, especially for the sake of any secular person. At last he went in to him; and when he saw a man formerly of such great power thus afflicted, he raised his eyes to God and said:

“You have humbled the proud man as one wounded.”

The duke, pierced by the abbot’s words, replied: “Dearest father, nothing is truer.” Breaking into tears and scarcely able to speak for sobbing, he made a pure confession to God before the abbot in expectation of death. Having made it, he ordered his sword brought to him and, with his son Godfrey standing by, amid unbroken groans of repentance presented it to the abbot, handing it over. He earnestly—indeed sorrowfully—called upon him to be his witness at God’s judgment of his renunciation of secular knighthood. [Col. 1366D–1367A] We have judged it better to leave to reflection than to relate how many tears that spectacle of such grief drew from the eyes of those standing around. For whose heart would not be softened, whose even inhuman feelings would not be moved, by the repentance, so devout and humble, of that man once so renowned: patrician of the city of Rome, prefect of Ancona, marquis of Pisa, lord of all Tuscany and Italy lying between, unconquered count of Verdun and duke of Lorraine, and for so many years Henry the emperor’s most strenuous adversary?

Not long afterward he ordered himself carried to the church of Saint Peter situated across the bridge, Abbot Theoderic, Gonzo of Florennes, Hermend of Verdun, his son Godfrey, and his nobles accompanying him. There he ordered an ivory casket brought to him, which had belonged to Marquis Boniface and was full of precious relics of saints. Among these were conspicuous a large portion of the Lord’s Cross and Pope John’s portable altar. Holding these in his hands before Saint Peter’s altar, he stood freely upon his feet without anyone’s support. Holding the aforesaid casket, he set forth in order that, by Pope Alexander’s decree, he had been separated from Margravine Beatrice; that, under the condition of that separation, he had vowed to God that he would establish a community of monks from the common possessions of both; and that the aforesaid pope had confirmed by a privilege of his authority those possessions, specified by the agreement of both, for assignment wherever the duke should choose. Since, weighed down by illness, he could not carry this out himself, he asked Abbot Theoderic to undertake on his behalf the task of fulfilling this vow.

Nearly all these possessions were held as fiefs by knights. Although they did not dare openly to oppose the duke’s ratification of them, they nevertheless murmured among themselves about it with the greatest indignation. The abbot perceived, from the cavils of those murmuring—and especially because in the very opposition of the duke’s son he discerned the image of filial affection already injured toward his father—that the duke was striving in vain for what he intended. Therefore, withdrawing farther away as though from the goal [Note: *ametando*, withdrawing, as if from a goal.], he replied that he could not carry out what the duke asked and that he should seek another whom he might appoint to manage his vows.

The duke was not unaware that the abbot was afraid. Bitterly calling his son, he reproached him for violating so shamelessly the rights of nature toward him, and for having so plainly shown himself degenerate that he failed his father’s welfare in this supreme necessity. He said that the son ought not make a spoil for his own crime of the few things which he destined for the redemption of his soul, when he left him very much, acquired through his own labor. When the son answered that he would in no respect fail his father’s will, the father said: “Come, give me a kiss on the condition that you keep this faith and promise, with your life and honor pledged as security.”

Thus, repeatedly called upon by both father and son, the abbot, believing the pledged undertaking which he had seen between them to be genuine, no longer hesitated to come at their summons, lest he seem, insofar as lay in him, in any way to have defrauded the sinner who trusted in him of the fruit of repentance.

As the abbot came nearer, the duke said: “Dearest father, through this casket”—and he handed it to him—“I entrust to you the care of this my devotion, that you may carry it out to the best of your power for the salvation of my soul.”

To his son he said: “To you I prescribe, under the faith owed and promised to your father, assistance, cooperation, and defense of this undertaking according to the admonition of this abbot.” He clasped the abbot’s right hand in his son’s right hand.

“I also assign in perpetuity to the monks to be established there this present church of Saint Peter the Apostle, which is my patrimony, and I confirm its mother church, Saltiacum Rivum, to their jurisdiction, utterly excluding the clerics who have hitherto held it. Besides the possessions which I have confirmed for this my devotion by the privilege and authority of Pope Alexander, with the agreement of my wife Beatrice, of you too, my dearest son, and of your betrothed Matilda, I have amassed from my movable goods a total of one thousand pounds in gold, silver, and various ornaments. I entrust these to your good faith, that they may advance the welfare of this church.”

The abbot, simple and upright as he was, believed that all these things, stipulated by the father and approved by the son, were settled. Without delay, he appointed to serve God there several very respectable members of his greater church: Alfred the custodian, Lambert the mayor, Liebert—afterward, under him, provost of that place—and Arnulf the chaplain. The duke was so comforted by their devout and honorable company that, although his illness constantly grew worse, whenever he heard the bells which marked the canonical hours according to monastic custom, he seemed to forget his illness and was refreshed by a certain cheerfulness of mind.

Meanwhile, wholly despairing of life, he resolved to have himself conveyed to Verdun, where he had once ordained that he should be buried in satisfaction, because he had set that city on fire in contempt of Emperor Henry [Note: A.D. 1047.]. On the day fixed for this journey, he first had himself carried to the church of Saint Peter [Note: At Bouillon.]. There, commending himself to its patronage and bidding a last tearful farewell to the abbot and brothers, he ordered his dinner prepared in the house of the common oven. When he had been brought there, with the abbot, his son, and many of his nobles following, and was set down before the oven at a place he himself had chosen, he said:

“I ought always to have been the manager of this workshop, if the divine favor had been willing to pardon me the many evils I have done.”

Having refreshed himself there with beggars who had gathered round him—for since he had begun to be ill he had wished to have no guests but the poor—he conveyed that very common oven workshop by lawful gift to Saint Peter, that it might forever serve the needs of the monks.

But, as with almost all his other acts, this was in vain. For when the abbot, as he had intended, had brought him to Verdun, his son lied to him, while he was still living there, about everything he had promised; forgetting mercy and truth, he brought harm upon his own life and honor. Once powerful through his paternal inheritance, he pretended not to remember what his father, in his presence and with his approval, had assigned for the redemption of his soul. Certain of his followers, truly faithless men, suggested to him, as though to curry favor, that he ought not lose the friendship of his knights, that his strength depended upon their hands, that his father had lost his senses at the end, and that he should attend to his own affairs rather than comply with the old man’s ravings.

Thus diverted from the resolve to preserve filial devotion, he craftily put off the abbot, who pressed him concerning the disposition of his father’s alms, for as long as his father lived. The latter survived nearly a month. At Verdun, thirteen days before the Kalends of January, the sky thundered terribly, and on the next day he died (A.D. 1069, 21 December).

Then at last the younger Godfrey showed what sort of man he was. When the abbot returned to him to arrange the dead father’s testament, he not only denied him counsel and help but even thought that he should be driven from him by threats and insults. Pressing him, he said that this affair was not for the present time; that it was not now expedient for him to establish a monastic community and postpone the military concerns of his duchy; and that the abbot should properly attend to what his father had entrusted to him, while he himself had other concerns to pursue.

The abbot was stunned by so great and sudden a change of circumstances and recoiled in indignation and horror from one so changed from what he had been, as from a monster. Yet lest he seem, after this refusal, to have failed in keeping his promised faith, he summoned Heribrand the elder and the other peers of the castle, whom he remembered had served the duke more faithfully, so that they might reason with Godfrey concerning his father’s business.

At last, overcome by shame, Godfrey answered that he neither wished nor could take away from the knights who held them as fiefs the specified possessions; but that he acknowledged and confirmed as his father’s alms Astinetum [Note: Assenoy and Givogne, near Sedan. Hancar.], with its ban, county, entire household, revenues, and the specified portion of Chevoni, as well as the common brew-house of the borough of Bouillon, since these were held of no fief. He said that he was willing to divide with the abbot, in their presence, the remaining treasure of his father’s movable goods; this should now suffice for the abbot, who should trouble him no further on these matters.

Urged by the others to accept in the meantime what was granted and not embitter a young man who might one day improve, the abbot yielded to their exhortations and, scarcely compelled, went with Godfrey to the chest to divide the treasure. Godfrey took from it seven hundred marks of silver in candlesticks, cups, small dishes, and various other utensils, and left the rest to the abbot, but on condition that he dispose of it with regard to Godfrey’s counsel.

On the advice, however, of Castellan Heribrand and his other faithful men, who urged him not so inhumanly to annul his father’s alms in addition to the aforesaid sum of silver, he assigned to the abbot and his successors Belle Vallée [Note: Belleveaux. R.], with its household, ban, all its boundaries, and acquisitions, for the use of the brothers serving God in the church of Saint Peter. This gift was held by them in peace for as long as Godfrey lived.

[Column 1370B] **24. (34.)** Not far from the greater church there was the royal estate of Caviniacus [Note: [Column 1369D] Chévigny. R.], from the inheritance of Countess Richeldis of Mons. After she had been widowed by Baldwin, the young count of Flanders (1070), she had lost Flanders when her son Arnulf was killed by his uncle Robert the Frisian (1071, February 22), by the hand of a certain Gerbod [Note: [Column 1369] Thus in manuscript 1.]. Not long afterward, Gerbod, troubled in conscience by so great an injustice and act of rashness, went to Rome and offered to Pope Gregory VII, as penance for that crime, the hands with which he had killed his lord, to be cut off. Gregory publicly entrusted the execution of this mutilation to his chief cook.

When Gerbod was brought out [Note: [Column 1369] Thus in manuscript 1.] for the punishment he had resolved to endure, the pope ordered the aforesaid officer [Column 1370C] to be recalled and secretly instructed him: if, after raising the sword, he in any way faltered while moving his hands, he was immediately to cut them off; but if Gerbod remained steadfast, he was to hold back the blow at once and spare him. Gerbod remained firm for the blow, and the executioner immediately presented him alive and unharmed to the pope. Rejoicing that Gerbod’s penance had turned out in this way, the pope judged that the hands which he had offered to be cut off were now no longer Gerbod’s but the Lord’s. He ordered him, on his return through Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to report the whole course of events to him and to place himself under his counsel. Gerbod went to the abbot, followed his exhortations, and later became renowned under him as an outstanding monk [Note: [Column 1370D] That Arnulf was killed by Gerbod, and the whole account of this is related in almost the same words by Gislebertus in the *Chronicle of Hainaut*, ed. Du Chasteler, pp. 6–7.].

The countess, however, in order to recover Flanders and avenge the killing of her son, summoned Philip, king of the Franks, Duke Godefrid himself, Count Albert of Namur, and many other princes of Lorraine and France against Robert, setting a stipulated price for each party to the agreement. The aforesaid abbot had long before been so familiar and beloved by both Baldwin and Richeldis that, often entreated by them, he stayed with them for some time in Flanders. Besides many gifts with which each of them honored him when he returned, he also deserved to obtain, by lawful donation, two allodial estates permanently granted to the church of Saint Hubert: Sulmodium [Note: [Column 1371D] Elsewhere *Smuz*. H.], quite close to the monastery, and Tavers in Hasbania [Note: [Column 1371D] The deed of donation was published by Foppens in Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* IV, 185, and by Martène and Durand, *Collectio amplissima* I, 487.].

Although the countess had been deprived of her former power, he nevertheless visited her repeatedly. Taking advantage of their former friendship and of the aforesaid agreement [Note: [Column 1371] Read *condictionis* (“of the agreement”) rather than *conductionis*.], she offered him the royal estate of Caviniacus, to be received in pledge through Lambert the mayor. The abbot was delighted that Caviniacus, which he had long desired to acquire for the church, was being offered to him. In the presence and with the consent of Duke Godefrid, he placed five hundred gold bezants from his father’s alms upon Caviniacus and accordingly, for the time being, accepted the same estate as a pledge in the presence of lawful witnesses—Segard, Arnulf, Gozuin, and Tietbold—[Column 1371B].

But when Richeldis had accomplished nothing despite so much expenditure, and when Philip, king of the Franks, had also been driven away by Robert the Frisian, she went to Lord Theoduin, bishop of Liège, and offered to him and to Saint Mary and Saint Lambert the castle of Mons, with all its dependent rights [Note: [Column 1371] The words *contradens* (“handing over”) seem to have dropped out.]. This purchase inflicted the churches of the bishopric with the greatest severity [Note: [Column 1371D] Gislebertus, p. 9, and Giles of the Golden Valley, chapter 3, have nearly the same words; the latter lists the losses of the greater church of Liège.], and also deprived our church for the most part. For the countess intended, with the bishop’s forces, to undertake some action against Robert, but she did not prevail. Nevertheless, she received the castle, with its appurtenances, back as a fief.

**25. (35.)** Meanwhile, a quarrel broke out between the abbot [Column 1371C] and the duke. The duke was entirely failing in the faith he had promised his father, while the abbot constantly demanded that he fulfill it by releasing the possessions he had pledged. Nor did the father’s curse fail—the curse which, as has been said, he laid upon his son at the point of death, imposing it under the condition of his son’s life and honor. For his wife Matilda, leaving him, returned to Lombardy. Although her husband repeatedly ordered her to return, she not only did not obey but told the messenger that he should come to her and bring her, as he would care for himself, the reliquary chest of her father Boniface.

Led astray by the hope of reconciling his wife to himself, he violently took from the abbot the aforesaid ivory chest containing the relics and brought it to Matilda, leaving behind, however, the altar that had belonged to Pope John [Column 1371D]. Yet even in this way he did not obtain marital favor from her. Rejected by her and unsuccessful, he returned from Italy to Lorraine. Aware that he had gravely offended the abbot by taking away the protection of the saints, and having himself gained nothing by it, he began, through a more cunning estrangement, to avoid more sharply the danger threatening him.

At last the abbot was forced to despair of him. Since he was a close friend of Lord Herimann, bishop of Metz, he arranged to go with him to Rome [Note: [Column 1371D] Compare *Life of Theoduin* IV, 47–49. There too he is said to have obtained from Gregory, while the pope was present, a privilege dated 1 May 1073. But in that year Gregory was elected on 22 April, and Easter Sunday fell on 31 March. Therefore, if the other details here are correctly reported, Theoderic left Rome before Gregory’s election. His journey must consequently be assigned to 1074, and perhaps the privilege as well. The year 1075 is excluded by the letter of Gregory mentioned shortly afterward.], wishing to consult Pope Gregory VII about the outcome of affairs and, on the way, to discuss the same matters with Marquess Beatrice (1074).

As they traveled, they were hastening to celebrate Easter in Rome, but, delayed by certain people who vied with one another in providing provisions for the bishop, they reached the port of Luna on Holy Thursday (April 17). There the envoy of Marquess Beatrice met them, bearing also requests from her daughter Matilda that they turn aside to Pisa and celebrate the approaching Easter with them. The bishop asked the abbot what he thought of this. He replied that he ought not to disregard the graciousness owed to so great a request, nor, when invited, delay going to meet them, since the business of visiting them concerned both of them.

Thus turning aside to Pisa, they were honorably received by mother and daughter and were regarded at that court as considerably more distinguished than the other courtiers. Seven bishops had gathered there to perform the Easter offices, and, setting all the others aside, the celebration of the Mass of the Lord’s Resurrection (1074, April 20) was assigned to Herimann, bishop of Metz. One could see, besides the manifold splendors of the crowds of secular people, a great gathering of clergy of various ranks, very many vessels of gold and silver for ecclesiastical service, and foreign garments of varied ceremonial dress; Beatrice and Matilda proceeded as though they were the governors [Column 1372C] of some dominion.

While the bishop celebrated Mass amid such pomp, the abbot hid himself in a corner. With his head covered, he devoted himself very humbly to psalmody with Lambert the elder and Lambert the younger. Matilda, looking around, noticed the abbot laboring in hiding and caring nothing for the display of such festive splendor. Assisting him in singing the psalms was Lord Anselm, appointed bishop of Lucca after Pope Alexander. He was an exceptionally religious man and, not long afterward, was taken by the Lord among the saints, his blessed death being accompanied by conspicuous miracles.

Matilda sent him to the abbot and ordered him to come up higher. When there was no seat available for the obedient man, Matilda rose and sent him her own seat, as it had been prepared, to the amazement of everyone, who wondered what person could possess such dignity in her eyes.

When he was to depart the next day (April 21), during the other conversations of their familiar association he complained to her that Godefrid had deceived him concerning his father’s alms [Note: [Column 1371] Something such as “or that something else was lacking” appears to be missing.]. She replied that on these matters he should consult the lord pope. To make it easier for him to obtain from the pope whatever he wished, she composed a letter of petition for him, which he was to deliver to the Apostolicus in Matilda’s name. She required him to return to her personally and report what happened to him.

Accordingly, he came to Rome with the bishop, presented Matilda’s letter to the Apostolicus, and, commended by it, was graciously received by him. After spending seven days in the City, during which the pope learned what kind of life and integrity he possessed, he became so beloved by the pope that one day, from the first hour, they sat alone together in the sacred chapel called Saint Lawrence [Note: [Column 1373D] In the Lateran palace.], where the heads of the apostles Peter and Paul are kept with the Lord’s sandals. They devoted themselves in friendly alternation to the divine utterances, continuing until night came on. Then, at the pope’s command, the armed prefect of the City escorted the abbot and his companions back to their lodging.

Among the other things that he requested from the pope as a favor of their intimacy, he also obtained a privilege of apostolic protection for his church, duly authorized. By the support and authority of the Roman Church, it was to remain forever in the monastic order with unshaken stability, and everything already given to it, or to be given in the future, was to remain firmly secured under an eternal anathema.

The pope subscribed this privilege, dictated by himself and publicly recognized and reread in the Lateran palace’s public consistory called *Ad speculum*, before many bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church, in his own hand:

> “Your mercies, Lord, are over all your works.”

When the abbot requested to be released from the promise he had exacted from Godefrid, because his son’s assistance was lacking for its fulfillment, the Apostolicus did not agree. Instead, he sent formally composed letters of apostolic authority to Anno, archbishop of Cologne, and Theoduin, bishop of Liège, so that they might either persuade Godefrid by counsel to fulfill what he had promised his dying father or compel him by ecclesiastical ministry, as one disobedient to it.

On his return, the abbot, as he had promised Matilda, thanked her for her recommendation and reported that everything had turned out for him according to her wishes before the pope. Although he was unwilling, she kept him with her for some time and honored him, as he was leaving, with a white chasuble that had belonged to Pope Leo IX and with a subdeacon’s tunic belonging to Pope Stephen, formerly called Frederick, who had been the brother of the elder Duke Godefrid [Column 1373D].

Nor was the favor of that court beneficial to our church only on this occasion. In the time of Pope Alexander II, when the same abbot, returning from Rome, turned aside to visit mother and daughter at Frassinoro [Note: [Column 1373D] Frassinoro, in the duchy of Modena.], where they had built a monastery for monks in the Apennine Alps, he was detained there for seven days and each day received from them a cloak as a gift. On the day of his departure they gave him a precious ivory chest containing relics of Claudius the martyr. He brought it back with him and, on the eve of the solemnity of Saint Hubert, carried it into the church in an honorable procession, while the responsory *Citizens of the Apostles* was sung. From that time, on the same day, together with the commemoration of Benignus, martyr of Dijon, he established, by the common consent of the community, that the feast of Claudius should also be celebrated.

**26. (36.)** After he had delivered to Theoduin, bishop of Liège, the pope’s letters sent to him concerning Godefrid, and had shortly afterward offered him, as though he were bringing good news, the Roman privilege that he had obtained through the bishop’s consent and commendation for the church of Saint Hubert, the archdeacon Boso took it from his hand. The bishop, already worn out by age, had entrusted all his affairs especially to Boso.

Boso had long been hostile to the abbot because he had sought, but failed to obtain, a prebend for a certain nephew of his, Nasania. He therefore sought more carefully an opportunity to avenge himself on the abbot after gathering his resentment. When the document had been unfolded, and Boso was offended by the unfamiliar characters in which privileges of Roman authority are written [Note: [Column 1373D] In Lombardic script.], he said:

> “There is no doubt that some deception lies hidden here, concealed by the barbarity of these characters.”

The word had scarcely left his mouth when the palace hounds, as though eager to please him, seized upon it, judging that the document had to be examined more carefully because its meaning seemed difficult and uncertain to read. At last, slowly scrutinizing the same characters, the men reputed among the clergy to be more perceptive discovered the matter as it truly was: the church of Saint Hubert had been especially committed to apostolic protection, and an eternal anathema had forbidden every person or power to presume to inflict damage or injury upon it, whether concerning possessions already acquired or those yet to be acquired. The monastic order was also to serve God there forever, free from every disturbance.

At this, Boso seized the opportunity to make an accusation. Shaking his head with sighs, and shouting in the indignation he had begun long before, he declared that Abbot Theoderic had utterly betrayed the abbey of Saint Hubert to the Roman pontiff; that the church of Liège had thereby incurred intolerable harm; and that, unless the bishop and his faithful men kept watch more carefully, nothing would remain to it of the great honor it had hitherto possessed.

The abbot understood that, out of private hatred, public hostility was being stirred up against him. Indignant that he was being accused against his conscience, he replied firmly that he had neither sought this malicious arrangement nor had the Apostolicus granted it. Let whichever men the church of Liège chose as its most trustworthy representatives come: he was ready to return to Rome and publicly prove there that the crime imputed to him was nothing. He stipulated only that, in accordance with the sacred canons, once he had cleared himself, the accusers should suffer the penalties for false accusation.

Boso foresaw that he would be caught in his own snare, and that he was finished if the abbot’s complaint were pursued at Rome [Note: [Column 1374D] This did in fact happen. In Letter II, 61, dated March 23, 1075, Gregory urges Theoduin no longer to trouble the abbot on account of that privilege: “It has become known to us,” he says, “that, on the advice of certain men, you have inflicted insults upon the abbot of Saint Hubert because of the privilege he received from us; but we excuse him, since he has done nothing against the welfare and honor of your church. Therefore we admonish and ask you to permit him to remain in peace and complete tranquility.”].

Accordingly, after consulting with his advisers, he said that he was not accustomed to Roman but to Liège judgment, and that no one was permitted to demand a hearing so suddenly unless he were being burdened by the judgment of his own bishop, especially that of his metropolitan. Although the bishop was old, he recognized that the abbot was being maliciously slandered. Nevertheless, so that he would not seem to pass over without investigation something believed harmful to the church, he appointed a day for its examination.

Keeping the privilege with him, he dismissed the abbot and summoned the other abbots of the bishopric, together with the archdeacons, to come on the appointed day. Meanwhile, Boso declaimed among the clergy and spread reports among the people about how great an evil the enemy had contrived against the holy man who had taken the abbey entrusted to him away from Saint Mary and Saint Lambert. As the abbot’s infamy circulated everywhere and was proclaimed as though it were true, he nevertheless knew within himself that his innocence was genuine. He was indignant, however, that the patience of a man deserving none of these things was being falsely burdened.

When the appointed day arrived and those summoned had assembled, the abbot himself also appeared with Provost Theoderic and both Lamberts, wholly confident in the truth. He brought with him a copy of the privilege to be examined, so that, since its slanderers had pretended that something monstrous was hidden in it beneath unfamiliar characters, it might become clear to everyone who wished to read it that it was written in the customary script.

The privilege was read aloud and reread, and the copy brought by the abbot was compared with it word for word. After prudent men had debated among themselves everything it contained, it was discovered that nothing had been taken away from the church of Liège and that the abbot had plotted nothing against it. Since the abbot’s case now depended not on Boso’s hatred but on the judgment of those summoned, the opinion of the greater and better men finally prevailed: it belonged to the Roman Church to judge all matters, and no one was permitted to reopen its judgments. The abbot was not to be blamed for securing the protection and assistance of apostolic authority for his church, since neither in meaning nor in wording had he excluded the due subjection of the church of Liège.

Indignant that his conjecture against the abbot had thus been weakened, Boso seized the privilege and withdrew from the midst of the assembly. Although the bishop and the others protested indignantly, asking why he wished to inflict such an injury on the abbot, Boso was compelled, whether he wished it or not, to return the privilege, which had been publicly commended and authenticated. The dispute ended, and the abbot departed acquitted. The credibility of the accusation brought against him had thus been emptied of substance, while the authority of Roman protection over our church had been confirmed.

This privilege is written on the preceding page, and is inserted here:

> **Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert, situated at Andage in the Ardennes, and to his successors who lawfully enter there, forever.**
>
> No member of the faithful is in doubt that the Apostolic See, because it is the universal mother and the prince of all churches, ought to preside over them all with rightful and dutiful care—not merely enclosing them within the unity of the Catholic religion, but also, by its general vigilance, preserving and defending them by its authority from whatever is promoted externally.
>
> Among these churches, however, many are found that, through a special and personal commendation, have entrusted themselves to the protection of that same Apostolic See, so that, embraced by the special affection and care of their mother, they might everywhere remain more secure and free from every attack. The Roman Church has received such churches as was fitting and has protected them everywhere with such great diligence that it has provided defenses of protection for all and has also granted some the favor of increasing their possessions.
>
> The holiest men who shone before us in that Apostolic See have left us very many examples of this. They were concerned for the honor and exaltation of the churches of God more than for their own life or safety: they received monasteries and venerable places under the protection of apostolic defense and confirmed them by their own privileges, so that, enjoying daily tranquility, they might advance more fervently in devotion to divine service and in every good work.
>
> The glory of those men shows us how piously and holily they acted in this matter, as does the fruitful grace of the matter itself. For when oratories remain in peace and tranquility, and ecclesiastical benefices nourish the poor of Christ, praise is then rightly offered to God, and remedies for sins are provided both to the living and to the dead.
>
> Therefore we, placed in that same Apostolic See not through our own merits but by divine grace, considering the duty of the office we have undertaken, have received the aforesaid monastery—which you, beloved son and aforementioned abbot, are recognized as governing—at your request under the protection of the Apostolic See, and under our defense and that of our successors. By the text of this present privilege we confirm and strengthen for it the church of Saint Mary situated above the Aisne [Note: [Column 1376D] At Eberneicourt.] and the church of Saint Sulpitius above the Meuse [Note: [Column 1376D] At Piren.], together with its other possessions, whether in villages, castles, or other churches, and whether cultivated or uncultivated lands, as well as all movable and immovable property that it now lawfully possesses [Note: [Column 1375] The surviving exemplar ends here.] or that, by God’s mercy, it may acquire in the future. Thus everything may always remain undisturbed and unimpaired for the common benefit of the brothers serving God there, under the rule and proper administration of you and your successors.
>
> If, however, any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed. Unless he restores whatever he has wickedly taken away or mourns it after performing worthy penance for his unlawful act, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ [Note: [Column 1377] Read “of God and of the Lord” (*Dei et domini*).], and let him be subjected at the final judgment to strict vengeance.
>
> But for all who preserve justice toward that place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.
>
> The lord pope himself subscribed in his own hand:
>
> > “Your mercies, Lord, are over all your works.”
>
> Farewell in good health. Given at the Lateran [Column 1377B] on an uncertain day of the Kalends of May [Note: The reading may be either I or III.], through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the first year of the pontificate of Gregory VII, pope, in the eleventh indiction.

**27. (38.)** Meanwhile, Godefrid was admonished by command of the pope, through both the bishop of Cologne and the bishop of Liège, to fulfill the truth and faith he had promised his father. Since he paid no attention to those who admonished or rebuked him, it happened that Lord Herimann, bishop of Metz, came to him at Bouillon.

It was the second Sunday of Advent, and, as was customary at that season, an exceptionally severe winter had spread everywhere. The duke received the bishop as befitted so great a prelate. After supper, while the bishop rested in the duke’s bedchamber and the duke slept on the other side of the same room, at the first cockcrow the brothers at Saint Peter’s [Column 1377C] rose for the vigils; Abbot Theoderic was then staying there with them.

The bishop was astonished to hear bells at such an hour and asked the duke what they were ringing for. The duke replied that the brothers at Saint Peter’s were rising for the vigils and that they had been established there through his father’s alms. At this the bishop sighed deeply and said:

> “Oh, how wretched we are, whom such vigils condemn while we lie resting amid such luxuries! Happy, by contrast, are those whom neither the torpor of midnight nor the terror of this most severe winter restrains from praising God, the creator of all. You too are more wretched than the most wretched, since neither fear of God nor love of your father has yet softened you—though you have defrauded him of his alms and have still withheld them from such devoted brothers!”

At this Godefrid, moved to repentance, burst into tears [Column 1377D]. Giving thanks for the bishop’s reasonable correction, he promised that from then on he would amend whatever he had neglected in this matter.

The next day both men summoned the abbot. When he arrived, the duke rose most courteously, and, before the bishop and some of his courtiers, offered the abbot, who expected nothing of the kind, a pledge of the humblest satisfaction on bended knee. He confessed that he had erred and sinned against God and his father, and declared that he would correct his error from then on.

The abbot was astonished and rejoiced in the Lord, who inclines the hearts of all human beings to whatever he wills. At the bishop’s urging, he restored to the duke the pledge he had offered him—the pledge consisting in the word of his father, who was still alive and had adjured him [Note: [Column 1377] Manuscript C reads *adjuverat* (“had helped”).], imposing the condition of his life and honor. Immediately, in compensation for what he had taken from the aforesaid treasure, the duke assigned Bellevaux to the abbot for the use of the brothers, and legally handed over to Saint Peter, to be possessed forever, the church of Montmédy [Note: [Column 1377D] Montmédy or Mairy.] together with three manses of land.

[Column 1378B] **28. (39.)** In the same year (1075, June 23), Theoduin, bishop of Liège, died. A dispute then arose among various powerful men over the conduct of the election; while several wished to become bishops, none of them succeeded in becoming bishop. For Duke Godefrid, who happened then to be staying with King Henry, had scarcely received the bare report that the bishop had died when he obtained from him, by his entreaties, that the grant of the bishopric should be given to no one except the man whom he himself should present to him. He immediately sent for Henry, archdeacon of Verdun [Note: [Column 1377] Giles adds: “his kinsman, a man most noble in life and birth, namely the son of Frederick, count of Toul.”], ordering him to come to him without any delay. Henry hastened to meet the duke, wholly uncertain what he wanted.

The people of Liège, however, since no election had yet been settled because of the aforesaid dispute, ordered Abbot Theoderic, somewhat tardily lest the delay in bringing the pontifical staff back should seem an affront to the king, to carry it back to him [Column 1378C]. Certain clerics, each getting ahead of the other, had meanwhile slipped into the court, each hoping either that the outcome would fall to himself or prepared, by way of reciprocal favor, to support another.

Meanwhile the duke informed the king that the cleric whom he had designated to receive the bishopric was present, and asked that the king, as befitted one making such a grant, should sit in judgment and, after summoning the people of Liège, appoint a bishop for them. When the people of Liège had been summoned, although they were secretly vexed that what they had hoped for had fallen to none of them, they nevertheless did not wish to seem to oppose the royal will, which carried greatest weight in the matter. On their counsel they charged Abbot Theoderic with announcing the election of Lord Henry. Standing with the others before the king, he was a man of polished urban manner and ready Latin eloquence, and said: “May God choose him; and we too have decreed that the man prechosen by Him shall be willingly chosen by us.”

**29. (41.)** Thus Lord Henry, having been granted the bishopric and favorably received into the city through the duke’s support, was not long afterward solemnly consecrated by Lord Anno, bishop of Cologne [Column 1379A]. Anno also adjured him, under the testimony of the blessing conferred upon him, to use his own words: “By the blessing of your father Anno, I adjure you to destroy the pride and insolence of Guolbodo.”

Guolbodo was abbot of the church of Saint Lawrence. Excessively confident in his glory and nobility [Note: [Column 1379] Giles inserts, “because he was exalting himself above the venerable”; the *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence* gives these words, chapter 43.], he conducted himself very differently from what befitted the monastic profession. The bishop did not long delay in correcting him by private admonitions. When he saw that he was making no progress and that Guolbodo, in indignation, was instead becoming still worse, he appointed a day for his public examination. When the abbots (October) and archdeacons had assembled, Guolbodo was unable to clear himself of the charges brought against him, and all his affairs were decreed to be in the bishop’s power and disposition [Column 1379B].

Lest, in hastening justice, he should seem to have set mercy aside, the bishop offered him a place and time for doing penance. He decreed that Guolbodo should withdraw for some time as a private person to Verdun, to Saint Agericus, and there, among the religious men recently gathered together [Note: [Column 1379D] A monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, founded by Rembert, bishop of Verdun, in 1037; hence the religious men are here said to have been recently gathered there. M.], demonstrate a satisfaction worthy of mercy. At first he agreed that he would submit to the judgment of wise men and to the episcopal decree; but after speaking privately with certain of his followers, he publicly refused to carry out what he had previously promised.

When the bishop demanded that judgment be passed upon this resistance and disobedience, the whole assembly decreed that he should acknowledge himself under his own sentence [Note: [Column 1379] That is, his sentence.], and that the bishop should freely dispose of the abbey as he pleased, since its abbot, convicted of crimes, would not obey him for his correction [Column 1379C]. Guolbodo lost no time in going to King Henry and attempted to defend himself against the bishop by the king’s violence. But in prostituting ecclesiastical justice to secular jurisdiction, he blocked for himself, according to the sacred canons, every avenue of restoration. Neither royal entreaties nor threats could induce the bishop to restore him; he declared that he would rather relinquish the bishopric for a time than endure such insolence without suitable satisfaction. Thus Guolbodo, in despair, went to Hungary; returning thence to the king while he was engaged in the Italian expedition, he remained with him until the death of Lord Henry, bishop.

[Column 1379D] **30. (42.)** After these things had been done at the synod of Liège, which is held on the feast of the apostles Simon and Jude [Note: [Column 1379D] The same account is in Giles, book I.], in the following Advent Lord Anno, the devout bishop, died at Cologne (December 4), to the great loss of that whole province [Note: [Column 1379D] “Province”; and he was buried in the monastery of Siegburg, which he had built at his own expense. Giles then turns to the events of Saint Trond. Compare the *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence*, chapter 44.], sending five marks of silver to our church as he lay dying [Column 1380A].

**31. (43.)** At the following solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, Duke Godefrid held his Christmas court with great splendor at Maastricht—certainly unhappy and far too heedless of himself, for this display of pomp was his last. Going down from there into Frisia, while staying at the castle of Vlaardingen, he was struck from behind in a secluded place by certain retainers of Robert, count of Flanders, and died (1076, February 27).

His death was indeed to be lamented, so ruinous was it for all Lorraine that justice and peace, which under him had prospered beyond the memory of those who lived in his time, failed with him when his loss soon came about. As he had directed while alive, his body was to be taken to Verdun for burial [Column 1380B]. When it was brought through Liège, Bishop Henry, deprived of so great a friend, went out to meet it in a procession of deepest grief with the clergy and people of the whole city; he ordered it to be carried in his own presence through each congregation, and, when it had been received, instituted the solemn celebration of Masses.

32. (44.) Then, having accompanied him as far as Vilance [Note: [Col. 1380D] Villance, two leagues from Saint-Hubert, where the remains of a feudal manor could still recently be seen. R.], he fell ill from excessive grief and could go no farther; he entrusted Theoderic the abbot with the task of escorting the body. He himself was carried to the church of Saint Hubert, where he remained until he recovered. He was there from the second Sunday of Lent until after the octave of Easter had been celebrated [Note: [Col. 1380D] That is, from 21 February to 3 April. But according to Lambert, Godefrid was killed on 26 February.]. For he was so delighted by the religious life of the brothers and by their proven sincere affection toward him that no suggestion from any of his men—whether clerics or princes—could prevail upon him to change his residence before the celebration of Easter.

At that time the younger Godefrid the marquis was staying with him. Deprived of his uncle’s assistance, he was under the protection of the same bishop. The bishop repeatedly reproached him concerning the allod of Telins, which the violence of the lord of Bouillon had long ago taken away from the church; he also said that he feared vengeance would overtake him for this injustice. On the advice and urging of his nobles, Godefrid yielded to the bishop and voluntarily acknowledged as belonging to Saint Hubert what was his own.

On the Sunday called Palm Sunday (20 March), after the solemn procession of the day, the two men, accompanied by their nobles, approached the high altar of Saint Peter the Apostle. The bishop held his pastoral staff, and Godefrid placed his right hand over the bishop’s right hand; together with him, he restored the aforesaid allod upon the altar without any dispute. The bishop also imposed upon himself the priestly stole and, lest anyone should again take it away from the church, forbade this under adjuration of the divine name and excommunicated the offender with the curse of eternal anathema. He absolved Godefrid, who humbly confessed his own fault and that of his predecessors; and, having publicly drawn up a charter of this acknowledgment, he confirmed it by his own assignment and by that of his men, who gave their assent.

On the following Thursday (24 March), at about the sixth hour, having prepared a seat for himself at the gates of the church, he reconciled to God with the greatest reverence and tears the penitents brought there from the bishopric, and restored them to the communion of the holy Church after they had been reconsigned to him through the hands of the archdeacons. Then, solemnly vested with the mitre and proceeding in episcopal fashion to celebrate Mass, he had chosen for the ecclesiastical ministry seven brothers from each order, while twelve priests in priestly vesture stood around him, awaiting the consecration of the sacred chrism during the canon itself.

At that time the religious community was so numerous that, even with these men removed from the convent for the performance of their duties, the conventual assembly did not seem diminished. The church possessed such an abundance of ornaments that each group proceeded in its order dressed in precious vestments. The bishop himself, setting aside his own vestments, put on a white chasuble that had belonged to Pope Leo and had been given, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1381D] Chapter 25], to Abbot Theoderic by Beatrice and Mathilda.

How devoutly he performed the Lord’s Passion and burial; with what eagerness, during the very Holy Saturday, he consecrated with his own mouth the fonts of holy baptism in the public procession of the brothers, while his archdeacons surrounded him; how, by his authority, he praised and approved this same privilege of the mother church; and with what glory and joy he celebrated the solemnity of Easter (27 March 1076)—all this, though it was recorded long ago, will scarcely seem credible to posterity.

Even the members of the episcopal household, leaving the city aside, were indignant that they had come to the bishop as though into a wilderness to visit him there; yet they were astonished that they found themselves diminished neither in the divine solemnities nor in the abundance of material provisions. The bishop also took pains to ensure that the religious order suffered no disturbance because of the presence of his household. Whenever he wished, for the sake of giving the brothers refreshment, to join them in reading or conversation, he dismissed his attendants at the very entrance of the cloister, shut the doors behind him, and, like a private man, joined those who respectfully rejoiced in his company.

33. (45.) When the middle of the feast had arrived, Herimannus, bishop of Metz, came to visit him. He was received by the bishop himself with an honorable procession, and seemed to have increased the joy of so great a solemnity. Since he had long been a very close friend of Abbot Theoderic, on the following day he presented himself quite cheerfully to the brothers’ assembly, saying that he wished to leave them some favor as a memorial of his visit.

Then, after common deliberation, Abbot Henry asked the bishop to permit him, with his consent, to dedicate to God the two altars that he had recently built. The bishop granting this, Lord Herimannus, on the Friday of Easter week (1 April), which fell on the Kalends of April, dedicated one chapel called “Holy Jerusalem,” because it had been constructed in the manner of the Lord’s tomb and represented its form for the devotion of the faithful. On the following Saturday he dedicated another, which was double: above it contained a memorial of Saint Nicholas, and below one of Saint Andrew the Apostle. The abbot had once built it especially so that the memory of the brothers might be commemorated there more particularly; their bodies had been transferred there from the cemetery that had been dug up to enlarge the crypt.

Although the abbot had decided to honor the bishop with prepared gifts for this favor bestowed upon the church, the bishop not only refused to accept anything from them but, on the contrary, offered to Saint Hubert his pontifical chasuble with stole and belt, two candlesticks, and a pallium.

34. (46.) When Easter week had ended and he was taking leave of the brothers as he departed, each of them began to weep on either side out of affection. Henry wept still more, as though he were being recalled from a rest he greatly desired to the manifold tumult of secular affairs.

35. (47.) A certain elderly man from Verdun, Eleutherius, was closely attached to him. He was indeed a religious man, and from the beginning of Henry’s life had instructed him in honorable and chaste conduct. Concerned for Henry’s salvation and honor, Eleutherius urged him more attentively to provide for the church of Saint Lawrence, which, having been without an abbot for some time, needed oversight.

While Eleutherius was staying with the bishop, he became familiar with the younger Lambert and with Berenger the prior. For a long time a bond of true charity in God had grown up between them, since their freely bestowed affection was independent of every necessity. When Eleutherius was often conversing with Lambert, the aforementioned abbey happened by chance to be mentioned. Eleutherius said that he had frequently discussed its administration with the bishop, and that the bishop was concerned but uncertain to whom he could suitably entrust it. Lambert replied that it ought best to be entrusted to Berenger, a wise man of tested virtue.

The moment he had seized upon the suggestion, Eleutherius gave thanks to the Lord and as soon as possible advised the bishop to ask Abbot Theoderic to lend him Berenger, whom he should meanwhile place over the church of Saint Lawrence as prior, until the passage of time provided him with a more certain decision concerning it. The bishop did not delay in asking for him. With difficulty he obtained him from the abbot, brought him in, and appointed him prior of the vacant church.

Berenger, being a discreet and prudent man, sought to arrange everything thoughtfully; he adapted himself to the character of each person, burdened no one as an importunate man, instructed the more serious by teaching and example, and meanwhile concealed the faults of the less serious with disciplinary patience, lest they be scandalized.

36. (48.) Not long afterward, when the feast of Saint Lambert arrived (17 September), the bishop announced to the abbots and archdeacons that they should give him their advice concerning the administration of the church of Saint Lawrence. They replied unanimously that the brothers of that congregation should be consulted and that a regular and legitimate election of an abbot should be offered to them.

The next day the bishop brought them with him to the place and commanded the brothers to elect an abbot for themselves. After deliberating, they elected Berenger with the unanimous consent of the abbots and archdeacons. The bishop rejoiced that their election agreed with his own desire and began strongly to urge Abbot Theoderic to release Berenger to him.

The abbot, however, objected that he neither wished nor was able to be deprived of such a man, and that Berenger was more suited to his own church than to another. The bishop scarcely obtained what he requested, even though the whole assembly supported him. At last, when Berenger had been brought before them, the bishop, despite the abbot’s long resistance, forcibly imposed the abbacy of Saint Lawrence upon him.
