In truth, this was arranged by the grace of God, which soon proved what it had arranged: through Berenger’s labor and ability, the congregation grew internally in excellent religious observance and externally acquired a manifold increase of ecclesiastical possessions.

37. (49.) [V. Theod. c. 4] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1076 [Note: [Col. 1383] Compare the Annals of Liège, 1076: Laub., and the Saxon Annalist, 1077.], an exceedingly severe winter set in. In Gaul it froze the very great rivers—the Arar, Rhône, Rhine, and Loire—and in Germany the Elbe, Vistula, and Danube; in Italy, the Eridanus—as for the lesser rivers, they may be left unmentioned—with such intense frost that, to the amazement of the inhabitants living nearby, they became passable as though across solid ground.

When this frost finally slackened in spring (1077), such dryness of the air followed that, with the fields parched, the harvest to come was almost despaired of. At that time Abbot Theoderic had gone to Rome during Lent for the sake of prayer. On his return, weary, he rested for some time in familiar surroundings at Saint Remigius in Reims.

When news of the arrival of so great a man had spread through the city, Manasses himself, then bishop of Reims, and nearly all the leading men of that metropolis came to him in supplication, asking that he give counsel to those despairing of the impending affliction and obtain through his prayers the help of divine consolation. Although unwilling, he was nevertheless overcome by the prayers of the supplicants and ordered a public assembly of the people to be held in the principal basilica of Saint Mary, ever-virgin, Mother of God.

During the solemn celebration of Mass he began a sermon and, in view of the danger, imposed upon everyone without distinction a continuous fast of one day, ordering them to give the poor what they withheld from themselves. The compassion of almighty God subsequently showed how deeply all had been moved by his exhortation—including the Jews themselves—and how eagerly they carried out the prescribed fast and almsgiving.

For on the following day, while the abbot was celebrating Mass, as soon as he had finished it, rain of such abundance and healthfulness burst forth that the fields everywhere became green again, and, by God’s grace, which bestowed what had long been despaired of, that year produced an exceedingly plentiful harvest.

38. (50.) At about the same time, a delegation from Elinand, bishop of Laon, came to Abbot Theoderic, asking that, if either he or the church entrusted to him could do anything, he grant them one of the brothers formed under his discipline, whom the bishop might appoint abbot of the church of Saint Vincent the Martyr.

The abbot altogether refused this. The bishop, however, demanded it again and again with increasing insistence. At last, after the matter had been reported for common consideration to the chapter, he brought Lord Adalbero to Laon by the unanimous election of the brothers and, in his presence, permitted him to be ordained abbot of the church of Saint Vincent.

39. (51.) To recall who this Adalbero was and where he came from: he was of noble Swabian lineage and a cleric of the church of Constance, learned in many fields. He had closely attached himself to the younger Duke Godefrid on his return from Italy; for as long as the duke lived, Adalbero was regarded by him as dearer than his dearest friends.

After Godefrid was killed, Adalbero joined the young Godefrid, whom his uncle, while still alive, had adopted as his heir. A most serious dispute arose between this Godefrid and Albert, count of Namur, over the castle of Bouillon. When the matter was discussed between them at Saint Hubert, Godefrid was present there, as was the cleric Adalbero.

Being perceptive in recognizing circumstances, Adalbero observed in the brothers an unremitting determination to carry out their religious discipline. He also saw clearly that, because of the very suitability of the place, it did not lack solitude for anyone who wished to serve God there. Moved by divine inspiration, he resolved within himself to reject the vanity of the world, which, being subject to so many contingencies, seemed durable to no one.

He therefore spoke with the abbot and arranged a day on which he would return to him entirely. After gathering together the possessions that were at hand, on the appointed day he prostrated himself in the chapter according to the custom of undertaking conversion. One could see no one able to restrain his tears when a young man who had enjoyed such great pleasures shortly before was suddenly so transformed and girded himself for contempt of the world that, of his own accord, he stripped off and cast away his most precious silk garments, together with his silk tunic. The golden rings pulled from his fingers and thrown upon the ground produced a clear ringing; and he himself could scarcely articulate his profession of conversion, so severely was he hindered by sobbing [Note: [Col. 1383] “Also” seems to have fallen out of the text.].

Not long afterward, as has been said, he was ordained abbot of the church of Saint Vincent at Laon-Chevresis. How much, with God’s help, he benefited that place is shown by the most noble religious community instituted and inwardly formed by him, as well as by the manifold external increase of its possessions and cells.

40. (52.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1081, in the fourth indiction, Abbot Theoderic summoned Bishop Henry to consecrate the crypt that he had built, and fixed the day of its consecration, namely, the Ides of January. The bishop gladly resolved to carry out what was requested. Accompanied by Franco, bishop of Bélograd, and by a very large company of his clerics and household, he came to the place on the Epiphany of the Lord.

If someone were to describe how great a gathering took place for the expectation of so great a solemnity—not only of relatives but also of outsiders, of both sexes and every age [Note: [Col. 1385] Something seems to have fallen out.]; with what devotion the aforesaid bishops acted; with what numbers and obedience the archdeacons of Liège attended; and with what lavish and manifold provisions the same consecration was celebrated, posterity would scarcely believe it, especially since, as the age degenerates, not only abundance but also the very integrity of morals and the ancient dignity of good conduct are everywhere failing.

41. (53.) At Calvitiacum there was a certain advocate named Albricus [Col. 1385B]. In exacting unlawful corvées [Note: [Col. 1385D] Corvée.] from the church’s household, he pressed them so severely that, while a poor man was plowing, one of his cows miscarried, and the poor man had to bear the yoke in its place for the entire day.

The abbot heard of this excessive and unjust exaction and was horrified by Albricus’s inhumanity. He hurried to Divum [Note: [Col. 1385D] Dun-sur-Meuse, five leagues from Montmédy. R.] and sought Adelo, explaining with considerable sorrow how his sub-advocate treated the church’s household, and declaring himself ready to prove that such forced labor was owed neither to him nor to anyone else.

Adelo was indignant against Albricus and was ashamed that he had done this. He fixed a day for the abbot to produce the requested proof. A certain Heribert, exceedingly faithful and upright, was then steward of Calvitiacum. On the appointed day, after giving lawful testimony under oath between the abbot and Adelo, he confirmed the same oath by judicial examination in water and proved that the advocates had imposed violent exactions, especially corvées that were wholly unjustly demanded of him.

Adelo of Die, Count Rainbald of Mussy [Note: [Col. 1386D] Mussy. R.], Peter of Mirowald, and many other nobles were present at this public proof. Done in the year of the incarnation of the Word 1081.

42. (54.) Not long afterward, Godefrid captured Count Theoderic, the son of Gerard the Fleming, who was also very close to King Henry and opposed the young man whenever he could. Godefrid had him taken to Bouillon and ordered that he be kept there with considerable liberality.

The younger Lambert, who was then provost of the church of Saint Peter, frequently visited the captive and served him in whatever ways he could. After remaining in that captivity for nearly half a year, Theoderic died there (1082). As he was dying, he instructed his relatives to carry him to Cologne. For he had long ago chosen burial for himself at Saint Gereon and had bestowed many of his possessions there.

Lambert, however, as he was always attentive to the interests of his mother church, arranged through Heribrand the castellan [Col. 1386A] and Tiebold that, by shortening the labor of so long a journey, Theoderic should be buried in the church of Saint Hubert. In gratitude for this, his sons Gerard and Gozwin legally granted to the church, to be held perpetually, six manses of allodial land at Brida [Note: [Col. 1386D] Brel. R.], which lies beneath Utrecht in the region of Taxandria. Done in the year of the incarnation of the Word 1082.

In that same year Bishop Henry rebuilt the castle of Mirvolt.

43. (55.) As the enmity between Albert of Namur and Godefrid of Bouillon increased, Albert secretly planned to rebuild the castle of Mirvolt for the war against Bouillon. When Bishop Henry discovered this—both because he favored Godefrid in every way and because he feared that the episcopal territory would thereby be harassed—he forestalled Albert’s intention.

From Richelde, countess of Mons, he purchased the mountain itself, together with the county, the ban, and its other dependencies, as well as two of her allods, namely Braz and Gruispont, with all their revenues and dependents, at an agreed price. In this way he rebuilt the castle at enormous expense.

When he assigned soldiers to it as though for the defense of the province, poverty compelled them to become public robbers. They harassed not only the poor of the villages but also the abbey of Saint Hubert itself with continual raids. This distressed Abbot Theoderic to the depths of his soul. He feared not only the danger threatening his own time but also that which would continue in the future. Frequently in person, and through whatever mediators he could, he entreated the bishop to dissolve so great an evil, which he had established for the destruction of the whole province, and to release him from the burden of such great fear.

He declared that he had labored in vain until then for the church of Saint Hubert, to which he would leave behind him a neighbor so close to certain desolation. The bishop was compelled to avoid inexorably offending so great a man, who pressed him so insistently and had long been held in such familiar friendship; he therefore sought somehow to lessen his grief and indignation. He legally transferred the castle, with all its dependencies, to the church for perpetual possession, and in the church of Saint Michael, which he had built and dedicated there, he installed brothers from the church of Saint Hubert. He also ordered that the abbot should hold the custody of the fortification that had been granted.

The abbot declared that he did not know how to guard a castle but a cloister. At last, overcome by his friends, and especially at the urging of the elder Lambert, lest they meanwhile provoke the anger of a powerful man, he accepted the appointed custody, stationing there faithful servants of the church.

44. (56.) At that time the marchioness Mathilda had added the abbey of Juvigny [Note: [Col. 1386D] Juvigny, between Stenay and Montmédy. R.] to the bishop of Verdun, so that [Note: [Col. 1385] Either “so that” should be deleted, or a word has fallen out.] Theoderic the bishop placed over it Galburga, a religious virgin whom he had forcibly drawn out of seclusion, though she resisted for a long time and with great determination.

When she found in that place a reliquary chest firmly fastened with iron chains, she sought through fasts and prayers to learn from the Lord what relics it contained. When it was divinely revealed to her that part of the body of Saint Benedict the abbot and of his sister, the virgin Scholastica, was contained there, she resolved to test the oracle more certainly and summoned Bishop Theoderic to the place so that the matter might be publicly examined.

The bishop appointed the opening for the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Not only neighboring people but also very many outsiders gathered in expectation. The younger Lambert was also present, sent by Bishop Henry and Abbot Theoderic to obtain relics of the saints.

With the assembly convened in an open field, the reliquary was opened there in the presence of the assembled people. Two heads were found—those, namely, of the aforementioned brother and sister—with bones of differing size. Some appeared to have masculine prominence, others feminine form.

The bishop tearfully displayed them for examination and then reverently replaced them. Solemn Masses were also celebrated in their honor. As a gift from the abbess, one joint of the finger of Saint Benedict and one tooth removed from the jaw of the virgin Scholastica came to this church [Note: [Col. 1387] Thus in two manuscripts; “uicna” in one.].

45. (57.) Meanwhile the bishop began frequently to visit the church of Saint Hubert, neglecting the episcopal residences, and to celebrate his Christmas courts and Easter festivities there. At the appropriate times he performed ecclesiastical offices there and lived familiarly with the brothers without any disturbance from his household.

The abbot sought by whatever services he could to please him and, while carrying out his duties, to test the bishop’s favor concerning the demolition of the castle. But the bishop cunningly evaded what was requested, sometimes replying that the matter had to be referred to the counsel of his nobles.

When the abbot, now weary, complained to the brothers that he was striving in vain, the whole congregation rose up in a great revolt against the bishop. He had imposed upon a church that had hitherto been completely free the intolerable yoke of this siege, like a great devil lying in wait for its sanctification.

Although they refrained from making this accusation to his face, they pressed it most sharply upon those whom they knew to be his principal men, so that, by reporting what had been said to them, they might either recall him to mercy or discover more certainly from him whether they should despair.

When his intimates, on the contrary, argued that a man of such power, who had until then been so friendly and humane toward them, should not be dishonored or provoked in this way, the younger Lambert, moved by zeal for his mother church, said: “When such friendship has brought us to this destruction [Note: [Col. 1387] Perhaps “end” should be read.], let it be despised with the same ease with which it is accepted.”

This remark was singled out above all the others. When it was reported to the bishop as a particular insult from the person who had spoken it, he seized the opportunity for what appeared to be a just outburst and began to rage and complain against the abbot and the brothers. He insisted that he had not deserved to be insulted in this way and that they should no longer be angry with him if, since his friendship had been wounded in this manner, he exercised hostility toward them.

The abbot understood that the bishop was willingly looking for pretexts so that he might refuse the requested demolition of the castle as though justly provoked. Forced to despair of the matter, he withdrew to France accompanied by both Lamberts.

While he was staying at the cell of Eberneicourt, Abbot Albero of Saint Vincent entreated him and obtained permission for the younger Lambert to remain with him. Not long afterward, when the bishop asked why he had been absent so long both from his place and from the bishop himself, Theoderic the provost, having been warned how to answer, replied that the abbot had decided to withdraw from him entirely. He no longer wished to preside over a place in which he could do no good; he grieved that he had lived so long as to see, while still alive, so many of his labors perish, while the castle he had fortified continued to stand.

Fearing both divine displeasure and the public disgrace arising from the departure of so great a man, the bishop ordered the provost to recall the abbot as soon as possible. He told him that he preferred to lose all the expense he had uselessly poured into the castle rather than offend God and provoke the abbot in such a way that he would depart; nevertheless, the matter could be undertaken at some time, with due regard to circumstances and reason.

At last the recalled abbot met the bishop at the castle itself. The bishop received him cheerfully and sat down with him. When the abbot complained that the bishop was pursuing and persecuting him excessively, he replied that nothing could be hurried enough for a mind eager for its desire. The bishop then promised him privately that the fulfillment of this desire would certainly be granted, although it could not yet suitably be done, lest the sudden overthrow of such great labor be attributed to his fickleness.

For the time being the abbot was comforted and remained silent, praying all the more earnestly that God would arrange a speedy fulfillment of what he awaited.

46. (58.) Lord Peter, venerable prior of the church of Saint Remigius, heard what had happened concerning the younger Lambert. He had formerly known that Lambert was staying with Lord Adalbero at Laon. Taking with him Thiebold, the cloister prior, and Humbert, the precentor, he advised Abbot Henry to send a delegation to Adalbero, asking that Lambert be lent to him and, since he needed a teacher, entrusting him with the direction of the schools.

The abbot, a man of great age and the highest integrity, did not delay. He sent Heribert, the succentor, instructing him first to ascertain Lambert’s mind: if Abbot Adalbero granted permission, would Lambert consent to come to Saint Remigius? Only then, with Lambert’s consent, was he to present the abbot with the letter of request written on his behalf.

When consulted according to the abbot’s command, Lambert replied that the matter was not within his own power; but, with Adalbero’s consent, he was ready to go wherever he was sent.

When the letter of supplication for Lambert had been delivered, Adalbero strongly objected to what was requested, asserting that he did not dare grant it without the will of Abbot Theoderic, who had entrusted Lambert to him on the understanding that he would return him to his own church.

Nevertheless, uncertain whether he should altogether reject the request of so important a church or return Lambert, who had been entrusted to him, to his own community, he asked for time to consider the matter and set a day for the messenger to return.

Meanwhile he began to sound out Lambert about what he preferred and urged him to free Adalbero from his fear by excusing him. Lambert persisted in his earlier response: that the decision did not belong to him, that Adalbero should command whatever he wished, and that Lambert was ready to obey him.

Adalbero then imposed upon him the condition that, if he were recalled by Abbot Theoderic, he should return to him as his man without excuse and place himself entirely at his disposal. He dismissed him, ordering him to return on the appointed day when the messenger from Saint Remigius came back for him.

Lambert was brought away honorably by God’s grace and received in a friendly manner. He was appointed teacher of the church’s schools, and not long afterward he was elected and installed as one of the seven cardinals of the high altar.

The dignity of this order had been established by a Roman privilege granted to that church by Lord Pope Leo when he dedicated it [Note: [Col. 1389D] In 1049. The privilege, dated 5 October, was published by Marlot, *History of Reims*, II, 107]. It provides that neither an archbishop, nor a bishop, nor any person of greater or lesser rank may celebrate Mass at that altar, except the archbishop of Reims and anyone to whom the abbot, not rashly but with the consent of the brothers, grants permission.

The seven cardinals appointed to this honor take precedence throughout the whole congregation by public election. Free from the other offices to which others are assigned in turn, they serve only the aforesaid altar. On feast days they use belts and have a procession consisting of three deacons, an equal number of subdeacons, and acolytes.

47. (59.) Everything that had happened concerning Lambert was heard at Saint Hubert. Abbot Theoderic had brought him away and entrusted him at Laon, as though to satisfy the bishop, who regarded Lambert as having insulted him by the careless remark previously made against him.

Everyone was indignant against Lambert, but the elder Lambert was more bitter than the others, because he thought that through the younger Lambert’s reckless simplicity this loss had come upon the church: a man nourished by [its own or his] resources was now serving the interests of another [Note: [Col. 1389] “His own or his” seems to have fallen out.]. The abbot therefore began to deliberate with himself whether he should order Adalbero to send Lambert back or seek Lambert for himself.

The dedication of the church of Ebernecourt was approaching; it takes place on Saint Martin’s Day [Col. 1389D]. When the abbot came there, he sent word to Lambert that he should meet him. Lambert heard the command at the third hour and came to him at the sixth hour with a delegation from the church of Saint Remigius.

The abbot rejoiced that Lambert had come to him so quickly, while some were put to shame who had asserted that he would not come, as though he were a rebel. When the abbot reproached him in person, saying that his mother church had not deserved from him that he should put it aside while serving the interests of others, Lambert replied that his accusers did not rightly understand his position.

“Wherever I may be,” he said, “I acknowledge myself entirely as a son of that church. And, so that you may know it more clearly, I have never until now lived according to my own judgment, nor do I wish to do so in the future. If you are pleased to test what you have already sufficiently tested, command authoritatively what you would have me do.”

At this the abbot looked around in astonishment at those sitting with him, because Lambert had so quickly and reasonably removed every accusation against himself. The delegation from Saint Remigius presented him with the following letter, expressing the same acknowledgment:

“To the venerable Abbot Theoderic, brother H. and the faithful congregation of Saint Remigius sends that which is salvation to the righteous from the Lord.

“In the true charity that we believe to be yours, brotherly confidence does not labor greatly to obtain what it asks. Let it therefore be the act of that same charity of yours to send Brother Lambert back to us with your favor.

“Nor should it be counted as a burden to you or to your church that what is proved to be an honor should be attributed to you; nor should it be reckoned a loss if a man nourished by your labor proves fit to serve in the archmonastery of the Apostle of the Franks, since in the judgment of the wise what is useful ought to yield to what is honorable.

“Farewell.”

At last, when the abbot had perceived that Lambert was prepared to obey him in everything, and also lest he offend a church of such dignity after it had made its request, he sent Lambert back to Saint Remigius with his favor. He himself also returned to his own monastery.

### 48. (62.)

Bishop Henry celebrated the approaching solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity at Saint-Hubert [Col. 1390C], where also, after completing the ordinations in the following Lent, he returned to Liège. [Note: [Col. 1389D] He celebrated it there in 1082, in the eighth year of his ordination; at that time he transferred the allod of Braz to Saint-Hubert by the lawful donation of Godfrey the duke and advocate of that same church, together with the ban, the thief, the court dues, and the pleas, but without the right of hunting. Miraei, *Opp. Dipl.* IV, 351; Martene, *Coll.* I, 517.]

But the abbot, who had long been troubled by the promise by which the bishop had agreed to demolish the castle for him, undertook to follow him to Liège, in order at last to learn the outcome of the matter. On Wednesday of Easter week, arriving at about the third hour at Tilleur, he heard from his men that the bishop was at Seraing [Note: [Col. 1390D] Tilleur and Seraing. R.]; he boarded a boat and came to him.

The bishop, standing at his own landing-place, recognized him from afar as he approached. When the abbot was already gliding toward the bank and the bishop called out to him by way of greeting, “The Lord has truly risen,” the abbot replied, “May he also appear to Henry today.”

The bishop received him kindly and led him into the chapel which he himself had built there with considerable elegance, admitting no one besides Provost Theoderic to the conference. After sitting for some time with his face and voice restrained, he raised his eyes, filled with tears, toward heaven and, turning to the abbot as though he were in agony, said:

“I know what you seek, dearest father; I know what you desire and what you fear for the future because of the wickedness that you see in the present age. So that this matter may not, as you often threaten, be counted against me before God, I today place at your will and power the castle which you wish to have demolished. I also legally transfer to your church, to possess forever, the mountain itself with its county and everything under its jurisdiction. In return for this exchange, I commit my whole self especially to you and your sons, to be commended by you to the Lord God.”

At once the abbot, weeping for joy, fell at his feet. The bishop lifted him up, himself bending his knee, and humbly reproved him for having done this.

The abbot did not delay. He sent Lambert the elder, whom he had left to guard the castle, a written account of the entire affair and commanded him under obedience to prepare, with whatever forces he could muster, to overthrow the height of Satan. The following morning, as soon as the letter had been delivered to him, Lambert mounted his horse and rode in every direction. By public levy he compelled everyone he could to assemble at the castle as quickly as possible. To prevent anyone from alleging an excuse for delay or evasion, he threateningly represented to each man, as though in anxious agitation, the urgent necessity of averting the impending danger, and threatened them with the loss of their property under the bishop’s ban unless they appeared to defend the fortification and strengthen the embankment.

A multitude of peasants was therefore roused, especially carpenters. At the ninth hour Lambert returned to the castle, and, first girding himself with the brothers who lived there, he climbed the tower and swore that he would not taste food until he had seen its summit thrown down. You would have seen the peasants, stirred by his example, rising eagerly as though avenging themselves upon the public enemy of the entire province: they rushed to the top of the tower, stripped away the roof with its beams, loosened the walls by breaking apart their joints, and utterly demolished the very ramparts and their defenses. With an immense crash of destruction, so much expense and so much labor collapsed within a short time.

On the following Friday, when the abbot was returning from the bishop, he looked toward the tower and did not see it where it had formerly been visible from afar. He raised his eyes to heaven, dismounted as quickly as possible, kissed the earth, and sang the *Te Deum laudamus* with the greatest devotion. When he reached the castle and found the bare embankment of the demolished tower before him, he raised his hand against it and said:

“May the power of almighty God dissolve you—the God who by his nod caused the walls of Jericho to fall.”

He did not desist until he had set aside twelve pounds of denarii for hiring workmen to level that same mound, in addition to those who had then been levied and assembled for the destruction of the castle.

### 49. (63.)

At about the same time, Countess Richeldis of Mons, returning from Rome, had decided to pass through her estate of Caviniacum. When Arnulf of Chiny learned of her journey, he pursued her and, in keeping with his bold wickedness, attempted to capture her. Escaping him with God’s help, she turned aside to the church of Saint-Hubert. There she was received with every courtesy by Abbot Theoderic and remained for a week, resting in the place.

Meanwhile, after carefully observing the brothers’ religious discipline and taking pleasure in the many services they cheerfully performed for her, she offered Caviniacum—which, as has been said, she had pledged to the abbot—to the church for outright purchase. Since this pleased the abbot and the entire congregation, by common agreement a day was appointed for carrying out the purchase, before the bishop at the castle of Fosses. The abbot also secured Count Albert for her; he escorted her back and placed her under his protection.

After collecting whatever silver could be found in the church, the abbot brought eighty marks with him to Fosses. Lambert the elder and Provost Theoderic had procured another three hundred, depositing pledges with the merchants and clerics of Liège. When Countess Richilde arrived with her son Baldwin, the agreement concerning Caviniacum was renewed before the bishop and Duke Godfrey. The bishop reduced the purchase price to three hundred marks, in addition to the seven hundred which the abbot had formerly added to the pledge. The mother and son then legally transferred the estate forever to the churches of Saint Peter and Saint-Hubert, by the turf and branch of that same allod, into the hands of the bishop, the abbot, and Duke Godfrey, the church’s advocate. In a public hearing each of them solemnly renounced all claim to it, both for himself and for his heirs. [Note: [Col. 1391D] Cf. Gislebert, *Chronicon Hanoniense*, p. 37.]

When the bishop saw that twenty marks were lacking for payment of the silver, he deposited with the countess two of his own candlesticks of that weight. Later, moved by love for the church, he redeemed them from his own resources. After the charter of this purchase had been drawn up and confirmed publicly in the presence of the bishop and the duke and had been authenticated by suitable witnesses, the abbot returned happily to the church. Receiving the lawful investiture through the hand of the duke, he seized Caviniacum in its entirety upon the altar of Saint Peter, together with its household, all its acquisitions and appurtenances, to be retained forever by the church as its own property, without any contradiction.

### 50. (64.)

Later, recalled by the bishop, the abbot came to Huy. He was retained there for some time by the bishop out of affection. When he was preparing to return, he suggested to the bishop that the church of Saint-Hubert possessed two mills near that town, and that it would be fitting for his grace to grant the monastery a site on which to build a third.

The bishop willingly consented. Summoning the officials and judges of the town, he mounted his horse and, at the abbot’s request, marked out an excellent site for a mill on the Hoyoux. He confirmed it by lawful gift, to be possessed by the church forever.

At that time Boso was archdeacon and abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Huy; Lambert, his nephew, was administrator and judge of public jurisdiction; and Dodo was steward of the episcopal table.

### 51. (65.)

To Braz and Gruispont, which he had formerly donated to the church in perpetuity [Note: [Col. 1393C] The first was in 1082, but Grupont only in 1087; see above, col. 1386, chapter 43.], he also added the portion of Arsia that belonged to his jurisdiction, from the allods that had belonged to Countess Richeldis. And, lest anyone should thereafter alter or remove these gifts of his, he condemned such an act with eternal anathema.

Cono of Hamerina takes this portion of Arsia from the church by force and unjustly.

### 52. (66.)

The mother church of Saint Monon the martyr at Nassogne [Note: [Col. 1393] “Vasanie” in witness 1.] had been given by Bishop Gualcaud [Note: [Col. 1393] “Gualco” in witness 1.] to the ancient church of Saint-Hubert with everything belonging to it, under the latter’s governing authority.

Although its clerics received prebends from the abbot, and this with the consent and approval of the brothers, and although the service owed in honor had been agreed upon and paid, they nevertheless thereafter insolently refused to submit to the abbot’s jurisdiction except in clerical councils under episcopal discipline.

At the abbot’s request, the bishop also abolished this insolence. Declaring the altar of that church free, he remitted forever to the church of Saint Peter and Saint-Hubert all episcopal and archidiaconal exactions and jurisdictions, with Archdeacon Boso present and joining him in the concession. He also authorized the same remission by a legally executed privilege.

But, to speak of the matter—not in reproach, but in compassion—for the peace of his blessed soul and holy memory, Theoderic and Lambert so dominated his simplicity that he trusted them completely in everything and, as though consulting God, listened to those same men as his advisers. Trusting these stewards, he was able to be more inwardly vigilant the more securely he slept regarding external matters.

Yet, since there is little difference in the fault between being able to deceive and being deceived, he mixed a very damaging crime into his glory: through their miserable persuasion, he imprudently allowed himself to be led astray. For whenever they wished, either through the favor of kinship or because of a payment received, to enfeoff someone newly [Note: [Col. 1393] That is, “to assign feudal holdings to him”; witness 1 reads *cassare*.], they did not hesitate to persuade the abbot to do this from the brothers’ prebend without their consent, and he did not delay obeying their persuasion.

In this way the church lost Vineias and Lesterneias from its ancient possessions, and, from acquisitions newly made by the same abbot, Sulmodium nearby and Tavers in Hesbaye.

### 53. (67.)

In the year of the Lord 1086 [1087], but in the thirty-second year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1393C] These statements appear mutually consistent, but the Laubach Annals and the author of the *Life* support the year 1087. The latter reports that he died before completing his eightieth year, having been born in 1007, on November 11. The charter of Gruispont also supports this, since it appears to have been issued while he was alive. On the other hand, Theoderic II is named in the donation of Raginoldus in Martene and Durand I, 519, issued in 1086, in the tenth indiction, the twenty-sixth year of Philip, and the third of Rainoldus. But Rainoldus reckoned the seventh year of his ordination in 1091 (*Gallia Christiana* X, 31), and the tenth indiction agrees with the year 1087.], Abbot Theoderic, exhausted not only by old age but also by fasts, prayers, vigils, and by the labors and cares of the pastoral office entrusted to him, began to fail in bodily strength, slight though it was, around the month of July. He therefore decided to withdraw to Piros for a little rest.

There, as he gradually felt his illness grow heavier and press him toward death, he ordered Provost Theoderic, who was staying there with him [Note: [Col. 1393] *secum* in witness 1: “there with him.”], to hasten his return to the monastery. He quickly sent messengers bearing letters—whether requests or admonitions, as seemed appropriate—to Adalbero, abbot of Laon; Guirede, provost of Épernay; Lambert, prior of Saint-Remi; Berenger, abbot of Saint-Laurent; and Henry himself, bishop of Liège [Col. 1394B]. He humbly begged them to come to him as quickly as possible and bid a final farewell to one who was dying.

When he had been carried from the cell to the opposite bank of the Meuse and was giving thanks to God, as though now nearer to the monastery for which he longed, Lambert the elder met him with equipment suitable for transporting him. On the following day, as he approached the monastery at about the ninth hour, he turned aside above the river Lomme, into a meadow in the surrounding forest, so that no popular lamentation or disturbance would arise on his account.

Thus avoiding the expectation of the people, he was received during the first watch of Sunday night [Note: [Col. 1394C] Sunday was August 22. According to the author of the *Life*, he arrived in the morning and died four days later, namely August 25, although the Alna manuscript there reads “the ninth day before the Kalends of September.” The eighth day before the Kalends of September is supported by the necrology of Saint-Maximin. Honth., *Prodromus*, p. 985, and the Stavelot Missal, manuscript.] amid the greatest sorrow of the brothers.

Very early in the morning the bishop arrived with Abbot Berenger. When they entered to see him, Theoderic, gathering his strength and sitting on his bed, gave thanks to God. After the stole had been placed upon him, he absolved his brothers, both those present and those absent, and commended them to divine mercy. Finally, according to ecclesiastical custom, he humbly offered himself to the bishop to be reconciled to God.

When all this had been completed at about the third hour, he thereafter devoted himself to silence and divine contemplation. At the same hour on the following day he departed to God, in the year 1087, on August 25.

As soon as his death had become known, Godfrey of Bouillon, Albert of Namur, Arnulf of Chiny, and Cono of Montaigu [Note: [Col. 1394C] Montaigu between Liège and Huy.] hastened together to the funeral of so great a man, along with courtiers [Note: [Col. 1393] Thus in witness 2; witness 1 has *qui*.] mingling indiscriminately with the common people, all lamenting together as though they had lost the father of their country [Note: [Col. 1393] Witness 1 reads *conquirentes*.].

After he had been watched over for two days, with solemn celebration of Masses and continuous chanting of psalms, he was finally buried on the third day [Note: [Col. 1394C] It was an ancient custom for abbots to be given burial only on the third day after their death, as we demonstrated in Book V, chapter 12, no. 6, of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*. MART.] in the new crypt which he had built in honor of blessed and glorious Mary, ever-virgin [Col. 1395A].

When the bishop could scarcely complete the funeral rites, his voice being interrupted by tears and groans, it will seem incredible to later generations how all the people roused themselves to such lamentation and how, with such cries, they collectively gave expression to their grief.

### 54. (68.)

After he had at last been buried, the bishop offered the brothers the choice of an abbot, declaring that he would not withdraw until he had appointed a father in place of the deceased. The election of the brothers, the testimony of the courtiers, and the acclamation of the people all converged upon one decision: that the abbacy should be given to Provost Theoderic.

Although he appeared to resist and admitted that he was not suited to so great an elevation, the favor of everyone, once aroused, grew so strong [Note: [Col. 1395] *clamor* is superscribed, or *favor* in witness 1.] that even the bishop could no longer reconsider the matter.

When the abbacy had been bestowed, he shook his head [Note: [Col. 1395] *quassabat* may perhaps be the reading.] and told his intimates, with great astonishment, that he feared the outcry of such favor would in the future prove to be a sign of some evil portent. Nor did the outcome disprove this statement; as will be related in its proper place, what he feared happened in due course.

Theoderic then escorted the departing bishop and was consecrated abbot by him according to custom. On the Kalends of September he was joyfully received by the brothers, who came out to meet him.

For, as someone says [Note: [Col. 1395D] Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 2.], “Authority is difficult to retain unless it is retained by the same arts by which it is acquired.” Still inexperienced in pastoral care, since until then he had been accustomed to the administration of external affairs, Theoderic at last remembered who he had been and what the office he had assumed now compelled him to become. He clearly found himself too unequal to the burden imposed upon him. He who had previously seemed to stand firmly on level ground began, once his foot had been set upon a precipice, to stagger gravely within himself.

Unable to master himself, he tried as best he could to follow in the footsteps of his predecessor, but he could in no way equal him. Gradually relaxing the strictness of discipline by which his predecessor had chiefly flourished to his glory, and bending too far toward everyone as though out of kindness, he soon fell into contempt through excessive familiarity.

Finally, wishing to be loved out of benevolence by those by whom, through reverence for his office, he ought to have been feared, he indiscriminately and imprudently promised everyone things they might hope for but which he could not grant [Note: [Col. 1395] That is, *dum promitteret speranda quae...* in witness 1.]. In this way he made even his old friends gratuitously hostile to him. “It is a very great part of a benefit quickly to refuse what ought not to be given” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II, 7), and a friend must be treated in such a way that he is thought capable of becoming an enemy.

Thus, when frequent disagreement arose between him and those entrusted to him, their mutual indignation burst out to such an extent that, as private hatred grew among them, the greatest public confusion of the church itself subsequently increased. But for the present, this must be left aside.

### 55. (69.)

The bishop, concerned for the place out of his ancient pious custom, heard from certain people what was taking place between the abbot and the brothers. Feigning ignorance of what he had heard, he hoped that the matter would be corrected either by time or by reason; but when this did not happen, he was indignant with himself over such an appointment and, in deep sorrow, said:

“Behold, what I feared has happened; behold how unhappy an outcome has arisen from such joyful beginnings!”

Nevertheless, he did not cease to revisit the place frequently, correct the brothers, take the greatest care that the church’s possessions should not be diminished, and support the abbot with his counsel and assistance whenever he found him less than adequate.

Refreshed by the bishop’s lively diligence, the abbot began to be more steadfast in the matters he had undertaken to manage, despite the defect that weighed upon him inwardly. Matters which he had previously found wearisome under a kind of lassitude because they were unfamiliar, he now attended to; and he not only retained what belonged to the church but also worked industriously to acquire certain things.

### 56. (70.)

A certain nobleman, Sigefridus, and his wife agreed to visit the church of Saint-Hubert for the sake of prayer. The abbot received them honorably and kept them there for three days. Moved by the goodwill shown to them, they offered the church the allod of Moroldiheis [Note: [Col. 1396D] Morhez. II.], which belonged to them, partly as a free gift and partly to be purchased from them.

The abbot rejoiced that he had found an opportunity for this acquisition. Before they departed, he weighed out twelve marks of silver for the man and his wife, and legally obtained the aforesaid possession, donated to the church forever together with its household and all its appurtenances.

### 57. (71.)

Stephen, castellan of Montaigu, had been enfeoffed to the church, having no heir among his sons or daughters. Since his nephews coveted his inheritance, the abbot redeemed from Stephen the feudal holding that belonged to the church and, five years before Stephen’s death, assigned the revenue received from it to the use of the sick.

He also built a hospice for receiving passing pilgrims and providing rest for poor invalids, assigning to it the mills of the estate of Caviniacum for their use. He further established an entire prebend to be added daily to the brothers’ common alms, specially designated for the salvation of the souls of this congregation.

### 58. (72.)

The tithe of the entire estate of Amberlaco—that is, of its demesne—belonged to the church situated at Ambra, dedicated to Saint Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1395] That is, “its own.”]. This had been so from the time of Abbot Beregis, by the gift of Pippin, who was mayor of the palace of King Theoderic.

In the time of Emperor Henry, surnamed the Pious, to whom Conrad succeeded in the kingdom because he had no heir, Countess Cunegondis—who had been the only daughter of Count Gozelo, lord of that estate [Col. 1397A]—married a certain Saxon named Otto. When an improper divorce occurred between them, a matter which it is not ours to recount, all Cunegondis’s patrimony passed by palatine law into the emperor’s hand.

Emperor Henry, the son of the aforesaid Conrad, lent the estate, together with the castle called the Rock of Seremannus, to Duke Frederick in exchange for certain of his possessions which were more useful to him in Saxony. Cunegondis, however, having become a recluse at the church of Saint Peter or Saint-Hubert, lived there with sufficient continence before the altar of Saint Martin, and after a long penance rested in Christ. She was buried beside [Note: [Col. 1397] The text is lacking in witness 1.] the body of her father Gozelo.

While she was still alive and was frequently visited by Duke Frederick out of charity, the duke, at her suggestion, fully recognized the aforesaid tithe as belonging to the church. And because he was a man of truth and justice, in compensation for the loss which he understood the place to have suffered in respect of that tithe through the aforementioned exchanges of the lords, he legally transferred Mount Pincio [Note: [Col. 1397D] Pinsamont, a village between Bastogne and Saint-Hubert. R.], together with its household and all its appurtenances, to blessed Hubert, to be possessed forever.

When he, still unfamiliar with the ancient and due custom, learned that all the first portions of each kind of wild animal from the annual hunting of the entire Ardennes forest had to be delivered to blessed Hubert, he took such care to pay them during his lifetime that once, when he had gone out with his hunters as they were bringing a boar to the monastery, he himself carried the boar’s head on his own shoulders into the church before our eyes and laid it before the altar of Saint Peter as an act of devotion.

Duke Godfrey, surnamed the Bearded, also went hunting one day in order to fulfill this custom toward blessed Hubert. He caught five stags and a wolf, and sent all of them—with their hides and the captured wolf still alive—to this church before our eyes.

After the aforementioned Frederick’s death in 1065, his wife Ida married Count Albert of Namur. The aforesaid tithe again began to be withdrawn from the church through the action of wicked and fraudulent officials, as though they trusted in the altered lordship. To reclaim it, the abbot appealed to the count on account of his wife. When Lambert the elder reasonably explained the sequence of events to them, the church recovered what was its own, with the assent of both of them, to possess forever.

### 59. (73.)

At the estate of Caviniacum there was a household of courtiers. Although it had formerly been acquired for the church together with the other inhabitants, it refused to acknowledge the church’s lordship as something newly imposed and disdained serving it.

The abbot therefore approached Count Baldwin of Mons, Richeldis’s son, accompanied by Lambert the elder, and reasonably urged him not to protect their insolence toward the church. The count reported the matter to his wife Ida and to his other faithful men who had been present at the transactions concerning Caviniacum mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1397D] Chapter 49.]. On the testimony of these men, he acknowledged that the abbot’s case was just, but he instructed him that he wished to be honored by receiving a payment in return for confirming that recognition.

The abbot promised him ten marks of silver and brought him to the castle of Tudiniacum [Note: [Col. 1397] Corrected by another hand from *Tud.* in witness 1.], namely Thuin [Note: [Col. 1398D] Thuin. R.], where the bishop was then staying with Duke Godfrey.

In their presence Baldwin recognized the aforesaid household of courtiers as belonging to the church of Saint-Hubert and completely withdrew his protection from them. By a public privilege executed there, he confirmed to the church all who appeared to be involved in this opposition, together with their male and female servants, their possessions, and their allods. He also had his own seal impressed upon the document along with the bishop’s seal. [Note: [Col. 1398D] That is, “his own.” Letters of this recognition survive, issued at Thuin in 1088. H.]

### 60.

The bishop told the duke that the church of Saint-Hubert would gain a considerable advantage if someone could also acquire the tithe of this estate, which belonged to the church of Prüm. At their advice and encouragement, Abbot Theoderic conceived the plan of carrying out this same business.

On his return, he sent both Lamberts to Prüm, dictating nothing to them either to say or to do, but entrusting them to test the outcome of the affair. They were honorably received by the venerable Abbot Wulfrannus, who kept them familiarly for a week. He became so attached to them through their witty conversation that, setting aside his own companions, he especially enjoyed their company.

Lambert the elder, who had been accustomed to courts from his youth, delighted the abbot by conversing with him in courtly jests. The younger Lambert, whenever there was an opportunity for him to speak, briefly introduced excerpts from the events of ancient annals. The abbot repeatedly asked him, as a source of amusement, to recount how the boy Papirius Praetextatus had outwitted his mother so as not to reveal a senatorial decree (Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, 6).

Papirius had secretly entered the Capitol beneath his father’s cloak. When he returned and presented himself to his mother, she asked him amid kisses where he had been for so long. After he replied that he had been in the senate with his father, she began pressing the boy with every argument to tell her what secret matter he had heard there.

Wearied by the persistence of her questioning, and having firmly resolved not to reveal the secrets of the Capitol, the boy cleverly invented the story that the senate had decreed that every man should have two wives, and that this decree would be confirmed at the next day’s session as a measure for the benefit of the state.

The woman, unable to tolerate any delay, left the house in agitation and stirred up the more powerful matrons of the city. Almost driven mad by such a rumor, they assembled the next day before the Capitol while the senate was in session. There, crying out in womanish fury that the senate should not reinforce its previous day’s decree against them but should instead decree that each woman should have two husbands, the senators asked what this unrestrained conduct of the women meant.

The senators were terrified and astonished at the portent of so great a matter: the shameless madness of the modest sex. Then the boy Papirius entered the senate house and dispelled the public fear, explaining how his importunate mother had pressed him and what he had falsely told her.

The senators, embracing the boy’s ingenuity, decreed that, in his honor, he should be surnamed Praetextatus because of his prudence in speaking and keeping silent; the following wording is textually uncertain: “in [the] *aetatem praetextatam*, [the] cause also and order of the affair” [Note: [Col. 1399] One should perhaps write either *vel supra* or *aetate praetextata*.]. Thus the shamelessness of feminine desire and fickleness was mocked, and Papirius Praetextatus, although still a boy, was granted the dignity of the senatorial order; from that time onward, other boys were excluded from the senate.

After Lambert had introduced these matters to the abbot’s satisfaction, he went on to relate what follows [Col. 1399B], whenever the occasion offered an entertaining story for his listener.

(Cicero, III, 9.) “Plato,” he said, “introduces a certain Gyges in the following story. Heavy rains opened up a fissure in the earth, and in it he encountered a bronze horse lying on the ground. When he opened its sides, he found inside a dead man who had a golden ring on his finger. He took the ring and put it on, then returned to the royal shepherds, since he himself was one of them.

When he happened to turn the bezel of the ring toward the palm of his hand, he saw everyone while remaining visible to no one. Having discovered the power of this marvel, he killed the king of the Lydians together with some of his leading men, and took possession of his wife and his kingdom.”

### 61. (74.)

“Another memorable story,” he says, “is told among philosophers about Damon and Pythias, namely two Pythagoreans. One of them, condemned to death by Dionysius, the Sicilian tyrant, asked him for a postponement so that he might arrange his affairs at home. The exceedingly cunning tyrant demanded from him a surety who would be executed in his place if he delayed. To demonstrate his trustworthiness in returning, the man calmly offered a companion as surety for his own death, prepared to die in his place if he did not return. On the appointed day of the threatened execution, the condemned man returned, while his companion was already eagerly prepared to die for his friend. Astonished that friendship was dearer to the philosophers than life, the tyrant remitted the sentence of death and invited both men into his own friendship, since he had proved them to be true friends in such danger.

The same tyrant, although he had punished many unjustly, is nevertheless praised for having punished one man entirely justly. For a certain bronze-worker, observing that he delighted in the tortures of human beings, thought he would please him if he devised for his madness a torture of some novelty. He therefore fashioned and cast a bronze bull, and presented it to the tyrant as a spectacle of a certain kind of pleasure. When asked by him for what purpose he had devised such a machine, the craftsman replied that those whom the tyrant destined for torture were to be put inside it; then, when a fire had been kindled beneath, they would produce a bellowing like that of a bull through the machine’s mouth. To this the tyrant replied: ‘I wish first to test that very thing on you, and it seems just to me that you should be the first to suffer what you prepared for others.’” [Col. 1399C–D; Col. 1400A]

“He mocked his gods as well to such an extent that he showed them to be more objects of contempt than of any veneration. For, entering the temple of Jupiter, he ordered the golden garment with which the statue was covered to be removed and a woollen one to be put in its place, joking that gold was cold in winter and burdensome in summer. [Note: [Col. 1399] We give the following narratives according to manuscript 1*.] (CICERO, *De natura deorum* III, 34.) He also ordered Aesculapius’ golden beard to be plucked off, saying that it was inappropriate for the son to appear bearded when his father Apollo, regarded as reborn every day, was beardless. He likewise took away the golden bowls held by the statues, declaring that human beings ought not to despise what was offered to them by the gods; (CICERO, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 21.) if gold was evil, the gods ought not to possess it, but if it was good, it was more suitable for those who knew how to use it. [Col. 1400B]

When a certain philosopher was praising him because such great power was available to him at his command, he invited him to dine that same day. He arranged an unusually sumptuous banquet, during which he ordered a naked sword to be suspended by a thin thread above the head of the philosopher reclining beside him. Seeing the sword hanging over him, the philosopher was terrified and abandoned the banquet; with such danger threatening him, he entirely excused himself from dining with the tyrant who had invited him. To this the tyrant replied: ‘Such is the security of the happiness which you falsely proclaimed to be mine, since either Fortune’s wheel suddenly casts the highest down among the lowest, or death itself, impending over all, is unwilling to spare anyone.’ (VALERIUS MAXIMUS III, 3, *Externa* 1.) [Col. 1399C–D; Col. 1400B–C]

“It is recorded that, while Alexander was sacrificing, a boy who was lighting the fire caught a live coal on his arm. Although his flesh was burned, he remained motionless and revealed neither pain nor a groan by any sign or movement. So great was the boy’s reverence for discipline that religious devotion overcame the sensation of nature.

“Diogenes the Cynic reclined in a barrel, which he honoured with the name of a palace, as though it were sufficient for him as a dwelling. He had arranged for the same barrel to be turned with the sun; by its rotation he avoided the sun when he needed to be cooled in summer, and sought it when he needed to be warmed in winter. (Cf. ibid. IV, 3, *Externa* 4; CICERO, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 32.) When Alexander the Great, passing by, contrary to the expectation of his nobles, visited him with lowered royal dignity, he found Diogenes in his ‘palace,’ seeking the winter sun. After greeting him with the utmost courtesy, Diogenes said: ‘While you are speaking, do not obstruct the sun for me, nor remove from me the source of warmth which you yourself cannot give.’ Alexander smiled at being held in such little regard by the philosopher and, turning to the princes who served him, said: ‘Look at the beast who has the whole world beneath his feet, the world we seek with such labour.’ When he then offered Diogenes garments as a royal gift, almost naked as he was, Diogenes threw them aside, asserting that the man born amid riches is the one for whom what he possesses is sufficient. (MACROBIUS, *Saturnalia* I, 11.)

“This man had been sold by barbarians from freedom into slavery. When Xeniades of Corinth wished to buy him and asked what craft he knew, Diogenes replied: ‘I know how to command free men.’ Astonished by his answer, Xeniades set him free after purchasing him and entrusted his sons to him, saying: ‘Take my children, and command them.’”

[Note: [Col. 1401] I do not know where he drew this from, although I remember having read it long ago.]

“When Alexander, travelling to the Brahmans, had learned long beforehand that this people was so restrained by natural law that those who publicly practised philosophy, through their devotion to virtue, knew no vices—especially lust and greed—he presented himself with considerable reverence to Didymus, the ruler of that province. Didymus received him in royal fashion and urged him to attend the next day the hearing of a case of justice between two neighbours.

“When the court had been set for the following day, Alexander sat with Didymus amid a crowd of people. Two neighbours also appeared, whose case was as follows. One had sold the other a field. While the purchaser was cultivating it, he found a treasure in it. He immediately returned to the seller of the field and urged him to take back his treasure, since he had sold him nothing except the field. The seller, on the contrary, argued that the treasure was no longer his, because, when he sold the field, he had also removed from himself the produce of the field. Alexander, astonished at this dispute free from all greed, said: ‘There would be no such litigation in my kingdom, because taxation would violently claim every discovery as public property.’

“Then Didymus asked him whether nature truly produced common resources there in abundance. Alexander replied: ‘Yes, in the greatest abundance.’ Didymus continued: ‘Although these gifts of the Creator arise there for the nourishment of the creatures living there, human beings would surely know that they are owed not merely to those who have earned them by their merits, but also to the birds and beasts that subsist in that same land.’” [Col. 1401A–C]

[Note: [Col. 1401] In 1* our chapter 63 follows here, then chapter 62, without any indication that the order should be changed. Since this plainly conflicts with the author’s intention, we have judged that the order must be altered. For the author seems to have committed to parchment here whatever, on various occasions in Lambert’s conversations, came into his mind that belonged to the same subject—or rather, to have later supplemented the text on a sewn-in slip. The scribe of 1* inserted that slip in the wrong place, after chapter 63.]

### 62.

Hannibal of Carthage, a refugee at the court of King Antiochus, made a very witty jest. (Ibid. II, 2.) The jest was of this kind. Antiochus displayed on the plain the enormous forces he had assembled to wage war against the Roman people. He paraded an army glittering with silver and gold standards; he brought out chariots with scythes, elephants with towers, horses with magnificent bridles and trappings, necklaces and military decorations. Elated by so large and splendid an army, the king addressed Hannibal [Note: [Col. 1401] *Hannibal* in 1*.]: “Do you think all this is enough for the Romans?” The Carthaginian, mocking the cowardice of the unmilitary troops and the value of their weapons, replied: “Clearly, I think this is enough for the Romans, even though they are exceedingly greedy.”

This was said not only wittily but also bitterly. The king had asked about the number of the army and its comparability with the Roman forces; Hannibal answered about the booty. [Col. 1401C–D]

(Ibid. II, 3.) Cicero’s biting wit also sharpened its tooth against Caesar in this fashion. After Caesar’s victory, when Cicero was asked why he had made a mistake in choosing sides, he replied: “His girding deceived me,” jesting about Caesar, who wore his toga girded in such a way that, by dragging the fold as he walked, he appeared soft and effeminate. Regarding him, the far-sighted Sulla had said to Pompey that he should beware of that boy.

Cicero likewise, while dining at Damasippus’ house, heard him serve a mediocre wine and say: “Drink this Falernian; it is forty years old.” Cicero replied: “It accurately reflects its age.” [Note: [Col. 1401] *fert* in Macrobius.]

When he saw his son-in-law, a man of short stature, girded with a long sword, he said: “Who tied my son-in-law to that sword?” Nor did he spare his own brother in his wit. His brother too was of small stature; when Cicero saw a shield-portrait of him with enormous features extending down to the chest, he said: “My brother is half again as large as he is in full.”

During the consulship of Vatinius, which lasted only a few days, he also joked in this way: “A great portent occurred [Note: [Col. 1401] *ostentum* in M.] in the year of Vatinius, in which there was neither winter nor spring nor summer nor autumn.” [Note: [Col. 1401] *Vaticum* in 1*; *Vatinii* in Macrobius.] [Col. 1401D; Col. 1402A–B]

(Ibid. II, 4.) Caesar Augustus heard that, among the boys whom Herod had ordered killed from the age of two years and under, his own son had also perished, and said: “I would rather be Herod’s pig than his son.”

The same Caesar, returning in triumph from the victory at Actium, was met among the people offering congratulations by a man holding a raven whom he had trained to say: “Hail, Caesar, victorious commander.” Astonished at the bird’s courteous greeting, Caesar bought it for twenty thousand coins. The craftsman’s associate, who had received nothing from that generosity, assured Caesar that the man had another bird as well, and asked him to make him bring it. When the raven was brought, it uttered the words it had learned: “Hail, victorious commander Antony.” Caesar, sufficiently angered, thought it sufficient [Note: [Col. 1401] *dixit*, “said,” in 1*.] to order the man to divide the gift with his associate. [Note: [Col. 1401] *provenerat* in 1*.] [Col. 1402B–C]

When a parrot greeted him in the same way, he ordered it to be purchased. Likewise, astonished by a magpie, he bought that bird too.

This example encouraged a poor shoemaker to train a raven to give the same greeting. After exhausting his resources, he would often say to the unresponsive bird: “My labour and expense are lost.” At last the raven began to utter the prescribed greeting. Augustus passed by after hearing it and replied: “I have enough such greeters at home.” The raven nevertheless retained enough memory to add the words it had often heard its complaining master say: “My labour and expense are lost.” At this Caesar laughed and ordered the bird to be bought for more than he had yet paid for any other. [Col. 1402C–D]

A little Greek used to offer Caesar some complimentary epigram whenever he came down from the palace. After doing so repeatedly in vain, he saw Augustus about to descend once more and, with his own hand, wrote a brief Greek epigram on a sheet of paper; as the Greek poet approached him, he sent it to meet him. The man read it and praised and admired it both in voice and expression. When Caesar had approached his seat, the Greek poet lowered his hand into a poor man’s purse and brought out a few coins to give the emperor, saying: “Not in accordance with your deed, Augustus, for if I had more, I would give more.” [Note: [Col. 1403D] Macrobius’ Greek is not translated correctly here; there it reads: Νὴ τὴν σὴν τύχην—“By your fortune.”] After everyone laughed, Caesar summoned his steward and ordered one hundred thousand sesterces to be counted out to the Greek poet. [Col. 1402D–Col. 1403A]

A certain veteran, in danger on a day appointed for him to answer a legal charge, approached Caesar publicly and asked him to assist him. Caesar immediately gave him an advocate whom he had thought should be chosen from his entourage, and recommended the litigant to him. The veteran cried out in a loud voice: “But when you, Caesar, were in danger in the Actian war, I did not seek a substitute; I fought for you!” He then exposed the scars impressed upon him. Caesar blushed and came to plead his case, since he feared appearing not only proud but also ungrateful. For in the greatest power there ought to be the least license: what is regarded as negligence in the case of lesser men is considered pride in the powerful. [Note: [Col. 1403] I have supplied this word from Macrobius.] [Col. 1403A–B]

(MACROBIUS II, 7.) Caesar invited a certain Laberius, a Roman knight of harsh freedom of speech, with five hundred thousand [sesterces] to come onto the stage and perform mimes that he had written in denunciation of others. [Note: [Col. 1403] *proderet niscenam* in 1*.] [Note: [Col. 1403] *nummos* in 1*; the reading is *mimos*.] [Note: [Col. 1403] *ita* in 1*.] But power compels not only when it invites, but even when it begs. Thus Laberius, declaring [Note: [Col. 1403] Added from Macrobius.] that Caesar had forced him, replied:

“Necessity, whose crosswise course and violence many have wished to escape, few have been able to evade. No ambition, no gift, could ever move me in my youth from the position of an excellent man; now, after sixty years have passed, with my mind driven out of itself, without a stain, it does not cast me down to break the summit of my reputation, flourishing in good and evil fortune, and to satisfy the people. Thus the old age of years, like ivy as it creeps, kills the strength of the tree.”

[Note: [Col. 1403] What follows is very corrupt.]

During the performance itself, from time to time, in whatever costume he could, as though beaten with whips and resembling a man being seized and dragged away [Note: [Col. 1403] I have supplied this from Macrobius.], he cried out, with a certain young Syrian named Publius placed over him: “Further, Romans, we are losing our freedom!” A little later, extending his finger and running about before Caesar, he added: “He whom many fear must fear many.”

At these words everyone turned eyes and faces toward Caesar alone, marking how his lack of restraint had been scourged by this sharp wit. Caesar nevertheless turned his anger into public favour, giving Publius the palm and Laberius a gold ring. [Col. 1403B–D]

Then Publius said to Laberius as he withdrew: “You whom you challenged as a writer, support him now as a spectator.” [Note: [Col. 1403] *Qui* in 2*.]

But Laberius added the following verses in a new mime:

> Not everyone can be first at every time.
>
> When you have reached the highest step of distinction,
>
> You will stand there with difficulty, and fall more quickly than you descend.
>
> I have fallen; he who follows will fall. Praise is public.
>
> In giving a benefit, the one who gives to a worthy person receives it.
>
> Bear, and do not blame, what cannot be changed. [Note: [Col. 1403] *non mutari* in 1*.]
>
> Whoever is allowed more than is proper wants more than is allowed.
>
> An eloquent companion on the road is a vehicle in place of a carriage.
>
> Frugality is poverty of good reputation.
>
> The heir’s tears beneath the mask are laughter. [Note: [Col. 1403] *Heroclis* in 1*.]
>
> Patience, when repeatedly injured, becomes madness.
>
> The man who makes shipwreck a second time
>
> Blames Neptune improperly. [Note: [Col. 1403] *verum* in 1*.]
>
> By arguing too much, truth is lost.
>
> Part of a benefit is what is requested, if you refuse it quickly.
>
> So possess a friend that you may suppose this man capable of becoming an enemy.
>
> By tolerating an old injury, you invite a new one.
>
> No danger is ever overcome without danger.
>
> Nothing is more fitting for a leader than to think about everything.”

[Col. 1403D–Col. 1404B]

### 63. (75.)

By these and similar witticisms the abbot had already become more favourably disposed, and he asked more privately what had brought them to him. They disclosed that they had been commissioned by the bishop and the duke, and also that the church of Saint Hubert was requesting the church of Caviniac in exchange.

When the abbot asked what reciprocal exchange they were offering for this alteration, they replied that they were offering the church of Melsin, together with one *mansus* of land on the border of Vilantia, which, because of its location, was more convenient for the church of Prüm, just as Caviniac would be more useful to the church of Saint Hubert. [Note: [Col. 1403D] Maissin. R.] [Note: [Col. 1403D] Vilantia, situated nearly three miles from Saint Hubert, was subject to the men of Prüm; see below, chapter 99.]

When the abbot had referred the matter to the hearing and counsel of the brethren, their common judgment decided that what was requested should be granted. Therefore, so that the delegation might be confirmed by the formal settlement of the matter, a day was appointed on which the abbots of both churches, with their advocates, would meet to determine and confirm it.

On the appointed day Duke Godfrey came to Prüm with Abbot Theoderic, and Count Berthold, summoned by Abbot Wulfrannus, was present. [Note: [Col. 1404D] Of Ham, on the river Prüm, advocate of the church of Prüm; see Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis* I, 479. But there must be an error in the dating, unless one says that these events took place under Theoderic I, which is supported by a. 1083, line 55, since Theoderic I did not die until 1087.]

Thus, in the public presence and by the common consent of the brethren, as well as of many nobles of the kingdom gathered with the aforementioned princes, the agreement concerning the aforesaid exchange between the two churches was legally transferred [Note: [Col. 1403] Or *tradita*, “delivered”?] and formally released, as well as confirmed, through the hands of the abbots and advocates, in the year 1083. [Col. 1404B–C]

### 64. (76.)

While Lord Abbot Theoderic the Elder was still alive, Roger of Macey, with the consent of his son Godfrey, had given to Saint Hubert whatever he possessed at Chevugy, in return for burial there and for the salvation of his soul. Four years after this donation, Roger having died and been buried there as he had requested, Rodulf, abbot of Mouzon [Note: [Col. 1405D] 1087–1106, according to the *Annals of Mouzon*, SS. III, p. 162.], suggested to Raginold [Note: [Col. 1405] *Raginoldi* in 1*.], archbishop of Reims, that the same Roger had once promised the aforesaid alms [Note: [Col. 1405] Two leaves are missing at this point in 1, but we have collated 1*.] to the church of Mouzon, and that it was consistent with its justice and honour for him to reclaim what had been promised for the abbey under his jurisdiction. [Col. 1404D–Col. 1405A]

The archbishop believed the abbot. Whatever belonged to Saint Hubert in the territory of Reims, he violently forbade it to the church unless the abbot acknowledged to him what the church of Mouzon was claiming. Compelled by this necessity, the abbot went to the archbishop and, taking with him Lambert, prior of the church of Saint Remigius, asked him why he had thus forbidden what belonged to Saint Hubert.

Reginold, being tenacious of a judgment once begun, especially in matters where he seemed to himself to be able to prevail, and also because he had taken little care to oppose greed wherever he hoped for some advantage, decided that the judgment in this dispute should be referred to the council of bishops which he had recently scheduled to take place at Soissons.

The abbot came to the council, bringing with him Godfrey, the son of the aforementioned Roger, prepared to establish legally the alms given by his father. When the abbot’s case, among other matters, was debated in the council, the bishops publicly settled the following judgment. Concerning the altars of the church of Reims that the church of Saint Hubert had acquired, the archbishop of Reims could lawfully bring a claim against the abbot; but concerning the abbey’s lands, the abbot owed him nothing [Note: [Col. 1405] *cuiquam* in 1*; perhaps *esse cuiquam*], except in the hearing of the church of Liège, to which the same abbey belonged, since the canons decree that no one is permitted to put his hand into another’s harvest. Thus the abbot’s case was concluded by the judgment of the bishops. [Col. 1405B–C]

Since he was fully aware that Raginold was hostile to him because no advantage had come to him from the source where he had hoped for one, the abbot so won him over with suitable gifts [Note: [Col. 1405] I suspect *inde* for *unde*; 1* has *provenire*.] [Note: [Col. 1405] *complacavit*; 1* has *placavit* “appeased,” with gifts] that, after the privilege had been confirmed and the person permanently excluded, he obtained the altar of Bedols as a donation to the church of Pyr. [Note: [Col. 1405D] Already in 1087; see above. It is scarcely credible that this occurred within so short an interval.] (1087). [Col. 1405C–D]

### 65. (77.)

Roger, count of Porcien, had also begun to build a church in honour of Saint Theobald before the castle of Porcien itself, across the river Aisne. Having assigned to it certain possessions of his own, which are enumerated in the privilege of that church, he intended, being a man of great generosity, to build there a monastery of considerable renown.

But after he had been betrayed by his own men and dishonoured in captivity, and saw that he could not continue what he had postponed for too long, he was also overcome by profound weariness at his humiliation. He gave his daughter Sibyl as wife to Godfrey, son of Count Albert of Namur, and sold the county of Porcien itself, with everything belonging to his jurisdiction, to father and son for a very large sum, which he received from them.

With their unanimous consent and by a legal donation, Abbot Theoderic of the church of Saint Hubert and Saint Peter obtained the aforesaid cell of Saint Theobald to be held in perpetuity, and established his monks there. The matter was publicly confirmed by a privilege deposited in the pontifical archive of the church of Reims, acknowledged and signed by Archbishop Raginold together with the clergy of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin. [Note: [Col. 1406D] 1087, indiction 10, in the twenty-eighth year of Philip. Published by Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* V, 662.] [Col. 1405D–Col. 1406A]

### 66. (78.)

He also acquired for the church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert, to be held in perpetuity, the cell of Cune [Note: [Col. 1406D] Cons-sur-la-Chière, near Longuyon.], which is dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel, together with all its appurtenances: namely, the possessions named in the privilege of that church; the churches subject to it; tithes; dependants; cultivated and uncultivated lands; meadows; woods; vineyards; waters; mills; fisheries; ovens; and the lawful donation of Walter and his brother Dodo, together with that of Walter’s wife Hawidis, daughter of Count Arnulf. [Note: [Col. 1406D] Of Chiny.]

With the consent of Engelbert, archbishop of Trier, he installed there as provost Robert, a monk of excellent character, formerly a cleric of the principal church of Verdun. Through his industry he enlarged that place in possessions and buildings. [Col. 1406A–B]

### 67. (79.)

Boso, abbot of Saint Agericus, a man of exceptionally devout religion, was staying at Jupille with his bishop, Theoderic of Verdun. [Note: [Col. 1406D] He died on 28 April 1088.] There he fell ill and, foreseeing that he would die, earnestly demanded with every kind of prayer from his own people that he be taken to Saint Hubert and buried there.

Certain nobles of the castle of Huy carried out his wishes—for he had been born of a good family there, being the nephew of the archdeacon Boso mentioned much earlier—and he was honourably buried in the church to the right of the altar of the blessed protomartyr Stephen. At that time Lord Henry, bishop of Liège, was residing there and performed the services for his funeral. By hereditary right from his parents, two houses worth twenty pounds in the market of Huy came to this church. [Col. 1406B–C]

### 68. (80.)

Bishop Henry, being a man intent on preserving virtue, had decided that a certain Obert, provost of the church of the Holy Cross, who had been convicted of crimes, should be expelled entirely from the city. [Note: [Col. 1405] *omnino* in 1*.] But Obert fled to Berenger, abbot of Saint Lawrence, and remained hidden with him for so long that, through Berenger’s support, he returned to the bishop’s favour.

Not long afterward, however, after collecting his possessions, he went to King Henry, who, having been excommunicated by Pope Gregory for ten years, was persecuting the Roman Church by every expedition within his power.
