For he had besieged and captured the City, driven Pope Gregory into exile, and, while Gregory was still alive, substituted Guibert of Ravenna in his place. Guibert too had long been excommunicated, yet had presumptuously dared to invade the apostolic see.

When Gregory died at Benevento, the cardinals of the Roman Church, with the agreement of the more religious citizens, substituted Odo, bishop of Ostia, in his place in the apostolic see. [Note: [Col. 1407D] That is, after Victor III.] They judged him, formerly a cleric of Reims and later a monk of Cluny, to be Pope Urban.

Thus, while priesthood and kingdom were at odds, and although the holy Church was generally endangered throughout the world, it was afflicted more particularly through Henry’s persistence. The pontiffs, setting justice aside and favouring themselves, either withdrew from Urban [Note: [Col. 1407] So in 1*; the editor reads *subtraheret et attraheret*] or drawing toward Guibert. [Note: [Col. 1407] So in 1*; the editor reads *subtraheret et attraheret*.]

While ecclesiastical justice languished under such dissension, in addition to the other losses of virtue, the simoniacal heresy grew widespread: those whom Urban excommunicated were absolved by Guibert, while Urban gathered the deserters of Guibert.

Meanwhile, while Henry still lived, Obert remained with the prince. Bringing gifts with him, he sought, as far as he could, by services and favours to win the prince’s support in obtaining some office of honour from him. [Col. 1406C–Col. 1407B]

### 69. (81.)

In the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1091, on 31 May, and in the sixteenth year of his episcopal ordination, Lord Henry died, to the detriment of the glory of Liège and the greatest loss of our solitude, which he had cultivated with particular devotion.

As soon as Obert heard of his death [Note: [Col. 1407] Here manuscript 1 continues.], he extorted the bishopric from the king without an ecclesiastical election, by means of very large contractual gifts; he nevertheless also swore fealty to him by an oath. [Col. 1407B–C]

### 70. (82.)

Two former pseudo-abbots, Guolbodo of Saint Lawrence and Leupo of Saint Trudo, had once gone to the same prince. After convicting them of proven crimes and excommunicating them, Lord Henry had expelled them from the bishopric of Liège. [Note: [Col. 1407] 1* is defective here.]

When they heard of Henry’s death, they were encouraged by the hope of recovering their honour and likewise promised money to the prince. Obert also swore to restore them to the prince’s favour and brought them with him to Liège (December 1091).

For the time being, however, he concealed what he intended to do, until, after being consecrated at Cologne on 1 February 1092, he would be more confident in carrying out his wickedness. [Note: [Col. 1407] A word seems to be missing again.]

On the very day of his return, he ordered Berenger, abbot of Saint Lawrence, to leave the church without delay and to surrender the abbey freely to Abbot Guolbodo.

So that Berenger might not reasonably be blamed for abandoning a church which he had lawfully undertaken to govern, he appeared before Obert the next day. Publicly, before the city’s leading men, he complained that he was being burdened with excessive injustice, that justice was being violently crushed without judgment, and that although he accepted either the divine will or the divine permission, he nevertheless wished it to be judged whether he deserved to be treated in this way.

When some shouted that this was exceedingly unjust and that he ought not to suffer such treatment, Obert replied that he himself fully recognized the same thing, but that he could not disregard the command of his lord, since he had sworn to him that he would carry it out, whether it was just or unjust.

Berenger, still more resolute, replied: “What is not possessed with great love is abandoned without great sorrow.”

As he departed, he took with him the pastoral staff he had held. Everyone, including Obert himself, testified that it rightfully belonged to him. Taking with him the brothers whom he wished, he withdrew to the church of Saint Hubert, which he fully recognized as the mother of his conversion and profession. [Col. 1407D–Col. 1408B]

There he was gratefully received. He reported not only the wrong inflicted upon himself but also the public disorders which Obert was rashly perpetrating, and discussed them with Abbot Theoderic and the brethren—namely, that Obert had seized the bishopric from an excommunicated man without a lawful election and by means of a monetary agreement; that, by expelling Berenger in this way and installing Guolbodo, he had betrayed justice; that he had sold the abbey of Florennes to Gislebert, provost of Hastière, and the abbey of Brogne to a certain Guiremundo, a monk of Saint James, for a publicly assessed price; and that he had polluted the church of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, formerly free and glorious.

Their indignation against Obert was aroused to such an extent that, by common agreement, they judged that, as though he were excommunicated, communion should no longer be maintained with him. [Col. 1408B–C]

Berenger, however, fearing for that church because of the danger of the times, and at the same time criticizing the abbot’s inadequate simplicity as insufficient for so great a defence, added that no one is defiled except by the consent of the mind. He himself had been violently expelled and therefore had to withdraw elsewhere; they should remain peacefully in their place and not rashly stir up any hostility against themselves, since no one had yet compelled them to do so. They should take great care not to begin such a course without sufficient consideration, lest they later regret having begun it.

The abbot replied that he too was concerned for himself and his people, and that he would rather offend Obert than God. “If anyone belongs to the Lord,” he said, “he will persevere with him, either remaining in the place or leaving the place with him.” [Col. 1408C–D]

When this judgment had therefore been jointly confirmed, Theoderic withdrew to France with Berenger. As they sought out Raginold, archbishop of Reims, to consult him about the outcome of events, he secretly sent Iheruin, bishop of Amiens, ahead of them and ordered him to tell those who were coming not to present themselves to him, because he would in no way communicate with them either by word or by kiss unless the bishop sent to them first absolved them from the Wibertine heresy and from communion with Obert, after they had confessed their fault.

Through this rebuke they became more certain of their own judgment. After being absolved by Iheruin, they were received with honour by Archbishop Raginold. He comforted and strengthened them to persist in defending the truth, and they withdrew to the cell of Eberneicourt.

Theoderic granted this place to Berenger so that he might remain there with his men while awaiting, through the passage of time, the end of the affair. He therefore sought the cell of Cume in order to stay there.

Meanwhile Berenger defamed Obert with accusations [Note: [Col. 1409] The editor suspects that *Obertum* has fallen out of the text.], disparaged his life and conduct, lamented in continual complaints that he had been treated so badly by him, and proclaimed that Obert had not been honoured by the episcopate but that the episcopate had been dishonoured through him.

Obert did not remain unaware of their judgment or of the disgrace of the public accusations against him; although he concealed it, his own conscience also testified to it. He therefore resolved to take revenge. But, so that he would not seem to have acted rashly, he summoned those whom he had made more loyal friends through rewards or promises.

There also gathered the abbots whom he had installed and restored: Guolbodo of Saint Lawrence, Leupo of Saint Trudo, Gislebert of Florennes, and Guarmundus of Brogne. They were prepared to condemn Abbot Theoderic, although, because they themselves were condemned by the decree of the canons, they had no authority to judge.

Nevertheless, so that they would not appear to have rushed alone into a reckless sentence, after consulting with the archdeacons they decided that the abbot should be prosecuted by lawful summonses, and that, unless he presented himself within the specified deadlines for episcopal judgment, he should justly be excommunicated or entirely deposed. [Col. 1409A–C]

Meanwhile Obert raged and grew angry against the abbot. He marvelled at the source of such firmness against the bishop of Liège and threatened to expel the monks from their place and distribute the abbey among his soldiers.

He sent Godiscalc, abbot of Hastière, and Guarmundus of Brogne to the monastery to announce this danger to the brethren, to shake them from their judgment, and under the pressure of fear to make them yield to his error.

The brethren remained firm and refused to communicate with the envoys, even by replying to them. When the local people heard of this threat, they complained that the abbot and monks were mad, that in their confusion they were dissenting from the bishop of Liège through new and unheard-of ravings, and that they would pay the penalties of this dissension. They declared that they would no longer serve either the church or the monks unless this novel dispute on both sides were brought to an end.

Moved by so many attacks and complaints, and being condemned by everyone as though he were a fugitive, the abbot resolved to expose himself to danger. Trusting in God’s help, he came to Liège, contrary to everyone’s expectation.

Astonished at his arrival, he presented himself on the appointed day before the assembly of his adversaries.

A fictitious charge was therefore brought in Obert’s place, and Abbot Theoderic was accused of the specified crimes: namely, of having admitted [Note: [Col. 1409] Martène added this word, since it is absent from the manuscript.] Pope Urban and Raginold, archbishop of Reims, into his counsels; of having, at their instigation, excommunicated his lord the emperor and Obert, his bishop; of thereby proving him to be excommunicated, because he had withdrawn himself and his people from communion with him; and likewise of having forbidden his own brothers to receive ordination from him. [Col. 1409D–Col. 1410A]

Moreover, he was accused of retaining Berenger as a public herald of his disgrace, to Obert’s injury.

The abbot, having been given an opportunity to answer for himself, summoned those whom he knew to be of sounder judgment and replied in good conscience, prepared to defend himself against the charges brought against him. He stated that he had in no way sought to have either the emperor or the bishop excommunicated, nor did he wish to prove them excommunicated. He had forbidden his brothers to receive ordination from him because those already ordained were sufficient for the church’s offices. He ought not to have cast out Berenger, who, after suffering so great a wrong and violence, had fled for refuge to his mother church—especially since the Apostle commands that we share in the needs of the saints. If anyone thought that he had sinned in any of these matters, he was ready to submit to their judgment.

When the individual defenses had been reported by Henry the archdeacon, the abbot was asked how he could substantiate his statements. After further consultation, the matter was debated until the following judgment was reached: since the monastic order belonged to an apostolic vocation, the abbot’s defense was sufficiently established by the authority of the Gospel, namely, that he had said “Yes and No” (Matthew 5:37), since the Lord absolutely forbids swearing oaths, and whatever goes beyond these words is from evil.

Obert, indignant [Col. 1410C] after so many insults to himself and so many threats arising from his anger, that the abbot had been given so easy a way of escape, sent word to him that the favor of the bishop of Liège was always necessary for the abbot of Saint-Hubert. He should endeavor to purchase it for himself at that moment with the greatest gifts, since he appeared not yet to have rendered any service. To this the abbot, conscious of his own innocence and desirous of a very different kind of glory, replied that the bishop of Liège would not lack the abbey’s service; but under the present dissension the church’s resources had been so diminished that they were insufficient to support either himself or the brothers.

After many hardships he was at last dismissed and returned to the monastery. There he suffered a grave scandal from the brothers, who believed that he had communicated with those with whom they had resolved, in good conscience, not to communicate. When they established more certainly that he had not done so, they decided that he should choose whichever brothers he wished, withdraw from the place and the occasion, and take with him the church’s more valuable ornaments, transferring them to more remote cells, lest Obert, on his arrival, seize them by force.

When the abbot replied that he did not wish to abandon the common danger, and that the evils feared individually were more serious than those endured together, the brothers added that they feared for him more than for themselves, since, as private persons, they owed nothing to the bishop. At last he agreed to follow their advice and took with him Lambert the elder and Wirede, who had voluntarily offered themselves for the defense of the faith.

He also carried with him the church’s more valuable ornaments to his own cell, which was safer, and withdrew to remain there in the castle of Cunens. Having received from Dodo, lord of the aforementioned castle, a pledge with hostages that the ornaments would be restored to the church, whatever might happen to him, he soon afterward wished to visit Abbot Berenger. Taking with him those who had come with him and Robert, prior of that cell, he set out and, arriving at the city of Reims, found Berenger at Saint Remigius.

Berenger recoiled from him, since he was visiting him out of charity, as though he had already become an apostate, and avoided him lest he be contaminated by him. Thus dissension arose between them. The abbot was indignant that the man whom he had hoped would be a like-minded friend had so changed toward him without cause. Berenger was afraid to trust a man whom he believed had communicated with excommunicated persons, and he was even prepared to withdraw with his own companions if the abbot wished to approach the cell entrusted to him.

But when, through an intervening discussion, it was established that the abbot was not at all what Berenger supposed him to be, they gave thanks and departed for Eberneicort. There they found brothers gravely scandalized by the accusation concerning the alleged communion. When they were assured that the matter was not as it had been represented, scarcely two of them could be brought to accept this explanation: Lambert and Heribrannus, monks of Saint Lawrence. At that time the name of Obert was so hateful to them that, whenever they heard it—even in ordinary conversation—they could not restrain themselves from spitting in indignation.

One of them, Lambert, was nevertheless overcome not long afterward by ambitious desire and was appointed by that same Obert [Col. 1411C] abbot of Florennes. But after a year he remembered what he had done, withdrew, and was deprived of that office.

As many as twenty-five monks, both from our own community and from the brothers of Saint Lawrence, had gathered at that same cell. They conducted themselves with such integrity and such well-ordered religious discipline that Raginald, bishop of Reims, and Helinand, bishop of Laon, moved by the fragrance of their good reputation, competed in supplying them with the necessities of life.

Abbot Berenger also worked to adapt himself so completely to the customs of those among whom he had come to live that he soon became most dear to everyone. Even Count Ebalus [Note: of Roucy.]—who was regarded as a common tyrant by the others—was gentle and humane toward him.

At that same time, at the urging of his wife Sibylla, Ebalus gave the church of Eberneicort a third part of the tithe, and by lawful authority confirmed permanently to that place the meadow called Regis.

Manasses, too, provost of the church of Reims, had gathered Berenger to himself with such affection that, when frequently summoned, he compelled him to remain with him for two or three days. He intended to promote him to the abbey [Col. 1412A] of Saint Remigius after Abbot Henry. He would indeed have done so after becoming archbishop, had Berenger not been recalled to his own abbey and returned to Liège.

### 71. (83.)

Meanwhile, after the church of Metz had been deprived of the venerable bishop Herimannus, it chose Burchard, provost of the church of Trier, to be ordained as its bishop [Note: He must have had two names. Herimannus died on 4 May 1090. According to the Annals of Metz, MGH SS III, 158, Poppo became bishop in 1090. In 1094 he was reckoning the fifth year of his episcopate, counting from his election; Gallia Christiana XIII, 736. According to Hugh of Flavigny above, col. 351, he was a cleric of Trier, ordained in the first week of Lent by the archbishop of Lyon and the bishops of Mâcon and Langres, together with the abbot of Dijon. [Col. 1412D] Bernold, however, reports under the year 1093 that, after Herimannus’s death, a Catholic bishop was elected and ordained by Gebehard of Constance on 27 March, in the middle of Lent. These accounts agree fairly well with one another and with ours. Poppo held the see until 1103. But who would believe that two bishops of the same party were ordained at the same time?].

He was received in the city without the consent of King Henry. Since he avoided being blessed by the bishop of Trier because that bishop supported Wibert whereas he himself supported Urban, he summoned Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Roman Church, to consecrate him.

Hugh, devoted as he was to the Catholic faith, fearlessly came to Metz in March 1093, accompanied by five bishops: the bishop of Constance [Note: Gebehard.], the bishop of Mâcon [Note: Landricus.], the bishop of Langres [Note: Robert.], the bishop of Toul [Note: Pibo.], and the bishop of Verdun [Note: Richer.], as well as Jeronta, abbot of Dijon. Formerly, when he had heard of the desolation of our church, Jeronta had written to Abbot Theoderic of Saint-Hubert the following letter of consolation:

> To Theoderic, abbot of Saint-Hubert, a man venerable through the religion granted by God, and to the whole congregation serving God under that father: Jerunta, abbot of Dijon, and the entire congregation of Saint Benignus send the spirit of Moses against Pharaoh and all his servants.
>
> Moses, the true servant of the Most High, preferred to profess the truth and suffer tribulation with the people of God rather than, by consenting to falsehood, be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.
>
> John the Baptist, whose right hand was worthy to touch the Savior’s most holy head, proved himself such a champion and friend of truth that he preferred the squalor of prison and the cutting off of his head to remaining silent in the face of an unjust king and failing to oppose his abominable marriage with the restraints of the law and the armor of justice [Note: Thus I have corrected the text; the manuscript reads “of the law and of justice … armor.”].
>
> John the Evangelist, intoxicated from the Savior’s fountain and foremost in the affection of all who love him, refused to apply the comfort of a bath to his aged limbs because he saw the heretic Cerinthus sitting among those bathing [Note: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History IV.14]. He believed that nothing was common with one who, through his unbelief, had withdrawn himself from the company of Christians. He taught that no communion should be maintained with those who, through heresy, cut themselves off from the body of Christ, and who through avarice become the arrows of the devil, teeth in the jaws of Antichrist, a treacherous offspring of vipers, and instruments of the ancient serpent.
>
> In what respect was Cerinthus worse than Obert [Note: The text reads sometimes “Cerinthus,” sometimes “Obert.”]?
>
> Cerinthus harmed the Catholic faith through fraud alone; by the cunning of his unbelief he drew as many as he could into agreement with his error. Obert gave money in order to become a heretic, so that, as a furnace of greed and avarice, he might overwhelm the temple of all religion and truth, and, infected with every kind of filth and defilement, contaminate the Holy of Holies with his curses, if one may so speak.
>
> Behold the true henchman of Antichrist, the chariot of Satan and his faithful charioteer, a true likeness of Simon Magus. He is plotting to destroy the kingdom of Christ while he does not cease persecuting the state of the holy mother Church and strives to drag into his own body those whom Christ redeemed, feeds, and gives drink with his blood.
>
> He wishes to empty the death of so great a head of its power, and he does not fear to hand over to the lion, which always thirsts for the blood of our souls, the sheep found through the Savior’s so great labor. Indeed, he hastens to hurl all of them with himself into forgetfulness of the truth and hatred of religion.
>
> Therefore, since the dangerous times foretold by the Apostle are now upon us, let everyone strive to be what he has professed to be. If the trumpet of Satan thunders loudly and threatens the loss of temporal goods, and even warns of punishments for the flesh that will one day die, let the charity of Christ gladly endure everything, so that neither death nor life nor any creature may frighten us away from defending the truth and zealously pursuing justice; so that we may not be torn from the bosom of mother Church or stray from the path of the Roman See.
>
> Therefore, friends of God, who until now have loved truth and holiness, do not abandon your place—that is, the Catholic faith. Drive out, as far as you can, the wolves rushing furiously into the Lord’s camp. Armed with faith and strengthened by hope of heavenly glory, regard every reproach endured for the name of Jesus as the highest honor. Receive with joy the seizure of your goods, and consider insults [Col. 1413C] and bodily tortures the surest medicine for your sins.
>
> Let Christ be glory and riches in your hearts. Let the good testimony of your conscience be your unfailing consolation. If you endure even a little for the truth, God is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, he will come—he will surely come and will not delay—and will provide a way for you to endure.
>
> But if you fear the lions’ molars, which the Lord will break in his anger, lest they devour you and somehow disturb the course of your simplicity, the house of Saint Benignus will kindly receive, through the grace of Christ, the flight of the children of the Church. As for our little poverty, we are ready—not, I will not say, to give it to your will, but as though it were yours—to return it or place it at your service [Note: Thus the first manuscript; another reads “our.”].
>
> Therefore, dearest brothers, maintain a manly spirit in God’s cause, and take every care not to fall away from the truth, which is Christ. Farewell.

At Israel’s departure from Egypt, true confession was sanctified by the Lord.

On the day appointed for the aforesaid blessing, Abbot Theoderic made every effort to attend this assembly. He was accompanied by Abbot Berenger, Lambert, Wirede, and Robert, intending to appeal to the legate of the Roman Church on behalf of himself and his people.

When Lord Hugh, legate of the Roman Church, had approved his case after it had been presented by the aforementioned Jerunta, abbot of Dijon, and Radulf, abbot of Verdun [Note: Of Saint Vannes.], and had commended it when it was brought before the assembly of bishops, he strengthened it still further by his authority. He blessed the church whose sons were such men—men who, when others failed, persisted in the Catholic and apostolic faith—and promised them the support of the Roman Church and of his own legation. He absolutely forbade them to submit to Obert or to communicate with him.

### 72. (86.)

Obert, embittered by the report of what had happened, as usual burst into anger. He repeatedly clapped his hands and reproached himself, either because, when he had once compelled the abbot, he had failed to extort from him permission to harm his party, together with an oath that he would oppose him in nothing; or because he had so far restrained himself and had not utterly disgraced the rebellious church of Saint-Hubert by violently expelling the brothers from it [Col. 1414B].

He could not conceal the anger he had conceived for long. He gathered an armed force and planned to come to the monastery. Having lodged at Nasania, he sent messengers ahead to the brothers announcing his arrival and ordering them to come out honorably to meet him the next day and to receive him as a visiting bishop of Liège ought to be received. He threatened to punish them unless they did so with greater care and solemnity than usual.

When the officers had been sent ahead and were coercively demanding this honor, no one gave a gracious reply. Yet, lest complete silence appear to arise from excessive indignation, Gislebert, the prior, said in a broken voice that he and the brothers would deliberate about the matter together and would do what they ought to do according to the circumstances and the time.

The next day, as they discussed the matter, although the state of some of the more tender faith secretly wavered, the better consensus of all reached this conclusion: a legitimate abbot presided over them, even though he happened to be absent; by their common agreement he dissented from the bishop; without his knowledge they ought not to consent to anyone, especially at the risk of their faith; they ought to obey God rather than man.

It was the feast of the Apostle John, in 1093, commemorating his being sent by the emperor Domitian before the Latin Gate into a cauldron of boiling oil, on 6 May.

The brothers therefore set aside their fear and carried out their order of worship. At the appointed time the principal Mass was already being celebrated when Obert suddenly arrived amid tumult and anger. He entered the open church and, without first offering the reverence of prayer, rushed furiously toward the upper chancel. Seizing the book from the deacon who was reading the Gospel, he closed it in his hands and, at the command of his anger, threateningly ordered the service that had begun to be interrupted.

Then, impatient of every delay, he seized a priestly stole, mounted the ambo [Note: One manuscript reads “umbonem.”], and without any reconsideration excommunicated by name the absent abbot and those who had left with him. He publicly alleged that the abbot had withdrawn the church’s better ornaments like a sacrilegious person, or—what troubled him more—that the abbot refused to communicate with him as though he were excommunicated.

The bystanders were astonished at such unbridled and immoderate conduct. Each was scandalized by what he saw, but the noble laymen who had come with Obert, and especially those who were more conscientious in maintaining loyalty to him, were filled with the greatest shame.

They could scarcely persuade him to speak with them as though in council. Through carefully prepared suggestions they tried to bring him back to his senses. They said that he was entirely justified in being angry, but that it was disgraceful for a wise man to be overcome by anger; that it seemed astonishing to everyone that he had closed the Gospel and thus shaken it away; that they neither wished nor were able to tolerate any further interruption of the service he had forbidden; and that such a matter required not rashness but deliberate consideration, especially since he possessed the power to impose whatever punishment he wished, though a more suitable vengeance would be preferable.

Obert was ashamed that he had presumed to do what, now more clear-minded, he wished he had not done. He publicly confessed that he had felt the greatest fear when he had suddenly looked back and seen the brothers standing in orderly formation in the choir, reverently serving God alone and setting aside all fear of him. He was indignant and amazed to find so many and such men there, when he had been told that very few had remained in the place.

He immediately made amends to them for having disturbed them in his thoughtlessness and humbly asked them to continue the service they had begun. Then he left the church.

That day he fully refreshed the troops who had come with him at a meal—not to thank those whom he had angered, but to soften with gifts those whom his threatened terrors had not shaken.

Moreover, through certain suitable agents of his party, he courted everyone with flatteries, tested the minds of each, deceived the stronger, sought out the weaker, and carefully commended humility and kindness toward them. He promised that he would be a common benefactor to their interests if they allowed him to be.

After his agents had thus tested the brothers, Obert presented himself to them the next day. Although they disdained to rise for him, he had learned to conceal his indignation. As though grieving for them, he began to ask how they were and to inquire into their needs as though they were his own. He said that he was ready to advise them in every matter, provided only that they would suppress all contention and agree with him; that they should prefer to experience his friendship rather than his hostility; and that they should consider the danger involved in ruining so great a church [Col. 1415D] and dispersing its ecclesiastical household.

Those who had come with him loudly exclaimed that the bishop had argued extremely well, that he had reasonably closed every mouth against him, and that it was not in their interest to lose such a man through their own fault—one who, having set aside the burden of his authority, humbly asked for what he could have violently compelled them to give.

Their defense of the truth, already almost overthrown, would have collapsed—not, as they say, by a sword smeared with honey [Note: Jerome is said to have used this expression; Erasmus records it in his Adages. It occurs again in chapter 89.]—unless the reason of their deliberation, delayed for a little while by shame alone, had come to their aid.

The brothers withdrew to one side in order to deliberate. After hesitating for some time about whether they should abandon or maintain their position, they finally agreed that nothing should be done without the abbot’s knowledge. They saw that he had not been deposed by any judgment of a legitimate trial, and they knew that he could not justly be deposed on the accusation of any crime. They should instead request a delay from the bishop until, after sending a delegation, they could consult the abbot about these matters; and, if they could obtain a guarantee of safe passage to come and go freely, they should bring him with them.

After they had obtained this only with difficulty and had sent three brothers to the abbot, certain men of Bouillon, meanwhile, gathered common retainers and lay in ambush in the forest at Gruispont. They blocked the roads and, seizing twelve wagons carrying the bishop’s baggage, confined them in the nearby castle of Mervolt until the wagons could be divided among them.

Rumor, which characteristically magnifies great things from small beginnings, announced to Obert that he and his men had been surrounded by enemies and that bands of hostile forces were hiding here and there in the woods—things that no one would dare unless he relied upon great strength.

Each person began to measure the dangers according to his own fear, and one urged another to flee. Thus, on the following night, Obert hired men familiar with the locality and, abandoning the undertaking for which he had come, withdrew by hidden and winding paths.

Those who had been sent to summon the abbot, in the presence of Dodo, reported the whole sequence of events to him. On Dodo’s advice, the abbot decided that he should not rashly expose himself to an enraged power; that one must sometimes yield to fortune and circumstance; and that no wise man could regard this as a crime, since the Lord himself commanded those suffering persecution to flee from city to city.

Meanwhile the abbot held back. When it was learned that Obert had withdrawn from the place, the abbot, now more secure, hastened to come to the monastery. After remaining there for some time with the brothers, he restored them to the position they had defended. Having arranged their affairs for the time being, he commended them to God and departed.

### 73. (87.)

At about the same time, to enlarge the episcopal possessions, Obert sought to buy the castle of Couvin [Col. 1416D] [Note: Couvin.], which was hereditary property of Count Baldwin [Note: Of Mons.]. He chose as executors of this business Arnulf and Wiger, brothers of the castle of Thuin [Note: Thuin. Wiger of Thuin appears among the witnesses to the purchase made at Liège on 14 June 1096, in Chapeavill II, 52. But this transaction took place earlier, since the Annals of Lobbes attest that Arnulf, abbot of Lobbes, died in 1094.], noblemen whom he considered all the more suitable for this task because, despite their proximity, they were more removed from the aforesaid count.

When they had completed the assignment and seemed to have served Obert sufficiently to win his favor, they suggested to him that they were prepared not only to waive their reward for carrying it out but also to add as much of their own property as he wished—provided only that he give the abbey of Saint-Hubert to one of their brothers, Ingobrand, a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter at Lobbes.

Since this seemed difficult to Obert while the legitimate abbot was still alive, although disobedient and opposed to him, Count Arnulf [Note: Of Chiny.], their nephew, who was present, added that if Obert was concerned about any obstacle to this plan, he should leave the matter to him. The abbey would be fortunate with such a procurator, and, once entrusted to his nephew, it would soon be restored to its former condition.

Obert was therefore wearied for some time by so many promises and appeals, and was also driven by anger and hatred of Theoderic to expel him in this manner. Although his conscience resisted and reason judged against it, he nevertheless agreed to undertake so great a disorder.

At last he sent word to Arnulf, abbot of Lobbes, that he should come to him as quickly as possible and bring his monk Ingobrand with him. He ordered that Ingobrand, once brought before him, be released, and, in his presence, appointed him abbot of the church of Saint-Hubert—without any preliminary canonical election by the brothers and without having established in him any merit of maturity or life.

Then, having sent a delegation, he informed the brothers that he had acted for their interests and their honor, had appointed them a noble and sufficiently humane abbot, and asked them, for love of him, to receive him voluntarily [Note: One manuscript reads “surpass them.”] and to come out to meet him with the fitting goodwill due to his arrival.

Everyone was disturbed by so sudden a change in affairs. After their initial astonishment had passed and each had returned to himself, it finally became evident how much love of virtue had previously prevailed in each of them, and how much dissimulation had been hidden by fear [Note: One manuscript reads “whatever had remained hidden.”]. They lamented that the enemy of the human race had so maliciously devised this plan against men of virtue, and they stirred up the censors of extinguished modesty because a profit from such affected novelty had come to them.

They scarcely had room to withdraw or time to deliberate, in proportion to the weight and significance of the matter. Some were restrained from departing too quickly from the common opinion only by shame, although the endurance of joys is very difficult to conceal.

Nevertheless, when they gathered together and sought collectively how they should prepare themselves for the immediate necessity, although the hearts of some were far from their lips, all nevertheless appeared to agree on this: that, by maintaining their position at least for a time, they should safeguard their reputation and good name, so that even those who intended to defect might seem to have done so under compulsion.

### 74. (88.)

Meanwhile Obert arrived, leading the man he had appointed. With him were Arnulf, abbot of Lobbes, Count Arnulf, and several other nobles of the episcopal territory.

Since he could scarcely restrain his anger and was indignant that no one had come out to meet him as he had ordered, the advice of his nobles compelled him to conceal it, lest he appear to provoke those among whom he had come to impose an unknown man.

He therefore summoned the brothers and ordered them to assemble together, saying that he wished to attend their meeting for the purpose of speaking with them.

### 75. (89.)

Leaving Ingobrand behind and taking with him those whom he knew to be suitable for the undertaking he intended, Obert went out to the brothers and, greeting them with a cheerful expression, sat down.

After first asking how they were and what outcome they hoped for amid all their troubles, he added that, with fatherly concern, he had provided what belonged to him: he had procured a suitable father for their desolation and had brought him to them.

When they remained silent and, as though accustomed to the expression of wounded devotion toward him, lowered their faces toward the ground, each of those who had assembled began, according to his own power, to rebuke the silent brothers.

They said that such conduct displayed the utmost savagery and immoderate contempt; that it seemed the height of madness for them to wish to resist the bishop of Liège in this way; that their excessive patience had caused him to be despised, even though he had tolerated their insolence with impunity for so long.

The brothers, on the other hand, publicly complained that they were being oppressed contrary to law. They said that it was plainly and manifestly unjust and injurious to impose another abbot upon men who already had an abbot, and that this was a matter within neither the knowledge nor the lawful election of any of them.

Obert was indignant that he and his men had been defeated by such evident reasoning. His appointment was now invalid unless he crushed those who opposed him by force, setting aside every canonical authority.

Lest he leave anything untried against those who resisted him, he twice attempted, although they restrained him, to throw himself at their feet, hoping that by so great a bowing of pontifical dignity he might overcome those whom his power had so far proved altogether unconquerable.

After many disputes and various objections and replies, he rose from the midst of the brothers, withdrew to his chamber, and, through the abbot of Lobbes and Count Arnulf, sent them this message: either they should willingly and gladly accept his decision, or, leaving his affairs to him, they should depart from the place.

When this cruel sentence had been pronounced, the brothers requested a delay so that they might summon the priors of the cells and deliberate with them collectively. They could obtain this delay only until the following day.

Meanwhile Count Arnulf approached each man individually, as he knew how, on behalf of his nephew. He promised his counsel and assistance to the church, while his son Otto, on that very day, invaded the estate of Couvin, carried away all its booty, and even killed some of its inhabitants, thereby contradicting the pledge of his father’s promises.

The brothers no longer had the strength to resist for long. The stronger had been wearied by so many assaults, and the weaker had been won over by so many promises.

Some resolved privately not to participate in this disorder, or to withdraw from the place when they could. Others, having been offered the hope of changing the situation, sought to obtain some advantageous office, or, now that liberty had been offered them, to pursue their own desires, whether leisure or activity.

Thus, while the brothers were divided among themselves—and, more importantly, were defecting from one another—Obert brought Ingobrand into the place. Leaving him there, he departed rejoicing that he had at last prevailed over those who had resisted him for so long.

### 76. (90.)

After all the anxieties caused by the contradiction directed against him, Ingobrand at last obtained what he desired. Being inexperienced and excessively simple-minded, he began to relax into leisure and youthful license, secure—or rather ignorant—of the task of governing a prelate’s office.

It is painful to remember how, amid these disasters, that most beautiful flower of the highest honor and dignity of this place was discolored and fell; how rapidly that long-established condition of the most seemly religious life, which at that time was praised as unique on this side of the Rhine, withered away. Its excellence had been so great that posterity will scarcely, or perhaps not at all, find it credible, since it is characteristic of human understanding—or rather of human error—to believe only slowly whatever excellence is attributed to its own inactivity [Note: Compare Sallust, Catiline 3.].

Ingobrand, lacking the unbroken rigor required to maintain virtue and excessively deficient in the discretion needed for moderation, attempted, contrary to the custom of his predecessors, to soften the fiercer spirits of religious men by a certain appearance of generosity. He sought the intimacy of young men, especially adolescents, and finally spared neither modesty nor expense, while making each of them, as though bound to him by favor, his loyal adherent [Note: Ibid., chapter 14.].

Although it is difficult to say how, in this way, the church’s revenues were reduced and almost exhausted, poverty in household affairs followed. When these resources were no longer sufficient to support the negligence of the imprudent, they compelled the negligent even to disregard their own loss and disgrace.

For, after twenty-five of the church ornaments that had remained there were dispersed—Abbot Theoderic having carried away the best in order to save them—and when they still could not thereby escape their need, they added to their losses by pledging or selling the mills and churches belonging to their possessions.

Moreover, while they were oppressed everywhere by the shortage of goods, what was more serious, they were also oppressed by the infamy of their neighbors. Those who, while their religious life flourished, had been a glory and an honor, were now, with that life languishing, a disgrace and a burden.

During these same days Berenger exercised such hostility toward the church, now apparently subject to Obert, that, forgetting his own conversion and profession, and ungrateful even for the preservation of himself and his followers during the persecution, he became irreparably harmful to the place.

For, following his customary practice of making rounds to solicit contributions, supposedly to support his brothers, he came to Ida, wife of Count Conon, and found her ill at Montaigu. She, sensing that death was near, was considering being buried at Saint-Hubert, where her father Lambert lay. Berenger absolutely opposed this and persuaded her instead, in order to avoid excommunicated persons on account of Obert’s authority, to seek burial at Stavelot and establish her alms there.

Her sons Lambert and Henry argued that the church of Stavelot seemed more free, since by a gift it was subject to King Henry and, in pastoral care, to Obert. Berenger’s opinion prevailed, and he permanently deprived the church of Saint-Hubert of an annual income of three pounds.

Theoderic and his followers also harassed the church’s possessions wherever they could. While they urged tyrants to burn and plunder them, they believed that they were rendering service to God.

Thus certain men, taking the opportunity to carry out tyranny against the place, began to call Ingobrand an impostor and the worst of men, to brand his supporters as deserters from the faith and traitors to religion, and therefore to declare that every evil should be inflicted upon them and that no good should henceforth be preserved for them. Whatever belonged to the church, they said, should be attributed solely to those who, moving from cell to cell, had avoided the contagion of wicked men.

Finally, whatever they could seize from their possessions, they seized with impunity, to such an extent that they carried out open plundering even from the monastery itself—something no one of that time had ever heard or seen happen.

Whatever belonged to the church in the episcopal territories of Reims or Laon, and likewise in those of Metz and Verdun, was peacefully available to Abbot Theoderic and the brothers subject to him, without regard for Obert or his Ingobrand. The dukes Godefrid and Theoderic forbade their men, whether seduced by entreaty or payment, to attempt to inflict any injury upon them.

Guiredus, too, having been granted authority to administer, took charge of Sulpeum and Nogaria together with Chevogy [Note: Souspy, Noyers, and Chévogy. R.], with such determination that, whenever any of Ingobrand’s officials tried to lead men of Mouzon or Bouillon there for payment [Note: One manuscript reads “tried” in the singular.], he either forestalled them by cunning or drove them away after gathering his forces.

Raginer, provost of Pierrepont, had also blocked the passage at Mézières for them with such diligence that no one from those regions dared to involve himself there in any business.

Robert, provost of Cunens, had likewise seized Chauvenoy, Flabeuville, and Gandrehengies [Note: Chauvenoy, Flabeuville, and Gandrehengies. R.] by force with Dodo’s support, and with their revenues he supported the brothers who had gathered there in greater numbers.

Whenever Ingobrand complained of this division of the abbey to Obert, Obert in turn sadly brought the matter before Duke Godefrid, as though he were the church’s advocate, reproaching him for allowing such things to happen.

The duke, however, responded that Obert was unjustly angry with him. No one could or ought to prevent his sons from enjoying what belonged to them in the church. Obert himself, rather, should be blamed: he had raised such confusion in a place that had until then been honorable and had imposed upon the legitimate abbot that particular adviser and administrator of his own.

Amid this confusion of the church, Lambert the younger, who was staying at the church of Saint Remigius, wrote the following letter to the brothers because of the circumstances of the time and situation [Note: The letter is missing from manuscript 1, either through the negligence of the copyist or because, in the original manuscript copied by 1, the author had intended to add it but had not done so].

### 77. (96)

At that time an irreconcilable rupture raged between Otbert and the count of Leuven [Note: [Col. 1421D] Apparently Henry the Younger, whom Godfrey succeeded in 1095. On the cause and conclusion of the dispute, see Aegidius, chapter 14.], and because of it the episcopate, lying between the two, was grievously oppressed: the count repeatedly attacked the city, while Otbert, having assembled an expedition, planned to make war upon the count. On this occasion the province’s leading men, summoned to a fixed day, had assembled in the city so that they might deliberate about the interests of the church amid such a division.

While they were deliberating, Obert stated that he had already excommunicated the aforesaid count, but that the count did not care about it at all. Duke Godfrey, smiling, added that the count had told him that Otbert’s excommunication had no validity with him unless Abbot Theoderic of Saint-Hubert authorized it for him—so that either he would demand to be absolved by Theoderic, or, as one excommunicated by him, he would be denied communion by the universal church.

At this Obert almost went mad, and, satisfying his fury in excessively unrestrained speech, swore indignantly that he would rather die than, on account of such a person, and such a contemptible one, be dishonored or despised, if he or his people had any power anywhere. When, in anger, he also reproached the leading men themselves for failing in their fidelity to Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, because they allowed the authority of the bishop of Liège to be so safely degraded—and said that they ought by no means to tolerate this if they had any concern for their own honor—the duke himself was first moved by this, as were also Albert, count of Namur, and Henry of Durbuy [Note: [Col. 1421D] Durbuy. Henry was the son of Henry, brother of Albert of Namur; see Ernst, *Des Comtes de Durbuy et de la Roche*. Liège, 1836, 8vo.], as well as Count Conon of Montaigu and the aforementioned Arnulf of Chiny, who, unlike himself, together with his son-in-law Dodo of Cunis, replied:

“We are indeed faithful to Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, but in this matter we have until now concealed that very fidelity with excessive patience, because we neglected to investigate the causes of this dissension.”

With unanimous agreement they therefore began to insist that Otbert appoint a day for a hearing between himself and the abbot, provided only that the abbot might safely bring and take back with him as many defenders of his position as he could, and that, in a public hearing of the church of Liège, with free permission to speak and hear in their presence, the truth, sifted out, might triumph [Col. 1421D].

Otbert was stunned, as though caught by what is called a “horned syllogism” [Note: [Col. 1422D] Jerome, *Epistle* 69.2.], and, since he could nowhere evade the matter, overcome by the authority of so many men, he reluctantly granted them a day for the hearing. But he could not be prevailed upon to allow the abbot safe passage there and back. When everyone protested that this was unjust and dishonorable to them, since it was sufficiently clear that by this pretext he wished to evade the hearing, he finally promised that he would consult with the duke about the matter and, through him, determine shortly whatever seemed to them should be done.

When Dodo returned and reported all this to the abbot, the latter rejoiced and gave thanks to the divine providence, hoping that an end would thereby come to the wavering dissension and that, with so many witnesses present, judgment of the truth would be brought to victory. Without delay he reported everything in order to Abbot Berenger and instructed him to bring defenders of the truth with him from his own region.

He himself, taking with him Lambert the elder and Robert, prior of Cunis, set out to travel through Metz, Toul, and Verdun. Explaining to his known and faithful friends the necessity that had arisen for defending the faith, and reminding them urgently that the matter to be conducted was not his but Christ’s, he urged them not to fail Christ’s testimony.

One would have seen, in each city, religious and powerful persons grieving over such a persecution for justice no less than those who were suffering it themselves. Secure in their own safety, they undertook to defend the cause of the once religious and honorable church of Andage, and none of them paused to consult another; rather, each in rivalry promised his assistance to the abbot.

Finally Paulinus, archdeacon of Metz, who was learned and accustomed to support defenses of this kind—for he had steadfastly fought through the long and numerous persecutions inflicted upon Bishop Herimann in defense of the faith—said:

“This outcome of events has wearied us for a long time, and we need no one’s encouragement to undertake these, as it were, new circumstances. We owe ourselves and all that is ours to Christ; the dishonor of this crime is shared by all who believe in him. It will certainly also be injurious if what ought to be voluntary appears, through any delay, to have been extorted, and if we postpone in assistance what we display in words. This business does not suit words dripping from the lips, but words carefully carved from the innermost depth of the heart. No reward will corrupt our tongues. This friendship will be honored by free services, and such favor will be valued by the deed itself, not by advantage.”

When Abbot Lanzo of Saint-Vincent said that he would indeed go willingly, but that some men had to be delayed because of the danger of famine, which was then at its height [Note: [Col. 1422D] In the year 1095, a famine long in preparation grew severe. *Annals of Liège*.], Paulinus replied:

“We shall each go at our own expense, because it is not perfect charity if, when something is to be carried out freely, you pursue it with assistance made burdensome against your friend.”

The same opinion stirred the people of Toul and Verdun to assist the abbot, and the same steadfastness encouraged them to proceed. Once the abbot, now equally secure because so many defenders had undertaken his cause, had arranged the proceedings, he returned to Cunis and instructed that a letter be sent to Abbot Berenger, who was staying at Eberneicourt, reporting how his affairs had progressed and whom he himself had secured.

Berenger replied that, through his efforts, the following were prepared to assemble for the appointed hearing: from the metropolitan church of Reims, Lord Manasses the provost, later made archbishop [Note: [Col. 1423D] Raginold died on 21 January 1096. *Necrology of Reims*, in Varin, *Archives administratives de la ville de Reims*.]; Roger, defender of the church and archdeacon; Rodulf, chancellor and later provost after Manasses [Note: [Col. 1423D] When Manasses died on 18 September 1106, he was elected archbishop, and in 1108 prevailed over his rival Gervasius.]; and Odalric, a scholar of the Roman Church, sufficiently well known and esteemed [Note: [Col. 1424D] In 1097 he served on a legation to Urban II. Marlot, *History of Reims* II, 214.]. From the church of Saint Remigius, Lambert the prior and whoever else he wished to bring with him; from the church of Soissons, Engelrannus [Note: [Col. 1423] Manuscript 1 has Emolrannum; below, Engelramnum.] the archdeacon, shortly afterward ordained bishop of Laon [Note: [Col. 1424D] In 1096. Sigebert’s *Laon Continuator*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS VI, 445.]; and from the church of Laon, Ebalus the archdeacon and Adalbero the abbot, together with anyone else whom he himself might deem suitable to accompany him.

He further informed him in the same letter that he had written and sent many communications, as circumstances and the occasion required, to Henry and Lanzo, the archdeacons, and to those members of the church of Liège whom he considered more reasonable. In these letters he argued that, seduced by Balaam’s reward, they had placed a scandal before the children of Israel, now accepting Otbert as bishop, although formerly they themselves detested him and had condemned him by the judgment of the most just opposition. He added, quoting some of Otbert’s own words:

“If you have done this rightly, rejoice today in Abimelech, and let him rejoice in you; but the Lord will rejoice in his works” (Judges 9:19).

The abbot reported all these arrangements for his defense to Dodo of Cunis, and by entreaties obtained from him that he meet Duke Godfrey, who was staying at Bouillon. He intended to ask the duke directly what he had arranged with Otbert concerning safe conduct for the hearing.

The duke replied that he had repeatedly approached Otbert about this, but that Otbert, by changing his words, had so far evaded giving a definite answer [Note: [Col. 1423] The words appear not to belong here, unless one prefers to interpret them as meaning “he avoided it by dissembling.”]. He said, however, that he would confer with him the following day at Vilantia, and asked Dodo to accompany him there; Dodo would then discover what should be believed concerning the message he was to report to the abbot.

Otbert, meanwhile, had learned that the abbot had zealously arranged his case, had stirred up so many hearers against him and his clerics, and that the people of Liège themselves were deeply offended that persons from other cities, as though more perceptive, were being brought in to dispute with them. Distrusting his own side if they came together for judgment, he resolved by any means to avoid the impending hearing, and therefore privately disclosed this same intention to the duke when the latter came to him.

When the duke heard this, he craftily pressed against Otbert the very thing Otbert feared, saying that the hearing ought not merely to be averted through his intervention but strengthened by his authority and safe conduct. In this way he compelled Otbert to double his original promise of money. Thus, as wickedness combined with greed, the attempt to ascertain and expose the truth was suppressed.

For when, under the duke’s protection and safe conduct, such a large and celebrated assembly was expected to meet at Liège as the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul approached (1095), Otbert publicly declared that on that very day he would be at Reims with Count Arnulf, in order to conduct his case before Archbishop Rainald and reach an agreement with him concerning the castle of Mouzon, which Otbert had burned and devastated [Note: [Col. 1424D] In 1092. *Annals of Mouzon*.].

Dodo, realizing that Otbert and the duke had failed in their duty to distinguish the truth, reported the same failure to the abbot, and, to one who had been hoping for better things, thereby deepened a wound of the greatest sorrow. For he did not grieve so much on his own behalf, deprived of the place where he might defend himself, as on behalf of those whom he had drawn into so great an expectation.

Soon afterward Abbot Berenger, taking the prior of Saint Remigius with him, had proceeded as far as Pirus, to inquire about securing safe conduct for those whom he himself had urged to come. While he was pausing there for a short time, Lambert the elder, sent by the abbot, met him and reported how Otbert and the duke, by their strategy, had frustrated their hopes—something he had not at all feared.

Indignant at this sudden overturning of events, Berenger immediately wrote, dictated by that same indignation, to the leaders of the church of Liège. He wrote that they had not properly looked after their reputation and honor, that they had shamefully failed in judgment and justice at their head, that they had proclaimed far and wide the disgrace of this failure by rejecting so many hearers [Col. 1424C], and yet, although they had thus frustrated the appointed hearing, had nonetheless accomplished the purposes of the proposed defense and the sifting of the truth.

Knowing also that Abbot Theoderic was suffering the deepest sorrow, he wrote him, in accordance with the tenderness of his own spirit, the following consolation among many other things:

“Prudence measures the outcomes of events, but, deceived by another’s error, we too for a while turn the wheel of fortune and expend great labors in vain, wearied by fruitless effort. Certainly it will belong to the eternal Judge to avenge this, for whose faith we have above all resolved to displease his enemies. You must take the greatest care to inform those whom you summoned of this as soon as possible, so that they may stay in their own places. On my return I too shall hasten to do the same. Farewell.”

Without delay, after arrangements had been made by both men that the summoned persons should withdraw when the hearing was abandoned, Berenger, returning to Reims, met the duke as soon as possible. Since, in view of the circumstances, the duke seemed to him a powerful person who should be cautiously appeased rather than sharply provoked, Berenger, when publicly complaining about the injury inflicted by Otbert upon the holy church, softened his manner of speech out of consideration for the duke, as though for his defender.

For while he accused Otbert of having shamefully evaded the appointed defense of the truth because he was conscious of his own guilt, he commended the duke instead for having compelled it to be arranged with the other leaders of the episcopate. The duke, flushed with shame and convicted by his conscience—for no guilty person is acquitted when his own conscience is the judge—was thereby exposed.

Archbishop Rainoldus, a most prudent man, who had been privately forewarned by Berenger, received these words and asked why he and the other defenders of the churches allowed the abbeys of the episcopate of Liège to perish in this way, when they could forcibly compel their Otbert to do whatever they wished, even against his will, or gently bend him if he were willing.

He sought to bring the duke, by reasonable arguments, to the point where he would promise that he would truly now labor for the defense of the churches and the restoration of the legitimate abbots. By this means, through the clemency of divine providence, the matter proceeded.

### 78. (97)

There was a castle between Huy and Liège called Mons clarus [Note: [Col. 1425D] Clermont, on the right bank of the Meuse, above Ingihoul.], and those who sailed along the Meuse complained to Otbert very frequently that it was exceedingly hostile to them. Since he had long been indignant at enduring so many complaints and injuries from them, he assembled his forces and resolved to besiege the castle.

He had summoned the duke of the episcopate and its leading men to arrange this siege, and, once the expedition had been organized, was already standing before the castle when suddenly the duke seized the opportunity, called Otbert to him, and publicly excused his counsel and assistance [Col. 1425C], unless Otbert restored the abbeys of Saint-Hubert and Saint-Laurent to their former condition and, after expelling the purchasers, freely appointed suitable persons to administer those he had sold [Note: [Col. 1426D] Compare the *History of Saint-Laurent* above, where you will see that these events took place in 1096 or earlier.].

“What assistance,” he said, “O fellow soldiers, shall we hope for from God, when, as his churches perish, we not only offer them no defense but also withdraw the free voice of opposition? Surely the most gracious ordering of the Creator has earned this from us: he made us ministers of his public cause, so that each of us, in his own person, should deny him the service for the protection of whose right his universal lordship has chosen us at this time.”

As he was preparing to say more, the assent of the leading men interrupted him. They all attacked Otbert together and began violently to demand that he fulfill the condition set by the duke: that the churches be restored and the legitimate abbots reinstated.

Some of the archdeacons and provosts of the episcopate had also assembled to arrange the same expedition. Seizing the opportunity created by this public attack, they intensified their private hostilities against Otbert, ostensibly out of zeal for defending justice, so that they might thereby establish fear of themselves in his eyes for the future. Without some advantage, they regarded his affection as useless and worthless.

When Otbert was constantly confronted with what canonical authority wholly forbids—namely, selling abbeys for a fixed price and selling ecclesiastical ministries that he ought to have bestowed freely for the care of souls—he was overwhelmed by such an unexpected demand. Although he understood that he had not acted rightly, he nevertheless tried to present not only a covering for his own wickedness but also a defense based on the established error of many prelates. He protested that he had not sold God’s grace in his blessings but had rather bestowed them freely; nor did it seem unjust to him to extract his own profit from ecclesiastical possessions, which he distributed to those who did not possess them so that they might possess them.

How detestable this plague, transferred from France to Lorraine, was, Peter Damian, in our own time, lamented in an attack of this kind addressed to Pope Alexander [Col. 1426B] [Note: [Col. 1425] It is not found in manuscript 1 or 1*; it is Letter I.13 in Cajetan’s edition.].

But to return to the sequence of events: Otbert, constrained by the aforesaid demand of the leading men, although he was being forced, as it were, with twisted arms to desire what he did not desire, nevertheless replied graciously for the moment concerning the restoration of the abbots and promised that he would do whatever the judgment of the proceedings determined.

It was immediately decreed that, without any delay, he should expel Wolbodo and Ingobrand and restore the legitimate abbots to their places. Otbert, however, fearing that such a sudden and ill-considered exchange of abbots might one day become a burden to him, reconsidered the matter with wiser men and decided that judgment should be held concerning them. Thus, once they had been reasonably convicted and expelled for their fault, he would then exclude the possibility of removing the source of contention at some future time.

Accordingly, on the appointed day, the abbots and archdeacons assembled to expedite the matter, and the court sat. Once the unjust displacement imposed upon each of them and the disorder of their conduct had been proved, both men were convicted and withdrew from the places they had invaded.

### 79. (98)

Otbert immediately wrote to Berenger that he thanked him, and that, after rejecting Wolbodo, he had decided concerning his monastery that it pleased him and his leading men that Berenger should return confidently and bring back with him the brothers who had fled to him.

He concealed this from Abbot Theoderic, although the same support and the same judgment had prevailed in the case, being exceedingly tenacious of the indignation he had conceived against him. He was also fully aware that Theoderic would not communicate with him.

Moreover, he dealt more secretly with those abbots and archdeacons who were more loyal to him, so that, since they had once judged Theoderic worthy of excommunication at Otbert’s command, although unjustly, they would in no way allow their judgment to be weakened unless Theoderic publicly sought absolution and favor from him.

Berenger, however, after receiving Otbert’s message, hesitated at first, uncertain whether he should persist in the defense he had begun or return and care for the church once entrusted to him, which was now entirely failing. He feared, with his conscience accusing him, the disgrace of public reproach: if he were reconciled with Otbert, he might appear an apostate to those who persevered in the true faith, since he had hitherto proclaimed Otbert’s apostasy in so many approved attacks.

But, on reconsidering the matter repeatedly, he concluded that such a changed and unexpected turn of events in circumstances had not occurred without the divine will. Taking some of his own men with him, he hurried to Liège.

There, when the archdeacons met him outside the city with the greatest courtesy, he presented himself to Otbert in their company. Otbert, wishing to draw him more affectionately to himself, offered him, before Duke Godfrey and the city’s leading men, a settlement for the injury he had inflicted upon the man departing from him.

Although Berenger appeared reluctant to accept it, he imposed this condition upon Otbert: whatever had been scattered and lost by Wolbodo was to be restored to the church. When Otbert agreed, Berenger kissed him, and Otbert restored him to his former seat beside himself.

Many were not only amazed but scandalized by so sudden a change in such a great man, whom they certainly believed could in no way be separated from his former judgment. Berenger, however, as he believed, acted with his conscience and intention secure before God—not out of ambition, but to assist the church in danger and the brothers dispersed from it.

### 80. (99)

When Abbot Theoderic, who was then staying at Cunis, heard this, he summoned his brothers to a council and asked what ought to be done in such a situation.

Lambert the elder, a man of counsel, together with Wiredus, Robert, and Rainer, replied to his inquiry that thanks should be given to the divine ordering, because, beyond everyone’s hope, it had opened a way for them to return to their church. He should return as quickly as possible, just as Berenger had done, lest some adverse event occur while he delayed; he should also bring back the church’s ornaments, which he had removed in order to preserve them.

The decision was therefore confirmed, a time was appointed for carrying it out, and, with Dodo’s agreement, Theoderic took the ornaments with him and left the castle at midnight. The following evening he came to Fredegorium [Note: [Col. 1427D] Freux, a league and a half from Saint-Hubert. R.].

The next day, after guards had been stationed at suitable points, he descended early in the morning into the oak grove overlooking the monastery. He sent Lambert the elder ahead to the brothers and instructed him to say that he wished to visit them with paternal affection, adding that they should not be afraid of him in any way, whatever they might have done amid such varied changes of circumstance.

At this, while some remained silent from conscious shame and others objected through fear of Otbert, lest they do what they did not wish to do, the consensus of the better men finally prevailed: they should do what was fitting, and attend to justice, truth, and honor; they should come gladly to meet the abbot, who had suffered exile for Christ, and, recognizing him as their abbot, honor him.

When this was reported to the abbot, the brothers came out to meet him. He presented himself humbly to them, and, followed by those who had left with him and by many others who had assembled after hearing of his return, entered the church with praises of God.

Then, after counting or publicly displaying the ornaments he had brought back, he entered the brothers’ assembly and imposed penance upon those who confessed their guilt both concerning communion with Otbert and concerning their subjection to Ingobrand. Having absolved them, he kissed them and restored them to the former judgment.

Regarding the aforementioned church treasure, he had entrusted it, on the pledge of his faith, to Rodulf of Vilantia: two copes and a Gospel book decorated with gold and gems, which had belonged to Emperor Charlemagne, and three ivory horns from the almsgiving of Duke Godfrey, called the Bearded.

This Rodulf, an impudent despiser of faith and truth, offered all these things as a gift to Lord Wulfram, abbot of Prüm, who was angry with him, in order to win his thanks. The abbot, astonished, asked where these objects had come from, since he clearly recognized the Gospel book from a procession once held by him.

At last Rodulf was convicted and forced to confess—or rather, to lie—that the objects had been sold to him from the dispersed treasure of Saint-Hubert.

At this the abbot shook his head and sighed sorrowfully over the scattering of so great a church. He sent two of the horns to his brother, the bishop of Utrecht [Note: [Col. 1428D] Conrad.], but returned the rest to Saint Hubert through Rodulf as an act of charity.

Rodulf, however, sold this charitable gift of the abbot to the church shamelessly, as though it had come from himself, demanding two horses for it. He was also convicted of this wickedness before the aforesaid abbot and lost the abbot’s favor.

### 81. (100)

Three days had now passed, and behold, Abbot Berenger was coming with the archdeacon Henry, in order, by Otbert’s command, to administer the abbey as though it were vacant. When they heard that the abbot had returned and had been received by the brothers, they turned aside to a church estate called Burs [Note: [Col. 1428D] Bure. R.].

When they returned to Otbert and reported the abbot’s return, he, in anger, forbade the church’s ministers to do anything for him. This prohibition, however, was weakened as readily as it had been pronounced, and the church’s ministers did not cease ministering to either the abbot or the brothers on that account.

As Otbert’s anger cooled for a while, he also pretended to forget what he recognized he had irrationally ordered. Nevertheless, his indignation against the abbot had become so obstinate that it could be calmed neither by time nor by reason.

Therefore, when Lambert the elder came to him on certain matters of the church and Otbert heard that the aforesaid abbot had fallen ill, he forbade the brothers to give him common burial, should he die as an excommunicate, unless he made satisfaction to him as his bishop or communicated with him.

The abbot, however, recovered from his illness. Now all the more secure, and all the more certain that Otbert’s malice against him had reached its completion, he wrote the following apologetic letter to the church of Liège. In it he proved that he had not been excommunicated and that no one could be excommunicated except when guilt required it:

“Since I have committed no crime worthy of anathema, I freely defend myself as unjustly excommunicated, because I am not and have not been a thief or sacrilegious person against that church which, by God’s grace, I govern. I have not despoiled the church of any of its possessions, nor have I sold or alienated anything from its estates, nor, so far as it lay within my power, have I permitted anyone to usurp anything.

“But when I saw the possessions of other churches being wickedly seized by their purchasers—that is, by Wolbodo, Leupodo [Note: [Col. 1429] Manuscript 1 and 1* have Leupodone.], Gislebert, and Warimund—and being most wickedly sold for the price of their simoniacal commerce, I feared that the possessions of our church might likewise be squandered by some usurper. On the advice of Duke Godfrey and other wise men, who feared what later happened, I entrusted the portion of the treasure for which I was most afraid to faithful men who were leaving the monastery with me. Together with them I preserved it faithfully, down to the last farthing, nowhere except within the possessions and estate of the church of Saint-Hubert. When God’s grace brought about my restoration, I returned to the church what belonged to it, not as a sacrilegious man but as a faithful guardian.

“Therefore, if any sentence of excommunication has been hurled against me, let the present testimonies of the holy Scriptures, which defend and protect me, judge it invalid.

“Jerome, explaining in his commentaries on Matthew the passage, ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16:9), says:

“‘Priests and bishops, not understanding this passage, assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or suppose that they can absolve the guilty, whereas before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the guilty that is examined. We read in Leviticus about lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests: “And if they have leprosy, then let them be declared unclean by the priest” (Leviticus 14:4). This does not mean that priests make lepers unclean, but that they possess knowledge of the leprous and the non-leprous and can discern who is clean and who is unclean. Therefore, just as the priest there makes the leper clean or unclean by uncovering him, so here the bishop or priest binds or absolves—not those who are innocent or guilty, but, in accordance with his office, when he has heard the various conditions of sinners, he knows who should be bound and who should be loosed.’”

Pope Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Caralis:

“Among many complaints, the illustrious man Isidore has complained to your fraternity that he was excommunicated by you. When we wished to learn from your cleric [Note: [Col. 1429] Manuscript 1 and 1* have *clero*, ‘the clergy’.], who was present, why this had been done, it became clear that it had been done for no other reason than that he had insulted you. This greatly distressed us, because, if this is so, you show that you think nothing of heavenly things; rather, you indicate that your conduct is earthly, since, in revenge for a personal insult, you have inflicted the curse of anathema, which the sacred rules forbid.

“Therefore, in future be watchful and careful, and do not presume again to inflict such things upon anyone in defense of your own injury; for if you do anything of this kind, know that it will be avenged upon you.”

Gregory also says in his treatises on the Gospels:

“Often the pastors of the church follow the impulses of their own will, rather than the merits of the cases, in binding and loosing. Thus the one who exercises this power according to his own wishes, not according to the conduct of his subjects, deprives himself of the power of binding and loosing. Often a pastor is moved toward his neighbor by hatred or favor. But those who follow their own hatred or favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly. The cases, therefore, must be weighed, and only then should the power of binding and loosing be exercised.”

### 82. (102)

At that time, at the urging of Pope Urban, one and the same purpose had stirred the Christian peoples of the entire West: namely, that armed men should go to Jerusalem, defeat the Medes and Persians who had invaded it, and subjugate the promised land so that they might hold it.

Not only common people of various ages but also the princes of the provinces themselves agreed to this expedition. Freely setting aside their wives and children, and either abandoning their honors and inheritances altogether or selling them for money, they hastened to pursue uncertainties in place of certainties.

Duke Godfrey had decided to go with them, and, in order to prepare supplies, had put the castle of Bouillon up for sale to Otbert.

To carry out this transaction, Ida, the duke’s mother, came to Bouillon. When she saw that the almsgiving of her father, the elder Godfrey, had perished, and that the monks had departed from the church of Saint Peter with the consent of her son Godfrey—who, after sending the brothers back to their mother church of Saint-Hubert at the urging of Lord Bishop Henry, had, by a renewed legal donation before suitable witnesses, transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Hubert whatever possessions, movable or immovable, belonged to the almsgiving of his aforesaid grandfather—she took the matter very seriously and sent for Abbot Theoderic.

She asked him sorrowfully why and how the memory of her father had vanished from that place. The abbot replied that this was to be attributed to her brother and her son, who, by withdrawing the revenues, had annihilated the place, and that he knew all its destroyers to be excommunicated in accordance with Pope Alexander’s privilege.
