But the virtuous woman, concerned both for the salvation of her father and for the absolution of her brother and son, approached the abbot with tears and begged him to resume responsibility for the church of Saint Peter, restore the brothers there, and absolve from danger those who had sinned against God and against her father.

When the abbot denied that he could do what he was being compelled to desire, the mother urged her son humbly to offer him a pledge of satisfaction. In order to obtain release from excommunication, Godfrey was to give him the mother church of Saltiacum rivus [Note: [Col. 1429D] Sansanruth. R.], with the chapels subject to it, as well as the chapel of Saint John and the prebends of the clerics serving there, together with all the movable and immovable property of that chapel.

The condition was that, when the clerics then living died, everything should be subject to the monks, with the abbot providing a chaplain [Note: [Col. 1431] Manuscript 1 and 1* have *capellano*, “by a chaplain”], who would serve the castle and the people’s parish, just as his grandfather, the elder Godfrey, had legally donated it to Saint Peter. Godfrey himself was also to acknowledge publicly that the brothers were to be restored there.

When Godfrey solemnly did this before his nobles, without any reconsideration or opposition, the countess Ida herself granted the mother church in the village of Basejo [Note: [Col. 1431D] Baisy. R.], which had long belonged to her own patrimony in Brabant and lay near Nivelles, to the church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert, to be held for the soul of her father Godfrey the Bearded, and likewise for the souls of her brother Godfrey and her son, who was present there.

She also obtained confirmation of this donation by a legal privilege and lawful witnesses [Note: [Col. 1431D] The privilege, in which mention is also made of the privilege granted by Pope Alexander II, was issued at Bouillon as early as 1094, indiction II; see Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 76. The chronological order is therefore disturbed here.]. She further obtained that the brothers be restored by the abbot, in her presence, to the church of Saint Peter.

[Col. 1431B] **83. (103).** Otbert, intent on his own glory, coveted the aforementioned castle that had been offered to him, and agreed with the duke on one thousand five hundred pounds of silver for it [Note: [Col. 1431D] Compare *The Triumph of Saint Lambert concerning the Castle of Bouillon*, chapter 1, which Aegidius copied out.]. To pay this sum, after he had proscribed the possessions of the episcopal communities for confiscation, he then, on this pretext, began to exercise the greatest hostility against the church of Saint Hubert. For when he had sent his own collectors, he caused the altar panel covered with gold to disappear, and broke up three golden crosses, scattering their precious stones. One of these, of considerable size, lord abbot Theoderic had recently had made through the efforts of Lambert the elder; and Bishop Henry had forbidden, under threat of anathema, that it be disposed of by anyone. From the remains of this plunder the aforesaid Lambert collected one and a half marks [Col. 1431C] of gold, and purchased for the church the allod of Felc, which is near Nassigny, from Count Conon, who was traveling with the duke to Jerusalem, in the presence of Bovo of Wahart and Walter of Amblève, by whom it had been donated.

Not long afterward, as the duke was traveling to Jerusalem [in August 1096], he sent us a game-set of crystal dice and brought with him many nobles and religious men. With their protection in view, the persecution by Otbert seemed in some measure tolerable to Abbot Theoderic. When they had departed, however, Theoderic was afflicted by prolonged and severe distress. Judging himself unequal to enduring so many such events, and telling no one what he had conceived, he went out for a time, as was his custom, and, bidding farewell to the brothers, withdrew to Saint Remigius at Reims to remain there.

Since he had decided this for himself, and because that place appeared to possess the greatest dignity and the highest esteem, he was all the more desirous of it because he had learned that a certain abbot named Robert had been appointed there, a monk of the Major Church [Note: [Col. 1431D] Marmoutier-les-Tours. Abbot Henry died on 16 March 1095. Robert is the author of the *Passage to the Holy Land*.], whom Archbishop Manasses had requested, at Pope Urban’s direction, in order to strengthen the religious observance there more strictly. How differently this turned out is testified by Hugh, bishop of Lyon and legate of the Roman Church, who wrote to Pope Urban about it as follows:

> To the most reverend father and lord, his lord Pope Urban, Hugh, servant of the church of Lyon, commends himself in all things.
>
> We suppose that the letter or embassy of a certain monk of the Major Monastery, named Robert, has already reached you. Brother Manasses, archbishop of Reims, obtained from his abbot, by the authority of your letters, what he could not accomplish by himself: that Robert should be appointed abbot of Saint Remigius. [Note: [Col. 1432D] Bernard. Lambert, bishop of Arras, wrote nearly the same things to the pope; see Baluzius, *Miscellanea* V, 304. Pope Urban, however, annulled the sentence pronounced against Robert; see his letter of 14 April 1097 in Marlot, *History of Reims* II, 221, and in Ducange, s.v. *Emancipatoriae*, as well as Robert’s own letter in Baluzius, *Miscellanea* V, 315. Compare Sybel, *History of the First Crusade*, p. 49.]
>
> Certain religious brothers were also assigned to him. Relying on their counsel and assistance, he was to shape the minds of his subordinate monks of Reims and instruct them in imitation of sacred religious life. But, as we have learned from the report of good men, he disregarded the counsel of those who had been given to him to help strengthen religious observance, and began to associate with companions in frivolity and to relax more leniently the strictness of regular life.
>
> When the archbishop of Reims learned this, he repeatedly admonished him, both personally and through other religious men, to be more diligent in correcting his order and those subject to him; but he accomplished nothing. Finally, recognizing that he had been deceived concerning the man whom he had thought religious and had consecrated as abbot, he informed the abbot of the Major Monastery of this matter and begged him to correct and reform Robert.
>
> The abbot, sending religious persons from his own side, rebuked him many times and admonished him more carefully not to dishonor, by living so negligently, the church from which he had come. He threatened that, unless he corrected himself, he would excommunicate him as disobedient and a transgressor of his profession.
>
> What more is there to say? Robert promised that on the appointed day he would go to the abbot and obey him as his father. But after speaking with his evil counselors, he scorned going. The abbot, as he had threatened, excommunicated him with the bishop’s consent.
>
> Robert, however, protested and declared that he was not at all bound by the abbot’s anathema. As though released from his obedience and profession, and restored—so it seemed to him—as a free man to the church of Reims, he was assigned a day by the archbishop on which the dispute would be settled by the judgment of bishops and abbots.
>
> On the appointed day the bishops, abbots, and many other religious persons assembled. The abbot of the Major Monastery and the prior of Cluny were also present. After the arguments and objections on both sides had been examined, it could not be proved that the monk Robert had been released from the bond of his first profession by his abbot, either in person or by letters bearing his seal, and had thus been granted as a free man to the archbishop of Reims. It was therefore judged that he had been excommunicated by his abbot and could not be retained by the bishop of Reims.
>
> When the judgment had ended, the aforementioned monk did not at all submit. Apparently seeking an opportunity to wander, he said that he was being oppressed and appealed to your hearing. Although the archbishop wished to retain him and return him to his abbot, because of his appeal he allowed him to go free.
>
> Robert immediately came to us and reported the sequence of events. From his account we learned that he could rightly be recalled by the abbot of the Major Monastery. He also told us that certain brothers of the Major Monastery would come to us on this matter. When we offered to wait for them so that, through their intercession—or restoration, if that could be done—they might assist his cause, he refused to remain and departed from us.
>
> On the third day after his departure, lord Hilgold, formerly bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 1433D] At that time a Cluniac monk.], and our brother Pontius, formerly known to us, together with Ralph, provost of the church of Reims, came to us. They narrated the affair to us in order and presented letters on behalf of the archbishop of Reims, begging that, with our advice, they might appoint another abbot for the church of Saint Remigius, lest it suffer from being without a ruler for a long time.
>
> We refused to do this solely because of your appeal, although we would judge that what had been done in so great an assembly and by such discerning persons was just. Therefore, since it is not our place to teach the prudence of your holiness, let your fatherhood consider how you should answer the aforesaid monk if he comes into your presence or sends letters to you.
>
> For if the church of Saint Remigius should come under the power of some irreligious man, it will be diminished both in temporal and spiritual matters, and the worship of divine religion there will be destroyed, with danger to souls.

**84. (105).** Hugh, abbot of Cluny, also wrote to the same Pope Urban about this affair:

> To our most loving and most reverend father, the supreme pontiff of the holy and apostolic see, lord Pope Urban, Brother Hugh of Cluny, together with our entire congregation, sends continual and most faithful prayers of devotion and perpetual peace.
>
> Many, lord father, have just and necessary reasons for wishing to visit your worthy presence, but they are hindered by various obstacles. Accordingly, some of them come at least to us, as to your own household, so that in some way their needs may be counseled or assisted.
>
> Among them, lord Manasses, bishop of Reims, your humble son and also our devoted friend, whom we commended to you in another letter, complained to us that he had appointed as abbot in the church of Saint Remigius a certain monk from the Major Monastery, and that, contrary to his expectation, the monk’s irreligiousness had caused the place enormous harm. He asked us to appeal to you about this.
>
> But since lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, has reported the entire sequence of events to you, as we have heard, we suggest to your reverence that, if this monk comes to you, he should not circumvent your prudence by any devices; rather, deal with him according to the wisdom that you have from God.
>
> May the Lord Christ preserve your most reverend and beloved fatherhood for us and for the universal Church, sound and unharmed.

**85. (106).** On the feast of Saint Giles, 1 September—the day on which his own appointment had formerly taken place—Abbot Theoderic left the monastery and remained at Reims. On the following solemnity of Saint Remigius, Rainer of Prisches, Robert of Couvin, and also Wired, provost of Évergnicourt, came to him to inquire more certainly about his intentions.

When they learned from him that he had voluntarily chosen a private life; that he could not endure so many persecutions by Otbert; that he wished to avoid the church’s being destroyed because of Otbert’s hostility toward him; that he no longer wished to preside; and that he was unable to be of sufficient help to those exposed to so many dangers, the brothers replied that this should not be done so rashly, but that the abbots who had gathered for the aforesaid feast should be consulted.

A time was therefore set for the matter. When they referred the matter to the abbot of Saint Remigius and to the others gathered there for the counsel of the church of Reims, and those men had discussed the well-known case of Abbot Theoderic in order to formulate their response, they reached this conclusion: since Theoderic wished to live as a private person so as not to be subject to Otbert, he should take care not to obstruct another person while freeing himself, nor to impose upon the aforesaid Otbert someone whom he had newly chosen to be consecrated in his place.

The abbot replied that he had taken counsel in this very matter for himself and his brothers, and that he had long ago designated as his successor Abbot Berenger of Saint Lawrence. Berenger had once been a monk of the church and had been lawfully consecrated by lord Bishop Henry; he therefore had no need of Otbert’s consecration.

The abbot was praised for having provided so wisely. With the agreement of the aforesaid brothers and those present, he wrote to Berenger, under the obligation of the profession he had made to the church, asking him to come to his aid in the present danger. He stated that he was willingly leaving him the abbacy entrusted to him, but inserted this absolute condition: setting aside all other considerations, he had chosen Berenger as his successor precisely so that Berenger would not need Otbert’s consecration.

He also wrote to the brothers collectively, instructing them to choose the man whom he had chosen. Thus, through the hands of Rainer of Prisches and Robert of Couvin, he sent the pastoral staff back to the church. They meanwhile left it at Prisches, after consultation, so that, as it were, it might anticipate a more certain decision among the dissenters concerning matters that were still unsettled, and so that they might choose Berenger’s assistance all the more quickly as the weariness of their desolation under Abbot Theoderic weighed upon them—especially because of Otbert’s persecution, which threatened to become more hostile to them the more unrestrainedly it acted against men left desolate.

**86. (107).** When Theoderic’s letter had been read aloud before the community [Col. 1435A], and either his voluntary resignation or Berenger’s prospective promotion had been announced, each man began, as happens when matters are being changed, to strive according to his own judgment. Dissension arose among them: some said that Theoderic had abandoned those entrusted to him in a disorderly manner; others that several men remained among them capable of governing the abbacy; others that Berenger alone could suffice for it; and others that they would in no way tolerate his presiding over them.

While the council remained undecided amid such varied disagreement, not long afterward the letter that Theoderic had sent to Berenger was delivered. When Berenger read in it that he had been chosen, and knew that he had already been rejected by the brothers, he smiled slightly and said: “Cato of Utica laughed on the day when he suffered rejection, and on the night when he was about to die he read.” [Note: [Col. 1435D] He took the words from Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, chapter 11.]

Although this rejection had entered his heart more deeply than anyone had thought, for the time being he replied as though graciously. He judged that those who had rejected him had acted with sufficient deliberation in deciding that they were sufficient for themselves; that each man serving in his own church was entitled to the honor due to him; and that he knew he did not fit their character. Let them seek someone for whom the flower of glory, now falling among them, might bloom again, and through whom their declining religious observance might rise anew.

Meanwhile Otbert heard the sequence of events. He summoned from the monastery those whom he knew to be the better men and said that he wondered why they had rejected Berenger, whom they ought already to have seized as a man so capable in ecclesiastical affairs. The same judgment about Berenger became widespread among clergy and laity, and they considered no one more suitable to the circumstances or to the church.

By then the brothers, overcome by so many affirmations, had also consented to his election. But he, because of the indignation conceived at his first rejection, could not be drawn to accept the administration offered to him by any entreaties from Otbert or by any acclamations of the brothers or clergy.

Thus, wearied by so many storms and so many delays in a church that was now almost failing, Otbert instructed the brothers to choose whichever of their own number they wished and present him for consecration as abbot.

**87. (109).** During these disputes, Lambert the elder fell ill unto death and sent for Berenger of Liège to be reconciled with him. He was anointed with the oil that he had reserved for himself from the consecration by Bishop Henry and died in the year of the Word made flesh 1099, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May [24 April].

He had been the energetic associate of Abbot Theoderic the elder in acquiring estates and ornaments, renewing and enlarging buildings, producing stained-glass windows and metalwork, arranging the brothers’ food and clothing, and in whatever other ecclesiastical improvements and advantages he could provide. When, under the younger Theoderic, he had been deprived of the dignity to which he was accustomed and had good reason to resent adolescents being placed above him, he was driven to such folly [Note: [Col. 1435] The text is missing at this point.] that, after that Theoderic’s departure, he caused the small shrine of Saint Hubert, which he had prepared with silver, to disappear, after also removing its golden cover of marvelous workmanship. When the bishop’s collectors were turning over the three golden crosses and the golden altar panel for the purchase of Bouillon, he handed them over. He lent Godefrid of Ham two back-hangings, one dalmatic, and one cope, and, during his final illness, he left Berenger part of the gold and a quantity of precious stones to be carried away from the place.

And lest anyone think that this mention of Lambert is either a condemnation of his crime as punishable before God or a judicial defamation before men, let that person know that he was provoked to do these things by bitter and prolonged grief. He had been treated and despised most dishonorably in his old age and grieved that all the labors of his youth had vanished among the ungrateful. For it is the most wretched kind of misfortune to have been happy and then to fall from sovereignty into servitude—or rather, into insults.

**88. (110).** In that same year [1097?] [Note: [Col. 1435D] This is an error, perhaps concealed in the number of the year, since Pope Urban, who died on 29 July 1099, still delivered a judgment concerning Wired’s election after this event.], on the Kalends of June [1 June], Otbert rebuilt the castle of Mirwart, situated not far from the monastery, to the desolation of the surrounding province. Bishop Henry had demolished it at the request of lord Theoderic the elder, under threat of perpetual anathema; he had also legally restored the mountain itself, which had belonged to the church of Saint Hubert from ancient times, confirming the privilege [Note: [Col. 1436D] See above, chapter 48], and, after building and dedicating there a church in honor of Saint Michael, had established brothers there in seclusion, to serve God in the wilderness.

The people of the region, fearing the desolation that they dreaded not only for themselves but also for their descendants, assembled on the appointed day at the church of Saint Hubert. With tears they demanded that his body be presented to Otbert, in the hope that perhaps even thus he might come to his senses and abandon the intention with which he had begun.

The brothers were compelled not only by the common necessity but also by a private necessity that weighed more heavily. Although they acted most imprudently, and in the tumultuous confusion of events, without preliminary fasts, vigils, or any preparation for this undertaking, they took up the holy man’s body and proceeded barefoot and with covered heads [Note: [Col. 1435] Perhaps *corpore* (“with the body”).]. You might have seen the crowds of those running together increasing everywhere [Note: [Col. 1435] Martène corrected this to *augeri*; the manuscript has *angeri*.], while the singing of litanies and psalms was subdued by the people’s mourning.

Otbert heard that he was being pursued by the authority of so great a pontiff. For a time concealing his fury, he mounted his horse and, together with his men, went out to meet those who were coming. After briefly displaying the reverence due to prayer and after the sprinkling of blessed water, he seized a staff prepared for this very purpose and, while incense was being burned, scattered the brothers through the forest, striking their heads and spilling their blood.

While the crowds marveled at the justice of the Most High over such great and outrageous insolence—for although he is patient in repaying, “according to the multitude of his anger” [Psalm X, 4], he does not seek repayment—the saint’s body was carried to the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, where the gathered brothers kept vigil over it.

On the following day Otbert planned to remove it by force. But when none of his own people would consent to such presumption, he recovered a more sound-minded judgment and brought it back with reverence and honor to its own place. Its removal had been exceedingly heavy, whereas its return proved extremely light; this showed that he had been displeased by the removal and pleased by the restoration.

The body was placed upon the altar of Saint Peter, and for eight days it could in no way be returned to its proper place, as though it were demanding some satisfaction for its removal.

Not long afterward, on the very anniversary of the day on which Otbert had inflicted the aforementioned injury upon Saint Hubert, Count Henry captured Otbert and drove him as far as Durbuy on a swift and exceedingly fierce horse. There Otbert was beaten most harshly and dishonorably and barely escaped death. From that time onward, for as long as he lived, he never lacked adversities and disgraceful oppression.

**89. (111).** While Otbert repeatedly pressed the brothers to choose an abbot, he finally set a day on which they were to settle the matter. At last, by the unanimous consent of all, a certain Gerard was elected and was being led to Liège. As they traveled, however, the escorts began discussing Otbert and saying that his appointment would in no way be lawful: first, because he was subject to the excommunicated King Henry; second, because he had rebuilt the aforementioned castle, which he was reconstructing in disregard of the anathema of Bishop Henry; and third, because with his own hand he had shed the blood of monks—or rather, of priests.

When this argument was reconsidered more attentively between Gislebert the dean and Wired, provost of Évergnicourt, they persuaded Gerard that he should meanwhile suspend the matter until they themselves went to Liège and consulted Abbot Berenger about it. Gerard, being a good man and desirous of no unjust promotion, simply yielded to these advisers, who willingly undertook the agreed task.

When they suggested this to Berenger, who was entirely unconcerned about giving them advice on the matter, and also mentioned to Otbert their fear that his appointment would not be lawful, Otbert regarded the remark as an insult to himself. He therefore summoned his leading men to a public hearing for the following day and told them to deliberate collectively whether he should completely annul the abbacy of Saint Hubert, which had so long been a source of injury to him, or whether he should appoint someone.

When everyone shouted that it ought rather to be appointed, Otbert repeatedly offered Berenger the administration [Note: [Col. 1437] The manuscript is defective here; Martène supplies the missing words.]. Since Berenger in no way accepted an office that he had once refused, he accepted the common judgment that he should designate, according to his own assessment, the person whom he knew to be most suitable to carry it out.

After hesitating briefly over this decision, which confronted him with opposing considerations, he replied that, for the present, he knew no one more suitable than Wired, a monk of that church who was present there. Wired was encouraged to come forward. Although, as often happens, he seemed for some time to resist, he nevertheless accepted the abbacy when Otbert granted it to him. Accompanied by Berenger and Frederick the provost, he came to Andage.

The brothers, indignant that their election had thus been frustrated and refusing, as is customary, to go out in procession to meet the newcomer, were approached by Berenger and Frederick. They supported their case as best they could by ingenuity and reason, so that the brothers would not continue to oppose a man who had until then been their brother but was now their father; even if it was not proper for him to endure this, it was not proper for them to do it. They urged the brothers to consider their own reputation, lest they appear to have acted too rashly, and to test first whether Wired was useful and should be retained, or useless and should be rejected.

At length, yielding for the moment to reason and suppressing their opposition temporarily, they allowed him to be present and to take part among them with equanimity. The same opposition could later become more justified if, after being consecrated by Otbert, he proved to be a deserter from the Roman judgment, whose most vehement defender he had previously been.

The church was still burdened by the greatest lack of resources from the time of Ingobrand’s accession. The stewards were handling its goods far too extravagantly, with no regard for fidelity, and the church’s revenues had been reduced by nearly twenty pounds since the accession of lord Theoderic the elder. New and unjust benefices had recently been granted—or even sold—from the brothers’ prebend without their consent, through the counsel and action, as stated above, of Lambert the elder and Theoderic the younger.

When the brothers’ frequent complaints before Wired lamented this injustice and loss, he shook his head and, clapping his hands, called down divine punishment and vengeance upon such advisers and perpetrators.

But how inexcusable is anyone who judges when he himself does the same thing! For, since—as the saying goes—the wills of kings are as changeable as they are vehement, not long afterward Wired summoned the aforesaid men who had recently been endowed with benefices, and, contrary to the public opposition of the brothers, endowed each of them anew for their private favor. Yet before his lawful consecration he could make no lawful grant to his own people.

For this reason the common judgment of the brothers grew stronger: he was to be regarded either as wholly invalid or as rejected. The privilege of Roman authority that Pope Gregory had specifically decreed for this church judged that such a usurper of power should be deprived of the dignity of his office—or, if he feared this, that he should submit himself to Otbert to be consecrated.

Sensing this, Wired withdrew for some time when Otbert offered him his consecration. To avoid more safely the burden of the necessity that was soon to threaten him, he turned toward France and began to stay at the cell of Évergnicourt.

Otbert, fully aware of the reason for this withdrawal, attempted to persuade him, judging from his own character that this would be all the easier and more agreeable: as matters stood, he supposed that Wired would not readily wish to lose the experience of an honor once tasted, whose grant he had refused from Otbert’s hand because that hand did not seem lawful to him at the time. [Note: [Col. 1437] It seems that *non deesse* is intended here: “not to be lacking.”]

From Liège he wrote to him as follows:

> Otbert, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Liège, sends his grace and true affection in Christ to Brother Wired, abbot of Saint Hubert.
>
> No one knows better than you how your promotion was made canonically and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict—how, I mean, human favor, worldly advantage, and all the other things by which unworthy men are customarily advanced unworthily to honors were far from us. We desire you to bring about, through yourselves, the restoration both of your temporal and of your spiritual commonwealth.
>
> Since I wish to keep the eye of right intention toward you always pure and always open, I wished to complete more successfully what had begun well in you and, with God’s help, I resolved to bring you shortly to the grace of benediction.
>
> At that time, however, you said that you were unprepared and that you were lamentably bound up in certain affairs. You said that, with the counsel and assistance of good men—and especially through the concord and unanimity of your brothers—you had to advance to so sublime a grace. You chose and requested a day for completing this matter and, with my consent, fixed it on the feast of Saint Andrew.
>
> But since we were not then at Liège, being occupied in serving the honor and favor of lord the emperor [Note: [Col. 1439D] He was then holding a conference at Mainz, as Ekkehard testifies.], we by no means attribute your failure to come to Liège at that time to negligence.
>
> Now, however, we announce to you by command, and admonish you through true obedience, that, once all obstacles have been removed, you must be at Liège on the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January 1098], that is, on the following Sunday [Note: [Col. 1440D] This agrees with the year 1098.], prepared to receive the benediction.
>
> We wish you to understand that you are being admonished in every way, by God and by Saint Hubert, that meanwhile you should seek or undertake nothing except what pertains to my honor and to the advantage of your church.
>
> Farewell.

Thus, as they say, with a sword smeared with honey, Otbert completely extinguished whatever steadfastness remained in Wired, and on the appointed day Wired came to Liège.

When Otbert reproached him for having evaded for so long the benediction offered to him, Wired, as though for a moment recovering his zeal to testify to the truth—or so that he might appear more excusable before the brothers concerning his consecration—presented this objection. In a public hearing he added openly that Otbert’s benediction did not seem advantageous to him: first, because Otbert had shown singular favor to King Henry, who was striving in such prolonged obstinacy against the apostolic see and its authority; second, because Wired feared that, if Otbert blessed him, his brothers would oppose him; and third, because Otbert had rebuilt the castle of Mirwart, thereby desolating the church of Saint Hubert, although Otbert’s predecessor Henry had forbidden anyone to do this under perpetual anathema.

Otbert replied that it was not merely the time for this discussion to be held. Concealing his indignation at such a sudden attack, he craftily resolved as though to withdraw his own benediction from Wired, now that Wired appeared unwilling to receive it.

Berenger, who was well aware of Otbert’s disposition, immediately intervened to settle the matter between them. He said that the benediction was not Otbert’s but God’s. Yet, on the other hand, the Lord says through Malachi concerning priests who displease him: “I will curse your blessings, because you have not taken it to heart to give glory to my name” (Malachi 2:2).

At that time a certain monk of Saint Lawrence, Lambert, had received the abbacy of Florennes from Otbert’s hand. As has already been said [Note: [Col. 1440D] Chapter 52.], for as long as he remained with Berenger at the cell of Évergnicourt, he could remember it only with the spitting of Otbert’s name.

The consecration of this man had been arranged together with Wired’s consecration. At that time, however, Berenger obtained, for Wired’s sake, that Lambert’s consecration be postponed until Stephen, abbot of Saint James, who had been sent ahead, should exhort the brothers of Saint Hubert, by pontifical authority, to consent to the benediction that was to be performed.

When Stephen arrived and obtained no result concerning his question, the brothers asked him during the proceedings to give them, according to his own understanding, a free counsel of truth and justice concerning this matter.

The abbot was astonished to find himself so trapped. Since he was being forced, as it were by a twisted neck, to give the testimony of truth and justice that he did not wish to give, he replied that he had not come to offer them testimony of truth and justice, but to report to those who had sent him their assent to the brothers’ will.

Thus compelled, he returned to Liège.

Wired, although concerned about the brothers’ opposition, was even more eager to retain his pre-eminence by whatever means. He voluntarily inserted himself into the consecration that was to be performed for the aforementioned Lambert.

Not long afterward, when his conscience reproached him, Lambert voluntarily abandoned the abbacy of Florennes. Wired once again took Frederick the provost with him and came to Andage. He entered the church after a procession, long hoped for but denied to him, had been refused.

In a public assembly of the brothers, in the presence of—and even to the indignation of—Frederick, he complained that this rejection was an injury not only to himself but also to Otbert and the church of Liège. He returned with Frederick to Liège to make this very complaint there.

Because at that time power was suppressing justice and will was suppressing reason, some of the brothers feared that violence would be inflicted upon them. Ten of them therefore departed together on a single day and withdrew to various cells.

Thus, as though relieved of a burden, Wired returned more secure and indeed more ferocious. Excessively ambitious for his own domination and wholly distrustful of the brothers’ administration, he entrusted the church’s administration to laymen, with himself as its sole overseer.

Accordingly, since he himself was impatient of labor and remained at home, and since he entrusted the church’s administration to men who sought their own interests rather than God’s or the brothers’, the fields began to deteriorate without anyone supervising them; the demesne buildings and barns began to collapse; the unfaithful ministers, supporting one another by mutual agreement, began in every way to rule as advocates over the church’s poor; lawful customs were twisted and altered according to their pleasure; improper provisions were demanded; voluntary exactions were imposed heavily upon the church; their own decrees were confirmed for the future through the coercive judgments of the *scabini*; and their pleading claims were violently exaggerated.

[Col. 1441A] 90. (114.) Meanwhile Theoderic was indignant that his election had been annulled because of Berenger, and he began to reclaim his abbacy, which he had relinquished only on the condition that someone should succeed him who would not need consecration from Obert. Therefore, strengthened by the counsel of Manasses, archbishop of Rheims [Note: [Col. 1441] I have written this in place of Raginold; for he was dead, and Manasses is already mentioned in chapter 83.], and of the abbots who had witnessed the aforesaid condition, he committed to writing and sent Wiredus a just complaint, saying that he was greatly and exceedingly astonished that Wiredus could so shamelessly become a monster of such divergent inconsistency, so quickly falling away as an apostate deserter from the position of which he had once been his most ardent defender. Therefore, he said, Wiredus had no claim to precedence in ecclesiastical dignities, since he had even betrayed the authority of the Apostolic See for the sake of the reward of this iniquity; or, if Obert had misled him by his counsel as one less learned, so that, after depriving him of his abbacy for the sake of the faith of Christ, he might fraudulently succeed him in his place, then, at the judgment of the Roman Church which he himself had arranged, the whole matter should be examined between them. He wrote to him as follows:

“Brother T. and the other brothers of the dispersed church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert, to W., who seeks his own glory with excessive ambition and thoughtlessness, and who, in this very matter, has people favoring him against God and the Apostolic See.

“The Son of the eternal Father, always coeternal and coequal with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit, ‘did not regard equality with God as something to be seized’; he emptied himself, and, having assumed the form of a servant without servile condition, refused the kingdom offered to him by fleeing from it, and, carrying his cross, freely descended for us unto death [Col. 1441C]. He established for his imitators the way of humility, not of arrogance. The same man, rising from the dead, entrusted to Peter, in a threefold confession of his love, the sheep whom he had redeemed with his blood. Peter, having received the power of binding and loosing, left that same authority and care to the Roman See.

“It is therefore certain that those who oppose Christ, refuse obedience to ecclesiastical authority and to the Apostolic See, and are found outside the ark of catholic unity, are engulfed in the flood of eternal death. To preserve this faith, Lord Berenger, together with his companions, instructed us—as did your own zeal, more learned and more fervent than that of the others, instructing us who were, as it were, simpler and slower—and, in its defense, armed us with your example even at the risk of our lives.

“How, then, did the enemy sow weeds over the word of God? How did the thorn and thistle of such inconsistency and dissimilarity sprout in the field of your heart? It is plainly a monstrous and altogether detestable inconsistency before God, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration, that the judgment we hold, established by the very men who defended it, should be perverted and weakened, as far as lies in them, by those same men now acting as deserters.

“For if, after so many testimonies of the Christian faith had been examined, you have thought against God in order to lead both us and yourselves astray, you are plainly proved to be heretics. Therefore, according to the sacred canons, you are to possess no promotion or authority in the Church of God; know that the sole place remaining for you is that of repentance, so that you may call upon Jesus, your teacher, from afar. But if, abandoning the glory of God and wishing to establish your own, you have become apostates, have you not—since the same judgment applies to those alike in this respect—become members of the devil, so that now the mystery of iniquity may work in you?

“And lest this judgment of ours seem to you excessively insulting, a judgment already long proved by your word and example, consult all the churches of catholic Christianity; consult also your own consciences within yourselves, and ask whether, in these endeavors of yours, they can either excuse or acquit you before God.

“And how has your strength and steadfastness failed—your strength and steadfastness which, with us, across foreign regions, appeared to endure for the love of Christ beggary and exile, displaying them before the eyes of men as though they were the palms of a kind of martyrdom? [Col. 1442B] How are the churches scandalized in your apostasy in their own places? The sees of Rheims, Laon, Metz, Verdun, and Toul are scandalized in you. At your proclamation they grieved, and they still grieve, over the disfigurement of the once most splendid and religious church of Liège, and also of our church of Andage.

“Moreover, that recent angel of that see, insufficiently concerned for us, at your instigation recently wrote to the archbishop of Rheims, asking him to close to us the open entrails of his charity and to exclude us from his boundaries and from our rightful possessions established there. Nor was it certainly enough for your glory to stir ecclesiastical persons against us, which might in some measure have been tolerable; but, through the support of your presence, you armed many secular tyrants with rewards and promises to persecute us, and, contrary to the decrees of the holy canons, you violently compelled us to appear before them.

“Those men, who were sufficiently humane toward us because of your charity, when they understood—or rather, when they were astonished [Note: [Col. 1441] Thus in manuscript 1.]—that we dissented from the truth’s earlier judgment, shrank from discussing among us what was not theirs to judge. When we protested against the hearing by either the church of Rheims or that of Laon, we finally assembled at Rheims, where we found, with Archbishop Manasses, Engelram, bishop of Laon, who had returned from Rome the day before. At their hearing, after a place had been given us to defend you [Note: [Col. 1441] Thus in manuscript 1.], and after we willingly agreed to submit to your judgment and to be subject to you, provided that, with the faith preserved, this could rightly be done to us [Note: [Col. 1441] Thus in manuscript 1.], you know by what judgment the two bishops concluded your case: namely, that you could in no way possess either the name or the office of abbot unless the Roman authority specifically adjudicated it to you, or confirmed it to you by a truthful legation bearing letters sealed there.

“We therefore pray, admonish, and entreat you, under adjuration and judgment in the divine name, by the authority granted to blessed Peter and to his Apostolic See, to take thought at last for the danger of both yourself and us, and, for discerning the cause of your disagreement, to present yourself with us at the Roman hearing on the coming feast of Simon and Jude. You should also bring us with you, as is just, from the stipends of our mother church, which are abundant for you [Col. 1443A], or graciously grant us the means by which we may meet you on the appointed day at that same hearing [Note: [Col. 1443] ‘with us’ in manuscript 1.].

“But if, in addition to the other injustices we suffer from you, you withdraw from us below the level of our appeal to the Roman hearing the stipend of our mother church—which you know belongs to us just as it belongs to you—believe for certain that, so far as lies in us, we shall not fail to attend the appointed hearing, even if we had nothing with which to carry this out except what we could obtain by begging.”

Wiredus scorned and neglected this summons when he had read it again, and did not wish to believe what he was indignant to fear. At that time Lambert was still staying at Rheims. When he learned, through Theoderic’s report, that the burden of so great a danger was weighing upon Wiredus and his subjects because of the Apostolic appeal [Col. 1443B], he felt deep sorrow for the brothers. He therefore sought, both personally and through wiser men wherever he could find them, to persuade Theoderic—who was exceptionally tender in disputes directed against him—to submit to counsel and reason and to desist from this admonition.

Many people, acting through Lambert, urged the same thing; even Archbishop Manasses inclined toward this suggestion: namely, that it was neither useful nor honorable for a church of such renown and once such great religious devotion to be so thoughtlessly oppressed by him through apostolic authority; and that, instead of pursuing so fiercely the man whom he had not designated as his successor, or whom he regarded as an invader of his former prelacy, it would be better for him to seek from someone a place where it might be preserved from complete destruction, since he himself detested subjection to Otbert.

At last Theoderic yielded to reason and circumstance, so far as to promise openly that, if Wiredus wished to trust him, he was prepared to go with him to Rome and, through his agency, to secure for him an uncontested abbacy from the Apostolic See. Since many people praised this promise, Lambert, for the sake of bringing about this settlement, sought out Wiredus and announced to him Theoderic’s aforesaid good will toward the church and toward those who cared for it, as well as Theoderic’s consent, if Wiredus were willing to trust him.

Wiredus replied: “I will never trust my enemy, nor can I in any way go to Rome without the consent of my bishop, since I am ready to undergo judgment before him together with Theoderic.”

When Lambert responded according to his earlier and true opinion of the matter—which he had once defended with the faithful of Christ—that Otbert was no one, being an adversary of the Apostolic See, Wiredus added: “He must necessarily be regarded as one’s own whom the church of Liège tolerates being called its bishop, whatever his character.”

When Theoderic heard this, he was deeply offended that Wiredus had sent him such a message. He also reproached his aforesaid advisers quite insultingly, saying that by offering such counsel they had wasted their words and that he had, as the saying goes, “washed a raw brick.” Thus anger and indignation arose between the two sides, and, with danger to souls and loss to ecclesiastical possessions, disagreement arose between the inner and outer brothers. The men of Castrum [Note: [Col. 1443D] That is, Saint Theobald’s at Porcinium Castle, as it is written in the privilege of Innocent II, book 1.], Pirres, Sancy [Note: [Col. 1443D] Sancy in Lorraine. H.], and Cugnon refused to be subject or united to Wiredus, and retained Theoderic in every way as abbot.

Theoderic, concerned for them as best he could, frequently visited those who depended upon his protection, and, living among them, urged each of them to labor for the advancement of his own place while preserving fidelity to the mother church of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert. Thus Emmo, provost of Pirres and later abbot of the monastery of Morin [Note: [Col. 1443D] That is, Saint John of Thérouanne, or at the Mount. [Col. 1444D] Apparently. I have found no mention of Emmo apart from this.], completed the church of Saint Mary and Saint Sulpicius, begun by Lord Rainer [Note: [Col. 1443] “Raigero” in manuscript 1.], bringing it to its present extent. The men of Castrum, Cugnon [Col. 1444B], and Sancy advanced their own settlements as each was able.

On the occasion of this disagreement, Dodo of Cugnon violently seized Calvitiacum and Flabotville and compelled their revenues to serve the brothers of his own cell. Meanwhile, with his supporters—or rather seducers—agreeing with him as though out of favor, Wiredus foolishly regarded as madness the summons to the Roman hearing which Theoderic had issued against him. For he did not believe that Theoderic, as an exile and a poor man, could carry out what he appeared to threaten, since he lacked the resources to accomplish it.

Theoderic, however, mindful of his own interests, earnestly appealed to men of known virtue to take pity on him and extend the hands of charity to carry out the business of his agency [Col. 1444C]. He soon obtained, through their generosity, sufficient support to travel honorably to Rome. Taking Heribrand with him, he sought Pope Urban, who was staying at Benevento [Note: [Col. 1444D] He was there toward the autumn of 1098.], and humbly presented him with the following petition for settlement:

“To Lord Urban, universal pope, the sons of the church of Saint Hubert, who, in defense of the true faith and its legitimate apostolate, have suffered dispersion before the eyes of God, as it is said: ‘While the Lord Jesus slept,’ etc.”

See this letter at the end of the letters of Urban II, in volume 151 of the *Patrologia*.

91. (118.) After the text of the petition had been read in the presence of Pope Urban and had been repeatedly and carefully examined by the Romans, they grieved that an abbot had been so dispossessed for his fidelity to the Roman Church. They decreed that Wiredus should be excommunicated without delay unless he repented and surrendered his position.

However, with Rainer’s support—he succeeded Urban in the papacy—the sentence of excommunication was at that time postponed until the day appointed for the hearing between the two parties, in case the hearing to be conducted might become more certain when Wiredus arrived. Since Wiredus remained at home, he was judged to have evaded the hearing appointed against him as one conscious of guilt. Therefore, on the feast of All Saints, the pope issued an excommunication against him, and, in his presence, delivered a letter of that excommunication:

“Urban, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the catholic brothers of the monastery of Saint Hubert of the Ardennes, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We have heard—and cannot hear it without grief—that, through the violence of the false bishop Otbert, our venerable son Theoderic, your abbot, has been expelled from your monastery for the sake of the catholic faith, and that Wiredus, a false monk, has been imposed over your heads through the violence of that same Otbert. Know that this is altogether displeasing to us.

“Therefore, greeting you by this present letter, we exhort you to preserve the steadfastness of your faith, and I grant you permission, if you cannot live in your monastery according to the rule of blessed Benedict and apostolic truth, to withdraw to whatever religious monastery you wish, until almighty God looks upon your place and restores it to its former condition according to his good pleasure.

“As for Wiredus, the invader of your monastery, together with all his subjects, we make known to you by this present writing that he is excommunicated by the holy Roman Church for as long as he does not desist from invading that monastery.

“Given …”

92. (120.) Pope Urban also sent the church of Liège the following letter on behalf of Theoderic:

“Urban, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the catholic clergy and people of Liège, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We grieve deeply for you, dearly beloved sons in Christ, because for so long the darkness of error has covered your church and alienated it from the truth of the Apostolic See. Therefore, as sons of my own heart, we correct you with fatherly affection, admonishing and beseeching you to lift the eyes of your minds toward the light of pure truth.

“Remove the evil from among yourselves. I mean that wolf and thief who did not enter through the door for your salvation, but climbed in from elsewhere, in order to slaughter, eat, and destroy. Therefore either drive from among yourselves the invader and occupier of the church—by Obert we mean the accomplice of Henry and Guibert—if this can in any way be done; or withdraw your obedience and fellowship from him as one alienated from and excommunicated by the holy Roman Church.

“We issue the same command concerning Wiredus, the false abbot, who through the violence of that same false bishop has occupied the monastery of Saint Hubert of the Ardennes. If anyone thereafter dares to communicate with them, until they have abandoned the oppression of the churches over which they preside and have made satisfaction to God and the Apostolic See, let him know that he is bound by the bond of the same excommunication.

“Let it also be known to you and to everyone else that we have granted the religious abbot Theoderic permission to absolve from the bond of excommunication those converts from the schismatics who flee to him.

“Given …”

When Theoderic returned in accordance with the pope’s command and publicly delivered this letter to the brothers of the church of Saint Hubert [Col. 1446A], Wiredus happened then to be absent. Realizing the common danger to their souls, each of them became scandalized at the absent man and feared, for his own part, subjection and communion with him. Thus, from the Sunday called Palm Sunday (1099, April 3) until Easter had fully passed, the church appeared almost entirely deserted.

Nevertheless, concealing his recognition of the obligation imposed upon him, Wiredus tried, as his own judge, to defend his obstinacy. He maintained that no one except his bishop could excommunicate him, and that he was ready to answer all his accusers in the bishop’s presence.

When Obert learned this, although the same accusation applied to him by decree of the Apostolic See, he nevertheless secretly smiled to himself. He saw that, on account of this necessity, Wiredus was at last recognizing him as the legitimate bishop, whereas for some time he had avoided him as though he were not legitimate. Meanwhile he ordered the brothers to suspend the dispute they had begun until he himself came and brought the matter to an end.

Wiredus, meanwhile, worked to make himself acceptable to those who opposed him, seeking to please each one according to the character by which he knew that person could be won over. In this way, little by little, the apostolic judgment became contemptible in the minds of those who were rashly tumultuous, and their fervor in defending the truth grew cold.

Although this impediment was postponed for a time, it was not entirely removed. Wiredus, now more secure, began, to the great detriment of the church, to seek free men and military tenants whom he could claim for himself, so that, once he had received their hands, he might vainly boast that they were his.

To the advocate John he gave the advocacy of Chauvency, and on that account John secured for himself the whole profit of Chauvency. He gave Walter of Ample to the allod of Seriel [Note: [Col. 1445] Or Senel.], which from ancient times had been assigned and recorded for the brothers’ prebend, together with three solidi. He gave to Bovo of Wahart [Note: [Col. 1445D] Castellan of Mirwart; see below, chapter 93, and Aegidius, chapter 19.] the mill at the lake and the valley of Gruispont. He returned to Ralph of Villers, as though to his own relative, the holdings of land which he himself had recovered for the church by lawful judgment. To Lambert of Revogne [Note: [Col. 1446D] Revogne. R.] he sold as a military tenancy his inheritance, which had been assigned to the brothers’ prebend. He sold to Goderan of Bure the small tithe of that same village, and to Duranne whatever land he held.

Having newly acquired these military tenants for himself from ecclesiastical property, permanently depriving the church of its resources, and wishing to appear stronger and more glorious, he found that matters proceeded very differently. Justice itself, under the direction of the Almighty, turned against him everything that it saw him uselessly plotting against God.

Those whom he had expected to be useful to him in counsel and assistance, and who frequently came to him as though to their lord, began to be a burden. Those whom he heard praising him at lavish banquets became, because of contempt arising from excessive familiarity, mockers when absent.

It also happened that he incurred Otbert’s resentment through some of these men. At one time, while dining with Otbert, they provoked him severely by saying that the abbot of Saint Hubert’s table was more abundant, indeed more sumptuous, than the table of the bishop of Liège. When some friends reported this to Wiredus and warned him to guard against it, he, angered, promised that no such thing would be permitted again. Nevertheless, habit prevailed, and he lacked the strength to resist, so that the extravagance which had begun continued.

93. (122.) In the year 1103 of the incarnate Word, Bovo, castellan of Mirwart, who appeared in such matters to be an exceptionally close friend of the table’s companions, rose up against the church and Wiredus. After violently seizing whatever revenues of the forest had hitherto belonged to the church, and also ravaging the peasants’ clearings because they had made them without his permission, he sent officials to seize the ecclesiastical fishermen who had been dispatched to the Lomme [Col. 1447B], and he committed them to custody in the castle.

When Wiredus, following the counsel of the brothers, excommunicated the instigators and perpetrators of this injury—for this church possesses, by authority of the Apostolic See, legitimate power to excommunicate unjust invaders of any of its rights—Bovo reported the matter to Obert as an unheard-of act of presumption, presenting it as harshly as he could. He claimed that the bishop’s household ought not to be excommunicated unless a complaint had first been brought before Obert.

With the greatest indignation, Obert summoned Wiredus on an appointed day to answer for this injury, and meanwhile forbade him in every way to interfere with the church’s two allods, namely Braz and Gruispont.

Wiredus, taking Lambert and Wido with him, came to the appointed hearing with the lawful privilege concerning the ecclesiastical possession placed under interdict against him [Col. 1447C]. He found that all the more powerful men of the city had assembled with Obert against him.

When the court had been arranged, the abbots and archdeacons sat on one side, and Obert and the laymen on the other. Wiredus was accused of having dared to excommunicate the bishop’s household—namely, the defenders of his castle—without waiting for a complaint first brought before Obert.

He replied that he had not considered the reckless deserters of justice, violent assailants of the church, and violators of the established peace to be members of that household [Note: [Col. 1447D] Established by Bishop Henry, who was consequently called “the Peaceful.”], nor had he rashly excommunicated them, as Obert alleged. Rather, he had confirmed by his own excommunication the excommunication imposed upon them for the violation of the peace.

The abbots and archdeacons remained silent and nodded at his reasonable answer. The laymen, however, resisting in favor of Obert, judged Wiredus altogether culpable on this account and therefore believed that he had incurred the bishop’s displeasure.

But Lambert, sitting with the archdeacons, said: “How has the honor of ecclesiastical and your own dignity been brought so low today [Note: [Col. 1447] Missing in the manuscript; added by Martène.], when a judgment that ought reasonably to have been decided by you has now been thrown into confusion so irrationally by lay presumption? Are laymen not to know what clerics do?”

Immediately, while the archdeacons grew indignant, a dispute arose against the laymen. Otbert, fearing the outcome of the quarrel, changed the place of the session and summoned only ecclesiastical assessors for consultation. He also told Wiredus to withdraw with his companions to the larger palace until he could decide his case with greater deliberation.

During the consultation, Otbert said that he wished to depose Wiredus, since he had so injured him, and to make the church’s allods of Braz and Gruispont tributary to the castle of Mirwart. Berenger resisted most firmly, asserting both that Wiredus did not deserve deposition and that the lawful donation of Bishop Henry, confirmed to the church by a public privilege bearing a seal, ought not to be overturned.

While some unjustly favored Obert and others rightly testified on Berenger’s behalf, Obert added that no privilege concerning the aforesaid donation existed—or, if one did exist, he wished to see it immediately. He thought that it was not present.

The two Henries [Note: [Col. 1447D] Archdeacons of the church of Liège, one also a dean and the other provost of Fosses; the latter was the son and the former the brother of Conon of Montaigu. See below, chapter 98; Hirsch, on Sigebert, p. 178.], being faithful to the church, went to Wiredus and asked about the privilege, saying that, if he had it, he should entrust it to them to bring to Obert.

After they had given and received a firm promise that they would return it, Wiredus entrusted the privilege to both of them. They offered it to Obert on condition that it be returned; but when he had received it, he tried, whether in jest or in earnest, to retain it. After unfolding it slowly, he began to read it even more slowly.

Berenger, alluding to Obert as though he were already becoming dim-sighted and therefore slow in reading, asked that the privilege be given to him to read. Obert, indignant at him, as though Berenger thought him unable to see properly, began to read more quickly, while Berenger repeatedly told him not to trouble himself. He relied on this very encouragement to make Obert read through to the anathema written at the end.

After the privilege had been read through, since the event was recent, those present testified [Note: [Col. 1447] Missing in the manuscript; added by Martène.] that it was genuine and that they had been present at Bishop Henry’s lawful donation, having seen and heard it. Wiredus was summoned, and they returned to him the privilege, publicly recognized as authentic. The judgment concerning the excommunication was postponed until the following feast of Saint Lambert (September 17).

When the bishops’ abbots had assembled and Wiredus’s case had been examined, they adjudicated peace to him because he had confirmed by his own excommunication the episcopal excommunication for the breach of peace. Obert, meanwhile, concealing his indignation, remained silent at that time [Col. 1448D] and repeatedly complained in private to his closest associates that he was suffering greatly.

One of them, Bruno, boasted that, as though he were archdeacon of that place, he would burden the church itself and Wiredus on any pretext. Obert urged him to carry this out with greater determination.

94. (123.) In the year 1104 of the incarnate Word, Bruno the archdeacon, having gathered a large number of priests and assembled soldiers, came to Andage, ostensibly to hold a synod, but rather to harass the church. He ordered Wiredus to provide food for him and his men.

When Wiredus heard that Bruno was coming on synodal business, he entirely refused him this service, which was not owed—namely, in accordance with an edict of blessed Pope Gregory, who absolutely forbids monasteries of monks to be disturbed by procurations imposed either by a bishop or by any episcopal person. Gualcaudus also prohibits this by the privilege of his authority.

Nevertheless, Wiredus sent word that, if Bruno were visiting the place out of charity, he would provide him hospitality as he did for other visitors; but if Bruno were troubling his parishes, he should direct his expectation not to Wiredus but to the procurators of those parishes.

Thus rejected in anger and indignation—for he had barely been admitted to the monastery for the sake of prayer—Bruno turned aside for lodging to the house of Obert, then a priest. On the following day (January 8), after holding the synod in the basilica of Saint Giles, which had formerly and from ancient times stood under the honor of Saint Dionysius the martyr, he turned aside to Bastogne [Col. 1449B].

There, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, he summoned the clergy of his archdeaconry by an announced council, chiefly to plot against and oppress the church of Saint Hubert.

In the castle formerly called Ambra, but called the monastery of Andage after Saint Beregisus, the mother church had stood from the beginning of Christianity’s emergence there under the honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. In this church, as was stated at length above, Bishop Gualcaudus of Liège, with the consent of Leo, Roman pontiff [Col. 1449C], and also on the advice of Hildebold, metropolitan of Cologne, and at the urging of Louis, most devout emperor and son of the great Charles, had established the order of monastic religion. According to canonical authority, it had thereafter remained for 325 years a settlement of monks free from every disturbance [Note: [Col. 1449D] Manifest error.].

As is proper to a mother church, it legitimately possesses its own baptistery, with fourteen churches subject to it as its endowment. Their liberty, authorized by a public privilege, owes no compliance to episcopal or archidiaconal exaction.

But because in our times, with priesthood and kingdom divided against each other, ecclesiastical authority was everywhere growing weak, and in the administration of lawful justice the will of each person dominated in place of reason, Bruno thought that he could change laws and times. Accordingly, at the aforesaid council of his men, he introduced as his principal complaint the charge that the church of Andage had treated him with excessive injury: he had suffered contemptible rejection there, and therefore wished, on any pretext, to satisfy the vengeance he had conceived.

Since he knew that, as the mother church, it could in no way be deprived of its legitimate baptistery, he nevertheless attempted to withdraw from it entirely the oil and chrism of his administration, violently to violate the churches hitherto free by imposing upon them the ban of subjection and protection, and, under the prompting of anger, ordered that the attempt to carry out this will of his be judged by their decision [Col. 1450A].

Wiredus, warned of these matters by certain faithful members of the church, went to the same council in order to remove any obstacle that Bruno might be contriving against it. Rising, he protested in free contradiction that such matters did not belong to their judgment, nor was it fitting for them to pass any judgment concerning a church of such authority and liberty. He also appealed to the written decision of this attempt among the fathers at a general synod, asking that it be respected.

Bruno, indignant that Wiredus had forestalled him by a lawful protest and synodal appeal, granted Wiredus a postponement, willingly or unwillingly.

Not long afterward, Obert sent his legation to Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, and obtained by entreaty that Manasses should come to meet him concerning the benefit he was seeking from him at Bouillon [Col. 1450A–B].

Accordingly, on the day appointed by both parties at Douzy [Note: [Col. 1449D] Douzy on the river Chiers.], Obert, eager to display who he was and what he could do, summoned his abbots and archdeacons, as well as all the more powerful men of the bishopric, and met the archbishop with considerable pomp, although the archbishop was concerned with no such display.

On the Monday of Rogations (May 24), after this meeting had concluded, each man hurried to the lodging where he expected to be received most familiarly, for the summer was more intense than usual. Wiredus took back with him the Liège abbots Berenger and Stephen, as well as the archdeacon Bruno, who had now become more favorable to him.

Sometimes time moderates what reason cannot moderate for the moment. While they were celebrating the Lord’s Ascension (May 25) with generous hospitality in the presence of the aforesaid abbots, the harassment which Bruno had inflicted upon the church was brought forward.

The abbots privately approached Bruno, gently rebuked him, and also presented him with a defense of the authority of the Apostolic See, supported by a specially confirmed privilege forbidding anyone to inflict injury unless the dignity of his honor and power had been suspended. Although Bruno resisted sufficiently, they finally drew him away from his judgment.

Thus Bruno, overcome by reason, publicly acknowledged and repented that he had acted unjustly in everything he had done or intended to do against the church—whether through his own effort or at another’s urging—including every undue exaction, every complaint, and every form of persecution or violation. By the authority of the ban he forbade anyone to do such things thereafter [Col. 1450D]. He also ordered Alard the dean, under obedience, to impose the same prohibition in the assembly of the priests subject to him.

At the following feast of the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul (June 29), after the priests had carried the processional crosses of the ban and Alard had discharged the offerings owed in devotion, the whole assembly publicly agreed to his judgment. Alard confirmed, by an archidiaconal ban, the decree concerning the recognized peace and liberty of the church of Saint Hubert, and excommunicated anyone who should thereafter violate that same ban.

95. (125.) In the year 1105 of the incarnate Word, a certain Richard, cardinal of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1450D] Bishop of Albano.], was exercising apostolic authority throughout Gaul, summoning councils. With Robert of Verdun, who was closely attached to him, supporting him, Theoderic proclaimed at these councils the circumstances of his deprivation.

When his case was examined, the same cardinal, following the judgment of faithful men, decreed that Theoderic neither ought nor could be deprived of the dignity of his prelacy, which he appeared to have relinquished very rashly in defense of the truth and fidelity to the Apostolic See. He also declared that Wiredus should know the abbacy of Andage to be entirely forbidden to him, or should certainly regard himself as excommunicated together with all his supporters and subjects.

Laurence, abbot of Saint Vanne [Note: [Col. 1451D] Of Verdun.], and Robert the monk intercepted this sentence of apostolic authority and announced it to Wiredus. When they had appointed a day and place for a meeting, but Wiredus failed to appear, they sent him the cardinal’s decree through Adelon, the provost [Col. 1451B]. Theoderic also, in letters sent to the brothers, intensified their awareness of the danger of the same excommunication.

During these attacks upon him, Wiredus approached Manasses, bishop of Rheims, and demanded the return of the altar of Sulpy, which he had withheld from the church for seven years. Manasses gave back not only what Wiredus had withheld but also the altar of Nogaria, removing the personal claim and making a public and lawful donation. With the consent of Gervasius the archdeacon and all his clergy, confirmed and sealed by a privilege, he handed both over to the church of Saint Hubert to be held in perpetuity for the solemn celebration of his anniversary from its revenues.

[Col. 1451C] **96. (126.)** Meanwhile Obertus, excessively bent on exercising domination, began at Liège to tear down the civil rights, alter the laws of his forebears, and annul the customs. In order that he might restrain the lesser men more freely, he meanwhile delayed provoking the greater ones; by gifts and promises as well he drew the more powerful into agreement with himself. Yet he could not long contain himself without revealing what he had postponed for the time being, and in the same oppression he became the same toward everyone.

Finally, he attempted violently to infringe the entire freedom of jurisdiction enjoyed by churches and clerics, to such an extent that he committed to custody the household servants of Frederic, provost of the church of Saint Lambert. Summoned from there by the complaint of the entire Liège clergy, he came to the palace at Aachen, until Frederic, metropolitan of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1451] Something appears to be missing or corrupt here.], announced that a public hearing for canonical examination of Obertus was to be held there.

Obertus arrived; a numerous Liège clergy also arrived, together with abbots and archdeacons. It was the year 1104 of the incarnate Word, Thursday of the first week of Lent (March 10). About these same days Wiredus had come to Liège to seek Obertus’s help concerning certain injustices inflicted upon our church. When he heard that so large an assembly had gathered at Aachen, he hastened to be present there, accompanied by Lambertus and Adelon.

Amazed that he had arrived unexpectedly, Henricus and Bruno, the archdeacons, came forward in the royal court [Col. 1452A]. After an address, they brought him into the palace and commended him to the bishop of Cologne. The bishop received and kissed him cheerfully, and asked why he had come. Wiredus, however, sighed deeply and remained silent for the moment—for Berengerus had already warned him that it would in no way benefit him, amid so many adversities, to add his own more serious case concerning Mirvolt against Obertus, who was already so heavily burdened.

The bishop then rose, summoned the abbots Berengerus and Stephanus aside, and under obedience ordered them to explain to him, in due sequence, the complaint of the man who was silently grieving. Berengerus, thoroughly informed about the matter and skilled in speaking, recounted what he had been ordered to say: namely, how the aforementioned castle, hostile to the entire surrounding province, had scarcely been overthrown by the strength of all Lotharingia, in accordance with the decree of Emperor Henricus [Col. 1452B]; how it had been rebuilt by Bishop Henricus and then destroyed again by him under threat of perpetual anathema; and how it now stood rebuilt for the ruin of the church of Saint Hubert.

When the bishop then asked why the abbot delayed making his complaint, Berengerus replied that he distrusted justice. The bishop seized upon the word “distrust” with indignation and swore that the abbot would distrust the administration of justice in vain, provided that life and prosperity remained to him.

About the sixth hour, when the Liège clergy had assembled against Obertus, one could see reason confused by tumultuous disagreement. Without any turn-taking in speaking and hearing, each man complained of the injuries he had suffered from Obertus, and canonical sentences were indiscriminately brought against him [Col. 1452C], until the bishop of Cologne, having brought Obertus in with him, took his seat.

At last the tumult was quieted, and judgment was given that one man should speak for all. Henricus the archdeacon, chosen to carry this out, stood in the midst and began to speak:

“This outcry which we must raise today against the lord bishop is not about his private life, of which God alone is witness and judge, but about ecclesiastical injustices, our laws, and public affairs. Specifically: that he has sold abbeys at a fixed price; that he has distributed for an agreed payment the ecclesiastical offices which preside over the care of souls and which, as gifts of the Holy Spirit, ought to be given and received freely; that, to the common detriment of all the churches of the province, he has so often changed or debased legitimate coinage [Col. 1452D] and, what is worse, has consented to its being debased; that he has attempted violently to violate the liberty of public law and the laws maintained by our forebears until now; that he has scorned to listen to us and to all the faithful of Saint Lambert who urged him not to do this; that, when the more powerful men of the bishopric demanded that he correct himself, he gave them his word that he would do so and then made that promise void; and that he has not yet been willing to restore the treasures of the churches which he despoiled, although he is able to do so.

“Since, therefore, this is the state of the public affairs of the Liège church, apart from the private complaints of many, which would take too long to proclaim, it is fitting that your authority should be attended by the spirit of counsel and fortitude, so that justice may be reformed under the direction of judgment, and that, once the complaints of her sons have been resolved, Mother Church may rejoice in their peace.”

The archbishop then spoke in council and returned to Obertus. After briefly preaching concerning the common complaint, he publicly rebuked Obertus, who was overwhelmed with shame—or rather with indignation—because of the accusations brought against him. He did not desist until Obertus agreed, with the counsel and judgment of his clergy, to correct the matters of which he was accused, and placed in the archbishop’s hand, as security for that agreement, his own pledge and episcopal authority.

The archbishop also set a date for Obertus to fulfill the aforesaid agreement before the council which he would hold at Cologne on the second Sunday after Easter. Thus, as evening was already approaching, he dissolved the hearing.

[Col. 1453B] **97. (127.)** At the following Easter, King Henricus celebrated the feast at Liège [Note: [Col. 1453D] He came to Liège after Easter, according to the *Annals of Hildesheim*.]. There Obertus, by providing the king with the greatest banquets, induced him not to allow the council appointed for Cologne to take place, because, while concealing the obligation of the pledged agreement, he feared the enforcement of the promised correction [the wording *direrectionis pactae* appears corrupt].

Finally, if he seemed to have achieved some correction among certain of the more powerful men, he had accomplished it not through carrying out either his pledge or his power, but in order to protect his reputation for a time. Thus, when the council failed because of the royal intervention, our expectation based on the archbishop’s promise was likewise frustrated.

Not long afterward God stirred up a most evil spirit between Henricus and his son. Henricus had been excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII for crimes clearly proven in a Roman synod in the year 1076 of the incarnate Word. From that time for nearly thirty years he had attacked the Apostolic See and, as far as lay in his power, had turned all who agreed with him away from reverence and fidelity toward it, to the peril of their souls.

After his son had already been crowned, many of the kingdom’s greatest princes suggested to him that he himself become the faithful defender of the Roman Church, against which his father had been such a long-standing aggressor; thus, by opposing his father, he might claim the defense of the better cause [Note: [Col. 1453] Read *praetenderet* for *praetenderetur*.]. The young man agreed to the suggestion, rejoicing that he was permitted to resist his father. Gathering certain supporters, he crossed the Rhine and persuaded the Saxons and all whom he knew to have previously suffered repeated injuries from his father to rebel with him (1105).

His father, taking Obertus with his followers from Liège, and also gathering those over whom he still seemed to exercise some authority, crossed the Rhine himself and pursued his son for fifteen days along the upper routes of the kingdom, urging the provincials to war. When he summoned the princes of the regions and personally ordered them to fight against his son, they replied that they neither ought nor could be compelled to do so, since he had bound them all collectively by an oath of fidelity to that same son [Col. 1454A].

Henricus, deceived in his hope of waging war—or rather, which was worse for him, intercepted amid enemies whom he had thought friends—fled to Lotharingia by continuous night marches, while his son pursued him in flight with torches and weapons. The son became so hostile to him that he shut him, while fleeing, into the castle of Becheneshem [Note: [Col. 1453D] Bockenheim.] on this side of the Rhine, and, after exacting the royal insignia from him, compelled him also to renounce the kingdom.
