These things took place in the year 1106 of the incarnate Word (December 31). Treated in this way by his son, and having scarcely escaped from his custody, the father came to Cologne. When the people there wished to escort him ceremonially, he did not consent; from there, as a private man and barefoot, he proceeded in the harshest winter to the palace at Aachen (1106).

Obertus, grieving that these things had happened to him, but fearing even more for himself if the son should prevail [Col. 1454B], went to meet him as though out of loyalty. Being a man of impetuous character, he brought him to Liège with excessive rashness and extreme imprudence, which he later wished to regret but was not permitted to do.

For, besides the expenses of the king and his followers, he was greatly burdened by the continual presence of the provincial princes who gathered there. He himself also summoned them voluntarily to aid the abandoned king, using both gifts and promises to prevent them from joining the son.

Meanwhile, since the son trusted the fidelity pledged to him by Obertus and the other princes, and had decided to celebrate Easter at Liège, he himself, remaining at Aachen, sent nearly three hundred of his leading men ahead to the city. This took place on Thursday of Holy Week (March 22).

Duke Henricus [Note: [Col. 1453D] Of Lotharingia.], drawn away from the son [Col. 1454C], was then staying with his father at Liège. At Obertus’s urging, at the time when the chrism was to be prepared, he gathered military auxiliaries and, having also withdrawn the forces of that same city, went to meet those who were approaching on this side of the bridge of Visé [Note: [Col. 1453D] Visé, on the Meuse, somewhat above Liège.]. After nearly killing and drowning them, he inflicted a great disaster upon the kingdom and brought upon himself and his countrymen implacable enmities.

**98. (129.)** In the same year, Arnulfus, count of Chisny, became a monk at this place on the Kalends of April and died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. Forty years earlier, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1454D] Chapter 15.], he had legally granted the cell of Pirenne to Saint Hubert to be held in perpetuity. As he was then dying, he gave the church the price of ten pounds as an alms.

Because his son Otto was then staying with Henricus at Cologne and could make no gift involving hereditary property without his consent, Arnulfus sent faithful servants to the absent son, instructing him, in fulfillment of the duty he owed his father, to grant for his father’s soul the tithe of Fescals and Mount Floheri [Note: [Col. 1454D] Feschaux and Flohimont. R.].

On the day before the Kalends of May, Count Cono [Note: [Col. 1454D] Of Montaigu.] died at the castle of Dolhem [Note: [Col. 1454D] Dalhem. R.] below Liège (1106, April 30). At his own request, he was carried from there and buried at Dinant, the place he had chosen for himself long before [Note: [Col. 1453] *dinan* in witness 1.].

Ten years earlier, when he was about to go to Jerusalem with Duke Godefridus, he had received ten ounces of our gold upon Felc, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1455B] Chapter 83.]. He had also arranged, by a legal charter, that the whole allod, including the portions which were his by right at Monz, Heis, and Cella [Note: [Col. 1455B] Mont, Heya, Salle. R.], together with the entire household belonging to it wherever it might be, should after his death belong perpetually to Saint Hubert, through the hands of guarantors—namely, Bovo W. and Boso.

After his funeral, his son Lambertus, having received the same alms back from the guarantors, legally transferred it to the church, in the presence there of his brother H., archdeacon, and his paternal uncle H., dean of the church of Saint Lambert [Note: [Col. 1455B] See above, chapter 93.], with the lawful testimony of many of his leading men [Col. 1455B].

[Col. 1456A] **99. (130.)** At Monz there was a certain knight named Udo, who was a tenant-holder (*casatus*). In mid-May, when he learned that a certain brother had arrived there to receive the rent, he came upon him in a fury, together with his nephew Thiebaldus, while the monk was still resting in the morning. He would have committed a sufficiently foul deed against the monk with his drawn sword, unless Thiebaldus had warded off the blow by thrusting forward his elbow.

After driving the brother away, Udo seized the rent; but this did not go unpunished for long. For when he had returned from there and was serving Count Henricus at dinner at La Roche [Note: [Col. 1456B] Henricus was the son of Albert, count of Namur.], as though insane he put his foot into a cauldron of meat that was still boiling, so that it might be burned. As a result of that burning, his entire body wasted away, and after publicly confessing his guilt [lacuna].
